Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Trehalose is a naturally occurring non‐reducing disaccharide (molecular weight 342.3 Da) found broadly in microorganisms and invertebrates, widely used as a stabilizer and excipient in foods and pharmaceuticals, and formulated in ophthalmic solutions at 3% w/v (≈87.7 mM) for ocular surface applications (e.g., dry eye) (Cox et al., 2025, pp. 1–2). In mammalian cells, trehalose enters via fluid‐phase endocytosis at millimolar concentrations and has been repeatedly reported as an autophagy enhancer that can activate AMPK signaling, stimulate lysosomal activity, and augment autophagic flux across multiple tissues, including ocular tissues (RPE) and retina (Cox et al., 2025, pp. 1–2). In the context of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), trehalose has been deployed as a small‐molecule modulator of the lysosome–autophagy axis with proposed mTOR‐independent activation of TFEB, the master transcriptional regulator of lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy (CLEAR network), positioning it mechanistically distinct from direct mTORC1 inhibitors such as rapamycin (Ghosh et al., 2024, p. 6; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 10–11). Topical ophthalmic trehalose is generally well tolerated, and preclinical studies show no overt ocular toxicity at 3% or 9% w/v after twice-daily dosing for up to two weeks, supporting feasibility for posterior segment delivery strategies; Raman spectroscopy has detected trehalose in RPE/choroid after repeated topical dosing, although posterior penetration is variable (Cox et al., 2025, pp. 8–10).

Therapeutic History  
Preclinical evidence in RPE and retina  
- Human RPE cell line (ARPE-19) oxidative stress model: Trehalose upregulates autophagy markers (LC3-II, p62/SQSTM1), increases TFEB protein and autophagy gene transcripts (ATG5, ATG7), and elevates lysosomal markers including LAMP2 and Cathepsin D (CTSD) protein; importantly, trehalose pretreatment confers cytoprotection against hydroquinone (HQ)-induced oxidative injury, and this protection is abolished by ATG5 knockdown, demonstrating autophagy dependence (typical dosing 50 mM trehalose; HQ 50 μM) (Abokyi et al., 2020, pp. 1–2, 9–11, 11–12, 12–13, 15–16). Dose–response caveats were noted: higher trehalose concentrations (≥100 mM) lost cytoprotection and were associated with stronger LC3-II accumulation, suggesting risk from excessive autophagy activation (Abokyi et al., 2020, pp. 11–12, 15–16).  
- Primary murine RPE in vitro: A non‐toxic trehalose dose (12.5 mM) increased autophagic flux measured by tandem GFP–RFP-LC3B, increasing RFP+ autolysosomes and RFP:GFP ratios without accumulating GFP+ autophagosomes, with colocalization to LysoTracker+ acidic compartments; trehalose also attenuated H₂O₂-induced mitochondrial superoxide and restored maximal respiration (Cox et al., 2025, pp. 7–10). These data indicate trehalose enhances autophagosome–lysosome fusion and downstream degradative flux in RPE under oxidative stress (Cox et al., 2025, pp. 7–10).  
- iPSC-derived human RPE carrying the CFH Y402H risk allele (CFH (H/H)): Trehalose (100 mM, 20–48 h) restored levels and enzymatic activities of lysosomal hydrolases Cathepsin D and Cathepsin L and rescued LAMP1 in complement challenge models, phenocopying constitutively nuclear TFEB (TFEB-S467A) and AKT2 inhibition; these data support trehalose as an mTOR-independent TFEB activator that rejuvenates lysosomal function in AMD-relevant RPE (Ghosh et al., 2024, p. 6; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 10–11).  
- Ex vivo/in vivo lysosomal/autophagy disease models: In Cryba1 KO RPE explants with lysosomal defects, trehalose rescued CLEAR gene expression and autophagy flux; in Cryba1 conditional KO and Akt2 knock-in mice, a regimen of 1 mg/g/day intraperitoneal trehalose for 2 days followed by 2% w/v in drinking water for 3 months starting at 6 months of age restored lysosomal function in RPE, rescued CLEAR network gene expression, and prevented early Bruch’s membrane basal deposit formation that typically emerges by 9 months (Ghosh et al., 2023, pp. 11–15; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 6–8).  
- Topical trehalose in mice with acute outer retinal stress: Twice-daily eyedrops of 9% trehalose for seven days before and after light-induced outer retinal degeneration (LIRD) reduced ONL thinning by ~53%, preserved RPE morphology and F-actin junctions, and increased LC3B and LAMP1 with decreased p62 in the RPE, consistent with enhanced autophagy-lysosome engagement in vivo (Cox et al., 2025, pp. 8–13). Clinical use  
- No clinical trials or clinical case series for trehalose in atrophic AMD or geographic atrophy (GA) are reported in the provided context (Abokyi et al., 2020, pp. 1–2; Cox et al., 2025, pp. 1–2). AMD-relevant lysosome–autophagy context in RPE  
- The RPE is exceptionally reliant on lysosomal degradation for both autophagy and daily heterophagy of photoreceptor outer segments (POS), and lysosomal ion homeostasis, including proton pump activity, determines acidification and hydrolase function; age-related lipofuscin accumulation, often oxidized and crosslinked, compromises lysosomal integrity and can promote lysosomal membrane permeabilization (LMP), driving cathepsin release and cell death cascades (Boya et al., 2023, pp. 3–4, 4–6). The mTORC1–TFEB/TFE3 axis regulates lysosomal biogenesis; TFEB dephosphorylation and nuclear translocation induce CLEAR network genes, including lysosomal hydrolases and V-ATPase subunits, while pathological signals (amino acid–Ragulator–Rag GTPases, AKT, and mTORC1) can sequester TFEB/TFE3 in the cytoplasm, thereby undermining lysosomal biogenesis (Boya et al., 2023, pp. 3–4, 4–6). In AMD models, impaired lysosomal acidification (e.g., via βA3/A1-crystallin deficits) and hyperactive mTORC1 reduce TFEB/TFE3 nuclear translocation, LAMP2 function, and degradative capacity, phenocopying AMD-relevant delays in phagosome degradation and lipofuscin handling (Boya et al., 2023, pp. 4–6). Human AMD RPE shows reduced CTSD and CTSL protein levels and activities, and increased TFEB phosphorylation with reduced nuclear TFEB staining, further linking impaired TFEB signaling and hydrolase deficiencies to AMD pathophysiology (Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7).

Trehalose: TFEB pathway engagement and autophagy–lysosome restoration

In ex vivo Cryba1 KO RPE (a lysosomal pH/ion-homeostasis-related defect model), trehalose rescued CLEAR gene expression and autophagy flux, and in vivo chronic trehalose treatment (IP loading followed by 2% oral) restored lysosomal function in RPE and prevented basal deposit formation, while not attenuating abnormal mTORC1 activation, consistent with an mTOR-independent route to TFEB activation (Ghosh et al., 2023, pp. 11–15; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 6–8).  
- In primary murine RPE, trehalose enhances autophagosome maturation and autolysosome formation (tandem GFP–RFP-LC3B reporter), with RFP colocalization to LysoTracker+ acidic compartments, indicating augmented flux through acidified lysosomes; this occurred at a low, non-toxic concentration (12.5 mM), and was functionally coupled to mitochondrial rescue under oxidative stress (Cox et al., 2025, pp. 7–8, 8–10). In ARPE-19 cells, trehalose increased TFEB protein levels, autophagy genes (ATG5, ATG7), LAMP2, LC3, p62, and Cathepsin D protein, and protection from HQ oxidant injury required intact autophagy (ATG5-dependent), illustrating an autophagy-centric cytoprotective mechanism in human RPE cells (Abokyi et al., 2020, pp. 1–2, 11–13).

Pharmacologic AKT2 inhibition or constitutively nuclear TFEB rescue CLEAR targets and degradative fusion; trehalose’s phenocopying of these interventions in the same models underscores TFEB pathway engagement, but again without direct trehalose-specific TFEB nuclear localization assays in RPE in the provided texts (Ghosh et al., 2024, p. 6; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 10–11).

Assay-linked molecular readouts and expression in RPE  
- TFEB/TFE3, LAMP1/2, LC3B, SQSTM1/p62, CTSD/CTSL, and V-ATPase subunits (e.g., ATP6V0A1) are expressed in RPE and are central to lysosomal/autophagic function, with CLEAR network control by TFEB; reduced nuclear TFEB and decreased CTSD/L activity are documented in AMD RPE (Boya et al., 2023, pp. 3–4, 4–6; Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7). Given these baselines, RPE is an appropriate cell type to measure trehalose-driven TFEB pathway engagement and lysosomal protease restoration (Boya et al., 2023, pp. 3–4, 4–6; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 10–11).

Translational expectations and delivery  
- Topical dosing: The 3%–9% trehalose eyedrop regimens are feasible and safe in preclinical studies, achieve measurable posterior exposure, and produced autophagy biomarker changes and structural protection in LIRD (Cox et al., 2025, pp. 8–10, 10–13). However, posterior ocular bioavailability is typically low and variable, and much drug is lost systemically, necessitating optimization of formulation and dosing frequency for consistent RPE exposure (Cox et al., 2025, pp. 10–13, 15–16).

Clinical translation will need to address trehalase metabolism and systemic exposure constraints (Cox et al., 2025, pp. 10–13).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Multi-modal preclinical evidence in RPE: Trehalose increases autophagy flux in human ARPE-19 and primary murine RPE, with autolysosome formation confirmed via tandem GFP–RFP-LC3 and LysoTracker colocalization, and cytoprotective effects depend on intact autophagy machinery (ATG5), directly aligning with the mechanistic target in RPE (Cox et al., 2025, pp. 7–8; Abokyi et al., 2020, pp. 1–2, 12–13).  
- Restoration of lysosomal hydrolase content and activity in human iPSC-RPE disease models: Trehalose rescued CTSD/L protein and activity and normalized LAMP1 under complement challenge in CFH Y402H RPE, mechanistically reversing disease-relevant lysosomal deficiencies (Ghosh et al., 2024, p. 6; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 10–11).  
- TFEB pathway engagement, mTOR-independent: Trehalose phenocopies constitutively nuclear TFEB and AKT2 inhibition in rescuing lysosomal/autophagy networks and function, and restores CLEAR transcripts in explants and in vivo without suppressing abnormal mTORC1 activation, suggesting lower risk of mTOR-related adverse effects (Ghosh et al., 2023, pp. 11–15; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 10–11).  
- In vivo efficacy signals: Topical trehalose improves autophagy markers in RPE and preserves ONL and RPE morphology after light stress; chronic systemic dosing prevents basal deposits and rescues lysosomal function in RPE in genetic lysosome-defect models (Cox et al., 2025, pp. 10–13; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 6–8; Ghosh et al., 2023, pp. 11–15).  
- Delivery feasibility and safety: Topical administration at high concentrations (3%–9%) is well tolerated and achieves posterior detection, creating a realistic translational route; topical dosing circumvents trehalase metabolism, a limitation for oral delivery (Cox et al., 2025, pp. 1–2, 8–10, 10–13).

Weaknesses and major gaps relative to the hypothesis  
- Lysosomal acidification not directly demonstrated: No quantitative lysosomal pH measurements with trehalose are reported in the provided RPE datasets; restoration of acidification remains an inference and must be demonstrated directly (Cox et al., 2025, pp. 7–8; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 10–11; Abokyi et al., 2020, pp. 1–2).  
- TFEB nuclear translocation under trehalose unproven in RPE: While trehalose is described as a TFEB activator and phenocopies TFEB-S467A, direct nuclear localization (imaging or fractionation) after trehalose in RPE is not shown here; this is a critical mechanistic gap (Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 10–11; Ghosh et al., 2023, pp. 11–15; Abokyi et al., 2020, pp. 16–17).  
- Lipofuscin/A2E clearance not demonstrated for trehalose: Although TFEB activation and mTOR inhibition are known to reduce A2E/lipofuscin-like granules in RPE models, trehalose-specific evidence for lipofuscin clearance is absent in the supplied materials (Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7).  
- Geographic atrophy endpoints lacking: There are no chronic GA model or clinical data showing trehalose slows lesion growth or preserves vision; LIRD is an acute stress model and does not recapitulate GA progression (Cox et al., 2025, pp. 1–2, 8–10).  
- Dosing translatability: Many in vitro effects were observed at 50–100 mM trehalose, which are high relative to likely in vivo intra-RPE exposures; dose–response optimization is needed, and excessive dosing risks autophagy-associated cytotoxicity (Abokyi et al., 2020, pp. 12–13, 15–16; Cox et al., 2025, pp. 7–8).  
- Source quality heterogeneity: Some supportive RPE studies come from lower-quality journals or preprints, warranting independent replication under rigorously controlled conditions (Abokyi et al., 2020, pp. 1–2; Ghosh et al., 2023, pp. 11–15).

Risk–benefit and development recommendations  
- Mechanistic verification package:  
  - Quantify lysosomal pH restoration with LysoSensor/DND-160 ratiometry and V-ATPase subunit/activity assays in RPE models ± trehalose, including disease-relevant stress (e.g., complement challenge, A2E loading) (Boya et al., 2023, pp. 3–4, 4–6).  
  - Directly quantify TFEB nuclear translocation (immunocytochemistry with nuclear segmentation; nuclear/cytosolic fractionation and immunoblotting) under trehalose vs. TFEB-S467A and vs. AKT2 inhibition, to confirm that trehalose’s phenotypic rescue is TFEB-dependent in RPE (Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 6, 10–11).  
  - CTSD/CTSL processing and activity: Extend the CFH (H/H) results by testing trehalose across primary human RPE and AMD-donor–derived RPE; relate CTSD activity rescue to autophagic flux endpoints (LC3 turnover, p62 degradation) and to substrate clearance (POS proteolysis kinetics) (Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 6, 10–11; Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7).  
  - Lipofuscin/A2E clearance: In A2E-loaded and POS-fed RPE, quantify autofluorescence granules and A2E mass spectrometry before/after trehalose, and test dependence on TFEB (siRNA/CRISPR) and lysosomal hydrolase inhibition (e.g., pepstatin-A for CTSD) (Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7, 7–9).  
- PK/PD and delivery optimization:  
  - For topical delivery, map trehalose concentration–time in RPE/choroid and retina with LC-MS or validated Raman signatures; explore permeation enhancers or sustained-release formulations to overcome low posterior bioavailability (Cox et al., 2025, pp. 8–10, 10–13, 15–16).  
  - Define an ocular PD biomarker panel (RPE LC3B/LAMP1 colocalization, p62 decrease, CTSD activity) and link to functional readouts (ERG, OCT metrics) in chronic complement- or lipofuscin-based models (Cox et al., 2025, pp. 10–13).  
- Comparative and combinatorial strategy:  
  - Benchmark trehalose against TFEB-centric comparators (e.g., rapalogs, Ezrin inhibitors) on shared endpoints (TFEB nuclear index, lysosomal pH, CTSD activity, lipofuscin clearance), given rapamycin’s ability to reduce A2E/lipofuscin via TFEB activation and the potential of ezrin blockade to increase lysosome number and cathepsin activity in RPE (Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7, 7–9; Boya et al., 2023, pp. 4–6).  
  - Consider combination with complement modulation where indicated, as complement stress contributes to AMD-relevant lysosomal dysfunction in CFH (H/H) RPE (Ghosh et al., 2024, p. 6).

Go/no-go criteria for advancement toward GA  
- Mechanistic Go: Demonstration in RPE that trehalose increases the TFEB nuclear index by >2-fold, lowers lysosomal pH toward physiological values, and increases CTSD activity by >30% over disease-state baseline, with concordant increases in LC3B–LAMP1 colocalization and p62 degradation; abrogation of effects by TFEB knockdown would confirm mechanism (Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 10–11; Cox et al., 2025, pp. 7–8; Boya et al., 2023, pp. 3–4).  
- Functional Go: Demonstrated reduction of A2E/lipofuscin by ≥25% in RPE models without cytotoxicity, and structural/functional rescue in a chronic AMD-relevant animal model (e.g., CFH-risk or complement-driven models) with durable effects beyond acute stress models (Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7; Cox et al., 2025, pp. 8–10; Ghosh et al., 2024, p. 6).  
- Safety Go: No evidence of autophagy-associated cytotoxicity at the intended exposure (maintained viability; absence of excessive LC3-II accumulation without flux; ocular histopathology clean) (Abokyi et al., 2020, pp. 15–16; Cox et al., 2025, pp. 8–10).

Conclusion  
The totality of evidence supports trehalose as a plausible, repurposable modulator of the TFEB–lysosome/autophagy axis in the RPE with multiple independent signals of autophagy flux enhancement, lysosomal hydrolase restoration (CTSD/L), and cytoprotection in oxidative/complement stress contexts, delivered via mechanisms that appear mTOR-independent and therefore potentially safer than broad mTORC1 inhibition (Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 10–11; Cox et al., 2025, pp. 7–8; Abokyi et al., 2020, pp. 1–2; Ghosh et al., 2023, pp. 11–15). However, the hypothesis’s most stringent claims—quantitative restoration of lysosomal acidification, trehalose-driven TFEB nuclear translocation in RPE, and direct lipofuscin/A2E clearance leading to slowed geographic atrophy progression—are not yet demonstrated in the supplied literature and require targeted mechanistic and disease-model validation (Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 10–11; Abokyi et al., 2020, pp. 16–17; Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7; Cox et al., 2025, pp. 8–10). Given strong biological plausibility and encouraging preclinical signals, a focused IND-enabling program that closes these gaps is justified, with early emphasis on mechanistic biomarkers (lysosomal pH, TFEB nuclear index, CTSD activity), pharmacokinetics of posterior delivery, and chronic AMD-relevant efficacy models before advancing to clinical study in GA (Boya et al., 2023, pp. 3–4; Cox et al., 2025, pp. 10–13; Ghosh et al., 2024, p. 6).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Tocilizumab (Actemra; Roche/Chugai) is a recombinant humanized monoclonal antibody that binds the human interleukin-6 receptor (IL-6R) and blocks IL-6 signal transduction, resulting in systemic anti-inflammatory effects characteristic of IL-6 pathway inhibition (class: humanized anti-IL-6R monoclonal antibody) (Shi, 2017a; Shi, 2017b; Zhujiang Hospital, 2025). In clinical development, tocilizumab has been administered intravenously at 8 mg/kg every 4 weeks and subcutaneously at 162 mg once weekly, with protocols reflecting the infectious, hepatic, hematologic, gastrointestinal, and reproductive safety considerations common to cytokine-targeted biologics (e.g., TB/hepatitis screening, neutrophil/platelet and transaminase thresholds, live-vaccine restrictions, diverticulitis history, and contraception requirements) (Shi, 2017b; University of Nebraska, 2016; Assistance Publique–Hôpitaux de Paris, 2017; Zhujiang Hospital, 2025). Ophthalmic interest in IL-6 blockade is evidenced by prospective trials in non-infectious uveitis and a withdrawn diabetic macular edema (DME) trial; those records establish feasible dosing, ophthalmic outcome collection, and safety oversight but do not provide efficacy data in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (Assistance Publique–Hôpitaux de Paris, 2017; University of Nebraska, 2016). At the disease-biology level, multiple clinical and literature-derived evidences associate IL-6 with AMD, including elevated ocular and systemic IL-6 in AMD populations and genetic associations in some cohorts; Open Targets ranks IL6 as the strongest among selected IL-6 pathway members for AMD relevance in the provided excerpt (Buniello et al., 2025).

Systemic uses and ophthalmic experience: Tocilizumab’s IL-6R blockade is well characterized clinically outside ophthalmology, and controlled ophthalmic trials have evaluated systemic tocilizumab as an investigational agent for posterior-segment, non-infectious uveitis (RUBI), using subcutaneous 162 mg weekly for 16 weeks with retinal structural and visual endpoints and active safety monitoring; the study is listed as completed in the registry excerpt but outcome data are not included here (Assistance Publique–Hôpitaux de Paris, 2017). Drug mechanism: Tocilizumab is a humanized monoclonal antibody that binds to IL-6R and blocks IL-6 signaling, thereby attenuating inflammatory pathways downstream of IL-6R engagement; mechanistic rationales in non-retinal disease emphasize IL-6–dependent survival and differentiation programs (e.g., plasma cells and autoantibody production in NMOSD), with dosing typically at 8 mg/kg IV every 4 weeks or 162 mg SC weekly in the studies cited (Shi, 2017a; Shi, 2017b; Assistance Publique–Hôpitaux de Paris, 2017).

Human retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells produce IL-6, secrete it in a polarized manner, and can engage autocrine/paracrine IL-6/IL-8 loops that drive RPE degeneration after inflammatory challenge (e.g., bacterial endotoxin), supporting the presence of IL-6–responsive circuits in retinal epithelia (Brandstetter, 2016).

AMD-relevant upstream injury nodes: The dominant mechanistic framework for dry AMD implicates chronic oxidative/photooxidative stress, age-related lysosomal decline, and intracellular clearance failure (autophagy/proteasome) in RPE, leading to lipofuscinogenesis, lysosomal membrane permeabilization (LMP), and activation of inflammasome pathways with downstream cytokine release and cell death (apoptosis vs pyroptosis depending on priming) (Brandstetter, 2016; Piippo, 2019). In primary human RPE and ARPE-19 cells, LMP induced chemically (Leu-Leu-OMe) or via blue-light irradiation of POS-derived lipofuscin activates the NLRP3 inflammasome with caspase-1–dependent maturation and release of IL-1β and IL-18; broader cytokine secretion includes IL-6, GM-CSF, and GRO, with IL-6 elevated ≈13.6-fold in a cytokine screen and partially suppressed by caspase-1 inhibition, indicating a secondary induction downstream of inflammasome activation (not direct inflammasome processing) (Brandstetter, 2016). Lysosomal proteases are mechanistically implicated: inhibition of cathepsin B and L suppresses LMP-triggered inflammasome activation in RPE, and cytosolic cathepsins in general, including cathepsin D, can promote apoptosis when released from the lysosome, underscoring the importance of lysosomal integrity in RPE survival (Brandstetter, 2016).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
T0901317 is a fully synthetic small‐molecule agonist originally identified through screening for compounds that activate liver X receptors (LXRs). It belongs to the class of nuclear receptor ligands and is structurally designed to mimic endogenous oxysterols, the natural activators of LXRs. LXRs, comprising two isoforms, LXRα (NR1H3) and LXRβ (NR1H2), are master transcriptional regulators of cholesterol, lipid, and glucose metabolism. T0901317 was first characterized for its capacity to bind and stimulate these receptors, thereby upregulating target genes involved in cholesterol efflux such as ATP-binding cassette transporter A1 (ABCA1) and apolipoprotein E (APOE) (Choudhary et al., 2020, pp. 15–16). The compound has been widely used in preclinical studies to investigate cholesterol homeostasis, inflammation modulation, and emerging neuroprotective pathways. Its chemical synthesis follows standard procedures for developing derivatives that confer high receptor affinity and bioactivity while allowing researchers to dissect LXR-dependent pathways in multiple cell types, including retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells. The rationale behind using such LXR agonists, including T0901317, in ocular disorders like dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) stems from their demonstrated ability to restore cholesterol efflux, ameliorate lipid deposition, and reduce inflammatory stress in target tissues (Choudhary et al., 2020, pp. 12–13).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, T0901317 has been utilized extensively within the biomedical research arena as a tool compound to elucidate the role of LXRs in metabolic and inflammatory diseases. Preclinical work has demonstrated that LXR activation in key tissues, including the retina, can reestablish lipid homeostasis and reduce pathological lipid accumulation. Several studies indicate that in LXR-deficient models, there is an accumulation of neutral lipids and extracellular deposits—features that are remarkably similar to drusen formation observed in early dry AMD (Choudhary et al., 2020, pp. 7–9; Terao et al., 2024, pp. 8–10). In animal models, particularly in mice lacking the Nr1h3 isoform, the phenotype includes RPE dysfunction, inflammatory microenvironment formation, and structural changes that closely mimic human dry AMD pathology (Choudhary et al., 2020, pp. 2–4). Although T0901317 has not advanced to clinical trials for AMD, its efficacy has been primarily established in vitro using human RPE cell models and in vivo in murine models. The compound has shown potential for correcting the dysregulated cholesterol metabolism that contributes to the chronic buildup of lipid-rich drusen—a central pathological hallmark of dry AMD (Choudhary et al., 2020, pp. 12–13, 15–16). Outside of ocular applications, compounds from this class have been investigated for atherosclerosis and neurodegeneration, further emphasizing the critical link between cholesterol metabolism and chronic inflammatory conditions (Malek & Lad, 2014, pp. 13–15).

Mechanism of Action:  
The mechanism of action of T0901317 is fundamentally tied to its role as a potent activator of LXRs. Upon binding to LXRα and LXRβ within retinal cells, T0901317 facilitates heterodimerization with retinoid X receptors (RXRs), forming a transcriptionally active complex that binds to LXR response elements (LXREs) in the promoter regions of target genes. This activation cascade results in upregulation of numerous genes critical for cholesterol efflux and lipid metabolism, most notably ABCA1 and APOE (Choudhary et al., 2020, pp. 15–16). Upregulation of ABCA1 increases the efflux of excess cholesterol and oxidized lipids from RPE cells into the extracellular environment, thereby reducing the intracellular lipid load that predisposes cells to toxicity and drusen accumulation (Choudhary et al., 2020, pp. 12–13; Wu et al., 2023, pp. 10–12).

Beyond cholesterol efflux, T0901317 activates additional gene networks that modulate lysosomal function and autophagy. Experimental data suggest that T0901317 enhances the expression of lysosomal hydrolases, including cathepsin D (CTSD), and promotes the assembly of vacuolar-type H⁺-ATPases (v-ATPase), essential for maintaining lysosomal acidity (Lei et al., 2017, pp. 13–17, 20–22). This increase in active lysosomal enzymes and reinforced acidification contributes to the improved clearance of debris, particularly drusen components composed of lipid and protein aggregates. Furthermore, LXR activation by T0901317 has been shown to increase autophagy gene expression, thereby inducing a mitophagy response that removes damaged organelles and supports cellular metabolic renewal (Terao et al., 2024, pp. 8–10; Xie et al., 2022, pp. 1–2). In addition, T0901317 exerts significant anti-inflammatory effects by downregulating NF-κB signaling. It has been observed to inhibit the phosphorylation of IκBα, which prevents the nuclear translocation of NF-κB and subsequent transcription of inflammatory cytokines such as TNF-α and IL-6 (Lei et al., 2017, pp. 13–17; Choudhary & Malek, 2016, pp. 4–6). This dual role in lipid regulation and inflammation attenuation is central to its therapeutic promise in AMD, where chronic inflammation and disrupted lipid processing are major determinants of disease progression.

Expected Effect:  
In the context of dry AMD, with its hallmark drusen deposits and RPE dysfunction, the expected therapeutic effect of T0901317 is multifold. By activating LXRs in RPE cells, T0901317 is expected to upregulate the expression of ABCA1 and other cholesterol efflux mediators, thereby reducing the intracellular build‐up of cholesterol and oxidized lipids that contribute to drusen formation (Choudhary et al., 2020, pp. 2–4). This increase in cholesterol efflux would allow the RPE to better clear lipid debris, lowering the overall lipid burden on Bruch’s membrane. Concomitantly, the drug’s capacity to augment lysosomal function is anticipated to result in improved clearance of extracellular drusen components via a cathepsin D–dependent mechanism. Enhanced v-ATPase assembly and lysosomal acidification, as demonstrated by increased CTSD activity in vitro, should restore the degradative capacity of the lysosomal system, thereby facilitating the removal of protein-lipid aggregates (Lei et al., 2017, pp. 25–33).

Furthermore, the activation of autophagy pathways and promotion of mitophagy are expected to counteract the mitochondrial dysfunction that characterizes aged RPE cells—an integral pathological feature of dry AMD (Choudhary et al., 2020, pp. 7–9, 2–4). The anticipated result is a restoration of cellular homeostasis, improved energy metabolism, and reduction in oxidative stress, all of which are essential for maintaining RPE cell integrity. RPE cells have been shown to express both LXRα and LXRβ, and their expression is frequently diminished in AMD-affected eyes (Choudhary et al., 2020, pp. 12–13; Lyssenko et al., 2018, pp. 1–3). Therefore, by boosting LXR activity, T0901317 not only counteracts lipid dysregulation but also provides a neuroprotective, anti-inflammatory benefit by modulating cytokine production and dampening microglial activation in the outer retina (Choudhary & Malek, 2016, pp. 4–6).

Overall Evaluation:  
The overall assessment of T0901317 as a therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration is cautiously optimistic, with several key strengths as well as notable limitations that warrant further investigation.  

Strengths:  
One of the primary advantages of T0901317 is its well-documented ability to activate LXRs and thereby induce a broad spectrum of beneficial responses relevant to dry AMD pathology. The compound’s capacity to upregulate ABCA1 expression is critical, as impaired cholesterol efflux is a central mechanism underlying the accumulation of lipid-rich drusen (Choudhary et al., 2020, pp. 15–16, 12–13). Moreover, its ability to enhance lysosomal enzyme expression and promote v-ATPase assembly is particularly promising for the restoration of lysosomal acidity—a key defect in aged RPE cells that contributes to decreased clearance of toxic lipid deposits (Lei et al., 2017, pp. 13–17, 20–22). In addition, the induction of autophagy and mitophagy following LXR activation offers a dual therapeutic benefit by promoting the removal of damaged mitochondria and reducing oxidative stress, thereby preserving RPE cell viability (Xie et al., 2022, pp. 1–2). The anti-inflammatory properties of T0901317, demonstrated by its inhibition of NF-κB signaling and reduction of pro-inflammatory cytokine production, further support its potential utility in addressing the chronic low-grade inflammation often observed in AMD (Choudhary & Malek, 2016, pp. 4–6). Collectively, these mechanisms directly target the multifactorial aspects of dry AMD pathology—namely, lipid dysregulation, lysosomal dysfunction, and inflammatory stress—making T0901317 an attractive candidate for repurposing in this indication (Choudhary et al., 2020, pp. 2–4).

Another significant strength is the potential for ocular delivery strategies to mitigate the systemic side effects associated with T0901317. Given that systemic administration of LXR agonists has been linked to adverse metabolic effects such as hypertriglyceridemia and off-target activation of nuclear receptors like FXR and PXR (Lei et al., 2017, pp. 20–22; Storti et al., 2019, pp. 15–16), localized ocular delivery could concentrate the drug’s therapeutic effects in the retina while minimizing systemic exposure. This approach may overcome one of the principal limitations of T0901317 and reposition it as a viable option specifically for retinal applications.

Weaknesses and Challenges:  
Despite these promising attributes, there are several challenges that temper the enthusiasm for T0901317 as a first-in-class therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. A well-recognized limitation of T0901317 is its lack of absolute specificity for LXRs. Its ability to activate other nuclear receptors such as FXR and PXR raises concerns about off-target effects that could lead to dysregulated lipid metabolism in non-ocular tissues, systemic toxicity, and unwanted metabolic side effects such as hepatic steatosis and hyperlipidemia (Lei et al., 2017, pp. 20–22). Moreover, while preclinical evidence in cell culture and murine models has shown that LXR activation can reverse lipid accumulation and partially restore RPE cell function, the translation of such effects to the human condition—especially over the chronic time course of dry AMD—remains to be conclusively demonstrated (Choudhary et al., 2020, pp. 12–13, 7–9).

Another challenge lies in the fact that many preclinical studies have used alternative LXR agonists such as GW3965, which may exhibit a more favorable safety profile compared to T0901317 (Choudhary et al., 2020, pp. 9–11; Peters et al., 2022, pp. 11–12). The potential differences in selectivity and off-target activity between T0901317 and these other compounds necessitate a careful comparison. It is possible that while T0901317 has provided invaluable mechanistic insights into LXR biology in the retina, compounds with improved specificity may eventually be more amenable to clinical development. Furthermore, the specific hypothesis regarding T0901317’s ability to enhance lysosomal acidity and cathepsin D-dependent clearance of drusen components is based on in vitro observations, and there is still a need for more comprehensive studies that document these effects in animal models that recapitulate the chronic aspects of dry AMD pathology (Lei et al., 2017, pp. 25–33; Choudhary et al., 2020, pp. 2–4).

Additionally, because the retinal environment is highly specialized and the RPE plays a central role in maintaining photoreceptor health, any therapeutic approach must carefully balance metabolic reprogramming with preservation of essential RPE functions. Overactivation of autophagy or lysosomal pathways might conceivably lead to other cellular stresses if not properly calibrated. Thus, while the theoretical framework for T0901317’s benefit in dry AMD is strong, detailed pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic studies in appropriate models are essential before moving this candidate further along the drug development pathway.

Conclusion:  
In conclusion, T0901317 demonstrates considerable promise as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration based on its ability to activate LXR in RPE cells, thereby inducing cholesterol efflux via ABCA1 upregulation, enhancing lysosomal function through increased expression of hydrolases like cathepsin D, promoting autophagy and mitophagy, and reducing inflammation by dampening NF-κB signaling (Choudhary et al., 2020, pp. 12–13; Terao et al., 2024, pp. 8–10).

The strengths of T0901317 lie in its robust mechanistic rationale, the preclinical evidence supporting LXR-mediated restoration of cholesterol homeostasis, and the potential for localized ocular delivery to minimize systemic toxicities. However, its known off-target effects, particularly activation of other nuclear receptor pathways that can lead to metabolic side effects, present a significant hurdle that must be addressed through formulation optimization and dosing strategies (Lei et al., 2017, pp. 20–22; Storti et al., 2019, pp. 15–16). Furthermore, while the mechanistic underpinnings are appealing, further in vivo validation in chronic, clinically relevant AMD models is essential to confirm that the improvements in cholesterol efflux and lysosomal function translate into meaningful therapeutic outcomes—in terms of slowing or reversing the progression of dry AMD. Overall, T0901317 represents a promising, though challenging, candidate for addressing the unmet need in dry AMD therapy. Investment in additional preclinical studies focusing on ocular bioavailability, long-term safety in the retinal microenvironment, and optimization of dosing regimens will be critical in determining whether T0901317 or a similarly acting, perhaps more selective, LXR agonist can progress into clinical evaluation for dry AMD. The strategic focus on lipid-driven dysfunction, particularly in lysosomal clearance pathways, offers a novel mechanism of action that could complement or serve as an alternative to current therapeutic approaches, making T0901317 (or its optimized derivatives) a compelling candidate for further investigation (Choudhary et al., 2020, pp. 2–4, 7–9, 13–17).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Eculizumab (Soliris, Alexion) is a humanized IgG monoclonal antibody derived from the murine anti–human C5 antibody m5G1 via CDR grafting and human framework engineering to reduce immunogenicity and extend serum half-life, designed to bind complement component C5 with high affinity and sterically prevent its cleavage by C5 convertases into C5a and C5b (thereby blocking terminal pathway activation and MAC assembly) (Park et al., 2019; Troutbeck et al., 2012; Yehoshua et al., 2014; Park et al., 2021). It belongs to the class of complement inhibitors that directly target an effector protein (C5) at the convergence of the classical, lectin, and alternative pathways, in contrast to upstream amplification-targeting agents (e.g., C3 or factor D inhibitors) (Park et al., 2019; Tzoumas et al., 2023). Systemically administered eculizumab has established clinical utility in complement-mediated hematologic and renal disorders, including paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria and atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome, and more recently generalized myasthenia gravis, reflecting a mature pharmacology and a well-characterized risk profile centered on increased susceptibility to encapsulated organisms (notably meningococcal infection) due to terminal pathway blockade (Park et al., 2019; Yehoshua et al., 2014).

Within ophthalmology, the terminal complement pathway is an attractive target for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) and geographic atrophy (GA) because C5a is a proinflammatory anaphylatoxin detected in drusen that can drive leukocyte recruitment and VEGF induction in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), and C5b nucleates formation of the membrane attack complex (MAC, C5b–C9), which accumulates with age and AMD in Bruch’s membrane and choriocapillaris and can lyse or sub-lytically activate choroidal endothelial and RPE cells (Kassa et al., 2019). The class of C5 inhibitors therefore aims to reduce both inflammatory signaling (via C5a) and cytolytic/proinflammatory MAC effects while preserving upstream opsonization and some host-defense functions mediated by C3b, potentially retaining aspects of immune competence relative to C3 inhibition (Halawa et al., 2021; Park et al., 2019).

Therapeutic History  
Approved indications and systemic pharmacology  
Eculizumab is FDA/EMA approved for paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria and atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome, where weight-based intravenous regimens achieve sustained trough serum concentrations and complete inhibition of hemolytic activity by blocking C5 cleavage; these regimens produce serum levels > 35 μg/mL and complete systemic C5 functional blockade, but require meningococcal vaccination to mitigate Neisseria risk inherent to terminal complement inhibition (Park et al., 2019; Yehoshua et al., 2014). In other complementopathies, clinical experience has highlighted a mechanism-consequent shift of pathology upstream (e.g., C3-loading and extravascular hemolysis in PNH under C5 blockade), underscoring that C5 inhibition leaves C3 activation intact (Hammadi et al., 2023).

Clinical investigation in geographic atrophy of dry AMD  
Eculizumab was investigated in the prospective, randomized, double-masked, single-center Phase 2 COMPLETE study that enrolled 30 participants with GA (primary cohort) plus an intermediate AMD/drusen cohort, randomized 2:1 to intravenous eculizumab versus saline over 24 weeks (with follow-up to 52 weeks) (Yehoshua et al., 2014). Two dosing regimens were tested: a low-dose arm (600 mg weekly × 4, then 900 mg every 2 weeks through week 24) and a high-dose arm with higher induction and maintenance dosing; all patients received meningococcal vaccination prior to first infusion (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Patel et al., 2022). Pharmacokinetically, systemic exposure and target engagement were confirmed: eculizumab concentrations were measurable at all assessed time points (mean ~ 65–189 μg/mL in low-dose and ~ 122–259 μg/mL in high-dose cohorts), with plasma C5 activity reduced to < 9% by week 1 and < 1% by week 2, indicating complete systemic terminal complement blockade sustained through treatment (Yehoshua et al., 2014).

Despite robust systemic pharmacodynamics, COMPLETE detected no effect on GA progression: at 26 weeks the change in square-root–transformed GA area was 0.19 ± 0.12 mm in eculizumab-treated eyes versus 0.18 ± 0.15 mm with placebo (P = 0.96), and at 52 weeks both arms exhibited ~ 0.37 mm enlargement (P ≈ 0.93), effectively excluding a large treatment effect (> 55% slowing) in this cohort (Yehoshua et al., 2014). Drusen volume endpoints in the intermediate AMD cohort were also negative (no participant achieved a 50% reduction), and fellow-eye analyses mirrored primary-eye results (Patel et al., 2022; Yehoshua et al., 2014). Visual function showed no durable benefit: a 26-week letter gain difference favoring eculizumab was attributed to a single outlier in placebo, and by 52 weeks there was no between-group difference; pooled estimates across small RCTs rated the certainty of BCVA effects as low-to-very-low with confidence intervals overlapping no effect (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Tzoumas et al., 2023). Safety was acceptable in the trial: no drug-related serious adverse events were identified through 52 weeks, and no eyes converted to neovascular AMD during the study; however, systemic C5 blockade requires vaccination and vigilance for meningococcal infection, and an independent systemic anti-C5 AMD trial was terminated early due to uncertainty about risk/benefit in light of reported meningococcal infections in real-world eculizumab users (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Tzoumas et al., 2023).

Interpretations from COMPLETE and subsequent reviews point to several plausible explanations for the null result: inadequate intraocular/RPE target engagement with systemic dosing due to blood–retinal and Bruch’s barriers; the possibility that C5 is the wrong target in GA given genetic associations that more strongly implicate proximal complement components (e.g., C3, CFH) rather than terminal pathway constituents; the short on-treatment window (24 weeks) and small sample size; and the biological reality that C5 inhibition preserves upstream C3a/C3b biology, which may continue to drive pathology (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Halawa et al., 2021; Hammadi et al., 2023; Tzoumas et al., 2023).

Comparative C5 and complement-targeting experience in AMD  
Intravitreal C5 inhibition has produced divergent results. LFG316 (tesidolumab), an anti-C5 monoclonal antibody administered intravitreally, failed to alter GA lesion growth or visual outcomes in a randomized phase 2 trial (Halawa et al., 2021; Park et al., 2019). By contrast, avacincaptad pegol (Zimura), an intravitreal C5 aptamer, reduced GA growth rates by approximately 27–30% over 12–18 months in pivotal trials, leading to FDA approval, although potential increased risk of macular neovascularization has been signaled and requires ongoing pharmacovigilance (Patel et al., 2022; Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023; Tzoumas et al., 2023). Upstream targeting at C3 with intravitreal pegcetacoplan (SYFOVRE) significantly slowed GA enlargement in phase 2–3 programs and achieved regulatory approval, but at the cost of increased rates of conversion to exudative AMD and, in the postmarketing setting, reports of occlusive retinal vasculitis, highlighting a target-dependent safety trade-off between efficacy and pro-angiogenic/immune-privilege perturbation risks (Halawa et al., 2021; Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023; Qin et al., 2024). Alternative-pathway inhibition via factor D (lampalizumab) produced a phase 2 signal but failed in two phase 3 trials, suggesting that partial pathway blockade may be insufficient in GA (Piri & Kaplan, 2023; Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023).

Taken together, these data place systemic eculizumab among C5-directed strategies where local delivery has demonstrated anatomic efficacy in GA, whereas systemic delivery has not, and they highlight that complement modulation can slow atrophy progression without improving visual function and may introduce target- and route-specific risks such as neovascularization or serious infection (Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023; Tzoumas et al., 2023).

Mechanism of Action  
Complement cascade biology and eculizumab target engagement  
Complement activation arises via classical, lectin, and alternative pathways, converging at the generation of C3 convertases that cleave C3 into C3a (anaphylatoxin) and C3b (opsonin/convertase component), with amplification by the alternative pathway accounting for the majority (80–90%) of downstream MAC generation in physiologic and pathologic settings (Tzoumas et al., 2023). C5 convertases (C4b2a3b for classical/lectin and C3bBbC3b for alternative pathway) cleave C5 into C5a, a potent anaphylatoxin that recruits/activates myeloid cells and stimulates RPE to produce VEGF and proinflammatory cytokines, and C5b, which seeds assembly of the terminal membrane attack complex (C5b–C9) on nearby membranes (Tzoumas et al., 2023; Kassa et al., 2019). Eculizumab binds C5 to prevent convertase-mediated cleavage, thereby abrogating both C5a generation and MAC formation independent of the initiating pathway; this preserves upstream C3 activation (C3a/C3b) and the alternative-pathway amplification loop while blunting terminal effector functions (Park et al., 2019; Halawa et al., 2021).

Ocular and RPE relevance of C5 and MAC  
Multiple lines of evidence implicate terminal pathway effectors in AMD pathophysiology at the RPE–choriocapillaris interface. Histopathology shows increasing MAC deposition with aging and AMD in Bruch’s membrane and the choriocapillaris; sub-lytic MAC on choroidal endothelial cells triggers pro-angiogenic/proteolytic responses (VEGF, MMPs), while high-level deposition can induce lysis of choroidal endothelial cells and bystander injury contributing to RPE atrophy (Kassa et al., 2019). C5a is present in drusen and is a strong inflammatory mediator that can recruit immune cells and induce VEGF release from RPE, linking terminal pathway activation to both atrophic and neovascular processes relevant to the AMD spectrum (Kassa et al., 2019). Additional experimental work demonstrates that sub-lytic C5b-9 can alter RPE function in ways consistent with AMD, including stress responses and secretory changes, reinforcing that terminal complement activation can be injurious to the RPE even in the absence of frank lysis (Park et al., 2019).

Complement production and regulation in the eye—and systemic versus local contributions  
Complement proteins are synthesized predominantly by the liver and circulate systemically, but they are also produced locally within ocular tissues (retina, RPE, choroid), with local activation and regulation shaped by cell-intrinsic complement regulatory proteins (e.g., CFH, CD46, CD59) and by oxidative stress effects that reduce cell-surface complement inhibition on RPE (Tzoumas et al., 2023; van Lookeren Campagne et al., 2016). Several studies highlight local complement expression and activation in retinal cells and macrophages, as well as increased local complement turnover preceding clinical disease, supporting the concept of an ocular complement “microenvironment” that can be dysregulated independent of systemic levels (Patel et al., 2022; Piri & Kaplan, 2023). Conversely, transcriptomic mapping suggests that posterior-pole tissues have limited local transcription of lectin and terminal pathway components (except C5 and C7), implying reliance on systemic sources for some terminal pathway proteins, which in principle could make systemic C5 blockade effective if sufficient intraocular penetration and target engagement are achieved (Troutbeck et al., 2012). These seemingly conflicting observations are reconciled by recognizing that both local production and systemic supply contribute to ocular complement biology, and that their relative importance likely varies by compartment (RPE, choriocapillaris, sub-RPE space), disease stage, and barrier integrity.

Genetic and biomarker context for C5 targeting in AMD  
GWAS and biomarker studies have repeatedly implicated complement dysregulation in AMD susceptibility and progression, including associations at CFH, C3, C2/CFB, CFI, and C9 loci, and elevated systemic and ocular concentrations of complement activation products (C3a, C5a, MAC) in AMD patients (Dascalu et al., 2024). However, the genetic signal is stronger and more consistent for proximal regulators (e.g., CFH, C3) than for C5, and at least one analysis noted C3 risk alleles do not necessarily correlate with GA progression (and in some contexts associated with decreased progression), emphasizing the complexity of translating susceptibility signals to progression biology and target selection in late AMD (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Halawa et al., 2021). Mechanistically, C5 blockade leaves upstream C3a/C3b biology intact; in extra-ocular diseases this can unmask C3-related pathophysiology under C5 inhibition, illustrating a general limitation of terminal pathway-only targeting (Hammadi et al., 2023). In GA, this implies that C3a/C3b-driven processes—chemoattraction, opsonization, and immune modulation—could continue in the outer retina/RPE even under complete C5 suppression, potentially blunting the benefit of C5-only therapy (Halawa et al., 2021; Tzoumas et al., 2023).

Therapeutic delivery constraints to ocular complement modulation with systemic C5 blockade  
Large biologics such as eculizumab face formidable physical barriers to ocular penetration, including the inner and outer blood–retina barriers and Bruch’s membrane/RPE tight junctions, whose permeability declines with increasing molecular weight and hydrophilicity (a profile characteristic of IgG antibodies), making intraocular access by systemic dosing uncertain without active transport mechanisms (Hammadi et al., 2023; Yehoshua et al., 2014). This is the most straightforward explanation for COMPLETE’s combination of complete systemic pharmacodynamic suppression with no effect on lesion enlargement: the effective intraocular concentration of antibody at relevant RPE–choroid interfaces was likely insufficient to inhibit terminal complement activation locally, a conclusion echoed by the trial investigators (Yehoshua et al., 2014).

Expected Effect  
Proposed pharmacologic and cellular effect  
Under the working hypothesis, systemic eculizumab would reduce MAC formation on RPE and choroidal endothelial surfaces and diminish C5a-driven inflammatory signaling, thereby protecting RPE cellular homeostasis and the RPE–choriocapillaris unit from complement-mediated injury and slowing expansion of GA lesions (Kassa et al., 2019; Park et al., 2019). Mechanistically, suppression of MAC would be expected to decrease lytic and sub-lytic injury to choroidal endothelial cells and RPE, attenuating downstream induction of VEGF and MMPs, and limiting bystander tissue damage around atrophic borders where complement activation is thought to be active (Tzoumas et al., 2023; Kassa et al., 2019). Reducing C5a generation could blunt recruitment and activation of myeloid cells and RPE proinflammatory cytokine production, decreasing local inflammatory amplification in the outer retina (Tzoumas et al., 2023; Kassa et al., 2019).

Expression and target presence in relevant cells/tissues  
C5 and terminal pathway components are present in the ocular compartments relevant to GA pathobiology: choriocapillaris/Bruch’s membrane deposition of MAC is well documented and increases with age and AMD, and C5a is detected within drusen; RPE-derived complement regulators (e.g., CD59) and choroidal endothelial susceptibility to MAC are described, establishing both target and downstream effectors within the disease-relevant tissues (Kassa et al., 2019). Complement components and regulators are expressed in retina, RPE, and choroid, with transcriptomic data indicating relatively higher choroidal expression and limited local transcription of some terminal components (except C5 and C7), consistent with both local and systemic sources contributing substrate for terminal pathway assembly (Troutbeck et al., 2012; Tzoumas et al., 2023).

Translational and clinical outcome expectations  
At the disease level, a therapy that meaningfully reduces local terminal complement activation in GA should slow the rate of GA lesion enlargement measured on fundus autofluorescence (FAF) and/or SD-OCT, endpoints accepted by the FDA/NEI and standard across GA trials; functional outcomes such as BCVA and low-luminance VA typically lag structural changes and may not improve even when lesion growth is slowed (Dascalu et al., 2024; Qin et al., 2024). In COMPLETE, these endpoints were precisely those evaluated; the absence of any measurable effect on square-root GA area at 26 and 52 weeks indicates that, at the tested systemic dosing regimens, eculizumab did not achieve sufficient intraocular target engagement to translate the mechanistic rationale into clinical benefit (Yehoshua et al., 2014).

Reasons for divergence between expected and observed effects  
Three non-exclusive explanations align with the totality of evidence:

  • Inadequate intraocular bioavailability from systemic dosing. Antibody size and hydrophilicity, combined with blood–retina and RPE–Bruch’s barriers, likely prevented sufficient drug from reaching the RPE–choriocapillaris compartment to inhibit local terminal pathway activation, despite verified systemic C5 suppression (Hammadi et al., 2023; Yehoshua et al., 2014; Tzoumas et al., 2023).

  • Target selection may be suboptimal for GA biology. The stronger genetic and pathophysiologic evidence for proximal complement dysregulation (e.g., C3, CFH) and the preservation of upstream activation under C5 blockade mean that C5-only inhibition may not adequately suppress the complement-driven processes that sustain GA border expansion, as supported by the comparatively stronger clinical signals with C3 inhibition and mixed-to-positive signals with intravitreal C5 inhibition (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Halawa et al., 2021; Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023).

  • Trial limitations. The COMPLETE cohort was small and on-treatment duration was six months, which may be insufficient to observe smaller effects on GA growth; however, confidence intervals excluded large effects, and lack of any trend over 52 weeks reduces the likelihood that longer dosing would have changed the outcome meaningfully (Yehoshua et al., 2014).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
  • Strong mechanistic rationale for terminal pathway blockade in AMD: C5a is proinflammatory and detected in drusen; MAC accumulates at the RPE–choriocapillaris interface with age/AMD and can injure choroidal endothelium and RPE via lytic and sub-lytic mechanisms, linking C5 effector functions directly to AMD pathophysiology (Kassa et al., 2019). Blocking C5 suppresses both MAC and C5a, targeting inflammatory and cytolytic arms while leaving upstream C3-mediated opsonization intact, an immunologic advantage over C3 blockade (Halawa et al., 2021; Park et al., 2019).

  • Mature systemic pharmacology with demonstrated ability to completely suppress plasma C5 activity at well-tolerated doses, including in AMD patients, making systemic development logistically straightforward and with known requirements (e.g., meningococcal vaccination) (Yehoshua et al., 2014).

  • Practical systemic-delivery advantages: single systemic therapy treats both eyes simultaneously and avoids intravitreal injection–related ocular risks (endophthalmitis, IOP spikes), which have nontrivial incidence in chronic IVT regimens (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Tzoumas et al., 2023).

  • External validation within the class: intravitreal C5 inhibition (avacincaptad pegol) has replicated GA-slowing effects in phase 2/3 programs, supporting the therapeutic value of suppressing terminal pathway activity in the outer retina if adequate local exposure is achieved (Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023).

Limitations  
  • Lack of efficacy in the definitive systemic eculizumab GA study. COMPLETE showed no reduction in GA lesion growth at 26 or 52 weeks despite complete systemic C5 blockade and adequate serum exposure, effectively excluding a large treatment effect and arguing strongly against systemic eculizumab as a viable GA therapy (Yehoshua et al., 2014).

  • Ocular pharmacokinetic barrier. The most parsimonious explanation for the COMPLETE result is inadequate intraocular target engagement from systemic dosing due to the blood–retina/RPE–Bruch’s barriers and the large size/hydrophilicity of IgG, an inherent limitation of systemic antibody delivery to the sub-RPE/choroidal compartment (Hammadi et al., 2023; Yehoshua et al., 2014).

  • Target-level uncertainties. Genetic and biomarker studies more consistently implicate proximal complement dysregulation (CFH/C3) than C5 in AMD susceptibility; moreover, C5 inhibition preserves upstream C3a/C3b activity, which may continue to drive border-zone inflammation and remodeling in GA (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Dascalu et al., 2024; Halawa et al., 2021). Clinical comparisons reinforce this: upstream C3 inhibition has produced larger and more consistent anatomic effects (with important safety trade-offs), whereas anti-C5 trials are split—systemic eculizumab negative; IVT LFG316 negative; IVT avacincaptad positive—pointing to delivery and target–context dependencies (Halawa et al., 2021; Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023).

  • Systemic safety constraints. While COMPLETE itself reported no drug-related serious adverse events over one year, terminal complement blockade carries a class risk of meningococcal infection requiring vaccination and risk mitigation; at least one planned AMD systemic anti-C5 trial was terminated early due to uncertainty regarding the systemic infection risk/benefit in this population (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Tzoumas et al., 2023).

  • Limited translatability of systemic complement activation to local disease control. Although systemic complement activation correlates with AMD and disease stage in several studies, the relative importance of local versus systemic complement sources—and the ability of systemic blockade to suppress complement activity at the RPE–choriocapillaris interface—is unresolved and likely unfavorable for large biologics, reducing the mechanistic plausibility of systemic C5 blockade for GA (Hammadi et al., 2023; Park et al., 2019).

Risk–benefit and competitive landscape assessment  
Eculizumab’s negative randomized, controlled data in GA, in the face of confirmed systemic pharmacodynamics, places a high bar against further systemic development for this indication, a conclusion explicitly drawn by the COMPLETE investigators who noted the linearity of GA growth and lack of signal as making additional systemic investigations with eculizumab unlikely (Yehoshua et al., 2014). In the evolving complement-therapeutic landscape, local (intravitreal) complement inhibitors have achieved regulatory approval (C3 inhibitor pegcetacoplan and C5 aptamer avacincaptad pegol), demonstrating that complement modulation can slow GA progression when adequate ocular exposure is achieved, albeit without functional vision improvement and with target-dependent safety liabilities (e.g., increased conversion to exudative AMD observed particularly with C3 inhibition) (Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023; Qin et al., 2024). Against this backdrop, systemic eculizumab offers no efficacy advantage, carries systemic infection risk and costs, and fails the core requirement of achieving ocular target engagement necessary for GA modification.

Operationally, even if one hypothesized that higher systemic dosing, longer exposure, or patient stratification could rescue efficacy, several facts weigh against that strategy: COMPLETE’s pharmacodynamics confirmed near-complete systemic C5 suppression within two weeks; genetic analyses within the trial found no association between at-risk alleles and GA growth or treatment response; and extended follow-up to a year showed no divergence in growth rates (Yehoshua et al., 2014). Moreover, retinal pharmacokinetics and barrier biology make it unlikely that increasing systemic doses would proportionally increase intraocular concentrations to therapeutic levels without exacerbating systemic risks (Hammadi et al., 2023). In addition, C5 may not be the optimal node for GA progression biology in many patients, given preserved upstream activity and the complex contributions of C3a/C3b, opsonization, and local complement production that may continue to drive border-zone degeneration independent of MAC inhibition (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Halawa et al., 2021; Piri & Kaplan, 2023).

Recommendation  
Based on the aggregate mechanistic, translational, and clinical evidence, eculizumab (systemic C5 inhibition) does not have compelling potential as a repurposed therapy for dry AMD/GA. The drug has a clear and relevant mechanism and an acceptable short-term tolerability profile in older adults, but it fails to slow GA lesion growth in a randomized, controlled trial despite complete systemic target engagement, and there are strong mechanistic and pharmacokinetic reasons to expect insufficient intraocular exposure with systemic delivery (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Hammadi et al., 2023). The therapeutic hypothesis—reducing MAC on RPE/choriocapillaris to preserve tissue integrity and slow atrophy—is supported conceptually and by local C5 inhibition successes; however, achieving that biology in vivo appears to require intraocular delivery or targeting upstream nodes, neither of which is compatible with systemic eculizumab administration (Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023; Halawa et al., 2021).

If complement-targeted strategies remain a program priority, resources should pivot to modalities with demonstrated ocular target engagement and anatomic efficacy (intravitreal C3 or C5 agents) while carefully managing known safety trade-offs (e.g., neovascularization risk), and to biomarker-driven questions (e.g., whether baseline low-luminance visual acuity deficit—correlated with faster GA growth in COMPLETE—can enrich for patients who derive greater anatomic benefit) (Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023; Tzoumas et al., 2023; Yehoshua et al., 2014). For systemic complement modulation in AMD more broadly, alternative targets with better ocular PK profiles (e.g., small-molecule systemic alternative-pathway inhibitors) and rigorous ocular target-engagement measurements would be required to justify late-stage development, but systemic C5 blockade with eculizumab itself should not be advanced further for GA (Hammadi et al., 2023; Tzoumas et al., 2023; Park et al., 2019).

In summary, while the mechanistic logic for terminal complement inhibition in AMD is robust, the totality of evidence argues against systemic eculizumab as a viable candidate to slow GA progression, and the development program should discontinue pursuit of this repurposing in favor of locally delivered complement inhibitors or alternative mechanisms better suited to the ocular compartment and GA pathobiology (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
T0901317 is a fully synthetic small‐molecule agonist originally identified through screening for compounds that activate liver X receptors (LXRs). It belongs to the class of nuclear receptor ligands and is structurally designed to mimic endogenous oxysterols, the natural activators of LXRs. LXRs, comprising two isoforms, LXRα (NR1H3) and LXRβ (NR1H2), are master transcriptional regulators of cholesterol, lipid, and glucose metabolism. T0901317 was first characterized for its capacity to bind and stimulate these receptors, thereby upregulating target genes involved in cholesterol efflux such as ATP-binding cassette transporter A1 (ABCA1) and apolipoprotein E (APOE) (Choudhary et al., 2020, pp. 15–16). The compound has been widely used in preclinical studies to investigate cholesterol homeostasis, inflammation modulation, and emerging neuroprotective pathways. Its chemical synthesis follows standard procedures for developing derivatives that confer high receptor affinity and bioactivity while allowing researchers to dissect LXR-dependent pathways in multiple cell types, including retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells. The rationale behind using such LXR agonists, including T0901317, in ocular disorders like dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) stems from their demonstrated ability to restore cholesterol efflux, ameliorate lipid deposition, and reduce inflammatory stress in target tissues (Choudhary et al., 2020, pp. 12–13).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, T0901317 has been utilized extensively within the biomedical research arena as a tool compound to elucidate the role of LXRs in metabolic and inflammatory diseases. Preclinical work has demonstrated that LXR activation in key tissues, including the retina, can reestablish lipid homeostasis and reduce pathological lipid accumulation. Several studies indicate that in LXR-deficient models, there is an accumulation of neutral lipids and extracellular deposits—features that are remarkably similar to drusen formation observed in early dry AMD (Choudhary et al., 2020, pp. 7–9; Terao et al., 2024, pp. 8–10). In animal models, particularly in mice lacking the Nr1h3 isoform, the phenotype includes RPE dysfunction, inflammatory microenvironment formation, and structural changes that closely mimic human dry AMD pathology (Choudhary et al., 2020, pp. 2–4). Although T0901317 has not advanced to clinical trials for AMD, its efficacy has been primarily established in vitro using human RPE cell models and in vivo in murine models. The compound has shown potential for correcting the dysregulated cholesterol metabolism that contributes to the chronic buildup of lipid-rich drusen—a central pathological hallmark of dry AMD (Choudhary et al., 2020, pp. 12–13, 15–16). Outside of ocular applications, compounds from this class have been investigated for atherosclerosis and neurodegeneration, further emphasizing the critical link between cholesterol metabolism and chronic inflammatory conditions (Malek & Lad, 2014, pp. 13–15).

Mechanism of Action:  
The mechanism of action of T0901317 is fundamentally tied to its role as a potent activator of LXRs. Upon binding to LXRα and LXRβ within retinal cells, T0901317 facilitates heterodimerization with retinoid X receptors (RXRs), forming a transcriptionally active complex that binds to LXR response elements (LXREs) in the promoter regions of target genes. This activation cascade results in upregulation of numerous genes critical for cholesterol efflux and lipid metabolism, most notably ABCA1 and APOE (Choudhary et al., 2020, pp. 15–16). Upregulation of ABCA1 increases the efflux of excess cholesterol and oxidized lipids from RPE cells into the extracellular environment, thereby reducing the intracellular lipid load that predisposes cells to toxicity and drusen accumulation (Choudhary et al., 2020, pp. 12–13; Wu et al., 2023, pp. 10–12).

Beyond cholesterol efflux, T0901317 activates additional gene networks that modulate lysosomal function and autophagy. Experimental data suggest that T0901317 enhances the expression of lysosomal hydrolases, including cathepsin D (CTSD), and promotes the assembly of vacuolar-type H⁺-ATPases (v-ATPase), essential for maintaining lysosomal acidity (Lei et al., 2017, pp. 13–17, 20–22). This increase in active lysosomal enzymes and reinforced acidification contributes to the improved clearance of debris, particularly drusen components composed of lipid and protein aggregates. Furthermore, LXR activation by T0901317 has been shown to increase autophagy gene expression, thereby inducing a mitophagy response that removes damaged organelles and supports cellular metabolic renewal (Terao et al., 2024, pp. 8–10; Xie et al., 2022, pp. 1–2). In addition, T0901317 exerts significant anti-inflammatory effects by downregulating NF-κB signaling. It has been observed to inhibit the phosphorylation of IκBα, which prevents the nuclear translocation of NF-κB and subsequent transcription of inflammatory cytokines such as TNF-α and IL-6 (Lei et al., 2017, pp. 13–17; Choudhary & Malek, 2016, pp. 4–6). This dual role in lipid regulation and inflammation attenuation is central to its therapeutic promise in AMD, where chronic inflammation and disrupted lipid processing are major determinants of disease progression.

Expected Effect:  
In the context of dry AMD, with its hallmark drusen deposits and RPE dysfunction, the expected therapeutic effect of T0901317 is multifold. By activating LXRs in RPE cells, T0901317 is expected to upregulate the expression of ABCA1 and other cholesterol efflux mediators, thereby reducing the intracellular build‐up of cholesterol and oxidized lipids that contribute to drusen formation (Choudhary et al., 2020, pp. 2–4). This increase in cholesterol efflux would allow the RPE to better clear lipid debris, lowering the overall lipid burden on Bruch’s membrane. Concomitantly, the drug’s capacity to augment lysosomal function is anticipated to result in improved clearance of extracellular drusen components via a cathepsin D–dependent mechanism. Enhanced v-ATPase assembly and lysosomal acidification, as demonstrated by increased CTSD activity in vitro, should restore the degradative capacity of the lysosomal system, thereby facilitating the removal of protein-lipid aggregates (Lei et al., 2017, pp. 25–33).

Furthermore, the activation of autophagy pathways and promotion of mitophagy are expected to counteract the mitochondrial dysfunction that characterizes aged RPE cells—an integral pathological feature of dry AMD (Choudhary et al., 2020, pp. 7–9, 2–4). The anticipated result is a restoration of cellular homeostasis, improved energy metabolism, and reduction in oxidative stress, all of which are essential for maintaining RPE cell integrity. RPE cells have been shown to express both LXRα and LXRβ, and their expression is frequently diminished in AMD-affected eyes (Choudhary et al., 2020, pp. 12–13; Lyssenko et al., 2018, pp. 1–3). Therefore, by boosting LXR activity, T0901317 not only counteracts lipid dysregulation but also provides a neuroprotective, anti-inflammatory benefit by modulating cytokine production and dampening microglial activation in the outer retina (Choudhary & Malek, 2016, pp. 4–6).

Overall Evaluation:  
The overall assessment of T0901317 as a therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration is cautiously optimistic, with several key strengths as well as notable limitations that warrant further investigation.  

Strengths:  
One of the primary advantages of T0901317 is its well-documented ability to activate LXRs and thereby induce a broad spectrum of beneficial responses relevant to dry AMD pathology. The compound’s capacity to upregulate ABCA1 expression is critical, as impaired cholesterol efflux is a central mechanism underlying the accumulation of lipid-rich drusen (Choudhary et al., 2020, pp. 15–16, 12–13). Moreover, its ability to enhance lysosomal enzyme expression and promote v-ATPase assembly is particularly promising for the restoration of lysosomal acidity—a key defect in aged RPE cells that contributes to decreased clearance of toxic lipid deposits (Lei et al., 2017, pp. 13–17, 20–22). In addition, the induction of autophagy and mitophagy following LXR activation offers a dual therapeutic benefit by promoting the removal of damaged mitochondria and reducing oxidative stress, thereby preserving RPE cell viability (Xie et al., 2022, pp. 1–2). The anti-inflammatory properties of T0901317, demonstrated by its inhibition of NF-κB signaling and reduction of pro-inflammatory cytokine production, further support its potential utility in addressing the chronic low-grade inflammation often observed in AMD (Choudhary & Malek, 2016, pp. 4–6). Collectively, these mechanisms directly target the multifactorial aspects of dry AMD pathology—namely, lipid dysregulation, lysosomal dysfunction, and inflammatory stress—making T0901317 an attractive candidate for repurposing in this indication (Choudhary et al., 2020, pp. 2–4).

Another significant strength is the potential for ocular delivery strategies to mitigate the systemic side effects associated with T0901317. Given that systemic administration of LXR agonists has been linked to adverse metabolic effects such as hypertriglyceridemia and off-target activation of nuclear receptors like FXR and PXR (Lei et al., 2017, pp. 20–22; Storti et al., 2019, pp. 15–16), localized ocular delivery could concentrate the drug’s therapeutic effects in the retina while minimizing systemic exposure. This approach may overcome one of the principal limitations of T0901317 and reposition it as a viable option specifically for retinal applications.

Weaknesses and Challenges:  
Despite these promising attributes, there are several challenges that temper the enthusiasm for T0901317 as a first-in-class therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. A well-recognized limitation of T0901317 is its lack of absolute specificity for LXRs. Its ability to activate other nuclear receptors such as FXR and PXR raises concerns about off-target effects that could lead to dysregulated lipid metabolism in non-ocular tissues, systemic toxicity, and unwanted metabolic side effects such as hepatic steatosis and hyperlipidemia (Lei et al., 2017, pp. 20–22). Moreover, while preclinical evidence in cell culture and murine models has shown that LXR activation can reverse lipid accumulation and partially restore RPE cell function, the translation of such effects to the human condition—especially over the chronic time course of dry AMD—remains to be conclusively demonstrated (Choudhary et al., 2020, pp. 12–13, 7–9).

Another challenge lies in the fact that many preclinical studies have used alternative LXR agonists such as GW3965, which may exhibit a more favorable safety profile compared to T0901317 (Choudhary et al., 2020, pp. 9–11; Peters et al., 2022, pp. 11–12). The potential differences in selectivity and off-target activity between T0901317 and these other compounds necessitate a careful comparison. It is possible that while T0901317 has provided invaluable mechanistic insights into LXR biology in the retina, compounds with improved specificity may eventually be more amenable to clinical development. Furthermore, the specific hypothesis regarding T0901317’s ability to enhance lysosomal acidity and cathepsin D-dependent clearance of drusen components is based on in vitro observations, and there is still a need for more comprehensive studies that document these effects in animal models that recapitulate the chronic aspects of dry AMD pathology (Lei et al., 2017, pp. 25–33; Choudhary et al., 2020, pp. 2–4).

Additionally, because the retinal environment is highly specialized and the RPE plays a central role in maintaining photoreceptor health, any therapeutic approach must carefully balance metabolic reprogramming with preservation of essential RPE functions. Overactivation of autophagy or lysosomal pathways might conceivably lead to other cellular stresses if not properly calibrated. Thus, while the theoretical framework for T0901317’s benefit in dry AMD is strong, detailed pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic studies in appropriate models are essential before moving this candidate further along the drug development pathway.

Conclusion:  
In conclusion, T0901317 demonstrates considerable promise as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration based on its ability to activate LXR in RPE cells, thereby inducing cholesterol efflux via ABCA1 upregulation, enhancing lysosomal function through increased expression of hydrolases like cathepsin D, promoting autophagy and mitophagy, and reducing inflammation by dampening NF-κB signaling (Choudhary et al., 2020, pp. 12–13; Terao et al., 2024, pp. 8–10).

The strengths of T0901317 lie in its robust mechanistic rationale, the preclinical evidence supporting LXR-mediated restoration of cholesterol homeostasis, and the potential for localized ocular delivery to minimize systemic toxicities. However, its known off-target effects, particularly activation of other nuclear receptor pathways that can lead to metabolic side effects, present a significant hurdle that must be addressed through formulation optimization and dosing strategies (Lei et al., 2017, pp. 20–22; Storti et al., 2019, pp. 15–16). Furthermore, while the mechanistic underpinnings are appealing, further in vivo validation in chronic, clinically relevant AMD models is essential to confirm that the improvements in cholesterol efflux and lysosomal function translate into meaningful therapeutic outcomes—in terms of slowing or reversing the progression of dry AMD. Overall, T0901317 represents a promising, though challenging, candidate for addressing the unmet need in dry AMD therapy. Investment in additional preclinical studies focusing on ocular bioavailability, long-term safety in the retinal microenvironment, and optimization of dosing regimens will be critical in determining whether T0901317 or a similarly acting, perhaps more selective, LXR agonist can progress into clinical evaluation for dry AMD. The strategic focus on lipid-driven dysfunction, particularly in lysosomal clearance pathways, offers a novel mechanism of action that could complement or serve as an alternative to current therapeutic approaches, making T0901317 (or its optimized derivatives) a compelling candidate for further investigation (Choudhary et al., 2020, pp. 2–4, 7–9, 13–17).
