─────────────────────────────  
Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
─────────────────────────────  
The miR-211 mimic is a synthetic, chemically modified oligonucleotide designed to recapitulate the function of the endogenous microRNA miR-211. As a member of the miRNA therapeutic class, this molecule belongs to a growing category of nucleic acid–based drugs that aim to modulate gene expression post-transcriptionally. Its design involves optimization of the nucleotide chemistry (for example, by including 2′-O-methyl modifications, phosphorothioate linkages, and sometimes locked nucleic acid (LNA) modifications) to improve stability, reduce degradation by nucleases, and minimize immune stimulation after ocular delivery. Such chemical modifications (collectively referred to as “agomir” chemistry) have been used successfully in preclinical models for other miRNA candidates, proving that the formulation and delivery of chemically stabilized miRNA mimics to ocular tissues is feasible (Boya et al., 2023; Intartaglia et al., 2021).

miR-211 was originally identified as a light-responsive microRNA in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and has been shown to regulate lysosomal biogenesis by targeting the mRNA of Ezrin, a cytoskeletal protein that also impacts cellular ion channel regulation. The candidate is repurposed from the naturally occurring miRNA sequence now “mimicked” by the synthetic therapeutic agent. Its design is based on the premise that the loss or downregulation of miR-211 in the diseased RPE contributes to defective lysosomal function and consequent accumulation of photoreceptor outer segment (POS) debris, which is a hallmark of dry AMD (Boya et al., 2023; Intartaglia et al., 2021).

As a therapeutic compound, the miR-211 mimic falls into the broader family of oligonucleotide drugs that have previously been used in various contexts such as oncology or viral diseases. In the ocular arena, similar approaches—including antisense oligonucleotides and small interfering RNAs (siRNAs)—have been deployed to modulate gene expression in models of ocular neovascularization and other retinal degenerations. In this way, the miR-211 agomir is both a repurposed and rationally designed candidate that leverages our growing understanding of miRNA-mediated regulation of lysosomal activity and intracellular clearance pathways (Naso et al., 2020).

─────────────────────────────  
Therapeutic History  
─────────────────────────────  
Although no miR-211 mimic as such has yet reached clinical trials in dry AMD, an increasing body of preclinical evidence supports the therapeutic potential of modulating miR-211 expression in the retina. In several rodent studies it has been demonstrated that global loss of miR-211 in mice leads to impaired lysosomal biogenesis, accumulation of lipofuscin-like granules, and defective processing of photoreceptor outer segments by the RPE (Naso et al., 2020). For example, mice with a genetic deletion of miR-211 exhibit phenotypes reminiscent of inherited retinal dystrophies and models of Stargardt’s disease, in which impaired degradative enzymes and lysosomal dysfunction are central features.

In parallel, pharmacological inhibition of Ezrin—a validated target of miR-211—using small molecule inhibitors such as NSC668394 has been shown to restore lysosomal activity, increase autophagic flux, and even rescue electrophysiological deficits in the rodent retina (Naso et al., 2020). These findings not only validate the molecular target (Ezrin) but also indirectly support the hypothesis that restoring miR-211 levels via an agomir should yield similar improvements in lysosomal function and cell clearance.

The use of chemically modified oligonucleotides (including agomirs) in ocular drug development is supported both by preclinical data and emerging clinical applications in other retinal diseases. While previous approaches in dry AMD have focused on antioxidants, complement inhibitors, or cell transplantation, the recent shift toward modulating intracellular clearance pathways and autophagy has created new opportunity. For instance, approaches to activate the transcription factor TFEB—which is the master regulator of lysosomal biogenesis—demonstrate that enhancement of the degradative pathway correlates with improved survival of the RPE and photoreceptor cells (Boya et al., 2023; Naso et al., 2020). Although direct use of a miR-211 mimic (as opposed to gene therapy or pharmacologic Ezrin inhibitors) has not yet been validated in clinical settings for AMD, the preclinical evidence for miR-211’s role in maintaining RPE homeostasis provides a strong rationale for advancing this candidate into further testing (Intartaglia et al., 2021; Naso et al., 2020).

─────────────────────────────  
Mechanism of Action  
─────────────────────────────  
The proposed molecular mechanism by which a miR-211 mimic would function in dry AMD is multifaceted, integrating several key cellular pathways that converge on the restoration of lysosomal biogenesis in the RPE. At its core, the therapeutic hypothesis centers on the ability of miR-211 to post-transcriptionally suppress Ezrin, a cytoskeletal linker protein that in the RPE is linked to disruptions in lysosomal function and cell clearance (Boya et al., 2023; Intartaglia et al., 2021).

Specifically, under physiological conditions miR-211 is induced in a light-dependent manner and directly binds to the 3′ untranslated region (UTR) of the Ezrin mRNA to repress its translation. In the context of dry AMD, miR-211 is downregulated—a change that leads to derepression of Ezrin. Elevated Ezrin levels are correlated with impaired lysosomal biogenesis, reduced cathepsin activity, and accumulation of metabolic debris (Boya et al., 2023; Naso et al., 2020). Once delivered to the RPE, the miR-211 mimic is expected to restore this regulatory inhibition, reducing Ezrin protein levels to a more physiologic state.

More intriguingly, this reduction in Ezrin is proposed to have downstream effects on lysosomal calcium signaling. Data indicate that when Ezrin is repressed, there is an increase in TRPML1 channel sensitivity at the lysosomal membrane, thereby generating a localized Ca²⁺ microdomain within these organelles (Naso et al., 2020). The increased lysosomal Ca²⁺ flux subsequently activates the Ca²⁺-dependent phosphatase calcineurin. Activated calcineurin dephosphorylates TFEB, a transcription factor that in its phosphorylated state is sequestered in the cytosol. Once dephosphorylated, TFEB can translocate into the nucleus where it functions as the master regulator of the Coordinated Lysosomal Expression and Regulation (CLEAR) gene network (Naso et al., 2020).

TFEB-driven transcription leads to enhanced expression of genes encoding lysosomal proteins, such as LAMP1, and digestive enzymes including cathepsin D, as well as proteins critical for autophagosome formation like LC3 and BECLIN. The net effect is an increase in the number and functionality of lysosomes, including improved acidification of these organelles—a crucial parameter for optimal enzymatic activity and degradation of engulfed materials (Du & Palczewski, 2022; Naso et al., 2020). The complete mechanistic cascade is thus: miR-211 mimic delivers a signal that downregulates Ezrin, alleviating its inhibitory effects on lysosomal biogenesis; this in turn potentiates TRPML1-mediated Ca²⁺ release, leading to calcineurin activation; calcineurin dephosphorylates TFEB, allowing its nuclear entry; and nuclear TFEB transcriptionally enhances lysosomal genes, culminating in improved cathepsin D expression and lysosomal acidification. This chain of events is hypothesized to restore the degradative capacity of the RPE and mitigate POS accumulation—a key pathogenic factor underlying dry AMD (Boya et al., 2023; Naso et al., 2020).

It is worth noting that similar signaling cascades have been observed in studies where Ezrin inhibition pharmacologically recapitulated the beneficial effects seen after TFEB activation, which indirectly supports this proposed miR-211–mediated mechanism (Naso et al., 2020). The convergence of genetic, pharmacologic, and mechanistic studies in preclinical rodent models reinforces confidence in the proposed chain-of-events, although direct demonstration of every step with a synthetic miR-211 agomir remains an area for future research.

─────────────────────────────  
Expected Effect  
─────────────────────────────  
When administrated to the retinal pigment epithelium via an appropriate ocular delivery method (such as intravitreal or subretinal injection, potentially formulated within lipid nanoparticles or other compatible carriers), the miR-211 mimic is expected to produce several beneficial effects that address the key pathological features of dry AMD. In in vitro assays using RPE cell lines or primary human RPE cultures, one would anticipate that treatment with the miR-211 agomir will lead to a measurable decrease in Ezrin mRNA and protein levels as confirmed by qRT-PCR and Western blot analyses, respectively (Boya et al., 2023; Intartaglia et al., 2021).

At the subcellular level, the downregulation of Ezrin is expected to relieve its inhibitory control on lysosomal Ca²⁺ dynamics. This should manifest as an increase in TRPML1 channel activity, resulting in a sustained and enhanced lysosomal Ca²⁺ signal, which can be quantified using calcium-sensitive dyes or genetically encoded Ca²⁺ indicators fused to lysosomal proteins (Naso et al., 2020). Following this, increased calcineurin activity is anticipated and can be monitored by assessing the phosphorylation status of downstream substrates including TFEB. In treated RPE cells, one would observe a redistribution of TFEB from the cytoplasm to the nucleus, a change that can be confirmed by immunocytochemistry and subcellular fractionation methods (Naso et al., 2020).

The nuclear translocation of TFEB should then promote transcriptional upregulation of lysosomal and autophagy-related genes, resulting in an increased number of lysosomes with enhanced acidification (as measured by pH-sensitive fluorescent probes) and increased activity of key lysosomal enzymes such as cathepsin D and cathepsin B. Ultrastructural analyses by electron microscopy might reveal a reduction in the number or size of accumulated phagolysosomes containing unprocessed POS, and a phenotypic rescue at the cellular level would be consistent with restored degradative function (Naso et al., 2020).

In animal models of dry AMD – particularly in miR-211 knockout mice or in models that replicate lipofuscin accumulation and reduced lysosomal function – treatment with the miR-211 mimic is expected to result in significant improvements in retinal structure and function. Outcomes could include a reduction in lipofuscin deposition in the RPE, improved clearance of dysfunctional or misfolded photoreceptor proteins, and ultimately functional improvements as measured by responses on electroretinography (ERG) and preservation of photoreceptor cell layers. The approach is expected to not only halt but also partially reverse the degenerative changes by boosting the intrinsic capacity of RPE cells to clear cellular debris and maintain homeostasis (Boya et al., 2023; Naso et al., 2020).

Furthermore, in preclinical experiments where pharmacological inhibition of Ezrin achieved similar results in terms of enhancing lysosomal markers and reducing pathological deposits, the miR-211 mimic is hypothesized to mimic these effects by acting upstream of the pathway. Given that there is evidence suggesting that downregulation of miR-211 in AMD leads to compromised visual function, restoring its levels should, in theory, improve RPE survival and enhance retinal performance (Naso et al., 2020). In summary, the expected effect of this therapeutic intervention is a robust enhancement of lysosomal biogenesis and function within the RPE, which in turn could restore degradative capacity, reduce debris accumulation, and preserve visual function in dry AMD.

─────────────────────────────  
Overall Evaluation  
─────────────────────────────  
The miR-211 mimic candidate for dry AMD represents an innovative approach that acts by rebalancing a key regulatory pathway implicated in lysosomal biogenesis and cellular clearance. Overall, there are several strengths and a number of challenges to consider:

Strengths:  
1. Rational Mechanistic Targeting:  
   The candidate is built on a clear mechanistic hypothesis. miR-211 has been shown in multiple preclinical studies to directly regulate Ezrin—a known inhibitor of lysosomal biogenesis—and its downregulation results in impaired degradation of POS in the RPE (Boya et al., 2023; Intartaglia et al., 2021). By restoring miR-211 levels, the cascade involving TRPML1-mediated Ca²⁺ release, calcineurin activation, and subsequent TFEB nuclear translocation is reactivated. This specificity in targeting a regulatory cascade central to intracellular clearance speaks to high precision in its design (Naso et al., 2020).

2. Preclinical Validation of the Concept:  
   Genetic models, such as miR-211 knockout mice, and pharmacologic approaches using Ezrin inhibitors have provided compelling evidence that manipulating this pathway can restore degradative capacity in the RPE (Naso et al., 2020). Although the miR-211 mimic itself has not yet been extensively tested in dry AMD models, these data provide a strong scientific rationale for its potential efficacy.

3. Established Chemical Modification Strategies:  
   The field of miRNA therapeutics has matured considerably, and the design of chemically modified agomirs is a well-established approach to increase in vivo stability and allow local ocular delivery. This is supported by multiple studies in ocular tissues showing that similar modifications lead to enhanced half-life and effective cellular uptake (Boya et al., 2023; Intartaglia et al., 2021).

4. Specificity for RPE Homeostasis:  
   The candidate is designed specifically for the RPE, the critical cell layer responsible for degrading old photoreceptor outer segments. Since RPE dysfunction is a hallmark of dry AMD, targeted restoration of its lysosomal capacity has a high potential to ameliorate disease progression and preserve vision (Naso et al., 2020).

Weaknesses/Challenges:  
1. Limited Direct Evidence with Agomirs:  
   Although there is substantial mechanistic preclinical evidence linking miR-211 to the regulation of lysosomal function via Ezrin repression, no data to date directly demonstrate the efficacy and safety of a chemically modified miR-211 mimic in relevant dry AMD models. It remains to be established whether the agomir will effectively reach the RPE, achieve the desired gene repression, and produce the biochemical cascade in vivo (Naso et al., 2020).

2. Delivery and Pharmacokinetic Hurdles:  
   Ocular delivery, while an area of active development, remains challenging. The RPE is separated from the vitreous by multiple biological barriers. Although intravitreal or subretinal injections are established, the pharmacokinetics, biodistribution, and long-term safety profile of a miRNA agomir in the human eye require thorough optimization. It will be necessary to confirm that the chemical modifications to the miR-211 mimic do not hinder its uptake by RPE cells or cause off-target effects (Naso et al., 2020; Boya et al., 2023).

3. Translational Gaps:  
   The preclinical studies have largely been performed in rodent models that, while informative, do not fully replicate human dry AMD. Scaling up from rodent to human necessitates careful consideration of dosing, frequency of administration, and long-term impact. In addition, the natural turnover and light-dependent regulation of miR-211 in the human RPE might be more complex than in animal models (Naso et al., 2020).

4. Potential Off-target Effects and Safety:  
   As with all nucleic acid–based therapies, off-target binding and unintended gene regulation are concerns. Although miR-211 is highly specific under endogenous conditions, the synthetic mimic may interact with unintended transcripts, potentially affecting other pathways in the RPE or neighboring retinal cells. Comprehensive in vitro and in vivo toxicity studies are essential to ensure that modulating the miR-211 network does not lead to adverse outcomes (Boya et al., 2023; Naso et al., 2020).

5. Regulatory and Manufacturing Issues:  
   The regulatory pathway for oligonucleotide therapeutics remains stringent, and the manufacturing process for chemically modified miRNAs must meet high quality and reproducibility standards. There is precedence in the field for similar agents, but each new candidate faces its own set of challenges regarding scalability and cost-effectiveness (Naso et al., 2020).

─────────────────────────────  
Overall Evaluation  
─────────────────────────────  
Based on the current literature and mechanistic rationale provided in the context, the miR-211 mimic candidate holds significant promise as a therapeutic agent for dry AMD. The strengths of this approach lie in its clearly defined mechanism of action, which ties the restoration of miR-211 levels directly to the re-establishment of lysosomal biogenesis—a critical process in RPE health. Preclinical data regarding miR-211’s role in repressing Ezrin and the downstream activation of the TRPML1–Ca²⁺–calcineurin–TFEB axis are compelling and suggest that correcting the deficiency of miR-211 could reverse the degradative defects observed in dry AMD (Boya et al., 2023; Intartaglia et al., 2021; Naso et al., 2020).

Moreover, the advances in chemical modification of miRNA mimics to generate agomirs provide a technical basis for formulating a stable and effective drug candidate. The specific targeting of the RPE—a key player in the pathophysiology of dry AMD—further strengthens the case for this candidate. In vitro and preclinical readouts, such as decreased expression of Ezrin, increases in TFEB nuclear translocation, upregulation of lysosomal markers (including cathepsin D), and consequent improvements in cell clearance, are all expected to translate into improved retinal structure and function (Naso et al., 2020; Boya et al., 2023).

However, significant work remains to address some of the translational challenges. There is a critical need for direct experimental validation using the chemically modified miR-211 agomir in relevant dry AMD models. Key studies will be required to evaluate pharmacodynamics, ocular biodistribution, and the long-term safety profile of the candidate. The potential for off-target effects and the challenges inherent in intraocular delivery further complicate the clinical development pathway. In addition, while the mechanistic pathway (miR-211 → Ezrin repression → TRPML1 activation → Ca²⁺ flux → calcineurin activation → TFEB nuclear translocation → lysosomal gene upregulation) is conceptually robust, some downstream biochemical events remain to be validated in the context of miR-211 agomir treatment (Naso et al., 2020; Boya et al., 2023).

In conclusion, the miR-211 mimic is an exciting repurposed candidate for dry AMD therapy that leverages a highly specific molecular mechanism with the potential to restore lysosomal function in RPE cells. Its strengths include a clear mechanistic rationale, a strong preclinical basis for targeting Ezrin and activating the TRPML1–Ca²⁺–calcineurin–TFEB pathway, and the availability of advanced chemical modification techniques for ocular delivery. The primary risks and challenges—such as the need for comprehensive in vivo validation, optimization of delivery methods, and a thorough safety assessment—are typical of emerging nucleic acid therapeutics but are not insurmountable given current technological advances. On balance, the available evidence supports further focused preclinical evaluation of the miR-211 agomir candidate as a promising therapeutic strategy for dry AMD (Boya et al., 2023; Intartaglia et al., 2021; Naso et al., 2020).

Given the potential to correct a key pathogenic deficiency in the RPE and restore essential degradative function, advancing this candidate into rigorous in vitro testing in human RPE models followed by in vivo testing in established animal models is a priority. Subsequent studies should focus on refining the chemical formulation, ensuring efficient and targeted delivery to the RPE, and establishing a clear safety profile while monitoring for improved lysosomal function and retinal structure/function rescue. This systematic approach will be critical in determining whether the miR-211 mimic can ultimately be developed into a viable therapeutic for patients with dry AMD.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
T0901317 is a fully synthetic small‐molecule agonist originally identified through screening for compounds that activate liver X receptors (LXRs). It belongs to the class of nuclear receptor ligands and is structurally designed to mimic endogenous oxysterols, the natural activators of LXRs. LXRs, comprising two isoforms, LXRα (NR1H3) and LXRβ (NR1H2), are master transcriptional regulators of cholesterol, lipid, and glucose metabolism. T0901317 was first characterized for its capacity to bind and stimulate these receptors, thereby upregulating target genes involved in cholesterol efflux such as ATP-binding cassette transporter A1 (ABCA1) and apolipoprotein E (APOE) (Choudhary et al., 2020, pp. 15–16). The compound has been widely used in preclinical studies to investigate cholesterol homeostasis, inflammation modulation, and emerging neuroprotective pathways. Its chemical synthesis follows standard procedures for developing derivatives that confer high receptor affinity and bioactivity while allowing researchers to dissect LXR-dependent pathways in multiple cell types, including retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells. The rationale behind using such LXR agonists, including T0901317, in ocular disorders like dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) stems from their demonstrated ability to restore cholesterol efflux, ameliorate lipid deposition, and reduce inflammatory stress in target tissues (Choudhary et al., 2020, pp. 12–13).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, T0901317 has been utilized extensively within the biomedical research arena as a tool compound to elucidate the role of LXRs in metabolic and inflammatory diseases. Preclinical work has demonstrated that LXR activation in key tissues, including the retina, can reestablish lipid homeostasis and reduce pathological lipid accumulation. Several studies indicate that in LXR-deficient models, there is an accumulation of neutral lipids and extracellular deposits—features that are remarkably similar to drusen formation observed in early dry AMD (Choudhary et al., 2020, pp. 7–9; Terao et al., 2024, pp. 8–10). In animal models, particularly in mice lacking the Nr1h3 isoform, the phenotype includes RPE dysfunction, inflammatory microenvironment formation, and structural changes that closely mimic human dry AMD pathology (Choudhary et al., 2020, pp. 2–4). Although T0901317 has not advanced to clinical trials for AMD, its efficacy has been primarily established in vitro using human RPE cell models and in vivo in murine models. The compound has shown potential for correcting the dysregulated cholesterol metabolism that contributes to the chronic buildup of lipid-rich drusen—a central pathological hallmark of dry AMD (Choudhary et al., 2020, pp. 12–13, 15–16). Outside of ocular applications, compounds from this class have been investigated for atherosclerosis and neurodegeneration, further emphasizing the critical link between cholesterol metabolism and chronic inflammatory conditions (Malek & Lad, 2014, pp. 13–15).

Mechanism of Action:  
The mechanism of action of T0901317 is fundamentally tied to its role as a potent activator of LXRs. Upon binding to LXRα and LXRβ within retinal cells, T0901317 facilitates heterodimerization with retinoid X receptors (RXRs), forming a transcriptionally active complex that binds to LXR response elements (LXREs) in the promoter regions of target genes. This activation cascade results in upregulation of numerous genes critical for cholesterol efflux and lipid metabolism, most notably ABCA1 and APOE (Choudhary et al., 2020, pp. 15–16). Upregulation of ABCA1 increases the efflux of excess cholesterol and oxidized lipids from RPE cells into the extracellular environment, thereby reducing the intracellular lipid load that predisposes cells to toxicity and drusen accumulation (Choudhary et al., 2020, pp. 12–13; Wu et al., 2023, pp. 10–12).

Beyond cholesterol efflux, T0901317 activates additional gene networks that modulate lysosomal function and autophagy. Experimental data suggest that T0901317 enhances the expression of lysosomal hydrolases, including cathepsin D (CTSD), and promotes the assembly of vacuolar-type H⁺-ATPases (v-ATPase), essential for maintaining lysosomal acidity (Lei et al., 2017, pp. 13–17, 20–22). This increase in active lysosomal enzymes and reinforced acidification contributes to the improved clearance of debris, particularly drusen components composed of lipid and protein aggregates. Furthermore, LXR activation by T0901317 has been shown to increase autophagy gene expression, thereby inducing a mitophagy response that removes damaged organelles and supports cellular metabolic renewal (Terao et al., 2024, pp. 8–10; Xie et al., 2022, pp. 1–2). In addition, T0901317 exerts significant anti-inflammatory effects by downregulating NF-κB signaling. It has been observed to inhibit the phosphorylation of IκBα, which prevents the nuclear translocation of NF-κB and subsequent transcription of inflammatory cytokines such as TNF-α and IL-6 (Lei et al., 2017, pp. 13–17; Choudhary & Malek, 2016, pp. 4–6). This dual role in lipid regulation and inflammation attenuation is central to its therapeutic promise in AMD, where chronic inflammation and disrupted lipid processing are major determinants of disease progression.

Expected Effect:  
In the context of dry AMD, with its hallmark drusen deposits and RPE dysfunction, the expected therapeutic effect of T0901317 is multifold. By activating LXRs in RPE cells, T0901317 is expected to upregulate the expression of ABCA1 and other cholesterol efflux mediators, thereby reducing the intracellular build‐up of cholesterol and oxidized lipids that contribute to drusen formation (Choudhary et al., 2020, pp. 2–4). This increase in cholesterol efflux would allow the RPE to better clear lipid debris, lowering the overall lipid burden on Bruch’s membrane. Concomitantly, the drug’s capacity to augment lysosomal function is anticipated to result in improved clearance of extracellular drusen components via a cathepsin D–dependent mechanism. Enhanced v-ATPase assembly and lysosomal acidification, as demonstrated by increased CTSD activity in vitro, should restore the degradative capacity of the lysosomal system, thereby facilitating the removal of protein-lipid aggregates (Lei et al., 2017, pp. 25–33).

The overall assessment of T0901317 as a therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration is cautiously optimistic, with several key strengths as well as notable limitations that warrant further investigation.  

Strengths:  
One of the primary advantages of T0901317 is its well-documented ability to activate LXRs and thereby induce a broad spectrum of beneficial responses relevant to dry AMD pathology. The compound’s capacity to upregulate ABCA1 expression is critical, as impaired cholesterol efflux is a central mechanism underlying the accumulation of lipid-rich drusen (Choudhary et al., 2020, pp. 15–16, 12–13). The anti-inflammatory properties of T0901317, demonstrated by its inhibition of NF-κB signaling and reduction of pro-inflammatory cytokine production, further support its potential utility in addressing the chronic low-grade inflammation often observed in AMD (Choudhary & Malek, 2016, pp. 4–6). Collectively, these mechanisms directly target the multifactorial aspects of dry AMD pathology—namely, lipid dysregulation, lysosomal dysfunction, and inflammatory stress—making T0901317 an attractive candidate for repurposing in this indication (Choudhary et al., 2020, pp. 2–4).

Another significant strength is the potential for ocular delivery strategies to mitigate the systemic side effects associated with T0901317. Given that systemic administration of LXR agonists has been linked to adverse metabolic effects such as hypertriglyceridemia and off-target activation of nuclear receptors like FXR and PXR (Lei et al., 2017, pp. 20–22; Storti et al., 2019, pp. 15–16), localized ocular delivery could concentrate the drug’s therapeutic effects in the retina while minimizing systemic exposure. Weaknesses and Challenges:  
Despite these promising attributes, there are several challenges that temper the enthusiasm for T0901317 as a first-in-class therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. Conclusion:  
In conclusion, T0901317 demonstrates considerable promise as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration based on its ability to activate LXR in RPE cells, thereby inducing cholesterol efflux via ABCA1 upregulation, enhancing lysosomal function through increased expression of hydrolases like cathepsin D, promoting autophagy and mitophagy, and reducing inflammation by dampening NF-κB signaling (Choudhary et al., 2020, pp. 12–13; Terao et al., 2024, pp. 8–10).

Furthermore, while the mechanistic underpinnings are appealing, further in vivo validation in chronic, clinically relevant AMD models is essential to confirm that the improvements in cholesterol efflux and lysosomal function translate into meaningful therapeutic outcomes—in terms of slowing or reversing the progression of dry AMD. Investment in additional preclinical studies focusing on ocular bioavailability, long-term safety in the retinal microenvironment, and optimization of dosing regimens will be critical in determining whether T0901317 or a similarly acting, perhaps more selective, LXR agonist can progress into clinical evaluation for dry AMD. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Calpeptin (Sigma C1571) is a synthetic, cell‐permeable peptidomimetic inhibitor originally developed to target calpain family proteases. It belongs to a class of small molecule calpain inhibitors that are designed to mimic specific peptide sequences found in the endogenous inhibitor calpastatin. These peptidomimetics have been refined chemically to enable cellular penetration and high-affinity binding to the calpain active site, thereby blocking its auto‐proteolytic activation process (Vu et al., 2022). Calpeptin was discovered through efforts aimed at identifying effective inhibitors of calcium‐dependent cysteine proteases that contribute to proteolytic events in pathogenic conditions. Its synthesis involves conventional organic synthesis techniques designed to yield a molecule with the critical chemical features—namely, an amide backbone that mimics peptide bonds and side chain substitutions that ensure selectivity and stability in biological systems. This compound has been widely adopted as a research tool to probe calpain‐dependent cellular processes, particularly in the context of neurodegeneration and ocular pathologies (Vu et al., 2022).

Therapeutic History:  
Calpeptin has a rich history as a biochemical tool in both in vitro and in vivo experimental paradigms. Within the realm of ocular disease research, calpain inhibitors similar in mechanism to calpeptin have been evaluated in multiple models of retinal degeneration. For example, studies using rodent models of inherited retinal degeneration, such as those employing the Rho P23H‐1 rat model, have demonstrated that calpeptin—alongside other calpain inhibitors—can reduce photoreceptor cell death and modulate apoptotic pathways (Azam & Jastrzebska, 2025). Although the majority of these studies have been conducted in the context of retinitis pigmentosa or other inherited forms of retinal degeneration, the underlying mechanism—namely, the inhibition of aberrant calpain activation leading to cell death—is also highly relevant to dry age‐related macular degeneration (Azam & Jastrzebska, 2025). In various experimental systems, such as in neuroblastoma cells and retinal cell cultures subject to stress (e.g., hypoxia or oxidative challenge), calpeptin has been shown to reduce calpain‐mediated cleavage of key substrates and inhibit caspase activation, which correlates with improved cell survival. Although direct clinical trials using calpeptin in dry AMD have not yet been reported, its use in ocular research, combined with evidence from preclinical models involving other calpain inhibitors (such as SNJ‐1945 and SJA6017), underscores the translational potential of this approach (Vu et al., 2022).

Mechanism of Action:  
Calpeptin functions by inhibiting the auto‐proteolytic activation of calpain isoforms, particularly cytosolic calpains such as CAPN1 and CAPN5. Under physiological conditions, calpains are maintained in an inactive state; however, under pathological conditions marked by calcium dysregulation—such as those encountered in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) during oxidative stress—calpains become activated and catalyze the proteolytic cleavage of vital cellular substrates. Calpeptin binds to the protease’s active site, thereby preventing the conformational changes necessary for auto‐activation and subsequent proteolytic activity (Vu et al., 2022).  
In the specific context of dry AMD, the hypothesis is that drusen accumulation leads to oxidative and metabolic stress in the RPE. This stress triggers calcium overload, which in turn activates calpains. One of the deleterious consequences of calpain activation is lysosomal membrane permeabilization (LMP). LMP destabilizes the lysosomal environment, leading to the dissipation of the proton gradient maintained by v-ATPase complexes and resulting in impaired acidification. This loss of lysosomal integrity negatively affects the processing and activity of lysosomal hydrolases, particularly cathepsin D (CTSD), which is essential for proper degradative and autophagic functions. By inhibiting calpain activity, calpeptin is expected to prevent the proteolytic degradation of components critical to lysosomal membrane stability, such as v-ATPase subunits, thereby preserving lysosomal pH and ensuring proper CTSD processing (Vu et al., 2022). The preservation of these lysosomal functions is crucial in the context of drusen-induced stress in dry AMD, as it directly addresses the underlying mechanism of lysosomal dysfunction and subsequent cell death.

Expected Effect:  
The proposed therapeutic application of calpeptin in dry AMD is based on its ability to mitigate calpain-mediated lysosomal damage in the retinal pigment epithelium. In an experimental setup where RPE cells are exposed to oxidative or drusen-like stress, one would expect calpeptin to reduce calpain activation, thereby decreasing lysosomal membrane permeabilization. This inhibition should lead to the stabilization of v-ATPase complexes, which are responsible for maintaining the acidic environment within lysosomes. Consequently, normal lysosomal acidification is preserved, allowing for proper activation and function of cathepsin D (CTSD), a critical enzyme in the degradation of photoreceptor outer segments and in cellular homeostasis (Azam & Jastrzebska, 2025; Vu et al., 2022).  
Furthermore, by blocking the calpain-driven cleavage events that would otherwise lead to cytoskeletal disorganization and cellular apoptosis, calpeptin is anticipated to reduce overall caspase activation and apoptotic signaling in RPE cells. Studies in other retinal disease models have demonstrated that calpain inhibition can restore cellular homeostasis by reducing markers of apoptosis and mitigating structural damage (Azam & Jastrzebska, 2025; Vu et al., 2022). Given that RPE cells are known to express significant levels of calpains and are highly susceptible to calcium dysregulation upon exposure to drusen and oxidative stress, the use of calpeptin is expected to yield improved cellular viability and function in these cells. This outcome would be assessed through indicators such as restored lysosomal pH, reduction in cytosolic release of lysosomal enzymes, and maintenance of normal CTSD processing, ultimately contributing to neuroprotection and preservation of retinal integrity in dry AMD (Vu et al., 2022).

Overall Evaluation:  
A comprehensive review of the literature suggests that calpeptin holds promise as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration. Its classification as a cell-permeable peptidomimetic inhibitor of calpain places it within a well-studied drug class known for modulating pathological proteolytic cascades initiated by calcium dysregulation. The strengths of calpeptin include its well-characterized mechanism of action—namely, the inhibition of calpain auto-proteolysis, which is pivotal for preventing the proteolytic breakdown of critical lysosomal components such as v-ATPase (Vu et al., 2022).  
Moreover, the therapeutic history of calpeptin and its analogues in various retinal degeneration models supports its potential applicability in dry AMD. Experimental evidence from studies in Rho P23H transgenic rat models, among others, demonstrates that calpain inhibitors can confer neuroprotection by reducing apoptotic pathways, preserving cellular integrity, and maintaining lysosomal function in stressed retinal cells (Azam & Jastrzebska, 2025). The existing knowledge regarding in vivo tolerability and the reversible nature of calpeptin’s inhibitory effects further bolster its candidacy for preclinical testing targeting dry AMD (Vu et al., 2022).

Despite these favorable attributes, several weaknesses and challenges must be acknowledged. First, while the mechanism underpinning calpeptin’s action—specifically, its inhibition of calpain-mediated lysosomal damage—is strongly supported by in vitro and retinal degeneration model data, direct evidence linking calpeptin to improved outcomes in dry AMD models remains limited (Azam & Jastrzebska, 2025; Vu et al., 2022). Furthermore, the hypothesized benefit of stabilizing v-ATPase complexes and preserving CTSD activity, although biologically plausible, requires further experimental validation in an AMD context to confirm that calpeptin’s inhibition of calpain is sufficient to counteract drusen-induced lysosomal stress.  
An additional concern relates to target selectivity. Calpain inhibitors, including calpeptin, can potentially exhibit off-target effects due to the conserved structure of the catalytic domains within the calpain family and related proteases. This lack of absolute specificity may lead to unintended inhibition of other proteases, such as certain cathepsins, which could compromise cellular function if not tightly regulated (Vu et al., 2022). Furthermore, chronic ocular delivery of small molecule inhibitors poses formulation challenges, as therapeutic concentrations must be maintained in the retina without eliciting local toxicity. The eye’s compartmentalized anatomy offers the advantage of localized delivery (e.g., via intravitreal injections or topical applications), yet achieving sustained and controlled drug release remains a technical hurdle that must be addressed in subsequent preclinical studies (Vu et al., 2022).  
Another potential weakness is the complexity of dry AMD pathophysiology itself. Dry AMD is characterized by a multifactorial etiology involving oxidative stress, complement dysregulation, and inflammatory processes, in addition to lysosomal dysfunction. While addressing calpain-mediated LMP directly targets one critical aspect of the disease mechanism, comprehensive protection of RPE cells may require combination approaches. Calpeptin’s role might be best viewed as a part of a broader therapeutic cocktail aimed at modulating multiple convergent pathways implicated in dry AMD progression (Vu et al., 2022).  
In summary, calpeptin shows considerable potential as a repurposed drug candidate for dry AMD based on its well-documented pharmacological profile and its mechanistic alignment with the proposed therapeutic strategy—namely, inhibiting calpain-mediated lysosomal destabilization in RPE cells. Its synthetic origin, cell-permeable nature, and established use in experimental models of retinal degeneration make it an attractive candidate for further preclinical evaluation. However, the absence of direct evidence in dry AMD models, in addition to concerns regarding specificity, delivery, and the need for combination intervention strategies, underscores the importance of rigorous preclinical studies to further validate calpeptin’s efficacy and safety in this indication (Vu et al., 2022; Azam & Jastrzebska, 2025). Overall, while promising, calpeptin will require targeted studies to evaluate its impact on lysosomal membrane permeabilization, v-ATPase stabilization, and cathepsin D activity in the context of drusen-induced oxidative stress, thereby confirming its potential to protect RPEs and mitigate the progression of dry age-related macular degeneration (Vu et al., 2022).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Nicotinamide riboside (NR), marketed as ChromaDex Niagen, belongs to the vitamin B3 family and is a naturally occurring precursor of nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+). Originally discovered in trace amounts in milk and other food sources, NR has been isolated and subsequently synthesized to yield a high‐purity form for nutritional and pharmaceutical applications. As a member of a class of compounds designed to elevate intracellular NAD+ levels, NR has attracted significant attention in the fields of metabolism, aging, and neuroprotection. Its chemical structure—a combination of a nicotinamide moiety bound to ribose—enables it to enter salvage pathways in cells with minimal metabolic conversion losses. In this regard, NR is comparable to other NAD+ boosters such as nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN), though differences in bioavailability and cellular transporter expression have been noted in some studies. Preclinical research has documented retinal distribution of NR in rodent models, suggesting that it reaches ocular tissues in pharmacologically relevant concentrations, an essential prerequisite for any agent intended to treat dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) (Abokyi & Tse, 2025; Braidy et al., 2019).

Therapeutic History:  
NR has been extensively investigated for its potential to modulate cellular energy metabolism and mitigate the effects of aging in diverse tissues. Early studies revealed that supplementation with NR effectively elevates NAD+ levels in multiple cell types, including neurons, skeletal muscle, and retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells, thereby enhancing mitochondrial function and cellular stress resistance (Dovijarski, 2019; Pîrvu et al., 2021). In the context of ocular research, while much of the direct experimental work has been performed using NMN, the close biochemical relationship between NMN and NR—as NAD+ precursors—has led investigators to propose that NR could produce similar outcomes in RPE cells. Models of retinal degeneration, including glaucoma and optic nerve injury, have demonstrated that NAD+ boosting via NR administration can ameliorate mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress, indirectly supporting its potential repurposing for dry AMD (Kitaoka et al., 2020; Mehmel et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2024). Moreover, clinical studies investigating NR’s safety in humans have shown that it is well tolerated at doses that elevate systemic NAD+ levels; doses in the gram-range have been employed without significant adverse effects (Jadeja et al., 2020). Although direct clinical trials targeting dry AMD are still forthcoming, the overall therapeutic history of NR—encompassing robust preclinical ocular benefit across neurodegenerative models and a favorable safety profile in human subjects—strongly supports further investigation for eye diseases where NAD+ depletion is a central pathophysiological feature (Dovijarski, 2019; Braidy et al., 2019; Pîrvu et al., 2021).

Mechanism of Action:  
The proposed mechanism of NR in dry AMD centers on its capacity to elevate intracellular NAD+ levels, thereby fueling a cascade of beneficial biochemical events. After cell entry, NR is phosphorylated by nicotinamide riboside kinases (NRKs) to generate NMN, which is subsequently converted to NAD+ through the activity of NMN adenylyltransferase. The resultant increase in NAD+ acts as a vital cofactor for sirtuins—primarily SIRT1 and SIRT3—which are NAD+-dependent deacetylases involved in regulating numerous cellular processes. SIRT1, in particular, has been implicated in deacetylating key transcription factors such as peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator-1α (PGC-1α) and transcription factor EB (TFEB). TFEB is a master regulator of lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy; its deacetylation leads to its nuclear translocation and binding to CLEAR (Coordinated Lysosomal Expression and Regulation) elements in the promoter regions of autophagy and lysosomal genes. Such activation promotes lysosomal acidification and increases the activity of hydrolases like cathepsin D, which are critical for the degradation of damaged proteins and organelles. Concurrently, SIRT3, which localizes predominantly to mitochondria, enhances mitochondrial function by deacetylating enzymes crucial for mitochondrial bioenergetics and reactive oxygen species (ROS) detoxification. The overall effect of NR supplementation is therefore hypothesized to be a restoration of cellular homeostasis in RPE cells—improving both autophagic clearance and mitochondrial function, two processes known to be compromised in dry AMD (Kitaoka et al., 2020; Mehmel et al., 2020; Lin & Apte, 2018; Jadeja et al., 2020). Such a mechanism is consistent with a substantial body of literature demonstrating that the NAD+-sirtuin axis plays a critical role in regulating neuroprotective and anti-aging functions across various tissues (Dovijarski, 2019; Jadeja et al., 2018; Pîrvu et al., 2021).

At the molecular level, the cascade initiated by NR begins with its metabolic conversion to NAD+, which then serves as an essential substrate for SIRT1 activation. Activated SIRT1 deacetylates TFEB, facilitating its nuclear accumulation and binding to the CLEAR network promoters, thereby upregulating genes responsible for autophagy, lysosomal biogenesis, and lysosomal acidification. This process is expected to boost cathepsin D activity and overall lysosomal proteolytic function. Parallel activation of SIRT3 in mitochondria further strengthens cellular defenses by enhancing mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation and reducing ROS generation through deacetylation of key metabolic enzymes. These reconstructed pathways directly address the deleterious effects of oxidative stress and metabolic dysfunction that drive RPE cell death in dry AMD (Kitaoka et al., 2020; Mehmel et al., 2020; Jadeja et al., 2018). While several studies using NMN have validated these pathways in RPE and retinal cells (Ren et al., 2022), the mechanistic rationale for NR’s effectiveness remains compelling given its similar mode of action and previously documented retinal distribution (Kitaoka et al., 2020; Jadeja et al., 2020).

Expected Effect:  
In the experimental setting, the administration of NR is expected to lead to a marked elevation of intracellular NAD+ levels within RPE cells, setting off a chain reaction of intracellular adjustments. The immediate consequence of increased NAD+ availability will be the enhanced activation of SIRT1 and SIRT3. Once activated, SIRT1 is anticipated to deacetylate TFEB, resulting in its translocation to the nucleus. In the nucleus, TFEB binds to target gene promoters, thereby upregulating a suite of genes involved in lysosomal biogenesis and the autophagic process. Critically, improvements in lysosomal acidification are expected to boost cathepsin D activity—a protease essential for the degradation of intracellular waste and damaged organelles. Simultaneously, SIRT3-mediated deacetylation events within the mitochondria are projected to improve mitochondrial respiratory capacity and enhance ATP production, while also reducing the production of ROS that ordinarily contribute to oxidative damage. The net effect of these cellular modifications should be an increase in RPE cell viability, particularly under conditions of induced oxidative stress (for example, H₂O₂ exposure), which mimics the pathological environment observed in dry AMD (Zhu et al., 2016; Tong et al., 2022).

Additionally, the NR-induced NAD+ boosting is hypothesized to initiate a beneficial feedback loop wherein improved mitochondrial function further supports cellular energy demands and sustains autophagic flux. This dual action—simultaneously targeting lysosomal and mitochondrial dysfunction—addresses two major hallmarks of dry AMD pathophysiology. RPE cells, which are crucial for the maintenance of photoreceptors, suffer from cumulative oxidative damage and impaired clearance of cellular debris as a result of aging and environmental stress. By restoring efficient autophagic processes and ensuring proper mitochondrial function, NR treatment is expected to reduce the accumulation of toxic protein aggregates and dysfunctional organelles, thereby staving off cellular senescence and death. This is especially salient given that recent studies have linked improved NAD+ metabolism to increased cellular resilience in models of age-related neurodegeneration (Jadeja et al., 2018; Jadeja et al., 2020). The expected outcomes in these assays include measurable increases in NAD+/NADH ratios, enhanced expression and nuclear localization of TFEB, elevated cathepsin D activity, and ultimately, improved cell survival following oxidative challenge. Such effects have been reported in various in vitro and in vivo studies employing NAD+ precursors, strengthening the biological plausibility of the NR hypothesis for treating dry AMD (Kitaoka et al., 2020; Mehmel et al., 2020; Dovijarski, 2019).

Overall Evaluation:  
An overall evaluation of NR as a candidate for treating dry AMD reveals both promising strengths and areas requiring further elucidation. Among the principal strengths is NR’s robust ability to elevate systemic and intracellular NAD+ levels, a key factor in numerous regulatory processes implicated in aging and cellular stress response. Its well-characterized pharmacokinetics, combined with documented safety in human supplementation studies, position NR as an attractive candidate for rapid clinical translation (Jadeja et al., 2020; Braidy et al., 2019). The underlying mechanism—that is, the activation of SIRT1 and SIRT3 leading to deacetylation and activation of TFEB—is supported by a breadth of biochemical and preclinical studies, albeit many of these have been performed with related compounds such as NMN. Nevertheless, the evidence suggests that the NAD+–sirtuin–TFEB axis is critical for autophagic and mitochondrial homeostasis in RPE cells—a process compromised in dry AMD (Kitaoka et al., 2020; Mehmel et al., 2020; Jadeja et al., 2018).

Further strengths include NR’s potential to confer dual-organellar benefit. Restoration of lysosomal function, as evidenced by improved acidification and protease activity (e.g., cathepsin D), is a novel therapeutic target that addresses the accumulation of cellular debris—a key factor in the progression of dry AMD. Concurrently, the enhancement of mitochondrial quality and bioenergetics through SIRT3 activation can mitigate oxidative stress and improve cell survival in metabolic stress conditions. Together, these actions provide a mechanistically coherent rationale for repurposing NR in a disease context that currently lacks effective treatments (Kitaoka et al., 2020; Mehmel et al., 2020).

However, several challenges and weaknesses must be acknowledged. First, while preclinical data offer promising insights, direct evidence of NR’s efficacy in RPE cells specifically challenged by dry AMD-like oxidative stress is still limited. Much of the supportive evidence comes from studies employing NMN or from models of other neurodegenerative conditions such as glaucoma and optic nerve degeneration (Lin et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2024). Given differences in uptake and metabolic processing between NR and NMN (Will-Orrego, 2020), it will be important to confirm that NR is adequately taken up by RPE and that its metabolic conversion is efficient in these cells.  

Furthermore, the full cascade—from NAD+ elevation through SIRT1/SIRT3 activation, subsequent TFEB deacetylation, and eventual lysosomal and mitochondrial improvements—remains to be validated within the specific context of dry AMD. Although the general biology of the NAD+–sirtuin axis is well established, its quantitative impact on TFEB activity and cathepsin D function in RPE under conditions of oxidative stress has not been directly demonstrated. This gap in the literature raises questions regarding the optimal dosing regimen, the timing of supplementation, and the potential for compensatory metabolic changes that might blunt the predicted benefits (Ren et al., 2022).

Another consideration is the heterogeneity inherent in dry AMD pathology. RPE cell dysfunction in AMD is multifactorial, involving not only oxidative stress and defective autophagy, but also inflammation, extracellular matrix alterations, and genetic predispositions. Whether NR’s NAD+ boosting effect alone can sufficiently address the multifaceted nature of dry AMD remains uncertain. There is also the possibility that chronic administration might lead to unforeseen metabolic imbalances or off-target effects, particularly if prolonged high-dose supplementation alters systemic NAD+ homeostasis or affects non-target tissues in unintended ways (Ghosh et al., 2023; Jadeja et al., 2018).

Despite these challenges, the candidate’s favorable safety profile and the mechanistic soundness of the NAD+–sirtuin–TFEB hypothesis underpin a strong case for further investigation. In vitro experiments using ARPE-19 cells and primary RPE cultures under oxidative stress conditions should be prioritized to determine whether NR supplementation can reproducibly induce TFEB nuclear translocation, enhance lysosomal acidification, and improve mitochondrial function. In addition, in vivo studies in animal models that recapitulate dry AMD pathology will be essential to assess the translational potential of NR. These studies might include detailed pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic analyses to ascertain the retinal bioavailability of NR, as well as dose-response studies to define the therapeutic window. Finally, controlled clinical trials in patients with early dry AMD would be necessary to confirm efficacy and to optimize treatment protocols (Martucci et al., 2025; Oshitari, 2024; Lin & Apte, 2018).

In summary, the current body of evidence suggests that NR is a promising repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. Its ability to efficiently elevate intracellular NAD+ levels, combined with the downstream activation of SIRT1 and SIRT3, provides a strong mechanistic rationale for improving both autophagic flux and mitochondrial function in RPE cells. These cellular processes are crucial for maintaining retinal health and combating the oxidative and metabolic stress that drives dry AMD progression. Moreover, the extensive preclinical investigation of NAD+ precursors and the favorable safety record of NR in human studies further support its potential for fast-tracking into clinical evaluation for retinal disorders (Kitaoka et al., 2020; Mehmel et al., 2020; Dovijarski, 2019; Jadeja et al., 2020; Pîrvu et al., 2021).

Nonetheless, key uncertainties remain regarding the direct applicability of NR’s effects to the complex microenvironment of the retina in dry AMD. Issues such as differential cellular uptake, the efficiency of NR’s metabolic conversion to NAD+ in RPE cells, and the precise threshold of NAD+ elevation required to trigger beneficial deacetylation of TFEB must be addressed. Furthermore, given the multifactorial nature of AMD pathology, combinatorial therapeutic approaches may ultimately be necessary to achieve clinically significant improvements. Therefore, while NR emerges as a highly promising candidate with a compelling mechanistic framework, rigorous experimental validation tailored specifically to the ocular setting is imperative. Future studies should elucidate whether the activation of the NAD+–sirtuin–TFEB axis translates into meaningful improvements in lysosomal acidification, cathepsin D activity, and RPE cell survival in both in vitro models of oxidative stress and in vivo models of dry AMD (Kitaoka et al., 2020; Jadeja et al., 2018; Will-Orrego, 2020).

Looking forward, systematic exploration through well-designed preclinical trials is recommended to confirm the predicted molecular events. These experiments should include detailed time-course and dose-response analyses of NAD+ levels, sirtuin activities, TFEB deacetylation status, and lysosomal function in retinal cells exposed to oxidative insults. Such data will not only clarify the effectiveness of NR in restoring cellular homeostasis but also help refine dosing strategies and identify potential biomarkers of response. Ultimately, if subsequent research affirms the predicted benefits of NR in improving RPE function and survival, this therapeutic candidate could represent a major advancement in the pharmacological management of dry AMD—a condition for which current treatment options remain notably limited (Kitaoka et al., 2020; Mehmel et al., 2020; Dovijarski, 2019; Jadeja et al., 2020; Pîrvu et al., 2021).

Overall, the promising preclinical evidence supporting the NAD+–sirtuin–TFEB pathway, combined with the safety profile demonstrated in human trials, renders NR a highly attractive candidate for drug development in dry AMD. While further direct experimental evidence is required to confirm its efficacy in retinal cells, the mechanistic insights gleaned from various studies provide a sound scientific basis for proceeding with additional preclinical and clinical investigations. Thus, repurposing nicotinamide riboside for dry AMD holds significant potential and merits further exploration as part of an integrated strategy to address the unmet therapeutic need in this degenerative retinal disease (Abokyi & Tse, 2025; Cimaglia et al., 2020; Ebeling et al., 2020; Jadeja et al., 2020; Pîrvu et al., 2021; Lin & Apte, 2018).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Vorinostat (suberoylanilide hydroxamic acid, SAHA; Selleckchem S1047) is a synthetic small molecule originally discovered through a screening process aimed at identifying inhibitors of histone deacetylases (HDACs) and belongs to the hydroxamic acid class of compounds. It was developed as an anticancer agent and later received U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approval for the treatment of cutaneous T cell lymphoma; its chemical synthesis involves derivatization of an anilide moiety with a hydroxamic acid function, enabling a high degree of specificity for the zinc-dependent catalytic pockets of HDAC enzymes. As a pan-HDAC inhibitor, Vorinostat is designed to modulate epigenetic regulation by binding to the active site of multiple HDAC isoforms, thereby increasing histone acetylation and altering the transcriptional profile of target genes. This class of compounds has been broadly used in oncology, where the modulation of chromatin structure reactivates suppressed tumor suppressor genes and triggers cell cycle arrest and apoptosis. In the context of drug repurposing, the rationale for exploring Vorinostat in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is centered on its potential to epigenetically reprogram retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells by enhancing the acetylation status and activation of key transcription factors such as TFEB and FOXO, which are critical regulators of lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy—a mechanism distinctly different from kinase inhibition strategies (Buniello et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2025).

Therapeutic History:  
Vorinostat’s clinical journey has predominantly revolved around its anticancer applications. Early-phase clinical trials in various solid tumors, including breast, colorectal, and non-small cell lung cancer, as well as studies in metastatic thyroid cancer, relapsed or refractory leukemia, and multiple myeloma, have provided a robust safety profile and dosing regimen for this therapeutic candidate (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2004, 2005, 2006; Ghosh et al., 2024). Although its use in oncology has been extensive—with studies demonstrating its ability to block cell growth by inhibiting key enzymes required for proliferation—the direct evidence for its application in ocular diseases, especially in dry AMD, remains limited. Nonetheless, the broader class of HDAC inhibitors has shown promising results in preclinical ocular models. For instance, several studies have demonstrated that HDAC inhibitors can attenuate choroidal neovascularization, protect retinal tissues from ischemic injury, and promote cellular differentiation in the retinal pigment epithelium (Luo et al., 2025). These findings provide an indirect validation of the concept that epigenetic modulators of HDAC activity may be repurposed to combat the autophagy and lysosomal dysfunction observed in dry AMD. Although Vorinostat itself has not been extensively studied in the context of dry AMD or similar RPE-driven degenerative diseases, its established pharmacological profile and ocular tolerability in other clinical contexts suggest that it could offer mechanistic benefits by modulating retinal epigenetic landscapes (Luo et al., 2025).

Mechanism of Action:  
Vorinostat exerts its biological effects by inhibiting the activity of zinc-dependent histone deacetylases. Under normal physiological conditions, HDACs remove acetyl groups from the lysine residues on histone tails, leading to chromatin condensation and transcriptional repression; by inhibiting these enzymes, Vorinostat results in the accumulation of acetylated histones and a more relaxed chromatin structure that promotes gene transcription. The current hypothesis contends that in RPE cells, Vorinostat-mediated HDAC inhibition will enhance the acetylation of the transcription factors TFEB (transcription factor EB) and members of the FOXO (forkhead box O) family. TFEB is a master regulator of the coordinated lysosomal expression and regulation (CLEAR) network, which governs the transcription of genes encoding lysosomal enzymes, including cathepsin D (CTSD), and other proteins necessary for autophagy and lysosomal acidification (Buniello et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2025). Similarly, FOXO transcription factors are implicated in cellular stress responses and can promote the expression of antioxidant enzymes as well as proteins involved in maintaining mitochondrial integrity. In neuronal models, HDAC inhibition has been linked to increased expression, acetylation, and nuclear localization of TFEB, leading to upregulation of lysosomal gene expression and enhanced autophagic flux (Buniello et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2025). It is anticipated that Vorinostat will operate through a similar mechanism in RPE cells by facilitating the dissociation of HDACs from the promoters of TFEB/FOXO target genes, thereby promoting their transcriptional activation. This would initiate a cascade of events that enhance lysosomal biogenesis, improve lysosomal acidification, and increase the activity of cathepsin D—the lysosomal protease that plays a critical role in degrading accumulated protein aggregates and damaged cellular organelles, which are pathognomonic of dry AMD pathology (Luo et al., 2025). Moreover, it is relevant that other HDAC inhibitors, such as trichostatin A (TSA) and valproic acid (VPA), have demonstrated the capacity to modulate similar pathways in retinal cells, thereby indirectly supporting the proposed mechanism of action for Vorinostat in restoring lysosomal function and autophagic balance in RPE cells (Luo et al., 2025).

Expected Effect:  
Based on the proposed mechanism of action, the expected effect of Vorinostat in the context of dry AMD is multifaceted. The compound is anticipated to inhibit HDAC activity in RPE cells, leading to an increase in overall protein acetylation, including that of histones and transcription factors. This epigenetic modulation should facilitate the nuclear translocation and activation of TFEB, thereby upregulating the CLEAR network of genes involved in lysosomal biogenesis, acidification, and autophagy. In turn, the increased expression and activity of cathepsin D will improve the degradative capacity of the lysosomes, fostering the clearance of lipofuscin and other deleterious protein aggregates that accumulate with age in RPE cells. Additionally, enhanced FOXO activity could promote an improved antioxidant response and mitigate mitochondrial dysfunction, which together would reduce oxidative stress—a key driver of RPE degeneration in dry AMD (Buniello et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2025).

The anticipated outcome in preclinical assays would be a measurable restoration of autophagic flux as evidenced by reductions in markers of cellular stress and accumulation of autophagy substrates. Cellular assays may demonstrate increased lysosomal enzyme activities, such as that of cathepsin D, and improved acidification of lysosomes in treated RPE cells. In animal models engineered or induced to exhibit dry AMD-like pathology, treatment with Vorinostat is expected to lead to an improvement in retinal structure and function, potentially assessed through morphological analyses and electroretinography. Furthermore, the restoration of TFEB/FOXO activity should enhance the overall cellular resilience of RPE, thereby delaying or preventing the progression of degenerative changes associated with dry AMD. Given Vorinostat’s established oral bioavailability and systemic tolerability in oncology patients, there is potential for its repurposing with adjusted dosing regimens aimed at achieving therapeutic concentrations in the retina with minimal systemic toxicity (Buniello et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2025).

Overall Evaluation:  
In evaluating Vorinostat as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, several strengths and weaknesses emerge. One of the principal strengths of Vorinostat is its well-characterized pharmacological profile, which is supported by extensive clinical data in oncology. Its FDA-approved status and known systemic tolerability provide a translational advantage over novel compounds that are still in early developmental stages. The robust mechanism of action of HDAC inhibitors, with demonstrated capacity to modulate gene expression through epigenetic reprogramming, aligns well with the pathobiology of dry AMD, where impaired autophagy and lysosomal dysfunction are central features. The specific hypothesis that Vorinostat will promote the acetylation and activation of TFEB and FOXO transcription factors to drive lysosomal biogenesis, improve acidification, and enhance cathepsin D activity addresses well-validated therapeutic targets in the disease process (Buniello et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2025).

However, there are also significant weaknesses and potential challenges that must be carefully considered. First, while the mechanistic rationale is compelling, direct experimental evidence supporting Vorinostat’s efficacy in RPE cells or animal models of dry AMD is currently sparse. Much of the supporting data is extrapolated from studies using other HDAC inhibitors such as TSA, VPA, or AN7, and from cancer studies where the cellular context differs substantially from that of the RPE (Luo et al., 2025). Second, the pharmacokinetic profile and ocular tissue penetration of Vorinostat when administered systemically remain uncertain. The blood–retinal barrier presents a formidable challenge to achieving therapeutic drug concentrations in the retina, and while clinical trials in oncology have established systemic dosing guidelines, it is unclear whether these doses will translate into efficacious levels within the RPE while maintaining safety. Third, the potential for off-target effects and retinal toxicity cannot be overlooked; certain HDAC inhibitors have been associated with deleterious retinal effects when administered at inappropriate doses or over prolonged periods, emphasizing the need for careful dose optimization and possibly localized (e.g., intravitreal) delivery strategies (Luo et al., 2025). Fourth, the complex interplay between various HDAC isoforms in the retina may necessitate a more selective approach than that offered by the broad-spectrum inhibition provided by Vorinostat, as indiscriminate inhibition could disrupt other acetylation-dependent regulatory mechanisms critical for normal retinal function (Luo et al., 2025).

In addition, while the hypothesis posits that Vorinostat will upregulate TFEB and FOXO to enhance autophagy and lysosomal function, the regulation of these transcription factors is multifactorial. For example, TFEB activity is tightly controlled by phosphorylation events mediated by mTORC1 and AKT2 signaling pathways, and the interplay between these kinases, deacetylases such as SIRT5, and HDACs remains an active area of investigation (Abokyi & Tse, 2025; Buniello et al., 2025; Ghosh et al., 2024). Thus, while there is mechanistic plausibility in promoting lysosomal biogenesis via HDAC inhibition, the precise molecular outcomes in the unique environment of aging RPE cells require further delineation. Furthermore, studies in other models have revealed that the beneficial effects of HDAC inhibition on autophagy and lysosomal function may vary depending on the timing, duration, and specific isoform selectivity of the inhibitor used (Luo et al., 2025).

Taking these factors into account, a cautious but optimistic view emerges regarding the repurposing of Vorinostat for dry AMD. The compound’s established clinical track record in oncology is a substantial advantage, providing a foundation for subsequent translational studies. The convergent evidence supporting the role of HDAC inhibition in enhancing autophagy and mitigating oxidative stress in retinal diseases further bolsters the rationale for this approach (Falcão et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2025). However, to fully validate the therapeutic potential of Vorinostat in dry AMD, rigorous preclinical studies are needed to (1) confirm its efficacy in restoring TFEB/FOXO activity and lysosomal function in RPE cells, (2) determine its pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic properties in ocular tissues, (3) assess its safety profile within the retina over chronic dosing schedules, and (4) establish optimized dosing strategies that achieve target engagement without compromising retinal integrity.

Moreover, future investigations might explore alternative delivery mechanisms, such as nanoparticle-based systems or sustained-release intravitreal formulations, to circumvent the challenges posed by the blood–retinal barrier and achieve localized drug concentrations that are both effective and safe. In parallel, combinatorial therapeutic strategies that pair Vorinostat with other agents that modulate complementary pathways—such as antioxidants, SIRT1 activators, or agents that specifically target mTORC1 signaling—could be considered to provide a multifaceted approach to treating dry AMD. These strategies would leverage the ability of Vorinostat to reprogram epigenetic signatures in RPE cells while simultaneously addressing other pathogenic mechanisms contributing to AMD progression (Buniello et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2025).

In summary, Vorinostat represents a promising candidate for drug repurposing in dry AMD due to its potent HDAC inhibitory activity, favorable clinical history in oncology, and a plausible mechanism by which it could restore lysosomal biogenesis and autophagic flux in RPE cells—a central defect in dry AMD pathogenesis. The strengths of this approach include the compound’s established approval and known pharmacology, coupled with emerging evidence that epigenetic modulation can address key cellular dysfunctions in retinal degeneration. Conversely, the critical weaknesses pertain to the lack of direct preclinical evidence in the context of AMD, uncertainties regarding effective ocular delivery, and potential risks of off-target effects in a delicate tissue such as the retina. A comprehensive series of translational studies, beginning with in vitro models of RPE dysfunction and progressing to in vivo dry AMD models, is essential to fully establish the therapeutic window, efficacy, and safety profile of Vorinostat for this new indication. If these studies yield positive results, Vorinostat could offer a novel, mechanistically precise approach to the treatment of dry AMD, addressing a significant unmet clinical need by restoring the autophagy–lysosome pathway and ultimately preserving vision in affected patients (Buniello et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2025).
