Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Fingolimod (FTY720) is a synthetic, sphingoid-base mimetic that is phosphorylated in vivo by sphingosine kinase 2 (SphK2) to yield the active metabolite FTY720-phosphate (FTY720-P), which binds sphingosine-1-phosphate receptors (S1PRs) with sub-micromolar affinity comparable to endogenous S1P (primarily S1PR1, S1PR3, S1PR4, and S1PR5) (Gupta et al., 2012; Gesualdo et al., 2021). As a small-molecule modulator of S1PRs, fingolimod belongs to the class of GPCR-targeting immunomodulators that regulate lymphocyte trafficking and vascular/endothelial signaling; this class has been deployed extensively in neuroinflammatory disease (e.g., multiple sclerosis) and investigated across ocular inflammatory and vascular pathologies (Gesualdo et al., 2021; Sorenson et al., 2022). In ocular biology, endogenous S1P signaling is pleiotropic: it is detected in, and acts upon, multiple retinal cell types including RPE, endothelium, neurons, and glia, where it can protect photoreceptors from oxidative stress–induced apoptosis and modulate wound repair and barrier function, underscoring the translational appeal of S1PR modulators for retinal degenerations (Gupta et al., 2012). At the same time, the S1P axis exhibits context-dependent outcomes—anti-S1P antibodies reduce subretinal fibrosis in AMD models—so receptor-subtype selectivity, ligand presentation (e.g., apoM/HDL-bound vs free), and cell-type–specific responses will be critical to therapeutic design (Gupta et al., 2012; Jung et al., 2025).

Therapeutic History  
Fingolimod is an approved oral therapy that reduces lesion formation in multiple sclerosis through S1PR-mediated immunomodulation, providing an extensive clinical safety and pharmacology dataset for potential repurposing (Mondal & Mandal, 2019). In ocular indications, preclinical studies demonstrate that S1PR pathway manipulation alters retinal/choroidal vascular pathology: intravitreally delivered S1P chaperoned by apolipoprotein M (apoM) activates endothelial S1PR1 and suppresses choroidal neovascularization (CNV) and vascular leak, and separate approaches show that anti-S1P antibodies or S1PR1-selective agonists can suppress CNV and stabilize endothelial barriers (Jung et al., 2025; Sorenson et al., 2022). Fingolimod itself (as FTY720) reduces choroidal endothelial migration and capillary morphogenesis in vitro and mitigates CNV in vivo, indicating that systemic or intraocular S1PR modulation impacts ocular neovascular disease biology (Sorenson et al., 2022). In diabetic retinopathy models, fingolimod reduces retinal angiogenesis and VEGFA levels, aligning with its anti-angiogenic/vascular-stabilizing profile (Gesualdo et al., 2021). Importantly for the dry AMD context, none of these studies directly evaluate atrophic AMD outcomes, RPE autophagy/lysosome endpoints, or complement-driven injury after fingolimod, and there is no prior clinical use of fingolimod for dry AMD (Jung et al., 2025; Sorenson et al., 2022). A material safety consideration for retinal indications is fingolimod-associated macular edema (FAME), reported in clinical settings and relevant to dosing, route, and patient selection if repurposed for macular disease (Mondal & Mandal, 2019).

Mechanism of Action  
Receptor pharmacology of fingolimod and ocular S1P biology. Fingolimod is phosphorylated by SphK2 to FTY720-P, which behaves as a functional agonist at S1PR1, S1PR4, and S1PR5 and a partial agonist at S1PR3, triggering receptor internalization and signaling adaptation that sequesters lymphocytes and modulates vascular responses (Gupta et al., 2012; Gesualdo et al., 2021). In ocular tissues, S1PR1 is prominently expressed in multiple cell types, with experimental evidence demonstrating S1PR1 expression in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) where S1PR1 appears as the predominant S1PR subtype alongside dynamic regulation of S1PR1/S1PR3 by oxygen tension (Sorenson et al., 2022). RPE also expresses the S1P-generating enzymes SphK1 and SphK2 and can synthesize and release S1P, providing the local pathway components to respond to pharmacologic S1PR modulation (Wang et al., 2023). S1P ligands elicit cell-type–specific responses in the retinal neurovascular unit: endothelial S1PR1 activation stabilizes adherens junctions and quells sprouting angiogenesis, apoM/HDL-bound S1P reduces choroidal leakage and CNV, and S1P/S1PR signaling influences RPE barrier function and angiogenic or inflammatory outputs (Jung et al., 2025; Sorenson et al., 2022). These features render S1PR1 a biologically plausible target in RPE and choroid for modulating disease-relevant pathways in AMD, while also highlighting that the net effect of S1P pathway modulation depends on receptor subtype and ligand context (Jung et al., 2025; Sorenson et al., 2022).

RPE autophagy–lysosome biology, lysosomal acidification, and AMD. The RPE is a post-mitotic, highly phagocytic epithelium that performs daily heterophagy of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) and constitutive macroautophagy, processes that converge on lysosomal degradation; failure at the lysosomal step produces lipofuscin accumulation, proteotoxic stress, and drusen formation that characterize AMD (Sinha et al., 2016). Lysosomal acidity, maintained by the vacuolar H^+-ATPase (V-ATPase), is essential for cathepsin activity and cargo hydrolysis; AMD-relevant lipofuscin bisretinoids such as A2E elevate lysosomal pH by inhibiting V-ATPase, impairing phagolysosomal digestion of POS and promoting a feed-forward cycle of oxidative stress and lysosomal dysfunction (Sinha et al., 2016). Lysosomal signaling couples to mTORC1 at the lysosomal surface via V-ATPase–Ragulator–Rag GTPase complexes, integrating luminal amino acids and energy status to regulate autophagy; in RPE, βA3/A1-crystallin (Cryba1) binds the V0 domain of V-ATPase and its loss produces mTORC1 hyperactivation, inefficient lysosomal clearance, and AMD-like pathology, functionally tying V-ATPase activity and mTORC1–TFEB signaling to disease (Sinha et al., 2016). Autophagy protects RPE from oxidative stress, and genetic or age-related declines in macroautophagy correlate with mitochondrial dysfunction, increased ROS, inflammasome activation, and lipofuscin accumulation in human AMD eyes and animal models (Sinha et al., 2016). These data establish that increasing autophagic flux and restoring lysosomal acidification are mechanistically central interventions for RPE protection in AMD.

The AMPK–mTOR–ULK1/TFEB axis: a mechanistic route to autophagy and lysosomal biogenesis. AMPK and mTOR are canonical, opposing regulators of autophagy: AMPK stimulates autophagy by activating ULK1 and inhibiting mTORC1 (including via TSC1/2–Rheb), whereas mTORC1 phosphorylates ULK1/Atg13 to block initiation and phosphorylates Atg14 to dampen nucleation (Wang et al., 2023). TFEB/TFE3 are master transcription factors of lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy; mTORC1 phosphorylation retains TFEB in the cytosol, and mTORC1 inhibition permits TFEB nuclear translocation to activate the CLEAR network of lysosomal and autophagy genes (Wang et al., 2023). AMPK-dependent phosphorylation is required for TFEB/TFE3 transcriptional activation, and AMPK activation increases V-ATPase assembly and activity under glucose starvation, providing a direct link from energy stress to lysosomal acidification machinery (Boya et al., 2023). In RPE/AMD-relevant systems, TFEB activation increases expression of V-ATPase subunits (e.g., ATP6V0A1), lysosomal proteins (LAMP2), and cathepsins (CTSB), and reduces accumulation of POS-dependent lipofuscin-like granules; trehalose- or rapamycin-mediated TFEB activation enhances autophagic flux and decreases A2E/lipofuscin load and inflammatory markers in RPE models (Falcão et al., 2025). Human AMD RPE displays increased TFEB phosphorylation and reduced nuclear TFEB, together with decreased cathepsin levels, consistent with mTORC1-mediated suppression of lysosomal function; TFEB reactivation in Cryba1-deficient RPE rescues CLEAR gene expression and degradative capacity, supporting TFEB as a viable target for lysosomal rejuvenation (Falcão et al., 2025).

Mitochondria–lysosome crosstalk, S1P, and oxidative damage. Mitochondrial quality control via PINK1/PRKN-driven mitophagy and mitochondria-derived vesicles (MDVs) is coordinated with lysosomal function; AMPK acts bidirectionally to couple mitochondrial stress to lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy competence (Boya et al., 2023). In RPE and AMD models, mitochondrial dysfunction (mtDNA damage, impaired mitophagy) increases ROS and sensitizes cells to inflammasome activation and downstream damage; restoring lysosomal/mitochondrial clearance reduces oxidative injury (Boya et al., 2023). S1P signaling can induce mitochondrial biogenesis and thereby influence immunometabolic homeostasis; combined with AMPK–TFEB activation, S1P-related pathways could theoretically enhance both mitochondrial and lysosomal resilience in stressed RPE (Boya et al., 2023).

Inflammation, complement, and autophagy–lysosome cross-talk in AMD. Autophagy negatively regulates inflammasome activation, and complement/inflammasome axes contribute to RPE pathology in AMD; for example, complement C5a primes inflammasomes, and high-risk CFH Y402H RPE exhibit swollen lysosomes with cathepsin D leakage and increased lysosomal C5b-9 deposition (Kaarniranta et al., 2023; Falcão et al., 2025). Complement-related lysosomal stress provides a plausible injury modality that could be mitigated by lysosomal stabilization and increased autophagic flux; indeed, complement modulation can restore lysosomal function in a CFH Y402H RPE model (Boya et al., 2023). Because impaired lysosome/autophagy promotes secretory autophagy of inflammatory cargo, including HMGB1 and possibly amyloid species, enhancing lysosomal degradation should also reduce extracellular pro-inflammatory signals that propagate AMD pathology (Kaarniranta et al., 2023; Sinha et al., 2016).

What is known—and unknown—about fingolimod and the AMPK/TFEB–lysosome axis. In human cell models outside the eye, fingolimod can increase LC3B-II and alter Akt signaling (dephosphorylating Akt1 at Ser473), consistent with autophagy induction; yet the same studies report TFEB downregulation and induction of an inhibitory phosphorylation mark on TFEB (Ser211), with overall interpretations suggesting potential for stalling/saturation of autophagy under some conditions, and cell-type–dependent lysosomal enlargement and membrane permeabilization have also been described (Relic et al., 2021). Across the RPE/AMD literature summarized here, there is no direct demonstration that fingolimod or S1PR agonists activate AMPK, mobilize TFEB to the nucleus, increase V-ATPase–dependent lysosomal acidification, or enhance autophagic flux in RPE; nor are there data showing that fingolimod reduces complement-driven RPE injury in dry AMD models (Boya et al., 2023; Falcão et al., 2025). These are critical gaps that must be addressed experimentally before the proposed mechanism can be accepted (Jung et al., 2025; Relic et al., 2021).

Expected Effect  
Target engagement and proximal signaling in RPE. Because S1PR1 is expressed in RPE and appears to be the predominant S1P receptor subtype in this cell type, fingolimod (as FTY720-P) should engage RPE S1PRs at pharmacologically relevant concentrations if present in the subretinal/choroidal milieu, although receptor subtype balance and receptor down-modulation dynamics will influence outcomes (Sorenson et al., 2022; Gesualdo et al., 2021). In the hypothesized AMPK→TFEB pathway, proximal readouts would include increased AMPK phosphorylation/activation, decreased mTORC1 activity (e.g., phospho-S6K/4EBP1), and enhanced nuclear localization of TFEB/TFE3, followed by transcriptional upregulation of CLEAR genes (e.g., LAMP1/2, ATP6V0A1, CTSB/D) (Boya et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2023; Falcão et al., 2025). Because S1PR signaling is pleiotropic, it is critical to test whether fingolimod in RPE shifts Akt and mTORC1 activities toward a TFEB-permissive state, as opposed to inducing the inhibitory TFEB Ser211 phosphorylation and autophagy stalling seen in some non-ocular cells (Relic et al., 2021).

Lysosomal acidification, degradative capacity, and autophagic flux. If fingolimod drives AMPK activation and TFEB nuclear translocation in RPE, predicted functional outcomes include increased V-ATPase assembly and activity (acidified lysosomes), higher cathepsin activity, and increased autophagic flux measurable by LC3-II turnover in the presence of bafilomycin or chloroquine, together with decreased steady-state p62/SQSTM1 under basal degradative conditions (Boya et al., 2023; Falcão et al., 2025). TFEB activation in RPE models reduces POS-dependent lipofuscin-like granule accumulation and increases lysosome number; pharmacologic TFEB induction (e.g., with trehalose) increases lysosomal biogenesis and autophagosome–lysosome fusion, so fingolimod engagement of this axis should phenocopy these protective changes if the postulated signaling is correct (Falcão et al., 2025). Restoration of lysosomal acidity would be expected to counteract A2E- and lipofuscin-induced V-ATPase inhibition, improving phagolysosomal degradation of POS and reducing waste buildup (Sinha et al., 2016).

Oxidative stress, mitochondrial homeostasis, and inflammasome/complement outputs. By increasing autophagic and mitophagic flux, and engaging TFEB-dependent antioxidant/clearance programs, the candidate mechanism should reduce mitochondrial ROS, stabilize mitochondrial biogenesis via AMPK–PGC-1 pathways, and decrease ROS-dependent priming of inflammasomes (Boya et al., 2023; Sinha et al., 2016). Autophagy mitigates inflammasome activation, and restoring lysosome function reduces the release of DAMPs and secretory autophagy cargo (e.g., HMGB1), which together would be expected to blunt complement pathway amplification in stressed RPE; complement deposition (C5b-9) within lysosomes, especially in CFH risk-allele RPE, may be reduced if lysosomal integrity is preserved and capacity is restored (Kaarniranta et al., 2023; Falcão et al., 2025). In aggregate, if fingolimod engages the AMPK–TFEB–lysosome axis in RPE as hypothesized, one would expect improvements in lysosomal pH, cathepsin activity (including CTSD), autophagic flux, reduced lipofuscin/A2E accumulation, lower mitochondrial ROS, and decreased inflammasome/complement readouts in RPE challenged with AMD-relevant stresses (oxidants, A2E, complement components) (Falcão et al., 2025; Sinha et al., 2016; Kaarniranta et al., 2023).

Caveats and contrary expectations. Fingolimod’s effects on TFEB and autophagy are cell- and context-dependent; in human synovial fibroblasts and HEK293 cells fingolimod induced TFEB Ser211 phosphorylation and TFEB downregulation despite LC3B-II accumulation, suggesting potential autophagy stalling and negative feedback on TFEB that could counter the desired lysosomal biogenesis in RPE (Relic et al., 2021). Moreover, S1P pathway manipulation can yield opposing outcomes in different compartments (e.g., anti-S1P strategies reduce ocular fibrosis/CNV), so nonselective S1PR modulation by fingolimod may not cleanly recapitulate the endothelial-protective, S1PR1-selective phenotypes observed with apoM/HDL–S1P delivery (Jung et al., 2025; Gupta et al., 2012). Finally, retinal safety signals—particularly macular edema—have been associated with fingolimod in clinical practice and would warrant stringent dose–exposure control and route optimization (e.g., local ocular delivery) in any AMD program (Mondal & Mandal, 2019).

Assay design implications. Given the mechanistic uncertainties, rigorous RPE-focused assays must be prioritized: (1) S1PR1/3/5 expression profiling in the chosen RPE system (primary human, iPSC-RPE) and receptor occupancy by fingolimod; (2) AMPK phosphorylation and mTORC1 readouts (p-AMPK, p-S6K, p-4EBP1) after fingolimod with and without S1PR antagonists; (3) TFEB/TFE3 nuclear translocation and CLEAR target induction; (4) lysosomal pH (ratiometric LysoSensor) and V-ATPase assembly/activity; (5) autophagic flux (LC3-II turnover ± lysosomal inhibitors; p62 dynamics); (6) cathepsin D/L activity assays; (7) oxidative stress resilience (mitoROS, mtDNA damage) and mitophagy markers; and (8) complement handling (C3 turnover, C5b-9 deposition) under CFH Y402H and amyloid/oxidant stress conditions (Falcão et al., 2025; Sinha et al., 2016; Falcão et al., 2025; Kaarniranta et al., 2023). Benchmarking to validated TFEB activators (e.g., trehalose) and lysosomal acidification restorers will contextualize fingolimod’s performance on the most disease-relevant axes (Falcão et al., 2025).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Strong disease–mechanism alignment: Dry AMD is characterized by impaired lysosomal acidification, defective autophagic clearance, and oxidative/complement stress in RPE; AMPK–mTOR–TFEB signaling and V-ATPase activity are validated nodal controllers of lysosomal competence in RPE and AMD models, providing clear mechanistic targets that, if engaged, should be disease-modifying (Sinha et al., 2016; Sinha et al., 2016; Falcão et al., 2025; Sinha et al., 2016).  
- On-target cellular expression: S1PR1 is present in RPE and is the predominant S1PR subtype, while RPE express SphK1/2, indicating the S1P/S1PR machinery required for pharmacologic modulation exists in the target cell (Sorenson et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2023).  
- Prior ocular efficacy signals via S1PR modulation: ApoM/HDL–S1P→S1PR1 suppresses CNV and leakage; FTY720 reduces choroidal endothelial angiogenic behaviors and mitigates CNV; in diabetic retinopathy, fingolimod decreases VEGF signaling—together confirming relevant ocular pharmacology and providing translational scaffolding for retinal use (Jung et al., 2025; Sorenson et al., 2022; Gesualdo et al., 2021).  
- Immunometabolic rationale: S1P signaling can promote mitochondrial biogenesis, and AMPK–TFEB signaling coordinates mitochondrial–lysosomal crosstalk; a single agent engaging the S1P–AMPK–TFEB axis might simultaneously improve mitochondrial and lysosomal resilience in oxidatively stressed RPE (Boya et al., 2023; Boya et al., 2023).  
- Repurposing tractability: Extensive human exposure, known PK/PD, and manageable formulation chemistry enable accelerated translational planning compared to de novo entities (Mondal & Mandal, 2019).

Weaknesses and risks  
- Mechanistic gap in the target cell: There is currently no direct evidence that fingolimod activates AMPK or TFEB in RPE, increases autophagic flux, or acidifies lysosomes; likewise, no data show fingolimod reduces complement-driven injury in RPE/dry AMD models, and this is the central premise of the hypothesis (Jung et al., 2025; Boya et al., 2023; Falcão et al., 2025).  
- Context dependence and potential for adverse lysosomal effects: In human non-ocular cells, fingolimod induced inhibitory TFEB phosphorylation and autophagy stalling, and lysosomal enlargement/permeabilization has been reported in some contexts—opposite to the desired lysosomal restoration—raising the possibility of deleterious effects in RPE unless carefully titrated (Relic et al., 2021).  
- Receptor- and ligand-context complexity: Beneficial vascular phenotypes are associated with endothelial S1PR1 stimulation—often via chaperone-bound S1P—while nonselective S1PR modulation or anti-S1P strategies can also be beneficial (e.g., anti-fibrotic effects in AMD), implying that fingolimod’s mixed S1PR agonism and functional antagonism could yield off-target or counterproductive outcomes in the RPE/choroid (Jung et al., 2025; Gupta et al., 2012; Sorenson et al., 2022).  
- Retinal safety concerns: Fingolimod-associated macular edema is a documented adverse effect in humans, which is particularly concerning in a macular disease; any development plan must incorporate delivery strategies and exposure limits that mitigate this risk (Mondal & Mandal, 2019).  
- Evidence base skew: Much of the directly AMD-relevant S1P/S1PR ocular literature concerns neovascular endpoints (wet AMD/CNV) or endothelium, not atrophic RPE biology; the best lysosome/autophagy data are robust but are not linked to S1PR pharmacology, necessitating bridging studies to validate the specific drug–mechanism–disease chain (Jung et al., 2025; Falcão et al., 2025).

Go/no-go perspective and experimental priorities  
On balance, fingolimod is a mechanistically plausible, but currently unvalidated, repurposing candidate for dry AMD via the proposed S1PR→AMPK→TFEB→lysosome axis. A limited, mechanism-first preclinical package in human RPE models is warranted before considering in vivo efficacy work. The minimum data package to de-risk the hypothesis should include:  
- Demonstration that fingolimod engages S1PRs on human RPE and increases AMPK activity while suppressing mTORC1, with consequent TFEB/TFE3 nuclear translocation and CLEAR gene induction; side-by-side with a S1PR1-selective agonist and apoM/HDL-S1P as positive controls for S1PR1 biology (Sorenson et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2023; Falcão et al., 2025; Jung et al., 2025).  
- Functional lysosomal rescue: increased V-ATPase assembly/activity, lower lysosomal pH, increased CTSD/CTSL activity, improved POS digestion, reduced A2E and lipofuscin-like autofluorescence under static and diurnal POS feeding paradigms (Sinha et al., 2016; Falcão et al., 2025).  
- Flux and mitochondrial outcomes: increased autophagic flux (LC3-II turnover, p62 dynamics), enhanced mitophagy under oxidant stress (PINK1/PRKN markers), and decreased mitoROS (Boya et al., 2023; Sinha et al., 2016).  
- Inflammation/complement endpoints: reduced IL1B release after MG-132/BafA challenges, lowered NLRP3 activation, decreased lysosomal C5b-9 deposition and improved lysosomal integrity in CFH Y402H iPSC-RPE exposed to complement (Piippo, 2019; Falcão et al., 2025).  
- Safety liabilities: absence of lysosomal membrane permeabilization, cathepsin leakage, or TFEB Ser211 inhibitory phosphorylation with autophagy stalling at therapeutic exposure in RPE, in contrast to adverse signatures reported in other cell types (Relic et al., 2021).

Depending on these in vitro outcomes, a focused in vivo test in a dry AMD-relevant model (e.g., NaIO3 injury or Cryba1 cKO) with intraocular delivery and a retinal safety assessment (OCT for edema, ERG, histology) would be the logical next step (Falcão et al., 2025; Sinha et al., 2016). If the AMPK–TFEB and lysosomal endpoints are not met, pivot to alternative S1PR strategies (S1PR1-selective agonists or apoM/HDL–S1P formulations) that have more consistent endothelial/retinal protective phenotypes may be warranted (Jung et al., 2025). If proximal signaling is partially engaged but lysosomal capacity remains limiting, combination approaches with validated TFEB activators (e.g., trehalose) or NRF2 activators that cross-reinforce lysosomal and antioxidant programs could be explored with attention to oncogenicity and cell specificity (Falcão et al., 2025).

Conclusion  
Fingolimod sits at the intersection of a compelling disease mechanism (lysosomal/autophagic failure in RPE), a plausible upstream target (S1PR1 in RPE), and a therapeutic class with ocular activity (S1PR modulators), but it lacks direct evidence for engaging the AMPK–TFEB–lysosomal biogenesis/acidification axis in RPE or for mitigating complement/oxidative injury in dry AMD models (Sorenson et al., 2022; Falcão et al., 2025; Jung et al., 2025). The strength of the lysosome/autophagy rationale and the existence of RPE S1PR1 expression support a mechanism-first exploration; however, cell-type–dependent fingolimod effects on TFEB and autophagy and the clinical risk of macular edema demand caution (Relic et al., 2021; Mondal & Mandal, 2019). Proceed only with a staged validation plan centered on RPE-intrinsic endpoints of AMPK/TFEB activation, lysosomal acidification, and complement/oxidative resilience; without those data, the hypothesis remains unsubstantiated for dry AMD, and alternative S1PR strategies or direct TFEB/lysosome-targeting interventions may be more tractable (Jung et al., 2025; Falcão et al., 2025).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
USP14 inhibitor IU1 (Sigma SML0010) is a synthetic small-molecule compound originally discovered through high-throughput screening efforts aimed at identifying inhibitors of deubiquitinating enzymes (DUBs) associated with the proteasome. IU1 belongs to the class of small-molecule DUB inhibitors that specifically target USP14, a proteasome-associated deubiquitinase responsible for trimming ubiquitin chains from substrates before their degradation by the 26S proteasome. Early medicinal chemistry studies led to the development of IU1 and its more potent analogs (such as IU1-47), which exploit structure–activity relationships on a benzene–dimethyl-pyrrole scaffold with tailored electron-withdrawing substitutions and lipophilic enhancements designed to improve potency, selectivity, and bioavailability (Lim et al., 2024; Boselli et al., 2017; Qin et al., 2024). These compounds are cell permeable and have been employed as chemical probes in multiple preclinical settings to modulate proteostasis via targeted inhibition of USP14. In essence, IU1 reflects a series of rationally designed molecules aimed at shifting the balance of proteasome-mediated degradation by preventing USP14’s “trimming” activity, thereby effectively accelerating the clearance of misfolded and aggregation-prone proteins.

Therapeutic History:  
The therapeutic history of USP14 inhibitors like IU1 is primarily rooted in preclinical research addressing proteostasis dysfunction in models of aging and neurodegeneration rather than in clinical or veterinary practice. In Drosophila models of proteostasis-associated aging, IU1 treatment was shown to reduce the accumulation of polyubiquitinated aggregates, increase autophagy markers such as LC3, improve behavioral phenotypes, and even extend lifespan, with these benefits abrogated when autophagy was experimentally disrupted (Lim et al., 2024). In mammalian cell proteotoxicity models—using stressors such as canavanine plus azetidine—IU1 has similarly been reported to reduce ubiquitin conjugate accumulation and enhance autophagic responses (Lim et al., 2024). Moreover, in primary neuronal cultures, more potent analogs like IU1-47 have been used to promote degradation of pathologic proteins such as tau, thereby supporting the concept that USP14 inhibition enhances proteasome-assisted clearance of aggregation-prone substrates (Boselli et al., 2017; Kiprowska, 2016). Despite these promising preclinical data in models of neurodegeneration and systemic aging, there is no direct evidence to date that IU1 or its analogs have been applied to treat dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or geographic atrophy specifically. However, given that several key observations in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells—such as evidence of impaired ubiquitin–proteasome system (UPS) and autophagy cross-talk, aggregate accumulation, and lysosomal dysfunction—are central to AMD pathology (Blasiak et al., 2019; Kaarniranta et al., 2023; Shang & Taylor, 2012), repurposing IU1 to restore proteostasis in RPE represents an innovative extension of its preclinical use.

Mechanism of Action:  
The known mechanism of IU1 centers on its inhibition of USP14, a deubiquitinating enzyme that transiently associates with the proteasome. USP14 normally functions by “trimming” ubiquitin chains on substrates as they enter the proteasome, an activity that can delay substrate degradation and allow for substrate rescue under stress conditions. IU1 and its optimized analogs (e.g., IU1-47) act through allosteric mechanisms—not by directly competing at the catalytic site but by binding a pocket distal (approximately 8.3 Å away) from the catalytic center, thereby perturbing USP14’s structural conformation and catalytic efficiency (Qin et al., 2024; Lim et al., 2024). Inhibition of USP14 by IU1 leads to a reduced removal of ubiquitin chains, effectively “locking in” the ubiquitin tag on misfolded and aggregation-prone proteins and facilitating their recognition and degradation by the 26S proteasome. Beyond its direct impact on proteasomal degradation, USP14 inhibition has been reported to modulate autophagy—evident from increased LC3 lipidation and autophagic flux in certain cellular contexts (Lim et al., 2024; Kim, 2020). Some studies suggest that USP14 may also indirectly influence autophagy by regulating the turnover of factors such as UVRAG, a key autophagy regulator, although these connections remain to be fully elucidated. Notably, while IU1 has been shown to accelerate aggregate clearance in neuronal and Drosophila models, a series of studies have also flagged potential off-target effects at higher concentrations, including inhibition of mitochondrial Complex I leading to ATP depletion and subsequent activation of calpain-mediated proteolysis (Kiprowska, 2016; Kiprowska et al., n.d.). Hence, the molecular interactions of IU1 are complex and highly context-dependent, with the potential to both enhance proteasomal degradation and, at non-optimized doses, induce metabolic perturbations.

Expected Effect:  
In the context of dry age-related macular degeneration, particularly geographic atrophy, the central hypothesis is that IU1 will inhibit USP14 in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells, thereby accelerating the proteasome-assisted clearance of misfolded, aggregation-prone proteins. RPE cells in AMD display defects in both the UPS and the autophagy/lysosomal systems, with studies documenting decreased proteasome activity, accumulation of ubiquitinated aggregates, elevated levels of the selective autophagy adaptor SQSTM1/p62, and lysosomal dysfunction including impaired acidification mediated by vacuolar ATPase (v-ATPase) (Blasiak et al., 2019; Kaarniranta et al., 2023; Shang & Taylor, 2012; Viiri, 2019). By inhibiting USP14, IU1 is expected to shift the proteostasis balance in RPE cells towards enhanced degradation of misfolded proteins via the proteasome. This would not only reduce the intracellular aggregate burden but also alleviate the overloading of the lysosomal pathway—in turn potentially restoring lysosomal functions such as proper acidification by v-ATPase activity. Improved lysosomal acidification is known to facilitate the maturation and activity of cathepsin D, a key lysosomal protease responsible for degrading various protein aggregates and damaged organelles (Kaarniranta et al., 2023). Moreover, preclinical findings in neuronal cells have demonstrated that USP14 inhibition reduces aggregate load (e.g., tau) and promotes autophagic flux (Boselli et al., 2017; Lim et al., 2024), lending indirect support to the concept that these effects might be recapitulated in RPE cells. Although no direct data exist for IU1 in RPE, the mechanistic parallels between proteostasis impairment in neurons and RPE—as documented in extensive AMD literature—suggest that IU1 could reduce aggregate accumulation and oxidative stress in RPE, thereby slowing the progression of geographic atrophy.

Overall Evaluation:  
The overall evaluation of USP14 inhibitor IU1 as a therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration is cautiously optimistic yet highlights several critical areas for further investigation. On the positive side, IU1 represents an innovative strategy targeting a central node in protein quality control—USP14—that regulates the degradation of misfolded, aggregation-prone proteins via the proteasome and modulates autophagic pathways. Preclinical evidence in Drosophila models and neuronal cultures demonstrates that pharmacological USP14 inhibition can enhance aggregate clearance, improve proteostasis, and even extend lifespan and motor function under proteotoxic stress conditions (Lim et al., 2024; Boselli et al., 2017). These findings support the concept that modulating the UPS–autophagy interplay may be beneficial in diseases where proteostasis failure is a key driver, such as dry AMD, in which RPE cells experience aggregate build-up, defective autophagy, and lysosomal dysfunction (Blasiak et al., 2019; Kaarniranta et al., 2023; Shang & Taylor, 2012).

Furthermore, the biochemical mechanism by which IU1 operates—namely, reducing the deubiquitinating activity of USP14 to promote ubiquitin-tag retention and substrate commitment to degradation—provides a theoretically attractive approach to simultaneously reduce the proteasomal backlog and relieve lysosomal burden. The potential secondary effects on autophagy, including improved LC3-II turnover and possibly upregulated clearance of aggregates through aggrephagy, add further appeal to the candidate as a multi-modal modulator of proteostasis. The cell-permeable, small-molecule nature of IU1, along with available more potent analogs (such as IU1-47), offers promising opportunities for medicinal chemistry optimization and dosage refinement, especially important given the need for safe application in delicate ocular tissues.

However, several weaknesses and challenges must be addressed before IU1 can be considered a viable therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. A significant concern originates from studies in neuronal systems that indicate off-target effects at higher concentrations—specifically, inhibition of mitochondrial Complex I, ATP depletion, and activation of calpain-mediated proteolysis (Kiprowska, 2016; Kiprowska et al., n.d.). These potential toxicities raise the possibility that a narrow therapeutic window may exist, necessitating thorough dose-response studies in RPE cell models to ensure efficacy without compromising cell viability. Moreover, no direct preclinical studies have yet evaluated IU1 in RPE cells or in animal models of geographic atrophy. As such, critical parameters—such as its ability to modulate v-ATPase function, maintain lysosomal acidification, boost cathepsin D activity, and ultimately clear RPE-specific aggregates such as lipofuscin or oxidized photoreceptor debris—remain to be validated (Kaarniranta et al., 2023; Shang & Taylor, 2012).

Additionally, while the mechanistic data from neurodegenerative models are compelling, the biochemical environment of RPE cells differs from that of neurons in several key respects. RPE cells are highly phagocytic, exposed to constant oxidative stress, and rely on a finely tuned balance between proteasomal and lysosomal pathways to manage the constant influx of photoreceptor outer segment material (Blasiak et al., 2019; Viiri, 2019). Thus, any intervention that modulates proteostasis must be carefully tailored to avoid unintended disruptions in these homeostatic processes. The current literature also underscores the complexity of deubiquitinase biology; while USP14 inhibition appears beneficial in some contexts, the intricate interplay with other DUBs and the broader UPS could lead to compensatory mechanisms that diminish the anticipated therapeutic effect or even trigger adverse consequences (Faber & Roepman, 2019; Kim, 2020).

In summary, USP14 inhibitor IU1 offers an innovative and potentially transformative approach to restoring proteostasis in RPE cells by enhancing proteasomal degradation and autophagic clearance of misfolded proteins—a strategy that directly addresses the pathobiology of dry AMD and geographic atrophy as defined by aggregate accumulation and lysosomal dysfunction (Lim et al., 2024; Blasiak et al., 2019; Kaarniranta et al., 2023). The strengths of this candidate include its robust preclinical data in non-RPE systems, its well-characterized mechanism of action, and its amenability to further chemical optimization. However, significant weaknesses, including potential off-target mitochondrial toxicity, an unestablished therapeutic window in RPE cells, and the lack of direct preclinical studies in AMD models, necessitate cautious and rigorous further investigation. To move forward, it will be essential to conduct targeted RPE-specific in vitro assays and in vivo studies—assessing proteasome activity, autophagy flux, lysosomal acidification (v-ATPase function), cathepsin D activity, and aggregate clearance—while carefully monitoring for cytotoxicity. Only with such detailed preclinical validation can the promise of IU1 as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD be fully assessed (Lim et al., 2024; Blasiak et al., 2019; Kiprowska, 2016; Shang & Taylor, 2012).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Everolimus (Afinitor; Novartis) is a semi‐synthetic derivative of sirolimus—a macrolide originally isolated from Streptomyces hygroscopicus—as evidenced by its chemical designation as 4-O-(2-hydroxyethyl)-rapamycin (Liu et al., 2023, pp. 11–12). By introducing a 2-hydroxyethyl group at position 40, everolimus achieves greater hydrophilicity and an increased oral bioavailability (from 10% to 16% relative to sirolimus) while retaining the core macrolactone structure that is characteristic of rapalogs (Liu et al., 2023, pp. 11–12; Weber, 2015, pp. 27–28). This compound belongs to the class of mTOR inhibitors—specifically, a first‐generation rapalog that selectively inhibits the mTOR complex 1 (mTORC1) while sparing mTORC2 (Liu et al., 2023, pp. 10–11; Weber, 2015, pp. 27–28). As a synthetic derivative of a naturally occurring product, everolimus represents the successful strategy of chemical modification to optimize pharmacokinetic properties and clinical tolerability. The design parameters underpinning everolimus’ synthesis have been guided by the goal of retaining potent immunosuppressive and anti‐proliferative effects while optimizing parameters such as solubility, half‐life, and tissue penetration, with the added advantage of an oral formulation already approved for several clinical indications (Liu et al., 2023, pp. 11–12; Wang et al., 2022, pp. 6–8).

Therapeutic History:  
Everolimus has a well‐established therapeutic history as an immunosuppressant and antineoplastic agent. Clinically, it is approved for treating advanced renal cell carcinoma, progressive neuroendocrine tumors of pancreatic origin, and subependymal giant cell astrocytoma in tuberous sclerosis complex patients who are not candidates for surgery (Wang et al., 2022, pp. 6–8; Weber, 2015, pp. 27–28). In these indications, its mechanism as an mTORC1 inhibitor serves to arrest cell cycle progression and inhibit angiogenesis, which are central to its antitumor activity (Kuo et al., 2018, pp. 5–7; Weber, 2015, pp. 27–28). The potential of everolimus as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD is supported by several compelling factors. First, its established clinical safety and efficacy in other indications—such as renal cell carcinoma and immunosuppression in transplantation—reduce the translational risk associated with drug repurposing (Weber, 2015, pp. 27–28; Wang et al., 2022, pp. 6–8). In addition, its selective inhibition of mTORC1 has a clear mechanistic rationale in the context of dry AMD. By specifically targeting the mTORC1–TFEB axis, everolimus may correct the impaired lysosomal degradation and autophagic dysfunction that underlie the accumulation of pathogenic debris in RPE cells (Kuo et al., 2018, p. 7; Nieto et al., 2015, pp. 28–32).

In ocular cell culture systems, everolimus has been shown to enhance LC3 turnover and promote CTSD maturation—both key markers of autophagic and lysosomal efficiency (Kuo et al., 2018, pp. 5–8). Additionally, its improved ocular penetration compared to its parent compound sirolimus suggests that even systemic administration might yield therapeutically relevant levels in the retina (Liu et al., 2023, pp. 11–14). This represents a significant advantage in the context of dry AMD, where achieving effective drug delivery to deeply situated retinal tissues is a persistent challenge.

However, several weaknesses must be acknowledged. Despite a sound mechanistic rationale, direct clinical evidence for everolimus’s efficacy in dry AMD is lacking. Existing clinical studies have primarily focused on other ocular conditions such as neovascular AMD and PVR, and the particular pathophysiology of dry AMD—with its complex interplay of oxidative stress, complement dysregulation, and chronic inflammation—may require a more nuanced therapeutic approach (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2009; Kuo et al., 2018, pp. 3–5). Although these adverse events are generally manageable in oncology and transplant settings, the chronic nature of dry AMD treatment may necessitate a careful balancing of therapeutic benefits against systemic risks. Another consideration relates to the multifactorial etiology of dry AMD. While lysosomal dysfunction is a critical aspect of the disease, it is accompanied by other pathological processes such as oxidative damage, chronic inflammation, and alterations in the complement cascade. Thus, monotherapy with an mTORC1 inhibitor may not be sufficiently robust to address all disease mechanisms. Combination therapies that target multiple pathological pathways might ultimately be necessary for effective disease modification. Lastly, discrepancies in the translation of preclinical findings to human disease remain a persistent challenge. For example, while certain animal models of retinal disease have demonstrated beneficial effects of mTOR inhibition, analogous results have not always been replicated in clinical settings (Kuo et al., 2018, pp. 3–5; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2009).

In summary, everolimus presents as a mechanistically intriguing candidate for repurposing in dry AMD due to its ability to inhibit mTORC1 and thereby promote TFEB‐mediated restoration of lysosomal function. Its solid record as an FDA‐approved drug with established dosing regimens and acceptable systemic safety lends additional support to its viability as a repurposing candidate. Preclinical data suggest that everolimus increases autophagic flux in RPE cells, enhancing LC3 turnover and CTSD maturation, which theoretically should facilitate the clearance of pathological debris that characterizes dry AMD (Kuo et al., 2018, pp. 5–8). Key limitations include the absence of direct clinical evidence for efficacy in dry AMD, potential systemic adverse effects associated with prolonged mTORC1 inhibition, and the inherent complexity of dry AMD pathology, which may require multimodal therapeutic strategies. Moreover, past experiences in ocular applications—such as studies in PVR models where everolimus did not yield a statistically significant clinical improvement—highlight the need for carefully controlled dose-finding and safety studies (Kuo et al., 2018, pp. 3–5). It will be crucial to establish that systemic dosing can achieve therapeutic retinal concentrations without eliciting unintended systemic toxicity or disrupting normal RPE physiology.

Overall, while mechanistic and preclinical data provide a strong rationale for repurposing everolimus to treat dry AMD, further rigorous preclinical studies specifically in models of dry AMD are warranted. A careful evaluation of dosing regimens, potential adverse effects, and efficacy endpoints will be essential in the translational development of everolimus for this indication. The mechanistic specificity for mTORC1 inhibition, combined with the ability to enhance autophagic clearance in RPE cells, represents a significant strength that could offer a novel approach to modifying the course of dry AMD. However, the challenges associated with systemic mTOR inhibition and the need for combination strategies or localized delivery systems must be addressed in subsequent research phases. In conclusion, everolimus is a promising, though not yet definitively validated, candidate for repurposing in dry AMD, and we recommend that further detailed studies be undertaken to fully elucidate its potential in restoring lysosomal function and ameliorating retinal degeneration in this patient population (Liu et al., 2023, pp. 11–12; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2009; Kuo et al., 2018, pp. 5–7; Weber, 2015, pp. 27–28; Wang et al., 2022, pp. 6–8; Kuo et al., 2018, pp. 7–8).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Pegcetacoplan (APL-2, now marketed as Syfovre) is a synthetically engineered, PEGylated cyclic peptide that belongs to the family of compstatin analogs designed to inhibit complement component C3. Its origins lie in early peptide discovery via phage‐display and random peptide library screening, and successive rounds of medicinal chemistry optimization were applied to improve its binding affinity, solubility, and pharmacokinetic profile through PEG conjugation (Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023; Ong et al., 2024). The PEGylation process not only grants enhanced resistance to enzymatic degradation but also prolongs the intravitreal residence time, an essential property for ocular applications requiring sustained drug exposure with limited dosing frequency (Tzoumas et al., 2023; Mastellos & Lambris, 2024). As a second‐generation compstatin analog, pegcetacoplan employs a bivalent design that enables high specificity for human C3, blocking its proteolytic cleavage into the active fragments C3a and C3b. These fragments are potent mediators that further amplify the inflammatory cascade through the formation of C3 convertases (Lamers et al., 2022). This therapeutic candidate is embedded within a broader class of complement inhibitors that have been actively explored in inflammatory disorders, and notably in ophthalmology for dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) where aberrant complement activation plays a central pathogenic role (Lamers et al., 2022; Mastellos & Lambris, 2024). Its synthetic nature, coupled with its targeted molecular design, positions pegcetacoplan as an attractive candidate for addressing the degenerative processes in geographic atrophy (GA) associated with dry AMD by directly modulating the complement cascade (Tzoumas et al., 2023; Patel et al., 2022).

Therapeutic History  
Historically, the evolution of pegcetacoplan reflects a successful translation from bench to bedside across multiple therapeutic domains. Initially, the compstatin class was primarily developed and evaluated in systemic disorders characterized by complement dysregulation, most notably in paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH). Early clinical trials in PNH provided critical safety and efficacy data that underscored the value of targeting C3, paving the way for the repurposing of these molecules in ocular disease (Lamers et al., 2022). With the conceptual framework and preclinical data in hand, pegcetacoplan was advanced into the ophthalmology space. The pivotal Phase II FILLY trial enrolled 246 patients with GA secondary to dry AMD, and the study demonstrated that monthly intravitreal injections of pegcetacoplan resulted in a statistically significant reduction of GA lesion growth by approximately 29%, while an every-other-month dosing regimen yielded a 20% reduction relative to sham-control treatment (Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023; Patel et al., 2022). These encouraging anatomical outcomes, evidenced by the slowed progression of GA and the concurrent reduction in photoreceptor loss as evaluated by SD-OCT imaging, provided a strong rationale for subsequent Phase III clinical trials (Regillo & Heier, n.d.; Patel et al., 2022).  
In addition to its use in dry AMD, pegcetacoplan’s earlier regulatory approval for PNH helped establish it as a viable molecule with a favorable safety profile. Its journey through successive clinical phases—from Phase I safety and tolerability studies to Phase II efficacy studies and ultimately Phase III confirmation—has offered compelling evidence that targeted complement inhibition can modify the disease course in conditions characterized by chronic complement activation (Tzoumas et al., 2023). However, clinical experience with pegcetacoplan has also identified potential safety signals, including an observed increase in the incidence of new-onset exudative (wet) AMD among certain subpopulations, a factor that necessitates careful patient selection and monitoring (Lamers et al., 2022; Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023). Overall, the therapeutic history of pegcetacoplan—spanning its origin from fundamental compstatin research to its current application in treating geographic atrophy—demonstrates its potential for repurposing as a disease-modifying therapy in ocular settings (Lamers et al., 2022; Desai & Dugel, 2022).

Mechanism of Action  
At the molecular level, the pathogenic cascade in dry AMD is tightly linked to dysregulated complement activation, and pegcetacoplan intervenes at one of the central nodes of this pathway by inhibiting complement component C3. Under physiological conditions, C3 is cleaved by C3 convertases into C3a—an anaphylatoxin that drives inflammation—and C3b, which functions as an opsonin and further propagates complement amplification (Yu & Wykoff, 2021). Pegcetacoplan binds to a key epitope on C3, thereby sterically hindering the enzyme-driven cleavage that would otherwise generate these active fragments. By effectively arresting this pivotal step in the complement cascade, the drug prevents downstream events such as the assembly of terminal complement complexes and the formation of the membrane attack complex (MAC) (Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023; Wu & Sun, 2019).  
The inhibition of C3 cleavage has several critical biochemical consequences. First, by lowering the concentrations of C3a and C3b, pegcetacoplan reduces the generation of pro-inflammatory mediators and the subsequent chemotactic recruitment of immune cells, which, in turn, diminishes local inflammation in the retinal environment (Regillo & Heier, n.d.; Tzoumas et al., 2023). Second, the reduction in C3b deposition directly limits the formation of MAC on retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) surfaces—a process that has been implicated in triggering lysosomal dysfunction within these critical cells (Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023; Park et al., 2021). The MAC, when deposited sublytically on RPE cells, can compromise the function of the vacuolar H⁺-ATPase (v-ATPase), the proton pump responsible for maintaining the acidic environment of lysosomes. Acidification of the lysosomal compartment is essential for optimal activity of proteolytic enzymes, such as cathepsin D, which are required to degrade photoreceptor outer segment debris and other cytotoxic by-products (Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023; Tzoumas et al., 2023).  
Thus, by preventing excessive complement activation and subsequent MAC formation, pegcetacoplan indirectly safeguards the intracellular degradative machinery of the RPE. This preservation of v-ATPase function ensures proper lysosomal acidification, which in turn maintains cathepsin D activity and reduces lysosomal overload—a key mechanism implicated in the progressive atrophy of the RPE observed in dry AMD (Mastellos & Lambris, 2024; Regillo & Heier, n.d.). Clinical trial data support this expectation: in the Phase II FILLY study, monthly intravitreal injections of pegcetacoplan were associated with a roughly 29% reduction in the rate of GA lesion growth relative to control, while an alternate-month regimen achieved a 20% reduction (Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023; Patel et al., 2022). Consequently, the expected biochemical outcome is that pegcetacoplan will reduce lysosomal overload and the accumulation of toxic metabolic by-products—a process thought to contribute to the formation of sub-RPE deposits that further exacerbate tissue atrophy in dry AMD (Lamers et al., 2022; Desai & Dugel, 2022).  
At the cellular level, maintaining cathepsin D activity is imperative because this protease is responsible for degrading intracellular waste products that accumulate in RPE cells, and its functionality is closely tied to the acidic environment provided by lysosomes. By preserving this aspect of lysosomal physiology, pegcetacoplan should contribute to RPE cell survival and thereby delay the progression of geographic atrophy (Patel et al., 2022). A comprehensive review of pegcetacoplan as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD reveals a well-substantiated rationale and a promising clinical profile, albeit with some challenges that must be addressed. One of the most compelling strengths of pegcetacoplan is its precise molecular targeting of complement component C3—a central mediator in the complement cascade. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
SB216763 is a synthetic small‐molecule inhibitor originally discovered during GlaxoSmithKline’s dedicated program in developing GSK-3 inhibitors. It belongs to the bisarylmaleimide class of compounds, with its chemical structure based on a pyrrole-2,5-dione core that is further substituted by aryl and indole moieties. In its initial characterization, SB216763 was identified as an ATP-competitive inhibitor of glycogen synthase kinase 3 beta (GSK3β), a central serine/threonine protein kinase implicated in multiple intracellular signaling cascades. The chemical class to which SB216763 belongs – maleimides – has been widely exploited across medicinal chemistry due to their synthetic tractability and ability to serve as potent inhibitors of enzymes, particularly kinases. This group of compounds has previously been used in various preclinical studies targeting neurodegenerative diseases and cell proliferative disorders by modulating cell signaling pathways such as the Wnt/β-catenin cascade, which is ubiquitously expressed in many tissues including the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and the central nervous system (Gianferrara et al., 2022; Ruiz & Eldar-Finkelman, 2022; Alhassan et al., 2025).

Therapeutic History:  
SB216763 has a well-established history in preclinical research, particularly in models of neurodegeneration. Several studies have deployed this compound in rodent models of Alzheimer’s disease, Parkinson’s disease, and other neurological insults to demonstrate its neuroprotective potential. In these models, SB216763 was shown to reduce tau hyperphosphorylation, protect neurons against both β-amyloid-mediated toxicity and radiation-induced apoptosis in hippocampal neurons, and promote beneficial modulation of signaling pathways linked to PI3K–Akt (Gianferrara et al., 2022; Ruiz & Eldar-Finkelman, 2022). Beyond its neuroprotective effects, SB216763 has been applied as a tool compound in cellular studies to activate canonical Wnt signaling through stabilization of beta-catenin by inhibiting GSK3β. Importantly, a radiolabeled derivative, [11C]SB216763, has been developed as a positron emission tomography (PET) probe, which confirmed its ability to cross the blood–brain barrier in rodent and nonhuman primate models, although significant selectivity issues have been noted with respect to off-target kinase inhibition (Gianferrara et al., 2022; Benn & Dawson, 2020). In addition, there is documented evidence of its application in ocular contexts; for instance, in an experimental ischemic retinal neuron model in rats, SB216763 was found to promote DNA repair by upregulating DNA ligase IV transcriptional activity. However, while it has been evaluated extensively in neurological and in vivo rodent models for central nervous system diseases, formal clinical deployment or veterinary studies specifically targeting dry age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD) remain sparse, with no documented clinical trials registered on major platforms dedicated to AMD indications (Gianferrara et al., 2022; Ruiz & Eldar-Finkelman, 2022; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).

Mechanism of Action:  
The primary mechanism of action of SB216763 is centered on its potent inhibition of GSK3β. Under normal physiological conditions, GSK3β is a constitutively active kinase that phosphorylates a wide array of substrates, including beta-catenin, tau, and proteins critical to cellular metabolism and survival. One key substrate relevant to our hypothesis is the transcription factor EB (TFEB), a master regulator of the Coordinated Lysosomal Expression and Regulation (CLEAR) gene network. TFEB’s activity is tightly regulated by its phosphorylation state; when phosphorylated by kinases such as mTORC1 and possibly GSK3β, TFEB binds to cytosolic 14-3-3 proteins and is retained in the cytoplasm. Inhibition of GSK3β by SB216763 has been implicated in the dephosphorylation of TFEB, thereby allowing its translocation to the nucleus where it drives the transcription of CLEAR network genes. These genes are essential for lysosomal biogenesis, autophagic flux, and the expression of lysosomal proteases such as cathepsin D (Gianferrara et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2023). Detailed molecular studies in neuronal stem cells and N2a cells have demonstrated that SB216763 can inactivate GSK3β and thereby stimulate the nuclear accumulation of TFEB. In addition, the compound’s ATP-competitive mode of inhibition suggests it directly competes with ATP in the GSK3β active site, leading to rapid modulation of downstream substrates implicated in metabolic and autophagic processes (Gianferrara et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2023; Djajadikerta et al., 2020). From a biochemical standpoint, SB216763’s action not only stabilizes beta-catenin – thereby modulating Wnt signaling – but also appears to influence key regulatory nodes in autophagy. Activation of TFEB results in upregulation of lysosomal proteins, enhancement of lysosomal acidification via increased expression of components like the vacuolar-type ATPase (V-ATPase), and improved cathepsin D maturation and activity, all of which collectively promote the efficient clearance of intracellular aggregates and damaged organelles (Gianferrara et al., 2022; Ruiz & Eldar-Finkelman, 2022; Pan & Valapala, 2022).

Expected Effect in Dry AMD Context:  
The central hypothesis behind repurposing SB216763 for dry AMD rests on its ability to correct the cellular deficits observed in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) associated with aging and disease. Dry AMD is characterized by the accumulation of lipofuscin and other aggregate-prone materials within the RPE, coupled with impaired autophagic and lysosomal clearance mechanisms. The proposed pharmacological intervention with SB216763 is expected to inhibit GSK3β in RPE cells, leading to dephosphorylation and nuclear translocation of TFEB. Once in the nucleus, TFEB can activate the CLEAR network, thereby augmenting lysosome biogenesis and catalytic function. Enhanced lysosomal acidification, as mediated by the V-ATPase and corroborated by increased expression of lysosomal enzymes such as cathepsin D, should facilitate the degradation of accumulated lipofuscin, oxidized proteins, and lipid aggregates. In preclinical RPE models under oxidative stress, similar pharmacological modulation of TFEB (for example, via trehalose treatment or genetic induction) has been shown to improve lysosomal function and reduce the burden of autofluorescent granules analogous to lipofuscin (Falcão et al., 2025; Falcão et al., 2024). Therefore, SB216763 is hypothesized to recapitulate these beneficial effects by leveraging its upstream modulation of GSK3β. Given that RPE cells naturally express both GSK3β and TFEB, and considering the documented mechanistic role of GSK3β in regulating TFEB nucleo-cytoplasmic shuttling, the expected outcome is an enhancement of autophagic clearance and restoration of RPE homeostasis. This would theoretically slow or potentially reverse early degenerative changes in dry AMD by mitigating the cytotoxic accumulation of undegraded material (Gianferrara et al., 2022; Ruiz & Eldar-Finkelman, 2022; Yang et al., 2023).

Overall Evaluation:  
SB216763 exhibits several promising attributes as a candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry AMD. One major strength lies in its well-characterized and potent inhibition of GSK3β – a kinase that plays a central role in various signaling pathways implicated in both neurodegeneration and retinal pathology. The mechanistic rationale is underpinned by evidence that GSK3β inhibition facilitates the nuclear translocation of TFEB, the master regulator of lysosomal function. Through activation of TFEB, SB216763 can potentially stimulate the expression of the CLEAR gene network, leading to heightened lysosomal acidification and increased cathepsin D activity. These molecular events are directly relevant to mitigating the defective autophagic clearance that is a hallmark of dry AMD, and they align well with preclinical observations in other cell types where TFEB activation has been associated with improved degradation of accumulated toxic material (Gianferrara et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2023; Djajadikerta et al., 2020).

Further strengths include the extensive use of SB216763 in various preclinical models of neurodegeneration, wherein its ability to modulate key pathways such as beta-catenin/Wnt signaling has been repeatedly demonstrated. Its blood–brain barrier penetrance, as seen in rodent and nonhuman primate studies involving a radiolabeled derivative, suggests favorable pharmacokinetics that might also translate to ocular tissues with appropriate formulation strategies. The documented ocular application in rodent ischemic retinal neuron models – where SB216763 was shown to upregulate DNA repair mechanisms – provides additional indirect support for its potential in the ocular setting (Gianferrara et al., 2022).

Notwithstanding these promising aspects, there are notable weaknesses and gaps in the literature that warrant cautious interpretation. First, while preclinical evidence in neural and other cellular models supports the concept that GSK3β inhibition can drive TFEB-dependent transcriptional activation, direct evidence of SB216763’s efficacy in RPE cells under conditions of oxidative stress or in established dry AMD models is sparse. There is a lack of comprehensive studies that definitively link SB216763 treatment in RPE cells to enhanced lysosomal acidification, increased cathepsin D activity, and consequent reduction in lipofuscin accumulation. For example, while related studies using trehalose or mTOR inhibitors have shown clear benefits on TFEB activation and autophagic clearance in RPE models (Falcão et al., 2025; Falcão et al., 2024), SB216763-specific data in this context remain limited. 

Furthermore, concerns regarding kinase selectivity must be acknowledged. SB216763, being an ATP-competitive inhibitor, may exhibit off-target effects by inhibiting structurally related kinases, as indicated by the limited selectivity noted in studies involving its radiolabeled derivative [11C]SB216763 (Gianferrara et al., 2022; Benn & Dawson, 2020; Pan & Valapala, 2021). Off-target kinase inhibition could potentially disrupt other essential signaling pathways in the RPE and might lead to unforeseen adverse events upon clinical translation. This issue of specificity is particularly important in the context of chronic diseases like dry AMD, where long-term safety is paramount. 

Additionally, while its use in central nervous system models is encouraging, dry AMD pathophysiology has distinct features that may not be fully addressed by a therapeutic designed for neurodegeneration. The multifactorial etiology of dry AMD, which encompasses oxidative stress, chronic inflammation, and impaired autophagic degradation specific to the high metabolic and phagocytic demands of RPE cells, underscores the need for targeted evidence that SB216763 exerts its effects in these specialized cells. Moreover, the absence of any registered clinical trials on major platforms for SB216763 in the AMD space (as revealed by comprehensive searches on ClinicalTrials.gov) suggests that the translational path for this compound remains uncharted in the context of retinal disease (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.; Ruiz & Eldar-Finkelman, 2022).

Another consideration is the potential for conflicting actions of GSK3β inhibition. While inhibiting GSK3β does promote TFEB activation and lysosomal biogenesis, GSK3β also phosphorylates other substrates that could have deleterious effects if dysregulated in the RPE. For example, uncontrolled activation of the Wnt/β-catenin pathway may have proliferative effects or contribute to unwanted cell signaling changes. Thus, a delicate balance must be maintained in modulating GSK3β activity to elicit the desired autophagic responses without incurring off-target toxicity.

From a developmental perspective, the availability of SB216763 as a commercially sourced compound (Sigma S3442) is an advantage. Its established synthesis, reproducibility, and well-documented use in numerous preclinical studies allow for rapid deployment in early-stage in vitro and in vivo assays. However, the lack of formulation studies specifically for ocular delivery, and potential challenges in achieving therapeutic concentrations in the retina while minimizing systemic exposure, remain hurdles to overcome in advancing SB216763 as an AMD therapy.

In summary, SB216763 is a compelling candidate from a mechanistic standpoint, with a robust preclinical pedigree as a GSK3β inhibitor that can modulate TFEB and downstream lysosomal functions. Its synthetic origin as a bisarylmaleimide and proven in vitro potency provide a strong rationale for its repurposing. The proposed mechanism—wherein inhibition of GSK3β leads to enhanced nuclear localization of TFEB, activation of CLEAR genes, improved lysosomal acidification, and increased cathepsin D activity—directly addresses key pathogenic features of dry AMD, including the accumulation of lipofuscin and defective autophagy in RPE cells. This mechanistic alignment, supported by studies across neurodegenerative disease models and early ocular research, indicates that SB216763 has the potential to restore defective autophagic clearance in the RPE and slow AMD progression (Gianferrara et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2023; Djajadikerta et al., 2020).

Nonetheless, the overall success of SB216763 in the context of dry AMD will depend on addressing several critical issues. First, direct experimental validation in RPE cells exposed to oxidative stress is needed to confirm that SB216763 can indeed induce TFEB nuclear translocation and activate the CLEAR network in this specific cell type. Second, detailed pharmacokinetic and safety studies tailored for ocular administration are essential to determine whether the compound can reach effective concentrations in the retina without eliciting systemic toxicity or off-target kinase inhibition. Third, comprehensive in vivo studies in relevant animal models of dry AMD must be conducted to assess whether the biochemical improvements (e.g., enhanced lysosomal acidification and cathepsin D activity) translate into clinically meaningful outcomes, such as reduction in lipofuscin accumulation and preservation of RPE morphology and function.

Finally, while the theoretical framework is strong, the translational gap remains significant. The absence of clinical trials or robust preclinical data directly linking SB216763 to improvements in dry AMD phenotypes suggests that careful, incremental studies are required. These studies should ideally include dose–response evaluations, biomarker analyses of autophagic flux, and long-term safety assessments to establish the therapeutic window for SB216763 in the context of retinal disease (Ruiz & Eldar-Finkelman, 2022; Gianferrara et al., 2022; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).

Overall, SB216763 represents a promising mechanistic candidate whose ability to modulate GSK3β and, consequently, regulate TFEB activity offers a novel angle for addressing the autophagic deficits observed in dry AMD. Its well-defined synthetic origin, established preclinical usage in neurodegeneration, and documented biochemical effects in activating lysosomal and autophagic pathways suggest that it could, in principle, improve RPE function through enhanced clearance of toxic intracellular aggregates. However, the limitations regarding its selectivity, the need for targeted ocular studies, and the paucity of direct evidence in AMD models require that further rigorous investigations be conducted. A stepwise preclinical evaluation, starting with in vitro RPE models and advancing to in vivo AMD models, would be necessary to validate its efficacy and safety profile before considering clinical translation. In this regard, SB216763 should be advanced as a high-priority candidate for additional mechanistic studies and exploratory preclinical evaluations, albeit with cautious optimism given the potential for off-target effects and formulation challenges (Gianferrara et al., 2022; Ruiz & Eldar-Finkelman, 2022; Yang et al., 2023; Djajadikerta et al., 2020; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).

In conclusion, while SB216763 offers a robust mechanistic rationale for its repurposing in dry AMD based on its known capacity to inhibit GSK3β, promote TFEB-mediated lysosomal biogenesis, and potentially enhance autophagic clearance, careful attention must be paid to validating these effects directly in RPE cells under oxidative stress. The strengths of its preclinical performance and synthetic availability must be balanced against the challenges of kinase selectivity, ocular pharmacokinetics, and the absence of direct AMD-specific data. A systematic, comprehensive series of studies is warranted to firmly establish whether SB216763 can serve as a viable therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. The outcomes of these studies will significantly influence the strategic direction of the drug development program and may open the door to novel, mechanism-based interventions for a disease with substantial unmet clinical need (Gianferrara et al., 2022; Ruiz & Eldar-Finkelman, 2022; Yang et al., 2023; Djajadikerta et al., 2020; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).
