Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Fenofibrate is a synthetic small‐molecule drug belonging to the fibrate class of compounds, originally developed and approved for the treatment of dyslipidemia. It acts predominantly as a peroxisome proliferator‐activated receptor alpha (PPARα) agonist. Fenofibrate itself is a prodrug that undergoes hepatic esterase hydrolysis to form its active metabolite, fenofibric acid, which binds to PPARα and modulates the transcription of genes involved in lipid metabolism. This drug class has historically been used for lowering serum triglycerides and increasing high‐density lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol, reflecting its well‐established lipid‐modulating properties. Although fenofibrate was not initially developed for ocular indications, its mechanism as a PPARα agonist has spurred interest for repurposing in retinal diseases. In particular, the broad class of fibrates has garnered attention because PPARα is expressed in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), and its activation can regulate lipid oxidation, autophagy, and inflammatory processes—all of which are critically disturbed in dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) (Fu et al., 2019; Falcão et al., 2025).

Therapeutic History:  
Fenofibrate has a robust clinical history in the management of dyslipidemia and cardiovascular risk reduction, with extensive use in millions of patients worldwide. Its ocular benefits became apparent with large clinical trials, such as the FIELD and ACCORD Eye studies, which demonstrated that fenofibrate can reduce the progression of diabetic retinopathy and decrease the need for retinal laser therapy in diabetic patients (Lu et al., 2014; Treacy & Hurst, 2012). Although these trials primarily addressed diabetic retinal disease, subsequent preclinical and clinical reports have indicated that the retina may benefit from the lipid‐modulatory, anti‐inflammatory, and neuroprotective actions of PPARα agonists. For instance, several studies have explored fenofibrate in animal models of retinal ischemia and neovascularization, showing protective effects on the retinal vasculature and RPE (Fu et al., 2020; Qiu et al., 2017). While the majority of these ocular studies have focused on diabetic retinopathy or neovascular AMD, emerging literature has pointed to the potential of targeting PPARα signaling to mitigate RPE dysfunction and lipid accumulation, which are hallmarks of dry AMD (da Ana et al., 2023; Dou & Duerfeldt, 2020). This history of fenofibrate in retinal disease, combined with its proven clinical safety for dyslipidemia and established ocular pharmacokinetics (including studies on topical delivery), provides a compelling rationale for its repurposing in dry AMD (Tomita et al., 2020; Lee et al., 2021).

Mechanism of Action:  
Fenofibrate’s mechanism of action is rooted in its role as a PPARα agonist. Upon conversion to fenofibric acid, the compound binds to PPARα—a nuclear receptor highly expressed in several tissues, including the liver and the retinal pigment epithelium. When activated, PPARα forms heterodimers with retinoid X receptors (RXR) and binds to peroxisome proliferator response elements (PPREs) within the promoters of target genes. This binding results in the upregulation of genes critical for fatty acid uptake, β-oxidation, and lipid catabolism. Key genes regulated by PPARα include those encoding enzymes that facilitate mitochondrial and peroxisomal fatty acid oxidation, which in turn reduces intracellular lipid accumulation and promotes energy homeostasis (Fu et al., 2019; Lee et al., 2023).

In the context of the RPE and dry AMD, the hypothesis is that fenofibrate will stimulate PPARα-mediated transcriptional programs that not only enhance lipid catabolism but also intersect with cellular degradative pathways. One of the central tenets of the proposed mechanism is the coactivation of transcription factor EB (TFEB). TFEB is recognized as a master regulator of lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy through the coordinated lysosomal expression and regulation (CLEAR) network. Under normal conditions, TFEB is kept inactive in the cytosol by phosphorylation mediated by mTORC1. Under stress conditions or when lysosomal function is impaired, TFEB translocates to the nucleus to upregulate genes involved in lysosomal acidification, autophagy, and lipid metabolism. The therapeutic hypothesis posits that fenofibrate, through PPARα activation in RPE cells, will indirectly coactivate TFEB. This may occur through changes in cellular metabolism that reduce mTORC1 activity or via direct transcriptional crosstalk between PPARα target genes and the CLEAR network (Falcão et al., 2025; da Ana et al., 2023).

Moreover, TFEB activation is expected to enhance lysosomal acidification—a process necessary for optimal degradation of phagocytosed outer segment debris and drusen precursors—and upregulate lysosomal hydrolases such as cathepsin D. In AMD, RPE cells often show lysosomal dysfunction characterized by deficient cathepsin D activity and lipofuscin accumulation. By improving lysosomal function, fenofibrate may facilitate the clearance of lipid-rich drusen precursors, thereby reducing RPE stress and preventing progression of dry AMD (Falcão et al., 2025; da Ana et al., 2023). In addition to these lysosome-centric effects, fenofibrate has anti-inflammatory properties, as PPARα activation suppresses NF-κB signaling, reduces the expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines (e.g., TNF-α and IL-1β), and alleviates oxidative stress—all of which are exacerbating factors in the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Lee et al., 2023; Treacy & Hurst, 2012). Furthermore, the modulation of the FGF21 pathway, occasionally observed with fenofibrate treatment, may contribute to neuroprotection and further support retinal homeostasis (Tomita et al., 2020; Lee et al., 2023). Taken together, the molecular interactions initiated by fenofibrate converge on restoring lipid homeostasis, enhancing autophagic flux, and mitigating inflammatory insults in RPE cells—a multifaceted approach that aligns with the pathophysiology of dry AMD (Treacy & Hurst, 2012; Lee et al., 2021).

Expected Effect:  
In the assays proposed to evaluate fenofibrate’s efficacy for dry AMD, one anticipates several measurable cellular and biochemical outcomes. First, treatment of RPE cells with fenofibrate should lead to a consistent activation of PPARα target genes, as demonstrated by upregulation of markers for fatty acid oxidation and lipid catabolism. Such molecular signatures can be quantified using gene expression analyses and reporter assays for PPRE activity (Fu et al., 2019; Tomita et al., 2021). Concurrently, it is expected that fenofibrate will enhance autophagic flux in RPE cells. This could be evident from increased LC3-II accumulation in the presence of lysosomal inhibitors and enhanced degradation of autophagic substrates, which would indicate an upregulation of the autophagic machinery (Falcão et al., 2025; da Ana et al., 2023).

A critical aspect of the proposed mechanism involves TFEB. Upon fenofibrate treatment, one should observe increased nuclear translocation of TFEB in RPE cells, which can be assessed by immunocytochemistry and subcellular fractionation. The activation of TFEB would then be expected to drive the transcriptional upregulation of genes encoding lysosomal proteins, such as lysosomal-associated membrane protein 2 (LAMP2) and various components of the V-ATPase complex, leading to enhanced lysosomal acidification. Lysotracker assays and measurements of intralysosomal pH could be deployed to confirm that fenofibrate-treated cells exhibit more acidic lysosomes (Falcão et al., 2025; da Ana et al., 2023).

Furthermore, increased cathepsin D activity is a pivotal expected outcome, serving as a surrogate marker for improved lysosomal enzyme function in degrading waste products, including drusen precursors. Biochemical assays to quantify cathepsin D activity, alongside immunostaining for its protein levels, would help to validate this aspect of the mechanism. Functionally, the cumulative effect of these molecular changes should be a reduction in the accumulation of lipofuscin and other drusen-associated lipid-protein aggregates within the RPE. This reduction could be observed using autofluorescence imaging techniques and electron microscopy to assess cytoplasmic inclusions (Falcão et al., 2025; Treacy & Hurst, 2012).

Additionally, given that fenofibrate has established anti-inflammatory properties, one might expect a decrease in the secretion or expression of inflammatory mediators in RPE cultures, as well as improved cellular resistance to oxidative stress challenges. Cytokine assays and measurements of reactive oxygen species (ROS) would serve as corroborative evidence for an anti-inflammatory and antioxidant effect. Importantly, because reduced autophagy and lysosomal dysfunction are central to dry AMD, the combined effect of enhanced lipid catabolism, improved lysosomal acidification, and increased cathepsin D activity should contribute to an overall reduction in cellular stress and preservation of RPE integrity (Falcão et al., 2025; Treacy & Hurst, 2012). Taken together, these expected effects would validate the therapeutic hypothesis and provide a strong rationale for advancing fenofibrate into further preclinical models of dry AMD.

Overall Evaluation:  
Fenofibrate emerges as a promising repurposed drug candidate for dry AMD based on several compelling lines of evidence. The drug’s long-established clinical safety profile and extensive use in dyslipidemia serve as major strengths in terms of its translational potential (Lu et al., 2014; Treacy & Hurst, 2012). Additionally, the documented success of fenofibrate in slowing the progression of diabetic retinopathy in large-scale clinical trials underscores its ability to exert beneficial effects in retinal tissues (Lu et al., 2014; Treacy & Hurst, 2012).

From a mechanistic standpoint, fenofibrate’s mode of action as a PPARα agonist is well characterized, and its ability to stimulate lipid oxidation and enhance fatty acid metabolism could directly address the lipid dysregulation observed in RPE cells in dry AMD (Fu et al., 2019; da Ana et al., 2023). Crucially, the hypothesis that fenofibrate may also coactivate TFEB, thereby promoting lysosomal biogenesis and function, positions it uniquely among therapeutic candidates. Improved lysosomal acidification and increased cathepsin D activity would facilitate the clearance of drusen precursors and reduce the cytotoxic accumulation of lipofuscin, which is a central pathogenic feature of dry AMD (Falcão et al., 2025; da Ana et al., 2023; Dou & Duerfeldt, 2020). The convergence of lipid catabolism enhancement, autophagy upregulation, and anti-inflammatory effects creates a multifaceted therapeutic profile that is particularly attractive for a complex, multifactorial disease such as dry AMD.

However, there are also notable weaknesses and challenges. Most of the current evidence supporting fenofibrate’s retinal benefits is derived from studies focusing on diabetic retinopathy or neovascular AMD rather than directly on dry AMD. Although there is supportive mechanistic rationale linking PPARα activation to improved lysosomal function in the RPE, direct evidence for fenofibrate’s efficacy in reducing drusen accumulation and alleviating RPE stress in dry AMD models remains sparse (Dou & Duerfeldt, 2020; da Ana et al., 2023). The specific involvement of TFEB activation by fenofibrate in RPE cells has not been fully elucidated in the existing literature, and further in vitro and in vivo studies are needed to validate this aspect of the mechanism. Additionally, while fenofibrate is generally safe when used systemically, there have been concerns regarding potential renal side effects, which may be particularly relevant in the elderly population that predominantly suffers from AMD (Treacy & Hurst, 2012; Tomita et al., 2021). Thus, optimizing the route of delivery—possibly via topical formulations or nanoparticle-based systems—may be necessary to ensure sufficient retinal bioavailability while minimizing systemic exposure (Huang et al., 2021; Lu et al., 2014).

Another potential limitation is the dose required to achieve sufficient PPARα activation in the RPE to modulate TFEB and lysosomal pathways effectively. Preclinical studies have sometimes required relatively high doses of fenofibrate to observe significant ocular effects, and the pharmacokinetic barriers posed by the blood-retinal barrier may further complicate translatability (Tomita et al., 2020; Lee et al., 2023). Moreover, the current body of literature underscores the need for more targeted studies to determine whether the benefits seen with fenofibrate in models of diabetic retinopathy and neovascular AMD can be replicated in models of dry AMD, where the pathogenic processes are distinct in their emphasis on lipid accumulation, oxidative stress, and RPE dysfunction (da Ana et al., 2023; Dou & Duerfeldt, 2020).

Despite these challenges, the overall evaluation remains cautiously optimistic. Fenofibrate’s mechanism of action aligns well with the pathophysiological features of dry AMD, particularly regarding the restoration of lipid homeostasis and the enhancement of lysosomal function. The dual potential for direct metabolic benefits via PPARα activation and indirect benefits through TFEB-mediated lysosomal enhancement represents an innovative therapeutic strategy that could fill a critical gap in the current treatment landscape for dry AMD (Falcão et al., 2025; Fu et al., 2019; da Ana et al., 2023; Dou & Duerfeldt, 2020; Lee et al., 2023). Additionally, the availability of various delivery platforms—including systemic administration, topical eye drops, and nanoparticle formulations—provides flexibility in addressing bioavailability challenges and minimizing adverse effects (Huang et al., 2021; Lu et al., 2014).

In conclusion, fenofibrate (Sigma F6020) possesses significant potential for repurposing as a drug candidate for dry AMD based on its well-established pharmacological profile, robust clinical safety record, and mechanistic actions that target key pathological processes in the RPE. While further preclinical studies specifically focused on dry AMD models are warranted to validate the hypothesized coactivation of TFEB and subsequent enhancement of lysosomal acidification and cathepsin D activity, the current literature provides a strong scientific basis for such investigations. The strengths of fenofibrate lie in its multifaceted mechanism—encompassing lipid catabolism, autophagy, anti-inflammatory, and possibly neuroprotective effects—which collectively offer a promising strategy to reduce drusen precursors and mitigate RPE stress. The primary weaknesses involve the need for direct evidence in dry AMD models, optimization of ocular delivery to overcome pharmacokinetic barriers, and careful monitoring of potential systemic side effects in an elderly population. Overall, fenofibrate represents a compelling and scientifically sound candidate that merits further exploration in the context of dry AMD, with the potential to significantly advance our therapeutic arsenal against this currently untreatable form of macular degeneration (Falcão et al., 2025; Fu et al., 2019; da Ana et al., 2023; Dou & Duerfeldt, 2020; Lee et al., 2023).

BAY 11-7082 exerts its pharmacological effects predominantly through irreversible covalent inhibition. Mechanistically, the compound forms covalent adducts with reactive cysteine residues on the NLRP3 protein, most likely within the ATPase domain—an essential activity domain required for inflammasome activation. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Pegcetacoplan (APL-2, now marketed as Syfovre) is a synthetically engineered, PEGylated cyclic peptide that belongs to the family of compstatin analogs designed to inhibit complement component C3. Its origins lie in early peptide discovery via phage‐display and random peptide library screening, and successive rounds of medicinal chemistry optimization were applied to improve its binding affinity, solubility, and pharmacokinetic profile through PEG conjugation (Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023; Ong et al., 2024). The PEGylation process not only grants enhanced resistance to enzymatic degradation but also prolongs the intravitreal residence time, an essential property for ocular applications requiring sustained drug exposure with limited dosing frequency (Tzoumas et al., 2023; Mastellos & Lambris, 2024). As a second‐generation compstatin analog, pegcetacoplan employs a bivalent design that enables high specificity for human C3, blocking its proteolytic cleavage into the active fragments C3a and C3b. These fragments are potent mediators that further amplify the inflammatory cascade through the formation of C3 convertases (Lamers et al., 2022). This therapeutic candidate is embedded within a broader class of complement inhibitors that have been actively explored in inflammatory disorders, and notably in ophthalmology for dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) where aberrant complement activation plays a central pathogenic role (Lamers et al., 2022; Mastellos & Lambris, 2024). Its synthetic nature, coupled with its targeted molecular design, positions pegcetacoplan as an attractive candidate for addressing the degenerative processes in geographic atrophy (GA) associated with dry AMD by directly modulating the complement cascade (Tzoumas et al., 2023; Patel et al., 2022).

Therapeutic History  
Historically, the evolution of pegcetacoplan reflects a successful translation from bench to bedside across multiple therapeutic domains. Initially, the compstatin class was primarily developed and evaluated in systemic disorders characterized by complement dysregulation, most notably in paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH). Early clinical trials in PNH provided critical safety and efficacy data that underscored the value of targeting C3, paving the way for the repurposing of these molecules in ocular disease (Lamers et al., 2022). With the conceptual framework and preclinical data in hand, pegcetacoplan was advanced into the ophthalmology space. The pivotal Phase II FILLY trial enrolled 246 patients with GA secondary to dry AMD, and the study demonstrated that monthly intravitreal injections of pegcetacoplan resulted in a statistically significant reduction of GA lesion growth by approximately 29%, while an every-other-month dosing regimen yielded a 20% reduction relative to sham-control treatment (Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023; Patel et al., 2022). These encouraging anatomical outcomes, evidenced by the slowed progression of GA and the concurrent reduction in photoreceptor loss as evaluated by SD-OCT imaging, provided a strong rationale for subsequent Phase III clinical trials (Regillo & Heier, n.d.; Patel et al., 2022).  
In addition to its use in dry AMD, pegcetacoplan’s earlier regulatory approval for PNH helped establish it as a viable molecule with a favorable safety profile. Its journey through successive clinical phases—from Phase I safety and tolerability studies to Phase II efficacy studies and ultimately Phase III confirmation—has offered compelling evidence that targeted complement inhibition can modify the disease course in conditions characterized by chronic complement activation (Tzoumas et al., 2023). However, clinical experience with pegcetacoplan has also identified potential safety signals, including an observed increase in the incidence of new-onset exudative (wet) AMD among certain subpopulations, a factor that necessitates careful patient selection and monitoring (Lamers et al., 2022; Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023). Overall, the therapeutic history of pegcetacoplan—spanning its origin from fundamental compstatin research to its current application in treating geographic atrophy—demonstrates its potential for repurposing as a disease-modifying therapy in ocular settings (Lamers et al., 2022; Desai & Dugel, 2022).

Mechanism of Action  
At the molecular level, the pathogenic cascade in dry AMD is tightly linked to dysregulated complement activation, and pegcetacoplan intervenes at one of the central nodes of this pathway by inhibiting complement component C3. Under physiological conditions, C3 is cleaved by C3 convertases into C3a—an anaphylatoxin that drives inflammation—and C3b, which functions as an opsonin and further propagates complement amplification (Yu & Wykoff, 2021). Pegcetacoplan binds to a key epitope on C3, thereby sterically hindering the enzyme-driven cleavage that would otherwise generate these active fragments. By effectively arresting this pivotal step in the complement cascade, the drug prevents downstream events such as the assembly of terminal complement complexes and the formation of the membrane attack complex (MAC) (Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023; Wu & Sun, 2019).  
The inhibition of C3 cleavage has several critical biochemical consequences. First, by lowering the concentrations of C3a and C3b, pegcetacoplan reduces the generation of pro-inflammatory mediators and the subsequent chemotactic recruitment of immune cells, which, in turn, diminishes local inflammation in the retinal environment (Regillo & Heier, n.d.; Tzoumas et al., 2023). Second, the reduction in C3b deposition directly limits the formation of MAC on retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) surfaces—a process that has been implicated in triggering lysosomal dysfunction within these critical cells (Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023; Park et al., 2021). The MAC, when deposited sublytically on RPE cells, can compromise the function of the vacuolar H⁺-ATPase (v-ATPase), the proton pump responsible for maintaining the acidic environment of lysosomes. Acidification of the lysosomal compartment is essential for optimal activity of proteolytic enzymes, such as cathepsin D, which are required to degrade photoreceptor outer segment debris and other cytotoxic by-products (Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023; Tzoumas et al., 2023).  
Thus, by preventing excessive complement activation and subsequent MAC formation, pegcetacoplan indirectly safeguards the intracellular degradative machinery of the RPE. This preservation of v-ATPase function ensures proper lysosomal acidification, which in turn maintains cathepsin D activity and reduces lysosomal overload—a key mechanism implicated in the progressive atrophy of the RPE observed in dry AMD (Mastellos & Lambris, 2024; Regillo & Heier, n.d.). Moreover, preclinical studies have demonstrated that complement blockade via agents such as pegcetacoplan lowers sub-RPE deposit formation and inflammasome priming, processes intimately linked to lysosomal dysfunction and chronic inflammation (Liao et al., 2020; Lamers et al., 2022). Collectively, the mechanism of action of pegcetacoplan encompasses both direct inhibition of complement-driven inflammatory processes and indirect protection of intracellular catabolic functions in the RPE, thereby addressing two core pathological contributors to geographic atrophy (Kassa et al., 2019; Rubner et al., 2022).

Expected Effect  
Based on its detailed mechanism of action, pegcetacoplan is expected to exert a dual beneficial effect in the management of dry AMD. First, by binding to and inhibiting complement C3, it should markedly reduce the formation of inflammatory mediators (C3a, C3b) as well as downstream terminal pathway components such as the MAC. Clinical trial data support this expectation: in the Phase II FILLY study, monthly intravitreal injections of pegcetacoplan were associated with a roughly 29% reduction in the rate of GA lesion growth relative to control, while an alternate-month regimen achieved a 20% reduction (Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023; Patel et al., 2022). These anatomical outcomes are presumed to correlate with a slowing of disease progression and a delay in the onset of irreversible retinal degeneration.  
Second, through the inhibition of MAC deposition on RPE cells, pegcetacoplan is anticipated to preserve the functional integrity of lysosomes by ensuring that v-ATPase activity is maintained and that cathepsin D retains its proteolytic function. The preservation of lysosomal function is critical not only for the proper degradation of photoreceptor outer segment debris but also for protecting RPE cells from metabolic stress and subsequent cell death (Liao et al., 2020; Desai & Dugel, 2022). Consequently, the expected biochemical outcome is that pegcetacoplan will reduce lysosomal overload and the accumulation of toxic metabolic by-products—a process thought to contribute to the formation of sub-RPE deposits that further exacerbate tissue atrophy in dry AMD (Lamers et al., 2022; Desai & Dugel, 2022).  
At the cellular level, maintaining cathepsin D activity is imperative because this protease is responsible for degrading intracellular waste products that accumulate in RPE cells, and its functionality is closely tied to the acidic environment provided by lysosomes. By preserving this aspect of lysosomal physiology, pegcetacoplan should contribute to RPE cell survival and thereby delay the progression of geographic atrophy (Patel et al., 2022). Although improvements in functional endpoints such as visual acuity have not been immediately evident in short-term clinical trials, the principal therapeutic endpoint remains the deceleration of structural degeneration. This structural preservation is expected to eventually translate into a longer period of maintained retinal function and a postponed deterioration in vision, ultimately extending the window during which patients can retain functional vision (Wu & Sun, 2019; Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023).  
Furthermore, the established dosing regimens—with monthly or alternate-month intravitreal injections—are designed to sustain local complement inhibition at therapeutic levels without causing excessive immunosuppression that might predispose patients to infections. However, some studies have raised concerns about an increased risk of conversion to exudative AMD (wet AMD) during treatment, signaling that while the inhibition of C3 can preserve RPE integrity, careful monitoring is warranted to manage potential adverse events (Regillo & Heier, n.d.; Rubner et al., 2022).

Overall Evaluation  
A comprehensive review of pegcetacoplan as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD reveals a well-substantiated rationale and a promising clinical profile, albeit with some challenges that must be addressed. One of the most compelling strengths of pegcetacoplan is its precise molecular targeting of complement component C3—a central mediator in the complement cascade. By inhibiting C3, pegcetacoplan effectively blocks the generation of both C3a and C3b, thereby reducing pro-inflammatory signaling and preventing the formation of the membrane attack complex (MAC) (Yu & Wykoff, 2021). This upstream blockade provides a broad-spectrum mechanism capable of modulating all three complement activation pathways (classical, lectin, and alternative), which is particularly important in a multifactorial disease such as dry AMD (Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023; Lamers et al., 2022).

These anatomical endpoints, while not immediately translating into measurable improvements in visual acuity, are critical surrogates for the long-term preservation of retinal structure and function—a key goal in the management of dry AMD (Regillo & Heier, n.d.; Patel et al., 2022).  
Biochemically, pegcetacoplan’s mechanism of action extends beyond the mere suppression of complement-mediated inflammation. Its ability to indirectly preserve lysosomal function by preventing MAC-induced dysfunction of the vacuolar H⁺-ATPase (v-ATPase) and maintaining cathepsin D activity introduces a novel paradigm in addressing the intracellular stress that accelerates RPE degeneration (Liao et al., 2020; Mastellos & Lambris, 2024). In dry AMD, the accumulation of metabolic by-products due to deficient lysosomal degradation leads to the formation of drusen and sub-RPE deposits, which further stimulate complement activation and create a vicious cycle of cellular damage. Pegcetacoplan, by protecting lysosomal integrity, offers the potential to break this cycle and slow the progression of geographic atrophy (Park et al., 2021; Kassa et al., 2019).  
There are, however, certain weaknesses and challenges that must be taken into account. One notable concern is the increased risk of new-onset exudative AMD that has been reported in some clinical studies. This adverse event appears to be dose-dependent and may reflect a complex interplay between complement inhibition and pro-angiogenic pathways in the retina (Wu & Sun, 2019; Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023). The occurrence of neovascular complications necessitates rigorous patient selection criteria, close imaging surveillance, and potentially the development of combination strategies to counterbalance this risk without compromising the therapeutic efficacy against GA (Lamers et al., 2022; Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Panobinostat (LBH589) is a fully synthetic small‐molecule compound originally developed by Novartis and characterized chemically as a cinnamic hydroxamic acid analogue formulated as its anhydrous lactate salt. This molecule belongs to the hydroxamate class of histone deacetylase inhibitors (HDACi), a group of compounds designed to inhibit the enzymatic activity of HDACs that regulate chromatin remodeling and transcription by catalyzing the removal of acetyl groups from histone proteins. Panobinostat’s chemical structure, defined by its hydroxamic acid moiety, is tailored to chelate the zinc ion in the catalytic domain of HDAC enzymes, thereby preventing deacetylation reactions that normally lead to a condensed chromatin state. In its initial development, panobinostat was formulated in multiple dosage forms, including oral hard capsules containing 10, 15, or 20 mg doses and earlier intravenous preparations, illustrating its versatility in administration routes for different clinical indications (Van Veggel, Westerman, & Hamberg, 2018; Libby et al., 2015; Dokmanovic, Clarke, & Marks, 2007). Compounds of this class have historically been employed in oncology, where their capacity to induce hyperacetylation of histone and non-histone substrates leads to altered gene transcription, cell cycle arrest, differentiation, and eventual apoptosis in malignant cells (Van Veggel et al., 2018; Cea et al., 2013). Moreover, the broad-spectrum inhibition of HDAC isoforms—spanning Classes I, II, and IV—distinguishes panobinostat as a “pan-HDAC inhibitor” with high potency at nanomolar concentrations, a characteristic that underlies its robust pharmacological profile and its subsequent regulatory approvals for certain cancer indications (Morabito et al., 2016).

Therapeutic History:  
Since its discovery, panobinostat has undergone extensive preclinical and clinical evaluation primarily targeting multiple myeloma and various hematologic malignancies. Early phase clinical trials established that, as a single agent, panobinostat had modest activity; however, its combination with proteasome inhibitors such as bortezomib and corticosteroids like dexamethasone produced synergistic effects that translated into significant improvements in progression‐free survival in relapsed and refractory multiple myeloma patients. This positive clinical efficacy culminated in its approval by both the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and the European Medicines Agency (EMA) in 2015 for the treatment of patients with multiple myeloma who had received at least two prior regimens (Van Veggel et al., 2018; Libby et al., 2015; Bondarev et al., 2021). Beyond multiple myeloma, panobinostat has been scrutinized in a variety of clinical settings—including cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, acute myeloid leukemia, diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, and several solid tumor malignancies—to explore its antitumor potential in combination therapies, given its capacity to potentiate the cytotoxic effects of other agents by modulating epigenetic regulation (Cea et al., 2013; Cinek & Karalı, 2021; Libby et al., 2015). Despite its demonstrated efficacy in cancer, there is no recorded use of panobinostat in ophthalmological diseases such as dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or in any similar degenerative condition. The extensive body of clinical research on HDAC inhibitors has predominantly focused on antineoplastic applications, and while some mechanistic parallels exist between the cellular processes targeted in cancer and those disrupted in degenerative retinal diseases, panobinostat’s utility in dry AMD remains an uncharted territory that has thus far not been explored in preclinical or clinical trials (Dokmanovic, Clarke, & Marks, 2007; Morabito et al., 2016; Libby et al., 2015).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, panobinostat exerts its biological effects primarily through the inhibition of histone deacetylase enzymes. The compound’s hydroxamic acid group binds with high affinity to the zinc ion located in the catalytic domain of HDAC enzymes, thereby blocking the deacetylation of lysine residues on histone tails as well as on several non-histone proteins. This blockade causes an accumulation of acetylated histones, which in turn results in a more open chromatin conformation that facilitates enhanced transcription of a multitude of genes, including those pivotal for cell cycle arrest, apoptosis, and cellular differentiation (Benedetti, Conte, & Altucci, 2015; Morabito et al., 2016). Beyond its classical role in modifying histone tail acetylation, panobinostat’s broad inhibition across HDAC classes implies that it can modulate the acetylation status of key transcription factors, chaperone proteins (such as heat shock protein 90), and structural proteins like α-tubulin. This wide-ranging impact on protein acetylation alters the functional activity of numerous signaling pathways and cellular processes, contributing to anti-proliferative and pro-apoptotic outcomes in cancer cells (Morabito et al., 2016). The pleiotropic nature of its action is further evidenced by the induction of autophagy in various tumor models, an effect thought to be mediated by the increased acetylation and transcriptional activation of master regulators of lysosomal biogenesis such as transcription factor EB (TFEB). Although the provided literature does not explicitly detail TFEB upregulation in response to panobinostat, the general tendency of HDAC inhibitors to enhance acetylation-dependent transcription supports the hypothesis that TFEB and its downstream lysosomal genes could be upregulated—thereby promoting autophagy and lysosomal clearance pathways (Cinek & Karalı, 2021; Libby et al., 2015). This complex interplay of molecular events not only underpins panobinostat’s established antitumor activity but also provides a rationale for its possible repurposing in degenerative diseases where enhanced cellular clearance mechanisms may be therapeutic (Van Veggel et al., 2018; Benedetti, Conte, & Altucci, 2015).

Expected Effect in Dry Age-Related Macular Degeneration (AMD):  
Dry age-related macular degeneration is characterized by the progressive dysfunction of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), which is responsible for the maintenance of photoreceptor health and the clearance of cellular debris. A central pathological hallmark of dry AMD is the accumulation of drusen deposits beneath the RPE, partly attributable to impaired lysosomal degradation and autophagy. In the context of this disease, the hypothesis proposes that localized ocular administration of panobinostat could inhibit HDAC activity in RPE cells, leading to a global increase in histone acetylation. This epigenetic modulation is expected to activate acetylation-dependent transcription factors such as TFEB—a master regulator of lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy—that, once activated, upregulates a network of genes involved in lysosomal acidification and cathepsin D expression (Van Veggel et al., 2018; Cinek & Karalı, 2021). Enhanced expression of these lysosomal components is anticipated to restore or improve the degradative capacity of the RPE, facilitating the clearance of drusen deposits and ameliorating the pathological buildup of cellular waste characteristic of dry AMD.

In preclinical oncology studies, panobinostat has consistently induced autophagy and promoted lysosomal function in cancer cells, leading to growth inhibition and apoptosis. If similar cellular responses occur in RPE cells, then panobinostat may stimulate a beneficial autophagic flux that targets accumulated proteins and lipids for degradation (Libby et al., 2015). The expression of cathepsin D—a lysosomal protease critical for the degradation of photoreceptor outer segments and other metabolic substrates—is well documented in RPE cells, and its activity is tightly regulated by lysosomal pH; thus, any intervention that improves lysosomal acidification is likely to have a favorable impact on RPE homeostasis (Mottamal et al., 2015; Morabito et al., 2016). These findings support the proposed mechanism whereby panobinostat’s inhibition of HDACs may indirectly enhance the transcriptional activation of TFEB, culminating in improved lysosomal biogenesis and function. From a translational perspective, it is crucial to recognize that systemic toxicity has been an important limitation of panobinostat in oncologic settings, where adverse effects such as gastrointestinal disturbances, thrombocytopenia, and cardiotoxicity (QT interval prolongation) have been observed. However, the concept of localized ocular dosing—via intravitreal injection or topical delivery—could potentially mitigate these risks by achieving high local drug concentrations with minimal systemic exposure (Libby et al., 2015; Karol et al., 2020). In the specific context of dry AMD, where chronic, localized pathology is present in the retina, targeted delivery of panobinostat could allow for the modulation of RPE cellular processes without triggering widespread adverse reactions. This targeted approach aligns with current trends in ocular pharmacotherapy, which increasingly favor local drug delivery systems designed to maximize therapeutic efficacy while minimizing systemic toxicity (Bondarev et al., 2021; Van Veggel et al., 2018). Ultimately, the expected outcome in the proposed assay is that panobinostat treatment will lead to measurable upregulation of lysosomal gene expression, restoration of lysosomal acidification, and enhanced activity of cathepsin D within RPE cells, thereby reducing the burden of drusen deposits and potentially slowing the progression of dry AMD (Cea et al., 2013; Libby et al., 2015).

Overall Evaluation:  
The repurposing of panobinostat for dry age-related macular degeneration presents an intriguing and biologically plausible strategy that leverages the compound’s well-documented HDAC inhibitory properties to modulate critical intracellular degradation pathways. One of the foremost strengths of this therapeutic candidate is its potent, broad-spectrum inhibition of HDAC enzymes at low nanomolar concentrations, which has been repeatedly demonstrated in various preclinical and clinical studies in oncology (Van Veggel et al., 2018; Morabito et al., 2016). The resultant hyperacetylation of histones and non-histone proteins not only promotes cell cycle arrest and apoptosis in malignant cells but also facilitates the transcriptional activation of autophagy- and lysosome-related genes—a pathway that could be harnessed to restore faithful lysosomal degradation in retinal pigment epithelial cells affected in dry AMD (Benedetti, Conte, & Altucci, 2015; Cinek & Karalı, 2021).

In terms of mechanistic specificity, the broad inhibitory profile of panobinostat could be seen as an advantage in the context of dry AMD, where multiple deacetylation pathways may contribute to the impaired clearance of cellular debris. By simultaneously inhibiting several HDAC isoforms, panobinostat is likely to achieve a more robust activation of TFEB and other transcription factors central to lysosomal biogenesis, thereby amplifying the cellular clearance mechanisms required to remove drusen deposits (Morabito et al., 2016; Carafa, Nebbioso, & Altucci, 2011). Additionally, the existing clinical experience with panobinostat in oncology provides a rich repository of pharmacokinetic, pharmacodynamic, and safety data that can inform dose optimization and risk management strategies—albeit with the caveat that ocular tissues may respond differently to HDAC inhibition than cancer cells (Bondarev et al., 2021; Libby et al., 2015).

Nevertheless, several significant weaknesses must be acknowledged in evaluating panobinostat as a candidate for dry AMD treatment. Chief among these is the potential for systemic toxicity. Panobinostat’s clinical utilization in cancer has been limited by adverse side effects including gastrointestinal toxicity, thrombocytopenia, and cardiac complications, and although localized ocular delivery may attenuate these concerns, the safety profile of panobinostat in retinal tissues remains largely unexplored (Libby et al., 2015; Karol et al., 2020). Moreover, the pharmacokinetic behavior of panobinostat when administered locally to the eye is unknown; challenges such as drug solubility, stability, and diffusion across retinal layers must be addressed rigorously in preclinical models. Another point of concern is the translational leap from oncology to ophthalmology. While the mechanistic rationale for using panobinostat to enhance autophagy and lysosomal function is supported by its effects in cancer cells, RPE cells possess distinctive metabolic and regulatory pathways that may not respond identically to HDAC inhibition. The degree to which TFEB and other autophagy or lysosomal genes are modulated by panobinostat in RPE cells has not yet been directly demonstrated, and significant differences in chromatin structure and gene expression profiles between cancer cells and differentiated RPE cells could impact both efficacy and safety outcomes (Morabito et al., 2016; Carafa, Nebbioso, & Altucci, 2011). From a drug development perspective, the strategy of repurposing panobinostat for dry AMD is compelling because it integrates a well-characterized molecular mode of action with an unmet clinical need. However, critical translational challenges must be overcome. These include reformulating panobinostat for localized ocular delivery, establishing appropriate dosing regimens that maximize local efficacy while minimizing toxicity, and conducting comprehensive preclinical evaluations in relevant in vitro and in vivo models of dry AMD. The potential benefit of enhancing lysosomal clearance through increased TFEB activation is a particularly attractive aspect of this proposal, as impaired autophagy and lysosomal dysfunction are recognized contributors to the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Cinek & Karalı, 2021; Morabito et al., 2016). Its ability to robustly inhibit multiple HDAC isoforms and thereby potentially activate TFEB and lysosomal gene networks aligns well with the therapeutic strategy of improving autophagic clearance in RPE cells. However, substantial gaps in knowledge remain regarding its direct effects on retinal cells and the feasibility of its long-term use in an ocular setting. Its established clinical use in oncology offers a wealth of pharmacological data and a precedent for potent HDAC inhibition, while the hypothesis that HDAC inhibitors can reactivate latent clearance pathways in RPE cells is both innovative and scientifically plausible. The strengths of panobinostat lie in its potency, broad-spectrum activity, and documented ability to elicit autophagic responses, which collectively suggest that, under the right conditions and with a carefully optimized ocular delivery system, it could address one of the major pathophysiological mechanisms underlying dry AMD. Nonetheless, the weaknesses, including potential off-target toxicity, uncertain ocular pharmacokinetics, and the need for a comprehensive reevaluation of its effects in non-malignant, differentiated cell types, must be thoroughly investigated before advancing into clinical studies. Therefore, data from directed preclinical experiments employing RPE cell cultures and animal models of dry AMD will be essential in determining whether the benefits of panobinostat can be safely and effectively harnessed to treat this common cause of vision loss in the elderly (Srinivas, 2017; Van Veggel et al., 2018; Bondarev et al., 2021; Carafa, Nebbioso, & Altucci, 2011).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Torin1 is a synthetic small‐molecule that belongs to the second‐generation, ATP‐competitive class of mTOR inhibitors, originally derived from a quinoline‐based scaffold. Its discovery originated from a high‐throughput compound library screen that identified quinolone hits with moderate mTOR activity, which were then optimized through iterative medicinal chemistry by introducing a six‐membered lactam to convert the initial quinolone into a tricyclic benzonaphthridinone scaffold (Guillem, 2015). This chemical modification yielded a molecule with exceptional biochemical potency—capable of inhibiting both mTOR complexes, mTORC1 and mTORC2, at very low (nanomolar to picomolar) concentrations—and with approximately 1000-fold improvement in cellular potency relative to the initial hits (Guillem, 2015). As an ATP-competitive inhibitor, Torin1 binds directly to the active (ATP-binding) site of mTOR, thereby circumventing the partial inhibition that is observed with first-generation mTOR inhibitors like rapamycin that act allosterically by binding FKBP12 (Liu et al., 2012). Torin1 has been widely used as a research tool to interrogate mTOR signaling in various cellular contexts, and its chemical lineage as a quinoline-derived molecule positions it within a well-characterized class of inhibitors that have been instrumental in expanding our understanding of mTOR-dependent regulation of autophagy and cellular metabolism (Liu et al., 2012).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, Torin1 has been employed predominantly as a research tool rather than as a clinical drug candidate. Extensive preclinical studies have demonstrated its robust ability to inhibit mTOR signaling in cancer models, autophagy-deficient systems, and metabolic studies. For instance, Torin1 was shown to potently inhibit mTOR signaling pathways in glioblastoma and prostate cancer cells, significantly reducing cell-cycle progression and inducing apoptosis in certain contexts (Gu, 2017; Liu et al., 2012). Its use as an autophagy inducer is well documented, as experiments utilizing Torin1 have demonstrated increased autophagic flux and elevated lysosomal activity in multiple cell lines (Li, 2018; Liu et al., 2012). Importantly, Torin1 is also used in studies with retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells, as evidenced by its ability to increase TFEB-driven luciferase reporter activity in ARPE-19 cells by effectively suppressing mTORC1 signaling (Huang et al., 2018). Despite these promising experimental findings, Torin1 has not advanced to clinical trials for any indication, including neurodegenerative disorders or dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD). Moreover, its intrinsic pharmacokinetic limitations—such as poor aqueous solubility, a short half-life, and low oral bioavailability—have been recognized in several studies, thereby limiting its potential as a direct therapeutic candidate without further structural optimization (Guillem, 2015; Wang et al., 2022).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, Torin1 functions by competing with ATP for binding to the catalytic domain of mTOR, effectively blocking the phosphorylation of downstream substrates. Its ATP-competitive nature allows Torin1 to inhibit both mTORC1 and mTORC2 complexes, thereby offering a broader inhibition profile than allosteric agents like rapamycin that primarily target mTORC1 (Guillem, 2015; Liu et al., 2012). Detailed molecular modeling and structure–activity relationship studies indicate that the tricyclic benzonaphthridinone core of Torin1 forms critical hinge-binding interactions with residues in the mTOR kinase domain (Liu et al., 2012). This interaction accounts for its high potency, as reflected in low nanomolar IC₅₀ values in cellular assays (Liu et al., 2012; Gros & Muller, 2014). Torin1 induces rapid dephosphorylation of canonical mTORC1 substrates, such as S6 kinase at Thr389 and 4E-BP1 at Thr37/46, which results in downregulation of protein synthesis and cellular growth signals (Misra & Pizzo, 2013). Moreover, by simultaneously inhibiting mTORC2, it reduces phosphorylation of Akt at Ser473—a site critical for full Akt activation—thus attenuating the feedback loops that typically reinvigorate upstream PI3K signaling in response to mTORC1 inhibition (Gu, 2017; Martina et al., 2014). A particularly notable feature of Torin1 is its slow off-rate, which leads to sustained inhibition of mTOR activity even after drug washout, a pharmacodynamic property that may confer prolonged downstream effects such as enhanced autophagic flux (Liu et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2013). The inhibition of mTOR by Torin1 correlates with dephosphorylation of transcription factors, particularly TFEB and TFE3; under normal nutrient-replete conditions, mTORC1 phosphorylates TFEB (e.g., on S211 in TFEB) and TFE3, sequestering them in the cytosol through binding with 14-3-3 proteins (Huang et al., 2018; Martina et al., 2014). Upon mTOR inhibition by Torin1, TFEB is dephosphorylated and translocates to the nucleus, where it induces the transcription of CLEAR (Coordinated Lysosomal Expression and Regulation) network genes that drive lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy (Li, 2018; Liu et al., 2013). This precise modulation of mTOR signaling and subsequent transcriptional reprogramming forms the biochemical basis for leveraging Torin1 as a candidate to ameliorate lysosomal clearance defects.

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis for repurposing Torin1 in the context of dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is that potent inhibition of mTORC1/2 in RPE cells can lift the repressive phosphorylation that normally limits the activity of TFEB and TFE3. In RPE cells, as demonstrated by studies in ARPE-19 cell models, mTOR inhibition via Torin1 not only leads to decreased phosphorylation of S6 kinase but also results in marked activation of TFEB-driven transcription (Huang et al., 2018). When TFEB translocates to the nucleus, it binds to CLEAR elements present in the promoters of genes responsible for lysosomal biogenesis, acidification (through the upregulation of V-ATPase subunits), and the maturation and activity of lysosomal enzymes such as cathepsin D (CTSD) (Huang et al., 2018; Li, 2018). In dry AMD, RPE cells exhibit a decline in lysosomal function along with accumulation of cellular debris and lipofuscin, which contribute to disease pathology. By inducing a robust CLEAR response, Torin1 is expected to restore lysosomal function through increased biogenesis, enhanced acidification, and elevated cathepsin D activity, thereby improving the clearance of toxic aggregates in RPE cells and ultimately mitigating the progression of dry AMD (Gu, 2017; Huang et al., 2018). Additionally, the sustained target engagement afforded by Torin1’s slow off-rate may provide prolonged therapeutic benefit even with intermittent dosing, an attractive feature given the chronic nature of AMD (Liu et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2013). Recent evidence from preclinical iPSC models and autophagy-deficiency studies underscores the potential translation of mTOR-targeted strategies in restoring cellular homeostasis in degenerative diseases, lending further credence to this expected mechanism (Guillem, 2015).

Overall Evaluation:  
In summary, Torin1 possesses a compelling mechanistic profile that aligns well with the therapeutic needs of dry AMD by targeting a fundamental pathway governing cellular homeostasis in RPE cells. Its origin from a quinoline-based scaffold and subsequent chemical optimization into a highly potent ATP-competitive mTOR inhibitor underline its status as a valuable chemical probe in preclinical settings (Guillem, 2015). The dual inhibition of both mTORC1 and mTORC2 by Torin1, combined with its slow off-rate and sustained downstream effects—including dephosphorylation and nuclear translocation of TFEB/TFE3—make it an ideal tool for inducing lysosomal biogenesis and enhancing autophagic clearance (Martina et al., 2014; Huang et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2012). In cellular models, including ARPE-19 RPE cells, Torin1 has already demonstrated the ability to activate TFEB and upregulate CLEAR gene expression, which is directly relevant to counteracting the lysosomal clearance defects observed in dry AMD (Huang et al., 2018; Li, 2018).

However, significant challenges remain regarding the translational applicability of Torin1 as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. Its reported poor aqueous solubility, short half-life, and low oral bioavailability present formidable barriers to clinical development unless addressed through formulation improvements or further medicinal chemistry optimization (Guillem, 2015; Wang et al., 2022). Moreover, while extensive preclinical literature supports its role as a robust mTOR inhibitor in cancer and autophagy research, there is a lack of direct in vivo evidence for its efficacy in ocular models, particularly in dry AMD or geographic atrophy (GA) mouse lines (Liu et al., 2013; Gu, 2017). Careful dosing will also be critical, as the broad and potent inhibition of mTOR can have unintended effects on cellular metabolism and protein synthesis beyond the intended enhancement of lysosomal function. Additionally, off-target effects have been observed in some biochemical screens at supraphysiologic concentrations, including binding to other PIKK family members such as ATR, ATM, and DNA-PK, although these are generally not manifested at the low nanomolar concentrations used in cellular assays (Settembre et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2012).

From the perspective of repurposing for dry AMD, Torin1’s deep mechanistic specificity is a double-edged sword: it offers a highly defined and robust approach to upregulating lysosomal biogenesis via the TFEB/TFE3 axis, yet its pharmacokinetic liabilities and the absence of any clinical history in ocular disease necessitate additional work. The promising in vitro data in RPE models (ARPE-19 cells) and iPSC-derived RPE systems provide valuable target validation, but before advancing to clinical trials a refined analog or an optimized delivery method (for example, local ocular administration to bypass systemic bioavailability issues) should be considered (Huang et al., 2018; Li, 2018; Wang et al., 2022).

In summary, Torin1 is an excellent candidate for preclinical proof-of-concept studies to validate mTOR inhibition as a strategy to combat lysosomal dysfunction in dry AMD; however, further optimization to improve its stability and bioavailability, alongside rigorous in vivo testing in relevant AMD models, will be essential prior to clinical development (Guillem, 2015; Gu, 2017). The strengths of Torin1 lie in its potent, dual mTOR inhibition and its ability to robustly induce TFEB activation, whereas its weaknesses center on its pharmacokinetic shortcomings and the current lack of efficacy data in ocular disease models. Overall, with focused optimization and targeted delivery strategies, Torin1 or its derivatives may offer a promising therapeutic avenue for ameliorating the lysosomal clearance defects that underlie dry AMD pathology (Liu et al., 2012; Huang et al., 2018).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
USP14 inhibitor IU1 (Sigma SML0010) is a synthetic small-molecule compound originally discovered through high-throughput screening efforts aimed at identifying inhibitors of deubiquitinating enzymes (DUBs) associated with the proteasome. IU1 belongs to the class of small-molecule DUB inhibitors that specifically target USP14, a proteasome-associated deubiquitinase responsible for trimming ubiquitin chains from substrates before their degradation by the 26S proteasome. Early medicinal chemistry studies led to the development of IU1 and its more potent analogs (such as IU1-47), which exploit structure–activity relationships on a benzene–dimethyl-pyrrole scaffold with tailored electron-withdrawing substitutions and lipophilic enhancements designed to improve potency, selectivity, and bioavailability (Lim et al., 2024; Boselli et al., 2017; Qin et al., 2024). These compounds are cell permeable and have been employed as chemical probes in multiple preclinical settings to modulate proteostasis via targeted inhibition of USP14. In essence, IU1 reflects a series of rationally designed molecules aimed at shifting the balance of proteasome-mediated degradation by preventing USP14’s “trimming” activity, thereby effectively accelerating the clearance of misfolded and aggregation-prone proteins.

Therapeutic History:  
The therapeutic history of USP14 inhibitors like IU1 is primarily rooted in preclinical research addressing proteostasis dysfunction in models of aging and neurodegeneration rather than in clinical or veterinary practice. In Drosophila models of proteostasis-associated aging, IU1 treatment was shown to reduce the accumulation of polyubiquitinated aggregates, increase autophagy markers such as LC3, improve behavioral phenotypes, and even extend lifespan, with these benefits abrogated when autophagy was experimentally disrupted (Lim et al., 2024). In mammalian cell proteotoxicity models—using stressors such as canavanine plus azetidine—IU1 has similarly been reported to reduce ubiquitin conjugate accumulation and enhance autophagic responses (Lim et al., 2024). Moreover, in primary neuronal cultures, more potent analogs like IU1-47 have been used to promote degradation of pathologic proteins such as tau, thereby supporting the concept that USP14 inhibition enhances proteasome-assisted clearance of aggregation-prone substrates (Boselli et al., 2017; Kiprowska, 2016). Despite these promising preclinical data in models of neurodegeneration and systemic aging, there is no direct evidence to date that IU1 or its analogs have been applied to treat dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or geographic atrophy specifically. However, given that several key observations in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells—such as evidence of impaired ubiquitin–proteasome system (UPS) and autophagy cross-talk, aggregate accumulation, and lysosomal dysfunction—are central to AMD pathology (Blasiak et al., 2019; Kaarniranta et al., 2023; Shang & Taylor, 2012), repurposing IU1 to restore proteostasis in RPE represents an innovative extension of its preclinical use.

Mechanism of Action:  
The known mechanism of IU1 centers on its inhibition of USP14, a deubiquitinating enzyme that transiently associates with the proteasome. USP14 normally functions by “trimming” ubiquitin chains on substrates as they enter the proteasome, an activity that can delay substrate degradation and allow for substrate rescue under stress conditions. IU1 and its optimized analogs (e.g., IU1-47) act through allosteric mechanisms—not by directly competing at the catalytic site but by binding a pocket distal (approximately 8.3 Å away) from the catalytic center, thereby perturbing USP14’s structural conformation and catalytic efficiency (Qin et al., 2024; Lim et al., 2024). Inhibition of USP14 by IU1 leads to a reduced removal of ubiquitin chains, effectively “locking in” the ubiquitin tag on misfolded and aggregation-prone proteins and facilitating their recognition and degradation by the 26S proteasome. Beyond its direct impact on proteasomal degradation, USP14 inhibition has been reported to modulate autophagy—evident from increased LC3 lipidation and autophagic flux in certain cellular contexts (Lim et al., 2024; Kim, 2020). Some studies suggest that USP14 may also indirectly influence autophagy by regulating the turnover of factors such as UVRAG, a key autophagy regulator, although these connections remain to be fully elucidated. Notably, while IU1 has been shown to accelerate aggregate clearance in neuronal and Drosophila models, a series of studies have also flagged potential off-target effects at higher concentrations, including inhibition of mitochondrial Complex I leading to ATP depletion and subsequent activation of calpain-mediated proteolysis (Kiprowska, 2016; Kiprowska et al., n.d.). Hence, the molecular interactions of IU1 are complex and highly context-dependent, with the potential to both enhance proteasomal degradation and, at non-optimized doses, induce metabolic perturbations.

Expected Effect:  
In the context of dry age-related macular degeneration, particularly geographic atrophy, the central hypothesis is that IU1 will inhibit USP14 in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells, thereby accelerating the proteasome-assisted clearance of misfolded, aggregation-prone proteins. RPE cells in AMD display defects in both the UPS and the autophagy/lysosomal systems, with studies documenting decreased proteasome activity, accumulation of ubiquitinated aggregates, elevated levels of the selective autophagy adaptor SQSTM1/p62, and lysosomal dysfunction including impaired acidification mediated by vacuolar ATPase (v-ATPase) (Blasiak et al., 2019; Kaarniranta et al., 2023; Shang & Taylor, 2012; Viiri, 2019). By inhibiting USP14, IU1 is expected to shift the proteostasis balance in RPE cells towards enhanced degradation of misfolded proteins via the proteasome. This would not only reduce the intracellular aggregate burden but also alleviate the overloading of the lysosomal pathway—in turn potentially restoring lysosomal functions such as proper acidification by v-ATPase activity. Improved lysosomal acidification is known to facilitate the maturation and activity of cathepsin D, a key lysosomal protease responsible for degrading various protein aggregates and damaged organelles (Kaarniranta et al., 2023). Moreover, preclinical findings in neuronal cells have demonstrated that USP14 inhibition reduces aggregate load (e.g., tau) and promotes autophagic flux (Boselli et al., 2017; Lim et al., 2024), lending indirect support to the concept that these effects might be recapitulated in RPE cells. Although no direct data exist for IU1 in RPE, the mechanistic parallels between proteostasis impairment in neurons and RPE—as documented in extensive AMD literature—suggest that IU1 could reduce aggregate accumulation and oxidative stress in RPE, thereby slowing the progression of geographic atrophy.

Overall Evaluation:  
The overall evaluation of USP14 inhibitor IU1 as a therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration is cautiously optimistic yet highlights several critical areas for further investigation. On the positive side, IU1 represents an innovative strategy targeting a central node in protein quality control—USP14—that regulates the degradation of misfolded, aggregation-prone proteins via the proteasome and modulates autophagic pathways. Preclinical evidence in Drosophila models and neuronal cultures demonstrates that pharmacological USP14 inhibition can enhance aggregate clearance, improve proteostasis, and even extend lifespan and motor function under proteotoxic stress conditions (Lim et al., 2024; Boselli et al., 2017). These findings support the concept that modulating the UPS–autophagy interplay may be beneficial in diseases where proteostasis failure is a key driver, such as dry AMD, in which RPE cells experience aggregate build-up, defective autophagy, and lysosomal dysfunction (Blasiak et al., 2019; Kaarniranta et al., 2023; Shang & Taylor, 2012).

Furthermore, the biochemical mechanism by which IU1 operates—namely, reducing the deubiquitinating activity of USP14 to promote ubiquitin-tag retention and substrate commitment to degradation—provides a theoretically attractive approach to simultaneously reduce the proteasomal backlog and relieve lysosomal burden. The potential secondary effects on autophagy, including improved LC3-II turnover and possibly upregulated clearance of aggregates through aggrephagy, add further appeal to the candidate as a multi-modal modulator of proteostasis. The cell-permeable, small-molecule nature of IU1, along with available more potent analogs (such as IU1-47), offers promising opportunities for medicinal chemistry optimization and dosage refinement, especially important given the need for safe application in delicate ocular tissues.

However, several weaknesses and challenges must be addressed before IU1 can be considered a viable therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. A significant concern originates from studies in neuronal systems that indicate off-target effects at higher concentrations—specifically, inhibition of mitochondrial Complex I, ATP depletion, and activation of calpain-mediated proteolysis (Kiprowska, 2016; Kiprowska et al., n.d.). These potential toxicities raise the possibility that a narrow therapeutic window may exist, necessitating thorough dose-response studies in RPE cell models to ensure efficacy without compromising cell viability. Moreover, no direct preclinical studies have yet evaluated IU1 in RPE cells or in animal models of geographic atrophy. As such, critical parameters—such as its ability to modulate v-ATPase function, maintain lysosomal acidification, boost cathepsin D activity, and ultimately clear RPE-specific aggregates such as lipofuscin or oxidized photoreceptor debris—remain to be validated (Kaarniranta et al., 2023; Shang & Taylor, 2012).

Additionally, while the mechanistic data from neurodegenerative models are compelling, the biochemical environment of RPE cells differs from that of neurons in several key respects. RPE cells are highly phagocytic, exposed to constant oxidative stress, and rely on a finely tuned balance between proteasomal and lysosomal pathways to manage the constant influx of photoreceptor outer segment material (Blasiak et al., 2019; Viiri, 2019). Thus, any intervention that modulates proteostasis must be carefully tailored to avoid unintended disruptions in these homeostatic processes. The current literature also underscores the complexity of deubiquitinase biology; while USP14 inhibition appears beneficial in some contexts, the intricate interplay with other DUBs and the broader UPS could lead to compensatory mechanisms that diminish the anticipated therapeutic effect or even trigger adverse consequences (Faber & Roepman, 2019; Kim, 2020).

In summary, USP14 inhibitor IU1 offers an innovative and potentially transformative approach to restoring proteostasis in RPE cells by enhancing proteasomal degradation and autophagic clearance of misfolded proteins—a strategy that directly addresses the pathobiology of dry AMD and geographic atrophy as defined by aggregate accumulation and lysosomal dysfunction (Lim et al., 2024; Blasiak et al., 2019; Kaarniranta et al., 2023). The strengths of this candidate include its robust preclinical data in non-RPE systems, its well-characterized mechanism of action, and its amenability to further chemical optimization. However, significant weaknesses, including potential off-target mitochondrial toxicity, an unestablished therapeutic window in RPE cells, and the lack of direct preclinical studies in AMD models, necessitate cautious and rigorous further investigation. To move forward, it will be essential to conduct targeted RPE-specific in vitro assays and in vivo studies—assessing proteasome activity, autophagy flux, lysosomal acidification (v-ATPase function), cathepsin D activity, and aggregate clearance—while carefully monitoring for cytotoxicity. Only with such detailed preclinical validation can the promise of IU1 as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD be fully assessed (Lim et al., 2024; Blasiak et al., 2019; Kiprowska, 2016; Shang & Taylor, 2012).
