Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Torin2 is a synthetic, second-generation ATP-competitive inhibitor of the mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) kinase designed to inhibit both mTOR complex 1 (mTORC1) and complex 2 (mTORC2) with high potency and favorable pharmacodynamic properties compared to first-generation allosteric mTOR inhibitors (rapamycin/rapalogs) and earlier catalytic mTOR kinase inhibitors (TORKi) such as PP242 and AZD8055 (Liu et al., 2013, pp. 7–10). Chemically optimized by structure-guided medicinal chemistry efforts, Torin2 exhibits rapid dephosphorylation of canonical mTORC1 substrates S6K1 (T389) and 4E-BP1 (T37/46) including rapamycin-insensitive sites, and of the mTORC2 substrate Akt (S473), reflecting dual-complex inhibition that is superior to rapamycin’s mTORC1-limited activity (with incomplete suppression of 4E-BP1) (Liu et al., 2013, pp. 7–10). In head-to-head comparisons with other ATP-competitive mTOR inhibitors, Torin2 maintains stronger and more sustained suppression of mTORC1/2 signaling after drug washout, attributable to its slow off-rate, with durable pathway inhibition persisting for approximately four hours in cellular assays, contrasting with rapid recovery observed with PP242 and shorter-duration suppression by AZD8055 (Liu et al., 2013, pp. 7–9). Torin2 is highly selective for mTOR over PI3K (>800-fold) and shows approximately 100-fold selectivity over the DNA damage response kinases ATM and ATR; these latter off-targets remain relevant at higher concentrations and inform safety margins and dose selection (Liu et al., 2013, pp. 9–10).

Mechanistically, Torin2 robustly induces autophagy across multiple cell lines (e.g., LC3-II accumulation, acridine-orange–positive acidic vesicle formation), consistent with its potent inhibition of mTORC1, a master negative regulator of autophagy initiation and flux (Liu et al., 2013, pp. 7–9). As a drug class, ATP-competitive TORKi have been widely investigated in oncology and proliferative diseases given their ability to fully suppress both mTOR complexes, thereby impacting protein synthesis, cell-cycle progression, metabolism, and survival signaling (Liu et al., 2013, pp. 7–10). Outside oncology, dual mTORC1/2 inhibition has demonstrated disease-modifying potential in organ systems where mTOR hyperactivation drives pathology; for example, Torin2 reduced S6 and 4E-BP1 phosphorylation and curtailed cyst burden in a mouse model of autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease, with efficacy comparable to sirolimus and a potentially more favorable side-effect profile (Holditch et al., 2019, pp. 6–7).

In the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), dysregulated mTOR signaling (particularly chronic mTORC1 activation with age) is strongly implicated in degradative/clearance failure, lysosomal dysfunction, metabolic reprogramming, and structural degeneration that recapitulate key features of dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD), including lipid-rich subretinal deposits and RPE dedifferentiation (Go et al., 2020, pp. 1–3, 11–13; Huang et al., 2019, pp. 1–2, 7–9; Zhao et al., 2011, pp. 10–11). RPE expresses and functionally engages both mTORC1 and mTORC2 complexes, providing a mechanistic rationale for evaluating dual-complex catalytic inhibitors like Torin2 as therapeutic candidates to correct core pathogenic processes in dry AMD (Intartaglia et al., 2022, pp. 15–17).

Therapeutic History  
The mTOR pathway has been studied extensively in retinal and RPE biology, with strong preclinical evidence linking mTOR hyperactivation to RPE degeneration and dry AMD-like pathology, and corresponding benefits from mTOR inhibition; however, direct ocular data with Torin2 itself are currently lacking and must be extrapolated from pharmacology in other tissues and from surrogates (Torin1, PP242, INK-128/MLN0128) and rapamycin (Liu et al., 2013, pp. 7–10; Holditch et al., 2019, pp. 6–7). Genetic and pharmacologic mTOR activation in RPE induces epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT), suppresses autophagy, disrupts metabolism, and yields an AMD-like phenotype; in a knock-in model that overexpresses mLST8 (a core mTORC component) in RPE, both mTORC1 and mTORC2 are upregulated, and dual-complex inhibition with TORIN1 (a TORKi closely related to Torin2) normalized signaling and restored autophagy and RPE function in vitro, including rescue of autophagy regulators Atg9b and Atg7 and recovery of autophagy flux (Chowdhury et al., 2025, pp. 1–2, 8–13). These data directly support the therapeutic relevance of dual mTORC1/2 inhibition in RPE conditions that model early AMD pathogenesis (Chowdhury et al., 2025, pp. 1–2, 8–13).

In a complementary RPE disease model focused on amyloid-β (Aβ)-induced lysosomal/autophagy impairment—a pathology linked to dry AMD—Torin (a first-generation mTOR inhibitor in this study; not explicitly Torin2) restored lysosomal activity via LAMP2 activation, corrected p62/SQSTM1 accumulation, facilitated Aβ aggregate clearance, and ameliorated Aβ-driven tight junction disruption in vitro and in Aβ-challenged mouse RPE in vivo, directly addressing the barrier degradation and clearance deficits central to AMD (Jo et al., 2023, pp. 1–2). In multiple RPE cell systems modeling autofluorescent granule (AFG) accumulation and lipofuscinogenesis after photoreceptor outer segment (POS) challenge, mTOR inhibition (rapamycin; INK-128) decreased AFG load by approximately 30% and activated a TFEB-dependent lysosome biogenesis program; these effects required intact lysosomal proteases/lipases and were associated with LAMP1 upregulation and GADD34 induction, supporting the concept that mTOR→TFEB pathway modulation can restore lysosomal clearance in RPE (albeit these studies were preprints and should be interpreted accordingly) (Falcão et al., 2024, pp. 1–6, 10–18). Constitutively active TFEB dramatically reduced POS-dependent AFGs in preventive and resolving paradigms, further validating TFEB activation as a mechanistic goal for pharmacologic mTOR inhibition in early AMD models (Falcão et al., 2024, pp. 1–6, 13–18).

In genetic models where RPE mTORC1 is hyperactivated through Tsc1 deletion, chronic mTORC1 activity causes progressive RPE degeneration, lipid accumulation, and subretinal drusenoid deposits, and rapamycin treatment restored RPE markers (e.g., RPE65), improved ERG responses, and partially normalized metabolomic derangements, providing in vivo proof-of-concept that mTOR pathway suppression improves RPE structure and function in AMD-like degeneration (Huang et al., 2019, pp. 1–2, 7–9; Zhao et al., 2011, pp. 10–11). At a mechanistic level, age-driven increases in lysosome mass and mTORC1 docking in RPE create a vicious cycle of mTORC1 hyperactivation that impairs phagolysosomal function, promotes lipogenesis, suppresses lipolysis, and degrades autophagy, converging on classic dry AMD phenotypes; mTOR inhibition breaks this cycle and restores degradative capacity (Go et al., 2020, pp. 1–3, 11–13).

Beyond ocular systems, Torin2 has been used preclinically in oncology and in non-ocular degenerative models; its dual mTORC1/2 suppression, sustained pharmacodynamics, and autophagy induction underlie anti-proliferative activity and apoptosis in cancer models, while in an ADPKD model Torin2 demonstrated pathway inhibition with efficacy comparable to sirolimus, suggesting that torin-class agents may be tolerable with appropriate dose and schedule selection (Liu et al., 2013, pp. 7–9; Holditch et al., 2019, pp. 6–7). Notably, second-generation mTOR inhibitors can be cytotoxic in RPE due to potent mTORC2 suppression with downstream Akt inhibition, a survival pathway for metabolically stressed RPE; this risk emphasizes the importance of dose titration and local ocular delivery strategies for Torin2 in AMD (Huang et al., 2018, pp. 7–8).

To our knowledge, Torin2 has not been reported in clinical trials for dry AMD or directly tested in RPE/retinal models in vivo; however, the strength of the translational prior—mTOR hyperactivation as a convergent mechanism in RPE degeneration; rescue with catalytic mTOR inhibitors such as TORIN1; and reversible ALP defects with Torin-class inhibition—warrants rigorous preclinical testing of Torin2 in dry AMD-relevant models (Chowdhury et al., 2025, pp. 1–2, 8–11; Jo et al., 2023, pp. 1–2).

Below is our detailed evaluation of GSK2656157 for repurposing in dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD), structured in the requested format.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
GSK2656157 is a small‐molecule inhibitor of PERK (protein kinase R–like endoplasmic reticulum kinase) that was discovered and optimized through medicinal‐chemistry efforts originally led by GlaxoSmithKline. This compound belongs to the class of ATP‐competitive, Type I inhibitors that target the kinase domain of PERK, binding within the ATP‐binding cleft and stabilizing a “DFG‐in, Cα‐helix shifted” conformation of the dephosphorylated kinase domain (Axten, 2017, pp. 15–19). Structurally, the compound is an indoline‐derived molecule; similar chemical series include the indoline/aminoquinazoline chemotypes that have been widely profiled for their high potency and kinase selectivity across panels exceeding 300 kinases (Axten, 2017, pp. 15–19). Originally, these inhibitors were developed as research tools to interrogate the role of PERK in the unfolded protein response (UPR) in oncology and neurodegeneration contexts, and in preclinical studies GSK2656157 demonstrated activity in suppressing tumor growth and angiogenesis in mouse xenograft models via inhibition of PERK autophosphorylation (Atkins et al., 2013, pp. 1–2, 8). As a synthetic small molecule, its origins lie in rational design based on X‐ray–guided structure–activity relationships, which enabled optimization for both high selectivity (with >100‐fold selectivity over related kinases including other eIF2α kinases as well as a broad kinome panel) and sufficient in vivo pharmacokinetics (Axten, 2017, pp. 15–19; Atkins et al., 2013, pp. 1–2). Thus, from a chemical and developmental perspective, GSK2656157 is a first‐in‐class PERK inhibitor that exemplifies how targeted kinase inhibition can be achieved by rational design.  

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, PERK inhibitors such as GSK2606414 and its more selective derivative GSK2656157 were developed primarily for indications in oncology and neurodegeneration. Preclinical studies in tumor xenograft models have demonstrated that oral dosing of GSK2656157 can suppress PERK-mediated signaling, resulting in attenuated phospho-eIF2α levels, diminished transcriptional responses of unfolded protein response (UPR) genes, and reduced tumor vascular density (Atkins et al., 2013, pp. 1–2, 8). In neurodegenerative models—for instance in prion and tauopathy mouse models—PERK inhibition has been shown to restore global protein synthesis, decrease the levels of phospho-tau, and produce mixed effects on behavior and neuronal survival (Rozpędek-Kamińska et al., 2020, pp. 17–19). Meanwhile, within the ocular space, experimental studies with the closely related PERK inhibitor GSK2606414 (a chemical analogue of GSK2656157) in in vitro retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cell models have demonstrated on-target inhibition of PERK signaling (evidenced by reduction in eIF2α phosphorylation) along with downstream alterations in stress markers such as CHOP and VEGF mRNA (Jiang et al., 2017, pp. 1–2). However, direct use of GSK2656157 in dry AMD or similar inflammatory/degenerative ocular conditions has not yet been reported in the literature. Some studies investigating retinal degeneration models, such as P23H rhodopsin transgenic rats, have suggested that PERK inhibition can worsen photoreceptor survival by enhancing misfolded protein aggregation, although these studies were typically conducted with compounds such as GSK2606414A (Athanasiou et al., 2017, pp. 1–2, 5–7). There is, therefore, limited clinical or preclinical history regarding the use of GSK2656157 specifically in AMD or related ocular diseases. In addition, while the compound has demonstrated acceptable pharmacokinetics and tolerability in preclinical oncology settings—with measurable systemic exposures—it is important to note that systemic PERK inhibition in multiple species has been associated with toxic liabilities such as pancreatic toxicity (Atkins et al., 2013, p. 8; Axten, 2017, pp. 1–7). Consequently, although the therapeutic class has a relatively rich history in oncology and neurodegeneration, its direct application to dry AMD remains a new and untested repurposing approach that requires careful consideration of pharmacodynamic impacts in ocular tissues and rigorous safety profiling.  

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, PERK functions as an endoplasmic reticulum (ER)–resident kinase that is activated upon the accumulation of misfolded proteins, a hallmark of chronic ER stress. Normally, when the ER’s folding capacity is overwhelmed, the molecular chaperone GRP78 dissociates from PERK, enabling PERK to oligomerize and autophosphorylate, which then enables it to phosphorylate the α subunit of eukaryotic initiation factor 2 (eIF2α) at serine-51 (Axten, 2017, pp. 7–11). Phosphorylation of eIF2α leads to a global reduction in protein synthesis—a protective adaptation that prevents further accumulation of misfolded proteins—and also selectively permits the translation of stress-induced genes, most notably ATF4. ATF4 subsequently upregulates transcription factors such as CHOP, which can drive pro-apoptotic signaling if ER stress persists (Axten, 2017, pp. 7–11; Chu et al., 2021, p. 8). In the context of dry AMD, chronic ER stress in RPE cells has been implicated in disrupting cellular proteostasis, where misfolded proteins—including subunits of key complexes like the vacuolar ATPase (v-ATPase)—may fail to fold properly, leading to impaired lysosomal acidification (Kaarniranta et al., 2018, pp. 1–4; Athanasiou et al., 2017, pp. 1–2). The hypothesis is that by inhibiting PERK with GSK2656157, the excessive phosphorylation of eIF2α and the maladaptive integrated stress response (ISR) can be attenuated. This would not only restore global protein synthesis but also prevent downstream consequences such as upregulation of CHOP and VEGF, thereby reducing pro-apoptotic as well as pro-inflammatory pathways (Jiang et al., 2017, pp. 1–2). Furthermore, it is posited that such normalization in the ISR could allow for proper folding and assembly of lysosomal enzymes and complexes, including the v-ATPase. Proper v-ATPase assembly is critical for maintaining low intraluminal pH in lysosomes, which is necessary for the activation and maturation of hydrolases like cathepsin D (Kaarniranta et al., 2018, pp. 1–4). In neuronal models, PERK inhibition has been associated with improvements in lysosomal function and proteostasis, indicating that reduction of chronic ER stress can indirectly favor the re-establishment of lysosomal homeostasis (Jiang et al., 2017, pp. 1–2). In essence, GSK2656157, by specifically targeting and inhibiting PERK, interferes with the pathological arm of the UPR (i.e. excessive eIF2α phosphorylation) that is hypothesized to contribute to impaired lysosomal acidification in RPE cells under chronic stress conditions—a mechanism that might be particularly relevant in the pathophysiology of dry AMD (Axten, 2017, pp. 24–28).  

Expected Effect:  
In the proposed assays, the primary expected effect of GSK2656157 is to inhibit PERK activity in RPE cells, as evidenced by reduced phosphorylation of eIF2α, and thereby dampen downstream signaling events that lead to the induction of ATF4, CHOP, and ultimately pro-apoptotic and proangiogenic factors such as VEGF. In vitro studies with analogues of GSK2656157 (such as GSK2606414) in ARPE-19 cells have shown dose-dependent inhibition of eIF2α phosphorylation with subsequent decreases in CHOP and VEGF mRNA expression without necessarily triggering apoptosis at higher doses (Jiang et al., 2017, pp. 1–2). These results provide a proof-of-concept that pharmacological inhibition of PERK can modulate this critical signaling pathway in RPE cells. The hypothesis for dry AMD is that chronic ER stress in the RPE disrupts lysosomal acidification via misfolding of v-ATPase subunits; under normal circumstances, proper v-ATPase function ensures that lysosomes maintain their acidic environment, which is essential for protease activation—including cathepsin D. Cathepsin D, in turn, is critical for lysosomal degradation of photoreceptor outer segments and for preventing lipofuscin accumulation, a pathological process in dry AMD (Kaarniranta et al., 2018, pp. 1–4). Thus, by reducing PERK activation through GSK2656157, it is expected that the overactive ISR would be tempered sufficiently to allow for the proper folding and assembly of v-ATPase complexes, thereby restoring lysosomal acidification (Chu et al., 2021, p. 8; Athanasiou et al., 2017, pp. 1–2). This restoration is anticipated to improve cathepsin D maturation and activity, leading to better clearance of intracellular debris and misfolded proteins, ultimately protecting RPE cells from stress-induced degeneration. On a cellular level, normalizing lysosomal pH would also promote autophagy flux, which is often impaired in the aged RPE, thereby mitigating one of the key contributing factors in the dry AMD phenotype (Kaarniranta et al., 2018, pp. 1–4; Athanasiou et al., 2017, pp. 1–2). Importantly, RPE cells are known to express PERK and components of the UPR, with studies demonstrating that ER stress markers, including phospho-PERK and phospho-eIF2α, are elevated in pathological states associated with AMD (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021, pp. 11–12; Chu et al., 2021, p. 8). Therefore, if GSK2656157 can achieve adequate ocular tissue exposure and inhibit PERK activity in the RPE, the expected outcome would be a reduction in cellular stress–mediated apoptosis and proliferation of protective pathways that maintain lysosomal and autophagy functions (Jiang et al., 2017, pp. 1–2; Rozpędek-Kamińska et al., 2020, pp. 17–19). Moreover, the compound’s known pharmacokinetic profile in preclinical oncology studies suggests that it is systemically bioavailable and, according to some reports, may achieve ocular tissue distribution; thus it is conceivable that with appropriate dosing and local delivery strategies, GSK2656157 could achieve effective concentrations in RPE cells (Atkins et al., 2013, pp. 1–2, 8).  

Overall Evaluation:  
Overall, GSK2656157 presents an intriguing therapeutic candidate for dry AMD based on a mechanistic hypothesis that links chronic ER stress to impaired lysosomal acidification—a process central to the pathogenesis of AMD. One of the primary strengths of GSK2656157 is its potent and selective inhibition of PERK, a critical mediator of the integrated stress response. The compound’s design as an ATP‐competitive PERK inhibitor places it squarely in a class of drugs that have been well characterized in terms of kinase selectivity and in vivo pharmacodynamics in oncology settings (Axten, 2017, pp. 15–19). The underlying biological rationale is that by attenuating the maladaptive PERK-mediated phosphorylation of eIF2α, it may be possible to relieve chronic translational suppression and dampen downstream deleterious signaling cascades—thereby re-establishing normal lysosomal function through proper v-ATPase assembly and restoration of cathepsin D activity (Axten, 2017, pp. 7–11; Chu et al., 2021, p. 8). There is supportive in vitro evidence from studies using related inhibitors (for example, GSK2606414 in ARPE-19 cells) that PERK inhibition can downregulate stress effectors such as CHOP and VEGF, which are both implicated in retinal degeneration and neovascularization (Jiang et al., 2017, pp. 1–2). Such studies underscore the potential of targeting the PERK/ISR axis in RPE cells to create a more favorable intracellular environment that could prevent progressive degeneration seen in dry AMD (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021, pp. 11–12; Chu et al., 2021, p. 8).

However, there are several notable weaknesses and caveats. First, while there is an extensive body of preclinical work on PERK inhibitors in oncology and neurodegeneration models, there is a significant lack of direct evidence in ocular disease models—especially chronic models of dry AMD—as well as an absence of published studies specifically evaluating GSK2656157 in RPE cells or in animal models of AMD (Athanasiou et al., 2017, pp. 5–7). In several studies using related PERK inhibitors in rod photoreceptor degeneration models (such as P23H rhodopsin transgenic rats), inhibition of PERK activity has been associated with worsened outcomes, suggesting that PERK activation may paradoxically be protective in certain contexts of protein misfolding (Athanasiou et al., 2017, pp. 1–2, 5–7). This dichotomous role of PERK—as both an adaptive and a pro-death signal depending on the context and duration of activation—raises concerns about whether inhibition will uniformly yield beneficial effects in the RPE, whose balance of ER stress responses may differ from that of neuronal or secretory tissues. Second, while the hypothesis postulates that chronic ER stress impairs lysosomal acidification by misfolding v-ATPase subunits, the direct link between PERK inhibition and restoration of v-ATPase assembly or cathepsin D maturation in RPE cells has not been firmly established in the literature. Data that explicitly demonstrate that PERK inhibition rescues lysosomal pH, enhances v-ATPase function, and improves cathepsin D activity in neuronal models may exist, yet similar studies in ocular models are limited (Chu et al., 2021, p. 8; Kaarniranta et al., 2018, pp. 1–4). Third, the systemic administration of PERK inhibitors such as GSK2656157 has been associated with pancreatic toxicity and other systemic adverse effects in preclinical studies, a liability that could be particularly problematic in chronic therapies such as those needed for dry AMD (Atkins et al., 2013, p. 8; Axten, 2017, pp. 1–7). Although strategies such as local (intravitreal) delivery might mitigate these systemic risks, ocular pharmacokinetic and tolerability data are sparse, and the tissue-specific distribution of GSK2656157 in the eye would need careful evaluation (Atkins et al., 2013, pp. 1–2, 8). Fourth, there is some concern over off-target effects; for example, early reports on similar GSK compounds noted possible inhibition of RIP1 kinase activity, although subsequent studies have argued that the effects observed were indeed mediated by PERK inhibition (Starr, 2019, pp. 133–137; Athanasiou et al., 2017, pp. 5–7). Nonetheless, affording absolute selectivity in a clinical candidate remains a challenge. In addition, chronic inhibition of the adaptive aspects of the ISR may inadvertently impair protective mechanisms in the retina, as transient ISR activation is known to mediate cellular adaptation during acute stress (Axten, 2017, pp. 7–11, 24–28).

In summary, while the mechanistic rationale for using GSK2656157 to address dry AMD is based on a conceptually appealing hypothesis—that PERK inhibition will relieve chronic ER stress, thereby restoring proper lysosomal acidification, enabling v-ATPase assembly, and rescuing cathepsin D activity in RPE cells—the current body of literature reveals both promising on-target effects in non-ocular systems and significant gaps in ocular-specific efficacy and safety data. Given the complex, context-dependent role of PERK signaling in retinal homeostasis and the potential for deleterious outcomes when PERK is inhibited in models of protein misfolding, further focused in vitro and in vivo studies are required to determine whether GSK2656157 can be safely and effectively repurposed for dry AMD. Strengths of this candidate include its potent, selective PERK inhibition and preclinical pharmacodynamic proof-of-concept in related disease models, while weaknesses center on limited ocular data, potential systemic and off-target toxicities, and an uncertain impact on lysosomal and proteostatic pathways in RPE cells. Ultimately, while GSK2656157 remains an attractive avenue for targeting an upstream stress node in dry AMD pathogenesis, careful optimization of dosing, targeted ocular delivery, and comprehensive evaluation in relevant AMD models will be essential before moving forward in clinical development (Axten, 2017, pp. 1–7, 15–19, 24–28; Atkins et al., 2013, pp. 1–2; Athanasiou et al., 2017, pp. 5–7; Jiang et al., 2017, pp. 1–2).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Resveratrol is a naturally occurring polyphenolic compound that belongs to the stilbene family and is most famously isolated from grape skins and red wine. Its chemical structure features two aromatic rings linked by an ethylene bridge, which confers potent antioxidant properties. Discovered over four decades ago, resveratrol (catalog number Sigma R5010) has been extensively studied for its diverse biological activities, including anti‐inflammatory, anti‐oxidative, and anti‐aging effects. As a member of natural polyphenols, resveratrol has been used both as a dietary supplement and as a laboratory tool to probe intracellular signaling and epigenetic regulation. This compound has been explored for therapeutic applications in cardiovascular diseases, metabolic disorders, and various age‐related conditions, thereby positioning it as an attractive lead for repurposing. Its natural origin, safety profile upon oral administration, and documented bioavailability in retinal tissues support its candidature for ocular indications, particularly in mitigating dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) pathology (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Delmas et al., 2021).

Therapeutic History:  
Numerous biochemical studies have established that resveratrol exerts its beneficial effects by modulating key intracellular pathways. Historically, resveratrol has been used as an anti‐oxidant in various cellular systems and has been investigated in preclinical models of neurodegeneration, cardiovascular disease, and metabolic syndrome. In the context of ophthalmology, several studies have evaluated its efficacy in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cell models. For instance, research using ARPE-19 cells, a well-established human RPE cell line, demonstrated that resveratrol activates SIRT1 to protect against oxidative stress and apoptosis induced by challenging stimuli such as sodium iodate, UVA radiation, acrolein, and A2E—a major component of lipofuscin implicated in drusen formation and AMD pathology (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Li et al., 2024; Alaimo et al., 2020). Additional investigations combined resveratrol with omega-3 fatty acids in formulations like Resvega® to induce autophagy and enhance cell survival under conditions simulating AMD (Delmas et al., 2021; Koskela et al., 2016). While much of the published literature has concentrated on resveratrol’s effects in oxidative stress, inflammatory responses, and autophagy promotion in RPE cells, a few reports have noted its capacity to counteract the toxic accumulation of intracellular debris that is a hallmark of dry AMD (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Pinelli et al., 2025). Moreover, preliminary clinical reports have suggested that long-term oral supplementation with resveratrol-containing nutraceuticals may contribute to anatomic restoration of retinal structure and improved visual function in elderly patients, thus further underpinning its translational potential. Notably, while there is extensive preclinical evidence in vitro and in animal models, resveratrol has not yet been unequivocally validated in advanced clinical trials targeting dry AMD specifically (Abu-Amero et al., 2016).

Mechanism of Action:  
A robust body of research supports that resveratrol acts principally through the activation of SIRT1 (sirtuin 1) and the energy sensor AMPK (AMP-activated protein kinase), both of which are critical for maintaining cellular homeostasis in the aging retina. At the molecular level, resveratrol has been reported to directly and indirectly stimulate SIRT1 activity in RPE cells, leading to the deacetylation of several downstream targets such as PGC-1α (peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator 1-alpha). This deacetylated PGC-1α, in turn, upregulates mitochondrial biogenesis and enhances cellular oxidative phosphorylation, thereby improving mitochondrial quality control and reducing the accumulation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Li et al., 2024; Buonfiglio et al., 2024). Concomitantly, resveratrol activates AMPK, albeit through complex mechanisms involving inhibition of phosphodiesterases and alterations in the intracellular AMP/ATP ratio. The resulting AMPK phosphorylation facilitates a myriad of downstream effects, notably the inhibition of mTOR signaling (a known suppressor of autophagy) and activation of ULK1, a serine/threonine kinase that initiates autophagosome formation (Li et al., 2024; Abu-Amero et al., 2016).

In RPE cells, the synergistic activation of SIRT1 and AMPK by resveratrol is believed to promote autophagy, as evidenced by increased LC3II/I ratios and decreased p62 expression. Autophagy is particularly critical in RPE cells to clear toxic cellular debris such as A2E and other protein aggregates that contribute to drusen accumulation in dry AMD (Alaimo et al., 2020; Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Pinelli et al., 2023). Furthermore, the prevailing hypothesis extends these autophagic benefits by suggesting that, downstream of AMPK/SIRT1 activation, resveratrol may induce TFEB dephosphorylation. TFEB is a transcription factor that, when dephosphorylated, translocates into the nucleus and upregulates the coordinated lysosomal expression and regulation (CLEAR) network. This results in enhanced lysosomal biogenesis, improved lysosomal acidification, and increased activation of lysosomal enzymes such as cathepsin D. Although direct experimental evidence linking resveratrol to TFEB dephosphorylation in RPE cells is not abundantly detailed in the current literature, several studies imply that agents that activate AMPK and inhibit mTOR can indirectly promote TFEB activity. In this context, resveratrol’s ability to inhibit mTOR, partly through AMPK activation, suggests a plausible mechanism for the promotion of TFEB-mediated lysosomal functions (Falcão et al., 2025; Pinelli et al., 2023). These molecular events are anticipated to bolster the autophagy-lysosomal system, thereby mitigating the drusen accumulation characteristic of dry AMD. Additionally, resveratrol exerts direct antioxidant effects by scavenging free radicals and modulating the expression of antioxidant enzymes such as superoxide dismutase, which contributes further to its protective milieu in the retina (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Abu-Amero et al., 2016).

Expected Effect:  
Based on its molecular pharmacology, the expected effect of resveratrol in preclinical models of dry AMD would be multifaceted. In assays utilizing ARPE-19 cells or primary human RPE cells, treatment with resveratrol is expected to enhance SIRT1 activity, as measured by increased deacetylation of SIRT1 substrates and upregulation of PGC-1α nuclear translocation. Concurrently, AMPK phosphorylation is anticipated to be elevated, leading to inhibition of the mTOR pathway; this would foster an increased autophagic flux, observable as a higher LC3II/I ratio and reduced levels of the autophagy substrate p62 (Li et al., 2024; Alaimo et al., 2020; Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021). Furthermore, the candidate is hypothesized to indirectly promote TFEB dephosphorylation, facilitating its nuclear translocation and subsequent upregulation of lysosomal genes. This could manifest as enhanced lysosomal biogenesis, improved acidification of the lysosomal compartment, and elevated activity of lysosomal proteases such as cathepsin D. The cumulative consequence of these events would be a more efficient clearance of intracellular debris, including lipofuscin and other drusen components, thereby ameliorating RPE dysfunction associated with dry AMD (Falcão et al., 2025; Pinelli et al., 2023).

It is also expected that resveratrol’s anti-inflammatory and anti-apoptotic actions would reduce the chronic low-grade inflammation that underpins AMD pathogenesis. In vivo, improved autophagic and lysosomal clearance should correlate with decreased accumulation of pathological deposits at the RPE-Bruch’s membrane interface, potentially reducing the progression of drusen formation and preserving retinal structure and function (Alaimo et al., 2020; Abu-Amero et al., 2016; Pinelli et al., 2025). Given that resveratrol is detectable in retinal tissue following oral administration, its systemic safety and potential for long-term use add to its attractiveness as a repurposed therapeutic agent for dry AMD. Moreover, the dual capacity to modulate both metabolic and epigenetic pathways may offer disease-modifying effects that extend beyond symptomatic relief and target the underlying cellular aging processes in the RPE (Subramani et al., 2017).

Overall Evaluation:  
Resveratrol emerges as a promising candidate for repurposing in the context of dry AMD owing to its well-documented ability to activate SIRT1 and AMPK, which are pivotal signaling nodes in the maintenance of cellular homeostasis and autophagy. One of the central strengths of resveratrol is its dual mechanism of action. By targeting SIRT1, resveratrol not only combats oxidative stress through the deacetylation of transcription factors and enhancement of mitochondrial biogenesis but also modulates anti-inflammatory pathways relevant to retinal preservation (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Li et al., 2024). Simultaneously, its activation of AMPK provides additional impetus for autophagy induction through mTOR inhibition and ULK1 activation. Such molecular actions are of particular relevance to RPE cells, in which impairment of the autophagy-lysosomal system is a key pathogenetic mechanism leading to the accumulation of cellular waste products such as drusen—a hallmark of dry AMD (Alaimo et al., 2020; Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021).

Furthermore, the hypothesis that resveratrol could foster TFEB dephosphorylation is especially intriguing. Although direct evidence linking resveratrol to TFEB activation in RPE cells is currently limited, the known interactions between AMPK/mTOR signaling and TFEB activity provide a strong conceptual framework. Activation of TFEB would result in enhanced lysosomal biogenesis, acidification, and increased cathepsin D activity—mechanisms that are critical for the proper degradation of accumulated photoreceptor-derived debris and toxic aggregates (Falcão et al., 2025; Pinelli et al., 2023). This potential to bolster a declining lysosomal-autophagy system with age might address the fundamental cellular dysfunction observed in dry AMD.

On the clinical side, resveratrol demonstrates a favorable safety profile with established oral bioavailability and experimental evidence suggesting retinal tissue penetration. Combined with its history of use as an anti-oxidative and anti-inflammatory agent in other disease contexts, these features support its translational potential. Several nutraceutical formulations incorporating resveratrol (often in combination with omega-3 fatty acids, as in Resvega®) have already reached early-phase clinical evaluation for ocular indications, providing preliminary signals of efficacy in improving retinal structure and function among aged patients (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Delmas et al., 2021).

Nevertheless, several weaknesses and gaps must be acknowledged. First, while there is abundant preclinical evidence of resveratrol’s activation of SIRT1/AMPK pathways and subsequent autophagy induction in RPE cells, the specific molecular events leading to TFEB dephosphorylation, enhanced lysosomal biogenesis, lysosomal acidification, and increased cathepsin D activity are not yet comprehensively elucidated. In other words, the critical mechanistic link between resveratrol treatment and lysosomal enhancement remains somewhat inferential rather than directly demonstrated in the existing literature (Falcão et al., 2025; Hyttinen et al., 2019). Second, much of the supporting data comes from in vitro studies or animal models, with limited robust clinical evidence explicitly addressing dry AMD. Although some pilot clinical studies with resveratrol-containing formulations show promise, their design, scale, and long-term outcomes are not sufficiently advanced to confirm therapeutic efficacy in a broad AMD population (Abu-Amero et al., 2016). Third, resveratrol is known to have issues with bioavailability due to rapid metabolism and low systemic concentrations after oral ingestion; therefore, optimizing its delivery to retinal tissues, perhaps via novel formulations or nanoparticle carriers, may be necessary to achieve therapeutic levels (Subramani et al., 2017; Pinelli et al., 2025). Additionally, while its pleiotropic activity is a strength in terms of targeting multiple pathogenic mechanisms, this same feature can pose challenges in ensuring specificity and avoiding off-target effects.

In summary, resveratrol presents a compelling case as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. Its ability to activate SIRT1 and AMPK, induce autophagy, and potentially stimulate TFEB-driven lysosomal biogenesis aligns well with the current understanding of the cellular derangements underlying AMD pathogenesis. The expected outcome would be improved clearance of toxic cellular debris and drusen, preservation of RPE integrity, and amelioration of oxidative stress and inflammation in the aging retina. However, to fully validate resveratrol as a viable treatment for dry AMD, further investigations are warranted to (a) directly demonstrate its effects on TFEB dephosphorylation and lysosomal function in RPE cells, (b) optimize its ocular bioavailability, and (c) establish robust clinical endpoints in well-designed trials. Overall, while promising and supported by a substantial body of preclinical evidence, additional targeted research is required to definitively establish resveratrol’s mechanistic effects on the autophagy-lysosomal pathway and its therapeutic potential in dry AMD (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Li et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2025; Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Abu-Amero et al., 2016).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Everolimus (Afinitor; Novartis) is a semi‐synthetic derivative of sirolimus—a macrolide originally isolated from Streptomyces hygroscopicus—as evidenced by its chemical designation as 4-O-(2-hydroxyethyl)-rapamycin (Liu et al., 2023, pp. 11–12). By introducing a 2-hydroxyethyl group at position 40, everolimus achieves greater hydrophilicity and an increased oral bioavailability (from 10% to 16% relative to sirolimus) while retaining the core macrolactone structure that is characteristic of rapalogs (Liu et al., 2023, pp. 11–12; Weber, 2015, pp. 27–28). This compound belongs to the class of mTOR inhibitors—specifically, a first‐generation rapalog that selectively inhibits the mTOR complex 1 (mTORC1) while sparing mTORC2 (Liu et al., 2023, pp. 10–11; Weber, 2015, pp. 27–28). As a synthetic derivative of a naturally occurring product, everolimus represents the successful strategy of chemical modification to optimize pharmacokinetic properties and clinical tolerability. The design parameters underpinning everolimus’ synthesis have been guided by the goal of retaining potent immunosuppressive and anti‐proliferative effects while optimizing parameters such as solubility, half‐life, and tissue penetration, with the added advantage of an oral formulation already approved for several clinical indications (Liu et al., 2023, pp. 11–12; Wang et al., 2022, pp. 6–8).

Therapeutic History:  
Everolimus has a well‐established therapeutic history as an immunosuppressant and antineoplastic agent. Clinically, it is approved for treating advanced renal cell carcinoma, progressive neuroendocrine tumors of pancreatic origin, and subependymal giant cell astrocytoma in tuberous sclerosis complex patients who are not candidates for surgery (Wang et al., 2022, pp. 6–8; Weber, 2015, pp. 27–28). In these indications, its mechanism as an mTORC1 inhibitor serves to arrest cell cycle progression and inhibit angiogenesis, which are central to its antitumor activity (Kuo et al., 2018, pp. 5–7; Weber, 2015, pp. 27–28). Moreover, everolimus has been effectively used in the context of organ transplantation to prevent allograft rejection by impairing helper T‐cell proliferation (Wang et al., 2022, pp. 6–8; Weber, 2015, pp. 27–28).

With regard to ocular applications, although everolimus has not been approved specifically for dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD), several preclinical studies have demonstrated its potential benefits in ocular cell types and models. For instance, in vitro investigations have highlighted that everolimus can inhibit the proliferation and migration of retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells and modulate mTOR signaling within retinal tissue—an effect critical to conditions such as proliferative vitreoretinopathy (PVR) (Kuo et al., 2018, pp. 5–8). Additionally, clinical trials such as the Phase 2 randomized trial for neovascular AMD (albeit focused on wet AMD) have assessed everolimus’s efficacy in combination with anti‐vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) agents (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2009), thereby providing indirect support for its ocular pharmacokinetic (PK) profile and safety profile. This background, combined with its well‐known systemic tolerability, underscores its candidacy for repurposing in nonexudative (dry) AMD—a disease area in which few pharmacologic treatments exist.

Mechanism of Action:  
Everolimus exerts its effects by binding to the intracellular receptor FKBP12, forming a complex that interacts with and inhibits mTORC1 (Liu et al., 2023, pp. 11–12; Weber, 2015, pp. 27–28). The inhibition of mTORC1 results in a downstream decrease in the phosphorylation of ribosomal protein S6 kinase (S6K1) and other substrates such as ribosomal protein S6 (RPS6), effectively suppressing cap‐dependent protein synthesis and cellular proliferation (Kuo et al., 2018, pp. 5–7; Liu et al., 2023, pp. 10–11). In the context of RPE cells, inhibition of mTORC1 plays a particularly critical role in modulating autophagic flux. Under normal conditions, mTORC1 phosphorylates and suppresses the transcription factor EB (TFEB), a master regulator of lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy. Inhibition of mTORC1 frees TFEB to translocate to the nucleus where it transactivates genes that codify for lysosomal proteins, such as the subunits of the vacuolar ATPase (V‐ATPase), and hydrolases including cathepsin D (Kuo et al., 2018, p. 7; Nieto et al., 2015, pp. 28–32). Preclinical studies have shown that in RPE culture systems, treatment with everolimus results in an increase in LC3 turnover—a marker of enhanced autophagic flux—and accelerates the maturation of cathepsin D (CTSD), which is essential for effective lysosomal degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (Kuo et al., 2018, pp. 5–8). Such modulation of the autophagy–lysosome pathway is mechanistically attractive in dry AMD because the accumulation of cellular debris and lipofuscin in RPE cells is implicated in disease pathogenesis. Furthermore, it has been reported that everolimus displays superior ocular tissue penetration compared with sirolimus in in vitro porcine corneal models, suggesting that its formulation could be optimized for direct ocular administration if required (Liu et al., 2023, pp. 11–14). Overall, the biochemical profile of everolimus supports the hypothesis that targeted mTORC1 inhibition in RPE cells could lead to enhanced TFEB activation and a subsequent restoration of lysosomal function—thereby addressing one of the key pathological features underlying dry AMD.

The hypothesis proposes that everolimus will inhibit mTORC1 in RPE cells, leading to the activation of TFEB, a critical step in lysosomal biogenesis and function. The V1 sector hydrolyzes ATP and the V0 sector conducts protons across the membrane, with subunit stoichiometries and regulatory dynamics (e.g., reversible V1–V0 association) that tune organelle pH; acidic pH ~4.5–5.0 is required for optimal lysosomal enzyme activity and membrane integrity (Chen et al., 2025, pp. 2–5). While reports outside the eye document multiple regulatory levers for v-ATPase assembly/activity (kinase control, accessory complexes, isoform selection), the provided sources do not identify a validated medicinal chemistry series that positively and directly activates v-ATPase in RPE or AMD models (Chen et al., 2025, pp. 22–23; Song et al., 2020, pp. 13–14).

Therapeutic History  
There is no documented clinical or veterinary use of SH-BC-893 in AMD or related retinal degeneration in the provided corpus, and the ClinicalTrials.gov query identified no trials in AMD with SH-BC-893 as an intervention (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.-a). Likewise, no AMD trials explicitly list “v-ATPase” as the intervention in the registry result provided (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.-b). Within ocular preclinical literature, restoration of lysosomal acidity and degradative capacity has been targeted by alternative pharmacologic or biophysical means, each reinforcing the disease rationale but not testing a v-ATPase activator per se. In ABCA4-mediated Stargardt models (human iPSC-RPE from STGD1 patients and Abca4⁻/⁻ mice), lysosomal alkalinization, impaired maturation of CTSD (accumulation of pro-CTSD), and reduced CTSD activity were demonstrated; pharmacologic lysosomal reacidification with the P2Y₁₂ antagonist ticagrelor lowered lysosomal pH, rescued CTSD maturation/activity, reduced CTSD aggregates, decreased autofluorescence, and protected photoreceptors, supporting therapeutic relevance of acidification in RPE disease (Ng et al., 2024, pp. 3–5, 10–12, 13–15). In these same systems, acidification was linked to restored degradation of outer segments (OS), a core RPE function degraded in AMD-like states (Ng et al., 2024, pp. 10–12, 13–15).

Independent strategies have shown that raising intracellular zinc with ionophores reacidifies A2E-alkalinized lysosomes, restores autophagic flux, reduces intracellular A2E burden, and protects ARPE-19 against A2E-induced cytotoxicity; in vivo chloroquine-induced alkalinization produced AMD-like pathology, again underscoring the central role of lysosomal pH (Choi et al., 2024, pp. 18–29, 29–36). The therapeutic hypothesis centers on allosteric stabilization and activation of the v-ATPase proton pump in RPE lysosomes to lower luminal pH and normalize the acid-hydrolase environment. RPE are uniquely burdened by daily phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments, and efficient lysosomal acidification is required to degrade these discs and recycle their components; impaired acidification disrupts heterophagy and autophagy, leading to lipofuscin and drusen accumulation recognized as core AMD cellular features (Kaarniranta et al., 2023, pp. 1–3; Sinha et al., 2016, pp. 1–3).

CTSD is the dominant lysosomal aspartyl protease in RPE, responsible for the bulk of rhodopsin proteolysis; its maturation (from preproenzyme to active heavy/light chains) and catalytic activity are sharply pH-dependent, with activity falling profoundly upon modest pH elevation (e.g., near pH 5.0) (Ng et al., 2024, pp. 13–15; Valapala et al., 2016, pp. 1–4). In patient-derived STGD1 iPSC-RPE and Abca4⁻/⁻ mice, lysosomal alkalinization is associated with accumulation of immature pro-CTSD, decreased mature CTSD, loss of CTSD activity, impaired OS digestion, protein aggregation (α-synuclein), and LAP/autophagy defects linked to perturbed phosphatidylethanolamine composition; pharmacologic reacidification restores CTSD maturation and proteolysis, reduces cathepsin aggregates, and improves degradative function, validating the causal sequence from pH to CTSD to flux (Ng et al., 2024, pp. 3–8, 10–15). These CTSD-centric dependencies underscore why direct v-ATPase activation could be an efficient lever: it addresses the proximal physical determinant (pH) needed for CTSD maturation and broad lysosomal hydrolase competency (Kaarniranta et al., 2023, pp. 2–3; Sinha et al., 2016, pp. 1–3).

Endogenous control of v-ATPase in RPE is exemplified by βA3/A1-crystallin, which binds ATP6V0A1 on the lysosomal membrane and appears to modulate catalytic efficiency; loss of βA3/A1-crystallin reduces v-ATPase activity, elevates pH, and diminishes CTSD activity with consequent degradative blockade and AMD-like retinal changes (Valapala et al., 2016, pp. 1–6). v-ATPase also participates in amino acid sensing and mTORC1 recruitment via the Ragulator–Rag GTPase axis; this signaling can suppress autophagy when hyperactivated, while TFEB—the master regulator of lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy genes—depends on mTORC1 dephosphorylation for nuclear entry and CLEAR-network activation (including ATP6V0A1 expression), placing v-ATPase at the hub of both acidification and signaling that set lysosomal capacity (Sinha et al., 2016, pp. 3–4; Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7). In AMD donor RPE, TFEB is more phosphorylated (cytosolic/inactive), and CTSD/CTSL protein levels and activities are reduced; constitutively active TFEB upregulates CLEAR genes (e.g., CTSB, LAMP2, ATP6V0A1) and reduces POS-dependent lipofuscin-like granules, while rapamycin reduces A2E and autofluorescent granules via TFEB activation and active lysosomal enzymes, reinforcing that increasing lysosomal gene expression and function rescues RPE degradative deficits (Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7).

The regulatory literature further indicates v-ATPase activity is controlled by signal-dependent assembly/disassembly, kinase phosphorylation, and accessory factors (RAVE, Rabconnectin-3, AMPK, PKA, AKT), as well as lipid and trafficking determinants; small-molecule perturbations in non-ocular contexts can modulate v-ATPase assembly or activity, though some agents cause over-acidification and cytotoxicity, emphasizing the need for precise tuning (Chen et al., 2025, pp. 22–23). None of the provided sources, however, describe SH-BC-893’s binding site, affinity, kinetics, effect on V1–V0 association, or selectivity across v-ATPase isoforms; nor do they document its effects on mitochondrial membrane potential, autophagic flux metrics, or ocular safety—these are central unknowns that would need to be established experimentally to substantiate the proposed allosteric-activation mechanism (Song et al., 2020, pp. 13–14; Chen et al., 2025, pp. 22–23).

Expected Effect  
If SH-BC-893 positively stabilizes and activates lysosomal v-ATPase in RPE, the expected sequence is: increased proton pumping → lower lysosomal pH toward physiologic (~4.5–5.0) → enhanced maturation of CTSD (and other cathepsins) → increased hydrolase activity → improved degradation of POS cargo in phagolysosomes and of autophagic substrates → reduction of lipofuscin/A2E accumulation and secondary inflammation → improved RPE homeostasis and photoreceptor support. This causal chain is strongly supported by multiple interventions that restore acidic pH or upregulate lysosomal capacity in RPE models. In STGD1 iPSC-RPE and Abca4⁻/⁻ mice, pharmacologic reacidification with ticagrelor lowered lysosomal pH, reduced pro-CTSD aggregates by roughly half, restored mature CTSD levels and enzymatic activity to near-normal, reduced autofluorescence, and protected photoreceptors—directly validating that reacidification rescues CTSD and degradative function in disease-relevant RPE (Ng et al., 2024, pp. 3–5, 10–12, 13–15). In ARPE-19, zinc ionophores reacidified A2E-alkalinized lysosomes, normalized autophagic flux (reduced p62/LC3-II accumulation), lowered A2E burden, and decreased cell death; conversely, chloroquine alkalinization generated AMD-like in vivo pathology, indicating bidirectional control and the importance of acidification for RPE viability (Choi et al., 2024, pp. 18–29, 29–36). Nevertheless, two mechanistic cautions should shape experimental expectations. First, v-ATPase also couples lysosomal amino acid sensing to mTORC1 activation through Ragulator–Rag GTPases; augmenting v-ATPase function could, context-dependently, promote mTORC1 signaling, which suppresses autophagy if chronically hyperactivated, potentially counteracting benefits unless managed (Sinha et al., 2016, pp. 3–4). Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
GSK2656157 is a small‐molecule inhibitor of PERK (protein kinase R–like endoplasmic reticulum kinase) that was discovered and optimized through medicinal‐chemistry efforts originally led by GlaxoSmithKline. This compound belongs to the class of ATP‐competitive, Type I inhibitors that target the kinase domain of PERK, binding within the ATP‐binding cleft and stabilizing a “DFG‐in, Cα‐helix shifted” conformation of the dephosphorylated kinase domain (Axten, 2017, pp. 15–19). Structurally, the compound is an indoline‐derived molecule; similar chemical series include the indoline/aminoquinazoline chemotypes that have been widely profiled for their high potency and kinase selectivity across panels exceeding 300 kinases (Axten, 2017, pp. 15–19). Originally, these inhibitors were developed as research tools to interrogate the role of PERK in the unfolded protein response (UPR) in oncology and neurodegeneration contexts, and in preclinical studies GSK2656157 demonstrated activity in suppressing tumor growth and angiogenesis in mouse xenograft models via inhibition of PERK autophosphorylation (Atkins et al., 2013, pp. 1–2, 8). As a synthetic small molecule, its origins lie in rational design based on X‐ray–guided structure–activity relationships, which enabled optimization for both high selectivity (with >100‐fold selectivity over related kinases including other eIF2α kinases as well as a broad kinome panel) and sufficient in vivo pharmacokinetics (Axten, 2017, pp. 15–19; Atkins et al., 2013, pp. 1–2). Thus, from a chemical and developmental perspective, GSK2656157 is a first‐in‐class PERK inhibitor that exemplifies how targeted kinase inhibition can be achieved by rational design.  

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, PERK inhibitors such as GSK2606414 and its more selective derivative GSK2656157 were developed primarily for indications in oncology and neurodegeneration. Preclinical studies in tumor xenograft models have demonstrated that oral dosing of GSK2656157 can suppress PERK-mediated signaling, resulting in attenuated phospho-eIF2α levels, diminished transcriptional responses of unfolded protein response (UPR) genes, and reduced tumor vascular density (Atkins et al., 2013, pp. 1–2, 8). In neurodegenerative models—for instance in prion and tauopathy mouse models—PERK inhibition has been shown to restore global protein synthesis, decrease the levels of phospho-tau, and produce mixed effects on behavior and neuronal survival (Rozpędek-Kamińska et al., 2020, pp. 17–19). Meanwhile, within the ocular space, experimental studies with the closely related PERK inhibitor GSK2606414 (a chemical analogue of GSK2656157) in in vitro retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cell models have demonstrated on-target inhibition of PERK signaling (evidenced by reduction in eIF2α phosphorylation) along with downstream alterations in stress markers such as CHOP and VEGF mRNA (Jiang et al., 2017, pp. 1–2). However, direct use of GSK2656157 in dry AMD or similar inflammatory/degenerative ocular conditions has not yet been reported in the literature. Some studies investigating retinal degeneration models, such as P23H rhodopsin transgenic rats, have suggested that PERK inhibition can worsen photoreceptor survival by enhancing misfolded protein aggregation, although these studies were typically conducted with compounds such as GSK2606414A (Athanasiou et al., 2017, pp. 1–2, 5–7). There is, therefore, limited clinical or preclinical history regarding the use of GSK2656157 specifically in AMD or related ocular diseases. In addition, while the compound has demonstrated acceptable pharmacokinetics and tolerability in preclinical oncology settings—with measurable systemic exposures—it is important to note that systemic PERK inhibition in multiple species has been associated with toxic liabilities such as pancreatic toxicity (Atkins et al., 2013, p. 8; Axten, 2017, pp. 1–7). Consequently, although the therapeutic class has a relatively rich history in oncology and neurodegeneration, its direct application to dry AMD remains a new and untested repurposing approach that requires careful consideration of pharmacodynamic impacts in ocular tissues and rigorous safety profiling.  

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, PERK functions as an endoplasmic reticulum (ER)–resident kinase that is activated upon the accumulation of misfolded proteins, a hallmark of chronic ER stress. Normally, when the ER’s folding capacity is overwhelmed, the molecular chaperone GRP78 dissociates from PERK, enabling PERK to oligomerize and autophosphorylate, which then enables it to phosphorylate the α subunit of eukaryotic initiation factor 2 (eIF2α) at serine-51 (Axten, 2017, pp. 7–11). Phosphorylation of eIF2α leads to a global reduction in protein synthesis—a protective adaptation that prevents further accumulation of misfolded proteins—and also selectively permits the translation of stress-induced genes, most notably ATF4. ATF4 subsequently upregulates transcription factors such as CHOP, which can drive pro-apoptotic signaling if ER stress persists (Axten, 2017, pp. 7–11; Chu et al., 2021, p. 8). In the context of dry AMD, chronic ER stress in RPE cells has been implicated in disrupting cellular proteostasis, where misfolded proteins—including subunits of key complexes like the vacuolar ATPase (v-ATPase)—may fail to fold properly, leading to impaired lysosomal acidification (Kaarniranta et al., 2018, pp. 1–4; Athanasiou et al., 2017, pp. 1–2). The hypothesis is that by inhibiting PERK with GSK2656157, the excessive phosphorylation of eIF2α and the maladaptive integrated stress response (ISR) can be attenuated. This would not only restore global protein synthesis but also prevent downstream consequences such as upregulation of CHOP and VEGF, thereby reducing pro-apoptotic as well as pro-inflammatory pathways (Jiang et al., 2017, pp. 1–2). Furthermore, it is posited that such normalization in the ISR could allow for proper folding and assembly of lysosomal enzymes and complexes, including the v-ATPase. Proper v-ATPase assembly is critical for maintaining low intraluminal pH in lysosomes, which is necessary for the activation and maturation of hydrolases like cathepsin D (Kaarniranta et al., 2018, pp. 1–4). In neuronal models, PERK inhibition has been associated with improvements in lysosomal function and proteostasis, indicating that reduction of chronic ER stress can indirectly favor the re-establishment of lysosomal homeostasis (Jiang et al., 2017, pp. 1–2). In essence, GSK2656157, by specifically targeting and inhibiting PERK, interferes with the pathological arm of the UPR (i.e. excessive eIF2α phosphorylation) that is hypothesized to contribute to impaired lysosomal acidification in RPE cells under chronic stress conditions—a mechanism that might be particularly relevant in the pathophysiology of dry AMD (Axten, 2017, pp. 24–28).  

Expected Effect:  
In the proposed assays, the primary expected effect of GSK2656157 is to inhibit PERK activity in RPE cells, as evidenced by reduced phosphorylation of eIF2α, and thereby dampen downstream signaling events that lead to the induction of ATF4, CHOP, and ultimately pro-apoptotic and proangiogenic factors such as VEGF. In vitro studies with analogues of GSK2656157 (such as GSK2606414) in ARPE-19 cells have shown dose-dependent inhibition of eIF2α phosphorylation with subsequent decreases in CHOP and VEGF mRNA expression without necessarily triggering apoptosis at higher doses (Jiang et al., 2017, pp. 1–2). These results provide a proof-of-concept that pharmacological inhibition of PERK can modulate this critical signaling pathway in RPE cells. The hypothesis for dry AMD is that chronic ER stress in the RPE disrupts lysosomal acidification via misfolding of v-ATPase subunits; under normal circumstances, proper v-ATPase function ensures that lysosomes maintain their acidic environment, which is essential for protease activation—including cathepsin D. Cathepsin D, in turn, is critical for lysosomal degradation of photoreceptor outer segments and for preventing lipofuscin accumulation, a pathological process in dry AMD (Kaarniranta et al., 2018, pp. 1–4). Thus, by reducing PERK activation through GSK2656157, it is expected that the overactive ISR would be tempered sufficiently to allow for the proper folding and assembly of v-ATPase complexes, thereby restoring lysosomal acidification (Chu et al., 2021, p. 8; Athanasiou et al., 2017, pp. 1–2). This restoration is anticipated to improve cathepsin D maturation and activity, leading to better clearance of intracellular debris and misfolded proteins, ultimately protecting RPE cells from stress-induced degeneration. On a cellular level, normalizing lysosomal pH would also promote autophagy flux, which is often impaired in the aged RPE, thereby mitigating one of the key contributing factors in the dry AMD phenotype (Kaarniranta et al., 2018, pp. 1–4; Athanasiou et al., 2017, pp. 1–2). Importantly, RPE cells are known to express PERK and components of the UPR, with studies demonstrating that ER stress markers, including phospho-PERK and phospho-eIF2α, are elevated in pathological states associated with AMD (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021, pp. 11–12; Chu et al., 2021, p. 8). Therefore, if GSK2656157 can achieve adequate ocular tissue exposure and inhibit PERK activity in the RPE, the expected outcome would be a reduction in cellular stress–mediated apoptosis and proliferation of protective pathways that maintain lysosomal and autophagy functions (Jiang et al., 2017, pp. 1–2; Rozpędek-Kamińska et al., 2020, pp. 17–19). Moreover, the compound’s known pharmacokinetic profile in preclinical oncology studies suggests that it is systemically bioavailable and, according to some reports, may achieve ocular tissue distribution; thus it is conceivable that with appropriate dosing and local delivery strategies, GSK2656157 could achieve effective concentrations in RPE cells (Atkins et al., 2013, pp. 1–2, 8).  

Overall Evaluation:  
Overall, GSK2656157 presents an intriguing therapeutic candidate for dry AMD based on a mechanistic hypothesis that links chronic ER stress to impaired lysosomal acidification—a process central to the pathogenesis of AMD. One of the primary strengths of GSK2656157 is its potent and selective inhibition of PERK, a critical mediator of the integrated stress response. The compound’s design as an ATP‐competitive PERK inhibitor places it squarely in a class of drugs that have been well characterized in terms of kinase selectivity and in vivo pharmacodynamics in oncology settings (Axten, 2017, pp. 15–19). The underlying biological rationale is that by attenuating the maladaptive PERK-mediated phosphorylation of eIF2α, it may be possible to relieve chronic translational suppression and dampen downstream deleterious signaling cascades—thereby re-establishing normal lysosomal function through proper v-ATPase assembly and restoration of cathepsin D activity (Axten, 2017, pp. 7–11; Chu et al., 2021, p. 8). There is supportive in vitro evidence from studies using related inhibitors (for example, GSK2606414 in ARPE-19 cells) that PERK inhibition can downregulate stress effectors such as CHOP and VEGF, which are both implicated in retinal degeneration and neovascularization (Jiang et al., 2017, pp. 1–2). Such studies underscore the potential of targeting the PERK/ISR axis in RPE cells to create a more favorable intracellular environment that could prevent progressive degeneration seen in dry AMD (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021, pp. 11–12; Chu et al., 2021, p. 8).

However, there are several notable weaknesses and caveats. First, while there is an extensive body of preclinical work on PERK inhibitors in oncology and neurodegeneration models, there is a significant lack of direct evidence in ocular disease models—especially chronic models of dry AMD—as well as an absence of published studies specifically evaluating GSK2656157 in RPE cells or in animal models of AMD (Athanasiou et al., 2017, pp. 5–7). In several studies using related PERK inhibitors in rod photoreceptor degeneration models (such as P23H rhodopsin transgenic rats), inhibition of PERK activity has been associated with worsened outcomes, suggesting that PERK activation may paradoxically be protective in certain contexts of protein misfolding (Athanasiou et al., 2017, pp. 1–2, 5–7). This dichotomous role of PERK—as both an adaptive and a pro-death signal depending on the context and duration of activation—raises concerns about whether inhibition will uniformly yield beneficial effects in the RPE, whose balance of ER stress responses may differ from that of neuronal or secretory tissues. Second, while the hypothesis postulates that chronic ER stress impairs lysosomal acidification by misfolding v-ATPase subunits, the direct link between PERK inhibition and restoration of v-ATPase assembly or cathepsin D maturation in RPE cells has not been firmly established in the literature. Data that explicitly demonstrate that PERK inhibition rescues lysosomal pH, enhances v-ATPase function, and improves cathepsin D activity in neuronal models may exist, yet similar studies in ocular models are limited (Chu et al., 2021, p. 8; Kaarniranta et al., 2018, pp. 1–4). Third, the systemic administration of PERK inhibitors such as GSK2656157 has been associated with pancreatic toxicity and other systemic adverse effects in preclinical studies, a liability that could be particularly problematic in chronic therapies such as those needed for dry AMD (Atkins et al., 2013, p. 8; Axten, 2017, pp. 1–7). Although strategies such as local (intravitreal) delivery might mitigate these systemic risks, ocular pharmacokinetic and tolerability data are sparse, and the tissue-specific distribution of GSK2656157 in the eye would need careful evaluation (Atkins et al., 2013, pp. 1–2, 8). Fourth, there is some concern over off-target effects; for example, early reports on similar GSK compounds noted possible inhibition of RIP1 kinase activity, although subsequent studies have argued that the effects observed were indeed mediated by PERK inhibition (Starr, 2019, pp. 133–137; Athanasiou et al., 2017, pp. 5–7). Nonetheless, affording absolute selectivity in a clinical candidate remains a challenge. In addition, chronic inhibition of the adaptive aspects of the ISR may inadvertently impair protective mechanisms in the retina, as transient ISR activation is known to mediate cellular adaptation during acute stress (Axten, 2017, pp. 7–11, 24–28).

In summary, while the mechanistic rationale for using GSK2656157 to address dry AMD is based on a conceptually appealing hypothesis—that PERK inhibition will relieve chronic ER stress, thereby restoring proper lysosomal acidification, enabling v-ATPase assembly, and rescuing cathepsin D activity in RPE cells—the current body of literature reveals both promising on-target effects in non-ocular systems and significant gaps in ocular-specific efficacy and safety data. Given the complex, context-dependent role of PERK signaling in retinal homeostasis and the potential for deleterious outcomes when PERK is inhibited in models of protein misfolding, further focused in vitro and in vivo studies are required to determine whether GSK2656157 can be safely and effectively repurposed for dry AMD. Strengths of this candidate include its potent, selective PERK inhibition and preclinical pharmacodynamic proof-of-concept in related disease models, while weaknesses center on limited ocular data, potential systemic and off-target toxicities, and an uncertain impact on lysosomal and proteostatic pathways in RPE cells. Ultimately, while GSK2656157 remains an attractive avenue for targeting an upstream stress node in dry AMD pathogenesis, careful optimization of dosing, targeted ocular delivery, and comprehensive evaluation in relevant AMD models will be essential before moving forward in clinical development (Axten, 2017, pp. 1–7, 15–19, 24–28; Atkins et al., 2013, pp. 1–2; Athanasiou et al., 2017, pp. 5–7; Jiang et al., 2017, pp. 1–2).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Lithium chloride (Sigma L9650) is an inorganic salt belonging to the family of lithium compounds that has been in use for several decades, primarily as a mood stabilizer in the treatment of bipolar disorder. It is synthesized by combining lithium carbonate or lithium hydroxide with hydrochloric acid, yielding a highly water‐soluble salt that is widely available for both clinical and experimental research purposes (Carmassi et al., 2016; Vallée et al., 2021). As a prototypical member of the lithium salts, lithium chloride has been repurposed in recent years as a candidate for neuroprotection because of its ability to inhibit glycogen synthase kinase-3β (GSK3β), a serine/threonine kinase involved in numerous intracellular signaling cascades. Lithium’s chemical simplicity belies its complex pharmacology; its effects extend well beyond mood stabilization to encompass modulation of cell survival, inflammatory responses, and protein degradation pathways. In this context, lithium salts are now recognized as small molecule modulators that can affect intracellular transcriptional programs, including nuclear import of factors such as transcription factor EB (TFEB) and β-catenin, which in turn control the expression of genes necessary for lysosomal biogenesis and autophagic flux (Carmassi et al., 2016; Vallée et al., 2021). These mechanistic insights, originally developed in studies of neurodegenerative and psychiatric diseases, have motivated investigations into whether lithium chloride might be repurposed to address the autophagic and lysosomal dysfunction observed in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD), particularly in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) (Carmassi et al., 2016; Vallée et al., 2021).

Therapeutic History:  
Lithium salts have a long-standing clinical history in psychiatry, especially in the management of bipolar disorder, where their dosing and long-term safety profiles have been thoroughly characterized. In addition, numerous preclinical studies in neuroscience have demonstrated that lithium can reduce tau phosphorylation and improve neuronal cell survival, partly by inhibiting GSK3β and modulating downstream targets such as β-catenin and Bcl-2 (Carmassi et al., 2016; Vallée et al., 2021). Lithium has been evaluated in several neurodegenerative contexts—for instance, it has been examined for its potential benefits in Alzheimer’s disease, Huntington’s disease, and Parkinson’s disease, with some studies reporting modest improvements in neuroprotection and behavioral outcomes, although clinical results have been mixed (Singh et al., 2022; Vallée et al., 2021). More specifically, preclinical data in the central nervous system have shown that prolonged exposure to lithium increases cortical grey matter and enhances neuronal markers such as N-acetyl-aspartate, suggesting that lithium exerts trophic and neuroprotective effects (Carmassi et al., 2016). In the ocular arena, while lithium’s use has been predominantly described in the context of glaucoma—in which its inhibition of GSK3β was shown to modulate WNT/β-catenin signaling in trabecular meshwork cells—the literature offers no direct clinical or in-depth preclinical evaluation of lithium chloride in dry AMD or for modulating autophagy specifically in RPE cells (Singh et al., 2022; Vallée et al., 2021). A search in clinical trial registries has not identified any trials using lithium chloride for macular degeneration, underscoring a notable gap between the neuroprotective models in which lithium has been studied and its potential application in dry AMD (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).

Mechanism of Action:  
Lithium chloride’s mechanisms of action are multifaceted, but a significant aspect relevant to the dry AMD hypothesis is its ability to inhibit GSK3β. GSK3β normally phosphorylates a variety of substrates including β-catenin and TFEB, leading to cytosolic retention and subsequent degradation; inhibition of GSK3β by lithium therefore results in stabilization and nuclear accumulation of β-catenin and promotes TFEB nuclear entry (Carmassi et al., 2016; Vallée et al., 2021). In detail, lithium binds directly to the magnesium-sensitive site of GSK3β and also promotes its inhibitory N-terminal serine phosphorylation, leading to a dose-dependent suppression of GSK3β activity (Carmassi et al., 2016). The release of β-catenin from the destruction complex allows it to accumulate in the nucleus, where it acts as a transcriptional coactivator for genes that contribute to cell survival and homeostasis, including those involved in lysosomal biogenesis (Carmassi et al., 2016; Vallée et al., 2021). Similarly, TFEB is a master transcription factor that coordinates the expression of a variety of genes encoding lysosomal enzymes and autophagy-related proteins. Under basal conditions, phosphorylation retains TFEB in the cytosol; inhibition of GSK3β can contribute to dephosphorylation of TFEB, thereby facilitating its nuclear translocation and transcriptional activation of targets such as cathepsin D (CTSD) and subunits of the vacuolar ATPase (v-ATPase) that are crucial for lysosomal acidification (Carmassi et al., 2016; Friedman et al., 2015). In neuronal models, lithium treatment has been demonstrated to increase levels of neurotrophic factors and cell survival molecules, as well as to enhance autophagy-mediated clearance of toxic proteins including aggregated forms of tau and other proteins implicated in neurodegenerative disease (Vallée et al., 2021). Furthermore, lithium’s inhibition of inositol monophosphatase further contributes to autophagy induction through an mTOR-independent mechanism, reinforcing its capacity to modulate autophagic flux (Friedman et al., 2015). Despite these promising mechanistic insights, it is important to note that most of the supporting data have been generated in neuronal or non-ocular cell systems; direct evidence for lithium chloride-mediated activation of TFEB/β-catenin signaling and upregulation of lysosomal acidification machinery specifically in RPE cells remains limited (Golestaneh et al., 2018; Guha et al., 2014).

Expected Effect:  
Based on the hypothesis, treatment with lithium chloride in RPE cells is anticipated to inhibit GSK3β, leading to a cascade of intracellular events that restore impaired autophagic flux—a major pathological hallmark in dry AMD. In the nucleus, these transcription factors can activate a broad transcriptional program that upregulates the synthesis of lysosomal proteins such as cathepsin D and components of the v-ATPase complex, ultimately leading to enhanced lysosomal acidification (Carmassi et al., 2016; Friedman et al., 2015). This improved lysosomal function is expected to accelerate the degradation of photoreceptor outer segment debris and other autophagic substrates, leading to a restoration of autophagic flux and a reduction in lipofuscin accumulation—a prominent feature of dry AMD pathology (Golestaneh et al., 2018). In parallel, lithium’s neuroprotective effects, including the upregulation of prosurvival factors like Bcl-2 and the attenuation of proinflammatory signaling pathways, may further support RPE cell survival and function under chronic oxidative stress conditions (Vallée et al., 2021).
