Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Fingolimod (FTY720) is a synthetic, sphingoid-base mimetic that is phosphorylated in vivo by sphingosine kinase 2 (SphK2) to yield the active metabolite FTY720-phosphate (FTY720-P), which binds sphingosine-1-phosphate receptors (S1PRs) with sub-micromolar affinity comparable to endogenous S1P (primarily S1PR1, S1PR3, S1PR4, and S1PR5) (Gupta et al., 2012; Gesualdo et al., 2021). As a small-molecule modulator of S1PRs, fingolimod belongs to the class of GPCR-targeting immunomodulators that regulate lymphocyte trafficking and vascular/endothelial signaling; this class has been deployed extensively in neuroinflammatory disease (e.g., multiple sclerosis) and investigated across ocular inflammatory and vascular pathologies (Gesualdo et al., 2021; Sorenson et al., 2022). In ocular biology, endogenous S1P signaling is pleiotropic: it is detected in, and acts upon, multiple retinal cell types including RPE, endothelium, neurons, and glia, where it can protect photoreceptors from oxidative stress–induced apoptosis and modulate wound repair and barrier function, underscoring the translational appeal of S1PR modulators for retinal degenerations (Gupta et al., 2012). At the same time, the S1P axis exhibits context-dependent outcomes—anti-S1P antibodies reduce subretinal fibrosis in AMD models—so receptor-subtype selectivity, ligand presentation (e.g., apoM/HDL-bound vs free), and cell-type–specific responses will be critical to therapeutic design (Gupta et al., 2012; Jung et al., 2025).

Therapeutic History  
Fingolimod is an approved oral therapy that reduces lesion formation in multiple sclerosis through S1PR-mediated immunomodulation, providing an extensive clinical safety and pharmacology dataset for potential repurposing (Mondal & Mandal, 2019). In ocular indications, preclinical studies demonstrate that S1PR pathway manipulation alters retinal/choroidal vascular pathology: intravitreally delivered S1P chaperoned by apolipoprotein M (apoM) activates endothelial S1PR1 and suppresses choroidal neovascularization (CNV) and vascular leak, and separate approaches show that anti-S1P antibodies or S1PR1-selective agonists can suppress CNV and stabilize endothelial barriers (Jung et al., 2025; Sorenson et al., 2022). Fingolimod itself (as FTY720) reduces choroidal endothelial migration and capillary morphogenesis in vitro and mitigates CNV in vivo, indicating that systemic or intraocular S1PR modulation impacts ocular neovascular disease biology (Sorenson et al., 2022). In diabetic retinopathy models, fingolimod reduces retinal angiogenesis and VEGFA levels, aligning with its anti-angiogenic/vascular-stabilizing profile (Gesualdo et al., 2021). Importantly for the dry AMD context, none of these studies directly evaluate atrophic AMD outcomes, RPE autophagy/lysosome endpoints, or complement-driven injury after fingolimod, and there is no prior clinical use of fingolimod for dry AMD (Jung et al., 2025; Sorenson et al., 2022). A material safety consideration for retinal indications is fingolimod-associated macular edema (FAME), reported in clinical settings and relevant to dosing, route, and patient selection if repurposed for macular disease (Mondal & Mandal, 2019).

Mechanism of Action  
Receptor pharmacology of fingolimod and ocular S1P biology. Fingolimod is phosphorylated by SphK2 to FTY720-P, which behaves as a functional agonist at S1PR1, S1PR4, and S1PR5 and a partial agonist at S1PR3, triggering receptor internalization and signaling adaptation that sequesters lymphocytes and modulates vascular responses (Gupta et al., 2012; Gesualdo et al., 2021). In ocular tissues, S1PR1 is prominently expressed in multiple cell types, with experimental evidence demonstrating S1PR1 expression in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) where S1PR1 appears as the predominant S1PR subtype alongside dynamic regulation of S1PR1/S1PR3 by oxygen tension (Sorenson et al., 2022). RPE also expresses the S1P-generating enzymes SphK1 and SphK2 and can synthesize and release S1P, providing the local pathway components to respond to pharmacologic S1PR modulation (Wang et al., 2023). S1P ligands elicit cell-type–specific responses in the retinal neurovascular unit: endothelial S1PR1 activation stabilizes adherens junctions and quells sprouting angiogenesis, apoM/HDL-bound S1P reduces choroidal leakage and CNV, and S1P/S1PR signaling influences RPE barrier function and angiogenic or inflammatory outputs (Jung et al., 2025; Sorenson et al., 2022). These features render S1PR1 a biologically plausible target in RPE and choroid for modulating disease-relevant pathways in AMD, while also highlighting that the net effect of S1P pathway modulation depends on receptor subtype and ligand context (Jung et al., 2025; Sorenson et al., 2022).

RPE autophagy–lysosome biology, lysosomal acidification, and AMD. The RPE is a post-mitotic, highly phagocytic epithelium that performs daily heterophagy of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) and constitutive macroautophagy, processes that converge on lysosomal degradation; failure at the lysosomal step produces lipofuscin accumulation, proteotoxic stress, and drusen formation that characterize AMD (Sinha et al., 2016). Lysosomal acidity, maintained by the vacuolar H^+-ATPase (V-ATPase), is essential for cathepsin activity and cargo hydrolysis; AMD-relevant lipofuscin bisretinoids such as A2E elevate lysosomal pH by inhibiting V-ATPase, impairing phagolysosomal digestion of POS and promoting a feed-forward cycle of oxidative stress and lysosomal dysfunction (Sinha et al., 2016). Lysosomal signaling couples to mTORC1 at the lysosomal surface via V-ATPase–Ragulator–Rag GTPase complexes, integrating luminal amino acids and energy status to regulate autophagy; in RPE, βA3/A1-crystallin (Cryba1) binds the V0 domain of V-ATPase and its loss produces mTORC1 hyperactivation, inefficient lysosomal clearance, and AMD-like pathology, functionally tying V-ATPase activity and mTORC1–TFEB signaling to disease (Sinha et al., 2016). Autophagy protects RPE from oxidative stress, and genetic or age-related declines in macroautophagy correlate with mitochondrial dysfunction, increased ROS, inflammasome activation, and lipofuscin accumulation in human AMD eyes and animal models (Sinha et al., 2016). These data establish that increasing autophagic flux and restoring lysosomal acidification are mechanistically central interventions for RPE protection in AMD.

The AMPK–mTOR–ULK1/TFEB axis: a mechanistic route to autophagy and lysosomal biogenesis. AMPK and mTOR are canonical, opposing regulators of autophagy: AMPK stimulates autophagy by activating ULK1 and inhibiting mTORC1 (including via TSC1/2–Rheb), whereas mTORC1 phosphorylates ULK1/Atg13 to block initiation and phosphorylates Atg14 to dampen nucleation (Wang et al., 2023). TFEB/TFE3 are master transcription factors of lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy; mTORC1 phosphorylation retains TFEB in the cytosol, and mTORC1 inhibition permits TFEB nuclear translocation to activate the CLEAR network of lysosomal and autophagy genes (Wang et al., 2023). AMPK-dependent phosphorylation is required for TFEB/TFE3 transcriptional activation, and AMPK activation increases V-ATPase assembly and activity under glucose starvation, providing a direct link from energy stress to lysosomal acidification machinery (Boya et al., 2023). In RPE/AMD-relevant systems, TFEB activation increases expression of V-ATPase subunits (e.g., ATP6V0A1), lysosomal proteins (LAMP2), and cathepsins (CTSB), and reduces accumulation of POS-dependent lipofuscin-like granules; trehalose- or rapamycin-mediated TFEB activation enhances autophagic flux and decreases A2E/lipofuscin load and inflammatory markers in RPE models (Falcão et al., 2025). Human AMD RPE displays increased TFEB phosphorylation and reduced nuclear TFEB, together with decreased cathepsin levels, consistent with mTORC1-mediated suppression of lysosomal function; TFEB reactivation in Cryba1-deficient RPE rescues CLEAR gene expression and degradative capacity, supporting TFEB as a viable target for lysosomal rejuvenation (Falcão et al., 2025).

Mitochondria–lysosome crosstalk, S1P, and oxidative damage. Mitochondrial quality control via PINK1/PRKN-driven mitophagy and mitochondria-derived vesicles (MDVs) is coordinated with lysosomal function; AMPK acts bidirectionally to couple mitochondrial stress to lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy competence (Boya et al., 2023). In RPE and AMD models, mitochondrial dysfunction (mtDNA damage, impaired mitophagy) increases ROS and sensitizes cells to inflammasome activation and downstream damage; restoring lysosomal/mitochondrial clearance reduces oxidative injury (Boya et al., 2023). S1P signaling can induce mitochondrial biogenesis and thereby influence immunometabolic homeostasis; combined with AMPK–TFEB activation, S1P-related pathways could theoretically enhance both mitochondrial and lysosomal resilience in stressed RPE (Boya et al., 2023).

Inflammation, complement, and autophagy–lysosome cross-talk in AMD. Autophagy negatively regulates inflammasome activation, and complement/inflammasome axes contribute to RPE pathology in AMD; for example, complement C5a primes inflammasomes, and high-risk CFH Y402H RPE exhibit swollen lysosomes with cathepsin D leakage and increased lysosomal C5b-9 deposition (Kaarniranta et al., 2023; Falcão et al., 2025). Complement-related lysosomal stress provides a plausible injury modality that could be mitigated by lysosomal stabilization and increased autophagic flux; indeed, complement modulation can restore lysosomal function in a CFH Y402H RPE model (Boya et al., 2023). Because impaired lysosome/autophagy promotes secretory autophagy of inflammatory cargo, including HMGB1 and possibly amyloid species, enhancing lysosomal degradation should also reduce extracellular pro-inflammatory signals that propagate AMD pathology (Kaarniranta et al., 2023; Sinha et al., 2016).

What is known—and unknown—about fingolimod and the AMPK/TFEB–lysosome axis. In human cell models outside the eye, fingolimod can increase LC3B-II and alter Akt signaling (dephosphorylating Akt1 at Ser473), consistent with autophagy induction; yet the same studies report TFEB downregulation and induction of an inhibitory phosphorylation mark on TFEB (Ser211), with overall interpretations suggesting potential for stalling/saturation of autophagy under some conditions, and cell-type–dependent lysosomal enlargement and membrane permeabilization have also been described (Relic et al., 2021). Across the RPE/AMD literature summarized here, there is no direct demonstration that fingolimod or S1PR agonists activate AMPK, mobilize TFEB to the nucleus, increase V-ATPase–dependent lysosomal acidification, or enhance autophagic flux in RPE; nor are there data showing that fingolimod reduces complement-driven RPE injury in dry AMD models (Boya et al., 2023; Falcão et al., 2025). These are critical gaps that must be addressed experimentally before the proposed mechanism can be accepted (Jung et al., 2025; Relic et al., 2021).

Expected Effect  
Target engagement and proximal signaling in RPE. Because S1PR1 is expressed in RPE and appears to be the predominant S1P receptor subtype in this cell type, fingolimod (as FTY720-P) should engage RPE S1PRs at pharmacologically relevant concentrations if present in the subretinal/choroidal milieu, although receptor subtype balance and receptor down-modulation dynamics will influence outcomes (Sorenson et al., 2022; Gesualdo et al., 2021). In the hypothesized AMPK→TFEB pathway, proximal readouts would include increased AMPK phosphorylation/activation, decreased mTORC1 activity (e.g., phospho-S6K/4EBP1), and enhanced nuclear localization of TFEB/TFE3, followed by transcriptional upregulation of CLEAR genes (e.g., LAMP1/2, ATP6V0A1, CTSB/D) (Boya et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2023; Falcão et al., 2025). Because S1PR signaling is pleiotropic, it is critical to test whether fingolimod in RPE shifts Akt and mTORC1 activities toward a TFEB-permissive state, as opposed to inducing the inhibitory TFEB Ser211 phosphorylation and autophagy stalling seen in some non-ocular cells (Relic et al., 2021).

Lysosomal acidification, degradative capacity, and autophagic flux. If fingolimod drives AMPK activation and TFEB nuclear translocation in RPE, predicted functional outcomes include increased V-ATPase assembly and activity (acidified lysosomes), higher cathepsin activity, and increased autophagic flux measurable by LC3-II turnover in the presence of bafilomycin or chloroquine, together with decreased steady-state p62/SQSTM1 under basal degradative conditions (Boya et al., 2023; Falcão et al., 2025). TFEB activation in RPE models reduces POS-dependent lipofuscin-like granule accumulation and increases lysosome number; pharmacologic TFEB induction (e.g., with trehalose) increases lysosomal biogenesis and autophagosome–lysosome fusion, so fingolimod engagement of this axis should phenocopy these protective changes if the postulated signaling is correct (Falcão et al., 2025). Restoration of lysosomal acidity would be expected to counteract A2E- and lipofuscin-induced V-ATPase inhibition, improving phagolysosomal degradation of POS and reducing waste buildup (Sinha et al., 2016).

Oxidative stress, mitochondrial homeostasis, and inflammasome/complement outputs. By increasing autophagic and mitophagic flux, and engaging TFEB-dependent antioxidant/clearance programs, the candidate mechanism should reduce mitochondrial ROS, stabilize mitochondrial biogenesis via AMPK–PGC-1 pathways, and decrease ROS-dependent priming of inflammasomes (Boya et al., 2023; Sinha et al., 2016). Autophagy mitigates inflammasome activation, and restoring lysosome function reduces the release of DAMPs and secretory autophagy cargo (e.g., HMGB1), which together would be expected to blunt complement pathway amplification in stressed RPE; complement deposition (C5b-9) within lysosomes, especially in CFH risk-allele RPE, may be reduced if lysosomal integrity is preserved and capacity is restored (Kaarniranta et al., 2023; Falcão et al., 2025). In aggregate, if fingolimod engages the AMPK–TFEB–lysosome axis in RPE as hypothesized, one would expect improvements in lysosomal pH, cathepsin activity (including CTSD), autophagic flux, reduced lipofuscin/A2E accumulation, lower mitochondrial ROS, and decreased inflammasome/complement readouts in RPE challenged with AMD-relevant stresses (oxidants, A2E, complement components) (Falcão et al., 2025; Sinha et al., 2016; Kaarniranta et al., 2023).

Caveats and contrary expectations. Fingolimod’s effects on TFEB and autophagy are cell- and context-dependent; in human synovial fibroblasts and HEK293 cells fingolimod induced TFEB Ser211 phosphorylation and TFEB downregulation despite LC3B-II accumulation, suggesting potential autophagy stalling and negative feedback on TFEB that could counter the desired lysosomal biogenesis in RPE (Relic et al., 2021). Moreover, S1P pathway manipulation can yield opposing outcomes in different compartments (e.g., anti-S1P strategies reduce ocular fibrosis/CNV), so nonselective S1PR modulation by fingolimod may not cleanly recapitulate the endothelial-protective, S1PR1-selective phenotypes observed with apoM/HDL–S1P delivery (Jung et al., 2025; Gupta et al., 2012). Finally, retinal safety signals—particularly macular edema—have been associated with fingolimod in clinical practice and would warrant stringent dose–exposure control and route optimization (e.g., local ocular delivery) in any AMD program (Mondal & Mandal, 2019).

Assay design implications. Given the mechanistic uncertainties, rigorous RPE-focused assays must be prioritized: (1) S1PR1/3/5 expression profiling in the chosen RPE system (primary human, iPSC-RPE) and receptor occupancy by fingolimod; (2) AMPK phosphorylation and mTORC1 readouts (p-AMPK, p-S6K, p-4EBP1) after fingolimod with and without S1PR antagonists; (3) TFEB/TFE3 nuclear translocation and CLEAR target induction; (4) lysosomal pH (ratiometric LysoSensor) and V-ATPase assembly/activity; (5) autophagic flux (LC3-II turnover ± lysosomal inhibitors; p62 dynamics); (6) cathepsin D/L activity assays; (7) oxidative stress resilience (mitoROS, mtDNA damage) and mitophagy markers; and (8) complement handling (C3 turnover, C5b-9 deposition) under CFH Y402H and amyloid/oxidant stress conditions (Falcão et al., 2025; Sinha et al., 2016; Falcão et al., 2025; Kaarniranta et al., 2023). Benchmarking to validated TFEB activators (e.g., trehalose) and lysosomal acidification restorers will contextualize fingolimod’s performance on the most disease-relevant axes (Falcão et al., 2025).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Strong disease–mechanism alignment: Dry AMD is characterized by impaired lysosomal acidification, defective autophagic clearance, and oxidative/complement stress in RPE; AMPK–mTOR–TFEB signaling and V-ATPase activity are validated nodal controllers of lysosomal competence in RPE and AMD models, providing clear mechanistic targets that, if engaged, should be disease-modifying (Sinha et al., 2016; Sinha et al., 2016; Falcão et al., 2025; Sinha et al., 2016).  
- On-target cellular expression: S1PR1 is present in RPE and is the predominant S1PR subtype, while RPE express SphK1/2, indicating the S1P/S1PR machinery required for pharmacologic modulation exists in the target cell (Sorenson et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2023).  
- Prior ocular efficacy signals via S1PR modulation: ApoM/HDL–S1P→S1PR1 suppresses CNV and leakage; FTY720 reduces choroidal endothelial angiogenic behaviors and mitigates CNV; in diabetic retinopathy, fingolimod decreases VEGF signaling—together confirming relevant ocular pharmacology and providing translational scaffolding for retinal use (Jung et al., 2025; Sorenson et al., 2022; Gesualdo et al., 2021).  
- Immunometabolic rationale: S1P signaling can promote mitochondrial biogenesis, and AMPK–TFEB signaling coordinates mitochondrial–lysosomal crosstalk; a single agent engaging the S1P–AMPK–TFEB axis might simultaneously improve mitochondrial and lysosomal resilience in oxidatively stressed RPE (Boya et al., 2023; Boya et al., 2023).  
- Repurposing tractability: Extensive human exposure, known PK/PD, and manageable formulation chemistry enable accelerated translational planning compared to de novo entities (Mondal & Mandal, 2019).

Weaknesses and risks  
- Mechanistic gap in the target cell: There is currently no direct evidence that fingolimod activates AMPK or TFEB in RPE, increases autophagic flux, or acidifies lysosomes; likewise, no data show fingolimod reduces complement-driven injury in RPE/dry AMD models, and this is the central premise of the hypothesis (Jung et al., 2025; Boya et al., 2023; Falcão et al., 2025).  
- Context dependence and potential for adverse lysosomal effects: In human non-ocular cells, fingolimod induced inhibitory TFEB phosphorylation and autophagy stalling, and lysosomal enlargement/permeabilization has been reported in some contexts—opposite to the desired lysosomal restoration—raising the possibility of deleterious effects in RPE unless carefully titrated (Relic et al., 2021).  
- Receptor- and ligand-context complexity: Beneficial vascular phenotypes are associated with endothelial S1PR1 stimulation—often via chaperone-bound S1P—while nonselective S1PR modulation or anti-S1P strategies can also be beneficial (e.g., anti-fibrotic effects in AMD), implying that fingolimod’s mixed S1PR agonism and functional antagonism could yield off-target or counterproductive outcomes in the RPE/choroid (Jung et al., 2025; Gupta et al., 2012; Sorenson et al., 2022).  
- Retinal safety concerns: Fingolimod-associated macular edema is a documented adverse effect in humans, which is particularly concerning in a macular disease; any development plan must incorporate delivery strategies and exposure limits that mitigate this risk (Mondal & Mandal, 2019).  
- Evidence base skew: Much of the directly AMD-relevant S1P/S1PR ocular literature concerns neovascular endpoints (wet AMD/CNV) or endothelium, not atrophic RPE biology; the best lysosome/autophagy data are robust but are not linked to S1PR pharmacology, necessitating bridging studies to validate the specific drug–mechanism–disease chain (Jung et al., 2025; Falcão et al., 2025).

Go/no-go perspective and experimental priorities  
On balance, fingolimod is a mechanistically plausible, but currently unvalidated, repurposing candidate for dry AMD via the proposed S1PR→AMPK→TFEB→lysosome axis. A limited, mechanism-first preclinical package in human RPE models is warranted before considering in vivo efficacy work. The minimum data package to de-risk the hypothesis should include:  
- Demonstration that fingolimod engages S1PRs on human RPE and increases AMPK activity while suppressing mTORC1, with consequent TFEB/TFE3 nuclear translocation and CLEAR gene induction; side-by-side with a S1PR1-selective agonist and apoM/HDL-S1P as positive controls for S1PR1 biology (Sorenson et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2023; Falcão et al., 2025; Jung et al., 2025).  
- Functional lysosomal rescue: increased V-ATPase assembly/activity, lower lysosomal pH, increased CTSD/CTSL activity, improved POS digestion, reduced A2E and lipofuscin-like autofluorescence under static and diurnal POS feeding paradigms (Sinha et al., 2016; Falcão et al., 2025).  
- Flux and mitochondrial outcomes: increased autophagic flux (LC3-II turnover, p62 dynamics), enhanced mitophagy under oxidant stress (PINK1/PRKN markers), and decreased mitoROS (Boya et al., 2023; Sinha et al., 2016).  
- Inflammation/complement endpoints: reduced IL1B release after MG-132/BafA challenges, lowered NLRP3 activation, decreased lysosomal C5b-9 deposition and improved lysosomal integrity in CFH Y402H iPSC-RPE exposed to complement (Piippo, 2019; Falcão et al., 2025).  
- Safety liabilities: absence of lysosomal membrane permeabilization, cathepsin leakage, or TFEB Ser211 inhibitory phosphorylation with autophagy stalling at therapeutic exposure in RPE, in contrast to adverse signatures reported in other cell types (Relic et al., 2021).

Depending on these in vitro outcomes, a focused in vivo test in a dry AMD-relevant model (e.g., NaIO3 injury or Cryba1 cKO) with intraocular delivery and a retinal safety assessment (OCT for edema, ERG, histology) would be the logical next step (Falcão et al., 2025; Sinha et al., 2016). If the AMPK–TFEB and lysosomal endpoints are not met, pivot to alternative S1PR strategies (S1PR1-selective agonists or apoM/HDL–S1P formulations) that have more consistent endothelial/retinal protective phenotypes may be warranted (Jung et al., 2025). If proximal signaling is partially engaged but lysosomal capacity remains limiting, combination approaches with validated TFEB activators (e.g., trehalose) or NRF2 activators that cross-reinforce lysosomal and antioxidant programs could be explored with attention to oncogenicity and cell specificity (Falcão et al., 2025).

Conclusion  
Fingolimod sits at the intersection of a compelling disease mechanism (lysosomal/autophagic failure in RPE), a plausible upstream target (S1PR1 in RPE), and a therapeutic class with ocular activity (S1PR modulators), but it lacks direct evidence for engaging the AMPK–TFEB–lysosomal biogenesis/acidification axis in RPE or for mitigating complement/oxidative injury in dry AMD models (Sorenson et al., 2022; Falcão et al., 2025; Jung et al., 2025). The strength of the lysosome/autophagy rationale and the existence of RPE S1PR1 expression support a mechanism-first exploration; however, cell-type–dependent fingolimod effects on TFEB and autophagy and the clinical risk of macular edema demand caution (Relic et al., 2021; Mondal & Mandal, 2019). Proceed only with a staged validation plan centered on RPE-intrinsic endpoints of AMPK/TFEB activation, lysosomal acidification, and complement/oxidative resilience; without those data, the hypothesis remains unsubstantiated for dry AMD, and alternative S1PR strategies or direct TFEB/lysosome-targeting interventions may be more tractable (Jung et al., 2025; Falcão et al., 2025).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Eculizumab (Soliris, Alexion) is a humanized IgG monoclonal antibody derived from the murine anti–human C5 antibody m5G1 via CDR grafting and human framework engineering to reduce immunogenicity and extend serum half-life, designed to bind complement component C5 with high affinity and sterically prevent its cleavage by C5 convertases into C5a and C5b (thereby blocking terminal pathway activation and MAC assembly) (Park et al., 2019; Troutbeck et al., 2012; Yehoshua et al., 2014; Park et al., 2021). It belongs to the class of complement inhibitors that directly target an effector protein (C5) at the convergence of the classical, lectin, and alternative pathways, in contrast to upstream amplification-targeting agents (e.g., C3 or factor D inhibitors) (Park et al., 2019; Tzoumas et al., 2023). Systemically administered eculizumab has established clinical utility in complement-mediated hematologic and renal disorders, including paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria and atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome, and more recently generalized myasthenia gravis, reflecting a mature pharmacology and a well-characterized risk profile centered on increased susceptibility to encapsulated organisms (notably meningococcal infection) due to terminal pathway blockade (Park et al., 2019; Yehoshua et al., 2014).

Within ophthalmology, the terminal complement pathway is an attractive target for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) and geographic atrophy (GA) because C5a is a proinflammatory anaphylatoxin detected in drusen that can drive leukocyte recruitment and VEGF induction in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), and C5b nucleates formation of the membrane attack complex (MAC, C5b–C9), which accumulates with age and AMD in Bruch’s membrane and choriocapillaris and can lyse or sub-lytically activate choroidal endothelial and RPE cells (Kassa et al., 2019). The class of C5 inhibitors therefore aims to reduce both inflammatory signaling (via C5a) and cytolytic/proinflammatory MAC effects while preserving upstream opsonization and some host-defense functions mediated by C3b, potentially retaining aspects of immune competence relative to C3 inhibition (Halawa et al., 2021; Park et al., 2019).

Therapeutic History  
Approved indications and systemic pharmacology  
Eculizumab is FDA/EMA approved for paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria and atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome, where weight-based intravenous regimens achieve sustained trough serum concentrations and complete inhibition of hemolytic activity by blocking C5 cleavage; these regimens produce serum levels > 35 μg/mL and complete systemic C5 functional blockade, but require meningococcal vaccination to mitigate Neisseria risk inherent to terminal complement inhibition (Park et al., 2019; Yehoshua et al., 2014). In other complementopathies, clinical experience has highlighted a mechanism-consequent shift of pathology upstream (e.g., C3-loading and extravascular hemolysis in PNH under C5 blockade), underscoring that C5 inhibition leaves C3 activation intact (Hammadi et al., 2023).

Clinical investigation in geographic atrophy of dry AMD  
Eculizumab was investigated in the prospective, randomized, double-masked, single-center Phase 2 COMPLETE study that enrolled 30 participants with GA (primary cohort) plus an intermediate AMD/drusen cohort, randomized 2:1 to intravenous eculizumab versus saline over 24 weeks (with follow-up to 52 weeks) (Yehoshua et al., 2014). Two dosing regimens were tested: a low-dose arm (600 mg weekly × 4, then 900 mg every 2 weeks through week 24) and a high-dose arm with higher induction and maintenance dosing; all patients received meningococcal vaccination prior to first infusion (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Patel et al., 2022). Pharmacokinetically, systemic exposure and target engagement were confirmed: eculizumab concentrations were measurable at all assessed time points (mean ~ 65–189 μg/mL in low-dose and ~ 122–259 μg/mL in high-dose cohorts), with plasma C5 activity reduced to < 9% by week 1 and < 1% by week 2, indicating complete systemic terminal complement blockade sustained through treatment (Yehoshua et al., 2014).

Despite robust systemic pharmacodynamics, COMPLETE detected no effect on GA progression: at 26 weeks the change in square-root–transformed GA area was 0.19 ± 0.12 mm in eculizumab-treated eyes versus 0.18 ± 0.15 mm with placebo (P = 0.96), and at 52 weeks both arms exhibited ~ 0.37 mm enlargement (P ≈ 0.93), effectively excluding a large treatment effect (> 55% slowing) in this cohort (Yehoshua et al., 2014). Drusen volume endpoints in the intermediate AMD cohort were also negative (no participant achieved a 50% reduction), and fellow-eye analyses mirrored primary-eye results (Patel et al., 2022; Yehoshua et al., 2014). Visual function showed no durable benefit: a 26-week letter gain difference favoring eculizumab was attributed to a single outlier in placebo, and by 52 weeks there was no between-group difference; pooled estimates across small RCTs rated the certainty of BCVA effects as low-to-very-low with confidence intervals overlapping no effect (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Tzoumas et al., 2023). Safety was acceptable in the trial: no drug-related serious adverse events were identified through 52 weeks, and no eyes converted to neovascular AMD during the study; however, systemic C5 blockade requires vaccination and vigilance for meningococcal infection, and an independent systemic anti-C5 AMD trial was terminated early due to uncertainty about risk/benefit in light of reported meningococcal infections in real-world eculizumab users (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Tzoumas et al., 2023).

Interpretations from COMPLETE and subsequent reviews point to several plausible explanations for the null result: inadequate intraocular/RPE target engagement with systemic dosing due to blood–retinal and Bruch’s barriers; the possibility that C5 is the wrong target in GA given genetic associations that more strongly implicate proximal complement components (e.g., C3, CFH) rather than terminal pathway constituents; the short on-treatment window (24 weeks) and small sample size; and the biological reality that C5 inhibition preserves upstream C3a/C3b biology, which may continue to drive pathology (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Halawa et al., 2021; Hammadi et al., 2023; Tzoumas et al., 2023).

Comparative C5 and complement-targeting experience in AMD  
Intravitreal C5 inhibition has produced divergent results. LFG316 (tesidolumab), an anti-C5 monoclonal antibody administered intravitreally, failed to alter GA lesion growth or visual outcomes in a randomized phase 2 trial (Halawa et al., 2021; Park et al., 2019). By contrast, avacincaptad pegol (Zimura), an intravitreal C5 aptamer, reduced GA growth rates by approximately 27–30% over 12–18 months in pivotal trials, leading to FDA approval, although potential increased risk of macular neovascularization has been signaled and requires ongoing pharmacovigilance (Patel et al., 2022; Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023; Tzoumas et al., 2023). Upstream targeting at C3 with intravitreal pegcetacoplan (SYFOVRE) significantly slowed GA enlargement in phase 2–3 programs and achieved regulatory approval, but at the cost of increased rates of conversion to exudative AMD and, in the postmarketing setting, reports of occlusive retinal vasculitis, highlighting a target-dependent safety trade-off between efficacy and pro-angiogenic/immune-privilege perturbation risks (Halawa et al., 2021; Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023; Qin et al., 2024). Alternative-pathway inhibition via factor D (lampalizumab) produced a phase 2 signal but failed in two phase 3 trials, suggesting that partial pathway blockade may be insufficient in GA (Piri & Kaplan, 2023; Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023).

Taken together, these data place systemic eculizumab among C5-directed strategies where local delivery has demonstrated anatomic efficacy in GA, whereas systemic delivery has not, and they highlight that complement modulation can slow atrophy progression without improving visual function and may introduce target- and route-specific risks such as neovascularization or serious infection (Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023; Tzoumas et al., 2023).

Mechanism of Action  
Complement cascade biology and eculizumab target engagement  
Complement activation arises via classical, lectin, and alternative pathways, converging at the generation of C3 convertases that cleave C3 into C3a (anaphylatoxin) and C3b (opsonin/convertase component), with amplification by the alternative pathway accounting for the majority (80–90%) of downstream MAC generation in physiologic and pathologic settings (Tzoumas et al., 2023). C5 convertases (C4b2a3b for classical/lectin and C3bBbC3b for alternative pathway) cleave C5 into C5a, a potent anaphylatoxin that recruits/activates myeloid cells and stimulates RPE to produce VEGF and proinflammatory cytokines, and C5b, which seeds assembly of the terminal membrane attack complex (C5b–C9) on nearby membranes (Tzoumas et al., 2023; Kassa et al., 2019). Eculizumab binds C5 to prevent convertase-mediated cleavage, thereby abrogating both C5a generation and MAC formation independent of the initiating pathway; this preserves upstream C3 activation (C3a/C3b) and the alternative-pathway amplification loop while blunting terminal effector functions (Park et al., 2019; Halawa et al., 2021).

Ocular and RPE relevance of C5 and MAC  
Multiple lines of evidence implicate terminal pathway effectors in AMD pathophysiology at the RPE–choriocapillaris interface. Histopathology shows increasing MAC deposition with aging and AMD in Bruch’s membrane and the choriocapillaris; sub-lytic MAC on choroidal endothelial cells triggers pro-angiogenic/proteolytic responses (VEGF, MMPs), while high-level deposition can induce lysis of choroidal endothelial cells and bystander injury contributing to RPE atrophy (Kassa et al., 2019). C5a is present in drusen and is a strong inflammatory mediator that can recruit immune cells and induce VEGF release from RPE, linking terminal pathway activation to both atrophic and neovascular processes relevant to the AMD spectrum (Kassa et al., 2019). Additional experimental work demonstrates that sub-lytic C5b-9 can alter RPE function in ways consistent with AMD, including stress responses and secretory changes, reinforcing that terminal complement activation can be injurious to the RPE even in the absence of frank lysis (Park et al., 2019).

Complement production and regulation in the eye—and systemic versus local contributions  
Complement proteins are synthesized predominantly by the liver and circulate systemically, but they are also produced locally within ocular tissues (retina, RPE, choroid), with local activation and regulation shaped by cell-intrinsic complement regulatory proteins (e.g., CFH, CD46, CD59) and by oxidative stress effects that reduce cell-surface complement inhibition on RPE (Tzoumas et al., 2023; van Lookeren Campagne et al., 2016). Several studies highlight local complement expression and activation in retinal cells and macrophages, as well as increased local complement turnover preceding clinical disease, supporting the concept of an ocular complement “microenvironment” that can be dysregulated independent of systemic levels (Patel et al., 2022; Piri & Kaplan, 2023). Conversely, transcriptomic mapping suggests that posterior-pole tissues have limited local transcription of lectin and terminal pathway components (except C5 and C7), implying reliance on systemic sources for some terminal pathway proteins, which in principle could make systemic C5 blockade effective if sufficient intraocular penetration and target engagement are achieved (Troutbeck et al., 2012). These seemingly conflicting observations are reconciled by recognizing that both local production and systemic supply contribute to ocular complement biology, and that their relative importance likely varies by compartment (RPE, choriocapillaris, sub-RPE space), disease stage, and barrier integrity.

Genetic and biomarker context for C5 targeting in AMD  
GWAS and biomarker studies have repeatedly implicated complement dysregulation in AMD susceptibility and progression, including associations at CFH, C3, C2/CFB, CFI, and C9 loci, and elevated systemic and ocular concentrations of complement activation products (C3a, C5a, MAC) in AMD patients (Dascalu et al., 2024). However, the genetic signal is stronger and more consistent for proximal regulators (e.g., CFH, C3) than for C5, and at least one analysis noted C3 risk alleles do not necessarily correlate with GA progression (and in some contexts associated with decreased progression), emphasizing the complexity of translating susceptibility signals to progression biology and target selection in late AMD (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Halawa et al., 2021). Mechanistically, C5 blockade leaves upstream C3a/C3b biology intact; in extra-ocular diseases this can unmask C3-related pathophysiology under C5 inhibition, illustrating a general limitation of terminal pathway-only targeting (Hammadi et al., 2023). In GA, this implies that C3a/C3b-driven processes—chemoattraction, opsonization, and immune modulation—could continue in the outer retina/RPE even under complete C5 suppression, potentially blunting the benefit of C5-only therapy (Halawa et al., 2021; Tzoumas et al., 2023).

Therapeutic delivery constraints to ocular complement modulation with systemic C5 blockade  
Large biologics such as eculizumab face formidable physical barriers to ocular penetration, including the inner and outer blood–retina barriers and Bruch’s membrane/RPE tight junctions, whose permeability declines with increasing molecular weight and hydrophilicity (a profile characteristic of IgG antibodies), making intraocular access by systemic dosing uncertain without active transport mechanisms (Hammadi et al., 2023; Yehoshua et al., 2014). This is the most straightforward explanation for COMPLETE’s combination of complete systemic pharmacodynamic suppression with no effect on lesion enlargement: the effective intraocular concentration of antibody at relevant RPE–choroid interfaces was likely insufficient to inhibit terminal complement activation locally, a conclusion echoed by the trial investigators (Yehoshua et al., 2014).

Expected Effect  
Proposed pharmacologic and cellular effect  
Under the working hypothesis, systemic eculizumab would reduce MAC formation on RPE and choroidal endothelial surfaces and diminish C5a-driven inflammatory signaling, thereby protecting RPE cellular homeostasis and the RPE–choriocapillaris unit from complement-mediated injury and slowing expansion of GA lesions (Kassa et al., 2019; Park et al., 2019). Mechanistically, suppression of MAC would be expected to decrease lytic and sub-lytic injury to choroidal endothelial cells and RPE, attenuating downstream induction of VEGF and MMPs, and limiting bystander tissue damage around atrophic borders where complement activation is thought to be active (Tzoumas et al., 2023; Kassa et al., 2019). Reducing C5a generation could blunt recruitment and activation of myeloid cells and RPE proinflammatory cytokine production, decreasing local inflammatory amplification in the outer retina (Tzoumas et al., 2023; Kassa et al., 2019).

Expression and target presence in relevant cells/tissues  
C5 and terminal pathway components are present in the ocular compartments relevant to GA pathobiology: choriocapillaris/Bruch’s membrane deposition of MAC is well documented and increases with age and AMD, and C5a is detected within drusen; RPE-derived complement regulators (e.g., CD59) and choroidal endothelial susceptibility to MAC are described, establishing both target and downstream effectors within the disease-relevant tissues (Kassa et al., 2019). Complement components and regulators are expressed in retina, RPE, and choroid, with transcriptomic data indicating relatively higher choroidal expression and limited local transcription of some terminal components (except C5 and C7), consistent with both local and systemic sources contributing substrate for terminal pathway assembly (Troutbeck et al., 2012; Tzoumas et al., 2023).

Translational and clinical outcome expectations  
At the disease level, a therapy that meaningfully reduces local terminal complement activation in GA should slow the rate of GA lesion enlargement measured on fundus autofluorescence (FAF) and/or SD-OCT, endpoints accepted by the FDA/NEI and standard across GA trials; functional outcomes such as BCVA and low-luminance VA typically lag structural changes and may not improve even when lesion growth is slowed (Dascalu et al., 2024; Qin et al., 2024). In COMPLETE, these endpoints were precisely those evaluated; the absence of any measurable effect on square-root GA area at 26 and 52 weeks indicates that, at the tested systemic dosing regimens, eculizumab did not achieve sufficient intraocular target engagement to translate the mechanistic rationale into clinical benefit (Yehoshua et al., 2014).

Reasons for divergence between expected and observed effects  
Three non-exclusive explanations align with the totality of evidence:

  • Inadequate intraocular bioavailability from systemic dosing. Antibody size and hydrophilicity, combined with blood–retina and RPE–Bruch’s barriers, likely prevented sufficient drug from reaching the RPE–choriocapillaris compartment to inhibit local terminal pathway activation, despite verified systemic C5 suppression (Hammadi et al., 2023; Yehoshua et al., 2014; Tzoumas et al., 2023).

  • Target selection may be suboptimal for GA biology. The stronger genetic and pathophysiologic evidence for proximal complement dysregulation (e.g., C3, CFH) and the preservation of upstream activation under C5 blockade mean that C5-only inhibition may not adequately suppress the complement-driven processes that sustain GA border expansion, as supported by the comparatively stronger clinical signals with C3 inhibition and mixed-to-positive signals with intravitreal C5 inhibition (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Halawa et al., 2021; Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023).

  • Trial limitations. The COMPLETE cohort was small and on-treatment duration was six months, which may be insufficient to observe smaller effects on GA growth; however, confidence intervals excluded large effects, and lack of any trend over 52 weeks reduces the likelihood that longer dosing would have changed the outcome meaningfully (Yehoshua et al., 2014).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
  • Strong mechanistic rationale for terminal pathway blockade in AMD: C5a is proinflammatory and detected in drusen; MAC accumulates at the RPE–choriocapillaris interface with age/AMD and can injure choroidal endothelium and RPE via lytic and sub-lytic mechanisms, linking C5 effector functions directly to AMD pathophysiology (Kassa et al., 2019). Blocking C5 suppresses both MAC and C5a, targeting inflammatory and cytolytic arms while leaving upstream C3-mediated opsonization intact, an immunologic advantage over C3 blockade (Halawa et al., 2021; Park et al., 2019).

  • Mature systemic pharmacology with demonstrated ability to completely suppress plasma C5 activity at well-tolerated doses, including in AMD patients, making systemic development logistically straightforward and with known requirements (e.g., meningococcal vaccination) (Yehoshua et al., 2014).

  • Practical systemic-delivery advantages: single systemic therapy treats both eyes simultaneously and avoids intravitreal injection–related ocular risks (endophthalmitis, IOP spikes), which have nontrivial incidence in chronic IVT regimens (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Tzoumas et al., 2023).

  • External validation within the class: intravitreal C5 inhibition (avacincaptad pegol) has replicated GA-slowing effects in phase 2/3 programs, supporting the therapeutic value of suppressing terminal pathway activity in the outer retina if adequate local exposure is achieved (Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023).

Limitations  
  • Lack of efficacy in the definitive systemic eculizumab GA study. COMPLETE showed no reduction in GA lesion growth at 26 or 52 weeks despite complete systemic C5 blockade and adequate serum exposure, effectively excluding a large treatment effect and arguing strongly against systemic eculizumab as a viable GA therapy (Yehoshua et al., 2014).

  • Ocular pharmacokinetic barrier. The most parsimonious explanation for the COMPLETE result is inadequate intraocular target engagement from systemic dosing due to the blood–retina/RPE–Bruch’s barriers and the large size/hydrophilicity of IgG, an inherent limitation of systemic antibody delivery to the sub-RPE/choroidal compartment (Hammadi et al., 2023; Yehoshua et al., 2014).

  • Target-level uncertainties. Genetic and biomarker studies more consistently implicate proximal complement dysregulation (CFH/C3) than C5 in AMD susceptibility; moreover, C5 inhibition preserves upstream C3a/C3b activity, which may continue to drive border-zone inflammation and remodeling in GA (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Dascalu et al., 2024; Halawa et al., 2021). Clinical comparisons reinforce this: upstream C3 inhibition has produced larger and more consistent anatomic effects (with important safety trade-offs), whereas anti-C5 trials are split—systemic eculizumab negative; IVT LFG316 negative; IVT avacincaptad positive—pointing to delivery and target–context dependencies (Halawa et al., 2021; Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023).

  • Systemic safety constraints. While COMPLETE itself reported no drug-related serious adverse events over one year, terminal complement blockade carries a class risk of meningococcal infection requiring vaccination and risk mitigation; at least one planned AMD systemic anti-C5 trial was terminated early due to uncertainty regarding the systemic infection risk/benefit in this population (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Tzoumas et al., 2023).

  • Limited translatability of systemic complement activation to local disease control. Although systemic complement activation correlates with AMD and disease stage in several studies, the relative importance of local versus systemic complement sources—and the ability of systemic blockade to suppress complement activity at the RPE–choriocapillaris interface—is unresolved and likely unfavorable for large biologics, reducing the mechanistic plausibility of systemic C5 blockade for GA (Hammadi et al., 2023; Park et al., 2019).

Risk–benefit and competitive landscape assessment  
Eculizumab’s negative randomized, controlled data in GA, in the face of confirmed systemic pharmacodynamics, places a high bar against further systemic development for this indication, a conclusion explicitly drawn by the COMPLETE investigators who noted the linearity of GA growth and lack of signal as making additional systemic investigations with eculizumab unlikely (Yehoshua et al., 2014). In the evolving complement-therapeutic landscape, local (intravitreal) complement inhibitors have achieved regulatory approval (C3 inhibitor pegcetacoplan and C5 aptamer avacincaptad pegol), demonstrating that complement modulation can slow GA progression when adequate ocular exposure is achieved, albeit without functional vision improvement and with target-dependent safety liabilities (e.g., increased conversion to exudative AMD observed particularly with C3 inhibition) (Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023; Qin et al., 2024). Against this backdrop, systemic eculizumab offers no efficacy advantage, carries systemic infection risk and costs, and fails the core requirement of achieving ocular target engagement necessary for GA modification.

Operationally, even if one hypothesized that higher systemic dosing, longer exposure, or patient stratification could rescue efficacy, several facts weigh against that strategy: COMPLETE’s pharmacodynamics confirmed near-complete systemic C5 suppression within two weeks; genetic analyses within the trial found no association between at-risk alleles and GA growth or treatment response; and extended follow-up to a year showed no divergence in growth rates (Yehoshua et al., 2014). Moreover, retinal pharmacokinetics and barrier biology make it unlikely that increasing systemic doses would proportionally increase intraocular concentrations to therapeutic levels without exacerbating systemic risks (Hammadi et al., 2023). In addition, C5 may not be the optimal node for GA progression biology in many patients, given preserved upstream activity and the complex contributions of C3a/C3b, opsonization, and local complement production that may continue to drive border-zone degeneration independent of MAC inhibition (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Halawa et al., 2021; Piri & Kaplan, 2023).

Recommendation  
Based on the aggregate mechanistic, translational, and clinical evidence, eculizumab (systemic C5 inhibition) does not have compelling potential as a repurposed therapy for dry AMD/GA. The drug has a clear and relevant mechanism and an acceptable short-term tolerability profile in older adults, but it fails to slow GA lesion growth in a randomized, controlled trial despite complete systemic target engagement, and there are strong mechanistic and pharmacokinetic reasons to expect insufficient intraocular exposure with systemic delivery (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Hammadi et al., 2023). The therapeutic hypothesis—reducing MAC on RPE/choriocapillaris to preserve tissue integrity and slow atrophy—is supported conceptually and by local C5 inhibition successes; however, achieving that biology in vivo appears to require intraocular delivery or targeting upstream nodes, neither of which is compatible with systemic eculizumab administration (Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023; Halawa et al., 2021).

If complement-targeted strategies remain a program priority, resources should pivot to modalities with demonstrated ocular target engagement and anatomic efficacy (intravitreal C3 or C5 agents) while carefully managing known safety trade-offs (e.g., neovascularization risk), and to biomarker-driven questions (e.g., whether baseline low-luminance visual acuity deficit—correlated with faster GA growth in COMPLETE—can enrich for patients who derive greater anatomic benefit) (Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023; Tzoumas et al., 2023; Yehoshua et al., 2014). For systemic complement modulation in AMD more broadly, alternative targets with better ocular PK profiles (e.g., small-molecule systemic alternative-pathway inhibitors) and rigorous ocular target-engagement measurements would be required to justify late-stage development, but systemic C5 blockade with eculizumab itself should not be advanced further for GA (Hammadi et al., 2023; Tzoumas et al., 2023; Park et al., 2019).

In summary, while the mechanistic logic for terminal complement inhibition in AMD is robust, the totality of evidence argues against systemic eculizumab as a viable candidate to slow GA progression, and the development program should discontinue pursuit of this repurposing in favor of locally delivered complement inhibitors or alternative mechanisms better suited to the ocular compartment and GA pathobiology (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023).

MCC950 was initially characterized in systemic inflammatory disease models, where it demonstrated remarkable efficacy in reducing the production of proinflammatory cytokines, such as interleukin (IL)-1β and IL-18, by directly inhibiting the activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome (Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018; Wooff et al., 2020). In the ocular arena, several studies have examined MCC950’s impact in diverse rodent models of retinal disease. For example, in laser-induced choroidal neovascularization (CNV) models, MCC950 administration led to reductions in IL-1β mRNA and secreted protein levels, albeit with a paradoxical increase in overall CNV lesion volume, suggesting a complex interplay between inflammasome inhibition and immune cell recruitment (Dieckmann et al., 2024). Mechanism of Action:  
MCC950 exerts its pharmacological effects by specifically targeting the NLRP3 inflammasome, a cytosolic multiprotein complex that mediates the innate immune response to both pathogen-associated and damage-associated molecular patterns (Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018). At the molecular level, MCC950 is believed to bind to the NACHT domain of NLRP3, thereby inhibiting its ATPase activity—a critical step required for the conformational changes and oligomerization that lead to the formation of the active inflammasome complex (Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2025). This blockade prevents the recruitment of the adaptor protein ASC, thus halting the maturation and activation of caspase-1 (Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018; Wooff et al., 2020). Consequently, the cleavage of pro-IL-1β and pro-IL-18 into their bioactive forms is suppressed, which results in diminished secretion of these potent proinflammatory cytokines (Wang et al., 2025; Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018). Importantly, MCC950’s mechanism is selective for NLRP3, as it does not interfere with the activation of other inflammasome platforms, such as those mediated by AIM2, NLRC4, or NLRP1 (Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018; Wooff et al., 2020). In the context of retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells—a cell type critical for the maintenance of the outer blood–retina barrier and implicated in the pathogenesis of dry AMD—NLRP3 activation has been linked to chronic inflammation, oxidative stress, and lysosomal destabilization. MCC950 offers several notable strengths as a potential therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. Preclinical studies have demonstrated that MCC950 can successfully reduce the release of IL-1β and IL-18 in various cell types, including retinal endothelial cells and RPE-like cells, which underscores its potential to ameliorate the chronic inflammatory environment observed in dry AMD (Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018; Li, 2020). Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Everolimus (Afinitor; Novartis) is a semi‐synthetic derivative of sirolimus—a macrolide originally isolated from Streptomyces hygroscopicus—as evidenced by its chemical designation as 4-O-(2-hydroxyethyl)-rapamycin (Liu et al., 2023, pp. 11–12). By introducing a 2-hydroxyethyl group at position 40, everolimus achieves greater hydrophilicity and an increased oral bioavailability (from 10% to 16% relative to sirolimus) while retaining the core macrolactone structure that is characteristic of rapalogs (Liu et al., 2023, pp. 11–12; Weber, 2015, pp. 27–28). This compound belongs to the class of mTOR inhibitors—specifically, a first‐generation rapalog that selectively inhibits the mTOR complex 1 (mTORC1) while sparing mTORC2 (Liu et al., 2023, pp. 10–11; Weber, 2015, pp. 27–28). As a synthetic derivative of a naturally occurring product, everolimus represents the successful strategy of chemical modification to optimize pharmacokinetic properties and clinical tolerability. The design parameters underpinning everolimus’ synthesis have been guided by the goal of retaining potent immunosuppressive and anti‐proliferative effects while optimizing parameters such as solubility, half‐life, and tissue penetration, with the added advantage of an oral formulation already approved for several clinical indications (Liu et al., 2023, pp. 11–12; Wang et al., 2022, pp. 6–8).

Therapeutic History:  
Everolimus has a well‐established therapeutic history as an immunosuppressant and antineoplastic agent. Clinically, it is approved for treating advanced renal cell carcinoma, progressive neuroendocrine tumors of pancreatic origin, and subependymal giant cell astrocytoma in tuberous sclerosis complex patients who are not candidates for surgery (Wang et al., 2022, pp. 6–8; Weber, 2015, pp. 27–28). In these indications, its mechanism as an mTORC1 inhibitor serves to arrest cell cycle progression and inhibit angiogenesis, which are central to its antitumor activity (Kuo et al., 2018, pp. 5–7; Weber, 2015, pp. 27–28). Moreover, everolimus has been effectively used in the context of organ transplantation to prevent allograft rejection by impairing helper T‐cell proliferation (Wang et al., 2022, pp. 6–8; Weber, 2015, pp. 27–28).

With regard to ocular applications, although everolimus has not been approved specifically for dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD), several preclinical studies have demonstrated its potential benefits in ocular cell types and models. For instance, in vitro investigations have highlighted that everolimus can inhibit the proliferation and migration of retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells and modulate mTOR signaling within retinal tissue—an effect critical to conditions such as proliferative vitreoretinopathy (PVR) (Kuo et al., 2018, pp. 5–8). Additionally, clinical trials such as the Phase 2 randomized trial for neovascular AMD (albeit focused on wet AMD) have assessed everolimus’s efficacy in combination with anti‐vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) agents (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2009), thereby providing indirect support for its ocular pharmacokinetic (PK) profile and safety profile. This background, combined with its well‐known systemic tolerability, underscores its candidacy for repurposing in nonexudative (dry) AMD—a disease area in which few pharmacologic treatments exist.

Mechanism of Action:  
Everolimus exerts its effects by binding to the intracellular receptor FKBP12, forming a complex that interacts with and inhibits mTORC1 (Liu et al., 2023, pp. 11–12; Weber, 2015, pp. 27–28). The inhibition of mTORC1 results in a downstream decrease in the phosphorylation of ribosomal protein S6 kinase (S6K1) and other substrates such as ribosomal protein S6 (RPS6), effectively suppressing cap‐dependent protein synthesis and cellular proliferation (Kuo et al., 2018, pp. 5–7; Liu et al., 2023, pp. 10–11). In the context of RPE cells, inhibition of mTORC1 plays a particularly critical role in modulating autophagic flux. Under normal conditions, mTORC1 phosphorylates and suppresses the transcription factor EB (TFEB), a master regulator of lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy. Inhibition of mTORC1 frees TFEB to translocate to the nucleus where it transactivates genes that codify for lysosomal proteins, such as the subunits of the vacuolar ATPase (V‐ATPase), and hydrolases including cathepsin D (Kuo et al., 2018, p. 7; Nieto et al., 2015, pp. 28–32). Thus, monotherapy with an mTORC1 inhibitor may not be sufficiently robust to address all disease mechanisms. Combination therapies that target multiple pathological pathways might ultimately be necessary for effective disease modification. Its solid record as an FDA‐approved drug with established dosing regimens and acceptable systemic safety lends additional support to its viability as a repurposing candidate. It will be crucial to establish that systemic dosing can achieve therapeutic retinal concentrations without eliciting unintended systemic toxicity or disrupting normal RPE physiology.

Overall, while mechanistic and preclinical data provide a strong rationale for repurposing everolimus to treat dry AMD, further rigorous preclinical studies specifically in models of dry AMD are warranted. A careful evaluation of dosing regimens, potential adverse effects, and efficacy endpoints will be essential in the translational development of everolimus for this indication. The mechanistic specificity for mTORC1 inhibition, combined with the ability to enhance autophagic clearance in RPE cells, represents a significant strength that could offer a novel approach to modifying the course of dry AMD. However, the challenges associated with systemic mTOR inhibition and the need for combination strategies or localized delivery systems must be addressed in subsequent research phases. In conclusion, everolimus is a promising, though not yet definitively validated, candidate for repurposing in dry AMD, and we recommend that further detailed studies be undertaken to fully elucidate its potential in restoring lysosomal function and ameliorating retinal degeneration in this patient population (Liu et al., 2023, pp. 11–12; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2009; Kuo et al., 2018, pp. 5–7; Weber, 2015, pp. 27–28; Wang et al., 2022, pp. 6–8; Kuo et al., 2018, pp. 7–8).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
GSK2656157 is a small‐molecule inhibitor of PERK (protein kinase R–like endoplasmic reticulum kinase) that was discovered and optimized through medicinal‐chemistry efforts originally led by GlaxoSmithKline. This compound belongs to the class of ATP‐competitive, Type I inhibitors that target the kinase domain of PERK, binding within the ATP‐binding cleft and stabilizing a “DFG‐in, Cα‐helix shifted” conformation of the dephosphorylated kinase domain (Axten, 2017, pp. 15–19). Structurally, the compound is an indoline‐derived molecule; similar chemical series include the indoline/aminoquinazoline chemotypes that have been widely profiled for their high potency and kinase selectivity across panels exceeding 300 kinases (Axten, 2017, pp. 15–19). Originally, these inhibitors were developed as research tools to interrogate the role of PERK in the unfolded protein response (UPR) in oncology and neurodegeneration contexts, and in preclinical studies GSK2656157 demonstrated activity in suppressing tumor growth and angiogenesis in mouse xenograft models via inhibition of PERK autophosphorylation (Atkins et al., 2013, pp. 1–2, 8). As a synthetic small molecule, its origins lie in rational design based on X‐ray–guided structure–activity relationships, which enabled optimization for both high selectivity (with >100‐fold selectivity over related kinases including other eIF2α kinases as well as a broad kinome panel) and sufficient in vivo pharmacokinetics (Axten, 2017, pp. 15–19; Atkins et al., 2013, pp. 1–2). Thus, from a chemical and developmental perspective, GSK2656157 is a first‐in‐class PERK inhibitor that exemplifies how targeted kinase inhibition can be achieved by rational design.  

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, PERK inhibitors such as GSK2606414 and its more selective derivative GSK2656157 were developed primarily for indications in oncology and neurodegeneration. Preclinical studies in tumor xenograft models have demonstrated that oral dosing of GSK2656157 can suppress PERK-mediated signaling, resulting in attenuated phospho-eIF2α levels, diminished transcriptional responses of unfolded protein response (UPR) genes, and reduced tumor vascular density (Atkins et al., 2013, pp. 1–2, 8). In neurodegenerative models—for instance in prion and tauopathy mouse models—PERK inhibition has been shown to restore global protein synthesis, decrease the levels of phospho-tau, and produce mixed effects on behavior and neuronal survival (Rozpędek-Kamińska et al., 2020, pp. 17–19). Meanwhile, within the ocular space, experimental studies with the closely related PERK inhibitor GSK2606414 (a chemical analogue of GSK2656157) in in vitro retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cell models have demonstrated on-target inhibition of PERK signaling (evidenced by reduction in eIF2α phosphorylation) along with downstream alterations in stress markers such as CHOP and VEGF mRNA (Jiang et al., 2017, pp. 1–2). However, direct use of GSK2656157 in dry AMD or similar inflammatory/degenerative ocular conditions has not yet been reported in the literature. Some studies investigating retinal degeneration models, such as P23H rhodopsin transgenic rats, have suggested that PERK inhibition can worsen photoreceptor survival by enhancing misfolded protein aggregation, although these studies were typically conducted with compounds such as GSK2606414A (Athanasiou et al., 2017, pp. 1–2, 5–7). There is, therefore, limited clinical or preclinical history regarding the use of GSK2656157 specifically in AMD or related ocular diseases. In addition, while the compound has demonstrated acceptable pharmacokinetics and tolerability in preclinical oncology settings—with measurable systemic exposures—it is important to note that systemic PERK inhibition in multiple species has been associated with toxic liabilities such as pancreatic toxicity (Atkins et al., 2013, p. 8; Axten, 2017, pp. 1–7). Consequently, although the therapeutic class has a relatively rich history in oncology and neurodegeneration, its direct application to dry AMD remains a new and untested repurposing approach that requires careful consideration of pharmacodynamic impacts in ocular tissues and rigorous safety profiling.  

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, PERK functions as an endoplasmic reticulum (ER)–resident kinase that is activated upon the accumulation of misfolded proteins, a hallmark of chronic ER stress. Normally, when the ER’s folding capacity is overwhelmed, the molecular chaperone GRP78 dissociates from PERK, enabling PERK to oligomerize and autophosphorylate, which then enables it to phosphorylate the α subunit of eukaryotic initiation factor 2 (eIF2α) at serine-51 (Axten, 2017, pp. 7–11). Phosphorylation of eIF2α leads to a global reduction in protein synthesis—a protective adaptation that prevents further accumulation of misfolded proteins—and also selectively permits the translation of stress-induced genes, most notably ATF4. ATF4 subsequently upregulates transcription factors such as CHOP, which can drive pro-apoptotic signaling if ER stress persists (Axten, 2017, pp. 7–11; Chu et al., 2021, p. 8). In the context of dry AMD, chronic ER stress in RPE cells has been implicated in disrupting cellular proteostasis, where misfolded proteins—including subunits of key complexes like the vacuolar ATPase (v-ATPase)—may fail to fold properly, leading to impaired lysosomal acidification (Kaarniranta et al., 2018, pp. 1–4; Athanasiou et al., 2017, pp. 1–2). The hypothesis is that by inhibiting PERK with GSK2656157, the excessive phosphorylation of eIF2α and the maladaptive integrated stress response (ISR) can be attenuated. This would not only restore global protein synthesis but also prevent downstream consequences such as upregulation of CHOP and VEGF, thereby reducing pro-apoptotic as well as pro-inflammatory pathways (Jiang et al., 2017, pp. 1–2). Furthermore, it is posited that such normalization in the ISR could allow for proper folding and assembly of lysosomal enzymes and complexes, including the v-ATPase. Proper v-ATPase assembly is critical for maintaining low intraluminal pH in lysosomes, which is necessary for the activation and maturation of hydrolases like cathepsin D (Kaarniranta et al., 2018, pp. 1–4). In neuronal models, PERK inhibition has been associated with improvements in lysosomal function and proteostasis, indicating that reduction of chronic ER stress can indirectly favor the re-establishment of lysosomal homeostasis (Jiang et al., 2017, pp. 1–2). In essence, GSK2656157, by specifically targeting and inhibiting PERK, interferes with the pathological arm of the UPR (i.e. excessive eIF2α phosphorylation) that is hypothesized to contribute to impaired lysosomal acidification in RPE cells under chronic stress conditions—a mechanism that might be particularly relevant in the pathophysiology of dry AMD (Axten, 2017, pp. 24–28).

In the proposed assays, the primary expected effect of GSK2656157 is to inhibit PERK activity in RPE cells, as evidenced by reduced phosphorylation of eIF2α, and thereby dampen downstream signaling events that lead to the induction of ATF4, CHOP, and ultimately pro-apoptotic and proangiogenic factors such as VEGF. In vitro studies with analogues of GSK2656157 (such as GSK2606414) in ARPE-19 cells have shown dose-dependent inhibition of eIF2α phosphorylation with subsequent decreases in CHOP and VEGF mRNA expression without necessarily triggering apoptosis at higher doses (Jiang et al., 2017, pp. 1–2). These results provide a proof-of-concept that pharmacological inhibition of PERK can modulate this critical signaling pathway in RPE cells. The hypothesis for dry AMD is that chronic ER stress in the RPE disrupts lysosomal acidification via misfolding of v-ATPase subunits; under normal circumstances, proper v-ATPase function ensures that lysosomes maintain their acidic environment, which is essential for protease activation—including cathepsin D. Cathepsin D, in turn, is critical for lysosomal degradation of photoreceptor outer segments and for preventing lipofuscin accumulation, a pathological process in dry AMD (Kaarniranta et al., 2018, pp. 1–4). Thus, by reducing PERK activation through GSK2656157, it is expected that the overactive ISR would be tempered sufficiently to allow for the proper folding and assembly of v-ATPase complexes, thereby restoring lysosomal acidification (Chu et al., 2021, p. 8; Athanasiou et al., 2017, pp. 1–2). This restoration is anticipated to improve cathepsin D maturation and activity, leading to better clearance of intracellular debris and misfolded proteins, ultimately protecting RPE cells from stress-induced degeneration. Therefore, if GSK2656157 can achieve adequate ocular tissue exposure and inhibit PERK activity in the RPE, the expected outcome would be a reduction in cellular stress–mediated apoptosis and proliferation of protective pathways that maintain lysosomal and autophagy functions (Jiang et al., 2017, pp. 1–2; Rozpędek-Kamińska et al., 2020, pp. 17–19). Overall, GSK2656157 presents an intriguing therapeutic candidate for dry AMD based on a mechanistic hypothesis that links chronic ER stress to impaired lysosomal acidification—a process central to the pathogenesis of AMD. One of the primary strengths of GSK2656157 is its potent and selective inhibition of PERK, a critical mediator of the integrated stress response. The compound’s design as an ATP‐competitive PERK inhibitor places it squarely in a class of drugs that have been well characterized in terms of kinase selectivity and in vivo pharmacodynamics in oncology settings (Axten, 2017, pp. 15–19). The underlying biological rationale is that by attenuating the maladaptive PERK-mediated phosphorylation of eIF2α, it may be possible to relieve chronic translational suppression and dampen downstream deleterious signaling cascades—thereby re-establishing normal lysosomal function through proper v-ATPase assembly and restoration of cathepsin D activity (Axten, 2017, pp. 7–11; Chu et al., 2021, p. 8). However, there are several notable weaknesses and caveats. First, while there is an extensive body of preclinical work on PERK inhibitors in oncology and neurodegeneration models, there is a significant lack of direct evidence in ocular disease models—especially chronic models of dry AMD—as well as an absence of published studies specifically evaluating GSK2656157 in RPE cells or in animal models of AMD (Athanasiou et al., 2017, pp. 5–7). In several studies using related PERK inhibitors in rod photoreceptor degeneration models (such as P23H rhodopsin transgenic rats), inhibition of PERK activity has been associated with worsened outcomes, suggesting that PERK activation may paradoxically be protective in certain contexts of protein misfolding (Athanasiou et al., 2017, pp. 1–2, 5–7). This dichotomous role of PERK—as both an adaptive and a pro-death signal depending on the context and duration of activation—raises concerns about whether inhibition will uniformly yield beneficial effects in the RPE, whose balance of ER stress responses may differ from that of neuronal or secretory tissues. Second, while the hypothesis postulates that chronic ER stress impairs lysosomal acidification by misfolding v-ATPase subunits, the direct link between PERK inhibition and restoration of v-ATPase assembly or cathepsin D maturation in RPE cells has not been firmly established in the literature. Data that explicitly demonstrate that PERK inhibition rescues lysosomal pH, enhances v-ATPase function, and improves cathepsin D activity in neuronal models may exist, yet similar studies in ocular models are limited (Chu et al., 2021, p. 8; Kaarniranta et al., 2018, pp. 1–4). Third, the systemic administration of PERK inhibitors such as GSK2656157 has been associated with pancreatic toxicity and other systemic adverse effects in preclinical studies, a liability that could be particularly problematic in chronic therapies such as those needed for dry AMD (Atkins et al., 2013, p. 8; Axten, 2017, pp. 1–7). Although strategies such as local (intravitreal) delivery might mitigate these systemic risks, ocular pharmacokinetic and tolerability data are sparse, and the tissue-specific distribution of GSK2656157 in the eye would need careful evaluation (Atkins et al., 2013, pp. 1–2, 8). Fourth, there is some concern over off-target effects; for example, early reports on similar GSK compounds noted possible inhibition of RIP1 kinase activity, although subsequent studies have argued that the effects observed were indeed mediated by PERK inhibition (Starr, 2019, pp. 133–137; Athanasiou et al., 2017, pp. 5–7). Nonetheless, affording absolute selectivity in a clinical candidate remains a challenge. In addition, chronic inhibition of the adaptive aspects of the ISR may inadvertently impair protective mechanisms in the retina, as transient ISR activation is known to mediate cellular adaptation during acute stress (Axten, 2017, pp. 7–11, 24–28).

In summary, while the mechanistic rationale for using GSK2656157 to address dry AMD is based on a conceptually appealing hypothesis—that PERK inhibition will relieve chronic ER stress, thereby restoring proper lysosomal acidification, enabling v-ATPase assembly, and rescuing cathepsin D activity in RPE cells—the current body of literature reveals both promising on-target effects in non-ocular systems and significant gaps in ocular-specific efficacy and safety data. Given the complex, context-dependent role of PERK signaling in retinal homeostasis and the potential for deleterious outcomes when PERK is inhibited in models of protein misfolding, further focused in vitro and in vivo studies are required to determine whether GSK2656157 can be safely and effectively repurposed for dry AMD. Strengths of this candidate include its potent, selective PERK inhibition and preclinical pharmacodynamic proof-of-concept in related disease models, while weaknesses center on limited ocular data, potential systemic and off-target toxicities, and an uncertain impact on lysosomal and proteostatic pathways in RPE cells. Ultimately, while GSK2656157 remains an attractive avenue for targeting an upstream stress node in dry AMD pathogenesis, careful optimization of dosing, targeted ocular delivery, and comprehensive evaluation in relevant AMD models will be essential before moving forward in clinical development (Axten, 2017, pp. 1–7, 15–19, 24–28; Atkins et al., 2013, pp. 1–2; Athanasiou et al., 2017, pp. 5–7; Jiang et al., 2017, pp. 1–2).

By contrast, there is considerable disease-relevant literature on CTSD biology in RPE and on pharmacological strategies that indirectly restore CTSD function by correcting upstream lysosomal defects. In the RPE/AMD literature, multiple lines of evidence support CTSD as a major lysosomal protease necessary for POS degradation and proteostasis. CTSD deficiency or pharmacologic inhibition impairs POS proteolysis, provokes accumulation of debris reminiscent of drusen, and is linked to retinal dysfunction in animal models, reinforcing its centrality to RPE homeostasis (Mahmud, 2019). A second therapeutic precedent relevant to “enhancing CTSD function” is enzyme augmentation. Recombinant pro-CTSD administration has been reported to correct proteolysis and autophagy defects in neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis (CLN10/CTSD deficiency), and intravitreal enzyme replacement strategies in other lysosomal storage diseases (e.g., TPP1 in CLN2) have preserved retinal structure/function in preclinical models, supporting feasibility of increasing lysosomal enzyme function in ocular tissues (Liu, 2021). These studies, while not in AMD and not small molecules, validate the general concept that augmenting CTSD can rescue lysosomal degradative failure in retina-derived tissues.

In summary, there is no therapeutic history for NSC19723 itself in the provided sources; however, there is an increasingly robust therapeutic precedent that pharmacological manipulation which restores CTSD maturation/activity in RPE improves degradative capacity and disease-relevant readouts in lipofuscin-accumulating retinal disorders, and that enzyme augmentation of lysosomal hydrolases can be effective in ocular degenerations driven by lysosomal insufficiency (Ng et al., 2024; Liu, 2021).

Mechanism of Action  
CTSD biosynthesis and maturation provide the mechanistic backdrop for a CTSD maturation enhancer. CTSD is synthesized as pre-procathepsin D with a signal peptide (for ER translocation) and a propeptide that maintains the zymogen in an inactive, folding-competent state; the protein acquires N-linked glycans and an M6P tag in the Golgi for M6P-receptor–mediated trafficking to late endosomes/lysosomes, where acidic pH facilitates removal of the propeptide, proteolytic processing, and generation of the mature, active enzyme (heavy and light chains) (Sharif, 2015). As an aspartic protease, CTSD employs two Asp residues to activate and position a water molecule for nucleophilic attack on the scissile peptide bond, a chemistry that requires acidic conditions for optimal catalysis; in neutral or alkaline environments, activity falls sharply, explaining why lysosomal alkalinization in disease states compromises both maturation and steady-state activity (Sharif, 2015; Ng et al., 2024).

Functionally, impaired CTSD maturation/activity correlates with delayed degradation of internalized POS and accumulation of aggregation-prone substrates such as α-synuclein, consistent with CTSD’s principal role in RPE proteolysis of rhodopsin and POS proteins; CTSD is reported to account for the majority of rhodopsin degradation in RPE and exhibits far higher proteolytic activity than cathepsin B against POS substrates (Ng et al., 2024). If achieved without broad, off-target activation of other proteases or perturbation of lysosomal pH/ion homeostasis, this mechanism would distinguish NSC19723 from autophagy inducers (e.g., rapamycin) or pH re-acidifiers (e.g., ticagrelor), while being convergent on the same functional outcome: restored CTSD proteolysis and lysosomal degradative capacity (Frost et al., 2014; Ng et al., 2024).

Mechanistic cross-talk and constraints that are relevant for a CTSD maturation enhancer include:  
- pH dependence: CTSD maturation and catalysis require acidic lysosomes; in alkaline lysosomes (e.g., due to bisretinoid accumulation), pro-CTSD processing is impaired even if total CTSD protein increases, so a maturation accelerator may be insufficient without concurrent restoration of lysosomal pH in some disease states (Ng et al., 2024).

Collectively, the mechanistic plausibility that a small molecule could stabilize a conformation of pro-CTSD that accelerates propeptide removal and activation in acidic lysosomes is strong, and a favorable on-target pharmacodynamic effect can be anchored to clearly measurable, disease-relevant biochemical endpoints in RPE (Ng et al., 2024). The key risk is that without correction of lysosomal pH, pro-CTSD processing bottlenecks may persist; therefore, a CTSD maturation enhancer may be best deployed in lysosomes that are sufficiently acidic or in combination with pH-restoring strategies (Ng et al., 2024).
