Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
SH-BC-893 is proposed as a small-molecule v-ATPase activator intended to allosterically stabilize the proton pump in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) lysosomes, thereby enhancing proton transport, reacidifying the lumen, and restoring cathepsin D (CTSD) maturation and activity to improve degradative flux relevant to dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) pathology. However, within the provided literature set there are no primary or review data naming SH-BC-893, describing its chemical class, discovery, or synthetic route, nor preclinical evaluations in ocular systems or other indications; moreover, no registered clinical trials in AMD list this agent on ClinicalTrials.gov, and no AMD trials list “v-ATPase” as an intervention term, indicating a lack of clinical development signals under those names in this registry at the time of the query (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.-a; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.-b). In contrast, the broader therapeutic class—agents that restore lysosomal acidity or augment lysosome/autophagy capacity—has been investigated in RPE disease models using several orthogonal strategies (e.g., cAMP-elevating ligands, zinc ionophores, TFEB activation, and acidifying nanoparticles), but none of the provided sources report a direct small-molecule v-ATPase activator tested in ocular models (RPE or AMD) or any mention of SH-BC-893 by name (Ng et al., 2024, pp. 3–5, 10–12, 13–15; Choi et al., 2024, pp. 18–29, 29–36; Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7; Li et al., 2025, pp. 17–20, 27–29). By mechanistic category, SH-BC-893 would fall under lysosomal function restorers that act directly on the lumenal acidification machinery; the central target, the vacuolar-type H⁺-ATPase (v-ATPase), is the multisubunit rotary proton pump that establishes lysosomal acidity required for hydrolase activity and autophagic/heterophagic flux in RPE, a post-mitotic, highly phagocytic epithelium that ingests and degrades photoreceptor outer segments daily (Kaarniranta et al., 2023, pp. 2–3; Sinha et al., 2016, pp. 1–3). The V1 sector hydrolyzes ATP and the V0 sector conducts protons across the membrane, with subunit stoichiometries and regulatory dynamics (e.g., reversible V1–V0 association) that tune organelle pH; acidic pH ~4.5–5.0 is required for optimal lysosomal enzyme activity and membrane integrity (Chen et al., 2025, pp. 2–5). While reports outside the eye document multiple regulatory levers for v-ATPase assembly/activity (kinase control, accessory complexes, isoform selection), the provided sources do not identify a validated medicinal chemistry series that positively and directly activates v-ATPase in RPE or AMD models (Chen et al., 2025, pp. 22–23; Song et al., 2020, pp. 13–14).

Therapeutic History  
There is no documented clinical or veterinary use of SH-BC-893 in AMD or related retinal degeneration in the provided corpus, and the ClinicalTrials.gov query identified no trials in AMD with SH-BC-893 as an intervention (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.-a). Likewise, no AMD trials explicitly list “v-ATPase” as the intervention in the registry result provided (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.-b). Within ocular preclinical literature, restoration of lysosomal acidity and degradative capacity has been targeted by alternative pharmacologic or biophysical means, each reinforcing the disease rationale but not testing a v-ATPase activator per se. In ABCA4-mediated Stargardt models (human iPSC-RPE from STGD1 patients and Abca4⁻/⁻ mice), lysosomal alkalinization, impaired maturation of CTSD (accumulation of pro-CTSD), and reduced CTSD activity were demonstrated; pharmacologic lysosomal reacidification with the P2Y₁₂ antagonist ticagrelor lowered lysosomal pH, rescued CTSD maturation/activity, reduced CTSD aggregates, decreased autofluorescence, and protected photoreceptors, supporting therapeutic relevance of acidification in RPE disease (Ng et al., 2024, pp. 3–5, 10–12, 13–15). In these same systems, acidification was linked to restored degradation of outer segments (OS), a core RPE function degraded in AMD-like states (Ng et al., 2024, pp. 10–12, 13–15).

Independent strategies have shown that raising intracellular zinc with ionophores reacidifies A2E-alkalinized lysosomes, restores autophagic flux, reduces intracellular A2E burden, and protects ARPE-19 against A2E-induced cytotoxicity; in vivo chloroquine-induced alkalinization produced AMD-like pathology, again underscoring the central role of lysosomal pH (Choi et al., 2024, pp. 18–29, 29–36). Nanoparticle delivery of acidic polymers (PLGA) has attenuated weak-base–induced lysosomal alkalinization and preserved CTSD activity in RPE and optic nerve astrocytes, demonstrating a delivery-based reacidification modality with high lysosomal colocalization (Li et al., 2025, pp. 17–20). Upstream enhancement of lysosomal biogenesis, acidification capacity, and hydrolase complement via TFEB activation (viral TFEB-S467A, trehalose) or AKT2 inhibition corrected CTSD/CTSL levels and improved lysosomal/autophagy markers in AMD-relevant RPE models, and rapamycin lowered A2E and lipofuscin-like material in POS-fed cells, with effects contingent on dephosphorylated, nuclear TFEB and active lysosomal enzymes (Ghosh et al., 2024, p. 6; Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7). In other inherited macular disease models (Best disease), inhibition of v-ATPase with bafilomycin phenocopied OS-degradation defects, and enhancing proteolysis/autophagy with valproic acid and rapamycin reduced rhodopsin burden after POS feeding and mitigated long-term autofluorescence accumulation in disease iPSC-RPE, albeit with acknowledged pleiotropy and translational constraints (Singh et al., 2015, pp. 6–7).

Mechanistically proximal genetic models further anchor v-ATPase to RPE health: βA3/A1-crystallin localizes to lysosomes and binds the V0 a1 subunit (ATP6V0A1), regulating v-ATPase activity. Conditional loss of βA3/A1-crystallin (Cryba1) in RPE elevates lysosomal pH, reduces CTSD activity, blocks degradation of ingested OS (despite normal ingestion), impairs autophagosome clearance, and produces vacuolation and retinal dysfunction—an AMD-like phenotype; these data highlight that v-ATPase activity is both necessary for acidification and functionally rate-limiting for RPE clearance pathways (Valapala et al., 2016, pp. 1–6). However, none of these ocular studies demonstrate rescue by pharmacologic or genetic activation of v-ATPase itself; rather, they leverage signaling, transcriptional, or physicochemical routes to restore lysosomal physiology (Boya et al., 2023, pp. 3–6). Outside the eye, enforced expression of the V0 subunit ATP6V0A2 restored lysosomal acidification and conferred protection from epirubicin-induced ferroptosis in cardiomyocytes, establishing that boosting v-ATPase can reacidify lysosomes and yield tissue-protective effects in vivo, but this evidence is in cardiac models and is not ocular (Chen et al., 2025, pp. 16–17).

Mechanism of Action  
The therapeutic hypothesis centers on allosteric stabilization and activation of the v-ATPase proton pump in RPE lysosomes to lower luminal pH and normalize the acid-hydrolase environment. This is well aligned with the biochemistry of RPE lysosomes and AMD pathobiology. v-ATPase is the principal proton pump creating the lysosomal pH gradient; the V1 sector (A3B3CDE3FG3H) hydrolyzes ATP, and the V0 sector (a c₉ c′′ d e along with ATP6AP1 and ATP6AP2) translocates protons into the lumen, thereby enabling activity of acidic hydrolases and supporting autophagy and phagolysosomal degradation (Chen et al., 2025, pp. 2–5). RPE are uniquely burdened by daily phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments, and efficient lysosomal acidification is required to degrade these discs and recycle their components; impaired acidification disrupts heterophagy and autophagy, leading to lipofuscin and drusen accumulation recognized as core AMD cellular features (Kaarniranta et al., 2023, pp. 1–3; Sinha et al., 2016, pp. 1–3).

CTSD is the dominant lysosomal aspartyl protease in RPE, responsible for the bulk of rhodopsin proteolysis; its maturation (from preproenzyme to active heavy/light chains) and catalytic activity are sharply pH-dependent, with activity falling profoundly upon modest pH elevation (e.g., near pH 5.0) (Ng et al., 2024, pp. 13–15; Valapala et al., 2016, pp. 1–4). In patient-derived STGD1 iPSC-RPE and Abca4⁻/⁻ mice, lysosomal alkalinization is associated with accumulation of immature pro-CTSD, decreased mature CTSD, loss of CTSD activity, impaired OS digestion, protein aggregation (α-synuclein), and LAP/autophagy defects linked to perturbed phosphatidylethanolamine composition; pharmacologic reacidification restores CTSD maturation and proteolysis, reduces cathepsin aggregates, and improves degradative function, validating the causal sequence from pH to CTSD to flux (Ng et al., 2024, pp. 3–8, 10–15). These CTSD-centric dependencies underscore why direct v-ATPase activation could be an efficient lever: it addresses the proximal physical determinant (pH) needed for CTSD maturation and broad lysosomal hydrolase competency (Kaarniranta et al., 2023, pp. 2–3; Sinha et al., 2016, pp. 1–3).

Endogenous control of v-ATPase in RPE is exemplified by βA3/A1-crystallin, which binds ATP6V0A1 on the lysosomal membrane and appears to modulate catalytic efficiency; loss of βA3/A1-crystallin reduces v-ATPase activity, elevates pH, and diminishes CTSD activity with consequent degradative blockade and AMD-like retinal changes (Valapala et al., 2016, pp. 1–6). v-ATPase also participates in amino acid sensing and mTORC1 recruitment via the Ragulator–Rag GTPase axis; this signaling can suppress autophagy when hyperactivated, while TFEB—the master regulator of lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy genes—depends on mTORC1 dephosphorylation for nuclear entry and CLEAR-network activation (including ATP6V0A1 expression), placing v-ATPase at the hub of both acidification and signaling that set lysosomal capacity (Sinha et al., 2016, pp. 3–4; Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7). In AMD donor RPE, TFEB is more phosphorylated (cytosolic/inactive), and CTSD/CTSL protein levels and activities are reduced; constitutively active TFEB upregulates CLEAR genes (e.g., CTSB, LAMP2, ATP6V0A1) and reduces POS-dependent lipofuscin-like granules, while rapamycin reduces A2E and autofluorescent granules via TFEB activation and active lysosomal enzymes, reinforcing that increasing lysosomal gene expression and function rescues RPE degradative deficits (Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7).

The regulatory literature further indicates v-ATPase activity is controlled by signal-dependent assembly/disassembly, kinase phosphorylation, and accessory factors (RAVE, Rabconnectin-3, AMPK, PKA, AKT), as well as lipid and trafficking determinants; small-molecule perturbations in non-ocular contexts can modulate v-ATPase assembly or activity, though some agents cause over-acidification and cytotoxicity, emphasizing the need for precise tuning (Chen et al., 2025, pp. 22–23). None of the provided sources, however, describe SH-BC-893’s binding site, affinity, kinetics, effect on V1–V0 association, or selectivity across v-ATPase isoforms; nor do they document its effects on mitochondrial membrane potential, autophagic flux metrics, or ocular safety—these are central unknowns that would need to be established experimentally to substantiate the proposed allosteric-activation mechanism (Song et al., 2020, pp. 13–14; Chen et al., 2025, pp. 22–23).

Expected Effect  
If SH-BC-893 positively stabilizes and activates lysosomal v-ATPase in RPE, the expected sequence is: increased proton pumping → lower lysosomal pH toward physiologic (~4.5–5.0) → enhanced maturation of CTSD (and other cathepsins) → increased hydrolase activity → improved degradation of POS cargo in phagolysosomes and of autophagic substrates → reduction of lipofuscin/A2E accumulation and secondary inflammation → improved RPE homeostasis and photoreceptor support. This causal chain is strongly supported by multiple interventions that restore acidic pH or upregulate lysosomal capacity in RPE models. In STGD1 iPSC-RPE and Abca4⁻/⁻ mice, pharmacologic reacidification with ticagrelor lowered lysosomal pH, reduced pro-CTSD aggregates by roughly half, restored mature CTSD levels and enzymatic activity to near-normal, reduced autofluorescence, and protected photoreceptors—directly validating that reacidification rescues CTSD and degradative function in disease-relevant RPE (Ng et al., 2024, pp. 3–5, 10–12, 13–15). In ARPE-19, zinc ionophores reacidified A2E-alkalinized lysosomes, normalized autophagic flux (reduced p62/LC3-II accumulation), lowered A2E burden, and decreased cell death; conversely, chloroquine alkalinization generated AMD-like in vivo pathology, indicating bidirectional control and the importance of acidification for RPE viability (Choi et al., 2024, pp. 18–29, 29–36). Acidic PLGA nanoparticles attenuated tamoxifen-induced lysosomal alkalinization and preserved CTSD catalytic-site binding by BODIPY FL-Pepstatin A, indicating restored CTSD activity in RPE and optic nerve astrocytes (Li et al., 2025, pp. 17–20). Activation of TFEB or mTOR inhibition increased CLEAR genes (including ATP6V0A1), reduced A2E and lipofuscin-like granules, and restored CTSD/CTSL abundance and activity together with lysosomal markers (LAMP1), consistent with enhanced lysosomal biogenesis/function and improved degradation (Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7; Ghosh et al., 2024, p. 6).

Expression of the relevant target machinery in the cell type is established: v-ATPase is the essential proton pump of lysosomes in RPE, and ATP6V0A1 (V0 a1) is a CLEAR gene upregulated by TFEB activation in these cells; CTSD and CTSL activities are reduced in AMD donor RPE, further underscoring the therapeutic importance of restoring lysosomal hydrolase function (Kaarniranta et al., 2023, pp. 2–3; Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7). Genetic data in Cryba1 cKO RPE demonstrate that reduced v-ATPase activity elevates lysosomal pH and decreases CTSD activity, blocking OS degradation and autophagic clearance, thereby establishing the proximal role of v-ATPase in RPE homeostasis (Valapala et al., 2016, pp. 1–6). Together, these data imply that a direct v-ATPase activator—if selective for lysosomes in RPE and capable of sufficient exposure—should lower lysosomal pH and increase CTSD activity, with predicted improvements in OS degradation, autophagic flux, and reductions in lipofuscin-like autofluorescence in dry AMD-relevant assays (Ng et al., 2024, pp. 3–5, 10–12, 13–15; Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7).

Nevertheless, two mechanistic cautions should shape experimental expectations. First, v-ATPase also couples lysosomal amino acid sensing to mTORC1 activation through Ragulator–Rag GTPases; augmenting v-ATPase function could, context-dependently, promote mTORC1 signaling, which suppresses autophagy if chronically hyperactivated, potentially counteracting benefits unless managed (Sinha et al., 2016, pp. 3–4). Second, inducing autophagy when lysosomal function is compromised can be cytotoxic; therefore, combination strategies that simultaneously stimulate autophagy and correct acidity must be balanced and staged to avoid flux–capacity mismatches (Boya et al., 2023, pp. 8–9).

Outside the eye, enforced ATP6V0A2 expression restored lysosomal acidification and conferred myocardial protection in cardiomyocytes, providing precedent that increasing v-ATPase function can reacidify lysosomes in vivo (Chen et al., 2025, pp. 16–17).

These cross-validate the target biology (lysosomal acidity, CTSD) while highlighting that pharmacologic v-ATPase activation has not yet been documented in these systems in the provided corpus.

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- High mechanistic plausibility in RPE: v-ATPase is the core determinant of lysosomal acidification; RPE requires robust lysosomal degradation for heterophagy and autophagy; and lysosomal alkalinization is a recurring lesion in AMD-like and Stargardt models (Kaarniranta et al., 2023, pp. 1–3; Sinha et al., 2016, pp. 1–3). Key Risks and Gaps  
- No evidence base for SH-BC-893: There are no publications or registry entries in the provided corpus documenting the identity, synthesis, class, binding site, target engagement, potency/selectivity, ocular PK/PD, or safety of SH-BC-893; consequently, the core claims about allosteric stabilization of the V0 domain and selective lysosomal activation in RPE cannot be substantiated here (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.-a; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.-b; Song et al., 2020, pp. 13–14).

- Target validity and disease linkage are strong: RPE lysosomal acidification defects and reduced CTSD function are documented in AMD donor tissue and in human disease-model RPE; reacidification restores CTSD and degradative function; v-ATPase sits at the mechanistic bottleneck (Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7; Ng et al., 2024, pp. 3–5, 10–12, 13–15; Kaarniranta et al., 2023, pp. 2–3).

- Establish compound identity and primary pharmacology: Because no SH-BC-893 data are available here, first confirm chemical identity, V0-domain binding, v-ATPase activation, and selectivity across organelles and tissues using biophysical assays and lysosomal pH measurements; define concentration–response for pH and CTSD activity in human iPSC-RPE derived from AMD donors or aged controls (Chen et al., 2025, pp. 2–5; Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7).

- Dissect signaling interactions: Quantify mTORC1 activity (p-S6K, p-4EBP1), TFEB localization, and CLEAR gene expression (including ATP6V0A1) to ensure that v-ATPase activation does not chronically hyperactivate mTORC1 and suppress autophagy; consider combination with TFEB-enhancing regimens if needed (Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7; Sinha et al., 2016, pp. 3–4).  
- Evaluate lysosomal membrane integrity and inflammation: Track LMP markers, cytosolic cathepsins, and inflammasome readouts to ensure acidification does not destabilize overloaded lysosomes; measure complement-related inflammation and secretory autophagy outputs, given their linkage to AMD (Boya et al., 2023, pp. 3–4).  
- In vivo pharmacology in RPE-driven models: Transition to models with documented lysosomal alkalinization and lipofuscin/A2E accumulation (e.g., Abca4⁻/⁻ mice), using ocular delivery to maximize RPE exposure; endpoints: in vivo RPE/retinal imaging of autofluorescence, ERG, photoreceptor survival, and RPE ultrastructure; pharmacodynamic tissue assays for pH and CTSD (Ng et al., 2024, pp. 3–5, 10–12, 13–15).

Conclusion  
On target biology, the rationale for lysosomal acidification in RPE as a disease-modifying strategy for dry AMD is compelling, and restoration of CTSD maturation/activity via pH correction is repeatedly shown to rescue degradative function and reduce toxic pigment accumulation in human RPE models and in vivo Stargardt systems (Ng et al., 2024, pp. 3–5, 10–12, 13–15; Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7). v-ATPase is the proximal driver of lysosomal acidity, genetically and mechanistically tied to RPE degradative competence and AMD-like phenotypes (Valapala et al., 2016, pp. 1–6). However, the specific drug candidate SH-BC-893 lacks any corroborating information in the provided literature set—no chemical identity, mechanism data, ocular pharmacology, or clinical development signals—so the central claims about its discovery and performance cannot be verified here (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.-a; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.-b). Therefore, while a v-ATPase activator remains an attractive therapeutic concept with strong biological underpinnings in RPE, SH-BC-893 should be considered unvalidated based on the sources provided, and a go/no-go decision would require de novo demonstration of selective v-ATPase activation, lysosomal reacidification, CTSD rescue, and durable functional benefit in RPE with a clear ocular safety margin (Boya et al., 2023, pp. 3–6; Sinha et al., 2016, pp. 3–4).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Lithium chloride (Sigma L9650) is an inorganic salt belonging to the family of lithium compounds that has been in use for several decades, primarily as a mood stabilizer in the treatment of bipolar disorder. It is synthesized by combining lithium carbonate or lithium hydroxide with hydrochloric acid, yielding a highly water‐soluble salt that is widely available for both clinical and experimental research purposes (Carmassi et al., 2016; Vallée et al., 2021). As a prototypical member of the lithium salts, lithium chloride has been repurposed in recent years as a candidate for neuroprotection because of its ability to inhibit glycogen synthase kinase-3β (GSK3β), a serine/threonine kinase involved in numerous intracellular signaling cascades. Lithium’s chemical simplicity belies its complex pharmacology; its effects extend well beyond mood stabilization to encompass modulation of cell survival, inflammatory responses, and protein degradation pathways. In this context, lithium salts are now recognized as small molecule modulators that can affect intracellular transcriptional programs, including nuclear import of factors such as transcription factor EB (TFEB) and β-catenin, which in turn control the expression of genes necessary for lysosomal biogenesis and autophagic flux (Carmassi et al., 2016; Vallée et al., 2021). These mechanistic insights, originally developed in studies of neurodegenerative and psychiatric diseases, have motivated investigations into whether lithium chloride might be repurposed to address the autophagic and lysosomal dysfunction observed in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD), particularly in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) (Carmassi et al., 2016; Vallée et al., 2021).

Therapeutic History:  
Lithium salts have a long-standing clinical history in psychiatry, especially in the management of bipolar disorder, where their dosing and long-term safety profiles have been thoroughly characterized. In addition, numerous preclinical studies in neuroscience have demonstrated that lithium can reduce tau phosphorylation and improve neuronal cell survival, partly by inhibiting GSK3β and modulating downstream targets such as β-catenin and Bcl-2 (Carmassi et al., 2016; Vallée et al., 2021). Lithium has been evaluated in several neurodegenerative contexts—for instance, it has been examined for its potential benefits in Alzheimer’s disease, Huntington’s disease, and Parkinson’s disease, with some studies reporting modest improvements in neuroprotection and behavioral outcomes, although clinical results have been mixed (Singh et al., 2022; Vallée et al., 2021). More specifically, preclinical data in the central nervous system have shown that prolonged exposure to lithium increases cortical grey matter and enhances neuronal markers such as N-acetyl-aspartate, suggesting that lithium exerts trophic and neuroprotective effects (Carmassi et al., 2016). In the ocular arena, while lithium’s use has been predominantly described in the context of glaucoma—in which its inhibition of GSK3β was shown to modulate WNT/β-catenin signaling in trabecular meshwork cells—the literature offers no direct clinical or in-depth preclinical evaluation of lithium chloride in dry AMD or for modulating autophagy specifically in RPE cells (Singh et al., 2022; Vallée et al., 2021). A search in clinical trial registries has not identified any trials using lithium chloride for macular degeneration, underscoring a notable gap between the neuroprotective models in which lithium has been studied and its potential application in dry AMD (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).

Mechanism of Action:  
Lithium chloride’s mechanisms of action are multifaceted, but a significant aspect relevant to the dry AMD hypothesis is its ability to inhibit GSK3β. GSK3β normally phosphorylates a variety of substrates including β-catenin and TFEB, leading to cytosolic retention and subsequent degradation; inhibition of GSK3β by lithium therefore results in stabilization and nuclear accumulation of β-catenin and promotes TFEB nuclear entry (Carmassi et al., 2016; Vallée et al., 2021). In detail, lithium binds directly to the magnesium-sensitive site of GSK3β and also promotes its inhibitory N-terminal serine phosphorylation, leading to a dose-dependent suppression of GSK3β activity (Carmassi et al., 2016). The release of β-catenin from the destruction complex allows it to accumulate in the nucleus, where it acts as a transcriptional coactivator for genes that contribute to cell survival and homeostasis, including those involved in lysosomal biogenesis (Carmassi et al., 2016; Vallée et al., 2021). Similarly, TFEB is a master transcription factor that coordinates the expression of a variety of genes encoding lysosomal enzymes and autophagy-related proteins. Under basal conditions, phosphorylation retains TFEB in the cytosol; inhibition of GSK3β can contribute to dephosphorylation of TFEB, thereby facilitating its nuclear translocation and transcriptional activation of targets such as cathepsin D (CTSD) and subunits of the vacuolar ATPase (v-ATPase) that are crucial for lysosomal acidification (Carmassi et al., 2016; Friedman et al., 2015). In neuronal models, lithium treatment has been demonstrated to increase levels of neurotrophic factors and cell survival molecules, as well as to enhance autophagy-mediated clearance of toxic proteins including aggregated forms of tau and other proteins implicated in neurodegenerative disease (Vallée et al., 2021). Furthermore, lithium’s inhibition of inositol monophosphatase further contributes to autophagy induction through an mTOR-independent mechanism, reinforcing its capacity to modulate autophagic flux (Friedman et al., 2015). Despite these promising mechanistic insights, it is important to note that most of the supporting data have been generated in neuronal or non-ocular cell systems; direct evidence for lithium chloride-mediated activation of TFEB/β-catenin signaling and upregulation of lysosomal acidification machinery specifically in RPE cells remains limited (Golestaneh et al., 2018; Guha et al., 2014).

Expected Effect:  
Based on the hypothesis, treatment with lithium chloride in RPE cells is anticipated to inhibit GSK3β, leading to a cascade of intracellular events that restore impaired autophagic flux—a major pathological hallmark in dry AMD. Specifically, inhibition of GSK3β should reduce the phosphorylation-dependent cytosolic retention of TFEB and β-catenin, thereby facilitating their nuclear import. In the nucleus, these transcription factors can activate a broad transcriptional program that upregulates the synthesis of lysosomal proteins such as cathepsin D and components of the v-ATPase complex, ultimately leading to enhanced lysosomal acidification (Carmassi et al., 2016; Friedman et al., 2015). This improved lysosomal function is expected to accelerate the degradation of photoreceptor outer segment debris and other autophagic substrates, leading to a restoration of autophagic flux and a reduction in lipofuscin accumulation—a prominent feature of dry AMD pathology (Golestaneh et al., 2018). In parallel, lithium’s neuroprotective effects, including the upregulation of prosurvival factors like Bcl-2 and the attenuation of proinflammatory signaling pathways, may further support RPE cell survival and function under chronic oxidative stress conditions (Vallée et al., 2021). Given that lysosomal alkalinization is known to impair cathepsin D activity and autophagic degradation in RPE cells, the upregulation of cathepsin D via TFEB activation represents a critical therapeutic target to counteract the reduced degradative capacity observed in dry AMD (Guha et al., 2014). Moreover, the candidate’s reported ocular penetration and long-term safety in other contexts provide a translational rationale, though the literature is notably deficient in direct measurements of RPE-specific outcomes—thus, further studies are required to validate that lithium chloride achieves effective intraocular concentrations without toxicity (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.; Vallée et al., 2021). The expected outcome in an in vitro assay would be an increase in nuclear TFEB and β-catenin as determined by immunocytochemistry and Western blot of nuclear extracts, an increase in mRNA and protein levels of lysosomal acidification machinery (e.g., v-ATPase subunits) and cathepsin D, restoration of autophagic flux as evidenced by normalized LC3-II/LC3-I ratios and p62 degradation, and improved clearance of photoreceptor outer segment-derived material in RPE cell culture models (Golestaneh et al., 2018).

Overall Evaluation:  
The repurposing of lithium chloride for dry age-related macular degeneration is based on a compelling mechanistic rationale that builds upon well-established aspects of lithium’s pharmacology. On one hand, the drug’s ability to inhibit GSK3β—and thereby to promote the nuclear translocation of TFEB and β-catenin—aligns well with the therapeutic goal of upregulating lysosomal gene expression and restoring autophagic flux in RPE cells (Golestaneh et al., 2018). Lithium’s longstanding use in psychiatric medicine has resulted in a rich and well-documented clinical safety profile, and its neuroprotective benefits in various models lend additional support to its potential utility in other degenerative conditions including ocular diseases (Carmassi et al., 2016; Vallée et al., 2021).

However, there are several notable weaknesses and gaps that must be addressed before lithium chloride can be considered a robust therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. First, while preclinical studies in neuronal models offer supportive evidence that lithium can modulate autophagy and enhance lysosomal function, there is a lack of direct data demonstrating these mechanisms in RPE cells specifically (Golestaneh et al., 2018). Second, the pharmacokinetic profile of lithium chloride in the eye—especially the extent to which it penetrates the RPE following systemic or local administration—remains poorly characterized, and this is a critical factor given the importance of achieving therapeutic concentrations in the retina without causing off-target toxicity (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.). Third, although lithium’s long-term safety has been established in psychiatric populations, its known systemic toxicities, including renal and thyroid effects, as well as its narrow therapeutic window, raise concerns about the potential risks of repurposing it for an ocular indication where localized delivery may be necessary to avoid systemic exposure (Singh et al., 2022; Vallée et al., 2021). Finally, the absence of any registered clinical trials or robust preclinical studies in an AMD model means that the translational viability of lithium chloride for this indication is still highly speculative (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).

Despite these concerns, the strengths of lithium chloride as a repurposed agent for dry AMD are significant. Its ability to target GSK3β provides a unique molecular entry point that could bypass some of the drawbacks of other autophagy modulators that primarily act through mTOR inhibition—a strategy that has yielded mixed clinical results (Friedman et al., 2015; Vallée et al., 2021). Moreover, the multi-modal action of lithium, which encompasses both anti-inflammatory and anti-excitotoxic effects in addition to its autophagy-promoting properties, suggests that it could provide a broad-spectrum protective effect in the stressed cellular environment of the RPE (Carmassi et al., 2016; Vallée et al., 2021). Nonetheless, given the complexity of RPE biology and the multifactorial nature of dry AMD pathogenesis—as evidenced by the alterations in lysosomal pH, reduced cathepsin activity, and compromised membrane trafficking in these cells—any candidate drug must be rigorously evaluated in appropriate RPE or AMD models before clinical translation is attempted (Golestaneh et al., 2018; Guha et al., 2014).

In summary, lithium chloride holds promise as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD through its inhibition of GSK3β and the subsequent activation of nuclear TFEB/β-catenin signaling pathways, which are anticipated to upregulate lysosomal acidification machinery and cathepsin D expression and thereby restore autophagic flux in the RPE. The candidate’s well-documented clinical history and long-term safety in other indications provide additional encouragement for its further preclinical exploration. However, critical issues—such as the need for direct experimental evidence in RPE system models, the establishment of effective and safe ocular dosing regimens with adequate retinal penetration, and thorough evaluations of potential systemic and ocular toxicities—must be rigorously addressed. Until these gaps are filled by focused preclinical and translational research, the use of lithium chloride for dry AMD remains a promising yet still unproven strategy that warrants additional investigation (Carmassi et al., 2016; Friedman et al., 2015; Golestaneh et al., 2018; Guha et al., 2014; Vallée et al., 2021; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.; Singh et al., 2022).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Anakinra (brand: Kineret) is a recombinant, non-glycosylated form of the human interleukin-1 receptor antagonist (IL-1Ra) that competitively binds the type I interleukin-1 receptor (IL-1RI) and prevents signaling by IL-1α and IL-1β, thereby broadly antagonizing downstream IL-1–dependent signal transduction cascades (notably NF-κB and MAPK) in responsive cells (Dabouz, 2024; Dabouz et al., 2020). IL-1Ra belongs to the class of anti-cytokine biologics that block pro-inflammatory cytokine signaling, a therapeutic strategy that has been validated across systemic autoinflammatory and autoimmune diseases; Kineret has an extensive human safety and pharmacology dossier as an approved product, with prescribing information available for systemic use (Mesquida, Drawnel, & Fauser, 2019). Within ophthalmology, IL-1 pathway blockade has been investigated in multiple preclinical ocular models and has seen clinical use for inflammatory eye diseases; routes explored include systemic administration of anakinra for uveitis and scleritis, topical IL-1 antagonists for ocular surface disease (e.g., isunakinra/EBI-005), and experimental ocular gene therapy encoding IL-1Ra (Fabiani et al., 2017). In posterior segment disease models, intravitreal recombinant IL-1Ra (anakinra) inhibited laser-induced choroidal neovascularization (CNV) in rodents in a dose-dependent fashion, establishing local ocular pharmacologic activity of IL-1R antagonism in retina/choroid (Fabiani et al., 2017; Sandhu, Lambert, Xu, & Kaplan, 2018).

Therapeutic History  
Systemic indications and ocular inflammatory experience. Anakinra has long been employed systemically in rheumatology and has been repurposed for ocular autoinflammatory and autoimmune conditions such as Behçet uveitis, Blau syndrome/CAPS phenotypes, and refractory scleritis, with reported improvements in intraocular inflammation and steroid-sparing in case series and retrospective cohorts; dosing regimens reported include 100–150 mg daily or weight-based 1–3 mg/kg daily subcutaneous dosing, with acceptable tolerability profiles dominated by mild injection-site reactions in the ocular cohorts cited (Fabiani et al., 2017; Korhonen, 2024). A practical constraint is anakinra’s short systemic half-life that necessitates daily dosing, with relapse reported upon dose reductions in some inflammatory eye disease cases—an important consideration for chronic indications (Fabiani et al., 2017; Korhonen, 2024). Topical isunakinra/IL-1Ra formulations for ocular surface disease demonstrated clinically meaningful symptom and sign improvements in randomized trials, high ocular receptor occupancy (~97%) at low doses, minimal systemic exposure (plasma below detection), and a favorable local safety signal, although these outcomes pertain to the anterior segment and cannot be extrapolated directly to the posterior segment (Fabiani et al., 2017).

Posterior segment and AMD-relevant preclinical work. Multiple animal studies substantiate that IL-1 signaling is active and targetable in the posterior segment. In a rat CNV model, intravitreal anakinra led to dose-dependent reductions in neovascular area; related IL-1β-targeted interventions prevented CNV without exacerbating photoreceptor degeneration, arguing against gross phototoxicity from IL-1 blockade in that setting (Sandhu et al., 2018; Fabiani et al., 2017). In a blue light–induced retinal degeneration model, systemic IL-1R antagonism with anakinra mitigated inflammatory readouts, reduced accumulation of subretinal macrophages, preserved photoreceptor structure, and maintained ERG function; an allosteric IL-1R modulator (rytvela) was somewhat superior, but anakinra nonetheless produced protective effects (Dabouz et al., 2020; Dabouz, 2024). Mechanistically, these studies localized IL-1β production to inflammasome-active subretinal mononuclear phagocytes (MPs) and mapped Il1r1 expression mainly to astroglia and vascular cells in mouse retina, supporting paracrine IL-1 signaling to neurovascular targets in the outer retina (Dabouz et al., 2020; Dabouz, 2024).

Human clinical evidence in dry AMD/geographic atrophy. No published human trials of anakinra for dry AMD/geographic atrophy (GA) were identified in the provided materials; a registry search string returned 18 ClinicalTrials.gov hits combining anakinra with retinal keywords, but no trial-level information (indication, route, dose, status, outcomes) was provided, and no AMD/GA trials of anakinra are documented here (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.). Systemic IL-1β blockade with canakinumab showed no effect in a diabetic retinopathy exploratory clinical context, underscoring translational uncertainty of systemic IL-1 pathway modulation for posterior segment disease (Korhonen, 2024).

Mechanistic rationale in RPE/AMD. Extensive literature supports that in AMD-relevant stress contexts the RPE and subretinal myeloid cells exhibit NLRP3 inflammasome activation, caspase-1–dependent maturation of IL-1β and IL-18, lysosomal membrane permeabilization (LMP) with cathepsin release, and altered autophagy/heterophagy—mechanistic substrates for chronic para-inflammation and cell death (apoptosis → pyroptosis shift) in RPE (Treanor, n.d.; Yerramothu, Vijay, & Willcox, 2018; Kaarniranta et al., 2023). IL-1β levels are elevated in AMD vitreous and plasma, and microglia/MP-derived IL-1β can drive chemokine and cytokine production by Müller cells and RPE, linking IL-1 to retinal inflammatory amplification (Nashine et al., 2022; Korhonen, 2024). The RPE itself produces IL-1Ra and uses IL-1Ra to limit immune activation: IL-1Ra suppresses necrosis-induced release of IL-6, IL-8, and MCP-1 from ARPE-19 and reduces antigen-presenting functions in RPE cocultures, indicating that IL-1 signaling is operational in RPE and that IL-1R antagonism can blunt RPE-mediated inflammatory outputs in vitro (Fabiani et al., 2017; Kaur & Singh, 2021).

Mechanism of Action  
Receptor pharmacology. IL-1β and IL-1α bind IL-1RI and recruit IL-1 receptor accessory protein (IL-1RAcP) to form a signaling complex that initiates MyD88-dependent activation of IRAKs, TRAF6, TAK1, and downstream MAPKs (JNK/p38) and NF-κB, driving expression of inflammatory mediators and cell-type–specific responses (Dabouz, 2024). Anakinra is a competitive orthosteric antagonist of IL-1RI that prevents IL-1α/β binding and thereby blocks the formation of the signaling complex with IL-1RAcP, “non-selectively” inhibiting downstream IL-1–dependent pathways across cell types expressing IL-1RI (Dabouz, 2024; Dabouz et al., 2020). In the blue-light retinal injury model, orthosteric antagonism with anakinra and allosteric modulation with rytvela each prevented IL-1–driven retinal inflammation and photoreceptor injury; mechanistically, both agents protected neuroretinal compartments that express IL-1R while not necessarily reducing IL-1β produced in macrophage conditioned media, consistent with receptor-level antagonism in responder cells (Dabouz et al., 2020; Dabouz, 2024).

Cellular sources/targets in retina. In injury models, Il1b is upregulated primarily in infiltrating subretinal mononuclear phagocytes that co-express NLRP3 and caspase-1, whereas Il1r1 expression is detected predominantly in astrocytes, pericytes, endothelial cells, and bipolar cells, with little to no detection in photoreceptors or MPs by scRNA-seq; this places the critical pharmacodynamic target of anakinra on neurovascular/astroglial elements rather than on the IL-1β-producing cells themselves (Dabouz et al., 2020; Dabouz, 2024). IL-1β is elevated in AMD patients’ vitreous and is a recognized biomarker of retinal inflammation; microglia-derived IL-1β amplifies chemokine signaling by Müller and RPE cells, indicating that RPE can serve as an IL-1–responsive amplifier of inflammation even if Il1r1 detection varies by model and assay (Nashine et al., 2022; Korhonen, 2024). RPE-derived endogenous IL-1Ra provides further evidence that IL-1 signaling—and its antagonism—are biologically relevant in the RPE microenvironment (Fabiani et al., 2017).

Inflammasome context and limitations of IL-1R blockade. In RPE and adjacent retinal cells, NLRP3 inflammasome activation is triggered by AMD-relevant stimuli including A2E/lipofuscin photooxidation, drusen components, DICER1/Alu RNA accumulation, oxidized lipoproteins, complement/cofactors, ROS, and lysosomal membrane permeabilization with cathepsin release (Treanor, n.d.; Yerramothu et al., 2018). Inflammasome activation requires priming (e.g., TLR-NF-κB–dependent upregulation of NLRP3/pro-IL-1β) followed by an activation signal (e.g., mtROS, LMP), culminating in caspase-1 activation and secretion of mature IL-1β and IL-18; inflammasome priming can shift RPE death from apoptosis to pyroptosis, increasing inflammatory cytokine release and DAMP extrusion (Treanor, n.d.; Kaarniranta et al., 2023). Critically, IL-1 pathway blockers such as anakinra do not inhibit upstream inflammasome assembly, caspase-1 activation, or IL-18 production; thus, IL-1R antagonism will block IL-1 signaling but will not shut down inflammasome-dependent IL-18 release or pyroptotic execution, which may continue to drive disease biology (Korhonen, 2024). Moreover, in some experimental paradigms, IL-18 can have protective or context-dependent roles in AMD models, complicating network-level predictions when only IL-1 signaling is blocked (Lim et al., 2020).

Evidence gaps regarding lysosomal targets. The working hypothesis posits that anakinra will prevent IL-1β-driven inflammasome amplification and lysosomal destabilization in RPE, preserving vacuolar H+-ATPase (v-ATPase) function and cathepsin D (CTSD) maturation/activity; however, the provided materials contain no direct experimental evidence that IL-1R antagonism rescues v-ATPase activity, lysosomal pH, or CTSD processing in RPE, nor that anakinra reduces lysosomal membrane permeabilization in these systems (Lim et al., 2020; Treanor, n.d.). While lysosomal destabilization and cathepsin B/L release are well-documented inflammasome triggers in RPE, and bafilomycin A1 (a v-ATPase inhibitor) has been used to model lysosomal/autophagic impairment that activates NLRP3 and IL-1β release, there is no reported dataset here demonstrating that IL-1R blockade restores lysosomal acidification or cathepsin D maturation in RPE (Yerramothu et al., 2018; Piippo, 2019). Consequently, the proposed IL-1→lysosome preservation claims remain conjectural in the absence of targeted RPE lysosomal measurements following anakinra treatment in AMD-relevant paradigms (Lim et al., 2020; Treanor, n.d.).

Expected Effect  
Assay-level effects in retinal/RPE systems. Based on the presented literature, IL-1R antagonism with anakinra is expected to reduce IL-1–driven inflammatory signaling in neuroretinal and gliovascular compartments, attenuate subretinal macrophage accumulation/activation, and preserve photoreceptor structure/function in acute inflammatory injury paradigms; these effects have been demonstrated in the blue light model (reduced GFAP, Il1b/Il6/Ccl2 transcripts, fewer subretinal MPs, more preserved ONL and ERG amplitudes) (Dabouz, 2024; Dabouz et al., 2020). In explant co-culture systems where LPS/ATP-activated macrophages produce IL-1β, IL-1R antagonists and anti-IL-1β antibodies abrogate photoreceptor death, supporting a causal role for IL-1β and a direct cytoprotective effect of IL-1 pathway blockade on IL-1RI-expressing retinal cells (Dabouz, 2024). In vitro RPE models show that IL-1Ra can suppress necrosis-induced secretion of IL-6, IL-8, and MCP-1 (likely via NF-κB), suggesting that anakinra may dampen autocrine/paracrine amplification in RPE cultures challenged with danger signals—though definitive RPE IL-1RI expression patterns in vivo remain incompletely defined in the cited mouse scRNA-seq data (Fabiani et al., 2017; Dabouz et al., 2020).

Inflammasome priming versus activation. IL-1 can contribute to priming (NF-κB–dependent) of inflammasome components; therefore, anakinra might indirectly reduce NLRP3 priming in some contexts by interrupting IL-1 positive feedback loops, leading to lower pro-IL-1β and possibly reduced susceptibility to subsequent activation triggers (Fabiani et al., 2017). However, because anakinra acts downstream of inflammasome assembly, it will not prevent caspase-1 activation, gasdermin D pore formation, pyroptosis, or IL-18 maturation/secretion once NLRP3 is engaged—which are all relevant to RPE and subretinal myeloid biology in AMD (Korhonen, 2024; Treanor, n.d.; Kaarniranta et al., 2023). Consequently, anakinra’s benefit in dry AMD models that are dominated by RPE-intrinsic inflammasome activation and pyroptosis may be partial, favoring reductions in IL-1–driven chemokine/cytokine cascades and immune cell recruitment over direct prevention of inflammasome-executed cell death (Korhonen, 2024; Treanor, n.d.).

Lysosomal endpoints. The proposed preservation of v-ATPase function and cathepsin D activity is not currently supported by primary data in the provided sources; no reports demonstrate that anakinra normalizes lysosomal pH, protease maturation (including CTSD), or membrane integrity in RPE subjected to AMD-relevant stressors (Lim et al., 2020; Treanor, n.d.; Piippo, 2019). While inhibiting IL-1 signaling may lower NF-κB–driven transcription of inflammatory mediators (and thus lessen secondary stressors to lysosomes), the extent to which this translates into measurable correction of lysosomal biology in RPE remains to be tested experimentally (Fabiani et al., 2017).

Translational dosing and safety in the eye. In mice, systemic anakinra at 4 mg/kg twice daily for 3 days produced retinal protection in the blue light model; this regimen emphasizes short-term systemic exposures in an acute injury context rather than chronic degenerative settings (Dabouz, 2024). In CNV rodents, intravitreal IL-1Ra reduced neovascularization without aggravating photoreceptor degeneration, providing proof-of-concept for posterior segment delivery and a supportive safety signal in that animal model (Sandhu et al., 2018). Clinically, systemic anakinra has an established safety profile in inflammatory eye disease cohorts, but no intravitreal human anakinra safety data in AMD/GA are presented here; systemic IL-1β blockade (canakinumab) did not improve retinopathy outcomes in a separate context, and anakinra’s daily dosing requirement remains a burden for chronic use unless long-acting ocular delivery is engineered (Korhonen, 2024; Fabiani et al., 2017).

Overall Evaluation  
Merits  
- Biological plausibility in AMD. AMD-relevant stressors activate NLRP3 in RPE and subretinal myeloid cells, elevating IL-1β and IL-18 and driving para-inflammatory cascades and pyroptosis; IL-1β is increased in AMD vitreous and plasma, and IL-1–producing MPs are present at sites of pathology, establishing IL-1 as a rational target for modulating retinal inflammation (Treanor, n.d.; Nashine et al., 2022; Korhonen, 2024).  
- Pharmacologic validation in retinal models. Anakinra significantly reduced inflammation and preserved retinal structure/function in a light-damage model and intravitreally suppressed CNV in rodents, indicating target engagement and protective potential in the posterior segment; IL-1β neutralization prevented CNV without exacerbating photoreceptor degeneration, arguing for a non-toxic profile in those contexts (Dabouz et al., 2020; Dabouz, 2024; Sandhu et al., 2018).  
- RPE-relevant immunobiology. RPE naturally produces IL-1Ra, and exogenous IL-1Ra reduces necrosis-induced inflammatory mediator release from RPE and suppresses dendritic-cell activation in RPE co-cultures, suggesting that anakinra could attenuate RPE-mediated inflammatory amplification in dry AMD (Fabiani et al., 2017; Kaur & Singh, 2021).  
- Clinical and formulation precedents. Systemic ocular use of anakinra in uveitis and scleritis shows clinical feasibility and manageable safety; topical IL-1 antagonists have robust ocular safety signals; gene therapy encoding IL-1Ra and intravitreal administration have been explored preclinically, supporting a spectrum of delivery options that could be adapted for posterior segment disease (Fabiani et al., 2017).

Limitations and risks  
- Mechanistic incompleteness vis-à-vis inflammasomes. IL-1R blockade will not prevent upstream NLRP3 activation, caspase-1 activity, gasdermin-mediated pyroptosis, or IL-18 production; in RPE-intrinsic inflammasome-dominant pathophysiology, anakinra would be expected to blunt downstream IL-1–mediated amplification and leukocyte recruitment but not stop the execution machinery of inflammasome-driven cell death (Korhonen, 2024; Treanor, n.d.; Kaarniranta et al., 2023).  
- Unsubstantiated lysosomal rescue claims. There is no evidence here that anakinra preserves lysosomal acidification (v-ATPase function), cathepsin D maturation/activity, or prevents LMP in RPE under AMD-relevant stress; this is a critical gap because the proposed therapeutic specificity hinges on cytokine–lysosome cross-talk that remains to be demonstrated (Lim et al., 2020; Treanor, n.d.; Piippo, 2019).  
- Target expression uncertainties. In mouse retina, Il1r1 is enriched in astroglia and vascular cells and not detected in photoreceptors or MPs by scRNA-seq, complicating assumptions about direct photoreceptor or RPE targeting by anakinra in vivo; while RPE responds to IL-1 in vitro and produces IL-1Ra, spatial and species differences in IL-1RI distribution may shape efficacy and delivery decisions (Dabouz et al., 2020; Dabouz, 2024; Fabiani et al., 2017).  
- Mixed translational signals. Systemic IL-1β blockade did not improve diabetic retinopathy outcomes in the cited study, and anakinra’s systemic short half-life imposes burdensome daily dosing for chronic disease; there is no documented human safety/efficacy experience with intravitreal anakinra in AMD/GA in the provided sources (Korhonen, 2024; Fabiani et al., 2017; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).  
- Network complexity. NLRP3/IL-18 can exert context-dependent protective or detrimental effects in AMD models; while anakinra does not block IL-18 signaling, its selective inhibition of IL-1 may not suffice to rebalance inflammasome-driven pathology if pyroptosis and IL-18-dependent pathways remain active (Lim et al., 2020).

Go/No-Go considerations and critical experiments  
- RPE-centric validation. Test anakinra in human RPE models exposed to A2E/blue-light, drusen components, DICER1/Alu RNA, or oxidized lipoproteins; quantify NLRP3 priming (NLRP3, pro-IL-1β), activation (ASC specks, caspase-1 cleavage), downstream cytokines (IL-1β, IL-18), and execution (GSDMD cleavage/pyroptosis markers), with and without anakinra to define points of pathway modulation (Treanor, n.d.; Yerramothu et al., 2018).  
- Lysosomal endpoints. Directly measure lysosomal pH, v-ATPase activity, LMP (galectin-3 puncta), cathepsin D maturation/activity, and autophagic flux in the same RPE paradigms ± anakinra to test the hypothesis that IL-1R blockade preserves lysosomal integrity and protease processing (Piippo, 2019).  
- In vivo GA-relevant models. Move from acute light injury to RPE-atrophy models (e.g., chronic photooxidative stress, Alu RNA/DICER1 disruption, lipofuscin models) to assess whether anakinra reduces rates of RPE atrophy, outer retinal thinning, and visual function decline; include comparators targeting the inflammasome (e.g., NLRP3 inhibitors) to benchmark effect sizes and mechanistic depth (Treanor, n.d.; Kaarniranta et al., 2023; Lim et al., 2020).  
- Ocular delivery and PK. Develop and test intravitreal dosing and, preferably, sustained-release formats for anakinra to overcome systemic short half-life; establish vitreous/retinal PK and receptor occupancy, and evaluate ocular safety (IOP, ERG, histopathology) and immunogenicity (anti-drug antibodies) in large-eye species (Korhonen, 2024; Fabiani et al., 2017).  
- Biomarker strategy. Use vitreous/plasma IL-1β and retinal inflammatory transcript signatures as pharmacodynamic biomarkers; consider scRNA-seq to confirm target cell engagement (Il1r1-expressing compartments) pre- and post-treatment (Nashine et al., 2022; Dabouz, 2024).

Positioning relative to alternatives  
Because anakinra does not interrupt inflammasome activation or execution, proximal inhibitors of the NLRP3 inflammasome (e.g., MCC950-class) may provide deeper control of IL-1β/IL-18 production and pyroptosis in RPE-driven disease, at the cost of potentially suppressing beneficial IL-18 signaling in some contexts; preclinical literature shows NLRP3 blockade can be protective in retinal models, meriting parallel evaluation (Lim et al., 2020). Conversely, allosteric IL-1R modulators (rytvela-type) have shown superior protection to anakinra in the light-damage model and may offer functional selectivity (e.g., sparing NF-κB while inhibiting JNK/p38/AP-1) with improved distribution and immunogenicity profiles; these properties deserve consideration if an IL-1-targeting approach is pursued (Dabouz, 2024; Dabouz et al., 2020).

Conclusions  
- Strength of rationale. There is robust evidence that IL-1β is elevated and pathogenic in retinal neuroinflammation and that IL-1R antagonism—including anakinra—can protect retina in preclinical models by reducing inflammatory signaling and immune cell recruitment; RPE-relevant IL-1 biology further supports plausibility (Dabouz et al., 2020; Dabouz, 2024; Fabiani et al., 2017).  
- Weakness of hypothesis specifics. The central claim that anakinra preserves v-ATPase function and cathepsin D maturation in RPE lacks support in the provided literature; moreover, IL-1R blockade cannot prevent upstream inflammasome activation or pyroptosis, limiting its capacity to halt RPE-intrinsic degenerative processes central to GA (Lim et al., 2020; Korhonen, 2024; Treanor, n.d.; Piippo, 2019).  
- Translational readiness. No human AMD/GA trials of anakinra are documented here; systemic IL-1β blockade has shown limited efficacy in retinal vascular disease, and anakinra’s dosing logistics are unfavorable for chronic ocular therapy without dedicated ocular delivery systems (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.; Korhonen, 2024).

Overall Evaluation  
Anakinra is a mechanistically credible anti-inflammatory candidate to blunt IL-1–driven retinal inflammation and leukocyte recruitment, with reproducible preclinical efficacy signals in posterior-segment injury models and supportive RPE-centric immunobiology; however, the specific hypothesis that it will mechanistically preserve lysosomal v-ATPase function and cathepsin D activity in RPE is currently unsupported by direct evidence, and IL-1R antagonism is unlikely to arrest inflammasome activation, IL-18 signaling, or pyroptotic cell death that contribute to RPE atrophy in dry AMD (Dabouz et al., 2020; Dabouz, 2024; Fabiani et al., 2017; Korhonen, 2024; Lim et al., 2020). Given the absence of clinical data in GA and delivery constraints, anakinra merits consideration as an adjunct anti-inflammatory approach contingent on (1) generation of RPE-focused data demonstrating modulation of inflammasome priming and lysosomal integrity, and (2) development of sustained intraocular delivery; in parallel, more proximal interventions (NLRP3 inhibitors) and IL-1R allosteric modulators with superior preclinical efficacy should be benchmarked as potentially higher-leverage strategies for disease modification in dry AMD (Lim et al., 2020; Dabouz et al., 2020).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
GDC-0941 (pictilisib) is a synthetic, orally bioavailable, ATP-competitive, pan–class I phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K) inhibitor discovered through structure-guided medicinal chemistry at Genentech as an optimization beyond early tool compounds and the dual PI3K/mTOR inhibitor PI-103, with substantially improved selectivity for class I PI3Ks and favorable pharmacokinetics (PK) suitable for systemic dosing in humans (Garces, n.d.; Zhao et al., 2017; Li et al., 2024). At the biochemical level, pictilisib exhibits low-nanomolar potency against p110α and p110δ, with activity across class I isoforms (representative IC₅₀s: α ≈ 3 nM, β ≈ 33 nM, δ ≈ 3 nM, γ ≈ 75 nM) and weak activity on mTOR (~0.58 μM), consistent with selective targeting of class I PI3Ks over mTOR kinase (Huang et al., 2023; Garces, n.d.; Josephs & Sarker, 2016; Zhao et al., 2017). Co-crystal structural analysis shows an ATP-mimetic thieno[3,2-d]pyrimidine core in which the morpholine oxygen donates a hinge hydrogen bond (Val882), the indazole engages an affinity pocket (Asp841/Tyr867), and a methanesulfonyl-piperazine tail projects toward solvent; these interactions underpin its potency and selectivity within the class I PI3K ATP site (PDB 3DBS) (Garces, n.d.). Pictilisib belongs to the pan-class I PI3K inhibitor class, a therapeutic category widely advanced in oncology to suppress the PI3K→AKT→mTOR signaling axis that governs cell growth, survival, and metabolism; multiple agents in this class have reached clinical testing or approval, providing a clear translational precedent for pathway engagement and safety management in humans (Schmitz et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2023; Li et al., 2024).

Therapeutic History  
The development history of pictilisib is anchored in oncology, where first-in-human Phase I trials established a recommended Phase II dose of 330 mg once daily, dose-proportional PK (Tₘₐₓ ≈ 2 h, t₁/₂ ≈ 13–24 h), and robust pharmacodynamic (PD) target engagement—up to ~90% inhibition of phosphorylated AKT (Ser473) in platelet-rich plasma within 1–3 h of dosing and suppression of p-AKT and p-S6 in tumor biopsies at sufficient exposure (AUC > 20 μM·h) (Sarker et al., 2015; Mishra et al., 2021). Across Phase I combination studies, pictilisib showed a manageable safety profile and some antitumor activity, with common adverse events including nausea, diarrhea, rash, fatigue, hyperglycemia, and cytopenias; dose-limiting toxicity in some settings was grade 3 maculopapular rash (Mishra et al., 2021; Josephs & Sarker, 2016; Sarker et al., 2015). Although pathway suppression was clear, randomized combination trials in breast and lung cancer variably met efficacy endpoints and broader development was limited by tolerability in multi-drug regimens and modest efficacy as monotherapy—experience that nonetheless provides clinically validated PK/PD tools and class-effect safety benchmarks (Mishra et al., 2021; Gao et al., 2017).

No preclinical or clinical use of pictilisib or other class I PI3K inhibitors has been reported for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or RPE-centered retinal disease models in the provided literature, and a recent review emphasizes that no ongoing clinical trials directly target autophagy in AMD, underscoring an evidence gap for PI3K inhibitors in this indication (Blasiak et al., 2025). By contrast, direct downstream pathway modulation in RPE—mTORC1 inhibition with rapamycin—has shown that activating the lysosome–TFEB axis reduces POS-derived autofluorescent granules in vitro in a hydrolase-dependent manner, but clinical testing in advanced AMD returned limited efficacy and adverse effects, illustrating both the mechanistic plausibility of modulating this pathway and translational challenges (Falcão et al., 2024). Collectively, the therapeutic history supports that class I PI3K inhibitors achieve systemic PI3K pathway inhibition in humans with tractable but nontrivial toxicities; however, there is no published RPE- or AMD-focused body of work with pictilisib to date in the provided context (Sarker et al., 2015; Mishra et al., 2021; Blasiak et al., 2025).

Mechanism of Action  
Class I PI3Ks phosphorylate PIP₂ to PIP₃, recruiting PH-domain effectors including PDK1 and AKT to the plasma membrane, where AKT is activated by phosphorylation at Thr308 (PDK1) and Ser473 (mTORC2) (Huang et al., 2023). Activated AKT phosphorylates multiple substrates that converge on mTORC1 activation (via TSC2/PRAS40), leading to phosphorylation of S6K1 and 4E-BP1 to promote protein synthesis and suppress autophagy, thereby integrating growth-factor status with anabolic programs (Huang et al., 2023; Castel et al., 2021). In retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), AKT/mTOR signaling is an established regulator of cell proliferation and autophagy; mTORC1 activation inhibits autophagy by blocking ULK1 signaling and autolysosomal biogenesis, whereas rapamycin-mediated mTORC1 inhibition activates autophagy and preserves photoreceptor function in preclinical models (Chang et al., 2015). PI3K inhibition upstream of AKT is thus expected to reduce PIP₃ generation, limit AKT membrane recruitment/activation, and secondarily depress mTORC1 signaling in RPE (Castel et al., 2021; Chang et al., 2015).

PI3K→AKT signaling intersects directly with TFEB/TFE3—the master transcription factors of lysosomal biogenesis and the CLEAR regulon—through both mTORC1-dependent and mTORC1-independent routes (Falcão et al., 2024; Ghosh et al., 2024). Nutrient-driven mTORC1 activity at the lysosome phosphorylates TFEB/TFE3 to retain them in the cytosol; conversely, mTORC1 inhibition permits TFEB nuclear translocation and induction of lysosomal/autophagy genes (Falcão et al., 2024). Importantly, AKT2 directly phosphorylates TFEB (at Ser467) and TFE3 (Ser321), promoting 14-3-3 binding and cytoplasmic sequestration independent of mTORC1, thereby repressing CLEAR gene expression and lysosomal programs in RPE (Ghosh et al., 2023; Ghosh et al., 2024). In AMD-relevant contexts—human dysmorphic macular RPE, CFH risk-allele iPSC-RPE, and Akt2 RPE-specific knock-in mice—AKT2 upregulation increases TFEB/TFE3 phosphorylation, reduces lysosomal hydrolases (cathepsin D/L) and CLEAR target expression, impairs autophagic flux, and shifts autophagy toward secretory pathways characterized by increased FKBP51/SNAP23, autophagosome fusion with the plasma membrane, and extracellular release of IL-1β/HMGB1 (Ghosh et al., 2023; Ghosh et al., 2024). TFEB rescue via a phospho-deficient TFEB-S467A mutant or pharmacologic TFEB activation with trehalose restores cathepsin D/L and autophagy genes, normalizes autophagosome–lysosome fusion, and improves RPE structure in AMD-like mouse models, establishing TFEB/TFE3 as actionable nodes downstream of AKT2 in RPE (Ghosh et al., 2023; Ghosh et al., 2024).

SIRT5 and mitochondrial metabolism integrate with AKT2–TFEB signaling in RPE. SIRT5 interacts with AKT2 and reduces lysine malonylation on AKT2, modulating AKT2 activity; AKT2, via inhibition of PGC-1α, downregulates SIRT5, creating a bidirectional circuit that affects TFEB-dependent lysosomal function and mitochondrial respiration (Ghosh et al., 2023). AKT2 upregulation impairs mitochondrial respiration (maximal and ATP-linked), which is rescued by SIRT5, linking mitochondrial–lysosomal crosstalk to RPE proteostasis (Ghosh et al., 2023). Functionally, failure of the AKT2/SIRT5/TFEB axis elevates secretory autophagy and likely contributes to drusen pathogenesis by exporting inflammatory cargo (Ghosh et al., 2023).

These mechanistic data converge with mTORC1→TFEB observations in POS-fed RPE models. Synchronous POS phagocytosis transiently activates mTORC1 early, with TFEB protein increasing but remaining phosphorylated during late maturation, indicating a bottleneck at TFEB activation (Falcão et al., 2024). Pharmacologic mTORC1 inhibition with rapamycin after AFGs have formed lowers POS-derived autofluorescence by ~30% in hfRPE/ARPE-19, reduces pS6, decreases the pTFEB/TFEB ratio, increases LAMP1, and requires active lysosomal hydrolases: cathepsin D knockout or protease/lipase inhibition abolishes the rapamycin effect (Falcão et al., 2024). Human AMD RPE exhibits hyperphosphorylated TFEB with decreased nuclear localization and lower cathepsin D/L protein levels and activities, consistent with impaired lysosome proteolysis; constitutively active TFEB boosts CLEAR genes, including hydrolases and V-ATPase subunits (e.g., ATP6V0A1), supporting enhanced acidification capacity (Falcão et al., 2025).

Pictilisib’s proximal pharmacology—ATP-competitive inhibition of class I PI3Ks—has been shown to produce substantial pathway suppression in human tissues (reduced pAKT, reduced pS6) and in tumor models; such upstream inhibition is expected to depress both AKT→mTORC1 signaling and AKT2-mediated TFEB phosphorylation, potentially enabling TFEB/TFE3 nuclear translocation and restoration of CLEAR programs in RPE (Sarker et al., 2015; Mishra et al., 2021; Castel et al., 2021; Ghosh et al., 2024). Two caveats are central. First, class III PI3K/VPS34 activity is required for autophagosome nucleation; thus class I–selective inhibition (as with pictilisib) is mechanistically appropriate, whereas class III inhibition would be detrimental to autophagy flux (Wang et al., 2023). Second, while AKT inhibitors (e.g., MK-2206) and TFEB activators (trehalose) have directly increased autophagy and TFEB nuclear translocation in RPE, no direct evidence of class I PI3K inhibitors reproducing these effects in RPE has been reported in the provided literature (Karim et al., 2020; Blasiak et al., 2025).

Expected Effect  
In RPE cell assays designed to model dry AMD–relevant lysosomal stress (e.g., POS feeding, A2E/oxidant exposure, or CFH risk-allele iPSC-RPE), pictilisib is expected to reduce PI3K-dependent PIP₃ generation, lowering membrane recruitment and phosphorylation of AKT, thereby secondarily suppressing mTORC1 and directly relieving AKT2-mediated phosphorylation of TFEB/TFE3 (Huang et al., 2023; Castel et al., 2021; Ghosh et al., 2024). Mechanistically, this should dephosphorylate TFEB/TFE3, promote nuclear translocation, and activate the CLEAR transcriptional program to increase components of lysosomal biogenesis and function (e.g., LAMP1/2, cathepsin D/L, and V-ATPase subunits), thereby enhancing degradative capacity and autophagic flux (Falcão et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2025; Falcão et al., 2024).

Operationally testable expected effects include:  
• Signaling: decreased pAKT (Ser473) and pS6 (Ser235/236) within hours of dosing in RPE, mirroring PD seen in tumors and platelet-rich plasma in human trials, establishing target engagement (Sarker et al., 2015; Mishra et al., 2021).  
• TFEB/TFE3 activation: reduction in pTFEB/TFEB ratio, increased nuclear TFEB/TFE3, and induction of CLEAR genes; in RPE systems, TFEB activation correlates with increased LAMP1 and rescue of lysosomal hydrolases and autophagy mediators (e.g., ATG9B), as seen upon TFEB S467A expression or trehalose treatment (Falcão et al., 2024; Ghosh et al., 2023; Ghosh et al., 2024).  
• Lysosomal function: increased abundance and maturation of cathepsin D (pro→intermediate→mature chain) and cathepsin L, and improved degradative flux, consistent with observations that AMD RPE shows diminished cathepsin levels/activities and that hydrolase function is required for rapamycin-mediated clearance of POS-derived AFGs (Falcão et al., 2025; Falcão et al., 2024).  
• Autophagic flux: increased LC3-II turnover (± bafilomycin A₁), reduced p62/SQSTM1 accumulation, restored autophagosome–lysosome fusion (e.g., GFP-LC3 and LysoTracker/LAMP1 colocalization), and decreased accumulation of double-membrane autophagosomes on EM, reversing the AKT2-driven flux block (Ghosh et al., 2023; Ghosh et al., 2024).  
• POS-derived autofluorescence: reduction in POS-dependent autofluorescent granules in preventive and resolving paradigms, analogous to mTORC1 inhibition or TFEB activation effects; efficacy will depend on intact lysosomal hydrolase activity (Falcão et al., 2024).  
• Secretory autophagy: decreased FKBP51/SNAP23 elevation, reduced plasma-membrane fusion of autophagosomes, and lower extracellular release of IL-1β and HMGB1 from RPE, mirroring effects seen with SIRT5 co-expression or AKT2 inhibition (Ghosh et al., 2023; Ghosh et al., 2024).  
• Acidification: although lysosomal pH has not been directly measured after class I PI3K inhibition in RPE, TFEB activation increases expression of V-ATPase subunits, and improved hydrolase activities imply normalization of the acidic lumen; direct pH assays (LysoSensor/LysoTracker) should be incorporated because efficacy of rapamycin/TFEB approaches depends on intact lysosomal acid hydrolases (Falcão et al., 2025; Falcão et al., 2024).

These expectations rest on the well-documented presence and dysregulation of the AKT2→TFEB/TFE3→CLEAR axis in RPE and the dependence of POS clearance on mTOR/TFEB-governed lysosomal function (Ghosh et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2024). AKT2 is upregulated in macular RPE from AMD donors and in AMD-like mouse models, and RPE-specific Akt2 overexpression is sufficient to induce AMD-like pathology, supporting target relevance in the cell type and disease context of interest (Ghosh et al., 2023; Ghosh et al., 2024). Because PI3K is upstream of AKT, class I PI3K inhibition should, in principle, reduce AKT2 activity and thereby favor TFEB activation; however, no direct studies in the provided literature demonstrate pictilisib (or any class I PI3K inhibitor) inducing TFEB nuclear translocation or improving cathepsin D maturation/activity in RPE, so these are testable, evidence-generating predictions rather than established facts (Blasiak et al., 2025; Chang et al., 2015; Karim et al., 2020).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Mechanistic alignment with disease biology: Dry AMD features impaired RPE autophagy–lysosome function, diminished cathepsin D/L levels/activities, and TFEB hyperphosphorylation with reduced nuclear TFEB, all of which converge on lysosomal insufficiency and accumulation of lipofuscin-like material and extracellular drusen; upstream PI3K inhibition is a coherent strategy to relieve AKT2- and mTORC1-mediated repression of TFEB/TFE3 and restore CLEAR-driven lysosomal biogenesis and flux (Falcão et al., 2025; Falcão et al., 2024; Ghosh et al., 2024).  
• Drug tractability and translational readiness: Pictilisib achieves robust systemic target engagement in humans (pAKT/pS6 suppression), has well-characterized PK/PD and class-effect safety, and is chemically and biophysically optimized, enabling accelerated preclinical testing and dosage/formulation exploration for ocular delivery or low systemic exposure strategies (Sarker et al., 2015; Mishra et al., 2021; Garces, n.d.).  
• Selectivity profile appropriate for autophagy enhancement: Because autophagosome nucleation requires class III PI3K/VPS34, class I selectivity of pictilisib avoids this liability while suppressing AKT→mTOR signaling and AKT2-dependent TFEB phosphorylation, in contrast to nonselective PI3K inhibition which would be deleterious (Wang et al., 2023; Castel et al., 2021).

Risks and Gaps  
• No direct RPE/AMD data with class I PI3K inhibitors: In contrast to clear benefits from rapamycin and TFEB activation, the literature presented contains no direct evidence that class I PI3K inhibition, or pictilisib specifically, improves TFEB activation/nuclear entry, lysosomal biogenesis, cathepsin D maturation/activity, lysosomal acidification, autophagy flux, or POS handling in RPE; thus, the central hypothesis remains unvalidated experimentally in the disease-relevant cell type (Blasiak et al., 2025; Chang et al., 2015; Falcão et al., 2024). By comparison, AKT inhibition (MK-2206) and trehalose have been shown to increase autophagy and nuclear TFEB in RPE, and AKT2 inhibitors reduced lipid/apoE in CFH(H/H) RPE, but these are not PI3K inhibitors and may differ in cellular selectivity and compensatory signaling (Karim et al., 2020; Ghosh et al., 2024).  
• Complexity of autophagy modulation and context dependence: Autophagy is a double-edged sword with biphasic responses to stress; overactivation or mistimed activation could exacerbate RPE stress or impair other retinal cell types, and some autophagy inhibitors display retinal toxicity (e.g., chloroquine class), emphasizing the need for precise control and safety profiling (Blasiak et al., 2025; Kaarniranta et al., 2013). Rapamycin has shown only limited clinical efficacy in advanced AMD despite mechanistic benefits in vitro, illustrating translational friction between pathway modulation and clinical outcomes (Falcão et al., 2024).  
• Safety, delivery, and exposure management: Systemic class I PI3K inhibition induces hyperglycemia, rash, and gastrointestinal toxicities; while these were generally manageable, ocular delivery strategies (intravitreal or periocular) and ocular pharmacokinetics for pictilisib are uncharacterized in the provided literature, and tissue-specific PD (e.g., drug levels at the RPE/Bruch’s complex) is likely to determine efficacy and safety (Josephs & Sarker, 2016; Sarker et al., 2015; Mishra et al., 2021). Tissue PD variability seen in tumors versus blood suggests careful intratissue PD assays are necessary (Sarker et al., 2015).  
• Isoform and cell-type specificity: AKT2 is the isoform implicated in RPE TFEB repression and secretory autophagy; upstream PI3K isoform contributions in RPE are not defined here, and pan-class I inhibition could affect neighboring retinal cells, choroidal endothelium, and immune cells, potentially altering retinal immunity and angiogenesis in unintended ways (Ghosh et al., 2024; Castel et al., 2021). Given the evidence favoring AKT2-selective inhibition or direct TFEB activation in RPE models, PI3K-level intervention may be broader than necessary and carry off-target tissue consequences (Ghosh et al., 2024; Karim et al., 2020).  
• Acidification endpoint uncertainty: The hypothesis specifically posits enhanced lysosomal acidification, yet none of the provided sources report direct lysosomal pH measurements after class I PI3K inhibition in RPE; while CLEAR induction can increase V-ATPase subunits and rapamycin-mediated clearance requires active hydrolases, direct acidification effects remain to be demonstrated (Falcão et al., 2025; Falcão et al., 2024; Blasiak et al., 2025).

Go/No-Go Evidence Plan  
Given the strong mechanistic rationale but absence of direct RPE data, a staged validation program is warranted:  
– In vitro RPE target engagement and TFEB activation: Demonstrate pictilisib decreases pAKT (Ser473) and pS6 in primary human fetal RPE, ARPE-19, and iPSC-RPE, and increases nuclear TFEB/TFE3 with induction of CLEAR genes (CTSD, CTSL, LAMP2, ATP6V0A1) assessed by Western, RT-qPCR, and ChIP-qPCR (Falcão et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2025; Ghosh et al., 2024).  
– Lysosome function readouts: Quantify cathepsin D maturation and enzymatic activity, LAMP1/2 abundance, and lysosomal pH using ratiometric probes; include hydrolase inhibition controls to assess dependence analogous to the rapamycin data (Falcão et al., 2024).  
– Autophagic flux and modality: Assess LC3-II turnover (± bafilomycin A₁), p62 dynamics, autolysosome number (LC3–LAMP1 colocalization), and EM confirmation; evaluate secretory-autophagy markers (FKBP51, SNAP23) and extracellular cargo (HMGB1, IL-1β) to test reversal of the AKT2-driven phenotype (Ghosh et al., 2023; Ghosh et al., 2024).  
– Functional disease readouts: Test POS-dependent autofluorescence reduction in preventive and resolving paradigms and POS degradation assays; evaluate lipid/apoE accumulation in CFH(H/H) iPSC-RPE and Cryba1 cKO explants to compare with reported trehalose and AKT2 inhibitor effects (Falcão et al., 2024; Ghosh et al., 2023; Ghosh et al., 2024).  
– In vivo and delivery: Establish ocular PK and tolerability for local delivery (intravitreal/periocular) in rodents, then test efficacy in RPE-driven AMD-like models (Akt2 KI, Cryba1 cKO, NaIO₃) with TFEB activation, lysosomal and functional endpoints (ERG/SD-OCT) (Ghosh et al., 2024; Ghosh et al., 2023; Falcão et al., 2025).  
– Benchmarking: Include rapamycin (mTORC1 inhibition), MK-2206 (AKT inhibition), and trehalose (mTOR-independent TFEB activation) comparators to position PI3K inhibition within the therapeutic landscape (Falcão et al., 2024; Karim et al., 2020; Ghosh et al., 2023).

Conclusion  
Pictilisib offers a mechanistically coherent, drug-like approach to modulate an RPE pathway of clear pathogenic relevance—AKT2/mTOR-mediated repression of TFEB/TFE3 and the CLEAR network—backed by robust human PK/PD experience and a selectivity profile compatible with enhancing autophagy without impeding VPS34-dependent nucleation (Ghosh et al., 2024; Sarker et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2023). However, the absence of direct evidence that class I PI3K inhibition rectifies TFEB activity, lysosomal hydrolase function (notably cathepsin D), lysosomal acidification, autophagic flux, or POS clearance in RPE is a critical gap that precludes immediate advancement; by contrast, downstream interventions (rapamycin, TFEB activation, AKT2 inhibition) already demonstrate these benefits in RPE models (Falcão et al., 2024; Ghosh et al., 2024). On balance, pictilisib is plausible and testable but not yet justified for translational progression without focused RPE and ocular studies; an AKT2-selective inhibitor or TFEB-directed strategies may offer a higher probability of effect with narrower network perturbation, and should be run in parallel as mechanistic benchmarks (Ghosh et al., 2024; Karim et al., 2020). If the proposed RPE experiments confirm that pictilisib restores TFEB-driven lysosomal programs, improves cathepsin D maturation/activity, normalizes autophagy flux, and reduces POS-derived autofluorescence with acceptable ocular tolerability, the candidate would merit advancement to in vivo ocular efficacy testing; absent such confirmation, resources should pivot to agents with demonstrated RPE TFEB engagement (Ghosh et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2024).
