Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Rapamycin (sirolimus), commercially available as Sigma R0395, is a macrocyclic lactone originally isolated from the bacterium Streptomyces hygroscopicus, a discovery that dates back to studies on soil samples from Easter Island. As a naturally derived compound now synthesized and purified for clinical use, rapamycin belongs to the macrolide class and is best known for its potent immunosuppressive properties, having been used extensively to prevent organ rejection in transplantation. Over time, its application expanded beyond transplantation to include areas such as oncology, neurodegeneration, and age-related diseases due to its ability to inhibit the mechanistic target of rapamycin complex 1 (mTORC1). The rationale for repurposing rapamycin in the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD), specifically geographic atrophy (GA), stems from its established pharmacological profile, extensive safety record, and well-characterized biochemical functions. Its clinical approval and long-term safety data in other contexts provide a solid foundation for exploring its potential in ocular indications, particularly given its capacity to modulate autophagy in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells (Wang et al., 2022).

Therapeutic History:  
Rapamycin’s development began with its use as an immunosuppressant in organ transplantation, and over the ensuing decades, its application has broadened considerably. Biochemical and preclinical studies have demonstrated that rapamycin is an effective inhibitor of mTORC1, a critical regulator not only of cell proliferation but also of autophagy and lysosomal biogenesis. Early investigations revealed that rapamycin could induce autophagy in various cell types, including RPE cells, by inhibiting mTORC1, thereby facilitating the clearance of toxic aggregates and damaged organelles. This mechanism has been explored extensively for neurodegenerative conditions, and more recently, there has been focused investigation into its utility for dry AMD. Clinical trials have tested rapamycin in forms ranging from intravitreal to subconjunctival injections in patients with GA; for example, a clinical trial by the National Eye Institute aimed to evaluate intravitreal injections of sirolimus for GA, although this study was terminated due to safety concerns (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2012). Similarly, other studies using subconjunctival injections demonstrated that while rapamycin appears safe and well-tolerated, significant benefits in terms of preventing GA progression have not been conclusively demonstrated (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2008, 2011). In animal studies and in vitro RPE models, rapamycin enhanced autophagic flux, increased the activity of cathepsin D (CTSD), and reduced the accumulation of toxic material such as A2E—an effect that is consistent with a potential for slowing GA progression (Wang et al., 2022; Falcão et al., 2024). Thus, rapamycin’s therapeutic history encompasses a combination of robust preclinical evidence supporting its mechanistic action and mixed clinical outcomes in ocular trials, setting the stage for further investigation into optimal dosing, delivery methods, and patient selection criteria (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2008, 2011).

Mechanism of Action:  
Rapamycin exerts its biological effects primarily through direct inhibition of mTORC1, a serine/threonine kinase complex that integrates signals from nutrients, growth factors, and cellular energy status to regulate cell growth, proliferation, and autophagy. In the absence of rapamycin, active mTORC1 phosphorylates downstream targets such as S6 kinase and 4E-BP1, thereby promoting anabolic processes and suppressing autophagy. When rapamycin binds to its intracellular receptor, FKBP12, the resulting complex interacts with the FKBP12-rapamycin binding (FRB) domain of mTORC1, leading to its inhibition. This inhibition results in dephosphorylation and subsequent activation of transcription factor EB (TFEB), a master regulator of lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy-related genes. Activated TFEB then translocates to the nucleus, where it enhances the expression of genes involved in lysosomal function, acidification, and the production of lysosomal enzymes such as cathepsin D (CTSD) (Falcão et al., 2025; Falcão et al., 2024; Sinha et al., 2016). In the context of dry AMD, the proposed mechanism hinges on rapamycin’s ability to restore cellular homeostasis in RPE cells by increasing autophagic flux and lysosomal clearance of accumulated drusen components, which include toxic aggregates like A2E. Preclinical studies have shown that treatment of RPE cells with rapamycin results in a marked reduction in the accumulation of autofluorescent granules (AFGs) that are indicative of impaired lysosomal degradation (Falcão et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2025). The cascade initiated by rapamycin—mTORC1 inhibition, TFEB activation, and enhanced expression of lysosome-associated proteins such as LAMP1 and pro-cathepsin D—forms the crux of its proposed therapeutic action in mitigating the progression of GA by promoting the dismantling and clearance of pathological deposits (Falcão et al., 2024).

Expected Effect:  
In RPE cells, the inhibition of mTORC1 by rapamycin is expected to release the inhibitory phosphorylation on TFEB, enabling its nuclear translocation and activation of a transcriptional program that drives lysosomal biogenesis, acidification, and the production of key lysosomal enzymes such as cathepsin D. This molecular shift is anticipated to markedly enhance the autophagic capacity of the RPE, leading to increased degradation of drusen components, including lipofuscin and A2E, which are hallmarks of dry AMD pathology. The activation of autophagy not only facilitates the clearance of accumulated toxic material but also mitigates oxidative stress by removing damaged mitochondria and other organelles that may contribute to reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation (Wang et al., 2022; Falcão et al., 2024). Moreover, preclinical evidence indicates that, in ARPE-19 cell models, rapamycin improves cellular viability in the face of oxidative injury and reduces markers of cellular senescence by enhancing autophagic flux. These cellular effects are directly linked to the expression of critical proteins in RPE cells; for example, TFEB is known to be expressed in these cells and its activation correlates with increased lysosomal gene expression and function (Falcão et al., 2024) while cathepsin D, a lysosomal protease, is vital for the degradation of phagocytosed photoreceptor outer segments (Chang et al., 2022; Sinha et al., 2016). The intended therapeutic outcome is to slow or potentially halt the progression of GA by reducing the burden of drusen and preserving RPE function, which could translate into better preservation of visual acuity over time. However, it is important to note that while these mechanisms are promising in vitro, clinical translation has encountered challenges related to dosing, delivery, and the stage of disease at which intervention occurs (Wang et al., 2022; Falcão et al., 2024).

Overall Evaluation:  
Rapamycin presents itself as a scientifically promising yet clinically challenging candidate for the treatment of dry AMD. One of the key strengths of rapamycin is its well-established mechanism of action: as a potent mTORC1 inhibitor, it leverages a well-characterized pathway involving TFEB activation that directly targets the core pathology observed in dry AMD—the accumulation of drusen components and impaired lysosomal function in RPE cells. Preclinical studies have consistently demonstrated that rapamycin can enhance autophagic flux, lower levels of toxic aggregates such as A2E, and increase the activity of lysosomal enzymes like cathepsin D, thereby supporting its target validation in the context of RPE health (Falcão et al., 2025; Falcão et al., 2024). Additionally, rapamycin has an extensive history of clinical use in other indications, and its safety profile, while not without concerns, is well documented from its use as an immunosuppressant in transplantation and in various oncology settings (Wang et al., 2022).

However, the clinical translation of rapamycin for dry AMD has not been straightforward. Multiple clinical trials have assessed its application using different routes of administration, such as intravitreal and subconjunctival injections, with mixed results. While safety and tolerability have generally been acceptable, the efficacy endpoints—specifically, the prevention or slowing of GA progression—have not been definitively met in these studies (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2008, 2011, 2012; Wang et al., 2022). Furthermore, some trials encountered complications such as sterile endophthalmitis or observed decreases in visual acuity relative to untreated eyes, suggesting that even if the underlying molecular mechanisms are engaged, the overall benefits in late-stage disease might be limited (Wang et al., 2022; Falcão et al., 2024).

Another potential weakness is the complexity inherent in mTOR signaling itself. The pathway plays a dual role in cellular homeostasis—while its inhibition can promote autophagy and lysosomal clearance, inappropriate or excessive inhibition could lead to adverse effects such as increased retinal neuron apoptosis, particularly in advanced stages of AMD where the cellular milieu is significantly altered (Wang et al., 2022; Chang et al., 2022). Moreover, the optimal dosing regimen and delivery method for achieving the desired ocular concentration without incurring systemic side effects remain unresolved. Some studies have suggested that modifications to the formulation, such as encapsulation in synthetic nanoparticles, could enhance ocular penetration and prolong the effective duration of rapamycin within the eye, thereby minimizing side effects and improving efficacy (Jo et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2022).

Despite these challenges, the strength of rapamycin’s mechanism—the inhibition of mTORC1 and consequent activation of TFEB leading to enhanced lysosomal biogenesis—remains compelling. The molecular rationale is robust, and the repeated demonstration of reduced levels of autofluorescent granules in RPE cells following rapamycin treatment is particularly encouraging (Falcão et al., 2024). The concept of using a repurposed, clinically approved drug to address a significant unmet need in dry AMD is attractive, especially given the limited treatment options currently available for this degenerative condition. In this light, further investigations—ideally, in earlier stages of AMD and with innovative delivery modalities—may reveal a niche where rapamycin can exert a clinically meaningful benefit (Wang et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2019).

In conclusion, while rapamycin has significant potential grounded in sound molecular pharmacology and extensive preclinical validation, its clinical application for dry AMD warrants careful optimization. The candidate’s strengths lie in its potent and well-understood mechanism of mTORC1 inhibition, the activation of TFEB, and subsequent improvements in lysosomal function and autophagic clearance in RPE cells. Conversely, clinical challenges including mixed efficacy outcomes in GA trials, potential adverse effects related to mTOR pathway modulation in vulnerable retinal neurons, and limitations in current dosing/delivery strategies represent hurdles that must be surmounted. Based on these comprehensive literature insights, rapamycin remains a promising candidate for further investigation, albeit with recommendations to explore its use in earlier disease stages and in combination with advanced ocular delivery systems to maximize its therapeutic benefit while minimizing risks (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2012; Wang et al., 2022; Falcão et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2025).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
USP14 inhibitor IU1 (Sigma SML0010) is a synthetic small-molecule compound originally discovered through high-throughput screening efforts aimed at identifying inhibitors of deubiquitinating enzymes (DUBs) associated with the proteasome. IU1 belongs to the class of small-molecule DUB inhibitors that specifically target USP14, a proteasome-associated deubiquitinase responsible for trimming ubiquitin chains from substrates before their degradation by the 26S proteasome. Early medicinal chemistry studies led to the development of IU1 and its more potent analogs (such as IU1-47), which exploit structure–activity relationships on a benzene–dimethyl-pyrrole scaffold with tailored electron-withdrawing substitutions and lipophilic enhancements designed to improve potency, selectivity, and bioavailability (Lim et al., 2024; Boselli et al., 2017; Qin et al., 2024). These compounds are cell permeable and have been employed as chemical probes in multiple preclinical settings to modulate proteostasis via targeted inhibition of USP14. In essence, IU1 reflects a series of rationally designed molecules aimed at shifting the balance of proteasome-mediated degradation by preventing USP14’s “trimming” activity, thereby effectively accelerating the clearance of misfolded and aggregation-prone proteins.

Therapeutic History:  
The therapeutic history of USP14 inhibitors like IU1 is primarily rooted in preclinical research addressing proteostasis dysfunction in models of aging and neurodegeneration rather than in clinical or veterinary practice. In Drosophila models of proteostasis-associated aging, IU1 treatment was shown to reduce the accumulation of polyubiquitinated aggregates, increase autophagy markers such as LC3, improve behavioral phenotypes, and even extend lifespan, with these benefits abrogated when autophagy was experimentally disrupted (Lim et al., 2024). In mammalian cell proteotoxicity models—using stressors such as canavanine plus azetidine—IU1 has similarly been reported to reduce ubiquitin conjugate accumulation and enhance autophagic responses (Lim et al., 2024). Moreover, in primary neuronal cultures, more potent analogs like IU1-47 have been used to promote degradation of pathologic proteins such as tau, thereby supporting the concept that USP14 inhibition enhances proteasome-assisted clearance of aggregation-prone substrates (Boselli et al., 2017; Kiprowska, 2016). Despite these promising preclinical data in models of neurodegeneration and systemic aging, there is no direct evidence to date that IU1 or its analogs have been applied to treat dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or geographic atrophy specifically. However, given that several key observations in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells—such as evidence of impaired ubiquitin–proteasome system (UPS) and autophagy cross-talk, aggregate accumulation, and lysosomal dysfunction—are central to AMD pathology (Blasiak et al., 2019; Kaarniranta et al., 2023; Shang & Taylor, 2012), repurposing IU1 to restore proteostasis in RPE represents an innovative extension of its preclinical use.

Mechanism of Action:  
The known mechanism of IU1 centers on its inhibition of USP14, a deubiquitinating enzyme that transiently associates with the proteasome. USP14 normally functions by “trimming” ubiquitin chains on substrates as they enter the proteasome, an activity that can delay substrate degradation and allow for substrate rescue under stress conditions. IU1 and its optimized analogs (e.g., IU1-47) act through allosteric mechanisms—not by directly competing at the catalytic site but by binding a pocket distal (approximately 8.3 Å away) from the catalytic center, thereby perturbing USP14’s structural conformation and catalytic efficiency (Qin et al., 2024; Lim et al., 2024). Inhibition of USP14 by IU1 leads to a reduced removal of ubiquitin chains, effectively “locking in” the ubiquitin tag on misfolded and aggregation-prone proteins and facilitating their recognition and degradation by the 26S proteasome. Beyond its direct impact on proteasomal degradation, USP14 inhibition has been reported to modulate autophagy—evident from increased LC3 lipidation and autophagic flux in certain cellular contexts (Lim et al., 2024; Kim, 2020). Some studies suggest that USP14 may also indirectly influence autophagy by regulating the turnover of factors such as UVRAG, a key autophagy regulator, although these connections remain to be fully elucidated. Notably, while IU1 has been shown to accelerate aggregate clearance in neuronal and Drosophila models, a series of studies have also flagged potential off-target effects at higher concentrations, including inhibition of mitochondrial Complex I leading to ATP depletion and subsequent activation of calpain-mediated proteolysis (Kiprowska, 2016; Kiprowska et al., n.d.). Hence, the molecular interactions of IU1 are complex and highly context-dependent, with the potential to both enhance proteasomal degradation and, at non-optimized doses, induce metabolic perturbations.

Expected Effect:  
In the context of dry age-related macular degeneration, particularly geographic atrophy, the central hypothesis is that IU1 will inhibit USP14 in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells, thereby accelerating the proteasome-assisted clearance of misfolded, aggregation-prone proteins. RPE cells in AMD display defects in both the UPS and the autophagy/lysosomal systems, with studies documenting decreased proteasome activity, accumulation of ubiquitinated aggregates, elevated levels of the selective autophagy adaptor SQSTM1/p62, and lysosomal dysfunction including impaired acidification mediated by vacuolar ATPase (v-ATPase) (Blasiak et al., 2019; Kaarniranta et al., 2023; Shang & Taylor, 2012; Viiri, 2019). By inhibiting USP14, IU1 is expected to shift the proteostasis balance in RPE cells towards enhanced degradation of misfolded proteins via the proteasome. This would not only reduce the intracellular aggregate burden but also alleviate the overloading of the lysosomal pathway—in turn potentially restoring lysosomal functions such as proper acidification by v-ATPase activity. Improved lysosomal acidification is known to facilitate the maturation and activity of cathepsin D, a key lysosomal protease responsible for degrading various protein aggregates and damaged organelles (Kaarniranta et al., 2023). Moreover, preclinical findings in neuronal cells have demonstrated that USP14 inhibition reduces aggregate load (e.g., tau) and promotes autophagic flux (Boselli et al., 2017; Lim et al., 2024), lending indirect support to the concept that these effects might be recapitulated in RPE cells. Although no direct data exist for IU1 in RPE, the mechanistic parallels between proteostasis impairment in neurons and RPE—as documented in extensive AMD literature—suggest that IU1 could reduce aggregate accumulation and oxidative stress in RPE, thereby slowing the progression of geographic atrophy.

Overall Evaluation:  
The overall evaluation of USP14 inhibitor IU1 as a therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration is cautiously optimistic yet highlights several critical areas for further investigation. On the positive side, IU1 represents an innovative strategy targeting a central node in protein quality control—USP14—that regulates the degradation of misfolded, aggregation-prone proteins via the proteasome and modulates autophagic pathways. Preclinical evidence in Drosophila models and neuronal cultures demonstrates that pharmacological USP14 inhibition can enhance aggregate clearance, improve proteostasis, and even extend lifespan and motor function under proteotoxic stress conditions (Lim et al., 2024; Boselli et al., 2017). These findings support the concept that modulating the UPS–autophagy interplay may be beneficial in diseases where proteostasis failure is a key driver, such as dry AMD, in which RPE cells experience aggregate build-up, defective autophagy, and lysosomal dysfunction (Blasiak et al., 2019; Kaarniranta et al., 2023; Shang & Taylor, 2012).

Furthermore, the biochemical mechanism by which IU1 operates—namely, reducing the deubiquitinating activity of USP14 to promote ubiquitin-tag retention and substrate commitment to degradation—provides a theoretically attractive approach to simultaneously reduce the proteasomal backlog and relieve lysosomal burden. The potential secondary effects on autophagy, including improved LC3-II turnover and possibly upregulated clearance of aggregates through aggrephagy, add further appeal to the candidate as a multi-modal modulator of proteostasis. The cell-permeable, small-molecule nature of IU1, along with available more potent analogs (such as IU1-47), offers promising opportunities for medicinal chemistry optimization and dosage refinement, especially important given the need for safe application in delicate ocular tissues.

However, several weaknesses and challenges must be addressed before IU1 can be considered a viable therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. A significant concern originates from studies in neuronal systems that indicate off-target effects at higher concentrations—specifically, inhibition of mitochondrial Complex I, ATP depletion, and activation of calpain-mediated proteolysis (Kiprowska, 2016; Kiprowska et al., n.d.). These potential toxicities raise the possibility that a narrow therapeutic window may exist, necessitating thorough dose-response studies in RPE cell models to ensure efficacy without compromising cell viability. Moreover, no direct preclinical studies have yet evaluated IU1 in RPE cells or in animal models of geographic atrophy. As such, critical parameters—such as its ability to modulate v-ATPase function, maintain lysosomal acidification, boost cathepsin D activity, and ultimately clear RPE-specific aggregates such as lipofuscin or oxidized photoreceptor debris—remain to be validated (Kaarniranta et al., 2023; Shang & Taylor, 2012).

Additionally, while the mechanistic data from neurodegenerative models are compelling, the biochemical environment of RPE cells differs from that of neurons in several key respects. RPE cells are highly phagocytic, exposed to constant oxidative stress, and rely on a finely tuned balance between proteasomal and lysosomal pathways to manage the constant influx of photoreceptor outer segment material (Blasiak et al., 2019; Viiri, 2019). Thus, any intervention that modulates proteostasis must be carefully tailored to avoid unintended disruptions in these homeostatic processes. The current literature also underscores the complexity of deubiquitinase biology; while USP14 inhibition appears beneficial in some contexts, the intricate interplay with other DUBs and the broader UPS could lead to compensatory mechanisms that diminish the anticipated therapeutic effect or even trigger adverse consequences (Faber & Roepman, 2019; Kim, 2020).

In summary, USP14 inhibitor IU1 offers an innovative and potentially transformative approach to restoring proteostasis in RPE cells by enhancing proteasomal degradation and autophagic clearance of misfolded proteins—a strategy that directly addresses the pathobiology of dry AMD and geographic atrophy as defined by aggregate accumulation and lysosomal dysfunction (Lim et al., 2024; Blasiak et al., 2019; Kaarniranta et al., 2023). The strengths of this candidate include its robust preclinical data in non-RPE systems, its well-characterized mechanism of action, and its amenability to further chemical optimization. However, significant weaknesses, including potential off-target mitochondrial toxicity, an unestablished therapeutic window in RPE cells, and the lack of direct preclinical studies in AMD models, necessitate cautious and rigorous further investigation. To move forward, it will be essential to conduct targeted RPE-specific in vitro assays and in vivo studies—assessing proteasome activity, autophagy flux, lysosomal acidification (v-ATPase function), cathepsin D activity, and aggregate clearance—while carefully monitoring for cytotoxicity. Only with such detailed preclinical validation can the promise of IU1 as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD be fully assessed (Lim et al., 2024; Blasiak et al., 2019; Kiprowska, 2016; Shang & Taylor, 2012).

It acts predominantly as a peroxisome proliferator‐activated receptor alpha (PPARα) agonist. Fenofibrate itself is a prodrug that undergoes hepatic esterase hydrolysis to form its active metabolite, fenofibric acid, which binds to PPARα and modulates the transcription of genes involved in lipid metabolism. This drug class has historically been used for lowering serum triglycerides and increasing high‐density lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol, reflecting its well‐established lipid‐modulating properties. Although fenofibrate was not initially developed for ocular indications, its mechanism as a PPARα agonist has spurred interest for repurposing in retinal diseases. In particular, the broad class of fibrates has garnered attention because PPARα is expressed in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), and its activation can regulate lipid oxidation, autophagy, and inflammatory processes—all of which are critically disturbed in dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) (Fu et al., 2019; Falcão et al., 2025).

Therapeutic History:  
Fenofibrate has a robust clinical history in the management of dyslipidemia and cardiovascular risk reduction, with extensive use in millions of patients worldwide. Its ocular benefits became apparent with large clinical trials, such as the FIELD and ACCORD Eye studies, which demonstrated that fenofibrate can reduce the progression of diabetic retinopathy and decrease the need for retinal laser therapy in diabetic patients (Lu et al., 2014; Treacy & Hurst, 2012). Although these trials primarily addressed diabetic retinal disease, subsequent preclinical and clinical reports have indicated that the retina may benefit from the lipid‐modulatory, anti‐inflammatory, and neuroprotective actions of PPARα agonists. For instance, several studies have explored fenofibrate in animal models of retinal ischemia and neovascularization, showing protective effects on the retinal vasculature and RPE (Fu et al., 2020; Qiu et al., 2017). While the majority of these ocular studies have focused on diabetic retinopathy or neovascular AMD, emerging literature has pointed to the potential of targeting PPARα signaling to mitigate RPE dysfunction and lipid accumulation, which are hallmarks of dry AMD (da Ana et al., 2023; Dou & Duerfeldt, 2020). This history of fenofibrate in retinal disease, combined with its proven clinical safety for dyslipidemia and established ocular pharmacokinetics (including studies on topical delivery), provides a compelling rationale for its repurposing in dry AMD (Tomita et al., 2020; Lee et al., 2021).

Mechanism of Action:  
Fenofibrate’s mechanism of action is rooted in its role as a PPARα agonist. Upon conversion to fenofibric acid, the compound binds to PPARα—a nuclear receptor highly expressed in several tissues, including the liver and the retinal pigment epithelium. When activated, PPARα forms heterodimers with retinoid X receptors (RXR) and binds to peroxisome proliferator response elements (PPREs) within the promoters of target genes. This binding results in the upregulation of genes critical for fatty acid uptake, β-oxidation, and lipid catabolism. Key genes regulated by PPARα include those encoding enzymes that facilitate mitochondrial and peroxisomal fatty acid oxidation, which in turn reduces intracellular lipid accumulation and promotes energy homeostasis (Fu et al., 2019; Lee et al., 2023).

In the context of the RPE and dry AMD, the hypothesis is that fenofibrate will stimulate PPARα-mediated transcriptional programs that not only enhance lipid catabolism but also intersect with cellular degradative pathways. One of the central tenets of the proposed mechanism is the coactivation of transcription factor EB (TFEB). TFEB is recognized as a master regulator of lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy through the coordinated lysosomal expression and regulation (CLEAR) network. Under normal conditions, TFEB is kept inactive in the cytosol by phosphorylation mediated by mTORC1. Under stress conditions or when lysosomal function is impaired, TFEB translocates to the nucleus to upregulate genes involved in lysosomal acidification, autophagy, and lipid metabolism. The therapeutic hypothesis posits that fenofibrate, through PPARα activation in RPE cells, will indirectly coactivate TFEB. This may occur through changes in cellular metabolism that reduce mTORC1 activity or via direct transcriptional crosstalk between PPARα target genes and the CLEAR network (Falcão et al., 2025; da Ana et al., 2023).

Moreover, TFEB activation is expected to enhance lysosomal acidification—a process necessary for optimal degradation of phagocytosed outer segment debris and drusen precursors—and upregulate lysosomal hydrolases such as cathepsin D. In AMD, RPE cells often show lysosomal dysfunction characterized by deficient cathepsin D activity and lipofuscin accumulation. By improving lysosomal function, fenofibrate may facilitate the clearance of lipid-rich drusen precursors, thereby reducing RPE stress and preventing progression of dry AMD (Falcão et al., 2025; da Ana et al., 2023). In addition to these lysosome-centric effects, fenofibrate has anti-inflammatory properties, as PPARα activation suppresses NF-κB signaling, reduces the expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines (e.g., TNF-α and IL-1β), and alleviates oxidative stress—all of which are exacerbating factors in the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Lee et al., 2023; Treacy & Hurst, 2012). Furthermore, the modulation of the FGF21 pathway, occasionally observed with fenofibrate treatment, may contribute to neuroprotection and further support retinal homeostasis (Tomita et al., 2020; Lee et al., 2023). Taken together, the molecular interactions initiated by fenofibrate converge on restoring lipid homeostasis, enhancing autophagic flux, and mitigating inflammatory insults in RPE cells—a multifaceted approach that aligns with the pathophysiology of dry AMD (Treacy & Hurst, 2012; Lee et al., 2021).

Expected Effect:  
In the assays proposed to evaluate fenofibrate’s efficacy for dry AMD, one anticipates several measurable cellular and biochemical outcomes. First, treatment of RPE cells with fenofibrate should lead to a consistent activation of PPARα target genes, as demonstrated by upregulation of markers for fatty acid oxidation and lipid catabolism. Such molecular signatures can be quantified using gene expression analyses and reporter assays for PPRE activity (Fu et al., 2019; Tomita et al., 2021). Concurrently, it is expected that fenofibrate will enhance autophagic flux in RPE cells. This could be evident from increased LC3-II accumulation in the presence of lysosomal inhibitors and enhanced degradation of autophagic substrates, which would indicate an upregulation of the autophagic machinery (Falcão et al., 2025; da Ana et al., 2023).

A critical aspect of the proposed mechanism involves TFEB. Upon fenofibrate treatment, one should observe increased nuclear translocation of TFEB in RPE cells, which can be assessed by immunocytochemistry and subcellular fractionation. The activation of TFEB would then be expected to drive the transcriptional upregulation of genes encoding lysosomal proteins, such as lysosomal-associated membrane protein 2 (LAMP2) and various components of the V-ATPase complex, leading to enhanced lysosomal acidification. Lysotracker assays and measurements of intralysosomal pH could be deployed to confirm that fenofibrate-treated cells exhibit more acidic lysosomes (Falcão et al., 2025; da Ana et al., 2023).

Furthermore, increased cathepsin D activity is a pivotal expected outcome, serving as a surrogate marker for improved lysosomal enzyme function in degrading waste products, including drusen precursors. Biochemical assays to quantify cathepsin D activity, alongside immunostaining for its protein levels, would help to validate this aspect of the mechanism. Functionally, the cumulative effect of these molecular changes should be a reduction in the accumulation of lipofuscin and other drusen-associated lipid-protein aggregates within the RPE. This reduction could be observed using autofluorescence imaging techniques and electron microscopy to assess cytoplasmic inclusions (Falcão et al., 2025; Treacy & Hurst, 2012).

Additionally, given that fenofibrate has established anti-inflammatory properties, one might expect a decrease in the secretion or expression of inflammatory mediators in RPE cultures, as well as improved cellular resistance to oxidative stress challenges. Cytokine assays and measurements of reactive oxygen species (ROS) would serve as corroborative evidence for an anti-inflammatory and antioxidant effect. Importantly, because reduced autophagy and lysosomal dysfunction are central to dry AMD, the combined effect of enhanced lipid catabolism, improved lysosomal acidification, and increased cathepsin D activity should contribute to an overall reduction in cellular stress and preservation of RPE integrity (Falcão et al., 2025; Treacy & Hurst, 2012). Taken together, these expected effects would validate the therapeutic hypothesis and provide a strong rationale for advancing fenofibrate into further preclinical models of dry AMD.

Overall Evaluation:  
Fenofibrate emerges as a promising repurposed drug candidate for dry AMD based on several compelling lines of evidence. The drug’s long-established clinical safety profile and extensive use in dyslipidemia serve as major strengths in terms of its translational potential (Lu et al., 2014; Treacy & Hurst, 2012). Additionally, the documented success of fenofibrate in slowing the progression of diabetic retinopathy in large-scale clinical trials underscores its ability to exert beneficial effects in retinal tissues (Lu et al., 2014; Treacy & Hurst, 2012).

From a mechanistic standpoint, fenofibrate’s mode of action as a PPARα agonist is well characterized, and its ability to stimulate lipid oxidation and enhance fatty acid metabolism could directly address the lipid dysregulation observed in RPE cells in dry AMD (Fu et al., 2019; da Ana et al., 2023). Crucially, the hypothesis that fenofibrate may also coactivate TFEB, thereby promoting lysosomal biogenesis and function, positions it uniquely among therapeutic candidates. Improved lysosomal acidification and increased cathepsin D activity would facilitate the clearance of drusen precursors and reduce the cytotoxic accumulation of lipofuscin, which is a central pathogenic feature of dry AMD (Falcão et al., 2025; da Ana et al., 2023; Dou & Duerfeldt, 2020). The convergence of lipid catabolism enhancement, autophagy upregulation, and anti-inflammatory effects creates a multifaceted therapeutic profile that is particularly attractive for a complex, multifactorial disease such as dry AMD.

However, there are also notable weaknesses and challenges. Most of the current evidence supporting fenofibrate’s retinal benefits is derived from studies focusing on diabetic retinopathy or neovascular AMD rather than directly on dry AMD. Although there is supportive mechanistic rationale linking PPARα activation to improved lysosomal function in the RPE, direct evidence for fenofibrate’s efficacy in reducing drusen accumulation and alleviating RPE stress in dry AMD models remains sparse (Dou & Duerfeldt, 2020; da Ana et al., 2023). The specific involvement of TFEB activation by fenofibrate in RPE cells has not been fully elucidated in the existing literature, and further in vitro and in vivo studies are needed to validate this aspect of the mechanism. Additionally, while fenofibrate is generally safe when used systemically, there have been concerns regarding potential renal side effects, which may be particularly relevant in the elderly population that predominantly suffers from AMD (Treacy & Hurst, 2012; Tomita et al., 2021). Thus, optimizing the route of delivery—possibly via topical formulations or nanoparticle-based systems—may be necessary to ensure sufficient retinal bioavailability while minimizing systemic exposure (Huang et al., 2021; Lu et al., 2014).

Another potential limitation is the dose required to achieve sufficient PPARα activation in the RPE to modulate TFEB and lysosomal pathways effectively. Preclinical studies have sometimes required relatively high doses of fenofibrate to observe significant ocular effects, and the pharmacokinetic barriers posed by the blood-retinal barrier may further complicate translatability (Tomita et al., 2020; Lee et al., 2023). Moreover, the current body of literature underscores the need for more targeted studies to determine whether the benefits seen with fenofibrate in models of diabetic retinopathy and neovascular AMD can be replicated in models of dry AMD, where the pathogenic processes are distinct in their emphasis on lipid accumulation, oxidative stress, and RPE dysfunction (da Ana et al., 2023; Dou & Duerfeldt, 2020).

Despite these challenges, the overall evaluation remains cautiously optimistic. Fenofibrate’s mechanism of action aligns well with the pathophysiological features of dry AMD, particularly regarding the restoration of lipid homeostasis and the enhancement of lysosomal function. The dual potential for direct metabolic benefits via PPARα activation and indirect benefits through TFEB-mediated lysosomal enhancement represents an innovative therapeutic strategy that could fill a critical gap in the current treatment landscape for dry AMD (Falcão et al., 2025; Fu et al., 2019; da Ana et al., 2023; Dou & Duerfeldt, 2020; Lee et al., 2023). Additionally, the availability of various delivery platforms—including systemic administration, topical eye drops, and nanoparticle formulations—provides flexibility in addressing bioavailability challenges and minimizing adverse effects (Huang et al., 2021; Lu et al., 2014).

In conclusion, fenofibrate (Sigma F6020) possesses significant potential for repurposing as a drug candidate for dry AMD based on its well-established pharmacological profile, robust clinical safety record, and mechanistic actions that target key pathological processes in the RPE. While further preclinical studies specifically focused on dry AMD models are warranted to validate the hypothesized coactivation of TFEB and subsequent enhancement of lysosomal acidification and cathepsin D activity, the current literature provides a strong scientific basis for such investigations. The strengths of fenofibrate lie in its multifaceted mechanism—encompassing lipid catabolism, autophagy, anti-inflammatory, and possibly neuroprotective effects—which collectively offer a promising strategy to reduce drusen precursors and mitigate RPE stress. The primary weaknesses involve the need for direct evidence in dry AMD models, optimization of ocular delivery to overcome pharmacokinetic barriers, and careful monitoring of potential systemic side effects in an elderly population. Overall, fenofibrate represents a compelling and scientifically sound candidate that merits further exploration in the context of dry AMD, with the potential to significantly advance our therapeutic arsenal against this currently untreatable form of macular degeneration (Falcão et al., 2025; Fu et al., 2019; da Ana et al., 2023; Dou & Duerfeldt, 2020; Lee et al., 2023).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
miR-204 is a highly conserved microRNA encoded within an intron of the TRPM3 locus and is among the most abundant miRNAs in human fetal retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) at roughly 10,000 copies per cell, with expression also present in neural retina and photoreceptors (Shiels, 2020; Karali et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2019). The proposed therapeutic candidate is a miR-204 mimic (agomir), i.e., a synthetic double-stranded RNA designed to reconstitute or augment mature miR-204 activity in target cells, thereby restoring sequence-specific repression of cognate mRNAs via Argonaute/RISC-mediated post-transcriptional regulation (Du & Palczewski, 2022). Agomirs are typically produced by solid-phase oligonucleotide synthesis and formulated with stabilizing chemical modifications and delivery moieties to resist nucleases and evade innate immune sensors; however, the present literature corpus specific to miR-204 provides no details on the chemical design or manufacturing of a miR-204 agomir used in ocular studies (Du & Palczewski, 2022; Karali et al., 2020). In vivo “gain-of-function” delivery of miR-204 has been achieved preclinically using adeno-associated viral (AAV) gene therapy vectors encoding the murine pre-miR-204 hairpin driven by ubiquitous (CMV) or photoreceptor-specific (RHO) promoters, establishing that increasing miR-204 activity is feasible and can confer neuroprotective and anti-inflammatory effects in degenerating retina (Karali et al., 2020). Separately, the agomir modality (chemically synthesized miR-204 mimic) has been used in ocular systems and vertebrate development: ocular injection of a miR-204 mimic in rat retina reduced GAP-43 expression, and double-stranded miR-204 mimic injection in medaka embryos caused microphthalmia and lens dysgenesis, demonstrating biological activity in vivo with potential context-dependent liabilities (Shiels, 2020).

Within the broader therapeutic class, miRNA modulation includes replacement (mimics/agomirs) and inhibition (antimiRs) and has been explored preclinically and clinically; the most advanced clinical precedent involves an antimiR of miR-122 (miravirsen) in hepatology, while miRNA mimics face delivery, stability, and innate-immune activation challenges that necessitate chemical modification and targeted delivery—issues directly relevant to deploying a miR-204 agomir in the eye (Parsi, 2016). In ophthalmology, miRNAs regulate essential RPE functions including phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments (POS), autophagy, endolysosomal trafficking, epithelial barrier integrity, and inflammatory signaling, making miR replacement an attractive strategy to correct multi-pathway dysfunctions typical of dry AMD (Du & Palczewski, 2022).

Therapeutic History  
- Ocular/retinal delivery of miR-204 by AAV gene therapy:  
  - In RHO-P347S and Aipl1−/− mouse models of inherited retinal degeneration (IRD), subretinal AAV2/8 vectors expressing pre-miR-204 preserved retinal function by ERG, reduced photoreceptor cell death (TUNEL), and dampened microglial activation and innate immune/inflammatory transcriptomes; luciferase data supported direct targeting of immune/apoptosis transcripts (Siglec1, Xaf1) by miR-204 (Karali et al., 2020). These effects persisted through at least PN60 when dosed at PN4 in the RHO-P347S model, and benefit tracked with ubiquitous expression (CMV) more than photoreceptor-restricted expression (RHO), consistent with non–cell-autonomous and multi-cell-type actions (Karali et al., 2020). The studies confirm feasibility and efficacy of miR-204 augmentation in murine retina, but they used viral expression rather than chemically synthesized mimics and were not performed in dry AMD models (Karali et al., 2020).  
- Ocular/neuronal use of miR-204 mimics/inhibitors:  
  - Direct ocular injection of a miR-204 mimic in rats decreased GAP-43 expression and, in the context of injury, increased retinal TUNEL-positive cells, while a miR-204 inhibitor increased GAP-43, indicating robust on-target modulation and context-dependent toxicity risk (Shiels, 2020). In medaka, overexpression of a miR-204 double-stranded mimic (agomir) produced microphthalmia and lens dysgenesis, underscoring the need for careful dose, spatial restriction, and developmental timing (Shiels, 2020).  
- Disease relevance of miR-204 to dry AMD biology:  
  - Genetic deletion of miR-204 in mice causes progressive, age-dependent RPE/retina pathology reminiscent of dry AMD: hyper-autofluorescent deposits, impaired POS degradation with rhodopsin accumulation in RPE, autophagosome accumulation, lysosomal deficits (lower LAMP2 signal), microglial migration to the RPE apical surface, increased proinflammatory cytokine secretion (apical IL-8), IPM disorganization, reduced ERG components (photoreceptor and RPE-driven), and downregulation of visual cycle genes (LRAT, RPE65, TTR) that would constrain retinoid recycling (Zhang et al., 2019; Intartaglia et al., 2021). Parallel anti-miR-204 knockdown in primary human fetal RPE recapitulates autophagy/lysosomal and phagolysosomal defects: reduced POS digestion without reduced uptake (~20% slower clearance), increased p62, accumulation of undigested autophagosomes, reduced LAMP2, and intracellular rhodopsin accumulation; Rab22a protein (an inhibitor of endosome maturation) rises in both anti-miR and KO settings, mechanistically linking the phenotype to a miR-204 → Rab22a axis (Zhang et al., 2019). These convergent in vivo/in vitro loss-of-function data provide the key mechanistic rationale to explore miR-204 augmentation as a corrective therapy in dry AMD-like RPE dysfunction (Zhang et al., 2019).  
- miRNA class precedent and translational trajectory:  
  - Reviews emphasize that RPE miRNAs control phagocytosis and lysosomal pathways and that specific miR:mRNA pairs (including miR-204→Rab22a) are central to vesicle trafficking; they also note that miR therapeutics can be delivered via viral vectors or nonviral carriers (e.g., nanoparticles), but that miRNA mimic programs face stability, delivery, and immune-activation challenges that will need to be mitigated (Du & Palczewski, 2022; Parsi, 2016). There are no reports of miR-204 agomir use in dry AMD patients or animal models of dry AMD; thus, clinical and AMD-specific preclinical history for a chemically synthesized miR-204 mimic is absent in the present corpus (Du & Palczewski, 2022; Karali et al., 2020).

Mechanism of Action  
At the biochemical level, mature miR-204 is loaded into the RISC and binds target 3′ UTR seed sites to repress translation and/or promote mRNA decay of specific transcripts that regulate RPE homeostasis (Du & Palczewski, 2022). The best-supported target in the context of endosomal maturation is Rab22a, a small GTPase that acts as an inhibitor of early-to-late endosomal progression and thereby impedes endosome–lysosome fusion necessary for proteolysis (Zhang et al., 2019). In miR-204 loss-of-function models (global KO mice and anti-miR-204–treated human fetal RPE), Rab22a protein levels are increased by immunostaining and western blot in RPE, particularly after POS feeding, and the authors interpret this as a dysregulation at the intersection of the autophagy and endosome pathways (Zhang et al., 2019). The mechanistic model is explicit: loss of miR-204 increases Rab22a expression, which impedes maturation of early autophagosomal/endosomal intermediates that fail to fuse with lysosomes, resulting in decreased phagocytic clearance and persistent accumulation of POS-derived rhodopsin in RPE (Zhang et al., 2019).

Functional correlates of this endosomal maturation block are well documented in RPE:  
- Phagolysosomal/autophagy markers: anti-miR-204 RPE shows increased p62/SQSTM1, increased number/size of undigested autophagosomes by TEM, and altered LC3B isoform distribution (increased LC3B-I without consistent LC3B-II accumulation), consistent with impaired maturation of degradative compartments rather than defective initiation of LC3-associated processes (Zhang et al., 2019). Anti-miR-204 reduces lysosomal content/function by ~1.6-fold lower LAMP2 in RPE relative to controls, consistent with fewer functional lysosomes available for phagosome fusion (Zhang et al., 2019).  
- Phagocytosis and digestion of POS: uptake per se is not impaired, but the digestion rate is slowed (~20% reduction in clearance in anti-miR-204 RPE by FACS-based pHrodo POS assays), directly supporting a degradative block downstream of engulfment (Zhang et al., 2019).  
- Rhodopsin accumulation: in miR-204−/− mice, rhodopsin-containing POS material accumulates within RPE at the peak of daily phagocytosis (8–10 a.m.) as measured by IF and western blot; anti-miR-204 hfRPE also accumulates rhodopsin after POS feeding (Zhang et al., 2019).  
- Secretory/inflammatory signaling: anti-miR-204 increases apical IL-8 secretion ~2-fold in hfRPE, creating a chemokine gradient predicted to attract retinal microglia to the RPE apical surface, which is observed in KO animals, and likely contributes to hyper-autofluorescent deposits and inflammatory retinal dysfunction (Zhang et al., 2019).  
- Electrophysiological and structural consequences: miR-204−/− mice exhibit reduced retinal photoreceptor and bipolar responses (ERG a- and b-wave), reduced RPE-derived DC-ERG components (c-wave and FO), age-dependent lipofuscin accumulation, interphotoreceptor matrix disorganization, and ultrastructural RPE defects, all consistent with chronic degradative deficiency and secondary degeneration (Zhang et al., 2019).

Beyond the Rab22a/endosome axis, miR-204 maintains epithelial identity and apical membrane physiology in RPE:  
- TGF-β signaling and EMT restraint: miR-204 directly targets TGFBR2 at the apical membrane; its inhibition upregulates TGF-β pathway genes (TGFBR2, SNAI2), collapses transepithelial resistance (~80% decrease), reduces claudins/tight junctions, and promotes EMT-like changes, linking miR-204 to barrier integrity and anti-fibrotic states (Shiels, 2020; Zhang et al., 2019).  
- Ion homeostasis: miR-204 loss indirectly reduces Kir7.1 expression and K+ efflux, leading to RPE cell swelling and subretinal space perturbations that can promote autophagy; these changes plausibly contribute to the reduced c-wave amplitude in KO animals (Zhang et al., 2019).  
- Visual cycle: miR-204 deficiency downregulates LRAT, RPE65, and TTR, impairing 11-cis-retinal regeneration and retinoid transport, thereby coupling endolysosomal deficits with phototransduction support failure (Intartaglia et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2019).

Inflammation can suppress miR-204 levels: IFN-γ downregulates miR-204 in ARPE-19, and miR-204 is coregulated with TRPM3; given that inflammation is a key driver in AMD, cytokine-driven miR-204 depletion provides a pathophysiological link to disease (Shiels, 2020).

In contrast to the detailed loss-of-function and in vitro mechanistic data, direct rescue experiments that re-introduce miR-204 in RPE to reverse Rab22a elevation, restore endosome–lysosome maturation, and normalize POS degradation have not been reported in the cited sources; the reported augmentation studies used AAV-miR-204 in IRD models and measured predominantly neuroinflammation and apoptosis endpoints rather than phagolysosomal rescue in RPE (Zhang et al., 2019; Karali et al., 2020).

Expected Effect  
If a chemically modified miR-204 agomir is delivered to RPE and achieves sufficient intracellular loading into Ago2/RISC, the expected molecular and cellular effects, by inversion of the validated loss-of-function phenotypes, are:  
- Target repression and endosomal maturation: Decrease Rab22a protein abundance in RPE, relieving its inhibitory effect on maturation of early endosomes/autophagosomal intermediates and permitting efficient endosome–lysosome fusion and phagolysosome function (Zhang et al., 2019).  
- Phagolysosomal/autophagy normalization: Increase functional lysosome content (e.g., rescue of LAMP2 levels), reduce p62 accumulation, decrease number/size of undigested autophagosomes, and accelerate degradation (but not uptake) of POS cargo in hfRPE digestion assays (e.g., increased pHrodo chase rate, reduced intracellular rhodopsin by IF/WB after standardized POS feeds) (Zhang et al., 2019).  
- Reduction of inflammatory signaling and microglial recruitment: Lower apical IL-8 secretion, diminishing chemotactic signals for resident microglia and reducing subretinal microglial accumulation; reduce hyper-autofluorescent material accrual over time, which is associated with impaired POS degradation (Zhang et al., 2019).  
- Functional recovery: Improve RPE and retinal electrophysiology (DC-ERG c-wave, FO; ERG a-/b-waves), contingent on sufficient rescue of POS handling and visual cycle support; maintain expression of visual cycle genes (LRAT, RPE65, TTR) and ion channel function (Kir7.1) through direct and indirect effects of miR-204 on apical physiology (Zhang et al., 2019; Intartaglia et al., 2021).

These expected effects are consistent with the mechanistic chain established in RPE: miR-204 controls Rab22a and endosomal maturation, which governs phagolysosomal processing of POS; failure at this node produces rhodopsin/undigested lipid accumulation, oxidative/proinflammatory stress, microglial activation, and electrophysiological decline—key features of dry AMD-like RPE dysfunction (Zhang et al., 2019). Notably, direct evidence that miR-204 augmentation in RPE increases cathepsin D activity or lysosomal acidification is not present in the cited literature; such outcomes are plausible secondary consequences of restored maturation but remain to be experimentally validated in this system (Zhang et al., 2019). Conversely, miR-204 augmentation has demonstrated capacity to downregulate proinflammatory/apoptotic signaling in degenerating retinas (AAV delivery in IRD), which may add non–phagolysosomal benefits in dry AMD by dampening microglia activation and apoptosis (Karali et al., 2020).

Assay-relevant expression and feasibility:  
- Rab22a is expressed in RPE and is upregulated when miR-204 is reduced, validating it as an RPE-relevant miR-204 target to monitor in pharmacodynamic assays (Zhang et al., 2019).  
- The RPE performs circadian POS phagocytosis and directs cargo to lysosomes; miRNAs regulate both uptake and downstream lysosomal breakdown, placing miR-204 within a well-defined physiological context where restoration should impact measurable endpoints (Du & Palczewski, 2022).  
- Established in vitro RPE models and in vivo mouse paradigms using exogenous POS feed, pHrodo uptake/chase, rhodopsin IF/WB, and endolysosomal markers (p62, LC3, LAMP2), as well as apical cytokine secretion and ERG readouts, provide a fit-for-purpose translational assay suite to test a miR-204 agomir (Zhang et al., 2019).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Mechanistic specificity linked to a central AMD-relevant pathway: The miR-204 → Rab22a axis is strongly supported in RPE by convergent mouse and human RPE data showing that miR-204 loss elevates Rab22a, blocks endosomal maturation, reduces phagolysosomal clearance (without impairing uptake), and causes intracellular rhodopsin/undigested autophagosome accumulation—key pathomechanisms implicated in dry AMD (Zhang et al., 2019). This provides a precise molecular rationale that a miR-204 mimic could correct a bottleneck in the RPE degradative axis central to disease biology (Du & Palczewski, 2022).  
- Strong phenotypic congruence with dry AMD: miR-204−/− mice develop age-related hyper-autofluorescent deposits, RPE/retina electrophysiological decline, microglial recruitment, and visual cycle impairment, aligning with multiple facets of dry AMD pathophysiology and supporting the translational relevance of restoring miR-204 in RPE (Zhang et al., 2019; Intartaglia et al., 2021).  
- High endogenous expression and biology in RPE: miR-204 is among the most abundant miRNAs in RPE and is induced during RPE differentiation; inflammation downregulates miR-204, plausibly contributing to disease, which rationalizes a replacement strategy (Shiels, 2020).

- Lack of direct rescue evidence for phagolysosomal function with miR-204 augmentation in RPE: The literature does not yet report that a miR-204 mimic (or even AAV miR-204) restores Rab22a levels, increases lysosomal maturation, improves POS degradation kinetics, or reduces rhodopsin/autophagosome accumulation in RPE in vivo; the mechanistic case is built from loss-of-function data with predictive inversion (Zhang et al., 2019).

The absence of agomir pharmacology in AMD-relevant models elevates translational risk relative to the AAV modality that already shows ocular efficacy (Karali et al., 2020).

Given miR-204’s pleiotropy in epithelial identity, ion transport, and neuronal circuits, off-target cell engagement or supra-physiological dosing could disrupt RPE and neuronal homeostasis (Shiels, 2020).  
- Disease-model scope: The strongest augmentation data for miR-204 come from IRD models; while these demonstrate anti-inflammatory and anti-apoptotic benefits, they do not directly test AMD-relevant endpoints such as drusen/lipofuscin dynamics, RPE atrophy trajectories, or aging/inflammation-driven POS handling failure (Karali et al., 2020).

Progress to aging/inflammation-driven RPE dysfunction models that recapitulate POS clearance deficits and lipofuscin/drusen-like pathology; assess fundus autofluorescence, rhodopsin accumulation, ERG/DC-ERG, and visual cycle gene expression after repeated agomir dosing (Zhang et al., 2019).

The totality of evidence supports miR-204 as a nodal regulator of RPE endosomal maturation and phagolysosomal clearance of photoreceptor outer segments via repression of Rab22a, with loss-of-function data in mice and human RPE showing degradative failure, inflammatory activation, and electrophysiological decline that recapitulate dry AMD-like features (Zhang et al., 2019). Although no study has yet demonstrated that a miR-204 agomir restores RPE phagolysosomal function in vivo in AMD-relevant models, augmentation with AAV-miR-204 achieves robust anti-inflammatory and anti-apoptotic effects and preserves retinal function in IRD models, indicating therapeutic potential of miR-204 enhancement and justifying further development (Karali et al., 2020). The agomir modality offers a nonviral, potentially titratable approach but currently lacks ocular pharmacology, delivery, and safety data; it also carries risks of off-target effects and context-dependent toxicity that must be mitigated by RPE-specific delivery and rigorous PD/PK control (Parsi, 2016; Shiels, 2020). Detailed Evaluation by Section  

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
miR-204 is an intronic miRNA within the TRPM3 locus, expressed at high levels in RPE and upregulated during RPE differentiation; it contributes to epithelial morphology, polarity, and tight junction integrity (Shiels, 2020). Synthetic miRNA mimics (agomirs) recreate the guide strand of the mature miRNA and, once delivered intracellularly, load into Ago2 to direct sequence-specific silencing of target mRNAs (Du & Palczewski, 2022). The literature shows that miR-204 function has been augmented in vivo using AAV2/8 delivery of pre-miR-204 to mouse retina and that direct agomir delivery has been performed in vertebrate ocular systems (rats and medaka), although specific chemistry and formulation details of the agomir are not provided (Karali et al., 2020; Shiels, 2020). In ophthalmic disease, miRNA-based modulation has emerged as a tool to adjust multi-gene networks; however, clinical experience with miRNA replacement is limited and will require attention to stability and innate immunity hazards typical of RNA therapeutics (Parsi, 2016).

Therapeutic History  
No prior clinical use of a miR-204 agomir in dry AMD has been reported; nevertheless, extensive preclinical loss-of-function evidence shows that miR-204 deficiency is sufficient to produce AMD-like phenotypes (accumulated autofluorescence, impaired POS clearance, inflammatory microglial recruitment, ERG deficits), supporting the pathophysiological premise that miR-204 restoration may be beneficial (Zhang et al., 2019). In primary human RPE, anti-miR-204 reduces POS digestion without affecting uptake and shifts endolysosomal markers in a manner consistent with a maturation block; Rab22a rises in both anti-miR and KO RPE (Zhang et al., 2019). In IRD models, AAV-delivered miR-204 improves ERG responses, reduces photoreceptor cell death, and downregulates inflammatory/apoptotic pathways (including direct repression of Siglec1 and Xaf1 by luciferase), establishing in vivo efficacy of miR-204 augmentation in degenerating retinas, albeit not in dry AMD models (Karali et al., 2020). Ocular administration of a miR-204 mimic in rats modulates neuronal markers (GAP-43) but can increase apoptosis in injury contexts, and embryonic overexpression in medaka causes eye malformations, highlighting potential safety concerns with unrestrained overexpression or ectopic exposure (Shiels, 2020).

Mechanism of Action  
The core molecular mechanism is the repression of Rab22a in RPE by miR-204, which relieves an inhibitory checkpoint in endosomal maturation and allows phagosomes to fuse with lysosomes, thereby promoting efficient POS proteolysis (Zhang et al., 2019). The downstream pathway is supported by multi-parameter readouts in KO and anti-miR RPE: impaired degradation (slower POS clearance, rhodopsin accumulation), autophagosome accumulation (p62+, LC3B-I elevation), reduced lysosomal marker LAMP2, and secondary inflammation (apical IL-8), culminating in microglial recruitment and electrophysiological decline (Zhang et al., 2019). miR-204 also sustains RPE barrier/ion physiology (TGFBR2/EMT restraint, Kir7.1), and its deficiency diminishes visual cycle gene expression that supports photoreceptor pigment regeneration (Shiels, 2020; Zhang et al., 2019; Intartaglia et al., 2021). The miRNA’s pleiotropy therefore suggests that restoration could concurrently benefit phagolysosomal function, barrier integrity, ionic balance, and retinoid handling, all implicated in dry AMD.

Expected Effect  
In vitro and in vivo assays of a miR-204 agomir should demonstrate molecular PD: reduced Rab22a protein in RPE (WB/IF), normalization of autophagy–endolysosomal markers (reduced p62, restored LC3B flux balance, increased LAMP2), and decreased apical IL-8 secretion (Zhang et al., 2019); functional PD: accelerated degradation of POS cargo in hfRPE pHrodo-chase assays and reduced intracellular rhodopsin accumulation post-feed (Zhang et al., 2019); and disease-relevant outcomes: in aged/inflammation-primed mice, decreased fundus autofluorescence and subretinal microglial accumulation, improved ERG/DC-ERG components, and maintenance of visual cycle gene expression (Zhang et al., 2019).

Overall Evaluation  
The miR-204 agomir is a mechanistically well-justified candidate for dry AMD, directly addressing a Rab22a-governed endosomal maturation defect that produces cardinal features of RPE failure seen in disease models and patient-like phenotypes (Zhang et al., 2019). The strength of the rationale is anchored in robust, cross-species loss-of-function data and in vitro human RPE phenocopying, as well as AAV-miR-204 augmentation data that validate the therapeutic value of increasing miR-204 in diseased retina (Zhang et al., 2019; Karali et al., 2020). However, the agomir modality lacks AMD-relevant in vivo rescue data and ocular pharmacology, and miRNA mimics pose delivery and safety challenges that necessitate careful formulation and RPE targeting (Parsi, 2016; Du & Palczewski, 2022). Given these considerations, the program should proceed with a staged preclinical plan emphasizing RPE-specific delivery, direct PD confirmation of Rab22a suppression and phagolysosomal restoration, AMD-relevant efficacy models, and rigorous safety/off-target profiling—including EMT/barrier and ion-channel endpoints—to de-risk translation (Zhang et al., 2019; Shiels, 2020; Karali et al., 2020).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Trehalose is a naturally occurring non‐reducing disaccharide (molecular weight 342.3 Da) found broadly in microorganisms and invertebrates, widely used as a stabilizer and excipient in foods and pharmaceuticals, and formulated in ophthalmic solutions at 3% w/v (≈87.7 mM) for ocular surface applications (e.g., dry eye) (Cox et al., 2025, pp. 1–2). In mammalian cells, trehalose enters via fluid‐phase endocytosis at millimolar concentrations and has been repeatedly reported as an autophagy enhancer that can activate AMPK signaling, stimulate lysosomal activity, and augment autophagic flux across multiple tissues, including ocular tissues (RPE) and retina (Cox et al., 2025, pp. 1–2). In the context of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), trehalose has been deployed as a small‐molecule modulator of the lysosome–autophagy axis with proposed mTOR‐independent activation of TFEB, the master transcriptional regulator of lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy (CLEAR network), positioning it mechanistically distinct from direct mTORC1 inhibitors such as rapamycin (Ghosh et al., 2024, p. 6; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 10–11). Topical ophthalmic trehalose is generally well tolerated, and preclinical studies show no overt ocular toxicity at 3% or 9% w/v after twice-daily dosing for up to two weeks, supporting feasibility for posterior segment delivery strategies; Raman spectroscopy has detected trehalose in RPE/choroid after repeated topical dosing, although posterior penetration is variable (Cox et al., 2025, pp. 8–10).

Preclinical evidence in RPE and retina

Dose–response caveats were noted: higher trehalose concentrations (≥100 mM) lost cytoprotection and were associated with stronger LC3-II accumulation, suggesting risk from excessive autophagy activation (Abokyi et al., 2020, pp. 11–12, 15–16).

- In vivo RPE/retinal structure preservation: In acute LIRD, topical trehalose preserved ONL thickness and RPE morphology; in chronic models with lysosomal defects, systemic trehalose prevented basal deposit formation and rescued RPE lysosomal function; hence, assays probing RPE structural resilience under oxidative or complement stress are likely to show benefit with trehalose (Cox et al., 2025, pp. 8–10, 10–13; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 6–8; Ghosh et al., 2023, pp. 11–15).

Assay-linked molecular readouts and expression in RPE  
- TFEB/TFE3, LAMP1/2, LC3B, SQSTM1/p62, CTSD/CTSL, and V-ATPase subunits (e.g., ATP6V0A1) are expressed in RPE and are central to lysosomal/autophagic function, with CLEAR network control by TFEB; reduced nuclear TFEB and decreased CTSD/L activity are documented in AMD RPE (Boya et al., 2023, pp. 3–4, 4–6; Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7). Given these baselines, RPE is an appropriate cell type to measure trehalose-driven TFEB pathway engagement and lysosomal protease restoration (Boya et al., 2023, pp. 3–4, 4–6; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 10–11).

Translational expectations and delivery  
- Topical dosing: The 3%–9% trehalose eyedrop regimens are feasible and safe in preclinical studies, achieve measurable posterior exposure, and produced autophagy biomarker changes and structural protection in LIRD (Cox et al., 2025, pp. 8–10, 10–13). However, posterior ocular bioavailability is typically low and variable, and much drug is lost systemically, necessitating optimization of formulation and dosing frequency for consistent RPE exposure (Cox et al., 2025, pp. 10–13, 15–16).  
- Systemic dosing: Oral trehalose can be degraded by trehalase, complicating systemic delivery; nonetheless, in mouse models (Cryba1 cKO and Akt2 KI), IP loading then 2% trehalose in drinking water for 3 months restored RPE lysosomal function and prevented deposit formation (Ghosh et al., 2023, pp. 11–15; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 6–8). Clinical translation will need to address trehalase metabolism and systemic exposure constraints (Cox et al., 2025, pp. 10–13).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Multi-modal preclinical evidence in RPE: Trehalose increases autophagy flux in human ARPE-19 and primary murine RPE, with autolysosome formation confirmed via tandem GFP–RFP-LC3 and LysoTracker colocalization, and cytoprotective effects depend on intact autophagy machinery (ATG5), directly aligning with the mechanistic target in RPE (Cox et al., 2025, pp. 7–8; Abokyi et al., 2020, pp. 1–2, 12–13).  
- Restoration of lysosomal hydrolase content and activity in human iPSC-RPE disease models: Trehalose rescued CTSD/L protein and activity and normalized LAMP1 under complement challenge in CFH Y402H RPE, mechanistically reversing disease-relevant lysosomal deficiencies (Ghosh et al., 2024, p. 6; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 10–11).  
- TFEB pathway engagement, mTOR-independent: Trehalose phenocopies constitutively nuclear TFEB and AKT2 inhibition in rescuing lysosomal/autophagy networks and function, and restores CLEAR transcripts in explants and in vivo without suppressing abnormal mTORC1 activation, suggesting lower risk of mTOR-related adverse effects (Ghosh et al., 2023, pp. 11–15; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 10–11).  
- In vivo efficacy signals: Topical trehalose improves autophagy markers in RPE and preserves ONL and RPE morphology after light stress; chronic systemic dosing prevents basal deposits and rescues lysosomal function in RPE in genetic lysosome-defect models (Cox et al., 2025, pp. 10–13; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 6–8; Ghosh et al., 2023, pp. 11–15).  
- Delivery feasibility and safety: Topical administration at high concentrations (3%–9%) is well tolerated and achieves posterior detection, creating a realistic translational route; topical dosing circumvents trehalase metabolism, a limitation for oral delivery (Cox et al., 2025, pp. 1–2, 8–10, 10–13).

Weaknesses and major gaps relative to the hypothesis  
- Lysosomal acidification not directly demonstrated: No quantitative lysosomal pH measurements with trehalose are reported in the provided RPE datasets; restoration of acidification remains an inference and must be demonstrated directly (Cox et al., 2025, pp. 7–8; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 10–11; Abokyi et al., 2020, pp. 1–2).  
- TFEB nuclear translocation under trehalose unproven in RPE: While trehalose is described as a TFEB activator and phenocopies TFEB-S467A, direct nuclear localization (imaging or fractionation) after trehalose in RPE is not shown here; this is a critical mechanistic gap (Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 10–11; Ghosh et al., 2023, pp. 11–15; Abokyi et al., 2020, pp. 16–17).  
- Lipofuscin/A2E clearance not demonstrated for trehalose: Although TFEB activation and mTOR inhibition are known to reduce A2E/lipofuscin-like granules in RPE models, trehalose-specific evidence for lipofuscin clearance is absent in the supplied materials (Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7).  
- Geographic atrophy endpoints lacking: There are no chronic GA model or clinical data showing trehalose slows lesion growth or preserves vision; LIRD is an acute stress model and does not recapitulate GA progression (Cox et al., 2025, pp. 1–2, 8–10).  
- Dosing translatability: Many in vitro effects were observed at 50–100 mM trehalose, which are high relative to likely in vivo intra-RPE exposures; dose–response optimization is needed, and excessive dosing risks autophagy-associated cytotoxicity (Abokyi et al., 2020, pp. 12–13, 15–16; Cox et al., 2025, pp. 7–8).  
- Source quality heterogeneity: Some supportive RPE studies come from lower-quality journals or preprints, warranting independent replication under rigorously controlled conditions (Abokyi et al., 2020, pp. 1–2; Ghosh et al., 2023, pp. 11–15).

Risk–benefit and development recommendations  
- Mechanistic verification package:  
  - Quantify lysosomal pH restoration with LysoSensor/DND-160 ratiometry and V-ATPase subunit/activity assays in RPE models ± trehalose, including disease-relevant stress (e.g., complement challenge, A2E loading) (Boya et al., 2023, pp. 3–4, 4–6).  
  - Directly quantify TFEB nuclear translocation (immunocytochemistry with nuclear segmentation; nuclear/cytosolic fractionation and immunoblotting) under trehalose vs. TFEB-S467A and vs. AKT2 inhibition, to confirm that trehalose’s phenotypic rescue is TFEB-dependent in RPE (Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 6, 10–11).  
  - CTSD/CTSL processing and activity: Extend the CFH (H/H) results by testing trehalose across primary human RPE and AMD-donor–derived RPE; relate CTSD activity rescue to autophagic flux endpoints (LC3 turnover, p62 degradation) and to substrate clearance (POS proteolysis kinetics) (Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 6, 10–11; Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7).  
  - Lipofuscin/A2E clearance: In A2E-loaded and POS-fed RPE, quantify autofluorescence granules and A2E mass spectrometry before/after trehalose, and test dependence on TFEB (siRNA/CRISPR) and lysosomal hydrolase inhibition (e.g., pepstatin-A for CTSD) (Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7, 7–9).  
- PK/PD and delivery optimization:  
  - For topical delivery, map trehalose concentration–time in RPE/choroid and retina with LC-MS or validated Raman signatures; explore permeation enhancers or sustained-release formulations to overcome low posterior bioavailability (Cox et al., 2025, pp. 8–10, 10–13, 15–16).  
  - Define an ocular PD biomarker panel (RPE LC3B/LAMP1 colocalization, p62 decrease, CTSD activity) and link to functional readouts (ERG, OCT metrics) in chronic complement- or lipofuscin-based models (Cox et al., 2025, pp. 10–13).  
- Comparative and combinatorial strategy:  
  - Benchmark trehalose against TFEB-centric comparators (e.g., rapalogs, Ezrin inhibitors) on shared endpoints (TFEB nuclear index, lysosomal pH, CTSD activity, lipofuscin clearance), given rapamycin’s ability to reduce A2E/lipofuscin via TFEB activation and the potential of ezrin blockade to increase lysosome number and cathepsin activity in RPE (Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7, 7–9; Boya et al., 2023, pp. 4–6).  
  - Consider combination with complement modulation where indicated, as complement stress contributes to AMD-relevant lysosomal dysfunction in CFH (H/H) RPE (Ghosh et al., 2024, p. 6).

Go/no-go criteria for advancement toward GA  
- Mechanistic Go: Demonstration in RPE that trehalose increases the TFEB nuclear index by >2-fold, lowers lysosomal pH toward physiological values, and increases CTSD activity by >30% over disease-state baseline, with concordant increases in LC3B–LAMP1 colocalization and p62 degradation; abrogation of effects by TFEB knockdown would confirm mechanism (Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 10–11; Cox et al., 2025, pp. 7–8; Boya et al., 2023, pp. 3–4).  
- Functional Go: Demonstrated reduction of A2E/lipofuscin by ≥25% in RPE models without cytotoxicity, and structural/functional rescue in a chronic AMD-relevant animal model (e.g., CFH-risk or complement-driven models) with durable effects beyond acute stress models (Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7; Cox et al., 2025, pp. 8–10; Ghosh et al., 2024, p. 6).  
- Safety Go: No evidence of autophagy-associated cytotoxicity at the intended exposure (maintained viability; absence of excessive LC3-II accumulation without flux; ocular histopathology clean) (Abokyi et al., 2020, pp. 15–16; Cox et al., 2025, pp. 8–10).

Conclusion  
The totality of evidence supports trehalose as a plausible, repurposable modulator of the TFEB–lysosome/autophagy axis in the RPE with multiple independent signals of autophagy flux enhancement, lysosomal hydrolase restoration (CTSD/L), and cytoprotection in oxidative/complement stress contexts, delivered via mechanisms that appear mTOR-independent and therefore potentially safer than broad mTORC1 inhibition (Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 10–11; Cox et al., 2025, pp. 7–8; Abokyi et al., 2020, pp. 1–2; Ghosh et al., 2023, pp. 11–15). However, the hypothesis’s most stringent claims—quantitative restoration of lysosomal acidification, trehalose-driven TFEB nuclear translocation in RPE, and direct lipofuscin/A2E clearance leading to slowed geographic atrophy progression—are not yet demonstrated in the supplied literature and require targeted mechanistic and disease-model validation (Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 10–11; Abokyi et al., 2020, pp. 16–17; Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7; Cox et al., 2025, pp. 8–10). Given strong biological plausibility and encouraging preclinical signals, a focused IND-enabling program that closes these gaps is justified, with early emphasis on mechanistic biomarkers (lysosomal pH, TFEB nuclear index, CTSD activity), pharmacokinetics of posterior delivery, and chronic AMD-relevant efficacy models before advancing to clinical study in GA (Boya et al., 2023, pp. 3–4; Cox et al., 2025, pp. 10–13; Ghosh et al., 2024, p. 6).
