Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
SB216763 is a synthetic small‐molecule inhibitor originally discovered during GlaxoSmithKline’s dedicated program in developing GSK-3 inhibitors. It belongs to the bisarylmaleimide class of compounds, with its chemical structure based on a pyrrole-2,5-dione core that is further substituted by aryl and indole moieties. In its initial characterization, SB216763 was identified as an ATP-competitive inhibitor of glycogen synthase kinase 3 beta (GSK3β), a central serine/threonine protein kinase implicated in multiple intracellular signaling cascades. The chemical class to which SB216763 belongs – maleimides – has been widely exploited across medicinal chemistry due to their synthetic tractability and ability to serve as potent inhibitors of enzymes, particularly kinases. This group of compounds has previously been used in various preclinical studies targeting neurodegenerative diseases and cell proliferative disorders by modulating cell signaling pathways such as the Wnt/β-catenin cascade, which is ubiquitously expressed in many tissues including the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and the central nervous system (Gianferrara et al., 2022; Ruiz & Eldar-Finkelman, 2022; Alhassan et al., 2025).

Therapeutic History:  
SB216763 has a well-established history in preclinical research, particularly in models of neurodegeneration. Several studies have deployed this compound in rodent models of Alzheimer’s disease, Parkinson’s disease, and other neurological insults to demonstrate its neuroprotective potential. In these models, SB216763 was shown to reduce tau hyperphosphorylation, protect neurons against both β-amyloid-mediated toxicity and radiation-induced apoptosis in hippocampal neurons, and promote beneficial modulation of signaling pathways linked to PI3K–Akt (Gianferrara et al., 2022; Ruiz & Eldar-Finkelman, 2022). Beyond its neuroprotective effects, SB216763 has been applied as a tool compound in cellular studies to activate canonical Wnt signaling through stabilization of beta-catenin by inhibiting GSK3β. Importantly, a radiolabeled derivative, [11C]SB216763, has been developed as a positron emission tomography (PET) probe, which confirmed its ability to cross the blood–brain barrier in rodent and nonhuman primate models, although significant selectivity issues have been noted with respect to off-target kinase inhibition (Gianferrara et al., 2022; Benn & Dawson, 2020). In addition, there is documented evidence of its application in ocular contexts; for instance, in an experimental ischemic retinal neuron model in rats, SB216763 was found to promote DNA repair by upregulating DNA ligase IV transcriptional activity. However, while it has been evaluated extensively in neurological and in vivo rodent models for central nervous system diseases, formal clinical deployment or veterinary studies specifically targeting dry age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD) remain sparse, with no documented clinical trials registered on major platforms dedicated to AMD indications (Gianferrara et al., 2022; Ruiz & Eldar-Finkelman, 2022; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).

Mechanism of Action:  
The primary mechanism of action of SB216763 is centered on its potent inhibition of GSK3β. Under normal physiological conditions, GSK3β is a constitutively active kinase that phosphorylates a wide array of substrates, including beta-catenin, tau, and proteins critical to cellular metabolism and survival. One key substrate relevant to our hypothesis is the transcription factor EB (TFEB), a master regulator of the Coordinated Lysosomal Expression and Regulation (CLEAR) gene network. TFEB’s activity is tightly regulated by its phosphorylation state; when phosphorylated by kinases such as mTORC1 and possibly GSK3β, TFEB binds to cytosolic 14-3-3 proteins and is retained in the cytoplasm. Inhibition of GSK3β by SB216763 has been implicated in the dephosphorylation of TFEB, thereby allowing its translocation to the nucleus where it drives the transcription of CLEAR network genes. These genes are essential for lysosomal biogenesis, autophagic flux, and the expression of lysosomal proteases such as cathepsin D (Gianferrara et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2023). Detailed molecular studies in neuronal stem cells and N2a cells have demonstrated that SB216763 can inactivate GSK3β and thereby stimulate the nuclear accumulation of TFEB. In addition, the compound’s ATP-competitive mode of inhibition suggests it directly competes with ATP in the GSK3β active site, leading to rapid modulation of downstream substrates implicated in metabolic and autophagic processes (Gianferrara et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2023; Djajadikerta et al., 2020). From a biochemical standpoint, SB216763’s action not only stabilizes beta-catenin – thereby modulating Wnt signaling – but also appears to influence key regulatory nodes in autophagy. Activation of TFEB results in upregulation of lysosomal proteins, enhancement of lysosomal acidification via increased expression of components like the vacuolar-type ATPase (V-ATPase), and improved cathepsin D maturation and activity, all of which collectively promote the efficient clearance of intracellular aggregates and damaged organelles (Gianferrara et al., 2022; Ruiz & Eldar-Finkelman, 2022; Pan & Valapala, 2022).

Expected Effect in Dry AMD Context:  
The central hypothesis behind repurposing SB216763 for dry AMD rests on its ability to correct the cellular deficits observed in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) associated with aging and disease. Dry AMD is characterized by the accumulation of lipofuscin and other aggregate-prone materials within the RPE, coupled with impaired autophagic and lysosomal clearance mechanisms. The proposed pharmacological intervention with SB216763 is expected to inhibit GSK3β in RPE cells, leading to dephosphorylation and nuclear translocation of TFEB. Once in the nucleus, TFEB can activate the CLEAR network, thereby augmenting lysosome biogenesis and catalytic function. Enhanced lysosomal acidification, as mediated by the V-ATPase and corroborated by increased expression of lysosomal enzymes such as cathepsin D, should facilitate the degradation of accumulated lipofuscin, oxidized proteins, and lipid aggregates. In preclinical RPE models under oxidative stress, similar pharmacological modulation of TFEB (for example, via trehalose treatment or genetic induction) has been shown to improve lysosomal function and reduce the burden of autofluorescent granules analogous to lipofuscin (Falcão et al., 2025; Falcão et al., 2024). Therefore, SB216763 is hypothesized to recapitulate these beneficial effects by leveraging its upstream modulation of GSK3β. Given that RPE cells naturally express both GSK3β and TFEB, and considering the documented mechanistic role of GSK3β in regulating TFEB nucleo-cytoplasmic shuttling, the expected outcome is an enhancement of autophagic clearance and restoration of RPE homeostasis. This would theoretically slow or potentially reverse early degenerative changes in dry AMD by mitigating the cytotoxic accumulation of undegraded material (Gianferrara et al., 2022; Ruiz & Eldar-Finkelman, 2022; Yang et al., 2023).

Overall Evaluation:  
SB216763 exhibits several promising attributes as a candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry AMD. One major strength lies in its well-characterized and potent inhibition of GSK3β – a kinase that plays a central role in various signaling pathways implicated in both neurodegeneration and retinal pathology. The mechanistic rationale is underpinned by evidence that GSK3β inhibition facilitates the nuclear translocation of TFEB, the master regulator of lysosomal function. Through activation of TFEB, SB216763 can potentially stimulate the expression of the CLEAR gene network, leading to heightened lysosomal acidification and increased cathepsin D activity. These molecular events are directly relevant to mitigating the defective autophagic clearance that is a hallmark of dry AMD, and they align well with preclinical observations in other cell types where TFEB activation has been associated with improved degradation of accumulated toxic material (Gianferrara et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2023; Djajadikerta et al., 2020).

Further strengths include the extensive use of SB216763 in various preclinical models of neurodegeneration, wherein its ability to modulate key pathways such as beta-catenin/Wnt signaling has been repeatedly demonstrated. Its blood–brain barrier penetrance, as seen in rodent and nonhuman primate studies involving a radiolabeled derivative, suggests favorable pharmacokinetics that might also translate to ocular tissues with appropriate formulation strategies. The documented ocular application in rodent ischemic retinal neuron models – where SB216763 was shown to upregulate DNA repair mechanisms – provides additional indirect support for its potential in the ocular setting (Gianferrara et al., 2022).

Notwithstanding these promising aspects, there are notable weaknesses and gaps in the literature that warrant cautious interpretation. First, while preclinical evidence in neural and other cellular models supports the concept that GSK3β inhibition can drive TFEB-dependent transcriptional activation, direct evidence of SB216763’s efficacy in RPE cells under conditions of oxidative stress or in established dry AMD models is sparse. There is a lack of comprehensive studies that definitively link SB216763 treatment in RPE cells to enhanced lysosomal acidification, increased cathepsin D activity, and consequent reduction in lipofuscin accumulation. For example, while related studies using trehalose or mTOR inhibitors have shown clear benefits on TFEB activation and autophagic clearance in RPE models (Falcão et al., 2025; Falcão et al., 2024), SB216763-specific data in this context remain limited. 

Furthermore, concerns regarding kinase selectivity must be acknowledged. SB216763, being an ATP-competitive inhibitor, may exhibit off-target effects by inhibiting structurally related kinases, as indicated by the limited selectivity noted in studies involving its radiolabeled derivative [11C]SB216763 (Gianferrara et al., 2022; Benn & Dawson, 2020; Pan & Valapala, 2021). Off-target kinase inhibition could potentially disrupt other essential signaling pathways in the RPE and might lead to unforeseen adverse events upon clinical translation. This issue of specificity is particularly important in the context of chronic diseases like dry AMD, where long-term safety is paramount. 

Additionally, while its use in central nervous system models is encouraging, dry AMD pathophysiology has distinct features that may not be fully addressed by a therapeutic designed for neurodegeneration. The multifactorial etiology of dry AMD, which encompasses oxidative stress, chronic inflammation, and impaired autophagic degradation specific to the high metabolic and phagocytic demands of RPE cells, underscores the need for targeted evidence that SB216763 exerts its effects in these specialized cells. Moreover, the absence of any registered clinical trials on major platforms for SB216763 in the AMD space (as revealed by comprehensive searches on ClinicalTrials.gov) suggests that the translational path for this compound remains uncharted in the context of retinal disease (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.; Ruiz & Eldar-Finkelman, 2022).

Another consideration is the potential for conflicting actions of GSK3β inhibition. While inhibiting GSK3β does promote TFEB activation and lysosomal biogenesis, GSK3β also phosphorylates other substrates that could have deleterious effects if dysregulated in the RPE. Its synthetic origin as a bisarylmaleimide and proven in vitro potency provide a strong rationale for its repurposing. The proposed mechanism—wherein inhibition of GSK3β leads to enhanced nuclear localization of TFEB, activation of CLEAR genes, improved lysosomal acidification, and increased cathepsin D activity—directly addresses key pathogenic features of dry AMD, including the accumulation of lipofuscin and defective autophagy in RPE cells. First, direct experimental validation in RPE cells exposed to oxidative stress is needed to confirm that SB216763 can indeed induce TFEB nuclear translocation and activate the CLEAR network in this specific cell type. Second, detailed pharmacokinetic and safety studies tailored for ocular administration are essential to determine whether the compound can reach effective concentrations in the retina without eliciting systemic toxicity or off-target kinase inhibition. Third, comprehensive in vivo studies in relevant animal models of dry AMD must be conducted to assess whether the biochemical improvements (e.g., enhanced lysosomal acidification and cathepsin D activity) translate into clinically meaningful outcomes, such as reduction in lipofuscin accumulation and preservation of RPE morphology and function.

Finally, while the theoretical framework is strong, the translational gap remains significant. The absence of clinical trials or robust preclinical data directly linking SB216763 to improvements in dry AMD phenotypes suggests that careful, incremental studies are required. These studies should ideally include dose–response evaluations, biomarker analyses of autophagic flux, and long-term safety assessments to establish the therapeutic window for SB216763 in the context of retinal disease (Ruiz & Eldar-Finkelman, 2022; Gianferrara et al., 2022; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).

Its well-defined synthetic origin, established preclinical usage in neurodegeneration, and documented biochemical effects in activating lysosomal and autophagic pathways suggest that it could, in principle, improve RPE function through enhanced clearance of toxic intracellular aggregates. A stepwise preclinical evaluation, starting with in vitro RPE models and advancing to in vivo AMD models, would be necessary to validate its efficacy and safety profile before considering clinical translation. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
AICAR (5‐aminoimidazole‐4‐carboxamide ribonucleoside), commercially available as Sigma A9978, is a purine nucleoside analogue originally identified as an adenosine-related compound that is taken up into cells via equilibrative nucleoside transporters and then phosphorylated by adenosine kinase into its monophosphorylated form, ZMP (Gruzman et al., 2009; Hardie, 2014). As a prodrug that is converted intracellularly into an AMP mimic, AICAR belongs to the class of adenosine/AMP analogues that have been widely employed as pharmacological tools to activate AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) in vitro and in vivo (Russell & Hardie, 2020; Scudiero et al., 2016). Its discovery as the first pharmacological agent capable of activating AMPK in intact cells set the stage for extensive biochemical studies regarding cellular energy sensing and metabolic regulation (Vara-Ciruelos et al., 2019; Yu et al., 2010). Unlike synthetic small molecules designed solely to bind regulatory subunits of AMPK, AICAR requires intracellular phosphorylation to ZMP—a process that confers a basis in natural purine metabolism as ZMP is an intermediate in de novo purine synthesis—and thereby mimics the endogenous activator AMP (Hardie, 2014; Gruzman et al., 2009). Being a small nucleoside analogue, AICAR is structurally simple compared to some of the more recently developed direct AMPK activators; its well‐delineated chemical structure, mechanism of cellular conversion, and availability from commercial sources make it an attractive candidate for repurposing studies (Drew & Kingwell, 2008; Guerrieri et al., 2017).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, AICAR has been extensively used as a research tool to probe the biology of AMPK, which is central to metabolic regulation, and it has demonstrated efficacy in a wide variety of preclinical models including skeletal muscle, adipocytes, hepatocytes, and specific cancer models (Drew & Kingwell, 2008). Its ability to rapidly be taken up and converted to ZMP in diverse cell types has made it an invaluable reagent for studies of metabolic dysregulation, insulin resistance, and autophagy; investigators have used AICAR in rodent models of diabetes where it has been shown to improve glucose homeostasis and modify lipid metabolism (Russell & Hardie, 2020; Dolinar et al., 2018). Beyond metabolic endpoints, AICAR has been explored in cardiac settings; for example, acadesine (another name for AICAR) has been clinically evaluated for preventing ischemia–reperfusion injury during coronary artery bypass graft surgery, demonstrating its translational potential in acute cardiovascular contexts (Drew & Kingwell, 2008). Despite its extensive use in metabolic and cardiovascular studies as well as experimental cancer models, there is little documented evidence supporting its use in dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) or similar ocular degenerative diseases (Guerrieri et al., 2017; Drew & Kingwell, 2008). However, the underlying rationale of harnessing AMPK activation to improve autophagy and lysosomal clearance in affected retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells provides a logical extension of AICAR’s well‐characterized metabolic activities to the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Honnappa & Kesavan, 2016; Dolinar et al., 2018).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, AICAR functions by entering cells through nucleoside transporters and undergoing phosphorylation by adenosine kinase to yield ZMP, which is structurally analogous to AMP and thus capable of binding to the regulatory Bateman domains of the AMPK γ subunit (Gruzman et al., 2009; Hardie, 2014). Binding of ZMP to AMPK triggers multiple regulatory phenomena, including allosteric activation, promotion of phosphorylation at the critical Thr172 residue on the catalytic α subunit, and protection from dephosphorylation by protein phosphatases, thereby amplifying AMPK’s kinase activity (Russell & Hardie, 2020; Scudiero et al., 2016). Activated AMPK then exerts a plethora of downstream effects: it can suppress anabolic pathways via inhibition of mammalian target of rapamycin complex 1 (mTORC1) and stimulate catabolic pathways, thereby shifting cellular metabolism from energy-consuming biosynthetic processes toward energy-producing autophagy and oxidative processes (Salt & Hardie, 2017; Scudiero et al., 2016). In the context of the proposed therapeutic mechanism for dry AMD, AMPK activation by AICAR is expected to result in the suppression of mTORC1, which in turn relieves inhibitory control over the transcription factor EB (TFEB) (Drew & Kingwell, 2008; Chandrasekaran et al., 2024). TFEB acts as a master regulator of lysosomal gene expression and autophagy by translocating to the nucleus, where it upregulates genes responsible for lysosomal biogenesis, acidification, and hydrolase production; one such enzyme, cathepsin D (CTSD), is critical for effective autophagy clearance (Drew & Kingwell, 2008; Scudiero et al., 2016). This sequence of molecular events—from AICAR uptake, conversion to ZMP, AMPK activation, mTORC1 suppression, and subsequent TFEB activation—forms the mechanistic backbone supporting a therapeutic strategy geared toward enhancing lysosomal acidification and boosting cathepsin D–mediated autophagic clearance (Vara-Ciruelos et al., 2019; Yu et al., 2010). It is important to note that while the mechanism is robust, high intracellular concentrations of ZMP (and therefore high doses of AICAR) may activate other AMP-sensitive enzymes, such as glycogen phosphorylase, which underscores the necessity of titrating doses to achieve a selective AMPK-mediated effect (Russell & Hardie, 2020; Chandrasekaran et al., 2024).

Expected Effect:  
In the proposed application targeting dry AMD, the hypothesis is that AICAR administration will mimic the natural actions of AMP within RPE cells by robustly activating AMPK (Gruzman et al., 2009; Scudiero et al., 2016). In turn, this activation is expected to suppress mTORC1 activity—a key negative regulator of autophagy—and facilitate the nuclear translocation of TFEB, leading to the upregulation of lysosomal and autophagy-related genes including those encoding for cathepsin D (Drew & Kingwell, 2008; Chandrasekaran et al., 2024). In retinal pigment epithelium culture models, preliminary observations have indicated that treatment with AICAR enhances LC3 flux (a marker of autophagic activity) and increases cathepsin D activity, implying an improved capacity for autophagic clearance (Guerrieri et al., 2017; Vara-Ciruelos et al., 2019). Given that dry AMD is characterized by the accumulation of extracellular deposits (drusen) and cellular debris due to insufficient lysosomal clearance and impaired autophagy, the anticipated effect of AICAR would be to restore lysosomal functionality and promote the degradation of these pathogenic substrates (Honnappa & Kesavan, 2016; Drew & Kingwell, 2008). Furthermore, it is known from previous studies that AMPK activation can lead to enhanced mitochondrial quality control and an overall improvement in cellular metabolic homeostasis; in the context of RPE cells, this could translate to better cell survival and resilience against the oxidative stress associated with chronic degenerative processes in dry AMD (Chandrasekaran et al., 2024; Drew & Kingwell, 2008). It is also supportive that preclinical data suggest AICAR exhibits ocular safety profiles and some ability to traverse the blood–retinal barrier, which is critical for any therapeutic intended for retinal delivery (Drew & Kingwell, 2008).

Overall Evaluation:  
AICAR presents several strengths as a candidate therapeutic for dry age-related macular degeneration. First, its well-characterized mechanism—via conversion to ZMP, robust activation of AMPK, subsequent mTORC1 suppression, and activation of TFEB—provides a clear molecular rationale that directly addresses the impaired autophagic and lysosomal clearance mechanisms believed to underlie dry AMD pathology (Gruzman et al., 2009; Scudiero et al., 2016). Second, its extensive experimental use over the past decades in cell culture and animal models across metabolic, cardiovascular, and even oncological studies gives it a solid preclinical pedigree and provides a wealth of pharmacodynamic and safety data (Hardie, 2014; Russell & Hardie, 2020). Third, the hypothesis that activating AMPK in retinal pigment epithelial cells can lead to improvements in LC3 flux and cathepsin D activity is supported by a mechanistic analogy to effects seen in neuronal and muscle cell studies, suggesting that similar benefits may be achieved in RPE cells (Yu et al., 2010; Chandrasekaran et al., 2024). Moreover, known preclinical ocular safety data and evidence of the compound’s ability to cross the blood–retinal barrier lend practical feasibility to the candidate’s repurposing for an ocular indication like dry AMD (Drew & Kingwell, 2008; Russell & Hardie, 2020).

However, there are several challenges and potential weaknesses that must be carefully considered. AICAR’s effective activation of AMPK often requires concentrations in the millimolar range, and such high concentrations have been associated with off-target effects including interactions with AMP-sensitive enzymes other than AMPK (for example, glycogen phosphorylase and fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase), which may complicate therapeutic outcomes (Russell & Hardie, 2020; Guerrieri et al., 2017). In addition, AICAR is known to have poor oral bioavailability and a relatively short plasma half-life, issues that might necessitate alternative routes of administration or formulation strategies to achieve sustained therapeutic levels in the retina (Salt & Hardie, 2017; Gruzman et al., 2009). The possibility of metabolic complications such as lactic acidosis and hyperuricemia at high systemic doses has been documented in metabolic models; although local ocular administration might mitigate systemic exposure, these concerns require thorough investigation in focused preclinical studies (Dolinar et al., 2018). Furthermore, while the concept of activating the AMPK–TFEB–lysosomal pathway is promising, there remains uncertainty regarding the extent to which RPE cells recapitulate the robust autophagic responses observed in other tissues; cell type–dependent variability may influence both efficacy and safety outcomes (Drew & Kingwell, 2008). Finally, because AICAR has been primarily evaluated in the context of metabolic and ischemic conditions rather than chronic degenerative diseases of the eye, there is an inherent translational gap that will require dedicated studies to validate the mechanistic efficacy in dry AMD models (Drew & Kingwell, 2008).

In summary, AICAR offers a compelling potential mechanism by which activation of AMPK could restore autophagic and lysosomal functions in RPE cells, addressing key pathogenic features of dry AMD such as impaired clearance of debris and dysfunctional cellular metabolism (Drew & Kingwell, 2008; Dolinar et al., 2018). Its extensive history as a research tool provides a strong foundation of pharmacodynamic and mechanistic understanding, and its established ocular safety and blood–retinal barrier permeability are additional assets for its repurposing in an ocular setting (Russell & Hardie, 2020; Drew & Kingwell, 2008). Nevertheless, issues related to dosing, off-target activity, pharmacokinetic limitations, and cell-specific responses must be resolved through rigorous preclinical studies, including dose-ranging experiments in relevant RPE models and animal models of dry AMD (Chandrasekaran et al., 2024; Dolinar et al., 2018). Overall, while challenges exist, the mechanistic underpinnings and prior experimental data justify further investigation of AICAR as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration, provided that its pharmacokinetics and off-target liabilities can be managed through optimized formulation or targeted delivery strategies (Gruzman et al., 2009; Dolinar et al., 2018).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Rapamycin (sirolimus), commercially available as Sigma R0395, is a macrocyclic lactone originally isolated from the bacterium Streptomyces hygroscopicus, a discovery that dates back to studies on soil samples from Easter Island. As a naturally derived compound now synthesized and purified for clinical use, rapamycin belongs to the macrolide class and is best known for its potent immunosuppressive properties, having been used extensively to prevent organ rejection in transplantation. Over time, its application expanded beyond transplantation to include areas such as oncology, neurodegeneration, and age-related diseases due to its ability to inhibit the mechanistic target of rapamycin complex 1 (mTORC1). The rationale for repurposing rapamycin in the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD), specifically geographic atrophy (GA), stems from its established pharmacological profile, extensive safety record, and well-characterized biochemical functions. Its clinical approval and long-term safety data in other contexts provide a solid foundation for exploring its potential in ocular indications, particularly given its capacity to modulate autophagy in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells (Wang et al., 2022).

Therapeutic History:  
Rapamycin’s development began with its use as an immunosuppressant in organ transplantation, and over the ensuing decades, its application has broadened considerably. Biochemical and preclinical studies have demonstrated that rapamycin is an effective inhibitor of mTORC1, a critical regulator not only of cell proliferation but also of autophagy and lysosomal biogenesis. Early investigations revealed that rapamycin could induce autophagy in various cell types, including RPE cells, by inhibiting mTORC1, thereby facilitating the clearance of toxic aggregates and damaged organelles. This mechanism has been explored extensively for neurodegenerative conditions, and more recently, there has been focused investigation into its utility for dry AMD. Clinical trials have tested rapamycin in forms ranging from intravitreal to subconjunctival injections in patients with GA; for example, a clinical trial by the National Eye Institute aimed to evaluate intravitreal injections of sirolimus for GA, although this study was terminated due to safety concerns (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2012). Similarly, other studies using subconjunctival injections demonstrated that while rapamycin appears safe and well-tolerated, significant benefits in terms of preventing GA progression have not been conclusively demonstrated (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2008, 2011). In animal studies and in vitro RPE models, rapamycin enhanced autophagic flux, increased the activity of cathepsin D (CTSD), and reduced the accumulation of toxic material such as A2E—an effect that is consistent with a potential for slowing GA progression (Wang et al., 2022; Falcão et al., 2024). Thus, rapamycin’s therapeutic history encompasses a combination of robust preclinical evidence supporting its mechanistic action and mixed clinical outcomes in ocular trials, setting the stage for further investigation into optimal dosing, delivery methods, and patient selection criteria (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2008, 2011).

Mechanism of Action:  
Rapamycin exerts its biological effects primarily through direct inhibition of mTORC1, a serine/threonine kinase complex that integrates signals from nutrients, growth factors, and cellular energy status to regulate cell growth, proliferation, and autophagy. In the absence of rapamycin, active mTORC1 phosphorylates downstream targets such as S6 kinase and 4E-BP1, thereby promoting anabolic processes and suppressing autophagy. When rapamycin binds to its intracellular receptor, FKBP12, the resulting complex interacts with the FKBP12-rapamycin binding (FRB) domain of mTORC1, leading to its inhibition. This inhibition results in dephosphorylation and subsequent activation of transcription factor EB (TFEB), a master regulator of lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy-related genes. Activated TFEB then translocates to the nucleus, where it enhances the expression of genes involved in lysosomal function, acidification, and the production of lysosomal enzymes such as cathepsin D (CTSD) (Falcão et al., 2025; Falcão et al., 2024; Sinha et al., 2016). In the context of dry AMD, the proposed mechanism hinges on rapamycin’s ability to restore cellular homeostasis in RPE cells by increasing autophagic flux and lysosomal clearance of accumulated drusen components, which include toxic aggregates like A2E. Preclinical studies have shown that treatment of RPE cells with rapamycin results in a marked reduction in the accumulation of autofluorescent granules (AFGs) that are indicative of impaired lysosomal degradation (Falcão et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2025). The cascade initiated by rapamycin—mTORC1 inhibition, TFEB activation, and enhanced expression of lysosome-associated proteins such as LAMP1 and pro-cathepsin D—forms the crux of its proposed therapeutic action in mitigating the progression of GA by promoting the dismantling and clearance of pathological deposits (Falcão et al., 2024).

Expected Effect:  
In RPE cells, the inhibition of mTORC1 by rapamycin is expected to release the inhibitory phosphorylation on TFEB, enabling its nuclear translocation and activation of a transcriptional program that drives lysosomal biogenesis, acidification, and the production of key lysosomal enzymes such as cathepsin D. This molecular shift is anticipated to markedly enhance the autophagic capacity of the RPE, leading to increased degradation of drusen components, including lipofuscin and A2E, which are hallmarks of dry AMD pathology. The activation of autophagy not only facilitates the clearance of accumulated toxic material but also mitigates oxidative stress by removing damaged mitochondria and other organelles that may contribute to reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation (Wang et al., 2022; Falcão et al., 2024). Moreover, preclinical evidence indicates that, in ARPE-19 cell models, rapamycin improves cellular viability in the face of oxidative injury and reduces markers of cellular senescence by enhancing autophagic flux. These cellular effects are directly linked to the expression of critical proteins in RPE cells; for example, TFEB is known to be expressed in these cells and its activation correlates with increased lysosomal gene expression and function (Falcão et al., 2024) while cathepsin D, a lysosomal protease, is vital for the degradation of phagocytosed photoreceptor outer segments (Chang et al., 2022; Sinha et al., 2016). The intended therapeutic outcome is to slow or potentially halt the progression of GA by reducing the burden of drusen and preserving RPE function, which could translate into better preservation of visual acuity over time. However, it is important to note that while these mechanisms are promising in vitro, clinical translation has encountered challenges related to dosing, delivery, and the stage of disease at which intervention occurs (Wang et al., 2022; Falcão et al., 2024).

Overall Evaluation:  
Rapamycin presents itself as a scientifically promising yet clinically challenging candidate for the treatment of dry AMD. One of the key strengths of rapamycin is its well-established mechanism of action: as a potent mTORC1 inhibitor, it leverages a well-characterized pathway involving TFEB activation that directly targets the core pathology observed in dry AMD—the accumulation of drusen components and impaired lysosomal function in RPE cells. Preclinical studies have consistently demonstrated that rapamycin can enhance autophagic flux, lower levels of toxic aggregates such as A2E, and increase the activity of lysosomal enzymes like cathepsin D, thereby supporting its target validation in the context of RPE health (Falcão et al., 2025; Falcão et al., 2024). Additionally, rapamycin has an extensive history of clinical use in other indications, and its safety profile, while not without concerns, is well documented from its use as an immunosuppressant in transplantation and in various oncology settings (Wang et al., 2022).

However, the clinical translation of rapamycin for dry AMD has not been straightforward. Multiple clinical trials have assessed its application using different routes of administration, such as intravitreal and subconjunctival injections, with mixed results. While safety and tolerability have generally been acceptable, the efficacy endpoints—specifically, the prevention or slowing of GA progression—have not been definitively met in these studies (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2008, 2011, 2012; Wang et al., 2022). Furthermore, some trials encountered complications such as sterile endophthalmitis or observed decreases in visual acuity relative to untreated eyes, suggesting that even if the underlying molecular mechanisms are engaged, the overall benefits in late-stage disease might be limited (Wang et al., 2022; Falcão et al., 2024).

Another potential weakness is the complexity inherent in mTOR signaling itself. The pathway plays a dual role in cellular homeostasis—while its inhibition can promote autophagy and lysosomal clearance, inappropriate or excessive inhibition could lead to adverse effects such as increased retinal neuron apoptosis, particularly in advanced stages of AMD where the cellular milieu is significantly altered (Wang et al., 2022; Chang et al., 2022). Moreover, the optimal dosing regimen and delivery method for achieving the desired ocular concentration without incurring systemic side effects remain unresolved. Some studies have suggested that modifications to the formulation, such as encapsulation in synthetic nanoparticles, could enhance ocular penetration and prolong the effective duration of rapamycin within the eye, thereby minimizing side effects and improving efficacy (Jo et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2022).

Despite these challenges, the strength of rapamycin’s mechanism—the inhibition of mTORC1 and consequent activation of TFEB leading to enhanced lysosomal biogenesis—remains compelling. The molecular rationale is robust, and the repeated demonstration of reduced levels of autofluorescent granules in RPE cells following rapamycin treatment is particularly encouraging (Falcão et al., 2024). The concept of using a repurposed, clinically approved drug to address a significant unmet need in dry AMD is attractive, especially given the limited treatment options currently available for this degenerative condition. In this light, further investigations—ideally, in earlier stages of AMD and with innovative delivery modalities—may reveal a niche where rapamycin can exert a clinically meaningful benefit (Wang et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2019).

In conclusion, while rapamycin has significant potential grounded in sound molecular pharmacology and extensive preclinical validation, its clinical application for dry AMD warrants careful optimization. The candidate’s strengths lie in its potent and well-understood mechanism of mTORC1 inhibition, the activation of TFEB, and subsequent improvements in lysosomal function and autophagic clearance in RPE cells. Conversely, clinical challenges including mixed efficacy outcomes in GA trials, potential adverse effects related to mTOR pathway modulation in vulnerable retinal neurons, and limitations in current dosing/delivery strategies represent hurdles that must be surmounted. Based on these comprehensive literature insights, rapamycin remains a promising candidate for further investigation, albeit with recommendations to explore its use in earlier disease stages and in combination with advanced ocular delivery systems to maximize its therapeutic benefit while minimizing risks (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2012; Wang et al., 2022; Falcão et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2025).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
ZLN005 is a synthetic, small-molecule benzimidazole identified by high-throughput screening of ~48,000 compounds using a HEK293 cell line harboring a human PGC-1α promoter–driven luciferase reporter; it was selected for its ability to transcriptionally induce the Ppargc1a (PGC-1α) gene and validated in follow-up orthogonal assays and cell types (Zhang et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2021). Chemically, ZLN005 is 2-(4-tert-butylphenyl)-1H-benzimidazole with a reported molecular weight of 250.3; it is repeatedly described as a “small-molecule PGC-1α transcriptional activator/agonist” and a “specific and selective transcriptional inducer of PGC-1α expression” (Bleckwehl et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2013; Maurice et al., 2022). The initial discovery campaign also yielded a related backbone compound (ZLN027) that showed cytotoxicity, whereas ZLN005 did not under the reported in vitro conditions, and ZLN005 was later found to inhibit luciferases—an assay interference red flag that necessitates careful interpretation of luciferase-based readouts (Zhang et al., 2013).

Pharmacologic class and precedent: ZLN005 belongs to the class of tool/investigational small molecules that transcriptionally upregulate PGC-1α and thereby stimulate mitochondrial biogenesis, oxidative phosphorylation, and fatty-acid oxidation in a tissue-selective fashion (Zhang et al., 2013). This class has been deployed broadly in preclinical systems—skeletal muscle, cardiomyocytes, neurons, kidney, lung epithelium, vascular smooth muscle, and retinal pigment epithelium (RPE)—to probe whether enhancing PGC-1α can restore mitochondrial capacity, reduce oxidative stress, and improve cell/tissue resilience (Zhang et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2020; Xu et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2021; Ma et al., 2023; Zou et al., 2025; Shu et al., 2021). A subset of studies emphasizes that ZLN005 acts upstream of AMPK→PGC-1α/MEF2 transcriptional circuits and engages canonical mitochondrial biogenesis regulators (NRF1/2, TFAM, ERRs), while in some tissues it promotes downstream fatty-acid oxidation via CPT-1α, aligning with the recognized role of PGC-1α as a master coactivator of oxidative metabolism (Zhang et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2020).

Therapeutic History  
ZLN005 has no reported clinical use. Its portfolio of preclinical applications includes:

- Metabolic disease: In diabetic db/db mice, chronic oral ZLN005 (15 mg/kg/day for 6 weeks) improved glucose tolerance, insulin sensitivity, and dyslipidemia, with induction of PGC-1α and mitochondrial/FAO gene programs in skeletal muscle and reduced hepatic gluconeogenic transcripts; AMPK/ACC phosphorylation rose in muscle but not liver, consistent with tissue selectivity (Zhang et al., 2013). Basic single-dose oral pharmacokinetics in db/db mice showed rapid plasma absorption and high initial liver exposure, with relatively stable muscle exposure over 4 hours (Zhang et al., 2013). A short-term rat safety study (75 mg/kg/day, 14 days) reported survival with no obvious changes in body weight gain or gross metabolic parameters (Zhang et al., 2013).

- Skeletal muscle cells: In L6 myotubes, ZLN005 dose-dependently increased PGC-1α mRNA, glucose uptake, and palmitate oxidation; AMPK and ACC phosphorylation increased, PGC-1α induction was AMPK-dependent (Compound C–sensitive), and MEF2 promoter integrity was required, consistent with a transcriptional mechanism (Zhang et al., 2013).

- Kidney ischemia–reperfusion injury (AKI): In mouse I/R models and H/R-injured renal tubular cells, ZLN005 restored PGC-1α and CPT-1α expression, improved mitochondrial ultrastructure/membrane potential, reduced ROS and lipid peroxidation (H₂O₂, MDA), lessened apoptosis, and required CPT-1α activity for benefit; high concentrations were toxic to HK2 cells (Wang et al., 2021).

- Neuronal injury: ZLN005 improved viability in OGD/R-injured PC12 cells, induced PGC-1α and antioxidant genes (SOD1/HO-1), and post-ischemia administration reduced infarct volume and neurological deficit in rat tMCAO, indicating neuroprotection likely via PGC-1α-driven mitochondrial and antioxidant programs; in a separate study, ZLN005 crossed the blood–brain barrier and protected against PBDE-47 neurotoxicity via PGC-1α-dependent mitochondrial biogenesis (Xu et al., 2018; Tian et al., 2023).

- Cardiomyocytes: In hESC-derived cardiomyocytes, brief ZLN005 exposure (10 μM, 48 h) increased PGC-1α and ERRγ, upregulated mitochondrial biogenesis and OXPHOS/FAO genes (NRF1, TFAM, respiratory subunits, CPT1b), increased mtDNA copy number, basal OCR and ATP, and drove structural/electrophysiological maturation (longer sarcomeres, more negative RMP, enhanced Ca²⁺ handling, increased CX43) (Liu et al., 2020).

- Lung epithelium/infection: In AECs (A549 and primary AEC2), ZLN005 increased PGC-1α and NRF1, improved mitochondrial bioenergetics, membrane potential, ATP, decreased ROS and senescence markers (p21, SA-β-gal), and these effects required PGC-1α (shPGC-1α attenuated benefit); in a P. aeruginosa pneumonia model, ZLN005 pretreatment (15 mg/kg × 3) reduced bacterial load and IL-1β and rescued SIRT3 in lung, consistent with PGC-1α–SIRT3 axis activation (Ma et al., 2023; Maurice et al., 2022).

- Vascular smooth muscle cells: ZLN005 increased PGC-1α, ESRRA, NRF1, mtDNA, and ATP, shifted mitochondrial dynamics toward fusion (↑MFN2, ↓DRP1), and dispersed perinuclear aggregates, indicating enhanced mitochondrial function (Zou et al., 2025).

- Retinal and RPE models: In ARPE-19, ZLN005 robustly increased PGC-1α, upregulated transcription factors, antioxidant enzymes and mitochondrial genes, improved basal/maximal respiration and spare capacity, and protected against oxidative insults (H₂O₂, oxLDL, NaIO₃); protection was PGC-1α-dependent; in primary human RPE (H-RPE), 10 μM ZLN005 selectively induced PGC-1α and blocked TGFβ₂-induced EMT and migration, with smaller fold-change than in ARPE-19 due to higher baseline PGC-1α (Tong et al., 2022; Shu et al., 2021). In ex vivo rd1 retinal explants (inherited photoreceptor degeneration), ZLN005 reduced overall calpain activity, shifted calpain isoform balance toward neuroprotective calpain-1 and away from calpain-2, and enhanced photoreceptor viability, supporting retinal neuroprotection via PGC-1α activation (Wang et al., 2025).

There are no reports that ZLN005 has been tested in dry age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD) animal models, nor direct demonstrations that it improves RPE phagosome clearance, lysosomal acidification, cathepsin D activity, lipofuscin burden, or drusen in AMD contexts; TFEB-targeted rescue of lysosomal function and cathepsin activity in RPE has been achieved with other agents (e.g., trehalose) or genetic TFEB activation, but ZLN005 has not been evaluated in those axes in RPE (Ghosh et al., 2024; Ghosh et al., 2023; Tong et al., 2022; Shu et al., 2021).

Mechanism of Action  
Transcriptional induction of PGC-1α. ZLN005 increases PGC-1α transcription via the PGC-1α promoter, requiring an intact MEF2 binding site; it increases PGC-1α mRNA and protein across multiple cell types where responsive, including myotubes, cardiomyocytes, lung epithelium, VSMCs, and RPE; reliance on MEF2 sites suggests ZLN005 engages upstream signaling and chromatin/transcriptional complexes that drive Ppargc1a expression (Zhang et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2020; Ma et al., 2023; Zou et al., 2025; Shu et al., 2021).

AMPK activation via mild mitochondrial uncoupling. In L6 myotubes, ZLN005 increases the cellular ADP:ATP ratio and mildly increases mitochondrial oxygen consumption in isolated mitochondria, consistent with weak uncoupling that activates AMPK; AMPK and ACC phosphorylation increase, and pharmacologic AMPK inhibition (Compound C) blocks PGC-1α induction and glucose uptake; the pathway is further modeled as AMPK-phosphorylated PGC-1α engaging MEF2C to amplify its own gene expression via positive feedback (Zhang et al., 2013). AMPK-dependence extends functionally: glucose uptake and PGC-1α induction in muscle cells require AMPK activation (Wang et al., 2021).

Downstream PGC-1α programs. Across tissues, ZLN005 induces the canonical PGC-1α program: coactivation of ERRs/PPARs/NRF1/2, upregulation of TFAM, increases in mtDNA copy number, OXPHOS complex gene products, fatty-acid oxidation enzymes (e.g., CPT-1, MCAD), and functional increases in basal/maximal OCR, ATP production, and mitochondrial content/number—data are robust in cardiomyocytes and skeletal muscle, and consistent in lung epithelial cells and RPE (Liu et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2013; Ma et al., 2023; Tong et al., 2022). In kidney I/R, PGC-1α induction by ZLN005 increased CPT-1α, restored mitochondrial FAO, reduced ROS and MDA, and decreased apoptosis; genetic or pharmacologic CPT-1α inhibition abrogated ZLN005 benefit, placing FAO downstream of PGC-1α as a necessary mediator of cytoprotection in that model (Wang et al., 2021).

PGC-1α–SIRT axis and anti-inflammatory effects. In lung infection models, ZLN005 activated the PGC-1α–SIRT3 axis, rescued SIRT3 expression, and lowered IL-1β expression in infected lungs, aligning with the role of SIRT3 in mitochondrial antioxidant function (activation of SOD2, glutathione system) and with PGC-1α’s coactivation of oxidative metabolism and antioxidant defense (Maurice et al., 2022).

Cell-type specificity and paradoxical tissue effects. ZLN005 shows a cell-type- and tissue-selective response: skeletal muscle and diverse non-hepatic cells robustly induce PGC-1α, whereas primary hepatocytes do not; in db/db mice, liver PGC-1α was paradoxically downregulated, with concurrent suppression of gluconeogenic genes, possibly via indirect systemic mechanisms (Zhang et al., 2013). In RPE, primary cells (H-RPE) exhibited modest PGC-1α fold-induction relative to ARPE-19 due to higher baseline PGC-1α expression, yet ZLN005 still blocked TGFβ₂-induced EMT and migration in H-RPE (Shu et al., 2021).

Assay caveats. ZLN005 potently inhibits luciferases, necessitating caution and orthogonal validation for any conclusions drawn from luciferase reporters, including those targeting TFEB/TFE3 or PGC-1α target promoters (Zhang et al., 2013).

Linking to TFEB/lysosomal axis: rationale vs evidence. AMPK primes lysosomal biogenesis and function partly by inducing TFEB/TFE3, while simultaneously regulating mitochondrial biogenesis via PGC-1α; a combined AMPK activation and mTORC1 inhibition strategy has been proposed as superior for mitochondrial disease contexts (Boya et al., 2023). In RPE/retina, genetic and pharmacologic activation of TFEB restores lysosomal hydrolases (CTSD, CTSL), improves autophagosome–lysosome fusion and catabolism, and reduces disease-relevant lipid accumulation; these TFEB-centered effects are well documented in RPE but have not been demonstrated for ZLN005 (Ghosh et al., 2024; Ghosh et al., 2023). Some evidence in non-retinal systems places PGC-1α upstream of TFEB-regulated lysosomal activity (e.g., in Huntington disease models), supporting a conceptual link between mitochondrial biogenesis and lysosomal/autophagy competence; however, ZLN005-specific co-activation of TFEB or enhancement of lysosomal acidification/CTSD in RPE has not been shown (Blasiak et al., 2021).

Expected Effect  
Dry AMD pathobiology—RPE mitochondrial–lysosomal dysfunction. Dry AMD features RPE oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction (mtDNA damage, reduced OXPHOS, fewer/disorganized mitochondria), defective mitophagy, impaired proteostasis, and lysosomal/autophagy defects that promote lipofuscin and drusen biogenesis (Hyttinen et al., 2023; Luján et al., 2022; Felszeghy et al., 2019). PGC-1α is highly expressed in retina/RPE and is a potent regulator of mitochondrial biogenesis and antioxidant defenses in these cells; genetic deficiency of PGC-1α (especially combined with NRF2 loss) fosters RPE degeneration with proteostatic/lysosomal stress reminiscent of dry AMD (Felszeghy et al., 2019; Hyttinen et al., 2018; Hyttinen et al., 2023). Mechanistically, AMPK→PGC-1α signaling induces mitochondrial biogenesis and interacts with NRF2/ARE antioxidant programs; reciprocally, AMPK can promote TFEB/TFE3-driven lysosomal biogenesis, providing a bidirectional mito–lyso coupling framework relevant to RPE homeostasis (Nita & Grzybowski, 2023; Boya et al., 2023).

What ZLN005 is expected to do in RPE assays. In ARPE-19 and H-RPE, ZLN005 selectively induces PGC-1α, improves mitochondrial respiration, upregulates mitochondrial/antioxidant gene expression, and protects against oxidative insults; PGC-1α dependence of cytoprotection has been demonstrated in ARPE-19 (Tong et al., 2022; Shu et al., 2021). In H-RPE, ZLN005 prevents TGFβ₂-induced EMT and migration, linking PGC-1α induction to preservation of epithelial phenotype and metabolic competence under stress (Shu et al., 2021). Based on these data, in RPE assays ZLN005 is expected to:

- Increase PGC-1α transcript/protein and downstream mitochondrial biogenesis (e.g., NRF1/TFAM/OXPHOS genes), raising basal/maximal respiration and spare capacity, and boosting ATP (Tong et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2020).  
- Lower ROS and improve mitochondrial membrane potential and structure, thereby reducing oxidative injury susceptibility (Tong et al., 2022; Ma et al., 2023).  
- Preserve epithelial features and reduce EMT/migration under profibrotic stress (TGFβ₂), maintaining RPE barrier function (Shu et al., 2021).

Hypothesized effects on lysosomes/TFEB/CTSD and phagosome clearance. The proposal posits that ZLN005 will “cooperate with TFEB to enhance lysosomal acidification and cathepsin D activity, thereby improving phagosome clearance” and that improved mito–lyso coupling will reduce lipofuscin. Available evidence supports the general biological framework—AMPK can activate TFEB/TFE3 and PGC-1α in parallel, PGC-1α/NRF2 promote mitochondrial homeostasis and antioxidant capacity in RPE, and TFEB activation restores lysosomal hydrolases and autophagic flux in diseased RPE—but there are no direct data that ZLN005 activates TFEB, increases lysosomal acidification, elevates cathepsin D activity, or enhances phagosome clearance in RPE (Boya et al., 2023; Ghosh et al., 2024; Tong et al., 2022; Shu et al., 2021). In fact, the TFEB-centric rescue of CTSD/LAMP1 and lysosome function in AMD-model RPE has been demonstrated with trehalose or genetic TFEB activation, not with ZLN005; therefore, any expectation that ZLN005 alone will enhance lysosomal acidification/CTSD or phagosome clearance is a plausible but unproven hypothesis that requires explicit testing with lysosomal pH probes, CTSD activity assays, and POS phagocytosis/phagosome clearance metrics in primary human RPE (Ghosh et al., 2024).

Important caveats for experimental design:  
- Reporter interference: ZLN005 inhibits luciferases and may confound TFEB/E-box luciferase or PGC-1α reporter assays; use non-luciferase readouts (e.g., immunoblots, qPCR, ChIP-qPCR, RNA-seq, proteomics, TFEB nuclear translocation imaging, LysoTracker/DQ-BSA/CTSD activity assays) (Zhang et al., 2013).  
- Primary vs cell line responsiveness: Primary H-RPE shows smaller PGC-1α fold-induction than ARPE-19 due to higher baseline PGC-1α; dosing windows and exposure times must be optimized in H-RPE to achieve functional gains without undue mitochondrial uncoupling (Shu et al., 2021).  
- Cross-talk assessment: If synergy with TFEB is a key aim, include a TFEB activator arm (e.g., trehalose) as comparator/combination and measure canonical TFEB outputs (CTSD/L, LAMP1/2, CLEAR network gene expression), while maintaining AMPK/mTORC1 pathway controls to dissect mechanism (Ghosh et al., 2024; Boya et al., 2023).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Direct RPE activity. ZLN005 selectively upregulates PGC-1α in ARPE-19 and primary H-RPE, enhances mitochondrial respiration, and protects ARPE-19 from oxidative stress in a PGC-1α-dependent manner; it also suppresses TGFβ₂-induced EMT/migration in H-RPE, linking mitochondrial competence to epithelial stability—both highly relevant to dry AMD pathophysiology (Tong et al., 2022; Shu et al., 2021).  
- Robust mitochondrial biogenesis/transcriptional program. Across cardiomyocytes, muscle, and lung epithelium, ZLN005 reproducibly induces PGC-1α and downstream transcriptional programs (NRF1/TFAM/OXPHOS/FAO), increasing mtDNA, OCR, and ATP, establishing a mechanistic basis for improving RPE mitochondrial deficits observed in dry AMD (Liu et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2013; Ma et al., 2023; Hyttinen et al., 2023).  
- Systems-level cytoprotection. In AKI and neuronal ischemia/toxicity models, ZLN005 reduces ROS and apoptosis, improves mitochondrial integrity, and requires key downstream effectors (CPT-1α in kidney), demonstrating that PGC-1α activation can translate to organ protection, which conceptually extends to RPE under oxidative/energetic stress (Wang et al., 2021; Xu et al., 2018; Tian et al., 2023).  
- Disease relevance of the target. Extensive genetic/pathophysiologic evidence places PGC-1α at the center of RPE mitochondrial biogenesis, antioxidant defense, and senescence control; PGC-1α or PGC-1α/NRF2 loss causes AMD-like degeneration, and AMPK→PGC-1α and NRF2/ARE axes are validated protective mechanisms in RPE (Felszeghy et al., 2019; Hyttinen et al., 2018; Hyttinen et al., 2023; Nita & Grzybowski, 2023).  
- Translational feasibility. ZLN005 has oral bioactivity with favorable metabolic endpoints in mice, rudimentary short-term rat safety, and a breadth of preclinical efficacy across tissues; it penetrates the CNS, implying some potential for ocular exposure via circulation, though eye PK is unknown (Zhang et al., 2013; Tian et al., 2023).

Limitations and risks  
- No direct evidence for TFEB/lysosomal activation by ZLN005. There are no data showing that ZLN005 increases TFEB activity, lysosomal acidification, cathepsin D activity, or phagosome clearance in RPE; TFEB-dependent improvements in lysosome function and CTSD have been demonstrated with other interventions (trehalose or genetic TFEB activation), not with ZLN005 (Ghosh et al., 2024; Tong et al., 2022; Shu et al., 2021). The hypothesized mito–lyso crosstalk is biologically plausible via AMPK signaling but remains to be demonstrated for this compound (Boya et al., 2023).  
- Potential pro-angiogenic signaling. PGC-1α/ERRα activation in RPE has been linked to VEGF upregulation under certain conditions; in a chronic retinal setting, inadvertent promotion of angiogenic signaling could be undesirable, especially near neovascular AMD thresholds; careful assessment of VEGF/angiogenic gene expression in RPE and choroid is warranted (Blasiak et al., 2021).  
- Dose window and uncoupling toxicity. ZLN005 acts at least partly via mild mitochondrial uncoupling to activate AMPK; while beneficial in moderation, uncoupling can exacerbate ROS and bioenergetic stress if overdosed; high ZLN005 concentrations were toxic in HK2 cells, underscoring the need for careful titration in primary H-RPE (Zhang et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2021).  
- Cell-type and species specificity. ZLN005 does not induce PGC-1α in primary hepatocytes and downregulated hepatic PGC-1α in db/db mice; responsiveness varies by cell context (e.g., smaller fold-change in H-RPE than ARPE-19), complicating dose translation and efficacy prediction in human RPE in vivo (Zhang et al., 2013; Shu et al., 2021).  
- Reporter assay interference. The compound inhibits luciferases; any reliance on luciferase readouts for PGC-1α or TFEB activity risks artifact and demands orthogonal assay confirmation (Zhang et al., 2013).  
- Ocular pharmacokinetics unknown. Oral PK demonstrates high liver exposure and moderate muscle exposure; there are no data on ocular distribution, RPE exposure, or retinal bioavailability, making formulation and dosing strategies for eye delivery an open question (Zhang et al., 2013).

Decision-critical gaps and suggested de-risking experiments  
- TFEB/lysosomal axis: Directly test whether ZLN005 increases TFEB nuclear translocation, CLEAR network gene expression, lysosomal pH acidification (ratiometric probes), CTSD/CTSL protein/activity, and autophagosome flux (LC3B-II/p62 turnover) in primary H-RPE; benchmark versus trehalose and/or genetic TFEB activation and evaluate additivity or synergy in ZLN005+trehalose combination, with AMPK/mTORC1 pathway readouts to mechanistically link signaling (Ghosh et al., 2024; Boya et al., 2023).  
- Phagosome processing: Quantify photoreceptor outer segment (POS) uptake and phagosome clearance kinetics, including cathepsin-dependent proteolysis and lipofuscinogenic adduct accumulation, under oxidative/complement stress ± ZLN005; include PGC-1α knockdown to confirm dependence (Tong et al., 2022; Felszeghy et al., 2019).  
- In vivo efficacy in AMD-relevant models: Test in complement/CFH risk allele iPSC-RPE xenograft or sodium iodate/aging mouse models focusing on RPE structure/function, lipofuscin proxies, sub-RPE deposit formation, and ERG endpoints; incorporate TFEB activation arms where possible to validate the dual-axis hypothesis (Ghosh et al., 2024; Luján et al., 2022).  
- Safety pharmacology: Titrate ZLN005 dosing in ocular delivery paradigms (intravitreal, periocular, or systemic) with eye PK, retinal/RPE exposure, retinal function (ERG), and VEGF expression profiling to exclude pro-angiogenic shifts; assess off-target mitochondrial stress at higher exposures in H-RPE (Blasiak et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2021).

Conclusion: fit for further evaluation with focused lysosome endpoints. ZLN005 has strong mechanistic and preclinical support as a PGC-1α activator that improves mitochondrial biogenesis and oxidative resilience in RPE and retina-adjacent systems, and it produces protective effects across diverse tissues via PGC-1α-dependent programs (Tong et al., 2022; Shu et al., 2021; Xu et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2021). However, the core elements of the present hypothesis—enhancement of TFEB activity, lysosomal acidification, cathepsin D activity, and phagosome clearance, plus reduction of lipofuscin and drusen—are not yet evidenced for ZLN005 and remain inferential based on pathway crosstalk (AMPK→TFEB/TFE3, PGC-1α–NRF2) and TFEB-targeted rescue in RPE by other agents (Boya et al., 2023; Ghosh et al., 2024). Consequently, ZLN005 is a promising mitochondrial-centric candidate for dry AMD that merits accelerated, targeted validation on lysosomal/phagosome endpoints and ocular delivery feasibility. The compound’s strengths—a validated mitochondrial biogenesis mechanism in RPE, demonstrated oxidative stress protection in ARPE-19, primary H-RPE EMT suppression, and broad cross-tissue efficacy—justify this investment, provided that the risks of off-target uncoupling, reporter assay interference, cell-type specificity, and potential pro-angiogenic signaling are actively managed in the experimental plan (Tong et al., 2022; Shu et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2013; Blasiak et al., 2021).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Everolimus (Afinitor; Novartis) is a semi‐synthetic derivative of sirolimus—a macrolide originally isolated from Streptomyces hygroscopicus—as evidenced by its chemical designation as 4-O-(2-hydroxyethyl)-rapamycin (Liu et al., 2023, pp. 11–12). By introducing a 2-hydroxyethyl group at position 40, everolimus achieves greater hydrophilicity and an increased oral bioavailability (from 10% to 16% relative to sirolimus) while retaining the core macrolactone structure that is characteristic of rapalogs (Liu et al., 2023, pp. 11–12; Weber, 2015, pp. 27–28). This compound belongs to the class of mTOR inhibitors—specifically, a first‐generation rapalog that selectively inhibits the mTOR complex 1 (mTORC1) while sparing mTORC2 (Liu et al., 2023, pp. 10–11; Weber, 2015, pp. 27–28). As a synthetic derivative of a naturally occurring product, everolimus represents the successful strategy of chemical modification to optimize pharmacokinetic properties and clinical tolerability. The design parameters underpinning everolimus’ synthesis have been guided by the goal of retaining potent immunosuppressive and anti‐proliferative effects while optimizing parameters such as solubility, half‐life, and tissue penetration, with the added advantage of an oral formulation already approved for several clinical indications (Liu et al., 2023, pp. 11–12; Wang et al., 2022, pp. 6–8).

Therapeutic History:  
Everolimus has a well‐established therapeutic history as an immunosuppressant and antineoplastic agent. Clinically, it is approved for treating advanced renal cell carcinoma, progressive neuroendocrine tumors of pancreatic origin, and subependymal giant cell astrocytoma in tuberous sclerosis complex patients who are not candidates for surgery (Wang et al., 2022, pp. 6–8; Weber, 2015, pp. 27–28). In these indications, its mechanism as an mTORC1 inhibitor serves to arrest cell cycle progression and inhibit angiogenesis, which are central to its antitumor activity (Kuo et al., 2018, pp. 5–7; Weber, 2015, pp. 27–28). Moreover, everolimus has been effectively used in the context of organ transplantation to prevent allograft rejection by impairing helper T‐cell proliferation (Wang et al., 2022, pp. 6–8; Weber, 2015, pp. 27–28).

With regard to ocular applications, although everolimus has not been approved specifically for dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD), several preclinical studies have demonstrated its potential benefits in ocular cell types and models. For instance, in vitro investigations have highlighted that everolimus can inhibit the proliferation and migration of retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells and modulate mTOR signaling within retinal tissue—an effect critical to conditions such as proliferative vitreoretinopathy (PVR) (Kuo et al., 2018, pp. 5–8). Additionally, clinical trials such as the Phase 2 randomized trial for neovascular AMD (albeit focused on wet AMD) have assessed everolimus’s efficacy in combination with anti‐vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) agents (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2009), thereby providing indirect support for its ocular pharmacokinetic (PK) profile and safety profile. This background, combined with its well‐known systemic tolerability, underscores its candidacy for repurposing in nonexudative (dry) AMD—a disease area in which few pharmacologic treatments exist.

Mechanism of Action:  
Everolimus exerts its effects by binding to the intracellular receptor FKBP12, forming a complex that interacts with and inhibits mTORC1 (Liu et al., 2023, pp. 11–12; Weber, 2015, pp. 27–28). The inhibition of mTORC1 results in a downstream decrease in the phosphorylation of ribosomal protein S6 kinase (S6K1) and other substrates such as ribosomal protein S6 (RPS6), effectively suppressing cap‐dependent protein synthesis and cellular proliferation (Kuo et al., 2018, pp. 5–7; Liu et al., 2023, pp. 10–11). In the context of RPE cells, inhibition of mTORC1 plays a particularly critical role in modulating autophagic flux. Under normal conditions, mTORC1 phosphorylates and suppresses the transcription factor EB (TFEB), a master regulator of lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy. Inhibition of mTORC1 frees TFEB to translocate to the nucleus where it transactivates genes that codify for lysosomal proteins, such as the subunits of the vacuolar ATPase (V‐ATPase), and hydrolases including cathepsin D (Kuo et al., 2018, p. 7; Nieto et al., 2015, pp. 28–32). Preclinical studies have shown that in RPE culture systems, treatment with everolimus results in an increase in LC3 turnover—a marker of enhanced autophagic flux—and accelerates the maturation of cathepsin D (CTSD), which is essential for effective lysosomal degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (Kuo et al., 2018, pp. 5–8). Such modulation of the autophagy–lysosome pathway is mechanistically attractive in dry AMD because the accumulation of cellular debris and lipofuscin in RPE cells is implicated in disease pathogenesis. Furthermore, it has been reported that everolimus displays superior ocular tissue penetration compared with sirolimus in in vitro porcine corneal models, suggesting that its formulation could be optimized for direct ocular administration if required (Liu et al., 2023, pp. 11–14). Overall, the biochemical profile of everolimus supports the hypothesis that targeted mTORC1 inhibition in RPE cells could lead to enhanced TFEB activation and a subsequent restoration of lysosomal function—thereby addressing one of the key pathological features underlying dry AMD.

Expected Effect:  
The hypothesis proposes that everolimus will inhibit mTORC1 in RPE cells, leading to the activation of TFEB, a critical step in lysosomal biogenesis and function. Upon release from mTORC1‐mediated phosphorylation constraints, TFEB translocates to the nucleus where it upregulates the expression of essential lysosomal genes, including those encoding V‐ATPase subunits (which are responsible for lysosomal acidification) and cathepsin D (CTSD), a protease required for the degradation of accumulated waste products (Kuo et al., 2018, p. 7; Nieto et al., 2015, pp. 28–32). This molecular cascade is expected to improve the clearance of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) and other cellular debris that accumulate in RPE cells owing to age‐related impairment of autophagy. In vitro data support that everolimus treatment increases LC3 turnover and facilitates the maturation of CTSD, both of which are indicative of enhanced autophagic flux and lysosomal functionality (Kuo et al., 2018, pp. 5–8). Given that RPE cells naturally express components of the mTOR signaling pathway—including high levels of mTORC1—and that dysfunctional lysosomal clearance is a hallmark of dry AMD (as exemplified by the accumulation of lipofuscin and drusen formation), the expected pharmacodynamic effect of everolimus would be to restore homeostasis in these cells. Successful activation of TFEB is anticipated to lead to improved degradation of damaged organelles and protein aggregates, potentially mitigating the progression of retinal degeneration characteristic of dry AMD. Moreover, the fact that everolimus is already formulated for oral administration with a known ocular PK profile further supports the translational potential of this candidate: systemic dosing may achieve sufficient retinal concentrations to exert the desired effects in RPE cells without necessitating invasive delivery methods (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2009; Liu et al., 2023, pp. 11–12).

Overall Evaluation:  
The potential of everolimus as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD is supported by several compelling factors. First, its established clinical safety and efficacy in other indications—such as renal cell carcinoma and immunosuppression in transplantation—reduce the translational risk associated with drug repurposing (Weber, 2015, pp. 27–28; Wang et al., 2022, pp. 6–8). The fact that everolimus is an FDA‐approved agent with an oral formulation makes it an attractive candidate for repurposing, as its dosing, systemic distribution, and side‐effect profile are already well characterized. In addition, its selective inhibition of mTORC1 has a clear mechanistic rationale in the context of dry AMD. Additionally, its improved ocular penetration compared to its parent compound sirolimus suggests that even systemic administration might yield therapeutically relevant levels in the retina (Liu et al., 2023, pp. 11–14). This represents a significant advantage in the context of dry AMD, where achieving effective drug delivery to deeply situated retinal tissues is a persistent challenge.

However, several weaknesses must be acknowledged. Despite a sound mechanistic rationale, direct clinical evidence for everolimus’s efficacy in dry AMD is lacking. Existing clinical studies have primarily focused on other ocular conditions such as neovascular AMD and PVR, and the particular pathophysiology of dry AMD—with its complex interplay of oxidative stress, complement dysregulation, and chronic inflammation—may require a more nuanced therapeutic approach (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2009; Kuo et al., 2018, pp. 3–5). Another consideration relates to the multifactorial etiology of dry AMD. While lysosomal dysfunction is a critical aspect of the disease, it is accompanied by other pathological processes such as oxidative damage, chronic inflammation, and alterations in the complement cascade. Thus, monotherapy with an mTORC1 inhibitor may not be sufficiently robust to address all disease mechanisms. Combination therapies that target multiple pathological pathways might ultimately be necessary for effective disease modification. Lastly, discrepancies in the translation of preclinical findings to human disease remain a persistent challenge. For example, while certain animal models of retinal disease have demonstrated beneficial effects of mTOR inhibition, analogous results have not always been replicated in clinical settings (Kuo et al., 2018, pp. 3–5; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2009).

In summary, everolimus presents as a mechanistically intriguing candidate for repurposing in dry AMD due to its ability to inhibit mTORC1 and thereby promote TFEB‐mediated restoration of lysosomal function. Its solid record as an FDA‐approved drug with established dosing regimens and acceptable systemic safety lends additional support to its viability as a repurposing candidate. Preclinical data suggest that everolimus increases autophagic flux in RPE cells, enhancing LC3 turnover and CTSD maturation, which theoretically should facilitate the clearance of pathological debris that characterizes dry AMD (Kuo et al., 2018, pp. 5–8). The advantages of an oral formulation and favorable ocular pharmacokinetics further underpin its translational potential (Liu et al., 2023, pp. 11–12; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2009).

Nonetheless, the candidate also faces important challenges. Key limitations include the absence of direct clinical evidence for efficacy in dry AMD, potential systemic adverse effects associated with prolonged mTORC1 inhibition, and the inherent complexity of dry AMD pathology, which may require multimodal therapeutic strategies. Moreover, past experiences in ocular applications—such as studies in PVR models where everolimus did not yield a statistically significant clinical improvement—highlight the need for carefully controlled dose-finding and safety studies (Kuo et al., 2018, pp. 3–5). It will be crucial to establish that systemic dosing can achieve therapeutic retinal concentrations without eliciting unintended systemic toxicity or disrupting normal RPE physiology.

Overall, while mechanistic and preclinical data provide a strong rationale for repurposing everolimus to treat dry AMD, further rigorous preclinical studies specifically in models of dry AMD are warranted. A careful evaluation of dosing regimens, potential adverse effects, and efficacy endpoints will be essential in the translational development of everolimus for this indication. The mechanistic specificity for mTORC1 inhibition, combined with the ability to enhance autophagic clearance in RPE cells, represents a significant strength that could offer a novel approach to modifying the course of dry AMD. However, the challenges associated with systemic mTOR inhibition and the need for combination strategies or localized delivery systems must be addressed in subsequent research phases. In conclusion, everolimus is a promising, though not yet definitively validated, candidate for repurposing in dry AMD, and we recommend that further detailed studies be undertaken to fully elucidate its potential in restoring lysosomal function and ameliorating retinal degeneration in this patient population (Liu et al., 2023, pp. 11–12; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2009; Kuo et al., 2018, pp. 5–7; Weber, 2015, pp. 27–28; Wang et al., 2022, pp. 6–8; Kuo et al., 2018, pp. 7–8).

BAY 11-7082 is a synthetic, small-molecule inhibitor originally discovered as an irreversible inhibitor of IκBα phosphorylation, which blocks NF-κB activation. This reactive electrophilic center enables the compound to covalently modify nucleophilic cysteine residues on target proteins. Early studies identified BAY 11-7082 for its capacity to inhibit NF-κB signaling in endothelial cells, and subsequent research expanded its profile to include inhibition of the NLRP3 inflammasome via cysteine alkylation of critical regulatory sites. In essence, BAY 11-7082 belongs to the class of covalent inhibitors that have been widely studied in the context of inflammatory and oncologic diseases, and its availability as Sigma B5556 has made it a common tool compound in preclinical research (Juliana et al., 2010; Marchetti, 2019; Yu et al., 2018).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, BAY 11-7082 has been utilized extensively in biochemical, cellular, and animal studies as an anti-inflammatory agent. Initial applications centered on its ability to block the phosphorylation and degradation of IκBα, thereby inhibiting downstream NF-κB–driven gene expression. This mechanism was exploited in models of endothelial inflammation and various cancer cell lines, including studies showing potent anticancer, neuroprotective, and anti-inflammatory effects (Lee et al., 2012; Melisi & Chiao, 2007). Furthermore, its repurposing has been explored in fields as diverse as hematologic malignancies, diabetes-related complications, and preclinical psoriasis models, where it served as a dual inhibitor of NF-κB and the NLRP3 inflammasome (Irrera et al., 2017; Kolati et al., 2015). Despite this broad research history, BAY 11-7082 has not been previously tested explicitly in the context of dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or diseases with a similar pathology in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE). However, its known capacity to reduce inflammatory cytokine production and preserve lysosomal integrity in nonocular cell types provides a rationale for evaluating its potential utility in dry AMD—a disease characterized by chronic inflammation, impaired lysosomal clearance, and inflammasome activation (Blevins et al., 2022; Irrera et al., 2017; Marchetti, 2019).

Mechanism of Action:  
BAY 11-7082 exerts its pharmacological effects predominantly through irreversible covalent inhibition. Its most well‐characterized mechanism is the blockade of NF-κB signaling by preventing the phosphorylation of the inhibitory protein IκBα. Under normal conditions, phosphorylation of IκBα triggers its degradation, thus allowing NF-κB (typically the p65/p50 heterodimer) to translocate into the nucleus and activate pro-inflammatory target genes. By inhibiting IκBα phosphorylation, BAY 11-7082 effectively sequesters NF-κB in the cytosol, thereby suppressing the expression of genes associated with inflammation such as IL-1β, TNF-α, and various chemokines (Marchetti, 2019; Melisi & Chiao, 2007).  

Moreover, BAY 11-7082 has been repurposed based on its ability to inhibit the NLRP3 inflammasome. Mechanistically, the compound forms covalent adducts with reactive cysteine residues on the NLRP3 protein, most likely within the ATPase domain—an essential activity domain required for inflammasome activation. This alkylation event, which proceeds via a Michael-type addition reaction, results in irreversible inactivation of NLRP3’s ATPase function, thereby preventing the assembly and subsequent activation of the inflammasome complex (Cocco et al., 2014; Juliana et al., 2010; Marchetti, 2019). In addition to these primary actions, BAY 11-7082 has been reported to inhibit other cysteine-dependent enzymes such as protein tyrosine phosphatases and even components like gasdermin D that contribute to pyroptosis. Consequently, the compound displays a broad-spectrum inhibitory profile that may diminish inflammatory cascades not only at the transcriptional (NF-κB) level but also at the inflammasome activation stage (Yu et al., 2018; Zahid et al., 2019).  

Expected Effect in Dry Age-Related Macular Degeneration:  
In the context of dry AMD, the hypothesis is that chronic inflammation in the RPE drives cellular dysfunction through mechanisms that include sustained NF-κB activation and priming of the NLRP3 inflammasome. Inflammatory cytokines and resultant oxidative stress contribute to lysosomal impairment, reducing the activity of v-ATPase and lysosomal proteases such as cathepsin D (CTSD), which are crucial for the clearance of cellular debris. BAY 11-7082 is expected to intervene at an early stage in this inflammatory cascade by inhibiting NF-κB signaling. In doing so, it would reduce the transcriptional upregulation of inflammasome components and pro-inflammatory cytokines, particularly IL-1β, a key mediator in inflammasome activation (Blevins et al., 2022; Marchetti, 2019).  

Experimental studies in macrophages and psoriasis models have demonstrated that NF-κB inhibition with BAY 11-7082 leads to a reduction in IL-1β production and preserves lysosomal integrity. Although these studies were conducted in nonocular tissues, the expression of NF-κB and NLRP3 inflammasome components in RPE cells is well-documented in the literature.
