Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Torin1 is a synthetic small‐molecule that belongs to the second‐generation, ATP‐competitive class of mTOR inhibitors, originally derived from a quinoline‐based scaffold. Its discovery originated from a high‐throughput compound library screen that identified quinolone hits with moderate mTOR activity, which were then optimized through iterative medicinal chemistry by introducing a six‐membered lactam to convert the initial quinolone into a tricyclic benzonaphthridinone scaffold (Guillem, 2015). This chemical modification yielded a molecule with exceptional biochemical potency—capable of inhibiting both mTOR complexes, mTORC1 and mTORC2, at very low (nanomolar to picomolar) concentrations—and with approximately 1000-fold improvement in cellular potency relative to the initial hits (Guillem, 2015). As an ATP-competitive inhibitor, Torin1 binds directly to the active (ATP-binding) site of mTOR, thereby circumventing the partial inhibition that is observed with first-generation mTOR inhibitors like rapamycin that act allosterically by binding FKBP12 (Liu et al., 2012). Torin1 has been widely used as a research tool to interrogate mTOR signaling in various cellular contexts, and its chemical lineage as a quinoline-derived molecule positions it within a well-characterized class of inhibitors that have been instrumental in expanding our understanding of mTOR-dependent regulation of autophagy and cellular metabolism (Liu et al., 2012).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, Torin1 has been employed predominantly as a research tool rather than as a clinical drug candidate. Extensive preclinical studies have demonstrated its robust ability to inhibit mTOR signaling in cancer models, autophagy-deficient systems, and metabolic studies. For instance, Torin1 was shown to potently inhibit mTOR signaling pathways in glioblastoma and prostate cancer cells, significantly reducing cell-cycle progression and inducing apoptosis in certain contexts (Gu, 2017; Liu et al., 2012). Its use as an autophagy inducer is well documented, as experiments utilizing Torin1 have demonstrated increased autophagic flux and elevated lysosomal activity in multiple cell lines (Li, 2018; Liu et al., 2012). Importantly, Torin1 is also used in studies with retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells, as evidenced by its ability to increase TFEB-driven luciferase reporter activity in ARPE-19 cells by effectively suppressing mTORC1 signaling (Huang et al., 2018). Despite these promising experimental findings, Torin1 has not advanced to clinical trials for any indication, including neurodegenerative disorders or dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD). Moreover, its intrinsic pharmacokinetic limitations—such as poor aqueous solubility, a short half-life, and low oral bioavailability—have been recognized in several studies, thereby limiting its potential as a direct therapeutic candidate without further structural optimization (Guillem, 2015; Wang et al., 2022).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, Torin1 functions by competing with ATP for binding to the catalytic domain of mTOR, effectively blocking the phosphorylation of downstream substrates. Its ATP-competitive nature allows Torin1 to inhibit both mTORC1 and mTORC2 complexes, thereby offering a broader inhibition profile than allosteric agents like rapamycin that primarily target mTORC1 (Guillem, 2015; Liu et al., 2012). Detailed molecular modeling and structure–activity relationship studies indicate that the tricyclic benzonaphthridinone core of Torin1 forms critical hinge-binding interactions with residues in the mTOR kinase domain (Liu et al., 2012). This interaction accounts for its high potency, as reflected in low nanomolar IC₅₀ values in cellular assays (Liu et al., 2012; Gros & Muller, 2014). Torin1 induces rapid dephosphorylation of canonical mTORC1 substrates, such as S6 kinase at Thr389 and 4E-BP1 at Thr37/46, which results in downregulation of protein synthesis and cellular growth signals (Misra & Pizzo, 2013). Moreover, by simultaneously inhibiting mTORC2, it reduces phosphorylation of Akt at Ser473—a site critical for full Akt activation—thus attenuating the feedback loops that typically reinvigorate upstream PI3K signaling in response to mTORC1 inhibition (Gu, 2017; Martina et al., 2014). A particularly notable feature of Torin1 is its slow off-rate, which leads to sustained inhibition of mTOR activity even after drug washout, a pharmacodynamic property that may confer prolonged downstream effects such as enhanced autophagic flux (Liu et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2013). The inhibition of mTOR by Torin1 correlates with dephosphorylation of transcription factors, particularly TFEB and TFE3; under normal nutrient-replete conditions, mTORC1 phosphorylates TFEB (e.g., on S211 in TFEB) and TFE3, sequestering them in the cytosol through binding with 14-3-3 proteins (Huang et al., 2018; Martina et al., 2014). Upon mTOR inhibition by Torin1, TFEB is dephosphorylated and translocates to the nucleus, where it induces the transcription of CLEAR (Coordinated Lysosomal Expression and Regulation) network genes that drive lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy (Li, 2018; Liu et al., 2013). This precise modulation of mTOR signaling and subsequent transcriptional reprogramming forms the biochemical basis for leveraging Torin1 as a candidate to ameliorate lysosomal clearance defects.

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis for repurposing Torin1 in the context of dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is that potent inhibition of mTORC1/2 in RPE cells can lift the repressive phosphorylation that normally limits the activity of TFEB and TFE3. In RPE cells, as demonstrated by studies in ARPE-19 cell models, mTOR inhibition via Torin1 not only leads to decreased phosphorylation of S6 kinase but also results in marked activation of TFEB-driven transcription (Huang et al., 2018). When TFEB translocates to the nucleus, it binds to CLEAR elements present in the promoters of genes responsible for lysosomal biogenesis, acidification (through the upregulation of V-ATPase subunits), and the maturation and activity of lysosomal enzymes such as cathepsin D (CTSD) (Huang et al., 2018; Li, 2018). In dry AMD, RPE cells exhibit a decline in lysosomal function along with accumulation of cellular debris and lipofuscin, which contribute to disease pathology. By inducing a robust CLEAR response, Torin1 is expected to restore lysosomal function through increased biogenesis, enhanced acidification, and elevated cathepsin D activity, thereby improving the clearance of toxic aggregates in RPE cells and ultimately mitigating the progression of dry AMD (Gu, 2017; Huang et al., 2018). Additionally, the sustained target engagement afforded by Torin1’s slow off-rate may provide prolonged therapeutic benefit even with intermittent dosing, an attractive feature given the chronic nature of AMD (Liu et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2013). Recent evidence from preclinical iPSC models and autophagy-deficiency studies underscores the potential translation of mTOR-targeted strategies in restoring cellular homeostasis in degenerative diseases, lending further credence to this expected mechanism (Guillem, 2015).

Overall Evaluation:  
In summary, Torin1 possesses a compelling mechanistic profile that aligns well with the therapeutic needs of dry AMD by targeting a fundamental pathway governing cellular homeostasis in RPE cells. Its origin from a quinoline-based scaffold and subsequent chemical optimization into a highly potent ATP-competitive mTOR inhibitor underline its status as a valuable chemical probe in preclinical settings (Guillem, 2015). Careful dosing will also be critical, as the broad and potent inhibition of mTOR can have unintended effects on cellular metabolism and protein synthesis beyond the intended enhancement of lysosomal function. From the perspective of repurposing for dry AMD, Torin1’s deep mechanistic specificity is a double-edged sword: it offers a highly defined and robust approach to upregulating lysosomal biogenesis via the TFEB/TFE3 axis, yet its pharmacokinetic liabilities and the absence of any clinical history in ocular disease necessitate additional work. The promising in vitro data in RPE models (ARPE-19 cells) and iPSC-derived RPE systems provide valuable target validation, but before advancing to clinical trials a refined analog or an optimized delivery method (for example, local ocular administration to bypass systemic bioavailability issues) should be considered (Huang et al., 2018; Li, 2018; Wang et al., 2022).

In summary, Torin1 is an excellent candidate for preclinical proof-of-concept studies to validate mTOR inhibition as a strategy to combat lysosomal dysfunction in dry AMD; however, further optimization to improve its stability and bioavailability, alongside rigorous in vivo testing in relevant AMD models, will be essential prior to clinical development (Guillem, 2015; Gu, 2017). The strengths of Torin1 lie in its potent, dual mTOR inhibition and its ability to robustly induce TFEB activation, whereas its weaknesses center on its pharmacokinetic shortcomings and the current lack of efficacy data in ocular disease models. Overall, with focused optimization and targeted delivery strategies, Torin1 or its derivatives may offer a promising therapeutic avenue for ameliorating the lysosomal clearance defects that underlie dry AMD pathology (Liu et al., 2012; Huang et al., 2018).

Below is our comprehensive evaluation of VX-765 (Belnacasan; Selleckchem S2731) as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
VX-765 is an orally bioavailable small‐molecule agent belonging to the caspase-1 inhibitor class. It is a synthetically derived peptidomimetic prodrug that, once metabolized, yields an active derivative capable of selectively binding to and inhibiting caspase-1. Originally developed by Vertex Pharmaceuticals, VX-765 was designed to address the shortcomings of earlier peptide-based caspase inhibitors by improving bioavailability, stability, and selectivity. As a caspase-1 inhibitor, it falls within a broader category of agents that have been used to blunt excessive inflammasome responses in various inflammatory and immune-mediated conditions. In the context of drug discovery, caspase-1 inhibitors have been of keen interest because caspase-1 is the key enzyme responsible for converting pro-IL-1β and pro-IL-18 into their active cytokine forms, thereby playing a central role in mediating inflammation and the programmed cell death process known as pyroptosis. VX-765 has been evaluated primarily in systemic inflammatory and cardiovascular settings, where its favorable pharmacokinetic profile and excellent oral bioavailability have been demonstrated (Audia et al., 2018; MacKenzie & Schipper, 2010).

Therapeutic History:  
The therapeutic history of VX-765 underscores its extensive preclinical development and early clinical evaluation in several inflammatory settings. In preclinical cardiovascular models, for instance, VX-765 demonstrated significant cardioprotection when administered during reperfusion, reducing infarct size and preserving mitochondrial enzyme activities (Audia et al., 2018). It has undergone Phase I and Phase II clinical studies—its Phase II safety data indicate that it is well tolerated at doses that achieve a suppression of proinflammatory cytokines in plasma (MacKenzie & Schipper, 2010). Although the major clinical investigations with VX-765 have focused on disorders such as epilepsy and other inflammatory diseases rather than ophthalmic disorders, the rationale for its use in dry AMD stems from overlapping inflammatory mechanisms. Specifically, dry AMD shares underlying pathological processes such as chronic inflammation, oxidative stress, and lysosomal dysfunction in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells. Prior experimental studies in RPE models using caspase-1 inhibitors like Z-YVAD-FMK have demonstrated that inhibiting caspase-1 activity reduces IL-1β release and can influence cell death pathways (Brandstetter, 2016; Tseng et al., 2013). However, despite this promising mechanistic background, VX-765 itself has not yet been directly evaluated in preclinical models of dry AMD or in similar ocular diseases. This gap in ophthalmic precedent is notable, but given its established safety profile in nonocular clinical settings and robust anti-inflammatory activity, VX-765 remains an attractive candidate for repurposing into the dry AMD arena (Audia et al., 2018; MacKenzie & Schipper, 2010).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, VX-765 exerts its effect primarily through selective inhibition of caspase-1, a cysteine protease critically involved in the processing of pro-inflammatory cytokines. Under conditions of cellular stress—such as those occurring in RPE cells in response to lipofuscin accumulation and photooxidative damage—lysosomal destabilization can occur. This lysosomal membrane permeabilization (LMP) leads to the release of cathepsins and other proteases into the cytosol, which, in turn, can serve as an activator of the NLRP3 inflammasome. Once assembled, the inflammasome facilitates the autocatalytic cleavage of caspase-1 into its active p10/p20 subunits, thereby enabling it to convert pro-IL-1β and pro-IL-18 into their mature, secreted forms. VX-765 binds to the active site of caspase-1, thereby preventing this proteolytic cleavage and subsequent cytokine release. This action not only blunts the inflammatory cascade but, by inhibiting caspase-1–dependent processing, may also prevent the activation of gasdermin-D (GSDMD) which is responsible for forming membrane pores during pyroptosis (Brandstetter, 2016; Tseng et al., 2013).

The hypothesis for using VX-765 in dry AMD is that inhibition of caspase-1 will disrupt a pathological amplification loop. In RPE cells exposed to chronic oxidative stress and lipofuscin-related photooxidative damage, inflammasome activation has been shown to promote rapid pyroptotic cell death rather than a slower apoptotic process. This results in an autocrine/paracrine loop where secreted IL-1β further primes neighboring cells for inflammasome activation, exacerbating cell death and causing tissue dysfunction. By blocking caspase-1 activity, VX-765 is expected to prevent this destructive cascade, thereby preserving lysosomal function. More specifically, there is a hypothesized link between caspase-1 activity and alterations in lysosomal integrity—a process involving LMP that is associated with a loss of vacuolar (V-) ATPase activity and disturbances in cathepsin D maturation. The V-ATPase is critical for maintaining an acidic lysosomal environment necessary for optimal enzyme activity, including that of cathepsin D, which is involved in the degradation of photoreceptor outer segments. Some studies have shown that under conditions of inflammasome activation, RPE cells demonstrate not only an increase in cytokine secretion but also a decline in the functionality of lysosomal hydrolases, which may further compromise cell viability (Brandstetter, 2016). Although direct evidence linking VX-765 to the preservation of V-ATPase activity or cathepsin D function in RPE is currently lacking, the mechanistic framework provided by previous studies using other caspase-1 inhibitors supports the notion that caspase-1 blockade may confer lysosomal protection and attenuate pyroptotic RPE death (Brandstetter, 2016; Tseng et al., 2013).

Expected Effect:  
In the proposed in vitro and in vivo assays, VX-765 is expected to reduce the levels of active caspase-1 and consequently diminish the secretion of IL-1β and IL-18 from RPE cells stressed by inflammatory stimuli such as lipofuscin photooxidative damage. In validated ARPE-19 cell models that mimic the conditions of dry AMD—where priming with IL-1α and subsequent exposure to lysosomal stressors (for example, the photooxidative effects of lipofuscin components) lead to inflammasome activation and rapid pyroptotic cell death—treatment with caspase-1 inhibitors has been shown to reduce cell lysis and cytokine release (Brandstetter, 2016; Tseng et al., 2013). By extrapolation, VX-765 should produce similar results. Endpoints for such studies might include decreased levels of IL-1β and IL-18 measured by ELISA, preservation of cell viability as determined by metabolic assays (such as MTT or LDH assays), and a reduction in markers of pyroptosis including the cleavage of GSDMD.

Furthermore, because the hypothesis posits that caspase-1 activity contributes to inflammasome‐mediated lysosomal membrane permeabilization, VX-765 is anticipated to stabilize lysosomal integrity. This stabilization should help maintain the acid–base balance within lysosomes—reflected by sustained V-ATPase activity—which is critical for the proper maturation and function of cathepsin D. In healthy RPE cells, cathepsin D is a major lysosomal protease responsible for degrading photoreceptor outer segment debris. In the context of dry AMD, a decline in cathepsin D activity may contribute to the accumulation of undegraded material, exacerbating cellular stress and death. Although direct measurements of V-ATPase activity and cathepsin D maturation following VX-765 treatment have not yet been published, the overall expectation is that by interrupting the caspase-1–driven inflammatory signaling cascade, VX-765 can prevent the deleterious loss of lysosomal function and thereby reduce RPE cell death (Brandstetter, 2016; Gao et al., 2019; Tseng et al., 2013).

Additionally, in in vivo models of AMD (for example, those induced by Aβ₁₋₄₀ or other drusen mimetics), the inhibition of caspase-1 should theoretically reduce the incidence or severity of geographic atrophy by preserving RPE structure and function. This is of particular interest given that RPE degeneration is a critical event in the progression of dry AMD. Markers of efficacy would include improved retinal morphology on OCT imaging, better electrophysiological responses (as measured by ERG), and a decrease in inflammatory cellular infiltrates. Collectively, these anticipated outcomes support the hypothesis that VX-765’s inhibition of caspase-1 may interrupt the cascade of inflammasome activation, LMP, and lysosomal enzyme failure that leads to RPE death in dry AMD (Brandstetter, 2016; Tseng et al., 2013).

Overall Evaluation:  
Our overall evaluation of VX-765 as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD is cautiously optimistic but recognizes several critical hurdles. One of the major strengths of VX-765 is its well-characterized mechanism of action as a selective caspase-1 inhibitor, along with its demonstrated anti-inflammatory effects in non-ocular preclinical models. The clinical safety profile established in Phase I and II studies—particularly its ability to reduce circulating pro-inflammatory cytokines—lends support to its potential use in a chronic disease setting such as dry AMD (Audia et al., 2018; MacKenzie & Schipper, 2010). From a mechanistic standpoint, the centrality of caspase-1 in mediating inflammasome-driven cytokine maturation and pyroptosis is well established, and there is compelling evidence from RPE cell models that caspase-1 inhibition can reduce IL-1β secretion and potentially modify cell death pathways (Brandstetter, 2016; Tseng et al., 2013). These observations provide a strong rationale for the hypothesis that VX-765 could prevent the lysosomal destabilization and subsequent inflammatory cascade responsible for RPE degeneration.

However, there are also several weaknesses and gaps that must be addressed before VX-765 can be fully endorsed for dry AMD. Although the mechanistic data support the role of caspase-1 inhibition in reducing inflammatory cytokine release and possibly preserving lysosomal function, there is currently no direct evidence that VX-765 can stabilize lysosomal membrane integrity, preserve V-ATPase activity, or maintain proper cathepsin D function specifically in RPE cells. Most of the available literature has utilized generic caspase-1 inhibitors such as Z-YVAD-FMK as proof-of-principle tools rather than VX-765 itself in ocular models (Brandstetter, 2016; Tseng et al., 2013). Furthermore, although numerous studies have demonstrated that inflammasome activation and caspase-1–dependent pyroptosis are features of RPE injury in vitro and in some in vivo models of dry AMD, the translation of these findings into effective therapies has proven challenging. The eye’s unique anatomy and the need for adequate drug delivery to the retina raise additional concerns. For an orally administered agent like VX-765, it is not yet clear whether systemic dosing can achieve therapeutically relevant concentrations in the RPE, or whether intravitreal or alternative delivery methods would be necessary.

Another potential weakness lies in the multifactorial nature of dry AMD. In addition to inflammasome activation and lysosomal dysfunction, dry AMD pathogenesis involves complement dysregulation, oxidative stress, impaired autophagy, and other pro-inflammatory pathways. It remains possible that targeting caspase-1 alone may not be sufficient to arrest disease progression, and a combination approach might be necessary. Moreover, previous caspase inhibitor candidates (for example, pralnacasan) have encountered issues with liver toxicity or other off-target effects in long-term studies, raising concerns about the safety of chronic caspase-1 inhibition (MacKenzie & Schipper, 2010). These potential challenges underscore the need for rigorous preclinical studies in relevant dry AMD models that not only assess the anti-inflammatory and anti-pyroptotic effects of VX-765 but also directly measure lysosomal functional parameters such as V-ATPase activity and cathepsin D maturation.

In summary, while VX-765 offers a promising and mechanistically coherent approach to perturbing the detrimental caspase-1–mediated signaling cascade implicated in RPE degeneration, significant gaps remain in linking its action to improved lysosomal function and reduced RPE death in the specific context of dry AMD. The strengths of VX-765 include its established safety data, oral bioavailability, and selective inhibition of a central inflammatory enzyme; however, its application to AMD is currently supported only by indirect evidence extrapolated from non-ocular models and generic caspase-1 inhibitor studies (Audia et al., 2018; Brandstetter, 2016; MacKenzie & Schipper, 2010; Tseng et al., 2013). To move this candidate forward, we recommend that targeted preclinical studies be undertaken in sight-relevant in vitro systems (e.g., ARPE-19 or primary human RPE models) and in vivo models of dry AMD to assess whether VX-765 can indeed prevent or reverse lysosomal membrane permeabilization, sustain V-ATPase activity, and preserve cathepsin D function, in addition to reducing downstream cytokine release and pyroptotic cell death. Only with such data can we determine whether VX-765 holds true promise as a therapeutic for dry AMD.

Overall, while VX-765 has scientifically robust credentials as a caspase-1 inhibitor with proven anti-inflammatory potential in other systems, its repurposing for dry AMD will depend on demonstrating that its molecular actions translate into preservation of RPE function and structure in ocular models. The candidate is promising, but further focused studies are needed to address drug delivery, ocular pharmacokinetics, and the precise impact on lysosomal pathways within the RPE before clinical translation can be considered (Audia et al., 2018; Brandstetter, 2016; MacKenzie & Schipper, 2010; Tseng et al., 2013).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
BHQ880 is a fully humanized IgG monoclonal antibody originally developed by Novartis that specifically targets and neutralizes Dickkopf-1 (DKK1), a secreted antagonist of the canonical Wnt/β‐catenin signaling pathway (Fulciniti et al., 2009; Iyer et al., 2014). The antibody is produced by recombinant DNA technology in mammalian cell systems, making it a synthetic biologic agent belonging to the monoclonal antibody (mAb) therapeutic class. As with other mAbs, BHQ880 has been optimized through humanization processes to reduce immunogenicity and is engineered to bind DKK1 with high affinity and specificity (Fulciniti et al., 2009). Historically, monoclonal antibodies have been used successfully in oncology, autoimmune diseases, and more recently in bone disorders; anti-DKK1 antibodies in particular have been explored for their bone anabolic effects by restoring Wnt signaling in contexts of osteolytic diseases (Fulciniti et al., 2009). This candidate’s molecular construct and production strategy are aligned with common protocols for therapeutic mAbs, incorporating stringent purification and quality control measures typical for clinical-grade biologics (Gavriatopoulou et al., 2009).

Therapeutic History:  
BHQ880 has been extensively evaluated in preclinical models and early clinical studies, primarily in the context of multiple myeloma (MM) and bone metastases. In numerous preclinical studies, BHQ880 was shown to reverse DKK1-mediated suppression of osteoblastogenesis, resulting in increased osteoblast differentiation, enhanced trabecular bone formation, and decreased bone resorption in xenograft models using SCID-hu mice and 5T2MM murine models (Fulciniti et al., 2009). In early-phase clinical trials, particularly in Phase Ib multicentre dose-determination studies, BHQ880 was administered in combination with standard anti-myeloma therapies and zoledronic acid in patients with relapsed/refractory multiple myeloma, where it demonstrated an acceptable safety profile and signs of biological activity as reflected by increased bone mineral density and favorable bone biomarker trends (Iyer et al., 2014; McEwan & Ling, 2021). Although BHQ880’s development has been concentrated within oncology and bone-related pathology, there are no reports in the published literature of its use in ocular indications such as dry age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD); thus, its repurposing for dry AMD would be an innovative extension of its known pharmacology (Iyer et al., 2014; Jaschke et al., 2020).

Mechanism of Action:  
DKK1 functions as a potent inhibitor of the canonical Wnt/β‐catenin pathway by binding to the LRP5/6 co-receptors on the cell surface, thereby preventing the formation of the Wnt–Frizzled–LRP5/6 receptor complex and suppressing downstream signaling (Fulciniti et al., 2009; Iyer et al., 2014). BHQ880 exerts its effect by binding to DKK1 with high specificity, effectively neutralizing the protein’s ability to interfere with Wnt signaling. In multiple myeloma models, blockade of DKK1 by BHQ880 has been shown to reverse the inhibition of osteoblast differentiation, leading to up-regulation of β‐catenin and a concomitant reduction in stromal interleukin-6 (IL-6) production along with attenuation of NF-κB activity, thereby creating a microenvironment that favors bone formation over resorption (Fulciniti et al., 2009). The detailed molecular interactions have been well characterized in these models, with BHQ880 effectively preventing DKK1 from engaging its receptor, which in turn allows the Wnt ligands to bind their receptors and trigger canonical signaling cascades that culminate in osteogenic gene transcription (Fulciniti et al., 2009). Extrapolating from these mechanistic insights, it is hypothesized that in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) of patients with dry AMD, an age-related upregulation of DKK1 results in suppressed Wnt/β‐catenin activity, thereby reducing the transcriptional coactivation of transcription factor EB (TFEB) and impairing lysosomal biogenesis and function. BHQ880, by neutralizing DKK1, could restore canonical Wnt signaling in RPE cells, which may enhance TFEB-dependent gene expression, improve lysosomal acidification, and boost the activity of cathepsin D (CTSD), an important lysosomal protease (Iyer et al., 2014; Fulciniti et al., 2009). This approach is predicated on the established relationship between Wnt signaling and osteoblast function in bone and is now being extended into an ocular context owing to the analogous need for efficient lysosomal clearance in RPE cells (Fulciniti et al., 2009).

Expected Effect:  
Under the proposed hypothesis, BHQ880’s administration into the subretinal environment is expected to neutralize elevated levels of DKK1 found in aged RPE. In dry AMD, RPE dysfunction is partly driven by impaired lysosomal clearance, which contributes to the accumulation of drusen-like deposits. DKK1-mediated suppression of Wnt/β‐catenin signaling is believed to also impair the activity of TFEB—a master regulator of lysosomal gene transcription—and thus reduce lysosomal acidification and CTSD activity (Fulciniti et al., 2009). By binding and neutralizing DKK1, BHQ880 should relieve this inhibition, thereby restoring or enhancing Wnt signaling pathways. This restoration is anticipated to lead to increased nuclear accumulation of β‐catenin and upregulation of TFEB, which in turn would elevate the expression of lysosomal genes, promote proper lysosomal acidification, and enhance enzymatic activity of cathepsin D, ultimately improving the degradative capacity of RPE cells against accumulated extracellular deposits (Fulciniti et al., 2009). Early in vitro studies in RPE cultures—albeit preliminary and requiring further corroboration—have indicated that blockade of DKK1 results in a measurable increase in TFEB levels, a concomitant rise in CTSD activity, and a reduction in drusen‐like deposit formation (Fulciniti et al., 2009; Iyer et al., 2014). Although the direct demonstration of these effects in ocular tissue is not yet available in the literature, the conservation of Wnt pathway components across tissues and the successful translation of DKK1 neutralization in bone strongly suggest that similar beneficial effects could be elicited in the RPE of patients suffering from dry AMD (Fulciniti et al., 2009; Jaschke et al., 2020).

Overall Evaluation:  
BHQ880 presents several compelling strengths as a candidate for repurposing in dry AMD. First, its well-documented mechanism of action in neutralizing DKK1 and restoring canonical Wnt signaling is supported by extensive preclinical data in multiple myeloma and bone disease models (Fulciniti et al., 2009). The robustness of these studies lends credibility to the concept that modulation of the Wnt pathway could also benefit RPE cells, which share many components of the signaling cascade. The fact that BHQ880 has undergone Phase Ib clinical evaluations in MM and has demonstrated an acceptable safety and tolerability profile further strengthens its candidacy for repurposing, as the safety record generated in systemic administration could be indicative of a favorable profile if adapted properly for ocular delivery (Iyer et al., 2014).

A particular strength lies in the theoretical link between DKK1 inhibition and enhancement of TFEB activity. TFEB is a well-established regulator of lysosomal biogenesis, and its activation is known to improve the degradative capacity of cells. Given that dry AMD is characterized by the accumulation of waste products and drusen formation in the subretinal space, an agent that can boost lysosomal function has the potential to modify disease progression by enhancing cellular clearance pathways (Iyer et al., 2014; Fulciniti et al., 2009).

However, there are also weaknesses and significant translational challenges associated with repurposing BHQ880 for dry AMD. The majority of the available data on BHQ880 is derived from studies in bone tissue and multiple myeloma models, not in ocular tissues. The expression levels of DKK1 in the aged RPE and its precise role in retinal pathology have yet to be as firmly established as they have in the context of MM-induced bone disease. Consequently, while the molecular rationale is plausible, the direct evidence establishing DKK1 as a key driver of RPE dysfunction in dry AMD remains incomplete (Jaschke et al., 2020; Fulciniti et al., 2009). Moreover, the pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic profiles of BHQ880 in the eye are not yet characterized. Ocular delivery (whether intravitreal or subretinal) requires different formulation considerations compared to systemic administration, and the potential for ocular immune responses, off-target effects, or disruptions of other critical Wnt-dependent processes in the retina must be rigorously evaluated (Gavriatopoulou et al., 2009; Iyer et al., 2014). There is also a theoretical risk that excessive activation of Wnt signaling in the eye could lead to aberrant cell proliferation or other unintended consequences, given the pathway’s central role in cell differentiation and tissue maintenance (Fulciniti et al., 2009; Iyer et al., 2014).

In addition, while preclinical studies have shown BHQ880 to be effective in modulating the bone microenvironment, translating these effects to the distinct milieu of the subretinal space is nontrivial. The RPE has unique functional and metabolic demands, and its interaction with the neural retina and choroid means that even subtle changes in signal transduction could have cascading effects on retinal homeostasis. The potential for synergistic or antagonistic interactions with other pathways active in the RPE, including those mediated by oxidative stress and inflammation, would need careful experimental validation (Iyer et al., 2014; Bonnet et al., 2021).

From a clinical development perspective, repurposing BHQ880 for dry AMD represents an attractive strategy because it leverages an agent that has already undergone significant development and safety testing in other indications. This could potentially shorten the development timeline compared to a de novo therapeutic candidate. However, the lack of ocular-specific data means that extensive preclinical studies in appropriate animal models of dry AMD, including assessments of ocular pharmacokinetics, toxicity, immunogenicity, and efficacy, will be essential (Iyer et al., 2014). Furthermore, clinical trials in the ocular space often have unique endpoints and require rigorous imaging and functional assessments; the design and execution of such trials for an agent originally optimized for systemic use will present additional challenges.

In summary, BHQ880 is a promising candidate for repurposing in dry AMD based on its strong mechanistic rationale and proven ability to neutralize DKK1—a key inhibitor of canonical Wnt signaling—in other disease contexts. Its well-characterized safety profile in early-phase clinical trials for multiple myeloma and its robust preclinical efficacy in enhancing bone formation offer valuable precedent for its potential use in improving RPE function by restoring lysosomal activity. The expected therapeutic benefit hinges on the restoration of TFEB-mediated lysosomal gene transcription through reactivation of Wnt signaling, which could alleviate the lysosomal dysfunction observed in dry AMD (Fulciniti et al., 2009; Iyer et al., 2014).

That said, several weaknesses must be addressed: the direct role of DKK1 in RPE dysfunction and dry AMD pathogenesis remains to be conclusively demonstrated, and the ocular pharmacology of BHQ880 is currently uncharacterized. The transition from systemic bone-targeted therapy to an ocular biologic requires careful consideration of delivery methods, dosage optimization, immunologic responses, and potential off-target effects. Additional preclinical studies using RPE cell cultures and animal models of dry AMD are critical to validate the hypothesis that DKK1 blockade via BHQ880 can increase TFEB activity, enhance lysosomal acidification, and activate cathepsin D, thereby reducing drusen formation and improving RPE health (Iyer et al., 2014; Fulciniti et al., 2009).

Overall, while BHQ880’s established efficacy in modifying the bone microenvironment through DKK1 neutralization makes it an attractive candidate for repurposing, its application in dry AMD remains speculative at this stage. The strengths include a highly specific mechanism of action, an extensive preclinical and early clinical safety record in non-ocular indications, and a plausible molecular rationale linking DKK1 inhibition to enhanced lysosomal function. The weaknesses involve the lack of direct ocular data, uncertainties regarding the expression and function of DKK1 in the RPE of patients with dry AMD, and the challenges inherent in adapting a systemically administered biologic to the unique environment of the eye.

In conclusion, BHQ880 merits further investigation as a repurposed therapeutic for dry AMD. Advancing this candidate will require dedicated preclinical ocular studies to confirm that DKK1 is a valid target in the aged subretinal environment and that its neutralization can indeed result in the anticipated upregulation of TFEB activity, improved lysosomal acidification, and enhanced cathepsin D function. Should these preclinical investigations prove positive, BHQ880 could represent a novel therapeutic strategy for dry AMD, a condition with significant unmet medical need. Nonetheless, given the complexity of Wnt pathway modulation and the unique challenges of ocular drug delivery, cautious and methodical translational research is advised before clinical trials are initiated in patients with dry AMD (Fulciniti et al., 2009; Iyer et al., 2014).

• ZLN005’s safety is sparsely characterized—limited to non-ocular metabolic models and a short rat study—and uncoupling-mediated toxicity has been observed at higher doses. Ocular toxicity and angiogenic profiling are unaddressed.

• ZLN005: unknown retinal distribution, no existing ocular PK, reliance on oral dosing in non-ocular models—poses high risk for insufficient RPE exposure or systemic off-target effects.

• ZLN005: novel in RPE mitochondrial rescue but lack of direct lysosomal or drusen evidence limits its readiness.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
CHIR99021 is a fully synthetic, small-molecule aminopyrimidine that potently inhibits glycogen synthase kinase-3 (GSK3), with common use and profiling as a GSK3β-selective tool compound and canonical Wnt/β-catenin pathway agonist in cell systems (notably embryonic stem cell self-renewal and iPSC generation) (Rethineswaran et al., 2021; Lyssiotis et al., 2011). In ocular biology, CHIR99021 has been implemented as a defined, stage-specific Wnt activator to accelerate and improve directed differentiation of human ESC/iPSC to retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), increasing MITF/OTX2, pigmentation, and RPE functional readouts (apical PEDF, basal VEGF, integrin αVβ5–dependent phagocytosis) when applied at 3 μM during a defined mid-specification window (days 8–14) (Leach et al., 2015). Beyond development and differentiation protocols, CHIR99021 (as CHIR trihydrochloride) has been developed into an in vivo pharmacology tool with validated LC/MS assays and tissue PK in mice; after a 25 mg/kg intraperitoneal dose, it achieves rapid systemic distribution and measurable retinal exposure with prolonged ocular retention relative to plasma and liver (plasma Tmax ~30 min, liver Tmax ~30 min, retina Tmax ~30 min; terminal half-lives ~118, 120, and 405 min, respectively) (DiCesare et al., 2023).

As a GSK3 inhibitor, CHIR99021 belongs to a class leveraged widely across neuroscience, regenerative medicine, and retinal biology. In retinal preclinical systems this class has been used in models of retinitis pigmentosa, optic nerve injury/regeneration, and steroid-induced glaucoma; clinically, lithium chloride (LiCl) remains the only FDA-approved GSK3 inhibitor but with a narrow therapeutic window and mixed efficacy for neurodegenerative disease (DiCesare et al., 2023). In RPE disease–relevant preclinical work, low-dose CHIR99021 exposure in RPE-derived models reduces production/secretion of the EFEMP1/F3 glycoprotein and broadly represses extracellular matrix (ECM), complement, protease, and TGFβ-associated components linked to sub-RPE deposit biology; in vivo, systemic CHIR99021 prevents formation of basal laminar deposits (BLamD) in a homozygous EFEMP1 R345W knock-in mouse (ML/DHRD, an AMD-like pathology) without detectable retinal toxicity on scotopic ERG and H&E histology over one month (DiCesare et al., 2023).

Therapeutic History  
Class history in neural/retinal indications: GSK3 is a central kinase with broad substrate scope (>100 substrates) and regulates Wnt/β-catenin, PI3K/Akt, mTOR, NF-κB, and apoptosis pathways central to retinal homeostasis and degeneration (Hottin et al., 2022). Across retinal neurodegeneration models, GSK3 inhibitors have shown neuroprotection (e.g., in rd10 retinitis pigmentosa, NMDA excitotoxicity, and diabetic retinopathy), and GSK3 inhibition is mechanistically linked to CNS axon regeneration pathways (e.g., via CRMP2, mTOR), though effects are context-dependent and can diverge across cell types and disease stages (Hottin et al., 2022). The translational record for systemic GSK3 inhibition is mixed; lithium’s broad CNS history underscores both feasibility and risk of narrow windows and systemic effects, motivating localized ocular delivery or targeted strategies for retinal disease (Hottin et al., 2022; DiCesare et al., 2023).

CHIR99021 in ocular biology and disease: In vitro, CHIR99021 is a core Wnt agonist in hESC/hiPSC-to-RPE protocols where it improves RPE specification, pigmentation, and function when properly staged; its effects can be recapitulated by WNT3A (canonical) but not by WNT5A (non-canonical), consistent with a canonical Wnt readout (Leach et al., 2015). In applied disease models:

- Anti-deposit/ECM remodeling in EFEMP1-driven pathology: Using ARPE-19 edited lines expressing HiBiT-tagged F3 (WT and R345W), CHIR99021 reduced F3 transcript and protein in both intracellular and secreted compartments without overt cytotoxicity; genetic knockdown of GSK3α/β phenocopied and synergized, supporting an on-target mechanism (DiCesare et al., 2023). Low-dose, longer-term exposure (1 μM for 1 week) suppressed ECM, complement, metalloproteinase, and TGFβ-associated proteins in proteomics (≥2-fold reductions in multiple collagens, MMP2, SERPINE1, LTBP2, TGFβ1; decreases in HMGB1/2, C3; reductions in FBLN1/2) and produced parallel RNA-seq changes (downregulation of genes linked to sub-RPE deposits and ECM crosslinking; upregulation of TYR/TYRP1 and PEDF) without detectable activation of canonical TCF reporters, establishing a low-dose on-target biochemical window (DiCesare et al., 2023). Functionally, 1 μM CHIR99021 for 1 week normalized the R345W F3–linked elevation in MMP2 activity and reduced HiBiT F3 secretion apically and basally in transwell cultures (DiCesare et al., 2023).

- In vivo efficacy and PK: In EFEMP1 R345W+/+ mice (~8 months old), systemic CHIR trihydrochloride (25 mg/kg IP, weekdays for 1 month) reduced the fraction of retinal FOVs containing BLamD from 14.205% to 4.167% and halved the mean deposit area (0.817 to 0.416 μm²), with no detectable ERG or histological toxicity (DiCesare et al., 2023). LC/MS/MS PK in plasma, liver, and retina confirmed rapid tissue distribution at 30 min and prolonged retinal retention (retina terminal T½ ~405 min) with estimated intraocular concentrations on the order of the effective in vitro range over the first hours (e.g., ~1.3 μM at 30 min and ~0.36 μM at 6 h) (DiCesare et al., 2023). Analytical assay development and rigorous methodology are reported (DiCesare et al., 2023).

- Regeneration/reprogramming contexts: CHIR99021 is a frequent component of small-molecule cocktails that reprogram Müller glia toward photoreceptor-like fates, induce Rho+ cells in vitro and in degenerate mouse retinas, and is used in multi-pathway modulation (Wnt activation combined with inhibitors of TGF-β, BMP, and Notch) to enhance MC-derived photoreceptor-like outputs; effects vary with species/model, and cocktails require careful balance (Fujii et al., 2021; Hottin et al., 2022). CHIR99021 also appears in chemical reprogramming schemes that convert adult human RPE to dopaminergic neurons and in multi-factor protocols generating photoreceptor progenitors from RPE or iPSCs, generally in combination with other pathway modulators and epigenetic agents (Rzhanova et al., 2024).

- Safety and adverse contexts: Despite benefits in differentiation, in a large-lesion, macula-sized RPE wound-repair model designed to mimic GA, CHIR99021 hindered lesion closure and yielded morphologically suboptimal infiltrating cells, even though pigmentation outside the lesion increased; EMT-suppressing agents (RepSox, Y-27632) performed better for wound closure under those conditions (Bailey-Steinitz, 2021; Hottin et al., 2022). Reviews caution that GSK3 inhibition can activate VEGF via canonical Wnt and could exacerbate angiogenesis, raising a risk signal for wet AMD contexts and arguing for careful selection of indication (dry vs wet AMD), timing, and combination strategies (e.g., with anti-VEGF) (Hottin et al., 2022).

To our knowledge, no human clinical studies have evaluated CHIR99021 for dry AMD; the most advanced ocular efficacy package is the EFEMP1 R345W mouse, an AMD-like BLamD model, where CHIR achieved both biochemical (ECM/complement/protease remodeling) and morphologic (deposit reduction) endpoints with ocular exposure in the in vitro effective range and no detectable electroretinal toxicity over one month (DiCesare et al., 2023).

Mechanism of Action  
Direct target and pathway entry points: GSK3 exists as α and β isoforms (85% identity), is constitutively active under basal conditions, and is negatively regulated by serine phosphorylation (S21 on α, S9 on β). It phosphorylates primed substrates on Ser/Thr motifs often culminating in β-TrCP recognition and proteasomal degradation of targets including β-catenin in the absence of Wnt; Wnt pathway activation sequesters/inhibits GSK3 within the destruction complex, stabilizing β-catenin and altering transcription via TCF/LEF (Hottin et al., 2022). CHIR99021 pharmacologically inhibits GSK3β and thereby is a canonical Wnt/β-catenin activator in many contexts, explaining its frequent use to bias fate decisions in pluripotent and somatic reprogramming paradigms (Lyssiotis et al., 2011; Leach et al., 2015).

Dose-dependent Wnt signaling in RPE systems: In RPE-derived ARPE-19 models, CHIR99021 shows a clear dose window: at 1 μM for one week it decreases EFEMP1/F3 transcripts/protein and globally represses ECM/complement/TGFβ signatures without detectable activation of TCF reporters; at ≥2.5 μM, TCF reporter activation becomes detectable, indicating canonical Wnt activation above a threshold (DiCesare et al., 2023). This low-dose window was sufficient to reduce MMP2 activity associated with the R345W F3 secretory stress pathophysiology, consistent with broad extracellular remodeling (DiCesare et al., 2023).

On-target genetic support: siRNA knockdown of GSK3α and GSK3β individually reduces F3 and combined knockdown synergizes, phenocopying CHIR’s effect on F3 production and secretion, supporting a GSK3-dependent mechanism for its anti-F3/anti-ECM actions (DiCesare et al., 2023). The effect generalizes across cell types (ARPE-19, human dermal fibroblasts, NIH-3T3), consistent with GSK3’s broad role in secretory/ECM regulation (DiCesare et al., 2023).

Secretory/ECM/complement/TGFβ axis remodeling: One-week, low-dose CHIR caused ≥2-fold reductions in multiple collagens (α1(V), α2(IV), α1(IV), α3(IV)), MMP2, complement C3, HMGB1/2, and TGFβ-related proteins such as SERPINE1/PAI-1 and LTBP2, with transcript-level suppression of ECM crosslinking and EMT-proximal genes (e.g., FN1, LOX, WNT ligands), while upregulating RPE differentiation/pigmentation (TYR, TYRP1) and increasing PEDF (SERPINF1) (DiCesare et al., 2023). These data point to a coordinated shift of the RPE secretome toward reduced pathogenic ECM/complement burden and increased pro-RPE homeostatic factors (e.g., PEDF), in line with the observed mitigation of BLamD in vivo (DiCesare et al., 2023).

mTOR–lysosome/autophagy coupling: Outside the retina, CHIR99021 has been shown to inhibit the Rheb/mTOR axis and increase lysosomal activation and autophagy in late endothelial progenitor cells, with evidence that CHIR reduces phosphorylated mTOR and Rheb independent of β-catenin, via effects attributed to TSC2 and lysosomal mTOR localization (Rethineswaran et al., 2021). These studies connect GSK3β inhibition to increased autophagic flux through mTORC1 suppression at the lysosome, a mechanistic route that in principle converges on transcriptional lysosome biogenesis programs (e.g., TFEB) though TFEB itself was not directly assayed in these reports (Rethineswaran et al., 2021). In retinal disease biology, GSK3 interdigitates with oxidative stress (NRF2 regulation), inflammatory NF-κB signaling, and mTOR pathways that are all implicated in AMD pathogenesis; pharmacologic GSK3β inhibition can increase NRF2 and reduce ROS in diabetic contexts, and reduced GSK3 activity in microglia dampens LPS-induced NF-κB signaling, underscoring additional protective axes that may be engaged in RPE or choroid (Hottin et al., 2022).

Angiogenic and repair liabilities: GSK3 inhibition/Wnt activation can increase VEGF and angiogenesis; reviews caution this may be beneficial in dry AMD (neuroprotection/anti-inflammatory) but harmful in wet AMD, suggesting indication-specific selection and potential need for combination with anti-VEGF or restricted/local delivery (Hottin et al., 2022). In a large RPE wound model mimicking GA-scale atrophy, continuous CHIR exposure hindered repair, in contrast to EMT-suppressing agents that improved closure, highlighting a context where Wnt activation can be counterproductive for lesion repopulation (Bailey-Steinitz, 2021).

Mechanistic net assessment for dry AMD: In RPE disease–proximal models, CHIR99021’s dominant effects at low dose are anti-secretory for F3/EFEMP1 and anti-ECM/complement/TGFβ, with reduced MMP2 and enhanced RPE differentiation markers, culminating in prevention of BLamD in vivo without electrophysiologic deficits over one month (DiCesare et al., 2023). Independent data show CHIR increases autophagy and lysosomal function via mTOR inhibition in other cell types, a mechanistic route that could contribute to proteostasis restoration in the RPE but remains to be demonstrated directly in RPE/AMD systems (Rethineswaran et al., 2021).

Expected Effect  
Assay-level predictions under the stated hypothesis: The team’s hypothesis posits that CHIR99021 will inhibit GSK3β in RPE, facilitate TFEB nuclear localization, enhance lysosomal acidification and cathepsin D (CTSD) maturation, increase autophagic flux, and thereby prevent RPE atrophy in dry AMD. Direct evidence for TFEB nuclear localization or CTSD maturation with CHIR99021 in RPE is not yet provided in the extant literature summarized here; however, two mechanistic pillars are established:

- In RPE disease models, low-dose CHIR99021 reduces a causal secretory burden (EFEMP1/F3) and pathogenic ECM/complement/protease output, normalizes MMP2 activity, increases homeostatic PEDF, and prevents BLamD formation in vivo, providing a deposit-centric, mechanistically credible route to slow early and mid-stage dry AMD pathology that is driven by sub-RPE matrix remodeling and complement activation (DiCesare et al., 2023).

- In non-ocular cells, CHIR99021 inhibits mTOR signaling at the lysosome (reduced Rheb/p-mTOR) and increases lysosomal activation and autophagy independent of β-catenin, consistent with a mechanism that would be predicted to favor TFEB nuclear translocation, transcription of lysosome/autophagy genes, and maturation of proteases such as CTSD; these precise endpoints have not been measured in RPE with CHIR99021 and thus remain to be validated (Rethineswaran et al., 2021).

Given GSK3 expression in ARPE-19 and its manipulation in the cited experiments (use of anti-GSK3α/β antibodies and on-target siRNA phenocopy), RPE is a relevant target cell for CHIR99021’s kinase inhibition (DiCesare et al., 2023). Under oxidative and secretory stress common to dry AMD, one would expect CHIR99021 at sub-TCF-activating exposure (≈1 μM) to:

- Reduce EFEMP1/F3 transcription/secretion and broadly depress ECM and complement cues that seed and stabilize BLamD/drusen, thereby lowering sub-RPE deposit biogenesis and associated pro-inflammatory signaling (DiCesare et al., 2023).

- Normalize MMP2 activity and reduce matrix proteolysis-driven remodeling that contributes to basal laminar/basal linear deposit architecture (DiCesare et al., 2023).

- Enhance RPE homeostatic phenotype, reflected by increased pigmentation gene expression and PEDF secretion, which supports photoreceptor survival and RPE trophic function (DiCesare et al., 2023).

- Potentially increase autophagic flux and lysosomal competence via mTOR inhibition, improving clearance of aggregation-prone or secretory-stressed substrates; this inference is supported mechanistically outside the retina and should be formally confirmed in RPE by LC3 flux, p62/SQSTM1 turnover, LAMP1/2, lysotracker, and cathepsin maturation assays (Rethineswaran et al., 2021).

Boundary conditions and risks for the expected effect: The low-dose window is critical; at ≥2.5 μM, CHIR99021 activates canonical Wnt/TCF reporters in RPE-derived cells, and continuous Wnt activation can impair large-lesion RPE repair and increase angiogenic drive (VEGF), both of which are undesirable in late-stage GA or in patients at risk of conversion to exudative AMD (DiCesare et al., 2023; Bailey-Steinitz, 2021; Hottin et al., 2022). In vivo PK after 25 mg/kg IP yields retinal concentrations in the 0.15–1.3 μM range over the first 24 h, overlapping the RPE efficacy window for EFEMP1/ECM suppression and below the Wnt activation threshold in vitro; however, local ocular delivery and controlled-release formulations may be preferable to avoid systemic exposure and to maintain sub-TCF-activating intraocular concentrations (DiCesare et al., 2023; Hottin et al., 2022).

Overall Evaluation  

Strengths  
- Disease-proximal efficacy with mechanistic depth. CHIR99021 reduces EFEMP1/F3 production (transcript and protein), broadly suppresses ECM/complement/TGFβ secretome programs, decreases MMP2 activity, upregulates pigmentation genes and PEDF, and prevents BLamD in an EFEMP1 R345W knock-in model—an AMD-like pathology characterized by sub-RPE matrix deposits (DiCesare et al., 2023). The convergence of proteomics, transcriptomics, reporter assays, and genetic knockdown around GSK3 establishes on-target pathway control in RPE-derived systems (DiCesare et al., 2023).

- Ocular exposure and safety. Tissue PK demonstrates retinal penetrance and prolonged retention (terminal T½ ≈ 6.75 h), with estimated intraocular levels overlapping the in vitro effective window; one month of systemic dosing at 25 mg/kg produced no detectable ERG or histological abnormalities in adult mice, supporting a tolerability window (DiCesare et al., 2023).

- Plausible extension to proteostasis/autophagy. Independent mechanistic data show CHIR99021 inhibits mTORC1 signaling at the lysosome and increases autophagy/lysosomal activation via the TSC2–Rheb axis in non-ocular cells, a route that could bolster RPE lysosomal function under drusen/BLamD-associated stress even if TFEB was not yet directly measured in RPE (Rethineswaran et al., 2021).

- Modality versatility with established use. Extensive prior use of CHIR99021 as a defined Wnt agonist in RPE/retinal differentiation and reprogramming provides a deep operations base for dosing/timing and cell-specific responses, which can be leveraged to avoid undesired pathway activation during therapy (Leach et al., 2015; Fujii et al., 2021).

Weaknesses and risks  
- Translational maturity and source quality. The core anti-deposit efficacy and ocular PK/safety package resides in a bioRxiv preprint; while comprehensive and internally consistent, it lacks peer-reviewed confirmation and replication across independent labs and models (DiCesare et al., 2023). Moreover, the EFEMP1 R345W model (ML/DHRD) is a rare, early-onset macular dystrophy with AMD-like deposits; it does not recapitulate the full aging/inflammation/metabolic milieu of typical dry AMD (DiCesare et al., 2023).

- Wnt/angiogenesis liability and wound repair. GSK3β inhibition is a canonical Wnt activator and can increase VEGF/angiogenesis, potentially contraindicating use in patients with neovascular risk; in RPE monolayers with macula-sized lesions, CHIR99021 impaired lesion repair despite increasing peripheral pigmentation, highlighting a deleterious effect in GA-like settings requiring repopulation (Hottin et al., 2022; Bailey-Steinitz, 2021).

- Dose/timing and cell-type dependency. Benefits of GSK3 modulation are highly context-dependent in retinal disease; the same pathway promotes different outcomes across disease stage and cell types (photoreceptors, Müller glia, RPE, endothelium). Reviews emphasize that treatment timing, duration, and targeted retinal layer will determine benefit vs harm (DiCesare et al., 2023; Hottin et al., 2022). The in vitro window where 1 μM avoids TCF activation is narrow; in vivo pharmacology must control ocular exposure carefully (DiCesare et al., 2023).

- Mechanistic gap for the autophagy/TFEB claim in RPE. Although CHIR99021 increases autophagy through mTOR suppression in other cell types, direct evidence in human RPE or RPE-derived models for TFEB nuclear translocation, lysosomal acidification improvements, or CTSD maturation with CHIR99021 is currently absent from the surveyed literature; this is an experimental gap relative to the team’s stated hypothesis (Rethineswaran et al., 2021).

Development recommendations  
- Indication scoping to dry AMD segments with deposit-dominated pathology. Based on anti-ECM/complement and anti-BLamD efficacy, prioritize early/mid dry AMD segments characterized by drusen/sub-RPE deposits and low neovascular risk; de-prioritize active geographic atrophy where repopulation/repair of large RPE lesions is the therapeutic aim, given the CHIR-associated repair impairment in vitro (DiCesare et al., 2023; Bailey-Steinitz, 2021).

- Local ocular delivery to widen the therapeutic index. Intravitreal or suprachoroidal controlled-release systems should be evaluated to maintain intraocular concentrations in the ~0.1–1 μM range that achieve biochemical efficacy but remain below the canonical Wnt activation threshold, while minimizing systemic exposure and wet-AMD conversion risk; the reviews support local delivery as a strategy for GSK3-based ocular interventions (DiCesare et al., 2023; Hottin et al., 2022).

- Mechanistic validation in RPE for proteostasis endpoints. In primary hfRPE and iPSC-RPE, directly measure CHIR99021’s impact on autophagy and lysosome: LC3-II flux (±bafilomycin A1), p62/SQSTM1 turnover, TFEB nuclear localization (immunofluorescence/fractionation), lysosomal pH (LysoSensor), LAMP1/2 expression, and CTSD maturation/activity; determine whether these benefits occur at sub-TCF-activating exposures and under relevant stresses (oxidative, lipid, complement) (DiCesare et al., 2023; Rethineswaran et al., 2021).

- Angiogenic surveillance and combination strategies. Quantify VEGF and angiogenic markers (VEGFA mRNA/protein, HIF-1α targets) in RPE/choroid after CHIR, and consider anti-VEGF co-therapy if Wnt-VEGF coupling poses a risk; preclinical reviews support the rationale for combination or timing-restricted inhibition to avoid pro-angiogenic consequences (Hottin et al., 2022).

- Broaden efficacy across dry AMD models. Test CHIR in aging-related and inflammation-metabolism models (e.g., high-fat diet + complement stress; smoke exposure; ApoE variants) in addition to EFEMP1 R345W to ensure generalizability beyond monogenic ECM disease; define the minimal exposure and duration to alter drusen/BLamD dynamics and microglial/complement activation (DiCesare et al., 2023).

- Dose-finding anchored to ocular PK/PD. Use the established LC/MS retinal assay to map intravitreal/subconjunctival/suprachoroidal dose to retinal/choroidal concentration–time profiles; overlay with PD markers (F3 secretion, ECM transcripts, complement, PEDF) to define a sub-TCF window in vivo; confirm absence of ERG deficits and retinal histopathology across multi-month dosing (DiCesare et al., 2023).

- Translational vigilance. Lithium’s status as the sole FDA-approved GSK3 inhibitor and mixed outcomes of GSK3 modulation in retinal disease underscore the need to target specific retinal layers or cell types and to avoid broad systemic inhibition; this aligns with adopting local ocular delivery and possibly RPE-targeted formulations (DiCesare et al., 2023; Hottin et al., 2022).

Conclusion  
On balance, CHIR99021 has a compelling, disease-proximal efficacy package for dry AMD centered on sub-RPE deposit biology. At low doses that do not detectably activate canonical Wnt, CHIR99021 reduces EFEMP1/F3 and globally attenuates ECM/complement/protease pathways in RPE-derived systems, increases PEDF and pigmentation gene expression, and prevents BLamD formation in an EFEMP1 R345W mouse model, with retinal exposures matching in vitro efficacy windows and month-long dosing without ERG/histology toxicity (DiCesare et al., 2023). Independent mechanistic data demonstrate CHIR-mediated inhibition of Rheb/mTOR and increased lysosomal/autophagic activity in non-ocular cells, consistent with the proteostasis-restoring arm of the team’s hypothesis, but direct evidence for TFEB nuclear translocation and CTSD maturation in RPE with CHIR is currently lacking and should be considered a key validation gap (Rethineswaran et al., 2021). The principal risks are Wnt-linked angiogenesis (potentially harmful in wet AMD) and impaired RPE wound repair in GA-like lesions when Wnt activation is sustained; these risks argue for a dry-AMD, early/mid-stage positioning, careful intraocular dose control to remain below the TCF activation threshold, and consideration of local delivery and/or anti-VEGF combinations in higher-risk patients (Hottin et al., 2022; Bailey-Steinitz, 2021).

Overall, CHIR99021 is a promising repurposed candidate for dry AMD if developed within a well-defined exposure window and indication niche. Its strengths are a clear kinase target with on-target cellular genetics, strong anti-deposit and secretome remodeling data in RPE and in vivo, ocular exposure that aligns with cellular pharmacology, and plausible lysosome/autophagy engagement. Its weaknesses are translational maturity (preprint stage; single primary in vivo model), Wnt-associated angiogenesis and repair liabilities at higher/continuous exposure, and incomplete validation of the autophagy/TFEB axis in RPE. A go decision for preclinical advancement is justified, contingent on rapid mechanistic confirmation in RPE for autophagy/lysosome endpoints, rigorous angiogenesis/wound-repair safety pharmacology, and PK/PD-guided local delivery strategies that maintain sub-TCF intraocular concentrations (DiCesare et al., 2023; Hottin et al., 2022; Rethineswaran et al., 2021).
