Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
GDC-0941 (pictilisib) is a synthetic, orally bioavailable, ATP-competitive, pan–class I phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K) inhibitor discovered through structure-guided medicinal chemistry at Genentech as an optimization beyond early tool compounds and the dual PI3K/mTOR inhibitor PI-103, with substantially improved selectivity for class I PI3Ks and favorable pharmacokinetics (PK) suitable for systemic dosing in humans (Garces, n.d.; Zhao et al., 2017; Li et al., 2024). At the biochemical level, pictilisib exhibits low-nanomolar potency against p110α and p110δ, with activity across class I isoforms (representative IC₅₀s: α ≈ 3 nM, β ≈ 33 nM, δ ≈ 3 nM, γ ≈ 75 nM) and weak activity on mTOR (~0.58 μM), consistent with selective targeting of class I PI3Ks over mTOR kinase (Huang et al., 2023; Garces, n.d.; Josephs & Sarker, 2016; Zhao et al., 2017). Co-crystal structural analysis shows an ATP-mimetic thieno[3,2-d]pyrimidine core in which the morpholine oxygen donates a hinge hydrogen bond (Val882), the indazole engages an affinity pocket (Asp841/Tyr867), and a methanesulfonyl-piperazine tail projects toward solvent; these interactions underpin its potency and selectivity within the class I PI3K ATP site (PDB 3DBS) (Garces, n.d.). Pictilisib belongs to the pan-class I PI3K inhibitor class, a therapeutic category widely advanced in oncology to suppress the PI3K→AKT→mTOR signaling axis that governs cell growth, survival, and metabolism; multiple agents in this class have reached clinical testing or approval, providing a clear translational precedent for pathway engagement and safety management in humans (Schmitz et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2023; Li et al., 2024).

Therapeutic History  
The development history of pictilisib is anchored in oncology, where first-in-human Phase I trials established a recommended Phase II dose of 330 mg once daily, dose-proportional PK (Tₘₐₓ ≈ 2 h, t₁/₂ ≈ 13–24 h), and robust pharmacodynamic (PD) target engagement—up to ~90% inhibition of phosphorylated AKT (Ser473) in platelet-rich plasma within 1–3 h of dosing and suppression of p-AKT and p-S6 in tumor biopsies at sufficient exposure (AUC > 20 μM·h) (Sarker et al., 2015; Mishra et al., 2021). Across Phase I combination studies, pictilisib showed a manageable safety profile and some antitumor activity, with common adverse events including nausea, diarrhea, rash, fatigue, hyperglycemia, and cytopenias; dose-limiting toxicity in some settings was grade 3 maculopapular rash (Mishra et al., 2021; Josephs & Sarker, 2016; Sarker et al., 2015). Although pathway suppression was clear, randomized combination trials in breast and lung cancer variably met efficacy endpoints and broader development was limited by tolerability in multi-drug regimens and modest efficacy as monotherapy—experience that nonetheless provides clinically validated PK/PD tools and class-effect safety benchmarks (Mishra et al., 2021; Gao et al., 2017).

No preclinical or clinical use of pictilisib or other class I PI3K inhibitors has been reported for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or RPE-centered retinal disease models in the provided literature, and a recent review emphasizes that no ongoing clinical trials directly target autophagy in AMD, underscoring an evidence gap for PI3K inhibitors in this indication (Blasiak et al., 2025). By contrast, direct downstream pathway modulation in RPE—mTORC1 inhibition with rapamycin—has shown that activating the lysosome–TFEB axis reduces POS-derived autofluorescent granules in vitro in a hydrolase-dependent manner, but clinical testing in advanced AMD returned limited efficacy and adverse effects, illustrating both the mechanistic plausibility of modulating this pathway and translational challenges (Falcão et al., 2024). Collectively, the therapeutic history supports that class I PI3K inhibitors achieve systemic PI3K pathway inhibition in humans with tractable but nontrivial toxicities; however, there is no published RPE- or AMD-focused body of work with pictilisib to date in the provided context (Sarker et al., 2015; Mishra et al., 2021; Blasiak et al., 2025).

Mechanism of Action  
Class I PI3Ks phosphorylate PIP₂ to PIP₃, recruiting PH-domain effectors including PDK1 and AKT to the plasma membrane, where AKT is activated by phosphorylation at Thr308 (PDK1) and Ser473 (mTORC2) (Huang et al., 2023). Activated AKT phosphorylates multiple substrates that converge on mTORC1 activation (via TSC2/PRAS40), leading to phosphorylation of S6K1 and 4E-BP1 to promote protein synthesis and suppress autophagy, thereby integrating growth-factor status with anabolic programs (Huang et al., 2023; Castel et al., 2021). In retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), AKT/mTOR signaling is an established regulator of cell proliferation and autophagy; mTORC1 activation inhibits autophagy by blocking ULK1 signaling and autolysosomal biogenesis, whereas rapamycin-mediated mTORC1 inhibition activates autophagy and preserves photoreceptor function in preclinical models (Chang et al., 2015). PI3K inhibition upstream of AKT is thus expected to reduce PIP₃ generation, limit AKT membrane recruitment/activation, and secondarily depress mTORC1 signaling in RPE (Castel et al., 2021; Chang et al., 2015).

PI3K→AKT signaling intersects directly with TFEB/TFE3—the master transcription factors of lysosomal biogenesis and the CLEAR regulon—through both mTORC1-dependent and mTORC1-independent routes (Falcão et al., 2024; Ghosh et al., 2024). Nutrient-driven mTORC1 activity at the lysosome phosphorylates TFEB/TFE3 to retain them in the cytosol; conversely, mTORC1 inhibition permits TFEB nuclear translocation and induction of lysosomal/autophagy genes (Falcão et al., 2024). Importantly, AKT2 directly phosphorylates TFEB (at Ser467) and TFE3 (Ser321), promoting 14-3-3 binding and cytoplasmic sequestration independent of mTORC1, thereby repressing CLEAR gene expression and lysosomal programs in RPE (Ghosh et al., 2023; Ghosh et al., 2024). In AMD-relevant contexts—human dysmorphic macular RPE, CFH risk-allele iPSC-RPE, and Akt2 RPE-specific knock-in mice—AKT2 upregulation increases TFEB/TFE3 phosphorylation, reduces lysosomal hydrolases (cathepsin D/L) and CLEAR target expression, impairs autophagic flux, and shifts autophagy toward secretory pathways characterized by increased FKBP51/SNAP23, autophagosome fusion with the plasma membrane, and extracellular release of IL-1β/HMGB1 (Ghosh et al., 2023; Ghosh et al., 2024). TFEB rescue via a phospho-deficient TFEB-S467A mutant or pharmacologic TFEB activation with trehalose restores cathepsin D/L and autophagy genes, normalizes autophagosome–lysosome fusion, and improves RPE structure in AMD-like mouse models, establishing TFEB/TFE3 as actionable nodes downstream of AKT2 in RPE (Ghosh et al., 2023; Ghosh et al., 2024).

SIRT5 and mitochondrial metabolism integrate with AKT2–TFEB signaling in RPE. SIRT5 interacts with AKT2 and reduces lysine malonylation on AKT2, modulating AKT2 activity; AKT2, via inhibition of PGC-1α, downregulates SIRT5, creating a bidirectional circuit that affects TFEB-dependent lysosomal function and mitochondrial respiration (Ghosh et al., 2023). AKT2 upregulation impairs mitochondrial respiration (maximal and ATP-linked), which is rescued by SIRT5, linking mitochondrial–lysosomal crosstalk to RPE proteostasis (Ghosh et al., 2023). Functionally, failure of the AKT2/SIRT5/TFEB axis elevates secretory autophagy and likely contributes to drusen pathogenesis by exporting inflammatory cargo (Ghosh et al., 2023).

These mechanistic data converge with mTORC1→TFEB observations in POS-fed RPE models. Synchronous POS phagocytosis transiently activates mTORC1 early, with TFEB protein increasing but remaining phosphorylated during late maturation, indicating a bottleneck at TFEB activation (Falcão et al., 2024). Pharmacologic mTORC1 inhibition with rapamycin after AFGs have formed lowers POS-derived autofluorescence by ~30% in hfRPE/ARPE-19, reduces pS6, decreases the pTFEB/TFEB ratio, increases LAMP1, and requires active lysosomal hydrolases: cathepsin D knockout or protease/lipase inhibition abolishes the rapamycin effect (Falcão et al., 2024). Human AMD RPE exhibits hyperphosphorylated TFEB with decreased nuclear localization and lower cathepsin D/L protein levels and activities, consistent with impaired lysosome proteolysis; constitutively active TFEB boosts CLEAR genes, including hydrolases and V-ATPase subunits (e.g., ATP6V0A1), supporting enhanced acidification capacity (Falcão et al., 2025).

Pictilisib’s proximal pharmacology—ATP-competitive inhibition of class I PI3Ks—has been shown to produce substantial pathway suppression in human tissues (reduced pAKT, reduced pS6) and in tumor models; such upstream inhibition is expected to depress both AKT→mTORC1 signaling and AKT2-mediated TFEB phosphorylation, potentially enabling TFEB/TFE3 nuclear translocation and restoration of CLEAR programs in RPE (Sarker et al., 2015; Mishra et al., 2021; Castel et al., 2021; Ghosh et al., 2024). Two caveats are central. First, class III PI3K/VPS34 activity is required for autophagosome nucleation; thus class I–selective inhibition (as with pictilisib) is mechanistically appropriate, whereas class III inhibition would be detrimental to autophagy flux (Wang et al., 2023). Second, while AKT inhibitors (e.g., MK-2206) and TFEB activators (trehalose) have directly increased autophagy and TFEB nuclear translocation in RPE, no direct evidence of class I PI3K inhibitors reproducing these effects in RPE has been reported in the provided literature (Karim et al., 2020; Blasiak et al., 2025).

Expected Effect  
In RPE cell assays designed to model dry AMD–relevant lysosomal stress (e.g., POS feeding, A2E/oxidant exposure, or CFH risk-allele iPSC-RPE), pictilisib is expected to reduce PI3K-dependent PIP₃ generation, lowering membrane recruitment and phosphorylation of AKT, thereby secondarily suppressing mTORC1 and directly relieving AKT2-mediated phosphorylation of TFEB/TFE3 (Huang et al., 2023; Castel et al., 2021; Ghosh et al., 2024). Mechanistically, this should dephosphorylate TFEB/TFE3, promote nuclear translocation, and activate the CLEAR transcriptional program to increase components of lysosomal biogenesis and function (e.g., LAMP1/2, cathepsin D/L, and V-ATPase subunits), thereby enhancing degradative capacity and autophagic flux (Falcão et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2025; Falcão et al., 2024).

Operationally testable expected effects include:  
• Signaling: decreased pAKT (Ser473) and pS6 (Ser235/236) within hours of dosing in RPE, mirroring PD seen in tumors and platelet-rich plasma in human trials, establishing target engagement (Sarker et al., 2015; Mishra et al., 2021).  
• TFEB/TFE3 activation: reduction in pTFEB/TFEB ratio, increased nuclear TFEB/TFE3, and induction of CLEAR genes; in RPE systems, TFEB activation correlates with increased LAMP1 and rescue of lysosomal hydrolases and autophagy mediators (e.g., ATG9B), as seen upon TFEB S467A expression or trehalose treatment (Falcão et al., 2024; Ghosh et al., 2023; Ghosh et al., 2024).  
• Lysosomal function: increased abundance and maturation of cathepsin D (pro→intermediate→mature chain) and cathepsin L, and improved degradative flux, consistent with observations that AMD RPE shows diminished cathepsin levels/activities and that hydrolase function is required for rapamycin-mediated clearance of POS-derived AFGs (Falcão et al., 2025; Falcão et al., 2024).  
• Autophagic flux: increased LC3-II turnover (± bafilomycin A₁), reduced p62/SQSTM1 accumulation, restored autophagosome–lysosome fusion (e.g., GFP-LC3 and LysoTracker/LAMP1 colocalization), and decreased accumulation of double-membrane autophagosomes on EM, reversing the AKT2-driven flux block (Ghosh et al., 2023; Ghosh et al., 2024).  
• POS-derived autofluorescence: reduction in POS-dependent autofluorescent granules in preventive and resolving paradigms, analogous to mTORC1 inhibition or TFEB activation effects; efficacy will depend on intact lysosomal hydrolase activity (Falcão et al., 2024).  
• Secretory autophagy: decreased FKBP51/SNAP23 elevation, reduced plasma-membrane fusion of autophagosomes, and lower extracellular release of IL-1β and HMGB1 from RPE, mirroring effects seen with SIRT5 co-expression or AKT2 inhibition (Ghosh et al., 2023; Ghosh et al., 2024).  
• Acidification: although lysosomal pH has not been directly measured after class I PI3K inhibition in RPE, TFEB activation increases expression of V-ATPase subunits, and improved hydrolase activities imply normalization of the acidic lumen; direct pH assays (LysoSensor/LysoTracker) should be incorporated because efficacy of rapamycin/TFEB approaches depends on intact lysosomal acid hydrolases (Falcão et al., 2025; Falcão et al., 2024).

These expectations rest on the well-documented presence and dysregulation of the AKT2→TFEB/TFE3→CLEAR axis in RPE and the dependence of POS clearance on mTOR/TFEB-governed lysosomal function (Ghosh et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2024). AKT2 is upregulated in macular RPE from AMD donors and in AMD-like mouse models, and RPE-specific Akt2 overexpression is sufficient to induce AMD-like pathology, supporting target relevance in the cell type and disease context of interest (Ghosh et al., 2023; Ghosh et al., 2024). Because PI3K is upstream of AKT, class I PI3K inhibition should, in principle, reduce AKT2 activity and thereby favor TFEB activation; however, no direct studies in the provided literature demonstrate pictilisib (or any class I PI3K inhibitor) inducing TFEB nuclear translocation or improving cathepsin D maturation/activity in RPE, so these are testable, evidence-generating predictions rather than established facts (Blasiak et al., 2025; Chang et al., 2015; Karim et al., 2020).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Mechanistic alignment with disease biology: Dry AMD features impaired RPE autophagy–lysosome function, diminished cathepsin D/L levels/activities, and TFEB hyperphosphorylation with reduced nuclear TFEB, all of which converge on lysosomal insufficiency and accumulation of lipofuscin-like material and extracellular drusen; upstream PI3K inhibition is a coherent strategy to relieve AKT2- and mTORC1-mediated repression of TFEB/TFE3 and restore CLEAR-driven lysosomal biogenesis and flux (Falcão et al., 2025; Falcão et al., 2024; Ghosh et al., 2024).  
• Drug tractability and translational readiness: Pictilisib achieves robust systemic target engagement in humans (pAKT/pS6 suppression), has well-characterized PK/PD and class-effect safety, and is chemically and biophysically optimized, enabling accelerated preclinical testing and dosage/formulation exploration for ocular delivery or low systemic exposure strategies (Sarker et al., 2015; Mishra et al., 2021; Garces, n.d.).  
• Selectivity profile appropriate for autophagy enhancement: Because autophagosome nucleation requires class III PI3K/VPS34, class I selectivity of pictilisib avoids this liability while suppressing AKT→mTOR signaling and AKT2-dependent TFEB phosphorylation, in contrast to nonselective PI3K inhibition which would be deleterious (Wang et al., 2023; Castel et al., 2021).

Risks and Gaps  
• No direct RPE/AMD data with class I PI3K inhibitors: In contrast to clear benefits from rapamycin and TFEB activation, the literature presented contains no direct evidence that class I PI3K inhibition, or pictilisib specifically, improves TFEB activation/nuclear entry, lysosomal biogenesis, cathepsin D maturation/activity, lysosomal acidification, autophagy flux, or POS handling in RPE; thus, the central hypothesis remains unvalidated experimentally in the disease-relevant cell type (Blasiak et al., 2025; Chang et al., 2015; Falcão et al., 2024). By comparison, AKT inhibition (MK-2206) and trehalose have been shown to increase autophagy and nuclear TFEB in RPE, and AKT2 inhibitors reduced lipid/apoE in CFH(H/H) RPE, but these are not PI3K inhibitors and may differ in cellular selectivity and compensatory signaling (Karim et al., 2020; Ghosh et al., 2024).  
• Complexity of autophagy modulation and context dependence: Autophagy is a double-edged sword with biphasic responses to stress; overactivation or mistimed activation could exacerbate RPE stress or impair other retinal cell types, and some autophagy inhibitors display retinal toxicity (e.g., chloroquine class), emphasizing the need for precise control and safety profiling (Blasiak et al., 2025; Kaarniranta et al., 2013). Rapamycin has shown only limited clinical efficacy in advanced AMD despite mechanistic benefits in vitro, illustrating translational friction between pathway modulation and clinical outcomes (Falcão et al., 2024).  
• Safety, delivery, and exposure management: Systemic class I PI3K inhibition induces hyperglycemia, rash, and gastrointestinal toxicities; while these were generally manageable, ocular delivery strategies (intravitreal or periocular) and ocular pharmacokinetics for pictilisib are uncharacterized in the provided literature, and tissue-specific PD (e.g., drug levels at the RPE/Bruch’s complex) is likely to determine efficacy and safety (Josephs & Sarker, 2016; Sarker et al., 2015; Mishra et al., 2021). Tissue PD variability seen in tumors versus blood suggests careful intratissue PD assays are necessary (Sarker et al., 2015).  
• Isoform and cell-type specificity: AKT2 is the isoform implicated in RPE TFEB repression and secretory autophagy; upstream PI3K isoform contributions in RPE are not defined here, and pan-class I inhibition could affect neighboring retinal cells, choroidal endothelium, and immune cells, potentially altering retinal immunity and angiogenesis in unintended ways (Ghosh et al., 2024; Castel et al., 2021). Given the evidence favoring AKT2-selective inhibition or direct TFEB activation in RPE models, PI3K-level intervention may be broader than necessary and carry off-target tissue consequences (Ghosh et al., 2024; Karim et al., 2020).  
• Acidification endpoint uncertainty: The hypothesis specifically posits enhanced lysosomal acidification, yet none of the provided sources report direct lysosomal pH measurements after class I PI3K inhibition in RPE; while CLEAR induction can increase V-ATPase subunits and rapamycin-mediated clearance requires active hydrolases, direct acidification effects remain to be demonstrated (Falcão et al., 2025; Falcão et al., 2024; Blasiak et al., 2025).

Go/No-Go Evidence Plan  
Given the strong mechanistic rationale but absence of direct RPE data, a staged validation program is warranted:  
– In vitro RPE target engagement and TFEB activation: Demonstrate pictilisib decreases pAKT (Ser473) and pS6 in primary human fetal RPE, ARPE-19, and iPSC-RPE, and increases nuclear TFEB/TFE3 with induction of CLEAR genes (CTSD, CTSL, LAMP2, ATP6V0A1) assessed by Western, RT-qPCR, and ChIP-qPCR (Falcão et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2025; Ghosh et al., 2024).  
– Lysosome function readouts: Quantify cathepsin D maturation and enzymatic activity, LAMP1/2 abundance, and lysosomal pH using ratiometric probes; include hydrolase inhibition controls to assess dependence analogous to the rapamycin data (Falcão et al., 2024).  
– Autophagic flux and modality: Assess LC3-II turnover (± bafilomycin A₁), p62 dynamics, autolysosome number (LC3–LAMP1 colocalization), and EM confirmation; evaluate secretory-autophagy markers (FKBP51, SNAP23) and extracellular cargo (HMGB1, IL-1β) to test reversal of the AKT2-driven phenotype (Ghosh et al., 2023; Ghosh et al., 2024).  
– Functional disease readouts: Test POS-dependent autofluorescence reduction in preventive and resolving paradigms and POS degradation assays; evaluate lipid/apoE accumulation in CFH(H/H) iPSC-RPE and Cryba1 cKO explants to compare with reported trehalose and AKT2 inhibitor effects (Falcão et al., 2024; Ghosh et al., 2023; Ghosh et al., 2024).  
– In vivo and delivery: Establish ocular PK and tolerability for local delivery (intravitreal/periocular) in rodents, then test efficacy in RPE-driven AMD-like models (Akt2 KI, Cryba1 cKO, NaIO₃) with TFEB activation, lysosomal and functional endpoints (ERG/SD-OCT) (Ghosh et al., 2024; Ghosh et al., 2023; Falcão et al., 2025).  
– Benchmarking: Include rapamycin (mTORC1 inhibition), MK-2206 (AKT inhibition), and trehalose (mTOR-independent TFEB activation) comparators to position PI3K inhibition within the therapeutic landscape (Falcão et al., 2024; Karim et al., 2020; Ghosh et al., 2023).

Conclusion  
Pictilisib offers a mechanistically coherent, drug-like approach to modulate an RPE pathway of clear pathogenic relevance—AKT2/mTOR-mediated repression of TFEB/TFE3 and the CLEAR network—backed by robust human PK/PD experience and a selectivity profile compatible with enhancing autophagy without impeding VPS34-dependent nucleation (Ghosh et al., 2024; Sarker et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2023). However, the absence of direct evidence that class I PI3K inhibition rectifies TFEB activity, lysosomal hydrolase function (notably cathepsin D), lysosomal acidification, autophagic flux, or POS clearance in RPE is a critical gap that precludes immediate advancement; by contrast, downstream interventions (rapamycin, TFEB activation, AKT2 inhibition) already demonstrate these benefits in RPE models (Falcão et al., 2024; Ghosh et al., 2024). On balance, pictilisib is plausible and testable but not yet justified for translational progression without focused RPE and ocular studies; an AKT2-selective inhibitor or TFEB-directed strategies may offer a higher probability of effect with narrower network perturbation, and should be run in parallel as mechanistic benchmarks (Ghosh et al., 2024; Karim et al., 2020). If the proposed RPE experiments confirm that pictilisib restores TFEB-driven lysosomal programs, improves cathepsin D maturation/activity, normalizes autophagy flux, and reduces POS-derived autofluorescence with acceptable ocular tolerability, the candidate would merit advancement to in vivo ocular efficacy testing; absent such confirmation, resources should pivot to agents with demonstrated RPE TFEB engagement (Ghosh et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2024).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Vorinostat (suberoylanilide hydroxamic acid, SAHA; Selleckchem S1047) is a synthetic small molecule originally discovered through a screening process aimed at identifying inhibitors of histone deacetylases (HDACs) and belongs to the hydroxamic acid class of compounds. It was developed as an anticancer agent and later received U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approval for the treatment of cutaneous T cell lymphoma; its chemical synthesis involves derivatization of an anilide moiety with a hydroxamic acid function, enabling a high degree of specificity for the zinc-dependent catalytic pockets of HDAC enzymes. As a pan-HDAC inhibitor, Vorinostat is designed to modulate epigenetic regulation by binding to the active site of multiple HDAC isoforms, thereby increasing histone acetylation and altering the transcriptional profile of target genes. This class of compounds has been broadly used in oncology, where the modulation of chromatin structure reactivates suppressed tumor suppressor genes and triggers cell cycle arrest and apoptosis. In the context of drug repurposing, the rationale for exploring Vorinostat in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is centered on its potential to epigenetically reprogram retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells by enhancing the acetylation status and activation of key transcription factors such as TFEB and FOXO, which are critical regulators of lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy—a mechanism distinctly different from kinase inhibition strategies (Buniello et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2025).

Therapeutic History:  
Vorinostat’s clinical journey has predominantly revolved around its anticancer applications. Early-phase clinical trials in various solid tumors, including breast, colorectal, and non-small cell lung cancer, as well as studies in metastatic thyroid cancer, relapsed or refractory leukemia, and multiple myeloma, have provided a robust safety profile and dosing regimen for this therapeutic candidate (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2004, 2005, 2006; Ghosh et al., 2024). Although its use in oncology has been extensive—with studies demonstrating its ability to block cell growth by inhibiting key enzymes required for proliferation—the direct evidence for its application in ocular diseases, especially in dry AMD, remains limited. Nonetheless, the broader class of HDAC inhibitors has shown promising results in preclinical ocular models. For instance, several studies have demonstrated that HDAC inhibitors can attenuate choroidal neovascularization, protect retinal tissues from ischemic injury, and promote cellular differentiation in the retinal pigment epithelium (Luo et al., 2025). These findings provide an indirect validation of the concept that epigenetic modulators of HDAC activity may be repurposed to combat the autophagy and lysosomal dysfunction observed in dry AMD. Although Vorinostat itself has not been extensively studied in the context of dry AMD or similar RPE-driven degenerative diseases, its established pharmacological profile and ocular tolerability in other clinical contexts suggest that it could offer mechanistic benefits by modulating retinal epigenetic landscapes (Luo et al., 2025).

Mechanism of Action:  
Vorinostat exerts its biological effects by inhibiting the activity of zinc-dependent histone deacetylases. Under normal physiological conditions, HDACs remove acetyl groups from the lysine residues on histone tails, leading to chromatin condensation and transcriptional repression; by inhibiting these enzymes, Vorinostat results in the accumulation of acetylated histones and a more relaxed chromatin structure that promotes gene transcription. The current hypothesis contends that in RPE cells, Vorinostat-mediated HDAC inhibition will enhance the acetylation of the transcription factors TFEB (transcription factor EB) and members of the FOXO (forkhead box O) family. TFEB is a master regulator of the coordinated lysosomal expression and regulation (CLEAR) network, which governs the transcription of genes encoding lysosomal enzymes, including cathepsin D (CTSD), and other proteins necessary for autophagy and lysosomal acidification (Buniello et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2025). Similarly, FOXO transcription factors are implicated in cellular stress responses and can promote the expression of antioxidant enzymes as well as proteins involved in maintaining mitochondrial integrity. In neuronal models, HDAC inhibition has been linked to increased expression, acetylation, and nuclear localization of TFEB, leading to upregulation of lysosomal gene expression and enhanced autophagic flux (Buniello et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2025). It is anticipated that Vorinostat will operate through a similar mechanism in RPE cells by facilitating the dissociation of HDACs from the promoters of TFEB/FOXO target genes, thereby promoting their transcriptional activation. This would initiate a cascade of events that enhance lysosomal biogenesis, improve lysosomal acidification, and increase the activity of cathepsin D—the lysosomal protease that plays a critical role in degrading accumulated protein aggregates and damaged cellular organelles, which are pathognomonic of dry AMD pathology (Luo et al., 2025). Moreover, it is relevant that other HDAC inhibitors, such as trichostatin A (TSA) and valproic acid (VPA), have demonstrated the capacity to modulate similar pathways in retinal cells, thereby indirectly supporting the proposed mechanism of action for Vorinostat in restoring lysosomal function and autophagic balance in RPE cells (Luo et al., 2025).

Expected Effect:  
Based on the proposed mechanism of action, the expected effect of Vorinostat in the context of dry AMD is multifaceted. The compound is anticipated to inhibit HDAC activity in RPE cells, leading to an increase in overall protein acetylation, including that of histones and transcription factors. This epigenetic modulation should facilitate the nuclear translocation and activation of TFEB, thereby upregulating the CLEAR network of genes involved in lysosomal biogenesis, acidification, and autophagy. In turn, the increased expression and activity of cathepsin D will improve the degradative capacity of the lysosomes, fostering the clearance of lipofuscin and other deleterious protein aggregates that accumulate with age in RPE cells. Additionally, enhanced FOXO activity could promote an improved antioxidant response and mitigate mitochondrial dysfunction, which together would reduce oxidative stress—a key driver of RPE degeneration in dry AMD (Buniello et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2025).

The anticipated outcome in preclinical assays would be a measurable restoration of autophagic flux as evidenced by reductions in markers of cellular stress and accumulation of autophagy substrates. Cellular assays may demonstrate increased lysosomal enzyme activities, such as that of cathepsin D, and improved acidification of lysosomes in treated RPE cells. In animal models engineered or induced to exhibit dry AMD-like pathology, treatment with Vorinostat is expected to lead to an improvement in retinal structure and function, potentially assessed through morphological analyses and electroretinography. Furthermore, the restoration of TFEB/FOXO activity should enhance the overall cellular resilience of RPE, thereby delaying or preventing the progression of degenerative changes associated with dry AMD. Given Vorinostat’s established oral bioavailability and systemic tolerability in oncology patients, there is potential for its repurposing with adjusted dosing regimens aimed at achieving therapeutic concentrations in the retina with minimal systemic toxicity (Buniello et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2025).

Overall Evaluation:  
In evaluating Vorinostat as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, several strengths and weaknesses emerge. One of the principal strengths of Vorinostat is its well-characterized pharmacological profile, which is supported by extensive clinical data in oncology. Its FDA-approved status and known systemic tolerability provide a translational advantage over novel compounds that are still in early developmental stages. The robust mechanism of action of HDAC inhibitors, with demonstrated capacity to modulate gene expression through epigenetic reprogramming, aligns well with the pathobiology of dry AMD, where impaired autophagy and lysosomal dysfunction are central features. The specific hypothesis that Vorinostat will promote the acetylation and activation of TFEB and FOXO transcription factors to drive lysosomal biogenesis, improve acidification, and enhance cathepsin D activity addresses well-validated therapeutic targets in the disease process (Buniello et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2025).

However, there are also significant weaknesses and potential challenges that must be carefully considered. First, while the mechanistic rationale is compelling, direct experimental evidence supporting Vorinostat’s efficacy in RPE cells or animal models of dry AMD is currently sparse. Much of the supporting data is extrapolated from studies using other HDAC inhibitors such as TSA, VPA, or AN7, and from cancer studies where the cellular context differs substantially from that of the RPE (Luo et al., 2025). Second, the pharmacokinetic profile and ocular tissue penetration of Vorinostat when administered systemically remain uncertain. The blood–retinal barrier presents a formidable challenge to achieving therapeutic drug concentrations in the retina, and while clinical trials in oncology have established systemic dosing guidelines, it is unclear whether these doses will translate into efficacious levels within the RPE while maintaining safety. Third, the potential for off-target effects and retinal toxicity cannot be overlooked; certain HDAC inhibitors have been associated with deleterious retinal effects when administered at inappropriate doses or over prolonged periods, emphasizing the need for careful dose optimization and possibly localized (e.g., intravitreal) delivery strategies (Luo et al., 2025). Fourth, the complex interplay between various HDAC isoforms in the retina may necessitate a more selective approach than that offered by the broad-spectrum inhibition provided by Vorinostat, as indiscriminate inhibition could disrupt other acetylation-dependent regulatory mechanisms critical for normal retinal function (Luo et al., 2025).

In addition, while the hypothesis posits that Vorinostat will upregulate TFEB and FOXO to enhance autophagy and lysosomal function, the regulation of these transcription factors is multifactorial. For example, TFEB activity is tightly controlled by phosphorylation events mediated by mTORC1 and AKT2 signaling pathways, and the interplay between these kinases, deacetylases such as SIRT5, and HDACs remains an active area of investigation (Abokyi & Tse, 2025; Buniello et al., 2025; Ghosh et al., 2024). Thus, while there is mechanistic plausibility in promoting lysosomal biogenesis via HDAC inhibition, the precise molecular outcomes in the unique environment of aging RPE cells require further delineation. Furthermore, studies in other models have revealed that the beneficial effects of HDAC inhibition on autophagy and lysosomal function may vary depending on the timing, duration, and specific isoform selectivity of the inhibitor used (Luo et al., 2025).

Taking these factors into account, a cautious but optimistic view emerges regarding the repurposing of Vorinostat for dry AMD. The compound’s established clinical track record in oncology is a substantial advantage, providing a foundation for subsequent translational studies. The convergent evidence supporting the role of HDAC inhibition in enhancing autophagy and mitigating oxidative stress in retinal diseases further bolsters the rationale for this approach (Falcão et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2025). However, to fully validate the therapeutic potential of Vorinostat in dry AMD, rigorous preclinical studies are needed to (1) confirm its efficacy in restoring TFEB/FOXO activity and lysosomal function in RPE cells, (2) determine its pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic properties in ocular tissues, (3) assess its safety profile within the retina over chronic dosing schedules, and (4) establish optimized dosing strategies that achieve target engagement without compromising retinal integrity.

Moreover, future investigations might explore alternative delivery mechanisms, such as nanoparticle-based systems or sustained-release intravitreal formulations, to circumvent the challenges posed by the blood–retinal barrier and achieve localized drug concentrations that are both effective and safe. In parallel, combinatorial therapeutic strategies that pair Vorinostat with other agents that modulate complementary pathways—such as antioxidants, SIRT1 activators, or agents that specifically target mTORC1 signaling—could be considered to provide a multifaceted approach to treating dry AMD. These strategies would leverage the ability of Vorinostat to reprogram epigenetic signatures in RPE cells while simultaneously addressing other pathogenic mechanisms contributing to AMD progression (Buniello et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2025).

In summary, Vorinostat represents a promising candidate for drug repurposing in dry AMD due to its potent HDAC inhibitory activity, favorable clinical history in oncology, and a plausible mechanism by which it could restore lysosomal biogenesis and autophagic flux in RPE cells—a central defect in dry AMD pathogenesis. The strengths of this approach include the compound’s established approval and known pharmacology, coupled with emerging evidence that epigenetic modulation can address key cellular dysfunctions in retinal degeneration. Conversely, the critical weaknesses pertain to the lack of direct preclinical evidence in the context of AMD, uncertainties regarding effective ocular delivery, and potential risks of off-target effects in a delicate tissue such as the retina. A comprehensive series of translational studies, beginning with in vitro models of RPE dysfunction and progressing to in vivo dry AMD models, is essential to fully establish the therapeutic window, efficacy, and safety profile of Vorinostat for this new indication. If these studies yield positive results, Vorinostat could offer a novel, mechanistically precise approach to the treatment of dry AMD, addressing a significant unmet clinical need by restoring the autophagy–lysosome pathway and ultimately preserving vision in affected patients (Buniello et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2025).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
CHIR99021 is a fully synthetic, small-molecule aminopyrimidine that potently inhibits glycogen synthase kinase-3 (GSK3), with common use and profiling as a GSK3β-selective tool compound and canonical Wnt/β-catenin pathway agonist in cell systems (notably embryonic stem cell self-renewal and iPSC generation) (Rethineswaran et al., 2021; Lyssiotis et al., 2011). In ocular biology, CHIR99021 has been implemented as a defined, stage-specific Wnt activator to accelerate and improve directed differentiation of human ESC/iPSC to retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), increasing MITF/OTX2, pigmentation, and RPE functional readouts (apical PEDF, basal VEGF, integrin αVβ5–dependent phagocytosis) when applied at 3 μM during a defined mid-specification window (days 8–14) (Leach et al., 2015). Beyond development and differentiation protocols, CHIR99021 (as CHIR trihydrochloride) has been developed into an in vivo pharmacology tool with validated LC/MS assays and tissue PK in mice; after a 25 mg/kg intraperitoneal dose, it achieves rapid systemic distribution and measurable retinal exposure with prolonged ocular retention relative to plasma and liver (plasma Tmax ~30 min, liver Tmax ~30 min, retina Tmax ~30 min; terminal half-lives ~118, 120, and 405 min, respectively) (DiCesare et al., 2023).

As a GSK3 inhibitor, CHIR99021 belongs to a class leveraged widely across neuroscience, regenerative medicine, and retinal biology. In retinal preclinical systems this class has been used in models of retinitis pigmentosa, optic nerve injury/regeneration, and steroid-induced glaucoma; clinically, lithium chloride (LiCl) remains the only FDA-approved GSK3 inhibitor but with a narrow therapeutic window and mixed efficacy for neurodegenerative disease (DiCesare et al., 2023). In RPE disease–relevant preclinical work, low-dose CHIR99021 exposure in RPE-derived models reduces production/secretion of the EFEMP1/F3 glycoprotein and broadly represses extracellular matrix (ECM), complement, protease, and TGFβ-associated components linked to sub-RPE deposit biology; in vivo, systemic CHIR99021 prevents formation of basal laminar deposits (BLamD) in a homozygous EFEMP1 R345W knock-in mouse (ML/DHRD, an AMD-like pathology) without detectable retinal toxicity on scotopic ERG and H&E histology over one month (DiCesare et al., 2023).

Therapeutic History  
Class history in neural/retinal indications: GSK3 is a central kinase with broad substrate scope (>100 substrates) and regulates Wnt/β-catenin, PI3K/Akt, mTOR, NF-κB, and apoptosis pathways central to retinal homeostasis and degeneration (Hottin et al., 2022). Across retinal neurodegeneration models, GSK3 inhibitors have shown neuroprotection (e.g., in rd10 retinitis pigmentosa, NMDA excitotoxicity, and diabetic retinopathy), and GSK3 inhibition is mechanistically linked to CNS axon regeneration pathways (e.g., via CRMP2, mTOR), though effects are context-dependent and can diverge across cell types and disease stages (Hottin et al., 2022). The translational record for systemic GSK3 inhibition is mixed; lithium’s broad CNS history underscores both feasibility and risk of narrow windows and systemic effects, motivating localized ocular delivery or targeted strategies for retinal disease (Hottin et al., 2022; DiCesare et al., 2023).

CHIR99021 in ocular biology and disease: In vitro, CHIR99021 is a core Wnt agonist in hESC/hiPSC-to-RPE protocols where it improves RPE specification, pigmentation, and function when properly staged; its effects can be recapitulated by WNT3A (canonical) but not by WNT5A (non-canonical), consistent with a canonical Wnt readout (Leach et al., 2015). In applied disease models:

- Anti-deposit/ECM remodeling in EFEMP1-driven pathology: Using ARPE-19 edited lines expressing HiBiT-tagged F3 (WT and R345W), CHIR99021 reduced F3 transcript and protein in both intracellular and secreted compartments without overt cytotoxicity; genetic knockdown of GSK3α/β phenocopied and synergized, supporting an on-target mechanism (DiCesare et al., 2023). Low-dose, longer-term exposure (1 μM for 1 week) suppressed ECM, complement, metalloproteinase, and TGFβ-associated proteins in proteomics (≥2-fold reductions in multiple collagens, MMP2, SERPINE1, LTBP2, TGFβ1; decreases in HMGB1/2, C3; reductions in FBLN1/2) and produced parallel RNA-seq changes (downregulation of genes linked to sub-RPE deposits and ECM crosslinking; upregulation of TYR/TYRP1 and PEDF) without detectable activation of canonical TCF reporters, establishing a low-dose on-target biochemical window (DiCesare et al., 2023). Functionally, 1 μM CHIR99021 for 1 week normalized the R345W F3–linked elevation in MMP2 activity and reduced HiBiT F3 secretion apically and basally in transwell cultures (DiCesare et al., 2023).

- In vivo efficacy and PK: In EFEMP1 R345W+/+ mice (~8 months old), systemic CHIR trihydrochloride (25 mg/kg IP, weekdays for 1 month) reduced the fraction of retinal FOVs containing BLamD from 14.205% to 4.167% and halved the mean deposit area (0.817 to 0.416 μm²), with no detectable ERG or histological toxicity (DiCesare et al., 2023). LC/MS/MS PK in plasma, liver, and retina confirmed rapid tissue distribution at 30 min and prolonged retinal retention (retina terminal T½ ~405 min) with estimated intraocular concentrations on the order of the effective in vitro range over the first hours (e.g., ~1.3 μM at 30 min and ~0.36 μM at 6 h) (DiCesare et al., 2023). Analytical assay development and rigorous methodology are reported (DiCesare et al., 2023).

- Regeneration/reprogramming contexts: CHIR99021 is a frequent component of small-molecule cocktails that reprogram Müller glia toward photoreceptor-like fates, induce Rho+ cells in vitro and in degenerate mouse retinas, and is used in multi-pathway modulation (Wnt activation combined with inhibitors of TGF-β, BMP, and Notch) to enhance MC-derived photoreceptor-like outputs; effects vary with species/model, and cocktails require careful balance (Fujii et al., 2021; Hottin et al., 2022). CHIR99021 also appears in chemical reprogramming schemes that convert adult human RPE to dopaminergic neurons and in multi-factor protocols generating photoreceptor progenitors from RPE or iPSCs, generally in combination with other pathway modulators and epigenetic agents (Rzhanova et al., 2024).

- Safety and adverse contexts: Despite benefits in differentiation, in a large-lesion, macula-sized RPE wound-repair model designed to mimic GA, CHIR99021 hindered lesion closure and yielded morphologically suboptimal infiltrating cells, even though pigmentation outside the lesion increased; EMT-suppressing agents (RepSox, Y-27632) performed better for wound closure under those conditions (Bailey-Steinitz, 2021; Hottin et al., 2022). Reviews caution that GSK3 inhibition can activate VEGF via canonical Wnt and could exacerbate angiogenesis, raising a risk signal for wet AMD contexts and arguing for careful selection of indication (dry vs wet AMD), timing, and combination strategies (e.g., with anti-VEGF) (Hottin et al., 2022).

To our knowledge, no human clinical studies have evaluated CHIR99021 for dry AMD; the most advanced ocular efficacy package is the EFEMP1 R345W mouse, an AMD-like BLamD model, where CHIR achieved both biochemical (ECM/complement/protease remodeling) and morphologic (deposit reduction) endpoints with ocular exposure in the in vitro effective range and no detectable electroretinal toxicity over one month (DiCesare et al., 2023).

Mechanism of Action  
Direct target and pathway entry points: GSK3 exists as α and β isoforms (85% identity), is constitutively active under basal conditions, and is negatively regulated by serine phosphorylation (S21 on α, S9 on β). It phosphorylates primed substrates on Ser/Thr motifs often culminating in β-TrCP recognition and proteasomal degradation of targets including β-catenin in the absence of Wnt; Wnt pathway activation sequesters/inhibits GSK3 within the destruction complex, stabilizing β-catenin and altering transcription via TCF/LEF (Hottin et al., 2022). CHIR99021 pharmacologically inhibits GSK3β and thereby is a canonical Wnt/β-catenin activator in many contexts, explaining its frequent use to bias fate decisions in pluripotent and somatic reprogramming paradigms (Lyssiotis et al., 2011; Leach et al., 2015).

Dose-dependent Wnt signaling in RPE systems: In RPE-derived ARPE-19 models, CHIR99021 shows a clear dose window: at 1 μM for one week it decreases EFEMP1/F3 transcripts/protein and globally represses ECM/complement/TGFβ signatures without detectable activation of TCF reporters; at ≥2.5 μM, TCF reporter activation becomes detectable, indicating canonical Wnt activation above a threshold (DiCesare et al., 2023). This low-dose window was sufficient to reduce MMP2 activity associated with the R345W F3 secretory stress pathophysiology, consistent with broad extracellular remodeling (DiCesare et al., 2023).

On-target genetic support: siRNA knockdown of GSK3α and GSK3β individually reduces F3 and combined knockdown synergizes, phenocopying CHIR’s effect on F3 production and secretion, supporting a GSK3-dependent mechanism for its anti-F3/anti-ECM actions (DiCesare et al., 2023). The effect generalizes across cell types (ARPE-19, human dermal fibroblasts, NIH-3T3), consistent with GSK3’s broad role in secretory/ECM regulation (DiCesare et al., 2023).

Secretory/ECM/complement/TGFβ axis remodeling: One-week, low-dose CHIR caused ≥2-fold reductions in multiple collagens (α1(V), α2(IV), α1(IV), α3(IV)), MMP2, complement C3, HMGB1/2, and TGFβ-related proteins such as SERPINE1/PAI-1 and LTBP2, with transcript-level suppression of ECM crosslinking and EMT-proximal genes (e.g., FN1, LOX, WNT ligands), while upregulating RPE differentiation/pigmentation (TYR, TYRP1) and increasing PEDF (SERPINF1) (DiCesare et al., 2023). These data point to a coordinated shift of the RPE secretome toward reduced pathogenic ECM/complement burden and increased pro-RPE homeostatic factors (e.g., PEDF), in line with the observed mitigation of BLamD in vivo (DiCesare et al., 2023).

mTOR–lysosome/autophagy coupling: Outside the retina, CHIR99021 has been shown to inhibit the Rheb/mTOR axis and increase lysosomal activation and autophagy in late endothelial progenitor cells, with evidence that CHIR reduces phosphorylated mTOR and Rheb independent of β-catenin, via effects attributed to TSC2 and lysosomal mTOR localization (Rethineswaran et al., 2021). These studies connect GSK3β inhibition to increased autophagic flux through mTORC1 suppression at the lysosome, a mechanistic route that in principle converges on transcriptional lysosome biogenesis programs (e.g., TFEB) though TFEB itself was not directly assayed in these reports (Rethineswaran et al., 2021). In retinal disease biology, GSK3 interdigitates with oxidative stress (NRF2 regulation), inflammatory NF-κB signaling, and mTOR pathways that are all implicated in AMD pathogenesis; pharmacologic GSK3β inhibition can increase NRF2 and reduce ROS in diabetic contexts, and reduced GSK3 activity in microglia dampens LPS-induced NF-κB signaling, underscoring additional protective axes that may be engaged in RPE or choroid (Hottin et al., 2022).

Angiogenic and repair liabilities: GSK3 inhibition/Wnt activation can increase VEGF and angiogenesis; reviews caution this may be beneficial in dry AMD (neuroprotection/anti-inflammatory) but harmful in wet AMD, suggesting indication-specific selection and potential need for combination with anti-VEGF or restricted/local delivery (Hottin et al., 2022). In a large RPE wound model mimicking GA-scale atrophy, continuous CHIR exposure hindered repair, in contrast to EMT-suppressing agents that improved closure, highlighting a context where Wnt activation can be counterproductive for lesion repopulation (Bailey-Steinitz, 2021).

Mechanistic net assessment for dry AMD: In RPE disease–proximal models, CHIR99021’s dominant effects at low dose are anti-secretory for F3/EFEMP1 and anti-ECM/complement/TGFβ, with reduced MMP2 and enhanced RPE differentiation markers, culminating in prevention of BLamD in vivo without electrophysiologic deficits over one month (DiCesare et al., 2023). Independent data show CHIR increases autophagy and lysosomal function via mTOR inhibition in other cell types, a mechanistic route that could contribute to proteostasis restoration in the RPE but remains to be demonstrated directly in RPE/AMD systems (Rethineswaran et al., 2021).

Expected Effect  
Assay-level predictions under the stated hypothesis: The team’s hypothesis posits that CHIR99021 will inhibit GSK3β in RPE, facilitate TFEB nuclear localization, enhance lysosomal acidification and cathepsin D (CTSD) maturation, increase autophagic flux, and thereby prevent RPE atrophy in dry AMD. Direct evidence for TFEB nuclear localization or CTSD maturation with CHIR99021 in RPE is not yet provided in the extant literature summarized here; however, two mechanistic pillars are established:

- In RPE disease models, low-dose CHIR99021 reduces a causal secretory burden (EFEMP1/F3) and pathogenic ECM/complement/protease output, normalizes MMP2 activity, increases homeostatic PEDF, and prevents BLamD formation in vivo, providing a deposit-centric, mechanistically credible route to slow early and mid-stage dry AMD pathology that is driven by sub-RPE matrix remodeling and complement activation (DiCesare et al., 2023).

- In non-ocular cells, CHIR99021 inhibits mTOR signaling at the lysosome (reduced Rheb/p-mTOR) and increases lysosomal activation and autophagy independent of β-catenin, consistent with a mechanism that would be predicted to favor TFEB nuclear translocation, transcription of lysosome/autophagy genes, and maturation of proteases such as CTSD; these precise endpoints have not been measured in RPE with CHIR99021 and thus remain to be validated (Rethineswaran et al., 2021).

Given GSK3 expression in ARPE-19 and its manipulation in the cited experiments (use of anti-GSK3α/β antibodies and on-target siRNA phenocopy), RPE is a relevant target cell for CHIR99021’s kinase inhibition (DiCesare et al., 2023). Under oxidative and secretory stress common to dry AMD, one would expect CHIR99021 at sub-TCF-activating exposure (≈1 μM) to:

- Reduce EFEMP1/F3 transcription/secretion and broadly depress ECM and complement cues that seed and stabilize BLamD/drusen, thereby lowering sub-RPE deposit biogenesis and associated pro-inflammatory signaling (DiCesare et al., 2023).

- Normalize MMP2 activity and reduce matrix proteolysis-driven remodeling that contributes to basal laminar/basal linear deposit architecture (DiCesare et al., 2023).

- Enhance RPE homeostatic phenotype, reflected by increased pigmentation gene expression and PEDF secretion, which supports photoreceptor survival and RPE trophic function (DiCesare et al., 2023).

- Potentially increase autophagic flux and lysosomal competence via mTOR inhibition, improving clearance of aggregation-prone or secretory-stressed substrates; this inference is supported mechanistically outside the retina and should be formally confirmed in RPE by LC3 flux, p62/SQSTM1 turnover, LAMP1/2, lysotracker, and cathepsin maturation assays (Rethineswaran et al., 2021).

Boundary conditions and risks for the expected effect: The low-dose window is critical; at ≥2.5 μM, CHIR99021 activates canonical Wnt/TCF reporters in RPE-derived cells, and continuous Wnt activation can impair large-lesion RPE repair and increase angiogenic drive (VEGF), both of which are undesirable in late-stage GA or in patients at risk of conversion to exudative AMD (DiCesare et al., 2023; Bailey-Steinitz, 2021; Hottin et al., 2022). In vivo PK after 25 mg/kg IP yields retinal concentrations in the 0.15–1.3 μM range over the first 24 h, overlapping the RPE efficacy window for EFEMP1/ECM suppression and below the Wnt activation threshold in vitro; however, local ocular delivery and controlled-release formulations may be preferable to avoid systemic exposure and to maintain sub-TCF-activating intraocular concentrations (DiCesare et al., 2023; Hottin et al., 2022).

Overall Evaluation  

Strengths  
- Disease-proximal efficacy with mechanistic depth. CHIR99021 reduces EFEMP1/F3 production (transcript and protein), broadly suppresses ECM/complement/TGFβ secretome programs, decreases MMP2 activity, upregulates pigmentation genes and PEDF, and prevents BLamD in an EFEMP1 R345W knock-in model—an AMD-like pathology characterized by sub-RPE matrix deposits (DiCesare et al., 2023). The convergence of proteomics, transcriptomics, reporter assays, and genetic knockdown around GSK3 establishes on-target pathway control in RPE-derived systems (DiCesare et al., 2023).

- Ocular exposure and safety. Tissue PK demonstrates retinal penetrance and prolonged retention (terminal T½ ≈ 6.75 h), with estimated intraocular levels overlapping the in vitro effective window; one month of systemic dosing at 25 mg/kg produced no detectable ERG or histological abnormalities in adult mice, supporting a tolerability window (DiCesare et al., 2023).

- Plausible extension to proteostasis/autophagy. Independent mechanistic data show CHIR99021 inhibits mTORC1 signaling at the lysosome and increases autophagy/lysosomal activation via the TSC2–Rheb axis in non-ocular cells, a route that could bolster RPE lysosomal function under drusen/BLamD-associated stress even if TFEB was not yet directly measured in RPE (Rethineswaran et al., 2021).

- Modality versatility with established use. Extensive prior use of CHIR99021 as a defined Wnt agonist in RPE/retinal differentiation and reprogramming provides a deep operations base for dosing/timing and cell-specific responses, which can be leveraged to avoid undesired pathway activation during therapy (Leach et al., 2015; Fujii et al., 2021).

Weaknesses and risks  
- Translational maturity and source quality. The core anti-deposit efficacy and ocular PK/safety package resides in a bioRxiv preprint; while comprehensive and internally consistent, it lacks peer-reviewed confirmation and replication across independent labs and models (DiCesare et al., 2023). Moreover, the EFEMP1 R345W model (ML/DHRD) is a rare, early-onset macular dystrophy with AMD-like deposits; it does not recapitulate the full aging/inflammation/metabolic milieu of typical dry AMD (DiCesare et al., 2023).

- Wnt/angiogenesis liability and wound repair. GSK3β inhibition is a canonical Wnt activator and can increase VEGF/angiogenesis, potentially contraindicating use in patients with neovascular risk; in RPE monolayers with macula-sized lesions, CHIR99021 impaired lesion repair despite increasing peripheral pigmentation, highlighting a deleterious effect in GA-like settings requiring repopulation (Hottin et al., 2022; Bailey-Steinitz, 2021).

- Dose/timing and cell-type dependency. Benefits of GSK3 modulation are highly context-dependent in retinal disease; the same pathway promotes different outcomes across disease stage and cell types (photoreceptors, Müller glia, RPE, endothelium). Reviews emphasize that treatment timing, duration, and targeted retinal layer will determine benefit vs harm (DiCesare et al., 2023; Hottin et al., 2022). The in vitro window where 1 μM avoids TCF activation is narrow; in vivo pharmacology must control ocular exposure carefully (DiCesare et al., 2023).

- Mechanistic gap for the autophagy/TFEB claim in RPE. Although CHIR99021 increases autophagy through mTOR suppression in other cell types, direct evidence in human RPE or RPE-derived models for TFEB nuclear translocation, lysosomal acidification improvements, or CTSD maturation with CHIR99021 is currently absent from the surveyed literature; this is an experimental gap relative to the team’s stated hypothesis (Rethineswaran et al., 2021).

Development recommendations  
- Indication scoping to dry AMD segments with deposit-dominated pathology. Based on anti-ECM/complement and anti-BLamD efficacy, prioritize early/mid dry AMD segments characterized by drusen/sub-RPE deposits and low neovascular risk; de-prioritize active geographic atrophy where repopulation/repair of large RPE lesions is the therapeutic aim, given the CHIR-associated repair impairment in vitro (DiCesare et al., 2023; Bailey-Steinitz, 2021).

- Local ocular delivery to widen the therapeutic index. Intravitreal or suprachoroidal controlled-release systems should be evaluated to maintain intraocular concentrations in the ~0.1–1 μM range that achieve biochemical efficacy but remain below the canonical Wnt activation threshold, while minimizing systemic exposure and wet-AMD conversion risk; the reviews support local delivery as a strategy for GSK3-based ocular interventions (DiCesare et al., 2023; Hottin et al., 2022).

- Mechanistic validation in RPE for proteostasis endpoints. In primary hfRPE and iPSC-RPE, directly measure CHIR99021’s impact on autophagy and lysosome: LC3-II flux (±bafilomycin A1), p62/SQSTM1 turnover, TFEB nuclear localization (immunofluorescence/fractionation), lysosomal pH (LysoSensor), LAMP1/2 expression, and CTSD maturation/activity; determine whether these benefits occur at sub-TCF-activating exposures and under relevant stresses (oxidative, lipid, complement) (DiCesare et al., 2023; Rethineswaran et al., 2021).

- Angiogenic surveillance and combination strategies. Quantify VEGF and angiogenic markers (VEGFA mRNA/protein, HIF-1α targets) in RPE/choroid after CHIR, and consider anti-VEGF co-therapy if Wnt-VEGF coupling poses a risk; preclinical reviews support the rationale for combination or timing-restricted inhibition to avoid pro-angiogenic consequences (Hottin et al., 2022).

- Broaden efficacy across dry AMD models. Test CHIR in aging-related and inflammation-metabolism models (e.g., high-fat diet + complement stress; smoke exposure; ApoE variants) in addition to EFEMP1 R345W to ensure generalizability beyond monogenic ECM disease; define the minimal exposure and duration to alter drusen/BLamD dynamics and microglial/complement activation (DiCesare et al., 2023).

- Dose-finding anchored to ocular PK/PD. Use the established LC/MS retinal assay to map intravitreal/subconjunctival/suprachoroidal dose to retinal/choroidal concentration–time profiles; overlay with PD markers (F3 secretion, ECM transcripts, complement, PEDF) to define a sub-TCF window in vivo; confirm absence of ERG deficits and retinal histopathology across multi-month dosing (DiCesare et al., 2023).

- Translational vigilance. Lithium’s status as the sole FDA-approved GSK3 inhibitor and mixed outcomes of GSK3 modulation in retinal disease underscore the need to target specific retinal layers or cell types and to avoid broad systemic inhibition; this aligns with adopting local ocular delivery and possibly RPE-targeted formulations (DiCesare et al., 2023; Hottin et al., 2022).

Conclusion  
On balance, CHIR99021 has a compelling, disease-proximal efficacy package for dry AMD centered on sub-RPE deposit biology. At low doses that do not detectably activate canonical Wnt, CHIR99021 reduces EFEMP1/F3 and globally attenuates ECM/complement/protease pathways in RPE-derived systems, increases PEDF and pigmentation gene expression, and prevents BLamD formation in an EFEMP1 R345W mouse model, with retinal exposures matching in vitro efficacy windows and month-long dosing without ERG/histology toxicity (DiCesare et al., 2023). Independent mechanistic data demonstrate CHIR-mediated inhibition of Rheb/mTOR and increased lysosomal/autophagic activity in non-ocular cells, consistent with the proteostasis-restoring arm of the team’s hypothesis, but direct evidence for TFEB nuclear translocation and CTSD maturation in RPE with CHIR is currently lacking and should be considered a key validation gap (Rethineswaran et al., 2021). The principal risks are Wnt-linked angiogenesis (potentially harmful in wet AMD) and impaired RPE wound repair in GA-like lesions when Wnt activation is sustained; these risks argue for a dry-AMD, early/mid-stage positioning, careful intraocular dose control to remain below the TCF activation threshold, and consideration of local delivery and/or anti-VEGF combinations in higher-risk patients (Hottin et al., 2022; Bailey-Steinitz, 2021).

Overall, CHIR99021 is a promising repurposed candidate for dry AMD if developed within a well-defined exposure window and indication niche. Its strengths are a clear kinase target with on-target cellular genetics, strong anti-deposit and secretome remodeling data in RPE and in vivo, ocular exposure that aligns with cellular pharmacology, and plausible lysosome/autophagy engagement. Its weaknesses are translational maturity (preprint stage; single primary in vivo model), Wnt-associated angiogenesis and repair liabilities at higher/continuous exposure, and incomplete validation of the autophagy/TFEB axis in RPE. A go decision for preclinical advancement is justified, contingent on rapid mechanistic confirmation in RPE for autophagy/lysosome endpoints, rigorous angiogenesis/wound-repair safety pharmacology, and PK/PD-guided local delivery strategies that maintain sub-TCF intraocular concentrations (DiCesare et al., 2023; Hottin et al., 2022; Rethineswaran et al., 2021).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Recombinant human pro-cathepsin D (rhCTSD), as exemplified by R&D Systems product 1869-CD, is a bioengineered form of a naturally occurring lysosomal aspartyl protease that is synthesized as an inactive precursor (pro-cathepsin D) (Sharif, 2015, pp. 60–64). This therapeutic candidate belongs to the enzyme replacement therapy (ERT) class, a category of biotherapeutics developed to supplement or correct deficient lysosomal enzymes in various disorders. The natural cathepsin D enzyme is normally produced and processed intracellularly through the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and Golgi apparatus, undergoing critical post-translational modifications—including the removal of the N-terminal signal peptide, glycosylation, and addition of a mannose-6-phosphate (M6P) tag—that are essential for its subsequent targeting to the lysosome (Sharif, 2015, pp. 60–64). The recombinant version is produced under conditions aimed at ensuring high purity and biological activity conforming to GMP standards, thus making it an attractive candidate for repurposing in conditions where lysosomal proteolytic capacity is compromised. The candidate has been designed in the context of neurodegenerative and lysosomal storage disorders, where enzyme supplementation has been shown to restore proteolytic flux by directly replacing a rate-limiting hydrolase (Bassal et al., 2021; Marques et al., 2020).

Therapeutic History:  
Enzyme replacement therapies have been a cornerstone in the management of several lysosomal storage disorders since the early 1990s, with the first approved treatment for Gaucher’s disease setting a precedent for this therapeutic strategy (Saftig, 2005; Lerussi et al., 2025). In the specific case of cathepsin D, recombinant forms have been employed in preclinical models of neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis (NCL) and other neurodegenerative lysosomal storage disorders, where the administration of exogenous pro-cathepsin D was able to rescue functional deficits associated with genetic CTSD deficiency (Bassal et al., 2021; Marques et al., 2020). Animal studies using CTSD-deficient mouse models have demonstrated that both intracranial and localized injections of recombinant CTSD can correct defects in proteolysis and autophagy, leading to improvements in neuropathological markers and even extending lifespan in treated animals (Bassal et al., 2021; Liu, 2021; Marques et al., 2020). Although most of these studies have focused on neurodegenerative conditions of the central nervous system, similar principles of lysosomal dysfunction apply to retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells, which are critical for maintaining retinal homeostasis in the context of age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (Klettner et al., 2013). Notably, the literature suggests that cathepsin D is highly expressed in RPE cells and plays a vital role in the degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (POS), with its deficiency or reduced function being implicated in the accumulation of toxic deposits and drusen formation—a hallmark of dry AMD (Klettner et al., 2013; Sharif, 2015). Despite the absence of direct clinical trials in dry AMD using rhCTSD, the extensive preclinical evidence from both neurodegenerative and retinal disease models provides a compelling rationale for exploring the repurposing of this enzyme replacement strategy in dry AMD (Liu, 2021; Marques et al., 2020).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, the mechanism of action of recombinant human pro-cathepsin D is rooted in its ability to restore lysosomal proteolytic function, which is often impaired in disease states such as dry AMD. Under physiological conditions, pro-cathepsin D is synthesized in the rough ER as an inactive precursor that undergoes several post-translational modifications, including the cleavage of an N-terminal signal peptide, N-linked glycosylation, and critical mannose-6-phosphate (M6P) tagging in the Golgi apparatus (Sharif, 2015). The M6P tag facilitates the binding of pro-cathepsin D to M6P receptors within the trans-Golgi network (TGN), directing the enzyme to late endosomes and, eventually, to lysosomes where the acidic environment promotes its maturation into its active form (Sharif, 2015). Once active, cathepsin D contributes to the degradation of a wide range of substrates, including the photoreceptor outer segments in RPE cells, thereby playing a crucial role in maintaining cellular homeostasis and preventing the accumulation of deleterious debris that can lead to drusen formation (Klettner et al., 2013). The proposed therapeutic strategy involves subretinal delivery of the recombinant enzyme to bypass systemic limitations such as the blood-brain barrier and to achieve localized uptake into RPE cells via the M6P receptor-mediated endocytosis pathway (Liu, 2021; Marques et al., 2020; Sharif, 2015). Once internalized, the enzyme can replenish endogenous levels of cathepsin D, thereby enhancing autophagic flux and proteolytic degradation processes that are essential for the health and function of the RPE (Klettner et al., 2013; Sharif, 2015). This targeted mechanism is a direct, molecularly specific approach that aims not only to compensate for maturation defects in the enzyme but also to overcome upstream acidification abnormalities that often hinder proper activation of endogenously produced cathepsin D in aging RPE cells (Liu, 2021; Marques et al., 2020; Sharif, 2015).

Expected Effect:  
The anticipated outcome of employing recombinant human pro-cathepsin D for the treatment of dry AMD is multifaceted. First, the subretinal administration of the enzyme is expected to lead to efficient uptake by RPE cells via the M6P receptor, thereby supplementing or restoring the lysosomal pool of active cathepsin D where it is most critically needed (Sharif, 2015). This direct enzyme replacement should result in improved degradation of cellular waste such as spent photoreceptor outer segments, mitigating the build-up of lipofuscin and drusen that are characteristic of dry AMD pathology (Klettner et al., 2013). In animal models of CTSD deficiency—specifically those that mimic aspects of neurodegenerative lysosomal storage disorders—the administration of exogenous pro-cathepsin D has yielded significant improvements in proteolytic function, reduction of pathological markers, and even extensions in lifespan (Bassal et al., 2021; Marques et al., 2020), which suggest that similar therapeutic benefits might be achievable in the context of dry AMD. Enhancing the proteolytic flux within the lysosomes of RPE cells is expected to restore autophagy and maintain cellular homeostasis, thereby reducing the incidence of apoptotic cell death and preserving retinal structure (Klettner et al., 2013; Sharif, 2015). Additionally, by compensating for potential maturation deficits and bypassing defective acidification processes through localized delivery, the therapeutic candidate offers a targeted approach that is likely to be both efficacious and specific compared to more indirect modulators of lysosomal function (Liu, 2021; Marques et al., 2020; Sharif, 2015). Ultimately, the expected effect is an overall improvement in RPE health, which should translate into slowed progression of dry AMD, decreased drusen accumulation, and preserved visual function.

Overall Evaluation:  
In evaluating recombinant human pro-cathepsin D as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, several strengths emerge from the literature, though some challenges remain. One of the primary strengths of this candidate lies in its specificity; unlike indirect modulators of lysosomal function, the exogenous delivery of a rate-limiting hydrolase such as CTSD offers a mechanistically driven, targeted replacement therapy that directly addresses a known biochemical deficit in the retinal pigment epithelium (Klettner et al., 2013; Liu, 2021). The robust body of preclinical evidence supporting the efficacy of recombinant pro-cathepsin D in models of neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis, where similar lysosomal impairments are present, lends further credence to its potential applicability in AMD (Bassal et al., 2021; Marques et al., 2020). Moreover, the formulation's GMP-compatibility and prior demonstration of safety in the context of genetic CTSD deficiency are significant advantages that can accelerate its translational potential (Marques et al., 2020; Liu, 2021).

The enzyme’s molecular mechanism, which involves uptake via mannose-6-phosphate receptor-mediated endocytosis and subsequent activation in the lysosomal compartment, is well-characterized and aligns with the pathological requirements for restoring RPE function in dry AMD (Sharif, 2015). This targeted approach provides a direct means to enhance proteolytic activity and autophagic flux, crucial processes that are disrupted in the aging retina and contribute to drusen accumulation (Klettner et al., 2013). The ability of the exogenously delivered pro-cathepsin D to overcome defects in lysosomal maturation and acidification further reinforces its potential role in reversing or mitigating the deleterious effects of the disease (Liu, 2021; Marques et al., 2020).

On the other hand, several weaknesses or challenges must be acknowledged. Although the mechanistic rationale is robust, the translation of preclinical successes in neurodegenerative and lysosomal storage disorder models to the complex, multifactorial pathology of dry AMD remains uncertain (Benes et al., 2008; Liu, 2021). Dry AMD is influenced by a host of factors—including oxidative stress, chronic inflammation, and genetic predispositions—that may not be fully addressed by simply supplementing CTSD activity. Therefore, while the normalization of proteolytic flux in RPE cells is a critical component, it may not suffice on its own in the context of the broader pathophysiological milieu present in AMD (Klettner et al., 2013; Sharif, 2015).

Furthermore, delivery challenges inherent to subretinal injections must be considered. Although localized delivery methods help bypass systemic barriers such as the blood-brain barrier, subretinal injections are technically demanding, carry inherent risks of infection, and may provoke local immune responses due to repeated interventions (Marques et al., 2020; Liu, 2021). The emergence of neutralizing antibodies, as observed in some ERT studies when alternative routes of administration were explored, could compromise the long-term efficacy of the therapy if systemic leakage occurs or if repeated dosing is required (Marques et al., 2020; Liu, 2021). Additionally, the stability and persistence of the enzyme in the subretinal space represent important pharmacokinetic questions that must be addressed through rigorous preclinical pharmacodynamic studies.

Another potential shortcoming is the specificity of the enzyme’s action. While cathepsin D is indeed a critical protease in RPE cells, there is an intricate interplay between cathepsin D and other lysosomal enzymes such as cathepsins B, L, and S, as well as regulatory proteins like cystatin C, which modulate proteolytic activity (Sharif, 2015). This interdependence implies that augmenting CTSD activity alone might lead to compensatory changes in other proteases that could either enhance the therapeutic effect or, conversely, result in unforeseen off-target consequences. Moreover, given the complexity of the RPE cell’s lysosomal network and the multifactorial nature of dry AMD pathogenesis, combination approaches targeting several aspects of lysosomal dysfunction might be necessary to achieve optimal clinical outcomes.

In summary, recombinant human pro-cathepsin D presents a therapeutically attractive and mechanistically rational candidate for the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration. Its origins as a naturally occurring lysosomal precursor that, when supplemented exogenously, has been shown to restore enzyme activity in preclinical models of lysosomal dysfunction (Bassal et al., 2021; Marques et al., 2020) underscores its potential for addressing the proteolytic deficits seen in RPE cells affected by dry AMD (Klettner et al., 2013). The candidate’s well-defined molecular processing pathway—from synthesis as an inactive proenzyme to activation within the acidic environment of the lysosome—ensures that it is both functionally and biologically suited to compensate for endogenous maturation deficits (Sharif, 2015). This detailed understanding of its biochemistry and cellular uptake mechanisms via the mannose-6-phosphate receptor supports the hypothesis that subretinal delivery of rhCTSD could enhance proteolytic flux, reduce drusen accumulation, and ultimately contribute to the preservation of retinal function in patients with dry AMD (Liu, 2021; Marques et al., 2020).

Despite these promising attributes, the candidate’s clinical translation will require addressing several key challenges. Future studies must rigorously evaluate the pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic profiles of subretinally delivered rhCTSD, with particular emphasis on its stability, local retention time in the subretinal space, and potential immunogenicity. It will also be critical to determine whether augmenting CTSD activity alone is sufficient to counteract the multi-factorial processes underlying dry AMD or if the therapeutic strategy should be integrated into a broader, combination-based treatment regimen. Additionally, long-term safety studies are necessary to monitor for potential adverse effects, such as immune-mediated clearance or detrimental off-target proteolytic activity that might impair retinal structure and function (Marques et al., 2020; Thiessen, 2023).

Ultimately, the overall evaluation is cautiously optimistic. The mechanistic rationale is strong—supported by extensive preclinical data from related neurodegenerative and lysosomal storage disorder models—and the therapeutic candidate is produced under rigorous, GMP-compliant conditions, offering a level of quality assurance that is imperative for clinical advancement (Marques et al., 2020; Liu, 2021). The specificity of recombinant pro-cathepsin D in directly addressing a rate-limiting step in lysosomal degradation makes it an especially compelling candidate in a disease setting where impaired autophagy and proteolysis are central to pathology (Klettner et al., 2013). However, challenges related to effective subretinal delivery, the potential for immune responses, and the need to integrate its action within the broader context of AMD pathogenesis must be rigorously addressed in subsequent preclinical and clinical studies before a definitive therapeutic benefit can be confirmed (Marques et al., 2020; Benes et al., 2008). In light of these considerations, recombinant human pro-cathepsin D stands out as a promising avenue for therapeutic intervention in dry AMD, meriting further investigation to delineate its efficacy, safety, and long-term benefits in the appropriate animal models and ultimately in clinical trials.
