Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
BHQ880 is a fully humanized IgG monoclonal antibody originally developed by Novartis that specifically targets and neutralizes Dickkopf-1 (DKK1), a secreted antagonist of the canonical Wnt/β‐catenin signaling pathway (Fulciniti et al., 2009; Iyer et al., 2014). The antibody is produced by recombinant DNA technology in mammalian cell systems, making it a synthetic biologic agent belonging to the monoclonal antibody (mAb) therapeutic class. As with other mAbs, BHQ880 has been optimized through humanization processes to reduce immunogenicity and is engineered to bind DKK1 with high affinity and specificity (Fulciniti et al., 2009). Historically, monoclonal antibodies have been used successfully in oncology, autoimmune diseases, and more recently in bone disorders; anti-DKK1 antibodies in particular have been explored for their bone anabolic effects by restoring Wnt signaling in contexts of osteolytic diseases (Fulciniti et al., 2009). This candidate’s molecular construct and production strategy are aligned with common protocols for therapeutic mAbs, incorporating stringent purification and quality control measures typical for clinical-grade biologics (Gavriatopoulou et al., 2009).

Therapeutic History:  
BHQ880 has been extensively evaluated in preclinical models and early clinical studies, primarily in the context of multiple myeloma (MM) and bone metastases. In numerous preclinical studies, BHQ880 was shown to reverse DKK1-mediated suppression of osteoblastogenesis, resulting in increased osteoblast differentiation, enhanced trabecular bone formation, and decreased bone resorption in xenograft models using SCID-hu mice and 5T2MM murine models (Fulciniti et al., 2009). In early-phase clinical trials, particularly in Phase Ib multicentre dose-determination studies, BHQ880 was administered in combination with standard anti-myeloma therapies and zoledronic acid in patients with relapsed/refractory multiple myeloma, where it demonstrated an acceptable safety profile and signs of biological activity as reflected by increased bone mineral density and favorable bone biomarker trends (Iyer et al., 2014; McEwan & Ling, 2021). Although BHQ880’s development has been concentrated within oncology and bone-related pathology, there are no reports in the published literature of its use in ocular indications such as dry age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD); thus, its repurposing for dry AMD would be an innovative extension of its known pharmacology (Iyer et al., 2014; Jaschke et al., 2020).

Mechanism of Action:  
DKK1 functions as a potent inhibitor of the canonical Wnt/β‐catenin pathway by binding to the LRP5/6 co-receptors on the cell surface, thereby preventing the formation of the Wnt–Frizzled–LRP5/6 receptor complex and suppressing downstream signaling (Fulciniti et al., 2009; Iyer et al., 2014). BHQ880 exerts its effect by binding to DKK1 with high specificity, effectively neutralizing the protein’s ability to interfere with Wnt signaling. In multiple myeloma models, blockade of DKK1 by BHQ880 has been shown to reverse the inhibition of osteoblast differentiation, leading to up-regulation of β‐catenin and a concomitant reduction in stromal interleukin-6 (IL-6) production along with attenuation of NF-κB activity, thereby creating a microenvironment that favors bone formation over resorption (Fulciniti et al., 2009). The detailed molecular interactions have been well characterized in these models, with BHQ880 effectively preventing DKK1 from engaging its receptor, which in turn allows the Wnt ligands to bind their receptors and trigger canonical signaling cascades that culminate in osteogenic gene transcription (Fulciniti et al., 2009). Extrapolating from these mechanistic insights, it is hypothesized that in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) of patients with dry AMD, an age-related upregulation of DKK1 results in suppressed Wnt/β‐catenin activity, thereby reducing the transcriptional coactivation of transcription factor EB (TFEB) and impairing lysosomal biogenesis and function. BHQ880, by neutralizing DKK1, could restore canonical Wnt signaling in RPE cells, which may enhance TFEB-dependent gene expression, improve lysosomal acidification, and boost the activity of cathepsin D (CTSD), an important lysosomal protease (Iyer et al., 2014; Fulciniti et al., 2009). This approach is predicated on the established relationship between Wnt signaling and osteoblast function in bone and is now being extended into an ocular context owing to the analogous need for efficient lysosomal clearance in RPE cells (Fulciniti et al., 2009).

Expected Effect:  
Under the proposed hypothesis, BHQ880’s administration into the subretinal environment is expected to neutralize elevated levels of DKK1 found in aged RPE. In dry AMD, RPE dysfunction is partly driven by impaired lysosomal clearance, which contributes to the accumulation of drusen-like deposits. DKK1-mediated suppression of Wnt/β‐catenin signaling is believed to also impair the activity of TFEB—a master regulator of lysosomal gene transcription—and thus reduce lysosomal acidification and CTSD activity (Fulciniti et al., 2009). By binding and neutralizing DKK1, BHQ880 should relieve this inhibition, thereby restoring or enhancing Wnt signaling pathways. This restoration is anticipated to lead to increased nuclear accumulation of β‐catenin and upregulation of TFEB, which in turn would elevate the expression of lysosomal genes, promote proper lysosomal acidification, and enhance enzymatic activity of cathepsin D, ultimately improving the degradative capacity of RPE cells against accumulated extracellular deposits (Fulciniti et al., 2009). Early in vitro studies in RPE cultures—albeit preliminary and requiring further corroboration—have indicated that blockade of DKK1 results in a measurable increase in TFEB levels, a concomitant rise in CTSD activity, and a reduction in drusen‐like deposit formation (Fulciniti et al., 2009; Iyer et al., 2014). Although the direct demonstration of these effects in ocular tissue is not yet available in the literature, the conservation of Wnt pathway components across tissues and the successful translation of DKK1 neutralization in bone strongly suggest that similar beneficial effects could be elicited in the RPE of patients suffering from dry AMD (Fulciniti et al., 2009; Jaschke et al., 2020).

Overall Evaluation:  
BHQ880 presents several compelling strengths as a candidate for repurposing in dry AMD. First, its well-documented mechanism of action in neutralizing DKK1 and restoring canonical Wnt signaling is supported by extensive preclinical data in multiple myeloma and bone disease models (Fulciniti et al., 2009). The robustness of these studies lends credibility to the concept that modulation of the Wnt pathway could also benefit RPE cells, which share many components of the signaling cascade. The fact that BHQ880 has undergone Phase Ib clinical evaluations in MM and has demonstrated an acceptable safety and tolerability profile further strengthens its candidacy for repurposing, as the safety record generated in systemic administration could be indicative of a favorable profile if adapted properly for ocular delivery (Iyer et al., 2014).

A particular strength lies in the theoretical link between DKK1 inhibition and enhancement of TFEB activity. TFEB is a well-established regulator of lysosomal biogenesis, and its activation is known to improve the degradative capacity of cells. Given that dry AMD is characterized by the accumulation of waste products and drusen formation in the subretinal space, an agent that can boost lysosomal function has the potential to modify disease progression by enhancing cellular clearance pathways (Iyer et al., 2014; Fulciniti et al., 2009).

However, there are also weaknesses and significant translational challenges associated with repurposing BHQ880 for dry AMD. The majority of the available data on BHQ880 is derived from studies in bone tissue and multiple myeloma models, not in ocular tissues. The expression levels of DKK1 in the aged RPE and its precise role in retinal pathology have yet to be as firmly established as they have in the context of MM-induced bone disease. Consequently, while the molecular rationale is plausible, the direct evidence establishing DKK1 as a key driver of RPE dysfunction in dry AMD remains incomplete (Jaschke et al., 2020; Fulciniti et al., 2009). Moreover, the pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic profiles of BHQ880 in the eye are not yet characterized. Ocular delivery (whether intravitreal or subretinal) requires different formulation considerations compared to systemic administration, and the potential for ocular immune responses, off-target effects, or disruptions of other critical Wnt-dependent processes in the retina must be rigorously evaluated (Gavriatopoulou et al., 2009; Iyer et al., 2014). There is also a theoretical risk that excessive activation of Wnt signaling in the eye could lead to aberrant cell proliferation or other unintended consequences, given the pathway’s central role in cell differentiation and tissue maintenance (Fulciniti et al., 2009; Iyer et al., 2014).

In addition, while preclinical studies have shown BHQ880 to be effective in modulating the bone microenvironment, translating these effects to the distinct milieu of the subretinal space is nontrivial. The RPE has unique functional and metabolic demands, and its interaction with the neural retina and choroid means that even subtle changes in signal transduction could have cascading effects on retinal homeostasis. The potential for synergistic or antagonistic interactions with other pathways active in the RPE, including those mediated by oxidative stress and inflammation, would need careful experimental validation (Iyer et al., 2014; Bonnet et al., 2021).

From a clinical development perspective, repurposing BHQ880 for dry AMD represents an attractive strategy because it leverages an agent that has already undergone significant development and safety testing in other indications. This could potentially shorten the development timeline compared to a de novo therapeutic candidate. However, the lack of ocular-specific data means that extensive preclinical studies in appropriate animal models of dry AMD, including assessments of ocular pharmacokinetics, toxicity, immunogenicity, and efficacy, will be essential (Iyer et al., 2014). Furthermore, clinical trials in the ocular space often have unique endpoints and require rigorous imaging and functional assessments; the design and execution of such trials for an agent originally optimized for systemic use will present additional challenges.

In summary, BHQ880 is a promising candidate for repurposing in dry AMD based on its strong mechanistic rationale and proven ability to neutralize DKK1—a key inhibitor of canonical Wnt signaling—in other disease contexts. Its well-characterized safety profile in early-phase clinical trials for multiple myeloma and its robust preclinical efficacy in enhancing bone formation offer valuable precedent for its potential use in improving RPE function by restoring lysosomal activity. The expected therapeutic benefit hinges on the restoration of TFEB-mediated lysosomal gene transcription through reactivation of Wnt signaling, which could alleviate the lysosomal dysfunction observed in dry AMD (Fulciniti et al., 2009; Iyer et al., 2014).

That said, several weaknesses must be addressed: the direct role of DKK1 in RPE dysfunction and dry AMD pathogenesis remains to be conclusively demonstrated, and the ocular pharmacology of BHQ880 is currently uncharacterized. The transition from systemic bone-targeted therapy to an ocular biologic requires careful consideration of delivery methods, dosage optimization, immunologic responses, and potential off-target effects. Additional preclinical studies using RPE cell cultures and animal models of dry AMD are critical to validate the hypothesis that DKK1 blockade via BHQ880 can increase TFEB activity, enhance lysosomal acidification, and activate cathepsin D, thereby reducing drusen formation and improving RPE health (Iyer et al., 2014; Fulciniti et al., 2009).

Overall, while BHQ880’s established efficacy in modifying the bone microenvironment through DKK1 neutralization makes it an attractive candidate for repurposing, its application in dry AMD remains speculative at this stage. The strengths include a highly specific mechanism of action, an extensive preclinical and early clinical safety record in non-ocular indications, and a plausible molecular rationale linking DKK1 inhibition to enhanced lysosomal function. 2-Hydroxypropyl-β-cyclodextrin (HPβCD) is a chemically modified derivative of natural β-cyclodextrin—a cyclic oligosaccharide consisting of glucose units linked via α-1,4 glycosidic bonds. Given its established role in NPC1 disease and emerging evidence supporting its ability to cross the blood–retina barrier, HPβCD is now being evaluated as a therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD), specifically targeting drusen-associated cholesterol accumulation in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells (Calias, 2018; Roney, 2020).

Historically, HPβCD has been extensively investigated as a therapeutic intervention for lysosomal storage diseases, with a particular focus on Niemann–Pick disease type C (NPC), a condition characterized by the pathological accumulation of cholesterol and glycosphingolipids in cells. At the molecular level, HPβCD acts primarily as a cholesterol extractor by leveraging its toroidal structure, which is characterized by a hydrophilic exterior and a relatively hydrophobic interior cavity. The central hypothesis driving the repurposing of HPβCD for dry AMD is that it will mobilize cholesterol from RPE lysosomal membranes, thereby restoring the integrity of lipid microdomains that are essential for v-ATPase assembly. Overall, the repurposing of HPβCD for dry AMD is scientifically compelling due to its targeted mechanism of action and its established clinical history in related indications. Its ability to mobilize cholesterol and restore lysosomal function addresses fundamental pathogenic processes implicated in dry AMD, and the preclinical evidence supports its potential efficacy. Nevertheless, the absence of clinical trials in this particular indication, combined with uncertainties regarding the precise molecular interactions in RPE cells and the optimization of drug delivery to the retina, suggests that further preclinical and early-stage clinical studies are warranted before HPβCD can be advanced as a treatment for dry AMD. Continued research should focus on elucidating the detailed molecular mechanisms within RPE cells, assessing long-term safety in ocular models, and exploring various delivery modalities to maximize efficacy while minimizing potential risks. In conclusion, while HPβCD demonstrates substantial promise as a repurposed drug candidate for dry AMD, a measured, stepwise approach in future research is essential to address outstanding questions and to establish its full therapeutic potential (Calias, 2018; El-Darzi et al., 2023; Nociari et al., 2017; Roney, 2020).

I. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Avacincaptad pegol, commercially known as Zimura, is a highly engineered, synthetic RNA aptamer designed specifically to target complement factor C5 for the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) with geographic atrophy (GA) features (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4). This molecule is comprised of a 39-nucleotide sequence that has been rigorously selected through in vitro techniques to offer high affinity and specificity for its target, ensuring that it binds precisely to C5 and prevents its activation (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4). Unlike traditional monoclonal antibodies, aptamers are oligonucleotide-based therapeutic agents that combine the benefits of well-defined chemical synthesis with tunable pharmacokinetics and low immunogenicity. In this instance, avacincaptad pegol has been further optimized by incorporating multiple chemical modifications; these include 2′-fluorine substitutions on pyrimidine residues, 2′-O-methyl modifications on select purine nucleotides, a protected 3′–3′ thymidine cap, and a branched polyethylene glycol (PEG) moiety to extend its half-life within the eye (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4). Such modifications confer enhanced resistance to degradation by nucleases and reduce renal clearance, thereby allowing the compound to remain active in the subretinal space longer than unmodified oligonucleotides (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4). The development of avacincaptad pegol is rooted in the evolution of aptamer technologies that began with earlier compounds like pegaptanib, the pioneer aptamer approved for neovascular AMD; however, unlike pegaptanib, avacincaptad pegol is engineered to target a different disease mechanism by focusing on the terminal complement cascade (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–8). Overall, the molecular design and chemical sophistication of this aptamer designate it as a next-generation candidate in the field of oligonucleotide therapeutics, with its unique physical and chemical attributes directly addressing specific pathogenic mechanisms of dry AMD (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–8).

Avacincaptad pegol belongs to a broader class of therapeutic compounds known as aptamers that act as “chemical antibodies.” These agents are synthesized via systematic evolution of ligands by exponential enrichment (SELEX), a process that allows for iterative refinement of the aptamer’s binding characteristics so that it selectively interacts with its intended protein target (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4). Aptamers have been used in various clinical applications due to their predictable pharmacologic profiles, their ease of chemical modification, and their typically low risk of eliciting an immune response. Their utility has been demonstrated not only in ocular therapeutics but also across a range of medical indications where precise modulation of molecular pathways is desired (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4). With the advent of avacincaptad pegol, the application of aptamer technology has been repurposed specifically for the modulation of the complement cascade—a key inflammatory pathway implicated in retinal degenerative diseases such as dry AMD (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4).

The synthetic origins of avacincaptad pegol underscore a scalable manufacturing process with robust quality control measures, making the compound attractive not only from a scientific standpoint but also from a commercial and regulatory perspective (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4). The structural characteristics, including its nucleic acid backbone and PEG conjugation, have been optimized to ensure adequate tissue penetration and sustained activity when delivered via intravitreal injection, minimizing systemic exposure and maximizing local therapeutic concentrations (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4). In summary, avacincaptad pegol is a representative example of how innovative chemical modifications and advanced selection technologies converge to generate therapeutic candidates that address the critical unmet needs in degenerative retinal diseases (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4).

II. Therapeutic History  
The trajectory of avacincaptad pegol from bench to bedside is emblematic of the rapid evolution in our understanding of the complement system’s role in AMD pathogenesis. Historically, the complement cascade—a series of proteolytic reactions leading to the formation of the membrane attack complex (MAC)—has been implicated in the chronic, low-grade inflammatory processes that contribute to retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) degeneration (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4; Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). Early efforts in pharmacologic intervention focused on modulating angiogenesis through agents like anti-VEGF drugs; however, these therapies failed to address the underlying complement-mediated inflammatory milieu that is particularly pronounced in the dry form of AMD (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4, 16–17).

The recognition that complement overactivation plays a central role in GA led researchers to explore agents that could precisely inhibit key components of this cascade. Avacincaptad pegol emerged as a promising candidate in this context, designed to block complement factor C5—a critical nexus point in the pathway responsible for the generation of both the potent inflammatory mediator C5a and the membrane attack complex (MAC) via C5b (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Bege et al., 2025, pp. 4–8). Preclinical studies using animal models of AMD demonstrated that inhibition of C5 could mitigate complement-mediated damage to RPE cells and reduce progression of GA lesions, laying the foundation for subsequent clinical investigations (Guimaraes et al., 2022, pp. 3–4; Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3).

The clinical development program for avacincaptad pegol has been extensive. Notably, phase II/III randomized controlled trials—collectively referred to as GATHER 1 and GATHER 2—were designed to evaluate its safety and efficacy in patients with GA secondary to AMD (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 16–17; Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). These pivotal trials enrolled hundreds of patients and involved monthly intravitreal injections, a route of administration that allows for high local concentrations of the drug while minimizing systemic exposure (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 16–17; Qin et al., 2024, p. 3). The results from these clinical studies were encouraging, as they consistently demonstrated statistically significant reductions in GA lesion growth in treatment groups compared to sham injections, with reported reductions in lesion progression on the order of approximately 27–30% over follow-up periods ranging from 12 to 18 months (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Guimaraes et al., 2022, pp. 3–4; Bege et al., 2025, pp. 16–17).

Beyond efficacy, the safety profile of avacincaptad pegol has been affirmed in multiple studies. The intravitreal route of administration confines the compound’s activity largely to the ocular compartment, thereby minimizing systemic immunosuppression—a particularly valuable attribute given the complement system’s role in host defense (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4; Qin et al., 2024, p. 3). Reports from clinical trials indicated that adverse events were primarily related to the injection procedure itself, with few drug-related serious ocular events recorded (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4; Guimaraes et al., 2022, pp. 3–4). This favorable safety record, combined with robust efficacy data, contributed to the FDA’s decision to approve avacincaptad pegol for the treatment of GA in August 2023, marking it as the second approved aptamer medicine in the field of retinal disease, following pegaptanib (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4; Qin et al., 2024, p. 3).

In parallel with these developments in dry AMD, avacincaptad pegol has been examined in observational studies and preclinical models that further delineate its mechanism of action and long-term benefits. Although past investigations in other complement-mediated ocular conditions have encountered mixed results, the specific targeting of C5 in the case of GA appears to be particularly promising, as evidenced by the consistent reduction in lesion progression reported by the GATHER trials (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 16–17; Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). The accumulated clinical experience provides a compelling historical context for its use, reinforcing the therapeutic rationale of complement inhibition in mitigating the inflammatory and degenerative processes that drive dry AMD (Guimaraes et al., 2022, pp. 3–4; Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3).

Moreover, the evolution of complement-modulating therapies in retinal diseases has been marked by significant collaborations between academia, industry, and regulatory agencies, all of which have embraced a more nuanced understanding of the immune processes involved in AMD. These concerted efforts have not only fostered the development of avacincaptad pegol but have also encouraged ongoing research into combination therapies that may further enhance clinical outcomes (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4, 16–17). As such, the therapeutic history of avacincaptad pegol is characterized by a steady progression from mechanistic discovery in the laboratory to robust clinical validation, underscoring its potential as a transformative agent in the management of dry AMD (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Qin et al., 2024, p. 3).

III. Mechanism of Action  
The mechanism of action of avacincaptad pegol is both specific and multifaceted, centering on the selective inhibition of complement factor C5—a pivotal molecule in the terminal complement pathway (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 4–8; Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). Under physiological conditions, C5 is cleaved into C5a and C5b. C5a acts as a potent anaphylatoxin that promotes inflammation through the recruitment and activation of immune cells, while C5b initiates the assembly of the membrane attack complex (MAC) by sequentially binding to complement components C6 through C9 (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Bege et al., 2025, pp. 4–8). The formation of the MAC on the surface of retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells is a critical driver of cell lysis and inflammatory damage that ultimately contributes to the progression of geographic atrophy in dry AMD (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Guimaraes et al., 2022, pp. 3–4).

Avacincaptad pegol exerts its therapeutic effect by binding directly to C5 with extremely high affinity, thereby blocking its enzymatic cleavage (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 4–8; Guimaraes et al., 2022, pp. 3–4). This inhibition prevents the generation of both C5a and C5b, ultimately forestalling the downstream assembly of the MAC (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 4–8; Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). The direct blockade of MAC formation is particularly beneficial in the subretinal microenvironment, where chronic complement activation is thought to contribute to lysosomal dysfunction in RPE cells (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Guimaraes et al., 2022, pp. 3–4). Specifically, when the MAC is deposited on RPE cell membranes, it can cause lysosomal membrane permeabilization (LMP), leading to impaired vacuolar ATPase (v-ATPase) activity and subsequent loss of lysosomal acidification (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 4–8; Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3).

Under normal circumstances, lysosomal acidification is essential for the proper maturation and activation of proteolytic enzymes such as cathepsin D (CTSD) (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Guimaraes et al., 2022, pp. 3–4). By preventing the formation of the MAC, avacincaptad pegol helps to preserve the proton gradient across the lysosomal membrane, thereby maintaining optimal conditions for lysosomal enzyme activity and ensuring adequate proteolytic clearance of debris within RPE cells (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 4–8; Guimaraes et al., 2022, pp. 3–4). This preservation of lysosomal function is of critical importance in preventing the accumulation of toxic byproducts, which have been implicated in the progressive degeneration of the retina observed in GA (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Guimaraes et al., 2022, pp. 3–4).

The detailed biochemistry underlying avacincaptad pegol’s activity was refined through iterative cycles of the SELEX process, during which the aptamer’s RNA sequence was optimized for maximal affinity toward C5 (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4; 4–8). The resulting aptamer exhibits a unique three-dimensional conformation that facilitates tight binding to a specific epitope on C5, effectively neutralizing its activity while sparing upstream complement components that may have beneficial roles in immune surveillance (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 4–8; 1–4). The high specificity of this interaction is essential because it limits off-target effects and reduces the risk of broader systemic immunosuppression—a concern that has previously complicated the development of complement inhibitors (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 4–8; Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3).

Furthermore, the localized administration of avacincaptad pegol via intravitreal injection ensures that its action is confined primarily to the retina, thereby concentrating its complement-inhibiting effects where they are most needed and minimizing the potential for systemic adverse events (Qin et al., 2024, p. 3; Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4). In preclinical studies, this targeted delivery was shown to result in marked reductions in the levels of C5 cleavage products, as well as diminished deposition of the MAC on the RPE, thereby validating the mechanistic rationale of the drug (Guimaraes et al., 2022, pp. 3–4; Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3).

In summary, avacincaptad pegol’s mode of action is rooted in its ability to effectively halt the terminal steps of the complement cascade by binding to C5, thereby preventing the formation of both pro-inflammatory C5a and the deleterious MAC (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 4–8; Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). Through this mechanism, it interrupts a key pathological process in dry AMD, offering a targeted strategy to preserve RPE cell function and maintain lysosomal integrity via sustained v-ATPase activity and proper cathepsin D maturation (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Guimaraes et al., 2022, pp. 3–4).

IV. Expected Effect  
Based on the mechanistic insights discussed above, the central hypothesis for avacincaptad pegol is that its inhibition of complement C5 activation will lead to a cascade of protective effects in the retinal microenvironment, ultimately decelerating the progression of GA associated with dry AMD (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Guimaraes et al., 2022, pp. 3–4). The expected effect in both in vitro and in vivo assays is multifactorial. Primarily, the aptamer is anticipated to reduce the generation of C5 cleavage products, thereby inhibiting the formation of the MAC on the surface of RPE cells. Such an effect is measurable via immunoassays that track the levels of C5a and related fragments, as well as by quantitative imaging techniques that assess MAC deposition (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Qin et al., 2024, pp. 2–3).

At the cellular level, the inhibition of MAC deposition is expected to translate into preserved lysosomal function within RPE cells—a critical factor given the reliance of these cells on lysosomal acidification for proper autophagic flux and metabolic homeostasis (Guimaraes et al., 2022, pp. 3–4; Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). In practical assay systems, one would anticipate that RPE cell cultures treated with avacincaptad pegol show maintained or even restored acidification of lysosomes as indicated by pH-sensitive fluorescent dyes, alongside intact activity of lysosomal enzymes such as cathepsin D (Guimaraes et al., 2022, pp. 3–4; Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). This preservation of lysosomal function is hypothesized to directly correlate with a reduced accumulation of cellular debris and toxic byproducts that accelerate the degenerative process in GA (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Bege et al., 2025, pp. 4–8).

Clinically, the outcome most often evaluated in trials of avacincaptad pegol is the deceleration of GA lesion enlargement, which is quantitatively assessed through imaging modalities such as fundus autofluorescence (FAF) and optical coherence tomography (OCT) (Qin et al., 2024, pp. 2–3; 3–3). In the pivotal GATHER 1 and GATHER 2 phase II/III studies, patients treated with monthly intravitreal injections of avacincaptad pegol exhibited reductions in GA progression rates of approximately 27% to 30% relative to sham-treated groups (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Bege et al., 2025, pp. 16–17). These anatomical endpoints serve as surrogate markers for the overall efficacy of the intervention, with the underlying assumption that slowing the expansion of GA lesions will eventually lead to stabilization of visual function (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Guimaraes et al., 2022, pp. 3–4).

At the molecular level, the expected effect also includes the restoration of critical lysosomal functions disrupted by excessive complement activation. Specifically, by preventing MAC-induced lysosomal membrane permeabilization, avacincaptad pegol is anticipated to maintain the proton gradient essential for v-ATPase function, thereby preserving the acidic environment required for optimal cathepsin D processing and other lysosomal enzymes (Guimaraes et al., 2022, pp. 3–4; Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). Such preservation is not only crucial for cellular clearance mechanisms but also plays a pivotal role in preventing intracellular accumulation of debris, which is a contributing factor in the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Guimaraes et al., 2022, pp. 3–4; Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3).

Moreover, since complement components, including C5, are expressed locally in the retina by RPE cells and resident immune cells, the targeted inhibition of C5 is expected to provide direct immunomodulatory benefits within the ocular microenvironment. This localized impact is critical because it addresses the pathophysiological cross-talk between complement activation and lysosomal dysfunction, which is thought to drive a vicious cycle of chronic inflammation and cellular degeneration (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Guimaraes et al., 2022, pp. 3–4). In theory, by reestablishing a balanced complement milieu, avacincaptad pegol may also help to curtail secondary inflammatory responses that otherwise exacerbate tissue damage, thereby preserving photoreceptor integrity and ultimately stabilizing visual acuity over time (Qin et al., 2024, pp. 2–3; 3–3).

In summary, the expected effects of avacincaptad pegol in the proposed assays and clinical settings are multi-layered. At the biochemical level, one should observe a pronounced reduction in C5 cleavage, diminished MAC formation on RPE membranes, and preserved lysosomal acidification and enzyme function. At the tissue level, these molecular events are predicted to culminate in a slowdown of GA lesion enlargement, which is widely regarded as a surrogate marker for the progression of dry AMD (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Qin et al., 2024, pp. 2–3). The overall hypothesis is that these combined effects will translate into meaningful clinical benefits, offering not only anatomical preservation but also the potential for stabilization—or even modest improvement—of visual function in affected patients (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3).

V. Overall Evaluation  
A comprehensive evaluation of avacincaptad pegol reveals a therapeutic candidate that is scientifically robust, mechanistically innovative, and clinically validated for the treatment of dry AMD with geographic atrophy. One of the major strengths of this therapeutic approach lies in its highly specific mechanism of action. By directly binding to and inhibiting complement factor C5, avacincaptad pegol interrupts a key pathological process at its source, namely the activation of the terminal complement cascade that results in the formation of the pro-inflammatory mediator C5a and the membrane attack complex (MAC) (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 4–8; Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). This level of specificity confers potential advantages over broader immunosuppressive agents, as it minimizes collateral inhibition of upstream complement components that may be protective. Such precise targeting results in reduced inflammation localized to the retinal tissues and lowers the risk of systemic adverse events (Guimaraes et al., 2022, pp. 3–4; Qin et al., 2024, pp. 3–3).

The extensive chemical modifications integrated into avacincaptad pegol’s structure—including 2′-fluoro and 2′-O-methyl substitutions, the incorporation of a 3′–3′ thymidine cap, and PEGylation—greatly enhance its stability and half-life in the intraocular environment (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4). These modifications are essential because they allow for sustained inhibition of C5 with relatively infrequent dosing, thereby improving the overall treatment regimen for a patient population that is often elderly and may struggle with stringent dosing schedules (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4; Qin et al., 2024, pp. 3–3). The aptamer-based nature of this drug also endows it with a low immunogenic risk profile, circumventing one of the potential pitfalls associated with protein-based therapies such as monoclonal antibodies (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4).

Clinically, the data emerging from the GATHER 1 and GATHER 2 phase II/III trials are particularly compelling. These studies have consistently demonstrated that patients receiving intravitreal injections of avacincaptad pegol experience a significant reduction in the rate of GA lesion growth, with observed reductions ranging from 27% to 30% compared to sham controls (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Bege et al., 2025, pp. 16–17). This tangible anatomical benefit, combined with the favorable safety profile—which includes minimal ocular adverse events—confirms the viability of C5 inhibition as a disease-modifying strategy in dry AMD (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4). Given that GA has long represented an area of substantial unmet clinical need, the regulatory approval of avacincaptad pegol by the FDA in August 2023 is a significant milestone that reinforces the credibility of this therapeutic approach (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4; Qin et al., 2024, pp. 3–3).

Another notable strength is the mechanistic rationale underpinning the expected therapeutic benefits. By preventing MAC formation on RPE membranes, avacincaptad pegol not only preserves the structural integrity of these cells but also protects lysosomal function by mitigating lysosomal membrane permeabilization (LMP) (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Bege et al., 2025, pp. 4–8). The preservation of lysosomal acidification and subsequent maintenance of autophagic and proteolytic function are critical factors in slowing the progression of GA, as they help to avert the accumulation of toxic metabolic byproducts that drive cellular degeneration (Guimaraes et al., 2022, pp. 3–4; Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). Thus, the therapeutic strategy is well anchored in a clear pathological framework that directly relates to the underlying disease process in dry AMD.

Despite the considerable promise of avacincaptad pegol, several potential weaknesses and challenges remain. One concern is the translation of anatomical benefits into meaningful functional improvements with respect to visual acuity. While reduction in GA lesion enlargement is an encouraging surrogate endpoint, there is a recognized challenge in correlating these anatomical outcomes with sustained improvements or stabilization of vision (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Qin et al., 2024, pp. 2–3). In some clinical trials involving complement inhibitors, the disconnect between reduced lesion growth and measurable improvements in best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) has raised questions about whether anatomical preservation will eventually lead to perceptible functional benefits for patients (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3).

Another potential challenge relates to the inherent complexity of the complement system. C5 is a critical component of the terminal cascade; however, the redundancy and cross-talk among multiple complement pathways may potentially compromise the overall efficacy of a monotherapeutic approach targeting only C5 (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 4–8; Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). There is a possibility that, even with effective C5 blockade, alternative inflammatory pathways may partially compensate for its inhibition, thereby limiting the long-term clinical benefit. This concern suggests that future treatment paradigms might require combination approaches that target both complement-mediated and non-complement-mediated mechanisms of retinal degeneration (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Bege et al., 2025, pp. 4–8).

The mode of delivery is another factor that merits consideration. Avacincaptad pegol is delivered via monthly intravitreal injections, which, while effective in ensuring localized drug activity, impose a significant treatment burden on an elderly patient population (Qin et al., 2024, pp. 3–3). Frequent intravitreal administration is associated with logistical challenges, including the risk of injection-related complications such as endophthalmitis or retinal detachment, albeit infrequent, and may negatively impact patient compliance over extended treatment periods (Qin et al., 2024, pp. 3–3; Bege et al., 2025, pp. 16–17). Future innovation in drug delivery systems—for example, sustained-release implants or alternative non-invasive administration routes—could be critical in overcoming this limitation and enhancing long-term treatment adherence (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 16–17; 1–4).

A further challenge lies in assessing the long-term safety of chronic complement inhibition within the ocular environment. Although the localized delivery method limits systemic exposure, the prolonged suppression of C5 activity in the retina may affect local immune surveillance and potentially predispose to subclinical infections or inflammatory dysregulation (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4; Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). Given that the complement system plays a nuanced role in both tissue repair and immune defense, extended studies are necessary to definitively characterize the long-term safety profile, particularly with respect to maintaining the delicate balance between controlling pathological inflammation and preserving protective immune functions (Qin et al., 2024, pp. 3–3; Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3).

Finally, the multifactorial nature of dry AMD suggests that while C5 inhibition may effectively slow the progression of GA, it might not fully address all aspects of this complex disease process. Oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and neurodegeneration are also critical contributors to AMD pathophysiology, and a monotherapy targeting the complement cascade may need to be integrated into a broader multimodal treatment strategy to achieve optimal clinical outcomes (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Bege et al., 2025, pp. 4–8). Such considerations imply that while avacincaptad pegol represents a significant advancement in the field, its maximal therapeutic potential may be realized only when used in combination with agents that address complementary pathological processes (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Bege et al., 2025, pp. 4–8).

In synthesizing these considerations, the overall evaluation of avacincaptad pegol is highly positive. Its unique molecular design, demonstrated clinical efficacy in reducing GA lesion growth, and favorable safety profile strongly support the hypothesis that targeted inhibition of complement C5 can provide a meaningful therapeutic benefit in dry AMD (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4; Qin et al., 2024, pp. 3–3). The strengths lie in both its mechanistic precision and the tangible clinical endpoints achieved in pivotal trials, which collectively underscore the validity of the hypothesis that disrupting terminal complement activation can preserve RPE integrity and lysosomal function (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3).

Nevertheless, the translation of these anatomical benefits into long-term preservation of vision, the challenges associated with the frequent intravitreal injection regimen, and the potential activation of alternative inflammatory pathways represent hurdles that warrant continued investigation (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). Addressing these challenges will likely require further mechanistic studies, extended clinical follow-up to capture functional outcomes, and possibly the development of innovative drug delivery systems that reduce the treatment burden on patients (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 16–17; Qin et al., 2024, pp. 3–3).

In conclusion, avacincaptad pegol emerges as a scientifically rigorous and clinically validated candidate for the treatment of dry AMD with geographic atrophy. Its ability to selectively inhibit complement C5 and thereby prevent MAC formation, lysosomal acidification loss, and subsequent RPE damage provides a mechanistic rationale that is well supported by both preclinical and clinical data (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Bege et al., 2025, pp. 4–8). Despite potential challenges in correlating anatomical preservation with functional visual improvements, the overall evidence supports further development and investment in this therapeutic candidate. The favorable risk–benefit profile observed to date, coupled with its innovative chemical design and robust clinical trial outcomes, positions avacincaptad pegol as one of the most promising agents in the evolving landscape of dry AMD therapy (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4; Qin et al., 2024, pp. 3–3).

Looking ahead, it is advisable that future research efforts focus on refining patient selection criteria through the identification of biomarkers predictive of complement activation and treatment response, as well as on exploring combinatorial approaches that might synergize the effects of C5 inhibition with agents addressing other facets of AMD pathogenesis (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Bege et al., 2025, pp. 4–8). The continued monitoring of long-term safety outcomes, particularly with respect to local immune function and the potential for injection-related complications, will also be crucial to ensure that the sustained administration of avacincaptad pegol remains both safe and effective over the extended treatment durations required in this chronic condition (Qin et al., 2024, pp. 3–3).

- Primary murine RPE in vitro: A non‐toxic trehalose dose (12.5 mM) increased autophagic flux measured by tandem GFP–RFP-LC3B, increasing RFP+ autolysosomes and RFP:GFP ratios without accumulating GFP+ autophagosomes, with colocalization to LysoTracker+ acidic compartments; trehalose also attenuated H₂O₂-induced mitochondrial superoxide and restored maximal respiration (Cox et al., 2025, pp. 7–10).   - Quantify lysosomal pH restoration with LysoSensor/DND-160 ratiometry and V-ATPase subunit/activity assays in RPE models ± trehalose, including disease-relevant stress (e.g., complement challenge, A2E loading) (Boya et al., 2023, pp. 3–4, 4–6).  
  - Directly quantify TFEB nuclear translocation (immunocytochemistry with nuclear segmentation; nuclear/cytosolic fractionation and immunoblotting) under trehalose vs. TFEB-S467A and vs. AKT2 inhibition, to confirm that trehalose’s phenotypic rescue is TFEB-dependent in RPE (Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 6, 10–11).  
  - CTSD/CTSL processing and activity: Extend the CFH (H/H) results by testing trehalose across primary human RPE and AMD-donor–derived RPE; relate CTSD activity rescue to autophagic flux endpoints (LC3 turnover, p62 degradation) and to substrate clearance (POS proteolysis kinetics) (Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 6, 10–11; Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7).  
  - Lipofuscin/A2E clearance: In A2E-loaded and POS-fed RPE, quantify autofluorescence granules and A2E mass spectrometry before/after trehalose, and test dependence on TFEB (siRNA/CRISPR) and lysosomal hydrolase inhibition (e.g., pepstatin-A for CTSD) (Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7, 7–9).  
- PK/PD and delivery optimization:  
  - For topical delivery, map trehalose concentration–time in RPE/choroid and retina with LC-MS or validated Raman signatures; explore permeation enhancers or sustained-release formulations to overcome low posterior bioavailability (Cox et al., 2025, pp. 8–10, 10–13, 15–16).  
  - Define an ocular PD biomarker panel (RPE LC3B/LAMP1 colocalization, p62 decrease, CTSD activity) and link to functional readouts (ERG, OCT metrics) in chronic complement- or lipofuscin-based models (Cox et al., 2025, pp. 10–13).  
- Comparative and combinatorial strategy:  
  - Benchmark trehalose against TFEB-centric comparators (e.g., rapalogs, Ezrin inhibitors) on shared endpoints (TFEB nuclear index, lysosomal pH, CTSD activity, lipofuscin clearance), given rapamycin’s ability to reduce A2E/lipofuscin via TFEB activation and the potential of ezrin blockade to increase lysosome number and cathepsin activity in RPE (Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7, 7–9; Boya et al., 2023, pp. 4–6).  
  - Consider combination with complement modulation where indicated, as complement stress contributes to AMD-relevant lysosomal dysfunction in CFH (H/H) RPE (Ghosh et al., 2024, p. 6).

Go/no-go criteria for advancement toward GA  
- Mechanistic Go: Demonstration in RPE that trehalose increases the TFEB nuclear index by >2-fold, lowers lysosomal pH toward physiological values, and increases CTSD activity by >30% over disease-state baseline, with concordant increases in LC3B–LAMP1 colocalization and p62 degradation; abrogation of effects by TFEB knockdown would confirm mechanism (Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 10–11; Cox et al., 2025, pp. 7–8; Boya et al., 2023, pp. 3–4).  
- Functional Go: Demonstrated reduction of A2E/lipofuscin by ≥25% in RPE models without cytotoxicity, and structural/functional rescue in a chronic AMD-relevant animal model (e.g., CFH-risk or complement-driven models) with durable effects beyond acute stress models (Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7; Cox et al., 2025, pp. 8–10; Ghosh et al., 2024, p. 6).  
- Safety Go: No evidence of autophagy-associated cytotoxicity at the intended exposure (maintained viability; absence of excessive LC3-II accumulation without flux; ocular histopathology clean) (Abokyi et al., 2020, pp. 15–16; Cox et al., 2025, pp. 8–10).

Conclusion  
The totality of evidence supports trehalose as a plausible, repurposable modulator of the TFEB–lysosome/autophagy axis in the RPE with multiple independent signals of autophagy flux enhancement, lysosomal hydrolase restoration (CTSD/L), and cytoprotection in oxidative/complement stress contexts, delivered via mechanisms that appear mTOR-independent and therefore potentially safer than broad mTORC1 inhibition (Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 10–11; Cox et al., 2025, pp. 7–8; Abokyi et al., 2020, pp. 1–2; Ghosh et al., 2023, pp. 11–15). However, the hypothesis’s most stringent claims—quantitative restoration of lysosomal acidification, trehalose-driven TFEB nuclear translocation in RPE, and direct lipofuscin/A2E clearance leading to slowed geographic atrophy progression—are not yet demonstrated in the supplied literature and require targeted mechanistic and disease-model validation (Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 10–11; Abokyi et al., 2020, pp. 16–17; Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7; Cox et al., 2025, pp. 8–10). Given strong biological plausibility and encouraging preclinical signals, a focused IND-enabling program that closes these gaps is justified, with early emphasis on mechanistic biomarkers (lysosomal pH, TFEB nuclear index, CTSD activity), pharmacokinetics of posterior delivery, and chronic AMD-relevant efficacy models before advancing to clinical study in GA (Boya et al., 2023, pp. 3–4; Cox et al., 2025, pp. 10–13; Ghosh et al., 2024, p. 6).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Anakinra (brand: Kineret) is a recombinant, non-glycosylated form of the human interleukin-1 receptor antagonist (IL-1Ra) that competitively binds the type I interleukin-1 receptor (IL-1RI) and prevents signaling by IL-1α and IL-1β, thereby broadly antagonizing downstream IL-1–dependent signal transduction cascades (notably NF-κB and MAPK) in responsive cells (Dabouz, 2024; Dabouz et al., 2020). IL-1Ra belongs to the class of anti-cytokine biologics that block pro-inflammatory cytokine signaling, a therapeutic strategy that has been validated across systemic autoinflammatory and autoimmune diseases; Kineret has an extensive human safety and pharmacology dossier as an approved product, with prescribing information available for systemic use (Mesquida, Drawnel, & Fauser, 2019). Within ophthalmology, IL-1 pathway blockade has been investigated in multiple preclinical ocular models and has seen clinical use for inflammatory eye diseases; routes explored include systemic administration of anakinra for uveitis and scleritis, topical IL-1 antagonists for ocular surface disease (e.g., isunakinra/EBI-005), and experimental ocular gene therapy encoding IL-1Ra (Fabiani et al., 2017). In posterior segment disease models, intravitreal recombinant IL-1Ra (anakinra) inhibited laser-induced choroidal neovascularization (CNV) in rodents in a dose-dependent fashion, establishing local ocular pharmacologic activity of IL-1R antagonism in retina/choroid (Fabiani et al., 2017; Sandhu, Lambert, Xu, & Kaplan, 2018).

Therapeutic History  
Systemic indications and ocular inflammatory experience. Anakinra has long been employed systemically in rheumatology and has been repurposed for ocular autoinflammatory and autoimmune conditions such as Behçet uveitis, Blau syndrome/CAPS phenotypes, and refractory scleritis, with reported improvements in intraocular inflammation and steroid-sparing in case series and retrospective cohorts; dosing regimens reported include 100–150 mg daily or weight-based 1–3 mg/kg daily subcutaneous dosing, with acceptable tolerability profiles dominated by mild injection-site reactions in the ocular cohorts cited (Fabiani et al., 2017; Korhonen, 2024). A practical constraint is anakinra’s short systemic half-life that necessitates daily dosing, with relapse reported upon dose reductions in some inflammatory eye disease cases—an important consideration for chronic indications (Fabiani et al., 2017; Korhonen, 2024). Topical isunakinra/IL-1Ra formulations for ocular surface disease demonstrated clinically meaningful symptom and sign improvements in randomized trials, high ocular receptor occupancy (~97%) at low doses, minimal systemic exposure (plasma below detection), and a favorable local safety signal, although these outcomes pertain to the anterior segment and cannot be extrapolated directly to the posterior segment (Fabiani et al., 2017).

Posterior segment and AMD-relevant preclinical work. Multiple animal studies substantiate that IL-1 signaling is active and targetable in the posterior segment. In a rat CNV model, intravitreal anakinra led to dose-dependent reductions in neovascular area; related IL-1β-targeted interventions prevented CNV without exacerbating photoreceptor degeneration, arguing against gross phototoxicity from IL-1 blockade in that setting (Sandhu et al., 2018; Fabiani et al., 2017). In a blue light–induced retinal degeneration model, systemic IL-1R antagonism with anakinra mitigated inflammatory readouts, reduced accumulation of subretinal macrophages, preserved photoreceptor structure, and maintained ERG function; an allosteric IL-1R modulator (rytvela) was somewhat superior, but anakinra nonetheless produced protective effects (Dabouz et al., 2020; Dabouz, 2024). Mechanistically, these studies localized IL-1β production to inflammasome-active subretinal mononuclear phagocytes (MPs) and mapped Il1r1 expression mainly to astroglia and vascular cells in mouse retina, supporting paracrine IL-1 signaling to neurovascular targets in the outer retina (Dabouz et al., 2020; Dabouz, 2024).

Human clinical evidence in dry AMD/geographic atrophy. No published human trials of anakinra for dry AMD/geographic atrophy (GA) were identified in the provided materials; a registry search string returned 18 ClinicalTrials.gov hits combining anakinra with retinal keywords, but no trial-level information (indication, route, dose, status, outcomes) was provided, and no AMD/GA trials of anakinra are documented here (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.). Systemic IL-1β blockade with canakinumab showed no effect in a diabetic retinopathy exploratory clinical context, underscoring translational uncertainty of systemic IL-1 pathway modulation for posterior segment disease (Korhonen, 2024).

Mechanistic rationale in RPE/AMD. Extensive literature supports that in AMD-relevant stress contexts the RPE and subretinal myeloid cells exhibit NLRP3 inflammasome activation, caspase-1–dependent maturation of IL-1β and IL-18, lysosomal membrane permeabilization (LMP) with cathepsin release, and altered autophagy/heterophagy—mechanistic substrates for chronic para-inflammation and cell death (apoptosis → pyroptosis shift) in RPE (Treanor, n.d.; Yerramothu, Vijay, & Willcox, 2018; Kaarniranta et al., 2023). IL-1β levels are elevated in AMD vitreous and plasma, and microglia/MP-derived IL-1β can drive chemokine and cytokine production by Müller cells and RPE, linking IL-1 to retinal inflammatory amplification (Nashine et al., 2022; Korhonen, 2024). The RPE itself produces IL-1Ra and uses IL-1Ra to limit immune activation: IL-1Ra suppresses necrosis-induced release of IL-6, IL-8, and MCP-1 from ARPE-19 and reduces antigen-presenting functions in RPE cocultures, indicating that IL-1 signaling is operational in RPE and that IL-1R antagonism can blunt RPE-mediated inflammatory outputs in vitro (Fabiani et al., 2017; Kaur & Singh, 2021).

Mechanism of Action  
Receptor pharmacology. IL-1β and IL-1α bind IL-1RI and recruit IL-1 receptor accessory protein (IL-1RAcP) to form a signaling complex that initiates MyD88-dependent activation of IRAKs, TRAF6, TAK1, and downstream MAPKs (JNK/p38) and NF-κB, driving expression of inflammatory mediators and cell-type–specific responses (Dabouz, 2024). Anakinra is a competitive orthosteric antagonist of IL-1RI that prevents IL-1α/β binding and thereby blocks the formation of the signaling complex with IL-1RAcP, “non-selectively” inhibiting downstream IL-1–dependent pathways across cell types expressing IL-1RI (Dabouz, 2024; Dabouz et al., 2020). In the blue-light retinal injury model, orthosteric antagonism with anakinra and allosteric modulation with rytvela each prevented IL-1–driven retinal inflammation and photoreceptor injury; mechanistically, both agents protected neuroretinal compartments that express IL-1R while not necessarily reducing IL-1β produced in macrophage conditioned media, consistent with receptor-level antagonism in responder cells (Dabouz et al., 2020; Dabouz, 2024).

Cellular sources/targets in retina. In injury models, Il1b is upregulated primarily in infiltrating subretinal mononuclear phagocytes that co-express NLRP3 and caspase-1, whereas Il1r1 expression is detected predominantly in astrocytes, pericytes, endothelial cells, and bipolar cells, with little to no detection in photoreceptors or MPs by scRNA-seq; this places the critical pharmacodynamic target of anakinra on neurovascular/astroglial elements rather than on the IL-1β-producing cells themselves (Dabouz et al., 2020; Dabouz, 2024). IL-1β is elevated in AMD patients’ vitreous and is a recognized biomarker of retinal inflammation; microglia-derived IL-1β amplifies chemokine signaling by Müller and RPE cells, indicating that RPE can serve as an IL-1–responsive amplifier of inflammation even if Il1r1 detection varies by model and assay (Nashine et al., 2022; Korhonen, 2024). RPE-derived endogenous IL-1Ra provides further evidence that IL-1 signaling—and its antagonism—are biologically relevant in the RPE microenvironment (Fabiani et al., 2017).

Inflammasome context and limitations of IL-1R blockade. In RPE and adjacent retinal cells, NLRP3 inflammasome activation is triggered by AMD-relevant stimuli including A2E/lipofuscin photooxidation, drusen components, DICER1/Alu RNA accumulation, oxidized lipoproteins, complement/cofactors, ROS, and lysosomal membrane permeabilization with cathepsin release (Treanor, n.d.; Yerramothu et al., 2018). Inflammasome activation requires priming (e.g., TLR-NF-κB–dependent upregulation of NLRP3/pro-IL-1β) followed by an activation signal (e.g., mtROS, LMP), culminating in caspase-1 activation and secretion of mature IL-1β and IL-18; inflammasome priming can shift RPE death from apoptosis to pyroptosis, increasing inflammatory cytokine release and DAMP extrusion (Treanor, n.d.; Kaarniranta et al., 2023). Critically, IL-1 pathway blockers such as anakinra do not inhibit upstream inflammasome assembly, caspase-1 activation, or IL-18 production; thus, IL-1R antagonism will block IL-1 signaling but will not shut down inflammasome-dependent IL-18 release or pyroptotic execution, which may continue to drive disease biology (Korhonen, 2024). Moreover, in some experimental paradigms, IL-18 can have protective or context-dependent roles in AMD models, complicating network-level predictions when only IL-1 signaling is blocked (Lim et al., 2020).

Evidence gaps regarding lysosomal targets. The working hypothesis posits that anakinra will prevent IL-1β-driven inflammasome amplification and lysosomal destabilization in RPE, preserving vacuolar H+-ATPase (v-ATPase) function and cathepsin D (CTSD) maturation/activity; however, the provided materials contain no direct experimental evidence that IL-1R antagonism rescues v-ATPase activity, lysosomal pH, or CTSD processing in RPE, nor that anakinra reduces lysosomal membrane permeabilization in these systems (Lim et al., 2020; Treanor, n.d.). While lysosomal destabilization and cathepsin B/L release are well-documented inflammasome triggers in RPE, and bafilomycin A1 (a v-ATPase inhibitor) has been used to model lysosomal/autophagic impairment that activates NLRP3 and IL-1β release, there is no reported dataset here demonstrating that IL-1R blockade restores lysosomal acidification or cathepsin D maturation in RPE (Yerramothu et al., 2018; Piippo, 2019). Consequently, the proposed IL-1→lysosome preservation claims remain conjectural in the absence of targeted RPE lysosomal measurements following anakinra treatment in AMD-relevant paradigms (Lim et al., 2020; Treanor, n.d.).

Expected Effect  
Assay-level effects in retinal/RPE systems. Based on the presented literature, IL-1R antagonism with anakinra is expected to reduce IL-1–driven inflammatory signaling in neuroretinal and gliovascular compartments, attenuate subretinal macrophage accumulation/activation, and preserve photoreceptor structure/function in acute inflammatory injury paradigms; these effects have been demonstrated in the blue light model (reduced GFAP, Il1b/Il6/Ccl2 transcripts, fewer subretinal MPs, more preserved ONL and ERG amplitudes) (Dabouz, 2024; Dabouz et al., 2020). In explant co-culture systems where LPS/ATP-activated macrophages produce IL-1β, IL-1R antagonists and anti-IL-1β antibodies abrogate photoreceptor death, supporting a causal role for IL-1β and a direct cytoprotective effect of IL-1 pathway blockade on IL-1RI-expressing retinal cells (Dabouz, 2024). In vitro RPE models show that IL-1Ra can suppress necrosis-induced secretion of IL-6, IL-8, and MCP-1 (likely via NF-κB), suggesting that anakinra may dampen autocrine/paracrine amplification in RPE cultures challenged with danger signals—though definitive RPE IL-1RI expression patterns in vivo remain incompletely defined in the cited mouse scRNA-seq data (Fabiani et al., 2017; Dabouz et al., 2020).

Inflammasome priming versus activation. IL-1 can contribute to priming (NF-κB–dependent) of inflammasome components; therefore, anakinra might indirectly reduce NLRP3 priming in some contexts by interrupting IL-1 positive feedback loops, leading to lower pro-IL-1β and possibly reduced susceptibility to subsequent activation triggers (Fabiani et al., 2017). However, because anakinra acts downstream of inflammasome assembly, it will not prevent caspase-1 activation, gasdermin D pore formation, pyroptosis, or IL-18 maturation/secretion once NLRP3 is engaged—which are all relevant to RPE and subretinal myeloid biology in AMD (Korhonen, 2024; Treanor, n.d.; Kaarniranta et al., 2023). Consequently, anakinra’s benefit in dry AMD models that are dominated by RPE-intrinsic inflammasome activation and pyroptosis may be partial, favoring reductions in IL-1–driven chemokine/cytokine cascades and immune cell recruitment over direct prevention of inflammasome-executed cell death (Korhonen, 2024; Treanor, n.d.).

Lysosomal endpoints. The proposed preservation of v-ATPase function and cathepsin D activity is not currently supported by primary data in the provided sources; no reports demonstrate that anakinra normalizes lysosomal pH, protease maturation (including CTSD), or membrane integrity in RPE subjected to AMD-relevant stressors (Lim et al., 2020; Treanor, n.d.; Piippo, 2019). While inhibiting IL-1 signaling may lower NF-κB–driven transcription of inflammatory mediators (and thus lessen secondary stressors to lysosomes), the extent to which this translates into measurable correction of lysosomal biology in RPE remains to be tested experimentally (Fabiani et al., 2017).

Translational dosing and safety in the eye. In mice, systemic anakinra at 4 mg/kg twice daily for 3 days produced retinal protection in the blue light model; this regimen emphasizes short-term systemic exposures in an acute injury context rather than chronic degenerative settings (Dabouz, 2024). In CNV rodents, intravitreal IL-1Ra reduced neovascularization without aggravating photoreceptor degeneration, providing proof-of-concept for posterior segment delivery and a supportive safety signal in that animal model (Sandhu et al., 2018). Clinically, systemic anakinra has an established safety profile in inflammatory eye disease cohorts, but no intravitreal human anakinra safety data in AMD/GA are presented here; systemic IL-1β blockade (canakinumab) did not improve retinopathy outcomes in a separate context, and anakinra’s daily dosing requirement remains a burden for chronic use unless long-acting ocular delivery is engineered (Korhonen, 2024; Fabiani et al., 2017).

Overall Evaluation  
Merits  
- Biological plausibility in AMD. AMD-relevant stressors activate NLRP3 in RPE and subretinal myeloid cells, elevating IL-1β and IL-18 and driving para-inflammatory cascades and pyroptosis; IL-1β is increased in AMD vitreous and plasma, and IL-1–producing MPs are present at sites of pathology, establishing IL-1 as a rational target for modulating retinal inflammation (Treanor, n.d.; Nashine et al., 2022; Korhonen, 2024).  
- Pharmacologic validation in retinal models. Anakinra significantly reduced inflammation and preserved retinal structure/function in a light-damage model and intravitreally suppressed CNV in rodents, indicating target engagement and protective potential in the posterior segment; IL-1β neutralization prevented CNV without exacerbating photoreceptor degeneration, arguing for a non-toxic profile in those contexts (Dabouz et al., 2020; Dabouz, 2024; Sandhu et al., 2018).  
- RPE-relevant immunobiology. RPE naturally produces IL-1Ra, and exogenous IL-1Ra reduces necrosis-induced inflammatory mediator release from RPE and suppresses dendritic-cell activation in RPE co-cultures, suggesting that anakinra could attenuate RPE-mediated inflammatory amplification in dry AMD (Fabiani et al., 2017; Kaur & Singh, 2021).  
- Clinical and formulation precedents. Systemic ocular use of anakinra in uveitis and scleritis shows clinical feasibility and manageable safety; topical IL-1 antagonists have robust ocular safety signals; gene therapy encoding IL-1Ra and intravitreal administration have been explored preclinically, supporting a spectrum of delivery options that could be adapted for posterior segment disease (Fabiani et al., 2017).

Limitations and risks  
- Mechanistic incompleteness vis-à-vis inflammasomes. IL-1R blockade will not prevent upstream NLRP3 activation, caspase-1 activity, gasdermin-mediated pyroptosis, or IL-18 production; in RPE-intrinsic inflammasome-dominant pathophysiology, anakinra would be expected to blunt downstream IL-1–mediated amplification and leukocyte recruitment but not stop the execution machinery of inflammasome-driven cell death (Korhonen, 2024; Treanor, n.d.; Kaarniranta et al., 2023).  
- Unsubstantiated lysosomal rescue claims. There is no evidence here that anakinra preserves lysosomal acidification (v-ATPase function), cathepsin D maturation/activity, or prevents LMP in RPE under AMD-relevant stress; this is a critical gap because the proposed therapeutic specificity hinges on cytokine–lysosome cross-talk that remains to be demonstrated (Lim et al., 2020; Treanor, n.d.; Piippo, 2019).  
- Target expression uncertainties. In mouse retina, Il1r1 is enriched in astroglia and vascular cells and not detected in photoreceptors or MPs by scRNA-seq, complicating assumptions about direct photoreceptor or RPE targeting by anakinra in vivo; while RPE responds to IL-1 in vitro and produces IL-1Ra, spatial and species differences in IL-1RI distribution may shape efficacy and delivery decisions (Dabouz et al., 2020; Dabouz, 2024; Fabiani et al., 2017).  
- Mixed translational signals. Systemic IL-1β blockade did not improve diabetic retinopathy outcomes in the cited study, and anakinra’s systemic short half-life imposes burdensome daily dosing for chronic disease; there is no documented human safety/efficacy experience with intravitreal anakinra in AMD/GA in the provided sources (Korhonen, 2024; Fabiani et al., 2017; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).  
- Network complexity. NLRP3/IL-18 can exert context-dependent protective or detrimental effects in AMD models; while anakinra does not block IL-18 signaling, its selective inhibition of IL-1 may not suffice to rebalance inflammasome-driven pathology if pyroptosis and IL-18-dependent pathways remain active (Lim et al., 2020).

Go/No-Go considerations and critical experiments  
- RPE-centric validation. Test anakinra in human RPE models exposed to A2E/blue-light, drusen components, DICER1/Alu RNA, or oxidized lipoproteins; quantify NLRP3 priming (NLRP3, pro-IL-1β), activation (ASC specks, caspase-1 cleavage), downstream cytokines (IL-1β, IL-18), and execution (GSDMD cleavage/pyroptosis markers), with and without anakinra to define points of pathway modulation (Treanor, n.d.; Yerramothu et al., 2018).  
- Lysosomal endpoints. Directly measure lysosomal pH, v-ATPase activity, LMP (galectin-3 puncta), cathepsin D maturation/activity, and autophagic flux in the same RPE paradigms ± anakinra to test the hypothesis that IL-1R blockade preserves lysosomal integrity and protease processing (Piippo, 2019).  
- In vivo GA-relevant models. Move from acute light injury to RPE-atrophy models (e.g., chronic photooxidative stress, Alu RNA/DICER1 disruption, lipofuscin models) to assess whether anakinra reduces rates of RPE atrophy, outer retinal thinning, and visual function decline; include comparators targeting the inflammasome (e.g., NLRP3 inhibitors) to benchmark effect sizes and mechanistic depth (Treanor, n.d.; Kaarniranta et al., 2023; Lim et al., 2020).  
- Ocular delivery and PK. Develop and test intravitreal dosing and, preferably, sustained-release formats for anakinra to overcome systemic short half-life; establish vitreous/retinal PK and receptor occupancy, and evaluate ocular safety (IOP, ERG, histopathology) and immunogenicity (anti-drug antibodies) in large-eye species (Korhonen, 2024; Fabiani et al., 2017).  
- Biomarker strategy. Use vitreous/plasma IL-1β and retinal inflammatory transcript signatures as pharmacodynamic biomarkers; consider scRNA-seq to confirm target cell engagement (Il1r1-expressing compartments) pre- and post-treatment (Nashine et al., 2022; Dabouz, 2024).

Positioning relative to alternatives  
Because anakinra does not interrupt inflammasome activation or execution, proximal inhibitors of the NLRP3 inflammasome (e.g., MCC950-class) may provide deeper control of IL-1β/IL-18 production and pyroptosis in RPE-driven disease, at the cost of potentially suppressing beneficial IL-18 signaling in some contexts; preclinical literature shows NLRP3 blockade can be protective in retinal models, meriting parallel evaluation (Lim et al., 2020). Conversely, allosteric IL-1R modulators (rytvela-type) have shown superior protection to anakinra in the light-damage model and may offer functional selectivity (e.g., sparing NF-κB while inhibiting JNK/p38/AP-1) with improved distribution and immunogenicity profiles; these properties deserve consideration if an IL-1-targeting approach is pursued (Dabouz, 2024; Dabouz et al., 2020).

Conclusions  
- Strength of rationale. There is robust evidence that IL-1β is elevated and pathogenic in retinal neuroinflammation and that IL-1R antagonism—including anakinra—can protect retina in preclinical models by reducing inflammatory signaling and immune cell recruitment; RPE-relevant IL-1 biology further supports plausibility (Dabouz et al., 2020; Dabouz, 2024; Fabiani et al., 2017).  
- Weakness of hypothesis specifics. The central claim that anakinra preserves v-ATPase function and cathepsin D maturation in RPE lacks support in the provided literature; moreover, IL-1R blockade cannot prevent upstream inflammasome activation or pyroptosis, limiting its capacity to halt RPE-intrinsic degenerative processes central to GA (Lim et al., 2020; Korhonen, 2024; Treanor, n.d.; Piippo, 2019).  
- Translational readiness. No human AMD/GA trials of anakinra are documented here; systemic IL-1β blockade has shown limited efficacy in retinal vascular disease, and anakinra’s dosing logistics are unfavorable for chronic ocular therapy without dedicated ocular delivery systems (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.; Korhonen, 2024).

Overall Evaluation  
Anakinra is a mechanistically credible anti-inflammatory candidate to blunt IL-1–driven retinal inflammation and leukocyte recruitment, with reproducible preclinical efficacy signals in posterior-segment injury models and supportive RPE-centric immunobiology; however, the specific hypothesis that it will mechanistically preserve lysosomal v-ATPase function and cathepsin D activity in RPE is currently unsupported by direct evidence, and IL-1R antagonism is unlikely to arrest inflammasome activation, IL-18 signaling, or pyroptotic cell death that contribute to RPE atrophy in dry AMD (Dabouz et al., 2020; Dabouz, 2024; Fabiani et al., 2017; Korhonen, 2024; Lim et al., 2020). Given the absence of clinical data in GA and delivery constraints, anakinra merits consideration as an adjunct anti-inflammatory approach contingent on (1) generation of RPE-focused data demonstrating modulation of inflammasome priming and lysosomal integrity, and (2) development of sustained intraocular delivery; in parallel, more proximal interventions (NLRP3 inhibitors) and IL-1R allosteric modulators with superior preclinical efficacy should be benchmarked as potentially higher-leverage strategies for disease modification in dry AMD (Lim et al., 2020; Dabouz et al., 2020).
