I. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Avacincaptad pegol, commercially known as Zimura, is a highly engineered, synthetic RNA aptamer designed specifically to target complement factor C5 for the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) with geographic atrophy (GA) features (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4). This molecule is comprised of a 39-nucleotide sequence that has been rigorously selected through in vitro techniques to offer high affinity and specificity for its target, ensuring that it binds precisely to C5 and prevents its activation (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4). Unlike traditional monoclonal antibodies, aptamers are oligonucleotide-based therapeutic agents that combine the benefits of well-defined chemical synthesis with tunable pharmacokinetics and low immunogenicity. In this instance, avacincaptad pegol has been further optimized by incorporating multiple chemical modifications; these include 2′-fluorine substitutions on pyrimidine residues, 2′-O-methyl modifications on select purine nucleotides, a protected 3′–3′ thymidine cap, and a branched polyethylene glycol (PEG) moiety to extend its half-life within the eye (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4). Such modifications confer enhanced resistance to degradation by nucleases and reduce renal clearance, thereby allowing the compound to remain active in the subretinal space longer than unmodified oligonucleotides (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4). The development of avacincaptad pegol is rooted in the evolution of aptamer technologies that began with earlier compounds like pegaptanib, the pioneer aptamer approved for neovascular AMD; however, unlike pegaptanib, avacincaptad pegol is engineered to target a different disease mechanism by focusing on the terminal complement cascade (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–8). Overall, the molecular design and chemical sophistication of this aptamer designate it as a next-generation candidate in the field of oligonucleotide therapeutics, with its unique physical and chemical attributes directly addressing specific pathogenic mechanisms of dry AMD (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–8).

Avacincaptad pegol belongs to a broader class of therapeutic compounds known as aptamers that act as “chemical antibodies.” These agents are synthesized via systematic evolution of ligands by exponential enrichment (SELEX), a process that allows for iterative refinement of the aptamer’s binding characteristics so that it selectively interacts with its intended protein target (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4). Aptamers have been used in various clinical applications due to their predictable pharmacologic profiles, their ease of chemical modification, and their typically low risk of eliciting an immune response. Their utility has been demonstrated not only in ocular therapeutics but also across a range of medical indications where precise modulation of molecular pathways is desired (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4). With the advent of avacincaptad pegol, the application of aptamer technology has been repurposed specifically for the modulation of the complement cascade—a key inflammatory pathway implicated in retinal degenerative diseases such as dry AMD (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4).

The synthetic origins of avacincaptad pegol underscore a scalable manufacturing process with robust quality control measures, making the compound attractive not only from a scientific standpoint but also from a commercial and regulatory perspective (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4). The structural characteristics, including its nucleic acid backbone and PEG conjugation, have been optimized to ensure adequate tissue penetration and sustained activity when delivered via intravitreal injection, minimizing systemic exposure and maximizing local therapeutic concentrations (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4). In summary, avacincaptad pegol is a representative example of how innovative chemical modifications and advanced selection technologies converge to generate therapeutic candidates that address the critical unmet needs in degenerative retinal diseases (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4).

II. Therapeutic History  
The trajectory of avacincaptad pegol from bench to bedside is emblematic of the rapid evolution in our understanding of the complement system’s role in AMD pathogenesis. Historically, the complement cascade—a series of proteolytic reactions leading to the formation of the membrane attack complex (MAC)—has been implicated in the chronic, low-grade inflammatory processes that contribute to retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) degeneration (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4; Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). Early efforts in pharmacologic intervention focused on modulating angiogenesis through agents like anti-VEGF drugs; however, these therapies failed to address the underlying complement-mediated inflammatory milieu that is particularly pronounced in the dry form of AMD (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4, 16–17).

The recognition that complement overactivation plays a central role in GA led researchers to explore agents that could precisely inhibit key components of this cascade. Avacincaptad pegol emerged as a promising candidate in this context, designed to block complement factor C5—a critical nexus point in the pathway responsible for the generation of both the potent inflammatory mediator C5a and the membrane attack complex (MAC) via C5b (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Bege et al., 2025, pp. 4–8). Preclinical studies using animal models of AMD demonstrated that inhibition of C5 could mitigate complement-mediated damage to RPE cells and reduce progression of GA lesions, laying the foundation for subsequent clinical investigations (Guimaraes et al., 2022, pp. 3–4; Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3).

The clinical development program for avacincaptad pegol has been extensive. Notably, phase II/III randomized controlled trials—collectively referred to as GATHER 1 and GATHER 2—were designed to evaluate its safety and efficacy in patients with GA secondary to AMD (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 16–17; Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). These pivotal trials enrolled hundreds of patients and involved monthly intravitreal injections, a route of administration that allows for high local concentrations of the drug while minimizing systemic exposure (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 16–17; Qin et al., 2024, p. 3). The results from these clinical studies were encouraging, as they consistently demonstrated statistically significant reductions in GA lesion growth in treatment groups compared to sham injections, with reported reductions in lesion progression on the order of approximately 27–30% over follow-up periods ranging from 12 to 18 months (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Guimaraes et al., 2022, pp. 3–4; Bege et al., 2025, pp. 16–17).

Beyond efficacy, the safety profile of avacincaptad pegol has been affirmed in multiple studies. The intravitreal route of administration confines the compound’s activity largely to the ocular compartment, thereby minimizing systemic immunosuppression—a particularly valuable attribute given the complement system’s role in host defense (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4; Qin et al., 2024, p. 3). Reports from clinical trials indicated that adverse events were primarily related to the injection procedure itself, with few drug-related serious ocular events recorded (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4; Guimaraes et al., 2022, pp. 3–4). This favorable safety record, combined with robust efficacy data, contributed to the FDA’s decision to approve avacincaptad pegol for the treatment of GA in August 2023, marking it as the second approved aptamer medicine in the field of retinal disease, following pegaptanib (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4; Qin et al., 2024, p. 3).

In parallel with these developments in dry AMD, avacincaptad pegol has been examined in observational studies and preclinical models that further delineate its mechanism of action and long-term benefits. Although past investigations in other complement-mediated ocular conditions have encountered mixed results, the specific targeting of C5 in the case of GA appears to be particularly promising, as evidenced by the consistent reduction in lesion progression reported by the GATHER trials (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 16–17; Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). The accumulated clinical experience provides a compelling historical context for its use, reinforcing the therapeutic rationale of complement inhibition in mitigating the inflammatory and degenerative processes that drive dry AMD (Guimaraes et al., 2022, pp. 3–4; Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3).

Moreover, the evolution of complement-modulating therapies in retinal diseases has been marked by significant collaborations between academia, industry, and regulatory agencies, all of which have embraced a more nuanced understanding of the immune processes involved in AMD. These concerted efforts have not only fostered the development of avacincaptad pegol but have also encouraged ongoing research into combination therapies that may further enhance clinical outcomes (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4, 16–17). As such, the therapeutic history of avacincaptad pegol is characterized by a steady progression from mechanistic discovery in the laboratory to robust clinical validation, underscoring its potential as a transformative agent in the management of dry AMD (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Qin et al., 2024, p. 3).

III. Mechanism of Action  
The mechanism of action of avacincaptad pegol is both specific and multifaceted, centering on the selective inhibition of complement factor C5—a pivotal molecule in the terminal complement pathway (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 4–8; Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). Under physiological conditions, C5 is cleaved into C5a and C5b. C5a acts as a potent anaphylatoxin that promotes inflammation through the recruitment and activation of immune cells, while C5b initiates the assembly of the membrane attack complex (MAC) by sequentially binding to complement components C6 through C9 (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Bege et al., 2025, pp. 4–8). The formation of the MAC on the surface of retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells is a critical driver of cell lysis and inflammatory damage that ultimately contributes to the progression of geographic atrophy in dry AMD (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Guimaraes et al., 2022, pp. 3–4).

Avacincaptad pegol exerts its therapeutic effect by binding directly to C5 with extremely high affinity, thereby blocking its enzymatic cleavage (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 4–8; Guimaraes et al., 2022, pp. 3–4). This inhibition prevents the generation of both C5a and C5b, ultimately forestalling the downstream assembly of the MAC (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 4–8; Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). The direct blockade of MAC formation is particularly beneficial in the subretinal microenvironment, where chronic complement activation is thought to contribute to lysosomal dysfunction in RPE cells (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Guimaraes et al., 2022, pp. 3–4). Specifically, when the MAC is deposited on RPE cell membranes, it can cause lysosomal membrane permeabilization (LMP), leading to impaired vacuolar ATPase (v-ATPase) activity and subsequent loss of lysosomal acidification (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 4–8; Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3).

Under normal circumstances, lysosomal acidification is essential for the proper maturation and activation of proteolytic enzymes such as cathepsin D (CTSD) (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Guimaraes et al., 2022, pp. 3–4). By preventing the formation of the MAC, avacincaptad pegol helps to preserve the proton gradient across the lysosomal membrane, thereby maintaining optimal conditions for lysosomal enzyme activity and ensuring adequate proteolytic clearance of debris within RPE cells (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 4–8; Guimaraes et al., 2022, pp. 3–4). This preservation of lysosomal function is of critical importance in preventing the accumulation of toxic byproducts, which have been implicated in the progressive degeneration of the retina observed in GA (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Guimaraes et al., 2022, pp. 3–4).

The detailed biochemistry underlying avacincaptad pegol’s activity was refined through iterative cycles of the SELEX process, during which the aptamer’s RNA sequence was optimized for maximal affinity toward C5 (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4; 4–8). The resulting aptamer exhibits a unique three-dimensional conformation that facilitates tight binding to a specific epitope on C5, effectively neutralizing its activity while sparing upstream complement components that may have beneficial roles in immune surveillance (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 4–8; 1–4). The high specificity of this interaction is essential because it limits off-target effects and reduces the risk of broader systemic immunosuppression—a concern that has previously complicated the development of complement inhibitors (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 4–8; Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3).

Furthermore, the localized administration of avacincaptad pegol via intravitreal injection ensures that its action is confined primarily to the retina, thereby concentrating its complement-inhibiting effects where they are most needed and minimizing the potential for systemic adverse events (Qin et al., 2024, p. 3; Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4). In preclinical studies, this targeted delivery was shown to result in marked reductions in the levels of C5 cleavage products, as well as diminished deposition of the MAC on the RPE, thereby validating the mechanistic rationale of the drug (Guimaraes et al., 2022, pp. 3–4; Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3).

In summary, avacincaptad pegol’s mode of action is rooted in its ability to effectively halt the terminal steps of the complement cascade by binding to C5, thereby preventing the formation of both pro-inflammatory C5a and the deleterious MAC (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 4–8; Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). Through this mechanism, it interrupts a key pathological process in dry AMD, offering a targeted strategy to preserve RPE cell function and maintain lysosomal integrity via sustained v-ATPase activity and proper cathepsin D maturation (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Guimaraes et al., 2022, pp. 3–4).

IV. Expected Effect  
Based on the mechanistic insights discussed above, the central hypothesis for avacincaptad pegol is that its inhibition of complement C5 activation will lead to a cascade of protective effects in the retinal microenvironment, ultimately decelerating the progression of GA associated with dry AMD (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Guimaraes et al., 2022, pp. 3–4). The expected effect in both in vitro and in vivo assays is multifactorial. Primarily, the aptamer is anticipated to reduce the generation of C5 cleavage products, thereby inhibiting the formation of the MAC on the surface of RPE cells. Such an effect is measurable via immunoassays that track the levels of C5a and related fragments, as well as by quantitative imaging techniques that assess MAC deposition (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Qin et al., 2024, pp. 2–3).

At the cellular level, the inhibition of MAC deposition is expected to translate into preserved lysosomal function within RPE cells—a critical factor given the reliance of these cells on lysosomal acidification for proper autophagic flux and metabolic homeostasis (Guimaraes et al., 2022, pp. 3–4; Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). In practical assay systems, one would anticipate that RPE cell cultures treated with avacincaptad pegol show maintained or even restored acidification of lysosomes as indicated by pH-sensitive fluorescent dyes, alongside intact activity of lysosomal enzymes such as cathepsin D (Guimaraes et al., 2022, pp. 3–4; Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). This preservation of lysosomal function is hypothesized to directly correlate with a reduced accumulation of cellular debris and toxic byproducts that accelerate the degenerative process in GA (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Bege et al., 2025, pp. 4–8).

Clinically, the outcome most often evaluated in trials of avacincaptad pegol is the deceleration of GA lesion enlargement, which is quantitatively assessed through imaging modalities such as fundus autofluorescence (FAF) and optical coherence tomography (OCT) (Qin et al., 2024, pp. 2–3; 3–3). In the pivotal GATHER 1 and GATHER 2 phase II/III studies, patients treated with monthly intravitreal injections of avacincaptad pegol exhibited reductions in GA progression rates of approximately 27% to 30% relative to sham-treated groups (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Bege et al., 2025, pp. 16–17). These anatomical endpoints serve as surrogate markers for the overall efficacy of the intervention, with the underlying assumption that slowing the expansion of GA lesions will eventually lead to stabilization of visual function (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Guimaraes et al., 2022, pp. 3–4).

At the molecular level, the expected effect also includes the restoration of critical lysosomal functions disrupted by excessive complement activation. Specifically, by preventing MAC-induced lysosomal membrane permeabilization, avacincaptad pegol is anticipated to maintain the proton gradient essential for v-ATPase function, thereby preserving the acidic environment required for optimal cathepsin D processing and other lysosomal enzymes (Guimaraes et al., 2022, pp. 3–4; Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). Such preservation is not only crucial for cellular clearance mechanisms but also plays a pivotal role in preventing intracellular accumulation of debris, which is a contributing factor in the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Guimaraes et al., 2022, pp. 3–4; Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3).

Moreover, since complement components, including C5, are expressed locally in the retina by RPE cells and resident immune cells, the targeted inhibition of C5 is expected to provide direct immunomodulatory benefits within the ocular microenvironment. This localized impact is critical because it addresses the pathophysiological cross-talk between complement activation and lysosomal dysfunction, which is thought to drive a vicious cycle of chronic inflammation and cellular degeneration (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Guimaraes et al., 2022, pp. 3–4). In theory, by reestablishing a balanced complement milieu, avacincaptad pegol may also help to curtail secondary inflammatory responses that otherwise exacerbate tissue damage, thereby preserving photoreceptor integrity and ultimately stabilizing visual acuity over time (Qin et al., 2024, pp. 2–3; 3–3).

In summary, the expected effects of avacincaptad pegol in the proposed assays and clinical settings are multi-layered. At the biochemical level, one should observe a pronounced reduction in C5 cleavage, diminished MAC formation on RPE membranes, and preserved lysosomal acidification and enzyme function. At the tissue level, these molecular events are predicted to culminate in a slowdown of GA lesion enlargement, which is widely regarded as a surrogate marker for the progression of dry AMD (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Qin et al., 2024, pp. 2–3). The overall hypothesis is that these combined effects will translate into meaningful clinical benefits, offering not only anatomical preservation but also the potential for stabilization—or even modest improvement—of visual function in affected patients (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3).

V. Overall Evaluation  
A comprehensive evaluation of avacincaptad pegol reveals a therapeutic candidate that is scientifically robust, mechanistically innovative, and clinically validated for the treatment of dry AMD with geographic atrophy. One of the major strengths of this therapeutic approach lies in its highly specific mechanism of action. By directly binding to and inhibiting complement factor C5, avacincaptad pegol interrupts a key pathological process at its source, namely the activation of the terminal complement cascade that results in the formation of the pro-inflammatory mediator C5a and the membrane attack complex (MAC) (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 4–8; Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). This level of specificity confers potential advantages over broader immunosuppressive agents, as it minimizes collateral inhibition of upstream complement components that may be protective. Such precise targeting results in reduced inflammation localized to the retinal tissues and lowers the risk of systemic adverse events (Guimaraes et al., 2022, pp. 3–4; Qin et al., 2024, pp. 3–3).

The extensive chemical modifications integrated into avacincaptad pegol’s structure—including 2′-fluoro and 2′-O-methyl substitutions, the incorporation of a 3′–3′ thymidine cap, and PEGylation—greatly enhance its stability and half-life in the intraocular environment (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4). These modifications are essential because they allow for sustained inhibition of C5 with relatively infrequent dosing, thereby improving the overall treatment regimen for a patient population that is often elderly and may struggle with stringent dosing schedules (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4; Qin et al., 2024, pp. 3–3). The aptamer-based nature of this drug also endows it with a low immunogenic risk profile, circumventing one of the potential pitfalls associated with protein-based therapies such as monoclonal antibodies (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4).

Clinically, the data emerging from the GATHER 1 and GATHER 2 phase II/III trials are particularly compelling. These studies have consistently demonstrated that patients receiving intravitreal injections of avacincaptad pegol experience a significant reduction in the rate of GA lesion growth, with observed reductions ranging from 27% to 30% compared to sham controls (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Bege et al., 2025, pp. 16–17). This tangible anatomical benefit, combined with the favorable safety profile—which includes minimal ocular adverse events—confirms the viability of C5 inhibition as a disease-modifying strategy in dry AMD (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4). Given that GA has long represented an area of substantial unmet clinical need, the regulatory approval of avacincaptad pegol by the FDA in August 2023 is a significant milestone that reinforces the credibility of this therapeutic approach (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4; Qin et al., 2024, pp. 3–3).

Another notable strength is the mechanistic rationale underpinning the expected therapeutic benefits. By preventing MAC formation on RPE membranes, avacincaptad pegol not only preserves the structural integrity of these cells but also protects lysosomal function by mitigating lysosomal membrane permeabilization (LMP) (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Bege et al., 2025, pp. 4–8). The preservation of lysosomal acidification and subsequent maintenance of autophagic and proteolytic function are critical factors in slowing the progression of GA, as they help to avert the accumulation of toxic metabolic byproducts that drive cellular degeneration (Guimaraes et al., 2022, pp. 3–4; Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). Thus, the therapeutic strategy is well anchored in a clear pathological framework that directly relates to the underlying disease process in dry AMD.

Despite the considerable promise of avacincaptad pegol, several potential weaknesses and challenges remain. One concern is the translation of anatomical benefits into meaningful functional improvements with respect to visual acuity. While reduction in GA lesion enlargement is an encouraging surrogate endpoint, there is a recognized challenge in correlating these anatomical outcomes with sustained improvements or stabilization of vision (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Qin et al., 2024, pp. 2–3). In some clinical trials involving complement inhibitors, the disconnect between reduced lesion growth and measurable improvements in best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) has raised questions about whether anatomical preservation will eventually lead to perceptible functional benefits for patients (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3).

Another potential challenge relates to the inherent complexity of the complement system. C5 is a critical component of the terminal cascade; however, the redundancy and cross-talk among multiple complement pathways may potentially compromise the overall efficacy of a monotherapeutic approach targeting only C5 (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 4–8; Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). There is a possibility that, even with effective C5 blockade, alternative inflammatory pathways may partially compensate for its inhibition, thereby limiting the long-term clinical benefit. This concern suggests that future treatment paradigms might require combination approaches that target both complement-mediated and non-complement-mediated mechanisms of retinal degeneration (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Bege et al., 2025, pp. 4–8).

The mode of delivery is another factor that merits consideration. Avacincaptad pegol is delivered via monthly intravitreal injections, which, while effective in ensuring localized drug activity, impose a significant treatment burden on an elderly patient population (Qin et al., 2024, pp. 3–3). Frequent intravitreal administration is associated with logistical challenges, including the risk of injection-related complications such as endophthalmitis or retinal detachment, albeit infrequent, and may negatively impact patient compliance over extended treatment periods (Qin et al., 2024, pp. 3–3; Bege et al., 2025, pp. 16–17). Future innovation in drug delivery systems—for example, sustained-release implants or alternative non-invasive administration routes—could be critical in overcoming this limitation and enhancing long-term treatment adherence (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 16–17; 1–4).

A further challenge lies in assessing the long-term safety of chronic complement inhibition within the ocular environment. Although the localized delivery method limits systemic exposure, the prolonged suppression of C5 activity in the retina may affect local immune surveillance and potentially predispose to subclinical infections or inflammatory dysregulation (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4; Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). Given that the complement system plays a nuanced role in both tissue repair and immune defense, extended studies are necessary to definitively characterize the long-term safety profile, particularly with respect to maintaining the delicate balance between controlling pathological inflammation and preserving protective immune functions (Qin et al., 2024, pp. 3–3; Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3).

Finally, the multifactorial nature of dry AMD suggests that while C5 inhibition may effectively slow the progression of GA, it might not fully address all aspects of this complex disease process. Oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and neurodegeneration are also critical contributors to AMD pathophysiology, and a monotherapy targeting the complement cascade may need to be integrated into a broader multimodal treatment strategy to achieve optimal clinical outcomes (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Bege et al., 2025, pp. 4–8). Such considerations imply that while avacincaptad pegol represents a significant advancement in the field, its maximal therapeutic potential may be realized only when used in combination with agents that address complementary pathological processes (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Bege et al., 2025, pp. 4–8).

In synthesizing these considerations, the overall evaluation of avacincaptad pegol is highly positive. Nevertheless, the translation of these anatomical benefits into long-term preservation of vision, the challenges associated with the frequent intravitreal injection regimen, and the potential activation of alternative inflammatory pathways represent hurdles that warrant continued investigation (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). Addressing these challenges will likely require further mechanistic studies, extended clinical follow-up to capture functional outcomes, and possibly the development of innovative drug delivery systems that reduce the treatment burden on patients (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 16–17; Qin et al., 2024, pp. 3–3).

In summary, avacincaptad pegol represents a landmark therapeutic innovation in the realm of retinal degenerative diseases. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Trehalose is a naturally occurring non‐reducing disaccharide (molecular weight 342.3 Da) found broadly in microorganisms and invertebrates, widely used as a stabilizer and excipient in foods and pharmaceuticals, and formulated in ophthalmic solutions at 3% w/v (≈87.7 mM) for ocular surface applications (e.g., dry eye) (Cox et al., 2025, pp. 1–2). In mammalian cells, trehalose enters via fluid‐phase endocytosis at millimolar concentrations and has been repeatedly reported as an autophagy enhancer that can activate AMPK signaling, stimulate lysosomal activity, and augment autophagic flux across multiple tissues, including ocular tissues (RPE) and retina (Cox et al., 2025, pp. 1–2). In the context of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), trehalose has been deployed as a small‐molecule modulator of the lysosome–autophagy axis with proposed mTOR‐independent activation of TFEB, the master transcriptional regulator of lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy (CLEAR network), positioning it mechanistically distinct from direct mTORC1 inhibitors such as rapamycin (Ghosh et al., 2024, p. 6; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 10–11). Topical ophthalmic trehalose is generally well tolerated, and preclinical studies show no overt ocular toxicity at 3% or 9% w/v after twice-daily dosing for up to two weeks, supporting feasibility for posterior segment delivery strategies; Raman spectroscopy has detected trehalose in RPE/choroid after repeated topical dosing, although posterior penetration is variable (Cox et al., 2025, pp. 8–10).

Therapeutic History  
Preclinical evidence in RPE and retina

Dose–response caveats were noted: higher trehalose concentrations (≥100 mM) lost cytoprotection and were associated with stronger LC3-II accumulation, suggesting risk from excessive autophagy activation (Abokyi et al., 2020, pp. 11–12, 15–16).  
- Primary murine RPE in vitro: A non‐toxic trehalose dose (12.5 mM) increased autophagic flux measured by tandem GFP–RFP-LC3B, increasing RFP+ autolysosomes and RFP:GFP ratios without accumulating GFP+ autophagosomes, with colocalization to LysoTracker+ acidic compartments; trehalose also attenuated H₂O₂-induced mitochondrial superoxide and restored maximal respiration (Cox et al., 2025, pp. 7–10). These data indicate trehalose enhances autophagosome–lysosome fusion and downstream degradative flux in RPE under oxidative stress (Cox et al., 2025, pp. 7–10).  
- iPSC-derived human RPE carrying the CFH Y402H risk allele (CFH (H/H)): Trehalose (100 mM, 20–48 h) restored levels and enzymatic activities of lysosomal hydrolases Cathepsin D and Cathepsin L and rescued LAMP1 in complement challenge models, phenocopying constitutively nuclear TFEB (TFEB-S467A) and AKT2 inhibition; these data support trehalose as an mTOR-independent TFEB activator that rejuvenates lysosomal function in AMD-relevant RPE (Ghosh et al., 2024, p. 6; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 10–11).

- Cathepsin D: In ARPE-19, trehalose increased CTSD protein levels (no enzymatic activity assay reported in those pages), whereas in CFH (H/H) iPSC-RPE trehalose significantly restored CTSD and CTSL activities, directly supporting trehalose-mediated hydrolase functional rescue in human RPE disease models (Abokyi et al., 2020, pp. 1–2; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 10–11). Given the reported decrease of CTSD/L protein and activity in human AMD RPE, restoration of CTSD activity aligns with a rational corrective mechanism (Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 10–11).  
- Lipofuscin/A2E clearance: Direct trehalose data are absent in the provided selection; however, TFEB activation and mTOR inhibition (rapamycin) reduce A2E accumulation and lipofuscin-like granules in RPE models in a manner dependent on active lysosomal enzymes and dephosphorylated TFEB, indicating that enhancing TFEB and lysosomal function can drive lipofuscin clearance mechanistically (Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7, 7–9). Whether trehalose replicates these outcomes in RPE remains to be tested explicitly.

Mechanistic risks and dose sensitivity  
- Dose-dependent overactivation of autophagy can erode cytoprotection; in ARPE-19, higher trehalose doses were associated with loss of protection against HQ despite ROS suppression, consistent with potential autophagy-associated cytotoxicity if overdosed (Abokyi et al., 2020, pp. 15–16). This argues for careful dose–response mapping and phasic exposure control in RPE (Abokyi et al., 2020, pp. 15–16).

Expected Effect  
Mechanistically expected effects in RPE assays aligned to the hypothesis  
- TFEB-dependent lysosome–autophagy augmentation: In RPE cell culture, trehalose is expected to increase expression of CLEAR network genes and lysosomal markers (e.g., LAMP1/2) and to enhance autophagic flux, evident by LC3 turnover dynamics and decreased p62/SQSTM1 as degradative flux improves; in multiple models, trehalose increased LC3B and LAMP markers and reduced p62, with autophagosome–lysosome fusion enhanced (GFP–RFP-LC3B, LysoTracker colocalization) (Cox et al., 2025, pp. 7–8; Cox et al., 2025, pp. 10–13; Abokyi et al., 2020, pp. 1–2). Given abundant TFEB expression in RPE and the centrality of TFEB to lysosomal gene programs, a TFEB-centric response to trehalose is plausible in RPE, although nuclear localization with trehalose should be measured directly (Boya et al., 2023, pp. 3–4, 4–6; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 10–11).  
- CTSD/CTSL functional rescue: In human iPSC-RPE with AMD-risk alleles, trehalose restored CTSD and CTSL abundance and enzymatic activity, suggesting that RPE harboring disease-related lysosomal deficits will show increased cathepsin activity with trehalose; therefore, in assays using disease-relevant RPE genetics or complement challenge, trehalose is expected to boost cathepsin activity (Ghosh et al., 2024, p. 6; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 10–11). Because CTSD and CTSL are reduced in human AMD RPE, this restoration aligns with a disease-relevant corrective effect (Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7).  
- Lysosomal acidification: While increased autolysosome formation and LysoTracker colocalization suggest engagement of acidic compartments, trehalose has not been shown here to quantitatively lower lysosomal pH; therefore, acidification restoration is a testable hypothesis requiring direct measurement (e.g., LysoSensor ratiometry, V-ATPase subunit expression/activity assays) (Cox et al., 2025, pp. 7–8; Boya et al., 2023, pp. 3–4).  
- Reduction of oxidative stress and mitochondrial rescue: Trehalose reduced basal ROS in ARPE-19 under resting conditions and decreased mitochondrial superoxide with restoration of maximal respiration under H₂O₂ stress in primary RPE, indicating that trehalose-mediated autophagy enhancement increases organelle quality control and redox homeostasis in RPE (Abokyi et al., 2020, pp. 12–13; Cox et al., 2025, pp. 8–10).  
- Lipofuscin/A2E clearance: Based on TFEB-dependent clearance data with rapamycin and TFEB-overexpression models, trehalose could reduce A2E and lipofuscin-like granules if it drives TFEB nuclear import and maintains lysosomal hydrolase function; however, explicit verification in RPE is lacking in the provided materials and should be included in the assay plan (e.g., A2E-loaded RPE with autofluorescence quantitation, POS-fed RPE granule counts) (Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7, 7–9).  
- In vivo RPE/retinal structure preservation: In acute LIRD, topical trehalose preserved ONL thickness and RPE morphology; in chronic models with lysosomal defects, systemic trehalose prevented basal deposit formation and rescued RPE lysosomal function; hence, assays probing RPE structural resilience under oxidative or complement stress are likely to show benefit with trehalose (Cox et al., 2025, pp. 8–10, 10–13; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 6–8; Ghosh et al., 2023, pp. 11–15).

Assay-linked molecular readouts and expression in RPE  
- TFEB/TFE3, LAMP1/2, LC3B, SQSTM1/p62, CTSD/CTSL, and V-ATPase subunits (e.g., ATP6V0A1) are expressed in RPE and are central to lysosomal/autophagic function, with CLEAR network control by TFEB; reduced nuclear TFEB and decreased CTSD/L activity are documented in AMD RPE (Boya et al., 2023, pp. 3–4, 4–6; Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7). Given these baselines, RPE is an appropriate cell type to measure trehalose-driven TFEB pathway engagement and lysosomal protease restoration (Boya et al., 2023, pp. 3–4, 4–6; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 10–11).

Translational expectations and delivery  
- Topical dosing: The 3%–9% trehalose eyedrop regimens are feasible and safe in preclinical studies, achieve measurable posterior exposure, and produced autophagy biomarker changes and structural protection in LIRD (Cox et al., 2025, pp. 8–10, 10–13). However, posterior ocular bioavailability is typically low and variable, and much drug is lost systemically, necessitating optimization of formulation and dosing frequency for consistent RPE exposure (Cox et al., 2025, pp. 10–13, 15–16).  
- Systemic dosing: Oral trehalose can be degraded by trehalase, complicating systemic delivery; nonetheless, in mouse models (Cryba1 cKO and Akt2 KI), IP loading then 2% trehalose in drinking water for 3 months restored RPE lysosomal function and prevented deposit formation (Ghosh et al., 2023, pp. 11–15; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 6–8). Clinical translation will need to address trehalase metabolism and systemic exposure constraints (Cox et al., 2025, pp. 10–13).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Multi-modal preclinical evidence in RPE: Trehalose increases autophagy flux in human ARPE-19 and primary murine RPE, with autolysosome formation confirmed via tandem GFP–RFP-LC3 and LysoTracker colocalization, and cytoprotective effects depend on intact autophagy machinery (ATG5), directly aligning with the mechanistic target in RPE (Cox et al., 2025, pp. 7–8; Abokyi et al., 2020, pp. 1–2, 12–13).  
- Restoration of lysosomal hydrolase content and activity in human iPSC-RPE disease models: Trehalose rescued CTSD/L protein and activity and normalized LAMP1 under complement challenge in CFH Y402H RPE, mechanistically reversing disease-relevant lysosomal deficiencies (Ghosh et al., 2024, p. 6; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 10–11).  
- TFEB pathway engagement, mTOR-independent: Trehalose phenocopies constitutively nuclear TFEB and AKT2 inhibition in rescuing lysosomal/autophagy networks and function, and restores CLEAR transcripts in explants and in vivo without suppressing abnormal mTORC1 activation, suggesting lower risk of mTOR-related adverse effects (Ghosh et al., 2023, pp. 11–15; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 10–11).  
- In vivo efficacy signals: Topical trehalose improves autophagy markers in RPE and preserves ONL and RPE morphology after light stress; chronic systemic dosing prevents basal deposits and rescues lysosomal function in RPE in genetic lysosome-defect models (Cox et al., 2025, pp. 10–13; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 6–8; Ghosh et al., 2023, pp. 11–15).  
- Delivery feasibility and safety: Topical administration at high concentrations (3%–9%) is well tolerated and achieves posterior detection, creating a realistic translational route; topical dosing circumvents trehalase metabolism, a limitation for oral delivery (Cox et al., 2025, pp. 1–2, 8–10, 10–13).

Weaknesses and major gaps relative to the hypothesis  
- Lysosomal acidification not directly demonstrated: No quantitative lysosomal pH measurements with trehalose are reported in the provided RPE datasets; restoration of acidification remains an inference and must be demonstrated directly (Cox et al., 2025, pp. 7–8; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 10–11; Abokyi et al., 2020, pp. 1–2).  
- TFEB nuclear translocation under trehalose unproven in RPE: While trehalose is described as a TFEB activator and phenocopies TFEB-S467A, direct nuclear localization (imaging or fractionation) after trehalose in RPE is not shown here; this is a critical mechanistic gap (Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 10–11; Ghosh et al., 2023, pp. 11–15; Abokyi et al., 2020, pp. 16–17).  
- Lipofuscin/A2E clearance not demonstrated for trehalose: Although TFEB activation and mTOR inhibition are known to reduce A2E/lipofuscin-like granules in RPE models, trehalose-specific evidence for lipofuscin clearance is absent in the supplied materials (Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7).  
- Geographic atrophy endpoints lacking: There are no chronic GA model or clinical data showing trehalose slows lesion growth or preserves vision; LIRD is an acute stress model and does not recapitulate GA progression (Cox et al., 2025, pp. 1–2, 8–10).  
- Dosing translatability: Many in vitro effects were observed at 50–100 mM trehalose, which are high relative to likely in vivo intra-RPE exposures; dose–response optimization is needed, and excessive dosing risks autophagy-associated cytotoxicity (Abokyi et al., 2020, pp. 12–13, 15–16; Cox et al., 2025, pp. 7–8).  
- Source quality heterogeneity: Some supportive RPE studies come from lower-quality journals or preprints, warranting independent replication under rigorously controlled conditions (Abokyi et al., 2020, pp. 1–2; Ghosh et al., 2023, pp. 11–15).

Risk–benefit and development recommendations  
- Mechanistic verification package:  
  - Quantify lysosomal pH restoration with LysoSensor/DND-160 ratiometry and V-ATPase subunit/activity assays in RPE models ± trehalose, including disease-relevant stress (e.g., complement challenge, A2E loading) (Boya et al., 2023, pp. 3–4, 4–6).  
  - Directly quantify TFEB nuclear translocation (immunocytochemistry with nuclear segmentation; nuclear/cytosolic fractionation and immunoblotting) under trehalose vs. TFEB-S467A and vs. AKT2 inhibition, to confirm that trehalose’s phenotypic rescue is TFEB-dependent in RPE (Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 6, 10–11).  
  - CTSD/CTSL processing and activity: Extend the CFH (H/H) results by testing trehalose across primary human RPE and AMD-donor–derived RPE; relate CTSD activity rescue to autophagic flux endpoints (LC3 turnover, p62 degradation) and to substrate clearance (POS proteolysis kinetics) (Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 6, 10–11; Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7).  
  - Lipofuscin/A2E clearance: In A2E-loaded and POS-fed RPE, quantify autofluorescence granules and A2E mass spectrometry before/after trehalose, and test dependence on TFEB (siRNA/CRISPR) and lysosomal hydrolase inhibition (e.g., pepstatin-A for CTSD) (Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7, 7–9).  
- PK/PD and delivery optimization:  
  - For topical delivery, map trehalose concentration–time in RPE/choroid and retina with LC-MS or validated Raman signatures; explore permeation enhancers or sustained-release formulations to overcome low posterior bioavailability (Cox et al., 2025, pp. 8–10, 10–13, 15–16).  
  - Define an ocular PD biomarker panel (RPE LC3B/LAMP1 colocalization, p62 decrease, CTSD activity) and link to functional readouts (ERG, OCT metrics) in chronic complement- or lipofuscin-based models (Cox et al., 2025, pp. 10–13).  
- Comparative and combinatorial strategy:  
  - Benchmark trehalose against TFEB-centric comparators (e.g., rapalogs, Ezrin inhibitors) on shared endpoints (TFEB nuclear index, lysosomal pH, CTSD activity, lipofuscin clearance), given rapamycin’s ability to reduce A2E/lipofuscin via TFEB activation and the potential of ezrin blockade to increase lysosome number and cathepsin activity in RPE (Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7, 7–9; Boya et al., 2023, pp. 4–6).  
  - Consider combination with complement modulation where indicated, as complement stress contributes to AMD-relevant lysosomal dysfunction in CFH (H/H) RPE (Ghosh et al., 2024, p. 6).

Go/no-go criteria for advancement toward GA  
- Mechanistic Go: Demonstration in RPE that trehalose increases the TFEB nuclear index by >2-fold, lowers lysosomal pH toward physiological values, and increases CTSD activity by >30% over disease-state baseline, with concordant increases in LC3B–LAMP1 colocalization and p62 degradation; abrogation of effects by TFEB knockdown would confirm mechanism (Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 10–11; Cox et al., 2025, pp. 7–8; Boya et al., 2023, pp. 3–4).  
- Functional Go: Demonstrated reduction of A2E/lipofuscin by ≥25% in RPE models without cytotoxicity, and structural/functional rescue in a chronic AMD-relevant animal model (e.g., CFH-risk or complement-driven models) with durable effects beyond acute stress models (Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7; Cox et al., 2025, pp. 8–10; Ghosh et al., 2024, p. 6).  
- Safety Go: No evidence of autophagy-associated cytotoxicity at the intended exposure (maintained viability; absence of excessive LC3-II accumulation without flux; ocular histopathology clean) (Abokyi et al., 2020, pp. 15–16; Cox et al., 2025, pp. 8–10).

Conclusion  
The totality of evidence supports trehalose as a plausible, repurposable modulator of the TFEB–lysosome/autophagy axis in the RPE with multiple independent signals of autophagy flux enhancement, lysosomal hydrolase restoration (CTSD/L), and cytoprotection in oxidative/complement stress contexts, delivered via mechanisms that appear mTOR-independent and therefore potentially safer than broad mTORC1 inhibition (Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 10–11; Cox et al., 2025, pp. 7–8; Abokyi et al., 2020, pp. 1–2; Ghosh et al., 2023, pp. 11–15). However, the hypothesis’s most stringent claims—quantitative restoration of lysosomal acidification, trehalose-driven TFEB nuclear translocation in RPE, and direct lipofuscin/A2E clearance leading to slowed geographic atrophy progression—are not yet demonstrated in the supplied literature and require targeted mechanistic and disease-model validation (Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 10–11; Abokyi et al., 2020, pp. 16–17; Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7; Cox et al., 2025, pp. 8–10). Given strong biological plausibility and encouraging preclinical signals, a focused IND-enabling program that closes these gaps is justified, with early emphasis on mechanistic biomarkers (lysosomal pH, TFEB nuclear index, CTSD activity), pharmacokinetics of posterior delivery, and chronic AMD-relevant efficacy models before advancing to clinical study in GA (Boya et al., 2023, pp. 3–4; Cox et al., 2025, pp. 10–13; Ghosh et al., 2024, p. 6).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Torin2 is a synthetic, second-generation ATP-competitive inhibitor of the mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) kinase designed to inhibit both mTOR complex 1 (mTORC1) and complex 2 (mTORC2) with high potency and favorable pharmacodynamic properties compared to first-generation allosteric mTOR inhibitors (rapamycin/rapalogs) and earlier catalytic mTOR kinase inhibitors (TORKi) such as PP242 and AZD8055 (Liu et al., 2013, pp. 7–10). Chemically optimized by structure-guided medicinal chemistry efforts, Torin2 exhibits rapid dephosphorylation of canonical mTORC1 substrates S6K1 (T389) and 4E-BP1 (T37/46) including rapamycin-insensitive sites, and of the mTORC2 substrate Akt (S473), reflecting dual-complex inhibition that is superior to rapamycin’s mTORC1-limited activity (with incomplete suppression of 4E-BP1) (Liu et al., 2013, pp. 7–10). In head-to-head comparisons with other ATP-competitive mTOR inhibitors, Torin2 maintains stronger and more sustained suppression of mTORC1/2 signaling after drug washout, attributable to its slow off-rate, with durable pathway inhibition persisting for approximately four hours in cellular assays, contrasting with rapid recovery observed with PP242 and shorter-duration suppression by AZD8055 (Liu et al., 2013, pp. 7–9). Torin2 is highly selective for mTOR over PI3K (>800-fold) and shows approximately 100-fold selectivity over the DNA damage response kinases ATM and ATR; these latter off-targets remain relevant at higher concentrations and inform safety margins and dose selection (Liu et al., 2013, pp. 9–10).

Mechanistically, Torin2 robustly induces autophagy across multiple cell lines (e.g., LC3-II accumulation, acridine-orange–positive acidic vesicle formation), consistent with its potent inhibition of mTORC1, a master negative regulator of autophagy initiation and flux (Liu et al., 2013, pp. 7–9). As a drug class, ATP-competitive TORKi have been widely investigated in oncology and proliferative diseases given their ability to fully suppress both mTOR complexes, thereby impacting protein synthesis, cell-cycle progression, metabolism, and survival signaling (Liu et al., 2013, pp. 7–10). Outside oncology, dual mTORC1/2 inhibition has demonstrated disease-modifying potential in organ systems where mTOR hyperactivation drives pathology; for example, Torin2 reduced S6 and 4E-BP1 phosphorylation and curtailed cyst burden in a mouse model of autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease, with efficacy comparable to sirolimus and a potentially more favorable side-effect profile (Holditch et al., 2019, pp. 6–7).

In the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), dysregulated mTOR signaling (particularly chronic mTORC1 activation with age) is strongly implicated in degradative/clearance failure, lysosomal dysfunction, metabolic reprogramming, and structural degeneration that recapitulate key features of dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD), including lipid-rich subretinal deposits and RPE dedifferentiation (Go et al., 2020, pp. 1–3, 11–13; Huang et al., 2019, pp. 1–2, 7–9; Zhao et al., 2011, pp. 10–11). RPE expresses and functionally engages both mTORC1 and mTORC2 complexes, providing a mechanistic rationale for evaluating dual-complex catalytic inhibitors like Torin2 as therapeutic candidates to correct core pathogenic processes in dry AMD (Intartaglia et al., 2022, pp. 15–17).

Therapeutic History  
The mTOR pathway has been studied extensively in retinal and RPE biology, with strong preclinical evidence linking mTOR hyperactivation to RPE degeneration and dry AMD-like pathology, and corresponding benefits from mTOR inhibition; however, direct ocular data with Torin2 itself are currently lacking and must be extrapolated from pharmacology in other tissues and from surrogates (Torin1, PP242, INK-128/MLN0128) and rapamycin (Liu et al., 2013, pp. 7–10; Holditch et al., 2019, pp. 6–7). Genetic and pharmacologic mTOR activation in RPE induces epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT), suppresses autophagy, disrupts metabolism, and yields an AMD-like phenotype; in a knock-in model that overexpresses mLST8 (a core mTORC component) in RPE, both mTORC1 and mTORC2 are upregulated, and dual-complex inhibition with TORIN1 (a TORKi closely related to Torin2) normalized signaling and restored autophagy and RPE function in vitro, including rescue of autophagy regulators Atg9b and Atg7 and recovery of autophagy flux (Chowdhury et al., 2025, pp. 1–2, 8–13). These data directly support the therapeutic relevance of dual mTORC1/2 inhibition in RPE conditions that model early AMD pathogenesis (Chowdhury et al., 2025, pp. 1–2, 8–13).

In a complementary RPE disease model focused on amyloid-β (Aβ)-induced lysosomal/autophagy impairment—a pathology linked to dry AMD—Torin (a first-generation mTOR inhibitor in this study; not explicitly Torin2) restored lysosomal activity via LAMP2 activation, corrected p62/SQSTM1 accumulation, facilitated Aβ aggregate clearance, and ameliorated Aβ-driven tight junction disruption in vitro and in Aβ-challenged mouse RPE in vivo, directly addressing the barrier degradation and clearance deficits central to AMD (Jo et al., 2023, pp. 1–2). In multiple RPE cell systems modeling autofluorescent granule (AFG) accumulation and lipofuscinogenesis after photoreceptor outer segment (POS) challenge, mTOR inhibition (rapamycin; INK-128) decreased AFG load by approximately 30% and activated a TFEB-dependent lysosome biogenesis program; these effects required intact lysosomal proteases/lipases and were associated with LAMP1 upregulation and GADD34 induction, supporting the concept that mTOR→TFEB pathway modulation can restore lysosomal clearance in RPE (albeit these studies were preprints and should be interpreted accordingly) (Falcão et al., 2024, pp. 1–6, 10–18). Constitutively active TFEB dramatically reduced POS-dependent AFGs in preventive and resolving paradigms, further validating TFEB activation as a mechanistic goal for pharmacologic mTOR inhibition in early AMD models (Falcão et al., 2024, pp. 1–6, 13–18).

In genetic models where RPE mTORC1 is hyperactivated through Tsc1 deletion, chronic mTORC1 activity causes progressive RPE degeneration, lipid accumulation, and subretinal drusenoid deposits, and rapamycin treatment restored RPE markers (e.g., RPE65), improved ERG responses, and partially normalized metabolomic derangements, providing in vivo proof-of-concept that mTOR pathway suppression improves RPE structure and function in AMD-like degeneration (Huang et al., 2019, pp. 1–2, 7–9; Zhao et al., 2011, pp. 10–11). At a mechanistic level, age-driven increases in lysosome mass and mTORC1 docking in RPE create a vicious cycle of mTORC1 hyperactivation that impairs phagolysosomal function, promotes lipogenesis, suppresses lipolysis, and degrades autophagy, converging on classic dry AMD phenotypes; mTOR inhibition breaks this cycle and restores degradative capacity (Go et al., 2020, pp. 1–3, 11–13).

Beyond ocular systems, Torin2 has been used preclinically in oncology and in non-ocular degenerative models; its dual mTORC1/2 suppression, sustained pharmacodynamics, and autophagy induction underlie anti-proliferative activity and apoptosis in cancer models, while in an ADPKD model Torin2 demonstrated pathway inhibition with efficacy comparable to sirolimus, suggesting that torin-class agents may be tolerable with appropriate dose and schedule selection (Liu et al., 2013, pp. 7–9; Holditch et al., 2019, pp. 6–7). Notably, second-generation mTOR inhibitors can be cytotoxic in RPE due to potent mTORC2 suppression with downstream Akt inhibition, a survival pathway for metabolically stressed RPE; this risk emphasizes the importance of dose titration and local ocular delivery strategies for Torin2 in AMD (Huang et al., 2018, pp. 7–8).

To our knowledge, Torin2 has not been reported in clinical trials for dry AMD or directly tested in RPE/retinal models in vivo; however, the strength of the translational prior—mTOR hyperactivation as a convergent mechanism in RPE degeneration; rescue with catalytic mTOR inhibitors such as TORIN1; and reversible ALP defects with Torin-class inhibition—warrants rigorous preclinical testing of Torin2 in dry AMD-relevant models (Chowdhury et al., 2025, pp. 1–2, 8–11; Jo et al., 2023, pp. 1–2).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Genistein is a naturally occurring isoflavone that was first isolated from soybeans and other leguminous plants. As a member of the phytoestrogen class, genistein possesses structural similarities to mammalian estrogens and can bind to estrogen receptors, albeit with much lower intrinsic potency than endogenous steroids. It is typically obtained from dietary sources such as soy, red clover, and other legumes, but high‐purity formulations have been developed and are commercially available (for example, Sigma G6649). Genistein belongs to a broader class of natural bioactive compounds that have been studied over the past several decades for their modulating effects on various cellular processes including antioxidant defense, differentiation, apoptosis, and proliferation. Historically, phytoestrogens like genistein have been investigated both for their hormone‐like activity and as specific inhibitors of protein tyrosine kinases. The compound has been utilized in research ranging from hormone replacement strategies in menopausal women to anticancer studies, and its ability to modulate several cell signaling pathways—including those associated with PI3K/AKT/mTOR—has attracted interest in other fields such as neurodegeneration and ocular health (Albulescu & Popovici, 2007).

Therapeutic History:  
The therapeutic history of genistein spans multiple domains. Clinically, phytoestrogens have been examined largely as potential alternatives to traditional estrogen replacement therapies for the alleviation of menopausal symptoms, with some studies reporting modest effects on vasomotor symptoms, menstrual cycle regulation, and quality‐of‐life indices (Glazier & Bowman, 2001; Albulescu & Popovici, 2007). In the veterinary and preclinical realm, high doses of phytoestrogens have been associated with reproductive toxicity in livestock such as sheep (the classical clover disease), while rodent studies have similarly documented endocrine disruptions when exposed to high concentrations (Glazier & Bowman, 2001). For bone health specifically, preclinical data have shown that ovariectomized rats fed genistein exhibit reduced rates of bone loss; this finding parallels clinical trials using the synthetic isoflavone derivative ipriflavone—which is related to the parent compounds in the isoflavone class—and has demonstrated benefits in slowing bone loss and increasing bone mineral density when given for periods of up to two years in postmenopausal women (Glazier & Bowman, 2001). Regarding ocular applications, there is emerging preclinical work to improve the solubility and corneal penetration of genistein; for example, encapsulating genistein in hyaluronic acid–modified MPEG-b-PAE polymeric micelles has been shown to improve its corneal permeability by approximately 1.5-fold compared to a simple drug solution (Li et al., 2018). Although genistein has not yet been extensively evaluated in clinical trials specifically targeting dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD), its broad modulatory effects on tyrosine kinases and downstream signaling pathways provide a rationale for repurposing it to address dry AMD pathophysiology, particularly given the significant unmet therapeutic need in this area (Glazier & Bowman, 2001).

Mechanism of Action:  
Genistein is widely recognized for its ability to inhibit protein tyrosine kinases. This inhibitory action extends to several receptors and intracellular kinases, thereby modulating key signaling cascades including the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway—a pathway that is critical for cell survival, proliferation, and metabolism. In many cell-based studies, genistein has been shown to suppress PI3K/AKT signaling, leading to downstream inhibition of mTOR complex 1 (mTORC1) activity. Since mTORC1 coordinates cellular anabolic processes and suppresses autophagy under nutrient-rich conditions, inhibiting this complex can trigger autophagic clearance mechanisms (Albulescu & Popovici, 2007). One of the pivotal regulators downstream of mTORC1 is the transcription factor EB (TFEB), which, when dephosphorylated due to mTORC1 inhibition, translocates into the nucleus and promotes the transcription of genes involved in lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy. There is evidence that genistein can modulate lysosomal metabolism and promote TFEB activation, as reported in studies highlighting the ability of flavonoids to enhance the clearance of substrate accumulations via TFEB-mediated transcriptional programs (Xu et al., 2020). In retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells, which play a crucial role in maintaining photoreceptor health through phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments (POS), enhanced autophagy and lysosomal function are essential for the degradation and removal of cellular debris, including drusen components characteristic of dry AMD (Falcão et al., 2024). Moreover, experimental reports have suggested that in RPE-like models, treatment with compounds that suppress the PI3K/AKT/mTOR axis leads to increased LC3 turnover and upregulation of cathepsin D (CTSD), a lysosomal aspartic protease essential for phagolysosomal digestion (Albulescu & Popovici, 2007; Jahan et al., 2022). In this context, genistein is hypothesized to function by inhibiting upstream tyrosine kinases that feed into PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling, thereby promoting TFEB activation. TFEB then orchestrates the transcription of lysosomal genes, leading to enhanced lysosomal acidification and increased enzymatic activities, including that of cathepsin D, which is imperative for effective degradation within phagolysosomes (Falcão et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2025).

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis posits that administration of genistein to RPE cells will lead to measurable inhibition of the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway, resulting in dephosphorylation and nuclear translocation of TFEB. This transcriptional activation is expected to upregulate a battery of lysosomal and autophagy-related genes, including those responsible for the maintenance of lysosomal acidification and the synthesis of key proteases such as cathepsin D (Falcão et al., 2024). In functional assays, an increase in LC3 turnover—a marker of enhanced autophagic flux—would be anticipated, alongside elevated levels of CTSD, providing the biochemical basis for improved phagolysosomal digestion. Consequently, in an in vitro RPE cell model subjected to a photoreceptor outer segment (POS) feeding assay, genistein treatment is expected to facilitate the clearance of POS-derived debris and reduce the accumulation of autofluorescent lipofuscin-like granules. This outcome mimics the effects observed with compounds like rapamycin, where mTOR inhibition leads to a significant, approximately 30% reduction of POS-dependent autofluorescence by improving lysosomal processing (Falcão et al., 2024). Moreover, in light of published observations demonstrating that effective activation of TFEB can restore lysosomal biogenesis and enhance cellular clearance, genistein’s dual inhibition of kinase activity and subsequent autophagy upregulation is predicted to result in a favorable impact on drusen clearance and overall RPE function in dry AMD settings (Falcão et al., 2024; Xu et al., 2020).

Overall Evaluation:  
Overall, genistein presents as an intriguing candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry AMD, particularly given its established history as a natural product with a favorable oral safety profile and its documented ability to modulate critical signaling pathways involved in cell survival and autophagy. One of the major strengths of genistein lies in its dual mechanism: as a selective inhibitor of tyrosine kinases, it can suppress the upstream activation of the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway, and as a modulator of lysosomal metabolism, it facilitates TFEB activation. This mechanistic duality offers a targeted approach to enhance the autophagic clearance capacity of RPE cells, which is critical in preventing the accumulation of intracellular debris and drusen associated with dry AMD (Falcão et al., 2024; Xu et al., 2020). Furthermore, the existing literature on phytoestrogens indicates that compounds in this chemical class are generally well tolerated when administered orally, and formulation strategies (such as encapsulation in hyaluronic acid–modified polymeric micelles) enhance ocular bioavailability, potentially enabling effective local delivery with minimal systemic adverse effects (Li et al., 2018).

However, several challenges and weaknesses must be addressed before advancing genistein as a therapy for dry AMD. First, while there is a substantial body of evidence supporting the role of genistein in modulating PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling in non-ocular tissues, direct evidence in RPE cells and in the context of dry AMD is sparse. Most published studies in the ocular domain have focused on formulation and delivery aspects rather than on detailed mechanism-of-action studies within RPE cells. Second, the estrogenic activity of genistein, although weak, raises potential concerns regarding off-target endocrine effects, particularly during long-term administration in older populations who may be susceptible to hormone-related side effects. These aspects would require rigorous assessment in preclinical and early-phase clinical trials. Additionally, the pharmacokinetics of genistein when administered via ocular routes (either topically or systemically) remain incompletely characterized, and comprehensive data on tissue distribution, especially to the retina or RPE, is limited. Such pharmacokinetic studies are crucial to ensure that therapeutic concentrations can be achieved and maintained in the target tissues without eliciting adverse effects (Glazier & Bowman, 2001; Li et al., 2018).

In light of the above considerations, genistein is promising as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD based on its capacity to inhibit upstream tyrosine kinases and suppress the PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling cascade, thereby promoting TFEB-mediated enhancement of lysosomal acidification and cathepsin D activity. Such a mechanism is directly relevant to improving phagolysosomal function in RPE cells and facilitating the clearance of drusen components—a critical unmet need in the management of dry AMD (Falcão et al., 2024; Xu et al., 2020). The dual actions of genistein offer mechanistic clarity that may translate into a therapeutic edge when compared to broad-spectrum autophagy inducers. Nonetheless, the current evidence base is still largely circumstantial, and further direct investigations are necessary to confirm that genistein induces the expected autophagic and lysosomal responses in RPE cells. Preclinical studies employing appropriate RPE models (such as POS feeding assays and chronic oxidative stress paradigms) should be prioritized to solidify the link between genistein treatment and improved clearance of lipofuscin-like deposits. Ultimately, detailed pharmacokinetic, efficacy, and safety studies—ideally complemented by early-phase clinical trials—will be required before genistein can be confidently advanced as a therapeutic modality for dry AMD (Albulescu & Popovici, 2007; Falcão et al., 2024).

In summary, genistein’s natural origin, established safety in other contexts, and its dual ability to inhibit relevant tyrosine kinase–mediated signaling and upregulate autophagy through TFEB activation collectively support its potential for repurposing in dry AMD. However, critical gaps in direct efficacy data in ocular models and a precise understanding of its tissue pharmacokinetics necessitate further investigation. This combination of promising mechanistic rationale and some supportive preclinical data argues that genistein merits further preclinical exploration in RPE models of dry AMD, with the expectation that if such studies confirm improved clearance of lipofuscin and drusen markers, subsequent early-phase clinical trials can be pursued to evaluate its therapeutic benefit in patients suffering from this blinding disease (Falcão et al., 2024; Glazier & Bowman, 2001; Li et al., 2018; Xu et al., 2020).
