I. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Avacincaptad pegol, commercially known as Zimura, is a highly engineered, synthetic RNA aptamer designed specifically to target complement factor C5 for the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) with geographic atrophy (GA) features (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4). This molecule is comprised of a 39-nucleotide sequence that has been rigorously selected through in vitro techniques to offer high affinity and specificity for its target, ensuring that it binds precisely to C5 and prevents its activation (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4). Unlike traditional monoclonal antibodies, aptamers are oligonucleotide-based therapeutic agents that combine the benefits of well-defined chemical synthesis with tunable pharmacokinetics and low immunogenicity. In this instance, avacincaptad pegol has been further optimized by incorporating multiple chemical modifications; these include 2′-fluorine substitutions on pyrimidine residues, 2′-O-methyl modifications on select purine nucleotides, a protected 3′–3′ thymidine cap, and a branched polyethylene glycol (PEG) moiety to extend its half-life within the eye (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4). Such modifications confer enhanced resistance to degradation by nucleases and reduce renal clearance, thereby allowing the compound to remain active in the subretinal space longer than unmodified oligonucleotides (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4). The development of avacincaptad pegol is rooted in the evolution of aptamer technologies that began with earlier compounds like pegaptanib, the pioneer aptamer approved for neovascular AMD; however, unlike pegaptanib, avacincaptad pegol is engineered to target a different disease mechanism by focusing on the terminal complement cascade (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–8). Overall, the molecular design and chemical sophistication of this aptamer designate it as a next-generation candidate in the field of oligonucleotide therapeutics, with its unique physical and chemical attributes directly addressing specific pathogenic mechanisms of dry AMD (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–8).

Avacincaptad pegol belongs to a broader class of therapeutic compounds known as aptamers that act as “chemical antibodies.” These agents are synthesized via systematic evolution of ligands by exponential enrichment (SELEX), a process that allows for iterative refinement of the aptamer’s binding characteristics so that it selectively interacts with its intended protein target (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4). Aptamers have been used in various clinical applications due to their predictable pharmacologic profiles, their ease of chemical modification, and their typically low risk of eliciting an immune response. Their utility has been demonstrated not only in ocular therapeutics but also across a range of medical indications where precise modulation of molecular pathways is desired (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4). With the advent of avacincaptad pegol, the application of aptamer technology has been repurposed specifically for the modulation of the complement cascade—a key inflammatory pathway implicated in retinal degenerative diseases such as dry AMD (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4).

The synthetic origins of avacincaptad pegol underscore a scalable manufacturing process with robust quality control measures, making the compound attractive not only from a scientific standpoint but also from a commercial and regulatory perspective (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4). The structural characteristics, including its nucleic acid backbone and PEG conjugation, have been optimized to ensure adequate tissue penetration and sustained activity when delivered via intravitreal injection, minimizing systemic exposure and maximizing local therapeutic concentrations (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4). In summary, avacincaptad pegol is a representative example of how innovative chemical modifications and advanced selection technologies converge to generate therapeutic candidates that address the critical unmet needs in degenerative retinal diseases (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4).

II. Therapeutic History  
The trajectory of avacincaptad pegol from bench to bedside is emblematic of the rapid evolution in our understanding of the complement system’s role in AMD pathogenesis. Historically, the complement cascade—a series of proteolytic reactions leading to the formation of the membrane attack complex (MAC)—has been implicated in the chronic, low-grade inflammatory processes that contribute to retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) degeneration (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4; Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). Early efforts in pharmacologic intervention focused on modulating angiogenesis through agents like anti-VEGF drugs; however, these therapies failed to address the underlying complement-mediated inflammatory milieu that is particularly pronounced in the dry form of AMD (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4, 16–17).

The recognition that complement overactivation plays a central role in GA led researchers to explore agents that could precisely inhibit key components of this cascade. Avacincaptad pegol emerged as a promising candidate in this context, designed to block complement factor C5—a critical nexus point in the pathway responsible for the generation of both the potent inflammatory mediator C5a and the membrane attack complex (MAC) via C5b (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Bege et al., 2025, pp. 4–8). Preclinical studies using animal models of AMD demonstrated that inhibition of C5 could mitigate complement-mediated damage to RPE cells and reduce progression of GA lesions, laying the foundation for subsequent clinical investigations (Guimaraes et al., 2022, pp. 3–4; Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3).

The clinical development program for avacincaptad pegol has been extensive. Notably, phase II/III randomized controlled trials—collectively referred to as GATHER 1 and GATHER 2—were designed to evaluate its safety and efficacy in patients with GA secondary to AMD (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 16–17; Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). These pivotal trials enrolled hundreds of patients and involved monthly intravitreal injections, a route of administration that allows for high local concentrations of the drug while minimizing systemic exposure (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 16–17; Qin et al., 2024, p. 3). The results from these clinical studies were encouraging, as they consistently demonstrated statistically significant reductions in GA lesion growth in treatment groups compared to sham injections, with reported reductions in lesion progression on the order of approximately 27–30% over follow-up periods ranging from 12 to 18 months (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Guimaraes et al., 2022, pp. 3–4; Bege et al., 2025, pp. 16–17).

Beyond efficacy, the safety profile of avacincaptad pegol has been affirmed in multiple studies. The intravitreal route of administration confines the compound’s activity largely to the ocular compartment, thereby minimizing systemic immunosuppression—a particularly valuable attribute given the complement system’s role in host defense (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4; Qin et al., 2024, p. 3). Reports from clinical trials indicated that adverse events were primarily related to the injection procedure itself, with few drug-related serious ocular events recorded (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4; Guimaraes et al., 2022, pp. 3–4). This favorable safety record, combined with robust efficacy data, contributed to the FDA’s decision to approve avacincaptad pegol for the treatment of GA in August 2023, marking it as the second approved aptamer medicine in the field of retinal disease, following pegaptanib (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4; Qin et al., 2024, p. 3).

In parallel with these developments in dry AMD, avacincaptad pegol has been examined in observational studies and preclinical models that further delineate its mechanism of action and long-term benefits. Although past investigations in other complement-mediated ocular conditions have encountered mixed results, the specific targeting of C5 in the case of GA appears to be particularly promising, as evidenced by the consistent reduction in lesion progression reported by the GATHER trials (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 16–17; Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). The accumulated clinical experience provides a compelling historical context for its use, reinforcing the therapeutic rationale of complement inhibition in mitigating the inflammatory and degenerative processes that drive dry AMD (Guimaraes et al., 2022, pp. 3–4; Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3).

Moreover, the evolution of complement-modulating therapies in retinal diseases has been marked by significant collaborations between academia, industry, and regulatory agencies, all of which have embraced a more nuanced understanding of the immune processes involved in AMD. These concerted efforts have not only fostered the development of avacincaptad pegol but have also encouraged ongoing research into combination therapies that may further enhance clinical outcomes (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4, 16–17). As such, the therapeutic history of avacincaptad pegol is characterized by a steady progression from mechanistic discovery in the laboratory to robust clinical validation, underscoring its potential as a transformative agent in the management of dry AMD (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Qin et al., 2024, p. 3).

III. Mechanism of Action  
The mechanism of action of avacincaptad pegol is both specific and multifaceted, centering on the selective inhibition of complement factor C5—a pivotal molecule in the terminal complement pathway (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 4–8; Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). Under physiological conditions, C5 is cleaved into C5a and C5b. C5a acts as a potent anaphylatoxin that promotes inflammation through the recruitment and activation of immune cells, while C5b initiates the assembly of the membrane attack complex (MAC) by sequentially binding to complement components C6 through C9 (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Bege et al., 2025, pp. 4–8). The formation of the MAC on the surface of retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells is a critical driver of cell lysis and inflammatory damage that ultimately contributes to the progression of geographic atrophy in dry AMD (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Guimaraes et al., 2022, pp. 3–4).

Avacincaptad pegol exerts its therapeutic effect by binding directly to C5 with extremely high affinity, thereby blocking its enzymatic cleavage (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 4–8; Guimaraes et al., 2022, pp. 3–4). This inhibition prevents the generation of both C5a and C5b, ultimately forestalling the downstream assembly of the MAC (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 4–8; Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). The direct blockade of MAC formation is particularly beneficial in the subretinal microenvironment, where chronic complement activation is thought to contribute to lysosomal dysfunction in RPE cells (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Guimaraes et al., 2022, pp. 3–4). Specifically, when the MAC is deposited on RPE cell membranes, it can cause lysosomal membrane permeabilization (LMP), leading to impaired vacuolar ATPase (v-ATPase) activity and subsequent loss of lysosomal acidification (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 4–8; Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3).

Under normal circumstances, lysosomal acidification is essential for the proper maturation and activation of proteolytic enzymes such as cathepsin D (CTSD) (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Guimaraes et al., 2022, pp. 3–4). By preventing the formation of the MAC, avacincaptad pegol helps to preserve the proton gradient across the lysosomal membrane, thereby maintaining optimal conditions for lysosomal enzyme activity and ensuring adequate proteolytic clearance of debris within RPE cells (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 4–8; Guimaraes et al., 2022, pp. 3–4). This preservation of lysosomal function is of critical importance in preventing the accumulation of toxic byproducts, which have been implicated in the progressive degeneration of the retina observed in GA (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Guimaraes et al., 2022, pp. 3–4).

The detailed biochemistry underlying avacincaptad pegol’s activity was refined through iterative cycles of the SELEX process, during which the aptamer’s RNA sequence was optimized for maximal affinity toward C5 (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4; 4–8). The resulting aptamer exhibits a unique three-dimensional conformation that facilitates tight binding to a specific epitope on C5, effectively neutralizing its activity while sparing upstream complement components that may have beneficial roles in immune surveillance (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 4–8; 1–4). The high specificity of this interaction is essential because it limits off-target effects and reduces the risk of broader systemic immunosuppression—a concern that has previously complicated the development of complement inhibitors (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 4–8; Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3).

Furthermore, the localized administration of avacincaptad pegol via intravitreal injection ensures that its action is confined primarily to the retina, thereby concentrating its complement-inhibiting effects where they are most needed and minimizing the potential for systemic adverse events (Qin et al., 2024, p. 3; Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4). In preclinical studies, this targeted delivery was shown to result in marked reductions in the levels of C5 cleavage products, as well as diminished deposition of the MAC on the RPE, thereby validating the mechanistic rationale of the drug (Guimaraes et al., 2022, pp. 3–4; Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3).

In summary, avacincaptad pegol’s mode of action is rooted in its ability to effectively halt the terminal steps of the complement cascade by binding to C5, thereby preventing the formation of both pro-inflammatory C5a and the deleterious MAC (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 4–8; Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). Through this mechanism, it interrupts a key pathological process in dry AMD, offering a targeted strategy to preserve RPE cell function and maintain lysosomal integrity via sustained v-ATPase activity and proper cathepsin D maturation (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Guimaraes et al., 2022, pp. 3–4).

IV. Expected Effect  
Based on the mechanistic insights discussed above, the central hypothesis for avacincaptad pegol is that its inhibition of complement C5 activation will lead to a cascade of protective effects in the retinal microenvironment, ultimately decelerating the progression of GA associated with dry AMD (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Guimaraes et al., 2022, pp. 3–4). The expected effect in both in vitro and in vivo assays is multifactorial. Primarily, the aptamer is anticipated to reduce the generation of C5 cleavage products, thereby inhibiting the formation of the MAC on the surface of RPE cells. Such an effect is measurable via immunoassays that track the levels of C5a and related fragments, as well as by quantitative imaging techniques that assess MAC deposition (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Qin et al., 2024, pp. 2–3).

At the cellular level, the inhibition of MAC deposition is expected to translate into preserved lysosomal function within RPE cells—a critical factor given the reliance of these cells on lysosomal acidification for proper autophagic flux and metabolic homeostasis (Guimaraes et al., 2022, pp. 3–4; Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). In practical assay systems, one would anticipate that RPE cell cultures treated with avacincaptad pegol show maintained or even restored acidification of lysosomes as indicated by pH-sensitive fluorescent dyes, alongside intact activity of lysosomal enzymes such as cathepsin D (Guimaraes et al., 2022, pp. 3–4; Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). This preservation of lysosomal function is hypothesized to directly correlate with a reduced accumulation of cellular debris and toxic byproducts that accelerate the degenerative process in GA (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Bege et al., 2025, pp. 4–8).

Clinically, the outcome most often evaluated in trials of avacincaptad pegol is the deceleration of GA lesion enlargement, which is quantitatively assessed through imaging modalities such as fundus autofluorescence (FAF) and optical coherence tomography (OCT) (Qin et al., 2024, pp. 2–3; 3–3). In the pivotal GATHER 1 and GATHER 2 phase II/III studies, patients treated with monthly intravitreal injections of avacincaptad pegol exhibited reductions in GA progression rates of approximately 27% to 30% relative to sham-treated groups (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Bege et al., 2025, pp. 16–17). These anatomical endpoints serve as surrogate markers for the overall efficacy of the intervention, with the underlying assumption that slowing the expansion of GA lesions will eventually lead to stabilization of visual function (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Guimaraes et al., 2022, pp. 3–4).

At the molecular level, the expected effect also includes the restoration of critical lysosomal functions disrupted by excessive complement activation. Specifically, by preventing MAC-induced lysosomal membrane permeabilization, avacincaptad pegol is anticipated to maintain the proton gradient essential for v-ATPase function, thereby preserving the acidic environment required for optimal cathepsin D processing and other lysosomal enzymes (Guimaraes et al., 2022, pp. 3–4; Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). Such preservation is not only crucial for cellular clearance mechanisms but also plays a pivotal role in preventing intracellular accumulation of debris, which is a contributing factor in the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Guimaraes et al., 2022, pp. 3–4; Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3).

Moreover, since complement components, including C5, are expressed locally in the retina by RPE cells and resident immune cells, the targeted inhibition of C5 is expected to provide direct immunomodulatory benefits within the ocular microenvironment. This localized impact is critical because it addresses the pathophysiological cross-talk between complement activation and lysosomal dysfunction, which is thought to drive a vicious cycle of chronic inflammation and cellular degeneration (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Guimaraes et al., 2022, pp. 3–4). In theory, by reestablishing a balanced complement milieu, avacincaptad pegol may also help to curtail secondary inflammatory responses that otherwise exacerbate tissue damage, thereby preserving photoreceptor integrity and ultimately stabilizing visual acuity over time (Qin et al., 2024, pp. 2–3; 3–3).

In summary, the expected effects of avacincaptad pegol in the proposed assays and clinical settings are multi-layered. At the biochemical level, one should observe a pronounced reduction in C5 cleavage, diminished MAC formation on RPE membranes, and preserved lysosomal acidification and enzyme function. At the tissue level, these molecular events are predicted to culminate in a slowdown of GA lesion enlargement, which is widely regarded as a surrogate marker for the progression of dry AMD (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Qin et al., 2024, pp. 2–3). The overall hypothesis is that these combined effects will translate into meaningful clinical benefits, offering not only anatomical preservation but also the potential for stabilization—or even modest improvement—of visual function in affected patients (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3).

V. Overall Evaluation  
A comprehensive evaluation of avacincaptad pegol reveals a therapeutic candidate that is scientifically robust, mechanistically innovative, and clinically validated for the treatment of dry AMD with geographic atrophy. One of the major strengths of this therapeutic approach lies in its highly specific mechanism of action. By directly binding to and inhibiting complement factor C5, avacincaptad pegol interrupts a key pathological process at its source, namely the activation of the terminal complement cascade that results in the formation of the pro-inflammatory mediator C5a and the membrane attack complex (MAC) (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 4–8; Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). This level of specificity confers potential advantages over broader immunosuppressive agents, as it minimizes collateral inhibition of upstream complement components that may be protective. Such precise targeting results in reduced inflammation localized to the retinal tissues and lowers the risk of systemic adverse events (Guimaraes et al., 2022, pp. 3–4; Qin et al., 2024, pp. 3–3).

The extensive chemical modifications integrated into avacincaptad pegol’s structure—including 2′-fluoro and 2′-O-methyl substitutions, the incorporation of a 3′–3′ thymidine cap, and PEGylation—greatly enhance its stability and half-life in the intraocular environment (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4). These modifications are essential because they allow for sustained inhibition of C5 with relatively infrequent dosing, thereby improving the overall treatment regimen for a patient population that is often elderly and may struggle with stringent dosing schedules (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4; Qin et al., 2024, pp. 3–3). The aptamer-based nature of this drug also endows it with a low immunogenic risk profile, circumventing one of the potential pitfalls associated with protein-based therapies such as monoclonal antibodies (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4).

Clinically, the data emerging from the GATHER 1 and GATHER 2 phase II/III trials are particularly compelling. These studies have consistently demonstrated that patients receiving intravitreal injections of avacincaptad pegol experience a significant reduction in the rate of GA lesion growth, with observed reductions ranging from 27% to 30% compared to sham controls (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Bege et al., 2025, pp. 16–17). This tangible anatomical benefit, combined with the favorable safety profile—which includes minimal ocular adverse events—confirms the viability of C5 inhibition as a disease-modifying strategy in dry AMD (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4). Given that GA has long represented an area of substantial unmet clinical need, the regulatory approval of avacincaptad pegol by the FDA in August 2023 is a significant milestone that reinforces the credibility of this therapeutic approach (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4; Qin et al., 2024, pp. 3–3).

Another notable strength is the mechanistic rationale underpinning the expected therapeutic benefits. By preventing MAC formation on RPE membranes, avacincaptad pegol not only preserves the structural integrity of these cells but also protects lysosomal function by mitigating lysosomal membrane permeabilization (LMP) (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Bege et al., 2025, pp. 4–8). The preservation of lysosomal acidification and subsequent maintenance of autophagic and proteolytic function are critical factors in slowing the progression of GA, as they help to avert the accumulation of toxic metabolic byproducts that drive cellular degeneration (Guimaraes et al., 2022, pp. 3–4; Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). Thus, the therapeutic strategy is well anchored in a clear pathological framework that directly relates to the underlying disease process in dry AMD.

Despite the considerable promise of avacincaptad pegol, several potential weaknesses and challenges remain. One concern is the translation of anatomical benefits into meaningful functional improvements with respect to visual acuity. While reduction in GA lesion enlargement is an encouraging surrogate endpoint, there is a recognized challenge in correlating these anatomical outcomes with sustained improvements or stabilization of vision (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Qin et al., 2024, pp. 2–3). In some clinical trials involving complement inhibitors, the disconnect between reduced lesion growth and measurable improvements in best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) has raised questions about whether anatomical preservation will eventually lead to perceptible functional benefits for patients (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3).

Another potential challenge relates to the inherent complexity of the complement system. C5 is a critical component of the terminal cascade; however, the redundancy and cross-talk among multiple complement pathways may potentially compromise the overall efficacy of a monotherapeutic approach targeting only C5 (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 4–8; Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). There is a possibility that, even with effective C5 blockade, alternative inflammatory pathways may partially compensate for its inhibition, thereby limiting the long-term clinical benefit. This concern suggests that future treatment paradigms might require combination approaches that target both complement-mediated and non-complement-mediated mechanisms of retinal degeneration (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Bege et al., 2025, pp. 4–8).

The mode of delivery is another factor that merits consideration. Avacincaptad pegol is delivered via monthly intravitreal injections, which, while effective in ensuring localized drug activity, impose a significant treatment burden on an elderly patient population (Qin et al., 2024, pp. 3–3). Frequent intravitreal administration is associated with logistical challenges, including the risk of injection-related complications such as endophthalmitis or retinal detachment, albeit infrequent, and may negatively impact patient compliance over extended treatment periods (Qin et al., 2024, pp. 3–3; Bege et al., 2025, pp. 16–17). Future innovation in drug delivery systems—for example, sustained-release implants or alternative non-invasive administration routes—could be critical in overcoming this limitation and enhancing long-term treatment adherence (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 16–17; 1–4).

A further challenge lies in assessing the long-term safety of chronic complement inhibition within the ocular environment. Although the localized delivery method limits systemic exposure, the prolonged suppression of C5 activity in the retina may affect local immune surveillance and potentially predispose to subclinical infections or inflammatory dysregulation (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4; Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). Given that the complement system plays a nuanced role in both tissue repair and immune defense, extended studies are necessary to definitively characterize the long-term safety profile, particularly with respect to maintaining the delicate balance between controlling pathological inflammation and preserving protective immune functions (Qin et al., 2024, pp. 3–3; Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3).

Finally, the multifactorial nature of dry AMD suggests that while C5 inhibition may effectively slow the progression of GA, it might not fully address all aspects of this complex disease process. Oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and neurodegeneration are also critical contributors to AMD pathophysiology, and a monotherapy targeting the complement cascade may need to be integrated into a broader multimodal treatment strategy to achieve optimal clinical outcomes (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Bege et al., 2025, pp. 4–8). Such considerations imply that while avacincaptad pegol represents a significant advancement in the field, its maximal therapeutic potential may be realized only when used in combination with agents that address complementary pathological processes (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Bege et al., 2025, pp. 4–8).

In synthesizing these considerations, the overall evaluation of avacincaptad pegol is highly positive. Its unique molecular design, demonstrated clinical efficacy in reducing GA lesion growth, and favorable safety profile strongly support the hypothesis that targeted inhibition of complement C5 can provide a meaningful therapeutic benefit in dry AMD (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4; Qin et al., 2024, pp. 3–3). The strengths lie in both its mechanistic precision and the tangible clinical endpoints achieved in pivotal trials, which collectively underscore the validity of the hypothesis that disrupting terminal complement activation can preserve RPE integrity and lysosomal function (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3).

Nevertheless, the translation of these anatomical benefits into long-term preservation of vision, the challenges associated with the frequent intravitreal injection regimen, and the potential activation of alternative inflammatory pathways represent hurdles that warrant continued investigation (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). Addressing these challenges will likely require further mechanistic studies, extended clinical follow-up to capture functional outcomes, and possibly the development of innovative drug delivery systems that reduce the treatment burden on patients (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 16–17; Qin et al., 2024, pp. 3–3).

In conclusion, avacincaptad pegol emerges as a scientifically rigorous and clinically validated candidate for the treatment of dry AMD with geographic atrophy. Its ability to selectively inhibit complement C5 and thereby prevent MAC formation, lysosomal acidification loss, and subsequent RPE damage provides a mechanistic rationale that is well supported by both preclinical and clinical data (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Bege et al., 2025, pp. 4–8). Despite potential challenges in correlating anatomical preservation with functional visual improvements, the overall evidence supports further development and investment in this therapeutic candidate. The favorable risk–benefit profile observed to date, coupled with its innovative chemical design and robust clinical trial outcomes, positions avacincaptad pegol as one of the most promising agents in the evolving landscape of dry AMD therapy (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4; Qin et al., 2024, pp. 3–3).

Looking ahead, it is advisable that future research efforts focus on refining patient selection criteria through the identification of biomarkers predictive of complement activation and treatment response, as well as on exploring combinatorial approaches that might synergize the effects of C5 inhibition with agents addressing other facets of AMD pathogenesis (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Bege et al., 2025, pp. 4–8). The continued monitoring of long-term safety outcomes, particularly with respect to local immune function and the potential for injection-related complications, will also be crucial to ensure that the sustained administration of avacincaptad pegol remains both safe and effective over the extended treatment durations required in this chronic condition (Qin et al., 2024, pp. 3–3).

Moreover, from a commercial and regulatory perspective, the recent FDA approval of avacincaptad pegol for GA marks a significant milestone that not only validates the scientific rationale for targeting complement C5 but also signals the readiness of the ocular therapeutic landscape to embrace novel molecular entities with differentiated mechanisms of action (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4; Qin et al., 2024, pp. 3–3). This regulatory endorsement, together with the mounting clinical evidence, provides a solid foundation for the continued expansion of complement inhibition strategies in the management of retinal degenerative diseases, especially in patients for whom current treatment options are severely limited or ineffective (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 16–17; Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3).

The strategic outlook for avacincaptad pegol involves a dual focus: firstly, on consolidating its clinical benefits through extended, long-term trials that aim to establish a clear correlation between anatomical preservation and visual function stabilization; and secondly, on integrating its use into combination treatment regimens that might include neuroprotective, antioxidant, or even adjunctive anti-VEGF therapies to comprehensively address the multifaceted nature of dry AMD (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Bege et al., 2025, pp. 4–8). Such an integrated approach has the potential to not only enhance the overall therapeutic efficacy but also to extend the duration of clinical benefits, ultimately improving the quality of life for patients suffering from this debilitating condition (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4).

In balancing these strengths and challenges, the overall assessment of avacincaptad pegol remains decidedly positive. Its molecular design is state-of-the-art, its mechanism of action is directly aligned with a critical pathogenic process in dry AMD, and its clinical performance to date offers substantive evidence of efficacy in slowing disease progression (Qin et al., 2024, pp. 3–3; Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4). While further research is needed to fully elucidate the long-term functional benefits and to optimize the dosing regimens, the current body of evidence establishes a compelling rationale for its continued development and potential integration into the standard of care for dry AMD (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4; Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3).

In summary, avacincaptad pegol represents a landmark therapeutic innovation in the realm of retinal degenerative diseases. Its targeted inhibition of complement C5 not only addresses a fundamental driver of retinal inflammation and degenerative cell death in GA but also offers a new paradigm in the treatment of a condition that has long been resistant to effective disease-modifying interventions (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4). The extensive clinical validation, marked by significant reductions in GA lesion growth and an acceptable safety profile, underscores its potential to significantly alter the natural history of dry AMD and improve patient outcomes (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Bege et al., 2025, pp. 16–17).

Considering all facets of its development—including chemical design, mechanistic efficacy, clinical performance, and future strategic directions—avacincaptad pegol stands as one of the most promising therapeutic candidates for addressing the unmet needs in dry AMD (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4; Qin et al., 2024, pp. 3–3). Continued investment in both clinical and translational research is warranted, as is the exploration of complementary therapeutic strategies that may further potentiate its benefits. As the field advances toward integrated, multimodal approaches to retinal disease, the therapeutic promise of avacincaptad pegol is likely to serve as a cornerstone for future innovations that collectively strive to preserve vision and enhance the quality of life for patients with dry AMD (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3).

Ultimately, the comprehensive evaluation presented here affirms that the repurposing and further clinical development of avacincaptad pegol is both scientifically grounded and clinically justified. Its ability to modulate the complement cascade, protect RPE cells from MAC-induced injury, maintain lysosomal function, and reduce the progression of GA lesions is supported by robust preclinical and clinical evidence (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Bege et al., 2025, pp. 4–8). The promising results from pivotal trials, together with a well-established safety profile and the advantages conferred by its aptamer-based design, mark avacincaptad pegol as a leading candidate in the ongoing battle against dry AMD (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 16–17; Qin et al., 2024, pp. 3–3).

In closing, while challenges remain—particularly in correlating anatomical improvements with sustained visual acuity and in managing the logistical hurdles associated with frequent intravitreal injections—the overall benefits of avacincaptad pegol are clear. It provides a targeted, innovative, and effective means of intervening in a condition that has historically lacked disease-modifying therapies. Its continued development promises to not only fill an unmet clinical need but also to serve as a model for the adaptation of aptamer technologies to other areas of degenerative and inflammatory diseases (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4). As research efforts progress, strategic collaborations and further optimization of its delivery and combination with other therapeutic modalities will be key to fully harnessing its potential, ultimately reshaping the therapeutic landscape for dry age-related macular degeneration (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Qin et al., 2024, pp. 3–3).

Given the significant strides made in understanding the complement system’s involvement in dry AMD pathogenesis and the robust clinical data supporting C5 inhibition, avacincaptad pegol stands poised not only as a transformative monotherapy but also as an integral component of future combination treatment strategies (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Bege et al., 2025, pp. 4–8). The scientific and clinical communities now have an opportunity to leverage this innovative approach to redefine patient care in a field where previous treatment options have been limited. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
GDC-0941 (pictilisib) is a synthetic, orally bioavailable, ATP-competitive, pan–class I phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K) inhibitor discovered through structure-guided medicinal chemistry at Genentech as an optimization beyond early tool compounds and the dual PI3K/mTOR inhibitor PI-103, with substantially improved selectivity for class I PI3Ks and favorable pharmacokinetics (PK) suitable for systemic dosing in humans (Garces, n.d.; Zhao et al., 2017; Li et al., 2024). At the biochemical level, pictilisib exhibits low-nanomolar potency against p110α and p110δ, with activity across class I isoforms (representative IC₅₀s: α ≈ 3 nM, β ≈ 33 nM, δ ≈ 3 nM, γ ≈ 75 nM) and weak activity on mTOR (~0.58 μM), consistent with selective targeting of class I PI3Ks over mTOR kinase (Huang et al., 2023; Garces, n.d.; Josephs & Sarker, 2016; Zhao et al., 2017). Co-crystal structural analysis shows an ATP-mimetic thieno[3,2-d]pyrimidine core in which the morpholine oxygen donates a hinge hydrogen bond (Val882), the indazole engages an affinity pocket (Asp841/Tyr867), and a methanesulfonyl-piperazine tail projects toward solvent; these interactions underpin its potency and selectivity within the class I PI3K ATP site (PDB 3DBS) (Garces, n.d.). Pictilisib belongs to the pan-class I PI3K inhibitor class, a therapeutic category widely advanced in oncology to suppress the PI3K→AKT→mTOR signaling axis that governs cell growth, survival, and metabolism; multiple agents in this class have reached clinical testing or approval, providing a clear translational precedent for pathway engagement and safety management in humans (Schmitz et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2023; Li et al., 2024).

Therapeutic History  
The development history of pictilisib is anchored in oncology, where first-in-human Phase I trials established a recommended Phase II dose of 330 mg once daily, dose-proportional PK (Tₘₐₓ ≈ 2 h, t₁/₂ ≈ 13–24 h), and robust pharmacodynamic (PD) target engagement—up to ~90% inhibition of phosphorylated AKT (Ser473) in platelet-rich plasma within 1–3 h of dosing and suppression of p-AKT and p-S6 in tumor biopsies at sufficient exposure (AUC > 20 μM·h) (Sarker et al., 2015; Mishra et al., 2021). Across Phase I combination studies, pictilisib showed a manageable safety profile and some antitumor activity, with common adverse events including nausea, diarrhea, rash, fatigue, hyperglycemia, and cytopenias; dose-limiting toxicity in some settings was grade 3 maculopapular rash (Mishra et al., 2021; Josephs & Sarker, 2016; Sarker et al., 2015). Although pathway suppression was clear, randomized combination trials in breast and lung cancer variably met efficacy endpoints and broader development was limited by tolerability in multi-drug regimens and modest efficacy as monotherapy—experience that nonetheless provides clinically validated PK/PD tools and class-effect safety benchmarks (Mishra et al., 2021; Gao et al., 2017).

No preclinical or clinical use of pictilisib or other class I PI3K inhibitors has been reported for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or RPE-centered retinal disease models in the provided literature, and a recent review emphasizes that no ongoing clinical trials directly target autophagy in AMD, underscoring an evidence gap for PI3K inhibitors in this indication (Blasiak et al., 2025). By contrast, direct downstream pathway modulation in RPE—mTORC1 inhibition with rapamycin—has shown that activating the lysosome–TFEB axis reduces POS-derived autofluorescent granules in vitro in a hydrolase-dependent manner, but clinical testing in advanced AMD returned limited efficacy and adverse effects, illustrating both the mechanistic plausibility of modulating this pathway and translational challenges (Falcão et al., 2024). Collectively, the therapeutic history supports that class I PI3K inhibitors achieve systemic PI3K pathway inhibition in humans with tractable but nontrivial toxicities; however, there is no published RPE- or AMD-focused body of work with pictilisib to date in the provided context (Sarker et al., 2015; Mishra et al., 2021; Blasiak et al., 2025).

Mechanism of Action  
Class I PI3Ks phosphorylate PIP₂ to PIP₃, recruiting PH-domain effectors including PDK1 and AKT to the plasma membrane, where AKT is activated by phosphorylation at Thr308 (PDK1) and Ser473 (mTORC2) (Huang et al., 2023). Activated AKT phosphorylates multiple substrates that converge on mTORC1 activation (via TSC2/PRAS40), leading to phosphorylation of S6K1 and 4E-BP1 to promote protein synthesis and suppress autophagy, thereby integrating growth-factor status with anabolic programs (Huang et al., 2023; Castel et al., 2021). In retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), AKT/mTOR signaling is an established regulator of cell proliferation and autophagy; mTORC1 activation inhibits autophagy by blocking ULK1 signaling and autolysosomal biogenesis, whereas rapamycin-mediated mTORC1 inhibition activates autophagy and preserves photoreceptor function in preclinical models (Chang et al., 2015). PI3K inhibition upstream of AKT is thus expected to reduce PIP₃ generation, limit AKT membrane recruitment/activation, and secondarily depress mTORC1 signaling in RPE (Castel et al., 2021; Chang et al., 2015).

PI3K→AKT signaling intersects directly with TFEB/TFE3—the master transcription factors of lysosomal biogenesis and the CLEAR regulon—through both mTORC1-dependent and mTORC1-independent routes (Falcão et al., 2024; Ghosh et al., 2024). Nutrient-driven mTORC1 activity at the lysosome phosphorylates TFEB/TFE3 to retain them in the cytosol; conversely, mTORC1 inhibition permits TFEB nuclear translocation and induction of lysosomal/autophagy genes (Falcão et al., 2024). Importantly, AKT2 directly phosphorylates TFEB (at Ser467) and TFE3 (Ser321), promoting 14-3-3 binding and cytoplasmic sequestration independent of mTORC1, thereby repressing CLEAR gene expression and lysosomal programs in RPE (Ghosh et al., 2023; Ghosh et al., 2024). In AMD-relevant contexts—human dysmorphic macular RPE, CFH risk-allele iPSC-RPE, and Akt2 RPE-specific knock-in mice—AKT2 upregulation increases TFEB/TFE3 phosphorylation, reduces lysosomal hydrolases (cathepsin D/L) and CLEAR target expression, impairs autophagic flux, and shifts autophagy toward secretory pathways characterized by increased FKBP51/SNAP23, autophagosome fusion with the plasma membrane, and extracellular release of IL-1β/HMGB1 (Ghosh et al., 2023; Ghosh et al., 2024). TFEB rescue via a phospho-deficient TFEB-S467A mutant or pharmacologic TFEB activation with trehalose restores cathepsin D/L and autophagy genes, normalizes autophagosome–lysosome fusion, and improves RPE structure in AMD-like mouse models, establishing TFEB/TFE3 as actionable nodes downstream of AKT2 in RPE (Ghosh et al., 2023; Ghosh et al., 2024).

SIRT5 and mitochondrial metabolism integrate with AKT2–TFEB signaling in RPE. SIRT5 interacts with AKT2 and reduces lysine malonylation on AKT2, modulating AKT2 activity; AKT2, via inhibition of PGC-1α, downregulates SIRT5, creating a bidirectional circuit that affects TFEB-dependent lysosomal function and mitochondrial respiration (Ghosh et al., 2023). AKT2 upregulation impairs mitochondrial respiration (maximal and ATP-linked), which is rescued by SIRT5, linking mitochondrial–lysosomal crosstalk to RPE proteostasis (Ghosh et al., 2023). Functionally, failure of the AKT2/SIRT5/TFEB axis elevates secretory autophagy and likely contributes to drusen pathogenesis by exporting inflammatory cargo (Ghosh et al., 2023).

These mechanistic data converge with mTORC1→TFEB observations in POS-fed RPE models. Synchronous POS phagocytosis transiently activates mTORC1 early, with TFEB protein increasing but remaining phosphorylated during late maturation, indicating a bottleneck at TFEB activation (Falcão et al., 2024). Pharmacologic mTORC1 inhibition with rapamycin after AFGs have formed lowers POS-derived autofluorescence by ~30% in hfRPE/ARPE-19, reduces pS6, decreases the pTFEB/TFEB ratio, increases LAMP1, and requires active lysosomal hydrolases: cathepsin D knockout or protease/lipase inhibition abolishes the rapamycin effect (Falcão et al., 2024). Human AMD RPE exhibits hyperphosphorylated TFEB with decreased nuclear localization and lower cathepsin D/L protein levels and activities, consistent with impaired lysosome proteolysis; constitutively active TFEB boosts CLEAR genes, including hydrolases and V-ATPase subunits (e.g., ATP6V0A1), supporting enhanced acidification capacity (Falcão et al., 2025).

Pictilisib’s proximal pharmacology—ATP-competitive inhibition of class I PI3Ks—has been shown to produce substantial pathway suppression in human tissues (reduced pAKT, reduced pS6) and in tumor models; such upstream inhibition is expected to depress both AKT→mTORC1 signaling and AKT2-mediated TFEB phosphorylation, potentially enabling TFEB/TFE3 nuclear translocation and restoration of CLEAR programs in RPE (Sarker et al., 2015; Mishra et al., 2021; Castel et al., 2021; Ghosh et al., 2024). Two caveats are central. First, class III PI3K/VPS34 activity is required for autophagosome nucleation; thus class I–selective inhibition (as with pictilisib) is mechanistically appropriate, whereas class III inhibition would be detrimental to autophagy flux (Wang et al., 2023). Second, while AKT inhibitors (e.g., MK-2206) and TFEB activators (trehalose) have directly increased autophagy and TFEB nuclear translocation in RPE, no direct evidence of class I PI3K inhibitors reproducing these effects in RPE has been reported in the provided literature (Karim et al., 2020; Blasiak et al., 2025).

Expected Effect  
In RPE cell assays designed to model dry AMD–relevant lysosomal stress (e.g., POS feeding, A2E/oxidant exposure, or CFH risk-allele iPSC-RPE), pictilisib is expected to reduce PI3K-dependent PIP₃ generation, lowering membrane recruitment and phosphorylation of AKT, thereby secondarily suppressing mTORC1 and directly relieving AKT2-mediated phosphorylation of TFEB/TFE3 (Huang et al., 2023; Castel et al., 2021; Ghosh et al., 2024). Mechanistically, this should dephosphorylate TFEB/TFE3, promote nuclear translocation, and activate the CLEAR transcriptional program to increase components of lysosomal biogenesis and function (e.g., LAMP1/2, cathepsin D/L, and V-ATPase subunits), thereby enhancing degradative capacity and autophagic flux (Falcão et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2025; Falcão et al., 2024).

Operationally testable expected effects include:  
• Signaling: decreased pAKT (Ser473) and pS6 (Ser235/236) within hours of dosing in RPE, mirroring PD seen in tumors and platelet-rich plasma in human trials, establishing target engagement (Sarker et al., 2015; Mishra et al., 2021).  
• TFEB/TFE3 activation: reduction in pTFEB/TFEB ratio, increased nuclear TFEB/TFE3, and induction of CLEAR genes; in RPE systems, TFEB activation correlates with increased LAMP1 and rescue of lysosomal hydrolases and autophagy mediators (e.g., ATG9B), as seen upon TFEB S467A expression or trehalose treatment (Falcão et al., 2024; Ghosh et al., 2023; Ghosh et al., 2024).  
• Lysosomal function: increased abundance and maturation of cathepsin D (pro→intermediate→mature chain) and cathepsin L, and improved degradative flux, consistent with observations that AMD RPE shows diminished cathepsin levels/activities and that hydrolase function is required for rapamycin-mediated clearance of POS-derived AFGs (Falcão et al., 2025; Falcão et al., 2024).  
• Autophagic flux: increased LC3-II turnover (± bafilomycin A₁), reduced p62/SQSTM1 accumulation, restored autophagosome–lysosome fusion (e.g., GFP-LC3 and LysoTracker/LAMP1 colocalization), and decreased accumulation of double-membrane autophagosomes on EM, reversing the AKT2-driven flux block (Ghosh et al., 2023; Ghosh et al., 2024).  
• POS-derived autofluorescence: reduction in POS-dependent autofluorescent granules in preventive and resolving paradigms, analogous to mTORC1 inhibition or TFEB activation effects; efficacy will depend on intact lysosomal hydrolase activity (Falcão et al., 2024).  
• Secretory autophagy: decreased FKBP51/SNAP23 elevation, reduced plasma-membrane fusion of autophagosomes, and lower extracellular release of IL-1β and HMGB1 from RPE, mirroring effects seen with SIRT5 co-expression or AKT2 inhibition (Ghosh et al., 2023; Ghosh et al., 2024).  
• Acidification: although lysosomal pH has not been directly measured after class I PI3K inhibition in RPE, TFEB activation increases expression of V-ATPase subunits, and improved hydrolase activities imply normalization of the acidic lumen; direct pH assays (LysoSensor/LysoTracker) should be incorporated because efficacy of rapamycin/TFEB approaches depends on intact lysosomal acid hydrolases (Falcão et al., 2025; Falcão et al., 2024).

These expectations rest on the well-documented presence and dysregulation of the AKT2→TFEB/TFE3→CLEAR axis in RPE and the dependence of POS clearance on mTOR/TFEB-governed lysosomal function (Ghosh et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2024). AKT2 is upregulated in macular RPE from AMD donors and in AMD-like mouse models, and RPE-specific Akt2 overexpression is sufficient to induce AMD-like pathology, supporting target relevance in the cell type and disease context of interest (Ghosh et al., 2023; Ghosh et al., 2024). Because PI3K is upstream of AKT, class I PI3K inhibition should, in principle, reduce AKT2 activity and thereby favor TFEB activation; however, no direct studies in the provided literature demonstrate pictilisib (or any class I PI3K inhibitor) inducing TFEB nuclear translocation or improving cathepsin D maturation/activity in RPE, so these are testable, evidence-generating predictions rather than established facts (Blasiak et al., 2025; Chang et al., 2015; Karim et al., 2020).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Mechanistic alignment with disease biology: Dry AMD features impaired RPE autophagy–lysosome function, diminished cathepsin D/L levels/activities, and TFEB hyperphosphorylation with reduced nuclear TFEB, all of which converge on lysosomal insufficiency and accumulation of lipofuscin-like material and extracellular drusen; upstream PI3K inhibition is a coherent strategy to relieve AKT2- and mTORC1-mediated repression of TFEB/TFE3 and restore CLEAR-driven lysosomal biogenesis and flux (Falcão et al., 2025; Falcão et al., 2024; Ghosh et al., 2024).  
• Drug tractability and translational readiness: Pictilisib achieves robust systemic target engagement in humans (pAKT/pS6 suppression), has well-characterized PK/PD and class-effect safety, and is chemically and biophysically optimized, enabling accelerated preclinical testing and dosage/formulation exploration for ocular delivery or low systemic exposure strategies (Sarker et al., 2015; Mishra et al., 2021; Garces, n.d.).  
• Selectivity profile appropriate for autophagy enhancement: Because autophagosome nucleation requires class III PI3K/VPS34, class I selectivity of pictilisib avoids this liability while suppressing AKT→mTOR signaling and AKT2-dependent TFEB phosphorylation, in contrast to nonselective PI3K inhibition which would be deleterious (Wang et al., 2023; Castel et al., 2021).

Risks and Gaps  
• No direct RPE/AMD data with class I PI3K inhibitors: In contrast to clear benefits from rapamycin and TFEB activation, the literature presented contains no direct evidence that class I PI3K inhibition, or pictilisib specifically, improves TFEB activation/nuclear entry, lysosomal biogenesis, cathepsin D maturation/activity, lysosomal acidification, autophagy flux, or POS handling in RPE; thus, the central hypothesis remains unvalidated experimentally in the disease-relevant cell type (Blasiak et al., 2025; Chang et al., 2015; Falcão et al., 2024). By comparison, AKT inhibition (MK-2206) and trehalose have been shown to increase autophagy and nuclear TFEB in RPE, and AKT2 inhibitors reduced lipid/apoE in CFH(H/H) RPE, but these are not PI3K inhibitors and may differ in cellular selectivity and compensatory signaling (Karim et al., 2020; Ghosh et al., 2024).  
• Complexity of autophagy modulation and context dependence: Autophagy is a double-edged sword with biphasic responses to stress; overactivation or mistimed activation could exacerbate RPE stress or impair other retinal cell types, and some autophagy inhibitors display retinal toxicity (e.g., chloroquine class), emphasizing the need for precise control and safety profiling (Blasiak et al., 2025; Kaarniranta et al., 2013). Rapamycin has shown only limited clinical efficacy in advanced AMD despite mechanistic benefits in vitro, illustrating translational friction between pathway modulation and clinical outcomes (Falcão et al., 2024).  
• Safety, delivery, and exposure management: Systemic class I PI3K inhibition induces hyperglycemia, rash, and gastrointestinal toxicities; while these were generally manageable, ocular delivery strategies (intravitreal or periocular) and ocular pharmacokinetics for pictilisib are uncharacterized in the provided literature, and tissue-specific PD (e.g., drug levels at the RPE/Bruch’s complex) is likely to determine efficacy and safety (Josephs & Sarker, 2016; Sarker et al., 2015; Mishra et al., 2021). Tissue PD variability seen in tumors versus blood suggests careful intratissue PD assays are necessary (Sarker et al., 2015).  
• Isoform and cell-type specificity: AKT2 is the isoform implicated in RPE TFEB repression and secretory autophagy; upstream PI3K isoform contributions in RPE are not defined here, and pan-class I inhibition could affect neighboring retinal cells, choroidal endothelium, and immune cells, potentially altering retinal immunity and angiogenesis in unintended ways (Ghosh et al., 2024; Castel et al., 2021). Given the evidence favoring AKT2-selective inhibition or direct TFEB activation in RPE models, PI3K-level intervention may be broader than necessary and carry off-target tissue consequences (Ghosh et al., 2024; Karim et al., 2020).  
• Acidification endpoint uncertainty: The hypothesis specifically posits enhanced lysosomal acidification, yet none of the provided sources report direct lysosomal pH measurements after class I PI3K inhibition in RPE; while CLEAR induction can increase V-ATPase subunits and rapamycin-mediated clearance requires active hydrolases, direct acidification effects remain to be demonstrated (Falcão et al., 2025; Falcão et al., 2024; Blasiak et al., 2025).

Go/No-Go Evidence Plan  
Given the strong mechanistic rationale but absence of direct RPE data, a staged validation program is warranted:  
– In vitro RPE target engagement and TFEB activation: Demonstrate pictilisib decreases pAKT (Ser473) and pS6 in primary human fetal RPE, ARPE-19, and iPSC-RPE, and increases nuclear TFEB/TFE3 with induction of CLEAR genes (CTSD, CTSL, LAMP2, ATP6V0A1) assessed by Western, RT-qPCR, and ChIP-qPCR (Falcão et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2025; Ghosh et al., 2024).  
– Lysosome function readouts: Quantify cathepsin D maturation and enzymatic activity, LAMP1/2 abundance, and lysosomal pH using ratiometric probes; include hydrolase inhibition controls to assess dependence analogous to the rapamycin data (Falcão et al., 2024).  
– Autophagic flux and modality: Assess LC3-II turnover (± bafilomycin A₁), p62 dynamics, autolysosome number (LC3–LAMP1 colocalization), and EM confirmation; evaluate secretory-autophagy markers (FKBP51, SNAP23) and extracellular cargo (HMGB1, IL-1β) to test reversal of the AKT2-driven phenotype (Ghosh et al., 2023; Ghosh et al., 2024).  
– Functional disease readouts: Test POS-dependent autofluorescence reduction in preventive and resolving paradigms and POS degradation assays; evaluate lipid/apoE accumulation in CFH(H/H) iPSC-RPE and Cryba1 cKO explants to compare with reported trehalose and AKT2 inhibitor effects (Falcão et al., 2024; Ghosh et al., 2023; Ghosh et al., 2024).  
– In vivo and delivery: Establish ocular PK and tolerability for local delivery (intravitreal/periocular) in rodents, then test efficacy in RPE-driven AMD-like models (Akt2 KI, Cryba1 cKO, NaIO₃) with TFEB activation, lysosomal and functional endpoints (ERG/SD-OCT) (Ghosh et al., 2024; Ghosh et al., 2023; Falcão et al., 2025).  
– Benchmarking: Include rapamycin (mTORC1 inhibition), MK-2206 (AKT inhibition), and trehalose (mTOR-independent TFEB activation) comparators to position PI3K inhibition within the therapeutic landscape (Falcão et al., 2024; Karim et al., 2020; Ghosh et al., 2023).

Conclusion  
Pictilisib offers a mechanistically coherent, drug-like approach to modulate an RPE pathway of clear pathogenic relevance—AKT2/mTOR-mediated repression of TFEB/TFE3 and the CLEAR network—backed by robust human PK/PD experience and a selectivity profile compatible with enhancing autophagy without impeding VPS34-dependent nucleation (Ghosh et al., 2024; Sarker et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2023). However, the absence of direct evidence that class I PI3K inhibition rectifies TFEB activity, lysosomal hydrolase function (notably cathepsin D), lysosomal acidification, autophagic flux, or POS clearance in RPE is a critical gap that precludes immediate advancement; by contrast, downstream interventions (rapamycin, TFEB activation, AKT2 inhibition) already demonstrate these benefits in RPE models (Falcão et al., 2024; Ghosh et al., 2024). On balance, pictilisib is plausible and testable but not yet justified for translational progression without focused RPE and ocular studies; an AKT2-selective inhibitor or TFEB-directed strategies may offer a higher probability of effect with narrower network perturbation, and should be run in parallel as mechanistic benchmarks (Ghosh et al., 2024; Karim et al., 2020). If the proposed RPE experiments confirm that pictilisib restores TFEB-driven lysosomal programs, improves cathepsin D maturation/activity, normalizes autophagy flux, and reduces POS-derived autofluorescence with acceptable ocular tolerability, the candidate would merit advancement to in vivo ocular efficacy testing; absent such confirmation, resources should pivot to agents with demonstrated RPE TFEB engagement (Ghosh et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2024).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
2-Hydroxypropyl-β-cyclodextrin (HPβCD) is a chemically modified derivative of natural β-cyclodextrin—a cyclic oligosaccharide consisting of glucose units linked via α-1,4 glycosidic bonds. This modification, achieved by the introduction of hydroxypropyl groups, improves its solubility and reduces its inherent cytotoxicity relative to unmodified cyclodextrins. HPβCD belongs to the cyclodextrin class, molecules that have been widely used in pharmaceutical formulations as solubilizing agents and excipients due to their ability to encapsulate hydrophobic molecules within their lipophilic interior, thereby increasing bioavailability. Over the years, these agents have gained attention as cholesterol-binding molecules, and HPβCD is no exception, being repurposed for diseases characterized by pathological cholesterol accumulation such as Niemann–Pick type C1 (NPC1). Its structural properties permit the formation of inclusion complexes with cholesterol and other lipids, facilitating their mobilization and removal from cells. Given its established role in NPC1 disease and emerging evidence supporting its ability to cross the blood–retina barrier, HPβCD is now being evaluated as a therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD), specifically targeting drusen-associated cholesterol accumulation in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells (Calias, 2018; Roney, 2020).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, HPβCD has been extensively investigated as a therapeutic intervention for lysosomal storage diseases, with a particular focus on Niemann–Pick disease type C (NPC), a condition characterized by the pathological accumulation of cholesterol and glycosphingolipids in cells. Preclinical studies in animal models have demonstrated that systemic administration of HPβCD can lower intracellular cholesterol levels, thereby ameliorating disease-related cellular dysfunction. However, its pharmacokinetic limitations—most notably, its minimal penetration of the blood–brain barrier (BBB) when administered intravenously—have necessitated alternative routes of delivery, such as intrathecal administration, to achieve sufficient central nervous system (CNS) exposure (Calias, 2018). In the context of retinal diseases, several studies have investigated the effects of HPβCD in animal models of retinal cholesterol dyshomeostasis. In these models, HPβCD treatment has been associated with significant reductions in cholesterol crystals, diminished lipid deposition in structures such as Bruch’s membrane, and decreased activation of retinal macrophages and microglial cells (El-Darzi et al., 2023). Although HPβCD has been repurposed from its application in NPC to target retinal pathologies, a focused investigation into its use for dry AMD remains to be performed clinically, as systematic searches on ClinicalTrials.gov indicate that no registered trials have specifically addressed cyclodextrin use in AMD (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, HPβCD acts primarily as a cholesterol extractor by leveraging its toroidal structure, which is characterized by a hydrophilic exterior and a relatively hydrophobic interior cavity. This unique architecture enables HPβCD to form inclusion complexes with cholesterol, effectively sequestering the lipid from cellular membranes. In the setting of RPE cells, where lysosomal cholesterol accumulation is implicated in the pathogenesis of dry AMD, HPβCD is hypothesized to mobilize cholesterol from lysosomal membranes. Excess cholesterol in these membranes disrupts the lipid microdomains necessary for the optimal assembly and functioning of protein complexes such as the vacuolar-type H⁺-ATPase (v-ATPase), which is essential for maintaining lysosomal acidity (Nociari, Kiss, & Rodriguez-Boulan, 2017). By extracting cholesterol, HPβCD is expected to restore these lipid microdomains, thereby facilitating the proper assembly and function of the v-ATPase complex. This normalization of v-ATPase assembly is critical for reestablishing an acidic environment within lysosomes, which in turn is necessary for the optimal activity of lysosomal hydrolases such as cathepsin D (CTSD).

In neurons and other cell types, studies have demonstrated that HPβCD treatment leads to a reduction in both luminal and membrane-associated cholesterol levels, a process that not only improves lysosomal trafficking but also induces lysosomal exocytosis under certain conditions (Roney, 2020). Furthermore, the improvement in lysosomal acidification following HPβCD-mediated cholesterol extraction has been correlated with enhanced autophagic flux due to increased CTSD-mediated proteolysis. Although direct evidence for this mechanism in RPE cells is still emerging, it is reasonable to extrapolate that similar molecular events would occur in retinal cells. The restoration of lysosomal pH and the subsequent improvement in autophagy are critical because they directly contribute to the clearance of intracellular debris, including drusen lipids, thereby potentially reducing the lipid burden that characterizes the progression of dry AMD (Nociari et al., 2017; Roney, 2020).

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis driving the repurposing of HPβCD for dry AMD is that it will mobilize cholesterol from RPE lysosomal membranes, thereby restoring the integrity of lipid microdomains that are essential for v-ATPase assembly. In practical terms, treatment with HPβCD is expected to yield several interrelated outcomes. First, the reduction in membrane cholesterol is anticipated to alleviate the inhibitory effect of cholesterol excess on v-ATPase assembly, leading to improved proton pump activity and a consequent normalization of lysosomal pH. Given that the activity of CTSD is pH-dependent—with optimal function occurring under acidic conditions—the normalization of lysosomal pH should enable enhanced CTSD activity and improved autophagic degradation of lipid aggregates (Nociari et al., 2017; Roney, 2020).

Second, by promoting the removal of excess cholesterol, HPβCD should reduce the formation of cholesterol crystals, a pathological hallmark associated with retinal lipid dyshomeostasis and drusen formation. Animal studies have demonstrated that HPβCD treatment leads to a significant reduction in the number of cholesterol crystals per unit area in retinal tissues, which is strongly correlated with improvements in retinal lipid processing and decreased inflammatory responses mediated by macrophage and microglial activation (El-Darzi et al., 2023).

Third, in laboratory assays using RPE cell cultures, one would expect to observe a decrease in the proportion of lipid-laden lysosomes, accompanied by measurable improvements in lysosomal acidification—parameters that serve as surrogate markers for enhanced autophagic capacity. Additionally, given the evidence that HPβCD can cross the blood–retina barrier when administered via systemic routes, there is a strong rationale for expecting that appropriate dosing regimens will yield sufficient retinal tissue concentrations to exert these beneficial effects (El-Darzi et al., 2023). Ultimately, these molecular and cellular changes are anticipated to culminate in the reduction of drusen lipid volumes, thereby slowing or potentially halting the progression of dry AMD (El-Darzi et al., 2023).

Overall Evaluation:  
The repurposing of HPβCD for the treatment of dry AMD is underpinned by a robust mechanistic rationale, a substantial preclinical history, and an acceptable clinical safety profile observed in other indications. One of the greatest strengths of HPβCD is its dual functionality: the ability to form effective inclusion complexes with cholesterol and the resultant improvement in lysosomal function. In several animal models of retinal cholesterol dyshomeostasis, HPβCD has yielded promising results by lowering total, unesterified, and esterified cholesterol levels, reducing the number of cholesterol crystals, and mitigating inflammatory responses in the retina (El-Darzi et al., 2023). These data provide a compelling basis for its evaluation in conditions such as dry AMD where drusen formation is closely linked to aberrant cholesterol metabolism. Furthermore, its prior use in the treatment of NPC—a condition that shares certain pathogenic features with AMD in terms of lysosomal dysfunction—adds credence to the hypothesis that HPβCD may exert similar therapeutic effects in RPE cells (Calias, 2018).

A significant advantage of HPβCD is its established safety record in clinical studies for NPC. Although challenges remain regarding optimal dosing—especially given the compound’s limited ability to cross the BBB when administered systemically—the retinal application appears more favorable, as preclinical studies suggest that HPβCD is capable of traversing the blood–retina barrier and achieving therapeutic concentrations in retinal tissues (El-Darzi et al., 2023). However, it should be noted that the safety profile in the context of chronic ocular exposure remains to be fully characterized. Notably, clinical studies in NPC have observed adverse effects such as hearing loss with certain routes of administration, and while these effects may not directly translate to ocular toxicity, rigorous ocular safety studies will be essential to ensure that any repurposing for dry AMD is both efficacious and safe (Calias, 2018).

Another potential strength lies in the specificity of the lipid‐targeting strategy. Unlike therapies that broadly modulate inflammatory or oxidative stress pathways, HPβCD acts directly on the cholesterol burden—the underlying driver of drusen lipid accumulation in dry AMD. This mechanistic specificity has the potential to result in a more direct impact on the disease process, rather than merely modifying secondary symptoms. Mechanistically, the extraction of cholesterol by HPβCD is anticipated to restore the lipid environment within RPE lysosomal membranes, thereby re-enabling the proper assembly of v-ATPase complexes. This, in turn, can lead to improved lysosomal acidification, enhanced cathepsin D activity, and accelerated autophagic clearance of damaged cellular components—a cascade of events that would address one of the root causes of retinal degeneration in AMD (Nociari et al., 2017; Roney, 2020).

Despite these strengths, several weaknesses and uncertainties must be acknowledged. First, while the preclinical data in animal models are promising, there remains a lack of clinical trial data specifically focusing on the use of HPβCD in dry AMD. A search using the relevant keywords indicates a paucity of clinical evidence in this particular indication (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.), which means that translational hurdles remain before HPβCD can be confidently recommended for dry AMD therapy. Second, although the mechanism by which HPβCD affects v-ATPase assembly and CTSD activity is supported by data in neuronal models, direct evidence of these molecular events in RPE cells is still emerging, leaving some uncertainty regarding the depth of its effects on lysosomal autophagy in the retinal environment (Nociari et al., 2017). Third, formulation and administration routes will be critical considerations. While systemic dosing has been used in other indications, the optimal approach for targeting the retina might require localized delivery techniques—such as intravitreal injection or the development of a sustained-release ocular formulation—to maximize retinal exposure while minimizing systemic exposure and off-target effects. Finally, the potential for adverse events, particularly those related to over-extraction of cholesterol or unintended disruption of lipid homeostasis, must be carefully evaluated in the context of chronic ocular treatment.

In summary, HPβCD is a well-characterized compound with a history of successful application in disorders of cholesterol accumulation, notably NPC. Its ability to extract cholesterol from cellular membranes, restore lipid microdomains, and thereby normalize lysosomal function forms a strong mechanistic basis for its evaluation as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. Preclinical studies in animal models provide encouraging evidence that HPβCD can reduce retinal cholesterol accumulation, lower the number of cholesterol crystals, and improve markers of lysosomal function in retinal tissues. This directly aligns with the therapeutic hypothesis that the mobilization of cholesterol from RPE lysosomal membranes will restore v-ATPase activity, normalize lysosomal pH, enhance cathepsin D activity, and ultimately reduce the drusen lipid burden characteristic of dry AMD (Calias, 2018; El-Darzi et al., 2023; Nociari et al., 2017; Roney, 2020).

However, the translation of these preclinical findings into a clinically effective therapy for dry AMD will require addressing several critical challenges. These include the absence of direct clinical data in AMD, the need for detailed mechanistic studies in RPE cells to confirm that the cholesterol-lowering effects observed in other tissues are recapitulated in the retina, and the optimization of dosing and delivery methods to ensure that therapeutic concentrations are achieved safely in the target tissue. Additionally, any potential side effects—such as those noted in NPC patients, including auditory toxicity—must be rigorously monitored in ocular studies to ensure that treatment remains safe over the long term (Calias, 2018).

Overall, the repurposing of HPβCD for dry AMD is scientifically compelling due to its targeted mechanism of action and its established clinical history in related indications. Its ability to mobilize cholesterol and restore lysosomal function addresses fundamental pathogenic processes implicated in dry AMD, and the preclinical evidence supports its potential efficacy. Nevertheless, the absence of clinical trials in this particular indication, combined with uncertainties regarding the precise molecular interactions in RPE cells and the optimization of drug delivery to the retina, suggests that further preclinical and early-stage clinical studies are warranted before HPβCD can be advanced as a treatment for dry AMD. Continued research should focus on elucidating the detailed molecular mechanisms within RPE cells, assessing long-term safety in ocular models, and exploring various delivery modalities to maximize efficacy while minimizing potential risks. In conclusion, while HPβCD demonstrates substantial promise as a repurposed drug candidate for dry AMD, a measured, stepwise approach in future research is essential to address outstanding questions and to establish its full therapeutic potential (Calias, 2018; El-Darzi et al., 2023; Nociari et al., 2017; Roney, 2020).

Pegcetacoplan (APL-2, now marketed as Syfovre) is a synthetically engineered, PEGylated cyclic peptide that belongs to the family of compstatin analogs designed to inhibit complement component C3. Its origins lie in early peptide discovery via phage‐display and random peptide library screening, and successive rounds of medicinal chemistry optimization were applied to improve its binding affinity, solubility, and pharmacokinetic profile through PEG conjugation (Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023; Ong et al., 2024). The PEGylation process not only grants enhanced resistance to enzymatic degradation but also prolongs the intravitreal residence time, an essential property for ocular applications requiring sustained drug exposure with limited dosing frequency (Tzoumas et al., 2023; Mastellos & Lambris, 2024). As a second‐generation compstatin analog, pegcetacoplan employs a bivalent design that enables high specificity for human C3, blocking its proteolytic cleavage into the active fragments C3a and C3b. These fragments are potent mediators that further amplify the inflammatory cascade through the formation of C3 convertases (Lamers et al., 2022). This therapeutic candidate is embedded within a broader class of complement inhibitors that have been actively explored in inflammatory disorders, and notably in ophthalmology for dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) where aberrant complement activation plays a central pathogenic role (Lamers et al., 2022; Mastellos & Lambris, 2024). Its synthetic nature, coupled with its targeted molecular design, positions pegcetacoplan as an attractive candidate for addressing the degenerative processes in geographic atrophy (GA) associated with dry AMD by directly modulating the complement cascade (Tzoumas et al., 2023; Patel et al., 2022).

Historically, the evolution of pegcetacoplan reflects a successful translation from bench to bedside across multiple therapeutic domains. Initially, the compstatin class was primarily developed and evaluated in systemic disorders characterized by complement dysregulation, most notably in paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH). Early clinical trials in PNH provided critical safety and efficacy data that underscored the value of targeting C3, paving the way for the repurposing of these molecules in ocular disease (Lamers et al., 2022). Mechanism of Action  
At the molecular level, the pathogenic cascade in dry AMD is tightly linked to dysregulated complement activation, and pegcetacoplan intervenes at one of the central nodes of this pathway by inhibiting complement component C3. Under physiological conditions, C3 is cleaved by C3 convertases into C3a—an anaphylatoxin that drives inflammation—and C3b, which functions as an opsonin and further propagates complement amplification (Yu & Wykoff, 2021). Pegcetacoplan binds to a key epitope on C3, thereby sterically hindering the enzyme-driven cleavage that would otherwise generate these active fragments. Collectively, the mechanism of action of pegcetacoplan encompasses both direct inhibition of complement-driven inflammatory processes and indirect protection of intracellular catabolic functions in the RPE, thereby addressing two core pathological contributors to geographic atrophy (Kassa et al., 2019; Rubner et al., 2022).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Fenofibrate is a synthetic small‐molecule drug belonging to the fibrate class of compounds, originally developed and approved for the treatment of dyslipidemia. It acts predominantly as a peroxisome proliferator‐activated receptor alpha (PPARα) agonist. Fenofibrate itself is a prodrug that undergoes hepatic esterase hydrolysis to form its active metabolite, fenofibric acid, which binds to PPARα and modulates the transcription of genes involved in lipid metabolism. This drug class has historically been used for lowering serum triglycerides and increasing high‐density lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol, reflecting its well‐established lipid‐modulating properties. Although fenofibrate was not initially developed for ocular indications, its mechanism as a PPARα agonist has spurred interest for repurposing in retinal diseases. In particular, the broad class of fibrates has garnered attention because PPARα is expressed in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), and its activation can regulate lipid oxidation, autophagy, and inflammatory processes—all of which are critically disturbed in dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) (Fu et al., 2019; Falcão et al., 2025).

Therapeutic History:  
Fenofibrate has a robust clinical history in the management of dyslipidemia and cardiovascular risk reduction, with extensive use in millions of patients worldwide. Its ocular benefits became apparent with large clinical trials, such as the FIELD and ACCORD Eye studies, which demonstrated that fenofibrate can reduce the progression of diabetic retinopathy and decrease the need for retinal laser therapy in diabetic patients (Lu et al., 2014; Treacy & Hurst, 2012). Although these trials primarily addressed diabetic retinal disease, subsequent preclinical and clinical reports have indicated that the retina may benefit from the lipid‐modulatory, anti‐inflammatory, and neuroprotective actions of PPARα agonists. While the majority of these ocular studies have focused on diabetic retinopathy or neovascular AMD, emerging literature has pointed to the potential of targeting PPARα signaling to mitigate RPE dysfunction and lipid accumulation, which are hallmarks of dry AMD (da Ana et al., 2023; Dou & Duerfeldt, 2020). This history of fenofibrate in retinal disease, combined with its proven clinical safety for dyslipidemia and established ocular pharmacokinetics (including studies on topical delivery), provides a compelling rationale for its repurposing in dry AMD (Tomita et al., 2020; Lee et al., 2021).
