Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
ML-SA1 is a synthetic, cell-permeable small-molecule agonist of the endolysosomal mucolipin/TRPML family, with primary pharmacological activity at TRPML1, the Ca2+-permeable cation channel encoded by MCOLN1 that resides on late endosome/lysosome membranes and mediates lysosomal Ca2+ efflux into the cytosol (Wang et al., 2023). ML-SA1 and chemically related “ML-SA” agonists emerged from small-molecule discovery programs aimed at pharmacologically restoring TRPML1 function; the compound is frequently referred to in the literature as “mucolipin synthetic agonist 1,” reflecting its origin as a tool compound class designed to activate TRPML channels rather than as a derivative of a natural product scaffold (Yan et al., 2021). Although the chemical structure and synthetic route for ML-SA1 are not detailed in the cited records, its provenance traces to a specialized small-molecule therapeutics effort at Calporta Therapeutics, a company subsequently acquired by Merck in 2019, signaling substantial translational interest in TRPML1 agonism for lysosomal storage and neurodegenerative disorders (Van Acker et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2023).

Functionally, ML-SA1 belongs to the broader class of TRPML1 agonists/activators that includes endogenous lipid ligands such as phosphatidylinositol-3,5-bisphosphate, PI(3,5)P2, and other synthetic small molecules (e.g., SF-22, MK6-83, and newer ML-SA chemotypes like ML-SA5), all of which gate TRPML channels to increase endolysosomal Ca2+ release (Wang et al., 2023; Más Gómez et al., 2018; Wünkhaus et al., 2024). Within this class, ML-SA1 is reported to activate TRPML1 with potency comparable to or greater than the endogenous PI(3,5)P2 under certain conditions and can act in conjunction with PI(3,5)P2 to potentiate channel opening, thereby rescuing endo-lysosomal morphology and function in cellular disease models that exhibit lysosomal stress (e.g., after PIKfyve inhibition) (Wang et al., 2023). Across preclinical research, TRPML1 agonists have been deployed as mechanistic probes and candidate therapeutics to restore lysosomal Ca2+ signaling, normalize lysosomal pH/acidification, promote autophagosome maturation and autolysosome formation, enhance lysosomal exocytosis, and induce TFEB-dependent lysosomal biogenesis in lysosomal storage and neurodegeneration models (Tedeschi et al., 2025; Pollmanns et al., 2022).

In ocular systems directly relevant to retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) biology, ML-SA1 has been used to interrogate TRPML1 function. In mouse primary RPE, human embryonic stem cell–derived RPE (hesRPE), and ARPE-19 cells, ML-SA1 produced rapid, robust, reversible increases in cytosolic Ca2+ that persisted in Ca2+-free external solutions and were blunted by lysosomal disruption, indicating a lysosomal Ca2+ source (Más Gómez et al., 2018). Critically, ML-SA1 failed to evoke Ca2+ signals in RPE from TRPML1 knockout mice, confirming channel specificity in this tissue (Más Gómez et al., 2018). The same study demonstrated that lysosomal lipid accumulation—induced pharmacologically or present in disease models—impairs ML-SA1-evoked TRPML1 Ca2+ release, mechanistically linking lysosomal lipidization to diminished TRPML1 function in RPE (Más Gómez et al., 2018). These data situate ML-SA1 squarely within a mechanistic toolkit for modulating RPE lysosomal physiology implicated in retinal degenerations associated with lipid/lipofuscin accrual (Más Gómez et al., 2018).

Therapeutic History  
There is no record in the provided corpus of ML-SA1 being used clinically in humans or specifically in trials for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or geographic atrophy (GA) (Más Gómez et al., 2018). However, extensive preclinical use across cell and animal models supports the biological rationale relevant to dry AMD. In RPE systems, ML-SA1 has been applied acutely to evoke TRPML1-dependent lysosomal Ca2+ release as described above (Más Gómez et al., 2018). In vivo, subretinal ML-SA1 administration in a rat retinal detachment model preserved outer nuclear layer thickness, reduced photoreceptor apoptosis, lessened cleaved caspase-3, increased autophagy markers (LC3-II/LC3-I and Beclin-1), decreased reactive oxygen species (ROS), and prevented TRPML1 degradation, collectively demonstrating functional rescue via autophagy activation and oxidative stress mitigation in injured retina (Yan et al., 2021).

Beyond the eye, multiple studies in neuronal and disease-model systems have used ML-SA1 to correct lysosomal/autophagy defects and proteostasis. In cultured neurons and HEK293T cells, ML-SA1 enhanced maturation of autophagosomes into acidic autolysosomes and reduced α-synuclein accumulation/aggregates; ML-SA1 could override bafilomycin-induced fusion/acidification blocks in both HEK293T cells and neurons, and these effects required lysosomal PI(3,5)P2 and cytosolic Ca2+ consistent with TRPML1 channel gating (Pollmanns et al., 2022). In primary cortical neurons, ML-SA1 rapidly acidified endolysosomes and prevented LDL-induced amyloidogenesis by reducing Aβ and BACE1 mislocalization/activity; TRPML1 knockdown abrogated ML-SA1’s effects and exacerbated LDL-driven Aβ production (Hui et al., 2019). In lysosomal storage disease (LSD) contexts, ML-SA1 was used as a TRPML1 activator to elicit lysosomal Ca2+ release responses that were impaired in Niemann–Pick type C (NPC1) patient fibroblasts; BK channel activation partially rescued the reduced ML-SA1 response, and BK upregulation lowered lipofuscin accumulation via lysosomal exocytosis, establishing pharmacological synergies that might be exploited in lipid storage states (Zhong et al., 2016).

Importantly for RPE-relevant lysosomal storage phenotypes, the more potent TRPML1 agonist ML-SA5 was used in ARPE-19 CLN3-knockout cells (a juvenile neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis model) to reduce lysosomal accumulation of subunit C of mitochondrial ATPase (SubC), Gb3, and lysosomal glycerophosphodiesters, accompanied by TFEB nuclear translocation and increased surface LAMP1 consistent with enhanced lysosomal exocytosis; however, BMP/LBPA lipid deficits and maturation of cathepsin D (CatD) and TPP1 remained impaired, indicating incomplete restoration of lysosomal hydrolase processing (Wünkhaus et al., 2024; Unknown Reference). Patch-clamp experiments in these cells confirmed that ML-SA1 variants evoke TRPML1 currents fully blocked by the antagonist ML-SI3, supporting pharmacological specificity in RPE lysosomes (Unknown Reference). Collectively, the body of preclinical work shows that TRPML1 agonism has repeatedly restored facets of lysosomal function (Ca2+ release, acidification, autophagosome–lysosome fusion, exocytosis, TFEB activation) across cell types and in injured retina, though complete correction of all lysosomal abnormalities (e.g., hydrolase maturation) is not assured in all disease contexts (Pollmanns et al., 2022; Yan et al., 2021; Unknown Reference).

No studies in the present corpus demonstrate ML-SA1 use in dry AMD animal models, in RPE models of drusen/lipofuscin accumulation specific to AMD, or in clinical AMD studies; however, in RPE, lipid accumulation was shown to blunt ML-SA1–evoked TRPML1 Ca2+ release, and TRPML1 KO RPE exhibited increased autofluorescence, mechanistically connecting TRPML1 functionality to handling of autofluorescent/neutral lipid material relevant to AMD pathophysiology (Más Gómez et al., 2018). The class of TRPML1 agonists (including ML-SA1) is being investigated preclinically for lysosomal storage and neurodegenerative indications, reinforcing translational plausibility even in the absence of AMD-specific studies (Wang et al., 2023).

Mechanism of Action  
TRPML1 is a lysosomal six-transmembrane TRP superfamily channel permeable to Ca2+ and other cations that localizes primarily to late endosomal/lysosomal membranes via cytosolic dileucine motifs, where it mediates lumen-to-cytosol ion efflux in response to endogenous and pharmacological gating (Wang et al., 2023; Unknown Reference). Physiological activation is conferred by the late endosomal/lysosomal phosphoinositide PI(3,5)P2, whose 3′ phosphate directly stabilizes an open-channel conformation; PI(4,5)P2 acts as an antagonist enriched at the plasma membrane, ensuring compartmental specificity (Wang et al., 2023). TRPML1-dependent lysosomal Ca2+ release acts as a master regulator of lysosomal/autophagic homeostasis via several calcium-sensitive effectors: calcineurin dephosphorylates TFEB to drive its nuclear translocation and induce the CLEAR network (lysosomal biogenesis and function genes), whereas CaMKKβ activation promotes autophagosome biogenesis; additional roles include regulation of vesicle trafficking, membrane fusion/fission, lysosomal reformation, exocytosis, and mitochondria–lysosome contacts (Wang et al., 2023; Tedeschi et al., 2025; Unknown Reference).

ML-SA1 is a synthetic agonist that binds TRPML channels and increases channel open probability, functionally mimicking or synergizing with PI(3,5)P2 to produce lysosomal Ca2+ efflux (Wang et al., 2023). In multiple cell systems, ML-SA1 triggers rapid lysosomal Ca2+ release measured by cytosolic Ca2+ reporters and genetically encoded TRPML1-proximal indicators; responses are abolished or blunted by TRPML1 gene knockout, lysosomal rupture, or pharmacological inhibitors, confirming that cytosolic Ca2+ rises originate from lysosomes through TRPML1 (Más Gómez et al., 2018). In RPE cells, ML-SA1-evoked Ca2+ signals were insensitive to extracellular Ca2+ removal and ER Ca2+ depletion with thapsigargin, but were eliminated by lysosomal disruption with GPN and absent in TRPML1−/− RPE, demonstrating the specificity and lysosomal source in the cell type of interest (Más Gómez et al., 2018).

Downstream of TRPML1 activation, ML-SA1 drives a coordinated set of lysosome-centric responses:  
- Autophagosome–lysosome fusion and maturation: ML-SA1 increases conversion of LC3-positive autophagosomes into acidic autolysosomes and shifts cargo (e.g., α-synuclein) into LAMP1-positive, acidified vesicles; notably, ML-SA1 can partially override bafilomycin A1 blocks on fusion/acidification, consistent with a Ca2+-dependent maturation/fusion mechanism (Pollmanns et al., 2022).  
- Lysosomal acidification: In primary neurons, ML-SA1 rapidly acidifies endolysosomes in a TRPML1-dependent manner, coincident with reduced LDL-induced amyloidogenesis and BACE1 localization/activity in endolysosomes (Hui et al., 2019).  
- TFEB signaling and lysosomal biogenesis/exocytosis: TRPML1 activation promotes TFEB nuclear translocation and transcription of lysosomal/autophagy genes; in ARPE-19 CLN3-KO cells, ML-SA5 triggered TFEB translocation and increased surface LAMP1 within 90 minutes, consistent with enhanced lysosomal exocytosis, and reduced lysosomal glycerophosphodiester loads (Tedeschi et al., 2025; Wünkhaus et al., 2024).  
- Proteostasis correction: ML-SA1 reduces α-synuclein protein/aggregates in cell models by steering cargo into maturing autolysosomes and promoting degradative flux; these effects require autophagy, PI(3,5)P2, and cytosolic Ca2+, aligning with TRPML1’s canonical signaling dependencies (Pollmanns et al., 2022).  
- Neuroprotection via autophagy induction and oxidative stress reduction: In vivo in retinal detachment, subretinal ML-SA1 increased LC3-II/LC3-I and Beclin-1, reduced cleaved caspase-3, decreased ROS, preserved photoreceptors, and prevented injury-induced TRPML1 degradation (Yan et al., 2021).

Two mechanism-linked constraints merit emphasis for AMD translation. First, lysosomal lipid accumulation impairs TRPML1 function in RPE: desipramine (ASM inhibition), PIKfyve inhibition (YM201636), and chloroquine/U18666A-induced neutral lipid/lipofuscin models decreased ML-SA1–evoked Ca2+ release without reducing TRPML1 mRNA or total lysosomal Ca2+, indicating functional channel inhibition by lipidized lysosomal membranes—an AMD-relevant condition (Más Gómez et al., 2018). Second, in CLN3-deficient RPE, TRPML1 activation improved substrate clearance and TFEB signaling but did not restore the mature, active forms of CatD and TPP1 despite increased transcripts and precursor/intermediate protein levels, pointing to persistent hydrolase processing defects not corrected by TRPML1 agonism alone (Unknown Reference). These observations suggest that while ML-SA1 should restore key steps (Ca2+ efflux, fusion/acidification, TFEB), lysosomal lipid environments typical of aged RPE may constrain efficacy, and hydrolase maturation deficits—if present in AMD—may not normalize solely via TRPML1 activation (Más Gómez et al., 2018; Unknown Reference).

Expected Effect  
Assay/System: RPE cells relevant to dry AMD pathophysiology, focusing on phagosome–lysosome fusion, lysosomal acidification, TFEB signaling, and clearance of drusen precursors.

Expected pharmacodynamic cascade:  
1) Channel activation and lysosomal Ca2+ efflux. ML-SA1 will directly activate TRPML1 on RPE lysosomes, eliciting cytosolic Ca2+ rises that persist in Ca2+-free external medium and are abolished by lysosomal disruption, as shown in mouse primary RPE, hesRPE, and ARPE-19 models; absence of response in TRPML1−/− RPE confirms target dependence (Más Gómez et al., 2018). TRPML1 expression in ARPE-19 is documented at the mRNA and functional current levels, supporting target presence in the proposed assay system (Wünkhaus et al., 2024; Unknown Reference).

2) Calcineurin-TFEB pathway activation and lysosomal program induction. TRPML1-mediated Ca2+ release will activate calcineurin, drive TFEB dephosphorylation and nuclear translocation, and upregulate CLEAR network genes that boost lysosomal biogenesis and function, as established for TRPML1 signaling; in RPE (CLN3-KO), ML-SA5 triggered TFEB nuclear import in both WT and mutant cells, indicating pathway engagement in ARPE-19 (Wang et al., 2023; Wünkhaus et al., 2024).

3) Lysosomal acidification and maturation of degradative organelles. ML-SA1 is expected to increase autophagosome–lysosome fusion and acidification, based on multiple cell models where ML-SA1 shifts LC3-positive vesicles toward acidic autolysosomes and augments LAMP1 colocalization; ML-SA1 also acidified neuronal endolysosomes within minutes in a TRPML1-dependent manner (Pollmanns et al., 2022; Hui et al., 2019). In retinal tissue in vivo (detachment model), TRPML1 activation promoted autolysosome formation by EM and upregulated LC3-II/LC3-I and Beclin-1, consistent with increased degradative flux (Yan et al., 2021).

4) Enhancement of degradative capacity and cargo clearance. By accelerating fusion and acidification, ML-SA1 should facilitate catabolic processing of outer segment phagosomes and lipoprotein-like cargoes that contribute to drusen precursors; in RPE knockout models of TRPML1, basal autofluorescence increases, supporting a role for TRPML1 in handling autofluorescent material, and ML-SA1-evoked TRPML1 activity is diminished by lysosomal lipid accumulation typical of aged RPE, highlighting both the therapeutic rationale and a potential barrier (Más Gómez et al., 2018; Wünkhaus et al., 2024; Unknown Reference).

Mechanistic uncertainties relevant to the hypothesis include the extent to which ML-SA1 will normalize hydrolase maturation (and consequently proteolysis) in aged or AMD RPE, given the CLN3-KO observation that mature CatD and TPP1 were not restored despite TFEB activation; while acidification generally supports protease activity, direct evidence of increased CatD activity post-TRPML1 activation in RPE is not provided here, and in CLN3-KO the maturation block persisted (Unknown Reference). Nevertheless, the acidic shift and fusion acceleration documented with ML-SA1 in neurons and the autophagy induction in retina argue for improved lysosomal degradative competence, which, together with increased exocytosis, should reduce accumulation of drusen precursors, albeit potentially incompletely if hydrolase processing bottlenecks remain (Hui et al., 2019; Yan et al., 2021; Wünkhaus et al., 2024).

Two context-specific modifiers should be anticipated:  
- Lysosomal lipid load: ML-SA1 responses are blunted by lysosomal lipid accumulation in RPE; thus, efficacy in dry AMD may require co-strategies that reduce lysosomal lipid burden or potentiate TRPML1 gating under lipidized conditions (e.g., via synergistic endogenous PI(3,5)P2, or adjuncts such as BK channel activators shown to enhance ML-SA1 responses in lipid storage contexts) (Más Gómez et al., 2018; Zhong et al., 2016).  
- TRPML isoform engagement: ML-SA1 can activate TRPML3 under certain expression conditions; while TRPML3’s role in RPE is less defined, off-target TRPML3 activation may modulate lysosomal transport and ion fluxes, warranting selectivity profiling in RPE (Unknown Reference).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Direct target validation in RPE: ML-SA1 elicits TRPML1-dependent lysosomal Ca2+ release in primary mouse RPE, hesRPE, and ARPE-19 cells, with responses absent in TRPML1−/− RPE and abolished by lysosomal disruption; this is the critical first step in the proposed mechanism and is robustly documented (Más Gómez et al., 2018).  
- Disease-mechanism alignment with AMD biology: Lysosomal lipid/lipofuscin accumulation—central to AMD—functionally inhibits TRPML1 signaling in RPE, directly linking a hallmark AMD stressor to the TRPML1 pathway that ML-SA1 targets; RPE from ABCA4−/− mice (linked to retinal lipid/lipofuscin pathology) exhibit impaired TRPML1-mediated Ca2+ release (Más Gómez et al., 2018). This alignment makes TRPML1 activation a rational corrective lever.  
- Downstream pathway evidence: ML-SA1/ML-SA agonism reproducibly enhances autophagosome–lysosome fusion and acidification, reduces proteotoxic burden (α-synuclein), and activates TFEB-dependent and TFEB-independent lysosomal functions across cell systems; in retina, subretinal ML-SA1 invokes autophagy, reduces ROS/apoptosis, and preserves structure/function after detachment, supporting ocular pharmacology and neuroprotection (Pollmanns et al., 2022; Yan et al., 2021).  
- Translational momentum: The TRPML1 agonist class is actively explored preclinically for LSD and neurodegenerative indications; Merck’s acquisition of Calporta underscores perceived therapeutic potential of TRPML1 agonism, supporting feasibility of a development path if RPE-specific efficacy is confirmed (Wang et al., 2023; Van Acker et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2023).

Limitations and risks  
- No AMD-specific in vivo data: There are no reports here of ML-SA1 tested in dry AMD or GA animal models, nor in clinical AMD studies; all AMD relevance is inferential from RPE biophysics, lipid-induced TRPML1 impairment, and generalized lysosomal/autophagy correction (Más Gómez et al., 2018). This gap means translational extrapolation to drusen clearance and GA slowing remains unproven.  
- Lipid-dependent resistance: Lysosomal lipid accumulation diminishes ML-SA1 responses in RPE without reducing TRPML1 expression or total lysosomal Ca2+, implying that aged/AMD RPE may exhibit attenuated pharmacodynamics; combination strategies or higher potency agonists (e.g., ML-SA5) may be needed to overcome lipidized lysosomal membranes (Más Gómez et al., 2018; Wünkhaus et al., 2024).  
- Hydrolase maturation not universally rescued: In CLN3-deficient RPE, TRPML1 activation failed to restore mature CatD and TPP1 despite TFEB induction, indicating that some degradative deficits—potentially relevant to AMD—may not normalize solely via TRPML1 activation; this could limit improvements in cathepsin-dependent proteolysis of drusen precursors (Unknown Reference).  
- Selectivity considerations: ML-SA1 can activate other TRPML family members (e.g., TRPML3) in overexpression systems, and pan-TRPML agonism in RPE may have uncharacterized effects on lysosomal trafficking and axonal transport; selectivity profiling in RPE and concentration-response mapping are needed to de-risk off-target TRPML isoform engagement (Unknown Reference).  
- Context-dependent acidification: ML-SA1 acidifies neuronal endolysosomes and enhances degradative flux, but direct demonstrations of increased CatD activity in RPE after ML-SA1 are not provided here; given the CLN3-KO findings on hydrolase maturation, reliance on acidification alone may not guarantee improved protease activity in diseased RPE (Hui et al., 2019; Unknown Reference).

Development guidance  
Given the strong RPE target validation and consistent downstream biology, ML-SA1 (or a more potent TRPML1 agonist such as ML-SA5) is a credible mechanistic candidate for dry AMD; however, AMD-relevant pharmacology must be demonstrated directly. The most decision-informative steps are:  
- Establish efficacy in AMD-relevant RPE contexts: Test ML-SA1 in iPSC-derived human RPE from older donors and/or RPE cultured with A2E/lipofuscin and oxidized lipids to recapitulate lysosomal lipidization; quantify TRPML1 Ca2+ responses, TFEB translocation, lysosomal pH, autophagosome–lysosome fusion, and cargo clearance (e.g., ApoE/cholesterol-rich particles, complement-containing deposits), benchmarking against the lipid-impairment reported in RPE (Más Gómez et al., 2018).  
- Measure hydrolase activity and maturation: Directly assay CatD and other cathepsin activities and maturation states post-ML-SA1 in lipidized RPE; if maturation remains deficient, evaluate combinations with agents that restore hydrolase processing (e.g., modulators of endolysosomal trafficking or mannose-6-phosphate receptor pathways) (Unknown Reference).  
- Explore potentiation strategies: Consider co-targeting known TRPML1 modulators to overcome lipidized lysosomal membranes—examples include augmenting PI(3,5)P2 availability or adding BK channel activators, which rescued impaired ML-SA1 responses and reduced storage in NPC-related settings (Wang et al., 2023; Zhong et al., 2016).  
- Prioritize potency and exposure: Given blunted responses in lipidized RPE, evaluate higher-potency ML-SA chemotypes (ML-SA5 EC50 ~80 nM in a TFE3/TFEB-related translocation assay vs. ML-SA1 in the µM range) for superior pharmacodynamics; subretinal tolerability is supported by RD studies but needs AMD-model confirmation (Wünkhaus et al., 2024; Yan et al., 2021).  
- In vivo validation in AMD models: Move to aged/multiple-hit models that accumulate sub-RPE deposits (e.g., high-fat diet, light exposure, Abca4−/− backgrounds) to test whether TRPML1 agonism reduces drusen-like material, preserves RPE function, and slows GA-like endpoints; note that Abca4−/− RPE exhibited impaired TRPML1 Ca2+ release, making it a relevant sensitized background to assay pharmacological rescue (Más Gómez et al., 2018).

Conclusion  
ML-SA1 is a tractable, mechanistically well-supported TRPML1 agonist with direct RPE target validation and robust evidence that its downstream effects—lysosomal Ca2+ release, TFEB activation, autophagosome–lysosome fusion/acidification, and exocytosis—can correct core lysosomal deficits that plausibly drive drusen precursor accumulation in dry AMD (Más Gómez et al., 2018; Pollmanns et al., 2022; Wünkhaus et al., 2024). The principal risks are the lipid-dependence of TRPML1 dysfunction in RPE and the incomplete rescue of hydrolase maturation observed in CLN3-deficient RPE, both of which may attenuate the magnitude of effect on complex AMD cargoes and necessitate combination strategies or use of more potent agonists (Más Gómez et al., 2018; Wünkhaus et al., 2024). On balance, the mechanistic specificity, ocular proof-of-concept in retinal detachment, and extensive preclinical precedent for lysosomal restoration argue that ML-SA1 (or next-generation TRPML1 agonists) merits prioritized evaluation in AMD-relevant RPE assays and in vivo models, with an early focus on overcoming lipidized lysosomal resistance and verifying improvements in both acidification and hydrolase function (Yan et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2023; Tedeschi et al., 2025).

Strength of evidence for the dry AMD hypothesis: moderate, driven by strong RPE target biology and retinal neuroprotection data but constrained by the absence of AMD-specific in vivo studies and by lipid-imposed pharmacodynamic limits (Más Gómez et al., 2018; Yan et al., 2021). If forthcoming AMD-relevant experiments confirm that TRPML1 activation restores lysosomal Ca2+ signaling and degradative capacity in lipidized RPE, and that drusen precursors are reduced, ML-SA1/ML-SA5 would represent a differentiated, mechanism-based approach compared with broad mTOR inhibition, with the potential to correct proximal lysosomal defects underlying GA progression (Wang et al., 2023; Pollmanns et al., 2022).

Detailed, component-wise assessment  

- Target presence and engagement in RPE: TRPML1 expression and function are present in ARPE-19 and primary RPE; ML-SA1 evokes lysosomal Ca2+ release that is TRPML1-dependent (absent in TRPML1−/− RPE), establishing on-target engagement (Más Gómez et al., 2018).  
- Relevance of TRPML1 signaling to AMD pathobiology: Lysosomal lipid/lipofuscin accumulation impairs TRPML1 function in RPE and is germane to AMD; RPE autofluorescence increases in TRPML1 KO, linking the channel to handling of drusen-like material (Más Gómez et al., 2018).  
- Downstream mechanisms aligned with therapeutic hypothesis: ML-SA1 triggers calcineurin-TFEB signaling, augments autophagosome–lysosome fusion and acidification, and enhances exocytosis—mechanisms expected to improve clearance of drusen precursors (Wang et al., 2023; Pollmanns et al., 2022).  
- Evidence for improved degradative flux: In neurons, ML-SA1 acidifies endolysosomes and reduces Aβ/BACE1 pathology; in retina in vivo, ML-SA1 increases autophagy markers and preserves photoreceptors; in RPE disease models, TRPML1 activation decreases stored substrates and reduces lysosomal surface area (Hui et al., 2019; Yan et al., 2021; Wünkhaus et al., 2024).  
- Constraints/unknowns: Lipid-imposed TRPML1 inhibition in RPE may limit efficacy; CatD/TPP1 maturation not rescued in CLN3-KO RPE; no direct AMD data; potential TRPML3 co-activation (Más Gómez et al., 2018; Unknown Reference).

Recommendation  
Advance ML-SA1 (and evaluate ML-SA5 as a higher-potency comparator) into AMD-relevant RPE assays with lipidized lysosomes, incorporating quantitative readouts of TRPML1 Ca2+ signaling, TFEB translocation, lysosomal pH, hydrolase maturation/activity, and cargo clearance, and then proceed to in vivo testing in drusen-accumulating models if in vitro data are supportive; in parallel, explore combination strategies (e.g., BK channel activation) to overcome lipid-dependent resistance to TRPML1 agonism (Más Gómez et al., 2018; Wünkhaus et al., 2024; Zhong et al., 2016).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Fingolimod (FTY720) is a synthetic, sphingoid-base mimetic that is phosphorylated in vivo by sphingosine kinase 2 (SphK2) to yield the active metabolite FTY720-phosphate (FTY720-P), which binds sphingosine-1-phosphate receptors (S1PRs) with sub-micromolar affinity comparable to endogenous S1P (primarily S1PR1, S1PR3, S1PR4, and S1PR5) (Gupta et al., 2012; Gesualdo et al., 2021). As a small-molecule modulator of S1PRs, fingolimod belongs to the class of GPCR-targeting immunomodulators that regulate lymphocyte trafficking and vascular/endothelial signaling; this class has been deployed extensively in neuroinflammatory disease (e.g., multiple sclerosis) and investigated across ocular inflammatory and vascular pathologies (Gesualdo et al., 2021; Sorenson et al., 2022). In ocular biology, endogenous S1P signaling is pleiotropic: it is detected in, and acts upon, multiple retinal cell types including RPE, endothelium, neurons, and glia, where it can protect photoreceptors from oxidative stress–induced apoptosis and modulate wound repair and barrier function, underscoring the translational appeal of S1PR modulators for retinal degenerations (Gupta et al., 2012). At the same time, the S1P axis exhibits context-dependent outcomes—anti-S1P antibodies reduce subretinal fibrosis in AMD models—so receptor-subtype selectivity, ligand presentation (e.g., apoM/HDL-bound vs free), and cell-type–specific responses will be critical to therapeutic design (Gupta et al., 2012; Jung et al., 2025).

Therapeutic History  
Fingolimod is an approved oral therapy that reduces lesion formation in multiple sclerosis through S1PR-mediated immunomodulation, providing an extensive clinical safety and pharmacology dataset for potential repurposing (Mondal & Mandal, 2019). In ocular indications, preclinical studies demonstrate that S1PR pathway manipulation alters retinal/choroidal vascular pathology: intravitreally delivered S1P chaperoned by apolipoprotein M (apoM) activates endothelial S1PR1 and suppresses choroidal neovascularization (CNV) and vascular leak, and separate approaches show that anti-S1P antibodies or S1PR1-selective agonists can suppress CNV and stabilize endothelial barriers (Jung et al., 2025; Sorenson et al., 2022). Fingolimod itself (as FTY720) reduces choroidal endothelial migration and capillary morphogenesis in vitro and mitigates CNV in vivo, indicating that systemic or intraocular S1PR modulation impacts ocular neovascular disease biology (Sorenson et al., 2022). In diabetic retinopathy models, fingolimod reduces retinal angiogenesis and VEGFA levels, aligning with its anti-angiogenic/vascular-stabilizing profile (Gesualdo et al., 2021). Importantly for the dry AMD context, none of these studies directly evaluate atrophic AMD outcomes, RPE autophagy/lysosome endpoints, or complement-driven injury after fingolimod, and there is no prior clinical use of fingolimod for dry AMD (Jung et al., 2025; Sorenson et al., 2022). A material safety consideration for retinal indications is fingolimod-associated macular edema (FAME), reported in clinical settings and relevant to dosing, route, and patient selection if repurposed for macular disease (Mondal & Mandal, 2019).

Mechanism of Action  
Receptor pharmacology of fingolimod and ocular S1P biology. Fingolimod is phosphorylated by SphK2 to FTY720-P, which behaves as a functional agonist at S1PR1, S1PR4, and S1PR5 and a partial agonist at S1PR3, triggering receptor internalization and signaling adaptation that sequesters lymphocytes and modulates vascular responses (Gupta et al., 2012; Gesualdo et al., 2021). In ocular tissues, S1PR1 is prominently expressed in multiple cell types, with experimental evidence demonstrating S1PR1 expression in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) where S1PR1 appears as the predominant S1PR subtype alongside dynamic regulation of S1PR1/S1PR3 by oxygen tension (Sorenson et al., 2022). RPE also expresses the S1P-generating enzymes SphK1 and SphK2 and can synthesize and release S1P, providing the local pathway components to respond to pharmacologic S1PR modulation (Wang et al., 2023). S1P ligands elicit cell-type–specific responses in the retinal neurovascular unit: endothelial S1PR1 activation stabilizes adherens junctions and quells sprouting angiogenesis, apoM/HDL-bound S1P reduces choroidal leakage and CNV, and S1P/S1PR signaling influences RPE barrier function and angiogenic or inflammatory outputs (Jung et al., 2025; Sorenson et al., 2022). These features render S1PR1 a biologically plausible target in RPE and choroid for modulating disease-relevant pathways in AMD, while also highlighting that the net effect of S1P pathway modulation depends on receptor subtype and ligand context (Jung et al., 2025; Sorenson et al., 2022).

RPE autophagy–lysosome biology, lysosomal acidification, and AMD. The RPE is a post-mitotic, highly phagocytic epithelium that performs daily heterophagy of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) and constitutive macroautophagy, processes that converge on lysosomal degradation; failure at the lysosomal step produces lipofuscin accumulation, proteotoxic stress, and drusen formation that characterize AMD (Sinha et al., 2016). Lysosomal acidity, maintained by the vacuolar H^+-ATPase (V-ATPase), is essential for cathepsin activity and cargo hydrolysis; AMD-relevant lipofuscin bisretinoids such as A2E elevate lysosomal pH by inhibiting V-ATPase, impairing phagolysosomal digestion of POS and promoting a feed-forward cycle of oxidative stress and lysosomal dysfunction (Sinha et al., 2016). Lysosomal signaling couples to mTORC1 at the lysosomal surface via V-ATPase–Ragulator–Rag GTPase complexes, integrating luminal amino acids and energy status to regulate autophagy; in RPE, βA3/A1-crystallin (Cryba1) binds the V0 domain of V-ATPase and its loss produces mTORC1 hyperactivation, inefficient lysosomal clearance, and AMD-like pathology, functionally tying V-ATPase activity and mTORC1–TFEB signaling to disease (Sinha et al., 2016). Autophagy protects RPE from oxidative stress, and genetic or age-related declines in macroautophagy correlate with mitochondrial dysfunction, increased ROS, inflammasome activation, and lipofuscin accumulation in human AMD eyes and animal models (Sinha et al., 2016). These data establish that increasing autophagic flux and restoring lysosomal acidification are mechanistically central interventions for RPE protection in AMD.

The AMPK–mTOR–ULK1/TFEB axis: a mechanistic route to autophagy and lysosomal biogenesis. AMPK and mTOR are canonical, opposing regulators of autophagy: AMPK stimulates autophagy by activating ULK1 and inhibiting mTORC1 (including via TSC1/2–Rheb), whereas mTORC1 phosphorylates ULK1/Atg13 to block initiation and phosphorylates Atg14 to dampen nucleation (Wang et al., 2023). TFEB/TFE3 are master transcription factors of lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy; mTORC1 phosphorylation retains TFEB in the cytosol, and mTORC1 inhibition permits TFEB nuclear translocation to activate the CLEAR network of lysosomal and autophagy genes (Wang et al., 2023). AMPK-dependent phosphorylation is required for TFEB/TFE3 transcriptional activation, and AMPK activation increases V-ATPase assembly and activity under glucose starvation, providing a direct link from energy stress to lysosomal acidification machinery (Boya et al., 2023). In RPE/AMD-relevant systems, TFEB activation increases expression of V-ATPase subunits (e.g., ATP6V0A1), lysosomal proteins (LAMP2), and cathepsins (CTSB), and reduces accumulation of POS-dependent lipofuscin-like granules; trehalose- or rapamycin-mediated TFEB activation enhances autophagic flux and decreases A2E/lipofuscin load and inflammatory markers in RPE models (Falcão et al., 2025). Human AMD RPE displays increased TFEB phosphorylation and reduced nuclear TFEB, together with decreased cathepsin levels, consistent with mTORC1-mediated suppression of lysosomal function; TFEB reactivation in Cryba1-deficient RPE rescues CLEAR gene expression and degradative capacity, supporting TFEB as a viable target for lysosomal rejuvenation (Falcão et al., 2025).

Mitochondria–lysosome crosstalk, S1P, and oxidative damage. Mitochondrial quality control via PINK1/PRKN-driven mitophagy and mitochondria-derived vesicles (MDVs) is coordinated with lysosomal function; AMPK acts bidirectionally to couple mitochondrial stress to lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy competence (Boya et al., 2023). In RPE and AMD models, mitochondrial dysfunction (mtDNA damage, impaired mitophagy) increases ROS and sensitizes cells to inflammasome activation and downstream damage; restoring lysosomal/mitochondrial clearance reduces oxidative injury (Boya et al., 2023). S1P signaling can induce mitochondrial biogenesis and thereby influence immunometabolic homeostasis; combined with AMPK–TFEB activation, S1P-related pathways could theoretically enhance both mitochondrial and lysosomal resilience in stressed RPE (Boya et al., 2023).

Inflammation, complement, and autophagy–lysosome cross-talk in AMD. Autophagy negatively regulates inflammasome activation, and complement/inflammasome axes contribute to RPE pathology in AMD; for example, complement C5a primes inflammasomes, and high-risk CFH Y402H RPE exhibit swollen lysosomes with cathepsin D leakage and increased lysosomal C5b-9 deposition (Kaarniranta et al., 2023; Falcão et al., 2025). Complement-related lysosomal stress provides a plausible injury modality that could be mitigated by lysosomal stabilization and increased autophagic flux; indeed, complement modulation can restore lysosomal function in a CFH Y402H RPE model (Boya et al., 2023). Because impaired lysosome/autophagy promotes secretory autophagy of inflammatory cargo, including HMGB1 and possibly amyloid species, enhancing lysosomal degradation should also reduce extracellular pro-inflammatory signals that propagate AMD pathology (Kaarniranta et al., 2023; Sinha et al., 2016).

What is known—and unknown—about fingolimod and the AMPK/TFEB–lysosome axis. In human cell models outside the eye, fingolimod can increase LC3B-II and alter Akt signaling (dephosphorylating Akt1 at Ser473), consistent with autophagy induction; yet the same studies report TFEB downregulation and induction of an inhibitory phosphorylation mark on TFEB (Ser211), with overall interpretations suggesting potential for stalling/saturation of autophagy under some conditions, and cell-type–dependent lysosomal enlargement and membrane permeabilization have also been described (Relic et al., 2021). Across the RPE/AMD literature summarized here, there is no direct demonstration that fingolimod or S1PR agonists activate AMPK, mobilize TFEB to the nucleus, increase V-ATPase–dependent lysosomal acidification, or enhance autophagic flux in RPE; nor are there data showing that fingolimod reduces complement-driven RPE injury in dry AMD models (Boya et al., 2023; Falcão et al., 2025). These are critical gaps that must be addressed experimentally before the proposed mechanism can be accepted (Jung et al., 2025; Relic et al., 2021).

Expected Effect  
Target engagement and proximal signaling in RPE. Because S1PR1 is expressed in RPE and appears to be the predominant S1P receptor subtype in this cell type, fingolimod (as FTY720-P) should engage RPE S1PRs at pharmacologically relevant concentrations if present in the subretinal/choroidal milieu, although receptor subtype balance and receptor down-modulation dynamics will influence outcomes (Sorenson et al., 2022; Gesualdo et al., 2021). In the hypothesized AMPK→TFEB pathway, proximal readouts would include increased AMPK phosphorylation/activation, decreased mTORC1 activity (e.g., phospho-S6K/4EBP1), and enhanced nuclear localization of TFEB/TFE3, followed by transcriptional upregulation of CLEAR genes (e.g., LAMP1/2, ATP6V0A1, CTSB/D) (Boya et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2023; Falcão et al., 2025). Because S1PR signaling is pleiotropic, it is critical to test whether fingolimod in RPE shifts Akt and mTORC1 activities toward a TFEB-permissive state, as opposed to inducing the inhibitory TFEB Ser211 phosphorylation and autophagy stalling seen in some non-ocular cells (Relic et al., 2021).

Lysosomal acidification, degradative capacity, and autophagic flux. If fingolimod drives AMPK activation and TFEB nuclear translocation in RPE, predicted functional outcomes include increased V-ATPase assembly and activity (acidified lysosomes), higher cathepsin activity, and increased autophagic flux measurable by LC3-II turnover in the presence of bafilomycin or chloroquine, together with decreased steady-state p62/SQSTM1 under basal degradative conditions (Boya et al., 2023; Falcão et al., 2025). TFEB activation in RPE models reduces POS-dependent lipofuscin-like granule accumulation and increases lysosome number; pharmacologic TFEB induction (e.g., with trehalose) increases lysosomal biogenesis and autophagosome–lysosome fusion, so fingolimod engagement of this axis should phenocopy these protective changes if the postulated signaling is correct (Falcão et al., 2025). Restoration of lysosomal acidity would be expected to counteract A2E- and lipofuscin-induced V-ATPase inhibition, improving phagolysosomal degradation of POS and reducing waste buildup (Sinha et al., 2016).

Oxidative stress, mitochondrial homeostasis, and inflammasome/complement outputs. By increasing autophagic and mitophagic flux, and engaging TFEB-dependent antioxidant/clearance programs, the candidate mechanism should reduce mitochondrial ROS, stabilize mitochondrial biogenesis via AMPK–PGC-1 pathways, and decrease ROS-dependent priming of inflammasomes (Boya et al., 2023; Sinha et al., 2016). Autophagy mitigates inflammasome activation, and restoring lysosome function reduces the release of DAMPs and secretory autophagy cargo (e.g., HMGB1), which together would be expected to blunt complement pathway amplification in stressed RPE; complement deposition (C5b-9) within lysosomes, especially in CFH risk-allele RPE, may be reduced if lysosomal integrity is preserved and capacity is restored (Kaarniranta et al., 2023; Falcão et al., 2025). In aggregate, if fingolimod engages the AMPK–TFEB–lysosome axis in RPE as hypothesized, one would expect improvements in lysosomal pH, cathepsin activity (including CTSD), autophagic flux, reduced lipofuscin/A2E accumulation, lower mitochondrial ROS, and decreased inflammasome/complement readouts in RPE challenged with AMD-relevant stresses (oxidants, A2E, complement components) (Falcão et al., 2025; Sinha et al., 2016; Kaarniranta et al., 2023).

Caveats and contrary expectations. Fingolimod’s effects on TFEB and autophagy are cell- and context-dependent; in human synovial fibroblasts and HEK293 cells fingolimod induced TFEB Ser211 phosphorylation and TFEB downregulation despite LC3B-II accumulation, suggesting potential autophagy stalling and negative feedback on TFEB that could counter the desired lysosomal biogenesis in RPE (Relic et al., 2021). Moreover, S1P pathway manipulation can yield opposing outcomes in different compartments (e.g., anti-S1P strategies reduce ocular fibrosis/CNV), so nonselective S1PR modulation by fingolimod may not cleanly recapitulate the endothelial-protective, S1PR1-selective phenotypes observed with apoM/HDL–S1P delivery (Jung et al., 2025; Gupta et al., 2012). Finally, retinal safety signals—particularly macular edema—have been associated with fingolimod in clinical practice and would warrant stringent dose–exposure control and route optimization (e.g., local ocular delivery) in any AMD program (Mondal & Mandal, 2019).

Assay design implications. Given the mechanistic uncertainties, rigorous RPE-focused assays must be prioritized: (1) S1PR1/3/5 expression profiling in the chosen RPE system (primary human, iPSC-RPE) and receptor occupancy by fingolimod; (2) AMPK phosphorylation and mTORC1 readouts (p-AMPK, p-S6K, p-4EBP1) after fingolimod with and without S1PR antagonists; (3) TFEB/TFE3 nuclear translocation and CLEAR target induction; (4) lysosomal pH (ratiometric LysoSensor) and V-ATPase assembly/activity; (5) autophagic flux (LC3-II turnover ± lysosomal inhibitors; p62 dynamics); (6) cathepsin D/L activity assays; (7) oxidative stress resilience (mitoROS, mtDNA damage) and mitophagy markers; and (8) complement handling (C3 turnover, C5b-9 deposition) under CFH Y402H and amyloid/oxidant stress conditions (Falcão et al., 2025; Sinha et al., 2016; Falcão et al., 2025; Kaarniranta et al., 2023). Benchmarking to validated TFEB activators (e.g., trehalose) and lysosomal acidification restorers will contextualize fingolimod’s performance on the most disease-relevant axes (Falcão et al., 2025).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Strong disease–mechanism alignment: Dry AMD is characterized by impaired lysosomal acidification, defective autophagic clearance, and oxidative/complement stress in RPE; AMPK–mTOR–TFEB signaling and V-ATPase activity are validated nodal controllers of lysosomal competence in RPE and AMD models, providing clear mechanistic targets that, if engaged, should be disease-modifying (Sinha et al., 2016; Sinha et al., 2016; Falcão et al., 2025; Sinha et al., 2016).  
- On-target cellular expression: S1PR1 is present in RPE and is the predominant S1PR subtype, while RPE express SphK1/2, indicating the S1P/S1PR machinery required for pharmacologic modulation exists in the target cell (Sorenson et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2023).  
- Prior ocular efficacy signals via S1PR modulation: ApoM/HDL–S1P→S1PR1 suppresses CNV and leakage; FTY720 reduces choroidal endothelial angiogenic behaviors and mitigates CNV; in diabetic retinopathy, fingolimod decreases VEGF signaling—together confirming relevant ocular pharmacology and providing translational scaffolding for retinal use (Jung et al., 2025; Sorenson et al., 2022; Gesualdo et al., 2021).  
- Immunometabolic rationale: S1P signaling can promote mitochondrial biogenesis, and AMPK–TFEB signaling coordinates mitochondrial–lysosomal crosstalk; a single agent engaging the S1P–AMPK–TFEB axis might simultaneously improve mitochondrial and lysosomal resilience in oxidatively stressed RPE (Boya et al., 2023; Boya et al., 2023).  
- Repurposing tractability: Extensive human exposure, known PK/PD, and manageable formulation chemistry enable accelerated translational planning compared to de novo entities (Mondal & Mandal, 2019).

Weaknesses and risks  
- Mechanistic gap in the target cell: There is currently no direct evidence that fingolimod activates AMPK or TFEB in RPE, increases autophagic flux, or acidifies lysosomes; likewise, no data show fingolimod reduces complement-driven injury in RPE/dry AMD models, and this is the central premise of the hypothesis (Jung et al., 2025; Boya et al., 2023; Falcão et al., 2025).  
- Context dependence and potential for adverse lysosomal effects: In human non-ocular cells, fingolimod induced inhibitory TFEB phosphorylation and autophagy stalling, and lysosomal enlargement/permeabilization has been reported in some contexts—opposite to the desired lysosomal restoration—raising the possibility of deleterious effects in RPE unless carefully titrated (Relic et al., 2021).  
- Receptor- and ligand-context complexity: Beneficial vascular phenotypes are associated with endothelial S1PR1 stimulation—often via chaperone-bound S1P—while nonselective S1PR modulation or anti-S1P strategies can also be beneficial (e.g., anti-fibrotic effects in AMD), implying that fingolimod’s mixed S1PR agonism and functional antagonism could yield off-target or counterproductive outcomes in the RPE/choroid (Jung et al., 2025; Gupta et al., 2012; Sorenson et al., 2022).  
- Retinal safety concerns: Fingolimod-associated macular edema is a documented adverse effect in humans, which is particularly concerning in a macular disease; any development plan must incorporate delivery strategies and exposure limits that mitigate this risk (Mondal & Mandal, 2019).  
- Evidence base skew: Much of the directly AMD-relevant S1P/S1PR ocular literature concerns neovascular endpoints (wet AMD/CNV) or endothelium, not atrophic RPE biology; the best lysosome/autophagy data are robust but are not linked to S1PR pharmacology, necessitating bridging studies to validate the specific drug–mechanism–disease chain (Jung et al., 2025; Falcão et al., 2025).

Go/no-go perspective and experimental priorities  
On balance, fingolimod is a mechanistically plausible, but currently unvalidated, repurposing candidate for dry AMD via the proposed S1PR→AMPK→TFEB→lysosome axis. A limited, mechanism-first preclinical package in human RPE models is warranted before considering in vivo efficacy work. The minimum data package to de-risk the hypothesis should include:  
- Demonstration that fingolimod engages S1PRs on human RPE and increases AMPK activity while suppressing mTORC1, with consequent TFEB/TFE3 nuclear translocation and CLEAR gene induction; side-by-side with a S1PR1-selective agonist and apoM/HDL-S1P as positive controls for S1PR1 biology (Sorenson et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2023; Falcão et al., 2025; Jung et al., 2025).  
- Functional lysosomal rescue: increased V-ATPase assembly/activity, lower lysosomal pH, increased CTSD/CTSL activity, improved POS digestion, reduced A2E and lipofuscin-like autofluorescence under static and diurnal POS feeding paradigms (Sinha et al., 2016; Falcão et al., 2025).  
- Flux and mitochondrial outcomes: increased autophagic flux (LC3-II turnover, p62 dynamics), enhanced mitophagy under oxidant stress (PINK1/PRKN markers), and decreased mitoROS (Boya et al., 2023; Sinha et al., 2016).  
- Inflammation/complement endpoints: reduced IL1B release after MG-132/BafA challenges, lowered NLRP3 activation, decreased lysosomal C5b-9 deposition and improved lysosomal integrity in CFH Y402H iPSC-RPE exposed to complement (Piippo, 2019; Falcão et al., 2025).  
- Safety liabilities: absence of lysosomal membrane permeabilization, cathepsin leakage, or TFEB Ser211 inhibitory phosphorylation with autophagy stalling at therapeutic exposure in RPE, in contrast to adverse signatures reported in other cell types (Relic et al., 2021).

Depending on these in vitro outcomes, a focused in vivo test in a dry AMD-relevant model (e.g., NaIO3 injury or Cryba1 cKO) with intraocular delivery and a retinal safety assessment (OCT for edema, ERG, histology) would be the logical next step (Falcão et al., 2025; Sinha et al., 2016). If the AMPK–TFEB and lysosomal endpoints are not met, pivot to alternative S1PR strategies (S1PR1-selective agonists or apoM/HDL–S1P formulations) that have more consistent endothelial/retinal protective phenotypes may be warranted (Jung et al., 2025). If proximal signaling is partially engaged but lysosomal capacity remains limiting, combination approaches with validated TFEB activators (e.g., trehalose) or NRF2 activators that cross-reinforce lysosomal and antioxidant programs could be explored with attention to oncogenicity and cell specificity (Falcão et al., 2025).

Conclusion  
Fingolimod sits at the intersection of a compelling disease mechanism (lysosomal/autophagic failure in RPE), a plausible upstream target (S1PR1 in RPE), and a therapeutic class with ocular activity (S1PR modulators), but it lacks direct evidence for engaging the AMPK–TFEB–lysosomal biogenesis/acidification axis in RPE or for mitigating complement/oxidative injury in dry AMD models (Sorenson et al., 2022; Falcão et al., 2025; Jung et al., 2025). The strength of the lysosome/autophagy rationale and the existence of RPE S1PR1 expression support a mechanism-first exploration; however, cell-type–dependent fingolimod effects on TFEB and autophagy and the clinical risk of macular edema demand caution (Relic et al., 2021; Mondal & Mandal, 2019). Proceed only with a staged validation plan centered on RPE-intrinsic endpoints of AMPK/TFEB activation, lysosomal acidification, and complement/oxidative resilience; without those data, the hypothesis remains unsubstantiated for dry AMD, and alternative S1PR strategies or direct TFEB/lysosome-targeting interventions may be more tractable (Jung et al., 2025; Falcão et al., 2025).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
GDC-0941 (pictilisib) is a synthetic, orally bioavailable, ATP-competitive, pan–class I phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K) inhibitor discovered through structure-guided medicinal chemistry at Genentech as an optimization beyond early tool compounds and the dual PI3K/mTOR inhibitor PI-103, with substantially improved selectivity for class I PI3Ks and favorable pharmacokinetics (PK) suitable for systemic dosing in humans (Garces, n.d.; Zhao et al., 2017; Li et al., 2024). At the biochemical level, pictilisib exhibits low-nanomolar potency against p110α and p110δ, with activity across class I isoforms (representative IC₅₀s: α ≈ 3 nM, β ≈ 33 nM, δ ≈ 3 nM, γ ≈ 75 nM) and weak activity on mTOR (~0.58 μM), consistent with selective targeting of class I PI3Ks over mTOR kinase (Huang et al., 2023; Garces, n.d.; Josephs & Sarker, 2016; Zhao et al., 2017). Co-crystal structural analysis shows an ATP-mimetic thieno[3,2-d]pyrimidine core in which the morpholine oxygen donates a hinge hydrogen bond (Val882), the indazole engages an affinity pocket (Asp841/Tyr867), and a methanesulfonyl-piperazine tail projects toward solvent; these interactions underpin its potency and selectivity within the class I PI3K ATP site (PDB 3DBS) (Garces, n.d.). Pictilisib belongs to the pan-class I PI3K inhibitor class, a therapeutic category widely advanced in oncology to suppress the PI3K→AKT→mTOR signaling axis that governs cell growth, survival, and metabolism; multiple agents in this class have reached clinical testing or approval, providing a clear translational precedent for pathway engagement and safety management in humans (Schmitz et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2023; Li et al., 2024).

Therapeutic History  
The development history of pictilisib is anchored in oncology, where first-in-human Phase I trials established a recommended Phase II dose of 330 mg once daily, dose-proportional PK (Tₘₐₓ ≈ 2 h, t₁/₂ ≈ 13–24 h), and robust pharmacodynamic (PD) target engagement—up to ~90% inhibition of phosphorylated AKT (Ser473) in platelet-rich plasma within 1–3 h of dosing and suppression of p-AKT and p-S6 in tumor biopsies at sufficient exposure (AUC > 20 μM·h) (Sarker et al., 2015; Mishra et al., 2021). Across Phase I combination studies, pictilisib showed a manageable safety profile and some antitumor activity, with common adverse events including nausea, diarrhea, rash, fatigue, hyperglycemia, and cytopenias; dose-limiting toxicity in some settings was grade 3 maculopapular rash (Mishra et al., 2021; Josephs & Sarker, 2016; Sarker et al., 2015). Although pathway suppression was clear, randomized combination trials in breast and lung cancer variably met efficacy endpoints and broader development was limited by tolerability in multi-drug regimens and modest efficacy as monotherapy—experience that nonetheless provides clinically validated PK/PD tools and class-effect safety benchmarks (Mishra et al., 2021; Gao et al., 2017).

No preclinical or clinical use of pictilisib or other class I PI3K inhibitors has been reported for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or RPE-centered retinal disease models in the provided literature, and a recent review emphasizes that no ongoing clinical trials directly target autophagy in AMD, underscoring an evidence gap for PI3K inhibitors in this indication (Blasiak et al., 2025). By contrast, direct downstream pathway modulation in RPE—mTORC1 inhibition with rapamycin—has shown that activating the lysosome–TFEB axis reduces POS-derived autofluorescent granules in vitro in a hydrolase-dependent manner, but clinical testing in advanced AMD returned limited efficacy and adverse effects, illustrating both the mechanistic plausibility of modulating this pathway and translational challenges (Falcão et al., 2024). Collectively, the therapeutic history supports that class I PI3K inhibitors achieve systemic PI3K pathway inhibition in humans with tractable but nontrivial toxicities; however, there is no published RPE- or AMD-focused body of work with pictilisib to date in the provided context (Sarker et al., 2015; Mishra et al., 2021; Blasiak et al., 2025).

Mechanism of Action  
Class I PI3Ks phosphorylate PIP₂ to PIP₃, recruiting PH-domain effectors including PDK1 and AKT to the plasma membrane, where AKT is activated by phosphorylation at Thr308 (PDK1) and Ser473 (mTORC2) (Huang et al., 2023). Activated AKT phosphorylates multiple substrates that converge on mTORC1 activation (via TSC2/PRAS40), leading to phosphorylation of S6K1 and 4E-BP1 to promote protein synthesis and suppress autophagy, thereby integrating growth-factor status with anabolic programs (Huang et al., 2023; Castel et al., 2021). In retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), AKT/mTOR signaling is an established regulator of cell proliferation and autophagy; mTORC1 activation inhibits autophagy by blocking ULK1 signaling and autolysosomal biogenesis, whereas rapamycin-mediated mTORC1 inhibition activates autophagy and preserves photoreceptor function in preclinical models (Chang et al., 2015). PI3K inhibition upstream of AKT is thus expected to reduce PIP₃ generation, limit AKT membrane recruitment/activation, and secondarily depress mTORC1 signaling in RPE (Castel et al., 2021; Chang et al., 2015).

PI3K→AKT signaling intersects directly with TFEB/TFE3—the master transcription factors of lysosomal biogenesis and the CLEAR regulon—through both mTORC1-dependent and mTORC1-independent routes (Falcão et al., 2024; Ghosh et al., 2024). Nutrient-driven mTORC1 activity at the lysosome phosphorylates TFEB/TFE3 to retain them in the cytosol; conversely, mTORC1 inhibition permits TFEB nuclear translocation and induction of lysosomal/autophagy genes (Falcão et al., 2024). Importantly, AKT2 directly phosphorylates TFEB (at Ser467) and TFE3 (Ser321), promoting 14-3-3 binding and cytoplasmic sequestration independent of mTORC1, thereby repressing CLEAR gene expression and lysosomal programs in RPE (Ghosh et al., 2023; Ghosh et al., 2024). In AMD-relevant contexts—human dysmorphic macular RPE, CFH risk-allele iPSC-RPE, and Akt2 RPE-specific knock-in mice—AKT2 upregulation increases TFEB/TFE3 phosphorylation, reduces lysosomal hydrolases (cathepsin D/L) and CLEAR target expression, impairs autophagic flux, and shifts autophagy toward secretory pathways characterized by increased FKBP51/SNAP23, autophagosome fusion with the plasma membrane, and extracellular release of IL-1β/HMGB1 (Ghosh et al., 2023; Ghosh et al., 2024). TFEB rescue via a phospho-deficient TFEB-S467A mutant or pharmacologic TFEB activation with trehalose restores cathepsin D/L and autophagy genes, normalizes autophagosome–lysosome fusion, and improves RPE structure in AMD-like mouse models, establishing TFEB/TFE3 as actionable nodes downstream of AKT2 in RPE (Ghosh et al., 2023; Ghosh et al., 2024).

SIRT5 and mitochondrial metabolism integrate with AKT2–TFEB signaling in RPE. SIRT5 interacts with AKT2 and reduces lysine malonylation on AKT2, modulating AKT2 activity; AKT2, via inhibition of PGC-1α, downregulates SIRT5, creating a bidirectional circuit that affects TFEB-dependent lysosomal function and mitochondrial respiration (Ghosh et al., 2023). AKT2 upregulation impairs mitochondrial respiration (maximal and ATP-linked), which is rescued by SIRT5, linking mitochondrial–lysosomal crosstalk to RPE proteostasis (Ghosh et al., 2023). Functionally, failure of the AKT2/SIRT5/TFEB axis elevates secretory autophagy and likely contributes to drusen pathogenesis by exporting inflammatory cargo (Ghosh et al., 2023).

These mechanistic data converge with mTORC1→TFEB observations in POS-fed RPE models. Synchronous POS phagocytosis transiently activates mTORC1 early, with TFEB protein increasing but remaining phosphorylated during late maturation, indicating a bottleneck at TFEB activation (Falcão et al., 2024). Pharmacologic mTORC1 inhibition with rapamycin after AFGs have formed lowers POS-derived autofluorescence by ~30% in hfRPE/ARPE-19, reduces pS6, decreases the pTFEB/TFEB ratio, increases LAMP1, and requires active lysosomal hydrolases: cathepsin D knockout or protease/lipase inhibition abolishes the rapamycin effect (Falcão et al., 2024). Human AMD RPE exhibits hyperphosphorylated TFEB with decreased nuclear localization and lower cathepsin D/L protein levels and activities, consistent with impaired lysosome proteolysis; constitutively active TFEB boosts CLEAR genes, including hydrolases and V-ATPase subunits (e.g., ATP6V0A1), supporting enhanced acidification capacity (Falcão et al., 2025).

Pictilisib’s proximal pharmacology—ATP-competitive inhibition of class I PI3Ks—has been shown to produce substantial pathway suppression in human tissues (reduced pAKT, reduced pS6) and in tumor models; such upstream inhibition is expected to depress both AKT→mTORC1 signaling and AKT2-mediated TFEB phosphorylation, potentially enabling TFEB/TFE3 nuclear translocation and restoration of CLEAR programs in RPE (Sarker et al., 2015; Mishra et al., 2021; Castel et al., 2021; Ghosh et al., 2024). Two caveats are central. First, class III PI3K/VPS34 activity is required for autophagosome nucleation; thus class I–selective inhibition (as with pictilisib) is mechanistically appropriate, whereas class III inhibition would be detrimental to autophagy flux (Wang et al., 2023). Second, while AKT inhibitors (e.g., MK-2206) and TFEB activators (trehalose) have directly increased autophagy and TFEB nuclear translocation in RPE, no direct evidence of class I PI3K inhibitors reproducing these effects in RPE has been reported in the provided literature (Karim et al., 2020; Blasiak et al., 2025).

Expected Effect  
In RPE cell assays designed to model dry AMD–relevant lysosomal stress (e.g., POS feeding, A2E/oxidant exposure, or CFH risk-allele iPSC-RPE), pictilisib is expected to reduce PI3K-dependent PIP₃ generation, lowering membrane recruitment and phosphorylation of AKT, thereby secondarily suppressing mTORC1 and directly relieving AKT2-mediated phosphorylation of TFEB/TFE3 (Huang et al., 2023; Castel et al., 2021; Ghosh et al., 2024). Mechanistically, this should dephosphorylate TFEB/TFE3, promote nuclear translocation, and activate the CLEAR transcriptional program to increase components of lysosomal biogenesis and function (e.g., LAMP1/2, cathepsin D/L, and V-ATPase subunits), thereby enhancing degradative capacity and autophagic flux (Falcão et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2025; Falcão et al., 2024).

Operationally testable expected effects include:  
• Signaling: decreased pAKT (Ser473) and pS6 (Ser235/236) within hours of dosing in RPE, mirroring PD seen in tumors and platelet-rich plasma in human trials, establishing target engagement (Sarker et al., 2015; Mishra et al., 2021).  
• TFEB/TFE3 activation: reduction in pTFEB/TFEB ratio, increased nuclear TFEB/TFE3, and induction of CLEAR genes; in RPE systems, TFEB activation correlates with increased LAMP1 and rescue of lysosomal hydrolases and autophagy mediators (e.g., ATG9B), as seen upon TFEB S467A expression or trehalose treatment (Falcão et al., 2024; Ghosh et al., 2023; Ghosh et al., 2024).  
• Lysosomal function: increased abundance and maturation of cathepsin D (pro→intermediate→mature chain) and cathepsin L, and improved degradative flux, consistent with observations that AMD RPE shows diminished cathepsin levels/activities and that hydrolase function is required for rapamycin-mediated clearance of POS-derived AFGs (Falcão et al., 2025; Falcão et al., 2024).  
• Autophagic flux: increased LC3-II turnover (± bafilomycin A₁), reduced p62/SQSTM1 accumulation, restored autophagosome–lysosome fusion (e.g., GFP-LC3 and LysoTracker/LAMP1 colocalization), and decreased accumulation of double-membrane autophagosomes on EM, reversing the AKT2-driven flux block (Ghosh et al., 2023; Ghosh et al., 2024).  
• POS-derived autofluorescence: reduction in POS-dependent autofluorescent granules in preventive and resolving paradigms, analogous to mTORC1 inhibition or TFEB activation effects; efficacy will depend on intact lysosomal hydrolase activity (Falcão et al., 2024).  
• Secretory autophagy: decreased FKBP51/SNAP23 elevation, reduced plasma-membrane fusion of autophagosomes, and lower extracellular release of IL-1β and HMGB1 from RPE, mirroring effects seen with SIRT5 co-expression or AKT2 inhibition (Ghosh et al., 2023; Ghosh et al., 2024).  
• Acidification: although lysosomal pH has not been directly measured after class I PI3K inhibition in RPE, TFEB activation increases expression of V-ATPase subunits, and improved hydrolase activities imply normalization of the acidic lumen; direct pH assays (LysoSensor/LysoTracker) should be incorporated because efficacy of rapamycin/TFEB approaches depends on intact lysosomal acid hydrolases (Falcão et al., 2025; Falcão et al., 2024).

These expectations rest on the well-documented presence and dysregulation of the AKT2→TFEB/TFE3→CLEAR axis in RPE and the dependence of POS clearance on mTOR/TFEB-governed lysosomal function (Ghosh et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2024). AKT2 is upregulated in macular RPE from AMD donors and in AMD-like mouse models, and RPE-specific Akt2 overexpression is sufficient to induce AMD-like pathology, supporting target relevance in the cell type and disease context of interest (Ghosh et al., 2023; Ghosh et al., 2024). Because PI3K is upstream of AKT, class I PI3K inhibition should, in principle, reduce AKT2 activity and thereby favor TFEB activation; however, no direct studies in the provided literature demonstrate pictilisib (or any class I PI3K inhibitor) inducing TFEB nuclear translocation or improving cathepsin D maturation/activity in RPE, so these are testable, evidence-generating predictions rather than established facts (Blasiak et al., 2025; Chang et al., 2015; Karim et al., 2020).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Mechanistic alignment with disease biology: Dry AMD features impaired RPE autophagy–lysosome function, diminished cathepsin D/L levels/activities, and TFEB hyperphosphorylation with reduced nuclear TFEB, all of which converge on lysosomal insufficiency and accumulation of lipofuscin-like material and extracellular drusen; upstream PI3K inhibition is a coherent strategy to relieve AKT2- and mTORC1-mediated repression of TFEB/TFE3 and restore CLEAR-driven lysosomal biogenesis and flux (Falcão et al., 2025; Falcão et al., 2024; Ghosh et al., 2024).  
• Drug tractability and translational readiness: Pictilisib achieves robust systemic target engagement in humans (pAKT/pS6 suppression), has well-characterized PK/PD and class-effect safety, and is chemically and biophysically optimized, enabling accelerated preclinical testing and dosage/formulation exploration for ocular delivery or low systemic exposure strategies (Sarker et al., 2015; Mishra et al., 2021; Garces, n.d.).  
• Selectivity profile appropriate for autophagy enhancement: Because autophagosome nucleation requires class III PI3K/VPS34, class I selectivity of pictilisib avoids this liability while suppressing AKT→mTOR signaling and AKT2-dependent TFEB phosphorylation, in contrast to nonselective PI3K inhibition which would be deleterious (Wang et al., 2023; Castel et al., 2021).

Risks and Gaps  
• No direct RPE/AMD data with class I PI3K inhibitors: In contrast to clear benefits from rapamycin and TFEB activation, the literature presented contains no direct evidence that class I PI3K inhibition, or pictilisib specifically, improves TFEB activation/nuclear entry, lysosomal biogenesis, cathepsin D maturation/activity, lysosomal acidification, autophagy flux, or POS handling in RPE; thus, the central hypothesis remains unvalidated experimentally in the disease-relevant cell type (Blasiak et al., 2025; Chang et al., 2015; Falcão et al., 2024). By comparison, AKT inhibition (MK-2206) and trehalose have been shown to increase autophagy and nuclear TFEB in RPE, and AKT2 inhibitors reduced lipid/apoE in CFH(H/H) RPE, but these are not PI3K inhibitors and may differ in cellular selectivity and compensatory signaling (Karim et al., 2020; Ghosh et al., 2024).  
• Complexity of autophagy modulation and context dependence: Autophagy is a double-edged sword with biphasic responses to stress; overactivation or mistimed activation could exacerbate RPE stress or impair other retinal cell types, and some autophagy inhibitors display retinal toxicity (e.g., chloroquine class), emphasizing the need for precise control and safety profiling (Blasiak et al., 2025; Kaarniranta et al., 2013). Rapamycin has shown only limited clinical efficacy in advanced AMD despite mechanistic benefits in vitro, illustrating translational friction between pathway modulation and clinical outcomes (Falcão et al., 2024).  
• Safety, delivery, and exposure management: Systemic class I PI3K inhibition induces hyperglycemia, rash, and gastrointestinal toxicities; while these were generally manageable, ocular delivery strategies (intravitreal or periocular) and ocular pharmacokinetics for pictilisib are uncharacterized in the provided literature, and tissue-specific PD (e.g., drug levels at the RPE/Bruch’s complex) is likely to determine efficacy and safety (Josephs & Sarker, 2016; Sarker et al., 2015; Mishra et al., 2021). Tissue PD variability seen in tumors versus blood suggests careful intratissue PD assays are necessary (Sarker et al., 2015).  
• Isoform and cell-type specificity: AKT2 is the isoform implicated in RPE TFEB repression and secretory autophagy; upstream PI3K isoform contributions in RPE are not defined here, and pan-class I inhibition could affect neighboring retinal cells, choroidal endothelium, and immune cells, potentially altering retinal immunity and angiogenesis in unintended ways (Ghosh et al., 2024; Castel et al., 2021). Given the evidence favoring AKT2-selective inhibition or direct TFEB activation in RPE models, PI3K-level intervention may be broader than necessary and carry off-target tissue consequences (Ghosh et al., 2024; Karim et al., 2020).  
• Acidification endpoint uncertainty: The hypothesis specifically posits enhanced lysosomal acidification, yet none of the provided sources report direct lysosomal pH measurements after class I PI3K inhibition in RPE; while CLEAR induction can increase V-ATPase subunits and rapamycin-mediated clearance requires active hydrolases, direct acidification effects remain to be demonstrated (Falcão et al., 2025; Falcão et al., 2024; Blasiak et al., 2025).

Go/No-Go Evidence Plan  
Given the strong mechanistic rationale but absence of direct RPE data, a staged validation program is warranted:  
– In vitro RPE target engagement and TFEB activation: Demonstrate pictilisib decreases pAKT (Ser473) and pS6 in primary human fetal RPE, ARPE-19, and iPSC-RPE, and increases nuclear TFEB/TFE3 with induction of CLEAR genes (CTSD, CTSL, LAMP2, ATP6V0A1) assessed by Western, RT-qPCR, and ChIP-qPCR (Falcão et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2025; Ghosh et al., 2024).  
– Lysosome function readouts: Quantify cathepsin D maturation and enzymatic activity, LAMP1/2 abundance, and lysosomal pH using ratiometric probes; include hydrolase inhibition controls to assess dependence analogous to the rapamycin data (Falcão et al., 2024).  
– Autophagic flux and modality: Assess LC3-II turnover (± bafilomycin A₁), p62 dynamics, autolysosome number (LC3–LAMP1 colocalization), and EM confirmation; evaluate secretory-autophagy markers (FKBP51, SNAP23) and extracellular cargo (HMGB1, IL-1β) to test reversal of the AKT2-driven phenotype (Ghosh et al., 2023; Ghosh et al., 2024).  
– Functional disease readouts: Test POS-dependent autofluorescence reduction in preventive and resolving paradigms and POS degradation assays; evaluate lipid/apoE accumulation in CFH(H/H) iPSC-RPE and Cryba1 cKO explants to compare with reported trehalose and AKT2 inhibitor effects (Falcão et al., 2024; Ghosh et al., 2023; Ghosh et al., 2024).  
– In vivo and delivery: Establish ocular PK and tolerability for local delivery (intravitreal/periocular) in rodents, then test efficacy in RPE-driven AMD-like models (Akt2 KI, Cryba1 cKO, NaIO₃) with TFEB activation, lysosomal and functional endpoints (ERG/SD-OCT) (Ghosh et al., 2024; Ghosh et al., 2023; Falcão et al., 2025).  
– Benchmarking: Include rapamycin (mTORC1 inhibition), MK-2206 (AKT inhibition), and trehalose (mTOR-independent TFEB activation) comparators to position PI3K inhibition within the therapeutic landscape (Falcão et al., 2024; Karim et al., 2020; Ghosh et al., 2023).

Conclusion  
Pictilisib offers a mechanistically coherent, drug-like approach to modulate an RPE pathway of clear pathogenic relevance—AKT2/mTOR-mediated repression of TFEB/TFE3 and the CLEAR network—backed by robust human PK/PD experience and a selectivity profile compatible with enhancing autophagy without impeding VPS34-dependent nucleation (Ghosh et al., 2024; Sarker et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2023). However, the absence of direct evidence that class I PI3K inhibition rectifies TFEB activity, lysosomal hydrolase function (notably cathepsin D), lysosomal acidification, autophagic flux, or POS clearance in RPE is a critical gap that precludes immediate advancement; by contrast, downstream interventions (rapamycin, TFEB activation, AKT2 inhibition) already demonstrate these benefits in RPE models (Falcão et al., 2024; Ghosh et al., 2024). On balance, pictilisib is plausible and testable but not yet justified for translational progression without focused RPE and ocular studies; an AKT2-selective inhibitor or TFEB-directed strategies may offer a higher probability of effect with narrower network perturbation, and should be run in parallel as mechanistic benchmarks (Ghosh et al., 2024; Karim et al., 2020). If the proposed RPE experiments confirm that pictilisib restores TFEB-driven lysosomal programs, improves cathepsin D maturation/activity, normalizes autophagy flux, and reduces POS-derived autofluorescence with acceptable ocular tolerability, the candidate would merit advancement to in vivo ocular efficacy testing; absent such confirmation, resources should pivot to agents with demonstrated RPE TFEB engagement (Ghosh et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2024).
