Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Temsirolimus (CCI-779; Torisel) is a semi-synthetic ester prodrug of sirolimus (rapamycin) discovered during rapamycin medicinal chemistry optimization to improve formulation properties and pharmacokinetics; it is a first-generation “rapalog” that inhibits mTOR by forming an intracellular complex with FKBP12 and binding the FRB domain of mTOR, thereby allosterically inhibiting mTORC1 catalytic signaling (and only indirectly affecting mTORC2) (Wang et al., 2022). As a class, rapalogs are derived from the natural macrolide rapamycin originally isolated from Streptomyces hygroscopicus; they have been used systemically as immunosuppressants and anti-proliferative/anti-angiogenic agents in oncology and transplant medicine by suppressing mTORC1-dependent growth and inflammatory programs (Wang et al., 2022; Johnson, 2013). mTORC1 is a lysosome-proximal signaling hub that integrates amino acid sufficiency via the Ragulator–Rag GTPase machinery and growth/energy signals via Rheb/AMPK, coordinating anabolism (protein synthesis via S6K and 4E-BP1), and repressing catabolism (autophagy and lysosomal biogenesis) (Johnson, 2013). In ocular biology, temsirolimus has been evaluated preclinically in human retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells and human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVEC), consistently demonstrating dose-dependent inhibition of proliferation and migration and decreased VEGF/PDGF expression through mTOR pathway inhibition, supporting target engagement in retinal cell types relevant to AMD pathogenesis (Liegl et al., 2014). Compared with rapamycin, temsirolimus has higher aqueous solubility and stability but is administered intravenously in approved oncology indications; adverse events include metabolic and mucosal toxicities typical of systemic mTOR inhibition (Wang et al., 2022).

Therapeutic History  
Rapamycin/sirolimus and rapalogs have a long clinical history across transplantation and oncology; in ophthalmology, mechanistic and translational work has targeted mTOR for AMD and other retinal diseases because mTORC1 suppresses autophagy/lysosomal programs and promotes inflammatory and angiogenic signaling (Wang et al., 2022; Nita & Grzybowski, 2023). In RPE models that recapitulate daily phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments (POS), mTORC1 activity is dynamically regulated: POS phagocytosis transiently activates mTORC1, followed by inhibition during phagosome maturation; however, in aged RPE and AMD, mTORC1 activity is relatively elevated and TFEB is retained in the phosphorylated cytosolic state, impairing lysosomal responses and favoring lipofuscin-like autofluorescent granule (AFG) accumulation (Falcão et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2025). In these systems, rapamycin reduces POS-dependent AFGs by about 30% while increasing TFEB activity and lysosomal biogenesis markers (e.g., LAMP1) in ARPE-19 and human fetal RPE cells; efficacy generalizes to other mTOR pathway inhibitors (e.g., INK-128), and constitutively active TFEB provides larger effects, supporting a TFEB-centric mechanism (Falcão et al., 2024). These effects require intact lysosomal proteolysis; pharmacologic blockade of lysosomal acid lipase, cathepsin inhibition, or cathepsin D (CTSD) knockout abrogates rapamycin’s benefit, highlighting a dependence on functional lysosomes (Falcão et al., 2024). Although these data do not directly test temsirolimus in lysosome-TFEB endpoints, temsirolimus is mechanistically a rapalog mTORC1 inhibitor, and in RPE it engages mTOR biology by suppressing growth factor signaling outputs (VEGF/PDGF) and cell motility/proliferation, thereby validating target engagement in the relevant cell type (Liegl et al., 2014).

Clinically, multiple sirolimus trials have evaluated mTOR inhibition in geographic atrophy (GA), a late stage of dry AMD, with disappointing outcomes. Subconjunctival sirolimus (440 µg every 3 months for 24 months) in a bilateral-eye, fellow-eye-control study did not slow GA enlargement and was associated with a treatment-associated decrease in visual acuity relative to untreated fellow eyes, despite an acceptable safety profile in that study (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2008; Wang et al., 2022). An intravitreal sirolimus Phase I/II study in bilateral GA was discontinued early, and separate trials reported ocular adverse events including accelerated retinal thinning, abnormal perilesional autofluorescence, and sterile endophthalmitis; overall, no structural or functional benefit was demonstrated across these programs (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2011; Wang et al., 2022). These clinical observations raise concern that chronic mTOR inhibition in established GA may be ineffective or even detrimental, potentially due to disease stage–specific network effects of autophagy and survival signaling in degenerating retina (Wang et al., 2022). In contrast, preclinical data in other retinal contexts (e.g., glaucoma) show neuroprotective correlates of mTOR inhibition, underscoring the context- and stage-dependence of therapeutic effects (Wang et al., 2022). For wet AMD and retinal vascular pathology, temsirolimus (and rapamycin) exert anti-angiogenic actions in vitro and in animal models by downregulating VEGF/PDGF and endothelial proliferation, which are less directly relevant to GA biology but establish ocular pharmacology for the class (Liegl et al., 2014; Johnson, 2013). Drug delivery innovations such as synthetic HDL nanoparticles carrying rapamycin have been explored preclinically to optimize ocular delivery, suggesting format-dependent translatability may be important for this class (Falcão et al., 2024).

Mechanism of Action  
Temsirolimus acts as a prototypical rapalog: it binds FKBP12 to form a gain-of-function complex that docks to the FKBP12-rapamycin binding (FRB) domain of mTOR and selectively inhibits mTORC1 signaling; mTORC2 is generally spared acutely, with potential indirect effects chronically depending on cellular context (Wang et al., 2022). mTORC1 normally phosphorylates TFEB on multiple serine residues, retaining it in the cytosol and preventing nuclear entry; when mTORC1 is inhibited, TFEB becomes dephosphorylated, translocates to the nucleus, and drives the CLEAR network that upregulates autophagy and lysosomal biogenesis genes (e.g., LAMP1), enhancing degradative capacity and organelle biogenesis (Falcão et al., 2025; Falcão et al., 2024). In RPE cells, POS phagocytosis engages mTORC1 transiently, but aged/AMD RPE exhibit enhanced mTORC1 activity that suppresses appropriate TFEB activation; rapamycin reverses this, promoting TFEB dephosphorylation, nuclear entry, GADD34 upregulation, and increased lysosomal mass, collectively reducing AFGs by approximately 30% in POS-challenged RPE (Falcão et al., 2024). The TFEB dependency has been functionally validated via TFEB gain-of-function, which markedly decreases AFGs in both preventive and “therapeutic” paradigms after lipofuscin-like material has already formed (Falcão et al., 2024). Pharmacologic relevance to mTOR pathway modulation beyond rapamycin was supported using INK-128 and other mTOR inhibitors, which replicated the AFG reduction and TFEB-lysosome signature (Falcão et al., 2024).

At the biochemical level, mTORC1 integrates amino acid signaling at the lysosomal surface via Ragulator-Rag GTPases and growth/energy cues via Rheb/AMPK, coordinating downstream phosphorylation of p70S6K and 4E-BP1 to activate translation while repressing catabolic programs including initiation of autophagy (partly by phosphorylating ULK1 at Ser757 and by blocking TFEB) (Johnson, 2013; Chang et al., 2022). In retinal tissues, mTOR inhibition is expected to relieve brakes on autophagy and lysosomal biogenesis; in diabetic retinopathy models, mTOR inhibition with rapamycin restored impaired lysosomal proteolysis by normalizing cathepsin L activity and autophagic flux, mechanistically consistent with TFEB-driven CLEAR network activation and improved lysosomal protease capacity (Wang et al., 2022). Although direct evidence for temsirolimus effects on RPE TFEB phosphorylation state, lysosomal acidification, or CTSD maturation is not available, the shared mechanism of FKBP12-dependent mTORC1 inhibition and the RPE-cell mTOR engagement demonstrated by temsirolimus (antiproliferative/anti-migratory, VEGF/PDGF suppression) support pathway perturbation in the correct cellular context (Liegl et al., 2014).

In the context of AMD pathophysiology, RPE lysosomal dysfunction and impaired clearance of POS-derived material drive lipofuscin accumulation and downstream toxicity; TFEB has emerged as a master regulator to restore lysosomal capacity, while AMD donor RPE show reduced cathepsin D and L levels/activities, highlighting protease insufficiency as a plausible node of therapeutic rescue (Falcão et al., 2025). Importantly, in POS-fed RPE, the rapamycin benefit is abolished by lysosomal protease inhibition or CTSD knockout, indicating that mTORC1 inhibition enhances clearance only when lysosomal protease function is preserved, and suggesting that concomitant strategies to support lysosomal acidification/protease maturation could be synergistic (Falcão et al., 2024). Finally, some reports have suggested low immunoreactivity of mTORC1/2 components in RPE, but this observation contrasts with multiple functional studies demonstrating mTORC1 signaling in RPE during POS handling and aging; taken together, functional responsiveness to mTOR inhibitors in RPE likely depends on model system and detection sensitivity (Wang et al., 2022; Falcão et al., 2024).

Expected Effect  
In a POS-pulse/chase AFG assay using ARPE-19 or human fetal RPE, temsirolimus is expected to inhibit mTORC1 (decreased pS6 phosphorylation), dephosphorylate TFEB, increase TFEB nuclear localization, upregulate CLEAR network/lysosomal biogenesis genes (e.g., GADD34, LAMP1), and reduce AFG burden by enhancing degradation of phagocytosed material; this mirrors rapamycin’s effects (~30% AFG reduction) and those of other mTOR inhibitors in these models (Falcão et al., 2024). To confirm on-target activity and pathway alignment, assays should include pS6/S6 and pTFEB/TFEB immunoblotting at 2–24 h, TFEB nuclear translocation imaging, LAMP1 immunostaining for lysosomal mass, and flow cytometry quantification of AFGs after 24–72 h chase, consistent with established methodologies (Falcão et al., 2024). Because rapamycin’s benefits are abolished by lysosomal protease blockade and in CTSD-deficient backgrounds, temsirolimus-dependent AFG reduction is predicted to require functional cathepsin D and lipases; co-assaying CTSD maturation (pro-/mature CTSD ratio), lysosomal pH, and acid lipase activity is therefore crucial to mechanistic validation (Falcão et al., 2024). In parallel, transcriptomic or targeted RT-qPCR panels for CLEAR genes will validate TFEB program engagement (Falcão et al., 2024).

Regarding lysosomal acidification and protease activity, there is mechanistic plausibility but no direct demonstration that temsirolimus enhances lysosomal pH or CTSD maturation in RPE; nevertheless, the TFEB-centric model predicts improved lysosomal proteostasis, and related retinal models show that mTOR inhibition can restore impaired lysosomal proteolysis (cathepsin L) and autophagic flux, supporting the hypothesis that temsirolimus could favorably influence protease maturation/activity in RPE (Wang et al., 2022; Falcão et al., 2025). Notably, independent approaches in RPE can acidify lysosomes and reduce AFGs, underscoring the tractability of the acidification axis, though this was not via mTOR inhibition; combining mTORC1-TFEB activation with direct acidification strategies could be additive (Falcão et al., 2024). The expectation for disease modification in GA derives from the idea that sustained enhancement of lysosomal clearance will reduce lipofuscin burden, preserve RPE function, and slow atrophic expansion; however, prior GA trials with sirolimus showed no benefit and potential harm, implying that either the disease stage, delivery/exposure, or network consequences of chronic mTORC1 inhibition negate the anticipated benefit in late disease (Wang et al., 2022).

Temsirolimus target expression and pharmacology in RPE are supported by in vitro data showing dose-dependent inhibition of RPE proliferation and migration and suppression of hypoxia-induced VEGF/PDGF increases without overt cytotoxicity at low micromolar to millimolar nominal concentrations; these endpoints corroborate mTOR pathway engagement in RPE and provide pharmacodynamic markers (e.g., VEGF suppression) that can be measured alongside TFEB-lysosomal readouts in AFG assays (Liegl et al., 2014). The drug class’s ocular delivery options range from systemic dosing (with significant class-typical adverse events) to local delivery; sirolimus trials used subconjunctival or intravitreal administration but encountered safety/tolerability signals including sterile endophthalmitis and accelerated retinal thinning with no efficacy in GA, emphasizing the need for alternative delivery technologies (e.g., nanoparticles) and stage-appropriate patient selection if pursuing this mechanism (Wang et al., 2022; Falcão et al., 2024). Finally, given AMD donor RPE deficiencies in cathepsins D/L, co-therapies or genetic activation strategies that more directly drive TFEB or augment lysosomal protease capacity could be required to realize the full benefit of mTORC1 inhibition in human disease (Falcão et al., 2025).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Mechanism-based rationale with cell-type congruence: RPE lysosomal dysfunction is central to AMD, and mTORC1 directly represses TFEB and lysosomal programs; in POS-fed RPE, mTORC1 inhibition with rapamycin reduces AFG burden by ~30%, increases lysosomal biogenesis (LAMP1), and requires intact lysosomal proteases, aligning precisely with the hypothesized MoA (Falcão et al., 2024). The effect generalizes across mTOR inhibitors and is amplified by TFEB gain-of-function, strengthening the pathway argument (Falcão et al., 2024).  
- Direct evidence that temsirolimus engages mTOR signaling in RPE: temsirolimus suppresses proliferation/migration and reduces VEGF/PDGF in primary human RPE, indicating pharmacodynamic activity and target engagement in the disease-relevant cell type (Liegl et al., 2014).  
- Broad mechanistic plausibility for enhancing lysosomal proteolysis: mTORC1 inhibition activates TFEB; retinal disease models show restoration of lysosomal protease activity (cathepsin L) and autophagic flux with rapamycin, consistent with improved lysosomal proteostasis, which could translate to better CTSD maturation in RPE even though that specific nexus is unproven for temsirolimus (Wang et al., 2022; Falcão et al., 2025).  
- Drug class knowledge base and formulation opportunities: extensive class experience informs safety risk assessment; emerging ocular delivery strategies (e.g., sHDL rapamycin nanoparticles) might overcome exposure constraints seen in prior sirolimus GA trials (Falcão et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2022).

Weaknesses and Risks  
- Negative/unsafe clinical precedents in GA with class analog: multiple sirolimus trials in GA failed to slow lesion growth and revealed adverse ocular events, including accelerated retinal thinning and procedure-related sterile endophthalmitis, suggesting either mechanistic inadequacy at late stages, harmful network effects of chronic mTORC1 inhibition, or delivery-related issues; this materially lowers clinical plausibility for GA-stage disease (Wang et al., 2022).  
- Absence of temsirolimus-specific TFEB/lysosome data in RPE: while rapamycin demonstrates TFEB activation, lysosomal biogenesis, and AFG reduction, comparable mechanistic data for temsirolimus in RPE are lacking; the program would therefore carry translatability risk until head-to-head, mechanistic RPE assays confirm TFEB engagement and AFG reduction with temsirolimus (Falcão et al., 2024; Liegl et al., 2014).  
- Dependence on intact lysosomes and proteases: rapamycin’s benefit disappears with lipase inhibition or CTSD deficiency; AMD donor RPE show reduced cathepsin D/L, implying that many patient retinas may not have sufficient residual lysosomal capacity for mTORC1 inhibition alone to succeed without adjuncts that restore acidification/protease maturation (Falcão et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2025).  
- Context and stage dependence of mTOR biology: autophagy upregulation that is protective in early disease can exacerbate neuronal apoptosis in late AMD; cell-type–specific and duration-dependent consequences of mTOR inhibition complicate chronic treatment in GA and may negate benefits or cause harm (Wang et al., 2022).  
- Systemic formulation constraints and ocular delivery safety: temsirolimus is an IV drug with known systemic toxicities; local ocular administration for a chronic indication must overcome prior safety/tolerability issues observed with sirolimus injections while achieving sustained, intraretinal/RPE-targeted exposure (Wang et al., 2022).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Temsirolimus (CCI-779; Torisel) is a semi-synthetic ester prodrug of sirolimus (rapamycin) discovered during rapamycin medicinal chemistry optimization to improve formulation properties and pharmacokinetics; it is a first-generation “rapalog” that inhibits mTOR by forming an intracellular complex with FKBP12 and binding the FRB domain of mTOR, thereby allosterically inhibiting mTORC1 catalytic signaling (and only indirectly affecting mTORC2) (Wang et al., 2022). As a class, rapalogs are derived from the natural macrolide rapamycin originally isolated from Streptomyces hygroscopicus; they have been used systemically as immunosuppressants and anti-proliferative/anti-angiogenic agents in oncology and transplant medicine by suppressing mTORC1-dependent growth and inflammatory programs (Wang et al., 2022; Johnson, 2013). mTORC1 is a lysosome-proximal signaling hub that integrates amino acid sufficiency via the Ragulator–Rag GTPase machinery and growth/energy signals via Rheb/AMPK, coordinating anabolism (protein synthesis via S6K and 4E-BP1), and repressing catabolism (autophagy and lysosomal biogenesis) (Johnson, 2013). In ocular biology, temsirolimus has been evaluated preclinically in human retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells and human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVEC), consistently demonstrating dose-dependent inhibition of proliferation and migration and decreased VEGF/PDGF expression through mTOR pathway inhibition, supporting target engagement in retinal cell types relevant to AMD pathogenesis (Liegl et al., 2014). Compared with rapamycin, temsirolimus has higher aqueous solubility and stability but is administered intravenously in approved oncology indications; adverse events include metabolic and mucosal toxicities typical of systemic mTOR inhibition (Wang et al., 2022).

Therapeutic History  
Rapamycin/sirolimus and rapalogs have a long clinical history across transplantation and oncology; in ophthalmology, mechanistic and translational work has targeted mTOR for AMD and other retinal diseases because mTORC1 suppresses autophagy/lysosomal programs and promotes inflammatory and angiogenic signaling (Wang et al., 2022; Nita & Grzybowski, 2023). In RPE models that recapitulate daily phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments (POS), mTORC1 activity is dynamically regulated: POS phagocytosis transiently activates mTORC1, followed by inhibition during phagosome maturation; however, in aged RPE and AMD, mTORC1 activity is relatively elevated and TFEB is retained in the phosphorylated cytosolic state, impairing lysosomal responses and favoring lipofuscin-like autofluorescent granule (AFG) accumulation (Falcão et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2025). In these systems, rapamycin reduces POS-dependent AFGs by about 30% while increasing TFEB activity and lysosomal biogenesis markers (e.g., LAMP1) in ARPE-19 and human fetal RPE cells; efficacy generalizes to other mTOR pathway inhibitors (e.g., INK-128), and constitutively active TFEB provides larger effects, supporting a TFEB-centric mechanism (Falcão et al., 2024). These effects require intact lysosomal proteolysis; pharmacologic blockade of lysosomal acid lipase, cathepsin inhibition, or cathepsin D (CTSD) knockout abrogates rapamycin’s benefit, highlighting a dependence on functional lysosomes (Falcão et al., 2024). Although these data do not directly test temsirolimus in lysosome-TFEB endpoints, temsirolimus is mechanistically a rapalog mTORC1 inhibitor, and in RPE it engages mTOR biology by suppressing growth factor signaling outputs (VEGF/PDGF) and cell motility/proliferation, thereby validating target engagement in the relevant cell type (Liegl et al., 2014).

Clinically, multiple sirolimus trials have evaluated mTOR inhibition in geographic atrophy (GA), a late stage of dry AMD, with disappointing outcomes. Subconjunctival sirolimus (440 µg every 3 months for 24 months) in a bilateral-eye, fellow-eye-control study did not slow GA enlargement and was associated with a treatment-associated decrease in visual acuity relative to untreated fellow eyes, despite an acceptable safety profile in that study (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2008; Wang et al., 2022). An intravitreal sirolimus Phase I/II study in bilateral GA was discontinued early, and separate trials reported ocular adverse events including accelerated retinal thinning, abnormal perilesional autofluorescence, and sterile endophthalmitis; overall, no structural or functional benefit was demonstrated across these programs (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2011; Wang et al., 2022). These clinical observations raise concern that chronic mTOR inhibition in established GA may be ineffective or even detrimental, potentially due to disease stage–specific network effects of autophagy and survival signaling in degenerating retina (Wang et al., 2022). In contrast, preclinical data in other retinal contexts (e.g., glaucoma) show neuroprotective correlates of mTOR inhibition, underscoring the context- and stage-dependence of therapeutic effects (Wang et al., 2022). For wet AMD and retinal vascular pathology, temsirolimus (and rapamycin) exert anti-angiogenic actions in vitro and in animal models by downregulating VEGF/PDGF and endothelial proliferation, which are less directly relevant to GA biology but establish ocular pharmacology for the class (Liegl et al., 2014; Johnson, 2013). Drug delivery innovations such as synthetic HDL nanoparticles carrying rapamycin have been explored preclinically to optimize ocular delivery, suggesting format-dependent translatability may be important for this class (Falcão et al., 2024).

Mechanism of Action  
Temsirolimus acts as a prototypical rapalog: it binds FKBP12 to form a gain-of-function complex that docks to the FKBP12-rapamycin binding (FRB) domain of mTOR and selectively inhibits mTORC1 signaling; mTORC2 is generally spared acutely, with potential indirect effects chronically depending on cellular context (Wang et al., 2022). mTORC1 normally phosphorylates TFEB on multiple serine residues, retaining it in the cytosol and preventing nuclear entry; when mTORC1 is inhibited, TFEB becomes dephosphorylated, translocates to the nucleus, and drives the CLEAR network that upregulates autophagy and lysosomal biogenesis genes (e.g., LAMP1), enhancing degradative capacity and organelle biogenesis (Falcão et al., 2025; Falcão et al., 2024). In RPE cells, POS phagocytosis engages mTORC1 transiently, but aged/AMD RPE exhibit enhanced mTORC1 activity that suppresses appropriate TFEB activation; rapamycin reverses this, promoting TFEB dephosphorylation, nuclear entry, GADD34 upregulation, and increased lysosomal mass, collectively reducing AFGs by approximately 30% in POS-challenged RPE (Falcão et al., 2024). The TFEB dependency has been functionally validated via TFEB gain-of-function, which markedly decreases AFGs in both preventive and “therapeutic” paradigms after lipofuscin-like material has already formed (Falcão et al., 2024). Pharmacologic relevance to mTOR pathway modulation beyond rapamycin was supported using INK-128 and other mTOR inhibitors, which replicated the AFG reduction and TFEB-lysosome signature (Falcão et al., 2024).

At the biochemical level, mTORC1 integrates amino acid signaling at the lysosomal surface via Ragulator-Rag GTPases and growth/energy cues via Rheb/AMPK, coordinating downstream phosphorylation of p70S6K and 4E-BP1 to activate translation while repressing catabolic programs including initiation of autophagy (partly by phosphorylating ULK1 at Ser757 and by blocking TFEB) (Johnson, 2013; Chang et al., 2022). In retinal tissues, mTOR inhibition is expected to relieve brakes on autophagy and lysosomal biogenesis; in diabetic retinopathy models, mTOR inhibition with rapamycin restored impaired lysosomal proteolysis by normalizing cathepsin L activity and autophagic flux, mechanistically consistent with TFEB-driven CLEAR network activation and improved lysosomal protease capacity (Wang et al., 2022). Although direct evidence for temsirolimus effects on RPE TFEB phosphorylation state, lysosomal acidification, or CTSD maturation is not available, the shared mechanism of FKBP12-dependent mTORC1 inhibition and the RPE-cell mTOR engagement demonstrated by temsirolimus (antiproliferative/anti-migratory, VEGF/PDGF suppression) support pathway perturbation in the correct cellular context (Liegl et al., 2014).

In the context of AMD pathophysiology, RPE lysosomal dysfunction and impaired clearance of POS-derived material drive lipofuscin accumulation and downstream toxicity; TFEB has emerged as a master regulator to restore lysosomal capacity, while AMD donor RPE show reduced cathepsin D and L levels/activities, highlighting protease insufficiency as a plausible node of therapeutic rescue (Falcão et al., 2025). Importantly, in POS-fed RPE, the rapamycin benefit is abolished by lysosomal protease inhibition or CTSD knockout, indicating that mTORC1 inhibition enhances clearance only when lysosomal protease function is preserved, and suggesting that concomitant strategies to support lysosomal acidification/protease maturation could be synergistic (Falcão et al., 2024). Finally, some reports have suggested low immunoreactivity of mTORC1/2 components in RPE, but this observation contrasts with multiple functional studies demonstrating mTORC1 signaling in RPE during POS handling and aging; taken together, functional responsiveness to mTOR inhibitors in RPE likely depends on model system and detection sensitivity (Wang et al., 2022; Falcão et al., 2024).

In parallel, transcriptomic or targeted RT-qPCR panels for CLEAR genes will validate TFEB program engagement (Falcão et al., 2024).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Eculizumab (Soliris, Alexion) is a humanized IgG monoclonal antibody derived from the murine anti–human C5 antibody m5G1 via CDR grafting and human framework engineering to reduce immunogenicity and extend serum half-life, designed to bind complement component C5 with high affinity and sterically prevent its cleavage by C5 convertases into C5a and C5b (thereby blocking terminal pathway activation and MAC assembly) (Park et al., 2019; Troutbeck et al., 2012; Yehoshua et al., 2014; Park et al., 2021). It belongs to the class of complement inhibitors that directly target an effector protein (C5) at the convergence of the classical, lectin, and alternative pathways, in contrast to upstream amplification-targeting agents (e.g., C3 or factor D inhibitors) (Park et al., 2019; Tzoumas et al., 2023). Systemically administered eculizumab has established clinical utility in complement-mediated hematologic and renal disorders, including paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria and atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome, and more recently generalized myasthenia gravis, reflecting a mature pharmacology and a well-characterized risk profile centered on increased susceptibility to encapsulated organisms (notably meningococcal infection) due to terminal pathway blockade (Park et al., 2019; Yehoshua et al., 2014).

Within ophthalmology, the terminal complement pathway is an attractive target for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) and geographic atrophy (GA) because C5a is a proinflammatory anaphylatoxin detected in drusen that can drive leukocyte recruitment and VEGF induction in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), and C5b nucleates formation of the membrane attack complex (MAC, C5b–C9), which accumulates with age and AMD in Bruch’s membrane and choriocapillaris and can lyse or sub-lytically activate choroidal endothelial and RPE cells (Kassa et al., 2019). The class of C5 inhibitors therefore aims to reduce both inflammatory signaling (via C5a) and cytolytic/proinflammatory MAC effects while preserving upstream opsonization and some host-defense functions mediated by C3b, potentially retaining aspects of immune competence relative to C3 inhibition (Halawa et al., 2021; Park et al., 2019).

Therapeutic History  
Approved indications and systemic pharmacology  
Eculizumab is FDA/EMA approved for paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria and atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome, where weight-based intravenous regimens achieve sustained trough serum concentrations and complete inhibition of hemolytic activity by blocking C5 cleavage; these regimens produce serum levels > 35 μg/mL and complete systemic C5 functional blockade, but require meningococcal vaccination to mitigate Neisseria risk inherent to terminal complement inhibition (Park et al., 2019; Yehoshua et al., 2014). In other complementopathies, clinical experience has highlighted a mechanism-consequent shift of pathology upstream (e.g., C3-loading and extravascular hemolysis in PNH under C5 blockade), underscoring that C5 inhibition leaves C3 activation intact (Hammadi et al., 2023).

Clinical investigation in geographic atrophy of dry AMD  
Eculizumab was investigated in the prospective, randomized, double-masked, single-center Phase 2 COMPLETE study that enrolled 30 participants with GA (primary cohort) plus an intermediate AMD/drusen cohort, randomized 2:1 to intravenous eculizumab versus saline over 24 weeks (with follow-up to 52 weeks) (Yehoshua et al., 2014). Two dosing regimens were tested: a low-dose arm (600 mg weekly × 4, then 900 mg every 2 weeks through week 24) and a high-dose arm with higher induction and maintenance dosing; all patients received meningococcal vaccination prior to first infusion (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Patel et al., 2022). Pharmacokinetically, systemic exposure and target engagement were confirmed: eculizumab concentrations were measurable at all assessed time points (mean ~ 65–189 μg/mL in low-dose and ~ 122–259 μg/mL in high-dose cohorts), with plasma C5 activity reduced to < 9% by week 1 and < 1% by week 2, indicating complete systemic terminal complement blockade sustained through treatment (Yehoshua et al., 2014).

Despite robust systemic pharmacodynamics, COMPLETE detected no effect on GA progression: at 26 weeks the change in square-root–transformed GA area was 0.19 ± 0.12 mm in eculizumab-treated eyes versus 0.18 ± 0.15 mm with placebo (P = 0.96), and at 52 weeks both arms exhibited ~ 0.37 mm enlargement (P ≈ 0.93), effectively excluding a large treatment effect (> 55% slowing) in this cohort (Yehoshua et al., 2014). Drusen volume endpoints in the intermediate AMD cohort were also negative (no participant achieved a 50% reduction), and fellow-eye analyses mirrored primary-eye results (Patel et al., 2022; Yehoshua et al., 2014). Visual function showed no durable benefit: a 26-week letter gain difference favoring eculizumab was attributed to a single outlier in placebo, and by 52 weeks there was no between-group difference; pooled estimates across small RCTs rated the certainty of BCVA effects as low-to-very-low with confidence intervals overlapping no effect (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Tzoumas et al., 2023). Safety was acceptable in the trial: no drug-related serious adverse events were identified through 52 weeks, and no eyes converted to neovascular AMD during the study; however, systemic C5 blockade requires vaccination and vigilance for meningococcal infection, and an independent systemic anti-C5 AMD trial was terminated early due to uncertainty about risk/benefit in light of reported meningococcal infections in real-world eculizumab users (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Tzoumas et al., 2023).

Interpretations from COMPLETE and subsequent reviews point to several plausible explanations for the null result: inadequate intraocular/RPE target engagement with systemic dosing due to blood–retinal and Bruch’s barriers; the possibility that C5 is the wrong target in GA given genetic associations that more strongly implicate proximal complement components (e.g., C3, CFH) rather than terminal pathway constituents; the short on-treatment window (24 weeks) and small sample size; and the biological reality that C5 inhibition preserves upstream C3a/C3b biology, which may continue to drive pathology (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Halawa et al., 2021; Hammadi et al., 2023; Tzoumas et al., 2023).

Comparative C5 and complement-targeting experience in AMD  
Intravitreal C5 inhibition has produced divergent results. LFG316 (tesidolumab), an anti-C5 monoclonal antibody administered intravitreally, failed to alter GA lesion growth or visual outcomes in a randomized phase 2 trial (Halawa et al., 2021; Park et al., 2019). By contrast, avacincaptad pegol (Zimura), an intravitreal C5 aptamer, reduced GA growth rates by approximately 27–30% over 12–18 months in pivotal trials, leading to FDA approval, although potential increased risk of macular neovascularization has been signaled and requires ongoing pharmacovigilance (Patel et al., 2022; Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023; Tzoumas et al., 2023). Upstream targeting at C3 with intravitreal pegcetacoplan (SYFOVRE) significantly slowed GA enlargement in phase 2–3 programs and achieved regulatory approval, but at the cost of increased rates of conversion to exudative AMD and, in the postmarketing setting, reports of occlusive retinal vasculitis, highlighting a target-dependent safety trade-off between efficacy and pro-angiogenic/immune-privilege perturbation risks (Halawa et al., 2021; Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023; Qin et al., 2024). Alternative-pathway inhibition via factor D (lampalizumab) produced a phase 2 signal but failed in two phase 3 trials, suggesting that partial pathway blockade may be insufficient in GA (Piri & Kaplan, 2023; Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023).

Taken together, these data place systemic eculizumab among C5-directed strategies where local delivery has demonstrated anatomic efficacy in GA, whereas systemic delivery has not, and they highlight that complement modulation can slow atrophy progression without improving visual function and may introduce target- and route-specific risks such as neovascularization or serious infection (Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023; Tzoumas et al., 2023).

Mechanism of Action  
Complement cascade biology and eculizumab target engagement  
Complement activation arises via classical, lectin, and alternative pathways, converging at the generation of C3 convertases that cleave C3 into C3a (anaphylatoxin) and C3b (opsonin/convertase component), with amplification by the alternative pathway accounting for the majority (80–90%) of downstream MAC generation in physiologic and pathologic settings (Tzoumas et al., 2023). C5 convertases (C4b2a3b for classical/lectin and C3bBbC3b for alternative pathway) cleave C5 into C5a, a potent anaphylatoxin that recruits/activates myeloid cells and stimulates RPE to produce VEGF and proinflammatory cytokines, and C5b, which seeds assembly of the terminal membrane attack complex (C5b–C9) on nearby membranes (Tzoumas et al., 2023; Kassa et al., 2019). Eculizumab binds C5 to prevent convertase-mediated cleavage, thereby abrogating both C5a generation and MAC formation independent of the initiating pathway; this preserves upstream C3 activation (C3a/C3b) and the alternative-pathway amplification loop while blunting terminal effector functions (Park et al., 2019; Halawa et al., 2021).

Ocular and RPE relevance of C5 and MAC  
Multiple lines of evidence implicate terminal pathway effectors in AMD pathophysiology at the RPE–choriocapillaris interface. Histopathology shows increasing MAC deposition with aging and AMD in Bruch’s membrane and the choriocapillaris; sub-lytic MAC on choroidal endothelial cells triggers pro-angiogenic/proteolytic responses (VEGF, MMPs), while high-level deposition can induce lysis of choroidal endothelial cells and bystander injury contributing to RPE atrophy (Kassa et al., 2019). C5a is present in drusen and is a strong inflammatory mediator that can recruit immune cells and induce VEGF release from RPE, linking terminal pathway activation to both atrophic and neovascular processes relevant to the AMD spectrum (Kassa et al., 2019). Additional experimental work demonstrates that sub-lytic C5b-9 can alter RPE function in ways consistent with AMD, including stress responses and secretory changes, reinforcing that terminal complement activation can be injurious to the RPE even in the absence of frank lysis (Park et al., 2019).

Complement production and regulation in the eye—and systemic versus local contributions  
Complement proteins are synthesized predominantly by the liver and circulate systemically, but they are also produced locally within ocular tissues (retina, RPE, choroid), with local activation and regulation shaped by cell-intrinsic complement regulatory proteins (e.g., CFH, CD46, CD59) and by oxidative stress effects that reduce cell-surface complement inhibition on RPE (Tzoumas et al., 2023; van Lookeren Campagne et al., 2016). Several studies highlight local complement expression and activation in retinal cells and macrophages, as well as increased local complement turnover preceding clinical disease, supporting the concept of an ocular complement “microenvironment” that can be dysregulated independent of systemic levels (Patel et al., 2022; Piri & Kaplan, 2023). Conversely, transcriptomic mapping suggests that posterior-pole tissues have limited local transcription of lectin and terminal pathway components (except C5 and C7), implying reliance on systemic sources for some terminal pathway proteins, which in principle could make systemic C5 blockade effective if sufficient intraocular penetration and target engagement are achieved (Troutbeck et al., 2012). These seemingly conflicting observations are reconciled by recognizing that both local production and systemic supply contribute to ocular complement biology, and that their relative importance likely varies by compartment (RPE, choriocapillaris, sub-RPE space), disease stage, and barrier integrity.

Genetic and biomarker context for C5 targeting in AMD  
GWAS and biomarker studies have repeatedly implicated complement dysregulation in AMD susceptibility and progression, including associations at CFH, C3, C2/CFB, CFI, and C9 loci, and elevated systemic and ocular concentrations of complement activation products (C3a, C5a, MAC) in AMD patients (Dascalu et al., 2024). However, the genetic signal is stronger and more consistent for proximal regulators (e.g., CFH, C3) than for C5, and at least one analysis noted C3 risk alleles do not necessarily correlate with GA progression (and in some contexts associated with decreased progression), emphasizing the complexity of translating susceptibility signals to progression biology and target selection in late AMD (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Halawa et al., 2021). Mechanistically, C5 blockade leaves upstream C3a/C3b biology intact; in extra-ocular diseases this can unmask C3-related pathophysiology under C5 inhibition, illustrating a general limitation of terminal pathway-only targeting (Hammadi et al., 2023). In GA, this implies that C3a/C3b-driven processes—chemoattraction, opsonization, and immune modulation—could continue in the outer retina/RPE even under complete C5 suppression, potentially blunting the benefit of C5-only therapy (Halawa et al., 2021; Tzoumas et al., 2023).

Therapeutic delivery constraints to ocular complement modulation with systemic C5 blockade  
Large biologics such as eculizumab face formidable physical barriers to ocular penetration, including the inner and outer blood–retina barriers and Bruch’s membrane/RPE tight junctions, whose permeability declines with increasing molecular weight and hydrophilicity (a profile characteristic of IgG antibodies), making intraocular access by systemic dosing uncertain without active transport mechanisms (Hammadi et al., 2023; Yehoshua et al., 2014). This is the most straightforward explanation for COMPLETE’s combination of complete systemic pharmacodynamic suppression with no effect on lesion enlargement: the effective intraocular concentration of antibody at relevant RPE–choroid interfaces was likely insufficient to inhibit terminal complement activation locally, a conclusion echoed by the trial investigators (Yehoshua et al., 2014).

Expected Effect  
Proposed pharmacologic and cellular effect  
Under the working hypothesis, systemic eculizumab would reduce MAC formation on RPE and choroidal endothelial surfaces and diminish C5a-driven inflammatory signaling, thereby protecting RPE cellular homeostasis and the RPE–choriocapillaris unit from complement-mediated injury and slowing expansion of GA lesions (Kassa et al., 2019; Park et al., 2019). Mechanistically, suppression of MAC would be expected to decrease lytic and sub-lytic injury to choroidal endothelial cells and RPE, attenuating downstream induction of VEGF and MMPs, and limiting bystander tissue damage around atrophic borders where complement activation is thought to be active (Tzoumas et al., 2023; Kassa et al., 2019). Reducing C5a generation could blunt recruitment and activation of myeloid cells and RPE proinflammatory cytokine production, decreasing local inflammatory amplification in the outer retina (Tzoumas et al., 2023; Kassa et al., 2019).

Expression and target presence in relevant cells/tissues  
C5 and terminal pathway components are present in the ocular compartments relevant to GA pathobiology: choriocapillaris/Bruch’s membrane deposition of MAC is well documented and increases with age and AMD, and C5a is detected within drusen; RPE-derived complement regulators (e.g., CD59) and choroidal endothelial susceptibility to MAC are described, establishing both target and downstream effectors within the disease-relevant tissues (Kassa et al., 2019). Complement components and regulators are expressed in retina, RPE, and choroid, with transcriptomic data indicating relatively higher choroidal expression and limited local transcription of some terminal components (except C5 and C7), consistent with both local and systemic sources contributing substrate for terminal pathway assembly (Troutbeck et al., 2012; Tzoumas et al., 2023).

Translational and clinical outcome expectations  
At the disease level, a therapy that meaningfully reduces local terminal complement activation in GA should slow the rate of GA lesion enlargement measured on fundus autofluorescence (FAF) and/or SD-OCT, endpoints accepted by the FDA/NEI and standard across GA trials; functional outcomes such as BCVA and low-luminance VA typically lag structural changes and may not improve even when lesion growth is slowed (Dascalu et al., 2024; Qin et al., 2024). In COMPLETE, these endpoints were precisely those evaluated; the absence of any measurable effect on square-root GA area at 26 and 52 weeks indicates that, at the tested systemic dosing regimens, eculizumab did not achieve sufficient intraocular target engagement to translate the mechanistic rationale into clinical benefit (Yehoshua et al., 2014).

Reasons for divergence between expected and observed effects  
Three non-exclusive explanations align with the totality of evidence:

  • Inadequate intraocular bioavailability from systemic dosing. Antibody size and hydrophilicity, combined with blood–retina and RPE–Bruch’s barriers, likely prevented sufficient drug from reaching the RPE–choriocapillaris compartment to inhibit local terminal pathway activation, despite verified systemic C5 suppression (Hammadi et al., 2023; Yehoshua et al., 2014; Tzoumas et al., 2023).

  • Target selection may be suboptimal for GA biology. The stronger genetic and pathophysiologic evidence for proximal complement dysregulation (e.g., C3, CFH) and the preservation of upstream activation under C5 blockade mean that C5-only inhibition may not adequately suppress the complement-driven processes that sustain GA border expansion, as supported by the comparatively stronger clinical signals with C3 inhibition and mixed-to-positive signals with intravitreal C5 inhibition (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Halawa et al., 2021; Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023).

  • Trial limitations. The COMPLETE cohort was small and on-treatment duration was six months, which may be insufficient to observe smaller effects on GA growth; however, confidence intervals excluded large effects, and lack of any trend over 52 weeks reduces the likelihood that longer dosing would have changed the outcome meaningfully (Yehoshua et al., 2014).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
  • Strong mechanistic rationale for terminal pathway blockade in AMD: C5a is proinflammatory and detected in drusen; MAC accumulates at the RPE–choriocapillaris interface with age/AMD and can injure choroidal endothelium and RPE via lytic and sub-lytic mechanisms, linking C5 effector functions directly to AMD pathophysiology (Kassa et al., 2019). Blocking C5 suppresses both MAC and C5a, targeting inflammatory and cytolytic arms while leaving upstream C3-mediated opsonization intact, an immunologic advantage over C3 blockade (Halawa et al., 2021; Park et al., 2019).

  • Mature systemic pharmacology with demonstrated ability to completely suppress plasma C5 activity at well-tolerated doses, including in AMD patients, making systemic development logistically straightforward and with known requirements (e.g., meningococcal vaccination) (Yehoshua et al., 2014).

  • Practical systemic-delivery advantages: single systemic therapy treats both eyes simultaneously and avoids intravitreal injection–related ocular risks (endophthalmitis, IOP spikes), which have nontrivial incidence in chronic IVT regimens (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Tzoumas et al., 2023).

  • External validation within the class: intravitreal C5 inhibition (avacincaptad pegol) has replicated GA-slowing effects in phase 2/3 programs, supporting the therapeutic value of suppressing terminal pathway activity in the outer retina if adequate local exposure is achieved (Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023).

Limitations  
  • Lack of efficacy in the definitive systemic eculizumab GA study. COMPLETE showed no reduction in GA lesion growth at 26 or 52 weeks despite complete systemic C5 blockade and adequate serum exposure, effectively excluding a large treatment effect and arguing strongly against systemic eculizumab as a viable GA therapy (Yehoshua et al., 2014).

  • Ocular pharmacokinetic barrier. The most parsimonious explanation for the COMPLETE result is inadequate intraocular target engagement from systemic dosing due to the blood–retina/RPE–Bruch’s barriers and the large size/hydrophilicity of IgG, an inherent limitation of systemic antibody delivery to the sub-RPE/choroidal compartment (Hammadi et al., 2023; Yehoshua et al., 2014).

  • Target-level uncertainties. Genetic and biomarker studies more consistently implicate proximal complement dysregulation (CFH/C3) than C5 in AMD susceptibility; moreover, C5 inhibition preserves upstream C3a/C3b activity, which may continue to drive border-zone inflammation and remodeling in GA (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Dascalu et al., 2024; Halawa et al., 2021). Clinical comparisons reinforce this: upstream C3 inhibition has produced larger and more consistent anatomic effects (with important safety trade-offs), whereas anti-C5 trials are split—systemic eculizumab negative; IVT LFG316 negative; IVT avacincaptad positive—pointing to delivery and target–context dependencies (Halawa et al., 2021; Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023).

  • Systemic safety constraints. While COMPLETE itself reported no drug-related serious adverse events over one year, terminal complement blockade carries a class risk of meningococcal infection requiring vaccination and risk mitigation; at least one planned AMD systemic anti-C5 trial was terminated early due to uncertainty regarding the systemic infection risk/benefit in this population (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Tzoumas et al., 2023).

  • Limited translatability of systemic complement activation to local disease control. Although systemic complement activation correlates with AMD and disease stage in several studies, the relative importance of local versus systemic complement sources—and the ability of systemic blockade to suppress complement activity at the RPE–choriocapillaris interface—is unresolved and likely unfavorable for large biologics, reducing the mechanistic plausibility of systemic C5 blockade for GA (Hammadi et al., 2023; Park et al., 2019).

Risk–benefit and competitive landscape assessment  
Eculizumab’s negative randomized, controlled data in GA, in the face of confirmed systemic pharmacodynamics, places a high bar against further systemic development for this indication, a conclusion explicitly drawn by the COMPLETE investigators who noted the linearity of GA growth and lack of signal as making additional systemic investigations with eculizumab unlikely (Yehoshua et al., 2014). In the evolving complement-therapeutic landscape, local (intravitreal) complement inhibitors have achieved regulatory approval (C3 inhibitor pegcetacoplan and C5 aptamer avacincaptad pegol), demonstrating that complement modulation can slow GA progression when adequate ocular exposure is achieved, albeit without functional vision improvement and with target-dependent safety liabilities (e.g., increased conversion to exudative AMD observed particularly with C3 inhibition) (Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023; Qin et al., 2024). Against this backdrop, systemic eculizumab offers no efficacy advantage, carries systemic infection risk and costs, and fails the core requirement of achieving ocular target engagement necessary for GA modification.

Operationally, even if one hypothesized that higher systemic dosing, longer exposure, or patient stratification could rescue efficacy, several facts weigh against that strategy: COMPLETE’s pharmacodynamics confirmed near-complete systemic C5 suppression within two weeks; genetic analyses within the trial found no association between at-risk alleles and GA growth or treatment response; and extended follow-up to a year showed no divergence in growth rates (Yehoshua et al., 2014). Moreover, retinal pharmacokinetics and barrier biology make it unlikely that increasing systemic doses would proportionally increase intraocular concentrations to therapeutic levels without exacerbating systemic risks (Hammadi et al., 2023). In addition, C5 may not be the optimal node for GA progression biology in many patients, given preserved upstream activity and the complex contributions of C3a/C3b, opsonization, and local complement production that may continue to drive border-zone degeneration independent of MAC inhibition (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Halawa et al., 2021; Piri & Kaplan, 2023).

Recommendation  
Based on the aggregate mechanistic, translational, and clinical evidence, eculizumab (systemic C5 inhibition) does not have compelling potential as a repurposed therapy for dry AMD/GA. The drug has a clear and relevant mechanism and an acceptable short-term tolerability profile in older adults, but it fails to slow GA lesion growth in a randomized, controlled trial despite complete systemic target engagement, and there are strong mechanistic and pharmacokinetic reasons to expect insufficient intraocular exposure with systemic delivery (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Hammadi et al., 2023). The therapeutic hypothesis—reducing MAC on RPE/choriocapillaris to preserve tissue integrity and slow atrophy—is supported conceptually and by local C5 inhibition successes; however, achieving that biology in vivo appears to require intraocular delivery or targeting upstream nodes, neither of which is compatible with systemic eculizumab administration (Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023; Halawa et al., 2021).

If complement-targeted strategies remain a program priority, resources should pivot to modalities with demonstrated ocular target engagement and anatomic efficacy (intravitreal C3 or C5 agents) while carefully managing known safety trade-offs (e.g., neovascularization risk), and to biomarker-driven questions (e.g., whether baseline low-luminance visual acuity deficit—correlated with faster GA growth in COMPLETE—can enrich for patients who derive greater anatomic benefit) (Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023; Tzoumas et al., 2023; Yehoshua et al., 2014). For systemic complement modulation in AMD more broadly, alternative targets with better ocular PK profiles (e.g., small-molecule systemic alternative-pathway inhibitors) and rigorous ocular target-engagement measurements would be required to justify late-stage development, but systemic C5 blockade with eculizumab itself should not be advanced further for GA (Hammadi et al., 2023; Tzoumas et al., 2023; Park et al., 2019).

In summary, while the mechanistic logic for terminal complement inhibition in AMD is robust, the totality of evidence argues against systemic eculizumab as a viable candidate to slow GA progression, and the development program should discontinue pursuit of this repurposing in favor of locally delivered complement inhibitors or alternative mechanisms better suited to the ocular compartment and GA pathobiology (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Eltanexor (also known as KPT-8602, MedKoo 406829) is a synthetic small‐molecule compound belonging to the class of “selective inhibitors of nuclear export” (SINE). These agents were developed by medicinal chemists to target the nuclear export protein exportin-1 (XPO1, also known as CRM1), which mediates the transport of a wide range of proteins from the nucleus to the cytoplasm. Eltanexor, like its predecessor Selinexor (KPT-330), functions by binding within the nuclear export signal (NES) recognition site of XPO1—most notably involving interaction with a conserved cysteine residue (Cys528) in XPO1’s NES‐binding pocket—and thereby preventing export of many regulatory proteins. However, Eltanexor has been engineered with modifications that confer improved tolerability along with oral bioavailability and a favorable pharmacokinetic profile, making it an attractive candidate for repurposing. SINE compounds have been extensively studied in oncology, where their ability to cause the nuclear retention of tumor suppressors has led to approved indications in certain hematological malignancies; accordingly, the synthetic origin of Eltanexor is rooted in efforts to optimize the drug‐like properties of early XPO1 inhibitors and to improve their clinical safety profile (Newell et al., 2024).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, the SINE class has been primarily associated with anticancer applications. Early compounds such as leptomycin B (LMB) were the first to demonstrate that inhibition of XPO1 could induce nuclear retention of proteins; however, issues with toxicity limited their clinical utility. Subsequent development efforts led to the creation of SINE compounds including Selinexor (KPT-330) and more recently Eltanexor (KPT-8602), which have undergone both preclinical and early-phase clinical trials in various cancer types. In these settings, XPO1 inhibition was shown to result in the nuclear accumulation of proteins that typically support cell survival, thereby selectively promoting apoptosis in cancer cells (Newell et al., 2024; Tang et al., 2025). Outside the field of oncology, mechanistic studies have indicated that inhibiting nuclear export can also impact proteins critically involved in autophagy regulation and lysosomal homeostasis. For instance, preclinical work in neuronal and glioblastoma models has shown that XPO1 inhibitors trigger nuclear retention of the master autophagy regulator TFEB, thereby enhancing autophagic flux and lysosomal biogenesis (Abokyi & Tse, 2025; Tang et al., 2025). To date, however, there is no published study that directly employs Eltanexor or other XPO1 inhibitors as therapeutic agents for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or related retinal degenerative conditions. In retinal research, extensive efforts have focused on modulating TFEB activity through alternative strategies—such as using trehalose, metformin, or genetic approaches—to restore lysosomal function in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells (Ghosh et al., 2024; Abokyi & Tse, 2025). Although the direct use of XPO1 inhibitors in RPE or dry AMD models has not been experimentally demonstrated, the established efficacy of SINE compounds in other contexts of neurodegeneration and autophagy dysregulation provides a compelling rationale for their repurposing in ocular diseases (Abokyi & Tse, 2025; Falcão et al., 2025).

Mechanism of Action:  
Under normal cellular conditions, XPO1 mediates the nuclear export of a diverse set of proteins by recognizing nuclear export signals (NES) present on cargo proteins. One critical cargo is the transcription factor TFEB, which regulates the expression of lysosomal hydrolases and autophagy-related genes by binding to CLEAR (coordinated lysosomal expression and regulation) elements within gene promoters. In nutrient-rich or stress-dysregulated states, TFEB undergoes phosphorylation by kinases such as mTORC1, resulting in cytoplasmic sequestration mediated by binding to 14-3-3 proteins and subsequent export from the nucleus via XPO1 (Pan & Valapala, 2022; La Spina et al., 2021; Li, 2018). Eltanexor’s mechanism of action is to bind within the NES-binding pocket of XPO1 and disrupt its interaction with such cargo proteins. The inhibition is achieved through covalent and slowly reversible binding to the Cys528 residue in XPO1, thereby preventing the nuclear export of target proteins. When export is blocked, TFEB (and likely its paralog TFE3) accumulates in the nucleus where it is free to activate transcription of CLEAR network genes. The resulting upregulation of lysosomal genes leads to increased lysosomal biogenesis, a lowering of lysosomal pH, and enhanced activation of hydrolases such as cathepsin D—all of which are critical to maintaining proteostasis and clearing damaged proteins and organelles (Abokyi & Tse, 2025; Pan & Valapala, 2022). Published data in glioblastoma models have shown that other XPO1 inhibitors such as Selinexor induce this type of nuclear trapping of TFEB, which correlates with an increase in autophagic flux and enhanced clearance mechanisms (Tang et al., 2025). Importantly, unlike pharmacological treatments that rely on mTOR inhibition (which can have widespread metabolic effects), the SINE approach works directly at the level of nuclear export, thereby selectively increasing TFEB activity independent of upstream mTOR/AKT signaling (Abokyi & Tse, 2025; Li, 2018).

Expected Effect in Dry AMD:  
Dry age-related macular degeneration is characterized by dysfunction of the RPE, resulting in diminished autophagic flux, accumulation of lipofuscin, and impaired degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (POS). In healthy RPE cells, nuclear TFEB orchestrates a transcriptional program that maintains lysosomal homeostasis by upregulating genes involved in lysosomal biogenesis, acidification, and cargo degradation. However, in aging and diseased RPE, TFEB becomes increasingly phosphorylated and sequestered in the cytoplasm, leading to reduced CLEAR network activity (Ghosh et al., 2024; Abokyi & Tse, 2025). The hypothesis behind repurposing Eltanexor for dry AMD is that by inhibiting XPO1 in RPE cells, the drug will promote nuclear retention of TFEB and TFE3. This nuclear accumulation is expected to drive upregulation of lysosomal gene expression, resulting in the restoration of lysosomal acidification and proteolytic capacity, particularly cathepsin D activity. An effective increase in autophagic flux and lysosomal biogenesis should aid in the degradation of accumulated toxic compounds such as lipofuscin and undegraded POS debris, ultimately improving RPE function and potentially slowing or reversing progression of dry AMD (Ghosh et al., 2024; Abokyi & Tse, 2025). In addition, preclinical studies in neurodegeneration and retinal models have demonstrated that enhancing TFEB activity—whether by trehalose treatment, gene therapy approaches, or by upstream modulation of kinases such as AKT2—can protect cells from oxidative and proteotoxic stress (Abokyi & Tse, 2025; Ghosh et al., 2024). Although direct evidence in RPE cells is still pending, the large body of mechanistic work linking nuclear TFEB accumulation to improved lysosomal function provides a strong rationale for expecting similar outcomes with Eltanexor in the context of dry AMD.

Overall Evaluation:  
Eltanexor presents several attractive features as a potential therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, especially given its novel mechanism of action and its ability to modulate a fundamental cellular process that is impaired in the disease. One of the major strengths of Eltanexor lies in its targeted inhibition of XPO1, which has been well validated in oncology and neurodegeneration studies as a means to induce nuclear retention of regulatory proteins. By preventing the export of TFEB and TFE3, Eltanexor is expected to allow these key transcription factors to reactivate the CLEAR network, thereby restoring lysosomal function, lowering lysosomal pH, and boosting the activity of cathepsin D-mediated degradation. This mechanism is particularly compelling for dry AMD because RPE cell dysfunction in the disease has been closely linked to defective autophagy and impaired clearance of toxic aggregates (Ghosh et al., 2024; Abokyi & Tse, 2025). Moreover, the proposed therapeutic approach bypasses some of the limitations of mTOR-based interventions, as it directly affects nucleocytoplasmic transport rather than broadly inhibiting upstream signaling pathways. This specificity provides an additional level of mechanistic precision that could translate into a better safety profile for chronic applications in an aging population.

Nevertheless, several weaknesses and challenges must be acknowledged. First, while there is abundant evidence that XPO1 inhibitors such as Selinexor induce TFEB nuclear retention and autophagy in glioblastoma and other non-ocular models (Tang et al., 2025), there is currently a lack of direct preclinical data evaluating Eltanexor or related compounds in retinal pigment epithelial cells or in animal models of dry AMD. The extrapolation of data from cancer and neuronal models to RPE cells, while mechanistically plausible, remains to be experimentally validated. Second, because XPO1 regulates the nuclear export of a wide range of proteins—not only TFEB and TFE3—there is a potential for off-target effects that could disrupt other cellular processes. This issue is particularly critical in the context of chronic administration in elderly patients, who may be more susceptible to systemic side effects. Third, the pharmacodynamic properties required to achieve effective nuclear retention of TFEB in the RPE may differ from those established in oncology trials. For example, the concentration of Eltanexor required to affect TFEB nuclear localization and lysosomal gene expression in RPE cells might be higher than that used in cancer models, necessitating further optimization of dosing and delivery strategies. Finally, while the oral bioavailability and existing Phase I safety data of Eltanexor support its clinical feasibility (Tang et al., 2025), localized and retina-specific delivery might ultimately prove necessary to maximize its therapeutic window and minimize systemic exposure.

In summary, Eltanexor’s mechanism of inhibiting XPO1 to promote nuclear retention of TFEB/TFE3 aligns very well with emerging therapeutic strategies aimed at correcting lysosomal dysfunction in dry AMD. The extensive literature on the role of TFEB in regulating autophagy and lysosomal biogenesis in RPE cells provides a strong mechanistic foundation for this approach (Ghosh et al., 2024; Abokyi & Tse, 2025). Additionally, the demonstrated ability of XPO1 inhibitors to induce autophagy in other preclinical models (Abokyi & Tse, 2025; Tang et al., 2025) reinforces the potential for repurposing Eltanexor in an ocular setting. However, to move forward, it will be essential to generate direct experimental evidence in primary RPE cultures and in vivo dry AMD models to verify that Eltanexor indeed promotes TFEB nuclear retention, enhances CLEAR network activity, lowers lysosomal pH, and increases cathepsin D–mediated cargo degradation in the retinal environment. Addressing these issues will not only validate the therapeutic concept but will also help to optimize dosing, delivery, and safety profiles tailored for the treatment of dry AMD.

Overall, while Eltanexor shows promise as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD owing to its targeted mechanism of action and favorable preclinical attributes in other disease models, further studies focused explicitly on retinal cell biology and AMD pathology are imperative before clinical translation can be considered. The strength of the candidate lies in its mechanistic specificity and the well-established role of TFEB/TFE3 in lysosomal function, whereas the main weaknesses revolve around the current lack of direct evidence in the target system and potential off-target effects associated with global nuclear export inhibition (Abokyi & Tse, 2025; Pan & Valapala, 2022; Ghosh et al., 2024).
