Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Recombinant human pro-cathepsin D (rhCTSD), as exemplified by R&D Systems product 1869-CD, is a bioengineered form of a naturally occurring lysosomal aspartyl protease that is synthesized as an inactive precursor (pro-cathepsin D) (Sharif, 2015, pp. 60–64). This therapeutic candidate belongs to the enzyme replacement therapy (ERT) class, a category of biotherapeutics developed to supplement or correct deficient lysosomal enzymes in various disorders. The natural cathepsin D enzyme is normally produced and processed intracellularly through the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and Golgi apparatus, undergoing critical post-translational modifications—including the removal of the N-terminal signal peptide, glycosylation, and addition of a mannose-6-phosphate (M6P) tag—that are essential for its subsequent targeting to the lysosome (Sharif, 2015, pp. 60–64). The recombinant version is produced under conditions aimed at ensuring high purity and biological activity conforming to GMP standards, thus making it an attractive candidate for repurposing in conditions where lysosomal proteolytic capacity is compromised. The candidate has been designed in the context of neurodegenerative and lysosomal storage disorders, where enzyme supplementation has been shown to restore proteolytic flux by directly replacing a rate-limiting hydrolase (Bassal et al., 2021; Marques et al., 2020).

Therapeutic History:  
Enzyme replacement therapies have been a cornerstone in the management of several lysosomal storage disorders since the early 1990s, with the first approved treatment for Gaucher’s disease setting a precedent for this therapeutic strategy (Saftig, 2005; Lerussi et al., 2025). In the specific case of cathepsin D, recombinant forms have been employed in preclinical models of neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis (NCL) and other neurodegenerative lysosomal storage disorders, where the administration of exogenous pro-cathepsin D was able to rescue functional deficits associated with genetic CTSD deficiency (Bassal et al., 2021; Marques et al., 2020). Animal studies using CTSD-deficient mouse models have demonstrated that both intracranial and localized injections of recombinant CTSD can correct defects in proteolysis and autophagy, leading to improvements in neuropathological markers and even extending lifespan in treated animals (Bassal et al., 2021; Liu, 2021; Marques et al., 2020). Although most of these studies have focused on neurodegenerative conditions of the central nervous system, similar principles of lysosomal dysfunction apply to retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells, which are critical for maintaining retinal homeostasis in the context of age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (Klettner et al., 2013). Notably, the literature suggests that cathepsin D is highly expressed in RPE cells and plays a vital role in the degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (POS), with its deficiency or reduced function being implicated in the accumulation of toxic deposits and drusen formation—a hallmark of dry AMD (Klettner et al., 2013; Sharif, 2015). Despite the absence of direct clinical trials in dry AMD using rhCTSD, the extensive preclinical evidence from both neurodegenerative and retinal disease models provides a compelling rationale for exploring the repurposing of this enzyme replacement strategy in dry AMD (Liu, 2021; Marques et al., 2020).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, the mechanism of action of recombinant human pro-cathepsin D is rooted in its ability to restore lysosomal proteolytic function, which is often impaired in disease states such as dry AMD. Under physiological conditions, pro-cathepsin D is synthesized in the rough ER as an inactive precursor that undergoes several post-translational modifications, including the cleavage of an N-terminal signal peptide, N-linked glycosylation, and critical mannose-6-phosphate (M6P) tagging in the Golgi apparatus (Sharif, 2015). The M6P tag facilitates the binding of pro-cathepsin D to M6P receptors within the trans-Golgi network (TGN), directing the enzyme to late endosomes and, eventually, to lysosomes where the acidic environment promotes its maturation into its active form (Sharif, 2015). Once active, cathepsin D contributes to the degradation of a wide range of substrates, including the photoreceptor outer segments in RPE cells, thereby playing a crucial role in maintaining cellular homeostasis and preventing the accumulation of deleterious debris that can lead to drusen formation (Klettner et al., 2013). The proposed therapeutic strategy involves subretinal delivery of the recombinant enzyme to bypass systemic limitations such as the blood-brain barrier and to achieve localized uptake into RPE cells via the M6P receptor-mediated endocytosis pathway (Liu, 2021; Marques et al., 2020; Sharif, 2015). Once internalized, the enzyme can replenish endogenous levels of cathepsin D, thereby enhancing autophagic flux and proteolytic degradation processes that are essential for the health and function of the RPE (Klettner et al., 2013; Sharif, 2015). This targeted mechanism is a direct, molecularly specific approach that aims not only to compensate for maturation defects in the enzyme but also to overcome upstream acidification abnormalities that often hinder proper activation of endogenously produced cathepsin D in aging RPE cells (Liu, 2021; Marques et al., 2020; Sharif, 2015).

Expected Effect:  
The anticipated outcome of employing recombinant human pro-cathepsin D for the treatment of dry AMD is multifaceted. First, the subretinal administration of the enzyme is expected to lead to efficient uptake by RPE cells via the M6P receptor, thereby supplementing or restoring the lysosomal pool of active cathepsin D where it is most critically needed (Sharif, 2015). This direct enzyme replacement should result in improved degradation of cellular waste such as spent photoreceptor outer segments, mitigating the build-up of lipofuscin and drusen that are characteristic of dry AMD pathology (Klettner et al., 2013). In animal models of CTSD deficiency—specifically those that mimic aspects of neurodegenerative lysosomal storage disorders—the administration of exogenous pro-cathepsin D has yielded significant improvements in proteolytic function, reduction of pathological markers, and even extensions in lifespan (Bassal et al., 2021; Marques et al., 2020), which suggest that similar therapeutic benefits might be achievable in the context of dry AMD. Enhancing the proteolytic flux within the lysosomes of RPE cells is expected to restore autophagy and maintain cellular homeostasis, thereby reducing the incidence of apoptotic cell death and preserving retinal structure (Klettner et al., 2013; Sharif, 2015). Additionally, by compensating for potential maturation deficits and bypassing defective acidification processes through localized delivery, the therapeutic candidate offers a targeted approach that is likely to be both efficacious and specific compared to more indirect modulators of lysosomal function (Liu, 2021; Marques et al., 2020; Sharif, 2015). Ultimately, the expected effect is an overall improvement in RPE health, which should translate into slowed progression of dry AMD, decreased drusen accumulation, and preserved visual function.

Overall Evaluation:  
In evaluating recombinant human pro-cathepsin D as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, several strengths emerge from the literature, though some challenges remain. One of the primary strengths of this candidate lies in its specificity; unlike indirect modulators of lysosomal function, the exogenous delivery of a rate-limiting hydrolase such as CTSD offers a mechanistically driven, targeted replacement therapy that directly addresses a known biochemical deficit in the retinal pigment epithelium (Klettner et al., 2013; Liu, 2021). The robust body of preclinical evidence supporting the efficacy of recombinant pro-cathepsin D in models of neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis, where similar lysosomal impairments are present, lends further credence to its potential applicability in AMD (Bassal et al., 2021; Marques et al., 2020). Moreover, the formulation's GMP-compatibility and prior demonstration of safety in the context of genetic CTSD deficiency are significant advantages that can accelerate its translational potential (Marques et al., 2020; Liu, 2021).

The enzyme’s molecular mechanism, which involves uptake via mannose-6-phosphate receptor-mediated endocytosis and subsequent activation in the lysosomal compartment, is well-characterized and aligns with the pathological requirements for restoring RPE function in dry AMD (Sharif, 2015). This targeted approach provides a direct means to enhance proteolytic activity and autophagic flux, crucial processes that are disrupted in the aging retina and contribute to drusen accumulation (Klettner et al., 2013). The ability of the exogenously delivered pro-cathepsin D to overcome defects in lysosomal maturation and acidification further reinforces its potential role in reversing or mitigating the deleterious effects of the disease (Liu, 2021; Marques et al., 2020).

On the other hand, several weaknesses or challenges must be acknowledged. Although the mechanistic rationale is robust, the translation of preclinical successes in neurodegenerative and lysosomal storage disorder models to the complex, multifactorial pathology of dry AMD remains uncertain (Benes et al., 2008; Liu, 2021). Dry AMD is influenced by a host of factors—including oxidative stress, chronic inflammation, and genetic predispositions—that may not be fully addressed by simply supplementing CTSD activity. Therefore, while the normalization of proteolytic flux in RPE cells is a critical component, it may not suffice on its own in the context of the broader pathophysiological milieu present in AMD (Klettner et al., 2013; Sharif, 2015).

Furthermore, delivery challenges inherent to subretinal injections must be considered. Although localized delivery methods help bypass systemic barriers such as the blood-brain barrier, subretinal injections are technically demanding, carry inherent risks of infection, and may provoke local immune responses due to repeated interventions (Marques et al., 2020; Liu, 2021). The emergence of neutralizing antibodies, as observed in some ERT studies when alternative routes of administration were explored, could compromise the long-term efficacy of the therapy if systemic leakage occurs or if repeated dosing is required (Marques et al., 2020; Liu, 2021). Additionally, the stability and persistence of the enzyme in the subretinal space represent important pharmacokinetic questions that must be addressed through rigorous preclinical pharmacodynamic studies.

Another potential shortcoming is the specificity of the enzyme’s action. While cathepsin D is indeed a critical protease in RPE cells, there is an intricate interplay between cathepsin D and other lysosomal enzymes such as cathepsins B, L, and S, as well as regulatory proteins like cystatin C, which modulate proteolytic activity (Sharif, 2015). This interdependence implies that augmenting CTSD activity alone might lead to compensatory changes in other proteases that could either enhance the therapeutic effect or, conversely, result in unforeseen off-target consequences. Moreover, given the complexity of the RPE cell’s lysosomal network and the multifactorial nature of dry AMD pathogenesis, combination approaches targeting several aspects of lysosomal dysfunction might be necessary to achieve optimal clinical outcomes.

In summary, recombinant human pro-cathepsin D presents a therapeutically attractive and mechanistically rational candidate for the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration. Its origins as a naturally occurring lysosomal precursor that, when supplemented exogenously, has been shown to restore enzyme activity in preclinical models of lysosomal dysfunction (Bassal et al., 2021; Marques et al., 2020) underscores its potential for addressing the proteolytic deficits seen in RPE cells affected by dry AMD (Klettner et al., 2013). The candidate’s well-defined molecular processing pathway—from synthesis as an inactive proenzyme to activation within the acidic environment of the lysosome—ensures that it is both functionally and biologically suited to compensate for endogenous maturation deficits (Sharif, 2015). This detailed understanding of its biochemistry and cellular uptake mechanisms via the mannose-6-phosphate receptor supports the hypothesis that subretinal delivery of rhCTSD could enhance proteolytic flux, reduce drusen accumulation, and ultimately contribute to the preservation of retinal function in patients with dry AMD (Liu, 2021; Marques et al., 2020).

Despite these promising attributes, the candidate’s clinical translation will require addressing several key challenges. Future studies must rigorously evaluate the pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic profiles of subretinally delivered rhCTSD, with particular emphasis on its stability, local retention time in the subretinal space, and potential immunogenicity. It will also be critical to determine whether augmenting CTSD activity alone is sufficient to counteract the multi-factorial processes underlying dry AMD or if the therapeutic strategy should be integrated into a broader, combination-based treatment regimen. Additionally, long-term safety studies are necessary to monitor for potential adverse effects, such as immune-mediated clearance or detrimental off-target proteolytic activity that might impair retinal structure and function (Marques et al., 2020; Thiessen, 2023).

Ultimately, the overall evaluation is cautiously optimistic. The mechanistic rationale is strong—supported by extensive preclinical data from related neurodegenerative and lysosomal storage disorder models—and the therapeutic candidate is produced under rigorous, GMP-compliant conditions, offering a level of quality assurance that is imperative for clinical advancement (Marques et al., 2020; Liu, 2021). The specificity of recombinant pro-cathepsin D in directly addressing a rate-limiting step in lysosomal degradation makes it an especially compelling candidate in a disease setting where impaired autophagy and proteolysis are central to pathology (Klettner et al., 2013). However, challenges related to effective subretinal delivery, the potential for immune responses, and the need to integrate its action within the broader context of AMD pathogenesis must be rigorously addressed in subsequent preclinical and clinical studies before a definitive therapeutic benefit can be confirmed (Marques et al., 2020; Benes et al., 2008). In light of these considerations, recombinant human pro-cathepsin D stands out as a promising avenue for therapeutic intervention in dry AMD, meriting further investigation to delineate its efficacy, safety, and long-term benefits in the appropriate animal models and ultimately in clinical trials.

I. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Avacincaptad pegol, commercially known as Zimura, is a highly engineered, synthetic RNA aptamer designed specifically to target complement factor C5 for the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) with geographic atrophy (GA) features (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4). This molecule is comprised of a 39-nucleotide sequence that has been rigorously selected through in vitro techniques to offer high affinity and specificity for its target, ensuring that it binds precisely to C5 and prevents its activation (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4). Unlike traditional monoclonal antibodies, aptamers are oligonucleotide-based therapeutic agents that combine the benefits of well-defined chemical synthesis with tunable pharmacokinetics and low immunogenicity. In this instance, avacincaptad pegol has been further optimized by incorporating multiple chemical modifications; these include 2′-fluorine substitutions on pyrimidine residues, 2′-O-methyl modifications on select purine nucleotides, a protected 3′–3′ thymidine cap, and a branched polyethylene glycol (PEG) moiety to extend its half-life within the eye (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4). Such modifications confer enhanced resistance to degradation by nucleases and reduce renal clearance, thereby allowing the compound to remain active in the subretinal space longer than unmodified oligonucleotides (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4). The development of avacincaptad pegol is rooted in the evolution of aptamer technologies that began with earlier compounds like pegaptanib, the pioneer aptamer approved for neovascular AMD; however, unlike pegaptanib, avacincaptad pegol is engineered to target a different disease mechanism by focusing on the terminal complement cascade (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–8). Overall, the molecular design and chemical sophistication of this aptamer designate it as a next-generation candidate in the field of oligonucleotide therapeutics, with its unique physical and chemical attributes directly addressing specific pathogenic mechanisms of dry AMD (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–8).

Avacincaptad pegol belongs to a broader class of therapeutic compounds known as aptamers that act as “chemical antibodies.” These agents are synthesized via systematic evolution of ligands by exponential enrichment (SELEX), a process that allows for iterative refinement of the aptamer’s binding characteristics so that it selectively interacts with its intended protein target (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4). Aptamers have been used in various clinical applications due to their predictable pharmacologic profiles, their ease of chemical modification, and their typically low risk of eliciting an immune response. Their utility has been demonstrated not only in ocular therapeutics but also across a range of medical indications where precise modulation of molecular pathways is desired (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4). With the advent of avacincaptad pegol, the application of aptamer technology has been repurposed specifically for the modulation of the complement cascade—a key inflammatory pathway implicated in retinal degenerative diseases such as dry AMD (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4).

The synthetic origins of avacincaptad pegol underscore a scalable manufacturing process with robust quality control measures, making the compound attractive not only from a scientific standpoint but also from a commercial and regulatory perspective (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4). The structural characteristics, including its nucleic acid backbone and PEG conjugation, have been optimized to ensure adequate tissue penetration and sustained activity when delivered via intravitreal injection, minimizing systemic exposure and maximizing local therapeutic concentrations (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4). In summary, avacincaptad pegol is a representative example of how innovative chemical modifications and advanced selection technologies converge to generate therapeutic candidates that address the critical unmet needs in degenerative retinal diseases (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4).

II. Therapeutic History  
The trajectory of avacincaptad pegol from bench to bedside is emblematic of the rapid evolution in our understanding of the complement system’s role in AMD pathogenesis. Historically, the complement cascade—a series of proteolytic reactions leading to the formation of the membrane attack complex (MAC)—has been implicated in the chronic, low-grade inflammatory processes that contribute to retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) degeneration (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4; Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). Early efforts in pharmacologic intervention focused on modulating angiogenesis through agents like anti-VEGF drugs; however, these therapies failed to address the underlying complement-mediated inflammatory milieu that is particularly pronounced in the dry form of AMD (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4, 16–17).

The recognition that complement overactivation plays a central role in GA led researchers to explore agents that could precisely inhibit key components of this cascade. Avacincaptad pegol emerged as a promising candidate in this context, designed to block complement factor C5—a critical nexus point in the pathway responsible for the generation of both the potent inflammatory mediator C5a and the membrane attack complex (MAC) via C5b (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Bege et al., 2025, pp. 4–8). Preclinical studies using animal models of AMD demonstrated that inhibition of C5 could mitigate complement-mediated damage to RPE cells and reduce progression of GA lesions, laying the foundation for subsequent clinical investigations (Guimaraes et al., 2022, pp. 3–4; Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3).

The clinical development program for avacincaptad pegol has been extensive. Notably, phase II/III randomized controlled trials—collectively referred to as GATHER 1 and GATHER 2—were designed to evaluate its safety and efficacy in patients with GA secondary to AMD (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 16–17; Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). These pivotal trials enrolled hundreds of patients and involved monthly intravitreal injections, a route of administration that allows for high local concentrations of the drug while minimizing systemic exposure (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 16–17; Qin et al., 2024, p. 3). The results from these clinical studies were encouraging, as they consistently demonstrated statistically significant reductions in GA lesion growth in treatment groups compared to sham injections, with reported reductions in lesion progression on the order of approximately 27–30% over follow-up periods ranging from 12 to 18 months (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Guimaraes et al., 2022, pp. 3–4; Bege et al., 2025, pp. 16–17).

Beyond efficacy, the safety profile of avacincaptad pegol has been affirmed in multiple studies. The intravitreal route of administration confines the compound’s activity largely to the ocular compartment, thereby minimizing systemic immunosuppression—a particularly valuable attribute given the complement system’s role in host defense (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4; Qin et al., 2024, p. 3). Reports from clinical trials indicated that adverse events were primarily related to the injection procedure itself, with few drug-related serious ocular events recorded (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4; Guimaraes et al., 2022, pp. 3–4). This favorable safety record, combined with robust efficacy data, contributed to the FDA’s decision to approve avacincaptad pegol for the treatment of GA in August 2023, marking it as the second approved aptamer medicine in the field of retinal disease, following pegaptanib (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4; Qin et al., 2024, p. 3).

In parallel with these developments in dry AMD, avacincaptad pegol has been examined in observational studies and preclinical models that further delineate its mechanism of action and long-term benefits. Although past investigations in other complement-mediated ocular conditions have encountered mixed results, the specific targeting of C5 in the case of GA appears to be particularly promising, as evidenced by the consistent reduction in lesion progression reported by the GATHER trials (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 16–17; Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). The accumulated clinical experience provides a compelling historical context for its use, reinforcing the therapeutic rationale of complement inhibition in mitigating the inflammatory and degenerative processes that drive dry AMD (Guimaraes et al., 2022, pp. 3–4; Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3).

Moreover, the evolution of complement-modulating therapies in retinal diseases has been marked by significant collaborations between academia, industry, and regulatory agencies, all of which have embraced a more nuanced understanding of the immune processes involved in AMD. These concerted efforts have not only fostered the development of avacincaptad pegol but have also encouraged ongoing research into combination therapies that may further enhance clinical outcomes (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4, 16–17). As such, the therapeutic history of avacincaptad pegol is characterized by a steady progression from mechanistic discovery in the laboratory to robust clinical validation, underscoring its potential as a transformative agent in the management of dry AMD (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Qin et al., 2024, p. 3).

III. Mechanism of Action  
The mechanism of action of avacincaptad pegol is both specific and multifaceted, centering on the selective inhibition of complement factor C5—a pivotal molecule in the terminal complement pathway (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 4–8; Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). Under physiological conditions, C5 is cleaved into C5a and C5b. C5a acts as a potent anaphylatoxin that promotes inflammation through the recruitment and activation of immune cells, while C5b initiates the assembly of the membrane attack complex (MAC) by sequentially binding to complement components C6 through C9 (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Bege et al., 2025, pp. 4–8). The formation of the MAC on the surface of retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells is a critical driver of cell lysis and inflammatory damage that ultimately contributes to the progression of geographic atrophy in dry AMD (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Guimaraes et al., 2022, pp. 3–4).

Avacincaptad pegol exerts its therapeutic effect by binding directly to C5 with extremely high affinity, thereby blocking its enzymatic cleavage (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 4–8; Guimaraes et al., 2022, pp. 3–4). This inhibition prevents the generation of both C5a and C5b, ultimately forestalling the downstream assembly of the MAC (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 4–8; Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). The direct blockade of MAC formation is particularly beneficial in the subretinal microenvironment, where chronic complement activation is thought to contribute to lysosomal dysfunction in RPE cells (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Guimaraes et al., 2022, pp. 3–4). Specifically, when the MAC is deposited on RPE cell membranes, it can cause lysosomal membrane permeabilization (LMP), leading to impaired vacuolar ATPase (v-ATPase) activity and subsequent loss of lysosomal acidification (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 4–8; Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3).

Under normal circumstances, lysosomal acidification is essential for the proper maturation and activation of proteolytic enzymes such as cathepsin D (CTSD) (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Guimaraes et al., 2022, pp. 3–4). By preventing the formation of the MAC, avacincaptad pegol helps to preserve the proton gradient across the lysosomal membrane, thereby maintaining optimal conditions for lysosomal enzyme activity and ensuring adequate proteolytic clearance of debris within RPE cells (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 4–8; Guimaraes et al., 2022, pp. 3–4). This preservation of lysosomal function is of critical importance in preventing the accumulation of toxic byproducts, which have been implicated in the progressive degeneration of the retina observed in GA (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Guimaraes et al., 2022, pp. 3–4).

The detailed biochemistry underlying avacincaptad pegol’s activity was refined through iterative cycles of the SELEX process, during which the aptamer’s RNA sequence was optimized for maximal affinity toward C5 (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4; 4–8). The resulting aptamer exhibits a unique three-dimensional conformation that facilitates tight binding to a specific epitope on C5, effectively neutralizing its activity while sparing upstream complement components that may have beneficial roles in immune surveillance (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 4–8; 1–4). The high specificity of this interaction is essential because it limits off-target effects and reduces the risk of broader systemic immunosuppression—a concern that has previously complicated the development of complement inhibitors (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 4–8; Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3).

Furthermore, the localized administration of avacincaptad pegol via intravitreal injection ensures that its action is confined primarily to the retina, thereby concentrating its complement-inhibiting effects where they are most needed and minimizing the potential for systemic adverse events (Qin et al., 2024, p. 3; Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4). In preclinical studies, this targeted delivery was shown to result in marked reductions in the levels of C5 cleavage products, as well as diminished deposition of the MAC on the RPE, thereby validating the mechanistic rationale of the drug (Guimaraes et al., 2022, pp. 3–4; Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3).

In summary, avacincaptad pegol’s mode of action is rooted in its ability to effectively halt the terminal steps of the complement cascade by binding to C5, thereby preventing the formation of both pro-inflammatory C5a and the deleterious MAC (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 4–8; Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). Through this mechanism, it interrupts a key pathological process in dry AMD, offering a targeted strategy to preserve RPE cell function and maintain lysosomal integrity via sustained v-ATPase activity and proper cathepsin D maturation (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Guimaraes et al., 2022, pp. 3–4).

IV. Expected Effect  
Based on the mechanistic insights discussed above, the central hypothesis for avacincaptad pegol is that its inhibition of complement C5 activation will lead to a cascade of protective effects in the retinal microenvironment, ultimately decelerating the progression of GA associated with dry AMD (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Guimaraes et al., 2022, pp. 3–4). The expected effect in both in vitro and in vivo assays is multifactorial. Primarily, the aptamer is anticipated to reduce the generation of C5 cleavage products, thereby inhibiting the formation of the MAC on the surface of RPE cells. Such an effect is measurable via immunoassays that track the levels of C5a and related fragments, as well as by quantitative imaging techniques that assess MAC deposition (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Qin et al., 2024, pp. 2–3).

At the cellular level, the inhibition of MAC deposition is expected to translate into preserved lysosomal function within RPE cells—a critical factor given the reliance of these cells on lysosomal acidification for proper autophagic flux and metabolic homeostasis (Guimaraes et al., 2022, pp. 3–4; Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). In practical assay systems, one would anticipate that RPE cell cultures treated with avacincaptad pegol show maintained or even restored acidification of lysosomes as indicated by pH-sensitive fluorescent dyes, alongside intact activity of lysosomal enzymes such as cathepsin D (Guimaraes et al., 2022, pp. 3–4; Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). This preservation of lysosomal function is hypothesized to directly correlate with a reduced accumulation of cellular debris and toxic byproducts that accelerate the degenerative process in GA (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Bege et al., 2025, pp. 4–8).

Clinically, the outcome most often evaluated in trials of avacincaptad pegol is the deceleration of GA lesion enlargement, which is quantitatively assessed through imaging modalities such as fundus autofluorescence (FAF) and optical coherence tomography (OCT) (Qin et al., 2024, pp. 2–3; 3–3). In the pivotal GATHER 1 and GATHER 2 phase II/III studies, patients treated with monthly intravitreal injections of avacincaptad pegol exhibited reductions in GA progression rates of approximately 27% to 30% relative to sham-treated groups (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Bege et al., 2025, pp. 16–17). These anatomical endpoints serve as surrogate markers for the overall efficacy of the intervention, with the underlying assumption that slowing the expansion of GA lesions will eventually lead to stabilization of visual function (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Guimaraes et al., 2022, pp. 3–4).

At the molecular level, the expected effect also includes the restoration of critical lysosomal functions disrupted by excessive complement activation. Specifically, by preventing MAC-induced lysosomal membrane permeabilization, avacincaptad pegol is anticipated to maintain the proton gradient essential for v-ATPase function, thereby preserving the acidic environment required for optimal cathepsin D processing and other lysosomal enzymes (Guimaraes et al., 2022, pp. 3–4; Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). Such preservation is not only crucial for cellular clearance mechanisms but also plays a pivotal role in preventing intracellular accumulation of debris, which is a contributing factor in the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Guimaraes et al., 2022, pp. 3–4; Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3).

Moreover, since complement components, including C5, are expressed locally in the retina by RPE cells and resident immune cells, the targeted inhibition of C5 is expected to provide direct immunomodulatory benefits within the ocular microenvironment. This localized impact is critical because it addresses the pathophysiological cross-talk between complement activation and lysosomal dysfunction, which is thought to drive a vicious cycle of chronic inflammation and cellular degeneration (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Guimaraes et al., 2022, pp. 3–4). In theory, by reestablishing a balanced complement milieu, avacincaptad pegol may also help to curtail secondary inflammatory responses that otherwise exacerbate tissue damage, thereby preserving photoreceptor integrity and ultimately stabilizing visual acuity over time (Qin et al., 2024, pp. 2–3; 3–3).

In summary, the expected effects of avacincaptad pegol in the proposed assays and clinical settings are multi-layered. At the biochemical level, one should observe a pronounced reduction in C5 cleavage, diminished MAC formation on RPE membranes, and preserved lysosomal acidification and enzyme function. At the tissue level, these molecular events are predicted to culminate in a slowdown of GA lesion enlargement, which is widely regarded as a surrogate marker for the progression of dry AMD (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Qin et al., 2024, pp. 2–3). The overall hypothesis is that these combined effects will translate into meaningful clinical benefits, offering not only anatomical preservation but also the potential for stabilization—or even modest improvement—of visual function in affected patients (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3).

V. Overall Evaluation  
A comprehensive evaluation of avacincaptad pegol reveals a therapeutic candidate that is scientifically robust, mechanistically innovative, and clinically validated for the treatment of dry AMD with geographic atrophy. One of the major strengths of this therapeutic approach lies in its highly specific mechanism of action. By directly binding to and inhibiting complement factor C5, avacincaptad pegol interrupts a key pathological process at its source, namely the activation of the terminal complement cascade that results in the formation of the pro-inflammatory mediator C5a and the membrane attack complex (MAC) (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 4–8; Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). This level of specificity confers potential advantages over broader immunosuppressive agents, as it minimizes collateral inhibition of upstream complement components that may be protective. Such precise targeting results in reduced inflammation localized to the retinal tissues and lowers the risk of systemic adverse events (Guimaraes et al., 2022, pp. 3–4; Qin et al., 2024, pp. 3–3).

The extensive chemical modifications integrated into avacincaptad pegol’s structure—including 2′-fluoro and 2′-O-methyl substitutions, the incorporation of a 3′–3′ thymidine cap, and PEGylation—greatly enhance its stability and half-life in the intraocular environment (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4). These modifications are essential because they allow for sustained inhibition of C5 with relatively infrequent dosing, thereby improving the overall treatment regimen for a patient population that is often elderly and may struggle with stringent dosing schedules (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4; Qin et al., 2024, pp. 3–3). The aptamer-based nature of this drug also endows it with a low immunogenic risk profile, circumventing one of the potential pitfalls associated with protein-based therapies such as monoclonal antibodies (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4).

Clinically, the data emerging from the GATHER 1 and GATHER 2 phase II/III trials are particularly compelling. These studies have consistently demonstrated that patients receiving intravitreal injections of avacincaptad pegol experience a significant reduction in the rate of GA lesion growth, with observed reductions ranging from 27% to 30% compared to sham controls (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Bege et al., 2025, pp. 16–17). This tangible anatomical benefit, combined with the favorable safety profile—which includes minimal ocular adverse events—confirms the viability of C5 inhibition as a disease-modifying strategy in dry AMD (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4). Given that GA has long represented an area of substantial unmet clinical need, the regulatory approval of avacincaptad pegol by the FDA in August 2023 is a significant milestone that reinforces the credibility of this therapeutic approach (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4; Qin et al., 2024, pp. 3–3).

Another notable strength is the mechanistic rationale underpinning the expected therapeutic benefits. By preventing MAC formation on RPE membranes, avacincaptad pegol not only preserves the structural integrity of these cells but also protects lysosomal function by mitigating lysosomal membrane permeabilization (LMP) (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Bege et al., 2025, pp. 4–8). The preservation of lysosomal acidification and subsequent maintenance of autophagic and proteolytic function are critical factors in slowing the progression of GA, as they help to avert the accumulation of toxic metabolic byproducts that drive cellular degeneration (Guimaraes et al., 2022, pp. 3–4; Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). Thus, the therapeutic strategy is well anchored in a clear pathological framework that directly relates to the underlying disease process in dry AMD.

Despite the considerable promise of avacincaptad pegol, several potential weaknesses and challenges remain. One concern is the translation of anatomical benefits into meaningful functional improvements with respect to visual acuity. While reduction in GA lesion enlargement is an encouraging surrogate endpoint, there is a recognized challenge in correlating these anatomical outcomes with sustained improvements or stabilization of vision (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Qin et al., 2024, pp. 2–3). In some clinical trials involving complement inhibitors, the disconnect between reduced lesion growth and measurable improvements in best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) has raised questions about whether anatomical preservation will eventually lead to perceptible functional benefits for patients (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3).

Another potential challenge relates to the inherent complexity of the complement system. C5 is a critical component of the terminal cascade; however, the redundancy and cross-talk among multiple complement pathways may potentially compromise the overall efficacy of a monotherapeutic approach targeting only C5 (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 4–8; Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). There is a possibility that, even with effective C5 blockade, alternative inflammatory pathways may partially compensate for its inhibition, thereby limiting the long-term clinical benefit. This concern suggests that future treatment paradigms might require combination approaches that target both complement-mediated and non-complement-mediated mechanisms of retinal degeneration (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Bege et al., 2025, pp. 4–8).

The mode of delivery is another factor that merits consideration. Avacincaptad pegol is delivered via monthly intravitreal injections, which, while effective in ensuring localized drug activity, impose a significant treatment burden on an elderly patient population (Qin et al., 2024, pp. 3–3). Frequent intravitreal administration is associated with logistical challenges, including the risk of injection-related complications such as endophthalmitis or retinal detachment, albeit infrequent, and may negatively impact patient compliance over extended treatment periods (Qin et al., 2024, pp. 3–3; Bege et al., 2025, pp. 16–17). Future innovation in drug delivery systems—for example, sustained-release implants or alternative non-invasive administration routes—could be critical in overcoming this limitation and enhancing long-term treatment adherence (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 16–17; 1–4).

A further challenge lies in assessing the long-term safety of chronic complement inhibition within the ocular environment. Although the localized delivery method limits systemic exposure, the prolonged suppression of C5 activity in the retina may affect local immune surveillance and potentially predispose to subclinical infections or inflammatory dysregulation (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4; Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). Given that the complement system plays a nuanced role in both tissue repair and immune defense, extended studies are necessary to definitively characterize the long-term safety profile, particularly with respect to maintaining the delicate balance between controlling pathological inflammation and preserving protective immune functions (Qin et al., 2024, pp. 3–3; Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3).

Finally, the multifactorial nature of dry AMD suggests that while C5 inhibition may effectively slow the progression of GA, it might not fully address all aspects of this complex disease process. Oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and neurodegeneration are also critical contributors to AMD pathophysiology, and a monotherapy targeting the complement cascade may need to be integrated into a broader multimodal treatment strategy to achieve optimal clinical outcomes (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Bege et al., 2025, pp. 4–8). Such considerations imply that while avacincaptad pegol represents a significant advancement in the field, its maximal therapeutic potential may be realized only when used in combination with agents that address complementary pathological processes (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Bege et al., 2025, pp. 4–8).

In synthesizing these considerations, the overall evaluation of avacincaptad pegol is highly positive. Its unique molecular design, demonstrated clinical efficacy in reducing GA lesion growth, and favorable safety profile strongly support the hypothesis that targeted inhibition of complement C5 can provide a meaningful therapeutic benefit in dry AMD (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4; Qin et al., 2024, pp. 3–3). The strengths lie in both its mechanistic precision and the tangible clinical endpoints achieved in pivotal trials, which collectively underscore the validity of the hypothesis that disrupting terminal complement activation can preserve RPE integrity and lysosomal function (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3).

Nevertheless, the translation of these anatomical benefits into long-term preservation of vision, the challenges associated with the frequent intravitreal injection regimen, and the potential activation of alternative inflammatory pathways represent hurdles that warrant continued investigation (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). Addressing these challenges will likely require further mechanistic studies, extended clinical follow-up to capture functional outcomes, and possibly the development of innovative drug delivery systems that reduce the treatment burden on patients (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 16–17; Qin et al., 2024, pp. 3–3).

In conclusion, avacincaptad pegol emerges as a scientifically rigorous and clinically validated candidate for the treatment of dry AMD with geographic atrophy. Its ability to selectively inhibit complement C5 and thereby prevent MAC formation, lysosomal acidification loss, and subsequent RPE damage provides a mechanistic rationale that is well supported by both preclinical and clinical data (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Bege et al., 2025, pp. 4–8). Moreover, from a commercial and regulatory perspective, the recent FDA approval of avacincaptad pegol for GA marks a significant milestone that not only validates the scientific rationale for targeting complement C5 but also signals the readiness of the ocular therapeutic landscape to embrace novel molecular entities with differentiated mechanisms of action (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4; Qin et al., 2024, pp. 3–3). Such an integrated approach has the potential to not only enhance the overall therapeutic efficacy but also to extend the duration of clinical benefits, ultimately improving the quality of life for patients suffering from this debilitating condition (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4).

In balancing these strengths and challenges, the overall assessment of avacincaptad pegol remains decidedly positive. Its molecular design is state-of-the-art, its mechanism of action is directly aligned with a critical pathogenic process in dry AMD, and its clinical performance to date offers substantive evidence of efficacy in slowing disease progression (Qin et al., 2024, pp. 3–3; Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4). In summary, avacincaptad pegol represents a landmark therapeutic innovation in the realm of retinal degenerative diseases. Its targeted inhibition of complement C5 not only addresses a fundamental driver of retinal inflammation and degenerative cell death in GA but also offers a new paradigm in the treatment of a condition that has long been resistant to effective disease-modifying interventions (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4). Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Pegcetacoplan (APL-2, now marketed as Syfovre) is a synthetically engineered, PEGylated cyclic peptide that belongs to the family of compstatin analogs designed to inhibit complement component C3. Its origins lie in early peptide discovery via phage‐display and random peptide library screening, and successive rounds of medicinal chemistry optimization were applied to improve its binding affinity, solubility, and pharmacokinetic profile through PEG conjugation (Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023; Ong et al., 2024). The PEGylation process not only grants enhanced resistance to enzymatic degradation but also prolongs the intravitreal residence time, an essential property for ocular applications requiring sustained drug exposure with limited dosing frequency (Tzoumas et al., 2023; Mastellos & Lambris, 2024). As a second‐generation compstatin analog, pegcetacoplan employs a bivalent design that enables high specificity for human C3, blocking its proteolytic cleavage into the active fragments C3a and C3b. These fragments are potent mediators that further amplify the inflammatory cascade through the formation of C3 convertases (Lamers et al., 2022). This therapeutic candidate is embedded within a broader class of complement inhibitors that have been actively explored in inflammatory disorders, and notably in ophthalmology for dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) where aberrant complement activation plays a central pathogenic role (Lamers et al., 2022; Mastellos & Lambris, 2024). Its synthetic nature, coupled with its targeted molecular design, positions pegcetacoplan as an attractive candidate for addressing the degenerative processes in geographic atrophy (GA) associated with dry AMD by directly modulating the complement cascade (Tzoumas et al., 2023; Patel et al., 2022).

Therapeutic History  
Historically, the evolution of pegcetacoplan reflects a successful translation from bench to bedside across multiple therapeutic domains. Initially, the compstatin class was primarily developed and evaluated in systemic disorders characterized by complement dysregulation, most notably in paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH). Early clinical trials in PNH provided critical safety and efficacy data that underscored the value of targeting C3, paving the way for the repurposing of these molecules in ocular disease (Lamers et al., 2022). With the conceptual framework and preclinical data in hand, pegcetacoplan was advanced into the ophthalmology space. The pivotal Phase II FILLY trial enrolled 246 patients with GA secondary to dry AMD, and the study demonstrated that monthly intravitreal injections of pegcetacoplan resulted in a statistically significant reduction of GA lesion growth by approximately 29%, while an every-other-month dosing regimen yielded a 20% reduction relative to sham-control treatment (Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023; Patel et al., 2022). These encouraging anatomical outcomes, evidenced by the slowed progression of GA and the concurrent reduction in photoreceptor loss as evaluated by SD-OCT imaging, provided a strong rationale for subsequent Phase III clinical trials (Regillo & Heier, n.d.; Patel et al., 2022).  
In addition to its use in dry AMD, pegcetacoplan’s earlier regulatory approval for PNH helped establish it as a viable molecule with a favorable safety profile. Its journey through successive clinical phases—from Phase I safety and tolerability studies to Phase II efficacy studies and ultimately Phase III confirmation—has offered compelling evidence that targeted complement inhibition can modify the disease course in conditions characterized by chronic complement activation (Tzoumas et al., 2023). However, clinical experience with pegcetacoplan has also identified potential safety signals, including an observed increase in the incidence of new-onset exudative (wet) AMD among certain subpopulations, a factor that necessitates careful patient selection and monitoring (Lamers et al., 2022; Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023). Overall, the therapeutic history of pegcetacoplan—spanning its origin from fundamental compstatin research to its current application in treating geographic atrophy—demonstrates its potential for repurposing as a disease-modifying therapy in ocular settings (Lamers et al., 2022; Desai & Dugel, 2022).

Mechanism of Action  
At the molecular level, the pathogenic cascade in dry AMD is tightly linked to dysregulated complement activation, and pegcetacoplan intervenes at one of the central nodes of this pathway by inhibiting complement component C3. Under physiological conditions, C3 is cleaved by C3 convertases into C3a—an anaphylatoxin that drives inflammation—and C3b, which functions as an opsonin and further propagates complement amplification (Yu & Wykoff, 2021). Pegcetacoplan binds to a key epitope on C3, thereby sterically hindering the enzyme-driven cleavage that would otherwise generate these active fragments. By effectively arresting this pivotal step in the complement cascade, the drug prevents downstream events such as the assembly of terminal complement complexes and the formation of the membrane attack complex (MAC) (Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023; Wu & Sun, 2019).  
The inhibition of C3 cleavage has several critical biochemical consequences. First, by lowering the concentrations of C3a and C3b, pegcetacoplan reduces the generation of pro-inflammatory mediators and the subsequent chemotactic recruitment of immune cells, which, in turn, diminishes local inflammation in the retinal environment (Regillo & Heier, n.d.; Tzoumas et al., 2023). Second, the reduction in C3b deposition directly limits the formation of MAC on retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) surfaces—a process that has been implicated in triggering lysosomal dysfunction within these critical cells (Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023; Park et al., 2021). The MAC, when deposited sublytically on RPE cells, can compromise the function of the vacuolar H⁺-ATPase (v-ATPase), the proton pump responsible for maintaining the acidic environment of lysosomes. Acidification of the lysosomal compartment is essential for optimal activity of proteolytic enzymes, such as cathepsin D, which are required to degrade photoreceptor outer segment debris and other cytotoxic by-products (Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023; Tzoumas et al., 2023).  
Thus, by preventing excessive complement activation and subsequent MAC formation, pegcetacoplan indirectly safeguards the intracellular degradative machinery of the RPE. This preservation of v-ATPase function ensures proper lysosomal acidification, which in turn maintains cathepsin D activity and reduces lysosomal overload—a key mechanism implicated in the progressive atrophy of the RPE observed in dry AMD (Mastellos & Lambris, 2024; Regillo & Heier, n.d.). Moreover, preclinical studies have demonstrated that complement blockade via agents such as pegcetacoplan lowers sub-RPE deposit formation and inflammasome priming, processes intimately linked to lysosomal dysfunction and chronic inflammation (Liao et al., 2020; Lamers et al., 2022). Collectively, the mechanism of action of pegcetacoplan encompasses both direct inhibition of complement-driven inflammatory processes and indirect protection of intracellular catabolic functions in the RPE, thereby addressing two core pathological contributors to geographic atrophy (Kassa et al., 2019; Rubner et al., 2022).

Expected Effect  
Based on its detailed mechanism of action, pegcetacoplan is expected to exert a dual beneficial effect in the management of dry AMD. First, by binding to and inhibiting complement C3, it should markedly reduce the formation of inflammatory mediators (C3a, C3b) as well as downstream terminal pathway components such as the MAC. At the cellular level, maintaining cathepsin D activity is imperative because this protease is responsible for degrading intracellular waste products that accumulate in RPE cells, and its functionality is closely tied to the acidic environment provided by lysosomes. By preserving this aspect of lysosomal physiology, pegcetacoplan should contribute to RPE cell survival and thereby delay the progression of geographic atrophy (Patel et al., 2022). A comprehensive review of pegcetacoplan as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD reveals a well-substantiated rationale and a promising clinical profile, albeit with some challenges that must be addressed. One of the most compelling strengths of pegcetacoplan is its precise molecular targeting of complement component C3—a central mediator in the complement cascade. By inhibiting C3, pegcetacoplan effectively blocks the generation of both C3a and C3b, thereby reducing pro-inflammatory signaling and preventing the formation of the membrane attack complex (MAC) (Yu & Wykoff, 2021). Another challenge is the logistical and patient adherence issues related to frequent intravitreal injections. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Nicotinamide riboside (NR), marketed as ChromaDex Niagen, belongs to the vitamin B3 family and is a naturally occurring precursor of nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+). Originally discovered in trace amounts in milk and other food sources, NR has been isolated and subsequently synthesized to yield a high‐purity form for nutritional and pharmaceutical applications. As a member of a class of compounds designed to elevate intracellular NAD+ levels, NR has attracted significant attention in the fields of metabolism, aging, and neuroprotection. Its chemical structure—a combination of a nicotinamide moiety bound to ribose—enables it to enter salvage pathways in cells with minimal metabolic conversion losses. In this regard, NR is comparable to other NAD+ boosters such as nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN), though differences in bioavailability and cellular transporter expression have been noted in some studies. Preclinical research has documented retinal distribution of NR in rodent models, suggesting that it reaches ocular tissues in pharmacologically relevant concentrations, an essential prerequisite for any agent intended to treat dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) (Abokyi & Tse, 2025; Braidy et al., 2019).

Therapeutic History:  
NR has been extensively investigated for its potential to modulate cellular energy metabolism and mitigate the effects of aging in diverse tissues. Early studies revealed that supplementation with NR effectively elevates NAD+ levels in multiple cell types, including neurons, skeletal muscle, and retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells, thereby enhancing mitochondrial function and cellular stress resistance (Dovijarski, 2019; Pîrvu et al., 2021). In the context of ocular research, while much of the direct experimental work has been performed using NMN, the close biochemical relationship between NMN and NR—as NAD+ precursors—has led investigators to propose that NR could produce similar outcomes in RPE cells. Models of retinal degeneration, including glaucoma and optic nerve injury, have demonstrated that NAD+ boosting via NR administration can ameliorate mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress, indirectly supporting its potential repurposing for dry AMD (Kitaoka et al., 2020; Mehmel et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2024). Moreover, clinical studies investigating NR’s safety in humans have shown that it is well tolerated at doses that elevate systemic NAD+ levels; doses in the gram-range have been employed without significant adverse effects (Jadeja et al., 2020). Although direct clinical trials targeting dry AMD are still forthcoming, the overall therapeutic history of NR—encompassing robust preclinical ocular benefit across neurodegenerative models and a favorable safety profile in human subjects—strongly supports further investigation for eye diseases where NAD+ depletion is a central pathophysiological feature (Dovijarski, 2019; Braidy et al., 2019; Pîrvu et al., 2021).

Mechanism of Action:  
The proposed mechanism of NR in dry AMD centers on its capacity to elevate intracellular NAD+ levels, thereby fueling a cascade of beneficial biochemical events. After cell entry, NR is phosphorylated by nicotinamide riboside kinases (NRKs) to generate NMN, which is subsequently converted to NAD+ through the activity of NMN adenylyltransferase. The resultant increase in NAD+ acts as a vital cofactor for sirtuins—primarily SIRT1 and SIRT3—which are NAD+-dependent deacetylases involved in regulating numerous cellular processes. SIRT1, in particular, has been implicated in deacetylating key transcription factors such as peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator-1α (PGC-1α) and transcription factor EB (TFEB). TFEB is a master regulator of lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy; its deacetylation leads to its nuclear translocation and binding to CLEAR (Coordinated Lysosomal Expression and Regulation) elements in the promoter regions of autophagy and lysosomal genes. Such activation promotes lysosomal acidification and increases the activity of hydrolases like cathepsin D, which are critical for the degradation of damaged proteins and organelles. Concurrently, SIRT3, which localizes predominantly to mitochondria, enhances mitochondrial function by deacetylating enzymes crucial for mitochondrial bioenergetics and reactive oxygen species (ROS) detoxification. The overall effect of NR supplementation is therefore hypothesized to be a restoration of cellular homeostasis in RPE cells—improving both autophagic clearance and mitochondrial function, two processes known to be compromised in dry AMD (Kitaoka et al., 2020; Mehmel et al., 2020; Lin & Apte, 2018; Jadeja et al., 2020). Such a mechanism is consistent with a substantial body of literature demonstrating that the NAD+-sirtuin axis plays a critical role in regulating neuroprotective and anti-aging functions across various tissues (Dovijarski, 2019; Jadeja et al., 2018; Pîrvu et al., 2021).

At the molecular level, the cascade initiated by NR begins with its metabolic conversion to NAD+, which then serves as an essential substrate for SIRT1 activation. This process is expected to boost cathepsin D activity and overall lysosomal proteolytic function. Parallel activation of SIRT3 in mitochondria further strengthens cellular defenses by enhancing mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation and reducing ROS generation through deacetylation of key metabolic enzymes. An overall evaluation of NR as a candidate for treating dry AMD reveals both promising strengths and areas requiring further elucidation. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Trehalose is a naturally occurring non‐reducing disaccharide (molecular weight 342.3 Da) found broadly in microorganisms and invertebrates, widely used as a stabilizer and excipient in foods and pharmaceuticals, and formulated in ophthalmic solutions at 3% w/v (≈87.7 mM) for ocular surface applications (e.g., dry eye) (Cox et al., 2025, pp. 1–2). In mammalian cells, trehalose enters via fluid‐phase endocytosis at millimolar concentrations and has been repeatedly reported as an autophagy enhancer that can activate AMPK signaling, stimulate lysosomal activity, and augment autophagic flux across multiple tissues, including ocular tissues (RPE) and retina (Cox et al., 2025, pp. 1–2). In the context of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), trehalose has been deployed as a small‐molecule modulator of the lysosome–autophagy axis with proposed mTOR‐independent activation of TFEB, the master transcriptional regulator of lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy (CLEAR network), positioning it mechanistically distinct from direct mTORC1 inhibitors such as rapamycin (Ghosh et al., 2024, p. 6; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 10–11). Topical ophthalmic trehalose is generally well tolerated, and preclinical studies show no overt ocular toxicity at 3% or 9% w/v after twice-daily dosing for up to two weeks, supporting feasibility for posterior segment delivery strategies; Raman spectroscopy has detected trehalose in RPE/choroid after repeated topical dosing, although posterior penetration is variable (Cox et al., 2025, pp. 8–10).

Therapeutic History  
Preclinical evidence in RPE and retina  
- Human RPE cell line (ARPE-19) oxidative stress model: Trehalose upregulates autophagy markers (LC3-II, p62/SQSTM1), increases TFEB protein and autophagy gene transcripts (ATG5, ATG7), and elevates lysosomal markers including LAMP2 and Cathepsin D (CTSD) protein; importantly, trehalose pretreatment confers cytoprotection against hydroquinone (HQ)-induced oxidative injury, and this protection is abolished by ATG5 knockdown, demonstrating autophagy dependence (typical dosing 50 mM trehalose; HQ 50 μM) (Abokyi et al., 2020, pp. 1–2, 9–11, 11–12, 12–13, 15–16). Dose–response caveats were noted: higher trehalose concentrations (≥100 mM) lost cytoprotection and were associated with stronger LC3-II accumulation, suggesting risk from excessive autophagy activation (Abokyi et al., 2020, pp. 11–12, 15–16).  
- Primary murine RPE in vitro: A non‐toxic trehalose dose (12.5 mM) increased autophagic flux measured by tandem GFP–RFP-LC3B, increasing RFP+ autolysosomes and RFP:GFP ratios without accumulating GFP+ autophagosomes, with colocalization to LysoTracker+ acidic compartments; trehalose also attenuated H₂O₂-induced mitochondrial superoxide and restored maximal respiration (Cox et al., 2025, pp. 7–10). These data indicate trehalose enhances autophagosome–lysosome fusion and downstream degradative flux in RPE under oxidative stress (Cox et al., 2025, pp. 7–10).  
- iPSC-derived human RPE carrying the CFH Y402H risk allele (CFH (H/H)): Trehalose (100 mM, 20–48 h) restored levels and enzymatic activities of lysosomal hydrolases Cathepsin D and Cathepsin L and rescued LAMP1 in complement challenge models, phenocopying constitutively nuclear TFEB (TFEB-S467A) and AKT2 inhibition; these data support trehalose as an mTOR-independent TFEB activator that rejuvenates lysosomal function in AMD-relevant RPE (Ghosh et al., 2024, p. 6; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 10–11).

- Mechanistic Go: Demonstration in RPE that trehalose increases the TFEB nuclear index by >2-fold, lowers lysosomal pH toward physiological values, and increases CTSD activity by >30% over disease-state baseline, with concordant increases in LC3B–LAMP1 colocalization and p62 degradation; abrogation of effects by TFEB knockdown would confirm mechanism (Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 10–11; Cox et al., 2025, pp. 7–8; Boya et al., 2023, pp. 3–4).

- Safety Go: No evidence of autophagy-associated cytotoxicity at the intended exposure (maintained viability; absence of excessive LC3-II accumulation without flux; ocular histopathology clean) (Abokyi et al., 2020, pp. 15–16; Cox et al., 2025, pp. 8–10).

The totality of evidence supports trehalose as a plausible, repurposable modulator of the TFEB–lysosome/autophagy axis in the RPE with multiple independent signals of autophagy flux enhancement, lysosomal hydrolase restoration (CTSD/L), and cytoprotection in oxidative/complement stress contexts, delivered via mechanisms that appear mTOR-independent and therefore potentially safer than broad mTORC1 inhibition (Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 10–11; Cox et al., 2025, pp. 7–8; Abokyi et al., 2020, pp. 1–2; Ghosh et al., 2023, pp. 11–15). However, the hypothesis’s most stringent claims—quantitative restoration of lysosomal acidification, trehalose-driven TFEB nuclear translocation in RPE, and direct lipofuscin/A2E clearance leading to slowed geographic atrophy progression—are not yet demonstrated in the supplied literature and require targeted mechanistic and disease-model validation (Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 10–11; Abokyi et al., 2020, pp. 16–17; Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7; Cox et al., 2025, pp. 8–10). Given strong biological plausibility and encouraging preclinical signals, a focused IND-enabling program that closes these gaps is justified, with early emphasis on mechanistic biomarkers (lysosomal pH, TFEB nuclear index, CTSD activity), pharmacokinetics of posterior delivery, and chronic AMD-relevant efficacy models before advancing to clinical study in GA (Boya et al., 2023, pp. 3–4; Cox et al., 2025, pp. 10–13; Ghosh et al., 2024, p. 6).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
USP14 inhibitor IU1 (Sigma SML0010) is a synthetic small-molecule compound originally discovered through high-throughput screening efforts aimed at identifying inhibitors of deubiquitinating enzymes (DUBs) associated with the proteasome. IU1 belongs to the class of small-molecule DUB inhibitors that specifically target USP14, a proteasome-associated deubiquitinase responsible for trimming ubiquitin chains from substrates before their degradation by the 26S proteasome. Early medicinal chemistry studies led to the development of IU1 and its more potent analogs (such as IU1-47), which exploit structure–activity relationships on a benzene–dimethyl-pyrrole scaffold with tailored electron-withdrawing substitutions and lipophilic enhancements designed to improve potency, selectivity, and bioavailability (Lim et al., 2024; Boselli et al., 2017; Qin et al., 2024). These compounds are cell permeable and have been employed as chemical probes in multiple preclinical settings to modulate proteostasis via targeted inhibition of USP14. In essence, IU1 reflects a series of rationally designed molecules aimed at shifting the balance of proteasome-mediated degradation by preventing USP14’s “trimming” activity, thereby effectively accelerating the clearance of misfolded and aggregation-prone proteins.

Therapeutic History:  
The therapeutic history of USP14 inhibitors like IU1 is primarily rooted in preclinical research addressing proteostasis dysfunction in models of aging and neurodegeneration rather than in clinical or veterinary practice. In Drosophila models of proteostasis-associated aging, IU1 treatment was shown to reduce the accumulation of polyubiquitinated aggregates, increase autophagy markers such as LC3, improve behavioral phenotypes, and even extend lifespan, with these benefits abrogated when autophagy was experimentally disrupted (Lim et al., 2024). In mammalian cell proteotoxicity models—using stressors such as canavanine plus azetidine—IU1 has similarly been reported to reduce ubiquitin conjugate accumulation and enhance autophagic responses (Lim et al., 2024). Moreover, in primary neuronal cultures, more potent analogs like IU1-47 have been used to promote degradation of pathologic proteins such as tau, thereby supporting the concept that USP14 inhibition enhances proteasome-assisted clearance of aggregation-prone substrates (Boselli et al., 2017; Kiprowska, 2016). Despite these promising preclinical data in models of neurodegeneration and systemic aging, there is no direct evidence to date that IU1 or its analogs have been applied to treat dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or geographic atrophy specifically. However, given that several key observations in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells—such as evidence of impaired ubiquitin–proteasome system (UPS) and autophagy cross-talk, aggregate accumulation, and lysosomal dysfunction—are central to AMD pathology (Blasiak et al., 2019; Kaarniranta et al., 2023; Shang & Taylor, 2012), repurposing IU1 to restore proteostasis in RPE represents an innovative extension of its preclinical use.

Mechanism of Action:  
The known mechanism of IU1 centers on its inhibition of USP14, a deubiquitinating enzyme that transiently associates with the proteasome. USP14 normally functions by “trimming” ubiquitin chains on substrates as they enter the proteasome, an activity that can delay substrate degradation and allow for substrate rescue under stress conditions. IU1 and its optimized analogs (e.g., IU1-47) act through allosteric mechanisms—not by directly competing at the catalytic site but by binding a pocket distal (approximately 8.3 Å away) from the catalytic center, thereby perturbing USP14’s structural conformation and catalytic efficiency (Qin et al., 2024; Lim et al., 2024). Inhibition of USP14 by IU1 leads to a reduced removal of ubiquitin chains, effectively “locking in” the ubiquitin tag on misfolded and aggregation-prone proteins and facilitating their recognition and degradation by the 26S proteasome. Beyond its direct impact on proteasomal degradation, USP14 inhibition has been reported to modulate autophagy—evident from increased LC3 lipidation and autophagic flux in certain cellular contexts (Lim et al., 2024; Kim, 2020). Some studies suggest that USP14 may also indirectly influence autophagy by regulating the turnover of factors such as UVRAG, a key autophagy regulator, although these connections remain to be fully elucidated. Notably, while IU1 has been shown to accelerate aggregate clearance in neuronal and Drosophila models, a series of studies have also flagged potential off-target effects at higher concentrations, including inhibition of mitochondrial Complex I leading to ATP depletion and subsequent activation of calpain-mediated proteolysis (Kiprowska, 2016; Kiprowska et al., n.d.). Hence, the molecular interactions of IU1 are complex and highly context-dependent, with the potential to both enhance proteasomal degradation and, at non-optimized doses, induce metabolic perturbations.

Expected Effect:  
In the context of dry age-related macular degeneration, particularly geographic atrophy, the central hypothesis is that IU1 will inhibit USP14 in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells, thereby accelerating the proteasome-assisted clearance of misfolded, aggregation-prone proteins. RPE cells in AMD display defects in both the UPS and the autophagy/lysosomal systems, with studies documenting decreased proteasome activity, accumulation of ubiquitinated aggregates, elevated levels of the selective autophagy adaptor SQSTM1/p62, and lysosomal dysfunction including impaired acidification mediated by vacuolar ATPase (v-ATPase) (Blasiak et al., 2019; Kaarniranta et al., 2023; Shang & Taylor, 2012; Viiri, 2019). By inhibiting USP14, IU1 is expected to shift the proteostasis balance in RPE cells towards enhanced degradation of misfolded proteins via the proteasome. This would not only reduce the intracellular aggregate burden but also alleviate the overloading of the lysosomal pathway—in turn potentially restoring lysosomal functions such as proper acidification by v-ATPase activity. Improved lysosomal acidification is known to facilitate the maturation and activity of cathepsin D, a key lysosomal protease responsible for degrading various protein aggregates and damaged organelles (Kaarniranta et al., 2023). Moreover, preclinical findings in neuronal cells have demonstrated that USP14 inhibition reduces aggregate load (e.g., tau) and promotes autophagic flux (Boselli et al., 2017; Lim et al., 2024), lending indirect support to the concept that these effects might be recapitulated in RPE cells. Although no direct data exist for IU1 in RPE, the mechanistic parallels between proteostasis impairment in neurons and RPE—as documented in extensive AMD literature—suggest that IU1 could reduce aggregate accumulation and oxidative stress in RPE, thereby slowing the progression of geographic atrophy.

Overall Evaluation:  
The overall evaluation of USP14 inhibitor IU1 as a therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration is cautiously optimistic yet highlights several critical areas for further investigation. On the positive side, IU1 represents an innovative strategy targeting a central node in protein quality control—USP14—that regulates the degradation of misfolded, aggregation-prone proteins via the proteasome and modulates autophagic pathways. Preclinical evidence in Drosophila models and neuronal cultures demonstrates that pharmacological USP14 inhibition can enhance aggregate clearance, improve proteostasis, and even extend lifespan and motor function under proteotoxic stress conditions (Lim et al., 2024; Boselli et al., 2017). These findings support the concept that modulating the UPS–autophagy interplay may be beneficial in diseases where proteostasis failure is a key driver, such as dry AMD, in which RPE cells experience aggregate build-up, defective autophagy, and lysosomal dysfunction (Blasiak et al., 2019; Kaarniranta et al., 2023; Shang & Taylor, 2012).

Furthermore, the biochemical mechanism by which IU1 operates—namely, reducing the deubiquitinating activity of USP14 to promote ubiquitin-tag retention and substrate commitment to degradation—provides a theoretically attractive approach to simultaneously reduce the proteasomal backlog and relieve lysosomal burden. The potential secondary effects on autophagy, including improved LC3-II turnover and possibly upregulated clearance of aggregates through aggrephagy, add further appeal to the candidate as a multi-modal modulator of proteostasis. The cell-permeable, small-molecule nature of IU1, along with available more potent analogs (such as IU1-47), offers promising opportunities for medicinal chemistry optimization and dosage refinement, especially important given the need for safe application in delicate ocular tissues.

However, several weaknesses and challenges must be addressed before IU1 can be considered a viable therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. A significant concern originates from studies in neuronal systems that indicate off-target effects at higher concentrations—specifically, inhibition of mitochondrial Complex I, ATP depletion, and activation of calpain-mediated proteolysis (Kiprowska, 2016; Kiprowska et al., n.d.). These potential toxicities raise the possibility that a narrow therapeutic window may exist, necessitating thorough dose-response studies in RPE cell models to ensure efficacy without compromising cell viability. Moreover, no direct preclinical studies have yet evaluated IU1 in RPE cells or in animal models of geographic atrophy. As such, critical parameters—such as its ability to modulate v-ATPase function, maintain lysosomal acidification, boost cathepsin D activity, and ultimately clear RPE-specific aggregates such as lipofuscin or oxidized photoreceptor debris—remain to be validated (Kaarniranta et al., 2023; Shang & Taylor, 2012).

Additionally, while the mechanistic data from neurodegenerative models are compelling, the biochemical environment of RPE cells differs from that of neurons in several key respects. RPE cells are highly phagocytic, exposed to constant oxidative stress, and rely on a finely tuned balance between proteasomal and lysosomal pathways to manage the constant influx of photoreceptor outer segment material (Blasiak et al., 2019; Viiri, 2019). Thus, any intervention that modulates proteostasis must be carefully tailored to avoid unintended disruptions in these homeostatic processes. The current literature also underscores the complexity of deubiquitinase biology; while USP14 inhibition appears beneficial in some contexts, the intricate interplay with other DUBs and the broader UPS could lead to compensatory mechanisms that diminish the anticipated therapeutic effect or even trigger adverse consequences (Faber & Roepman, 2019; Kim, 2020).

In summary, USP14 inhibitor IU1 offers an innovative and potentially transformative approach to restoring proteostasis in RPE cells by enhancing proteasomal degradation and autophagic clearance of misfolded proteins—a strategy that directly addresses the pathobiology of dry AMD and geographic atrophy as defined by aggregate accumulation and lysosomal dysfunction (Lim et al., 2024; Blasiak et al., 2019; Kaarniranta et al., 2023). The strengths of this candidate include its robust preclinical data in non-RPE systems, its well-characterized mechanism of action, and its amenability to further chemical optimization. However, significant weaknesses, including potential off-target mitochondrial toxicity, an unestablished therapeutic window in RPE cells, and the lack of direct preclinical studies in AMD models, necessitate cautious and rigorous further investigation. To move forward, it will be essential to conduct targeted RPE-specific in vitro assays and in vivo studies—assessing proteasome activity, autophagy flux, lysosomal acidification (v-ATPase function), cathepsin D activity, and aggregate clearance—while carefully monitoring for cytotoxicity. Only with such detailed preclinical validation can the promise of IU1 as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD be fully assessed (Lim et al., 2024; Blasiak et al., 2019; Kiprowska, 2016; Shang & Taylor, 2012).
