Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
AZD9056 is a small‐molecule, orally active P2X7 receptor antagonist developed by AstraZeneca that belongs to the class of synthetic adamantane‐based compounds. Although its precise chemical structure has not been fully disclosed in the public domain, multiple reports indicate that it emerges from a medicinal chemistry program focused on adamantyl benzamide scaffolds discovered through high‐throughput screening and subsequent structure–activity relationship (SAR) optimization (Chrovian et al., 2014; Gunosewoyo et al., 2007). The compound is understood to maintain the essential adamantane moiety linked through a methylene spacer to an aromatic benzamide, which is thought to force a twist in the benzamide conformation critical for high P2X7 antagonism (Chrovian et al., 2014; Gunosewoyo et al., 2007). In general, the adamantane class of compounds has been explored for its lipophilic and sterically constrained properties that can impart favorable bioavailability and receptor selectivity; indeed, the adamantane scaffold has also been exploited in a number of antiviral and anti-inflammatory agents. In the case of AZD9056, this design strategy was implemented to yield a molecule that potently blocks the ATP‐driven activity of the P2X7 receptor—a ligand‐gated ion channel implicated in inflammation and cell death—while offering the oral bioavailability and acceptable pharmacokinetic properties required for systemic application (Chrovian et al., 2014; Eser et al., 2015). The overall discovery process appears to have combined hit identification with parallel synthetic approaches in order to establish an SAR profile that ultimately led to a candidate with nanomolar potency in cell‐based assays of P2X7 function, such as inhibition of Bz-ATP–induced Ca2+ influx and dye uptake, although the specific synthetic steps remain proprietary (Chrovian et al., 2014; Gunosewoyo et al., 2007).  

Therapeutic History:  
AZD9056 has been evaluated extensively in non‐ocular inflammatory disease contexts. Early-phase clinical trials established its safety and tolerability in healthy volunteers through single- and multiple-dose studies that characterized its pharmacokinetic profile, with parameters such as a moderate oral bioavailability (~62%), a terminal half-life in the range of 16–18 hours, and the capacity for once-daily dosing (Arulkumaran et al., 2011). Its development program initially focused on rheumatoid arthritis (RA). In a 4-week phase IIa trial in RA patients, AZD9056 was found to be safe and well tolerated at the doses assessed, and target engagement was evidenced by significant inhibition of ex vivo ATP-induced monocyte IL-1β release (Chrovian et al., 2014). However, a subsequent larger phase IIb study in RA, enrolling up to 385 or more patients and including an open etanercept comparator arm, failed to demonstrate superior clinical efficacy over placebo across several objective endpoints, even though tolerability remained acceptable (Arulkumaran et al., 2011; Chrovian et al., 2014; Lepre et al., 2023). In parallel with its RA development, AZD9056 also underwent evaluation for inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), specifically in patients with Crohn's disease, where a phase IIa trial using a 200 mg once-daily regimen showed nominal improvements in the Crohn’s Disease Activity Index (CDAI) but no accompanying improvement in inflammatory biomarkers (Arulkumaran et al., 2011; Rech et al., 2016). Aside from these clinical endeavors in systemic inflammatory disorders, a dedicated ocular safety study was conducted in healthy volunteers; in this randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover study, retinal function was directly assessed by measures including electroretinography and visual acuity—an indication that the eye was considered as a potential compartment of interest, even though no efficacy studies in ocular disease states such as dry age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD) have been reported (Arulkumaran et al., 2011). Overall, while the compound has been repurposed extensively for anti-inflammatory indications and has an established human safety profile, its clinical history thus far has not included a trial specifically targeting dry AMD or any direct veterinary employments for ocular diseases (Arulkumaran et al., 2011; Guile et al., 2009).  

Mechanism of Action:  
The P2X7 receptor (P2X7R) is an ATP-gated, nonselective cation channel predominantly expressed on immune cells and, importantly for the intended application, on the retinal pigmented epithelium (RPE) (Calzaferri et al., 2020). Under physiological conditions, P2X7R is quiescent; however, in the presence of elevated extracellular ATP—a phenomenon noted in inflammatory and degenerative conditions, including AMD—the receptor becomes activated, mediating several deleterious downstream events. Upon activation, P2X7R undergoes a conformational change that not only allows the influx of Ca2+ and Na+ but also promotes the formation of large membrane pores owing to its ability to transition into a state that permits the passage of molecules as large as 900 Da (Chrovian et al., 2014; Eser et al., 2015). This pore formation results in cytotoxic calcium overload and is directly linked to the activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome, a multiprotein complex responsible for the processing of pro-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-1β and IL-18 (Calzaferri et al., 2020; Gu & Wiley, 2018). In the retinal pigment epithelium, this ATP-driven activation has been shown to contribute to lysosomal alkalization—a process that impairs the optimal acidic environment required by lysosomal enzymes, including cathepsins—and ultimately leads to defective clearance of cellular debris (Calzaferri et al., 2020; Tempest-Roe, 2017). Specifically, experimental studies in ARPE-19 cells (a human RPE cell line) have demonstrated that stimulation of P2X7 induces lysosomal dysfunction; conversely, pharmacological inhibition of P2X7 using antagonists such as Brilliant Blue G (BBG) can reverse this lysosomal impairment (Tempest-Roe, 2017). Mechanistically, AZD9056 is designed to bind to the P2X7 receptor with high potency and selectivity, thereby preventing the receptor’s activation by ATP. By doing so, it is anticipated to block the cascade of events that lead from receptor activation to pore formation, inflammasome assembly, and subsequent IL-1β release (Calzaferri et al., 2020; Gu & Wiley, 2018; Lee et al., 2023). Although the exact molecular binding mode of AZD9056 has not been detailed in available literature, it is presumed to interact with key residues involved in channel gating and pore formation, thereby stabilizing the receptor in a closed, inactive conformation (Chrovian et al., 2014; Lee et al., 2023). Additionally, its ability to reduce ex vivo ATP-induced monocyte IL-1β release in healthy volunteers has served as a functional biomarker for target engagement, reinforcing the hypothesis that P2X7 antagonism can modulate inflammasome-driven inflammatory signaling (Chrovian et al., 2014; Lee et al., 2023).  

Expected Effect:  
In the context of dry age-related macular degeneration, the central hypothesis for repurposing AZD9056 is that it will antagonize P2X7 receptors on retinal pigmented epithelium cells, thereby preventing a cascade of ATP-driven pathological events. Elevated extracellular ATP levels have been documented in the vitreous of AMD patients, which suggests a pathological activation of purinergic signaling in the retina (Calzaferri et al., 2020). When ATP activates P2X7 receptors on RPE cells, it leads to two major deleterious outcomes. First, the receptor’s activation results in sustained Ca2+ influx and large pore formation, triggering cytotoxicity and subsequent cell death mechanisms, including apoptotic and inflammasome-dependent cell death pathways (Calzaferri et al., 2020; Gu & Wiley, 2018). Second, P2X7 activation has been mechanistically linked to lysosomal alkalization in RPE cells, which impairs the activity of lysosomal proteases such as cathepsin D; this enzyme is critical for the degradation of photoreceptor outer segments and other cellular debris (Gu & Wiley, 2018; Tempest-Roe, 2017). The hypothesis posits that by blocking P2X7 receptor activation with AZD9056, one would preserve the normal acidic environment of the lysosomes, thereby maintaining or even restoring optimal cathepsin D activity. In turn, these effects are anticipated to protect the RPE from inflammasome-mediated apoptosis and lysosomal dysfunction, which are key drivers of geographic atrophy, the advanced clinical manifestation of dry AMD (Gu & Wiley, 2018; Calzaferri et al., 2020). Preclinical studies support the role of P2X7 in mediating RPE degeneration; for example, genetic knockout of P2X7 in mouse models has been shown to protect against Alu RNA-induced RPE toxicity, an established model of dry AMD pathology (Calzaferri et al., 2020; Gu & Wiley, 2018). Furthermore, in vitro studies using human RPE cell cultures have indicated that P2X7 receptor blockade can reverse lysosomal impairment, suggesting that AZD9056 could produce measurable improvements in functional assays that evaluate lysosomal protease activity, such as cathepsin D activity assays, and overall RPE viability assays (Calzaferri et al., 2020; Tempest-Roe, 2017). Ultimately, if the protective effects seen in preclinical studies translate into the clinical setting, AZD9056 may reduce the accumulation of undigested cellular debris (drusen) and slow or halt the progression of geographic atrophy in patients with dry AMD by dampening the inflamed state and preserving RPE function (Calzaferri et al., 2020; Gu & Wiley, 2018).  

Overall Evaluation:  
From a drug development perspective, the repurposing of AZD9056 for dry AMD presents a compelling but challenging opportunity. One of the primary strengths of this therapeutic candidate lies in its robust mechanistic rationale. The P2X7 receptor plays a central role in mediating ATP-induced inflammasome activation, lysosomal dysfunction, and subsequent RPE cell death—pathophysiological processes that have been repeatedly implicated in dry AMD and geographic atrophy models (Calzaferri et al., 2020; Gu & Wiley, 2018; Tempest-Roe, 2017). The ability of P2X7 antagonists to block these processes has been demonstrated in various in vitro and in vivo models, where blockade of the receptor reduces IL-1β release, reverses lysosomal alkalization, and confers protection against RPE degeneration (Calzaferri et al., 2020; Gu & Wiley, 2018; Tempest-Roe, 2017). Furthermore, AZD9056 has gone through extensive clinical safety evaluations in multiple inflammatory disease indications; its pharmacokinetic profile—characterized by acceptable oral bioavailability and a half-life conducive to once-daily dosing—has been well established in early phase studies (Arulkumaran et al., 2011; Chrovian et al., 2014). This pre-existing clinical safety data is an asset in reducing the risk profile typically associated with novel drug candidates and may streamline early-stage clinical trial designs for an ocular indication. Additionally, preliminary ocular safety assessments in healthy volunteers, which included measures such as retinal electroretinography and visual acuity testing, suggest that systemic administration of AZD9056 does not produce overt ocular toxicity—an encouraging sign for its potential repurposing in dry AMD (Arulkumaran et al., 2011).  

Nevertheless, there are several notable limitations and challenges associated with using AZD9056 in the treatment of dry AMD. First, the prior clinical development history of AZD9056 in rheumatoid arthritis and Crohn’s disease revealed limited or inconsistent efficacy despite demonstrable target engagement. In the phase IIb studies for RA, the compound failed to outperform placebo across objective outcome measures even though safety endpoints were met (Arulkumaran et al., 2011; Chrovian et al., 2014). This raises concerns about whether P2X7 receptor blockade alone is sufficient to generate a meaningful clinical outcome, particularly in a complex and multifactorial disease process such as dry AMD. Moreover, the inflammatory milieu in rheumatoid arthritis or IBD differs significantly from that in the retina, and systemic inflammation may not accurately recapitulate the localized, chronic degenerative processes occurring in the RPE (Arulkumaran et al., 2011; Guile et al., 2009).  

Another concern relates to the dual and sometimes paradoxical roles of the P2X7 receptor. While its pathological activation is linked to pro-inflammatory signaling, P2X7 also appears to have a scavenger or phagocytic function under conditions of low ATP levels (Calzaferri et al., 2020; Newman, 2024). In the context of the RPE, which is specialized for high-volume phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments, complete blockade of P2X7 might inadvertently impair beneficial clearance processes that serve to prevent debris accumulation. In animal models, alternative data has shown that the loss of P2X7 function can result in changes reminiscent of early AMD, such as reduced phagocytosis, suggesting that finely balanced modulation rather than total inhibition may be necessary (Calzaferri et al., 2020; Gu & Wiley, 2018). Such duality underscores the potential risk that while AZD9056 may ameliorate inflammasome activation and lysosomal destabilization, it might simultaneously disrupt physiologic functions of RPE cells that are critical for maintaining retinal homeostasis.  

The lack of direct evidence for AZD9056’s efficacy in ocular models of dry AMD is another major gap. While the preclinical literature supports a role for P2X7 signaling in RPE dysfunction and geographic atrophy (Calzaferri et al., 2020; Tempest-Roe, 2017), the specific application of AZD9056 in these models remains largely inferential. There are no published studies documenting that AZD9056, when administered at doses achieving retinal penetration, effectively preserves cathepsin D activity or prevents RPE cell death in animal models of dry AMD. Furthermore, the translation of systemic pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic data to ocular compartments is nontrivial; disparities in drug distribution, blood–retinal barrier permeability, and local metabolism could limit effective target engagement in the retina even if systemic safety is acceptable (Arulkumaran et al., 2011). The undisclosed chemical structure of AZD9056 also complicates any efforts to optimize the compound specifically for ocular bioavailability or to better understand its off-target profile relative to other P2X7 antagonists that have been more thoroughly characterized in the literature (Chrovian et al., 2014; Gunosewoyo et al., 2007).  

In summary, the overall evaluation of AZD9056 for treatment of dry AMD is one of cautious enthusiasm tempered by several unresolved questions. On the strength side, the compound leverages a clear mechanistic rationale by antagonizing the P2X7 receptor—a key mediator of ATP-induced inflammasome activation and lysosomal dysfunction known to be active in the RPE of AMD patients—and it comes with an established clinical safety record in inflammatory disorders (Calzaferri et al., 2020; Chrovian et al., 2014; Gu & Wiley, 2018). Its ability to suppress IL-1β release in ex vivo assays supports its functional engagement with the P2X7/IL-1β pathway, and preclinical data suggest that P2X7 inhibition can protect against RPE degeneration (Gu & Wiley, 2018; Tempest-Roe, 2017). However, significant challenges persist: prior clinical trials in RA and IBD have yielded mixed efficacy results, casting doubt on whether P2X7 blockade alone can significantly modify disease progression in complex conditions; the potential for interference with beneficial receptor functions in the RPE may compromise its utility; and the lack of direct preclinical data in dry AMD models means that much of the benefit remains theoretical at this stage (Arulkumaran et al., 2011; Chrovian et al., 2014; Gu & Wiley, 2018; Territo & Zarrinmayeh, 2021). Additionally, uncertainties related to ocular pharmacokinetics and the inability to adjust the synthetic structure for improved retinal targeting (given the proprietary nature of the molecule’s chemistry) further complicate its repositioning for an ocular indication (Chrovian et al., 2014; Eser et al., 2015).  

Given the current state of the literature, it would be advisable to conduct targeted preclinical studies that specifically address the effects of AZD9056 on RPE cells and retinal tissue. These studies should include assays for lysosomal pH stability, cathepsin D activity, inflammasome assembly (e.g., NLRP3 activation and caspase-1 processing), and overall RPE cell viability under conditions of ATP stress. Furthermore, careful evaluation of retinal drug levels following systemic dosing—or the development of a topical formulation—might be necessary to ensure that sufficient drug concentrations can be achieved in the retina without systemic toxicity. A parallel investigation into the potential compensatory roles of P2X7 in RPE phagocytosis would also be warranted to minimize any risk of disrupting beneficial cellular functions (Calzaferri et al., 2020; Gu & Wiley, 2018; Arulkumaran et al., 2011).  

Overall, while AZD9056’s strong mechanistic basis and favorable early-phase clinical safety profile make it an attractive candidate for repurposing, the translational challenges and previous clinical setbacks in other indications necessitate rigorous preclinical validation in dry AMD models before further clinical development is considered. The compound’s capacity to specifically maintain lysosomal function and cathepsin D activity in the RPE represents a promising therapeutic opportunity if these effects can be reliably recapitulated in the ocular setting. However, caution is advised due to the dual roles of P2X7 signaling in both pathological and physiologic processes and the potential non-optimal receptor occupancy in the retina. In conclusion, the repurposing of AZD9056 for dry AMD holds potential but would require a focused, mechanistically guided preclinical program to address the unique challenges posed by the ocular environment and the complex biology of the P2X7 receptor (Arulkumaran et al., 2011; Chrovian et al., 2014; Calzaferri et al., 2020; Tempest-Roe, 2017).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Tocilizumab (Actemra; Roche/Chugai) is a recombinant humanized monoclonal antibody that binds the human interleukin-6 receptor (IL-6R) and blocks IL-6 signal transduction, resulting in systemic anti-inflammatory effects characteristic of IL-6 pathway inhibition (class: humanized anti-IL-6R monoclonal antibody) (Shi, 2017a; Shi, 2017b; Zhujiang Hospital, 2025). In clinical development, tocilizumab has been administered intravenously at 8 mg/kg every 4 weeks and subcutaneously at 162 mg once weekly, with protocols reflecting the infectious, hepatic, hematologic, gastrointestinal, and reproductive safety considerations common to cytokine-targeted biologics (e.g., TB/hepatitis screening, neutrophil/platelet and transaminase thresholds, live-vaccine restrictions, diverticulitis history, and contraception requirements) (Shi, 2017b; University of Nebraska, 2016; Assistance Publique–Hôpitaux de Paris, 2017; Zhujiang Hospital, 2025). Ophthalmic interest in IL-6 blockade is evidenced by prospective trials in non-infectious uveitis and a withdrawn diabetic macular edema (DME) trial; those records establish feasible dosing, ophthalmic outcome collection, and safety oversight but do not provide efficacy data in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (Assistance Publique–Hôpitaux de Paris, 2017; University of Nebraska, 2016). At the disease-biology level, multiple clinical and literature-derived evidences associate IL-6 with AMD, including elevated ocular and systemic IL-6 in AMD populations and genetic associations in some cohorts; Open Targets ranks IL6 as the strongest among selected IL-6 pathway members for AMD relevance in the provided excerpt (Buniello et al., 2025).

Therapeutic History  
Systemic uses and ophthalmic experience: Tocilizumab’s IL-6R blockade is well characterized clinically outside ophthalmology, and controlled ophthalmic trials have evaluated systemic tocilizumab as an investigational agent for posterior-segment, non-infectious uveitis (RUBI), using subcutaneous 162 mg weekly for 16 weeks with retinal structural and visual endpoints and active safety monitoring; the study is listed as completed in the registry excerpt but outcome data are not included here (Assistance Publique–Hôpitaux de Paris, 2017). A single-center, open-label Behçet’s uveitis trial planned to assess 6 months of tocilizumab while maintaining background immunosuppression, but it enrolled only three participants and was terminated early based on its measured outcomes, limiting inferences on efficacy; this protocol reiterates standard immunosuppression-related exclusions (active TB/hepatitis, malignancy, pregnancy) (Zheng, 2018). In DME, the READ-4 protocol designed a Phase 2 evaluation of monthly IV tocilizumab (8 mg/kg) alone or combined with monthly intravitreal ranibizumab through Month 6, with safety and OCT central retinal thickness as primary outcomes; the trial was withdrawn before enrollment due to loss of funding, yielding no clinical data (University of Nebraska, 2016). A registry query identified 10 ClinicalTrials.gov records linking “tocilizumab” with retina/macular degeneration terms, but no identifiers or results are available in the excerpt to inform AMD-specific evidence (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.). Beyond retinal disease, randomized and single-arm neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (NMOSD) studies used IV tocilizumab 8 mg/kg every 4 weeks (or every 4–6 weeks) and incorporated ocular structural and visual function endpoints among secondaries; these trials demonstrate feasibility of systemic dosing with ophthalmic measurements but are mechanistically distinct from retinal degenerations such as dry AMD (Shi, 2017b; Shi, 2017a). Collectively, the corpus establishes operational feasibility and safety monitoring frameworks for systemic tocilizumab in ophthalmic settings but contains no clinical evidence in dry AMD (University of Nebraska, 2016; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).

Mechanism of Action  
Drug mechanism: Tocilizumab is a humanized monoclonal antibody that binds to IL-6R and blocks IL-6 signaling, thereby attenuating inflammatory pathways downstream of IL-6R engagement; mechanistic rationales in non-retinal disease emphasize IL-6–dependent survival and differentiation programs (e.g., plasma cells and autoantibody production in NMOSD), with dosing typically at 8 mg/kg IV every 4 weeks or 162 mg SC weekly in the studies cited (Shi, 2017a; Shi, 2017b; Assistance Publique–Hôpitaux de Paris, 2017).

Retinal IL-6 biology and RPE sources/targets: Multiple lines of evidence link IL-6 to AMD: clinical reports of elevated serum and ocular IL-6 in AMD versus controls, genetic association signals in some cohorts, and IL-6’s role in inflammation and neovascularization in advanced disease; Open Targets assigns IL6 the strongest association among queried IL-6 pathway components in the excerpt, while evidence for STAT3 and IL6ST is comparatively weak (Buniello et al., 2025). Human retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells produce IL-6, secrete it in a polarized manner, and can engage autocrine/paracrine IL-6/IL-8 loops that drive RPE degeneration after inflammatory challenge (e.g., bacterial endotoxin), supporting the presence of IL-6–responsive circuits in retinal epithelia (Brandstetter, 2016).

AMD-relevant upstream injury nodes: The dominant mechanistic framework for dry AMD implicates chronic oxidative/photooxidative stress, age-related lysosomal decline, and intracellular clearance failure (autophagy/proteasome) in RPE, leading to lipofuscinogenesis, lysosomal membrane permeabilization (LMP), and activation of inflammasome pathways with downstream cytokine release and cell death (apoptosis vs pyroptosis depending on priming) (Brandstetter, 2016; Piippo, 2019). In primary human RPE and ARPE-19 cells, LMP induced chemically (Leu-Leu-OMe) or via blue-light irradiation of POS-derived lipofuscin activates the NLRP3 inflammasome with caspase-1–dependent maturation and release of IL-1β and IL-18; broader cytokine secretion includes IL-6, GM-CSF, and GRO, with IL-6 elevated ≈13.6-fold in a cytokine screen and partially suppressed by caspase-1 inhibition, indicating a secondary induction downstream of inflammasome activation (not direct inflammasome processing) (Brandstetter, 2016). Cytokine release is apically polarized, and conditioned media from inflammasome-activated RPE is chemotactic for microglia, linking RPE lysosomal injury to neuroretinal immune activation (Brandstetter, 2016). Complement C5a serves as a physiologically relevant priming agent in RPE by activating NF-κB and inducing pro-IL-1β, which permits subsequent LMP-triggered NLRP3 activation; C5a priming and IL-1α priming also shift cell death from apoptosis to pyroptosis after lipofuscin phototoxicity (Brandstetter, 2016). Lysosomal proteases are mechanistically implicated: inhibition of cathepsin B and L suppresses LMP-triggered inflammasome activation in RPE, and cytosolic cathepsins in general, including cathepsin D, can promote apoptosis when released from the lysosome, underscoring the importance of lysosomal integrity in RPE survival (Brandstetter, 2016).

Intracellular clearance failure and mitochondrial stress as alternative inflammasome drivers: Independent RPE models that combine proteasome inhibition (MG-132) with autophagy/lysosome blockade (bafilomycin A₁) activate NLRP3 via oxidative stress, producing caspase-1–dependent IL-1β secretion without evidence that lysosomal rupture/cathepsin leakage is the primary driver; Hsp90 stabilizes NLRP3 in this setting, and Hsp90 inhibition promotes autophagic degradation of NLRP3 when autophagy remains functional (Piippo, 2019). Mitochondrial dysfunction induced by antimycin A activates both NLRP3 and AIM2 inflammasomes in human RPE lines via mitochondrial ROS and cytosolic DNA, with AIM2 showing dominant control of IL-1β/IL-18 in some contexts, broadening the repertoire of upstream hazards beyond lysosomal damage (Korhonen, 2024).

Mechanistic gaps for IL-6R control of lysosomes/autophagy: Crucially, the provided materials do not furnish direct mechanistic or biochemical evidence that IL-6 or IL-6R signaling modulates RPE autophagic flux, lysosomal acidification (v-ATPase function), or cathepsin D enzymatic activity, and several excerpts explicitly note the absence of IL-6R blockade studies interrogating autophagy/lysosome endpoints in RPE/AMD models (Buniello et al., 2025; Brandstetter, 2016). In additional RPE experiments modulating autophagy and p62/SQSTM1, cytokine shifts were observed for MCP-1 and IL-8, while IL-6 did not exhibit consistent dependency on p62 state, arguing against a simple autophagy→IL-6 coupling that would predict lysosomal rescue by IL-6R blockade (Korhonen, 2024). Within this corpus, IL-6 behaves as part of a downstream inflammatory secretome during RPE stress rather than an upstream determinant of lysosomal health (Brandstetter, 2016).

Expected Effect  
Assay-level expectations under AMD-relevant stress paradigms should be aligned with the causal structure supported by the evidence.

- What IL-6R blockade should do: Given that RPE secrete IL-6 and can engage IL-6/IL-8 autocrine degenerative signaling in inflammatory contexts, tocilizumab is expected to abrogate IL-6–dependent downstream signaling in RPE and neighboring cells, dampening IL-6–responsive gene expression and paracrine effects where IL-6 is a driver (Brandstetter, 2016). In LMP/blue-light or impaired-clearance inflammasome models, IL-6 is robustly induced alongside IL-1β/IL-18 and partially depends on caspase-1–driven pathways, so tocilizumab would be expected to reduce IL-6-mediated signaling outputs but would not suppress upstream lysosomal damage, cathepsin leakage, inflammasome assembly, or caspase-1 activation per se (Brandstetter, 2016). Because inflammasome activation in these models also reduces constitutive VEGF secretion and polarizes cytokine release apically, IL-6R blockade might modestly alter the inflammatory milieu without restoring basal angiogenic signaling from RPE or preventing microglial chemotaxis induced by the broader cytokine secretome (Brandstetter, 2016).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Fenofibrate is a synthetic small‐molecule drug belonging to the fibrate class of compounds, originally developed and approved for the treatment of dyslipidemia. It acts predominantly as a peroxisome proliferator‐activated receptor alpha (PPARα) agonist. Fenofibrate itself is a prodrug that undergoes hepatic esterase hydrolysis to form its active metabolite, fenofibric acid, which binds to PPARα and modulates the transcription of genes involved in lipid metabolism. This drug class has historically been used for lowering serum triglycerides and increasing high‐density lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol, reflecting its well‐established lipid‐modulating properties. Although fenofibrate was not initially developed for ocular indications, its mechanism as a PPARα agonist has spurred interest for repurposing in retinal diseases. In particular, the broad class of fibrates has garnered attention because PPARα is expressed in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), and its activation can regulate lipid oxidation, autophagy, and inflammatory processes—all of which are critically disturbed in dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) (Fu et al., 2019; Falcão et al., 2025).

Therapeutic History:  
Fenofibrate has a robust clinical history in the management of dyslipidemia and cardiovascular risk reduction, with extensive use in millions of patients worldwide. Its ocular benefits became apparent with large clinical trials, such as the FIELD and ACCORD Eye studies, which demonstrated that fenofibrate can reduce the progression of diabetic retinopathy and decrease the need for retinal laser therapy in diabetic patients (Lu et al., 2014; Treacy & Hurst, 2012). Although these trials primarily addressed diabetic retinal disease, subsequent preclinical and clinical reports have indicated that the retina may benefit from the lipid‐modulatory, anti‐inflammatory, and neuroprotective actions of PPARα agonists. For instance, several studies have explored fenofibrate in animal models of retinal ischemia and neovascularization, showing protective effects on the retinal vasculature and RPE (Fu et al., 2020; Qiu et al., 2017). While the majority of these ocular studies have focused on diabetic retinopathy or neovascular AMD, emerging literature has pointed to the potential of targeting PPARα signaling to mitigate RPE dysfunction and lipid accumulation, which are hallmarks of dry AMD (da Ana et al., 2023; Dou & Duerfeldt, 2020). This history of fenofibrate in retinal disease, combined with its proven clinical safety for dyslipidemia and established ocular pharmacokinetics (including studies on topical delivery), provides a compelling rationale for its repurposing in dry AMD (Tomita et al., 2020; Lee et al., 2021).

Mechanism of Action:  
Fenofibrate’s mechanism of action is rooted in its role as a PPARα agonist. Upon conversion to fenofibric acid, the compound binds to PPARα—a nuclear receptor highly expressed in several tissues, including the liver and the retinal pigment epithelium. When activated, PPARα forms heterodimers with retinoid X receptors (RXR) and binds to peroxisome proliferator response elements (PPREs) within the promoters of target genes. This binding results in the upregulation of genes critical for fatty acid uptake, β-oxidation, and lipid catabolism. Key genes regulated by PPARα include those encoding enzymes that facilitate mitochondrial and peroxisomal fatty acid oxidation, which in turn reduces intracellular lipid accumulation and promotes energy homeostasis (Fu et al., 2019; Lee et al., 2023).

In the context of the RPE and dry AMD, the hypothesis is that fenofibrate will stimulate PPARα-mediated transcriptional programs that not only enhance lipid catabolism but also intersect with cellular degradative pathways. One of the central tenets of the proposed mechanism is the coactivation of transcription factor EB (TFEB). TFEB is recognized as a master regulator of lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy through the coordinated lysosomal expression and regulation (CLEAR) network. Under normal conditions, TFEB is kept inactive in the cytosol by phosphorylation mediated by mTORC1. Under stress conditions or when lysosomal function is impaired, TFEB translocates to the nucleus to upregulate genes involved in lysosomal acidification, autophagy, and lipid metabolism. The therapeutic hypothesis posits that fenofibrate, through PPARα activation in RPE cells, will indirectly coactivate TFEB. This may occur through changes in cellular metabolism that reduce mTORC1 activity or via direct transcriptional crosstalk between PPARα target genes and the CLEAR network (Falcão et al., 2025; da Ana et al., 2023).

Moreover, TFEB activation is expected to enhance lysosomal acidification—a process necessary for optimal degradation of phagocytosed outer segment debris and drusen precursors—and upregulate lysosomal hydrolases such as cathepsin D. In AMD, RPE cells often show lysosomal dysfunction characterized by deficient cathepsin D activity and lipofuscin accumulation. By improving lysosomal function, fenofibrate may facilitate the clearance of lipid-rich drusen precursors, thereby reducing RPE stress and preventing progression of dry AMD (Falcão et al., 2025; da Ana et al., 2023). In addition to these lysosome-centric effects, fenofibrate has anti-inflammatory properties, as PPARα activation suppresses NF-κB signaling, reduces the expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines (e.g., TNF-α and IL-1β), and alleviates oxidative stress—all of which are exacerbating factors in the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Lee et al., 2023; Treacy & Hurst, 2012). Furthermore, the modulation of the FGF21 pathway, occasionally observed with fenofibrate treatment, may contribute to neuroprotection and further support retinal homeostasis (Tomita et al., 2020; Lee et al., 2023). Taken together, the molecular interactions initiated by fenofibrate converge on restoring lipid homeostasis, enhancing autophagic flux, and mitigating inflammatory insults in RPE cells—a multifaceted approach that aligns with the pathophysiology of dry AMD (Treacy & Hurst, 2012; Lee et al., 2021).

Expected Effect:  
In the assays proposed to evaluate fenofibrate’s efficacy for dry AMD, one anticipates several measurable cellular and biochemical outcomes. First, treatment of RPE cells with fenofibrate should lead to a consistent activation of PPARα target genes, as demonstrated by upregulation of markers for fatty acid oxidation and lipid catabolism. Such molecular signatures can be quantified using gene expression analyses and reporter assays for PPRE activity (Fu et al., 2019; Tomita et al., 2021). Concurrently, it is expected that fenofibrate will enhance autophagic flux in RPE cells. This could be evident from increased LC3-II accumulation in the presence of lysosomal inhibitors and enhanced degradation of autophagic substrates, which would indicate an upregulation of the autophagic machinery (Falcão et al., 2025; da Ana et al., 2023).

A critical aspect of the proposed mechanism involves TFEB. Upon fenofibrate treatment, one should observe increased nuclear translocation of TFEB in RPE cells, which can be assessed by immunocytochemistry and subcellular fractionation. The activation of TFEB would then be expected to drive the transcriptional upregulation of genes encoding lysosomal proteins, such as lysosomal-associated membrane protein 2 (LAMP2) and various components of the V-ATPase complex, leading to enhanced lysosomal acidification. Lysotracker assays and measurements of intralysosomal pH could be deployed to confirm that fenofibrate-treated cells exhibit more acidic lysosomes (Falcão et al., 2025; da Ana et al., 2023).

Furthermore, increased cathepsin D activity is a pivotal expected outcome, serving as a surrogate marker for improved lysosomal enzyme function in degrading waste products, including drusen precursors. Biochemical assays to quantify cathepsin D activity, alongside immunostaining for its protein levels, would help to validate this aspect of the mechanism. Functionally, the cumulative effect of these molecular changes should be a reduction in the accumulation of lipofuscin and other drusen-associated lipid-protein aggregates within the RPE. This reduction could be observed using autofluorescence imaging techniques and electron microscopy to assess cytoplasmic inclusions (Falcão et al., 2025; Treacy & Hurst, 2012).

Additionally, given that fenofibrate has established anti-inflammatory properties, one might expect a decrease in the secretion or expression of inflammatory mediators in RPE cultures, as well as improved cellular resistance to oxidative stress challenges. Cytokine assays and measurements of reactive oxygen species (ROS) would serve as corroborative evidence for an anti-inflammatory and antioxidant effect. Importantly, because reduced autophagy and lysosomal dysfunction are central to dry AMD, the combined effect of enhanced lipid catabolism, improved lysosomal acidification, and increased cathepsin D activity should contribute to an overall reduction in cellular stress and preservation of RPE integrity (Falcão et al., 2025; Treacy & Hurst, 2012). Taken together, these expected effects would validate the therapeutic hypothesis and provide a strong rationale for advancing fenofibrate into further preclinical models of dry AMD.

Overall Evaluation:  
Fenofibrate emerges as a promising repurposed drug candidate for dry AMD based on several compelling lines of evidence. The drug’s long-established clinical safety profile and extensive use in dyslipidemia serve as major strengths in terms of its translational potential (Lu et al., 2014; Treacy & Hurst, 2012). Additionally, the documented success of fenofibrate in slowing the progression of diabetic retinopathy in large-scale clinical trials underscores its ability to exert beneficial effects in retinal tissues (Lu et al., 2014; Treacy & Hurst, 2012).

From a mechanistic standpoint, fenofibrate’s mode of action as a PPARα agonist is well characterized, and its ability to stimulate lipid oxidation and enhance fatty acid metabolism could directly address the lipid dysregulation observed in RPE cells in dry AMD (Fu et al., 2019; da Ana et al., 2023). Crucially, the hypothesis that fenofibrate may also coactivate TFEB, thereby promoting lysosomal biogenesis and function, positions it uniquely among therapeutic candidates. Improved lysosomal acidification and increased cathepsin D activity would facilitate the clearance of drusen precursors and reduce the cytotoxic accumulation of lipofuscin, which is a central pathogenic feature of dry AMD (Falcão et al., 2025; da Ana et al., 2023; Dou & Duerfeldt, 2020). The convergence of lipid catabolism enhancement, autophagy upregulation, and anti-inflammatory effects creates a multifaceted therapeutic profile that is particularly attractive for a complex, multifactorial disease such as dry AMD.

However, there are also notable weaknesses and challenges. Most of the current evidence supporting fenofibrate’s retinal benefits is derived from studies focusing on diabetic retinopathy or neovascular AMD rather than directly on dry AMD. Although there is supportive mechanistic rationale linking PPARα activation to improved lysosomal function in the RPE, direct evidence for fenofibrate’s efficacy in reducing drusen accumulation and alleviating RPE stress in dry AMD models remains sparse (Dou & Duerfeldt, 2020; da Ana et al., 2023). The specific involvement of TFEB activation by fenofibrate in RPE cells has not been fully elucidated in the existing literature, and further in vitro and in vivo studies are needed to validate this aspect of the mechanism. Additionally, while fenofibrate is generally safe when used systemically, there have been concerns regarding potential renal side effects, which may be particularly relevant in the elderly population that predominantly suffers from AMD (Treacy & Hurst, 2012; Tomita et al., 2021). Thus, optimizing the route of delivery—possibly via topical formulations or nanoparticle-based systems—may be necessary to ensure sufficient retinal bioavailability while minimizing systemic exposure (Huang et al., 2021; Lu et al., 2014).

Another potential limitation is the dose required to achieve sufficient PPARα activation in the RPE to modulate TFEB and lysosomal pathways effectively. Preclinical studies have sometimes required relatively high doses of fenofibrate to observe significant ocular effects, and the pharmacokinetic barriers posed by the blood-retinal barrier may further complicate translatability (Tomita et al., 2020; Lee et al., 2023). Moreover, the current body of literature underscores the need for more targeted studies to determine whether the benefits seen with fenofibrate in models of diabetic retinopathy and neovascular AMD can be replicated in models of dry AMD, where the pathogenic processes are distinct in their emphasis on lipid accumulation, oxidative stress, and RPE dysfunction (da Ana et al., 2023; Dou & Duerfeldt, 2020).

Despite these challenges, the overall evaluation remains cautiously optimistic. Fenofibrate’s mechanism of action aligns well with the pathophysiological features of dry AMD, particularly regarding the restoration of lipid homeostasis and the enhancement of lysosomal function. The dual potential for direct metabolic benefits via PPARα activation and indirect benefits through TFEB-mediated lysosomal enhancement represents an innovative therapeutic strategy that could fill a critical gap in the current treatment landscape for dry AMD (Falcão et al., 2025; Fu et al., 2019; da Ana et al., 2023; Dou & Duerfeldt, 2020; Lee et al., 2023). Additionally, the availability of various delivery platforms—including systemic administration, topical eye drops, and nanoparticle formulations—provides flexibility in addressing bioavailability challenges and minimizing adverse effects (Huang et al., 2021; Lu et al., 2014).

In conclusion, fenofibrate (Sigma F6020) possesses significant potential for repurposing as a drug candidate for dry AMD based on its well-established pharmacological profile, robust clinical safety record, and mechanistic actions that target key pathological processes in the RPE. While further preclinical studies specifically focused on dry AMD models are warranted to validate the hypothesized coactivation of TFEB and subsequent enhancement of lysosomal acidification and cathepsin D activity, the current literature provides a strong scientific basis for such investigations. The strengths of fenofibrate lie in its multifaceted mechanism—encompassing lipid catabolism, autophagy, anti-inflammatory, and possibly neuroprotective effects—which collectively offer a promising strategy to reduce drusen precursors and mitigate RPE stress. The primary weaknesses involve the need for direct evidence in dry AMD models, optimization of ocular delivery to overcome pharmacokinetic barriers, and careful monitoring of potential systemic side effects in an elderly population. Overall, fenofibrate represents a compelling and scientifically sound candidate that merits further exploration in the context of dry AMD, with the potential to significantly advance our therapeutic arsenal against this currently untreatable form of macular degeneration (Falcão et al., 2025; Fu et al., 2019; da Ana et al., 2023; Dou & Duerfeldt, 2020; Lee et al., 2023).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
AZD9056 is a small‐molecule, orally active P2X7 receptor antagonist developed by AstraZeneca that belongs to the class of synthetic adamantane‐based compounds. Although its precise chemical structure has not been fully disclosed in the public domain, multiple reports indicate that it emerges from a medicinal chemistry program focused on adamantyl benzamide scaffolds discovered through high‐throughput screening and subsequent structure–activity relationship (SAR) optimization (Chrovian et al., 2014; Gunosewoyo et al., 2007). The compound is understood to maintain the essential adamantane moiety linked through a methylene spacer to an aromatic benzamide, which is thought to force a twist in the benzamide conformation critical for high P2X7 antagonism (Chrovian et al., 2014; Gunosewoyo et al., 2007). In general, the adamantane class of compounds has been explored for its lipophilic and sterically constrained properties that can impart favorable bioavailability and receptor selectivity; indeed, the adamantane scaffold has also been exploited in a number of antiviral and anti-inflammatory agents. In the case of AZD9056, this design strategy was implemented to yield a molecule that potently blocks the ATP‐driven activity of the P2X7 receptor—a ligand‐gated ion channel implicated in inflammation and cell death—while offering the oral bioavailability and acceptable pharmacokinetic properties required for systemic application (Chrovian et al., 2014; Eser et al., 2015). The overall discovery process appears to have combined hit identification with parallel synthetic approaches in order to establish an SAR profile that ultimately led to a candidate with nanomolar potency in cell‐based assays of P2X7 function, such as inhibition of Bz-ATP–induced Ca2+ influx and dye uptake, although the specific synthetic steps remain proprietary (Chrovian et al., 2014; Gunosewoyo et al., 2007).  

Therapeutic History:  
AZD9056 has been evaluated extensively in non‐ocular inflammatory disease contexts. Early-phase clinical trials established its safety and tolerability in healthy volunteers through single- and multiple-dose studies that characterized its pharmacokinetic profile, with parameters such as a moderate oral bioavailability (~62%), a terminal half-life in the range of 16–18 hours, and the capacity for once-daily dosing (Arulkumaran et al., 2011). Its development program initially focused on rheumatoid arthritis (RA). In a 4-week phase IIa trial in RA patients, AZD9056 was found to be safe and well tolerated at the doses assessed, and target engagement was evidenced by significant inhibition of ex vivo ATP-induced monocyte IL-1β release (Chrovian et al., 2014). However, a subsequent larger phase IIb study in RA, enrolling up to 385 or more patients and including an open etanercept comparator arm, failed to demonstrate superior clinical efficacy over placebo across several objective endpoints, even though tolerability remained acceptable (Arulkumaran et al., 2011; Chrovian et al., 2014; Lepre et al., 2023). In parallel with its RA development, AZD9056 also underwent evaluation for inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), specifically in patients with Crohn's disease, where a phase IIa trial using a 200 mg once-daily regimen showed nominal improvements in the Crohn’s Disease Activity Index (CDAI) but no accompanying improvement in inflammatory biomarkers (Arulkumaran et al., 2011; Rech et al., 2016). Aside from these clinical endeavors in systemic inflammatory disorders, a dedicated ocular safety study was conducted in healthy volunteers; in this randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover study, retinal function was directly assessed by measures including electroretinography and visual acuity—an indication that the eye was considered as a potential compartment of interest, even though no efficacy studies in ocular disease states such as dry age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD) have been reported (Arulkumaran et al., 2011). Overall, while the compound has been repurposed extensively for anti-inflammatory indications and has an established human safety profile, its clinical history thus far has not included a trial specifically targeting dry AMD or any direct veterinary employments for ocular diseases (Arulkumaran et al., 2011; Guile et al., 2009).  

Mechanism of Action:  
The P2X7 receptor (P2X7R) is an ATP-gated, nonselective cation channel predominantly expressed on immune cells and, importantly for the intended application, on the retinal pigmented epithelium (RPE) (Calzaferri et al., 2020). Under physiological conditions, P2X7R is quiescent; however, in the presence of elevated extracellular ATP—a phenomenon noted in inflammatory and degenerative conditions, including AMD—the receptor becomes activated, mediating several deleterious downstream events. Upon activation, P2X7R undergoes a conformational change that not only allows the influx of Ca2+ and Na+ but also promotes the formation of large membrane pores owing to its ability to transition into a state that permits the passage of molecules as large as 900 Da (Chrovian et al., 2014; Eser et al., 2015). This pore formation results in cytotoxic calcium overload and is directly linked to the activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome, a multiprotein complex responsible for the processing of pro-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-1β and IL-18 (Calzaferri et al., 2020; Gu & Wiley, 2018). In the retinal pigment epithelium, this ATP-driven activation has been shown to contribute to lysosomal alkalization—a process that impairs the optimal acidic environment required by lysosomal enzymes, including cathepsins—and ultimately leads to defective clearance of cellular debris (Calzaferri et al., 2020; Tempest-Roe, 2017). Specifically, experimental studies in ARPE-19 cells (a human RPE cell line) have demonstrated that stimulation of P2X7 induces lysosomal dysfunction; conversely, pharmacological inhibition of P2X7 using antagonists such as Brilliant Blue G (BBG) can reverse this lysosomal impairment (Tempest-Roe, 2017). Mechanistically, AZD9056 is designed to bind to the P2X7 receptor with high potency and selectivity, thereby preventing the receptor’s activation by ATP. By doing so, it is anticipated to block the cascade of events that lead from receptor activation to pore formation, inflammasome assembly, and subsequent IL-1β release (Calzaferri et al., 2020; Gu & Wiley, 2018; Lee et al., 2023). Although the exact molecular binding mode of AZD9056 has not been detailed in available literature, it is presumed to interact with key residues involved in channel gating and pore formation, thereby stabilizing the receptor in a closed, inactive conformation (Chrovian et al., 2014; Lee et al., 2023). Additionally, its ability to reduce ex vivo ATP-induced monocyte IL-1β release in healthy volunteers has served as a functional biomarker for target engagement, reinforcing the hypothesis that P2X7 antagonism can modulate inflammasome-driven inflammatory signaling (Chrovian et al., 2014; Lee et al., 2023).  

Expected Effect:  
In the context of dry age-related macular degeneration, the central hypothesis for repurposing AZD9056 is that it will antagonize P2X7 receptors on retinal pigmented epithelium cells, thereby preventing a cascade of ATP-driven pathological events. Elevated extracellular ATP levels have been documented in the vitreous of AMD patients, which suggests a pathological activation of purinergic signaling in the retina (Calzaferri et al., 2020). When ATP activates P2X7 receptors on RPE cells, it leads to two major deleterious outcomes. First, the receptor’s activation results in sustained Ca2+ influx and large pore formation, triggering cytotoxicity and subsequent cell death mechanisms, including apoptotic and inflammasome-dependent cell death pathways (Calzaferri et al., 2020; Gu & Wiley, 2018). Second, P2X7 activation has been mechanistically linked to lysosomal alkalization in RPE cells, which impairs the activity of lysosomal proteases such as cathepsin D; this enzyme is critical for the degradation of photoreceptor outer segments and other cellular debris (Gu & Wiley, 2018; Tempest-Roe, 2017). The hypothesis posits that by blocking P2X7 receptor activation with AZD9056, one would preserve the normal acidic environment of the lysosomes, thereby maintaining or even restoring optimal cathepsin D activity. In turn, these effects are anticipated to protect the RPE from inflammasome-mediated apoptosis and lysosomal dysfunction, which are key drivers of geographic atrophy, the advanced clinical manifestation of dry AMD (Gu & Wiley, 2018; Calzaferri et al., 2020). Preclinical studies support the role of P2X7 in mediating RPE degeneration; for example, genetic knockout of P2X7 in mouse models has been shown to protect against Alu RNA-induced RPE toxicity, an established model of dry AMD pathology (Calzaferri et al., 2020; Gu & Wiley, 2018). Furthermore, in vitro studies using human RPE cell cultures have indicated that P2X7 receptor blockade can reverse lysosomal impairment, suggesting that AZD9056 could produce measurable improvements in functional assays that evaluate lysosomal protease activity, such as cathepsin D activity assays, and overall RPE viability assays (Calzaferri et al., 2020; Tempest-Roe, 2017). Ultimately, if the protective effects seen in preclinical studies translate into the clinical setting, AZD9056 may reduce the accumulation of undigested cellular debris (drusen) and slow or halt the progression of geographic atrophy in patients with dry AMD by dampening the inflamed state and preserving RPE function (Calzaferri et al., 2020; Gu & Wiley, 2018).  

Overall Evaluation:  
From a drug development perspective, the repurposing of AZD9056 for dry AMD presents a compelling but challenging opportunity. One of the primary strengths of this therapeutic candidate lies in its robust mechanistic rationale. The P2X7 receptor plays a central role in mediating ATP-induced inflammasome activation, lysosomal dysfunction, and subsequent RPE cell death—pathophysiological processes that have been repeatedly implicated in dry AMD and geographic atrophy models (Calzaferri et al., 2020; Gu & Wiley, 2018; Tempest-Roe, 2017). The ability of P2X7 antagonists to block these processes has been demonstrated in various in vitro and in vivo models, where blockade of the receptor reduces IL-1β release, reverses lysosomal alkalization, and confers protection against RPE degeneration (Calzaferri et al., 2020; Gu & Wiley, 2018; Tempest-Roe, 2017). Furthermore, AZD9056 has gone through extensive clinical safety evaluations in multiple inflammatory disease indications; its pharmacokinetic profile—characterized by acceptable oral bioavailability and a half-life conducive to once-daily dosing—has been well established in early phase studies (Arulkumaran et al., 2011; Chrovian et al., 2014). This pre-existing clinical safety data is an asset in reducing the risk profile typically associated with novel drug candidates and may streamline early-stage clinical trial designs for an ocular indication. Additionally, preliminary ocular safety assessments in healthy volunteers, which included measures such as retinal electroretinography and visual acuity testing, suggest that systemic administration of AZD9056 does not produce overt ocular toxicity—an encouraging sign for its potential repurposing in dry AMD (Arulkumaran et al., 2011).  

Nevertheless, there are several notable limitations and challenges associated with using AZD9056 in the treatment of dry AMD. First, the prior clinical development history of AZD9056 in rheumatoid arthritis and Crohn’s disease revealed limited or inconsistent efficacy despite demonstrable target engagement. In the phase IIb studies for RA, the compound failed to outperform placebo across objective outcome measures even though safety endpoints were met (Arulkumaran et al., 2011; Chrovian et al., 2014). This raises concerns about whether P2X7 receptor blockade alone is sufficient to generate a meaningful clinical outcome, particularly in a complex and multifactorial disease process such as dry AMD. Moreover, the inflammatory milieu in rheumatoid arthritis or IBD differs significantly from that in the retina, and systemic inflammation may not accurately recapitulate the localized, chronic degenerative processes occurring in the RPE (Arulkumaran et al., 2011; Guile et al., 2009).  

Another concern relates to the dual and sometimes paradoxical roles of the P2X7 receptor. While its pathological activation is linked to pro-inflammatory signaling, P2X7 also appears to have a scavenger or phagocytic function under conditions of low ATP levels (Calzaferri et al., 2020; Newman, 2024). In the context of the RPE, which is specialized for high-volume phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments, complete blockade of P2X7 might inadvertently impair beneficial clearance processes that serve to prevent debris accumulation. In animal models, alternative data has shown that the loss of P2X7 function can result in changes reminiscent of early AMD, such as reduced phagocytosis, suggesting that finely balanced modulation rather than total inhibition may be necessary (Calzaferri et al., 2020; Gu & Wiley, 2018). Such duality underscores the potential risk that while AZD9056 may ameliorate inflammasome activation and lysosomal destabilization, it might simultaneously disrupt physiologic functions of RPE cells that are critical for maintaining retinal homeostasis.  

The lack of direct evidence for AZD9056’s efficacy in ocular models of dry AMD is another major gap. While the preclinical literature supports a role for P2X7 signaling in RPE dysfunction and geographic atrophy (Calzaferri et al., 2020; Tempest-Roe, 2017), the specific application of AZD9056 in these models remains largely inferential. There are no published studies documenting that AZD9056, when administered at doses achieving retinal penetration, effectively preserves cathepsin D activity or prevents RPE cell death in animal models of dry AMD. The undisclosed chemical structure of AZD9056 also complicates any efforts to optimize the compound specifically for ocular bioavailability or to better understand its off-target profile relative to other P2X7 antagonists that have been more thoroughly characterized in the literature (Chrovian et al., 2014; Gunosewoyo et al., 2007).  

In summary, the overall evaluation of AZD9056 for treatment of dry AMD is one of cautious enthusiasm tempered by several unresolved questions. On the strength side, the compound leverages a clear mechanistic rationale by antagonizing the P2X7 receptor—a key mediator of ATP-induced inflammasome activation and lysosomal dysfunction known to be active in the RPE of AMD patients—and it comes with an established clinical safety record in inflammatory disorders (Calzaferri et al., 2020; Chrovian et al., 2014; Gu & Wiley, 2018). Given the current state of the literature, it would be advisable to conduct targeted preclinical studies that specifically address the effects of AZD9056 on RPE cells and retinal tissue. These studies should include assays for lysosomal pH stability, cathepsin D activity, inflammasome assembly (e.g., NLRP3 activation and caspase-1 processing), and overall RPE cell viability under conditions of ATP stress. Furthermore, careful evaluation of retinal drug levels following systemic dosing—or the development of a topical formulation—might be necessary to ensure that sufficient drug concentrations can be achieved in the retina without systemic toxicity. A parallel investigation into the potential compensatory roles of P2X7 in RPE phagocytosis would also be warranted to minimize any risk of disrupting beneficial cellular functions (Calzaferri et al., 2020; Gu & Wiley, 2018; Arulkumaran et al., 2011).  

Overall, while AZD9056’s strong mechanistic basis and favorable early-phase clinical safety profile make it an attractive candidate for repurposing, the translational challenges and previous clinical setbacks in other indications necessitate rigorous preclinical validation in dry AMD models before further clinical development is considered. The compound’s capacity to specifically maintain lysosomal function and cathepsin D activity in the RPE represents a promising therapeutic opportunity if these effects can be reliably recapitulated in the ocular setting. However, caution is advised due to the dual roles of P2X7 signaling in both pathological and physiologic processes and the potential non-optimal receptor occupancy in the retina. In conclusion, the repurposing of AZD9056 for dry AMD holds potential but would require a focused, mechanistically guided preclinical program to address the unique challenges posed by the ocular environment and the complex biology of the P2X7 receptor (Arulkumaran et al., 2011; Chrovian et al., 2014; Calzaferri et al., 2020; Tempest-Roe, 2017).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
miR-204 is a highly conserved microRNA encoded within an intron of the TRPM3 locus and is among the most abundant miRNAs in human fetal retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) at roughly 10,000 copies per cell, with expression also present in neural retina and photoreceptors (Shiels, 2020; Karali et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2019). The proposed therapeutic candidate is a miR-204 mimic (agomir), i.e., a synthetic double-stranded RNA designed to reconstitute or augment mature miR-204 activity in target cells, thereby restoring sequence-specific repression of cognate mRNAs via Argonaute/RISC-mediated post-transcriptional regulation (Du & Palczewski, 2022). Agomirs are typically produced by solid-phase oligonucleotide synthesis and formulated with stabilizing chemical modifications and delivery moieties to resist nucleases and evade innate immune sensors; however, the present literature corpus specific to miR-204 provides no details on the chemical design or manufacturing of a miR-204 agomir used in ocular studies (Du & Palczewski, 2022; Karali et al., 2020). In vivo “gain-of-function” delivery of miR-204 has been achieved preclinically using adeno-associated viral (AAV) gene therapy vectors encoding the murine pre-miR-204 hairpin driven by ubiquitous (CMV) or photoreceptor-specific (RHO) promoters, establishing that increasing miR-204 activity is feasible and can confer neuroprotective and anti-inflammatory effects in degenerating retina (Karali et al., 2020). Separately, the agomir modality (chemically synthesized miR-204 mimic) has been used in ocular systems and vertebrate development: ocular injection of a miR-204 mimic in rat retina reduced GAP-43 expression, and double-stranded miR-204 mimic injection in medaka embryos caused microphthalmia and lens dysgenesis, demonstrating biological activity in vivo with potential context-dependent liabilities (Shiels, 2020).

Within the broader therapeutic class, miRNA modulation includes replacement (mimics/agomirs) and inhibition (antimiRs) and has been explored preclinically and clinically; the most advanced clinical precedent involves an antimiR of miR-122 (miravirsen) in hepatology, while miRNA mimics face delivery, stability, and innate-immune activation challenges that necessitate chemical modification and targeted delivery—issues directly relevant to deploying a miR-204 agomir in the eye (Parsi, 2016). In ophthalmology, miRNAs regulate essential RPE functions including phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments (POS), autophagy, endolysosomal trafficking, epithelial barrier integrity, and inflammatory signaling, making miR replacement an attractive strategy to correct multi-pathway dysfunctions typical of dry AMD (Du & Palczewski, 2022).

Therapeutic History  
- Ocular/retinal delivery of miR-204 by AAV gene therapy:  
  - In RHO-P347S and Aipl1−/− mouse models of inherited retinal degeneration (IRD), subretinal AAV2/8 vectors expressing pre-miR-204 preserved retinal function by ERG, reduced photoreceptor cell death (TUNEL), and dampened microglial activation and innate immune/inflammatory transcriptomes; luciferase data supported direct targeting of immune/apoptosis transcripts (Siglec1, Xaf1) by miR-204 (Karali et al., 2020). These effects persisted through at least PN60 when dosed at PN4 in the RHO-P347S model, and benefit tracked with ubiquitous expression (CMV) more than photoreceptor-restricted expression (RHO), consistent with non–cell-autonomous and multi-cell-type actions (Karali et al., 2020). The studies confirm feasibility and efficacy of miR-204 augmentation in murine retina, but they used viral expression rather than chemically synthesized mimics and were not performed in dry AMD models (Karali et al., 2020).  
- Ocular/neuronal use of miR-204 mimics/inhibitors:  
  - Direct ocular injection of a miR-204 mimic in rats decreased GAP-43 expression and, in the context of injury, increased retinal TUNEL-positive cells, while a miR-204 inhibitor increased GAP-43, indicating robust on-target modulation and context-dependent toxicity risk (Shiels, 2020). In medaka, overexpression of a miR-204 double-stranded mimic (agomir) produced microphthalmia and lens dysgenesis, underscoring the need for careful dose, spatial restriction, and developmental timing (Shiels, 2020).  
- Disease relevance of miR-204 to dry AMD biology:  
  - Genetic deletion of miR-204 in mice causes progressive, age-dependent RPE/retina pathology reminiscent of dry AMD: hyper-autofluorescent deposits, impaired POS degradation with rhodopsin accumulation in RPE, autophagosome accumulation, lysosomal deficits (lower LAMP2 signal), microglial migration to the RPE apical surface, increased proinflammatory cytokine secretion (apical IL-8), IPM disorganization, reduced ERG components (photoreceptor and RPE-driven), and downregulation of visual cycle genes (LRAT, RPE65, TTR) that would constrain retinoid recycling (Zhang et al., 2019; Intartaglia et al., 2021). Parallel anti-miR-204 knockdown in primary human fetal RPE recapitulates autophagy/lysosomal and phagolysosomal defects: reduced POS digestion without reduced uptake (~20% slower clearance), increased p62, accumulation of undigested autophagosomes, reduced LAMP2, and intracellular rhodopsin accumulation; Rab22a protein (an inhibitor of endosome maturation) rises in both anti-miR and KO settings, mechanistically linking the phenotype to a miR-204 → Rab22a axis (Zhang et al., 2019). These convergent in vivo/in vitro loss-of-function data provide the key mechanistic rationale to explore miR-204 augmentation as a corrective therapy in dry AMD-like RPE dysfunction (Zhang et al., 2019).  
- miRNA class precedent and translational trajectory:  
  - Reviews emphasize that RPE miRNAs control phagocytosis and lysosomal pathways and that specific miR:mRNA pairs (including miR-204→Rab22a) are central to vesicle trafficking; they also note that miR therapeutics can be delivered via viral vectors or nonviral carriers (e.g., nanoparticles), but that miRNA mimic programs face stability, delivery, and immune-activation challenges that will need to be mitigated (Du & Palczewski, 2022; Parsi, 2016). There are no reports of miR-204 agomir use in dry AMD patients or animal models of dry AMD; thus, clinical and AMD-specific preclinical history for a chemically synthesized miR-204 mimic is absent in the present corpus (Du & Palczewski, 2022; Karali et al., 2020).

Mechanism of Action  
At the biochemical level, mature miR-204 is loaded into the RISC and binds target 3′ UTR seed sites to repress translation and/or promote mRNA decay of specific transcripts that regulate RPE homeostasis (Du & Palczewski, 2022). The best-supported target in the context of endosomal maturation is Rab22a, a small GTPase that acts as an inhibitor of early-to-late endosomal progression and thereby impedes endosome–lysosome fusion necessary for proteolysis (Zhang et al., 2019). In miR-204 loss-of-function models (global KO mice and anti-miR-204–treated human fetal RPE), Rab22a protein levels are increased by immunostaining and western blot in RPE, particularly after POS feeding, and the authors interpret this as a dysregulation at the intersection of the autophagy and endosome pathways (Zhang et al., 2019). The mechanistic model is explicit: loss of miR-204 increases Rab22a expression, which impedes maturation of early autophagosomal/endosomal intermediates that fail to fuse with lysosomes, resulting in decreased phagocytic clearance and persistent accumulation of POS-derived rhodopsin in RPE (Zhang et al., 2019).

Functional correlates of this endosomal maturation block are well documented in RPE:  
- Phagolysosomal/autophagy markers: anti-miR-204 RPE shows increased p62/SQSTM1, increased number/size of undigested autophagosomes by TEM, and altered LC3B isoform distribution (increased LC3B-I without consistent LC3B-II accumulation), consistent with impaired maturation of degradative compartments rather than defective initiation of LC3-associated processes (Zhang et al., 2019). Anti-miR-204 reduces lysosomal content/function by ~1.6-fold lower LAMP2 in RPE relative to controls, consistent with fewer functional lysosomes available for phagosome fusion (Zhang et al., 2019).  
- Phagocytosis and digestion of POS: uptake per se is not impaired, but the digestion rate is slowed (~20% reduction in clearance in anti-miR-204 RPE by FACS-based pHrodo POS assays), directly supporting a degradative block downstream of engulfment (Zhang et al., 2019).  
- Rhodopsin accumulation: in miR-204−/− mice, rhodopsin-containing POS material accumulates within RPE at the peak of daily phagocytosis (8–10 a.m.) as measured by IF and western blot; anti-miR-204 hfRPE also accumulates rhodopsin after POS feeding (Zhang et al., 2019).  
- Secretory/inflammatory signaling: anti-miR-204 increases apical IL-8 secretion ~2-fold in hfRPE, creating a chemokine gradient predicted to attract retinal microglia to the RPE apical surface, which is observed in KO animals, and likely contributes to hyper-autofluorescent deposits and inflammatory retinal dysfunction (Zhang et al., 2019).  
- Electrophysiological and structural consequences: miR-204−/− mice exhibit reduced retinal photoreceptor and bipolar responses (ERG a- and b-wave), reduced RPE-derived DC-ERG components (c-wave and FO), age-dependent lipofuscin accumulation, interphotoreceptor matrix disorganization, and ultrastructural RPE defects, all consistent with chronic degradative deficiency and secondary degeneration (Zhang et al., 2019).

Beyond the Rab22a/endosome axis, miR-204 maintains epithelial identity and apical membrane physiology in RPE:  
- TGF-β signaling and EMT restraint: miR-204 directly targets TGFBR2 at the apical membrane; its inhibition upregulates TGF-β pathway genes (TGFBR2, SNAI2), collapses transepithelial resistance (~80% decrease), reduces claudins/tight junctions, and promotes EMT-like changes, linking miR-204 to barrier integrity and anti-fibrotic states (Shiels, 2020; Zhang et al., 2019).  
- Ion homeostasis: miR-204 loss indirectly reduces Kir7.1 expression and K+ efflux, leading to RPE cell swelling and subretinal space perturbations that can promote autophagy; these changes plausibly contribute to the reduced c-wave amplitude in KO animals (Zhang et al., 2019).  
- Visual cycle: miR-204 deficiency downregulates LRAT, RPE65, and TTR, impairing 11-cis-retinal regeneration and retinoid transport, thereby coupling endolysosomal deficits with phototransduction support failure (Intartaglia et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2019).

Inflammation can suppress miR-204 levels: IFN-γ downregulates miR-204 in ARPE-19, and miR-204 is coregulated with TRPM3; given that inflammation is a key driver in AMD, cytokine-driven miR-204 depletion provides a pathophysiological link to disease (Shiels, 2020).

In contrast to the detailed loss-of-function and in vitro mechanistic data, direct rescue experiments that re-introduce miR-204 in RPE to reverse Rab22a elevation, restore endosome–lysosome maturation, and normalize POS degradation have not been reported in the cited sources; the reported augmentation studies used AAV-miR-204 in IRD models and measured predominantly neuroinflammation and apoptosis endpoints rather than phagolysosomal rescue in RPE (Zhang et al., 2019; Karali et al., 2020).

Expected Effect  
If a chemically modified miR-204 agomir is delivered to RPE and achieves sufficient intracellular loading into Ago2/RISC, the expected molecular and cellular effects, by inversion of the validated loss-of-function phenotypes, are:  
- Target repression and endosomal maturation: Decrease Rab22a protein abundance in RPE, relieving its inhibitory effect on maturation of early endosomes/autophagosomal intermediates and permitting efficient endosome–lysosome fusion and phagolysosome function (Zhang et al., 2019).  
- Phagolysosomal/autophagy normalization: Increase functional lysosome content (e.g., rescue of LAMP2 levels), reduce p62 accumulation, decrease number/size of undigested autophagosomes, and accelerate degradation (but not uptake) of POS cargo in hfRPE digestion assays (e.g., increased pHrodo chase rate, reduced intracellular rhodopsin by IF/WB after standardized POS feeds) (Zhang et al., 2019).  
- Reduction of inflammatory signaling and microglial recruitment: Lower apical IL-8 secretion, diminishing chemotactic signals for resident microglia and reducing subretinal microglial accumulation; reduce hyper-autofluorescent material accrual over time, which is associated with impaired POS degradation (Zhang et al., 2019).  
- Functional recovery: Improve RPE and retinal electrophysiology (DC-ERG c-wave, FO; ERG a-/b-waves), contingent on sufficient rescue of POS handling and visual cycle support; maintain expression of visual cycle genes (LRAT, RPE65, TTR) and ion channel function (Kir7.1) through direct and indirect effects of miR-204 on apical physiology (Zhang et al., 2019; Intartaglia et al., 2021).

These expected effects are consistent with the mechanistic chain established in RPE: miR-204 controls Rab22a and endosomal maturation, which governs phagolysosomal processing of POS; failure at this node produces rhodopsin/undigested lipid accumulation, oxidative/proinflammatory stress, microglial activation, and electrophysiological decline—key features of dry AMD-like RPE dysfunction (Zhang et al., 2019). Notably, direct evidence that miR-204 augmentation in RPE increases cathepsin D activity or lysosomal acidification is not present in the cited literature; such outcomes are plausible secondary consequences of restored maturation but remain to be experimentally validated in this system (Zhang et al., 2019). Conversely, miR-204 augmentation has demonstrated capacity to downregulate proinflammatory/apoptotic signaling in degenerating retinas (AAV delivery in IRD), which may add non–phagolysosomal benefits in dry AMD by dampening microglia activation and apoptosis (Karali et al., 2020).

Assay-relevant expression and feasibility:  
- Rab22a is expressed in RPE and is upregulated when miR-204 is reduced, validating it as an RPE-relevant miR-204 target to monitor in pharmacodynamic assays (Zhang et al., 2019).  
- The RPE performs circadian POS phagocytosis and directs cargo to lysosomes; miRNAs regulate both uptake and downstream lysosomal breakdown, placing miR-204 within a well-defined physiological context where restoration should impact measurable endpoints (Du & Palczewski, 2022).  
- Established in vitro RPE models and in vivo mouse paradigms using exogenous POS feed, pHrodo uptake/chase, rhodopsin IF/WB, and endolysosomal markers (p62, LC3, LAMP2), as well as apical cytokine secretion and ERG readouts, provide a fit-for-purpose translational assay suite to test a miR-204 agomir (Zhang et al., 2019).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Mechanistic specificity linked to a central AMD-relevant pathway: The miR-204 → Rab22a axis is strongly supported in RPE by convergent mouse and human RPE data showing that miR-204 loss elevates Rab22a, blocks endosomal maturation, reduces phagolysosomal clearance (without impairing uptake), and causes intracellular rhodopsin/undigested autophagosome accumulation—key pathomechanisms implicated in dry AMD (Zhang et al., 2019). This provides a precise molecular rationale that a miR-204 mimic could correct a bottleneck in the RPE degradative axis central to disease biology (Du & Palczewski, 2022).  
- Strong phenotypic congruence with dry AMD: miR-204−/− mice develop age-related hyper-autofluorescent deposits, RPE/retina electrophysiological decline, microglial recruitment, and visual cycle impairment, aligning with multiple facets of dry AMD pathophysiology and supporting the translational relevance of restoring miR-204 in RPE (Zhang et al., 2019; Intartaglia et al., 2021).  
- High endogenous expression and biology in RPE: miR-204 is among the most abundant miRNAs in RPE and is induced during RPE differentiation; inflammation downregulates miR-204, plausibly contributing to disease, which rationalizes a replacement strategy (Shiels, 2020).  
- Modality precedent and in vivo efficacy: Although not a mimic per se, AAV-mediated miR-204 augmentation confers neuroprotection, anti-inflammatory effects, and partial functional rescue in IRD models, indicating therapeutic potential of miR-204 augmentation in retinal disease and providing insight into safety, dose timing, and target engagement in vivo (Karali et al., 2020).  
- Multiplexed benefits beyond endosomes: miR-204 regulates EMT/barrier pathways (TGFBR2, claudins), apical ion homeostasis (Kir7.1), and visual cycle gene expression (LRAT, RPE65, TTR), potentially addressing several RPE dysfunction axes simultaneously—a desirable property in multifactorial dry AMD (Shiels, 2020; Zhang et al., 2019; Intartaglia et al., 2021).
