─────────────────────────────  
Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
─────────────────────────────  
The miR-211 mimic is a synthetic, chemically modified oligonucleotide designed to recapitulate the function of the endogenous microRNA miR-211. As a member of the miRNA therapeutic class, this molecule belongs to a growing category of nucleic acid–based drugs that aim to modulate gene expression post-transcriptionally. Its design involves optimization of the nucleotide chemistry (for example, by including 2′-O-methyl modifications, phosphorothioate linkages, and sometimes locked nucleic acid (LNA) modifications) to improve stability, reduce degradation by nucleases, and minimize immune stimulation after ocular delivery. Such chemical modifications (collectively referred to as “agomir” chemistry) have been used successfully in preclinical models for other miRNA candidates, proving that the formulation and delivery of chemically stabilized miRNA mimics to ocular tissues is feasible (Boya et al., 2023; Intartaglia et al., 2021).

miR-211 was originally identified as a light-responsive microRNA in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and has been shown to regulate lysosomal biogenesis by targeting the mRNA of Ezrin, a cytoskeletal protein that also impacts cellular ion channel regulation. The candidate is repurposed from the naturally occurring miRNA sequence now “mimicked” by the synthetic therapeutic agent. Its design is based on the premise that the loss or downregulation of miR-211 in the diseased RPE contributes to defective lysosomal function and consequent accumulation of photoreceptor outer segment (POS) debris, which is a hallmark of dry AMD (Boya et al., 2023; Intartaglia et al., 2021).

As a therapeutic compound, the miR-211 mimic falls into the broader family of oligonucleotide drugs that have previously been used in various contexts such as oncology or viral diseases. In the ocular arena, similar approaches—including antisense oligonucleotides and small interfering RNAs (siRNAs)—have been deployed to modulate gene expression in models of ocular neovascularization and other retinal degenerations. In this way, the miR-211 agomir is both a repurposed and rationally designed candidate that leverages our growing understanding of miRNA-mediated regulation of lysosomal activity and intracellular clearance pathways (Naso et al., 2020).

─────────────────────────────  
Therapeutic History  
─────────────────────────────  
Although no miR-211 mimic as such has yet reached clinical trials in dry AMD, an increasing body of preclinical evidence supports the therapeutic potential of modulating miR-211 expression in the retina. In several rodent studies it has been demonstrated that global loss of miR-211 in mice leads to impaired lysosomal biogenesis, accumulation of lipofuscin-like granules, and defective processing of photoreceptor outer segments by the RPE (Naso et al., 2020). For example, mice with a genetic deletion of miR-211 exhibit phenotypes reminiscent of inherited retinal dystrophies and models of Stargardt’s disease, in which impaired degradative enzymes and lysosomal dysfunction are central features.

In parallel, pharmacological inhibition of Ezrin—a validated target of miR-211—using small molecule inhibitors such as NSC668394 has been shown to restore lysosomal activity, increase autophagic flux, and even rescue electrophysiological deficits in the rodent retina (Naso et al., 2020). These findings not only validate the molecular target (Ezrin) but also indirectly support the hypothesis that restoring miR-211 levels via an agomir should yield similar improvements in lysosomal function and cell clearance.

The use of chemically modified oligonucleotides (including agomirs) in ocular drug development is supported both by preclinical data and emerging clinical applications in other retinal diseases. While previous approaches in dry AMD have focused on antioxidants, complement inhibitors, or cell transplantation, the recent shift toward modulating intracellular clearance pathways and autophagy has created new opportunity. For instance, approaches to activate the transcription factor TFEB—which is the master regulator of lysosomal biogenesis—demonstrate that enhancement of the degradative pathway correlates with improved survival of the RPE and photoreceptor cells (Boya et al., 2023; Naso et al., 2020). Although direct use of a miR-211 mimic (as opposed to gene therapy or pharmacologic Ezrin inhibitors) has not yet been validated in clinical settings for AMD, the preclinical evidence for miR-211’s role in maintaining RPE homeostasis provides a strong rationale for advancing this candidate into further testing (Intartaglia et al., 2021; Naso et al., 2020).

─────────────────────────────  
Mechanism of Action  
─────────────────────────────  
The proposed molecular mechanism by which a miR-211 mimic would function in dry AMD is multifaceted, integrating several key cellular pathways that converge on the restoration of lysosomal biogenesis in the RPE. At its core, the therapeutic hypothesis centers on the ability of miR-211 to post-transcriptionally suppress Ezrin, a cytoskeletal linker protein that in the RPE is linked to disruptions in lysosomal function and cell clearance (Boya et al., 2023; Intartaglia et al., 2021).

Specifically, under physiological conditions miR-211 is induced in a light-dependent manner and directly binds to the 3′ untranslated region (UTR) of the Ezrin mRNA to repress its translation. In the context of dry AMD, miR-211 is downregulated—a change that leads to derepression of Ezrin. Elevated Ezrin levels are correlated with impaired lysosomal biogenesis, reduced cathepsin activity, and accumulation of metabolic debris (Boya et al., 2023; Naso et al., 2020). Once delivered to the RPE, the miR-211 mimic is expected to restore this regulatory inhibition, reducing Ezrin protein levels to a more physiologic state.

More intriguingly, this reduction in Ezrin is proposed to have downstream effects on lysosomal calcium signaling. Data indicate that when Ezrin is repressed, there is an increase in TRPML1 channel sensitivity at the lysosomal membrane, thereby generating a localized Ca²⁺ microdomain within these organelles (Naso et al., 2020). The increased lysosomal Ca²⁺ flux subsequently activates the Ca²⁺-dependent phosphatase calcineurin. Activated calcineurin dephosphorylates TFEB, a transcription factor that in its phosphorylated state is sequestered in the cytosol. Once dephosphorylated, TFEB can translocate into the nucleus where it functions as the master regulator of the Coordinated Lysosomal Expression and Regulation (CLEAR) gene network (Naso et al., 2020).

TFEB-driven transcription leads to enhanced expression of genes encoding lysosomal proteins, such as LAMP1, and digestive enzymes including cathepsin D, as well as proteins critical for autophagosome formation like LC3 and BECLIN. The net effect is an increase in the number and functionality of lysosomes, including improved acidification of these organelles—a crucial parameter for optimal enzymatic activity and degradation of engulfed materials (Du & Palczewski, 2022; Naso et al., 2020). The complete mechanistic cascade is thus: miR-211 mimic delivers a signal that downregulates Ezrin, alleviating its inhibitory effects on lysosomal biogenesis; this in turn potentiates TRPML1-mediated Ca²⁺ release, leading to calcineurin activation; calcineurin dephosphorylates TFEB, allowing its nuclear entry; and nuclear TFEB transcriptionally enhances lysosomal genes, culminating in improved cathepsin D expression and lysosomal acidification. This chain of events is hypothesized to restore the degradative capacity of the RPE and mitigate POS accumulation—a key pathogenic factor underlying dry AMD (Boya et al., 2023; Naso et al., 2020).

It is worth noting that similar signaling cascades have been observed in studies where Ezrin inhibition pharmacologically recapitulated the beneficial effects seen after TFEB activation, which indirectly supports this proposed miR-211–mediated mechanism (Naso et al., 2020). The convergence of genetic, pharmacologic, and mechanistic studies in preclinical rodent models reinforces confidence in the proposed chain-of-events, although direct demonstration of every step with a synthetic miR-211 agomir remains an area for future research.

─────────────────────────────  
Expected Effect  
─────────────────────────────  
When administrated to the retinal pigment epithelium via an appropriate ocular delivery method (such as intravitreal or subretinal injection, potentially formulated within lipid nanoparticles or other compatible carriers), the miR-211 mimic is expected to produce several beneficial effects that address the key pathological features of dry AMD. In in vitro assays using RPE cell lines or primary human RPE cultures, one would anticipate that treatment with the miR-211 agomir will lead to a measurable decrease in Ezrin mRNA and protein levels as confirmed by qRT-PCR and Western blot analyses, respectively (Boya et al., 2023; Intartaglia et al., 2021).

At the subcellular level, the downregulation of Ezrin is expected to relieve its inhibitory control on lysosomal Ca²⁺ dynamics. This should manifest as an increase in TRPML1 channel activity, resulting in a sustained and enhanced lysosomal Ca²⁺ signal, which can be quantified using calcium-sensitive dyes or genetically encoded Ca²⁺ indicators fused to lysosomal proteins (Naso et al., 2020). Following this, increased calcineurin activity is anticipated and can be monitored by assessing the phosphorylation status of downstream substrates including TFEB. In treated RPE cells, one would observe a redistribution of TFEB from the cytoplasm to the nucleus, a change that can be confirmed by immunocytochemistry and subcellular fractionation methods (Naso et al., 2020).

The nuclear translocation of TFEB should then promote transcriptional upregulation of lysosomal and autophagy-related genes, resulting in an increased number of lysosomes with enhanced acidification (as measured by pH-sensitive fluorescent probes) and increased activity of key lysosomal enzymes such as cathepsin D and cathepsin B. Ultrastructural analyses by electron microscopy might reveal a reduction in the number or size of accumulated phagolysosomes containing unprocessed POS, and a phenotypic rescue at the cellular level would be consistent with restored degradative function (Naso et al., 2020).

In animal models of dry AMD – particularly in miR-211 knockout mice or in models that replicate lipofuscin accumulation and reduced lysosomal function – treatment with the miR-211 mimic is expected to result in significant improvements in retinal structure and function. Outcomes could include a reduction in lipofuscin deposition in the RPE, improved clearance of dysfunctional or misfolded photoreceptor proteins, and ultimately functional improvements as measured by responses on electroretinography (ERG) and preservation of photoreceptor cell layers. The approach is expected to not only halt but also partially reverse the degenerative changes by boosting the intrinsic capacity of RPE cells to clear cellular debris and maintain homeostasis (Boya et al., 2023; Naso et al., 2020).

Furthermore, in preclinical experiments where pharmacological inhibition of Ezrin achieved similar results in terms of enhancing lysosomal markers and reducing pathological deposits, the miR-211 mimic is hypothesized to mimic these effects by acting upstream of the pathway. Given that there is evidence suggesting that downregulation of miR-211 in AMD leads to compromised visual function, restoring its levels should, in theory, improve RPE survival and enhance retinal performance (Naso et al., 2020). In summary, the expected effect of this therapeutic intervention is a robust enhancement of lysosomal biogenesis and function within the RPE, which in turn could restore degradative capacity, reduce debris accumulation, and preserve visual function in dry AMD.

─────────────────────────────  
Overall Evaluation  
─────────────────────────────  
The miR-211 mimic candidate for dry AMD represents an innovative approach that acts by rebalancing a key regulatory pathway implicated in lysosomal biogenesis and cellular clearance. Overall, there are several strengths and a number of challenges to consider:

Strengths:  
1. Rational Mechanistic Targeting:  
   The candidate is built on a clear mechanistic hypothesis. miR-211 has been shown in multiple preclinical studies to directly regulate Ezrin—a known inhibitor of lysosomal biogenesis—and its downregulation results in impaired degradation of POS in the RPE (Boya et al., 2023; Intartaglia et al., 2021). By restoring miR-211 levels, the cascade involving TRPML1-mediated Ca²⁺ release, calcineurin activation, and subsequent TFEB nuclear translocation is reactivated. This specificity in targeting a regulatory cascade central to intracellular clearance speaks to high precision in its design (Naso et al., 2020).

2. Preclinical Validation of the Concept:  
   Genetic models, such as miR-211 knockout mice, and pharmacologic approaches using Ezrin inhibitors have provided compelling evidence that manipulating this pathway can restore degradative capacity in the RPE (Naso et al., 2020). Although the miR-211 mimic itself has not yet been extensively tested in dry AMD models, these data provide a strong scientific rationale for its potential efficacy.

3. Established Chemical Modification Strategies:  
   The field of miRNA therapeutics has matured considerably, and the design of chemically modified agomirs is a well-established approach to increase in vivo stability and allow local ocular delivery. This is supported by multiple studies in ocular tissues showing that similar modifications lead to enhanced half-life and effective cellular uptake (Boya et al., 2023; Intartaglia et al., 2021).

4. Specificity for RPE Homeostasis:  
   The candidate is designed specifically for the RPE, the critical cell layer responsible for degrading old photoreceptor outer segments. Since RPE dysfunction is a hallmark of dry AMD, targeted restoration of its lysosomal capacity has a high potential to ameliorate disease progression and preserve vision (Naso et al., 2020).

Weaknesses/Challenges:  
1. Limited Direct Evidence with Agomirs:  
   Although there is substantial mechanistic preclinical evidence linking miR-211 to the regulation of lysosomal function via Ezrin repression, no data to date directly demonstrate the efficacy and safety of a chemically modified miR-211 mimic in relevant dry AMD models. It remains to be established whether the agomir will effectively reach the RPE, achieve the desired gene repression, and produce the biochemical cascade in vivo (Naso et al., 2020).

2. Delivery and Pharmacokinetic Hurdles:  
   Ocular delivery, while an area of active development, remains challenging. The RPE is separated from the vitreous by multiple biological barriers. Although intravitreal or subretinal injections are established, the pharmacokinetics, biodistribution, and long-term safety profile of a miRNA agomir in the human eye require thorough optimization. It will be necessary to confirm that the chemical modifications to the miR-211 mimic do not hinder its uptake by RPE cells or cause off-target effects (Naso et al., 2020; Boya et al., 2023).

3. Translational Gaps:  
   The preclinical studies have largely been performed in rodent models that, while informative, do not fully replicate human dry AMD. Scaling up from rodent to human necessitates careful consideration of dosing, frequency of administration, and long-term impact. In addition, the natural turnover and light-dependent regulation of miR-211 in the human RPE might be more complex than in animal models (Naso et al., 2020).

4. Potential Off-target Effects and Safety:  
   As with all nucleic acid–based therapies, off-target binding and unintended gene regulation are concerns. Although miR-211 is highly specific under endogenous conditions, the synthetic mimic may interact with unintended transcripts, potentially affecting other pathways in the RPE or neighboring retinal cells. Comprehensive in vitro and in vivo toxicity studies are essential to ensure that modulating the miR-211 network does not lead to adverse outcomes (Boya et al., 2023; Naso et al., 2020).

5. Regulatory and Manufacturing Issues:  
   The regulatory pathway for oligonucleotide therapeutics remains stringent, and the manufacturing process for chemically modified miRNAs must meet high quality and reproducibility standards. There is precedence in the field for similar agents, but each new candidate faces its own set of challenges regarding scalability and cost-effectiveness (Naso et al., 2020).

─────────────────────────────  
Overall Evaluation  
─────────────────────────────  
Based on the current literature and mechanistic rationale provided in the context, the miR-211 mimic candidate holds significant promise as a therapeutic agent for dry AMD. The strengths of this approach lie in its clearly defined mechanism of action, which ties the restoration of miR-211 levels directly to the re-establishment of lysosomal biogenesis—a critical process in RPE health. Preclinical data regarding miR-211’s role in repressing Ezrin and the downstream activation of the TRPML1–Ca²⁺–calcineurin–TFEB axis are compelling and suggest that correcting the deficiency of miR-211 could reverse the degradative defects observed in dry AMD (Boya et al., 2023; Intartaglia et al., 2021; Naso et al., 2020).

Moreover, the advances in chemical modification of miRNA mimics to generate agomirs provide a technical basis for formulating a stable and effective drug candidate. The specific targeting of the RPE—a key player in the pathophysiology of dry AMD—further strengthens the case for this candidate. In vitro and preclinical readouts, such as decreased expression of Ezrin, increases in TFEB nuclear translocation, upregulation of lysosomal markers (including cathepsin D), and consequent improvements in cell clearance, are all expected to translate into improved retinal structure and function (Naso et al., 2020; Boya et al., 2023).

However, significant work remains to address some of the translational challenges. There is a critical need for direct experimental validation using the chemically modified miR-211 agomir in relevant dry AMD models. Key studies will be required to evaluate pharmacodynamics, ocular biodistribution, and the long-term safety profile of the candidate. The potential for off-target effects and the challenges inherent in intraocular delivery further complicate the clinical development pathway. In addition, while the mechanistic pathway (miR-211 → Ezrin repression → TRPML1 activation → Ca²⁺ flux → calcineurin activation → TFEB nuclear translocation → lysosomal gene upregulation) is conceptually robust, some downstream biochemical events remain to be validated in the context of miR-211 agomir treatment (Naso et al., 2020; Boya et al., 2023).

In conclusion, the miR-211 mimic is an exciting repurposed candidate for dry AMD therapy that leverages a highly specific molecular mechanism with the potential to restore lysosomal function in RPE cells. Its strengths include a clear mechanistic rationale, a strong preclinical basis for targeting Ezrin and activating the TRPML1–Ca²⁺–calcineurin–TFEB pathway, and the availability of advanced chemical modification techniques for ocular delivery. The primary risks and challenges—such as the need for comprehensive in vivo validation, optimization of delivery methods, and a thorough safety assessment—are typical of emerging nucleic acid therapeutics but are not insurmountable given current technological advances. On balance, the available evidence supports further focused preclinical evaluation of the miR-211 agomir candidate as a promising therapeutic strategy for dry AMD (Boya et al., 2023; Intartaglia et al., 2021; Naso et al., 2020).

Given the potential to correct a key pathogenic deficiency in the RPE and restore essential degradative function, advancing this candidate into rigorous in vitro testing in human RPE models followed by in vivo testing in established animal models is a priority. Subsequent studies should focus on refining the chemical formulation, ensuring efficient and targeted delivery to the RPE, and establishing a clear safety profile while monitoring for improved lysosomal function and retinal structure/function rescue. This systematic approach will be critical in determining whether the miR-211 mimic can ultimately be developed into a viable therapeutic for patients with dry AMD.

Below is our detailed evaluation of GSK2656157 for repurposing in dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD), structured in the requested format.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
GSK2656157 is a small‐molecule inhibitor of PERK (protein kinase R–like endoplasmic reticulum kinase) that was discovered and optimized through medicinal‐chemistry efforts originally led by GlaxoSmithKline. This compound belongs to the class of ATP‐competitive, Type I inhibitors that target the kinase domain of PERK, binding within the ATP‐binding cleft and stabilizing a “DFG‐in, Cα‐helix shifted” conformation of the dephosphorylated kinase domain (Axten, 2017, pp. 15–19). Structurally, the compound is an indoline‐derived molecule; similar chemical series include the indoline/aminoquinazoline chemotypes that have been widely profiled for their high potency and kinase selectivity across panels exceeding 300 kinases (Axten, 2017, pp. 15–19). Originally, these inhibitors were developed as research tools to interrogate the role of PERK in the unfolded protein response (UPR) in oncology and neurodegeneration contexts, and in preclinical studies GSK2656157 demonstrated activity in suppressing tumor growth and angiogenesis in mouse xenograft models via inhibition of PERK autophosphorylation (Atkins et al., 2013, pp. 1–2, 8). As a synthetic small molecule, its origins lie in rational design based on X‐ray–guided structure–activity relationships, which enabled optimization for both high selectivity (with >100‐fold selectivity over related kinases including other eIF2α kinases as well as a broad kinome panel) and sufficient in vivo pharmacokinetics (Axten, 2017, pp. 15–19; Atkins et al., 2013, pp. 1–2). Thus, from a chemical and developmental perspective, GSK2656157 is a first‐in‐class PERK inhibitor that exemplifies how targeted kinase inhibition can be achieved by rational design.  

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, PERK inhibitors such as GSK2606414 and its more selective derivative GSK2656157 were developed primarily for indications in oncology and neurodegeneration. Preclinical studies in tumor xenograft models have demonstrated that oral dosing of GSK2656157 can suppress PERK-mediated signaling, resulting in attenuated phospho-eIF2α levels, diminished transcriptional responses of unfolded protein response (UPR) genes, and reduced tumor vascular density (Atkins et al., 2013, pp. 1–2, 8). In neurodegenerative models—for instance in prion and tauopathy mouse models—PERK inhibition has been shown to restore global protein synthesis, decrease the levels of phospho-tau, and produce mixed effects on behavior and neuronal survival (Rozpędek-Kamińska et al., 2020, pp. 17–19). Meanwhile, within the ocular space, experimental studies with the closely related PERK inhibitor GSK2606414 (a chemical analogue of GSK2656157) in in vitro retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cell models have demonstrated on-target inhibition of PERK signaling (evidenced by reduction in eIF2α phosphorylation) along with downstream alterations in stress markers such as CHOP and VEGF mRNA (Jiang et al., 2017, pp. 1–2). However, direct use of GSK2656157 in dry AMD or similar inflammatory/degenerative ocular conditions has not yet been reported in the literature. Some studies investigating retinal degeneration models, such as P23H rhodopsin transgenic rats, have suggested that PERK inhibition can worsen photoreceptor survival by enhancing misfolded protein aggregation, although these studies were typically conducted with compounds such as GSK2606414A (Athanasiou et al., 2017, pp. 1–2, 5–7). There is, therefore, limited clinical or preclinical history regarding the use of GSK2656157 specifically in AMD or related ocular diseases. In addition, while the compound has demonstrated acceptable pharmacokinetics and tolerability in preclinical oncology settings—with measurable systemic exposures—it is important to note that systemic PERK inhibition in multiple species has been associated with toxic liabilities such as pancreatic toxicity (Atkins et al., 2013, p. 8; Axten, 2017, pp. 1–7). Consequently, although the therapeutic class has a relatively rich history in oncology and neurodegeneration, its direct application to dry AMD remains a new and untested repurposing approach that requires careful consideration of pharmacodynamic impacts in ocular tissues and rigorous safety profiling.  

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, PERK functions as an endoplasmic reticulum (ER)–resident kinase that is activated upon the accumulation of misfolded proteins, a hallmark of chronic ER stress. Normally, when the ER’s folding capacity is overwhelmed, the molecular chaperone GRP78 dissociates from PERK, enabling PERK to oligomerize and autophosphorylate, which then enables it to phosphorylate the α subunit of eukaryotic initiation factor 2 (eIF2α) at serine-51 (Axten, 2017, pp. 7–11). Phosphorylation of eIF2α leads to a global reduction in protein synthesis—a protective adaptation that prevents further accumulation of misfolded proteins—and also selectively permits the translation of stress-induced genes, most notably ATF4. ATF4 subsequently upregulates transcription factors such as CHOP, which can drive pro-apoptotic signaling if ER stress persists (Axten, 2017, pp. 7–11; Chu et al., 2021, p. 8). In the context of dry AMD, chronic ER stress in RPE cells has been implicated in disrupting cellular proteostasis, where misfolded proteins—including subunits of key complexes like the vacuolar ATPase (v-ATPase)—may fail to fold properly, leading to impaired lysosomal acidification (Kaarniranta et al., 2018, pp. 1–4; Athanasiou et al., 2017, pp. 1–2). The hypothesis is that by inhibiting PERK with GSK2656157, the excessive phosphorylation of eIF2α and the maladaptive integrated stress response (ISR) can be attenuated. This would not only restore global protein synthesis but also prevent downstream consequences such as upregulation of CHOP and VEGF, thereby reducing pro-apoptotic as well as pro-inflammatory pathways (Jiang et al., 2017, pp. 1–2). Furthermore, it is posited that such normalization in the ISR could allow for proper folding and assembly of lysosomal enzymes and complexes, including the v-ATPase. Proper v-ATPase assembly is critical for maintaining low intraluminal pH in lysosomes, which is necessary for the activation and maturation of hydrolases like cathepsin D (Kaarniranta et al., 2018, pp. 1–4). In neuronal models, PERK inhibition has been associated with improvements in lysosomal function and proteostasis, indicating that reduction of chronic ER stress can indirectly favor the re-establishment of lysosomal homeostasis (Jiang et al., 2017, pp. 1–2). In essence, GSK2656157, by specifically targeting and inhibiting PERK, interferes with the pathological arm of the UPR (i.e. excessive eIF2α phosphorylation) that is hypothesized to contribute to impaired lysosomal acidification in RPE cells under chronic stress conditions—a mechanism that might be particularly relevant in the pathophysiology of dry AMD (Axten, 2017, pp. 24–28).  

Expected Effect:  
In the proposed assays, the primary expected effect of GSK2656157 is to inhibit PERK activity in RPE cells, as evidenced by reduced phosphorylation of eIF2α, and thereby dampen downstream signaling events that lead to the induction of ATF4, CHOP, and ultimately pro-apoptotic and proangiogenic factors such as VEGF. In vitro studies with analogues of GSK2656157 (such as GSK2606414) in ARPE-19 cells have shown dose-dependent inhibition of eIF2α phosphorylation with subsequent decreases in CHOP and VEGF mRNA expression without necessarily triggering apoptosis at higher doses (Jiang et al., 2017, pp. 1–2). These results provide a proof-of-concept that pharmacological inhibition of PERK can modulate this critical signaling pathway in RPE cells. The hypothesis for dry AMD is that chronic ER stress in the RPE disrupts lysosomal acidification via misfolding of v-ATPase subunits; under normal circumstances, proper v-ATPase function ensures that lysosomes maintain their acidic environment, which is essential for protease activation—including cathepsin D. Cathepsin D, in turn, is critical for lysosomal degradation of photoreceptor outer segments and for preventing lipofuscin accumulation, a pathological process in dry AMD (Kaarniranta et al., 2018, pp. 1–4). Thus, by reducing PERK activation through GSK2656157, it is expected that the overactive ISR would be tempered sufficiently to allow for the proper folding and assembly of v-ATPase complexes, thereby restoring lysosomal acidification (Chu et al., 2021, p. 8; Athanasiou et al., 2017, pp. 1–2). This restoration is anticipated to improve cathepsin D maturation and activity, leading to better clearance of intracellular debris and misfolded proteins, ultimately protecting RPE cells from stress-induced degeneration. On a cellular level, normalizing lysosomal pH would also promote autophagy flux, which is often impaired in the aged RPE, thereby mitigating one of the key contributing factors in the dry AMD phenotype (Kaarniranta et al., 2018, pp. 1–4; Athanasiou et al., 2017, pp. 1–2). Importantly, RPE cells are known to express PERK and components of the UPR, with studies demonstrating that ER stress markers, including phospho-PERK and phospho-eIF2α, are elevated in pathological states associated with AMD (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021, pp. 11–12; Chu et al., 2021, p. 8). Therefore, if GSK2656157 can achieve adequate ocular tissue exposure and inhibit PERK activity in the RPE, the expected outcome would be a reduction in cellular stress–mediated apoptosis and proliferation of protective pathways that maintain lysosomal and autophagy functions (Jiang et al., 2017, pp. 1–2; Rozpędek-Kamińska et al., 2020, pp. 17–19). Moreover, the compound’s known pharmacokinetic profile in preclinical oncology studies suggests that it is systemically bioavailable and, according to some reports, may achieve ocular tissue distribution; thus it is conceivable that with appropriate dosing and local delivery strategies, GSK2656157 could achieve effective concentrations in RPE cells (Atkins et al., 2013, pp. 1–2, 8).  

Overall Evaluation:  
Overall, GSK2656157 presents an intriguing therapeutic candidate for dry AMD based on a mechanistic hypothesis that links chronic ER stress to impaired lysosomal acidification—a process central to the pathogenesis of AMD. One of the primary strengths of GSK2656157 is its potent and selective inhibition of PERK, a critical mediator of the integrated stress response. The compound’s design as an ATP‐competitive PERK inhibitor places it squarely in a class of drugs that have been well characterized in terms of kinase selectivity and in vivo pharmacodynamics in oncology settings (Axten, 2017, pp. 15–19). The underlying biological rationale is that by attenuating the maladaptive PERK-mediated phosphorylation of eIF2α, it may be possible to relieve chronic translational suppression and dampen downstream deleterious signaling cascades—thereby re-establishing normal lysosomal function through proper v-ATPase assembly and restoration of cathepsin D activity (Axten, 2017, pp. 7–11; Chu et al., 2021, p. 8). There is supportive in vitro evidence from studies using related inhibitors (for example, GSK2606414 in ARPE-19 cells) that PERK inhibition can downregulate stress effectors such as CHOP and VEGF, which are both implicated in retinal degeneration and neovascularization (Jiang et al., 2017, pp. 1–2). Such studies underscore the potential of targeting the PERK/ISR axis in RPE cells to create a more favorable intracellular environment that could prevent progressive degeneration seen in dry AMD (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021, pp. 11–12; Chu et al., 2021, p. 8).

However, there are several notable weaknesses and caveats. First, while there is an extensive body of preclinical work on PERK inhibitors in oncology and neurodegeneration models, there is a significant lack of direct evidence in ocular disease models—especially chronic models of dry AMD—as well as an absence of published studies specifically evaluating GSK2656157 in RPE cells or in animal models of AMD (Athanasiou et al., 2017, pp. 5–7). In several studies using related PERK inhibitors in rod photoreceptor degeneration models (such as P23H rhodopsin transgenic rats), inhibition of PERK activity has been associated with worsened outcomes, suggesting that PERK activation may paradoxically be protective in certain contexts of protein misfolding (Athanasiou et al., 2017, pp. 1–2, 5–7). This dichotomous role of PERK—as both an adaptive and a pro-death signal depending on the context and duration of activation—raises concerns about whether inhibition will uniformly yield beneficial effects in the RPE, whose balance of ER stress responses may differ from that of neuronal or secretory tissues. Second, while the hypothesis postulates that chronic ER stress impairs lysosomal acidification by misfolding v-ATPase subunits, the direct link between PERK inhibition and restoration of v-ATPase assembly or cathepsin D maturation in RPE cells has not been firmly established in the literature. Data that explicitly demonstrate that PERK inhibition rescues lysosomal pH, enhances v-ATPase function, and improves cathepsin D activity in neuronal models may exist, yet similar studies in ocular models are limited (Chu et al., 2021, p. 8; Kaarniranta et al., 2018, pp. 1–4). Third, the systemic administration of PERK inhibitors such as GSK2656157 has been associated with pancreatic toxicity and other systemic adverse effects in preclinical studies, a liability that could be particularly problematic in chronic therapies such as those needed for dry AMD (Atkins et al., 2013, p. 8; Axten, 2017, pp. 1–7). Although strategies such as local (intravitreal) delivery might mitigate these systemic risks, ocular pharmacokinetic and tolerability data are sparse, and the tissue-specific distribution of GSK2656157 in the eye would need careful evaluation (Atkins et al., 2013, pp. 1–2, 8). Fourth, there is some concern over off-target effects; for example, early reports on similar GSK compounds noted possible inhibition of RIP1 kinase activity, although subsequent studies have argued that the effects observed were indeed mediated by PERK inhibition (Starr, 2019, pp. 133–137; Athanasiou et al., 2017, pp. 5–7). Nonetheless, affording absolute selectivity in a clinical candidate remains a challenge. In addition, chronic inhibition of the adaptive aspects of the ISR may inadvertently impair protective mechanisms in the retina, as transient ISR activation is known to mediate cellular adaptation during acute stress (Axten, 2017, pp. 7–11, 24–28).

In summary, while the mechanistic rationale for using GSK2656157 to address dry AMD is based on a conceptually appealing hypothesis—that PERK inhibition will relieve chronic ER stress, thereby restoring proper lysosomal acidification, enabling v-ATPase assembly, and rescuing cathepsin D activity in RPE cells—the current body of literature reveals both promising on-target effects in non-ocular systems and significant gaps in ocular-specific efficacy and safety data. Given the complex, context-dependent role of PERK signaling in retinal homeostasis and the potential for deleterious outcomes when PERK is inhibited in models of protein misfolding, further focused in vitro and in vivo studies are required to determine whether GSK2656157 can be safely and effectively repurposed for dry AMD. Strengths of this candidate include its potent, selective PERK inhibition and preclinical pharmacodynamic proof-of-concept in related disease models, while weaknesses center on limited ocular data, potential systemic and off-target toxicities, and an uncertain impact on lysosomal and proteostatic pathways in RPE cells. Ultimately, while GSK2656157 remains an attractive avenue for targeting an upstream stress node in dry AMD pathogenesis, careful optimization of dosing, targeted ocular delivery, and comprehensive evaluation in relevant AMD models will be essential before moving forward in clinical development (Axten, 2017, pp. 1–7, 15–19, 24–28; Atkins et al., 2013, pp. 1–2; Athanasiou et al., 2017, pp. 5–7; Jiang et al., 2017, pp. 1–2).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Eculizumab (Soliris, Alexion) is a humanized IgG monoclonal antibody derived from the murine anti–human C5 antibody m5G1 via CDR grafting and human framework engineering to reduce immunogenicity and extend serum half-life, designed to bind complement component C5 with high affinity and sterically prevent its cleavage by C5 convertases into C5a and C5b (thereby blocking terminal pathway activation and MAC assembly) (Park et al., 2019; Troutbeck et al., 2012; Yehoshua et al., 2014; Park et al., 2021). It belongs to the class of complement inhibitors that directly target an effector protein (C5) at the convergence of the classical, lectin, and alternative pathways, in contrast to upstream amplification-targeting agents (e.g., C3 or factor D inhibitors) (Park et al., 2019; Tzoumas et al., 2023). Systemically administered eculizumab has established clinical utility in complement-mediated hematologic and renal disorders, including paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria and atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome, and more recently generalized myasthenia gravis, reflecting a mature pharmacology and a well-characterized risk profile centered on increased susceptibility to encapsulated organisms (notably meningococcal infection) due to terminal pathway blockade (Park et al., 2019; Yehoshua et al., 2014).

Within ophthalmology, the terminal complement pathway is an attractive target for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) and geographic atrophy (GA) because C5a is a proinflammatory anaphylatoxin detected in drusen that can drive leukocyte recruitment and VEGF induction in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), and C5b nucleates formation of the membrane attack complex (MAC, C5b–C9), which accumulates with age and AMD in Bruch’s membrane and choriocapillaris and can lyse or sub-lytically activate choroidal endothelial and RPE cells (Kassa et al., 2019). The class of C5 inhibitors therefore aims to reduce both inflammatory signaling (via C5a) and cytolytic/proinflammatory MAC effects while preserving upstream opsonization and some host-defense functions mediated by C3b, potentially retaining aspects of immune competence relative to C3 inhibition (Halawa et al., 2021; Park et al., 2019).

Therapeutic History  
Approved indications and systemic pharmacology  
Eculizumab is FDA/EMA approved for paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria and atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome, where weight-based intravenous regimens achieve sustained trough serum concentrations and complete inhibition of hemolytic activity by blocking C5 cleavage; these regimens produce serum levels > 35 μg/mL and complete systemic C5 functional blockade, but require meningococcal vaccination to mitigate Neisseria risk inherent to terminal complement inhibition (Park et al., 2019; Yehoshua et al., 2014). In other complementopathies, clinical experience has highlighted a mechanism-consequent shift of pathology upstream (e.g., C3-loading and extravascular hemolysis in PNH under C5 blockade), underscoring that C5 inhibition leaves C3 activation intact (Hammadi et al., 2023).

Clinical investigation in geographic atrophy of dry AMD  
Eculizumab was investigated in the prospective, randomized, double-masked, single-center Phase 2 COMPLETE study that enrolled 30 participants with GA (primary cohort) plus an intermediate AMD/drusen cohort, randomized 2:1 to intravenous eculizumab versus saline over 24 weeks (with follow-up to 52 weeks) (Yehoshua et al., 2014). Two dosing regimens were tested: a low-dose arm (600 mg weekly × 4, then 900 mg every 2 weeks through week 24) and a high-dose arm with higher induction and maintenance dosing; all patients received meningococcal vaccination prior to first infusion (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Patel et al., 2022). Pharmacokinetically, systemic exposure and target engagement were confirmed: eculizumab concentrations were measurable at all assessed time points (mean ~ 65–189 μg/mL in low-dose and ~ 122–259 μg/mL in high-dose cohorts), with plasma C5 activity reduced to < 9% by week 1 and < 1% by week 2, indicating complete systemic terminal complement blockade sustained through treatment (Yehoshua et al., 2014).

Despite robust systemic pharmacodynamics, COMPLETE detected no effect on GA progression: at 26 weeks the change in square-root–transformed GA area was 0.19 ± 0.12 mm in eculizumab-treated eyes versus 0.18 ± 0.15 mm with placebo (P = 0.96), and at 52 weeks both arms exhibited ~ 0.37 mm enlargement (P ≈ 0.93), effectively excluding a large treatment effect (> 55% slowing) in this cohort (Yehoshua et al., 2014). Drusen volume endpoints in the intermediate AMD cohort were also negative (no participant achieved a 50% reduction), and fellow-eye analyses mirrored primary-eye results (Patel et al., 2022; Yehoshua et al., 2014). Visual function showed no durable benefit: a 26-week letter gain difference favoring eculizumab was attributed to a single outlier in placebo, and by 52 weeks there was no between-group difference; pooled estimates across small RCTs rated the certainty of BCVA effects as low-to-very-low with confidence intervals overlapping no effect (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Tzoumas et al., 2023). Safety was acceptable in the trial: no drug-related serious adverse events were identified through 52 weeks, and no eyes converted to neovascular AMD during the study; however, systemic C5 blockade requires vaccination and vigilance for meningococcal infection, and an independent systemic anti-C5 AMD trial was terminated early due to uncertainty about risk/benefit in light of reported meningococcal infections in real-world eculizumab users (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Tzoumas et al., 2023).

Interpretations from COMPLETE and subsequent reviews point to several plausible explanations for the null result: inadequate intraocular/RPE target engagement with systemic dosing due to blood–retinal and Bruch’s barriers; the possibility that C5 is the wrong target in GA given genetic associations that more strongly implicate proximal complement components (e.g., C3, CFH) rather than terminal pathway constituents; the short on-treatment window (24 weeks) and small sample size; and the biological reality that C5 inhibition preserves upstream C3a/C3b biology, which may continue to drive pathology (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Halawa et al., 2021; Hammadi et al., 2023; Tzoumas et al., 2023).

Comparative C5 and complement-targeting experience in AMD  
Intravitreal C5 inhibition has produced divergent results. LFG316 (tesidolumab), an anti-C5 monoclonal antibody administered intravitreally, failed to alter GA lesion growth or visual outcomes in a randomized phase 2 trial (Halawa et al., 2021; Park et al., 2019). By contrast, avacincaptad pegol (Zimura), an intravitreal C5 aptamer, reduced GA growth rates by approximately 27–30% over 12–18 months in pivotal trials, leading to FDA approval, although potential increased risk of macular neovascularization has been signaled and requires ongoing pharmacovigilance (Patel et al., 2022; Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023; Tzoumas et al., 2023). Upstream targeting at C3 with intravitreal pegcetacoplan (SYFOVRE) significantly slowed GA enlargement in phase 2–3 programs and achieved regulatory approval, but at the cost of increased rates of conversion to exudative AMD and, in the postmarketing setting, reports of occlusive retinal vasculitis, highlighting a target-dependent safety trade-off between efficacy and pro-angiogenic/immune-privilege perturbation risks (Halawa et al., 2021; Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023; Qin et al., 2024). Alternative-pathway inhibition via factor D (lampalizumab) produced a phase 2 signal but failed in two phase 3 trials, suggesting that partial pathway blockade may be insufficient in GA (Piri & Kaplan, 2023; Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023).

Taken together, these data place systemic eculizumab among C5-directed strategies where local delivery has demonstrated anatomic efficacy in GA, whereas systemic delivery has not, and they highlight that complement modulation can slow atrophy progression without improving visual function and may introduce target- and route-specific risks such as neovascularization or serious infection (Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023; Tzoumas et al., 2023).

Mechanism of Action  
Complement cascade biology and eculizumab target engagement  
Complement activation arises via classical, lectin, and alternative pathways, converging at the generation of C3 convertases that cleave C3 into C3a (anaphylatoxin) and C3b (opsonin/convertase component), with amplification by the alternative pathway accounting for the majority (80–90%) of downstream MAC generation in physiologic and pathologic settings (Tzoumas et al., 2023). C5 convertases (C4b2a3b for classical/lectin and C3bBbC3b for alternative pathway) cleave C5 into C5a, a potent anaphylatoxin that recruits/activates myeloid cells and stimulates RPE to produce VEGF and proinflammatory cytokines, and C5b, which seeds assembly of the terminal membrane attack complex (C5b–C9) on nearby membranes (Tzoumas et al., 2023; Kassa et al., 2019). Eculizumab binds C5 to prevent convertase-mediated cleavage, thereby abrogating both C5a generation and MAC formation independent of the initiating pathway; this preserves upstream C3 activation (C3a/C3b) and the alternative-pathway amplification loop while blunting terminal effector functions (Park et al., 2019; Halawa et al., 2021).

Ocular and RPE relevance of C5 and MAC  
Multiple lines of evidence implicate terminal pathway effectors in AMD pathophysiology at the RPE–choriocapillaris interface. Histopathology shows increasing MAC deposition with aging and AMD in Bruch’s membrane and the choriocapillaris; sub-lytic MAC on choroidal endothelial cells triggers pro-angiogenic/proteolytic responses (VEGF, MMPs), while high-level deposition can induce lysis of choroidal endothelial cells and bystander injury contributing to RPE atrophy (Kassa et al., 2019). C5a is present in drusen and is a strong inflammatory mediator that can recruit immune cells and induce VEGF release from RPE, linking terminal pathway activation to both atrophic and neovascular processes relevant to the AMD spectrum (Kassa et al., 2019). Additional experimental work demonstrates that sub-lytic C5b-9 can alter RPE function in ways consistent with AMD, including stress responses and secretory changes, reinforcing that terminal complement activation can be injurious to the RPE even in the absence of frank lysis (Park et al., 2019).

Complement production and regulation in the eye—and systemic versus local contributions  
Complement proteins are synthesized predominantly by the liver and circulate systemically, but they are also produced locally within ocular tissues (retina, RPE, choroid), with local activation and regulation shaped by cell-intrinsic complement regulatory proteins (e.g., CFH, CD46, CD59) and by oxidative stress effects that reduce cell-surface complement inhibition on RPE (Tzoumas et al., 2023; van Lookeren Campagne et al., 2016). Several studies highlight local complement expression and activation in retinal cells and macrophages, as well as increased local complement turnover preceding clinical disease, supporting the concept of an ocular complement “microenvironment” that can be dysregulated independent of systemic levels (Patel et al., 2022; Piri & Kaplan, 2023). Conversely, transcriptomic mapping suggests that posterior-pole tissues have limited local transcription of lectin and terminal pathway components (except C5 and C7), implying reliance on systemic sources for some terminal pathway proteins, which in principle could make systemic C5 blockade effective if sufficient intraocular penetration and target engagement are achieved (Troutbeck et al., 2012). These seemingly conflicting observations are reconciled by recognizing that both local production and systemic supply contribute to ocular complement biology, and that their relative importance likely varies by compartment (RPE, choriocapillaris, sub-RPE space), disease stage, and barrier integrity.

Genetic and biomarker context for C5 targeting in AMD  
GWAS and biomarker studies have repeatedly implicated complement dysregulation in AMD susceptibility and progression, including associations at CFH, C3, C2/CFB, CFI, and C9 loci, and elevated systemic and ocular concentrations of complement activation products (C3a, C5a, MAC) in AMD patients (Dascalu et al., 2024). However, the genetic signal is stronger and more consistent for proximal regulators (e.g., CFH, C3) than for C5, and at least one analysis noted C3 risk alleles do not necessarily correlate with GA progression (and in some contexts associated with decreased progression), emphasizing the complexity of translating susceptibility signals to progression biology and target selection in late AMD (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Halawa et al., 2021). Mechanistically, C5 blockade leaves upstream C3a/C3b biology intact; in extra-ocular diseases this can unmask C3-related pathophysiology under C5 inhibition, illustrating a general limitation of terminal pathway-only targeting (Hammadi et al., 2023). In GA, this implies that C3a/C3b-driven processes—chemoattraction, opsonization, and immune modulation—could continue in the outer retina/RPE even under complete C5 suppression, potentially blunting the benefit of C5-only therapy (Halawa et al., 2021; Tzoumas et al., 2023).

Therapeutic delivery constraints to ocular complement modulation with systemic C5 blockade  
Large biologics such as eculizumab face formidable physical barriers to ocular penetration, including the inner and outer blood–retina barriers and Bruch’s membrane/RPE tight junctions, whose permeability declines with increasing molecular weight and hydrophilicity (a profile characteristic of IgG antibodies), making intraocular access by systemic dosing uncertain without active transport mechanisms (Hammadi et al., 2023; Yehoshua et al., 2014). This is the most straightforward explanation for COMPLETE’s combination of complete systemic pharmacodynamic suppression with no effect on lesion enlargement: the effective intraocular concentration of antibody at relevant RPE–choroid interfaces was likely insufficient to inhibit terminal complement activation locally, a conclusion echoed by the trial investigators (Yehoshua et al., 2014).

Expected Effect  
Proposed pharmacologic and cellular effect  
Under the working hypothesis, systemic eculizumab would reduce MAC formation on RPE and choroidal endothelial surfaces and diminish C5a-driven inflammatory signaling, thereby protecting RPE cellular homeostasis and the RPE–choriocapillaris unit from complement-mediated injury and slowing expansion of GA lesions (Kassa et al., 2019; Park et al., 2019). Mechanistically, suppression of MAC would be expected to decrease lytic and sub-lytic injury to choroidal endothelial cells and RPE, attenuating downstream induction of VEGF and MMPs, and limiting bystander tissue damage around atrophic borders where complement activation is thought to be active (Tzoumas et al., 2023; Kassa et al., 2019). Reducing C5a generation could blunt recruitment and activation of myeloid cells and RPE proinflammatory cytokine production, decreasing local inflammatory amplification in the outer retina (Tzoumas et al., 2023; Kassa et al., 2019).

Expression and target presence in relevant cells/tissues  
C5 and terminal pathway components are present in the ocular compartments relevant to GA pathobiology: choriocapillaris/Bruch’s membrane deposition of MAC is well documented and increases with age and AMD, and C5a is detected within drusen; RPE-derived complement regulators (e.g., CD59) and choroidal endothelial susceptibility to MAC are described, establishing both target and downstream effectors within the disease-relevant tissues (Kassa et al., 2019). Complement components and regulators are expressed in retina, RPE, and choroid, with transcriptomic data indicating relatively higher choroidal expression and limited local transcription of some terminal components (except C5 and C7), consistent with both local and systemic sources contributing substrate for terminal pathway assembly (Troutbeck et al., 2012; Tzoumas et al., 2023).

Translational and clinical outcome expectations  
At the disease level, a therapy that meaningfully reduces local terminal complement activation in GA should slow the rate of GA lesion enlargement measured on fundus autofluorescence (FAF) and/or SD-OCT, endpoints accepted by the FDA/NEI and standard across GA trials; functional outcomes such as BCVA and low-luminance VA typically lag structural changes and may not improve even when lesion growth is slowed (Dascalu et al., 2024; Qin et al., 2024). In COMPLETE, these endpoints were precisely those evaluated; the absence of any measurable effect on square-root GA area at 26 and 52 weeks indicates that, at the tested systemic dosing regimens, eculizumab did not achieve sufficient intraocular target engagement to translate the mechanistic rationale into clinical benefit (Yehoshua et al., 2014).

Reasons for divergence between expected and observed effects  
Three non-exclusive explanations align with the totality of evidence:

  • Inadequate intraocular bioavailability from systemic dosing. Antibody size and hydrophilicity, combined with blood–retina and RPE–Bruch’s barriers, likely prevented sufficient drug from reaching the RPE–choriocapillaris compartment to inhibit local terminal pathway activation, despite verified systemic C5 suppression (Hammadi et al., 2023; Yehoshua et al., 2014; Tzoumas et al., 2023).

  • Target selection may be suboptimal for GA biology. The stronger genetic and pathophysiologic evidence for proximal complement dysregulation (e.g., C3, CFH) and the preservation of upstream activation under C5 blockade mean that C5-only inhibition may not adequately suppress the complement-driven processes that sustain GA border expansion, as supported by the comparatively stronger clinical signals with C3 inhibition and mixed-to-positive signals with intravitreal C5 inhibition (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Halawa et al., 2021; Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023).

  • Trial limitations. The COMPLETE cohort was small and on-treatment duration was six months, which may be insufficient to observe smaller effects on GA growth; however, confidence intervals excluded large effects, and lack of any trend over 52 weeks reduces the likelihood that longer dosing would have changed the outcome meaningfully (Yehoshua et al., 2014).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
  • Strong mechanistic rationale for terminal pathway blockade in AMD: C5a is proinflammatory and detected in drusen; MAC accumulates at the RPE–choriocapillaris interface with age/AMD and can injure choroidal endothelium and RPE via lytic and sub-lytic mechanisms, linking C5 effector functions directly to AMD pathophysiology (Kassa et al., 2019). Blocking C5 suppresses both MAC and C5a, targeting inflammatory and cytolytic arms while leaving upstream C3-mediated opsonization intact, an immunologic advantage over C3 blockade (Halawa et al., 2021; Park et al., 2019).

  • Mature systemic pharmacology with demonstrated ability to completely suppress plasma C5 activity at well-tolerated doses, including in AMD patients, making systemic development logistically straightforward and with known requirements (e.g., meningococcal vaccination) (Yehoshua et al., 2014).

  • Practical systemic-delivery advantages: single systemic therapy treats both eyes simultaneously and avoids intravitreal injection–related ocular risks (endophthalmitis, IOP spikes), which have nontrivial incidence in chronic IVT regimens (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Tzoumas et al., 2023).

  • External validation within the class: intravitreal C5 inhibition (avacincaptad pegol) has replicated GA-slowing effects in phase 2/3 programs, supporting the therapeutic value of suppressing terminal pathway activity in the outer retina if adequate local exposure is achieved (Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023).

Limitations  
  • Lack of efficacy in the definitive systemic eculizumab GA study. COMPLETE showed no reduction in GA lesion growth at 26 or 52 weeks despite complete systemic C5 blockade and adequate serum exposure, effectively excluding a large treatment effect and arguing strongly against systemic eculizumab as a viable GA therapy (Yehoshua et al., 2014).

  • Ocular pharmacokinetic barrier. The most parsimonious explanation for the COMPLETE result is inadequate intraocular target engagement from systemic dosing due to the blood–retina/RPE–Bruch’s barriers and the large size/hydrophilicity of IgG, an inherent limitation of systemic antibody delivery to the sub-RPE/choroidal compartment (Hammadi et al., 2023; Yehoshua et al., 2014).

  • Target-level uncertainties. Genetic and biomarker studies more consistently implicate proximal complement dysregulation (CFH/C3) than C5 in AMD susceptibility; moreover, C5 inhibition preserves upstream C3a/C3b activity, which may continue to drive border-zone inflammation and remodeling in GA (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Dascalu et al., 2024; Halawa et al., 2021). Clinical comparisons reinforce this: upstream C3 inhibition has produced larger and more consistent anatomic effects (with important safety trade-offs), whereas anti-C5 trials are split—systemic eculizumab negative; IVT LFG316 negative; IVT avacincaptad positive—pointing to delivery and target–context dependencies (Halawa et al., 2021; Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023).

  • Systemic safety constraints. While COMPLETE itself reported no drug-related serious adverse events over one year, terminal complement blockade carries a class risk of meningococcal infection requiring vaccination and risk mitigation; at least one planned AMD systemic anti-C5 trial was terminated early due to uncertainty regarding the systemic infection risk/benefit in this population (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Tzoumas et al., 2023).

  • Limited translatability of systemic complement activation to local disease control. Although systemic complement activation correlates with AMD and disease stage in several studies, the relative importance of local versus systemic complement sources—and the ability of systemic blockade to suppress complement activity at the RPE–choriocapillaris interface—is unresolved and likely unfavorable for large biologics, reducing the mechanistic plausibility of systemic C5 blockade for GA (Hammadi et al., 2023; Park et al., 2019).

Risk–benefit and competitive landscape assessment  
Eculizumab’s negative randomized, controlled data in GA, in the face of confirmed systemic pharmacodynamics, places a high bar against further systemic development for this indication, a conclusion explicitly drawn by the COMPLETE investigators who noted the linearity of GA growth and lack of signal as making additional systemic investigations with eculizumab unlikely (Yehoshua et al., 2014). Against this backdrop, systemic eculizumab offers no efficacy advantage, carries systemic infection risk and costs, and fails the core requirement of achieving ocular target engagement necessary for GA modification.

Operationally, even if one hypothesized that higher systemic dosing, longer exposure, or patient stratification could rescue efficacy, several facts weigh against that strategy: COMPLETE’s pharmacodynamics confirmed near-complete systemic C5 suppression within two weeks; genetic analyses within the trial found no association between at-risk alleles and GA growth or treatment response; and extended follow-up to a year showed no divergence in growth rates (Yehoshua et al., 2014). Moreover, retinal pharmacokinetics and barrier biology make it unlikely that increasing systemic doses would proportionally increase intraocular concentrations to therapeutic levels without exacerbating systemic risks (Hammadi et al., 2023). In addition, C5 may not be the optimal node for GA progression biology in many patients, given preserved upstream activity and the complex contributions of C3a/C3b, opsonization, and local complement production that may continue to drive border-zone degeneration independent of MAC inhibition (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Halawa et al., 2021; Piri & Kaplan, 2023).

Recommendation  
Based on the aggregate mechanistic, translational, and clinical evidence, eculizumab (systemic C5 inhibition) does not have compelling potential as a repurposed therapy for dry AMD/GA. The drug has a clear and relevant mechanism and an acceptable short-term tolerability profile in older adults, but it fails to slow GA lesion growth in a randomized, controlled trial despite complete systemic target engagement, and there are strong mechanistic and pharmacokinetic reasons to expect insufficient intraocular exposure with systemic delivery (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Hammadi et al., 2023). The therapeutic hypothesis—reducing MAC on RPE/choriocapillaris to preserve tissue integrity and slow atrophy—is supported conceptually and by local C5 inhibition successes; however, achieving that biology in vivo appears to require intraocular delivery or targeting upstream nodes, neither of which is compatible with systemic eculizumab administration (Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023; Halawa et al., 2021).

If complement-targeted strategies remain a program priority, resources should pivot to modalities with demonstrated ocular target engagement and anatomic efficacy (intravitreal C3 or C5 agents) while carefully managing known safety trade-offs (e.g., neovascularization risk), and to biomarker-driven questions (e.g., whether baseline low-luminance visual acuity deficit—correlated with faster GA growth in COMPLETE—can enrich for patients who derive greater anatomic benefit) (Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023; Tzoumas et al., 2023; Yehoshua et al., 2014). For systemic complement modulation in AMD more broadly, alternative targets with better ocular PK profiles (e.g., small-molecule systemic alternative-pathway inhibitors) and rigorous ocular target-engagement measurements would be required to justify late-stage development, but systemic C5 blockade with eculizumab itself should not be advanced further for GA (Hammadi et al., 2023; Tzoumas et al., 2023; Park et al., 2019).

In summary, while the mechanistic logic for terminal complement inhibition in AMD is robust, the totality of evidence argues against systemic eculizumab as a viable candidate to slow GA progression, and the development program should discontinue pursuit of this repurposing in favor of locally delivered complement inhibitors or alternative mechanisms better suited to the ocular compartment and GA pathobiology (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023).

Overall, metformin is a biologically plausible, low-cost, and generally safe repurposing candidate for dry AMD that warrants mechanistic confirmation in RPE for lysosome-centric endpoints and rigorous randomized trials across AMD stages (Amin et al., 2022; Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Moir et al., 2023).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Metformin is a small-molecule biguanide synthesized as a derivative of galegine, a guanidine-class alkaloid originally isolated from the plant Galega officinalis; clinically it has been used for more than 60 years as the most commonly prescribed oral antihyperglycemic agent worldwide (class: biguanides) (Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Amin et al., 2022). Chemically, metformin comprises two coupled guanidine moieties conferring cationic, hydrophilic properties and cellular accumulation via organic cation transporters, consistent with mitochondrial complex I engagement and AMPK pathway activation described in mechanistic literature (Augustin & Atorf, 2023). Beyond glycemic control, metformin exhibits pleiotropic effects—anti-inflammatory, anti-oxidative, anti-angiogenic, anti-apoptotic and anti-senescence—reported in diverse cell types and tissues, many of which intersect with pathways implicated in AMD pathogenesis (oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, impaired proteostasis/autophagy, para-inflammation, vascular dysregulation) (Amin et al., 2022; Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Kozlowski, 2023). In ocular contexts, preclinical work indicates that metformin activates AMPK in RPE and neural retina and can preserve retinal structure and function under oxidative, metabolic, and phototoxic stressors (Amin et al., 2022). Collectively, these properties position metformin as a rational repurposing candidate for dry AMD, wherein RPE dysfunction, impaired autophagy/lysosomal clearance, mitochondrial stress, and chronic inflammation are central pathogenic nodes (Amin et al., 2022; Buonfiglio et al., 2024).

Therapeutic History  
Systemic use: Metformin is established first-line therapy for type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) and has been investigated broadly for aging-related conditions due to putative geroprotective effects; long-term safety has been documented, including in the Diabetes Prevention Program (DPP) where gastrointestinal intolerance is the most common adverse event and lactic acidosis was not observed under trial conditions, though B12 deficiency can occur with chronic use (Amin et al., 2022; Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Zhou & Xue, 2024). Preclinical ocular use: In retinal models, metformin has been tested systemically (oral/IP) and intravitreally, demonstrating protective effects in RPE and photoreceptors across light-damage, iodate-induced injury, inherited retinal degeneration (rd1/rd10), and oxygen-induced retinopathy (OIR) with readouts including preserved RPE tight junctions (ZO-1, occludin), outer nuclear layer thickness, and ERG amplitudes; notable anti-angiogenic activity includes decreased CNV lesion size and VEGF/VEGFR signaling modulation in several models (Amin et al., 2022). In these preclinical settings, metformin’s ocular benefits are frequently attributed to AMPK activation and downstream autophagy/mitochondrial and anti-inflammatory pathways, without overt ocular toxicity reported in rodents; however, human ocular safety data and pharmacokinetics under intravitreal or high-dose local exposure are not detailed in the excerpts (Amin et al., 2022).

Clinical/epidemiologic AMD history: Observational epidemiology offers mixed signals. Several large retrospective cohorts and case–control analyses associate metformin use with reduced odds or risk of any AMD or early AMD, with dose–duration trends in some datasets (e.g., MarketScan/claims OR 0.93 and propensity-matched HR 0.57; Taiwanese cohorts HR ~0.54 with stronger protection at >4 years and higher average daily doses), and lower odds reported in multiple studies across US, Europe, and Asia (Amin et al., 2022; Jiang et al., 2022; Kozlowski, 2023; Moir et al., 2023). Other datasets report null or complex associations: a high-quality UK T2DM cohort found no differential AMD risk with metformin using time-varying exposure models; a U.S. claims analysis focusing on dry AMD reported current use slightly increased dry AMD risk while prior use trended protective; additional analyses show no association or heterogeneity by diabetic retinopathy status (Eton et al., 2022; Gokhale et al., 2023; Liang et al., 2022). Meta-analyses also conflict: a systematic review of diabetics suggested decreased odds of AMD with metformin, whereas a broader 2024 meta-analysis concluded no overall prophylactic/treatment role; a European meta-analysis of antidiabetic/lipid-lowering drugs found reduced AMD prevalence overall but not for late-stage AMD specifically (Elhalag et al., 2024; Mauschitz et al., 2023). Importantly, these retrospective designs face confounding (e.g., smoking, comorbidities, health-care utilization), outcome misclassification (wet vs dry AMD), and exposure misclassification (adherence), limiting causal inference and stage-specific conclusions (Brown et al., 2019; Gokhale et al., 2023; Moir et al., 2023). Prospective interventional testing for dry AMD is underway: a randomized, single-blind Phase II trial of metformin to slow geographic atrophy (GA) progression has been conducted, with publication reported in 2024 (Shen et al., 2024); however, the excerpts do not provide efficacy outcomes in GA and emphasize that randomized evidence remains needed (Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Shen et al., 2024).

No regulatory approval exists for metformin in AMD (dry or wet), and the totality of evidence remains preclinical and observational for efficacy, with one randomized GA study reported but without effect-size details here; therefore, clinical utility in dry AMD is presently unproven (Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Shen et al., 2024).

Mechanism of Action  
Canonical pharmacology: Metformin partially inhibits mitochondrial respiratory complex I, reducing hepatic ATP and increasing AMP/ADP, thereby activating AMPK, the cellular energy sensor that shifts metabolism toward ATP-generating pathways; AMPK-dependent and ‑independent mechanisms operate systemically, including reduced hepatic gluconeogenesis, increased enterocyte glucose uptake/GLP-1 secretion, and microbiome modulation with potential systemic anti-inflammatory effects (Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Kozlowski, 2023).

Retinal/RPE mechanisms: In RPE cell lines (e.g., ARPE-19), metformin increases pAMPK and triggers autophagy, reduces ROS, decreases apoptosis, and preserves tight junction proteins (ZO-1, occludin), thereby maintaining barrier integrity under oxidative challenges (Amin et al., 2022; Augustin & Atorf, 2023). At the molecular level, treatment increases Sirt1 and multiple mitochondrial biogenesis and antioxidant markers (SOD-2, Nrf1, Tfam, PGC-1α, COX-II), restores NADH:NAD+ ratios and ATP, and lowers inflammatory mediators (NF-κB signaling, IL-6) (Amin et al., 2022). These signatures are consistent with AMPK’s coordinate regulation of autophagy and mitochondrial homeostasis observed in RPE/retinal contexts, contributing to improved proteostasis and reduced oxidative stress—key failure modes in dry AMD (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Amin et al., 2022).

In vivo, systemic or intravitreal metformin preserves photoreceptors and RPE structure/function in light-damage, iodate injury, and inherited degeneration models (rd1, rd10), with ERG preservation and ONL maintenance; mechanistically, AMPK activation is necessary for light-damage protection in an isoform-specific manner (AMPKα2 dependency), and retina-specific Pparδ is not required, supporting an AMPK-centric retinal mechanism rather than PPARδ signaling (Amin et al., 2022). Without these data, the proposed AMPK–TFEB–lysosome axis remains inferential in RPE.
- Heterogeneous and contradictory epidemiology: While many retrospective datasets suggest benefit (often in T2DM cohorts), high-quality time-varying analyses and some claims datasets report null or even an increased risk signal for current users regarding dry AMD; meta-analyses differ in conclusions, and late-stage AMD associations are particularly uncertain (Elhalag et al., 2024; Gokhale et al., 2023; Liang et al., 2022; Mauschitz et al., 2023). Confounding (smoking, DR severity, comedications), misclassification (wet vs dry), and exposure uncertainty limit inferential strength (Brown et al., 2019; Moir et al., 2023; Gokhale et al., 2023).
- Limited randomized clinical efficacy data in dry AMD: A GA randomized trial has been reported, but efficacy outcomes are not detailed in the excerpts; prior DPP follow-up imaging showed no significant AMD prevalence difference between metformin, lifestyle, and placebo, though that study was not designed for AMD endpoints; consequently, clinical efficacy remains unproven (Moir et al., 2023; Shen et al., 2024).
- Context dependence and dose constraints: Retinal benefits can be model- and isoform-specific (AMPKα2 dependence) and mixed in metabolic DR models; some analyses suggest suprapharmacologic concentrations may be necessary for robust AMPK activation in vitro, raising translational questions regarding retinal exposure at tolerated systemic doses, and arguing for ocular PK and target-engagement studies (Amin et al., 2022; Moir et al., 2023).
- Ocular safety and pharmacokinetics: Human ocular safety data for chronic exposure (systemic or local) in older non-diabetic AMD patients are not detailed here; intravitreal metformin safety in humans is uncharacterized in these excerpts, necessitating staged ocular toxicology and PK prior to (or within) clinical trials (Amin et al., 2022; Moir et al., 2023).

Development Implications and Recommendations  
- Mechanism validation in RPE: Prioritize targeted studies in human iPSC-RPE and donor-derived RPE to test the hypothesized AMPK→mTORC1→TFEB→lysosome axis. Required assays: TFEB nuclear localization (immunocytochemistry, subcellular fractionation), lysosomal pH (LysoSensor/LysoTracker), V-ATPase subunit expression and activity (ATPase assays), CTSD maturation (pro/mature CTSD Western) and enzymatic activity, autophagic flux (LC3 turnover with/without lysosomal blockade), and rescue experiments with AMPK and TFEB perturbation (e.g., CRISPRi/siRNA) (Amin et al., 2022; Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Ebeling et al., 2022).
- Translational pharmacology: Define retinal/RPE exposure–response using clinically relevant systemic concentrations and ocular distribution modeling; consider topical/periocular/intravitreal delivery if systemic exposure is insufficient for retinal AMPK engagement and lysosome-centric endpoints, with rigorous ocular toxicology (Moir et al., 2023).
- Indication and stage targeting: Given epidemiologic signals skew toward early/non-exudative AMD and limited evidence for late AMD benefit, prioritize early/intermediate AMD cohorts and GA progression trials with mechanistic biomarkers (RPE autofluorescence dynamics, OCT-based RPE/ONL metrics, aqueous humor cytokines/miRNAs) to increase sensitivity to disease-modifying effects (Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Liang et al., 2022; Moir et al., 2023).
- Clinical trial design: Incorporate robust confounder control and stratification (smoking, DR status, renal function, OCT1 polymorphisms) and embed target engagement (e.g., peripheral blood or aqueous biomarkers of AMPK/mTOR/autophagy) and safety surveillance (B12 levels, GI tolerability, lactate in at-risk) to bridge mechanism to clinical outcome (Gokhale et al., 2023; Zhou & Xue, 2024).
- Combination/adjunct strategies: Given non-overlapping mechanisms with anti-VEGF and complement inhibitors, explore combinatorial approaches in late-stage disease (e.g., GA with complement inhibition) if target engagement and safety are demonstrated (Amin et al., 2022; Shen et al., 2024).

Conclusion: Metformin is a credible repurposing candidate for dry AMD on the strength of convergent mechanistic rationale (AMPK activation, autophagy/mitochondrial support, anti-inflammatory/anti-senescence actions), robust preclinical retinal protection across models, and suggestive—but inconsistent—observational human data; however, decisive gaps remain for the central lysosome-centric hypothesis (TFEB/V-ATPase/CTSD in RPE) and for randomized clinical efficacy, especially in GA. The program should proceed with focused mechanistic validation of TFEB/lysosome endpoints in RPE, retinal target engagement and pharmacology at clinically feasible exposures, and staged, biomarker-rich randomized trials in early/intermediate AMD and GA to quantify efficacy and safety. Until lysosomal endpoints are confirmed and clinical benefit demonstrated, the hypothesis that metformin restores RPE autophagic flux via TFEB/V-ATPase/CTSD to prevent dry AMD remains plausible but unproven (Amin et al., 2022; Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Shen et al., 2024; Gokhale et al., 2023; Elhalag et al., 2024).
