Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Urolithin A is a naturally derived small molecule that originates from the gut microbial metabolism of dietary polyphenols, particularly ellagitannins and ellagic acid, which are abundant in fruits such as pomegranates, berries, and nuts (Djedjibegović et al., 2020; Heilman et al., 2017). Unlike synthetic drug candidates, Urolithin A is generated endogenously following dietary intake, a process that relies on a healthy gut microbiome to convert these precursors into bioactive urolithins. This compound belongs to the broader class of nutraceuticals and microbiota‐derived metabolites that have been widely investigated for their capacity to modulate mitochondrial function and cellular homeostasis (Djedjibegović et al., 2020; Jayatunga et al., 2021). These compounds, which have historically been explored mostly within the context of nutritional interventions and age-related muscle decline, are now being repurposed as potential drugs for other degenerative conditions. Urolithin A, in particular, has attracted significant attention due to its ability to enhance mitochondrial quality control through the activation of pathways such as PINK1/Parkin and modulation of autophagy-related mechanisms. Its synthesis in the human body, as well as its isolation from natural sources for research-grade applications such as Sigma SML1791, underscores its dual status as both a naturally occurring metabolite and a drug candidate with therapeutic potential across a variety of disease models (Jayatunga et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2025). Moreover, as a member of this emerging class, Urolithin A has been shown to be well tolerated, which gives it an advantage over many synthetic compounds that may pose safety concerns due to their off-target toxicities (Wang & Yu, 2025; Zhang et al., 2025). The natural origin and well-characterized safety profile of Urolithin A lend support to its development as a repurposed therapeutic agent, particularly for diseases like dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD), where mitochondrial dysfunction and impaired lysosomal clearance play central roles.

Therapeutic History:  
The therapeutic history of Urolithin A spans several preclinical and clinical studies that have established its safety, bioavailability, and efficacy in improving mitochondrial function. In numerous animal studies, Urolithin A has demonstrated a high no‐observed‐adverse‐effect level (NOAEL), with doses in the range of several thousand mg/kg demonstrating a remarkable safety margin (Djedjibegović et al., 2020). Early-phase clinical trials, including randomized placebo-controlled studies in healthy elderly subjects, have corroborated its safety; these trials reported no serious adverse events even at doses as high as 2000 mg, and significant improvements were observed in mitochondrial gene expression and muscle function (Jayatunga et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2025). This safety profile has been further supported by work that shows Urolithin A’s favorable pharmacokinetic properties. For instance, following oral administration, Urolithin A is rapidly absorbed, with peak plasma concentrations reached around 6 hours post-dose and a half-life of approximately 17–22 hours for the compound and its glucuronide conjugates (Djedjibegović et al., 2020; Raimundo et al., 2021). Its systemic bioavailability is advantageous when considering repurposing for systemic degenerative conditions such as AMD.

Historically, the focus of Urolithin A research has been on its role in mitigating age-associated muscle decline by improving mitochondrial quality, a property that has been linked to its induction of mitophagy, which is the selective removal of damaged mitochondria (Jayatunga et al., 2021; Singh et al., 2019). However, growing evidence from both in vitro studies and animal models indicates that Urolithin A’s benefits extend to other tissues, particularly those that are highly dependent on mitochondrial health such as the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) in the eye (Hyttinen et al., 2018; Jiménez-Loygorri et al., 2024). Although direct clinical studies using Urolithin A for dry AMD are still pending, the preclinical data suggest that its ability to improve mitochondrial function by promoting mitophagy and lysosomal clearance mechanisms could be beneficial in counteracting RPE degeneration, a hallmark of dry AMD. The therapeutic candidate thus finds support from both its legacy in muscle studies and emerging evidence in neurodegenerative disease models, including studies related to Alzheimer’s disease and Parkinson’s disease, where mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress are central themes (Jayatunga et al., 2021; Skeie et al., 2021). This therapeutic history, spanning several decades of research on mitochondrial modulators, positions Urolithin A as a promising candidate for repurposing toward diseases that involve similar cellular and molecular derangements.

Mechanism of Action:  
The mechanism of action of Urolithin A is multifaceted and central to its potential as a therapeutic agent for dry AMD. At a molecular level, Urolithin A functions primarily as a mitophagy enhancer. In cells experiencing mitochondrial damage or oxidative stress, the kinase PINK1 accumulates on the outer mitochondrial membrane, thereby recruiting the E3 ubiquitin ligase Parkin; together, they tag dysfunctional mitochondria for autophagic degradation (Borsky et al., 2025; Jiménez-Loygorri et al., 2024). This PINK1/Parkin-mediated pathway is essential for maintaining mitochondrial quality and cellular energy metabolism, particularly in high-energy demanding tissues such as the RPE where mitochondria are crucial for photoreceptor support (Hyttinen et al., 2018; Borsky et al., 2025). In addition to inducing mitophagy through PINK1/Parkin signaling, Urolithin A has been shown to activate AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK), a key energy sensor in cells. AMPK activation leads to the phosphorylation and subsequent nuclear translocation of transcription factor EB (TFEB), which acts as a master regulator of lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy (Zhang et al., 2025; Borsky et al., 2025). Once translocated into the nucleus, TFEB upregulates the expression of genes encoding lysosomal proteins such as LAMP1 and cathepsin D (CTSD), thereby enhancing the capacity of cells to clear autophagic cargo through improved lysosomal degradation (D’Amico et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2025).

The biochemical interactions involved in these processes are well supported by in vitro data showing that Urolithin A not only reduces mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (ROS) but also ameliorates the disruption of autophagic flux that is often observed under oxidative stress conditions (Djedjibegović et al., 2020; Jayatunga et al., 2021). This reduction of oxidative stress is particularly relevant for the RPE because elevated oxidative damage is a significant contributor to cellular senescence and apoptosis in patients with dry AMD. Furthermore, Urolithin A has been noted to induce p62-dependent lysophagy, a specialized form of autophagy that targets lysosomal components for recycling and repair, ensuring that even when conventional lysosomal biogenesis is impaired, cellular proteostasis can be maintained (Jiménez-Loygorri et al., 2024). The dual activation of mitophagy and lysosomal biogenesis creates a synergistic effect, where damaged mitochondria are efficiently recognized, isolated, and degraded, and the lysosomal compartment is concurrently replenished with new, fully functional enzymes, ensuring an optimal degradative environment (Auguste, 2022; Borsky et al., 2025). Moreover, studies have shown that Urolithin A can favorably influence other signaling pathways that contribute to mitochondrial biogenesis, such as the SIRT1/PGC-1α axis, further supporting its role in restoring mitochondrial homeostasis (Borsky et al., 2025; D’Amico et al., 2021). In summary, Urolithin A’s multifaceted mechanism—which encompasses the induction of PINK1/Parkin-mediated mitophagy, activation of AMPK–TFEB signaling to enhance lysosomal biogenesis, and reduction of oxidative stress—forms a robust foundation for its proposed therapeutic application in the treatment of dry AMD.

Expected Effect:  
The therapeutic hypothesis for Urolithin A in dry AMD rests on its ability to restore mitochondrial quality and enhance lysosomal clearance in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE). In the proposed assay, Urolithin A is expected to activate the PINK1/Parkin pathway in RPE cells, thus facilitating the selective removal of damaged mitochondria that contribute to oxidative stress and cellular dysfunction (Borsky et al., 2025). Concurrently, through the activation of AMPK, Urolithin A is anticipated to drive the nuclear translocation of TFEB, thereby upregulating lysosomal genes such as LAMP1 and cathepsin D. This upregulation is expected to enhance lysosomal acidification, an essential component for the proper degradation of autophagic cargo, including damaged mitochondria and photoreceptor outer segments (POS) that accumulate with age (Zhang et al., 2025; Borsky et al., 2025).

The PEGylation process not only grants enhanced resistance to enzymatic degradation but also prolongs the intravitreal residence time, an essential property for ocular applications requiring sustained drug exposure with limited dosing frequency (Tzoumas et al., 2023; Mastellos & Lambris, 2024). As a second‐generation compstatin analog, pegcetacoplan employs a bivalent design that enables high specificity for human C3, blocking its proteolytic cleavage into the active fragments C3a and C3b. These fragments are potent mediators that further amplify the inflammatory cascade through the formation of C3 convertases (Lamers et al., 2022). This therapeutic candidate is embedded within a broader class of complement inhibitors that have been actively explored in inflammatory disorders, and notably in ophthalmology for dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) where aberrant complement activation plays a central pathogenic role (Lamers et al., 2022; Mastellos & Lambris, 2024). Its synthetic nature, coupled with its targeted molecular design, positions pegcetacoplan as an attractive candidate for addressing the degenerative processes in geographic atrophy (GA) associated with dry AMD by directly modulating the complement cascade (Tzoumas et al., 2023; Patel et al., 2022).

Overall, the therapeutic history of pegcetacoplan—spanning its origin from fundamental compstatin research to its current application in treating geographic atrophy—demonstrates its potential for repurposing as a disease-modifying therapy in ocular settings (Lamers et al., 2022; Desai & Dugel, 2022).

Mechanism of Action  
At the molecular level, the pathogenic cascade in dry AMD is tightly linked to dysregulated complement activation, and pegcetacoplan intervenes at one of the central nodes of this pathway by inhibiting complement component C3. Under physiological conditions, C3 is cleaved by C3 convertases into C3a—an anaphylatoxin that drives inflammation—and C3b, which functions as an opsonin and further propagates complement amplification (Yu & Wykoff, 2021). Pegcetacoplan binds to a key epitope on C3, thereby sterically hindering the enzyme-driven cleavage that would otherwise generate these active fragments. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Rapamycin (sirolimus), commercially available as Sigma R0395, is a macrocyclic lactone originally isolated from the bacterium Streptomyces hygroscopicus, a discovery that dates back to studies on soil samples from Easter Island. As a naturally derived compound now synthesized and purified for clinical use, rapamycin belongs to the macrolide class and is best known for its potent immunosuppressive properties, having been used extensively to prevent organ rejection in transplantation. Over time, its application expanded beyond transplantation to include areas such as oncology, neurodegeneration, and age-related diseases due to its ability to inhibit the mechanistic target of rapamycin complex 1 (mTORC1). The rationale for repurposing rapamycin in the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD), specifically geographic atrophy (GA), stems from its established pharmacological profile, extensive safety record, and well-characterized biochemical functions. Its clinical approval and long-term safety data in other contexts provide a solid foundation for exploring its potential in ocular indications, particularly given its capacity to modulate autophagy in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells (Wang et al., 2022).

Therapeutic History:  
Rapamycin’s development began with its use as an immunosuppressant in organ transplantation, and over the ensuing decades, its application has broadened considerably. Biochemical and preclinical studies have demonstrated that rapamycin is an effective inhibitor of mTORC1, a critical regulator not only of cell proliferation but also of autophagy and lysosomal biogenesis. Early investigations revealed that rapamycin could induce autophagy in various cell types, including RPE cells, by inhibiting mTORC1, thereby facilitating the clearance of toxic aggregates and damaged organelles. This mechanism has been explored extensively for neurodegenerative conditions, and more recently, there has been focused investigation into its utility for dry AMD. Clinical trials have tested rapamycin in forms ranging from intravitreal to subconjunctival injections in patients with GA; for example, a clinical trial by the National Eye Institute aimed to evaluate intravitreal injections of sirolimus for GA, although this study was terminated due to safety concerns (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2012). Similarly, other studies using subconjunctival injections demonstrated that while rapamycin appears safe and well-tolerated, significant benefits in terms of preventing GA progression have not been conclusively demonstrated (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2008, 2011). In animal studies and in vitro RPE models, rapamycin enhanced autophagic flux, increased the activity of cathepsin D (CTSD), and reduced the accumulation of toxic material such as A2E—an effect that is consistent with a potential for slowing GA progression (Wang et al., 2022; Falcão et al., 2024). Thus, rapamycin’s therapeutic history encompasses a combination of robust preclinical evidence supporting its mechanistic action and mixed clinical outcomes in ocular trials, setting the stage for further investigation into optimal dosing, delivery methods, and patient selection criteria (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2008, 2011).

Mechanism of Action:  
Rapamycin exerts its biological effects primarily through direct inhibition of mTORC1, a serine/threonine kinase complex that integrates signals from nutrients, growth factors, and cellular energy status to regulate cell growth, proliferation, and autophagy. In the absence of rapamycin, active mTORC1 phosphorylates downstream targets such as S6 kinase and 4E-BP1, thereby promoting anabolic processes and suppressing autophagy. When rapamycin binds to its intracellular receptor, FKBP12, the resulting complex interacts with the FKBP12-rapamycin binding (FRB) domain of mTORC1, leading to its inhibition. This inhibition results in dephosphorylation and subsequent activation of transcription factor EB (TFEB), a master regulator of lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy-related genes. Activated TFEB then translocates to the nucleus, where it enhances the expression of genes involved in lysosomal function, acidification, and the production of lysosomal enzymes such as cathepsin D (CTSD) (Falcão et al., 2025; Falcão et al., 2024; Sinha et al., 2016). In the context of dry AMD, the proposed mechanism hinges on rapamycin’s ability to restore cellular homeostasis in RPE cells by increasing autophagic flux and lysosomal clearance of accumulated drusen components, which include toxic aggregates like A2E. Preclinical studies have shown that treatment of RPE cells with rapamycin results in a marked reduction in the accumulation of autofluorescent granules (AFGs) that are indicative of impaired lysosomal degradation (Falcão et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2025). The cascade initiated by rapamycin—mTORC1 inhibition, TFEB activation, and enhanced expression of lysosome-associated proteins such as LAMP1 and pro-cathepsin D—forms the crux of its proposed therapeutic action in mitigating the progression of GA by promoting the dismantling and clearance of pathological deposits (Falcão et al., 2024).

Expected Effect:  
In RPE cells, the inhibition of mTORC1 by rapamycin is expected to release the inhibitory phosphorylation on TFEB, enabling its nuclear translocation and activation of a transcriptional program that drives lysosomal biogenesis, acidification, and the production of key lysosomal enzymes such as cathepsin D. This molecular shift is anticipated to markedly enhance the autophagic capacity of the RPE, leading to increased degradation of drusen components, including lipofuscin and A2E, which are hallmarks of dry AMD pathology. The activation of autophagy not only facilitates the clearance of accumulated toxic material but also mitigates oxidative stress by removing damaged mitochondria and other organelles that may contribute to reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation (Wang et al., 2022; Falcão et al., 2024). Moreover, preclinical evidence indicates that, in ARPE-19 cell models, rapamycin improves cellular viability in the face of oxidative injury and reduces markers of cellular senescence by enhancing autophagic flux. These cellular effects are directly linked to the expression of critical proteins in RPE cells; for example, TFEB is known to be expressed in these cells and its activation correlates with increased lysosomal gene expression and function (Falcão et al., 2024) while cathepsin D, a lysosomal protease, is vital for the degradation of phagocytosed photoreceptor outer segments (Chang et al., 2022; Sinha et al., 2016). The intended therapeutic outcome is to slow or potentially halt the progression of GA by reducing the burden of drusen and preserving RPE function, which could translate into better preservation of visual acuity over time. However, it is important to note that while these mechanisms are promising in vitro, clinical translation has encountered challenges related to dosing, delivery, and the stage of disease at which intervention occurs (Wang et al., 2022; Falcão et al., 2024).

Overall Evaluation:  
Rapamycin presents itself as a scientifically promising yet clinically challenging candidate for the treatment of dry AMD. One of the key strengths of rapamycin is its well-established mechanism of action: as a potent mTORC1 inhibitor, it leverages a well-characterized pathway involving TFEB activation that directly targets the core pathology observed in dry AMD—the accumulation of drusen components and impaired lysosomal function in RPE cells. Preclinical studies have consistently demonstrated that rapamycin can enhance autophagic flux, lower levels of toxic aggregates such as A2E, and increase the activity of lysosomal enzymes like cathepsin D, thereby supporting its target validation in the context of RPE health (Falcão et al., 2025; Falcão et al., 2024). Additionally, rapamycin has an extensive history of clinical use in other indications, and its safety profile, while not without concerns, is well documented from its use as an immunosuppressant in transplantation and in various oncology settings (Wang et al., 2022).

However, the clinical translation of rapamycin for dry AMD has not been straightforward. Multiple clinical trials have assessed its application using different routes of administration, such as intravitreal and subconjunctival injections, with mixed results. While safety and tolerability have generally been acceptable, the efficacy endpoints—specifically, the prevention or slowing of GA progression—have not been definitively met in these studies (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2008, 2011, 2012; Wang et al., 2022). Furthermore, some trials encountered complications such as sterile endophthalmitis or observed decreases in visual acuity relative to untreated eyes, suggesting that even if the underlying molecular mechanisms are engaged, the overall benefits in late-stage disease might be limited (Wang et al., 2022; Falcão et al., 2024).

Another potential weakness is the complexity inherent in mTOR signaling itself. The pathway plays a dual role in cellular homeostasis—while its inhibition can promote autophagy and lysosomal clearance, inappropriate or excessive inhibition could lead to adverse effects such as increased retinal neuron apoptosis, particularly in advanced stages of AMD where the cellular milieu is significantly altered (Wang et al., 2022; Chang et al., 2022). Moreover, the optimal dosing regimen and delivery method for achieving the desired ocular concentration without incurring systemic side effects remain unresolved. Some studies have suggested that modifications to the formulation, such as encapsulation in synthetic nanoparticles, could enhance ocular penetration and prolong the effective duration of rapamycin within the eye, thereby minimizing side effects and improving efficacy (Jo et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2022).

Despite these challenges, the strength of rapamycin’s mechanism—the inhibition of mTORC1 and consequent activation of TFEB leading to enhanced lysosomal biogenesis—remains compelling. The molecular rationale is robust, and the repeated demonstration of reduced levels of autofluorescent granules in RPE cells following rapamycin treatment is particularly encouraging (Falcão et al., 2024). The concept of using a repurposed, clinically approved drug to address a significant unmet need in dry AMD is attractive, especially given the limited treatment options currently available for this degenerative condition. In this light, further investigations—ideally, in earlier stages of AMD and with innovative delivery modalities—may reveal a niche where rapamycin can exert a clinically meaningful benefit (Wang et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2019).

In conclusion, while rapamycin has significant potential grounded in sound molecular pharmacology and extensive preclinical validation, its clinical application for dry AMD warrants careful optimization. The candidate’s strengths lie in its potent and well-understood mechanism of mTORC1 inhibition, the activation of TFEB, and subsequent improvements in lysosomal function and autophagic clearance in RPE cells. Conversely, clinical challenges including mixed efficacy outcomes in GA trials, potential adverse effects related to mTOR pathway modulation in vulnerable retinal neurons, and limitations in current dosing/delivery strategies represent hurdles that must be surmounted. Based on these comprehensive literature insights, rapamycin remains a promising candidate for further investigation, albeit with recommendations to explore its use in earlier disease stages and in combination with advanced ocular delivery systems to maximize its therapeutic benefit while minimizing risks (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2012; Wang et al., 2022; Falcão et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2025).

Below is a comprehensive evaluation of the miR-211 mimic (chemically modified agomir) candidate for dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD), structured as requested.

─────────────────────────────  
Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
─────────────────────────────  
The miR-211 mimic is a synthetic, chemically modified oligonucleotide designed to recapitulate the function of the endogenous microRNA miR-211. As a member of the miRNA therapeutic class, this molecule belongs to a growing category of nucleic acid–based drugs that aim to modulate gene expression post-transcriptionally. Its design involves optimization of the nucleotide chemistry (for example, by including 2′-O-methyl modifications, phosphorothioate linkages, and sometimes locked nucleic acid (LNA) modifications) to improve stability, reduce degradation by nucleases, and minimize immune stimulation after ocular delivery. Such chemical modifications (collectively referred to as “agomir” chemistry) have been used successfully in preclinical models for other miRNA candidates, proving that the formulation and delivery of chemically stabilized miRNA mimics to ocular tissues is feasible (Boya et al., 2023; Intartaglia et al., 2021).

miR-211 was originally identified as a light-responsive microRNA in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and has been shown to regulate lysosomal biogenesis by targeting the mRNA of Ezrin, a cytoskeletal protein that also impacts cellular ion channel regulation. The candidate is repurposed from the naturally occurring miRNA sequence now “mimicked” by the synthetic therapeutic agent. Its design is based on the premise that the loss or downregulation of miR-211 in the diseased RPE contributes to defective lysosomal function and consequent accumulation of photoreceptor outer segment (POS) debris, which is a hallmark of dry AMD (Boya et al., 2023; Intartaglia et al., 2021).

As a therapeutic compound, the miR-211 mimic falls into the broader family of oligonucleotide drugs that have previously been used in various contexts such as oncology or viral diseases. In the ocular arena, similar approaches—including antisense oligonucleotides and small interfering RNAs (siRNAs)—have been deployed to modulate gene expression in models of ocular neovascularization and other retinal degenerations. In this way, the miR-211 agomir is both a repurposed and rationally designed candidate that leverages our growing understanding of miRNA-mediated regulation of lysosomal activity and intracellular clearance pathways (Naso et al., 2020).

─────────────────────────────  
Therapeutic History  
─────────────────────────────  
Although no miR-211 mimic as such has yet reached clinical trials in dry AMD, an increasing body of preclinical evidence supports the therapeutic potential of modulating miR-211 expression in the retina. In several rodent studies it has been demonstrated that global loss of miR-211 in mice leads to impaired lysosomal biogenesis, accumulation of lipofuscin-like granules, and defective processing of photoreceptor outer segments by the RPE (Naso et al., 2020). For example, mice with a genetic deletion of miR-211 exhibit phenotypes reminiscent of inherited retinal dystrophies and models of Stargardt’s disease, in which impaired degradative enzymes and lysosomal dysfunction are central features.

In parallel, pharmacological inhibition of Ezrin—a validated target of miR-211—using small molecule inhibitors such as NSC668394 has been shown to restore lysosomal activity, increase autophagic flux, and even rescue electrophysiological deficits in the rodent retina (Naso et al., 2020). These findings not only validate the molecular target (Ezrin) but also indirectly support the hypothesis that restoring miR-211 levels via an agomir should yield similar improvements in lysosomal function and cell clearance.

The use of chemically modified oligonucleotides (including agomirs) in ocular drug development is supported both by preclinical data and emerging clinical applications in other retinal diseases. While previous approaches in dry AMD have focused on antioxidants, complement inhibitors, or cell transplantation, the recent shift toward modulating intracellular clearance pathways and autophagy has created new opportunity. For instance, approaches to activate the transcription factor TFEB—which is the master regulator of lysosomal biogenesis—demonstrate that enhancement of the degradative pathway correlates with improved survival of the RPE and photoreceptor cells (Boya et al., 2023; Naso et al., 2020). Although direct use of a miR-211 mimic (as opposed to gene therapy or pharmacologic Ezrin inhibitors) has not yet been validated in clinical settings for AMD, the preclinical evidence for miR-211’s role in maintaining RPE homeostasis provides a strong rationale for advancing this candidate into further testing (Intartaglia et al., 2021; Naso et al., 2020).

─────────────────────────────  
Mechanism of Action  
─────────────────────────────  
The proposed molecular mechanism by which a miR-211 mimic would function in dry AMD is multifaceted, integrating several key cellular pathways that converge on the restoration of lysosomal biogenesis in the RPE. At its core, the therapeutic hypothesis centers on the ability of miR-211 to post-transcriptionally suppress Ezrin, a cytoskeletal linker protein that in the RPE is linked to disruptions in lysosomal function and cell clearance (Boya et al., 2023; Intartaglia et al., 2021).

Specifically, under physiological conditions miR-211 is induced in a light-dependent manner and directly binds to the 3′ untranslated region (UTR) of the Ezrin mRNA to repress its translation. In the context of dry AMD, miR-211 is downregulated—a change that leads to derepression of Ezrin. Elevated Ezrin levels are correlated with impaired lysosomal biogenesis, reduced cathepsin activity, and accumulation of metabolic debris (Boya et al., 2023; Naso et al., 2020). Once delivered to the RPE, the miR-211 mimic is expected to restore this regulatory inhibition, reducing Ezrin protein levels to a more physiologic state.

More intriguingly, this reduction in Ezrin is proposed to have downstream effects on lysosomal calcium signaling. Data indicate that when Ezrin is repressed, there is an increase in TRPML1 channel sensitivity at the lysosomal membrane, thereby generating a localized Ca²⁺ microdomain within these organelles (Naso et al., 2020). The increased lysosomal Ca²⁺ flux subsequently activates the Ca²⁺-dependent phosphatase calcineurin. Activated calcineurin dephosphorylates TFEB, a transcription factor that in its phosphorylated state is sequestered in the cytosol. Once dephosphorylated, TFEB can translocate into the nucleus where it functions as the master regulator of the Coordinated Lysosomal Expression and Regulation (CLEAR) gene network (Naso et al., 2020).

TFEB-driven transcription leads to enhanced expression of genes encoding lysosomal proteins, such as LAMP1, and digestive enzymes including cathepsin D, as well as proteins critical for autophagosome formation like LC3 and BECLIN. The net effect is an increase in the number and functionality of lysosomes, including improved acidification of these organelles—a crucial parameter for optimal enzymatic activity and degradation of engulfed materials (Du & Palczewski, 2022; Naso et al., 2020). The complete mechanistic cascade is thus: miR-211 mimic delivers a signal that downregulates Ezrin, alleviating its inhibitory effects on lysosomal biogenesis; this in turn potentiates TRPML1-mediated Ca²⁺ release, leading to calcineurin activation; calcineurin dephosphorylates TFEB, allowing its nuclear entry; and nuclear TFEB transcriptionally enhances lysosomal genes, culminating in improved cathepsin D expression and lysosomal acidification. This chain of events is hypothesized to restore the degradative capacity of the RPE and mitigate POS accumulation—a key pathogenic factor underlying dry AMD (Boya et al., 2023; Naso et al., 2020).

It is worth noting that similar signaling cascades have been observed in studies where Ezrin inhibition pharmacologically recapitulated the beneficial effects seen after TFEB activation, which indirectly supports this proposed miR-211–mediated mechanism (Naso et al., 2020). The convergence of genetic, pharmacologic, and mechanistic studies in preclinical rodent models reinforces confidence in the proposed chain-of-events, although direct demonstration of every step with a synthetic miR-211 agomir remains an area for future research.

─────────────────────────────  
Expected Effect  
─────────────────────────────  
When administrated to the retinal pigment epithelium via an appropriate ocular delivery method (such as intravitreal or subretinal injection, potentially formulated within lipid nanoparticles or other compatible carriers), the miR-211 mimic is expected to produce several beneficial effects that address the key pathological features of dry AMD. In in vitro assays using RPE cell lines or primary human RPE cultures, one would anticipate that treatment with the miR-211 agomir will lead to a measurable decrease in Ezrin mRNA and protein levels as confirmed by qRT-PCR and Western blot analyses, respectively (Boya et al., 2023; Intartaglia et al., 2021).

At the subcellular level, the downregulation of Ezrin is expected to relieve its inhibitory control on lysosomal Ca²⁺ dynamics. This should manifest as an increase in TRPML1 channel activity, resulting in a sustained and enhanced lysosomal Ca²⁺ signal, which can be quantified using calcium-sensitive dyes or genetically encoded Ca²⁺ indicators fused to lysosomal proteins (Naso et al., 2020). Following this, increased calcineurin activity is anticipated and can be monitored by assessing the phosphorylation status of downstream substrates including TFEB. In treated RPE cells, one would observe a redistribution of TFEB from the cytoplasm to the nucleus, a change that can be confirmed by immunocytochemistry and subcellular fractionation methods (Naso et al., 2020).

The nuclear translocation of TFEB should then promote transcriptional upregulation of lysosomal and autophagy-related genes, resulting in an increased number of lysosomes with enhanced acidification (as measured by pH-sensitive fluorescent probes) and increased activity of key lysosomal enzymes such as cathepsin D and cathepsin B. Ultrastructural analyses by electron microscopy might reveal a reduction in the number or size of accumulated phagolysosomes containing unprocessed POS, and a phenotypic rescue at the cellular level would be consistent with restored degradative function (Naso et al., 2020).

In animal models of dry AMD – particularly in miR-211 knockout mice or in models that replicate lipofuscin accumulation and reduced lysosomal function – treatment with the miR-211 mimic is expected to result in significant improvements in retinal structure and function. Outcomes could include a reduction in lipofuscin deposition in the RPE, improved clearance of dysfunctional or misfolded photoreceptor proteins, and ultimately functional improvements as measured by responses on electroretinography (ERG) and preservation of photoreceptor cell layers. The approach is expected to not only halt but also partially reverse the degenerative changes by boosting the intrinsic capacity of RPE cells to clear cellular debris and maintain homeostasis (Boya et al., 2023; Naso et al., 2020).

Furthermore, in preclinical experiments where pharmacological inhibition of Ezrin achieved similar results in terms of enhancing lysosomal markers and reducing pathological deposits, the miR-211 mimic is hypothesized to mimic these effects by acting upstream of the pathway. Given that there is evidence suggesting that downregulation of miR-211 in AMD leads to compromised visual function, restoring its levels should, in theory, improve RPE survival and enhance retinal performance (Naso et al., 2020). In summary, the expected effect of this therapeutic intervention is a robust enhancement of lysosomal biogenesis and function within the RPE, which in turn could restore degradative capacity, reduce debris accumulation, and preserve visual function in dry AMD.

─────────────────────────────  
Overall Evaluation  
─────────────────────────────  
The miR-211 mimic candidate for dry AMD represents an innovative approach that acts by rebalancing a key regulatory pathway implicated in lysosomal biogenesis and cellular clearance. Overall, there are several strengths and a number of challenges to consider:

Strengths:  
1. Rational Mechanistic Targeting:  
   The candidate is built on a clear mechanistic hypothesis. miR-211 has been shown in multiple preclinical studies to directly regulate Ezrin—a known inhibitor of lysosomal biogenesis—and its downregulation results in impaired degradation of POS in the RPE (Boya et al., 2023; Intartaglia et al., 2021). By restoring miR-211 levels, the cascade involving TRPML1-mediated Ca²⁺ release, calcineurin activation, and subsequent TFEB nuclear translocation is reactivated. This specificity in targeting a regulatory cascade central to intracellular clearance speaks to high precision in its design (Naso et al., 2020).

2. Preclinical Validation of the Concept:  
   Genetic models, such as miR-211 knockout mice, and pharmacologic approaches using Ezrin inhibitors have provided compelling evidence that manipulating this pathway can restore degradative capacity in the RPE (Naso et al., 2020). Although the miR-211 mimic itself has not yet been extensively tested in dry AMD models, these data provide a strong scientific rationale for its potential efficacy.

3. Established Chemical Modification Strategies:  
   The field of miRNA therapeutics has matured considerably, and the design of chemically modified agomirs is a well-established approach to increase in vivo stability and allow local ocular delivery. This is supported by multiple studies in ocular tissues showing that similar modifications lead to enhanced half-life and effective cellular uptake (Boya et al., 2023; Intartaglia et al., 2021).

4. Specificity for RPE Homeostasis:

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Lithium chloride (Sigma L9650) is an inorganic salt belonging to the family of lithium compounds that has been in use for several decades, primarily as a mood stabilizer in the treatment of bipolar disorder. It is synthesized by combining lithium carbonate or lithium hydroxide with hydrochloric acid, yielding a highly water‐soluble salt that is widely available for both clinical and experimental research purposes (Carmassi et al., 2016; Vallée et al., 2021). As a prototypical member of the lithium salts, lithium chloride has been repurposed in recent years as a candidate for neuroprotection because of its ability to inhibit glycogen synthase kinase-3β (GSK3β), a serine/threonine kinase involved in numerous intracellular signaling cascades. Lithium’s chemical simplicity belies its complex pharmacology; its effects extend well beyond mood stabilization to encompass modulation of cell survival, inflammatory responses, and protein degradation pathways. In this context, lithium salts are now recognized as small molecule modulators that can affect intracellular transcriptional programs, including nuclear import of factors such as transcription factor EB (TFEB) and β-catenin, which in turn control the expression of genes necessary for lysosomal biogenesis and autophagic flux (Carmassi et al., 2016; Vallée et al., 2021). Therapeutic History:  
Lithium salts have a long-standing clinical history in psychiatry, especially in the management of bipolar disorder, where their dosing and long-term safety profiles have been thoroughly characterized. In addition, numerous preclinical studies in neuroscience have demonstrated that lithium can reduce tau phosphorylation and improve neuronal cell survival, partly by inhibiting GSK3β and modulating downstream targets such as β-catenin and Bcl-2 (Carmassi et al., 2016; Vallée et al., 2021). Lithium has been evaluated in several neurodegenerative contexts—for instance, it has been examined for its potential benefits in Alzheimer’s disease, Huntington’s disease, and Parkinson’s disease, with some studies reporting modest improvements in neuroprotection and behavioral outcomes, although clinical results have been mixed (Singh et al., 2022; Vallée et al., 2021). More specifically, preclinical data in the central nervous system have shown that prolonged exposure to lithium increases cortical grey matter and enhances neuronal markers such as N-acetyl-aspartate, suggesting that lithium exerts trophic and neuroprotective effects (Carmassi et al., 2016). In the ocular arena, while lithium’s use has been predominantly described in the context of glaucoma—in which its inhibition of GSK3β was shown to modulate WNT/β-catenin signaling in trabecular meshwork cells—the literature offers no direct clinical or in-depth preclinical evaluation of lithium chloride in dry AMD or for modulating autophagy specifically in RPE cells (Singh et al., 2022; Vallée et al., 2021). Lithium chloride’s mechanisms of action are multifaceted, but a significant aspect relevant to the dry AMD hypothesis is its ability to inhibit GSK3β. GSK3β normally phosphorylates a variety of substrates including β-catenin and TFEB, leading to cytosolic retention and subsequent degradation; inhibition of GSK3β by lithium therefore results in stabilization and nuclear accumulation of β-catenin and promotes TFEB nuclear entry (Carmassi et al., 2016; Vallée et al., 2021). In detail, lithium binds directly to the magnesium-sensitive site of GSK3β and also promotes its inhibitory N-terminal serine phosphorylation, leading to a dose-dependent suppression of GSK3β activity (Carmassi et al., 2016). The release of β-catenin from the destruction complex allows it to accumulate in the nucleus, where it acts as a transcriptional coactivator for genes that contribute to cell survival and homeostasis, including those involved in lysosomal biogenesis (Carmassi et al., 2016; Vallée et al., 2021). Similarly, TFEB is a master transcription factor that coordinates the expression of a variety of genes encoding lysosomal enzymes and autophagy-related proteins. Under basal conditions, phosphorylation retains TFEB in the cytosol; inhibition of GSK3β can contribute to dephosphorylation of TFEB, thereby facilitating its nuclear translocation and transcriptional activation of targets such as cathepsin D (CTSD) and subunits of the vacuolar ATPase (v-ATPase) that are crucial for lysosomal acidification (Carmassi et al., 2016; Friedman et al., 2015). Finally, the absence of any registered clinical trials or robust preclinical studies in an AMD model means that the translational viability of lithium chloride for this indication is still highly speculative (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).

Despite these concerns, the strengths of lithium chloride as a repurposed agent for dry AMD are significant. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
AZD9056 is a small‐molecule, orally active P2X7 receptor antagonist developed by AstraZeneca that belongs to the class of synthetic adamantane‐based compounds. Although its precise chemical structure has not been fully disclosed in the public domain, multiple reports indicate that it emerges from a medicinal chemistry program focused on adamantyl benzamide scaffolds discovered through high‐throughput screening and subsequent structure–activity relationship (SAR) optimization (Chrovian et al., 2014; Gunosewoyo et al., 2007). The compound is understood to maintain the essential adamantane moiety linked through a methylene spacer to an aromatic benzamide, which is thought to force a twist in the benzamide conformation critical for high P2X7 antagonism (Chrovian et al., 2014; Gunosewoyo et al., 2007). In general, the adamantane class of compounds has been explored for its lipophilic and sterically constrained properties that can impart favorable bioavailability and receptor selectivity; indeed, the adamantane scaffold has also been exploited in a number of antiviral and anti-inflammatory agents. In the case of AZD9056, this design strategy was implemented to yield a molecule that potently blocks the ATP‐driven activity of the P2X7 receptor—a ligand‐gated ion channel implicated in inflammation and cell death—while offering the oral bioavailability and acceptable pharmacokinetic properties required for systemic application (Chrovian et al., 2014; Eser et al., 2015). The overall discovery process appears to have combined hit identification with parallel synthetic approaches in order to establish an SAR profile that ultimately led to a candidate with nanomolar potency in cell‐based assays of P2X7 function, such as inhibition of Bz-ATP–induced Ca2+ influx and dye uptake, although the specific synthetic steps remain proprietary (Chrovian et al., 2014; Gunosewoyo et al., 2007).  

Therapeutic History:  
AZD9056 has been evaluated extensively in non‐ocular inflammatory disease contexts. Early-phase clinical trials established its safety and tolerability in healthy volunteers through single- and multiple-dose studies that characterized its pharmacokinetic profile, with parameters such as a moderate oral bioavailability (~62%), a terminal half-life in the range of 16–18 hours, and the capacity for once-daily dosing (Arulkumaran et al., 2011). Its development program initially focused on rheumatoid arthritis (RA). In a 4-week phase IIa trial in RA patients, AZD9056 was found to be safe and well tolerated at the doses assessed, and target engagement was evidenced by significant inhibition of ex vivo ATP-induced monocyte IL-1β release (Chrovian et al., 2014). However, a subsequent larger phase IIb study in RA, enrolling up to 385 or more patients and including an open etanercept comparator arm, failed to demonstrate superior clinical efficacy over placebo across several objective endpoints, even though tolerability remained acceptable (Arulkumaran et al., 2011; Chrovian et al., 2014; Lepre et al., 2023). In parallel with its RA development, AZD9056 also underwent evaluation for inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), specifically in patients with Crohn's disease, where a phase IIa trial using a 200 mg once-daily regimen showed nominal improvements in the Crohn’s Disease Activity Index (CDAI) but no accompanying improvement in inflammatory biomarkers (Arulkumaran et al., 2011; Rech et al., 2016). Aside from these clinical endeavors in systemic inflammatory disorders, a dedicated ocular safety study was conducted in healthy volunteers; in this randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover study, retinal function was directly assessed by measures including electroretinography and visual acuity—an indication that the eye was considered as a potential compartment of interest, even though no efficacy studies in ocular disease states such as dry age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD) have been reported (Arulkumaran et al., 2011). Overall, while the compound has been repurposed extensively for anti-inflammatory indications and has an established human safety profile, its clinical history thus far has not included a trial specifically targeting dry AMD or any direct veterinary employments for ocular diseases (Arulkumaran et al., 2011; Guile et al., 2009).  

Mechanism of Action:  
The P2X7 receptor (P2X7R) is an ATP-gated, nonselective cation channel predominantly expressed on immune cells and, importantly for the intended application, on the retinal pigmented epithelium (RPE) (Calzaferri et al., 2020). Under physiological conditions, P2X7R is quiescent; however, in the presence of elevated extracellular ATP—a phenomenon noted in inflammatory and degenerative conditions, including AMD—the receptor becomes activated, mediating several deleterious downstream events. Upon activation, P2X7R undergoes a conformational change that not only allows the influx of Ca2+ and Na+ but also promotes the formation of large membrane pores owing to its ability to transition into a state that permits the passage of molecules as large as 900 Da (Chrovian et al., 2014; Eser et al., 2015). This pore formation results in cytotoxic calcium overload and is directly linked to the activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome, a multiprotein complex responsible for the processing of pro-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-1β and IL-18 (Calzaferri et al., 2020; Gu & Wiley, 2018). In the retinal pigment epithelium, this ATP-driven activation has been shown to contribute to lysosomal alkalization—a process that impairs the optimal acidic environment required by lysosomal enzymes, including cathepsins—and ultimately leads to defective clearance of cellular debris (Calzaferri et al., 2020; Tempest-Roe, 2017). Specifically, experimental studies in ARPE-19 cells (a human RPE cell line) have demonstrated that stimulation of P2X7 induces lysosomal dysfunction; conversely, pharmacological inhibition of P2X7 using antagonists such as Brilliant Blue G (BBG) can reverse this lysosomal impairment (Tempest-Roe, 2017). Mechanistically, AZD9056 is designed to bind to the P2X7 receptor with high potency and selectivity, thereby preventing the receptor’s activation by ATP. By doing so, it is anticipated to block the cascade of events that lead from receptor activation to pore formation, inflammasome assembly, and subsequent IL-1β release (Calzaferri et al., 2020; Gu & Wiley, 2018; Lee et al., 2023). Although the exact molecular binding mode of AZD9056 has not been detailed in available literature, it is presumed to interact with key residues involved in channel gating and pore formation, thereby stabilizing the receptor in a closed, inactive conformation (Chrovian et al., 2014; Lee et al., 2023). Elevated extracellular ATP levels have been documented in the vitreous of AMD patients, which suggests a pathological activation of purinergic signaling in the retina (Calzaferri et al., 2020). When ATP activates P2X7 receptors on RPE cells, it leads to two major deleterious outcomes. First, the receptor’s activation results in sustained Ca2+ influx and large pore formation, triggering cytotoxicity and subsequent cell death mechanisms, including apoptotic and inflammasome-dependent cell death pathways (Calzaferri et al., 2020; Gu & Wiley, 2018). From a drug development perspective, the repurposing of AZD9056 for dry AMD presents a compelling but challenging opportunity. One of the primary strengths of this therapeutic candidate lies in its robust mechanistic rationale. The P2X7 receptor plays a central role in mediating ATP-induced inflammasome activation, lysosomal dysfunction, and subsequent RPE cell death—pathophysiological processes that have been repeatedly implicated in dry AMD and geographic atrophy models (Calzaferri et al., 2020; Gu & Wiley, 2018; Tempest-Roe, 2017). The ability of P2X7 antagonists to block these processes has been demonstrated in various in vitro and in vivo models, where blockade of the receptor reduces IL-1β release, reverses lysosomal alkalization, and confers protection against RPE degeneration (Calzaferri et al., 2020; Gu & Wiley, 2018; Tempest-Roe, 2017). Furthermore, AZD9056 has gone through extensive clinical safety evaluations in multiple inflammatory disease indications; its pharmacokinetic profile—characterized by acceptable oral bioavailability and a half-life conducive to once-daily dosing—has been well established in early phase studies (Arulkumaran et al., 2011; Chrovian et al., 2014). This pre-existing clinical safety data is an asset in reducing the risk profile typically associated with novel drug candidates and may streamline early-stage clinical trial designs for an ocular indication. Additionally, preliminary ocular safety assessments in healthy volunteers, which included measures such as retinal electroretinography and visual acuity testing, suggest that systemic administration of AZD9056 does not produce overt ocular toxicity—an encouraging sign for its potential repurposing in dry AMD (Arulkumaran et al., 2011).  

Nevertheless, there are several notable limitations and challenges associated with using AZD9056 in the treatment of dry AMD. First, the prior clinical development history of AZD9056 in rheumatoid arthritis and Crohn’s disease revealed limited or inconsistent efficacy despite demonstrable target engagement. In the phase IIb studies for RA, the compound failed to outperform placebo across objective outcome measures even though safety endpoints were met (Arulkumaran et al., 2011; Chrovian et al., 2014). This raises concerns about whether P2X7 receptor blockade alone is sufficient to generate a meaningful clinical outcome, particularly in a complex and multifactorial disease process such as dry AMD. Moreover, the inflammatory milieu in rheumatoid arthritis or IBD differs significantly from that in the retina, and systemic inflammation may not accurately recapitulate the localized, chronic degenerative processes occurring in the RPE (Arulkumaran et al., 2011; Guile et al., 2009).  

Another concern relates to the dual and sometimes paradoxical roles of the P2X7 receptor. While its pathological activation is linked to pro-inflammatory signaling, P2X7 also appears to have a scavenger or phagocytic function under conditions of low ATP levels (Calzaferri et al., 2020; Newman, 2024). In the context of the RPE, which is specialized for high-volume phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments, complete blockade of P2X7 might inadvertently impair beneficial clearance processes that serve to prevent debris accumulation. In animal models, alternative data has shown that the loss of P2X7 function can result in changes reminiscent of early AMD, such as reduced phagocytosis, suggesting that finely balanced modulation rather than total inhibition may be necessary (Calzaferri et al., 2020; Gu & Wiley, 2018). Such duality underscores the potential risk that while AZD9056 may ameliorate inflammasome activation and lysosomal destabilization, it might simultaneously disrupt physiologic functions of RPE cells that are critical for maintaining retinal homeostasis.  

The lack of direct evidence for AZD9056’s efficacy in ocular models of dry AMD is another major gap. While the preclinical literature supports a role for P2X7 signaling in RPE dysfunction and geographic atrophy (Calzaferri et al., 2020; Tempest-Roe, 2017), the specific application of AZD9056 in these models remains largely inferential. There are no published studies documenting that AZD9056, when administered at doses achieving retinal penetration, effectively preserves cathepsin D activity or prevents RPE cell death in animal models of dry AMD. Furthermore, the translation of systemic pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic data to ocular compartments is nontrivial; disparities in drug distribution, blood–retinal barrier permeability, and local metabolism could limit effective target engagement in the retina even if systemic safety is acceptable (Arulkumaran et al., 2011). The undisclosed chemical structure of AZD9056 also complicates any efforts to optimize the compound specifically for ocular bioavailability or to better understand its off-target profile relative to other P2X7 antagonists that have been more thoroughly characterized in the literature (Chrovian et al., 2014; Gunosewoyo et al., 2007).  

In summary, the overall evaluation of AZD9056 for treatment of dry AMD is one of cautious enthusiasm tempered by several unresolved questions. On the strength side, the compound leverages a clear mechanistic rationale by antagonizing the P2X7 receptor—a key mediator of ATP-induced inflammasome activation and lysosomal dysfunction known to be active in the RPE of AMD patients—and it comes with an established clinical safety record in inflammatory disorders (Calzaferri et al., 2020; Chrovian et al., 2014; Gu & Wiley, 2018). Its ability to suppress IL-1β release in ex vivo assays supports its functional engagement with the P2X7/IL-1β pathway, and preclinical data suggest that P2X7 inhibition can protect against RPE degeneration (Gu & Wiley, 2018; Tempest-Roe, 2017). However, significant challenges persist: prior clinical trials in RA and IBD have yielded mixed efficacy results, casting doubt on whether P2X7 blockade alone can significantly modify disease progression in complex conditions; the potential for interference with beneficial receptor functions in the RPE may compromise its utility; and the lack of direct preclinical data in dry AMD models means that much of the benefit remains theoretical at this stage (Arulkumaran et al., 2011; Chrovian et al., 2014; Gu & Wiley, 2018; Territo & Zarrinmayeh, 2021). Additionally, uncertainties related to ocular pharmacokinetics and the inability to adjust the synthetic structure for improved retinal targeting (given the proprietary nature of the molecule’s chemistry) further complicate its repositioning for an ocular indication (Chrovian et al., 2014; Eser et al., 2015).  

Given the current state of the literature, it would be advisable to conduct targeted preclinical studies that specifically address the effects of AZD9056 on RPE cells and retinal tissue. These studies should include assays for lysosomal pH stability, cathepsin D activity, inflammasome assembly (e.g., NLRP3 activation and caspase-1 processing), and overall RPE cell viability under conditions of ATP stress. Furthermore, careful evaluation of retinal drug levels following systemic dosing—or the development of a topical formulation—might be necessary to ensure that sufficient drug concentrations can be achieved in the retina without systemic toxicity. A parallel investigation into the potential compensatory roles of P2X7 in RPE phagocytosis would also be warranted to minimize any risk of disrupting beneficial cellular functions (Calzaferri et al., 2020; Gu & Wiley, 2018; Arulkumaran et al., 2011).  

Overall, while AZD9056’s strong mechanistic basis and favorable early-phase clinical safety profile make it an attractive candidate for repurposing, the translational challenges and previous clinical setbacks in other indications necessitate rigorous preclinical validation in dry AMD models before further clinical development is considered. The compound’s capacity to specifically maintain lysosomal function and cathepsin D activity in the RPE represents a promising therapeutic opportunity if these effects can be reliably recapitulated in the ocular setting. However, caution is advised due to the dual roles of P2X7 signaling in both pathological and physiologic processes and the potential non-optimal receptor occupancy in the retina. In conclusion, the repurposing of AZD9056 for dry AMD holds potential but would require a focused, mechanistically guided preclinical program to address the unique challenges posed by the ocular environment and the complex biology of the P2X7 receptor (Arulkumaran et al., 2011; Chrovian et al., 2014; Calzaferri et al., 2020; Tempest-Roe, 2017).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Calpeptin (Sigma C1571) is a synthetic, cell‐permeable peptidomimetic inhibitor originally developed to target calpain family proteases. It belongs to a class of small molecule calpain inhibitors that are designed to mimic specific peptide sequences found in the endogenous inhibitor calpastatin. These peptidomimetics have been refined chemically to enable cellular penetration and high-affinity binding to the calpain active site, thereby blocking its auto‐proteolytic activation process (Vu et al., 2022). Calpeptin was discovered through efforts aimed at identifying effective inhibitors of calcium‐dependent cysteine proteases that contribute to proteolytic events in pathogenic conditions. Its synthesis involves conventional organic synthesis techniques designed to yield a molecule with the critical chemical features—namely, an amide backbone that mimics peptide bonds and side chain substitutions that ensure selectivity and stability in biological systems. This compound has been widely adopted as a research tool to probe calpain‐dependent cellular processes, particularly in the context of neurodegeneration and ocular pathologies (Vu et al., 2022).

Therapeutic History:  
Calpeptin has a rich history as a biochemical tool in both in vitro and in vivo experimental paradigms. Within the realm of ocular disease research, calpain inhibitors similar in mechanism to calpeptin have been evaluated in multiple models of retinal degeneration. For example, studies using rodent models of inherited retinal degeneration, such as those employing the Rho P23H‐1 rat model, have demonstrated that calpeptin—alongside other calpain inhibitors—can reduce photoreceptor cell death and modulate apoptotic pathways (Azam & Jastrzebska, 2025). Although the majority of these studies have been conducted in the context of retinitis pigmentosa or other inherited forms of retinal degeneration, the underlying mechanism—namely, the inhibition of aberrant calpain activation leading to cell death—is also highly relevant to dry age‐related macular degeneration (Azam & Jastrzebska, 2025). In various experimental systems, such as in neuroblastoma cells and retinal cell cultures subject to stress (e.g., hypoxia or oxidative challenge), calpeptin has been shown to reduce calpain‐mediated cleavage of key substrates and inhibit caspase activation, which correlates with improved cell survival. Although direct clinical trials using calpeptin in dry AMD have not yet been reported, its use in ocular research, combined with evidence from preclinical models involving other calpain inhibitors (such as SNJ‐1945 and SJA6017), underscores the translational potential of this approach (Vu et al., 2022).

Mechanism of Action:  
Calpeptin functions by inhibiting the auto‐proteolytic activation of calpain isoforms, particularly cytosolic calpains such as CAPN1 and CAPN5. Under physiological conditions, calpains are maintained in an inactive state; however, under pathological conditions marked by calcium dysregulation—such as those encountered in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) during oxidative stress—calpains become activated and catalyze the proteolytic cleavage of vital cellular substrates. Calpeptin binds to the protease’s active site, thereby preventing the conformational changes necessary for auto‐activation and subsequent proteolytic activity (Vu et al., 2022).  
In the specific context of dry AMD, the hypothesis is that drusen accumulation leads to oxidative and metabolic stress in the RPE. This stress triggers calcium overload, which in turn activates calpains. One of the deleterious consequences of calpain activation is lysosomal membrane permeabilization (LMP). LMP destabilizes the lysosomal environment, leading to the dissipation of the proton gradient maintained by v-ATPase complexes and resulting in impaired acidification. This loss of lysosomal integrity negatively affects the processing and activity of lysosomal hydrolases, particularly cathepsin D (CTSD), which is essential for proper degradative and autophagic functions. By inhibiting calpain activity, calpeptin is expected to prevent the proteolytic degradation of components critical to lysosomal membrane stability, such as v-ATPase subunits, thereby preserving lysosomal pH and ensuring proper CTSD processing (Vu et al., 2022). The preservation of these lysosomal functions is crucial in the context of drusen-induced stress in dry AMD, as it directly addresses the underlying mechanism of lysosomal dysfunction and subsequent cell death.

Expected Effect:  
The proposed therapeutic application of calpeptin in dry AMD is based on its ability to mitigate calpain-mediated lysosomal damage in the retinal pigment epithelium. In an experimental setup where RPE cells are exposed to oxidative or drusen-like stress, one would expect calpeptin to reduce calpain activation, thereby decreasing lysosomal membrane permeabilization. This inhibition should lead to the stabilization of v-ATPase complexes, which are responsible for maintaining the acidic environment within lysosomes. Consequently, normal lysosomal acidification is preserved, allowing for proper activation and function of cathepsin D (CTSD), a critical enzyme in the degradation of photoreceptor outer segments and in cellular homeostasis (Azam & Jastrzebska, 2025; Vu et al., 2022).  
Furthermore, by blocking the calpain-driven cleavage events that would otherwise lead to cytoskeletal disorganization and cellular apoptosis, calpeptin is anticipated to reduce overall caspase activation and apoptotic signaling in RPE cells. Studies in other retinal disease models have demonstrated that calpain inhibition can restore cellular homeostasis by reducing markers of apoptosis and mitigating structural damage (Azam & Jastrzebska, 2025; Vu et al., 2022). Given that RPE cells are known to express significant levels of calpains and are highly susceptible to calcium dysregulation upon exposure to drusen and oxidative stress, the use of calpeptin is expected to yield improved cellular viability and function in these cells. This outcome would be assessed through indicators such as restored lysosomal pH, reduction in cytosolic release of lysosomal enzymes, and maintenance of normal CTSD processing, ultimately contributing to neuroprotection and preservation of retinal integrity in dry AMD (Vu et al., 2022).

Overall Evaluation:  
A comprehensive review of the literature suggests that calpeptin holds promise as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration. Its classification as a cell-permeable peptidomimetic inhibitor of calpain places it within a well-studied drug class known for modulating pathological proteolytic cascades initiated by calcium dysregulation. The strengths of calpeptin include its well-characterized mechanism of action—namely, the inhibition of calpain auto-proteolysis, which is pivotal for preventing the proteolytic breakdown of critical lysosomal components such as v-ATPase (Vu et al., 2022).  
Moreover, the therapeutic history of calpeptin and its analogues in various retinal degeneration models supports its potential applicability in dry AMD. Experimental evidence from studies in Rho P23H transgenic rat models, among others, demonstrates that calpain inhibitors can confer neuroprotection by reducing apoptotic pathways, preserving cellular integrity, and maintaining lysosomal function in stressed retinal cells (Azam & Jastrzebska, 2025). The existing knowledge regarding in vivo tolerability and the reversible nature of calpeptin’s inhibitory effects further bolster its candidacy for preclinical testing targeting dry AMD (Vu et al., 2022).

Despite these favorable attributes, several weaknesses and challenges must be acknowledged. First, while the mechanism underpinning calpeptin’s action—specifically, its inhibition of calpain-mediated lysosomal damage—is strongly supported by in vitro and retinal degeneration model data, direct evidence linking calpeptin to improved outcomes in dry AMD models remains limited (Azam & Jastrzebska, 2025; Vu et al., 2022). Furthermore, the hypothesized benefit of stabilizing v-ATPase complexes and preserving CTSD activity, although biologically plausible, requires further experimental validation in an AMD context to confirm that calpeptin’s inhibition of calpain is sufficient to counteract drusen-induced lysosomal stress.  
An additional concern relates to target selectivity. Calpain inhibitors, including calpeptin, can potentially exhibit off-target effects due to the conserved structure of the catalytic domains within the calpain family and related proteases. This lack of absolute specificity may lead to unintended inhibition of other proteases, such as certain cathepsins, which could compromise cellular function if not tightly regulated (Vu et al., 2022). Furthermore, chronic ocular delivery of small molecule inhibitors poses formulation challenges, as therapeutic concentrations must be maintained in the retina without eliciting local toxicity. The eye’s compartmentalized anatomy offers the advantage of localized delivery (e.g., via intravitreal injections or topical applications), yet achieving sustained and controlled drug release remains a technical hurdle that must be addressed in subsequent preclinical studies (Vu et al., 2022).  
Another potential weakness is the complexity of dry AMD pathophysiology itself. Dry AMD is characterized by a multifactorial etiology involving oxidative stress, complement dysregulation, and inflammatory processes, in addition to lysosomal dysfunction. While addressing calpain-mediated LMP directly targets one critical aspect of the disease mechanism, comprehensive protection of RPE cells may require combination approaches. Calpeptin’s role might be best viewed as a part of a broader therapeutic cocktail aimed at modulating multiple convergent pathways implicated in dry AMD progression (Vu et al., 2022).  
In summary, calpeptin shows considerable potential as a repurposed drug candidate for dry AMD based on its well-documented pharmacological profile and its mechanistic alignment with the proposed therapeutic strategy—namely, inhibiting calpain-mediated lysosomal destabilization in RPE cells. Its synthetic origin, cell-permeable nature, and established use in experimental models of retinal degeneration make it an attractive candidate for further preclinical evaluation. However, the absence of direct evidence in dry AMD models, in addition to concerns regarding specificity, delivery, and the need for combination intervention strategies, underscores the importance of rigorous preclinical studies to further validate calpeptin’s efficacy and safety in this indication (Vu et al., 2022; Azam & Jastrzebska, 2025). Overall, while promising, calpeptin will require targeted studies to evaluate its impact on lysosomal membrane permeabilization, v-ATPase stabilization, and cathepsin D activity in the context of drusen-induced oxidative stress, thereby confirming its potential to protect RPEs and mitigate the progression of dry age-related macular degeneration (Vu et al., 2022).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Torin2 is a synthetic, second-generation ATP-competitive inhibitor of the mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) kinase designed to inhibit both mTOR complex 1 (mTORC1) and complex 2 (mTORC2) with high potency and favorable pharmacodynamic properties compared to first-generation allosteric mTOR inhibitors (rapamycin/rapalogs) and earlier catalytic mTOR kinase inhibitors (TORKi) such as PP242 and AZD8055 (Liu et al., 2013, pp. 7–10). Chemically optimized by structure-guided medicinal chemistry efforts, Torin2 exhibits rapid dephosphorylation of canonical mTORC1 substrates S6K1 (T389) and 4E-BP1 (T37/46) including rapamycin-insensitive sites, and of the mTORC2 substrate Akt (S473), reflecting dual-complex inhibition that is superior to rapamycin’s mTORC1-limited activity (with incomplete suppression of 4E-BP1) (Liu et al., 2013, pp. 7–10). In head-to-head comparisons with other ATP-competitive mTOR inhibitors, Torin2 maintains stronger and more sustained suppression of mTORC1/2 signaling after drug washout, attributable to its slow off-rate, with durable pathway inhibition persisting for approximately four hours in cellular assays, contrasting with rapid recovery observed with PP242 and shorter-duration suppression by AZD8055 (Liu et al., 2013, pp. 7–9). Torin2 is highly selective for mTOR over PI3K (>800-fold) and shows approximately 100-fold selectivity over the DNA damage response kinases ATM and ATR; these latter off-targets remain relevant at higher concentrations and inform safety margins and dose selection (Liu et al., 2013, pp. 9–10).

Mechanistically, Torin2 robustly induces autophagy across multiple cell lines (e.g., LC3-II accumulation, acridine-orange–positive acidic vesicle formation), consistent with its potent inhibition of mTORC1, a master negative regulator of autophagy initiation and flux (Liu et al., 2013, pp. 7–9). As a drug class, ATP-competitive TORKi have been widely investigated in oncology and proliferative diseases given their ability to fully suppress both mTOR complexes, thereby impacting protein synthesis, cell-cycle progression, metabolism, and survival signaling (Liu et al., 2013, pp. 7–10). Outside oncology, dual mTORC1/2 inhibition has demonstrated disease-modifying potential in organ systems where mTOR hyperactivation drives pathology; for example, Torin2 reduced S6 and 4E-BP1 phosphorylation and curtailed cyst burden in a mouse model of autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease, with efficacy comparable to sirolimus and a potentially more favorable side-effect profile (Holditch et al., 2019, pp. 6–7).

In the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), dysregulated mTOR signaling (particularly chronic mTORC1 activation with age) is strongly implicated in degradative/clearance failure, lysosomal dysfunction, metabolic reprogramming, and structural degeneration that recapitulate key features of dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD), including lipid-rich subretinal deposits and RPE dedifferentiation (Go et al., 2020, pp. 1–3, 11–13; Huang et al., 2019, pp. 1–2, 7–9; Zhao et al., 2011, pp. 10–11). RPE expresses and functionally engages both mTORC1 and mTORC2 complexes, providing a mechanistic rationale for evaluating dual-complex catalytic inhibitors like Torin2 as therapeutic candidates to correct core pathogenic processes in dry AMD (Intartaglia et al., 2022, pp. 15–17).

Therapeutic History  
The mTOR pathway has been studied extensively in retinal and RPE biology, with strong preclinical evidence linking mTOR hyperactivation to RPE degeneration and dry AMD-like pathology, and corresponding benefits from mTOR inhibition; however, direct ocular data with Torin2 itself are currently lacking and must be extrapolated from pharmacology in other tissues and from surrogates (Torin1, PP242, INK-128/MLN0128) and rapamycin (Liu et al., 2013, pp. 7–10; Holditch et al., 2019, pp. 6–7). Genetic and pharmacologic mTOR activation in RPE induces epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT), suppresses autophagy, disrupts metabolism, and yields an AMD-like phenotype; in a knock-in model that overexpresses mLST8 (a core mTORC component) in RPE, both mTORC1 and mTORC2 are upregulated, and dual-complex inhibition with TORIN1 (a TORKi closely related to Torin2) normalized signaling and restored autophagy and RPE function in vitro, including rescue of autophagy regulators Atg9b and Atg7 and recovery of autophagy flux (Chowdhury et al., 2025, pp. 1–2, 8–13). These data directly support the therapeutic relevance of dual mTORC1/2 inhibition in RPE conditions that model early AMD pathogenesis (Chowdhury et al., 2025, pp. 1–2, 8–13).

In a complementary RPE disease model focused on amyloid-β (Aβ)-induced lysosomal/autophagy impairment—a pathology linked to dry AMD—Torin (a first-generation mTOR inhibitor in this study; not explicitly Torin2) restored lysosomal activity via LAMP2 activation, corrected p62/SQSTM1 accumulation, facilitated Aβ aggregate clearance, and ameliorated Aβ-driven tight junction disruption in vitro and in Aβ-challenged mouse RPE in vivo, directly addressing the barrier degradation and clearance deficits central to AMD (Jo et al., 2023, pp. 1–2). In multiple RPE cell systems modeling autofluorescent granule (AFG) accumulation and lipofuscinogenesis after photoreceptor outer segment (POS) challenge, mTOR inhibition (rapamycin; INK-128) decreased AFG load by approximately 30% and activated a TFEB-dependent lysosome biogenesis program; these effects required intact lysosomal proteases/lipases and were associated with LAMP1 upregulation and GADD34 induction, supporting the concept that mTOR→TFEB pathway modulation can restore lysosomal clearance in RPE (albeit these studies were preprints and should be interpreted accordingly) (Falcão et al., 2024, pp. 1–6, 10–18). Constitutively active TFEB dramatically reduced POS-dependent AFGs in preventive and resolving paradigms, further validating TFEB activation as a mechanistic goal for pharmacologic mTOR inhibition in early AMD models (Falcão et al., 2024, pp. 1–6, 13–18).

In genetic models where RPE mTORC1 is hyperactivated through Tsc1 deletion, chronic mTORC1 activity causes progressive RPE degeneration, lipid accumulation, and subretinal drusenoid deposits, and rapamycin treatment restored RPE markers (e.g., RPE65), improved ERG responses, and partially normalized metabolomic derangements, providing in vivo proof-of-concept that mTOR pathway suppression improves RPE structure and function in AMD-like degeneration (Huang et al., 2019, pp. 1–2, 7–9; Zhao et al., 2011, pp. 10–11). At a mechanistic level, age-driven increases in lysosome mass and mTORC1 docking in RPE create a vicious cycle of mTORC1 hyperactivation that impairs phagolysosomal function, promotes lipogenesis, suppresses lipolysis, and degrades autophagy, converging on classic dry AMD phenotypes; mTOR inhibition breaks this cycle and restores degradative capacity (Go et al., 2020, pp. 1–3, 11–13).

Beyond ocular systems, Torin2 has been used preclinically in oncology and in non-ocular degenerative models; its dual mTORC1/2 suppression, sustained pharmacodynamics, and autophagy induction underlie anti-proliferative activity and apoptosis in cancer models, while in an ADPKD model Torin2 demonstrated pathway inhibition with efficacy comparable to sirolimus, suggesting that torin-class agents may be tolerable with appropriate dose and schedule selection (Liu et al., 2013, pp. 7–9; Holditch et al., 2019, pp. 6–7). Notably, second-generation mTOR inhibitors can be cytotoxic in RPE due to potent mTORC2 suppression with downstream Akt inhibition, a survival pathway for metabolically stressed RPE; this risk emphasizes the importance of dose titration and local ocular delivery strategies for Torin2 in AMD (Huang et al., 2018, pp. 7–8).

To our knowledge, Torin2 has not been reported in clinical trials for dry AMD or directly tested in RPE/retinal models in vivo; however, the strength of the translational prior—mTOR hyperactivation as a convergent mechanism in RPE degeneration; rescue with catalytic mTOR inhibitors such as TORIN1; and reversible ALP defects with Torin-class inhibition—warrants rigorous preclinical testing of Torin2 in dry AMD-relevant models (Chowdhury et al., 2025, pp. 1–2, 8–11; Jo et al., 2023, pp. 1–2).
