Lipofuscin and its photoproducts can further inhibit lysosomal proton pumps or hydrolases and promote lysosomal membrane permeabilization, coupling storage to organelle damage and propagating autophagy-lysosomal dysfunction and inflammatory signaling (Si et al., 2023, pp. 5–7; Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 2–4).

Signal control of lysosomal biogenesis and acidification in RPE: The V-ATPase–mTORC1–TFEB axis is central in RPE lysosomal homeostasis; CRYBA1/βA3/A1-crystallin directly regulates the V-ATPase and signals to mTORC1 at the lysosomal membrane, where mTORC1 activity controls TFEB phosphorylation and localization (phosphorylated TFEB is cytosolic; dephosphorylation permits nuclear translocation and activation of CLEAR network genes) (Kaarniranta et al., 2023, pp. 2–3; Markitantova & Simirskii, 2025, pp. 9–11; Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7). Pharmacologic mTOR inhibition (e.g., rapamycin) shifts TFEB toward an active dephosphorylated state, increases autophagic flux, reduces A2E, and decreases lipofuscin-like granules in RPE and POS-fed models, with the reduction in storage material being dependent on active lysosomal enzymes and TFEB activation (Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7). Trehalose also augments autophagy markers and flux with cytoprotective effects in RPE insult models, supporting the druggability of lysosome–autophagy axes (Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7).

What is known and unknown about ambroxol in RPE/AMD: The provided literature contains no experimental data showing that ambroxol binds, stabilizes, or otherwise directly modulates RPE cathepsin D or V-ATPase, nor does it report ambroxol’s effects on lysosomal pH, TFEB activity, or CLEAR network gene expression in RPE models (Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7; Markitantova & Simirskii, 2025, pp. 9–11). While small-molecule interventions can restore lysosomal acidity (e.g., acidic nanoparticles) or, conversely, deacidify lysosomes (e.g., chloroquine, quinacrine), these examples do not involve ambroxol and serve primarily to illustrate the malleability of lysosomal pH by pharmacological means (Alhowyan & Harisa, 2025, pp. 12–15). Importantly, antimalarial lysosomotropic agents that raise lysosomal pH carry ocular toxicity risks, providing a cautionary context for any lysosome-acting small molecule in ophthalmology, although ambroxol’s lysosomotropism and ocular toxicity profile are not defined in the provided excerpts (Alhowyan & Harisa, 2025, pp. 14–15). The context explicitly notes that no small-molecule pharmacological chaperones targeting cathepsin D deficiency or V-ATPase impairment in RPE/AMD models are presented, and there is no direct evidence described for ambroxol enhancing cathepsin D activity or drusen clearance in dry AMD (Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7).

Expected Effect  
Pathway-level expectation if the hypothesis holds: If ambroxol acts as a pharmacological chaperone for lysosomal enzymes expressed in RPE and indirectly improves V-ATPase-dependent acidification, one would expect increased lysosomal hydrolase maturation/activity (including CTSD), restoration of acidic lysosomal pH, improved autophagosome–lysosome fusion and autophagic flux, and enhanced clearance of POS-derived material and lipofuscin components (Si et al., 2023, pp. 4–7; Markitantova & Simirskii, 2025, pp. 9–11). In RPE cells subjected to AMD-relevant stressors (e.g., A2E loading, AGEs-modified substrates), improved acidification and hydrolase function should reduce accumulation of autofluorescent granules and mitigate the need for exosome-mediated egress of undegraded material implicated in drusen formation (Sharif, 2015, pp. 68–72, 199–202; Grilo, 2014, pp. 42–46). Assay predictions and measurable readouts: In RPE-like cells (ARPE-19, primary human RPE), relevant readouts to substantiate the hypothesis include:  
- Lysosomal pH measurements showing acidification relative to stressed controls; for comparison, A2E raises lysosomal pH via V-ATPase inhibition in RPE (Wang et al., 2023, pp. 11–13).  
- CTSD maturation (pro-CTSD to mature CTSD) and enzymatic activity assays, given RPE dependence on CTSD for POS degradation and its documented reduction in AMD RPE (Si et al., 2023, pp. 4–5; Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7).

Strength of biological rationale: The centrality of lysosomal dysfunction to RPE degeneration in dry AMD is well-supported: lysosomal enzyme activity declines with aging and stress, lipofuscin accumulates and inhibits proton pumps/hydrolases, lysosomal acidification is critical for hydrolase function, and impaired lysosome–autophagy flux contributes to intracellular overload, exosome-mediated debris export, drusen formation, and inflammation (Kaarniranta et al., 2023, pp. 2–5; Si et al., 2023, pp. 5–7; Sharif, 2015, pp. 199–202). A rigorous, staged preclinical plan is warranted:  
- In vitro RPE assays under A2E and POS-fed conditions to quantify lysosomal pH, V-ATPase subunit expression (ATP6VOA1), TFEB nuclear translocation/CLEAR activation, CTSD maturation/activity, POS degradation kinetics, and lipofuscin-like autofluorescence, with rapamycin and trehalose as mechanistically validated comparators (Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7; Wang et al., 2023, pp. 11–13).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
CHIR99021 is a fully synthetic, small-molecule aminopyrimidine that potently inhibits glycogen synthase kinase-3 (GSK3), with common use and profiling as a GSK3β-selective tool compound and canonical Wnt/β-catenin pathway agonist in cell systems (notably embryonic stem cell self-renewal and iPSC generation) (Rethineswaran et al., 2021; Lyssiotis et al., 2011). In ocular biology, CHIR99021 has been implemented as a defined, stage-specific Wnt activator to accelerate and improve directed differentiation of human ESC/iPSC to retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), increasing MITF/OTX2, pigmentation, and RPE functional readouts (apical PEDF, basal VEGF, integrin αVβ5–dependent phagocytosis) when applied at 3 μM during a defined mid-specification window (days 8–14) (Leach et al., 2015). Beyond development and differentiation protocols, CHIR99021 (as CHIR trihydrochloride) has been developed into an in vivo pharmacology tool with validated LC/MS assays and tissue PK in mice; after a 25 mg/kg intraperitoneal dose, it achieves rapid systemic distribution and measurable retinal exposure with prolonged ocular retention relative to plasma and liver (plasma Tmax ~30 min, liver Tmax ~30 min, retina Tmax ~30 min; terminal half-lives ~118, 120, and 405 min, respectively) (DiCesare et al., 2023).

As a GSK3 inhibitor, CHIR99021 belongs to a class leveraged widely across neuroscience, regenerative medicine, and retinal biology. In retinal preclinical systems this class has been used in models of retinitis pigmentosa, optic nerve injury/regeneration, and steroid-induced glaucoma; clinically, lithium chloride (LiCl) remains the only FDA-approved GSK3 inhibitor but with a narrow therapeutic window and mixed efficacy for neurodegenerative disease (DiCesare et al., 2023). In RPE disease–relevant preclinical work, low-dose CHIR99021 exposure in RPE-derived models reduces production/secretion of the EFEMP1/F3 glycoprotein and broadly represses extracellular matrix (ECM), complement, protease, and TGFβ-associated components linked to sub-RPE deposit biology; in vivo, systemic CHIR99021 prevents formation of basal laminar deposits (BLamD) in a homozygous EFEMP1 R345W knock-in mouse (ML/DHRD, an AMD-like pathology) without detectable retinal toxicity on scotopic ERG and H&E histology over one month (DiCesare et al., 2023).

Therapeutic History  
Class history in neural/retinal indications: GSK3 is a central kinase with broad substrate scope (>100 substrates) and regulates Wnt/β-catenin, PI3K/Akt, mTOR, NF-κB, and apoptosis pathways central to retinal homeostasis and degeneration (Hottin et al., 2022). Across retinal neurodegeneration models, GSK3 inhibitors have shown neuroprotection (e.g., in rd10 retinitis pigmentosa, NMDA excitotoxicity, and diabetic retinopathy), and GSK3 inhibition is mechanistically linked to CNS axon regeneration pathways (e.g., via CRMP2, mTOR), though effects are context-dependent and can diverge across cell types and disease stages (Hottin et al., 2022). The translational record for systemic GSK3 inhibition is mixed; lithium’s broad CNS history underscores both feasibility and risk of narrow windows and systemic effects, motivating localized ocular delivery or targeted strategies for retinal disease (Hottin et al., 2022; DiCesare et al., 2023).

CHIR99021 in ocular biology and disease: In vitro, CHIR99021 is a core Wnt agonist in hESC/hiPSC-to-RPE protocols where it improves RPE specification, pigmentation, and function when properly staged; its effects can be recapitulated by WNT3A (canonical) but not by WNT5A (non-canonical), consistent with a canonical Wnt readout (Leach et al., 2015). In applied disease models:

- Anti-deposit/ECM remodeling in EFEMP1-driven pathology: Using ARPE-19 edited lines expressing HiBiT-tagged F3 (WT and R345W), CHIR99021 reduced F3 transcript and protein in both intracellular and secreted compartments without overt cytotoxicity; genetic knockdown of GSK3α/β phenocopied and synergized, supporting an on-target mechanism (DiCesare et al., 2023). Low-dose, longer-term exposure (1 μM for 1 week) suppressed ECM, complement, metalloproteinase, and TGFβ-associated proteins in proteomics (≥2-fold reductions in multiple collagens, MMP2, SERPINE1, LTBP2, TGFβ1; decreases in HMGB1/2, C3; reductions in FBLN1/2) and produced parallel RNA-seq changes (downregulation of genes linked to sub-RPE deposits and ECM crosslinking; upregulation of TYR/TYRP1 and PEDF) without detectable activation of canonical TCF reporters, establishing a low-dose on-target biochemical window (DiCesare et al., 2023). Functionally, 1 μM CHIR99021 for 1 week normalized the R345W F3–linked elevation in MMP2 activity and reduced HiBiT F3 secretion apically and basally in transwell cultures (DiCesare et al., 2023).

- In vivo efficacy and PK: In EFEMP1 R345W+/+ mice (~8 months old), systemic CHIR trihydrochloride (25 mg/kg IP, weekdays for 1 month) reduced the fraction of retinal FOVs containing BLamD from 14.205% to 4.167% and halved the mean deposit area (0.817 to 0.416 μm²), with no detectable ERG or histological toxicity (DiCesare et al., 2023). LC/MS/MS PK in plasma, liver, and retina confirmed rapid tissue distribution at 30 min and prolonged retinal retention (retina terminal T½ ~405 min) with estimated intraocular concentrations on the order of the effective in vitro range over the first hours (e.g., ~1.3 μM at 30 min and ~0.36 μM at 6 h) (DiCesare et al., 2023). Analytical assay development and rigorous methodology are reported (DiCesare et al., 2023).

- Regeneration/reprogramming contexts: CHIR99021 is a frequent component of small-molecule cocktails that reprogram Müller glia toward photoreceptor-like fates, induce Rho+ cells in vitro and in degenerate mouse retinas, and is used in multi-pathway modulation (Wnt activation combined with inhibitors of TGF-β, BMP, and Notch) to enhance MC-derived photoreceptor-like outputs; effects vary with species/model, and cocktails require careful balance (Fujii et al., 2021; Hottin et al., 2022). CHIR99021 also appears in chemical reprogramming schemes that convert adult human RPE to dopaminergic neurons and in multi-factor protocols generating photoreceptor progenitors from RPE or iPSCs, generally in combination with other pathway modulators and epigenetic agents (Rzhanova et al., 2024).

- Safety and adverse contexts: Despite benefits in differentiation, in a large-lesion, macula-sized RPE wound-repair model designed to mimic GA, CHIR99021 hindered lesion closure and yielded morphologically suboptimal infiltrating cells, even though pigmentation outside the lesion increased; EMT-suppressing agents (RepSox, Y-27632) performed better for wound closure under those conditions (Bailey-Steinitz, 2021; Hottin et al., 2022). Reviews caution that GSK3 inhibition can activate VEGF via canonical Wnt and could exacerbate angiogenesis, raising a risk signal for wet AMD contexts and arguing for careful selection of indication (dry vs wet AMD), timing, and combination strategies (e.g., with anti-VEGF) (Hottin et al., 2022).

To our knowledge, no human clinical studies have evaluated CHIR99021 for dry AMD; the most advanced ocular efficacy package is the EFEMP1 R345W mouse, an AMD-like BLamD model, where CHIR achieved both biochemical (ECM/complement/protease remodeling) and morphologic (deposit reduction) endpoints with ocular exposure in the in vitro effective range and no detectable electroretinal toxicity over one month (DiCesare et al., 2023).

Mechanism of Action  
Direct target and pathway entry points: GSK3 exists as α and β isoforms (85% identity), is constitutively active under basal conditions, and is negatively regulated by serine phosphorylation (S21 on α, S9 on β). It phosphorylates primed substrates on Ser/Thr motifs often culminating in β-TrCP recognition and proteasomal degradation of targets including β-catenin in the absence of Wnt; Wnt pathway activation sequesters/inhibits GSK3 within the destruction complex, stabilizing β-catenin and altering transcription via TCF/LEF (Hottin et al., 2022). CHIR99021 pharmacologically inhibits GSK3β and thereby is a canonical Wnt/β-catenin activator in many contexts, explaining its frequent use to bias fate decisions in pluripotent and somatic reprogramming paradigms (Lyssiotis et al., 2011; Leach et al., 2015).

Dose-dependent Wnt signaling in RPE systems: In RPE-derived ARPE-19 models, CHIR99021 shows a clear dose window: at 1 μM for one week it decreases EFEMP1/F3 transcripts/protein and globally represses ECM/complement/TGFβ signatures without detectable activation of TCF reporters; at ≥2.5 μM, TCF reporter activation becomes detectable, indicating canonical Wnt activation above a threshold (DiCesare et al., 2023). This low-dose window was sufficient to reduce MMP2 activity associated with the R345W F3 secretory stress pathophysiology, consistent with broad extracellular remodeling (DiCesare et al., 2023).

On-target genetic support: siRNA knockdown of GSK3α and GSK3β individually reduces F3 and combined knockdown synergizes, phenocopying CHIR’s effect on F3 production and secretion, supporting a GSK3-dependent mechanism for its anti-F3/anti-ECM actions (DiCesare et al., 2023). The effect generalizes across cell types (ARPE-19, human dermal fibroblasts, NIH-3T3), consistent with GSK3’s broad role in secretory/ECM regulation (DiCesare et al., 2023).

Secretory/ECM/complement/TGFβ axis remodeling: One-week, low-dose CHIR caused ≥2-fold reductions in multiple collagens (α1(V), α2(IV), α1(IV), α3(IV)), MMP2, complement C3, HMGB1/2, and TGFβ-related proteins such as SERPINE1/PAI-1 and LTBP2, with transcript-level suppression of ECM crosslinking and EMT-proximal genes (e.g., FN1, LOX, WNT ligands), while upregulating RPE differentiation/pigmentation (TYR, TYRP1) and increasing PEDF (SERPINF1) (DiCesare et al., 2023). These data point to a coordinated shift of the RPE secretome toward reduced pathogenic ECM/complement burden and increased pro-RPE homeostatic factors (e.g., PEDF), in line with the observed mitigation of BLamD in vivo (DiCesare et al., 2023).

mTOR–lysosome/autophagy coupling: Outside the retina, CHIR99021 has been shown to inhibit the Rheb/mTOR axis and increase lysosomal activation and autophagy in late endothelial progenitor cells, with evidence that CHIR reduces phosphorylated mTOR and Rheb independent of β-catenin, via effects attributed to TSC2 and lysosomal mTOR localization (Rethineswaran et al., 2021). These studies connect GSK3β inhibition to increased autophagic flux through mTORC1 suppression at the lysosome, a mechanistic route that in principle converges on transcriptional lysosome biogenesis programs (e.g., TFEB) though TFEB itself was not directly assayed in these reports (Rethineswaran et al., 2021). In retinal disease biology, GSK3 interdigitates with oxidative stress (NRF2 regulation), inflammatory NF-κB signaling, and mTOR pathways that are all implicated in AMD pathogenesis; pharmacologic GSK3β inhibition can increase NRF2 and reduce ROS in diabetic contexts, and reduced GSK3 activity in microglia dampens LPS-induced NF-κB signaling, underscoring additional protective axes that may be engaged in RPE or choroid (Hottin et al., 2022).

Angiogenic and repair liabilities: GSK3 inhibition/Wnt activation can increase VEGF and angiogenesis; reviews caution this may be beneficial in dry AMD (neuroprotection/anti-inflammatory) but harmful in wet AMD, suggesting indication-specific selection and potential need for combination with anti-VEGF or restricted/local delivery (Hottin et al., 2022). In a large RPE wound model mimicking GA-scale atrophy, continuous CHIR exposure hindered repair, in contrast to EMT-suppressing agents that improved closure, highlighting a context where Wnt activation can be counterproductive for lesion repopulation (Bailey-Steinitz, 2021).

Mechanistic net assessment for dry AMD: In RPE disease–proximal models, CHIR99021’s dominant effects at low dose are anti-secretory for F3/EFEMP1 and anti-ECM/complement/TGFβ, with reduced MMP2 and enhanced RPE differentiation markers, culminating in prevention of BLamD in vivo without electrophysiologic deficits over one month (DiCesare et al., 2023). Independent data show CHIR increases autophagy and lysosomal function via mTOR inhibition in other cell types, a mechanistic route that could contribute to proteostasis restoration in the RPE but remains to be demonstrated directly in RPE/AMD systems (Rethineswaran et al., 2021).

Expected Effect  
Assay-level predictions under the stated hypothesis: The team’s hypothesis posits that CHIR99021 will inhibit GSK3β in RPE, facilitate TFEB nuclear localization, enhance lysosomal acidification and cathepsin D (CTSD) maturation, increase autophagic flux, and thereby prevent RPE atrophy in dry AMD. Direct evidence for TFEB nuclear localization or CTSD maturation with CHIR99021 in RPE is not yet provided in the extant literature summarized here; however, two mechanistic pillars are established:

- In RPE disease models, low-dose CHIR99021 reduces a causal secretory burden (EFEMP1/F3) and pathogenic ECM/complement/protease output, normalizes MMP2 activity, increases homeostatic PEDF, and prevents BLamD formation in vivo, providing a deposit-centric, mechanistically credible route to slow early and mid-stage dry AMD pathology that is driven by sub-RPE matrix remodeling and complement activation (DiCesare et al., 2023).

- In non-ocular cells, CHIR99021 inhibits mTOR signaling at the lysosome (reduced Rheb/p-mTOR) and increases lysosomal activation and autophagy independent of β-catenin, consistent with a mechanism that would be predicted to favor TFEB nuclear translocation, transcription of lysosome/autophagy genes, and maturation of proteases such as CTSD; these precise endpoints have not been measured in RPE with CHIR99021 and thus remain to be validated (Rethineswaran et al., 2021).

Given GSK3 expression in ARPE-19 and its manipulation in the cited experiments (use of anti-GSK3α/β antibodies and on-target siRNA phenocopy), RPE is a relevant target cell for CHIR99021’s kinase inhibition (DiCesare et al., 2023). Under oxidative and secretory stress common to dry AMD, one would expect CHIR99021 at sub-TCF-activating exposure (≈1 μM) to:

- Reduce EFEMP1/F3 transcription/secretion and broadly depress ECM and complement cues that seed and stabilize BLamD/drusen, thereby lowering sub-RPE deposit biogenesis and associated pro-inflammatory signaling (DiCesare et al., 2023).

- Normalize MMP2 activity and reduce matrix proteolysis-driven remodeling that contributes to basal laminar/basal linear deposit architecture (DiCesare et al., 2023).

- Enhance RPE homeostatic phenotype, reflected by increased pigmentation gene expression and PEDF secretion, which supports photoreceptor survival and RPE trophic function (DiCesare et al., 2023).

- Potentially increase autophagic flux and lysosomal competence via mTOR inhibition, improving clearance of aggregation-prone or secretory-stressed substrates; this inference is supported mechanistically outside the retina and should be formally confirmed in RPE by LC3 flux, p62/SQSTM1 turnover, LAMP1/2, lysotracker, and cathepsin maturation assays (Rethineswaran et al., 2021).

Boundary conditions and risks for the expected effect: The low-dose window is critical; at ≥2.5 μM, CHIR99021 activates canonical Wnt/TCF reporters in RPE-derived cells, and continuous Wnt activation can impair large-lesion RPE repair and increase angiogenic drive (VEGF), both of which are undesirable in late-stage GA or in patients at risk of conversion to exudative AMD (DiCesare et al., 2023; Bailey-Steinitz, 2021; Hottin et al., 2022). In vivo PK after 25 mg/kg IP yields retinal concentrations in the 0.15–1.3 μM range over the first 24 h, overlapping the RPE efficacy window for EFEMP1/ECM suppression and below the Wnt activation threshold in vitro; however, local ocular delivery and controlled-release formulations may be preferable to avoid systemic exposure and to maintain sub-TCF-activating intraocular concentrations (DiCesare et al., 2023; Hottin et al., 2022).

Overall Evaluation  

Strengths  
- Disease-proximal efficacy with mechanistic depth. CHIR99021 reduces EFEMP1/F3 production (transcript and protein), broadly suppresses ECM/complement/TGFβ secretome programs, decreases MMP2 activity, upregulates pigmentation genes and PEDF, and prevents BLamD in an EFEMP1 R345W knock-in model—an AMD-like pathology characterized by sub-RPE matrix deposits (DiCesare et al., 2023). The convergence of proteomics, transcriptomics, reporter assays, and genetic knockdown around GSK3 establishes on-target pathway control in RPE-derived systems (DiCesare et al., 2023).

- Ocular exposure and safety. Tissue PK demonstrates retinal penetrance and prolonged retention (terminal T½ ≈ 6.75 h), with estimated intraocular levels overlapping the in vitro effective window; one month of systemic dosing at 25 mg/kg produced no detectable ERG or histological abnormalities in adult mice, supporting a tolerability window (DiCesare et al., 2023).

- Plausible extension to proteostasis/autophagy. Independent mechanistic data show CHIR99021 inhibits mTORC1 signaling at the lysosome and increases autophagy/lysosomal activation via the TSC2–Rheb axis in non-ocular cells, a route that could bolster RPE lysosomal function under drusen/BLamD-associated stress even if TFEB was not yet directly measured in RPE (Rethineswaran et al., 2021).

- Modality versatility with established use. Extensive prior use of CHIR99021 as a defined Wnt agonist in RPE/retinal differentiation and reprogramming provides a deep operations base for dosing/timing and cell-specific responses, which can be leveraged to avoid undesired pathway activation during therapy (Leach et al., 2015; Fujii et al., 2021).

Weaknesses and risks  
- Translational maturity and source quality. The core anti-deposit efficacy and ocular PK/safety package resides in a bioRxiv preprint; while comprehensive and internally consistent, it lacks peer-reviewed confirmation and replication across independent labs and models (DiCesare et al., 2023). Moreover, the EFEMP1 R345W model (ML/DHRD) is a rare, early-onset macular dystrophy with AMD-like deposits; it does not recapitulate the full aging/inflammation/metabolic milieu of typical dry AMD (DiCesare et al., 2023).

- Wnt/angiogenesis liability and wound repair. GSK3β inhibition is a canonical Wnt activator and can increase VEGF/angiogenesis, potentially contraindicating use in patients with neovascular risk; in RPE monolayers with macula-sized lesions, CHIR99021 impaired lesion repair despite increasing peripheral pigmentation, highlighting a deleterious effect in GA-like settings requiring repopulation (Hottin et al., 2022; Bailey-Steinitz, 2021).

- Dose/timing and cell-type dependency. Benefits of GSK3 modulation are highly context-dependent in retinal disease; the same pathway promotes different outcomes across disease stage and cell types (photoreceptors, Müller glia, RPE, endothelium). Reviews emphasize that treatment timing, duration, and targeted retinal layer will determine benefit vs harm (DiCesare et al., 2023; Hottin et al., 2022). The in vitro window where 1 μM avoids TCF activation is narrow; in vivo pharmacology must control ocular exposure carefully (DiCesare et al., 2023).

- Mechanistic gap for the autophagy/TFEB claim in RPE. Although CHIR99021 increases autophagy through mTOR suppression in other cell types, direct evidence in human RPE or RPE-derived models for TFEB nuclear translocation, lysosomal acidification improvements, or CTSD maturation with CHIR99021 is currently absent from the surveyed literature; this is an experimental gap relative to the team’s stated hypothesis (Rethineswaran et al., 2021).

Development recommendations  
- Indication scoping to dry AMD segments with deposit-dominated pathology. Based on anti-ECM/complement and anti-BLamD efficacy, prioritize early/mid dry AMD segments characterized by drusen/sub-RPE deposits and low neovascular risk; de-prioritize active geographic atrophy where repopulation/repair of large RPE lesions is the therapeutic aim, given the CHIR-associated repair impairment in vitro (DiCesare et al., 2023; Bailey-Steinitz, 2021).

- Local ocular delivery to widen the therapeutic index. Intravitreal or suprachoroidal controlled-release systems should be evaluated to maintain intraocular concentrations in the ~0.1–1 μM range that achieve biochemical efficacy but remain below the canonical Wnt activation threshold, while minimizing systemic exposure and wet-AMD conversion risk; the reviews support local delivery as a strategy for GSK3-based ocular interventions (DiCesare et al., 2023; Hottin et al., 2022).

- Mechanistic validation in RPE for proteostasis endpoints. In primary hfRPE and iPSC-RPE, directly measure CHIR99021’s impact on autophagy and lysosome: LC3-II flux (±bafilomycin A1), p62/SQSTM1 turnover, TFEB nuclear localization (immunofluorescence/fractionation), lysosomal pH (LysoSensor), LAMP1/2 expression, and CTSD maturation/activity; determine whether these benefits occur at sub-TCF-activating exposures and under relevant stresses (oxidative, lipid, complement) (DiCesare et al., 2023; Rethineswaran et al., 2021).

- Angiogenic surveillance and combination strategies. Quantify VEGF and angiogenic markers (VEGFA mRNA/protein, HIF-1α targets) in RPE/choroid after CHIR, and consider anti-VEGF co-therapy if Wnt-VEGF coupling poses a risk; preclinical reviews support the rationale for combination or timing-restricted inhibition to avoid pro-angiogenic consequences (Hottin et al., 2022).

- Broaden efficacy across dry AMD models. Test CHIR in aging-related and inflammation-metabolism models (e.g., high-fat diet + complement stress; smoke exposure; ApoE variants) in addition to EFEMP1 R345W to ensure generalizability beyond monogenic ECM disease; define the minimal exposure and duration to alter drusen/BLamD dynamics and microglial/complement activation (DiCesare et al., 2023).

- Dose-finding anchored to ocular PK/PD. Use the established LC/MS retinal assay to map intravitreal/subconjunctival/suprachoroidal dose to retinal/choroidal concentration–time profiles; overlay with PD markers (F3 secretion, ECM transcripts, complement, PEDF) to define a sub-TCF window in vivo; confirm absence of ERG deficits and retinal histopathology across multi-month dosing (DiCesare et al., 2023).

- Translational vigilance. Lithium’s status as the sole FDA-approved GSK3 inhibitor and mixed outcomes of GSK3 modulation in retinal disease underscore the need to target specific retinal layers or cell types and to avoid broad systemic inhibition; this aligns with adopting local ocular delivery and possibly RPE-targeted formulations (DiCesare et al., 2023; Hottin et al., 2022).

Conclusion  
On balance, CHIR99021 has a compelling, disease-proximal efficacy package for dry AMD centered on sub-RPE deposit biology. At low doses that do not detectably activate canonical Wnt, CHIR99021 reduces EFEMP1/F3 and globally attenuates ECM/complement/protease pathways in RPE-derived systems, increases PEDF and pigmentation gene expression, and prevents BLamD formation in an EFEMP1 R345W mouse model, with retinal exposures matching in vitro efficacy windows and month-long dosing without ERG/histology toxicity (DiCesare et al., 2023). Independent mechanistic data demonstrate CHIR-mediated inhibition of Rheb/mTOR and increased lysosomal/autophagic activity in non-ocular cells, consistent with the proteostasis-restoring arm of the team’s hypothesis, but direct evidence for TFEB nuclear translocation and CTSD maturation in RPE with CHIR is currently lacking and should be considered a key validation gap (Rethineswaran et al., 2021). The principal risks are Wnt-linked angiogenesis (potentially harmful in wet AMD) and impaired RPE wound repair in GA-like lesions when Wnt activation is sustained; these risks argue for a dry-AMD, early/mid-stage positioning, careful intraocular dose control to remain below the TCF activation threshold, and consideration of local delivery and/or anti-VEGF combinations in higher-risk patients (Hottin et al., 2022; Bailey-Steinitz, 2021).

Overall, CHIR99021 is a promising repurposed candidate for dry AMD if developed within a well-defined exposure window and indication niche. Its strengths are a clear kinase target with on-target cellular genetics, strong anti-deposit and secretome remodeling data in RPE and in vivo, ocular exposure that aligns with cellular pharmacology, and plausible lysosome/autophagy engagement. Its weaknesses are translational maturity (preprint stage; single primary in vivo model), Wnt-associated angiogenesis and repair liabilities at higher/continuous exposure, and incomplete validation of the autophagy/TFEB axis in RPE. A go decision for preclinical advancement is justified, contingent on rapid mechanistic confirmation in RPE for autophagy/lysosome endpoints, rigorous angiogenesis/wound-repair safety pharmacology, and PK/PD-guided local delivery strategies that maintain sub-TCF intraocular concentrations (DiCesare et al., 2023; Hottin et al., 2022; Rethineswaran et al., 2021).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
T0901317 is a fully synthetic small‐molecule agonist originally identified through screening for compounds that activate liver X receptors (LXRs). It belongs to the class of nuclear receptor ligands and is structurally designed to mimic endogenous oxysterols, the natural activators of LXRs. LXRs, comprising two isoforms, LXRα (NR1H3) and LXRβ (NR1H2), are master transcriptional regulators of cholesterol, lipid, and glucose metabolism. T0901317 was first characterized for its capacity to bind and stimulate these receptors, thereby upregulating target genes involved in cholesterol efflux such as ATP-binding cassette transporter A1 (ABCA1) and apolipoprotein E (APOE) (Choudhary et al., 2020, pp. 15–16). The compound has been widely used in preclinical studies to investigate cholesterol homeostasis, inflammation modulation, and emerging neuroprotective pathways. Its chemical synthesis follows standard procedures for developing derivatives that confer high receptor affinity and bioactivity while allowing researchers to dissect LXR-dependent pathways in multiple cell types, including retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells. The rationale behind using such LXR agonists, including T0901317, in ocular disorders like dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) stems from their demonstrated ability to restore cholesterol efflux, ameliorate lipid deposition, and reduce inflammatory stress in target tissues (Choudhary et al., 2020, pp. 12–13).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, T0901317 has been utilized extensively within the biomedical research arena as a tool compound to elucidate the role of LXRs in metabolic and inflammatory diseases. Preclinical work has demonstrated that LXR activation in key tissues, including the retina, can reestablish lipid homeostasis and reduce pathological lipid accumulation. Several studies indicate that in LXR-deficient models, there is an accumulation of neutral lipids and extracellular deposits—features that are remarkably similar to drusen formation observed in early dry AMD (Choudhary et al., 2020, pp. 7–9; Terao et al., 2024, pp. 8–10). In animal models, particularly in mice lacking the Nr1h3 isoform, the phenotype includes RPE dysfunction, inflammatory microenvironment formation, and structural changes that closely mimic human dry AMD pathology (Choudhary et al., 2020, pp. 2–4). Although T0901317 has not advanced to clinical trials for AMD, its efficacy has been primarily established in vitro using human RPE cell models and in vivo in murine models. The compound has shown potential for correcting the dysregulated cholesterol metabolism that contributes to the chronic buildup of lipid-rich drusen—a central pathological hallmark of dry AMD (Choudhary et al., 2020, pp. 12–13, 15–16). Outside of ocular applications, compounds from this class have been investigated for atherosclerosis and neurodegeneration, further emphasizing the critical link between cholesterol metabolism and chronic inflammatory conditions (Malek & Lad, 2014, pp. 13–15).

Mechanism of Action:  
The mechanism of action of T0901317 is fundamentally tied to its role as a potent activator of LXRs. Upon binding to LXRα and LXRβ within retinal cells, T0901317 facilitates heterodimerization with retinoid X receptors (RXRs), forming a transcriptionally active complex that binds to LXR response elements (LXREs) in the promoter regions of target genes. This activation cascade results in upregulation of numerous genes critical for cholesterol efflux and lipid metabolism, most notably ABCA1 and APOE (Choudhary et al., 2020, pp. 15–16). Upregulation of ABCA1 increases the efflux of excess cholesterol and oxidized lipids from RPE cells into the extracellular environment, thereby reducing the intracellular lipid load that predisposes cells to toxicity and drusen accumulation (Choudhary et al., 2020, pp. 12–13; Wu et al., 2023, pp. 10–12).

Beyond cholesterol efflux, T0901317 activates additional gene networks that modulate lysosomal function and autophagy. Experimental data suggest that T0901317 enhances the expression of lysosomal hydrolases, including cathepsin D (CTSD), and promotes the assembly of vacuolar-type H⁺-ATPases (v-ATPase), essential for maintaining lysosomal acidity (Lei et al., 2017, pp. 13–17, 20–22). This increase in active lysosomal enzymes and reinforced acidification contributes to the improved clearance of debris, particularly drusen components composed of lipid and protein aggregates. Furthermore, LXR activation by T0901317 has been shown to increase autophagy gene expression, thereby inducing a mitophagy response that removes damaged organelles and supports cellular metabolic renewal (Terao et al., 2024, pp. 8–10; Xie et al., 2022, pp. 1–2). In addition, T0901317 exerts significant anti-inflammatory effects by downregulating NF-κB signaling. It has been observed to inhibit the phosphorylation of IκBα, which prevents the nuclear translocation of NF-κB and subsequent transcription of inflammatory cytokines such as TNF-α and IL-6 (Lei et al., 2017, pp. 13–17; Choudhary & Malek, 2016, pp. 4–6). This dual role in lipid regulation and inflammation attenuation is central to its therapeutic promise in AMD, where chronic inflammation and disrupted lipid processing are major determinants of disease progression.

Expected Effect:  
In the context of dry AMD, with its hallmark drusen deposits and RPE dysfunction, the expected therapeutic effect of T0901317 is multifold. By activating LXRs in RPE cells, T0901317 is expected to upregulate the expression of ABCA1 and other cholesterol efflux mediators, thereby reducing the intracellular build‐up of cholesterol and oxidized lipids that contribute to drusen formation (Choudhary et al., 2020, pp. 2–4). This increase in cholesterol efflux would allow the RPE to better clear lipid debris, lowering the overall lipid burden on Bruch’s membrane. Concomitantly, the drug’s capacity to augment lysosomal function is anticipated to result in improved clearance of extracellular drusen components via a cathepsin D–dependent mechanism. Enhanced v-ATPase assembly and lysosomal acidification, as demonstrated by increased CTSD activity in vitro, should restore the degradative capacity of the lysosomal system, thereby facilitating the removal of protein-lipid aggregates (Lei et al., 2017, pp. 25–33).

Furthermore, the activation of autophagy pathways and promotion of mitophagy are expected to counteract the mitochondrial dysfunction that characterizes aged RPE cells—an integral pathological feature of dry AMD (Choudhary et al., 2020, pp. 7–9, 2–4). The anticipated result is a restoration of cellular homeostasis, improved energy metabolism, and reduction in oxidative stress, all of which are essential for maintaining RPE cell integrity. RPE cells have been shown to express both LXRα and LXRβ, and their expression is frequently diminished in AMD-affected eyes (Choudhary et al., 2020, pp. 12–13; Lyssenko et al., 2018, pp. 1–3). Therefore, by boosting LXR activity, T0901317 not only counteracts lipid dysregulation but also provides a neuroprotective, anti-inflammatory benefit by modulating cytokine production and dampening microglial activation in the outer retina (Choudhary & Malek, 2016, pp. 4–6).

Overall Evaluation:  
The overall assessment of T0901317 as a therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration is cautiously optimistic, with several key strengths as well as notable limitations that warrant further investigation.  

Strengths:  
One of the primary advantages of T0901317 is its well-documented ability to activate LXRs and thereby induce a broad spectrum of beneficial responses relevant to dry AMD pathology. The compound’s capacity to upregulate ABCA1 expression is critical, as impaired cholesterol efflux is a central mechanism underlying the accumulation of lipid-rich drusen (Choudhary et al., 2020, pp. 15–16, 12–13). Moreover, its ability to enhance lysosomal enzyme expression and promote v-ATPase assembly is particularly promising for the restoration of lysosomal acidity—a key defect in aged RPE cells that contributes to decreased clearance of toxic lipid deposits (Lei et al., 2017, pp. 13–17, 20–22). In addition, the induction of autophagy and mitophagy following LXR activation offers a dual therapeutic benefit by promoting the removal of damaged mitochondria and reducing oxidative stress, thereby preserving RPE cell viability (Xie et al., 2022, pp. 1–2). The anti-inflammatory properties of T0901317, demonstrated by its inhibition of NF-κB signaling and reduction of pro-inflammatory cytokine production, further support its potential utility in addressing the chronic low-grade inflammation often observed in AMD (Choudhary & Malek, 2016, pp. 4–6). Collectively, these mechanisms directly target the multifactorial aspects of dry AMD pathology—namely, lipid dysregulation, lysosomal dysfunction, and inflammatory stress—making T0901317 an attractive candidate for repurposing in this indication (Choudhary et al., 2020, pp. 2–4).

Another significant strength is the potential for ocular delivery strategies to mitigate the systemic side effects associated with T0901317. Given that systemic administration of LXR agonists has been linked to adverse metabolic effects such as hypertriglyceridemia and off-target activation of nuclear receptors like FXR and PXR (Lei et al., 2017, pp. 20–22; Storti et al., 2019, pp. 15–16), localized ocular delivery could concentrate the drug’s therapeutic effects in the retina while minimizing systemic exposure. Despite these promising attributes, there are several challenges that temper the enthusiasm for T0901317 as a first-in-class therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. Furthermore, while the mechanistic underpinnings are appealing, further in vivo validation in chronic, clinically relevant AMD models is essential to confirm that the improvements in cholesterol efflux and lysosomal function translate into meaningful therapeutic outcomes—in terms of slowing or reversing the progression of dry AMD. Overall, T0901317 represents a promising, though challenging, candidate for addressing the unmet need in dry AMD therapy. Investment in additional preclinical studies focusing on ocular bioavailability, long-term safety in the retinal microenvironment, and optimization of dosing regimens will be critical in determining whether T0901317 or a similarly acting, perhaps more selective, LXR agonist can progress into clinical evaluation for dry AMD. The strategic focus on lipid-driven dysfunction, particularly in lysosomal clearance pathways, offers a novel mechanism of action that could complement or serve as an alternative to current therapeutic approaches, making T0901317 (or its optimized derivatives) a compelling candidate for further investigation (Choudhary et al., 2020, pp. 2–4, 7–9, 13–17).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
VX-765 is an orally bioavailable small‐molecule agent belonging to the caspase-1 inhibitor class. Originally developed by Vertex Pharmaceuticals, VX-765 was designed to address the shortcomings of earlier peptide-based caspase inhibitors by improving bioavailability, stability, and selectivity. As a caspase-1 inhibitor, it falls within a broader category of agents that have been used to blunt excessive inflammasome responses in various inflammatory and immune-mediated conditions. In the context of drug discovery, caspase-1 inhibitors have been of keen interest because caspase-1 is the key enzyme responsible for converting pro-IL-1β and pro-IL-18 into their active cytokine forms, thereby playing a central role in mediating inflammation and the programmed cell death process known as pyroptosis. VX-765 has been evaluated primarily in systemic inflammatory and cardiovascular settings, where its favorable pharmacokinetic profile and excellent oral bioavailability have been demonstrated (Audia et al., 2018; MacKenzie & Schipper, 2010).

Therapeutic History:  
The therapeutic history of VX-765 underscores its extensive preclinical development and early clinical evaluation in several inflammatory settings. In preclinical cardiovascular models, for instance, VX-765 demonstrated significant cardioprotection when administered during reperfusion, reducing infarct size and preserving mitochondrial enzyme activities (Audia et al., 2018). It has undergone Phase I and Phase II clinical studies—its Phase II safety data indicate that it is well tolerated at doses that achieve a suppression of proinflammatory cytokines in plasma (MacKenzie & Schipper, 2010). Although the major clinical investigations with VX-765 have focused on disorders such as epilepsy and other inflammatory diseases rather than ophthalmic disorders, the rationale for its use in dry AMD stems from overlapping inflammatory mechanisms. Specifically, dry AMD shares underlying pathological processes such as chronic inflammation, oxidative stress, and lysosomal dysfunction in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells. Prior experimental studies in RPE models using caspase-1 inhibitors like Z-YVAD-FMK have demonstrated that inhibiting caspase-1 activity reduces IL-1β release and can influence cell death pathways (Brandstetter, 2016; Tseng et al., 2013). However, despite this promising mechanistic background, VX-765 itself has not yet been directly evaluated in preclinical models of dry AMD or in similar ocular diseases. This gap in ophthalmic precedent is notable, but given its established safety profile in nonocular clinical settings and robust anti-inflammatory activity, VX-765 remains an attractive candidate for repurposing into the dry AMD arena (Audia et al., 2018; MacKenzie & Schipper, 2010).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, VX-765 exerts its effect primarily through selective inhibition of caspase-1, a cysteine protease critically involved in the processing of pro-inflammatory cytokines. Under conditions of cellular stress—such as those occurring in RPE cells in response to lipofuscin accumulation and photooxidative damage—lysosomal destabilization can occur. This lysosomal membrane permeabilization (LMP) leads to the release of cathepsins and other proteases into the cytosol, which, in turn, can serve as an activator of the NLRP3 inflammasome. Once assembled, the inflammasome facilitates the autocatalytic cleavage of caspase-1 into its active p10/p20 subunits, thereby enabling it to convert pro-IL-1β and pro-IL-18 into their mature, secreted forms. VX-765 binds to the active site of caspase-1, thereby preventing this proteolytic cleavage and subsequent cytokine release. This action not only blunts the inflammatory cascade but, by inhibiting caspase-1–dependent processing, may also prevent the activation of gasdermin-D (GSDMD) which is responsible for forming membrane pores during pyroptosis (Brandstetter, 2016; Tseng et al., 2013).

The hypothesis for using VX-765 in dry AMD is that inhibition of caspase-1 will disrupt a pathological amplification loop. In RPE cells exposed to chronic oxidative stress and lipofuscin-related photooxidative damage, inflammasome activation has been shown to promote rapid pyroptotic cell death rather than a slower apoptotic process. This results in an autocrine/paracrine loop where secreted IL-1β further primes neighboring cells for inflammasome activation, exacerbating cell death and causing tissue dysfunction. By blocking caspase-1 activity, VX-765 is expected to prevent this destructive cascade, thereby preserving lysosomal function. More specifically, there is a hypothesized link between caspase-1 activity and alterations in lysosomal integrity—a process involving LMP that is associated with a loss of vacuolar (V-) ATPase activity and disturbances in cathepsin D maturation. The V-ATPase is critical for maintaining an acidic lysosomal environment necessary for optimal enzyme activity, including that of cathepsin D, which is involved in the degradation of photoreceptor outer segments. Some studies have shown that under conditions of inflammasome activation, RPE cells demonstrate not only an increase in cytokine secretion but also a decline in the functionality of lysosomal hydrolases, which may further compromise cell viability (Brandstetter, 2016). Although direct evidence linking VX-765 to the preservation of V-ATPase activity or cathepsin D function in RPE is currently lacking, the mechanistic framework provided by previous studies using other caspase-1 inhibitors supports the notion that caspase-1 blockade may confer lysosomal protection and attenuate pyroptotic RPE death (Brandstetter, 2016; Tseng et al., 2013).

In healthy RPE cells, cathepsin D is a major lysosomal protease responsible for degrading photoreceptor outer segment debris. Although direct measurements of V-ATPase activity and cathepsin D maturation following VX-765 treatment have not yet been published, the overall expectation is that by interrupting the caspase-1–driven inflammatory signaling cascade, VX-765 can prevent the deleterious loss of lysosomal function and thereby reduce RPE cell death (Brandstetter, 2016; Gao et al., 2019; Tseng et al., 2013).

Markers of efficacy would include improved retinal morphology on OCT imaging, better electrophysiological responses (as measured by ERG), and a decrease in inflammatory cellular infiltrates. Collectively, these anticipated outcomes support the hypothesis that VX-765’s inhibition of caspase-1 may interrupt the cascade of inflammasome activation, LMP, and lysosomal enzyme failure that leads to RPE death in dry AMD (Brandstetter, 2016; Tseng et al., 2013).

Our overall evaluation of VX-765 as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD is cautiously optimistic but recognizes several critical hurdles. One of the major strengths of VX-765 is its well-characterized mechanism of action as a selective caspase-1 inhibitor, along with its demonstrated anti-inflammatory effects in non-ocular preclinical models. The clinical safety profile established in Phase I and II studies—particularly its ability to reduce circulating pro-inflammatory cytokines—lends support to its potential use in a chronic disease setting such as dry AMD (Audia et al., 2018; MacKenzie & Schipper, 2010). From a mechanistic standpoint, the centrality of caspase-1 in mediating inflammasome-driven cytokine maturation and pyroptosis is well established, and there is compelling evidence from RPE cell models that caspase-1 inhibition can reduce IL-1β secretion and potentially modify cell death pathways (Brandstetter, 2016; Tseng et al., 2013). These observations provide a strong rationale for the hypothesis that VX-765 could prevent the lysosomal destabilization and subsequent inflammatory cascade responsible for RPE degeneration.

However, there are also several weaknesses and gaps that must be addressed before VX-765 can be fully endorsed for dry AMD. Although the mechanistic data support the role of caspase-1 inhibition in reducing inflammatory cytokine release and possibly preserving lysosomal function, there is currently no direct evidence that VX-765 can stabilize lysosomal membrane integrity, preserve V-ATPase activity, or maintain proper cathepsin D function specifically in RPE cells. Most of the available literature has utilized generic caspase-1 inhibitors such as Z-YVAD-FMK as proof-of-principle tools rather than VX-765 itself in ocular models (Brandstetter, 2016; Tseng et al., 2013). In addition to inflammasome activation and lysosomal dysfunction, dry AMD pathogenesis involves complement dysregulation, oxidative stress, impaired autophagy, and other pro-inflammatory pathways. Only with such data can we determine whether VX-765 holds true promise as a therapeutic for dry AMD.

Overall, while VX-765 has scientifically robust credentials as a caspase-1 inhibitor with proven anti-inflammatory potential in other systems, its repurposing for dry AMD will depend on demonstrating that its molecular actions translate into preservation of RPE function and structure in ocular models. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
AZD9056 is a small‐molecule, orally active P2X7 receptor antagonist developed by AstraZeneca that belongs to the class of synthetic adamantane‐based compounds. Although its precise chemical structure has not been fully disclosed in the public domain, multiple reports indicate that it emerges from a medicinal chemistry program focused on adamantyl benzamide scaffolds discovered through high‐throughput screening and subsequent structure–activity relationship (SAR) optimization (Chrovian et al., 2014; Gunosewoyo et al., 2007). The compound is understood to maintain the essential adamantane moiety linked through a methylene spacer to an aromatic benzamide, which is thought to force a twist in the benzamide conformation critical for high P2X7 antagonism (Chrovian et al., 2014; Gunosewoyo et al., 2007). In general, the adamantane class of compounds has been explored for its lipophilic and sterically constrained properties that can impart favorable bioavailability and receptor selectivity; indeed, the adamantane scaffold has also been exploited in a number of antiviral and anti-inflammatory agents. In the case of AZD9056, this design strategy was implemented to yield a molecule that potently blocks the ATP‐driven activity of the P2X7 receptor—a ligand‐gated ion channel implicated in inflammation and cell death—while offering the oral bioavailability and acceptable pharmacokinetic properties required for systemic application (Chrovian et al., 2014; Eser et al., 2015). The overall discovery process appears to have combined hit identification with parallel synthetic approaches in order to establish an SAR profile that ultimately led to a candidate with nanomolar potency in cell‐based assays of P2X7 function, such as inhibition of Bz-ATP–induced Ca2+ influx and dye uptake, although the specific synthetic steps remain proprietary (Chrovian et al., 2014; Gunosewoyo et al., 2007).  

Therapeutic History:  
AZD9056 has been evaluated extensively in non‐ocular inflammatory disease contexts. Early-phase clinical trials established its safety and tolerability in healthy volunteers through single- and multiple-dose studies that characterized its pharmacokinetic profile, with parameters such as a moderate oral bioavailability (~62%), a terminal half-life in the range of 16–18 hours, and the capacity for once-daily dosing (Arulkumaran et al., 2011). Its development program initially focused on rheumatoid arthritis (RA). In a 4-week phase IIa trial in RA patients, AZD9056 was found to be safe and well tolerated at the doses assessed, and target engagement was evidenced by significant inhibition of ex vivo ATP-induced monocyte IL-1β release (Chrovian et al., 2014). However, a subsequent larger phase IIb study in RA, enrolling up to 385 or more patients and including an open etanercept comparator arm, failed to demonstrate superior clinical efficacy over placebo across several objective endpoints, even though tolerability remained acceptable (Arulkumaran et al., 2011; Chrovian et al., 2014; Lepre et al., 2023). In parallel with its RA development, AZD9056 also underwent evaluation for inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), specifically in patients with Crohn's disease, where a phase IIa trial using a 200 mg once-daily regimen showed nominal improvements in the Crohn’s Disease Activity Index (CDAI) but no accompanying improvement in inflammatory biomarkers (Arulkumaran et al., 2011; Rech et al., 2016). Aside from these clinical endeavors in systemic inflammatory disorders, a dedicated ocular safety study was conducted in healthy volunteers; in this randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover study, retinal function was directly assessed by measures including electroretinography and visual acuity—an indication that the eye was considered as a potential compartment of interest, even though no efficacy studies in ocular disease states such as dry age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD) have been reported (Arulkumaran et al., 2011). Overall, while the compound has been repurposed extensively for anti-inflammatory indications and has an established human safety profile, its clinical history thus far has not included a trial specifically targeting dry AMD or any direct veterinary employments for ocular diseases (Arulkumaran et al., 2011; Guile et al., 2009).  

Mechanism of Action:  
The P2X7 receptor (P2X7R) is an ATP-gated, nonselective cation channel predominantly expressed on immune cells and, importantly for the intended application, on the retinal pigmented epithelium (RPE) (Calzaferri et al., 2020). Under physiological conditions, P2X7R is quiescent; however, in the presence of elevated extracellular ATP—a phenomenon noted in inflammatory and degenerative conditions, including AMD—the receptor becomes activated, mediating several deleterious downstream events. Upon activation, P2X7R undergoes a conformational change that not only allows the influx of Ca2+ and Na+ but also promotes the formation of large membrane pores owing to its ability to transition into a state that permits the passage of molecules as large as 900 Da (Chrovian et al., 2014; Eser et al., 2015). This pore formation results in cytotoxic calcium overload and is directly linked to the activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome, a multiprotein complex responsible for the processing of pro-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-1β and IL-18 (Calzaferri et al., 2020; Gu & Wiley, 2018). In the retinal pigment epithelium, this ATP-driven activation has been shown to contribute to lysosomal alkalization—a process that impairs the optimal acidic environment required by lysosomal enzymes, including cathepsins—and ultimately leads to defective clearance of cellular debris (Calzaferri et al., 2020; Tempest-Roe, 2017). Specifically, experimental studies in ARPE-19 cells (a human RPE cell line) have demonstrated that stimulation of P2X7 induces lysosomal dysfunction; conversely, pharmacological inhibition of P2X7 using antagonists such as Brilliant Blue G (BBG) can reverse this lysosomal impairment (Tempest-Roe, 2017). Mechanistically, AZD9056 is designed to bind to the P2X7 receptor with high potency and selectivity, thereby preventing the receptor’s activation by ATP. By doing so, it is anticipated to block the cascade of events that lead from receptor activation to pore formation, inflammasome assembly, and subsequent IL-1β release (Calzaferri et al., 2020; Gu & Wiley, 2018; Lee et al., 2023). Although the exact molecular binding mode of AZD9056 has not been detailed in available literature, it is presumed to interact with key residues involved in channel gating and pore formation, thereby stabilizing the receptor in a closed, inactive conformation (Chrovian et al., 2014; Lee et al., 2023). Additionally, its ability to reduce ex vivo ATP-induced monocyte IL-1β release in healthy volunteers has served as a functional biomarker for target engagement, reinforcing the hypothesis that P2X7 antagonism can modulate inflammasome-driven inflammatory signaling (Chrovian et al., 2014; Lee et al., 2023).  

Expected Effect:  
In the context of dry age-related macular degeneration, the central hypothesis for repurposing AZD9056 is that it will antagonize P2X7 receptors on retinal pigmented epithelium cells, thereby preventing a cascade of ATP-driven pathological events. Elevated extracellular ATP levels have been documented in the vitreous of AMD patients, which suggests a pathological activation of purinergic signaling in the retina (Calzaferri et al., 2020). When ATP activates P2X7 receptors on RPE cells, it leads to two major deleterious outcomes. First, the receptor’s activation results in sustained Ca2+ influx and large pore formation, triggering cytotoxicity and subsequent cell death mechanisms, including apoptotic and inflammasome-dependent cell death pathways (Calzaferri et al., 2020; Gu & Wiley, 2018). Second, P2X7 activation has been mechanistically linked to lysosomal alkalization in RPE cells, which impairs the activity of lysosomal proteases such as cathepsin D; this enzyme is critical for the degradation of photoreceptor outer segments and other cellular debris (Gu & Wiley, 2018; Tempest-Roe, 2017). The hypothesis posits that by blocking P2X7 receptor activation with AZD9056, one would preserve the normal acidic environment of the lysosomes, thereby maintaining or even restoring optimal cathepsin D activity. In turn, these effects are anticipated to protect the RPE from inflammasome-mediated apoptosis and lysosomal dysfunction, which are key drivers of geographic atrophy, the advanced clinical manifestation of dry AMD (Gu & Wiley, 2018; Calzaferri et al., 2020). Preclinical studies support the role of P2X7 in mediating RPE degeneration; for example, genetic knockout of P2X7 in mouse models has been shown to protect against Alu RNA-induced RPE toxicity, an established model of dry AMD pathology (Calzaferri et al., 2020; Gu & Wiley, 2018). Furthermore, in vitro studies using human RPE cell cultures have indicated that P2X7 receptor blockade can reverse lysosomal impairment, suggesting that AZD9056 could produce measurable improvements in functional assays that evaluate lysosomal protease activity, such as cathepsin D activity assays, and overall RPE viability assays (Calzaferri et al., 2020; Tempest-Roe, 2017). Ultimately, if the protective effects seen in preclinical studies translate into the clinical setting, AZD9056 may reduce the accumulation of undigested cellular debris (drusen) and slow or halt the progression of geographic atrophy in patients with dry AMD by dampening the inflamed state and preserving RPE function (Calzaferri et al., 2020; Gu & Wiley, 2018).  

Overall Evaluation:  
From a drug development perspective, the repurposing of AZD9056 for dry AMD presents a compelling but challenging opportunity. One of the primary strengths of this therapeutic candidate lies in its robust mechanistic rationale. The P2X7 receptor plays a central role in mediating ATP-induced inflammasome activation, lysosomal dysfunction, and subsequent RPE cell death—pathophysiological processes that have been repeatedly implicated in dry AMD and geographic atrophy models (Calzaferri et al., 2020; Gu & Wiley, 2018; Tempest-Roe, 2017). The ability of P2X7 antagonists to block these processes has been demonstrated in various in vitro and in vivo models, where blockade of the receptor reduces IL-1β release, reverses lysosomal alkalization, and confers protection against RPE degeneration (Calzaferri et al., 2020; Gu & Wiley, 2018; Tempest-Roe, 2017). Furthermore, AZD9056 has gone through extensive clinical safety evaluations in multiple inflammatory disease indications; its pharmacokinetic profile—characterized by acceptable oral bioavailability and a half-life conducive to once-daily dosing—has been well established in early phase studies (Arulkumaran et al., 2011; Chrovian et al., 2014). This pre-existing clinical safety data is an asset in reducing the risk profile typically associated with novel drug candidates and may streamline early-stage clinical trial designs for an ocular indication. Additionally, preliminary ocular safety assessments in healthy volunteers, which included measures such as retinal electroretinography and visual acuity testing, suggest that systemic administration of AZD9056 does not produce overt ocular toxicity—an encouraging sign for its potential repurposing in dry AMD (Arulkumaran et al., 2011).  

Nevertheless, there are several notable limitations and challenges associated with using AZD9056 in the treatment of dry AMD. First, the prior clinical development history of AZD9056 in rheumatoid arthritis and Crohn’s disease revealed limited or inconsistent efficacy despite demonstrable target engagement. In the phase IIb studies for RA, the compound failed to outperform placebo across objective outcome measures even though safety endpoints were met (Arulkumaran et al., 2011; Chrovian et al., 2014). This raises concerns about whether P2X7 receptor blockade alone is sufficient to generate a meaningful clinical outcome, particularly in a complex and multifactorial disease process such as dry AMD. Moreover, the inflammatory milieu in rheumatoid arthritis or IBD differs significantly from that in the retina, and systemic inflammation may not accurately recapitulate the localized, chronic degenerative processes occurring in the RPE (Arulkumaran et al., 2011; Guile et al., 2009).  

Another concern relates to the dual and sometimes paradoxical roles of the P2X7 receptor. While its pathological activation is linked to pro-inflammatory signaling, P2X7 also appears to have a scavenger or phagocytic function under conditions of low ATP levels (Calzaferri et al., 2020; Newman, 2024). In the context of the RPE, which is specialized for high-volume phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments, complete blockade of P2X7 might inadvertently impair beneficial clearance processes that serve to prevent debris accumulation. In animal models, alternative data has shown that the loss of P2X7 function can result in changes reminiscent of early AMD, such as reduced phagocytosis, suggesting that finely balanced modulation rather than total inhibition may be necessary (Calzaferri et al., 2020; Gu & Wiley, 2018). Such duality underscores the potential risk that while AZD9056 may ameliorate inflammasome activation and lysosomal destabilization, it might simultaneously disrupt physiologic functions of RPE cells that are critical for maintaining retinal homeostasis.  

The lack of direct evidence for AZD9056’s efficacy in ocular models of dry AMD is another major gap. While the preclinical literature supports a role for P2X7 signaling in RPE dysfunction and geographic atrophy (Calzaferri et al., 2020; Tempest-Roe, 2017), the specific application of AZD9056 in these models remains largely inferential. There are no published studies documenting that AZD9056, when administered at doses achieving retinal penetration, effectively preserves cathepsin D activity or prevents RPE cell death in animal models of dry AMD. Furthermore, the translation of systemic pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic data to ocular compartments is nontrivial; disparities in drug distribution, blood–retinal barrier permeability, and local metabolism could limit effective target engagement in the retina even if systemic safety is acceptable (Arulkumaran et al., 2011). The undisclosed chemical structure of AZD9056 also complicates any efforts to optimize the compound specifically for ocular bioavailability or to better understand its off-target profile relative to other P2X7 antagonists that have been more thoroughly characterized in the literature (Chrovian et al., 2014; Gunosewoyo et al., 2007).  

In summary, the overall evaluation of AZD9056 for treatment of dry AMD is one of cautious enthusiasm tempered by several unresolved questions. On the strength side, the compound leverages a clear mechanistic rationale by antagonizing the P2X7 receptor—a key mediator of ATP-induced inflammasome activation and lysosomal dysfunction known to be active in the RPE of AMD patients—and it comes with an established clinical safety record in inflammatory disorders (Calzaferri et al., 2020; Chrovian et al., 2014; Gu & Wiley, 2018). Its ability to suppress IL-1β release in ex vivo assays supports its functional engagement with the P2X7/IL-1β pathway, and preclinical data suggest that P2X7 inhibition can protect against RPE degeneration (Gu & Wiley, 2018; Tempest-Roe, 2017). However, significant challenges persist: prior clinical trials in RA and IBD have yielded mixed efficacy results, casting doubt on whether P2X7 blockade alone can significantly modify disease progression in complex conditions; the potential for interference with beneficial receptor functions in the RPE may compromise its utility; and the lack of direct preclinical data in dry AMD models means that much of the benefit remains theoretical at this stage (Arulkumaran et al., 2011; Chrovian et al., 2014; Gu & Wiley, 2018; Territo & Zarrinmayeh, 2021). Additionally, uncertainties related to ocular pharmacokinetics and the inability to adjust the synthetic structure for improved retinal targeting (given the proprietary nature of the molecule’s chemistry) further complicate its repositioning for an ocular indication (Chrovian et al., 2014; Eser et al., 2015).  

Given the current state of the literature, it would be advisable to conduct targeted preclinical studies that specifically address the effects of AZD9056 on RPE cells and retinal tissue. These studies should include assays for lysosomal pH stability, cathepsin D activity, inflammasome assembly (e.g., NLRP3 activation and caspase-1 processing), and overall RPE cell viability under conditions of ATP stress. Furthermore, careful evaluation of retinal drug levels following systemic dosing—or the development of a topical formulation—might be necessary to ensure that sufficient drug concentrations can be achieved in the retina without systemic toxicity. A parallel investigation into the potential compensatory roles of P2X7 in RPE phagocytosis would also be warranted to minimize any risk of disrupting beneficial cellular functions (Calzaferri et al., 2020; Gu & Wiley, 2018; Arulkumaran et al., 2011).  

Overall, while AZD9056’s strong mechanistic basis and favorable early-phase clinical safety profile make it an attractive candidate for repurposing, the translational challenges and previous clinical setbacks in other indications necessitate rigorous preclinical validation in dry AMD models before further clinical development is considered. The compound’s capacity to specifically maintain lysosomal function and cathepsin D activity in the RPE represents a promising therapeutic opportunity if these effects can be reliably recapitulated in the ocular setting. However, caution is advised due to the dual roles of P2X7 signaling in both pathological and physiologic processes and the potential non-optimal receptor occupancy in the retina. In conclusion, the repurposing of AZD9056 for dry AMD holds potential but would require a focused, mechanistically guided preclinical program to address the unique challenges posed by the ocular environment and the complex biology of the P2X7 receptor (Arulkumaran et al., 2011; Chrovian et al., 2014; Calzaferri et al., 2020; Tempest-Roe, 2017).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
AICAR (5‐aminoimidazole‐4‐carboxamide ribonucleoside), commercially available as Sigma A9978, is a purine nucleoside analogue originally identified as an adenosine-related compound that is taken up into cells via equilibrative nucleoside transporters and then phosphorylated by adenosine kinase into its monophosphorylated form, ZMP (Gruzman et al., 2009; Hardie, 2014). As a prodrug that is converted intracellularly into an AMP mimic, AICAR belongs to the class of adenosine/AMP analogues that have been widely employed as pharmacological tools to activate AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) in vitro and in vivo (Russell & Hardie, 2020; Scudiero et al., 2016). Its discovery as the first pharmacological agent capable of activating AMPK in intact cells set the stage for extensive biochemical studies regarding cellular energy sensing and metabolic regulation (Vara-Ciruelos et al., 2019; Yu et al., 2010). Unlike synthetic small molecules designed solely to bind regulatory subunits of AMPK, AICAR requires intracellular phosphorylation to ZMP—a process that confers a basis in natural purine metabolism as ZMP is an intermediate in de novo purine synthesis—and thereby mimics the endogenous activator AMP (Hardie, 2014; Gruzman et al., 2009). Being a small nucleoside analogue, AICAR is structurally simple compared to some of the more recently developed direct AMPK activators; its well‐delineated chemical structure, mechanism of cellular conversion, and availability from commercial sources make it an attractive candidate for repurposing studies (Drew & Kingwell, 2008; Guerrieri et al., 2017).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, AICAR has been extensively used as a research tool to probe the biology of AMPK, which is central to metabolic regulation, and it has demonstrated efficacy in a wide variety of preclinical models including skeletal muscle, adipocytes, hepatocytes, and specific cancer models (Drew & Kingwell, 2008). Its ability to rapidly be taken up and converted to ZMP in diverse cell types has made it an invaluable reagent for studies of metabolic dysregulation, insulin resistance, and autophagy; investigators have used AICAR in rodent models of diabetes where it has been shown to improve glucose homeostasis and modify lipid metabolism (Russell & Hardie, 2020; Dolinar et al., 2018). Beyond metabolic endpoints, AICAR has been explored in cardiac settings; for example, acadesine (another name for AICAR) has been clinically evaluated for preventing ischemia–reperfusion injury during coronary artery bypass graft surgery, demonstrating its translational potential in acute cardiovascular contexts (Drew & Kingwell, 2008). Despite its extensive use in metabolic and cardiovascular studies as well as experimental cancer models, there is little documented evidence supporting its use in dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) or similar ocular degenerative diseases (Guerrieri et al., 2017; Drew & Kingwell, 2008). However, the underlying rationale of harnessing AMPK activation to improve autophagy and lysosomal clearance in affected retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells provides a logical extension of AICAR’s well‐characterized metabolic activities to the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Honnappa & Kesavan, 2016; Dolinar et al., 2018).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, AICAR functions by entering cells through nucleoside transporters and undergoing phosphorylation by adenosine kinase to yield ZMP, which is structurally analogous to AMP and thus capable of binding to the regulatory Bateman domains of the AMPK γ subunit (Gruzman et al., 2009; Hardie, 2014). Binding of ZMP to AMPK triggers multiple regulatory phenomena, including allosteric activation, promotion of phosphorylation at the critical Thr172 residue on the catalytic α subunit, and protection from dephosphorylation by protein phosphatases, thereby amplifying AMPK’s kinase activity (Russell & Hardie, 2020; Scudiero et al., 2016). Activated AMPK then exerts a plethora of downstream effects: it can suppress anabolic pathways via inhibition of mammalian target of rapamycin complex 1 (mTORC1) and stimulate catabolic pathways, thereby shifting cellular metabolism from energy-consuming biosynthetic processes toward energy-producing autophagy and oxidative processes (Salt & Hardie, 2017; Scudiero et al., 2016). In the context of the proposed therapeutic mechanism for dry AMD, AMPK activation by AICAR is expected to result in the suppression of mTORC1, which in turn relieves inhibitory control over the transcription factor EB (TFEB) (Drew & Kingwell, 2008; Chandrasekaran et al., 2024). TFEB acts as a master regulator of lysosomal gene expression and autophagy by translocating to the nucleus, where it upregulates genes responsible for lysosomal biogenesis, acidification, and hydrolase production; one such enzyme, cathepsin D (CTSD), is critical for effective autophagy clearance (Drew & Kingwell, 2008; Scudiero et al., 2016). This sequence of molecular events—from AICAR uptake, conversion to ZMP, AMPK activation, mTORC1 suppression, and subsequent TFEB activation—forms the mechanistic backbone supporting a therapeutic strategy geared toward enhancing lysosomal acidification and boosting cathepsin D–mediated autophagic clearance (Vara-Ciruelos et al., 2019; Yu et al., 2010). It is important to note that while the mechanism is robust, high intracellular concentrations of ZMP (and therefore high doses of AICAR) may activate other AMP-sensitive enzymes, such as glycogen phosphorylase, which underscores the necessity of titrating doses to achieve a selective AMPK-mediated effect (Russell & Hardie, 2020; Chandrasekaran et al., 2024).

Expected Effect:  
In the proposed application targeting dry AMD, the hypothesis is that AICAR administration will mimic the natural actions of AMP within RPE cells by robustly activating AMPK (Gruzman et al., 2009; Scudiero et al., 2016). In turn, this activation is expected to suppress mTORC1 activity—a key negative regulator of autophagy—and facilitate the nuclear translocation of TFEB, leading to the upregulation of lysosomal and autophagy-related genes including those encoding for cathepsin D (Drew & Kingwell, 2008; Chandrasekaran et al., 2024). In retinal pigment epithelium culture models, preliminary observations have indicated that treatment with AICAR enhances LC3 flux (a marker of autophagic activity) and increases cathepsin D activity, implying an improved capacity for autophagic clearance (Guerrieri et al., 2017; Vara-Ciruelos et al., 2019). Given that dry AMD is characterized by the accumulation of extracellular deposits (drusen) and cellular debris due to insufficient lysosomal clearance and impaired autophagy, the anticipated effect of AICAR would be to restore lysosomal functionality and promote the degradation of these pathogenic substrates (Honnappa & Kesavan, 2016; Drew & Kingwell, 2008). Furthermore, it is known from previous studies that AMPK activation can lead to enhanced mitochondrial quality control and an overall improvement in cellular metabolic homeostasis; in the context of RPE cells, this could translate to better cell survival and resilience against the oxidative stress associated with chronic degenerative processes in dry AMD (Chandrasekaran et al., 2024; Drew & Kingwell, 2008).
