Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
SB216763 is a synthetic small‐molecule inhibitor originally discovered during GlaxoSmithKline’s dedicated program in developing GSK-3 inhibitors. It belongs to the bisarylmaleimide class of compounds, with its chemical structure based on a pyrrole-2,5-dione core that is further substituted by aryl and indole moieties. In its initial characterization, SB216763 was identified as an ATP-competitive inhibitor of glycogen synthase kinase 3 beta (GSK3β), a central serine/threonine protein kinase implicated in multiple intracellular signaling cascades. The chemical class to which SB216763 belongs – maleimides – has been widely exploited across medicinal chemistry due to their synthetic tractability and ability to serve as potent inhibitors of enzymes, particularly kinases. This group of compounds has previously been used in various preclinical studies targeting neurodegenerative diseases and cell proliferative disorders by modulating cell signaling pathways such as the Wnt/β-catenin cascade, which is ubiquitously expressed in many tissues including the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and the central nervous system (Gianferrara et al., 2022; Ruiz & Eldar-Finkelman, 2022; Alhassan et al., 2025).

Therapeutic History:  
SB216763 has a well-established history in preclinical research, particularly in models of neurodegeneration. Several studies have deployed this compound in rodent models of Alzheimer’s disease, Parkinson’s disease, and other neurological insults to demonstrate its neuroprotective potential. In these models, SB216763 was shown to reduce tau hyperphosphorylation, protect neurons against both β-amyloid-mediated toxicity and radiation-induced apoptosis in hippocampal neurons, and promote beneficial modulation of signaling pathways linked to PI3K–Akt (Gianferrara et al., 2022; Ruiz & Eldar-Finkelman, 2022). Beyond its neuroprotective effects, SB216763 has been applied as a tool compound in cellular studies to activate canonical Wnt signaling through stabilization of beta-catenin by inhibiting GSK3β. Importantly, a radiolabeled derivative, [11C]SB216763, has been developed as a positron emission tomography (PET) probe, which confirmed its ability to cross the blood–brain barrier in rodent and nonhuman primate models, although significant selectivity issues have been noted with respect to off-target kinase inhibition (Gianferrara et al., 2022; Benn & Dawson, 2020). In addition, there is documented evidence of its application in ocular contexts; for instance, in an experimental ischemic retinal neuron model in rats, SB216763 was found to promote DNA repair by upregulating DNA ligase IV transcriptional activity. However, while it has been evaluated extensively in neurological and in vivo rodent models for central nervous system diseases, formal clinical deployment or veterinary studies specifically targeting dry age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD) remain sparse, with no documented clinical trials registered on major platforms dedicated to AMD indications (Gianferrara et al., 2022; Ruiz & Eldar-Finkelman, 2022; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).

Mechanism of Action:  
The primary mechanism of action of SB216763 is centered on its potent inhibition of GSK3β. Under normal physiological conditions, GSK3β is a constitutively active kinase that phosphorylates a wide array of substrates, including beta-catenin, tau, and proteins critical to cellular metabolism and survival. One key substrate relevant to our hypothesis is the transcription factor EB (TFEB), a master regulator of the Coordinated Lysosomal Expression and Regulation (CLEAR) gene network. TFEB’s activity is tightly regulated by its phosphorylation state; when phosphorylated by kinases such as mTORC1 and possibly GSK3β, TFEB binds to cytosolic 14-3-3 proteins and is retained in the cytoplasm. Inhibition of GSK3β by SB216763 has been implicated in the dephosphorylation of TFEB, thereby allowing its translocation to the nucleus where it drives the transcription of CLEAR network genes. These genes are essential for lysosomal biogenesis, autophagic flux, and the expression of lysosomal proteases such as cathepsin D (Gianferrara et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2023). Detailed molecular studies in neuronal stem cells and N2a cells have demonstrated that SB216763 can inactivate GSK3β and thereby stimulate the nuclear accumulation of TFEB. In addition, the compound’s ATP-competitive mode of inhibition suggests it directly competes with ATP in the GSK3β active site, leading to rapid modulation of downstream substrates implicated in metabolic and autophagic processes (Gianferrara et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2023; Djajadikerta et al., 2020). From a biochemical standpoint, SB216763’s action not only stabilizes beta-catenin – thereby modulating Wnt signaling – but also appears to influence key regulatory nodes in autophagy. Activation of TFEB results in upregulation of lysosomal proteins, enhancement of lysosomal acidification via increased expression of components like the vacuolar-type ATPase (V-ATPase), and improved cathepsin D maturation and activity, all of which collectively promote the efficient clearance of intracellular aggregates and damaged organelles (Gianferrara et al., 2022; Ruiz & Eldar-Finkelman, 2022; Pan & Valapala, 2022).

Expected Effect in Dry AMD Context:  
The central hypothesis behind repurposing SB216763 for dry AMD rests on its ability to correct the cellular deficits observed in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) associated with aging and disease. Dry AMD is characterized by the accumulation of lipofuscin and other aggregate-prone materials within the RPE, coupled with impaired autophagic and lysosomal clearance mechanisms. The proposed pharmacological intervention with SB216763 is expected to inhibit GSK3β in RPE cells, leading to dephosphorylation and nuclear translocation of TFEB. Once in the nucleus, TFEB can activate the CLEAR network, thereby augmenting lysosome biogenesis and catalytic function. Enhanced lysosomal acidification, as mediated by the V-ATPase and corroborated by increased expression of lysosomal enzymes such as cathepsin D, should facilitate the degradation of accumulated lipofuscin, oxidized proteins, and lipid aggregates. In preclinical RPE models under oxidative stress, similar pharmacological modulation of TFEB (for example, via trehalose treatment or genetic induction) has been shown to improve lysosomal function and reduce the burden of autofluorescent granules analogous to lipofuscin (Falcão et al., 2025; Falcão et al., 2024). Therefore, SB216763 is hypothesized to recapitulate these beneficial effects by leveraging its upstream modulation of GSK3β. Given that RPE cells naturally express both GSK3β and TFEB, and considering the documented mechanistic role of GSK3β in regulating TFEB nucleo-cytoplasmic shuttling, the expected outcome is an enhancement of autophagic clearance and restoration of RPE homeostasis. This would theoretically slow or potentially reverse early degenerative changes in dry AMD by mitigating the cytotoxic accumulation of undegraded material (Gianferrara et al., 2022; Ruiz & Eldar-Finkelman, 2022; Yang et al., 2023).

Overall Evaluation:  
SB216763 exhibits several promising attributes as a candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry AMD. One major strength lies in its well-characterized and potent inhibition of GSK3β – a kinase that plays a central role in various signaling pathways implicated in both neurodegeneration and retinal pathology. The mechanistic rationale is underpinned by evidence that GSK3β inhibition facilitates the nuclear translocation of TFEB, the master regulator of lysosomal function. Through activation of TFEB, SB216763 can potentially stimulate the expression of the CLEAR gene network, leading to heightened lysosomal acidification and increased cathepsin D activity. These molecular events are directly relevant to mitigating the defective autophagic clearance that is a hallmark of dry AMD, and they align well with preclinical observations in other cell types where TFEB activation has been associated with improved degradation of accumulated toxic material (Gianferrara et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2023; Djajadikerta et al., 2020).

Further strengths include the extensive use of SB216763 in various preclinical models of neurodegeneration, wherein its ability to modulate key pathways such as beta-catenin/Wnt signaling has been repeatedly demonstrated. Its blood–brain barrier penetrance, as seen in rodent and nonhuman primate studies involving a radiolabeled derivative, suggests favorable pharmacokinetics that might also translate to ocular tissues with appropriate formulation strategies. The documented ocular application in rodent ischemic retinal neuron models – where SB216763 was shown to upregulate DNA repair mechanisms – provides additional indirect support for its potential in the ocular setting (Gianferrara et al., 2022).

Notwithstanding these promising aspects, there are notable weaknesses and gaps in the literature that warrant cautious interpretation. First, while preclinical evidence in neural and other cellular models supports the concept that GSK3β inhibition can drive TFEB-dependent transcriptional activation, direct evidence of SB216763’s efficacy in RPE cells under conditions of oxidative stress or in established dry AMD models is sparse. There is a lack of comprehensive studies that definitively link SB216763 treatment in RPE cells to enhanced lysosomal acidification, increased cathepsin D activity, and consequent reduction in lipofuscin accumulation. For example, while related studies using trehalose or mTOR inhibitors have shown clear benefits on TFEB activation and autophagic clearance in RPE models (Falcão et al., 2025; Falcão et al., 2024), SB216763-specific data in this context remain limited. 

Furthermore, concerns regarding kinase selectivity must be acknowledged. SB216763, being an ATP-competitive inhibitor, may exhibit off-target effects by inhibiting structurally related kinases, as indicated by the limited selectivity noted in studies involving its radiolabeled derivative [11C]SB216763 (Gianferrara et al., 2022; Benn & Dawson, 2020; Pan & Valapala, 2021). Off-target kinase inhibition could potentially disrupt other essential signaling pathways in the RPE and might lead to unforeseen adverse events upon clinical translation. This issue of specificity is particularly important in the context of chronic diseases like dry AMD, where long-term safety is paramount. 

Additionally, while its use in central nervous system models is encouraging, dry AMD pathophysiology has distinct features that may not be fully addressed by a therapeutic designed for neurodegeneration. The multifactorial etiology of dry AMD, which encompasses oxidative stress, chronic inflammation, and impaired autophagic degradation specific to the high metabolic and phagocytic demands of RPE cells, underscores the need for targeted evidence that SB216763 exerts its effects in these specialized cells. In summary, SB216763 is a compelling candidate from a mechanistic standpoint, with a robust preclinical pedigree as a GSK3β inhibitor that can modulate TFEB and downstream lysosomal functions. Its synthetic origin as a bisarylmaleimide and proven in vitro potency provide a strong rationale for its repurposing. The proposed mechanism—wherein inhibition of GSK3β leads to enhanced nuclear localization of TFEB, activation of CLEAR genes, improved lysosomal acidification, and increased cathepsin D activity—directly addresses key pathogenic features of dry AMD, including the accumulation of lipofuscin and defective autophagy in RPE cells. This mechanistic alignment, supported by studies across neurodegenerative disease models and early ocular research, indicates that SB216763 has the potential to restore defective autophagic clearance in the RPE and slow AMD progression (Gianferrara et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2023; Djajadikerta et al., 2020).

Nonetheless, the overall success of SB216763 in the context of dry AMD will depend on addressing several critical issues. First, direct experimental validation in RPE cells exposed to oxidative stress is needed to confirm that SB216763 can indeed induce TFEB nuclear translocation and activate the CLEAR network in this specific cell type. Second, detailed pharmacokinetic and safety studies tailored for ocular administration are essential to determine whether the compound can reach effective concentrations in the retina without eliciting systemic toxicity or off-target kinase inhibition. Third, comprehensive in vivo studies in relevant animal models of dry AMD must be conducted to assess whether the biochemical improvements (e.g., enhanced lysosomal acidification and cathepsin D activity) translate into clinically meaningful outcomes, such as reduction in lipofuscin accumulation and preservation of RPE morphology and function.

Finally, while the theoretical framework is strong, the translational gap remains significant. The absence of clinical trials or robust preclinical data directly linking SB216763 to improvements in dry AMD phenotypes suggests that careful, incremental studies are required. These studies should ideally include dose–response evaluations, biomarker analyses of autophagic flux, and long-term safety assessments to establish the therapeutic window for SB216763 in the context of retinal disease (Ruiz & Eldar-Finkelman, 2022; Gianferrara et al., 2022; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).

Overall, SB216763 represents a promising mechanistic candidate whose ability to modulate GSK3β and, consequently, regulate TFEB activity offers a novel angle for addressing the autophagic deficits observed in dry AMD. Its well-defined synthetic origin, established preclinical usage in neurodegeneration, and documented biochemical effects in activating lysosomal and autophagic pathways suggest that it could, in principle, improve RPE function through enhanced clearance of toxic intracellular aggregates. However, the limitations regarding its selectivity, the need for targeted ocular studies, and the paucity of direct evidence in AMD models require that further rigorous investigations be conducted. A stepwise preclinical evaluation, starting with in vitro RPE models and advancing to in vivo AMD models, would be necessary to validate its efficacy and safety profile before considering clinical translation. In this regard, SB216763 should be advanced as a high-priority candidate for additional mechanistic studies and exploratory preclinical evaluations, albeit with cautious optimism given the potential for off-target effects and formulation challenges (Gianferrara et al., 2022; Ruiz & Eldar-Finkelman, 2022; Yang et al., 2023; Djajadikerta et al., 2020; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).

In conclusion, while SB216763 offers a robust mechanistic rationale for its repurposing in dry AMD based on its known capacity to inhibit GSK3β, promote TFEB-mediated lysosomal biogenesis, and potentially enhance autophagic clearance, careful attention must be paid to validating these effects directly in RPE cells under oxidative stress. The strengths of its preclinical performance and synthetic availability must be balanced against the challenges of kinase selectivity, ocular pharmacokinetics, and the absence of direct AMD-specific data. A systematic, comprehensive series of studies is warranted to firmly establish whether SB216763 can serve as a viable therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. The outcomes of these studies will significantly influence the strategic direction of the drug development program and may open the door to novel, mechanism-based interventions for a disease with substantial unmet clinical need (Gianferrara et al., 2022; Ruiz & Eldar-Finkelman, 2022; Yang et al., 2023; Djajadikerta et al., 2020; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).

Below is our comprehensive evaluation of SB290157 as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD), with a focus on its chemical origin, its therapeutic history, the detailed mechanism of action at the molecular level, the expected pharmacological effects in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) models, and an overall assessment of strengths and weaknesses.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
SB290157 is a fully synthetic, nonpeptidic small‐molecule agent originally discovered as a selective antagonist of the complement anaphylatoxin C3a receptor (C3aR). Chemically, it is defined as N2-[(2,2-diphenylethoxy)acetyl]-L-arginine and was identified via high-throughput screening of chemical libraries using membranes from cells stably expressing human C3aR, such as RBL-2H3 cells (Ames et al., 2001). The lead compound was chemically optimized from an initial hit (SKF 63649) to improve affinity and potency, and its synthesis has been well described using peptide–like solid‐phase synthetic strategies (e.g., Fmoc protecting group chemistry on Wang resin) thereby yielding a compound with high purity (≥95%) and reproducible physicochemical properties (Ames et al., 2001). SB290157 belongs to a class of compounds that modulate G protein–coupled receptors (GPCRs), in this case a complement receptor, and similar nonpeptidic small‐molecule ligands have been employed in preclinical studies to probe inflammatory pathways in various disease states (Iyer et al., 2017; Ames et al., 2001). Its discovery set an important precedent for the therapeutic targeting of complement receptors, especially given the historical absence of potent, selective C3aR antagonists, and it has been widely used as a research tool in animal models and cell-based assays to interrogate the physiological roles of C3a/C3aR signaling (Ames et al., 2001).

Therapeutic History:  
SB290157 has been extensively employed in preclinical models to examine the role of C3aR in inflammation and immune modulation. In early studies, it was shown to antagonize C3a-induced intracellular calcium mobilization and receptor internalization in RBL-2H3 cells and human neutrophils, with reported IC50 values in the low-nanomolar range (approximately 27–30 nM), suggesting robust antagonism under defined experimental conditions (Ames et al., 2001). In vivo, SB290157 demonstrated antiinflammatory efficacy by reducing neutrophil recruitment in guinea pig models of lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-induced airway neutrophilia and by decreasing paw edema in rat adjuvant-induced arthritis models through intraperitoneal dosing (Ames et al., 2001). Although valuable as a pharmacological probe, its history is mired by concerns as several subsequent investigations indicated that SB290157 can exhibit partial agonist activity—depending on the assay system and receptor expression context—and even engage an off-target complement receptor, C5aR2, to induce β-arrestin recruitment (Coulthard, 2015; Li et al., 2021; Mathieu et al., 2005). With more than 70 publications referencing its use, SB290157 remains one of the most commonly used C3aR inhibitors; however, it is essentially confined to the research arena and has never reached clinical development for AMD or other indications (Li et al., 2021).  
There is emerging evidence in ophthalmologic research relevant to dry AMD. For example, an in vitro human fetal RPE cell model has shown that complement fragment C3a can drive the formation of sub-retinal pigment epithelium deposits via dysregulation of the ubiquitin proteasome pathway; importantly, co-application of SB290157 with recombinant C3a in these cultures prevented the abnormal deposit formation, suggesting that C3aR blockade can modulate key pathological events relevant to AMD pathogenesis (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). Despite this promising mechanistic link, SB290157 itself has not been advanced clinically, and its use in retinal models remains primarily exploratory. Moreover, the existence of antagonistic and agonistic properties in various assay systems necessitates careful interpretation of its efficacy when contemplating the translation to human ocular diseases (Iyer et al., 2017; Li et al., 2021).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, SB290157 has been characterized as a competitive antagonist that binds to the orthosteric site of the C3a receptor, thereby inhibiting the native ligand, C3a, from eliciting its downstream signaling responses. In classic radioligand binding assays using 125I-labeled C3a, SB290157 displaces the radiolabeled peptide with an IC50 of ~200 nM, indicating it competes effectively with C3a (Ames et al., 2001). Functionally, this displacement correlates with inhibition of C3a-induced intracellular calcium mobilization, a key second messenger response mediated via G-protein coupling to pertussis-toxin–sensitive Gi/o proteins (Ames et al., 2001). Additionally, SB290157 has been shown to block C3a-mediated receptor internalization in immune cells, further supporting its role in antagonizing C3aR activation (Ames et al., 2001; Iyer et al., 2017).  
Beyond the canonical receptor blockade, several studies have pointed out that SB290157’s activity is highly context-dependent. In systems where C3aR is overexpressed—such as recombinant CHO or transfected RBL cells—SB290157 can paradoxically act as an agonist to trigger intracellular signaling cascades like ERK phosphorylation, potentially due to rapid receptor desensitization or kinetic differences in ligand-receptor interaction (Coulthard, 2015; Li et al., 2021; Mathieu et al., 2005). Moreover, its off-target partial agonism at the closely related receptor C5aR2 has been documented, wherein it mediates β-arrestin recruitment at higher concentrations, thereby dampening C5a-induced ERK signaling in primary macrophages (Li et al., 2021; Mathieu et al., 2005). Such dual or biased pharmacological properties underscore that SB290157’s molecular actions cannot be solely categorized as pure antagonism without considering assay conditions and cell contexts (Li et al., 2021; Mathieu et al., 2005).  
In the context of RPE cells, C3a binding to C3aR is hypothesized to disrupt intracellular calcium homeostasis, leading to lysosomal alkalinization—a key factor that impairs the maturation and proteolytic activity of lysosomal enzymes such as cathepsin D (CTSD). Cathepsin D is critical for proper turnover of extracellular matrix (ECM) components and degradation of proteinaceous aggregates; its dysfunction is implicated in drusen formation, a hallmark of dry AMD (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). By competitively inhibiting C3a binding, SB290157 is expected to mitigate abnormal Ca2+ signaling, maintain lysosomal acidification, and therefore preserve CTSD processing and activity, which in turn would prevent or lessen the accumulation of drusen-like deposits (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018; Iyer et al., 2017). This proposed mechanism is supported by the observation that in hfRPE cultures, SB290157 co-application with C3a prevented both the upregulation of C3aR expression and the subsequent deposition of abnormal ECM structures (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). Nonetheless, the precise molecular interactions at the receptor—the positioning of the diphenylethoxy moiety and arginine side chain—is critical for binding affinity and selectivity (Iyer et al., 2017; Mishra et al., 2025), and minor alterations in these interactions might contribute to the observed functional variability.

Expected Effect:  
Based on the hypothesis for dry AMD, SB290157 is expected to act on RPE cells by antagonizing the C3aR, thereby preventing the cascade of intracellular events that lead to lysosomal stress. In a typical RPE culture assay where C3a is exogenously added—thereby simulating enhanced complement activity as observed in AMD—SB290157 should block C3a binding, which would normally result in the perturbation of lysosomal pH homeostasis. The blockade of this receptor is envisaged to preserve the normally acidic lysosomal environment required for the optimal maturation and proteolytic function of cathepsin D (CTSD), an enzyme whose dysfunction is implicated in the formation of drusen and the progression of dry AMD (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018; Iyer et al., 2017).  
Furthermore, by preserving lysosomal function, SB290157 is expected to reduce subsequent activation of the inflammasome—a multi-protein complex that is triggered when lysosomal destabilization occurs—and thus attenuate the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-1β. This cascade is particularly relevant because chronic inflammation is thought to drive many of the degenerative changes associated with AMD (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). In vitro, RPE cells pre-treated with SB290157 before C3a challenge would be anticipated to maintain normal lysosomal acidity (measured by appropriate pH-sensitive dyes), exhibit proper CTSD processing (as observed by Western blot analysis for mature cathepsin D forms), and display reduced markers of inflammasome activation such as caspase-1 cleavage and IL-1β release. Gene expression studies in these cells might also reveal normalized levels of key ECM components and proteases, ultimately leading to a reduction in sub-RPE deposit accumulation (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018).  
It is important to note that C3aR is expressed on RPE cells and its activation has been implicated in additional downstream effects—including modulation of the ubiquitin proteasome pathway and extracellular matrix turnover—which further contribute to cell dysfunction and deposit formation. Therefore, antagonism of C3aR by SB290157, if effective and selective, could theoretically interrupt this pathogenic cascade and offer a protective effect against drusen-mediated RPE degeneration in dry AMD (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018; Ames et al., 2001).

Overall Evaluation:  
SB290157 offers a compelling mechanistic rationale for repurposing in dry AMD given the central role of complement dysregulation in the pathogenesis of the disease. Among its strengths is a well-documented ability to block C3a-induced signaling events across multiple preclinical models. Early characterizations demonstrated that SB290157 effectively inhibited intracellular Ca2+ mobilization, receptor internalization, and other pro-inflammatory events in both immune cells and engineered cell systems (Ames et al., 2001). Its application in an hfRPE model demonstrated that C3a-induced sub-RPE deposit formation can be reversed upon treatment with SB290157, underscoring its potential utility in preventing one of the critical pathological features of dry AMD (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). Furthermore, the known rodent tolerability and defined in vivo pharmacokinetics observed in other disease models—such as LPS-induced airway inflammation and adjuvant-induced arthritis—support the concept that SB290157 can be delivered systemically with demonstrable pharmacodynamic effects (Ames et al., 2001).  

However, several weaknesses temper enthusiasm for immediate clinical translation. A significant concern is the compound’s context-dependent pharmacology. Multiple studies have reported that SB290157 can function as a partial or even full agonist under certain conditions, particularly in overexpression systems, and paradoxically activate C3aR instead of inhibiting it (Coulthard, 2015; Li et al., 2021; Mathieu et al., 2005). Such functional divergence is critical when considering a therapy designed to block a deleterious signal in a delicate tissue such as the retina. Moreover, SB290157 has been shown to exhibit off-target effects, including partial agonism at C5aR2—a related complement receptor—which may confound downstream anti-inflammatory responses and produce unintended biological effects (Li et al., 2021; Mathieu et al., 2005).  
Additionally, while there is evidence of efficacy in non-ocular models and even in an hfRPE culture system, there is a paucity of robust in vivo data specifically demonstrating efficacy in ocular or AMD preclinical models. Modern translational approaches demand rigorous evaluation of pharmacokinetics, tissue penetration, ocular tolerability, and local off-target activity in the complex microenvironment of the eye—data that remain limited for SB290157 in the AMD setting (Iyer et al., 2017; Li et al., 2021). Furthermore, owing to its reputation as a “controversial” tool compound, some in the field recommend the use of complementary genetic models (e.g., C3aR knockout mice) to validate findings derived from its use (Coulthard, 2015; Li et al., 2021). This underscores the need for next-generation C3aR antagonists with improved selectivity and a more predictable pharmacodynamic profile if the goal is clinical translation for dry AMD.  

In summary, SB290157 has strong theoretical appeal as a means to interrupt a pathological complement cascade that leads to lysosomal dysfunction, impaired CTSD maturation, and ultimately drusen formation in dry AMD. Its prior use in various inflammatory and in vitro RPE models, along with the biochemistry linking C3aR activation to intracellular Ca2+ dysregulation and lysosomal stress, supports the hypothesis that C3aR blockade may be beneficial in preserving RPE function (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018; Iyer et al., 2017). Nonetheless, the intrinsic limitations of SB290157—including its potential for agonistic behavior, off-target C5aR2 activity, and inconsistent effects across different cellular contexts—present significant challenges that must be addressed prior to advancing this candidate into clinical trials for AMD (Ames et al., 2001; Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018; Li et al., 2021).

Overall Evaluation:  
In conclusion, SB290157 is a well-characterized research tool with documented efficacy in blocking complement-mediated inflammatory responses in several animal models as well as in an hfRPE culture system, making it a promising candidate to test the hypothesis that C3aR blockade can prevent lysosomal alkalinization and CTSD dysfunction in dry AMD. Its strengths include a defined mechanism of competitive antagonism at C3aR, cross-species activity, and experimentally demonstrated protective effects against abnormal sub-RPE deposit formation. However, its context-dependent agonist behavior and off-target activation of C5aR2 raise significant concerns about its selectivity and reliability as a clinical therapeutic. Additionally, the limited data regarding ocular pharmacokinetics and direct efficacy in robust in vivo dry AMD models suggest that further validation is required. Thus, while the underlying rationale for targeting complement-mediated lysosomal dysfunction remains compelling, SB290157 is best viewed as a stepping stone toward the development of next-generation C3aR antagonists with improved pharmacological profiles for potential clinical application in dry AMD (Ames et al., 2001; Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018; Li et al., 2021).

Historically, BAY 11-7082 has been utilized extensively in biochemical, cellular, and animal studies as an anti-inflammatory agent. Initial applications centered on its ability to block the phosphorylation and degradation of IκBα, thereby inhibiting downstream NF-κB–driven gene expression. This mechanism was exploited in models of endothelial inflammation and various cancer cell lines, including studies showing potent anticancer, neuroprotective, and anti-inflammatory effects (Lee et al., 2012; Melisi & Chiao, 2007). Furthermore, its repurposing has been explored in fields as diverse as hematologic malignancies, diabetes-related complications, and preclinical psoriasis models, where it served as a dual inhibitor of NF-κB and the NLRP3 inflammasome (Irrera et al., 2017; Kolati et al., 2015). Despite this broad research history, BAY 11-7082 has not been previously tested explicitly in the context of dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or diseases with a similar pathology in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE). However, its known capacity to reduce inflammatory cytokine production and preserve lysosomal integrity in nonocular cell types provides a rationale for evaluating its potential utility in dry AMD—a disease characterized by chronic inflammation, impaired lysosomal clearance, and inflammasome activation (Blevins et al., 2022; Irrera et al., 2017; Marchetti, 2019).

Mechanism of Action:  
BAY 11-7082 exerts its pharmacological effects predominantly through irreversible covalent inhibition. Its most well‐characterized mechanism is the blockade of NF-κB signaling by preventing the phosphorylation of the inhibitory protein IκBα. Under normal conditions, phosphorylation of IκBα triggers its degradation, thus allowing NF-κB (typically the p65/p50 heterodimer) to translocate into the nucleus and activate pro-inflammatory target genes. By inhibiting IκBα phosphorylation, BAY 11-7082 effectively sequesters NF-κB in the cytosol, thereby suppressing the expression of genes associated with inflammation such as IL-1β, TNF-α, and various chemokines (Marchetti, 2019; Melisi & Chiao, 2007).  

Moreover, BAY 11-7082 has been repurposed based on its ability to inhibit the NLRP3 inflammasome. Mechanistically, the compound forms covalent adducts with reactive cysteine residues on the NLRP3 protein, most likely within the ATPase domain—an essential activity domain required for inflammasome activation. This alkylation event, which proceeds via a Michael-type addition reaction, results in irreversible inactivation of NLRP3’s ATPase function, thereby preventing the assembly and subsequent activation of the inflammasome complex (Cocco et al., 2014; Juliana et al., 2010; Marchetti, 2019). In addition to these primary actions, BAY 11-7082 has been reported to inhibit other cysteine-dependent enzymes such as protein tyrosine phosphatases and even components like gasdermin D that contribute to pyroptosis. Consequently, the compound displays a broad-spectrum inhibitory profile that may diminish inflammatory cascades not only at the transcriptional (NF-κB) level but also at the inflammasome activation stage (Yu et al., 2018; Zahid et al., 2019).  

Expected Effect in Dry Age-Related Macular Degeneration:  
In the context of dry AMD, the hypothesis is that chronic inflammation in the RPE drives cellular dysfunction through mechanisms that include sustained NF-κB activation and priming of the NLRP3 inflammasome. Inflammatory cytokines and resultant oxidative stress contribute to lysosomal impairment, reducing the activity of v-ATPase and lysosomal proteases such as cathepsin D (CTSD), which are crucial for the clearance of cellular debris. BAY 11-7082 is expected to intervene at an early stage in this inflammatory cascade by inhibiting NF-κB signaling. In doing so, it would reduce the transcriptional upregulation of inflammasome components and pro-inflammatory cytokines, particularly IL-1β, a key mediator in inflammasome activation (Blevins et al., 2022; Marchetti, 2019).  

Experimental studies in macrophages and psoriasis models have demonstrated that NF-κB inhibition with BAY 11-7082 leads to a reduction in IL-1β production and preserves lysosomal integrity. Although these studies were conducted in nonocular tissues, the expression of NF-κB and NLRP3 inflammasome components in RPE cells is well-documented in the literature. Therefore, it is reasonable to propose that BAY 11-7082, when applied to RPE cell models, could diminish the priming of the NLRP3 inflammasome. This reduction in inflammasome activity is expected to mitigate downstream lysosomal damage, preserve v-ATPase function, and maintain cathepsin D–mediated clearance. Ultimately, these cellular improvements could slow the degenerative progression characteristic of dry AMD (Cocco et al., 2014; Irrera et al., 2017).  

The proposed testing strategy leverages the rapid on–off pharmacology observed in cell culture models, facilitating dose optimization to achieve sufficient anti-inflammatory activity while minimizing potential toxicity. Importantly, targeting an upstream event, namely NF-κB activation and inflammasome priming, distinguishes BAY 11-7082 from therapeutic strategies that focus on downstream caspase inhibition. In retinal cells, preservation of lysosomal function is critical; thus, preventing inflammasome-triggered lysosomal rupture could have a marked protective effect on RPE health (Ajetunmobi et al., 2023; Zahid et al., 2019).

Overall Evaluation:  
BAY 11-7082 presents a compelling therapeutic candidate for dry AMD based on its dual mechanism of action. One of its primary strengths is that it targets two key upstream pathways—inhibition of NF-κB signaling and direct inactivation of the NLRP3 inflammasome—which are critically implicated in the inflammatory processes that drive RPE dysfunction and subsequent retinal degeneration in dry AMD. This upstream intervention could, in theory, reduce the chronic production of pro-inflammatory cytokines and prevent lysosomal abnormalities that compromise the clearance of metabolic waste in RPE cells. The promising preclinical data from psoriasis, diabetic nephropathy, and other inflammatory disease models provide an encouraging foundation regarding its anti-inflammatory capacity (Blevins et al., 2022; Irrera et al., 2017; Marchetti, 2019).

However, there are several potential weaknesses and challenges to consider. First, BAY 11-7082 operates via irreversible covalent binding through its Michael acceptor; while this can yield sustained inhibition, it also raises significant concerns regarding off-target effects and general toxicity due to the potential for nonselective alkylation of other cysteine-containing proteins. Such promiscuous reactivity has been observed in studies involving diverse cell types, and cellular toxicity in contexts such as platelets or myeloma cells has been reported, albeit at higher concentrations (Coles et al., 2021; Paul et al., 2017; Rauert-Wunderlich et al., 2013). Second, although extensive preclinical data exist demonstrating its anti-inflammatory and anti-cancer activity, BAY 11-7082 has not been previously evaluated in ocular tissues. The unique physiology of the eye, particularly the retinal pigment epithelium, could result in significantly different pharmacokinetics and tissue-specific toxicity profiles. The documented rapid on–off pharmacology in cell culture is encouraging, yet extrapolation to an in vivo retinal environment must be approached cautiously (Paul et al., 2017; Zahid et al., 2019).  

Another consideration is the narrow therapeutic window that may exist; while doses in animal models have been optimized for systemic inflammation or cancer, achieving effective local concentrations in the RPE without compromising cell viability is a delicate balance. Previous studies in nonocular systems suggest that BAY 11-7082 can function without overt toxicity at concentrations up to 20 μM in cell culture and 20 mg/kg/day in animal models, but whether similar dosing regimens would be applicable for ocular delivery remains to be determined (Mabuchi et al., 2004; Paul et al., 2017). Additionally, because BAY 11-7082 modulates ubiquitin system components beyond NF-κB and NLRP3 inflammasome targets, there is a risk of unintended interference with normal protein turnover and cellular homeostasis, potentially exacerbating cellular stress in a tissue already vulnerable to degenerative processes, as seen in dry AMD (Coles et al., 2021; Strickson et al., 2013).

In summary, BAY 11-7082 shows promise as a candidate repurposed for dry AMD because it strategically targets early inflammatory events that have been implicated in RPE dysfunction, including NF-κB–mediated inflammasome priming and consequent lysosomal impairment. The compound’s established anti-inflammatory effects in various preclinical models lend strong support to the hypothesis that its use in RPE could preserve lysosomal function and enhance CTSD-mediated clearance. Nonetheless, the inherent risks associated with its covalent, irreversible mechanism demand rigorous ocular-specific toxicity and pharmacokinetics investigations. If dose optimization and targeted delivery—perhaps through localized ocular formulations—can mitigate off-target effects, BAY 11-7082 might offer a novel approach that differentiates itself from therapies focused solely on downstream caspase inhibition. Overall, while the repurposing of BAY 11-7082 for dry AMD is mechanistically attractive and supported by a broad preclinical research history in nonocular inflammatory models (Blevins et al., 2022; Irrera et al., 2017; Marchetti, 2019), further dedicated studies in retinal cell models and in vivo ocular systems are essential to fully validate its potential and safety profile for this indication.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Sulforaphane (SFN) is a naturally occurring isothiocyanate derived from glucoraphanin in cruciferous vegetables via myrosinase-mediated hydrolysis; as an electrophilic small molecule, SFN was identified through its unusually potent induction of phase II detoxification enzymes and antioxidant defenses in mammalian tissues via the KEAP1–NFE2L2/NRF2 stress-response axis (classically termed “phase 2 induction”) (Qin, 2007; Hyttinen et al., 2019). Isothiocyanates and related electrophiles covalently modify reactive cysteine residues on KEAP1, disrupting the KEAP1–NRF2 “hinge-and-latch” ubiquitin ligase complex and stabilizing NRF2 to drive ARE-dependent transcription of cytoprotective enzymes including NQO1, GCLM, HO-1, and glutathione pathway genes (Hyttinen et al., 2019; Qin, 2007). Beyond canonical NRF2 activation, SFN is now recognized to engage lysosome-centered adaptive transcription by inducing nuclear translocation and activation of TFEB/TFE3 through a mild, ROS-triggered Ca²⁺–calcineurin pathway that is largely MTOR-independent, thereby upregulating CLEAR-network genes controlling lysosome and autophagy biogenesis (Li et al., 2021). In ocular contexts, SFN has been used experimentally as a cytoprotective agent in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) models subjected to oxidative or phototoxic stress, and as a modulator of autophagy markers, situating SFN within a dual-modality class that can activate antioxidant defenses and augment lysosome-autophagy function (Yang et al., 2021; Li et al., 2021).

Therapeutic History  
SFN and other NRF2 activators have been widely studied as cytoprotective chemopreventive agents and as protectants in oxidative-stress paradigms across tissues; in RPE models, SFN has repeatedly demonstrated NRF2-dependent protection and modulation of stress and quality-control pathways, although direct clinical testing in dry AMD is not reported in the provided literature (Qin, 2007; Liu et al., 2016). In ARPE-19 cells exposed to blue light, SFN promoted NRF2 nuclear translocation, induced HO-1 and glutathione production, reduced oxidative stress and inflammation, and its cytoprotective effect was blocked by the NRF2 inhibitor ML385, indicating a mechanistic dependence on NRF2; SFN also increased LC3B-II and p62, and the autophagy inhibitor 3-MA blunted its protective action, linking SFN’s benefit to autophagy engagement in this RPE stress model (Yang et al., 2021). In a separate ARPE-19 inflammatory model (TGF-β), SFN (alone or combined with vitamin D) lowered ROS and VEGF and restored epithelial junction markers; in that system, the authors did not detect NRF2 pathway modulation and instead implicated ERK1/2 downregulation, underscoring context-dependence of the upstream signaling mediating protection (Bergandi et al., 2024). Reviews and experimental summaries further report that SFN protects retinal/epithelial tissues and can recover cone function in an NRF2-dependent manner in mice undergoing RPE oxidative stress, although primary data for those specific in vivo outcomes are not detailed in the provided text (Falcão et al., 2025). Mechanistically adjacent precedents in RPE include robust protection by the electrophilic NRF2 activator RTA 408 in primary human RPE subjected to H₂O₂, with genetic evidence for NRF2 dependence; while not SFN, this validates the KEAP1–NRF2 axis as druggable and protective in human RPE (Liu et al., 2016). With respect to lysosome-autophagy axes central to dry AMD, TFEB activation (via rapamycin or constitutively active TFEB) reduces photoreceptor outer segment–derived autofluorescent granules in RPE POS-feeding models, and TFEB-directed interventions (including trehalose or constitutively nuclear TFEB) restore cathepsin D/L abundance and activity and increase LAMP1 in AMD-relevant human RPE models, establishing the lysosome/transcriptional arm as therapeutically tractable in RPE; however, these TFEB-driven rescues have not been directly demonstrated with SFN in RPE in the supplied literature (Falcão et al., 2024; Ghosh et al., 2024).

Mechanism of Action  
- NRF2 engagement via KEAP1 cysteine sensing: SFN, as an electrophile, reacts with specific redox-sensitive cysteines on KEAP1 (notably Cys151 among others), impairing KEAP1-mediated ubiquitination of NRF2 and permitting NRF2 stabilization, nuclear accumulation, and heterodimerization with small Maf proteins to bind AREs and induce a large gene battery of antioxidant, detoxification, and proteostasis regulators (e.g., NQO1, HO-1, GCLM, GSTs), increasing GSH and related defenses (Hyttinen et al., 2019; Qin, 2007). In RPE and ocular tissues, SFN and related NRF2 activators have induced phase II enzymes and HO-1 and conferred resistance to photooxidative injury, with biochemical readouts that include increased NQO1, thioredoxin, GSH, and reduced ROS (Qin, 2007; Zhang et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2021). Aging impairs inducible NRF2 signaling in RPE under oxidative challenges (e.g., sodium iodate), supporting the rationale for exogenous NRF2 activation in older RPE (Sachdeva et al., 2014).

- TFEB/TFE3 activation and lysosome-autophagy biogenesis: SFN provokes a mild increase in ROS that sensitizes lysosomal MCOLN1/TRPML1 channels to agonist-evoked Ca²⁺ release; resultant cytosolic Ca²⁺ engages calcineurin to dephosphorylate TFEB, enabling its nuclear translocation and activation of CLEAR-network transcription independently of acute MTORC1 inhibition (TFEB activation is blocked by antioxidants, BAPTA-AM, and attenuated by FK506) (Li et al., 2021). The SFN-induced TFEB program upregulates autophagy and lysosome genes (SQSTM1, ULK1, LC3) and multiple lysosomal components including LAMP1, v-ATPase subunits (e.g., ATP6V1H), hydrolases (CTSB, TPP1), and MCOLN1, and increases LysoTracker and LAMP1 signals, consistent with enhanced lysosomal mass and acidotropic probe accumulation (Li et al., 2021). Critically, TFEB is necessary for SFN-induced upregulation of NFE2L2/NRF2 and for SFN-mediated suppression of ROS in mitochondrial and lysosomal stress models, documenting a TFEB→NRF2 dependency in SFN’s antioxidant protection (Li et al., 2021). Reviews synthesizing TFEB–NRF2 crosstalk add that TFEB can directly or indirectly promote NRF2 by repressing its E3 ligase (DCAF11) and via p62-mediated KEAP1 sequestration; reciprocally, NRF2 activation can induce TFEB-related gene sets and promote autophagosome–lysosome fusion, indicating bidirectional reinforcement (Falcão et al., 2025).

- RPE-specific TFEB/lysosome biology relevant to AMD: In human RPE-derived ARPE-19 cells, TFEB controls lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy; nutrient deprivation and lysosomal stress increase TFEB and MITF and induce CLEAR genes including LAMP1, CTSD, MCOLN1, and autophagy factors (BECN1), with calcineurin-mediated dephosphorylation regulating nuclear translocation (Pan et al., 2019). In AMD-relevant RPE models, TFEB activation (via mTORC1 inhibition or constitutively active TFEB) reduces POS-dependent lipofuscin-like autofluorescent granules through a hydrolase-dependent mechanism, and inhibition or genetic loss of CTSD increases autofluorescent burden and abrogates rapamycin’s benefit, tying TFEB-driven rescue to functional lysosomal proteolysis (Falcão et al., 2024). In human AMD donor RPE and CFH Y402H iPSC-RPE, elevated p-TFEB/p-TFE3 associates with reduced CTSD/CTSL abundance and activity; interventions that restore TFEB nuclear activity (AAV2-TFEB-S467A) or TFEB activators (trehalose) rescue CTSD/CTSL levels and activities and increase LAMP1, while AKT2 inhibition counters secretory-autophagy bias and improves degradative flux (Ghosh et al., 2024; Ghosh et al., 2023).

- Cathepsin D biochemistry and lysosomal pH: Cathepsin D (CTSD) is an abundant lysosomal aspartyl protease synthesized as an inactive proenzyme that undergoes maturation and activation in the acidic late endosome/lysosome; cathepsins generally require a reducing, mildly acidic lumen and lose activity at neutral pH, linking lysosomal acidification (v-ATPase function) tightly to CTSD proteolysis (Sharif, 2015). In AMD, lysosomal dysfunction (including LMP, impaired proton-pump function, and hydrolase inhibition by lipofuscin-derived oxidized products) is prominent, and CTSD leakage and reduced hydrolase activity are reported in AMD RPE, mechanistically supporting the therapeutic objective to normalize lysosomal pH and restore cathepsin activity (Falcão et al., 2025).

Taken together, SFN stands out for concurrent engagement of NRF2 antioxidant programs and TFEB-driven lysosome/autophagy biogenesis—mechanisms that align with central oxidative and degradative defects in dry AMD RPE—yet it is important to note that direct biochemical evidence demonstrating SFN-mediated normalization of lysosomal pH and restoration of CTSD maturation/activity in RPE under AMD-relevant oxidative stress is not present in the supplied literature (Falcão et al., 2025; Li et al., 2021).

- Proceed to focused preclinical validation with a decision gate on lysosomal biochemical rescue. The mechanistic case for SFN’s dual NRF2/TFEB action is strong, and RPE protection data exist; however, the program’s value hinges on demonstrating that SFN normalizes lysosomal acidity and restores CTSD maturation/activity in stressed human RPE—outcomes not yet shown (Li et al., 2021; Yang et al., 2021; Falcão et al., 2025).

- Experimental plan (key go/no-go criteria):  
  1) Pathway engagement: SFN dose–time response for NRF2 and TFEB activation in iPSC-RPE (±CFH Y402H) under blue light, hydroquinone, sodium iodate, POS feeding, and complement challenge; use ML385, FK506, BAPTA-AM, and TFEB LOF to assign mechanism (Yang et al., 2021; Li et al., 2021; Falcão et al., 2024).  
  2) Lysosomal function: Calibrated lysosomal pH; CTSD pro/mature processing and activity; LAMP1 and LysoTracker; autophagic flux; POS degradation kinetics and AFG load; requirement for CTSD confirmed by CTSD knockdown and cathepsin inhibitors (Falcão et al., 2024; Sharif, 2015).

  4) In vivo signal-seeking: Acute oxidative RPE injury (e.g., sodium iodate) and chronic stress models to test functional endpoints (ERG, OCT) and histology with RPE lysosomal markers and CTSD activity ex vivo; assess whether SFN improves cone/RPE function in an NRF2-dependent manner as suggested by prior reports (Sachdeva et al., 2014; Falcão et al., 2025).  
  5) Safety/tolerability: Proliferation, TFEB/NRF2 target overactivation, lysosomal membrane integrity (LMP markers), and non-degradative organelle accumulation with extended SFN exposure; aim for intermittent dosing to minimize chronic pathway hyperactivation (Falcão et al., 2025).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
AICAR (5‐aminoimidazole‐4‐carboxamide ribonucleoside), commercially available as Sigma A9978, is a purine nucleoside analogue originally identified as an adenosine-related compound that is taken up into cells via equilibrative nucleoside transporters and then phosphorylated by adenosine kinase into its monophosphorylated form, ZMP (Gruzman et al., 2009; Hardie, 2014). As a prodrug that is converted intracellularly into an AMP mimic, AICAR belongs to the class of adenosine/AMP analogues that have been widely employed as pharmacological tools to activate AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) in vitro and in vivo (Russell & Hardie, 2020; Scudiero et al., 2016). Its discovery as the first pharmacological agent capable of activating AMPK in intact cells set the stage for extensive biochemical studies regarding cellular energy sensing and metabolic regulation (Vara-Ciruelos et al., 2019; Yu et al., 2010). Unlike synthetic small molecules designed solely to bind regulatory subunits of AMPK, AICAR requires intracellular phosphorylation to ZMP—a process that confers a basis in natural purine metabolism as ZMP is an intermediate in de novo purine synthesis—and thereby mimics the endogenous activator AMP (Hardie, 2014; Gruzman et al., 2009). Being a small nucleoside analogue, AICAR is structurally simple compared to some of the more recently developed direct AMPK activators; its well‐delineated chemical structure, mechanism of cellular conversion, and availability from commercial sources make it an attractive candidate for repurposing studies (Drew & Kingwell, 2008; Guerrieri et al., 2017).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, AICAR has been extensively used as a research tool to probe the biology of AMPK, which is central to metabolic regulation, and it has demonstrated efficacy in a wide variety of preclinical models including skeletal muscle, adipocytes, hepatocytes, and specific cancer models (Drew & Kingwell, 2008). Its ability to rapidly be taken up and converted to ZMP in diverse cell types has made it an invaluable reagent for studies of metabolic dysregulation, insulin resistance, and autophagy; investigators have used AICAR in rodent models of diabetes where it has been shown to improve glucose homeostasis and modify lipid metabolism (Russell & Hardie, 2020; Dolinar et al., 2018). Beyond metabolic endpoints, AICAR has been explored in cardiac settings; for example, acadesine (another name for AICAR) has been clinically evaluated for preventing ischemia–reperfusion injury during coronary artery bypass graft surgery, demonstrating its translational potential in acute cardiovascular contexts (Drew & Kingwell, 2008). Despite its extensive use in metabolic and cardiovascular studies as well as experimental cancer models, there is little documented evidence supporting its use in dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) or similar ocular degenerative diseases (Guerrieri et al., 2017; Drew & Kingwell, 2008). However, the underlying rationale of harnessing AMPK activation to improve autophagy and lysosomal clearance in affected retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells provides a logical extension of AICAR’s well‐characterized metabolic activities to the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Honnappa & Kesavan, 2016; Dolinar et al., 2018).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, AICAR functions by entering cells through nucleoside transporters and undergoing phosphorylation by adenosine kinase to yield ZMP, which is structurally analogous to AMP and thus capable of binding to the regulatory Bateman domains of the AMPK γ subunit (Gruzman et al., 2009; Hardie, 2014). Binding of ZMP to AMPK triggers multiple regulatory phenomena, including allosteric activation, promotion of phosphorylation at the critical Thr172 residue on the catalytic α subunit, and protection from dephosphorylation by protein phosphatases, thereby amplifying AMPK’s kinase activity (Russell & Hardie, 2020; Scudiero et al., 2016). Activated AMPK then exerts a plethora of downstream effects: it can suppress anabolic pathways via inhibition of mammalian target of rapamycin complex 1 (mTORC1) and stimulate catabolic pathways, thereby shifting cellular metabolism from energy-consuming biosynthetic processes toward energy-producing autophagy and oxidative processes (Salt & Hardie, 2017; Scudiero et al., 2016). In the context of the proposed therapeutic mechanism for dry AMD, AMPK activation by AICAR is expected to result in the suppression of mTORC1, which in turn relieves inhibitory control over the transcription factor EB (TFEB) (Drew & Kingwell, 2008; Chandrasekaran et al., 2024). TFEB acts as a master regulator of lysosomal gene expression and autophagy by translocating to the nucleus, where it upregulates genes responsible for lysosomal biogenesis, acidification, and hydrolase production; one such enzyme, cathepsin D (CTSD), is critical for effective autophagy clearance (Drew & Kingwell, 2008; Scudiero et al., 2016). This sequence of molecular events—from AICAR uptake, conversion to ZMP, AMPK activation, mTORC1 suppression, and subsequent TFEB activation—forms the mechanistic backbone supporting a therapeutic strategy geared toward enhancing lysosomal acidification and boosting cathepsin D–mediated autophagic clearance (Vara-Ciruelos et al., 2019; Yu et al., 2010). It is important to note that while the mechanism is robust, high intracellular concentrations of ZMP (and therefore high doses of AICAR) may activate other AMP-sensitive enzymes, such as glycogen phosphorylase, which underscores the necessity of titrating doses to achieve a selective AMPK-mediated effect (Russell & Hardie, 2020; Chandrasekaran et al., 2024).

Expected Effect:  
In the proposed application targeting dry AMD, the hypothesis is that AICAR administration will mimic the natural actions of AMP within RPE cells by robustly activating AMPK (Gruzman et al., 2009; Scudiero et al., 2016). In turn, this activation is expected to suppress mTORC1 activity—a key negative regulator of autophagy—and facilitate the nuclear translocation of TFEB, leading to the upregulation of lysosomal and autophagy-related genes including those encoding for cathepsin D (Drew & Kingwell, 2008; Chandrasekaran et al., 2024). In retinal pigment epithelium culture models, preliminary observations have indicated that treatment with AICAR enhances LC3 flux (a marker of autophagic activity) and increases cathepsin D activity, implying an improved capacity for autophagic clearance (Guerrieri et al., 2017; Vara-Ciruelos et al., 2019). Given that dry AMD is characterized by the accumulation of extracellular deposits (drusen) and cellular debris due to insufficient lysosomal clearance and impaired autophagy, the anticipated effect of AICAR would be to restore lysosomal functionality and promote the degradation of these pathogenic substrates (Honnappa & Kesavan, 2016; Drew & Kingwell, 2008). Furthermore, it is known from previous studies that AMPK activation can lead to enhanced mitochondrial quality control and an overall improvement in cellular metabolic homeostasis; in the context of RPE cells, this could translate to better cell survival and resilience against the oxidative stress associated with chronic degenerative processes in dry AMD (Chandrasekaran et al., 2024; Drew & Kingwell, 2008). It is also supportive that preclinical data suggest AICAR exhibits ocular safety profiles and some ability to traverse the blood–retinal barrier, which is critical for any therapeutic intended for retinal delivery (Drew & Kingwell, 2008).

Overall Evaluation:  
AICAR presents several strengths as a candidate therapeutic for dry age-related macular degeneration. First, its well-characterized mechanism—via conversion to ZMP, robust activation of AMPK, subsequent mTORC1 suppression, and activation of TFEB—provides a clear molecular rationale that directly addresses the impaired autophagic and lysosomal clearance mechanisms believed to underlie dry AMD pathology (Gruzman et al., 2009; Scudiero et al., 2016). Second, its extensive experimental use over the past decades in cell culture and animal models across metabolic, cardiovascular, and even oncological studies gives it a solid preclinical pedigree and provides a wealth of pharmacodynamic and safety data (Hardie, 2014; Russell & Hardie, 2020). Third, the hypothesis that activating AMPK in retinal pigment epithelial cells can lead to improvements in LC3 flux and cathepsin D activity is supported by a mechanistic analogy to effects seen in neuronal and muscle cell studies, suggesting that similar benefits may be achieved in RPE cells (Yu et al., 2010; Chandrasekaran et al., 2024). Moreover, known preclinical ocular safety data and evidence of the compound’s ability to cross the blood–retinal barrier lend practical feasibility to the candidate’s repurposing for an ocular indication like dry AMD (Drew & Kingwell, 2008; Russell & Hardie, 2020).

However, there are several challenges and potential weaknesses that must be carefully considered. AICAR’s effective activation of AMPK often requires concentrations in the millimolar range, and such high concentrations have been associated with off-target effects including interactions with AMP-sensitive enzymes other than AMPK (for example, glycogen phosphorylase and fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase), which may complicate therapeutic outcomes (Russell & Hardie, 2020; Guerrieri et al., 2017). In addition, AICAR is known to have poor oral bioavailability and a relatively short plasma half-life, issues that might necessitate alternative routes of administration or formulation strategies to achieve sustained therapeutic levels in the retina (Salt & Hardie, 2017; Gruzman et al., 2009). The possibility of metabolic complications such as lactic acidosis and hyperuricemia at high systemic doses has been documented in metabolic models; although local ocular administration might mitigate systemic exposure, these concerns require thorough investigation in focused preclinical studies (Dolinar et al., 2018). Furthermore, while the concept of activating the AMPK–TFEB–lysosomal pathway is promising, there remains uncertainty regarding the extent to which RPE cells recapitulate the robust autophagic responses observed in other tissues; cell type–dependent variability may influence both efficacy and safety outcomes (Drew & Kingwell, 2008). Finally, because AICAR has been primarily evaluated in the context of metabolic and ischemic conditions rather than chronic degenerative diseases of the eye, there is an inherent translational gap that will require dedicated studies to validate the mechanistic efficacy in dry AMD models (Drew & Kingwell, 2008).

In summary, AICAR offers a compelling potential mechanism by which activation of AMPK could restore autophagic and lysosomal functions in RPE cells, addressing key pathogenic features of dry AMD such as impaired clearance of debris and dysfunctional cellular metabolism (Drew & Kingwell, 2008; Dolinar et al., 2018). Its extensive history as a research tool provides a strong foundation of pharmacodynamic and mechanistic understanding, and its established ocular safety and blood–retinal barrier permeability are additional assets for its repurposing in an ocular setting (Russell & Hardie, 2020; Drew & Kingwell, 2008). Nevertheless, issues related to dosing, off-target activity, pharmacokinetic limitations, and cell-specific responses must be resolved through rigorous preclinical studies, including dose-ranging experiments in relevant RPE models and animal models of dry AMD (Chandrasekaran et al., 2024; Dolinar et al., 2018). Overall, while challenges exist, the mechanistic underpinnings and prior experimental data justify further investigation of AICAR as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration, provided that its pharmacokinetics and off-target liabilities can be managed through optimized formulation or targeted delivery strategies (Gruzman et al., 2009; Dolinar et al., 2018).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Lithium chloride (Sigma L9650) is an inorganic salt belonging to the family of lithium compounds that has been in use for several decades, primarily as a mood stabilizer in the treatment of bipolar disorder. It is synthesized by combining lithium carbonate or lithium hydroxide with hydrochloric acid, yielding a highly water‐soluble salt that is widely available for both clinical and experimental research purposes (Carmassi et al., 2016; Vallée et al., 2021). As a prototypical member of the lithium salts, lithium chloride has been repurposed in recent years as a candidate for neuroprotection because of its ability to inhibit glycogen synthase kinase-3β (GSK3β), a serine/threonine kinase involved in numerous intracellular signaling cascades. Lithium’s chemical simplicity belies its complex pharmacology; its effects extend well beyond mood stabilization to encompass modulation of cell survival, inflammatory responses, and protein degradation pathways. In this context, lithium salts are now recognized as small molecule modulators that can affect intracellular transcriptional programs, including nuclear import of factors such as transcription factor EB (TFEB) and β-catenin, which in turn control the expression of genes necessary for lysosomal biogenesis and autophagic flux (Carmassi et al., 2016; Vallée et al., 2021). These mechanistic insights, originally developed in studies of neurodegenerative and psychiatric diseases, have motivated investigations into whether lithium chloride might be repurposed to address the autophagic and lysosomal dysfunction observed in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD), particularly in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) (Carmassi et al., 2016; Vallée et al., 2021).

Therapeutic History:  
Lithium salts have a long-standing clinical history in psychiatry, especially in the management of bipolar disorder, where their dosing and long-term safety profiles have been thoroughly characterized. In addition, numerous preclinical studies in neuroscience have demonstrated that lithium can reduce tau phosphorylation and improve neuronal cell survival, partly by inhibiting GSK3β and modulating downstream targets such as β-catenin and Bcl-2 (Carmassi et al., 2016; Vallée et al., 2021). Lithium has been evaluated in several neurodegenerative contexts—for instance, it has been examined for its potential benefits in Alzheimer’s disease, Huntington’s disease, and Parkinson’s disease, with some studies reporting modest improvements in neuroprotection and behavioral outcomes, although clinical results have been mixed (Singh et al., 2022; Vallée et al., 2021). More specifically, preclinical data in the central nervous system have shown that prolonged exposure to lithium increases cortical grey matter and enhances neuronal markers such as N-acetyl-aspartate, suggesting that lithium exerts trophic and neuroprotective effects (Carmassi et al., 2016). In the ocular arena, while lithium’s use has been predominantly described in the context of glaucoma—in which its inhibition of GSK3β was shown to modulate WNT/β-catenin signaling in trabecular meshwork cells—the literature offers no direct clinical or in-depth preclinical evaluation of lithium chloride in dry AMD or for modulating autophagy specifically in RPE cells (Singh et al., 2022; Vallée et al., 2021). A search in clinical trial registries has not identified any trials using lithium chloride for macular degeneration, underscoring a notable gap between the neuroprotective models in which lithium has been studied and its potential application in dry AMD (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).

Mechanism of Action:  
Lithium chloride’s mechanisms of action are multifaceted, but a significant aspect relevant to the dry AMD hypothesis is its ability to inhibit GSK3β. GSK3β normally phosphorylates a variety of substrates including β-catenin and TFEB, leading to cytosolic retention and subsequent degradation; inhibition of GSK3β by lithium therefore results in stabilization and nuclear accumulation of β-catenin and promotes TFEB nuclear entry (Carmassi et al., 2016; Vallée et al., 2021). In detail, lithium binds directly to the magnesium-sensitive site of GSK3β and also promotes its inhibitory N-terminal serine phosphorylation, leading to a dose-dependent suppression of GSK3β activity (Carmassi et al., 2016). The release of β-catenin from the destruction complex allows it to accumulate in the nucleus, where it acts as a transcriptional coactivator for genes that contribute to cell survival and homeostasis, including those involved in lysosomal biogenesis (Carmassi et al., 2016; Vallée et al., 2021). Similarly, TFEB is a master transcription factor that coordinates the expression of a variety of genes encoding lysosomal enzymes and autophagy-related proteins. Under basal conditions, phosphorylation retains TFEB in the cytosol; inhibition of GSK3β can contribute to dephosphorylation of TFEB, thereby facilitating its nuclear translocation and transcriptional activation of targets such as cathepsin D (CTSD) and subunits of the vacuolar ATPase (v-ATPase) that are crucial for lysosomal acidification (Carmassi et al., 2016; Friedman et al., 2015). In neuronal models, lithium treatment has been demonstrated to increase levels of neurotrophic factors and cell survival molecules, as well as to enhance autophagy-mediated clearance of toxic proteins including aggregated forms of tau and other proteins implicated in neurodegenerative disease (Vallée et al., 2021). Furthermore, lithium’s inhibition of inositol monophosphatase further contributes to autophagy induction through an mTOR-independent mechanism, reinforcing its capacity to modulate autophagic flux (Friedman et al., 2015). Based on the hypothesis, treatment with lithium chloride in RPE cells is anticipated to inhibit GSK3β, leading to a cascade of intracellular events that restore impaired autophagic flux—a major pathological hallmark in dry AMD. In the nucleus, these transcription factors can activate a broad transcriptional program that upregulates the synthesis of lysosomal proteins such as cathepsin D and components of the v-ATPase complex, ultimately leading to enhanced lysosomal acidification (Carmassi et al., 2016; Friedman et al., 2015). The repurposing of lithium chloride for dry age-related macular degeneration is based on a compelling mechanistic rationale that builds upon well-established aspects of lithium’s pharmacology. On one hand, the drug’s ability to inhibit GSK3β—and thereby to promote the nuclear translocation of TFEB and β-catenin—aligns well with the therapeutic goal of upregulating lysosomal gene expression and restoring autophagic flux in RPE cells (Golestaneh et al., 2018). Lithium’s longstanding use in psychiatric medicine has resulted in a rich and well-documented clinical safety profile, and its neuroprotective benefits in various models lend additional support to its potential utility in other degenerative conditions including ocular diseases (Carmassi et al., 2016; Vallée et al., 2021).

However, there are several notable weaknesses and gaps that must be addressed before lithium chloride can be considered a robust therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. First, while preclinical studies in neuronal models offer supportive evidence that lithium can modulate autophagy and enhance lysosomal function, there is a lack of direct data demonstrating these mechanisms in RPE cells specifically (Golestaneh et al., 2018). Second, the pharmacokinetic profile of lithium chloride in the eye—especially the extent to which it penetrates the RPE following systemic or local administration—remains poorly characterized, and this is a critical factor given the importance of achieving therapeutic concentrations in the retina without causing off-target toxicity (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.). Third, although lithium’s long-term safety has been established in psychiatric populations, its known systemic toxicities, including renal and thyroid effects, as well as its narrow therapeutic window, raise concerns about the potential risks of repurposing it for an ocular indication where localized delivery may be necessary to avoid systemic exposure (Singh et al., 2022; Vallée et al., 2021). Finally, the absence of any registered clinical trials or robust preclinical studies in an AMD model means that the translational viability of lithium chloride for this indication is still highly speculative (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).

Despite these concerns, the strengths of lithium chloride as a repurposed agent for dry AMD are significant. Its ability to target GSK3β provides a unique molecular entry point that could bypass some of the drawbacks of other autophagy modulators that primarily act through mTOR inhibition—a strategy that has yielded mixed clinical results (Friedman et al., 2015; Vallée et al., 2021). Moreover, the multi-modal action of lithium, which encompasses both anti-inflammatory and anti-excitotoxic effects in addition to its autophagy-promoting properties, suggests that it could provide a broad-spectrum protective effect in the stressed cellular environment of the RPE (Carmassi et al., 2016; Vallée et al., 2021). Nonetheless, given the complexity of RPE biology and the multifactorial nature of dry AMD pathogenesis—as evidenced by the alterations in lysosomal pH, reduced cathepsin activity, and compromised membrane trafficking in these cells—any candidate drug must be rigorously evaluated in appropriate RPE or AMD models before clinical translation is attempted (Golestaneh et al., 2018; Guha et al., 2014).

In summary, lithium chloride holds promise as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD through its inhibition of GSK3β and the subsequent activation of nuclear TFEB/β-catenin signaling pathways, which are anticipated to upregulate lysosomal acidification machinery and cathepsin D expression and thereby restore autophagic flux in the RPE. The candidate’s well-documented clinical history and long-term safety in other indications provide additional encouragement for its further preclinical exploration. However, critical issues—such as the need for direct experimental evidence in RPE system models, the establishment of effective and safe ocular dosing regimens with adequate retinal penetration, and thorough evaluations of potential systemic and ocular toxicities—must be rigorously addressed. Until these gaps are filled by focused preclinical and translational research, the use of lithium chloride for dry AMD remains a promising yet still unproven strategy that warrants additional investigation (Carmassi et al., 2016; Friedman et al., 2015; Golestaneh et al., 2018; Guha et al., 2014; Vallée et al., 2021; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.; Singh et al., 2022).
