Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
SRT1720 is a first-generation synthetic small-molecule sirtuin 1 (SIRT1)–activating compound (STAC) originally discovered by high-throughput screening at Sirtris Pharmaceuticals and optimized around an imidazo[1,2-b]thiazole chemotype to yield higher apparent potency and selectivity than the natural product resveratrol in early assay systems (Chang et al., 2024; Mazzone, 2018). Subsequent mechanistic work across the STAC class resolved that many apparent activation signals were substrate/context dependent and, in some assay configurations, artifactual; nevertheless, later kinetic/biophysical and structural studies established that STACs can directly engage SIRT1 via an assisted allosteric mechanism that stabilizes the enzyme–substrate complex, with mutational data showing that E230K/A SIRT1 variants abolish both binding and activation by STACs (Lee et al., 2021; Mazzone, 2018). While most STACs are SIRT1-selective, SRT1720 exhibits notable polypharmacology, including reported inhibitory activity against Sirt3, highlighting potential off-target risks intrinsic to this first-generation class (Mazzone, 2018). As a class, STACs have been widely evaluated for metabolic, inflammatory, neurodegenerative, and aging phenotypes predicated on SIRT1’s broad substrate repertoire (for example, PGC-1α, NF-κB p65/RelA, FOXO family, p53), which link to mitochondrial biogenesis, anti-inflammatory signaling, oxidative stress responses, and cell survival programs (Chang et al., 2024; Mazzone, 2018).

Therapeutic History  
SRT1720 has extensive preclinical use, but there is no evidence in the provided corpus that it has been tested in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), in the eye, or in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) models (cellular or in vivo) (Ji et al., 2021; Ding et al., 2017; Bononi et al., 2022). In non-ocular systems, SRT1720 increased mitochondrial biogenesis and rescued mitochondrial function after oxidant injury in renal proximal tubule cells, providing proof-of-concept that STAC activation can drive PGC-1α–linked mitochondrial programs in mammalian cells under oxidative stress (Ji et al., 2021). In metabolic disease models, SRT1720 is reported to improve hepatic lipid metabolism via SIRT1-dependent pathways regulating PGC-1α, AMPK, PPARα, FOXO1, SREBP-1c and FGF21, with consistent decreases in lipogenesis and inflammation and increases in fatty-acid β-oxidation in NAFLD models (Ding et al., 2017). Multiple lifespan/healthspan studies reported benefits in mice—improved survival and healthspan in diet-induced obese animals and lifespan extension on standard diet—again consistent with systemic SIRT1-axis engagement (Mazzone, 2018). At the same time, substantial controversy surrounds both mechanism and safety. Pacholec et al. argued SRT1720 (and related first-generation STACs) are not direct SIRT1 activators under specific biochemical conditions, although later work provided structural and kinetic support for allosteric activation with specific substrates (Lee et al., 2021; Bononi et al., 2022). Importantly for repurposing risk, SRT1720 promoted tumor cell migration and lung metastasis in a breast cancer model, and SRT1720 can trigger SIRT1-independent cytotoxicity in some hematologic malignancy cells, underscoring unresolved off-target liabilities (Bononi et al., 2022; Chang et al., 2024). No pharmacokinetic (PK), ADME, or clinical tolerability data for SRT1720 are supplied in the present corpus; by contrast, the second-generation STAC SRT2104 has human PK/tolerability and multiple preclinical and clinical signals across diseases, including ocular/neurologic models (but those data cannot be extrapolated to SRT1720 without qualification) (Bononi et al., 2022; Chang et al., 2024). Collectively, the historical record supports that SRT1720 is a pharmacologically active first-generation STAC with broad preclinical use, mixed mechanistic interpretations, and safety concerns; critically, there is no published use in AMD or RPE models in the material provided here (Ji et al., 2021; Bononi et al., 2022).

Mechanism of Action  
- Biochemical pharmacology and target engagement: SRT1720 belongs to the STAC class that can directly activate SIRT1 through an assisted allosteric mechanism requiring specific substrate motifs; mutating SIRT1 E230 disrupts both activator binding and activation, and co-crystal structures of SIRT1 with SRT-like activators support an allosteric binding pocket that enhances deacetylation efficiency in a substrate-dependent manner (Lee et al., 2021; Mazzone, 2018). Early reports of direct activation were contested due to labeled peptide assay artifacts, but subsequent kinetic and structural data reconciled these findings with an allosteric model; nonetheless, the field recognizes pharmacological caveats including context-dependent activation and off-targets, such as reported Sirt3 inhibition by SRT1720 (Mazzone, 2018; Lee et al., 2021).  
- Canonical SIRT1 substrates and pathway biology: SIRT1 deacetylates transcriptional regulators and autophagy/mitophagy machinery that converge on mitochondrial quality control, oxidative stress defense, and inflammatory tone—each relevant to AMD pathogenesis. These include PGC-1α (mitochondrial biogenesis/oxidative metabolism), FOXO1/FOXO3a (antioxidant/autophagy transcription), NF-κB p65/RelA (inflammatory gene programs), p53 (apoptosis/senescence), and Nrf2 (antioxidant transcription), as well as autophagy proteins (e.g., ATG family members and LC3) and trafficking nodes such as Rab7 that promote autophagosome–lysosome fusion (Chang et al., 2024; Luján et al., 2022; Luo et al., 2025). In multiple cell types, SIRT1 activation or NAD⁺ elevation increases PGC-1α activity and mitochondrial biogenesis and can suppress NF-κB signaling via p65 deacetylation, consistent with anti-oxidative and anti-inflammatory effects that are therapeutically desirable in RPE (Ding et al., 2017; Luo et al., 2025).  
- RPE-specific SIRT1/autophagy linkage: In ARPE-19 cells under oxidative stress, PARP1 activation depletes NAD⁺, inhibits SIRT1 (elevated p53 acetylation), and selectively impairs late-stage autophagy by blocking autolysosome formation without preventing autophagosome formation; restoring NAD⁺ or inhibiting PARP1 preserves SIRT1 activity and rescues late autophagic flux, whereas PARP1 inhibition fails to rescue autophagy when SIRT1 is depleted—placing SIRT1 as the essential downstream effector for recovering autophagy in oxidatively stressed RPE (Jang et al., 2020). In vivo, PARP1 inhibition protected the retina in sodium iodate (SI) injury and the benefit was autophagy-dependent, reinforcing the PARP1→NAD⁺→SIRT1→autophagy axis as a mechanistic driver of RPE/retinal resilience (Jang et al., 2020). AMD donor RPE exhibits decreased NAD⁺, reduced SIRT1 levels, increased acetylated (inactive) PGC-1α, impaired AMPK signaling, and hyperactive mTOR—all changes expected to depress SIRT1-dependent autophagy and mitochondrial biogenesis and to contribute to lysosomal/autophagic abnormalities (Zhang et al., 2020).  
- TFEB/CLEAR and lysosomal acidification context: TFEB is the master transcription factor for lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy gene networks (CLEAR), whose nuclear translocation is negatively regulated by mTORC1; CLEAR target upregulation increases lysosomal capacity and flux, while lysosomal ion/pH homeostasis (v-ATPase–dependent proton pumping) determines enzyme activation, including cathepsins such as CTSD (Boya et al., 2023; Falcão et al., 2025; Kaarniranta et al., 2023). In AMD/RPE-relevant literature, TFEB/CLEAR is positioned as a principal lever for lysosomal rejuvenation, and lysosomal acidity and calcium handling are identified as key determinants of autophagic flux and RPE health (Boya et al., 2023). Although sirtuin family members can intersect TFEB signaling (e.g., AKT2/SIRT5/TFEB axis in non-neovascular AMD), direct evidence for SIRT1-driven TFEB deacetylation/activation is not provided in the present corpus; however, PGC-1α has been placed upstream of TFEB in other disease contexts, linking SIRT1→PGC-1α activity to potential TFEB–CLEAR induction by inference (not by direct RPE data) (Falcão et al., 2025).  
- Critical gaps relevant to the working hypothesis: Within the provided literature, there is no direct evidence that SRT1720 activates SIRT1 in RPE, no demonstration that SRT1720 promotes TFEB deacetylation or nuclear activation, and no reports that SRT1720 enhances lysosomal acidification or cathepsin D (CTSD) activity in RPE or AMD models; any such assertions remain unsubstantiated by the references supplied here (Ji et al., 2021; Mazzone, 2018; Kaarniranta et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2020). Therefore, while the SIRT1→autophagy/mitophagy rationale in RPE is strong, the specific mechanistic chain “SRT1720→SIRT1 activation in RPE→TFEB deacetylation→CLEAR upregulation→lysosomal acidification/CTSD enhancement” lacks direct experimental support in RPE/AMD contexts in these sources and should be treated as a testable, not established, hypothesis (Falcão et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2020).

Therapeutic biology of the disease target supports SIRT1 activation in RPE. Multiple AMD-relevant datasets show NAD⁺ depletion and SIRT1 downregulation in AMD RPE (primary donor-derived cultures and iPSC-RPE), accompanied by impaired PGC-1α activity, AMPK suppression, and mTOR hyperactivation, together with autophagy/lysosome structural and functional abnormalities; the PARP1-dependent late-autophagy block under oxidative stress in RPE is SIRT1-dependent for rescue, further bolstering SIRT1 as a target for restoring autophagic flux and organelle quality control (Zhang et al., 2020; Jang et al., 2020). However, these observations do not establish which pharmacologic SIRT1 activator is optimal for RPE/AMD, and they do not establish TFEB deacetylation as a SIRT1-dependent event in RPE (Jang et al., 2020; Falcão et al., 2025).

Therapeutic History in Related Ocular Systems (Class Precedent)  
Although direct SRT1720 ocular data are absent here, SRT2104—a second-generation STAC with improved specificity and exposure—shows SIRT1-linked protection in retinal ischemia/reperfusion and TNF-induced optic nerve injury, including deacetylation of canonical SIRT1 substrates (p53, NF-κB p65, STAT3), reduced apoptosis/inflammation, and induction of autophagy in optic nerve, which provides class-level ocular precedent that SIRT1 activation can be neuroprotective and autophagy-enhancing in the visual system (Chang et al., 2024). These results should not be extrapolated to SRT1720 without direct data, but they reinforce the biological plausibility that a STAC could benefit retinal tissues if target engagement and safety can be achieved (Chang et al., 2024).

Expected Effect  
The proposed assay hypothesis is that SRT1720 will activate SIRT1 in RPE, leading to TFEB deacetylation/activation, increased lysosomal acidification and CTSD activity, and improved clearance of photoreceptor outer segment (POS) material. Based on the literature provided here, the following expectations are reasonable and aligned with evidence, and several components are speculative:

- Supported expectations tied to SIRT1 biology in RPE:

- Plausible, but not demonstrated within the provided literature:
  - TFEB deacetylation/activation: the present corpus does not document SIRT1-dependent TFEB deacetylation or STAC-induced TFEB activation in RPE. TFEB/CLEAR is a validated master lysosomal program, and PGC-1α can lie upstream of TFEB in other disease contexts, so an indirect route “SIRT1→PGC-1α→TFEB→CLEAR” is biologically plausible but remains unproven in RPE here and should be tested directly (Falcão et al., 2025).

On balance, the therapeutic rationale “activate SIRT1 to restore autophagy/mitophagy and lysosomal competence in RPE for dry AMD” is well-supported by AMD-relevant cell biology and human donor data; however, the specific choice of SRT1720 has substantial evidentiary and safety gaps relative to alternatives in the STAC space, and the asserted TFEB/lysosome mechanistic specifics are not demonstrated in the provided literature.

- Given the safety concerns and off-target profile of SRT1720, and the existence of a later-generation STAC (SRT2104) with human PK and ocular neuroprotection, SRT1720 should not be advanced beyond in vitro RPE validation until it demonstrates clear, on-target superiority in RPE assays and acceptable safety margins; otherwise, the team should prioritize either SRT2104 or NAD⁺ augmentation/PARP1 modulation for translational efforts (Chang et al., 2024; Bononi et al., 2022; Jang et al., 2020).

- Pros: Strong disease–target alignment in RPE; robust class biology for SIRT1-driven autophagy/mitophagy; SRT1720 can activate SIRT1 pathways in other oxidative-stress contexts; feasible, discriminating assays exist to test the MoA (Zhang et al., 2020; Jang et al., 2020; Ji et al., 2021; Boya et al., 2023).

Decision guidance: Proceed with a narrowly scoped, mechanism-first in vitro validation of SRT1720 in human RPE focused on SIRT1 target engagement and late-stage autophagy rescue under oxidative/phagolysosomal stress, with explicit tests for TFEB/CLEAR activation and lysosomal acidification/CTSD activity; in parallel, benchmark against SRT2104 and NAD⁺ repletion, and use pre-specified go/no-go criteria tied to on-target mechanistic readouts and safety signals to decide whether SRT1720 merits in vivo exploration in retinal degeneration models (Jang et al., 2020; Chang et al., 2024; Boya et al., 2023).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
MCC950 (AdipoGen AG‐CRID3) is a synthetic small‐molecule inhibitor that belongs to the diarylsulfonylurea chemical class and was originally discovered during investigations aimed at identifying potent inhibitors of the NLRP3 inflammasome complex (Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018). This compound has been synthetically optimized for high potency, with reported effective concentrations in the nanomolar range in various disease models, and its structure–activity relationship has been refined in numerous preclinical studies over the past several years (Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018; Wooff et al., 2020). As a representative of its drug class, diarylsulfonylureas have been broadly explored in inflammatory contexts due to their capacity to modulate innate immune pathways; however, MCC950 has emerged as a prototype NLRP3-targeting agent with potential applications across inflammatory and degenerative diseases, including those affecting ocular tissues (Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018; Wooff et al., 2020).

MCC950 was initially characterized in systemic inflammatory disease models, where it demonstrated remarkable efficacy in reducing the production of proinflammatory cytokines, such as interleukin (IL)-1β and IL-18, by directly inhibiting the activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome (Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018; Wooff et al., 2020). Preclinical evaluations in nonocular contexts—such as experimental colitis, myocardial infarction, and atherosclerosis—have consistently shown that MCC950 can markedly mitigate pathology by blocking the inflammasome cascade (Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018; Wooff et al., 2020). In the ocular arena, several studies have examined MCC950’s impact in diverse rodent models of retinal disease. For example, in laser-induced choroidal neovascularization (CNV) models, MCC950 administration led to reductions in IL-1β mRNA and secreted protein levels, albeit with a paradoxical increase in overall CNV lesion volume, suggesting a complex interplay between inflammasome inhibition and immune cell recruitment (Dieckmann et al., 2024). Furthermore, intravitreal delivery of MCC950 in an OPTN(E50K) mouse model of normal-tension glaucoma (NTG) showed functional and structural retinal improvements through decreased expression of inflammasome components and glial activation markers (Wang et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2023). In vitro investigations using ARPE-19 and R28 retinal cell lines have also highlighted MCC950's ability to decrease NLRP3, caspase-1, IL-1β, and IL-18 levels, thus attenuating inflammasome-mediated inflammatory responses (Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018; Li, 2020). Despite these promising preclinical data in models of retinal inflammation and vascular dysfunction, MCC950 has not yet progressed into clinical trials for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or geographic atrophy (GA), and its use in ocular conditions remains primarily in the preclinical and exploratory phase (Wooff et al., 2020).

Mechanism of Action:  
MCC950 exerts its pharmacological effects by specifically targeting the NLRP3 inflammasome, a cytosolic multiprotein complex that mediates the innate immune response to both pathogen-associated and damage-associated molecular patterns (Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018). At the molecular level, MCC950 is believed to bind to the NACHT domain of NLRP3, thereby inhibiting its ATPase activity—a critical step required for the conformational changes and oligomerization that lead to the formation of the active inflammasome complex (Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2025). This blockade prevents the recruitment of the adaptor protein ASC, thus halting the maturation and activation of caspase-1 (Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018; Wooff et al., 2020). Consequently, the cleavage of pro-IL-1β and pro-IL-18 into their bioactive forms is suppressed, which results in diminished secretion of these potent proinflammatory cytokines (Wang et al., 2025; Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018). Importantly, MCC950’s mechanism is selective for NLRP3, as it does not interfere with the activation of other inflammasome platforms, such as those mediated by AIM2, NLRC4, or NLRP1 (Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018; Wooff et al., 2020). In the context of retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells—a cell type critical for the maintenance of the outer blood–retina barrier and implicated in the pathogenesis of dry AMD—NLRP3 activation has been linked to chronic inflammation, oxidative stress, and lysosomal destabilization. Inhibition of NLRP3 by MCC950 is postulated to preserve lysosomal integrity by preventing excessive caspase-1 activation, which is known to contribute to lysosomal membrane permeabilization and the subsequent loss of v-ATPase–dependent acidification along with aberrant cathepsin D (CTSD) activity (Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018; Korhonen, 2024). MCC950 offers several notable strengths as a potential therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. Preclinical studies have demonstrated that MCC950 can successfully reduce the release of IL-1β and IL-18 in various cell types, including retinal endothelial cells and RPE-like cells, which underscores its potential to ameliorate the chronic inflammatory environment observed in dry AMD (Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018; Li, 2020). However, several weaknesses and challenges must be considered before advancing MCC950 as a therapy for dry AMD. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Panobinostat (LBH589) is a fully synthetic small‐molecule compound originally developed by Novartis and characterized chemically as a cinnamic hydroxamic acid analogue formulated as its anhydrous lactate salt. This molecule belongs to the hydroxamate class of histone deacetylase inhibitors (HDACi), a group of compounds designed to inhibit the enzymatic activity of HDACs that regulate chromatin remodeling and transcription by catalyzing the removal of acetyl groups from histone proteins. Panobinostat’s chemical structure, defined by its hydroxamic acid moiety, is tailored to chelate the zinc ion in the catalytic domain of HDAC enzymes, thereby preventing deacetylation reactions that normally lead to a condensed chromatin state. In its initial development, panobinostat was formulated in multiple dosage forms, including oral hard capsules containing 10, 15, or 20 mg doses and earlier intravenous preparations, illustrating its versatility in administration routes for different clinical indications (Van Veggel, Westerman, & Hamberg, 2018; Libby et al., 2015; Dokmanovic, Clarke, & Marks, 2007). Compounds of this class have historically been employed in oncology, where their capacity to induce hyperacetylation of histone and non-histone substrates leads to altered gene transcription, cell cycle arrest, differentiation, and eventual apoptosis in malignant cells (Van Veggel et al., 2018; Cea et al., 2013). Moreover, the broad-spectrum inhibition of HDAC isoforms—spanning Classes I, II, and IV—distinguishes panobinostat as a “pan-HDAC inhibitor” with high potency at nanomolar concentrations, a characteristic that underlies its robust pharmacological profile and its subsequent regulatory approvals for certain cancer indications (Morabito et al., 2016).

Therapeutic History:  
Since its discovery, panobinostat has undergone extensive preclinical and clinical evaluation primarily targeting multiple myeloma and various hematologic malignancies. Early phase clinical trials established that, as a single agent, panobinostat had modest activity; however, its combination with proteasome inhibitors such as bortezomib and corticosteroids like dexamethasone produced synergistic effects that translated into significant improvements in progression‐free survival in relapsed and refractory multiple myeloma patients. This positive clinical efficacy culminated in its approval by both the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and the European Medicines Agency (EMA) in 2015 for the treatment of patients with multiple myeloma who had received at least two prior regimens (Van Veggel et al., 2018; Libby et al., 2015; Bondarev et al., 2021). Beyond multiple myeloma, panobinostat has been scrutinized in a variety of clinical settings—including cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, acute myeloid leukemia, diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, and several solid tumor malignancies—to explore its antitumor potential in combination therapies, given its capacity to potentiate the cytotoxic effects of other agents by modulating epigenetic regulation (Cea et al., 2013; Cinek & Karalı, 2021; Libby et al., 2015). Despite its demonstrated efficacy in cancer, there is no recorded use of panobinostat in ophthalmological diseases such as dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or in any similar degenerative condition. The extensive body of clinical research on HDAC inhibitors has predominantly focused on antineoplastic applications, and while some mechanistic parallels exist between the cellular processes targeted in cancer and those disrupted in degenerative retinal diseases, panobinostat’s utility in dry AMD remains an uncharted territory that has thus far not been explored in preclinical or clinical trials (Dokmanovic, Clarke, & Marks, 2007; Morabito et al., 2016; Libby et al., 2015).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, panobinostat exerts its biological effects primarily through the inhibition of histone deacetylase enzymes. The compound’s hydroxamic acid group binds with high affinity to the zinc ion located in the catalytic domain of HDAC enzymes, thereby blocking the deacetylation of lysine residues on histone tails as well as on several non-histone proteins. This blockade causes an accumulation of acetylated histones, which in turn results in a more open chromatin conformation that facilitates enhanced transcription of a multitude of genes, including those pivotal for cell cycle arrest, apoptosis, and cellular differentiation (Benedetti, Conte, & Altucci, 2015; Morabito et al., 2016). Beyond its classical role in modifying histone tail acetylation, panobinostat’s broad inhibition across HDAC classes implies that it can modulate the acetylation status of key transcription factors, chaperone proteins (such as heat shock protein 90), and structural proteins like α-tubulin. This wide-ranging impact on protein acetylation alters the functional activity of numerous signaling pathways and cellular processes, contributing to anti-proliferative and pro-apoptotic outcomes in cancer cells (Morabito et al., 2016). The pleiotropic nature of its action is further evidenced by the induction of autophagy in various tumor models, an effect thought to be mediated by the increased acetylation and transcriptional activation of master regulators of lysosomal biogenesis such as transcription factor EB (TFEB). Although the provided literature does not explicitly detail TFEB upregulation in response to panobinostat, the general tendency of HDAC inhibitors to enhance acetylation-dependent transcription supports the hypothesis that TFEB and its downstream lysosomal genes could be upregulated—thereby promoting autophagy and lysosomal clearance pathways (Cinek & Karalı, 2021; Libby et al., 2015). This complex interplay of molecular events not only underpins panobinostat’s established antitumor activity but also provides a rationale for its possible repurposing in degenerative diseases where enhanced cellular clearance mechanisms may be therapeutic (Van Veggel et al., 2018; Benedetti, Conte, & Altucci, 2015).

Expected Effect in Dry Age-Related Macular Degeneration (AMD):  
Dry age-related macular degeneration is characterized by the progressive dysfunction of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), which is responsible for the maintenance of photoreceptor health and the clearance of cellular debris. A central pathological hallmark of dry AMD is the accumulation of drusen deposits beneath the RPE, partly attributable to impaired lysosomal degradation and autophagy. In the context of this disease, the hypothesis proposes that localized ocular administration of panobinostat could inhibit HDAC activity in RPE cells, leading to a global increase in histone acetylation. This epigenetic modulation is expected to activate acetylation-dependent transcription factors such as TFEB—a master regulator of lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy—that, once activated, upregulates a network of genes involved in lysosomal acidification and cathepsin D expression (Van Veggel et al., 2018; Cinek & Karalı, 2021). Enhanced expression of these lysosomal components is anticipated to restore or improve the degradative capacity of the RPE, facilitating the clearance of drusen deposits and ameliorating the pathological buildup of cellular waste characteristic of dry AMD.

In preclinical oncology studies, panobinostat has consistently induced autophagy and promoted lysosomal function in cancer cells, leading to growth inhibition and apoptosis. If similar cellular responses occur in RPE cells, then panobinostat may stimulate a beneficial autophagic flux that targets accumulated proteins and lipids for degradation (Libby et al., 2015). The expression of cathepsin D—a lysosomal protease critical for the degradation of photoreceptor outer segments and other metabolic substrates—is well documented in RPE cells, and its activity is tightly regulated by lysosomal pH; thus, any intervention that improves lysosomal acidification is likely to have a favorable impact on RPE homeostasis (Mottamal et al., 2015; Morabito et al., 2016). These findings support the proposed mechanism whereby panobinostat’s inhibition of HDACs may indirectly enhance the transcriptional activation of TFEB, culminating in improved lysosomal biogenesis and function. Moreover, the broad HDAC inhibitory profile of panobinostat ensures that multiple redundant deacetylation pathways are targeted simultaneously, offering the potential for robust and sustained activation of the cellular clearance machinery compared to more selective agents (Morabito et al., 2016; Carafa, Nebbioso, & Altucci, 2011).

However, the concept of localized ocular dosing—via intravitreal injection or topical delivery—could potentially mitigate these risks by achieving high local drug concentrations with minimal systemic exposure (Libby et al., 2015; Karol et al., 2020). In the specific context of dry AMD, where chronic, localized pathology is present in the retina, targeted delivery of panobinostat could allow for the modulation of RPE cellular processes without triggering widespread adverse reactions. This targeted approach aligns with current trends in ocular pharmacotherapy, which increasingly favor local drug delivery systems designed to maximize therapeutic efficacy while minimizing systemic toxicity (Bondarev et al., 2021; Van Veggel et al., 2018). Ultimately, the expected outcome in the proposed assay is that panobinostat treatment will lead to measurable upregulation of lysosomal gene expression, restoration of lysosomal acidification, and enhanced activity of cathepsin D within RPE cells, thereby reducing the burden of drusen deposits and potentially slowing the progression of dry AMD (Cea et al., 2013; Libby et al., 2015).

Overall Evaluation:  
The repurposing of panobinostat for dry age-related macular degeneration presents an intriguing and biologically plausible strategy that leverages the compound’s well-documented HDAC inhibitory properties to modulate critical intracellular degradation pathways. One of the foremost strengths of this therapeutic candidate is its potent, broad-spectrum inhibition of HDAC enzymes at low nanomolar concentrations, which has been repeatedly demonstrated in various preclinical and clinical studies in oncology (Van Veggel et al., 2018; Morabito et al., 2016). The resultant hyperacetylation of histones and non-histone proteins not only promotes cell cycle arrest and apoptosis in malignant cells but also facilitates the transcriptional activation of autophagy- and lysosome-related genes—a pathway that could be harnessed to restore faithful lysosomal degradation in retinal pigment epithelial cells affected in dry AMD (Benedetti, Conte, & Altucci, 2015; Cinek & Karalı, 2021).

In terms of mechanistic specificity, the broad inhibitory profile of panobinostat could be seen as an advantage in the context of dry AMD, where multiple deacetylation pathways may contribute to the impaired clearance of cellular debris. By simultaneously inhibiting several HDAC isoforms, panobinostat is likely to achieve a more robust activation of TFEB and other transcription factors central to lysosomal biogenesis, thereby amplifying the cellular clearance mechanisms required to remove drusen deposits (Morabito et al., 2016; Carafa, Nebbioso, & Altucci, 2011). Additionally, the existing clinical experience with panobinostat in oncology provides a rich repository of pharmacokinetic, pharmacodynamic, and safety data that can inform dose optimization and risk management strategies—albeit with the caveat that ocular tissues may respond differently to HDAC inhibition than cancer cells (Bondarev et al., 2021; Libby et al., 2015).

Nevertheless, several significant weaknesses must be acknowledged in evaluating panobinostat as a candidate for dry AMD treatment. Chief among these is the potential for systemic toxicity. Panobinostat’s clinical utilization in cancer has been limited by adverse side effects including gastrointestinal toxicity, thrombocytopenia, and cardiac complications, and although localized ocular delivery may attenuate these concerns, the safety profile of panobinostat in retinal tissues remains largely unexplored (Libby et al., 2015; Karol et al., 2020). Moreover, the pharmacokinetic behavior of panobinostat when administered locally to the eye is unknown; challenges such as drug solubility, stability, and diffusion across retinal layers must be addressed rigorously in preclinical models. There is also the possibility of off-target effects in retinal cells that could exacerbate retinal stress or contribute to unwanted inflammation, particularly given the complex interplay of epigenetic regulation in non-dividing, highly specialized cells like the RPE (Cea et al., 2013; Benedetti, Conte, & Altucci, 2015).

Another point of concern is the translational leap from oncology to ophthalmology. While the mechanistic rationale for using panobinostat to enhance autophagy and lysosomal function is supported by its effects in cancer cells, RPE cells possess distinctive metabolic and regulatory pathways that may not respond identically to HDAC inhibition. The degree to which TFEB and other autophagy or lysosomal genes are modulated by panobinostat in RPE cells has not yet been directly demonstrated, and significant differences in chromatin structure and gene expression profiles between cancer cells and differentiated RPE cells could impact both efficacy and safety outcomes (Morabito et al., 2016; Carafa, Nebbioso, & Altucci, 2011). In addition, the chronic nature of dry AMD necessitates long-term treatment, and the potential cumulative effects of continuous HDAC inhibition in ocular tissues raise concerns regarding retinal integrity, visual function, and overall ocular health over extended periods—a consideration that remains entirely speculative without targeted preclinical studies (Dokmanovic, Clarke, & Marks, 2007; Morabito et al., 2016).

From a drug development perspective, the strategy of repurposing panobinostat for dry AMD is compelling because it integrates a well-characterized molecular mode of action with an unmet clinical need. However, critical translational challenges must be overcome. These include reformulating panobinostat for localized ocular delivery, establishing appropriate dosing regimens that maximize local efficacy while minimizing toxicity, and conducting comprehensive preclinical evaluations in relevant in vitro and in vivo models of dry AMD. The potential benefit of enhancing lysosomal clearance through increased TFEB activation is a particularly attractive aspect of this proposal, as impaired autophagy and lysosomal dysfunction are recognized contributors to the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Cinek & Karalı, 2021; Morabito et al., 2016). Nonetheless, a careful balance must be maintained, as excessive activation of autophagy pathways in non-proliferative tissues may inadvertently trigger cell death or exacerbated stress responses.

In summary, while panobinostat’s established efficacy in oncology and its well-documented ability to induce broad epigenetic changes provide a strong scientific foundation for its potential repurposing, a number of critical challenges remain. On the positive side, panobinostat is among the most potent HDAC inhibitors available, capable of eliciting profound changes in gene expression that might restore lysosomal function in RPE cells and thereby clear accumulated drusen deposits. In addition, modern advances in ocular drug delivery—such as intravitreal injections, biodegradable implants, or topical formulations enhanced by nanocarrier systems—offer promising routes to achieve the necessary drug concentrations in the retina while mitigating systemic exposure and toxicity (Van Veggel et al., 2018; Morabito et al., 2016).

Conversely, the risk of adverse effects related to HDAC inhibition, the unknown ocular pharmacokinetics, and the potential differences in cellular responses between cancerous and retinal cells represent significant hurdles that must be rigorously addressed through targeted preclinical research. Furthermore, given that panobinostat’s clinical track record is largely confined to oncology, its application in a degenerative ocular disease such as dry AMD would require new, dedicated studies to validate its safety, efficacy, and optimal delivery modality in this context (Libby et al., 2015; Afifi et al., 2015).

Overall, panobinostat emerges as a promising yet challenging candidate for repurposing in dry age‐related macular degeneration. Its ability to robustly inhibit multiple HDAC isoforms and thereby potentially activate TFEB and lysosomal gene networks aligns well with the therapeutic strategy of improving autophagic clearance in RPE cells. However, substantial gaps in knowledge remain regarding its direct effects on retinal cells and the feasibility of its long-term use in an ocular setting. Consequently, while the mechanistic rationale is strong and the preclinical evidence from oncology provides useful insights, extensive additional research is needed to assess the translational potential, determine safe and efficacious ocular dosing parameters, and ultimately validate this approach in models that reliably mimic the pathophysiology of dry AMD (Prince et al., 2009; Morabito et al., 2016; Benedetti, Conte, & Altucci, 2015; Bondarev et al., 2021).

In conclusion, panobinostat’s repurposing for dry AMD is grounded in a robust understanding of epigenetic regulation and lysosomal biology. Its established clinical use in oncology offers a wealth of pharmacological data and a precedent for potent HDAC inhibition, while the hypothesis that HDAC inhibitors can reactivate latent clearance pathways in RPE cells is both innovative and scientifically plausible. The strengths of panobinostat lie in its potency, broad-spectrum activity, and documented ability to elicit autophagic responses, which collectively suggest that, under the right conditions and with a carefully optimized ocular delivery system, it could address one of the major pathophysiological mechanisms underlying dry AMD. Nonetheless, the weaknesses, including potential off-target toxicity, uncertain ocular pharmacokinetics, and the need for a comprehensive reevaluation of its effects in non-malignant, differentiated cell types, must be thoroughly investigated before advancing into clinical studies. Therefore, data from directed preclinical experiments employing RPE cell cultures and animal models of dry AMD will be essential in determining whether the benefits of panobinostat can be safely and effectively harnessed to treat this common cause of vision loss in the elderly (Srinivas, 2017; Van Veggel et al., 2018; Bondarev et al., 2021; Carafa, Nebbioso, & Altucci, 2011).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Everolimus (Afinitor; Novartis) is a semi‐synthetic derivative of sirolimus—a macrolide originally isolated from Streptomyces hygroscopicus—as evidenced by its chemical designation as 4-O-(2-hydroxyethyl)-rapamycin (Liu et al., 2023, pp. 11–12). By introducing a 2-hydroxyethyl group at position 40, everolimus achieves greater hydrophilicity and an increased oral bioavailability (from 10% to 16% relative to sirolimus) while retaining the core macrolactone structure that is characteristic of rapalogs (Liu et al., 2023, pp. 11–12; Weber, 2015, pp. 27–28). This compound belongs to the class of mTOR inhibitors—specifically, a first‐generation rapalog that selectively inhibits the mTOR complex 1 (mTORC1) while sparing mTORC2 (Liu et al., 2023, pp. 10–11; Weber, 2015, pp. 27–28). As a synthetic derivative of a naturally occurring product, everolimus represents the successful strategy of chemical modification to optimize pharmacokinetic properties and clinical tolerability. The design parameters underpinning everolimus’ synthesis have been guided by the goal of retaining potent immunosuppressive and anti‐proliferative effects while optimizing parameters such as solubility, half‐life, and tissue penetration, with the added advantage of an oral formulation already approved for several clinical indications (Liu et al., 2023, pp. 11–12; Wang et al., 2022, pp. 6–8).

Therapeutic History:  
Everolimus has a well‐established therapeutic history as an immunosuppressant and antineoplastic agent. Clinically, it is approved for treating advanced renal cell carcinoma, progressive neuroendocrine tumors of pancreatic origin, and subependymal giant cell astrocytoma in tuberous sclerosis complex patients who are not candidates for surgery (Wang et al., 2022, pp. 6–8; Weber, 2015, pp. 27–28). In these indications, its mechanism as an mTORC1 inhibitor serves to arrest cell cycle progression and inhibit angiogenesis, which are central to its antitumor activity (Kuo et al., 2018, pp. 5–7; Weber, 2015, pp. 27–28). Moreover, everolimus has been effectively used in the context of organ transplantation to prevent allograft rejection by impairing helper T‐cell proliferation (Wang et al., 2022, pp. 6–8; Weber, 2015, pp. 27–28).

With regard to ocular applications, although everolimus has not been approved specifically for dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD), several preclinical studies have demonstrated its potential benefits in ocular cell types and models. For instance, in vitro investigations have highlighted that everolimus can inhibit the proliferation and migration of retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells and modulate mTOR signaling within retinal tissue—an effect critical to conditions such as proliferative vitreoretinopathy (PVR) (Kuo et al., 2018, pp. 5–8). Additionally, clinical trials such as the Phase 2 randomized trial for neovascular AMD (albeit focused on wet AMD) have assessed everolimus’s efficacy in combination with anti‐vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) agents (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2009), thereby providing indirect support for its ocular pharmacokinetic (PK) profile and safety profile. This background, combined with its well‐known systemic tolerability, underscores its candidacy for repurposing in nonexudative (dry) AMD—a disease area in which few pharmacologic treatments exist.

Mechanism of Action:  
Everolimus exerts its effects by binding to the intracellular receptor FKBP12, forming a complex that interacts with and inhibits mTORC1 (Liu et al., 2023, pp. 11–12; Weber, 2015, pp. 27–28). The inhibition of mTORC1 results in a downstream decrease in the phosphorylation of ribosomal protein S6 kinase (S6K1) and other substrates such as ribosomal protein S6 (RPS6), effectively suppressing cap‐dependent protein synthesis and cellular proliferation (Kuo et al., 2018, pp. 5–7; Liu et al., 2023, pp. 10–11). In the context of RPE cells, inhibition of mTORC1 plays a particularly critical role in modulating autophagic flux. Under normal conditions, mTORC1 phosphorylates and suppresses the transcription factor EB (TFEB), a master regulator of lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy. Inhibition of mTORC1 frees TFEB to translocate to the nucleus where it transactivates genes that codify for lysosomal proteins, such as the subunits of the vacuolar ATPase (V‐ATPase), and hydrolases including cathepsin D (Kuo et al., 2018, p. 7; Nieto et al., 2015, pp. 28–32). Preclinical studies have shown that in RPE culture systems, treatment with everolimus results in an increase in LC3 turnover—a marker of enhanced autophagic flux—and accelerates the maturation of cathepsin D (CTSD), which is essential for effective lysosomal degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (Kuo et al., 2018, pp. 5–8). Such modulation of the autophagy–lysosome pathway is mechanistically attractive in dry AMD because the accumulation of cellular debris and lipofuscin in RPE cells is implicated in disease pathogenesis. Furthermore, it has been reported that everolimus displays superior ocular tissue penetration compared with sirolimus in in vitro porcine corneal models, suggesting that its formulation could be optimized for direct ocular administration if required (Liu et al., 2023, pp. 11–14). Overall, the biochemical profile of everolimus supports the hypothesis that targeted mTORC1 inhibition in RPE cells could lead to enhanced TFEB activation and a subsequent restoration of lysosomal function—thereby addressing one of the key pathological features underlying dry AMD.

Expected Effect:  
The hypothesis proposes that everolimus will inhibit mTORC1 in RPE cells, leading to the activation of TFEB, a critical step in lysosomal biogenesis and function. Upon release from mTORC1‐mediated phosphorylation constraints, TFEB translocates to the nucleus where it upregulates the expression of essential lysosomal genes, including those encoding V‐ATPase subunits (which are responsible for lysosomal acidification) and cathepsin D (CTSD), a protease required for the degradation of accumulated waste products (Kuo et al., 2018, p. 7; Nieto et al., 2015, pp. 28–32). This molecular cascade is expected to improve the clearance of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) and other cellular debris that accumulate in RPE cells owing to age‐related impairment of autophagy. In vitro data support that everolimus treatment increases LC3 turnover and facilitates the maturation of CTSD, both of which are indicative of enhanced autophagic flux and lysosomal functionality (Kuo et al., 2018, pp. 5–8). Given that RPE cells naturally express components of the mTOR signaling pathway—including high levels of mTORC1—and that dysfunctional lysosomal clearance is a hallmark of dry AMD (as exemplified by the accumulation of lipofuscin and drusen formation), the expected pharmacodynamic effect of everolimus would be to restore homeostasis in these cells. Successful activation of TFEB is anticipated to lead to improved degradation of damaged organelles and protein aggregates, potentially mitigating the progression of retinal degeneration characteristic of dry AMD. Moreover, the fact that everolimus is already formulated for oral administration with a known ocular PK profile further supports the translational potential of this candidate: systemic dosing may achieve sufficient retinal concentrations to exert the desired effects in RPE cells without necessitating invasive delivery methods (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2009; Liu et al., 2023, pp. 11–12).

Overall Evaluation:  
The potential of everolimus as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD is supported by several compelling factors. First, its established clinical safety and efficacy in other indications—such as renal cell carcinoma and immunosuppression in transplantation—reduce the translational risk associated with drug repurposing (Weber, 2015, pp. 27–28; Wang et al., 2022, pp. 6–8). The fact that everolimus is an FDA‐approved agent with an oral formulation makes it an attractive candidate for repurposing, as its dosing, systemic distribution, and side‐effect profile are already well characterized. In addition, its selective inhibition of mTORC1 has a clear mechanistic rationale in the context of dry AMD. By specifically targeting the mTORC1–TFEB axis, everolimus may correct the impaired lysosomal degradation and autophagic dysfunction that underlie the accumulation of pathogenic debris in RPE cells (Kuo et al., 2018, p. 7; Nieto et al., 2015, pp. 28–32).

A major strength of everolimus is the robust preclinical evidence indicative of its capacity to modulate autophagy. In ocular cell culture systems, everolimus has been shown to enhance LC3 turnover and promote CTSD maturation—both key markers of autophagic and lysosomal efficiency (Kuo et al., 2018, pp. 5–8). Additionally, its improved ocular penetration compared to its parent compound sirolimus suggests that even systemic administration might yield therapeutically relevant levels in the retina (Liu et al., 2023, pp. 11–14). This represents a significant advantage in the context of dry AMD, where achieving effective drug delivery to deeply situated retinal tissues is a persistent challenge.

However, several weaknesses must be acknowledged. Despite a sound mechanistic rationale, direct clinical evidence for everolimus’s efficacy in dry AMD is lacking. Existing clinical studies have primarily focused on other ocular conditions such as neovascular AMD and PVR, and the particular pathophysiology of dry AMD—with its complex interplay of oxidative stress, complement dysregulation, and chronic inflammation—may require a more nuanced therapeutic approach (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2009; Kuo et al., 2018, pp. 3–5). It is also important to consider the potential systemic side effects of mTOR inhibition, which include hyperglycemia, dyslipidemia, stomatitis, and, in some cases, immunosuppression (Weber, 2015, pp. 27–28, 28–29). Although these adverse events are generally manageable in oncology and transplant settings, the chronic nature of dry AMD treatment may necessitate a careful balancing of therapeutic benefits against systemic risks. Moreover, while everolimus selectively inhibits mTORC1, prolonged inhibition of this pathway could potentially interfere with homeostatic cellular processes beyond autophagy, raising concerns about long‐term retinal safety.

Another consideration relates to the multifactorial etiology of dry AMD. While lysosomal dysfunction is a critical aspect of the disease, it is accompanied by other pathological processes such as oxidative damage, chronic inflammation, and alterations in the complement cascade. Thus, monotherapy with an mTORC1 inhibitor may not be sufficiently robust to address all disease mechanisms. Combination therapies that target multiple pathological pathways might ultimately be necessary for effective disease modification. Lastly, discrepancies in the translation of preclinical findings to human disease remain a persistent challenge. For example, while certain animal models of retinal disease have demonstrated beneficial effects of mTOR inhibition, analogous results have not always been replicated in clinical settings (Kuo et al., 2018, pp. 3–5; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2009).

In summary, everolimus presents as a mechanistically intriguing candidate for repurposing in dry AMD due to its ability to inhibit mTORC1 and thereby promote TFEB‐mediated restoration of lysosomal function. Its solid record as an FDA‐approved drug with established dosing regimens and acceptable systemic safety lends additional support to its viability as a repurposing candidate. Preclinical data suggest that everolimus increases autophagic flux in RPE cells, enhancing LC3 turnover and CTSD maturation, which theoretically should facilitate the clearance of pathological debris that characterizes dry AMD (Kuo et al., 2018, pp. 5–8). The advantages of an oral formulation and favorable ocular pharmacokinetics further underpin its translational potential (Liu et al., 2023, pp. 11–12; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2009).

Nonetheless, the candidate also faces important challenges. Key limitations include the absence of direct clinical evidence for efficacy in dry AMD, potential systemic adverse effects associated with prolonged mTORC1 inhibition, and the inherent complexity of dry AMD pathology, which may require multimodal therapeutic strategies. Moreover, past experiences in ocular applications—such as studies in PVR models where everolimus did not yield a statistically significant clinical improvement—highlight the need for carefully controlled dose-finding and safety studies (Kuo et al., 2018, pp. 3–5). It will be crucial to establish that systemic dosing can achieve therapeutic retinal concentrations without eliciting unintended systemic toxicity or disrupting normal RPE physiology.

Overall, while mechanistic and preclinical data provide a strong rationale for repurposing everolimus to treat dry AMD, further rigorous preclinical studies specifically in models of dry AMD are warranted. A careful evaluation of dosing regimens, potential adverse effects, and efficacy endpoints will be essential in the translational development of everolimus for this indication. The mechanistic specificity for mTORC1 inhibition, combined with the ability to enhance autophagic clearance in RPE cells, represents a significant strength that could offer a novel approach to modifying the course of dry AMD. However, the challenges associated with systemic mTOR inhibition and the need for combination strategies or localized delivery systems must be addressed in subsequent research phases. In conclusion, everolimus is a promising, though not yet definitively validated, candidate for repurposing in dry AMD, and we recommend that further detailed studies be undertaken to fully elucidate its potential in restoring lysosomal function and ameliorating retinal degeneration in this patient population (Liu et al., 2023, pp. 11–12; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2009; Kuo et al., 2018, pp. 5–7; Weber, 2015, pp. 27–28; Wang et al., 2022, pp. 6–8; Kuo et al., 2018, pp. 7–8).

Abstract—Metformin, a synthetic biguanide derived from galegine (French lilac), is widely used as first-line therapy for type 2 diabetes mellitus and has pleiotropic cellular effects that intersect with age-related macular degeneration (AMD) biology, including AMPK activation, modulation of mTOR signaling, autophagy induction, anti-inflammatory actions, mitochondrial support, anti-senescence effects, and anti-angiogenic signaling in retinal models (Amin et al., 2022). Multiple preclinical studies in RPE cell lines and rodent retinal injury/degeneration models show that metformin preserves RPE barrier integrity, reduces oxidative and inflammatory stress, supports mitochondrial biogenesis, and maintains photoreceptor structure/function, largely via AMPK-dependent pathways; however, dry AMD–specific randomized clinical efficacy data remain limited and observational epidemiology is heterogeneous, with mixed associations across populations, exposure definitions, and AMD subtypes (Amin et al., 2022; Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Gokhale et al., 2023; Liang et al., 2022; Moir et al., 2023; Romdhoniyyah et al., 2021). Critically, while AMPK→mTORC1→autophagy is well-supported in retinal contexts, direct evidence for metformin-driven TFEB nuclear translocation, V-ATPase upregulation, or cathepsin D (CTSD) maturation in human RPE/AMD models is not demonstrated in the excerpted literature, representing material gaps for the central hypothesis (Amin et al., 2022; Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Buonfiglio et al., 2024). Overall, metformin is a biologically plausible, low-cost, and generally safe repurposing candidate for dry AMD that warrants mechanistic confirmation in RPE for lysosome-centric endpoints and rigorous randomized trials across AMD stages (Amin et al., 2022; Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Moir et al., 2023).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Metformin is a small-molecule biguanide synthesized as a derivative of galegine, a guanidine-class alkaloid originally isolated from the plant Galega officinalis; clinically it has been used for more than 60 years as the most commonly prescribed oral antihyperglycemic agent worldwide (class: biguanides) (Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Amin et al., 2022). Chemically, metformin comprises two coupled guanidine moieties conferring cationic, hydrophilic properties and cellular accumulation via organic cation transporters, consistent with mitochondrial complex I engagement and AMPK pathway activation described in mechanistic literature (Augustin & Atorf, 2023). Beyond glycemic control, metformin exhibits pleiotropic effects—anti-inflammatory, anti-oxidative, anti-angiogenic, anti-apoptotic and anti-senescence—reported in diverse cell types and tissues, many of which intersect with pathways implicated in AMD pathogenesis (oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, impaired proteostasis/autophagy, para-inflammation, vascular dysregulation) (Amin et al., 2022; Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Kozlowski, 2023). In ocular contexts, preclinical work indicates that metformin activates AMPK in RPE and neural retina and can preserve retinal structure and function under oxidative, metabolic, and phototoxic stressors (Amin et al., 2022). Collectively, these properties position metformin as a rational repurposing candidate for dry AMD, wherein RPE dysfunction, impaired autophagy/lysosomal clearance, mitochondrial stress, and chronic inflammation are central pathogenic nodes (Amin et al., 2022; Buonfiglio et al., 2024).

Therapeutic History  
Systemic use: Metformin is established first-line therapy for type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) and has been investigated broadly for aging-related conditions due to putative geroprotective effects; long-term safety has been documented, including in the Diabetes Prevention Program (DPP) where gastrointestinal intolerance is the most common adverse event and lactic acidosis was not observed under trial conditions, though B12 deficiency can occur with chronic use (Amin et al., 2022; Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Zhou & Xue, 2024). Preclinical ocular use: In retinal models, metformin has been tested systemically (oral/IP) and intravitreally, demonstrating protective effects in RPE and photoreceptors across light-damage, iodate-induced injury, inherited retinal degeneration (rd1/rd10), and oxygen-induced retinopathy (OIR) with readouts including preserved RPE tight junctions (ZO-1, occludin), outer nuclear layer thickness, and ERG amplitudes; notable anti-angiogenic activity includes decreased CNV lesion size and VEGF/VEGFR signaling modulation in several models (Amin et al., 2022). In these preclinical settings, metformin’s ocular benefits are frequently attributed to AMPK activation and downstream autophagy/mitochondrial and anti-inflammatory pathways, without overt ocular toxicity reported in rodents; however, human ocular safety data and pharmacokinetics under intravitreal or high-dose local exposure are not detailed in the excerpts (Amin et al., 2022).

Clinical/epidemiologic AMD history: Observational epidemiology offers mixed signals. Several large retrospective cohorts and case–control analyses associate metformin use with reduced odds or risk of any AMD or early AMD, with dose–duration trends in some datasets (e.g., MarketScan/claims OR 0.93 and propensity-matched HR 0.57; Taiwanese cohorts HR ~0.54 with stronger protection at >4 years and higher average daily doses), and lower odds reported in multiple studies across US, Europe, and Asia (Amin et al., 2022; Jiang et al., 2022; Kozlowski, 2023; Moir et al., 2023). Other datasets report null or complex associations: a high-quality UK T2DM cohort found no differential AMD risk with metformin using time-varying exposure models; a U.S. claims analysis focusing on dry AMD reported current use slightly increased dry AMD risk while prior use trended protective; additional analyses show no association or heterogeneity by diabetic retinopathy status (Eton et al., 2022; Gokhale et al., 2023; Liang et al., 2022). Meta-analyses also conflict: a systematic review of diabetics suggested decreased odds of AMD with metformin, whereas a broader 2024 meta-analysis concluded no overall prophylactic/treatment role; a European meta-analysis of antidiabetic/lipid-lowering drugs found reduced AMD prevalence overall but not for late-stage AMD specifically (Elhalag et al., 2024; Mauschitz et al., 2023). Importantly, these retrospective designs face confounding (e.g., smoking, comorbidities, health-care utilization), outcome misclassification (wet vs dry AMD), and exposure misclassification (adherence), limiting causal inference and stage-specific conclusions (Brown et al., 2019; Gokhale et al., 2023; Moir et al., 2023). Prospective interventional testing for dry AMD is underway: a randomized, single-blind Phase II trial of metformin to slow geographic atrophy (GA) progression has been conducted, with publication reported in 2024 (Shen et al., 2024); however, the excerpts do not provide efficacy outcomes in GA and emphasize that randomized evidence remains needed (Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Shen et al., 2024).

No regulatory approval exists for metformin in AMD (dry or wet), and the totality of evidence remains preclinical and observational for efficacy, with one randomized GA study reported but without effect-size details here; therefore, clinical utility in dry AMD is presently unproven (Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Shen et al., 2024).

Mechanism of Action  
Canonical pharmacology: Metformin partially inhibits mitochondrial respiratory complex I, reducing hepatic ATP and increasing AMP/ADP, thereby activating AMPK, the cellular energy sensor that shifts metabolism toward ATP-generating pathways; AMPK-dependent and ‑independent mechanisms operate systemically, including reduced hepatic gluconeogenesis, increased enterocyte glucose uptake/GLP-1 secretion, and microbiome modulation with potential systemic anti-inflammatory effects (Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Kozlowski, 2023).

Retinal/RPE mechanisms: In RPE cell lines (e.g., ARPE-19), metformin increases pAMPK and triggers autophagy, reduces ROS, decreases apoptosis, and preserves tight junction proteins (ZO-1, occludin), thereby maintaining barrier integrity under oxidative challenges (Amin et al., 2022; Augustin & Atorf, 2023). At the molecular level, treatment increases Sirt1 and multiple mitochondrial biogenesis and antioxidant markers (SOD-2, Nrf1, Tfam, PGC-1α, COX-II), restores NADH:NAD+ ratios and ATP, and lowers inflammatory mediators (NF-κB signaling, IL-6) (Amin et al., 2022). These signatures are consistent with AMPK’s coordinate regulation of autophagy and mitochondrial homeostasis observed in RPE/retinal contexts, contributing to improved proteostasis and reduced oxidative stress—key failure modes in dry AMD (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Amin et al., 2022).

In vivo, systemic or intravitreal metformin preserves photoreceptors and RPE structure/function in light-damage, iodate injury, and inherited degeneration models (rd1, rd10), with ERG preservation and ONL maintenance; mechanistically, AMPK activation is necessary for light-damage protection in an isoform-specific manner (AMPKα2 dependency), and retina-specific Pparδ is not required, supporting an AMPK-centric retinal mechanism rather than PPARδ signaling (Amin et al., 2022). Metformin also dampens retinal senescence and SASP in OIR after intravitreal dosing, with decreased cdkn1a/cdkn2a and NF-κB/IL-6 signaling, implicating anti-senescence immunomodulation as an additional neurovascular protective mechanism (Amin et al., 2022). Anti-angiogenic actions involve AMPK-dependent and ‑independent pathways: decreased VEGFR2 via enhanced ubiquitin–proteasome degradation, altered VEGF-A isoform splicing toward less angiogenic forms, reduced Flk-1 expression, and inhibition of ALK1-mediated angiogenesis; collectively these actions reduce CNV lesion size, endothelial proliferation/migration/tube formation, and neovascularization in OIR, diabetic, and laser-CNV models (Amin et al., 2022; Augustin & Atorf, 2023). Inflammatory suppression includes reductions in ICAM-1/MCP-1 (AMPK-dependent) and NF-κB p65/IL-8 (AMPK-independent), accompanied by decreased leukostasis and cytokines across models; NLRP3 inflammasome inhibition and modulation of macrophage polarization further contribute to reduced para-inflammation (Amin et al., 2022; Dang et al., 2021; Augustin & Atorf, 2023).

mTOR/autophagy axis: AMPK activation by metformin can inhibit mTORC1, activate the ULK complex, and initiate autophagy, which in RPE promotes clearance of damaged organelles, reduces ROS, and protects against oxidative injury—mechanistically vital for countering autophagy/lysosomal dysfunction in AMD (Dang et al., 2021; Zhou & Xue, 2024). Several retinal studies report AMPK-linked increases in autophagosome formation, and some contextual discussion references mTOR modulation in retinal protection, including translational control via EF2K and general proteostasis benefits (e.g., mutant opsin trafficking) with mixed in vivo translation (Amin et al., 2022). While AMPK→mTOR→autophagy activation is strongly implicated, explicit experimental confirmation in the provided corpus for metformin-driven TFEB nuclear translocation, V-ATPase upregulation, or increased cathepsin D maturation/activity in RPE is lacking; several reviews and excerpts explicitly note these as gaps requiring targeted mechanistic studies (Amin et al., 2022; Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Buonfiglio et al., 2024).

Dose/context dependence and AMPK-independent considerations: Some analyses suggest that AMPK activation by metformin in vitro can require suprapharmacologic concentrations and that certain systemic antihyperglycemic effects are AMPK-independent in hepatocytes; in retinal contexts, isoform-specific AMPKα2 dependence is observed for photoreceptor protection, yet disease models can yield mixed outcomes (e.g., limited benefit or worse function in some HFD diabetic retinopathy paradigms), underscoring the need to define dosing, timing, and disease-stage context for retinal efficacy (Amin et al., 2022; Moir et al., 2023). These data caution against assuming uniform AMPK-mediated benefit across all retinal diseases or AMD stages and highlight the importance of pharmacokinetics, tissue exposure, and therapeutic window in the eye (Moir et al., 2023).

Translational addenda—microbiome and lipid handling: Metformin alters gut microbiota and systemic metabolites, which has been linked to reduced retinal neovascularization through a putative “gut–retina axis,” and may also reduce OxLDL uptake and promote cholesterol efflux via AMPK/LXR–ABCA1/G1 signaling, potentially limiting drusen-related lipid accumulation and NLRP3 activation in RPE (Dang et al., 2021; Zhou & Xue, 2024).

Summary of mechanistic sufficiency for the hypothesis: The literature robustly supports metformin’s activation of AMPK in RPE/retina, inhibition of inflammatory and oxidative pathways, modulation of mTOR/autophagy, and preservation of RPE and photoreceptor function in multiple preclinical models—mechanistic axes consistent with dry AMD biology (Amin et al., 2022; Zhou & Xue, 2024). However, direct experimental evidence in the provided corpus for metformin-induced TFEB nuclear translocation, increased V-ATPase expression, or enhanced cathepsin D maturation/activity in human RPE is not shown; several reviews explicitly note TFEB/V-ATPase/CTSD endpoints as critical gaps that merit targeted validation in AMD-relevant assays (Amin et al., 2022; Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Buonfiglio et al., 2024).

Expected Effect  
Assay-level predictions for RPE models: In human RPE cell lines and iPSC-RPE, metformin at concentrations compatible with cellular AMPK activation is expected to increase pAMPK (Thr172), reduce mTORC1 activity (e.g., decreased pS6 and p4EBP1), and initiate autophagy (increased LC3-II with enhanced flux in the presence of bafilomycin, reduction in p62/SQSTM1 under steady-state), while decreasing ROS and apoptosis under oxidative stress (e.g., H2O2), preserving tight junction integrity (occludin, ZO-1), and improving mitochondrial function (increased ATP, restored NADH:NAD+ ratio, increased PGC-1α/Tfam/Nrf1 and SOD-2) (Amin et al., 2022). Published in vitro data already support many of these endpoints: metformin reduced ROS and apoptosis, increased pAMPK and antioxidative molecules including Sirt1/Nrf2, and preserved occludin/ZO-1 in ARPE-19 challenged with H2O2 or glyoxal; AMPK inhibition abrogated the protection, indicating dependence on AMPK signaling (Amin et al., 2022). In oxidant or lipid-rich RPE conditions, decreased NF-κB activation and inflammasome signaling (e.g., NLRP3) would be anticipated, consistent with prior reports of metformin inhibiting NF-κB and NLRP3 activation in ocular/immune models (Augustin & Atorf, 2023).

Hypothesized lysosomal/TFEB endpoints: The working hypothesis proposes that AMPK activation by metformin will inhibit mTORC1, promote TFEB nuclear translocation, increase V-ATPase expression, enhance lysosomal acidification, and increase cathepsin D (CTSD) maturation, restoring autophagic flux and preventing RPE degeneration. While the AMPK→mTORC1→autophagy cascade is supported in RPE and retina, the provided literature does not directly demonstrate metformin-induced TFEB nuclear translocation, V-ATPase upregulation, or CTSD maturation increases in RPE; thus, these are testable predictions rather than established metformin actions in RPE (Amin et al., 2022; Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Augustin & Atorf, 2023). Given TFEB’s role in lysosomal biogenesis and function, metformin’s dampening of mTORC1 could plausibly facilitate TFEB nuclear entry, but explicit experimental validation (e.g., TFEB nuclear localization quantification, lysosomal pH assays, V-ATPase subunit expression/activity, pro-CTSD→mature CTSD processing and enzymatic activity assays) is needed to confirm the hypothesized mechanism in AMD-relevant RPE models (Dang et al., 2021; Ebeling et al., 2022).

Target expression plausibility: AMPK is expressed in RPE and retina; stimulation prevents RPE and photoreceptor degeneration in multiple mouse models, and metformin increases pAMPK in human RPE cell lines—indicating sufficient expression and pathway competence for drug action in the assay system (Elhalag et al., 2024; Amin et al., 2022). Downstream readouts of autophagy and mitochondrial biogenesis/antioxidant pathways (LC3-II, PGC-1α, SOD-2, Nrf1, Tfam) have been measured and improved with metformin in RPE/retinal models, supporting assay feasibility and expected directions of effect (Amin et al., 2022).

In vivo expected effects in dry-AMD–relevant models: In toxin- and stress-driven models of RPE/photoreceptor degeneration (e.g., sodium iodate, light-induced damage) and inherited retinal degeneration, metformin is expected to preserve RPE morphology and function, maintain ONL thickness, and preserve ERG signals, consistent with reported benefits mediated by AMPK activation; however, model- and disease-stage–specific responses can vary, and negative/neutral results have been documented in some diabetic retinopathy paradigms, underscoring the need to test across multiple AMD-relevant models and to incorporate timing and dose-response studies (Amin et al., 2022). In models of para-inflammation and senescence, metformin is expected to reduce SASP mediators and senescent RPE or retinal cells, aligning with intravitreal metformin effects in OIR and broader anti-senescence literature (Amin et al., 2022; Kozlowski, 2023).

Clinical expected effects: Based on observational associations, any protective effect may be stronger for early or non-exudative AMD and may display dose–duration dependence; however, epidemiologic heterogeneity and potential confounding mean that no specific effect size can be assumed, and randomized trial confirmation in geographic atrophy and earlier AMD stages is necessary to define clinical benefit and exposure requirements (Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Liang et al., 2022).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Mechanistic convergence on AMD biology: Metformin engages AMPK-dependent and ‑independent processes that directly counter core dry AMD pathomechanisms—oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, impaired autophagy/proteostasis, para-inflammation/senescence, and, secondarily, maladaptive vascular/angio-inflammatory signaling—supported by coherent molecular readouts (pAMPK↑, autophagy induction, mitochondrial biogenesis markers↑, NF-κB/NLRP3↓) in RPE and retinal models (Amin et al., 2022; Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Zhou & Xue, 2024). Preclinical efficacy in preserving RPE barrier proteins and photoreceptor function across multiple insults strengthens biological plausibility for dry AMD (Amin et al., 2022).
- Epidemiologic signal and translational momentum: Multiple large retrospective analyses show reduced odds/risk of AMD—often with dose–duration trends—among metformin users, and a randomized GA trial has been conducted, indicating clinical interest and feasibility for prospective testing (Amin et al., 2022; Jiang et al., 2022; Moir et al., 2023; Shen et al., 2024). Meta-analytic work in diabetics suggests potential protective associations, especially in early AMD, reinforcing the rationale to test in non-diabetic AMD populations with controlled exposure (Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Liang et al., 2022).
- Favorable systemic safety and low cost: Decades of broad clinical use, with well-characterized safety signals (GI intolerance, B12 deficiency; rare lactic acidosis risk under renal/hepatic compromise), make metformin attractive from a risk–benefit and access perspective for an elderly AMD population, assuming ocular safety is confirmed (Amin et al., 2022; Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Zhou & Xue, 2024).
- Ocular delivery flexibility and mechanistic redundancy: Both systemic and intravitreal dosing have produced retinal benefits in animals; intravitreal delivery achieved senescence suppression independent of anti-VEGF effects, suggesting non-overlapping mechanisms that could complement existing therapies (Amin et al., 2022). Mechanistic redundancy (anti-oxidant, autophagy, anti-inflammatory, anti-angiogenic) could enhance robustness in multifactorial AMD pathophysiology (Amin et al., 2022; Dang et al., 2021).

Weaknesses and Gaps  
- Critical mechanistic gaps relative to the hypothesis: Direct evidence in human RPE/AMD-relevant systems for metformin-driven TFEB nuclear translocation, increases in V-ATPase expression/activity, and enhanced cathepsin D maturation/activity is absent in the provided literature; several reviews explicitly highlight TFEB/V-ATPase/CTSD endpoints as missing and necessary to establish lysosome-centric restoration of autophagic flux (Amin et al., 2022; Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Buonfiglio et al., 2024). Without these data, the proposed AMPK–TFEB–lysosome axis remains inferential in RPE.
- Heterogeneous and contradictory epidemiology: While many retrospective datasets suggest benefit (often in T2DM cohorts), high-quality time-varying analyses and some claims datasets report null or even an increased risk signal for current users regarding dry AMD; meta-analyses differ in conclusions, and late-stage AMD associations are particularly uncertain (Elhalag et al., 2024; Gokhale et al., 2023; Liang et al., 2022; Mauschitz et al., 2023). Confounding (smoking, DR severity, comedications), misclassification (wet vs dry), and exposure uncertainty limit inferential strength (Brown et al., 2019; Moir et al., 2023; Gokhale et al., 2023).
- Limited randomized clinical efficacy data in dry AMD: A GA randomized trial has been reported, but efficacy outcomes are not detailed in the excerpts; prior DPP follow-up imaging showed no significant AMD prevalence difference between metformin, lifestyle, and placebo, though that study was not designed for AMD endpoints; consequently, clinical efficacy remains unproven (Moir et al., 2023; Shen et al., 2024).
- Context dependence and dose constraints: Retinal benefits can be model- and isoform-specific (AMPKα2 dependence) and mixed in metabolic DR models; some analyses suggest suprapharmacologic concentrations may be necessary for robust AMPK activation in vitro, raising translational questions regarding retinal exposure at tolerated systemic doses, and arguing for ocular PK and target-engagement studies (Amin et al., 2022; Moir et al., 2023).
- Ocular safety and pharmacokinetics: Human ocular safety data for chronic exposure (systemic or local) in older non-diabetic AMD patients are not detailed here; intravitreal metformin safety in humans is uncharacterized in these excerpts, necessitating staged ocular toxicology and PK prior to (or within) clinical trials (Amin et al., 2022; Moir et al., 2023).

Development Implications and Recommendations  
- Mechanism validation in RPE: Prioritize targeted studies in human iPSC-RPE and donor-derived RPE to test the hypothesized AMPK→mTORC1→TFEB→lysosome axis. Required assays: TFEB nuclear localization (immunocytochemistry, subcellular fractionation), lysosomal pH (LysoSensor/LysoTracker), V-ATPase subunit expression and activity (ATPase assays), CTSD maturation (pro/mature CTSD Western) and enzymatic activity, autophagic flux (LC3 turnover with/without lysosomal blockade), and rescue experiments with AMPK and TFEB perturbation (e.g., CRISPRi/siRNA) (Amin et al., 2022; Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Ebeling et al., 2022).
- Translational pharmacology: Define retinal/RPE exposure–response using clinically relevant systemic concentrations and ocular distribution modeling; consider topical/periocular/intravitreal delivery if systemic exposure is insufficient for retinal AMPK engagement and lysosome-centric endpoints, with rigorous ocular toxicology (Moir et al., 2023).
- Indication and stage targeting: Given epidemiologic signals skew toward early/non-exudative AMD and limited evidence for late AMD benefit, prioritize early/intermediate AMD cohorts and GA progression trials with mechanistic biomarkers (RPE autofluorescence dynamics, OCT-based RPE/ONL metrics, aqueous humor cytokines/miRNAs) to increase sensitivity to disease-modifying effects (Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Liang et al., 2022; Moir et al., 2023).
- Clinical trial design: Incorporate robust confounder control and stratification (smoking, DR status, renal function, OCT1 polymorphisms) and embed target engagement (e.g., peripheral blood or aqueous biomarkers of AMPK/mTOR/autophagy) and safety surveillance (B12 levels, GI tolerability, lactate in at-risk) to bridge mechanism to clinical outcome (Gokhale et al., 2023; Zhou & Xue, 2024).
- Combination/adjunct strategies: Given non-overlapping mechanisms with anti-VEGF and complement inhibitors, explore combinatorial approaches in late-stage disease (e.g., GA with complement inhibition) if target engagement and safety are demonstrated (Amin et al., 2022; Shen et al., 2024).

Conclusion: Metformin is a credible repurposing candidate for dry AMD on the strength of convergent mechanistic rationale (AMPK activation, autophagy/mitochondrial support, anti-inflammatory/anti-senescence actions), robust preclinical retinal protection across models, and suggestive—but inconsistent—observational human data; however, decisive gaps remain for the central lysosome-centric hypothesis (TFEB/V-ATPase/CTSD in RPE) and for randomized clinical efficacy, especially in GA. The program should proceed with focused mechanistic validation of TFEB/lysosome endpoints in RPE, retinal target engagement and pharmacology at clinically feasible exposures, and staged, biomarker-rich randomized trials in early/intermediate AMD and GA to quantify efficacy and safety. Until lysosomal endpoints are confirmed and clinical benefit demonstrated, the hypothesis that metformin restores RPE autophagic flux via TFEB/V-ATPase/CTSD to prevent dry AMD remains plausible but unproven (Amin et al., 2022; Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Shen et al., 2024; Gokhale et al., 2023; Elhalag et al., 2024).
