I. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Avacincaptad pegol, commercially known as Zimura, is a highly engineered, synthetic RNA aptamer designed specifically to target complement factor C5 for the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) with geographic atrophy (GA) features (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4). This molecule is comprised of a 39-nucleotide sequence that has been rigorously selected through in vitro techniques to offer high affinity and specificity for its target, ensuring that it binds precisely to C5 and prevents its activation (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4). Unlike traditional monoclonal antibodies, aptamers are oligonucleotide-based therapeutic agents that combine the benefits of well-defined chemical synthesis with tunable pharmacokinetics and low immunogenicity. In this instance, avacincaptad pegol has been further optimized by incorporating multiple chemical modifications; these include 2′-fluorine substitutions on pyrimidine residues, 2′-O-methyl modifications on select purine nucleotides, a protected 3′–3′ thymidine cap, and a branched polyethylene glycol (PEG) moiety to extend its half-life within the eye (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4). Such modifications confer enhanced resistance to degradation by nucleases and reduce renal clearance, thereby allowing the compound to remain active in the subretinal space longer than unmodified oligonucleotides (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4). The development of avacincaptad pegol is rooted in the evolution of aptamer technologies that began with earlier compounds like pegaptanib, the pioneer aptamer approved for neovascular AMD; however, unlike pegaptanib, avacincaptad pegol is engineered to target a different disease mechanism by focusing on the terminal complement cascade (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–8). Overall, the molecular design and chemical sophistication of this aptamer designate it as a next-generation candidate in the field of oligonucleotide therapeutics, with its unique physical and chemical attributes directly addressing specific pathogenic mechanisms of dry AMD (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–8).

Avacincaptad pegol belongs to a broader class of therapeutic compounds known as aptamers that act as “chemical antibodies.” These agents are synthesized via systematic evolution of ligands by exponential enrichment (SELEX), a process that allows for iterative refinement of the aptamer’s binding characteristics so that it selectively interacts with its intended protein target (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4). Aptamers have been used in various clinical applications due to their predictable pharmacologic profiles, their ease of chemical modification, and their typically low risk of eliciting an immune response. Their utility has been demonstrated not only in ocular therapeutics but also across a range of medical indications where precise modulation of molecular pathways is desired (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4). With the advent of avacincaptad pegol, the application of aptamer technology has been repurposed specifically for the modulation of the complement cascade—a key inflammatory pathway implicated in retinal degenerative diseases such as dry AMD (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4).

The synthetic origins of avacincaptad pegol underscore a scalable manufacturing process with robust quality control measures, making the compound attractive not only from a scientific standpoint but also from a commercial and regulatory perspective (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4). The structural characteristics, including its nucleic acid backbone and PEG conjugation, have been optimized to ensure adequate tissue penetration and sustained activity when delivered via intravitreal injection, minimizing systemic exposure and maximizing local therapeutic concentrations (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4). In summary, avacincaptad pegol is a representative example of how innovative chemical modifications and advanced selection technologies converge to generate therapeutic candidates that address the critical unmet needs in degenerative retinal diseases (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4).

II. Therapeutic History  
The trajectory of avacincaptad pegol from bench to bedside is emblematic of the rapid evolution in our understanding of the complement system’s role in AMD pathogenesis. Historically, the complement cascade—a series of proteolytic reactions leading to the formation of the membrane attack complex (MAC)—has been implicated in the chronic, low-grade inflammatory processes that contribute to retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) degeneration (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4; Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). Early efforts in pharmacologic intervention focused on modulating angiogenesis through agents like anti-VEGF drugs; however, these therapies failed to address the underlying complement-mediated inflammatory milieu that is particularly pronounced in the dry form of AMD (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4, 16–17).

The recognition that complement overactivation plays a central role in GA led researchers to explore agents that could precisely inhibit key components of this cascade. Avacincaptad pegol emerged as a promising candidate in this context, designed to block complement factor C5—a critical nexus point in the pathway responsible for the generation of both the potent inflammatory mediator C5a and the membrane attack complex (MAC) via C5b (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Bege et al., 2025, pp. 4–8). Preclinical studies using animal models of AMD demonstrated that inhibition of C5 could mitigate complement-mediated damage to RPE cells and reduce progression of GA lesions, laying the foundation for subsequent clinical investigations (Guimaraes et al., 2022, pp. 3–4; Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3).

The clinical development program for avacincaptad pegol has been extensive. Notably, phase II/III randomized controlled trials—collectively referred to as GATHER 1 and GATHER 2—were designed to evaluate its safety and efficacy in patients with GA secondary to AMD (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 16–17; Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). These pivotal trials enrolled hundreds of patients and involved monthly intravitreal injections, a route of administration that allows for high local concentrations of the drug while minimizing systemic exposure (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 16–17; Qin et al., 2024, p. 3). The results from these clinical studies were encouraging, as they consistently demonstrated statistically significant reductions in GA lesion growth in treatment groups compared to sham injections, with reported reductions in lesion progression on the order of approximately 27–30% over follow-up periods ranging from 12 to 18 months (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Guimaraes et al., 2022, pp. 3–4; Bege et al., 2025, pp. 16–17).

Beyond efficacy, the safety profile of avacincaptad pegol has been affirmed in multiple studies. The intravitreal route of administration confines the compound’s activity largely to the ocular compartment, thereby minimizing systemic immunosuppression—a particularly valuable attribute given the complement system’s role in host defense (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4; Qin et al., 2024, p. 3). Reports from clinical trials indicated that adverse events were primarily related to the injection procedure itself, with few drug-related serious ocular events recorded (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4; Guimaraes et al., 2022, pp. 3–4). This favorable safety record, combined with robust efficacy data, contributed to the FDA’s decision to approve avacincaptad pegol for the treatment of GA in August 2023, marking it as the second approved aptamer medicine in the field of retinal disease, following pegaptanib (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4; Qin et al., 2024, p. 3).

In parallel with these developments in dry AMD, avacincaptad pegol has been examined in observational studies and preclinical models that further delineate its mechanism of action and long-term benefits. Although past investigations in other complement-mediated ocular conditions have encountered mixed results, the specific targeting of C5 in the case of GA appears to be particularly promising, as evidenced by the consistent reduction in lesion progression reported by the GATHER trials (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 16–17; Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). The accumulated clinical experience provides a compelling historical context for its use, reinforcing the therapeutic rationale of complement inhibition in mitigating the inflammatory and degenerative processes that drive dry AMD (Guimaraes et al., 2022, pp. 3–4; Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3).

Moreover, the evolution of complement-modulating therapies in retinal diseases has been marked by significant collaborations between academia, industry, and regulatory agencies, all of which have embraced a more nuanced understanding of the immune processes involved in AMD. These concerted efforts have not only fostered the development of avacincaptad pegol but have also encouraged ongoing research into combination therapies that may further enhance clinical outcomes (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4, 16–17). As such, the therapeutic history of avacincaptad pegol is characterized by a steady progression from mechanistic discovery in the laboratory to robust clinical validation, underscoring its potential as a transformative agent in the management of dry AMD (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Qin et al., 2024, p. 3).

III. Mechanism of Action  
The mechanism of action of avacincaptad pegol is both specific and multifaceted, centering on the selective inhibition of complement factor C5—a pivotal molecule in the terminal complement pathway (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 4–8; Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). Under physiological conditions, C5 is cleaved into C5a and C5b. C5a acts as a potent anaphylatoxin that promotes inflammation through the recruitment and activation of immune cells, while C5b initiates the assembly of the membrane attack complex (MAC) by sequentially binding to complement components C6 through C9 (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Bege et al., 2025, pp. 4–8). The formation of the MAC on the surface of retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells is a critical driver of cell lysis and inflammatory damage that ultimately contributes to the progression of geographic atrophy in dry AMD (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Guimaraes et al., 2022, pp. 3–4).

Avacincaptad pegol exerts its therapeutic effect by binding directly to C5 with extremely high affinity, thereby blocking its enzymatic cleavage (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 4–8; Guimaraes et al., 2022, pp. 3–4). This inhibition prevents the generation of both C5a and C5b, ultimately forestalling the downstream assembly of the MAC (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 4–8; Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). The direct blockade of MAC formation is particularly beneficial in the subretinal microenvironment, where chronic complement activation is thought to contribute to lysosomal dysfunction in RPE cells (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Guimaraes et al., 2022, pp. 3–4). Specifically, when the MAC is deposited on RPE cell membranes, it can cause lysosomal membrane permeabilization (LMP), leading to impaired vacuolar ATPase (v-ATPase) activity and subsequent loss of lysosomal acidification (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 4–8; Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3).

Under normal circumstances, lysosomal acidification is essential for the proper maturation and activation of proteolytic enzymes such as cathepsin D (CTSD) (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Guimaraes et al., 2022, pp. 3–4). By preventing the formation of the MAC, avacincaptad pegol helps to preserve the proton gradient across the lysosomal membrane, thereby maintaining optimal conditions for lysosomal enzyme activity and ensuring adequate proteolytic clearance of debris within RPE cells (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 4–8; Guimaraes et al., 2022, pp. 3–4). This preservation of lysosomal function is of critical importance in preventing the accumulation of toxic byproducts, which have been implicated in the progressive degeneration of the retina observed in GA (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Guimaraes et al., 2022, pp. 3–4).

The detailed biochemistry underlying avacincaptad pegol’s activity was refined through iterative cycles of the SELEX process, during which the aptamer’s RNA sequence was optimized for maximal affinity toward C5 (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4; 4–8). The resulting aptamer exhibits a unique three-dimensional conformation that facilitates tight binding to a specific epitope on C5, effectively neutralizing its activity while sparing upstream complement components that may have beneficial roles in immune surveillance (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 4–8; 1–4). The high specificity of this interaction is essential because it limits off-target effects and reduces the risk of broader systemic immunosuppression—a concern that has previously complicated the development of complement inhibitors (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 4–8; Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3).

Furthermore, the localized administration of avacincaptad pegol via intravitreal injection ensures that its action is confined primarily to the retina, thereby concentrating its complement-inhibiting effects where they are most needed and minimizing the potential for systemic adverse events (Qin et al., 2024, p. 3; Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4). In preclinical studies, this targeted delivery was shown to result in marked reductions in the levels of C5 cleavage products, as well as diminished deposition of the MAC on the RPE, thereby validating the mechanistic rationale of the drug (Guimaraes et al., 2022, pp. 3–4; Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3).

In summary, avacincaptad pegol’s mode of action is rooted in its ability to effectively halt the terminal steps of the complement cascade by binding to C5, thereby preventing the formation of both pro-inflammatory C5a and the deleterious MAC (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 4–8; Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). Through this mechanism, it interrupts a key pathological process in dry AMD, offering a targeted strategy to preserve RPE cell function and maintain lysosomal integrity via sustained v-ATPase activity and proper cathepsin D maturation (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Guimaraes et al., 2022, pp. 3–4).

IV. Expected Effect  
Based on the mechanistic insights discussed above, the central hypothesis for avacincaptad pegol is that its inhibition of complement C5 activation will lead to a cascade of protective effects in the retinal microenvironment, ultimately decelerating the progression of GA associated with dry AMD (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Guimaraes et al., 2022, pp. 3–4). The expected effect in both in vitro and in vivo assays is multifactorial. Primarily, the aptamer is anticipated to reduce the generation of C5 cleavage products, thereby inhibiting the formation of the MAC on the surface of RPE cells. Such an effect is measurable via immunoassays that track the levels of C5a and related fragments, as well as by quantitative imaging techniques that assess MAC deposition (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Qin et al., 2024, pp. 2–3).

At the cellular level, the inhibition of MAC deposition is expected to translate into preserved lysosomal function within RPE cells—a critical factor given the reliance of these cells on lysosomal acidification for proper autophagic flux and metabolic homeostasis (Guimaraes et al., 2022, pp. 3–4; Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). In practical assay systems, one would anticipate that RPE cell cultures treated with avacincaptad pegol show maintained or even restored acidification of lysosomes as indicated by pH-sensitive fluorescent dyes, alongside intact activity of lysosomal enzymes such as cathepsin D (Guimaraes et al., 2022, pp. 3–4; Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). This preservation of lysosomal function is hypothesized to directly correlate with a reduced accumulation of cellular debris and toxic byproducts that accelerate the degenerative process in GA (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Bege et al., 2025, pp. 4–8).

Clinically, the outcome most often evaluated in trials of avacincaptad pegol is the deceleration of GA lesion enlargement, which is quantitatively assessed through imaging modalities such as fundus autofluorescence (FAF) and optical coherence tomography (OCT) (Qin et al., 2024, pp. 2–3; 3–3). In the pivotal GATHER 1 and GATHER 2 phase II/III studies, patients treated with monthly intravitreal injections of avacincaptad pegol exhibited reductions in GA progression rates of approximately 27% to 30% relative to sham-treated groups (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Bege et al., 2025, pp. 16–17). These anatomical endpoints serve as surrogate markers for the overall efficacy of the intervention, with the underlying assumption that slowing the expansion of GA lesions will eventually lead to stabilization of visual function (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Guimaraes et al., 2022, pp. 3–4).

At the molecular level, the expected effect also includes the restoration of critical lysosomal functions disrupted by excessive complement activation. Specifically, by preventing MAC-induced lysosomal membrane permeabilization, avacincaptad pegol is anticipated to maintain the proton gradient essential for v-ATPase function, thereby preserving the acidic environment required for optimal cathepsin D processing and other lysosomal enzymes (Guimaraes et al., 2022, pp. 3–4; Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). Such preservation is not only crucial for cellular clearance mechanisms but also plays a pivotal role in preventing intracellular accumulation of debris, which is a contributing factor in the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Guimaraes et al., 2022, pp. 3–4; Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3).

Moreover, since complement components, including C5, are expressed locally in the retina by RPE cells and resident immune cells, the targeted inhibition of C5 is expected to provide direct immunomodulatory benefits within the ocular microenvironment. This localized impact is critical because it addresses the pathophysiological cross-talk between complement activation and lysosomal dysfunction, which is thought to drive a vicious cycle of chronic inflammation and cellular degeneration (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Guimaraes et al., 2022, pp. 3–4). In theory, by reestablishing a balanced complement milieu, avacincaptad pegol may also help to curtail secondary inflammatory responses that otherwise exacerbate tissue damage, thereby preserving photoreceptor integrity and ultimately stabilizing visual acuity over time (Qin et al., 2024, pp. 2–3; 3–3).

In summary, the expected effects of avacincaptad pegol in the proposed assays and clinical settings are multi-layered. At the biochemical level, one should observe a pronounced reduction in C5 cleavage, diminished MAC formation on RPE membranes, and preserved lysosomal acidification and enzyme function. At the tissue level, these molecular events are predicted to culminate in a slowdown of GA lesion enlargement, which is widely regarded as a surrogate marker for the progression of dry AMD (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Qin et al., 2024, pp. 2–3). The overall hypothesis is that these combined effects will translate into meaningful clinical benefits, offering not only anatomical preservation but also the potential for stabilization—or even modest improvement—of visual function in affected patients (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3).

V. Overall Evaluation  
A comprehensive evaluation of avacincaptad pegol reveals a therapeutic candidate that is scientifically robust, mechanistically innovative, and clinically validated for the treatment of dry AMD with geographic atrophy. One of the major strengths of this therapeutic approach lies in its highly specific mechanism of action. By directly binding to and inhibiting complement factor C5, avacincaptad pegol interrupts a key pathological process at its source, namely the activation of the terminal complement cascade that results in the formation of the pro-inflammatory mediator C5a and the membrane attack complex (MAC) (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 4–8; Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). This level of specificity confers potential advantages over broader immunosuppressive agents, as it minimizes collateral inhibition of upstream complement components that may be protective. Such precise targeting results in reduced inflammation localized to the retinal tissues and lowers the risk of systemic adverse events (Guimaraes et al., 2022, pp. 3–4; Qin et al., 2024, pp. 3–3).

The extensive chemical modifications integrated into avacincaptad pegol’s structure—including 2′-fluoro and 2′-O-methyl substitutions, the incorporation of a 3′–3′ thymidine cap, and PEGylation—greatly enhance its stability and half-life in the intraocular environment (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4). These modifications are essential because they allow for sustained inhibition of C5 with relatively infrequent dosing, thereby improving the overall treatment regimen for a patient population that is often elderly and may struggle with stringent dosing schedules (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4; Qin et al., 2024, pp. 3–3). The aptamer-based nature of this drug also endows it with a low immunogenic risk profile, circumventing one of the potential pitfalls associated with protein-based therapies such as monoclonal antibodies (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4).

Clinically, the data emerging from the GATHER 1 and GATHER 2 phase II/III trials are particularly compelling. These studies have consistently demonstrated that patients receiving intravitreal injections of avacincaptad pegol experience a significant reduction in the rate of GA lesion growth, with observed reductions ranging from 27% to 30% compared to sham controls (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Bege et al., 2025, pp. 16–17). This tangible anatomical benefit, combined with the favorable safety profile—which includes minimal ocular adverse events—confirms the viability of C5 inhibition as a disease-modifying strategy in dry AMD (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4). Given that GA has long represented an area of substantial unmet clinical need, the regulatory approval of avacincaptad pegol by the FDA in August 2023 is a significant milestone that reinforces the credibility of this therapeutic approach (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4; Qin et al., 2024, pp. 3–3).

Another notable strength is the mechanistic rationale underpinning the expected therapeutic benefits. By preventing MAC formation on RPE membranes, avacincaptad pegol not only preserves the structural integrity of these cells but also protects lysosomal function by mitigating lysosomal membrane permeabilization (LMP) (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Bege et al., 2025, pp. 4–8). The preservation of lysosomal acidification and subsequent maintenance of autophagic and proteolytic function are critical factors in slowing the progression of GA, as they help to avert the accumulation of toxic metabolic byproducts that drive cellular degeneration (Guimaraes et al., 2022, pp. 3–4; Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). Thus, the therapeutic strategy is well anchored in a clear pathological framework that directly relates to the underlying disease process in dry AMD.

Despite the considerable promise of avacincaptad pegol, several potential weaknesses and challenges remain. One concern is the translation of anatomical benefits into meaningful functional improvements with respect to visual acuity. While reduction in GA lesion enlargement is an encouraging surrogate endpoint, there is a recognized challenge in correlating these anatomical outcomes with sustained improvements or stabilization of vision (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Qin et al., 2024, pp. 2–3). In some clinical trials involving complement inhibitors, the disconnect between reduced lesion growth and measurable improvements in best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) has raised questions about whether anatomical preservation will eventually lead to perceptible functional benefits for patients (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3).

Another potential challenge relates to the inherent complexity of the complement system. C5 is a critical component of the terminal cascade; however, the redundancy and cross-talk among multiple complement pathways may potentially compromise the overall efficacy of a monotherapeutic approach targeting only C5 (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 4–8; Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). There is a possibility that, even with effective C5 blockade, alternative inflammatory pathways may partially compensate for its inhibition, thereby limiting the long-term clinical benefit. This concern suggests that future treatment paradigms might require combination approaches that target both complement-mediated and non-complement-mediated mechanisms of retinal degeneration (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Bege et al., 2025, pp. 4–8).

The mode of delivery is another factor that merits consideration. Avacincaptad pegol is delivered via monthly intravitreal injections, which, while effective in ensuring localized drug activity, impose a significant treatment burden on an elderly patient population (Qin et al., 2024, pp. 3–3). Frequent intravitreal administration is associated with logistical challenges, including the risk of injection-related complications such as endophthalmitis or retinal detachment, albeit infrequent, and may negatively impact patient compliance over extended treatment periods (Qin et al., 2024, pp. 3–3; Bege et al., 2025, pp. 16–17). Future innovation in drug delivery systems—for example, sustained-release implants or alternative non-invasive administration routes—could be critical in overcoming this limitation and enhancing long-term treatment adherence (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 16–17; 1–4).

A further challenge lies in assessing the long-term safety of chronic complement inhibition within the ocular environment. Although the localized delivery method limits systemic exposure, the prolonged suppression of C5 activity in the retina may affect local immune surveillance and potentially predispose to subclinical infections or inflammatory dysregulation (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4; Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). Given that the complement system plays a nuanced role in both tissue repair and immune defense, extended studies are necessary to definitively characterize the long-term safety profile, particularly with respect to maintaining the delicate balance between controlling pathological inflammation and preserving protective immune functions (Qin et al., 2024, pp. 3–3; Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3).

Finally, the multifactorial nature of dry AMD suggests that while C5 inhibition may effectively slow the progression of GA, it might not fully address all aspects of this complex disease process. Oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and neurodegeneration are also critical contributors to AMD pathophysiology, and a monotherapy targeting the complement cascade may need to be integrated into a broader multimodal treatment strategy to achieve optimal clinical outcomes (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Bege et al., 2025, pp. 4–8). Such considerations imply that while avacincaptad pegol represents a significant advancement in the field, its maximal therapeutic potential may be realized only when used in combination with agents that address complementary pathological processes (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Bege et al., 2025, pp. 4–8).

In synthesizing these considerations, the overall evaluation of avacincaptad pegol is highly positive. Its unique molecular design, demonstrated clinical efficacy in reducing GA lesion growth, and favorable safety profile strongly support the hypothesis that targeted inhibition of complement C5 can provide a meaningful therapeutic benefit in dry AMD (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4; Qin et al., 2024, pp. 3–3). The strengths lie in both its mechanistic precision and the tangible clinical endpoints achieved in pivotal trials, which collectively underscore the validity of the hypothesis that disrupting terminal complement activation can preserve RPE integrity and lysosomal function (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3).

Nevertheless, the translation of these anatomical benefits into long-term preservation of vision, the challenges associated with the frequent intravitreal injection regimen, and the potential activation of alternative inflammatory pathways represent hurdles that warrant continued investigation (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). Addressing these challenges will likely require further mechanistic studies, extended clinical follow-up to capture functional outcomes, and possibly the development of innovative drug delivery systems that reduce the treatment burden on patients (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 16–17; Qin et al., 2024, pp. 3–3).

In conclusion, avacincaptad pegol emerges as a scientifically rigorous and clinically validated candidate for the treatment of dry AMD with geographic atrophy. Its ability to selectively inhibit complement C5 and thereby prevent MAC formation, lysosomal acidification loss, and subsequent RPE damage provides a mechanistic rationale that is well supported by both preclinical and clinical data (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Bege et al., 2025, pp. 4–8). Despite potential challenges in correlating anatomical preservation with functional visual improvements, the overall evidence supports further development and investment in this therapeutic candidate. The favorable risk–benefit profile observed to date, coupled with its innovative chemical design and robust clinical trial outcomes, positions avacincaptad pegol as one of the most promising agents in the evolving landscape of dry AMD therapy (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4; Qin et al., 2024, pp. 3–3).

Looking ahead, it is advisable that future research efforts focus on refining patient selection criteria through the identification of biomarkers predictive of complement activation and treatment response, as well as on exploring combinatorial approaches that might synergize the effects of C5 inhibition with agents addressing other facets of AMD pathogenesis (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Bege et al., 2025, pp. 4–8). The continued monitoring of long-term safety outcomes, particularly with respect to local immune function and the potential for injection-related complications, will also be crucial to ensure that the sustained administration of avacincaptad pegol remains both safe and effective over the extended treatment durations required in this chronic condition (Qin et al., 2024, pp. 3–3).

Moreover, from a commercial and regulatory perspective, the recent FDA approval of avacincaptad pegol for GA marks a significant milestone that not only validates the scientific rationale for targeting complement C5 but also signals the readiness of the ocular therapeutic landscape to embrace novel molecular entities with differentiated mechanisms of action (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4; Qin et al., 2024, pp. 3–3). This regulatory endorsement, together with the mounting clinical evidence, provides a solid foundation for the continued expansion of complement inhibition strategies in the management of retinal degenerative diseases, especially in patients for whom current treatment options are severely limited or ineffective (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 16–17; Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3).

The strategic outlook for avacincaptad pegol involves a dual focus: firstly, on consolidating its clinical benefits through extended, long-term trials that aim to establish a clear correlation between anatomical preservation and visual function stabilization; and secondly, on integrating its use into combination treatment regimens that might include neuroprotective, antioxidant, or even adjunctive anti-VEGF therapies to comprehensively address the multifaceted nature of dry AMD (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Bege et al., 2025, pp. 4–8). Such an integrated approach has the potential to not only enhance the overall therapeutic efficacy but also to extend the duration of clinical benefits, ultimately improving the quality of life for patients suffering from this debilitating condition (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4).

In balancing these strengths and challenges, the overall assessment of avacincaptad pegol remains decidedly positive. Its molecular design is state-of-the-art, its mechanism of action is directly aligned with a critical pathogenic process in dry AMD, and its clinical performance to date offers substantive evidence of efficacy in slowing disease progression (Qin et al., 2024, pp. 3–3; Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4). While further research is needed to fully elucidate the long-term functional benefits and to optimize the dosing regimens, the current body of evidence establishes a compelling rationale for its continued development and potential integration into the standard of care for dry AMD (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4; Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3).

In summary, avacincaptad pegol represents a landmark therapeutic innovation in the realm of retinal degenerative diseases. Its targeted inhibition of complement C5 not only addresses a fundamental driver of retinal inflammation and degenerative cell death in GA but also offers a new paradigm in the treatment of a condition that has long been resistant to effective disease-modifying interventions (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4). The extensive clinical validation, marked by significant reductions in GA lesion growth and an acceptable safety profile, underscores its potential to significantly alter the natural history of dry AMD and improve patient outcomes (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Bege et al., 2025, pp. 16–17).

Considering all facets of its development—including chemical design, mechanistic efficacy, clinical performance, and future strategic directions—avacincaptad pegol stands as one of the most promising therapeutic candidates for addressing the unmet needs in dry AMD (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4; Qin et al., 2024, pp. 3–3). Continued investment in both clinical and translational research is warranted, as is the exploration of complementary therapeutic strategies that may further potentiate its benefits. As the field advances toward integrated, multimodal approaches to retinal disease, the therapeutic promise of avacincaptad pegol is likely to serve as a cornerstone for future innovations that collectively strive to preserve vision and enhance the quality of life for patients with dry AMD (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3).

Ultimately, the comprehensive evaluation presented here affirms that the repurposing and further clinical development of avacincaptad pegol is both scientifically grounded and clinically justified. Its ability to modulate the complement cascade, protect RPE cells from MAC-induced injury, maintain lysosomal function, and reduce the progression of GA lesions is supported by robust preclinical and clinical evidence (Ewing et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Bege et al., 2025, pp. 4–8). The promising results from pivotal trials, together with a well-established safety profile and the advantages conferred by its aptamer-based design, mark avacincaptad pegol as a leading candidate in the ongoing battle against dry AMD (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 16–17; Qin et al., 2024, pp. 3–3).

In closing, while challenges remain—particularly in correlating anatomical improvements with sustained visual acuity and in managing the logistical hurdles associated with frequent intravitreal injections—the overall benefits of avacincaptad pegol are clear. It provides a targeted, innovative, and effective means of intervening in a condition that has historically lacked disease-modifying therapies. Its continued development promises to not only fill an unmet clinical need but also to serve as a model for the adaptation of aptamer technologies to other areas of degenerative and inflammatory diseases (Bege et al., 2025, pp. 1–4). Trehalose is a naturally occurring non‐reducing disaccharide (molecular weight 342.3 Da) found broadly in microorganisms and invertebrates, widely used as a stabilizer and excipient in foods and pharmaceuticals, and formulated in ophthalmic solutions at 3% w/v (≈87.7 mM) for ocular surface applications (e.g., dry eye) (Cox et al., 2025, pp. 1–2). In mammalian cells, trehalose enters via fluid‐phase endocytosis at millimolar concentrations and has been repeatedly reported as an autophagy enhancer that can activate AMPK signaling, stimulate lysosomal activity, and augment autophagic flux across multiple tissues, including ocular tissues (RPE) and retina (Cox et al., 2025, pp. 1–2). In the context of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), trehalose has been deployed as a small‐molecule modulator of the lysosome–autophagy axis with proposed mTOR‐independent activation of TFEB, the master transcriptional regulator of lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy (CLEAR network), positioning it mechanistically distinct from direct mTORC1 inhibitors such as rapamycin (Ghosh et al., 2024, p. 6; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 10–11). Topical ophthalmic trehalose is generally well tolerated, and preclinical studies show no overt ocular toxicity at 3% or 9% w/v after twice-daily dosing for up to two weeks, supporting feasibility for posterior segment delivery strategies; Raman spectroscopy has detected trehalose in RPE/choroid after repeated topical dosing, although posterior penetration is variable (Cox et al., 2025, pp. 8–10).

Preclinical evidence in RPE and retina

Dose–response caveats were noted: higher trehalose concentrations (≥100 mM) lost cytoprotection and were associated with stronger LC3-II accumulation, suggesting risk from excessive autophagy activation (Abokyi et al., 2020, pp. 11–12, 15–16).  
- Primary murine RPE in vitro: A non‐toxic trehalose dose (12.5 mM) increased autophagic flux measured by tandem GFP–RFP-LC3B, increasing RFP+ autolysosomes and RFP:GFP ratios without accumulating GFP+ autophagosomes, with colocalization to LysoTracker+ acidic compartments; trehalose also attenuated H₂O₂-induced mitochondrial superoxide and restored maximal respiration (Cox et al., 2025, pp. 7–10). - Mechanistic verification package:

- Mechanistic Go: Demonstration in RPE that trehalose increases the TFEB nuclear index by >2-fold, lowers lysosomal pH toward physiological values, and increases CTSD activity by >30% over disease-state baseline, with concordant increases in LC3B–LAMP1 colocalization and p62 degradation; abrogation of effects by TFEB knockdown would confirm mechanism (Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 10–11; Cox et al., 2025, pp. 7–8; Boya et al., 2023, pp. 3–4).

- Safety Go: No evidence of autophagy-associated cytotoxicity at the intended exposure (maintained viability; absence of excessive LC3-II accumulation without flux; ocular histopathology clean) (Abokyi et al., 2020, pp. 15–16; Cox et al., 2025, pp. 8–10).

Conclusion  
The totality of evidence supports trehalose as a plausible, repurposable modulator of the TFEB–lysosome/autophagy axis in the RPE with multiple independent signals of autophagy flux enhancement, lysosomal hydrolase restoration (CTSD/L), and cytoprotection in oxidative/complement stress contexts, delivered via mechanisms that appear mTOR-independent and therefore potentially safer than broad mTORC1 inhibition (Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 10–11; Cox et al., 2025, pp. 7–8; Abokyi et al., 2020, pp. 1–2; Ghosh et al., 2023, pp. 11–15). However, the hypothesis’s most stringent claims—quantitative restoration of lysosomal acidification, trehalose-driven TFEB nuclear translocation in RPE, and direct lipofuscin/A2E clearance leading to slowed geographic atrophy progression—are not yet demonstrated in the supplied literature and require targeted mechanistic and disease-model validation (Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 10–11; Abokyi et al., 2020, pp. 16–17; Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7; Cox et al., 2025, pp. 8–10). Given strong biological plausibility and encouraging preclinical signals, a focused IND-enabling program that closes these gaps is justified, with early emphasis on mechanistic biomarkers (lysosomal pH, TFEB nuclear index, CTSD activity), pharmacokinetics of posterior delivery, and chronic AMD-relevant efficacy models before advancing to clinical study in GA (Boya et al., 2023, pp. 3–4; Cox et al., 2025, pp. 10–13; Ghosh et al., 2024, p. 6).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN) is an endogenous intermediate in the mammalian NAD⁺ salvage pathway, generated by nicotinamide phosphoribosyltransferase (NAMPT) from nicotinamide (NAM) and 5-phosphoribosyl‐1‐pyrophosphate (PRPP) and converted to NAD⁺ by nicotinamide mononucleotide adenylyltransferases (NMNAT1–3) (Jadeja et al., 2020; Cimaglia et al., 2020). NMN belongs to the vitamin B3–derived NAD⁺ precursor class and is one of several precursors (others include nicotinamide [NAM], nicotinic acid [NA], and nicotinamide riboside [NR]) used to augment cellular NAD⁺ pools in aging and disease (Cimaglia et al., 2020). NMN was prioritized as a practical intervention because direct NAD⁺ delivery to tissues is not straightforward, whereas in vivo administration of NMN elevates tissue NAD⁺ and supports mitochondrial function and cellular stress defenses in multiple systems (Ebeling et al., 2020; Rahman et al., 2024). Transport and uptake mechanisms include the Slc12a8 transporter described in mouse small intestine, as well as extracellular dephosphorylation to NR followed by NR uptake via equilibrative nucleoside transporters; intracellular NR is re‐phosphorylated by NRK1 to NMN for resynthesis of NAD⁺ (Will‐Orrego, 2020a; Rahman et al., 2024). Notably for RPE models, ARPE‐19 cells have been reported to express transporters supporting NMN uptake but not NR uptake, favoring NMN over NR in this system (Will‐Orrego, 2020b). In RPE and retinal contexts, NMN and related precursors have been deployed preclinically to restore NAD⁺, improve mitochondrial function, modulate sirtuin‐dependent pathways, and mitigate features of neurodegeneration and cellular senescence (Jadeja et al., 2018; Ebeling et al., 2020; Lin, 2020).

Therapeutic History  
NAD⁺ decline with age is conserved across tissues, including the retina and RPE, and is mechanistically linked to impaired mitochondrial function, heightened oxidative stress, and increased susceptibility to degeneration (Jadeja et al., 2018; Cimaglia et al., 2020). In the outer retina, rod‐ or cone‐specific Nampt deletion produces NAD⁺ deficiency and photoreceptor degeneration; systemic NMN at 150 mg/kg i.p. restored retinal function by ERG and preserved photoreceptor structure, establishing that exogenous NMN can replenish retinal NAD⁺ and mitigate degeneration linked to impaired salvage (Lin, 2020). NMN also protected in models of acute retinal injury: daily systemic NMN reduced photoreceptor death and oxidative stress after retinal detachment and increased retinal SIRT1 and HO‐1, consistent with NAD⁺‐dependent sirtuin activation in vivo (Chen et al., 2020). In ischemia models, NMN administration protected against retinal dysfunction (Lee et al., 2022; Lee et al., 2024). In a cholesterol efflux–deficient murine model that recapitulates key dry AMD features driven by senescent subretinal macrophages (Abca1/g1‐deficient), systemic NMN reduced subretinal drusenoid deposits (SDDs), decreased lipofuscin‐positive macrophage burden, and improved electrophysiological and structural endpoints, supporting a role for NAD⁺ augmentation in reversing senescence‐driven outer retinal pathology in vivo (Terao et al., 2024). In RPE‐directed models, pharmacologic NAMPT inhibition with FK866 is widely used to mimic age‐related NAD⁺ decline; in ARPE‐19 and primary RPE, NMN co‐treatment preserved NAD⁺, SIRT1 protein, viability, and reduced senescence markers, and in vivo systemic NMN preserved RPE NAD⁺ and SIRT1 after subretinal FK866 (Jadeja et al., 2018). Oxidant injury with sodium iodate (NaIO₃) induced RPE senescence, NAD⁺ depletion, mitochondrial dysfunction, and subretinal inflammation; NMN restored RPE NAD⁺, reduced DNA damage and senescence markers, improved mitochondrial membrane potential and ATP in ARPE‐19, and reduced inflammatory cell recruitment in vivo, with intact Sirt1 signaling required for NMN benefit (Ren et al., 2022). Outside strictly RPE biology, NMN improved RPE phagocytosis and mitochondrial ultrastructure in the RCS rat model of retinal degeneration, with a mechanistic link to a NAD⁺/GAPDH axis that modulated actin/cytoskeletal phagocytosis machinery in RPE; GAPDH knockdown abrogated NMN’s benefits, supporting a causal chain from NAD⁺ repletion to enhanced RPE POS clearance via GAPDH‐dependent pathways (Zhang et al., 2024).

Clinical translation of NAD⁺ precursors has begun with nicotinamide and NR in ophthalmology-adjacent indications (e.g., glaucoma), demonstrating tolerability and retinal functional protection in mice, and documenting NAD⁺ elevation in adult humans, but direct clinical data for NMN in dry AMD are not available in the provided context (Cimaglia et al., 2020; Rahman et al., 2024). Long-term NMN treatment in mice mitigated age-associated physiological decline systemically and reportedly ameliorated eye function, but detailed ocular pharmacology and human NMN ocular safety are not established here (Rahman et al., 2024). Collectively, the preclinical record supports NMN as an NAD⁺ augmenting therapy with demonstrated efficacy in retina and RPE-relevant models of NAD⁺ deficiency, oxidative injury, and senescence; however, there is no direct published clinical trial evidence in dry AMD patients in this context set (Jadeja et al., 2018; Lin, 2020; Chen et al., 2020; Terao et al., 2024).

Mechanism of Action  
Core biochemistry  
- NAD⁺ salvage. In mammalian cells, the salvage pathway supplies most NAD⁺ (~80%), with NAMPT catalyzing NAM → NMN and NMNAT1–3 completing NMN → NAD⁺; this pool fuels redox reactions and serves as substrate for NAD⁺‐consuming enzymes including sirtuins, PARPs, and the NAD glycohydrolase CD38 (Cimaglia et al., 2020; Jadeja et al., 2020). NAMPT-mediated biosynthesis is essential for vision, and its decline in RPE with age causally links to reduced NAD⁺, reduced SIRT1 expression/activity, and enhanced cellular senescence (Jadeja et al., 2018).  
- Uptake and intracellular handling. NMN can enter cells via specific transporters (Slc12a8 shown in mouse gut) and/or after extracellular dephosphorylation to NR with re-phosphorylation by NRK1, routes that are cell type–dependent; ARPE-19 preferentially transport NMN in vitro, supporting the choice of NMN over NR in these RPE models (Will‐Orrego, 2020a; Will‐Orrego, 2020b; Rahman et al., 2024).

Downstream signaling nodes relevant to RPE and dry AMD  
- Sirtuins. NAD⁺ is an obligate co-substrate for sirtuins; increased NAD⁺ drives sirtuin deacetylase/deacylase activities across SIRT1–7 with consequences for mitochondrial function, antioxidant defenses, DNA repair, and autophagy/mitophagy (Cimaglia et al., 2020). In aging RPE, NAD⁺ and SIRT1 decline in parallel; restoring NAD⁺ with NMN rescues SIRT1 protein and activity in vitro and in vivo, and reduces senescence markers p16^INK4a and p21^Waf/Cip1 (Jadeja et al., 2018). SIRT3, the mitochondrial sirtuin, maintains mitochondrial integrity by deacetylating and activating SOD2 and coordinating antioxidant responses, mitophagy, and UPR^mt; retinal NAD⁺ deficiency impairs SIRT3, linking NAD⁺ loss to mitochondrial vulnerability (Cimaglia et al., 2020; Lin, 2020). In a retinal detachment model, systemic NMN increased SIRT1 protein and HO‐1, with mechanistic in vitro data supporting a SIRT1 → HO‐1 protective axis (Chen et al., 2020).  
- AMPK and NAMPT/SIRT1 crosstalk. AMPK upregulates NAMPT expression and thus supports NAD⁺ salvage; reciprocally, SIRT1 deacetylates/stabilizes LKB1 to activate AMPK, forming a positive feedback loop that coordinates energy sensing and catabolic responses (Luján et al., 2022). In RPE senescence induced by NaIO₃, AMPK activation occurs downstream of ATP depletion and is modulated by NMN treatment, though overactivation of Sirt1 by a direct agonist (SRT1720) produced mitochondrial hyperfusion and stress signaling, arguing for physiological NAD⁺‐driven Sirt1 activation rather than pharmacologic overdrive (Ren et al., 2022).  
- Autophagy/mitophagy and mitochondrial biogenesis. SIRT1 promotes autophagosome formation and Rab7‐dependent autophagosome–lysosome fusion; together with AMPK, it enhances expression of mitophagy effectors (PINK1, Parkin) and co-activates PGC‐1α to drive mitochondrial biogenesis programs via transcriptional partners (NRF‐1, ERRα, PPARα) (Luján et al., 2022). Reviews and preclinical observations indicate that NAD⁺ repletion can restore mitophagy, activate UPR^mt, and normalize mitochondrial metabolic profiles, including evidence that “NAD⁺ inhibits the metabolic reprogramming of RPE cells in early AMD by upregulating mitophagy,” supporting the hypothesis that NMN-driven NAD⁺ gain could favorably reprogram RPE mitochondrial quality control (Rahman et al., 2024; Jadeja et al., 2020). In primary AMD donor RPE, NMN improved mitochondrial function in vitro; the same study used mitophagy reporter assays (mKeima-mito), underscoring the feasibility of measuring NMN’s effects on mitophagy in human RPE although specific NMN → mitophagy data were not detailed in the excerpt (Fisher et al., 2022; Ebeling et al., 2020).  
- PARP and CD38 as NAD⁺ sinks. DNA damage and SASP/inflammation drive PARP and CD38 activities that deplete NAD⁺; CD38 in particular contributes to age-related NAD⁺ decline and mitochondrial dysfunction and is induced by LXR signaling and SASP, creating a self-reinforcing senescence–NAD⁺ depletion loop (Cimaglia et al., 2020; Terao et al., 2024). In photoreceptor cells, PARP inhibition partially rescues viability under NAMPT inhibition, highlighting the vulnerability of NAD⁺ pools to consumption pathways and the value of reducing NAD⁺ sinks in parallel with NMN supplementation (Lin & Apte, 2018).  
- Inflammation and inflammasome. NAD⁺ augmentation via NMN or increased NAMPT/NAD⁺ can reduce NLRP3 inflammasome activation and downstream IL-1β/IL-18 via a SIRT1‐dependent mechanism in RPE aging models, pointing to anti‐inflammatory benefits of the NAMPT/NAD⁺/SIRT1 axis (Wu et al., 2021). In the Abca1/g1 macrophage senescence model of dry AMD, NAD⁺ repletion (NMN or CD38 inhibition) eliminated senescent macrophages and reversed drusenoid pathology and RPE functional deficits, extending the anti‐senescence and anti‐inflammatory reach of NAD⁺ augmentation to subretinal immune cells central to AMD pathobiology (Terao et al., 2024).

Critically, although TFEB (a master regulator of lysosomal biogenesis) and lysosomal proteases such as cathepsin D (CTSD) are highly relevant to RPE oxidative‐debris clearance in dry AMD, the provided literature does not demonstrate direct NMN‐induced TFEB activation, lysosomal acidification, or increased CTSD activity in RPE or retina; these remain plausible but unproven links in this context set (Falcão et al., 2025; Will‐Orrego, 2020a; Ebeling et al., 2020; Cimaglia et al., 2020).

Expected Effect  
Assay-level expectations in RPE models of dry AMD  
- NAD⁺ repletion in RPE. In ARPE‐19 and primary RPE, co‐treatment with NMN restores cellular NAD⁺ reduced by NAMPT inhibition, with partial to robust recovery depending on media and dosing; in ARPE‐19, FK866 sharply lowers NAD⁺/NADH and ATP, while NMN rescues both metrics and normalizes OXPHOS/glycolysis balance measured by Seahorse assays (Will‐Orrego, 2020b, 2020c). ARPE‐19 cells express NMN but not NR transporters, predicting superior uptake and intracellular conversion for NMN in this model (Will‐Orrego, 2020b). In NaIO₃‐stressed ARPE‐19, 800–1,000 µM NMN restored NAD⁺, mitochondrial membrane potential, and ATP, reduced ROS and DNA damage, and reduced senescence markers, with Sirt1 activity required for these benefits (Ren et al., 2022).  
- Sirtuin engagement. In FK866‐inhibited RPE, NMN co‐treatment restored SIRT1 protein and activity in vitro and in vivo; in photoreceptor injury, NMN increased retinal SIRT1 and induced HO-1, suggesting a SIRT1‐dependent antioxidant arm (Jadeja et al., 2018; Chen et al., 2020). In primary AMD donor RPE, NMN improved mitochondrial function, consistent with engagement of mitochondrial sirtuins and/or PGC-1α programs, though specific sirtuin readouts were not reported in that excerpt (Ebeling et al., 2020).  
- AMPK and mitophagy. AMPK will be sensitive to changes in ATP/AMP driven by mitochondrial recovery after NMN; in RPE senescence models, AMPK activation was observed under oxidant injury and modulated by NMN, and the NAD⁺/Sirt1/AMPK network is positioned to restore mitophagy via ULK1 activation, mTORC1 attenuation, and PINK1/Parkin induction (Ren et al., 2022; Luján et al., 2022). The hypothesis that NAD⁺ supplementation restores RPE metabolic dysfunction by inducing mitophagy is supported conceptually and by limited preclinical data cited for NAD⁺ effects on RPE mitophagy, making mitophagy flux (e.g., mKeima‐mito) a reasonable expected readout under NMN treatment (Jadeja et al., 2020; Fisher et al., 2022).  
- Autophagy-lysosome system and debris clearance. TFEB governs lysosomal biogenesis and function and is a rational target in dry AMD; Sirt1 and AMPK facilitate autophagosome formation and autophagosome–lysosome fusion (Rab7) and thus could secondarily enhance lysosomal throughput after NMN (Falcão et al., 2025; Luján et al., 2022). However, direct evidence that NMN increases lysosomal number, lysosomal acidification, TFEB nuclear translocation, or CTSD activity in RPE is not provided here; these are testable but as yet unvalidated expectations (Falcão et al., 2025; Will‐Orrego, 2020a). By contrast, NMN increased RPE phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments and restored actin‐mediated phagocytic machinery in vivo in the RCS rat, revealing a complementary route by which NMN could improve outer segment turnover independent of direct TFEB activation (Zhang et al., 2024).  
- Anti‐senescence and anti‐inflammatory effects. In RPE and subretinal myeloid cells, NMN suppresses senescence phenotypes and reduces inflammatory mediators, which should reduce SASP‐driven bystander stress on RPE and photoreceptors and may indirectly lower CD38‐mediated NAD⁺ depletion in the subretinal compartment (Jadeja et al., 2018; Terao et al., 2024).

Collectively, in an RPE assay aligned to dry AMD pathophysiology, NMN is expected to: (1) restore NAD⁺ and ATP; (2) engage Sirt1/Sirt3 and normalize mitochondrial function; (3) reduce senescence and inflammatory signaling; and (4) enhance POS phagocytosis via cytoskeletal machinery, with plausible but unproven enhancement of lysosomal biogenesis/function via Sirt1/AMPK-mediated autophagy pathways and TFEB cross-talk (Will‐Orrego, 2020b; Jadeja et al., 2018; Ren et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2025; Luján et al., 2022).

Assay design notes  
- Use ARPE‐19 and primary human RPE including AMD donor–derived cultures for translational relevance; confirm NMN uptake advantages versus NR in each model (Will‐Orrego, 2020b; Ebeling et al., 2020).  
- Quantify NAD⁺ by enzymatic assay, SIRT1 activity fluorometrically, mitochondrial ATP production via Seahorse ATP rate assay, and senescence markers (SA‐β‐gal, p16, p21) per established protocols (Jadeja et al., 2018; Will‐Orrego, 2020b).  
- Test TFEB nuclear translocation (immunocytochemistry), lysosomal mass (LAMP1/2), acidification (LysoSensor/LysoTracker), and cathepsin D maturation/activity explicitly, recognizing these endpoints are not yet shown for NMN in RPE (Falcão et al., 2025).  
- Assay mitophagy flux (mKeima‐mito), PINK1/Parkin expression, and autophagosome–lysosome fusion (LC3‐II, p62, Rab7 localization) (Fisher et al., 2022; Luján et al., 2022).  
- Measure RPE phagocytosis of POS and handling of phototoxic bisretinoids/lipofuscin surrogates to capture clearance outcomes (Zhang et al., 2024).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Strong disease‐mechanism alignment. Dry AMD is characterized by RPE mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, impaired autophagy/lysosomal clearance, and chronic para‐inflammation; age‐associated NAD⁺ decline in RPE and retina connects this pathobiology to a targetable metabolic axis (NAMPT/NAD⁺), and restoring NAD⁺ is causally protective in multiple retinal models (Jadeja et al., 2018; Cimaglia et al., 2020; Lin, 2020). In vitro and in vivo, NMN replenishes NAD⁺ in RPE and retina, rescues SIRT1 and mitochondrial function, and reduces senescence and inflammation—key drivers of RPE failure in dry AMD (Jadeja et al., 2018; Ren et al., 2022; Chen et al., 2020).  
- Direct RPE benefits with functional readouts. Under NAMPT inhibition and oxidant stress, NMN restores NAD⁺/ATP, normalizes OXPHOS/glycolysis, rescues RPE gene expression, lowers ROS and DNA damage, and blunts senescence markers; in RCS rats, NMN enhances RPE POS phagocytosis through a NAD⁺/GAPDH-actin axis (Will‐Orrego, 2020c; Ren et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2024).  
- Reversal of senescence-driven dry AMD phenotypes in vivo. In the Abca1/g1 model where subretinal macrophage senescence drives SDDs and RPE dysfunction, NAD⁺ augmentation by NMN reduces SDDs, lipofuscin‐positive macrophages, and functional/structural pathology, demonstrating disease‐relevant efficacy in a model that captures hallmark dry AMD features (Terao et al., 2024).  
- Mechanistic tractability and biomarkerability. The NAMPT/NMN → NAD⁺ → sirtuin/AMPK network is well studied and offers clear pharmacodynamic biomarkers (NAD⁺ levels, SIRT1 activity, mitochondrial respiration) and pathophysiological readouts (senescence markers, mitophagy flux), supporting a high‐confidence translational path (Jadeja et al., 2018; Luján et al., 2022; Ebeling et al., 2020).  
- RPE uptake feasibility. ARPE‐19 transport NMN but not NR, favoring NMN for in vitro RPE work; broader literature identifies NMN transport and NR conversion pathways that together ensure NMN bioavailability in ocular cell types (Will‐Orrego, 2020b, 2020a).

Limitations and risks  
- TFEB/lysosome claims remain unproven for NMN in RPE. While TFEB‐driven lysosomal biogenesis/function is a compelling therapeutic target in dry AMD, direct evidence that NMN activates TFEB, increases lysosomal number/acidification, or enhances cathepsin D activity in RPE is not present in the provided literature; these are critical, testable hypotheses that should not be presupposed in development plans (Falcão et al., 2025; Will‐Orrego, 2020a; Ebeling et al., 2020; Cimaglia et al., 2020).  
- Context‐dependent AMPK/Sirt1 dynamics. In NaIO₃‐induced RPE senescence, AMPK activation accompanied ATP loss and was suppressed upon NMN treatment; further, pharmacologic Sirt1 overactivation caused mitochondrial hyperfusion and stress signaling, underscoring that pathway set points matter and that NMN’s benefits likely hinge on physiologic tuning rather than maximal activation (Ren et al., 2022). This complexity argues for careful titration of NMN exposure and for avoiding assumptions about AMPK activation being uniformly beneficial in all RPE contexts.  
- Model caveats. ARPE‐19 harbor genomic abnormalities and do not recapitulate all RPE functions (e.g., missing RPE65), and media composition strongly modulates metabolic readouts; corroboration in primary human RPE (including AMD donors) and in vivo models is essential (Will‐Orrego, 2020c; Will‐Orrego, 2020b; Ebeling et al., 2020).  
- Target competition with NAD⁺ sinks. PARPs and CD38 can drain NAD⁺; in photoreceptors and macrophages these sinks materially influence disease, suggesting that combining NMN with PARP/CD38 modulation may be superior to NMN alone in some settings, and that patient subgroups with high NAD⁺ consumption (e.g., inflammatory phenotypes) may require tailored strategies (Lin & Apte, 2018; Terao et al., 2024).  
- Translation and clinical data gaps. Although nicotinamide and NR have human safety/PK data, direct human ocular PK/PD and safety data for NMN are limited here, and no clinical testing in dry AMD is documented in the provided sources (Cimaglia et al., 2020; Rahman et al., 2024). Dosing translation must reconcile effective rodent exposures (150–1,000 mg/kg/day in various models) with human tolerability and ocular exposure (Lin, 2020; Chen et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2024).

Program implications and next steps  
- Mechanistic validation in RPE. Prioritize experiments that directly test the unproven parts of the hypothesis: TFEB activation (nuclear translocation), lysosomal biogenesis (LAMP1/2), acidification (LysoSensor), and cathepsin D maturation/activity after NMN in primary human RPE from AMD and non‐AMD donors, and in iPSC‐RPE, with parallel readouts of NAD⁺, SIRT1, SIRT3, and AMPK (Falcão et al., 2025; Ebeling et al., 2020).  
- Mitochondria–lysosome crosstalk. Quantify mitophagy flux (mKeima‐mito), autophagosome–lysosome fusion (Rab7 co‐localization), and PINK1/Parkin dynamics under NMN, leveraging assays already applied in AMD donor RPE studies (Fisher et al., 2022; Luján et al., 2022).  
- Functional clearance endpoints. Test NMN effects on RPE POS phagocytosis, lipofuscin/bisretinoid handling, and oxidative debris clearance in vitro and in vivo, building on the strong RCS rat evidence for NMN‐mediated enhancement of RPE phagocytosis via a GAPDH‐actin mechanism (Zhang et al., 2024).  
- Inflammation and senescence. Extend evaluation to subretinal macrophage phenotypes and SASP factors in RPE–macrophage co‐culture and in vivo, given NMN’s ability to eliminate senescent macrophages and reverse SDDs in the Abca1/g1 model (Terao et al., 2024).  
- Dosing/PD strategy. Calibrate NMN dose–response carefully: in ARPE‐19 and primary RPE, co‐treatment with 0.05–1.0 mM NMN rescued FK866‐induced NAD⁺ loss within 72 h, while NMN alone did not elevate ATP above baseline; in NaIO₃ ARPE‐19, 800–1,000 µM was required to adequately restore NAD⁺ (Jadeja et al., 2018; Will‐Orrego, 2020b; Ren et al., 2022). In vivo, effective rodent doses ranged from 150 mg/kg i.p. to 1,000 mg/kg oral depending on model and endpoint (Lin, 2020; Zhang et al., 2024). Engage PK/PD modeling to bridge to human‐equivalent dosing and to support ocular exposure.  
- Combination hypotheses. Consider rational combinations with PARP inhibition (to reduce NAD⁺ consumption) or CD38 inhibition in inflammatory phenotypes, consistent with partial rescue by PARP inhibitors in NAMPT‐deficient contexts and CD38’s role in macrophage senescence (Lin & Apte, 2018; Terao et al., 2024). Also consider pairing with agents that more directly activate TFEB where justified, while monitoring for unintended mTORC1 perturbations (Falcão et al., 2025).

Conclusion  
NMN is a biologically credible and mechanistically tractable candidate for dry AMD focused on RPE rescue through NAD⁺ repletion and sirtuin‐centric mitochondrial restoration, with strong preclinical support in RPE senescence, oxidant injury, and phagocytosis assays, and compelling in vivo evidence in retinal injury and senescence‐driven dry‐AMD–like pathology (Jadeja et al., 2018; Ren et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2024; Terao et al., 2024). The hypothesized downstream impacts on TFEB, lysosomal biogenesis, acidification, and cathepsin D activity are plausible given the Sirt1/AMPK/autophagy network architecture but remain unvalidated in RPE after NMN and should be explicitly de‐risked experimentally before clinical translation (Falcão et al., 2025; Luján et al., 2022; Ebeling et al., 2020). Strengths include a coherent disease‐mechanism target, measurable PD, multi‐compartment benefits (RPE, photoreceptors, subretinal macrophages), and favorable uptake in RPE models; weaknesses include reliance on models with limitations, the need to control for NAD⁺ sinks and pathway set points, and gaps in lysosome‐specific mechanistic evidence and human ocular PK/PD (Will‐Orrego, 2020b, 2020c; Lin & Apte, 2018; Rahman et al., 2024). Overall, NMN merits advancement to a rigorous preclinical validation package focused on lysosome‐mitophagy endpoints in primary human RPE and AMD‐relevant in vivo models, with a translational plan that integrates mitochondrial function, senescence/inflammation control, and debris clearance readouts as co‐primary pharmacology objectives (Ebeling et al., 2020; Fisher et al., 2022; Terao et al., 2024).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Vorinostat (suberoylanilide hydroxamic acid, SAHA; Selleckchem S1047) is a synthetic small molecule originally discovered through a screening process aimed at identifying inhibitors of histone deacetylases (HDACs) and belongs to the hydroxamic acid class of compounds. It was developed as an anticancer agent and later received U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approval for the treatment of cutaneous T cell lymphoma; its chemical synthesis involves derivatization of an anilide moiety with a hydroxamic acid function, enabling a high degree of specificity for the zinc-dependent catalytic pockets of HDAC enzymes. As a pan-HDAC inhibitor, Vorinostat is designed to modulate epigenetic regulation by binding to the active site of multiple HDAC isoforms, thereby increasing histone acetylation and altering the transcriptional profile of target genes. This class of compounds has been broadly used in oncology, where the modulation of chromatin structure reactivates suppressed tumor suppressor genes and triggers cell cycle arrest and apoptosis. In the context of drug repurposing, the rationale for exploring Vorinostat in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is centered on its potential to epigenetically reprogram retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells by enhancing the acetylation status and activation of key transcription factors such as TFEB and FOXO, which are critical regulators of lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy—a mechanism distinctly different from kinase inhibition strategies (Buniello et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2025).

Therapeutic History:  
Vorinostat’s clinical journey has predominantly revolved around its anticancer applications. Early-phase clinical trials in various solid tumors, including breast, colorectal, and non-small cell lung cancer, as well as studies in metastatic thyroid cancer, relapsed or refractory leukemia, and multiple myeloma, have provided a robust safety profile and dosing regimen for this therapeutic candidate (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2004, 2005, 2006; Ghosh et al., 2024). Although its use in oncology has been extensive—with studies demonstrating its ability to block cell growth by inhibiting key enzymes required for proliferation—the direct evidence for its application in ocular diseases, especially in dry AMD, remains limited. Nonetheless, the broader class of HDAC inhibitors has shown promising results in preclinical ocular models. For instance, several studies have demonstrated that HDAC inhibitors can attenuate choroidal neovascularization, protect retinal tissues from ischemic injury, and promote cellular differentiation in the retinal pigment epithelium (Luo et al., 2025). These findings provide an indirect validation of the concept that epigenetic modulators of HDAC activity may be repurposed to combat the autophagy and lysosomal dysfunction observed in dry AMD. Although Vorinostat itself has not been extensively studied in the context of dry AMD or similar RPE-driven degenerative diseases, its established pharmacological profile and ocular tolerability in other clinical contexts suggest that it could offer mechanistic benefits by modulating retinal epigenetic landscapes (Luo et al., 2025).

Mechanism of Action:  
Vorinostat exerts its biological effects by inhibiting the activity of zinc-dependent histone deacetylases. Under normal physiological conditions, HDACs remove acetyl groups from the lysine residues on histone tails, leading to chromatin condensation and transcriptional repression; by inhibiting these enzymes, Vorinostat results in the accumulation of acetylated histones and a more relaxed chromatin structure that promotes gene transcription. The current hypothesis contends that in RPE cells, Vorinostat-mediated HDAC inhibition will enhance the acetylation of the transcription factors TFEB (transcription factor EB) and members of the FOXO (forkhead box O) family. TFEB is a master regulator of the coordinated lysosomal expression and regulation (CLEAR) network, which governs the transcription of genes encoding lysosomal enzymes, including cathepsin D (CTSD), and other proteins necessary for autophagy and lysosomal acidification (Buniello et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2025). Similarly, FOXO transcription factors are implicated in cellular stress responses and can promote the expression of antioxidant enzymes as well as proteins involved in maintaining mitochondrial integrity. In neuronal models, HDAC inhibition has been linked to increased expression, acetylation, and nuclear localization of TFEB, leading to upregulation of lysosomal gene expression and enhanced autophagic flux (Buniello et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2025). It is anticipated that Vorinostat will operate through a similar mechanism in RPE cells by facilitating the dissociation of HDACs from the promoters of TFEB/FOXO target genes, thereby promoting their transcriptional activation. This would initiate a cascade of events that enhance lysosomal biogenesis, improve lysosomal acidification, and increase the activity of cathepsin D—the lysosomal protease that plays a critical role in degrading accumulated protein aggregates and damaged cellular organelles, which are pathognomonic of dry AMD pathology (Luo et al., 2025). Moreover, it is relevant that other HDAC inhibitors, such as trichostatin A (TSA) and valproic acid (VPA), have demonstrated the capacity to modulate similar pathways in retinal cells, thereby indirectly supporting the proposed mechanism of action for Vorinostat in restoring lysosomal function and autophagic balance in RPE cells (Luo et al., 2025).

Expected Effect:  
Based on the proposed mechanism of action, the expected effect of Vorinostat in the context of dry AMD is multifaceted. The compound is anticipated to inhibit HDAC activity in RPE cells, leading to an increase in overall protein acetylation, including that of histones and transcription factors. This epigenetic modulation should facilitate the nuclear translocation and activation of TFEB, thereby upregulating the CLEAR network of genes involved in lysosomal biogenesis, acidification, and autophagy. In turn, the increased expression and activity of cathepsin D will improve the degradative capacity of the lysosomes, fostering the clearance of lipofuscin and other deleterious protein aggregates that accumulate with age in RPE cells. Additionally, enhanced FOXO activity could promote an improved antioxidant response and mitigate mitochondrial dysfunction, which together would reduce oxidative stress—a key driver of RPE degeneration in dry AMD (Buniello et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2025).

The anticipated outcome in preclinical assays would be a measurable restoration of autophagic flux as evidenced by reductions in markers of cellular stress and accumulation of autophagy substrates. Cellular assays may demonstrate increased lysosomal enzyme activities, such as that of cathepsin D, and improved acidification of lysosomes in treated RPE cells. In animal models engineered or induced to exhibit dry AMD-like pathology, treatment with Vorinostat is expected to lead to an improvement in retinal structure and function, potentially assessed through morphological analyses and electroretinography. Furthermore, the restoration of TFEB/FOXO activity should enhance the overall cellular resilience of RPE, thereby delaying or preventing the progression of degenerative changes associated with dry AMD. Given Vorinostat’s established oral bioavailability and systemic tolerability in oncology patients, there is potential for its repurposing with adjusted dosing regimens aimed at achieving therapeutic concentrations in the retina with minimal systemic toxicity (Buniello et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2025).

Overall Evaluation:  
In evaluating Vorinostat as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, several strengths and weaknesses emerge. One of the principal strengths of Vorinostat is its well-characterized pharmacological profile, which is supported by extensive clinical data in oncology. Its FDA-approved status and known systemic tolerability provide a translational advantage over novel compounds that are still in early developmental stages. The robust mechanism of action of HDAC inhibitors, with demonstrated capacity to modulate gene expression through epigenetic reprogramming, aligns well with the pathobiology of dry AMD, where impaired autophagy and lysosomal dysfunction are central features. The specific hypothesis that Vorinostat will promote the acetylation and activation of TFEB and FOXO transcription factors to drive lysosomal biogenesis, improve acidification, and enhance cathepsin D activity addresses well-validated therapeutic targets in the disease process (Buniello et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2025).

However, there are also significant weaknesses and potential challenges that must be carefully considered. First, while the mechanistic rationale is compelling, direct experimental evidence supporting Vorinostat’s efficacy in RPE cells or animal models of dry AMD is currently sparse. Much of the supporting data is extrapolated from studies using other HDAC inhibitors such as TSA, VPA, or AN7, and from cancer studies where the cellular context differs substantially from that of the RPE (Luo et al., 2025). Second, the pharmacokinetic profile and ocular tissue penetration of Vorinostat when administered systemically remain uncertain. The blood–retinal barrier presents a formidable challenge to achieving therapeutic drug concentrations in the retina, and while clinical trials in oncology have established systemic dosing guidelines, it is unclear whether these doses will translate into efficacious levels within the RPE while maintaining safety. Third, the potential for off-target effects and retinal toxicity cannot be overlooked; certain HDAC inhibitors have been associated with deleterious retinal effects when administered at inappropriate doses or over prolonged periods, emphasizing the need for careful dose optimization and possibly localized (e.g., intravitreal) delivery strategies (Luo et al., 2025). Fourth, the complex interplay between various HDAC isoforms in the retina may necessitate a more selective approach than that offered by the broad-spectrum inhibition provided by Vorinostat, as indiscriminate inhibition could disrupt other acetylation-dependent regulatory mechanisms critical for normal retinal function (Luo et al., 2025).

In addition, while the hypothesis posits that Vorinostat will upregulate TFEB and FOXO to enhance autophagy and lysosomal function, the regulation of these transcription factors is multifactorial. For example, TFEB activity is tightly controlled by phosphorylation events mediated by mTORC1 and AKT2 signaling pathways, and the interplay between these kinases, deacetylases such as SIRT5, and HDACs remains an active area of investigation (Abokyi & Tse, 2025; Buniello et al., 2025; Ghosh et al., 2024). Thus, while there is mechanistic plausibility in promoting lysosomal biogenesis via HDAC inhibition, the precise molecular outcomes in the unique environment of aging RPE cells require further delineation. Furthermore, studies in other models have revealed that the beneficial effects of HDAC inhibition on autophagy and lysosomal function may vary depending on the timing, duration, and specific isoform selectivity of the inhibitor used (Luo et al., 2025).

Taking these factors into account, a cautious but optimistic view emerges regarding the repurposing of Vorinostat for dry AMD. The compound’s established clinical track record in oncology is a substantial advantage, providing a foundation for subsequent translational studies. The convergent evidence supporting the role of HDAC inhibition in enhancing autophagy and mitigating oxidative stress in retinal diseases further bolsters the rationale for this approach (Falcão et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2025). However, to fully validate the therapeutic potential of Vorinostat in dry AMD, rigorous preclinical studies are needed to (1) confirm its efficacy in restoring TFEB/FOXO activity and lysosomal function in RPE cells, (2) determine its pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic properties in ocular tissues, (3) assess its safety profile within the retina over chronic dosing schedules, and (4) establish optimized dosing strategies that achieve target engagement without compromising retinal integrity.

Moreover, future investigations might explore alternative delivery mechanisms, such as nanoparticle-based systems or sustained-release intravitreal formulations, to circumvent the challenges posed by the blood–retinal barrier and achieve localized drug concentrations that are both effective and safe. In parallel, combinatorial therapeutic strategies that pair Vorinostat with other agents that modulate complementary pathways—such as antioxidants, SIRT1 activators, or agents that specifically target mTORC1 signaling—could be considered to provide a multifaceted approach to treating dry AMD. These strategies would leverage the ability of Vorinostat to reprogram epigenetic signatures in RPE cells while simultaneously addressing other pathogenic mechanisms contributing to AMD progression (Buniello et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2025).

In summary, Vorinostat represents a promising candidate for drug repurposing in dry AMD due to its potent HDAC inhibitory activity, favorable clinical history in oncology, and a plausible mechanism by which it could restore lysosomal biogenesis and autophagic flux in RPE cells—a central defect in dry AMD pathogenesis. The strengths of this approach include the compound’s established approval and known pharmacology, coupled with emerging evidence that epigenetic modulation can address key cellular dysfunctions in retinal degeneration. Conversely, the critical weaknesses pertain to the lack of direct preclinical evidence in the context of AMD, uncertainties regarding effective ocular delivery, and potential risks of off-target effects in a delicate tissue such as the retina. A comprehensive series of translational studies, beginning with in vitro models of RPE dysfunction and progressing to in vivo dry AMD models, is essential to fully establish the therapeutic window, efficacy, and safety profile of Vorinostat for this new indication. If these studies yield positive results, Vorinostat could offer a novel, mechanistically precise approach to the treatment of dry AMD, addressing a significant unmet clinical need by restoring the autophagy–lysosome pathway and ultimately preserving vision in affected patients (Buniello et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2025).
