Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Harmine is a naturally occurring β-carboline alkaloid that is abundant in Peganum harmala L., and has been investigated for neuropharmacological activities including acetylcholinesterase (AChE) inhibition, antioxidant activity, and anti-inflammatory effects, with related β-carbolines such as harmaline frequently studied alongside it (Singh et al., 2024). As an alkaloid, harmine belongs to a class of nitrogen-containing, basic, often polycyclic natural products that have historically provided a rich source of neuroactive scaffolds and approved therapeutics across neurodegenerative diseases (NDDs), with the literature situating harmine within a broader set of “neuroprotective alkaloids” considered for NDD drug discovery (Singh et al., 2024). In preclinical pharmacology, water-soluble salt forms such as harmine hydrochloride have been used, and medicinal chemistry analogs with higher potency than the parent have been reported, supporting tractability for formulation and structure–activity optimization (Singh et al., 2024).

The mechanistic disease context relevant to dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is dominated by lysosomal and autophagy dysfunction in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), where impaired lysosomal degradation, phagosome–lysosome fusion, and autophagic flux promote lipofuscin accumulation, oxidative stress, complement/inflammasome activation, and RPE death (Boya et al., 2023; Kaarniranta et al., 2023). Master regulators of lysosomal biogenesis and degradative capacity include TFEB/TFE3, which are controlled by mTORC1, AMPK, Ca2+/calcineurin, and lysosomal signaling nodes; TFEB drives expression of the CLEAR gene network to expand lysosomal/autophagy capacity and has been repeatedly highlighted as a central therapeutic axis for restoring RPE degradative function (Boya et al., 2023). The CLEAR program directly impacts lysosomal membrane proteins such as LAMP2 and proteases like cathepsins, and TFEB activity is constrained by nutrient-sensing mTORC1 signaling on the lysosomal surface (Boya et al., 2023). Because LAMP2 deficiency impairs photoreceptor outer segment (POS) degradation and yields AMD-like phenotypes, and cathepsin D (CTSD) is the primary POS protease in RPE, TFEB-mediated enhancement of these systems is mechanistically aligned with dry AMD pathobiology (Boya et al., 2023; Si et al., 2023; Kaarniranta et al., 2013). Note, however, that the provided evidence base contains no direct data linking harmine to TFEB activation, CLEAR gene induction, or DYRK1A inhibition in RPE or neural cells; those specific connections are absent in the cited retinal/lysosome literature excerpts (Boya et al., 2023).

Therapeutic History  
No registered clinical trials were identified on ClinicalTrials.gov for the search terms “Harmine retinal pigment epithelium” or “Harmine dry age-related macular degeneration,” indicating no publicly registered clinical evaluation of harmine for dry AMD or closely related RPE indications under those exact phrases (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.). The negative registry findings were reiterated in independent queries and associated summaries, which emphasize that these are specific to the exact search terms and this registry, and do not exclude preclinical studies, trials registered elsewhere, or studies indexed under alternative nomenclature; nonetheless, they demonstrate a lack of registered clinical activity for harmine in dry AMD on this platform (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).

Outside ophthalmology, harmine has a preclinical pharmacology history in neurodegenerative disease models, including antiparkinsonian activity comparable in some studies to levodopa, anti-cataleptogenic effects in haloperidol models at 2.5–5 mg/kg, and reduction of MPTP-induced oligokinesia, with some analogs achieving desired effects at 2 mg/kg compared with 20 mg/kg for harmine (Singh et al., 2024). Mechanistically, harmine promotes time- and dose-dependent degradation of α-synuclein species via upregulation of the PSMD1 subunit of the ubiquitin–proteasome system and enhanced PKA phosphorylation, supporting a proteostasis-modulating mechanism in CNS models (Singh et al., 2024). Additional pharmacology reported in the literature includes MAO and AChE inhibition in preclinical models, consistent with multi-target neuromodulatory activity of β-carbolines (Singh et al., 2024). The excerpts provided here do not document any prior use of harmine in ocular disease models or clinical settings for retinal disease, nor do they offer ocular pharmacokinetic/tissue exposure or ocular tolerability data (Singh et al., 2024).

Mechanism of Action  
Known pharmacology of harmine in the supplied materials centers on: (1) enhancement of proteasome-dependent clearance of aggregation-prone proteins through upregulation of the PSMD1 subunit and PKA-mediated mechanisms, leading to time- and dose-dependent degradation of α-synuclein species; and (2) inhibition of monoamine oxidase (MAO) and acetylcholinesterase (AChE), along with reported antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects in diverse preclinical systems (Singh et al., 2024). These activities position harmine as a multi-modal agent influencing proteostasis and neurotransmitter pathways in the CNS (Singh et al., 2024).

By contrast, the specific hypothesis under evaluation—that harmine will inhibit DYRK1A in RPE, increase TFEB dephosphorylation and nuclear translocation, and thereby promote CLEAR-driven lysosomal biogenesis, acidification, and CTSD activity—is not supported by direct evidence in the provided context; the retinal/lysosomal references explicitly discuss TFEB/TFE3 regulation, RPE lysosome biology, and autophagy dysfunction in AMD, but do not report DYRK1A involvement or link harmine to TFEB modulation (Boya et al., 2023). The mechanistic literature excerpts instead highlight established regulatory routes by which TFEB/TFE3 control lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy: mTORC1-dependent phosphorylation prevents TFEB nuclear import, whereas AMPK activation and lysosomal Ca2+/calcineurin signaling can promote TFEB/TFE3 dephosphorylation and nuclear translocation to induce the CLEAR program (Boya et al., 2023). In the RPE, upstream lysosomal amino-acid sensing via V-ATPase–Ragulator–Rag GTPases coordinates mTORC1 activity at the lysosomal membrane, and disruptions in these nodes (e.g., βA3/A1-crystallin deficits) impair TFEB/TFE3 nuclear translocation and CLEAR gene expression, contributing to AMD-like phenotypes (Boya et al., 2023; Sinha et al., 2016).

The RPE’s degradative workload is extraordinary—daily heterophagy of shed photoreceptor outer segments and continuous autophagy—so lysosomal membrane proteins and hydrolytic enzyme systems are critical to homeostasis: LAMP2 is a TFEB/CLEAR target whose deficiency delays POS degradation and produces AMD-like retinal changes, and CTSD is the principal lysosomal protease mediating POS/rhodopsin degradation; impaired phagosome–lysosome fusion and elevated lysosomal pH (e.g., due to A2E or lipofuscin) reduce cathepsin activity and drive lipofuscinogenesis and RPE degeneration (Boya et al., 2023; Si et al., 2023; Kaarniranta et al., 2013). Consequences of lysosomal failure include LMP with cytosolic release of cathepsins, DAMP emission, complement activation, and necroptotic cell death; interventions that stabilize lysosomal membranes (e.g., Hsp70 induction) or normalize pH have restored lysosomal function and reduced retinal degeneration in preclinical models, underscoring the therapeutic relevance of lysosome-centric strategies (Boya et al., 2023). In summary, while TFEB activation and lysosomal rejuvenation are compelling, disease-relevant mechanisms for dry AMD, the materials provided do not document harmine as a DYRK1A inhibitor in RPE, or as an agent that increases TFEB nuclear translocation, CLEAR gene expression, LAMP1/2 abundance, or CTSD activity in ocular systems; these specific mechanistic links remain unsubstantiated in this evidence set (Boya et al., 2023).

If the hypothesized mechanism were correct—that harmine inhibits a TFEB-restraining kinase and thereby drives TFEB nuclear translocation and CLEAR gene activation in RPE—the expected cellular outcomes would include increased lysosomal biogenesis, improved lysosomal acidification and ion homeostasis, higher LAMP2/LAMP1 expression, augmented cathepsin content and activity (including CTSD), enhanced autophagic flux, and improved phagosome–lysosome fusion and degradation of POS, together leading to reduced lipofuscin burden, mitigation of LMP, and protection from necroptosis and chronic inflammation (Boya et al., 2023; Si et al., 2023). Autophagy and mitophagy readouts should similarly improve: TFEB/CLEAR activation increases autophagosome formation and lysosomal fusion, restoring autophagic flux diminished with age and in AMD, and reducing SQSTM1/p62 accumulation and associated proteostatic stress (Kaarniranta et al., 2023). Enhanced lysosomal function is expected to reduce DAMP release and intracellular complement activation, attenuate inflammasome/ferroptosis cascades associated with reduced autophagy, and stabilize mitochondrial–lysosomal crosstalk via AMPK-dependent signaling and TFEB-induced biogenesis (Boya et al., 2023). Because mTORC1 hyperactivation in the RPE causes lysosomal dysfunction and AMD-like degeneration, an agent that indirectly reduces mTORC1 activity or relieves TFEB from mTORC1/AKT constraints could restore lysosomal-autophagic balance and improve RPE survival (Boya et al., 2023).

Strengths  
- Mechanistic alignment with RPE pathobiology: The dry AMD literature strongly implicates lysosomal dysfunction, autophagy decline, impaired phagosome–lysosome fusion, and defective degradative capacity in RPE degeneration; TFEB-directed lysosomal biogenesis and restoration of lysosomal pH/ion homeostasis are repeatedly identified as rational therapeutic axes (Boya et al., 2023). - Potential upside: If harmine or an optimized analog demonstrates robust TFEB/CLEAR activation and lysosomal rejuvenation in RPE—with measurable restoration of LAMP2 and CTSD activity, improved POS clearance, reduced lipofuscin/LMP, and downstream anti-inflammatory benefits—then it would sit squarely on a well-validated pathophysiological axis in dry AMD, akin to other successful lysosome-targeted interventions in retinal models (Boya et al., 2023).

Harmine presents as a proteostasis-active, neuropharmacologically tractable scaffold with preclinical in vivo CNS efficacy and formulation/medicinal chemistry precedent, but the specific mechanism-of-action proposed for dry AMD—DYRK1A inhibition leading to TFEB/CLEAR-mediated lysosomal rejuvenation in RPE—lacks direct support in the provided evidence base, and there is no ocular pharmacokinetic or tolerability information to enable translational planning (Singh et al., 2024; Boya et al., 2023). Multiple preclinical studies in RPE cell lines and rodent retinal injury/degeneration models show that metformin preserves RPE barrier integrity, reduces oxidative and inflammatory stress, supports mitochondrial biogenesis, and maintains photoreceptor structure/function, largely via AMPK-dependent pathways; however, dry AMD–specific randomized clinical efficacy data remain limited and observational epidemiology is heterogeneous, with mixed associations across populations, exposure definitions, and AMD subtypes (Amin et al., 2022; Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Gokhale et al., 2023; Liang et al., 2022; Moir et al., 2023; Romdhoniyyah et al., 2021). Critically, while AMPK→mTORC1→autophagy is well-supported in retinal contexts, direct evidence for metformin-driven TFEB nuclear translocation, V-ATPase upregulation, or cathepsin D (CTSD) maturation in human RPE/AMD models is not demonstrated in the excerpted literature, representing material gaps for the central hypothesis (Amin et al., 2022; Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Buonfiglio et al., 2024). Overall, metformin is a biologically plausible, low-cost, and generally safe repurposing candidate for dry AMD that warrants mechanistic confirmation in RPE for lysosome-centric endpoints and rigorous randomized trials across AMD stages (Amin et al., 2022; Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Moir et al., 2023).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Metformin is a small-molecule biguanide synthesized as a derivative of galegine, a guanidine-class alkaloid originally isolated from the plant Galega officinalis; clinically it has been used for more than 60 years as the most commonly prescribed oral antihyperglycemic agent worldwide (class: biguanides) (Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Amin et al., 2022). Chemically, metformin comprises two coupled guanidine moieties conferring cationic, hydrophilic properties and cellular accumulation via organic cation transporters, consistent with mitochondrial complex I engagement and AMPK pathway activation described in mechanistic literature (Augustin & Atorf, 2023). Beyond glycemic control, metformin exhibits pleiotropic effects—anti-inflammatory, anti-oxidative, anti-angiogenic, anti-apoptotic and anti-senescence—reported in diverse cell types and tissues, many of which intersect with pathways implicated in AMD pathogenesis (oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, impaired proteostasis/autophagy, para-inflammation, vascular dysregulation) (Amin et al., 2022; Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Kozlowski, 2023). In ocular contexts, preclinical work indicates that metformin activates AMPK in RPE and neural retina and can preserve retinal structure and function under oxidative, metabolic, and phototoxic stressors (Amin et al., 2022). Collectively, these properties position metformin as a rational repurposing candidate for dry AMD, wherein RPE dysfunction, impaired autophagy/lysosomal clearance, mitochondrial stress, and chronic inflammation are central pathogenic nodes (Amin et al., 2022; Buonfiglio et al., 2024).

Therapeutic History  
Systemic use: Metformin is established first-line therapy for type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) and has been investigated broadly for aging-related conditions due to putative geroprotective effects; long-term safety has been documented, including in the Diabetes Prevention Program (DPP) where gastrointestinal intolerance is the most common adverse event and lactic acidosis was not observed under trial conditions, though B12 deficiency can occur with chronic use (Amin et al., 2022; Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Zhou & Xue, 2024). Preclinical ocular use: In retinal models, metformin has been tested systemically (oral/IP) and intravitreally, demonstrating protective effects in RPE and photoreceptors across light-damage, iodate-induced injury, inherited retinal degeneration (rd1/rd10), and oxygen-induced retinopathy (OIR) with readouts including preserved RPE tight junctions (ZO-1, occludin), outer nuclear layer thickness, and ERG amplitudes; notable anti-angiogenic activity includes decreased CNV lesion size and VEGF/VEGFR signaling modulation in several models (Amin et al., 2022). In these preclinical settings, metformin’s ocular benefits are frequently attributed to AMPK activation and downstream autophagy/mitochondrial and anti-inflammatory pathways, without overt ocular toxicity reported in rodents; however, human ocular safety data and pharmacokinetics under intravitreal or high-dose local exposure are not detailed in the excerpts (Amin et al., 2022).

Clinical/epidemiologic AMD history: Observational epidemiology offers mixed signals. Several large retrospective cohorts and case–control analyses associate metformin use with reduced odds or risk of any AMD or early AMD, with dose–duration trends in some datasets (e.g., MarketScan/claims OR 0.93 and propensity-matched HR 0.57; Taiwanese cohorts HR ~0.54 with stronger protection at >4 years and higher average daily doses), and lower odds reported in multiple studies across US, Europe, and Asia (Amin et al., 2022; Jiang et al., 2022; Kozlowski, 2023; Moir et al., 2023). Other datasets report null or complex associations: a high-quality UK T2DM cohort found no differential AMD risk with metformin using time-varying exposure models; a U.S. claims analysis focusing on dry AMD reported current use slightly increased dry AMD risk while prior use trended protective; additional analyses show no association or heterogeneity by diabetic retinopathy status (Eton et al., 2022; Gokhale et al., 2023; Liang et al., 2022). Meta-analyses also conflict: a systematic review of diabetics suggested decreased odds of AMD with metformin, whereas a broader 2024 meta-analysis concluded no overall prophylactic/treatment role; a European meta-analysis of antidiabetic/lipid-lowering drugs found reduced AMD prevalence overall but not for late-stage AMD specifically (Elhalag et al., 2024; Mauschitz et al., 2023). Importantly, these retrospective designs face confounding (e.g., smoking, comorbidities, health-care utilization), outcome misclassification (wet vs dry AMD), and exposure misclassification (adherence), limiting causal inference and stage-specific conclusions (Brown et al., 2019; Gokhale et al., 2023; Moir et al., 2023). Prospective interventional testing for dry AMD is underway: a randomized, single-blind Phase II trial of metformin to slow geographic atrophy (GA) progression has been conducted, with publication reported in 2024 (Shen et al., 2024); however, the excerpts do not provide efficacy outcomes in GA and emphasize that randomized evidence remains needed (Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Shen et al., 2024).

No regulatory approval exists for metformin in AMD (dry or wet), and the totality of evidence remains preclinical and observational for efficacy, with one randomized GA study reported but without effect-size details here; therefore, clinical utility in dry AMD is presently unproven (Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Shen et al., 2024).

Mechanism of Action  
Canonical pharmacology: Metformin partially inhibits mitochondrial respiratory complex I, reducing hepatic ATP and increasing AMP/ADP, thereby activating AMPK, the cellular energy sensor that shifts metabolism toward ATP-generating pathways; AMPK-dependent and ‑independent mechanisms operate systemically, including reduced hepatic gluconeogenesis, increased enterocyte glucose uptake/GLP-1 secretion, and microbiome modulation with potential systemic anti-inflammatory effects (Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Kozlowski, 2023).

Retinal/RPE mechanisms: In RPE cell lines (e.g., ARPE-19), metformin increases pAMPK and triggers autophagy, reduces ROS, decreases apoptosis, and preserves tight junction proteins (ZO-1, occludin), thereby maintaining barrier integrity under oxidative challenges (Amin et al., 2022; Augustin & Atorf, 2023). At the molecular level, treatment increases Sirt1 and multiple mitochondrial biogenesis and antioxidant markers (SOD-2, Nrf1, Tfam, PGC-1α, COX-II), restores NADH:NAD+ ratios and ATP, and lowers inflammatory mediators (NF-κB signaling, IL-6) (Amin et al., 2022). These signatures are consistent with AMPK’s coordinate regulation of autophagy and mitochondrial homeostasis observed in RPE/retinal contexts, contributing to improved proteostasis and reduced oxidative stress—key failure modes in dry AMD (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Amin et al., 2022).

In vivo, systemic or intravitreal metformin preserves photoreceptors and RPE structure/function in light-damage, iodate injury, and inherited degeneration models (rd1, rd10), with ERG preservation and ONL maintenance; mechanistically, AMPK activation is necessary for light-damage protection in an isoform-specific manner (AMPKα2 dependency), and retina-specific Pparδ is not required, supporting an AMPK-centric retinal mechanism rather than PPARδ signaling (Amin et al., 2022). Metformin also dampens retinal senescence and SASP in OIR after intravitreal dosing, with decreased cdkn1a/cdkn2a and NF-κB/IL-6 signaling, implicating anti-senescence immunomodulation as an additional neurovascular protective mechanism (Amin et al., 2022). Anti-angiogenic actions involve AMPK-dependent and ‑independent pathways: decreased VEGFR2 via enhanced ubiquitin–proteasome degradation, altered VEGF-A isoform splicing toward less angiogenic forms, reduced Flk-1 expression, and inhibition of ALK1-mediated angiogenesis; collectively these actions reduce CNV lesion size, endothelial proliferation/migration/tube formation, and neovascularization in OIR, diabetic, and laser-CNV models (Amin et al., 2022; Augustin & Atorf, 2023). Inflammatory suppression includes reductions in ICAM-1/MCP-1 (AMPK-dependent) and NF-κB p65/IL-8 (AMPK-independent), accompanied by decreased leukostasis and cytokines across models; NLRP3 inflammasome inhibition and modulation of macrophage polarization further contribute to reduced para-inflammation (Amin et al., 2022; Dang et al., 2021; Augustin & Atorf, 2023).

mTOR/autophagy axis: AMPK activation by metformin can inhibit mTORC1, activate the ULK complex, and initiate autophagy, which in RPE promotes clearance of damaged organelles, reduces ROS, and protects against oxidative injury—mechanistically vital for countering autophagy/lysosomal dysfunction in AMD (Dang et al., 2021; Zhou & Xue, 2024). Several retinal studies report AMPK-linked increases in autophagosome formation, and some contextual discussion references mTOR modulation in retinal protection, including translational control via EF2K and general proteostasis benefits (e.g., mutant opsin trafficking) with mixed in vivo translation (Amin et al., 2022). While AMPK→mTOR→autophagy activation is strongly implicated, explicit experimental confirmation in the provided corpus for metformin-driven TFEB nuclear translocation, V-ATPase upregulation, or increased cathepsin D maturation/activity in RPE is lacking; several reviews and excerpts explicitly note these as gaps requiring targeted mechanistic studies (Amin et al., 2022; Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Buonfiglio et al., 2024).

Dose/context dependence and AMPK-independent considerations: Some analyses suggest that AMPK activation by metformin in vitro can require suprapharmacologic concentrations and that certain systemic antihyperglycemic effects are AMPK-independent in hepatocytes; in retinal contexts, isoform-specific AMPKα2 dependence is observed for photoreceptor protection, yet disease models can yield mixed outcomes (e.g., limited benefit or worse function in some HFD diabetic retinopathy paradigms), underscoring the need to define dosing, timing, and disease-stage context for retinal efficacy (Amin et al., 2022; Moir et al., 2023). These data caution against assuming uniform AMPK-mediated benefit across all retinal diseases or AMD stages and highlight the importance of pharmacokinetics, tissue exposure, and therapeutic window in the eye (Moir et al., 2023).

Translational addenda—microbiome and lipid handling: Metformin alters gut microbiota and systemic metabolites, which has been linked to reduced retinal neovascularization through a putative “gut–retina axis,” and may also reduce OxLDL uptake and promote cholesterol efflux via AMPK/LXR–ABCA1/G1 signaling, potentially limiting drusen-related lipid accumulation and NLRP3 activation in RPE (Dang et al., 2021; Zhou & Xue, 2024).

Summary of mechanistic sufficiency for the hypothesis: The literature robustly supports metformin’s activation of AMPK in RPE/retina, inhibition of inflammatory and oxidative pathways, modulation of mTOR/autophagy, and preservation of RPE and photoreceptor function in multiple preclinical models—mechanistic axes consistent with dry AMD biology (Amin et al., 2022; Zhou & Xue, 2024). However, direct experimental evidence in the provided corpus for metformin-induced TFEB nuclear translocation, increased V-ATPase expression, or enhanced cathepsin D maturation/activity in human RPE is not shown; several reviews explicitly note TFEB/V-ATPase/CTSD endpoints as critical gaps that merit targeted validation in AMD-relevant assays (Amin et al., 2022; Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Buonfiglio et al., 2024).

Expected Effect  
Assay-level predictions for RPE models: In human RPE cell lines and iPSC-RPE, metformin at concentrations compatible with cellular AMPK activation is expected to increase pAMPK (Thr172), reduce mTORC1 activity (e.g., decreased pS6 and p4EBP1), and initiate autophagy (increased LC3-II with enhanced flux in the presence of bafilomycin, reduction in p62/SQSTM1 under steady-state), while decreasing ROS and apoptosis under oxidative stress (e.g., H2O2), preserving tight junction integrity (occludin, ZO-1), and improving mitochondrial function (increased ATP, restored NADH:NAD+ ratio, increased PGC-1α/Tfam/Nrf1 and SOD-2) (Amin et al., 2022). Published in vitro data already support many of these endpoints: metformin reduced ROS and apoptosis, increased pAMPK and antioxidative molecules including Sirt1/Nrf2, and preserved occludin/ZO-1 in ARPE-19 challenged with H2O2 or glyoxal; AMPK inhibition abrogated the protection, indicating dependence on AMPK signaling (Amin et al., 2022). In oxidant or lipid-rich RPE conditions, decreased NF-κB activation and inflammasome signaling (e.g., NLRP3) would be anticipated, consistent with prior reports of metformin inhibiting NF-κB and NLRP3 activation in ocular/immune models (Augustin & Atorf, 2023).

Hypothesized lysosomal/TFEB endpoints: The working hypothesis proposes that AMPK activation by metformin will inhibit mTORC1, promote TFEB nuclear translocation, increase V-ATPase expression, enhance lysosomal acidification, and increase cathepsin D (CTSD) maturation, restoring autophagic flux and preventing RPE degeneration. While the AMPK→mTORC1→autophagy cascade is supported in RPE and retina, the provided literature does not directly demonstrate metformin-induced TFEB nuclear translocation, V-ATPase upregulation, or CTSD maturation increases in RPE; thus, these are testable predictions rather than established metformin actions in RPE (Amin et al., 2022; Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Augustin & Atorf, 2023). Given TFEB’s role in lysosomal biogenesis and function, metformin’s dampening of mTORC1 could plausibly facilitate TFEB nuclear entry, but explicit experimental validation (e.g., TFEB nuclear localization quantification, lysosomal pH assays, V-ATPase subunit expression/activity, pro-CTSD→mature CTSD processing and enzymatic activity assays) is needed to confirm the hypothesized mechanism in AMD-relevant RPE models (Dang et al., 2021; Ebeling et al., 2022).

Target expression plausibility: AMPK is expressed in RPE and retina; stimulation prevents RPE and photoreceptor degeneration in multiple mouse models, and metformin increases pAMPK in human RPE cell lines—indicating sufficient expression and pathway competence for drug action in the assay system (Elhalag et al., 2024; Amin et al., 2022). Downstream readouts of autophagy and mitochondrial biogenesis/antioxidant pathways (LC3-II, PGC-1α, SOD-2, Nrf1, Tfam) have been measured and improved with metformin in RPE/retinal models, supporting assay feasibility and expected directions of effect (Amin et al., 2022).

In vivo expected effects in dry-AMD–relevant models: In toxin- and stress-driven models of RPE/photoreceptor degeneration (e.g., sodium iodate, light-induced damage) and inherited retinal degeneration, metformin is expected to preserve RPE morphology and function, maintain ONL thickness, and preserve ERG signals, consistent with reported benefits mediated by AMPK activation; however, model- and disease-stage–specific responses can vary, and negative/neutral results have been documented in some diabetic retinopathy paradigms, underscoring the need to test across multiple AMD-relevant models and to incorporate timing and dose-response studies (Amin et al., 2022). In models of para-inflammation and senescence, metformin is expected to reduce SASP mediators and senescent RPE or retinal cells, aligning with intravitreal metformin effects in OIR and broader anti-senescence literature (Amin et al., 2022; Kozlowski, 2023).

Clinical expected effects: Based on observational associations, any protective effect may be stronger for early or non-exudative AMD and may display dose–duration dependence; however, epidemiologic heterogeneity and potential confounding mean that no specific effect size can be assumed, and randomized trial confirmation in geographic atrophy and earlier AMD stages is necessary to define clinical benefit and exposure requirements (Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Liang et al., 2022).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Mechanistic convergence on AMD biology: Metformin engages AMPK-dependent and ‑independent processes that directly counter core dry AMD pathomechanisms—oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, impaired autophagy/proteostasis, para-inflammation/senescence, and, secondarily, maladaptive vascular/angio-inflammatory signaling—supported by coherent molecular readouts (pAMPK↑, autophagy induction, mitochondrial biogenesis markers↑, NF-κB/NLRP3↓) in RPE and retinal models (Amin et al., 2022; Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Zhou & Xue, 2024). Preclinical efficacy in preserving RPE barrier proteins and photoreceptor function across multiple insults strengthens biological plausibility for dry AMD (Amin et al., 2022).
- Epidemiologic signal and translational momentum: Multiple large retrospective analyses show reduced odds/risk of AMD—often with dose–duration trends—among metformin users, and a randomized GA trial has been conducted, indicating clinical interest and feasibility for prospective testing (Amin et al., 2022; Jiang et al., 2022; Moir et al., 2023; Shen et al., 2024). Meta-analytic work in diabetics suggests potential protective associations, especially in early AMD, reinforcing the rationale to test in non-diabetic AMD populations with controlled exposure (Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Liang et al., 2022).
- Favorable systemic safety and low cost: Decades of broad clinical use, with well-characterized safety signals (GI intolerance, B12 deficiency; rare lactic acidosis risk under renal/hepatic compromise), make metformin attractive from a risk–benefit and access perspective for an elderly AMD population, assuming ocular safety is confirmed (Amin et al., 2022; Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Zhou & Xue, 2024).
- Ocular delivery flexibility and mechanistic redundancy: Both systemic and intravitreal dosing have produced retinal benefits in animals; intravitreal delivery achieved senescence suppression independent of anti-VEGF effects, suggesting non-overlapping mechanisms that could complement existing therapies (Amin et al., 2022). Mechanistic redundancy (anti-oxidant, autophagy, anti-inflammatory, anti-angiogenic) could enhance robustness in multifactorial AMD pathophysiology (Amin et al., 2022; Dang et al., 2021).

Weaknesses and Gaps  
- Critical mechanistic gaps relative to the hypothesis: Direct evidence in human RPE/AMD-relevant systems for metformin-driven TFEB nuclear translocation, increases in V-ATPase expression/activity, and enhanced cathepsin D maturation/activity is absent in the provided literature; several reviews explicitly highlight TFEB/V-ATPase/CTSD endpoints as missing and necessary to establish lysosome-centric restoration of autophagic flux (Amin et al., 2022; Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Buonfiglio et al., 2024). Without these data, the proposed AMPK–TFEB–lysosome axis remains inferential in RPE.
- Heterogeneous and contradictory epidemiology: While many retrospective datasets suggest benefit (often in T2DM cohorts), high-quality time-varying analyses and some claims datasets report null or even an increased risk signal for current users regarding dry AMD; meta-analyses differ in conclusions, and late-stage AMD associations are particularly uncertain (Elhalag et al., 2024; Gokhale et al., 2023; Liang et al., 2022; Mauschitz et al., 2023). Confounding (smoking, DR severity, comedications), misclassification (wet vs dry), and exposure uncertainty limit inferential strength (Brown et al., 2019; Moir et al., 2023; Gokhale et al., 2023).
- Limited randomized clinical efficacy data in dry AMD: A GA randomized trial has been reported, but efficacy outcomes are not detailed in the excerpts; prior DPP follow-up imaging showed no significant AMD prevalence difference between metformin, lifestyle, and placebo, though that study was not designed for AMD endpoints; consequently, clinical efficacy remains unproven (Moir et al., 2023; Shen et al., 2024).
- Context dependence and dose constraints: Retinal benefits can be model- and isoform-specific (AMPKα2 dependence) and mixed in metabolic DR models; some analyses suggest suprapharmacologic concentrations may be necessary for robust AMPK activation in vitro, raising translational questions regarding retinal exposure at tolerated systemic doses, and arguing for ocular PK and target-engagement studies (Amin et al., 2022; Moir et al., 2023).
- Ocular safety and pharmacokinetics: Human ocular safety data for chronic exposure (systemic or local) in older non-diabetic AMD patients are not detailed here; intravitreal metformin safety in humans is uncharacterized in these excerpts, necessitating staged ocular toxicology and PK prior to (or within) clinical trials (Amin et al., 2022; Moir et al., 2023).

Development Implications and Recommendations  
- Mechanism validation in RPE: Prioritize targeted studies in human iPSC-RPE and donor-derived RPE to test the hypothesized AMPK→mTORC1→TFEB→lysosome axis. Required assays: TFEB nuclear localization (immunocytochemistry, subcellular fractionation), lysosomal pH (LysoSensor/LysoTracker), V-ATPase subunit expression and activity (ATPase assays), CTSD maturation (pro/mature CTSD Western) and enzymatic activity, autophagic flux (LC3 turnover with/without lysosomal blockade), and rescue experiments with AMPK and TFEB perturbation (e.g., CRISPRi/siRNA) (Amin et al., 2022; Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Ebeling et al., 2022).
- Translational pharmacology: Define retinal/RPE exposure–response using clinically relevant systemic concentrations and ocular distribution modeling; consider topical/periocular/intravitreal delivery if systemic exposure is insufficient for retinal AMPK engagement and lysosome-centric endpoints, with rigorous ocular toxicology (Moir et al., 2023).
- Indication and stage targeting: Given epidemiologic signals skew toward early/non-exudative AMD and limited evidence for late AMD benefit, prioritize early/intermediate AMD cohorts and GA progression trials with mechanistic biomarkers (RPE autofluorescence dynamics, OCT-based RPE/ONL metrics, aqueous humor cytokines/miRNAs) to increase sensitivity to disease-modifying effects (Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Liang et al., 2022; Moir et al., 2023).
- Clinical trial design: Incorporate robust confounder control and stratification (smoking, DR status, renal function, OCT1 polymorphisms) and embed target engagement (e.g., peripheral blood or aqueous biomarkers of AMPK/mTOR/autophagy) and safety surveillance (B12 levels, GI tolerability, lactate in at-risk) to bridge mechanism to clinical outcome (Gokhale et al., 2023; Zhou & Xue, 2024).
- Combination/adjunct strategies: Given non-overlapping mechanisms with anti-VEGF and complement inhibitors, explore combinatorial approaches in late-stage disease (e.g., GA with complement inhibition) if target engagement and safety are demonstrated (Amin et al., 2022; Shen et al., 2024).

Conclusion: Metformin is a credible repurposing candidate for dry AMD on the strength of convergent mechanistic rationale (AMPK activation, autophagy/mitochondrial support, anti-inflammatory/anti-senescence actions), robust preclinical retinal protection across models, and suggestive—but inconsistent—observational human data; however, decisive gaps remain for the central lysosome-centric hypothesis (TFEB/V-ATPase/CTSD in RPE) and for randomized clinical efficacy, especially in GA. The program should proceed with focused mechanistic validation of TFEB/lysosome endpoints in RPE, retinal target engagement and pharmacology at clinically feasible exposures, and staged, biomarker-rich randomized trials in early/intermediate AMD and GA to quantify efficacy and safety. Until lysosomal endpoints are confirmed and clinical benefit demonstrated, the hypothesis that metformin restores RPE autophagic flux via TFEB/V-ATPase/CTSD to prevent dry AMD remains plausible but unproven (Amin et al., 2022; Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Shen et al., 2024; Gokhale et al., 2023; Elhalag et al., 2024).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
VX-765 is an orally bioavailable small‐molecule agent belonging to the caspase-1 inhibitor class. It is a synthetically derived peptidomimetic prodrug that, once metabolized, yields an active derivative capable of selectively binding to and inhibiting caspase-1. Originally developed by Vertex Pharmaceuticals, VX-765 was designed to address the shortcomings of earlier peptide-based caspase inhibitors by improving bioavailability, stability, and selectivity. As a caspase-1 inhibitor, it falls within a broader category of agents that have been used to blunt excessive inflammasome responses in various inflammatory and immune-mediated conditions. In the context of drug discovery, caspase-1 inhibitors have been of keen interest because caspase-1 is the key enzyme responsible for converting pro-IL-1β and pro-IL-18 into their active cytokine forms, thereby playing a central role in mediating inflammation and the programmed cell death process known as pyroptosis. VX-765 has been evaluated primarily in systemic inflammatory and cardiovascular settings, where its favorable pharmacokinetic profile and excellent oral bioavailability have been demonstrated (Audia et al., 2018; MacKenzie & Schipper, 2010).

Therapeutic History:  
The therapeutic history of VX-765 underscores its extensive preclinical development and early clinical evaluation in several inflammatory settings. In preclinical cardiovascular models, for instance, VX-765 demonstrated significant cardioprotection when administered during reperfusion, reducing infarct size and preserving mitochondrial enzyme activities (Audia et al., 2018). It has undergone Phase I and Phase II clinical studies—its Phase II safety data indicate that it is well tolerated at doses that achieve a suppression of proinflammatory cytokines in plasma (MacKenzie & Schipper, 2010). Although the major clinical investigations with VX-765 have focused on disorders such as epilepsy and other inflammatory diseases rather than ophthalmic disorders, the rationale for its use in dry AMD stems from overlapping inflammatory mechanisms. Specifically, dry AMD shares underlying pathological processes such as chronic inflammation, oxidative stress, and lysosomal dysfunction in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells. Prior experimental studies in RPE models using caspase-1 inhibitors like Z-YVAD-FMK have demonstrated that inhibiting caspase-1 activity reduces IL-1β release and can influence cell death pathways (Brandstetter, 2016; Tseng et al., 2013). However, despite this promising mechanistic background, VX-765 itself has not yet been directly evaluated in preclinical models of dry AMD or in similar ocular diseases. This gap in ophthalmic precedent is notable, but given its established safety profile in nonocular clinical settings and robust anti-inflammatory activity, VX-765 remains an attractive candidate for repurposing into the dry AMD arena (Audia et al., 2018; MacKenzie & Schipper, 2010).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, VX-765 exerts its effect primarily through selective inhibition of caspase-1, a cysteine protease critically involved in the processing of pro-inflammatory cytokines. Under conditions of cellular stress—such as those occurring in RPE cells in response to lipofuscin accumulation and photooxidative damage—lysosomal destabilization can occur. This lysosomal membrane permeabilization (LMP) leads to the release of cathepsins and other proteases into the cytosol, which, in turn, can serve as an activator of the NLRP3 inflammasome. Once assembled, the inflammasome facilitates the autocatalytic cleavage of caspase-1 into its active p10/p20 subunits, thereby enabling it to convert pro-IL-1β and pro-IL-18 into their mature, secreted forms. VX-765 binds to the active site of caspase-1, thereby preventing this proteolytic cleavage and subsequent cytokine release. This action not only blunts the inflammatory cascade but, by inhibiting caspase-1–dependent processing, may also prevent the activation of gasdermin-D (GSDMD) which is responsible for forming membrane pores during pyroptosis (Brandstetter, 2016; Tseng et al., 2013).

The hypothesis for using VX-765 in dry AMD is that inhibition of caspase-1 will disrupt a pathological amplification loop. In RPE cells exposed to chronic oxidative stress and lipofuscin-related photooxidative damage, inflammasome activation has been shown to promote rapid pyroptotic cell death rather than a slower apoptotic process. This results in an autocrine/paracrine loop where secreted IL-1β further primes neighboring cells for inflammasome activation, exacerbating cell death and causing tissue dysfunction. By blocking caspase-1 activity, VX-765 is expected to prevent this destructive cascade, thereby preserving lysosomal function. More specifically, there is a hypothesized link between caspase-1 activity and alterations in lysosomal integrity—a process involving LMP that is associated with a loss of vacuolar (V-) ATPase activity and disturbances in cathepsin D maturation. The V-ATPase is critical for maintaining an acidic lysosomal environment necessary for optimal enzyme activity, including that of cathepsin D, which is involved in the degradation of photoreceptor outer segments. Some studies have shown that under conditions of inflammasome activation, RPE cells demonstrate not only an increase in cytokine secretion but also a decline in the functionality of lysosomal hydrolases, which may further compromise cell viability (Brandstetter, 2016). Although direct evidence linking VX-765 to the preservation of V-ATPase activity or cathepsin D function in RPE is currently lacking, the mechanistic framework provided by previous studies using other caspase-1 inhibitors supports the notion that caspase-1 blockade may confer lysosomal protection and attenuate pyroptotic RPE death (Brandstetter, 2016; Tseng et al., 2013).

Expected Effect:  
In the proposed in vitro and in vivo assays, VX-765 is expected to reduce the levels of active caspase-1 and consequently diminish the secretion of IL-1β and IL-18 from RPE cells stressed by inflammatory stimuli such as lipofuscin photooxidative damage. In validated ARPE-19 cell models that mimic the conditions of dry AMD—where priming with IL-1α and subsequent exposure to lysosomal stressors (for example, the photooxidative effects of lipofuscin components) lead to inflammasome activation and rapid pyroptotic cell death—treatment with caspase-1 inhibitors has been shown to reduce cell lysis and cytokine release (Brandstetter, 2016; Tseng et al., 2013). By extrapolation, VX-765 should produce similar results. Endpoints for such studies might include decreased levels of IL-1β and IL-18 measured by ELISA, preservation of cell viability as determined by metabolic assays (such as MTT or LDH assays), and a reduction in markers of pyroptosis including the cleavage of GSDMD.

Furthermore, because the hypothesis posits that caspase-1 activity contributes to inflammasome‐mediated lysosomal membrane permeabilization, VX-765 is anticipated to stabilize lysosomal integrity. This stabilization should help maintain the acid–base balance within lysosomes—reflected by sustained V-ATPase activity—which is critical for the proper maturation and function of cathepsin D. In healthy RPE cells, cathepsin D is a major lysosomal protease responsible for degrading photoreceptor outer segment debris. In the context of dry AMD, a decline in cathepsin D activity may contribute to the accumulation of undegraded material, exacerbating cellular stress and death. Although direct measurements of V-ATPase activity and cathepsin D maturation following VX-765 treatment have not yet been published, the overall expectation is that by interrupting the caspase-1–driven inflammatory signaling cascade, VX-765 can prevent the deleterious loss of lysosomal function and thereby reduce RPE cell death (Brandstetter, 2016; Gao et al., 2019; Tseng et al., 2013).

Our overall evaluation of VX-765 as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD is cautiously optimistic but recognizes several critical hurdles. One of the major strengths of VX-765 is its well-characterized mechanism of action as a selective caspase-1 inhibitor, along with its demonstrated anti-inflammatory effects in non-ocular preclinical models. The clinical safety profile established in Phase I and II studies—particularly its ability to reduce circulating pro-inflammatory cytokines—lends support to its potential use in a chronic disease setting such as dry AMD (Audia et al., 2018; MacKenzie & Schipper, 2010). From a mechanistic standpoint, the centrality of caspase-1 in mediating inflammasome-driven cytokine maturation and pyroptosis is well established, and there is compelling evidence from RPE cell models that caspase-1 inhibition can reduce IL-1β secretion and potentially modify cell death pathways (Brandstetter, 2016; Tseng et al., 2013). These observations provide a strong rationale for the hypothesis that VX-765 could prevent the lysosomal destabilization and subsequent inflammatory cascade responsible for RPE degeneration.

However, there are also several weaknesses and gaps that must be addressed before VX-765 can be fully endorsed for dry AMD. Although the mechanistic data support the role of caspase-1 inhibition in reducing inflammatory cytokine release and possibly preserving lysosomal function, there is currently no direct evidence that VX-765 can stabilize lysosomal membrane integrity, preserve V-ATPase activity, or maintain proper cathepsin D function specifically in RPE cells. Most of the available literature has utilized generic caspase-1 inhibitors such as Z-YVAD-FMK as proof-of-principle tools rather than VX-765 itself in ocular models (Brandstetter, 2016; Tseng et al., 2013). Furthermore, although numerous studies have demonstrated that inflammasome activation and caspase-1–dependent pyroptosis are features of RPE injury in vitro and in some in vivo models of dry AMD, the translation of these findings into effective therapies has proven challenging. The eye’s unique anatomy and the need for adequate drug delivery to the retina raise additional concerns. For an orally administered agent like VX-765, it is not yet clear whether systemic dosing can achieve therapeutically relevant concentrations in the RPE, or whether intravitreal or alternative delivery methods would be necessary.

Another potential weakness lies in the multifactorial nature of dry AMD. In addition to inflammasome activation and lysosomal dysfunction, dry AMD pathogenesis involves complement dysregulation, oxidative stress, impaired autophagy, and other pro-inflammatory pathways. It remains possible that targeting caspase-1 alone may not be sufficient to arrest disease progression, and a combination approach might be necessary. Moreover, previous caspase inhibitor candidates (for example, pralnacasan) have encountered issues with liver toxicity or other off-target effects in long-term studies, raising concerns about the safety of chronic caspase-1 inhibition (MacKenzie & Schipper, 2010). These potential challenges underscore the need for rigorous preclinical studies in relevant dry AMD models that not only assess the anti-inflammatory and anti-pyroptotic effects of VX-765 but also directly measure lysosomal functional parameters such as V-ATPase activity and cathepsin D maturation.

In summary, while VX-765 offers a promising and mechanistically coherent approach to perturbing the detrimental caspase-1–mediated signaling cascade implicated in RPE degeneration, significant gaps remain in linking its action to improved lysosomal function and reduced RPE death in the specific context of dry AMD. The strengths of VX-765 include its established safety data, oral bioavailability, and selective inhibition of a central inflammatory enzyme; however, its application to AMD is currently supported only by indirect evidence extrapolated from non-ocular models and generic caspase-1 inhibitor studies (Audia et al., 2018; Brandstetter, 2016; MacKenzie & Schipper, 2010; Tseng et al., 2013). To move this candidate forward, we recommend that targeted preclinical studies be undertaken in sight-relevant in vitro systems (e.g., ARPE-19 or primary human RPE models) and in vivo models of dry AMD to assess whether VX-765 can indeed prevent or reverse lysosomal membrane permeabilization, sustain V-ATPase activity, and preserve cathepsin D function, in addition to reducing downstream cytokine release and pyroptotic cell death. Only with such data can we determine whether VX-765 holds true promise as a therapeutic for dry AMD.

Overall, while VX-765 has scientifically robust credentials as a caspase-1 inhibitor with proven anti-inflammatory potential in other systems, its repurposing for dry AMD will depend on demonstrating that its molecular actions translate into preservation of RPE function and structure in ocular models. The candidate is promising, but further focused studies are needed to address drug delivery, ocular pharmacokinetics, and the precise impact on lysosomal pathways within the RPE before clinical translation can be considered (Audia et al., 2018; Brandstetter, 2016; MacKenzie & Schipper, 2010; Tseng et al., 2013).

Below is our detailed evaluation of GW501516 as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
GW501516 is a fully synthetic small‐molecule agonist of peroxisome proliferator–activated receptor delta (PPARδ, also known as PPARβ/δ) developed during intensive medicinal–chemistry programs for metabolic diseases. Its synthesis and optimization were driven by the need to generate a molecule with high binding affinity for the spacious ligand–binding pocket of PPARδ, a receptor known for its promiscuity with respect to ligand chemical structure (Acharya, 2017). GW501516 belongs to a class of synthetic PPARδ agonists that emerged alongside compounds such as GW0742, with these molecules originally explored for their ability to improve lipid metabolism, increase fatty acid β–oxidation, and modulate inflammatory responses in tissues such as skeletal muscle, heart, and vascular endothelium (Acharya, 2017; Choudhary et al., 2016). As a representative of this chemical class—and marketed historically under the Sigma catalog number G3536—the compound has been a subject of numerous preclinical studies and has been tested in rodent models to assess its metabolic and anti–inflammatory effects (Acharya, 2017). Its synthetic origin and structural design allow it to bind selectively to PPARδ in order to elicit transcriptional responses that adjust cellular energy metabolism, including the regulation of fatty acid oxidation and mitochondrial biogenesis. Given that the PPAR family acts as obligate heterodimers with the retinoid X receptor (RXR) to regulate gene expression through peroxisome proliferator response elements (PPREs), GW501516’s design confers it the ability to influence transcriptional networks important not only in metabolic tissues, but potentially also in ocular tissues such as the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) (Acharya, 2017; Choudhary et al., 2016).

Therapeutic History:  
Originally, GW501516 was investigated extensively as a therapeutic candidate for metabolic disorders, such as dyslipidemia, insulin resistance, and atherosclerosis. Preclinical studies demonstrated that it could increase serum high–density lipoprotein (HDL) levels, reduce adiposity, and even improve glucose tolerance in rodent models (Acharya, 2017; Choudhary et al., 2016). The compound advanced into phase 2 clinical trials for metabolic indications; despite promising metabolic effects in animal studies, it has not been approved due mainly to safety concerns—in particular, rodent carcinogenicity that emerged in long–term studies (Acharya, 2017; Choudhary et al., 2016). While the focus of its initial development was in the realm of systemic metabolic disease, later investigations have expanded the scope of PPARδ agonists to other pathology areas. For instance, PPARδ has been found to regulate angiogenic cell behaviors, and its modulation has been implicated in experimental models of retinal neovascularization and oxygen–induced retinopathy (Choudhary et al., 2016; Dou & Duerfeldt, 2020). In ocular contexts, research by Choudhary et al. has shown that ligand activation of PPARδ can reduce intracellular lipid accumulation in RPE cells and that genetic ablation of PPARδ in mice exacerbates early dry AMD–like phenotypes while reducing choroidal neovascularization (Choudhary et al., 2016). Furthermore, selective PPARδ modulators including GW501516 have been listed among candidates in reviews discussing lipid–activated nuclear receptors and their potential role in modulating microglia and extracellular matrix turnover in AMD (Choudhary et al., 2016; Choudhary & Malek, 2016). Although no prior clinical studies have directly evaluated GW501516 for dry AMD or related RPE disorders, its history in metabolic research and its identification in ocular-focused preclinical studies support its consideration as a repurposed agent. Notably, it must be borne in mind that while metabolic endpoints were favorable in early studies, systemic administration in humans was halted because of potential carcinogenic events in rodent models, suggesting that if GW501516 is to be advanced for ocular use, localized delivery may be required to mitigate such risks (Acharya, 2017; Choudhary et al., 2016).

Mechanism of Action:  
Mechanistically, GW501516 functions by binding to the ligand–binding domain of PPARδ, thereby inducing a conformational change that releases associated corepressors and enables the recruitment of transcriptional coactivators such as PPARγ coactivator 1 alpha (PGC-1α). This heterodimeric complex, formed with RXR, then binds to specific peroxisome proliferator response elements (PPREs) in target gene promoters to modulate gene expression (Acharya, 2017). In metabolic tissues, this cascade leads to the upregulation of genes implicated in fatty acid β–oxidation (e.g., pyruvate dehydrogenase kinase isozyme 4 (PDK4)) and genes involved in the regulation of lipid handling such as angiopoietin-like 4 (ANGPTL4) (Choudhary et al., 2016). In the context of retinal pigment epithelium, the hypothesis is that GW501516-induced activation of PPARδ would similarly upregulate genes involved in fatty acid oxidation. Such metabolic reprogramming is thought to reduce intracellular lipid accumulation and may simultaneously promote enhancement of mitochondrial function through PGC-1α–dependent pathways. Not only does PGC-1α drive mitochondrial biogenesis, but it also interacts with other transcription factor networks such as the transcription factor EB (TFEB), a master regulator of lysosomal biogenesis and function (Ji et al., 2021). In theory, the activation of these pathways would lead to enhanced autophagic flux and lysosomal acidification, thereby upregulating cathepsin D activity—the lysosomal protease crucial for metabolizing complex lipid species. Such a biochemical cascade would be particularly beneficial in the setting of dry AMD, where drusen formation is in part the result of impaired lipid clearance in the RPE (Choudhary et al., 2016). However, a note of caution comes from studies in rodent retinal degeneration models. Organotypic retinal explants from rd1 mice showed that while PPARα and PPARγ agonists reduced photoreceptor cell death, activation of PPARδ using GW501516 (often abbreviated as GW516 in these studies) failed to protect and even worsened cell viability in wild–type explants, indicating that the tissue–specific role of PPARδ in the retina may be more complex than that seen in metabolic tissues (Wang et al., 2025). Nonetheless, the proposed mechanism in RPE focuses on reducing drusen lipid burden by promoting mitochondrial β–oxidation and improving lysosomal degradation via enhanced TFEB and cathepsin D activity—a pathway that has analogies in other cell types and disease models (Choudhary et al., 2016).

Expected Effect:  
Based on the hypothesis for using GW501516 in dry AMD, its anticipated effects in RPE cells would be multifold. First, activation of PPARδ by GW501516 is expected to increase the transcription of genes involved in fatty acid oxidation, essentially reprogramming the metabolic machinery of RPE cells to enhance the catabolism of long–chain fatty acids. Such a shift would theoretically lead to a decrease in intracellular lipid accumulation, which is a key pathological hallmark observed in dry AMD as drusen and sub–RPE deposits (Choudhary et al., 2016). Second, by triggering the release and/or upregulation of coactivators like PGC-1α, GW501516 would facilitate not only mitochondrial biogenesis and function but also might potentiate the activity of TFEB—a central regulator of lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy. The cooperative action of PGC-1α and TFEB is believed to enhance lysosomal acidification and increase the activity of cathepsin D, thereby accelerating the clearance of aggregated lipids and proteinaceous debris within the RPE (Ji et al., 2021; Choudhary et al., 2016). Third, improved lysosomal and mitochondrial function would ultimately support the homeostatic balance within RPE cells, potentially slowing or reversing the degenerative process characteristic of dry AMD. Importantly, expression data indicate that PPARδ and its coactivators are indeed present in AMD-vulnerable cells—including primary RPE cells and choroidal endothelial cells—suggesting that the molecular targets of GW501516 are accessible in the intended tissue (Choudhary et al., 2016). On the other hand, preclinical animal models of retinal degeneration (such as the rd1 explant studies) have shown that PPARδ activation with GW501516 did not confer protection to photoreceptors and was even toxic at certain concentrations (Wang et al., 2025); however, these models focused primarily on photoreceptor survival in retinal degeneration rather than lipid clearance in RPE. Therefore, while the expected effect in the RPE is an enhancement of fatty acid oxidation and lysosomal processing leading to reduced drusen formation, the exact dose and delivery modality will be critical, particularly to avoid adverse effects observed in other retinal cell types and to bypass the systemic carcinogenicity that halted previous clinical development (Choudhary et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2025).

Overall Evaluation:  
In summary, GW501516 presents both promising and challenging attributes as a potential repurposed agent for dry AMD. One of its chief strengths is its well-defined mechanism in metabolic regulation: as a highly selective PPARδ agonist, it robustly stimulates pathways leading to increased fatty acid oxidation, mitochondrial biogenesis, and—in theory—the enhancement of lysosomal function via cross-talk with PGC-1α and TFEB (Acharya, 2017; Choudhary et al., 2016; Ji et al., 2021). In the paradigm of dry AMD, where defective lipid metabolism and impaired autophagy contribute to drusen formation and RPE dysfunction, the metabolic–lysosomal axis targeted by GW501516 is particularly attractive (Choudhary et al., 2016). Moreover, the underlying rationale is supported by studies showing that ligand activation of PPARδ in RPE cells can diminish lipid accumulation—a finding directly relevant to reducing the drusen burden associated with dry AMD (Choudhary et al., 2016).  

However, notable weaknesses temper the enthusiasm for GW501516. Historically, its systemic administration in metabolic disease trials was halted due to carcinogenicity observed in rodents, raising significant safety concerns that would have to be mitigated by strategies such as localized ocular delivery (Acharya, 2017; Choudhary et al., 2016). The risk of adverse systemic effects could be minimized by intravitreal injection or by employing sustained-release formulations such as ocular hydrogels or nanocarriers, but such approaches require extensive preclinical safety validation. Another critical point is that the beneficial effects of PPARδ activation in ocular cells have not been uniformly observed. For instance, in rd1 organotypic retinal explant studies—which, while focused on photoreceptor degeneration rather than RPE lipid clearance—PPARδ agonism with GW501516 did not reduce photoreceptor death and even increased toxicity in wild-type retinal tissue (Choudhary et al., 2016; Dou & Duerfeldt, 2020). Additionally, while the hypothesis posits that GW501516 will operate through a metabolic–lysosomal mechanism involving PGC-1α and TFEB to enhance lysosomal acidification and cathepsin D activity, direct evidence in RPE models linking these endpoints is sparse. Much of the molecular framework comes from studies in muscle, neuronal, and systemic metabolic contexts rather than from robust ocular models (Ji et al., 2021; Choudhary et al., 2016).  

Furthermore, it remains to be rigorously established whether PPARδ activation in the RPE would indeed result in a meaningful reduction in drusen lipid burden in dry AMD patients. Preclinical studies have indicated that genetic knockouts of PPARδ can lead to early dry AMD–like pathology in mice (Choudhary et al., 2016), supporting the idea that proper receptor function is necessary for lipid homeostasis; yet pharmacologic activation may not recapitulate the complete spectrum of protective effects observed with endogenous receptor function. Moreover, the carcinogenicity concerns associated with GW501516 underscore a key translational hurdle. Even if localized delivery can theoretically reduce systemic exposure, the long-term risk of oncogenic transformation in ocular cells must be assessed with extreme caution given the potential for even low-level systemic distribution or local proliferative effects that could increase melanocytic or retinal tumor risk (Acharya, 2017; Choudhary et al., 2016). Lastly, efficacy in a multifactorial disease such as dry AMD is unlikely to be achieved with a single-target approach. While modulating the metabolic–lysosomal axis is compelling, dry AMD is characterized by inflammation, oxidative stress, and extracellular matrix remodeling as well. Thus, combining GW501516 with other agents that target complementary pathways might offer greater clinical benefit than monotherapy, albeit with additional complexity in evaluating drug–drug interactions and compounded safety risks (Choudhary et al., 2016).

Overall, while GW501516 shows promise in theory by linking PPARδ activation to enhanced fatty acid oxidation and lysosomal capacity—a mechanistic pathway that could, if properly harnessed, ameliorate the drusen lipid burden in the RPE—the existing literature suggests several areas of concern. These include its historical carcinogenicity in long-term systemic studies, mixed and sometimes adverse effects in retinal explant models, and a relative paucity of direct evidence in RPE cells regarding TFEB and cathepsin D upregulation. Before advancing GW501516 as a candidate for dry AMD, further targeted studies are necessary. Such studies would need to assess the molecular effects of localized ocular delivery on lysosomal biogenesis and acidification in human RPE cells, confirm proper engagement of the PGC-1α/TFEB axis, and determine whether any measurable reduction in drusen formation can be achieved without deleterious off-target effects in the retina. In parallel, robust toxicology studies using localized dosing schemes must be performed to address the historical safety concerns. In conclusion, while the metabolic–lysosomal hypothesis for treating dry AMD is scientifically attractive and GW501516 embodies some key attributes that support this approach, its previous toxicity profile and mixed preclinical ocular findings advise caution and the need for significant additional research (Acharya, 2017; Choudhary et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2025).

Taken together, our comprehensive literature review indicates that GW501516 has a sound mechanistic rationale—through activation of PPARδ to enhance fatty acid oxidation and possibly upregulate autophagy–lysosomal functions via cooperation with PGC-1α and TFEB. However, its therapeutic history is marred by safety concerns due to rodent carcinogenicity, and ocular preclinical models have shown variable results that necessitate careful dose optimization and targeted delivery. Ultimately, GW501516 may have potential for treating dry AMD if its adverse systemic effects can be mitigated by localized ocular formulations and if future studies confirm that activation of the metabolic–lysosomal axis within RPE cells translates into meaningful clinical benefit. Further research should focus on detailed in vitro assays in human RPE cells, animal models using localized delivery to the retina, and comprehensive toxicology studies in ocular tissues before committing to clinical trials.

Everolimus has a well‐established therapeutic history as an immunosuppressant and antineoplastic agent. Clinically, it is approved for treating advanced renal cell carcinoma, progressive neuroendocrine tumors of pancreatic origin, and subependymal giant cell astrocytoma in tuberous sclerosis complex patients who are not candidates for surgery (Wang et al., 2022, pp. 6–8; Weber, 2015, pp. 27–28). In these indications, its mechanism as an mTORC1 inhibitor serves to arrest cell cycle progression and inhibit angiogenesis, which are central to its antitumor activity (Kuo et al., 2018, pp. 5–7; Weber, 2015, pp. 27–28). Moreover, everolimus has been effectively used in the context of organ transplantation to prevent allograft rejection by impairing helper T‐cell proliferation (Wang et al., 2022, pp. 6–8; Weber, 2015, pp. 27–28).

With regard to ocular applications, although everolimus has not been approved specifically for dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD), several preclinical studies have demonstrated its potential benefits in ocular cell types and models. For instance, in vitro investigations have highlighted that everolimus can inhibit the proliferation and migration of retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells and modulate mTOR signaling within retinal tissue—an effect critical to conditions such as proliferative vitreoretinopathy (PVR) (Kuo et al., 2018, pp. 5–8). Additionally, clinical trials such as the Phase 2 randomized trial for neovascular AMD (albeit focused on wet AMD) have assessed everolimus’s efficacy in combination with anti‐vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) agents (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2009), thereby providing indirect support for its ocular pharmacokinetic (PK) profile and safety profile. This background, combined with its well‐known systemic tolerability, underscores its candidacy for repurposing in nonexudative (dry) AMD—a disease area in which few pharmacologic treatments exist.

Mechanism of Action:  
Everolimus exerts its effects by binding to the intracellular receptor FKBP12, forming a complex that interacts with and inhibits mTORC1 (Liu et al., 2023, pp. 11–12; Weber, 2015, pp. 27–28). The inhibition of mTORC1 results in a downstream decrease in the phosphorylation of ribosomal protein S6 kinase (S6K1) and other substrates such as ribosomal protein S6 (RPS6), effectively suppressing cap‐dependent protein synthesis and cellular proliferation (Kuo et al., 2018, pp. 5–7; Liu et al., 2023, pp. 10–11). In the context of RPE cells, inhibition of mTORC1 plays a particularly critical role in modulating autophagic flux. Under normal conditions, mTORC1 phosphorylates and suppresses the transcription factor EB (TFEB), a master regulator of lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy. Inhibition of mTORC1 frees TFEB to translocate to the nucleus where it transactivates genes that codify for lysosomal proteins, such as the subunits of the vacuolar ATPase (V‐ATPase), and hydrolases including cathepsin D (Kuo et al., 2018, p. 7; Nieto et al., 2015, pp. 28–32). Preclinical studies have shown that in RPE culture systems, treatment with everolimus results in an increase in LC3 turnover—a marker of enhanced autophagic flux—and accelerates the maturation of cathepsin D (CTSD), which is essential for effective lysosomal degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (Kuo et al., 2018, pp. 5–8). Such modulation of the autophagy–lysosome pathway is mechanistically attractive in dry AMD because the accumulation of cellular debris and lipofuscin in RPE cells is implicated in disease pathogenesis. Furthermore, it has been reported that everolimus displays superior ocular tissue penetration compared with sirolimus in in vitro porcine corneal models, suggesting that its formulation could be optimized for direct ocular administration if required (Liu et al., 2023, pp. 11–14). Overall, the biochemical profile of everolimus supports the hypothesis that targeted mTORC1 inhibition in RPE cells could lead to enhanced TFEB activation and a subsequent restoration of lysosomal function—thereby addressing one of the key pathological features underlying dry AMD.

Expected Effect:  
The hypothesis proposes that everolimus will inhibit mTORC1 in RPE cells, leading to the activation of TFEB, a critical step in lysosomal biogenesis and function. Upon release from mTORC1‐mediated phosphorylation constraints, TFEB translocates to the nucleus where it upregulates the expression of essential lysosomal genes, including those encoding V‐ATPase subunits (which are responsible for lysosomal acidification) and cathepsin D (CTSD), a protease required for the degradation of accumulated waste products (Kuo et al., 2018, p. 7; Nieto et al., 2015, pp. 28–32). This molecular cascade is expected to improve the clearance of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) and other cellular debris that accumulate in RPE cells owing to age‐related impairment of autophagy. In vitro data support that everolimus treatment increases LC3 turnover and facilitates the maturation of CTSD, both of which are indicative of enhanced autophagic flux and lysosomal functionality (Kuo et al., 2018, pp. 5–8). Given that RPE cells naturally express components of the mTOR signaling pathway—including high levels of mTORC1—and that dysfunctional lysosomal clearance is a hallmark of dry AMD (as exemplified by the accumulation of lipofuscin and drusen formation), the expected pharmacodynamic effect of everolimus would be to restore homeostasis in these cells. Successful activation of TFEB is anticipated to lead to improved degradation of damaged organelles and protein aggregates, potentially mitigating the progression of retinal degeneration characteristic of dry AMD. Moreover, the fact that everolimus is already formulated for oral administration with a known ocular PK profile further supports the translational potential of this candidate: systemic dosing may achieve sufficient retinal concentrations to exert the desired effects in RPE cells without necessitating invasive delivery methods (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2009; Liu et al., 2023, pp. 11–12).

Overall Evaluation:  
The potential of everolimus as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD is supported by several compelling factors. First, its established clinical safety and efficacy in other indications—such as renal cell carcinoma and immunosuppression in transplantation—reduce the translational risk associated with drug repurposing (Weber, 2015, pp. 27–28; Wang et al., 2022, pp. 6–8). The fact that everolimus is an FDA‐approved agent with an oral formulation makes it an attractive candidate for repurposing, as its dosing, systemic distribution, and side‐effect profile are already well characterized. In addition, its selective inhibition of mTORC1 has a clear mechanistic rationale in the context of dry AMD. By specifically targeting the mTORC1–TFEB axis, everolimus may correct the impaired lysosomal degradation and autophagic dysfunction that underlie the accumulation of pathogenic debris in RPE cells (Kuo et al., 2018, p. 7; Nieto et al., 2015, pp. 28–32).

A major strength of everolimus is the robust preclinical evidence indicative of its capacity to modulate autophagy. In ocular cell culture systems, everolimus has been shown to enhance LC3 turnover and promote CTSD maturation—both key markers of autophagic and lysosomal efficiency (Kuo et al., 2018, pp. 5–8). Additionally, its improved ocular penetration compared to its parent compound sirolimus suggests that even systemic administration might yield therapeutically relevant levels in the retina (Liu et al., 2023, pp. 11–14). This represents a significant advantage in the context of dry AMD, where achieving effective drug delivery to deeply situated retinal tissues is a persistent challenge.

However, several weaknesses must be acknowledged. Despite a sound mechanistic rationale, direct clinical evidence for everolimus’s efficacy in dry AMD is lacking. Existing clinical studies have primarily focused on other ocular conditions such as neovascular AMD and PVR, and the particular pathophysiology of dry AMD—with its complex interplay of oxidative stress, complement dysregulation, and chronic inflammation—may require a more nuanced therapeutic approach (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2009; Kuo et al., 2018, pp. 3–5). It is also important to consider the potential systemic side effects of mTOR inhibition, which include hyperglycemia, dyslipidemia, stomatitis, and, in some cases, immunosuppression (Weber, 2015, pp. 27–28, 28–29). Although these adverse events are generally manageable in oncology and transplant settings, the chronic nature of dry AMD treatment may necessitate a careful balancing of therapeutic benefits against systemic risks. Moreover, while everolimus selectively inhibits mTORC1, prolonged inhibition of this pathway could potentially interfere with homeostatic cellular processes beyond autophagy, raising concerns about long‐term retinal safety.

Another consideration relates to the multifactorial etiology of dry AMD. While lysosomal dysfunction is a critical aspect of the disease, it is accompanied by other pathological processes such as oxidative damage, chronic inflammation, and alterations in the complement cascade. Thus, monotherapy with an mTORC1 inhibitor may not be sufficiently robust to address all disease mechanisms. Combination therapies that target multiple pathological pathways might ultimately be necessary for effective disease modification. Lastly, discrepancies in the translation of preclinical findings to human disease remain a persistent challenge. For example, while certain animal models of retinal disease have demonstrated beneficial effects of mTOR inhibition, analogous results have not always been replicated in clinical settings (Kuo et al., 2018, pp. 3–5; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2009).

In summary, everolimus presents as a mechanistically intriguing candidate for repurposing in dry AMD due to its ability to inhibit mTORC1 and thereby promote TFEB‐mediated restoration of lysosomal function. Its solid record as an FDA‐approved drug with established dosing regimens and acceptable systemic safety lends additional support to its viability as a repurposing candidate. Preclinical data suggest that everolimus increases autophagic flux in RPE cells, enhancing LC3 turnover and CTSD maturation, which theoretically should facilitate the clearance of pathological debris that characterizes dry AMD (Kuo et al., 2018, pp. 5–8). The advantages of an oral formulation and favorable ocular pharmacokinetics further underpin its translational potential (Liu et al., 2023, pp. 11–12; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2009).

Nonetheless, the candidate also faces important challenges. Key limitations include the absence of direct clinical evidence for efficacy in dry AMD, potential systemic adverse effects associated with prolonged mTORC1 inhibition, and the inherent complexity of dry AMD pathology, which may require multimodal therapeutic strategies. Moreover, past experiences in ocular applications—such as studies in PVR models where everolimus did not yield a statistically significant clinical improvement—highlight the need for carefully controlled dose-finding and safety studies (Kuo et al., 2018, pp. 3–5). It will be crucial to establish that systemic dosing can achieve therapeutic retinal concentrations without eliciting unintended systemic toxicity or disrupting normal RPE physiology.

Overall, while mechanistic and preclinical data provide a strong rationale for repurposing everolimus to treat dry AMD, further rigorous preclinical studies specifically in models of dry AMD are warranted. A careful evaluation of dosing regimens, potential adverse effects, and efficacy endpoints will be essential in the translational development of everolimus for this indication. The mechanistic specificity for mTORC1 inhibition, combined with the ability to enhance autophagic clearance in RPE cells, represents a significant strength that could offer a novel approach to modifying the course of dry AMD. However, the challenges associated with systemic mTOR inhibition and the need for combination strategies or localized delivery systems must be addressed in subsequent research phases. In conclusion, everolimus is a promising, though not yet definitively validated, candidate for repurposing in dry AMD, and we recommend that further detailed studies be undertaken to fully elucidate its potential in restoring lysosomal function and ameliorating retinal degeneration in this patient population (Liu et al., 2023, pp. 11–12; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2009; Kuo et al., 2018, pp. 5–7; Weber, 2015, pp. 27–28; Wang et al., 2022, pp. 6–8; Kuo et al., 2018, pp. 7–8).
