Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Recombinant human pro-cathepsin D (rhCTSD), as exemplified by R&D Systems product 1869-CD, is a bioengineered form of a naturally occurring lysosomal aspartyl protease that is synthesized as an inactive precursor (pro-cathepsin D) (Sharif, 2015, pp. 60–64). This therapeutic candidate belongs to the enzyme replacement therapy (ERT) class, a category of biotherapeutics developed to supplement or correct deficient lysosomal enzymes in various disorders. The natural cathepsin D enzyme is normally produced and processed intracellularly through the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and Golgi apparatus, undergoing critical post-translational modifications—including the removal of the N-terminal signal peptide, glycosylation, and addition of a mannose-6-phosphate (M6P) tag—that are essential for its subsequent targeting to the lysosome (Sharif, 2015, pp. 60–64). The recombinant version is produced under conditions aimed at ensuring high purity and biological activity conforming to GMP standards, thus making it an attractive candidate for repurposing in conditions where lysosomal proteolytic capacity is compromised. The candidate has been designed in the context of neurodegenerative and lysosomal storage disorders, where enzyme supplementation has been shown to restore proteolytic flux by directly replacing a rate-limiting hydrolase (Bassal et al., 2021; Marques et al., 2020).

Therapeutic History:  
Enzyme replacement therapies have been a cornerstone in the management of several lysosomal storage disorders since the early 1990s, with the first approved treatment for Gaucher’s disease setting a precedent for this therapeutic strategy (Saftig, 2005; Lerussi et al., 2025). In the specific case of cathepsin D, recombinant forms have been employed in preclinical models of neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis (NCL) and other neurodegenerative lysosomal storage disorders, where the administration of exogenous pro-cathepsin D was able to rescue functional deficits associated with genetic CTSD deficiency (Bassal et al., 2021; Marques et al., 2020). Animal studies using CTSD-deficient mouse models have demonstrated that both intracranial and localized injections of recombinant CTSD can correct defects in proteolysis and autophagy, leading to improvements in neuropathological markers and even extending lifespan in treated animals (Bassal et al., 2021; Liu, 2021; Marques et al., 2020). Although most of these studies have focused on neurodegenerative conditions of the central nervous system, similar principles of lysosomal dysfunction apply to retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells, which are critical for maintaining retinal homeostasis in the context of age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (Klettner et al., 2013). Notably, the literature suggests that cathepsin D is highly expressed in RPE cells and plays a vital role in the degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (POS), with its deficiency or reduced function being implicated in the accumulation of toxic deposits and drusen formation—a hallmark of dry AMD (Klettner et al., 2013; Sharif, 2015). Despite the absence of direct clinical trials in dry AMD using rhCTSD, the extensive preclinical evidence from both neurodegenerative and retinal disease models provides a compelling rationale for exploring the repurposing of this enzyme replacement strategy in dry AMD (Liu, 2021; Marques et al., 2020).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, the mechanism of action of recombinant human pro-cathepsin D is rooted in its ability to restore lysosomal proteolytic function, which is often impaired in disease states such as dry AMD. Under physiological conditions, pro-cathepsin D is synthesized in the rough ER as an inactive precursor that undergoes several post-translational modifications, including the cleavage of an N-terminal signal peptide, N-linked glycosylation, and critical mannose-6-phosphate (M6P) tagging in the Golgi apparatus (Sharif, 2015). The M6P tag facilitates the binding of pro-cathepsin D to M6P receptors within the trans-Golgi network (TGN), directing the enzyme to late endosomes and, eventually, to lysosomes where the acidic environment promotes its maturation into its active form (Sharif, 2015). Once active, cathepsin D contributes to the degradation of a wide range of substrates, including the photoreceptor outer segments in RPE cells, thereby playing a crucial role in maintaining cellular homeostasis and preventing the accumulation of deleterious debris that can lead to drusen formation (Klettner et al., 2013). The proposed therapeutic strategy involves subretinal delivery of the recombinant enzyme to bypass systemic limitations such as the blood-brain barrier and to achieve localized uptake into RPE cells via the M6P receptor-mediated endocytosis pathway (Liu, 2021; Marques et al., 2020; Sharif, 2015). Once internalized, the enzyme can replenish endogenous levels of cathepsin D, thereby enhancing autophagic flux and proteolytic degradation processes that are essential for the health and function of the RPE (Klettner et al., 2013; Sharif, 2015). This targeted mechanism is a direct, molecularly specific approach that aims not only to compensate for maturation defects in the enzyme but also to overcome upstream acidification abnormalities that often hinder proper activation of endogenously produced cathepsin D in aging RPE cells (Liu, 2021; Marques et al., 2020; Sharif, 2015).

Expected Effect:  
The anticipated outcome of employing recombinant human pro-cathepsin D for the treatment of dry AMD is multifaceted. First, the subretinal administration of the enzyme is expected to lead to efficient uptake by RPE cells via the M6P receptor, thereby supplementing or restoring the lysosomal pool of active cathepsin D where it is most critically needed (Sharif, 2015). This direct enzyme replacement should result in improved degradation of cellular waste such as spent photoreceptor outer segments, mitigating the build-up of lipofuscin and drusen that are characteristic of dry AMD pathology (Klettner et al., 2013). In animal models of CTSD deficiency—specifically those that mimic aspects of neurodegenerative lysosomal storage disorders—the administration of exogenous pro-cathepsin D has yielded significant improvements in proteolytic function, reduction of pathological markers, and even extensions in lifespan (Bassal et al., 2021; Marques et al., 2020), which suggest that similar therapeutic benefits might be achievable in the context of dry AMD. Enhancing the proteolytic flux within the lysosomes of RPE cells is expected to restore autophagy and maintain cellular homeostasis, thereby reducing the incidence of apoptotic cell death and preserving retinal structure (Klettner et al., 2013; Sharif, 2015). Additionally, by compensating for potential maturation deficits and bypassing defective acidification processes through localized delivery, the therapeutic candidate offers a targeted approach that is likely to be both efficacious and specific compared to more indirect modulators of lysosomal function (Liu, 2021; Marques et al., 2020; Sharif, 2015). Ultimately, the expected effect is an overall improvement in RPE health, which should translate into slowed progression of dry AMD, decreased drusen accumulation, and preserved visual function.

Overall Evaluation:  
In evaluating recombinant human pro-cathepsin D as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, several strengths emerge from the literature, though some challenges remain. One of the primary strengths of this candidate lies in its specificity; unlike indirect modulators of lysosomal function, the exogenous delivery of a rate-limiting hydrolase such as CTSD offers a mechanistically driven, targeted replacement therapy that directly addresses a known biochemical deficit in the retinal pigment epithelium (Klettner et al., 2013; Liu, 2021). The robust body of preclinical evidence supporting the efficacy of recombinant pro-cathepsin D in models of neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis, where similar lysosomal impairments are present, lends further credence to its potential applicability in AMD (Bassal et al., 2021; Marques et al., 2020). Moreover, the formulation's GMP-compatibility and prior demonstration of safety in the context of genetic CTSD deficiency are significant advantages that can accelerate its translational potential (Marques et al., 2020; Liu, 2021).

The enzyme’s molecular mechanism, which involves uptake via mannose-6-phosphate receptor-mediated endocytosis and subsequent activation in the lysosomal compartment, is well-characterized and aligns with the pathological requirements for restoring RPE function in dry AMD (Sharif, 2015). This targeted approach provides a direct means to enhance proteolytic activity and autophagic flux, crucial processes that are disrupted in the aging retina and contribute to drusen accumulation (Klettner et al., 2013). The ability of the exogenously delivered pro-cathepsin D to overcome defects in lysosomal maturation and acidification further reinforces its potential role in reversing or mitigating the deleterious effects of the disease (Liu, 2021; Marques et al., 2020).

On the other hand, several weaknesses or challenges must be acknowledged. Although the mechanistic rationale is robust, the translation of preclinical successes in neurodegenerative and lysosomal storage disorder models to the complex, multifactorial pathology of dry AMD remains uncertain (Benes et al., 2008; Liu, 2021). Dry AMD is influenced by a host of factors—including oxidative stress, chronic inflammation, and genetic predispositions—that may not be fully addressed by simply supplementing CTSD activity. Therefore, while the normalization of proteolytic flux in RPE cells is a critical component, it may not suffice on its own in the context of the broader pathophysiological milieu present in AMD (Klettner et al., 2013; Sharif, 2015).

Furthermore, delivery challenges inherent to subretinal injections must be considered. Although localized delivery methods help bypass systemic barriers such as the blood-brain barrier, subretinal injections are technically demanding, carry inherent risks of infection, and may provoke local immune responses due to repeated interventions (Marques et al., 2020; Liu, 2021). The emergence of neutralizing antibodies, as observed in some ERT studies when alternative routes of administration were explored, could compromise the long-term efficacy of the therapy if systemic leakage occurs or if repeated dosing is required (Marques et al., 2020; Liu, 2021). Additionally, the stability and persistence of the enzyme in the subretinal space represent important pharmacokinetic questions that must be addressed through rigorous preclinical pharmacodynamic studies.

Another potential shortcoming is the specificity of the enzyme’s action. While cathepsin D is indeed a critical protease in RPE cells, there is an intricate interplay between cathepsin D and other lysosomal enzymes such as cathepsins B, L, and S, as well as regulatory proteins like cystatin C, which modulate proteolytic activity (Sharif, 2015). This interdependence implies that augmenting CTSD activity alone might lead to compensatory changes in other proteases that could either enhance the therapeutic effect or, conversely, result in unforeseen off-target consequences. Moreover, given the complexity of the RPE cell’s lysosomal network and the multifactorial nature of dry AMD pathogenesis, combination approaches targeting several aspects of lysosomal dysfunction might be necessary to achieve optimal clinical outcomes.

In summary, recombinant human pro-cathepsin D presents a therapeutically attractive and mechanistically rational candidate for the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration. Its origins as a naturally occurring lysosomal precursor that, when supplemented exogenously, has been shown to restore enzyme activity in preclinical models of lysosomal dysfunction (Bassal et al., 2021; Marques et al., 2020) underscores its potential for addressing the proteolytic deficits seen in RPE cells affected by dry AMD (Klettner et al., 2013). The candidate’s well-defined molecular processing pathway—from synthesis as an inactive proenzyme to activation within the acidic environment of the lysosome—ensures that it is both functionally and biologically suited to compensate for endogenous maturation deficits (Sharif, 2015). This detailed understanding of its biochemistry and cellular uptake mechanisms via the mannose-6-phosphate receptor supports the hypothesis that subretinal delivery of rhCTSD could enhance proteolytic flux, reduce drusen accumulation, and ultimately contribute to the preservation of retinal function in patients with dry AMD (Liu, 2021; Marques et al., 2020).

Despite these promising attributes, the candidate’s clinical translation will require addressing several key challenges. Future studies must rigorously evaluate the pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic profiles of subretinally delivered rhCTSD, with particular emphasis on its stability, local retention time in the subretinal space, and potential immunogenicity. It will also be critical to determine whether augmenting CTSD activity alone is sufficient to counteract the multi-factorial processes underlying dry AMD or if the therapeutic strategy should be integrated into a broader, combination-based treatment regimen. Additionally, long-term safety studies are necessary to monitor for potential adverse effects, such as immune-mediated clearance or detrimental off-target proteolytic activity that might impair retinal structure and function (Marques et al., 2020; Thiessen, 2023).

Ultimately, the overall evaluation is cautiously optimistic. The mechanistic rationale is strong—supported by extensive preclinical data from related neurodegenerative and lysosomal storage disorder models—and the therapeutic candidate is produced under rigorous, GMP-compliant conditions, offering a level of quality assurance that is imperative for clinical advancement (Marques et al., 2020; Liu, 2021). The specificity of recombinant pro-cathepsin D in directly addressing a rate-limiting step in lysosomal degradation makes it an especially compelling candidate in a disease setting where impaired autophagy and proteolysis are central to pathology (Klettner et al., 2013). However, challenges related to effective subretinal delivery, the potential for immune responses, and the need to integrate its action within the broader context of AMD pathogenesis must be rigorously addressed in subsequent preclinical and clinical studies before a definitive therapeutic benefit can be confirmed (Marques et al., 2020; Benes et al., 2008). In light of these considerations, recombinant human pro-cathepsin D stands out as a promising avenue for therapeutic intervention in dry AMD, meriting further investigation to delineate its efficacy, safety, and long-term benefits in the appropriate animal models and ultimately in clinical trials.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
2-Hydroxypropyl-β-cyclodextrin (HPβCD) is a chemically modified derivative of natural β-cyclodextrin—a cyclic oligosaccharide consisting of glucose units linked via α-1,4 glycosidic bonds. This modification, achieved by the introduction of hydroxypropyl groups, improves its solubility and reduces its inherent cytotoxicity relative to unmodified cyclodextrins. HPβCD belongs to the cyclodextrin class, molecules that have been widely used in pharmaceutical formulations as solubilizing agents and excipients due to their ability to encapsulate hydrophobic molecules within their lipophilic interior, thereby increasing bioavailability. Over the years, these agents have gained attention as cholesterol-binding molecules, and HPβCD is no exception, being repurposed for diseases characterized by pathological cholesterol accumulation such as Niemann–Pick type C1 (NPC1). Its structural properties permit the formation of inclusion complexes with cholesterol and other lipids, facilitating their mobilization and removal from cells. Given its established role in NPC1 disease and emerging evidence supporting its ability to cross the blood–retina barrier, HPβCD is now being evaluated as a therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD), specifically targeting drusen-associated cholesterol accumulation in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells (Calias, 2018; Roney, 2020).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, HPβCD has been extensively investigated as a therapeutic intervention for lysosomal storage diseases, with a particular focus on Niemann–Pick disease type C (NPC), a condition characterized by the pathological accumulation of cholesterol and glycosphingolipids in cells. Preclinical studies in animal models have demonstrated that systemic administration of HPβCD can lower intracellular cholesterol levels, thereby ameliorating disease-related cellular dysfunction. However, its pharmacokinetic limitations—most notably, its minimal penetration of the blood–brain barrier (BBB) when administered intravenously—have necessitated alternative routes of delivery, such as intrathecal administration, to achieve sufficient central nervous system (CNS) exposure (Calias, 2018). In the context of retinal diseases, several studies have investigated the effects of HPβCD in animal models of retinal cholesterol dyshomeostasis. In these models, HPβCD treatment has been associated with significant reductions in cholesterol crystals, diminished lipid deposition in structures such as Bruch’s membrane, and decreased activation of retinal macrophages and microglial cells (El-Darzi et al., 2023). Although HPβCD has been repurposed from its application in NPC to target retinal pathologies, a focused investigation into its use for dry AMD remains to be performed clinically, as systematic searches on ClinicalTrials.gov indicate that no registered trials have specifically addressed cyclodextrin use in AMD (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, HPβCD acts primarily as a cholesterol extractor by leveraging its toroidal structure, which is characterized by a hydrophilic exterior and a relatively hydrophobic interior cavity. This unique architecture enables HPβCD to form inclusion complexes with cholesterol, effectively sequestering the lipid from cellular membranes. In the setting of RPE cells, where lysosomal cholesterol accumulation is implicated in the pathogenesis of dry AMD, HPβCD is hypothesized to mobilize cholesterol from lysosomal membranes. Excess cholesterol in these membranes disrupts the lipid microdomains necessary for the optimal assembly and functioning of protein complexes such as the vacuolar-type H⁺-ATPase (v-ATPase), which is essential for maintaining lysosomal acidity (Nociari, Kiss, & Rodriguez-Boulan, 2017). By extracting cholesterol, HPβCD is expected to restore these lipid microdomains, thereby facilitating the proper assembly and function of the v-ATPase complex. This normalization of v-ATPase assembly is critical for reestablishing an acidic environment within lysosomes, which in turn is necessary for the optimal activity of lysosomal hydrolases such as cathepsin D (CTSD).

In neurons and other cell types, studies have demonstrated that HPβCD treatment leads to a reduction in both luminal and membrane-associated cholesterol levels, a process that not only improves lysosomal trafficking but also induces lysosomal exocytosis under certain conditions (Roney, 2020). Furthermore, the improvement in lysosomal acidification following HPβCD-mediated cholesterol extraction has been correlated with enhanced autophagic flux due to increased CTSD-mediated proteolysis. Although direct evidence for this mechanism in RPE cells is still emerging, it is reasonable to extrapolate that similar molecular events would occur in retinal cells. The restoration of lysosomal pH and the subsequent improvement in autophagy are critical because they directly contribute to the clearance of intracellular debris, including drusen lipids, thereby potentially reducing the lipid burden that characterizes the progression of dry AMD (Nociari et al., 2017; Roney, 2020).

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis driving the repurposing of HPβCD for dry AMD is that it will mobilize cholesterol from RPE lysosomal membranes, thereby restoring the integrity of lipid microdomains that are essential for v-ATPase assembly. In practical terms, treatment with HPβCD is expected to yield several interrelated outcomes. First, the reduction in membrane cholesterol is anticipated to alleviate the inhibitory effect of cholesterol excess on v-ATPase assembly, leading to improved proton pump activity and a consequent normalization of lysosomal pH. Given that the activity of CTSD is pH-dependent—with optimal function occurring under acidic conditions—the normalization of lysosomal pH should enable enhanced CTSD activity and improved autophagic degradation of lipid aggregates (Nociari et al., 2017; Roney, 2020).

Second, by promoting the removal of excess cholesterol, HPβCD should reduce the formation of cholesterol crystals, a pathological hallmark associated with retinal lipid dyshomeostasis and drusen formation. Animal studies have demonstrated that HPβCD treatment leads to a significant reduction in the number of cholesterol crystals per unit area in retinal tissues, which is strongly correlated with improvements in retinal lipid processing and decreased inflammatory responses mediated by macrophage and microglial activation (El-Darzi et al., 2023).

Third, in laboratory assays using RPE cell cultures, one would expect to observe a decrease in the proportion of lipid-laden lysosomes, accompanied by measurable improvements in lysosomal acidification—parameters that serve as surrogate markers for enhanced autophagic capacity. The repurposing of HPβCD for the treatment of dry AMD is underpinned by a robust mechanistic rationale, a substantial preclinical history, and an acceptable clinical safety profile observed in other indications. One of the greatest strengths of HPβCD is its dual functionality: the ability to form effective inclusion complexes with cholesterol and the resultant improvement in lysosomal function. In several animal models of retinal cholesterol dyshomeostasis, HPβCD has yielded promising results by lowering total, unesterified, and esterified cholesterol levels, reducing the number of cholesterol crystals, and mitigating inflammatory responses in the retina (El-Darzi et al., 2023). These data provide a compelling basis for its evaluation in conditions such as dry AMD where drusen formation is closely linked to aberrant cholesterol metabolism. Furthermore, its prior use in the treatment of NPC—a condition that shares certain pathogenic features with AMD in terms of lysosomal dysfunction—adds credence to the hypothesis that HPβCD may exert similar therapeutic effects in RPE cells (Calias, 2018).

A significant advantage of HPβCD is its established safety record in clinical studies for NPC. Although challenges remain regarding optimal dosing—especially given the compound’s limited ability to cross the BBB when administered systemically—the retinal application appears more favorable, as preclinical studies suggest that HPβCD is capable of traversing the blood–retina barrier and achieving therapeutic concentrations in retinal tissues (El-Darzi et al., 2023). However, it should be noted that the safety profile in the context of chronic ocular exposure remains to be fully characterized. Notably, clinical studies in NPC have observed adverse effects such as hearing loss with certain routes of administration, and while these effects may not directly translate to ocular toxicity, rigorous ocular safety studies will be essential to ensure that any repurposing for dry AMD is both efficacious and safe (Calias, 2018).

Another potential strength lies in the specificity of the lipid‐targeting strategy. Unlike therapies that broadly modulate inflammatory or oxidative stress pathways, HPβCD acts directly on the cholesterol burden—the underlying driver of drusen lipid accumulation in dry AMD. This mechanistic specificity has the potential to result in a more direct impact on the disease process, rather than merely modifying secondary symptoms. Mechanistically, the extraction of cholesterol by HPβCD is anticipated to restore the lipid environment within RPE lysosomal membranes, thereby re-enabling the proper assembly of v-ATPase complexes. This, in turn, can lead to improved lysosomal acidification, enhanced cathepsin D activity, and accelerated autophagic clearance of damaged cellular components—a cascade of events that would address one of the root causes of retinal degeneration in AMD (Nociari et al., 2017; Roney, 2020).

Despite these strengths, several weaknesses and uncertainties must be acknowledged. First, while the preclinical data in animal models are promising, there remains a lack of clinical trial data specifically focusing on the use of HPβCD in dry AMD. A search using the relevant keywords indicates a paucity of clinical evidence in this particular indication (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.), which means that translational hurdles remain before HPβCD can be confidently recommended for dry AMD therapy. Second, although the mechanism by which HPβCD affects v-ATPase assembly and CTSD activity is supported by data in neuronal models, direct evidence of these molecular events in RPE cells is still emerging, leaving some uncertainty regarding the depth of its effects on lysosomal autophagy in the retinal environment (Nociari et al., 2017). Third, formulation and administration routes will be critical considerations. While systemic dosing has been used in other indications, the optimal approach for targeting the retina might require localized delivery techniques—such as intravitreal injection or the development of a sustained-release ocular formulation—to maximize retinal exposure while minimizing systemic exposure and off-target effects. Finally, the potential for adverse events, particularly those related to over-extraction of cholesterol or unintended disruption of lipid homeostasis, must be carefully evaluated in the context of chronic ocular treatment.

In summary, HPβCD is a well-characterized compound with a history of successful application in disorders of cholesterol accumulation, notably NPC. Its ability to extract cholesterol from cellular membranes, restore lipid microdomains, and thereby normalize lysosomal function forms a strong mechanistic basis for its evaluation as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. Preclinical studies in animal models provide encouraging evidence that HPβCD can reduce retinal cholesterol accumulation, lower the number of cholesterol crystals, and improve markers of lysosomal function in retinal tissues. This directly aligns with the therapeutic hypothesis that the mobilization of cholesterol from RPE lysosomal membranes will restore v-ATPase activity, normalize lysosomal pH, enhance cathepsin D activity, and ultimately reduce the drusen lipid burden characteristic of dry AMD (Calias, 2018; El-Darzi et al., 2023; Nociari et al., 2017; Roney, 2020).

However, the translation of these preclinical findings into a clinically effective therapy for dry AMD will require addressing several critical challenges. These include the absence of direct clinical data in AMD, the need for detailed mechanistic studies in RPE cells to confirm that the cholesterol-lowering effects observed in other tissues are recapitulated in the retina, and the optimization of dosing and delivery methods to ensure that therapeutic concentrations are achieved safely in the target tissue. Additionally, any potential side effects—such as those noted in NPC patients, including auditory toxicity—must be rigorously monitored in ocular studies to ensure that treatment remains safe over the long term (Calias, 2018).

Overall, the repurposing of HPβCD for dry AMD is scientifically compelling due to its targeted mechanism of action and its established clinical history in related indications. Its ability to mobilize cholesterol and restore lysosomal function addresses fundamental pathogenic processes implicated in dry AMD, and the preclinical evidence supports its potential efficacy. Nevertheless, the absence of clinical trials in this particular indication, combined with uncertainties regarding the precise molecular interactions in RPE cells and the optimization of drug delivery to the retina, suggests that further preclinical and early-stage clinical studies are warranted before HPβCD can be advanced as a treatment for dry AMD. Continued research should focus on elucidating the detailed molecular mechanisms within RPE cells, assessing long-term safety in ocular models, and exploring various delivery modalities to maximize efficacy while minimizing potential risks. In conclusion, while HPβCD demonstrates substantial promise as a repurposed drug candidate for dry AMD, a measured, stepwise approach in future research is essential to address outstanding questions and to establish its full therapeutic potential (Calias, 2018; El-Darzi et al., 2023; Nociari et al., 2017; Roney, 2020).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Ambroxol is a small-molecule mucolytic historically used to thin airway mucus and has been repurposed as a pharmacological chaperone for the lysosomal enzyme glucocerebrosidase (GCase) in Gaucher disease, where it selectively binds misfolded GCase to aid folding and trafficking to lysosomes for substrate degradation (Alhowyan & Harisa, 2025, pp. 17–18). Ambroxol is further characterized by its ability to cross the blood–brain barrier, a property relevant for neuronopathic lysosomal storage disorders and attractive for central nervous system or ocular indications where access is otherwise constrained (Alhowyan & Harisa, 2025, pp. 17–18). Within the broader landscape of lysosomal therapeutics, small molecules also act as proteostasis regulators and modulators of lysosomal signaling and biogenesis; however, off-target actions remain a central limitation of small-molecule therapy in this domain (Alhowyan & Harisa, 2025, pp. 17–18).

The therapeutic hypothesis for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) posits that ambroxol could act as a pharmacological chaperone for lysosomal enzymes in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), stabilize or enhance vacuolar H+-ATPase (V-ATPase) function, improve lysosomal acidification, and thereby augment cathepsin D (CTSD) activity to clear lipofuscin/drusen components characteristic of dry AMD (Kaarniranta et al., 2023, pp. 2–3; Si et al., 2023, pp. 4–7). This rationale is grounded in the centrality of lysosomal function to RPE homeostasis and AMD pathogenesis: RPE lysosomes sustain heavy heterophagic and autophagic loads from daily photoreceptor outer-segment (POS) digestion, and impaired lysosomal acidification and hydrolase function contribute to lipofuscin accumulation, exosome-driven drusen formation, and progressive degeneration (Kaarniranta et al., 2023, pp. 2–3; Si et al., 2023, pp. 2–4, 5–7; Sharif, 2015, pp. 199–202). Notably, in AMD models and donor RPE, TFEB—the master transcriptional driver of lysosomal/autophagy biogenesis—is dysregulated, V-ATPase-related transcripts (e.g., ATP6VOA1) and cathepsin abundance/activity are linked to lysosomal competence, and TFEB activation or mTOR inhibition reduces toxic storage material such as A2E and POS-derived autofluorescent granules (Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7).

Conventional use: Ambroxol is primarily used clinically as a mucolytic agent to reduce mucus viscosity in respiratory disease (Alhowyan & Harisa, 2025, pp. 17–18). Beyond its mucolytic effects, ambroxol has been investigated in lysosomal storage diseases as a pharmacological chaperone for glucocerebrosidase; it binds misfolded GCase, promotes its proper folding/trafficking to lysosomes, and facilitates substrate clearance, with reported neurological benefits in neuronopathic Gaucher disease and demonstrated blood–brain barrier penetration (Alhowyan & Harisa, 2025, pp. 17–18). Clinically observed improvements in neurological symptoms such as myoclonus and seizures have been reported in pilot studies, and reviews summarize safety/efficacy observations in Gaucher populations, albeit with the caveat of potential off-target toxicities innate to small-molecule approaches (Alhowyan & Harisa, 2025, pp. 17–18, 33–35).

CTSD biosynthesis and maturation provide the mechanistic backdrop for a CTSD maturation enhancer. Mechanistic cross-talk and constraints that are relevant for a CTSD maturation enhancer include:  
- pH dependence: CTSD maturation and catalysis require acidic lysosomes; in alkaline lysosomes (e.g., due to bisretinoid accumulation), pro-CTSD processing is impaired even if total CTSD protein increases, so a maturation accelerator may be insufficient without concurrent restoration of lysosomal pH in some disease states (Ng et al., 2024).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Anakinra (brand: Kineret) is a recombinant, non-glycosylated form of the human interleukin-1 receptor antagonist (IL-1Ra) that competitively binds the type I interleukin-1 receptor (IL-1RI) and prevents signaling by IL-1α and IL-1β, thereby broadly antagonizing downstream IL-1–dependent signal transduction cascades (notably NF-κB and MAPK) in responsive cells (Dabouz, 2024; Dabouz et al., 2020). IL-1Ra belongs to the class of anti-cytokine biologics that block pro-inflammatory cytokine signaling, a therapeutic strategy that has been validated across systemic autoinflammatory and autoimmune diseases; Kineret has an extensive human safety and pharmacology dossier as an approved product, with prescribing information available for systemic use (Mesquida, Drawnel, & Fauser, 2019). Within ophthalmology, IL-1 pathway blockade has been investigated in multiple preclinical ocular models and has seen clinical use for inflammatory eye diseases; routes explored include systemic administration of anakinra for uveitis and scleritis, topical IL-1 antagonists for ocular surface disease (e.g., isunakinra/EBI-005), and experimental ocular gene therapy encoding IL-1Ra (Fabiani et al., 2017). In posterior segment disease models, intravitreal recombinant IL-1Ra (anakinra) inhibited laser-induced choroidal neovascularization (CNV) in rodents in a dose-dependent fashion, establishing local ocular pharmacologic activity of IL-1R antagonism in retina/choroid (Fabiani et al., 2017; Sandhu, Lambert, Xu, & Kaplan, 2018).

Therapeutic History  
Systemic indications and ocular inflammatory experience. Anakinra has long been employed systemically in rheumatology and has been repurposed for ocular autoinflammatory and autoimmune conditions such as Behçet uveitis, Blau syndrome/CAPS phenotypes, and refractory scleritis, with reported improvements in intraocular inflammation and steroid-sparing in case series and retrospective cohorts; dosing regimens reported include 100–150 mg daily or weight-based 1–3 mg/kg daily subcutaneous dosing, with acceptable tolerability profiles dominated by mild injection-site reactions in the ocular cohorts cited (Fabiani et al., 2017; Korhonen, 2024). A practical constraint is anakinra’s short systemic half-life that necessitates daily dosing, with relapse reported upon dose reductions in some inflammatory eye disease cases—an important consideration for chronic indications (Fabiani et al., 2017; Korhonen, 2024). Topical isunakinra/IL-1Ra formulations for ocular surface disease demonstrated clinically meaningful symptom and sign improvements in randomized trials, high ocular receptor occupancy (~97%) at low doses, minimal systemic exposure (plasma below detection), and a favorable local safety signal, although these outcomes pertain to the anterior segment and cannot be extrapolated directly to the posterior segment (Fabiani et al., 2017).

Posterior segment and AMD-relevant preclinical work. Multiple animal studies substantiate that IL-1 signaling is active and targetable in the posterior segment. In a rat CNV model, intravitreal anakinra led to dose-dependent reductions in neovascular area; related IL-1β-targeted interventions prevented CNV without exacerbating photoreceptor degeneration, arguing against gross phototoxicity from IL-1 blockade in that setting (Sandhu et al., 2018; Fabiani et al., 2017). In a blue light–induced retinal degeneration model, systemic IL-1R antagonism with anakinra mitigated inflammatory readouts, reduced accumulation of subretinal macrophages, preserved photoreceptor structure, and maintained ERG function; an allosteric IL-1R modulator (rytvela) was somewhat superior, but anakinra nonetheless produced protective effects (Dabouz et al., 2020; Dabouz, 2024). Mechanistically, these studies localized IL-1β production to inflammasome-active subretinal mononuclear phagocytes (MPs) and mapped Il1r1 expression mainly to astroglia and vascular cells in mouse retina, supporting paracrine IL-1 signaling to neurovascular targets in the outer retina (Dabouz et al., 2020; Dabouz, 2024).

Human clinical evidence in dry AMD/geographic atrophy. No published human trials of anakinra for dry AMD/geographic atrophy (GA) were identified in the provided materials; a registry search string returned 18 ClinicalTrials.gov hits combining anakinra with retinal keywords, but no trial-level information (indication, route, dose, status, outcomes) was provided, and no AMD/GA trials of anakinra are documented here (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.). Systemic IL-1β blockade with canakinumab showed no effect in a diabetic retinopathy exploratory clinical context, underscoring translational uncertainty of systemic IL-1 pathway modulation for posterior segment disease (Korhonen, 2024).

Mechanistic rationale in RPE/AMD. Extensive literature supports that in AMD-relevant stress contexts the RPE and subretinal myeloid cells exhibit NLRP3 inflammasome activation, caspase-1–dependent maturation of IL-1β and IL-18, lysosomal membrane permeabilization (LMP) with cathepsin release, and altered autophagy/heterophagy—mechanistic substrates for chronic para-inflammation and cell death (apoptosis → pyroptosis shift) in RPE (Treanor, n.d.; Yerramothu, Vijay, & Willcox, 2018; Kaarniranta et al., 2023). IL-1β levels are elevated in AMD vitreous and plasma, and microglia/MP-derived IL-1β can drive chemokine and cytokine production by Müller cells and RPE, linking IL-1 to retinal inflammatory amplification (Nashine et al., 2022; Korhonen, 2024). The RPE itself produces IL-1Ra and uses IL-1Ra to limit immune activation: IL-1Ra suppresses necrosis-induced release of IL-6, IL-8, and MCP-1 from ARPE-19 and reduces antigen-presenting functions in RPE cocultures, indicating that IL-1 signaling is operational in RPE and that IL-1R antagonism can blunt RPE-mediated inflammatory outputs in vitro (Fabiani et al., 2017; Kaur & Singh, 2021).

In the blue-light retinal injury model, orthosteric antagonism with anakinra and allosteric modulation with rytvela each prevented IL-1–driven retinal inflammation and photoreceptor injury; mechanistically, both agents protected neuroretinal compartments that express IL-1R while not necessarily reducing IL-1β produced in macrophage conditioned media, consistent with receptor-level antagonism in responder cells (Dabouz et al., 2020; Dabouz, 2024).

Cellular sources/targets in retina. In injury models, Il1b is upregulated primarily in infiltrating subretinal mononuclear phagocytes that co-express NLRP3 and caspase-1, whereas Il1r1 expression is detected predominantly in astrocytes, pericytes, endothelial cells, and bipolar cells, with little to no detection in photoreceptors or MPs by scRNA-seq; this places the critical pharmacodynamic target of anakinra on neurovascular/astroglial elements rather than on the IL-1β-producing cells themselves (Dabouz et al., 2020; Dabouz, 2024). IL-1β is elevated in AMD patients’ vitreous and is a recognized biomarker of retinal inflammation; microglia-derived IL-1β amplifies chemokine signaling by Müller and RPE cells, indicating that RPE can serve as an IL-1–responsive amplifier of inflammation even if Il1r1 detection varies by model and assay (Nashine et al., 2022; Korhonen, 2024). RPE-derived endogenous IL-1Ra provides further evidence that IL-1 signaling—and its antagonism—are biologically relevant in the RPE microenvironment (Fabiani et al., 2017).

Inflammasome context and limitations of IL-1R blockade. In RPE and adjacent retinal cells, NLRP3 inflammasome activation is triggered by AMD-relevant stimuli including A2E/lipofuscin photooxidation, drusen components, DICER1/Alu RNA accumulation, oxidized lipoproteins, complement/cofactors, ROS, and lysosomal membrane permeabilization with cathepsin release (Treanor, n.d.; Yerramothu et al., 2018). Inflammasome activation requires priming (e.g., TLR-NF-κB–dependent upregulation of NLRP3/pro-IL-1β) followed by an activation signal (e.g., mtROS, LMP), culminating in caspase-1 activation and secretion of mature IL-1β and IL-18; inflammasome priming can shift RPE death from apoptosis to pyroptosis, increasing inflammatory cytokine release and DAMP extrusion (Treanor, n.d.; Kaarniranta et al., 2023). Critically, IL-1 pathway blockers such as anakinra do not inhibit upstream inflammasome assembly, caspase-1 activation, or IL-18 production; thus, IL-1R antagonism will block IL-1 signaling but will not shut down inflammasome-dependent IL-18 release or pyroptotic execution, which may continue to drive disease biology (Korhonen, 2024). Moreover, in some experimental paradigms, IL-18 can have protective or context-dependent roles in AMD models, complicating network-level predictions when only IL-1 signaling is blocked (Lim et al., 2020).

Evidence gaps regarding lysosomal targets. The working hypothesis posits that anakinra will prevent IL-1β-driven inflammasome amplification and lysosomal destabilization in RPE, preserving vacuolar H+-ATPase (v-ATPase) function and cathepsin D (CTSD) maturation/activity; however, the provided materials contain no direct experimental evidence that IL-1R antagonism rescues v-ATPase activity, lysosomal pH, or CTSD processing in RPE, nor that anakinra reduces lysosomal membrane permeabilization in these systems (Lim et al., 2020; Treanor, n.d.). While lysosomal destabilization and cathepsin B/L release are well-documented inflammasome triggers in RPE, and bafilomycin A1 (a v-ATPase inhibitor) has been used to model lysosomal/autophagic impairment that activates NLRP3 and IL-1β release, there is no reported dataset here demonstrating that IL-1R blockade restores lysosomal acidification or cathepsin D maturation in RPE (Yerramothu et al., 2018; Piippo, 2019). Consequently, the proposed IL-1→lysosome preservation claims remain conjectural in the absence of targeted RPE lysosomal measurements following anakinra treatment in AMD-relevant paradigms (Lim et al., 2020; Treanor, n.d.).

Expected Effect  
Assay-level effects in retinal/RPE systems. Based on the presented literature, IL-1R antagonism with anakinra is expected to reduce IL-1–driven inflammatory signaling in neuroretinal and gliovascular compartments, attenuate subretinal macrophage accumulation/activation, and preserve photoreceptor structure/function in acute inflammatory injury paradigms; these effects have been demonstrated in the blue light model (reduced GFAP, Il1b/Il6/Ccl2 transcripts, fewer subretinal MPs, more preserved ONL and ERG amplitudes) (Dabouz, 2024; Dabouz et al., 2020). In explant co-culture systems where LPS/ATP-activated macrophages produce IL-1β, IL-1R antagonists and anti-IL-1β antibodies abrogate photoreceptor death, supporting a causal role for IL-1β and a direct cytoprotective effect of IL-1 pathway blockade on IL-1RI-expressing retinal cells (Dabouz, 2024). In vitro RPE models show that IL-1Ra can suppress necrosis-induced secretion of IL-6, IL-8, and MCP-1 (likely via NF-κB), suggesting that anakinra may dampen autocrine/paracrine amplification in RPE cultures challenged with danger signals—though definitive RPE IL-1RI expression patterns in vivo remain incompletely defined in the cited mouse scRNA-seq data (Fabiani et al., 2017; Dabouz et al., 2020).

Inflammasome priming versus activation. IL-1 can contribute to priming (NF-κB–dependent) of inflammasome components; therefore, anakinra might indirectly reduce NLRP3 priming in some contexts by interrupting IL-1 positive feedback loops, leading to lower pro-IL-1β and possibly reduced susceptibility to subsequent activation triggers (Fabiani et al., 2017). However, because anakinra acts downstream of inflammasome assembly, it will not prevent caspase-1 activation, gasdermin D pore formation, pyroptosis, or IL-18 maturation/secretion once NLRP3 is engaged—which are all relevant to RPE and subretinal myeloid biology in AMD (Korhonen, 2024; Treanor, n.d.; Kaarniranta et al., 2023). Consequently, anakinra’s benefit in dry AMD models that are dominated by RPE-intrinsic inflammasome activation and pyroptosis may be partial, favoring reductions in IL-1–driven chemokine/cytokine cascades and immune cell recruitment over direct prevention of inflammasome-executed cell death (Korhonen, 2024; Treanor, n.d.).

Lysosomal endpoints. The proposed preservation of v-ATPase function and cathepsin D activity is not currently supported by primary data in the provided sources; no reports demonstrate that anakinra normalizes lysosomal pH, protease maturation (including CTSD), or membrane integrity in RPE subjected to AMD-relevant stressors (Lim et al., 2020; Treanor, n.d.; Piippo, 2019). While inhibiting IL-1 signaling may lower NF-κB–driven transcription of inflammatory mediators (and thus lessen secondary stressors to lysosomes), the extent to which this translates into measurable correction of lysosomal biology in RPE remains to be tested experimentally (Fabiani et al., 2017).

Translational dosing and safety in the eye. In mice, systemic anakinra at 4 mg/kg twice daily for 3 days produced retinal protection in the blue light model; this regimen emphasizes short-term systemic exposures in an acute injury context rather than chronic degenerative settings (Dabouz, 2024). In CNV rodents, intravitreal IL-1Ra reduced neovascularization without aggravating photoreceptor degeneration, providing proof-of-concept for posterior segment delivery and a supportive safety signal in that animal model (Sandhu et al., 2018). Clinically, systemic anakinra has an established safety profile in inflammatory eye disease cohorts, but no intravitreal human anakinra safety data in AMD/GA are presented here; systemic IL-1β blockade (canakinumab) did not improve retinopathy outcomes in a separate context, and anakinra’s daily dosing requirement remains a burden for chronic use unless long-acting ocular delivery is engineered (Korhonen, 2024; Fabiani et al., 2017).

Overall Evaluation  
Merits  
- Biological plausibility in AMD. AMD-relevant stressors activate NLRP3 in RPE and subretinal myeloid cells, elevating IL-1β and IL-18 and driving para-inflammatory cascades and pyroptosis; IL-1β is increased in AMD vitreous and plasma, and IL-1–producing MPs are present at sites of pathology, establishing IL-1 as a rational target for modulating retinal inflammation (Treanor, n.d.; Nashine et al., 2022; Korhonen, 2024).  
- Pharmacologic validation in retinal models. Anakinra significantly reduced inflammation and preserved retinal structure/function in a light-damage model and intravitreally suppressed CNV in rodents, indicating target engagement and protective potential in the posterior segment; IL-1β neutralization prevented CNV without exacerbating photoreceptor degeneration, arguing for a non-toxic profile in those contexts (Dabouz et al., 2020; Dabouz, 2024; Sandhu et al., 2018).  
- RPE-relevant immunobiology. RPE naturally produces IL-1Ra, and exogenous IL-1Ra reduces necrosis-induced inflammatory mediator release from RPE and suppresses dendritic-cell activation in RPE co-cultures, suggesting that anakinra could attenuate RPE-mediated inflammatory amplification in dry AMD (Fabiani et al., 2017; Kaur & Singh, 2021).  
- Clinical and formulation precedents. Systemic ocular use of anakinra in uveitis and scleritis shows clinical feasibility and manageable safety; topical IL-1 antagonists have robust ocular safety signals; gene therapy encoding IL-1Ra and intravitreal administration have been explored preclinically, supporting a spectrum of delivery options that could be adapted for posterior segment disease (Fabiani et al., 2017).

Limitations and risks  
- Mechanistic incompleteness vis-à-vis inflammasomes. IL-1R blockade will not prevent upstream NLRP3 activation, caspase-1 activity, gasdermin-mediated pyroptosis, or IL-18 production; in RPE-intrinsic inflammasome-dominant pathophysiology, anakinra would be expected to blunt downstream IL-1–mediated amplification and leukocyte recruitment but not stop the execution machinery of inflammasome-driven cell death (Korhonen, 2024; Treanor, n.d.; Kaarniranta et al., 2023).  
- Unsubstantiated lysosomal rescue claims. There is no evidence here that anakinra preserves lysosomal acidification (v-ATPase function), cathepsin D maturation/activity, or prevents LMP in RPE under AMD-relevant stress; this is a critical gap because the proposed therapeutic specificity hinges on cytokine–lysosome cross-talk that remains to be demonstrated (Lim et al., 2020; Treanor, n.d.; Piippo, 2019).  
- Target expression uncertainties. In mouse retina, Il1r1 is enriched in astroglia and vascular cells and not detected in photoreceptors or MPs by scRNA-seq, complicating assumptions about direct photoreceptor or RPE targeting by anakinra in vivo; while RPE responds to IL-1 in vitro and produces IL-1Ra, spatial and species differences in IL-1RI distribution may shape efficacy and delivery decisions (Dabouz et al., 2020; Dabouz, 2024; Fabiani et al., 2017).  
- Mixed translational signals. Systemic IL-1β blockade did not improve diabetic retinopathy outcomes in the cited study, and anakinra’s systemic short half-life imposes burdensome daily dosing for chronic disease; there is no documented human safety/efficacy experience with intravitreal anakinra in AMD/GA in the provided sources (Korhonen, 2024; Fabiani et al., 2017; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).  
- Network complexity. NLRP3/IL-18 can exert context-dependent protective or detrimental effects in AMD models; while anakinra does not block IL-18 signaling, its selective inhibition of IL-1 may not suffice to rebalance inflammasome-driven pathology if pyroptosis and IL-18-dependent pathways remain active (Lim et al., 2020).

Go/No-Go considerations and critical experiments  
- RPE-centric validation. Test anakinra in human RPE models exposed to A2E/blue-light, drusen components, DICER1/Alu RNA, or oxidized lipoproteins; quantify NLRP3 priming (NLRP3, pro-IL-1β), activation (ASC specks, caspase-1 cleavage), downstream cytokines (IL-1β, IL-18), and execution (GSDMD cleavage/pyroptosis markers), with and without anakinra to define points of pathway modulation (Treanor, n.d.; Yerramothu et al., 2018).  
- Lysosomal endpoints. Directly measure lysosomal pH, v-ATPase activity, LMP (galectin-3 puncta), cathepsin D maturation/activity, and autophagic flux in the same RPE paradigms ± anakinra to test the hypothesis that IL-1R blockade preserves lysosomal integrity and protease processing (Piippo, 2019).  
- In vivo GA-relevant models. Move from acute light injury to RPE-atrophy models (e.g., chronic photooxidative stress, Alu RNA/DICER1 disruption, lipofuscin models) to assess whether anakinra reduces rates of RPE atrophy, outer retinal thinning, and visual function decline; include comparators targeting the inflammasome (e.g., NLRP3 inhibitors) to benchmark effect sizes and mechanistic depth (Treanor, n.d.; Kaarniranta et al., 2023; Lim et al., 2020).  
- Ocular delivery and PK. Develop and test intravitreal dosing and, preferably, sustained-release formats for anakinra to overcome systemic short half-life; establish vitreous/retinal PK and receptor occupancy, and evaluate ocular safety (IOP, ERG, histopathology) and immunogenicity (anti-drug antibodies) in large-eye species (Korhonen, 2024; Fabiani et al., 2017).  
- Biomarker strategy. Use vitreous/plasma IL-1β and retinal inflammatory transcript signatures as pharmacodynamic biomarkers; consider scRNA-seq to confirm target cell engagement (Il1r1-expressing compartments) pre- and post-treatment (Nashine et al., 2022; Dabouz, 2024).

Positioning relative to alternatives  
Because anakinra does not interrupt inflammasome activation or execution, proximal inhibitors of the NLRP3 inflammasome (e.g., MCC950-class) may provide deeper control of IL-1β/IL-18 production and pyroptosis in RPE-driven disease, at the cost of potentially suppressing beneficial IL-18 signaling in some contexts; preclinical literature shows NLRP3 blockade can be protective in retinal models, meriting parallel evaluation (Lim et al., 2020). Conversely, allosteric IL-1R modulators (rytvela-type) have shown superior protection to anakinra in the light-damage model and may offer functional selectivity (e.g., sparing NF-κB while inhibiting JNK/p38/AP-1) with improved distribution and immunogenicity profiles; these properties deserve consideration if an IL-1-targeting approach is pursued (Dabouz, 2024; Dabouz et al., 2020).

Conclusions  
- Strength of rationale. There is robust evidence that IL-1β is elevated and pathogenic in retinal neuroinflammation and that IL-1R antagonism—including anakinra—can protect retina in preclinical models by reducing inflammatory signaling and immune cell recruitment; RPE-relevant IL-1 biology further supports plausibility (Dabouz et al., 2020; Dabouz, 2024; Fabiani et al., 2017).  
- Weakness of hypothesis specifics. The central claim that anakinra preserves v-ATPase function and cathepsin D maturation in RPE lacks support in the provided literature; moreover, IL-1R blockade cannot prevent upstream inflammasome activation or pyroptosis, limiting its capacity to halt RPE-intrinsic degenerative processes central to GA (Lim et al., 2020; Korhonen, 2024; Treanor, n.d.; Piippo, 2019).  
- Translational readiness. No human AMD/GA trials of anakinra are documented here; systemic IL-1β blockade has shown limited efficacy in retinal vascular disease, and anakinra’s dosing logistics are unfavorable for chronic ocular therapy without dedicated ocular delivery systems (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.; Korhonen, 2024).

Overall Evaluation  
Anakinra is a mechanistically credible anti-inflammatory candidate to blunt IL-1–driven retinal inflammation and leukocyte recruitment, with reproducible preclinical efficacy signals in posterior-segment injury models and supportive RPE-centric immunobiology; however, the specific hypothesis that it will mechanistically preserve lysosomal v-ATPase function and cathepsin D activity in RPE is currently unsupported by direct evidence, and IL-1R antagonism is unlikely to arrest inflammasome activation, IL-18 signaling, or pyroptotic cell death that contribute to RPE atrophy in dry AMD (Dabouz et al., 2020; Dabouz, 2024; Fabiani et al., 2017; Korhonen, 2024; Lim et al., 2020). Given the absence of clinical data in GA and delivery constraints, anakinra merits consideration as an adjunct anti-inflammatory approach contingent on (1) generation of RPE-focused data demonstrating modulation of inflammasome priming and lysosomal integrity, and (2) development of sustained intraocular delivery; in parallel, more proximal interventions (NLRP3 inhibitors) and IL-1R allosteric modulators with superior preclinical efficacy should be benchmarked as potentially higher-leverage strategies for disease modification in dry AMD (Lim et al., 2020; Dabouz et al., 2020).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Ambroxol is a small-molecule mucolytic historically used to thin airway mucus and has been repurposed as a pharmacological chaperone for the lysosomal enzyme glucocerebrosidase (GCase) in Gaucher disease, where it selectively binds misfolded GCase to aid folding and trafficking to lysosomes for substrate degradation (Alhowyan & Harisa, 2025, pp. 17–18). Pharmacological chaperones constitute a class of small molecules that stabilize specific mutant lysosomal enzymes conformationally in the endoplasmic reticulum, enabling correct processing and lysosomal delivery; a paradigmatic example is migalastat, an alpha-galactosidase A chaperone approved for Fabry disease with amenable variants (Alhowyan & Harisa, 2025, pp. 17–18). Ambroxol is further characterized by its ability to cross the blood–brain barrier, a property relevant for neuronopathic lysosomal storage disorders and attractive for central nervous system or ocular indications where access is otherwise constrained (Alhowyan & Harisa, 2025, pp. 17–18). Within the broader landscape of lysosomal therapeutics, small molecules also act as proteostasis regulators and modulators of lysosomal signaling and biogenesis; however, off-target actions remain a central limitation of small-molecule therapy in this domain (Alhowyan & Harisa, 2025, pp. 17–18).

The therapeutic hypothesis for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) posits that ambroxol could act as a pharmacological chaperone for lysosomal enzymes in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), stabilize or enhance vacuolar H+-ATPase (V-ATPase) function, improve lysosomal acidification, and thereby augment cathepsin D (CTSD) activity to clear lipofuscin/drusen components characteristic of dry AMD (Kaarniranta et al., 2023, pp. 2–3; Si et al., 2023, pp. 4–7). This rationale is grounded in the centrality of lysosomal function to RPE homeostasis and AMD pathogenesis: RPE lysosomes sustain heavy heterophagic and autophagic loads from daily photoreceptor outer-segment (POS) digestion, and impaired lysosomal acidification and hydrolase function contribute to lipofuscin accumulation, exosome-driven drusen formation, and progressive degeneration (Kaarniranta et al., 2023, pp. 2–3; Si et al., 2023, pp. 2–4, 5–7; Sharif, 2015, pp. 199–202). Notably, in AMD models and donor RPE, TFEB—the master transcriptional driver of lysosomal/autophagy biogenesis—is dysregulated, V-ATPase-related transcripts (e.g., ATP6VOA1) and cathepsin abundance/activity are linked to lysosomal competence, and TFEB activation or mTOR inhibition reduces toxic storage material such as A2E and POS-derived autofluorescent granules (Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7).

Therapeutic History  
Conventional use: Ambroxol is primarily used clinically as a mucolytic agent to reduce mucus viscosity in respiratory disease (Alhowyan & Harisa, 2025, pp. 17–18). Beyond its mucolytic effects, ambroxol has been investigated in lysosomal storage diseases as a pharmacological chaperone for glucocerebrosidase; it binds misfolded GCase, promotes its proper folding/trafficking to lysosomes, and facilitates substrate clearance, with reported neurological benefits in neuronopathic Gaucher disease and demonstrated blood–brain barrier penetration (Alhowyan & Harisa, 2025, pp. 17–18). Clinically observed improvements in neurological symptoms such as myoclonus and seizures have been reported in pilot studies, and reviews summarize safety/efficacy observations in Gaucher populations, albeit with the caveat of potential off-target toxicities innate to small-molecule approaches (Alhowyan & Harisa, 2025, pp. 17–18, 33–35).

Use in ophthalmology and AMD: A targeted search of ClinicalTrials.gov for ambroxol in macular degeneration, AMD, or retinal conditions returned zero registered trials, indicating a lack of clinical testing for ambroxol in AMD or retina-specific indications within that registry (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.). The provided literature excerpts contain no preclinical or clinical data demonstrating ambroxol use in RPE, retinal degeneration models, or AMD, and they do not report ocular distribution or ocular pharmacokinetics for ambroxol (Alhowyan & Harisa, 2025, pp. 17–18; Si et al., 2023, pp. 2–4; Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7). In contrast, other small-molecule interventions that modulate lysosomal/autophagy function in RPE have been reported: mTOR inhibition with rapamycin decreases A2E and lipofuscin-like granules and reduces inflammatory/angiogenic proteins; trehalose increases autophagy markers and flux and exhibits cytoprotective effects, although limitations in clinical efficacy and adverse effects are noted for mTOR inhibitors (Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7). More broadly, pharmacologic restoration of lysosomal pH and regulatory control of V-ATPase–mTORC1 signaling in RPE have been explored mechanistically, underscoring the translational target plausibility but not implicating ambroxol specifically (Kaarniranta et al., 2023, pp. 2–3; Markitantova & Simirskii, 2025, pp. 24–25).

Mechanism of Action  
Ambroxol as a pharmacological chaperone: Ambroxol binds selectively to misfolded glucocerebrosidase (GCase), stabilizing its conformation in the biosynthetic pathway and enabling correct trafficking to lysosomes, where it restores enzymatic degradation of GCase substrates (Alhowyan & Harisa, 2025, pp. 17–18). This canonical chaperone mechanism increases lysosomal GCase activity and substrate turnover and has been linked to functional improvements in Gaucher disease models and patient reports, with additional indications that ambroxol can enhance mitochondrial function in patient-derived cells (Alhowyan & Harisa, 2025, pp. 17–18). The drug’s small-molecule nature and CNS penetrance differentiate it from enzyme-replacement approaches and position it within a class of proteostasis-modulating agents where target-specific engagement can produce organelle-level functional rescue but also carries risk of off-target interactions (Alhowyan & Harisa, 2025, pp. 17–18).

RPE lysosomal biology relevant to the hypothesis: In the RPE, lysosomal acidification is primarily established by the V-ATPase proton pump and is essential for optimal activity of luminal hydrolases including cathepsins; most lysosomal enzymes are exquisitely pH-dependent and lose activity when lysosomal pH is elevated (Markitantova & Simirskii, 2025, pp. 9–11; Kaarniranta et al., 2023, pp. 2–3). RPE lysosomes operate at the nexus of two degradative streams: heterophagy of POS (requiring efficient phagosome–lysosome fusion and acidic hydrolase activity) and macroautophagy/CMA for damaged proteins and organelles, both of which are dysregulated with aging and AMD-relevant stresses such as oxidative damage and advanced glycation end-products (AGEs) (Si et al., 2023, pp. 4–5; Kaarniranta et al., 2023, pp. 2–3; Sharif, 2015, pp. 199–202). CTSD is a key RPE lysosomal aspartic protease and the principal POS-degrading enzyme; CTSD loss causes retinal degeneration in mice, underscoring its nonredundant role (Si et al., 2023, pp. 4–5). In AMD, human donor RPE show decreased CTSD and CTSL levels/activities, increased TFEB phosphorylation with reduced nuclear localization, and impaired degradative capacity with accumulation of POS-dependent lipofuscin-like granules; activating TFEB in RPE increases CLEAR network gene expression including ATP6VOA1 (a V-ATPase subunit) and reduces POS-derived lipofuscin-like granules (Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7). Oxidized bisretinoids such as A2E, a major lipofuscin component, inhibit V-ATPase and raise lysosomal pH in RPE, which decreases lysosomal enzyme function and impairs cargo hydrolysis—a direct mechanism linking storage material to acidification defects (Wang et al., 2023, pp. 11–13). Lipofuscin and its photoproducts can further inhibit lysosomal proton pumps or hydrolases and promote lysosomal membrane permeabilization, coupling storage to organelle damage and propagating autophagy-lysosomal dysfunction and inflammatory signaling (Si et al., 2023, pp. 5–7; Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 2–4).

Signal control of lysosomal biogenesis and acidification in RPE: The V-ATPase–mTORC1–TFEB axis is central in RPE lysosomal homeostasis; CRYBA1/βA3/A1-crystallin directly regulates the V-ATPase and signals to mTORC1 at the lysosomal membrane, where mTORC1 activity controls TFEB phosphorylation and localization (phosphorylated TFEB is cytosolic; dephosphorylation permits nuclear translocation and activation of CLEAR network genes) (Kaarniranta et al., 2023, pp. 2–3; Markitantova & Simirskii, 2025, pp. 9–11; Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7). Pharmacologic mTOR inhibition (e.g., rapamycin) shifts TFEB toward an active dephosphorylated state, increases autophagic flux, reduces A2E, and decreases lipofuscin-like granules in RPE and POS-fed models, with the reduction in storage material being dependent on active lysosomal enzymes and TFEB activation (Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7). Trehalose also augments autophagy markers and flux with cytoprotective effects in RPE insult models, supporting the druggability of lysosome–autophagy axes (Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7).

What is known and unknown about ambroxol in RPE/AMD: The provided literature contains no experimental data showing that ambroxol binds, stabilizes, or otherwise directly modulates RPE cathepsin D or V-ATPase, nor does it report ambroxol’s effects on lysosomal pH, TFEB activity, or CLEAR network gene expression in RPE models (Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7; Markitantova & Simirskii, 2025, pp. 9–11). While small-molecule interventions can restore lysosomal acidity (e.g., acidic nanoparticles) or, conversely, deacidify lysosomes (e.g., chloroquine, quinacrine), these examples do not involve ambroxol and serve primarily to illustrate the malleability of lysosomal pH by pharmacological means (Alhowyan & Harisa, 2025, pp. 12–15). Importantly, antimalarial lysosomotropic agents that raise lysosomal pH carry ocular toxicity risks, providing a cautionary context for any lysosome-acting small molecule in ophthalmology, although ambroxol’s lysosomotropism and ocular toxicity profile are not defined in the provided excerpts (Alhowyan & Harisa, 2025, pp. 14–15). The context explicitly notes that no small-molecule pharmacological chaperones targeting cathepsin D deficiency or V-ATPase impairment in RPE/AMD models are presented, and there is no direct evidence described for ambroxol enhancing cathepsin D activity or drusen clearance in dry AMD (Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7).

Expected Effect  
Pathway-level expectation if the hypothesis holds: If ambroxol acts as a pharmacological chaperone for lysosomal enzymes expressed in RPE and indirectly improves V-ATPase-dependent acidification, one would expect increased lysosomal hydrolase maturation/activity (including CTSD), restoration of acidic lysosomal pH, improved autophagosome–lysosome fusion and autophagic flux, and enhanced clearance of POS-derived material and lipofuscin components (Si et al., 2023, pp. 4–7; Markitantova & Simirskii, 2025, pp. 9–11). In RPE cells subjected to AMD-relevant stressors (e.g., A2E loading, AGEs-modified substrates), improved acidification and hydrolase function should reduce accumulation of autofluorescent granules and mitigate the need for exosome-mediated egress of undegraded material implicated in drusen formation (Sharif, 2015, pp. 68–72, 199–202; Grilo, 2014, pp. 42–46). Because TFEB activation robustly upregulates lysosomal biogenesis and can decrease lipofuscin-like material, intersecting ambroxol effects with TFEB–mTORC1 signaling and V-ATPase subunit expression (e.g., ATP6VOA1) would be logical endpoints for mechanistic alignment, even though ambroxol has not been shown to modulate TFEB in RPE (Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7).

Assay predictions and measurable readouts: In RPE-like cells (ARPE-19, primary human RPE), relevant readouts to substantiate the hypothesis include:  
- Lysosomal pH measurements showing acidification relative to stressed controls; for comparison, A2E raises lysosomal pH via V-ATPase inhibition in RPE (Wang et al., 2023, pp. 11–13).  
- CTSD maturation (pro-CTSD to mature CTSD) and enzymatic activity assays, given RPE dependence on CTSD for POS degradation and its documented reduction in AMD RPE (Si et al., 2023, pp. 4–5; Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7).  
- V-ATPase function and expression, including ATP6VOA1 transcript/protein, as TFEB target and acidification determinant (Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7).  
- TFEB localization and CLEAR network gene expression, to assess upstream biogenesis signaling that correlates with lysosomal competence (Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7).  
- POS degradation capacity and lipofuscin-like autofluorescent granule burden after POS feeding, a disease-relevant functional output sensitive to lysosomal hydrolase and acidification status (Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7; Sharif, 2015, pp. 189–192).  
- Drusen-relevant surrogate readouts such as exosome marker release (CD63, CD81) and extracellular debris deposition under conditions of impaired lysosomal flux versus pharmacologic rescue (Grilo, 2014, pp. 42–46; Sharif, 2015, pp. 199–202).  
- In genetic/stress backgrounds that exacerbate lysosomal dysfunction (e.g., CFH Y402H), examine CTSD leakage and lysosomal fragility as phenotypes that might be normalized by improved acidification/hydrolase function (Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 4–5).

Importantly, these expectations derive from RPE lysosome–autophagy biology and the mechanistic success of TFEB activation or mTOR inhibition in reducing storage material, not from any demonstrated ambroxol activity in RPE models; thus, ambroxol-specific efficacy remains speculative in this context (Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7).

Evidence gaps and comparators: The literature does not report ambroxol enhancing lysosomal acidification, V-ATPase stability, or CTSD activity in RPE; preclinical evaluation would therefore require rigorous head-to-head comparisons with pathway-validating controls such as rapamycin (mTOR/TFEB activation) and trehalose (autophagy enhancer) that have shown reductions in A2E and lipofuscin-like granules or increased autophagy markers in RPE models (Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7). Given the sensitivity of RPE hydrolases to lysosomal pH and the pathogenic role of A2E-mediated V-ATPase inhibition, an explicit demonstration that ambroxol reverses A2E-induced deacidification and restores hydrolase activity is a critical bar for translational plausibility (Wang et al., 2023, pp. 11–13; Markitantova & Simirskii, 2025, pp. 9–11).

Overall Evaluation  
Strength of biological rationale: The centrality of lysosomal dysfunction to RPE degeneration in dry AMD is well-supported: lysosomal enzyme activity declines with aging and stress, lipofuscin accumulates and inhibits proton pumps/hydrolases, lysosomal acidification is critical for hydrolase function, and impaired lysosome–autophagy flux contributes to intracellular overload, exosome-mediated debris export, drusen formation, and inflammation (Kaarniranta et al., 2023, pp. 2–5; Si et al., 2023, pp. 5–7; Sharif, 2015, pp. 199–202). CTSD is a principal POS-degrading protease in RPE and is reduced in human AMD donor tissue, making strategies that restore CTSD maturation/activity and lysosomal acidification compelling (Si et al., 2023, pp. 4–5; Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7). The V-ATPase–mTORC1–TFEB axis offers convergent control over lysosomal biogenesis and acidification, and experimental activation of TFEB or mTOR inhibition in RPE produces the desired phenotypes—elevated lysosomal gene expression (including ATP6VOA1), increased autophagic capacity, reduced A2E, and decreased lipofuscin-like granules—validating this biology as druggable in principle (Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7). Against this backdrop, small-molecule chaperones are an attractive modality because they can enhance endogenous lysosomal enzyme folding/trafficking and potentially boost organelle function without gene transfer; ambroxol exemplifies this approach in GCase biology, with CNS penetration and clinical observations supporting feasibility in lysosomal disease (Alhowyan & Harisa, 2025, pp. 17–18).

Evidence weaknesses specific to ambroxol in AMD: Despite the strong organelle-level rationale, the ambroxol-specific data package for AMD is essentially absent in the provided record: no RPE cell data, no measurements of lysosomal pH or V-ATPase stabilization, no CTSD maturation/activity rescue, no POS degradation assays, no lipofuscin/A2E clearance, and no in vivo retinal outcomes are reported here (Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7; Markitantova & Simirskii, 2025, pp. 9–11). There are no registered clinical trials for ambroxol in macular degeneration or retinal indications on ClinicalTrials.gov per the specified query, and the excerpts contain no ocular distribution or pharmacokinetics information for ambroxol (Alhowyan & Harisa, 2025, pp. 17–18; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.). The mechanistic extrapolation—ambroxol chaperoning broadly for lysosomal enzymes in RPE and stabilizing V-ATPase—is unsubstantiated; ambroxol’s demonstrated chaperone target is GCase, not CTSD or V-ATPase, and the literature provided explicitly notes the lack of small-molecule pharmacological chaperones targeting CTSD deficiency or V-ATPase impairment in RPE/AMD models (Alhowyan & Harisa, 2025, pp. 17–18; Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7). Furthermore, while small molecules can manipulate lysosomal pH in either direction (e.g., chloroquine deacidifies; acidic nanoparticles re-acidify), these findings emphasize the need for target-specific validation and caution regarding retinal toxicity from lysosomotropic agents; none of these pharmacologies have been tied to ambroxol in RPE (Alhowyan & Harisa, 2025, pp. 14–15).

Translational considerations and risk: The absence of ocular PK and target engagement data is a major liability for advancing ambroxol toward AMD; lysosomal pharmacology in post-mitotic RPE under chronic oxidative and lipofuscin stress likely differs from LSD contexts, and direct evidence of RPE target engagement is needed to justify escalation (Si et al., 2023, pp. 2–4; Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 2–4). It is also noteworthy that mTOR inhibitors—which validated TFEB-mediated lysosomal rescue in RPE models—have shown limited efficacy and adverse effects in clinical settings, highlighting the translational friction even when mechanisms are strong (Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7). Given that CTSD is pH-dependent and V-ATPase inhibition by lipofuscin bisretinoids is a proximal defect in AMD RPE, any candidate must demonstrate re-acidification and hydrolase restoration under A2E load to be credible; absent such data for ambroxol, the mechanistic chain remains hypothetical (Wang et al., 2023, pp. 11–13; Markitantova & Simirskii, 2025, pp. 9–11). Finally, because impaired lysosomal clearance increases exosome release and contributes to drusen, measuring exosome markers and extracellular deposit proxies will be important to link intracellular rescue to extracellular AMD hallmarks, but ambroxol lacks such evidence here (Sharif, 2015, pp. 199–202; Grilo, 2014, pp. 42–46).

Programmatic recommendation and experimental path: At this stage, ambroxol should not advance directly to in vivo retinal studies or clinical exploration for dry AMD without foundational RPE data demonstrating lysosomal acidification rescue and CTSD activity enhancement under AMD-relevant stressors (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.). A rigorous, staged preclinical plan is warranted:  
- In vitro RPE assays under A2E and POS-fed conditions to quantify lysosomal pH, V-ATPase subunit expression (ATP6VOA1), TFEB nuclear translocation/CLEAR activation, CTSD maturation/activity, POS degradation kinetics, and lipofuscin-like autofluorescence, with rapamycin and trehalose as mechanistically validated comparators (Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7; Wang et al., 2023, pp. 11–13).  
- Lysosomal membrane integrity tests and CTSD leakage assessment in CFH Y402H RPE models to probe stabilization of lysosomal compartments under genetic risk backgrounds (Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 4–5).  
- Exosome marker release and extracellular deposit assays to link intracellular lysosomal rescue to drusen-relevant phenotypes (Grilo, 2014, pp. 42–46).  
- Ocular exposure assessment to confirm ambroxol reaches RPE at pharmacologically active concentrations using appropriate delivery routes; absent ocular PK data in the provided literature, this becomes a gating requirement (Alhowyan & Harisa, 2025, pp. 17–18).

Overall, ambroxol’s demonstrated chaperone activity for GCase, BBB penetration, and clinical observations in Gaucher disease establish it as a plausible proteostasis-modulating scaffold, but the lack of any RPE/AMD-directed mechanistic or efficacy evidence and the absence of ocular PK data create a high translational risk profile for dry AMD (Alhowyan & Harisa, 2025, pp. 17–18; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.). By contrast, interventions that directly activate TFEB or modulate mTOR have documented efficacy in RPE models, though clinical translation hurdles remain, and this suggests that ambroxol should be benchmarked against these pathways in a preclinical setting before any programmatic commitment (Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7).
