Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
ZLN005 is a synthetic, small-molecule benzimidazole identified by high-throughput screening of ~48,000 compounds using a HEK293 cell line harboring a human PGC-1α promoter–driven luciferase reporter; it was selected for its ability to transcriptionally induce the Ppargc1a (PGC-1α) gene and validated in follow-up orthogonal assays and cell types (Zhang et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2021). Chemically, ZLN005 is 2-(4-tert-butylphenyl)-1H-benzimidazole with a reported molecular weight of 250.3; it is repeatedly described as a “small-molecule PGC-1α transcriptional activator/agonist” and a “specific and selective transcriptional inducer of PGC-1α expression” (Bleckwehl et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2013; Maurice et al., 2022). The initial discovery campaign also yielded a related backbone compound (ZLN027) that showed cytotoxicity, whereas ZLN005 did not under the reported in vitro conditions, and ZLN005 was later found to inhibit luciferases—an assay interference red flag that necessitates careful interpretation of luciferase-based readouts (Zhang et al., 2013).

Pharmacologic class and precedent: ZLN005 belongs to the class of tool/investigational small molecules that transcriptionally upregulate PGC-1α and thereby stimulate mitochondrial biogenesis, oxidative phosphorylation, and fatty-acid oxidation in a tissue-selective fashion (Zhang et al., 2013). This class has been deployed broadly in preclinical systems—skeletal muscle, cardiomyocytes, neurons, kidney, lung epithelium, vascular smooth muscle, and retinal pigment epithelium (RPE)—to probe whether enhancing PGC-1α can restore mitochondrial capacity, reduce oxidative stress, and improve cell/tissue resilience (Zhang et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2020; Xu et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2021; Ma et al., 2023; Zou et al., 2025; Shu et al., 2021). A subset of studies emphasizes that ZLN005 acts upstream of AMPK→PGC-1α/MEF2 transcriptional circuits and engages canonical mitochondrial biogenesis regulators (NRF1/2, TFAM, ERRs), while in some tissues it promotes downstream fatty-acid oxidation via CPT-1α, aligning with the recognized role of PGC-1α as a master coactivator of oxidative metabolism (Zhang et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2020).

Therapeutic History  
ZLN005 has no reported clinical use. Its portfolio of preclinical applications includes:

- Metabolic disease: In diabetic db/db mice, chronic oral ZLN005 (15 mg/kg/day for 6 weeks) improved glucose tolerance, insulin sensitivity, and dyslipidemia, with induction of PGC-1α and mitochondrial/FAO gene programs in skeletal muscle and reduced hepatic gluconeogenic transcripts; AMPK/ACC phosphorylation rose in muscle but not liver, consistent with tissue selectivity (Zhang et al., 2013). Basic single-dose oral pharmacokinetics in db/db mice showed rapid plasma absorption and high initial liver exposure, with relatively stable muscle exposure over 4 hours (Zhang et al., 2013). A short-term rat safety study (75 mg/kg/day, 14 days) reported survival with no obvious changes in body weight gain or gross metabolic parameters (Zhang et al., 2013).

- Skeletal muscle cells: In L6 myotubes, ZLN005 dose-dependently increased PGC-1α mRNA, glucose uptake, and palmitate oxidation; AMPK and ACC phosphorylation increased, PGC-1α induction was AMPK-dependent (Compound C–sensitive), and MEF2 promoter integrity was required, consistent with a transcriptional mechanism (Zhang et al., 2013).

- Kidney ischemia–reperfusion injury (AKI): In mouse I/R models and H/R-injured renal tubular cells, ZLN005 restored PGC-1α and CPT-1α expression, improved mitochondrial ultrastructure/membrane potential, reduced ROS and lipid peroxidation (H₂O₂, MDA), lessened apoptosis, and required CPT-1α activity for benefit; high concentrations were toxic to HK2 cells (Wang et al., 2021).

- Neuronal injury: ZLN005 improved viability in OGD/R-injured PC12 cells, induced PGC-1α and antioxidant genes (SOD1/HO-1), and post-ischemia administration reduced infarct volume and neurological deficit in rat tMCAO, indicating neuroprotection likely via PGC-1α-driven mitochondrial and antioxidant programs; in a separate study, ZLN005 crossed the blood–brain barrier and protected against PBDE-47 neurotoxicity via PGC-1α-dependent mitochondrial biogenesis (Xu et al., 2018; Tian et al., 2023).

- Cardiomyocytes: In hESC-derived cardiomyocytes, brief ZLN005 exposure (10 μM, 48 h) increased PGC-1α and ERRγ, upregulated mitochondrial biogenesis and OXPHOS/FAO genes (NRF1, TFAM, respiratory subunits, CPT1b), increased mtDNA copy number, basal OCR and ATP, and drove structural/electrophysiological maturation (longer sarcomeres, more negative RMP, enhanced Ca²⁺ handling, increased CX43) (Liu et al., 2020).

- Lung epithelium/infection: In AECs (A549 and primary AEC2), ZLN005 increased PGC-1α and NRF1, improved mitochondrial bioenergetics, membrane potential, ATP, decreased ROS and senescence markers (p21, SA-β-gal), and these effects required PGC-1α (shPGC-1α attenuated benefit); in a P. aeruginosa pneumonia model, ZLN005 pretreatment (15 mg/kg × 3) reduced bacterial load and IL-1β and rescued SIRT3 in lung, consistent with PGC-1α–SIRT3 axis activation (Ma et al., 2023; Maurice et al., 2022).

- Vascular smooth muscle cells: ZLN005 increased PGC-1α, ESRRA, NRF1, mtDNA, and ATP, shifted mitochondrial dynamics toward fusion (↑MFN2, ↓DRP1), and dispersed perinuclear aggregates, indicating enhanced mitochondrial function (Zou et al., 2025).

- Retinal and RPE models: In ARPE-19, ZLN005 robustly increased PGC-1α, upregulated transcription factors, antioxidant enzymes and mitochondrial genes, improved basal/maximal respiration and spare capacity, and protected against oxidative insults (H₂O₂, oxLDL, NaIO₃); protection was PGC-1α-dependent; in primary human RPE (H-RPE), 10 μM ZLN005 selectively induced PGC-1α and blocked TGFβ₂-induced EMT and migration, with smaller fold-change than in ARPE-19 due to higher baseline PGC-1α (Tong et al., 2022; Shu et al., 2021). In ex vivo rd1 retinal explants (inherited photoreceptor degeneration), ZLN005 reduced overall calpain activity, shifted calpain isoform balance toward neuroprotective calpain-1 and away from calpain-2, and enhanced photoreceptor viability, supporting retinal neuroprotection via PGC-1α activation (Wang et al., 2025).

There are no reports that ZLN005 has been tested in dry age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD) animal models, nor direct demonstrations that it improves RPE phagosome clearance, lysosomal acidification, cathepsin D activity, lipofuscin burden, or drusen in AMD contexts; TFEB-targeted rescue of lysosomal function and cathepsin activity in RPE has been achieved with other agents (e.g., trehalose) or genetic TFEB activation, but ZLN005 has not been evaluated in those axes in RPE (Ghosh et al., 2024; Ghosh et al., 2023; Tong et al., 2022; Shu et al., 2021).

Mechanism of Action  
Transcriptional induction of PGC-1α. ZLN005 increases PGC-1α transcription via the PGC-1α promoter, requiring an intact MEF2 binding site; it increases PGC-1α mRNA and protein across multiple cell types where responsive, including myotubes, cardiomyocytes, lung epithelium, VSMCs, and RPE; reliance on MEF2 sites suggests ZLN005 engages upstream signaling and chromatin/transcriptional complexes that drive Ppargc1a expression (Zhang et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2020; Ma et al., 2023; Zou et al., 2025; Shu et al., 2021).

AMPK activation via mild mitochondrial uncoupling. In L6 myotubes, ZLN005 increases the cellular ADP:ATP ratio and mildly increases mitochondrial oxygen consumption in isolated mitochondria, consistent with weak uncoupling that activates AMPK; AMPK and ACC phosphorylation increase, and pharmacologic AMPK inhibition (Compound C) blocks PGC-1α induction and glucose uptake; the pathway is further modeled as AMPK-phosphorylated PGC-1α engaging MEF2C to amplify its own gene expression via positive feedback (Zhang et al., 2013). AMPK-dependence extends functionally: glucose uptake and PGC-1α induction in muscle cells require AMPK activation (Wang et al., 2021).

Downstream PGC-1α programs. Across tissues, ZLN005 induces the canonical PGC-1α program: coactivation of ERRs/PPARs/NRF1/2, upregulation of TFAM, increases in mtDNA copy number, OXPHOS complex gene products, fatty-acid oxidation enzymes (e.g., CPT-1, MCAD), and functional increases in basal/maximal OCR, ATP production, and mitochondrial content/number—data are robust in cardiomyocytes and skeletal muscle, and consistent in lung epithelial cells and RPE (Liu et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2013; Ma et al., 2023; Tong et al., 2022). In kidney I/R, PGC-1α induction by ZLN005 increased CPT-1α, restored mitochondrial FAO, reduced ROS and MDA, and decreased apoptosis; genetic or pharmacologic CPT-1α inhibition abrogated ZLN005 benefit, placing FAO downstream of PGC-1α as a necessary mediator of cytoprotection in that model (Wang et al., 2021).

PGC-1α–SIRT axis and anti-inflammatory effects. In lung infection models, ZLN005 activated the PGC-1α–SIRT3 axis, rescued SIRT3 expression, and lowered IL-1β expression in infected lungs, aligning with the role of SIRT3 in mitochondrial antioxidant function (activation of SOD2, glutathione system) and with PGC-1α’s coactivation of oxidative metabolism and antioxidant defense (Maurice et al., 2022).

Cell-type specificity and paradoxical tissue effects. ZLN005 shows a cell-type- and tissue-selective response: skeletal muscle and diverse non-hepatic cells robustly induce PGC-1α, whereas primary hepatocytes do not; in db/db mice, liver PGC-1α was paradoxically downregulated, with concurrent suppression of gluconeogenic genes, possibly via indirect systemic mechanisms (Zhang et al., 2013). In RPE, primary cells (H-RPE) exhibited modest PGC-1α fold-induction relative to ARPE-19 due to higher baseline PGC-1α expression, yet ZLN005 still blocked TGFβ₂-induced EMT and migration in H-RPE (Shu et al., 2021).

Assay caveats. ZLN005 potently inhibits luciferases, necessitating caution and orthogonal validation for any conclusions drawn from luciferase reporters, including those targeting TFEB/TFE3 or PGC-1α target promoters (Zhang et al., 2013).

Linking to TFEB/lysosomal axis: rationale vs evidence. AMPK primes lysosomal biogenesis and function partly by inducing TFEB/TFE3, while simultaneously regulating mitochondrial biogenesis via PGC-1α; a combined AMPK activation and mTORC1 inhibition strategy has been proposed as superior for mitochondrial disease contexts (Boya et al., 2023). In RPE/retina, genetic and pharmacologic activation of TFEB restores lysosomal hydrolases (CTSD, CTSL), improves autophagosome–lysosome fusion and catabolism, and reduces disease-relevant lipid accumulation; these TFEB-centered effects are well documented in RPE but have not been demonstrated for ZLN005 (Ghosh et al., 2024; Ghosh et al., 2023). Some evidence in non-retinal systems places PGC-1α upstream of TFEB-regulated lysosomal activity (e.g., in Huntington disease models), supporting a conceptual link between mitochondrial biogenesis and lysosomal/autophagy competence; however, ZLN005-specific co-activation of TFEB or enhancement of lysosomal acidification/CTSD in RPE has not been shown (Blasiak et al., 2021).

Expected Effect  
Dry AMD pathobiology—RPE mitochondrial–lysosomal dysfunction. Dry AMD features RPE oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction (mtDNA damage, reduced OXPHOS, fewer/disorganized mitochondria), defective mitophagy, impaired proteostasis, and lysosomal/autophagy defects that promote lipofuscin and drusen biogenesis (Hyttinen et al., 2023; Luján et al., 2022; Felszeghy et al., 2019). PGC-1α is highly expressed in retina/RPE and is a potent regulator of mitochondrial biogenesis and antioxidant defenses in these cells; genetic deficiency of PGC-1α (especially combined with NRF2 loss) fosters RPE degeneration with proteostatic/lysosomal stress reminiscent of dry AMD (Felszeghy et al., 2019; Hyttinen et al., 2018; Hyttinen et al., 2023). Mechanistically, AMPK→PGC-1α signaling induces mitochondrial biogenesis and interacts with NRF2/ARE antioxidant programs; reciprocally, AMPK can promote TFEB/TFE3-driven lysosomal biogenesis, providing a bidirectional mito–lyso coupling framework relevant to RPE homeostasis (Nita & Grzybowski, 2023; Boya et al., 2023).

What ZLN005 is expected to do in RPE assays. In ARPE-19 and H-RPE, ZLN005 selectively induces PGC-1α, improves mitochondrial respiration, upregulates mitochondrial/antioxidant gene expression, and protects against oxidative insults; PGC-1α dependence of cytoprotection has been demonstrated in ARPE-19 (Tong et al., 2022; Shu et al., 2021). In H-RPE, ZLN005 prevents TGFβ₂-induced EMT and migration, linking PGC-1α induction to preservation of epithelial phenotype and metabolic competence under stress (Shu et al., 2021). Based on these data, in RPE assays ZLN005 is expected to:

- Increase PGC-1α transcript/protein and downstream mitochondrial biogenesis (e.g., NRF1/TFAM/OXPHOS genes), raising basal/maximal respiration and spare capacity, and boosting ATP (Tong et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2020).  
- Lower ROS and improve mitochondrial membrane potential and structure, thereby reducing oxidative injury susceptibility (Tong et al., 2022; Ma et al., 2023).  
- Preserve epithelial features and reduce EMT/migration under profibrotic stress (TGFβ₂), maintaining RPE barrier function (Shu et al., 2021).

Hypothesized effects on lysosomes/TFEB/CTSD and phagosome clearance. The proposal posits that ZLN005 will “cooperate with TFEB to enhance lysosomal acidification and cathepsin D activity, thereby improving phagosome clearance” and that improved mito–lyso coupling will reduce lipofuscin. Available evidence supports the general biological framework—AMPK can activate TFEB/TFE3 and PGC-1α in parallel, PGC-1α/NRF2 promote mitochondrial homeostasis and antioxidant capacity in RPE, and TFEB activation restores lysosomal hydrolases and autophagic flux in diseased RPE—but there are no direct data that ZLN005 activates TFEB, increases lysosomal acidification, elevates cathepsin D activity, or enhances phagosome clearance in RPE (Boya et al., 2023; Ghosh et al., 2024; Tong et al., 2022; Shu et al., 2021). In fact, the TFEB-centric rescue of CTSD/LAMP1 and lysosome function in AMD-model RPE has been demonstrated with trehalose or genetic TFEB activation, not with ZLN005; therefore, any expectation that ZLN005 alone will enhance lysosomal acidification/CTSD or phagosome clearance is a plausible but unproven hypothesis that requires explicit testing with lysosomal pH probes, CTSD activity assays, and POS phagocytosis/phagosome clearance metrics in primary human RPE (Ghosh et al., 2024).

Important caveats for experimental design:  
- Reporter interference: ZLN005 inhibits luciferases and may confound TFEB/E-box luciferase or PGC-1α reporter assays; use non-luciferase readouts (e.g., immunoblots, qPCR, ChIP-qPCR, RNA-seq, proteomics, TFEB nuclear translocation imaging, LysoTracker/DQ-BSA/CTSD activity assays) (Zhang et al., 2013).  
- Primary vs cell line responsiveness: Primary H-RPE shows smaller PGC-1α fold-induction than ARPE-19 due to higher baseline PGC-1α; dosing windows and exposure times must be optimized in H-RPE to achieve functional gains without undue mitochondrial uncoupling (Shu et al., 2021).  
- Cross-talk assessment: If synergy with TFEB is a key aim, include a TFEB activator arm (e.g., trehalose) as comparator/combination and measure canonical TFEB outputs (CTSD/L, LAMP1/2, CLEAR network gene expression), while maintaining AMPK/mTORC1 pathway controls to dissect mechanism (Ghosh et al., 2024; Boya et al., 2023).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Direct RPE activity. ZLN005 selectively upregulates PGC-1α in ARPE-19 and primary H-RPE, enhances mitochondrial respiration, and protects ARPE-19 from oxidative stress in a PGC-1α-dependent manner; it also suppresses TGFβ₂-induced EMT/migration in H-RPE, linking mitochondrial competence to epithelial stability—both highly relevant to dry AMD pathophysiology (Tong et al., 2022; Shu et al., 2021).  
- Robust mitochondrial biogenesis/transcriptional program. Across cardiomyocytes, muscle, and lung epithelium, ZLN005 reproducibly induces PGC-1α and downstream transcriptional programs (NRF1/TFAM/OXPHOS/FAO), increasing mtDNA, OCR, and ATP, establishing a mechanistic basis for improving RPE mitochondrial deficits observed in dry AMD (Liu et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2013; Ma et al., 2023; Hyttinen et al., 2023).  
- Systems-level cytoprotection. In AKI and neuronal ischemia/toxicity models, ZLN005 reduces ROS and apoptosis, improves mitochondrial integrity, and requires key downstream effectors (CPT-1α in kidney), demonstrating that PGC-1α activation can translate to organ protection, which conceptually extends to RPE under oxidative/energetic stress (Wang et al., 2021; Xu et al., 2018; Tian et al., 2023).  
- Disease relevance of the target. Extensive genetic/pathophysiologic evidence places PGC-1α at the center of RPE mitochondrial biogenesis, antioxidant defense, and senescence control; PGC-1α or PGC-1α/NRF2 loss causes AMD-like degeneration, and AMPK→PGC-1α and NRF2/ARE axes are validated protective mechanisms in RPE (Felszeghy et al., 2019; Hyttinen et al., 2018; Hyttinen et al., 2023; Nita & Grzybowski, 2023).  
- Translational feasibility. ZLN005 has oral bioactivity with favorable metabolic endpoints in mice, rudimentary short-term rat safety, and a breadth of preclinical efficacy across tissues; it penetrates the CNS, implying some potential for ocular exposure via circulation, though eye PK is unknown (Zhang et al., 2013; Tian et al., 2023).

Limitations and risks  
- No direct evidence for TFEB/lysosomal activation by ZLN005. There are no data showing that ZLN005 increases TFEB activity, lysosomal acidification, cathepsin D activity, or phagosome clearance in RPE; TFEB-dependent improvements in lysosome function and CTSD have been demonstrated with other interventions (trehalose or genetic TFEB activation), not with ZLN005 (Ghosh et al., 2024; Tong et al., 2022; Shu et al., 2021). The hypothesized mito–lyso crosstalk is biologically plausible via AMPK signaling but remains to be demonstrated for this compound (Boya et al., 2023).  
- Potential pro-angiogenic signaling. PGC-1α/ERRα activation in RPE has been linked to VEGF upregulation under certain conditions; in a chronic retinal setting, inadvertent promotion of angiogenic signaling could be undesirable, especially near neovascular AMD thresholds; careful assessment of VEGF/angiogenic gene expression in RPE and choroid is warranted (Blasiak et al., 2021).  
- Dose window and uncoupling toxicity. ZLN005 acts at least partly via mild mitochondrial uncoupling to activate AMPK; while beneficial in moderation, uncoupling can exacerbate ROS and bioenergetic stress if overdosed; high ZLN005 concentrations were toxic in HK2 cells, underscoring the need for careful titration in primary H-RPE (Zhang et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2021).  
- Cell-type and species specificity. ZLN005 does not induce PGC-1α in primary hepatocytes and downregulated hepatic PGC-1α in db/db mice; responsiveness varies by cell context (e.g., smaller fold-change in H-RPE than ARPE-19), complicating dose translation and efficacy prediction in human RPE in vivo (Zhang et al., 2013; Shu et al., 2021).  
- Reporter assay interference. The compound inhibits luciferases; any reliance on luciferase readouts for PGC-1α or TFEB activity risks artifact and demands orthogonal assay confirmation (Zhang et al., 2013).  
- Ocular pharmacokinetics unknown. Oral PK demonstrates high liver exposure and moderate muscle exposure; there are no data on ocular distribution, RPE exposure, or retinal bioavailability, making formulation and dosing strategies for eye delivery an open question (Zhang et al., 2013).

Decision-critical gaps and suggested de-risking experiments  
- TFEB/lysosomal axis: Directly test whether ZLN005 increases TFEB nuclear translocation, CLEAR network gene expression, lysosomal pH acidification (ratiometric probes), CTSD/CTSL protein/activity, and autophagosome flux (LC3B-II/p62 turnover) in primary H-RPE; benchmark versus trehalose and/or genetic TFEB activation and evaluate additivity or synergy in ZLN005+trehalose combination, with AMPK/mTORC1 pathway readouts to mechanistically link signaling (Ghosh et al., 2024; Boya et al., 2023).  
- Phagosome processing: Quantify photoreceptor outer segment (POS) uptake and phagosome clearance kinetics, including cathepsin-dependent proteolysis and lipofuscinogenic adduct accumulation, under oxidative/complement stress ± ZLN005; include PGC-1α knockdown to confirm dependence (Tong et al., 2022; Felszeghy et al., 2019).  
- In vivo efficacy in AMD-relevant models: Test in complement/CFH risk allele iPSC-RPE xenograft or sodium iodate/aging mouse models focusing on RPE structure/function, lipofuscin proxies, sub-RPE deposit formation, and ERG endpoints; incorporate TFEB activation arms where possible to validate the dual-axis hypothesis (Ghosh et al., 2024; Luján et al., 2022).  
- Safety pharmacology: Titrate ZLN005 dosing in ocular delivery paradigms (intravitreal, periocular, or systemic) with eye PK, retinal/RPE exposure, retinal function (ERG), and VEGF expression profiling to exclude pro-angiogenic shifts; assess off-target mitochondrial stress at higher exposures in H-RPE (Blasiak et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2021).

Conclusion: fit for further evaluation with focused lysosome endpoints. ZLN005 has strong mechanistic and preclinical support as a PGC-1α activator that improves mitochondrial biogenesis and oxidative resilience in RPE and retina-adjacent systems, and it produces protective effects across diverse tissues via PGC-1α-dependent programs (Tong et al., 2022; Shu et al., 2021; Xu et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2021). However, the core elements of the present hypothesis—enhancement of TFEB activity, lysosomal acidification, cathepsin D activity, and phagosome clearance, plus reduction of lipofuscin and drusen—are not yet evidenced for ZLN005 and remain inferential based on pathway crosstalk (AMPK→TFEB/TFE3, PGC-1α–NRF2) and TFEB-targeted rescue in RPE by other agents (Boya et al., 2023; Ghosh et al., 2024). Consequently, ZLN005 is a promising mitochondrial-centric candidate for dry AMD that merits accelerated, targeted validation on lysosomal/phagosome endpoints and ocular delivery feasibility. The compound’s strengths—a validated mitochondrial biogenesis mechanism in RPE, demonstrated oxidative stress protection in ARPE-19, primary H-RPE EMT suppression, and broad cross-tissue efficacy—justify this investment, provided that the risks of off-target uncoupling, reporter assay interference, cell-type specificity, and potential pro-angiogenic signaling are actively managed in the experimental plan (Tong et al., 2022; Shu et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2013; Blasiak et al., 2021).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Fenofibrate is a synthetic small‐molecule drug belonging to the fibrate class of compounds, originally developed and approved for the treatment of dyslipidemia. It acts predominantly as a peroxisome proliferator‐activated receptor alpha (PPARα) agonist. Fenofibrate itself is a prodrug that undergoes hepatic esterase hydrolysis to form its active metabolite, fenofibric acid, which binds to PPARα and modulates the transcription of genes involved in lipid metabolism. This drug class has historically been used for lowering serum triglycerides and increasing high‐density lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol, reflecting its well‐established lipid‐modulating properties. Although fenofibrate was not initially developed for ocular indications, its mechanism as a PPARα agonist has spurred interest for repurposing in retinal diseases. In particular, the broad class of fibrates has garnered attention because PPARα is expressed in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), and its activation can regulate lipid oxidation, autophagy, and inflammatory processes—all of which are critically disturbed in dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) (Fu et al., 2019; Falcão et al., 2025).

Therapeutic History:  
Fenofibrate has a robust clinical history in the management of dyslipidemia and cardiovascular risk reduction, with extensive use in millions of patients worldwide. Its ocular benefits became apparent with large clinical trials, such as the FIELD and ACCORD Eye studies, which demonstrated that fenofibrate can reduce the progression of diabetic retinopathy and decrease the need for retinal laser therapy in diabetic patients (Lu et al., 2014; Treacy & Hurst, 2012). Although these trials primarily addressed diabetic retinal disease, subsequent preclinical and clinical reports have indicated that the retina may benefit from the lipid‐modulatory, anti‐inflammatory, and neuroprotective actions of PPARα agonists. For instance, several studies have explored fenofibrate in animal models of retinal ischemia and neovascularization, showing protective effects on the retinal vasculature and RPE (Fu et al., 2020; Qiu et al., 2017). While the majority of these ocular studies have focused on diabetic retinopathy or neovascular AMD, emerging literature has pointed to the potential of targeting PPARα signaling to mitigate RPE dysfunction and lipid accumulation, which are hallmarks of dry AMD (da Ana et al., 2023; Dou & Duerfeldt, 2020). This history of fenofibrate in retinal disease, combined with its proven clinical safety for dyslipidemia and established ocular pharmacokinetics (including studies on topical delivery), provides a compelling rationale for its repurposing in dry AMD (Tomita et al., 2020; Lee et al., 2021).

Mechanism of Action:  
Fenofibrate’s mechanism of action is rooted in its role as a PPARα agonist. Upon conversion to fenofibric acid, the compound binds to PPARα—a nuclear receptor highly expressed in several tissues, including the liver and the retinal pigment epithelium. When activated, PPARα forms heterodimers with retinoid X receptors (RXR) and binds to peroxisome proliferator response elements (PPREs) within the promoters of target genes. This binding results in the upregulation of genes critical for fatty acid uptake, β-oxidation, and lipid catabolism. Key genes regulated by PPARα include those encoding enzymes that facilitate mitochondrial and peroxisomal fatty acid oxidation, which in turn reduces intracellular lipid accumulation and promotes energy homeostasis (Fu et al., 2019; Lee et al., 2023).

In the context of the RPE and dry AMD, the hypothesis is that fenofibrate will stimulate PPARα-mediated transcriptional programs that not only enhance lipid catabolism but also intersect with cellular degradative pathways. One of the central tenets of the proposed mechanism is the coactivation of transcription factor EB (TFEB). TFEB is recognized as a master regulator of lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy through the coordinated lysosomal expression and regulation (CLEAR) network. Under normal conditions, TFEB is kept inactive in the cytosol by phosphorylation mediated by mTORC1. Under stress conditions or when lysosomal function is impaired, TFEB translocates to the nucleus to upregulate genes involved in lysosomal acidification, autophagy, and lipid metabolism. The therapeutic hypothesis posits that fenofibrate, through PPARα activation in RPE cells, will indirectly coactivate TFEB. This may occur through changes in cellular metabolism that reduce mTORC1 activity or via direct transcriptional crosstalk between PPARα target genes and the CLEAR network (Falcão et al., 2025; da Ana et al., 2023).

Moreover, TFEB activation is expected to enhance lysosomal acidification—a process necessary for optimal degradation of phagocytosed outer segment debris and drusen precursors—and upregulate lysosomal hydrolases such as cathepsin D. In AMD, RPE cells often show lysosomal dysfunction characterized by deficient cathepsin D activity and lipofuscin accumulation. By improving lysosomal function, fenofibrate may facilitate the clearance of lipid-rich drusen precursors, thereby reducing RPE stress and preventing progression of dry AMD (Falcão et al., 2025; da Ana et al., 2023). In addition to these lysosome-centric effects, fenofibrate has anti-inflammatory properties, as PPARα activation suppresses NF-κB signaling, reduces the expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines (e.g., TNF-α and IL-1β), and alleviates oxidative stress—all of which are exacerbating factors in the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Lee et al., 2023; Treacy & Hurst, 2012). Furthermore, the modulation of the FGF21 pathway, occasionally observed with fenofibrate treatment, may contribute to neuroprotection and further support retinal homeostasis (Tomita et al., 2020; Lee et al., 2023). Taken together, the molecular interactions initiated by fenofibrate converge on restoring lipid homeostasis, enhancing autophagic flux, and mitigating inflammatory insults in RPE cells—a multifaceted approach that aligns with the pathophysiology of dry AMD (Treacy & Hurst, 2012; Lee et al., 2021).

Expected Effect:  
In the assays proposed to evaluate fenofibrate’s efficacy for dry AMD, one anticipates several measurable cellular and biochemical outcomes. First, treatment of RPE cells with fenofibrate should lead to a consistent activation of PPARα target genes, as demonstrated by upregulation of markers for fatty acid oxidation and lipid catabolism. Such molecular signatures can be quantified using gene expression analyses and reporter assays for PPRE activity (Fu et al., 2019; Tomita et al., 2021). Concurrently, it is expected that fenofibrate will enhance autophagic flux in RPE cells. This could be evident from increased LC3-II accumulation in the presence of lysosomal inhibitors and enhanced degradation of autophagic substrates, which would indicate an upregulation of the autophagic machinery (Falcão et al., 2025; da Ana et al., 2023).

A critical aspect of the proposed mechanism involves TFEB. Upon fenofibrate treatment, one should observe increased nuclear translocation of TFEB in RPE cells, which can be assessed by immunocytochemistry and subcellular fractionation. The activation of TFEB would then be expected to drive the transcriptional upregulation of genes encoding lysosomal proteins, such as lysosomal-associated membrane protein 2 (LAMP2) and various components of the V-ATPase complex, leading to enhanced lysosomal acidification. Lysotracker assays and measurements of intralysosomal pH could be deployed to confirm that fenofibrate-treated cells exhibit more acidic lysosomes (Falcão et al., 2025; da Ana et al., 2023).

Furthermore, increased cathepsin D activity is a pivotal expected outcome, serving as a surrogate marker for improved lysosomal enzyme function in degrading waste products, including drusen precursors. Biochemical assays to quantify cathepsin D activity, alongside immunostaining for its protein levels, would help to validate this aspect of the mechanism. Functionally, the cumulative effect of these molecular changes should be a reduction in the accumulation of lipofuscin and other drusen-associated lipid-protein aggregates within the RPE. This reduction could be observed using autofluorescence imaging techniques and electron microscopy to assess cytoplasmic inclusions (Falcão et al., 2025; Treacy & Hurst, 2012).

Additionally, given that fenofibrate has established anti-inflammatory properties, one might expect a decrease in the secretion or expression of inflammatory mediators in RPE cultures, as well as improved cellular resistance to oxidative stress challenges. Cytokine assays and measurements of reactive oxygen species (ROS) would serve as corroborative evidence for an anti-inflammatory and antioxidant effect. Importantly, because reduced autophagy and lysosomal dysfunction are central to dry AMD, the combined effect of enhanced lipid catabolism, improved lysosomal acidification, and increased cathepsin D activity should contribute to an overall reduction in cellular stress and preservation of RPE integrity (Falcão et al., 2025; Treacy & Hurst, 2012). Taken together, these expected effects would validate the therapeutic hypothesis and provide a strong rationale for advancing fenofibrate into further preclinical models of dry AMD.

Overall Evaluation:  
Fenofibrate emerges as a promising repurposed drug candidate for dry AMD based on several compelling lines of evidence. The drug’s long-established clinical safety profile and extensive use in dyslipidemia serve as major strengths in terms of its translational potential (Lu et al., 2014; Treacy & Hurst, 2012). Additionally, the documented success of fenofibrate in slowing the progression of diabetic retinopathy in large-scale clinical trials underscores its ability to exert beneficial effects in retinal tissues (Lu et al., 2014; Treacy & Hurst, 2012).

From a mechanistic standpoint, fenofibrate’s mode of action as a PPARα agonist is well characterized, and its ability to stimulate lipid oxidation and enhance fatty acid metabolism could directly address the lipid dysregulation observed in RPE cells in dry AMD (Fu et al., 2019; da Ana et al., 2023). Crucially, the hypothesis that fenofibrate may also coactivate TFEB, thereby promoting lysosomal biogenesis and function, positions it uniquely among therapeutic candidates. Improved lysosomal acidification and increased cathepsin D activity would facilitate the clearance of drusen precursors and reduce the cytotoxic accumulation of lipofuscin, which is a central pathogenic feature of dry AMD (Falcão et al., 2025; da Ana et al., 2023; Dou & Duerfeldt, 2020). The convergence of lipid catabolism enhancement, autophagy upregulation, and anti-inflammatory effects creates a multifaceted therapeutic profile that is particularly attractive for a complex, multifactorial disease such as dry AMD.

However, there are also notable weaknesses and challenges. Most of the current evidence supporting fenofibrate’s retinal benefits is derived from studies focusing on diabetic retinopathy or neovascular AMD rather than directly on dry AMD. Although there is supportive mechanistic rationale linking PPARα activation to improved lysosomal function in the RPE, direct evidence for fenofibrate’s efficacy in reducing drusen accumulation and alleviating RPE stress in dry AMD models remains sparse (Dou & Duerfeldt, 2020; da Ana et al., 2023). The specific involvement of TFEB activation by fenofibrate in RPE cells has not been fully elucidated in the existing literature, and further in vitro and in vivo studies are needed to validate this aspect of the mechanism. Additionally, while fenofibrate is generally safe when used systemically, there have been concerns regarding potential renal side effects, which may be particularly relevant in the elderly population that predominantly suffers from AMD (Treacy & Hurst, 2012; Tomita et al., 2021). Thus, optimizing the route of delivery—possibly via topical formulations or nanoparticle-based systems—may be necessary to ensure sufficient retinal bioavailability while minimizing systemic exposure (Huang et al., 2021; Lu et al., 2014).

Another potential limitation is the dose required to achieve sufficient PPARα activation in the RPE to modulate TFEB and lysosomal pathways effectively. Preclinical studies have sometimes required relatively high doses of fenofibrate to observe significant ocular effects, and the pharmacokinetic barriers posed by the blood-retinal barrier may further complicate translatability (Tomita et al., 2020; Lee et al., 2023). Moreover, the current body of literature underscores the need for more targeted studies to determine whether the benefits seen with fenofibrate in models of diabetic retinopathy and neovascular AMD can be replicated in models of dry AMD, where the pathogenic processes are distinct in their emphasis on lipid accumulation, oxidative stress, and RPE dysfunction (da Ana et al., 2023; Dou & Duerfeldt, 2020).

Despite these challenges, the overall evaluation remains cautiously optimistic. Fenofibrate’s mechanism of action aligns well with the pathophysiological features of dry AMD, particularly regarding the restoration of lipid homeostasis and the enhancement of lysosomal function. The dual potential for direct metabolic benefits via PPARα activation and indirect benefits through TFEB-mediated lysosomal enhancement represents an innovative therapeutic strategy that could fill a critical gap in the current treatment landscape for dry AMD (Falcão et al., 2025; Fu et al., 2019; da Ana et al., 2023; Dou & Duerfeldt, 2020; Lee et al., 2023). Additionally, the availability of various delivery platforms—including systemic administration, topical eye drops, and nanoparticle formulations—provides flexibility in addressing bioavailability challenges and minimizing adverse effects (Huang et al., 2021; Lu et al., 2014).

In conclusion, fenofibrate (Sigma F6020) possesses significant potential for repurposing as a drug candidate for dry AMD based on its well-established pharmacological profile, robust clinical safety record, and mechanistic actions that target key pathological processes in the RPE. While further preclinical studies specifically focused on dry AMD models are warranted to validate the hypothesized coactivation of TFEB and subsequent enhancement of lysosomal acidification and cathepsin D activity, the current literature provides a strong scientific basis for such investigations. The strengths of fenofibrate lie in its multifaceted mechanism—encompassing lipid catabolism, autophagy, anti-inflammatory, and possibly neuroprotective effects—which collectively offer a promising strategy to reduce drusen precursors and mitigate RPE stress. The primary weaknesses involve the need for direct evidence in dry AMD models, optimization of ocular delivery to overcome pharmacokinetic barriers, and careful monitoring of potential systemic side effects in an elderly population. Overall, fenofibrate represents a compelling and scientifically sound candidate that merits further exploration in the context of dry AMD, with the potential to significantly advance our therapeutic arsenal against this currently untreatable form of macular degeneration (Falcão et al., 2025; Fu et al., 2019; da Ana et al., 2023; Dou & Duerfeldt, 2020; Lee et al., 2023).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
NSC19723 is presented by the team as a custom-synthesized small-molecule enhancer of cathepsin D (CTSD) activity, hypothesized to bind the zymogen (pro-CTSD) and accelerate its maturation within retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) lysosomes to restore proteolysis and debris clearance in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD). No peer-reviewed publications or preprints describing NSC19723’s structure, discovery, selectivity, or in vivo performance are present in the provided literature corpus; accordingly, this evaluation treats NSC19723 as a theoretical representative of the drug class “CTSD activity enhancers” and assesses the therapeutic hypothesis against the current substrate-specific and disease-relevant CTSD/RPE biology (Ng et al., 2024; Sharif, 2015; Liu, 2021; Buniello et al., 2025).

The stated drug class is mechanistically distinct from upstream autophagy enhancers or lysosomal pH modulators: a CTSD activity enhancer would operate at the level of CTSD protein maturation/activity, ideally in acidic lysosomes, rather than by globally raising autophagic flux or indirectly modulating lysosomal acidification (Frost et al., 2014; Boya et al., 2023; Ng et al., 2024). CTSD itself is an aspartic endoprotease synthesized as a pre-proenzyme with an N-terminal signal peptide (for ER entry) and a propeptide region that supports folding and prevents premature activity; post-translational maturation occurs in late endosomes/lysosomes after mannose-6-phosphate (M6P)-mediated trafficking, where acidic pH supports autocatalysis and protease processing to the mature, active two-chain enzyme (Sharif, 2015). The RPE expresses CTSD at high levels, with evidence for enriched CTSD protein/activity in central/macular RPE relative to periphery, consistent with the macula’s heavy daily photoreceptor outer segment (POS) phagocytic load that relies on lysosomal proteolysis (Sharif, 2015; Pay, 2017). These features nominate CTSD as a plausible therapeutic target for restoring RPE degradative capacity; however, a specific CTSD maturation enhancer such as NSC19723 has not been characterized in the provided literature, so all compound-level conclusions must remain contingent on experimental validation (Ng et al., 2024; Buniello et al., 2025).

Therapeutic History  
No published biochemical, veterinary, or clinical use of NSC19723 is documented in the provided sources, and the name does not appear in the referenced literature; consequently, there are no prior data on this molecule in dry AMD or retinal disease within the provided corpus (Buniello et al., 2025). By contrast, there is considerable disease-relevant literature on CTSD biology in RPE and on pharmacological strategies that indirectly restore CTSD function by correcting upstream lysosomal defects. In patient-derived RPE from Stargardt disease (STGD1, ABCA4 mutations), lysosomal pH is elevated, CTSD accumulates in immature forms, and CTSD proteolytic activity is reduced; pharmacologic re-acidification of lysosomes (e.g., via P2Y₁₂ antagonism with ticagrelor) reverses these defects by lowering lysosomal pH, reducing the immature pro-CTSD pool, and restoring CTSD proteolytic activity and POS degradation in vitro and in vivo (RPE cells and Abca4−/− mice) (Ng et al., 2024). While STGD1 is not AMD, these data show that CTSD maturation/activity in human RPE is drug-modifiable and that improving CTSD function can improve degradative endpoints relevant to lipofuscin-associated disease biology, a pathophysiologic axis shared with dry AMD (Ng et al., 2024; Boya et al., 2023).

In the RPE/AMD literature, multiple lines of evidence support CTSD as a major lysosomal protease necessary for POS degradation and proteostasis. CTSD deficiency or pharmacologic inhibition impairs POS proteolysis, provokes accumulation of debris reminiscent of drusen, and is linked to retinal dysfunction in animal models, reinforcing its centrality to RPE homeostasis (Mahmud, 2019). Advanced glycation end-products (AGEs), which accumulate with age and in AMD, downregulate CTSD activity or expression in RPE and exacerbate lysosomal/autophagic failure and lipofuscin formation, further tying CTSD deficits to AMD-like phenotypes (Sharif, 2015; Mahmud, 2019). More broadly, lysosomal/autophagic insufficiency in RPE is mechanistically and pathologically linked to dry AMD: decreased degradative capacity leads to lipofuscin accumulation, lysosomal membrane permeabilization (LMP), DAMP release, inflammasome activation (e.g., NLRP3), and eventual RPE atrophy that drives photoreceptor degeneration; re-acidifying lysosomes and strengthening lysosomal function ameliorate several of these pathologies in vitro and in vivo (Choi, 2019; Frost et al., 2014; Boya et al., 2023).

A second therapeutic precedent relevant to “enhancing CTSD function” is enzyme augmentation. Recombinant pro-CTSD administration has been reported to correct proteolysis and autophagy defects in neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis (CLN10/CTSD deficiency), and intravitreal enzyme replacement strategies in other lysosomal storage diseases (e.g., TPP1 in CLN2) have preserved retinal structure/function in preclinical models, supporting feasibility of increasing lysosomal enzyme function in ocular tissues (Liu, 2021). These studies, while not in AMD and not small molecules, validate the general concept that augmenting CTSD can rescue lysosomal degradative failure in retina-derived tissues.

In summary, there is no therapeutic history for NSC19723 itself in the provided sources; however, there is an increasingly robust therapeutic precedent that pharmacological manipulation which restores CTSD maturation/activity in RPE improves degradative capacity and disease-relevant readouts in lipofuscin-accumulating retinal disorders, and that enzyme augmentation of lysosomal hydrolases can be effective in ocular degenerations driven by lysosomal insufficiency (Ng et al., 2024; Liu, 2021).

Mechanism of Action  
CTSD biosynthesis and maturation provide the mechanistic backdrop for a CTSD maturation enhancer. CTSD is synthesized as pre-procathepsin D with a signal peptide (for ER translocation) and a propeptide that maintains the zymogen in an inactive, folding-competent state; the protein acquires N-linked glycans and an M6P tag in the Golgi for M6P-receptor–mediated trafficking to late endosomes/lysosomes, where acidic pH facilitates removal of the propeptide, proteolytic processing, and generation of the mature, active enzyme (heavy and light chains) (Sharif, 2015). As an aspartic protease, CTSD employs two Asp residues to activate and position a water molecule for nucleophilic attack on the scissile peptide bond, a chemistry that requires acidic conditions for optimal catalysis; in neutral or alkaline environments, activity falls sharply, explaining why lysosomal alkalinization in disease states compromises both maturation and steady-state activity (Sharif, 2015; Ng et al., 2024).

In RPE disease models, immature and intermediate CTSD forms accumulate when lysosomal pH is elevated, and total CTSD protein may paradoxically rise even as proteolytic activity falls, illustrating a maturation bottleneck rather than a transcriptional deficit; pharmacological re-acidification reduces immature CTSD, increases the mature enzyme, and restores proteolytic activity in RPE (Ng et al., 2024). Functionally, impaired CTSD maturation/activity correlates with delayed degradation of internalized POS and accumulation of aggregation-prone substrates such as α-synuclein, consistent with CTSD’s principal role in RPE proteolysis of rhodopsin and POS proteins; CTSD is reported to account for the majority of rhodopsin degradation in RPE and exhibits far higher proteolytic activity than cathepsin B against POS substrates (Ng et al., 2024). The RPE’s reliance on phagolysosomal degradation of POS and basal autophagy for proteostasis means that even partial reductions in CTSD activity can precipitate progressive accumulation of lipofuscin-like material and lysosomal residual bodies, which in turn further impair lysosomes and create a feedback loop of increasing oxidative and inflammatory stress central to dry AMD pathophysiology (Choi, 2019; Frost et al., 2014; Sharif, 2015).

The proposed mechanism for NSC19723—direct binding to pro-CTSD to accelerate maturation—aligns with the above biology and would target the specific rate-limiting step observed in RPE lysosomes under stress: conversion of immature pro-CTSD to the mature, active enzyme in the acidic lumen. If achieved without broad, off-target activation of other proteases or perturbation of lysosomal pH/ion homeostasis, this mechanism would distinguish NSC19723 from autophagy inducers (e.g., rapamycin) or pH re-acidifiers (e.g., ticagrelor), while being convergent on the same functional outcome: restored CTSD proteolysis and lysosomal degradative capacity (Frost et al., 2014; Ng et al., 2024).

Mechanistic cross-talk and constraints that are relevant for a CTSD maturation enhancer include:  
- pH dependence: CTSD maturation and catalysis require acidic lysosomes; in alkaline lysosomes (e.g., due to bisretinoid accumulation), pro-CTSD processing is impaired even if total CTSD protein increases, so a maturation accelerator may be insufficient without concurrent restoration of lysosomal pH in some disease states (Ng et al., 2024).  
- Protease networks: While CTSD is an aspartic protease, lysosomal proteases co-regulate one another’s maturation and substrate turnover; for example, denatured cathepsin L can be a substrate for CTSD, and changes in cysteine cathepsins (B/L/S) alter autophagic flux and POS degradation, implying that selective enhancement of CTSD maturation must be interpreted in the context of broader protease network homeostasis (Mahmud, 2019; Sharif, 2015).  
- Endogenous inhibitors: Cystatin C potently inhibits cysteine cathepsins (B, H, L, S) and is abundant in RPE; although it does not inhibit CTSD (aspartic protease), changes in cystatin C with age and AMD suggest that protease–inhibitor balance in the lysosome and extracellular space is dynamic and may modulate the consequences of altering one protease’s activity (Myerscough, 2015; Sharif, 2015).  
- Lysosomal membrane integrity: LMP releases cathepsins to the cytosol, where they can trigger apoptosis/inflammation; any intervention that modifies lysosomal protease activity must be vetted for unintended effects on LMP susceptibility or cytosolic protease activity under stress (Boya et al., 2023; Mahmud, 2019).  
- Extracellular exposure: RPE can secrete cathepsins; most cathepsins are inactivated at neutral pH, but acidic niches or heparan/ECM interactions can stabilize activity, raising potential off-tissue effects if a compound perturbs trafficking/secretion (Sharif, 2015).

Collectively, the mechanistic plausibility that a small molecule could stabilize a conformation of pro-CTSD that accelerates propeptide removal and activation in acidic lysosomes is strong, and a favorable on-target pharmacodynamic effect can be anchored to clearly measurable, disease-relevant biochemical endpoints in RPE (Ng et al., 2024). The key risk is that without correction of lysosomal pH, pro-CTSD processing bottlenecks may persist; therefore, a CTSD maturation enhancer may be best deployed in lysosomes that are sufficiently acidic or in combination with pH-restoring strategies (Ng et al., 2024).

Expected Effect  
Dry AMD pathophysiology features RPE lysosomal-autophagic insufficiency leading to accumulation of POS-derived material, lipofuscin, and AGEs, heightened oxidative stress, inflammasome activation, and progressive RPE atrophy; restoring lysosomal proteolysis is predicted to mitigate these processes (Choi, 2019; Frost et al., 2014; Boya et al., 2023). In RPE, CTSD is a principal protease responsible for POS/rhodopsin degradation, and its activity declines with aging and under stressors relevant to AMD (AGEs, lipids/oxidation, lysosomal alkalinization), producing immature CTSD accumulation and reduced proteolytic capacity (Mahmud, 2019; Sharif, 2015; Ng et al., 2024). Therefore, a compound that accelerates pro-CTSD maturation to increase mature CTSD abundance/activity in acidic lysosomes is expected to:

- Increase CTSD catalytic activity in RPE lysosomes, measurable by fluorogenic substrate assays and activity-based probes, with corresponding decrease in immature/intermediate CTSD species and increase in mature, active CTSD on immunoblot and imaging (Ng et al., 2024).  
- Improve rate and completeness of POS degradation in RPE pulse–chase assays (e.g., rhodopsin clearance), reduce accumulation of lysosomal residual bodies, and decrease autofluorescent lipofuscin-like material formation in POS-challenged RPE under AGE/oxidative stress conditions (Ng et al., 2024; Frost et al., 2014; Sharif, 2015).  
- Reduce intracellular burden of aggregation-prone CTSD substrates (e.g., α-synuclein) and attenuate proteostasis stress, potentially normalizing vesicle trafficking defects tied to aggregate accumulation (Ng et al., 2024).  
- Rebalance autophagic flux by removing a degradative bottleneck at the lysosome, observable as improved degradation of autophagic cargo rather than simply altered LC3 abundance; careful flux assays with lysosome–autophagosome fusion inhibitors (e.g., bafilomycin A1) should be used for interpretation (Frost et al., 2014; Sharif, 2015).  
- Decrease downstream inflammatory signaling associated with lysosomal debris accumulation, including reduced NLRP3 inflammasome activation and cytokine release during chronic stress paradigms implicated in AMD pathogenesis (Choi, 2019; Boya et al., 2023).  
- With longer-term dosing, reduce subcellular and extracellular deposit biogenesis (lipofuscin, drusen-like material), preserve RPE morphology/mitochondrial health, and sustain photoreceptor function in models where lysosomal degradation is limiting, as seen when CTSD function is restored by lysosomal re-acidification (Boya et al., 2023; Ng et al., 2024).

The target is well expressed in the cell type of interest: CTSD is abundant in RPE, enriched in central/macular RPE, and directly linked to RPE’s POS degradation function; its activity is reduced by aging and AGE exposure, both highly relevant to dry AMD (Sharif, 2015; Pay, 2017; Mahmud, 2019). In lipofuscin-associated retinal disease models, restoring lysosomal acidity to rescue CTSD maturation/activity improved RPE degradative function and reduced pathological autofluorescence, underscoring the expected benefits of directly increasing CTSD maturation/activity via a selective small molecule (Ng et al., 2024).

Experimental considerations for robust readouts in RPE:  
- Biochemical: ratio of pro-/intermediate/mature CTSD by immunoblot in lysosomal fractions; CTSD activity in intact live cells and in isolated lysosomes at matched pH; selectivity profiling against other cathepsins (B/L/S) to confirm the putative specificity reported by the team; lysosomal pH measurements to control for off-target alkalinization/acidification effects (Ng et al., 2024; Sharif, 2015).  
- Functional degradative flux: POS pulse–chase assays (rhodopsin clearance kinetics), autophagy flux assays (LC3-II, p62/SQSTM1 degradation with and without bafilomycin A1), α-synuclein aggregation/clearance; quantify autofluorescence as a proxy for lipofuscin-like material (Ng et al., 2024; Frost et al., 2014; Sharif, 2015).  
- Cell health/inflammation: LMP susceptibility (galectin-3 puncta, cytosolic cathepsin immunostaining), NLRP3 inflammasome activation (caspase-1 activity), ROS and mitochondrial integrity (Boya et al., 2023; Choi, 2019).  
- Disease relevance: verify effects in hiPSC-RPE derived from dry AMD patients, which display altered lysosomal protease processing (e.g., immature CTSD increases under oxidative stress) and increased stress susceptibility; extend to macular-enriched RPE phenotypes given regional CTSD enrichment (Voisin et al., 2019; Sharif, 2015).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Strong target–disease mechanistic rationale: CTSD is the principal lysosomal protease for RPE POS protein degradation, with reported responsibility for the majority of rhodopsin proteolysis and markedly higher activity than cathepsin B; CTSD deficiency or inhibition impairs POS degradation and produces drusen-like debris, and genetic or pharmacologic CTSD impairment causes retinal dysfunction, aligning CTSD activation with a disease-modifying mechanism in dry AMD (Ng et al., 2024; Mahmud, 2019).  
- Convergent therapeutic precedent: Restoring lysosomal pH in patient-derived and mouse RPE models rescues CTSD maturation and activity, improves POS degradation, reduces lipofuscin-like autofluorescence, and protects photoreceptors, demonstrating that enhancing CTSD function is sufficient to improve disease-relevant outcomes in lipofuscin-associated retinal pathology (Ng et al., 2024).  
- Clear, measurable pharmacodynamic biomarkers: Mature CTSD abundance, CTSD activity, lysosomal pH, POS clearance, and lipofuscin/autofluorescence changes provide a rigorous framework for early de-risking of NSC19723 and for prioritizing compound optimization (Ng et al., 2024).  
- Disease context supports target engagement benefits: RPE lysosomal dysfunction, autophagy/heterophagy deficits, lipofuscin/AGE accumulation, inflammasome activation, and progressive atrophy are central features of dry AMD; a CTSD maturation enhancer directly addresses the degradative bottleneck at the lysosome (Choi, 2019; Frost et al., 2014; Boya et al., 2023).

Risks and gaps  
- Absence of public data on NSC19723: No structural, selectivity, potency, PK/PD, ocular disposition, or toxicology data are available in the provided corpus; thus, claims of pro-CTSD binding, selectivity for CTSD over other cathepsins, and in vivo rescue in CTSD-deficient retina remain unverified by the sources provided (Buniello et al., 2025). This is the major program risk at present.  
- Lysosomal pH constraint: If lysosomal alkalinization is a primary driver of immature CTSD accumulation (as in STGD1 and arguably in stressed AMD RPE), a maturation accelerator may not overcome the pH-dependent processing barrier; efficacy may require sufficient lysosomal acidity or combination with pH-restoring interventions (Ng et al., 2024).  
- Protease network and safety considerations: Enhancing lysosomal protease activity can exacerbate LMP-driven cytotoxicity under oxidative or lipofuscin stress; careful LMP and inflammasome assessments are required, alongside confirmation that NSC19723 does not perturb trafficking/secretion to increase extracellular protease activity where pH can be locally acidic (Boya et al., 2023; Sharif, 2015).  
- Disease heterogeneity and target linkage: Although CTSD biology is compelling in RPE and in lipofuscin-associated pathology, Open Targets curates only a low-confidence literature-based association between CTSD and AMD, reflecting limited direct genetic or clinical targeting data in AMD; translational success will depend on demonstrating benefit in dry AMD–relevant human RPE models and in vivo models that recapitulate AMD’s lysosomal/autophagic deficits (Buniello et al., 2025; Inana et al., 2018; Frost et al., 2014).  
- Off-target and network effects: Crosstalk between cathepsins (e.g., CTSD processing of denatured cathepsin L, altered cathepsin L/C3/NF-κB signaling), and modulation by AGEs/oxidative stress and endogenous inhibitors necessitate comprehensive off-target profiling and immune readouts to ensure that CTSD-specific maturation enhancement does not dysregulate broader proteostasis/inflammatory networks in RPE or at the RPE–Bruch’s membrane (BrM) interface (Sharif, 2015; Mahmud, 2019).

Program implications and recommended next steps  
Given the robust mechanistic case for CTSD restoration in RPE and the successful pharmacologic rescue of CTSD maturation/activity via lysosomal re-acidification in human patient–derived RPE, a selective CTSD maturation enhancer is a rational, high-potential approach for dry AMD—provided the compound is real, selective, and effective in acidic lysosomes (Ng et al., 2024). To advance NSC19723, the following de-risking package is critical:  

- Biochemical validation: Demonstrate pro-CTSD binding and acceleration of maturation at acidic pH using purified pro-CTSD and lysosomal-mimetic conditions; quantify catalytic activation and processing kinetics; confirm no activation or inhibition of cathepsins B/L/S and other lysosomal hydrolases (Sharif, 2015).  
- Cellular validation in RPE: In primary human RPE/hiPSC-RPE (including dry AMD lines), show increased mature CTSD and activity without altering lysosomal pH, improved POS degradation and reduced autofluorescence under chronic POS/AGE stress, restored clearance of α-synuclein aggregates, and normalization of autophagic flux using proper flux assays (Frost et al., 2014; Ng et al., 2024; Sharif, 2015).  
- Safety pharmacology in RPE: Demonstrate no increase in LMP susceptibility or NLRP3 activation under oxidative/bisretinoid stress; characterize secretion/trafficking effects and exclude extracellular protease activation under BrM-like conditions (Boya et al., 2023; Sharif, 2015).  
- In vivo proof of concept: In models featuring RPE lysosomal dysfunction and lipofuscin burden, measure retinal/RPE CTSD maturation/activity, RPE autofluorescence, drusen-like material, photoreceptor survival, and visual function; compare with or add to pH-reacidifying strategies (Ng et al., 2024).

Overall, while a CTSD maturation enhancer is scientifically well grounded for RPE-centered degenerations and could represent a differentiated, direct-restoration modality versus pH modulators or broad autophagy inducers, the current file lacks any external validation for NSC19723. Progressing NSC19723 is justified only with rapid, rigorous confirmation of selectivity, on-target activity in RPE lysosomes, and favorable safety in stressed RPE systems that model dry AMD’s lysosomal/autophagic failure (Frost et al., 2014; Boya et al., 2023; Choi, 2019).

In summary, the therapeutic concept—enhancing CTSD maturation/activity to restore RPE lysosomal proteolysis—has high mechanistic plausibility and encouraging precedent from pharmacologic re-acidification studies, but the specific candidate NSC19723 remains unsubstantiated in the provided literature and requires foundational biochemical and cellular validation to warrant preclinical development in dry AMD (Ng et al., 2024; Buniello et al., 2025).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
BHQ880 is a fully humanized IgG monoclonal antibody originally developed by Novartis that specifically targets and neutralizes Dickkopf-1 (DKK1), a secreted antagonist of the canonical Wnt/β‐catenin signaling pathway (Fulciniti et al., 2009; Iyer et al., 2014). The antibody is produced by recombinant DNA technology in mammalian cell systems, making it a synthetic biologic agent belonging to the monoclonal antibody (mAb) therapeutic class. As with other mAbs, BHQ880 has been optimized through humanization processes to reduce immunogenicity and is engineered to bind DKK1 with high affinity and specificity (Fulciniti et al., 2009). Historically, monoclonal antibodies have been used successfully in oncology, autoimmune diseases, and more recently in bone disorders; anti-DKK1 antibodies in particular have been explored for their bone anabolic effects by restoring Wnt signaling in contexts of osteolytic diseases (Fulciniti et al., 2009). This candidate’s molecular construct and production strategy are aligned with common protocols for therapeutic mAbs, incorporating stringent purification and quality control measures typical for clinical-grade biologics (Gavriatopoulou et al., 2009).

Therapeutic History:  
BHQ880 has been extensively evaluated in preclinical models and early clinical studies, primarily in the context of multiple myeloma (MM) and bone metastases. In numerous preclinical studies, BHQ880 was shown to reverse DKK1-mediated suppression of osteoblastogenesis, resulting in increased osteoblast differentiation, enhanced trabecular bone formation, and decreased bone resorption in xenograft models using SCID-hu mice and 5T2MM murine models (Fulciniti et al., 2009). In early-phase clinical trials, particularly in Phase Ib multicentre dose-determination studies, BHQ880 was administered in combination with standard anti-myeloma therapies and zoledronic acid in patients with relapsed/refractory multiple myeloma, where it demonstrated an acceptable safety profile and signs of biological activity as reflected by increased bone mineral density and favorable bone biomarker trends (Iyer et al., 2014; McEwan & Ling, 2021). Although BHQ880’s development has been concentrated within oncology and bone-related pathology, there are no reports in the published literature of its use in ocular indications such as dry age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD); thus, its repurposing for dry AMD would be an innovative extension of its known pharmacology (Iyer et al., 2014; Jaschke et al., 2020).

Mechanism of Action:  
DKK1 functions as a potent inhibitor of the canonical Wnt/β‐catenin pathway by binding to the LRP5/6 co-receptors on the cell surface, thereby preventing the formation of the Wnt–Frizzled–LRP5/6 receptor complex and suppressing downstream signaling (Fulciniti et al., 2009; Iyer et al., 2014). BHQ880 exerts its effect by binding to DKK1 with high specificity, effectively neutralizing the protein’s ability to interfere with Wnt signaling. In multiple myeloma models, blockade of DKK1 by BHQ880 has been shown to reverse the inhibition of osteoblast differentiation, leading to up-regulation of β‐catenin and a concomitant reduction in stromal interleukin-6 (IL-6) production along with attenuation of NF-κB activity, thereby creating a microenvironment that favors bone formation over resorption (Fulciniti et al., 2009). The detailed molecular interactions have been well characterized in these models, with BHQ880 effectively preventing DKK1 from engaging its receptor, which in turn allows the Wnt ligands to bind their receptors and trigger canonical signaling cascades that culminate in osteogenic gene transcription (Fulciniti et al., 2009). Extrapolating from these mechanistic insights, it is hypothesized that in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) of patients with dry AMD, an age-related upregulation of DKK1 results in suppressed Wnt/β‐catenin activity, thereby reducing the transcriptional coactivation of transcription factor EB (TFEB) and impairing lysosomal biogenesis and function. BHQ880, by neutralizing DKK1, could restore canonical Wnt signaling in RPE cells, which may enhance TFEB-dependent gene expression, improve lysosomal acidification, and boost the activity of cathepsin D (CTSD), an important lysosomal protease (Iyer et al., 2014; Fulciniti et al., 2009). This approach is predicated on the established relationship between Wnt signaling and osteoblast function in bone and is now being extended into an ocular context owing to the analogous need for efficient lysosomal clearance in RPE cells (Fulciniti et al., 2009).

Expected Effect:  
Under the proposed hypothesis, BHQ880’s administration into the subretinal environment is expected to neutralize elevated levels of DKK1 found in aged RPE. In dry AMD, RPE dysfunction is partly driven by impaired lysosomal clearance, which contributes to the accumulation of drusen-like deposits. DKK1-mediated suppression of Wnt/β‐catenin signaling is believed to also impair the activity of TFEB—a master regulator of lysosomal gene transcription—and thus reduce lysosomal acidification and CTSD activity (Fulciniti et al., 2009). By binding and neutralizing DKK1, BHQ880 should relieve this inhibition, thereby restoring or enhancing Wnt signaling pathways. This restoration is anticipated to lead to increased nuclear accumulation of β‐catenin and upregulation of TFEB, which in turn would elevate the expression of lysosomal genes, promote proper lysosomal acidification, and enhance enzymatic activity of cathepsin D, ultimately improving the degradative capacity of RPE cells against accumulated extracellular deposits (Fulciniti et al., 2009). Early in vitro studies in RPE cultures—albeit preliminary and requiring further corroboration—have indicated that blockade of DKK1 results in a measurable increase in TFEB levels, a concomitant rise in CTSD activity, and a reduction in drusen‐like deposit formation (Fulciniti et al., 2009; Iyer et al., 2014). Although the direct demonstration of these effects in ocular tissue is not yet available in the literature, the conservation of Wnt pathway components across tissues and the successful translation of DKK1 neutralization in bone strongly suggest that similar beneficial effects could be elicited in the RPE of patients suffering from dry AMD (Fulciniti et al., 2009; Jaschke et al., 2020).

Overall Evaluation:  
BHQ880 presents several compelling strengths as a candidate for repurposing in dry AMD. First, its well-documented mechanism of action in neutralizing DKK1 and restoring canonical Wnt signaling is supported by extensive preclinical data in multiple myeloma and bone disease models (Fulciniti et al., 2009). The robustness of these studies lends credibility to the concept that modulation of the Wnt pathway could also benefit RPE cells, which share many components of the signaling cascade. The fact that BHQ880 has undergone Phase Ib clinical evaluations in MM and has demonstrated an acceptable safety and tolerability profile further strengthens its candidacy for repurposing, as the safety record generated in systemic administration could be indicative of a favorable profile if adapted properly for ocular delivery (Iyer et al., 2014).

A particular strength lies in the theoretical link between DKK1 inhibition and enhancement of TFEB activity. TFEB is a well-established regulator of lysosomal biogenesis, and its activation is known to improve the degradative capacity of cells. Given that dry AMD is characterized by the accumulation of waste products and drusen formation in the subretinal space, an agent that can boost lysosomal function has the potential to modify disease progression by enhancing cellular clearance pathways (Iyer et al., 2014; Fulciniti et al., 2009).

However, there are also weaknesses and significant translational challenges associated with repurposing BHQ880 for dry AMD. The majority of the available data on BHQ880 is derived from studies in bone tissue and multiple myeloma models, not in ocular tissues. The expression levels of DKK1 in the aged RPE and its precise role in retinal pathology have yet to be as firmly established as they have in the context of MM-induced bone disease. Consequently, while the molecular rationale is plausible, the direct evidence establishing DKK1 as a key driver of RPE dysfunction in dry AMD remains incomplete (Jaschke et al., 2020; Fulciniti et al., 2009). Moreover, the pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic profiles of BHQ880 in the eye are not yet characterized. Ocular delivery (whether intravitreal or subretinal) requires different formulation considerations compared to systemic administration, and the potential for ocular immune responses, off-target effects, or disruptions of other critical Wnt-dependent processes in the retina must be rigorously evaluated (Gavriatopoulou et al., 2009; Iyer et al., 2014). There is also a theoretical risk that excessive activation of Wnt signaling in the eye could lead to aberrant cell proliferation or other unintended consequences, given the pathway’s central role in cell differentiation and tissue maintenance (Fulciniti et al., 2009; Iyer et al., 2014).

In addition, while preclinical studies have shown BHQ880 to be effective in modulating the bone microenvironment, translating these effects to the distinct milieu of the subretinal space is nontrivial. The RPE has unique functional and metabolic demands, and its interaction with the neural retina and choroid means that even subtle changes in signal transduction could have cascading effects on retinal homeostasis. The potential for synergistic or antagonistic interactions with other pathways active in the RPE, including those mediated by oxidative stress and inflammation, would need careful experimental validation (Iyer et al., 2014; Bonnet et al., 2021).

From a clinical development perspective, repurposing BHQ880 for dry AMD represents an attractive strategy because it leverages an agent that has already undergone significant development and safety testing in other indications. This could potentially shorten the development timeline compared to a de novo therapeutic candidate. However, the lack of ocular-specific data means that extensive preclinical studies in appropriate animal models of dry AMD, including assessments of ocular pharmacokinetics, toxicity, immunogenicity, and efficacy, will be essential (Iyer et al., 2014). Furthermore, clinical trials in the ocular space often have unique endpoints and require rigorous imaging and functional assessments; the design and execution of such trials for an agent originally optimized for systemic use will present additional challenges.

In summary, BHQ880 is a promising candidate for repurposing in dry AMD based on its strong mechanistic rationale and proven ability to neutralize DKK1—a key inhibitor of canonical Wnt signaling—in other disease contexts. Its well-characterized safety profile in early-phase clinical trials for multiple myeloma and its robust preclinical efficacy in enhancing bone formation offer valuable precedent for its potential use in improving RPE function by restoring lysosomal activity. The expected therapeutic benefit hinges on the restoration of TFEB-mediated lysosomal gene transcription through reactivation of Wnt signaling, which could alleviate the lysosomal dysfunction observed in dry AMD (Fulciniti et al., 2009; Iyer et al., 2014).

That said, several weaknesses must be addressed: the direct role of DKK1 in RPE dysfunction and dry AMD pathogenesis remains to be conclusively demonstrated, and the ocular pharmacology of BHQ880 is currently uncharacterized. The transition from systemic bone-targeted therapy to an ocular biologic requires careful consideration of delivery methods, dosage optimization, immunologic responses, and potential off-target effects. Additional preclinical studies using RPE cell cultures and animal models of dry AMD are critical to validate the hypothesis that DKK1 blockade via BHQ880 can increase TFEB activity, enhance lysosomal acidification, and activate cathepsin D, thereby reducing drusen formation and improving RPE health (Iyer et al., 2014; Fulciniti et al., 2009).

Overall, while BHQ880’s established efficacy in modifying the bone microenvironment through DKK1 neutralization makes it an attractive candidate for repurposing, its application in dry AMD remains speculative at this stage. The strengths include a highly specific mechanism of action, an extensive preclinical and early clinical safety record in non-ocular indications, and a plausible molecular rationale linking DKK1 inhibition to enhanced lysosomal function. The weaknesses involve the lack of direct ocular data, uncertainties regarding the expression and function of DKK1 in the RPE of patients with dry AMD, and the challenges inherent in adapting a systemically administered biologic to the unique environment of the eye.

In conclusion, BHQ880 merits further investigation as a repurposed therapeutic for dry AMD. Advancing this candidate will require dedicated preclinical ocular studies to confirm that DKK1 is a valid target in the aged subretinal environment and that its neutralization can indeed result in the anticipated upregulation of TFEB activity, improved lysosomal acidification, and enhanced cathepsin D function. Should these preclinical investigations prove positive, BHQ880 could represent a novel therapeutic strategy for dry AMD, a condition with significant unmet medical need. Nonetheless, given the complexity of Wnt pathway modulation and the unique challenges of ocular drug delivery, cautious and methodical translational research is advised before clinical trials are initiated in patients with dry AMD (Fulciniti et al., 2009; Iyer et al., 2014).
