Chemically, it is defined as N2-[(2,2-diphenylethoxy)acetyl]-L-arginine and was identified via high-throughput screening of chemical libraries using membranes from cells stably expressing human C3aR, such as RBL-2H3 cells (Ames et al., 2001). The lead compound was chemically optimized from an initial hit (SKF 63649) to improve affinity and potency, and its synthesis has been well described using peptide–like solid‐phase synthetic strategies (e.g., Fmoc protecting group chemistry on Wang resin) thereby yielding a compound with high purity (≥95%) and reproducible physicochemical properties (Ames et al., 2001). SB290157 belongs to a class of compounds that modulate G protein–coupled receptors (GPCRs), in this case a complement receptor, and similar nonpeptidic small‐molecule ligands have been employed in preclinical studies to probe inflammatory pathways in various disease states (Iyer et al., 2017; Ames et al., 2001). Its discovery set an important precedent for the therapeutic targeting of complement receptors, especially given the historical absence of potent, selective C3aR antagonists, and it has been widely used as a research tool in animal models and cell-based assays to interrogate the physiological roles of C3a/C3aR signaling (Ames et al., 2001).

Therapeutic History:  
SB290157 has been extensively employed in preclinical models to examine the role of C3aR in inflammation and immune modulation. In early studies, it was shown to antagonize C3a-induced intracellular calcium mobilization and receptor internalization in RBL-2H3 cells and human neutrophils, with reported IC50 values in the low-nanomolar range (approximately 27–30 nM), suggesting robust antagonism under defined experimental conditions (Ames et al., 2001). In vivo, SB290157 demonstrated antiinflammatory efficacy by reducing neutrophil recruitment in guinea pig models of lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-induced airway neutrophilia and by decreasing paw edema in rat adjuvant-induced arthritis models through intraperitoneal dosing (Ames et al., 2001). Although valuable as a pharmacological probe, its history is mired by concerns as several subsequent investigations indicated that SB290157 can exhibit partial agonist activity—depending on the assay system and receptor expression context—and even engage an off-target complement receptor, C5aR2, to induce β-arrestin recruitment (Coulthard, 2015; Li et al., 2021; Mathieu et al., 2005). With more than 70 publications referencing its use, SB290157 remains one of the most commonly used C3aR inhibitors; however, it is essentially confined to the research arena and has never reached clinical development for AMD or other indications (Li et al., 2021).  
There is emerging evidence in ophthalmologic research relevant to dry AMD. For example, an in vitro human fetal RPE cell model has shown that complement fragment C3a can drive the formation of sub-retinal pigment epithelium deposits via dysregulation of the ubiquitin proteasome pathway; importantly, co-application of SB290157 with recombinant C3a in these cultures prevented the abnormal deposit formation, suggesting that C3aR blockade can modulate key pathological events relevant to AMD pathogenesis (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). Despite this promising mechanistic link, SB290157 itself has not been advanced clinically, and its use in retinal models remains primarily exploratory. Moreover, the existence of antagonistic and agonistic properties in various assay systems necessitates careful interpretation of its efficacy when contemplating the translation to human ocular diseases (Iyer et al., 2017; Li et al., 2021).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, SB290157 has been characterized as a competitive antagonist that binds to the orthosteric site of the C3a receptor, thereby inhibiting the native ligand, C3a, from eliciting its downstream signaling responses. In classic radioligand binding assays using 125I-labeled C3a, SB290157 displaces the radiolabeled peptide with an IC50 of ~200 nM, indicating it competes effectively with C3a (Ames et al., 2001). Functionally, this displacement correlates with inhibition of C3a-induced intracellular calcium mobilization, a key second messenger response mediated via G-protein coupling to pertussis-toxin–sensitive Gi/o proteins (Ames et al., 2001). Additionally, SB290157 has been shown to block C3a-mediated receptor internalization in immune cells, further supporting its role in antagonizing C3aR activation (Ames et al., 2001; Iyer et al., 2017).  
Beyond the canonical receptor blockade, several studies have pointed out that SB290157’s activity is highly context-dependent. In systems where C3aR is overexpressed—such as recombinant CHO or transfected RBL cells—SB290157 can paradoxically act as an agonist to trigger intracellular signaling cascades like ERK phosphorylation, potentially due to rapid receptor desensitization or kinetic differences in ligand-receptor interaction (Coulthard, 2015; Li et al., 2021; Mathieu et al., 2005). Moreover, its off-target partial agonism at the closely related receptor C5aR2 has been documented, wherein it mediates β-arrestin recruitment at higher concentrations, thereby dampening C5a-induced ERK signaling in primary macrophages (Li et al., 2021; Mathieu et al., 2005). Such dual or biased pharmacological properties underscore that SB290157’s molecular actions cannot be solely categorized as pure antagonism without considering assay conditions and cell contexts (Li et al., 2021; Mathieu et al., 2005).  
In the context of RPE cells, C3a binding to C3aR is hypothesized to disrupt intracellular calcium homeostasis, leading to lysosomal alkalinization—a key factor that impairs the maturation and proteolytic activity of lysosomal enzymes such as cathepsin D (CTSD). Cathepsin D is critical for proper turnover of extracellular matrix (ECM) components and degradation of proteinaceous aggregates; its dysfunction is implicated in drusen formation, a hallmark of dry AMD (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). By competitively inhibiting C3a binding, SB290157 is expected to mitigate abnormal Ca2+ signaling, maintain lysosomal acidification, and therefore preserve CTSD processing and activity, which in turn would prevent or lessen the accumulation of drusen-like deposits (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018; Iyer et al., 2017). This proposed mechanism is supported by the observation that in hfRPE cultures, SB290157 co-application with C3a prevented both the upregulation of C3aR expression and the subsequent deposition of abnormal ECM structures (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). Nonetheless, the precise molecular interactions at the receptor—the positioning of the diphenylethoxy moiety and arginine side chain—is critical for binding affinity and selectivity (Iyer et al., 2017; Mishra et al., 2025), and minor alterations in these interactions might contribute to the observed functional variability.

Expected Effect:  
Based on the hypothesis for dry AMD, SB290157 is expected to act on RPE cells by antagonizing the C3aR, thereby preventing the cascade of intracellular events that lead to lysosomal stress. In a typical RPE culture assay where C3a is exogenously added—thereby simulating enhanced complement activity as observed in AMD—SB290157 should block C3a binding, which would normally result in the perturbation of lysosomal pH homeostasis. The blockade of this receptor is envisaged to preserve the normally acidic lysosomal environment required for the optimal maturation and proteolytic function of cathepsin D (CTSD), an enzyme whose dysfunction is implicated in the formation of drusen and the progression of dry AMD (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018; Iyer et al., 2017).  
Furthermore, by preserving lysosomal function, SB290157 is expected to reduce subsequent activation of the inflammasome—a multi-protein complex that is triggered when lysosomal destabilization occurs—and thus attenuate the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-1β. This cascade is particularly relevant because chronic inflammation is thought to drive many of the degenerative changes associated with AMD (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). In vitro, RPE cells pre-treated with SB290157 before C3a challenge would be anticipated to maintain normal lysosomal acidity (measured by appropriate pH-sensitive dyes), exhibit proper CTSD processing (as observed by Western blot analysis for mature cathepsin D forms), and display reduced markers of inflammasome activation such as caspase-1 cleavage and IL-1β release. Gene expression studies in these cells might also reveal normalized levels of key ECM components and proteases, ultimately leading to a reduction in sub-RPE deposit accumulation (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018).  
It is important to note that C3aR is expressed on RPE cells and its activation has been implicated in additional downstream effects—including modulation of the ubiquitin proteasome pathway and extracellular matrix turnover—which further contribute to cell dysfunction and deposit formation. Therefore, antagonism of C3aR by SB290157, if effective and selective, could theoretically interrupt this pathogenic cascade and offer a protective effect against drusen-mediated RPE degeneration in dry AMD (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018; Ames et al., 2001).

SB290157 offers a compelling mechanistic rationale for repurposing in dry AMD given the central role of complement dysregulation in the pathogenesis of the disease. Among its strengths is a well-documented ability to block C3a-induced signaling events across multiple preclinical models. Early characterizations demonstrated that SB290157 effectively inhibited intracellular Ca2+ mobilization, receptor internalization, and other pro-inflammatory events in both immune cells and engineered cell systems (Ames et al., 2001). Its application in an hfRPE model demonstrated that C3a-induced sub-RPE deposit formation can be reversed upon treatment with SB290157, underscoring its potential utility in preventing one of the critical pathological features of dry AMD (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). Furthermore, the known rodent tolerability and defined in vivo pharmacokinetics observed in other disease models—such as LPS-induced airway inflammation and adjuvant-induced arthritis—support the concept that SB290157 can be delivered systemically with demonstrable pharmacodynamic effects (Ames et al., 2001).  

However, several weaknesses temper enthusiasm for immediate clinical translation. A significant concern is the compound’s context-dependent pharmacology. Multiple studies have reported that SB290157 can function as a partial or even full agonist under certain conditions, particularly in overexpression systems, and paradoxically activate C3aR instead of inhibiting it (Coulthard, 2015; Li et al., 2021; Mathieu et al., 2005). Such functional divergence is critical when considering a therapy designed to block a deleterious signal in a delicate tissue such as the retina. Moreover, SB290157 has been shown to exhibit off-target effects, including partial agonism at C5aR2—a related complement receptor—which may confound downstream anti-inflammatory responses and produce unintended biological effects (Li et al., 2021; Mathieu et al., 2005).  
Additionally, while there is evidence of efficacy in non-ocular models and even in an hfRPE culture system, there is a paucity of robust in vivo data specifically demonstrating efficacy in ocular or AMD preclinical models. Modern translational approaches demand rigorous evaluation of pharmacokinetics, tissue penetration, ocular tolerability, and local off-target activity in the complex microenvironment of the eye—data that remain limited for SB290157 in the AMD setting (Iyer et al., 2017; Li et al., 2021). Furthermore, owing to its reputation as a “controversial” tool compound, some in the field recommend the use of complementary genetic models (e.g., C3aR knockout mice) to validate findings derived from its use (Coulthard, 2015; Li et al., 2021). This underscores the need for next-generation C3aR antagonists with improved selectivity and a more predictable pharmacodynamic profile if the goal is clinical translation for dry AMD.  

In summary, SB290157 has strong theoretical appeal as a means to interrupt a pathological complement cascade that leads to lysosomal dysfunction, impaired CTSD maturation, and ultimately drusen formation in dry AMD. Its prior use in various inflammatory and in vitro RPE models, along with the biochemistry linking C3aR activation to intracellular Ca2+ dysregulation and lysosomal stress, supports the hypothesis that C3aR blockade may be beneficial in preserving RPE function (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018; Iyer et al., 2017). Nonetheless, the intrinsic limitations of SB290157—including its potential for agonistic behavior, off-target C5aR2 activity, and inconsistent effects across different cellular contexts—present significant challenges that must be addressed prior to advancing this candidate into clinical trials for AMD (Ames et al., 2001; Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018; Li et al., 2021).

In conclusion, SB290157 is a well-characterized research tool with documented efficacy in blocking complement-mediated inflammatory responses in several animal models as well as in an hfRPE culture system, making it a promising candidate to test the hypothesis that C3aR blockade can prevent lysosomal alkalinization and CTSD dysfunction in dry AMD. Its strengths include a defined mechanism of competitive antagonism at C3aR, cross-species activity, and experimentally demonstrated protective effects against abnormal sub-RPE deposit formation. However, its context-dependent agonist behavior and off-target activation of C5aR2 raise significant concerns about its selectivity and reliability as a clinical therapeutic. Additionally, the limited data regarding ocular pharmacokinetics and direct efficacy in robust in vivo dry AMD models suggest that further validation is required. Thus, while the underlying rationale for targeting complement-mediated lysosomal dysfunction remains compelling, SB290157 is best viewed as a stepping stone toward the development of next-generation C3aR antagonists with improved pharmacological profiles for potential clinical application in dry AMD (Ames et al., 2001; Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018; Li et al., 2021).

The use of chemically modified oligonucleotides (including agomirs) in ocular drug development is supported both by preclinical data and emerging clinical applications in other retinal diseases. For instance, approaches to activate the transcription factor TFEB—which is the master regulator of lysosomal biogenesis—demonstrate that enhancement of the degradative pathway correlates with improved survival of the RPE and photoreceptor cells (Boya et al., 2023; Naso et al., 2020). Although direct use of a miR-211 mimic (as opposed to gene therapy or pharmacologic Ezrin inhibitors) has not yet been validated in clinical settings for AMD, the preclinical evidence for miR-211’s role in maintaining RPE homeostasis provides a strong rationale for advancing this candidate into further testing (Intartaglia et al., 2021; Naso et al., 2020).

─────────────────────────────  
Mechanism of Action  
─────────────────────────────  
The proposed molecular mechanism by which a miR-211 mimic would function in dry AMD is multifaceted, integrating several key cellular pathways that converge on the restoration of lysosomal biogenesis in the RPE. At its core, the therapeutic hypothesis centers on the ability of miR-211 to post-transcriptionally suppress Ezrin, a cytoskeletal linker protein that in the RPE is linked to disruptions in lysosomal function and cell clearance (Boya et al., 2023; Intartaglia et al., 2021).

Specifically, under physiological conditions miR-211 is induced in a light-dependent manner and directly binds to the 3′ untranslated region (UTR) of the Ezrin mRNA to repress its translation. In the context of dry AMD, miR-211 is downregulated—a change that leads to derepression of Ezrin. Elevated Ezrin levels are correlated with impaired lysosomal biogenesis, reduced cathepsin activity, and accumulation of metabolic debris (Boya et al., 2023; Naso et al., 2020). Once delivered to the RPE, the miR-211 mimic is expected to restore this regulatory inhibition, reducing Ezrin protein levels to a more physiologic state.

More intriguingly, this reduction in Ezrin is proposed to have downstream effects on lysosomal calcium signaling. Data indicate that when Ezrin is repressed, there is an increase in TRPML1 channel sensitivity at the lysosomal membrane, thereby generating a localized Ca²⁺ microdomain within these organelles (Naso et al., 2020). The increased lysosomal Ca²⁺ flux subsequently activates the Ca²⁺-dependent phosphatase calcineurin. Activated calcineurin dephosphorylates TFEB, a transcription factor that in its phosphorylated state is sequestered in the cytosol. Once dephosphorylated, TFEB can translocate into the nucleus where it functions as the master regulator of the Coordinated Lysosomal Expression and Regulation (CLEAR) gene network (Naso et al., 2020).

TFEB-driven transcription leads to enhanced expression of genes encoding lysosomal proteins, such as LAMP1, and digestive enzymes including cathepsin D, as well as proteins critical for autophagosome formation like LC3 and BECLIN. The net effect is an increase in the number and functionality of lysosomes, including improved acidification of these organelles—a crucial parameter for optimal enzymatic activity and degradation of engulfed materials (Du & Palczewski, 2022; Naso et al., 2020). The complete mechanistic cascade is thus: miR-211 mimic delivers a signal that downregulates Ezrin, alleviating its inhibitory effects on lysosomal biogenesis; this in turn potentiates TRPML1-mediated Ca²⁺ release, leading to calcineurin activation; calcineurin dephosphorylates TFEB, allowing its nuclear entry; and nuclear TFEB transcriptionally enhances lysosomal genes, culminating in improved cathepsin D expression and lysosomal acidification. This chain of events is hypothesized to restore the degradative capacity of the RPE and mitigate POS accumulation—a key pathogenic factor underlying dry AMD (Boya et al., 2023; Naso et al., 2020).

It is worth noting that similar signaling cascades have been observed in studies where Ezrin inhibition pharmacologically recapitulated the beneficial effects seen after TFEB activation, which indirectly supports this proposed miR-211–mediated mechanism (Naso et al., 2020). The convergence of genetic, pharmacologic, and mechanistic studies in preclinical rodent models reinforces confidence in the proposed chain-of-events, although direct demonstration of every step with a synthetic miR-211 agomir remains an area for future research.

─────────────────────────────  
Expected Effect  
─────────────────────────────  
When administrated to the retinal pigment epithelium via an appropriate ocular delivery method (such as intravitreal or subretinal injection, potentially formulated within lipid nanoparticles or other compatible carriers), the miR-211 mimic is expected to produce several beneficial effects that address the key pathological features of dry AMD. In in vitro assays using RPE cell lines or primary human RPE cultures, one would anticipate that treatment with the miR-211 agomir will lead to a measurable decrease in Ezrin mRNA and protein levels as confirmed by qRT-PCR and Western blot analyses, respectively (Boya et al., 2023; Intartaglia et al., 2021).

At the subcellular level, the downregulation of Ezrin is expected to relieve its inhibitory control on lysosomal Ca²⁺ dynamics. This should manifest as an increase in TRPML1 channel activity, resulting in a sustained and enhanced lysosomal Ca²⁺ signal, which can be quantified using calcium-sensitive dyes or genetically encoded Ca²⁺ indicators fused to lysosomal proteins (Naso et al., 2020). Following this, increased calcineurin activity is anticipated and can be monitored by assessing the phosphorylation status of downstream substrates including TFEB. In treated RPE cells, one would observe a redistribution of TFEB from the cytoplasm to the nucleus, a change that can be confirmed by immunocytochemistry and subcellular fractionation methods (Naso et al., 2020).

The nuclear translocation of TFEB should then promote transcriptional upregulation of lysosomal and autophagy-related genes, resulting in an increased number of lysosomes with enhanced acidification (as measured by pH-sensitive fluorescent probes) and increased activity of key lysosomal enzymes such as cathepsin D and cathepsin B. Ultrastructural analyses by electron microscopy might reveal a reduction in the number or size of accumulated phagolysosomes containing unprocessed POS, and a phenotypic rescue at the cellular level would be consistent with restored degradative function (Naso et al., 2020).

In animal models of dry AMD – particularly in miR-211 knockout mice or in models that replicate lipofuscin accumulation and reduced lysosomal function – treatment with the miR-211 mimic is expected to result in significant improvements in retinal structure and function. Outcomes could include a reduction in lipofuscin deposition in the RPE, improved clearance of dysfunctional or misfolded photoreceptor proteins, and ultimately functional improvements as measured by responses on electroretinography (ERG) and preservation of photoreceptor cell layers. The approach is expected to not only halt but also partially reverse the degenerative changes by boosting the intrinsic capacity of RPE cells to clear cellular debris and maintain homeostasis (Boya et al., 2023; Naso et al., 2020).

Furthermore, in preclinical experiments where pharmacological inhibition of Ezrin achieved similar results in terms of enhancing lysosomal markers and reducing pathological deposits, the miR-211 mimic is hypothesized to mimic these effects by acting upstream of the pathway. Given that there is evidence suggesting that downregulation of miR-211 in AMD leads to compromised visual function, restoring its levels should, in theory, improve RPE survival and enhance retinal performance (Naso et al., 2020). In summary, the expected effect of this therapeutic intervention is a robust enhancement of lysosomal biogenesis and function within the RPE, which in turn could restore degradative capacity, reduce debris accumulation, and preserve visual function in dry AMD.

─────────────────────────────  
Overall Evaluation  
─────────────────────────────  
The miR-211 mimic candidate for dry AMD represents an innovative approach that acts by rebalancing a key regulatory pathway implicated in lysosomal biogenesis and cellular clearance. Overall, there are several strengths and a number of challenges to consider:

Strengths:  
1. Rational Mechanistic Targeting:  
   The candidate is built on a clear mechanistic hypothesis. miR-211 has been shown in multiple preclinical studies to directly regulate Ezrin—a known inhibitor of lysosomal biogenesis—and its downregulation results in impaired degradation of POS in the RPE (Boya et al., 2023; Intartaglia et al., 2021). By restoring miR-211 levels, the cascade involving TRPML1-mediated Ca²⁺ release, calcineurin activation, and subsequent TFEB nuclear translocation is reactivated. This specificity in targeting a regulatory cascade central to intracellular clearance speaks to high precision in its design (Naso et al., 2020).

2. Preclinical Validation of the Concept:  
   Genetic models, such as miR-211 knockout mice, and pharmacologic approaches using Ezrin inhibitors have provided compelling evidence that manipulating this pathway can restore degradative capacity in the RPE (Naso et al., 2020). Although the miR-211 mimic itself has not yet been extensively tested in dry AMD models, these data provide a strong scientific rationale for its potential efficacy.

3. Established Chemical Modification Strategies:  
   The field of miRNA therapeutics has matured considerably, and the design of chemically modified agomirs is a well-established approach to increase in vivo stability and allow local ocular delivery. This is supported by multiple studies in ocular tissues showing that similar modifications lead to enhanced half-life and effective cellular uptake (Boya et al., 2023; Intartaglia et al., 2021).

4. Specificity for RPE Homeostasis:  
   The candidate is designed specifically for the RPE, the critical cell layer responsible for degrading old photoreceptor outer segments. Since RPE dysfunction is a hallmark of dry AMD, targeted restoration of its lysosomal capacity has a high potential to ameliorate disease progression and preserve vision (Naso et al., 2020).

Weaknesses/Challenges:  
1. Limited Direct Evidence with Agomirs:  
   Although there is substantial mechanistic preclinical evidence linking miR-211 to the regulation of lysosomal function via Ezrin repression, no data to date directly demonstrate the efficacy and safety of a chemically modified miR-211 mimic in relevant dry AMD models. It remains to be established whether the agomir will effectively reach the RPE, achieve the desired gene repression, and produce the biochemical cascade in vivo (Naso et al., 2020).

2. Delivery and Pharmacokinetic Hurdles:  
   Ocular delivery, while an area of active development, remains challenging. The RPE is separated from the vitreous by multiple biological barriers. Although intravitreal or subretinal injections are established, the pharmacokinetics, biodistribution, and long-term safety profile of a miRNA agomir in the human eye require thorough optimization. It will be necessary to confirm that the chemical modifications to the miR-211 mimic do not hinder its uptake by RPE cells or cause off-target effects (Naso et al., 2020; Boya et al., 2023).

3. Translational Gaps:  
   The preclinical studies have largely been performed in rodent models that, while informative, do not fully replicate human dry AMD. Scaling up from rodent to human necessitates careful consideration of dosing, frequency of administration, and long-term impact. In addition, the natural turnover and light-dependent regulation of miR-211 in the human RPE might be more complex than in animal models (Naso et al., 2020).

4. Potential Off-target Effects and Safety:  
   As with all nucleic acid–based therapies, off-target binding and unintended gene regulation are concerns. Although miR-211 is highly specific under endogenous conditions, the synthetic mimic may interact with unintended transcripts, potentially affecting other pathways in the RPE or neighboring retinal cells. Comprehensive in vitro and in vivo toxicity studies are essential to ensure that modulating the miR-211 network does not lead to adverse outcomes (Boya et al., 2023; Naso et al., 2020).

5. Regulatory and Manufacturing Issues:  
   The regulatory pathway for oligonucleotide therapeutics remains stringent, and the manufacturing process for chemically modified miRNAs must meet high quality and reproducibility standards. There is precedence in the field for similar agents, but each new candidate faces its own set of challenges regarding scalability and cost-effectiveness (Naso et al., 2020).

─────────────────────────────  
Overall Evaluation  
─────────────────────────────  
Based on the current literature and mechanistic rationale provided in the context, the miR-211 mimic candidate holds significant promise as a therapeutic agent for dry AMD. The strengths of this approach lie in its clearly defined mechanism of action, which ties the restoration of miR-211 levels directly to the re-establishment of lysosomal biogenesis—a critical process in RPE health. Preclinical data regarding miR-211’s role in repressing Ezrin and the downstream activation of the TRPML1–Ca²⁺–calcineurin–TFEB axis are compelling and suggest that correcting the deficiency of miR-211 could reverse the degradative defects observed in dry AMD (Boya et al., 2023; Intartaglia et al., 2021; Naso et al., 2020).

Moreover, the advances in chemical modification of miRNA mimics to generate agomirs provide a technical basis for formulating a stable and effective drug candidate. The specific targeting of the RPE—a key player in the pathophysiology of dry AMD—further strengthens the case for this candidate. In vitro and preclinical readouts, such as decreased expression of Ezrin, increases in TFEB nuclear translocation, upregulation of lysosomal markers (including cathepsin D), and consequent improvements in cell clearance, are all expected to translate into improved retinal structure and function (Naso et al., 2020; Boya et al., 2023).

However, significant work remains to address some of the translational challenges. There is a critical need for direct experimental validation using the chemically modified miR-211 agomir in relevant dry AMD models. Key studies will be required to evaluate pharmacodynamics, ocular biodistribution, and the long-term safety profile of the candidate. The potential for off-target effects and the challenges inherent in intraocular delivery further complicate the clinical development pathway. In addition, while the mechanistic pathway (miR-211 → Ezrin repression → TRPML1 activation → Ca²⁺ flux → calcineurin activation → TFEB nuclear translocation → lysosomal gene upregulation) is conceptually robust, some downstream biochemical events remain to be validated in the context of miR-211 agomir treatment (Naso et al., 2020; Boya et al., 2023).

In conclusion, the miR-211 mimic is an exciting repurposed candidate for dry AMD therapy that leverages a highly specific molecular mechanism with the potential to restore lysosomal function in RPE cells. Its strengths include a clear mechanistic rationale, a strong preclinical basis for targeting Ezrin and activating the TRPML1–Ca²⁺–calcineurin–TFEB pathway, and the availability of advanced chemical modification techniques for ocular delivery. The primary risks and challenges—such as the need for comprehensive in vivo validation, optimization of delivery methods, and a thorough safety assessment—are typical of emerging nucleic acid therapeutics but are not insurmountable given current technological advances. On balance, the available evidence supports further focused preclinical evaluation of the miR-211 agomir candidate as a promising therapeutic strategy for dry AMD (Boya et al., 2023; Intartaglia et al., 2021; Naso et al., 2020).

Given the potential to correct a key pathogenic deficiency in the RPE and restore essential degradative function, advancing this candidate into rigorous in vitro testing in human RPE models followed by in vivo testing in established animal models is a priority. Subsequent studies should focus on refining the chemical formulation, ensuring efficient and targeted delivery to the RPE, and establishing a clear safety profile while monitoring for improved lysosomal function and retinal structure/function rescue. This systematic approach will be critical in determining whether the miR-211 mimic can ultimately be developed into a viable therapeutic for patients with dry AMD.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Anakinra (brand: Kineret) is a recombinant, non-glycosylated form of the human interleukin-1 receptor antagonist (IL-1Ra) that competitively binds the type I interleukin-1 receptor (IL-1RI) and prevents signaling by IL-1α and IL-1β, thereby broadly antagonizing downstream IL-1–dependent signal transduction cascades (notably NF-κB and MAPK) in responsive cells (Dabouz, 2024; Dabouz et al., 2020). IL-1Ra belongs to the class of anti-cytokine biologics that block pro-inflammatory cytokine signaling, a therapeutic strategy that has been validated across systemic autoinflammatory and autoimmune diseases; Kineret has an extensive human safety and pharmacology dossier as an approved product, with prescribing information available for systemic use (Mesquida, Drawnel, & Fauser, 2019). Within ophthalmology, IL-1 pathway blockade has been investigated in multiple preclinical ocular models and has seen clinical use for inflammatory eye diseases; routes explored include systemic administration of anakinra for uveitis and scleritis, topical IL-1 antagonists for ocular surface disease (e.g., isunakinra/EBI-005), and experimental ocular gene therapy encoding IL-1Ra (Fabiani et al., 2017). In posterior segment disease models, intravitreal recombinant IL-1Ra (anakinra) inhibited laser-induced choroidal neovascularization (CNV) in rodents in a dose-dependent fashion, establishing local ocular pharmacologic activity of IL-1R antagonism in retina/choroid (Fabiani et al., 2017; Sandhu, Lambert, Xu, & Kaplan, 2018).

Therapeutic History  
Systemic indications and ocular inflammatory experience. Anakinra has long been employed systemically in rheumatology and has been repurposed for ocular autoinflammatory and autoimmune conditions such as Behçet uveitis, Blau syndrome/CAPS phenotypes, and refractory scleritis, with reported improvements in intraocular inflammation and steroid-sparing in case series and retrospective cohorts; dosing regimens reported include 100–150 mg daily or weight-based 1–3 mg/kg daily subcutaneous dosing, with acceptable tolerability profiles dominated by mild injection-site reactions in the ocular cohorts cited (Fabiani et al., 2017; Korhonen, 2024). A practical constraint is anakinra’s short systemic half-life that necessitates daily dosing, with relapse reported upon dose reductions in some inflammatory eye disease cases—an important consideration for chronic indications (Fabiani et al., 2017; Korhonen, 2024). Topical isunakinra/IL-1Ra formulations for ocular surface disease demonstrated clinically meaningful symptom and sign improvements in randomized trials, high ocular receptor occupancy (~97%) at low doses, minimal systemic exposure (plasma below detection), and a favorable local safety signal, although these outcomes pertain to the anterior segment and cannot be extrapolated directly to the posterior segment (Fabiani et al., 2017).

Posterior segment and AMD-relevant preclinical work. Multiple animal studies substantiate that IL-1 signaling is active and targetable in the posterior segment. In a rat CNV model, intravitreal anakinra led to dose-dependent reductions in neovascular area; related IL-1β-targeted interventions prevented CNV without exacerbating photoreceptor degeneration, arguing against gross phototoxicity from IL-1 blockade in that setting (Sandhu et al., 2018; Fabiani et al., 2017). In a blue light–induced retinal degeneration model, systemic IL-1R antagonism with anakinra mitigated inflammatory readouts, reduced accumulation of subretinal macrophages, preserved photoreceptor structure, and maintained ERG function; an allosteric IL-1R modulator (rytvela) was somewhat superior, but anakinra nonetheless produced protective effects (Dabouz et al., 2020; Dabouz, 2024). Mechanistically, these studies localized IL-1β production to inflammasome-active subretinal mononuclear phagocytes (MPs) and mapped Il1r1 expression mainly to astroglia and vascular cells in mouse retina, supporting paracrine IL-1 signaling to neurovascular targets in the outer retina (Dabouz et al., 2020; Dabouz, 2024).

Human clinical evidence in dry AMD/geographic atrophy. No published human trials of anakinra for dry AMD/geographic atrophy (GA) were identified in the provided materials; a registry search string returned 18 ClinicalTrials.gov hits combining anakinra with retinal keywords, but no trial-level information (indication, route, dose, status, outcomes) was provided, and no AMD/GA trials of anakinra are documented here (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.). Systemic IL-1β blockade with canakinumab showed no effect in a diabetic retinopathy exploratory clinical context, underscoring translational uncertainty of systemic IL-1 pathway modulation for posterior segment disease (Korhonen, 2024).

Mechanistic rationale in RPE/AMD. Extensive literature supports that in AMD-relevant stress contexts the RPE and subretinal myeloid cells exhibit NLRP3 inflammasome activation, caspase-1–dependent maturation of IL-1β and IL-18, lysosomal membrane permeabilization (LMP) with cathepsin release, and altered autophagy/heterophagy—mechanistic substrates for chronic para-inflammation and cell death (apoptosis → pyroptosis shift) in RPE (Treanor, n.d.; Yerramothu, Vijay, & Willcox, 2018; Kaarniranta et al., 2023). RPE-derived endogenous IL-1Ra provides further evidence that IL-1 signaling—and its antagonism—are biologically relevant in the RPE microenvironment (Fabiani et al., 2017).

Inflammasome context and limitations of IL-1R blockade. In RPE and adjacent retinal cells, NLRP3 inflammasome activation is triggered by AMD-relevant stimuli including A2E/lipofuscin photooxidation, drusen components, DICER1/Alu RNA accumulation, oxidized lipoproteins, complement/cofactors, ROS, and lysosomal membrane permeabilization with cathepsin release (Treanor, n.d.; Yerramothu et al., 2018). Critically, IL-1 pathway blockers such as anakinra do not inhibit upstream inflammasome assembly, caspase-1 activation, or IL-18 production; thus, IL-1R antagonism will block IL-1 signaling but will not shut down inflammasome-dependent IL-18 release or pyroptotic execution, which may continue to drive disease biology (Korhonen, 2024). Assay-level effects in retinal/RPE systems. IL-1 can contribute to priming (NF-κB–dependent) of inflammasome components; therefore, anakinra might indirectly reduce NLRP3 priming in some contexts by interrupting IL-1 positive feedback loops, leading to lower pro-IL-1β and possibly reduced susceptibility to subsequent activation triggers (Fabiani et al., 2017). In mice, systemic anakinra at 4 mg/kg twice daily for 3 days produced retinal protection in the blue light model; this regimen emphasizes short-term systemic exposures in an acute injury context rather than chronic degenerative settings (Dabouz, 2024). Overall Evaluation  
Merits  
- Biological plausibility in AMD. AMD-relevant stressors activate NLRP3 in RPE and subretinal myeloid cells, elevating IL-1β and IL-18 and driving para-inflammatory cascades and pyroptosis; IL-1β is increased in AMD vitreous and plasma, and IL-1–producing MPs are present at sites of pathology, establishing IL-1 as a rational target for modulating retinal inflammation (Treanor, n.d.; Nashine et al., 2022; Korhonen, 2024).  
- Pharmacologic validation in retinal models. Anakinra significantly reduced inflammation and preserved retinal structure/function in a light-damage model and intravitreally suppressed CNV in rodents, indicating target engagement and protective potential in the posterior segment; IL-1β neutralization prevented CNV without exacerbating photoreceptor degeneration, arguing for a non-toxic profile in those contexts (Dabouz et al., 2020; Dabouz, 2024; Sandhu et al., 2018).  
- RPE-relevant immunobiology. RPE naturally produces IL-1Ra, and exogenous IL-1Ra reduces necrosis-induced inflammatory mediator release from RPE and suppresses dendritic-cell activation in RPE co-cultures, suggesting that anakinra could attenuate RPE-mediated inflammatory amplification in dry AMD (Fabiani et al., 2017; Kaur & Singh, 2021).  
- Clinical and formulation precedents. Systemic ocular use of anakinra in uveitis and scleritis shows clinical feasibility and manageable safety; topical IL-1 antagonists have robust ocular safety signals; gene therapy encoding IL-1Ra and intravitreal administration have been explored preclinically, supporting a spectrum of delivery options that could be adapted for posterior segment disease (Fabiani et al., 2017).

Limitations and risks  
- Mechanistic incompleteness vis-à-vis inflammasomes. IL-1R blockade will not prevent upstream NLRP3 activation, caspase-1 activity, gasdermin-mediated pyroptosis, or IL-18 production; in RPE-intrinsic inflammasome-dominant pathophysiology, anakinra would be expected to blunt downstream IL-1–mediated amplification and leukocyte recruitment but not stop the execution machinery of inflammasome-driven cell death (Korhonen, 2024; Treanor, n.d.; Kaarniranta et al., 2023).  
- Unsubstantiated lysosomal rescue claims. There is no evidence here that anakinra preserves lysosomal acidification (v-ATPase function), cathepsin D maturation/activity, or prevents LMP in RPE under AMD-relevant stress; this is a critical gap because the proposed therapeutic specificity hinges on cytokine–lysosome cross-talk that remains to be demonstrated (Lim et al., 2020; Treanor, n.d.; Piippo, 2019).  
- Target expression uncertainties. In mouse retina, Il1r1 is enriched in astroglia and vascular cells and not detected in photoreceptors or MPs by scRNA-seq, complicating assumptions about direct photoreceptor or RPE targeting by anakinra in vivo; while RPE responds to IL-1 in vitro and produces IL-1Ra, spatial and species differences in IL-1RI distribution may shape efficacy and delivery decisions (Dabouz et al., 2020; Dabouz, 2024; Fabiani et al., 2017).  
- Mixed translational signals. Systemic IL-1β blockade did not improve diabetic retinopathy outcomes in the cited study, and anakinra’s systemic short half-life imposes burdensome daily dosing for chronic disease; there is no documented human safety/efficacy experience with intravitreal anakinra in AMD/GA in the provided sources (Korhonen, 2024; Fabiani et al., 2017; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).  
- Network complexity. NLRP3/IL-18 can exert context-dependent protective or detrimental effects in AMD models; while anakinra does not block IL-18 signaling, its selective inhibition of IL-1 may not suffice to rebalance inflammasome-driven pathology if pyroptosis and IL-18-dependent pathways remain active (Lim et al., 2020).

Go/No-Go considerations and critical experiments  
- RPE-centric validation. Test anakinra in human RPE models exposed to A2E/blue-light, drusen components, DICER1/Alu RNA, or oxidized lipoproteins; quantify NLRP3 priming (NLRP3, pro-IL-1β), activation (ASC specks, caspase-1 cleavage), downstream cytokines (IL-1β, IL-18), and execution (GSDMD cleavage/pyroptosis markers), with and without anakinra to define points of pathway modulation (Treanor, n.d.; Yerramothu et al., 2018).  
- Lysosomal endpoints. Directly measure lysosomal pH, v-ATPase activity, LMP (galectin-3 puncta), cathepsin D maturation/activity, and autophagic flux in the same RPE paradigms ± anakinra to test the hypothesis that IL-1R blockade preserves lysosomal integrity and protease processing (Piippo, 2019).  
- In vivo GA-relevant models. Move from acute light injury to RPE-atrophy models (e.g., chronic photooxidative stress, Alu RNA/DICER1 disruption, lipofuscin models) to assess whether anakinra reduces rates of RPE atrophy, outer retinal thinning, and visual function decline; include comparators targeting the inflammasome (e.g., NLRP3 inhibitors) to benchmark effect sizes and mechanistic depth (Treanor, n.d.; Kaarniranta et al., 2023; Lim et al., 2020).  
- Ocular delivery and PK. Develop and test intravitreal dosing and, preferably, sustained-release formats for anakinra to overcome systemic short half-life; establish vitreous/retinal PK and receptor occupancy, and evaluate ocular safety (IOP, ERG, histopathology) and immunogenicity (anti-drug antibodies) in large-eye species (Korhonen, 2024; Fabiani et al., 2017).  
- Biomarker strategy. Use vitreous/plasma IL-1β and retinal inflammatory transcript signatures as pharmacodynamic biomarkers; consider scRNA-seq to confirm target cell engagement (Il1r1-expressing compartments) pre- and post-treatment (Nashine et al., 2022; Dabouz, 2024).

Positioning relative to alternatives  
Because anakinra does not interrupt inflammasome activation or execution, proximal inhibitors of the NLRP3 inflammasome (e.g., MCC950-class) may provide deeper control of IL-1β/IL-18 production and pyroptosis in RPE-driven disease, at the cost of potentially suppressing beneficial IL-18 signaling in some contexts; preclinical literature shows NLRP3 blockade can be protective in retinal models, meriting parallel evaluation (Lim et al., 2020). Conversely, allosteric IL-1R modulators (rytvela-type) have shown superior protection to anakinra in the light-damage model and may offer functional selectivity (e.g., sparing NF-κB while inhibiting JNK/p38/AP-1) with improved distribution and immunogenicity profiles; these properties deserve consideration if an IL-1-targeting approach is pursued (Dabouz, 2024; Dabouz et al., 2020).

Conclusions  
- Strength of rationale. There is robust evidence that IL-1β is elevated and pathogenic in retinal neuroinflammation and that IL-1R antagonism—including anakinra—can protect retina in preclinical models by reducing inflammatory signaling and immune cell recruitment; RPE-relevant IL-1 biology further supports plausibility (Dabouz et al., 2020; Dabouz, 2024; Fabiani et al., 2017).  
- Weakness of hypothesis specifics. The central claim that anakinra preserves v-ATPase function and cathepsin D maturation in RPE lacks support in the provided literature; moreover, IL-1R blockade cannot prevent upstream inflammasome activation or pyroptosis, limiting its capacity to halt RPE-intrinsic degenerative processes central to GA (Lim et al., 2020; Korhonen, 2024; Treanor, n.d.; Piippo, 2019).  
- Translational readiness. No human AMD/GA trials of anakinra are documented here; systemic IL-1β blockade has shown limited efficacy in retinal vascular disease, and anakinra’s dosing logistics are unfavorable for chronic ocular therapy without dedicated ocular delivery systems (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.; Korhonen, 2024).

Overall Evaluation  
Anakinra is a mechanistically credible anti-inflammatory candidate to blunt IL-1–driven retinal inflammation and leukocyte recruitment, with reproducible preclinical efficacy signals in posterior-segment injury models and supportive RPE-centric immunobiology; however, the specific hypothesis that it will mechanistically preserve lysosomal v-ATPase function and cathepsin D activity in RPE is currently unsupported by direct evidence, and IL-1R antagonism is unlikely to arrest inflammasome activation, IL-18 signaling, or pyroptotic cell death that contribute to RPE atrophy in dry AMD (Dabouz et al., 2020; Dabouz, 2024; Fabiani et al., 2017; Korhonen, 2024; Lim et al., 2020). Given the absence of clinical data in GA and delivery constraints, anakinra merits consideration as an adjunct anti-inflammatory approach contingent on (1) generation of RPE-focused data demonstrating modulation of inflammasome priming and lysosomal integrity, and (2) development of sustained intraocular delivery; in parallel, more proximal interventions (NLRP3 inhibitors) and IL-1R allosteric modulators with superior preclinical efficacy should be benchmarked as potentially higher-leverage strategies for disease modification in dry AMD (Lim et al., 2020; Dabouz et al., 2020).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Panobinostat (LBH589) is a fully synthetic small‐molecule compound originally developed by Novartis and characterized chemically as a cinnamic hydroxamic acid analogue formulated as its anhydrous lactate salt. This molecule belongs to the hydroxamate class of histone deacetylase inhibitors (HDACi), a group of compounds designed to inhibit the enzymatic activity of HDACs that regulate chromatin remodeling and transcription by catalyzing the removal of acetyl groups from histone proteins. Panobinostat’s chemical structure, defined by its hydroxamic acid moiety, is tailored to chelate the zinc ion in the catalytic domain of HDAC enzymes, thereby preventing deacetylation reactions that normally lead to a condensed chromatin state. In its initial development, panobinostat was formulated in multiple dosage forms, including oral hard capsules containing 10, 15, or 20 mg doses and earlier intravenous preparations, illustrating its versatility in administration routes for different clinical indications (Van Veggel, Westerman, & Hamberg, 2018; Libby et al., 2015; Dokmanovic, Clarke, & Marks, 2007). Compounds of this class have historically been employed in oncology, where their capacity to induce hyperacetylation of histone and non-histone substrates leads to altered gene transcription, cell cycle arrest, differentiation, and eventual apoptosis in malignant cells (Van Veggel et al., 2018; Cea et al., 2013). Moreover, the broad-spectrum inhibition of HDAC isoforms—spanning Classes I, II, and IV—distinguishes panobinostat as a “pan-HDAC inhibitor” with high potency at nanomolar concentrations, a characteristic that underlies its robust pharmacological profile and its subsequent regulatory approvals for certain cancer indications (Morabito et al., 2016).

Therapeutic History:  
Since its discovery, panobinostat has undergone extensive preclinical and clinical evaluation primarily targeting multiple myeloma and various hematologic malignancies. Early phase clinical trials established that, as a single agent, panobinostat had modest activity; however, its combination with proteasome inhibitors such as bortezomib and corticosteroids like dexamethasone produced synergistic effects that translated into significant improvements in progression‐free survival in relapsed and refractory multiple myeloma patients. This positive clinical efficacy culminated in its approval by both the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and the European Medicines Agency (EMA) in 2015 for the treatment of patients with multiple myeloma who had received at least two prior regimens (Van Veggel et al., 2018; Libby et al., 2015; Bondarev et al., 2021). Beyond multiple myeloma, panobinostat has been scrutinized in a variety of clinical settings—including cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, acute myeloid leukemia, diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, and several solid tumor malignancies—to explore its antitumor potential in combination therapies, given its capacity to potentiate the cytotoxic effects of other agents by modulating epigenetic regulation (Cea et al., 2013; Cinek & Karalı, 2021; Libby et al., 2015). Despite its demonstrated efficacy in cancer, there is no recorded use of panobinostat in ophthalmological diseases such as dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or in any similar degenerative condition. The extensive body of clinical research on HDAC inhibitors has predominantly focused on antineoplastic applications, and while some mechanistic parallels exist between the cellular processes targeted in cancer and those disrupted in degenerative retinal diseases, panobinostat’s utility in dry AMD remains an uncharted territory that has thus far not been explored in preclinical or clinical trials (Dokmanovic, Clarke, & Marks, 2007; Morabito et al., 2016; Libby et al., 2015).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, panobinostat exerts its biological effects primarily through the inhibition of histone deacetylase enzymes. The compound’s hydroxamic acid group binds with high affinity to the zinc ion located in the catalytic domain of HDAC enzymes, thereby blocking the deacetylation of lysine residues on histone tails as well as on several non-histone proteins. This blockade causes an accumulation of acetylated histones, which in turn results in a more open chromatin conformation that facilitates enhanced transcription of a multitude of genes, including those pivotal for cell cycle arrest, apoptosis, and cellular differentiation (Benedetti, Conte, & Altucci, 2015; Morabito et al., 2016). Beyond its classical role in modifying histone tail acetylation, panobinostat’s broad inhibition across HDAC classes implies that it can modulate the acetylation status of key transcription factors, chaperone proteins (such as heat shock protein 90), and structural proteins like α-tubulin. This wide-ranging impact on protein acetylation alters the functional activity of numerous signaling pathways and cellular processes, contributing to anti-proliferative and pro-apoptotic outcomes in cancer cells (Morabito et al., 2016). The pleiotropic nature of its action is further evidenced by the induction of autophagy in various tumor models, an effect thought to be mediated by the increased acetylation and transcriptional activation of master regulators of lysosomal biogenesis such as transcription factor EB (TFEB). The repurposing of panobinostat for dry age-related macular degeneration presents an intriguing and biologically plausible strategy that leverages the compound’s well-documented HDAC inhibitory properties to modulate critical intracellular degradation pathways. One of the foremost strengths of this therapeutic candidate is its potent, broad-spectrum inhibition of HDAC enzymes at low nanomolar concentrations, which has been repeatedly demonstrated in various preclinical and clinical studies in oncology (Van Veggel et al., 2018; Morabito et al., 2016). The resultant hyperacetylation of histones and non-histone proteins not only promotes cell cycle arrest and apoptosis in malignant cells but also facilitates the transcriptional activation of autophagy- and lysosome-related genes—a pathway that could be harnessed to restore faithful lysosomal degradation in retinal pigment epithelial cells affected in dry AMD (Benedetti, Conte, & Altucci, 2015; Cinek & Karalı, 2021).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
2-Hydroxypropyl-β-cyclodextrin (HPβCD) is a chemically modified derivative of natural β-cyclodextrin—a cyclic oligosaccharide consisting of glucose units linked via α-1,4 glycosidic bonds. This modification, achieved by the introduction of hydroxypropyl groups, improves its solubility and reduces its inherent cytotoxicity relative to unmodified cyclodextrins. HPβCD belongs to the cyclodextrin class, molecules that have been widely used in pharmaceutical formulations as solubilizing agents and excipients due to their ability to encapsulate hydrophobic molecules within their lipophilic interior, thereby increasing bioavailability. Over the years, these agents have gained attention as cholesterol-binding molecules, and HPβCD is no exception, being repurposed for diseases characterized by pathological cholesterol accumulation such as Niemann–Pick type C1 (NPC1). Its structural properties permit the formation of inclusion complexes with cholesterol and other lipids, facilitating their mobilization and removal from cells. Given its established role in NPC1 disease and emerging evidence supporting its ability to cross the blood–retina barrier, HPβCD is now being evaluated as a therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD), specifically targeting drusen-associated cholesterol accumulation in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells (Calias, 2018; Roney, 2020).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, HPβCD has been extensively investigated as a therapeutic intervention for lysosomal storage diseases, with a particular focus on Niemann–Pick disease type C (NPC), a condition characterized by the pathological accumulation of cholesterol and glycosphingolipids in cells. Preclinical studies in animal models have demonstrated that systemic administration of HPβCD can lower intracellular cholesterol levels, thereby ameliorating disease-related cellular dysfunction. However, its pharmacokinetic limitations—most notably, its minimal penetration of the blood–brain barrier (BBB) when administered intravenously—have necessitated alternative routes of delivery, such as intrathecal administration, to achieve sufficient central nervous system (CNS) exposure (Calias, 2018). In the context of retinal diseases, several studies have investigated the effects of HPβCD in animal models of retinal cholesterol dyshomeostasis. In these models, HPβCD treatment has been associated with significant reductions in cholesterol crystals, diminished lipid deposition in structures such as Bruch’s membrane, and decreased activation of retinal macrophages and microglial cells (El-Darzi et al., 2023). Although HPβCD has been repurposed from its application in NPC to target retinal pathologies, a focused investigation into its use for dry AMD remains to be performed clinically, as systematic searches on ClinicalTrials.gov indicate that no registered trials have specifically addressed cyclodextrin use in AMD (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, HPβCD acts primarily as a cholesterol extractor by leveraging its toroidal structure, which is characterized by a hydrophilic exterior and a relatively hydrophobic interior cavity. This unique architecture enables HPβCD to form inclusion complexes with cholesterol, effectively sequestering the lipid from cellular membranes. In the setting of RPE cells, where lysosomal cholesterol accumulation is implicated in the pathogenesis of dry AMD, HPβCD is hypothesized to mobilize cholesterol from lysosomal membranes. Excess cholesterol in these membranes disrupts the lipid microdomains necessary for the optimal assembly and functioning of protein complexes such as the vacuolar-type H⁺-ATPase (v-ATPase), which is essential for maintaining lysosomal acidity (Nociari, Kiss, & Rodriguez-Boulan, 2017). By extracting cholesterol, HPβCD is expected to restore these lipid microdomains, thereby facilitating the proper assembly and function of the v-ATPase complex. This normalization of v-ATPase assembly is critical for reestablishing an acidic environment within lysosomes, which in turn is necessary for the optimal activity of lysosomal hydrolases such as cathepsin D (CTSD).

In neurons and other cell types, studies have demonstrated that HPβCD treatment leads to a reduction in both luminal and membrane-associated cholesterol levels, a process that not only improves lysosomal trafficking but also induces lysosomal exocytosis under certain conditions (Roney, 2020). Furthermore, the improvement in lysosomal acidification following HPβCD-mediated cholesterol extraction has been correlated with enhanced autophagic flux due to increased CTSD-mediated proteolysis. Although direct evidence for this mechanism in RPE cells is still emerging, it is reasonable to extrapolate that similar molecular events would occur in retinal cells. The restoration of lysosomal pH and the subsequent improvement in autophagy are critical because they directly contribute to the clearance of intracellular debris, including drusen lipids, thereby potentially reducing the lipid burden that characterizes the progression of dry AMD (Nociari et al., 2017; Roney, 2020).

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis driving the repurposing of HPβCD for dry AMD is that it will mobilize cholesterol from RPE lysosomal membranes, thereby restoring the integrity of lipid microdomains that are essential for v-ATPase assembly. In practical terms, treatment with HPβCD is expected to yield several interrelated outcomes. First, the reduction in membrane cholesterol is anticipated to alleviate the inhibitory effect of cholesterol excess on v-ATPase assembly, leading to improved proton pump activity and a consequent normalization of lysosomal pH. Given that the activity of CTSD is pH-dependent—with optimal function occurring under acidic conditions—the normalization of lysosomal pH should enable enhanced CTSD activity and improved autophagic degradation of lipid aggregates (Nociari et al., 2017; Roney, 2020).

Second, by promoting the removal of excess cholesterol, HPβCD should reduce the formation of cholesterol crystals, a pathological hallmark associated with retinal lipid dyshomeostasis and drusen formation. Animal studies have demonstrated that HPβCD treatment leads to a significant reduction in the number of cholesterol crystals per unit area in retinal tissues, which is strongly correlated with improvements in retinal lipid processing and decreased inflammatory responses mediated by macrophage and microglial activation (El-Darzi et al., 2023).

Third, in laboratory assays using RPE cell cultures, one would expect to observe a decrease in the proportion of lipid-laden lysosomes, accompanied by measurable improvements in lysosomal acidification—parameters that serve as surrogate markers for enhanced autophagic capacity. Ultimately, these molecular and cellular changes are anticipated to culminate in the reduction of drusen lipid volumes, thereby slowing or potentially halting the progression of dry AMD (El-Darzi et al., 2023).

The repurposing of HPβCD for the treatment of dry AMD is underpinned by a robust mechanistic rationale, a substantial preclinical history, and an acceptable clinical safety profile observed in other indications. In several animal models of retinal cholesterol dyshomeostasis, HPβCD has yielded promising results by lowering total, unesterified, and esterified cholesterol levels, reducing the number of cholesterol crystals, and mitigating inflammatory responses in the retina (El-Darzi et al., 2023). These data provide a compelling basis for its evaluation in conditions such as dry AMD where drusen formation is closely linked to aberrant cholesterol metabolism. Furthermore, its prior use in the treatment of NPC—a condition that shares certain pathogenic features with AMD in terms of lysosomal dysfunction—adds credence to the hypothesis that HPβCD may exert similar therapeutic effects in RPE cells (Calias, 2018).

A significant advantage of HPβCD is its established safety record in clinical studies for NPC. Unlike therapies that broadly modulate inflammatory or oxidative stress pathways, HPβCD acts directly on the cholesterol burden—the underlying driver of drusen lipid accumulation in dry AMD. This mechanistic specificity has the potential to result in a more direct impact on the disease process, rather than merely modifying secondary symptoms. Mechanistically, the extraction of cholesterol by HPβCD is anticipated to restore the lipid environment within RPE lysosomal membranes, thereby re-enabling the proper assembly of v-ATPase complexes. This, in turn, can lead to improved lysosomal acidification, enhanced cathepsin D activity, and accelerated autophagic clearance of damaged cellular components—a cascade of events that would address one of the root causes of retinal degeneration in AMD (Nociari et al., 2017; Roney, 2020).

Despite these strengths, several weaknesses and uncertainties must be acknowledged. First, while the preclinical data in animal models are promising, there remains a lack of clinical trial data specifically focusing on the use of HPβCD in dry AMD. A search using the relevant keywords indicates a paucity of clinical evidence in this particular indication (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.), which means that translational hurdles remain before HPβCD can be confidently recommended for dry AMD therapy. Second, although the mechanism by which HPβCD affects v-ATPase assembly and CTSD activity is supported by data in neuronal models, direct evidence of these molecular events in RPE cells is still emerging, leaving some uncertainty regarding the depth of its effects on lysosomal autophagy in the retinal environment (Nociari et al., 2017). Third, formulation and administration routes will be critical considerations. While systemic dosing has been used in other indications, the optimal approach for targeting the retina might require localized delivery techniques—such as intravitreal injection or the development of a sustained-release ocular formulation—to maximize retinal exposure while minimizing systemic exposure and off-target effects. Finally, the potential for adverse events, particularly those related to over-extraction of cholesterol or unintended disruption of lipid homeostasis, must be carefully evaluated in the context of chronic ocular treatment.

In summary, HPβCD is a well-characterized compound with a history of successful application in disorders of cholesterol accumulation, notably NPC. Its ability to extract cholesterol from cellular membranes, restore lipid microdomains, and thereby normalize lysosomal function forms a strong mechanistic basis for its evaluation as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. Preclinical studies in animal models provide encouraging evidence that HPβCD can reduce retinal cholesterol accumulation, lower the number of cholesterol crystals, and improve markers of lysosomal function in retinal tissues. This directly aligns with the therapeutic hypothesis that the mobilization of cholesterol from RPE lysosomal membranes will restore v-ATPase activity, normalize lysosomal pH, enhance cathepsin D activity, and ultimately reduce the drusen lipid burden characteristic of dry AMD (Calias, 2018; El-Darzi et al., 2023; Nociari et al., 2017; Roney, 2020).

However, the translation of these preclinical findings into a clinically effective therapy for dry AMD will require addressing several critical challenges. These include the absence of direct clinical data in AMD, the need for detailed mechanistic studies in RPE cells to confirm that the cholesterol-lowering effects observed in other tissues are recapitulated in the retina, and the optimization of dosing and delivery methods to ensure that therapeutic concentrations are achieved safely in the target tissue. Additionally, any potential side effects—such as those noted in NPC patients, including auditory toxicity—must be rigorously monitored in ocular studies to ensure that treatment remains safe over the long term (Calias, 2018).

Overall, the repurposing of HPβCD for dry AMD is scientifically compelling due to its targeted mechanism of action and its established clinical history in related indications. Its ability to mobilize cholesterol and restore lysosomal function addresses fundamental pathogenic processes implicated in dry AMD, and the preclinical evidence supports its potential efficacy. Nevertheless, the absence of clinical trials in this particular indication, combined with uncertainties regarding the precise molecular interactions in RPE cells and the optimization of drug delivery to the retina, suggests that further preclinical and early-stage clinical studies are warranted before HPβCD can be advanced as a treatment for dry AMD. Continued research should focus on elucidating the detailed molecular mechanisms within RPE cells, assessing long-term safety in ocular models, and exploring various delivery modalities to maximize efficacy while minimizing potential risks.
