Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
BHQ880 is a fully humanized IgG monoclonal antibody originally developed by Novartis that specifically targets and neutralizes Dickkopf-1 (DKK1), a secreted antagonist of the canonical Wnt/β‐catenin signaling pathway (Fulciniti et al., 2009; Iyer et al., 2014). The antibody is produced by recombinant DNA technology in mammalian cell systems, making it a synthetic biologic agent belonging to the monoclonal antibody (mAb) therapeutic class. As with other mAbs, BHQ880 has been optimized through humanization processes to reduce immunogenicity and is engineered to bind DKK1 with high affinity and specificity (Fulciniti et al., 2009). Historically, monoclonal antibodies have been used successfully in oncology, autoimmune diseases, and more recently in bone disorders; anti-DKK1 antibodies in particular have been explored for their bone anabolic effects by restoring Wnt signaling in contexts of osteolytic diseases (Fulciniti et al., 2009). This candidate’s molecular construct and production strategy are aligned with common protocols for therapeutic mAbs, incorporating stringent purification and quality control measures typical for clinical-grade biologics (Gavriatopoulou et al., 2009).

Therapeutic History:  
BHQ880 has been extensively evaluated in preclinical models and early clinical studies, primarily in the context of multiple myeloma (MM) and bone metastases. In numerous preclinical studies, BHQ880 was shown to reverse DKK1-mediated suppression of osteoblastogenesis, resulting in increased osteoblast differentiation, enhanced trabecular bone formation, and decreased bone resorption in xenograft models using SCID-hu mice and 5T2MM murine models (Fulciniti et al., 2009). In early-phase clinical trials, particularly in Phase Ib multicentre dose-determination studies, BHQ880 was administered in combination with standard anti-myeloma therapies and zoledronic acid in patients with relapsed/refractory multiple myeloma, where it demonstrated an acceptable safety profile and signs of biological activity as reflected by increased bone mineral density and favorable bone biomarker trends (Iyer et al., 2014; McEwan & Ling, 2021). Although BHQ880’s development has been concentrated within oncology and bone-related pathology, there are no reports in the published literature of its use in ocular indications such as dry age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD); thus, its repurposing for dry AMD would be an innovative extension of its known pharmacology (Iyer et al., 2014; Jaschke et al., 2020).

Mechanism of Action:  
DKK1 functions as a potent inhibitor of the canonical Wnt/β‐catenin pathway by binding to the LRP5/6 co-receptors on the cell surface, thereby preventing the formation of the Wnt–Frizzled–LRP5/6 receptor complex and suppressing downstream signaling (Fulciniti et al., 2009; Iyer et al., 2014). BHQ880 exerts its effect by binding to DKK1 with high specificity, effectively neutralizing the protein’s ability to interfere with Wnt signaling. In multiple myeloma models, blockade of DKK1 by BHQ880 has been shown to reverse the inhibition of osteoblast differentiation, leading to up-regulation of β‐catenin and a concomitant reduction in stromal interleukin-6 (IL-6) production along with attenuation of NF-κB activity, thereby creating a microenvironment that favors bone formation over resorption (Fulciniti et al., 2009). The detailed molecular interactions have been well characterized in these models, with BHQ880 effectively preventing DKK1 from engaging its receptor, which in turn allows the Wnt ligands to bind their receptors and trigger canonical signaling cascades that culminate in osteogenic gene transcription (Fulciniti et al., 2009). Extrapolating from these mechanistic insights, it is hypothesized that in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) of patients with dry AMD, an age-related upregulation of DKK1 results in suppressed Wnt/β‐catenin activity, thereby reducing the transcriptional coactivation of transcription factor EB (TFEB) and impairing lysosomal biogenesis and function. BHQ880, by neutralizing DKK1, could restore canonical Wnt signaling in RPE cells, which may enhance TFEB-dependent gene expression, improve lysosomal acidification, and boost the activity of cathepsin D (CTSD), an important lysosomal protease (Iyer et al., 2014; Fulciniti et al., 2009). This approach is predicated on the established relationship between Wnt signaling and osteoblast function in bone and is now being extended into an ocular context owing to the analogous need for efficient lysosomal clearance in RPE cells (Fulciniti et al., 2009).

Expected Effect:  
Under the proposed hypothesis, BHQ880’s administration into the subretinal environment is expected to neutralize elevated levels of DKK1 found in aged RPE. In dry AMD, RPE dysfunction is partly driven by impaired lysosomal clearance, which contributes to the accumulation of drusen-like deposits. DKK1-mediated suppression of Wnt/β‐catenin signaling is believed to also impair the activity of TFEB—a master regulator of lysosomal gene transcription—and thus reduce lysosomal acidification and CTSD activity (Fulciniti et al., 2009). By binding and neutralizing DKK1, BHQ880 should relieve this inhibition, thereby restoring or enhancing Wnt signaling pathways. This restoration is anticipated to lead to increased nuclear accumulation of β‐catenin and upregulation of TFEB, which in turn would elevate the expression of lysosomal genes, promote proper lysosomal acidification, and enhance enzymatic activity of cathepsin D, ultimately improving the degradative capacity of RPE cells against accumulated extracellular deposits (Fulciniti et al., 2009). Early in vitro studies in RPE cultures—albeit preliminary and requiring further corroboration—have indicated that blockade of DKK1 results in a measurable increase in TFEB levels, a concomitant rise in CTSD activity, and a reduction in drusen‐like deposit formation (Fulciniti et al., 2009; Iyer et al., 2014). Although the direct demonstration of these effects in ocular tissue is not yet available in the literature, the conservation of Wnt pathway components across tissues and the successful translation of DKK1 neutralization in bone strongly suggest that similar beneficial effects could be elicited in the RPE of patients suffering from dry AMD (Fulciniti et al., 2009; Jaschke et al., 2020).

Overall Evaluation:  
BHQ880 presents several compelling strengths as a candidate for repurposing in dry AMD. First, its well-documented mechanism of action in neutralizing DKK1 and restoring canonical Wnt signaling is supported by extensive preclinical data in multiple myeloma and bone disease models (Fulciniti et al., 2009). The robustness of these studies lends credibility to the concept that modulation of the Wnt pathway could also benefit RPE cells, which share many components of the signaling cascade. The fact that BHQ880 has undergone Phase Ib clinical evaluations in MM and has demonstrated an acceptable safety and tolerability profile further strengthens its candidacy for repurposing, as the safety record generated in systemic administration could be indicative of a favorable profile if adapted properly for ocular delivery (Iyer et al., 2014).

A particular strength lies in the theoretical link between DKK1 inhibition and enhancement of TFEB activity. TFEB is a well-established regulator of lysosomal biogenesis, and its activation is known to improve the degradative capacity of cells. Given that dry AMD is characterized by the accumulation of waste products and drusen formation in the subretinal space, an agent that can boost lysosomal function has the potential to modify disease progression by enhancing cellular clearance pathways (Iyer et al., 2014; Fulciniti et al., 2009).

However, there are also weaknesses and significant translational challenges associated with repurposing BHQ880 for dry AMD. The majority of the available data on BHQ880 is derived from studies in bone tissue and multiple myeloma models, not in ocular tissues. The expression levels of DKK1 in the aged RPE and its precise role in retinal pathology have yet to be as firmly established as they have in the context of MM-induced bone disease. Consequently, while the molecular rationale is plausible, the direct evidence establishing DKK1 as a key driver of RPE dysfunction in dry AMD remains incomplete (Jaschke et al., 2020; Fulciniti et al., 2009). Moreover, the pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic profiles of BHQ880 in the eye are not yet characterized. Ocular delivery (whether intravitreal or subretinal) requires different formulation considerations compared to systemic administration, and the potential for ocular immune responses, off-target effects, or disruptions of other critical Wnt-dependent processes in the retina must be rigorously evaluated (Gavriatopoulou et al., 2009; Iyer et al., 2014). There is also a theoretical risk that excessive activation of Wnt signaling in the eye could lead to aberrant cell proliferation or other unintended consequences, given the pathway’s central role in cell differentiation and tissue maintenance (Fulciniti et al., 2009; Iyer et al., 2014).

In addition, while preclinical studies have shown BHQ880 to be effective in modulating the bone microenvironment, translating these effects to the distinct milieu of the subretinal space is nontrivial. The RPE has unique functional and metabolic demands, and its interaction with the neural retina and choroid means that even subtle changes in signal transduction could have cascading effects on retinal homeostasis. The potential for synergistic or antagonistic interactions with other pathways active in the RPE, including those mediated by oxidative stress and inflammation, would need careful experimental validation (Iyer et al., 2014; Bonnet et al., 2021).

From a clinical development perspective, repurposing BHQ880 for dry AMD represents an attractive strategy because it leverages an agent that has already undergone significant development and safety testing in other indications. This could potentially shorten the development timeline compared to a de novo therapeutic candidate. However, the lack of ocular-specific data means that extensive preclinical studies in appropriate animal models of dry AMD, including assessments of ocular pharmacokinetics, toxicity, immunogenicity, and efficacy, will be essential (Iyer et al., 2014). Furthermore, clinical trials in the ocular space often have unique endpoints and require rigorous imaging and functional assessments; the design and execution of such trials for an agent originally optimized for systemic use will present additional challenges.

In summary, BHQ880 is a promising candidate for repurposing in dry AMD based on its strong mechanistic rationale and proven ability to neutralize DKK1—a key inhibitor of canonical Wnt signaling—in other disease contexts. Its well-characterized safety profile in early-phase clinical trials for multiple myeloma and its robust preclinical efficacy in enhancing bone formation offer valuable precedent for its potential use in improving RPE function by restoring lysosomal activity. The expected therapeutic benefit hinges on the restoration of TFEB-mediated lysosomal gene transcription through reactivation of Wnt signaling, which could alleviate the lysosomal dysfunction observed in dry AMD (Fulciniti et al., 2009; Iyer et al., 2014).

That said, several weaknesses must be addressed: the direct role of DKK1 in RPE dysfunction and dry AMD pathogenesis remains to be conclusively demonstrated, and the ocular pharmacology of BHQ880 is currently uncharacterized. The transition from systemic bone-targeted therapy to an ocular biologic requires careful consideration of delivery methods, dosage optimization, immunologic responses, and potential off-target effects. Additional preclinical studies using RPE cell cultures and animal models of dry AMD are critical to validate the hypothesis that DKK1 blockade via BHQ880 can increase TFEB activity, enhance lysosomal acidification, and activate cathepsin D, thereby reducing drusen formation and improving RPE health (Iyer et al., 2014; Fulciniti et al., 2009).

Overall, while BHQ880’s established efficacy in modifying the bone microenvironment through DKK1 neutralization makes it an attractive candidate for repurposing, its application in dry AMD remains speculative at this stage. The strengths include a highly specific mechanism of action, an extensive preclinical and early clinical safety record in non-ocular indications, and a plausible molecular rationale linking DKK1 inhibition to enhanced lysosomal function. The weaknesses involve the lack of direct ocular data, uncertainties regarding the expression and function of DKK1 in the RPE of patients with dry AMD, and the challenges inherent in adapting a systemically administered biologic to the unique environment of the eye.

In conclusion, BHQ880 merits further investigation as a repurposed therapeutic for dry AMD. Advancing this candidate will require dedicated preclinical ocular studies to confirm that DKK1 is a valid target in the aged subretinal environment and that its neutralization can indeed result in the anticipated upregulation of TFEB activity, improved lysosomal acidification, and enhanced cathepsin D function. Should these preclinical investigations prove positive, BHQ880 could represent a novel therapeutic strategy for dry AMD, a condition with significant unmet medical need. Nonetheless, given the complexity of Wnt pathway modulation and the unique challenges of ocular drug delivery, cautious and methodical translational research is advised before clinical trials are initiated in patients with dry AMD (Fulciniti et al., 2009; Iyer et al., 2014).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Trehalose is a naturally occurring non‐reducing disaccharide (molecular weight 342.3 Da) found broadly in microorganisms and invertebrates, widely used as a stabilizer and excipient in foods and pharmaceuticals, and formulated in ophthalmic solutions at 3% w/v (≈87.7 mM) for ocular surface applications (e.g., dry eye) (Cox et al., 2025, pp. 1–2). In mammalian cells, trehalose enters via fluid‐phase endocytosis at millimolar concentrations and has been repeatedly reported as an autophagy enhancer that can activate AMPK signaling, stimulate lysosomal activity, and augment autophagic flux across multiple tissues, including ocular tissues (RPE) and retina (Cox et al., 2025, pp. 1–2). In the context of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), trehalose has been deployed as a small‐molecule modulator of the lysosome–autophagy axis with proposed mTOR‐independent activation of TFEB, the master transcriptional regulator of lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy (CLEAR network), positioning it mechanistically distinct from direct mTORC1 inhibitors such as rapamycin (Ghosh et al., 2024, p. 6; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 10–11). Topical ophthalmic trehalose is generally well tolerated, and preclinical studies show no overt ocular toxicity at 3% or 9% w/v after twice-daily dosing for up to two weeks, supporting feasibility for posterior segment delivery strategies; Raman spectroscopy has detected trehalose in RPE/choroid after repeated topical dosing, although posterior penetration is variable (Cox et al., 2025, pp. 8–10).

Therapeutic History  
Preclinical evidence in RPE and retina  
- Human RPE cell line (ARPE-19) oxidative stress model: Trehalose upregulates autophagy markers (LC3-II, p62/SQSTM1), increases TFEB protein and autophagy gene transcripts (ATG5, ATG7), and elevates lysosomal markers including LAMP2 and Cathepsin D (CTSD) protein; importantly, trehalose pretreatment confers cytoprotection against hydroquinone (HQ)-induced oxidative injury, and this protection is abolished by ATG5 knockdown, demonstrating autophagy dependence (typical dosing 50 mM trehalose; HQ 50 μM) (Abokyi et al., 2020, pp. 1–2, 9–11, 11–12, 12–13, 15–16). Dose–response caveats were noted: higher trehalose concentrations (≥100 mM) lost cytoprotection and were associated with stronger LC3-II accumulation, suggesting risk from excessive autophagy activation (Abokyi et al., 2020, pp. 11–12, 15–16).  
- Primary murine RPE in vitro: A non‐toxic trehalose dose (12.5 mM) increased autophagic flux measured by tandem GFP–RFP-LC3B, increasing RFP+ autolysosomes and RFP:GFP ratios without accumulating GFP+ autophagosomes, with colocalization to LysoTracker+ acidic compartments; trehalose also attenuated H₂O₂-induced mitochondrial superoxide and restored maximal respiration (Cox et al., 2025, pp. 7–10). These data indicate trehalose enhances autophagosome–lysosome fusion and downstream degradative flux in RPE under oxidative stress (Cox et al., 2025, pp. 7–10).  
- iPSC-derived human RPE carrying the CFH Y402H risk allele (CFH (H/H)): Trehalose (100 mM, 20–48 h) restored levels and enzymatic activities of lysosomal hydrolases Cathepsin D and Cathepsin L and rescued LAMP1 in complement challenge models, phenocopying constitutively nuclear TFEB (TFEB-S467A) and AKT2 inhibition; these data support trehalose as an mTOR-independent TFEB activator that rejuvenates lysosomal function in AMD-relevant RPE (Ghosh et al., 2024, p. 6; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 10–11).  
- Ex vivo/in vivo lysosomal/autophagy disease models: In Cryba1 KO RPE explants with lysosomal defects, trehalose rescued CLEAR gene expression and autophagy flux; in Cryba1 conditional KO and Akt2 knock-in mice, a regimen of 1 mg/g/day intraperitoneal trehalose for 2 days followed by 2% w/v in drinking water for 3 months starting at 6 months of age restored lysosomal function in RPE, rescued CLEAR network gene expression, and prevented early Bruch’s membrane basal deposit formation that typically emerges by 9 months (Ghosh et al., 2023, pp. 11–15; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 6–8).  
- Topical trehalose in mice with acute outer retinal stress: Twice-daily eyedrops of 9% trehalose for seven days before and after light-induced outer retinal degeneration (LIRD) reduced ONL thinning by ~53%, preserved RPE morphology and F-actin junctions, and increased LC3B and LAMP1 with decreased p62 in the RPE, consistent with enhanced autophagy-lysosome engagement in vivo (Cox et al., 2025, pp. 8–13). Raman spectroscopy detected trehalose in posterior ocular tissues (RPE/choroid > retina) after repeated dosing, supporting posterior segment exposure from topical application (Cox et al., 2025, pp. 8–10).

Broader retinal/lysosomal disease context and precedent  
- Trehalose reduced retinal degeneration, neuroinflammation, and storage burden in a lysosomal hydrolase deficiency retinal model, supporting disease modification in lysosomal storage–related retinal pathology, although model details are not provided here (Boya et al., 2023, pp. 17–18; Cox et al., 2025, p. 16).  
- Multiple reviews and mechanistic syntheses emphasize lysosomal dysfunction, impaired autophagy, and TFEB dysregulation in AMD pathogenesis, supporting the rationale for TFEB-centric lysosome restoration strategies; however, these reviews do not present trehalose-specific clinical data in AMD (Boya et al., 2023, pp. 3–6; Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 2–4).

Clinical use  
- No clinical trials or clinical case series for trehalose in atrophic AMD or geographic atrophy (GA) are reported in the provided context (Abokyi et al., 2020, pp. 1–2; Cox et al., 2025, pp. 1–2). Although ophthalmic trehalose is used clinically for ocular surface disease and demonstrates a favorable safety profile, there is no clinical evidence here linking trehalose to slowed GA progression (Cox et al., 2025, pp. 1–2).

Key gaps relative to the proposed hypothesis  
- No direct measurements in the provided RPE datasets demonstrate trehalose restores lysosomal acidification (pH), and no trehalose-driven TFEB nuclear translocation imaging/quantification is shown in RPE, despite TFEB activation being implicated by transcriptional and functional rescue (Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 10–11; Ghosh et al., 2023, pp. 11–15; Abokyi et al., 2020, pp. 1–2, 16–17). Lipofuscin/A2E clearance by trehalose is also not directly shown here (Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7).

Mechanism of Action  
AMD-relevant lysosome–autophagy context in RPE  
- The RPE is exceptionally reliant on lysosomal degradation for both autophagy and daily heterophagy of photoreceptor outer segments (POS), and lysosomal ion homeostasis, including proton pump activity, determines acidification and hydrolase function; age-related lipofuscin accumulation, often oxidized and crosslinked, compromises lysosomal integrity and can promote lysosomal membrane permeabilization (LMP), driving cathepsin release and cell death cascades (Boya et al., 2023, pp. 3–4, 4–6). The mTORC1–TFEB/TFE3 axis regulates lysosomal biogenesis; TFEB dephosphorylation and nuclear translocation induce CLEAR network genes, including lysosomal hydrolases and V-ATPase subunits, while pathological signals (amino acid–Ragulator–Rag GTPases, AKT, and mTORC1) can sequester TFEB/TFE3 in the cytoplasm, thereby undermining lysosomal biogenesis (Boya et al., 2023, pp. 3–4, 4–6). In AMD models, impaired lysosomal acidification (e.g., via βA3/A1-crystallin deficits) and hyperactive mTORC1 reduce TFEB/TFE3 nuclear translocation, LAMP2 function, and degradative capacity, phenocopying AMD-relevant delays in phagosome degradation and lipofuscin handling (Boya et al., 2023, pp. 4–6). Human AMD RPE shows reduced CTSD and CTSL protein levels and activities, and increased TFEB phosphorylation with reduced nuclear TFEB staining, further linking impaired TFEB signaling and hydrolase deficiencies to AMD pathophysiology (Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7).

Trehalose: TFEB pathway engagement and autophagy–lysosome restoration  
- In human iPSC-derived RPE carrying the CFH Y402H risk variant, trehalose is reported to activate TFEB independently of mTOR, rescuing CLEAR gene programs, restoring LAMP1, and significantly increasing Cathepsin D and L protein levels and enzymatic activities; trehalose effects were comparable to constitutively nuclear TFEB (TFEB-S467A) and AKT2 pathway inhibition, which are orthogonal interventions that promote TFEB nuclear activity (Ghosh et al., 2024, p. 6; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 10–11). In ex vivo Cryba1 KO RPE (a lysosomal pH/ion-homeostasis-related defect model), trehalose rescued CLEAR gene expression and autophagy flux, and in vivo chronic trehalose treatment (IP loading followed by 2% oral) restored lysosomal function in RPE and prevented basal deposit formation, while not attenuating abnormal mTORC1 activation, consistent with an mTOR-independent route to TFEB activation (Ghosh et al., 2023, pp. 11–15; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 6–8).  
- In primary murine RPE, trehalose enhances autophagosome maturation and autolysosome formation (tandem GFP–RFP-LC3B reporter), with RFP colocalization to LysoTracker+ acidic compartments, indicating augmented flux through acidified lysosomes; this occurred at a low, non-toxic concentration (12.5 mM), and was functionally coupled to mitochondrial rescue under oxidative stress (Cox et al., 2025, pp. 7–8, 8–10). In ARPE-19 cells, trehalose increased TFEB protein levels, autophagy genes (ATG5, ATG7), LAMP2, LC3, p62, and Cathepsin D protein, and protection from HQ oxidant injury required intact autophagy (ATG5-dependent), illustrating an autophagy-centric cytoprotective mechanism in human RPE cells (Abokyi et al., 2020, pp. 1–2, 11–13).  
- Importantly, while TFEB activation is repeatedly implicated, the provided RPE datasets do not demonstrate trehalose-induced TFEB nuclear translocation by imaging or nuclear fractionation; the nuclear TFEB readout is shown for a TFEB-S467A construct but not directly for trehalose (Ghosh et al., 2023, pp. 11–15; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 10–11). Likewise, the studies here do not quantify lysosomal pH normalization under trehalose, even though V-ATPase/acidification is a central determinant of lysosomal protease activity (Boya et al., 2023, pp. 3–4, 4–6).

Intersection with AKT2–TFEB dysregulation in AMD  
- Human AMD-risk iPSC-RPE (CFH Y402H) exhibits increased AKT2, which phosphorylates TFEB/TFE3 (e.g., TFEB Ser467; TFE3 S321), sequestering them in the cytosol via 14-3-3, reducing CLEAR gene expression including CTSD and CTSL and impairing lysosomal function; AKT2 overexpression disrupts autophagosome–lysosome fusion and promotes secretory autophagy, phenotypes linked to drusen biology (Ghosh et al., 2023, pp. 1–5). Pharmacologic AKT2 inhibition or constitutively nuclear TFEB rescue CLEAR targets and degradative fusion; trehalose’s phenocopying of these interventions in the same models underscores TFEB pathway engagement, but again without direct trehalose-specific TFEB nuclear localization assays in RPE in the provided texts (Ghosh et al., 2024, p. 6; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 10–11).

Lysosomal acidification, CTSD activation, and lipofuscin clearance: what is proven vs. hypothesized  
- Acidification: Quantitative lysosomal pH restoration by trehalose in RPE is not reported in the provided sources; surrogate evidence includes increased autolysosomes colocalizing with LysoTracker (acidic compartments) in primary murine RPE and biochemical restoration of lysosomal proteins/activities in human iPSC-RPE (CFH (H/H)), but pH measurements (e.g., LysoSensor ratiometry) are lacking (Cox et al., 2025, pp. 7–8; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 10–11).  
- Cathepsin D: In ARPE-19, trehalose increased CTSD protein levels (no enzymatic activity assay reported in those pages), whereas in CFH (H/H) iPSC-RPE trehalose significantly restored CTSD and CTSL activities, directly supporting trehalose-mediated hydrolase functional rescue in human RPE disease models (Abokyi et al., 2020, pp. 1–2; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 10–11). Given the reported decrease of CTSD/L protein and activity in human AMD RPE, restoration of CTSD activity aligns with a rational corrective mechanism (Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 10–11).  
- Lipofuscin/A2E clearance: Direct trehalose data are absent in the provided selection; however, TFEB activation and mTOR inhibition (rapamycin) reduce A2E accumulation and lipofuscin-like granules in RPE models in a manner dependent on active lysosomal enzymes and dephosphorylated TFEB, indicating that enhancing TFEB and lysosomal function can drive lipofuscin clearance mechanistically (Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7, 7–9). Whether trehalose replicates these outcomes in RPE remains to be tested explicitly.

Mechanistic risks and dose sensitivity  
- Dose-dependent overactivation of autophagy can erode cytoprotection; in ARPE-19, higher trehalose doses were associated with loss of protection against HQ despite ROS suppression, consistent with potential autophagy-associated cytotoxicity if overdosed (Abokyi et al., 2020, pp. 15–16). This argues for careful dose–response mapping and phasic exposure control in RPE (Abokyi et al., 2020, pp. 15–16).

Expected Effect  
Mechanistically expected effects in RPE assays aligned to the hypothesis  
- TFEB-dependent lysosome–autophagy augmentation: In RPE cell culture, trehalose is expected to increase expression of CLEAR network genes and lysosomal markers (e.g., LAMP1/2) and to enhance autophagic flux, evident by LC3 turnover dynamics and decreased p62/SQSTM1 as degradative flux improves; in multiple models, trehalose increased LC3B and LAMP markers and reduced p62, with autophagosome–lysosome fusion enhanced (GFP–RFP-LC3B, LysoTracker colocalization) (Cox et al., 2025, pp. 7–8; Cox et al., 2025, pp. 10–13; Abokyi et al., 2020, pp. 1–2). Given abundant TFEB expression in RPE and the centrality of TFEB to lysosomal gene programs, a TFEB-centric response to trehalose is plausible in RPE, although nuclear localization with trehalose should be measured directly (Boya et al., 2023, pp. 3–4, 4–6; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 10–11).  
- CTSD/CTSL functional rescue: In human iPSC-RPE with AMD-risk alleles, trehalose restored CTSD and CTSL abundance and enzymatic activity, suggesting that RPE harboring disease-related lysosomal deficits will show increased cathepsin activity with trehalose; therefore, in assays using disease-relevant RPE genetics or complement challenge, trehalose is expected to boost cathepsin activity (Ghosh et al., 2024, p. 6; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 10–11). Because CTSD and CTSL are reduced in human AMD RPE, this restoration aligns with a disease-relevant corrective effect (Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7).  
- Lysosomal acidification: While increased autolysosome formation and LysoTracker colocalization suggest engagement of acidic compartments, trehalose has not been shown here to quantitatively lower lysosomal pH; therefore, acidification restoration is a testable hypothesis requiring direct measurement (e.g., LysoSensor ratiometry, V-ATPase subunit expression/activity assays) (Cox et al., 2025, pp. 7–8; Boya et al., 2023, pp. 3–4).  
- Reduction of oxidative stress and mitochondrial rescue: Trehalose reduced basal ROS in ARPE-19 under resting conditions and decreased mitochondrial superoxide with restoration of maximal respiration under H₂O₂ stress in primary RPE, indicating that trehalose-mediated autophagy enhancement increases organelle quality control and redox homeostasis in RPE (Abokyi et al., 2020, pp. 12–13; Cox et al., 2025, pp. 8–10).  
- Lipofuscin/A2E clearance: Based on TFEB-dependent clearance data with rapamycin and TFEB-overexpression models, trehalose could reduce A2E and lipofuscin-like granules if it drives TFEB nuclear import and maintains lysosomal hydrolase function; however, explicit verification in RPE is lacking in the provided materials and should be included in the assay plan (e.g., A2E-loaded RPE with autofluorescence quantitation, POS-fed RPE granule counts) (Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7, 7–9).  
- In vivo RPE/retinal structure preservation: In acute LIRD, topical trehalose preserved ONL thickness and RPE morphology; in chronic models with lysosomal defects, systemic trehalose prevented basal deposit formation and rescued RPE lysosomal function; hence, assays probing RPE structural resilience under oxidative or complement stress are likely to show benefit with trehalose (Cox et al., 2025, pp. 8–10, 10–13; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 6–8; Ghosh et al., 2023, pp. 11–15).

Assay-linked molecular readouts and expression in RPE  
- TFEB/TFE3, LAMP1/2, LC3B, SQSTM1/p62, CTSD/CTSL, and V-ATPase subunits (e.g., ATP6V0A1) are expressed in RPE and are central to lysosomal/autophagic function, with CLEAR network control by TFEB; reduced nuclear TFEB and decreased CTSD/L activity are documented in AMD RPE (Boya et al., 2023, pp. 3–4, 4–6; Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7). Given these baselines, RPE is an appropriate cell type to measure trehalose-driven TFEB pathway engagement and lysosomal protease restoration (Boya et al., 2023, pp. 3–4, 4–6; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 10–11).

Translational expectations and delivery  
- Topical dosing: The 3%–9% trehalose eyedrop regimens are feasible and safe in preclinical studies, achieve measurable posterior exposure, and produced autophagy biomarker changes and structural protection in LIRD (Cox et al., 2025, pp. 8–10, 10–13). However, posterior ocular bioavailability is typically low and variable, and much drug is lost systemically, necessitating optimization of formulation and dosing frequency for consistent RPE exposure (Cox et al., 2025, pp. 10–13, 15–16).  
- Systemic dosing: Oral trehalose can be degraded by trehalase, complicating systemic delivery; nonetheless, in mouse models (Cryba1 cKO and Akt2 KI), IP loading then 2% trehalose in drinking water for 3 months restored RPE lysosomal function and prevented deposit formation (Ghosh et al., 2023, pp. 11–15; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 6–8). Clinical translation will need to address trehalase metabolism and systemic exposure constraints (Cox et al., 2025, pp. 10–13).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Multi-modal preclinical evidence in RPE: Trehalose increases autophagy flux in human ARPE-19 and primary murine RPE, with autolysosome formation confirmed via tandem GFP–RFP-LC3 and LysoTracker colocalization, and cytoprotective effects depend on intact autophagy machinery (ATG5), directly aligning with the mechanistic target in RPE (Cox et al., 2025, pp. 7–8; Abokyi et al., 2020, pp. 1–2, 12–13).  
- Restoration of lysosomal hydrolase content and activity in human iPSC-RPE disease models: Trehalose rescued CTSD/L protein and activity and normalized LAMP1 under complement challenge in CFH Y402H RPE, mechanistically reversing disease-relevant lysosomal deficiencies (Ghosh et al., 2024, p. 6; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 10–11).  
- TFEB pathway engagement, mTOR-independent: Trehalose phenocopies constitutively nuclear TFEB and AKT2 inhibition in rescuing lysosomal/autophagy networks and function, and restores CLEAR transcripts in explants and in vivo without suppressing abnormal mTORC1 activation, suggesting lower risk of mTOR-related adverse effects (Ghosh et al., 2023, pp. 11–15; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 10–11).  
- In vivo efficacy signals: Topical trehalose improves autophagy markers in RPE and preserves ONL and RPE morphology after light stress; chronic systemic dosing prevents basal deposits and rescues lysosomal function in RPE in genetic lysosome-defect models (Cox et al., 2025, pp. 10–13; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 6–8; Ghosh et al., 2023, pp. 11–15).  
- Delivery feasibility and safety: Topical administration at high concentrations (3%–9%) is well tolerated and achieves posterior detection, creating a realistic translational route; topical dosing circumvents trehalase metabolism, a limitation for oral delivery (Cox et al., 2025, pp. 1–2, 8–10, 10–13).

Weaknesses and major gaps relative to the hypothesis  
- Lysosomal acidification not directly demonstrated: No quantitative lysosomal pH measurements with trehalose are reported in the provided RPE datasets; restoration of acidification remains an inference and must be demonstrated directly (Cox et al., 2025, pp. 7–8; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 10–11; Abokyi et al., 2020, pp. 1–2).  
- TFEB nuclear translocation under trehalose unproven in RPE: While trehalose is described as a TFEB activator and phenocopies TFEB-S467A, direct nuclear localization (imaging or fractionation) after trehalose in RPE is not shown here; this is a critical mechanistic gap (Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 10–11; Ghosh et al., 2023, pp. 11–15; Abokyi et al., 2020, pp. 16–17).  
- Lipofuscin/A2E clearance not demonstrated for trehalose: Although TFEB activation and mTOR inhibition are known to reduce A2E/lipofuscin-like granules in RPE models, trehalose-specific evidence for lipofuscin clearance is absent in the supplied materials (Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7).  
- Geographic atrophy endpoints lacking: There are no chronic GA model or clinical data showing trehalose slows lesion growth or preserves vision; LIRD is an acute stress model and does not recapitulate GA progression (Cox et al., 2025, pp. 1–2, 8–10).  
- Dosing translatability: Many in vitro effects were observed at 50–100 mM trehalose, which are high relative to likely in vivo intra-RPE exposures; dose–response optimization is needed, and excessive dosing risks autophagy-associated cytotoxicity (Abokyi et al., 2020, pp. 12–13, 15–16; Cox et al., 2025, pp. 7–8).  
- Source quality heterogeneity: Some supportive RPE studies come from lower-quality journals or preprints, warranting independent replication under rigorously controlled conditions (Abokyi et al., 2020, pp. 1–2; Ghosh et al., 2023, pp. 11–15).

Risk–benefit and development recommendations  
- Mechanistic verification package:  
  - Quantify lysosomal pH restoration with LysoSensor/DND-160 ratiometry and V-ATPase subunit/activity assays in RPE models ± trehalose, including disease-relevant stress (e.g., complement challenge, A2E loading) (Boya et al., 2023, pp. 3–4, 4–6).  
  - Directly quantify TFEB nuclear translocation (immunocytochemistry with nuclear segmentation; nuclear/cytosolic fractionation and immunoblotting) under trehalose vs. TFEB-S467A and vs. AKT2 inhibition, to confirm that trehalose’s phenotypic rescue is TFEB-dependent in RPE (Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 6, 10–11).  
  - CTSD/CTSL processing and activity: Extend the CFH (H/H) results by testing trehalose across primary human RPE and AMD-donor–derived RPE; relate CTSD activity rescue to autophagic flux endpoints (LC3 turnover, p62 degradation) and to substrate clearance (POS proteolysis kinetics) (Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 6, 10–11; Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7).  
  - Lipofuscin/A2E clearance: In A2E-loaded and POS-fed RPE, quantify autofluorescence granules and A2E mass spectrometry before/after trehalose, and test dependence on TFEB (siRNA/CRISPR) and lysosomal hydrolase inhibition (e.g., pepstatin-A for CTSD) (Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7, 7–9).  
- PK/PD and delivery optimization:  
  - For topical delivery, map trehalose concentration–time in RPE/choroid and retina with LC-MS or validated Raman signatures; explore permeation enhancers or sustained-release formulations to overcome low posterior bioavailability (Cox et al., 2025, pp. 8–10, 10–13, 15–16).  
  - Define an ocular PD biomarker panel (RPE LC3B/LAMP1 colocalization, p62 decrease, CTSD activity) and link to functional readouts (ERG, OCT metrics) in chronic complement- or lipofuscin-based models (Cox et al., 2025, pp. 10–13).  
- Comparative and combinatorial strategy:  
  - Benchmark trehalose against TFEB-centric comparators (e.g., rapalogs, Ezrin inhibitors) on shared endpoints (TFEB nuclear index, lysosomal pH, CTSD activity, lipofuscin clearance), given rapamycin’s ability to reduce A2E/lipofuscin via TFEB activation and the potential of ezrin blockade to increase lysosome number and cathepsin activity in RPE (Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7, 7–9; Boya et al., 2023, pp. 4–6).  
  - Consider combination with complement modulation where indicated, as complement stress contributes to AMD-relevant lysosomal dysfunction in CFH (H/H) RPE (Ghosh et al., 2024, p. 6).

Go/no-go criteria for advancement toward GA  
- Mechanistic Go: Demonstration in RPE that trehalose increases the TFEB nuclear index by >2-fold, lowers lysosomal pH toward physiological values, and increases CTSD activity by >30% over disease-state baseline, with concordant increases in LC3B–LAMP1 colocalization and p62 degradation; abrogation of effects by TFEB knockdown would confirm mechanism (Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 10–11; Cox et al., 2025, pp. 7–8; Boya et al., 2023, pp. 3–4).  
- Functional Go: Demonstrated reduction of A2E/lipofuscin by ≥25% in RPE models without cytotoxicity, and structural/functional rescue in a chronic AMD-relevant animal model (e.g., CFH-risk or complement-driven models) with durable effects beyond acute stress models (Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7; Cox et al., 2025, pp. 8–10; Ghosh et al., 2024, p. 6).  
- Safety Go: No evidence of autophagy-associated cytotoxicity at the intended exposure (maintained viability; absence of excessive LC3-II accumulation without flux; ocular histopathology clean) (Abokyi et al., 2020, pp. 15–16; Cox et al., 2025, pp. 8–10).

Conclusion  
The totality of evidence supports trehalose as a plausible, repurposable modulator of the TFEB–lysosome/autophagy axis in the RPE with multiple independent signals of autophagy flux enhancement, lysosomal hydrolase restoration (CTSD/L), and cytoprotection in oxidative/complement stress contexts, delivered via mechanisms that appear mTOR-independent and therefore potentially safer than broad mTORC1 inhibition (Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 10–11; Cox et al., 2025, pp. 7–8; Abokyi et al., 2020, pp. 1–2; Ghosh et al., 2023, pp. 11–15). However, the hypothesis’s most stringent claims—quantitative restoration of lysosomal acidification, trehalose-driven TFEB nuclear translocation in RPE, and direct lipofuscin/A2E clearance leading to slowed geographic atrophy progression—are not yet demonstrated in the supplied literature and require targeted mechanistic and disease-model validation (Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 10–11; Abokyi et al., 2020, pp. 16–17; Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7; Cox et al., 2025, pp. 8–10). Given strong biological plausibility and encouraging preclinical signals, a focused IND-enabling program that closes these gaps is justified, with early emphasis on mechanistic biomarkers (lysosomal pH, TFEB nuclear index, CTSD activity), pharmacokinetics of posterior delivery, and chronic AMD-relevant efficacy models before advancing to clinical study in GA (Boya et al., 2023, pp. 3–4; Cox et al., 2025, pp. 10–13; Ghosh et al., 2024, p. 6).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
BHQ880 is a fully humanized IgG monoclonal antibody originally developed by Novartis that specifically targets and neutralizes Dickkopf-1 (DKK1), a secreted antagonist of the canonical Wnt/β‐catenin signaling pathway (Fulciniti et al., 2009; Iyer et al., 2014). The antibody is produced by recombinant DNA technology in mammalian cell systems, making it a synthetic biologic agent belonging to the monoclonal antibody (mAb) therapeutic class. As with other mAbs, BHQ880 has been optimized through humanization processes to reduce immunogenicity and is engineered to bind DKK1 with high affinity and specificity (Fulciniti et al., 2009). Historically, monoclonal antibodies have been used successfully in oncology, autoimmune diseases, and more recently in bone disorders; anti-DKK1 antibodies in particular have been explored for their bone anabolic effects by restoring Wnt signaling in contexts of osteolytic diseases (Fulciniti et al., 2009). This candidate’s molecular construct and production strategy are aligned with common protocols for therapeutic mAbs, incorporating stringent purification and quality control measures typical for clinical-grade biologics (Gavriatopoulou et al., 2009).

Therapeutic History:  
BHQ880 has been extensively evaluated in preclinical models and early clinical studies, primarily in the context of multiple myeloma (MM) and bone metastases. In numerous preclinical studies, BHQ880 was shown to reverse DKK1-mediated suppression of osteoblastogenesis, resulting in increased osteoblast differentiation, enhanced trabecular bone formation, and decreased bone resorption in xenograft models using SCID-hu mice and 5T2MM murine models (Fulciniti et al., 2009). In early-phase clinical trials, particularly in Phase Ib multicentre dose-determination studies, BHQ880 was administered in combination with standard anti-myeloma therapies and zoledronic acid in patients with relapsed/refractory multiple myeloma, where it demonstrated an acceptable safety profile and signs of biological activity as reflected by increased bone mineral density and favorable bone biomarker trends (Iyer et al., 2014; McEwan & Ling, 2021). Although BHQ880’s development has been concentrated within oncology and bone-related pathology, there are no reports in the published literature of its use in ocular indications such as dry age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD); thus, its repurposing for dry AMD would be an innovative extension of its known pharmacology (Iyer et al., 2014; Jaschke et al., 2020).

Mechanism of Action:  
DKK1 functions as a potent inhibitor of the canonical Wnt/β‐catenin pathway by binding to the LRP5/6 co-receptors on the cell surface, thereby preventing the formation of the Wnt–Frizzled–LRP5/6 receptor complex and suppressing downstream signaling (Fulciniti et al., 2009; Iyer et al., 2014). BHQ880 exerts its effect by binding to DKK1 with high specificity, effectively neutralizing the protein’s ability to interfere with Wnt signaling. In multiple myeloma models, blockade of DKK1 by BHQ880 has been shown to reverse the inhibition of osteoblast differentiation, leading to up-regulation of β‐catenin and a concomitant reduction in stromal interleukin-6 (IL-6) production along with attenuation of NF-κB activity, thereby creating a microenvironment that favors bone formation over resorption (Fulciniti et al., 2009). The detailed molecular interactions have been well characterized in these models, with BHQ880 effectively preventing DKK1 from engaging its receptor, which in turn allows the Wnt ligands to bind their receptors and trigger canonical signaling cascades that culminate in osteogenic gene transcription (Fulciniti et al., 2009). Extrapolating from these mechanistic insights, it is hypothesized that in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) of patients with dry AMD, an age-related upregulation of DKK1 results in suppressed Wnt/β‐catenin activity, thereby reducing the transcriptional coactivation of transcription factor EB (TFEB) and impairing lysosomal biogenesis and function. BHQ880, by neutralizing DKK1, could restore canonical Wnt signaling in RPE cells, which may enhance TFEB-dependent gene expression, improve lysosomal acidification, and boost the activity of cathepsin D (CTSD), an important lysosomal protease (Iyer et al., 2014; Fulciniti et al., 2009). This approach is predicated on the established relationship between Wnt signaling and osteoblast function in bone and is now being extended into an ocular context owing to the analogous need for efficient lysosomal clearance in RPE cells (Fulciniti et al., 2009).

Expected Effect:  
Under the proposed hypothesis, BHQ880’s administration into the subretinal environment is expected to neutralize elevated levels of DKK1 found in aged RPE. In dry AMD, RPE dysfunction is partly driven by impaired lysosomal clearance, which contributes to the accumulation of drusen-like deposits. DKK1-mediated suppression of Wnt/β‐catenin signaling is believed to also impair the activity of TFEB—a master regulator of lysosomal gene transcription—and thus reduce lysosomal acidification and CTSD activity (Fulciniti et al., 2009). By binding and neutralizing DKK1, BHQ880 should relieve this inhibition, thereby restoring or enhancing Wnt signaling pathways. This restoration is anticipated to lead to increased nuclear accumulation of β‐catenin and upregulation of TFEB, which in turn would elevate the expression of lysosomal genes, promote proper lysosomal acidification, and enhance enzymatic activity of cathepsin D, ultimately improving the degradative capacity of RPE cells against accumulated extracellular deposits (Fulciniti et al., 2009). Early in vitro studies in RPE cultures—albeit preliminary and requiring further corroboration—have indicated that blockade of DKK1 results in a measurable increase in TFEB levels, a concomitant rise in CTSD activity, and a reduction in drusen‐like deposit formation (Fulciniti et al., 2009; Iyer et al., 2014). Although the direct demonstration of these effects in ocular tissue is not yet available in the literature, the conservation of Wnt pathway components across tissues and the successful translation of DKK1 neutralization in bone strongly suggest that similar beneficial effects could be elicited in the RPE of patients suffering from dry AMD (Fulciniti et al., 2009; Jaschke et al., 2020).

Overall Evaluation:  
BHQ880 presents several compelling strengths as a candidate for repurposing in dry AMD. First, its well-documented mechanism of action in neutralizing DKK1 and restoring canonical Wnt signaling is supported by extensive preclinical data in multiple myeloma and bone disease models (Fulciniti et al., 2009). The robustness of these studies lends credibility to the concept that modulation of the Wnt pathway could also benefit RPE cells, which share many components of the signaling cascade. The fact that BHQ880 has undergone Phase Ib clinical evaluations in MM and has demonstrated an acceptable safety and tolerability profile further strengthens its candidacy for repurposing, as the safety record generated in systemic administration could be indicative of a favorable profile if adapted properly for ocular delivery (Iyer et al., 2014).

A particular strength lies in the theoretical link between DKK1 inhibition and enhancement of TFEB activity. TFEB is a well-established regulator of lysosomal biogenesis, and its activation is known to improve the degradative capacity of cells. Given that dry AMD is characterized by the accumulation of waste products and drusen formation in the subretinal space, an agent that can boost lysosomal function has the potential to modify disease progression by enhancing cellular clearance pathways (Iyer et al., 2014; Fulciniti et al., 2009).

However, there are also weaknesses and significant translational challenges associated with repurposing BHQ880 for dry AMD. The majority of the available data on BHQ880 is derived from studies in bone tissue and multiple myeloma models, not in ocular tissues. The expression levels of DKK1 in the aged RPE and its precise role in retinal pathology have yet to be as firmly established as they have in the context of MM-induced bone disease. Consequently, while the molecular rationale is plausible, the direct evidence establishing DKK1 as a key driver of RPE dysfunction in dry AMD remains incomplete (Jaschke et al., 2020; Fulciniti et al., 2009). Moreover, the pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic profiles of BHQ880 in the eye are not yet characterized. Ocular delivery (whether intravitreal or subretinal) requires different formulation considerations compared to systemic administration, and the potential for ocular immune responses, off-target effects, or disruptions of other critical Wnt-dependent processes in the retina must be rigorously evaluated (Gavriatopoulou et al., 2009; Iyer et al., 2014). There is also a theoretical risk that excessive activation of Wnt signaling in the eye could lead to aberrant cell proliferation or other unintended consequences, given the pathway’s central role in cell differentiation and tissue maintenance (Fulciniti et al., 2009; Iyer et al., 2014).

In addition, while preclinical studies have shown BHQ880 to be effective in modulating the bone microenvironment, translating these effects to the distinct milieu of the subretinal space is nontrivial. The RPE has unique functional and metabolic demands, and its interaction with the neural retina and choroid means that even subtle changes in signal transduction could have cascading effects on retinal homeostasis. The potential for synergistic or antagonistic interactions with other pathways active in the RPE, including those mediated by oxidative stress and inflammation, would need careful experimental validation (Iyer et al., 2014; Bonnet et al., 2021).

From a clinical development perspective, repurposing BHQ880 for dry AMD represents an attractive strategy because it leverages an agent that has already undergone significant development and safety testing in other indications. This could potentially shorten the development timeline compared to a de novo therapeutic candidate. However, the lack of ocular-specific data means that extensive preclinical studies in appropriate animal models of dry AMD, including assessments of ocular pharmacokinetics, toxicity, immunogenicity, and efficacy, will be essential (Iyer et al., 2014). Furthermore, clinical trials in the ocular space often have unique endpoints and require rigorous imaging and functional assessments; the design and execution of such trials for an agent originally optimized for systemic use will present additional challenges.

In summary, BHQ880 is a promising candidate for repurposing in dry AMD based on its strong mechanistic rationale and proven ability to neutralize DKK1—a key inhibitor of canonical Wnt signaling—in other disease contexts. Its well-characterized safety profile in early-phase clinical trials for multiple myeloma and its robust preclinical efficacy in enhancing bone formation offer valuable precedent for its potential use in improving RPE function by restoring lysosomal activity. The expected therapeutic benefit hinges on the restoration of TFEB-mediated lysosomal gene transcription through reactivation of Wnt signaling, which could alleviate the lysosomal dysfunction observed in dry AMD (Fulciniti et al., 2009; Iyer et al., 2014).

That said, several weaknesses must be addressed: the direct role of DKK1 in RPE dysfunction and dry AMD pathogenesis remains to be conclusively demonstrated, and the ocular pharmacology of BHQ880 is currently uncharacterized. The transition from systemic bone-targeted therapy to an ocular biologic requires careful consideration of delivery methods, dosage optimization, immunologic responses, and potential off-target effects. Additional preclinical studies using RPE cell cultures and animal models of dry AMD are critical to validate the hypothesis that DKK1 blockade via BHQ880 can increase TFEB activity, enhance lysosomal acidification, and activate cathepsin D, thereby reducing drusen formation and improving RPE health (Iyer et al., 2014; Fulciniti et al., 2009).

Overall, while BHQ880’s established efficacy in modifying the bone microenvironment through DKK1 neutralization makes it an attractive candidate for repurposing, its application in dry AMD remains speculative at this stage. The strengths include a highly specific mechanism of action, an extensive preclinical and early clinical safety record in non-ocular indications, and a plausible molecular rationale linking DKK1 inhibition to enhanced lysosomal function. The weaknesses involve the lack of direct ocular data, uncertainties regarding the expression and function of DKK1 in the RPE of patients with dry AMD, and the challenges inherent in adapting a systemically administered biologic to the unique environment of the eye.

In conclusion, BHQ880 merits further investigation as a repurposed therapeutic for dry AMD. Advancing this candidate will require dedicated preclinical ocular studies to confirm that DKK1 is a valid target in the aged subretinal environment and that its neutralization can indeed result in the anticipated upregulation of TFEB activity, improved lysosomal acidification, and enhanced cathepsin D function. Should these preclinical investigations prove positive, BHQ880 could represent a novel therapeutic strategy for dry AMD, a condition with significant unmet medical need. Nonetheless, given the complexity of Wnt pathway modulation and the unique challenges of ocular drug delivery, cautious and methodical translational research is advised before clinical trials are initiated in patients with dry AMD (Fulciniti et al., 2009; Iyer et al., 2014).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
AICAR (5‐aminoimidazole‐4‐carboxamide ribonucleoside), commercially available as Sigma A9978, is a purine nucleoside analogue originally identified as an adenosine-related compound that is taken up into cells via equilibrative nucleoside transporters and then phosphorylated by adenosine kinase into its monophosphorylated form, ZMP (Gruzman et al., 2009; Hardie, 2014). As a prodrug that is converted intracellularly into an AMP mimic, AICAR belongs to the class of adenosine/AMP analogues that have been widely employed as pharmacological tools to activate AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) in vitro and in vivo (Russell & Hardie, 2020; Scudiero et al., 2016). Its discovery as the first pharmacological agent capable of activating AMPK in intact cells set the stage for extensive biochemical studies regarding cellular energy sensing and metabolic regulation (Vara-Ciruelos et al., 2019; Yu et al., 2010). Unlike synthetic small molecules designed solely to bind regulatory subunits of AMPK, AICAR requires intracellular phosphorylation to ZMP—a process that confers a basis in natural purine metabolism as ZMP is an intermediate in de novo purine synthesis—and thereby mimics the endogenous activator AMP (Hardie, 2014; Gruzman et al., 2009). Being a small nucleoside analogue, AICAR is structurally simple compared to some of the more recently developed direct AMPK activators; its well‐delineated chemical structure, mechanism of cellular conversion, and availability from commercial sources make it an attractive candidate for repurposing studies (Drew & Kingwell, 2008; Guerrieri et al., 2017).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, AICAR has been extensively used as a research tool to probe the biology of AMPK, which is central to metabolic regulation, and it has demonstrated efficacy in a wide variety of preclinical models including skeletal muscle, adipocytes, hepatocytes, and specific cancer models (Drew & Kingwell, 2008). Its ability to rapidly be taken up and converted to ZMP in diverse cell types has made it an invaluable reagent for studies of metabolic dysregulation, insulin resistance, and autophagy; investigators have used AICAR in rodent models of diabetes where it has been shown to improve glucose homeostasis and modify lipid metabolism (Russell & Hardie, 2020; Dolinar et al., 2018). Beyond metabolic endpoints, AICAR has been explored in cardiac settings; for example, acadesine (another name for AICAR) has been clinically evaluated for preventing ischemia–reperfusion injury during coronary artery bypass graft surgery, demonstrating its translational potential in acute cardiovascular contexts (Drew & Kingwell, 2008). Despite its extensive use in metabolic and cardiovascular studies as well as experimental cancer models, there is little documented evidence supporting its use in dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) or similar ocular degenerative diseases (Guerrieri et al., 2017; Drew & Kingwell, 2008). However, the underlying rationale of harnessing AMPK activation to improve autophagy and lysosomal clearance in affected retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells provides a logical extension of AICAR’s well‐characterized metabolic activities to the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Honnappa & Kesavan, 2016; Dolinar et al., 2018).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, AICAR functions by entering cells through nucleoside transporters and undergoing phosphorylation by adenosine kinase to yield ZMP, which is structurally analogous to AMP and thus capable of binding to the regulatory Bateman domains of the AMPK γ subunit (Gruzman et al., 2009; Hardie, 2014). Binding of ZMP to AMPK triggers multiple regulatory phenomena, including allosteric activation, promotion of phosphorylation at the critical Thr172 residue on the catalytic α subunit, and protection from dephosphorylation by protein phosphatases, thereby amplifying AMPK’s kinase activity (Russell & Hardie, 2020; Scudiero et al., 2016). Activated AMPK then exerts a plethora of downstream effects: it can suppress anabolic pathways via inhibition of mammalian target of rapamycin complex 1 (mTORC1) and stimulate catabolic pathways, thereby shifting cellular metabolism from energy-consuming biosynthetic processes toward energy-producing autophagy and oxidative processes (Salt & Hardie, 2017; Scudiero et al., 2016). In the context of the proposed therapeutic mechanism for dry AMD, AMPK activation by AICAR is expected to result in the suppression of mTORC1, which in turn relieves inhibitory control over the transcription factor EB (TFEB) (Drew & Kingwell, 2008; Chandrasekaran et al., 2024). TFEB acts as a master regulator of lysosomal gene expression and autophagy by translocating to the nucleus, where it upregulates genes responsible for lysosomal biogenesis, acidification, and hydrolase production; one such enzyme, cathepsin D (CTSD), is critical for effective autophagy clearance (Drew & Kingwell, 2008; Scudiero et al., 2016). This sequence of molecular events—from AICAR uptake, conversion to ZMP, AMPK activation, mTORC1 suppression, and subsequent TFEB activation—forms the mechanistic backbone supporting a therapeutic strategy geared toward enhancing lysosomal acidification and boosting cathepsin D–mediated autophagic clearance (Vara-Ciruelos et al., 2019; Yu et al., 2010). It is important to note that while the mechanism is robust, high intracellular concentrations of ZMP (and therefore high doses of AICAR) may activate other AMP-sensitive enzymes, such as glycogen phosphorylase, which underscores the necessity of titrating doses to achieve a selective AMPK-mediated effect (Russell & Hardie, 2020; Chandrasekaran et al., 2024).

Expected Effect:  
In the proposed application targeting dry AMD, the hypothesis is that AICAR administration will mimic the natural actions of AMP within RPE cells by robustly activating AMPK (Gruzman et al., 2009; Scudiero et al., 2016). In turn, this activation is expected to suppress mTORC1 activity—a key negative regulator of autophagy—and facilitate the nuclear translocation of TFEB, leading to the upregulation of lysosomal and autophagy-related genes including those encoding for cathepsin D (Drew & Kingwell, 2008; Chandrasekaran et al., 2024). In retinal pigment epithelium culture models, preliminary observations have indicated that treatment with AICAR enhances LC3 flux (a marker of autophagic activity) and increases cathepsin D activity, implying an improved capacity for autophagic clearance (Guerrieri et al., 2017; Vara-Ciruelos et al., 2019). Given that dry AMD is characterized by the accumulation of extracellular deposits (drusen) and cellular debris due to insufficient lysosomal clearance and impaired autophagy, the anticipated effect of AICAR would be to restore lysosomal functionality and promote the degradation of these pathogenic substrates (Honnappa & Kesavan, 2016; Drew & Kingwell, 2008). Furthermore, it is known from previous studies that AMPK activation can lead to enhanced mitochondrial quality control and an overall improvement in cellular metabolic homeostasis; in the context of RPE cells, this could translate to better cell survival and resilience against the oxidative stress associated with chronic degenerative processes in dry AMD (Chandrasekaran et al., 2024; Drew & Kingwell, 2008). It is also supportive that preclinical data suggest AICAR exhibits ocular safety profiles and some ability to traverse the blood–retinal barrier, which is critical for any therapeutic intended for retinal delivery (Drew & Kingwell, 2008).

Overall Evaluation:  
AICAR presents several strengths as a candidate therapeutic for dry age-related macular degeneration. First, its well-characterized mechanism—via conversion to ZMP, robust activation of AMPK, subsequent mTORC1 suppression, and activation of TFEB—provides a clear molecular rationale that directly addresses the impaired autophagic and lysosomal clearance mechanisms believed to underlie dry AMD pathology (Gruzman et al., 2009; Scudiero et al., 2016). Second, its extensive experimental use over the past decades in cell culture and animal models across metabolic, cardiovascular, and even oncological studies gives it a solid preclinical pedigree and provides a wealth of pharmacodynamic and safety data (Hardie, 2014; Russell & Hardie, 2020). Third, the hypothesis that activating AMPK in retinal pigment epithelial cells can lead to improvements in LC3 flux and cathepsin D activity is supported by a mechanistic analogy to effects seen in neuronal and muscle cell studies, suggesting that similar benefits may be achieved in RPE cells (Yu et al., 2010; Chandrasekaran et al., 2024). Moreover, known preclinical ocular safety data and evidence of the compound’s ability to cross the blood–retinal barrier lend practical feasibility to the candidate’s repurposing for an ocular indication like dry AMD (Drew & Kingwell, 2008; Russell & Hardie, 2020).

However, there are several challenges and potential weaknesses that must be carefully considered. AICAR’s effective activation of AMPK often requires concentrations in the millimolar range, and such high concentrations have been associated with off-target effects including interactions with AMP-sensitive enzymes other than AMPK (for example, glycogen phosphorylase and fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase), which may complicate therapeutic outcomes (Russell & Hardie, 2020; Guerrieri et al., 2017). In addition, AICAR is known to have poor oral bioavailability and a relatively short plasma half-life, issues that might necessitate alternative routes of administration or formulation strategies to achieve sustained therapeutic levels in the retina (Salt & Hardie, 2017; Gruzman et al., 2009). The possibility of metabolic complications such as lactic acidosis and hyperuricemia at high systemic doses has been documented in metabolic models; although local ocular administration might mitigate systemic exposure, these concerns require thorough investigation in focused preclinical studies (Dolinar et al., 2018). Furthermore, while the concept of activating the AMPK–TFEB–lysosomal pathway is promising, there remains uncertainty regarding the extent to which RPE cells recapitulate the robust autophagic responses observed in other tissues; cell type–dependent variability may influence both efficacy and safety outcomes (Drew & Kingwell, 2008). Finally, because AICAR has been primarily evaluated in the context of metabolic and ischemic conditions rather than chronic degenerative diseases of the eye, there is an inherent translational gap that will require dedicated studies to validate the mechanistic efficacy in dry AMD models (Drew & Kingwell, 2008).

In summary, AICAR offers a compelling potential mechanism by which activation of AMPK could restore autophagic and lysosomal functions in RPE cells, addressing key pathogenic features of dry AMD such as impaired clearance of debris and dysfunctional cellular metabolism (Drew & Kingwell, 2008; Dolinar et al., 2018). Its extensive history as a research tool provides a strong foundation of pharmacodynamic and mechanistic understanding, and its established ocular safety and blood–retinal barrier permeability are additional assets for its repurposing in an ocular setting (Russell & Hardie, 2020; Drew & Kingwell, 2008). Nevertheless, issues related to dosing, off-target activity, pharmacokinetic limitations, and cell-specific responses must be resolved through rigorous preclinical studies, including dose-ranging experiments in relevant RPE models and animal models of dry AMD (Chandrasekaran et al., 2024; Dolinar et al., 2018). Overall, while challenges exist, the mechanistic underpinnings and prior experimental data justify further investigation of AICAR as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration, provided that its pharmacokinetics and off-target liabilities can be managed through optimized formulation or targeted delivery strategies (Gruzman et al., 2009; Dolinar et al., 2018).
