Below is a detailed evaluation of MK-2206 as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD), structured into five sections.

─────────────────────────────  
Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
─────────────────────────────  
MK-2206 is a synthetically derived, orally bioavailable small‐molecule inhibitor that functions as an allosteric modulator of the serine/threonine kinase AKT. Unlike classical ATP‐competitive agents, MK-2206 binds to an allosteric site outside the catalytic pocket, thereby altering the conformation of AKT and preventing its full activation. Originally discovered and optimized for oncological indications, its development was driven by the need to inhibit aberrant AKT signaling observed in multiple cancers. The compound belongs to a class of drugs known as allosteric AKT inhibitors, which historically have been explored for their ability to modulate critical intracellular signaling pathways that govern cellular proliferation, survival, and metabolism. More specifically, MK-2206 has been demonstrated in vitro to reduce the phosphorylation of AKT at key regulatory residues (for example, S473) in multiple cell types, including primary retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cultures where its application at 1 μM for 24 hours was shown to inhibit AKT phosphorylation and promote nuclear translocation of TFEB (Transcription Factor EB) – the master regulator of lysosomal gene expression (Karim et al., 2020). Although the detailed synthetic route is not fully delineated within our context, the compound has been thoroughly characterized for its bioavailability, metabolic stability, and cell‐penetrant properties during its extensive preclinical and clinical evaluation in oncology (Guo et al., 2021; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2009). These attributes underpin its suitability for repurposing; its well‐defined medicinal chemistry profile and advanced clinical development stage (availability of Phase I data) position MK-2206 as an attractive candidate for investigating autophagy regulation in non‐oncologic contexts such as AMD (Karim et al., 2020).

─────────────────────────────  
Therapeutic History  
─────────────────────────────  
Historically, MK-2206 has been developed and evaluated predominantly as an anticancer agent. During its clinical evolution, it was subjected to multiple Phase I and combination Phase I/II clinical trials in patients with advanced solid tumors, HER2-positive cancers, and other malignancies. The compound has been administered on both an every-other-day (QOD) schedule and on a once-weekly (QW) regimen in dose‐escalation studies (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2008; 2010). These early clinical studies provided valuable safety, tolerability, and pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic (PK/PD) data that have now established an acceptable safety profile in humans. Outside the field of oncology, no published clinical study has yet directly evaluated MK-2206 in ocular indications. However, a separate body of preclinical research has increasingly linked dysregulated AKT activation in RPE cells with impaired lysosomal function and defective autophagy – two pathological hallmarks of dry AMD (Karim et al., 2020). In immunoproteasome‐deficient RPE models (for example, LMP2 knockout [KO] cells), hyper‐phosphorylation of AKT is associated with reduced nuclear TFEB and compromised autophagic flux, features that correlate with RPE stress and lipofuscin accumulation (Karim et al., 2020). Preclinical in vitro data have demonstrated that pharmacological inhibition of AKT using MK-2206 leads to decreased AKT phosphorylation, increased nuclear TFEB localization, and enhanced autophagy flux in RPE, rescuing some of the defects observed in these models (Karim et al., 2020). Although MK-2206 per se has not been directly tested in animal models of AMD, related preclinical evidence based on the modulation of the AKT–TFEB axis in RPE supports its potential utility in the AMD context (Karim et al., 2020). In addition, several patent reviews have discussed MK-2206 within the broader portfolio of AKT inhibitors that are being repurposed for indications beyond oncology, further reinforcing the plausibility of using MK-2206 to target cellular pathways implicated in AMD (Guo et al., 2021).

─────────────────────────────  
Mechanism of Action  
─────────────────────────────  
The established mechanism of MK-2206 is anchored in its ability to inhibit AKT signaling through an allosteric mechanism. Under normal conditions, the AKT kinase is activated by phosphorylation events – typically at threonine 308 and serine 473 – in response to upstream signals from receptor tyrosine kinases and phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K) pathways. AKT then phosphorylates a wide range of substrates that control cell survival, growth, and metabolism. One of the downstream effects of activated AKT is the phosphorylation of TFEB (and possibly other MiT/TFE family members such as TFE3) at specific serine residues (for example, S467). This phosphorylation event hampers TFEB’s capacity to translocate from the cytosol to the nucleus, thereby repressing its transcriptional activity on the CLEAR (Coordinated Lysosomal Expression and Regulation) network, a gene set that drives lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy (Karim et al., 2020).

MK-2206 exerts its effect by binding to an allosteric site on AKT, a mode of inhibition that distinguishes it from ATP‐competitive inhibitors. In doing so, it reduces the phosphorylation of AKT at Ser473, thereby lowering its kinase activity (Karim et al., 2020). In RPE cells – particularly under pathogenic conditions such as immunoproteasome deficiency that leads to AKT hyper‐phosphorylation – MK-2206 administration has been shown to result in a marked decrease in AKT activity. This decrease, in turn, permits the dephosphorylation of TFEB, facilitating its nuclear import (Karim et al., 2020). Once in the nucleus, TFEB upregulates the transcription of genes involved in lysosomal function, autophagosome formation, and the expression of critical enzymes such as cathepsin D and components of the V-ATPase, which are necessary for maintaining lysosomal acidification (Karim et al., 2020).

Although the research cited does not explicitly verify isoform‐specific inhibition of AKT2 by MK-2206, the underlying hypothesis – that AKT2 hyperactivity in RPE suppresses TFEB nuclear localization – provides a strong rationale for repurposing MK-2206 in AMD. Some studies have proposed that AKT2, among the three isoforms, may predominantly drive the inflammatory and autophagy‐related deficits encountered in RPE in AMD models (Ghosh et al., 2019). This hypothesis is further supported by evidence showing that AKT2 inhibition can attenuate inflammatory cascades (such as IFNλ–LCN-2–driven neutrophil infiltration) that contribute to early RPE pathology (Ghosh et al., 2019). Thus, the mechanism of action of MK-2206 – namely, its ability to allosterically inhibit AKT activity leading to increased nuclear translocation of TFEB and subsequent upregulation of lysosomal/autophagy pathways – directly addresses key pathobiological mechanisms implicated in dry AMD.

─────────────────────────────  
Expected Effect  
─────────────────────────────  
Based on the hypothesis under review, the administration of MK-2206 to RPE cells is expected to yield several critical downstream effects that are therapeutically desirable in the context of dry AMD. First, MK-2206 should decrease the hyper‐phosphorylation of AKT observed in stressed or disease‐impacted RPE, which is thought to be a major contributing factor to the suppression of TFEB nuclear localization in these cells (Karim et al., 2020). By relieving this inhibitory phosphorylation, MK-2206 should facilitate the dephosphorylation and subsequent nuclear translocation of TFEB. Once TFEB is allowed to enter the nucleus, it can promote the transcription of a broad array of genes responsible for lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy, including those involved in the expression of vacuolar H-ATPase (V-ATPase) components and cathepsin D (CTSD) (Karim et al., 2020).

The restoration of nuclear TFEB activity is expected to lead to several beneficial cellular effects. In the RPE – which relies on robust autophagy for the clearance of photoreceptor outer segments and maintenance of cellular homeostasis – enhanced TFEB‐driven gene expression should improve lysosomal acidification and enzymatic activity, including that of cathepsin D (a key lysosomal protease) (Karim et al., 2020). Improved lysosomal acidification is critical for the maturation and function of cathepsin D, which in turn is essential for the degradation of protein aggregates and lipofuscin. Since drusen and lipofuscin accumulation represent major pathological hallmarks of dry AMD, the normalization of cathepsin D function could help to clear these toxic deposits, potentially slowing or reversing disease progression (Karim et al., 2020; Ghosh et al., 2019).

Furthermore, other reports suggest that AKT activation in RPE not only hinders autophagy but also promotes pro‐inflammatory pathways that contribute to tissue degeneration (Ghosh et al., 2019). Thus, the inhibition of AKT signaling by MK-2206 is anticipated to diminish such inflammatory cascades (Ghosh et al., 2019). In aggregate, the expected net effect is a re‐establishment of cellular proteostasis within the RPE via two interrelated mechanisms: (1) an enhancement of autophagic flux and lysosomal clearance via the TFEB pathway, and (2) a reduction in deleterious inflammatory and stress responses mediated by aberrant AKT2 signaling. Given that RPE dysfunction, lipofuscin accumulation, and drusen formation underlie the pathogenesis of dry AMD, MK-2206 could thereby serve to counteract disease progression at a mechanistic level (Karim et al., 2020).

─────────────────────────────  
Overall Evaluation  
─────────────────────────────  
In evaluating MK-2206 as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, several key points emerge. On the strength side, MK-2206 is a well-characterized small-molecule allosteric inhibitor of the AKT pathway – a pathway increasingly implicated in the regulation of autophagy and lysosomal function in RPE cells. Preclinical studies in immunoproteasome-deficient RPE have demonstrated that MK-2206 can inhibit AKT phosphorylation, restore nuclear TFEB localization, and promote autophagic flux (Karim et al., 2020). This mechanistic link is especially relevant, as dry AMD is characterized by reduced autophagy, impaired lysosomal clearance, and resultant accumulation of drusen and lipofuscin. Moreover, the rationale that AKT2 hyperactivity in RPE cells suppresses TFEB function – thereby weakening the cell’s proteolytic capacity – is well supported by the available preclinical data (Ghosh et al., 2019). In addition, MK-2206 has already been through several Phase I oncology trials, meaning that its safety and pharmacokinetic profiles are largely established in humans, which dramatically de-risks its repurposing for a different indication such as AMD (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2008; 2010). This could accelerate the clinical development timeline, as much of the initial toxicity and dosing work has been completed.

Nonetheless, there are several challenges and potential weaknesses to be addressed. First, while the available studies support that MK-2206 can modulate the AKT–TFEB axis in RPE cells under preclinical conditions, many of these studies do not provide isoform‐specific data; our hypothesis hinges on the idea that AKT2 is the critical isoform to be inhibited. MK-2206 is generally described as a pan-AKT inhibitor, which means that it may also affect AKT1 and AKT3. The lack of isoform specificity could lead to unanticipated off-target effects or impact cellular processes in non-RPE tissues if systemic exposure is not tightly controlled (Karim et al., 2020). Second, although the mechanism of promoting nuclear TFEB activity through AKT inhibition is conceptually sound and supported by cellular data, direct measurements of downstream endpoints critical to AMD – such as lysosomal acidification (e.g., via V-ATPase activity assays) and cathepsin D maturation or activity – are limited or indirect in the current literature (Karim et al., 2020). Without robust evidence that MK-2206 improves these specific lysosomal functions in RPE cells, the link between restored autophagy and actual therapeutic benefit in terms of drusen clearance remains inferential. Third, previous clinical development of MK-2206 in oncology has encountered variable efficacy when used as a monotherapy, prompting its evaluation predominantly in combination regimens (Guo et al., 2021; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2009). The implications of these findings for a non‐oncologic, degenerative condition such as AMD are not straightforward, and careful attention must be paid to optimizing both delivery routes (for example, local versus systemic administration) and dosing strategies that are tailored to the ocular microenvironment.

Furthermore, while the literature provides a strong rationale linking AKT hyperactivation to impaired autophagy in RPE, dry AMD is a multifactorial disease with complex pathophysiology that includes oxidative stress, inflammation, and genetic risk factors such as CFH variants. It is not yet fully clear whether correcting the autophagy defect alone will suffice to produce clinically meaningful outcomes in all patients with dry AMD. In addition, toxicity concerns must be carefully revisited: although MK-2206’s safety profile is defined in the context of oncology, potential ocular toxicity – such as RPE cell toxicity, off-target retinal effects, or interference with normal retinal cellular turnover – must be rigorously evaluated via dedicated preclinical ocular studies before clinical translation. Finally, the intellectual property and regulatory landscape for repurposing a cancer drug to treat an ocular disease will require further scrutiny, although the existing clinical data on MK-2206 do provide an important head-start compared to wholly novel compounds (Guo et al., 2021; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2009).

In summary, the strengths of MK-2206 as a candidate for repurposing in dry AMD include:  
• A well-characterized mechanism of action that aligns with pathobiological insights from RPE autophagy studies, namely the inhibition of aberrant AKT signaling leading to enhanced nuclear TFEB activity and autophagy restoration (Karim et al., 2020).  
• Established clinical safety and PK data from multiple Phase I oncology trials, which reduce translational risk and may accelerate repurposing efforts (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2008; 2010).  
• A plausible hypothesis that links AKT2 hyperactivity in RPE (observed in CFH-risk models and immunoproteasome-deficient systems) to lysosomal dysfunction, drusen accumulation, and ultimately, AMD pathology (Ghosh et al., 2019).

Conversely, potential weaknesses include:  
• Limited evidence regarding isoform specificity toward AKT2, as MK-2206 is generally considered a pan-AKT inhibitor, which may inadvertently modulate other AKT isoforms and lead to systemic side effects (Karim et al., 2020).  
• Incomplete preclinical data linking MK-2206 directly to improvements in lysosomal acidification and cathepsin D activity in RPE, which remain key therapeutic endpoints predicted to counteract drusen formation (Karim et al., 2020).  
• The challenge of adapting systemic dosing regimens used in oncology to the ocular setting, where achieving therapeutic retinal concentrations without causing off-target toxicity is paramount (Guo et al., 2021; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2009).  
• The multifactorial nature of dry AMD that may require combination approaches, meaning that modulation of the AKT–TFEB axis alone might not be sufficient to achieve robust clinical benefit in all patients.

Overall, MK-2206 represents a promising candidate to repurpose for dry AMD based on its ability to allosterically inhibit AKT, a central node in a pathway that has been implicated in RPE autophagy and lysosomal dysfunction. The preclinical rationale – that inhibition of AKT releases the block on TFEB nuclear translocation, thereby improving lysosomal acidification and cathepsin D activity – is well founded in the literature (Karim et al., 2020). Moreover, the favorable clinical safety profile gleaned from its extensive evaluation in oncology serves as an important asset when considering repurposing strategies. However, critical questions remain regarding isoform specificity, the optimal route and dosing for ocular application, and whether restoring autophagy via this pathway is sufficient to reverse or halt the progression of dry AMD in patients. Future studies should focus on establishing robust preclinical data in AMD-relevant animal models —including direct measures of lysosomal acidification, cathepsin D function, and drusen clearance —as well as refining ocular delivery strategies that minimize systemic exposure. Addressing these gaps will be essential for de-risking MK-2206’s application in the AMD setting and for paving the way toward clinical trials specifically targeting the AKT–TFEB pathway in the context of retinal degeneration.

─────────────────────────────  
Conclusion  
─────────────────────────────  
In conclusion, our comprehensive literature review supports the repurposing of MK-2206 for dry AMD on the following grounds: it is a well‐studied allosteric AKT inhibitor with a known safety profile from Phase I oncology trials; preclinical investigations in RPE models implicate AKT hyperactivation in the suppression of TFEB nuclear localization and consequent lysosomal dysfunction; and mechanistic hypotheses derived from these models suggest that inhibiting AKT (and, by extension, AKT2) can restore autophagy, improve lysosomal acidification, boost cathepsin D activity, and potentially counteract drusen accumulation – a key driver of dry AMD pathology. While challenges remain, particularly with respect to isoform selectivity and the translation of dosing paradigms from oncology to ocular applications, the existing data provide a strong rationale for advancing MK-2206 into more focused preclinical studies for dry AMD. Such work should include detailed analyses of lysosomal pH, cathepsin D activity, and the overall impact on RPE proteostasis in in vivo models that recapitulate the human disease. With these additional studies, MK-2206 could emerge as a viable candidate in our therapeutic pipeline for addressing the unmet need in dry AMD (Karim et al., 2020; Ghosh et al., 2019; Guo et al., 2021).

In the absence of rapamycin, active mTORC1 phosphorylates downstream targets such as S6 kinase and 4E-BP1, thereby promoting anabolic processes and suppressing autophagy. Preclinical studies have shown that treatment of RPE cells with rapamycin results in a marked reduction in the accumulation of autofluorescent granules (AFGs) that are indicative of impaired lysosomal degradation (Falcão et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2025). These cellular effects are directly linked to the expression of critical proteins in RPE cells; for example, TFEB is known to be expressed in these cells and its activation correlates with increased lysosomal gene expression and function (Falcão et al., 2024) while cathepsin D, a lysosomal protease, is vital for the degradation of phagocytosed photoreceptor outer segments (Chang et al., 2022; Sinha et al., 2016). The intended therapeutic outcome is to slow or potentially halt the progression of GA by reducing the burden of drusen and preserving RPE function, which could translate into better preservation of visual acuity over time. However, it is important to note that while these mechanisms are promising in vitro, clinical translation has encountered challenges related to dosing, delivery, and the stage of disease at which intervention occurs (Wang et al., 2022; Falcão et al., 2024).

Overall Evaluation:  
Rapamycin presents itself as a scientifically promising yet clinically challenging candidate for the treatment of dry AMD. One of the key strengths of rapamycin is its well-established mechanism of action: as a potent mTORC1 inhibitor, it leverages a well-characterized pathway involving TFEB activation that directly targets the core pathology observed in dry AMD—the accumulation of drusen components and impaired lysosomal function in RPE cells. Preclinical studies have consistently demonstrated that rapamycin can enhance autophagic flux, lower levels of toxic aggregates such as A2E, and increase the activity of lysosomal enzymes like cathepsin D, thereby supporting its target validation in the context of RPE health (Falcão et al., 2025; Falcão et al., 2024). Additionally, rapamycin has an extensive history of clinical use in other indications, and its safety profile, while not without concerns, is well documented from its use as an immunosuppressant in transplantation and in various oncology settings (Wang et al., 2022).

However, the clinical translation of rapamycin for dry AMD has not been straightforward. Multiple clinical trials have assessed its application using different routes of administration, such as intravitreal and subconjunctival injections, with mixed results. While safety and tolerability have generally been acceptable, the efficacy endpoints—specifically, the prevention or slowing of GA progression—have not been definitively met in these studies (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2008, 2011, 2012; Wang et al., 2022). Furthermore, some trials encountered complications such as sterile endophthalmitis or observed decreases in visual acuity relative to untreated eyes, suggesting that even if the underlying molecular mechanisms are engaged, the overall benefits in late-stage disease might be limited (Wang et al., 2022; Falcão et al., 2024).

Another potential weakness is the complexity inherent in mTOR signaling itself. The pathway plays a dual role in cellular homeostasis—while its inhibition can promote autophagy and lysosomal clearance, inappropriate or excessive inhibition could lead to adverse effects such as increased retinal neuron apoptosis, particularly in advanced stages of AMD where the cellular milieu is significantly altered (Wang et al., 2022; Chang et al., 2022). Moreover, the optimal dosing regimen and delivery method for achieving the desired ocular concentration without incurring systemic side effects remain unresolved. Some studies have suggested that modifications to the formulation, such as encapsulation in synthetic nanoparticles, could enhance ocular penetration and prolong the effective duration of rapamycin within the eye, thereby minimizing side effects and improving efficacy (Jo et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2022).

Despite these challenges, the strength of rapamycin’s mechanism—the inhibition of mTORC1 and consequent activation of TFEB leading to enhanced lysosomal biogenesis—remains compelling. The molecular rationale is robust, and the repeated demonstration of reduced levels of autofluorescent granules in RPE cells following rapamycin treatment is particularly encouraging (Falcão et al., 2024). The concept of using a repurposed, clinically approved drug to address a significant unmet need in dry AMD is attractive, especially given the limited treatment options currently available for this degenerative condition. In this light, further investigations—ideally, in earlier stages of AMD and with innovative delivery modalities—may reveal a niche where rapamycin can exert a clinically meaningful benefit (Wang et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2019).

In conclusion, while rapamycin has significant potential grounded in sound molecular pharmacology and extensive preclinical validation, its clinical application for dry AMD warrants careful optimization. The candidate’s strengths lie in its potent and well-understood mechanism of mTORC1 inhibition, the activation of TFEB, and subsequent improvements in lysosomal function and autophagic clearance in RPE cells. Conversely, clinical challenges including mixed efficacy outcomes in GA trials, potential adverse effects related to mTOR pathway modulation in vulnerable retinal neurons, and limitations in current dosing/delivery strategies represent hurdles that must be surmounted. Based on these comprehensive literature insights, rapamycin remains a promising candidate for further investigation, albeit with recommendations to explore its use in earlier disease stages and in combination with advanced ocular delivery systems to maximize its therapeutic benefit while minimizing risks (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2012; Wang et al., 2022; Falcão et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2025).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Torin1 is a synthetic small‐molecule that belongs to the second‐generation, ATP‐competitive class of mTOR inhibitors, originally derived from a quinoline‐based scaffold. Its discovery originated from a high‐throughput compound library screen that identified quinolone hits with moderate mTOR activity, which were then optimized through iterative medicinal chemistry by introducing a six‐membered lactam to convert the initial quinolone into a tricyclic benzonaphthridinone scaffold (Guillem, 2015). This chemical modification yielded a molecule with exceptional biochemical potency—capable of inhibiting both mTOR complexes, mTORC1 and mTORC2, at very low (nanomolar to picomolar) concentrations—and with approximately 1000-fold improvement in cellular potency relative to the initial hits (Guillem, 2015). As an ATP-competitive inhibitor, Torin1 binds directly to the active (ATP-binding) site of mTOR, thereby circumventing the partial inhibition that is observed with first-generation mTOR inhibitors like rapamycin that act allosterically by binding FKBP12 (Liu et al., 2012). Torin1 has been widely used as a research tool to interrogate mTOR signaling in various cellular contexts, and its chemical lineage as a quinoline-derived molecule positions it within a well-characterized class of inhibitors that have been instrumental in expanding our understanding of mTOR-dependent regulation of autophagy and cellular metabolism (Liu et al., 2012).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, Torin1 has been employed predominantly as a research tool rather than as a clinical drug candidate. Extensive preclinical studies have demonstrated its robust ability to inhibit mTOR signaling in cancer models, autophagy-deficient systems, and metabolic studies. For instance, Torin1 was shown to potently inhibit mTOR signaling pathways in glioblastoma and prostate cancer cells, significantly reducing cell-cycle progression and inducing apoptosis in certain contexts (Gu, 2017; Liu et al., 2012). Its use as an autophagy inducer is well documented, as experiments utilizing Torin1 have demonstrated increased autophagic flux and elevated lysosomal activity in multiple cell lines (Li, 2018; Liu et al., 2012). Importantly, Torin1 is also used in studies with retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells, as evidenced by its ability to increase TFEB-driven luciferase reporter activity in ARPE-19 cells by effectively suppressing mTORC1 signaling (Huang et al., 2018). Despite these promising experimental findings, Torin1 has not advanced to clinical trials for any indication, including neurodegenerative disorders or dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD). Moreover, its intrinsic pharmacokinetic limitations—such as poor aqueous solubility, a short half-life, and low oral bioavailability—have been recognized in several studies, thereby limiting its potential as a direct therapeutic candidate without further structural optimization (Guillem, 2015; Wang et al., 2022).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, Torin1 functions by competing with ATP for binding to the catalytic domain of mTOR, effectively blocking the phosphorylation of downstream substrates. Its ATP-competitive nature allows Torin1 to inhibit both mTORC1 and mTORC2 complexes, thereby offering a broader inhibition profile than allosteric agents like rapamycin that primarily target mTORC1 (Guillem, 2015; Liu et al., 2012). Detailed molecular modeling and structure–activity relationship studies indicate that the tricyclic benzonaphthridinone core of Torin1 forms critical hinge-binding interactions with residues in the mTOR kinase domain (Liu et al., 2012). This interaction accounts for its high potency, as reflected in low nanomolar IC₅₀ values in cellular assays (Liu et al., 2012; Gros & Muller, 2014). Torin1 induces rapid dephosphorylation of canonical mTORC1 substrates, such as S6 kinase at Thr389 and 4E-BP1 at Thr37/46, which results in downregulation of protein synthesis and cellular growth signals (Misra & Pizzo, 2013). Moreover, by simultaneously inhibiting mTORC2, it reduces phosphorylation of Akt at Ser473—a site critical for full Akt activation—thus attenuating the feedback loops that typically reinvigorate upstream PI3K signaling in response to mTORC1 inhibition (Gu, 2017; Martina et al., 2014). A particularly notable feature of Torin1 is its slow off-rate, which leads to sustained inhibition of mTOR activity even after drug washout, a pharmacodynamic property that may confer prolonged downstream effects such as enhanced autophagic flux (Liu et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2013). The inhibition of mTOR by Torin1 correlates with dephosphorylation of transcription factors, particularly TFEB and TFE3; under normal nutrient-replete conditions, mTORC1 phosphorylates TFEB (e.g., on S211 in TFEB) and TFE3, sequestering them in the cytosol through binding with 14-3-3 proteins (Huang et al., 2018; Martina et al., 2014). Upon mTOR inhibition by Torin1, TFEB is dephosphorylated and translocates to the nucleus, where it induces the transcription of CLEAR (Coordinated Lysosomal Expression and Regulation) network genes that drive lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy (Li, 2018; Liu et al., 2013). This precise modulation of mTOR signaling and subsequent transcriptional reprogramming forms the biochemical basis for leveraging Torin1 as a candidate to ameliorate lysosomal clearance defects.

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis for repurposing Torin1 in the context of dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is that potent inhibition of mTORC1/2 in RPE cells can lift the repressive phosphorylation that normally limits the activity of TFEB and TFE3. In RPE cells, as demonstrated by studies in ARPE-19 cell models, mTOR inhibition via Torin1 not only leads to decreased phosphorylation of S6 kinase but also results in marked activation of TFEB-driven transcription (Huang et al., 2018). When TFEB translocates to the nucleus, it binds to CLEAR elements present in the promoters of genes responsible for lysosomal biogenesis, acidification (through the upregulation of V-ATPase subunits), and the maturation and activity of lysosomal enzymes such as cathepsin D (CTSD) (Huang et al., 2018; Li, 2018). In dry AMD, RPE cells exhibit a decline in lysosomal function along with accumulation of cellular debris and lipofuscin, which contribute to disease pathology. By inducing a robust CLEAR response, Torin1 is expected to restore lysosomal function through increased biogenesis, enhanced acidification, and elevated cathepsin D activity, thereby improving the clearance of toxic aggregates in RPE cells and ultimately mitigating the progression of dry AMD (Gu, 2017; Huang et al., 2018). Additionally, the sustained target engagement afforded by Torin1’s slow off-rate may provide prolonged therapeutic benefit even with intermittent dosing, an attractive feature given the chronic nature of AMD (Liu et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2013). Recent evidence from preclinical iPSC models and autophagy-deficiency studies underscores the potential translation of mTOR-targeted strategies in restoring cellular homeostasis in degenerative diseases, lending further credence to this expected mechanism (Guillem, 2015).

Overall Evaluation:  
In summary, Torin1 possesses a compelling mechanistic profile that aligns well with the therapeutic needs of dry AMD by targeting a fundamental pathway governing cellular homeostasis in RPE cells. Its origin from a quinoline-based scaffold and subsequent chemical optimization into a highly potent ATP-competitive mTOR inhibitor underline its status as a valuable chemical probe in preclinical settings (Guillem, 2015). The dual inhibition of both mTORC1 and mTORC2 by Torin1, combined with its slow off-rate and sustained downstream effects—including dephosphorylation and nuclear translocation of TFEB/TFE3—make it an ideal tool for inducing lysosomal biogenesis and enhancing autophagic clearance (Martina et al., 2014; Huang et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2012). In cellular models, including ARPE-19 RPE cells, Torin1 has already demonstrated the ability to activate TFEB and upregulate CLEAR gene expression, which is directly relevant to counteracting the lysosomal clearance defects observed in dry AMD (Huang et al., 2018; Li, 2018).

However, significant challenges remain regarding the translational applicability of Torin1 as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. Its reported poor aqueous solubility, short half-life, and low oral bioavailability present formidable barriers to clinical development unless addressed through formulation improvements or further medicinal chemistry optimization (Guillem, 2015; Wang et al., 2022). Moreover, while extensive preclinical literature supports its role as a robust mTOR inhibitor in cancer and autophagy research, there is a lack of direct in vivo evidence for its efficacy in ocular models, particularly in dry AMD or geographic atrophy (GA) mouse lines (Liu et al., 2013; Gu, 2017). Careful dosing will also be critical, as the broad and potent inhibition of mTOR can have unintended effects on cellular metabolism and protein synthesis beyond the intended enhancement of lysosomal function. Additionally, off-target effects have been observed in some biochemical screens at supraphysiologic concentrations, including binding to other PIKK family members such as ATR, ATM, and DNA-PK, although these are generally not manifested at the low nanomolar concentrations used in cellular assays (Settembre et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2012).

From the perspective of repurposing for dry AMD, Torin1’s deep mechanistic specificity is a double-edged sword: it offers a highly defined and robust approach to upregulating lysosomal biogenesis via the TFEB/TFE3 axis, yet its pharmacokinetic liabilities and the absence of any clinical history in ocular disease necessitate additional work. The promising in vitro data in RPE models (ARPE-19 cells) and iPSC-derived RPE systems provide valuable target validation, but before advancing to clinical trials a refined analog or an optimized delivery method (for example, local ocular administration to bypass systemic bioavailability issues) should be considered (Huang et al., 2018; Li, 2018; Wang et al., 2022).

In summary, Torin1 is an excellent candidate for preclinical proof-of-concept studies to validate mTOR inhibition as a strategy to combat lysosomal dysfunction in dry AMD; however, further optimization to improve its stability and bioavailability, alongside rigorous in vivo testing in relevant AMD models, will be essential prior to clinical development (Guillem, 2015; Gu, 2017). The strengths of Torin1 lie in its potent, dual mTOR inhibition and its ability to robustly induce TFEB activation, whereas its weaknesses center on its pharmacokinetic shortcomings and the current lack of efficacy data in ocular disease models. Overall, with focused optimization and targeted delivery strategies, Torin1 or its derivatives may offer a promising therapeutic avenue for ameliorating the lysosomal clearance defects that underlie dry AMD pathology (Liu et al., 2012; Huang et al., 2018).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Lithium chloride (Sigma L9650) is an inorganic salt belonging to the family of lithium compounds that has been in use for several decades, primarily as a mood stabilizer in the treatment of bipolar disorder. It is synthesized by combining lithium carbonate or lithium hydroxide with hydrochloric acid, yielding a highly water‐soluble salt that is widely available for both clinical and experimental research purposes (Carmassi et al., 2016; Vallée et al., 2021). As a prototypical member of the lithium salts, lithium chloride has been repurposed in recent years as a candidate for neuroprotection because of its ability to inhibit glycogen synthase kinase-3β (GSK3β), a serine/threonine kinase involved in numerous intracellular signaling cascades. Lithium’s chemical simplicity belies its complex pharmacology; its effects extend well beyond mood stabilization to encompass modulation of cell survival, inflammatory responses, and protein degradation pathways. In this context, lithium salts are now recognized as small molecule modulators that can affect intracellular transcriptional programs, including nuclear import of factors such as transcription factor EB (TFEB) and β-catenin, which in turn control the expression of genes necessary for lysosomal biogenesis and autophagic flux (Carmassi et al., 2016; Vallée et al., 2021). These mechanistic insights, originally developed in studies of neurodegenerative and psychiatric diseases, have motivated investigations into whether lithium chloride might be repurposed to address the autophagic and lysosomal dysfunction observed in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD), particularly in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) (Carmassi et al., 2016; Vallée et al., 2021).

Therapeutic History:  
Lithium salts have a long-standing clinical history in psychiatry, especially in the management of bipolar disorder, where their dosing and long-term safety profiles have been thoroughly characterized. In addition, numerous preclinical studies in neuroscience have demonstrated that lithium can reduce tau phosphorylation and improve neuronal cell survival, partly by inhibiting GSK3β and modulating downstream targets such as β-catenin and Bcl-2 (Carmassi et al., 2016; Vallée et al., 2021). Lithium has been evaluated in several neurodegenerative contexts—for instance, it has been examined for its potential benefits in Alzheimer’s disease, Huntington’s disease, and Parkinson’s disease, with some studies reporting modest improvements in neuroprotection and behavioral outcomes, although clinical results have been mixed (Singh et al., 2022; Vallée et al., 2021). More specifically, preclinical data in the central nervous system have shown that prolonged exposure to lithium increases cortical grey matter and enhances neuronal markers such as N-acetyl-aspartate, suggesting that lithium exerts trophic and neuroprotective effects (Carmassi et al., 2016). In the ocular arena, while lithium’s use has been predominantly described in the context of glaucoma—in which its inhibition of GSK3β was shown to modulate WNT/β-catenin signaling in trabecular meshwork cells—the literature offers no direct clinical or in-depth preclinical evaluation of lithium chloride in dry AMD or for modulating autophagy specifically in RPE cells (Singh et al., 2022; Vallée et al., 2021). A search in clinical trial registries has not identified any trials using lithium chloride for macular degeneration, underscoring a notable gap between the neuroprotective models in which lithium has been studied and its potential application in dry AMD (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).

Mechanism of Action:  
Lithium chloride’s mechanisms of action are multifaceted, but a significant aspect relevant to the dry AMD hypothesis is its ability to inhibit GSK3β. GSK3β normally phosphorylates a variety of substrates including β-catenin and TFEB, leading to cytosolic retention and subsequent degradation; inhibition of GSK3β by lithium therefore results in stabilization and nuclear accumulation of β-catenin and promotes TFEB nuclear entry (Carmassi et al., 2016; Vallée et al., 2021). In detail, lithium binds directly to the magnesium-sensitive site of GSK3β and also promotes its inhibitory N-terminal serine phosphorylation, leading to a dose-dependent suppression of GSK3β activity (Carmassi et al., 2016). The release of β-catenin from the destruction complex allows it to accumulate in the nucleus, where it acts as a transcriptional coactivator for genes that contribute to cell survival and homeostasis, including those involved in lysosomal biogenesis (Carmassi et al., 2016; Vallée et al., 2021). Similarly, TFEB is a master transcription factor that coordinates the expression of a variety of genes encoding lysosomal enzymes and autophagy-related proteins. Under basal conditions, phosphorylation retains TFEB in the cytosol; inhibition of GSK3β can contribute to dephosphorylation of TFEB, thereby facilitating its nuclear translocation and transcriptional activation of targets such as cathepsin D (CTSD) and subunits of the vacuolar ATPase (v-ATPase) that are crucial for lysosomal acidification (Carmassi et al., 2016; Friedman et al., 2015). In neuronal models, lithium treatment has been demonstrated to increase levels of neurotrophic factors and cell survival molecules, as well as to enhance autophagy-mediated clearance of toxic proteins including aggregated forms of tau and other proteins implicated in neurodegenerative disease (Vallée et al., 2021). Furthermore, lithium’s inhibition of inositol monophosphatase further contributes to autophagy induction through an mTOR-independent mechanism, reinforcing its capacity to modulate autophagic flux (Friedman et al., 2015). Despite these promising mechanistic insights, it is important to note that most of the supporting data have been generated in neuronal or non-ocular cell systems; direct evidence for lithium chloride-mediated activation of TFEB/β-catenin signaling and upregulation of lysosomal acidification machinery specifically in RPE cells remains limited (Golestaneh et al., 2018; Guha et al., 2014).

Expected Effect:  
Based on the hypothesis, treatment with lithium chloride in RPE cells is anticipated to inhibit GSK3β, leading to a cascade of intracellular events that restore impaired autophagic flux—a major pathological hallmark in dry AMD. Specifically, inhibition of GSK3β should reduce the phosphorylation-dependent cytosolic retention of TFEB and β-catenin, thereby facilitating their nuclear import. In the nucleus, these transcription factors can activate a broad transcriptional program that upregulates the synthesis of lysosomal proteins such as cathepsin D and components of the v-ATPase complex, ultimately leading to enhanced lysosomal acidification (Carmassi et al., 2016; Friedman et al., 2015). This improved lysosomal function is expected to accelerate the degradation of photoreceptor outer segment debris and other autophagic substrates, leading to a restoration of autophagic flux and a reduction in lipofuscin accumulation—a prominent feature of dry AMD pathology (Golestaneh et al., 2018). In parallel, lithium’s neuroprotective effects, including the upregulation of prosurvival factors like Bcl-2 and the attenuation of proinflammatory signaling pathways, may further support RPE cell survival and function under chronic oxidative stress conditions (Vallée et al., 2021). Given that lysosomal alkalinization is known to impair cathepsin D activity and autophagic degradation in RPE cells, the upregulation of cathepsin D via TFEB activation represents a critical therapeutic target to counteract the reduced degradative capacity observed in dry AMD (Guha et al., 2014). Moreover, the candidate’s reported ocular penetration and long-term safety in other contexts provide a translational rationale, though the literature is notably deficient in direct measurements of RPE-specific outcomes—thus, further studies are required to validate that lithium chloride achieves effective intraocular concentrations without toxicity (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.; Vallée et al., 2021). The expected outcome in an in vitro assay would be an increase in nuclear TFEB and β-catenin as determined by immunocytochemistry and Western blot of nuclear extracts, an increase in mRNA and protein levels of lysosomal acidification machinery (e.g., v-ATPase subunits) and cathepsin D, restoration of autophagic flux as evidenced by normalized LC3-II/LC3-I ratios and p62 degradation, and improved clearance of photoreceptor outer segment-derived material in RPE cell culture models (Golestaneh et al., 2018).

Overall Evaluation:  
The repurposing of lithium chloride for dry age-related macular degeneration is based on a compelling mechanistic rationale that builds upon well-established aspects of lithium’s pharmacology. On one hand, the drug’s ability to inhibit GSK3β—and thereby to promote the nuclear translocation of TFEB and β-catenin—aligns well with the therapeutic goal of upregulating lysosomal gene expression and restoring autophagic flux in RPE cells (Golestaneh et al., 2018). Lithium’s longstanding use in psychiatric medicine has resulted in a rich and well-documented clinical safety profile, and its neuroprotective benefits in various models lend additional support to its potential utility in other degenerative conditions including ocular diseases (Carmassi et al., 2016; Vallée et al., 2021).

However, there are several notable weaknesses and gaps that must be addressed before lithium chloride can be considered a robust therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. First, while preclinical studies in neuronal models offer supportive evidence that lithium can modulate autophagy and enhance lysosomal function, there is a lack of direct data demonstrating these mechanisms in RPE cells specifically (Golestaneh et al., 2018). Second, the pharmacokinetic profile of lithium chloride in the eye—especially the extent to which it penetrates the RPE following systemic or local administration—remains poorly characterized, and this is a critical factor given the importance of achieving therapeutic concentrations in the retina without causing off-target toxicity (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.). Third, although lithium’s long-term safety has been established in psychiatric populations, its known systemic toxicities, including renal and thyroid effects, as well as its narrow therapeutic window, raise concerns about the potential risks of repurposing it for an ocular indication where localized delivery may be necessary to avoid systemic exposure (Singh et al., 2022; Vallée et al., 2021). Finally, the absence of any registered clinical trials or robust preclinical studies in an AMD model means that the translational viability of lithium chloride for this indication is still highly speculative (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).

Despite these concerns, the strengths of lithium chloride as a repurposed agent for dry AMD are significant. Its ability to target GSK3β provides a unique molecular entry point that could bypass some of the drawbacks of other autophagy modulators that primarily act through mTOR inhibition—a strategy that has yielded mixed clinical results (Friedman et al., 2015; Vallée et al., 2021). Moreover, the multi-modal action of lithium, which encompasses both anti-inflammatory and anti-excitotoxic effects in addition to its autophagy-promoting properties, suggests that it could provide a broad-spectrum protective effect in the stressed cellular environment of the RPE (Carmassi et al., 2016; Vallée et al., 2021). Nonetheless, given the complexity of RPE biology and the multifactorial nature of dry AMD pathogenesis—as evidenced by the alterations in lysosomal pH, reduced cathepsin activity, and compromised membrane trafficking in these cells—any candidate drug must be rigorously evaluated in appropriate RPE or AMD models before clinical translation is attempted (Golestaneh et al., 2018; Guha et al., 2014).

In summary, lithium chloride holds promise as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD through its inhibition of GSK3β and the subsequent activation of nuclear TFEB/β-catenin signaling pathways, which are anticipated to upregulate lysosomal acidification machinery and cathepsin D expression and thereby restore autophagic flux in the RPE. The candidate’s well-documented clinical history and long-term safety in other indications provide additional encouragement for its further preclinical exploration. However, critical issues—such as the need for direct experimental evidence in RPE system models, the establishment of effective and safe ocular dosing regimens with adequate retinal penetration, and thorough evaluations of potential systemic and ocular toxicities—must be rigorously addressed. Until these gaps are filled by focused preclinical and translational research, the use of lithium chloride for dry AMD remains a promising yet still unproven strategy that warrants additional investigation (Carmassi et al., 2016; Friedman et al., 2015; Golestaneh et al., 2018; Guha et al., 2014; Vallée et al., 2021; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.; Singh et al., 2022).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
GDC-0941 (pictilisib) is a synthetic, orally bioavailable, ATP-competitive, pan–class I phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K) inhibitor discovered through structure-guided medicinal chemistry at Genentech as an optimization beyond early tool compounds and the dual PI3K/mTOR inhibitor PI-103, with substantially improved selectivity for class I PI3Ks and favorable pharmacokinetics (PK) suitable for systemic dosing in humans (Garces, n.d.; Zhao et al., 2017; Li et al., 2024). At the biochemical level, pictilisib exhibits low-nanomolar potency against p110α and p110δ, with activity across class I isoforms (representative IC₅₀s: α ≈ 3 nM, β ≈ 33 nM, δ ≈ 3 nM, γ ≈ 75 nM) and weak activity on mTOR (~0.58 μM), consistent with selective targeting of class I PI3Ks over mTOR kinase (Huang et al., 2023; Garces, n.d.; Josephs & Sarker, 2016; Zhao et al., 2017). Co-crystal structural analysis shows an ATP-mimetic thieno[3,2-d]pyrimidine core in which the morpholine oxygen donates a hinge hydrogen bond (Val882), the indazole engages an affinity pocket (Asp841/Tyr867), and a methanesulfonyl-piperazine tail projects toward solvent; these interactions underpin its potency and selectivity within the class I PI3K ATP site (PDB 3DBS) (Garces, n.d.). Pictilisib belongs to the pan-class I PI3K inhibitor class, a therapeutic category widely advanced in oncology to suppress the PI3K→AKT→mTOR signaling axis that governs cell growth, survival, and metabolism; multiple agents in this class have reached clinical testing or approval, providing a clear translational precedent for pathway engagement and safety management in humans (Schmitz et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2023; Li et al., 2024).

Therapeutic History  
The development history of pictilisib is anchored in oncology, where first-in-human Phase I trials established a recommended Phase II dose of 330 mg once daily, dose-proportional PK (Tₘₐₓ ≈ 2 h, t₁/₂ ≈ 13–24 h), and robust pharmacodynamic (PD) target engagement—up to ~90% inhibition of phosphorylated AKT (Ser473) in platelet-rich plasma within 1–3 h of dosing and suppression of p-AKT and p-S6 in tumor biopsies at sufficient exposure (AUC > 20 μM·h) (Sarker et al., 2015; Mishra et al., 2021). Across Phase I combination studies, pictilisib showed a manageable safety profile and some antitumor activity, with common adverse events including nausea, diarrhea, rash, fatigue, hyperglycemia, and cytopenias; dose-limiting toxicity in some settings was grade 3 maculopapular rash (Mishra et al., 2021; Josephs & Sarker, 2016; Sarker et al., 2015). Although pathway suppression was clear, randomized combination trials in breast and lung cancer variably met efficacy endpoints and broader development was limited by tolerability in multi-drug regimens and modest efficacy as monotherapy—experience that nonetheless provides clinically validated PK/PD tools and class-effect safety benchmarks (Mishra et al., 2021; Gao et al., 2017).

No preclinical or clinical use of pictilisib or other class I PI3K inhibitors has been reported for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or RPE-centered retinal disease models in the provided literature, and a recent review emphasizes that no ongoing clinical trials directly target autophagy in AMD, underscoring an evidence gap for PI3K inhibitors in this indication (Blasiak et al., 2025). By contrast, direct downstream pathway modulation in RPE—mTORC1 inhibition with rapamycin—has shown that activating the lysosome–TFEB axis reduces POS-derived autofluorescent granules in vitro in a hydrolase-dependent manner, but clinical testing in advanced AMD returned limited efficacy and adverse effects, illustrating both the mechanistic plausibility of modulating this pathway and translational challenges (Falcão et al., 2024). Collectively, the therapeutic history supports that class I PI3K inhibitors achieve systemic PI3K pathway inhibition in humans with tractable but nontrivial toxicities; however, there is no published RPE- or AMD-focused body of work with pictilisib to date in the provided context (Sarker et al., 2015; Mishra et al., 2021; Blasiak et al., 2025).

Mechanism of Action  
Class I PI3Ks phosphorylate PIP₂ to PIP₃, recruiting PH-domain effectors including PDK1 and AKT to the plasma membrane, where AKT is activated by phosphorylation at Thr308 (PDK1) and Ser473 (mTORC2) (Huang et al., 2023). Activated AKT phosphorylates multiple substrates that converge on mTORC1 activation (via TSC2/PRAS40), leading to phosphorylation of S6K1 and 4E-BP1 to promote protein synthesis and suppress autophagy, thereby integrating growth-factor status with anabolic programs (Huang et al., 2023; Castel et al., 2021). In retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), AKT/mTOR signaling is an established regulator of cell proliferation and autophagy; mTORC1 activation inhibits autophagy by blocking ULK1 signaling and autolysosomal biogenesis, whereas rapamycin-mediated mTORC1 inhibition activates autophagy and preserves photoreceptor function in preclinical models (Chang et al., 2015). PI3K inhibition upstream of AKT is thus expected to reduce PIP₃ generation, limit AKT membrane recruitment/activation, and secondarily depress mTORC1 signaling in RPE (Castel et al., 2021; Chang et al., 2015).

PI3K→AKT signaling intersects directly with TFEB/TFE3—the master transcription factors of lysosomal biogenesis and the CLEAR regulon—through both mTORC1-dependent and mTORC1-independent routes (Falcão et al., 2024; Ghosh et al., 2024). Nutrient-driven mTORC1 activity at the lysosome phosphorylates TFEB/TFE3 to retain them in the cytosol; conversely, mTORC1 inhibition permits TFEB nuclear translocation and induction of lysosomal/autophagy genes (Falcão et al., 2024). Importantly, AKT2 directly phosphorylates TFEB (at Ser467) and TFE3 (Ser321), promoting 14-3-3 binding and cytoplasmic sequestration independent of mTORC1, thereby repressing CLEAR gene expression and lysosomal programs in RPE (Ghosh et al., 2023; Ghosh et al., 2024). In AMD-relevant contexts—human dysmorphic macular RPE, CFH risk-allele iPSC-RPE, and Akt2 RPE-specific knock-in mice—AKT2 upregulation increases TFEB/TFE3 phosphorylation, reduces lysosomal hydrolases (cathepsin D/L) and CLEAR target expression, impairs autophagic flux, and shifts autophagy toward secretory pathways characterized by increased FKBP51/SNAP23, autophagosome fusion with the plasma membrane, and extracellular release of IL-1β/HMGB1 (Ghosh et al., 2023; Ghosh et al., 2024). TFEB rescue via a phospho-deficient TFEB-S467A mutant or pharmacologic TFEB activation with trehalose restores cathepsin D/L and autophagy genes, normalizes autophagosome–lysosome fusion, and improves RPE structure in AMD-like mouse models, establishing TFEB/TFE3 as actionable nodes downstream of AKT2 in RPE (Ghosh et al., 2023; Ghosh et al., 2024).

SIRT5 and mitochondrial metabolism integrate with AKT2–TFEB signaling in RPE. SIRT5 interacts with AKT2 and reduces lysine malonylation on AKT2, modulating AKT2 activity; AKT2, via inhibition of PGC-1α, downregulates SIRT5, creating a bidirectional circuit that affects TFEB-dependent lysosomal function and mitochondrial respiration (Ghosh et al., 2023). AKT2 upregulation impairs mitochondrial respiration (maximal and ATP-linked), which is rescued by SIRT5, linking mitochondrial–lysosomal crosstalk to RPE proteostasis (Ghosh et al., 2023). Functionally, failure of the AKT2/SIRT5/TFEB axis elevates secretory autophagy and likely contributes to drusen pathogenesis by exporting inflammatory cargo (Ghosh et al., 2023).

These mechanistic data converge with mTORC1→TFEB observations in POS-fed RPE models. Synchronous POS phagocytosis transiently activates mTORC1 early, with TFEB protein increasing but remaining phosphorylated during late maturation, indicating a bottleneck at TFEB activation (Falcão et al., 2024). Pharmacologic mTORC1 inhibition with rapamycin after AFGs have formed lowers POS-derived autofluorescence by ~30% in hfRPE/ARPE-19, reduces pS6, decreases the pTFEB/TFEB ratio, increases LAMP1, and requires active lysosomal hydrolases: cathepsin D knockout or protease/lipase inhibition abolishes the rapamycin effect (Falcão et al., 2024). Human AMD RPE exhibits hyperphosphorylated TFEB with decreased nuclear localization and lower cathepsin D/L protein levels and activities, consistent with impaired lysosome proteolysis; constitutively active TFEB boosts CLEAR genes, including hydrolases and V-ATPase subunits (e.g., ATP6V0A1), supporting enhanced acidification capacity (Falcão et al., 2025).

Pictilisib’s proximal pharmacology—ATP-competitive inhibition of class I PI3Ks—has been shown to produce substantial pathway suppression in human tissues (reduced pAKT, reduced pS6) and in tumor models; such upstream inhibition is expected to depress both AKT→mTORC1 signaling and AKT2-mediated TFEB phosphorylation, potentially enabling TFEB/TFE3 nuclear translocation and restoration of CLEAR programs in RPE (Sarker et al., 2015; Mishra et al., 2021; Castel et al., 2021; Ghosh et al., 2024). Two caveats are central. First, class III PI3K/VPS34 activity is required for autophagosome nucleation; thus class I–selective inhibition (as with pictilisib) is mechanistically appropriate, whereas class III inhibition would be detrimental to autophagy flux (Wang et al., 2023). Second, while AKT inhibitors (e.g., MK-2206) and TFEB activators (trehalose) have directly increased autophagy and TFEB nuclear translocation in RPE, no direct evidence of class I PI3K inhibitors reproducing these effects in RPE has been reported in the provided literature (Karim et al., 2020; Blasiak et al., 2025).

Expected Effect  
In RPE cell assays designed to model dry AMD–relevant lysosomal stress (e.g., POS feeding, A2E/oxidant exposure, or CFH risk-allele iPSC-RPE), pictilisib is expected to reduce PI3K-dependent PIP₃ generation, lowering membrane recruitment and phosphorylation of AKT, thereby secondarily suppressing mTORC1 and directly relieving AKT2-mediated phosphorylation of TFEB/TFE3 (Huang et al., 2023; Castel et al., 2021; Ghosh et al., 2024). Mechanistically, this should dephosphorylate TFEB/TFE3, promote nuclear translocation, and activate the CLEAR transcriptional program to increase components of lysosomal biogenesis and function (e.g., LAMP1/2, cathepsin D/L, and V-ATPase subunits), thereby enhancing degradative capacity and autophagic flux (Falcão et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2025; Falcão et al., 2024).

Operationally testable expected effects include:  
• Signaling: decreased pAKT (Ser473) and pS6 (Ser235/236) within hours of dosing in RPE, mirroring PD seen in tumors and platelet-rich plasma in human trials, establishing target engagement (Sarker et al., 2015; Mishra et al., 2021).  
• TFEB/TFE3 activation: reduction in pTFEB/TFEB ratio, increased nuclear TFEB/TFE3, and induction of CLEAR genes; in RPE systems, TFEB activation correlates with increased LAMP1 and rescue of lysosomal hydrolases and autophagy mediators (e.g., ATG9B), as seen upon TFEB S467A expression or trehalose treatment (Falcão et al., 2024; Ghosh et al., 2023; Ghosh et al., 2024).  
• Lysosomal function: increased abundance and maturation of cathepsin D (pro→intermediate→mature chain) and cathepsin L, and improved degradative flux, consistent with observations that AMD RPE shows diminished cathepsin levels/activities and that hydrolase function is required for rapamycin-mediated clearance of POS-derived AFGs (Falcão et al., 2025; Falcão et al., 2024).  
• Autophagic flux: increased LC3-II turnover (± bafilomycin A₁), reduced p62/SQSTM1 accumulation, restored autophagosome–lysosome fusion (e.g., GFP-LC3 and LysoTracker/LAMP1 colocalization), and decreased accumulation of double-membrane autophagosomes on EM, reversing the AKT2-driven flux block (Ghosh et al., 2023; Ghosh et al., 2024).  
• POS-derived autofluorescence: reduction in POS-dependent autofluorescent granules in preventive and resolving paradigms, analogous to mTORC1 inhibition or TFEB activation effects; efficacy will depend on intact lysosomal hydrolase activity (Falcão et al., 2024).  
• Secretory autophagy: decreased FKBP51/SNAP23 elevation, reduced plasma-membrane fusion of autophagosomes, and lower extracellular release of IL-1β and HMGB1 from RPE, mirroring effects seen with SIRT5 co-expression or AKT2 inhibition (Ghosh et al., 2023; Ghosh et al., 2024).  
• Acidification: although lysosomal pH has not been directly measured after class I PI3K inhibition in RPE, TFEB activation increases expression of V-ATPase subunits, and improved hydrolase activities imply normalization of the acidic lumen; direct pH assays (LysoSensor/LysoTracker) should be incorporated because efficacy of rapamycin/TFEB approaches depends on intact lysosomal acid hydrolases (Falcão et al., 2025; Falcão et al., 2024).

These expectations rest on the well-documented presence and dysregulation of the AKT2→TFEB/TFE3→CLEAR axis in RPE and the dependence of POS clearance on mTOR/TFEB-governed lysosomal function (Ghosh et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2024). AKT2 is upregulated in macular RPE from AMD donors and in AMD-like mouse models, and RPE-specific Akt2 overexpression is sufficient to induce AMD-like pathology, supporting target relevance in the cell type and disease context of interest (Ghosh et al., 2023; Ghosh et al., 2024). Because PI3K is upstream of AKT, class I PI3K inhibition should, in principle, reduce AKT2 activity and thereby favor TFEB activation; however, no direct studies in the provided literature demonstrate pictilisib (or any class I PI3K inhibitor) inducing TFEB nuclear translocation or improving cathepsin D maturation/activity in RPE, so these are testable, evidence-generating predictions rather than established facts (Blasiak et al., 2025; Chang et al., 2015; Karim et al., 2020).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Mechanistic alignment with disease biology: Dry AMD features impaired RPE autophagy–lysosome function, diminished cathepsin D/L levels/activities, and TFEB hyperphosphorylation with reduced nuclear TFEB, all of which converge on lysosomal insufficiency and accumulation of lipofuscin-like material and extracellular drusen; upstream PI3K inhibition is a coherent strategy to relieve AKT2- and mTORC1-mediated repression of TFEB/TFE3 and restore CLEAR-driven lysosomal biogenesis and flux (Falcão et al., 2025; Falcão et al., 2024; Ghosh et al., 2024).  
• Drug tractability and translational readiness: Pictilisib achieves robust systemic target engagement in humans (pAKT/pS6 suppression), has well-characterized PK/PD and class-effect safety, and is chemically and biophysically optimized, enabling accelerated preclinical testing and dosage/formulation exploration for ocular delivery or low systemic exposure strategies (Sarker et al., 2015; Mishra et al., 2021; Garces, n.d.).  
• Selectivity profile appropriate for autophagy enhancement: Because autophagosome nucleation requires class III PI3K/VPS34, class I selectivity of pictilisib avoids this liability while suppressing AKT→mTOR signaling and AKT2-dependent TFEB phosphorylation, in contrast to nonselective PI3K inhibition which would be deleterious (Wang et al., 2023; Castel et al., 2021).

Risks and Gaps  
• No direct RPE/AMD data with class I PI3K inhibitors: In contrast to clear benefits from rapamycin and TFEB activation, the literature presented contains no direct evidence that class I PI3K inhibition, or pictilisib specifically, improves TFEB activation/nuclear entry, lysosomal biogenesis, cathepsin D maturation/activity, lysosomal acidification, autophagy flux, or POS handling in RPE; thus, the central hypothesis remains unvalidated experimentally in the disease-relevant cell type (Blasiak et al., 2025; Chang et al., 2015; Falcão et al., 2024). By comparison, AKT inhibition (MK-2206) and trehalose have been shown to increase autophagy and nuclear TFEB in RPE, and AKT2 inhibitors reduced lipid/apoE in CFH(H/H) RPE, but these are not PI3K inhibitors and may differ in cellular selectivity and compensatory signaling (Karim et al., 2020; Ghosh et al., 2024).  
• Complexity of autophagy modulation and context dependence: Autophagy is a double-edged sword with biphasic responses to stress; overactivation or mistimed activation could exacerbate RPE stress or impair other retinal cell types, and some autophagy inhibitors display retinal toxicity (e.g., chloroquine class), emphasizing the need for precise control and safety profiling (Blasiak et al., 2025; Kaarniranta et al., 2013). Rapamycin has shown only limited clinical efficacy in advanced AMD despite mechanistic benefits in vitro, illustrating translational friction between pathway modulation and clinical outcomes (Falcão et al., 2024).  
• Safety, delivery, and exposure management: Systemic class I PI3K inhibition induces hyperglycemia, rash, and gastrointestinal toxicities; while these were generally manageable, ocular delivery strategies (intravitreal or periocular) and ocular pharmacokinetics for pictilisib are uncharacterized in the provided literature, and tissue-specific PD (e.g., drug levels at the RPE/Bruch’s complex) is likely to determine efficacy and safety (Josephs & Sarker, 2016; Sarker et al., 2015; Mishra et al., 2021). Tissue PD variability seen in tumors versus blood suggests careful intratissue PD assays are necessary (Sarker et al., 2015).  
• Isoform and cell-type specificity: AKT2 is the isoform implicated in RPE TFEB repression and secretory autophagy; upstream PI3K isoform contributions in RPE are not defined here, and pan-class I inhibition could affect neighboring retinal cells, choroidal endothelium, and immune cells, potentially altering retinal immunity and angiogenesis in unintended ways (Ghosh et al., 2024; Castel et al., 2021). Given the evidence favoring AKT2-selective inhibition or direct TFEB activation in RPE models, PI3K-level intervention may be broader than necessary and carry off-target tissue consequences (Ghosh et al., 2024; Karim et al., 2020).  
• Acidification endpoint uncertainty: The hypothesis specifically posits enhanced lysosomal acidification, yet none of the provided sources report direct lysosomal pH measurements after class I PI3K inhibition in RPE; while CLEAR induction can increase V-ATPase subunits and rapamycin-mediated clearance requires active hydrolases, direct acidification effects remain to be demonstrated (Falcão et al., 2025; Falcão et al., 2024; Blasiak et al., 2025).

Go/No-Go Evidence Plan  
Given the strong mechanistic rationale but absence of direct RPE data, a staged validation program is warranted:  
– In vitro RPE target engagement and TFEB activation: Demonstrate pictilisib decreases pAKT (Ser473) and pS6 in primary human fetal RPE, ARPE-19, and iPSC-RPE, and increases nuclear TFEB/TFE3 with induction of CLEAR genes (CTSD, CTSL, LAMP2, ATP6V0A1) assessed by Western, RT-qPCR, and ChIP-qPCR (Falcão et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2025; Ghosh et al., 2024).  
– Lysosome function readouts: Quantify cathepsin D maturation and enzymatic activity, LAMP1/2 abundance, and lysosomal pH using ratiometric probes; include hydrolase inhibition controls to assess dependence analogous to the rapamycin data (Falcão et al., 2024).  
– Autophagic flux and modality: Assess LC3-II turnover (± bafilomycin A₁), p62 dynamics, autolysosome number (LC3–LAMP1 colocalization), and EM confirmation; evaluate secretory-autophagy markers (FKBP51, SNAP23) and extracellular cargo (HMGB1, IL-1β) to test reversal of the AKT2-driven phenotype (Ghosh et al., 2023; Ghosh et al., 2024).  
– Functional disease readouts: Test POS-dependent autofluorescence reduction in preventive and resolving paradigms and POS degradation assays; evaluate lipid/apoE accumulation in CFH(H/H) iPSC-RPE and Cryba1 cKO explants to compare with reported trehalose and AKT2 inhibitor effects (Falcão et al., 2024; Ghosh et al., 2023; Ghosh et al., 2024).  
– In vivo and delivery: Establish ocular PK and tolerability for local delivery (intravitreal/periocular) in rodents, then test efficacy in RPE-driven AMD-like models (Akt2 KI, Cryba1 cKO, NaIO₃) with TFEB activation, lysosomal and functional endpoints (ERG/SD-OCT) (Ghosh et al., 2024; Ghosh et al., 2023; Falcão et al., 2025).  
– Benchmarking: Include rapamycin (mTORC1 inhibition), MK-2206 (AKT inhibition), and trehalose (mTOR-independent TFEB activation) comparators to position PI3K inhibition within the therapeutic landscape (Falcão et al., 2024; Karim et al., 2020; Ghosh et al., 2023).

Conclusion  
Pictilisib offers a mechanistically coherent, drug-like approach to modulate an RPE pathway of clear pathogenic relevance—AKT2/mTOR-mediated repression of TFEB/TFE3 and the CLEAR network—backed by robust human PK/PD experience and a selectivity profile compatible with enhancing autophagy without impeding VPS34-dependent nucleation (Ghosh et al., 2024; Sarker et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2023). However, the absence of direct evidence that class I PI3K inhibition rectifies TFEB activity, lysosomal hydrolase function (notably cathepsin D), lysosomal acidification, autophagic flux, or POS clearance in RPE is a critical gap that precludes immediate advancement; by contrast, downstream interventions (rapamycin, TFEB activation, AKT2 inhibition) already demonstrate these benefits in RPE models (Falcão et al., 2024; Ghosh et al., 2024). On balance, pictilisib is plausible and testable but not yet justified for translational progression without focused RPE and ocular studies; an AKT2-selective inhibitor or TFEB-directed strategies may offer a higher probability of effect with narrower network perturbation, and should be run in parallel as mechanistic benchmarks (Ghosh et al., 2024; Karim et al., 2020). If the proposed RPE experiments confirm that pictilisib restores TFEB-driven lysosomal programs, improves cathepsin D maturation/activity, normalizes autophagy flux, and reduces POS-derived autofluorescence with acceptable ocular tolerability, the candidate would merit advancement to in vivo ocular efficacy testing; absent such confirmation, resources should pivot to agents with demonstrated RPE TFEB engagement (Ghosh et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2024).
