Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
GDC-0941 (pictilisib) is a synthetic, orally bioavailable, ATP-competitive, pan–class I phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K) inhibitor discovered through structure-guided medicinal chemistry at Genentech as an optimization beyond early tool compounds and the dual PI3K/mTOR inhibitor PI-103, with substantially improved selectivity for class I PI3Ks and favorable pharmacokinetics (PK) suitable for systemic dosing in humans (Garces, n.d.; Zhao et al., 2017; Li et al., 2024). At the biochemical level, pictilisib exhibits low-nanomolar potency against p110α and p110δ, with activity across class I isoforms (representative IC₅₀s: α ≈ 3 nM, β ≈ 33 nM, δ ≈ 3 nM, γ ≈ 75 nM) and weak activity on mTOR (~0.58 μM), consistent with selective targeting of class I PI3Ks over mTOR kinase (Huang et al., 2023; Garces, n.d.; Josephs & Sarker, 2016; Zhao et al., 2017). Co-crystal structural analysis shows an ATP-mimetic thieno[3,2-d]pyrimidine core in which the morpholine oxygen donates a hinge hydrogen bond (Val882), the indazole engages an affinity pocket (Asp841/Tyr867), and a methanesulfonyl-piperazine tail projects toward solvent; these interactions underpin its potency and selectivity within the class I PI3K ATP site (PDB 3DBS) (Garces, n.d.). Pictilisib belongs to the pan-class I PI3K inhibitor class, a therapeutic category widely advanced in oncology to suppress the PI3K→AKT→mTOR signaling axis that governs cell growth, survival, and metabolism; multiple agents in this class have reached clinical testing or approval, providing a clear translational precedent for pathway engagement and safety management in humans (Schmitz et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2023; Li et al., 2024).

Therapeutic History  
The development history of pictilisib is anchored in oncology, where first-in-human Phase I trials established a recommended Phase II dose of 330 mg once daily, dose-proportional PK (Tₘₐₓ ≈ 2 h, t₁/₂ ≈ 13–24 h), and robust pharmacodynamic (PD) target engagement—up to ~90% inhibition of phosphorylated AKT (Ser473) in platelet-rich plasma within 1–3 h of dosing and suppression of p-AKT and p-S6 in tumor biopsies at sufficient exposure (AUC > 20 μM·h) (Sarker et al., 2015; Mishra et al., 2021). Across Phase I combination studies, pictilisib showed a manageable safety profile and some antitumor activity, with common adverse events including nausea, diarrhea, rash, fatigue, hyperglycemia, and cytopenias; dose-limiting toxicity in some settings was grade 3 maculopapular rash (Mishra et al., 2021; Josephs & Sarker, 2016; Sarker et al., 2015). Although pathway suppression was clear, randomized combination trials in breast and lung cancer variably met efficacy endpoints and broader development was limited by tolerability in multi-drug regimens and modest efficacy as monotherapy—experience that nonetheless provides clinically validated PK/PD tools and class-effect safety benchmarks (Mishra et al., 2021; Gao et al., 2017).

No preclinical or clinical use of pictilisib or other class I PI3K inhibitors has been reported for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or RPE-centered retinal disease models in the provided literature, and a recent review emphasizes that no ongoing clinical trials directly target autophagy in AMD, underscoring an evidence gap for PI3K inhibitors in this indication (Blasiak et al., 2025). By contrast, direct downstream pathway modulation in RPE—mTORC1 inhibition with rapamycin—has shown that activating the lysosome–TFEB axis reduces POS-derived autofluorescent granules in vitro in a hydrolase-dependent manner, but clinical testing in advanced AMD returned limited efficacy and adverse effects, illustrating both the mechanistic plausibility of modulating this pathway and translational challenges (Falcão et al., 2024). Collectively, the therapeutic history supports that class I PI3K inhibitors achieve systemic PI3K pathway inhibition in humans with tractable but nontrivial toxicities; however, there is no published RPE- or AMD-focused body of work with pictilisib to date in the provided context (Sarker et al., 2015; Mishra et al., 2021; Blasiak et al., 2025).

Mechanism of Action  
Class I PI3Ks phosphorylate PIP₂ to PIP₃, recruiting PH-domain effectors including PDK1 and AKT to the plasma membrane, where AKT is activated by phosphorylation at Thr308 (PDK1) and Ser473 (mTORC2) (Huang et al., 2023). Activated AKT phosphorylates multiple substrates that converge on mTORC1 activation (via TSC2/PRAS40), leading to phosphorylation of S6K1 and 4E-BP1 to promote protein synthesis and suppress autophagy, thereby integrating growth-factor status with anabolic programs (Huang et al., 2023; Castel et al., 2021). In retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), AKT/mTOR signaling is an established regulator of cell proliferation and autophagy; mTORC1 activation inhibits autophagy by blocking ULK1 signaling and autolysosomal biogenesis, whereas rapamycin-mediated mTORC1 inhibition activates autophagy and preserves photoreceptor function in preclinical models (Chang et al., 2015). PI3K inhibition upstream of AKT is thus expected to reduce PIP₃ generation, limit AKT membrane recruitment/activation, and secondarily depress mTORC1 signaling in RPE (Castel et al., 2021; Chang et al., 2015).

PI3K→AKT signaling intersects directly with TFEB/TFE3—the master transcription factors of lysosomal biogenesis and the CLEAR regulon—through both mTORC1-dependent and mTORC1-independent routes (Falcão et al., 2024; Ghosh et al., 2024). Nutrient-driven mTORC1 activity at the lysosome phosphorylates TFEB/TFE3 to retain them in the cytosol; conversely, mTORC1 inhibition permits TFEB nuclear translocation and induction of lysosomal/autophagy genes (Falcão et al., 2024). Importantly, AKT2 directly phosphorylates TFEB (at Ser467) and TFE3 (Ser321), promoting 14-3-3 binding and cytoplasmic sequestration independent of mTORC1, thereby repressing CLEAR gene expression and lysosomal programs in RPE (Ghosh et al., 2023; Ghosh et al., 2024). In AMD-relevant contexts—human dysmorphic macular RPE, CFH risk-allele iPSC-RPE, and Akt2 RPE-specific knock-in mice—AKT2 upregulation increases TFEB/TFE3 phosphorylation, reduces lysosomal hydrolases (cathepsin D/L) and CLEAR target expression, impairs autophagic flux, and shifts autophagy toward secretory pathways characterized by increased FKBP51/SNAP23, autophagosome fusion with the plasma membrane, and extracellular release of IL-1β/HMGB1 (Ghosh et al., 2023; Ghosh et al., 2024). TFEB rescue via a phospho-deficient TFEB-S467A mutant or pharmacologic TFEB activation with trehalose restores cathepsin D/L and autophagy genes, normalizes autophagosome–lysosome fusion, and improves RPE structure in AMD-like mouse models, establishing TFEB/TFE3 as actionable nodes downstream of AKT2 in RPE (Ghosh et al., 2023; Ghosh et al., 2024).

SIRT5 and mitochondrial metabolism integrate with AKT2–TFEB signaling in RPE. SIRT5 interacts with AKT2 and reduces lysine malonylation on AKT2, modulating AKT2 activity; AKT2, via inhibition of PGC-1α, downregulates SIRT5, creating a bidirectional circuit that affects TFEB-dependent lysosomal function and mitochondrial respiration (Ghosh et al., 2023). AKT2 upregulation impairs mitochondrial respiration (maximal and ATP-linked), which is rescued by SIRT5, linking mitochondrial–lysosomal crosstalk to RPE proteostasis (Ghosh et al., 2023). Functionally, failure of the AKT2/SIRT5/TFEB axis elevates secretory autophagy and likely contributes to drusen pathogenesis by exporting inflammatory cargo (Ghosh et al., 2023).

These mechanistic data converge with mTORC1→TFEB observations in POS-fed RPE models. Synchronous POS phagocytosis transiently activates mTORC1 early, with TFEB protein increasing but remaining phosphorylated during late maturation, indicating a bottleneck at TFEB activation (Falcão et al., 2024). Pharmacologic mTORC1 inhibition with rapamycin after AFGs have formed lowers POS-derived autofluorescence by ~30% in hfRPE/ARPE-19, reduces pS6, decreases the pTFEB/TFEB ratio, increases LAMP1, and requires active lysosomal hydrolases: cathepsin D knockout or protease/lipase inhibition abolishes the rapamycin effect (Falcão et al., 2024). Human AMD RPE exhibits hyperphosphorylated TFEB with decreased nuclear localization and lower cathepsin D/L protein levels and activities, consistent with impaired lysosome proteolysis; constitutively active TFEB boosts CLEAR genes, including hydrolases and V-ATPase subunits (e.g., ATP6V0A1), supporting enhanced acidification capacity (Falcão et al., 2025).

Pictilisib’s proximal pharmacology—ATP-competitive inhibition of class I PI3Ks—has been shown to produce substantial pathway suppression in human tissues (reduced pAKT, reduced pS6) and in tumor models; such upstream inhibition is expected to depress both AKT→mTORC1 signaling and AKT2-mediated TFEB phosphorylation, potentially enabling TFEB/TFE3 nuclear translocation and restoration of CLEAR programs in RPE (Sarker et al., 2015; Mishra et al., 2021; Castel et al., 2021; Ghosh et al., 2024). Two caveats are central. First, class III PI3K/VPS34 activity is required for autophagosome nucleation; thus class I–selective inhibition (as with pictilisib) is mechanistically appropriate, whereas class III inhibition would be detrimental to autophagy flux (Wang et al., 2023). Second, while AKT inhibitors (e.g., MK-2206) and TFEB activators (trehalose) have directly increased autophagy and TFEB nuclear translocation in RPE, no direct evidence of class I PI3K inhibitors reproducing these effects in RPE has been reported in the provided literature (Karim et al., 2020; Blasiak et al., 2025).

Expected Effect  
In RPE cell assays designed to model dry AMD–relevant lysosomal stress (e.g., POS feeding, A2E/oxidant exposure, or CFH risk-allele iPSC-RPE), pictilisib is expected to reduce PI3K-dependent PIP₃ generation, lowering membrane recruitment and phosphorylation of AKT, thereby secondarily suppressing mTORC1 and directly relieving AKT2-mediated phosphorylation of TFEB/TFE3 (Huang et al., 2023; Castel et al., 2021; Ghosh et al., 2024). Mechanistically, this should dephosphorylate TFEB/TFE3, promote nuclear translocation, and activate the CLEAR transcriptional program to increase components of lysosomal biogenesis and function (e.g., LAMP1/2, cathepsin D/L, and V-ATPase subunits), thereby enhancing degradative capacity and autophagic flux (Falcão et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2025; Falcão et al., 2024).

Operationally testable expected effects include:  
• Signaling: decreased pAKT (Ser473) and pS6 (Ser235/236) within hours of dosing in RPE, mirroring PD seen in tumors and platelet-rich plasma in human trials, establishing target engagement (Sarker et al., 2015; Mishra et al., 2021).  
• TFEB/TFE3 activation: reduction in pTFEB/TFEB ratio, increased nuclear TFEB/TFE3, and induction of CLEAR genes; in RPE systems, TFEB activation correlates with increased LAMP1 and rescue of lysosomal hydrolases and autophagy mediators (e.g., ATG9B), as seen upon TFEB S467A expression or trehalose treatment (Falcão et al., 2024; Ghosh et al., 2023; Ghosh et al., 2024).  
• Lysosomal function: increased abundance and maturation of cathepsin D (pro→intermediate→mature chain) and cathepsin L, and improved degradative flux, consistent with observations that AMD RPE shows diminished cathepsin levels/activities and that hydrolase function is required for rapamycin-mediated clearance of POS-derived AFGs (Falcão et al., 2025; Falcão et al., 2024).  
• Autophagic flux: increased LC3-II turnover (± bafilomycin A₁), reduced p62/SQSTM1 accumulation, restored autophagosome–lysosome fusion (e.g., GFP-LC3 and LysoTracker/LAMP1 colocalization), and decreased accumulation of double-membrane autophagosomes on EM, reversing the AKT2-driven flux block (Ghosh et al., 2023; Ghosh et al., 2024).  
• POS-derived autofluorescence: reduction in POS-dependent autofluorescent granules in preventive and resolving paradigms, analogous to mTORC1 inhibition or TFEB activation effects; efficacy will depend on intact lysosomal hydrolase activity (Falcão et al., 2024).  
• Secretory autophagy: decreased FKBP51/SNAP23 elevation, reduced plasma-membrane fusion of autophagosomes, and lower extracellular release of IL-1β and HMGB1 from RPE, mirroring effects seen with SIRT5 co-expression or AKT2 inhibition (Ghosh et al., 2023; Ghosh et al., 2024).  
• Acidification: although lysosomal pH has not been directly measured after class I PI3K inhibition in RPE, TFEB activation increases expression of V-ATPase subunits, and improved hydrolase activities imply normalization of the acidic lumen; direct pH assays (LysoSensor/LysoTracker) should be incorporated because efficacy of rapamycin/TFEB approaches depends on intact lysosomal acid hydrolases (Falcão et al., 2025; Falcão et al., 2024).

These expectations rest on the well-documented presence and dysregulation of the AKT2→TFEB/TFE3→CLEAR axis in RPE and the dependence of POS clearance on mTOR/TFEB-governed lysosomal function (Ghosh et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2024). AKT2 is upregulated in macular RPE from AMD donors and in AMD-like mouse models, and RPE-specific Akt2 overexpression is sufficient to induce AMD-like pathology, supporting target relevance in the cell type and disease context of interest (Ghosh et al., 2023; Ghosh et al., 2024). Because PI3K is upstream of AKT, class I PI3K inhibition should, in principle, reduce AKT2 activity and thereby favor TFEB activation; however, no direct studies in the provided literature demonstrate pictilisib (or any class I PI3K inhibitor) inducing TFEB nuclear translocation or improving cathepsin D maturation/activity in RPE, so these are testable, evidence-generating predictions rather than established facts (Blasiak et al., 2025; Chang et al., 2015; Karim et al., 2020).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Mechanistic alignment with disease biology: Dry AMD features impaired RPE autophagy–lysosome function, diminished cathepsin D/L levels/activities, and TFEB hyperphosphorylation with reduced nuclear TFEB, all of which converge on lysosomal insufficiency and accumulation of lipofuscin-like material and extracellular drusen; upstream PI3K inhibition is a coherent strategy to relieve AKT2- and mTORC1-mediated repression of TFEB/TFE3 and restore CLEAR-driven lysosomal biogenesis and flux (Falcão et al., 2025; Falcão et al., 2024; Ghosh et al., 2024).  
• Drug tractability and translational readiness: Pictilisib achieves robust systemic target engagement in humans (pAKT/pS6 suppression), has well-characterized PK/PD and class-effect safety, and is chemically and biophysically optimized, enabling accelerated preclinical testing and dosage/formulation exploration for ocular delivery or low systemic exposure strategies (Sarker et al., 2015; Mishra et al., 2021; Garces, n.d.).  
• Selectivity profile appropriate for autophagy enhancement: Because autophagosome nucleation requires class III PI3K/VPS34, class I selectivity of pictilisib avoids this liability while suppressing AKT→mTOR signaling and AKT2-dependent TFEB phosphorylation, in contrast to nonselective PI3K inhibition which would be deleterious (Wang et al., 2023; Castel et al., 2021).

Risks and Gaps  
• No direct RPE/AMD data with class I PI3K inhibitors: In contrast to clear benefits from rapamycin and TFEB activation, the literature presented contains no direct evidence that class I PI3K inhibition, or pictilisib specifically, improves TFEB activation/nuclear entry, lysosomal biogenesis, cathepsin D maturation/activity, lysosomal acidification, autophagy flux, or POS handling in RPE; thus, the central hypothesis remains unvalidated experimentally in the disease-relevant cell type (Blasiak et al., 2025; Chang et al., 2015; Falcão et al., 2024). By comparison, AKT inhibition (MK-2206) and trehalose have been shown to increase autophagy and nuclear TFEB in RPE, and AKT2 inhibitors reduced lipid/apoE in CFH(H/H) RPE, but these are not PI3K inhibitors and may differ in cellular selectivity and compensatory signaling (Karim et al., 2020; Ghosh et al., 2024).  
• Complexity of autophagy modulation and context dependence: Autophagy is a double-edged sword with biphasic responses to stress; overactivation or mistimed activation could exacerbate RPE stress or impair other retinal cell types, and some autophagy inhibitors display retinal toxicity (e.g., chloroquine class), emphasizing the need for precise control and safety profiling (Blasiak et al., 2025; Kaarniranta et al., 2013). Rapamycin has shown only limited clinical efficacy in advanced AMD despite mechanistic benefits in vitro, illustrating translational friction between pathway modulation and clinical outcomes (Falcão et al., 2024).  
• Safety, delivery, and exposure management: Systemic class I PI3K inhibition induces hyperglycemia, rash, and gastrointestinal toxicities; while these were generally manageable, ocular delivery strategies (intravitreal or periocular) and ocular pharmacokinetics for pictilisib are uncharacterized in the provided literature, and tissue-specific PD (e.g., drug levels at the RPE/Bruch’s complex) is likely to determine efficacy and safety (Josephs & Sarker, 2016; Sarker et al., 2015; Mishra et al., 2021). Tissue PD variability seen in tumors versus blood suggests careful intratissue PD assays are necessary (Sarker et al., 2015).  
• Isoform and cell-type specificity: AKT2 is the isoform implicated in RPE TFEB repression and secretory autophagy; upstream PI3K isoform contributions in RPE are not defined here, and pan-class I inhibition could affect neighboring retinal cells, choroidal endothelium, and immune cells, potentially altering retinal immunity and angiogenesis in unintended ways (Ghosh et al., 2024; Castel et al., 2021). Given the evidence favoring AKT2-selective inhibition or direct TFEB activation in RPE models, PI3K-level intervention may be broader than necessary and carry off-target tissue consequences (Ghosh et al., 2024; Karim et al., 2020).  
• Acidification endpoint uncertainty: The hypothesis specifically posits enhanced lysosomal acidification, yet none of the provided sources report direct lysosomal pH measurements after class I PI3K inhibition in RPE; while CLEAR induction can increase V-ATPase subunits and rapamycin-mediated clearance requires active hydrolases, direct acidification effects remain to be demonstrated (Falcão et al., 2025; Falcão et al., 2024; Blasiak et al., 2025).

Go/No-Go Evidence Plan  
Given the strong mechanistic rationale but absence of direct RPE data, a staged validation program is warranted:  
– In vitro RPE target engagement and TFEB activation: Demonstrate pictilisib decreases pAKT (Ser473) and pS6 in primary human fetal RPE, ARPE-19, and iPSC-RPE, and increases nuclear TFEB/TFE3 with induction of CLEAR genes (CTSD, CTSL, LAMP2, ATP6V0A1) assessed by Western, RT-qPCR, and ChIP-qPCR (Falcão et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2025; Ghosh et al., 2024).  
– Lysosome function readouts: Quantify cathepsin D maturation and enzymatic activity, LAMP1/2 abundance, and lysosomal pH using ratiometric probes; include hydrolase inhibition controls to assess dependence analogous to the rapamycin data (Falcão et al., 2024).  
– Autophagic flux and modality: Assess LC3-II turnover (± bafilomycin A₁), p62 dynamics, autolysosome number (LC3–LAMP1 colocalization), and EM confirmation; evaluate secretory-autophagy markers (FKBP51, SNAP23) and extracellular cargo (HMGB1, IL-1β) to test reversal of the AKT2-driven phenotype (Ghosh et al., 2023; Ghosh et al., 2024).  
– Functional disease readouts: Test POS-dependent autofluorescence reduction in preventive and resolving paradigms and POS degradation assays; evaluate lipid/apoE accumulation in CFH(H/H) iPSC-RPE and Cryba1 cKO explants to compare with reported trehalose and AKT2 inhibitor effects (Falcão et al., 2024; Ghosh et al., 2023; Ghosh et al., 2024).  
– In vivo and delivery: Establish ocular PK and tolerability for local delivery (intravitreal/periocular) in rodents, then test efficacy in RPE-driven AMD-like models (Akt2 KI, Cryba1 cKO, NaIO₃) with TFEB activation, lysosomal and functional endpoints (ERG/SD-OCT) (Ghosh et al., 2024; Ghosh et al., 2023; Falcão et al., 2025).  
– Benchmarking: Include rapamycin (mTORC1 inhibition), MK-2206 (AKT inhibition), and trehalose (mTOR-independent TFEB activation) comparators to position PI3K inhibition within the therapeutic landscape (Falcão et al., 2024; Karim et al., 2020; Ghosh et al., 2023).

Conclusion  
Pictilisib offers a mechanistically coherent, drug-like approach to modulate an RPE pathway of clear pathogenic relevance—AKT2/mTOR-mediated repression of TFEB/TFE3 and the CLEAR network—backed by robust human PK/PD experience and a selectivity profile compatible with enhancing autophagy without impeding VPS34-dependent nucleation (Ghosh et al., 2024; Sarker et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2023). However, the absence of direct evidence that class I PI3K inhibition rectifies TFEB activity, lysosomal hydrolase function (notably cathepsin D), lysosomal acidification, autophagic flux, or POS clearance in RPE is a critical gap that precludes immediate advancement; by contrast, downstream interventions (rapamycin, TFEB activation, AKT2 inhibition) already demonstrate these benefits in RPE models (Falcão et al., 2024; Ghosh et al., 2024). On balance, pictilisib is plausible and testable but not yet justified for translational progression without focused RPE and ocular studies; an AKT2-selective inhibitor or TFEB-directed strategies may offer a higher probability of effect with narrower network perturbation, and should be run in parallel as mechanistic benchmarks (Ghosh et al., 2024; Karim et al., 2020). If the proposed RPE experiments confirm that pictilisib restores TFEB-driven lysosomal programs, improves cathepsin D maturation/activity, normalizes autophagy flux, and reduces POS-derived autofluorescence with acceptable ocular tolerability, the candidate would merit advancement to in vivo ocular efficacy testing; absent such confirmation, resources should pivot to agents with demonstrated RPE TFEB engagement (Ghosh et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2024).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
ZLN005 is a synthetic, small-molecule benzimidazole identified by high-throughput screening of ~48,000 compounds using a HEK293 cell line harboring a human PGC-1α promoter–driven luciferase reporter; it was selected for its ability to transcriptionally induce the Ppargc1a (PGC-1α) gene and validated in follow-up orthogonal assays and cell types (Zhang et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2021). Chemically, ZLN005 is 2-(4-tert-butylphenyl)-1H-benzimidazole with a reported molecular weight of 250.3; it is repeatedly described as a “small-molecule PGC-1α transcriptional activator/agonist” and a “specific and selective transcriptional inducer of PGC-1α expression” (Bleckwehl et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2013; Maurice et al., 2022). The initial discovery campaign also yielded a related backbone compound (ZLN027) that showed cytotoxicity, whereas ZLN005 did not under the reported in vitro conditions, and ZLN005 was later found to inhibit luciferases—an assay interference red flag that necessitates careful interpretation of luciferase-based readouts (Zhang et al., 2013).

Pharmacologic class and precedent: ZLN005 belongs to the class of tool/investigational small molecules that transcriptionally upregulate PGC-1α and thereby stimulate mitochondrial biogenesis, oxidative phosphorylation, and fatty-acid oxidation in a tissue-selective fashion (Zhang et al., 2013). This class has been deployed broadly in preclinical systems—skeletal muscle, cardiomyocytes, neurons, kidney, lung epithelium, vascular smooth muscle, and retinal pigment epithelium (RPE)—to probe whether enhancing PGC-1α can restore mitochondrial capacity, reduce oxidative stress, and improve cell/tissue resilience (Zhang et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2020; Xu et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2021; Ma et al., 2023; Zou et al., 2025; Shu et al., 2021). A subset of studies emphasizes that ZLN005 acts upstream of AMPK→PGC-1α/MEF2 transcriptional circuits and engages canonical mitochondrial biogenesis regulators (NRF1/2, TFAM, ERRs), while in some tissues it promotes downstream fatty-acid oxidation via CPT-1α, aligning with the recognized role of PGC-1α as a master coactivator of oxidative metabolism (Zhang et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2020).

Therapeutic History  
ZLN005 has no reported clinical use. Its portfolio of preclinical applications includes:

- Metabolic disease: In diabetic db/db mice, chronic oral ZLN005 (15 mg/kg/day for 6 weeks) improved glucose tolerance, insulin sensitivity, and dyslipidemia, with induction of PGC-1α and mitochondrial/FAO gene programs in skeletal muscle and reduced hepatic gluconeogenic transcripts; AMPK/ACC phosphorylation rose in muscle but not liver, consistent with tissue selectivity (Zhang et al., 2013). Basic single-dose oral pharmacokinetics in db/db mice showed rapid plasma absorption and high initial liver exposure, with relatively stable muscle exposure over 4 hours (Zhang et al., 2013). A short-term rat safety study (75 mg/kg/day, 14 days) reported survival with no obvious changes in body weight gain or gross metabolic parameters (Zhang et al., 2013).

- Skeletal muscle cells: In L6 myotubes, ZLN005 dose-dependently increased PGC-1α mRNA, glucose uptake, and palmitate oxidation; AMPK and ACC phosphorylation increased, PGC-1α induction was AMPK-dependent (Compound C–sensitive), and MEF2 promoter integrity was required, consistent with a transcriptional mechanism (Zhang et al., 2013).

- Kidney ischemia–reperfusion injury (AKI): In mouse I/R models and H/R-injured renal tubular cells, ZLN005 restored PGC-1α and CPT-1α expression, improved mitochondrial ultrastructure/membrane potential, reduced ROS and lipid peroxidation (H₂O₂, MDA), lessened apoptosis, and required CPT-1α activity for benefit; high concentrations were toxic to HK2 cells (Wang et al., 2021).

- Neuronal injury: ZLN005 improved viability in OGD/R-injured PC12 cells, induced PGC-1α and antioxidant genes (SOD1/HO-1), and post-ischemia administration reduced infarct volume and neurological deficit in rat tMCAO, indicating neuroprotection likely via PGC-1α-driven mitochondrial and antioxidant programs; in a separate study, ZLN005 crossed the blood–brain barrier and protected against PBDE-47 neurotoxicity via PGC-1α-dependent mitochondrial biogenesis (Xu et al., 2018; Tian et al., 2023).

- Cardiomyocytes: In hESC-derived cardiomyocytes, brief ZLN005 exposure (10 μM, 48 h) increased PGC-1α and ERRγ, upregulated mitochondrial biogenesis and OXPHOS/FAO genes (NRF1, TFAM, respiratory subunits, CPT1b), increased mtDNA copy number, basal OCR and ATP, and drove structural/electrophysiological maturation (longer sarcomeres, more negative RMP, enhanced Ca²⁺ handling, increased CX43) (Liu et al., 2020).

- Lung epithelium/infection: In AECs (A549 and primary AEC2), ZLN005 increased PGC-1α and NRF1, improved mitochondrial bioenergetics, membrane potential, ATP, decreased ROS and senescence markers (p21, SA-β-gal), and these effects required PGC-1α (shPGC-1α attenuated benefit); in a P. aeruginosa pneumonia model, ZLN005 pretreatment (15 mg/kg × 3) reduced bacterial load and IL-1β and rescued SIRT3 in lung, consistent with PGC-1α–SIRT3 axis activation (Ma et al., 2023; Maurice et al., 2022).

- Vascular smooth muscle cells: ZLN005 increased PGC-1α, ESRRA, NRF1, mtDNA, and ATP, shifted mitochondrial dynamics toward fusion (↑MFN2, ↓DRP1), and dispersed perinuclear aggregates, indicating enhanced mitochondrial function (Zou et al., 2025).

- Retinal and RPE models: In ARPE-19, ZLN005 robustly increased PGC-1α, upregulated transcription factors, antioxidant enzymes and mitochondrial genes, improved basal/maximal respiration and spare capacity, and protected against oxidative insults (H₂O₂, oxLDL, NaIO₃); protection was PGC-1α-dependent; in primary human RPE (H-RPE), 10 μM ZLN005 selectively induced PGC-1α and blocked TGFβ₂-induced EMT and migration, with smaller fold-change than in ARPE-19 due to higher baseline PGC-1α (Tong et al., 2022; Shu et al., 2021). In ex vivo rd1 retinal explants (inherited photoreceptor degeneration), ZLN005 reduced overall calpain activity, shifted calpain isoform balance toward neuroprotective calpain-1 and away from calpain-2, and enhanced photoreceptor viability, supporting retinal neuroprotection via PGC-1α activation (Wang et al., 2025).

There are no reports that ZLN005 has been tested in dry age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD) animal models, nor direct demonstrations that it improves RPE phagosome clearance, lysosomal acidification, cathepsin D activity, lipofuscin burden, or drusen in AMD contexts; TFEB-targeted rescue of lysosomal function and cathepsin activity in RPE has been achieved with other agents (e.g., trehalose) or genetic TFEB activation, but ZLN005 has not been evaluated in those axes in RPE (Ghosh et al., 2024; Ghosh et al., 2023; Tong et al., 2022; Shu et al., 2021).

Mechanism of Action  
Transcriptional induction of PGC-1α. ZLN005 increases PGC-1α transcription via the PGC-1α promoter, requiring an intact MEF2 binding site; it increases PGC-1α mRNA and protein across multiple cell types where responsive, including myotubes, cardiomyocytes, lung epithelium, VSMCs, and RPE; reliance on MEF2 sites suggests ZLN005 engages upstream signaling and chromatin/transcriptional complexes that drive Ppargc1a expression (Zhang et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2020; Ma et al., 2023; Zou et al., 2025; Shu et al., 2021).

AMPK activation via mild mitochondrial uncoupling. In L6 myotubes, ZLN005 increases the cellular ADP:ATP ratio and mildly increases mitochondrial oxygen consumption in isolated mitochondria, consistent with weak uncoupling that activates AMPK; AMPK and ACC phosphorylation increase, and pharmacologic AMPK inhibition (Compound C) blocks PGC-1α induction and glucose uptake; the pathway is further modeled as AMPK-phosphorylated PGC-1α engaging MEF2C to amplify its own gene expression via positive feedback (Zhang et al., 2013). AMPK-dependence extends functionally: glucose uptake and PGC-1α induction in muscle cells require AMPK activation (Wang et al., 2021).

Downstream PGC-1α programs. Across tissues, ZLN005 induces the canonical PGC-1α program: coactivation of ERRs/PPARs/NRF1/2, upregulation of TFAM, increases in mtDNA copy number, OXPHOS complex gene products, fatty-acid oxidation enzymes (e.g., CPT-1, MCAD), and functional increases in basal/maximal OCR, ATP production, and mitochondrial content/number—data are robust in cardiomyocytes and skeletal muscle, and consistent in lung epithelial cells and RPE (Liu et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2013; Ma et al., 2023; Tong et al., 2022). In kidney I/R, PGC-1α induction by ZLN005 increased CPT-1α, restored mitochondrial FAO, reduced ROS and MDA, and decreased apoptosis; genetic or pharmacologic CPT-1α inhibition abrogated ZLN005 benefit, placing FAO downstream of PGC-1α as a necessary mediator of cytoprotection in that model (Wang et al., 2021).

PGC-1α–SIRT axis and anti-inflammatory effects. In lung infection models, ZLN005 activated the PGC-1α–SIRT3 axis, rescued SIRT3 expression, and lowered IL-1β expression in infected lungs, aligning with the role of SIRT3 in mitochondrial antioxidant function (activation of SOD2, glutathione system) and with PGC-1α’s coactivation of oxidative metabolism and antioxidant defense (Maurice et al., 2022).

Cell-type specificity and paradoxical tissue effects. ZLN005 shows a cell-type- and tissue-selective response: skeletal muscle and diverse non-hepatic cells robustly induce PGC-1α, whereas primary hepatocytes do not; in db/db mice, liver PGC-1α was paradoxically downregulated, with concurrent suppression of gluconeogenic genes, possibly via indirect systemic mechanisms (Zhang et al., 2013). In RPE, primary cells (H-RPE) exhibited modest PGC-1α fold-induction relative to ARPE-19 due to higher baseline PGC-1α expression, yet ZLN005 still blocked TGFβ₂-induced EMT and migration in H-RPE (Shu et al., 2021).

Assay caveats. ZLN005 potently inhibits luciferases, necessitating caution and orthogonal validation for any conclusions drawn from luciferase reporters, including those targeting TFEB/TFE3 or PGC-1α target promoters (Zhang et al., 2013).

Linking to TFEB/lysosomal axis: rationale vs evidence. AMPK primes lysosomal biogenesis and function partly by inducing TFEB/TFE3, while simultaneously regulating mitochondrial biogenesis via PGC-1α; a combined AMPK activation and mTORC1 inhibition strategy has been proposed as superior for mitochondrial disease contexts (Boya et al., 2023). In RPE/retina, genetic and pharmacologic activation of TFEB restores lysosomal hydrolases (CTSD, CTSL), improves autophagosome–lysosome fusion and catabolism, and reduces disease-relevant lipid accumulation; these TFEB-centered effects are well documented in RPE but have not been demonstrated for ZLN005 (Ghosh et al., 2024; Ghosh et al., 2023). Some evidence in non-retinal systems places PGC-1α upstream of TFEB-regulated lysosomal activity (e.g., in Huntington disease models), supporting a conceptual link between mitochondrial biogenesis and lysosomal/autophagy competence; however, ZLN005-specific co-activation of TFEB or enhancement of lysosomal acidification/CTSD in RPE has not been shown (Blasiak et al., 2021).

Expected Effect  
Dry AMD pathobiology—RPE mitochondrial–lysosomal dysfunction. Dry AMD features RPE oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction (mtDNA damage, reduced OXPHOS, fewer/disorganized mitochondria), defective mitophagy, impaired proteostasis, and lysosomal/autophagy defects that promote lipofuscin and drusen biogenesis (Hyttinen et al., 2023; Luján et al., 2022; Felszeghy et al., 2019). PGC-1α is highly expressed in retina/RPE and is a potent regulator of mitochondrial biogenesis and antioxidant defenses in these cells; genetic deficiency of PGC-1α (especially combined with NRF2 loss) fosters RPE degeneration with proteostatic/lysosomal stress reminiscent of dry AMD (Felszeghy et al., 2019; Hyttinen et al., 2018; Hyttinen et al., 2023). Mechanistically, AMPK→PGC-1α signaling induces mitochondrial biogenesis and interacts with NRF2/ARE antioxidant programs; reciprocally, AMPK can promote TFEB/TFE3-driven lysosomal biogenesis, providing a bidirectional mito–lyso coupling framework relevant to RPE homeostasis (Nita & Grzybowski, 2023; Boya et al., 2023).

What ZLN005 is expected to do in RPE assays. In ARPE-19 and H-RPE, ZLN005 selectively induces PGC-1α, improves mitochondrial respiration, upregulates mitochondrial/antioxidant gene expression, and protects against oxidative insults; PGC-1α dependence of cytoprotection has been demonstrated in ARPE-19 (Tong et al., 2022; Shu et al., 2021). In H-RPE, ZLN005 prevents TGFβ₂-induced EMT and migration, linking PGC-1α induction to preservation of epithelial phenotype and metabolic competence under stress (Shu et al., 2021). Based on these data, in RPE assays ZLN005 is expected to:

- Increase PGC-1α transcript/protein and downstream mitochondrial biogenesis (e.g., NRF1/TFAM/OXPHOS genes), raising basal/maximal respiration and spare capacity, and boosting ATP (Tong et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2020).  
- Lower ROS and improve mitochondrial membrane potential and structure, thereby reducing oxidative injury susceptibility (Tong et al., 2022; Ma et al., 2023).  
- Preserve epithelial features and reduce EMT/migration under profibrotic stress (TGFβ₂), maintaining RPE barrier function (Shu et al., 2021).

Hypothesized effects on lysosomes/TFEB/CTSD and phagosome clearance. The proposal posits that ZLN005 will “cooperate with TFEB to enhance lysosomal acidification and cathepsin D activity, thereby improving phagosome clearance” and that improved mito–lyso coupling will reduce lipofuscin. Available evidence supports the general biological framework—AMPK can activate TFEB/TFE3 and PGC-1α in parallel, PGC-1α/NRF2 promote mitochondrial homeostasis and antioxidant capacity in RPE, and TFEB activation restores lysosomal hydrolases and autophagic flux in diseased RPE—but there are no direct data that ZLN005 activates TFEB, increases lysosomal acidification, elevates cathepsin D activity, or enhances phagosome clearance in RPE (Boya et al., 2023; Ghosh et al., 2024; Tong et al., 2022; Shu et al., 2021). In fact, the TFEB-centric rescue of CTSD/LAMP1 and lysosome function in AMD-model RPE has been demonstrated with trehalose or genetic TFEB activation, not with ZLN005; therefore, any expectation that ZLN005 alone will enhance lysosomal acidification/CTSD or phagosome clearance is a plausible but unproven hypothesis that requires explicit testing with lysosomal pH probes, CTSD activity assays, and POS phagocytosis/phagosome clearance metrics in primary human RPE (Ghosh et al., 2024).

Important caveats for experimental design:  
- Reporter interference: ZLN005 inhibits luciferases and may confound TFEB/E-box luciferase or PGC-1α reporter assays; use non-luciferase readouts (e.g., immunoblots, qPCR, ChIP-qPCR, RNA-seq, proteomics, TFEB nuclear translocation imaging, LysoTracker/DQ-BSA/CTSD activity assays) (Zhang et al., 2013).  
- Primary vs cell line responsiveness: Primary H-RPE shows smaller PGC-1α fold-induction than ARPE-19 due to higher baseline PGC-1α; dosing windows and exposure times must be optimized in H-RPE to achieve functional gains without undue mitochondrial uncoupling (Shu et al., 2021).  
- Cross-talk assessment: If synergy with TFEB is a key aim, include a TFEB activator arm (e.g., trehalose) as comparator/combination and measure canonical TFEB outputs (CTSD/L, LAMP1/2, CLEAR network gene expression), while maintaining AMPK/mTORC1 pathway controls to dissect mechanism (Ghosh et al., 2024; Boya et al., 2023).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Direct RPE activity. ZLN005 selectively upregulates PGC-1α in ARPE-19 and primary H-RPE, enhances mitochondrial respiration, and protects ARPE-19 from oxidative stress in a PGC-1α-dependent manner; it also suppresses TGFβ₂-induced EMT/migration in H-RPE, linking mitochondrial competence to epithelial stability—both highly relevant to dry AMD pathophysiology (Tong et al., 2022; Shu et al., 2021).  
- Robust mitochondrial biogenesis/transcriptional program. Across cardiomyocytes, muscle, and lung epithelium, ZLN005 reproducibly induces PGC-1α and downstream transcriptional programs (NRF1/TFAM/OXPHOS/FAO), increasing mtDNA, OCR, and ATP, establishing a mechanistic basis for improving RPE mitochondrial deficits observed in dry AMD (Liu et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2013; Ma et al., 2023; Hyttinen et al., 2023).  
- Systems-level cytoprotection. In AKI and neuronal ischemia/toxicity models, ZLN005 reduces ROS and apoptosis, improves mitochondrial integrity, and requires key downstream effectors (CPT-1α in kidney), demonstrating that PGC-1α activation can translate to organ protection, which conceptually extends to RPE under oxidative/energetic stress (Wang et al., 2021; Xu et al., 2018; Tian et al., 2023).  
- Disease relevance of the target. Extensive genetic/pathophysiologic evidence places PGC-1α at the center of RPE mitochondrial biogenesis, antioxidant defense, and senescence control; PGC-1α or PGC-1α/NRF2 loss causes AMD-like degeneration, and AMPK→PGC-1α and NRF2/ARE axes are validated protective mechanisms in RPE (Felszeghy et al., 2019; Hyttinen et al., 2018; Hyttinen et al., 2023; Nita & Grzybowski, 2023).  
- Translational feasibility. ZLN005 has oral bioactivity with favorable metabolic endpoints in mice, rudimentary short-term rat safety, and a breadth of preclinical efficacy across tissues; it penetrates the CNS, implying some potential for ocular exposure via circulation, though eye PK is unknown (Zhang et al., 2013; Tian et al., 2023).

Limitations and risks  
- No direct evidence for TFEB/lysosomal activation by ZLN005. There are no data showing that ZLN005 increases TFEB activity, lysosomal acidification, cathepsin D activity, or phagosome clearance in RPE; TFEB-dependent improvements in lysosome function and CTSD have been demonstrated with other interventions (trehalose or genetic TFEB activation), not with ZLN005 (Ghosh et al., 2024; Tong et al., 2022; Shu et al., 2021). The hypothesized mito–lyso crosstalk is biologically plausible via AMPK signaling but remains to be demonstrated for this compound (Boya et al., 2023).  
- Potential pro-angiogenic signaling. PGC-1α/ERRα activation in RPE has been linked to VEGF upregulation under certain conditions; in a chronic retinal setting, inadvertent promotion of angiogenic signaling could be undesirable, especially near neovascular AMD thresholds; careful assessment of VEGF/angiogenic gene expression in RPE and choroid is warranted (Blasiak et al., 2021).  
- Dose window and uncoupling toxicity. ZLN005 acts at least partly via mild mitochondrial uncoupling to activate AMPK; while beneficial in moderation, uncoupling can exacerbate ROS and bioenergetic stress if overdosed; high ZLN005 concentrations were toxic in HK2 cells, underscoring the need for careful titration in primary H-RPE (Zhang et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2021).  
- Cell-type and species specificity. ZLN005 does not induce PGC-1α in primary hepatocytes and downregulated hepatic PGC-1α in db/db mice; responsiveness varies by cell context (e.g., smaller fold-change in H-RPE than ARPE-19), complicating dose translation and efficacy prediction in human RPE in vivo (Zhang et al., 2013; Shu et al., 2021).  
- Reporter assay interference. The compound inhibits luciferases; any reliance on luciferase readouts for PGC-1α or TFEB activity risks artifact and demands orthogonal assay confirmation (Zhang et al., 2013).  
- Ocular pharmacokinetics unknown. Oral PK demonstrates high liver exposure and moderate muscle exposure; there are no data on ocular distribution, RPE exposure, or retinal bioavailability, making formulation and dosing strategies for eye delivery an open question (Zhang et al., 2013).

Decision-critical gaps and suggested de-risking experiments  
- TFEB/lysosomal axis: Directly test whether ZLN005 increases TFEB nuclear translocation, CLEAR network gene expression, lysosomal pH acidification (ratiometric probes), CTSD/CTSL protein/activity, and autophagosome flux (LC3B-II/p62 turnover) in primary H-RPE; benchmark versus trehalose and/or genetic TFEB activation and evaluate additivity or synergy in ZLN005+trehalose combination, with AMPK/mTORC1 pathway readouts to mechanistically link signaling (Ghosh et al., 2024; Boya et al., 2023).  
- Phagosome processing: Quantify photoreceptor outer segment (POS) uptake and phagosome clearance kinetics, including cathepsin-dependent proteolysis and lipofuscinogenic adduct accumulation, under oxidative/complement stress ± ZLN005; include PGC-1α knockdown to confirm dependence (Tong et al., 2022; Felszeghy et al., 2019).  
- In vivo efficacy in AMD-relevant models: Test in complement/CFH risk allele iPSC-RPE xenograft or sodium iodate/aging mouse models focusing on RPE structure/function, lipofuscin proxies, sub-RPE deposit formation, and ERG endpoints; incorporate TFEB activation arms where possible to validate the dual-axis hypothesis (Ghosh et al., 2024; Luján et al., 2022).  
- Safety pharmacology: Titrate ZLN005 dosing in ocular delivery paradigms (intravitreal, periocular, or systemic) with eye PK, retinal/RPE exposure, retinal function (ERG), and VEGF expression profiling to exclude pro-angiogenic shifts; assess off-target mitochondrial stress at higher exposures in H-RPE (Blasiak et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2021).

Conclusion: fit for further evaluation with focused lysosome endpoints. ZLN005 has strong mechanistic and preclinical support as a PGC-1α activator that improves mitochondrial biogenesis and oxidative resilience in RPE and retina-adjacent systems, and it produces protective effects across diverse tissues via PGC-1α-dependent programs (Tong et al., 2022; Shu et al., 2021; Xu et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2021). However, the core elements of the present hypothesis—enhancement of TFEB activity, lysosomal acidification, cathepsin D activity, and phagosome clearance, plus reduction of lipofuscin and drusen—are not yet evidenced for ZLN005 and remain inferential based on pathway crosstalk (AMPK→TFEB/TFE3, PGC-1α–NRF2) and TFEB-targeted rescue in RPE by other agents (Boya et al., 2023; Ghosh et al., 2024). Consequently, ZLN005 is a promising mitochondrial-centric candidate for dry AMD that merits accelerated, targeted validation on lysosomal/phagosome endpoints and ocular delivery feasibility. The compound’s strengths—a validated mitochondrial biogenesis mechanism in RPE, demonstrated oxidative stress protection in ARPE-19, primary H-RPE EMT suppression, and broad cross-tissue efficacy—justify this investment, provided that the risks of off-target uncoupling, reporter assay interference, cell-type specificity, and potential pro-angiogenic signaling are actively managed in the experimental plan (Tong et al., 2022; Shu et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2013; Blasiak et al., 2021).

Although lithium’s clinical history is extensive, the translational gap into dry AMD remains speculative, with no registered trials or direct RPE evidence. Urolithin A’s alignment with core AMD pathology (mitochondrial and lysosomal dysfunction), strong safety profile, and existing RPE-relevant data make it the superior candidate for preclinical advancement.

Lithium’s MoA in non-ocular systems and lack of RPE/AMD data, combined with its known systemic liabilities, create substantial translational risk. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Urolithin A is a naturally derived small molecule that originates from the gut microbial metabolism of dietary polyphenols, particularly ellagitannins and ellagic acid, which are abundant in fruits such as pomegranates, berries, and nuts (Djedjibegović et al., 2020; Heilman et al., 2017). Unlike synthetic drug candidates, Urolithin A is generated endogenously following dietary intake, a process that relies on a healthy gut microbiome to convert these precursors into bioactive urolithins. This compound belongs to the broader class of nutraceuticals and microbiota‐derived metabolites that have been widely investigated for their capacity to modulate mitochondrial function and cellular homeostasis (Djedjibegović et al., 2020; Jayatunga et al., 2021). These compounds, which have historically been explored mostly within the context of nutritional interventions and age-related muscle decline, are now being repurposed as potential drugs for other degenerative conditions. Urolithin A, in particular, has attracted significant attention due to its ability to enhance mitochondrial quality control through the activation of pathways such as PINK1/Parkin and modulation of autophagy-related mechanisms. Its synthesis in the human body, as well as its isolation from natural sources for research-grade applications such as Sigma SML1791, underscores its dual status as both a naturally occurring metabolite and a drug candidate with therapeutic potential across a variety of disease models (Jayatunga et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2025). Moreover, as a member of this emerging class, Urolithin A has been shown to be well tolerated, which gives it an advantage over many synthetic compounds that may pose safety concerns due to their off-target toxicities (Wang & Yu, 2025; Zhang et al., 2025). The natural origin and well-characterized safety profile of Urolithin A lend support to its development as a repurposed therapeutic agent, particularly for diseases like dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD), where mitochondrial dysfunction and impaired lysosomal clearance play central roles.

Therapeutic History:  
The therapeutic history of Urolithin A spans several preclinical and clinical studies that have established its safety, bioavailability, and efficacy in improving mitochondrial function. In numerous animal studies, Urolithin A has demonstrated a high no‐observed‐adverse‐effect level (NOAEL), with doses in the range of several thousand mg/kg demonstrating a remarkable safety margin (Djedjibegović et al., 2020). Early-phase clinical trials, including randomized placebo-controlled studies in healthy elderly subjects, have corroborated its safety; these trials reported no serious adverse events even at doses as high as 2000 mg, and significant improvements were observed in mitochondrial gene expression and muscle function (Jayatunga et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2025). This safety profile has been further supported by work that shows Urolithin A’s favorable pharmacokinetic properties. For instance, following oral administration, Urolithin A is rapidly absorbed, with peak plasma concentrations reached around 6 hours post-dose and a half-life of approximately 17–22 hours for the compound and its glucuronide conjugates (Djedjibegović et al., 2020; Raimundo et al., 2021). Its systemic bioavailability is advantageous when considering repurposing for systemic degenerative conditions such as AMD.

Historically, the focus of Urolithin A research has been on its role in mitigating age-associated muscle decline by improving mitochondrial quality, a property that has been linked to its induction of mitophagy, which is the selective removal of damaged mitochondria (Jayatunga et al., 2021; Singh et al., 2019). However, growing evidence from both in vitro studies and animal models indicates that Urolithin A’s benefits extend to other tissues, particularly those that are highly dependent on mitochondrial health such as the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) in the eye (Hyttinen et al., 2018; Jiménez-Loygorri et al., 2024). Although direct clinical studies using Urolithin A for dry AMD are still pending, the preclinical data suggest that its ability to improve mitochondrial function by promoting mitophagy and lysosomal clearance mechanisms could be beneficial in counteracting RPE degeneration, a hallmark of dry AMD. The therapeutic candidate thus finds support from both its legacy in muscle studies and emerging evidence in neurodegenerative disease models, including studies related to Alzheimer’s disease and Parkinson’s disease, where mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress are central themes (Jayatunga et al., 2021; Skeie et al., 2021). This therapeutic history, spanning several decades of research on mitochondrial modulators, positions Urolithin A as a promising candidate for repurposing toward diseases that involve similar cellular and molecular derangements.

Mechanism of Action:  
The mechanism of action of Urolithin A is multifaceted and central to its potential as a therapeutic agent for dry AMD. At a molecular level, Urolithin A functions primarily as a mitophagy enhancer. In cells experiencing mitochondrial damage or oxidative stress, the kinase PINK1 accumulates on the outer mitochondrial membrane, thereby recruiting the E3 ubiquitin ligase Parkin; together, they tag dysfunctional mitochondria for autophagic degradation (Borsky et al., 2025; Jiménez-Loygorri et al., 2024). This PINK1/Parkin-mediated pathway is essential for maintaining mitochondrial quality and cellular energy metabolism, particularly in high-energy demanding tissues such as the RPE where mitochondria are crucial for photoreceptor support (Hyttinen et al., 2018; Borsky et al., 2025). In addition to inducing mitophagy through PINK1/Parkin signaling, Urolithin A has been shown to activate AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK), a key energy sensor in cells. AMPK activation leads to the phosphorylation and subsequent nuclear translocation of transcription factor EB (TFEB), which acts as a master regulator of lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy (Zhang et al., 2025; Borsky et al., 2025). Once translocated into the nucleus, TFEB upregulates the expression of genes encoding lysosomal proteins such as LAMP1 and cathepsin D (CTSD), thereby enhancing the capacity of cells to clear autophagic cargo through improved lysosomal degradation (D’Amico et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2025).

The biochemical interactions involved in these processes are well supported by in vitro data showing that Urolithin A not only reduces mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (ROS) but also ameliorates the disruption of autophagic flux that is often observed under oxidative stress conditions (Djedjibegović et al., 2020; Jayatunga et al., 2021). This reduction of oxidative stress is particularly relevant for the RPE because elevated oxidative damage is a significant contributor to cellular senescence and apoptosis in patients with dry AMD. Furthermore, Urolithin A has been noted to induce p62-dependent lysophagy, a specialized form of autophagy that targets lysosomal components for recycling and repair, ensuring that even when conventional lysosomal biogenesis is impaired, cellular proteostasis can be maintained (Jiménez-Loygorri et al., 2024). The dual activation of mitophagy and lysosomal biogenesis creates a synergistic effect, where damaged mitochondria are efficiently recognized, isolated, and degraded, and the lysosomal compartment is concurrently replenished with new, fully functional enzymes, ensuring an optimal degradative environment (Auguste, 2022; Borsky et al., 2025). Moreover, studies have shown that Urolithin A can favorably influence other signaling pathways that contribute to mitochondrial biogenesis, such as the SIRT1/PGC-1α axis, further supporting its role in restoring mitochondrial homeostasis (Borsky et al., 2025; D’Amico et al., 2021). In summary, Urolithin A’s multifaceted mechanism—which encompasses the induction of PINK1/Parkin-mediated mitophagy, activation of AMPK–TFEB signaling to enhance lysosomal biogenesis, and reduction of oxidative stress—forms a robust foundation for its proposed therapeutic application in the treatment of dry AMD.

Expected Effect:  
The therapeutic hypothesis for Urolithin A in dry AMD rests on its ability to restore mitochondrial quality and enhance lysosomal clearance in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE). In the proposed assay, Urolithin A is expected to activate the PINK1/Parkin pathway in RPE cells, thus facilitating the selective removal of damaged mitochondria that contribute to oxidative stress and cellular dysfunction (Borsky et al., 2025). Concurrently, through the activation of AMPK, Urolithin A is anticipated to drive the nuclear translocation of TFEB, thereby upregulating lysosomal genes such as LAMP1 and cathepsin D. This upregulation is expected to enhance lysosomal acidification, an essential component for the proper degradation of autophagic cargo, including damaged mitochondria and photoreceptor outer segments (POS) that accumulate with age (Zhang et al., 2025; Borsky et al., 2025).

In oxidative stress RPE models, where mitochondrial ROS levels are elevated due to chronic insult, Urolithin A is projected to reduce ROS production by promoting the clearance of dysfunctional mitochondria, thereby mitigating the cascade of oxidative damage (Djedjibegović et al., 2020; Jayatunga et al., 2021). This is expected to result in the stabilization of mitochondrial membrane potential and the maintenance of energy homeostasis, both of which are crucial for the survival of RPE cells under stress. Additionally, the enhanced lysosomal function driven by TFEB activation is likely to lead to increased activity of cathepsin D, a lysosomal protease that plays a pivotal role in degrading autophagosomal substrates and in processing debris from phagocytosis of POS (D’Amico et al., 2021; Jiménez-Loygorri et al., 2024). The net effect of these actions would be a reduction in cellular stress markers, improved cellular clearance, and preservation of RPE cell integrity, which are fundamental in slowing down the progression of dry AMD.

The expected pharmacological outcomes are supported by prior studies demonstrating that Urolithin A can modulate key proteins known to be expressed in RPE cells. For instance, PINK1 is well documented to be present in RPE cells and plays an essential role in initiating mitophagy in response to mitochondrial damage (Hyttinen et al., 2018; García‐Villalba et al., 2020). Similarly, proteins such as LAMP1 and CTSD are integral to the function of the lysosomal system in RPE cells, and their upregulation has been associated with improved cellular clearance and resistance to stress-induced apoptosis (Zhang et al., 2025; Borsky et al., 2025). Thus, by simultaneously targeting both the mitophagic and lysosomal arms of the cellular clearance machinery, Urolithin A is expected to exert a comprehensive protective effect in the diseased state. This integrative approach is particularly relevant in dry AMD, wherein the accumulation of damaged cellular components and impaired lysosomal degradation are key pathological features (Makarov & Korkotian, 2023; Jiménez-Loygorri et al., 2024). Ultimately, the anticipated effects of Urolithin A administration include enhanced mitochondrial turnover, reduced oxidative stress, reinvigorated lysosomal function, and overall RPE cell survival, all of which are envisioned to culminate in a slowing or possible arrest of the degenerative processes underlying dry AMD.

Overall Evaluation:  
In evaluating Urolithin A as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, several strengths emerge that underscore its potential while also highlighting critical areas that warrant further investigation. One of the most significant strengths of Urolithin A is its well-established safety profile. Preclinical toxicology studies have demonstrated that Urolithin A has a high NOAEL, and early-phase human clinical trials have shown that it is effectively tolerated at doses ranging from 250 to 2000 mg without significant adverse events (Jayatunga et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2025). This establishes a favorable risk–benefit ratio that is particularly advantageous when considering the chronic administration likely required for a degenerative condition such as dry AMD. Additionally, its oral bioavailability and favorable pharmacokinetic parameters, including a consistent half-life and effective systemic distribution, further support its potential for use as a repurposed drug (Zhang et al., 2025; Raimundo et al., 2021).

Mechanistically, Urolithin A addresses two core pathological processes implicated in dry AMD: mitochondrial dysfunction and lysosomal insufficiency. Its ability to trigger the PINK1/Parkin pathway ensures that damaged mitochondria are selectively removed, thereby reducing mitochondrial ROS production and mitigating oxidative injury—a process that is particularly beneficial in the energy-intensive environment of the RPE (Borsky et al., 2025). Simultaneously, the activation of AMPK and subsequent nuclear translocation of TFEB primes the lysosomal system for enhanced biogenesis and improved degradative capacity, thus tackling the accumulation of cellular debris and phagocytosed POS that are hallmarks of AMD pathology (Zhang et al., 2025; Borsky et al., 2025).

From a translational perspective, the therapeutic history of Urolithin A provides a strong foundation for its repurposing. Although much of the direct evidence pertains to skeletal muscle and neurodegenerative models, the underlying mechanisms—mitochondrial clearance and autophagic enhancement—are universally relevant to cellular systems burdened by degenerative stress, including the RPE (Hyttinen et al., 2018; Jiménez-Loygorri et al., 2024). However, a notable limitation remains in the current literature: there is a paucity of direct experimental data specifically utilizing RPE models or clinical cohorts with dry AMD. Although the extrapolation from other systems is promising, targeted studies are needed to validate the efficacy and optimize the dosing regimen for ocular applications (Zhang et al., 2025; Makarov & Korkotian, 2023).

Another potential challenge is the inherent variability in the bioactivation of ellagitannins to Urolithins among individuals, owing to differences in gut microbiota composition. While direct administration of Urolithin A circumvents this challenge, variability in metabolic processing and individual pharmacodynamic responses may still influence therapeutic outcomes (Wang & Yu, 2025; Zhang et al., 2025). Moreover, the translation of systemic improvements in mitochondrial function to localized effects within the retina is not entirely straightforward; the blood–retinal barrier and unique ocular microenvironment may affect drug distribution and efficacy (Makarov & Korkotian, 2023; Harper, 2023). These challenges underscore the need for comprehensive ocular pharmacokinetic studies and the development of delivery strategies that ensure adequate drug concentration in the RPE.

Despite these limitations, the overall evidence supports the advancement of Urolithin A as a candidate for treating dry AMD. Its dual mechanism of enhancing both mitophagy and lysosomal function is particularly well-suited to counteracting the complex pathophysiology of AMD, where mitochondrial decay and lysosomal failure converge to induce cellular apoptosis and dysfunction (Auguste, 2022; Borsky et al., 2025). In addition, the compound’s ability to reduce oxidative stress, a critical driver of AMD progression, further bolsters the rationale for its use (Djedjibegović et al., 2020; Jayatunga et al., 2021). Importantly, the wealth of preclinical data demonstrating Urolithin A’s beneficial effects in animal models and cell culture systems provides a compelling argument for its continued evaluation in ocular models of AMD (Hyttinen et al., 2018; Jiménez-Loygorri et al., 2024).

In summary, Urolithin A presents a highly promising therapeutic candidate for repurposing against dry AMD. Its natural origin, excellent safety profile, favorable pharmacokinetics, and robust mechanism of action—characterized by the activation of PINK1/Parkin-mediated mitophagy and AMPK–TFEB-mediated lysosomal biogenesis—render it an attractive candidate for further investigation. The expected beneficial effects in reducing oxidative stress, clearing damaged mitochondria, and re-establishing lysosomal function in RPE cells align well with the therapeutic needs in dry AMD. Nevertheless, critical gaps remain in direct evidence from ocular models and in addressing potential interindividual variability in drug response. If these challenges are successfully navigated through targeted preclinical and early-phase clinical studies, Urolithin A could fill a significant unmet need in the treatment of dry AMD, offering a novel, mechanism-based intervention that targets the underlying cellular dysfunctions driving the disease (Jayatunga et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2025; Borsky et al., 2025; Hyttinen et al., 2018). Ultimately, while further research is necessary to refine dosing strategies and confirm ocular efficacy, the overall evaluation indicates that Urolithin A is a strong candidate worthy of pursuit in the quest for effective therapies for dry age-related macular degeneration.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Lithium chloride (Sigma L9650) is an inorganic salt belonging to the family of lithium compounds that has been in use for several decades, primarily as a mood stabilizer in the treatment of bipolar disorder. It is synthesized by combining lithium carbonate or lithium hydroxide with hydrochloric acid, yielding a highly water‐soluble salt that is widely available for both clinical and experimental research purposes (Carmassi et al., 2016; Vallée et al., 2021). As a prototypical member of the lithium salts, lithium chloride has been repurposed in recent years as a candidate for neuroprotection because of its ability to inhibit glycogen synthase kinase-3β (GSK3β), a serine/threonine kinase involved in numerous intracellular signaling cascades. Lithium’s chemical simplicity belies its complex pharmacology; its effects extend well beyond mood stabilization to encompass modulation of cell survival, inflammatory responses, and protein degradation pathways. In this context, lithium salts are now recognized as small molecule modulators that can affect intracellular transcriptional programs, including nuclear import of factors such as transcription factor EB (TFEB) and β-catenin, which in turn control the expression of genes necessary for lysosomal biogenesis and autophagic flux (Carmassi et al., 2016; Vallée et al., 2021). These mechanistic insights, originally developed in studies of neurodegenerative and psychiatric diseases, have motivated investigations into whether lithium chloride might be repurposed to address the autophagic and lysosomal dysfunction observed in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD), particularly in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) (Carmassi et al., 2016; Vallée et al., 2021).

Therapeutic History:  
Lithium salts have a long-standing clinical history in psychiatry, especially in the management of bipolar disorder, where their dosing and long-term safety profiles have been thoroughly characterized. In addition, numerous preclinical studies in neuroscience have demonstrated that lithium can reduce tau phosphorylation and improve neuronal cell survival, partly by inhibiting GSK3β and modulating downstream targets such as β-catenin and Bcl-2 (Carmassi et al., 2016; Vallée et al., 2021). Lithium has been evaluated in several neurodegenerative contexts—for instance, it has been examined for its potential benefits in Alzheimer’s disease, Huntington’s disease, and Parkinson’s disease, with some studies reporting modest improvements in neuroprotection and behavioral outcomes, although clinical results have been mixed (Singh et al., 2022; Vallée et al., 2021). More specifically, preclinical data in the central nervous system have shown that prolonged exposure to lithium increases cortical grey matter and enhances neuronal markers such as N-acetyl-aspartate, suggesting that lithium exerts trophic and neuroprotective effects (Carmassi et al., 2016). In the ocular arena, while lithium’s use has been predominantly described in the context of glaucoma—in which its inhibition of GSK3β was shown to modulate WNT/β-catenin signaling in trabecular meshwork cells—the literature offers no direct clinical or in-depth preclinical evaluation of lithium chloride in dry AMD or for modulating autophagy specifically in RPE cells (Singh et al., 2022; Vallée et al., 2021). A search in clinical trial registries has not identified any trials using lithium chloride for macular degeneration, underscoring a notable gap between the neuroprotective models in which lithium has been studied and its potential application in dry AMD (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).

Mechanism of Action:  
Lithium chloride’s mechanisms of action are multifaceted, but a significant aspect relevant to the dry AMD hypothesis is its ability to inhibit GSK3β. GSK3β normally phosphorylates a variety of substrates including β-catenin and TFEB, leading to cytosolic retention and subsequent degradation; inhibition of GSK3β by lithium therefore results in stabilization and nuclear accumulation of β-catenin and promotes TFEB nuclear entry (Carmassi et al., 2016; Vallée et al., 2021). In detail, lithium binds directly to the magnesium-sensitive site of GSK3β and also promotes its inhibitory N-terminal serine phosphorylation, leading to a dose-dependent suppression of GSK3β activity (Carmassi et al., 2016). The release of β-catenin from the destruction complex allows it to accumulate in the nucleus, where it acts as a transcriptional coactivator for genes that contribute to cell survival and homeostasis, including those involved in lysosomal biogenesis (Carmassi et al., 2016; Vallée et al., 2021). Similarly, TFEB is a master transcription factor that coordinates the expression of a variety of genes encoding lysosomal enzymes and autophagy-related proteins. Under basal conditions, phosphorylation retains TFEB in the cytosol; inhibition of GSK3β can contribute to dephosphorylation of TFEB, thereby facilitating its nuclear translocation and transcriptional activation of targets such as cathepsin D (CTSD) and subunits of the vacuolar ATPase (v-ATPase) that are crucial for lysosomal acidification (Carmassi et al., 2016; Friedman et al., 2015). In neuronal models, lithium treatment has been demonstrated to increase levels of neurotrophic factors and cell survival molecules, as well as to enhance autophagy-mediated clearance of toxic proteins including aggregated forms of tau and other proteins implicated in neurodegenerative disease (Vallée et al., 2021). Furthermore, lithium’s inhibition of inositol monophosphatase further contributes to autophagy induction through an mTOR-independent mechanism, reinforcing its capacity to modulate autophagic flux (Friedman et al., 2015). Despite these promising mechanistic insights, it is important to note that most of the supporting data have been generated in neuronal or non-ocular cell systems; direct evidence for lithium chloride-mediated activation of TFEB/β-catenin signaling and upregulation of lysosomal acidification machinery specifically in RPE cells remains limited (Golestaneh et al., 2018; Guha et al., 2014).

Expected Effect:  
Based on the hypothesis, treatment with lithium chloride in RPE cells is anticipated to inhibit GSK3β, leading to a cascade of intracellular events that restore impaired autophagic flux—a major pathological hallmark in dry AMD. Specifically, inhibition of GSK3β should reduce the phosphorylation-dependent cytosolic retention of TFEB and β-catenin, thereby facilitating their nuclear import. In the nucleus, these transcription factors can activate a broad transcriptional program that upregulates the synthesis of lysosomal proteins such as cathepsin D and components of the v-ATPase complex, ultimately leading to enhanced lysosomal acidification (Carmassi et al., 2016; Friedman et al., 2015). This improved lysosomal function is expected to accelerate the degradation of photoreceptor outer segment debris and other autophagic substrates, leading to a restoration of autophagic flux and a reduction in lipofuscin accumulation—a prominent feature of dry AMD pathology (Golestaneh et al., 2018). In parallel, lithium’s neuroprotective effects, including the upregulation of prosurvival factors like Bcl-2 and the attenuation of proinflammatory signaling pathways, may further support RPE cell survival and function under chronic oxidative stress conditions (Vallée et al., 2021). Given that lysosomal alkalinization is known to impair cathepsin D activity and autophagic degradation in RPE cells, the upregulation of cathepsin D via TFEB activation represents a critical therapeutic target to counteract the reduced degradative capacity observed in dry AMD (Guha et al., 2014). Moreover, the candidate’s reported ocular penetration and long-term safety in other contexts provide a translational rationale, though the literature is notably deficient in direct measurements of RPE-specific outcomes—thus, further studies are required to validate that lithium chloride achieves effective intraocular concentrations without toxicity (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.; Vallée et al., 2021). The expected outcome in an in vitro assay would be an increase in nuclear TFEB and β-catenin as determined by immunocytochemistry and Western blot of nuclear extracts, an increase in mRNA and protein levels of lysosomal acidification machinery (e.g., v-ATPase subunits) and cathepsin D, restoration of autophagic flux as evidenced by normalized LC3-II/LC3-I ratios and p62 degradation, and improved clearance of photoreceptor outer segment-derived material in RPE cell culture models (Golestaneh et al., 2018).

Overall Evaluation:  
The repurposing of lithium chloride for dry age-related macular degeneration is based on a compelling mechanistic rationale that builds upon well-established aspects of lithium’s pharmacology. On one hand, the drug’s ability to inhibit GSK3β—and thereby to promote the nuclear translocation of TFEB and β-catenin—aligns well with the therapeutic goal of upregulating lysosomal gene expression and restoring autophagic flux in RPE cells (Golestaneh et al., 2018). Lithium’s longstanding use in psychiatric medicine has resulted in a rich and well-documented clinical safety profile, and its neuroprotective benefits in various models lend additional support to its potential utility in other degenerative conditions including ocular diseases (Carmassi et al., 2016; Vallée et al., 2021).

However, there are several notable weaknesses and gaps that must be addressed before lithium chloride can be considered a robust therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. First, while preclinical studies in neuronal models offer supportive evidence that lithium can modulate autophagy and enhance lysosomal function, there is a lack of direct data demonstrating these mechanisms in RPE cells specifically (Golestaneh et al., 2018). Second, the pharmacokinetic profile of lithium chloride in the eye—especially the extent to which it penetrates the RPE following systemic or local administration—remains poorly characterized, and this is a critical factor given the importance of achieving therapeutic concentrations in the retina without causing off-target toxicity (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.). Third, although lithium’s long-term safety has been established in psychiatric populations, its known systemic toxicities, including renal and thyroid effects, as well as its narrow therapeutic window, raise concerns about the potential risks of repurposing it for an ocular indication where localized delivery may be necessary to avoid systemic exposure (Singh et al., 2022; Vallée et al., 2021). Finally, the absence of any registered clinical trials or robust preclinical studies in an AMD model means that the translational viability of lithium chloride for this indication is still highly speculative (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).

Despite these concerns, the strengths of lithium chloride as a repurposed agent for dry AMD are significant. Its ability to target GSK3β provides a unique molecular entry point that could bypass some of the drawbacks of other autophagy modulators that primarily act through mTOR inhibition—a strategy that has yielded mixed clinical results (Friedman et al., 2015; Vallée et al., 2021). Moreover, the multi-modal action of lithium, which encompasses both anti-inflammatory and anti-excitotoxic effects in addition to its autophagy-promoting properties, suggests that it could provide a broad-spectrum protective effect in the stressed cellular environment of the RPE (Carmassi et al., 2016; Vallée et al., 2021). Nonetheless, given the complexity of RPE biology and the multifactorial nature of dry AMD pathogenesis—as evidenced by the alterations in lysosomal pH, reduced cathepsin activity, and compromised membrane trafficking in these cells—any candidate drug must be rigorously evaluated in appropriate RPE or AMD models before clinical translation is attempted (Golestaneh et al., 2018; Guha et al., 2014).

In summary, lithium chloride holds promise as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD through its inhibition of GSK3β and the subsequent activation of nuclear TFEB/β-catenin signaling pathways, which are anticipated to upregulate lysosomal acidification machinery and cathepsin D expression and thereby restore autophagic flux in the RPE. The candidate’s well-documented clinical history and long-term safety in other indications provide additional encouragement for its further preclinical exploration. However, critical issues—such as the need for direct experimental evidence in RPE system models, the establishment of effective and safe ocular dosing regimens with adequate retinal penetration, and thorough evaluations of potential systemic and ocular toxicities—must be rigorously addressed. Until these gaps are filled by focused preclinical and translational research, the use of lithium chloride for dry AMD remains a promising yet still unproven strategy that warrants additional investigation (Carmassi et al., 2016; Friedman et al., 2015; Golestaneh et al., 2018; Guha et al., 2014; Vallée et al., 2021; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.; Singh et al., 2022).
