Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Torin1 is a synthetic small‐molecule that belongs to the second‐generation, ATP‐competitive class of mTOR inhibitors, originally derived from a quinoline‐based scaffold. Its discovery originated from a high‐throughput compound library screen that identified quinolone hits with moderate mTOR activity, which were then optimized through iterative medicinal chemistry by introducing a six‐membered lactam to convert the initial quinolone into a tricyclic benzonaphthridinone scaffold (Guillem, 2015). This chemical modification yielded a molecule with exceptional biochemical potency—capable of inhibiting both mTOR complexes, mTORC1 and mTORC2, at very low (nanomolar to picomolar) concentrations—and with approximately 1000-fold improvement in cellular potency relative to the initial hits (Guillem, 2015). As an ATP-competitive inhibitor, Torin1 binds directly to the active (ATP-binding) site of mTOR, thereby circumventing the partial inhibition that is observed with first-generation mTOR inhibitors like rapamycin that act allosterically by binding FKBP12 (Liu et al., 2012). Torin1 has been widely used as a research tool to interrogate mTOR signaling in various cellular contexts, and its chemical lineage as a quinoline-derived molecule positions it within a well-characterized class of inhibitors that have been instrumental in expanding our understanding of mTOR-dependent regulation of autophagy and cellular metabolism (Liu et al., 2012).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, Torin1 has been employed predominantly as a research tool rather than as a clinical drug candidate. Extensive preclinical studies have demonstrated its robust ability to inhibit mTOR signaling in cancer models, autophagy-deficient systems, and metabolic studies. For instance, Torin1 was shown to potently inhibit mTOR signaling pathways in glioblastoma and prostate cancer cells, significantly reducing cell-cycle progression and inducing apoptosis in certain contexts (Gu, 2017; Liu et al., 2012). Its use as an autophagy inducer is well documented, as experiments utilizing Torin1 have demonstrated increased autophagic flux and elevated lysosomal activity in multiple cell lines (Li, 2018; Liu et al., 2012). Importantly, Torin1 is also used in studies with retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells, as evidenced by its ability to increase TFEB-driven luciferase reporter activity in ARPE-19 cells by effectively suppressing mTORC1 signaling (Huang et al., 2018). Despite these promising experimental findings, Torin1 has not advanced to clinical trials for any indication, including neurodegenerative disorders or dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD). Moreover, its intrinsic pharmacokinetic limitations—such as poor aqueous solubility, a short half-life, and low oral bioavailability—have been recognized in several studies, thereby limiting its potential as a direct therapeutic candidate without further structural optimization (Guillem, 2015; Wang et al., 2022).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, Torin1 functions by competing with ATP for binding to the catalytic domain of mTOR, effectively blocking the phosphorylation of downstream substrates. Its ATP-competitive nature allows Torin1 to inhibit both mTORC1 and mTORC2 complexes, thereby offering a broader inhibition profile than allosteric agents like rapamycin that primarily target mTORC1 (Guillem, 2015; Liu et al., 2012). Detailed molecular modeling and structure–activity relationship studies indicate that the tricyclic benzonaphthridinone core of Torin1 forms critical hinge-binding interactions with residues in the mTOR kinase domain (Liu et al., 2012). This interaction accounts for its high potency, as reflected in low nanomolar IC₅₀ values in cellular assays (Liu et al., 2012; Gros & Muller, 2014). Torin1 induces rapid dephosphorylation of canonical mTORC1 substrates, such as S6 kinase at Thr389 and 4E-BP1 at Thr37/46, which results in downregulation of protein synthesis and cellular growth signals (Misra & Pizzo, 2013). Moreover, by simultaneously inhibiting mTORC2, it reduces phosphorylation of Akt at Ser473—a site critical for full Akt activation—thus attenuating the feedback loops that typically reinvigorate upstream PI3K signaling in response to mTORC1 inhibition (Gu, 2017; Martina et al., 2014). A particularly notable feature of Torin1 is its slow off-rate, which leads to sustained inhibition of mTOR activity even after drug washout, a pharmacodynamic property that may confer prolonged downstream effects such as enhanced autophagic flux (Liu et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2013). The inhibition of mTOR by Torin1 correlates with dephosphorylation of transcription factors, particularly TFEB and TFE3; under normal nutrient-replete conditions, mTORC1 phosphorylates TFEB (e.g., on S211 in TFEB) and TFE3, sequestering them in the cytosol through binding with 14-3-3 proteins (Huang et al., 2018; Martina et al., 2014). Upon mTOR inhibition by Torin1, TFEB is dephosphorylated and translocates to the nucleus, where it induces the transcription of CLEAR (Coordinated Lysosomal Expression and Regulation) network genes that drive lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy (Li, 2018; Liu et al., 2013). This precise modulation of mTOR signaling and subsequent transcriptional reprogramming forms the biochemical basis for leveraging Torin1 as a candidate to ameliorate lysosomal clearance defects.

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis for repurposing Torin1 in the context of dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is that potent inhibition of mTORC1/2 in RPE cells can lift the repressive phosphorylation that normally limits the activity of TFEB and TFE3. In RPE cells, as demonstrated by studies in ARPE-19 cell models, mTOR inhibition via Torin1 not only leads to decreased phosphorylation of S6 kinase but also results in marked activation of TFEB-driven transcription (Huang et al., 2018). When TFEB translocates to the nucleus, it binds to CLEAR elements present in the promoters of genes responsible for lysosomal biogenesis, acidification (through the upregulation of V-ATPase subunits), and the maturation and activity of lysosomal enzymes such as cathepsin D (CTSD) (Huang et al., 2018; Li, 2018). In dry AMD, RPE cells exhibit a decline in lysosomal function along with accumulation of cellular debris and lipofuscin, which contribute to disease pathology. By inducing a robust CLEAR response, Torin1 is expected to restore lysosomal function through increased biogenesis, enhanced acidification, and elevated cathepsin D activity, thereby improving the clearance of toxic aggregates in RPE cells and ultimately mitigating the progression of dry AMD (Gu, 2017; Huang et al., 2018). Additionally, the sustained target engagement afforded by Torin1’s slow off-rate may provide prolonged therapeutic benefit even with intermittent dosing, an attractive feature given the chronic nature of AMD (Liu et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2013). Recent evidence from preclinical iPSC models and autophagy-deficiency studies underscores the potential translation of mTOR-targeted strategies in restoring cellular homeostasis in degenerative diseases, lending further credence to this expected mechanism (Guillem, 2015).

Overall Evaluation:  
In summary, Torin1 possesses a compelling mechanistic profile that aligns well with the therapeutic needs of dry AMD by targeting a fundamental pathway governing cellular homeostasis in RPE cells. Its origin from a quinoline-based scaffold and subsequent chemical optimization into a highly potent ATP-competitive mTOR inhibitor underline its status as a valuable chemical probe in preclinical settings (Guillem, 2015). The dual inhibition of both mTORC1 and mTORC2 by Torin1, combined with its slow off-rate and sustained downstream effects—including dephosphorylation and nuclear translocation of TFEB/TFE3—make it an ideal tool for inducing lysosomal biogenesis and enhancing autophagic clearance (Martina et al., 2014; Huang et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2012). In cellular models, including ARPE-19 RPE cells, Torin1 has already demonstrated the ability to activate TFEB and upregulate CLEAR gene expression, which is directly relevant to counteracting the lysosomal clearance defects observed in dry AMD (Huang et al., 2018; Li, 2018).

However, significant challenges remain regarding the translational applicability of Torin1 as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. Its reported poor aqueous solubility, short half-life, and low oral bioavailability present formidable barriers to clinical development unless addressed through formulation improvements or further medicinal chemistry optimization (Guillem, 2015; Wang et al., 2022). Moreover, while extensive preclinical literature supports its role as a robust mTOR inhibitor in cancer and autophagy research, there is a lack of direct in vivo evidence for its efficacy in ocular models, particularly in dry AMD or geographic atrophy (GA) mouse lines (Liu et al., 2013; Gu, 2017). In summary, Torin1 is an excellent candidate for preclinical proof-of-concept studies to validate mTOR inhibition as a strategy to combat lysosomal dysfunction in dry AMD; however, further optimization to improve its stability and bioavailability, alongside rigorous in vivo testing in relevant AMD models, will be essential prior to clinical development (Guillem, 2015; Gu, 2017). The strengths of Torin1 lie in its potent, dual mTOR inhibition and its ability to robustly induce TFEB activation, whereas its weaknesses center on its pharmacokinetic shortcomings and the current lack of efficacy data in ocular disease models. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Nicotinamide riboside (NR), marketed as ChromaDex Niagen, belongs to the vitamin B3 family and is a naturally occurring precursor of nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+). Originally discovered in trace amounts in milk and other food sources, NR has been isolated and subsequently synthesized to yield a high‐purity form for nutritional and pharmaceutical applications. As a member of a class of compounds designed to elevate intracellular NAD+ levels, NR has attracted significant attention in the fields of metabolism, aging, and neuroprotection. Its chemical structure—a combination of a nicotinamide moiety bound to ribose—enables it to enter salvage pathways in cells with minimal metabolic conversion losses. In this regard, NR is comparable to other NAD+ boosters such as nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN), though differences in bioavailability and cellular transporter expression have been noted in some studies. Preclinical research has documented retinal distribution of NR in rodent models, suggesting that it reaches ocular tissues in pharmacologically relevant concentrations, an essential prerequisite for any agent intended to treat dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) (Abokyi & Tse, 2025; Braidy et al., 2019).

Therapeutic History:  
NR has been extensively investigated for its potential to modulate cellular energy metabolism and mitigate the effects of aging in diverse tissues. Early studies revealed that supplementation with NR effectively elevates NAD+ levels in multiple cell types, including neurons, skeletal muscle, and retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells, thereby enhancing mitochondrial function and cellular stress resistance (Dovijarski, 2019; Pîrvu et al., 2021). In the context of ocular research, while much of the direct experimental work has been performed using NMN, the close biochemical relationship between NMN and NR—as NAD+ precursors—has led investigators to propose that NR could produce similar outcomes in RPE cells. Models of retinal degeneration, including glaucoma and optic nerve injury, have demonstrated that NAD+ boosting via NR administration can ameliorate mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress, indirectly supporting its potential repurposing for dry AMD (Kitaoka et al., 2020; Mehmel et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2024). Moreover, clinical studies investigating NR’s safety in humans have shown that it is well tolerated at doses that elevate systemic NAD+ levels; doses in the gram-range have been employed without significant adverse effects (Jadeja et al., 2020). Although direct clinical trials targeting dry AMD are still forthcoming, the overall therapeutic history of NR—encompassing robust preclinical ocular benefit across neurodegenerative models and a favorable safety profile in human subjects—strongly supports further investigation for eye diseases where NAD+ depletion is a central pathophysiological feature (Dovijarski, 2019; Braidy et al., 2019; Pîrvu et al., 2021).

Mechanism of Action:  
The proposed mechanism of NR in dry AMD centers on its capacity to elevate intracellular NAD+ levels, thereby fueling a cascade of beneficial biochemical events. After cell entry, NR is phosphorylated by nicotinamide riboside kinases (NRKs) to generate NMN, which is subsequently converted to NAD+ through the activity of NMN adenylyltransferase. The resultant increase in NAD+ acts as a vital cofactor for sirtuins—primarily SIRT1 and SIRT3—which are NAD+-dependent deacetylases involved in regulating numerous cellular processes. SIRT1, in particular, has been implicated in deacetylating key transcription factors such as peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator-1α (PGC-1α) and transcription factor EB (TFEB). TFEB is a master regulator of lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy; its deacetylation leads to its nuclear translocation and binding to CLEAR (Coordinated Lysosomal Expression and Regulation) elements in the promoter regions of autophagy and lysosomal genes. Such activation promotes lysosomal acidification and increases the activity of hydrolases like cathepsin D, which are critical for the degradation of damaged proteins and organelles. Concurrently, SIRT3, which localizes predominantly to mitochondria, enhances mitochondrial function by deacetylating enzymes crucial for mitochondrial bioenergetics and reactive oxygen species (ROS) detoxification. The overall effect of NR supplementation is therefore hypothesized to be a restoration of cellular homeostasis in RPE cells—improving both autophagic clearance and mitochondrial function, two processes known to be compromised in dry AMD (Kitaoka et al., 2020; Mehmel et al., 2020; Lin & Apte, 2018; Jadeja et al., 2020). Such a mechanism is consistent with a substantial body of literature demonstrating that the NAD+-sirtuin axis plays a critical role in regulating neuroprotective and anti-aging functions across various tissues (Dovijarski, 2019; Jadeja et al., 2018; Pîrvu et al., 2021).

At the molecular level, the cascade initiated by NR begins with its metabolic conversion to NAD+, which then serves as an essential substrate for SIRT1 activation. Activated SIRT1 deacetylates TFEB, facilitating its nuclear accumulation and binding to the CLEAR network promoters, thereby upregulating genes responsible for autophagy, lysosomal biogenesis, and lysosomal acidification. This process is expected to boost cathepsin D activity and overall lysosomal proteolytic function. Parallel activation of SIRT3 in mitochondria further strengthens cellular defenses by enhancing mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation and reducing ROS generation through deacetylation of key metabolic enzymes. These reconstructed pathways directly address the deleterious effects of oxidative stress and metabolic dysfunction that drive RPE cell death in dry AMD (Kitaoka et al., 2020; Mehmel et al., 2020; Jadeja et al., 2018). While several studies using NMN have validated these pathways in RPE and retinal cells (Ren et al., 2022), the mechanistic rationale for NR’s effectiveness remains compelling given its similar mode of action and previously documented retinal distribution (Kitaoka et al., 2020; Jadeja et al., 2020).

Expected Effect:  
In the experimental setting, the administration of NR is expected to lead to a marked elevation of intracellular NAD+ levels within RPE cells, setting off a chain reaction of intracellular adjustments. The immediate consequence of increased NAD+ availability will be the enhanced activation of SIRT1 and SIRT3. Once activated, SIRT1 is anticipated to deacetylate TFEB, resulting in its translocation to the nucleus. In the nucleus, TFEB binds to target gene promoters, thereby upregulating a suite of genes involved in lysosomal biogenesis and the autophagic process. Critically, improvements in lysosomal acidification are expected to boost cathepsin D activity—a protease essential for the degradation of intracellular waste and damaged organelles. Simultaneously, SIRT3-mediated deacetylation events within the mitochondria are projected to improve mitochondrial respiratory capacity and enhance ATP production, while also reducing the production of ROS that ordinarily contribute to oxidative damage. The net effect of these cellular modifications should be an increase in RPE cell viability, particularly under conditions of induced oxidative stress (for example, H₂O₂ exposure), which mimics the pathological environment observed in dry AMD (Zhu et al., 2016; Tong et al., 2022).

Additionally, the NR-induced NAD+ boosting is hypothesized to initiate a beneficial feedback loop wherein improved mitochondrial function further supports cellular energy demands and sustains autophagic flux. This dual action—simultaneously targeting lysosomal and mitochondrial dysfunction—addresses two major hallmarks of dry AMD pathophysiology. RPE cells, which are crucial for the maintenance of photoreceptors, suffer from cumulative oxidative damage and impaired clearance of cellular debris as a result of aging and environmental stress. By restoring efficient autophagic processes and ensuring proper mitochondrial function, NR treatment is expected to reduce the accumulation of toxic protein aggregates and dysfunctional organelles, thereby staving off cellular senescence and death. This is especially salient given that recent studies have linked improved NAD+ metabolism to increased cellular resilience in models of age-related neurodegeneration (Jadeja et al., 2018; Jadeja et al., 2020). The expected outcomes in these assays include measurable increases in NAD+/NADH ratios, enhanced expression and nuclear localization of TFEB, elevated cathepsin D activity, and ultimately, improved cell survival following oxidative challenge. Such effects have been reported in various in vitro and in vivo studies employing NAD+ precursors, strengthening the biological plausibility of the NR hypothesis for treating dry AMD (Kitaoka et al., 2020; Mehmel et al., 2020; Dovijarski, 2019).

Overall Evaluation:  
An overall evaluation of NR as a candidate for treating dry AMD reveals both promising strengths and areas requiring further elucidation. Among the principal strengths is NR’s robust ability to elevate systemic and intracellular NAD+ levels, a key factor in numerous regulatory processes implicated in aging and cellular stress response. Its well-characterized pharmacokinetics, combined with documented safety in human supplementation studies, position NR as an attractive candidate for rapid clinical translation (Jadeja et al., 2020; Braidy et al., 2019). The underlying mechanism—that is, the activation of SIRT1 and SIRT3 leading to deacetylation and activation of TFEB—is supported by a breadth of biochemical and preclinical studies, albeit many of these have been performed with related compounds such as NMN. Nevertheless, the evidence suggests that the NAD+–sirtuin–TFEB axis is critical for autophagic and mitochondrial homeostasis in RPE cells—a process compromised in dry AMD (Kitaoka et al., 2020; Mehmel et al., 2020; Jadeja et al., 2018).

Further strengths include NR’s potential to confer dual-organellar benefit. Restoration of lysosomal function, as evidenced by improved acidification and protease activity (e.g., cathepsin D), is a novel therapeutic target that addresses the accumulation of cellular debris—a key factor in the progression of dry AMD. Concurrently, the enhancement of mitochondrial quality and bioenergetics through SIRT3 activation can mitigate oxidative stress and improve cell survival in metabolic stress conditions. Together, these actions provide a mechanistically coherent rationale for repurposing NR in a disease context that currently lacks effective treatments (Kitaoka et al., 2020; Mehmel et al., 2020).

First, while preclinical data offer promising insights, direct evidence of NR’s efficacy in RPE cells specifically challenged by dry AMD-like oxidative stress is still limited. Looking forward, systematic exploration through well-designed preclinical trials is recommended to confirm the predicted molecular events. These experiments should include detailed time-course and dose-response analyses of NAD+ levels, sirtuin activities, TFEB deacetylation status, and lysosomal function in retinal cells exposed to oxidative insults. Such data will not only clarify the effectiveness of NR in restoring cellular homeostasis but also help refine dosing strategies and identify potential biomarkers of response. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
AICAR (5‐aminoimidazole‐4‐carboxamide ribonucleoside), commercially available as Sigma A9978, is a purine nucleoside analogue originally identified as an adenosine-related compound that is taken up into cells via equilibrative nucleoside transporters and then phosphorylated by adenosine kinase into its monophosphorylated form, ZMP (Gruzman et al., 2009; Hardie, 2014). Unlike synthetic small molecules designed solely to bind regulatory subunits of AMPK, AICAR requires intracellular phosphorylation to ZMP—a process that confers a basis in natural purine metabolism as ZMP is an intermediate in de novo purine synthesis—and thereby mimics the endogenous activator AMP (Hardie, 2014; Gruzman et al., 2009). Being a small nucleoside analogue, AICAR is structurally simple compared to some of the more recently developed direct AMPK activators; its well‐delineated chemical structure, mechanism of cellular conversion, and availability from commercial sources make it an attractive candidate for repurposing studies (Drew & Kingwell, 2008; Guerrieri et al., 2017).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, AICAR has been extensively used as a research tool to probe the biology of AMPK, which is central to metabolic regulation, and it has demonstrated efficacy in a wide variety of preclinical models including skeletal muscle, adipocytes, hepatocytes, and specific cancer models (Drew & Kingwell, 2008). However, the underlying rationale of harnessing AMPK activation to improve autophagy and lysosomal clearance in affected retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells provides a logical extension of AICAR’s well‐characterized metabolic activities to the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Honnappa & Kesavan, 2016; Dolinar et al., 2018).

At the molecular level, AICAR functions by entering cells through nucleoside transporters and undergoing phosphorylation by adenosine kinase to yield ZMP, which is structurally analogous to AMP and thus capable of binding to the regulatory Bateman domains of the AMPK γ subunit (Gruzman et al., 2009; Hardie, 2014). Binding of ZMP to AMPK triggers multiple regulatory phenomena, including allosteric activation, promotion of phosphorylation at the critical Thr172 residue on the catalytic α subunit, and protection from dephosphorylation by protein phosphatases, thereby amplifying AMPK’s kinase activity (Russell & Hardie, 2020; Scudiero et al., 2016). Activated AMPK then exerts a plethora of downstream effects: it can suppress anabolic pathways via inhibition of mammalian target of rapamycin complex 1 (mTORC1) and stimulate catabolic pathways, thereby shifting cellular metabolism from energy-consuming biosynthetic processes toward energy-producing autophagy and oxidative processes (Salt & Hardie, 2017; Scudiero et al., 2016). In the context of the proposed therapeutic mechanism for dry AMD, AMPK activation by AICAR is expected to result in the suppression of mTORC1, which in turn relieves inhibitory control over the transcription factor EB (TFEB) (Drew & Kingwell, 2008; Chandrasekaran et al., 2024). TFEB acts as a master regulator of lysosomal gene expression and autophagy by translocating to the nucleus, where it upregulates genes responsible for lysosomal biogenesis, acidification, and hydrolase production; one such enzyme, cathepsin D (CTSD), is critical for effective autophagy clearance (Drew & Kingwell, 2008; Scudiero et al., 2016). This sequence of molecular events—from AICAR uptake, conversion to ZMP, AMPK activation, mTORC1 suppression, and subsequent TFEB activation—forms the mechanistic backbone supporting a therapeutic strategy geared toward enhancing lysosomal acidification and boosting cathepsin D–mediated autophagic clearance (Vara-Ciruelos et al., 2019; Yu et al., 2010). It is important to note that while the mechanism is robust, high intracellular concentrations of ZMP (and therefore high doses of AICAR) may activate other AMP-sensitive enzymes, such as glycogen phosphorylase, which underscores the necessity of titrating doses to achieve a selective AMPK-mediated effect (Russell & Hardie, 2020; Chandrasekaran et al., 2024).

Expected Effect:  
In the proposed application targeting dry AMD, the hypothesis is that AICAR administration will mimic the natural actions of AMP within RPE cells by robustly activating AMPK (Gruzman et al., 2009; Scudiero et al., 2016). In turn, this activation is expected to suppress mTORC1 activity—a key negative regulator of autophagy—and facilitate the nuclear translocation of TFEB, leading to the upregulation of lysosomal and autophagy-related genes including those encoding for cathepsin D (Drew & Kingwell, 2008; Chandrasekaran et al., 2024). In retinal pigment epithelium culture models, preliminary observations have indicated that treatment with AICAR enhances LC3 flux (a marker of autophagic activity) and increases cathepsin D activity, implying an improved capacity for autophagic clearance (Guerrieri et al., 2017; Vara-Ciruelos et al., 2019). Given that dry AMD is characterized by the accumulation of extracellular deposits (drusen) and cellular debris due to insufficient lysosomal clearance and impaired autophagy, the anticipated effect of AICAR would be to restore lysosomal functionality and promote the degradation of these pathogenic substrates (Honnappa & Kesavan, 2016; Drew & Kingwell, 2008). Furthermore, it is known from previous studies that AMPK activation can lead to enhanced mitochondrial quality control and an overall improvement in cellular metabolic homeostasis; in the context of RPE cells, this could translate to better cell survival and resilience against the oxidative stress associated with chronic degenerative processes in dry AMD (Chandrasekaran et al., 2024; Drew & Kingwell, 2008). It is also supportive that preclinical data suggest AICAR exhibits ocular safety profiles and some ability to traverse the blood–retinal barrier, which is critical for any therapeutic intended for retinal delivery (Drew & Kingwell, 2008).

Overall Evaluation:  
AICAR presents several strengths as a candidate therapeutic for dry age-related macular degeneration. First, its well-characterized mechanism—via conversion to ZMP, robust activation of AMPK, subsequent mTORC1 suppression, and activation of TFEB—provides a clear molecular rationale that directly addresses the impaired autophagic and lysosomal clearance mechanisms believed to underlie dry AMD pathology (Gruzman et al., 2009; Scudiero et al., 2016). Second, its extensive experimental use over the past decades in cell culture and animal models across metabolic, cardiovascular, and even oncological studies gives it a solid preclinical pedigree and provides a wealth of pharmacodynamic and safety data (Hardie, 2014; Russell & Hardie, 2020). Third, the hypothesis that activating AMPK in retinal pigment epithelial cells can lead to improvements in LC3 flux and cathepsin D activity is supported by a mechanistic analogy to effects seen in neuronal and muscle cell studies, suggesting that similar benefits may be achieved in RPE cells (Yu et al., 2010; Chandrasekaran et al., 2024). Moreover, known preclinical ocular safety data and evidence of the compound’s ability to cross the blood–retinal barrier lend practical feasibility to the candidate’s repurposing for an ocular indication like dry AMD (Drew & Kingwell, 2008; Russell & Hardie, 2020).

However, there are several challenges and potential weaknesses that must be carefully considered. AICAR’s effective activation of AMPK often requires concentrations in the millimolar range, and such high concentrations have been associated with off-target effects including interactions with AMP-sensitive enzymes other than AMPK (for example, glycogen phosphorylase and fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase), which may complicate therapeutic outcomes (Russell & Hardie, 2020; Guerrieri et al., 2017). In addition, AICAR is known to have poor oral bioavailability and a relatively short plasma half-life, issues that might necessitate alternative routes of administration or formulation strategies to achieve sustained therapeutic levels in the retina (Salt & Hardie, 2017; Gruzman et al., 2009). The possibility of metabolic complications such as lactic acidosis and hyperuricemia at high systemic doses has been documented in metabolic models; although local ocular administration might mitigate systemic exposure, these concerns require thorough investigation in focused preclinical studies (Dolinar et al., 2018). Furthermore, while the concept of activating the AMPK–TFEB–lysosomal pathway is promising, there remains uncertainty regarding the extent to which RPE cells recapitulate the robust autophagic responses observed in other tissues; cell type–dependent variability may influence both efficacy and safety outcomes (Drew & Kingwell, 2008). Finally, because AICAR has been primarily evaluated in the context of metabolic and ischemic conditions rather than chronic degenerative diseases of the eye, there is an inherent translational gap that will require dedicated studies to validate the mechanistic efficacy in dry AMD models (Drew & Kingwell, 2008).

In summary, AICAR offers a compelling potential mechanism by which activation of AMPK could restore autophagic and lysosomal functions in RPE cells, addressing key pathogenic features of dry AMD such as impaired clearance of debris and dysfunctional cellular metabolism (Drew & Kingwell, 2008; Dolinar et al., 2018). Its extensive history as a research tool provides a strong foundation of pharmacodynamic and mechanistic understanding, and its established ocular safety and blood–retinal barrier permeability are additional assets for its repurposing in an ocular setting (Russell & Hardie, 2020; Drew & Kingwell, 2008). Nevertheless, issues related to dosing, off-target activity, pharmacokinetic limitations, and cell-specific responses must be resolved through rigorous preclinical studies, including dose-ranging experiments in relevant RPE models and animal models of dry AMD (Chandrasekaran et al., 2024; Dolinar et al., 2018). Overall, while challenges exist, the mechanistic underpinnings and prior experimental data justify further investigation of AICAR as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration, provided that its pharmacokinetics and off-target liabilities can be managed through optimized formulation or targeted delivery strategies (Gruzman et al., 2009; Dolinar et al., 2018).

While most STACs are SIRT1-selective, SRT1720 exhibits notable polypharmacology, including reported inhibitory activity against Sirt3, highlighting potential off-target risks intrinsic to this first-generation class (Mazzone, 2018). As a class, STACs have been widely evaluated for metabolic, inflammatory, neurodegenerative, and aging phenotypes predicated on SIRT1’s broad substrate repertoire (for example, PGC-1α, NF-κB p65/RelA, FOXO family, p53), which link to mitochondrial biogenesis, anti-inflammatory signaling, oxidative stress responses, and cell survival programs (Chang et al., 2024; Mazzone, 2018).

Therapeutic History  
SRT1720 has extensive preclinical use, but there is no evidence in the provided corpus that it has been tested in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), in the eye, or in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) models (cellular or in vivo) (Ji et al., 2021; Ding et al., 2017; Bononi et al., 2022). In non-ocular systems, SRT1720 increased mitochondrial biogenesis and rescued mitochondrial function after oxidant injury in renal proximal tubule cells, providing proof-of-concept that STAC activation can drive PGC-1α–linked mitochondrial programs in mammalian cells under oxidative stress (Ji et al., 2021). In metabolic disease models, SRT1720 is reported to improve hepatic lipid metabolism via SIRT1-dependent pathways regulating PGC-1α, AMPK, PPARα, FOXO1, SREBP-1c and FGF21, with consistent decreases in lipogenesis and inflammation and increases in fatty-acid β-oxidation in NAFLD models (Ding et al., 2017). Multiple lifespan/healthspan studies reported benefits in mice—improved survival and healthspan in diet-induced obese animals and lifespan extension on standard diet—again consistent with systemic SIRT1-axis engagement (Mazzone, 2018). At the same time, substantial controversy surrounds both mechanism and safety. Pacholec et al. argued SRT1720 (and related first-generation STACs) are not direct SIRT1 activators under specific biochemical conditions, although later work provided structural and kinetic support for allosteric activation with specific substrates (Lee et al., 2021; Bononi et al., 2022). Importantly for repurposing risk, SRT1720 promoted tumor cell migration and lung metastasis in a breast cancer model, and SRT1720 can trigger SIRT1-independent cytotoxicity in some hematologic malignancy cells, underscoring unresolved off-target liabilities (Bononi et al., 2022; Chang et al., 2024). - Biochemical pharmacology and target engagement: SRT1720 belongs to the STAC class that can directly activate SIRT1 through an assisted allosteric mechanism requiring specific substrate motifs; mutating SIRT1 E230 disrupts both activator binding and activation, and co-crystal structures of SIRT1 with SRT-like activators support an allosteric binding pocket that enhances deacetylation efficiency in a substrate-dependent manner (Lee et al., 2021; Mazzone, 2018). Early reports of direct activation were contested due to labeled peptide assay artifacts, but subsequent kinetic and structural data reconciled these findings with an allosteric model; nonetheless, the field recognizes pharmacological caveats including context-dependent activation and off-targets, such as reported Sirt3 inhibition by SRT1720 (Mazzone, 2018; Lee et al., 2021).

The proposed therapeutic candidate is a miR-204 mimic (agomir), i.e., a synthetic double-stranded RNA designed to reconstitute or augment mature miR-204 activity in target cells, thereby restoring sequence-specific repression of cognate mRNAs via Argonaute/RISC-mediated post-transcriptional regulation (Du & Palczewski, 2022). Agomirs are typically produced by solid-phase oligonucleotide synthesis and formulated with stabilizing chemical modifications and delivery moieties to resist nucleases and evade innate immune sensors; however, the present literature corpus specific to miR-204 provides no details on the chemical design or manufacturing of a miR-204 agomir used in ocular studies (Du & Palczewski, 2022; Karali et al., 2020). In vivo “gain-of-function” delivery of miR-204 has been achieved preclinically using adeno-associated viral (AAV) gene therapy vectors encoding the murine pre-miR-204 hairpin driven by ubiquitous (CMV) or photoreceptor-specific (RHO) promoters, establishing that increasing miR-204 activity is feasible and can confer neuroprotective and anti-inflammatory effects in degenerating retina (Karali et al., 2020). Separately, the agomir modality (chemically synthesized miR-204 mimic) has been used in ocular systems and vertebrate development: ocular injection of a miR-204 mimic in rat retina reduced GAP-43 expression, and double-stranded miR-204 mimic injection in medaka embryos caused microphthalmia and lens dysgenesis, demonstrating biological activity in vivo with potential context-dependent liabilities (Shiels, 2020).

Within the broader therapeutic class, miRNA modulation includes replacement (mimics/agomirs) and inhibition (antimiRs) and has been explored preclinically and clinically; the most advanced clinical precedent involves an antimiR of miR-122 (miravirsen) in hepatology, while miRNA mimics face delivery, stability, and innate-immune activation challenges that necessitate chemical modification and targeted delivery—issues directly relevant to deploying a miR-204 agomir in the eye (Parsi, 2016). In ophthalmology, miRNAs regulate essential RPE functions including phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments (POS), autophagy, endolysosomal trafficking, epithelial barrier integrity, and inflammatory signaling, making miR replacement an attractive strategy to correct multi-pathway dysfunctions typical of dry AMD (Du & Palczewski, 2022).

Therapeutic History  
- Ocular/retinal delivery of miR-204 by AAV gene therapy:  
  - In RHO-P347S and Aipl1−/− mouse models of inherited retinal degeneration (IRD), subretinal AAV2/8 vectors expressing pre-miR-204 preserved retinal function by ERG, reduced photoreceptor cell death (TUNEL), and dampened microglial activation and innate immune/inflammatory transcriptomes; luciferase data supported direct targeting of immune/apoptosis transcripts (Siglec1, Xaf1) by miR-204 (Karali et al., 2020). These effects persisted through at least PN60 when dosed at PN4 in the RHO-P347S model, and benefit tracked with ubiquitous expression (CMV) more than photoreceptor-restricted expression (RHO), consistent with non–cell-autonomous and multi-cell-type actions (Karali et al., 2020). The studies confirm feasibility and efficacy of miR-204 augmentation in murine retina, but they used viral expression rather than chemically synthesized mimics and were not performed in dry AMD models (Karali et al., 2020).  
- Ocular/neuronal use of miR-204 mimics/inhibitors:  
  - Direct ocular injection of a miR-204 mimic in rats decreased GAP-43 expression and, in the context of injury, increased retinal TUNEL-positive cells, while a miR-204 inhibitor increased GAP-43, indicating robust on-target modulation and context-dependent toxicity risk (Shiels, 2020). In medaka, overexpression of a miR-204 double-stranded mimic (agomir) produced microphthalmia and lens dysgenesis, underscoring the need for careful dose, spatial restriction, and developmental timing (Shiels, 2020).  
- Disease relevance of miR-204 to dry AMD biology:  
  - Genetic deletion of miR-204 in mice causes progressive, age-dependent RPE/retina pathology reminiscent of dry AMD: hyper-autofluorescent deposits, impaired POS degradation with rhodopsin accumulation in RPE, autophagosome accumulation, lysosomal deficits (lower LAMP2 signal), microglial migration to the RPE apical surface, increased proinflammatory cytokine secretion (apical IL-8), IPM disorganization, reduced ERG components (photoreceptor and RPE-driven), and downregulation of visual cycle genes (LRAT, RPE65, TTR) that would constrain retinoid recycling (Zhang et al., 2019; Intartaglia et al., 2021). Parallel anti-miR-204 knockdown in primary human fetal RPE recapitulates autophagy/lysosomal and phagolysosomal defects: reduced POS digestion without reduced uptake (~20% slower clearance), increased p62, accumulation of undigested autophagosomes, reduced LAMP2, and intracellular rhodopsin accumulation; Rab22a protein (an inhibitor of endosome maturation) rises in both anti-miR and KO settings, mechanistically linking the phenotype to a miR-204 → Rab22a axis (Zhang et al., 2019). These convergent in vivo/in vitro loss-of-function data provide the key mechanistic rationale to explore miR-204 augmentation as a corrective therapy in dry AMD-like RPE dysfunction (Zhang et al., 2019).  
- miRNA class precedent and translational trajectory:  
  - Reviews emphasize that RPE miRNAs control phagocytosis and lysosomal pathways and that specific miR:mRNA pairs (including miR-204→Rab22a) are central to vesicle trafficking; they also note that miR therapeutics can be delivered via viral vectors or nonviral carriers (e.g., nanoparticles), but that miRNA mimic programs face stability, delivery, and immune-activation challenges that will need to be mitigated (Du & Palczewski, 2022; Parsi, 2016). There are no reports of miR-204 agomir use in dry AMD patients or animal models of dry AMD; thus, clinical and AMD-specific preclinical history for a chemically synthesized miR-204 mimic is absent in the present corpus (Du & Palczewski, 2022; Karali et al., 2020).

Mechanism of Action  
At the biochemical level, mature miR-204 is loaded into the RISC and binds target 3′ UTR seed sites to repress translation and/or promote mRNA decay of specific transcripts that regulate RPE homeostasis (Du & Palczewski, 2022). The best-supported target in the context of endosomal maturation is Rab22a, a small GTPase that acts as an inhibitor of early-to-late endosomal progression and thereby impedes endosome–lysosome fusion necessary for proteolysis (Zhang et al., 2019). In miR-204 loss-of-function models (global KO mice and anti-miR-204–treated human fetal RPE), Rab22a protein levels are increased by immunostaining and western blot in RPE, particularly after POS feeding, and the authors interpret this as a dysregulation at the intersection of the autophagy and endosome pathways (Zhang et al., 2019). The mechanistic model is explicit: loss of miR-204 increases Rab22a expression, which impedes maturation of early autophagosomal/endosomal intermediates that fail to fuse with lysosomes, resulting in decreased phagocytic clearance and persistent accumulation of POS-derived rhodopsin in RPE (Zhang et al., 2019).

Functional correlates of this endosomal maturation block are well documented in RPE:  
- Phagolysosomal/autophagy markers: anti-miR-204 RPE shows increased p62/SQSTM1, increased number/size of undigested autophagosomes by TEM, and altered LC3B isoform distribution (increased LC3B-I without consistent LC3B-II accumulation), consistent with impaired maturation of degradative compartments rather than defective initiation of LC3-associated processes (Zhang et al., 2019). Anti-miR-204 reduces lysosomal content/function by ~1.6-fold lower LAMP2 in RPE relative to controls, consistent with fewer functional lysosomes available for phagosome fusion (Zhang et al., 2019).  
- Phagocytosis and digestion of POS: uptake per se is not impaired, but the digestion rate is slowed (~20% reduction in clearance in anti-miR-204 RPE by FACS-based pHrodo POS assays), directly supporting a degradative block downstream of engulfment (Zhang et al., 2019).  
- Rhodopsin accumulation: in miR-204−/− mice, rhodopsin-containing POS material accumulates within RPE at the peak of daily phagocytosis (8–10 a.m.) as measured by IF and western blot; anti-miR-204 hfRPE also accumulates rhodopsin after POS feeding (Zhang et al., 2019).  
- Secretory/inflammatory signaling: anti-miR-204 increases apical IL-8 secretion ~2-fold in hfRPE, creating a chemokine gradient predicted to attract retinal microglia to the RPE apical surface, which is observed in KO animals, and likely contributes to hyper-autofluorescent deposits and inflammatory retinal dysfunction (Zhang et al., 2019).  
- Electrophysiological and structural consequences: miR-204−/− mice exhibit reduced retinal photoreceptor and bipolar responses (ERG a- and b-wave), reduced RPE-derived DC-ERG components (c-wave and FO), age-dependent lipofuscin accumulation, interphotoreceptor matrix disorganization, and ultrastructural RPE defects, all consistent with chronic degradative deficiency and secondary degeneration (Zhang et al., 2019).

Beyond the Rab22a/endosome axis, miR-204 maintains epithelial identity and apical membrane physiology in RPE:  
- TGF-β signaling and EMT restraint: miR-204 directly targets TGFBR2 at the apical membrane; its inhibition upregulates TGF-β pathway genes (TGFBR2, SNAI2), collapses transepithelial resistance (~80% decrease), reduces claudins/tight junctions, and promotes EMT-like changes, linking miR-204 to barrier integrity and anti-fibrotic states (Shiels, 2020; Zhang et al., 2019).  
- Ion homeostasis: miR-204 loss indirectly reduces Kir7.1 expression and K+ efflux, leading to RPE cell swelling and subretinal space perturbations that can promote autophagy; these changes plausibly contribute to the reduced c-wave amplitude in KO animals (Zhang et al., 2019).  
- Visual cycle: miR-204 deficiency downregulates LRAT, RPE65, and TTR, impairing 11-cis-retinal regeneration and retinoid transport, thereby coupling endolysosomal deficits with phototransduction support failure (Intartaglia et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2019).

Inflammation can suppress miR-204 levels: IFN-γ downregulates miR-204 in ARPE-19, and miR-204 is coregulated with TRPM3; given that inflammation is a key driver in AMD, cytokine-driven miR-204 depletion provides a pathophysiological link to disease (Shiels, 2020).

In contrast to the detailed loss-of-function and in vitro mechanistic data, direct rescue experiments that re-introduce miR-204 in RPE to reverse Rab22a elevation, restore endosome–lysosome maturation, and normalize POS degradation have not been reported in the cited sources; the reported augmentation studies used AAV-miR-204 in IRD models and measured predominantly neuroinflammation and apoptosis endpoints rather than phagolysosomal rescue in RPE (Zhang et al., 2019; Karali et al., 2020).

Expected Effect  
If a chemically modified miR-204 agomir is delivered to RPE and achieves sufficient intracellular loading into Ago2/RISC, the expected molecular and cellular effects, by inversion of the validated loss-of-function phenotypes, are:  
- Target repression and endosomal maturation: Decrease Rab22a protein abundance in RPE, relieving its inhibitory effect on maturation of early endosomes/autophagosomal intermediates and permitting efficient endosome–lysosome fusion and phagolysosome function (Zhang et al., 2019).  
- Phagolysosomal/autophagy normalization: Increase functional lysosome content (e.g., rescue of LAMP2 levels), reduce p62 accumulation, decrease number/size of undigested autophagosomes, and accelerate degradation (but not uptake) of POS cargo in hfRPE digestion assays (e.g., increased pHrodo chase rate, reduced intracellular rhodopsin by IF/WB after standardized POS feeds) (Zhang et al., 2019).  
- Reduction of inflammatory signaling and microglial recruitment: Lower apical IL-8 secretion, diminishing chemotactic signals for resident microglia and reducing subretinal microglial accumulation; reduce hyper-autofluorescent material accrual over time, which is associated with impaired POS degradation (Zhang et al., 2019).  
- Functional recovery: Improve RPE and retinal electrophysiology (DC-ERG c-wave, FO; ERG a-/b-waves), contingent on sufficient rescue of POS handling and visual cycle support; maintain expression of visual cycle genes (LRAT, RPE65, TTR) and ion channel function (Kir7.1) through direct and indirect effects of miR-204 on apical physiology (Zhang et al., 2019; Intartaglia et al., 2021).

These expected effects are consistent with the mechanistic chain established in RPE: miR-204 controls Rab22a and endosomal maturation, which governs phagolysosomal processing of POS; failure at this node produces rhodopsin/undigested lipid accumulation, oxidative/proinflammatory stress, microglial activation, and electrophysiological decline—key features of dry AMD-like RPE dysfunction (Zhang et al., 2019). Notably, direct evidence that miR-204 augmentation in RPE increases cathepsin D activity or lysosomal acidification is not present in the cited literature; such outcomes are plausible secondary consequences of restored maturation but remain to be experimentally validated in this system (Zhang et al., 2019). Conversely, miR-204 augmentation has demonstrated capacity to downregulate proinflammatory/apoptotic signaling in degenerating retinas (AAV delivery in IRD), which may add non–phagolysosomal benefits in dry AMD by dampening microglia activation and apoptosis (Karali et al., 2020).

Assay-relevant expression and feasibility:  
- Rab22a is expressed in RPE and is upregulated when miR-204 is reduced, validating it as an RPE-relevant miR-204 target to monitor in pharmacodynamic assays (Zhang et al., 2019).  
- The RPE performs circadian POS phagocytosis and directs cargo to lysosomes; miRNAs regulate both uptake and downstream lysosomal breakdown, placing miR-204 within a well-defined physiological context where restoration should impact measurable endpoints (Du & Palczewski, 2022).  
- Established in vitro RPE models and in vivo mouse paradigms using exogenous POS feed, pHrodo uptake/chase, rhodopsin IF/WB, and endolysosomal markers (p62, LC3, LAMP2), as well as apical cytokine secretion and ERG readouts, provide a fit-for-purpose translational assay suite to test a miR-204 agomir (Zhang et al., 2019).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Mechanistic specificity linked to a central AMD-relevant pathway: The miR-204 → Rab22a axis is strongly supported in RPE by convergent mouse and human RPE data showing that miR-204 loss elevates Rab22a, blocks endosomal maturation, reduces phagolysosomal clearance (without impairing uptake), and causes intracellular rhodopsin/undigested autophagosome accumulation—key pathomechanisms implicated in dry AMD (Zhang et al., 2019). This provides a precise molecular rationale that a miR-204 mimic could correct a bottleneck in the RPE degradative axis central to disease biology (Du & Palczewski, 2022).  
- Strong phenotypic congruence with dry AMD: miR-204−/− mice develop age-related hyper-autofluorescent deposits, RPE/retina electrophysiological decline, microglial recruitment, and visual cycle impairment, aligning with multiple facets of dry AMD pathophysiology and supporting the translational relevance of restoring miR-204 in RPE (Zhang et al., 2019; Intartaglia et al., 2021).  
- High endogenous expression and biology in RPE: miR-204 is among the most abundant miRNAs in RPE and is induced during RPE differentiation; inflammation downregulates miR-204, plausibly contributing to disease, which rationalizes a replacement strategy (Shiels, 2020).  
- Modality precedent and in vivo efficacy: Although not a mimic per se, AAV-mediated miR-204 augmentation confers neuroprotection, anti-inflammatory effects, and partial functional rescue in IRD models, indicating therapeutic potential of miR-204 augmentation in retinal disease and providing insight into safety, dose timing, and target engagement in vivo (Karali et al., 2020).  
- Multiplexed benefits beyond endosomes: miR-204 regulates EMT/barrier pathways (TGFBR2, claudins), apical ion homeostasis (Kir7.1), and visual cycle gene expression (LRAT, RPE65, TTR), potentially addressing several RPE dysfunction axes simultaneously—a desirable property in multifactorial dry AMD (Shiels, 2020; Zhang et al., 2019; Intartaglia et al., 2021).

Weaknesses and Gaps  
- Lack of direct rescue evidence for phagolysosomal function with miR-204 augmentation in RPE: The literature does not yet report that a miR-204 mimic (or even AAV miR-204) restores Rab22a levels, increases lysosomal maturation, improves POS degradation kinetics, or reduces rhodopsin/autophagosome accumulation in RPE in vivo; the mechanistic case is built from loss-of-function data with predictive inversion (Zhang et al., 2019).  
- Modality-specific uncertainties: No chemical design, stability, or delivery data exist for a miR-204 agomir in ocular models; miRNA mimics face known hurdles (nuclease stability, RISC loading efficiency, innate immune activation via TLRs, off-targeting), and eye-specific delivery vehicles (e.g., lipid nanoparticles, conjugates) require optimization for RPE targeting via subretinal or intravitreal routes (Parsi, 2016; Du & Palczewski, 2022). The absence of agomir pharmacology in AMD-relevant models elevates translational risk relative to the AAV modality that already shows ocular efficacy (Karali et al., 2020).  
- Context-dependent safety signals: Ocular delivery of miR-204 mimics in rats reduced GAP-43 but, in conjunction with injury, increased retinal apoptosis; overexpression in medaka produced ocular developmental defects, indicating potential toxicity if miR-204 is overexpressed in non-target cells or at inappropriate developmental stages (Shiels, 2020). Given miR-204’s pleiotropy in epithelial identity, ion transport, and neuronal circuits, off-target cell engagement or supra-physiological dosing could disrupt RPE and neuronal homeostasis (Shiels, 2020).  
- Disease-model scope: The strongest augmentation data for miR-204 come from IRD models; while these demonstrate anti-inflammatory and anti-apoptotic benefits, they do not directly test AMD-relevant endpoints such as drusen/lipofuscin dynamics, RPE atrophy trajectories, or aging/inflammation-driven POS handling failure (Karali et al., 2020).  
- Specific biochemical endpoints in hypothesis not yet supported: The hypothesis posits improved acidic vesicle trafficking and cathepsin D activity; the supplied literature does not report lysosomal pH or cathepsin D assays in miR-204 perturbations, so these remain to be demonstrated experimentally (Zhang et al., 2019).

Risk mitigation and development plan considerations  
- Prioritize RPE-specific delivery and dose control. Given the sensitivity of neuronal tissues to miR-204 overexpression and the broad target set, subretinal delivery of an RPE-targeted agomir formulation or RPE-tropic carrier should be favored over diffuse intravitreal exposure to minimize photoreceptor or ganglion cell transduction (Shiels, 2020; Karali et al., 2020).  
- Establish pharmacodynamic linkage. In hfRPE and in vivo, measure Rab22a suppression, restoration of LAMP2, reduced p62, improved POS digestion, and decreased apical IL-8 post-dose; these PD markers are available and directly read out the proposed mechanism (Zhang et al., 2019).  
- Compare to genetic augmentation. Benchmark agomir against AAV-pre-miR-204 in identical readouts to de-risk modality differences and clarify whether non–phagolysosomal benefits (e.g., anti-inflammatory network modulation) are preserved with transient synthetic dosing (Karali et al., 2020).  
- Off-target and safety profiling. Use Argonaute CLIP or related approaches in RPE to map miR-204 on-targets under agomir exposure; monitor EMT markers, tight junctions, Kir7.1, and TRPM3-linked pathways to avoid epithelial or ionic dysregulation; evaluate microglial activation states and apoptotic markers to detect adverse network effects (Du & Palczewski, 2022; Shiels, 2020; Zhang et al., 2019; Karali et al., 2020).  
- AMD-relevant efficacy models. Progress to aging/inflammation-driven RPE dysfunction models that recapitulate POS clearance deficits and lipofuscin/drusen-like pathology; assess fundus autofluorescence, rhodopsin accumulation, ERG/DC-ERG, and visual cycle gene expression after repeated agomir dosing (Zhang et al., 2019).

Conclusion  
The totality of evidence supports miR-204 as a nodal regulator of RPE endosomal maturation and phagolysosomal clearance of photoreceptor outer segments via repression of Rab22a, with loss-of-function data in mice and human RPE showing degradative failure, inflammatory activation, and electrophysiological decline that recapitulate dry AMD-like features (Zhang et al., 2019). Although no study has yet demonstrated that a miR-204 agomir restores RPE phagolysosomal function in vivo in AMD-relevant models, augmentation with AAV-miR-204 achieves robust anti-inflammatory and anti-apoptotic effects and preserves retinal function in IRD models, indicating therapeutic potential of miR-204 enhancement and justifying further development (Karali et al., 2020). The agomir modality offers a nonviral, potentially titratable approach but currently lacks ocular pharmacology, delivery, and safety data; it also carries risks of off-target effects and context-dependent toxicity that must be mitigated by RPE-specific delivery and rigorous PD/PK control (Parsi, 2016; Shiels, 2020). On balance, a chemically modified miR-204 mimic targeted to RPE is a mechanistically compelling candidate for dry AMD that addresses a validated maturation bottleneck in the RPE degradative axis, with multiple additional benefits expected on barrier/ion homeostasis and the visual cycle; however, the program requires foundational preclinical work to demonstrate rescue of endosomal maturation and POS clearance in RPE, establish ocular delivery and dosing, and define safety margins before advancing toward IND-enabling studies (Zhang et al., 2019; Du & Palczewski, 2022).

Detailed Evaluation by Section  

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
miR-204 is an intronic miRNA within the TRPM3 locus, expressed at high levels in RPE and upregulated during RPE differentiation; it contributes to epithelial morphology, polarity, and tight junction integrity (Shiels, 2020). Synthetic miRNA mimics (agomirs) recreate the guide strand of the mature miRNA and, once delivered intracellularly, load into Ago2 to direct sequence-specific silencing of target mRNAs (Du & Palczewski, 2022). The literature shows that miR-204 function has been augmented in vivo using AAV2/8 delivery of pre-miR-204 to mouse retina and that direct agomir delivery has been performed in vertebrate ocular systems (rats and medaka), although specific chemistry and formulation details of the agomir are not provided (Karali et al., 2020; Shiels, 2020). In ophthalmic disease, miRNA-based modulation has emerged as a tool to adjust multi-gene networks; however, clinical experience with miRNA replacement is limited and will require attention to stability and innate immunity hazards typical of RNA therapeutics (Parsi, 2016).

Therapeutic History  
No prior clinical use of a miR-204 agomir in dry AMD has been reported; nevertheless, extensive preclinical loss-of-function evidence shows that miR-204 deficiency is sufficient to produce AMD-like phenotypes (accumulated autofluorescence, impaired POS clearance, inflammatory microglial recruitment, ERG deficits), supporting the pathophysiological premise that miR-204 restoration may be beneficial (Zhang et al., 2019). In primary human RPE, anti-miR-204 reduces POS digestion without affecting uptake and shifts endolysosomal markers in a manner consistent with a maturation block; Rab22a rises in both anti-miR and KO RPE (Zhang et al., 2019). In IRD models, AAV-delivered miR-204 improves ERG responses, reduces photoreceptor cell death, and downregulates inflammatory/apoptotic pathways (including direct repression of Siglec1 and Xaf1 by luciferase), establishing in vivo efficacy of miR-204 augmentation in degenerating retinas, albeit not in dry AMD models (Karali et al., 2020). Ocular administration of a miR-204 mimic in rats modulates neuronal markers (GAP-43) but can increase apoptosis in injury contexts, and embryonic overexpression in medaka causes eye malformations, highlighting potential safety concerns with unrestrained overexpression or ectopic exposure (Shiels, 2020).

Mechanism of Action  
The core molecular mechanism is the repression of Rab22a in RPE by miR-204, which relieves an inhibitory checkpoint in endosomal maturation and allows phagosomes to fuse with lysosomes, thereby promoting efficient POS proteolysis (Zhang et al., 2019). The downstream pathway is supported by multi-parameter readouts in KO and anti-miR RPE: impaired degradation (slower POS clearance, rhodopsin accumulation), autophagosome accumulation (p62+, LC3B-I elevation), reduced lysosomal marker LAMP2, and secondary inflammation (apical IL-8), culminating in microglial recruitment and electrophysiological decline (Zhang et al., 2019). miR-204 also sustains RPE barrier/ion physiology (TGFBR2/EMT restraint, Kir7.1), and its deficiency diminishes visual cycle gene expression that supports photoreceptor pigment regeneration (Shiels, 2020; Zhang et al., 2019; Intartaglia et al., 2021). The miRNA’s pleiotropy therefore suggests that restoration could concurrently benefit phagolysosomal function, barrier integrity, ionic balance, and retinoid handling, all implicated in dry AMD.

Expected Effect  
In vitro and in vivo assays of a miR-204 agomir should demonstrate molecular PD: reduced Rab22a protein in RPE (WB/IF), normalization of autophagy–endolysosomal markers (reduced p62, restored LC3B flux balance, increased LAMP2), and decreased apical IL-8 secretion (Zhang et al., 2019); functional PD: accelerated degradation of POS cargo in hfRPE pHrodo-chase assays and reduced intracellular rhodopsin accumulation post-feed (Zhang et al., 2019); and disease-relevant outcomes: in aged/inflammation-primed mice, decreased fundus autofluorescence and subretinal microglial accumulation, improved ERG/DC-ERG components, and maintenance of visual cycle gene expression (Zhang et al., 2019).

Overall Evaluation  
The miR-204 agomir is a mechanistically well-justified candidate for dry AMD, directly addressing a Rab22a-governed endosomal maturation defect that produces cardinal features of RPE failure seen in disease models and patient-like phenotypes (Zhang et al., 2019). The strength of the rationale is anchored in robust, cross-species loss-of-function data and in vitro human RPE phenocopying, as well as AAV-miR-204 augmentation data that validate the therapeutic value of increasing miR-204 in diseased retina (Zhang et al., 2019; Karali et al., 2020). However, the agomir modality lacks AMD-relevant in vivo rescue data and ocular pharmacology, and miRNA mimics pose delivery and safety challenges that necessitate careful formulation and RPE targeting (Parsi, 2016; Du & Palczewski, 2022). Given these considerations, the program should proceed with a staged preclinical plan emphasizing RPE-specific delivery, direct PD confirmation of Rab22a suppression and phagolysosomal restoration, AMD-relevant efficacy models, and rigorous safety/off-target profiling—including EMT/barrier and ion-channel endpoints—to de-risk translation (Zhang et al., 2019; Shiels, 2020; Karali et al., 2020).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Torin1 is a synthetic small‐molecule that belongs to the second‐generation, ATP‐competitive class of mTOR inhibitors, originally derived from a quinoline‐based scaffold. Its discovery originated from a high‐throughput compound library screen that identified quinolone hits with moderate mTOR activity, which were then optimized through iterative medicinal chemistry by introducing a six‐membered lactam to convert the initial quinolone into a tricyclic benzonaphthridinone scaffold (Guillem, 2015). This chemical modification yielded a molecule with exceptional biochemical potency—capable of inhibiting both mTOR complexes, mTORC1 and mTORC2, at very low (nanomolar to picomolar) concentrations—and with approximately 1000-fold improvement in cellular potency relative to the initial hits (Guillem, 2015). As an ATP-competitive inhibitor, Torin1 binds directly to the active (ATP-binding) site of mTOR, thereby circumventing the partial inhibition that is observed with first-generation mTOR inhibitors like rapamycin that act allosterically by binding FKBP12 (Liu et al., 2012). Torin1 has been widely used as a research tool to interrogate mTOR signaling in various cellular contexts, and its chemical lineage as a quinoline-derived molecule positions it within a well-characterized class of inhibitors that have been instrumental in expanding our understanding of mTOR-dependent regulation of autophagy and cellular metabolism (Liu et al., 2012).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, Torin1 has been employed predominantly as a research tool rather than as a clinical drug candidate. Extensive preclinical studies have demonstrated its robust ability to inhibit mTOR signaling in cancer models, autophagy-deficient systems, and metabolic studies. For instance, Torin1 was shown to potently inhibit mTOR signaling pathways in glioblastoma and prostate cancer cells, significantly reducing cell-cycle progression and inducing apoptosis in certain contexts (Gu, 2017; Liu et al., 2012). Its use as an autophagy inducer is well documented, as experiments utilizing Torin1 have demonstrated increased autophagic flux and elevated lysosomal activity in multiple cell lines (Li, 2018; Liu et al., 2012). Importantly, Torin1 is also used in studies with retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells, as evidenced by its ability to increase TFEB-driven luciferase reporter activity in ARPE-19 cells by effectively suppressing mTORC1 signaling (Huang et al., 2018). Despite these promising experimental findings, Torin1 has not advanced to clinical trials for any indication, including neurodegenerative disorders or dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD). Moreover, its intrinsic pharmacokinetic limitations—such as poor aqueous solubility, a short half-life, and low oral bioavailability—have been recognized in several studies, thereby limiting its potential as a direct therapeutic candidate without further structural optimization (Guillem, 2015; Wang et al., 2022).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, Torin1 functions by competing with ATP for binding to the catalytic domain of mTOR, effectively blocking the phosphorylation of downstream substrates. Its ATP-competitive nature allows Torin1 to inhibit both mTORC1 and mTORC2 complexes, thereby offering a broader inhibition profile than allosteric agents like rapamycin that primarily target mTORC1 (Guillem, 2015; Liu et al., 2012). Detailed molecular modeling and structure–activity relationship studies indicate that the tricyclic benzonaphthridinone core of Torin1 forms critical hinge-binding interactions with residues in the mTOR kinase domain (Liu et al., 2012). This interaction accounts for its high potency, as reflected in low nanomolar IC₅₀ values in cellular assays (Liu et al., 2012; Gros & Muller, 2014). Torin1 induces rapid dephosphorylation of canonical mTORC1 substrates, such as S6 kinase at Thr389 and 4E-BP1 at Thr37/46, which results in downregulation of protein synthesis and cellular growth signals (Misra & Pizzo, 2013). Moreover, by simultaneously inhibiting mTORC2, it reduces phosphorylation of Akt at Ser473—a site critical for full Akt activation—thus attenuating the feedback loops that typically reinvigorate upstream PI3K signaling in response to mTORC1 inhibition (Gu, 2017; Martina et al., 2014). A particularly notable feature of Torin1 is its slow off-rate, which leads to sustained inhibition of mTOR activity even after drug washout, a pharmacodynamic property that may confer prolonged downstream effects such as enhanced autophagic flux (Liu et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2013). The inhibition of mTOR by Torin1 correlates with dephosphorylation of transcription factors, particularly TFEB and TFE3; under normal nutrient-replete conditions, mTORC1 phosphorylates TFEB (e.g., on S211 in TFEB) and TFE3, sequestering them in the cytosol through binding with 14-3-3 proteins (Huang et al., 2018; Martina et al., 2014). Upon mTOR inhibition by Torin1, TFEB is dephosphorylated and translocates to the nucleus, where it induces the transcription of CLEAR (Coordinated Lysosomal Expression and Regulation) network genes that drive lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy (Li, 2018; Liu et al., 2013). This precise modulation of mTOR signaling and subsequent transcriptional reprogramming forms the biochemical basis for leveraging Torin1 as a candidate to ameliorate lysosomal clearance defects.

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis for repurposing Torin1 in the context of dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is that potent inhibition of mTORC1/2 in RPE cells can lift the repressive phosphorylation that normally limits the activity of TFEB and TFE3. In RPE cells, as demonstrated by studies in ARPE-19 cell models, mTOR inhibition via Torin1 not only leads to decreased phosphorylation of S6 kinase but also results in marked activation of TFEB-driven transcription (Huang et al., 2018). When TFEB translocates to the nucleus, it binds to CLEAR elements present in the promoters of genes responsible for lysosomal biogenesis, acidification (through the upregulation of V-ATPase subunits), and the maturation and activity of lysosomal enzymes such as cathepsin D (CTSD) (Huang et al., 2018; Li, 2018). In dry AMD, RPE cells exhibit a decline in lysosomal function along with accumulation of cellular debris and lipofuscin, which contribute to disease pathology. By inducing a robust CLEAR response, Torin1 is expected to restore lysosomal function through increased biogenesis, enhanced acidification, and elevated cathepsin D activity, thereby improving the clearance of toxic aggregates in RPE cells and ultimately mitigating the progression of dry AMD (Gu, 2017; Huang et al., 2018). Additionally, the sustained target engagement afforded by Torin1’s slow off-rate may provide prolonged therapeutic benefit even with intermittent dosing, an attractive feature given the chronic nature of AMD (Liu et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2013). Recent evidence from preclinical iPSC models and autophagy-deficiency studies underscores the potential translation of mTOR-targeted strategies in restoring cellular homeostasis in degenerative diseases, lending further credence to this expected mechanism (Guillem, 2015).

Overall Evaluation:  
In summary, Torin1 possesses a compelling mechanistic profile that aligns well with the therapeutic needs of dry AMD by targeting a fundamental pathway governing cellular homeostasis in RPE cells. Its origin from a quinoline-based scaffold and subsequent chemical optimization into a highly potent ATP-competitive mTOR inhibitor underline its status as a valuable chemical probe in preclinical settings (Guillem, 2015). The dual inhibition of both mTORC1 and mTORC2 by Torin1, combined with its slow off-rate and sustained downstream effects—including dephosphorylation and nuclear translocation of TFEB/TFE3—make it an ideal tool for inducing lysosomal biogenesis and enhancing autophagic clearance (Martina et al., 2014; Huang et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2012). In cellular models, including ARPE-19 RPE cells, Torin1 has already demonstrated the ability to activate TFEB and upregulate CLEAR gene expression, which is directly relevant to counteracting the lysosomal clearance defects observed in dry AMD (Huang et al., 2018; Li, 2018).

However, significant challenges remain regarding the translational applicability of Torin1 as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. Its reported poor aqueous solubility, short half-life, and low oral bioavailability present formidable barriers to clinical development unless addressed through formulation improvements or further medicinal chemistry optimization (Guillem, 2015; Wang et al., 2022). Moreover, while extensive preclinical literature supports its role as a robust mTOR inhibitor in cancer and autophagy research, there is a lack of direct in vivo evidence for its efficacy in ocular models, particularly in dry AMD or geographic atrophy (GA) mouse lines (Liu et al., 2013; Gu, 2017). Careful dosing will also be critical, as the broad and potent inhibition of mTOR can have unintended effects on cellular metabolism and protein synthesis beyond the intended enhancement of lysosomal function. Additionally, off-target effects have been observed in some biochemical screens at supraphysiologic concentrations, including binding to other PIKK family members such as ATR, ATM, and DNA-PK, although these are generally not manifested at the low nanomolar concentrations used in cellular assays (Settembre et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2012).

From the perspective of repurposing for dry AMD, Torin1’s deep mechanistic specificity is a double-edged sword: it offers a highly defined and robust approach to upregulating lysosomal biogenesis via the TFEB/TFE3 axis, yet its pharmacokinetic liabilities and the absence of any clinical history in ocular disease necessitate additional work. The promising in vitro data in RPE models (ARPE-19 cells) and iPSC-derived RPE systems provide valuable target validation, but before advancing to clinical trials a refined analog or an optimized delivery method (for example, local ocular administration to bypass systemic bioavailability issues) should be considered (Huang et al., 2018; Li, 2018; Wang et al., 2022).

In summary, Torin1 is an excellent candidate for preclinical proof-of-concept studies to validate mTOR inhibition as a strategy to combat lysosomal dysfunction in dry AMD; however, further optimization to improve its stability and bioavailability, alongside rigorous in vivo testing in relevant AMD models, will be essential prior to clinical development (Guillem, 2015; Gu, 2017). The strengths of Torin1 lie in its potent, dual mTOR inhibition and its ability to robustly induce TFEB activation, whereas its weaknesses center on its pharmacokinetic shortcomings and the current lack of efficacy data in ocular disease models. Overall, with focused optimization and targeted delivery strategies, Torin1 or its derivatives may offer a promising therapeutic avenue for ameliorating the lysosomal clearance defects that underlie dry AMD pathology (Liu et al., 2012; Huang et al., 2018).
