Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Resveratrol is a naturally occurring polyphenolic compound that belongs to the stilbene family and is most famously isolated from grape skins and red wine. Its chemical structure features two aromatic rings linked by an ethylene bridge, which confers potent antioxidant properties. Discovered over four decades ago, resveratrol (catalog number Sigma R5010) has been extensively studied for its diverse biological activities, including anti‐inflammatory, anti‐oxidative, and anti‐aging effects. As a member of natural polyphenols, resveratrol has been used both as a dietary supplement and as a laboratory tool to probe intracellular signaling and epigenetic regulation. This compound has been explored for therapeutic applications in cardiovascular diseases, metabolic disorders, and various age‐related conditions, thereby positioning it as an attractive lead for repurposing. Its natural origin, safety profile upon oral administration, and documented bioavailability in retinal tissues support its candidature for ocular indications, particularly in mitigating dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) pathology (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Delmas et al., 2021).

Therapeutic History:  
Numerous biochemical studies have established that resveratrol exerts its beneficial effects by modulating key intracellular pathways. Historically, resveratrol has been used as an anti‐oxidant in various cellular systems and has been investigated in preclinical models of neurodegeneration, cardiovascular disease, and metabolic syndrome. In the context of ophthalmology, several studies have evaluated its efficacy in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cell models. For instance, research using ARPE-19 cells, a well-established human RPE cell line, demonstrated that resveratrol activates SIRT1 to protect against oxidative stress and apoptosis induced by challenging stimuli such as sodium iodate, UVA radiation, acrolein, and A2E—a major component of lipofuscin implicated in drusen formation and AMD pathology (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Li et al., 2024; Alaimo et al., 2020). Additional investigations combined resveratrol with omega-3 fatty acids in formulations like Resvega® to induce autophagy and enhance cell survival under conditions simulating AMD (Delmas et al., 2021; Koskela et al., 2016). While much of the published literature has concentrated on resveratrol’s effects in oxidative stress, inflammatory responses, and autophagy promotion in RPE cells, a few reports have noted its capacity to counteract the toxic accumulation of intracellular debris that is a hallmark of dry AMD (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Pinelli et al., 2025). Moreover, preliminary clinical reports have suggested that long-term oral supplementation with resveratrol-containing nutraceuticals may contribute to anatomic restoration of retinal structure and improved visual function in elderly patients, thus further underpinning its translational potential. Notably, while there is extensive preclinical evidence in vitro and in animal models, resveratrol has not yet been unequivocally validated in advanced clinical trials targeting dry AMD specifically (Abu-Amero et al., 2016).

Mechanism of Action:  
A robust body of research supports that resveratrol acts principally through the activation of SIRT1 (sirtuin 1) and the energy sensor AMPK (AMP-activated protein kinase), both of which are critical for maintaining cellular homeostasis in the aging retina. At the molecular level, resveratrol has been reported to directly and indirectly stimulate SIRT1 activity in RPE cells, leading to the deacetylation of several downstream targets such as PGC-1α (peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator 1-alpha). This deacetylated PGC-1α, in turn, upregulates mitochondrial biogenesis and enhances cellular oxidative phosphorylation, thereby improving mitochondrial quality control and reducing the accumulation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Li et al., 2024; Buonfiglio et al., 2024). Concomitantly, resveratrol activates AMPK, albeit through complex mechanisms involving inhibition of phosphodiesterases and alterations in the intracellular AMP/ATP ratio. The resulting AMPK phosphorylation facilitates a myriad of downstream effects, notably the inhibition of mTOR signaling (a known suppressor of autophagy) and activation of ULK1, a serine/threonine kinase that initiates autophagosome formation (Li et al., 2024; Abu-Amero et al., 2016).

In RPE cells, the synergistic activation of SIRT1 and AMPK by resveratrol is believed to promote autophagy, as evidenced by increased LC3II/I ratios and decreased p62 expression. Autophagy is particularly critical in RPE cells to clear toxic cellular debris such as A2E and other protein aggregates that contribute to drusen accumulation in dry AMD (Alaimo et al., 2020; Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Pinelli et al., 2023). Furthermore, the prevailing hypothesis extends these autophagic benefits by suggesting that, downstream of AMPK/SIRT1 activation, resveratrol may induce TFEB dephosphorylation. TFEB is a transcription factor that, when dephosphorylated, translocates into the nucleus and upregulates the coordinated lysosomal expression and regulation (CLEAR) network. This results in enhanced lysosomal biogenesis, improved lysosomal acidification, and increased activation of lysosomal enzymes such as cathepsin D. Although direct experimental evidence linking resveratrol to TFEB dephosphorylation in RPE cells is not abundantly detailed in the current literature, several studies imply that agents that activate AMPK and inhibit mTOR can indirectly promote TFEB activity. In this context, resveratrol’s ability to inhibit mTOR, partly through AMPK activation, suggests a plausible mechanism for the promotion of TFEB-mediated lysosomal functions (Falcão et al., 2025; Pinelli et al., 2023). These molecular events are anticipated to bolster the autophagy-lysosomal system, thereby mitigating the drusen accumulation characteristic of dry AMD. Additionally, resveratrol exerts direct antioxidant effects by scavenging free radicals and modulating the expression of antioxidant enzymes such as superoxide dismutase, which contributes further to its protective milieu in the retina (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Abu-Amero et al., 2016).

Expected Effect:  
Based on its molecular pharmacology, the expected effect of resveratrol in preclinical models of dry AMD would be multifaceted. In assays utilizing ARPE-19 cells or primary human RPE cells, treatment with resveratrol is expected to enhance SIRT1 activity, as measured by increased deacetylation of SIRT1 substrates and upregulation of PGC-1α nuclear translocation. Concurrently, AMPK phosphorylation is anticipated to be elevated, leading to inhibition of the mTOR pathway; this would foster an increased autophagic flux, observable as a higher LC3II/I ratio and reduced levels of the autophagy substrate p62 (Li et al., 2024; Alaimo et al., 2020; Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021). Furthermore, the candidate is hypothesized to indirectly promote TFEB dephosphorylation, facilitating its nuclear translocation and subsequent upregulation of lysosomal genes. This could manifest as enhanced lysosomal biogenesis, improved acidification of the lysosomal compartment, and elevated activity of lysosomal proteases such as cathepsin D. The cumulative consequence of these events would be a more efficient clearance of intracellular debris, including lipofuscin and other drusen components, thereby ameliorating RPE dysfunction associated with dry AMD (Falcão et al., 2025; Pinelli et al., 2023).

It is also expected that resveratrol’s anti-inflammatory and anti-apoptotic actions would reduce the chronic low-grade inflammation that underpins AMD pathogenesis. In vivo, improved autophagic and lysosomal clearance should correlate with decreased accumulation of pathological deposits at the RPE-Bruch’s membrane interface, potentially reducing the progression of drusen formation and preserving retinal structure and function (Alaimo et al., 2020; Abu-Amero et al., 2016; Pinelli et al., 2025). Given that resveratrol is detectable in retinal tissue following oral administration, its systemic safety and potential for long-term use add to its attractiveness as a repurposed therapeutic agent for dry AMD. Moreover, the dual capacity to modulate both metabolic and epigenetic pathways may offer disease-modifying effects that extend beyond symptomatic relief and target the underlying cellular aging processes in the RPE (Subramani et al., 2017).

Overall Evaluation:  
Resveratrol emerges as a promising candidate for repurposing in the context of dry AMD owing to its well-documented ability to activate SIRT1 and AMPK, which are pivotal signaling nodes in the maintenance of cellular homeostasis and autophagy. One of the central strengths of resveratrol is its dual mechanism of action. By targeting SIRT1, resveratrol not only combats oxidative stress through the deacetylation of transcription factors and enhancement of mitochondrial biogenesis but also modulates anti-inflammatory pathways relevant to retinal preservation (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Li et al., 2024). Simultaneously, its activation of AMPK provides additional impetus for autophagy induction through mTOR inhibition and ULK1 activation. Such molecular actions are of particular relevance to RPE cells, in which impairment of the autophagy-lysosomal system is a key pathogenetic mechanism leading to the accumulation of cellular waste products such as drusen—a hallmark of dry AMD (Alaimo et al., 2020; Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021).

Furthermore, the hypothesis that resveratrol could foster TFEB dephosphorylation is especially intriguing. Although direct evidence linking resveratrol to TFEB activation in RPE cells is currently limited, the known interactions between AMPK/mTOR signaling and TFEB activity provide a strong conceptual framework. Activation of TFEB would result in enhanced lysosomal biogenesis, acidification, and increased cathepsin D activity—mechanisms that are critical for the proper degradation of accumulated photoreceptor-derived debris and toxic aggregates (Falcão et al., 2025; Pinelli et al., 2023). This potential to bolster a declining lysosomal-autophagy system with age might address the fundamental cellular dysfunction observed in dry AMD.

On the clinical side, resveratrol demonstrates a favorable safety profile with established oral bioavailability and experimental evidence suggesting retinal tissue penetration. Combined with its history of use as an anti-oxidative and anti-inflammatory agent in other disease contexts, these features support its translational potential. Several nutraceutical formulations incorporating resveratrol (often in combination with omega-3 fatty acids, as in Resvega®) have already reached early-phase clinical evaluation for ocular indications, providing preliminary signals of efficacy in improving retinal structure and function among aged patients (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Delmas et al., 2021).

Nevertheless, several weaknesses and gaps must be acknowledged. First, while there is abundant preclinical evidence of resveratrol’s activation of SIRT1/AMPK pathways and subsequent autophagy induction in RPE cells, the specific molecular events leading to TFEB dephosphorylation, enhanced lysosomal biogenesis, lysosomal acidification, and increased cathepsin D activity are not yet comprehensively elucidated. In other words, the critical mechanistic link between resveratrol treatment and lysosomal enhancement remains somewhat inferential rather than directly demonstrated in the existing literature (Falcão et al., 2025; Hyttinen et al., 2019). Second, much of the supporting data comes from in vitro studies or animal models, with limited robust clinical evidence explicitly addressing dry AMD. Although some pilot clinical studies with resveratrol-containing formulations show promise, their design, scale, and long-term outcomes are not sufficiently advanced to confirm therapeutic efficacy in a broad AMD population (Abu-Amero et al., 2016). Third, resveratrol is known to have issues with bioavailability due to rapid metabolism and low systemic concentrations after oral ingestion; therefore, optimizing its delivery to retinal tissues, perhaps via novel formulations or nanoparticle carriers, may be necessary to achieve therapeutic levels (Subramani et al., 2017; Pinelli et al., 2025). Additionally, while its pleiotropic activity is a strength in terms of targeting multiple pathogenic mechanisms, this same feature can pose challenges in ensuring specificity and avoiding off-target effects.

In summary, resveratrol presents a compelling case as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. Its ability to activate SIRT1 and AMPK, induce autophagy, and potentially stimulate TFEB-driven lysosomal biogenesis aligns well with the current understanding of the cellular derangements underlying AMD pathogenesis. The expected outcome would be improved clearance of toxic cellular debris and drusen, preservation of RPE integrity, and amelioration of oxidative stress and inflammation in the aging retina. However, to fully validate resveratrol as a viable treatment for dry AMD, further investigations are warranted to (a) directly demonstrate its effects on TFEB dephosphorylation and lysosomal function in RPE cells, (b) optimize its ocular bioavailability, and (c) establish robust clinical endpoints in well-designed trials. Overall, while promising and supported by a substantial body of preclinical evidence, additional targeted research is required to definitively establish resveratrol’s mechanistic effects on the autophagy-lysosomal pathway and its therapeutic potential in dry AMD (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Li et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2025; Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Abu-Amero et al., 2016).

Abstract—Metformin, a synthetic biguanide derived from galegine (French lilac), is widely used as first-line therapy for type 2 diabetes mellitus and has pleiotropic cellular effects that intersect with age-related macular degeneration (AMD) biology, including AMPK activation, modulation of mTOR signaling, autophagy induction, anti-inflammatory actions, mitochondrial support, anti-senescence effects, and anti-angiogenic signaling in retinal models (Amin et al., 2022). Critically, while AMPK→mTORC1→autophagy is well-supported in retinal contexts, direct evidence for metformin-driven TFEB nuclear translocation, V-ATPase upregulation, or cathepsin D (CTSD) maturation in human RPE/AMD models is not demonstrated in the excerpted literature, representing material gaps for the central hypothesis (Amin et al., 2022; Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Buonfiglio et al., 2024). Overall, metformin is a biologically plausible, low-cost, and generally safe repurposing candidate for dry AMD that warrants mechanistic confirmation in RPE for lysosome-centric endpoints and rigorous randomized trials across AMD stages (Amin et al., 2022; Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Moir et al., 2023).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Metformin is a small-molecule biguanide synthesized as a derivative of galegine, a guanidine-class alkaloid originally isolated from the plant Galega officinalis; clinically it has been used for more than 60 years as the most commonly prescribed oral antihyperglycemic agent worldwide (class: biguanides) (Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Amin et al., 2022). Chemically, metformin comprises two coupled guanidine moieties conferring cationic, hydrophilic properties and cellular accumulation via organic cation transporters, consistent with mitochondrial complex I engagement and AMPK pathway activation described in mechanistic literature (Augustin & Atorf, 2023). Beyond glycemic control, metformin exhibits pleiotropic effects—anti-inflammatory, anti-oxidative, anti-angiogenic, anti-apoptotic and anti-senescence—reported in diverse cell types and tissues, many of which intersect with pathways implicated in AMD pathogenesis (oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, impaired proteostasis/autophagy, para-inflammation, vascular dysregulation) (Amin et al., 2022; Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Kozlowski, 2023). In ocular contexts, preclinical work indicates that metformin activates AMPK in RPE and neural retina and can preserve retinal structure and function under oxidative, metabolic, and phototoxic stressors (Amin et al., 2022). Collectively, these properties position metformin as a rational repurposing candidate for dry AMD, wherein RPE dysfunction, impaired autophagy/lysosomal clearance, mitochondrial stress, and chronic inflammation are central pathogenic nodes (Amin et al., 2022; Buonfiglio et al., 2024).

Therapeutic History  
Systemic use: Metformin is established first-line therapy for type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) and has been investigated broadly for aging-related conditions due to putative geroprotective effects; long-term safety has been documented, including in the Diabetes Prevention Program (DPP) where gastrointestinal intolerance is the most common adverse event and lactic acidosis was not observed under trial conditions, though B12 deficiency can occur with chronic use (Amin et al., 2022; Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Zhou & Xue, 2024). Preclinical ocular use: In retinal models, metformin has been tested systemically (oral/IP) and intravitreally, demonstrating protective effects in RPE and photoreceptors across light-damage, iodate-induced injury, inherited retinal degeneration (rd1/rd10), and oxygen-induced retinopathy (OIR) with readouts including preserved RPE tight junctions (ZO-1, occludin), outer nuclear layer thickness, and ERG amplitudes; notable anti-angiogenic activity includes decreased CNV lesion size and VEGF/VEGFR signaling modulation in several models (Amin et al., 2022). In these preclinical settings, metformin’s ocular benefits are frequently attributed to AMPK activation and downstream autophagy/mitochondrial and anti-inflammatory pathways, without overt ocular toxicity reported in rodents; however, human ocular safety data and pharmacokinetics under intravitreal or high-dose local exposure are not detailed in the excerpts (Amin et al., 2022).

Clinical/epidemiologic AMD history: Observational epidemiology offers mixed signals. Several large retrospective cohorts and case–control analyses associate metformin use with reduced odds or risk of any AMD or early AMD, with dose–duration trends in some datasets (e.g., MarketScan/claims OR 0.93 and propensity-matched HR 0.57; Taiwanese cohorts HR ~0.54 with stronger protection at >4 years and higher average daily doses), and lower odds reported in multiple studies across US, Europe, and Asia (Amin et al., 2022; Jiang et al., 2022; Kozlowski, 2023; Moir et al., 2023). Other datasets report null or complex associations: a high-quality UK T2DM cohort found no differential AMD risk with metformin using time-varying exposure models; a U.S. claims analysis focusing on dry AMD reported current use slightly increased dry AMD risk while prior use trended protective; additional analyses show no association or heterogeneity by diabetic retinopathy status (Eton et al., 2022; Gokhale et al., 2023; Liang et al., 2022). Meta-analyses also conflict: a systematic review of diabetics suggested decreased odds of AMD with metformin, whereas a broader 2024 meta-analysis concluded no overall prophylactic/treatment role; a European meta-analysis of antidiabetic/lipid-lowering drugs found reduced AMD prevalence overall but not for late-stage AMD specifically (Elhalag et al., 2024; Mauschitz et al., 2023). Importantly, these retrospective designs face confounding (e.g., smoking, comorbidities, health-care utilization), outcome misclassification (wet vs dry AMD), and exposure misclassification (adherence), limiting causal inference and stage-specific conclusions (Brown et al., 2019; Gokhale et al., 2023; Moir et al., 2023). Prospective interventional testing for dry AMD is underway: a randomized, single-blind Phase II trial of metformin to slow geographic atrophy (GA) progression has been conducted, with publication reported in 2024 (Shen et al., 2024); however, the excerpts do not provide efficacy outcomes in GA and emphasize that randomized evidence remains needed (Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Shen et al., 2024).

No regulatory approval exists for metformin in AMD (dry or wet), and the totality of evidence remains preclinical and observational for efficacy, with one randomized GA study reported but without effect-size details here; therefore, clinical utility in dry AMD is presently unproven (Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Shen et al., 2024).

Mechanism of Action  
Canonical pharmacology: Metformin partially inhibits mitochondrial respiratory complex I, reducing hepatic ATP and increasing AMP/ADP, thereby activating AMPK, the cellular energy sensor that shifts metabolism toward ATP-generating pathways; AMPK-dependent and ‑independent mechanisms operate systemically, including reduced hepatic gluconeogenesis, increased enterocyte glucose uptake/GLP-1 secretion, and microbiome modulation with potential systemic anti-inflammatory effects (Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Kozlowski, 2023).

Retinal/RPE mechanisms: In RPE cell lines (e.g., ARPE-19), metformin increases pAMPK and triggers autophagy, reduces ROS, decreases apoptosis, and preserves tight junction proteins (ZO-1, occludin), thereby maintaining barrier integrity under oxidative challenges (Amin et al., 2022; Augustin & Atorf, 2023). At the molecular level, treatment increases Sirt1 and multiple mitochondrial biogenesis and antioxidant markers (SOD-2, Nrf1, Tfam, PGC-1α, COX-II), restores NADH:NAD+ ratios and ATP, and lowers inflammatory mediators (NF-κB signaling, IL-6) (Amin et al., 2022). These signatures are consistent with AMPK’s coordinate regulation of autophagy and mitochondrial homeostasis observed in RPE/retinal contexts, contributing to improved proteostasis and reduced oxidative stress—key failure modes in dry AMD (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Amin et al., 2022).

In vivo, systemic or intravitreal metformin preserves photoreceptors and RPE structure/function in light-damage, iodate injury, and inherited degeneration models (rd1, rd10), with ERG preservation and ONL maintenance; mechanistically, AMPK activation is necessary for light-damage protection in an isoform-specific manner (AMPKα2 dependency), and retina-specific Pparδ is not required, supporting an AMPK-centric retinal mechanism rather than PPARδ signaling (Amin et al., 2022). Metformin also dampens retinal senescence and SASP in OIR after intravitreal dosing, with decreased cdkn1a/cdkn2a and NF-κB/IL-6 signaling, implicating anti-senescence immunomodulation as an additional neurovascular protective mechanism (Amin et al., 2022). Anti-angiogenic actions involve AMPK-dependent and ‑independent pathways: decreased VEGFR2 via enhanced ubiquitin–proteasome degradation, altered VEGF-A isoform splicing toward less angiogenic forms, reduced Flk-1 expression, and inhibition of ALK1-mediated angiogenesis; collectively these actions reduce CNV lesion size, endothelial proliferation/migration/tube formation, and neovascularization in OIR, diabetic, and laser-CNV models (Amin et al., 2022; Augustin & Atorf, 2023). Inflammatory suppression includes reductions in ICAM-1/MCP-1 (AMPK-dependent) and NF-κB p65/IL-8 (AMPK-independent), accompanied by decreased leukostasis and cytokines across models; NLRP3 inflammasome inhibition and modulation of macrophage polarization further contribute to reduced para-inflammation (Amin et al., 2022; Dang et al., 2021; Augustin & Atorf, 2023).

mTOR/autophagy axis: AMPK activation by metformin can inhibit mTORC1, activate the ULK complex, and initiate autophagy, which in RPE promotes clearance of damaged organelles, reduces ROS, and protects against oxidative injury—mechanistically vital for countering autophagy/lysosomal dysfunction in AMD (Dang et al., 2021; Zhou & Xue, 2024). Several retinal studies report AMPK-linked increases in autophagosome formation, and some contextual discussion references mTOR modulation in retinal protection, including translational control via EF2K and general proteostasis benefits (e.g., mutant opsin trafficking) with mixed in vivo translation (Amin et al., 2022). While AMPK→mTOR→autophagy activation is strongly implicated, explicit experimental confirmation in the provided corpus for metformin-driven TFEB nuclear translocation, V-ATPase upregulation, or increased cathepsin D maturation/activity in RPE is lacking; several reviews and excerpts explicitly note these as gaps requiring targeted mechanistic studies (Amin et al., 2022; Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Buonfiglio et al., 2024).

Dose/context dependence and AMPK-independent considerations: Some analyses suggest that AMPK activation by metformin in vitro can require suprapharmacologic concentrations and that certain systemic antihyperglycemic effects are AMPK-independent in hepatocytes; in retinal contexts, isoform-specific AMPKα2 dependence is observed for photoreceptor protection, yet disease models can yield mixed outcomes (e.g., limited benefit or worse function in some HFD diabetic retinopathy paradigms), underscoring the need to define dosing, timing, and disease-stage context for retinal efficacy (Amin et al., 2022; Moir et al., 2023). These data caution against assuming uniform AMPK-mediated benefit across all retinal diseases or AMD stages and highlight the importance of pharmacokinetics, tissue exposure, and therapeutic window in the eye (Moir et al., 2023).

Translational addenda—microbiome and lipid handling: Metformin alters gut microbiota and systemic metabolites, which has been linked to reduced retinal neovascularization through a putative “gut–retina axis,” and may also reduce OxLDL uptake and promote cholesterol efflux via AMPK/LXR–ABCA1/G1 signaling, potentially limiting drusen-related lipid accumulation and NLRP3 activation in RPE (Dang et al., 2021; Zhou & Xue, 2024).

Summary of mechanistic sufficiency for the hypothesis: The literature robustly supports metformin’s activation of AMPK in RPE/retina, inhibition of inflammatory and oxidative pathways, modulation of mTOR/autophagy, and preservation of RPE and photoreceptor function in multiple preclinical models—mechanistic axes consistent with dry AMD biology (Amin et al., 2022; Zhou & Xue, 2024). Expected Effect  
Assay-level predictions for RPE models: In human RPE cell lines and iPSC-RPE, metformin at concentrations compatible with cellular AMPK activation is expected to increase pAMPK (Thr172), reduce mTORC1 activity (e.g., decreased pS6 and p4EBP1), and initiate autophagy (increased LC3-II with enhanced flux in the presence of bafilomycin, reduction in p62/SQSTM1 under steady-state), while decreasing ROS and apoptosis under oxidative stress (e.g., H2O2), preserving tight junction integrity (occludin, ZO-1), and improving mitochondrial function (increased ATP, restored NADH:NAD+ ratio, increased PGC-1α/Tfam/Nrf1 and SOD-2) (Amin et al., 2022). Published in vitro data already support many of these endpoints: metformin reduced ROS and apoptosis, increased pAMPK and antioxidative molecules including Sirt1/Nrf2, and preserved occludin/ZO-1 in ARPE-19 challenged with H2O2 or glyoxal; AMPK inhibition abrogated the protection, indicating dependence on AMPK signaling (Amin et al., 2022). In oxidant or lipid-rich RPE conditions, decreased NF-κB activation and inflammasome signaling (e.g., NLRP3) would be anticipated, consistent with prior reports of metformin inhibiting NF-κB and NLRP3 activation in ocular/immune models (Augustin & Atorf, 2023).

Hypothesized lysosomal/TFEB endpoints: The working hypothesis proposes that AMPK activation by metformin will inhibit mTORC1, promote TFEB nuclear translocation, increase V-ATPase expression, enhance lysosomal acidification, and increase cathepsin D (CTSD) maturation, restoring autophagic flux and preventing RPE degeneration. Given TFEB’s role in lysosomal biogenesis and function, metformin’s dampening of mTORC1 could plausibly facilitate TFEB nuclear entry, but explicit experimental validation (e.g., TFEB nuclear localization quantification, lysosomal pH assays, V-ATPase subunit expression/activity, pro-CTSD→mature CTSD processing and enzymatic activity assays) is needed to confirm the hypothesized mechanism in AMD-relevant RPE models (Dang et al., 2021; Ebeling et al., 2022).

Target expression plausibility: AMPK is expressed in RPE and retina; stimulation prevents RPE and photoreceptor degeneration in multiple mouse models, and metformin increases pAMPK in human RPE cell lines—indicating sufficient expression and pathway competence for drug action in the assay system (Elhalag et al., 2024; Amin et al., 2022). In vivo expected effects in dry-AMD–relevant models: In toxin- and stress-driven models of RPE/photoreceptor degeneration (e.g., sodium iodate, light-induced damage) and inherited retinal degeneration, metformin is expected to preserve RPE morphology and function, maintain ONL thickness, and preserve ERG signals, consistent with reported benefits mediated by AMPK activation; however, model- and disease-stage–specific responses can vary, and negative/neutral results have been documented in some diabetic retinopathy paradigms, underscoring the need to test across multiple AMD-relevant models and to incorporate timing and dose-response studies (Amin et al., 2022). Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Mechanistic convergence on AMD biology: Metformin engages AMPK-dependent and ‑independent processes that directly counter core dry AMD pathomechanisms—oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, impaired autophagy/proteostasis, para-inflammation/senescence, and, secondarily, maladaptive vascular/angio-inflammatory signaling—supported by coherent molecular readouts (pAMPK↑, autophagy induction, mitochondrial biogenesis markers↑, NF-κB/NLRP3↓) in RPE and retinal models (Amin et al., 2022; Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Zhou & Xue, 2024). Preclinical efficacy in preserving RPE barrier proteins and photoreceptor function across multiple insults strengthens biological plausibility for dry AMD (Amin et al., 2022).
- Epidemiologic signal and translational momentum: Multiple large retrospective analyses show reduced odds/risk of AMD—often with dose–duration trends—among metformin users, and a randomized GA trial has been conducted, indicating clinical interest and feasibility for prospective testing (Amin et al., 2022; Jiang et al., 2022; Moir et al., 2023; Shen et al., 2024). Meta-analytic work in diabetics suggests potential protective associations, especially in early AMD, reinforcing the rationale to test in non-diabetic AMD populations with controlled exposure (Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Liang et al., 2022).
- Favorable systemic safety and low cost: Decades of broad clinical use, with well-characterized safety signals (GI intolerance, B12 deficiency; rare lactic acidosis risk under renal/hepatic compromise), make metformin attractive from a risk–benefit and access perspective for an elderly AMD population, assuming ocular safety is confirmed (Amin et al., 2022; Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Zhou & Xue, 2024).
- Ocular delivery flexibility and mechanistic redundancy: Both systemic and intravitreal dosing have produced retinal benefits in animals; intravitreal delivery achieved senescence suppression independent of anti-VEGF effects, suggesting non-overlapping mechanisms that could complement existing therapies (Amin et al., 2022). Mechanistic redundancy (anti-oxidant, autophagy, anti-inflammatory, anti-angiogenic) could enhance robustness in multifactorial AMD pathophysiology (Amin et al., 2022; Dang et al., 2021).

- Critical mechanistic gaps relative to the hypothesis: Direct evidence in human RPE/AMD-relevant systems for metformin-driven TFEB nuclear translocation, increases in V-ATPase expression/activity, and enhanced cathepsin D maturation/activity is absent in the provided literature; several reviews explicitly highlight TFEB/V-ATPase/CTSD endpoints as missing and necessary to establish lysosome-centric restoration of autophagic flux (Amin et al., 2022; Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Buonfiglio et al., 2024). Without these data, the proposed AMPK–TFEB–lysosome axis remains inferential in RPE.
- Heterogeneous and contradictory epidemiology: While many retrospective datasets suggest benefit (often in T2DM cohorts), high-quality time-varying analyses and some claims datasets report null or even an increased risk signal for current users regarding dry AMD; meta-analyses differ in conclusions, and late-stage AMD associations are particularly uncertain (Elhalag et al., 2024; Gokhale et al., 2023; Liang et al., 2022; Mauschitz et al., 2023). Confounding (smoking, DR severity, comedications), misclassification (wet vs dry), and exposure uncertainty limit inferential strength (Brown et al., 2019; Moir et al., 2023; Gokhale et al., 2023).
- Limited randomized clinical efficacy data in dry AMD: A GA randomized trial has been reported, but efficacy outcomes are not detailed in the excerpts; prior DPP follow-up imaging showed no significant AMD prevalence difference between metformin, lifestyle, and placebo, though that study was not designed for AMD endpoints; consequently, clinical efficacy remains unproven (Moir et al., 2023; Shen et al., 2024).

Development Implications and Recommendations  
- Mechanism validation in RPE: Prioritize targeted studies in human iPSC-RPE and donor-derived RPE to test the hypothesized AMPK→mTORC1→TFEB→lysosome axis. Required assays: TFEB nuclear localization (immunocytochemistry, subcellular fractionation), lysosomal pH (LysoSensor/LysoTracker), V-ATPase subunit expression and activity (ATPase assays), CTSD maturation (pro/mature CTSD Western) and enzymatic activity, autophagic flux (LC3 turnover with/without lysosomal blockade), and rescue experiments with AMPK and TFEB perturbation (e.g., CRISPRi/siRNA) (Amin et al., 2022; Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Ebeling et al., 2022).
- Translational pharmacology: Define retinal/RPE exposure–response using clinically relevant systemic concentrations and ocular distribution modeling; consider topical/periocular/intravitreal delivery if systemic exposure is insufficient for retinal AMPK engagement and lysosome-centric endpoints, with rigorous ocular toxicology (Moir et al., 2023).
- Indication and stage targeting: Given epidemiologic signals skew toward early/non-exudative AMD and limited evidence for late AMD benefit, prioritize early/intermediate AMD cohorts and GA progression trials with mechanistic biomarkers (RPE autofluorescence dynamics, OCT-based RPE/ONL metrics, aqueous humor cytokines/miRNAs) to increase sensitivity to disease-modifying effects (Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Liang et al., 2022; Moir et al., 2023).
- Clinical trial design: Incorporate robust confounder control and stratification (smoking, DR status, renal function, OCT1 polymorphisms) and embed target engagement (e.g., peripheral blood or aqueous biomarkers of AMPK/mTOR/autophagy) and safety surveillance (B12 levels, GI tolerability, lactate in at-risk) to bridge mechanism to clinical outcome (Gokhale et al., 2023; Zhou & Xue, 2024).

The program should proceed with focused mechanistic validation of TFEB/lysosome endpoints in RPE, retinal target engagement and pharmacology at clinically feasible exposures, and staged, biomarker-rich randomized trials in early/intermediate AMD and GA to quantify efficacy and safety. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Calpeptin (Sigma C1571) is a synthetic, cell‐permeable peptidomimetic inhibitor originally developed to target calpain family proteases. It belongs to a class of small molecule calpain inhibitors that are designed to mimic specific peptide sequences found in the endogenous inhibitor calpastatin. These peptidomimetics have been refined chemically to enable cellular penetration and high-affinity binding to the calpain active site, thereby blocking its auto‐proteolytic activation process (Vu et al., 2022). Calpeptin was discovered through efforts aimed at identifying effective inhibitors of calcium‐dependent cysteine proteases that contribute to proteolytic events in pathogenic conditions. Its synthesis involves conventional organic synthesis techniques designed to yield a molecule with the critical chemical features—namely, an amide backbone that mimics peptide bonds and side chain substitutions that ensure selectivity and stability in biological systems. This compound has been widely adopted as a research tool to probe calpain‐dependent cellular processes, particularly in the context of neurodegeneration and ocular pathologies (Vu et al., 2022).

Therapeutic History:  
Calpeptin has a rich history as a biochemical tool in both in vitro and in vivo experimental paradigms. Within the realm of ocular disease research, calpain inhibitors similar in mechanism to calpeptin have been evaluated in multiple models of retinal degeneration. For example, studies using rodent models of inherited retinal degeneration, such as those employing the Rho P23H‐1 rat model, have demonstrated that calpeptin—alongside other calpain inhibitors—can reduce photoreceptor cell death and modulate apoptotic pathways (Azam & Jastrzebska, 2025). Although the majority of these studies have been conducted in the context of retinitis pigmentosa or other inherited forms of retinal degeneration, the underlying mechanism—namely, the inhibition of aberrant calpain activation leading to cell death—is also highly relevant to dry age‐related macular degeneration (Azam & Jastrzebska, 2025). In various experimental systems, such as in neuroblastoma cells and retinal cell cultures subject to stress (e.g., hypoxia or oxidative challenge), calpeptin has been shown to reduce calpain‐mediated cleavage of key substrates and inhibit caspase activation, which correlates with improved cell survival. Although direct clinical trials using calpeptin in dry AMD have not yet been reported, its use in ocular research, combined with evidence from preclinical models involving other calpain inhibitors (such as SNJ‐1945 and SJA6017), underscores the translational potential of this approach (Vu et al., 2022).

Mechanism of Action:  
Calpeptin functions by inhibiting the auto‐proteolytic activation of calpain isoforms, particularly cytosolic calpains such as CAPN1 and CAPN5. Under physiological conditions, calpains are maintained in an inactive state; however, under pathological conditions marked by calcium dysregulation—such as those encountered in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) during oxidative stress—calpains become activated and catalyze the proteolytic cleavage of vital cellular substrates. Calpeptin binds to the protease’s active site, thereby preventing the conformational changes necessary for auto‐activation and subsequent proteolytic activity (Vu et al., 2022).  
In the specific context of dry AMD, the hypothesis is that drusen accumulation leads to oxidative and metabolic stress in the RPE. This stress triggers calcium overload, which in turn activates calpains. One of the deleterious consequences of calpain activation is lysosomal membrane permeabilization (LMP). LMP destabilizes the lysosomal environment, leading to the dissipation of the proton gradient maintained by v-ATPase complexes and resulting in impaired acidification. This loss of lysosomal integrity negatively affects the processing and activity of lysosomal hydrolases, particularly cathepsin D (CTSD), which is essential for proper degradative and autophagic functions. By inhibiting calpain activity, calpeptin is expected to prevent the proteolytic degradation of components critical to lysosomal membrane stability, such as v-ATPase subunits, thereby preserving lysosomal pH and ensuring proper CTSD processing (Vu et al., 2022). The preservation of these lysosomal functions is crucial in the context of drusen-induced stress in dry AMD, as it directly addresses the underlying mechanism of lysosomal dysfunction and subsequent cell death.

Expected Effect:  
The proposed therapeutic application of calpeptin in dry AMD is based on its ability to mitigate calpain-mediated lysosomal damage in the retinal pigment epithelium. In an experimental setup where RPE cells are exposed to oxidative or drusen-like stress, one would expect calpeptin to reduce calpain activation, thereby decreasing lysosomal membrane permeabilization. This inhibition should lead to the stabilization of v-ATPase complexes, which are responsible for maintaining the acidic environment within lysosomes. Consequently, normal lysosomal acidification is preserved, allowing for proper activation and function of cathepsin D (CTSD), a critical enzyme in the degradation of photoreceptor outer segments and in cellular homeostasis (Azam & Jastrzebska, 2025; Vu et al., 2022).  
Furthermore, by blocking the calpain-driven cleavage events that would otherwise lead to cytoskeletal disorganization and cellular apoptosis, calpeptin is anticipated to reduce overall caspase activation and apoptotic signaling in RPE cells. Studies in other retinal disease models have demonstrated that calpain inhibition can restore cellular homeostasis by reducing markers of apoptosis and mitigating structural damage (Azam & Jastrzebska, 2025; Vu et al., 2022). Given that RPE cells are known to express significant levels of calpains and are highly susceptible to calcium dysregulation upon exposure to drusen and oxidative stress, the use of calpeptin is expected to yield improved cellular viability and function in these cells. This outcome would be assessed through indicators such as restored lysosomal pH, reduction in cytosolic release of lysosomal enzymes, and maintenance of normal CTSD processing, ultimately contributing to neuroprotection and preservation of retinal integrity in dry AMD (Vu et al., 2022).

Overall Evaluation:  
A comprehensive review of the literature suggests that calpeptin holds promise as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration. Its classification as a cell-permeable peptidomimetic inhibitor of calpain places it within a well-studied drug class known for modulating pathological proteolytic cascades initiated by calcium dysregulation. The strengths of calpeptin include its well-characterized mechanism of action—namely, the inhibition of calpain auto-proteolysis, which is pivotal for preventing the proteolytic breakdown of critical lysosomal components such as v-ATPase (Vu et al., 2022).  
Moreover, the therapeutic history of calpeptin and its analogues in various retinal degeneration models supports its potential applicability in dry AMD. Experimental evidence from studies in Rho P23H transgenic rat models, among others, demonstrates that calpain inhibitors can confer neuroprotection by reducing apoptotic pathways, preserving cellular integrity, and maintaining lysosomal function in stressed retinal cells (Azam & Jastrzebska, 2025). The existing knowledge regarding in vivo tolerability and the reversible nature of calpeptin’s inhibitory effects further bolster its candidacy for preclinical testing targeting dry AMD (Vu et al., 2022).

Despite these favorable attributes, several weaknesses and challenges must be acknowledged. First, while the mechanism underpinning calpeptin’s action—specifically, its inhibition of calpain-mediated lysosomal damage—is strongly supported by in vitro and retinal degeneration model data, direct evidence linking calpeptin to improved outcomes in dry AMD models remains limited (Azam & Jastrzebska, 2025; Vu et al., 2022). Furthermore, the hypothesized benefit of stabilizing v-ATPase complexes and preserving CTSD activity, although biologically plausible, requires further experimental validation in an AMD context to confirm that calpeptin’s inhibition of calpain is sufficient to counteract drusen-induced lysosomal stress.  
An additional concern relates to target selectivity. Calpain inhibitors, including calpeptin, can potentially exhibit off-target effects due to the conserved structure of the catalytic domains within the calpain family and related proteases. This lack of absolute specificity may lead to unintended inhibition of other proteases, such as certain cathepsins, which could compromise cellular function if not tightly regulated (Vu et al., 2022). Furthermore, chronic ocular delivery of small molecule inhibitors poses formulation challenges, as therapeutic concentrations must be maintained in the retina without eliciting local toxicity. The eye’s compartmentalized anatomy offers the advantage of localized delivery (e.g., via intravitreal injections or topical applications), yet achieving sustained and controlled drug release remains a technical hurdle that must be addressed in subsequent preclinical studies (Vu et al., 2022).  
Another potential weakness is the complexity of dry AMD pathophysiology itself. Dry AMD is characterized by a multifactorial etiology involving oxidative stress, complement dysregulation, and inflammatory processes, in addition to lysosomal dysfunction. While addressing calpain-mediated LMP directly targets one critical aspect of the disease mechanism, comprehensive protection of RPE cells may require combination approaches. Calpeptin’s role might be best viewed as a part of a broader therapeutic cocktail aimed at modulating multiple convergent pathways implicated in dry AMD progression (Vu et al., 2022).  
In summary, calpeptin shows considerable potential as a repurposed drug candidate for dry AMD based on its well-documented pharmacological profile and its mechanistic alignment with the proposed therapeutic strategy—namely, inhibiting calpain-mediated lysosomal destabilization in RPE cells. Its synthetic origin, cell-permeable nature, and established use in experimental models of retinal degeneration make it an attractive candidate for further preclinical evaluation. However, the absence of direct evidence in dry AMD models, in addition to concerns regarding specificity, delivery, and the need for combination intervention strategies, underscores the importance of rigorous preclinical studies to further validate calpeptin’s efficacy and safety in this indication (Vu et al., 2022; Azam & Jastrzebska, 2025). Overall, while promising, calpeptin will require targeted studies to evaluate its impact on lysosomal membrane permeabilization, v-ATPase stabilization, and cathepsin D activity in the context of drusen-induced oxidative stress, thereby confirming its potential to protect RPEs and mitigate the progression of dry age-related macular degeneration (Vu et al., 2022).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Vorinostat (suberoylanilide hydroxamic acid, SAHA; Selleckchem S1047) is a synthetic small molecule originally discovered through a screening process aimed at identifying inhibitors of histone deacetylases (HDACs) and belongs to the hydroxamic acid class of compounds. It was developed as an anticancer agent and later received U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approval for the treatment of cutaneous T cell lymphoma; its chemical synthesis involves derivatization of an anilide moiety with a hydroxamic acid function, enabling a high degree of specificity for the zinc-dependent catalytic pockets of HDAC enzymes. As a pan-HDAC inhibitor, Vorinostat is designed to modulate epigenetic regulation by binding to the active site of multiple HDAC isoforms, thereby increasing histone acetylation and altering the transcriptional profile of target genes. This class of compounds has been broadly used in oncology, where the modulation of chromatin structure reactivates suppressed tumor suppressor genes and triggers cell cycle arrest and apoptosis. In the context of drug repurposing, the rationale for exploring Vorinostat in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is centered on its potential to epigenetically reprogram retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells by enhancing the acetylation status and activation of key transcription factors such as TFEB and FOXO, which are critical regulators of lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy—a mechanism distinctly different from kinase inhibition strategies (Buniello et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2025).

Therapeutic History:  
Vorinostat’s clinical journey has predominantly revolved around its anticancer applications. Early-phase clinical trials in various solid tumors, including breast, colorectal, and non-small cell lung cancer, as well as studies in metastatic thyroid cancer, relapsed or refractory leukemia, and multiple myeloma, have provided a robust safety profile and dosing regimen for this therapeutic candidate (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2004, 2005, 2006; Ghosh et al., 2024). Although its use in oncology has been extensive—with studies demonstrating its ability to block cell growth by inhibiting key enzymes required for proliferation—the direct evidence for its application in ocular diseases, especially in dry AMD, remains limited. Nonetheless, the broader class of HDAC inhibitors has shown promising results in preclinical ocular models. For instance, several studies have demonstrated that HDAC inhibitors can attenuate choroidal neovascularization, protect retinal tissues from ischemic injury, and promote cellular differentiation in the retinal pigment epithelium (Luo et al., 2025). These findings provide an indirect validation of the concept that epigenetic modulators of HDAC activity may be repurposed to combat the autophagy and lysosomal dysfunction observed in dry AMD. Although Vorinostat itself has not been extensively studied in the context of dry AMD or similar RPE-driven degenerative diseases, its established pharmacological profile and ocular tolerability in other clinical contexts suggest that it could offer mechanistic benefits by modulating retinal epigenetic landscapes (Luo et al., 2025).

Mechanism of Action:  
Vorinostat exerts its biological effects by inhibiting the activity of zinc-dependent histone deacetylases. Under normal physiological conditions, HDACs remove acetyl groups from the lysine residues on histone tails, leading to chromatin condensation and transcriptional repression; by inhibiting these enzymes, Vorinostat results in the accumulation of acetylated histones and a more relaxed chromatin structure that promotes gene transcription. The current hypothesis contends that in RPE cells, Vorinostat-mediated HDAC inhibition will enhance the acetylation of the transcription factors TFEB (transcription factor EB) and members of the FOXO (forkhead box O) family. TFEB is a master regulator of the coordinated lysosomal expression and regulation (CLEAR) network, which governs the transcription of genes encoding lysosomal enzymes, including cathepsin D (CTSD), and other proteins necessary for autophagy and lysosomal acidification (Buniello et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2025). Similarly, FOXO transcription factors are implicated in cellular stress responses and can promote the expression of antioxidant enzymes as well as proteins involved in maintaining mitochondrial integrity. In neuronal models, HDAC inhibition has been linked to increased expression, acetylation, and nuclear localization of TFEB, leading to upregulation of lysosomal gene expression and enhanced autophagic flux (Buniello et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2025). It is anticipated that Vorinostat will operate through a similar mechanism in RPE cells by facilitating the dissociation of HDACs from the promoters of TFEB/FOXO target genes, thereby promoting their transcriptional activation. This would initiate a cascade of events that enhance lysosomal biogenesis, improve lysosomal acidification, and increase the activity of cathepsin D—the lysosomal protease that plays a critical role in degrading accumulated protein aggregates and damaged cellular organelles, which are pathognomonic of dry AMD pathology (Luo et al., 2025). Moreover, it is relevant that other HDAC inhibitors, such as trichostatin A (TSA) and valproic acid (VPA), have demonstrated the capacity to modulate similar pathways in retinal cells, thereby indirectly supporting the proposed mechanism of action for Vorinostat in restoring lysosomal function and autophagic balance in RPE cells (Luo et al., 2025).

Expected Effect:  
Based on the proposed mechanism of action, the expected effect of Vorinostat in the context of dry AMD is multifaceted. The compound is anticipated to inhibit HDAC activity in RPE cells, leading to an increase in overall protein acetylation, including that of histones and transcription factors. This epigenetic modulation should facilitate the nuclear translocation and activation of TFEB, thereby upregulating the CLEAR network of genes involved in lysosomal biogenesis, acidification, and autophagy. In turn, the increased expression and activity of cathepsin D will improve the degradative capacity of the lysosomes, fostering the clearance of lipofuscin and other deleterious protein aggregates that accumulate with age in RPE cells. Additionally, enhanced FOXO activity could promote an improved antioxidant response and mitigate mitochondrial dysfunction, which together would reduce oxidative stress—a key driver of RPE degeneration in dry AMD (Buniello et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2025).

The anticipated outcome in preclinical assays would be a measurable restoration of autophagic flux as evidenced by reductions in markers of cellular stress and accumulation of autophagy substrates. Cellular assays may demonstrate increased lysosomal enzyme activities, such as that of cathepsin D, and improved acidification of lysosomes in treated RPE cells. In animal models engineered or induced to exhibit dry AMD-like pathology, treatment with Vorinostat is expected to lead to an improvement in retinal structure and function, potentially assessed through morphological analyses and electroretinography. Furthermore, the restoration of TFEB/FOXO activity should enhance the overall cellular resilience of RPE, thereby delaying or preventing the progression of degenerative changes associated with dry AMD. Given Vorinostat’s established oral bioavailability and systemic tolerability in oncology patients, there is potential for its repurposing with adjusted dosing regimens aimed at achieving therapeutic concentrations in the retina with minimal systemic toxicity (Buniello et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2025).

Overall Evaluation:  
In evaluating Vorinostat as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, several strengths and weaknesses emerge. One of the principal strengths of Vorinostat is its well-characterized pharmacological profile, which is supported by extensive clinical data in oncology. Its FDA-approved status and known systemic tolerability provide a translational advantage over novel compounds that are still in early developmental stages. The robust mechanism of action of HDAC inhibitors, with demonstrated capacity to modulate gene expression through epigenetic reprogramming, aligns well with the pathobiology of dry AMD, where impaired autophagy and lysosomal dysfunction are central features. The specific hypothesis that Vorinostat will promote the acetylation and activation of TFEB and FOXO transcription factors to drive lysosomal biogenesis, improve acidification, and enhance cathepsin D activity addresses well-validated therapeutic targets in the disease process (Buniello et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2025).

However, there are also significant weaknesses and potential challenges that must be carefully considered. First, while the mechanistic rationale is compelling, direct experimental evidence supporting Vorinostat’s efficacy in RPE cells or animal models of dry AMD is currently sparse. Much of the supporting data is extrapolated from studies using other HDAC inhibitors such as TSA, VPA, or AN7, and from cancer studies where the cellular context differs substantially from that of the RPE (Luo et al., 2025). Second, the pharmacokinetic profile and ocular tissue penetration of Vorinostat when administered systemically remain uncertain. The blood–retinal barrier presents a formidable challenge to achieving therapeutic drug concentrations in the retina, and while clinical trials in oncology have established systemic dosing guidelines, it is unclear whether these doses will translate into efficacious levels within the RPE while maintaining safety. Third, the potential for off-target effects and retinal toxicity cannot be overlooked; certain HDAC inhibitors have been associated with deleterious retinal effects when administered at inappropriate doses or over prolonged periods, emphasizing the need for careful dose optimization and possibly localized (e.g., intravitreal) delivery strategies (Luo et al., 2025). Fourth, the complex interplay between various HDAC isoforms in the retina may necessitate a more selective approach than that offered by the broad-spectrum inhibition provided by Vorinostat, as indiscriminate inhibition could disrupt other acetylation-dependent regulatory mechanisms critical for normal retinal function (Luo et al., 2025).

In addition, while the hypothesis posits that Vorinostat will upregulate TFEB and FOXO to enhance autophagy and lysosomal function, the regulation of these transcription factors is multifactorial. For example, TFEB activity is tightly controlled by phosphorylation events mediated by mTORC1 and AKT2 signaling pathways, and the interplay between these kinases, deacetylases such as SIRT5, and HDACs remains an active area of investigation (Abokyi & Tse, 2025; Buniello et al., 2025; Ghosh et al., 2024). Thus, while there is mechanistic plausibility in promoting lysosomal biogenesis via HDAC inhibition, the precise molecular outcomes in the unique environment of aging RPE cells require further delineation. Furthermore, studies in other models have revealed that the beneficial effects of HDAC inhibition on autophagy and lysosomal function may vary depending on the timing, duration, and specific isoform selectivity of the inhibitor used (Luo et al., 2025).

Taking these factors into account, a cautious but optimistic view emerges regarding the repurposing of Vorinostat for dry AMD. The compound’s established clinical track record in oncology is a substantial advantage, providing a foundation for subsequent translational studies. The convergent evidence supporting the role of HDAC inhibition in enhancing autophagy and mitigating oxidative stress in retinal diseases further bolsters the rationale for this approach (Falcão et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2025). However, to fully validate the therapeutic potential of Vorinostat in dry AMD, rigorous preclinical studies are needed to (1) confirm its efficacy in restoring TFEB/FOXO activity and lysosomal function in RPE cells, (2) determine its pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic properties in ocular tissues, (3) assess its safety profile within the retina over chronic dosing schedules, and (4) establish optimized dosing strategies that achieve target engagement without compromising retinal integrity.

Moreover, future investigations might explore alternative delivery mechanisms, such as nanoparticle-based systems or sustained-release intravitreal formulations, to circumvent the challenges posed by the blood–retinal barrier and achieve localized drug concentrations that are both effective and safe. In parallel, combinatorial therapeutic strategies that pair Vorinostat with other agents that modulate complementary pathways—such as antioxidants, SIRT1 activators, or agents that specifically target mTORC1 signaling—could be considered to provide a multifaceted approach to treating dry AMD. These strategies would leverage the ability of Vorinostat to reprogram epigenetic signatures in RPE cells while simultaneously addressing other pathogenic mechanisms contributing to AMD progression (Buniello et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2025).

In summary, Vorinostat represents a promising candidate for drug repurposing in dry AMD due to its potent HDAC inhibitory activity, favorable clinical history in oncology, and a plausible mechanism by which it could restore lysosomal biogenesis and autophagic flux in RPE cells—a central defect in dry AMD pathogenesis. The strengths of this approach include the compound’s established approval and known pharmacology, coupled with emerging evidence that epigenetic modulation can address key cellular dysfunctions in retinal degeneration. Conversely, the critical weaknesses pertain to the lack of direct preclinical evidence in the context of AMD, uncertainties regarding effective ocular delivery, and potential risks of off-target effects in a delicate tissue such as the retina. A comprehensive series of translational studies, beginning with in vitro models of RPE dysfunction and progressing to in vivo dry AMD models, is essential to fully establish the therapeutic window, efficacy, and safety profile of Vorinostat for this new indication. If these studies yield positive results, Vorinostat could offer a novel, mechanistically precise approach to the treatment of dry AMD, addressing a significant unmet clinical need by restoring the autophagy–lysosome pathway and ultimately preserving vision in affected patients (Buniello et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2025).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Lithium chloride (Sigma L9650) is an inorganic salt belonging to the family of lithium compounds that has been in use for several decades, primarily as a mood stabilizer in the treatment of bipolar disorder. It is synthesized by combining lithium carbonate or lithium hydroxide with hydrochloric acid, yielding a highly water‐soluble salt that is widely available for both clinical and experimental research purposes (Carmassi et al., 2016; Vallée et al., 2021). As a prototypical member of the lithium salts, lithium chloride has been repurposed in recent years as a candidate for neuroprotection because of its ability to inhibit glycogen synthase kinase-3β (GSK3β), a serine/threonine kinase involved in numerous intracellular signaling cascades. Lithium’s chemical simplicity belies its complex pharmacology; its effects extend well beyond mood stabilization to encompass modulation of cell survival, inflammatory responses, and protein degradation pathways. In this context, lithium salts are now recognized as small molecule modulators that can affect intracellular transcriptional programs, including nuclear import of factors such as transcription factor EB (TFEB) and β-catenin, which in turn control the expression of genes necessary for lysosomal biogenesis and autophagic flux (Carmassi et al., 2016; Vallée et al., 2021). These mechanistic insights, originally developed in studies of neurodegenerative and psychiatric diseases, have motivated investigations into whether lithium chloride might be repurposed to address the autophagic and lysosomal dysfunction observed in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD), particularly in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) (Carmassi et al., 2016; Vallée et al., 2021).

Therapeutic History:  
Lithium salts have a long-standing clinical history in psychiatry, especially in the management of bipolar disorder, where their dosing and long-term safety profiles have been thoroughly characterized. In addition, numerous preclinical studies in neuroscience have demonstrated that lithium can reduce tau phosphorylation and improve neuronal cell survival, partly by inhibiting GSK3β and modulating downstream targets such as β-catenin and Bcl-2 (Carmassi et al., 2016; Vallée et al., 2021). Lithium has been evaluated in several neurodegenerative contexts—for instance, it has been examined for its potential benefits in Alzheimer’s disease, Huntington’s disease, and Parkinson’s disease, with some studies reporting modest improvements in neuroprotection and behavioral outcomes, although clinical results have been mixed (Singh et al., 2022; Vallée et al., 2021). More specifically, preclinical data in the central nervous system have shown that prolonged exposure to lithium increases cortical grey matter and enhances neuronal markers such as N-acetyl-aspartate, suggesting that lithium exerts trophic and neuroprotective effects (Carmassi et al., 2016). In the ocular arena, while lithium’s use has been predominantly described in the context of glaucoma—in which its inhibition of GSK3β was shown to modulate WNT/β-catenin signaling in trabecular meshwork cells—the literature offers no direct clinical or in-depth preclinical evaluation of lithium chloride in dry AMD or for modulating autophagy specifically in RPE cells (Singh et al., 2022; Vallée et al., 2021). A search in clinical trial registries has not identified any trials using lithium chloride for macular degeneration, underscoring a notable gap between the neuroprotective models in which lithium has been studied and its potential application in dry AMD (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).

Mechanism of Action:  
Lithium chloride’s mechanisms of action are multifaceted, but a significant aspect relevant to the dry AMD hypothesis is its ability to inhibit GSK3β. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:

VX-765 has been evaluated primarily in systemic inflammatory and cardiovascular settings, where its favorable pharmacokinetic profile and excellent oral bioavailability have been demonstrated (Audia et al., 2018; MacKenzie & Schipper, 2010).

The therapeutic history of VX-765 underscores its extensive preclinical development and early clinical evaluation in several inflammatory settings. Specifically, dry AMD shares underlying pathological processes such as chronic inflammation, oxidative stress, and lysosomal dysfunction in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells. Prior experimental studies in RPE models using caspase-1 inhibitors like Z-YVAD-FMK have demonstrated that inhibiting caspase-1 activity reduces IL-1β release and can influence cell death pathways (Brandstetter, 2016; Tseng et al., 2013). However, despite this promising mechanistic background, VX-765 itself has not yet been directly evaluated in preclinical models of dry AMD or in similar ocular diseases. At the molecular level, VX-765 exerts its effect primarily through selective inhibition of caspase-1, a cysteine protease critically involved in the processing of pro-inflammatory cytokines. More specifically, there is a hypothesized link between caspase-1 activity and alterations in lysosomal integrity—a process involving LMP that is associated with a loss of vacuolar (V-) ATPase activity and disturbances in cathepsin D maturation. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Tocilizumab (Actemra; Roche/Chugai) is a recombinant humanized monoclonal antibody that binds the human interleukin-6 receptor (IL-6R) and blocks IL-6 signal transduction, resulting in systemic anti-inflammatory effects characteristic of IL-6 pathway inhibition (class: humanized anti-IL-6R monoclonal antibody) (Shi, 2017a; Shi, 2017b; Zhujiang Hospital, 2025). AMD-relevant upstream injury nodes: The dominant mechanistic framework for dry AMD implicates chronic oxidative/photooxidative stress, age-related lysosomal decline, and intracellular clearance failure (autophagy/proteasome) in RPE, leading to lipofuscinogenesis, lysosomal membrane permeabilization (LMP), and activation of inflammasome pathways with downstream cytokine release and cell death (apoptosis vs pyroptosis depending on priming) (Brandstetter, 2016; Piippo, 2019). In primary human RPE and ARPE-19 cells, LMP induced chemically (Leu-Leu-OMe) or via blue-light irradiation of POS-derived lipofuscin activates the NLRP3 inflammasome with caspase-1–dependent maturation and release of IL-1β and IL-18; broader cytokine secretion includes IL-6, GM-CSF, and GRO, with IL-6 elevated ≈13.6-fold in a cytokine screen and partially suppressed by caspase-1 inhibition, indicating a secondary induction downstream of inflammasome activation (not direct inflammasome processing) (Brandstetter, 2016). Cytokine release is apically polarized, and conditioned media from inflammasome-activated RPE is chemotactic for microglia, linking RPE lysosomal injury to neuroretinal immune activation (Brandstetter, 2016). Complement C5a serves as a physiologically relevant priming agent in RPE by activating NF-κB and inducing pro-IL-1β, which permits subsequent LMP-triggered NLRP3 activation; C5a priming and IL-1α priming also shift cell death from apoptosis to pyroptosis after lipofuscin phototoxicity (Brandstetter, 2016). Lysosomal proteases are mechanistically implicated: inhibition of cathepsin B and L suppresses LMP-triggered inflammasome activation in RPE, and cytosolic cathepsins in general, including cathepsin D, can promote apoptosis when released from the lysosome, underscoring the importance of lysosomal integrity in RPE survival (Brandstetter, 2016).

Intracellular clearance failure and mitochondrial stress as alternative inflammasome drivers: Independent RPE models that combine proteasome inhibition (MG-132) with autophagy/lysosome blockade (bafilomycin A₁) activate NLRP3 via oxidative stress, producing caspase-1–dependent IL-1β secretion without evidence that lysosomal rupture/cathepsin leakage is the primary driver; Hsp90 stabilizes NLRP3 in this setting, and Hsp90 inhibition promotes autophagic degradation of NLRP3 when autophagy remains functional (Piippo, 2019). Mitochondrial dysfunction induced by antimycin A activates both NLRP3 and AIM2 inflammasomes in human RPE lines via mitochondrial ROS and cytosolic DNA, with AIM2 showing dominant control of IL-1β/IL-18 in some contexts, broadening the repertoire of upstream hazards beyond lysosomal damage (Korhonen, 2024).

Mechanistic gaps for IL-6R control of lysosomes/autophagy: Crucially, the provided materials do not furnish direct mechanistic or biochemical evidence that IL-6 or IL-6R signaling modulates RPE autophagic flux, lysosomal acidification (v-ATPase function), or cathepsin D enzymatic activity, and several excerpts explicitly note the absence of IL-6R blockade studies interrogating autophagy/lysosome endpoints in RPE/AMD models (Buniello et al., 2025; Brandstetter, 2016). In additional RPE experiments modulating autophagy and p62/SQSTM1, cytokine shifts were observed for MCP-1 and IL-8, while IL-6 did not exhibit consistent dependency on p62 state, arguing against a simple autophagy→IL-6 coupling that would predict lysosomal rescue by IL-6R blockade (Korhonen, 2024). Within this corpus, IL-6 behaves as part of a downstream inflammatory secretome during RPE stress rather than an upstream determinant of lysosomal health (Brandstetter, 2016).

Expected Effect  
Assay-level expectations under AMD-relevant stress paradigms should be aligned with the causal structure supported by the evidence.

- What IL-6R blockade should do: Given that RPE secrete IL-6 and can engage IL-6/IL-8 autocrine degenerative signaling in inflammatory contexts, tocilizumab is expected to abrogate IL-6–dependent downstream signaling in RPE and neighboring cells, dampening IL-6–responsive gene expression and paracrine effects where IL-6 is a driver (Brandstetter, 2016). In LMP/blue-light or impaired-clearance inflammasome models, IL-6 is robustly induced alongside IL-1β/IL-18 and partially depends on caspase-1–driven pathways, so tocilizumab would be expected to reduce IL-6-mediated signaling outputs but would not suppress upstream lysosomal damage, cathepsin leakage, inflammasome assembly, or caspase-1 activation per se (Brandstetter, 2016). Because inflammasome activation in these models also reduces constitutive VEGF secretion and polarizes cytokine release apically, IL-6R blockade might modestly alter the inflammatory milieu without restoring basal angiogenic signaling from RPE or preventing microglial chemotaxis induced by the broader cytokine secretome (Brandstetter, 2016).

- Unsupported elements of the working hypothesis: The claim that tocilizumab will prevent v-ATPase downregulation, preserve lysosomal pH, and maintain cathepsin D activity to slow RPE atrophy is not supported by the present corpus; none of the provided sources demonstrate that IL-6 or IL-6R signaling directly regulates v-ATPase subunits, lysosomal acidification, or CTSD activity in RPE, nor that IL-6R blockade restores these parameters in AMD-relevant assays (Buniello et al., 2025; Brandstetter, 2016). In contrast, interventions that directly target inflammasome priming/assembly or its stability (e.g., Hsp90 inhibition enabling autophagic degradation of NLRP3 when autophagy is intact) have demonstrated impact on inflammasome outputs in RPE models, emphasizing that upstream proteostasis/oxidative stress rather than IL-6 drives inflammasome activation in those settings (Piippo, 2019).

- Target expression and pathway verification in assay design: The corpus documents RPE production of IL-6, but it does not provide direct evidence of IL-6R expression/function or JAK/STAT3 activation in the specific RPE models used for AMD-relevant stress paradigms, and the Open Targets excerpt shows weaker curated AMD evidence for STAT3 than for IL6 itself (Brandstetter, 2016; Buniello et al., 2025). Therefore, prior to efficacy testing, verify IL-6R expression and IL-6–induced pathway activation (e.g., STAT3 phosphorylation and transcriptional targets) in the chosen human RPE model and confirm that tocilizumab blocks these readouts (Brandstetter, 2016; Buniello et al., 2025).

- Net biological effect in dry AMD context: Dry AMD progression is mechanistically rooted in upstream lysosomal/photooxidative injury, complement-driven NF-κB priming, and NLRP3/AIM2 inflammasome activation that governs IL-1β/IL-18 release and shifts death modes toward pyroptosis; IL-6 is a downstream secretome component rather than a proximal trigger in these paradigms (Brandstetter, 2016). Consequently, tocilizumab is more likely to modulate inflammatory tone than to prevent the initiating RPE lysosomal failure that drives atrophy in dry AMD (Brandstetter, 2016; Piippo, 2019).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Biologic plausibility at the cytokine level: IL-6 is elevated in AMD and produced by RPE, and RPE inflammasome activation produces a pronounced IL-6 response (≈13.6-fold increase) together with IL-1β/IL-18 under AMD-relevant stresses; IL-6 can participate in autocrine degenerative loops in RPE after inflammatory stimuli (Buniello et al., 2025; Brandstetter, 2016). This supports testing whether IL-6/IL-6R signaling contributes to maladaptive inflammatory reinforcement in diseased RPE (Buniello et al., 2025).  
- Validated pharmacology and established clinical operations: Tocilizumab’s IL-6R blockade is mechanistically defined, and systemic dosing regimens (IV 8 mg/kg q4w, SC 162 mg weekly) and safety frameworks are standardized; ophthalmic trials have successfully embedded retinal structural and visual endpoints under systemic IL-6R blockade, providing a feasible operational scaffold (Assistance Publique–Hôpitaux de Paris, 2017; Shi, 2017b; Shi, 2017a).  
- Ocular inflammatory precedent and safety monitoring: Prospective uveitis trials and the planned DME study demonstrate translational interest in IL-6 blockade in eye disease and detail immunosuppression-oriented screening and monitoring relevant to an elderly population (TB/hepatitis screening, neutrophil/platelet/hepatic thresholds, live-vaccine restrictions, diverticulitis caution, reproductive precautions) (University of Nebraska, 2016; Assistance Publique–Hôpitaux de Paris, 2017; Zhujiang Hospital, 2025).

Weaknesses and risks  
- Lack of mechanistic linkage to lysosomal rescue: No evidence in the corpus shows that IL-6/IL-6R signaling controls v-ATPase function, lysosomal pH, autophagic flux, or cathepsin D activity in RPE; multiple excerpts explicitly note the absence of IL-6R blockade studies addressing autophagy/lysosome endpoints in RPE models (Buniello et al., 2025; Brandstetter, 2016). By contrast, RPE inflammasome activation arises from upstream lysosomal damage, proteostasis failure, oxidative stress, and complement priming—nodes not expected to be corrected by IL-6R blockade (Brandstetter, 2016; Piippo, 2019; Brandstetter, 2016; Brandstetter, 2016).  
- Downstream positioning of IL-6 in AMD-relevant cascades: In LMP/blue-light and impaired-clearance models, IL-6 is part of a downstream secretome secondary to caspase-1–dependent pathways, whereas proximal determinants of RPE fate include lysosomal integrity, cathepsin activity, inflammasome assembly, and priming signals; targeting IL-6R is therefore unlikely to interrupt the initiating injury that drives RPE atrophy (Brandstetter, 2016).  
- No clinical evidence in dry AMD and uncertain ocular route: The materials contain no clinical trials of tocilizumab in dry AMD, and the only retina-focused interventional protocol in the corpus (READ-4 for DME) was withdrawn before enrollment; registry-level hits lack extractable information here (University of Nebraska, 2016; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.). Intravitreal data for tocilizumab are not provided, and systemic use in an elderly AMD population carries non-trivial risks (serious infections, cytopenias, hepatic injury, GI perforation risk, vaccine restrictions) that may outweigh an unproven benefit (University of Nebraska, 2016; Assistance Publique–Hôpitaux de Paris, 2017; Zhujiang Hospital, 2025).  
- Limited curated evidence for IL-6R/STAT3 in AMD: The Open Targets excerpt underscores that while IL6 is strongly associated with AMD literature, STAT3 (a principal IL-6R effector) has minimal curated AMD evidence in this dataset, weakening confidence that IL-6R blockade will materially modulate the NF-κB priming required for inflammasome activation in RPE (Buniello et al., 2025).

Development recommendation  
- Given the current evidence, tocilizumab is not a priority candidate for slowing RPE atrophy in dry AMD via lysosomal preservation, because the mechanistic chain posited—IL-6R blockade preserving v-ATPase and cathepsin D activity—lacks experimental support in RPE/AMD models in this corpus, while disease-proximal injury nodes are driven by lysosomal/photooxidative damage, intracellular clearance failure, complement-driven NF-κB priming, and NLRP3/AIM2 activation (Brandstetter, 2016; Piippo, 2019; Korhonen, 2024).  
- If pursued at all, the program should begin with narrow mechanistic validation in human RPE: verify IL-6R expression and functional IL-6→JAK/STAT signaling; quantify whether tocilizumab reduces IL-6–dependent outputs in AMD-relevant RPE stress assays (lipofuscin/blue-light LMP, MG-132+BafA proteostasis failure, antimycin A mitochondrial stress) while measuring lysosomal pH, v-ATPase subunit expression, cathepsin D activity, caspase-1 activity, IL-1β/IL-18 release, and RPE death mode; a priori, expect effects restricted to IL-6-responsive readouts without rescue of lysosome/inflammasome metrics (Brandstetter, 2016; Piippo, 2019; Korhonen, 2024).  
- Benchmark tocilizumab against mechanistically proximal modulators (e.g., NLRP3 pathway inhibitors, IL-1 pathway blockade, Hsp90 inhibition enabling NLRP3 degradation when autophagy is intact) to determine whether IL-6R blockade adds independent benefit on RPE survival beyond dampening IL-6 signaling (Piippo, 2019; Brandstetter, 2016).  
- Absent compelling preclinical data showing that IL-6R blockade favorably modifies lysosomal function or decisively improves RPE survival in AMD-relevant paradigms, deprioritize tocilizumab in favor of targets that directly modulate the proximal injury axis (lysosome integrity, complement-NF-κB priming, and inflammasome assembly) (Brandstetter, 2016; Piippo, 2019).
