Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Biologic plausibility at the cytokine level: IL-6 is elevated in AMD and produced by RPE, and RPE inflammasome activation produces a pronounced IL-6 response (≈13.6-fold increase) together with IL-1β/IL-18 under AMD-relevant stresses; IL-6 can participate in autocrine degenerative loops in RPE after inflammatory stimuli (Buniello et al., 2025; Brandstetter, 2016). - Lack of mechanistic linkage to lysosomal rescue: No evidence in the corpus shows that IL-6/IL-6R signaling controls v-ATPase function, lysosomal pH, autophagic flux, or cathepsin D activity in RPE; multiple excerpts explicitly note the absence of IL-6R blockade studies addressing autophagy/lysosome endpoints in RPE models (Buniello et al., 2025; Brandstetter, 2016). - Downstream positioning of IL-6 in AMD-relevant cascades: In LMP/blue-light and impaired-clearance models, IL-6 is part of a downstream secretome secondary to caspase-1–dependent pathways, whereas proximal determinants of RPE fate include lysosomal integrity, cathepsin activity, inflammasome assembly, and priming signals; targeting IL-6R is therefore unlikely to interrupt the initiating injury that drives RPE atrophy (Brandstetter, 2016).

- Limited curated evidence for IL-6R/STAT3 in AMD: The Open Targets excerpt underscores that while IL6 is strongly associated with AMD literature, STAT3 (a principal IL-6R effector) has minimal curated AMD evidence in this dataset, weakening confidence that IL-6R blockade will materially modulate the NF-κB priming required for inflammasome activation in RPE (Buniello et al., 2025).

Development recommendation  
- Given the current evidence, tocilizumab is not a priority candidate for slowing RPE atrophy in dry AMD via lysosomal preservation, because the mechanistic chain posited—IL-6R blockade preserving v-ATPase and cathepsin D activity—lacks experimental support in RPE/AMD models in this corpus, while disease-proximal injury nodes are driven by lysosomal/photooxidative damage, intracellular clearance failure, complement-driven NF-κB priming, and NLRP3/AIM2 activation (Brandstetter, 2016; Piippo, 2019; Korhonen, 2024).

- Benchmark tocilizumab against mechanistically proximal modulators (e.g., NLRP3 pathway inhibitors, IL-1 pathway blockade, Hsp90 inhibition enabling NLRP3 degradation when autophagy is intact) to determine whether IL-6R blockade adds independent benefit on RPE survival beyond dampening IL-6 signaling (Piippo, 2019; Brandstetter, 2016).  
- Absent compelling preclinical data showing that IL-6R blockade favorably modifies lysosomal function or decisively improves RPE survival in AMD-relevant paradigms, deprioritize tocilizumab in favor of targets that directly modulate the proximal injury axis (lysosome integrity, complement-NF-κB priming, and inflammasome assembly) (Brandstetter, 2016; Piippo, 2019).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Temsirolimus (CCI-779; Torisel) is a semi-synthetic ester prodrug of sirolimus (rapamycin) discovered during rapamycin medicinal chemistry optimization to improve formulation properties and pharmacokinetics; it is a first-generation “rapalog” that inhibits mTOR by forming an intracellular complex with FKBP12 and binding the FRB domain of mTOR, thereby allosterically inhibiting mTORC1 catalytic signaling (and only indirectly affecting mTORC2) (Wang et al., 2022). As a class, rapalogs are derived from the natural macrolide rapamycin originally isolated from Streptomyces hygroscopicus; they have been used systemically as immunosuppressants and anti-proliferative/anti-angiogenic agents in oncology and transplant medicine by suppressing mTORC1-dependent growth and inflammatory programs (Wang et al., 2022; Johnson, 2013). mTORC1 is a lysosome-proximal signaling hub that integrates amino acid sufficiency via the Ragulator–Rag GTPase machinery and growth/energy signals via Rheb/AMPK, coordinating anabolism (protein synthesis via S6K and 4E-BP1), and repressing catabolism (autophagy and lysosomal biogenesis) (Johnson, 2013). In ocular biology, temsirolimus has been evaluated preclinically in human retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells and human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVEC), consistently demonstrating dose-dependent inhibition of proliferation and migration and decreased VEGF/PDGF expression through mTOR pathway inhibition, supporting target engagement in retinal cell types relevant to AMD pathogenesis (Liegl et al., 2014). Compared with rapamycin, temsirolimus has higher aqueous solubility and stability but is administered intravenously in approved oncology indications; adverse events include metabolic and mucosal toxicities typical of systemic mTOR inhibition (Wang et al., 2022).

Therapeutic History  
Rapamycin/sirolimus and rapalogs have a long clinical history across transplantation and oncology; in ophthalmology, mechanistic and translational work has targeted mTOR for AMD and other retinal diseases because mTORC1 suppresses autophagy/lysosomal programs and promotes inflammatory and angiogenic signaling (Wang et al., 2022; Nita & Grzybowski, 2023). In RPE models that recapitulate daily phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments (POS), mTORC1 activity is dynamically regulated: POS phagocytosis transiently activates mTORC1, followed by inhibition during phagosome maturation; however, in aged RPE and AMD, mTORC1 activity is relatively elevated and TFEB is retained in the phosphorylated cytosolic state, impairing lysosomal responses and favoring lipofuscin-like autofluorescent granule (AFG) accumulation (Falcão et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2025). In these systems, rapamycin reduces POS-dependent AFGs by about 30% while increasing TFEB activity and lysosomal biogenesis markers (e.g., LAMP1) in ARPE-19 and human fetal RPE cells; efficacy generalizes to other mTOR pathway inhibitors (e.g., INK-128), and constitutively active TFEB provides larger effects, supporting a TFEB-centric mechanism (Falcão et al., 2024). These effects require intact lysosomal proteolysis; pharmacologic blockade of lysosomal acid lipase, cathepsin inhibition, or cathepsin D (CTSD) knockout abrogates rapamycin’s benefit, highlighting a dependence on functional lysosomes (Falcão et al., 2024). Although these data do not directly test temsirolimus in lysosome-TFEB endpoints, temsirolimus is mechanistically a rapalog mTORC1 inhibitor, and in RPE it engages mTOR biology by suppressing growth factor signaling outputs (VEGF/PDGF) and cell motility/proliferation, thereby validating target engagement in the relevant cell type (Liegl et al., 2014).

Clinically, multiple sirolimus trials have evaluated mTOR inhibition in geographic atrophy (GA), a late stage of dry AMD, with disappointing outcomes. Subconjunctival sirolimus (440 µg every 3 months for 24 months) in a bilateral-eye, fellow-eye-control study did not slow GA enlargement and was associated with a treatment-associated decrease in visual acuity relative to untreated fellow eyes, despite an acceptable safety profile in that study (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2008; Wang et al., 2022). An intravitreal sirolimus Phase I/II study in bilateral GA was discontinued early, and separate trials reported ocular adverse events including accelerated retinal thinning, abnormal perilesional autofluorescence, and sterile endophthalmitis; overall, no structural or functional benefit was demonstrated across these programs (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2011; Wang et al., 2022). These clinical observations raise concern that chronic mTOR inhibition in established GA may be ineffective or even detrimental, potentially due to disease stage–specific network effects of autophagy and survival signaling in degenerating retina (Wang et al., 2022). In contrast, preclinical data in other retinal contexts (e.g., glaucoma) show neuroprotective correlates of mTOR inhibition, underscoring the context- and stage-dependence of therapeutic effects (Wang et al., 2022). For wet AMD and retinal vascular pathology, temsirolimus (and rapamycin) exert anti-angiogenic actions in vitro and in animal models by downregulating VEGF/PDGF and endothelial proliferation, which are less directly relevant to GA biology but establish ocular pharmacology for the class (Liegl et al., 2014; Johnson, 2013). Drug delivery innovations such as synthetic HDL nanoparticles carrying rapamycin have been explored preclinically to optimize ocular delivery, suggesting format-dependent translatability may be important for this class (Falcão et al., 2024).

Mechanism of Action  
Temsirolimus acts as a prototypical rapalog: it binds FKBP12 to form a gain-of-function complex that docks to the FKBP12-rapamycin binding (FRB) domain of mTOR and selectively inhibits mTORC1 signaling; mTORC2 is generally spared acutely, with potential indirect effects chronically depending on cellular context (Wang et al., 2022). mTORC1 normally phosphorylates TFEB on multiple serine residues, retaining it in the cytosol and preventing nuclear entry; when mTORC1 is inhibited, TFEB becomes dephosphorylated, translocates to the nucleus, and drives the CLEAR network that upregulates autophagy and lysosomal biogenesis genes (e.g., LAMP1), enhancing degradative capacity and organelle biogenesis (Falcão et al., 2025; Falcão et al., 2024). In RPE cells, POS phagocytosis engages mTORC1 transiently, but aged/AMD RPE exhibit enhanced mTORC1 activity that suppresses appropriate TFEB activation; rapamycin reverses this, promoting TFEB dephosphorylation, nuclear entry, GADD34 upregulation, and increased lysosomal mass, collectively reducing AFGs by approximately 30% in POS-challenged RPE (Falcão et al., 2024). The TFEB dependency has been functionally validated via TFEB gain-of-function, which markedly decreases AFGs in both preventive and “therapeutic” paradigms after lipofuscin-like material has already formed (Falcão et al., 2024). Pharmacologic relevance to mTOR pathway modulation beyond rapamycin was supported using INK-128 and other mTOR inhibitors, which replicated the AFG reduction and TFEB-lysosome signature (Falcão et al., 2024).

At the biochemical level, mTORC1 integrates amino acid signaling at the lysosomal surface via Ragulator-Rag GTPases and growth/energy cues via Rheb/AMPK, coordinating downstream phosphorylation of p70S6K and 4E-BP1 to activate translation while repressing catabolic programs including initiation of autophagy (partly by phosphorylating ULK1 at Ser757 and by blocking TFEB) (Johnson, 2013; Chang et al., 2022). In retinal tissues, mTOR inhibition is expected to relieve brakes on autophagy and lysosomal biogenesis; in diabetic retinopathy models, mTOR inhibition with rapamycin restored impaired lysosomal proteolysis by normalizing cathepsin L activity and autophagic flux, mechanistically consistent with TFEB-driven CLEAR network activation and improved lysosomal protease capacity (Wang et al., 2022). Although direct evidence for temsirolimus effects on RPE TFEB phosphorylation state, lysosomal acidification, or CTSD maturation is not available, the shared mechanism of FKBP12-dependent mTORC1 inhibition and the RPE-cell mTOR engagement demonstrated by temsirolimus (antiproliferative/anti-migratory, VEGF/PDGF suppression) support pathway perturbation in the correct cellular context (Liegl et al., 2014).

In the context of AMD pathophysiology, RPE lysosomal dysfunction and impaired clearance of POS-derived material drive lipofuscin accumulation and downstream toxicity; TFEB has emerged as a master regulator to restore lysosomal capacity, while AMD donor RPE show reduced cathepsin D and L levels/activities, highlighting protease insufficiency as a plausible node of therapeutic rescue (Falcão et al., 2025). Importantly, in POS-fed RPE, the rapamycin benefit is abolished by lysosomal protease inhibition or CTSD knockout, indicating that mTORC1 inhibition enhances clearance only when lysosomal protease function is preserved, and suggesting that concomitant strategies to support lysosomal acidification/protease maturation could be synergistic (Falcão et al., 2024). Finally, some reports have suggested low immunoreactivity of mTORC1/2 components in RPE, but this observation contrasts with multiple functional studies demonstrating mTORC1 signaling in RPE during POS handling and aging; taken together, functional responsiveness to mTOR inhibitors in RPE likely depends on model system and detection sensitivity (Wang et al., 2022; Falcão et al., 2024).

Expected Effect  
In a POS-pulse/chase AFG assay using ARPE-19 or human fetal RPE, temsirolimus is expected to inhibit mTORC1 (decreased pS6 phosphorylation), dephosphorylate TFEB, increase TFEB nuclear localization, upregulate CLEAR network/lysosomal biogenesis genes (e.g., GADD34, LAMP1), and reduce AFG burden by enhancing degradation of phagocytosed material; this mirrors rapamycin’s effects (~30% AFG reduction) and those of other mTOR inhibitors in these models (Falcão et al., 2024). To confirm on-target activity and pathway alignment, assays should include pS6/S6 and pTFEB/TFEB immunoblotting at 2–24 h, TFEB nuclear translocation imaging, LAMP1 immunostaining for lysosomal mass, and flow cytometry quantification of AFGs after 24–72 h chase, consistent with established methodologies (Falcão et al., 2024). Because rapamycin’s benefits are abolished by lysosomal protease blockade and in CTSD-deficient backgrounds, temsirolimus-dependent AFG reduction is predicted to require functional cathepsin D and lipases; co-assaying CTSD maturation (pro-/mature CTSD ratio), lysosomal pH, and acid lipase activity is therefore crucial to mechanistic validation (Falcão et al., 2024). In parallel, transcriptomic or targeted RT-qPCR panels for CLEAR genes will validate TFEB program engagement (Falcão et al., 2024).

Regarding lysosomal acidification and protease activity, there is mechanistic plausibility but no direct demonstration that temsirolimus enhances lysosomal pH or CTSD maturation in RPE; nevertheless, the TFEB-centric model predicts improved lysosomal proteostasis, and related retinal models show that mTOR inhibition can restore impaired lysosomal proteolysis (cathepsin L) and autophagic flux, supporting the hypothesis that temsirolimus could favorably influence protease maturation/activity in RPE (Wang et al., 2022; Falcão et al., 2025). Notably, independent approaches in RPE can acidify lysosomes and reduce AFGs, underscoring the tractability of the acidification axis, though this was not via mTOR inhibition; combining mTORC1-TFEB activation with direct acidification strategies could be additive (Falcão et al., 2024). The expectation for disease modification in GA derives from the idea that sustained enhancement of lysosomal clearance will reduce lipofuscin burden, preserve RPE function, and slow atrophic expansion; however, prior GA trials with sirolimus showed no benefit and potential harm, implying that either the disease stage, delivery/exposure, or network consequences of chronic mTORC1 inhibition negate the anticipated benefit in late disease (Wang et al., 2022).

Temsirolimus target expression and pharmacology in RPE are supported by in vitro data showing dose-dependent inhibition of RPE proliferation and migration and suppression of hypoxia-induced VEGF/PDGF increases without overt cytotoxicity at low micromolar to millimolar nominal concentrations; these endpoints corroborate mTOR pathway engagement in RPE and provide pharmacodynamic markers (e.g., VEGF suppression) that can be measured alongside TFEB-lysosomal readouts in AFG assays (Liegl et al., 2014). The drug class’s ocular delivery options range from systemic dosing (with significant class-typical adverse events) to local delivery; sirolimus trials used subconjunctival or intravitreal administration but encountered safety/tolerability signals including sterile endophthalmitis and accelerated retinal thinning with no efficacy in GA, emphasizing the need for alternative delivery technologies (e.g., nanoparticles) and stage-appropriate patient selection if pursuing this mechanism (Wang et al., 2022; Falcão et al., 2024). Finally, given AMD donor RPE deficiencies in cathepsins D/L, co-therapies or genetic activation strategies that more directly drive TFEB or augment lysosomal protease capacity could be required to realize the full benefit of mTORC1 inhibition in human disease (Falcão et al., 2025).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Mechanism-based rationale with cell-type congruence: RPE lysosomal dysfunction is central to AMD, and mTORC1 directly represses TFEB and lysosomal programs; in POS-fed RPE, mTORC1 inhibition with rapamycin reduces AFG burden by ~30%, increases lysosomal biogenesis (LAMP1), and requires intact lysosomal proteases, aligning precisely with the hypothesized MoA (Falcão et al., 2024). The effect generalizes across mTOR inhibitors and is amplified by TFEB gain-of-function, strengthening the pathway argument (Falcão et al., 2024).  
- Direct evidence that temsirolimus engages mTOR signaling in RPE: temsirolimus suppresses proliferation/migration and reduces VEGF/PDGF in primary human RPE, indicating pharmacodynamic activity and target engagement in the disease-relevant cell type (Liegl et al., 2014).  
- Broad mechanistic plausibility for enhancing lysosomal proteolysis: mTORC1 inhibition activates TFEB; retinal disease models show restoration of lysosomal protease activity (cathepsin L) and autophagic flux with rapamycin, consistent with improved lysosomal proteostasis, which could translate to better CTSD maturation in RPE even though that specific nexus is unproven for temsirolimus (Wang et al., 2022; Falcão et al., 2025).  
- Drug class knowledge base and formulation opportunities: extensive class experience informs safety risk assessment; emerging ocular delivery strategies (e.g., sHDL rapamycin nanoparticles) might overcome exposure constraints seen in prior sirolimus GA trials (Falcão et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2022).

Weaknesses and Risks  
- Negative/unsafe clinical precedents in GA with class analog: multiple sirolimus trials in GA failed to slow lesion growth and revealed adverse ocular events, including accelerated retinal thinning and procedure-related sterile endophthalmitis, suggesting either mechanistic inadequacy at late stages, harmful network effects of chronic mTORC1 inhibition, or delivery-related issues; this materially lowers clinical plausibility for GA-stage disease (Wang et al., 2022).  
- Absence of temsirolimus-specific TFEB/lysosome data in RPE: while rapamycin demonstrates TFEB activation, lysosomal biogenesis, and AFG reduction, comparable mechanistic data for temsirolimus in RPE are lacking; the program would therefore carry translatability risk until head-to-head, mechanistic RPE assays confirm TFEB engagement and AFG reduction with temsirolimus (Falcão et al., 2024; Liegl et al., 2014).  
- Dependence on intact lysosomes and proteases: rapamycin’s benefit disappears with lipase inhibition or CTSD deficiency; AMD donor RPE show reduced cathepsin D/L, implying that many patient retinas may not have sufficient residual lysosomal capacity for mTORC1 inhibition alone to succeed without adjuncts that restore acidification/protease maturation (Falcão et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2025).  
- Context and stage dependence of mTOR biology: autophagy upregulation that is protective in early disease can exacerbate neuronal apoptosis in late AMD; cell-type–specific and duration-dependent consequences of mTOR inhibition complicate chronic treatment in GA and may negate benefits or cause harm (Wang et al., 2022).  
- Systemic formulation constraints and ocular delivery safety: temsirolimus is an IV drug with known systemic toxicities; local ocular administration for a chronic indication must overcome prior safety/tolerability issues observed with sirolimus injections while achieving sustained, intraretinal/RPE-targeted exposure (Wang et al., 2022).

Go/No-Go Perspective and Development Recommendations  
- Indication selection: Given the negative GA clinical history with sirolimus, prioritize early/intermediate dry AMD with measurable lipofuscin/AFG burden and residual RPE lysosomal capacity, rather than established GA, where class effects have been neutral or detrimental (Falcão et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2022).  
- Mechanistic bridging for temsirolimus: Run definitive RPE mechanistic studies comparing temsirolimus to rapamycin and an ATP-competitive mTOR inhibitor (e.g., INK-128) using POS-pulse/chase AFG assays, pS6/pTFEB readouts, TFEB nuclear localization, LAMP1, lysosomal pH, acid lipase, and CTSD maturation/activity, with rescue and block experiments to confirm TFEB dependence and lysosome-requirement (Falcão et al., 2024).  
- Combination strategies: Evaluate temsirolimus with lysosome-acidifying agents or TFEB-direct activators/gene transfer to overcome the protease dependency bottleneck evident in AMD RPE; mechanistic review suggests dual TFEB/mTOR and NRF2/KEAP1 modulation could be synergistic but requires careful control to avoid oncogenic risk (Falcão et al., 2025).  
- Delivery innovation: Avoid frequent intravitreal bolusing; explore sustained-release local delivery or targeted nanoparticles (e.g., sHDL-like) to deliver rapalogs selectively to RPE/retina at sub-toxic exposures, learning from prior sirolimus delivery failures (Falcão et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2022).  
- Translational biomarkers: In early clinical exploration, incorporate pharmacodynamic biomarkers of TFEB activation (e.g., aqueous humor proteomics for CLEAR targets, retinal LAMP1 imaging if feasible), structural endpoints sensitive to RPE health (fundus autofluorescence for lipofuscin load), and stringent safety monitoring for retinal thinning and inflammation to detect class-typical adverse signals early (Falcão et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2022).

Bottom line: The TFEB-lysosome rationale is robust at the cellular level in RPE, but the rapalog class has failed to translate benefit in GA; temsirolimus lacks direct RPE TFEB/lysosomal evidence and carries delivery/safety liabilities observed with sirolimus in GA. As a repurposing candidate, temsirolimus merits mechanistic validation in RPE with TFEB/lysosome endpoints and, if positive, a carefully designed, stage-appropriate pilot in early/intermediate dry AMD using optimized delivery; it is not a priority candidate for GA without compelling new mechanistic and translational data that overcome the class’s negative clinical precedent (Falcão et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2022).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Recombinant human pro-cathepsin D (rhCTSD), as exemplified by R&D Systems product 1869-CD, is a bioengineered form of a naturally occurring lysosomal aspartyl protease that is synthesized as an inactive precursor (pro-cathepsin D) (Sharif, 2015, pp. 60–64). This therapeutic candidate belongs to the enzyme replacement therapy (ERT) class, a category of biotherapeutics developed to supplement or correct deficient lysosomal enzymes in various disorders. The natural cathepsin D enzyme is normally produced and processed intracellularly through the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and Golgi apparatus, undergoing critical post-translational modifications—including the removal of the N-terminal signal peptide, glycosylation, and addition of a mannose-6-phosphate (M6P) tag—that are essential for its subsequent targeting to the lysosome (Sharif, 2015, pp. 60–64). The recombinant version is produced under conditions aimed at ensuring high purity and biological activity conforming to GMP standards, thus making it an attractive candidate for repurposing in conditions where lysosomal proteolytic capacity is compromised. The candidate has been designed in the context of neurodegenerative and lysosomal storage disorders, where enzyme supplementation has been shown to restore proteolytic flux by directly replacing a rate-limiting hydrolase (Bassal et al., 2021; Marques et al., 2020).

Therapeutic History:  
Enzyme replacement therapies have been a cornerstone in the management of several lysosomal storage disorders since the early 1990s, with the first approved treatment for Gaucher’s disease setting a precedent for this therapeutic strategy (Saftig, 2005; Lerussi et al., 2025). In the specific case of cathepsin D, recombinant forms have been employed in preclinical models of neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis (NCL) and other neurodegenerative lysosomal storage disorders, where the administration of exogenous pro-cathepsin D was able to rescue functional deficits associated with genetic CTSD deficiency (Bassal et al., 2021; Marques et al., 2020). Animal studies using CTSD-deficient mouse models have demonstrated that both intracranial and localized injections of recombinant CTSD can correct defects in proteolysis and autophagy, leading to improvements in neuropathological markers and even extending lifespan in treated animals (Bassal et al., 2021; Liu, 2021; Marques et al., 2020). Although most of these studies have focused on neurodegenerative conditions of the central nervous system, similar principles of lysosomal dysfunction apply to retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells, which are critical for maintaining retinal homeostasis in the context of age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (Klettner et al., 2013). Notably, the literature suggests that cathepsin D is highly expressed in RPE cells and plays a vital role in the degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (POS), with its deficiency or reduced function being implicated in the accumulation of toxic deposits and drusen formation—a hallmark of dry AMD (Klettner et al., 2013; Sharif, 2015). Despite the absence of direct clinical trials in dry AMD using rhCTSD, the extensive preclinical evidence from both neurodegenerative and retinal disease models provides a compelling rationale for exploring the repurposing of this enzyme replacement strategy in dry AMD (Liu, 2021; Marques et al., 2020).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, the mechanism of action of recombinant human pro-cathepsin D is rooted in its ability to restore lysosomal proteolytic function, which is often impaired in disease states such as dry AMD. Under physiological conditions, pro-cathepsin D is synthesized in the rough ER as an inactive precursor that undergoes several post-translational modifications, including the cleavage of an N-terminal signal peptide, N-linked glycosylation, and critical mannose-6-phosphate (M6P) tagging in the Golgi apparatus (Sharif, 2015). The M6P tag facilitates the binding of pro-cathepsin D to M6P receptors within the trans-Golgi network (TGN), directing the enzyme to late endosomes and, eventually, to lysosomes where the acidic environment promotes its maturation into its active form (Sharif, 2015). Once active, cathepsin D contributes to the degradation of a wide range of substrates, including the photoreceptor outer segments in RPE cells, thereby playing a crucial role in maintaining cellular homeostasis and preventing the accumulation of deleterious debris that can lead to drusen formation (Klettner et al., 2013). The proposed therapeutic strategy involves subretinal delivery of the recombinant enzyme to bypass systemic limitations such as the blood-brain barrier and to achieve localized uptake into RPE cells via the M6P receptor-mediated endocytosis pathway (Liu, 2021; Marques et al., 2020; Sharif, 2015). Once internalized, the enzyme can replenish endogenous levels of cathepsin D, thereby enhancing autophagic flux and proteolytic degradation processes that are essential for the health and function of the RPE (Klettner et al., 2013; Sharif, 2015). This targeted mechanism is a direct, molecularly specific approach that aims not only to compensate for maturation defects in the enzyme but also to overcome upstream acidification abnormalities that often hinder proper activation of endogenously produced cathepsin D in aging RPE cells (Liu, 2021; Marques et al., 2020; Sharif, 2015).

Expected Effect:  
The anticipated outcome of employing recombinant human pro-cathepsin D for the treatment of dry AMD is multifaceted. First, the subretinal administration of the enzyme is expected to lead to efficient uptake by RPE cells via the M6P receptor, thereby supplementing or restoring the lysosomal pool of active cathepsin D where it is most critically needed (Sharif, 2015). This direct enzyme replacement should result in improved degradation of cellular waste such as spent photoreceptor outer segments, mitigating the build-up of lipofuscin and drusen that are characteristic of dry AMD pathology (Klettner et al., 2013). In animal models of CTSD deficiency—specifically those that mimic aspects of neurodegenerative lysosomal storage disorders—the administration of exogenous pro-cathepsin D has yielded significant improvements in proteolytic function, reduction of pathological markers, and even extensions in lifespan (Bassal et al., 2021; Marques et al., 2020), which suggest that similar therapeutic benefits might be achievable in the context of dry AMD. Enhancing the proteolytic flux within the lysosomes of RPE cells is expected to restore autophagy and maintain cellular homeostasis, thereby reducing the incidence of apoptotic cell death and preserving retinal structure (Klettner et al., 2013; Sharif, 2015). Additionally, by compensating for potential maturation deficits and bypassing defective acidification processes through localized delivery, the therapeutic candidate offers a targeted approach that is likely to be both efficacious and specific compared to more indirect modulators of lysosomal function (Liu, 2021; Marques et al., 2020; Sharif, 2015). Ultimately, the expected effect is an overall improvement in RPE health, which should translate into slowed progression of dry AMD, decreased drusen accumulation, and preserved visual function.

Overall Evaluation:  
In evaluating recombinant human pro-cathepsin D as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, several strengths emerge from the literature, though some challenges remain. One of the primary strengths of this candidate lies in its specificity; unlike indirect modulators of lysosomal function, the exogenous delivery of a rate-limiting hydrolase such as CTSD offers a mechanistically driven, targeted replacement therapy that directly addresses a known biochemical deficit in the retinal pigment epithelium (Klettner et al., 2013; Liu, 2021). The robust body of preclinical evidence supporting the efficacy of recombinant pro-cathepsin D in models of neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis, where similar lysosomal impairments are present, lends further credence to its potential applicability in AMD (Bassal et al., 2021; Marques et al., 2020). Moreover, the formulation's GMP-compatibility and prior demonstration of safety in the context of genetic CTSD deficiency are significant advantages that can accelerate its translational potential (Marques et al., 2020; Liu, 2021).

The enzyme’s molecular mechanism, which involves uptake via mannose-6-phosphate receptor-mediated endocytosis and subsequent activation in the lysosomal compartment, is well-characterized and aligns with the pathological requirements for restoring RPE function in dry AMD (Sharif, 2015). This targeted approach provides a direct means to enhance proteolytic activity and autophagic flux, crucial processes that are disrupted in the aging retina and contribute to drusen accumulation (Klettner et al., 2013). The ability of the exogenously delivered pro-cathepsin D to overcome defects in lysosomal maturation and acidification further reinforces its potential role in reversing or mitigating the deleterious effects of the disease (Liu, 2021; Marques et al., 2020).

On the other hand, several weaknesses or challenges must be acknowledged. Although the mechanistic rationale is robust, the translation of preclinical successes in neurodegenerative and lysosomal storage disorder models to the complex, multifactorial pathology of dry AMD remains uncertain (Benes et al., 2008; Liu, 2021). Dry AMD is influenced by a host of factors—including oxidative stress, chronic inflammation, and genetic predispositions—that may not be fully addressed by simply supplementing CTSD activity. Therefore, while the normalization of proteolytic flux in RPE cells is a critical component, it may not suffice on its own in the context of the broader pathophysiological milieu present in AMD (Klettner et al., 2013; Sharif, 2015).

Furthermore, delivery challenges inherent to subretinal injections must be considered. Although localized delivery methods help bypass systemic barriers such as the blood-brain barrier, subretinal injections are technically demanding, carry inherent risks of infection, and may provoke local immune responses due to repeated interventions (Marques et al., 2020; Liu, 2021). The emergence of neutralizing antibodies, as observed in some ERT studies when alternative routes of administration were explored, could compromise the long-term efficacy of the therapy if systemic leakage occurs or if repeated dosing is required (Marques et al., 2020; Liu, 2021). Additionally, the stability and persistence of the enzyme in the subretinal space represent important pharmacokinetic questions that must be addressed through rigorous preclinical pharmacodynamic studies.

Another potential shortcoming is the specificity of the enzyme’s action. While cathepsin D is indeed a critical protease in RPE cells, there is an intricate interplay between cathepsin D and other lysosomal enzymes such as cathepsins B, L, and S, as well as regulatory proteins like cystatin C, which modulate proteolytic activity (Sharif, 2015). This interdependence implies that augmenting CTSD activity alone might lead to compensatory changes in other proteases that could either enhance the therapeutic effect or, conversely, result in unforeseen off-target consequences. Moreover, given the complexity of the RPE cell’s lysosomal network and the multifactorial nature of dry AMD pathogenesis, combination approaches targeting several aspects of lysosomal dysfunction might be necessary to achieve optimal clinical outcomes.

In summary, recombinant human pro-cathepsin D presents a therapeutically attractive and mechanistically rational candidate for the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration. Its origins as a naturally occurring lysosomal precursor that, when supplemented exogenously, has been shown to restore enzyme activity in preclinical models of lysosomal dysfunction (Bassal et al., 2021; Marques et al., 2020) underscores its potential for addressing the proteolytic deficits seen in RPE cells affected by dry AMD (Klettner et al., 2013). The candidate’s well-defined molecular processing pathway—from synthesis as an inactive proenzyme to activation within the acidic environment of the lysosome—ensures that it is both functionally and biologically suited to compensate for endogenous maturation deficits (Sharif, 2015). This detailed understanding of its biochemistry and cellular uptake mechanisms via the mannose-6-phosphate receptor supports the hypothesis that subretinal delivery of rhCTSD could enhance proteolytic flux, reduce drusen accumulation, and ultimately contribute to the preservation of retinal function in patients with dry AMD (Liu, 2021; Marques et al., 2020).

Despite these promising attributes, the candidate’s clinical translation will require addressing several key challenges. Future studies must rigorously evaluate the pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic profiles of subretinally delivered rhCTSD, with particular emphasis on its stability, local retention time in the subretinal space, and potential immunogenicity. It will also be critical to determine whether augmenting CTSD activity alone is sufficient to counteract the multi-factorial processes underlying dry AMD or if the therapeutic strategy should be integrated into a broader, combination-based treatment regimen. Additionally, long-term safety studies are necessary to monitor for potential adverse effects, such as immune-mediated clearance or detrimental off-target proteolytic activity that might impair retinal structure and function (Marques et al., 2020; Thiessen, 2023).

Ultimately, the overall evaluation is cautiously optimistic. The mechanistic rationale is strong—supported by extensive preclinical data from related neurodegenerative and lysosomal storage disorder models—and the therapeutic candidate is produced under rigorous, GMP-compliant conditions, offering a level of quality assurance that is imperative for clinical advancement (Marques et al., 2020; Liu, 2021). The specificity of recombinant pro-cathepsin D in directly addressing a rate-limiting step in lysosomal degradation makes it an especially compelling candidate in a disease setting where impaired autophagy and proteolysis are central to pathology (Klettner et al., 2013). However, challenges related to effective subretinal delivery, the potential for immune responses, and the need to integrate its action within the broader context of AMD pathogenesis must be rigorously addressed in subsequent preclinical and clinical studies before a definitive therapeutic benefit can be confirmed (Marques et al., 2020; Benes et al., 2008). In light of these considerations, recombinant human pro-cathepsin D stands out as a promising avenue for therapeutic intervention in dry AMD, meriting further investigation to delineate its efficacy, safety, and long-term benefits in the appropriate animal models and ultimately in clinical trials.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
BAY 11-7082 is a synthetic, small-molecule inhibitor originally discovered as an irreversible inhibitor of IκBα phosphorylation, which blocks NF-κB activation. Chemically, it is classified as a phenyl vinyl sulfone compound featuring an α,β-unsaturated moiety that functions as a Michael acceptor. This reactive electrophilic center enables the compound to covalently modify nucleophilic cysteine residues on target proteins. Early studies identified BAY 11-7082 for its capacity to inhibit NF-κB signaling in endothelial cells, and subsequent research expanded its profile to include inhibition of the NLRP3 inflammasome via cysteine alkylation of critical regulatory sites. In essence, BAY 11-7082 belongs to the class of covalent inhibitors that have been widely studied in the context of inflammatory and oncologic diseases, and its availability as Sigma B5556 has made it a common tool compound in preclinical research (Juliana et al., 2010; Marchetti, 2019; Yu et al., 2018).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, BAY 11-7082 has been utilized extensively in biochemical, cellular, and animal studies as an anti-inflammatory agent. Initial applications centered on its ability to block the phosphorylation and degradation of IκBα, thereby inhibiting downstream NF-κB–driven gene expression. This mechanism was exploited in models of endothelial inflammation and various cancer cell lines, including studies showing potent anticancer, neuroprotective, and anti-inflammatory effects (Lee et al., 2012; Melisi & Chiao, 2007). Furthermore, its repurposing has been explored in fields as diverse as hematologic malignancies, diabetes-related complications, and preclinical psoriasis models, where it served as a dual inhibitor of NF-κB and the NLRP3 inflammasome (Irrera et al., 2017; Kolati et al., 2015). Despite this broad research history, BAY 11-7082 has not been previously tested explicitly in the context of dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or diseases with a similar pathology in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE). However, its known capacity to reduce inflammatory cytokine production and preserve lysosomal integrity in nonocular cell types provides a rationale for evaluating its potential utility in dry AMD—a disease characterized by chronic inflammation, impaired lysosomal clearance, and inflammasome activation (Blevins et al., 2022; Irrera et al., 2017; Marchetti, 2019).

Mechanism of Action:  
BAY 11-7082 exerts its pharmacological effects predominantly through irreversible covalent inhibition. Its most well‐characterized mechanism is the blockade of NF-κB signaling by preventing the phosphorylation of the inhibitory protein IκBα. Under normal conditions, phosphorylation of IκBα triggers its degradation, thus allowing NF-κB (typically the p65/p50 heterodimer) to translocate into the nucleus and activate pro-inflammatory target genes. By inhibiting IκBα phosphorylation, BAY 11-7082 effectively sequesters NF-κB in the cytosol, thereby suppressing the expression of genes associated with inflammation such as IL-1β, TNF-α, and various chemokines (Marchetti, 2019; Melisi & Chiao, 2007).  

Moreover, BAY 11-7082 has been repurposed based on its ability to inhibit the NLRP3 inflammasome. Mechanistically, the compound forms covalent adducts with reactive cysteine residues on the NLRP3 protein, most likely within the ATPase domain—an essential activity domain required for inflammasome activation. This alkylation event, which proceeds via a Michael-type addition reaction, results in irreversible inactivation of NLRP3’s ATPase function, thereby preventing the assembly and subsequent activation of the inflammasome complex (Cocco et al., 2014; Juliana et al., 2010; Marchetti, 2019). In addition to these primary actions, BAY 11-7082 has been reported to inhibit other cysteine-dependent enzymes such as protein tyrosine phosphatases and even components like gasdermin D that contribute to pyroptosis. Consequently, the compound displays a broad-spectrum inhibitory profile that may diminish inflammatory cascades not only at the transcriptional (NF-κB) level but also at the inflammasome activation stage (Yu et al., 2018; Zahid et al., 2019).  

Expected Effect in Dry Age-Related Macular Degeneration:  
In the context of dry AMD, the hypothesis is that chronic inflammation in the RPE drives cellular dysfunction through mechanisms that include sustained NF-κB activation and priming of the NLRP3 inflammasome. Inflammatory cytokines and resultant oxidative stress contribute to lysosomal impairment, reducing the activity of v-ATPase and lysosomal proteases such as cathepsin D (CTSD), which are crucial for the clearance of cellular debris. BAY 11-7082 is expected to intervene at an early stage in this inflammatory cascade by inhibiting NF-κB signaling. In doing so, it would reduce the transcriptional upregulation of inflammasome components and pro-inflammatory cytokines, particularly IL-1β, a key mediator in inflammasome activation (Blevins et al., 2022; Marchetti, 2019).  

Experimental studies in macrophages and psoriasis models have demonstrated that NF-κB inhibition with BAY 11-7082 leads to a reduction in IL-1β production and preserves lysosomal integrity. Although these studies were conducted in nonocular tissues, the expression of NF-κB and NLRP3 inflammasome components in RPE cells is well-documented in the literature. Therefore, it is reasonable to propose that BAY 11-7082, when applied to RPE cell models, could diminish the priming of the NLRP3 inflammasome. This reduction in inflammasome activity is expected to mitigate downstream lysosomal damage, preserve v-ATPase function, and maintain cathepsin D–mediated clearance. Ultimately, these cellular improvements could slow the degenerative progression characteristic of dry AMD (Cocco et al., 2014; Irrera et al., 2017).  

The proposed testing strategy leverages the rapid on–off pharmacology observed in cell culture models, facilitating dose optimization to achieve sufficient anti-inflammatory activity while minimizing potential toxicity. Importantly, targeting an upstream event, namely NF-κB activation and inflammasome priming, distinguishes BAY 11-7082 from therapeutic strategies that focus on downstream caspase inhibition. In retinal cells, preservation of lysosomal function is critical; thus, preventing inflammasome-triggered lysosomal rupture could have a marked protective effect on RPE health (Ajetunmobi et al., 2023; Zahid et al., 2019).

Overall Evaluation:  
BAY 11-7082 presents a compelling therapeutic candidate for dry AMD based on its dual mechanism of action. One of its primary strengths is that it targets two key upstream pathways—inhibition of NF-κB signaling and direct inactivation of the NLRP3 inflammasome—which are critically implicated in the inflammatory processes that drive RPE dysfunction and subsequent retinal degeneration in dry AMD. This upstream intervention could, in theory, reduce the chronic production of pro-inflammatory cytokines and prevent lysosomal abnormalities that compromise the clearance of metabolic waste in RPE cells. The promising preclinical data from psoriasis, diabetic nephropathy, and other inflammatory disease models provide an encouraging foundation regarding its anti-inflammatory capacity (Blevins et al., 2022; Irrera et al., 2017; Marchetti, 2019).

However, there are several potential weaknesses and challenges to consider. First, BAY 11-7082 operates via irreversible covalent binding through its Michael acceptor; while this can yield sustained inhibition, it also raises significant concerns regarding off-target effects and general toxicity due to the potential for nonselective alkylation of other cysteine-containing proteins. Such promiscuous reactivity has been observed in studies involving diverse cell types, and cellular toxicity in contexts such as platelets or myeloma cells has been reported, albeit at higher concentrations (Coles et al., 2021; Paul et al., 2017; Rauert-Wunderlich et al., 2013). Second, although extensive preclinical data exist demonstrating its anti-inflammatory and anti-cancer activity, BAY 11-7082 has not been previously evaluated in ocular tissues. The unique physiology of the eye, particularly the retinal pigment epithelium, could result in significantly different pharmacokinetics and tissue-specific toxicity profiles. The documented rapid on–off pharmacology in cell culture is encouraging, yet extrapolation to an in vivo retinal environment must be approached cautiously (Paul et al., 2017; Zahid et al., 2019).  

Another consideration is the narrow therapeutic window that may exist; while doses in animal models have been optimized for systemic inflammation or cancer, achieving effective local concentrations in the RPE without compromising cell viability is a delicate balance. Previous studies in nonocular systems suggest that BAY 11-7082 can function without overt toxicity at concentrations up to 20 μM in cell culture and 20 mg/kg/day in animal models, but whether similar dosing regimens would be applicable for ocular delivery remains to be determined (Mabuchi et al., 2004; Paul et al., 2017). Additionally, because BAY 11-7082 modulates ubiquitin system components beyond NF-κB and NLRP3 inflammasome targets, there is a risk of unintended interference with normal protein turnover and cellular homeostasis, potentially exacerbating cellular stress in a tissue already vulnerable to degenerative processes, as seen in dry AMD (Coles et al., 2021; Strickson et al., 2013).

In summary, BAY 11-7082 shows promise as a candidate repurposed for dry AMD because it strategically targets early inflammatory events that have been implicated in RPE dysfunction, including NF-κB–mediated inflammasome priming and consequent lysosomal impairment. The compound’s established anti-inflammatory effects in various preclinical models lend strong support to the hypothesis that its use in RPE could preserve lysosomal function and enhance CTSD-mediated clearance. Nonetheless, the inherent risks associated with its covalent, irreversible mechanism demand rigorous ocular-specific toxicity and pharmacokinetics investigations. If dose optimization and targeted delivery—perhaps through localized ocular formulations—can mitigate off-target effects, BAY 11-7082 might offer a novel approach that differentiates itself from therapies focused solely on downstream caspase inhibition. Overall, while the repurposing of BAY 11-7082 for dry AMD is mechanistically attractive and supported by a broad preclinical research history in nonocular inflammatory models (Blevins et al., 2022; Irrera et al., 2017; Marchetti, 2019), further dedicated studies in retinal cell models and in vivo ocular systems are essential to fully validate its potential and safety profile for this indication.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
NSC19723 is presented by the team as a custom-synthesized small-molecule enhancer of cathepsin D (CTSD) activity, hypothesized to bind the zymogen (pro-CTSD) and accelerate its maturation within retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) lysosomes to restore proteolysis and debris clearance in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD). No peer-reviewed publications or preprints describing NSC19723’s structure, discovery, selectivity, or in vivo performance are present in the provided literature corpus; accordingly, this evaluation treats NSC19723 as a theoretical representative of the drug class “CTSD activity enhancers” and assesses the therapeutic hypothesis against the current substrate-specific and disease-relevant CTSD/RPE biology (Ng et al., 2024; Sharif, 2015; Liu, 2021; Buniello et al., 2025).

The stated drug class is mechanistically distinct from upstream autophagy enhancers or lysosomal pH modulators: a CTSD activity enhancer would operate at the level of CTSD protein maturation/activity, ideally in acidic lysosomes, rather than by globally raising autophagic flux or indirectly modulating lysosomal acidification (Frost et al., 2014; Boya et al., 2023; Ng et al., 2024). CTSD itself is an aspartic endoprotease synthesized as a pre-proenzyme with an N-terminal signal peptide (for ER entry) and a propeptide region that supports folding and prevents premature activity; post-translational maturation occurs in late endosomes/lysosomes after mannose-6-phosphate (M6P)-mediated trafficking, where acidic pH supports autocatalysis and protease processing to the mature, active two-chain enzyme (Sharif, 2015). The RPE expresses CTSD at high levels, with evidence for enriched CTSD protein/activity in central/macular RPE relative to periphery, consistent with the macula’s heavy daily photoreceptor outer segment (POS) phagocytic load that relies on lysosomal proteolysis (Sharif, 2015; Pay, 2017). These features nominate CTSD as a plausible therapeutic target for restoring RPE degradative capacity; however, a specific CTSD maturation enhancer such as NSC19723 has not been characterized in the provided literature, so all compound-level conclusions must remain contingent on experimental validation (Ng et al., 2024; Buniello et al., 2025).

Therapeutic History  
No published biochemical, veterinary, or clinical use of NSC19723 is documented in the provided sources, and the name does not appear in the referenced literature; consequently, there are no prior data on this molecule in dry AMD or retinal disease within the provided corpus (Buniello et al., 2025). By contrast, there is considerable disease-relevant literature on CTSD biology in RPE and on pharmacological strategies that indirectly restore CTSD function by correcting upstream lysosomal defects. In patient-derived RPE from Stargardt disease (STGD1, ABCA4 mutations), lysosomal pH is elevated, CTSD accumulates in immature forms, and CTSD proteolytic activity is reduced; pharmacologic re-acidification of lysosomes (e.g., via P2Y₁₂ antagonism with ticagrelor) reverses these defects by lowering lysosomal pH, reducing the immature pro-CTSD pool, and restoring CTSD proteolytic activity and POS degradation in vitro and in vivo (RPE cells and Abca4−/− mice) (Ng et al., 2024). While STGD1 is not AMD, these data show that CTSD maturation/activity in human RPE is drug-modifiable and that improving CTSD function can improve degradative endpoints relevant to lipofuscin-associated disease biology, a pathophysiologic axis shared with dry AMD (Ng et al., 2024; Boya et al., 2023).

In the RPE/AMD literature, multiple lines of evidence support CTSD as a major lysosomal protease necessary for POS degradation and proteostasis. CTSD deficiency or pharmacologic inhibition impairs POS proteolysis, provokes accumulation of debris reminiscent of drusen, and is linked to retinal dysfunction in animal models, reinforcing its centrality to RPE homeostasis (Mahmud, 2019). Advanced glycation end-products (AGEs), which accumulate with age and in AMD, downregulate CTSD activity or expression in RPE and exacerbate lysosomal/autophagic failure and lipofuscin formation, further tying CTSD deficits to AMD-like phenotypes (Sharif, 2015; Mahmud, 2019). More broadly, lysosomal/autophagic insufficiency in RPE is mechanistically and pathologically linked to dry AMD: decreased degradative capacity leads to lipofuscin accumulation, lysosomal membrane permeabilization (LMP), DAMP release, inflammasome activation (e.g., NLRP3), and eventual RPE atrophy that drives photoreceptor degeneration; re-acidifying lysosomes and strengthening lysosomal function ameliorate several of these pathologies in vitro and in vivo (Choi, 2019; Frost et al., 2014; Boya et al., 2023).

A second therapeutic precedent relevant to “enhancing CTSD function” is enzyme augmentation. Recombinant pro-CTSD administration has been reported to correct proteolysis and autophagy defects in neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis (CLN10/CTSD deficiency), and intravitreal enzyme replacement strategies in other lysosomal storage diseases (e.g., TPP1 in CLN2) have preserved retinal structure/function in preclinical models, supporting feasibility of increasing lysosomal enzyme function in ocular tissues (Liu, 2021). These studies, while not in AMD and not small molecules, validate the general concept that augmenting CTSD can rescue lysosomal degradative failure in retina-derived tissues.

In summary, there is no therapeutic history for NSC19723 itself in the provided sources; however, there is an increasingly robust therapeutic precedent that pharmacological manipulation which restores CTSD maturation/activity in RPE improves degradative capacity and disease-relevant readouts in lipofuscin-accumulating retinal disorders, and that enzyme augmentation of lysosomal hydrolases can be effective in ocular degenerations driven by lysosomal insufficiency (Ng et al., 2024; Liu, 2021).

Mechanism of Action  
CTSD biosynthesis and maturation provide the mechanistic backdrop for a CTSD maturation enhancer. CTSD is synthesized as pre-procathepsin D with a signal peptide (for ER translocation) and a propeptide that maintains the zymogen in an inactive, folding-competent state; the protein acquires N-linked glycans and an M6P tag in the Golgi for M6P-receptor–mediated trafficking to late endosomes/lysosomes, where acidic pH facilitates removal of the propeptide, proteolytic processing, and generation of the mature, active enzyme (heavy and light chains) (Sharif, 2015). As an aspartic protease, CTSD employs two Asp residues to activate and position a water molecule for nucleophilic attack on the scissile peptide bond, a chemistry that requires acidic conditions for optimal catalysis; in neutral or alkaline environments, activity falls sharply, explaining why lysosomal alkalinization in disease states compromises both maturation and steady-state activity (Sharif, 2015; Ng et al., 2024).

In RPE disease models, immature and intermediate CTSD forms accumulate when lysosomal pH is elevated, and total CTSD protein may paradoxically rise even as proteolytic activity falls, illustrating a maturation bottleneck rather than a transcriptional deficit; pharmacological re-acidification reduces immature CTSD, increases the mature enzyme, and restores proteolytic activity in RPE (Ng et al., 2024). Functionally, impaired CTSD maturation/activity correlates with delayed degradation of internalized POS and accumulation of aggregation-prone substrates such as α-synuclein, consistent with CTSD’s principal role in RPE proteolysis of rhodopsin and POS proteins; CTSD is reported to account for the majority of rhodopsin degradation in RPE and exhibits far higher proteolytic activity than cathepsin B against POS substrates (Ng et al., 2024). The RPE’s reliance on phagolysosomal degradation of POS and basal autophagy for proteostasis means that even partial reductions in CTSD activity can precipitate progressive accumulation of lipofuscin-like material and lysosomal residual bodies, which in turn further impair lysosomes and create a feedback loop of increasing oxidative and inflammatory stress central to dry AMD pathophysiology (Choi, 2019; Frost et al., 2014; Sharif, 2015).

The proposed mechanism for NSC19723—direct binding to pro-CTSD to accelerate maturation—aligns with the above biology and would target the specific rate-limiting step observed in RPE lysosomes under stress: conversion of immature pro-CTSD to the mature, active enzyme in the acidic lumen. If achieved without broad, off-target activation of other proteases or perturbation of lysosomal pH/ion homeostasis, this mechanism would distinguish NSC19723 from autophagy inducers (e.g., rapamycin) or pH re-acidifiers (e.g., ticagrelor), while being convergent on the same functional outcome: restored CTSD proteolysis and lysosomal degradative capacity (Frost et al., 2014; Ng et al., 2024).

Mechanistic cross-talk and constraints that are relevant for a CTSD maturation enhancer include:  
- pH dependence: CTSD maturation and catalysis require acidic lysosomes; in alkaline lysosomes (e.g., due to bisretinoid accumulation), pro-CTSD processing is impaired even if total CTSD protein increases, so a maturation accelerator may be insufficient without concurrent restoration of lysosomal pH in some disease states (Ng et al., 2024).  
- Protease networks: While CTSD is an aspartic protease, lysosomal proteases co-regulate one another’s maturation and substrate turnover; for example, denatured cathepsin L can be a substrate for CTSD, and changes in cysteine cathepsins (B/L/S) alter autophagic flux and POS degradation, implying that selective enhancement of CTSD maturation must be interpreted in the context of broader protease network homeostasis (Mahmud, 2019; Sharif, 2015).  
- Endogenous inhibitors: Cystatin C potently inhibits cysteine cathepsins (B, H, L, S) and is abundant in RPE; although it does not inhibit CTSD (aspartic protease), changes in cystatin C with age and AMD suggest that protease–inhibitor balance in the lysosome and extracellular space is dynamic and may modulate the consequences of altering one protease’s activity (Myerscough, 2015; Sharif, 2015).  
- Lysosomal membrane integrity: LMP releases cathepsins to the cytosol, where they can trigger apoptosis/inflammation; any intervention that modifies lysosomal protease activity must be vetted for unintended effects on LMP susceptibility or cytosolic protease activity under stress (Boya et al., 2023; Mahmud, 2019).  
- Extracellular exposure: RPE can secrete cathepsins; most cathepsins are inactivated at neutral pH, but acidic niches or heparan/ECM interactions can stabilize activity, raising potential off-tissue effects if a compound perturbs trafficking/secretion (Sharif, 2015).

Collectively, the mechanistic plausibility that a small molecule could stabilize a conformation of pro-CTSD that accelerates propeptide removal and activation in acidic lysosomes is strong, and a favorable on-target pharmacodynamic effect can be anchored to clearly measurable, disease-relevant biochemical endpoints in RPE (Ng et al., 2024). The key risk is that without correction of lysosomal pH, pro-CTSD processing bottlenecks may persist; therefore, a CTSD maturation enhancer may be best deployed in lysosomes that are sufficiently acidic or in combination with pH-restoring strategies (Ng et al., 2024).

Expected Effect  
Dry AMD pathophysiology features RPE lysosomal-autophagic insufficiency leading to accumulation of POS-derived material, lipofuscin, and AGEs, heightened oxidative stress, inflammasome activation, and progressive RPE atrophy; restoring lysosomal proteolysis is predicted to mitigate these processes (Choi, 2019; Frost et al., 2014; Boya et al., 2023). In RPE, CTSD is a principal protease responsible for POS/rhodopsin degradation, and its activity declines with aging and under stressors relevant to AMD (AGEs, lipids/oxidation, lysosomal alkalinization), producing immature CTSD accumulation and reduced proteolytic capacity (Mahmud, 2019; Sharif, 2015; Ng et al., 2024). Therefore, a compound that accelerates pro-CTSD maturation to increase mature CTSD abundance/activity in acidic lysosomes is expected to:

- Increase CTSD catalytic activity in RPE lysosomes, measurable by fluorogenic substrate assays and activity-based probes, with corresponding decrease in immature/intermediate CTSD species and increase in mature, active CTSD on immunoblot and imaging (Ng et al., 2024).  
- Improve rate and completeness of POS degradation in RPE pulse–chase assays (e.g., rhodopsin clearance), reduce accumulation of lysosomal residual bodies, and decrease autofluorescent lipofuscin-like material formation in POS-challenged RPE under AGE/oxidative stress conditions (Ng et al., 2024; Frost et al., 2014; Sharif, 2015).  
- Reduce intracellular burden of aggregation-prone CTSD substrates (e.g., α-synuclein) and attenuate proteostasis stress, potentially normalizing vesicle trafficking defects tied to aggregate accumulation (Ng et al., 2024).  
- Rebalance autophagic flux by removing a degradative bottleneck at the lysosome, observable as improved degradation of autophagic cargo rather than simply altered LC3 abundance; careful flux assays with lysosome–autophagosome fusion inhibitors (e.g., bafilomycin A1) should be used for interpretation (Frost et al., 2014; Sharif, 2015).  
- Decrease downstream inflammatory signaling associated with lysosomal debris accumulation, including reduced NLRP3 inflammasome activation and cytokine release during chronic stress paradigms implicated in AMD pathogenesis (Choi, 2019; Boya et al., 2023).  
- With longer-term dosing, reduce subcellular and extracellular deposit biogenesis (lipofuscin, drusen-like material), preserve RPE morphology/mitochondrial health, and sustain photoreceptor function in models where lysosomal degradation is limiting, as seen when CTSD function is restored by lysosomal re-acidification (Boya et al., 2023; Ng et al., 2024).

The target is well expressed in the cell type of interest: CTSD is abundant in RPE, enriched in central/macular RPE, and directly linked to RPE’s POS degradation function; its activity is reduced by aging and AGE exposure, both highly relevant to dry AMD (Sharif, 2015; Pay, 2017; Mahmud, 2019). In lipofuscin-associated retinal disease models, restoring lysosomal acidity to rescue CTSD maturation/activity improved RPE degradative function and reduced pathological autofluorescence, underscoring the expected benefits of directly increasing CTSD maturation/activity via a selective small molecule (Ng et al., 2024).

Experimental considerations for robust readouts in RPE:  
- Biochemical: ratio of pro-/intermediate/mature CTSD by immunoblot in lysosomal fractions; CTSD activity in intact live cells and in isolated lysosomes at matched pH; selectivity profiling against other cathepsins (B/L/S) to confirm the putative specificity reported by the team; lysosomal pH measurements to control for off-target alkalinization/acidification effects (Ng et al., 2024; Sharif, 2015).  
- Functional degradative flux: POS pulse–chase assays (rhodopsin clearance kinetics), autophagy flux assays (LC3-II, p62/SQSTM1 degradation with and without bafilomycin A1), α-synuclein aggregation/clearance; quantify autofluorescence as a proxy for lipofuscin-like material (Ng et al., 2024; Frost et al., 2014; Sharif, 2015).  
- Cell health/inflammation: LMP susceptibility (galectin-3 puncta, cytosolic cathepsin immunostaining), NLRP3 inflammasome activation (caspase-1 activity), ROS and mitochondrial integrity (Boya et al., 2023; Choi, 2019).  
- Disease relevance: verify effects in hiPSC-RPE derived from dry AMD patients, which display altered lysosomal protease processing (e.g., immature CTSD increases under oxidative stress) and increased stress susceptibility; extend to macular-enriched RPE phenotypes given regional CTSD enrichment (Voisin et al., 2019; Sharif, 2015).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Strong target–disease mechanistic rationale: CTSD is the principal lysosomal protease for RPE POS protein degradation, with reported responsibility for the majority of rhodopsin proteolysis and markedly higher activity than cathepsin B; CTSD deficiency or inhibition impairs POS degradation and produces drusen-like debris, and genetic or pharmacologic CTSD impairment causes retinal dysfunction, aligning CTSD activation with a disease-modifying mechanism in dry AMD (Ng et al., 2024; Mahmud, 2019).  
- Convergent therapeutic precedent: Restoring lysosomal pH in patient-derived and mouse RPE models rescues CTSD maturation and activity, improves POS degradation, reduces lipofuscin-like autofluorescence, and protects photoreceptors, demonstrating that enhancing CTSD function is sufficient to improve disease-relevant outcomes in lipofuscin-associated retinal pathology (Ng et al., 2024).  
- Clear, measurable pharmacodynamic biomarkers: Mature CTSD abundance, CTSD activity, lysosomal pH, POS clearance, and lipofuscin/autofluorescence changes provide a rigorous framework for early de-risking of NSC19723 and for prioritizing compound optimization (Ng et al., 2024).  
- Disease context supports target engagement benefits: RPE lysosomal dysfunction, autophagy/heterophagy deficits, lipofuscin/AGE accumulation, inflammasome activation, and progressive atrophy are central features of dry AMD; a CTSD maturation enhancer directly addresses the degradative bottleneck at the lysosome (Choi, 2019; Frost et al., 2014; Boya et al., 2023).

Risks and gaps  
- Absence of public data on NSC19723: No structural, selectivity, potency, PK/PD, ocular disposition, or toxicology data are available in the provided corpus; thus, claims of pro-CTSD binding, selectivity for CTSD over other cathepsins, and in vivo rescue in CTSD-deficient retina remain unverified by the sources provided (Buniello et al., 2025). This is the major program risk at present.  
- Lysosomal pH constraint: If lysosomal alkalinization is a primary driver of immature CTSD accumulation (as in STGD1 and arguably in stressed AMD RPE), a maturation accelerator may not overcome the pH-dependent processing barrier; efficacy may require sufficient lysosomal acidity or combination with pH-restoring interventions (Ng et al., 2024).  
- Protease network and safety considerations: Enhancing lysosomal protease activity can exacerbate LMP-driven cytotoxicity under oxidative or lipofuscin stress; careful LMP and inflammasome assessments are required, alongside confirmation that NSC19723 does not perturb trafficking/secretion to increase extracellular protease activity where pH can be locally acidic (Boya et al., 2023; Sharif, 2015).  
- Disease heterogeneity and target linkage: Although CTSD biology is compelling in RPE and in lipofuscin-associated pathology, Open Targets curates only a low-confidence literature-based association between CTSD and AMD, reflecting limited direct genetic or clinical targeting data in AMD; translational success will depend on demonstrating benefit in dry AMD–relevant human RPE models and in vivo models that recapitulate AMD’s lysosomal/autophagic deficits (Buniello et al., 2025; Inana et al., 2018; Frost et al., 2014).  
- Off-target and network effects: Crosstalk between cathepsins (e.g., CTSD processing of denatured cathepsin L, altered cathepsin L/C3/NF-κB signaling), and modulation by AGEs/oxidative stress and endogenous inhibitors necessitate comprehensive off-target profiling and immune readouts to ensure that CTSD-specific maturation enhancement does not dysregulate broader proteostasis/inflammatory networks in RPE or at the RPE–Bruch’s membrane (BrM) interface (Sharif, 2015; Mahmud, 2019).

Program implications and recommended next steps  
Given the robust mechanistic case for CTSD restoration in RPE and the successful pharmacologic rescue of CTSD maturation/activity via lysosomal re-acidification in human patient–derived RPE, a selective CTSD maturation enhancer is a rational, high-potential approach for dry AMD—provided the compound is real, selective, and effective in acidic lysosomes (Ng et al., 2024). To advance NSC19723, the following de-risking package is critical:  

- Biochemical validation: Demonstrate pro-CTSD binding and acceleration of maturation at acidic pH using purified pro-CTSD and lysosomal-mimetic conditions; quantify catalytic activation and processing kinetics; confirm no activation or inhibition of cathepsins B/L/S and other lysosomal hydrolases (Sharif, 2015).  
- Cellular validation in RPE: In primary human RPE/hiPSC-RPE (including dry AMD lines), show increased mature CTSD and activity without altering lysosomal pH, improved POS degradation and reduced autofluorescence under chronic POS/AGE stress, restored clearance of α-synuclein aggregates, and normalization of autophagic flux using proper flux assays (Frost et al., 2014; Ng et al., 2024; Sharif, 2015).  
- Safety pharmacology in RPE: Demonstrate no increase in LMP susceptibility or NLRP3 activation under oxidative/bisretinoid stress; characterize secretion/trafficking effects and exclude extracellular protease activation under BrM-like conditions (Boya et al., 2023; Sharif, 2015).  
- In vivo proof of concept: In models featuring RPE lysosomal dysfunction and lipofuscin burden, measure retinal/RPE CTSD maturation/activity, RPE autofluorescence, drusen-like material, photoreceptor survival, and visual function; compare with or add to pH-reacidifying strategies (Ng et al., 2024).

Overall, while a CTSD maturation enhancer is scientifically well grounded for RPE-centered degenerations and could represent a differentiated, direct-restoration modality versus pH modulators or broad autophagy inducers, the current file lacks any external validation for NSC19723. Progressing NSC19723 is justified only with rapid, rigorous confirmation of selectivity, on-target activity in RPE lysosomes, and favorable safety in stressed RPE systems that model dry AMD’s lysosomal/autophagic failure (Frost et al., 2014; Boya et al., 2023; Choi, 2019).

In summary, the therapeutic concept—enhancing CTSD maturation/activity to restore RPE lysosomal proteolysis—has high mechanistic plausibility and encouraging precedent from pharmacologic re-acidification studies, but the specific candidate NSC19723 remains unsubstantiated in the provided literature and requires foundational biochemical and cellular validation to warrant preclinical development in dry AMD (Ng et al., 2024; Buniello et al., 2025).
