Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN) is an endogenous intermediate in the mammalian NAD⁺ salvage pathway, generated by nicotinamide phosphoribosyltransferase (NAMPT) from nicotinamide (NAM) and 5-phosphoribosyl‐1‐pyrophosphate (PRPP) and converted to NAD⁺ by nicotinamide mononucleotide adenylyltransferases (NMNAT1–3) (Jadeja et al., 2020; Cimaglia et al., 2020). NMN belongs to the vitamin B3–derived NAD⁺ precursor class and is one of several precursors (others include nicotinamide [NAM], nicotinic acid [NA], and nicotinamide riboside [NR]) used to augment cellular NAD⁺ pools in aging and disease (Cimaglia et al., 2020). NMN was prioritized as a practical intervention because direct NAD⁺ delivery to tissues is not straightforward, whereas in vivo administration of NMN elevates tissue NAD⁺ and supports mitochondrial function and cellular stress defenses in multiple systems (Ebeling et al., 2020; Rahman et al., 2024). Transport and uptake mechanisms include the Slc12a8 transporter described in mouse small intestine, as well as extracellular dephosphorylation to NR followed by NR uptake via equilibrative nucleoside transporters; intracellular NR is re‐phosphorylated by NRK1 to NMN for resynthesis of NAD⁺ (Will‐Orrego, 2020a; Rahman et al., 2024). Notably for RPE models, ARPE‐19 cells have been reported to express transporters supporting NMN uptake but not NR uptake, favoring NMN over NR in this system (Will‐Orrego, 2020b). In RPE and retinal contexts, NMN and related precursors have been deployed preclinically to restore NAD⁺, improve mitochondrial function, modulate sirtuin‐dependent pathways, and mitigate features of neurodegeneration and cellular senescence (Jadeja et al., 2018; Ebeling et al., 2020; Lin, 2020).

Therapeutic History  
NAD⁺ decline with age is conserved across tissues, including the retina and RPE, and is mechanistically linked to impaired mitochondrial function, heightened oxidative stress, and increased susceptibility to degeneration (Jadeja et al., 2018; Cimaglia et al., 2020). In the outer retina, rod‐ or cone‐specific Nampt deletion produces NAD⁺ deficiency and photoreceptor degeneration; systemic NMN at 150 mg/kg i.p. restored retinal function by ERG and preserved photoreceptor structure, establishing that exogenous NMN can replenish retinal NAD⁺ and mitigate degeneration linked to impaired salvage (Lin, 2020). NMN also protected in models of acute retinal injury: daily systemic NMN reduced photoreceptor death and oxidative stress after retinal detachment and increased retinal SIRT1 and HO‐1, consistent with NAD⁺‐dependent sirtuin activation in vivo (Chen et al., 2020). In ischemia models, NMN administration protected against retinal dysfunction (Lee et al., 2022; Lee et al., 2024). In a cholesterol efflux–deficient murine model that recapitulates key dry AMD features driven by senescent subretinal macrophages (Abca1/g1‐deficient), systemic NMN reduced subretinal drusenoid deposits (SDDs), decreased lipofuscin‐positive macrophage burden, and improved electrophysiological and structural endpoints, supporting a role for NAD⁺ augmentation in reversing senescence‐driven outer retinal pathology in vivo (Terao et al., 2024). In RPE‐directed models, pharmacologic NAMPT inhibition with FK866 is widely used to mimic age‐related NAD⁺ decline; in ARPE‐19 and primary RPE, NMN co‐treatment preserved NAD⁺, SIRT1 protein, viability, and reduced senescence markers, and in vivo systemic NMN preserved RPE NAD⁺ and SIRT1 after subretinal FK866 (Jadeja et al., 2018). Oxidant injury with sodium iodate (NaIO₃) induced RPE senescence, NAD⁺ depletion, mitochondrial dysfunction, and subretinal inflammation; NMN restored RPE NAD⁺, reduced DNA damage and senescence markers, improved mitochondrial membrane potential and ATP in ARPE‐19, and reduced inflammatory cell recruitment in vivo, with intact Sirt1 signaling required for NMN benefit (Ren et al., 2022). Outside strictly RPE biology, NMN improved RPE phagocytosis and mitochondrial ultrastructure in the RCS rat model of retinal degeneration, with a mechanistic link to a NAD⁺/GAPDH axis that modulated actin/cytoskeletal phagocytosis machinery in RPE; GAPDH knockdown abrogated NMN’s benefits, supporting a causal chain from NAD⁺ repletion to enhanced RPE POS clearance via GAPDH‐dependent pathways (Zhang et al., 2024).

Clinical translation of NAD⁺ precursors has begun with nicotinamide and NR in ophthalmology-adjacent indications (e.g., glaucoma), demonstrating tolerability and retinal functional protection in mice, and documenting NAD⁺ elevation in adult humans, but direct clinical data for NMN in dry AMD are not available in the provided context (Cimaglia et al., 2020; Rahman et al., 2024). Long-term NMN treatment in mice mitigated age-associated physiological decline systemically and reportedly ameliorated eye function, but detailed ocular pharmacology and human NMN ocular safety are not established here (Rahman et al., 2024). Collectively, the preclinical record supports NMN as an NAD⁺ augmenting therapy with demonstrated efficacy in retina and RPE-relevant models of NAD⁺ deficiency, oxidative injury, and senescence; however, there is no direct published clinical trial evidence in dry AMD patients in this context set (Jadeja et al., 2018; Lin, 2020; Chen et al., 2020; Terao et al., 2024).

Mechanism of Action  
Core biochemistry  
- NAD⁺ salvage. In mammalian cells, the salvage pathway supplies most NAD⁺ (~80%), with NAMPT catalyzing NAM → NMN and NMNAT1–3 completing NMN → NAD⁺; this pool fuels redox reactions and serves as substrate for NAD⁺‐consuming enzymes including sirtuins, PARPs, and the NAD glycohydrolase CD38 (Cimaglia et al., 2020; Jadeja et al., 2020). NAMPT-mediated biosynthesis is essential for vision, and its decline in RPE with age causally links to reduced NAD⁺, reduced SIRT1 expression/activity, and enhanced cellular senescence (Jadeja et al., 2018).  
- Uptake and intracellular handling. NMN can enter cells via specific transporters (Slc12a8 shown in mouse gut) and/or after extracellular dephosphorylation to NR with re-phosphorylation by NRK1, routes that are cell type–dependent; ARPE-19 preferentially transport NMN in vitro, supporting the choice of NMN over NR in these RPE models (Will‐Orrego, 2020a; Will‐Orrego, 2020b; Rahman et al., 2024).

Downstream signaling nodes relevant to RPE and dry AMD  
- Sirtuins. NAD⁺ is an obligate co-substrate for sirtuins; increased NAD⁺ drives sirtuin deacetylase/deacylase activities across SIRT1–7 with consequences for mitochondrial function, antioxidant defenses, DNA repair, and autophagy/mitophagy (Cimaglia et al., 2020). In aging RPE, NAD⁺ and SIRT1 decline in parallel; restoring NAD⁺ with NMN rescues SIRT1 protein and activity in vitro and in vivo, and reduces senescence markers p16^INK4a and p21^Waf/Cip1 (Jadeja et al., 2018). SIRT3, the mitochondrial sirtuin, maintains mitochondrial integrity by deacetylating and activating SOD2 and coordinating antioxidant responses, mitophagy, and UPR^mt; retinal NAD⁺ deficiency impairs SIRT3, linking NAD⁺ loss to mitochondrial vulnerability (Cimaglia et al., 2020; Lin, 2020). In a retinal detachment model, systemic NMN increased SIRT1 protein and HO‐1, with mechanistic in vitro data supporting a SIRT1 → HO‐1 protective axis (Chen et al., 2020).  
- AMPK and NAMPT/SIRT1 crosstalk. AMPK upregulates NAMPT expression and thus supports NAD⁺ salvage; reciprocally, SIRT1 deacetylates/stabilizes LKB1 to activate AMPK, forming a positive feedback loop that coordinates energy sensing and catabolic responses (Luján et al., 2022). In RPE senescence induced by NaIO₃, AMPK activation occurs downstream of ATP depletion and is modulated by NMN treatment, though overactivation of Sirt1 by a direct agonist (SRT1720) produced mitochondrial hyperfusion and stress signaling, arguing for physiological NAD⁺‐driven Sirt1 activation rather than pharmacologic overdrive (Ren et al., 2022).  
- Autophagy/mitophagy and mitochondrial biogenesis. SIRT1 promotes autophagosome formation and Rab7‐dependent autophagosome–lysosome fusion; together with AMPK, it enhances expression of mitophagy effectors (PINK1, Parkin) and co-activates PGC‐1α to drive mitochondrial biogenesis programs via transcriptional partners (NRF‐1, ERRα, PPARα) (Luján et al., 2022). Reviews and preclinical observations indicate that NAD⁺ repletion can restore mitophagy, activate UPR^mt, and normalize mitochondrial metabolic profiles, including evidence that “NAD⁺ inhibits the metabolic reprogramming of RPE cells in early AMD by upregulating mitophagy,” supporting the hypothesis that NMN-driven NAD⁺ gain could favorably reprogram RPE mitochondrial quality control (Rahman et al., 2024; Jadeja et al., 2020). In primary AMD donor RPE, NMN improved mitochondrial function in vitro; the same study used mitophagy reporter assays (mKeima-mito), underscoring the feasibility of measuring NMN’s effects on mitophagy in human RPE although specific NMN → mitophagy data were not detailed in the excerpt (Fisher et al., 2022; Ebeling et al., 2020).  
- PARP and CD38 as NAD⁺ sinks. DNA damage and SASP/inflammation drive PARP and CD38 activities that deplete NAD⁺; CD38 in particular contributes to age-related NAD⁺ decline and mitochondrial dysfunction and is induced by LXR signaling and SASP, creating a self-reinforcing senescence–NAD⁺ depletion loop (Cimaglia et al., 2020; Terao et al., 2024). In photoreceptor cells, PARP inhibition partially rescues viability under NAMPT inhibition, highlighting the vulnerability of NAD⁺ pools to consumption pathways and the value of reducing NAD⁺ sinks in parallel with NMN supplementation (Lin & Apte, 2018).  
- Inflammation and inflammasome. NAD⁺ augmentation via NMN or increased NAMPT/NAD⁺ can reduce NLRP3 inflammasome activation and downstream IL-1β/IL-18 via a SIRT1‐dependent mechanism in RPE aging models, pointing to anti‐inflammatory benefits of the NAMPT/NAD⁺/SIRT1 axis (Wu et al., 2021). In the Abca1/g1 macrophage senescence model of dry AMD, NAD⁺ repletion (NMN or CD38 inhibition) eliminated senescent macrophages and reversed drusenoid pathology and RPE functional deficits, extending the anti‐senescence and anti‐inflammatory reach of NAD⁺ augmentation to subretinal immune cells central to AMD pathobiology (Terao et al., 2024).

Critically, although TFEB (a master regulator of lysosomal biogenesis) and lysosomal proteases such as cathepsin D (CTSD) are highly relevant to RPE oxidative‐debris clearance in dry AMD, the provided literature does not demonstrate direct NMN‐induced TFEB activation, lysosomal acidification, or increased CTSD activity in RPE or retina; these remain plausible but unproven links in this context set (Falcão et al., 2025; Will‐Orrego, 2020a; Ebeling et al., 2020; Cimaglia et al., 2020).

Expected Effect  
Assay-level expectations in RPE models of dry AMD  
- NAD⁺ repletion in RPE. In ARPE‐19 and primary RPE, co‐treatment with NMN restores cellular NAD⁺ reduced by NAMPT inhibition, with partial to robust recovery depending on media and dosing; in ARPE‐19, FK866 sharply lowers NAD⁺/NADH and ATP, while NMN rescues both metrics and normalizes OXPHOS/glycolysis balance measured by Seahorse assays (Will‐Orrego, 2020b, 2020c). ARPE‐19 cells express NMN but not NR transporters, predicting superior uptake and intracellular conversion for NMN in this model (Will‐Orrego, 2020b). In NaIO₃‐stressed ARPE‐19, 800–1,000 µM NMN restored NAD⁺, mitochondrial membrane potential, and ATP, reduced ROS and DNA damage, and reduced senescence markers, with Sirt1 activity required for these benefits (Ren et al., 2022).  
- Sirtuin engagement. In FK866‐inhibited RPE, NMN co‐treatment restored SIRT1 protein and activity in vitro and in vivo; in photoreceptor injury, NMN increased retinal SIRT1 and induced HO-1, suggesting a SIRT1‐dependent antioxidant arm (Jadeja et al., 2018; Chen et al., 2020). In primary AMD donor RPE, NMN improved mitochondrial function, consistent with engagement of mitochondrial sirtuins and/or PGC-1α programs, though specific sirtuin readouts were not reported in that excerpt (Ebeling et al., 2020).  
- AMPK and mitophagy. AMPK will be sensitive to changes in ATP/AMP driven by mitochondrial recovery after NMN; in RPE senescence models, AMPK activation was observed under oxidant injury and modulated by NMN, and the NAD⁺/Sirt1/AMPK network is positioned to restore mitophagy via ULK1 activation, mTORC1 attenuation, and PINK1/Parkin induction (Ren et al., 2022; Luján et al., 2022). The hypothesis that NAD⁺ supplementation restores RPE metabolic dysfunction by inducing mitophagy is supported conceptually and by limited preclinical data cited for NAD⁺ effects on RPE mitophagy, making mitophagy flux (e.g., mKeima‐mito) a reasonable expected readout under NMN treatment (Jadeja et al., 2020; Fisher et al., 2022).  
- Autophagy-lysosome system and debris clearance. TFEB governs lysosomal biogenesis and function and is a rational target in dry AMD; Sirt1 and AMPK facilitate autophagosome formation and autophagosome–lysosome fusion (Rab7) and thus could secondarily enhance lysosomal throughput after NMN (Falcão et al., 2025; Luján et al., 2022). However, direct evidence that NMN increases lysosomal number, lysosomal acidification, TFEB nuclear translocation, or CTSD activity in RPE is not provided here; these are testable but as yet unvalidated expectations (Falcão et al., 2025; Will‐Orrego, 2020a). By contrast, NMN increased RPE phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments and restored actin‐mediated phagocytic machinery in vivo in the RCS rat, revealing a complementary route by which NMN could improve outer segment turnover independent of direct TFEB activation (Zhang et al., 2024).  
- Anti‐senescence and anti‐inflammatory effects. In RPE and subretinal myeloid cells, NMN suppresses senescence phenotypes and reduces inflammatory mediators, which should reduce SASP‐driven bystander stress on RPE and photoreceptors and may indirectly lower CD38‐mediated NAD⁺ depletion in the subretinal compartment (Jadeja et al., 2018; Terao et al., 2024).

Collectively, in an RPE assay aligned to dry AMD pathophysiology, NMN is expected to: (1) restore NAD⁺ and ATP; (2) engage Sirt1/Sirt3 and normalize mitochondrial function; (3) reduce senescence and inflammatory signaling; and (4) enhance POS phagocytosis via cytoskeletal machinery, with plausible but unproven enhancement of lysosomal biogenesis/function via Sirt1/AMPK-mediated autophagy pathways and TFEB cross-talk (Will‐Orrego, 2020b; Jadeja et al., 2018; Ren et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2025; Luján et al., 2022).

Assay design notes  
- Use ARPE‐19 and primary human RPE including AMD donor–derived cultures for translational relevance; confirm NMN uptake advantages versus NR in each model (Will‐Orrego, 2020b; Ebeling et al., 2020).  
- Quantify NAD⁺ by enzymatic assay, SIRT1 activity fluorometrically, mitochondrial ATP production via Seahorse ATP rate assay, and senescence markers (SA‐β‐gal, p16, p21) per established protocols (Jadeja et al., 2018; Will‐Orrego, 2020b).  
- Test TFEB nuclear translocation (immunocytochemistry), lysosomal mass (LAMP1/2), acidification (LysoSensor/LysoTracker), and cathepsin D maturation/activity explicitly, recognizing these endpoints are not yet shown for NMN in RPE (Falcão et al., 2025).  
- Assay mitophagy flux (mKeima‐mito), PINK1/Parkin expression, and autophagosome–lysosome fusion (LC3‐II, p62, Rab7 localization) (Fisher et al., 2022; Luján et al., 2022).  
- Measure RPE phagocytosis of POS and handling of phototoxic bisretinoids/lipofuscin surrogates to capture clearance outcomes (Zhang et al., 2024).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Strong disease‐mechanism alignment. Dry AMD is characterized by RPE mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, impaired autophagy/lysosomal clearance, and chronic para‐inflammation; age‐associated NAD⁺ decline in RPE and retina connects this pathobiology to a targetable metabolic axis (NAMPT/NAD⁺), and restoring NAD⁺ is causally protective in multiple retinal models (Jadeja et al., 2018; Cimaglia et al., 2020; Lin, 2020). In vitro and in vivo, NMN replenishes NAD⁺ in RPE and retina, rescues SIRT1 and mitochondrial function, and reduces senescence and inflammation—key drivers of RPE failure in dry AMD (Jadeja et al., 2018; Ren et al., 2022; Chen et al., 2020).  
- Direct RPE benefits with functional readouts. Under NAMPT inhibition and oxidant stress, NMN restores NAD⁺/ATP, normalizes OXPHOS/glycolysis, rescues RPE gene expression, lowers ROS and DNA damage, and blunts senescence markers; in RCS rats, NMN enhances RPE POS phagocytosis through a NAD⁺/GAPDH-actin axis (Will‐Orrego, 2020c; Ren et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2024).  
- Reversal of senescence-driven dry AMD phenotypes in vivo. In the Abca1/g1 model where subretinal macrophage senescence drives SDDs and RPE dysfunction, NAD⁺ augmentation by NMN reduces SDDs, lipofuscin‐positive macrophages, and functional/structural pathology, demonstrating disease‐relevant efficacy in a model that captures hallmark dry AMD features (Terao et al., 2024).  
- Mechanistic tractability and biomarkerability. The NAMPT/NMN → NAD⁺ → sirtuin/AMPK network is well studied and offers clear pharmacodynamic biomarkers (NAD⁺ levels, SIRT1 activity, mitochondrial respiration) and pathophysiological readouts (senescence markers, mitophagy flux), supporting a high‐confidence translational path (Jadeja et al., 2018; Luján et al., 2022; Ebeling et al., 2020).  
- RPE uptake feasibility. ARPE‐19 transport NMN but not NR, favoring NMN for in vitro RPE work; broader literature identifies NMN transport and NR conversion pathways that together ensure NMN bioavailability in ocular cell types (Will‐Orrego, 2020b, 2020a).

Limitations and risks  
- TFEB/lysosome claims remain unproven for NMN in RPE. While TFEB‐driven lysosomal biogenesis/function is a compelling therapeutic target in dry AMD, direct evidence that NMN activates TFEB, increases lysosomal number/acidification, or enhances cathepsin D activity in RPE is not present in the provided literature; these are critical, testable hypotheses that should not be presupposed in development plans (Falcão et al., 2025; Will‐Orrego, 2020a; Ebeling et al., 2020; Cimaglia et al., 2020).  
- Context‐dependent AMPK/Sirt1 dynamics. In NaIO₃‐induced RPE senescence, AMPK activation accompanied ATP loss and was suppressed upon NMN treatment; further, pharmacologic Sirt1 overactivation caused mitochondrial hyperfusion and stress signaling, underscoring that pathway set points matter and that NMN’s benefits likely hinge on physiologic tuning rather than maximal activation (Ren et al., 2022). This complexity argues for careful titration of NMN exposure and for avoiding assumptions about AMPK activation being uniformly beneficial in all RPE contexts.  
- Model caveats. ARPE‐19 harbor genomic abnormalities and do not recapitulate all RPE functions (e.g., missing RPE65), and media composition strongly modulates metabolic readouts; corroboration in primary human RPE (including AMD donors) and in vivo models is essential (Will‐Orrego, 2020c; Will‐Orrego, 2020b; Ebeling et al., 2020).  
- Target competition with NAD⁺ sinks. PARPs and CD38 can drain NAD⁺; in photoreceptors and macrophages these sinks materially influence disease, suggesting that combining NMN with PARP/CD38 modulation may be superior to NMN alone in some settings, and that patient subgroups with high NAD⁺ consumption (e.g., inflammatory phenotypes) may require tailored strategies (Lin & Apte, 2018; Terao et al., 2024).  
- Translation and clinical data gaps. Although nicotinamide and NR have human safety/PK data, direct human ocular PK/PD and safety data for NMN are limited here, and no clinical testing in dry AMD is documented in the provided sources (Cimaglia et al., 2020; Rahman et al., 2024). Dosing translation must reconcile effective rodent exposures (150–1,000 mg/kg/day in various models) with human tolerability and ocular exposure (Lin, 2020; Chen et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2024).

Program implications and next steps  
- Mechanistic validation in RPE. Prioritize experiments that directly test the unproven parts of the hypothesis: TFEB activation (nuclear translocation), lysosomal biogenesis (LAMP1/2), acidification (LysoSensor), and cathepsin D maturation/activity after NMN in primary human RPE from AMD and non‐AMD donors, and in iPSC‐RPE, with parallel readouts of NAD⁺, SIRT1, SIRT3, and AMPK (Falcão et al., 2025; Ebeling et al., 2020).  
- Mitochondria–lysosome crosstalk. Quantify mitophagy flux (mKeima‐mito), autophagosome–lysosome fusion (Rab7 co‐localization), and PINK1/Parkin dynamics under NMN, leveraging assays already applied in AMD donor RPE studies (Fisher et al., 2022; Luján et al., 2022).  
- Functional clearance endpoints. Test NMN effects on RPE POS phagocytosis, lipofuscin/bisretinoid handling, and oxidative debris clearance in vitro and in vivo, building on the strong RCS rat evidence for NMN‐mediated enhancement of RPE phagocytosis via a GAPDH‐actin mechanism (Zhang et al., 2024).  
- Inflammation and senescence. Extend evaluation to subretinal macrophage phenotypes and SASP factors in RPE–macrophage co‐culture and in vivo, given NMN’s ability to eliminate senescent macrophages and reverse SDDs in the Abca1/g1 model (Terao et al., 2024).  
- Dosing/PD strategy. Calibrate NMN dose–response carefully: in ARPE‐19 and primary RPE, co‐treatment with 0.05–1.0 mM NMN rescued FK866‐induced NAD⁺ loss within 72 h, while NMN alone did not elevate ATP above baseline; in NaIO₃ ARPE‐19, 800–1,000 µM was required to adequately restore NAD⁺ (Jadeja et al., 2018; Will‐Orrego, 2020b; Ren et al., 2022). In vivo, effective rodent doses ranged from 150 mg/kg i.p. to 1,000 mg/kg oral depending on model and endpoint (Lin, 2020; Zhang et al., 2024). Engage PK/PD modeling to bridge to human‐equivalent dosing and to support ocular exposure.  
- Combination hypotheses. Consider rational combinations with PARP inhibition (to reduce NAD⁺ consumption) or CD38 inhibition in inflammatory phenotypes, consistent with partial rescue by PARP inhibitors in NAMPT‐deficient contexts and CD38’s role in macrophage senescence (Lin & Apte, 2018; Terao et al., 2024). Also consider pairing with agents that more directly activate TFEB where justified, while monitoring for unintended mTORC1 perturbations (Falcão et al., 2025).

Conclusion  
NMN is a biologically credible and mechanistically tractable candidate for dry AMD focused on RPE rescue through NAD⁺ repletion and sirtuin‐centric mitochondrial restoration, with strong preclinical support in RPE senescence, oxidant injury, and phagocytosis assays, and compelling in vivo evidence in retinal injury and senescence‐driven dry‐AMD–like pathology (Jadeja et al., 2018; Ren et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2024; Terao et al., 2024). The hypothesized downstream impacts on TFEB, lysosomal biogenesis, acidification, and cathepsin D activity are plausible given the Sirt1/AMPK/autophagy network architecture but remain unvalidated in RPE after NMN and should be explicitly de‐risked experimentally before clinical translation (Falcão et al., 2025; Luján et al., 2022; Ebeling et al., 2020). Strengths include a coherent disease‐mechanism target, measurable PD, multi‐compartment benefits (RPE, photoreceptors, subretinal macrophages), and favorable uptake in RPE models; weaknesses include reliance on models with limitations, the need to control for NAD⁺ sinks and pathway set points, and gaps in lysosome‐specific mechanistic evidence and human ocular PK/PD (Will‐Orrego, 2020b, 2020c; Lin & Apte, 2018; Rahman et al., 2024). Overall, NMN merits advancement to a rigorous preclinical validation package focused on lysosome‐mitophagy endpoints in primary human RPE and AMD‐relevant in vivo models, with a translational plan that integrates mitochondrial function, senescence/inflammation control, and debris clearance readouts as co‐primary pharmacology objectives (Ebeling et al., 2020; Fisher et al., 2022; Terao et al., 2024).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Bexarotene, commercially known as Targretin and referenced here as Sigma B1269, is a fully synthetic rexinoid that was originally designed as a selective agonist for the retinoid X receptor (RXR). It is structurally distinct from naturally occurring retinoids such as 9‐cis‐retinoic acid; its chemical structure consists of a lipophilic tetramethyltetralin moiety connected through an ethynyl linker to a benzoic acid group, a design that confers high binding affinity (nanomolar EC50 values) and specificity for RXR subtypes (de Almeida & Conda‐Sheridan, 2019, pp. 8–9; Jurutka et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). As a member of the rexinoid class, bexarotene belongs to a group of therapeutic compounds that were developed to overcome the limitations of pan‐retinoid receptor activation by offering a more targeted means of modulating nuclear receptor signaling. RXRs have the unique ability to form either homodimers or heterodimers with a wide range of nuclear receptors—including peroxisome proliferator‐activated receptors (PPARs), liver X receptors (LXRs), thyroid hormone receptors (TRs), and vitamin D receptors (VDRs)—thereby influencing diverse gene expression programs that control cell growth, differentiation, and lipid metabolism (de Almeida & Conda‐Sheridan, 2019, pp. 8–9; Heck et al., 2016, pp. 1–2; Lalloyer et al., 2009, pp. 1–2). The synthetic origin of bexarotene, achieved through sophisticated organic synthesis that optimizes its lipophilic and acidic domains, enables it to engage conserved ligand‐binding residues (for example, key arginine and hydrophobic amino acids) in the RXR ligand‐binding domain, ensuring potent activation of the receptor (Chitranshi et al., 2019, p. 9; de Almeida & Conda‐Sheridan, 2019, pp. 11–13). This profile not only underlies its efficacy in its original oncologic indications but also supports its potential for repurposing in other diseases where RXR signaling is of therapeutic interest.

Therapeutic History:  
Bexarotene is well established in clinical practice as the first FDA-approved RXR-selective agonist, primarily indicated for the treatment of refractory cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (CTCL) in patients who have failed at least one systemic therapy (de Almeida & Conda‐Sheridan, 2019, pp. 8–9; Jurutka et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). Over the years, extensive clinical experience with bexarotene has been accrued in oncology, with studies demonstrating its capacity to induce cancer cell arrest, differentiation, and apoptosis by modulating the transcriptional landscape via RXR-mediated gene regulation (Heck et al., 2016, pp. 1–2, 9–10). Beyond its original role in oncology, bexarotene has been investigated in various other contexts; preclinical studies have explored its effects in non-small cell lung cancer, acute myeloid leukemia, and even in some hormone-sensitive malignancies—owing to its ability to interfere with proliferative signaling pathways (Marshall et al., 2015, pp. 2–3; Dheer et al., 2018, pp. 1–2). Notably, recent investigations have also assessed bexarotene in neurodegenerative disease models, particularly Alzheimer’s disease and Parkinson’s disease, where its RXR-mediated upregulation of apolipoprotein E (ApoE) and cholesterol transporters such as ABCA1 have been postulated to facilitate amyloid-beta clearance and neuronal protection (Marshall et al., 2015, pp. 2–3; Mallick et al., 2021, pp. 1–2). Although the compound has not been directly tested in clinical trials for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD), its mechanism of action—centered on modulating lipid metabolism and cellular clearance pathways—suggests that its repurposing for dry AMD is scientifically plausible, especially given the involvement of dysregulated lipid homeostasis and lysosomal dysfunction in this condition (Chitranshi et al., 2019, pp. 1–2; de Almeida & Conda‐Sheridan, 2019, pp. 8–9). Furthermore, RXR signaling is known to be critical in maintaining retinal homeostasis, and studies in animal models have shown that disruption of RXR function can lead to retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) abnormalities, providing an indirect rationale for evaluating RXR agonists like bexarotene in ocular applications (Chitranshi et al., 2019, pp. 1–2; Lalloyer et al., 2009, pp. 1–2).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, bexarotene exerts its effects by binding selectively to the ligand-binding domain of RXRs with high affinity, thereby promoting conformational changes that favor the release of co-repressor proteins and the recruitment of co-activators containing LxxLL motifs. This binding event induces RXR to function either as a homodimer or, more importantly, as a heterodimer with other nuclear receptors such as LXR and PPAR, which are central to the regulation of lipid homeostasis and inflammatory responses (de Almeida & Conda‐Sheridan, 2019, pp. 8–9; Marshall et al., 2015, pp. 2–3). In its role as an RXR agonist, bexarotene has been shown to markedly upregulate the transcription of genes involved in cholesterol efflux, including those coding for ATP-binding cassette transporters like ABCA1 and for apolipoproteins such as ApoE; these factors are critical for mobilizing and clearing excess cholesterol in various tissues (Marshall et al., 2015, pp. 2–3; Mallick et al., 2021, pp. 2–3). Furthermore, RXR agonism by bexarotene can stimulate the activity of permissive heterodimers—such as RXR/PPARα—which are known to play pivotal roles in fatty acid oxidation and energy metabolism. This activation is hypothesized to extend to downstream transcriptional regulators like TFEB, the master regulator of lysosomal biogenesis, though direct evidence in retinal cells is still emerging (Marshall et al., 2015, pp. 2–3; Dheer et al., 2018, pp. 1–2). In several preclinical models, bexarotene has been associated with the modulation of lysosomal pathways; for instance, it can alleviate endoplasmic reticulum stress and prevent the activation of pro-apoptotic proteins, which are important contributors to intracellular lipid accumulation and cellular dysfunction (Farol & Hymes, 2004, pp. 1–2; Lalloyer et al., 2009, pp. 1–2). Moreover, its selective RXR activity circumvents the adverse effects associated with pan-retinoid receptor activation, particularly the hypercalcemic and other toxicities seen with non-selective retinoids, by limiting cross-reactivity with RARs (Jurutka et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Mallick et al., 2021, pp. 2–3). In summary, bexarotene’s multifaceted mechanism includes (1) robust activation of RXR-mediated transcription of lipid transporter genes, (2) modulation of heterodimer partners such as PPARα and LXR that indirectly regulate lipid metabolism and energy balance, and (3) potential upregulation of lysosomal biogenesis and function via TFEB-associated pathways—collectively contributing to improved cellular lipid clearance and metabolic homeostasis (Marshall et al., 2015, pp. 2–3; Mallick et al., 2021, pp. 1–2; Heck et al., 2016, pp. 7–9).

Expected Effect in Dry Age-related Macular Degeneration:  
The central hypothesis driving the evaluation of bexarotene for dry AMD posits that activation of RXR in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells will lead to beneficial metabolic remodeling, specifically through enhancing cholesterol efflux and promoting lysosomal function. In the context of dry AMD, pathologic drusen formation is largely a consequence of chronic accumulation of lipids and misprocessed extracellular debris under the RPE. Through the activation of RXR, bexarotene is expected to upregulate key mediators of cholesterol transport such as ABCA1 and ApoE, thereby facilitating the removal of excess cholesterol and lipid deposits from the RPE (Marshall et al., 2015, pp. 2–3; Chitranshi et al., 2019, pp. 1–2). In addition, RXR activation, particularly when partnered with PPARα, has been associated with the induction of a lysosomal program that involves enhanced expression of genes regulating lysosomal acidification—potentially via the upregulation of vacuolar ATPase (V-ATPase) subunits—and the activation of lysosomal enzymes such as cathepsin D (CTSD) (Marshall et al., 2015, pp. 2–3; Mallick et al., 2021, pp. 2–3). Although direct demonstrations of TFEB activation in RPE models with bexarotene treatment are limited in the provided literature, the established role of RXR agonists in modulating lipid-rich, lysosomal compartments in other cell types supports the likelihood that a similar upregulation would occur in RPE cells (Marshall et al., 2015, pp. 2–3; Dheer et al., 2018, pp. 1–2). Given that TFEB is a master regulator of lysosomal biogenesis and function, its coactivation alongside PPARα could enhance the degradative capacity of the cell, resulting in improved clearance of drusen-associated lipid aggregates. This dual action—promoting cholesterol efflux while simultaneously enhancing lysosomal catabolism—addresses two of the key pathogenic mechanisms underlying dry AMD (Marshall et al., 2015, pp. 2–3; Mallick et al., 2021, pp. 1–2). In vitro, one might anticipate that bexarotene treatment of cultured RPE cells will lead to increased transcript and protein levels of ABC transporters, elevated markers of lysosomal acidification such as V-ATPase subunits, and enhanced activity of cathepsin D, collectively contributing to the reduction of lipid overload at a cellular level (Marshall et al., 2015, pp. 2–3; de Almeida & Conda‐Sheridan, 2019, pp. 8–9). Moreover, given its extensive clinical use in oncology with a tolerable ocular safety profile, bexarotene is well situated for repurposing, provided that its systemic adverse effects (e.g., hyperlipidemia, hypothyroidism) can be managed or mitigated through controlled dosing strategies or targeted delivery approaches (de Almeida & Conda‐Sheridan, 2019, pp. 8–9; Marshall et al., 2015, pp. 2–3).

Overall Evaluation:  
Bexarotene emerges as a promising therapeutic candidate for dry AMD based on its well-characterized pharmacological profile and multifaceted mechanism of action. One of its primary strengths lies in its selective activation of RXR, which has been shown to trigger transcriptional programs that enhance cholesterol efflux via the upregulation of key transporters such as ABCA1 and ApoE—pathways that are directly relevant to the clearance of drusen-associated lipids in dry AMD (Marshall et al., 2015, pp. 2–3; Mallick et al., 2021, pp. 1–2). In addition, the potential for RXR agonism to engage PPARα and, by extension, coactivate TFEB offers a novel approach to correcting lysosomal dysfunction—a critical factor in the pathogenesis of dry AMD. This dual action addresses both the extracellular accumulation of lipids and the intracellular deficits in degradative capacity that contribute to RPE dysfunction. The extensive clinical experience with bexarotene in cancer therapy provides an added advantage, as its pharmacokinetics, dosing regimens, and safety profiles are well documented, thereby facilitating a more rapid transition into repurposing studies. However, several challenges and weaknesses need to be acknowledged. Bexarotene is known to cause significant metabolic side effects, including hyperlipidemia and hypothyroidism, which may necessitate adjunctive treatments (such as lipid-lowering agents) or the development of targeted ocular delivery systems to minimize systemic exposure (de Almeida & Conda‐Sheridan, 2019, pp. 8–9; Mallick et al., 2021, pp. 2–3). Furthermore, although preclinical data in neurodegenerative models have demonstrated beneficial effects on lipid metabolism and lysosomal pathways, direct evidence in retinal pigment epithelial models is still limited. This gap underscores the need for rigorous in vitro and in vivo studies specifically designed to evaluate bexarotene’s efficacy in RPE cells and animal models of dry AMD (Chitranshi et al., 2019, pp. 1–2; Lalloyer et al., 2009, pp. 1–2). Another potential risk involves the compound’s polypharmacological nature; while its ability to interact with multiple nuclear receptors can be advantageous for targeting complex diseases, it also raises the possibility of off-target effects, such as its documented antagonism at PPARγ in certain contexts, which could have unforeseen impacts on retinal cell physiology (Marciano et al., 2015, pp. 1–2; Heck et al., 2016, pp. 7–9). The balance between therapeutic benefits and adverse effects will need to be carefully managed, perhaps by optimizing dosing regimens or by designing analogues with improved selectivity and reduced side effect profiles. In summary, the repurposing of bexarotene for dry AMD is supported by its robust activation of RXR-driven pathways related to lipid efflux and lysosomal function, as well as by its safe clinical history in ocular settings when used topically or in controlled systemic regimens. Nonetheless, additional preclinical work is essential to directly demonstrate its efficacy in RPE models and to delineate any ocular-specific pharmacodynamic parameters. Overall, the candidate shows promise as a multi‐pathway therapeutic approach for dry AMD, with strengths including its defined mechanism of action and extensive clinical history, and weaknesses largely centered on potential systemic side effects and the need for targeted delivery strategies (de Almeida & Conda‐Sheridan, 2019, pp. 8–9; Marshall et al., 2015, pp. 2–3; Chitranshi et al., 2019, pp. 1–2; Mallick et al., 2021, pp. 1–2; Marciano et al., 2015, pp. 1–2).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Torin1 is a synthetic small‐molecule that belongs to the second‐generation, ATP‐competitive class of mTOR inhibitors, originally derived from a quinoline‐based scaffold. Its discovery originated from a high‐throughput compound library screen that identified quinolone hits with moderate mTOR activity, which were then optimized through iterative medicinal chemistry by introducing a six‐membered lactam to convert the initial quinolone into a tricyclic benzonaphthridinone scaffold (Guillem, 2015). This chemical modification yielded a molecule with exceptional biochemical potency—capable of inhibiting both mTOR complexes, mTORC1 and mTORC2, at very low (nanomolar to picomolar) concentrations—and with approximately 1000-fold improvement in cellular potency relative to the initial hits (Guillem, 2015). As an ATP-competitive inhibitor, Torin1 binds directly to the active (ATP-binding) site of mTOR, thereby circumventing the partial inhibition that is observed with first-generation mTOR inhibitors like rapamycin that act allosterically by binding FKBP12 (Liu et al., 2012). Torin1 has been widely used as a research tool to interrogate mTOR signaling in various cellular contexts, and its chemical lineage as a quinoline-derived molecule positions it within a well-characterized class of inhibitors that have been instrumental in expanding our understanding of mTOR-dependent regulation of autophagy and cellular metabolism (Liu et al., 2012).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, Torin1 has been employed predominantly as a research tool rather than as a clinical drug candidate. Extensive preclinical studies have demonstrated its robust ability to inhibit mTOR signaling in cancer models, autophagy-deficient systems, and metabolic studies. For instance, Torin1 was shown to potently inhibit mTOR signaling pathways in glioblastoma and prostate cancer cells, significantly reducing cell-cycle progression and inducing apoptosis in certain contexts (Gu, 2017; Liu et al., 2012). Its use as an autophagy inducer is well documented, as experiments utilizing Torin1 have demonstrated increased autophagic flux and elevated lysosomal activity in multiple cell lines (Li, 2018; Liu et al., 2012). Importantly, Torin1 is also used in studies with retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells, as evidenced by its ability to increase TFEB-driven luciferase reporter activity in ARPE-19 cells by effectively suppressing mTORC1 signaling (Huang et al., 2018). Despite these promising experimental findings, Torin1 has not advanced to clinical trials for any indication, including neurodegenerative disorders or dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD). Moreover, its intrinsic pharmacokinetic limitations—such as poor aqueous solubility, a short half-life, and low oral bioavailability—have been recognized in several studies, thereby limiting its potential as a direct therapeutic candidate without further structural optimization (Guillem, 2015; Wang et al., 2022).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, Torin1 functions by competing with ATP for binding to the catalytic domain of mTOR, effectively blocking the phosphorylation of downstream substrates. Its ATP-competitive nature allows Torin1 to inhibit both mTORC1 and mTORC2 complexes, thereby offering a broader inhibition profile than allosteric agents like rapamycin that primarily target mTORC1 (Guillem, 2015; Liu et al., 2012). Detailed molecular modeling and structure–activity relationship studies indicate that the tricyclic benzonaphthridinone core of Torin1 forms critical hinge-binding interactions with residues in the mTOR kinase domain (Liu et al., 2012). This interaction accounts for its high potency, as reflected in low nanomolar IC₅₀ values in cellular assays (Liu et al., 2012; Gros & Muller, 2014). Torin1 induces rapid dephosphorylation of canonical mTORC1 substrates, such as S6 kinase at Thr389 and 4E-BP1 at Thr37/46, which results in downregulation of protein synthesis and cellular growth signals (Misra & Pizzo, 2013). Moreover, by simultaneously inhibiting mTORC2, it reduces phosphorylation of Akt at Ser473—a site critical for full Akt activation—thus attenuating the feedback loops that typically reinvigorate upstream PI3K signaling in response to mTORC1 inhibition (Gu, 2017; Martina et al., 2014). A particularly notable feature of Torin1 is its slow off-rate, which leads to sustained inhibition of mTOR activity even after drug washout, a pharmacodynamic property that may confer prolonged downstream effects such as enhanced autophagic flux (Liu et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2013). The inhibition of mTOR by Torin1 correlates with dephosphorylation of transcription factors, particularly TFEB and TFE3; under normal nutrient-replete conditions, mTORC1 phosphorylates TFEB (e.g., on S211 in TFEB) and TFE3, sequestering them in the cytosol through binding with 14-3-3 proteins (Huang et al., 2018; Martina et al., 2014). Upon mTOR inhibition by Torin1, TFEB is dephosphorylated and translocates to the nucleus, where it induces the transcription of CLEAR (Coordinated Lysosomal Expression and Regulation) network genes that drive lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy (Li, 2018; Liu et al., 2013). This precise modulation of mTOR signaling and subsequent transcriptional reprogramming forms the biochemical basis for leveraging Torin1 as a candidate to ameliorate lysosomal clearance defects.

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis for repurposing Torin1 in the context of dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is that potent inhibition of mTORC1/2 in RPE cells can lift the repressive phosphorylation that normally limits the activity of TFEB and TFE3. In RPE cells, as demonstrated by studies in ARPE-19 cell models, mTOR inhibition via Torin1 not only leads to decreased phosphorylation of S6 kinase but also results in marked activation of TFEB-driven transcription (Huang et al., 2018). When TFEB translocates to the nucleus, it binds to CLEAR elements present in the promoters of genes responsible for lysosomal biogenesis, acidification (through the upregulation of V-ATPase subunits), and the maturation and activity of lysosomal enzymes such as cathepsin D (CTSD) (Huang et al., 2018; Li, 2018). In dry AMD, RPE cells exhibit a decline in lysosomal function along with accumulation of cellular debris and lipofuscin, which contribute to disease pathology. By inducing a robust CLEAR response, Torin1 is expected to restore lysosomal function through increased biogenesis, enhanced acidification, and elevated cathepsin D activity, thereby improving the clearance of toxic aggregates in RPE cells and ultimately mitigating the progression of dry AMD (Gu, 2017; Huang et al., 2018). Additionally, the sustained target engagement afforded by Torin1’s slow off-rate may provide prolonged therapeutic benefit even with intermittent dosing, an attractive feature given the chronic nature of AMD (Liu et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2013). Recent evidence from preclinical iPSC models and autophagy-deficiency studies underscores the potential translation of mTOR-targeted strategies in restoring cellular homeostasis in degenerative diseases, lending further credence to this expected mechanism (Guillem, 2015).

Overall Evaluation:  
In summary, Torin1 possesses a compelling mechanistic profile that aligns well with the therapeutic needs of dry AMD by targeting a fundamental pathway governing cellular homeostasis in RPE cells. Its origin from a quinoline-based scaffold and subsequent chemical optimization into a highly potent ATP-competitive mTOR inhibitor underline its status as a valuable chemical probe in preclinical settings (Guillem, 2015). The dual inhibition of both mTORC1 and mTORC2 by Torin1, combined with its slow off-rate and sustained downstream effects—including dephosphorylation and nuclear translocation of TFEB/TFE3—make it an ideal tool for inducing lysosomal biogenesis and enhancing autophagic clearance (Martina et al., 2014; Huang et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2012). In cellular models, including ARPE-19 RPE cells, Torin1 has already demonstrated the ability to activate TFEB and upregulate CLEAR gene expression, which is directly relevant to counteracting the lysosomal clearance defects observed in dry AMD (Huang et al., 2018; Li, 2018).

However, significant challenges remain regarding the translational applicability of Torin1 as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. Its reported poor aqueous solubility, short half-life, and low oral bioavailability present formidable barriers to clinical development unless addressed through formulation improvements or further medicinal chemistry optimization (Guillem, 2015; Wang et al., 2022). Moreover, while extensive preclinical literature supports its role as a robust mTOR inhibitor in cancer and autophagy research, there is a lack of direct in vivo evidence for its efficacy in ocular models, particularly in dry AMD or geographic atrophy (GA) mouse lines (Liu et al., 2013; Gu, 2017). Careful dosing will also be critical, as the broad and potent inhibition of mTOR can have unintended effects on cellular metabolism and protein synthesis beyond the intended enhancement of lysosomal function. Additionally, off-target effects have been observed in some biochemical screens at supraphysiologic concentrations, including binding to other PIKK family members such as ATR, ATM, and DNA-PK, although these are generally not manifested at the low nanomolar concentrations used in cellular assays (Settembre et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2012).

From the perspective of repurposing for dry AMD, Torin1’s deep mechanistic specificity is a double-edged sword: it offers a highly defined and robust approach to upregulating lysosomal biogenesis via the TFEB/TFE3 axis, yet its pharmacokinetic liabilities and the absence of any clinical history in ocular disease necessitate additional work. The promising in vitro data in RPE models (ARPE-19 cells) and iPSC-derived RPE systems provide valuable target validation, but before advancing to clinical trials a refined analog or an optimized delivery method (for example, local ocular administration to bypass systemic bioavailability issues) should be considered (Huang et al., 2018; Li, 2018; Wang et al., 2022).

In summary, Torin1 is an excellent candidate for preclinical proof-of-concept studies to validate mTOR inhibition as a strategy to combat lysosomal dysfunction in dry AMD; however, further optimization to improve its stability and bioavailability, alongside rigorous in vivo testing in relevant AMD models, will be essential prior to clinical development (Guillem, 2015; Gu, 2017). The strengths of Torin1 lie in its potent, dual mTOR inhibition and its ability to robustly induce TFEB activation, whereas its weaknesses center on its pharmacokinetic shortcomings and the current lack of efficacy data in ocular disease models. Overall, with focused optimization and targeted delivery strategies, Torin1 or its derivatives may offer a promising therapeutic avenue for ameliorating the lysosomal clearance defects that underlie dry AMD pathology (Liu et al., 2012; Huang et al., 2018).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Tocilizumab (Actemra; Roche/Chugai) is a recombinant humanized monoclonal antibody that binds the human interleukin-6 receptor (IL-6R) and blocks IL-6 signal transduction, resulting in systemic anti-inflammatory effects characteristic of IL-6 pathway inhibition (class: humanized anti-IL-6R monoclonal antibody) (Shi, 2017a; Shi, 2017b; Zhujiang Hospital, 2025). In clinical development, tocilizumab has been administered intravenously at 8 mg/kg every 4 weeks and subcutaneously at 162 mg once weekly, with protocols reflecting the infectious, hepatic, hematologic, gastrointestinal, and reproductive safety considerations common to cytokine-targeted biologics (e.g., TB/hepatitis screening, neutrophil/platelet and transaminase thresholds, live-vaccine restrictions, diverticulitis history, and contraception requirements) (Shi, 2017b; University of Nebraska, 2016; Assistance Publique–Hôpitaux de Paris, 2017; Zhujiang Hospital, 2025). Ophthalmic interest in IL-6 blockade is evidenced by prospective trials in non-infectious uveitis and a withdrawn diabetic macular edema (DME) trial; those records establish feasible dosing, ophthalmic outcome collection, and safety oversight but do not provide efficacy data in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (Assistance Publique–Hôpitaux de Paris, 2017; University of Nebraska, 2016). At the disease-biology level, multiple clinical and literature-derived evidences associate IL-6 with AMD, including elevated ocular and systemic IL-6 in AMD populations and genetic associations in some cohorts; Open Targets ranks IL6 as the strongest among selected IL-6 pathway members for AMD relevance in the provided excerpt (Buniello et al., 2025).

Therapeutic History  
Systemic uses and ophthalmic experience: Tocilizumab’s IL-6R blockade is well characterized clinically outside ophthalmology, and controlled ophthalmic trials have evaluated systemic tocilizumab as an investigational agent for posterior-segment, non-infectious uveitis (RUBI), using subcutaneous 162 mg weekly for 16 weeks with retinal structural and visual endpoints and active safety monitoring; the study is listed as completed in the registry excerpt but outcome data are not included here (Assistance Publique–Hôpitaux de Paris, 2017). A single-center, open-label Behçet’s uveitis trial planned to assess 6 months of tocilizumab while maintaining background immunosuppression, but it enrolled only three participants and was terminated early based on its measured outcomes, limiting inferences on efficacy; this protocol reiterates standard immunosuppression-related exclusions (active TB/hepatitis, malignancy, pregnancy) (Zheng, 2018). In DME, the READ-4 protocol designed a Phase 2 evaluation of monthly IV tocilizumab (8 mg/kg) alone or combined with monthly intravitreal ranibizumab through Month 6, with safety and OCT central retinal thickness as primary outcomes; the trial was withdrawn before enrollment due to loss of funding, yielding no clinical data (University of Nebraska, 2016). A registry query identified 10 ClinicalTrials.gov records linking “tocilizumab” with retina/macular degeneration terms, but no identifiers or results are available in the excerpt to inform AMD-specific evidence (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.). Beyond retinal disease, randomized and single-arm neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (NMOSD) studies used IV tocilizumab 8 mg/kg every 4 weeks (or every 4–6 weeks) and incorporated ocular structural and visual function endpoints among secondaries; these trials demonstrate feasibility of systemic dosing with ophthalmic measurements but are mechanistically distinct from retinal degenerations such as dry AMD (Shi, 2017b; Shi, 2017a). Collectively, the corpus establishes operational feasibility and safety monitoring frameworks for systemic tocilizumab in ophthalmic settings but contains no clinical evidence in dry AMD (University of Nebraska, 2016; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).

Mechanism of Action  
Drug mechanism: Tocilizumab is a humanized monoclonal antibody that binds to IL-6R and blocks IL-6 signaling, thereby attenuating inflammatory pathways downstream of IL-6R engagement; mechanistic rationales in non-retinal disease emphasize IL-6–dependent survival and differentiation programs (e.g., plasma cells and autoantibody production in NMOSD), with dosing typically at 8 mg/kg IV every 4 weeks or 162 mg SC weekly in the studies cited (Shi, 2017a; Shi, 2017b; Assistance Publique–Hôpitaux de Paris, 2017).

Retinal IL-6 biology and RPE sources/targets: Multiple lines of evidence link IL-6 to AMD: clinical reports of elevated serum and ocular IL-6 in AMD versus controls, genetic association signals in some cohorts, and IL-6’s role in inflammation and neovascularization in advanced disease; Open Targets assigns IL6 the strongest association among queried IL-6 pathway components in the excerpt, while evidence for STAT3 and IL6ST is comparatively weak (Buniello et al., 2025). Human retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells produce IL-6, secrete it in a polarized manner, and can engage autocrine/paracrine IL-6/IL-8 loops that drive RPE degeneration after inflammatory challenge (e.g., bacterial endotoxin), supporting the presence of IL-6–responsive circuits in retinal epithelia (Brandstetter, 2016).

AMD-relevant upstream injury nodes: The dominant mechanistic framework for dry AMD implicates chronic oxidative/photooxidative stress, age-related lysosomal decline, and intracellular clearance failure (autophagy/proteasome) in RPE, leading to lipofuscinogenesis, lysosomal membrane permeabilization (LMP), and activation of inflammasome pathways with downstream cytokine release and cell death (apoptosis vs pyroptosis depending on priming) (Brandstetter, 2016; Piippo, 2019). In primary human RPE and ARPE-19 cells, LMP induced chemically (Leu-Leu-OMe) or via blue-light irradiation of POS-derived lipofuscin activates the NLRP3 inflammasome with caspase-1–dependent maturation and release of IL-1β and IL-18; broader cytokine secretion includes IL-6, GM-CSF, and GRO, with IL-6 elevated ≈13.6-fold in a cytokine screen and partially suppressed by caspase-1 inhibition, indicating a secondary induction downstream of inflammasome activation (not direct inflammasome processing) (Brandstetter, 2016). Cytokine release is apically polarized, and conditioned media from inflammasome-activated RPE is chemotactic for microglia, linking RPE lysosomal injury to neuroretinal immune activation (Brandstetter, 2016). Complement C5a serves as a physiologically relevant priming agent in RPE by activating NF-κB and inducing pro-IL-1β, which permits subsequent LMP-triggered NLRP3 activation; C5a priming and IL-1α priming also shift cell death from apoptosis to pyroptosis after lipofuscin phototoxicity (Brandstetter, 2016). Lysosomal proteases are mechanistically implicated: inhibition of cathepsin B and L suppresses LMP-triggered inflammasome activation in RPE, and cytosolic cathepsins in general, including cathepsin D, can promote apoptosis when released from the lysosome, underscoring the importance of lysosomal integrity in RPE survival (Brandstetter, 2016).

Intracellular clearance failure and mitochondrial stress as alternative inflammasome drivers: Independent RPE models that combine proteasome inhibition (MG-132) with autophagy/lysosome blockade (bafilomycin A₁) activate NLRP3 via oxidative stress, producing caspase-1–dependent IL-1β secretion without evidence that lysosomal rupture/cathepsin leakage is the primary driver; Hsp90 stabilizes NLRP3 in this setting, and Hsp90 inhibition promotes autophagic degradation of NLRP3 when autophagy remains functional (Piippo, 2019). Mitochondrial dysfunction induced by antimycin A activates both NLRP3 and AIM2 inflammasomes in human RPE lines via mitochondrial ROS and cytosolic DNA, with AIM2 showing dominant control of IL-1β/IL-18 in some contexts, broadening the repertoire of upstream hazards beyond lysosomal damage (Korhonen, 2024).

Mechanistic gaps for IL-6R control of lysosomes/autophagy: Crucially, the provided materials do not furnish direct mechanistic or biochemical evidence that IL-6 or IL-6R signaling modulates RPE autophagic flux, lysosomal acidification (v-ATPase function), or cathepsin D enzymatic activity, and several excerpts explicitly note the absence of IL-6R blockade studies interrogating autophagy/lysosome endpoints in RPE/AMD models (Buniello et al., 2025; Brandstetter, 2016). In additional RPE experiments modulating autophagy and p62/SQSTM1, cytokine shifts were observed for MCP-1 and IL-8, while IL-6 did not exhibit consistent dependency on p62 state, arguing against a simple autophagy→IL-6 coupling that would predict lysosomal rescue by IL-6R blockade (Korhonen, 2024). Within this corpus, IL-6 behaves as part of a downstream inflammatory secretome during RPE stress rather than an upstream determinant of lysosomal health (Brandstetter, 2016).

Expected Effect  
Assay-level expectations under AMD-relevant stress paradigms should be aligned with the causal structure supported by the evidence.

- What IL-6R blockade should do: Given that RPE secrete IL-6 and can engage IL-6/IL-8 autocrine degenerative signaling in inflammatory contexts, tocilizumab is expected to abrogate IL-6–dependent downstream signaling in RPE and neighboring cells, dampening IL-6–responsive gene expression and paracrine effects where IL-6 is a driver (Brandstetter, 2016). In LMP/blue-light or impaired-clearance inflammasome models, IL-6 is robustly induced alongside IL-1β/IL-18 and partially depends on caspase-1–driven pathways, so tocilizumab would be expected to reduce IL-6-mediated signaling outputs but would not suppress upstream lysosomal damage, cathepsin leakage, inflammasome assembly, or caspase-1 activation per se (Brandstetter, 2016). Because inflammasome activation in these models also reduces constitutive VEGF secretion and polarizes cytokine release apically, IL-6R blockade might modestly alter the inflammatory milieu without restoring basal angiogenic signaling from RPE or preventing microglial chemotaxis induced by the broader cytokine secretome (Brandstetter, 2016).

- Unsupported elements of the working hypothesis: The claim that tocilizumab will prevent v-ATPase downregulation, preserve lysosomal pH, and maintain cathepsin D activity to slow RPE atrophy is not supported by the present corpus; none of the provided sources demonstrate that IL-6 or IL-6R signaling directly regulates v-ATPase subunits, lysosomal acidification, or CTSD activity in RPE, nor that IL-6R blockade restores these parameters in AMD-relevant assays (Buniello et al., 2025; Brandstetter, 2016). In contrast, interventions that directly target inflammasome priming/assembly or its stability (e.g., Hsp90 inhibition enabling autophagic degradation of NLRP3 when autophagy is intact) have demonstrated impact on inflammasome outputs in RPE models, emphasizing that upstream proteostasis/oxidative stress rather than IL-6 drives inflammasome activation in those settings (Piippo, 2019).

- Target expression and pathway verification in assay design: The corpus documents RPE production of IL-6, but it does not provide direct evidence of IL-6R expression/function or JAK/STAT3 activation in the specific RPE models used for AMD-relevant stress paradigms, and the Open Targets excerpt shows weaker curated AMD evidence for STAT3 than for IL6 itself (Brandstetter, 2016; Buniello et al., 2025). Therefore, prior to efficacy testing, verify IL-6R expression and IL-6–induced pathway activation (e.g., STAT3 phosphorylation and transcriptional targets) in the chosen human RPE model and confirm that tocilizumab blocks these readouts (Brandstetter, 2016; Buniello et al., 2025).

- Net biological effect in dry AMD context: Dry AMD progression is mechanistically rooted in upstream lysosomal/photooxidative injury, complement-driven NF-κB priming, and NLRP3/AIM2 inflammasome activation that governs IL-1β/IL-18 release and shifts death modes toward pyroptosis; IL-6 is a downstream secretome component rather than a proximal trigger in these paradigms (Brandstetter, 2016). Consequently, tocilizumab is more likely to modulate inflammatory tone than to prevent the initiating RPE lysosomal failure that drives atrophy in dry AMD (Brandstetter, 2016; Piippo, 2019).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Biologic plausibility at the cytokine level: IL-6 is elevated in AMD and produced by RPE, and RPE inflammasome activation produces a pronounced IL-6 response (≈13.6-fold increase) together with IL-1β/IL-18 under AMD-relevant stresses; IL-6 can participate in autocrine degenerative loops in RPE after inflammatory stimuli (Buniello et al., 2025; Brandstetter, 2016). This supports testing whether IL-6/IL-6R signaling contributes to maladaptive inflammatory reinforcement in diseased RPE (Buniello et al., 2025).  
- Validated pharmacology and established clinical operations: Tocilizumab’s IL-6R blockade is mechanistically defined, and systemic dosing regimens (IV 8 mg/kg q4w, SC 162 mg weekly) and safety frameworks are standardized; ophthalmic trials have successfully embedded retinal structural and visual endpoints under systemic IL-6R blockade, providing a feasible operational scaffold (Assistance Publique–Hôpitaux de Paris, 2017; Shi, 2017b; Shi, 2017a).  
- Ocular inflammatory precedent and safety monitoring: Prospective uveitis trials and the planned DME study demonstrate translational interest in IL-6 blockade in eye disease and detail immunosuppression-oriented screening and monitoring relevant to an elderly population (TB/hepatitis screening, neutrophil/platelet/hepatic thresholds, live-vaccine restrictions, diverticulitis caution, reproductive precautions) (University of Nebraska, 2016; Assistance Publique–Hôpitaux de Paris, 2017; Zhujiang Hospital, 2025).

Weaknesses and risks  
- Lack of mechanistic linkage to lysosomal rescue: No evidence in the corpus shows that IL-6/IL-6R signaling controls v-ATPase function, lysosomal pH, autophagic flux, or cathepsin D activity in RPE; multiple excerpts explicitly note the absence of IL-6R blockade studies addressing autophagy/lysosome endpoints in RPE models (Buniello et al., 2025; Brandstetter, 2016). By contrast, RPE inflammasome activation arises from upstream lysosomal damage, proteostasis failure, oxidative stress, and complement priming—nodes not expected to be corrected by IL-6R blockade (Brandstetter, 2016; Piippo, 2019; Brandstetter, 2016; Brandstetter, 2016).  
- Downstream positioning of IL-6 in AMD-relevant cascades: In LMP/blue-light and impaired-clearance models, IL-6 is part of a downstream secretome secondary to caspase-1–dependent pathways, whereas proximal determinants of RPE fate include lysosomal integrity, cathepsin activity, inflammasome assembly, and priming signals; targeting IL-6R is therefore unlikely to interrupt the initiating injury that drives RPE atrophy (Brandstetter, 2016).  
- No clinical evidence in dry AMD and uncertain ocular route: The materials contain no clinical trials of tocilizumab in dry AMD, and the only retina-focused interventional protocol in the corpus (READ-4 for DME) was withdrawn before enrollment; registry-level hits lack extractable information here (University of Nebraska, 2016; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.). Intravitreal data for tocilizumab are not provided, and systemic use in an elderly AMD population carries non-trivial risks (serious infections, cytopenias, hepatic injury, GI perforation risk, vaccine restrictions) that may outweigh an unproven benefit (University of Nebraska, 2016; Assistance Publique–Hôpitaux de Paris, 2017; Zhujiang Hospital, 2025).  
- Limited curated evidence for IL-6R/STAT3 in AMD: The Open Targets excerpt underscores that while IL6 is strongly associated with AMD literature, STAT3 (a principal IL-6R effector) has minimal curated AMD evidence in this dataset, weakening confidence that IL-6R blockade will materially modulate the NF-κB priming required for inflammasome activation in RPE (Buniello et al., 2025).

Development recommendation  
- Given the current evidence, tocilizumab is not a priority candidate for slowing RPE atrophy in dry AMD via lysosomal preservation, because the mechanistic chain posited—IL-6R blockade preserving v-ATPase and cathepsin D activity—lacks experimental support in RPE/AMD models in this corpus, while disease-proximal injury nodes are driven by lysosomal/photooxidative damage, intracellular clearance failure, complement-driven NF-κB priming, and NLRP3/AIM2 activation (Brandstetter, 2016; Piippo, 2019; Korhonen, 2024).  
- If pursued at all, the program should begin with narrow mechanistic validation in human RPE: verify IL-6R expression and functional IL-6→JAK/STAT signaling; quantify whether tocilizumab reduces IL-6–dependent outputs in AMD-relevant RPE stress assays (lipofuscin/blue-light LMP, MG-132+BafA proteostasis failure, antimycin A mitochondrial stress) while measuring lysosomal pH, v-ATPase subunit expression, cathepsin D activity, caspase-1 activity, IL-1β/IL-18 release, and RPE death mode; a priori, expect effects restricted to IL-6-responsive readouts without rescue of lysosome/inflammasome metrics (Brandstetter, 2016; Piippo, 2019; Korhonen, 2024).  
- Benchmark tocilizumab against mechanistically proximal modulators (e.g., NLRP3 pathway inhibitors, IL-1 pathway blockade, Hsp90 inhibition enabling NLRP3 degradation when autophagy is intact) to determine whether IL-6R blockade adds independent benefit on RPE survival beyond dampening IL-6 signaling (Piippo, 2019; Brandstetter, 2016).  
- Absent compelling preclinical data showing that IL-6R blockade favorably modifies lysosomal function or decisively improves RPE survival in AMD-relevant paradigms, deprioritize tocilizumab in favor of targets that directly modulate the proximal injury axis (lysosome integrity, complement-NF-κB priming, and inflammasome assembly) (Brandstetter, 2016; Piippo, 2019).

Analysis: Candidate 1 (NMN) and Candidate 2 (T0901317) both address core pathological features of dry AMD but differ markedly in evidence strength, safety profile, and translational feasibility. NMN is an endogenous NAD+ precursor with extensive preclinical validation in RPE and retinal models, including primary human RPE, ARPE-19, and multiple in vivo mouse models recapitulating NAD+ decline, photoreceptor injury, senescence, drusenoid deposit formation, and RPE phagocytosis deficits. NMN consistently restores NAD+ pools, engages SIRT1/SIRT3, improves mitochondrial function, reduces oxidative stress and senescence markers, and demonstrably mitigates subretinal drusenoid deposits in a cholesterol efflux–deficient dry AMD model. Although direct TFEB/lysosomal data are pending, the mechanistic network (NAMPT→NMN→NAD+→sirtuin/AMPK→mitophagy/autophagy) is well established with clear PD biomarkers and minimal safety concerns given NMN’s status as a vitamin B3–derived metabolite with human tolerability data for related precursors. Drug delivery to RPE is plausible via systemic dosing, and dose translation strategies exist. In contrast, T0901317 is a potent synthetic LXR agonist that upregulates ABCA1/APOE, promotes lysosomal enzymes and acidification, and exerts anti-inflammatory effects via NF-κB inhibition. However, T0901317 suffers from off-target activation of FXR/PXR, known systemic metabolic liabilities (hypertriglyceridemia, hepatic steatosis), and limited ocular PK/PD or clinical data in AMD. Its preclinical evidence in AMD models is largely in vitro or in acute murine settings, with no direct demonstration of drusen clearance or long-term disease modification. Local ocular delivery could mitigate systemic exposure but requires substantial formulation development. Thus, NMN offers superior direct disease alignment, mechanistic clarity, safety, and translational readiness compared to T0901317.
Reasoning: Between the two candidates, NMN is supported by robust, disease-relevant in vitro and in vivo data demonstrating efficacy across multiple AMD-aligned endpoints (NAD+ repletion, mitochondrial rescue, senescence suppression, RPE phagocytosis, drusenoid deposit reduction). Its mechanism is centered on a well-characterized metabolic axis with clear biomarkers, and its safety profile is favorable given endogenous nature and clinical use of related NAD+ precursors. T0901317, while mechanistically attractive for lipid efflux and lysosomal enhancement, carries significant off-target risks, metabolic side effects, and lacks direct, long-term AMD model validation or clinical ocular data. Therefore, NMN delivers both higher probability of successful experimental outcome and a clearer path toward translation into a viable dry AMD therapy.
