Numerous biochemical studies have established that resveratrol exerts its beneficial effects by modulating key intracellular pathways. Historically, resveratrol has been used as an anti‐oxidant in various cellular systems and has been investigated in preclinical models of neurodegeneration, cardiovascular disease, and metabolic syndrome. In the context of ophthalmology, several studies have evaluated its efficacy in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cell models. For instance, research using ARPE-19 cells, a well-established human RPE cell line, demonstrated that resveratrol activates SIRT1 to protect against oxidative stress and apoptosis induced by challenging stimuli such as sodium iodate, UVA radiation, acrolein, and A2E—a major component of lipofuscin implicated in drusen formation and AMD pathology (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Li et al., 2024; Alaimo et al., 2020). Additional investigations combined resveratrol with omega-3 fatty acids in formulations like Resvega® to induce autophagy and enhance cell survival under conditions simulating AMD (Delmas et al., 2021; Koskela et al., 2016). While much of the published literature has concentrated on resveratrol’s effects in oxidative stress, inflammatory responses, and autophagy promotion in RPE cells, a few reports have noted its capacity to counteract the toxic accumulation of intracellular debris that is a hallmark of dry AMD (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Pinelli et al., 2025). Moreover, preliminary clinical reports have suggested that long-term oral supplementation with resveratrol-containing nutraceuticals may contribute to anatomic restoration of retinal structure and improved visual function in elderly patients, thus further underpinning its translational potential. Notably, while there is extensive preclinical evidence in vitro and in animal models, resveratrol has not yet been unequivocally validated in advanced clinical trials targeting dry AMD specifically (Abu-Amero et al., 2016).

Mechanism of Action:  
A robust body of research supports that resveratrol acts principally through the activation of SIRT1 (sirtuin 1) and the energy sensor AMPK (AMP-activated protein kinase), both of which are critical for maintaining cellular homeostasis in the aging retina. At the molecular level, resveratrol has been reported to directly and indirectly stimulate SIRT1 activity in RPE cells, leading to the deacetylation of several downstream targets such as PGC-1α (peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator 1-alpha). This deacetylated PGC-1α, in turn, upregulates mitochondrial biogenesis and enhances cellular oxidative phosphorylation, thereby improving mitochondrial quality control and reducing the accumulation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Li et al., 2024; Buonfiglio et al., 2024). Concomitantly, resveratrol activates AMPK, albeit through complex mechanisms involving inhibition of phosphodiesterases and alterations in the intracellular AMP/ATP ratio. The resulting AMPK phosphorylation facilitates a myriad of downstream effects, notably the inhibition of mTOR signaling (a known suppressor of autophagy) and activation of ULK1, a serine/threonine kinase that initiates autophagosome formation (Li et al., 2024; Abu-Amero et al., 2016).

In RPE cells, the synergistic activation of SIRT1 and AMPK by resveratrol is believed to promote autophagy, as evidenced by increased LC3II/I ratios and decreased p62 expression. Autophagy is particularly critical in RPE cells to clear toxic cellular debris such as A2E and other protein aggregates that contribute to drusen accumulation in dry AMD (Alaimo et al., 2020; Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Pinelli et al., 2023). Furthermore, the prevailing hypothesis extends these autophagic benefits by suggesting that, downstream of AMPK/SIRT1 activation, resveratrol may induce TFEB dephosphorylation. TFEB is a transcription factor that, when dephosphorylated, translocates into the nucleus and upregulates the coordinated lysosomal expression and regulation (CLEAR) network. This results in enhanced lysosomal biogenesis, improved lysosomal acidification, and increased activation of lysosomal enzymes such as cathepsin D. Although direct experimental evidence linking resveratrol to TFEB dephosphorylation in RPE cells is not abundantly detailed in the current literature, several studies imply that agents that activate AMPK and inhibit mTOR can indirectly promote TFEB activity. In this context, resveratrol’s ability to inhibit mTOR, partly through AMPK activation, suggests a plausible mechanism for the promotion of TFEB-mediated lysosomal functions (Falcão et al., 2025; Pinelli et al., 2023). These molecular events are anticipated to bolster the autophagy-lysosomal system, thereby mitigating the drusen accumulation characteristic of dry AMD. Additionally, resveratrol exerts direct antioxidant effects by scavenging free radicals and modulating the expression of antioxidant enzymes such as superoxide dismutase, which contributes further to its protective milieu in the retina (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Abu-Amero et al., 2016).

Expected Effect:  
Based on its molecular pharmacology, the expected effect of resveratrol in preclinical models of dry AMD would be multifaceted. In assays utilizing ARPE-19 cells or primary human RPE cells, treatment with resveratrol is expected to enhance SIRT1 activity, as measured by increased deacetylation of SIRT1 substrates and upregulation of PGC-1α nuclear translocation. Concurrently, AMPK phosphorylation is anticipated to be elevated, leading to inhibition of the mTOR pathway; this would foster an increased autophagic flux, observable as a higher LC3II/I ratio and reduced levels of the autophagy substrate p62 (Li et al., 2024; Alaimo et al., 2020; Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021). Furthermore, the candidate is hypothesized to indirectly promote TFEB dephosphorylation, facilitating its nuclear translocation and subsequent upregulation of lysosomal genes. This could manifest as enhanced lysosomal biogenesis, improved acidification of the lysosomal compartment, and elevated activity of lysosomal proteases such as cathepsin D. The cumulative consequence of these events would be a more efficient clearance of intracellular debris, including lipofuscin and other drusen components, thereby ameliorating RPE dysfunction associated with dry AMD (Falcão et al., 2025; Pinelli et al., 2023).

It is also expected that resveratrol’s anti-inflammatory and anti-apoptotic actions would reduce the chronic low-grade inflammation that underpins AMD pathogenesis. In vivo, improved autophagic and lysosomal clearance should correlate with decreased accumulation of pathological deposits at the RPE-Bruch’s membrane interface, potentially reducing the progression of drusen formation and preserving retinal structure and function (Alaimo et al., 2020; Abu-Amero et al., 2016; Pinelli et al., 2025). Given that resveratrol is detectable in retinal tissue following oral administration, its systemic safety and potential for long-term use add to its attractiveness as a repurposed therapeutic agent for dry AMD. Moreover, the dual capacity to modulate both metabolic and epigenetic pathways may offer disease-modifying effects that extend beyond symptomatic relief and target the underlying cellular aging processes in the RPE (Subramani et al., 2017).

Overall Evaluation:  
Resveratrol emerges as a promising candidate for repurposing in the context of dry AMD owing to its well-documented ability to activate SIRT1 and AMPK, which are pivotal signaling nodes in the maintenance of cellular homeostasis and autophagy. One of the central strengths of resveratrol is its dual mechanism of action. By targeting SIRT1, resveratrol not only combats oxidative stress through the deacetylation of transcription factors and enhancement of mitochondrial biogenesis but also modulates anti-inflammatory pathways relevant to retinal preservation (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Li et al., 2024). Simultaneously, its activation of AMPK provides additional impetus for autophagy induction through mTOR inhibition and ULK1 activation. Such molecular actions are of particular relevance to RPE cells, in which impairment of the autophagy-lysosomal system is a key pathogenetic mechanism leading to the accumulation of cellular waste products such as drusen—a hallmark of dry AMD (Alaimo et al., 2020; Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021).

Furthermore, the hypothesis that resveratrol could foster TFEB dephosphorylation is especially intriguing. Although direct evidence linking resveratrol to TFEB activation in RPE cells is currently limited, the known interactions between AMPK/mTOR signaling and TFEB activity provide a strong conceptual framework. Activation of TFEB would result in enhanced lysosomal biogenesis, acidification, and increased cathepsin D activity—mechanisms that are critical for the proper degradation of accumulated photoreceptor-derived debris and toxic aggregates (Falcão et al., 2025; Pinelli et al., 2023). This potential to bolster a declining lysosomal-autophagy system with age might address the fundamental cellular dysfunction observed in dry AMD.

On the clinical side, resveratrol demonstrates a favorable safety profile with established oral bioavailability and experimental evidence suggesting retinal tissue penetration. Combined with its history of use as an anti-oxidative and anti-inflammatory agent in other disease contexts, these features support its translational potential. Several nutraceutical formulations incorporating resveratrol (often in combination with omega-3 fatty acids, as in Resvega®) have already reached early-phase clinical evaluation for ocular indications, providing preliminary signals of efficacy in improving retinal structure and function among aged patients (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Delmas et al., 2021).

Nevertheless, several weaknesses and gaps must be acknowledged. First, while there is abundant preclinical evidence of resveratrol’s activation of SIRT1/AMPK pathways and subsequent autophagy induction in RPE cells, the specific molecular events leading to TFEB dephosphorylation, enhanced lysosomal biogenesis, lysosomal acidification, and increased cathepsin D activity are not yet comprehensively elucidated. In other words, the critical mechanistic link between resveratrol treatment and lysosomal enhancement remains somewhat inferential rather than directly demonstrated in the existing literature (Falcão et al., 2025; Hyttinen et al., 2019). Second, much of the supporting data comes from in vitro studies or animal models, with limited robust clinical evidence explicitly addressing dry AMD. Although some pilot clinical studies with resveratrol-containing formulations show promise, their design, scale, and long-term outcomes are not sufficiently advanced to confirm therapeutic efficacy in a broad AMD population (Abu-Amero et al., 2016). Third, resveratrol is known to have issues with bioavailability due to rapid metabolism and low systemic concentrations after oral ingestion; therefore, optimizing its delivery to retinal tissues, perhaps via novel formulations or nanoparticle carriers, may be necessary to achieve therapeutic levels (Subramani et al., 2017; Pinelli et al., 2025). Additionally, while its pleiotropic activity is a strength in terms of targeting multiple pathogenic mechanisms, this same feature can pose challenges in ensuring specificity and avoiding off-target effects.

In summary, resveratrol presents a compelling case as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. Its ability to activate SIRT1 and AMPK, induce autophagy, and potentially stimulate TFEB-driven lysosomal biogenesis aligns well with the current understanding of the cellular derangements underlying AMD pathogenesis. The expected outcome would be improved clearance of toxic cellular debris and drusen, preservation of RPE integrity, and amelioration of oxidative stress and inflammation in the aging retina. However, to fully validate resveratrol as a viable treatment for dry AMD, further investigations are warranted to (a) directly demonstrate its effects on TFEB dephosphorylation and lysosomal function in RPE cells, (b) optimize its ocular bioavailability, and (c) establish robust clinical endpoints in well-designed trials. Overall, while promising and supported by a substantial body of preclinical evidence, additional targeted research is required to definitively establish resveratrol’s mechanistic effects on the autophagy-lysosomal pathway and its therapeutic potential in dry AMD (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Li et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2025; Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Abu-Amero et al., 2016).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Torin2 is a synthetic, second-generation ATP-competitive inhibitor of the mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) kinase designed to inhibit both mTOR complex 1 (mTORC1) and complex 2 (mTORC2) with high potency and favorable pharmacodynamic properties compared to first-generation allosteric mTOR inhibitors (rapamycin/rapalogs) and earlier catalytic mTOR kinase inhibitors (TORKi) such as PP242 and AZD8055 (Liu et al., 2013, pp. 7–10). Chemically optimized by structure-guided medicinal chemistry efforts, Torin2 exhibits rapid dephosphorylation of canonical mTORC1 substrates S6K1 (T389) and 4E-BP1 (T37/46) including rapamycin-insensitive sites, and of the mTORC2 substrate Akt (S473), reflecting dual-complex inhibition that is superior to rapamycin’s mTORC1-limited activity (with incomplete suppression of 4E-BP1) (Liu et al., 2013, pp. 7–10). In head-to-head comparisons with other ATP-competitive mTOR inhibitors, Torin2 maintains stronger and more sustained suppression of mTORC1/2 signaling after drug washout, attributable to its slow off-rate, with durable pathway inhibition persisting for approximately four hours in cellular assays, contrasting with rapid recovery observed with PP242 and shorter-duration suppression by AZD8055 (Liu et al., 2013, pp. 7–9). Torin2 is highly selective for mTOR over PI3K (>800-fold) and shows approximately 100-fold selectivity over the DNA damage response kinases ATM and ATR; these latter off-targets remain relevant at higher concentrations and inform safety margins and dose selection (Liu et al., 2013, pp. 9–10).

Mechanistically, Torin2 robustly induces autophagy across multiple cell lines (e.g., LC3-II accumulation, acridine-orange–positive acidic vesicle formation), consistent with its potent inhibition of mTORC1, a master negative regulator of autophagy initiation and flux (Liu et al., 2013, pp. 7–9). As a drug class, ATP-competitive TORKi have been widely investigated in oncology and proliferative diseases given their ability to fully suppress both mTOR complexes, thereby impacting protein synthesis, cell-cycle progression, metabolism, and survival signaling (Liu et al., 2013, pp. 7–10). Outside oncology, dual mTORC1/2 inhibition has demonstrated disease-modifying potential in organ systems where mTOR hyperactivation drives pathology; for example, Torin2 reduced S6 and 4E-BP1 phosphorylation and curtailed cyst burden in a mouse model of autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease, with efficacy comparable to sirolimus and a potentially more favorable side-effect profile (Holditch et al., 2019, pp. 6–7).

In the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), dysregulated mTOR signaling (particularly chronic mTORC1 activation with age) is strongly implicated in degradative/clearance failure, lysosomal dysfunction, metabolic reprogramming, and structural degeneration that recapitulate key features of dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD), including lipid-rich subretinal deposits and RPE dedifferentiation (Go et al., 2020, pp. 1–3, 11–13; Huang et al., 2019, pp. 1–2, 7–9; Zhao et al., 2011, pp. 10–11). RPE expresses and functionally engages both mTORC1 and mTORC2 complexes, providing a mechanistic rationale for evaluating dual-complex catalytic inhibitors like Torin2 as therapeutic candidates to correct core pathogenic processes in dry AMD (Intartaglia et al., 2022, pp. 15–17).

Therapeutic History  
The mTOR pathway has been studied extensively in retinal and RPE biology, with strong preclinical evidence linking mTOR hyperactivation to RPE degeneration and dry AMD-like pathology, and corresponding benefits from mTOR inhibition; however, direct ocular data with Torin2 itself are currently lacking and must be extrapolated from pharmacology in other tissues and from surrogates (Torin1, PP242, INK-128/MLN0128) and rapamycin (Liu et al., 2013, pp. 7–10; Holditch et al., 2019, pp. 6–7). Genetic and pharmacologic mTOR activation in RPE induces epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT), suppresses autophagy, disrupts metabolism, and yields an AMD-like phenotype; in a knock-in model that overexpresses mLST8 (a core mTORC component) in RPE, both mTORC1 and mTORC2 are upregulated, and dual-complex inhibition with TORIN1 (a TORKi closely related to Torin2) normalized signaling and restored autophagy and RPE function in vitro, including rescue of autophagy regulators Atg9b and Atg7 and recovery of autophagy flux (Chowdhury et al., 2025, pp. 1–2, 8–13). These data directly support the therapeutic relevance of dual mTORC1/2 inhibition in RPE conditions that model early AMD pathogenesis (Chowdhury et al., 2025, pp. 1–2, 8–13).

In a complementary RPE disease model focused on amyloid-β (Aβ)-induced lysosomal/autophagy impairment—a pathology linked to dry AMD—Torin (a first-generation mTOR inhibitor in this study; not explicitly Torin2) restored lysosomal activity via LAMP2 activation, corrected p62/SQSTM1 accumulation, facilitated Aβ aggregate clearance, and ameliorated Aβ-driven tight junction disruption in vitro and in Aβ-challenged mouse RPE in vivo, directly addressing the barrier degradation and clearance deficits central to AMD (Jo et al., 2023, pp. 1–2). In multiple RPE cell systems modeling autofluorescent granule (AFG) accumulation and lipofuscinogenesis after photoreceptor outer segment (POS) challenge, mTOR inhibition (rapamycin; INK-128) decreased AFG load by approximately 30% and activated a TFEB-dependent lysosome biogenesis program; these effects required intact lysosomal proteases/lipases and were associated with LAMP1 upregulation and GADD34 induction, supporting the concept that mTOR→TFEB pathway modulation can restore lysosomal clearance in RPE (albeit these studies were preprints and should be interpreted accordingly) (Falcão et al., 2024, pp. 1–6, 10–18). Constitutively active TFEB dramatically reduced POS-dependent AFGs in preventive and resolving paradigms, further validating TFEB activation as a mechanistic goal for pharmacologic mTOR inhibition in early AMD models (Falcão et al., 2024, pp. 1–6, 13–18).

In genetic models where RPE mTORC1 is hyperactivated through Tsc1 deletion, chronic mTORC1 activity causes progressive RPE degeneration, lipid accumulation, and subretinal drusenoid deposits, and rapamycin treatment restored RPE markers (e.g., RPE65), improved ERG responses, and partially normalized metabolomic derangements, providing in vivo proof-of-concept that mTOR pathway suppression improves RPE structure and function in AMD-like degeneration (Huang et al., 2019, pp. 1–2, 7–9; Zhao et al., 2011, pp. 10–11). At a mechanistic level, age-driven increases in lysosome mass and mTORC1 docking in RPE create a vicious cycle of mTORC1 hyperactivation that impairs phagolysosomal function, promotes lipogenesis, suppresses lipolysis, and degrades autophagy, converging on classic dry AMD phenotypes; mTOR inhibition breaks this cycle and restores degradative capacity (Go et al., 2020, pp. 1–3, 11–13).

Beyond ocular systems, Torin2 has been used preclinically in oncology and in non-ocular degenerative models; its dual mTORC1/2 suppression, sustained pharmacodynamics, and autophagy induction underlie anti-proliferative activity and apoptosis in cancer models, while in an ADPKD model Torin2 demonstrated pathway inhibition with efficacy comparable to sirolimus, suggesting that torin-class agents may be tolerable with appropriate dose and schedule selection (Liu et al., 2013, pp. 7–9; Holditch et al., 2019, pp. 6–7). Notably, second-generation mTOR inhibitors can be cytotoxic in RPE due to potent mTORC2 suppression with downstream Akt inhibition, a survival pathway for metabolically stressed RPE; this risk emphasizes the importance of dose titration and local ocular delivery strategies for Torin2 in AMD (Huang et al., 2018, pp. 7–8).

To our knowledge, Torin2 has not been reported in clinical trials for dry AMD or directly tested in RPE/retinal models in vivo; however, the strength of the translational prior—mTOR hyperactivation as a convergent mechanism in RPE degeneration; rescue with catalytic mTOR inhibitors such as TORIN1; and reversible ALP defects with Torin-class inhibition—warrants rigorous preclinical testing of Torin2 in dry AMD-relevant models (Chowdhury et al., 2025, pp. 1–2, 8–11; Jo et al., 2023, pp. 1–2).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Eltanexor (also known as KPT-8602, MedKoo 406829) is a synthetic small‐molecule compound belonging to the class of “selective inhibitors of nuclear export” (SINE). These agents were developed by medicinal chemists to target the nuclear export protein exportin-1 (XPO1, also known as CRM1), which mediates the transport of a wide range of proteins from the nucleus to the cytoplasm. Eltanexor, like its predecessor Selinexor (KPT-330), functions by binding within the nuclear export signal (NES) recognition site of XPO1—most notably involving interaction with a conserved cysteine residue (Cys528) in XPO1’s NES‐binding pocket—and thereby preventing export of many regulatory proteins. However, Eltanexor has been engineered with modifications that confer improved tolerability along with oral bioavailability and a favorable pharmacokinetic profile, making it an attractive candidate for repurposing. SINE compounds have been extensively studied in oncology, where their ability to cause the nuclear retention of tumor suppressors has led to approved indications in certain hematological malignancies; accordingly, the synthetic origin of Eltanexor is rooted in efforts to optimize the drug‐like properties of early XPO1 inhibitors and to improve their clinical safety profile (Newell et al., 2024).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, the SINE class has been primarily associated with anticancer applications. Early compounds such as leptomycin B (LMB) were the first to demonstrate that inhibition of XPO1 could induce nuclear retention of proteins; however, issues with toxicity limited their clinical utility. Subsequent development efforts led to the creation of SINE compounds including Selinexor (KPT-330) and more recently Eltanexor (KPT-8602), which have undergone both preclinical and early-phase clinical trials in various cancer types. In these settings, XPO1 inhibition was shown to result in the nuclear accumulation of proteins that typically support cell survival, thereby selectively promoting apoptosis in cancer cells (Newell et al., 2024; Tang et al., 2025). Outside the field of oncology, mechanistic studies have indicated that inhibiting nuclear export can also impact proteins critically involved in autophagy regulation and lysosomal homeostasis. For instance, preclinical work in neuronal and glioblastoma models has shown that XPO1 inhibitors trigger nuclear retention of the master autophagy regulator TFEB, thereby enhancing autophagic flux and lysosomal biogenesis (Abokyi & Tse, 2025; Tang et al., 2025). To date, however, there is no published study that directly employs Eltanexor or other XPO1 inhibitors as therapeutic agents for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or related retinal degenerative conditions. In retinal research, extensive efforts have focused on modulating TFEB activity through alternative strategies—such as using trehalose, metformin, or genetic approaches—to restore lysosomal function in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells (Ghosh et al., 2024; Abokyi & Tse, 2025). Although the direct use of XPO1 inhibitors in RPE or dry AMD models has not been experimentally demonstrated, the established efficacy of SINE compounds in other contexts of neurodegeneration and autophagy dysregulation provides a compelling rationale for their repurposing in ocular diseases (Abokyi & Tse, 2025; Falcão et al., 2025).

Mechanism of Action:  
Under normal cellular conditions, XPO1 mediates the nuclear export of a diverse set of proteins by recognizing nuclear export signals (NES) present on cargo proteins. One critical cargo is the transcription factor TFEB, which regulates the expression of lysosomal hydrolases and autophagy-related genes by binding to CLEAR (coordinated lysosomal expression and regulation) elements within gene promoters. In nutrient-rich or stress-dysregulated states, TFEB undergoes phosphorylation by kinases such as mTORC1, resulting in cytoplasmic sequestration mediated by binding to 14-3-3 proteins and subsequent export from the nucleus via XPO1 (Pan & Valapala, 2022; La Spina et al., 2021; Li, 2018). Eltanexor’s mechanism of action is to bind within the NES-binding pocket of XPO1 and disrupt its interaction with such cargo proteins. The inhibition is achieved through covalent and slowly reversible binding to the Cys528 residue in XPO1, thereby preventing the nuclear export of target proteins. When export is blocked, TFEB (and likely its paralog TFE3) accumulates in the nucleus where it is free to activate transcription of CLEAR network genes. The resulting upregulation of lysosomal genes leads to increased lysosomal biogenesis, a lowering of lysosomal pH, and enhanced activation of hydrolases such as cathepsin D—all of which are critical to maintaining proteostasis and clearing damaged proteins and organelles (Abokyi & Tse, 2025; Pan & Valapala, 2022). Published data in glioblastoma models have shown that other XPO1 inhibitors such as Selinexor induce this type of nuclear trapping of TFEB, which correlates with an increase in autophagic flux and enhanced clearance mechanisms (Tang et al., 2025). Importantly, unlike pharmacological treatments that rely on mTOR inhibition (which can have widespread metabolic effects), the SINE approach works directly at the level of nuclear export, thereby selectively increasing TFEB activity independent of upstream mTOR/AKT signaling (Abokyi & Tse, 2025; Li, 2018).

Expected Effect in Dry AMD:  
Dry age-related macular degeneration is characterized by dysfunction of the RPE, resulting in diminished autophagic flux, accumulation of lipofuscin, and impaired degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (POS). In healthy RPE cells, nuclear TFEB orchestrates a transcriptional program that maintains lysosomal homeostasis by upregulating genes involved in lysosomal biogenesis, acidification, and cargo degradation. However, in aging and diseased RPE, TFEB becomes increasingly phosphorylated and sequestered in the cytoplasm, leading to reduced CLEAR network activity (Ghosh et al., 2024; Abokyi & Tse, 2025). The hypothesis behind repurposing Eltanexor for dry AMD is that by inhibiting XPO1 in RPE cells, the drug will promote nuclear retention of TFEB and TFE3. This nuclear accumulation is expected to drive upregulation of lysosomal gene expression, resulting in the restoration of lysosomal acidification and proteolytic capacity, particularly cathepsin D activity. An effective increase in autophagic flux and lysosomal biogenesis should aid in the degradation of accumulated toxic compounds such as lipofuscin and undegraded POS debris, ultimately improving RPE function and potentially slowing or reversing progression of dry AMD (Ghosh et al., 2024; Abokyi & Tse, 2025). In addition, preclinical studies in neurodegeneration and retinal models have demonstrated that enhancing TFEB activity—whether by trehalose treatment, gene therapy approaches, or by upstream modulation of kinases such as AKT2—can protect cells from oxidative and proteotoxic stress (Abokyi & Tse, 2025; Ghosh et al., 2024). Although direct evidence in RPE cells is still pending, the large body of mechanistic work linking nuclear TFEB accumulation to improved lysosomal function provides a strong rationale for expecting similar outcomes with Eltanexor in the context of dry AMD.

Overall Evaluation:  
Eltanexor presents several attractive features as a potential therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, especially given its novel mechanism of action and its ability to modulate a fundamental cellular process that is impaired in the disease. One of the major strengths of Eltanexor lies in its targeted inhibition of XPO1, which has been well validated in oncology and neurodegeneration studies as a means to induce nuclear retention of regulatory proteins. By preventing the export of TFEB and TFE3, Eltanexor is expected to allow these key transcription factors to reactivate the CLEAR network, thereby restoring lysosomal function, lowering lysosomal pH, and boosting the activity of cathepsin D-mediated degradation. This mechanism is particularly compelling for dry AMD because RPE cell dysfunction in the disease has been closely linked to defective autophagy and impaired clearance of toxic aggregates (Ghosh et al., 2024; Abokyi & Tse, 2025). Moreover, the proposed therapeutic approach bypasses some of the limitations of mTOR-based interventions, as it directly affects nucleocytoplasmic transport rather than broadly inhibiting upstream signaling pathways. This specificity provides an additional level of mechanistic precision that could translate into a better safety profile for chronic applications in an aging population.

Nevertheless, several weaknesses and challenges must be acknowledged. First, while there is abundant evidence that XPO1 inhibitors such as Selinexor induce TFEB nuclear retention and autophagy in glioblastoma and other non-ocular models (Tang et al., 2025), there is currently a lack of direct preclinical data evaluating Eltanexor or related compounds in retinal pigment epithelial cells or in animal models of dry AMD. The extrapolation of data from cancer and neuronal models to RPE cells, while mechanistically plausible, remains to be experimentally validated. Second, because XPO1 regulates the nuclear export of a wide range of proteins—not only TFEB and TFE3—there is a potential for off-target effects that could disrupt other cellular processes. This issue is particularly critical in the context of chronic administration in elderly patients, who may be more susceptible to systemic side effects. Third, the pharmacodynamic properties required to achieve effective nuclear retention of TFEB in the RPE may differ from those established in oncology trials. For example, the concentration of Eltanexor required to affect TFEB nuclear localization and lysosomal gene expression in RPE cells might be higher than that used in cancer models, necessitating further optimization of dosing and delivery strategies. Finally, while the oral bioavailability and existing Phase I safety data of Eltanexor support its clinical feasibility (Tang et al., 2025), localized and retina-specific delivery might ultimately prove necessary to maximize its therapeutic window and minimize systemic exposure.

In summary, Eltanexor’s mechanism of inhibiting XPO1 to promote nuclear retention of TFEB/TFE3 aligns very well with emerging therapeutic strategies aimed at correcting lysosomal dysfunction in dry AMD. The extensive literature on the role of TFEB in regulating autophagy and lysosomal biogenesis in RPE cells provides a strong mechanistic foundation for this approach (Ghosh et al., 2024; Abokyi & Tse, 2025). Additionally, the demonstrated ability of XPO1 inhibitors to induce autophagy in other preclinical models (Abokyi & Tse, 2025; Tang et al., 2025) reinforces the potential for repurposing Eltanexor in an ocular setting. However, to move forward, it will be essential to generate direct experimental evidence in primary RPE cultures and in vivo dry AMD models to verify that Eltanexor indeed promotes TFEB nuclear retention, enhances CLEAR network activity, lowers lysosomal pH, and increases cathepsin D–mediated cargo degradation in the retinal environment. Addressing these issues will not only validate the therapeutic concept but will also help to optimize dosing, delivery, and safety profiles tailored for the treatment of dry AMD.

Overall, while Eltanexor shows promise as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD owing to its targeted mechanism of action and favorable preclinical attributes in other disease models, further studies focused explicitly on retinal cell biology and AMD pathology are imperative before clinical translation can be considered. The strength of the candidate lies in its mechanistic specificity and the well-established role of TFEB/TFE3 in lysosomal function, whereas the main weaknesses revolve around the current lack of direct evidence in the target system and potential off-target effects associated with global nuclear export inhibition (Abokyi & Tse, 2025; Pan & Valapala, 2022; Ghosh et al., 2024).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Pegcetacoplan (APL-2, now marketed as Syfovre) is a synthetically engineered, PEGylated cyclic peptide that belongs to the family of compstatin analogs designed to inhibit complement component C3. Its origins lie in early peptide discovery via phage‐display and random peptide library screening, and successive rounds of medicinal chemistry optimization were applied to improve its binding affinity, solubility, and pharmacokinetic profile through PEG conjugation (Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023; Ong et al., 2024). The PEGylation process not only grants enhanced resistance to enzymatic degradation but also prolongs the intravitreal residence time, an essential property for ocular applications requiring sustained drug exposure with limited dosing frequency (Tzoumas et al., 2023; Mastellos & Lambris, 2024). As a second‐generation compstatin analog, pegcetacoplan employs a bivalent design that enables high specificity for human C3, blocking its proteolytic cleavage into the active fragments C3a and C3b. These fragments are potent mediators that further amplify the inflammatory cascade through the formation of C3 convertases (Lamers et al., 2022). This therapeutic candidate is embedded within a broader class of complement inhibitors that have been actively explored in inflammatory disorders, and notably in ophthalmology for dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) where aberrant complement activation plays a central pathogenic role (Lamers et al., 2022; Mastellos & Lambris, 2024). Its synthetic nature, coupled with its targeted molecular design, positions pegcetacoplan as an attractive candidate for addressing the degenerative processes in geographic atrophy (GA) associated with dry AMD by directly modulating the complement cascade (Tzoumas et al., 2023; Patel et al., 2022).

Therapeutic History  
Historically, the evolution of pegcetacoplan reflects a successful translation from bench to bedside across multiple therapeutic domains. Initially, the compstatin class was primarily developed and evaluated in systemic disorders characterized by complement dysregulation, most notably in paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH). Early clinical trials in PNH provided critical safety and efficacy data that underscored the value of targeting C3, paving the way for the repurposing of these molecules in ocular disease (Lamers et al., 2022). With the conceptual framework and preclinical data in hand, pegcetacoplan was advanced into the ophthalmology space. The pivotal Phase II FILLY trial enrolled 246 patients with GA secondary to dry AMD, and the study demonstrated that monthly intravitreal injections of pegcetacoplan resulted in a statistically significant reduction of GA lesion growth by approximately 29%, while an every-other-month dosing regimen yielded a 20% reduction relative to sham-control treatment (Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023; Patel et al., 2022). These encouraging anatomical outcomes, evidenced by the slowed progression of GA and the concurrent reduction in photoreceptor loss as evaluated by SD-OCT imaging, provided a strong rationale for subsequent Phase III clinical trials (Regillo & Heier, n.d.; Patel et al., 2022).  
In addition to its use in dry AMD, pegcetacoplan’s earlier regulatory approval for PNH helped establish it as a viable molecule with a favorable safety profile. Its journey through successive clinical phases—from Phase I safety and tolerability studies to Phase II efficacy studies and ultimately Phase III confirmation—has offered compelling evidence that targeted complement inhibition can modify the disease course in conditions characterized by chronic complement activation (Tzoumas et al., 2023). However, clinical experience with pegcetacoplan has also identified potential safety signals, including an observed increase in the incidence of new-onset exudative (wet) AMD among certain subpopulations, a factor that necessitates careful patient selection and monitoring (Lamers et al., 2022; Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023). Overall, the therapeutic history of pegcetacoplan—spanning its origin from fundamental compstatin research to its current application in treating geographic atrophy—demonstrates its potential for repurposing as a disease-modifying therapy in ocular settings (Lamers et al., 2022; Desai & Dugel, 2022).

Mechanism of Action  
At the molecular level, the pathogenic cascade in dry AMD is tightly linked to dysregulated complement activation, and pegcetacoplan intervenes at one of the central nodes of this pathway by inhibiting complement component C3. Under physiological conditions, C3 is cleaved by C3 convertases into C3a—an anaphylatoxin that drives inflammation—and C3b, which functions as an opsonin and further propagates complement amplification (Yu & Wykoff, 2021). Pegcetacoplan binds to a key epitope on C3, thereby sterically hindering the enzyme-driven cleavage that would otherwise generate these active fragments. By effectively arresting this pivotal step in the complement cascade, the drug prevents downstream events such as the assembly of terminal complement complexes and the formation of the membrane attack complex (MAC) (Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023; Wu & Sun, 2019).  
The inhibition of C3 cleavage has several critical biochemical consequences. First, by lowering the concentrations of C3a and C3b, pegcetacoplan reduces the generation of pro-inflammatory mediators and the subsequent chemotactic recruitment of immune cells, which, in turn, diminishes local inflammation in the retinal environment (Regillo & Heier, n.d.; Tzoumas et al., 2023). Second, the reduction in C3b deposition directly limits the formation of MAC on retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) surfaces—a process that has been implicated in triggering lysosomal dysfunction within these critical cells (Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023; Park et al., 2021). The MAC, when deposited sublytically on RPE cells, can compromise the function of the vacuolar H⁺-ATPase (v-ATPase), the proton pump responsible for maintaining the acidic environment of lysosomes. Acidification of the lysosomal compartment is essential for optimal activity of proteolytic enzymes, such as cathepsin D, which are required to degrade photoreceptor outer segment debris and other cytotoxic by-products (Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023; Tzoumas et al., 2023).  
Thus, by preventing excessive complement activation and subsequent MAC formation, pegcetacoplan indirectly safeguards the intracellular degradative machinery of the RPE. This preservation of v-ATPase function ensures proper lysosomal acidification, which in turn maintains cathepsin D activity and reduces lysosomal overload—a key mechanism implicated in the progressive atrophy of the RPE observed in dry AMD (Mastellos & Lambris, 2024; Regillo & Heier, n.d.). Moreover, preclinical studies have demonstrated that complement blockade via agents such as pegcetacoplan lowers sub-RPE deposit formation and inflammasome priming, processes intimately linked to lysosomal dysfunction and chronic inflammation (Liao et al., 2020; Lamers et al., 2022). Collectively, the mechanism of action of pegcetacoplan encompasses both direct inhibition of complement-driven inflammatory processes and indirect protection of intracellular catabolic functions in the RPE, thereby addressing two core pathological contributors to geographic atrophy (Kassa et al., 2019; Rubner et al., 2022).

Expected Effect  
Based on its detailed mechanism of action, pegcetacoplan is expected to exert a dual beneficial effect in the management of dry AMD. First, by binding to and inhibiting complement C3, it should markedly reduce the formation of inflammatory mediators (C3a, C3b) as well as downstream terminal pathway components such as the MAC. Clinical trial data support this expectation: in the Phase II FILLY study, monthly intravitreal injections of pegcetacoplan were associated with a roughly 29% reduction in the rate of GA lesion growth relative to control, while an alternate-month regimen achieved a 20% reduction (Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023; Patel et al., 2022). These anatomical outcomes are presumed to correlate with a slowing of disease progression and a delay in the onset of irreversible retinal degeneration.  
Second, through the inhibition of MAC deposition on RPE cells, pegcetacoplan is anticipated to preserve the functional integrity of lysosomes by ensuring that v-ATPase activity is maintained and that cathepsin D retains its proteolytic function. The preservation of lysosomal function is critical not only for the proper degradation of photoreceptor outer segment debris but also for protecting RPE cells from metabolic stress and subsequent cell death (Liao et al., 2020; Desai & Dugel, 2022). Consequently, the expected biochemical outcome is that pegcetacoplan will reduce lysosomal overload and the accumulation of toxic metabolic by-products—a process thought to contribute to the formation of sub-RPE deposits that further exacerbate tissue atrophy in dry AMD (Lamers et al., 2022; Desai & Dugel, 2022).  
At the cellular level, maintaining cathepsin D activity is imperative because this protease is responsible for degrading intracellular waste products that accumulate in RPE cells, and its functionality is closely tied to the acidic environment provided by lysosomes. By preserving this aspect of lysosomal physiology, pegcetacoplan should contribute to RPE cell survival and thereby delay the progression of geographic atrophy (Patel et al., 2022). Although improvements in functional endpoints such as visual acuity have not been immediately evident in short-term clinical trials, the principal therapeutic endpoint remains the deceleration of structural degeneration. This structural preservation is expected to eventually translate into a longer period of maintained retinal function and a postponed deterioration in vision, ultimately extending the window during which patients can retain functional vision (Wu & Sun, 2019; Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023).  
Furthermore, the established dosing regimens—with monthly or alternate-month intravitreal injections—are designed to sustain local complement inhibition at therapeutic levels without causing excessive immunosuppression that might predispose patients to infections. However, some studies have raised concerns about an increased risk of conversion to exudative AMD (wet AMD) during treatment, signaling that while the inhibition of C3 can preserve RPE integrity, careful monitoring is warranted to manage potential adverse events (Regillo & Heier, n.d.; Rubner et al., 2022).

Overall Evaluation  
A comprehensive review of pegcetacoplan as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD reveals a well-substantiated rationale and a promising clinical profile, albeit with some challenges that must be addressed. One of the most compelling strengths of pegcetacoplan is its precise molecular targeting of complement component C3—a central mediator in the complement cascade. By inhibiting C3, pegcetacoplan effectively blocks the generation of both C3a and C3b, thereby reducing pro-inflammatory signaling and preventing the formation of the membrane attack complex (MAC) (Yu & Wykoff, 2021). This upstream blockade provides a broad-spectrum mechanism capable of modulating all three complement activation pathways (classical, lectin, and alternative), which is particularly important in a multifactorial disease such as dry AMD (Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023; Lamers et al., 2022).  
Clinically, the results from the Phase II FILLY study are extremely encouraging, demonstrating a 29% reduction in GA lesion growth with monthly intravitreal administration and a 20% reduction with alternate-month dosing, outcomes that have been replicated in additional studies and served as the basis for progressing to Phase III evaluations (Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023; Patel et al., 2022; Desai & Dugel, 2022). These anatomical endpoints, while not immediately translating into measurable improvements in visual acuity, are critical surrogates for the long-term preservation of retinal structure and function—a key goal in the management of dry AMD (Regillo & Heier, n.d.; Patel et al., 2022).  
Biochemically, pegcetacoplan’s mechanism of action extends beyond the mere suppression of complement-mediated inflammation. Its ability to indirectly preserve lysosomal function by preventing MAC-induced dysfunction of the vacuolar H⁺-ATPase (v-ATPase) and maintaining cathepsin D activity introduces a novel paradigm in addressing the intracellular stress that accelerates RPE degeneration (Liao et al., 2020; Mastellos & Lambris, 2024). In dry AMD, the accumulation of metabolic by-products due to deficient lysosomal degradation leads to the formation of drusen and sub-RPE deposits, which further stimulate complement activation and create a vicious cycle of cellular damage. Pegcetacoplan, by protecting lysosomal integrity, offers the potential to break this cycle and slow the progression of geographic atrophy (Park et al., 2021; Kassa et al., 2019).  
There are, however, certain weaknesses and challenges that must be taken into account. One notable concern is the increased risk of new-onset exudative AMD that has been reported in some clinical studies. This adverse event appears to be dose-dependent and may reflect a complex interplay between complement inhibition and pro-angiogenic pathways in the retina (Wu & Sun, 2019; Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023). The occurrence of neovascular complications necessitates rigorous patient selection criteria, close imaging surveillance, and potentially the development of combination strategies to counterbalance this risk without compromising the therapeutic efficacy against GA (Lamers et al., 2022; Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023).  
Another challenge is the logistical and patient adherence issues related to frequent intravitreal injections. Although the PEGylation of pegcetacoplan aids in prolonging its ocular residence, the need for repeated injections every month or every other month represents a significant treatment burden. This may affect patient compliance and overall treatment outcomes, particularly when compared to therapies that require less frequent dosing or alternative delivery modalities (Piri & Kaplan, 2023; Petrukhin, 2020). Future work aimed at developing sustained-release formulations or implantable devices could potentially alleviate this drawback (Lamers et al., 2022; Patel et al., 2022).  
From a mechanistic standpoint, while the inhibition of C3 is expected to preserve lysosomal function by protecting v-ATPase activity and sustaining cathepsin D levels, further research is needed to fully elucidate the downstream biochemical consequences of long-term complement inhibition. Detailed studies evaluating biomarkers of lysosomal function—including cathepsin D activity, lysosomal pH, and the turnover of sub-RPE deposits—will be instrumental in correlating these molecular effects with clinical outcomes (Desai & Dugel, 2022; Rubner et al., 2022). Such investigations are essential not only for optimizing dosing regimens but also for refining patient selection strategies, ensuring that those most likely to benefit from complement inhibition are appropriately targeted (Rubner et al., 2022; Patel et al., 2022).  
In addition, it is worth noting that while the current clinical evidence has predominantly focused on anatomical endpoints such as GA lesion size, translating these findings into meaningful improvements in vision remains an ongoing challenge. The disconnect between structural preservation and functional outcomes is a well-recognized issue in dry AMD research and may require additional therapeutic interventions or combination approaches to achieve robust clinical benefits (Patel et al., 2022; Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023).  
Overall, the benefit–risk profile of pegcetacoplan remains favorable when considered in the context of a disease with a profound unmet medical need. Its dual-action mechanism—combining potent complement inhibition with the preservation of intracellular lysosomal function—addresses both extracellular inflammatory processes and the intracellular degradative pathways that contribute to RPE cell loss and GA progression (Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023; Mastellos & Lambris, 2024). Moreover, the clinical trial data, particularly the significant reduction in GA lesion progression observed in the FILLY study, provide a compelling rationale for further investment in pegcetacoplan’s development for dry AMD (Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023; Patel et al., 2022).

Further optimization of the dosing regimen, exploration of sustained-release formulations, and rigorous monitoring for conversion to exudative AMD are critical next steps that will determine the long-term viability of this agent in clinical practice (Tzoumas et al., 2023; Lamers et al., 2022). In addition, combination therapies targeting complementary pathogenic pathways—such as oxidative stress and dysregulated angiogenesis—may augment the efficacy of pegcetacoplan and help mitigate its potential adverse effects (Halawa et al., 2021; Qin et al., 2021).

It has been observed to inhibit the phosphorylation of IκBα, which prevents the nuclear translocation of NF-κB and subsequent transcription of inflammatory cytokines such as TNF-α and IL-6 (Lei et al., 2017, pp. 13–17; Choudhary & Malek, 2016, pp. 4–6). This dual role in lipid regulation and inflammation attenuation is central to its therapeutic promise in AMD, where chronic inflammation and disrupted lipid processing are major determinants of disease progression.

Expected Effect:  
In the context of dry AMD, with its hallmark drusen deposits and RPE dysfunction, the expected therapeutic effect of T0901317 is multifold. By activating LXRs in RPE cells, T0901317 is expected to upregulate the expression of ABCA1 and other cholesterol efflux mediators, thereby reducing the intracellular build‐up of cholesterol and oxidized lipids that contribute to drusen formation (Choudhary et al., 2020, pp. 2–4). This increase in cholesterol efflux would allow the RPE to better clear lipid debris, lowering the overall lipid burden on Bruch’s membrane. Concomitantly, the drug’s capacity to augment lysosomal function is anticipated to result in improved clearance of extracellular drusen components via a cathepsin D–dependent mechanism. Enhanced v-ATPase assembly and lysosomal acidification, as demonstrated by increased CTSD activity in vitro, should restore the degradative capacity of the lysosomal system, thereby facilitating the removal of protein-lipid aggregates (Lei et al., 2017, pp. 25–33).

Furthermore, the activation of autophagy pathways and promotion of mitophagy are expected to counteract the mitochondrial dysfunction that characterizes aged RPE cells—an integral pathological feature of dry AMD (Choudhary et al., 2020, pp. 7–9, 2–4). The anticipated result is a restoration of cellular homeostasis, improved energy metabolism, and reduction in oxidative stress, all of which are essential for maintaining RPE cell integrity. RPE cells have been shown to express both LXRα and LXRβ, and their expression is frequently diminished in AMD-affected eyes (Choudhary et al., 2020, pp. 12–13; Lyssenko et al., 2018, pp. 1–3). Therefore, by boosting LXR activity, T0901317 not only counteracts lipid dysregulation but also provides a neuroprotective, anti-inflammatory benefit by modulating cytokine production and dampening microglial activation in the outer retina (Choudhary & Malek, 2016, pp. 4–6).

Overall Evaluation:  
The overall assessment of T0901317 as a therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration is cautiously optimistic, with several key strengths as well as notable limitations that warrant further investigation.  

Strengths:  
One of the primary advantages of T0901317 is its well-documented ability to activate LXRs and thereby induce a broad spectrum of beneficial responses relevant to dry AMD pathology. The compound’s capacity to upregulate ABCA1 expression is critical, as impaired cholesterol efflux is a central mechanism underlying the accumulation of lipid-rich drusen (Choudhary et al., 2020, pp. 15–16, 12–13). Moreover, its ability to enhance lysosomal enzyme expression and promote v-ATPase assembly is particularly promising for the restoration of lysosomal acidity—a key defect in aged RPE cells that contributes to decreased clearance of toxic lipid deposits (Lei et al., 2017, pp. 13–17, 20–22). In addition, the induction of autophagy and mitophagy following LXR activation offers a dual therapeutic benefit by promoting the removal of damaged mitochondria and reducing oxidative stress, thereby preserving RPE cell viability (Xie et al., 2022, pp. 1–2). The anti-inflammatory properties of T0901317, demonstrated by its inhibition of NF-κB signaling and reduction of pro-inflammatory cytokine production, further support its potential utility in addressing the chronic low-grade inflammation often observed in AMD (Choudhary & Malek, 2016, pp. 4–6). Collectively, these mechanisms directly target the multifactorial aspects of dry AMD pathology—namely, lipid dysregulation, lysosomal dysfunction, and inflammatory stress—making T0901317 an attractive candidate for repurposing in this indication (Choudhary et al., 2020, pp. 2–4).

Another significant strength is the potential for ocular delivery strategies to mitigate the systemic side effects associated with T0901317. Given that systemic administration of LXR agonists has been linked to adverse metabolic effects such as hypertriglyceridemia and off-target activation of nuclear receptors like FXR and PXR (Lei et al., 2017, pp. 20–22; Storti et al., 2019, pp. 15–16), localized ocular delivery could concentrate the drug’s therapeutic effects in the retina while minimizing systemic exposure. This approach may overcome one of the principal limitations of T0901317 and reposition it as a viable option specifically for retinal applications.

Weaknesses and Challenges:  
Despite these promising attributes, there are several challenges that temper the enthusiasm for T0901317 as a first-in-class therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. A well-recognized limitation of T0901317 is its lack of absolute specificity for LXRs. Its ability to activate other nuclear receptors such as FXR and PXR raises concerns about off-target effects that could lead to dysregulated lipid metabolism in non-ocular tissues, systemic toxicity, and unwanted metabolic side effects such as hepatic steatosis and hyperlipidemia (Lei et al., 2017, pp. 20–22). Moreover, while preclinical evidence in cell culture and murine models has shown that LXR activation can reverse lipid accumulation and partially restore RPE cell function, the translation of such effects to the human condition—especially over the chronic time course of dry AMD—remains to be conclusively demonstrated (Choudhary et al., 2020, pp. 12–13, 7–9).

Another challenge lies in the fact that many preclinical studies have used alternative LXR agonists such as GW3965, which may exhibit a more favorable safety profile compared to T0901317 (Choudhary et al., 2020, pp. 9–11; Peters et al., 2022, pp. 11–12). The potential differences in selectivity and off-target activity between T0901317 and these other compounds necessitate a careful comparison. It is possible that while T0901317 has provided invaluable mechanistic insights into LXR biology in the retina, compounds with improved specificity may eventually be more amenable to clinical development. Furthermore, the specific hypothesis regarding T0901317’s ability to enhance lysosomal acidity and cathepsin D-dependent clearance of drusen components is based on in vitro observations, and there is still a need for more comprehensive studies that document these effects in animal models that recapitulate the chronic aspects of dry AMD pathology (Lei et al., 2017, pp. 25–33; Choudhary et al., 2020, pp. 2–4).

Additionally, because the retinal environment is highly specialized and the RPE plays a central role in maintaining photoreceptor health, any therapeutic approach must carefully balance metabolic reprogramming with preservation of essential RPE functions. Overactivation of autophagy or lysosomal pathways might conceivably lead to other cellular stresses if not properly calibrated. Thus, while the theoretical framework for T0901317’s benefit in dry AMD is strong, detailed pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic studies in appropriate models are essential before moving this candidate further along the drug development pathway.

Conclusion:  
In conclusion, T0901317 demonstrates considerable promise as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration based on its ability to activate LXR in RPE cells, thereby inducing cholesterol efflux via ABCA1 upregulation, enhancing lysosomal function through increased expression of hydrolases like cathepsin D, promoting autophagy and mitophagy, and reducing inflammation by dampening NF-κB signaling (Choudhary et al., 2020, pp. 12–13; Terao et al., 2024, pp. 8–10).

The strengths of T0901317 lie in its robust mechanistic rationale, the preclinical evidence supporting LXR-mediated restoration of cholesterol homeostasis, and the potential for localized ocular delivery to minimize systemic toxicities. However, its known off-target effects, particularly activation of other nuclear receptor pathways that can lead to metabolic side effects, present a significant hurdle that must be addressed through formulation optimization and dosing strategies (Lei et al., 2017, pp. 20–22; Storti et al., 2019, pp. 15–16). Furthermore, while the mechanistic underpinnings are appealing, further in vivo validation in chronic, clinically relevant AMD models is essential to confirm that the improvements in cholesterol efflux and lysosomal function translate into meaningful therapeutic outcomes—in terms of slowing or reversing the progression of dry AMD. Overall, T0901317 represents a promising, though challenging, candidate for addressing the unmet need in dry AMD therapy. Investment in additional preclinical studies focusing on ocular bioavailability, long-term safety in the retinal microenvironment, and optimization of dosing regimens will be critical in determining whether T0901317 or a similarly acting, perhaps more selective, LXR agonist can progress into clinical evaluation for dry AMD. The strategic focus on lipid-driven dysfunction, particularly in lysosomal clearance pathways, offers a novel mechanism of action that could complement or serve as an alternative to current therapeutic approaches, making T0901317 (or its optimized derivatives) a compelling candidate for further investigation (Choudhary et al., 2020, pp. 2–4, 7–9, 13–17).

Below is our comprehensive evaluation of SB290157 as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD), with a focus on its chemical origin, its therapeutic history, the detailed mechanism of action at the molecular level, the expected pharmacological effects in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) models, and an overall assessment of strengths and weaknesses.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
SB290157 is a fully synthetic, nonpeptidic small‐molecule agent originally discovered as a selective antagonist of the complement anaphylatoxin C3a receptor (C3aR). Chemically, it is defined as N2-[(2,2-diphenylethoxy)acetyl]-L-arginine and was identified via high-throughput screening of chemical libraries using membranes from cells stably expressing human C3aR, such as RBL-2H3 cells (Ames et al., 2001). The lead compound was chemically optimized from an initial hit (SKF 63649) to improve affinity and potency, and its synthesis has been well described using peptide–like solid‐phase synthetic strategies (e.g., Fmoc protecting group chemistry on Wang resin) thereby yielding a compound with high purity (≥95%) and reproducible physicochemical properties (Ames et al., 2001). SB290157 belongs to a class of compounds that modulate G protein–coupled receptors (GPCRs), in this case a complement receptor, and similar nonpeptidic small‐molecule ligands have been employed in preclinical studies to probe inflammatory pathways in various disease states (Iyer et al., 2017; Ames et al., 2001). Its discovery set an important precedent for the therapeutic targeting of complement receptors, especially given the historical absence of potent, selective C3aR antagonists, and it has been widely used as a research tool in animal models and cell-based assays to interrogate the physiological roles of C3a/C3aR signaling (Ames et al., 2001).

Therapeutic History:  
SB290157 has been extensively employed in preclinical models to examine the role of C3aR in inflammation and immune modulation. In early studies, it was shown to antagonize C3a-induced intracellular calcium mobilization and receptor internalization in RBL-2H3 cells and human neutrophils, with reported IC50 values in the low-nanomolar range (approximately 27–30 nM), suggesting robust antagonism under defined experimental conditions (Ames et al., 2001). In vivo, SB290157 demonstrated antiinflammatory efficacy by reducing neutrophil recruitment in guinea pig models of lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-induced airway neutrophilia and by decreasing paw edema in rat adjuvant-induced arthritis models through intraperitoneal dosing (Ames et al., 2001). Although valuable as a pharmacological probe, its history is mired by concerns as several subsequent investigations indicated that SB290157 can exhibit partial agonist activity—depending on the assay system and receptor expression context—and even engage an off-target complement receptor, C5aR2, to induce β-arrestin recruitment (Coulthard, 2015; Li et al., 2021; Mathieu et al., 2005). With more than 70 publications referencing its use, SB290157 remains one of the most commonly used C3aR inhibitors; however, it is essentially confined to the research arena and has never reached clinical development for AMD or other indications (Li et al., 2021).  
There is emerging evidence in ophthalmologic research relevant to dry AMD. For example, an in vitro human fetal RPE cell model has shown that complement fragment C3a can drive the formation of sub-retinal pigment epithelium deposits via dysregulation of the ubiquitin proteasome pathway; importantly, co-application of SB290157 with recombinant C3a in these cultures prevented the abnormal deposit formation, suggesting that C3aR blockade can modulate key pathological events relevant to AMD pathogenesis (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). Despite this promising mechanistic link, SB290157 itself has not been advanced clinically, and its use in retinal models remains primarily exploratory. Moreover, the existence of antagonistic and agonistic properties in various assay systems necessitates careful interpretation of its efficacy when contemplating the translation to human ocular diseases (Iyer et al., 2017; Li et al., 2021).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, SB290157 has been characterized as a competitive antagonist that binds to the orthosteric site of the C3a receptor, thereby inhibiting the native ligand, C3a, from eliciting its downstream signaling responses. In classic radioligand binding assays using 125I-labeled C3a, SB290157 displaces the radiolabeled peptide with an IC50 of ~200 nM, indicating it competes effectively with C3a (Ames et al., 2001). Functionally, this displacement correlates with inhibition of C3a-induced intracellular calcium mobilization, a key second messenger response mediated via G-protein coupling to pertussis-toxin–sensitive Gi/o proteins (Ames et al., 2001). Additionally, SB290157 has been shown to block C3a-mediated receptor internalization in immune cells, further supporting its role in antagonizing C3aR activation (Ames et al., 2001; Iyer et al., 2017).  
Beyond the canonical receptor blockade, several studies have pointed out that SB290157’s activity is highly context-dependent. In systems where C3aR is overexpressed—such as recombinant CHO or transfected RBL cells—SB290157 can paradoxically act as an agonist to trigger intracellular signaling cascades like ERK phosphorylation, potentially due to rapid receptor desensitization or kinetic differences in ligand-receptor interaction (Coulthard, 2015; Li et al., 2021; Mathieu et al., 2005). Moreover, its off-target partial agonism at the closely related receptor C5aR2 has been documented, wherein it mediates β-arrestin recruitment at higher concentrations, thereby dampening C5a-induced ERK signaling in primary macrophages (Li et al., 2021; Mathieu et al., 2005). Such dual or biased pharmacological properties underscore that SB290157’s molecular actions cannot be solely categorized as pure antagonism without considering assay conditions and cell contexts (Li et al., 2021; Mathieu et al., 2005).  
In the context of RPE cells, C3a binding to C3aR is hypothesized to disrupt intracellular calcium homeostasis, leading to lysosomal alkalinization—a key factor that impairs the maturation and proteolytic activity of lysosomal enzymes such as cathepsin D (CTSD). Cathepsin D is critical for proper turnover of extracellular matrix (ECM) components and degradation of proteinaceous aggregates; its dysfunction is implicated in drusen formation, a hallmark of dry AMD (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). By competitively inhibiting C3a binding, SB290157 is expected to mitigate abnormal Ca2+ signaling, maintain lysosomal acidification, and therefore preserve CTSD processing and activity, which in turn would prevent or lessen the accumulation of drusen-like deposits (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018; Iyer et al., 2017). This proposed mechanism is supported by the observation that in hfRPE cultures, SB290157 co-application with C3a prevented both the upregulation of C3aR expression and the subsequent deposition of abnormal ECM structures (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). Nonetheless, the precise molecular interactions at the receptor—the positioning of the diphenylethoxy moiety and arginine side chain—is critical for binding affinity and selectivity (Iyer et al., 2017; Mishra et al., 2025), and minor alterations in these interactions might contribute to the observed functional variability.

Expected Effect:  
Based on the hypothesis for dry AMD, SB290157 is expected to act on RPE cells by antagonizing the C3aR, thereby preventing the cascade of intracellular events that lead to lysosomal stress. In a typical RPE culture assay where C3a is exogenously added—thereby simulating enhanced complement activity as observed in AMD—SB290157 should block C3a binding, which would normally result in the perturbation of lysosomal pH homeostasis. The blockade of this receptor is envisaged to preserve the normally acidic lysosomal environment required for the optimal maturation and proteolytic function of cathepsin D (CTSD), an enzyme whose dysfunction is implicated in the formation of drusen and the progression of dry AMD (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018; Iyer et al., 2017).  
Furthermore, by preserving lysosomal function, SB290157 is expected to reduce subsequent activation of the inflammasome—a multi-protein complex that is triggered when lysosomal destabilization occurs—and thus attenuate the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-1β. This cascade is particularly relevant because chronic inflammation is thought to drive many of the degenerative changes associated with AMD (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). In vitro, RPE cells pre-treated with SB290157 before C3a challenge would be anticipated to maintain normal lysosomal acidity (measured by appropriate pH-sensitive dyes), exhibit proper CTSD processing (as observed by Western blot analysis for mature cathepsin D forms), and display reduced markers of inflammasome activation such as caspase-1 cleavage and IL-1β release. Gene expression studies in these cells might also reveal normalized levels of key ECM components and proteases, ultimately leading to a reduction in sub-RPE deposit accumulation (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018).  
It is important to note that C3aR is expressed on RPE cells and its activation has been implicated in additional downstream effects—including modulation of the ubiquitin proteasome pathway and extracellular matrix turnover—which further contribute to cell dysfunction and deposit formation. Therefore, antagonism of C3aR by SB290157, if effective and selective, could theoretically interrupt this pathogenic cascade and offer a protective effect against drusen-mediated RPE degeneration in dry AMD (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018; Ames et al., 2001).

Overall Evaluation:  
SB290157 offers a compelling mechanistic rationale for repurposing in dry AMD given the central role of complement dysregulation in the pathogenesis of the disease. Among its strengths is a well-documented ability to block C3a-induced signaling events across multiple preclinical models. Early characterizations demonstrated that SB290157 effectively inhibited intracellular Ca2+ mobilization, receptor internalization, and other pro-inflammatory events in both immune cells and engineered cell systems (Ames et al., 2001). Its application in an hfRPE model demonstrated that C3a-induced sub-RPE deposit formation can be reversed upon treatment with SB290157, underscoring its potential utility in preventing one of the critical pathological features of dry AMD (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). Furthermore, the known rodent tolerability and defined in vivo pharmacokinetics observed in other disease models—such as LPS-induced airway inflammation and adjuvant-induced arthritis—support the concept that SB290157 can be delivered systemically with demonstrable pharmacodynamic effects (Ames et al., 2001).  

However, several weaknesses temper enthusiasm for immediate clinical translation. A significant concern is the compound’s context-dependent pharmacology. Multiple studies have reported that SB290157 can function as a partial or even full agonist under certain conditions, particularly in overexpression systems, and paradoxically activate C3aR instead of inhibiting it (Coulthard, 2015; Li et al., 2021; Mathieu et al., 2005). Such functional divergence is critical when considering a therapy designed to block a deleterious signal in a delicate tissue such as the retina. Moreover, SB290157 has been shown to exhibit off-target effects, including partial agonism at C5aR2—a related complement receptor—which may confound downstream anti-inflammatory responses and produce unintended biological effects (Li et al., 2021; Mathieu et al., 2005).  
Additionally, while there is evidence of efficacy in non-ocular models and even in an hfRPE culture system, there is a paucity of robust in vivo data specifically demonstrating efficacy in ocular or AMD preclinical models. Modern translational approaches demand rigorous evaluation of pharmacokinetics, tissue penetration, ocular tolerability, and local off-target activity in the complex microenvironment of the eye—data that remain limited for SB290157 in the AMD setting (Iyer et al., 2017; Li et al., 2021). Furthermore, owing to its reputation as a “controversial” tool compound, some in the field recommend the use of complementary genetic models (e.g., C3aR knockout mice) to validate findings derived from its use (Coulthard, 2015; Li et al., 2021). This underscores the need for next-generation C3aR antagonists with improved selectivity and a more predictable pharmacodynamic profile if the goal is clinical translation for dry AMD.  

In summary, SB290157 has strong theoretical appeal as a means to interrupt a pathological complement cascade that leads to lysosomal dysfunction, impaired CTSD maturation, and ultimately drusen formation in dry AMD. Its prior use in various inflammatory and in vitro RPE models, along with the biochemistry linking C3aR activation to intracellular Ca2+ dysregulation and lysosomal stress, supports the hypothesis that C3aR blockade may be beneficial in preserving RPE function (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018; Iyer et al., 2017). Nonetheless, the intrinsic limitations of SB290157—including its potential for agonistic behavior, off-target C5aR2 activity, and inconsistent effects across different cellular contexts—present significant challenges that must be addressed prior to advancing this candidate into clinical trials for AMD (Ames et al., 2001; Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018; Li et al., 2021).

Overall Evaluation:  
In conclusion, SB290157 is a well-characterized research tool with documented efficacy in blocking complement-mediated inflammatory responses in several animal models as well as in an hfRPE culture system, making it a promising candidate to test the hypothesis that C3aR blockade can prevent lysosomal alkalinization and CTSD dysfunction in dry AMD. Its strengths include a defined mechanism of competitive antagonism at C3aR, cross-species activity, and experimentally demonstrated protective effects against abnormal sub-RPE deposit formation. However, its context-dependent agonist behavior and off-target activation of C5aR2 raise significant concerns about its selectivity and reliability as a clinical therapeutic. Additionally, the limited data regarding ocular pharmacokinetics and direct efficacy in robust in vivo dry AMD models suggest that further validation is required. Thus, while the underlying rationale for targeting complement-mediated lysosomal dysfunction remains compelling, SB290157 is best viewed as a stepping stone toward the development of next-generation C3aR antagonists with improved pharmacological profiles for potential clinical application in dry AMD (Ames et al., 2001; Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018; Li et al., 2021).

Analysis: Candidate 1 (Ambroxol, ID 23) offers an attractive conceptual approach by leveraging pharmacological chaperone activity to improve lysosomal enzyme folding, acidification, and cathepsin D activity in RPE cells, addressing a central AMD pathology. It has established safety as a mucolytic and CNS penetrance, but zero direct preclinical or clinical data in RPE or AMD models; no ocular PK or target‐engagement evidence; and its canonical target is GCase, not CTSD or V‐ATPase in RPE. Extensive evidence gaps undermine translatability, and ocular delivery/toxicity remain uncharacterized. Candidate 2 (Temsirolimus, ID 33) embodies a well‐defined, target‐based MoA—mTORC1 inhibition to activate TFEB, upregulate lysosomal biogenesis, and enhance autophagic clearance—directly validated by rapamycin in multiple RPE AFG models (~30% lipofuscin reduction) and by temsirolimus in RPE/ endothelial cell proliferation, migration, and VEGF/PDGF assays. Temsirolimus carries known systemic and ocular injection risks and prior sirolimus GA trials failed, but its mechanism is clear, the evidence in relevant cell types is strong, and class‐based translational tools (nanoparticles, local delivery) are emerging. Overall, Temsirolimus has far stronger mechanistic and preclinical support specific to RPE/AMD, despite safety/delivery challenges, whereas Ambroxol remains speculative without any AMD‐relevant data.
Reasoning: Based on the prioritization of direct, disease‐relevant preclinical evidence, mechanism clarity, and target engagement in RPE models, Temsirolimus is the superior candidate. It has been mechanistically validated in RPE cells and POS‐fed assays to activate TFEB/lysosome programs and reduce autofluorescent granules, addressing core AMD pathology. Although prior GA trials with sirolimus were negative and ocular safety issues exist, these can be addressed by optimized delivery and stage selection. In contrast, Ambroxol’s rationale relies entirely on extrapolation from Gaucher disease GCase chaperoning and lysosomal biology without any demonstration of CTSD or V‐ATPase modulation in RPE, no ocular PK, and no AMD‐model efficacy. Therefore, Temsirolimus presents a more actionable, evidence‐backed path to experimental success and clinical translation.
