Ambroxol is a small-molecule mucolytic historically used to thin airway mucus and has been repurposed as a pharmacological chaperone for the lysosomal enzyme glucocerebrosidase (GCase) in Gaucher disease, where it selectively binds misfolded GCase to aid folding and trafficking to lysosomes for substrate degradation (Alhowyan & Harisa, 2025, pp. 17–18). Pharmacological chaperones constitute a class of small molecules that stabilize specific mutant lysosomal enzymes conformationally in the endoplasmic reticulum, enabling correct processing and lysosomal delivery; a paradigmatic example is migalastat, an alpha-galactosidase A chaperone approved for Fabry disease with amenable variants (Alhowyan & Harisa, 2025, pp. 17–18). Ambroxol is further characterized by its ability to cross the blood–brain barrier, a property relevant for neuronopathic lysosomal storage disorders and attractive for central nervous system or ocular indications where access is otherwise constrained (Alhowyan & Harisa, 2025, pp. 17–18). Within the broader landscape of lysosomal therapeutics, small molecules also act as proteostasis regulators and modulators of lysosomal signaling and biogenesis; however, off-target actions remain a central limitation of small-molecule therapy in this domain (Alhowyan & Harisa, 2025, pp. 17–18).

The therapeutic hypothesis for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) posits that ambroxol could act as a pharmacological chaperone for lysosomal enzymes in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), stabilize or enhance vacuolar H+-ATPase (V-ATPase) function, improve lysosomal acidification, and thereby augment cathepsin D (CTSD) activity to clear lipofuscin/drusen components characteristic of dry AMD (Kaarniranta et al., 2023, pp. 2–3; Si et al., 2023, pp. 4–7). This rationale is grounded in the centrality of lysosomal function to RPE homeostasis and AMD pathogenesis: RPE lysosomes sustain heavy heterophagic and autophagic loads from daily photoreceptor outer-segment (POS) digestion, and impaired lysosomal acidification and hydrolase function contribute to lipofuscin accumulation, exosome-driven drusen formation, and progressive degeneration (Kaarniranta et al., 2023, pp. 2–3; Si et al., 2023, pp. 2–4, 5–7; Sharif, 2015, pp. 199–202). Notably, in AMD models and donor RPE, TFEB—the master transcriptional driver of lysosomal/autophagy biogenesis—is dysregulated, V-ATPase-related transcripts (e.g., ATP6VOA1) and cathepsin abundance/activity are linked to lysosomal competence, and TFEB activation or mTOR inhibition reduces toxic storage material such as A2E and POS-derived autofluorescent granules (Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7).

Therapeutic History  
Conventional use: Ambroxol is primarily used clinically as a mucolytic agent to reduce mucus viscosity in respiratory disease (Alhowyan & Harisa, 2025, pp. 17–18). Beyond its mucolytic effects, ambroxol has been investigated in lysosomal storage diseases as a pharmacological chaperone for glucocerebrosidase; it binds misfolded GCase, promotes its proper folding/trafficking to lysosomes, and facilitates substrate clearance, with reported neurological benefits in neuronopathic Gaucher disease and demonstrated blood–brain barrier penetration (Alhowyan & Harisa, 2025, pp. 17–18). Clinically observed improvements in neurological symptoms such as myoclonus and seizures have been reported in pilot studies, and reviews summarize safety/efficacy observations in Gaucher populations, albeit with the caveat of potential off-target toxicities innate to small-molecule approaches (Alhowyan & Harisa, 2025, pp. 17–18, 33–35).

Use in ophthalmology and AMD: A targeted search of ClinicalTrials.gov for ambroxol in macular degeneration, AMD, or retinal conditions returned zero registered trials, indicating a lack of clinical testing for ambroxol in AMD or retina-specific indications within that registry (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.). The provided literature excerpts contain no preclinical or clinical data demonstrating ambroxol use in RPE, retinal degeneration models, or AMD, and they do not report ocular distribution or ocular pharmacokinetics for ambroxol (Alhowyan & Harisa, 2025, pp. 17–18; Si et al., 2023, pp. 2–4; Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7). In contrast, other small-molecule interventions that modulate lysosomal/autophagy function in RPE have been reported: mTOR inhibition with rapamycin decreases A2E and lipofuscin-like granules and reduces inflammatory/angiogenic proteins; trehalose increases autophagy markers and flux and exhibits cytoprotective effects, although limitations in clinical efficacy and adverse effects are noted for mTOR inhibitors (Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7). Mechanism of Action  
Ambroxol as a pharmacological chaperone: Ambroxol binds selectively to misfolded glucocerebrosidase (GCase), stabilizing its conformation in the biosynthetic pathway and enabling correct trafficking to lysosomes, where it restores enzymatic degradation of GCase substrates (Alhowyan & Harisa, 2025, pp. 17–18). This canonical chaperone mechanism increases lysosomal GCase activity and substrate turnover and has been linked to functional improvements in Gaucher disease models and patient reports, with additional indications that ambroxol can enhance mitochondrial function in patient-derived cells (Alhowyan & Harisa, 2025, pp. 17–18). The drug’s small-molecule nature and CNS penetrance differentiate it from enzyme-replacement approaches and position it within a class of proteostasis-modulating agents where target-specific engagement can produce organelle-level functional rescue but also carries risk of off-target interactions (Alhowyan & Harisa, 2025, pp. 17–18).

RPE lysosomal biology relevant to the hypothesis: In the RPE, lysosomal acidification is primarily established by the V-ATPase proton pump and is essential for optimal activity of luminal hydrolases including cathepsins; most lysosomal enzymes are exquisitely pH-dependent and lose activity when lysosomal pH is elevated (Markitantova & Simirskii, 2025, pp. 9–11; Kaarniranta et al., 2023, pp. 2–3). RPE lysosomes operate at the nexus of two degradative streams: heterophagy of POS (requiring efficient phagosome–lysosome fusion and acidic hydrolase activity) and macroautophagy/CMA for damaged proteins and organelles, both of which are dysregulated with aging and AMD-relevant stresses such as oxidative damage and advanced glycation end-products (AGEs) (Si et al., 2023, pp. 4–5; Kaarniranta et al., 2023, pp. 2–3; Sharif, 2015, pp. 199–202). CTSD is a key RPE lysosomal aspartic protease and the principal POS-degrading enzyme; CTSD loss causes retinal degeneration in mice, underscoring its nonredundant role (Si et al., 2023, pp. 4–5). In AMD, human donor RPE show decreased CTSD and CTSL levels/activities, increased TFEB phosphorylation with reduced nuclear localization, and impaired degradative capacity with accumulation of POS-dependent lipofuscin-like granules; activating TFEB in RPE increases CLEAR network gene expression including ATP6VOA1 (a V-ATPase subunit) and reduces POS-derived lipofuscin-like granules (Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7). Oxidized bisretinoids such as A2E, a major lipofuscin component, inhibit V-ATPase and raise lysosomal pH in RPE, which decreases lysosomal enzyme function and impairs cargo hydrolysis—a direct mechanism linking storage material to acidification defects (Wang et al., 2023, pp. 11–13). Lipofuscin and its photoproducts can further inhibit lysosomal proton pumps or hydrolases and promote lysosomal membrane permeabilization, coupling storage to organelle damage and propagating autophagy-lysosomal dysfunction and inflammatory signaling (Si et al., 2023, pp. 5–7; Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 2–4).

Signal control of lysosomal biogenesis and acidification in RPE: The V-ATPase–mTORC1–TFEB axis is central in RPE lysosomal homeostasis; CRYBA1/βA3/A1-crystallin directly regulates the V-ATPase and signals to mTORC1 at the lysosomal membrane, where mTORC1 activity controls TFEB phosphorylation and localization (phosphorylated TFEB is cytosolic; dephosphorylation permits nuclear translocation and activation of CLEAR network genes) (Kaarniranta et al., 2023, pp. 2–3; Markitantova & Simirskii, 2025, pp. 9–11; Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7). Pharmacologic mTOR inhibition (e.g., rapamycin) shifts TFEB toward an active dephosphorylated state, increases autophagic flux, reduces A2E, and decreases lipofuscin-like granules in RPE and POS-fed models, with the reduction in storage material being dependent on active lysosomal enzymes and TFEB activation (Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7). Expected Effect  
Pathway-level expectation if the hypothesis holds: If ambroxol acts as a pharmacological chaperone for lysosomal enzymes expressed in RPE and indirectly improves V-ATPase-dependent acidification, one would expect increased lysosomal hydrolase maturation/activity (including CTSD), restoration of acidic lysosomal pH, improved autophagosome–lysosome fusion and autophagic flux, and enhanced clearance of POS-derived material and lipofuscin components (Si et al., 2023, pp. 4–7; Markitantova & Simirskii, 2025, pp. 9–11). In RPE cells subjected to AMD-relevant stressors (e.g., A2E loading, AGEs-modified substrates), improved acidification and hydrolase function should reduce accumulation of autofluorescent granules and mitigate the need for exosome-mediated egress of undegraded material implicated in drusen formation (Sharif, 2015, pp. 68–72, 199–202; Grilo, 2014, pp. 42–46). Because TFEB activation robustly upregulates lysosomal biogenesis and can decrease lipofuscin-like material, intersecting ambroxol effects with TFEB–mTORC1 signaling and V-ATPase subunit expression (e.g., ATP6VOA1) would be logical endpoints for mechanistic alignment, even though ambroxol has not been shown to modulate TFEB in RPE (Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7).

Assay predictions and measurable readouts: In RPE-like cells (ARPE-19, primary human RPE), relevant readouts to substantiate the hypothesis include:  
- Lysosomal pH measurements showing acidification relative to stressed controls; for comparison, A2E raises lysosomal pH via V-ATPase inhibition in RPE (Wang et al., 2023, pp. 11–13).  
- CTSD maturation (pro-CTSD to mature CTSD) and enzymatic activity assays, given RPE dependence on CTSD for POS degradation and its documented reduction in AMD RPE (Si et al., 2023, pp. 4–5; Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7).  
- V-ATPase function and expression, including ATP6VOA1 transcript/protein, as TFEB target and acidification determinant (Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7).  
- TFEB localization and CLEAR network gene expression, to assess upstream biogenesis signaling that correlates with lysosomal competence (Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7).  
- POS degradation capacity and lipofuscin-like autofluorescent granule burden after POS feeding, a disease-relevant functional output sensitive to lysosomal hydrolase and acidification status (Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7; Sharif, 2015, pp. 189–192).  
- Drusen-relevant surrogate readouts such as exosome marker release (CD63, CD81) and extracellular debris deposition under conditions of impaired lysosomal flux versus pharmacologic rescue (Grilo, 2014, pp. 42–46; Sharif, 2015, pp. 199–202).

Strength of biological rationale: The centrality of lysosomal dysfunction to RPE degeneration in dry AMD is well-supported: lysosomal enzyme activity declines with aging and stress, lipofuscin accumulates and inhibits proton pumps/hydrolases, lysosomal acidification is critical for hydrolase function, and impaired lysosome–autophagy flux contributes to intracellular overload, exosome-mediated debris export, drusen formation, and inflammation (Kaarniranta et al., 2023, pp. 2–5; Si et al., 2023, pp. 5–7; Sharif, 2015, pp. 199–202). CTSD is a principal POS-degrading protease in RPE and is reduced in human AMD donor tissue, making strategies that restore CTSD maturation/activity and lysosomal acidification compelling (Si et al., 2023, pp. 4–5; Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7). Against this backdrop, small-molecule chaperones are an attractive modality because they can enhance endogenous lysosomal enzyme folding/trafficking and potentially boost organelle function without gene transfer; ambroxol exemplifies this approach in GCase biology, with CNS penetration and clinical observations supporting feasibility in lysosomal disease (Alhowyan & Harisa, 2025, pp. 17–18).

Evidence weaknesses specific to ambroxol in AMD: Despite the strong organelle-level rationale, the ambroxol-specific data package for AMD is essentially absent in the provided record: no RPE cell data, no measurements of lysosomal pH or V-ATPase stabilization, no CTSD maturation/activity rescue, no POS degradation assays, no lipofuscin/A2E clearance, and no in vivo retinal outcomes are reported here (Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7; Markitantova & Simirskii, 2025, pp. 9–11). The mechanistic extrapolation—ambroxol chaperoning broadly for lysosomal enzymes in RPE and stabilizing V-ATPase—is unsubstantiated; ambroxol’s demonstrated chaperone target is GCase, not CTSD or V-ATPase, and the literature provided explicitly notes the lack of small-molecule pharmacological chaperones targeting CTSD deficiency or V-ATPase impairment in RPE/AMD models (Alhowyan & Harisa, 2025, pp. 17–18; Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7). Furthermore, while small molecules can manipulate lysosomal pH in either direction (e.g., chloroquine deacidifies; acidic nanoparticles re-acidify), these findings emphasize the need for target-specific validation and caution regarding retinal toxicity from lysosomotropic agents; none of these pharmacologies have been tied to ambroxol in RPE (Alhowyan & Harisa, 2025, pp. 14–15).

Translational considerations and risk: The absence of ocular PK and target engagement data is a major liability for advancing ambroxol toward AMD; lysosomal pharmacology in post-mitotic RPE under chronic oxidative and lipofuscin stress likely differs from LSD contexts, and direct evidence of RPE target engagement is needed to justify escalation (Si et al., 2023, pp. 2–4; Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 2–4). It is also noteworthy that mTOR inhibitors—which validated TFEB-mediated lysosomal rescue in RPE models—have shown limited efficacy and adverse effects in clinical settings, highlighting the translational friction even when mechanisms are strong (Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7). Given that CTSD is pH-dependent and V-ATPase inhibition by lipofuscin bisretinoids is a proximal defect in AMD RPE, any candidate must demonstrate re-acidification and hydrolase restoration under A2E load to be credible; absent such data for ambroxol, the mechanistic chain remains hypothetical (Wang et al., 2023, pp. 11–13; Markitantova & Simirskii, 2025, pp. 9–11). Finally, because impaired lysosomal clearance increases exosome release and contributes to drusen, measuring exosome markers and extracellular deposit proxies will be important to link intracellular rescue to extracellular AMD hallmarks, but ambroxol lacks such evidence here (Sharif, 2015, pp. 199–202; Grilo, 2014, pp. 42–46).

Programmatic recommendation and experimental path: At this stage, ambroxol should not advance directly to in vivo retinal studies or clinical exploration for dry AMD without foundational RPE data demonstrating lysosomal acidification rescue and CTSD activity enhancement under AMD-relevant stressors (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.). A rigorous, staged preclinical plan is warranted:  
- In vitro RPE assays under A2E and POS-fed conditions to quantify lysosomal pH, V-ATPase subunit expression (ATP6VOA1), TFEB nuclear translocation/CLEAR activation, CTSD maturation/activity, POS degradation kinetics, and lipofuscin-like autofluorescence, with rapamycin and trehalose as mechanistically validated comparators (Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7; Wang et al., 2023, pp. 11–13).  
- Lysosomal membrane integrity tests and CTSD leakage assessment in CFH Y402H RPE models to probe stabilization of lysosomal compartments under genetic risk backgrounds (Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 4–5).  
- Exosome marker release and extracellular deposit assays to link intracellular lysosomal rescue to drusen-relevant phenotypes (Grilo, 2014, pp. 42–46).  
- Ocular exposure assessment to confirm ambroxol reaches RPE at pharmacologically active concentrations using appropriate delivery routes; absent ocular PK data in the provided literature, this becomes a gating requirement (Alhowyan & Harisa, 2025, pp. 17–18).

Overall, ambroxol’s demonstrated chaperone activity for GCase, BBB penetration, and clinical observations in Gaucher disease establish it as a plausible proteostasis-modulating scaffold, but the lack of any RPE/AMD-directed mechanistic or efficacy evidence and the absence of ocular PK data create a high translational risk profile for dry AMD (Alhowyan & Harisa, 2025, pp. 17–18; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.). By contrast, interventions that directly activate TFEB or modulate mTOR have documented efficacy in RPE models, though clinical translation hurdles remain, and this suggests that ambroxol should be benchmarked against these pathways in a preclinical setting before any programmatic commitment (Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Temsirolimus (CCI-779; Torisel) is a semi-synthetic ester prodrug of sirolimus (rapamycin) discovered during rapamycin medicinal chemistry optimization to improve formulation properties and pharmacokinetics; it is a first-generation “rapalog” that inhibits mTOR by forming an intracellular complex with FKBP12 and binding the FRB domain of mTOR, thereby allosterically inhibiting mTORC1 catalytic signaling (and only indirectly affecting mTORC2) (Wang et al., 2022). As a class, rapalogs are derived from the natural macrolide rapamycin originally isolated from Streptomyces hygroscopicus; they have been used systemically as immunosuppressants and anti-proliferative/anti-angiogenic agents in oncology and transplant medicine by suppressing mTORC1-dependent growth and inflammatory programs (Wang et al., 2022; Johnson, 2013). mTORC1 is a lysosome-proximal signaling hub that integrates amino acid sufficiency via the Ragulator–Rag GTPase machinery and growth/energy signals via Rheb/AMPK, coordinating anabolism (protein synthesis via S6K and 4E-BP1), and repressing catabolism (autophagy and lysosomal biogenesis) (Johnson, 2013). In ocular biology, temsirolimus has been evaluated preclinically in human retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells and human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVEC), consistently demonstrating dose-dependent inhibition of proliferation and migration and decreased VEGF/PDGF expression through mTOR pathway inhibition, supporting target engagement in retinal cell types relevant to AMD pathogenesis (Liegl et al., 2014). Compared with rapamycin, temsirolimus has higher aqueous solubility and stability but is administered intravenously in approved oncology indications; adverse events include metabolic and mucosal toxicities typical of systemic mTOR inhibition (Wang et al., 2022).

Therapeutic History  
Rapamycin/sirolimus and rapalogs have a long clinical history across transplantation and oncology; in ophthalmology, mechanistic and translational work has targeted mTOR for AMD and other retinal diseases because mTORC1 suppresses autophagy/lysosomal programs and promotes inflammatory and angiogenic signaling (Wang et al., 2022; Nita & Grzybowski, 2023). In RPE models that recapitulate daily phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments (POS), mTORC1 activity is dynamically regulated: POS phagocytosis transiently activates mTORC1, followed by inhibition during phagosome maturation; however, in aged RPE and AMD, mTORC1 activity is relatively elevated and TFEB is retained in the phosphorylated cytosolic state, impairing lysosomal responses and favoring lipofuscin-like autofluorescent granule (AFG) accumulation (Falcão et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2025). In these systems, rapamycin reduces POS-dependent AFGs by about 30% while increasing TFEB activity and lysosomal biogenesis markers (e.g., LAMP1) in ARPE-19 and human fetal RPE cells; efficacy generalizes to other mTOR pathway inhibitors (e.g., INK-128), and constitutively active TFEB provides larger effects, supporting a TFEB-centric mechanism (Falcão et al., 2024). These effects require intact lysosomal proteolysis; pharmacologic blockade of lysosomal acid lipase, cathepsin inhibition, or cathepsin D (CTSD) knockout abrogates rapamycin’s benefit, highlighting a dependence on functional lysosomes (Falcão et al., 2024). Although these data do not directly test temsirolimus in lysosome-TFEB endpoints, temsirolimus is mechanistically a rapalog mTORC1 inhibitor, and in RPE it engages mTOR biology by suppressing growth factor signaling outputs (VEGF/PDGF) and cell motility/proliferation, thereby validating target engagement in the relevant cell type (Liegl et al., 2014).

Clinically, multiple sirolimus trials have evaluated mTOR inhibition in geographic atrophy (GA), a late stage of dry AMD, with disappointing outcomes. Subconjunctival sirolimus (440 µg every 3 months for 24 months) in a bilateral-eye, fellow-eye-control study did not slow GA enlargement and was associated with a treatment-associated decrease in visual acuity relative to untreated fellow eyes, despite an acceptable safety profile in that study (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2008; Wang et al., 2022). An intravitreal sirolimus Phase I/II study in bilateral GA was discontinued early, and separate trials reported ocular adverse events including accelerated retinal thinning, abnormal perilesional autofluorescence, and sterile endophthalmitis; overall, no structural or functional benefit was demonstrated across these programs (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2011; Wang et al., 2022). These clinical observations raise concern that chronic mTOR inhibition in established GA may be ineffective or even detrimental, potentially due to disease stage–specific network effects of autophagy and survival signaling in degenerating retina (Wang et al., 2022). In contrast, preclinical data in other retinal contexts (e.g., glaucoma) show neuroprotective correlates of mTOR inhibition, underscoring the context- and stage-dependence of therapeutic effects (Wang et al., 2022). For wet AMD and retinal vascular pathology, temsirolimus (and rapamycin) exert anti-angiogenic actions in vitro and in animal models by downregulating VEGF/PDGF and endothelial proliferation, which are less directly relevant to GA biology but establish ocular pharmacology for the class (Liegl et al., 2014; Johnson, 2013). Drug delivery innovations such as synthetic HDL nanoparticles carrying rapamycin have been explored preclinically to optimize ocular delivery, suggesting format-dependent translatability may be important for this class (Falcão et al., 2024).

Mechanism of Action  
Temsirolimus acts as a prototypical rapalog: it binds FKBP12 to form a gain-of-function complex that docks to the FKBP12-rapamycin binding (FRB) domain of mTOR and selectively inhibits mTORC1 signaling; mTORC2 is generally spared acutely, with potential indirect effects chronically depending on cellular context (Wang et al., 2022). mTORC1 normally phosphorylates TFEB on multiple serine residues, retaining it in the cytosol and preventing nuclear entry; when mTORC1 is inhibited, TFEB becomes dephosphorylated, translocates to the nucleus, and drives the CLEAR network that upregulates autophagy and lysosomal biogenesis genes (e.g., LAMP1), enhancing degradative capacity and organelle biogenesis (Falcão et al., 2025; Falcão et al., 2024). In RPE cells, POS phagocytosis engages mTORC1 transiently, but aged/AMD RPE exhibit enhanced mTORC1 activity that suppresses appropriate TFEB activation; rapamycin reverses this, promoting TFEB dephosphorylation, nuclear entry, GADD34 upregulation, and increased lysosomal mass, collectively reducing AFGs by approximately 30% in POS-challenged RPE (Falcão et al., 2024). The TFEB dependency has been functionally validated via TFEB gain-of-function, which markedly decreases AFGs in both preventive and “therapeutic” paradigms after lipofuscin-like material has already formed (Falcão et al., 2024). Pharmacologic relevance to mTOR pathway modulation beyond rapamycin was supported using INK-128 and other mTOR inhibitors, which replicated the AFG reduction and TFEB-lysosome signature (Falcão et al., 2024).

At the biochemical level, mTORC1 integrates amino acid signaling at the lysosomal surface via Ragulator-Rag GTPases and growth/energy cues via Rheb/AMPK, coordinating downstream phosphorylation of p70S6K and 4E-BP1 to activate translation while repressing catabolic programs including initiation of autophagy (partly by phosphorylating ULK1 at Ser757 and by blocking TFEB) (Johnson, 2013; Chang et al., 2022). In retinal tissues, mTOR inhibition is expected to relieve brakes on autophagy and lysosomal biogenesis; in diabetic retinopathy models, mTOR inhibition with rapamycin restored impaired lysosomal proteolysis by normalizing cathepsin L activity and autophagic flux, mechanistically consistent with TFEB-driven CLEAR network activation and improved lysosomal protease capacity (Wang et al., 2022). Although direct evidence for temsirolimus effects on RPE TFEB phosphorylation state, lysosomal acidification, or CTSD maturation is not available, the shared mechanism of FKBP12-dependent mTORC1 inhibition and the RPE-cell mTOR engagement demonstrated by temsirolimus (antiproliferative/anti-migratory, VEGF/PDGF suppression) support pathway perturbation in the correct cellular context (Liegl et al., 2014).

In the context of AMD pathophysiology, RPE lysosomal dysfunction and impaired clearance of POS-derived material drive lipofuscin accumulation and downstream toxicity; TFEB has emerged as a master regulator to restore lysosomal capacity, while AMD donor RPE show reduced cathepsin D and L levels/activities, highlighting protease insufficiency as a plausible node of therapeutic rescue (Falcão et al., 2025). Importantly, in POS-fed RPE, the rapamycin benefit is abolished by lysosomal protease inhibition or CTSD knockout, indicating that mTORC1 inhibition enhances clearance only when lysosomal protease function is preserved, and suggesting that concomitant strategies to support lysosomal acidification/protease maturation could be synergistic (Falcão et al., 2024). Finally, some reports have suggested low immunoreactivity of mTORC1/2 components in RPE, but this observation contrasts with multiple functional studies demonstrating mTORC1 signaling in RPE during POS handling and aging; taken together, functional responsiveness to mTOR inhibitors in RPE likely depends on model system and detection sensitivity (Wang et al., 2022; Falcão et al., 2024).

Expected Effect  
In a POS-pulse/chase AFG assay using ARPE-19 or human fetal RPE, temsirolimus is expected to inhibit mTORC1 (decreased pS6 phosphorylation), dephosphorylate TFEB, increase TFEB nuclear localization, upregulate CLEAR network/lysosomal biogenesis genes (e.g., GADD34, LAMP1), and reduce AFG burden by enhancing degradation of phagocytosed material; this mirrors rapamycin’s effects (~30% AFG reduction) and those of other mTOR inhibitors in these models (Falcão et al., 2024). To confirm on-target activity and pathway alignment, assays should include pS6/S6 and pTFEB/TFEB immunoblotting at 2–24 h, TFEB nuclear translocation imaging, LAMP1 immunostaining for lysosomal mass, and flow cytometry quantification of AFGs after 24–72 h chase, consistent with established methodologies (Falcão et al., 2024). Because rapamycin’s benefits are abolished by lysosomal protease blockade and in CTSD-deficient backgrounds, temsirolimus-dependent AFG reduction is predicted to require functional cathepsin D and lipases; co-assaying CTSD maturation (pro-/mature CTSD ratio), lysosomal pH, and acid lipase activity is therefore crucial to mechanistic validation (Falcão et al., 2024). In parallel, transcriptomic or targeted RT-qPCR panels for CLEAR genes will validate TFEB program engagement (Falcão et al., 2024).

Regarding lysosomal acidification and protease activity, there is mechanistic plausibility but no direct demonstration that temsirolimus enhances lysosomal pH or CTSD maturation in RPE; nevertheless, the TFEB-centric model predicts improved lysosomal proteostasis, and related retinal models show that mTOR inhibition can restore impaired lysosomal proteolysis (cathepsin L) and autophagic flux, supporting the hypothesis that temsirolimus could favorably influence protease maturation/activity in RPE (Wang et al., 2022; Falcão et al., 2025). Notably, independent approaches in RPE can acidify lysosomes and reduce AFGs, underscoring the tractability of the acidification axis, though this was not via mTOR inhibition; combining mTORC1-TFEB activation with direct acidification strategies could be additive (Falcão et al., 2024). The expectation for disease modification in GA derives from the idea that sustained enhancement of lysosomal clearance will reduce lipofuscin burden, preserve RPE function, and slow atrophic expansion; however, prior GA trials with sirolimus showed no benefit and potential harm, implying that either the disease stage, delivery/exposure, or network consequences of chronic mTORC1 inhibition negate the anticipated benefit in late disease (Wang et al., 2022).

Temsirolimus target expression and pharmacology in RPE are supported by in vitro data showing dose-dependent inhibition of RPE proliferation and migration and suppression of hypoxia-induced VEGF/PDGF increases without overt cytotoxicity at low micromolar to millimolar nominal concentrations; these endpoints corroborate mTOR pathway engagement in RPE and provide pharmacodynamic markers (e.g., VEGF suppression) that can be measured alongside TFEB-lysosomal readouts in AFG assays (Liegl et al., 2014). The drug class’s ocular delivery options range from systemic dosing (with significant class-typical adverse events) to local delivery; sirolimus trials used subconjunctival or intravitreal administration but encountered safety/tolerability signals including sterile endophthalmitis and accelerated retinal thinning with no efficacy in GA, emphasizing the need for alternative delivery technologies (e.g., nanoparticles) and stage-appropriate patient selection if pursuing this mechanism (Wang et al., 2022; Falcão et al., 2024). Finally, given AMD donor RPE deficiencies in cathepsins D/L, co-therapies or genetic activation strategies that more directly drive TFEB or augment lysosomal protease capacity could be required to realize the full benefit of mTORC1 inhibition in human disease (Falcão et al., 2025).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Mechanism-based rationale with cell-type congruence: RPE lysosomal dysfunction is central to AMD, and mTORC1 directly represses TFEB and lysosomal programs; in POS-fed RPE, mTORC1 inhibition with rapamycin reduces AFG burden by ~30%, increases lysosomal biogenesis (LAMP1), and requires intact lysosomal proteases, aligning precisely with the hypothesized MoA (Falcão et al., 2024). The effect generalizes across mTOR inhibitors and is amplified by TFEB gain-of-function, strengthening the pathway argument (Falcão et al., 2024).  
- Direct evidence that temsirolimus engages mTOR signaling in RPE: temsirolimus suppresses proliferation/migration and reduces VEGF/PDGF in primary human RPE, indicating pharmacodynamic activity and target engagement in the disease-relevant cell type (Liegl et al., 2014).  
- Broad mechanistic plausibility for enhancing lysosomal proteolysis: mTORC1 inhibition activates TFEB; retinal disease models show restoration of lysosomal protease activity (cathepsin L) and autophagic flux with rapamycin, consistent with improved lysosomal proteostasis, which could translate to better CTSD maturation in RPE even though that specific nexus is unproven for temsirolimus (Wang et al., 2022; Falcão et al., 2025).  
- Drug class knowledge base and formulation opportunities: extensive class experience informs safety risk assessment; emerging ocular delivery strategies (e.g., sHDL rapamycin nanoparticles) might overcome exposure constraints seen in prior sirolimus GA trials (Falcão et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2022).

Weaknesses and Risks  
- Negative/unsafe clinical precedents in GA with class analog: multiple sirolimus trials in GA failed to slow lesion growth and revealed adverse ocular events, including accelerated retinal thinning and procedure-related sterile endophthalmitis, suggesting either mechanistic inadequacy at late stages, harmful network effects of chronic mTORC1 inhibition, or delivery-related issues; this materially lowers clinical plausibility for GA-stage disease (Wang et al., 2022).  
- Absence of temsirolimus-specific TFEB/lysosome data in RPE: while rapamycin demonstrates TFEB activation, lysosomal biogenesis, and AFG reduction, comparable mechanistic data for temsirolimus in RPE are lacking; the program would therefore carry translatability risk until head-to-head, mechanistic RPE assays confirm TFEB engagement and AFG reduction with temsirolimus (Falcão et al., 2024; Liegl et al., 2014).  
- Dependence on intact lysosomes and proteases: rapamycin’s benefit disappears with lipase inhibition or CTSD deficiency; AMD donor RPE show reduced cathepsin D/L, implying that many patient retinas may not have sufficient residual lysosomal capacity for mTORC1 inhibition alone to succeed without adjuncts that restore acidification/protease maturation (Falcão et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2025).  
- Context and stage dependence of mTOR biology: autophagy upregulation that is protective in early disease can exacerbate neuronal apoptosis in late AMD; cell-type–specific and duration-dependent consequences of mTOR inhibition complicate chronic treatment in GA and may negate benefits or cause harm (Wang et al., 2022).  
- Systemic formulation constraints and ocular delivery safety: temsirolimus is an IV drug with known systemic toxicities; local ocular administration for a chronic indication must overcome prior safety/tolerability issues observed with sirolimus injections while achieving sustained, intraretinal/RPE-targeted exposure (Wang et al., 2022).

Go/No-Go Perspective and Development Recommendations  
- Indication selection: Given the negative GA clinical history with sirolimus, prioritize early/intermediate dry AMD with measurable lipofuscin/AFG burden and residual RPE lysosomal capacity, rather than established GA, where class effects have been neutral or detrimental (Falcão et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2022).  
- Mechanistic bridging for temsirolimus: Run definitive RPE mechanistic studies comparing temsirolimus to rapamycin and an ATP-competitive mTOR inhibitor (e.g., INK-128) using POS-pulse/chase AFG assays, pS6/pTFEB readouts, TFEB nuclear localization, LAMP1, lysosomal pH, acid lipase, and CTSD maturation/activity, with rescue and block experiments to confirm TFEB dependence and lysosome-requirement (Falcão et al., 2024).  
- Combination strategies: Evaluate temsirolimus with lysosome-acidifying agents or TFEB-direct activators/gene transfer to overcome the protease dependency bottleneck evident in AMD RPE; mechanistic review suggests dual TFEB/mTOR and NRF2/KEAP1 modulation could be synergistic but requires careful control to avoid oncogenic risk (Falcão et al., 2025).  
- Delivery innovation: Avoid frequent intravitreal bolusing; explore sustained-release local delivery or targeted nanoparticles (e.g., sHDL-like) to deliver rapalogs selectively to RPE/retina at sub-toxic exposures, learning from prior sirolimus delivery failures (Falcão et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2022).  
- Translational biomarkers: In early clinical exploration, incorporate pharmacodynamic biomarkers of TFEB activation (e.g., aqueous humor proteomics for CLEAR targets, retinal LAMP1 imaging if feasible), structural endpoints sensitive to RPE health (fundus autofluorescence for lipofuscin load), and stringent safety monitoring for retinal thinning and inflammation to detect class-typical adverse signals early (Falcão et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2022).

Bottom line: The TFEB-lysosome rationale is robust at the cellular level in RPE, but the rapalog class has failed to translate benefit in GA; temsirolimus lacks direct RPE TFEB/lysosomal evidence and carries delivery/safety liabilities observed with sirolimus in GA. As a repurposing candidate, temsirolimus merits mechanistic validation in RPE with TFEB/lysosome endpoints and, if positive, a carefully designed, stage-appropriate pilot in early/intermediate dry AMD using optimized delivery; it is not a priority candidate for GA without compelling new mechanistic and translational data that overcome the class’s negative clinical precedent (Falcão et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2022).

Abstract—Metformin, a synthetic biguanide derived from galegine (French lilac), is widely used as first-line therapy for type 2 diabetes mellitus and has pleiotropic cellular effects that intersect with age-related macular degeneration (AMD) biology, including AMPK activation, modulation of mTOR signaling, autophagy induction, anti-inflammatory actions, mitochondrial support, anti-senescence effects, and anti-angiogenic signaling in retinal models (Amin et al., 2022). Multiple preclinical studies in RPE cell lines and rodent retinal injury/degeneration models show that metformin preserves RPE barrier integrity, reduces oxidative and inflammatory stress, supports mitochondrial biogenesis, and maintains photoreceptor structure/function, largely via AMPK-dependent pathways; however, dry AMD–specific randomized clinical efficacy data remain limited and observational epidemiology is heterogeneous, with mixed associations across populations, exposure definitions, and AMD subtypes (Amin et al., 2022; Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Gokhale et al., 2023; Liang et al., 2022; Moir et al., 2023; Romdhoniyyah et al., 2021). Critically, while AMPK→mTORC1→autophagy is well-supported in retinal contexts, direct evidence for metformin-driven TFEB nuclear translocation, V-ATPase upregulation, or cathepsin D (CTSD) maturation in human RPE/AMD models is not demonstrated in the excerpted literature, representing material gaps for the central hypothesis (Amin et al., 2022; Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Buonfiglio et al., 2024). Overall, metformin is a biologically plausible, low-cost, and generally safe repurposing candidate for dry AMD that warrants mechanistic confirmation in RPE for lysosome-centric endpoints and rigorous randomized trials across AMD stages (Amin et al., 2022; Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Moir et al., 2023).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Metformin is a small-molecule biguanide synthesized as a derivative of galegine, a guanidine-class alkaloid originally isolated from the plant Galega officinalis; clinically it has been used for more than 60 years as the most commonly prescribed oral antihyperglycemic agent worldwide (class: biguanides) (Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Amin et al., 2022). Chemically, metformin comprises two coupled guanidine moieties conferring cationic, hydrophilic properties and cellular accumulation via organic cation transporters, consistent with mitochondrial complex I engagement and AMPK pathway activation described in mechanistic literature (Augustin & Atorf, 2023). Beyond glycemic control, metformin exhibits pleiotropic effects—anti-inflammatory, anti-oxidative, anti-angiogenic, anti-apoptotic and anti-senescence—reported in diverse cell types and tissues, many of which intersect with pathways implicated in AMD pathogenesis (oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, impaired proteostasis/autophagy, para-inflammation, vascular dysregulation) (Amin et al., 2022; Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Kozlowski, 2023). In ocular contexts, preclinical work indicates that metformin activates AMPK in RPE and neural retina and can preserve retinal structure and function under oxidative, metabolic, and phototoxic stressors (Amin et al., 2022). Collectively, these properties position metformin as a rational repurposing candidate for dry AMD, wherein RPE dysfunction, impaired autophagy/lysosomal clearance, mitochondrial stress, and chronic inflammation are central pathogenic nodes (Amin et al., 2022; Buonfiglio et al., 2024).

Therapeutic History  
Systemic use: Metformin is established first-line therapy for type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) and has been investigated broadly for aging-related conditions due to putative geroprotective effects; long-term safety has been documented, including in the Diabetes Prevention Program (DPP) where gastrointestinal intolerance is the most common adverse event and lactic acidosis was not observed under trial conditions, though B12 deficiency can occur with chronic use (Amin et al., 2022; Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Zhou & Xue, 2024). Preclinical ocular use: In retinal models, metformin has been tested systemically (oral/IP) and intravitreally, demonstrating protective effects in RPE and photoreceptors across light-damage, iodate-induced injury, inherited retinal degeneration (rd1/rd10), and oxygen-induced retinopathy (OIR) with readouts including preserved RPE tight junctions (ZO-1, occludin), outer nuclear layer thickness, and ERG amplitudes; notable anti-angiogenic activity includes decreased CNV lesion size and VEGF/VEGFR signaling modulation in several models (Amin et al., 2022). In these preclinical settings, metformin’s ocular benefits are frequently attributed to AMPK activation and downstream autophagy/mitochondrial and anti-inflammatory pathways, without overt ocular toxicity reported in rodents; however, human ocular safety data and pharmacokinetics under intravitreal or high-dose local exposure are not detailed in the excerpts (Amin et al., 2022).

Clinical/epidemiologic AMD history: Observational epidemiology offers mixed signals. Several large retrospective cohorts and case–control analyses associate metformin use with reduced odds or risk of any AMD or early AMD, with dose–duration trends in some datasets (e.g., MarketScan/claims OR 0.93 and propensity-matched HR 0.57; Taiwanese cohorts HR ~0.54 with stronger protection at >4 years and higher average daily doses), and lower odds reported in multiple studies across US, Europe, and Asia (Amin et al., 2022; Jiang et al., 2022; Kozlowski, 2023; Moir et al., 2023). Other datasets report null or complex associations: a high-quality UK T2DM cohort found no differential AMD risk with metformin using time-varying exposure models; a U.S. claims analysis focusing on dry AMD reported current use slightly increased dry AMD risk while prior use trended protective; additional analyses show no association or heterogeneity by diabetic retinopathy status (Eton et al., 2022; Gokhale et al., 2023; Liang et al., 2022). Meta-analyses also conflict: a systematic review of diabetics suggested decreased odds of AMD with metformin, whereas a broader 2024 meta-analysis concluded no overall prophylactic/treatment role; a European meta-analysis of antidiabetic/lipid-lowering drugs found reduced AMD prevalence overall but not for late-stage AMD specifically (Elhalag et al., 2024; Mauschitz et al., 2023). Importantly, these retrospective designs face confounding (e.g., smoking, comorbidities, health-care utilization), outcome misclassification (wet vs dry AMD), and exposure misclassification (adherence), limiting causal inference and stage-specific conclusions (Brown et al., 2019; Gokhale et al., 2023; Moir et al., 2023). Prospective interventional testing for dry AMD is underway: a randomized, single-blind Phase II trial of metformin to slow geographic atrophy (GA) progression has been conducted, with publication reported in 2024 (Shen et al., 2024); however, the excerpts do not provide efficacy outcomes in GA and emphasize that randomized evidence remains needed (Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Shen et al., 2024).

No regulatory approval exists for metformin in AMD (dry or wet), and the totality of evidence remains preclinical and observational for efficacy, with one randomized GA study reported but without effect-size details here; therefore, clinical utility in dry AMD is presently unproven (Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Shen et al., 2024).

Mechanism of Action  
Canonical pharmacology: Metformin partially inhibits mitochondrial respiratory complex I, reducing hepatic ATP and increasing AMP/ADP, thereby activating AMPK, the cellular energy sensor that shifts metabolism toward ATP-generating pathways; AMPK-dependent and ‑independent mechanisms operate systemically, including reduced hepatic gluconeogenesis, increased enterocyte glucose uptake/GLP-1 secretion, and microbiome modulation with potential systemic anti-inflammatory effects (Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Kozlowski, 2023).

Retinal/RPE mechanisms: In RPE cell lines (e.g., ARPE-19), metformin increases pAMPK and triggers autophagy, reduces ROS, decreases apoptosis, and preserves tight junction proteins (ZO-1, occludin), thereby maintaining barrier integrity under oxidative challenges (Amin et al., 2022; Augustin & Atorf, 2023). At the molecular level, treatment increases Sirt1 and multiple mitochondrial biogenesis and antioxidant markers (SOD-2, Nrf1, Tfam, PGC-1α, COX-II), restores NADH:NAD+ ratios and ATP, and lowers inflammatory mediators (NF-κB signaling, IL-6) (Amin et al., 2022). These signatures are consistent with AMPK’s coordinate regulation of autophagy and mitochondrial homeostasis observed in RPE/retinal contexts, contributing to improved proteostasis and reduced oxidative stress—key failure modes in dry AMD (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Amin et al., 2022).

In vivo, systemic or intravitreal metformin preserves photoreceptors and RPE structure/function in light-damage, iodate injury, and inherited degeneration models (rd1, rd10), with ERG preservation and ONL maintenance; mechanistically, AMPK activation is necessary for light-damage protection in an isoform-specific manner (AMPKα2 dependency), and retina-specific Pparδ is not required, supporting an AMPK-centric retinal mechanism rather than PPARδ signaling (Amin et al., 2022). Metformin also dampens retinal senescence and SASP in OIR after intravitreal dosing, with decreased cdkn1a/cdkn2a and NF-κB/IL-6 signaling, implicating anti-senescence immunomodulation as an additional neurovascular protective mechanism (Amin et al., 2022). Anti-angiogenic actions involve AMPK-dependent and ‑independent pathways: decreased VEGFR2 via enhanced ubiquitin–proteasome degradation, altered VEGF-A isoform splicing toward less angiogenic forms, reduced Flk-1 expression, and inhibition of ALK1-mediated angiogenesis; collectively these actions reduce CNV lesion size, endothelial proliferation/migration/tube formation, and neovascularization in OIR, diabetic, and laser-CNV models (Amin et al., 2022; Augustin & Atorf, 2023). Inflammatory suppression includes reductions in ICAM-1/MCP-1 (AMPK-dependent) and NF-κB p65/IL-8 (AMPK-independent), accompanied by decreased leukostasis and cytokines across models; NLRP3 inflammasome inhibition and modulation of macrophage polarization further contribute to reduced para-inflammation (Amin et al., 2022; Dang et al., 2021; Augustin & Atorf, 2023).

mTOR/autophagy axis: AMPK activation by metformin can inhibit mTORC1, activate the ULK complex, and initiate autophagy, which in RPE promotes clearance of damaged organelles, reduces ROS, and protects against oxidative injury—mechanistically vital for countering autophagy/lysosomal dysfunction in AMD (Dang et al., 2021; Zhou & Xue, 2024). Several retinal studies report AMPK-linked increases in autophagosome formation, and some contextual discussion references mTOR modulation in retinal protection, including translational control via EF2K and general proteostasis benefits (e.g., mutant opsin trafficking) with mixed in vivo translation (Amin et al., 2022). While AMPK→mTOR→autophagy activation is strongly implicated, explicit experimental confirmation in the provided corpus for metformin-driven TFEB nuclear translocation, V-ATPase upregulation, or increased cathepsin D maturation/activity in RPE is lacking; several reviews and excerpts explicitly note these as gaps requiring targeted mechanistic studies (Amin et al., 2022; Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Buonfiglio et al., 2024).

These data caution against assuming uniform AMPK-mediated benefit across all retinal diseases or AMD stages and highlight the importance of pharmacokinetics, tissue exposure, and therapeutic window in the eye (Moir et al., 2023).

Translational addenda—microbiome and lipid handling: Metformin alters gut microbiota and systemic metabolites, which has been linked to reduced retinal neovascularization through a putative “gut–retina axis,” and may also reduce OxLDL uptake and promote cholesterol efflux via AMPK/LXR–ABCA1/G1 signaling, potentially limiting drusen-related lipid accumulation and NLRP3 activation in RPE (Dang et al., 2021; Zhou & Xue, 2024).

Published in vitro data already support many of these endpoints: metformin reduced ROS and apoptosis, increased pAMPK and antioxidative molecules including Sirt1/Nrf2, and preserved occludin/ZO-1 in ARPE-19 challenged with H2O2 or glyoxal; AMPK inhibition abrogated the protection, indicating dependence on AMPK signaling (Amin et al., 2022). While the AMPK→mTORC1→autophagy cascade is supported in RPE and retina, the provided literature does not directly demonstrate metformin-induced TFEB nuclear translocation, V-ATPase upregulation, or CTSD maturation increases in RPE; thus, these are testable predictions rather than established metformin actions in RPE (Amin et al., 2022; Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Augustin & Atorf, 2023). Given TFEB’s role in lysosomal biogenesis and function, metformin’s dampening of mTORC1 could plausibly facilitate TFEB nuclear entry, but explicit experimental validation (e.g., TFEB nuclear localization quantification, lysosomal pH assays, V-ATPase subunit expression/activity, pro-CTSD→mature CTSD processing and enzymatic activity assays) is needed to confirm the hypothesized mechanism in AMD-relevant RPE models (Dang et al., 2021; Ebeling et al., 2022).

Downstream readouts of autophagy and mitochondrial biogenesis/antioxidant pathways (LC3-II, PGC-1α, SOD-2, Nrf1, Tfam) have been measured and improved with metformin in RPE/retinal models, supporting assay feasibility and expected directions of effect (Amin et al., 2022).

In vivo expected effects in dry-AMD–relevant models: In toxin- and stress-driven models of RPE/photoreceptor degeneration (e.g., sodium iodate, light-induced damage) and inherited retinal degeneration, metformin is expected to preserve RPE morphology and function, maintain ONL thickness, and preserve ERG signals, consistent with reported benefits mediated by AMPK activation; however, model- and disease-stage–specific responses can vary, and negative/neutral results have been documented in some diabetic retinopathy paradigms, underscoring the need to test across multiple AMD-relevant models and to incorporate timing and dose-response studies (Amin et al., 2022). Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Mechanistic convergence on AMD biology: Metformin engages AMPK-dependent and ‑independent processes that directly counter core dry AMD pathomechanisms—oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, impaired autophagy/proteostasis, para-inflammation/senescence, and, secondarily, maladaptive vascular/angio-inflammatory signaling—supported by coherent molecular readouts (pAMPK↑, autophagy induction, mitochondrial biogenesis markers↑, NF-κB/NLRP3↓) in RPE and retinal models (Amin et al., 2022; Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Zhou & Xue, 2024). Preclinical efficacy in preserving RPE barrier proteins and photoreceptor function across multiple insults strengthens biological plausibility for dry AMD (Amin et al., 2022).
- Epidemiologic signal and translational momentum: Multiple large retrospective analyses show reduced odds/risk of AMD—often with dose–duration trends—among metformin users, and a randomized GA trial has been conducted, indicating clinical interest and feasibility for prospective testing (Amin et al., 2022; Jiang et al., 2022; Moir et al., 2023; Shen et al., 2024). Meta-analytic work in diabetics suggests potential protective associations, especially in early AMD, reinforcing the rationale to test in non-diabetic AMD populations with controlled exposure (Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Liang et al., 2022).
- Favorable systemic safety and low cost: Decades of broad clinical use, with well-characterized safety signals (GI intolerance, B12 deficiency; rare lactic acidosis risk under renal/hepatic compromise), make metformin attractive from a risk–benefit and access perspective for an elderly AMD population, assuming ocular safety is confirmed (Amin et al., 2022; Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Zhou & Xue, 2024).
- Ocular delivery flexibility and mechanistic redundancy: Both systemic and intravitreal dosing have produced retinal benefits in animals; intravitreal delivery achieved senescence suppression independent of anti-VEGF effects, suggesting non-overlapping mechanisms that could complement existing therapies (Amin et al., 2022). Mechanistic redundancy (anti-oxidant, autophagy, anti-inflammatory, anti-angiogenic) could enhance robustness in multifactorial AMD pathophysiology (Amin et al., 2022; Dang et al., 2021).

Weaknesses and Gaps  
- Critical mechanistic gaps relative to the hypothesis: Direct evidence in human RPE/AMD-relevant systems for metformin-driven TFEB nuclear translocation, increases in V-ATPase expression/activity, and enhanced cathepsin D maturation/activity is absent in the provided literature; several reviews explicitly highlight TFEB/V-ATPase/CTSD endpoints as missing and necessary to establish lysosome-centric restoration of autophagic flux (Amin et al., 2022; Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Buonfiglio et al., 2024). Without these data, the proposed AMPK–TFEB–lysosome axis remains inferential in RPE.
- Heterogeneous and contradictory epidemiology: While many retrospective datasets suggest benefit (often in T2DM cohorts), high-quality time-varying analyses and some claims datasets report null or even an increased risk signal for current users regarding dry AMD; meta-analyses differ in conclusions, and late-stage AMD associations are particularly uncertain (Elhalag et al., 2024; Gokhale et al., 2023; Liang et al., 2022; Mauschitz et al., 2023). Confounding (smoking, DR severity, comedications), misclassification (wet vs dry), and exposure uncertainty limit inferential strength (Brown et al., 2019; Moir et al., 2023; Gokhale et al., 2023).
- Limited randomized clinical efficacy data in dry AMD: A GA randomized trial has been reported, but efficacy outcomes are not detailed in the excerpts; prior DPP follow-up imaging showed no significant AMD prevalence difference between metformin, lifestyle, and placebo, though that study was not designed for AMD endpoints; consequently, clinical efficacy remains unproven (Moir et al., 2023; Shen et al., 2024).
- Context dependence and dose constraints: Retinal benefits can be model- and isoform-specific (AMPKα2 dependence) and mixed in metabolic DR models; some analyses suggest suprapharmacologic concentrations may be necessary for robust AMPK activation in vitro, raising translational questions regarding retinal exposure at tolerated systemic doses, and arguing for ocular PK and target-engagement studies (Amin et al., 2022; Moir et al., 2023).
- Ocular safety and pharmacokinetics: Human ocular safety data for chronic exposure (systemic or local) in older non-diabetic AMD patients are not detailed here; intravitreal metformin safety in humans is uncharacterized in these excerpts, necessitating staged ocular toxicology and PK prior to (or within) clinical trials (Amin et al., 2022; Moir et al., 2023).

Development Implications and Recommendations  
- Mechanism validation in RPE: Prioritize targeted studies in human iPSC-RPE and donor-derived RPE to test the hypothesized AMPK→mTORC1→TFEB→lysosome axis. Required assays: TFEB nuclear localization (immunocytochemistry, subcellular fractionation), lysosomal pH (LysoSensor/LysoTracker), V-ATPase subunit expression and activity (ATPase assays), CTSD maturation (pro/mature CTSD Western) and enzymatic activity, autophagic flux (LC3 turnover with/without lysosomal blockade), and rescue experiments with AMPK and TFEB perturbation (e.g., CRISPRi/siRNA) (Amin et al., 2022; Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Ebeling et al., 2022).
- Translational pharmacology: Define retinal/RPE exposure–response using clinically relevant systemic concentrations and ocular distribution modeling; consider topical/periocular/intravitreal delivery if systemic exposure is insufficient for retinal AMPK engagement and lysosome-centric endpoints, with rigorous ocular toxicology (Moir et al., 2023).
- Indication and stage targeting: Given epidemiologic signals skew toward early/non-exudative AMD and limited evidence for late AMD benefit, prioritize early/intermediate AMD cohorts and GA progression trials with mechanistic biomarkers (RPE autofluorescence dynamics, OCT-based RPE/ONL metrics, aqueous humor cytokines/miRNAs) to increase sensitivity to disease-modifying effects (Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Liang et al., 2022; Moir et al., 2023).
- Clinical trial design: Incorporate robust confounder control and stratification (smoking, DR status, renal function, OCT1 polymorphisms) and embed target engagement (e.g., peripheral blood or aqueous biomarkers of AMPK/mTOR/autophagy) and safety surveillance (B12 levels, GI tolerability, lactate in at-risk) to bridge mechanism to clinical outcome (Gokhale et al., 2023; Zhou & Xue, 2024).
- Combination/adjunct strategies: Given non-overlapping mechanisms with anti-VEGF and complement inhibitors, explore combinatorial approaches in late-stage disease (e.g., GA with complement inhibition) if target engagement and safety are demonstrated (Amin et al., 2022; Shen et al., 2024).

Conclusion: Metformin is a credible repurposing candidate for dry AMD on the strength of convergent mechanistic rationale (AMPK activation, autophagy/mitochondrial support, anti-inflammatory/anti-senescence actions), robust preclinical retinal protection across models, and suggestive—but inconsistent—observational human data; however, decisive gaps remain for the central lysosome-centric hypothesis (TFEB/V-ATPase/CTSD in RPE) and for randomized clinical efficacy, especially in GA. The program should proceed with focused mechanistic validation of TFEB/lysosome endpoints in RPE, retinal target engagement and pharmacology at clinically feasible exposures, and staged, biomarker-rich randomized trials in early/intermediate AMD and GA to quantify efficacy and safety. Until lysosomal endpoints are confirmed and clinical benefit demonstrated, the hypothesis that metformin restores RPE autophagic flux via TFEB/V-ATPase/CTSD to prevent dry AMD remains plausible but unproven (Amin et al., 2022; Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Shen et al., 2024; Gokhale et al., 2023; Elhalag et al., 2024).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Tocilizumab (Actemra; Roche/Chugai) is a recombinant humanized monoclonal antibody that binds the human interleukin-6 receptor (IL-6R) and blocks IL-6 signal transduction, resulting in systemic anti-inflammatory effects characteristic of IL-6 pathway inhibition (class: humanized anti-IL-6R monoclonal antibody) (Shi, 2017a; Shi, 2017b; Zhujiang Hospital, 2025). In clinical development, tocilizumab has been administered intravenously at 8 mg/kg every 4 weeks and subcutaneously at 162 mg once weekly, with protocols reflecting the infectious, hepatic, hematologic, gastrointestinal, and reproductive safety considerations common to cytokine-targeted biologics (e.g., TB/hepatitis screening, neutrophil/platelet and transaminase thresholds, live-vaccine restrictions, diverticulitis history, and contraception requirements) (Shi, 2017b; University of Nebraska, 2016; Assistance Publique–Hôpitaux de Paris, 2017; Zhujiang Hospital, 2025). Ophthalmic interest in IL-6 blockade is evidenced by prospective trials in non-infectious uveitis and a withdrawn diabetic macular edema (DME) trial; those records establish feasible dosing, ophthalmic outcome collection, and safety oversight but do not provide efficacy data in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (Assistance Publique–Hôpitaux de Paris, 2017; University of Nebraska, 2016). At the disease-biology level, multiple clinical and literature-derived evidences associate IL-6 with AMD, including elevated ocular and systemic IL-6 in AMD populations and genetic associations in some cohorts; Open Targets ranks IL6 as the strongest among selected IL-6 pathway members for AMD relevance in the provided excerpt (Buniello et al., 2025).

Therapeutic History  
Systemic uses and ophthalmic experience: Tocilizumab’s IL-6R blockade is well characterized clinically outside ophthalmology, and controlled ophthalmic trials have evaluated systemic tocilizumab as an investigational agent for posterior-segment, non-infectious uveitis (RUBI), using subcutaneous 162 mg weekly for 16 weeks with retinal structural and visual endpoints and active safety monitoring; the study is listed as completed in the registry excerpt but outcome data are not included here (Assistance Publique–Hôpitaux de Paris, 2017). A single-center, open-label Behçet’s uveitis trial planned to assess 6 months of tocilizumab while maintaining background immunosuppression, but it enrolled only three participants and was terminated early based on its measured outcomes, limiting inferences on efficacy; this protocol reiterates standard immunosuppression-related exclusions (active TB/hepatitis, malignancy, pregnancy) (Zheng, 2018). In DME, the READ-4 protocol designed a Phase 2 evaluation of monthly IV tocilizumab (8 mg/kg) alone or combined with monthly intravitreal ranibizumab through Month 6, with safety and OCT central retinal thickness as primary outcomes; the trial was withdrawn before enrollment due to loss of funding, yielding no clinical data (University of Nebraska, 2016). A registry query identified 10 ClinicalTrials.gov records linking “tocilizumab” with retina/macular degeneration terms, but no identifiers or results are available in the excerpt to inform AMD-specific evidence (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.). Beyond retinal disease, randomized and single-arm neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (NMOSD) studies used IV tocilizumab 8 mg/kg every 4 weeks (or every 4–6 weeks) and incorporated ocular structural and visual function endpoints among secondaries; these trials demonstrate feasibility of systemic dosing with ophthalmic measurements but are mechanistically distinct from retinal degenerations such as dry AMD (Shi, 2017b; Shi, 2017a). Collectively, the corpus establishes operational feasibility and safety monitoring frameworks for systemic tocilizumab in ophthalmic settings but contains no clinical evidence in dry AMD (University of Nebraska, 2016; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).

Mechanism of Action  
Drug mechanism: Tocilizumab is a humanized monoclonal antibody that binds to IL-6R and blocks IL-6 signaling, thereby attenuating inflammatory pathways downstream of IL-6R engagement; mechanistic rationales in non-retinal disease emphasize IL-6–dependent survival and differentiation programs (e.g., plasma cells and autoantibody production in NMOSD), with dosing typically at 8 mg/kg IV every 4 weeks or 162 mg SC weekly in the studies cited (Shi, 2017a; Shi, 2017b; Assistance Publique–Hôpitaux de Paris, 2017).

Retinal IL-6 biology and RPE sources/targets: Multiple lines of evidence link IL-6 to AMD: clinical reports of elevated serum and ocular IL-6 in AMD versus controls, genetic association signals in some cohorts, and IL-6’s role in inflammation and neovascularization in advanced disease; Open Targets assigns IL6 the strongest association among queried IL-6 pathway components in the excerpt, while evidence for STAT3 and IL6ST is comparatively weak (Buniello et al., 2025). Human retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells produce IL-6, secrete it in a polarized manner, and can engage autocrine/paracrine IL-6/IL-8 loops that drive RPE degeneration after inflammatory challenge (e.g., bacterial endotoxin), supporting the presence of IL-6–responsive circuits in retinal epithelia (Brandstetter, 2016).

AMD-relevant upstream injury nodes: The dominant mechanistic framework for dry AMD implicates chronic oxidative/photooxidative stress, age-related lysosomal decline, and intracellular clearance failure (autophagy/proteasome) in RPE, leading to lipofuscinogenesis, lysosomal membrane permeabilization (LMP), and activation of inflammasome pathways with downstream cytokine release and cell death (apoptosis vs pyroptosis depending on priming) (Brandstetter, 2016; Piippo, 2019). In primary human RPE and ARPE-19 cells, LMP induced chemically (Leu-Leu-OMe) or via blue-light irradiation of POS-derived lipofuscin activates the NLRP3 inflammasome with caspase-1–dependent maturation and release of IL-1β and IL-18; broader cytokine secretion includes IL-6, GM-CSF, and GRO, with IL-6 elevated ≈13.6-fold in a cytokine screen and partially suppressed by caspase-1 inhibition, indicating a secondary induction downstream of inflammasome activation (not direct inflammasome processing) (Brandstetter, 2016). Cytokine release is apically polarized, and conditioned media from inflammasome-activated RPE is chemotactic for microglia, linking RPE lysosomal injury to neuroretinal immune activation (Brandstetter, 2016). Complement C5a serves as a physiologically relevant priming agent in RPE by activating NF-κB and inducing pro-IL-1β, which permits subsequent LMP-triggered NLRP3 activation; C5a priming and IL-1α priming also shift cell death from apoptosis to pyroptosis after lipofuscin phototoxicity (Brandstetter, 2016). Lysosomal proteases are mechanistically implicated: inhibition of cathepsin B and L suppresses LMP-triggered inflammasome activation in RPE, and cytosolic cathepsins in general, including cathepsin D, can promote apoptosis when released from the lysosome, underscoring the importance of lysosomal integrity in RPE survival (Brandstetter, 2016).

Intracellular clearance failure and mitochondrial stress as alternative inflammasome drivers: Independent RPE models that combine proteasome inhibition (MG-132) with autophagy/lysosome blockade (bafilomycin A₁) activate NLRP3 via oxidative stress, producing caspase-1–dependent IL-1β secretion without evidence that lysosomal rupture/cathepsin leakage is the primary driver; Hsp90 stabilizes NLRP3 in this setting, and Hsp90 inhibition promotes autophagic degradation of NLRP3 when autophagy remains functional (Piippo, 2019). Mitochondrial dysfunction induced by antimycin A activates both NLRP3 and AIM2 inflammasomes in human RPE lines via mitochondrial ROS and cytosolic DNA, with AIM2 showing dominant control of IL-1β/IL-18 in some contexts, broadening the repertoire of upstream hazards beyond lysosomal damage (Korhonen, 2024).

Mechanistic gaps for IL-6R control of lysosomes/autophagy: Crucially, the provided materials do not furnish direct mechanistic or biochemical evidence that IL-6 or IL-6R signaling modulates RPE autophagic flux, lysosomal acidification (v-ATPase function), or cathepsin D enzymatic activity, and several excerpts explicitly note the absence of IL-6R blockade studies interrogating autophagy/lysosome endpoints in RPE/AMD models (Buniello et al., 2025; Brandstetter, 2016). In additional RPE experiments modulating autophagy and p62/SQSTM1, cytokine shifts were observed for MCP-1 and IL-8, while IL-6 did not exhibit consistent dependency on p62 state, arguing against a simple autophagy→IL-6 coupling that would predict lysosomal rescue by IL-6R blockade (Korhonen, 2024). Within this corpus, IL-6 behaves as part of a downstream inflammatory secretome during RPE stress rather than an upstream determinant of lysosomal health (Brandstetter, 2016).

Expected Effect  
Assay-level expectations under AMD-relevant stress paradigms should be aligned with the causal structure supported by the evidence.

- What IL-6R blockade should do: Given that RPE secrete IL-6 and can engage IL-6/IL-8 autocrine degenerative signaling in inflammatory contexts, tocilizumab is expected to abrogate IL-6–dependent downstream signaling in RPE and neighboring cells, dampening IL-6–responsive gene expression and paracrine effects where IL-6 is a driver (Brandstetter, 2016). In LMP/blue-light or impaired-clearance inflammasome models, IL-6 is robustly induced alongside IL-1β/IL-18 and partially depends on caspase-1–driven pathways, so tocilizumab would be expected to reduce IL-6-mediated signaling outputs but would not suppress upstream lysosomal damage, cathepsin leakage, inflammasome assembly, or caspase-1 activation per se (Brandstetter, 2016). Because inflammasome activation in these models also reduces constitutive VEGF secretion and polarizes cytokine release apically, IL-6R blockade might modestly alter the inflammatory milieu without restoring basal angiogenic signaling from RPE or preventing microglial chemotaxis induced by the broader cytokine secretome (Brandstetter, 2016).

- Unsupported elements of the working hypothesis: The claim that tocilizumab will prevent v-ATPase downregulation, preserve lysosomal pH, and maintain cathepsin D activity to slow RPE atrophy is not supported by the present corpus; none of the provided sources demonstrate that IL-6 or IL-6R signaling directly regulates v-ATPase subunits, lysosomal acidification, or CTSD activity in RPE, nor that IL-6R blockade restores these parameters in AMD-relevant assays (Buniello et al., 2025; Brandstetter, 2016). In contrast, interventions that directly target inflammasome priming/assembly or its stability (e.g., Hsp90 inhibition enabling autophagic degradation of NLRP3 when autophagy is intact) have demonstrated impact on inflammasome outputs in RPE models, emphasizing that upstream proteostasis/oxidative stress rather than IL-6 drives inflammasome activation in those settings (Piippo, 2019).

Consequently, tocilizumab is more likely to modulate inflammatory tone than to prevent the initiating RPE lysosomal failure that drives atrophy in dry AMD (Brandstetter, 2016; Piippo, 2019).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Biologic plausibility at the cytokine level: IL-6 is elevated in AMD and produced by RPE, and RPE inflammasome activation produces a pronounced IL-6 response (≈13.6-fold increase) together with IL-1β/IL-18 under AMD-relevant stresses; IL-6 can participate in autocrine degenerative loops in RPE after inflammatory stimuli (Buniello et al., 2025; Brandstetter, 2016). This supports testing whether IL-6/IL-6R signaling contributes to maladaptive inflammatory reinforcement in diseased RPE (Buniello et al., 2025).  
- Validated pharmacology and established clinical operations: Tocilizumab’s IL-6R blockade is mechanistically defined, and systemic dosing regimens (IV 8 mg/kg q4w, SC 162 mg weekly) and safety frameworks are standardized; ophthalmic trials have successfully embedded retinal structural and visual endpoints under systemic IL-6R blockade, providing a feasible operational scaffold (Assistance Publique–Hôpitaux de Paris, 2017; Shi, 2017b; Shi, 2017a).

- Lack of mechanistic linkage to lysosomal rescue: No evidence in the corpus shows that IL-6/IL-6R signaling controls v-ATPase function, lysosomal pH, autophagic flux, or cathepsin D activity in RPE; multiple excerpts explicitly note the absence of IL-6R blockade studies addressing autophagy/lysosome endpoints in RPE models (Buniello et al., 2025; Brandstetter, 2016). - Downstream positioning of IL-6 in AMD-relevant cascades: In LMP/blue-light and impaired-clearance models, IL-6 is part of a downstream secretome secondary to caspase-1–dependent pathways, whereas proximal determinants of RPE fate include lysosomal integrity, cathepsin activity, inflammasome assembly, and priming signals; targeting IL-6R is therefore unlikely to interrupt the initiating injury that drives RPE atrophy (Brandstetter, 2016).

Intravitreal data for tocilizumab are not provided, and systemic use in an elderly AMD population carries non-trivial risks (serious infections, cytopenias, hepatic injury, GI perforation risk, vaccine restrictions) that may outweigh an unproven benefit (University of Nebraska, 2016; Assistance Publique–Hôpitaux de Paris, 2017; Zhujiang Hospital, 2025).

- Given the current evidence, tocilizumab is not a priority candidate for slowing RPE atrophy in dry AMD via lysosomal preservation, because the mechanistic chain posited—IL-6R blockade preserving v-ATPase and cathepsin D activity—lacks experimental support in RPE/AMD models in this corpus, while disease-proximal injury nodes are driven by lysosomal/photooxidative damage, intracellular clearance failure, complement-driven NF-κB priming, and NLRP3/AIM2 activation (Brandstetter, 2016; Piippo, 2019; Korhonen, 2024).

- Absent compelling preclinical data showing that IL-6R blockade favorably modifies lysosomal function or decisively improves RPE survival in AMD-relevant paradigms, deprioritize tocilizumab in favor of targets that directly modulate the proximal injury axis (lysosome integrity, complement-NF-κB priming, and inflammasome assembly) (Brandstetter, 2016; Piippo, 2019).

Analysis: Candidate 1 (GDC-0941) and Candidate 2 (VX-765) both present mechanistically coherent approaches to dry AMD, but they differ sharply in evidence strength, safety, and translational readiness. GDC-0941 is a pan–class I PI3K inhibitor with robust human PK/PD and deep oncology experience. Its mechanistic rationale hinges on upstream suppression of PI3K→AKT2→mTORC1 signaling to relieve TFEB/TFE3 repression, thereby restoring lysosomal biogenesis and autophagic flux in RPE cells. This aligns closely with known dry AMD pathology—TFEB hyperphosphorylation, cathepsin D/L deficiency, impaired POS clearance—but no direct preclinical data validate pictilisib’s effects on TFEB activation, lysosomal acidification, or POS-derived autofluorescence in RPE. Moreover, systemic class I PI3K inhibition carries known liabilities (hyperglycemia, rash, GI toxicities), and ocular delivery/PK remain uncharacterized. By contrast, VX-765 is a well-tolerated, orally bioavailable caspase-1 inhibitor with Phase I/II safety and pharmacology. Inflammation and NLRP3/caspase-1–driven pyroptosis are firmly implicated in RPE injury and drusen pathogenesis. Generic caspase-1 inhibitors (e.g., Z-YVAD-FMK) have demonstrably reduced IL-1β release, stabilized lysosomal integrity, and improved RPE survival in AMD-relevant in vitro models. Although VX-765 itself lacks direct ocular data, its safety profile, selectivity for caspase-1, and central position in the inflammasome–pyroptosis axis give it a higher probability of successful preclinical validation and repurposing. Compared head-to-head, VX-765 has both more directly relevant biological precedent in RPE models and a cleaner human safety record. GDC-0941’s broad pathway targeting and toxicity concerns, combined with the absence of any RPE-specific data, make it riskier and less ready for translation without extensive de novo validation.
Reasoning: VX-765 outperforms GDC-0941 because it targets a discrete, disease-relevant node—caspase-1–mediated inflammasome activation and pyroptosis—that has been directly implicated in RPE pathology and validated with caspase inhibitors in AMD models. VX-765’s established human safety and oral bioavailability further de-risk its repurposing. In contrast, while GDC-0941 has high-quality clinical PK/PD data and plausible mechanistic linkage to autophagy/TFEB activation, it lacks any direct RPE/AMD evidence and carries known systemic toxicities. Its broad PI3K network perturbation may also introduce off-target liabilities in the retina. Therefore, VX-765 presents a more focused, evidence-backed, and safer path toward a viable dry AMD therapy.
