Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Eltanexor (also known as KPT-8602, MedKoo 406829) is a synthetic small‐molecule compound belonging to the class of “selective inhibitors of nuclear export” (SINE). These agents were developed by medicinal chemists to target the nuclear export protein exportin-1 (XPO1, also known as CRM1), which mediates the transport of a wide range of proteins from the nucleus to the cytoplasm. Eltanexor, like its predecessor Selinexor (KPT-330), functions by binding within the nuclear export signal (NES) recognition site of XPO1—most notably involving interaction with a conserved cysteine residue (Cys528) in XPO1’s NES‐binding pocket—and thereby preventing export of many regulatory proteins. However, Eltanexor has been engineered with modifications that confer improved tolerability along with oral bioavailability and a favorable pharmacokinetic profile, making it an attractive candidate for repurposing. SINE compounds have been extensively studied in oncology, where their ability to cause the nuclear retention of tumor suppressors has led to approved indications in certain hematological malignancies; accordingly, the synthetic origin of Eltanexor is rooted in efforts to optimize the drug‐like properties of early XPO1 inhibitors and to improve their clinical safety profile (Newell et al., 2024).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, the SINE class has been primarily associated with anticancer applications. Early compounds such as leptomycin B (LMB) were the first to demonstrate that inhibition of XPO1 could induce nuclear retention of proteins; however, issues with toxicity limited their clinical utility. Subsequent development efforts led to the creation of SINE compounds including Selinexor (KPT-330) and more recently Eltanexor (KPT-8602), which have undergone both preclinical and early-phase clinical trials in various cancer types. In these settings, XPO1 inhibition was shown to result in the nuclear accumulation of proteins that typically support cell survival, thereby selectively promoting apoptosis in cancer cells (Newell et al., 2024; Tang et al., 2025). Outside the field of oncology, mechanistic studies have indicated that inhibiting nuclear export can also impact proteins critically involved in autophagy regulation and lysosomal homeostasis. For instance, preclinical work in neuronal and glioblastoma models has shown that XPO1 inhibitors trigger nuclear retention of the master autophagy regulator TFEB, thereby enhancing autophagic flux and lysosomal biogenesis (Abokyi & Tse, 2025; Tang et al., 2025). To date, however, there is no published study that directly employs Eltanexor or other XPO1 inhibitors as therapeutic agents for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or related retinal degenerative conditions. In retinal research, extensive efforts have focused on modulating TFEB activity through alternative strategies—such as using trehalose, metformin, or genetic approaches—to restore lysosomal function in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells (Ghosh et al., 2024; Abokyi & Tse, 2025). Although the direct use of XPO1 inhibitors in RPE or dry AMD models has not been experimentally demonstrated, the established efficacy of SINE compounds in other contexts of neurodegeneration and autophagy dysregulation provides a compelling rationale for their repurposing in ocular diseases (Abokyi & Tse, 2025; Falcão et al., 2025).

Mechanism of Action:  
Under normal cellular conditions, XPO1 mediates the nuclear export of a diverse set of proteins by recognizing nuclear export signals (NES) present on cargo proteins. One critical cargo is the transcription factor TFEB, which regulates the expression of lysosomal hydrolases and autophagy-related genes by binding to CLEAR (coordinated lysosomal expression and regulation) elements within gene promoters. In nutrient-rich or stress-dysregulated states, TFEB undergoes phosphorylation by kinases such as mTORC1, resulting in cytoplasmic sequestration mediated by binding to 14-3-3 proteins and subsequent export from the nucleus via XPO1 (Pan & Valapala, 2022; La Spina et al., 2021; Li, 2018). Eltanexor’s mechanism of action is to bind within the NES-binding pocket of XPO1 and disrupt its interaction with such cargo proteins. The inhibition is achieved through covalent and slowly reversible binding to the Cys528 residue in XPO1, thereby preventing the nuclear export of target proteins. When export is blocked, TFEB (and likely its paralog TFE3) accumulates in the nucleus where it is free to activate transcription of CLEAR network genes. The resulting upregulation of lysosomal genes leads to increased lysosomal biogenesis, a lowering of lysosomal pH, and enhanced activation of hydrolases such as cathepsin D—all of which are critical to maintaining proteostasis and clearing damaged proteins and organelles (Abokyi & Tse, 2025; Pan & Valapala, 2022). Published data in glioblastoma models have shown that other XPO1 inhibitors such as Selinexor induce this type of nuclear trapping of TFEB, which correlates with an increase in autophagic flux and enhanced clearance mechanisms (Tang et al., 2025). Importantly, unlike pharmacological treatments that rely on mTOR inhibition (which can have widespread metabolic effects), the SINE approach works directly at the level of nuclear export, thereby selectively increasing TFEB activity independent of upstream mTOR/AKT signaling (Abokyi & Tse, 2025; Li, 2018).

Expected Effect in Dry AMD:  
Dry age-related macular degeneration is characterized by dysfunction of the RPE, resulting in diminished autophagic flux, accumulation of lipofuscin, and impaired degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (POS). In healthy RPE cells, nuclear TFEB orchestrates a transcriptional program that maintains lysosomal homeostasis by upregulating genes involved in lysosomal biogenesis, acidification, and cargo degradation. However, in aging and diseased RPE, TFEB becomes increasingly phosphorylated and sequestered in the cytoplasm, leading to reduced CLEAR network activity (Ghosh et al., 2024; Abokyi & Tse, 2025). The hypothesis behind repurposing Eltanexor for dry AMD is that by inhibiting XPO1 in RPE cells, the drug will promote nuclear retention of TFEB and TFE3. This nuclear accumulation is expected to drive upregulation of lysosomal gene expression, resulting in the restoration of lysosomal acidification and proteolytic capacity, particularly cathepsin D activity. An effective increase in autophagic flux and lysosomal biogenesis should aid in the degradation of accumulated toxic compounds such as lipofuscin and undegraded POS debris, ultimately improving RPE function and potentially slowing or reversing progression of dry AMD (Ghosh et al., 2024; Abokyi & Tse, 2025). In addition, preclinical studies in neurodegeneration and retinal models have demonstrated that enhancing TFEB activity—whether by trehalose treatment, gene therapy approaches, or by upstream modulation of kinases such as AKT2—can protect cells from oxidative and proteotoxic stress (Abokyi & Tse, 2025; Ghosh et al., 2024). Although direct evidence in RPE cells is still pending, the large body of mechanistic work linking nuclear TFEB accumulation to improved lysosomal function provides a strong rationale for expecting similar outcomes with Eltanexor in the context of dry AMD.

Overall Evaluation:  
Eltanexor presents several attractive features as a potential therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, especially given its novel mechanism of action and its ability to modulate a fundamental cellular process that is impaired in the disease. One of the major strengths of Eltanexor lies in its targeted inhibition of XPO1, which has been well validated in oncology and neurodegeneration studies as a means to induce nuclear retention of regulatory proteins. By preventing the export of TFEB and TFE3, Eltanexor is expected to allow these key transcription factors to reactivate the CLEAR network, thereby restoring lysosomal function, lowering lysosomal pH, and boosting the activity of cathepsin D-mediated degradation. This mechanism is particularly compelling for dry AMD because RPE cell dysfunction in the disease has been closely linked to defective autophagy and impaired clearance of toxic aggregates (Ghosh et al., 2024; Abokyi & Tse, 2025). Moreover, the proposed therapeutic approach bypasses some of the limitations of mTOR-based interventions, as it directly affects nucleocytoplasmic transport rather than broadly inhibiting upstream signaling pathways. This specificity provides an additional level of mechanistic precision that could translate into a better safety profile for chronic applications in an aging population.

Nevertheless, several weaknesses and challenges must be acknowledged. First, while there is abundant evidence that XPO1 inhibitors such as Selinexor induce TFEB nuclear retention and autophagy in glioblastoma and other non-ocular models (Tang et al., 2025), there is currently a lack of direct preclinical data evaluating Eltanexor or related compounds in retinal pigment epithelial cells or in animal models of dry AMD. The extrapolation of data from cancer and neuronal models to RPE cells, while mechanistically plausible, remains to be experimentally validated. Second, because XPO1 regulates the nuclear export of a wide range of proteins—not only TFEB and TFE3—there is a potential for off-target effects that could disrupt other cellular processes. This issue is particularly critical in the context of chronic administration in elderly patients, who may be more susceptible to systemic side effects. Third, the pharmacodynamic properties required to achieve effective nuclear retention of TFEB in the RPE may differ from those established in oncology trials. For example, the concentration of Eltanexor required to affect TFEB nuclear localization and lysosomal gene expression in RPE cells might be higher than that used in cancer models, necessitating further optimization of dosing and delivery strategies. Finally, while the oral bioavailability and existing Phase I safety data of Eltanexor support its clinical feasibility (Tang et al., 2025), localized and retina-specific delivery might ultimately prove necessary to maximize its therapeutic window and minimize systemic exposure.

In summary, Eltanexor’s mechanism of inhibiting XPO1 to promote nuclear retention of TFEB/TFE3 aligns very well with emerging therapeutic strategies aimed at correcting lysosomal dysfunction in dry AMD. The extensive literature on the role of TFEB in regulating autophagy and lysosomal biogenesis in RPE cells provides a strong mechanistic foundation for this approach (Ghosh et al., 2024; Abokyi & Tse, 2025). Additionally, the demonstrated ability of XPO1 inhibitors to induce autophagy in other preclinical models (Abokyi & Tse, 2025; Tang et al., 2025) reinforces the potential for repurposing Eltanexor in an ocular setting. However, to move forward, it will be essential to generate direct experimental evidence in primary RPE cultures and in vivo dry AMD models to verify that Eltanexor indeed promotes TFEB nuclear retention, enhances CLEAR network activity, lowers lysosomal pH, and increases cathepsin D–mediated cargo degradation in the retinal environment. Addressing these issues will not only validate the therapeutic concept but will also help to optimize dosing, delivery, and safety profiles tailored for the treatment of dry AMD.

Overall, while Eltanexor shows promise as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD owing to its targeted mechanism of action and favorable preclinical attributes in other disease models, further studies focused explicitly on retinal cell biology and AMD pathology are imperative before clinical translation can be considered. The strength of the candidate lies in its mechanistic specificity and the well-established role of TFEB/TFE3 in lysosomal function, whereas the main weaknesses revolve around the current lack of direct evidence in the target system and potential off-target effects associated with global nuclear export inhibition (Abokyi & Tse, 2025; Pan & Valapala, 2022; Ghosh et al., 2024).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Lithium chloride (Sigma L9650) is an inorganic salt belonging to the family of lithium compounds that has been in use for several decades, primarily as a mood stabilizer in the treatment of bipolar disorder. It is synthesized by combining lithium carbonate or lithium hydroxide with hydrochloric acid, yielding a highly water‐soluble salt that is widely available for both clinical and experimental research purposes (Carmassi et al., 2016; Vallée et al., 2021). As a prototypical member of the lithium salts, lithium chloride has been repurposed in recent years as a candidate for neuroprotection because of its ability to inhibit glycogen synthase kinase-3β (GSK3β), a serine/threonine kinase involved in numerous intracellular signaling cascades. Lithium’s chemical simplicity belies its complex pharmacology; its effects extend well beyond mood stabilization to encompass modulation of cell survival, inflammatory responses, and protein degradation pathways. In this context, lithium salts are now recognized as small molecule modulators that can affect intracellular transcriptional programs, including nuclear import of factors such as transcription factor EB (TFEB) and β-catenin, which in turn control the expression of genes necessary for lysosomal biogenesis and autophagic flux (Carmassi et al., 2016; Vallée et al., 2021). These mechanistic insights, originally developed in studies of neurodegenerative and psychiatric diseases, have motivated investigations into whether lithium chloride might be repurposed to address the autophagic and lysosomal dysfunction observed in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD), particularly in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) (Carmassi et al., 2016; Vallée et al., 2021).

Therapeutic History:  
Lithium salts have a long-standing clinical history in psychiatry, especially in the management of bipolar disorder, where their dosing and long-term safety profiles have been thoroughly characterized. In addition, numerous preclinical studies in neuroscience have demonstrated that lithium can reduce tau phosphorylation and improve neuronal cell survival, partly by inhibiting GSK3β and modulating downstream targets such as β-catenin and Bcl-2 (Carmassi et al., 2016; Vallée et al., 2021). Lithium has been evaluated in several neurodegenerative contexts—for instance, it has been examined for its potential benefits in Alzheimer’s disease, Huntington’s disease, and Parkinson’s disease, with some studies reporting modest improvements in neuroprotection and behavioral outcomes, although clinical results have been mixed (Singh et al., 2022; Vallée et al., 2021). More specifically, preclinical data in the central nervous system have shown that prolonged exposure to lithium increases cortical grey matter and enhances neuronal markers such as N-acetyl-aspartate, suggesting that lithium exerts trophic and neuroprotective effects (Carmassi et al., 2016). In the ocular arena, while lithium’s use has been predominantly described in the context of glaucoma—in which its inhibition of GSK3β was shown to modulate WNT/β-catenin signaling in trabecular meshwork cells—the literature offers no direct clinical or in-depth preclinical evaluation of lithium chloride in dry AMD or for modulating autophagy specifically in RPE cells (Singh et al., 2022; Vallée et al., 2021). A search in clinical trial registries has not identified any trials using lithium chloride for macular degeneration, underscoring a notable gap between the neuroprotective models in which lithium has been studied and its potential application in dry AMD (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).

Mechanism of Action:  
Lithium chloride’s mechanisms of action are multifaceted, but a significant aspect relevant to the dry AMD hypothesis is its ability to inhibit GSK3β. GSK3β normally phosphorylates a variety of substrates including β-catenin and TFEB, leading to cytosolic retention and subsequent degradation; inhibition of GSK3β by lithium therefore results in stabilization and nuclear accumulation of β-catenin and promotes TFEB nuclear entry (Carmassi et al., 2016; Vallée et al., 2021). In detail, lithium binds directly to the magnesium-sensitive site of GSK3β and also promotes its inhibitory N-terminal serine phosphorylation, leading to a dose-dependent suppression of GSK3β activity (Carmassi et al., 2016). The release of β-catenin from the destruction complex allows it to accumulate in the nucleus, where it acts as a transcriptional coactivator for genes that contribute to cell survival and homeostasis, including those involved in lysosomal biogenesis (Carmassi et al., 2016; Vallée et al., 2021). Similarly, TFEB is a master transcription factor that coordinates the expression of a variety of genes encoding lysosomal enzymes and autophagy-related proteins. Under basal conditions, phosphorylation retains TFEB in the cytosol; inhibition of GSK3β can contribute to dephosphorylation of TFEB, thereby facilitating its nuclear translocation and transcriptional activation of targets such as cathepsin D (CTSD) and subunits of the vacuolar ATPase (v-ATPase) that are crucial for lysosomal acidification (Carmassi et al., 2016; Friedman et al., 2015). In neuronal models, lithium treatment has been demonstrated to increase levels of neurotrophic factors and cell survival molecules, as well as to enhance autophagy-mediated clearance of toxic proteins including aggregated forms of tau and other proteins implicated in neurodegenerative disease (Vallée et al., 2021). Furthermore, lithium’s inhibition of inositol monophosphatase further contributes to autophagy induction through an mTOR-independent mechanism, reinforcing its capacity to modulate autophagic flux (Friedman et al., 2015). Despite these promising mechanistic insights, it is important to note that most of the supporting data have been generated in neuronal or non-ocular cell systems; direct evidence for lithium chloride-mediated activation of TFEB/β-catenin signaling and upregulation of lysosomal acidification machinery specifically in RPE cells remains limited (Golestaneh et al., 2018; Guha et al., 2014).

Expected Effect:  
Based on the hypothesis, treatment with lithium chloride in RPE cells is anticipated to inhibit GSK3β, leading to a cascade of intracellular events that restore impaired autophagic flux—a major pathological hallmark in dry AMD. Specifically, inhibition of GSK3β should reduce the phosphorylation-dependent cytosolic retention of TFEB and β-catenin, thereby facilitating their nuclear import. In the nucleus, these transcription factors can activate a broad transcriptional program that upregulates the synthesis of lysosomal proteins such as cathepsin D and components of the v-ATPase complex, ultimately leading to enhanced lysosomal acidification (Carmassi et al., 2016; Friedman et al., 2015). This improved lysosomal function is expected to accelerate the degradation of photoreceptor outer segment debris and other autophagic substrates, leading to a restoration of autophagic flux and a reduction in lipofuscin accumulation—a prominent feature of dry AMD pathology (Golestaneh et al., 2018). In parallel, lithium’s neuroprotective effects, including the upregulation of prosurvival factors like Bcl-2 and the attenuation of proinflammatory signaling pathways, may further support RPE cell survival and function under chronic oxidative stress conditions (Vallée et al., 2021). Given that lysosomal alkalinization is known to impair cathepsin D activity and autophagic degradation in RPE cells, the upregulation of cathepsin D via TFEB activation represents a critical therapeutic target to counteract the reduced degradative capacity observed in dry AMD (Guha et al., 2014). Moreover, the candidate’s reported ocular penetration and long-term safety in other contexts provide a translational rationale, though the literature is notably deficient in direct measurements of RPE-specific outcomes—thus, further studies are required to validate that lithium chloride achieves effective intraocular concentrations without toxicity (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.; Vallée et al., 2021). The expected outcome in an in vitro assay would be an increase in nuclear TFEB and β-catenin as determined by immunocytochemistry and Western blot of nuclear extracts, an increase in mRNA and protein levels of lysosomal acidification machinery (e.g., v-ATPase subunits) and cathepsin D, restoration of autophagic flux as evidenced by normalized LC3-II/LC3-I ratios and p62 degradation, and improved clearance of photoreceptor outer segment-derived material in RPE cell culture models (Golestaneh et al., 2018).

Overall Evaluation:  
The repurposing of lithium chloride for dry age-related macular degeneration is based on a compelling mechanistic rationale that builds upon well-established aspects of lithium’s pharmacology. On one hand, the drug’s ability to inhibit GSK3β—and thereby to promote the nuclear translocation of TFEB and β-catenin—aligns well with the therapeutic goal of upregulating lysosomal gene expression and restoring autophagic flux in RPE cells (Golestaneh et al., 2018). Lithium’s longstanding use in psychiatric medicine has resulted in a rich and well-documented clinical safety profile, and its neuroprotective benefits in various models lend additional support to its potential utility in other degenerative conditions including ocular diseases (Carmassi et al., 2016; Vallée et al., 2021).

However, there are several notable weaknesses and gaps that must be addressed before lithium chloride can be considered a robust therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. First, while preclinical studies in neuronal models offer supportive evidence that lithium can modulate autophagy and enhance lysosomal function, there is a lack of direct data demonstrating these mechanisms in RPE cells specifically (Golestaneh et al., 2018). Second, the pharmacokinetic profile of lithium chloride in the eye—especially the extent to which it penetrates the RPE following systemic or local administration—remains poorly characterized, and this is a critical factor given the importance of achieving therapeutic concentrations in the retina without causing off-target toxicity (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.). Third, although lithium’s long-term safety has been established in psychiatric populations, its known systemic toxicities, including renal and thyroid effects, as well as its narrow therapeutic window, raise concerns about the potential risks of repurposing it for an ocular indication where localized delivery may be necessary to avoid systemic exposure (Singh et al., 2022; Vallée et al., 2021). Finally, the absence of any registered clinical trials or robust preclinical studies in an AMD model means that the translational viability of lithium chloride for this indication is still highly speculative (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).

Despite these concerns, the strengths of lithium chloride as a repurposed agent for dry AMD are significant. Its ability to target GSK3β provides a unique molecular entry point that could bypass some of the drawbacks of other autophagy modulators that primarily act through mTOR inhibition—a strategy that has yielded mixed clinical results (Friedman et al., 2015; Vallée et al., 2021). Moreover, the multi-modal action of lithium, which encompasses both anti-inflammatory and anti-excitotoxic effects in addition to its autophagy-promoting properties, suggests that it could provide a broad-spectrum protective effect in the stressed cellular environment of the RPE (Carmassi et al., 2016; Vallée et al., 2021). Nonetheless, given the complexity of RPE biology and the multifactorial nature of dry AMD pathogenesis—as evidenced by the alterations in lysosomal pH, reduced cathepsin activity, and compromised membrane trafficking in these cells—any candidate drug must be rigorously evaluated in appropriate RPE or AMD models before clinical translation is attempted (Golestaneh et al., 2018; Guha et al., 2014).

In summary, lithium chloride holds promise as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD through its inhibition of GSK3β and the subsequent activation of nuclear TFEB/β-catenin signaling pathways, which are anticipated to upregulate lysosomal acidification machinery and cathepsin D expression and thereby restore autophagic flux in the RPE. The candidate’s well-documented clinical history and long-term safety in other indications provide additional encouragement for its further preclinical exploration. However, critical issues—such as the need for direct experimental evidence in RPE system models, the establishment of effective and safe ocular dosing regimens with adequate retinal penetration, and thorough evaluations of potential systemic and ocular toxicities—must be rigorously addressed. Until these gaps are filled by focused preclinical and translational research, the use of lithium chloride for dry AMD remains a promising yet still unproven strategy that warrants additional investigation (Carmassi et al., 2016; Friedman et al., 2015; Golestaneh et al., 2018; Guha et al., 2014; Vallée et al., 2021; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.; Singh et al., 2022).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Everolimus (Afinitor; Novartis) is a semi‐synthetic derivative of sirolimus—a macrolide originally isolated from Streptomyces hygroscopicus—as evidenced by its chemical designation as 4-O-(2-hydroxyethyl)-rapamycin (Liu et al., 2023, pp. 11–12). By introducing a 2-hydroxyethyl group at position 40, everolimus achieves greater hydrophilicity and an increased oral bioavailability (from 10% to 16% relative to sirolimus) while retaining the core macrolactone structure that is characteristic of rapalogs (Liu et al., 2023, pp. 11–12; Weber, 2015, pp. 27–28). This compound belongs to the class of mTOR inhibitors—specifically, a first‐generation rapalog that selectively inhibits the mTOR complex 1 (mTORC1) while sparing mTORC2 (Liu et al., 2023, pp. 10–11; Weber, 2015, pp. 27–28). As a synthetic derivative of a naturally occurring product, everolimus represents the successful strategy of chemical modification to optimize pharmacokinetic properties and clinical tolerability. The design parameters underpinning everolimus’ synthesis have been guided by the goal of retaining potent immunosuppressive and anti‐proliferative effects while optimizing parameters such as solubility, half‐life, and tissue penetration, with the added advantage of an oral formulation already approved for several clinical indications (Liu et al., 2023, pp. 11–12; Wang et al., 2022, pp. 6–8).

Therapeutic History:  
Everolimus has a well‐established therapeutic history as an immunosuppressant and antineoplastic agent. Clinically, it is approved for treating advanced renal cell carcinoma, progressive neuroendocrine tumors of pancreatic origin, and subependymal giant cell astrocytoma in tuberous sclerosis complex patients who are not candidates for surgery (Wang et al., 2022, pp. 6–8; Weber, 2015, pp. 27–28). In these indications, its mechanism as an mTORC1 inhibitor serves to arrest cell cycle progression and inhibit angiogenesis, which are central to its antitumor activity (Kuo et al., 2018, pp. 5–7; Weber, 2015, pp. 27–28). Moreover, everolimus has been effectively used in the context of organ transplantation to prevent allograft rejection by impairing helper T‐cell proliferation (Wang et al., 2022, pp. 6–8; Weber, 2015, pp. 27–28).

With regard to ocular applications, although everolimus has not been approved specifically for dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD), several preclinical studies have demonstrated its potential benefits in ocular cell types and models. For instance, in vitro investigations have highlighted that everolimus can inhibit the proliferation and migration of retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells and modulate mTOR signaling within retinal tissue—an effect critical to conditions such as proliferative vitreoretinopathy (PVR) (Kuo et al., 2018, pp. 5–8). Additionally, clinical trials such as the Phase 2 randomized trial for neovascular AMD (albeit focused on wet AMD) have assessed everolimus’s efficacy in combination with anti‐vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) agents (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2009), thereby providing indirect support for its ocular pharmacokinetic (PK) profile and safety profile. This background, combined with its well‐known systemic tolerability, underscores its candidacy for repurposing in nonexudative (dry) AMD—a disease area in which few pharmacologic treatments exist.

Mechanism of Action:  
Everolimus exerts its effects by binding to the intracellular receptor FKBP12, forming a complex that interacts with and inhibits mTORC1 (Liu et al., 2023, pp. 11–12; Weber, 2015, pp. 27–28). The inhibition of mTORC1 results in a downstream decrease in the phosphorylation of ribosomal protein S6 kinase (S6K1) and other substrates such as ribosomal protein S6 (RPS6), effectively suppressing cap‐dependent protein synthesis and cellular proliferation (Kuo et al., 2018, pp. 5–7; Liu et al., 2023, pp. 10–11). In the context of RPE cells, inhibition of mTORC1 plays a particularly critical role in modulating autophagic flux. Under normal conditions, mTORC1 phosphorylates and suppresses the transcription factor EB (TFEB), a master regulator of lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy. Inhibition of mTORC1 frees TFEB to translocate to the nucleus where it transactivates genes that codify for lysosomal proteins, such as the subunits of the vacuolar ATPase (V‐ATPase), and hydrolases including cathepsin D (Kuo et al., 2018, p. 7; Nieto et al., 2015, pp. 28–32). Preclinical studies have shown that in RPE culture systems, treatment with everolimus results in an increase in LC3 turnover—a marker of enhanced autophagic flux—and accelerates the maturation of cathepsin D (CTSD), which is essential for effective lysosomal degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (Kuo et al., 2018, pp. 5–8). Such modulation of the autophagy–lysosome pathway is mechanistically attractive in dry AMD because the accumulation of cellular debris and lipofuscin in RPE cells is implicated in disease pathogenesis. Furthermore, it has been reported that everolimus displays superior ocular tissue penetration compared with sirolimus in in vitro porcine corneal models, suggesting that its formulation could be optimized for direct ocular administration if required (Liu et al., 2023, pp. 11–14). Overall, the biochemical profile of everolimus supports the hypothesis that targeted mTORC1 inhibition in RPE cells could lead to enhanced TFEB activation and a subsequent restoration of lysosomal function—thereby addressing one of the key pathological features underlying dry AMD.

Expected Effect:  
The hypothesis proposes that everolimus will inhibit mTORC1 in RPE cells, leading to the activation of TFEB, a critical step in lysosomal biogenesis and function. Upon release from mTORC1‐mediated phosphorylation constraints, TFEB translocates to the nucleus where it upregulates the expression of essential lysosomal genes, including those encoding V‐ATPase subunits (which are responsible for lysosomal acidification) and cathepsin D (CTSD), a protease required for the degradation of accumulated waste products (Kuo et al., 2018, p. 7; Nieto et al., 2015, pp. 28–32). This molecular cascade is expected to improve the clearance of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) and other cellular debris that accumulate in RPE cells owing to age‐related impairment of autophagy. In vitro data support that everolimus treatment increases LC3 turnover and facilitates the maturation of CTSD, both of which are indicative of enhanced autophagic flux and lysosomal functionality (Kuo et al., 2018, pp. 5–8). Given that RPE cells naturally express components of the mTOR signaling pathway—including high levels of mTORC1—and that dysfunctional lysosomal clearance is a hallmark of dry AMD (as exemplified by the accumulation of lipofuscin and drusen formation), the expected pharmacodynamic effect of everolimus would be to restore homeostasis in these cells. Successful activation of TFEB is anticipated to lead to improved degradation of damaged organelles and protein aggregates, potentially mitigating the progression of retinal degeneration characteristic of dry AMD. Moreover, the fact that everolimus is already formulated for oral administration with a known ocular PK profile further supports the translational potential of this candidate: systemic dosing may achieve sufficient retinal concentrations to exert the desired effects in RPE cells without necessitating invasive delivery methods (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2009; Liu et al., 2023, pp. 11–12).

Overall Evaluation:  
The potential of everolimus as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD is supported by several compelling factors. First, its established clinical safety and efficacy in other indications—such as renal cell carcinoma and immunosuppression in transplantation—reduce the translational risk associated with drug repurposing (Weber, 2015, pp. 27–28; Wang et al., 2022, pp. 6–8). The fact that everolimus is an FDA‐approved agent with an oral formulation makes it an attractive candidate for repurposing, as its dosing, systemic distribution, and side‐effect profile are already well characterized. In addition, its selective inhibition of mTORC1 has a clear mechanistic rationale in the context of dry AMD. By specifically targeting the mTORC1–TFEB axis, everolimus may correct the impaired lysosomal degradation and autophagic dysfunction that underlie the accumulation of pathogenic debris in RPE cells (Kuo et al., 2018, p. 7; Nieto et al., 2015, pp. 28–32).

A major strength of everolimus is the robust preclinical evidence indicative of its capacity to modulate autophagy. In ocular cell culture systems, everolimus has been shown to enhance LC3 turnover and promote CTSD maturation—both key markers of autophagic and lysosomal efficiency (Kuo et al., 2018, pp. 5–8). Additionally, its improved ocular penetration compared to its parent compound sirolimus suggests that even systemic administration might yield therapeutically relevant levels in the retina (Liu et al., 2023, pp. 11–14). This represents a significant advantage in the context of dry AMD, where achieving effective drug delivery to deeply situated retinal tissues is a persistent challenge.

However, several weaknesses must be acknowledged. Despite a sound mechanistic rationale, direct clinical evidence for everolimus’s efficacy in dry AMD is lacking. Existing clinical studies have primarily focused on other ocular conditions such as neovascular AMD and PVR, and the particular pathophysiology of dry AMD—with its complex interplay of oxidative stress, complement dysregulation, and chronic inflammation—may require a more nuanced therapeutic approach (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2009; Kuo et al., 2018, pp. 3–5). It is also important to consider the potential systemic side effects of mTOR inhibition, which include hyperglycemia, dyslipidemia, stomatitis, and, in some cases, immunosuppression (Weber, 2015, pp. 27–28, 28–29). Although these adverse events are generally manageable in oncology and transplant settings, the chronic nature of dry AMD treatment may necessitate a careful balancing of therapeutic benefits against systemic risks. Moreover, while everolimus selectively inhibits mTORC1, prolonged inhibition of this pathway could potentially interfere with homeostatic cellular processes beyond autophagy, raising concerns about long‐term retinal safety.

Another consideration relates to the multifactorial etiology of dry AMD. While lysosomal dysfunction is a critical aspect of the disease, it is accompanied by other pathological processes such as oxidative damage, chronic inflammation, and alterations in the complement cascade. Thus, monotherapy with an mTORC1 inhibitor may not be sufficiently robust to address all disease mechanisms. Combination therapies that target multiple pathological pathways might ultimately be necessary for effective disease modification. Lastly, discrepancies in the translation of preclinical findings to human disease remain a persistent challenge. For example, while certain animal models of retinal disease have demonstrated beneficial effects of mTOR inhibition, analogous results have not always been replicated in clinical settings (Kuo et al., 2018, pp. 3–5; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2009).

In summary, everolimus presents as a mechanistically intriguing candidate for repurposing in dry AMD due to its ability to inhibit mTORC1 and thereby promote TFEB‐mediated restoration of lysosomal function. Its solid record as an FDA‐approved drug with established dosing regimens and acceptable systemic safety lends additional support to its viability as a repurposing candidate. Preclinical data suggest that everolimus increases autophagic flux in RPE cells, enhancing LC3 turnover and CTSD maturation, which theoretically should facilitate the clearance of pathological debris that characterizes dry AMD (Kuo et al., 2018, pp. 5–8). The advantages of an oral formulation and favorable ocular pharmacokinetics further underpin its translational potential (Liu et al., 2023, pp. 11–12; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2009).

Nonetheless, the candidate also faces important challenges. Key limitations include the absence of direct clinical evidence for efficacy in dry AMD, potential systemic adverse effects associated with prolonged mTORC1 inhibition, and the inherent complexity of dry AMD pathology, which may require multimodal therapeutic strategies. Moreover, past experiences in ocular applications—such as studies in PVR models where everolimus did not yield a statistically significant clinical improvement—highlight the need for carefully controlled dose-finding and safety studies (Kuo et al., 2018, pp. 3–5). It will be crucial to establish that systemic dosing can achieve therapeutic retinal concentrations without eliciting unintended systemic toxicity or disrupting normal RPE physiology.

Overall, while mechanistic and preclinical data provide a strong rationale for repurposing everolimus to treat dry AMD, further rigorous preclinical studies specifically in models of dry AMD are warranted. A careful evaluation of dosing regimens, potential adverse effects, and efficacy endpoints will be essential in the translational development of everolimus for this indication. The mechanistic specificity for mTORC1 inhibition, combined with the ability to enhance autophagic clearance in RPE cells, represents a significant strength that could offer a novel approach to modifying the course of dry AMD. However, the challenges associated with systemic mTOR inhibition and the need for combination strategies or localized delivery systems must be addressed in subsequent research phases. In conclusion, everolimus is a promising, though not yet definitively validated, candidate for repurposing in dry AMD, and we recommend that further detailed studies be undertaken to fully elucidate its potential in restoring lysosomal function and ameliorating retinal degeneration in this patient population (Liu et al., 2023, pp. 11–12; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2009; Kuo et al., 2018, pp. 5–7; Weber, 2015, pp. 27–28; Wang et al., 2022, pp. 6–8; Kuo et al., 2018, pp. 7–8).

Below is our detailed evaluation of GSK2656157 for repurposing in dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD), structured in the requested format.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
GSK2656157 is a small‐molecule inhibitor of PERK (protein kinase R–like endoplasmic reticulum kinase) that was discovered and optimized through medicinal‐chemistry efforts originally led by GlaxoSmithKline. This compound belongs to the class of ATP‐competitive, Type I inhibitors that target the kinase domain of PERK, binding within the ATP‐binding cleft and stabilizing a “DFG‐in, Cα‐helix shifted” conformation of the dephosphorylated kinase domain (Axten, 2017, pp. 15–19). Structurally, the compound is an indoline‐derived molecule; similar chemical series include the indoline/aminoquinazoline chemotypes that have been widely profiled for their high potency and kinase selectivity across panels exceeding 300 kinases (Axten, 2017, pp. 15–19). Originally, these inhibitors were developed as research tools to interrogate the role of PERK in the unfolded protein response (UPR) in oncology and neurodegeneration contexts, and in preclinical studies GSK2656157 demonstrated activity in suppressing tumor growth and angiogenesis in mouse xenograft models via inhibition of PERK autophosphorylation (Atkins et al., 2013, pp. 1–2, 8). As a synthetic small molecule, its origins lie in rational design based on X‐ray–guided structure–activity relationships, which enabled optimization for both high selectivity (with >100‐fold selectivity over related kinases including other eIF2α kinases as well as a broad kinome panel) and sufficient in vivo pharmacokinetics (Axten, 2017, pp. 15–19; Atkins et al., 2013, pp. 1–2). Thus, from a chemical and developmental perspective, GSK2656157 is a first‐in‐class PERK inhibitor that exemplifies how targeted kinase inhibition can be achieved by rational design.  

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, PERK inhibitors such as GSK2606414 and its more selective derivative GSK2656157 were developed primarily for indications in oncology and neurodegeneration. Preclinical studies in tumor xenograft models have demonstrated that oral dosing of GSK2656157 can suppress PERK-mediated signaling, resulting in attenuated phospho-eIF2α levels, diminished transcriptional responses of unfolded protein response (UPR) genes, and reduced tumor vascular density (Atkins et al., 2013, pp. 1–2, 8). In neurodegenerative models—for instance in prion and tauopathy mouse models—PERK inhibition has been shown to restore global protein synthesis, decrease the levels of phospho-tau, and produce mixed effects on behavior and neuronal survival (Rozpędek-Kamińska et al., 2020, pp. 17–19). Meanwhile, within the ocular space, experimental studies with the closely related PERK inhibitor GSK2606414 (a chemical analogue of GSK2656157) in in vitro retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cell models have demonstrated on-target inhibition of PERK signaling (evidenced by reduction in eIF2α phosphorylation) along with downstream alterations in stress markers such as CHOP and VEGF mRNA (Jiang et al., 2017, pp. 1–2). However, direct use of GSK2656157 in dry AMD or similar inflammatory/degenerative ocular conditions has not yet been reported in the literature. Some studies investigating retinal degeneration models, such as P23H rhodopsin transgenic rats, have suggested that PERK inhibition can worsen photoreceptor survival by enhancing misfolded protein aggregation, although these studies were typically conducted with compounds such as GSK2606414A (Athanasiou et al., 2017, pp. 1–2, 5–7). There is, therefore, limited clinical or preclinical history regarding the use of GSK2656157 specifically in AMD or related ocular diseases. In addition, while the compound has demonstrated acceptable pharmacokinetics and tolerability in preclinical oncology settings—with measurable systemic exposures—it is important to note that systemic PERK inhibition in multiple species has been associated with toxic liabilities such as pancreatic toxicity (Atkins et al., 2013, p. 8; Axten, 2017, pp. 1–7). Consequently, although the therapeutic class has a relatively rich history in oncology and neurodegeneration, its direct application to dry AMD remains a new and untested repurposing approach that requires careful consideration of pharmacodynamic impacts in ocular tissues and rigorous safety profiling.  

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, PERK functions as an endoplasmic reticulum (ER)–resident kinase that is activated upon the accumulation of misfolded proteins, a hallmark of chronic ER stress. Normally, when the ER’s folding capacity is overwhelmed, the molecular chaperone GRP78 dissociates from PERK, enabling PERK to oligomerize and autophosphorylate, which then enables it to phosphorylate the α subunit of eukaryotic initiation factor 2 (eIF2α) at serine-51 (Axten, 2017, pp. 7–11). Phosphorylation of eIF2α leads to a global reduction in protein synthesis—a protective adaptation that prevents further accumulation of misfolded proteins—and also selectively permits the translation of stress-induced genes, most notably ATF4. ATF4 subsequently upregulates transcription factors such as CHOP, which can drive pro-apoptotic signaling if ER stress persists (Axten, 2017, pp. 7–11; Chu et al., 2021, p. 8). In the context of dry AMD, chronic ER stress in RPE cells has been implicated in disrupting cellular proteostasis, where misfolded proteins—including subunits of key complexes like the vacuolar ATPase (v-ATPase)—may fail to fold properly, leading to impaired lysosomal acidification (Kaarniranta et al., 2018, pp. 1–4; Athanasiou et al., 2017, pp. 1–2). The hypothesis is that by inhibiting PERK with GSK2656157, the excessive phosphorylation of eIF2α and the maladaptive integrated stress response (ISR) can be attenuated. This would not only restore global protein synthesis but also prevent downstream consequences such as upregulation of CHOP and VEGF, thereby reducing pro-apoptotic as well as pro-inflammatory pathways (Jiang et al., 2017, pp. 1–2). Furthermore, it is posited that such normalization in the ISR could allow for proper folding and assembly of lysosomal enzymes and complexes, including the v-ATPase. Proper v-ATPase assembly is critical for maintaining low intraluminal pH in lysosomes, which is necessary for the activation and maturation of hydrolases like cathepsin D (Kaarniranta et al., 2018, pp. 1–4). In neuronal models, PERK inhibition has been associated with improvements in lysosomal function and proteostasis, indicating that reduction of chronic ER stress can indirectly favor the re-establishment of lysosomal homeostasis (Jiang et al., 2017, pp. 1–2). In essence, GSK2656157, by specifically targeting and inhibiting PERK, interferes with the pathological arm of the UPR (i.e. excessive eIF2α phosphorylation) that is hypothesized to contribute to impaired lysosomal acidification in RPE cells under chronic stress conditions—a mechanism that might be particularly relevant in the pathophysiology of dry AMD (Axten, 2017, pp. 24–28).  

Expected Effect:  
In the proposed assays, the primary expected effect of GSK2656157 is to inhibit PERK activity in RPE cells, as evidenced by reduced phosphorylation of eIF2α, and thereby dampen downstream signaling events that lead to the induction of ATF4, CHOP, and ultimately pro-apoptotic and proangiogenic factors such as VEGF. In vitro studies with analogues of GSK2656157 (such as GSK2606414) in ARPE-19 cells have shown dose-dependent inhibition of eIF2α phosphorylation with subsequent decreases in CHOP and VEGF mRNA expression without necessarily triggering apoptosis at higher doses (Jiang et al., 2017, pp. 1–2). These results provide a proof-of-concept that pharmacological inhibition of PERK can modulate this critical signaling pathway in RPE cells. The hypothesis for dry AMD is that chronic ER stress in the RPE disrupts lysosomal acidification via misfolding of v-ATPase subunits; under normal circumstances, proper v-ATPase function ensures that lysosomes maintain their acidic environment, which is essential for protease activation—including cathepsin D. Cathepsin D, in turn, is critical for lysosomal degradation of photoreceptor outer segments and for preventing lipofuscin accumulation, a pathological process in dry AMD (Kaarniranta et al., 2018, pp. 1–4). Thus, by reducing PERK activation through GSK2656157, it is expected that the overactive ISR would be tempered sufficiently to allow for the proper folding and assembly of v-ATPase complexes, thereby restoring lysosomal acidification (Chu et al., 2021, p. 8; Athanasiou et al., 2017, pp. 1–2). This restoration is anticipated to improve cathepsin D maturation and activity, leading to better clearance of intracellular debris and misfolded proteins, ultimately protecting RPE cells from stress-induced degeneration. On a cellular level, normalizing lysosomal pH would also promote autophagy flux, which is often impaired in the aged RPE, thereby mitigating one of the key contributing factors in the dry AMD phenotype (Kaarniranta et al., 2018, pp. 1–4; Athanasiou et al., 2017, pp. 1–2). Importantly, RPE cells are known to express PERK and components of the UPR, with studies demonstrating that ER stress markers, including phospho-PERK and phospho-eIF2α, are elevated in pathological states associated with AMD (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021, pp. 11–12; Chu et al., 2021, p. 8). Therefore, if GSK2656157 can achieve adequate ocular tissue exposure and inhibit PERK activity in the RPE, the expected outcome would be a reduction in cellular stress–mediated apoptosis and proliferation of protective pathways that maintain lysosomal and autophagy functions (Jiang et al., 2017, pp. 1–2; Rozpędek-Kamińska et al., 2020, pp. 17–19). Moreover, the compound’s known pharmacokinetic profile in preclinical oncology studies suggests that it is systemically bioavailable and, according to some reports, may achieve ocular tissue distribution; thus it is conceivable that with appropriate dosing and local delivery strategies, GSK2656157 could achieve effective concentrations in RPE cells (Atkins et al., 2013, pp. 1–2, 8).  

Overall Evaluation:  
Overall, GSK2656157 presents an intriguing therapeutic candidate for dry AMD based on a mechanistic hypothesis that links chronic ER stress to impaired lysosomal acidification—a process central to the pathogenesis of AMD. One of the primary strengths of GSK2656157 is its potent and selective inhibition of PERK, a critical mediator of the integrated stress response. The compound’s design as an ATP‐competitive PERK inhibitor places it squarely in a class of drugs that have been well characterized in terms of kinase selectivity and in vivo pharmacodynamics in oncology settings (Axten, 2017, pp. 15–19). The underlying biological rationale is that by attenuating the maladaptive PERK-mediated phosphorylation of eIF2α, it may be possible to relieve chronic translational suppression and dampen downstream deleterious signaling cascades—thereby re-establishing normal lysosomal function through proper v-ATPase assembly and restoration of cathepsin D activity (Axten, 2017, pp. 7–11; Chu et al., 2021, p. 8). There is supportive in vitro evidence from studies using related inhibitors (for example, GSK2606414 in ARPE-19 cells) that PERK inhibition can downregulate stress effectors such as CHOP and VEGF, which are both implicated in retinal degeneration and neovascularization (Jiang et al., 2017, pp. 1–2). Such studies underscore the potential of targeting the PERK/ISR axis in RPE cells to create a more favorable intracellular environment that could prevent progressive degeneration seen in dry AMD (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021, pp. 11–12; Chu et al., 2021, p. 8).

However, there are several notable weaknesses and caveats. First, while there is an extensive body of preclinical work on PERK inhibitors in oncology and neurodegeneration models, there is a significant lack of direct evidence in ocular disease models—especially chronic models of dry AMD—as well as an absence of published studies specifically evaluating GSK2656157 in RPE cells or in animal models of AMD (Athanasiou et al., 2017, pp. 5–7). In several studies using related PERK inhibitors in rod photoreceptor degeneration models (such as P23H rhodopsin transgenic rats), inhibition of PERK activity has been associated with worsened outcomes, suggesting that PERK activation may paradoxically be protective in certain contexts of protein misfolding (Athanasiou et al., 2017, pp. 1–2, 5–7). This dichotomous role of PERK—as both an adaptive and a pro-death signal depending on the context and duration of activation—raises concerns about whether inhibition will uniformly yield beneficial effects in the RPE, whose balance of ER stress responses may differ from that of neuronal or secretory tissues. Second, while the hypothesis postulates that chronic ER stress impairs lysosomal acidification by misfolding v-ATPase subunits, the direct link between PERK inhibition and restoration of v-ATPase assembly or cathepsin D maturation in RPE cells has not been firmly established in the literature. Data that explicitly demonstrate that PERK inhibition rescues lysosomal pH, enhances v-ATPase function, and improves cathepsin D activity in neuronal models may exist, yet similar studies in ocular models are limited (Chu et al., 2021, p. 8; Kaarniranta et al., 2018, pp. 1–4). Third, the systemic administration of PERK inhibitors such as GSK2656157 has been associated with pancreatic toxicity and other systemic adverse effects in preclinical studies, a liability that could be particularly problematic in chronic therapies such as those needed for dry AMD (Atkins et al., 2013, p. 8; Axten, 2017, pp. 1–7). Although strategies such as local (intravitreal) delivery might mitigate these systemic risks, ocular pharmacokinetic and tolerability data are sparse, and the tissue-specific distribution of GSK2656157 in the eye would need careful evaluation (Atkins et al., 2013, pp. 1–2, 8). Fourth, there is some concern over off-target effects; for example, early reports on similar GSK compounds noted possible inhibition of RIP1 kinase activity, although subsequent studies have argued that the effects observed were indeed mediated by PERK inhibition (Starr, 2019, pp. 133–137; Athanasiou et al., 2017, pp. 5–7). Nonetheless, affording absolute selectivity in a clinical candidate remains a challenge. In addition, chronic inhibition of the adaptive aspects of the ISR may inadvertently impair protective mechanisms in the retina, as transient ISR activation is known to mediate cellular adaptation during acute stress (Axten, 2017, pp. 7–11, 24–28).

In summary, while the mechanistic rationale for using GSK2656157 to address dry AMD is based on a conceptually appealing hypothesis—that PERK inhibition will relieve chronic ER stress, thereby restoring proper lysosomal acidification, enabling v-ATPase assembly, and rescuing cathepsin D activity in RPE cells—the current body of literature reveals both promising on-target effects in non-ocular systems and significant gaps in ocular-specific efficacy and safety data. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Bexarotene, commercially known as Targretin and referenced here as Sigma B1269, is a fully synthetic rexinoid that was originally designed as a selective agonist for the retinoid X receptor (RXR). It is structurally distinct from naturally occurring retinoids such as 9‐cis‐retinoic acid; its chemical structure consists of a lipophilic tetramethyltetralin moiety connected through an ethynyl linker to a benzoic acid group, a design that confers high binding affinity (nanomolar EC50 values) and specificity for RXR subtypes (de Almeida & Conda‐Sheridan, 2019, pp. 8–9; Jurutka et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). As a member of the rexinoid class, bexarotene belongs to a group of therapeutic compounds that were developed to overcome the limitations of pan‐retinoid receptor activation by offering a more targeted means of modulating nuclear receptor signaling. RXRs have the unique ability to form either homodimers or heterodimers with a wide range of nuclear receptors—including peroxisome proliferator‐activated receptors (PPARs), liver X receptors (LXRs), thyroid hormone receptors (TRs), and vitamin D receptors (VDRs)—thereby influencing diverse gene expression programs that control cell growth, differentiation, and lipid metabolism (de Almeida & Conda‐Sheridan, 2019, pp. 8–9; Heck et al., 2016, pp. 1–2; Lalloyer et al., 2009, pp. 1–2). The synthetic origin of bexarotene, achieved through sophisticated organic synthesis that optimizes its lipophilic and acidic domains, enables it to engage conserved ligand‐binding residues (for example, key arginine and hydrophobic amino acids) in the RXR ligand‐binding domain, ensuring potent activation of the receptor (Chitranshi et al., 2019, p. 9; de Almeida & Conda‐Sheridan, 2019, pp. 11–13). This profile not only underlies its efficacy in its original oncologic indications but also supports its potential for repurposing in other diseases where RXR signaling is of therapeutic interest.

Therapeutic History:  
Bexarotene is well established in clinical practice as the first FDA-approved RXR-selective agonist, primarily indicated for the treatment of refractory cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (CTCL) in patients who have failed at least one systemic therapy (de Almeida & Conda‐Sheridan, 2019, pp. 8–9; Jurutka et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). Over the years, extensive clinical experience with bexarotene has been accrued in oncology, with studies demonstrating its capacity to induce cancer cell arrest, differentiation, and apoptosis by modulating the transcriptional landscape via RXR-mediated gene regulation (Heck et al., 2016, pp. 1–2, 9–10). Beyond its original role in oncology, bexarotene has been investigated in various other contexts; preclinical studies have explored its effects in non-small cell lung cancer, acute myeloid leukemia, and even in some hormone-sensitive malignancies—owing to its ability to interfere with proliferative signaling pathways (Marshall et al., 2015, pp. 2–3; Dheer et al., 2018, pp. 1–2). Notably, recent investigations have also assessed bexarotene in neurodegenerative disease models, particularly Alzheimer’s disease and Parkinson’s disease, where its RXR-mediated upregulation of apolipoprotein E (ApoE) and cholesterol transporters such as ABCA1 have been postulated to facilitate amyloid-beta clearance and neuronal protection (Marshall et al., 2015, pp. 2–3; Mallick et al., 2021, pp. 1–2). Although the compound has not been directly tested in clinical trials for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD), its mechanism of action—centered on modulating lipid metabolism and cellular clearance pathways—suggests that its repurposing for dry AMD is scientifically plausible, especially given the involvement of dysregulated lipid homeostasis and lysosomal dysfunction in this condition (Chitranshi et al., 2019, pp. 1–2; de Almeida & Conda‐Sheridan, 2019, pp. 8–9). Furthermore, RXR signaling is known to be critical in maintaining retinal homeostasis, and studies in animal models have shown that disruption of RXR function can lead to retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) abnormalities, providing an indirect rationale for evaluating RXR agonists like bexarotene in ocular applications (Chitranshi et al., 2019, pp. 1–2; Lalloyer et al., 2009, pp. 1–2).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, bexarotene exerts its effects by binding selectively to the ligand-binding domain of RXRs with high affinity, thereby promoting conformational changes that favor the release of co-repressor proteins and the recruitment of co-activators containing LxxLL motifs. This binding event induces RXR to function either as a homodimer or, more importantly, as a heterodimer with other nuclear receptors such as LXR and PPAR, which are central to the regulation of lipid homeostasis and inflammatory responses (de Almeida & Conda‐Sheridan, 2019, pp. 8–9; Marshall et al., 2015, pp. 2–3). In its role as an RXR agonist, bexarotene has been shown to markedly upregulate the transcription of genes involved in cholesterol efflux, including those coding for ATP-binding cassette transporters like ABCA1 and for apolipoproteins such as ApoE; these factors are critical for mobilizing and clearing excess cholesterol in various tissues (Marshall et al., 2015, pp. 2–3; Mallick et al., 2021, pp. 2–3). Furthermore, RXR agonism by bexarotene can stimulate the activity of permissive heterodimers—such as RXR/PPARα—which are known to play pivotal roles in fatty acid oxidation and energy metabolism. This activation is hypothesized to extend to downstream transcriptional regulators like TFEB, the master regulator of lysosomal biogenesis, though direct evidence in retinal cells is still emerging (Marshall et al., 2015, pp. 2–3; Dheer et al., 2018, pp. 1–2). In several preclinical models, bexarotene has been associated with the modulation of lysosomal pathways; for instance, it can alleviate endoplasmic reticulum stress and prevent the activation of pro-apoptotic proteins, which are important contributors to intracellular lipid accumulation and cellular dysfunction (Farol & Hymes, 2004, pp. 1–2; Lalloyer et al., 2009, pp. 1–2). Moreover, its selective RXR activity circumvents the adverse effects associated with pan-retinoid receptor activation, particularly the hypercalcemic and other toxicities seen with non-selective retinoids, by limiting cross-reactivity with RARs (Jurutka et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Mallick et al., 2021, pp. 2–3). Expected Effect in Dry Age-related Macular Degeneration:  
The central hypothesis driving the evaluation of bexarotene for dry AMD posits that activation of RXR in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells will lead to beneficial metabolic remodeling, specifically through enhancing cholesterol efflux and promoting lysosomal function. In the context of dry AMD, pathologic drusen formation is largely a consequence of chronic accumulation of lipids and misprocessed extracellular debris under the RPE. Through the activation of RXR, bexarotene is expected to upregulate key mediators of cholesterol transport such as ABCA1 and ApoE, thereby facilitating the removal of excess cholesterol and lipid deposits from the RPE (Marshall et al., 2015, pp. 2–3; Chitranshi et al., 2019, pp. 1–2). In addition, RXR activation, particularly when partnered with PPARα, has been associated with the induction of a lysosomal program that involves enhanced expression of genes regulating lysosomal acidification—potentially via the upregulation of vacuolar ATPase (V-ATPase) subunits—and the activation of lysosomal enzymes such as cathepsin D (CTSD) (Marshall et al., 2015, pp. 2–3; Mallick et al., 2021, pp. 2–3). Given that TFEB is a master regulator of lysosomal biogenesis and function, its coactivation alongside PPARα could enhance the degradative capacity of the cell, resulting in improved clearance of drusen-associated lipid aggregates. This dual action—promoting cholesterol efflux while simultaneously enhancing lysosomal catabolism—addresses two of the key pathogenic mechanisms underlying dry AMD (Marshall et al., 2015, pp. 2–3; Mallick et al., 2021, pp. 1–2). In vitro, one might anticipate that bexarotene treatment of cultured RPE cells will lead to increased transcript and protein levels of ABC transporters, elevated markers of lysosomal acidification such as V-ATPase subunits, and enhanced activity of cathepsin D, collectively contributing to the reduction of lipid overload at a cellular level (Marshall et al., 2015, pp. 2–3; de Almeida & Conda‐Sheridan, 2019, pp. 8–9). Moreover, given its extensive clinical use in oncology with a tolerable ocular safety profile, bexarotene is well situated for repurposing, provided that its systemic adverse effects (e.g., hyperlipidemia, hypothyroidism) can be managed or mitigated through controlled dosing strategies or targeted delivery approaches (de Almeida & Conda‐Sheridan, 2019, pp. 8–9; Marshall et al., 2015, pp. 2–3).

Overall Evaluation:  
Bexarotene emerges as a promising therapeutic candidate for dry AMD based on its well-characterized pharmacological profile and multifaceted mechanism of action. One of its primary strengths lies in its selective activation of RXR, which has been shown to trigger transcriptional programs that enhance cholesterol efflux via the upregulation of key transporters such as ABCA1 and ApoE—pathways that are directly relevant to the clearance of drusen-associated lipids in dry AMD (Marshall et al., 2015, pp. 2–3; Mallick et al., 2021, pp. 1–2). This dual action addresses both the extracellular accumulation of lipids and the intracellular deficits in degradative capacity that contribute to RPE dysfunction. The extensive clinical experience with bexarotene in cancer therapy provides an added advantage, as its pharmacokinetics, dosing regimens, and safety profiles are well documented, thereby facilitating a more rapid transition into repurposing studies. Bexarotene is known to cause significant metabolic side effects, including hyperlipidemia and hypothyroidism, which may necessitate adjunctive treatments (such as lipid-lowering agents) or the development of targeted ocular delivery systems to minimize systemic exposure (de Almeida & Conda‐Sheridan, 2019, pp. 8–9; Mallick et al., 2021, pp. 2–3). Nonetheless, additional preclinical work is essential to directly demonstrate its efficacy in RPE models and to delineate any ocular-specific pharmacodynamic parameters. Overall, the candidate shows promise as a multi‐pathway therapeutic approach for dry AMD, with strengths including its defined mechanism of action and extensive clinical history, and weaknesses largely centered on potential systemic side effects and the need for targeted delivery strategies (de Almeida & Conda‐Sheridan, 2019, pp. 8–9; Marshall et al., 2015, pp. 2–3; Chitranshi et al., 2019, pp. 1–2; Mallick et al., 2021, pp. 1–2; Marciano et al., 2015, pp. 1–2).
