Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
NSC19723 is presented by the team as a custom-synthesized small-molecule enhancer of cathepsin D (CTSD) activity, hypothesized to bind the zymogen (pro-CTSD) and accelerate its maturation within retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) lysosomes to restore proteolysis and debris clearance in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD). No peer-reviewed publications or preprints describing NSC19723’s structure, discovery, selectivity, or in vivo performance are present in the provided literature corpus; accordingly, this evaluation treats NSC19723 as a theoretical representative of the drug class “CTSD activity enhancers” and assesses the therapeutic hypothesis against the current substrate-specific and disease-relevant CTSD/RPE biology (Ng et al., 2024; Sharif, 2015; Liu, 2021; Buniello et al., 2025).

The stated drug class is mechanistically distinct from upstream autophagy enhancers or lysosomal pH modulators: a CTSD activity enhancer would operate at the level of CTSD protein maturation/activity, ideally in acidic lysosomes, rather than by globally raising autophagic flux or indirectly modulating lysosomal acidification (Frost et al., 2014; Boya et al., 2023; Ng et al., 2024). CTSD itself is an aspartic endoprotease synthesized as a pre-proenzyme with an N-terminal signal peptide (for ER entry) and a propeptide region that supports folding and prevents premature activity; post-translational maturation occurs in late endosomes/lysosomes after mannose-6-phosphate (M6P)-mediated trafficking, where acidic pH supports autocatalysis and protease processing to the mature, active two-chain enzyme (Sharif, 2015). The RPE expresses CTSD at high levels, with evidence for enriched CTSD protein/activity in central/macular RPE relative to periphery, consistent with the macula’s heavy daily photoreceptor outer segment (POS) phagocytic load that relies on lysosomal proteolysis (Sharif, 2015; Pay, 2017). These features nominate CTSD as a plausible therapeutic target for restoring RPE degradative capacity; however, a specific CTSD maturation enhancer such as NSC19723 has not been characterized in the provided literature, so all compound-level conclusions must remain contingent on experimental validation (Ng et al., 2024; Buniello et al., 2025).

Therapeutic History  
No published biochemical, veterinary, or clinical use of NSC19723 is documented in the provided sources, and the name does not appear in the referenced literature; consequently, there are no prior data on this molecule in dry AMD or retinal disease within the provided corpus (Buniello et al., 2025). By contrast, there is considerable disease-relevant literature on CTSD biology in RPE and on pharmacological strategies that indirectly restore CTSD function by correcting upstream lysosomal defects. In patient-derived RPE from Stargardt disease (STGD1, ABCA4 mutations), lysosomal pH is elevated, CTSD accumulates in immature forms, and CTSD proteolytic activity is reduced; pharmacologic re-acidification of lysosomes (e.g., via P2Y₁₂ antagonism with ticagrelor) reverses these defects by lowering lysosomal pH, reducing the immature pro-CTSD pool, and restoring CTSD proteolytic activity and POS degradation in vitro and in vivo (RPE cells and Abca4−/− mice) (Ng et al., 2024). While STGD1 is not AMD, these data show that CTSD maturation/activity in human RPE is drug-modifiable and that improving CTSD function can improve degradative endpoints relevant to lipofuscin-associated disease biology, a pathophysiologic axis shared with dry AMD (Ng et al., 2024; Boya et al., 2023).

In the RPE/AMD literature, multiple lines of evidence support CTSD as a major lysosomal protease necessary for POS degradation and proteostasis. CTSD deficiency or pharmacologic inhibition impairs POS proteolysis, provokes accumulation of debris reminiscent of drusen, and is linked to retinal dysfunction in animal models, reinforcing its centrality to RPE homeostasis (Mahmud, 2019). Advanced glycation end-products (AGEs), which accumulate with age and in AMD, downregulate CTSD activity or expression in RPE and exacerbate lysosomal/autophagic failure and lipofuscin formation, further tying CTSD deficits to AMD-like phenotypes (Sharif, 2015; Mahmud, 2019). More broadly, lysosomal/autophagic insufficiency in RPE is mechanistically and pathologically linked to dry AMD: decreased degradative capacity leads to lipofuscin accumulation, lysosomal membrane permeabilization (LMP), DAMP release, inflammasome activation (e.g., NLRP3), and eventual RPE atrophy that drives photoreceptor degeneration; re-acidifying lysosomes and strengthening lysosomal function ameliorate several of these pathologies in vitro and in vivo (Choi, 2019; Frost et al., 2014; Boya et al., 2023).

A second therapeutic precedent relevant to “enhancing CTSD function” is enzyme augmentation. Recombinant pro-CTSD administration has been reported to correct proteolysis and autophagy defects in neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis (CLN10/CTSD deficiency), and intravitreal enzyme replacement strategies in other lysosomal storage diseases (e.g., TPP1 in CLN2) have preserved retinal structure/function in preclinical models, supporting feasibility of increasing lysosomal enzyme function in ocular tissues (Liu, 2021). These studies, while not in AMD and not small molecules, validate the general concept that augmenting CTSD can rescue lysosomal degradative failure in retina-derived tissues.

In summary, there is no therapeutic history for NSC19723 itself in the provided sources; however, there is an increasingly robust therapeutic precedent that pharmacological manipulation which restores CTSD maturation/activity in RPE improves degradative capacity and disease-relevant readouts in lipofuscin-accumulating retinal disorders, and that enzyme augmentation of lysosomal hydrolases can be effective in ocular degenerations driven by lysosomal insufficiency (Ng et al., 2024; Liu, 2021).

Mechanism of Action  
CTSD biosynthesis and maturation provide the mechanistic backdrop for a CTSD maturation enhancer. CTSD is synthesized as pre-procathepsin D with a signal peptide (for ER translocation) and a propeptide that maintains the zymogen in an inactive, folding-competent state; the protein acquires N-linked glycans and an M6P tag in the Golgi for M6P-receptor–mediated trafficking to late endosomes/lysosomes, where acidic pH facilitates removal of the propeptide, proteolytic processing, and generation of the mature, active enzyme (heavy and light chains) (Sharif, 2015). As an aspartic protease, CTSD employs two Asp residues to activate and position a water molecule for nucleophilic attack on the scissile peptide bond, a chemistry that requires acidic conditions for optimal catalysis; in neutral or alkaline environments, activity falls sharply, explaining why lysosomal alkalinization in disease states compromises both maturation and steady-state activity (Sharif, 2015; Ng et al., 2024).

In RPE disease models, immature and intermediate CTSD forms accumulate when lysosomal pH is elevated, and total CTSD protein may paradoxically rise even as proteolytic activity falls, illustrating a maturation bottleneck rather than a transcriptional deficit; pharmacological re-acidification reduces immature CTSD, increases the mature enzyme, and restores proteolytic activity in RPE (Ng et al., 2024). Functionally, impaired CTSD maturation/activity correlates with delayed degradation of internalized POS and accumulation of aggregation-prone substrates such as α-synuclein, consistent with CTSD’s principal role in RPE proteolysis of rhodopsin and POS proteins; CTSD is reported to account for the majority of rhodopsin degradation in RPE and exhibits far higher proteolytic activity than cathepsin B against POS substrates (Ng et al., 2024). The RPE’s reliance on phagolysosomal degradation of POS and basal autophagy for proteostasis means that even partial reductions in CTSD activity can precipitate progressive accumulation of lipofuscin-like material and lysosomal residual bodies, which in turn further impair lysosomes and create a feedback loop of increasing oxidative and inflammatory stress central to dry AMD pathophysiology (Choi, 2019; Frost et al., 2014; Sharif, 2015).

The proposed mechanism for NSC19723—direct binding to pro-CTSD to accelerate maturation—aligns with the above biology and would target the specific rate-limiting step observed in RPE lysosomes under stress: conversion of immature pro-CTSD to the mature, active enzyme in the acidic lumen. If achieved without broad, off-target activation of other proteases or perturbation of lysosomal pH/ion homeostasis, this mechanism would distinguish NSC19723 from autophagy inducers (e.g., rapamycin) or pH re-acidifiers (e.g., ticagrelor), while being convergent on the same functional outcome: restored CTSD proteolysis and lysosomal degradative capacity (Frost et al., 2014; Ng et al., 2024).

Mechanistic cross-talk and constraints that are relevant for a CTSD maturation enhancer include:  
- pH dependence: CTSD maturation and catalysis require acidic lysosomes; in alkaline lysosomes (e.g., due to bisretinoid accumulation), pro-CTSD processing is impaired even if total CTSD protein increases, so a maturation accelerator may be insufficient without concurrent restoration of lysosomal pH in some disease states (Ng et al., 2024).  
- Protease networks: While CTSD is an aspartic protease, lysosomal proteases co-regulate one another’s maturation and substrate turnover; for example, denatured cathepsin L can be a substrate for CTSD, and changes in cysteine cathepsins (B/L/S) alter autophagic flux and POS degradation, implying that selective enhancement of CTSD maturation must be interpreted in the context of broader protease network homeostasis (Mahmud, 2019; Sharif, 2015).  
- Endogenous inhibitors: Cystatin C potently inhibits cysteine cathepsins (B, H, L, S) and is abundant in RPE; although it does not inhibit CTSD (aspartic protease), changes in cystatin C with age and AMD suggest that protease–inhibitor balance in the lysosome and extracellular space is dynamic and may modulate the consequences of altering one protease’s activity (Myerscough, 2015; Sharif, 2015).  
- Lysosomal membrane integrity: LMP releases cathepsins to the cytosol, where they can trigger apoptosis/inflammation; any intervention that modifies lysosomal protease activity must be vetted for unintended effects on LMP susceptibility or cytosolic protease activity under stress (Boya et al., 2023; Mahmud, 2019).  
- Extracellular exposure: RPE can secrete cathepsins; most cathepsins are inactivated at neutral pH, but acidic niches or heparan/ECM interactions can stabilize activity, raising potential off-tissue effects if a compound perturbs trafficking/secretion (Sharif, 2015).

Collectively, the mechanistic plausibility that a small molecule could stabilize a conformation of pro-CTSD that accelerates propeptide removal and activation in acidic lysosomes is strong, and a favorable on-target pharmacodynamic effect can be anchored to clearly measurable, disease-relevant biochemical endpoints in RPE (Ng et al., 2024). The key risk is that without correction of lysosomal pH, pro-CTSD processing bottlenecks may persist; therefore, a CTSD maturation enhancer may be best deployed in lysosomes that are sufficiently acidic or in combination with pH-restoring strategies (Ng et al., 2024).

Expected Effect  
Dry AMD pathophysiology features RPE lysosomal-autophagic insufficiency leading to accumulation of POS-derived material, lipofuscin, and AGEs, heightened oxidative stress, inflammasome activation, and progressive RPE atrophy; restoring lysosomal proteolysis is predicted to mitigate these processes (Choi, 2019; Frost et al., 2014; Boya et al., 2023). In RPE, CTSD is a principal protease responsible for POS/rhodopsin degradation, and its activity declines with aging and under stressors relevant to AMD (AGEs, lipids/oxidation, lysosomal alkalinization), producing immature CTSD accumulation and reduced proteolytic capacity (Mahmud, 2019; Sharif, 2015; Ng et al., 2024). Therefore, a compound that accelerates pro-CTSD maturation to increase mature CTSD abundance/activity in acidic lysosomes is expected to:

- Increase CTSD catalytic activity in RPE lysosomes, measurable by fluorogenic substrate assays and activity-based probes, with corresponding decrease in immature/intermediate CTSD species and increase in mature, active CTSD on immunoblot and imaging (Ng et al., 2024).  
- Improve rate and completeness of POS degradation in RPE pulse–chase assays (e.g., rhodopsin clearance), reduce accumulation of lysosomal residual bodies, and decrease autofluorescent lipofuscin-like material formation in POS-challenged RPE under AGE/oxidative stress conditions (Ng et al., 2024; Frost et al., 2014; Sharif, 2015).  
- Reduce intracellular burden of aggregation-prone CTSD substrates (e.g., α-synuclein) and attenuate proteostasis stress, potentially normalizing vesicle trafficking defects tied to aggregate accumulation (Ng et al., 2024).  
- Rebalance autophagic flux by removing a degradative bottleneck at the lysosome, observable as improved degradation of autophagic cargo rather than simply altered LC3 abundance; careful flux assays with lysosome–autophagosome fusion inhibitors (e.g., bafilomycin A1) should be used for interpretation (Frost et al., 2014; Sharif, 2015).  
- Decrease downstream inflammatory signaling associated with lysosomal debris accumulation, including reduced NLRP3 inflammasome activation and cytokine release during chronic stress paradigms implicated in AMD pathogenesis (Choi, 2019; Boya et al., 2023).  
- With longer-term dosing, reduce subcellular and extracellular deposit biogenesis (lipofuscin, drusen-like material), preserve RPE morphology/mitochondrial health, and sustain photoreceptor function in models where lysosomal degradation is limiting, as seen when CTSD function is restored by lysosomal re-acidification (Boya et al., 2023; Ng et al., 2024).

The target is well expressed in the cell type of interest: CTSD is abundant in RPE, enriched in central/macular RPE, and directly linked to RPE’s POS degradation function; its activity is reduced by aging and AGE exposure, both highly relevant to dry AMD (Sharif, 2015; Pay, 2017; Mahmud, 2019). In lipofuscin-associated retinal disease models, restoring lysosomal acidity to rescue CTSD maturation/activity improved RPE degradative function and reduced pathological autofluorescence, underscoring the expected benefits of directly increasing CTSD maturation/activity via a selective small molecule (Ng et al., 2024).

Experimental considerations for robust readouts in RPE:  
- Biochemical: ratio of pro-/intermediate/mature CTSD by immunoblot in lysosomal fractions; CTSD activity in intact live cells and in isolated lysosomes at matched pH; selectivity profiling against other cathepsins (B/L/S) to confirm the putative specificity reported by the team; lysosomal pH measurements to control for off-target alkalinization/acidification effects (Ng et al., 2024; Sharif, 2015).  
- Functional degradative flux: POS pulse–chase assays (rhodopsin clearance kinetics), autophagy flux assays (LC3-II, p62/SQSTM1 degradation with and without bafilomycin A1), α-synuclein aggregation/clearance; quantify autofluorescence as a proxy for lipofuscin-like material (Ng et al., 2024; Frost et al., 2014; Sharif, 2015).  
- Cell health/inflammation: LMP susceptibility (galectin-3 puncta, cytosolic cathepsin immunostaining), NLRP3 inflammasome activation (caspase-1 activity), ROS and mitochondrial integrity (Boya et al., 2023; Choi, 2019).  
- Disease relevance: verify effects in hiPSC-RPE derived from dry AMD patients, which display altered lysosomal protease processing (e.g., immature CTSD increases under oxidative stress) and increased stress susceptibility; extend to macular-enriched RPE phenotypes given regional CTSD enrichment (Voisin et al., 2019; Sharif, 2015).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Strong target–disease mechanistic rationale: CTSD is the principal lysosomal protease for RPE POS protein degradation, with reported responsibility for the majority of rhodopsin proteolysis and markedly higher activity than cathepsin B; CTSD deficiency or inhibition impairs POS degradation and produces drusen-like debris, and genetic or pharmacologic CTSD impairment causes retinal dysfunction, aligning CTSD activation with a disease-modifying mechanism in dry AMD (Ng et al., 2024; Mahmud, 2019).  
- Convergent therapeutic precedent: Restoring lysosomal pH in patient-derived and mouse RPE models rescues CTSD maturation and activity, improves POS degradation, reduces lipofuscin-like autofluorescence, and protects photoreceptors, demonstrating that enhancing CTSD function is sufficient to improve disease-relevant outcomes in lipofuscin-associated retinal pathology (Ng et al., 2024).  
- Clear, measurable pharmacodynamic biomarkers: Mature CTSD abundance, CTSD activity, lysosomal pH, POS clearance, and lipofuscin/autofluorescence changes provide a rigorous framework for early de-risking of NSC19723 and for prioritizing compound optimization (Ng et al., 2024).  
- Disease context supports target engagement benefits: RPE lysosomal dysfunction, autophagy/heterophagy deficits, lipofuscin/AGE accumulation, inflammasome activation, and progressive atrophy are central features of dry AMD; a CTSD maturation enhancer directly addresses the degradative bottleneck at the lysosome (Choi, 2019; Frost et al., 2014; Boya et al., 2023).

Risks and gaps  
- Absence of public data on NSC19723: No structural, selectivity, potency, PK/PD, ocular disposition, or toxicology data are available in the provided corpus; thus, claims of pro-CTSD binding, selectivity for CTSD over other cathepsins, and in vivo rescue in CTSD-deficient retina remain unverified by the sources provided (Buniello et al., 2025). This is the major program risk at present.  
- Lysosomal pH constraint: If lysosomal alkalinization is a primary driver of immature CTSD accumulation (as in STGD1 and arguably in stressed AMD RPE), a maturation accelerator may not overcome the pH-dependent processing barrier; efficacy may require sufficient lysosomal acidity or combination with pH-restoring interventions (Ng et al., 2024).  
- Protease network and safety considerations: Enhancing lysosomal protease activity can exacerbate LMP-driven cytotoxicity under oxidative or lipofuscin stress; careful LMP and inflammasome assessments are required, alongside confirmation that NSC19723 does not perturb trafficking/secretion to increase extracellular protease activity where pH can be locally acidic (Boya et al., 2023; Sharif, 2015).

Program implications and recommended next steps  
Given the robust mechanistic case for CTSD restoration in RPE and the successful pharmacologic rescue of CTSD maturation/activity via lysosomal re-acidification in human patient–derived RPE, a selective CTSD maturation enhancer is a rational, high-potential approach for dry AMD—provided the compound is real, selective, and effective in acidic lysosomes (Ng et al., 2024). To advance NSC19723, the following de-risking package is critical:  

- Biochemical validation: Demonstrate pro-CTSD binding and acceleration of maturation at acidic pH using purified pro-CTSD and lysosomal-mimetic conditions; quantify catalytic activation and processing kinetics; confirm no activation or inhibition of cathepsins B/L/S and other lysosomal hydrolases (Sharif, 2015).  
- Cellular validation in RPE: In primary human RPE/hiPSC-RPE (including dry AMD lines), show increased mature CTSD and activity without altering lysosomal pH, improved POS degradation and reduced autofluorescence under chronic POS/AGE stress, restored clearance of α-synuclein aggregates, and normalization of autophagic flux using proper flux assays (Frost et al., 2014; Ng et al., 2024; Sharif, 2015).  
- Safety pharmacology in RPE: Demonstrate no increase in LMP susceptibility or NLRP3 activation under oxidative/bisretinoid stress; characterize secretion/trafficking effects and exclude extracellular protease activation under BrM-like conditions (Boya et al., 2023; Sharif, 2015).  
- In vivo proof of concept: In models featuring RPE lysosomal dysfunction and lipofuscin burden, measure retinal/RPE CTSD maturation/activity, RPE autofluorescence, drusen-like material, photoreceptor survival, and visual function; compare with or add to pH-reacidifying strategies (Ng et al., 2024).

Overall, while a CTSD maturation enhancer is scientifically well grounded for RPE-centered degenerations and could represent a differentiated, direct-restoration modality versus pH modulators or broad autophagy inducers, the current file lacks any external validation for NSC19723. Progressing NSC19723 is justified only with rapid, rigorous confirmation of selectivity, on-target activity in RPE lysosomes, and favorable safety in stressed RPE systems that model dry AMD’s lysosomal/autophagic failure (Frost et al., 2014; Boya et al., 2023; Choi, 2019).

In summary, the therapeutic concept—enhancing CTSD maturation/activity to restore RPE lysosomal proteolysis—has high mechanistic plausibility and encouraging precedent from pharmacologic re-acidification studies, but the specific candidate NSC19723 remains unsubstantiated in the provided literature and requires foundational biochemical and cellular validation to warrant preclinical development in dry AMD (Ng et al., 2024; Buniello et al., 2025).

Below is our detailed evaluation of GW501516 as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
GW501516 is a fully synthetic small‐molecule agonist of peroxisome proliferator–activated receptor delta (PPARδ, also known as PPARβ/δ) developed during intensive medicinal–chemistry programs for metabolic diseases. Its synthesis and optimization were driven by the need to generate a molecule with high binding affinity for the spacious ligand–binding pocket of PPARδ, a receptor known for its promiscuity with respect to ligand chemical structure (Acharya, 2017). GW501516 belongs to a class of synthetic PPARδ agonists that emerged alongside compounds such as GW0742, with these molecules originally explored for their ability to improve lipid metabolism, increase fatty acid β–oxidation, and modulate inflammatory responses in tissues such as skeletal muscle, heart, and vascular endothelium (Acharya, 2017; Choudhary et al., 2016). As a representative of this chemical class—and marketed historically under the Sigma catalog number G3536—the compound has been a subject of numerous preclinical studies and has been tested in rodent models to assess its metabolic and anti–inflammatory effects (Acharya, 2017). Its synthetic origin and structural design allow it to bind selectively to PPARδ in order to elicit transcriptional responses that adjust cellular energy metabolism, including the regulation of fatty acid oxidation and mitochondrial biogenesis. Given that the PPAR family acts as obligate heterodimers with the retinoid X receptor (RXR) to regulate gene expression through peroxisome proliferator response elements (PPREs), GW501516’s design confers it the ability to influence transcriptional networks important not only in metabolic tissues, but potentially also in ocular tissues such as the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) (Acharya, 2017; Choudhary et al., 2016).

Therapeutic History:  
Originally, GW501516 was investigated extensively as a therapeutic candidate for metabolic disorders, such as dyslipidemia, insulin resistance, and atherosclerosis. Preclinical studies demonstrated that it could increase serum high–density lipoprotein (HDL) levels, reduce adiposity, and even improve glucose tolerance in rodent models (Acharya, 2017; Choudhary et al., 2016). The compound advanced into phase 2 clinical trials for metabolic indications; despite promising metabolic effects in animal studies, it has not been approved due mainly to safety concerns—in particular, rodent carcinogenicity that emerged in long–term studies (Acharya, 2017; Choudhary et al., 2016). While the focus of its initial development was in the realm of systemic metabolic disease, later investigations have expanded the scope of PPARδ agonists to other pathology areas. For instance, PPARδ has been found to regulate angiogenic cell behaviors, and its modulation has been implicated in experimental models of retinal neovascularization and oxygen–induced retinopathy (Choudhary et al., 2016; Dou & Duerfeldt, 2020). In ocular contexts, research by Choudhary et al. has shown that ligand activation of PPARδ can reduce intracellular lipid accumulation in RPE cells and that genetic ablation of PPARδ in mice exacerbates early dry AMD–like phenotypes while reducing choroidal neovascularization (Choudhary et al., 2016). Furthermore, selective PPARδ modulators including GW501516 have been listed among candidates in reviews discussing lipid–activated nuclear receptors and their potential role in modulating microglia and extracellular matrix turnover in AMD (Choudhary et al., 2016; Choudhary & Malek, 2016). Although no prior clinical studies have directly evaluated GW501516 for dry AMD or related RPE disorders, its history in metabolic research and its identification in ocular-focused preclinical studies support its consideration as a repurposed agent. Notably, it must be borne in mind that while metabolic endpoints were favorable in early studies, systemic administration in humans was halted because of potential carcinogenic events in rodent models, suggesting that if GW501516 is to be advanced for ocular use, localized delivery may be required to mitigate such risks (Acharya, 2017; Choudhary et al., 2016).

Mechanism of Action:  
Mechanistically, GW501516 functions by binding to the ligand–binding domain of PPARδ, thereby inducing a conformational change that releases associated corepressors and enables the recruitment of transcriptional coactivators such as PPARγ coactivator 1 alpha (PGC-1α). This heterodimeric complex, formed with RXR, then binds to specific peroxisome proliferator response elements (PPREs) in target gene promoters to modulate gene expression (Acharya, 2017). In metabolic tissues, this cascade leads to the upregulation of genes implicated in fatty acid β–oxidation (e.g., pyruvate dehydrogenase kinase isozyme 4 (PDK4)) and genes involved in the regulation of lipid handling such as angiopoietin-like 4 (ANGPTL4) (Choudhary et al., 2016). In the context of retinal pigment epithelium, the hypothesis is that GW501516-induced activation of PPARδ would similarly upregulate genes involved in fatty acid oxidation. Such metabolic reprogramming is thought to reduce intracellular lipid accumulation and may simultaneously promote enhancement of mitochondrial function through PGC-1α–dependent pathways. Not only does PGC-1α drive mitochondrial biogenesis, but it also interacts with other transcription factor networks such as the transcription factor EB (TFEB), a master regulator of lysosomal biogenesis and function (Ji et al., 2021). In theory, the activation of these pathways would lead to enhanced autophagic flux and lysosomal acidification, thereby upregulating cathepsin D activity—the lysosomal protease crucial for metabolizing complex lipid species. Such a biochemical cascade would be particularly beneficial in the setting of dry AMD, where drusen formation is in part the result of impaired lipid clearance in the RPE (Choudhary et al., 2016). However, a note of caution comes from studies in rodent retinal degeneration models. Organotypic retinal explants from rd1 mice showed that while PPARα and PPARγ agonists reduced photoreceptor cell death, activation of PPARδ using GW501516 (often abbreviated as GW516 in these studies) failed to protect and even worsened cell viability in wild–type explants, indicating that the tissue–specific role of PPARδ in the retina may be more complex than that seen in metabolic tissues (Wang et al., 2025). Nonetheless, the proposed mechanism in RPE focuses on reducing drusen lipid burden by promoting mitochondrial β–oxidation and improving lysosomal degradation via enhanced TFEB and cathepsin D activity—a pathway that has analogies in other cell types and disease models (Choudhary et al., 2016).

Expected Effect:  
Based on the hypothesis for using GW501516 in dry AMD, its anticipated effects in RPE cells would be multifold. First, activation of PPARδ by GW501516 is expected to increase the transcription of genes involved in fatty acid oxidation, essentially reprogramming the metabolic machinery of RPE cells to enhance the catabolism of long–chain fatty acids. Such a shift would theoretically lead to a decrease in intracellular lipid accumulation, which is a key pathological hallmark observed in dry AMD as drusen and sub–RPE deposits (Choudhary et al., 2016). Second, by triggering the release and/or upregulation of coactivators like PGC-1α, GW501516 would facilitate not only mitochondrial biogenesis and function but also might potentiate the activity of TFEB—a central regulator of lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy. The cooperative action of PGC-1α and TFEB is believed to enhance lysosomal acidification and increase the activity of cathepsin D, thereby accelerating the clearance of aggregated lipids and proteinaceous debris within the RPE (Ji et al., 2021; Choudhary et al., 2016). Third, improved lysosomal and mitochondrial function would ultimately support the homeostatic balance within RPE cells, potentially slowing or reversing the degenerative process characteristic of dry AMD. Importantly, expression data indicate that PPARδ and its coactivators are indeed present in AMD-vulnerable cells—including primary RPE cells and choroidal endothelial cells—suggesting that the molecular targets of GW501516 are accessible in the intended tissue (Choudhary et al., 2016). On the other hand, preclinical animal models of retinal degeneration (such as the rd1 explant studies) have shown that PPARδ activation with GW501516 did not confer protection to photoreceptors and was even toxic at certain concentrations (Wang et al., 2025); however, these models focused primarily on photoreceptor survival in retinal degeneration rather than lipid clearance in RPE. Therefore, while the expected effect in the RPE is an enhancement of fatty acid oxidation and lysosomal processing leading to reduced drusen formation, the exact dose and delivery modality will be critical, particularly to avoid adverse effects observed in other retinal cell types and to bypass the systemic carcinogenicity that halted previous clinical development (Choudhary et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2025).

Overall Evaluation:  
In summary, GW501516 presents both promising and challenging attributes as a potential repurposed agent for dry AMD. One of its chief strengths is its well-defined mechanism in metabolic regulation: as a highly selective PPARδ agonist, it robustly stimulates pathways leading to increased fatty acid oxidation, mitochondrial biogenesis, and—in theory—the enhancement of lysosomal function via cross-talk with PGC-1α and TFEB (Acharya, 2017; Choudhary et al., 2016; Ji et al., 2021). In the paradigm of dry AMD, where defective lipid metabolism and impaired autophagy contribute to drusen formation and RPE dysfunction, the metabolic–lysosomal axis targeted by GW501516 is particularly attractive (Choudhary et al., 2016). Moreover, the underlying rationale is supported by studies showing that ligand activation of PPARδ in RPE cells can diminish lipid accumulation—a finding directly relevant to reducing the drusen burden associated with dry AMD (Choudhary et al., 2016).  

However, notable weaknesses temper the enthusiasm for GW501516. Historically, its systemic administration in metabolic disease trials was halted due to carcinogenicity observed in rodents, raising significant safety concerns that would have to be mitigated by strategies such as localized ocular delivery (Acharya, 2017; Choudhary et al., 2016). The risk of adverse systemic effects could be minimized by intravitreal injection or by employing sustained-release formulations such as ocular hydrogels or nanocarriers, but such approaches require extensive preclinical safety validation. Another critical point is that the beneficial effects of PPARδ activation in ocular cells have not been uniformly observed. For instance, in rd1 organotypic retinal explant studies—which, while focused on photoreceptor degeneration rather than RPE lipid clearance—PPARδ agonism with GW501516 did not reduce photoreceptor death and even increased toxicity in wild-type retinal tissue (Choudhary et al., 2016; Dou & Duerfeldt, 2020). Additionally, while the hypothesis posits that GW501516 will operate through a metabolic–lysosomal mechanism involving PGC-1α and TFEB to enhance lysosomal acidification and cathepsin D activity, direct evidence in RPE models linking these endpoints is sparse. Much of the molecular framework comes from studies in muscle, neuronal, and systemic metabolic contexts rather than from robust ocular models (Ji et al., 2021; Choudhary et al., 2016).  

Furthermore, it remains to be rigorously established whether PPARδ activation in the RPE would indeed result in a meaningful reduction in drusen lipid burden in dry AMD patients. Preclinical studies have indicated that genetic knockouts of PPARδ can lead to early dry AMD–like pathology in mice (Choudhary et al., 2016), supporting the idea that proper receptor function is necessary for lipid homeostasis; yet pharmacologic activation may not recapitulate the complete spectrum of protective effects observed with endogenous receptor function. Moreover, the carcinogenicity concerns associated with GW501516 underscore a key translational hurdle. Even if localized delivery can theoretically reduce systemic exposure, the long-term risk of oncogenic transformation in ocular cells must be assessed with extreme caution given the potential for even low-level systemic distribution or local proliferative effects that could increase melanocytic or retinal tumor risk (Acharya, 2017; Choudhary et al., 2016). Lastly, efficacy in a multifactorial disease such as dry AMD is unlikely to be achieved with a single-target approach. While modulating the metabolic–lysosomal axis is compelling, dry AMD is characterized by inflammation, oxidative stress, and extracellular matrix remodeling as well. Thus, combining GW501516 with other agents that target complementary pathways might offer greater clinical benefit than monotherapy, albeit with additional complexity in evaluating drug–drug interactions and compounded safety risks (Choudhary et al., 2016).

Overall, while GW501516 shows promise in theory by linking PPARδ activation to enhanced fatty acid oxidation and lysosomal capacity—a mechanistic pathway that could, if properly harnessed, ameliorate the drusen lipid burden in the RPE—the existing literature suggests several areas of concern. These include its historical carcinogenicity in long-term systemic studies, mixed and sometimes adverse effects in retinal explant models, and a relative paucity of direct evidence in RPE cells regarding TFEB and cathepsin D upregulation. Before advancing GW501516 as a candidate for dry AMD, further targeted studies are necessary. Such studies would need to assess the molecular effects of localized ocular delivery on lysosomal biogenesis and acidification in human RPE cells, confirm proper engagement of the PGC-1α/TFEB axis, and determine whether any measurable reduction in drusen formation can be achieved without deleterious off-target effects in the retina. In parallel, robust toxicology studies using localized dosing schemes must be performed to address the historical safety concerns. In conclusion, while the metabolic–lysosomal hypothesis for treating dry AMD is scientifically attractive and GW501516 embodies some key attributes that support this approach, its previous toxicity profile and mixed preclinical ocular findings advise caution and the need for significant additional research (Acharya, 2017; Choudhary et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2025).

Taken together, our comprehensive literature review indicates that GW501516 has a sound mechanistic rationale—through activation of PPARδ to enhance fatty acid oxidation and possibly upregulate autophagy–lysosomal functions via cooperation with PGC-1α and TFEB. However, its therapeutic history is marred by safety concerns due to rodent carcinogenicity, and ocular preclinical models have shown variable results that necessitate careful dose optimization and targeted delivery. Ultimately, GW501516 may have potential for treating dry AMD if its adverse systemic effects can be mitigated by localized ocular formulations and if future studies confirm that activation of the metabolic–lysosomal axis within RPE cells translates into meaningful clinical benefit. Further research should focus on detailed in vitro assays in human RPE cells, animal models using localized delivery to the retina, and comprehensive toxicology studies in ocular tissues before committing to clinical trials.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
SB216763 is a synthetic small‐molecule inhibitor originally discovered during GlaxoSmithKline’s dedicated program in developing GSK-3 inhibitors. It belongs to the bisarylmaleimide class of compounds, with its chemical structure based on a pyrrole-2,5-dione core that is further substituted by aryl and indole moieties. In its initial characterization, SB216763 was identified as an ATP-competitive inhibitor of glycogen synthase kinase 3 beta (GSK3β), a central serine/threonine protein kinase implicated in multiple intracellular signaling cascades. The chemical class to which SB216763 belongs – maleimides – has been widely exploited across medicinal chemistry due to their synthetic tractability and ability to serve as potent inhibitors of enzymes, particularly kinases. This group of compounds has previously been used in various preclinical studies targeting neurodegenerative diseases and cell proliferative disorders by modulating cell signaling pathways such as the Wnt/β-catenin cascade, which is ubiquitously expressed in many tissues including the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and the central nervous system (Gianferrara et al., 2022; Ruiz & Eldar-Finkelman, 2022; Alhassan et al., 2025).

Therapeutic History:  
SB216763 has a well-established history in preclinical research, particularly in models of neurodegeneration. Several studies have deployed this compound in rodent models of Alzheimer’s disease, Parkinson’s disease, and other neurological insults to demonstrate its neuroprotective potential. In these models, SB216763 was shown to reduce tau hyperphosphorylation, protect neurons against both β-amyloid-mediated toxicity and radiation-induced apoptosis in hippocampal neurons, and promote beneficial modulation of signaling pathways linked to PI3K–Akt (Gianferrara et al., 2022; Ruiz & Eldar-Finkelman, 2022). Beyond its neuroprotective effects, SB216763 has been applied as a tool compound in cellular studies to activate canonical Wnt signaling through stabilization of beta-catenin by inhibiting GSK3β. Importantly, a radiolabeled derivative, [11C]SB216763, has been developed as a positron emission tomography (PET) probe, which confirmed its ability to cross the blood–brain barrier in rodent and nonhuman primate models, although significant selectivity issues have been noted with respect to off-target kinase inhibition (Gianferrara et al., 2022; Benn & Dawson, 2020). In addition, there is documented evidence of its application in ocular contexts; for instance, in an experimental ischemic retinal neuron model in rats, SB216763 was found to promote DNA repair by upregulating DNA ligase IV transcriptional activity. However, while it has been evaluated extensively in neurological and in vivo rodent models for central nervous system diseases, formal clinical deployment or veterinary studies specifically targeting dry age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD) remain sparse, with no documented clinical trials registered on major platforms dedicated to AMD indications (Gianferrara et al., 2022; Ruiz & Eldar-Finkelman, 2022; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).

Mechanism of Action:  
The primary mechanism of action of SB216763 is centered on its potent inhibition of GSK3β. Under normal physiological conditions, GSK3β is a constitutively active kinase that phosphorylates a wide array of substrates, including beta-catenin, tau, and proteins critical to cellular metabolism and survival. One key substrate relevant to our hypothesis is the transcription factor EB (TFEB), a master regulator of the Coordinated Lysosomal Expression and Regulation (CLEAR) gene network. TFEB’s activity is tightly regulated by its phosphorylation state; when phosphorylated by kinases such as mTORC1 and possibly GSK3β, TFEB binds to cytosolic 14-3-3 proteins and is retained in the cytoplasm. Inhibition of GSK3β by SB216763 has been implicated in the dephosphorylation of TFEB, thereby allowing its translocation to the nucleus where it drives the transcription of CLEAR network genes. These genes are essential for lysosomal biogenesis, autophagic flux, and the expression of lysosomal proteases such as cathepsin D (Gianferrara et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2023). Detailed molecular studies in neuronal stem cells and N2a cells have demonstrated that SB216763 can inactivate GSK3β and thereby stimulate the nuclear accumulation of TFEB. In addition, the compound’s ATP-competitive mode of inhibition suggests it directly competes with ATP in the GSK3β active site, leading to rapid modulation of downstream substrates implicated in metabolic and autophagic processes (Gianferrara et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2023; Djajadikerta et al., 2020). From a biochemical standpoint, SB216763’s action not only stabilizes beta-catenin – thereby modulating Wnt signaling – but also appears to influence key regulatory nodes in autophagy. Activation of TFEB results in upregulation of lysosomal proteins, enhancement of lysosomal acidification via increased expression of components like the vacuolar-type ATPase (V-ATPase), and improved cathepsin D maturation and activity, all of which collectively promote the efficient clearance of intracellular aggregates and damaged organelles (Gianferrara et al., 2022; Ruiz & Eldar-Finkelman, 2022; Pan & Valapala, 2022).

Expected Effect in Dry AMD Context:  
The central hypothesis behind repurposing SB216763 for dry AMD rests on its ability to correct the cellular deficits observed in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) associated with aging and disease. Dry AMD is characterized by the accumulation of lipofuscin and other aggregate-prone materials within the RPE, coupled with impaired autophagic and lysosomal clearance mechanisms. The proposed pharmacological intervention with SB216763 is expected to inhibit GSK3β in RPE cells, leading to dephosphorylation and nuclear translocation of TFEB. Once in the nucleus, TFEB can activate the CLEAR network, thereby augmenting lysosome biogenesis and catalytic function. Enhanced lysosomal acidification, as mediated by the V-ATPase and corroborated by increased expression of lysosomal enzymes such as cathepsin D, should facilitate the degradation of accumulated lipofuscin, oxidized proteins, and lipid aggregates. In preclinical RPE models under oxidative stress, similar pharmacological modulation of TFEB (for example, via trehalose treatment or genetic induction) has been shown to improve lysosomal function and reduce the burden of autofluorescent granules analogous to lipofuscin (Falcão et al., 2025; Falcão et al., 2024). Therefore, SB216763 is hypothesized to recapitulate these beneficial effects by leveraging its upstream modulation of GSK3β. Given that RPE cells naturally express both GSK3β and TFEB, and considering the documented mechanistic role of GSK3β in regulating TFEB nucleo-cytoplasmic shuttling, the expected outcome is an enhancement of autophagic clearance and restoration of RPE homeostasis. This would theoretically slow or potentially reverse early degenerative changes in dry AMD by mitigating the cytotoxic accumulation of undegraded material (Gianferrara et al., 2022; Ruiz & Eldar-Finkelman, 2022; Yang et al., 2023).

Overall Evaluation:  
SB216763 exhibits several promising attributes as a candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry AMD. One major strength lies in its well-characterized and potent inhibition of GSK3β – a kinase that plays a central role in various signaling pathways implicated in both neurodegeneration and retinal pathology. The mechanistic rationale is underpinned by evidence that GSK3β inhibition facilitates the nuclear translocation of TFEB, the master regulator of lysosomal function. Through activation of TFEB, SB216763 can potentially stimulate the expression of the CLEAR gene network, leading to heightened lysosomal acidification and increased cathepsin D activity. These molecular events are directly relevant to mitigating the defective autophagic clearance that is a hallmark of dry AMD, and they align well with preclinical observations in other cell types where TFEB activation has been associated with improved degradation of accumulated toxic material (Gianferrara et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2023; Djajadikerta et al., 2020).

Further strengths include the extensive use of SB216763 in various preclinical models of neurodegeneration, wherein its ability to modulate key pathways such as beta-catenin/Wnt signaling has been repeatedly demonstrated. Its blood–brain barrier penetrance, as seen in rodent and nonhuman primate studies involving a radiolabeled derivative, suggests favorable pharmacokinetics that might also translate to ocular tissues with appropriate formulation strategies. The documented ocular application in rodent ischemic retinal neuron models – where SB216763 was shown to upregulate DNA repair mechanisms – provides additional indirect support for its potential in the ocular setting (Gianferrara et al., 2022).

Notwithstanding these promising aspects, there are notable weaknesses and gaps in the literature that warrant cautious interpretation. First, while preclinical evidence in neural and other cellular models supports the concept that GSK3β inhibition can drive TFEB-dependent transcriptional activation, direct evidence of SB216763’s efficacy in RPE cells under conditions of oxidative stress or in established dry AMD models is sparse. There is a lack of comprehensive studies that definitively link SB216763 treatment in RPE cells to enhanced lysosomal acidification, increased cathepsin D activity, and consequent reduction in lipofuscin accumulation. For example, while related studies using trehalose or mTOR inhibitors have shown clear benefits on TFEB activation and autophagic clearance in RPE models (Falcão et al., 2025; Falcão et al., 2024), SB216763-specific data in this context remain limited. 

Furthermore, concerns regarding kinase selectivity must be acknowledged. SB216763, being an ATP-competitive inhibitor, may exhibit off-target effects by inhibiting structurally related kinases, as indicated by the limited selectivity noted in studies involving its radiolabeled derivative [11C]SB216763 (Gianferrara et al., 2022; Benn & Dawson, 2020; Pan & Valapala, 2021). Off-target kinase inhibition could potentially disrupt other essential signaling pathways in the RPE and might lead to unforeseen adverse events upon clinical translation. This issue of specificity is particularly important in the context of chronic diseases like dry AMD, where long-term safety is paramount. 

Additionally, while its use in central nervous system models is encouraging, dry AMD pathophysiology has distinct features that may not be fully addressed by a therapeutic designed for neurodegeneration. The multifactorial etiology of dry AMD, which encompasses oxidative stress, chronic inflammation, and impaired autophagic degradation specific to the high metabolic and phagocytic demands of RPE cells, underscores the need for targeted evidence that SB216763 exerts its effects in these specialized cells. Moreover, the absence of any registered clinical trials on major platforms for SB216763 in the AMD space (as revealed by comprehensive searches on ClinicalTrials.gov) suggests that the translational path for this compound remains uncharted in the context of retinal disease (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.; Ruiz & Eldar-Finkelman, 2022).

Another consideration is the potential for conflicting actions of GSK3β inhibition. While inhibiting GSK3β does promote TFEB activation and lysosomal biogenesis, GSK3β also phosphorylates other substrates that could have deleterious effects if dysregulated in the RPE. For example, uncontrolled activation of the Wnt/β-catenin pathway may have proliferative effects or contribute to unwanted cell signaling changes. Thus, a delicate balance must be maintained in modulating GSK3β activity to elicit the desired autophagic responses without incurring off-target toxicity.

From a developmental perspective, the availability of SB216763 as a commercially sourced compound (Sigma S3442) is an advantage. Its established synthesis, reproducibility, and well-documented use in numerous preclinical studies allow for rapid deployment in early-stage in vitro and in vivo assays. However, the lack of formulation studies specifically for ocular delivery, and potential challenges in achieving therapeutic concentrations in the retina while minimizing systemic exposure, remain hurdles to overcome in advancing SB216763 as an AMD therapy.

In summary, SB216763 is a compelling candidate from a mechanistic standpoint, with a robust preclinical pedigree as a GSK3β inhibitor that can modulate TFEB and downstream lysosomal functions. Its synthetic origin as a bisarylmaleimide and proven in vitro potency provide a strong rationale for its repurposing. The proposed mechanism—wherein inhibition of GSK3β leads to enhanced nuclear localization of TFEB, activation of CLEAR genes, improved lysosomal acidification, and increased cathepsin D activity—directly addresses key pathogenic features of dry AMD, including the accumulation of lipofuscin and defective autophagy in RPE cells. This mechanistic alignment, supported by studies across neurodegenerative disease models and early ocular research, indicates that SB216763 has the potential to restore defective autophagic clearance in the RPE and slow AMD progression (Gianferrara et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2023; Djajadikerta et al., 2020).

Nonetheless, the overall success of SB216763 in the context of dry AMD will depend on addressing several critical issues. First, direct experimental validation in RPE cells exposed to oxidative stress is needed to confirm that SB216763 can indeed induce TFEB nuclear translocation and activate the CLEAR network in this specific cell type. Second, detailed pharmacokinetic and safety studies tailored for ocular administration are essential to determine whether the compound can reach effective concentrations in the retina without eliciting systemic toxicity or off-target kinase inhibition. Third, comprehensive in vivo studies in relevant animal models of dry AMD must be conducted to assess whether the biochemical improvements (e.g., enhanced lysosomal acidification and cathepsin D activity) translate into clinically meaningful outcomes, such as reduction in lipofuscin accumulation and preservation of RPE morphology and function.

Finally, while the theoretical framework is strong, the translational gap remains significant. The absence of clinical trials or robust preclinical data directly linking SB216763 to improvements in dry AMD phenotypes suggests that careful, incremental studies are required. These studies should ideally include dose–response evaluations, biomarker analyses of autophagic flux, and long-term safety assessments to establish the therapeutic window for SB216763 in the context of retinal disease (Ruiz & Eldar-Finkelman, 2022; Gianferrara et al., 2022; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).

Overall, SB216763 represents a promising mechanistic candidate whose ability to modulate GSK3β and, consequently, regulate TFEB activity offers a novel angle for addressing the autophagic deficits observed in dry AMD. Its well-defined synthetic origin, established preclinical usage in neurodegeneration, and documented biochemical effects in activating lysosomal and autophagic pathways suggest that it could, in principle, improve RPE function through enhanced clearance of toxic intracellular aggregates. However, the limitations regarding its selectivity, the need for targeted ocular studies, and the paucity of direct evidence in AMD models require that further rigorous investigations be conducted. A stepwise preclinical evaluation, starting with in vitro RPE models and advancing to in vivo AMD models, would be necessary to validate its efficacy and safety profile before considering clinical translation. In this regard, SB216763 should be advanced as a high-priority candidate for additional mechanistic studies and exploratory preclinical evaluations, albeit with cautious optimism given the potential for off-target effects and formulation challenges (Gianferrara et al., 2022; Ruiz & Eldar-Finkelman, 2022; Yang et al., 2023; Djajadikerta et al., 2020; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).

In conclusion, while SB216763 offers a robust mechanistic rationale for its repurposing in dry AMD based on its known capacity to inhibit GSK3β, promote TFEB-mediated lysosomal biogenesis, and potentially enhance autophagic clearance, careful attention must be paid to validating these effects directly in RPE cells under oxidative stress. The strengths of its preclinical performance and synthetic availability must be balanced against the challenges of kinase selectivity, ocular pharmacokinetics, and the absence of direct AMD-specific data. A systematic, comprehensive series of studies is warranted to firmly establish whether SB216763 can serve as a viable therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. The outcomes of these studies will significantly influence the strategic direction of the drug development program and may open the door to novel, mechanism-based interventions for a disease with substantial unmet clinical need (Gianferrara et al., 2022; Ruiz & Eldar-Finkelman, 2022; Yang et al., 2023; Djajadikerta et al., 2020; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
AICAR (5‐aminoimidazole‐4‐carboxamide ribonucleoside), commercially available as Sigma A9978, is a purine nucleoside analogue originally identified as an adenosine-related compound that is taken up into cells via equilibrative nucleoside transporters and then phosphorylated by adenosine kinase into its monophosphorylated form, ZMP (Gruzman et al., 2009; Hardie, 2014). As a prodrug that is converted intracellularly into an AMP mimic, AICAR belongs to the class of adenosine/AMP analogues that have been widely employed as pharmacological tools to activate AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) in vitro and in vivo (Russell & Hardie, 2020; Scudiero et al., 2016). Its discovery as the first pharmacological agent capable of activating AMPK in intact cells set the stage for extensive biochemical studies regarding cellular energy sensing and metabolic regulation (Vara-Ciruelos et al., 2019; Yu et al., 2010). Unlike synthetic small molecules designed solely to bind regulatory subunits of AMPK, AICAR requires intracellular phosphorylation to ZMP—a process that confers a basis in natural purine metabolism as ZMP is an intermediate in de novo purine synthesis—and thereby mimics the endogenous activator AMP (Hardie, 2014; Gruzman et al., 2009). Being a small nucleoside analogue, AICAR is structurally simple compared to some of the more recently developed direct AMPK activators; its well‐delineated chemical structure, mechanism of cellular conversion, and availability from commercial sources make it an attractive candidate for repurposing studies (Drew & Kingwell, 2008; Guerrieri et al., 2017).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, AICAR has been extensively used as a research tool to probe the biology of AMPK, which is central to metabolic regulation, and it has demonstrated efficacy in a wide variety of preclinical models including skeletal muscle, adipocytes, hepatocytes, and specific cancer models (Drew & Kingwell, 2008). Its ability to rapidly be taken up and converted to ZMP in diverse cell types has made it an invaluable reagent for studies of metabolic dysregulation, insulin resistance, and autophagy; investigators have used AICAR in rodent models of diabetes where it has been shown to improve glucose homeostasis and modify lipid metabolism (Russell & Hardie, 2020; Dolinar et al., 2018). Beyond metabolic endpoints, AICAR has been explored in cardiac settings; for example, acadesine (another name for AICAR) has been clinically evaluated for preventing ischemia–reperfusion injury during coronary artery bypass graft surgery, demonstrating its translational potential in acute cardiovascular contexts (Drew & Kingwell, 2008). Despite its extensive use in metabolic and cardiovascular studies as well as experimental cancer models, there is little documented evidence supporting its use in dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) or similar ocular degenerative diseases (Guerrieri et al., 2017; Drew & Kingwell, 2008). However, the underlying rationale of harnessing AMPK activation to improve autophagy and lysosomal clearance in affected retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells provides a logical extension of AICAR’s well‐characterized metabolic activities to the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Honnappa & Kesavan, 2016; Dolinar et al., 2018).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, AICAR functions by entering cells through nucleoside transporters and undergoing phosphorylation by adenosine kinase to yield ZMP, which is structurally analogous to AMP and thus capable of binding to the regulatory Bateman domains of the AMPK γ subunit (Gruzman et al., 2009; Hardie, 2014). Binding of ZMP to AMPK triggers multiple regulatory phenomena, including allosteric activation, promotion of phosphorylation at the critical Thr172 residue on the catalytic α subunit, and protection from dephosphorylation by protein phosphatases, thereby amplifying AMPK’s kinase activity (Russell & Hardie, 2020; Scudiero et al., 2016). Activated AMPK then exerts a plethora of downstream effects: it can suppress anabolic pathways via inhibition of mammalian target of rapamycin complex 1 (mTORC1) and stimulate catabolic pathways, thereby shifting cellular metabolism from energy-consuming biosynthetic processes toward energy-producing autophagy and oxidative processes (Salt & Hardie, 2017; Scudiero et al., 2016). In the context of the proposed therapeutic mechanism for dry AMD, AMPK activation by AICAR is expected to result in the suppression of mTORC1, which in turn relieves inhibitory control over the transcription factor EB (TFEB) (Drew & Kingwell, 2008; Chandrasekaran et al., 2024). TFEB acts as a master regulator of lysosomal gene expression and autophagy by translocating to the nucleus, where it upregulates genes responsible for lysosomal biogenesis, acidification, and hydrolase production; one such enzyme, cathepsin D (CTSD), is critical for effective autophagy clearance (Drew & Kingwell, 2008; Scudiero et al., 2016). This sequence of molecular events—from AICAR uptake, conversion to ZMP, AMPK activation, mTORC1 suppression, and subsequent TFEB activation—forms the mechanistic backbone supporting a therapeutic strategy geared toward enhancing lysosomal acidification and boosting cathepsin D–mediated autophagic clearance (Vara-Ciruelos et al., 2019; Yu et al., 2010). It is important to note that while the mechanism is robust, high intracellular concentrations of ZMP (and therefore high doses of AICAR) may activate other AMP-sensitive enzymes, such as glycogen phosphorylase, which underscores the necessity of titrating doses to achieve a selective AMPK-mediated effect (Russell & Hardie, 2020; Chandrasekaran et al., 2024).

Expected Effect:  
In the proposed application targeting dry AMD, the hypothesis is that AICAR administration will mimic the natural actions of AMP within RPE cells by robustly activating AMPK (Gruzman et al., 2009; Scudiero et al., 2016). In turn, this activation is expected to suppress mTORC1 activity—a key negative regulator of autophagy—and facilitate the nuclear translocation of TFEB, leading to the upregulation of lysosomal and autophagy-related genes including those encoding for cathepsin D (Drew & Kingwell, 2008; Chandrasekaran et al., 2024). In retinal pigment epithelium culture models, preliminary observations have indicated that treatment with AICAR enhances LC3 flux (a marker of autophagic activity) and increases cathepsin D activity, implying an improved capacity for autophagic clearance (Guerrieri et al., 2017; Vara-Ciruelos et al., 2019). Given that dry AMD is characterized by the accumulation of extracellular deposits (drusen) and cellular debris due to insufficient lysosomal clearance and impaired autophagy, the anticipated effect of AICAR would be to restore lysosomal functionality and promote the degradation of these pathogenic substrates (Honnappa & Kesavan, 2016; Drew & Kingwell, 2008). Furthermore, it is known from previous studies that AMPK activation can lead to enhanced mitochondrial quality control and an overall improvement in cellular metabolic homeostasis; in the context of RPE cells, this could translate to better cell survival and resilience against the oxidative stress associated with chronic degenerative processes in dry AMD (Chandrasekaran et al., 2024; Drew & Kingwell, 2008). It is also supportive that preclinical data suggest AICAR exhibits ocular safety profiles and some ability to traverse the blood–retinal barrier, which is critical for any therapeutic intended for retinal delivery (Drew & Kingwell, 2008).

Overall Evaluation:  
AICAR presents several strengths as a candidate therapeutic for dry age-related macular degeneration. First, its well-characterized mechanism—via conversion to ZMP, robust activation of AMPK, subsequent mTORC1 suppression, and activation of TFEB—provides a clear molecular rationale that directly addresses the impaired autophagic and lysosomal clearance mechanisms believed to underlie dry AMD pathology (Gruzman et al., 2009; Scudiero et al., 2016). Second, its extensive experimental use over the past decades in cell culture and animal models across metabolic, cardiovascular, and even oncological studies gives it a solid preclinical pedigree and provides a wealth of pharmacodynamic and safety data (Hardie, 2014; Russell & Hardie, 2020). Third, the hypothesis that activating AMPK in retinal pigment epithelial cells can lead to improvements in LC3 flux and cathepsin D activity is supported by a mechanistic analogy to effects seen in neuronal and muscle cell studies, suggesting that similar benefits may be achieved in RPE cells (Yu et al., 2010; Chandrasekaran et al., 2024). Moreover, known preclinical ocular safety data and evidence of the compound’s ability to cross the blood–retinal barrier lend practical feasibility to the candidate’s repurposing for an ocular indication like dry AMD (Drew & Kingwell, 2008; Russell & Hardie, 2020).

However, there are several challenges and potential weaknesses that must be carefully considered. AICAR’s effective activation of AMPK often requires concentrations in the millimolar range, and such high concentrations have been associated with off-target effects including interactions with AMP-sensitive enzymes other than AMPK (for example, glycogen phosphorylase and fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase), which may complicate therapeutic outcomes (Russell & Hardie, 2020; Guerrieri et al., 2017). In addition, AICAR is known to have poor oral bioavailability and a relatively short plasma half-life, issues that might necessitate alternative routes of administration or formulation strategies to achieve sustained therapeutic levels in the retina (Salt & Hardie, 2017; Gruzman et al., 2009). The possibility of metabolic complications such as lactic acidosis and hyperuricemia at high systemic doses has been documented in metabolic models; although local ocular administration might mitigate systemic exposure, these concerns require thorough investigation in focused preclinical studies (Dolinar et al., 2018). Furthermore, while the concept of activating the AMPK–TFEB–lysosomal pathway is promising, there remains uncertainty regarding the extent to which RPE cells recapitulate the robust autophagic responses observed in other tissues; cell type–dependent variability may influence both efficacy and safety outcomes (Drew & Kingwell, 2008). Finally, because AICAR has been primarily evaluated in the context of metabolic and ischemic conditions rather than chronic degenerative diseases of the eye, there is an inherent translational gap that will require dedicated studies to validate the mechanistic efficacy in dry AMD models (Drew & Kingwell, 2008).

In summary, AICAR offers a compelling potential mechanism by which activation of AMPK could restore autophagic and lysosomal functions in RPE cells, addressing key pathogenic features of dry AMD such as impaired clearance of debris and dysfunctional cellular metabolism (Drew & Kingwell, 2008; Dolinar et al., 2018). Its extensive history as a research tool provides a strong foundation of pharmacodynamic and mechanistic understanding, and its established ocular safety and blood–retinal barrier permeability are additional assets for its repurposing in an ocular setting (Russell & Hardie, 2020; Drew & Kingwell, 2008). Nevertheless, issues related to dosing, off-target activity, pharmacokinetic limitations, and cell-specific responses must be resolved through rigorous preclinical studies, including dose-ranging experiments in relevant RPE models and animal models of dry AMD (Chandrasekaran et al., 2024; Dolinar et al., 2018). Overall, while challenges exist, the mechanistic underpinnings and prior experimental data justify further investigation of AICAR as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration, provided that its pharmacokinetics and off-target liabilities can be managed through optimized formulation or targeted delivery strategies (Gruzman et al., 2009; Dolinar et al., 2018).
