Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Everolimus (Afinitor; Novartis) is a semi‐synthetic derivative of sirolimus—a macrolide originally isolated from Streptomyces hygroscopicus—as evidenced by its chemical designation as 4-O-(2-hydroxyethyl)-rapamycin (Liu et al., 2023, pp. 11–12). By introducing a 2-hydroxyethyl group at position 40, everolimus achieves greater hydrophilicity and an increased oral bioavailability (from 10% to 16% relative to sirolimus) while retaining the core macrolactone structure that is characteristic of rapalogs (Liu et al., 2023, pp. 11–12; Weber, 2015, pp. 27–28). This compound belongs to the class of mTOR inhibitors—specifically, a first‐generation rapalog that selectively inhibits the mTOR complex 1 (mTORC1) while sparing mTORC2 (Liu et al., 2023, pp. 10–11; Weber, 2015, pp. 27–28). As a synthetic derivative of a naturally occurring product, everolimus represents the successful strategy of chemical modification to optimize pharmacokinetic properties and clinical tolerability. The design parameters underpinning everolimus’ synthesis have been guided by the goal of retaining potent immunosuppressive and anti‐proliferative effects while optimizing parameters such as solubility, half‐life, and tissue penetration, with the added advantage of an oral formulation already approved for several clinical indications (Liu et al., 2023, pp. 11–12; Wang et al., 2022, pp. 6–8).

Therapeutic History:  
Everolimus has a well‐established therapeutic history as an immunosuppressant and antineoplastic agent. Clinically, it is approved for treating advanced renal cell carcinoma, progressive neuroendocrine tumors of pancreatic origin, and subependymal giant cell astrocytoma in tuberous sclerosis complex patients who are not candidates for surgery (Wang et al., 2022, pp. 6–8; Weber, 2015, pp. 27–28). In these indications, its mechanism as an mTORC1 inhibitor serves to arrest cell cycle progression and inhibit angiogenesis, which are central to its antitumor activity (Kuo et al., 2018, pp. 5–7; Weber, 2015, pp. 27–28). Moreover, everolimus has been effectively used in the context of organ transplantation to prevent allograft rejection by impairing helper T‐cell proliferation (Wang et al., 2022, pp. 6–8; Weber, 2015, pp. 27–28).

With regard to ocular applications, although everolimus has not been approved specifically for dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD), several preclinical studies have demonstrated its potential benefits in ocular cell types and models. For instance, in vitro investigations have highlighted that everolimus can inhibit the proliferation and migration of retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells and modulate mTOR signaling within retinal tissue—an effect critical to conditions such as proliferative vitreoretinopathy (PVR) (Kuo et al., 2018, pp. 5–8). Additionally, clinical trials such as the Phase 2 randomized trial for neovascular AMD (albeit focused on wet AMD) have assessed everolimus’s efficacy in combination with anti‐vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) agents (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2009), thereby providing indirect support for its ocular pharmacokinetic (PK) profile and safety profile. This background, combined with its well‐known systemic tolerability, underscores its candidacy for repurposing in nonexudative (dry) AMD—a disease area in which few pharmacologic treatments exist.

Mechanism of Action:  
Everolimus exerts its effects by binding to the intracellular receptor FKBP12, forming a complex that interacts with and inhibits mTORC1 (Liu et al., 2023, pp. 11–12; Weber, 2015, pp. 27–28). The inhibition of mTORC1 results in a downstream decrease in the phosphorylation of ribosomal protein S6 kinase (S6K1) and other substrates such as ribosomal protein S6 (RPS6), effectively suppressing cap‐dependent protein synthesis and cellular proliferation (Kuo et al., 2018, pp. 5–7; Liu et al., 2023, pp. 10–11). In the context of RPE cells, inhibition of mTORC1 plays a particularly critical role in modulating autophagic flux. Under normal conditions, mTORC1 phosphorylates and suppresses the transcription factor EB (TFEB), a master regulator of lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy. Inhibition of mTORC1 frees TFEB to translocate to the nucleus where it transactivates genes that codify for lysosomal proteins, such as the subunits of the vacuolar ATPase (V‐ATPase), and hydrolases including cathepsin D (Kuo et al., 2018, p. 7; Nieto et al., 2015, pp. 28–32). Preclinical studies have shown that in RPE culture systems, treatment with everolimus results in an increase in LC3 turnover—a marker of enhanced autophagic flux—and accelerates the maturation of cathepsin D (CTSD), which is essential for effective lysosomal degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (Kuo et al., 2018, pp. 5–8). Such modulation of the autophagy–lysosome pathway is mechanistically attractive in dry AMD because the accumulation of cellular debris and lipofuscin in RPE cells is implicated in disease pathogenesis. Furthermore, it has been reported that everolimus displays superior ocular tissue penetration compared with sirolimus in in vitro porcine corneal models, suggesting that its formulation could be optimized for direct ocular administration if required (Liu et al., 2023, pp. 11–14). Overall, the biochemical profile of everolimus supports the hypothesis that targeted mTORC1 inhibition in RPE cells could lead to enhanced TFEB activation and a subsequent restoration of lysosomal function—thereby addressing one of the key pathological features underlying dry AMD.

Expected Effect:  
The hypothesis proposes that everolimus will inhibit mTORC1 in RPE cells, leading to the activation of TFEB, a critical step in lysosomal biogenesis and function. Upon release from mTORC1‐mediated phosphorylation constraints, TFEB translocates to the nucleus where it upregulates the expression of essential lysosomal genes, including those encoding V‐ATPase subunits (which are responsible for lysosomal acidification) and cathepsin D (CTSD), a protease required for the degradation of accumulated waste products (Kuo et al., 2018, p. 7; Nieto et al., 2015, pp. 28–32). This molecular cascade is expected to improve the clearance of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) and other cellular debris that accumulate in RPE cells owing to age‐related impairment of autophagy. In vitro data support that everolimus treatment increases LC3 turnover and facilitates the maturation of CTSD, both of which are indicative of enhanced autophagic flux and lysosomal functionality (Kuo et al., 2018, pp. 5–8). Given that RPE cells naturally express components of the mTOR signaling pathway—including high levels of mTORC1—and that dysfunctional lysosomal clearance is a hallmark of dry AMD (as exemplified by the accumulation of lipofuscin and drusen formation), the expected pharmacodynamic effect of everolimus would be to restore homeostasis in these cells. Successful activation of TFEB is anticipated to lead to improved degradation of damaged organelles and protein aggregates, potentially mitigating the progression of retinal degeneration characteristic of dry AMD. Moreover, the fact that everolimus is already formulated for oral administration with a known ocular PK profile further supports the translational potential of this candidate: systemic dosing may achieve sufficient retinal concentrations to exert the desired effects in RPE cells without necessitating invasive delivery methods (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2009; Liu et al., 2023, pp. 11–12).

Overall Evaluation:  
The potential of everolimus as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD is supported by several compelling factors. First, its established clinical safety and efficacy in other indications—such as renal cell carcinoma and immunosuppression in transplantation—reduce the translational risk associated with drug repurposing (Weber, 2015, pp. 27–28; Wang et al., 2022, pp. 6–8). The fact that everolimus is an FDA‐approved agent with an oral formulation makes it an attractive candidate for repurposing, as its dosing, systemic distribution, and side‐effect profile are already well characterized. In addition, its selective inhibition of mTORC1 has a clear mechanistic rationale in the context of dry AMD. By specifically targeting the mTORC1–TFEB axis, everolimus may correct the impaired lysosomal degradation and autophagic dysfunction that underlie the accumulation of pathogenic debris in RPE cells (Kuo et al., 2018, p. 7; Nieto et al., 2015, pp. 28–32).

A major strength of everolimus is the robust preclinical evidence indicative of its capacity to modulate autophagy. In ocular cell culture systems, everolimus has been shown to enhance LC3 turnover and promote CTSD maturation—both key markers of autophagic and lysosomal efficiency (Kuo et al., 2018, pp. 5–8). Additionally, its improved ocular penetration compared to its parent compound sirolimus suggests that even systemic administration might yield therapeutically relevant levels in the retina (Liu et al., 2023, pp. 11–14). This represents a significant advantage in the context of dry AMD, where achieving effective drug delivery to deeply situated retinal tissues is a persistent challenge.

However, several weaknesses must be acknowledged. Despite a sound mechanistic rationale, direct clinical evidence for everolimus’s efficacy in dry AMD is lacking. Existing clinical studies have primarily focused on other ocular conditions such as neovascular AMD and PVR, and the particular pathophysiology of dry AMD—with its complex interplay of oxidative stress, complement dysregulation, and chronic inflammation—may require a more nuanced therapeutic approach (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2009; Kuo et al., 2018, pp. 3–5). It is also important to consider the potential systemic side effects of mTOR inhibition, which include hyperglycemia, dyslipidemia, stomatitis, and, in some cases, immunosuppression (Weber, 2015, pp. 27–28, 28–29). Although these adverse events are generally manageable in oncology and transplant settings, the chronic nature of dry AMD treatment may necessitate a careful balancing of therapeutic benefits against systemic risks. Moreover, while everolimus selectively inhibits mTORC1, prolonged inhibition of this pathway could potentially interfere with homeostatic cellular processes beyond autophagy, raising concerns about long‐term retinal safety.

Another consideration relates to the multifactorial etiology of dry AMD. While lysosomal dysfunction is a critical aspect of the disease, it is accompanied by other pathological processes such as oxidative damage, chronic inflammation, and alterations in the complement cascade. Thus, monotherapy with an mTORC1 inhibitor may not be sufficiently robust to address all disease mechanisms. Combination therapies that target multiple pathological pathways might ultimately be necessary for effective disease modification. Lastly, discrepancies in the translation of preclinical findings to human disease remain a persistent challenge. For example, while certain animal models of retinal disease have demonstrated beneficial effects of mTOR inhibition, analogous results have not always been replicated in clinical settings (Kuo et al., 2018, pp. 3–5; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2009).

In summary, everolimus presents as a mechanistically intriguing candidate for repurposing in dry AMD due to its ability to inhibit mTORC1 and thereby promote TFEB‐mediated restoration of lysosomal function. Its solid record as an FDA‐approved drug with established dosing regimens and acceptable systemic safety lends additional support to its viability as a repurposing candidate. Preclinical data suggest that everolimus increases autophagic flux in RPE cells, enhancing LC3 turnover and CTSD maturation, which theoretically should facilitate the clearance of pathological debris that characterizes dry AMD (Kuo et al., 2018, pp. 5–8). The advantages of an oral formulation and favorable ocular pharmacokinetics further underpin its translational potential (Liu et al., 2023, pp. 11–12; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2009).

Nonetheless, the candidate also faces important challenges. Key limitations include the absence of direct clinical evidence for efficacy in dry AMD, potential systemic adverse effects associated with prolonged mTORC1 inhibition, and the inherent complexity of dry AMD pathology, which may require multimodal therapeutic strategies. Moreover, past experiences in ocular applications—such as studies in PVR models where everolimus did not yield a statistically significant clinical improvement—highlight the need for carefully controlled dose-finding and safety studies (Kuo et al., 2018, pp. 3–5). It will be crucial to establish that systemic dosing can achieve therapeutic retinal concentrations without eliciting unintended systemic toxicity or disrupting normal RPE physiology.

Overall, while mechanistic and preclinical data provide a strong rationale for repurposing everolimus to treat dry AMD, further rigorous preclinical studies specifically in models of dry AMD are warranted. A careful evaluation of dosing regimens, potential adverse effects, and efficacy endpoints will be essential in the translational development of everolimus for this indication. The mechanistic specificity for mTORC1 inhibition, combined with the ability to enhance autophagic clearance in RPE cells, represents a significant strength that could offer a novel approach to modifying the course of dry AMD. However, the challenges associated with systemic mTOR inhibition and the need for combination strategies or localized delivery systems must be addressed in subsequent research phases. In conclusion, everolimus is a promising, though not yet definitively validated, candidate for repurposing in dry AMD, and we recommend that further detailed studies be undertaken to fully elucidate its potential in restoring lysosomal function and ameliorating retinal degeneration in this patient population (Liu et al., 2023, pp. 11–12; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2009; Kuo et al., 2018, pp. 5–7; Weber, 2015, pp. 27–28; Wang et al., 2022, pp. 6–8; Kuo et al., 2018, pp. 7–8).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
MCC950 (AdipoGen AG‐CRID3) is a synthetic small‐molecule inhibitor that belongs to the diarylsulfonylurea chemical class and was originally discovered during investigations aimed at identifying potent inhibitors of the NLRP3 inflammasome complex (Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018). Its chemical scaffold was designed to specifically interfere with the ATPase function of the NLRP3 NACHT domain, thereby preventing the oligomerization of NLRP3 and subsequent formation of the ASC speck complex that is essential for inflammasome activation (Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2025). This compound has been synthetically optimized for high potency, with reported effective concentrations in the nanomolar range in various disease models, and its structure–activity relationship has been refined in numerous preclinical studies over the past several years (Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018; Wooff et al., 2020). As a representative of its drug class, diarylsulfonylureas have been broadly explored in inflammatory contexts due to their capacity to modulate innate immune pathways; however, MCC950 has emerged as a prototype NLRP3-targeting agent with potential applications across inflammatory and degenerative diseases, including those affecting ocular tissues (Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018; Wooff et al., 2020).

Therapeutic History:  
MCC950 was initially characterized in systemic inflammatory disease models, where it demonstrated remarkable efficacy in reducing the production of proinflammatory cytokines, such as interleukin (IL)-1β and IL-18, by directly inhibiting the activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome (Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018; Wooff et al., 2020). Preclinical evaluations in nonocular contexts—such as experimental colitis, myocardial infarction, and atherosclerosis—have consistently shown that MCC950 can markedly mitigate pathology by blocking the inflammasome cascade (Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018; Wooff et al., 2020). In the ocular arena, several studies have examined MCC950’s impact in diverse rodent models of retinal disease. For example, in laser-induced choroidal neovascularization (CNV) models, MCC950 administration led to reductions in IL-1β mRNA and secreted protein levels, albeit with a paradoxical increase in overall CNV lesion volume, suggesting a complex interplay between inflammasome inhibition and immune cell recruitment (Dieckmann et al., 2024). Furthermore, intravitreal delivery of MCC950 in an OPTN(E50K) mouse model of normal-tension glaucoma (NTG) showed functional and structural retinal improvements through decreased expression of inflammasome components and glial activation markers (Wang et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2023). In vitro investigations using ARPE-19 and R28 retinal cell lines have also highlighted MCC950's ability to decrease NLRP3, caspase-1, IL-1β, and IL-18 levels, thus attenuating inflammasome-mediated inflammatory responses (Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018; Li, 2020). Despite these promising preclinical data in models of retinal inflammation and vascular dysfunction, MCC950 has not yet progressed into clinical trials for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or geographic atrophy (GA), and its use in ocular conditions remains primarily in the preclinical and exploratory phase (Wooff et al., 2020).

Mechanism of Action:  
MCC950 exerts its pharmacological effects by specifically targeting the NLRP3 inflammasome, a cytosolic multiprotein complex that mediates the innate immune response to both pathogen-associated and damage-associated molecular patterns (Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018). At the molecular level, MCC950 is believed to bind to the NACHT domain of NLRP3, thereby inhibiting its ATPase activity—a critical step required for the conformational changes and oligomerization that lead to the formation of the active inflammasome complex (Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2025). This blockade prevents the recruitment of the adaptor protein ASC, thus halting the maturation and activation of caspase-1 (Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018; Wooff et al., 2020). Consequently, the cleavage of pro-IL-1β and pro-IL-18 into their bioactive forms is suppressed, which results in diminished secretion of these potent proinflammatory cytokines (Wang et al., 2025; Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018). Importantly, MCC950’s mechanism is selective for NLRP3, as it does not interfere with the activation of other inflammasome platforms, such as those mediated by AIM2, NLRC4, or NLRP1 (Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018; Wooff et al., 2020). In the context of retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells—a cell type critical for the maintenance of the outer blood–retina barrier and implicated in the pathogenesis of dry AMD—NLRP3 activation has been linked to chronic inflammation, oxidative stress, and lysosomal destabilization. Inhibition of NLRP3 by MCC950 is postulated to preserve lysosomal integrity by preventing excessive caspase-1 activation, which is known to contribute to lysosomal membrane permeabilization and the subsequent loss of v-ATPase–dependent acidification along with aberrant cathepsin D (CTSD) activity (Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018; Korhonen, 2024). Although direct experimental evidence demonstrating the preservation of CTSD activity or v-ATPase function by MCC950 in RPE cells is not yet firmly established in the literature provided, the underlying rationale is supported by the well-documented role of caspase-1 in mediating pyroptosis and lysosomal dysfunction in models of RPE degeneration (Korhonen, 2024; Ildefonso et al., 2016).

Expected Effect:  
In a therapeutic scenario for dry AMD, the expected effect of MCC950 is to inhibit NLRP3 inflammasome activation within RPE cells, thereby reducing the downstream activation of caspase-1 and the cleavage of proinflammatory cytokines IL-1β and IL-18. This dampening of the inflammatory cascade is anticipated to prevent or attenuate the lysosomal membrane destabilization that is often observed in RPE cells under stress conditions such as those induced by Alu RNA accumulation secondary to DICER1 deficiency—an event that has been strongly implicated in geographic atrophy (Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018; Korhonen, 2024). With reduced caspase-1 activity, it is hypothesized that MCC950 will preserve the integrity of the lysosomal compartment by maintaining proper v-ATPase function and ensuring that cathepsin D is correctly matured and compartmentalized, thereby mitigating autophagic and lysosomal stress (Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018; Ildefonso et al., 2016). In preclinical RPE models, inhibitors of NLRP3 have been shown to decrease IL-1β/IL-18 release and reduce inflammatory cell death (pyroptosis), which in turn supports cellular homeostasis and may prevent the progressive loss of RPE cells that drives the clinical progression of dry AMD (Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018; Wooff et al., 2020). Although direct evidence of MCC950 restoring lysosomal enzyme activity or preventing v-ATPase dysfunction in the context of AMD is currently limited, the compound has demonstrated efficacy in reducing inflammatory biomarker levels in retinal cell cultures and animal models, which is consistent with the desired outcome in a dry AMD setting (Li, 2020; Wooff et al., 2020). In addition to its biochemical effects, it is anticipated that the suppression of chronic inflammation by MCC950 will translate into preserved retinal architecture and function, as observed in some glaucoma models where intravitreal administration improved retinal ganglion cell survival and visual behavioral outcomes (Wang et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2023). Therefore, integrating both molecular and functional endpoints, MCC950 is expected to mitigate the inflammatory processes that underlie RPE loss, preserve key lysosomal functions, and ultimately slow or prevent the progression of geographic atrophy in dry AMD (Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018; Wooff et al., 2020).

Overall Evaluation:  
MCC950 offers several notable strengths as a potential therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. Foremost among these is its high potency and selectivity as an inhibitor of the NLRP3 inflammasome, a central mediator of innate immune inflammatory responses that has been implicated in the pathogenesis of various retinal degenerative disorders, including AMD (Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018). Its mechanism of action—binding to the NACHT domain to inhibit ATPase activity and subsequently block caspase-1 activation—provides a targeted approach that directly addresses a proximal event in the inflammatory cascade (Wang et al., 2025; Wooff et al., 2020). Preclinical studies have demonstrated that MCC950 can successfully reduce the release of IL-1β and IL-18 in various cell types, including retinal endothelial cells and RPE-like cells, which underscores its potential to ameliorate the chronic inflammatory environment observed in dry AMD (Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018; Li, 2020). Moreover, the use of MCC950 in ocular models—albeit primarily in glaucoma and CNV studies—has yielded promising outcomes in terms of reducing retinal inflammation, glial activation, and, in the case of intravitreal delivery in aged mouse models, improving retinal morphology and visual function (Wang et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2023). This provides an encouraging proof-of-concept that NLRP3 inhibition can have beneficial effects on retinal structure and function.

However, several weaknesses and challenges must be considered before advancing MCC950 as a therapy for dry AMD. While the compound effectively reduces inflammasome activity in multiple settings, its performance in models that closely recapitulate dry AMD pathology, particularly those focusing on geographic atrophy and RPE degeneration, remains to be conclusively demonstrated (Wooff et al., 2020). In some preclinical models, such as the photo-oxidative damage study, MCC950 failed to rescue photoreceptor cell death or improve overall retinal function, and higher doses were associated with adverse functional effects, suggesting a narrow therapeutic window or model-specific limitations (Wooff et al., 2020; Zha et al., 2022). Furthermore, while the hypothesis that MCC950 will preserve lysosomal v-ATPase function and cathepsin D activity is compelling, the current literature does not present direct experimental evidence confirming that these specific endpoints are restored in RPE cells following NLRP3 inhibition by MCC950 (Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018; Ildefonso et al., 2016). This gap is critical, given that lysosomal dysfunction and impaired autophagy are central to the chronic inflammation and RPE loss observed in dry AMD. Additionally, there are reports of paradoxical effects in certain ocular models—such as increased lesion volume in laser-induced CNV models despite reductions in IL-1β levels—which hint at the complex biology of the inflammasome and suggest that blocking NLRP3 may have unintended consequences on immune cell recruitment and neovascular dynamics (Dieckmann et al., 2024).

A further limitation is the relative paucity of data regarding the pharmacokinetic properties and ocular bioavailability of MCC950 when administered via routes that would be clinically relevant for AMD, such as intravitreal or topical delivery. Although some studies have begun to characterize its ocular distribution and short-term safety in rodent models (Chen et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2025), comprehensive long-term toxicity profiles, dose–response evaluations, and assessments of potential off-target effects in the highly specialized environment of the eye have yet to be established. These studies are essential not only for confirming the anti-inflammatory efficacy of MCC950 in RPE cells but also for ensuring that long-term inhibition of NLRP3 does not inadvertently impair other cellular processes critical for retinal health.

In summary, the evaluation of MCC950 as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD is promising yet remains preliminary. Its well-characterized ability to selectively inhibit the NLRP3 inflammasome, reducing caspase-1 activation and downstream IL-1β/IL-18 release, aligns with the mechanistic rationale for targeting chronic inflammation in RPE cells—a key driver of geographic atrophy in dry AMD (Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018; Korhonen, 2024). The compound’s preclinical efficacy in reducing inflammatory biomarkers in various ocular and non-ocular models supports the hypothesis that MCC950 may alleviate the inflammatory milieu that underlies RPE degeneration and lysosomal dysfunction. However, mixed outcomes observed in certain retinal models, along with the absence of direct evidence linking MCC950 to improved lysosomal v-ATPase function and cathepsin D maturation in RPE cells, underscore the need for further detailed studies (Wooff et al., 2020). Moreover, optimizing the ocular delivery method, establishing a robust pharmacokinetic profile in the eye, and conducting dedicated preclinical trials in models that accurately mimic dry AMD pathophysiology are critical next steps before this candidate can be considered for clinical translation. 

Overall, while MCC950 exhibits significant mechanistic and pharmacological strengths that support its evaluation as a potential treatment for dry AMD, its clinical viability will depend on resolving several key uncertainties. These include (1) the demonstration of its capacity to restore and maintain lysosomal integrity and CTSD activity in stressed RPE cells, (2) the establishment of an optimal dosing regimen with minimal ocular toxicity, and (3) clarification of the complex immunological consequences of long-term NLRP3 inhibition within the retinal environment. Addressing these questions through a comprehensive series of biochemical, cellular, and animal studies will be essential for determining whether MCC950 can be effectively repurposed to combat the progressive RPE loss and chronic inflammatory state that drive geographic atrophy in dry AMD (Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018; Wooff et al., 2020; Ildefonso et al., 2016).

In conclusion, MCC950 is a highly attractive candidate from a drug development perspective due to its potent, selective inhibition of the NLRP3 inflammasome—a pathway increasingly implicated in the inflammatory cascade that underlies dry AMD. Its synthetic origins as a diarylsulfonylurea and its extensive preclinical evaluation in inflammatory disease models lend strong support to its potential utility. Nevertheless, the complex biology of the retinal environment and the conflicting preclinical results observed in some models necessitate cautious optimism. Further targeted studies that rigorously assess MCC950’s effects on RPE-specific endpoints—including lysosomal acidification, v-ATPase function, and cathepsin D maturation—will be pivotal in establishing its efficacy for dry AMD. Additionally, comprehensive ocular safety and pharmacokinetic studies are required to ensure that the benefits of MCC950 can be realized without incurring off-target toxicities in this delicate tissue. Based on the current literature, MCC950 holds promise as a means to directly address inflammasome-driven inflammation in dry AMD; however, its advancement into clinical trials will depend on the outcomes of these critical preclinical investigations (Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018; Wooff et al., 2020; Li, 2020; Ildefonso et al., 2016; Dieckmann et al., 2024).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Harmine is a naturally occurring β-carboline alkaloid that is abundant in Peganum harmala L., and has been investigated for neuropharmacological activities including acetylcholinesterase (AChE) inhibition, antioxidant activity, and anti-inflammatory effects, with related β-carbolines such as harmaline frequently studied alongside it (Singh et al., 2024). In preclinical pharmacology, water-soluble salt forms such as harmine hydrochloride have been used, and medicinal chemistry analogs with higher potency than the parent have been reported, supporting tractability for formulation and structure–activity optimization (Singh et al., 2024).

The mechanistic disease context relevant to dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is dominated by lysosomal and autophagy dysfunction in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), where impaired lysosomal degradation, phagosome–lysosome fusion, and autophagic flux promote lipofuscin accumulation, oxidative stress, complement/inflammasome activation, and RPE death (Boya et al., 2023; Kaarniranta et al., 2023). Master regulators of lysosomal biogenesis and degradative capacity include TFEB/TFE3, which are controlled by mTORC1, AMPK, Ca2+/calcineurin, and lysosomal signaling nodes; TFEB drives expression of the CLEAR gene network to expand lysosomal/autophagy capacity and has been repeatedly highlighted as a central therapeutic axis for restoring RPE degradative function (Boya et al., 2023). Because LAMP2 deficiency impairs photoreceptor outer segment (POS) degradation and yields AMD-like phenotypes, and cathepsin D (CTSD) is the primary POS protease in RPE, TFEB-mediated enhancement of these systems is mechanistically aligned with dry AMD pathobiology (Boya et al., 2023; Si et al., 2023; Kaarniranta et al., 2013). Torin1 is a synthetic small‐molecule that belongs to the second‐generation, ATP‐competitive class of mTOR inhibitors, originally derived from a quinoline‐based scaffold. This chemical modification yielded a molecule with exceptional biochemical potency—capable of inhibiting both mTOR complexes, mTORC1 and mTORC2, at very low (nanomolar to picomolar) concentrations—and with approximately 1000-fold improvement in cellular potency relative to the initial hits (Guillem, 2015). As an ATP-competitive inhibitor, Torin1 binds directly to the active (ATP-binding) site of mTOR, thereby circumventing the partial inhibition that is observed with first-generation mTOR inhibitors like rapamycin that act allosterically by binding FKBP12 (Liu et al., 2012). Torin1 has been widely used as a research tool to interrogate mTOR signaling in various cellular contexts, and its chemical lineage as a quinoline-derived molecule positions it within a well-characterized class of inhibitors that have been instrumental in expanding our understanding of mTOR-dependent regulation of autophagy and cellular metabolism (Liu et al., 2012).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, Torin1 has been employed predominantly as a research tool rather than as a clinical drug candidate. Extensive preclinical studies have demonstrated its robust ability to inhibit mTOR signaling in cancer models, autophagy-deficient systems, and metabolic studies. For instance, Torin1 was shown to potently inhibit mTOR signaling pathways in glioblastoma and prostate cancer cells, significantly reducing cell-cycle progression and inducing apoptosis in certain contexts (Gu, 2017; Liu et al., 2012). Its use as an autophagy inducer is well documented, as experiments utilizing Torin1 have demonstrated increased autophagic flux and elevated lysosomal activity in multiple cell lines (Li, 2018; Liu et al., 2012). Importantly, Torin1 is also used in studies with retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells, as evidenced by its ability to increase TFEB-driven luciferase reporter activity in ARPE-19 cells by effectively suppressing mTORC1 signaling (Huang et al., 2018). Despite these promising experimental findings, Torin1 has not advanced to clinical trials for any indication, including neurodegenerative disorders or dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD). Moreover, its intrinsic pharmacokinetic limitations—such as poor aqueous solubility, a short half-life, and low oral bioavailability—have been recognized in several studies, thereby limiting its potential as a direct therapeutic candidate without further structural optimization (Guillem, 2015; Wang et al., 2022).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, Torin1 functions by competing with ATP for binding to the catalytic domain of mTOR, effectively blocking the phosphorylation of downstream substrates. Its ATP-competitive nature allows Torin1 to inhibit both mTORC1 and mTORC2 complexes, thereby offering a broader inhibition profile than allosteric agents like rapamycin that primarily target mTORC1 (Guillem, 2015; Liu et al., 2012). Detailed molecular modeling and structure–activity relationship studies indicate that the tricyclic benzonaphthridinone core of Torin1 forms critical hinge-binding interactions with residues in the mTOR kinase domain (Liu et al., 2012). This interaction accounts for its high potency, as reflected in low nanomolar IC₅₀ values in cellular assays (Liu et al., 2012; Gros & Muller, 2014). Torin1 induces rapid dephosphorylation of canonical mTORC1 substrates, such as S6 kinase at Thr389 and 4E-BP1 at Thr37/46, which results in downregulation of protein synthesis and cellular growth signals (Misra & Pizzo, 2013). Moreover, by simultaneously inhibiting mTORC2, it reduces phosphorylation of Akt at Ser473—a site critical for full Akt activation—thus attenuating the feedback loops that typically reinvigorate upstream PI3K signaling in response to mTORC1 inhibition (Gu, 2017; Martina et al., 2014). A particularly notable feature of Torin1 is its slow off-rate, which leads to sustained inhibition of mTOR activity even after drug washout, a pharmacodynamic property that may confer prolonged downstream effects such as enhanced autophagic flux (Liu et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2013). The inhibition of mTOR by Torin1 correlates with dephosphorylation of transcription factors, particularly TFEB and TFE3; under normal nutrient-replete conditions, mTORC1 phosphorylates TFEB (e.g., on S211 in TFEB) and TFE3, sequestering them in the cytosol through binding with 14-3-3 proteins (Huang et al., 2018; Martina et al., 2014). Upon mTOR inhibition by Torin1, TFEB is dephosphorylated and translocates to the nucleus, where it induces the transcription of CLEAR (Coordinated Lysosomal Expression and Regulation) network genes that drive lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy (Li, 2018; Liu et al., 2013). This precise modulation of mTOR signaling and subsequent transcriptional reprogramming forms the biochemical basis for leveraging Torin1 as a candidate to ameliorate lysosomal clearance defects.

The central hypothesis for repurposing Torin1 in the context of dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is that potent inhibition of mTORC1/2 in RPE cells can lift the repressive phosphorylation that normally limits the activity of TFEB and TFE3. In RPE cells, as demonstrated by studies in ARPE-19 cell models, mTOR inhibition via Torin1 not only leads to decreased phosphorylation of S6 kinase but also results in marked activation of TFEB-driven transcription (Huang et al., 2018). In summary, Torin1 possesses a compelling mechanistic profile that aligns well with the therapeutic needs of dry AMD by targeting a fundamental pathway governing cellular homeostasis in RPE cells. Its origin from a quinoline-based scaffold and subsequent chemical optimization into a highly potent ATP-competitive mTOR inhibitor underline its status as a valuable chemical probe in preclinical settings (Guillem, 2015). The dual inhibition of both mTORC1 and mTORC2 by Torin1, combined with its slow off-rate and sustained downstream effects—including dephosphorylation and nuclear translocation of TFEB/TFE3—make it an ideal tool for inducing lysosomal biogenesis and enhancing autophagic clearance (Martina et al., 2014; Huang et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2012). In cellular models, including ARPE-19 RPE cells, Torin1 has already demonstrated the ability to activate TFEB and upregulate CLEAR gene expression, which is directly relevant to counteracting the lysosomal clearance defects observed in dry AMD (Huang et al., 2018; Li, 2018).

However, significant challenges remain regarding the translational applicability of Torin1 as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. Its reported poor aqueous solubility, short half-life, and low oral bioavailability present formidable barriers to clinical development unless addressed through formulation improvements or further medicinal chemistry optimization (Guillem, 2015; Wang et al., 2022). Moreover, while extensive preclinical literature supports its role as a robust mTOR inhibitor in cancer and autophagy research, there is a lack of direct in vivo evidence for its efficacy in ocular models, particularly in dry AMD or geographic atrophy (GA) mouse lines (Liu et al., 2013; Gu, 2017). Careful dosing will also be critical, as the broad and potent inhibition of mTOR can have unintended effects on cellular metabolism and protein synthesis beyond the intended enhancement of lysosomal function. Additionally, off-target effects have been observed in some biochemical screens at supraphysiologic concentrations, including binding to other PIKK family members such as ATR, ATM, and DNA-PK, although these are generally not manifested at the low nanomolar concentrations used in cellular assays (Settembre et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2012).

From the perspective of repurposing for dry AMD, Torin1’s deep mechanistic specificity is a double-edged sword: it offers a highly defined and robust approach to upregulating lysosomal biogenesis via the TFEB/TFE3 axis, yet its pharmacokinetic liabilities and the absence of any clinical history in ocular disease necessitate additional work. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Ambroxol is a small-molecule mucolytic historically used to thin airway mucus and has been repurposed as a pharmacological chaperone for the lysosomal enzyme glucocerebrosidase (GCase) in Gaucher disease, where it selectively binds misfolded GCase to aid folding and trafficking to lysosomes for substrate degradation (Alhowyan & Harisa, 2025, pp. 17–18). Pharmacological chaperones constitute a class of small molecules that stabilize specific mutant lysosomal enzymes conformationally in the endoplasmic reticulum, enabling correct processing and lysosomal delivery; a paradigmatic example is migalastat, an alpha-galactosidase A chaperone approved for Fabry disease with amenable variants (Alhowyan & Harisa, 2025, pp. 17–18). Ambroxol is further characterized by its ability to cross the blood–brain barrier, a property relevant for neuronopathic lysosomal storage disorders and attractive for central nervous system or ocular indications where access is otherwise constrained (Alhowyan & Harisa, 2025, pp. 17–18). Within the broader landscape of lysosomal therapeutics, small molecules also act as proteostasis regulators and modulators of lysosomal signaling and biogenesis; however, off-target actions remain a central limitation of small-molecule therapy in this domain (Alhowyan & Harisa, 2025, pp. 17–18).

The therapeutic hypothesis for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) posits that ambroxol could act as a pharmacological chaperone for lysosomal enzymes in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), stabilize or enhance vacuolar H+-ATPase (V-ATPase) function, improve lysosomal acidification, and thereby augment cathepsin D (CTSD) activity to clear lipofuscin/drusen components characteristic of dry AMD (Kaarniranta et al., 2023, pp. 2–3; Si et al., 2023, pp. 4–7). This rationale is grounded in the centrality of lysosomal function to RPE homeostasis and AMD pathogenesis: RPE lysosomes sustain heavy heterophagic and autophagic loads from daily photoreceptor outer-segment (POS) digestion, and impaired lysosomal acidification and hydrolase function contribute to lipofuscin accumulation, exosome-driven drusen formation, and progressive degeneration (Kaarniranta et al., 2023, pp. 2–3; Si et al., 2023, pp. 2–4, 5–7; Sharif, 2015, pp. 199–202). Notably, in AMD models and donor RPE, TFEB—the master transcriptional driver of lysosomal/autophagy biogenesis—is dysregulated, V-ATPase-related transcripts (e.g., ATP6VOA1) and cathepsin abundance/activity are linked to lysosomal competence, and TFEB activation or mTOR inhibition reduces toxic storage material such as A2E and POS-derived autofluorescent granules (Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7).

Conventional use: Ambroxol is primarily used clinically as a mucolytic agent to reduce mucus viscosity in respiratory disease (Alhowyan & Harisa, 2025, pp. 17–18). Beyond its mucolytic effects, ambroxol has been investigated in lysosomal storage diseases as a pharmacological chaperone for glucocerebrosidase; it binds misfolded GCase, promotes its proper folding/trafficking to lysosomes, and facilitates substrate clearance, with reported neurological benefits in neuronopathic Gaucher disease and demonstrated blood–brain barrier penetration (Alhowyan & Harisa, 2025, pp. 17–18). Clinically observed improvements in neurological symptoms such as myoclonus and seizures have been reported in pilot studies, and reviews summarize safety/efficacy observations in Gaucher populations, albeit with the caveat of potential off-target toxicities innate to small-molecule approaches (Alhowyan & Harisa, 2025, pp. 17–18, 33–35).

Use in ophthalmology and AMD: A targeted search of ClinicalTrials.gov for ambroxol in macular degeneration, AMD, or retinal conditions returned zero registered trials, indicating a lack of clinical testing for ambroxol in AMD or retina-specific indications within that registry (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.). The provided literature excerpts contain no preclinical or clinical data demonstrating ambroxol use in RPE, retinal degeneration models, or AMD, and they do not report ocular distribution or ocular pharmacokinetics for ambroxol (Alhowyan & Harisa, 2025, pp. 17–18; Si et al., 2023, pp. 2–4; Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7). In contrast, other small-molecule interventions that modulate lysosomal/autophagy function in RPE have been reported: mTOR inhibition with rapamycin decreases A2E and lipofuscin-like granules and reduces inflammatory/angiogenic proteins; trehalose increases autophagy markers and flux and exhibits cytoprotective effects, although limitations in clinical efficacy and adverse effects are noted for mTOR inhibitors (Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7). More broadly, pharmacologic restoration of lysosomal pH and regulatory control of V-ATPase–mTORC1 signaling in RPE have been explored mechanistically, underscoring the translational target plausibility but not implicating ambroxol specifically (Kaarniranta et al., 2023, pp. 2–3; Markitantova & Simirskii, 2025, pp. 24–25).

Mechanism of Action  
Ambroxol as a pharmacological chaperone: Ambroxol binds selectively to misfolded glucocerebrosidase (GCase), stabilizing its conformation in the biosynthetic pathway and enabling correct trafficking to lysosomes, where it restores enzymatic degradation of GCase substrates (Alhowyan & Harisa, 2025, pp. 17–18). This canonical chaperone mechanism increases lysosomal GCase activity and substrate turnover and has been linked to functional improvements in Gaucher disease models and patient reports, with additional indications that ambroxol can enhance mitochondrial function in patient-derived cells (Alhowyan & Harisa, 2025, pp. 17–18). The drug’s small-molecule nature and CNS penetrance differentiate it from enzyme-replacement approaches and position it within a class of proteostasis-modulating agents where target-specific engagement can produce organelle-level functional rescue but also carries risk of off-target interactions (Alhowyan & Harisa, 2025, pp. 17–18).

RPE lysosomal biology relevant to the hypothesis: In the RPE, lysosomal acidification is primarily established by the V-ATPase proton pump and is essential for optimal activity of luminal hydrolases including cathepsins; most lysosomal enzymes are exquisitely pH-dependent and lose activity when lysosomal pH is elevated (Markitantova & Simirskii, 2025, pp. 9–11; Kaarniranta et al., 2023, pp. 2–3). RPE lysosomes operate at the nexus of two degradative streams: heterophagy of POS (requiring efficient phagosome–lysosome fusion and acidic hydrolase activity) and macroautophagy/CMA for damaged proteins and organelles, both of which are dysregulated with aging and AMD-relevant stresses such as oxidative damage and advanced glycation end-products (AGEs) (Si et al., 2023, pp. 4–5; Kaarniranta et al., 2023, pp. 2–3; Sharif, 2015, pp. 199–202). CTSD is a key RPE lysosomal aspartic protease and the principal POS-degrading enzyme; CTSD loss causes retinal degeneration in mice, underscoring its nonredundant role (Si et al., 2023, pp. 4–5). Finally, because impaired lysosomal clearance increases exosome release and contributes to drusen, measuring exosome markers and extracellular deposit proxies will be important to link intracellular rescue to extracellular AMD hallmarks, but ambroxol lacks such evidence here (Sharif, 2015, pp. 199–202; Grilo, 2014, pp. 42–46).

Programmatic recommendation and experimental path: At this stage, ambroxol should not advance directly to in vivo retinal studies or clinical exploration for dry AMD without foundational RPE data demonstrating lysosomal acidification rescue and CTSD activity enhancement under AMD-relevant stressors (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.). A rigorous, staged preclinical plan is warranted:  
- In vitro RPE assays under A2E and POS-fed conditions to quantify lysosomal pH, V-ATPase subunit expression (ATP6VOA1), TFEB nuclear translocation/CLEAR activation, CTSD maturation/activity, POS degradation kinetics, and lipofuscin-like autofluorescence, with rapamycin and trehalose as mechanistically validated comparators (Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7; Wang et al., 2023, pp. 11–13).  
- Lysosomal membrane integrity tests and CTSD leakage assessment in CFH Y402H RPE models to probe stabilization of lysosomal compartments under genetic risk backgrounds (Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 4–5).  
- Exosome marker release and extracellular deposit assays to link intracellular lysosomal rescue to drusen-relevant phenotypes (Grilo, 2014, pp. 42–46).  
- Ocular exposure assessment to confirm ambroxol reaches RPE at pharmacologically active concentrations using appropriate delivery routes; absent ocular PK data in the provided literature, this becomes a gating requirement (Alhowyan & Harisa, 2025, pp. 17–18).

Overall, ambroxol’s demonstrated chaperone activity for GCase, BBB penetration, and clinical observations in Gaucher disease establish it as a plausible proteostasis-modulating scaffold, but the lack of any RPE/AMD-directed mechanistic or efficacy evidence and the absence of ocular PK data create a high translational risk profile for dry AMD (Alhowyan & Harisa, 2025, pp. 17–18; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.). By contrast, interventions that directly activate TFEB or modulate mTOR have documented efficacy in RPE models, though clinical translation hurdles remain, and this suggests that ambroxol should be benchmarked against these pathways in a preclinical setting before any programmatic commitment (Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
SRT1720 is a first-generation synthetic small-molecule sirtuin 1 (SIRT1)–activating compound (STAC) originally discovered by high-throughput screening at Sirtris Pharmaceuticals and optimized around an imidazo[1,2-b]thiazole chemotype to yield higher apparent potency and selectivity than the natural product resveratrol in early assay systems (Chang et al., 2024; Mazzone, 2018). Subsequent mechanistic work across the STAC class resolved that many apparent activation signals were substrate/context dependent and, in some assay configurations, artifactual; nevertheless, later kinetic/biophysical and structural studies established that STACs can directly engage SIRT1 via an assisted allosteric mechanism that stabilizes the enzyme–substrate complex, with mutational data showing that E230K/A SIRT1 variants abolish both binding and activation by STACs (Lee et al., 2021; Mazzone, 2018). While most STACs are SIRT1-selective, SRT1720 exhibits notable polypharmacology, including reported inhibitory activity against Sirt3, highlighting potential off-target risks intrinsic to this first-generation class (Mazzone, 2018). As a class, STACs have been widely evaluated for metabolic, inflammatory, neurodegenerative, and aging phenotypes predicated on SIRT1’s broad substrate repertoire (for example, PGC-1α, NF-κB p65/RelA, FOXO family, p53), which link to mitochondrial biogenesis, anti-inflammatory signaling, oxidative stress responses, and cell survival programs (Chang et al., 2024; Mazzone, 2018).

Therapeutic History  
SRT1720 has extensive preclinical use, but there is no evidence in the provided corpus that it has been tested in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), in the eye, or in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) models (cellular or in vivo) (Ji et al., 2021; Ding et al., 2017; Bononi et al., 2022). In non-ocular systems, SRT1720 increased mitochondrial biogenesis and rescued mitochondrial function after oxidant injury in renal proximal tubule cells, providing proof-of-concept that STAC activation can drive PGC-1α–linked mitochondrial programs in mammalian cells under oxidative stress (Ji et al., 2021). In metabolic disease models, SRT1720 is reported to improve hepatic lipid metabolism via SIRT1-dependent pathways regulating PGC-1α, AMPK, PPARα, FOXO1, SREBP-1c and FGF21, with consistent decreases in lipogenesis and inflammation and increases in fatty-acid β-oxidation in NAFLD models (Ding et al., 2017). Multiple lifespan/healthspan studies reported benefits in mice—improved survival and healthspan in diet-induced obese animals and lifespan extension on standard diet—again consistent with systemic SIRT1-axis engagement (Mazzone, 2018). At the same time, substantial controversy surrounds both mechanism and safety. Pacholec et al. argued SRT1720 (and related first-generation STACs) are not direct SIRT1 activators under specific biochemical conditions, although later work provided structural and kinetic support for allosteric activation with specific substrates (Lee et al., 2021; Bononi et al., 2022). Importantly for repurposing risk, SRT1720 promoted tumor cell migration and lung metastasis in a breast cancer model, and SRT1720 can trigger SIRT1-independent cytotoxicity in some hematologic malignancy cells, underscoring unresolved off-target liabilities (Bononi et al., 2022; Chang et al., 2024). No pharmacokinetic (PK), ADME, or clinical tolerability data for SRT1720 are supplied in the present corpus; by contrast, the second-generation STAC SRT2104 has human PK/tolerability and multiple preclinical and clinical signals across diseases, including ocular/neurologic models (but those data cannot be extrapolated to SRT1720 without qualification) (Bononi et al., 2022; Chang et al., 2024). Collectively, the historical record supports that SRT1720 is a pharmacologically active first-generation STAC with broad preclinical use, mixed mechanistic interpretations, and safety concerns; critically, there is no published use in AMD or RPE models in the material provided here (Ji et al., 2021; Bononi et al., 2022).

Mechanism of Action  
- Biochemical pharmacology and target engagement: SRT1720 belongs to the STAC class that can directly activate SIRT1 through an assisted allosteric mechanism requiring specific substrate motifs; mutating SIRT1 E230 disrupts both activator binding and activation, and co-crystal structures of SIRT1 with SRT-like activators support an allosteric binding pocket that enhances deacetylation efficiency in a substrate-dependent manner (Lee et al., 2021; Mazzone, 2018). Early reports of direct activation were contested due to labeled peptide assay artifacts, but subsequent kinetic and structural data reconciled these findings with an allosteric model; nonetheless, the field recognizes pharmacological caveats including context-dependent activation and off-targets, such as reported Sirt3 inhibition by SRT1720 (Mazzone, 2018; Lee et al., 2021).  
- Canonical SIRT1 substrates and pathway biology: SIRT1 deacetylates transcriptional regulators and autophagy/mitophagy machinery that converge on mitochondrial quality control, oxidative stress defense, and inflammatory tone—each relevant to AMD pathogenesis. These include PGC-1α (mitochondrial biogenesis/oxidative metabolism), FOXO1/FOXO3a (antioxidant/autophagy transcription), NF-κB p65/RelA (inflammatory gene programs), p53 (apoptosis/senescence), and Nrf2 (antioxidant transcription), as well as autophagy proteins (e.g., ATG family members and LC3) and trafficking nodes such as Rab7 that promote autophagosome–lysosome fusion (Chang et al., 2024; Luján et al., 2022; Luo et al., 2025). In multiple cell types, SIRT1 activation or NAD⁺ elevation increases PGC-1α activity and mitochondrial biogenesis and can suppress NF-κB signaling via p65 deacetylation, consistent with anti-oxidative and anti-inflammatory effects that are therapeutically desirable in RPE (Ding et al., 2017; Luo et al., 2025).  
- RPE-specific SIRT1/autophagy linkage: In ARPE-19 cells under oxidative stress, PARP1 activation depletes NAD⁺, inhibits SIRT1 (elevated p53 acetylation), and selectively impairs late-stage autophagy by blocking autolysosome formation without preventing autophagosome formation; restoring NAD⁺ or inhibiting PARP1 preserves SIRT1 activity and rescues late autophagic flux, whereas PARP1 inhibition fails to rescue autophagy when SIRT1 is depleted—placing SIRT1 as the essential downstream effector for recovering autophagy in oxidatively stressed RPE (Jang et al., 2020). In vivo, PARP1 inhibition protected the retina in sodium iodate (SI) injury and the benefit was autophagy-dependent, reinforcing the PARP1→NAD⁺→SIRT1→autophagy axis as a mechanistic driver of RPE/retinal resilience (Jang et al., 2020). AMD donor RPE exhibits decreased NAD⁺, reduced SIRT1 levels, increased acetylated (inactive) PGC-1α, impaired AMPK signaling, and hyperactive mTOR—all changes expected to depress SIRT1-dependent autophagy and mitochondrial biogenesis and to contribute to lysosomal/autophagic abnormalities (Zhang et al., 2020).  
- TFEB/CLEAR and lysosomal acidification context: TFEB is the master transcription factor for lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy gene networks (CLEAR), whose nuclear translocation is negatively regulated by mTORC1; CLEAR target upregulation increases lysosomal capacity and flux, while lysosomal ion/pH homeostasis (v-ATPase–dependent proton pumping) determines enzyme activation, including cathepsins such as CTSD (Boya et al., 2023; Falcão et al., 2025; Kaarniranta et al., 2023). In AMD/RPE-relevant literature, TFEB/CLEAR is positioned as a principal lever for lysosomal rejuvenation, and lysosomal acidity and calcium handling are identified as key determinants of autophagic flux and RPE health (Boya et al., 2023). Although sirtuin family members can intersect TFEB signaling (e.g., AKT2/SIRT5/TFEB axis in non-neovascular AMD), direct evidence for SIRT1-driven TFEB deacetylation/activation is not provided in the present corpus; however, PGC-1α has been placed upstream of TFEB in other disease contexts, linking SIRT1→PGC-1α activity to potential TFEB–CLEAR induction by inference (not by direct RPE data) (Falcão et al., 2025).  
- Critical gaps relevant to the working hypothesis: Within the provided literature, there is no direct evidence that SRT1720 activates SIRT1 in RPE, no demonstration that SRT1720 promotes TFEB deacetylation or nuclear activation, and no reports that SRT1720 enhances lysosomal acidification or cathepsin D (CTSD) activity in RPE or AMD models; any such assertions remain unsubstantiated by the references supplied here (Ji et al., 2021; Mazzone, 2018; Kaarniranta et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2020). Therefore, while the SIRT1→autophagy/mitophagy rationale in RPE is strong, the specific mechanistic chain “SRT1720→SIRT1 activation in RPE→TFEB deacetylation→CLEAR upregulation→lysosomal acidification/CTSD enhancement” lacks direct experimental support in RPE/AMD contexts in these sources and should be treated as a testable, not established, hypothesis (Falcão et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2020).

Therapeutic biology of the disease target supports SIRT1 activation in RPE. Multiple AMD-relevant datasets show NAD⁺ depletion and SIRT1 downregulation in AMD RPE (primary donor-derived cultures and iPSC-RPE), accompanied by impaired PGC-1α activity, AMPK suppression, and mTOR hyperactivation, together with autophagy/lysosome structural and functional abnormalities; the PARP1-dependent late-autophagy block under oxidative stress in RPE is SIRT1-dependent for rescue, further bolstering SIRT1 as a target for restoring autophagic flux and organelle quality control (Zhang et al., 2020; Jang et al., 2020). However, these observations do not establish which pharmacologic SIRT1 activator is optimal for RPE/AMD, and they do not establish TFEB deacetylation as a SIRT1-dependent event in RPE (Jang et al., 2020; Falcão et al., 2025).

Therapeutic History in Related Ocular Systems (Class Precedent)  
Although direct SRT1720 ocular data are absent here, SRT2104—a second-generation STAC with improved specificity and exposure—shows SIRT1-linked protection in retinal ischemia/reperfusion and TNF-induced optic nerve injury, including deacetylation of canonical SIRT1 substrates (p53, NF-κB p65, STAT3), reduced apoptosis/inflammation, and induction of autophagy in optic nerve, which provides class-level ocular precedent that SIRT1 activation can be neuroprotective and autophagy-enhancing in the visual system (Chang et al., 2024). These results should not be extrapolated to SRT1720 without direct data, but they reinforce the biological plausibility that a STAC could benefit retinal tissues if target engagement and safety can be achieved (Chang et al., 2024).

Expected Effect  
The proposed assay hypothesis is that SRT1720 will activate SIRT1 in RPE, leading to TFEB deacetylation/activation, increased lysosomal acidification and CTSD activity, and improved clearance of photoreceptor outer segment (POS) material. Based on the literature provided here, the following expectations are reasonable and aligned with evidence, and several components are speculative:

- Supported expectations tied to SIRT1 biology in RPE:
  - If SRT1720 achieves bona fide SIRT1 activation and target engagement in RPE, it should decrease acetylation of canonical SIRT1 substrates (for example, p53 K382ac, p65 K310ac, PGC-1α), restore late-stage autophagic flux under oxidative stress, and enhance autophagosome–lysosome fusion, given the demonstrated requirement for SIRT1 to rescue late-stage autophagy in H₂O₂-stressed ARPE-19 cells (Jang et al., 2020; Luo et al., 2025).  
  - Biomarkers: recovery of p62 turnover, normalization of LC3-II/LC3-I dynamics in flux assays, increased autolysosome signal in tandem RFP-GFP-LC3 imaging, and potentially increased Rab7 activity/localization to autophagosomes are anticipated if SRT1720 strengthens late-stage autophagy via SIRT1 (Jang et al., 2020; Luján et al., 2022).  
  - Mitochondrial endpoints: increased PGC-1α deacetylation/activity and improved mitophagy markers (PINK1, Parkin induction) would be consistent with SIRT1 activation; SRT1720 has driven PGC-1α–dependent mitochondrial biogenesis after oxidant injury in renal cells, supporting feasibility of this axis in oxidatively stressed epithelia (Ji et al., 2021; Luján et al., 2022).  

- Plausible, but not demonstrated within the provided literature:
  - TFEB deacetylation/activation: the present corpus does not document SIRT1-dependent TFEB deacetylation or STAC-induced TFEB activation in RPE. TFEB/CLEAR is a validated master lysosomal program, and PGC-1α can lie upstream of TFEB in other disease contexts, so an indirect route “SIRT1→PGC-1α→TFEB→CLEAR” is biologically plausible but remains unproven in RPE here and should be tested directly (Falcão et al., 2025).  
  - Lysosomal acidification and CTSD activity: lysosomal pH and hydrolase activation are central to RPE proteostasis and AMD; however, no experiment in the supplied sources demonstrates that SRT1720 or any STAC increases lysosomal acidification or CTSD activity in RPE. These readouts (e.g., LysoTracker/LysoSensor ratio, DQ-BSA, cathepsin activity assays) should be considered exploratory endpoints for SRT1720, not expected outcomes (Boya et al., 2023; Kaarniranta et al., 2023).  
  - LAMP2 expression: likewise, no provided reference shows SRT1720 increasing LAMP2 in RPE. While CLEAR activation generally elevates lysosomal genes (e.g., LAMP family, cathepsins), this requires evidence of TFEB activation in the same system and has not been shown for SRT1720 in RPE in the available literature (Boya et al., 2023; Falcão et al., 2025).  

- Target presence/assay feasibility:
  - SIRT1 is expressed in human RPE and is reduced in AMD donor RPE and AMD iPSC-RPE models, with associated increases in acetylated PGC-1α and deficits in mitochondrial/autophagic programs, confirming the presence of the pharmacological target and a disease-relevant deficit that SIRT1 activation could address (Golestaneh et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2020).  
  - The disease cell biology is well-aligned with a SIRT1-centric intervention: in RPE, autophagy and phagocytic digestion converge on lysosomes to clear POS; impaired lysosomal enzyme activity and acidification reduce flux and increase oxidative stress and protein/organelle damage—phenotypes linked to AMD and to which SIRT1’s autophagy/mitophagy-promoting actions are mechanistically relevant (Kaarniranta et al., 2023; Boya et al., 2023).

Overall Evaluation  
On balance, the therapeutic rationale “activate SIRT1 to restore autophagy/mitophagy and lysosomal competence in RPE for dry AMD” is well-supported by AMD-relevant cell biology and human donor data; however, the specific choice of SRT1720 has substantial evidentiary and safety gaps relative to alternatives in the STAC space, and the asserted TFEB/lysosome mechanistic specifics are not demonstrated in the provided literature.

Strengths  
- Strong target biology and disease alignment in RPE and AMD: Multiple independent datasets demonstrate that AMD RPE exhibit decreased NAD⁺, reduced SIRT1, increased acetylated PGC-1α, impaired AMPK signaling, and mTOR hyperactivity concurrent with autophagy/lysosomal abnormalities, which together point to an actionable SIRT1 deficit in AMD pathology (Zhang et al., 2020; Jang et al., 2020). In oxidatively stressed ARPE-19 cells and an SI mouse model, preserving NAD⁺ and thereby SIRT1 activity was necessary and sufficient to rescue late-stage autophagy and protect retina, placing SIRT1 centrally in autophagy restoration and retinal resilience (Jang et al., 2020).  
- Class-level ocular precedent for SIRT1 activation: SRT2104, a later-generation STAC with better drug-like properties, increases SIRT1 activity in retina/optic nerve, promotes SIRT1-mediated deacetylation of p53, NF-κB p65, and STAT3, reduces apoptosis/inflammation, and upregulates autophagy in optic nerve, establishing that STAC-mediated SIRT1 activation can be protective and autophagy-enhancing in ocular tissues (Chang et al., 2024).  
- Mitochondrial stress/biogenesis axis engagement by SRT1720: In non-ocular epithelia, SRT1720 induces PGC-1α–dependent mitochondrial biogenesis and rescues function after oxidant injury, a desirable capability for stressed RPE; SRT1720 also modulates metabolic signaling via SIRT1–PGC-1α/AMPK/PPARα/FOXO1 pathways, consistent with correcting mitochondrial oxidative metabolism defects that characterize AMD RPE (Ji et al., 2021; Ding et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2020).  
- Therapeutic tractability of lysosome/autophagy endpoints: TFEB/CLEAR biology, lysosomal acidification, and cathepsin function are well-defined levers in RPE; measuring autophagic flux (LC3, p62, RFP-GFP-LC3), lysosomal pH (LysoSensor), and hydrolase activity (e.g., CTSD) is straightforward and interpretable in RPE assays, enabling rapid validation of the hypothesis in vitro (Boya et al., 2023; Kaarniranta et al., 2023).

Weaknesses and Risks  
- Absence of direct RPE/AMD data for SRT1720: No provided reference shows SRT1720 engaging SIRT1 in RPE, improving autophagic flux in RPE, activating TFEB/CLEAR in RPE, or enhancing lysosomal acidification/CTSD activity in RPE or AMD-like models. The core elements of the hypothesis (TFEB deacetylation and CLEAR induction by SRT1720 in RPE) are not documented here and require de novo demonstration (Ji et al., 2021; Falcão et al., 2025; Kaarniranta et al., 2023).  
- Mechanistic controversy and off-targets: The STAC field’s historical assay artifacts, substrate dependence, and the assisted allosteric mechanism place a premium on rigorous target engagement readouts in the specific cellular context; SRT1720 additionally shows Sirt3 inhibitory activity and has been associated with SIRT1-independent cytotoxicity in certain cells, complicating mechanistic attribution (Mazzone, 2018; Chang et al., 2024).  
- Safety signal: SRT1720 increased tumor cell migration and metastasis in a breast cancer mouse model; while AMD is not a malignancy, a pro-migratory/pro-metastatic signal raises a red flag for systemic exposure and suggests careful ocular delivery strategies and off-target profiling if pursued (Bononi et al., 2022; Mazzone, 2018).  
- Lack of PK/ADME and clinical data for SRT1720 in this corpus: Unlike SRT2104, which has human PK/tolerability data and CNS/retinal preclinical activity, SRT1720 lacks disclosed PK/ADME and clinical reports here, hindering translational assessment and dose/exposure design for ocular studies (Bononi et al., 2022; Chang et al., 2024).  
- TFEB/lysosome-specific uncertainty: While CLEAR network activation and lysosomal acidification are compelling RPE targets, the present sources do not show SIRT1-dependent TFEB deacetylation in RPE, nor do they link STACs to lysosomal pH regulation or CTSD activation in RPE; asserting this mechanism is premature without experimental support (Falcão et al., 2025; Boya et al., 2023; Kaarniranta et al., 2023).

Recommendation and Development Path  
- Scientific merit: Pursuing SIRT1 activation to normalize late-stage autophagy and mitochondrial quality control in RPE is well-justified by the PARP1→NAD⁺→SIRT1 axis in RPE and AMD donor biology; however, SRT1720 is not, on current evidence, the optimal first-in-class molecule to test this hypothesis in RPE (Jang et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2020).  
- Prioritization: If the team’s objective is target validation, consider tool-compound triage: compare SRT1720 with a second-generation clinical-stage STAC (SRT2104) and with an orthogonal approach that is known to restore SIRT1 activity in RPE (e.g., NAD⁺ boosting) in parallel RPE assays, using target-engagement and autophagy/lysosome endpoints defined a priori (Chang et al., 2024; Jang et al., 2020).  
- Minimal dataset to proceed (go/no-go):  
  1) Demonstrate SIRT1 activation in human RPE by SRT1720 at non-toxic concentrations via decreased acetyl-p53 (K382), decreased acetyl-PGC-1α, and decreased acetyl-p65 (K310), with rescue by SIRT1 knockdown or a SIRT1-dead mutant to confirm on-target action (Luo et al., 2025; Jang et al., 2020).  
  2) Show restoration of late-stage autophagy under H₂O₂ or A2E stress: increased autolysosome formation in tandem RFP-GFP-LC3, decreased p62, and restored LC3-II flux in the presence/absence of lysosomal inhibitors; confirm loss of effect with SIRT1 knockdown (Jang et al., 2020).  
  3) Test TFEB/CLEAR explicitly: TFEB nuclear translocation, TFEB transcriptional reporter, and CLEAR target induction (e.g., LAMP2 and CTSD mRNA/protein) with and without mTORC1 modulation; test necessity of SIRT1 by knockdown and sufficiency by PGC-1α gain-of-function to probe the SIRT1→PGC-1α→TFEB chain (Boya et al., 2023; Falcão et al., 2025).  
  4) Quantify lysosomal acidification and hydrolase activity: LysoSensor/LysoTracker measurements and CTSD activity assays; relate outcomes to TFEB activation and to autophagic flux to determine whether SRT1720 enhances lysosomal function or acts predominantly on pre-lysosomal steps (Kaarniranta et al., 2023; Boya et al., 2023).  
  5) Evaluate mitophagy and mitochondrial function: PINK1/Parkin recruitment, mt-Keima flux, mitochondrial respiration/ATP, and ROS after SRT1720 in stressed RPE to connect SIRT1–PGC-1α engagement to mitochondrial quality control (Kaarniranta et al., 2023; Luján et al., 2022).  
  6) Safety pharmacology in RPE: assess proliferation/migration, EMT markers, and off-target sirtuin activity (Sirt3) to de-risk pro-migratory liabilities observed in cancer models (Bononi et al., 2022; Mazzone, 2018).  

- If SRT1720 fails to deliver on TFEB/CLEAR and lysosomal pH/hydrolase endpoints but still rescues late-stage autophagic flux, the program can pivot to an autophagy-centric mechanism of action (MoA) without TFEB claims; conversely, if TFEB/CLEAR induction is robust, the candidate may differentiate from mTOR inhibitors via epigenetic/cofactor-driven CLEAR activation, contingent on confirming SIRT1 dependency (Boya et al., 2023; Falcão et al., 2025).  
- For in vivo progression, the SI model used to establish PARP1→SIRT1/autophagy dependency provides a tractable retinal degeneration context, but ocular delivery and safety (especially with first-generation STACs) will require localized dosing strategies (intravitreal/subretinal) and careful dosing to minimize systemic exposure (Jang et al., 2020).

Bottom Line  
- The hypothesis that SRT1720 can correct RPE proteostasis in dry AMD via SIRT1 activation is mechanistically credible with respect to autophagy/mitophagy restoration, but the specific claims of TFEB deacetylation, CLEAR network activation, and enhancement of lysosomal acidification/CTSD activity by SRT1720 in RPE are not supported by the present literature and must be treated as untested (Jang et al., 2020; Falcão et al., 2025; Boya et al., 2023).  
- Given the safety concerns and off-target profile of SRT1720, and the existence of a later-generation STAC (SRT2104) with human PK and ocular neuroprotection, SRT1720 should not be advanced beyond in vitro RPE validation until it demonstrates clear, on-target superiority in RPE assays and acceptable safety margins; otherwise, the team should prioritize either SRT2104 or NAD⁺ augmentation/PARP1 modulation for translational efforts (Chang et al., 2024; Bononi et al., 2022; Jang et al., 2020).  

Summary assessment  
- Pros: Strong disease–target alignment in RPE; robust class biology for SIRT1-driven autophagy/mitophagy; SRT1720 can activate SIRT1 pathways in other oxidative-stress contexts; feasible, discriminating assays exist to test the MoA (Zhang et al., 2020; Jang et al., 2020; Ji et al., 2021; Boya et al., 2023).  
- Cons: No direct evidence of efficacy/mechanism in RPE; TFEB/lysosome mechanistic claims unsupported; safety/off-target risks; no PK/clinical data in this corpus; better-characterized STAC alternatives exist (Falcão et al., 2025; Bononi et al., 2022; Chang et al., 2024).  

Decision guidance: Proceed with a narrowly scoped, mechanism-first in vitro validation of SRT1720 in human RPE focused on SIRT1 target engagement and late-stage autophagy rescue under oxidative/phagolysosomal stress, with explicit tests for TFEB/CLEAR activation and lysosomal acidification/CTSD activity; in parallel, benchmark against SRT2104 and NAD⁺ repletion, and use pre-specified go/no-go criteria tied to on-target mechanistic readouts and safety signals to decide whether SRT1720 merits in vivo exploration in retinal degeneration models (Jang et al., 2020; Chang et al., 2024; Boya et al., 2023).
