This reactive electrophilic center enables the compound to covalently modify nucleophilic cysteine residues on target proteins. Early studies identified BAY 11-7082 for its capacity to inhibit NF-κB signaling in endothelial cells, and subsequent research expanded its profile to include inhibition of the NLRP3 inflammasome via cysteine alkylation of critical regulatory sites. In essence, BAY 11-7082 belongs to the class of covalent inhibitors that have been widely studied in the context of inflammatory and oncologic diseases, and its availability as Sigma B5556 has made it a common tool compound in preclinical research (Juliana et al., 2010; Marchetti, 2019; Yu et al., 2018).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, BAY 11-7082 has been utilized extensively in biochemical, cellular, and animal studies as an anti-inflammatory agent. Initial applications centered on its ability to block the phosphorylation and degradation of IκBα, thereby inhibiting downstream NF-κB–driven gene expression. This mechanism was exploited in models of endothelial inflammation and various cancer cell lines, including studies showing potent anticancer, neuroprotective, and anti-inflammatory effects (Lee et al., 2012; Melisi & Chiao, 2007). Furthermore, its repurposing has been explored in fields as diverse as hematologic malignancies, diabetes-related complications, and preclinical psoriasis models, where it served as a dual inhibitor of NF-κB and the NLRP3 inflammasome (Irrera et al., 2017; Kolati et al., 2015). Despite this broad research history, BAY 11-7082 has not been previously tested explicitly in the context of dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or diseases with a similar pathology in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE). However, its known capacity to reduce inflammatory cytokine production and preserve lysosomal integrity in nonocular cell types provides a rationale for evaluating its potential utility in dry AMD—a disease characterized by chronic inflammation, impaired lysosomal clearance, and inflammasome activation (Blevins et al., 2022; Irrera et al., 2017; Marchetti, 2019).

Mechanism of Action:  
BAY 11-7082 exerts its pharmacological effects predominantly through irreversible covalent inhibition. Its most well‐characterized mechanism is the blockade of NF-κB signaling by preventing the phosphorylation of the inhibitory protein IκBα. Under normal conditions, phosphorylation of IκBα triggers its degradation, thus allowing NF-κB (typically the p65/p50 heterodimer) to translocate into the nucleus and activate pro-inflammatory target genes. By inhibiting IκBα phosphorylation, BAY 11-7082 effectively sequesters NF-κB in the cytosol, thereby suppressing the expression of genes associated with inflammation such as IL-1β, TNF-α, and various chemokines (Marchetti, 2019; Melisi & Chiao, 2007).  

Moreover, BAY 11-7082 has been repurposed based on its ability to inhibit the NLRP3 inflammasome. Mechanistically, the compound forms covalent adducts with reactive cysteine residues on the NLRP3 protein, most likely within the ATPase domain—an essential activity domain required for inflammasome activation. This alkylation event, which proceeds via a Michael-type addition reaction, results in irreversible inactivation of NLRP3’s ATPase function, thereby preventing the assembly and subsequent activation of the inflammasome complex (Cocco et al., 2014; Juliana et al., 2010; Marchetti, 2019). In addition to these primary actions, BAY 11-7082 has been reported to inhibit other cysteine-dependent enzymes such as protein tyrosine phosphatases and even components like gasdermin D that contribute to pyroptosis. Consequently, the compound displays a broad-spectrum inhibitory profile that may diminish inflammatory cascades not only at the transcriptional (NF-κB) level but also at the inflammasome activation stage (Yu et al., 2018; Zahid et al., 2019).  

Expected Effect in Dry Age-Related Macular Degeneration:  
In the context of dry AMD, the hypothesis is that chronic inflammation in the RPE drives cellular dysfunction through mechanisms that include sustained NF-κB activation and priming of the NLRP3 inflammasome. Inflammatory cytokines and resultant oxidative stress contribute to lysosomal impairment, reducing the activity of v-ATPase and lysosomal proteases such as cathepsin D (CTSD), which are crucial for the clearance of cellular debris. BAY 11-7082 is expected to intervene at an early stage in this inflammatory cascade by inhibiting NF-κB signaling. In doing so, it would reduce the transcriptional upregulation of inflammasome components and pro-inflammatory cytokines, particularly IL-1β, a key mediator in inflammasome activation (Blevins et al., 2022; Marchetti, 2019).  

Experimental studies in macrophages and psoriasis models have demonstrated that NF-κB inhibition with BAY 11-7082 leads to a reduction in IL-1β production and preserves lysosomal integrity. Although these studies were conducted in nonocular tissues, the expression of NF-κB and NLRP3 inflammasome components in RPE cells is well-documented in the literature. Therefore, it is reasonable to propose that BAY 11-7082, when applied to RPE cell models, could diminish the priming of the NLRP3 inflammasome. This reduction in inflammasome activity is expected to mitigate downstream lysosomal damage, preserve v-ATPase function, and maintain cathepsin D–mediated clearance. Ultimately, these cellular improvements could slow the degenerative progression characteristic of dry AMD (Cocco et al., 2014; Irrera et al., 2017).  

The proposed testing strategy leverages the rapid on–off pharmacology observed in cell culture models, facilitating dose optimization to achieve sufficient anti-inflammatory activity while minimizing potential toxicity. Importantly, targeting an upstream event, namely NF-κB activation and inflammasome priming, distinguishes BAY 11-7082 from therapeutic strategies that focus on downstream caspase inhibition. In retinal cells, preservation of lysosomal function is critical; thus, preventing inflammasome-triggered lysosomal rupture could have a marked protective effect on RPE health (Ajetunmobi et al., 2023; Zahid et al., 2019).

Overall Evaluation:  
BAY 11-7082 presents a compelling therapeutic candidate for dry AMD based on its dual mechanism of action. One of its primary strengths is that it targets two key upstream pathways—inhibition of NF-κB signaling and direct inactivation of the NLRP3 inflammasome—which are critically implicated in the inflammatory processes that drive RPE dysfunction and subsequent retinal degeneration in dry AMD. This upstream intervention could, in theory, reduce the chronic production of pro-inflammatory cytokines and prevent lysosomal abnormalities that compromise the clearance of metabolic waste in RPE cells. The promising preclinical data from psoriasis, diabetic nephropathy, and other inflammatory disease models provide an encouraging foundation regarding its anti-inflammatory capacity (Blevins et al., 2022; Irrera et al., 2017; Marchetti, 2019).

However, there are several potential weaknesses and challenges to consider. First, BAY 11-7082 operates via irreversible covalent binding through its Michael acceptor; while this can yield sustained inhibition, it also raises significant concerns regarding off-target effects and general toxicity due to the potential for nonselective alkylation of other cysteine-containing proteins. Such promiscuous reactivity has been observed in studies involving diverse cell types, and cellular toxicity in contexts such as platelets or myeloma cells has been reported, albeit at higher concentrations (Coles et al., 2021; Paul et al., 2017; Rauert-Wunderlich et al., 2013). Second, although extensive preclinical data exist demonstrating its anti-inflammatory and anti-cancer activity, BAY 11-7082 has not been previously evaluated in ocular tissues. The unique physiology of the eye, particularly the retinal pigment epithelium, could result in significantly different pharmacokinetics and tissue-specific toxicity profiles. The documented rapid on–off pharmacology in cell culture is encouraging, yet extrapolation to an in vivo retinal environment must be approached cautiously (Paul et al., 2017; Zahid et al., 2019).  

Another consideration is the narrow therapeutic window that may exist; while doses in animal models have been optimized for systemic inflammation or cancer, achieving effective local concentrations in the RPE without compromising cell viability is a delicate balance. Previous studies in nonocular systems suggest that BAY 11-7082 can function without overt toxicity at concentrations up to 20 μM in cell culture and 20 mg/kg/day in animal models, but whether similar dosing regimens would be applicable for ocular delivery remains to be determined (Mabuchi et al., 2004; Paul et al., 2017). Additionally, because BAY 11-7082 modulates ubiquitin system components beyond NF-κB and NLRP3 inflammasome targets, there is a risk of unintended interference with normal protein turnover and cellular homeostasis, potentially exacerbating cellular stress in a tissue already vulnerable to degenerative processes, as seen in dry AMD (Coles et al., 2021; Strickson et al., 2013).

In summary, BAY 11-7082 shows promise as a candidate repurposed for dry AMD because it strategically targets early inflammatory events that have been implicated in RPE dysfunction, including NF-κB–mediated inflammasome priming and consequent lysosomal impairment. The compound’s established anti-inflammatory effects in various preclinical models lend strong support to the hypothesis that its use in RPE could preserve lysosomal function and enhance CTSD-mediated clearance. Nonetheless, the inherent risks associated with its covalent, irreversible mechanism demand rigorous ocular-specific toxicity and pharmacokinetics investigations. If dose optimization and targeted delivery—perhaps through localized ocular formulations—can mitigate off-target effects, BAY 11-7082 might offer a novel approach that differentiates itself from therapies focused solely on downstream caspase inhibition. Overall, while the repurposing of BAY 11-7082 for dry AMD is mechanistically attractive and supported by a broad preclinical research history in nonocular inflammatory models (Blevins et al., 2022; Irrera et al., 2017; Marchetti, 2019), further dedicated studies in retinal cell models and in vivo ocular systems are essential to fully validate its potential and safety profile for this indication.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
ML-SA1 is a synthetic, cell-permeable small-molecule agonist of the endolysosomal mucolipin/TRPML family, with primary pharmacological activity at TRPML1, the Ca2+-permeable cation channel encoded by MCOLN1 that resides on late endosome/lysosome membranes and mediates lysosomal Ca2+ efflux into the cytosol (Wang et al., 2023). ML-SA1 and chemically related “ML-SA” agonists emerged from small-molecule discovery programs aimed at pharmacologically restoring TRPML1 function; the compound is frequently referred to in the literature as “mucolipin synthetic agonist 1,” reflecting its origin as a tool compound class designed to activate TRPML channels rather than as a derivative of a natural product scaffold (Yan et al., 2021). Although the chemical structure and synthetic route for ML-SA1 are not detailed in the cited records, its provenance traces to a specialized small-molecule therapeutics effort at Calporta Therapeutics, a company subsequently acquired by Merck in 2019, signaling substantial translational interest in TRPML1 agonism for lysosomal storage and neurodegenerative disorders (Van Acker et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2023).

Functionally, ML-SA1 belongs to the broader class of TRPML1 agonists/activators that includes endogenous lipid ligands such as phosphatidylinositol-3,5-bisphosphate, PI(3,5)P2, and other synthetic small molecules (e.g., SF-22, MK6-83, and newer ML-SA chemotypes like ML-SA5), all of which gate TRPML channels to increase endolysosomal Ca2+ release (Wang et al., 2023; Más Gómez et al., 2018; Wünkhaus et al., 2024). Within this class, ML-SA1 is reported to activate TRPML1 with potency comparable to or greater than the endogenous PI(3,5)P2 under certain conditions and can act in conjunction with PI(3,5)P2 to potentiate channel opening, thereby rescuing endo-lysosomal morphology and function in cellular disease models that exhibit lysosomal stress (e.g., after PIKfyve inhibition) (Wang et al., 2023). Across preclinical research, TRPML1 agonists have been deployed as mechanistic probes and candidate therapeutics to restore lysosomal Ca2+ signaling, normalize lysosomal pH/acidification, promote autophagosome maturation and autolysosome formation, enhance lysosomal exocytosis, and induce TFEB-dependent lysosomal biogenesis in lysosomal storage and neurodegeneration models (Tedeschi et al., 2025; Pollmanns et al., 2022).

In ocular systems directly relevant to retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) biology, ML-SA1 has been used to interrogate TRPML1 function. In mouse primary RPE, human embryonic stem cell–derived RPE (hesRPE), and ARPE-19 cells, ML-SA1 produced rapid, robust, reversible increases in cytosolic Ca2+ that persisted in Ca2+-free external solutions and were blunted by lysosomal disruption, indicating a lysosomal Ca2+ source (Más Gómez et al., 2018). Critically, ML-SA1 failed to evoke Ca2+ signals in RPE from TRPML1 knockout mice, confirming channel specificity in this tissue (Más Gómez et al., 2018). The same study demonstrated that lysosomal lipid accumulation—induced pharmacologically or present in disease models—impairs ML-SA1-evoked TRPML1 Ca2+ release, mechanistically linking lysosomal lipidization to diminished TRPML1 function in RPE (Más Gómez et al., 2018). These data situate ML-SA1 squarely within a mechanistic toolkit for modulating RPE lysosomal physiology implicated in retinal degenerations associated with lipid/lipofuscin accrual (Más Gómez et al., 2018).

Therapeutic History  
There is no record in the provided corpus of ML-SA1 being used clinically in humans or specifically in trials for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or geographic atrophy (GA) (Más Gómez et al., 2018). However, extensive preclinical use across cell and animal models supports the biological rationale relevant to dry AMD. In RPE systems, ML-SA1 has been applied acutely to evoke TRPML1-dependent lysosomal Ca2+ release as described above (Más Gómez et al., 2018). In vivo, subretinal ML-SA1 administration in a rat retinal detachment model preserved outer nuclear layer thickness, reduced photoreceptor apoptosis, lessened cleaved caspase-3, increased autophagy markers (LC3-II/LC3-I and Beclin-1), decreased reactive oxygen species (ROS), and prevented TRPML1 degradation, collectively demonstrating functional rescue via autophagy activation and oxidative stress mitigation in injured retina (Yan et al., 2021).

Beyond the eye, multiple studies in neuronal and disease-model systems have used ML-SA1 to correct lysosomal/autophagy defects and proteostasis. In cultured neurons and HEK293T cells, ML-SA1 enhanced maturation of autophagosomes into acidic autolysosomes and reduced α-synuclein accumulation/aggregates; ML-SA1 could override bafilomycin-induced fusion/acidification blocks in both HEK293T cells and neurons, and these effects required lysosomal PI(3,5)P2 and cytosolic Ca2+ consistent with TRPML1 channel gating (Pollmanns et al., 2022). In primary cortical neurons, ML-SA1 rapidly acidified endolysosomes and prevented LDL-induced amyloidogenesis by reducing Aβ and BACE1 mislocalization/activity; TRPML1 knockdown abrogated ML-SA1’s effects and exacerbated LDL-driven Aβ production (Hui et al., 2019). In lysosomal storage disease (LSD) contexts, ML-SA1 was used as a TRPML1 activator to elicit lysosomal Ca2+ release responses that were impaired in Niemann–Pick type C (NPC1) patient fibroblasts; BK channel activation partially rescued the reduced ML-SA1 response, and BK upregulation lowered lipofuscin accumulation via lysosomal exocytosis, establishing pharmacological synergies that might be exploited in lipid storage states (Zhong et al., 2016).

Importantly for RPE-relevant lysosomal storage phenotypes, the more potent TRPML1 agonist ML-SA5 was used in ARPE-19 CLN3-knockout cells (a juvenile neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis model) to reduce lysosomal accumulation of subunit C of mitochondrial ATPase (SubC), Gb3, and lysosomal glycerophosphodiesters, accompanied by TFEB nuclear translocation and increased surface LAMP1 consistent with enhanced lysosomal exocytosis; however, BMP/LBPA lipid deficits and maturation of cathepsin D (CatD) and TPP1 remained impaired, indicating incomplete restoration of lysosomal hydrolase processing (Wünkhaus et al., 2024; Unknown Reference). Patch-clamp experiments in these cells confirmed that ML-SA1 variants evoke TRPML1 currents fully blocked by the antagonist ML-SI3, supporting pharmacological specificity in RPE lysosomes (Unknown Reference). The class of TRPML1 agonists (including ML-SA1) is being investigated preclinically for lysosomal storage and neurodegenerative indications, reinforcing translational plausibility even in the absence of AMD-specific studies (Wang et al., 2023).

Mechanism of Action  
TRPML1 is a lysosomal six-transmembrane TRP superfamily channel permeable to Ca2+ and other cations that localizes primarily to late endosomal/lysosomal membranes via cytosolic dileucine motifs, where it mediates lumen-to-cytosol ion efflux in response to endogenous and pharmacological gating (Wang et al., 2023; Unknown Reference). Physiological activation is conferred by the late endosomal/lysosomal phosphoinositide PI(3,5)P2, whose 3′ phosphate directly stabilizes an open-channel conformation; PI(4,5)P2 acts as an antagonist enriched at the plasma membrane, ensuring compartmental specificity (Wang et al., 2023). TRPML1-dependent lysosomal Ca2+ release acts as a master regulator of lysosomal/autophagic homeostasis via several calcium-sensitive effectors: calcineurin dephosphorylates TFEB to drive its nuclear translocation and induce the CLEAR network (lysosomal biogenesis and function genes), whereas CaMKKβ activation promotes autophagosome biogenesis; additional roles include regulation of vesicle trafficking, membrane fusion/fission, lysosomal reformation, exocytosis, and mitochondria–lysosome contacts (Wang et al., 2023; Tedeschi et al., 2025; Unknown Reference).

ML-SA1 is a synthetic agonist that binds TRPML channels and increases channel open probability, functionally mimicking or synergizing with PI(3,5)P2 to produce lysosomal Ca2+ efflux (Wang et al., 2023). In multiple cell systems, ML-SA1 triggers rapid lysosomal Ca2+ release measured by cytosolic Ca2+ reporters and genetically encoded TRPML1-proximal indicators; responses are abolished or blunted by TRPML1 gene knockout, lysosomal rupture, or pharmacological inhibitors, confirming that cytosolic Ca2+ rises originate from lysosomes through TRPML1 (Más Gómez et al., 2018). In RPE cells, ML-SA1-evoked Ca2+ signals were insensitive to extracellular Ca2+ removal and ER Ca2+ depletion with thapsigargin, but were eliminated by lysosomal disruption with GPN and absent in TRPML1−/− RPE, demonstrating the specificity and lysosomal source in the cell type of interest (Más Gómez et al., 2018).

Downstream of TRPML1 activation, ML-SA1 drives a coordinated set of lysosome-centric responses:  
- Autophagosome–lysosome fusion and maturation: ML-SA1 increases conversion of LC3-positive autophagosomes into acidic autolysosomes and shifts cargo (e.g., α-synuclein) into LAMP1-positive, acidified vesicles; notably, ML-SA1 can partially override bafilomycin A1 blocks on fusion/acidification, consistent with a Ca2+-dependent maturation/fusion mechanism (Pollmanns et al., 2022).  
- Lysosomal acidification: In primary neurons, ML-SA1 rapidly acidifies endolysosomes in a TRPML1-dependent manner, coincident with reduced LDL-induced amyloidogenesis and BACE1 localization/activity in endolysosomes (Hui et al., 2019).  
- TFEB signaling and lysosomal biogenesis/exocytosis: TRPML1 activation promotes TFEB nuclear translocation and transcription of lysosomal/autophagy genes; in ARPE-19 CLN3-KO cells, ML-SA5 triggered TFEB translocation and increased surface LAMP1 within 90 minutes, consistent with enhanced lysosomal exocytosis, and reduced lysosomal glycerophosphodiester loads (Tedeschi et al., 2025; Wünkhaus et al., 2024).  
- Proteostasis correction: ML-SA1 reduces α-synuclein protein/aggregates in cell models by steering cargo into maturing autolysosomes and promoting degradative flux; these effects require autophagy, PI(3,5)P2, and cytosolic Ca2+, aligning with TRPML1’s canonical signaling dependencies (Pollmanns et al., 2022).  
- Neuroprotection via autophagy induction and oxidative stress reduction: In vivo in retinal detachment, subretinal ML-SA1 increased LC3-II/LC3-I and Beclin-1, reduced cleaved caspase-3, decreased ROS, preserved photoreceptors, and prevented injury-induced TRPML1 degradation (Yan et al., 2021).

First, lysosomal lipid accumulation impairs TRPML1 function in RPE: desipramine (ASM inhibition), PIKfyve inhibition (YM201636), and chloroquine/U18666A-induced neutral lipid/lipofuscin models decreased ML-SA1–evoked Ca2+ release without reducing TRPML1 mRNA or total lysosomal Ca2+, indicating functional channel inhibition by lipidized lysosomal membranes—an AMD-relevant condition (Más Gómez et al., 2018). Second, in CLN3-deficient RPE, TRPML1 activation improved substrate clearance and TFEB signaling but did not restore the mature, active forms of CatD and TPP1 despite increased transcripts and precursor/intermediate protein levels, pointing to persistent hydrolase processing defects not corrected by TRPML1 agonism alone (Unknown Reference). These observations suggest that while ML-SA1 should restore key steps (Ca2+ efflux, fusion/acidification, TFEB), lysosomal lipid environments typical of aged RPE may constrain efficacy, and hydrolase maturation deficits—if present in AMD—may not normalize solely via TRPML1 activation (Más Gómez et al., 2018; Unknown Reference).

In retinal tissue in vivo (detachment model), TRPML1 activation promoted autolysosome formation by EM and upregulated LC3-II/LC3-I and Beclin-1, consistent with increased degradative flux (Yan et al., 2021).

4) Enhancement of degradative capacity and cargo clearance. By accelerating fusion and acidification, ML-SA1 should facilitate catabolic processing of outer segment phagosomes and lipoprotein-like cargoes that contribute to drusen precursors; in RPE knockout models of TRPML1, basal autofluorescence increases, supporting a role for TRPML1 in handling autofluorescent material, and ML-SA1-evoked TRPML1 activity is diminished by lysosomal lipid accumulation typical of aged RPE, highlighting both the therapeutic rationale and a potential barrier (Más Gómez et al., 2018; Wünkhaus et al., 2024; Unknown Reference).

Mechanistic uncertainties relevant to the hypothesis include the extent to which ML-SA1 will normalize hydrolase maturation (and consequently proteolysis) in aged or AMD RPE, given the CLN3-KO observation that mature CatD and TPP1 were not restored despite TFEB activation; while acidification generally supports protease activity, direct evidence of increased CatD activity post-TRPML1 activation in RPE is not provided here, and in CLN3-KO the maturation block persisted (Unknown Reference). Nevertheless, the acidic shift and fusion acceleration documented with ML-SA1 in neurons and the autophagy induction in retina argue for improved lysosomal degradative competence, which, together with increased exocytosis, should reduce accumulation of drusen precursors, albeit potentially incompletely if hydrolase processing bottlenecks remain (Hui et al., 2019; Yan et al., 2021; Wünkhaus et al., 2024).

Two context-specific modifiers should be anticipated:  
- Lysosomal lipid load: ML-SA1 responses are blunted by lysosomal lipid accumulation in RPE; thus, efficacy in dry AMD may require co-strategies that reduce lysosomal lipid burden or potentiate TRPML1 gating under lipidized conditions (e.g., via synergistic endogenous PI(3,5)P2, or adjuncts such as BK channel activators shown to enhance ML-SA1 responses in lipid storage contexts) (Más Gómez et al., 2018; Zhong et al., 2016).  
- TRPML isoform engagement: ML-SA1 can activate TRPML3 under certain expression conditions; while TRPML3’s role in RPE is less defined, off-target TRPML3 activation may modulate lysosomal transport and ion fluxes, warranting selectivity profiling in RPE (Unknown Reference).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Direct target validation in RPE: ML-SA1 elicits TRPML1-dependent lysosomal Ca2+ release in primary mouse RPE, hesRPE, and ARPE-19 cells, with responses absent in TRPML1−/− RPE and abolished by lysosomal disruption; this is the critical first step in the proposed mechanism and is robustly documented (Más Gómez et al., 2018).  
- Disease-mechanism alignment with AMD biology: Lysosomal lipid/lipofuscin accumulation—central to AMD—functionally inhibits TRPML1 signaling in RPE, directly linking a hallmark AMD stressor to the TRPML1 pathway that ML-SA1 targets; RPE from ABCA4−/− mice (linked to retinal lipid/lipofuscin pathology) exhibit impaired TRPML1-mediated Ca2+ release (Más Gómez et al., 2018). This alignment makes TRPML1 activation a rational corrective lever.  
- Downstream pathway evidence: ML-SA1/ML-SA agonism reproducibly enhances autophagosome–lysosome fusion and acidification, reduces proteotoxic burden (α-synuclein), and activates TFEB-dependent and TFEB-independent lysosomal functions across cell systems; in retina, subretinal ML-SA1 invokes autophagy, reduces ROS/apoptosis, and preserves structure/function after detachment, supporting ocular pharmacology and neuroprotection (Pollmanns et al., 2022; Yan et al., 2021).  
- Translational momentum: The TRPML1 agonist class is actively explored preclinically for LSD and neurodegenerative indications; Merck’s acquisition of Calporta underscores perceived therapeutic potential of TRPML1 agonism, supporting feasibility of a development path if RPE-specific efficacy is confirmed (Wang et al., 2023; Van Acker et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2023).

Limitations and risks  
- No AMD-specific in vivo data: There are no reports here of ML-SA1 tested in dry AMD or GA animal models, nor in clinical AMD studies; all AMD relevance is inferential from RPE biophysics, lipid-induced TRPML1 impairment, and generalized lysosomal/autophagy correction (Más Gómez et al., 2018). This gap means translational extrapolation to drusen clearance and GA slowing remains unproven.  
- Lipid-dependent resistance: Lysosomal lipid accumulation diminishes ML-SA1 responses in RPE without reducing TRPML1 expression or total lysosomal Ca2+, implying that aged/AMD RPE may exhibit attenuated pharmacodynamics; combination strategies or higher potency agonists (e.g., ML-SA5) may be needed to overcome lipidized lysosomal membranes (Más Gómez et al., 2018; Wünkhaus et al., 2024).  
- Hydrolase maturation not universally rescued: In CLN3-deficient RPE, TRPML1 activation failed to restore mature CatD and TPP1 despite TFEB induction, indicating that some degradative deficits—potentially relevant to AMD—may not normalize solely via TRPML1 activation; this could limit improvements in cathepsin-dependent proteolysis of drusen precursors (Unknown Reference).  
- Selectivity considerations: ML-SA1 can activate other TRPML family members (e.g., TRPML3) in overexpression systems, and pan-TRPML agonism in RPE may have uncharacterized effects on lysosomal trafficking and axonal transport; selectivity profiling in RPE and concentration-response mapping are needed to de-risk off-target TRPML isoform engagement (Unknown Reference).  
- Context-dependent acidification: ML-SA1 acidifies neuronal endolysosomes and enhances degradative flux, but direct demonstrations of increased CatD activity in RPE after ML-SA1 are not provided here; given the CLN3-KO findings on hydrolase maturation, reliance on acidification alone may not guarantee improved protease activity in diseased RPE (Hui et al., 2019; Unknown Reference).

Development guidance  
Given the strong RPE target validation and consistent downstream biology, ML-SA1 (or a more potent TRPML1 agonist such as ML-SA5) is a credible mechanistic candidate for dry AMD; however, AMD-relevant pharmacology must be demonstrated directly. The most decision-informative steps are:  
- Establish efficacy in AMD-relevant RPE contexts: Test ML-SA1 in iPSC-derived human RPE from older donors and/or RPE cultured with A2E/lipofuscin and oxidized lipids to recapitulate lysosomal lipidization; quantify TRPML1 Ca2+ responses, TFEB translocation, lysosomal pH, autophagosome–lysosome fusion, and cargo clearance (e.g., ApoE/cholesterol-rich particles, complement-containing deposits), benchmarking against the lipid-impairment reported in RPE (Más Gómez et al., 2018).  
- Measure hydrolase activity and maturation: Directly assay CatD and other cathepsin activities and maturation states post-ML-SA1 in lipidized RPE; if maturation remains deficient, evaluate combinations with agents that restore hydrolase processing (e.g., modulators of endolysosomal trafficking or mannose-6-phosphate receptor pathways) (Unknown Reference).  
- Explore potentiation strategies: Consider co-targeting known TRPML1 modulators to overcome lipidized lysosomal membranes—examples include augmenting PI(3,5)P2 availability or adding BK channel activators, which rescued impaired ML-SA1 responses and reduced storage in NPC-related settings (Wang et al., 2023; Zhong et al., 2016).  
- Prioritize potency and exposure: Given blunted responses in lipidized RPE, evaluate higher-potency ML-SA chemotypes (ML-SA5 EC50 ~80 nM in a TFE3/TFEB-related translocation assay vs. ML-SA1 in the µM range) for superior pharmacodynamics; subretinal tolerability is supported by RD studies but needs AMD-model confirmation (Wünkhaus et al., 2024; Yan et al., 2021).  
- In vivo validation in AMD models: Move to aged/multiple-hit models that accumulate sub-RPE deposits (e.g., high-fat diet, light exposure, Abca4−/− backgrounds) to test whether TRPML1 agonism reduces drusen-like material, preserves RPE function, and slows GA-like endpoints; note that Abca4−/− RPE exhibited impaired TRPML1 Ca2+ release, making it a relevant sensitized background to assay pharmacological rescue (Más Gómez et al., 2018).

Conclusion  
ML-SA1 is a tractable, mechanistically well-supported TRPML1 agonist with direct RPE target validation and robust evidence that its downstream effects—lysosomal Ca2+ release, TFEB activation, autophagosome–lysosome fusion/acidification, and exocytosis—can correct core lysosomal deficits that plausibly drive drusen precursor accumulation in dry AMD (Más Gómez et al., 2018; Pollmanns et al., 2022; Wünkhaus et al., 2024). The principal risks are the lipid-dependence of TRPML1 dysfunction in RPE and the incomplete rescue of hydrolase maturation observed in CLN3-deficient RPE, both of which may attenuate the magnitude of effect on complex AMD cargoes and necessitate combination strategies or use of more potent agonists (Más Gómez et al., 2018; Wünkhaus et al., 2024). On balance, the mechanistic specificity, ocular proof-of-concept in retinal detachment, and extensive preclinical precedent for lysosomal restoration argue that ML-SA1 (or next-generation TRPML1 agonists) merits prioritized evaluation in AMD-relevant RPE assays and in vivo models, with an early focus on overcoming lipidized lysosomal resistance and verifying improvements in both acidification and hydrolase function (Yan et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2023; Tedeschi et al., 2025).

Strength of evidence for the dry AMD hypothesis: moderate, driven by strong RPE target biology and retinal neuroprotection data but constrained by the absence of AMD-specific in vivo studies and by lipid-imposed pharmacodynamic limits (Más Gómez et al., 2018; Yan et al., 2021). If forthcoming AMD-relevant experiments confirm that TRPML1 activation restores lysosomal Ca2+ signaling and degradative capacity in lipidized RPE, and that drusen precursors are reduced, ML-SA1/ML-SA5 would represent a differentiated, mechanism-based approach compared with broad mTOR inhibition, with the potential to correct proximal lysosomal defects underlying GA progression (Wang et al., 2023; Pollmanns et al., 2022).

Detailed, component-wise assessment  

- Target presence and engagement in RPE: TRPML1 expression and function are present in ARPE-19 and primary RPE; ML-SA1 evokes lysosomal Ca2+ release that is TRPML1-dependent (absent in TRPML1−/− RPE), establishing on-target engagement (Más Gómez et al., 2018).  
- Relevance of TRPML1 signaling to AMD pathobiology: Lysosomal lipid/lipofuscin accumulation impairs TRPML1 function in RPE and is germane to AMD; RPE autofluorescence increases in TRPML1 KO, linking the channel to handling of drusen-like material (Más Gómez et al., 2018).  
- Downstream mechanisms aligned with therapeutic hypothesis: ML-SA1 triggers calcineurin-TFEB signaling, augments autophagosome–lysosome fusion and acidification, and enhances exocytosis—mechanisms expected to improve clearance of drusen precursors (Wang et al., 2023; Pollmanns et al., 2022).  
- Evidence for improved degradative flux: In neurons, ML-SA1 acidifies endolysosomes and reduces Aβ/BACE1 pathology; in retina in vivo, ML-SA1 increases autophagy markers and preserves photoreceptors; in RPE disease models, TRPML1 activation decreases stored substrates and reduces lysosomal surface area (Hui et al., 2019; Yan et al., 2021; Wünkhaus et al., 2024).  
- Constraints/unknowns: Lipid-imposed TRPML1 inhibition in RPE may limit efficacy; CatD/TPP1 maturation not rescued in CLN3-KO RPE; no direct AMD data; potential TRPML3 co-activation (Más Gómez et al., 2018; Unknown Reference).

Recommendation  
Advance ML-SA1 (and evaluate ML-SA5 as a higher-potency comparator) into AMD-relevant RPE assays with lipidized lysosomes, incorporating quantitative readouts of TRPML1 Ca2+ signaling, TFEB translocation, lysosomal pH, hydrolase maturation/activity, and cargo clearance, and then proceed to in vivo testing in drusen-accumulating models if in vitro data are supportive; in parallel, explore combination strategies (e.g., BK channel activation) to overcome lipid-dependent resistance to TRPML1 agonism (Más Gómez et al., 2018; Wünkhaus et al., 2024; Zhong et al., 2016).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Resveratrol is a naturally occurring polyphenolic compound that belongs to the stilbene family and is most famously isolated from grape skins and red wine. Its chemical structure features two aromatic rings linked by an ethylene bridge, which confers potent antioxidant properties. Discovered over four decades ago, resveratrol (catalog number Sigma R5010) has been extensively studied for its diverse biological activities, including anti‐inflammatory, anti‐oxidative, and anti‐aging effects. As a member of natural polyphenols, resveratrol has been used both as a dietary supplement and as a laboratory tool to probe intracellular signaling and epigenetic regulation. This compound has been explored for therapeutic applications in cardiovascular diseases, metabolic disorders, and various age‐related conditions, thereby positioning it as an attractive lead for repurposing. Its natural origin, safety profile upon oral administration, and documented bioavailability in retinal tissues support its candidature for ocular indications, particularly in mitigating dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) pathology (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Delmas et al., 2021).

Therapeutic History:  
Numerous biochemical studies have established that resveratrol exerts its beneficial effects by modulating key intracellular pathways. Historically, resveratrol has been used as an anti‐oxidant in various cellular systems and has been investigated in preclinical models of neurodegeneration, cardiovascular disease, and metabolic syndrome. In the context of ophthalmology, several studies have evaluated its efficacy in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cell models. For instance, research using ARPE-19 cells, a well-established human RPE cell line, demonstrated that resveratrol activates SIRT1 to protect against oxidative stress and apoptosis induced by challenging stimuli such as sodium iodate, UVA radiation, acrolein, and A2E—a major component of lipofuscin implicated in drusen formation and AMD pathology (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Li et al., 2024; Alaimo et al., 2020). Additional investigations combined resveratrol with omega-3 fatty acids in formulations like Resvega® to induce autophagy and enhance cell survival under conditions simulating AMD (Delmas et al., 2021; Koskela et al., 2016). While much of the published literature has concentrated on resveratrol’s effects in oxidative stress, inflammatory responses, and autophagy promotion in RPE cells, a few reports have noted its capacity to counteract the toxic accumulation of intracellular debris that is a hallmark of dry AMD (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Pinelli et al., 2025). Moreover, preliminary clinical reports have suggested that long-term oral supplementation with resveratrol-containing nutraceuticals may contribute to anatomic restoration of retinal structure and improved visual function in elderly patients, thus further underpinning its translational potential. Notably, while there is extensive preclinical evidence in vitro and in animal models, resveratrol has not yet been unequivocally validated in advanced clinical trials targeting dry AMD specifically (Abu-Amero et al., 2016).

Mechanism of Action:  
A robust body of research supports that resveratrol acts principally through the activation of SIRT1 (sirtuin 1) and the energy sensor AMPK (AMP-activated protein kinase), both of which are critical for maintaining cellular homeostasis in the aging retina. At the molecular level, resveratrol has been reported to directly and indirectly stimulate SIRT1 activity in RPE cells, leading to the deacetylation of several downstream targets such as PGC-1α (peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator 1-alpha). This deacetylated PGC-1α, in turn, upregulates mitochondrial biogenesis and enhances cellular oxidative phosphorylation, thereby improving mitochondrial quality control and reducing the accumulation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Li et al., 2024; Buonfiglio et al., 2024). Concomitantly, resveratrol activates AMPK, albeit through complex mechanisms involving inhibition of phosphodiesterases and alterations in the intracellular AMP/ATP ratio. The resulting AMPK phosphorylation facilitates a myriad of downstream effects, notably the inhibition of mTOR signaling (a known suppressor of autophagy) and activation of ULK1, a serine/threonine kinase that initiates autophagosome formation (Li et al., 2024; Abu-Amero et al., 2016).

In RPE cells, the synergistic activation of SIRT1 and AMPK by resveratrol is believed to promote autophagy, as evidenced by increased LC3II/I ratios and decreased p62 expression. Autophagy is particularly critical in RPE cells to clear toxic cellular debris such as A2E and other protein aggregates that contribute to drusen accumulation in dry AMD (Alaimo et al., 2020; Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Pinelli et al., 2023). Furthermore, the prevailing hypothesis extends these autophagic benefits by suggesting that, downstream of AMPK/SIRT1 activation, resveratrol may induce TFEB dephosphorylation. TFEB is a transcription factor that, when dephosphorylated, translocates into the nucleus and upregulates the coordinated lysosomal expression and regulation (CLEAR) network. This results in enhanced lysosomal biogenesis, improved lysosomal acidification, and increased activation of lysosomal enzymes such as cathepsin D. Although direct experimental evidence linking resveratrol to TFEB dephosphorylation in RPE cells is not abundantly detailed in the current literature, several studies imply that agents that activate AMPK and inhibit mTOR can indirectly promote TFEB activity. In this context, resveratrol’s ability to inhibit mTOR, partly through AMPK activation, suggests a plausible mechanism for the promotion of TFEB-mediated lysosomal functions (Falcão et al., 2025; Pinelli et al., 2023). These molecular events are anticipated to bolster the autophagy-lysosomal system, thereby mitigating the drusen accumulation characteristic of dry AMD. Additionally, resveratrol exerts direct antioxidant effects by scavenging free radicals and modulating the expression of antioxidant enzymes such as superoxide dismutase, which contributes further to its protective milieu in the retina (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Abu-Amero et al., 2016).

Expected Effect:  
Based on its molecular pharmacology, the expected effect of resveratrol in preclinical models of dry AMD would be multifaceted. In assays utilizing ARPE-19 cells or primary human RPE cells, treatment with resveratrol is expected to enhance SIRT1 activity, as measured by increased deacetylation of SIRT1 substrates and upregulation of PGC-1α nuclear translocation. Concurrently, AMPK phosphorylation is anticipated to be elevated, leading to inhibition of the mTOR pathway; this would foster an increased autophagic flux, observable as a higher LC3II/I ratio and reduced levels of the autophagy substrate p62 (Li et al., 2024; Alaimo et al., 2020; Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021). Furthermore, the candidate is hypothesized to indirectly promote TFEB dephosphorylation, facilitating its nuclear translocation and subsequent upregulation of lysosomal genes. This could manifest as enhanced lysosomal biogenesis, improved acidification of the lysosomal compartment, and elevated activity of lysosomal proteases such as cathepsin D. The cumulative consequence of these events would be a more efficient clearance of intracellular debris, including lipofuscin and other drusen components, thereby ameliorating RPE dysfunction associated with dry AMD (Falcão et al., 2025; Pinelli et al., 2023).

It is also expected that resveratrol’s anti-inflammatory and anti-apoptotic actions would reduce the chronic low-grade inflammation that underpins AMD pathogenesis. In vivo, improved autophagic and lysosomal clearance should correlate with decreased accumulation of pathological deposits at the RPE-Bruch’s membrane interface, potentially reducing the progression of drusen formation and preserving retinal structure and function (Alaimo et al., 2020; Abu-Amero et al., 2016; Pinelli et al., 2025). Given that resveratrol is detectable in retinal tissue following oral administration, its systemic safety and potential for long-term use add to its attractiveness as a repurposed therapeutic agent for dry AMD. Moreover, the dual capacity to modulate both metabolic and epigenetic pathways may offer disease-modifying effects that extend beyond symptomatic relief and target the underlying cellular aging processes in the RPE (Subramani et al., 2017).

Overall Evaluation:  
Resveratrol emerges as a promising candidate for repurposing in the context of dry AMD owing to its well-documented ability to activate SIRT1 and AMPK, which are pivotal signaling nodes in the maintenance of cellular homeostasis and autophagy. One of the central strengths of resveratrol is its dual mechanism of action. By targeting SIRT1, resveratrol not only combats oxidative stress through the deacetylation of transcription factors and enhancement of mitochondrial biogenesis but also modulates anti-inflammatory pathways relevant to retinal preservation (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Li et al., 2024). Simultaneously, its activation of AMPK provides additional impetus for autophagy induction through mTOR inhibition and ULK1 activation. Such molecular actions are of particular relevance to RPE cells, in which impairment of the autophagy-lysosomal system is a key pathogenetic mechanism leading to the accumulation of cellular waste products such as drusen—a hallmark of dry AMD (Alaimo et al., 2020; Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021).

Furthermore, the hypothesis that resveratrol could foster TFEB dephosphorylation is especially intriguing. Although direct evidence linking resveratrol to TFEB activation in RPE cells is currently limited, the known interactions between AMPK/mTOR signaling and TFEB activity provide a strong conceptual framework. Activation of TFEB would result in enhanced lysosomal biogenesis, acidification, and increased cathepsin D activity—mechanisms that are critical for the proper degradation of accumulated photoreceptor-derived debris and toxic aggregates (Falcão et al., 2025; Pinelli et al., 2023). This potential to bolster a declining lysosomal-autophagy system with age might address the fundamental cellular dysfunction observed in dry AMD.

On the clinical side, resveratrol demonstrates a favorable safety profile with established oral bioavailability and experimental evidence suggesting retinal tissue penetration. Combined with its history of use as an anti-oxidative and anti-inflammatory agent in other disease contexts, these features support its translational potential. Several nutraceutical formulations incorporating resveratrol (often in combination with omega-3 fatty acids, as in Resvega®) have already reached early-phase clinical evaluation for ocular indications, providing preliminary signals of efficacy in improving retinal structure and function among aged patients (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Delmas et al., 2021).

Nevertheless, several weaknesses and gaps must be acknowledged. First, while there is abundant preclinical evidence of resveratrol’s activation of SIRT1/AMPK pathways and subsequent autophagy induction in RPE cells, the specific molecular events leading to TFEB dephosphorylation, enhanced lysosomal biogenesis, lysosomal acidification, and increased cathepsin D activity are not yet comprehensively elucidated. In other words, the critical mechanistic link between resveratrol treatment and lysosomal enhancement remains somewhat inferential rather than directly demonstrated in the existing literature (Falcão et al., 2025; Hyttinen et al., 2019). Second, much of the supporting data comes from in vitro studies or animal models, with limited robust clinical evidence explicitly addressing dry AMD. Although some pilot clinical studies with resveratrol-containing formulations show promise, their design, scale, and long-term outcomes are not sufficiently advanced to confirm therapeutic efficacy in a broad AMD population (Abu-Amero et al., 2016). Third, resveratrol is known to have issues with bioavailability due to rapid metabolism and low systemic concentrations after oral ingestion; therefore, optimizing its delivery to retinal tissues, perhaps via novel formulations or nanoparticle carriers, may be necessary to achieve therapeutic levels (Subramani et al., 2017; Pinelli et al., 2025). Additionally, while its pleiotropic activity is a strength in terms of targeting multiple pathogenic mechanisms, this same feature can pose challenges in ensuring specificity and avoiding off-target effects.

In summary, resveratrol presents a compelling case as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. Its ability to activate SIRT1 and AMPK, induce autophagy, and potentially stimulate TFEB-driven lysosomal biogenesis aligns well with the current understanding of the cellular derangements underlying AMD pathogenesis. The expected outcome would be improved clearance of toxic cellular debris and drusen, preservation of RPE integrity, and amelioration of oxidative stress and inflammation in the aging retina. However, to fully validate resveratrol as a viable treatment for dry AMD, further investigations are warranted to (a) directly demonstrate its effects on TFEB dephosphorylation and lysosomal function in RPE cells, (b) optimize its ocular bioavailability, and (c) establish robust clinical endpoints in well-designed trials. Overall, while promising and supported by a substantial body of preclinical evidence, additional targeted research is required to definitively establish resveratrol’s mechanistic effects on the autophagy-lysosomal pathway and its therapeutic potential in dry AMD (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Li et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2025; Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Abu-Amero et al., 2016).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Nicotinamide riboside (NR), marketed as ChromaDex Niagen, belongs to the vitamin B3 family and is a naturally occurring precursor of nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+). Originally discovered in trace amounts in milk and other food sources, NR has been isolated and subsequently synthesized to yield a high‐purity form for nutritional and pharmaceutical applications. As a member of a class of compounds designed to elevate intracellular NAD+ levels, NR has attracted significant attention in the fields of metabolism, aging, and neuroprotection. Its chemical structure—a combination of a nicotinamide moiety bound to ribose—enables it to enter salvage pathways in cells with minimal metabolic conversion losses. In this regard, NR is comparable to other NAD+ boosters such as nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN), though differences in bioavailability and cellular transporter expression have been noted in some studies. Preclinical research has documented retinal distribution of NR in rodent models, suggesting that it reaches ocular tissues in pharmacologically relevant concentrations, an essential prerequisite for any agent intended to treat dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) (Abokyi & Tse, 2025; Braidy et al., 2019).

Therapeutic History:  
NR has been extensively investigated for its potential to modulate cellular energy metabolism and mitigate the effects of aging in diverse tissues. Early studies revealed that supplementation with NR effectively elevates NAD+ levels in multiple cell types, including neurons, skeletal muscle, and retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells, thereby enhancing mitochondrial function and cellular stress resistance (Dovijarski, 2019; Pîrvu et al., 2021). In the context of ocular research, while much of the direct experimental work has been performed using NMN, the close biochemical relationship between NMN and NR—as NAD+ precursors—has led investigators to propose that NR could produce similar outcomes in RPE cells. Models of retinal degeneration, including glaucoma and optic nerve injury, have demonstrated that NAD+ boosting via NR administration can ameliorate mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress, indirectly supporting its potential repurposing for dry AMD (Kitaoka et al., 2020; Mehmel et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2024). Moreover, clinical studies investigating NR’s safety in humans have shown that it is well tolerated at doses that elevate systemic NAD+ levels; doses in the gram-range have been employed without significant adverse effects (Jadeja et al., 2020). Although direct clinical trials targeting dry AMD are still forthcoming, the overall therapeutic history of NR—encompassing robust preclinical ocular benefit across neurodegenerative models and a favorable safety profile in human subjects—strongly supports further investigation for eye diseases where NAD+ depletion is a central pathophysiological feature (Dovijarski, 2019; Braidy et al., 2019; Pîrvu et al., 2021).

Mechanism of Action:  
The proposed mechanism of NR in dry AMD centers on its capacity to elevate intracellular NAD+ levels, thereby fueling a cascade of beneficial biochemical events. After cell entry, NR is phosphorylated by nicotinamide riboside kinases (NRKs) to generate NMN, which is subsequently converted to NAD+ through the activity of NMN adenylyltransferase. The resultant increase in NAD+ acts as a vital cofactor for sirtuins—primarily SIRT1 and SIRT3—which are NAD+-dependent deacetylases involved in regulating numerous cellular processes. SIRT1, in particular, has been implicated in deacetylating key transcription factors such as peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator-1α (PGC-1α) and transcription factor EB (TFEB). TFEB is a master regulator of lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy; its deacetylation leads to its nuclear translocation and binding to CLEAR (Coordinated Lysosomal Expression and Regulation) elements in the promoter regions of autophagy and lysosomal genes. Such activation promotes lysosomal acidification and increases the activity of hydrolases like cathepsin D, which are critical for the degradation of damaged proteins and organelles. Concurrently, SIRT3, which localizes predominantly to mitochondria, enhances mitochondrial function by deacetylating enzymes crucial for mitochondrial bioenergetics and reactive oxygen species (ROS) detoxification. The overall effect of NR supplementation is therefore hypothesized to be a restoration of cellular homeostasis in RPE cells—improving both autophagic clearance and mitochondrial function, two processes known to be compromised in dry AMD (Kitaoka et al., 2020; Mehmel et al., 2020; Lin & Apte, 2018; Jadeja et al., 2020). Such a mechanism is consistent with a substantial body of literature demonstrating that the NAD+-sirtuin axis plays a critical role in regulating neuroprotective and anti-aging functions across various tissues (Dovijarski, 2019; Jadeja et al., 2018; Pîrvu et al., 2021).

At the molecular level, the cascade initiated by NR begins with its metabolic conversion to NAD+, which then serves as an essential substrate for SIRT1 activation. Activated SIRT1 deacetylates TFEB, facilitating its nuclear accumulation and binding to the CLEAR network promoters, thereby upregulating genes responsible for autophagy, lysosomal biogenesis, and lysosomal acidification. This process is expected to boost cathepsin D activity and overall lysosomal proteolytic function. Parallel activation of SIRT3 in mitochondria further strengthens cellular defenses by enhancing mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation and reducing ROS generation through deacetylation of key metabolic enzymes. These reconstructed pathways directly address the deleterious effects of oxidative stress and metabolic dysfunction that drive RPE cell death in dry AMD (Kitaoka et al., 2020; Mehmel et al., 2020; Jadeja et al., 2018). While several studies using NMN have validated these pathways in RPE and retinal cells (Ren et al., 2022), the mechanistic rationale for NR’s effectiveness remains compelling given its similar mode of action and previously documented retinal distribution (Kitaoka et al., 2020; Jadeja et al., 2020).

Expected Effect:  
In the experimental setting, the administration of NR is expected to lead to a marked elevation of intracellular NAD+ levels within RPE cells, setting off a chain reaction of intracellular adjustments. The immediate consequence of increased NAD+ availability will be the enhanced activation of SIRT1 and SIRT3. Once activated, SIRT1 is anticipated to deacetylate TFEB, resulting in its translocation to the nucleus. In the nucleus, TFEB binds to target gene promoters, thereby upregulating a suite of genes involved in lysosomal biogenesis and the autophagic process. Critically, improvements in lysosomal acidification are expected to boost cathepsin D activity—a protease essential for the degradation of intracellular waste and damaged organelles. Simultaneously, SIRT3-mediated deacetylation events within the mitochondria are projected to improve mitochondrial respiratory capacity and enhance ATP production, while also reducing the production of ROS that ordinarily contribute to oxidative damage. The net effect of these cellular modifications should be an increase in RPE cell viability, particularly under conditions of induced oxidative stress (for example, H₂O₂ exposure), which mimics the pathological environment observed in dry AMD (Zhu et al., 2016; Tong et al., 2022).

Additionally, the NR-induced NAD+ boosting is hypothesized to initiate a beneficial feedback loop wherein improved mitochondrial function further supports cellular energy demands and sustains autophagic flux. This dual action—simultaneously targeting lysosomal and mitochondrial dysfunction—addresses two major hallmarks of dry AMD pathophysiology. RPE cells, which are crucial for the maintenance of photoreceptors, suffer from cumulative oxidative damage and impaired clearance of cellular debris as a result of aging and environmental stress. By restoring efficient autophagic processes and ensuring proper mitochondrial function, NR treatment is expected to reduce the accumulation of toxic protein aggregates and dysfunctional organelles, thereby staving off cellular senescence and death. This is especially salient given that recent studies have linked improved NAD+ metabolism to increased cellular resilience in models of age-related neurodegeneration (Jadeja et al., 2018; Jadeja et al., 2020). The expected outcomes in these assays include measurable increases in NAD+/NADH ratios, enhanced expression and nuclear localization of TFEB, elevated cathepsin D activity, and ultimately, improved cell survival following oxidative challenge. Such effects have been reported in various in vitro and in vivo studies employing NAD+ precursors, strengthening the biological plausibility of the NR hypothesis for treating dry AMD (Kitaoka et al., 2020; Mehmel et al., 2020; Dovijarski, 2019).

Overall Evaluation:  
An overall evaluation of NR as a candidate for treating dry AMD reveals both promising strengths and areas requiring further elucidation. Among the principal strengths is NR’s robust ability to elevate systemic and intracellular NAD+ levels, a key factor in numerous regulatory processes implicated in aging and cellular stress response. Its well-characterized pharmacokinetics, combined with documented safety in human supplementation studies, position NR as an attractive candidate for rapid clinical translation (Jadeja et al., 2020; Braidy et al., 2019). The underlying mechanism—that is, the activation of SIRT1 and SIRT3 leading to deacetylation and activation of TFEB—is supported by a breadth of biochemical and preclinical studies, albeit many of these have been performed with related compounds such as NMN. Nevertheless, the evidence suggests that the NAD+–sirtuin–TFEB axis is critical for autophagic and mitochondrial homeostasis in RPE cells—a process compromised in dry AMD (Kitaoka et al., 2020; Mehmel et al., 2020; Jadeja et al., 2018).

Further strengths include NR’s potential to confer dual-organellar benefit. Restoration of lysosomal function, as evidenced by improved acidification and protease activity (e.g., cathepsin D), is a novel therapeutic target that addresses the accumulation of cellular debris—a key factor in the progression of dry AMD. Concurrently, the enhancement of mitochondrial quality and bioenergetics through SIRT3 activation can mitigate oxidative stress and improve cell survival in metabolic stress conditions. Together, these actions provide a mechanistically coherent rationale for repurposing NR in a disease context that currently lacks effective treatments (Kitaoka et al., 2020; Mehmel et al., 2020).

However, several challenges and weaknesses must be acknowledged. First, while preclinical data offer promising insights, direct evidence of NR’s efficacy in RPE cells specifically challenged by dry AMD-like oxidative stress is still limited. Much of the supportive evidence comes from studies employing NMN or from models of other neurodegenerative conditions such as glaucoma and optic nerve degeneration (Lin et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2024). Given differences in uptake and metabolic processing between NR and NMN (Will-Orrego, 2020), it will be important to confirm that NR is adequately taken up by RPE and that its metabolic conversion is efficient in these cells.  

Furthermore, the full cascade—from NAD+ elevation through SIRT1/SIRT3 activation, subsequent TFEB deacetylation, and eventual lysosomal and mitochondrial improvements—remains to be validated within the specific context of dry AMD. Although the general biology of the NAD+–sirtuin axis is well established, its quantitative impact on TFEB activity and cathepsin D function in RPE under conditions of oxidative stress has not been directly demonstrated. This gap in the literature raises questions regarding the optimal dosing regimen, the timing of supplementation, and the potential for compensatory metabolic changes that might blunt the predicted benefits (Ren et al., 2022).

Another consideration is the heterogeneity inherent in dry AMD pathology. RPE cell dysfunction in AMD is multifactorial, involving not only oxidative stress and defective autophagy, but also inflammation, extracellular matrix alterations, and genetic predispositions. Whether NR’s NAD+ boosting effect alone can sufficiently address the multifaceted nature of dry AMD remains uncertain. There is also the possibility that chronic administration might lead to unforeseen metabolic imbalances or off-target effects, particularly if prolonged high-dose supplementation alters systemic NAD+ homeostasis or affects non-target tissues in unintended ways (Ghosh et al., 2023; Jadeja et al., 2018).

Despite these challenges, the candidate’s favorable safety profile and the mechanistic soundness of the NAD+–sirtuin–TFEB hypothesis underpin a strong case for further investigation. In vitro experiments using ARPE-19 cells and primary RPE cultures under oxidative stress conditions should be prioritized to determine whether NR supplementation can reproducibly induce TFEB nuclear translocation, enhance lysosomal acidification, and improve mitochondrial function. In addition, in vivo studies in animal models that recapitulate dry AMD pathology will be essential to assess the translational potential of NR. These studies might include detailed pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic analyses to ascertain the retinal bioavailability of NR, as well as dose-response studies to define the therapeutic window. Finally, controlled clinical trials in patients with early dry AMD would be necessary to confirm efficacy and to optimize treatment protocols (Martucci et al., 2025; Oshitari, 2024; Lin & Apte, 2018).

In summary, the current body of evidence suggests that NR is a promising repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. Its ability to efficiently elevate intracellular NAD+ levels, combined with the downstream activation of SIRT1 and SIRT3, provides a strong mechanistic rationale for improving both autophagic flux and mitochondrial function in RPE cells. These cellular processes are crucial for maintaining retinal health and combating the oxidative and metabolic stress that drives dry AMD progression. Moreover, the extensive preclinical investigation of NAD+ precursors and the favorable safety record of NR in human studies further support its potential for fast-tracking into clinical evaluation for retinal disorders (Kitaoka et al., 2020; Mehmel et al., 2020; Dovijarski, 2019; Jadeja et al., 2020; Pîrvu et al., 2021).

Nonetheless, key uncertainties remain regarding the direct applicability of NR’s effects to the complex microenvironment of the retina in dry AMD. Issues such as differential cellular uptake, the efficiency of NR’s metabolic conversion to NAD+ in RPE cells, and the precise threshold of NAD+ elevation required to trigger beneficial deacetylation of TFEB must be addressed. Furthermore, given the multifactorial nature of AMD pathology, combinatorial therapeutic approaches may ultimately be necessary to achieve clinically significant improvements. Therefore, while NR emerges as a highly promising candidate with a compelling mechanistic framework, rigorous experimental validation tailored specifically to the ocular setting is imperative. Future studies should elucidate whether the activation of the NAD+–sirtuin–TFEB axis translates into meaningful improvements in lysosomal acidification, cathepsin D activity, and RPE cell survival in both in vitro models of oxidative stress and in vivo models of dry AMD (Kitaoka et al., 2020; Jadeja et al., 2018; Will-Orrego, 2020).

Looking forward, systematic exploration through well-designed preclinical trials is recommended to confirm the predicted molecular events. These experiments should include detailed time-course and dose-response analyses of NAD+ levels, sirtuin activities, TFEB deacetylation status, and lysosomal function in retinal cells exposed to oxidative insults. Such data will not only clarify the effectiveness of NR in restoring cellular homeostasis but also help refine dosing strategies and identify potential biomarkers of response. Ultimately, if subsequent research affirms the predicted benefits of NR in improving RPE function and survival, this therapeutic candidate could represent a major advancement in the pharmacological management of dry AMD—a condition for which current treatment options remain notably limited (Kitaoka et al., 2020; Mehmel et al., 2020; Dovijarski, 2019; Jadeja et al., 2020; Pîrvu et al., 2021).

Overall, the promising preclinical evidence supporting the NAD+–sirtuin–TFEB pathway, combined with the safety profile demonstrated in human trials, renders NR a highly attractive candidate for drug development in dry AMD. While further direct experimental evidence is required to confirm its efficacy in retinal cells, the mechanistic insights gleaned from various studies provide a sound scientific basis for proceeding with additional preclinical and clinical investigations. Thus, repurposing nicotinamide riboside for dry AMD holds significant potential and merits further exploration as part of an integrated strategy to address the unmet therapeutic need in this degenerative retinal disease (Abokyi & Tse, 2025; Cimaglia et al., 2020; Ebeling et al., 2020; Jadeja et al., 2020; Pîrvu et al., 2021; Lin & Apte, 2018).
