Below is our comprehensive evaluation of SB290157 as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD), with a focus on its chemical origin, its therapeutic history, the detailed mechanism of action at the molecular level, the expected pharmacological effects in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) models, and an overall assessment of strengths and weaknesses.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
SB290157 is a fully synthetic, nonpeptidic small‐molecule agent originally discovered as a selective antagonist of the complement anaphylatoxin C3a receptor (C3aR). Chemically, it is defined as N2-[(2,2-diphenylethoxy)acetyl]-L-arginine and was identified via high-throughput screening of chemical libraries using membranes from cells stably expressing human C3aR, such as RBL-2H3 cells (Ames et al., 2001). The lead compound was chemically optimized from an initial hit (SKF 63649) to improve affinity and potency, and its synthesis has been well described using peptide–like solid‐phase synthetic strategies (e.g., Fmoc protecting group chemistry on Wang resin) thereby yielding a compound with high purity (≥95%) and reproducible physicochemical properties (Ames et al., 2001). SB290157 belongs to a class of compounds that modulate G protein–coupled receptors (GPCRs), in this case a complement receptor, and similar nonpeptidic small‐molecule ligands have been employed in preclinical studies to probe inflammatory pathways in various disease states (Iyer et al., 2017; Ames et al., 2001). Its discovery set an important precedent for the therapeutic targeting of complement receptors, especially given the historical absence of potent, selective C3aR antagonists, and it has been widely used as a research tool in animal models and cell-based assays to interrogate the physiological roles of C3a/C3aR signaling (Ames et al., 2001).

Therapeutic History:  
SB290157 has been extensively employed in preclinical models to examine the role of C3aR in inflammation and immune modulation. In early studies, it was shown to antagonize C3a-induced intracellular calcium mobilization and receptor internalization in RBL-2H3 cells and human neutrophils, with reported IC50 values in the low-nanomolar range (approximately 27–30 nM), suggesting robust antagonism under defined experimental conditions (Ames et al., 2001). In vivo, SB290157 demonstrated antiinflammatory efficacy by reducing neutrophil recruitment in guinea pig models of lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-induced airway neutrophilia and by decreasing paw edema in rat adjuvant-induced arthritis models through intraperitoneal dosing (Ames et al., 2001). Although valuable as a pharmacological probe, its history is mired by concerns as several subsequent investigations indicated that SB290157 can exhibit partial agonist activity—depending on the assay system and receptor expression context—and even engage an off-target complement receptor, C5aR2, to induce β-arrestin recruitment (Coulthard, 2015; Li et al., 2021; Mathieu et al., 2005). With more than 70 publications referencing its use, SB290157 remains one of the most commonly used C3aR inhibitors; however, it is essentially confined to the research arena and has never reached clinical development for AMD or other indications (Li et al., 2021).  
There is emerging evidence in ophthalmologic research relevant to dry AMD. For example, an in vitro human fetal RPE cell model has shown that complement fragment C3a can drive the formation of sub-retinal pigment epithelium deposits via dysregulation of the ubiquitin proteasome pathway; importantly, co-application of SB290157 with recombinant C3a in these cultures prevented the abnormal deposit formation, suggesting that C3aR blockade can modulate key pathological events relevant to AMD pathogenesis (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). Despite this promising mechanistic link, SB290157 itself has not been advanced clinically, and its use in retinal models remains primarily exploratory. Moreover, the existence of antagonistic and agonistic properties in various assay systems necessitates careful interpretation of its efficacy when contemplating the translation to human ocular diseases (Iyer et al., 2017; Li et al., 2021).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, SB290157 has been characterized as a competitive antagonist that binds to the orthosteric site of the C3a receptor, thereby inhibiting the native ligand, C3a, from eliciting its downstream signaling responses. In classic radioligand binding assays using 125I-labeled C3a, SB290157 displaces the radiolabeled peptide with an IC50 of ~200 nM, indicating it competes effectively with C3a (Ames et al., 2001). Functionally, this displacement correlates with inhibition of C3a-induced intracellular calcium mobilization, a key second messenger response mediated via G-protein coupling to pertussis-toxin–sensitive Gi/o proteins (Ames et al., 2001). Additionally, SB290157 has been shown to block C3a-mediated receptor internalization in immune cells, further supporting its role in antagonizing C3aR activation (Ames et al., 2001; Iyer et al., 2017).  
Beyond the canonical receptor blockade, several studies have pointed out that SB290157’s activity is highly context-dependent. In systems where C3aR is overexpressed—such as recombinant CHO or transfected RBL cells—SB290157 can paradoxically act as an agonist to trigger intracellular signaling cascades like ERK phosphorylation, potentially due to rapid receptor desensitization or kinetic differences in ligand-receptor interaction (Coulthard, 2015; Li et al., 2021; Mathieu et al., 2005). Moreover, its off-target partial agonism at the closely related receptor C5aR2 has been documented, wherein it mediates β-arrestin recruitment at higher concentrations, thereby dampening C5a-induced ERK signaling in primary macrophages (Li et al., 2021; Mathieu et al., 2005). Such dual or biased pharmacological properties underscore that SB290157’s molecular actions cannot be solely categorized as pure antagonism without considering assay conditions and cell contexts (Li et al., 2021; Mathieu et al., 2005).  
In the context of RPE cells, C3a binding to C3aR is hypothesized to disrupt intracellular calcium homeostasis, leading to lysosomal alkalinization—a key factor that impairs the maturation and proteolytic activity of lysosomal enzymes such as cathepsin D (CTSD). Cathepsin D is critical for proper turnover of extracellular matrix (ECM) components and degradation of proteinaceous aggregates; its dysfunction is implicated in drusen formation, a hallmark of dry AMD (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). By competitively inhibiting C3a binding, SB290157 is expected to mitigate abnormal Ca2+ signaling, maintain lysosomal acidification, and therefore preserve CTSD processing and activity, which in turn would prevent or lessen the accumulation of drusen-like deposits (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018; Iyer et al., 2017). This proposed mechanism is supported by the observation that in hfRPE cultures, SB290157 co-application with C3a prevented both the upregulation of C3aR expression and the subsequent deposition of abnormal ECM structures (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). Nonetheless, the precise molecular interactions at the receptor—the positioning of the diphenylethoxy moiety and arginine side chain—is critical for binding affinity and selectivity (Iyer et al., 2017; Mishra et al., 2025), and minor alterations in these interactions might contribute to the observed functional variability.

Expected Effect:  
Based on the hypothesis for dry AMD, SB290157 is expected to act on RPE cells by antagonizing the C3aR, thereby preventing the cascade of intracellular events that lead to lysosomal stress. In a typical RPE culture assay where C3a is exogenously added—thereby simulating enhanced complement activity as observed in AMD—SB290157 should block C3a binding, which would normally result in the perturbation of lysosomal pH homeostasis. The blockade of this receptor is envisaged to preserve the normally acidic lysosomal environment required for the optimal maturation and proteolytic function of cathepsin D (CTSD), an enzyme whose dysfunction is implicated in the formation of drusen and the progression of dry AMD (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018; Iyer et al., 2017).  
Furthermore, by preserving lysosomal function, SB290157 is expected to reduce subsequent activation of the inflammasome—a multi-protein complex that is triggered when lysosomal destabilization occurs—and thus attenuate the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-1β. This cascade is particularly relevant because chronic inflammation is thought to drive many of the degenerative changes associated with AMD (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). In vitro, RPE cells pre-treated with SB290157 before C3a challenge would be anticipated to maintain normal lysosomal acidity (measured by appropriate pH-sensitive dyes), exhibit proper CTSD processing (as observed by Western blot analysis for mature cathepsin D forms), and display reduced markers of inflammasome activation such as caspase-1 cleavage and IL-1β release. Gene expression studies in these cells might also reveal normalized levels of key ECM components and proteases, ultimately leading to a reduction in sub-RPE deposit accumulation (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018).  
It is important to note that C3aR is expressed on RPE cells and its activation has been implicated in additional downstream effects—including modulation of the ubiquitin proteasome pathway and extracellular matrix turnover—which further contribute to cell dysfunction and deposit formation. Therefore, antagonism of C3aR by SB290157, if effective and selective, could theoretically interrupt this pathogenic cascade and offer a protective effect against drusen-mediated RPE degeneration in dry AMD (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018; Ames et al., 2001).

Overall Evaluation:  
SB290157 offers a compelling mechanistic rationale for repurposing in dry AMD given the central role of complement dysregulation in the pathogenesis of the disease. Among its strengths is a well-documented ability to block C3a-induced signaling events across multiple preclinical models. Early characterizations demonstrated that SB290157 effectively inhibited intracellular Ca2+ mobilization, receptor internalization, and other pro-inflammatory events in both immune cells and engineered cell systems (Ames et al., 2001). Its application in an hfRPE model demonstrated that C3a-induced sub-RPE deposit formation can be reversed upon treatment with SB290157, underscoring its potential utility in preventing one of the critical pathological features of dry AMD (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). Furthermore, the known rodent tolerability and defined in vivo pharmacokinetics observed in other disease models—such as LPS-induced airway inflammation and adjuvant-induced arthritis—support the concept that SB290157 can be delivered systemically with demonstrable pharmacodynamic effects (Ames et al., 2001).  

However, several weaknesses temper enthusiasm for immediate clinical translation. A significant concern is the compound’s context-dependent pharmacology. Multiple studies have reported that SB290157 can function as a partial or even full agonist under certain conditions, particularly in overexpression systems, and paradoxically activate C3aR instead of inhibiting it (Coulthard, 2015; Li et al., 2021; Mathieu et al., 2005). Such functional divergence is critical when considering a therapy designed to block a deleterious signal in a delicate tissue such as the retina. Moreover, SB290157 has been shown to exhibit off-target effects, including partial agonism at C5aR2—a related complement receptor—which may confound downstream anti-inflammatory responses and produce unintended biological effects (Li et al., 2021; Mathieu et al., 2005).  
Additionally, while there is evidence of efficacy in non-ocular models and even in an hfRPE culture system, there is a paucity of robust in vivo data specifically demonstrating efficacy in ocular or AMD preclinical models. Modern translational approaches demand rigorous evaluation of pharmacokinetics, tissue penetration, ocular tolerability, and local off-target activity in the complex microenvironment of the eye—data that remain limited for SB290157 in the AMD setting (Iyer et al., 2017; Li et al., 2021). Furthermore, owing to its reputation as a “controversial” tool compound, some in the field recommend the use of complementary genetic models (e.g., C3aR knockout mice) to validate findings derived from its use (Coulthard, 2015; Li et al., 2021). This underscores the need for next-generation C3aR antagonists with improved selectivity and a more predictable pharmacodynamic profile if the goal is clinical translation for dry AMD.  

In summary, SB290157 has strong theoretical appeal as a means to interrupt a pathological complement cascade that leads to lysosomal dysfunction, impaired CTSD maturation, and ultimately drusen formation in dry AMD. Its prior use in various inflammatory and in vitro RPE models, along with the biochemistry linking C3aR activation to intracellular Ca2+ dysregulation and lysosomal stress, supports the hypothesis that C3aR blockade may be beneficial in preserving RPE function (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018; Iyer et al., 2017). Nonetheless, the intrinsic limitations of SB290157—including its potential for agonistic behavior, off-target C5aR2 activity, and inconsistent effects across different cellular contexts—present significant challenges that must be addressed prior to advancing this candidate into clinical trials for AMD (Ames et al., 2001; Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018; Li et al., 2021).

Overall Evaluation:  
In conclusion, SB290157 is a well-characterized research tool with documented efficacy in blocking complement-mediated inflammatory responses in several animal models as well as in an hfRPE culture system, making it a promising candidate to test the hypothesis that C3aR blockade can prevent lysosomal alkalinization and CTSD dysfunction in dry AMD. Its strengths include a defined mechanism of competitive antagonism at C3aR, cross-species activity, and experimentally demonstrated protective effects against abnormal sub-RPE deposit formation. However, its context-dependent agonist behavior and off-target activation of C5aR2 raise significant concerns about its selectivity and reliability as a clinical therapeutic. Additionally, the limited data regarding ocular pharmacokinetics and direct efficacy in robust in vivo dry AMD models suggest that further validation is required. Thus, while the underlying rationale for targeting complement-mediated lysosomal dysfunction remains compelling, SB290157 is best viewed as a stepping stone toward the development of next-generation C3aR antagonists with improved pharmacological profiles for potential clinical application in dry AMD (Ames et al., 2001; Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018; Li et al., 2021).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
CHIR99021 is a fully synthetic, small-molecule aminopyrimidine that potently inhibits glycogen synthase kinase-3 (GSK3), with common use and profiling as a GSK3β-selective tool compound and canonical Wnt/β-catenin pathway agonist in cell systems (notably embryonic stem cell self-renewal and iPSC generation) (Rethineswaran et al., 2021; Lyssiotis et al., 2011). In ocular biology, CHIR99021 has been implemented as a defined, stage-specific Wnt activator to accelerate and improve directed differentiation of human ESC/iPSC to retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), increasing MITF/OTX2, pigmentation, and RPE functional readouts (apical PEDF, basal VEGF, integrin αVβ5–dependent phagocytosis) when applied at 3 μM during a defined mid-specification window (days 8–14) (Leach et al., 2015). Beyond development and differentiation protocols, CHIR99021 (as CHIR trihydrochloride) has been developed into an in vivo pharmacology tool with validated LC/MS assays and tissue PK in mice; after a 25 mg/kg intraperitoneal dose, it achieves rapid systemic distribution and measurable retinal exposure with prolonged ocular retention relative to plasma and liver (plasma Tmax ~30 min, liver Tmax ~30 min, retina Tmax ~30 min; terminal half-lives ~118, 120, and 405 min, respectively) (DiCesare et al., 2023).

As a GSK3 inhibitor, CHIR99021 belongs to a class leveraged widely across neuroscience, regenerative medicine, and retinal biology. In retinal preclinical systems this class has been used in models of retinitis pigmentosa, optic nerve injury/regeneration, and steroid-induced glaucoma; clinically, lithium chloride (LiCl) remains the only FDA-approved GSK3 inhibitor but with a narrow therapeutic window and mixed efficacy for neurodegenerative disease (DiCesare et al., 2023). In RPE disease–relevant preclinical work, low-dose CHIR99021 exposure in RPE-derived models reduces production/secretion of the EFEMP1/F3 glycoprotein and broadly represses extracellular matrix (ECM), complement, protease, and TGFβ-associated components linked to sub-RPE deposit biology; in vivo, systemic CHIR99021 prevents formation of basal laminar deposits (BLamD) in a homozygous EFEMP1 R345W knock-in mouse (ML/DHRD, an AMD-like pathology) without detectable retinal toxicity on scotopic ERG and H&E histology over one month (DiCesare et al., 2023).

Therapeutic History  
Class history in neural/retinal indications: GSK3 is a central kinase with broad substrate scope (>100 substrates) and regulates Wnt/β-catenin, PI3K/Akt, mTOR, NF-κB, and apoptosis pathways central to retinal homeostasis and degeneration (Hottin et al., 2022). Across retinal neurodegeneration models, GSK3 inhibitors have shown neuroprotection (e.g., in rd10 retinitis pigmentosa, NMDA excitotoxicity, and diabetic retinopathy), and GSK3 inhibition is mechanistically linked to CNS axon regeneration pathways (e.g., via CRMP2, mTOR), though effects are context-dependent and can diverge across cell types and disease stages (Hottin et al., 2022). The translational record for systemic GSK3 inhibition is mixed; lithium’s broad CNS history underscores both feasibility and risk of narrow windows and systemic effects, motivating localized ocular delivery or targeted strategies for retinal disease (Hottin et al., 2022; DiCesare et al., 2023).

CHIR99021 in ocular biology and disease: In vitro, CHIR99021 is a core Wnt agonist in hESC/hiPSC-to-RPE protocols where it improves RPE specification, pigmentation, and function when properly staged; its effects can be recapitulated by WNT3A (canonical) but not by WNT5A (non-canonical), consistent with a canonical Wnt readout (Leach et al., 2015). In applied disease models:

- Anti-deposit/ECM remodeling in EFEMP1-driven pathology: Using ARPE-19 edited lines expressing HiBiT-tagged F3 (WT and R345W), CHIR99021 reduced F3 transcript and protein in both intracellular and secreted compartments without overt cytotoxicity; genetic knockdown of GSK3α/β phenocopied and synergized, supporting an on-target mechanism (DiCesare et al., 2023). Low-dose, longer-term exposure (1 μM for 1 week) suppressed ECM, complement, metalloproteinase, and TGFβ-associated proteins in proteomics (≥2-fold reductions in multiple collagens, MMP2, SERPINE1, LTBP2, TGFβ1; decreases in HMGB1/2, C3; reductions in FBLN1/2) and produced parallel RNA-seq changes (downregulation of genes linked to sub-RPE deposits and ECM crosslinking; upregulation of TYR/TYRP1 and PEDF) without detectable activation of canonical TCF reporters, establishing a low-dose on-target biochemical window (DiCesare et al., 2023). Functionally, 1 μM CHIR99021 for 1 week normalized the R345W F3–linked elevation in MMP2 activity and reduced HiBiT F3 secretion apically and basally in transwell cultures (DiCesare et al., 2023).

- In vivo efficacy and PK: In EFEMP1 R345W+/+ mice (~8 months old), systemic CHIR trihydrochloride (25 mg/kg IP, weekdays for 1 month) reduced the fraction of retinal FOVs containing BLamD from 14.205% to 4.167% and halved the mean deposit area (0.817 to 0.416 μm²), with no detectable ERG or histological toxicity (DiCesare et al., 2023). LC/MS/MS PK in plasma, liver, and retina confirmed rapid tissue distribution at 30 min and prolonged retinal retention (retina terminal T½ ~405 min) with estimated intraocular concentrations on the order of the effective in vitro range over the first hours (e.g., ~1.3 μM at 30 min and ~0.36 μM at 6 h) (DiCesare et al., 2023). Analytical assay development and rigorous methodology are reported (DiCesare et al., 2023).

- Regeneration/reprogramming contexts: CHIR99021 is a frequent component of small-molecule cocktails that reprogram Müller glia toward photoreceptor-like fates, induce Rho+ cells in vitro and in degenerate mouse retinas, and is used in multi-pathway modulation (Wnt activation combined with inhibitors of TGF-β, BMP, and Notch) to enhance MC-derived photoreceptor-like outputs; effects vary with species/model, and cocktails require careful balance (Fujii et al., 2021; Hottin et al., 2022). CHIR99021 also appears in chemical reprogramming schemes that convert adult human RPE to dopaminergic neurons and in multi-factor protocols generating photoreceptor progenitors from RPE or iPSCs, generally in combination with other pathway modulators and epigenetic agents (Rzhanova et al., 2024).

- Safety and adverse contexts: Despite benefits in differentiation, in a large-lesion, macula-sized RPE wound-repair model designed to mimic GA, CHIR99021 hindered lesion closure and yielded morphologically suboptimal infiltrating cells, even though pigmentation outside the lesion increased; EMT-suppressing agents (RepSox, Y-27632) performed better for wound closure under those conditions (Bailey-Steinitz, 2021; Hottin et al., 2022). Reviews caution that GSK3 inhibition can activate VEGF via canonical Wnt and could exacerbate angiogenesis, raising a risk signal for wet AMD contexts and arguing for careful selection of indication (dry vs wet AMD), timing, and combination strategies (e.g., with anti-VEGF) (Hottin et al., 2022).

To our knowledge, no human clinical studies have evaluated CHIR99021 for dry AMD; the most advanced ocular efficacy package is the EFEMP1 R345W mouse, an AMD-like BLamD model, where CHIR achieved both biochemical (ECM/complement/protease remodeling) and morphologic (deposit reduction) endpoints with ocular exposure in the in vitro effective range and no detectable electroretinal toxicity over one month (DiCesare et al., 2023).

Mechanism of Action  
Direct target and pathway entry points: GSK3 exists as α and β isoforms (85% identity), is constitutively active under basal conditions, and is negatively regulated by serine phosphorylation (S21 on α, S9 on β). It phosphorylates primed substrates on Ser/Thr motifs often culminating in β-TrCP recognition and proteasomal degradation of targets including β-catenin in the absence of Wnt; Wnt pathway activation sequesters/inhibits GSK3 within the destruction complex, stabilizing β-catenin and altering transcription via TCF/LEF (Hottin et al., 2022). CHIR99021 pharmacologically inhibits GSK3β and thereby is a canonical Wnt/β-catenin activator in many contexts, explaining its frequent use to bias fate decisions in pluripotent and somatic reprogramming paradigms (Lyssiotis et al., 2011; Leach et al., 2015).

Dose-dependent Wnt signaling in RPE systems: In RPE-derived ARPE-19 models, CHIR99021 shows a clear dose window: at 1 μM for one week it decreases EFEMP1/F3 transcripts/protein and globally represses ECM/complement/TGFβ signatures without detectable activation of TCF reporters; at ≥2.5 μM, TCF reporter activation becomes detectable, indicating canonical Wnt activation above a threshold (DiCesare et al., 2023). This low-dose window was sufficient to reduce MMP2 activity associated with the R345W F3 secretory stress pathophysiology, consistent with broad extracellular remodeling (DiCesare et al., 2023).

On-target genetic support: siRNA knockdown of GSK3α and GSK3β individually reduces F3 and combined knockdown synergizes, phenocopying CHIR’s effect on F3 production and secretion, supporting a GSK3-dependent mechanism for its anti-F3/anti-ECM actions (DiCesare et al., 2023). The effect generalizes across cell types (ARPE-19, human dermal fibroblasts, NIH-3T3), consistent with GSK3’s broad role in secretory/ECM regulation (DiCesare et al., 2023).

Secretory/ECM/complement/TGFβ axis remodeling: One-week, low-dose CHIR caused ≥2-fold reductions in multiple collagens (α1(V), α2(IV), α1(IV), α3(IV)), MMP2, complement C3, HMGB1/2, and TGFβ-related proteins such as SERPINE1/PAI-1 and LTBP2, with transcript-level suppression of ECM crosslinking and EMT-proximal genes (e.g., FN1, LOX, WNT ligands), while upregulating RPE differentiation/pigmentation (TYR, TYRP1) and increasing PEDF (SERPINF1) (DiCesare et al., 2023). These data point to a coordinated shift of the RPE secretome toward reduced pathogenic ECM/complement burden and increased pro-RPE homeostatic factors (e.g., PEDF), in line with the observed mitigation of BLamD in vivo (DiCesare et al., 2023).

mTOR–lysosome/autophagy coupling: Outside the retina, CHIR99021 has been shown to inhibit the Rheb/mTOR axis and increase lysosomal activation and autophagy in late endothelial progenitor cells, with evidence that CHIR reduces phosphorylated mTOR and Rheb independent of β-catenin, via effects attributed to TSC2 and lysosomal mTOR localization (Rethineswaran et al., 2021). These studies connect GSK3β inhibition to increased autophagic flux through mTORC1 suppression at the lysosome, a mechanistic route that in principle converges on transcriptional lysosome biogenesis programs (e.g., TFEB) though TFEB itself was not directly assayed in these reports (Rethineswaran et al., 2021). In retinal disease biology, GSK3 interdigitates with oxidative stress (NRF2 regulation), inflammatory NF-κB signaling, and mTOR pathways that are all implicated in AMD pathogenesis; pharmacologic GSK3β inhibition can increase NRF2 and reduce ROS in diabetic contexts, and reduced GSK3 activity in microglia dampens LPS-induced NF-κB signaling, underscoring additional protective axes that may be engaged in RPE or choroid (Hottin et al., 2022).

Angiogenic and repair liabilities: GSK3 inhibition/Wnt activation can increase VEGF and angiogenesis; reviews caution this may be beneficial in dry AMD (neuroprotection/anti-inflammatory) but harmful in wet AMD, suggesting indication-specific selection and potential need for combination with anti-VEGF or restricted/local delivery (Hottin et al., 2022). In a large RPE wound model mimicking GA-scale atrophy, continuous CHIR exposure hindered repair, in contrast to EMT-suppressing agents that improved closure, highlighting a context where Wnt activation can be counterproductive for lesion repopulation (Bailey-Steinitz, 2021).

Mechanistic net assessment for dry AMD: In RPE disease–proximal models, CHIR99021’s dominant effects at low dose are anti-secretory for F3/EFEMP1 and anti-ECM/complement/TGFβ, with reduced MMP2 and enhanced RPE differentiation markers, culminating in prevention of BLamD in vivo without electrophysiologic deficits over one month (DiCesare et al., 2023). Independent data show CHIR increases autophagy and lysosomal function via mTOR inhibition in other cell types, a mechanistic route that could contribute to proteostasis restoration in the RPE but remains to be demonstrated directly in RPE/AMD systems (Rethineswaran et al., 2021).

Expected Effect  
Assay-level predictions under the stated hypothesis: The team’s hypothesis posits that CHIR99021 will inhibit GSK3β in RPE, facilitate TFEB nuclear localization, enhance lysosomal acidification and cathepsin D (CTSD) maturation, increase autophagic flux, and thereby prevent RPE atrophy in dry AMD. Direct evidence for TFEB nuclear localization or CTSD maturation with CHIR99021 in RPE is not yet provided in the extant literature summarized here; however, two mechanistic pillars are established:

- In RPE disease models, low-dose CHIR99021 reduces a causal secretory burden (EFEMP1/F3) and pathogenic ECM/complement/protease output, normalizes MMP2 activity, increases homeostatic PEDF, and prevents BLamD formation in vivo, providing a deposit-centric, mechanistically credible route to slow early and mid-stage dry AMD pathology that is driven by sub-RPE matrix remodeling and complement activation (DiCesare et al., 2023).

- In non-ocular cells, CHIR99021 inhibits mTOR signaling at the lysosome (reduced Rheb/p-mTOR) and increases lysosomal activation and autophagy independent of β-catenin, consistent with a mechanism that would be predicted to favor TFEB nuclear translocation, transcription of lysosome/autophagy genes, and maturation of proteases such as CTSD; these precise endpoints have not been measured in RPE with CHIR99021 and thus remain to be validated (Rethineswaran et al., 2021).

Given GSK3 expression in ARPE-19 and its manipulation in the cited experiments (use of anti-GSK3α/β antibodies and on-target siRNA phenocopy), RPE is a relevant target cell for CHIR99021’s kinase inhibition (DiCesare et al., 2023). Under oxidative and secretory stress common to dry AMD, one would expect CHIR99021 at sub-TCF-activating exposure (≈1 μM) to:

- Reduce EFEMP1/F3 transcription/secretion and broadly depress ECM and complement cues that seed and stabilize BLamD/drusen, thereby lowering sub-RPE deposit biogenesis and associated pro-inflammatory signaling (DiCesare et al., 2023).

- Normalize MMP2 activity and reduce matrix proteolysis-driven remodeling that contributes to basal laminar/basal linear deposit architecture (DiCesare et al., 2023).

- Enhance RPE homeostatic phenotype, reflected by increased pigmentation gene expression and PEDF secretion, which supports photoreceptor survival and RPE trophic function (DiCesare et al., 2023).

- Potentially increase autophagic flux and lysosomal competence via mTOR inhibition, improving clearance of aggregation-prone or secretory-stressed substrates; this inference is supported mechanistically outside the retina and should be formally confirmed in RPE by LC3 flux, p62/SQSTM1 turnover, LAMP1/2, lysotracker, and cathepsin maturation assays (Rethineswaran et al., 2021).

Boundary conditions and risks for the expected effect: The low-dose window is critical; at ≥2.5 μM, CHIR99021 activates canonical Wnt/TCF reporters in RPE-derived cells, and continuous Wnt activation can impair large-lesion RPE repair and increase angiogenic drive (VEGF), both of which are undesirable in late-stage GA or in patients at risk of conversion to exudative AMD (DiCesare et al., 2023; Bailey-Steinitz, 2021; Hottin et al., 2022). In vivo PK after 25 mg/kg IP yields retinal concentrations in the 0.15–1.3 μM range over the first 24 h, overlapping the RPE efficacy window for EFEMP1/ECM suppression and below the Wnt activation threshold in vitro; however, local ocular delivery and controlled-release formulations may be preferable to avoid systemic exposure and to maintain sub-TCF-activating intraocular concentrations (DiCesare et al., 2023; Hottin et al., 2022).

Overall Evaluation  

Strengths  
- Disease-proximal efficacy with mechanistic depth. CHIR99021 reduces EFEMP1/F3 production (transcript and protein), broadly suppresses ECM/complement/TGFβ secretome programs, decreases MMP2 activity, upregulates pigmentation genes and PEDF, and prevents BLamD in an EFEMP1 R345W knock-in model—an AMD-like pathology characterized by sub-RPE matrix deposits (DiCesare et al., 2023). The convergence of proteomics, transcriptomics, reporter assays, and genetic knockdown around GSK3 establishes on-target pathway control in RPE-derived systems (DiCesare et al., 2023).

- Ocular exposure and safety. Tissue PK demonstrates retinal penetrance and prolonged retention (terminal T½ ≈ 6.75 h), with estimated intraocular levels overlapping the in vitro effective window; one month of systemic dosing at 25 mg/kg produced no detectable ERG or histological abnormalities in adult mice, supporting a tolerability window (DiCesare et al., 2023).

- Plausible extension to proteostasis/autophagy. Independent mechanistic data show CHIR99021 inhibits mTORC1 signaling at the lysosome and increases autophagy/lysosomal activation via the TSC2–Rheb axis in non-ocular cells, a route that could bolster RPE lysosomal function under drusen/BLamD-associated stress even if TFEB was not yet directly measured in RPE (Rethineswaran et al., 2021).

- Modality versatility with established use. Extensive prior use of CHIR99021 as a defined Wnt agonist in RPE/retinal differentiation and reprogramming provides a deep operations base for dosing/timing and cell-specific responses, which can be leveraged to avoid undesired pathway activation during therapy (Leach et al., 2015; Fujii et al., 2021).

Weaknesses and risks  
- Translational maturity and source quality. The core anti-deposit efficacy and ocular PK/safety package resides in a bioRxiv preprint; while comprehensive and internally consistent, it lacks peer-reviewed confirmation and replication across independent labs and models (DiCesare et al., 2023). Moreover, the EFEMP1 R345W model (ML/DHRD) is a rare, early-onset macular dystrophy with AMD-like deposits; it does not recapitulate the full aging/inflammation/metabolic milieu of typical dry AMD (DiCesare et al., 2023).

- Wnt/angiogenesis liability and wound repair. GSK3β inhibition is a canonical Wnt activator and can increase VEGF/angiogenesis, potentially contraindicating use in patients with neovascular risk; in RPE monolayers with macula-sized lesions, CHIR99021 impaired lesion repair despite increasing peripheral pigmentation, highlighting a deleterious effect in GA-like settings requiring repopulation (Hottin et al., 2022; Bailey-Steinitz, 2021).

- Dose/timing and cell-type dependency. Benefits of GSK3 modulation are highly context-dependent in retinal disease; the same pathway promotes different outcomes across disease stage and cell types (photoreceptors, Müller glia, RPE, endothelium). Reviews emphasize that treatment timing, duration, and targeted retinal layer will determine benefit vs harm (DiCesare et al., 2023; Hottin et al., 2022). The in vitro window where 1 μM avoids TCF activation is narrow; in vivo pharmacology must control ocular exposure carefully (DiCesare et al., 2023).

- Mechanistic gap for the autophagy/TFEB claim in RPE. Although CHIR99021 increases autophagy through mTOR suppression in other cell types, direct evidence in human RPE or RPE-derived models for TFEB nuclear translocation, lysosomal acidification improvements, or CTSD maturation with CHIR99021 is currently absent from the surveyed literature; this is an experimental gap relative to the team’s stated hypothesis (Rethineswaran et al., 2021).

Development recommendations  
- Indication scoping to dry AMD segments with deposit-dominated pathology. Based on anti-ECM/complement and anti-BLamD efficacy, prioritize early/mid dry AMD segments characterized by drusen/sub-RPE deposits and low neovascular risk; de-prioritize active geographic atrophy where repopulation/repair of large RPE lesions is the therapeutic aim, given the CHIR-associated repair impairment in vitro (DiCesare et al., 2023; Bailey-Steinitz, 2021).

- Local ocular delivery to widen the therapeutic index. Intravitreal or suprachoroidal controlled-release systems should be evaluated to maintain intraocular concentrations in the ~0.1–1 μM range that achieve biochemical efficacy but remain below the canonical Wnt activation threshold, while minimizing systemic exposure and wet-AMD conversion risk; the reviews support local delivery as a strategy for GSK3-based ocular interventions (DiCesare et al., 2023; Hottin et al., 2022).

- Mechanistic validation in RPE for proteostasis endpoints. Quantify VEGF and angiogenic markers (VEGFA mRNA/protein, HIF-1α targets) in RPE/choroid after CHIR, and consider anti-VEGF co-therapy if Wnt-VEGF coupling poses a risk; preclinical reviews support the rationale for combination or timing-restricted inhibition to avoid pro-angiogenic consequences (Hottin et al., 2022).

Test CHIR in aging-related and inflammation-metabolism models (e.g., high-fat diet + complement stress; smoke exposure; ApoE variants) in addition to EFEMP1 R345W to ensure generalizability beyond monogenic ECM disease; define the minimal exposure and duration to alter drusen/BLamD dynamics and microglial/complement activation (DiCesare et al., 2023).

- Dose-finding anchored to ocular PK/PD. Use the established LC/MS retinal assay to map intravitreal/subconjunctival/suprachoroidal dose to retinal/choroidal concentration–time profiles; overlay with PD markers (F3 secretion, ECM transcripts, complement, PEDF) to define a sub-TCF window in vivo; confirm absence of ERG deficits and retinal histopathology across multi-month dosing (DiCesare et al., 2023).

Lithium’s status as the sole FDA-approved GSK3 inhibitor and mixed outcomes of GSK3 modulation in retinal disease underscore the need to target specific retinal layers or cell types and to avoid broad systemic inhibition; this aligns with adopting local ocular delivery and possibly RPE-targeted formulations (DiCesare et al., 2023; Hottin et al., 2022).

Conclusion  
On balance, CHIR99021 has a compelling, disease-proximal efficacy package for dry AMD centered on sub-RPE deposit biology. At low doses that do not detectably activate canonical Wnt, CHIR99021 reduces EFEMP1/F3 and globally attenuates ECM/complement/protease pathways in RPE-derived systems, increases PEDF and pigmentation gene expression, and prevents BLamD formation in an EFEMP1 R345W mouse model, with retinal exposures matching in vitro efficacy windows and month-long dosing without ERG/histology toxicity (DiCesare et al., 2023). Independent mechanistic data demonstrate CHIR-mediated inhibition of Rheb/mTOR and increased lysosomal/autophagic activity in non-ocular cells, consistent with the proteostasis-restoring arm of the team’s hypothesis, but direct evidence for TFEB nuclear translocation and CTSD maturation in RPE with CHIR is currently lacking and should be considered a key validation gap (Rethineswaran et al., 2021). The principal risks are Wnt-linked angiogenesis (potentially harmful in wet AMD) and impaired RPE wound repair in GA-like lesions when Wnt activation is sustained; these risks argue for a dry-AMD, early/mid-stage positioning, careful intraocular dose control to remain below the TCF activation threshold, and consideration of local delivery and/or anti-VEGF combinations in higher-risk patients (Hottin et al., 2022; Bailey-Steinitz, 2021).

Overall, CHIR99021 is a promising repurposed candidate for dry AMD if developed within a well-defined exposure window and indication niche. Its strengths are a clear kinase target with on-target cellular genetics, strong anti-deposit and secretome remodeling data in RPE and in vivo, ocular exposure that aligns with cellular pharmacology, and plausible lysosome/autophagy engagement. Its weaknesses are translational maturity (preprint stage; single primary in vivo model), Wnt-associated angiogenesis and repair liabilities at higher/continuous exposure, and incomplete validation of the autophagy/TFEB axis in RPE. A go decision for preclinical advancement is justified, contingent on rapid mechanistic confirmation in RPE for autophagy/lysosome endpoints, rigorous angiogenesis/wound-repair safety pharmacology, and PK/PD-guided local delivery strategies that maintain sub-TCF intraocular concentrations (DiCesare et al., 2023; Hottin et al., 2022; Rethineswaran et al., 2021).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Ambroxol is a small-molecule mucolytic historically used to thin airway mucus and has been repurposed as a pharmacological chaperone for the lysosomal enzyme glucocerebrosidase (GCase) in Gaucher disease, where it selectively binds misfolded GCase to aid folding and trafficking to lysosomes for substrate degradation (Alhowyan & Harisa, 2025, pp. 17–18). Pharmacological chaperones constitute a class of small molecules that stabilize specific mutant lysosomal enzymes conformationally in the endoplasmic reticulum, enabling correct processing and lysosomal delivery; a paradigmatic example is migalastat, an alpha-galactosidase A chaperone approved for Fabry disease with amenable variants (Alhowyan & Harisa, 2025, pp. 17–18). Ambroxol is further characterized by its ability to cross the blood–brain barrier, a property relevant for neuronopathic lysosomal storage disorders and attractive for central nervous system or ocular indications where access is otherwise constrained (Alhowyan & Harisa, 2025, pp. 17–18). Within the broader landscape of lysosomal therapeutics, small molecules also act as proteostasis regulators and modulators of lysosomal signaling and biogenesis; however, off-target actions remain a central limitation of small-molecule therapy in this domain (Alhowyan & Harisa, 2025, pp. 17–18).

The therapeutic hypothesis for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) posits that ambroxol could act as a pharmacological chaperone for lysosomal enzymes in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), stabilize or enhance vacuolar H+-ATPase (V-ATPase) function, improve lysosomal acidification, and thereby augment cathepsin D (CTSD) activity to clear lipofuscin/drusen components characteristic of dry AMD (Kaarniranta et al., 2023, pp. 2–3; Si et al., 2023, pp. 4–7). This rationale is grounded in the centrality of lysosomal function to RPE homeostasis and AMD pathogenesis: RPE lysosomes sustain heavy heterophagic and autophagic loads from daily photoreceptor outer-segment (POS) digestion, and impaired lysosomal acidification and hydrolase function contribute to lipofuscin accumulation, exosome-driven drusen formation, and progressive degeneration (Kaarniranta et al., 2023, pp. 2–3; Si et al., 2023, pp. 2–4, 5–7; Sharif, 2015, pp. 199–202). Notably, in AMD models and donor RPE, TFEB—the master transcriptional driver of lysosomal/autophagy biogenesis—is dysregulated, V-ATPase-related transcripts (e.g., ATP6VOA1) and cathepsin abundance/activity are linked to lysosomal competence, and TFEB activation or mTOR inhibition reduces toxic storage material such as A2E and POS-derived autofluorescent granules (Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7).

Therapeutic History  
Conventional use: Ambroxol is primarily used clinically as a mucolytic agent to reduce mucus viscosity in respiratory disease (Alhowyan & Harisa, 2025, pp. 17–18). Beyond its mucolytic effects, ambroxol has been investigated in lysosomal storage diseases as a pharmacological chaperone for glucocerebrosidase; it binds misfolded GCase, promotes its proper folding/trafficking to lysosomes, and facilitates substrate clearance, with reported neurological benefits in neuronopathic Gaucher disease and demonstrated blood–brain barrier penetration (Alhowyan & Harisa, 2025, pp. 17–18). Clinically observed improvements in neurological symptoms such as myoclonus and seizures have been reported in pilot studies, and reviews summarize safety/efficacy observations in Gaucher populations, albeit with the caveat of potential off-target toxicities innate to small-molecule approaches (Alhowyan & Harisa, 2025, pp. 17–18, 33–35).

Use in ophthalmology and AMD: A targeted search of ClinicalTrials.gov for ambroxol in macular degeneration, AMD, or retinal conditions returned zero registered trials, indicating a lack of clinical testing for ambroxol in AMD or retina-specific indications within that registry (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.). The provided literature excerpts contain no preclinical or clinical data demonstrating ambroxol use in RPE, retinal degeneration models, or AMD, and they do not report ocular distribution or ocular pharmacokinetics for ambroxol (Alhowyan & Harisa, 2025, pp. 17–18; Si et al., 2023, pp. 2–4; Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7). In contrast, other small-molecule interventions that modulate lysosomal/autophagy function in RPE have been reported: mTOR inhibition with rapamycin decreases A2E and lipofuscin-like granules and reduces inflammatory/angiogenic proteins; trehalose increases autophagy markers and flux and exhibits cytoprotective effects, although limitations in clinical efficacy and adverse effects are noted for mTOR inhibitors (Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7). More broadly, pharmacologic restoration of lysosomal pH and regulatory control of V-ATPase–mTORC1 signaling in RPE have been explored mechanistically, underscoring the translational target plausibility but not implicating ambroxol specifically (Kaarniranta et al., 2023, pp. 2–3; Markitantova & Simirskii, 2025, pp. 24–25).

Mechanism of Action  
Ambroxol as a pharmacological chaperone: Ambroxol binds selectively to misfolded glucocerebrosidase (GCase), stabilizing its conformation in the biosynthetic pathway and enabling correct trafficking to lysosomes, where it restores enzymatic degradation of GCase substrates (Alhowyan & Harisa, 2025, pp. 17–18). This canonical chaperone mechanism increases lysosomal GCase activity and substrate turnover and has been linked to functional improvements in Gaucher disease models and patient reports, with additional indications that ambroxol can enhance mitochondrial function in patient-derived cells (Alhowyan & Harisa, 2025, pp. 17–18). The drug’s small-molecule nature and CNS penetrance differentiate it from enzyme-replacement approaches and position it within a class of proteostasis-modulating agents where target-specific engagement can produce organelle-level functional rescue but also carries risk of off-target interactions (Alhowyan & Harisa, 2025, pp. 17–18).

RPE lysosomal biology relevant to the hypothesis: In the RPE, lysosomal acidification is primarily established by the V-ATPase proton pump and is essential for optimal activity of luminal hydrolases including cathepsins; most lysosomal enzymes are exquisitely pH-dependent and lose activity when lysosomal pH is elevated (Markitantova & Simirskii, 2025, pp. 9–11; Kaarniranta et al., 2023, pp. 2–3). RPE lysosomes operate at the nexus of two degradative streams: heterophagy of POS (requiring efficient phagosome–lysosome fusion and acidic hydrolase activity) and macroautophagy/CMA for damaged proteins and organelles, both of which are dysregulated with aging and AMD-relevant stresses such as oxidative damage and advanced glycation end-products (AGEs) (Si et al., 2023, pp. 4–5; Kaarniranta et al., 2023, pp. 2–3; Sharif, 2015, pp. 199–202). CTSD is a key RPE lysosomal aspartic protease and the principal POS-degrading enzyme; CTSD loss causes retinal degeneration in mice, underscoring its nonredundant role (Si et al., 2023, pp. 4–5). In AMD, human donor RPE show decreased CTSD and CTSL levels/activities, increased TFEB phosphorylation with reduced nuclear localization, and impaired degradative capacity with accumulation of POS-dependent lipofuscin-like granules; activating TFEB in RPE increases CLEAR network gene expression including ATP6VOA1 (a V-ATPase subunit) and reduces POS-derived lipofuscin-like granules (Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7). Oxidized bisretinoids such as A2E, a major lipofuscin component, inhibit V-ATPase and raise lysosomal pH in RPE, which decreases lysosomal enzyme function and impairs cargo hydrolysis—a direct mechanism linking storage material to acidification defects (Wang et al., 2023, pp. 11–13). Lipofuscin and its photoproducts can further inhibit lysosomal proton pumps or hydrolases and promote lysosomal membrane permeabilization, coupling storage to organelle damage and propagating autophagy-lysosomal dysfunction and inflammatory signaling (Si et al., 2023, pp. 5–7; Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 2–4).

Signal control of lysosomal biogenesis and acidification in RPE: The V-ATPase–mTORC1–TFEB axis is central in RPE lysosomal homeostasis; CRYBA1/βA3/A1-crystallin directly regulates the V-ATPase and signals to mTORC1 at the lysosomal membrane, where mTORC1 activity controls TFEB phosphorylation and localization (phosphorylated TFEB is cytosolic; dephosphorylation permits nuclear translocation and activation of CLEAR network genes) (Kaarniranta et al., 2023, pp. 2–3; Markitantova & Simirskii, 2025, pp. 9–11; Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7). Pharmacologic mTOR inhibition (e.g., rapamycin) shifts TFEB toward an active dephosphorylated state, increases autophagic flux, reduces A2E, and decreases lipofuscin-like granules in RPE and POS-fed models, with the reduction in storage material being dependent on active lysosomal enzymes and TFEB activation (Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7). Trehalose also augments autophagy markers and flux with cytoprotective effects in RPE insult models, supporting the druggability of lysosome–autophagy axes (Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7).

A rigorous, staged preclinical plan is warranted:  
- In vitro RPE assays under A2E and POS-fed conditions to quantify lysosomal pH, V-ATPase subunit expression (ATP6VOA1), TFEB nuclear translocation/CLEAR activation, CTSD maturation/activity, POS degradation kinetics, and lipofuscin-like autofluorescence, with rapamycin and trehalose as mechanistically validated comparators (Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7; Wang et al., 2023, pp. 11–13).

Overall, ambroxol’s demonstrated chaperone activity for GCase, BBB penetration, and clinical observations in Gaucher disease establish it as a plausible proteostasis-modulating scaffold, but the lack of any RPE/AMD-directed mechanistic or efficacy evidence and the absence of ocular PK data create a high translational risk profile for dry AMD (Alhowyan & Harisa, 2025, pp. 17–18; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.). AICAR (5‐aminoimidazole‐4‐carboxamide ribonucleoside), commercially available as Sigma A9978, is a purine nucleoside analogue originally identified as an adenosine-related compound that is taken up into cells via equilibrative nucleoside transporters and then phosphorylated by adenosine kinase into its monophosphorylated form, ZMP (Gruzman et al., 2009; Hardie, 2014). Unlike synthetic small molecules designed solely to bind regulatory subunits of AMPK, AICAR requires intracellular phosphorylation to ZMP—a process that confers a basis in natural purine metabolism as ZMP is an intermediate in de novo purine synthesis—and thereby mimics the endogenous activator AMP (Hardie, 2014; Gruzman et al., 2009). Being a small nucleoside analogue, AICAR is structurally simple compared to some of the more recently developed direct AMPK activators; its well‐delineated chemical structure, mechanism of cellular conversion, and availability from commercial sources make it an attractive candidate for repurposing studies (Drew & Kingwell, 2008; Guerrieri et al., 2017).

Historically, AICAR has been extensively used as a research tool to probe the biology of AMPK, which is central to metabolic regulation, and it has demonstrated efficacy in a wide variety of preclinical models including skeletal muscle, adipocytes, hepatocytes, and specific cancer models (Drew & Kingwell, 2008). At the molecular level, AICAR functions by entering cells through nucleoside transporters and undergoing phosphorylation by adenosine kinase to yield ZMP, which is structurally analogous to AMP and thus capable of binding to the regulatory Bateman domains of the AMPK γ subunit (Gruzman et al., 2009; Hardie, 2014). Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
USP14 inhibitor IU1 (Sigma SML0010) is a synthetic small-molecule compound originally discovered through high-throughput screening efforts aimed at identifying inhibitors of deubiquitinating enzymes (DUBs) associated with the proteasome. IU1 belongs to the class of small-molecule DUB inhibitors that specifically target USP14, a proteasome-associated deubiquitinase responsible for trimming ubiquitin chains from substrates before their degradation by the 26S proteasome. Early medicinal chemistry studies led to the development of IU1 and its more potent analogs (such as IU1-47), which exploit structure–activity relationships on a benzene–dimethyl-pyrrole scaffold with tailored electron-withdrawing substitutions and lipophilic enhancements designed to improve potency, selectivity, and bioavailability (Lim et al., 2024; Boselli et al., 2017; Qin et al., 2024). These compounds are cell permeable and have been employed as chemical probes in multiple preclinical settings to modulate proteostasis via targeted inhibition of USP14. In essence, IU1 reflects a series of rationally designed molecules aimed at shifting the balance of proteasome-mediated degradation by preventing USP14’s “trimming” activity, thereby effectively accelerating the clearance of misfolded and aggregation-prone proteins.

Therapeutic History:  
The therapeutic history of USP14 inhibitors like IU1 is primarily rooted in preclinical research addressing proteostasis dysfunction in models of aging and neurodegeneration rather than in clinical or veterinary practice. In Drosophila models of proteostasis-associated aging, IU1 treatment was shown to reduce the accumulation of polyubiquitinated aggregates, increase autophagy markers such as LC3, improve behavioral phenotypes, and even extend lifespan, with these benefits abrogated when autophagy was experimentally disrupted (Lim et al., 2024). In mammalian cell proteotoxicity models—using stressors such as canavanine plus azetidine—IU1 has similarly been reported to reduce ubiquitin conjugate accumulation and enhance autophagic responses (Lim et al., 2024). Moreover, in primary neuronal cultures, more potent analogs like IU1-47 have been used to promote degradation of pathologic proteins such as tau, thereby supporting the concept that USP14 inhibition enhances proteasome-assisted clearance of aggregation-prone substrates (Boselli et al., 2017; Kiprowska, 2016). Despite these promising preclinical data in models of neurodegeneration and systemic aging, there is no direct evidence to date that IU1 or its analogs have been applied to treat dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or geographic atrophy specifically. However, given that several key observations in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells—such as evidence of impaired ubiquitin–proteasome system (UPS) and autophagy cross-talk, aggregate accumulation, and lysosomal dysfunction—are central to AMD pathology (Blasiak et al., 2019; Kaarniranta et al., 2023; Shang & Taylor, 2012), repurposing IU1 to restore proteostasis in RPE represents an innovative extension of its preclinical use.

Mechanism of Action:  
The known mechanism of IU1 centers on its inhibition of USP14, a deubiquitinating enzyme that transiently associates with the proteasome. USP14 normally functions by “trimming” ubiquitin chains on substrates as they enter the proteasome, an activity that can delay substrate degradation and allow for substrate rescue under stress conditions. IU1 and its optimized analogs (e.g., IU1-47) act through allosteric mechanisms—not by directly competing at the catalytic site but by binding a pocket distal (approximately 8.3 Å away) from the catalytic center, thereby perturbing USP14’s structural conformation and catalytic efficiency (Qin et al., 2024; Lim et al., 2024). Inhibition of USP14 by IU1 leads to a reduced removal of ubiquitin chains, effectively “locking in” the ubiquitin tag on misfolded and aggregation-prone proteins and facilitating their recognition and degradation by the 26S proteasome. Beyond its direct impact on proteasomal degradation, USP14 inhibition has been reported to modulate autophagy—evident from increased LC3 lipidation and autophagic flux in certain cellular contexts (Lim et al., 2024; Kim, 2020). Some studies suggest that USP14 may also indirectly influence autophagy by regulating the turnover of factors such as UVRAG, a key autophagy regulator, although these connections remain to be fully elucidated. Notably, while IU1 has been shown to accelerate aggregate clearance in neuronal and Drosophila models, a series of studies have also flagged potential off-target effects at higher concentrations, including inhibition of mitochondrial Complex I leading to ATP depletion and subsequent activation of calpain-mediated proteolysis (Kiprowska, 2016; Kiprowska et al., n.d.). Hence, the molecular interactions of IU1 are complex and highly context-dependent, with the potential to both enhance proteasomal degradation and, at non-optimized doses, induce metabolic perturbations.

Expected Effect:  
In the context of dry age-related macular degeneration, particularly geographic atrophy, the central hypothesis is that IU1 will inhibit USP14 in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells, thereby accelerating the proteasome-assisted clearance of misfolded, aggregation-prone proteins. RPE cells in AMD display defects in both the UPS and the autophagy/lysosomal systems, with studies documenting decreased proteasome activity, accumulation of ubiquitinated aggregates, elevated levels of the selective autophagy adaptor SQSTM1/p62, and lysosomal dysfunction including impaired acidification mediated by vacuolar ATPase (v-ATPase) (Blasiak et al., 2019; Kaarniranta et al., 2023; Shang & Taylor, 2012; Viiri, 2019). By inhibiting USP14, IU1 is expected to shift the proteostasis balance in RPE cells towards enhanced degradation of misfolded proteins via the proteasome. This would not only reduce the intracellular aggregate burden but also alleviate the overloading of the lysosomal pathway—in turn potentially restoring lysosomal functions such as proper acidification by v-ATPase activity. Improved lysosomal acidification is known to facilitate the maturation and activity of cathepsin D, a key lysosomal protease responsible for degrading various protein aggregates and damaged organelles (Kaarniranta et al., 2023). The overall evaluation of USP14 inhibitor IU1 as a therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration is cautiously optimistic yet highlights several critical areas for further investigation. On the positive side, IU1 represents an innovative strategy targeting a central node in protein quality control—USP14—that regulates the degradation of misfolded, aggregation-prone proteins via the proteasome and modulates autophagic pathways. Preclinical evidence in Drosophila models and neuronal cultures demonstrates that pharmacological USP14 inhibition can enhance aggregate clearance, improve proteostasis, and even extend lifespan and motor function under proteotoxic stress conditions (Lim et al., 2024; Boselli et al., 2017). These findings support the concept that modulating the UPS–autophagy interplay may be beneficial in diseases where proteostasis failure is a key driver, such as dry AMD, in which RPE cells experience aggregate build-up, defective autophagy, and lysosomal dysfunction (Blasiak et al., 2019; Kaarniranta et al., 2023; Shang & Taylor, 2012).

Furthermore, the biochemical mechanism by which IU1 operates—namely, reducing the deubiquitinating activity of USP14 to promote ubiquitin-tag retention and substrate commitment to degradation—provides a theoretically attractive approach to simultaneously reduce the proteasomal backlog and relieve lysosomal burden. The potential secondary effects on autophagy, including improved LC3-II turnover and possibly upregulated clearance of aggregates through aggrephagy, add further appeal to the candidate as a multi-modal modulator of proteostasis. The cell-permeable, small-molecule nature of IU1, along with available more potent analogs (such as IU1-47), offers promising opportunities for medicinal chemistry optimization and dosage refinement, especially important given the need for safe application in delicate ocular tissues.

However, several weaknesses and challenges must be addressed before IU1 can be considered a viable therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. A significant concern originates from studies in neuronal systems that indicate off-target effects at higher concentrations—specifically, inhibition of mitochondrial Complex I, ATP depletion, and activation of calpain-mediated proteolysis (Kiprowska, 2016; Kiprowska et al., n.d.). These potential toxicities raise the possibility that a narrow therapeutic window may exist, necessitating thorough dose-response studies in RPE cell models to ensure efficacy without compromising cell viability. Moreover, no direct preclinical studies have yet evaluated IU1 in RPE cells or in animal models of geographic atrophy. As such, critical parameters—such as its ability to modulate v-ATPase function, maintain lysosomal acidification, boost cathepsin D activity, and ultimately clear RPE-specific aggregates such as lipofuscin or oxidized photoreceptor debris—remain to be validated (Kaarniranta et al., 2023; Shang & Taylor, 2012).

Additionally, while the mechanistic data from neurodegenerative models are compelling, the biochemical environment of RPE cells differs from that of neurons in several key respects. RPE cells are highly phagocytic, exposed to constant oxidative stress, and rely on a finely tuned balance between proteasomal and lysosomal pathways to manage the constant influx of photoreceptor outer segment material (Blasiak et al., 2019; Viiri, 2019). Thus, any intervention that modulates proteostasis must be carefully tailored to avoid unintended disruptions in these homeostatic processes. The current literature also underscores the complexity of deubiquitinase biology; while USP14 inhibition appears beneficial in some contexts, the intricate interplay with other DUBs and the broader UPS could lead to compensatory mechanisms that diminish the anticipated therapeutic effect or even trigger adverse consequences (Faber & Roepman, 2019; Kim, 2020).

In summary, USP14 inhibitor IU1 offers an innovative and potentially transformative approach to restoring proteostasis in RPE cells by enhancing proteasomal degradation and autophagic clearance of misfolded proteins—a strategy that directly addresses the pathobiology of dry AMD and geographic atrophy as defined by aggregate accumulation and lysosomal dysfunction (Lim et al., 2024; Blasiak et al., 2019; Kaarniranta et al., 2023). The strengths of this candidate include its robust preclinical data in non-RPE systems, its well-characterized mechanism of action, and its amenability to further chemical optimization. However, significant weaknesses, including potential off-target mitochondrial toxicity, an unestablished therapeutic window in RPE cells, and the lack of direct preclinical studies in AMD models, necessitate cautious and rigorous further investigation. To move forward, it will be essential to conduct targeted RPE-specific in vitro assays and in vivo studies—assessing proteasome activity, autophagy flux, lysosomal acidification (v-ATPase function), cathepsin D activity, and aggregate clearance—while carefully monitoring for cytotoxicity. Only with such detailed preclinical validation can the promise of IU1 as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD be fully assessed (Lim et al., 2024; Blasiak et al., 2019; Kiprowska, 2016; Shang & Taylor, 2012).
