Subsequent mechanistic work across the STAC class resolved that many apparent activation signals were substrate/context dependent and, in some assay configurations, artifactual; nevertheless, later kinetic/biophysical and structural studies established that STACs can directly engage SIRT1 via an assisted allosteric mechanism that stabilizes the enzyme–substrate complex, with mutational data showing that E230K/A SIRT1 variants abolish both binding and activation by STACs (Lee et al., 2021; Mazzone, 2018). While most STACs are SIRT1-selective, SRT1720 exhibits notable polypharmacology, including reported inhibitory activity against Sirt3, highlighting potential off-target risks intrinsic to this first-generation class (Mazzone, 2018). As a class, STACs have been widely evaluated for metabolic, inflammatory, neurodegenerative, and aging phenotypes predicated on SIRT1’s broad substrate repertoire (for example, PGC-1α, NF-κB p65/RelA, FOXO family, p53), which link to mitochondrial biogenesis, anti-inflammatory signaling, oxidative stress responses, and cell survival programs (Chang et al., 2024; Mazzone, 2018).

Therapeutic History  
SRT1720 has extensive preclinical use, but there is no evidence in the provided corpus that it has been tested in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), in the eye, or in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) models (cellular or in vivo) (Ji et al., 2021; Ding et al., 2017; Bononi et al., 2022). In non-ocular systems, SRT1720 increased mitochondrial biogenesis and rescued mitochondrial function after oxidant injury in renal proximal tubule cells, providing proof-of-concept that STAC activation can drive PGC-1α–linked mitochondrial programs in mammalian cells under oxidative stress (Ji et al., 2021). In metabolic disease models, SRT1720 is reported to improve hepatic lipid metabolism via SIRT1-dependent pathways regulating PGC-1α, AMPK, PPARα, FOXO1, SREBP-1c and FGF21, with consistent decreases in lipogenesis and inflammation and increases in fatty-acid β-oxidation in NAFLD models (Ding et al., 2017). Multiple lifespan/healthspan studies reported benefits in mice—improved survival and healthspan in diet-induced obese animals and lifespan extension on standard diet—again consistent with systemic SIRT1-axis engagement (Mazzone, 2018). At the same time, substantial controversy surrounds both mechanism and safety. Pacholec et al. argued SRT1720 (and related first-generation STACs) are not direct SIRT1 activators under specific biochemical conditions, although later work provided structural and kinetic support for allosteric activation with specific substrates (Lee et al., 2021; Bononi et al., 2022). Importantly for repurposing risk, SRT1720 promoted tumor cell migration and lung metastasis in a breast cancer model, and SRT1720 can trigger SIRT1-independent cytotoxicity in some hematologic malignancy cells, underscoring unresolved off-target liabilities (Bononi et al., 2022; Chang et al., 2024). No pharmacokinetic (PK), ADME, or clinical tolerability data for SRT1720 are supplied in the present corpus; by contrast, the second-generation STAC SRT2104 has human PK/tolerability and multiple preclinical and clinical signals across diseases, including ocular/neurologic models (but those data cannot be extrapolated to SRT1720 without qualification) (Bononi et al., 2022; Chang et al., 2024). Collectively, the historical record supports that SRT1720 is a pharmacologically active first-generation STAC with broad preclinical use, mixed mechanistic interpretations, and safety concerns; critically, there is no published use in AMD or RPE models in the material provided here (Ji et al., 2021; Bononi et al., 2022).

Mechanism of Action  
- Biochemical pharmacology and target engagement: SRT1720 belongs to the STAC class that can directly activate SIRT1 through an assisted allosteric mechanism requiring specific substrate motifs; mutating SIRT1 E230 disrupts both activator binding and activation, and co-crystal structures of SIRT1 with SRT-like activators support an allosteric binding pocket that enhances deacetylation efficiency in a substrate-dependent manner (Lee et al., 2021; Mazzone, 2018). Early reports of direct activation were contested due to labeled peptide assay artifacts, but subsequent kinetic and structural data reconciled these findings with an allosteric model; nonetheless, the field recognizes pharmacological caveats including context-dependent activation and off-targets, such as reported Sirt3 inhibition by SRT1720 (Mazzone, 2018; Lee et al., 2021).  
- Canonical SIRT1 substrates and pathway biology: SIRT1 deacetylates transcriptional regulators and autophagy/mitophagy machinery that converge on mitochondrial quality control, oxidative stress defense, and inflammatory tone—each relevant to AMD pathogenesis. These include PGC-1α (mitochondrial biogenesis/oxidative metabolism), FOXO1/FOXO3a (antioxidant/autophagy transcription), NF-κB p65/RelA (inflammatory gene programs), p53 (apoptosis/senescence), and Nrf2 (antioxidant transcription), as well as autophagy proteins (e.g., ATG family members and LC3) and trafficking nodes such as Rab7 that promote autophagosome–lysosome fusion (Chang et al., 2024; Luján et al., 2022; Luo et al., 2025). In multiple cell types, SIRT1 activation or NAD⁺ elevation increases PGC-1α activity and mitochondrial biogenesis and can suppress NF-κB signaling via p65 deacetylation, consistent with anti-oxidative and anti-inflammatory effects that are therapeutically desirable in RPE (Ding et al., 2017; Luo et al., 2025).  
- RPE-specific SIRT1/autophagy linkage: In ARPE-19 cells under oxidative stress, PARP1 activation depletes NAD⁺, inhibits SIRT1 (elevated p53 acetylation), and selectively impairs late-stage autophagy by blocking autolysosome formation without preventing autophagosome formation; restoring NAD⁺ or inhibiting PARP1 preserves SIRT1 activity and rescues late autophagic flux, whereas PARP1 inhibition fails to rescue autophagy when SIRT1 is depleted—placing SIRT1 as the essential downstream effector for recovering autophagy in oxidatively stressed RPE (Jang et al., 2020). In vivo, PARP1 inhibition protected the retina in sodium iodate (SI) injury and the benefit was autophagy-dependent, reinforcing the PARP1→NAD⁺→SIRT1→autophagy axis as a mechanistic driver of RPE/retinal resilience (Jang et al., 2020). AMD donor RPE exhibits decreased NAD⁺, reduced SIRT1 levels, increased acetylated (inactive) PGC-1α, impaired AMPK signaling, and hyperactive mTOR—all changes expected to depress SIRT1-dependent autophagy and mitochondrial biogenesis and to contribute to lysosomal/autophagic abnormalities (Zhang et al., 2020).  
- TFEB/CLEAR and lysosomal acidification context: TFEB is the master transcription factor for lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy gene networks (CLEAR), whose nuclear translocation is negatively regulated by mTORC1; CLEAR target upregulation increases lysosomal capacity and flux, while lysosomal ion/pH homeostasis (v-ATPase–dependent proton pumping) determines enzyme activation, including cathepsins such as CTSD (Boya et al., 2023; Falcão et al., 2025; Kaarniranta et al., 2023). In AMD/RPE-relevant literature, TFEB/CLEAR is positioned as a principal lever for lysosomal rejuvenation, and lysosomal acidity and calcium handling are identified as key determinants of autophagic flux and RPE health (Boya et al., 2023). Although sirtuin family members can intersect TFEB signaling (e.g., AKT2/SIRT5/TFEB axis in non-neovascular AMD), direct evidence for SIRT1-driven TFEB deacetylation/activation is not provided in the present corpus; however, PGC-1α has been placed upstream of TFEB in other disease contexts, linking SIRT1→PGC-1α activity to potential TFEB–CLEAR induction by inference (not by direct RPE data) (Falcão et al., 2025).  
- Critical gaps relevant to the working hypothesis: Within the provided literature, there is no direct evidence that SRT1720 activates SIRT1 in RPE, no demonstration that SRT1720 promotes TFEB deacetylation or nuclear activation, and no reports that SRT1720 enhances lysosomal acidification or cathepsin D (CTSD) activity in RPE or AMD models; any such assertions remain unsubstantiated by the references supplied here (Ji et al., 2021; Mazzone, 2018; Kaarniranta et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2020). Therefore, while the SIRT1→autophagy/mitophagy rationale in RPE is strong, the specific mechanistic chain “SRT1720→SIRT1 activation in RPE→TFEB deacetylation→CLEAR upregulation→lysosomal acidification/CTSD enhancement” lacks direct experimental support in RPE/AMD contexts in these sources and should be treated as a testable, not established, hypothesis (Falcão et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2020).

Therapeutic biology of the disease target supports SIRT1 activation in RPE. Multiple AMD-relevant datasets show NAD⁺ depletion and SIRT1 downregulation in AMD RPE (primary donor-derived cultures and iPSC-RPE), accompanied by impaired PGC-1α activity, AMPK suppression, and mTOR hyperactivation, together with autophagy/lysosome structural and functional abnormalities; the PARP1-dependent late-autophagy block under oxidative stress in RPE is SIRT1-dependent for rescue, further bolstering SIRT1 as a target for restoring autophagic flux and organelle quality control (Zhang et al., 2020; Jang et al., 2020). However, these observations do not establish which pharmacologic SIRT1 activator is optimal for RPE/AMD, and they do not establish TFEB deacetylation as a SIRT1-dependent event in RPE (Jang et al., 2020; Falcão et al., 2025).

Therapeutic History in Related Ocular Systems (Class Precedent)  
Although direct SRT1720 ocular data are absent here, SRT2104—a second-generation STAC with improved specificity and exposure—shows SIRT1-linked protection in retinal ischemia/reperfusion and TNF-induced optic nerve injury, including deacetylation of canonical SIRT1 substrates (p53, NF-κB p65, STAT3), reduced apoptosis/inflammation, and induction of autophagy in optic nerve, which provides class-level ocular precedent that SIRT1 activation can be neuroprotective and autophagy-enhancing in the visual system (Chang et al., 2024). These results should not be extrapolated to SRT1720 without direct data, but they reinforce the biological plausibility that a STAC could benefit retinal tissues if target engagement and safety can be achieved (Chang et al., 2024).

Expected Effect  
The proposed assay hypothesis is that SRT1720 will activate SIRT1 in RPE, leading to TFEB deacetylation/activation, increased lysosomal acidification and CTSD activity, and improved clearance of photoreceptor outer segment (POS) material. Based on the literature provided here, the following expectations are reasonable and aligned with evidence, and several components are speculative:

- Supported expectations tied to SIRT1 biology in RPE:
  - If SRT1720 achieves bona fide SIRT1 activation and target engagement in RPE, it should decrease acetylation of canonical SIRT1 substrates (for example, p53 K382ac, p65 K310ac, PGC-1α), restore late-stage autophagic flux under oxidative stress, and enhance autophagosome–lysosome fusion, given the demonstrated requirement for SIRT1 to rescue late-stage autophagy in H₂O₂-stressed ARPE-19 cells (Jang et al., 2020; Luo et al., 2025).  
  - Biomarkers: recovery of p62 turnover, normalization of LC3-II/LC3-I dynamics in flux assays, increased autolysosome signal in tandem RFP-GFP-LC3 imaging, and potentially increased Rab7 activity/localization to autophagosomes are anticipated if SRT1720 strengthens late-stage autophagy via SIRT1 (Jang et al., 2020; Luján et al., 2022).  
  - Mitochondrial endpoints: increased PGC-1α deacetylation/activity and improved mitophagy markers (PINK1, Parkin induction) would be consistent with SIRT1 activation; SRT1720 has driven PGC-1α–dependent mitochondrial biogenesis after oxidant injury in renal cells, supporting feasibility of this axis in oxidatively stressed epithelia (Ji et al., 2021; Luján et al., 2022).  

- Plausible, but not demonstrated within the provided literature:
  - TFEB deacetylation/activation: the present corpus does not document SIRT1-dependent TFEB deacetylation or STAC-induced TFEB activation in RPE. TFEB/CLEAR is a validated master lysosomal program, and PGC-1α can lie upstream of TFEB in other disease contexts, so an indirect route “SIRT1→PGC-1α→TFEB→CLEAR” is biologically plausible but remains unproven in RPE here and should be tested directly (Falcão et al., 2025).  
  - Lysosomal acidification and CTSD activity: lysosomal pH and hydrolase activation are central to RPE proteostasis and AMD; however, no experiment in the supplied sources demonstrates that SRT1720 or any STAC increases lysosomal acidification or CTSD activity in RPE. These readouts (e.g., LysoTracker/LysoSensor ratio, DQ-BSA, cathepsin activity assays) should be considered exploratory endpoints for SRT1720, not expected outcomes (Boya et al., 2023; Kaarniranta et al., 2023).  
  - LAMP2 expression: likewise, no provided reference shows SRT1720 increasing LAMP2 in RPE. While CLEAR activation generally elevates lysosomal genes (e.g., LAMP family, cathepsins), this requires evidence of TFEB activation in the same system and has not been shown for SRT1720 in RPE in the available literature (Boya et al., 2023; Falcão et al., 2025).  

- Target presence/assay feasibility:
  - SIRT1 is expressed in human RPE and is reduced in AMD donor RPE and AMD iPSC-RPE models, with associated increases in acetylated PGC-1α and deficits in mitochondrial/autophagic programs, confirming the presence of the pharmacological target and a disease-relevant deficit that SIRT1 activation could address (Golestaneh et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2020).  
  - The disease cell biology is well-aligned with a SIRT1-centric intervention: in RPE, autophagy and phagocytic digestion converge on lysosomes to clear POS; impaired lysosomal enzyme activity and acidification reduce flux and increase oxidative stress and protein/organelle damage—phenotypes linked to AMD and to which SIRT1’s autophagy/mitophagy-promoting actions are mechanistically relevant (Kaarniranta et al., 2023; Boya et al., 2023).

Overall Evaluation  
On balance, the therapeutic rationale “activate SIRT1 to restore autophagy/mitophagy and lysosomal competence in RPE for dry AMD” is well-supported by AMD-relevant cell biology and human donor data; however, the specific choice of SRT1720 has substantial evidentiary and safety gaps relative to alternatives in the STAC space, and the asserted TFEB/lysosome mechanistic specifics are not demonstrated in the provided literature.

Strengths  
- Strong target biology and disease alignment in RPE and AMD: Multiple independent datasets demonstrate that AMD RPE exhibit decreased NAD⁺, reduced SIRT1, increased acetylated PGC-1α, impaired AMPK signaling, and mTOR hyperactivity concurrent with autophagy/lysosomal abnormalities, which together point to an actionable SIRT1 deficit in AMD pathology (Zhang et al., 2020; Jang et al., 2020). In oxidatively stressed ARPE-19 cells and an SI mouse model, preserving NAD⁺ and thereby SIRT1 activity was necessary and sufficient to rescue late-stage autophagy and protect retina, placing SIRT1 centrally in autophagy restoration and retinal resilience (Jang et al., 2020).  
- Class-level ocular precedent for SIRT1 activation: SRT2104, a later-generation STAC with better drug-like properties, increases SIRT1 activity in retina/optic nerve, promotes SIRT1-mediated deacetylation of p53, NF-κB p65, and STAT3, reduces apoptosis/inflammation, and upregulates autophagy in optic nerve, establishing that STAC-mediated SIRT1 activation can be protective and autophagy-enhancing in ocular tissues (Chang et al., 2024).  
- Mitochondrial stress/biogenesis axis engagement by SRT1720: In non-ocular epithelia, SRT1720 induces PGC-1α–dependent mitochondrial biogenesis and rescues function after oxidant injury, a desirable capability for stressed RPE; SRT1720 also modulates metabolic signaling via SIRT1–PGC-1α/AMPK/PPARα/FOXO1 pathways, consistent with correcting mitochondrial oxidative metabolism defects that characterize AMD RPE (Ji et al., 2021; Ding et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2020).  
- Therapeutic tractability of lysosome/autophagy endpoints: TFEB/CLEAR biology, lysosomal acidification, and cathepsin function are well-defined levers in RPE; measuring autophagic flux (LC3, p62, RFP-GFP-LC3), lysosomal pH (LysoSensor), and hydrolase activity (e.g., CTSD) is straightforward and interpretable in RPE assays, enabling rapid validation of the hypothesis in vitro (Boya et al., 2023; Kaarniranta et al., 2023).

Weaknesses and Risks  
- Absence of direct RPE/AMD data for SRT1720: No provided reference shows SRT1720 engaging SIRT1 in RPE, improving autophagic flux in RPE, activating TFEB/CLEAR in RPE, or enhancing lysosomal acidification/CTSD activity in RPE or AMD-like models. The core elements of the hypothesis (TFEB deacetylation and CLEAR induction by SRT1720 in RPE) are not documented here and require de novo demonstration (Ji et al., 2021; Falcão et al., 2025; Kaarniranta et al., 2023).  
- Mechanistic controversy and off-targets: The STAC field’s historical assay artifacts, substrate dependence, and the assisted allosteric mechanism place a premium on rigorous target engagement readouts in the specific cellular context; SRT1720 additionally shows Sirt3 inhibitory activity and has been associated with SIRT1-independent cytotoxicity in certain cells, complicating mechanistic attribution (Mazzone, 2018; Chang et al., 2024).  
- Safety signal: SRT1720 increased tumor cell migration and metastasis in a breast cancer mouse model; while AMD is not a malignancy, a pro-migratory/pro-metastatic signal raises a red flag for systemic exposure and suggests careful ocular delivery strategies and off-target profiling if pursued (Bononi et al., 2022; Mazzone, 2018).  
- Lack of PK/ADME and clinical data for SRT1720 in this corpus: Unlike SRT2104, which has human PK/tolerability data and CNS/retinal preclinical activity, SRT1720 lacks disclosed PK/ADME and clinical reports here, hindering translational assessment and dose/exposure design for ocular studies (Bononi et al., 2022; Chang et al., 2024).  
- TFEB/lysosome-specific uncertainty: While CLEAR network activation and lysosomal acidification are compelling RPE targets, the present sources do not show SIRT1-dependent TFEB deacetylation in RPE, nor do they link STACs to lysosomal pH regulation or CTSD activation in RPE; asserting this mechanism is premature without experimental support (Falcão et al., 2025; Boya et al., 2023; Kaarniranta et al., 2023).

Recommendation and Development Path  
- Scientific merit: Pursuing SIRT1 activation to normalize late-stage autophagy and mitochondrial quality control in RPE is well-justified by the PARP1→NAD⁺→SIRT1 axis in RPE and AMD donor biology; however, SRT1720 is not, on current evidence, the optimal first-in-class molecule to test this hypothesis in RPE (Jang et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2020).  
- Prioritization: If the team’s objective is target validation, consider tool-compound triage: compare SRT1720 with a second-generation clinical-stage STAC (SRT2104) and with an orthogonal approach that is known to restore SIRT1 activity in RPE (e.g., NAD⁺ boosting) in parallel RPE assays, using target-engagement and autophagy/lysosome endpoints defined a priori (Chang et al., 2024; Jang et al., 2020).  
- Minimal dataset to proceed (go/no-go):  
  1) Demonstrate SIRT1 activation in human RPE by SRT1720 at non-toxic concentrations via decreased acetyl-p53 (K382), decreased acetyl-PGC-1α, and decreased acetyl-p65 (K310), with rescue by SIRT1 knockdown or a SIRT1-dead mutant to confirm on-target action (Luo et al., 2025; Jang et al., 2020).  
  2) Show restoration of late-stage autophagy under H₂O₂ or A2E stress: increased autolysosome formation in tandem RFP-GFP-LC3, decreased p62, and restored LC3-II flux in the presence/absence of lysosomal inhibitors; confirm loss of effect with SIRT1 knockdown (Jang et al., 2020).  
  3) Test TFEB/CLEAR explicitly: TFEB nuclear translocation, TFEB transcriptional reporter, and CLEAR target induction (e.g., LAMP2 and CTSD mRNA/protein) with and without mTORC1 modulation; test necessity of SIRT1 by knockdown and sufficiency by PGC-1α gain-of-function to probe the SIRT1→PGC-1α→TFEB chain (Boya et al., 2023; Falcão et al., 2025).  
  4) Quantify lysosomal acidification and hydrolase activity: LysoSensor/LysoTracker measurements and CTSD activity assays; relate outcomes to TFEB activation and to autophagic flux to determine whether SRT1720 enhances lysosomal function or acts predominantly on pre-lysosomal steps (Kaarniranta et al., 2023; Boya et al., 2023).  
  5) Evaluate mitophagy and mitochondrial function: PINK1/Parkin recruitment, mt-Keima flux, mitochondrial respiration/ATP, and ROS after SRT1720 in stressed RPE to connect SIRT1–PGC-1α engagement to mitochondrial quality control (Kaarniranta et al., 2023; Luján et al., 2022).  
  6) Safety pharmacology in RPE: assess proliferation/migration, EMT markers, and off-target sirtuin activity (Sirt3) to de-risk pro-migratory liabilities observed in cancer models (Bononi et al., 2022; Mazzone, 2018).  

- If SRT1720 fails to deliver on TFEB/CLEAR and lysosomal pH/hydrolase endpoints but still rescues late-stage autophagic flux, the program can pivot to an autophagy-centric mechanism of action (MoA) without TFEB claims; conversely, if TFEB/CLEAR induction is robust, the candidate may differentiate from mTOR inhibitors via epigenetic/cofactor-driven CLEAR activation, contingent on confirming SIRT1 dependency (Boya et al., 2023; Falcão et al., 2025).  
- For in vivo progression, the SI model used to establish PARP1→SIRT1/autophagy dependency provides a tractable retinal degeneration context, but ocular delivery and safety (especially with first-generation STACs) will require localized dosing strategies (intravitreal/subretinal) and careful dosing to minimize systemic exposure (Jang et al., 2020).

Bottom Line  
- The hypothesis that SRT1720 can correct RPE proteostasis in dry AMD via SIRT1 activation is mechanistically credible with respect to autophagy/mitophagy restoration, but the specific claims of TFEB deacetylation, CLEAR network activation, and enhancement of lysosomal acidification/CTSD activity by SRT1720 in RPE are not supported by the present literature and must be treated as untested (Jang et al., 2020; Falcão et al., 2025; Boya et al., 2023).  
- Given the safety concerns and off-target profile of SRT1720, and the existence of a later-generation STAC (SRT2104) with human PK and ocular neuroprotection, SRT1720 should not be advanced beyond in vitro RPE validation until it demonstrates clear, on-target superiority in RPE assays and acceptable safety margins; otherwise, the team should prioritize either SRT2104 or NAD⁺ augmentation/PARP1 modulation for translational efforts (Chang et al., 2024; Bononi et al., 2022; Jang et al., 2020).  

Summary assessment  
- Pros: Strong disease–target alignment in RPE; robust class biology for SIRT1-driven autophagy/mitophagy; SRT1720 can activate SIRT1 pathways in other oxidative-stress contexts; feasible, discriminating assays exist to test the MoA (Zhang et al., 2020; Jang et al., 2020; Ji et al., 2021; Boya et al., 2023).  
- Cons: No direct evidence of efficacy/mechanism in RPE; TFEB/lysosome mechanistic claims unsupported; safety/off-target risks; no PK/clinical data in this corpus; better-characterized STAC alternatives exist (Falcão et al., 2025; Bononi et al., 2022; Chang et al., 2024).  

Decision guidance: Proceed with a narrowly scoped, mechanism-first in vitro validation of SRT1720 in human RPE focused on SIRT1 target engagement and late-stage autophagy rescue under oxidative/phagolysosomal stress, with explicit tests for TFEB/CLEAR activation and lysosomal acidification/CTSD activity; in parallel, benchmark against SRT2104 and NAD⁺ repletion, and use pre-specified go/no-go criteria tied to on-target mechanistic readouts and safety signals to decide whether SRT1720 merits in vivo exploration in retinal degeneration models (Jang et al., 2020; Chang et al., 2024; Boya et al., 2023).

Below is our detailed evaluation of GSK2656157 for repurposing in dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD), structured in the requested format.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
GSK2656157 is a small‐molecule inhibitor of PERK (protein kinase R–like endoplasmic reticulum kinase) that was discovered and optimized through medicinal‐chemistry efforts originally led by GlaxoSmithKline. This compound belongs to the class of ATP‐competitive, Type I inhibitors that target the kinase domain of PERK, binding within the ATP‐binding cleft and stabilizing a “DFG‐in, Cα‐helix shifted” conformation of the dephosphorylated kinase domain (Axten, 2017, pp. 15–19). Structurally, the compound is an indoline‐derived molecule; similar chemical series include the indoline/aminoquinazoline chemotypes that have been widely profiled for their high potency and kinase selectivity across panels exceeding 300 kinases (Axten, 2017, pp. 15–19). Originally, these inhibitors were developed as research tools to interrogate the role of PERK in the unfolded protein response (UPR) in oncology and neurodegeneration contexts, and in preclinical studies GSK2656157 demonstrated activity in suppressing tumor growth and angiogenesis in mouse xenograft models via inhibition of PERK autophosphorylation (Atkins et al., 2013, pp. 1–2, 8). As a synthetic small molecule, its origins lie in rational design based on X‐ray–guided structure–activity relationships, which enabled optimization for both high selectivity (with >100‐fold selectivity over related kinases including other eIF2α kinases as well as a broad kinome panel) and sufficient in vivo pharmacokinetics (Axten, 2017, pp. 15–19; Atkins et al., 2013, pp. 1–2). Thus, from a chemical and developmental perspective, GSK2656157 is a first‐in‐class PERK inhibitor that exemplifies how targeted kinase inhibition can be achieved by rational design.  

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, PERK inhibitors such as GSK2606414 and its more selective derivative GSK2656157 were developed primarily for indications in oncology and neurodegeneration. Preclinical studies in tumor xenograft models have demonstrated that oral dosing of GSK2656157 can suppress PERK-mediated signaling, resulting in attenuated phospho-eIF2α levels, diminished transcriptional responses of unfolded protein response (UPR) genes, and reduced tumor vascular density (Atkins et al., 2013, pp. 1–2, 8). In neurodegenerative models—for instance in prion and tauopathy mouse models—PERK inhibition has been shown to restore global protein synthesis, decrease the levels of phospho-tau, and produce mixed effects on behavior and neuronal survival (Rozpędek-Kamińska et al., 2020, pp. 17–19). Meanwhile, within the ocular space, experimental studies with the closely related PERK inhibitor GSK2606414 (a chemical analogue of GSK2656157) in in vitro retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cell models have demonstrated on-target inhibition of PERK signaling (evidenced by reduction in eIF2α phosphorylation) along with downstream alterations in stress markers such as CHOP and VEGF mRNA (Jiang et al., 2017, pp. 1–2). However, direct use of GSK2656157 in dry AMD or similar inflammatory/degenerative ocular conditions has not yet been reported in the literature. Some studies investigating retinal degeneration models, such as P23H rhodopsin transgenic rats, have suggested that PERK inhibition can worsen photoreceptor survival by enhancing misfolded protein aggregation, although these studies were typically conducted with compounds such as GSK2606414A (Athanasiou et al., 2017, pp. 1–2, 5–7). There is, therefore, limited clinical or preclinical history regarding the use of GSK2656157 specifically in AMD or related ocular diseases. In addition, while the compound has demonstrated acceptable pharmacokinetics and tolerability in preclinical oncology settings—with measurable systemic exposures—it is important to note that systemic PERK inhibition in multiple species has been associated with toxic liabilities such as pancreatic toxicity (Atkins et al., 2013, p. 8; Axten, 2017, pp. 1–7). Consequently, although the therapeutic class has a relatively rich history in oncology and neurodegeneration, its direct application to dry AMD remains a new and untested repurposing approach that requires careful consideration of pharmacodynamic impacts in ocular tissues and rigorous safety profiling.  

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, PERK functions as an endoplasmic reticulum (ER)–resident kinase that is activated upon the accumulation of misfolded proteins, a hallmark of chronic ER stress. Normally, when the ER’s folding capacity is overwhelmed, the molecular chaperone GRP78 dissociates from PERK, enabling PERK to oligomerize and autophosphorylate, which then enables it to phosphorylate the α subunit of eukaryotic initiation factor 2 (eIF2α) at serine-51 (Axten, 2017, pp. 7–11). Phosphorylation of eIF2α leads to a global reduction in protein synthesis—a protective adaptation that prevents further accumulation of misfolded proteins—and also selectively permits the translation of stress-induced genes, most notably ATF4. ATF4 subsequently upregulates transcription factors such as CHOP, which can drive pro-apoptotic signaling if ER stress persists (Axten, 2017, pp. 7–11; Chu et al., 2021, p. 8). In the context of dry AMD, chronic ER stress in RPE cells has been implicated in disrupting cellular proteostasis, where misfolded proteins—including subunits of key complexes like the vacuolar ATPase (v-ATPase)—may fail to fold properly, leading to impaired lysosomal acidification (Kaarniranta et al., 2018, pp. 1–4; Athanasiou et al., 2017, pp. 1–2). The hypothesis is that by inhibiting PERK with GSK2656157, the excessive phosphorylation of eIF2α and the maladaptive integrated stress response (ISR) can be attenuated. This would not only restore global protein synthesis but also prevent downstream consequences such as upregulation of CHOP and VEGF, thereby reducing pro-apoptotic as well as pro-inflammatory pathways (Jiang et al., 2017, pp. 1–2). Furthermore, it is posited that such normalization in the ISR could allow for proper folding and assembly of lysosomal enzymes and complexes, including the v-ATPase. Proper v-ATPase assembly is critical for maintaining low intraluminal pH in lysosomes, which is necessary for the activation and maturation of hydrolases like cathepsin D (Kaarniranta et al., 2018, pp. 1–4). In neuronal models, PERK inhibition has been associated with improvements in lysosomal function and proteostasis, indicating that reduction of chronic ER stress can indirectly favor the re-establishment of lysosomal homeostasis (Jiang et al., 2017, pp. 1–2). In essence, GSK2656157, by specifically targeting and inhibiting PERK, interferes with the pathological arm of the UPR (i.e. excessive eIF2α phosphorylation) that is hypothesized to contribute to impaired lysosomal acidification in RPE cells under chronic stress conditions—a mechanism that might be particularly relevant in the pathophysiology of dry AMD (Axten, 2017, pp. 24–28).  

Expected Effect:  
In the proposed assays, the primary expected effect of GSK2656157 is to inhibit PERK activity in RPE cells, as evidenced by reduced phosphorylation of eIF2α, and thereby dampen downstream signaling events that lead to the induction of ATF4, CHOP, and ultimately pro-apoptotic and proangiogenic factors such as VEGF. In vitro studies with analogues of GSK2656157 (such as GSK2606414) in ARPE-19 cells have shown dose-dependent inhibition of eIF2α phosphorylation with subsequent decreases in CHOP and VEGF mRNA expression without necessarily triggering apoptosis at higher doses (Jiang et al., 2017, pp. 1–2). These results provide a proof-of-concept that pharmacological inhibition of PERK can modulate this critical signaling pathway in RPE cells. The hypothesis for dry AMD is that chronic ER stress in the RPE disrupts lysosomal acidification via misfolding of v-ATPase subunits; under normal circumstances, proper v-ATPase function ensures that lysosomes maintain their acidic environment, which is essential for protease activation—including cathepsin D. Cathepsin D, in turn, is critical for lysosomal degradation of photoreceptor outer segments and for preventing lipofuscin accumulation, a pathological process in dry AMD (Kaarniranta et al., 2018, pp. 1–4). Thus, by reducing PERK activation through GSK2656157, it is expected that the overactive ISR would be tempered sufficiently to allow for the proper folding and assembly of v-ATPase complexes, thereby restoring lysosomal acidification (Chu et al., 2021, p. 8; Athanasiou et al., 2017, pp. 1–2). This restoration is anticipated to improve cathepsin D maturation and activity, leading to better clearance of intracellular debris and misfolded proteins, ultimately protecting RPE cells from stress-induced degeneration. On a cellular level, normalizing lysosomal pH would also promote autophagy flux, which is often impaired in the aged RPE, thereby mitigating one of the key contributing factors in the dry AMD phenotype (Kaarniranta et al., 2018, pp. 1–4; Athanasiou et al., 2017, pp. 1–2). Importantly, RPE cells are known to express PERK and components of the UPR, with studies demonstrating that ER stress markers, including phospho-PERK and phospho-eIF2α, are elevated in pathological states associated with AMD (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021, pp. 11–12; Chu et al., 2021, p. 8). Therefore, if GSK2656157 can achieve adequate ocular tissue exposure and inhibit PERK activity in the RPE, the expected outcome would be a reduction in cellular stress–mediated apoptosis and proliferation of protective pathways that maintain lysosomal and autophagy functions (Jiang et al., 2017, pp. 1–2; Rozpędek-Kamińska et al., 2020, pp. 17–19). Moreover, the compound’s known pharmacokinetic profile in preclinical oncology studies suggests that it is systemically bioavailable and, according to some reports, may achieve ocular tissue distribution; thus it is conceivable that with appropriate dosing and local delivery strategies, GSK2656157 could achieve effective concentrations in RPE cells (Atkins et al., 2013, pp. 1–2, 8).  

Overall Evaluation:  
Overall, GSK2656157 presents an intriguing therapeutic candidate for dry AMD based on a mechanistic hypothesis that links chronic ER stress to impaired lysosomal acidification—a process central to the pathogenesis of AMD. One of the primary strengths of GSK2656157 is its potent and selective inhibition of PERK, a critical mediator of the integrated stress response. The compound’s design as an ATP‐competitive PERK inhibitor places it squarely in a class of drugs that have been well characterized in terms of kinase selectivity and in vivo pharmacodynamics in oncology settings (Axten, 2017, pp. 15–19). The underlying biological rationale is that by attenuating the maladaptive PERK-mediated phosphorylation of eIF2α, it may be possible to relieve chronic translational suppression and dampen downstream deleterious signaling cascades—thereby re-establishing normal lysosomal function through proper v-ATPase assembly and restoration of cathepsin D activity (Axten, 2017, pp. 7–11; Chu et al., 2021, p. 8). There is supportive in vitro evidence from studies using related inhibitors (for example, GSK2606414 in ARPE-19 cells) that PERK inhibition can downregulate stress effectors such as CHOP and VEGF, which are both implicated in retinal degeneration and neovascularization (Jiang et al., 2017, pp. 1–2). Such studies underscore the potential of targeting the PERK/ISR axis in RPE cells to create a more favorable intracellular environment that could prevent progressive degeneration seen in dry AMD (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021, pp. 11–12; Chu et al., 2021, p. 8).

However, there are several notable weaknesses and caveats. First, while there is an extensive body of preclinical work on PERK inhibitors in oncology and neurodegeneration models, there is a significant lack of direct evidence in ocular disease models—especially chronic models of dry AMD—as well as an absence of published studies specifically evaluating GSK2656157 in RPE cells or in animal models of AMD (Athanasiou et al., 2017, pp. 5–7). In several studies using related PERK inhibitors in rod photoreceptor degeneration models (such as P23H rhodopsin transgenic rats), inhibition of PERK activity has been associated with worsened outcomes, suggesting that PERK activation may paradoxically be protective in certain contexts of protein misfolding (Athanasiou et al., 2017, pp. 1–2, 5–7). This dichotomous role of PERK—as both an adaptive and a pro-death signal depending on the context and duration of activation—raises concerns about whether inhibition will uniformly yield beneficial effects in the RPE, whose balance of ER stress responses may differ from that of neuronal or secretory tissues. Second, while the hypothesis postulates that chronic ER stress impairs lysosomal acidification by misfolding v-ATPase subunits, the direct link between PERK inhibition and restoration of v-ATPase assembly or cathepsin D maturation in RPE cells has not been firmly established in the literature. Data that explicitly demonstrate that PERK inhibition rescues lysosomal pH, enhances v-ATPase function, and improves cathepsin D activity in neuronal models may exist, yet similar studies in ocular models are limited (Chu et al., 2021, p. 8; Kaarniranta et al., 2018, pp. 1–4). Third, the systemic administration of PERK inhibitors such as GSK2656157 has been associated with pancreatic toxicity and other systemic adverse effects in preclinical studies, a liability that could be particularly problematic in chronic therapies such as those needed for dry AMD (Atkins et al., 2013, p. 8; Axten, 2017, pp. 1–7). Although strategies such as local (intravitreal) delivery might mitigate these systemic risks, ocular pharmacokinetic and tolerability data are sparse, and the tissue-specific distribution of GSK2656157 in the eye would need careful evaluation (Atkins et al., 2013, pp. 1–2, 8). Fourth, there is some concern over off-target effects; for example, early reports on similar GSK compounds noted possible inhibition of RIP1 kinase activity, although subsequent studies have argued that the effects observed were indeed mediated by PERK inhibition (Starr, 2019, pp. 133–137; Athanasiou et al., 2017, pp. 5–7). Nonetheless, affording absolute selectivity in a clinical candidate remains a challenge. In addition, chronic inhibition of the adaptive aspects of the ISR may inadvertently impair protective mechanisms in the retina, as transient ISR activation is known to mediate cellular adaptation during acute stress (Axten, 2017, pp. 7–11, 24–28).

In summary, while the mechanistic rationale for using GSK2656157 to address dry AMD is based on a conceptually appealing hypothesis—that PERK inhibition will relieve chronic ER stress, thereby restoring proper lysosomal acidification, enabling v-ATPase assembly, and rescuing cathepsin D activity in RPE cells—the current body of literature reveals both promising on-target effects in non-ocular systems and significant gaps in ocular-specific efficacy and safety data. Given the complex, context-dependent role of PERK signaling in retinal homeostasis and the potential for deleterious outcomes when PERK is inhibited in models of protein misfolding, further focused in vitro and in vivo studies are required to determine whether GSK2656157 can be safely and effectively repurposed for dry AMD. Strengths of this candidate include its potent, selective PERK inhibition and preclinical pharmacodynamic proof-of-concept in related disease models, while weaknesses center on limited ocular data, potential systemic and off-target toxicities, and an uncertain impact on lysosomal and proteostatic pathways in RPE cells. Ultimately, while GSK2656157 remains an attractive avenue for targeting an upstream stress node in dry AMD pathogenesis, careful optimization of dosing, targeted ocular delivery, and comprehensive evaluation in relevant AMD models will be essential before moving forward in clinical development (Axten, 2017, pp. 1–7, 15–19, 24–28; Atkins et al., 2013, pp. 1–2; Athanasiou et al., 2017, pp. 5–7; Jiang et al., 2017, pp. 1–2).

Abstract—Metformin, a synthetic biguanide derived from galegine (French lilac), is widely used as first-line therapy for type 2 diabetes mellitus and has pleiotropic cellular effects that intersect with age-related macular degeneration (AMD) biology, including AMPK activation, modulation of mTOR signaling, autophagy induction, anti-inflammatory actions, mitochondrial support, anti-senescence effects, and anti-angiogenic signaling in retinal models (Amin et al., 2022). Multiple preclinical studies in RPE cell lines and rodent retinal injury/degeneration models show that metformin preserves RPE barrier integrity, reduces oxidative and inflammatory stress, supports mitochondrial biogenesis, and maintains photoreceptor structure/function, largely via AMPK-dependent pathways; however, dry AMD–specific randomized clinical efficacy data remain limited and observational epidemiology is heterogeneous, with mixed associations across populations, exposure definitions, and AMD subtypes (Amin et al., 2022; Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Gokhale et al., 2023; Liang et al., 2022; Moir et al., 2023; Romdhoniyyah et al., 2021). Critically, while AMPK→mTORC1→autophagy is well-supported in retinal contexts, direct evidence for metformin-driven TFEB nuclear translocation, V-ATPase upregulation, or cathepsin D (CTSD) maturation in human RPE/AMD models is not demonstrated in the excerpted literature, representing material gaps for the central hypothesis (Amin et al., 2022; Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Buonfiglio et al., 2024). Overall, metformin is a biologically plausible, low-cost, and generally safe repurposing candidate for dry AMD that warrants mechanistic confirmation in RPE for lysosome-centric endpoints and rigorous randomized trials across AMD stages (Amin et al., 2022; Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Moir et al., 2023).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Metformin is a small-molecule biguanide synthesized as a derivative of galegine, a guanidine-class alkaloid originally isolated from the plant Galega officinalis; clinically it has been used for more than 60 years as the most commonly prescribed oral antihyperglycemic agent worldwide (class: biguanides) (Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Amin et al., 2022). Chemically, metformin comprises two coupled guanidine moieties conferring cationic, hydrophilic properties and cellular accumulation via organic cation transporters, consistent with mitochondrial complex I engagement and AMPK pathway activation described in mechanistic literature (Augustin & Atorf, 2023). Beyond glycemic control, metformin exhibits pleiotropic effects—anti-inflammatory, anti-oxidative, anti-angiogenic, anti-apoptotic and anti-senescence—reported in diverse cell types and tissues, many of which intersect with pathways implicated in AMD pathogenesis (oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, impaired proteostasis/autophagy, para-inflammation, vascular dysregulation) (Amin et al., 2022; Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Kozlowski, 2023). In ocular contexts, preclinical work indicates that metformin activates AMPK in RPE and neural retina and can preserve retinal structure and function under oxidative, metabolic, and phototoxic stressors (Amin et al., 2022). Collectively, these properties position metformin as a rational repurposing candidate for dry AMD, wherein RPE dysfunction, impaired autophagy/lysosomal clearance, mitochondrial stress, and chronic inflammation are central pathogenic nodes (Amin et al., 2022; Buonfiglio et al., 2024).

Therapeutic History  
Systemic use: Metformin is established first-line therapy for type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) and has been investigated broadly for aging-related conditions due to putative geroprotective effects; long-term safety has been documented, including in the Diabetes Prevention Program (DPP) where gastrointestinal intolerance is the most common adverse event and lactic acidosis was not observed under trial conditions, though B12 deficiency can occur with chronic use (Amin et al., 2022; Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Zhou & Xue, 2024). Preclinical ocular use: In retinal models, metformin has been tested systemically (oral/IP) and intravitreally, demonstrating protective effects in RPE and photoreceptors across light-damage, iodate-induced injury, inherited retinal degeneration (rd1/rd10), and oxygen-induced retinopathy (OIR) with readouts including preserved RPE tight junctions (ZO-1, occludin), outer nuclear layer thickness, and ERG amplitudes; notable anti-angiogenic activity includes decreased CNV lesion size and VEGF/VEGFR signaling modulation in several models (Amin et al., 2022). In these preclinical settings, metformin’s ocular benefits are frequently attributed to AMPK activation and downstream autophagy/mitochondrial and anti-inflammatory pathways, without overt ocular toxicity reported in rodents; however, human ocular safety data and pharmacokinetics under intravitreal or high-dose local exposure are not detailed in the excerpts (Amin et al., 2022).

Clinical/epidemiologic AMD history: Observational epidemiology offers mixed signals. Several large retrospective cohorts and case–control analyses associate metformin use with reduced odds or risk of any AMD or early AMD, with dose–duration trends in some datasets (e.g., MarketScan/claims OR 0.93 and propensity-matched HR 0.57; Taiwanese cohorts HR ~0.54 with stronger protection at >4 years and higher average daily doses), and lower odds reported in multiple studies across US, Europe, and Asia (Amin et al., 2022; Jiang et al., 2022; Kozlowski, 2023; Moir et al., 2023). Other datasets report null or complex associations: a high-quality UK T2DM cohort found no differential AMD risk with metformin using time-varying exposure models; a U.S. claims analysis focusing on dry AMD reported current use slightly increased dry AMD risk while prior use trended protective; additional analyses show no association or heterogeneity by diabetic retinopathy status (Eton et al., 2022; Gokhale et al., 2023; Liang et al., 2022). Meta-analyses also conflict: a systematic review of diabetics suggested decreased odds of AMD with metformin, whereas a broader 2024 meta-analysis concluded no overall prophylactic/treatment role; a European meta-analysis of antidiabetic/lipid-lowering drugs found reduced AMD prevalence overall but not for late-stage AMD specifically (Elhalag et al., 2024; Mauschitz et al., 2023). Importantly, these retrospective designs face confounding (e.g., smoking, comorbidities, health-care utilization), outcome misclassification (wet vs dry AMD), and exposure misclassification (adherence), limiting causal inference and stage-specific conclusions (Brown et al., 2019; Gokhale et al., 2023; Moir et al., 2023). Prospective interventional testing for dry AMD is underway: a randomized, single-blind Phase II trial of metformin to slow geographic atrophy (GA) progression has been conducted, with publication reported in 2024 (Shen et al., 2024); however, the excerpts do not provide efficacy outcomes in GA and emphasize that randomized evidence remains needed (Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Shen et al., 2024).

No regulatory approval exists for metformin in AMD (dry or wet), and the totality of evidence remains preclinical and observational for efficacy, with one randomized GA study reported but without effect-size details here; therefore, clinical utility in dry AMD is presently unproven (Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Shen et al., 2024).

Mechanism of Action  
Canonical pharmacology: Metformin partially inhibits mitochondrial respiratory complex I, reducing hepatic ATP and increasing AMP/ADP, thereby activating AMPK, the cellular energy sensor that shifts metabolism toward ATP-generating pathways; AMPK-dependent and ‑independent mechanisms operate systemically, including reduced hepatic gluconeogenesis, increased enterocyte glucose uptake/GLP-1 secretion, and microbiome modulation with potential systemic anti-inflammatory effects (Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Kozlowski, 2023).

Retinal/RPE mechanisms: In RPE cell lines (e.g., ARPE-19), metformin increases pAMPK and triggers autophagy, reduces ROS, decreases apoptosis, and preserves tight junction proteins (ZO-1, occludin), thereby maintaining barrier integrity under oxidative challenges (Amin et al., 2022; Augustin & Atorf, 2023). At the molecular level, treatment increases Sirt1 and multiple mitochondrial biogenesis and antioxidant markers (SOD-2, Nrf1, Tfam, PGC-1α, COX-II), restores NADH:NAD+ ratios and ATP, and lowers inflammatory mediators (NF-κB signaling, IL-6) (Amin et al., 2022). These signatures are consistent with AMPK’s coordinate regulation of autophagy and mitochondrial homeostasis observed in RPE/retinal contexts, contributing to improved proteostasis and reduced oxidative stress—key failure modes in dry AMD (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Amin et al., 2022).

In vivo, systemic or intravitreal metformin preserves photoreceptors and RPE structure/function in light-damage, iodate injury, and inherited degeneration models (rd1, rd10), with ERG preservation and ONL maintenance; mechanistically, AMPK activation is necessary for light-damage protection in an isoform-specific manner (AMPKα2 dependency), and retina-specific Pparδ is not required, supporting an AMPK-centric retinal mechanism rather than PPARδ signaling (Amin et al., 2022). Metformin also dampens retinal senescence and SASP in OIR after intravitreal dosing, with decreased cdkn1a/cdkn2a and NF-κB/IL-6 signaling, implicating anti-senescence immunomodulation as an additional neurovascular protective mechanism (Amin et al., 2022). Anti-angiogenic actions involve AMPK-dependent and ‑independent pathways: decreased VEGFR2 via enhanced ubiquitin–proteasome degradation, altered VEGF-A isoform splicing toward less angiogenic forms, reduced Flk-1 expression, and inhibition of ALK1-mediated angiogenesis; collectively these actions reduce CNV lesion size, endothelial proliferation/migration/tube formation, and neovascularization in OIR, diabetic, and laser-CNV models (Amin et al., 2022; Augustin & Atorf, 2023). Inflammatory suppression includes reductions in ICAM-1/MCP-1 (AMPK-dependent) and NF-κB p65/IL-8 (AMPK-independent), accompanied by decreased leukostasis and cytokines across models; NLRP3 inflammasome inhibition and modulation of macrophage polarization further contribute to reduced para-inflammation (Amin et al., 2022; Dang et al., 2021; Augustin & Atorf, 2023).

mTOR/autophagy axis: AMPK activation by metformin can inhibit mTORC1, activate the ULK complex, and initiate autophagy, which in RPE promotes clearance of damaged organelles, reduces ROS, and protects against oxidative injury—mechanistically vital for countering autophagy/lysosomal dysfunction in AMD (Dang et al., 2021; Zhou & Xue, 2024). Several retinal studies report AMPK-linked increases in autophagosome formation, and some contextual discussion references mTOR modulation in retinal protection, including translational control via EF2K and general proteostasis benefits (e.g., mutant opsin trafficking) with mixed in vivo translation (Amin et al., 2022). While AMPK→mTOR→autophagy activation is strongly implicated, explicit experimental confirmation in the provided corpus for metformin-driven TFEB nuclear translocation, V-ATPase upregulation, or increased cathepsin D maturation/activity in RPE is lacking; several reviews and excerpts explicitly note these as gaps requiring targeted mechanistic studies (Amin et al., 2022; Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Buonfiglio et al., 2024).

These data caution against assuming uniform AMPK-mediated benefit across all retinal diseases or AMD stages and highlight the importance of pharmacokinetics, tissue exposure, and therapeutic window in the eye (Moir et al., 2023).

Translational addenda—microbiome and lipid handling: Metformin alters gut microbiota and systemic metabolites, which has been linked to reduced retinal neovascularization through a putative “gut–retina axis,” and may also reduce OxLDL uptake and promote cholesterol efflux via AMPK/LXR–ABCA1/G1 signaling, potentially limiting drusen-related lipid accumulation and NLRP3 activation in RPE (Dang et al., 2021; Zhou & Xue, 2024).

However, direct experimental evidence in the provided corpus for metformin-induced TFEB nuclear translocation, increased V-ATPase expression, or enhanced cathepsin D maturation/activity in human RPE is not shown; several reviews explicitly note TFEB/V-ATPase/CTSD endpoints as critical gaps that merit targeted validation in AMD-relevant assays (Amin et al., 2022; Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Buonfiglio et al., 2024).

Expected Effect

Published in vitro data already support many of these endpoints: metformin reduced ROS and apoptosis, increased pAMPK and antioxidative molecules including Sirt1/Nrf2, and preserved occludin/ZO-1 in ARPE-19 challenged with H2O2 or glyoxal; AMPK inhibition abrogated the protection, indicating dependence on AMPK signaling (Amin et al., 2022). In oxidant or lipid-rich RPE conditions, decreased NF-κB activation and inflammasome signaling (e.g., NLRP3) would be anticipated, consistent with prior reports of metformin inhibiting NF-κB and NLRP3 activation in ocular/immune models (Augustin & Atorf, 2023).

Hypothesized lysosomal/TFEB endpoints: The working hypothesis proposes that AMPK activation by metformin will inhibit mTORC1, promote TFEB nuclear translocation, increase V-ATPase expression, enhance lysosomal acidification, and increase cathepsin D (CTSD) maturation, restoring autophagic flux and preventing RPE degeneration. While the AMPK→mTORC1→autophagy cascade is supported in RPE and retina, the provided literature does not directly demonstrate metformin-induced TFEB nuclear translocation, V-ATPase upregulation, or CTSD maturation increases in RPE; thus, these are testable predictions rather than established metformin actions in RPE (Amin et al., 2022; Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Augustin & Atorf, 2023). Given TFEB’s role in lysosomal biogenesis and function, metformin’s dampening of mTORC1 could plausibly facilitate TFEB nuclear entry, but explicit experimental validation (e.g., TFEB nuclear localization quantification, lysosomal pH assays, V-ATPase subunit expression/activity, pro-CTSD→mature CTSD processing and enzymatic activity assays) is needed to confirm the hypothesized mechanism in AMD-relevant RPE models (Dang et al., 2021; Ebeling et al., 2022).

Target expression plausibility: AMPK is expressed in RPE and retina; stimulation prevents RPE and photoreceptor degeneration in multiple mouse models, and metformin increases pAMPK in human RPE cell lines—indicating sufficient expression and pathway competence for drug action in the assay system (Elhalag et al., 2024; Amin et al., 2022). Downstream readouts of autophagy and mitochondrial biogenesis/antioxidant pathways (LC3-II, PGC-1α, SOD-2, Nrf1, Tfam) have been measured and improved with metformin in RPE/retinal models, supporting assay feasibility and expected directions of effect (Amin et al., 2022).

In vivo expected effects in dry-AMD–relevant models: In toxin- and stress-driven models of RPE/photoreceptor degeneration (e.g., sodium iodate, light-induced damage) and inherited retinal degeneration, metformin is expected to preserve RPE morphology and function, maintain ONL thickness, and preserve ERG signals, consistent with reported benefits mediated by AMPK activation; however, model- and disease-stage–specific responses can vary, and negative/neutral results have been documented in some diabetic retinopathy paradigms, underscoring the need to test across multiple AMD-relevant models and to incorporate timing and dose-response studies (Amin et al., 2022). In models of para-inflammation and senescence, metformin is expected to reduce SASP mediators and senescent RPE or retinal cells, aligning with intravitreal metformin effects in OIR and broader anti-senescence literature (Amin et al., 2022; Kozlowski, 2023).

Clinical expected effects: Based on observational associations, any protective effect may be stronger for early or non-exudative AMD and may display dose–duration dependence; however, epidemiologic heterogeneity and potential confounding mean that no specific effect size can be assumed, and randomized trial confirmation in geographic atrophy and earlier AMD stages is necessary to define clinical benefit and exposure requirements (Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Liang et al., 2022).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Mechanistic convergence on AMD biology: Metformin engages AMPK-dependent and ‑independent processes that directly counter core dry AMD pathomechanisms—oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, impaired autophagy/proteostasis, para-inflammation/senescence, and, secondarily, maladaptive vascular/angio-inflammatory signaling—supported by coherent molecular readouts (pAMPK↑, autophagy induction, mitochondrial biogenesis markers↑, NF-κB/NLRP3↓) in RPE and retinal models (Amin et al., 2022; Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Zhou & Xue, 2024). Preclinical efficacy in preserving RPE barrier proteins and photoreceptor function across multiple insults strengthens biological plausibility for dry AMD (Amin et al., 2022).
- Epidemiologic signal and translational momentum: Multiple large retrospective analyses show reduced odds/risk of AMD—often with dose–duration trends—among metformin users, and a randomized GA trial has been conducted, indicating clinical interest and feasibility for prospective testing (Amin et al., 2022; Jiang et al., 2022; Moir et al., 2023; Shen et al., 2024). Meta-analytic work in diabetics suggests potential protective associations, especially in early AMD, reinforcing the rationale to test in non-diabetic AMD populations with controlled exposure (Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Liang et al., 2022).
- Favorable systemic safety and low cost: Decades of broad clinical use, with well-characterized safety signals (GI intolerance, B12 deficiency; rare lactic acidosis risk under renal/hepatic compromise), make metformin attractive from a risk–benefit and access perspective for an elderly AMD population, assuming ocular safety is confirmed (Amin et al., 2022; Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Zhou & Xue, 2024).
- Ocular delivery flexibility and mechanistic redundancy: Both systemic and intravitreal dosing have produced retinal benefits in animals; intravitreal delivery achieved senescence suppression independent of anti-VEGF effects, suggesting non-overlapping mechanisms that could complement existing therapies (Amin et al., 2022). Mechanistic redundancy (anti-oxidant, autophagy, anti-inflammatory, anti-angiogenic) could enhance robustness in multifactorial AMD pathophysiology (Amin et al., 2022; Dang et al., 2021).

Weaknesses and Gaps  
- Critical mechanistic gaps relative to the hypothesis: Direct evidence in human RPE/AMD-relevant systems for metformin-driven TFEB nuclear translocation, increases in V-ATPase expression/activity, and enhanced cathepsin D maturation/activity is absent in the provided literature; several reviews explicitly highlight TFEB/V-ATPase/CTSD endpoints as missing and necessary to establish lysosome-centric restoration of autophagic flux (Amin et al., 2022; Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Buonfiglio et al., 2024). Without these data, the proposed AMPK–TFEB–lysosome axis remains inferential in RPE.
- Heterogeneous and contradictory epidemiology: While many retrospective datasets suggest benefit (often in T2DM cohorts), high-quality time-varying analyses and some claims datasets report null or even an increased risk signal for current users regarding dry AMD; meta-analyses differ in conclusions, and late-stage AMD associations are particularly uncertain (Elhalag et al., 2024; Gokhale et al., 2023; Liang et al., 2022; Mauschitz et al., 2023). Confounding (smoking, DR severity, comedications), misclassification (wet vs dry), and exposure uncertainty limit inferential strength (Brown et al., 2019; Moir et al., 2023; Gokhale et al., 2023).
- Limited randomized clinical efficacy data in dry AMD: A GA randomized trial has been reported, but efficacy outcomes are not detailed in the excerpts; prior DPP follow-up imaging showed no significant AMD prevalence difference between metformin, lifestyle, and placebo, though that study was not designed for AMD endpoints; consequently, clinical efficacy remains unproven (Moir et al., 2023; Shen et al., 2024).
- Context dependence and dose constraints: Retinal benefits can be model- and isoform-specific (AMPKα2 dependence) and mixed in metabolic DR models; some analyses suggest suprapharmacologic concentrations may be necessary for robust AMPK activation in vitro, raising translational questions regarding retinal exposure at tolerated systemic doses, and arguing for ocular PK and target-engagement studies (Amin et al., 2022; Moir et al., 2023).
- Ocular safety and pharmacokinetics: Human ocular safety data for chronic exposure (systemic or local) in older non-diabetic AMD patients are not detailed here; intravitreal metformin safety in humans is uncharacterized in these excerpts, necessitating staged ocular toxicology and PK prior to (or within) clinical trials (Amin et al., 2022; Moir et al., 2023).

Development Implications and Recommendations  
- Mechanism validation in RPE: Prioritize targeted studies in human iPSC-RPE and donor-derived RPE to test the hypothesized AMPK→mTORC1→TFEB→lysosome axis. Required assays: TFEB nuclear localization (immunocytochemistry, subcellular fractionation), lysosomal pH (LysoSensor/LysoTracker), V-ATPase subunit expression and activity (ATPase assays), CTSD maturation (pro/mature CTSD Western) and enzymatic activity, autophagic flux (LC3 turnover with/without lysosomal blockade), and rescue experiments with AMPK and TFEB perturbation (e.g., CRISPRi/siRNA) (Amin et al., 2022; Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Ebeling et al., 2022).
- Translational pharmacology: Define retinal/RPE exposure–response using clinically relevant systemic concentrations and ocular distribution modeling; consider topical/periocular/intravitreal delivery if systemic exposure is insufficient for retinal AMPK engagement and lysosome-centric endpoints, with rigorous ocular toxicology (Moir et al., 2023).
- Indication and stage targeting: Given epidemiologic signals skew toward early/non-exudative AMD and limited evidence for late AMD benefit, prioritize early/intermediate AMD cohorts and GA progression trials with mechanistic biomarkers (RPE autofluorescence dynamics, OCT-based RPE/ONL metrics, aqueous humor cytokines/miRNAs) to increase sensitivity to disease-modifying effects (Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Liang et al., 2022; Moir et al., 2023).
- Clinical trial design: Incorporate robust confounder control and stratification (smoking, DR status, renal function, OCT1 polymorphisms) and embed target engagement (e.g., peripheral blood or aqueous biomarkers of AMPK/mTOR/autophagy) and safety surveillance (B12 levels, GI tolerability, lactate in at-risk) to bridge mechanism to clinical outcome (Gokhale et al., 2023; Zhou & Xue, 2024).
- Combination/adjunct strategies: Given non-overlapping mechanisms with anti-VEGF and complement inhibitors, explore combinatorial approaches in late-stage disease (e.g., GA with complement inhibition) if target engagement and safety are demonstrated (Amin et al., 2022; Shen et al., 2024).

Conclusion: Metformin is a credible repurposing candidate for dry AMD on the strength of convergent mechanistic rationale (AMPK activation, autophagy/mitochondrial support, anti-inflammatory/anti-senescence actions), robust preclinical retinal protection across models, and suggestive—but inconsistent—observational human data; however, decisive gaps remain for the central lysosome-centric hypothesis (TFEB/V-ATPase/CTSD in RPE) and for randomized clinical efficacy, especially in GA. The program should proceed with focused mechanistic validation of TFEB/lysosome endpoints in RPE, retinal target engagement and pharmacology at clinically feasible exposures, and staged, biomarker-rich randomized trials in early/intermediate AMD and GA to quantify efficacy and safety. Until lysosomal endpoints are confirmed and clinical benefit demonstrated, the hypothesis that metformin restores RPE autophagic flux via TFEB/V-ATPase/CTSD to prevent dry AMD remains plausible but unproven (Amin et al., 2022; Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Shen et al., 2024; Gokhale et al., 2023; Elhalag et al., 2024).
