Within this corpus, IL-6 behaves as part of a downstream inflammatory secretome during RPE stress rather than an upstream determinant of lysosomal health (Brandstetter, 2016).

Assay-level expectations under AMD-relevant stress paradigms should be aligned with the causal structure supported by the evidence.

- What IL-6R blockade should do: Given that RPE secrete IL-6 and can engage IL-6/IL-8 autocrine degenerative signaling in inflammatory contexts, tocilizumab is expected to abrogate IL-6–dependent downstream signaling in RPE and neighboring cells, dampening IL-6–responsive gene expression and paracrine effects where IL-6 is a driver (Brandstetter, 2016). In LMP/blue-light or impaired-clearance inflammasome models, IL-6 is robustly induced alongside IL-1β/IL-18 and partially depends on caspase-1–driven pathways, so tocilizumab would be expected to reduce IL-6-mediated signaling outputs but would not suppress upstream lysosomal damage, cathepsin leakage, inflammasome assembly, or caspase-1 activation per se (Brandstetter, 2016). Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Bexarotene, commercially known as Targretin and referenced here as Sigma B1269, is a fully synthetic rexinoid that was originally designed as a selective agonist for the retinoid X receptor (RXR). It is structurally distinct from naturally occurring retinoids such as 9‐cis‐retinoic acid; its chemical structure consists of a lipophilic tetramethyltetralin moiety connected through an ethynyl linker to a benzoic acid group, a design that confers high binding affinity (nanomolar EC50 values) and specificity for RXR subtypes (de Almeida & Conda‐Sheridan, 2019, pp. 8–9; Jurutka et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). As a member of the rexinoid class, bexarotene belongs to a group of therapeutic compounds that were developed to overcome the limitations of pan‐retinoid receptor activation by offering a more targeted means of modulating nuclear receptor signaling. RXRs have the unique ability to form either homodimers or heterodimers with a wide range of nuclear receptors—including peroxisome proliferator‐activated receptors (PPARs), liver X receptors (LXRs), thyroid hormone receptors (TRs), and vitamin D receptors (VDRs)—thereby influencing diverse gene expression programs that control cell growth, differentiation, and lipid metabolism (de Almeida & Conda‐Sheridan, 2019, pp. 8–9; Heck et al., 2016, pp. 1–2; Lalloyer et al., 2009, pp. 1–2). The synthetic origin of bexarotene, achieved through sophisticated organic synthesis that optimizes its lipophilic and acidic domains, enables it to engage conserved ligand‐binding residues (for example, key arginine and hydrophobic amino acids) in the RXR ligand‐binding domain, ensuring potent activation of the receptor (Chitranshi et al., 2019, p. 9; de Almeida & Conda‐Sheridan, 2019, pp. 11–13). This profile not only underlies its efficacy in its original oncologic indications but also supports its potential for repurposing in other diseases where RXR signaling is of therapeutic interest.

Therapeutic History:  
Bexarotene is well established in clinical practice as the first FDA-approved RXR-selective agonist, primarily indicated for the treatment of refractory cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (CTCL) in patients who have failed at least one systemic therapy (de Almeida & Conda‐Sheridan, 2019, pp. 8–9; Jurutka et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). Over the years, extensive clinical experience with bexarotene has been accrued in oncology, with studies demonstrating its capacity to induce cancer cell arrest, differentiation, and apoptosis by modulating the transcriptional landscape via RXR-mediated gene regulation (Heck et al., 2016, pp. 1–2, 9–10). Beyond its original role in oncology, bexarotene has been investigated in various other contexts; preclinical studies have explored its effects in non-small cell lung cancer, acute myeloid leukemia, and even in some hormone-sensitive malignancies—owing to its ability to interfere with proliferative signaling pathways (Marshall et al., 2015, pp. 2–3; Dheer et al., 2018, pp. 1–2). Notably, recent investigations have also assessed bexarotene in neurodegenerative disease models, particularly Alzheimer’s disease and Parkinson’s disease, where its RXR-mediated upregulation of apolipoprotein E (ApoE) and cholesterol transporters such as ABCA1 have been postulated to facilitate amyloid-beta clearance and neuronal protection (Marshall et al., 2015, pp. 2–3; Mallick et al., 2021, pp. 1–2). Although the compound has not been directly tested in clinical trials for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD), its mechanism of action—centered on modulating lipid metabolism and cellular clearance pathways—suggests that its repurposing for dry AMD is scientifically plausible, especially given the involvement of dysregulated lipid homeostasis and lysosomal dysfunction in this condition (Chitranshi et al., 2019, pp. 1–2; de Almeida & Conda‐Sheridan, 2019, pp. 8–9). Furthermore, RXR signaling is known to be critical in maintaining retinal homeostasis, and studies in animal models have shown that disruption of RXR function can lead to retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) abnormalities, providing an indirect rationale for evaluating RXR agonists like bexarotene in ocular applications (Chitranshi et al., 2019, pp. 1–2; Lalloyer et al., 2009, pp. 1–2).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, bexarotene exerts its effects by binding selectively to the ligand-binding domain of RXRs with high affinity, thereby promoting conformational changes that favor the release of co-repressor proteins and the recruitment of co-activators containing LxxLL motifs. This binding event induces RXR to function either as a homodimer or, more importantly, as a heterodimer with other nuclear receptors such as LXR and PPAR, which are central to the regulation of lipid homeostasis and inflammatory responses (de Almeida & Conda‐Sheridan, 2019, pp. 8–9; Marshall et al., 2015, pp. 2–3). In its role as an RXR agonist, bexarotene has been shown to markedly upregulate the transcription of genes involved in cholesterol efflux, including those coding for ATP-binding cassette transporters like ABCA1 and for apolipoproteins such as ApoE; these factors are critical for mobilizing and clearing excess cholesterol in various tissues (Marshall et al., 2015, pp. 2–3; Mallick et al., 2021, pp. 2–3). Furthermore, RXR agonism by bexarotene can stimulate the activity of permissive heterodimers—such as RXR/PPARα—which are known to play pivotal roles in fatty acid oxidation and energy metabolism. This activation is hypothesized to extend to downstream transcriptional regulators like TFEB, the master regulator of lysosomal biogenesis, though direct evidence in retinal cells is still emerging (Marshall et al., 2015, pp. 2–3; Dheer et al., 2018, pp. 1–2). In several preclinical models, bexarotene has been associated with the modulation of lysosomal pathways; for instance, it can alleviate endoplasmic reticulum stress and prevent the activation of pro-apoptotic proteins, which are important contributors to intracellular lipid accumulation and cellular dysfunction (Farol & Hymes, 2004, pp. 1–2; Lalloyer et al., 2009, pp. 1–2). Moreover, its selective RXR activity circumvents the adverse effects associated with pan-retinoid receptor activation, particularly the hypercalcemic and other toxicities seen with non-selective retinoids, by limiting cross-reactivity with RARs (Jurutka et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Mallick et al., 2021, pp. 2–3). In summary, bexarotene’s multifaceted mechanism includes (1) robust activation of RXR-mediated transcription of lipid transporter genes, (2) modulation of heterodimer partners such as PPARα and LXR that indirectly regulate lipid metabolism and energy balance, and (3) potential upregulation of lysosomal biogenesis and function via TFEB-associated pathways—collectively contributing to improved cellular lipid clearance and metabolic homeostasis (Marshall et al., 2015, pp. 2–3; Mallick et al., 2021, pp. 1–2; Heck et al., 2016, pp. 7–9).

Expected Effect in Dry Age-related Macular Degeneration:  
The central hypothesis driving the evaluation of bexarotene for dry AMD posits that activation of RXR in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells will lead to beneficial metabolic remodeling, specifically through enhancing cholesterol efflux and promoting lysosomal function. In the context of dry AMD, pathologic drusen formation is largely a consequence of chronic accumulation of lipids and misprocessed extracellular debris under the RPE. Through the activation of RXR, bexarotene is expected to upregulate key mediators of cholesterol transport such as ABCA1 and ApoE, thereby facilitating the removal of excess cholesterol and lipid deposits from the RPE (Marshall et al., 2015, pp. 2–3; Chitranshi et al., 2019, pp. 1–2). In addition, RXR activation, particularly when partnered with PPARα, has been associated with the induction of a lysosomal program that involves enhanced expression of genes regulating lysosomal acidification—potentially via the upregulation of vacuolar ATPase (V-ATPase) subunits—and the activation of lysosomal enzymes such as cathepsin D (CTSD) (Marshall et al., 2015, pp. 2–3; Mallick et al., 2021, pp. 2–3). Although direct demonstrations of TFEB activation in RPE models with bexarotene treatment are limited in the provided literature, the established role of RXR agonists in modulating lipid-rich, lysosomal compartments in other cell types supports the likelihood that a similar upregulation would occur in RPE cells (Marshall et al., 2015, pp. 2–3; Dheer et al., 2018, pp. 1–2). Given that TFEB is a master regulator of lysosomal biogenesis and function, its coactivation alongside PPARα could enhance the degradative capacity of the cell, resulting in improved clearance of drusen-associated lipid aggregates. This dual action—promoting cholesterol efflux while simultaneously enhancing lysosomal catabolism—addresses two of the key pathogenic mechanisms underlying dry AMD (Marshall et al., 2015, pp. 2–3; Mallick et al., 2021, pp. 1–2). In vitro, one might anticipate that bexarotene treatment of cultured RPE cells will lead to increased transcript and protein levels of ABC transporters, elevated markers of lysosomal acidification such as V-ATPase subunits, and enhanced activity of cathepsin D, collectively contributing to the reduction of lipid overload at a cellular level (Marshall et al., 2015, pp. 2–3; de Almeida & Conda‐Sheridan, 2019, pp. 8–9). Moreover, given its extensive clinical use in oncology with a tolerable ocular safety profile, bexarotene is well situated for repurposing, provided that its systemic adverse effects (e.g., hyperlipidemia, hypothyroidism) can be managed or mitigated through controlled dosing strategies or targeted delivery approaches (de Almeida & Conda‐Sheridan, 2019, pp. 8–9; Marshall et al., 2015, pp. 2–3).

Overall Evaluation:  
Bexarotene emerges as a promising therapeutic candidate for dry AMD based on its well-characterized pharmacological profile and multifaceted mechanism of action. One of its primary strengths lies in its selective activation of RXR, which has been shown to trigger transcriptional programs that enhance cholesterol efflux via the upregulation of key transporters such as ABCA1 and ApoE—pathways that are directly relevant to the clearance of drusen-associated lipids in dry AMD (Marshall et al., 2015, pp. 2–3; Mallick et al., 2021, pp. 1–2). In addition, the potential for RXR agonism to engage PPARα and, by extension, coactivate TFEB offers a novel approach to correcting lysosomal dysfunction—a critical factor in the pathogenesis of dry AMD. This dual action addresses both the extracellular accumulation of lipids and the intracellular deficits in degradative capacity that contribute to RPE dysfunction. The extensive clinical experience with bexarotene in cancer therapy provides an added advantage, as its pharmacokinetics, dosing regimens, and safety profiles are well documented, thereby facilitating a more rapid transition into repurposing studies. However, several challenges and weaknesses need to be acknowledged. Bexarotene is known to cause significant metabolic side effects, including hyperlipidemia and hypothyroidism, which may necessitate adjunctive treatments (such as lipid-lowering agents) or the development of targeted ocular delivery systems to minimize systemic exposure (de Almeida & Conda‐Sheridan, 2019, pp. 8–9; Mallick et al., 2021, pp. 2–3). Furthermore, although preclinical data in neurodegenerative models have demonstrated beneficial effects on lipid metabolism and lysosomal pathways, direct evidence in retinal pigment epithelial models is still limited. This gap underscores the need for rigorous in vitro and in vivo studies specifically designed to evaluate bexarotene’s efficacy in RPE cells and animal models of dry AMD (Chitranshi et al., 2019, pp. 1–2; Lalloyer et al., 2009, pp. 1–2). Another potential risk involves the compound’s polypharmacological nature; while its ability to interact with multiple nuclear receptors can be advantageous for targeting complex diseases, it also raises the possibility of off-target effects, such as its documented antagonism at PPARγ in certain contexts, which could have unforeseen impacts on retinal cell physiology (Marciano et al., 2015, pp. 1–2; Heck et al., 2016, pp. 7–9). The balance between therapeutic benefits and adverse effects will need to be carefully managed, perhaps by optimizing dosing regimens or by designing analogues with improved selectivity and reduced side effect profiles. In summary, the repurposing of bexarotene for dry AMD is supported by its robust activation of RXR-driven pathways related to lipid efflux and lysosomal function, as well as by its safe clinical history in ocular settings when used topically or in controlled systemic regimens. Nonetheless, additional preclinical work is essential to directly demonstrate its efficacy in RPE models and to delineate any ocular-specific pharmacodynamic parameters. Overall, the candidate shows promise as a multi‐pathway therapeutic approach for dry AMD, with strengths including its defined mechanism of action and extensive clinical history, and weaknesses largely centered on potential systemic side effects and the need for targeted delivery strategies (de Almeida & Conda‐Sheridan, 2019, pp. 8–9; Marshall et al., 2015, pp. 2–3; Chitranshi et al., 2019, pp. 1–2; Mallick et al., 2021, pp. 1–2; Marciano et al., 2015, pp. 1–2).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Sulforaphane (SFN) is a naturally occurring isothiocyanate derived from glucoraphanin in cruciferous vegetables via myrosinase-mediated hydrolysis; as an electrophilic small molecule, SFN was identified through its unusually potent induction of phase II detoxification enzymes and antioxidant defenses in mammalian tissues via the KEAP1–NFE2L2/NRF2 stress-response axis (classically termed “phase 2 induction”) (Qin, 2007; Hyttinen et al., 2019). Isothiocyanates and related electrophiles covalently modify reactive cysteine residues on KEAP1, disrupting the KEAP1–NRF2 “hinge-and-latch” ubiquitin ligase complex and stabilizing NRF2 to drive ARE-dependent transcription of cytoprotective enzymes including NQO1, GCLM, HO-1, and glutathione pathway genes (Hyttinen et al., 2019; Qin, 2007). Beyond canonical NRF2 activation, SFN is now recognized to engage lysosome-centered adaptive transcription by inducing nuclear translocation and activation of TFEB/TFE3 through a mild, ROS-triggered Ca²⁺–calcineurin pathway that is largely MTOR-independent, thereby upregulating CLEAR-network genes controlling lysosome and autophagy biogenesis (Li et al., 2021). In ocular contexts, SFN has been used experimentally as a cytoprotective agent in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) models subjected to oxidative or phototoxic stress, and as a modulator of autophagy markers, situating SFN within a dual-modality class that can activate antioxidant defenses and augment lysosome-autophagy function (Yang et al., 2021; Li et al., 2021).

Therapeutic History  
SFN and other NRF2 activators have been widely studied as cytoprotective chemopreventive agents and as protectants in oxidative-stress paradigms across tissues; in RPE models, SFN has repeatedly demonstrated NRF2-dependent protection and modulation of stress and quality-control pathways, although direct clinical testing in dry AMD is not reported in the provided literature (Qin, 2007; Liu et al., 2016). In ARPE-19 cells exposed to blue light, SFN promoted NRF2 nuclear translocation, induced HO-1 and glutathione production, reduced oxidative stress and inflammation, and its cytoprotective effect was blocked by the NRF2 inhibitor ML385, indicating a mechanistic dependence on NRF2; SFN also increased LC3B-II and p62, and the autophagy inhibitor 3-MA blunted its protective action, linking SFN’s benefit to autophagy engagement in this RPE stress model (Yang et al., 2021). In a separate ARPE-19 inflammatory model (TGF-β), SFN (alone or combined with vitamin D) lowered ROS and VEGF and restored epithelial junction markers; in that system, the authors did not detect NRF2 pathway modulation and instead implicated ERK1/2 downregulation, underscoring context-dependence of the upstream signaling mediating protection (Bergandi et al., 2024). Reviews and experimental summaries further report that SFN protects retinal/epithelial tissues and can recover cone function in an NRF2-dependent manner in mice undergoing RPE oxidative stress, although primary data for those specific in vivo outcomes are not detailed in the provided text (Falcão et al., 2025). Mechanistically adjacent precedents in RPE include robust protection by the electrophilic NRF2 activator RTA 408 in primary human RPE subjected to H₂O₂, with genetic evidence for NRF2 dependence; while not SFN, this validates the KEAP1–NRF2 axis as druggable and protective in human RPE (Liu et al., 2016). With respect to lysosome-autophagy axes central to dry AMD, TFEB activation (via rapamycin or constitutively active TFEB) reduces photoreceptor outer segment–derived autofluorescent granules in RPE POS-feeding models, and TFEB-directed interventions (including trehalose or constitutively nuclear TFEB) restore cathepsin D/L abundance and activity and increase LAMP1 in AMD-relevant human RPE models, establishing the lysosome/transcriptional arm as therapeutically tractable in RPE; however, these TFEB-driven rescues have not been directly demonstrated with SFN in RPE in the supplied literature (Falcão et al., 2024; Ghosh et al., 2024).

Mechanism of Action  
- NRF2 engagement via KEAP1 cysteine sensing: SFN, as an electrophile, reacts with specific redox-sensitive cysteines on KEAP1 (notably Cys151 among others), impairing KEAP1-mediated ubiquitination of NRF2 and permitting NRF2 stabilization, nuclear accumulation, and heterodimerization with small Maf proteins to bind AREs and induce a large gene battery of antioxidant, detoxification, and proteostasis regulators (e.g., NQO1, HO-1, GCLM, GSTs), increasing GSH and related defenses (Hyttinen et al., 2019; Qin, 2007). In RPE and ocular tissues, SFN and related NRF2 activators have induced phase II enzymes and HO-1 and conferred resistance to photooxidative injury, with biochemical readouts that include increased NQO1, thioredoxin, GSH, and reduced ROS (Qin, 2007; Zhang et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2021). Aging impairs inducible NRF2 signaling in RPE under oxidative challenges (e.g., sodium iodate), supporting the rationale for exogenous NRF2 activation in older RPE (Sachdeva et al., 2014).

- TFEB/TFE3 activation and lysosome-autophagy biogenesis: SFN provokes a mild increase in ROS that sensitizes lysosomal MCOLN1/TRPML1 channels to agonist-evoked Ca²⁺ release; resultant cytosolic Ca²⁺ engages calcineurin to dephosphorylate TFEB, enabling its nuclear translocation and activation of CLEAR-network transcription independently of acute MTORC1 inhibition (TFEB activation is blocked by antioxidants, BAPTA-AM, and attenuated by FK506) (Li et al., 2021). The SFN-induced TFEB program upregulates autophagy and lysosome genes (SQSTM1, ULK1, LC3) and multiple lysosomal components including LAMP1, v-ATPase subunits (e.g., ATP6V1H), hydrolases (CTSB, TPP1), and MCOLN1, and increases LysoTracker and LAMP1 signals, consistent with enhanced lysosomal mass and acidotropic probe accumulation (Li et al., 2021). Critically, TFEB is necessary for SFN-induced upregulation of NFE2L2/NRF2 and for SFN-mediated suppression of ROS in mitochondrial and lysosomal stress models, documenting a TFEB→NRF2 dependency in SFN’s antioxidant protection (Li et al., 2021). Reviews synthesizing TFEB–NRF2 crosstalk add that TFEB can directly or indirectly promote NRF2 by repressing its E3 ligase (DCAF11) and via p62-mediated KEAP1 sequestration; reciprocally, NRF2 activation can induce TFEB-related gene sets and promote autophagosome–lysosome fusion, indicating bidirectional reinforcement (Falcão et al., 2025).

- RPE-specific TFEB/lysosome biology relevant to AMD: In human RPE-derived ARPE-19 cells, TFEB controls lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy; nutrient deprivation and lysosomal stress increase TFEB and MITF and induce CLEAR genes including LAMP1, CTSD, MCOLN1, and autophagy factors (BECN1), with calcineurin-mediated dephosphorylation regulating nuclear translocation (Pan et al., 2019). In AMD-relevant RPE models, TFEB activation (via mTORC1 inhibition or constitutively active TFEB) reduces POS-dependent lipofuscin-like autofluorescent granules through a hydrolase-dependent mechanism, and inhibition or genetic loss of CTSD increases autofluorescent burden and abrogates rapamycin’s benefit, tying TFEB-driven rescue to functional lysosomal proteolysis (Falcão et al., 2024). In human AMD donor RPE and CFH Y402H iPSC-RPE, elevated p-TFEB/p-TFE3 associates with reduced CTSD/CTSL abundance and activity; interventions that restore TFEB nuclear activity (AAV2-TFEB-S467A) or TFEB activators (trehalose) rescue CTSD/CTSL levels and activities and increase LAMP1, while AKT2 inhibition counters secretory-autophagy bias and improves degradative flux (Ghosh et al., 2024; Ghosh et al., 2023).

- Cathepsin D biochemistry and lysosomal pH: Cathepsin D (CTSD) is an abundant lysosomal aspartyl protease synthesized as an inactive proenzyme that undergoes maturation and activation in the acidic late endosome/lysosome; cathepsins generally require a reducing, mildly acidic lumen and lose activity at neutral pH, linking lysosomal acidification (v-ATPase function) tightly to CTSD proteolysis (Sharif, 2015). In AMD, lysosomal dysfunction (including LMP, impaired proton-pump function, and hydrolase inhibition by lipofuscin-derived oxidized products) is prominent, and CTSD leakage and reduced hydrolase activity are reported in AMD RPE, mechanistically supporting the therapeutic objective to normalize lysosomal pH and restore cathepsin activity (Falcão et al., 2025).

- Safety and pathway caveats: Constitutive or excessive activation of NRF2 or TFEB can carry oncogenic or maladaptive risks, and chronic KEAP1–NRF2 perturbation can yield accumulation of non-degradative organelles, emphasizing the need for cell-specific, dose-titrated modulation and rigorous safety assessment in the AMD context (Falcão et al., 2025).

Taken together, SFN stands out for concurrent engagement of NRF2 antioxidant programs and TFEB-driven lysosome/autophagy biogenesis—mechanisms that align with central oxidative and degradative defects in dry AMD RPE—yet it is important to note that direct biochemical evidence demonstrating SFN-mediated normalization of lysosomal pH and restoration of CTSD maturation/activity in RPE under AMD-relevant oxidative stress is not present in the supplied literature (Falcão et al., 2025; Li et al., 2021).

Expected Effect  
Under the stated hypothesis—SFN engages NRF2 and TFEB in oxidatively stressed RPE to normalize lysosomal pH and restore CTSD proteolysis—the expected proximate and downstream effects in rigorously designed assays are:  
- Antioxidant response and ROS control: SFN should increase NRF2 nuclear accumulation and ARE target expression (HO-1, NQO1, GCLM, Trx1, GSH biosynthesis enzymes) in RPE cells subjected to oxidative paradigms (e.g., blue light, sodium iodate, hydroquinone, or POS feeding with photooxidative stress), lowering ROS burden and oxidative damage; this is strongly supported in ARPE-19 under blue light (and in other epithelial systems), and the effect shows functional dependence on NRF2 (ML385-sensitive) (Yang et al., 2021; Qin, 2007). Aging-associated defects in inducible NRF2 signaling suggest exogenous NRF2 activation may be especially beneficial in aged RPE, further motivating this outcome measure (Sachdeva et al., 2014).

- TFEB activation and lysosome-autophagy program: SFN should induce TFEB nuclear translocation through ROS→Ca²⁺→calcineurin signaling, upregulate CLEAR-network transcripts (including LAMP1, CTSD, ATP6V1H, MCOLN1, ULK1, SQSTM1, LC3), increase lysosomal biogenesis and LysoTracker staining, and enhance autophagic flux; these outcomes are well documented for SFN in multiple human cell models and provide mechanistic plausibility for analogous effects in RPE (Li et al., 2021). In RPE specifically, TFEB is inducible and drives LAMP1 and CTSD expression under stress, while TFEB activation improves degradative capacity in AMD-relevant settings, supporting the assay logic to monitor TFEB localization and CLEAR targets in RPE (Pan et al., 2019; Falcão et al., 2024).

- Lysosomal acidification and CTSD proteolysis: If SFN increases v-ATPase subunit expression and lysosomal mass (as in other cells), one would expect improved lysosomal acidification (lower pH) and more efficient CTSD maturation (pro- to intermediate- to mature forms) and activity, read out by calibrated pH probes (e.g., LysoSensor or ratiometric genetically encoded sensors), Western blots for CTSD processing, and fluorometric CTSD activity assays. This is biologically plausible given SFN-induced lysosomal gene expression and LysoTracker increases in vitro, and given that TFEB activation rescues hydrolase-dependent POS processing in RPE; however, direct evidence that SFN normalizes lysosomal pH and increases CTSD maturation/activity in RPE under oxidative stress is not shown in the provided literature and must be generated (Li et al., 2021; Falcão et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2025).

- Functional RPE outcomes: Improved degradative clearance of POS-derived material and reduced accumulation of autofluorescent granules (lipofuscin-like AFG) are expected functional correlates. Rapamycin and constitutively active TFEB reduce AFG in RPE POS-feeding models in a hydrolase-dependent manner, and TFEB activation or AKT2 inhibition restores CTSD/CTSL activity and LAMP1 levels in human AMD RPE models; SFN could converge on these endpoints via TFEB activation, but this remains to be established experimentally (Falcão et al., 2024; Ghosh et al., 2024).

Assay implementation considerations:  
- Cell systems and paradigms: iPSC-derived human RPE (including CFH Y402H risk background) and ARPE-19, subjected to blue light, hydroquinone/cigarette smoke mimetics, sodium iodate, POS feeding, and/or complement challenge, to model oxidative and degradative stress relevant to dry AMD (Yang et al., 2021; Ghosh et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2024).

- Readouts: NRF2 nuclear translocation and ARE target induction; TFEB nuclear translocation and phosphorylation state; CLEAR-network gene expression (LAMP1, CTSD, ATP6V1H, MCOLN1, ULK1, SQSTM1); lysosomal pH (calibrated probes); lysosomal mass (LAMP1 immunostaining, LysoTracker); CTSD processing (pro/mature Western blots) and enzymatic activity; autophagic flux (LC3 turnover with and without lysosomal inhibitors); POS processing kinetics and AFG quantification (Li et al., 2021; Pan et al., 2019; Falcão et al., 2024).

- Controls and mechanism validation: Antioxidant blockade (NAC, catalase) to test ROS-dependence of TFEB activation; Ca²⁺ chelation (BAPTA-AM) and calcineurin inhibition (FK506) to probe TFEB activation pathway; NRF2 inhibitor (ML385) to test NRF2 dependence; TFEB loss-of-function (siRNA/CRISPR) to test TFEB dependence; rapamycin/trehalose/AAV-TFEB as positive controls for lysosomal biogenesis; cathepsin inhibitors and CTSD KO/knockdown to test hydrolase dependence; use of AKT2 pathway modulators to deconvolve TFEB repression in AMD-relevant models (Li et al., 2021; Yang et al., 2021; Ghosh et al., 2024).

- Dosing: Based on mechanistic studies, SFN at 5–15 µM for 4–9 h is effective for TFEB activation in several cell lines; in ARPE-19 blue-light studies, SFN modulated NRF2 and autophagy markers, and in TGF-β models, SFN was tested at 1–10 µM with ERK pathway modulation observed (Li et al., 2021; Yang et al., 2021; Bergandi et al., 2024).

- Interpretation caveats: In TGF-β–treated RPE, investigators did not detect NRF2 modulation with SFN, implying model-specific pathway engagement; this further justifies running multiple oxidative-stress paradigms and confirming pathway activation per condition (Bergandi et al., 2024).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Mechanistic alignment with AMD pathobiology: SFN targets two validated, convergent axes implicated in non-neovascular AMD—NRF2-mediated antioxidant defense and TFEB-driven lysosomal-autophagy competence—addressing both oxidative injury and impaired degradative capacity in RPE (Pinelli et al., 2020; Pan et al., 2019; Falcão et al., 2024). The KEAP1–NRF2 pathway is protective in RPE and becomes inducibly impaired with age, and TFEB activation restores lysosomal hydrolase function and reduces POS-derived autofluorescence in RPE models (Sachdeva et al., 2014; Ghosh et al., 2024).

- Robust cellular mechanism for dual-pathway engagement: High-quality mechanistic studies show SFN activates TFEB via ROS→Ca²⁺→calcineurin independent of acute MTORC1 inhibition, induces CLEAR genes, increases lysosomal mass and LysoTracker staining, and requires TFEB to drive NFE2L2 transcription and antioxidant protection; this dual activation positions SFN to coordinate detoxification and lysosomal biogenesis (Li et al., 2021).

- RPE-relevant efficacy signals: In ARPE-19 blue-light stress, SFN confers NRF2-dependent cytoprotection and requires autophagy; SFN also reduces ROS and preserves epithelial integrity in an inflammatory RPE model (albeit via ERK1/2 modulation), indicating protective breadth across RPE-relevant stressors (Yang et al., 2021; Bergandi et al., 2024).

- Translational plausibility: SFN (and class analogs) have measurable bioavailability in humans and have long been explored as chemopreventive agents, supporting feasibility of repurposing if ocular exposure and dosing can be optimized; as a comparator, RTA 408’s efficacy in primary RPE confirms the druggability of KEAP1–NRF2 in human RPE (Qin, 2007; Liu et al., 2016).

Weaknesses and Gaps  
- No direct evidence for lysosomal pH normalization or CTSD rescue by SFN in RPE: Although SFN upregulates lysosomal genes and LysoTracker signal in other cell types, the literature provided does not report calibrated lysosomal pH measurements, CTSD maturation patterns, or CTSD enzymatic activity in RPE after SFN under AMD-relevant oxidative stress; this is the critical gap relative to the stated hypothesis (Falcão et al., 2025; Li et al., 2021).

- Model-dependent pathway engagement: In TGF-β ARPE-19, SFN protection tracked with ERK1/2 modulation rather than detectable NRF2 activation, underscoring that the upstream route by which SFN confers benefit can vary with the stressor and cellular context; robust pathway biomarker panels will be required in each model (Bergandi et al., 2024).

- Safety and liability considerations: Persistent activation of NRF2 or TFEB may carry oncogenic or maladaptive risks; KEAP1–NRF2 dysregulation can drive accumulation of non-degradative organelles, and TFEB activation must be titrated to avoid excessive catabolic or proliferative shifts; this risk profile necessitates careful dose finding, exposure control, and long-term safety assessment (Falcão et al., 2025).

- Ocular delivery/exposure unknowns: The provided literature notes systemic bioavailability with detection in non-ocular tissues; however, data establishing therapeutic concentrations in the RPE/choroid following systemic or local administration are absent here and will need to be generated to support translational feasibility (Qin, 2007).

- Disease-network complexity: In AMD-relevant RPE, AKT2 upregulation suppresses TFEB/TFE3 and reduces cathepsin expression/activity, while complement dysregulation, iron overload, and lipofuscin-associated proton-pump/hydrolase inhibition further stress lysosomes; whether SFN’s TFEB activation suffices under these multi-hit conditions, or whether combination with AKT2/MTOR modulators is required, remains to be determined (Ghosh et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2025; Ghosh et al., 2023).

Programmatic recommendation  
- Proceed to focused preclinical validation with a decision gate on lysosomal biochemical rescue. The mechanistic case for SFN’s dual NRF2/TFEB action is strong, and RPE protection data exist; however, the program’s value hinges on demonstrating that SFN normalizes lysosomal acidity and restores CTSD maturation/activity in stressed human RPE—outcomes not yet shown (Li et al., 2021; Yang et al., 2021; Falcão et al., 2025).

- Experimental plan (key go/no-go criteria):  
  1) Pathway engagement: SFN dose–time response for NRF2 and TFEB activation in iPSC-RPE (±CFH Y402H) under blue light, hydroquinone, sodium iodate, POS feeding, and complement challenge; use ML385, FK506, BAPTA-AM, and TFEB LOF to assign mechanism (Yang et al., 2021; Li et al., 2021; Falcão et al., 2024).  
  2) Lysosomal function: Calibrated lysosomal pH; CTSD pro/mature processing and activity; LAMP1 and LysoTracker; autophagic flux; POS degradation kinetics and AFG load; requirement for CTSD confirmed by CTSD knockdown and cathepsin inhibitors (Falcão et al., 2024; Sharif, 2015).  
  3) Comparative controls: Rapamycin, trehalose, and AAV2-TFEB-S467A as positive controls for lysosomal rescue; AKT2 inhibition as a disease-relevant comparator; RTA 408 or DMF as NRF2-pathway comparators (Ghosh et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2016).  
  4) In vivo signal-seeking: Acute oxidative RPE injury (e.g., sodium iodate) and chronic stress models to test functional endpoints (ERG, OCT) and histology with RPE lysosomal markers and CTSD activity ex vivo; assess whether SFN improves cone/RPE function in an NRF2-dependent manner as suggested by prior reports (Sachdeva et al., 2014; Falcão et al., 2025).  
  5) Safety/tolerability: Proliferation, TFEB/NRF2 target overactivation, lysosomal membrane integrity (LMP markers), and non-degradative organelle accumulation with extended SFN exposure; aim for intermittent dosing to minimize chronic pathway hyperactivation (Falcão et al., 2025).

If SFN demonstrates robust TFEB/NRF2 engagement in human RPE, normalizes lysosomal pH, and restores CTSD maturation/activity with concomitant functional improvements in POS clearance and AFG reduction, it would represent a differentiated candidate addressing both oxidative and degradative lesions central to geographic atrophy; absent those biochemical rescues, SFN should be deprioritized in favor of TFEB-directed agents (e.g., trehalose or gene-based TFEB activation) or combinations that address AKT2–TFEB repression and complement-driven lysosomal injury (Ghosh et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2024; Ghosh et al., 2023).

In summary, sulforaphane is a scientifically credible, mechanistically dual-action candidate for dry AMD based on strong evidence of NRF2 activation in RPE and TFEB-driven lysosome-autophagy induction in multiple cell systems, with supportive RPE protection data; yet the decisive evidence that SFN normalizes lysosomal acidity and rescues cathepsin D proteolysis in oxidatively stressed human RPE is currently lacking in the provided literature and must be established to justify advancement (Yang et al., 2021; Li et al., 2021; Falcão et al., 2025).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Genistein is a naturally occurring isoflavone that was first isolated from soybeans and other leguminous plants. As a member of the phytoestrogen class, genistein possesses structural similarities to mammalian estrogens and can bind to estrogen receptors, albeit with much lower intrinsic potency than endogenous steroids. It is typically obtained from dietary sources such as soy, red clover, and other legumes, but high‐purity formulations have been developed and are commercially available (for example, Sigma G6649). Genistein belongs to a broader class of natural bioactive compounds that have been studied over the past several decades for their modulating effects on various cellular processes including antioxidant defense, differentiation, apoptosis, and proliferation. Historically, phytoestrogens like genistein have been investigated both for their hormone‐like activity and as specific inhibitors of protein tyrosine kinases. The compound has been utilized in research ranging from hormone replacement strategies in menopausal women to anticancer studies, and its ability to modulate several cell signaling pathways—including those associated with PI3K/AKT/mTOR—has attracted interest in other fields such as neurodegeneration and ocular health (Albulescu & Popovici, 2007).

Therapeutic History:  
The therapeutic history of genistein spans multiple domains. Clinically, phytoestrogens have been examined largely as potential alternatives to traditional estrogen replacement therapies for the alleviation of menopausal symptoms, with some studies reporting modest effects on vasomotor symptoms, menstrual cycle regulation, and quality‐of‐life indices (Glazier & Bowman, 2001; Albulescu & Popovici, 2007). In the veterinary and preclinical realm, high doses of phytoestrogens have been associated with reproductive toxicity in livestock such as sheep (the classical clover disease), while rodent studies have similarly documented endocrine disruptions when exposed to high concentrations (Glazier & Bowman, 2001). For bone health specifically, preclinical data have shown that ovariectomized rats fed genistein exhibit reduced rates of bone loss; this finding parallels clinical trials using the synthetic isoflavone derivative ipriflavone—which is related to the parent compounds in the isoflavone class—and has demonstrated benefits in slowing bone loss and increasing bone mineral density when given for periods of up to two years in postmenopausal women (Glazier & Bowman, 2001). Regarding ocular applications, there is emerging preclinical work to improve the solubility and corneal penetration of genistein; for example, encapsulating genistein in hyaluronic acid–modified MPEG-b-PAE polymeric micelles has been shown to improve its corneal permeability by approximately 1.5-fold compared to a simple drug solution (Li et al., 2018). Although genistein has not yet been extensively evaluated in clinical trials specifically targeting dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD), its broad modulatory effects on tyrosine kinases and downstream signaling pathways provide a rationale for repurposing it to address dry AMD pathophysiology, particularly given the significant unmet therapeutic need in this area (Glazier & Bowman, 2001).

Mechanism of Action:  
Genistein is widely recognized for its ability to inhibit protein tyrosine kinases. This inhibitory action extends to several receptors and intracellular kinases, thereby modulating key signaling cascades including the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway—a pathway that is critical for cell survival, proliferation, and metabolism. In many cell-based studies, genistein has been shown to suppress PI3K/AKT signaling, leading to downstream inhibition of mTOR complex 1 (mTORC1) activity. Since mTORC1 coordinates cellular anabolic processes and suppresses autophagy under nutrient-rich conditions, inhibiting this complex can trigger autophagic clearance mechanisms (Albulescu & Popovici, 2007). One of the pivotal regulators downstream of mTORC1 is the transcription factor EB (TFEB), which, when dephosphorylated due to mTORC1 inhibition, translocates into the nucleus and promotes the transcription of genes involved in lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy. There is evidence that genistein can modulate lysosomal metabolism and promote TFEB activation, as reported in studies highlighting the ability of flavonoids to enhance the clearance of substrate accumulations via TFEB-mediated transcriptional programs (Xu et al., 2020). In retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells, which play a crucial role in maintaining photoreceptor health through phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments (POS), enhanced autophagy and lysosomal function are essential for the degradation and removal of cellular debris, including drusen components characteristic of dry AMD (Falcão et al., 2024). Moreover, experimental reports have suggested that in RPE-like models, treatment with compounds that suppress the PI3K/AKT/mTOR axis leads to increased LC3 turnover and upregulation of cathepsin D (CTSD), a lysosomal aspartic protease essential for phagolysosomal digestion (Albulescu & Popovici, 2007; Jahan et al., 2022). In this context, genistein is hypothesized to function by inhibiting upstream tyrosine kinases that feed into PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling, thereby promoting TFEB activation. TFEB then orchestrates the transcription of lysosomal genes, leading to enhanced lysosomal acidification and increased enzymatic activities, including that of cathepsin D, which is imperative for effective degradation within phagolysosomes (Falcão et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2025).

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis posits that administration of genistein to RPE cells will lead to measurable inhibition of the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway, resulting in dephosphorylation and nuclear translocation of TFEB. This transcriptional activation is expected to upregulate a battery of lysosomal and autophagy-related genes, including those responsible for the maintenance of lysosomal acidification and the synthesis of key proteases such as cathepsin D (Falcão et al., 2024). In functional assays, an increase in LC3 turnover—a marker of enhanced autophagic flux—would be anticipated, alongside elevated levels of CTSD, providing the biochemical basis for improved phagolysosomal digestion. Consequently, in an in vitro RPE cell model subjected to a photoreceptor outer segment (POS) feeding assay, genistein treatment is expected to facilitate the clearance of POS-derived debris and reduce the accumulation of autofluorescent lipofuscin-like granules. This outcome mimics the effects observed with compounds like rapamycin, where mTOR inhibition leads to a significant, approximately 30% reduction of POS-dependent autofluorescence by improving lysosomal processing (Falcão et al., 2024). Moreover, in light of published observations demonstrating that effective activation of TFEB can restore lysosomal biogenesis and enhance cellular clearance, genistein’s dual inhibition of kinase activity and subsequent autophagy upregulation is predicted to result in a favorable impact on drusen clearance and overall RPE function in dry AMD settings (Falcão et al., 2024; Xu et al., 2020).

Overall Evaluation:  
Overall, genistein presents as an intriguing candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry AMD, particularly given its established history as a natural product with a favorable oral safety profile and its documented ability to modulate critical signaling pathways involved in cell survival and autophagy. One of the major strengths of genistein lies in its dual mechanism: as a selective inhibitor of tyrosine kinases, it can suppress the upstream activation of the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway, and as a modulator of lysosomal metabolism, it facilitates TFEB activation. This mechanistic duality offers a targeted approach to enhance the autophagic clearance capacity of RPE cells, which is critical in preventing the accumulation of intracellular debris and drusen associated with dry AMD (Falcão et al., 2024; Xu et al., 2020). Furthermore, the existing literature on phytoestrogens indicates that compounds in this chemical class are generally well tolerated when administered orally, and formulation strategies (such as encapsulation in hyaluronic acid–modified polymeric micelles) enhance ocular bioavailability, potentially enabling effective local delivery with minimal systemic adverse effects (Li et al., 2018).

However, several challenges and weaknesses must be addressed before advancing genistein as a therapy for dry AMD. First, while there is a substantial body of evidence supporting the role of genistein in modulating PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling in non-ocular tissues, direct evidence in RPE cells and in the context of dry AMD is sparse. Most published studies in the ocular domain have focused on formulation and delivery aspects rather than on detailed mechanism-of-action studies within RPE cells. Second, the estrogenic activity of genistein, although weak, raises potential concerns regarding off-target endocrine effects, particularly during long-term administration in older populations who may be susceptible to hormone-related side effects. These aspects would require rigorous assessment in preclinical and early-phase clinical trials. Additionally, the pharmacokinetics of genistein when administered via ocular routes (either topically or systemically) remain incompletely characterized, and comprehensive data on tissue distribution, especially to the retina or RPE, is limited. Such pharmacokinetic studies are crucial to ensure that therapeutic concentrations can be achieved and maintained in the target tissues without eliciting adverse effects (Glazier & Bowman, 2001; Li et al., 2018).

In light of the above considerations, genistein is promising as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD based on its capacity to inhibit upstream tyrosine kinases and suppress the PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling cascade, thereby promoting TFEB-mediated enhancement of lysosomal acidification and cathepsin D activity. Such a mechanism is directly relevant to improving phagolysosomal function in RPE cells and facilitating the clearance of drusen components—a critical unmet need in the management of dry AMD (Falcão et al., 2024; Xu et al., 2020). The dual actions of genistein offer mechanistic clarity that may translate into a therapeutic edge when compared to broad-spectrum autophagy inducers. Nonetheless, the current evidence base is still largely circumstantial, and further direct investigations are necessary to confirm that genistein induces the expected autophagic and lysosomal responses in RPE cells. Preclinical studies employing appropriate RPE models (such as POS feeding assays and chronic oxidative stress paradigms) should be prioritized to solidify the link between genistein treatment and improved clearance of lipofuscin-like deposits. Ultimately, detailed pharmacokinetic, efficacy, and safety studies—ideally complemented by early-phase clinical trials—will be required before genistein can be confidently advanced as a therapeutic modality for dry AMD (Albulescu & Popovici, 2007; Falcão et al., 2024).

In summary, genistein’s natural origin, established safety in other contexts, and its dual ability to inhibit relevant tyrosine kinase–mediated signaling and upregulate autophagy through TFEB activation collectively support its potential for repurposing in dry AMD. However, critical gaps in direct efficacy data in ocular models and a precise understanding of its tissue pharmacokinetics necessitate further investigation. This combination of promising mechanistic rationale and some supportive preclinical data argues that genistein merits further preclinical exploration in RPE models of dry AMD, with the expectation that if such studies confirm improved clearance of lipofuscin and drusen markers, subsequent early-phase clinical trials can be pursued to evaluate its therapeutic benefit in patients suffering from this blinding disease (Falcão et al., 2024; Glazier & Bowman, 2001; Li et al., 2018; Xu et al., 2020).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Fenofibrate is a synthetic small‐molecule drug belonging to the fibrate class of compounds, originally developed and approved for the treatment of dyslipidemia. It acts predominantly as a peroxisome proliferator‐activated receptor alpha (PPARα) agonist. Fenofibrate itself is a prodrug that undergoes hepatic esterase hydrolysis to form its active metabolite, fenofibric acid, which binds to PPARα and modulates the transcription of genes involved in lipid metabolism. This drug class has historically been used for lowering serum triglycerides and increasing high‐density lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol, reflecting its well‐established lipid‐modulating properties. Although fenofibrate was not initially developed for ocular indications, its mechanism as a PPARα agonist has spurred interest for repurposing in retinal diseases. In particular, the broad class of fibrates has garnered attention because PPARα is expressed in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), and its activation can regulate lipid oxidation, autophagy, and inflammatory processes—all of which are critically disturbed in dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) (Fu et al., 2019; Falcão et al., 2025).

Therapeutic History:  
Fenofibrate has a robust clinical history in the management of dyslipidemia and cardiovascular risk reduction, with extensive use in millions of patients worldwide. Its ocular benefits became apparent with large clinical trials, such as the FIELD and ACCORD Eye studies, which demonstrated that fenofibrate can reduce the progression of diabetic retinopathy and decrease the need for retinal laser therapy in diabetic patients (Lu et al., 2014; Treacy & Hurst, 2012). Although these trials primarily addressed diabetic retinal disease, subsequent preclinical and clinical reports have indicated that the retina may benefit from the lipid‐modulatory, anti‐inflammatory, and neuroprotective actions of PPARα agonists. For instance, several studies have explored fenofibrate in animal models of retinal ischemia and neovascularization, showing protective effects on the retinal vasculature and RPE (Fu et al., 2020; Qiu et al., 2017). While the majority of these ocular studies have focused on diabetic retinopathy or neovascular AMD, emerging literature has pointed to the potential of targeting PPARα signaling to mitigate RPE dysfunction and lipid accumulation, which are hallmarks of dry AMD (da Ana et al., 2023; Dou & Duerfeldt, 2020). This history of fenofibrate in retinal disease, combined with its proven clinical safety for dyslipidemia and established ocular pharmacokinetics (including studies on topical delivery), provides a compelling rationale for its repurposing in dry AMD (Tomita et al., 2020; Lee et al., 2021).

Mechanism of Action:  
Fenofibrate’s mechanism of action is rooted in its role as a PPARα agonist. Upon conversion to fenofibric acid, the compound binds to PPARα—a nuclear receptor highly expressed in several tissues, including the liver and the retinal pigment epithelium. When activated, PPARα forms heterodimers with retinoid X receptors (RXR) and binds to peroxisome proliferator response elements (PPREs) within the promoters of target genes. This binding results in the upregulation of genes critical for fatty acid uptake, β-oxidation, and lipid catabolism. Key genes regulated by PPARα include those encoding enzymes that facilitate mitochondrial and peroxisomal fatty acid oxidation, which in turn reduces intracellular lipid accumulation and promotes energy homeostasis (Fu et al., 2019; Lee et al., 2023).

In the context of the RPE and dry AMD, the hypothesis is that fenofibrate will stimulate PPARα-mediated transcriptional programs that not only enhance lipid catabolism but also intersect with cellular degradative pathways. One of the central tenets of the proposed mechanism is the coactivation of transcription factor EB (TFEB). TFEB is recognized as a master regulator of lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy through the coordinated lysosomal expression and regulation (CLEAR) network. Under normal conditions, TFEB is kept inactive in the cytosol by phosphorylation mediated by mTORC1. Under stress conditions or when lysosomal function is impaired, TFEB translocates to the nucleus to upregulate genes involved in lysosomal acidification, autophagy, and lipid metabolism. The therapeutic hypothesis posits that fenofibrate, through PPARα activation in RPE cells, will indirectly coactivate TFEB. This may occur through changes in cellular metabolism that reduce mTORC1 activity or via direct transcriptional crosstalk between PPARα target genes and the CLEAR network (Falcão et al., 2025; da Ana et al., 2023).

Moreover, TFEB activation is expected to enhance lysosomal acidification—a process necessary for optimal degradation of phagocytosed outer segment debris and drusen precursors—and upregulate lysosomal hydrolases such as cathepsin D. In AMD, RPE cells often show lysosomal dysfunction characterized by deficient cathepsin D activity and lipofuscin accumulation. By improving lysosomal function, fenofibrate may facilitate the clearance of lipid-rich drusen precursors, thereby reducing RPE stress and preventing progression of dry AMD (Falcão et al., 2025; da Ana et al., 2023). In addition to these lysosome-centric effects, fenofibrate has anti-inflammatory properties, as PPARα activation suppresses NF-κB signaling, reduces the expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines (e.g., TNF-α and IL-1β), and alleviates oxidative stress—all of which are exacerbating factors in the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Lee et al., 2023; Treacy & Hurst, 2012). Furthermore, the modulation of the FGF21 pathway, occasionally observed with fenofibrate treatment, may contribute to neuroprotection and further support retinal homeostasis (Tomita et al., 2020; Lee et al., 2023). Taken together, the molecular interactions initiated by fenofibrate converge on restoring lipid homeostasis, enhancing autophagic flux, and mitigating inflammatory insults in RPE cells—a multifaceted approach that aligns with the pathophysiology of dry AMD (Treacy & Hurst, 2012; Lee et al., 2021).

Expected Effect:  
In the assays proposed to evaluate fenofibrate’s efficacy for dry AMD, one anticipates several measurable cellular and biochemical outcomes. First, treatment of RPE cells with fenofibrate should lead to a consistent activation of PPARα target genes, as demonstrated by upregulation of markers for fatty acid oxidation and lipid catabolism. Such molecular signatures can be quantified using gene expression analyses and reporter assays for PPRE activity (Fu et al., 2019; Tomita et al., 2021). Concurrently, it is expected that fenofibrate will enhance autophagic flux in RPE cells. This could be evident from increased LC3-II accumulation in the presence of lysosomal inhibitors and enhanced degradation of autophagic substrates, which would indicate an upregulation of the autophagic machinery (Falcão et al., 2025; da Ana et al., 2023).

A critical aspect of the proposed mechanism involves TFEB. Upon fenofibrate treatment, one should observe increased nuclear translocation of TFEB in RPE cells, which can be assessed by immunocytochemistry and subcellular fractionation. The activation of TFEB would then be expected to drive the transcriptional upregulation of genes encoding lysosomal proteins, such as lysosomal-associated membrane protein 2 (LAMP2) and various components of the V-ATPase complex, leading to enhanced lysosomal acidification. Lysotracker assays and measurements of intralysosomal pH could be deployed to confirm that fenofibrate-treated cells exhibit more acidic lysosomes (Falcão et al., 2025; da Ana et al., 2023).

Furthermore, increased cathepsin D activity is a pivotal expected outcome, serving as a surrogate marker for improved lysosomal enzyme function in degrading waste products, including drusen precursors. Biochemical assays to quantify cathepsin D activity, alongside immunostaining for its protein levels, would help to validate this aspect of the mechanism. Functionally, the cumulative effect of these molecular changes should be a reduction in the accumulation of lipofuscin and other drusen-associated lipid-protein aggregates within the RPE. This reduction could be observed using autofluorescence imaging techniques and electron microscopy to assess cytoplasmic inclusions (Falcão et al., 2025; Treacy & Hurst, 2012).

Additionally, given that fenofibrate has established anti-inflammatory properties, one might expect a decrease in the secretion or expression of inflammatory mediators in RPE cultures, as well as improved cellular resistance to oxidative stress challenges. Cytokine assays and measurements of reactive oxygen species (ROS) would serve as corroborative evidence for an anti-inflammatory and antioxidant effect. Importantly, because reduced autophagy and lysosomal dysfunction are central to dry AMD, the combined effect of enhanced lipid catabolism, improved lysosomal acidification, and increased cathepsin D activity should contribute to an overall reduction in cellular stress and preservation of RPE integrity (Falcão et al., 2025; Treacy & Hurst, 2012). Taken together, these expected effects would validate the therapeutic hypothesis and provide a strong rationale for advancing fenofibrate into further preclinical models of dry AMD.

Overall Evaluation:  
Fenofibrate emerges as a promising repurposed drug candidate for dry AMD based on several compelling lines of evidence. The drug’s long-established clinical safety profile and extensive use in dyslipidemia serve as major strengths in terms of its translational potential (Lu et al., 2014; Treacy & Hurst, 2012). Additionally, the documented success of fenofibrate in slowing the progression of diabetic retinopathy in large-scale clinical trials underscores its ability to exert beneficial effects in retinal tissues (Lu et al., 2014; Treacy & Hurst, 2012).

From a mechanistic standpoint, fenofibrate’s mode of action as a PPARα agonist is well characterized, and its ability to stimulate lipid oxidation and enhance fatty acid metabolism could directly address the lipid dysregulation observed in RPE cells in dry AMD (Fu et al., 2019; da Ana et al., 2023). Crucially, the hypothesis that fenofibrate may also coactivate TFEB, thereby promoting lysosomal biogenesis and function, positions it uniquely among therapeutic candidates. Improved lysosomal acidification and increased cathepsin D activity would facilitate the clearance of drusen precursors and reduce the cytotoxic accumulation of lipofuscin, which is a central pathogenic feature of dry AMD (Falcão et al., 2025; da Ana et al., 2023; Dou & Duerfeldt, 2020). The convergence of lipid catabolism enhancement, autophagy upregulation, and anti-inflammatory effects creates a multifaceted therapeutic profile that is particularly attractive for a complex, multifactorial disease such as dry AMD.

However, there are also notable weaknesses and challenges. Most of the current evidence supporting fenofibrate’s retinal benefits is derived from studies focusing on diabetic retinopathy or neovascular AMD rather than directly on dry AMD. Although there is supportive mechanistic rationale linking PPARα activation to improved lysosomal function in the RPE, direct evidence for fenofibrate’s efficacy in reducing drusen accumulation and alleviating RPE stress in dry AMD models remains sparse (Dou & Duerfeldt, 2020; da Ana et al., 2023). The specific involvement of TFEB activation by fenofibrate in RPE cells has not been fully elucidated in the existing literature, and further in vitro and in vivo studies are needed to validate this aspect of the mechanism. Additionally, while fenofibrate is generally safe when used systemically, there have been concerns regarding potential renal side effects, which may be particularly relevant in the elderly population that predominantly suffers from AMD (Treacy & Hurst, 2012; Tomita et al., 2021). Thus, optimizing the route of delivery—possibly via topical formulations or nanoparticle-based systems—may be necessary to ensure sufficient retinal bioavailability while minimizing systemic exposure (Huang et al., 2021; Lu et al., 2014).

Another potential limitation is the dose required to achieve sufficient PPARα activation in the RPE to modulate TFEB and lysosomal pathways effectively. Preclinical studies have sometimes required relatively high doses of fenofibrate to observe significant ocular effects, and the pharmacokinetic barriers posed by the blood-retinal barrier may further complicate translatability (Tomita et al., 2020; Lee et al., 2023). Moreover, the current body of literature underscores the need for more targeted studies to determine whether the benefits seen with fenofibrate in models of diabetic retinopathy and neovascular AMD can be replicated in models of dry AMD, where the pathogenic processes are distinct in their emphasis on lipid accumulation, oxidative stress, and RPE dysfunction (da Ana et al., 2023; Dou & Duerfeldt, 2020).

Despite these challenges, the overall evaluation remains cautiously optimistic. Fenofibrate’s mechanism of action aligns well with the pathophysiological features of dry AMD, particularly regarding the restoration of lipid homeostasis and the enhancement of lysosomal function. The dual potential for direct metabolic benefits via PPARα activation and indirect benefits through TFEB-mediated lysosomal enhancement represents an innovative therapeutic strategy that could fill a critical gap in the current treatment landscape for dry AMD (Falcão et al., 2025; Fu et al., 2019; da Ana et al., 2023; Dou & Duerfeldt, 2020; Lee et al., 2023). Additionally, the availability of various delivery platforms—including systemic administration, topical eye drops, and nanoparticle formulations—provides flexibility in addressing bioavailability challenges and minimizing adverse effects (Huang et al., 2021; Lu et al., 2014).

In conclusion, fenofibrate (Sigma F6020) possesses significant potential for repurposing as a drug candidate for dry AMD based on its well-established pharmacological profile, robust clinical safety record, and mechanistic actions that target key pathological processes in the RPE. While further preclinical studies specifically focused on dry AMD models are warranted to validate the hypothesized coactivation of TFEB and subsequent enhancement of lysosomal acidification and cathepsin D activity, the current literature provides a strong scientific basis for such investigations. The strengths of fenofibrate lie in its multifaceted mechanism—encompassing lipid catabolism, autophagy, anti-inflammatory, and possibly neuroprotective effects—which collectively offer a promising strategy to reduce drusen precursors and mitigate RPE stress. The primary weaknesses involve the need for direct evidence in dry AMD models, optimization of ocular delivery to overcome pharmacokinetic barriers, and careful monitoring of potential systemic side effects in an elderly population. Overall, fenofibrate represents a compelling and scientifically sound candidate that merits further exploration in the context of dry AMD, with the potential to significantly advance our therapeutic arsenal against this currently untreatable form of macular degeneration (Falcão et al., 2025; Fu et al., 2019; da Ana et al., 2023; Dou & Duerfeldt, 2020; Lee et al., 2023).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Rapamycin (sirolimus), commercially available as Sigma R0395, is a macrocyclic lactone originally isolated from the bacterium Streptomyces hygroscopicus, a discovery that dates back to studies on soil samples from Easter Island. As a naturally derived compound now synthesized and purified for clinical use, rapamycin belongs to the macrolide class and is best known for its potent immunosuppressive properties, having been used extensively to prevent organ rejection in transplantation. Over time, its application expanded beyond transplantation to include areas such as oncology, neurodegeneration, and age-related diseases due to its ability to inhibit the mechanistic target of rapamycin complex 1 (mTORC1). The rationale for repurposing rapamycin in the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD), specifically geographic atrophy (GA), stems from its established pharmacological profile, extensive safety record, and well-characterized biochemical functions. Its clinical approval and long-term safety data in other contexts provide a solid foundation for exploring its potential in ocular indications, particularly given its capacity to modulate autophagy in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells (Wang et al., 2022).

Therapeutic History:  
Rapamycin’s development began with its use as an immunosuppressant in organ transplantation, and over the ensuing decades, its application has broadened considerably. Biochemical and preclinical studies have demonstrated that rapamycin is an effective inhibitor of mTORC1, a critical regulator not only of cell proliferation but also of autophagy and lysosomal biogenesis. Early investigations revealed that rapamycin could induce autophagy in various cell types, including RPE cells, by inhibiting mTORC1, thereby facilitating the clearance of toxic aggregates and damaged organelles. This mechanism has been explored extensively for neurodegenerative conditions, and more recently, there has been focused investigation into its utility for dry AMD. Clinical trials have tested rapamycin in forms ranging from intravitreal to subconjunctival injections in patients with GA; for example, a clinical trial by the National Eye Institute aimed to evaluate intravitreal injections of sirolimus for GA, although this study was terminated due to safety concerns (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2012). Similarly, other studies using subconjunctival injections demonstrated that while rapamycin appears safe and well-tolerated, significant benefits in terms of preventing GA progression have not been conclusively demonstrated (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2008, 2011). In animal studies and in vitro RPE models, rapamycin enhanced autophagic flux, increased the activity of cathepsin D (CTSD), and reduced the accumulation of toxic material such as A2E—an effect that is consistent with a potential for slowing GA progression (Wang et al., 2022; Falcão et al., 2024). Thus, rapamycin’s therapeutic history encompasses a combination of robust preclinical evidence supporting its mechanistic action and mixed clinical outcomes in ocular trials, setting the stage for further investigation into optimal dosing, delivery methods, and patient selection criteria (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2008, 2011).

Mechanism of Action:  
Rapamycin exerts its biological effects primarily through direct inhibition of mTORC1, a serine/threonine kinase complex that integrates signals from nutrients, growth factors, and cellular energy status to regulate cell growth, proliferation, and autophagy. In the absence of rapamycin, active mTORC1 phosphorylates downstream targets such as S6 kinase and 4E-BP1, thereby promoting anabolic processes and suppressing autophagy. When rapamycin binds to its intracellular receptor, FKBP12, the resulting complex interacts with the FKBP12-rapamycin binding (FRB) domain of mTORC1, leading to its inhibition. This inhibition results in dephosphorylation and subsequent activation of transcription factor EB (TFEB), a master regulator of lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy-related genes. Activated TFEB then translocates to the nucleus, where it enhances the expression of genes involved in lysosomal function, acidification, and the production of lysosomal enzymes such as cathepsin D (CTSD) (Falcão et al., 2025; Falcão et al., 2024; Sinha et al., 2016). In the context of dry AMD, the proposed mechanism hinges on rapamycin’s ability to restore cellular homeostasis in RPE cells by increasing autophagic flux and lysosomal clearance of accumulated drusen components, which include toxic aggregates like A2E. Preclinical studies have shown that treatment of RPE cells with rapamycin results in a marked reduction in the accumulation of autofluorescent granules (AFGs) that are indicative of impaired lysosomal degradation (Falcão et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2025). The cascade initiated by rapamycin—mTORC1 inhibition, TFEB activation, and enhanced expression of lysosome-associated proteins such as LAMP1 and pro-cathepsin D—forms the crux of its proposed therapeutic action in mitigating the progression of GA by promoting the dismantling and clearance of pathological deposits (Falcão et al., 2024).

Expected Effect:  
In RPE cells, the inhibition of mTORC1 by rapamycin is expected to release the inhibitory phosphorylation on TFEB, enabling its nuclear translocation and activation of a transcriptional program that drives lysosomal biogenesis, acidification, and the production of key lysosomal enzymes such as cathepsin D. This molecular shift is anticipated to markedly enhance the autophagic capacity of the RPE, leading to increased degradation of drusen components, including lipofuscin and A2E, which are hallmarks of dry AMD pathology. The activation of autophagy not only facilitates the clearance of accumulated toxic material but also mitigates oxidative stress by removing damaged mitochondria and other organelles that may contribute to reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation (Wang et al., 2022; Falcão et al., 2024). Moreover, preclinical evidence indicates that, in ARPE-19 cell models, rapamycin improves cellular viability in the face of oxidative injury and reduces markers of cellular senescence by enhancing autophagic flux. These cellular effects are directly linked to the expression of critical proteins in RPE cells; for example, TFEB is known to be expressed in these cells and its activation correlates with increased lysosomal gene expression and function (Falcão et al., 2024) while cathepsin D, a lysosomal protease, is vital for the degradation of phagocytosed photoreceptor outer segments (Chang et al., 2022; Sinha et al., 2016). The intended therapeutic outcome is to slow or potentially halt the progression of GA by reducing the burden of drusen and preserving RPE function, which could translate into better preservation of visual acuity over time. Overall Evaluation:  
Rapamycin presents itself as a scientifically promising yet clinically challenging candidate for the treatment of dry AMD. One of the key strengths of rapamycin is its well-established mechanism of action: as a potent mTORC1 inhibitor, it leverages a well-characterized pathway involving TFEB activation that directly targets the core pathology observed in dry AMD—the accumulation of drusen components and impaired lysosomal function in RPE cells. Preclinical studies have consistently demonstrated that rapamycin can enhance autophagic flux, lower levels of toxic aggregates such as A2E, and increase the activity of lysosomal enzymes like cathepsin D, thereby supporting its target validation in the context of RPE health (Falcão et al., 2025; Falcão et al., 2024). Additionally, rapamycin has an extensive history of clinical use in other indications, and its safety profile, while not without concerns, is well documented from its use as an immunosuppressant in transplantation and in various oncology settings (Wang et al., 2022).

However, the clinical translation of rapamycin for dry AMD has not been straightforward. Multiple clinical trials have assessed its application using different routes of administration, such as intravitreal and subconjunctival injections, with mixed results. While safety and tolerability have generally been acceptable, the efficacy endpoints—specifically, the prevention or slowing of GA progression—have not been definitively met in these studies (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2008, 2011, 2012; Wang et al., 2022). Furthermore, some trials encountered complications such as sterile endophthalmitis or observed decreases in visual acuity relative to untreated eyes, suggesting that even if the underlying molecular mechanisms are engaged, the overall benefits in late-stage disease might be limited (Wang et al., 2022; Falcão et al., 2024).

Another potential weakness is the complexity inherent in mTOR signaling itself. The pathway plays a dual role in cellular homeostasis—while its inhibition can promote autophagy and lysosomal clearance, inappropriate or excessive inhibition could lead to adverse effects such as increased retinal neuron apoptosis, particularly in advanced stages of AMD where the cellular milieu is significantly altered (Wang et al., 2022; Chang et al., 2022). Moreover, the optimal dosing regimen and delivery method for achieving the desired ocular concentration without incurring systemic side effects remain unresolved. Some studies have suggested that modifications to the formulation, such as encapsulation in synthetic nanoparticles, could enhance ocular penetration and prolong the effective duration of rapamycin within the eye, thereby minimizing side effects and improving efficacy (Jo et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2022).

Despite these challenges, the strength of rapamycin’s mechanism—the inhibition of mTORC1 and consequent activation of TFEB leading to enhanced lysosomal biogenesis—remains compelling. The molecular rationale is robust, and the repeated demonstration of reduced levels of autofluorescent granules in RPE cells following rapamycin treatment is particularly encouraging (Falcão et al., 2024). The concept of using a repurposed, clinically approved drug to address a significant unmet need in dry AMD is attractive, especially given the limited treatment options currently available for this degenerative condition. In this light, further investigations—ideally, in earlier stages of AMD and with innovative delivery modalities—may reveal a niche where rapamycin can exert a clinically meaningful benefit (Wang et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2019).

In conclusion, while rapamycin has significant potential grounded in sound molecular pharmacology and extensive preclinical validation, its clinical application for dry AMD warrants careful optimization. The candidate’s strengths lie in its potent and well-understood mechanism of mTORC1 inhibition, the activation of TFEB, and subsequent improvements in lysosomal function and autophagic clearance in RPE cells. Conversely, clinical challenges including mixed efficacy outcomes in GA trials, potential adverse effects related to mTOR pathway modulation in vulnerable retinal neurons, and limitations in current dosing/delivery strategies represent hurdles that must be surmounted. Based on these comprehensive literature insights, rapamycin remains a promising candidate for further investigation, albeit with recommendations to explore its use in earlier disease stages and in combination with advanced ocular delivery systems to maximize its therapeutic benefit while minimizing risks (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2012; Wang et al., 2022; Falcão et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2025).
