Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
2-Hydroxypropyl-β-cyclodextrin (HPβCD) is a chemically modified derivative of natural β-cyclodextrin—a cyclic oligosaccharide consisting of glucose units linked via α-1,4 glycosidic bonds. This modification, achieved by the introduction of hydroxypropyl groups, improves its solubility and reduces its inherent cytotoxicity relative to unmodified cyclodextrins. HPβCD belongs to the cyclodextrin class, molecules that have been widely used in pharmaceutical formulations as solubilizing agents and excipients due to their ability to encapsulate hydrophobic molecules within their lipophilic interior, thereby increasing bioavailability. Over the years, these agents have gained attention as cholesterol-binding molecules, and HPβCD is no exception, being repurposed for diseases characterized by pathological cholesterol accumulation such as Niemann–Pick type C1 (NPC1). Its structural properties permit the formation of inclusion complexes with cholesterol and other lipids, facilitating their mobilization and removal from cells. Given its established role in NPC1 disease and emerging evidence supporting its ability to cross the blood–retina barrier, HPβCD is now being evaluated as a therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD), specifically targeting drusen-associated cholesterol accumulation in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells (Calias, 2018; Roney, 2020).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, HPβCD has been extensively investigated as a therapeutic intervention for lysosomal storage diseases, with a particular focus on Niemann–Pick disease type C (NPC), a condition characterized by the pathological accumulation of cholesterol and glycosphingolipids in cells. Preclinical studies in animal models have demonstrated that systemic administration of HPβCD can lower intracellular cholesterol levels, thereby ameliorating disease-related cellular dysfunction. However, its pharmacokinetic limitations—most notably, its minimal penetration of the blood–brain barrier (BBB) when administered intravenously—have necessitated alternative routes of delivery, such as intrathecal administration, to achieve sufficient central nervous system (CNS) exposure (Calias, 2018). In the context of retinal diseases, several studies have investigated the effects of HPβCD in animal models of retinal cholesterol dyshomeostasis. In these models, HPβCD treatment has been associated with significant reductions in cholesterol crystals, diminished lipid deposition in structures such as Bruch’s membrane, and decreased activation of retinal macrophages and microglial cells (El-Darzi et al., 2023). Although HPβCD has been repurposed from its application in NPC to target retinal pathologies, a focused investigation into its use for dry AMD remains to be performed clinically, as systematic searches on ClinicalTrials.gov indicate that no registered trials have specifically addressed cyclodextrin use in AMD (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, HPβCD acts primarily as a cholesterol extractor by leveraging its toroidal structure, which is characterized by a hydrophilic exterior and a relatively hydrophobic interior cavity. This unique architecture enables HPβCD to form inclusion complexes with cholesterol, effectively sequestering the lipid from cellular membranes. In the setting of RPE cells, where lysosomal cholesterol accumulation is implicated in the pathogenesis of dry AMD, HPβCD is hypothesized to mobilize cholesterol from lysosomal membranes. Excess cholesterol in these membranes disrupts the lipid microdomains necessary for the optimal assembly and functioning of protein complexes such as the vacuolar-type H⁺-ATPase (v-ATPase), which is essential for maintaining lysosomal acidity (Nociari, Kiss, & Rodriguez-Boulan, 2017). By extracting cholesterol, HPβCD is expected to restore these lipid microdomains, thereby facilitating the proper assembly and function of the v-ATPase complex. This normalization of v-ATPase assembly is critical for reestablishing an acidic environment within lysosomes, which in turn is necessary for the optimal activity of lysosomal hydrolases such as cathepsin D (CTSD).

In neurons and other cell types, studies have demonstrated that HPβCD treatment leads to a reduction in both luminal and membrane-associated cholesterol levels, a process that not only improves lysosomal trafficking but also induces lysosomal exocytosis under certain conditions (Roney, 2020). Furthermore, the improvement in lysosomal acidification following HPβCD-mediated cholesterol extraction has been correlated with enhanced autophagic flux due to increased CTSD-mediated proteolysis. Although direct evidence for this mechanism in RPE cells is still emerging, it is reasonable to extrapolate that similar molecular events would occur in retinal cells. The restoration of lysosomal pH and the subsequent improvement in autophagy are critical because they directly contribute to the clearance of intracellular debris, including drusen lipids, thereby potentially reducing the lipid burden that characterizes the progression of dry AMD (Nociari et al., 2017; Roney, 2020).

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis driving the repurposing of HPβCD for dry AMD is that it will mobilize cholesterol from RPE lysosomal membranes, thereby restoring the integrity of lipid microdomains that are essential for v-ATPase assembly. In practical terms, treatment with HPβCD is expected to yield several interrelated outcomes. First, the reduction in membrane cholesterol is anticipated to alleviate the inhibitory effect of cholesterol excess on v-ATPase assembly, leading to improved proton pump activity and a consequent normalization of lysosomal pH. Given that the activity of CTSD is pH-dependent—with optimal function occurring under acidic conditions—the normalization of lysosomal pH should enable enhanced CTSD activity and improved autophagic degradation of lipid aggregates (Nociari et al., 2017; Roney, 2020).

Second, by promoting the removal of excess cholesterol, HPβCD should reduce the formation of cholesterol crystals, a pathological hallmark associated with retinal lipid dyshomeostasis and drusen formation. Animal studies have demonstrated that HPβCD treatment leads to a significant reduction in the number of cholesterol crystals per unit area in retinal tissues, which is strongly correlated with improvements in retinal lipid processing and decreased inflammatory responses mediated by macrophage and microglial activation (El-Darzi et al., 2023).

Third, in laboratory assays using RPE cell cultures, one would expect to observe a decrease in the proportion of lipid-laden lysosomes, accompanied by measurable improvements in lysosomal acidification—parameters that serve as surrogate markers for enhanced autophagic capacity. Additionally, given the evidence that HPβCD can cross the blood–retina barrier when administered via systemic routes, there is a strong rationale for expecting that appropriate dosing regimens will yield sufficient retinal tissue concentrations to exert these beneficial effects (El-Darzi et al., 2023). Ultimately, these molecular and cellular changes are anticipated to culminate in the reduction of drusen lipid volumes, thereby slowing or potentially halting the progression of dry AMD (El-Darzi et al., 2023).

Overall Evaluation:  
The repurposing of HPβCD for the treatment of dry AMD is underpinned by a robust mechanistic rationale, a substantial preclinical history, and an acceptable clinical safety profile observed in other indications. One of the greatest strengths of HPβCD is its dual functionality: the ability to form effective inclusion complexes with cholesterol and the resultant improvement in lysosomal function. In several animal models of retinal cholesterol dyshomeostasis, HPβCD has yielded promising results by lowering total, unesterified, and esterified cholesterol levels, reducing the number of cholesterol crystals, and mitigating inflammatory responses in the retina (El-Darzi et al., 2023). These data provide a compelling basis for its evaluation in conditions such as dry AMD where drusen formation is closely linked to aberrant cholesterol metabolism. Furthermore, its prior use in the treatment of NPC—a condition that shares certain pathogenic features with AMD in terms of lysosomal dysfunction—adds credence to the hypothesis that HPβCD may exert similar therapeutic effects in RPE cells (Calias, 2018).

A significant advantage of HPβCD is its established safety record in clinical studies for NPC. Although challenges remain regarding optimal dosing—especially given the compound’s limited ability to cross the BBB when administered systemically—the retinal application appears more favorable, as preclinical studies suggest that HPβCD is capable of traversing the blood–retina barrier and achieving therapeutic concentrations in retinal tissues (El-Darzi et al., 2023). However, it should be noted that the safety profile in the context of chronic ocular exposure remains to be fully characterized. Notably, clinical studies in NPC have observed adverse effects such as hearing loss with certain routes of administration, and while these effects may not directly translate to ocular toxicity, rigorous ocular safety studies will be essential to ensure that any repurposing for dry AMD is both efficacious and safe (Calias, 2018).

Another potential strength lies in the specificity of the lipid‐targeting strategy. Unlike therapies that broadly modulate inflammatory or oxidative stress pathways, HPβCD acts directly on the cholesterol burden—the underlying driver of drusen lipid accumulation in dry AMD. This mechanistic specificity has the potential to result in a more direct impact on the disease process, rather than merely modifying secondary symptoms. Mechanistically, the extraction of cholesterol by HPβCD is anticipated to restore the lipid environment within RPE lysosomal membranes, thereby re-enabling the proper assembly of v-ATPase complexes. This, in turn, can lead to improved lysosomal acidification, enhanced cathepsin D activity, and accelerated autophagic clearance of damaged cellular components—a cascade of events that would address one of the root causes of retinal degeneration in AMD (Nociari et al., 2017; Roney, 2020).

Despite these strengths, several weaknesses and uncertainties must be acknowledged. First, while the preclinical data in animal models are promising, there remains a lack of clinical trial data specifically focusing on the use of HPβCD in dry AMD. A search using the relevant keywords indicates a paucity of clinical evidence in this particular indication (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.), which means that translational hurdles remain before HPβCD can be confidently recommended for dry AMD therapy. Second, although the mechanism by which HPβCD affects v-ATPase assembly and CTSD activity is supported by data in neuronal models, direct evidence of these molecular events in RPE cells is still emerging, leaving some uncertainty regarding the depth of its effects on lysosomal autophagy in the retinal environment (Nociari et al., 2017). Third, formulation and administration routes will be critical considerations. While systemic dosing has been used in other indications, the optimal approach for targeting the retina might require localized delivery techniques—such as intravitreal injection or the development of a sustained-release ocular formulation—to maximize retinal exposure while minimizing systemic exposure and off-target effects. Finally, the potential for adverse events, particularly those related to over-extraction of cholesterol or unintended disruption of lipid homeostasis, must be carefully evaluated in the context of chronic ocular treatment.

In summary, HPβCD is a well-characterized compound with a history of successful application in disorders of cholesterol accumulation, notably NPC. Its ability to extract cholesterol from cellular membranes, restore lipid microdomains, and thereby normalize lysosomal function forms a strong mechanistic basis for its evaluation as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. Preclinical studies in animal models provide encouraging evidence that HPβCD can reduce retinal cholesterol accumulation, lower the number of cholesterol crystals, and improve markers of lysosomal function in retinal tissues. This directly aligns with the therapeutic hypothesis that the mobilization of cholesterol from RPE lysosomal membranes will restore v-ATPase activity, normalize lysosomal pH, enhance cathepsin D activity, and ultimately reduce the drusen lipid burden characteristic of dry AMD (Calias, 2018; El-Darzi et al., 2023; Nociari et al., 2017; Roney, 2020).

However, the translation of these preclinical findings into a clinically effective therapy for dry AMD will require addressing several critical challenges. These include the absence of direct clinical data in AMD, the need for detailed mechanistic studies in RPE cells to confirm that the cholesterol-lowering effects observed in other tissues are recapitulated in the retina, and the optimization of dosing and delivery methods to ensure that therapeutic concentrations are achieved safely in the target tissue. Additionally, any potential side effects—such as those noted in NPC patients, including auditory toxicity—must be rigorously monitored in ocular studies to ensure that treatment remains safe over the long term (Calias, 2018).

Overall, the repurposing of HPβCD for dry AMD is scientifically compelling due to its targeted mechanism of action and its established clinical history in related indications. Its ability to mobilize cholesterol and restore lysosomal function addresses fundamental pathogenic processes implicated in dry AMD, and the preclinical evidence supports its potential efficacy. Nevertheless, the absence of clinical trials in this particular indication, combined with uncertainties regarding the precise molecular interactions in RPE cells and the optimization of drug delivery to the retina, suggests that further preclinical and early-stage clinical studies are warranted before HPβCD can be advanced as a treatment for dry AMD. Continued research should focus on elucidating the detailed molecular mechanisms within RPE cells, assessing long-term safety in ocular models, and exploring various delivery modalities to maximize efficacy while minimizing potential risks. Below is a detailed evaluation of MK-2206 as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD), structured into five sections.

─────────────────────────────  
Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
─────────────────────────────  
MK-2206 is a synthetically derived, orally bioavailable small‐molecule inhibitor that functions as an allosteric modulator of the serine/threonine kinase AKT. Unlike classical ATP‐competitive agents, MK-2206 binds to an allosteric site outside the catalytic pocket, thereby altering the conformation of AKT and preventing its full activation. Originally discovered and optimized for oncological indications, its development was driven by the need to inhibit aberrant AKT signaling observed in multiple cancers. The compound belongs to a class of drugs known as allosteric AKT inhibitors, which historically have been explored for their ability to modulate critical intracellular signaling pathways that govern cellular proliferation, survival, and metabolism. More specifically, MK-2206 has been demonstrated in vitro to reduce the phosphorylation of AKT at key regulatory residues (for example, S473) in multiple cell types, including primary retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cultures where its application at 1 μM for 24 hours was shown to inhibit AKT phosphorylation and promote nuclear translocation of TFEB (Transcription Factor EB) – the master regulator of lysosomal gene expression (Karim et al., 2020). Although the detailed synthetic route is not fully delineated within our context, the compound has been thoroughly characterized for its bioavailability, metabolic stability, and cell‐penetrant properties during its extensive preclinical and clinical evaluation in oncology (Guo et al., 2021; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2009). These attributes underpin its suitability for repurposing; its well‐defined medicinal chemistry profile and advanced clinical development stage (availability of Phase I data) position MK-2206 as an attractive candidate for investigating autophagy regulation in non‐oncologic contexts such as AMD (Karim et al., 2020).

─────────────────────────────  
Therapeutic History  
─────────────────────────────  
Historically, MK-2206 has been developed and evaluated predominantly as an anticancer agent. During its clinical evolution, it was subjected to multiple Phase I and combination Phase I/II clinical trials in patients with advanced solid tumors, HER2-positive cancers, and other malignancies. The compound has been administered on both an every-other-day (QOD) schedule and on a once-weekly (QW) regimen in dose‐escalation studies (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2008; 2010). These early clinical studies provided valuable safety, tolerability, and pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic (PK/PD) data that have now established an acceptable safety profile in humans. Outside the field of oncology, no published clinical study has yet directly evaluated MK-2206 in ocular indications. However, a separate body of preclinical research has increasingly linked dysregulated AKT activation in RPE cells with impaired lysosomal function and defective autophagy – two pathological hallmarks of dry AMD (Karim et al., 2020). In immunoproteasome‐deficient RPE models (for example, LMP2 knockout [KO] cells), hyper‐phosphorylation of AKT is associated with reduced nuclear TFEB and compromised autophagic flux, features that correlate with RPE stress and lipofuscin accumulation (Karim et al., 2020). Preclinical in vitro data have demonstrated that pharmacological inhibition of AKT using MK-2206 leads to decreased AKT phosphorylation, increased nuclear TFEB localization, and enhanced autophagy flux in RPE, rescuing some of the defects observed in these models (Karim et al., 2020). Although MK-2206 per se has not been directly tested in animal models of AMD, related preclinical evidence based on the modulation of the AKT–TFEB axis in RPE supports its potential utility in the AMD context (Karim et al., 2020). In addition, several patent reviews have discussed MK-2206 within the broader portfolio of AKT inhibitors that are being repurposed for indications beyond oncology, further reinforcing the plausibility of using MK-2206 to target cellular pathways implicated in AMD (Guo et al., 2021).

─────────────────────────────  
Mechanism of Action  
─────────────────────────────  
The established mechanism of MK-2206 is anchored in its ability to inhibit AKT signaling through an allosteric mechanism. Under normal conditions, the AKT kinase is activated by phosphorylation events – typically at threonine 308 and serine 473 – in response to upstream signals from receptor tyrosine kinases and phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K) pathways. AKT then phosphorylates a wide range of substrates that control cell survival, growth, and metabolism. One of the downstream effects of activated AKT is the phosphorylation of TFEB (and possibly other MiT/TFE family members such as TFE3) at specific serine residues (for example, S467). This phosphorylation event hampers TFEB’s capacity to translocate from the cytosol to the nucleus, thereby repressing its transcriptional activity on the CLEAR (Coordinated Lysosomal Expression and Regulation) network, a gene set that drives lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy (Karim et al., 2020).

MK-2206 exerts its effect by binding to an allosteric site on AKT, a mode of inhibition that distinguishes it from ATP‐competitive inhibitors. In doing so, it reduces the phosphorylation of AKT at Ser473, thereby lowering its kinase activity (Karim et al., 2020). In RPE cells – particularly under pathogenic conditions such as immunoproteasome deficiency that leads to AKT hyper‐phosphorylation – MK-2206 administration has been shown to result in a marked decrease in AKT activity. This decrease, in turn, permits the dephosphorylation of TFEB, facilitating its nuclear import (Karim et al., 2020). Once in the nucleus, TFEB upregulates the transcription of genes involved in lysosomal function, autophagosome formation, and the expression of critical enzymes such as cathepsin D and components of the V-ATPase, which are necessary for maintaining lysosomal acidification (Karim et al., 2020).

Although the research cited does not explicitly verify isoform‐specific inhibition of AKT2 by MK-2206, the underlying hypothesis – that AKT2 hyperactivity in RPE suppresses TFEB nuclear localization – provides a strong rationale for repurposing MK-2206 in AMD. Some studies have proposed that AKT2, among the three isoforms, may predominantly drive the inflammatory and autophagy‐related deficits encountered in RPE in AMD models (Ghosh et al., 2019). This hypothesis is further supported by evidence showing that AKT2 inhibition can attenuate inflammatory cascades (such as IFNλ–LCN-2–driven neutrophil infiltration) that contribute to early RPE pathology (Ghosh et al., 2019). Thus, the mechanism of action of MK-2206 – namely, its ability to allosterically inhibit AKT activity leading to increased nuclear translocation of TFEB and subsequent upregulation of lysosomal/autophagy pathways – directly addresses key pathobiological mechanisms implicated in dry AMD.

─────────────────────────────  
Expected Effect  
─────────────────────────────  
Based on the hypothesis under review, the administration of MK-2206 to RPE cells is expected to yield several critical downstream effects that are therapeutically desirable in the context of dry AMD. First, MK-2206 should decrease the hyper‐phosphorylation of AKT observed in stressed or disease‐impacted RPE, which is thought to be a major contributing factor to the suppression of TFEB nuclear localization in these cells (Karim et al., 2020). By relieving this inhibitory phosphorylation, MK-2206 should facilitate the dephosphorylation and subsequent nuclear translocation of TFEB. Once TFEB is allowed to enter the nucleus, it can promote the transcription of a broad array of genes responsible for lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy, including those involved in the expression of vacuolar H-ATPase (V-ATPase) components and cathepsin D (CTSD) (Karim et al., 2020).

The restoration of nuclear TFEB activity is expected to lead to several beneficial cellular effects. In the RPE – which relies on robust autophagy for the clearance of photoreceptor outer segments and maintenance of cellular homeostasis – enhanced TFEB‐driven gene expression should improve lysosomal acidification and enzymatic activity, including that of cathepsin D (a key lysosomal protease) (Karim et al., 2020). Improved lysosomal acidification is critical for the maturation and function of cathepsin D, which in turn is essential for the degradation of protein aggregates and lipofuscin. Since drusen and lipofuscin accumulation represent major pathological hallmarks of dry AMD, the normalization of cathepsin D function could help to clear these toxic deposits, potentially slowing or reversing disease progression (Karim et al., 2020; Ghosh et al., 2019).

Furthermore, other reports suggest that AKT activation in RPE not only hinders autophagy but also promotes pro‐inflammatory pathways that contribute to tissue degeneration (Ghosh et al., 2019). Thus, the inhibition of AKT signaling by MK-2206 is anticipated to diminish such inflammatory cascades (Ghosh et al., 2019). In aggregate, the expected net effect is a re‐establishment of cellular proteostasis within the RPE via two interrelated mechanisms: (1) an enhancement of autophagic flux and lysosomal clearance via the TFEB pathway, and (2) a reduction in deleterious inflammatory and stress responses mediated by aberrant AKT2 signaling. Given that RPE dysfunction, lipofuscin accumulation, and drusen formation underlie the pathogenesis of dry AMD, MK-2206 could thereby serve to counteract disease progression at a mechanistic level (Karim et al., 2020).

─────────────────────────────  
Overall Evaluation  
─────────────────────────────  
In evaluating MK-2206 as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, several key points emerge. On the strength side, MK-2206 is a well-characterized small-molecule allosteric inhibitor of the AKT pathway – a pathway increasingly implicated in the regulation of autophagy and lysosomal function in RPE cells. Preclinical studies in immunoproteasome-deficient RPE have demonstrated that MK-2206 can inhibit AKT phosphorylation, restore nuclear TFEB localization, and promote autophagic flux (Karim et al., 2020). This mechanistic link is especially relevant, as dry AMD is characterized by reduced autophagy, impaired lysosomal clearance, and resultant accumulation of drusen and lipofuscin. Moreover, the rationale that AKT2 hyperactivity in RPE cells suppresses TFEB function – thereby weakening the cell’s proteolytic capacity – is well supported by the available preclinical data (Ghosh et al., 2019). In addition, MK-2206 has already been through several Phase I oncology trials, meaning that its safety and pharmacokinetic profiles are largely established in humans, which dramatically de-risks its repurposing for a different indication such as AMD (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2008; 2010). This could accelerate the clinical development timeline, as much of the initial toxicity and dosing work has been completed.

Nonetheless, there are several challenges and potential weaknesses to be addressed. First, while the available studies support that MK-2206 can modulate the AKT–TFEB axis in RPE cells under preclinical conditions, many of these studies do not provide isoform‐specific data; our hypothesis hinges on the idea that AKT2 is the critical isoform to be inhibited. MK-2206 is generally described as a pan-AKT inhibitor, which means that it may also affect AKT1 and AKT3. The lack of isoform specificity could lead to unanticipated off-target effects or impact cellular processes in non-RPE tissues if systemic exposure is not tightly controlled (Karim et al., 2020). Second, although the mechanism of promoting nuclear TFEB activity through AKT inhibition is conceptually sound and supported by cellular data, direct measurements of downstream endpoints critical to AMD – such as lysosomal acidification (e.g., via V-ATPase activity assays) and cathepsin D maturation or activity – are limited or indirect in the current literature (Karim et al., 2020). Without robust evidence that MK-2206 improves these specific lysosomal functions in RPE cells, the link between restored autophagy and actual therapeutic benefit in terms of drusen clearance remains inferential. Third, previous clinical development of MK-2206 in oncology has encountered variable efficacy when used as a monotherapy, prompting its evaluation predominantly in combination regimens (Guo et al., 2021; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2009). The implications of these findings for a non‐oncologic, degenerative condition such as AMD are not straightforward, and careful attention must be paid to optimizing both delivery routes (for example, local versus systemic administration) and dosing strategies that are tailored to the ocular microenvironment.

Furthermore, while the literature provides a strong rationale linking AKT hyperactivation to impaired autophagy in RPE, dry AMD is a multifactorial disease with complex pathophysiology that includes oxidative stress, inflammation, and genetic risk factors such as CFH variants. It is not yet fully clear whether correcting the autophagy defect alone will suffice to produce clinically meaningful outcomes in all patients with dry AMD. In addition, toxicity concerns must be carefully revisited: although MK-2206’s safety profile is defined in the context of oncology, potential ocular toxicity – such as RPE cell toxicity, off-target retinal effects, or interference with normal retinal cellular turnover – must be rigorously evaluated via dedicated preclinical ocular studies before clinical translation. Finally, the intellectual property and regulatory landscape for repurposing a cancer drug to treat an ocular disease will require further scrutiny, although the existing clinical data on MK-2206 do provide an important head-start compared to wholly novel compounds (Guo et al., 2021; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2009).

In summary, the strengths of MK-2206 as a candidate for repurposing in dry AMD include:  
• A well-characterized mechanism of action that aligns with pathobiological insights from RPE autophagy studies, namely the inhibition of aberrant AKT signaling leading to enhanced nuclear TFEB activity and autophagy restoration (Karim et al., 2020).  
• Established clinical safety and PK data from multiple Phase I oncology trials, which reduce translational risk and may accelerate repurposing efforts (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2008; 2010).  
• A plausible hypothesis that links AKT2 hyperactivity in RPE (observed in CFH-risk models and immunoproteasome-deficient systems) to lysosomal dysfunction, drusen accumulation, and ultimately, AMD pathology (Ghosh et al., 2019).

Conversely, potential weaknesses include:  
• Limited evidence regarding isoform specificity toward AKT2, as MK-2206 is generally considered a pan-AKT inhibitor, which may inadvertently modulate other AKT isoforms and lead to systemic side effects (Karim et al., 2020).  
• Incomplete preclinical data linking MK-2206 directly to improvements in lysosomal acidification and cathepsin D activity in RPE, which remain key therapeutic endpoints predicted to counteract drusen formation (Karim et al., 2020).  
• The challenge of adapting systemic dosing regimens used in oncology to the ocular setting, where achieving therapeutic retinal concentrations without causing off-target toxicity is paramount (Guo et al., 2021; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2009).  
• The multifactorial nature of dry AMD that may require combination approaches, meaning that modulation of the AKT–TFEB axis alone might not be sufficient to achieve robust clinical benefit in all patients.

Overall, MK-2206 represents a promising candidate to repurpose for dry AMD based on its ability to allosterically inhibit AKT, a central node in a pathway that has been implicated in RPE autophagy and lysosomal dysfunction. The preclinical rationale – that inhibition of AKT releases the block on TFEB nuclear translocation, thereby improving lysosomal acidification and cathepsin D activity – is well founded in the literature (Karim et al., 2020). Moreover, the favorable clinical safety profile gleaned from its extensive evaluation in oncology serves as an important asset when considering repurposing strategies. However, critical questions remain regarding isoform specificity, the optimal route and dosing for ocular application, and whether restoring autophagy via this pathway is sufficient to reverse or halt the progression of dry AMD in patients. Future studies should focus on establishing robust preclinical data in AMD-relevant animal models —including direct measures of lysosomal acidification, cathepsin D function, and drusen clearance —as well as refining ocular delivery strategies that minimize systemic exposure. Addressing these gaps will be essential for de-risking MK-2206’s application in the AMD setting and for paving the way toward clinical trials specifically targeting the AKT–TFEB pathway in the context of retinal degeneration.

─────────────────────────────  
Conclusion  
─────────────────────────────  
In conclusion, our comprehensive literature review supports the repurposing of MK-2206 for dry AMD on the following grounds: it is a well‐studied allosteric AKT inhibitor with a known safety profile from Phase I oncology trials; preclinical investigations in RPE models implicate AKT hyperactivation in the suppression of TFEB nuclear localization and consequent lysosomal dysfunction; and mechanistic hypotheses derived from these models suggest that inhibiting AKT (and, by extension, AKT2) can restore autophagy, improve lysosomal acidification, boost cathepsin D activity, and potentially counteract drusen accumulation – a key driver of dry AMD pathology. While challenges remain, particularly with respect to isoform selectivity and the translation of dosing paradigms from oncology to ocular applications, the existing data provide a strong rationale for advancing MK-2206 into more focused preclinical studies for dry AMD. Such work should include detailed analyses of lysosomal pH, cathepsin D activity, and the overall impact on RPE proteostasis in in vivo models that recapitulate the human disease. With these additional studies, MK-2206 could emerge as a viable candidate in our therapeutic pipeline for addressing the unmet need in dry AMD (Karim et al., 2020; Ghosh et al., 2019; Guo et al., 2021).

The therapeutic hypothesis centers on allosteric stabilization and activation of the v-ATPase proton pump in RPE lysosomes to lower luminal pH and normalize the acid-hydrolase environment. CTSD is the dominant lysosomal aspartyl protease in RPE, responsible for the bulk of rhodopsin proteolysis; its maturation (from preproenzyme to active heavy/light chains) and catalytic activity are sharply pH-dependent, with activity falling profoundly upon modest pH elevation (e.g., near pH 5.0) (Ng et al., 2024, pp. 13–15; Valapala et al., 2016, pp. 1–4). - Flux–capacity mismatch: Augmenting autophagy when lysosomal function is still suboptimal can be cytotoxic; conversely, rapid acidification in lysosomes loaded with lipofuscin could risk lysosomal membrane permeabilization cascades in extreme stress contexts; staging, dose selection, and markers of lysosomal membrane integrity (e.g., LMP assays) should be integrated into development (Boya et al., 2023, pp. 8–9).  
- Translational pharmacology: Related agents (e.g., rapamycin, valproic acid) show in vitro benefits but present systemic tolerability limits in vivo; although nanoparticles and ocular routes can localize exposure, there are no data for SH-BC-893 ocular dosing, distribution, or durability in this corpus (Singh et al., 2015, pp. 6–7; Li et al., 2025, pp. 17–20).

Decision Drivers for Advancement  
- Target validity and disease linkage are strong: RPE lysosomal acidification defects and reduced CTSD function are documented in AMD donor tissue and in human disease-model RPE; reacidification restores CTSD and degradative function; v-ATPase sits at the mechanistic bottleneck (Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7; Ng et al., 2024, pp. 3–5, 10–12, 13–15; Kaarniranta et al., 2023, pp. 2–3).  
- Modality novelty: A direct, positive v-ATPase modulator could provide a rapid and proximal correction compared to upstream signaling or biogenesis approaches, potentially synergizing with TFEB activation or complement-modulating strategies; however, because this is an unvalidated modality in ocular models within the provided data, the risk is considerable (Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7; Boya et al., 2023, pp. 3–6).  
- Feasibility signals from other systems: Enforced expression of ATP6V0A2 restored lysosomal acidity and protected cardiomyocytes in vivo, supporting the general concept that increasing v-ATPase function can correct deacidification in disease—but chemical activation and ocular translation remain to be demonstrated (Chen et al., 2025, pp. 16–17).

Program Recommendations (evidence-based)  
- Establish compound identity and primary pharmacology: Because no SH-BC-893 data are available here, first confirm chemical identity, V0-domain binding, v-ATPase activation, and selectivity across organelles and tissues using biophysical assays and lysosomal pH measurements; define concentration–response for pH and CTSD activity in human iPSC-RPE derived from AMD donors or aged controls (Chen et al., 2025, pp. 2–5; Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7).  
- Demonstrate on-mechanism rescue in RPE: Replicate the acidification–CTSD–flux triad demonstrated for ticagrelor, zinc ionophores, and nanoparticles using SH-BC-893, with readouts including LysoSensor pH, CTSD maturation/activity, OS uptake/degradation kinetics, LC3/p62 flux, and autofluorescent granule burden under POS feeding; benchmark against ticagrelor or trehalose/TFEB activation arms (Ng et al., 2024, pp. 3–5, 10–12, 13–15; Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7; Li et al., 2025, pp. 17–20).  
- Dissect signaling interactions: Quantify mTORC1 activity (p-S6K, p-4EBP1), TFEB localization, and CLEAR gene expression (including ATP6V0A1) to ensure that v-ATPase activation does not chronically hyperactivate mTORC1 and suppress autophagy; consider combination with TFEB-enhancing regimens if needed (Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7; Sinha et al., 2016, pp. 3–4).  
- Evaluate lysosomal membrane integrity and inflammation: Track LMP markers, cytosolic cathepsins, and inflammasome readouts to ensure acidification does not destabilize overloaded lysosomes; measure complement-related inflammation and secretory autophagy outputs, given their linkage to AMD (Boya et al., 2023, pp. 3–4).  
- In vivo pharmacology in RPE-driven models: Transition to models with documented lysosomal alkalinization and lipofuscin/A2E accumulation (e.g., Abca4⁻/⁻ mice), using ocular delivery to maximize RPE exposure; endpoints: in vivo RPE/retinal imaging of autofluorescence, ERG, photoreceptor survival, and RPE ultrastructure; pharmacodynamic tissue assays for pH and CTSD (Ng et al., 2024, pp. 3–5, 10–12, 13–15).  
- Safety pharmacology: Because v-ATPase is ubiquitous and controls multiple organellar pH-dependent processes, perform local tolerability, ocular histopathology, and systemic safety with emphasis on tissues sensitive to altered endo-lysosomal pH (cardiac, kidney, immune), guided by precedents that modulation of v-ATPase assembly can have profound non-ocular effects (Chen et al., 2025, pp. 16–17, 22–23).

Conclusion  
On target biology, the rationale for lysosomal acidification in RPE as a disease-modifying strategy for dry AMD is compelling, and restoration of CTSD maturation/activity via pH correction is repeatedly shown to rescue degradative function and reduce toxic pigment accumulation in human RPE models and in vivo Stargardt systems (Ng et al., 2024, pp. 3–5, 10–12, 13–15; Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7). v-ATPase is the proximal driver of lysosomal acidity, genetically and mechanistically tied to RPE degradative competence and AMD-like phenotypes (Valapala et al., 2016, pp. 1–6). However, the specific drug candidate SH-BC-893 lacks any corroborating information in the provided literature set—no chemical identity, mechanism data, ocular pharmacology, or clinical development signals—so the central claims about its discovery and performance cannot be verified here (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.-a; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.-b). Therefore, while a v-ATPase activator remains an attractive therapeutic concept with strong biological underpinnings in RPE, SH-BC-893 should be considered unvalidated based on the sources provided, and a go/no-go decision would require de novo demonstration of selective v-ATPase activation, lysosomal reacidification, CTSD rescue, and durable functional benefit in RPE with a clear ocular safety margin (Boya et al., 2023, pp. 3–6; Sinha et al., 2016, pp. 3–4).

Analysis: Candidate 1, eculizumab (ID 38), is a systemic anti-C5 monoclonal antibody with extensive clinical history in complement-mediated diseases and a clear MoA of preventing C5 cleavage and MAC formation. However, a pivotal Phase 2 trial in geographic atrophy (COMPLETE) demonstrated no slowing of GA lesion growth despite confirmed systemic C5 blockade, and mechanistic and pharmacokinetic barriers (blood–retina and Bruch’s barriers) strongly limit ocular target engagement. Intravitreal C5 agents have shown some efficacy, but systemic eculizumab carries infection risk and has failed in the indication. Candidate 2, recombinant human pro-cathepsin D (rhCTSD, ID 50), is an enzyme replacement approach to restore lysosomal proteolysis in RPE cells via subretinal delivery. Preclinical data in CTSD-deficient models demonstrate restoration of autophagy and reduction of pathological markers; cathepsin D is implicated in photoreceptor outer segment degradation, and its deficiency correlates with drusen formation in AMD. While direct in vivo AMD data are lacking, the mechanism is upstream of core RPE pathology, uses a plausible ocular delivery route, and addresses a known biochemical deficit that contributes to drusen accumulation. Subretinal administration bypasses systemic barriers and leverages M6P-receptor uptake. Key risks include immunogenicity, subretinal procedural complications, and the multifactorial nature of AMD that may require combination strategies.
Reasoning: Eculizumab has definitive negative clinical data in dry AMD, with no anatomical or functional benefit and strong evidence of inadequate ocular exposure when dosed systemically. Conversely, rhCTSD offers a novel, directly targeted replacement of a lysosomal enzyme whose deficiency is mechanistically linked to drusen accumulation and RPE dysfunction. Although rhCTSD lacks direct AMD clinical data, its strong preclinical proof-of-concept in related lysosomal disorders, a rational ocular delivery strategy, and the absence of definitive failures in this indication give it higher translational potential. Therefore, recombinant human pro-cathepsin D (ID 50) is the more promising candidate for further development in dry AMD.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Eculizumab (Soliris, Alexion) is a humanized IgG monoclonal antibody derived from the murine anti–human C5 antibody m5G1 via CDR grafting and human framework engineering to reduce immunogenicity and extend serum half-life, designed to bind complement component C5 with high affinity and sterically prevent its cleavage by C5 convertases into C5a and C5b (thereby blocking terminal pathway activation and MAC assembly) (Park et al., 2019; Troutbeck et al., 2012; Yehoshua et al., 2014; Park et al., 2021). It belongs to the class of complement inhibitors that directly target an effector protein (C5) at the convergence of the classical, lectin, and alternative pathways, in contrast to upstream amplification-targeting agents (e.g., C3 or factor D inhibitors) (Park et al., 2019; Tzoumas et al., 2023). Systemically administered eculizumab has established clinical utility in complement-mediated hematologic and renal disorders, including paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria and atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome, and more recently generalized myasthenia gravis, reflecting a mature pharmacology and a well-characterized risk profile centered on increased susceptibility to encapsulated organisms (notably meningococcal infection) due to terminal pathway blockade (Park et al., 2019; Yehoshua et al., 2014).

Within ophthalmology, the terminal complement pathway is an attractive target for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) and geographic atrophy (GA) because C5a is a proinflammatory anaphylatoxin detected in drusen that can drive leukocyte recruitment and VEGF induction in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), and C5b nucleates formation of the membrane attack complex (MAC, C5b–C9), which accumulates with age and AMD in Bruch’s membrane and choriocapillaris and can lyse or sub-lytically activate choroidal endothelial and RPE cells (Kassa et al., 2019). The class of C5 inhibitors therefore aims to reduce both inflammatory signaling (via C5a) and cytolytic/proinflammatory MAC effects while preserving upstream opsonization and some host-defense functions mediated by C3b, potentially retaining aspects of immune competence relative to C3 inhibition (Halawa et al., 2021; Park et al., 2019).

Therapeutic History  
Approved indications and systemic pharmacology  
Eculizumab is FDA/EMA approved for paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria and atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome, where weight-based intravenous regimens achieve sustained trough serum concentrations and complete inhibition of hemolytic activity by blocking C5 cleavage; these regimens produce serum levels > 35 μg/mL and complete systemic C5 functional blockade, but require meningococcal vaccination to mitigate Neisseria risk inherent to terminal complement inhibition (Park et al., 2019; Yehoshua et al., 2014). In other complementopathies, clinical experience has highlighted a mechanism-consequent shift of pathology upstream (e.g., C3-loading and extravascular hemolysis in PNH under C5 blockade), underscoring that C5 inhibition leaves C3 activation intact (Hammadi et al., 2023).

Clinical investigation in geographic atrophy of dry AMD  
Eculizumab was investigated in the prospective, randomized, double-masked, single-center Phase 2 COMPLETE study that enrolled 30 participants with GA (primary cohort) plus an intermediate AMD/drusen cohort, randomized 2:1 to intravenous eculizumab versus saline over 24 weeks (with follow-up to 52 weeks) (Yehoshua et al., 2014). Two dosing regimens were tested: a low-dose arm (600 mg weekly × 4, then 900 mg every 2 weeks through week 24) and a high-dose arm with higher induction and maintenance dosing; all patients received meningococcal vaccination prior to first infusion (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Patel et al., 2022). Pharmacokinetically, systemic exposure and target engagement were confirmed: eculizumab concentrations were measurable at all assessed time points (mean ~ 65–189 μg/mL in low-dose and ~ 122–259 μg/mL in high-dose cohorts), with plasma C5 activity reduced to < 9% by week 1 and < 1% by week 2, indicating complete systemic terminal complement blockade sustained through treatment (Yehoshua et al., 2014).

Despite robust systemic pharmacodynamics, COMPLETE detected no effect on GA progression: at 26 weeks the change in square-root–transformed GA area was 0.19 ± 0.12 mm in eculizumab-treated eyes versus 0.18 ± 0.15 mm with placebo (P = 0.96), and at 52 weeks both arms exhibited ~ 0.37 mm enlargement (P ≈ 0.93), effectively excluding a large treatment effect (> 55% slowing) in this cohort (Yehoshua et al., 2014). Drusen volume endpoints in the intermediate AMD cohort were also negative (no participant achieved a 50% reduction), and fellow-eye analyses mirrored primary-eye results (Patel et al., 2022; Yehoshua et al., 2014). Visual function showed no durable benefit: a 26-week letter gain difference favoring eculizumab was attributed to a single outlier in placebo, and by 52 weeks there was no between-group difference; pooled estimates across small RCTs rated the certainty of BCVA effects as low-to-very-low with confidence intervals overlapping no effect (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Tzoumas et al., 2023). Safety was acceptable in the trial: no drug-related serious adverse events were identified through 52 weeks, and no eyes converted to neovascular AMD during the study; however, systemic C5 blockade requires vaccination and vigilance for meningococcal infection, and an independent systemic anti-C5 AMD trial was terminated early due to uncertainty about risk/benefit in light of reported meningococcal infections in real-world eculizumab users (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Tzoumas et al., 2023).

Interpretations from COMPLETE and subsequent reviews point to several plausible explanations for the null result: inadequate intraocular/RPE target engagement with systemic dosing due to blood–retinal and Bruch’s barriers; the possibility that C5 is the wrong target in GA given genetic associations that more strongly implicate proximal complement components (e.g., C3, CFH) rather than terminal pathway constituents; the short on-treatment window (24 weeks) and small sample size; and the biological reality that C5 inhibition preserves upstream C3a/C3b biology, which may continue to drive pathology (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Halawa et al., 2021; Hammadi et al., 2023; Tzoumas et al., 2023).

Comparative C5 and complement-targeting experience in AMD  
Intravitreal C5 inhibition has produced divergent results. LFG316 (tesidolumab), an anti-C5 monoclonal antibody administered intravitreally, failed to alter GA lesion growth or visual outcomes in a randomized phase 2 trial (Halawa et al., 2021; Park et al., 2019). By contrast, avacincaptad pegol (Zimura), an intravitreal C5 aptamer, reduced GA growth rates by approximately 27–30% over 12–18 months in pivotal trials, leading to FDA approval, although potential increased risk of macular neovascularization has been signaled and requires ongoing pharmacovigilance (Patel et al., 2022; Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023; Tzoumas et al., 2023). Upstream targeting at C3 with intravitreal pegcetacoplan (SYFOVRE) significantly slowed GA enlargement in phase 2–3 programs and achieved regulatory approval, but at the cost of increased rates of conversion to exudative AMD and, in the postmarketing setting, reports of occlusive retinal vasculitis, highlighting a target-dependent safety trade-off between efficacy and pro-angiogenic/immune-privilege perturbation risks (Halawa et al., 2021; Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023; Qin et al., 2024). Alternative-pathway inhibition via factor D (lampalizumab) produced a phase 2 signal but failed in two phase 3 trials, suggesting that partial pathway blockade may be insufficient in GA (Piri & Kaplan, 2023; Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023).

Taken together, these data place systemic eculizumab among C5-directed strategies where local delivery has demonstrated anatomic efficacy in GA, whereas systemic delivery has not, and they highlight that complement modulation can slow atrophy progression without improving visual function and may introduce target- and route-specific risks such as neovascularization or serious infection (Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023; Tzoumas et al., 2023).

Mechanism of Action  
Complement cascade biology and eculizumab target engagement  
Complement activation arises via classical, lectin, and alternative pathways, converging at the generation of C3 convertases that cleave C3 into C3a (anaphylatoxin) and C3b (opsonin/convertase component), with amplification by the alternative pathway accounting for the majority (80–90%) of downstream MAC generation in physiologic and pathologic settings (Tzoumas et al., 2023). C5 convertases (C4b2a3b for classical/lectin and C3bBbC3b for alternative pathway) cleave C5 into C5a, a potent anaphylatoxin that recruits/activates myeloid cells and stimulates RPE to produce VEGF and proinflammatory cytokines, and C5b, which seeds assembly of the terminal membrane attack complex (C5b–C9) on nearby membranes (Tzoumas et al., 2023; Kassa et al., 2019). Eculizumab binds C5 to prevent convertase-mediated cleavage, thereby abrogating both C5a generation and MAC formation independent of the initiating pathway; this preserves upstream C3 activation (C3a/C3b) and the alternative-pathway amplification loop while blunting terminal effector functions (Park et al., 2019; Halawa et al., 2021).

Ocular and RPE relevance of C5 and MAC  
Multiple lines of evidence implicate terminal pathway effectors in AMD pathophysiology at the RPE–choriocapillaris interface. Histopathology shows increasing MAC deposition with aging and AMD in Bruch’s membrane and the choriocapillaris; sub-lytic MAC on choroidal endothelial cells triggers pro-angiogenic/proteolytic responses (VEGF, MMPs), while high-level deposition can induce lysis of choroidal endothelial cells and bystander injury contributing to RPE atrophy (Kassa et al., 2019). C5a is present in drusen and is a strong inflammatory mediator that can recruit immune cells and induce VEGF release from RPE, linking terminal pathway activation to both atrophic and neovascular processes relevant to the AMD spectrum (Kassa et al., 2019). Additional experimental work demonstrates that sub-lytic C5b-9 can alter RPE function in ways consistent with AMD, including stress responses and secretory changes, reinforcing that terminal complement activation can be injurious to the RPE even in the absence of frank lysis (Park et al., 2019).

Complement production and regulation in the eye—and systemic versus local contributions  
Complement proteins are synthesized predominantly by the liver and circulate systemically, but they are also produced locally within ocular tissues (retina, RPE, choroid), with local activation and regulation shaped by cell-intrinsic complement regulatory proteins (e.g., CFH, CD46, CD59) and by oxidative stress effects that reduce cell-surface complement inhibition on RPE (Tzoumas et al., 2023; van Lookeren Campagne et al., 2016). Several studies highlight local complement expression and activation in retinal cells and macrophages, as well as increased local complement turnover preceding clinical disease, supporting the concept of an ocular complement “microenvironment” that can be dysregulated independent of systemic levels (Patel et al., 2022; Piri & Kaplan, 2023). Conversely, transcriptomic mapping suggests that posterior-pole tissues have limited local transcription of lectin and terminal pathway components (except C5 and C7), implying reliance on systemic sources for some terminal pathway proteins, which in principle could make systemic C5 blockade effective if sufficient intraocular penetration and target engagement are achieved (Troutbeck et al., 2012). These seemingly conflicting observations are reconciled by recognizing that both local production and systemic supply contribute to ocular complement biology, and that their relative importance likely varies by compartment (RPE, choriocapillaris, sub-RPE space), disease stage, and barrier integrity.

Genetic and biomarker context for C5 targeting in AMD  
GWAS and biomarker studies have repeatedly implicated complement dysregulation in AMD susceptibility and progression, including associations at CFH, C3, C2/CFB, CFI, and C9 loci, and elevated systemic and ocular concentrations of complement activation products (C3a, C5a, MAC) in AMD patients (Dascalu et al., 2024). However, the genetic signal is stronger and more consistent for proximal regulators (e.g., CFH, C3) than for C5, and at least one analysis noted C3 risk alleles do not necessarily correlate with GA progression (and in some contexts associated with decreased progression), emphasizing the complexity of translating susceptibility signals to progression biology and target selection in late AMD (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Halawa et al., 2021). Mechanistically, C5 blockade leaves upstream C3a/C3b biology intact; in extra-ocular diseases this can unmask C3-related pathophysiology under C5 inhibition, illustrating a general limitation of terminal pathway-only targeting (Hammadi et al., 2023). In GA, this implies that C3a/C3b-driven processes—chemoattraction, opsonization, and immune modulation—could continue in the outer retina/RPE even under complete C5 suppression, potentially blunting the benefit of C5-only therapy (Halawa et al., 2021; Tzoumas et al., 2023).

Therapeutic delivery constraints to ocular complement modulation with systemic C5 blockade  
Large biologics such as eculizumab face formidable physical barriers to ocular penetration, including the inner and outer blood–retina barriers and Bruch’s membrane/RPE tight junctions, whose permeability declines with increasing molecular weight and hydrophilicity (a profile characteristic of IgG antibodies), making intraocular access by systemic dosing uncertain without active transport mechanisms (Hammadi et al., 2023; Yehoshua et al., 2014). This is the most straightforward explanation for COMPLETE’s combination of complete systemic pharmacodynamic suppression with no effect on lesion enlargement: the effective intraocular concentration of antibody at relevant RPE–choroid interfaces was likely insufficient to inhibit terminal complement activation locally, a conclusion echoed by the trial investigators (Yehoshua et al., 2014).

Expected Effect  
Proposed pharmacologic and cellular effect  
Under the working hypothesis, systemic eculizumab would reduce MAC formation on RPE and choroidal endothelial surfaces and diminish C5a-driven inflammatory signaling, thereby protecting RPE cellular homeostasis and the RPE–choriocapillaris unit from complement-mediated injury and slowing expansion of GA lesions (Kassa et al., 2019; Park et al., 2019). Mechanistically, suppression of MAC would be expected to decrease lytic and sub-lytic injury to choroidal endothelial cells and RPE, attenuating downstream induction of VEGF and MMPs, and limiting bystander tissue damage around atrophic borders where complement activation is thought to be active (Tzoumas et al., 2023; Kassa et al., 2019). Reducing C5a generation could blunt recruitment and activation of myeloid cells and RPE proinflammatory cytokine production, decreasing local inflammatory amplification in the outer retina (Tzoumas et al., 2023; Kassa et al., 2019).

Expression and target presence in relevant cells/tissues  
C5 and terminal pathway components are present in the ocular compartments relevant to GA pathobiology: choriocapillaris/Bruch’s membrane deposition of MAC is well documented and increases with age and AMD, and C5a is detected within drusen; RPE-derived complement regulators (e.g., CD59) and choroidal endothelial susceptibility to MAC are described, establishing both target and downstream effectors within the disease-relevant tissues (Kassa et al., 2019). Complement components and regulators are expressed in retina, RPE, and choroid, with transcriptomic data indicating relatively higher choroidal expression and limited local transcription of some terminal components (except C5 and C7), consistent with both local and systemic sources contributing substrate for terminal pathway assembly (Troutbeck et al., 2012; Tzoumas et al., 2023).

Translational and clinical outcome expectations  
At the disease level, a therapy that meaningfully reduces local terminal complement activation in GA should slow the rate of GA lesion enlargement measured on fundus autofluorescence (FAF) and/or SD-OCT, endpoints accepted by the FDA/NEI and standard across GA trials; functional outcomes such as BCVA and low-luminance VA typically lag structural changes and may not improve even when lesion growth is slowed (Dascalu et al., 2024; Qin et al., 2024). In COMPLETE, these endpoints were precisely those evaluated; the absence of any measurable effect on square-root GA area at 26 and 52 weeks indicates that, at the tested systemic dosing regimens, eculizumab did not achieve sufficient intraocular target engagement to translate the mechanistic rationale into clinical benefit (Yehoshua et al., 2014).

Reasons for divergence between expected and observed effects  
Three non-exclusive explanations align with the totality of evidence:

  • Inadequate intraocular bioavailability from systemic dosing. Antibody size and hydrophilicity, combined with blood–retina and RPE–Bruch’s barriers, likely prevented sufficient drug from reaching the RPE–choriocapillaris compartment to inhibit local terminal pathway activation, despite verified systemic C5 suppression (Hammadi et al., 2023; Yehoshua et al., 2014; Tzoumas et al., 2023).

  • Target selection may be suboptimal for GA biology. The stronger genetic and pathophysiologic evidence for proximal complement dysregulation (e.g., C3, CFH) and the preservation of upstream activation under C5 blockade mean that C5-only inhibition may not adequately suppress the complement-driven processes that sustain GA border expansion, as supported by the comparatively stronger clinical signals with C3 inhibition and mixed-to-positive signals with intravitreal C5 inhibition (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Halawa et al., 2021; Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023).

  • Trial limitations. The COMPLETE cohort was small and on-treatment duration was six months, which may be insufficient to observe smaller effects on GA growth; however, confidence intervals excluded large effects, and lack of any trend over 52 weeks reduces the likelihood that longer dosing would have changed the outcome meaningfully (Yehoshua et al., 2014).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
  • Strong mechanistic rationale for terminal pathway blockade in AMD: C5a is proinflammatory and detected in drusen; MAC accumulates at the RPE–choriocapillaris interface with age/AMD and can injure choroidal endothelium and RPE via lytic and sub-lytic mechanisms, linking C5 effector functions directly to AMD pathophysiology (Kassa et al., 2019). Blocking C5 suppresses both MAC and C5a, targeting inflammatory and cytolytic arms while leaving upstream C3-mediated opsonization intact, an immunologic advantage over C3 blockade (Halawa et al., 2021; Park et al., 2019).

  • Mature systemic pharmacology with demonstrated ability to completely suppress plasma C5 activity at well-tolerated doses, including in AMD patients, making systemic development logistically straightforward and with known requirements (e.g., meningococcal vaccination) (Yehoshua et al., 2014).

  • Practical systemic-delivery advantages: single systemic therapy treats both eyes simultaneously and avoids intravitreal injection–related ocular risks (endophthalmitis, IOP spikes), which have nontrivial incidence in chronic IVT regimens (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Tzoumas et al., 2023).

  • External validation within the class: intravitreal C5 inhibition (avacincaptad pegol) has replicated GA-slowing effects in phase 2/3 programs, supporting the therapeutic value of suppressing terminal pathway activity in the outer retina if adequate local exposure is achieved (Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023).

Limitations  
  • Lack of efficacy in the definitive systemic eculizumab GA study. COMPLETE showed no reduction in GA lesion growth at 26 or 52 weeks despite complete systemic C5 blockade and adequate serum exposure, effectively excluding a large treatment effect and arguing strongly against systemic eculizumab as a viable GA therapy (Yehoshua et al., 2014).

  • Ocular pharmacokinetic barrier. The most parsimonious explanation for the COMPLETE result is inadequate intraocular target engagement from systemic dosing due to the blood–retina/RPE–Bruch’s barriers and the large size/hydrophilicity of IgG, an inherent limitation of systemic antibody delivery to the sub-RPE/choroidal compartment (Hammadi et al., 2023; Yehoshua et al., 2014).

  • Target-level uncertainties. Genetic and biomarker studies more consistently implicate proximal complement dysregulation (CFH/C3) than C5 in AMD susceptibility; moreover, C5 inhibition preserves upstream C3a/C3b activity, which may continue to drive border-zone inflammation and remodeling in GA (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Dascalu et al., 2024; Halawa et al., 2021). Clinical comparisons reinforce this: upstream C3 inhibition has produced larger and more consistent anatomic effects (with important safety trade-offs), whereas anti-C5 trials are split—systemic eculizumab negative; IVT LFG316 negative; IVT avacincaptad positive—pointing to delivery and target–context dependencies (Halawa et al., 2021; Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023).

  • Systemic safety constraints. While COMPLETE itself reported no drug-related serious adverse events over one year, terminal complement blockade carries a class risk of meningococcal infection requiring vaccination and risk mitigation; at least one planned AMD systemic anti-C5 trial was terminated early due to uncertainty regarding the systemic infection risk/benefit in this population (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Tzoumas et al., 2023).

  • Limited translatability of systemic complement activation to local disease control. Although systemic complement activation correlates with AMD and disease stage in several studies, the relative importance of local versus systemic complement sources—and the ability of systemic blockade to suppress complement activity at the RPE–choriocapillaris interface—is unresolved and likely unfavorable for large biologics, reducing the mechanistic plausibility of systemic C5 blockade for GA (Hammadi et al., 2023; Park et al., 2019).

Risk–benefit and competitive landscape assessment  
Eculizumab’s negative randomized, controlled data in GA, in the face of confirmed systemic pharmacodynamics, places a high bar against further systemic development for this indication, a conclusion explicitly drawn by the COMPLETE investigators who noted the linearity of GA growth and lack of signal as making additional systemic investigations with eculizumab unlikely (Yehoshua et al., 2014). In the evolving complement-therapeutic landscape, local (intravitreal) complement inhibitors have achieved regulatory approval (C3 inhibitor pegcetacoplan and C5 aptamer avacincaptad pegol), demonstrating that complement modulation can slow GA progression when adequate ocular exposure is achieved, albeit without functional vision improvement and with target-dependent safety liabilities (e.g., increased conversion to exudative AMD observed particularly with C3 inhibition) (Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023; Qin et al., 2024). Against this backdrop, systemic eculizumab offers no efficacy advantage, carries systemic infection risk and costs, and fails the core requirement of achieving ocular target engagement necessary for GA modification.

Operationally, even if one hypothesized that higher systemic dosing, longer exposure, or patient stratification could rescue efficacy, several facts weigh against that strategy: COMPLETE’s pharmacodynamics confirmed near-complete systemic C5 suppression within two weeks; genetic analyses within the trial found no association between at-risk alleles and GA growth or treatment response; and extended follow-up to a year showed no divergence in growth rates (Yehoshua et al., 2014). Moreover, retinal pharmacokinetics and barrier biology make it unlikely that increasing systemic doses would proportionally increase intraocular concentrations to therapeutic levels without exacerbating systemic risks (Hammadi et al., 2023). In addition, C5 may not be the optimal node for GA progression biology in many patients, given preserved upstream activity and the complex contributions of C3a/C3b, opsonization, and local complement production that may continue to drive border-zone degeneration independent of MAC inhibition (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Halawa et al., 2021; Piri & Kaplan, 2023).

Recommendation  
Based on the aggregate mechanistic, translational, and clinical evidence, eculizumab (systemic C5 inhibition) does not have compelling potential as a repurposed therapy for dry AMD/GA. The drug has a clear and relevant mechanism and an acceptable short-term tolerability profile in older adults, but it fails to slow GA lesion growth in a randomized, controlled trial despite complete systemic target engagement, and there are strong mechanistic and pharmacokinetic reasons to expect insufficient intraocular exposure with systemic delivery (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Hammadi et al., 2023). The therapeutic hypothesis—reducing MAC on RPE/choriocapillaris to preserve tissue integrity and slow atrophy—is supported conceptually and by local C5 inhibition successes; however, achieving that biology in vivo appears to require intraocular delivery or targeting upstream nodes, neither of which is compatible with systemic eculizumab administration (Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023; Halawa et al., 2021).

If complement-targeted strategies remain a program priority, resources should pivot to modalities with demonstrated ocular target engagement and anatomic efficacy (intravitreal C3 or C5 agents) while carefully managing known safety trade-offs (e.g., neovascularization risk), and to biomarker-driven questions (e.g., whether baseline low-luminance visual acuity deficit—correlated with faster GA growth in COMPLETE—can enrich for patients who derive greater anatomic benefit) (Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023; Tzoumas et al., 2023; Yehoshua et al., 2014). For systemic complement modulation in AMD more broadly, alternative targets with better ocular PK profiles (e.g., small-molecule systemic alternative-pathway inhibitors) and rigorous ocular target-engagement measurements would be required to justify late-stage development, but systemic C5 blockade with eculizumab itself should not be advanced further for GA (Hammadi et al., 2023; Tzoumas et al., 2023; Park et al., 2019).

In summary, while the mechanistic logic for terminal complement inhibition in AMD is robust, the totality of evidence argues against systemic eculizumab as a viable candidate to slow GA progression, and the development program should discontinue pursuit of this repurposing in favor of locally delivered complement inhibitors or alternative mechanisms better suited to the ocular compartment and GA pathobiology (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023).
