Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Recombinant human pro-cathepsin D (rhCTSD), as exemplified by R&D Systems product 1869-CD, is a bioengineered form of a naturally occurring lysosomal aspartyl protease that is synthesized as an inactive precursor (pro-cathepsin D) (Sharif, 2015, pp. 60–64). This therapeutic candidate belongs to the enzyme replacement therapy (ERT) class, a category of biotherapeutics developed to supplement or correct deficient lysosomal enzymes in various disorders. The natural cathepsin D enzyme is normally produced and processed intracellularly through the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and Golgi apparatus, undergoing critical post-translational modifications—including the removal of the N-terminal signal peptide, glycosylation, and addition of a mannose-6-phosphate (M6P) tag—that are essential for its subsequent targeting to the lysosome (Sharif, 2015, pp. 60–64). The recombinant version is produced under conditions aimed at ensuring high purity and biological activity conforming to GMP standards, thus making it an attractive candidate for repurposing in conditions where lysosomal proteolytic capacity is compromised. The candidate has been designed in the context of neurodegenerative and lysosomal storage disorders, where enzyme supplementation has been shown to restore proteolytic flux by directly replacing a rate-limiting hydrolase (Bassal et al., 2021; Marques et al., 2020).

Therapeutic History:  
Enzyme replacement therapies have been a cornerstone in the management of several lysosomal storage disorders since the early 1990s, with the first approved treatment for Gaucher’s disease setting a precedent for this therapeutic strategy (Saftig, 2005; Lerussi et al., 2025). In the specific case of cathepsin D, recombinant forms have been employed in preclinical models of neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis (NCL) and other neurodegenerative lysosomal storage disorders, where the administration of exogenous pro-cathepsin D was able to rescue functional deficits associated with genetic CTSD deficiency (Bassal et al., 2021; Marques et al., 2020). Animal studies using CTSD-deficient mouse models have demonstrated that both intracranial and localized injections of recombinant CTSD can correct defects in proteolysis and autophagy, leading to improvements in neuropathological markers and even extending lifespan in treated animals (Bassal et al., 2021; Liu, 2021; Marques et al., 2020). Although most of these studies have focused on neurodegenerative conditions of the central nervous system, similar principles of lysosomal dysfunction apply to retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells, which are critical for maintaining retinal homeostasis in the context of age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (Klettner et al., 2013). Notably, the literature suggests that cathepsin D is highly expressed in RPE cells and plays a vital role in the degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (POS), with its deficiency or reduced function being implicated in the accumulation of toxic deposits and drusen formation—a hallmark of dry AMD (Klettner et al., 2013; Sharif, 2015). Despite the absence of direct clinical trials in dry AMD using rhCTSD, the extensive preclinical evidence from both neurodegenerative and retinal disease models provides a compelling rationale for exploring the repurposing of this enzyme replacement strategy in dry AMD (Liu, 2021; Marques et al., 2020).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, the mechanism of action of recombinant human pro-cathepsin D is rooted in its ability to restore lysosomal proteolytic function, which is often impaired in disease states such as dry AMD. Under physiological conditions, pro-cathepsin D is synthesized in the rough ER as an inactive precursor that undergoes several post-translational modifications, including the cleavage of an N-terminal signal peptide, N-linked glycosylation, and critical mannose-6-phosphate (M6P) tagging in the Golgi apparatus (Sharif, 2015). The M6P tag facilitates the binding of pro-cathepsin D to M6P receptors within the trans-Golgi network (TGN), directing the enzyme to late endosomes and, eventually, to lysosomes where the acidic environment promotes its maturation into its active form (Sharif, 2015). Once active, cathepsin D contributes to the degradation of a wide range of substrates, including the photoreceptor outer segments in RPE cells, thereby playing a crucial role in maintaining cellular homeostasis and preventing the accumulation of deleterious debris that can lead to drusen formation (Klettner et al., 2013). The proposed therapeutic strategy involves subretinal delivery of the recombinant enzyme to bypass systemic limitations such as the blood-brain barrier and to achieve localized uptake into RPE cells via the M6P receptor-mediated endocytosis pathway (Liu, 2021; Marques et al., 2020; Sharif, 2015). Once internalized, the enzyme can replenish endogenous levels of cathepsin D, thereby enhancing autophagic flux and proteolytic degradation processes that are essential for the health and function of the RPE (Klettner et al., 2013; Sharif, 2015). This targeted mechanism is a direct, molecularly specific approach that aims not only to compensate for maturation defects in the enzyme but also to overcome upstream acidification abnormalities that often hinder proper activation of endogenously produced cathepsin D in aging RPE cells (Liu, 2021; Marques et al., 2020; Sharif, 2015).

Expected Effect:  
The anticipated outcome of employing recombinant human pro-cathepsin D for the treatment of dry AMD is multifaceted. First, the subretinal administration of the enzyme is expected to lead to efficient uptake by RPE cells via the M6P receptor, thereby supplementing or restoring the lysosomal pool of active cathepsin D where it is most critically needed (Sharif, 2015). This direct enzyme replacement should result in improved degradation of cellular waste such as spent photoreceptor outer segments, mitigating the build-up of lipofuscin and drusen that are characteristic of dry AMD pathology (Klettner et al., 2013). In animal models of CTSD deficiency—specifically those that mimic aspects of neurodegenerative lysosomal storage disorders—the administration of exogenous pro-cathepsin D has yielded significant improvements in proteolytic function, reduction of pathological markers, and even extensions in lifespan (Bassal et al., 2021; Marques et al., 2020), which suggest that similar therapeutic benefits might be achievable in the context of dry AMD. Enhancing the proteolytic flux within the lysosomes of RPE cells is expected to restore autophagy and maintain cellular homeostasis, thereby reducing the incidence of apoptotic cell death and preserving retinal structure (Klettner et al., 2013; Sharif, 2015). Additionally, by compensating for potential maturation deficits and bypassing defective acidification processes through localized delivery, the therapeutic candidate offers a targeted approach that is likely to be both efficacious and specific compared to more indirect modulators of lysosomal function (Liu, 2021; Marques et al., 2020; Sharif, 2015). Ultimately, the expected effect is an overall improvement in RPE health, which should translate into slowed progression of dry AMD, decreased drusen accumulation, and preserved visual function.

Overall Evaluation:  
In evaluating recombinant human pro-cathepsin D as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, several strengths emerge from the literature, though some challenges remain. One of the primary strengths of this candidate lies in its specificity; unlike indirect modulators of lysosomal function, the exogenous delivery of a rate-limiting hydrolase such as CTSD offers a mechanistically driven, targeted replacement therapy that directly addresses a known biochemical deficit in the retinal pigment epithelium (Klettner et al., 2013; Liu, 2021). The robust body of preclinical evidence supporting the efficacy of recombinant pro-cathepsin D in models of neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis, where similar lysosomal impairments are present, lends further credence to its potential applicability in AMD (Bassal et al., 2021; Marques et al., 2020). Moreover, the formulation's GMP-compatibility and prior demonstration of safety in the context of genetic CTSD deficiency are significant advantages that can accelerate its translational potential (Marques et al., 2020; Liu, 2021).

The enzyme’s molecular mechanism, which involves uptake via mannose-6-phosphate receptor-mediated endocytosis and subsequent activation in the lysosomal compartment, is well-characterized and aligns with the pathological requirements for restoring RPE function in dry AMD (Sharif, 2015). This targeted approach provides a direct means to enhance proteolytic activity and autophagic flux, crucial processes that are disrupted in the aging retina and contribute to drusen accumulation (Klettner et al., 2013). The ability of the exogenously delivered pro-cathepsin D to overcome defects in lysosomal maturation and acidification further reinforces its potential role in reversing or mitigating the deleterious effects of the disease (Liu, 2021; Marques et al., 2020).

On the other hand, several weaknesses or challenges must be acknowledged. Although the mechanistic rationale is robust, the translation of preclinical successes in neurodegenerative and lysosomal storage disorder models to the complex, multifactorial pathology of dry AMD remains uncertain (Benes et al., 2008; Liu, 2021). Dry AMD is influenced by a host of factors—including oxidative stress, chronic inflammation, and genetic predispositions—that may not be fully addressed by simply supplementing CTSD activity. Therefore, while the normalization of proteolytic flux in RPE cells is a critical component, it may not suffice on its own in the context of the broader pathophysiological milieu present in AMD (Klettner et al., 2013; Sharif, 2015).

Furthermore, delivery challenges inherent to subretinal injections must be considered. Although localized delivery methods help bypass systemic barriers such as the blood-brain barrier, subretinal injections are technically demanding, carry inherent risks of infection, and may provoke local immune responses due to repeated interventions (Marques et al., 2020; Liu, 2021). The emergence of neutralizing antibodies, as observed in some ERT studies when alternative routes of administration were explored, could compromise the long-term efficacy of the therapy if systemic leakage occurs or if repeated dosing is required (Marques et al., 2020; Liu, 2021). Additionally, the stability and persistence of the enzyme in the subretinal space represent important pharmacokinetic questions that must be addressed through rigorous preclinical pharmacodynamic studies.

Another potential shortcoming is the specificity of the enzyme’s action. While cathepsin D is indeed a critical protease in RPE cells, there is an intricate interplay between cathepsin D and other lysosomal enzymes such as cathepsins B, L, and S, as well as regulatory proteins like cystatin C, which modulate proteolytic activity (Sharif, 2015). This interdependence implies that augmenting CTSD activity alone might lead to compensatory changes in other proteases that could either enhance the therapeutic effect or, conversely, result in unforeseen off-target consequences. Moreover, given the complexity of the RPE cell’s lysosomal network and the multifactorial nature of dry AMD pathogenesis, combination approaches targeting several aspects of lysosomal dysfunction might be necessary to achieve optimal clinical outcomes.

In summary, recombinant human pro-cathepsin D presents a therapeutically attractive and mechanistically rational candidate for the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration. Its origins as a naturally occurring lysosomal precursor that, when supplemented exogenously, has been shown to restore enzyme activity in preclinical models of lysosomal dysfunction (Bassal et al., 2021; Marques et al., 2020) underscores its potential for addressing the proteolytic deficits seen in RPE cells affected by dry AMD (Klettner et al., 2013). The candidate’s well-defined molecular processing pathway—from synthesis as an inactive proenzyme to activation within the acidic environment of the lysosome—ensures that it is both functionally and biologically suited to compensate for endogenous maturation deficits (Sharif, 2015). This detailed understanding of its biochemistry and cellular uptake mechanisms via the mannose-6-phosphate receptor supports the hypothesis that subretinal delivery of rhCTSD could enhance proteolytic flux, reduce drusen accumulation, and ultimately contribute to the preservation of retinal function in patients with dry AMD (Liu, 2021; Marques et al., 2020).

Despite these promising attributes, the candidate’s clinical translation will require addressing several key challenges. Future studies must rigorously evaluate the pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic profiles of subretinally delivered rhCTSD, with particular emphasis on its stability, local retention time in the subretinal space, and potential immunogenicity. It will also be critical to determine whether augmenting CTSD activity alone is sufficient to counteract the multi-factorial processes underlying dry AMD or if the therapeutic strategy should be integrated into a broader, combination-based treatment regimen. Additionally, long-term safety studies are necessary to monitor for potential adverse effects, such as immune-mediated clearance or detrimental off-target proteolytic activity that might impair retinal structure and function (Marques et al., 2020; Thiessen, 2023).

Ultimately, the overall evaluation is cautiously optimistic. The mechanistic rationale is strong—supported by extensive preclinical data from related neurodegenerative and lysosomal storage disorder models—and the therapeutic candidate is produced under rigorous, GMP-compliant conditions, offering a level of quality assurance that is imperative for clinical advancement (Marques et al., 2020; Liu, 2021). The specificity of recombinant pro-cathepsin D in directly addressing a rate-limiting step in lysosomal degradation makes it an especially compelling candidate in a disease setting where impaired autophagy and proteolysis are central to pathology (Klettner et al., 2013). However, challenges related to effective subretinal delivery, the potential for immune responses, and the need to integrate its action within the broader context of AMD pathogenesis must be rigorously addressed in subsequent preclinical and clinical studies before a definitive therapeutic benefit can be confirmed (Marques et al., 2020; Benes et al., 2008). In light of these considerations, recombinant human pro-cathepsin D stands out as a promising avenue for therapeutic intervention in dry AMD, meriting further investigation to delineate its efficacy, safety, and long-term benefits in the appropriate animal models and ultimately in clinical trials.

Collectively, these properties position metformin as a rational repurposing candidate for dry AMD, wherein RPE dysfunction, impaired autophagy/lysosomal clearance, mitochondrial stress, and chronic inflammation are central pathogenic nodes (Amin et al., 2022; Buonfiglio et al., 2024).

Therapeutic History  
Systemic use: Metformin is established first-line therapy for type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) and has been investigated broadly for aging-related conditions due to putative geroprotective effects; long-term safety has been documented, including in the Diabetes Prevention Program (DPP) where gastrointestinal intolerance is the most common adverse event and lactic acidosis was not observed under trial conditions, though B12 deficiency can occur with chronic use (Amin et al., 2022; Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Zhou & Xue, 2024). Preclinical ocular use: In retinal models, metformin has been tested systemically (oral/IP) and intravitreally, demonstrating protective effects in RPE and photoreceptors across light-damage, iodate-induced injury, inherited retinal degeneration (rd1/rd10), and oxygen-induced retinopathy (OIR) with readouts including preserved RPE tight junctions (ZO-1, occludin), outer nuclear layer thickness, and ERG amplitudes; notable anti-angiogenic activity includes decreased CNV lesion size and VEGF/VEGFR signaling modulation in several models (Amin et al., 2022). In these preclinical settings, metformin’s ocular benefits are frequently attributed to AMPK activation and downstream autophagy/mitochondrial and anti-inflammatory pathways, without overt ocular toxicity reported in rodents; however, human ocular safety data and pharmacokinetics under intravitreal or high-dose local exposure are not detailed in the excerpts (Amin et al., 2022).

Clinical/epidemiologic AMD history: Observational epidemiology offers mixed signals. Several large retrospective cohorts and case–control analyses associate metformin use with reduced odds or risk of any AMD or early AMD, with dose–duration trends in some datasets (e.g., MarketScan/claims OR 0.93 and propensity-matched HR 0.57; Taiwanese cohorts HR ~0.54 with stronger protection at >4 years and higher average daily doses), and lower odds reported in multiple studies across US, Europe, and Asia (Amin et al., 2022; Jiang et al., 2022; Kozlowski, 2023; Moir et al., 2023). Other datasets report null or complex associations: a high-quality UK T2DM cohort found no differential AMD risk with metformin using time-varying exposure models; a U.S. claims analysis focusing on dry AMD reported current use slightly increased dry AMD risk while prior use trended protective; additional analyses show no association or heterogeneity by diabetic retinopathy status (Eton et al., 2022; Gokhale et al., 2023; Liang et al., 2022). Meta-analyses also conflict: a systematic review of diabetics suggested decreased odds of AMD with metformin, whereas a broader 2024 meta-analysis concluded no overall prophylactic/treatment role; a European meta-analysis of antidiabetic/lipid-lowering drugs found reduced AMD prevalence overall but not for late-stage AMD specifically (Elhalag et al., 2024; Mauschitz et al., 2023). Importantly, these retrospective designs face confounding (e.g., smoking, comorbidities, health-care utilization), outcome misclassification (wet vs dry AMD), and exposure misclassification (adherence), limiting causal inference and stage-specific conclusions (Brown et al., 2019; Gokhale et al., 2023; Moir et al., 2023). Prospective interventional testing for dry AMD is underway: a randomized, single-blind Phase II trial of metformin to slow geographic atrophy (GA) progression has been conducted, with publication reported in 2024 (Shen et al., 2024); however, the excerpts do not provide efficacy outcomes in GA and emphasize that randomized evidence remains needed (Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Shen et al., 2024).

No regulatory approval exists for metformin in AMD (dry or wet), and the totality of evidence remains preclinical and observational for efficacy, with one randomized GA study reported but without effect-size details here; therefore, clinical utility in dry AMD is presently unproven (Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Shen et al., 2024).

Mechanism of Action  
Canonical pharmacology: Metformin partially inhibits mitochondrial respiratory complex I, reducing hepatic ATP and increasing AMP/ADP, thereby activating AMPK, the cellular energy sensor that shifts metabolism toward ATP-generating pathways; AMPK-dependent and ‑independent mechanisms operate systemically, including reduced hepatic gluconeogenesis, increased enterocyte glucose uptake/GLP-1 secretion, and microbiome modulation with potential systemic anti-inflammatory effects (Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Kozlowski, 2023).

Retinal/RPE mechanisms: In RPE cell lines (e.g., ARPE-19), metformin increases pAMPK and triggers autophagy, reduces ROS, decreases apoptosis, and preserves tight junction proteins (ZO-1, occludin), thereby maintaining barrier integrity under oxidative challenges (Amin et al., 2022; Augustin & Atorf, 2023). At the molecular level, treatment increases Sirt1 and multiple mitochondrial biogenesis and antioxidant markers (SOD-2, Nrf1, Tfam, PGC-1α, COX-II), restores NADH:NAD+ ratios and ATP, and lowers inflammatory mediators (NF-κB signaling, IL-6) (Amin et al., 2022). These signatures are consistent with AMPK’s coordinate regulation of autophagy and mitochondrial homeostasis observed in RPE/retinal contexts, contributing to improved proteostasis and reduced oxidative stress—key failure modes in dry AMD (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Amin et al., 2022).

In vivo, systemic or intravitreal metformin preserves photoreceptors and RPE structure/function in light-damage, iodate injury, and inherited degeneration models (rd1, rd10), with ERG preservation and ONL maintenance; mechanistically, AMPK activation is necessary for light-damage protection in an isoform-specific manner (AMPKα2 dependency), and retina-specific Pparδ is not required, supporting an AMPK-centric retinal mechanism rather than PPARδ signaling (Amin et al., 2022). Metformin also dampens retinal senescence and SASP in OIR after intravitreal dosing, with decreased cdkn1a/cdkn2a and NF-κB/IL-6 signaling, implicating anti-senescence immunomodulation as an additional neurovascular protective mechanism (Amin et al., 2022). Anti-angiogenic actions involve AMPK-dependent and ‑independent pathways: decreased VEGFR2 via enhanced ubiquitin–proteasome degradation, altered VEGF-A isoform splicing toward less angiogenic forms, reduced Flk-1 expression, and inhibition of ALK1-mediated angiogenesis; collectively these actions reduce CNV lesion size, endothelial proliferation/migration/tube formation, and neovascularization in OIR, diabetic, and laser-CNV models (Amin et al., 2022; Augustin & Atorf, 2023). Inflammatory suppression includes reductions in ICAM-1/MCP-1 (AMPK-dependent) and NF-κB p65/IL-8 (AMPK-independent), accompanied by decreased leukostasis and cytokines across models; NLRP3 inflammasome inhibition and modulation of macrophage polarization further contribute to reduced para-inflammation (Amin et al., 2022; Dang et al., 2021; Augustin & Atorf, 2023).

mTOR/autophagy axis: AMPK activation by metformin can inhibit mTORC1, activate the ULK complex, and initiate autophagy, which in RPE promotes clearance of damaged organelles, reduces ROS, and protects against oxidative injury—mechanistically vital for countering autophagy/lysosomal dysfunction in AMD (Dang et al., 2021; Zhou & Xue, 2024). Several retinal studies report AMPK-linked increases in autophagosome formation, and some contextual discussion references mTOR modulation in retinal protection, including translational control via EF2K and general proteostasis benefits (e.g., mutant opsin trafficking) with mixed in vivo translation (Amin et al., 2022). While AMPK→mTOR→autophagy activation is strongly implicated, explicit experimental confirmation in the provided corpus for metformin-driven TFEB nuclear translocation, V-ATPase upregulation, or increased cathepsin D maturation/activity in RPE is lacking; several reviews and excerpts explicitly note these as gaps requiring targeted mechanistic studies (Amin et al., 2022; Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Buonfiglio et al., 2024).

Dose/context dependence and AMPK-independent considerations: Some analyses suggest that AMPK activation by metformin in vitro can require suprapharmacologic concentrations and that certain systemic antihyperglycemic effects are AMPK-independent in hepatocytes; in retinal contexts, isoform-specific AMPKα2 dependence is observed for photoreceptor protection, yet disease models can yield mixed outcomes (e.g., limited benefit or worse function in some HFD diabetic retinopathy paradigms), underscoring the need to define dosing, timing, and disease-stage context for retinal efficacy (Amin et al., 2022; Moir et al., 2023). These data caution against assuming uniform AMPK-mediated benefit across all retinal diseases or AMD stages and highlight the importance of pharmacokinetics, tissue exposure, and therapeutic window in the eye (Moir et al., 2023).

Translational addenda—microbiome and lipid handling: Metformin alters gut microbiota and systemic metabolites, which has been linked to reduced retinal neovascularization through a putative “gut–retina axis,” and may also reduce OxLDL uptake and promote cholesterol efflux via AMPK/LXR–ABCA1/G1 signaling, potentially limiting drusen-related lipid accumulation and NLRP3 activation in RPE (Dang et al., 2021; Zhou & Xue, 2024).

Summary of mechanistic sufficiency for the hypothesis: The literature robustly supports metformin’s activation of AMPK in RPE/retina, inhibition of inflammatory and oxidative pathways, modulation of mTOR/autophagy, and preservation of RPE and photoreceptor function in multiple preclinical models—mechanistic axes consistent with dry AMD biology (Amin et al., 2022; Zhou & Xue, 2024). However, direct experimental evidence in the provided corpus for metformin-induced TFEB nuclear translocation, increased V-ATPase expression, or enhanced cathepsin D maturation/activity in human RPE is not shown; several reviews explicitly note TFEB/V-ATPase/CTSD endpoints as critical gaps that merit targeted validation in AMD-relevant assays (Amin et al., 2022; Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Buonfiglio et al., 2024).

Expected Effect  
Assay-level predictions for RPE models: In human RPE cell lines and iPSC-RPE, metformin at concentrations compatible with cellular AMPK activation is expected to increase pAMPK (Thr172), reduce mTORC1 activity (e.g., decreased pS6 and p4EBP1), and initiate autophagy (increased LC3-II with enhanced flux in the presence of bafilomycin, reduction in p62/SQSTM1 under steady-state), while decreasing ROS and apoptosis under oxidative stress (e.g., H2O2), preserving tight junction integrity (occludin, ZO-1), and improving mitochondrial function (increased ATP, restored NADH:NAD+ ratio, increased PGC-1α/Tfam/Nrf1 and SOD-2) (Amin et al., 2022). Published in vitro data already support many of these endpoints: metformin reduced ROS and apoptosis, increased pAMPK and antioxidative molecules including Sirt1/Nrf2, and preserved occludin/ZO-1 in ARPE-19 challenged with H2O2 or glyoxal; AMPK inhibition abrogated the protection, indicating dependence on AMPK signaling (Amin et al., 2022). In oxidant or lipid-rich RPE conditions, decreased NF-κB activation and inflammasome signaling (e.g., NLRP3) would be anticipated, consistent with prior reports of metformin inhibiting NF-κB and NLRP3 activation in ocular/immune models (Augustin & Atorf, 2023).

Hypothesized lysosomal/TFEB endpoints: The working hypothesis proposes that AMPK activation by metformin will inhibit mTORC1, promote TFEB nuclear translocation, increase V-ATPase expression, enhance lysosomal acidification, and increase cathepsin D (CTSD) maturation, restoring autophagic flux and preventing RPE degeneration. While the AMPK→mTORC1→autophagy cascade is supported in RPE and retina, the provided literature does not directly demonstrate metformin-induced TFEB nuclear translocation, V-ATPase upregulation, or CTSD maturation increases in RPE; thus, these are testable predictions rather than established metformin actions in RPE (Amin et al., 2022; Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Augustin & Atorf, 2023). Given TFEB’s role in lysosomal biogenesis and function, metformin’s dampening of mTORC1 could plausibly facilitate TFEB nuclear entry, but explicit experimental validation (e.g., TFEB nuclear localization quantification, lysosomal pH assays, V-ATPase subunit expression/activity, pro-CTSD→mature CTSD processing and enzymatic activity assays) is needed to confirm the hypothesized mechanism in AMD-relevant RPE models (Dang et al., 2021; Ebeling et al., 2022).

Target expression plausibility: AMPK is expressed in RPE and retina; stimulation prevents RPE and photoreceptor degeneration in multiple mouse models, and metformin increases pAMPK in human RPE cell lines—indicating sufficient expression and pathway competence for drug action in the assay system (Elhalag et al., 2024; Amin et al., 2022). Downstream readouts of autophagy and mitochondrial biogenesis/antioxidant pathways (LC3-II, PGC-1α, SOD-2, Nrf1, Tfam) have been measured and improved with metformin in RPE/retinal models, supporting assay feasibility and expected directions of effect (Amin et al., 2022).

In vivo expected effects in dry-AMD–relevant models: In toxin- and stress-driven models of RPE/photoreceptor degeneration (e.g., sodium iodate, light-induced damage) and inherited retinal degeneration, metformin is expected to preserve RPE morphology and function, maintain ONL thickness, and preserve ERG signals, consistent with reported benefits mediated by AMPK activation; however, model- and disease-stage–specific responses can vary, and negative/neutral results have been documented in some diabetic retinopathy paradigms, underscoring the need to test across multiple AMD-relevant models and to incorporate timing and dose-response studies (Amin et al., 2022). In models of para-inflammation and senescence, metformin is expected to reduce SASP mediators and senescent RPE or retinal cells, aligning with intravitreal metformin effects in OIR and broader anti-senescence literature (Amin et al., 2022; Kozlowski, 2023).

Clinical expected effects: Based on observational associations, any protective effect may be stronger for early or non-exudative AMD and may display dose–duration dependence; however, epidemiologic heterogeneity and potential confounding mean that no specific effect size can be assumed, and randomized trial confirmation in geographic atrophy and earlier AMD stages is necessary to define clinical benefit and exposure requirements (Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Liang et al., 2022).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Mechanistic convergence on AMD biology: Metformin engages AMPK-dependent and ‑independent processes that directly counter core dry AMD pathomechanisms—oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, impaired autophagy/proteostasis, para-inflammation/senescence, and, secondarily, maladaptive vascular/angio-inflammatory signaling—supported by coherent molecular readouts (pAMPK↑, autophagy induction, mitochondrial biogenesis markers↑, NF-κB/NLRP3↓) in RPE and retinal models (Amin et al., 2022; Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Zhou & Xue, 2024). Preclinical efficacy in preserving RPE barrier proteins and photoreceptor function across multiple insults strengthens biological plausibility for dry AMD (Amin et al., 2022).
- Epidemiologic signal and translational momentum: Multiple large retrospective analyses show reduced odds/risk of AMD—often with dose–duration trends—among metformin users, and a randomized GA trial has been conducted, indicating clinical interest and feasibility for prospective testing (Amin et al., 2022; Jiang et al., 2022; Moir et al., 2023; Shen et al., 2024). Meta-analytic work in diabetics suggests potential protective associations, especially in early AMD, reinforcing the rationale to test in non-diabetic AMD populations with controlled exposure (Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Liang et al., 2022).
- Favorable systemic safety and low cost: Decades of broad clinical use, with well-characterized safety signals (GI intolerance, B12 deficiency; rare lactic acidosis risk under renal/hepatic compromise), make metformin attractive from a risk–benefit and access perspective for an elderly AMD population, assuming ocular safety is confirmed (Amin et al., 2022; Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Zhou & Xue, 2024).
- Ocular delivery flexibility and mechanistic redundancy: Both systemic and intravitreal dosing have produced retinal benefits in animals; intravitreal delivery achieved senescence suppression independent of anti-VEGF effects, suggesting non-overlapping mechanisms that could complement existing therapies (Amin et al., 2022). Mechanistic redundancy (anti-oxidant, autophagy, anti-inflammatory, anti-angiogenic) could enhance robustness in multifactorial AMD pathophysiology (Amin et al., 2022; Dang et al., 2021).

Weaknesses and Gaps  
- Critical mechanistic gaps relative to the hypothesis: Direct evidence in human RPE/AMD-relevant systems for metformin-driven TFEB nuclear translocation, increases in V-ATPase expression/activity, and enhanced cathepsin D maturation/activity is absent in the provided literature; several reviews explicitly highlight TFEB/V-ATPase/CTSD endpoints as missing and necessary to establish lysosome-centric restoration of autophagic flux (Amin et al., 2022; Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Buonfiglio et al., 2024). Without these data, the proposed AMPK–TFEB–lysosome axis remains inferential in RPE.
- Heterogeneous and contradictory epidemiology: While many retrospective datasets suggest benefit (often in T2DM cohorts), high-quality time-varying analyses and some claims datasets report null or even an increased risk signal for current users regarding dry AMD; meta-analyses differ in conclusions, and late-stage AMD associations are particularly uncertain (Elhalag et al., 2024; Gokhale et al., 2023; Liang et al., 2022; Mauschitz et al., 2023). Confounding (smoking, DR severity, comedications), misclassification (wet vs dry), and exposure uncertainty limit inferential strength (Brown et al., 2019; Moir et al., 2023; Gokhale et al., 2023).
- Limited randomized clinical efficacy data in dry AMD: A GA randomized trial has been reported, but efficacy outcomes are not detailed in the excerpts; prior DPP follow-up imaging showed no significant AMD prevalence difference between metformin, lifestyle, and placebo, though that study was not designed for AMD endpoints; consequently, clinical efficacy remains unproven (Moir et al., 2023; Shen et al., 2024).
- Context dependence and dose constraints: Retinal benefits can be model- and isoform-specific (AMPKα2 dependence) and mixed in metabolic DR models; some analyses suggest suprapharmacologic concentrations may be necessary for robust AMPK activation in vitro, raising translational questions regarding retinal exposure at tolerated systemic doses, and arguing for ocular PK and target-engagement studies (Amin et al., 2022; Moir et al., 2023).
- Ocular safety and pharmacokinetics: Human ocular safety data for chronic exposure (systemic or local) in older non-diabetic AMD patients are not detailed here; intravitreal metformin safety in humans is uncharacterized in these excerpts, necessitating staged ocular toxicology and PK prior to (or within) clinical trials (Amin et al., 2022; Moir et al., 2023).

Development Implications and Recommendations  
- Mechanism validation in RPE: Prioritize targeted studies in human iPSC-RPE and donor-derived RPE to test the hypothesized AMPK→mTORC1→TFEB→lysosome axis. Required assays: TFEB nuclear localization (immunocytochemistry, subcellular fractionation), lysosomal pH (LysoSensor/LysoTracker), V-ATPase subunit expression and activity (ATPase assays), CTSD maturation (pro/mature CTSD Western) and enzymatic activity, autophagic flux (LC3 turnover with/without lysosomal blockade), and rescue experiments with AMPK and TFEB perturbation (e.g., CRISPRi/siRNA) (Amin et al., 2022; Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Ebeling et al., 2022).
- Translational pharmacology: Define retinal/RPE exposure–response using clinically relevant systemic concentrations and ocular distribution modeling; consider topical/periocular/intravitreal delivery if systemic exposure is insufficient for retinal AMPK engagement and lysosome-centric endpoints, with rigorous ocular toxicology (Moir et al., 2023).
- Indication and stage targeting: Given epidemiologic signals skew toward early/non-exudative AMD and limited evidence for late AMD benefit, prioritize early/intermediate AMD cohorts and GA progression trials with mechanistic biomarkers (RPE autofluorescence dynamics, OCT-based RPE/ONL metrics, aqueous humor cytokines/miRNAs) to increase sensitivity to disease-modifying effects (Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Liang et al., 2022; Moir et al., 2023).
- Clinical trial design: Incorporate robust confounder control and stratification (smoking, DR status, renal function, OCT1 polymorphisms) and embed target engagement (e.g., peripheral blood or aqueous biomarkers of AMPK/mTOR/autophagy) and safety surveillance (B12 levels, GI tolerability, lactate in at-risk) to bridge mechanism to clinical outcome (Gokhale et al., 2023; Zhou & Xue, 2024).
- Combination/adjunct strategies: Given non-overlapping mechanisms with anti-VEGF and complement inhibitors, explore combinatorial approaches in late-stage disease (e.g., GA with complement inhibition) if target engagement and safety are demonstrated (Amin et al., 2022; Shen et al., 2024).

Conclusion: Metformin is a credible repurposing candidate for dry AMD on the strength of convergent mechanistic rationale (AMPK activation, autophagy/mitochondrial support, anti-inflammatory/anti-senescence actions), robust preclinical retinal protection across models, and suggestive—but inconsistent—observational human data; however, decisive gaps remain for the central lysosome-centric hypothesis (TFEB/V-ATPase/CTSD in RPE) and for randomized clinical efficacy, especially in GA. The program should proceed with focused mechanistic validation of TFEB/lysosome endpoints in RPE, retinal target engagement and pharmacology at clinically feasible exposures, and staged, biomarker-rich randomized trials in early/intermediate AMD and GA to quantify efficacy and safety. Until lysosomal endpoints are confirmed and clinical benefit demonstrated, the hypothesis that metformin restores RPE autophagic flux via TFEB/V-ATPase/CTSD to prevent dry AMD remains plausible but unproven (Amin et al., 2022; Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Shen et al., 2024; Gokhale et al., 2023; Elhalag et al., 2024).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Panobinostat (LBH589) is a fully synthetic small‐molecule compound originally developed by Novartis and characterized chemically as a cinnamic hydroxamic acid analogue formulated as its anhydrous lactate salt. This molecule belongs to the hydroxamate class of histone deacetylase inhibitors (HDACi), a group of compounds designed to inhibit the enzymatic activity of HDACs that regulate chromatin remodeling and transcription by catalyzing the removal of acetyl groups from histone proteins. Panobinostat’s chemical structure, defined by its hydroxamic acid moiety, is tailored to chelate the zinc ion in the catalytic domain of HDAC enzymes, thereby preventing deacetylation reactions that normally lead to a condensed chromatin state. In its initial development, panobinostat was formulated in multiple dosage forms, including oral hard capsules containing 10, 15, or 20 mg doses and earlier intravenous preparations, illustrating its versatility in administration routes for different clinical indications (Van Veggel, Westerman, & Hamberg, 2018; Libby et al., 2015; Dokmanovic, Clarke, & Marks, 2007). Compounds of this class have historically been employed in oncology, where their capacity to induce hyperacetylation of histone and non-histone substrates leads to altered gene transcription, cell cycle arrest, differentiation, and eventual apoptosis in malignant cells (Van Veggel et al., 2018; Cea et al., 2013). Moreover, the broad-spectrum inhibition of HDAC isoforms—spanning Classes I, II, and IV—distinguishes panobinostat as a “pan-HDAC inhibitor” with high potency at nanomolar concentrations, a characteristic that underlies its robust pharmacological profile and its subsequent regulatory approvals for certain cancer indications (Morabito et al., 2016).

Therapeutic History:  
Since its discovery, panobinostat has undergone extensive preclinical and clinical evaluation primarily targeting multiple myeloma and various hematologic malignancies. Early phase clinical trials established that, as a single agent, panobinostat had modest activity; however, its combination with proteasome inhibitors such as bortezomib and corticosteroids like dexamethasone produced synergistic effects that translated into significant improvements in progression‐free survival in relapsed and refractory multiple myeloma patients. This positive clinical efficacy culminated in its approval by both the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and the European Medicines Agency (EMA) in 2015 for the treatment of patients with multiple myeloma who had received at least two prior regimens (Van Veggel et al., 2018; Libby et al., 2015; Bondarev et al., 2021). Beyond multiple myeloma, panobinostat has been scrutinized in a variety of clinical settings—including cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, acute myeloid leukemia, diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, and several solid tumor malignancies—to explore its antitumor potential in combination therapies, given its capacity to potentiate the cytotoxic effects of other agents by modulating epigenetic regulation (Cea et al., 2013; Cinek & Karalı, 2021; Libby et al., 2015). Despite its demonstrated efficacy in cancer, there is no recorded use of panobinostat in ophthalmological diseases such as dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or in any similar degenerative condition. The extensive body of clinical research on HDAC inhibitors has predominantly focused on antineoplastic applications, and while some mechanistic parallels exist between the cellular processes targeted in cancer and those disrupted in degenerative retinal diseases, panobinostat’s utility in dry AMD remains an uncharted territory that has thus far not been explored in preclinical or clinical trials (Dokmanovic, Clarke, & Marks, 2007; Morabito et al., 2016; Libby et al., 2015).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, panobinostat exerts its biological effects primarily through the inhibition of histone deacetylase enzymes. The compound’s hydroxamic acid group binds with high affinity to the zinc ion located in the catalytic domain of HDAC enzymes, thereby blocking the deacetylation of lysine residues on histone tails as well as on several non-histone proteins. This blockade causes an accumulation of acetylated histones, which in turn results in a more open chromatin conformation that facilitates enhanced transcription of a multitude of genes, including those pivotal for cell cycle arrest, apoptosis, and cellular differentiation (Benedetti, Conte, & Altucci, 2015; Morabito et al., 2016). Beyond its classical role in modifying histone tail acetylation, panobinostat’s broad inhibition across HDAC classes implies that it can modulate the acetylation status of key transcription factors, chaperone proteins (such as heat shock protein 90), and structural proteins like α-tubulin. This wide-ranging impact on protein acetylation alters the functional activity of numerous signaling pathways and cellular processes, contributing to anti-proliferative and pro-apoptotic outcomes in cancer cells (Morabito et al., 2016). Expected Effect in Dry Age-Related Macular Degeneration (AMD):  
Dry age-related macular degeneration is characterized by the progressive dysfunction of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), which is responsible for the maintenance of photoreceptor health and the clearance of cellular debris. A central pathological hallmark of dry AMD is the accumulation of drusen deposits beneath the RPE, partly attributable to impaired lysosomal degradation and autophagy. In the context of this disease, the hypothesis proposes that localized ocular administration of panobinostat could inhibit HDAC activity in RPE cells, leading to a global increase in histone acetylation. This epigenetic modulation is expected to activate acetylation-dependent transcription factors such as TFEB—a master regulator of lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy—that, once activated, upregulates a network of genes involved in lysosomal acidification and cathepsin D expression (Van Veggel et al., 2018; Cinek & Karalı, 2021). Enhanced expression of these lysosomal components is anticipated to restore or improve the degradative capacity of the RPE, facilitating the clearance of drusen deposits and ameliorating the pathological buildup of cellular waste characteristic of dry AMD.

In preclinical oncology studies, panobinostat has consistently induced autophagy and promoted lysosomal function in cancer cells, leading to growth inhibition and apoptosis. If similar cellular responses occur in RPE cells, then panobinostat may stimulate a beneficial autophagic flux that targets accumulated proteins and lipids for degradation (Libby et al., 2015). The expression of cathepsin D—a lysosomal protease critical for the degradation of photoreceptor outer segments and other metabolic substrates—is well documented in RPE cells, and its activity is tightly regulated by lysosomal pH; thus, any intervention that improves lysosomal acidification is likely to have a favorable impact on RPE homeostasis (Mottamal et al., 2015; Morabito et al., 2016). These findings support the proposed mechanism whereby panobinostat’s inhibition of HDACs may indirectly enhance the transcriptional activation of TFEB, culminating in improved lysosomal biogenesis and function. Moreover, the broad HDAC inhibitory profile of panobinostat ensures that multiple redundant deacetylation pathways are targeted simultaneously, offering the potential for robust and sustained activation of the cellular clearance machinery compared to more selective agents (Morabito et al., 2016; Carafa, Nebbioso, & Altucci, 2011).

From a translational perspective, it is crucial to recognize that systemic toxicity has been an important limitation of panobinostat in oncologic settings, where adverse effects such as gastrointestinal disturbances, thrombocytopenia, and cardiotoxicity (QT interval prolongation) have been observed. However, the concept of localized ocular dosing—via intravitreal injection or topical delivery—could potentially mitigate these risks by achieving high local drug concentrations with minimal systemic exposure (Libby et al., 2015; Karol et al., 2020). In the specific context of dry AMD, where chronic, localized pathology is present in the retina, targeted delivery of panobinostat could allow for the modulation of RPE cellular processes without triggering widespread adverse reactions. This targeted approach aligns with current trends in ocular pharmacotherapy, which increasingly favor local drug delivery systems designed to maximize therapeutic efficacy while minimizing systemic toxicity (Bondarev et al., 2021; Van Veggel et al., 2018). Ultimately, the expected outcome in the proposed assay is that panobinostat treatment will lead to measurable upregulation of lysosomal gene expression, restoration of lysosomal acidification, and enhanced activity of cathepsin D within RPE cells, thereby reducing the burden of drusen deposits and potentially slowing the progression of dry AMD (Cea et al., 2013; Libby et al., 2015).

Overall Evaluation:  
The repurposing of panobinostat for dry age-related macular degeneration presents an intriguing and biologically plausible strategy that leverages the compound’s well-documented HDAC inhibitory properties to modulate critical intracellular degradation pathways. One of the foremost strengths of this therapeutic candidate is its potent, broad-spectrum inhibition of HDAC enzymes at low nanomolar concentrations, which has been repeatedly demonstrated in various preclinical and clinical studies in oncology (Van Veggel et al., 2018; Morabito et al., 2016). The resultant hyperacetylation of histones and non-histone proteins not only promotes cell cycle arrest and apoptosis in malignant cells but also facilitates the transcriptional activation of autophagy- and lysosome-related genes—a pathway that could be harnessed to restore faithful lysosomal degradation in retinal pigment epithelial cells affected in dry AMD (Benedetti, Conte, & Altucci, 2015; Cinek & Karalı, 2021).

In terms of mechanistic specificity, the broad inhibitory profile of panobinostat could be seen as an advantage in the context of dry AMD, where multiple deacetylation pathways may contribute to the impaired clearance of cellular debris. By simultaneously inhibiting several HDAC isoforms, panobinostat is likely to achieve a more robust activation of TFEB and other transcription factors central to lysosomal biogenesis, thereby amplifying the cellular clearance mechanisms required to remove drusen deposits (Morabito et al., 2016; Carafa, Nebbioso, & Altucci, 2011). Additionally, the existing clinical experience with panobinostat in oncology provides a rich repository of pharmacokinetic, pharmacodynamic, and safety data that can inform dose optimization and risk management strategies—albeit with the caveat that ocular tissues may respond differently to HDAC inhibition than cancer cells (Bondarev et al., 2021; Libby et al., 2015).

Nevertheless, several significant weaknesses must be acknowledged in evaluating panobinostat as a candidate for dry AMD treatment. Chief among these is the potential for systemic toxicity. Panobinostat’s clinical utilization in cancer has been limited by adverse side effects including gastrointestinal toxicity, thrombocytopenia, and cardiac complications, and although localized ocular delivery may attenuate these concerns, the safety profile of panobinostat in retinal tissues remains largely unexplored (Libby et al., 2015; Karol et al., 2020). Moreover, the pharmacokinetic behavior of panobinostat when administered locally to the eye is unknown; challenges such as drug solubility, stability, and diffusion across retinal layers must be addressed rigorously in preclinical models. There is also the possibility of off-target effects in retinal cells that could exacerbate retinal stress or contribute to unwanted inflammation, particularly given the complex interplay of epigenetic regulation in non-dividing, highly specialized cells like the RPE (Cea et al., 2013; Benedetti, Conte, & Altucci, 2015).

Another point of concern is the translational leap from oncology to ophthalmology. While the mechanistic rationale for using panobinostat to enhance autophagy and lysosomal function is supported by its effects in cancer cells, RPE cells possess distinctive metabolic and regulatory pathways that may not respond identically to HDAC inhibition. The degree to which TFEB and other autophagy or lysosomal genes are modulated by panobinostat in RPE cells has not yet been directly demonstrated, and significant differences in chromatin structure and gene expression profiles between cancer cells and differentiated RPE cells could impact both efficacy and safety outcomes (Morabito et al., 2016; Carafa, Nebbioso, & Altucci, 2011). In addition, the chronic nature of dry AMD necessitates long-term treatment, and the potential cumulative effects of continuous HDAC inhibition in ocular tissues raise concerns regarding retinal integrity, visual function, and overall ocular health over extended periods—a consideration that remains entirely speculative without targeted preclinical studies (Dokmanovic, Clarke, & Marks, 2007; Morabito et al., 2016).

From a drug development perspective, the strategy of repurposing panobinostat for dry AMD is compelling because it integrates a well-characterized molecular mode of action with an unmet clinical need. However, critical translational challenges must be overcome. These include reformulating panobinostat for localized ocular delivery, establishing appropriate dosing regimens that maximize local efficacy while minimizing toxicity, and conducting comprehensive preclinical evaluations in relevant in vitro and in vivo models of dry AMD. The potential benefit of enhancing lysosomal clearance through increased TFEB activation is a particularly attractive aspect of this proposal, as impaired autophagy and lysosomal dysfunction are recognized contributors to the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Cinek & Karalı, 2021; Morabito et al., 2016). Nonetheless, a careful balance must be maintained, as excessive activation of autophagy pathways in non-proliferative tissues may inadvertently trigger cell death or exacerbated stress responses.

In summary, while panobinostat’s established efficacy in oncology and its well-documented ability to induce broad epigenetic changes provide a strong scientific foundation for its potential repurposing, a number of critical challenges remain. On the positive side, panobinostat is among the most potent HDAC inhibitors available, capable of eliciting profound changes in gene expression that might restore lysosomal function in RPE cells and thereby clear accumulated drusen deposits. In addition, modern advances in ocular drug delivery—such as intravitreal injections, biodegradable implants, or topical formulations enhanced by nanocarrier systems—offer promising routes to achieve the necessary drug concentrations in the retina while mitigating systemic exposure and toxicity (Van Veggel et al., 2018; Morabito et al., 2016).

Conversely, the risk of adverse effects related to HDAC inhibition, the unknown ocular pharmacokinetics, and the potential differences in cellular responses between cancerous and retinal cells represent significant hurdles that must be rigorously addressed through targeted preclinical research. Furthermore, given that panobinostat’s clinical track record is largely confined to oncology, its application in a degenerative ocular disease such as dry AMD would require new, dedicated studies to validate its safety, efficacy, and optimal delivery modality in this context (Libby et al., 2015; Afifi et al., 2015).

Overall, panobinostat emerges as a promising yet challenging candidate for repurposing in dry age‐related macular degeneration. Its ability to robustly inhibit multiple HDAC isoforms and thereby potentially activate TFEB and lysosomal gene networks aligns well with the therapeutic strategy of improving autophagic clearance in RPE cells. However, substantial gaps in knowledge remain regarding its direct effects on retinal cells and the feasibility of its long-term use in an ocular setting. Consequently, while the mechanistic rationale is strong and the preclinical evidence from oncology provides useful insights, extensive additional research is needed to assess the translational potential, determine safe and efficacious ocular dosing parameters, and ultimately validate this approach in models that reliably mimic the pathophysiology of dry AMD (Prince et al., 2009; Morabito et al., 2016; Benedetti, Conte, & Altucci, 2015; Bondarev et al., 2021).

In conclusion, panobinostat’s repurposing for dry AMD is grounded in a robust understanding of epigenetic regulation and lysosomal biology. Its established clinical use in oncology offers a wealth of pharmacological data and a precedent for potent HDAC inhibition, while the hypothesis that HDAC inhibitors can reactivate latent clearance pathways in RPE cells is both innovative and scientifically plausible. The strengths of panobinostat lie in its potency, broad-spectrum activity, and documented ability to elicit autophagic responses, which collectively suggest that, under the right conditions and with a carefully optimized ocular delivery system, it could address one of the major pathophysiological mechanisms underlying dry AMD. Nonetheless, the weaknesses, including potential off-target toxicity, uncertain ocular pharmacokinetics, and the need for a comprehensive reevaluation of its effects in non-malignant, differentiated cell types, must be thoroughly investigated before advancing into clinical studies. Therefore, data from directed preclinical experiments employing RPE cell cultures and animal models of dry AMD will be essential in determining whether the benefits of panobinostat can be safely and effectively harnessed to treat this common cause of vision loss in the elderly (Srinivas, 2017; Van Veggel et al., 2018; Bondarev et al., 2021; Carafa, Nebbioso, & Altucci, 2011).

The likelihood of achieving meaningful disease modification is higher for GSK126, provided its hypothesized TFEB/CLEAR network activation is confirmed, whereas Tocilizumab’s impact on disease progression is highly speculative.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
GSK126 is a small‐molecule, synthetic compound originally developed as a selective inhibitor of the enhancer of zeste homolog 2 (EZH2) enzyme. As a S-adenosyl-L-methionine (SAM)-competitive inhibitor, GSK126 belongs to the class of epigenetic modulators that work by impairing the catalytic activity of EZH2, a methyltransferase that deposits H3K27me3 repressive marks on chromatin. These compounds were discovered and optimized initially for use in cancer, where aberrant EZH2 activity drives tumor progression through silencing of tumor suppressor genes. The chemical structure of GSK126 and its mode of synthesis have been well characterized in the oncology literature, and the compound has been extensively used in preclinical models and early phase clinical studies to assess its ability to relieve polycomb repressive complex 2 (PRC2)-mediated gene silencing (Shu et al., 2023, pp. 16–17). As such, GSK126 represents a prototypical member of a therapeutic class that has been used predominantly in oncology, with recent efforts to repurpose its epigenetic modulatory properties to other diseases where aberrant gene repression plays a role.

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, the development of EZH2 inhibitors such as GSK126 has been focused predominantly on oncological applications. Several clinical trials have evaluated EZH2 inhibitors in hematologic malignancies and solid tumors, where deregulated EZH2 activity supports cancer cell proliferation and survival. For example, while related compounds (e.g., GSK2816126) were investigated in dose escalation studies in patients with hematologic malignancies and solid tumors, GSK126 itself has been studied preclinically and in clinical contexts for its anti-proliferative effects in cancer models (GlaxoSmithKline, 2014). In addition, high-content screening initiatives in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells have identified EZH2 inhibitors among a range of epigenetic drug candidates, with studies reporting that GSK126 can upregulate p16 expression in RPE models as part of broader efforts to identify modulators of senescence (Coryell, 2019, pp. 48–53). However, there is no published record to date of GSK126 being deployed specifically for the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or for directly targeting lysosomal dysfunction in ocular tissues. Open Targets Platform data reveal a very weak association between EZH2 and AMD, with minimal documented evidence tying EZH2 activity directly to disease pathogenesis in the retina (Buniello et al., 2025). Thus, while extensive preclinical and clinical data substantiate the use of EZH2 inhibitors in cancer, their specific application to dry AMD remains an emerging hypothesis that has not yet been validated either in biochemical in vitro studies or in in vivo ocular models.

Mechanism of Action:  
The primary mechanism of action of GSK126 is based on its inhibition of EZH2 activity. EZH2 is the catalytic subunit of the polycomb repressive complex 2 (PRC2) that methylates lysine 27 on histone H3 (H3K27me3), a modification generally associated with transcriptional silencing of target genes. By competitively binding to the SAM-binding pocket of EZH2, GSK126 prevents the addition of methyl groups to H3K27, thereby reducing the global levels of H3K27me3 and leading to a derepression of genes normally silenced by this epigenetic mark (Shu et al., 2023, pp. 16–17). In cancer cells, this mechanism leads to reactivation of tumor suppressor genes such as p16, and similar findings have been observed in epigenetic drug screens using RPE cells where treatment with GSK126 resulted in upregulation of p16 expression (Coryell, 2019, pp. 48–53).

The repurposing hypothesis for dry AMD suggests that similar chromatin-level mechanisms could be exploited in RPE cells to relieve the suppression of the CLEAR (Coordinated Lysosomal Expression and Regulation) network, a collection of genes regulated by the master transcription factor TFEB responsible for lysosomal biogenesis and function. Under stress conditions, the epigenetic repression mediated by EZH2 via H3K27me3 may contribute to the diminished expression of lysosomal genes, including those coding for components of the acidification machinery such as vacuolar ATPase (V-ATPase) subunits and lysosomal proteases like cathepsin D (Abokyi & Tse, 2025, pp. 2–3; Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7). The rationale is that inhibition of EZH2 with GSK126 will alleviate H3K27me3 deposition at promoters of lysosomal genes, allowing TFEB to more effectively activate the transcription of these CLEAR genes. In cancer models, related observations have been made where EZH2 inhibition leads to increased expression of V-ATPase subunits and CTSD (cathepsin D) as well as enhancement of autophagy (Coryell, 2019, pp. 48–53; Shu et al., 2023, pp. 16–17, 22–23). Although most of these studies have been conducted in cancer or other non-ocular cell types, the underlying biochemical interactions between EZH2, histone modifications, and gene expression remain consistent and serve as the basis for the proposed mechanism in RPE cells. In summary, by reducing H3K27me3-mediated repression, GSK126 is expected to derepress genes that are essential for maintaining proper lysosomal acidification, proteolysis, and overall cell homeostasis, thereby addressing one potential pathogenic mechanism in dry AMD.

Expected Effect:  
The therapeutic hypothesis posits that in the context of dry AMD, RPE cells suffer from lysosomal dysfunction—manifested by aberrant acidification and insufficient activity of lysosomal proteases such as cathepsin D—that contributes to the accumulation of toxic protein aggregates and cellular debris. TFEB, a transcription factor known to drive the expression of the CLEAR network, plays a critical role in regulating lysosomal biogenesis and function. Notably, in aging retina and AMD, the activation of TFEB-mediated gene expression is impaired, leading to reduced levels of essential lysosomal enzymes and V-ATPase subunits, as well as the accumulation of lipofuscin-like material (Abokyi & Tse, 2025, pp. 9–10). The proposed effect of GSK126 in RPE cells is to inhibit EZH2 and relieve the epigenetic repression imposed by H3K27me3 at lysosomal gene promoters. This derepression should allow TFEB to more robustly activate the transcription of its target genes, thereby enhancing the expression of V-ATPase subunits and cathepsin D. Enhanced V-ATPase expression will improve lysosomal acidification—a key determinant of lysosome function—while increased levels of cathepsin D will bolster the degradative capacity of the lysosome. In other cellular contexts, such as in certain cancer cell lines, EZH2 inhibition has been shown to upregulate autophagy-related genes, including those involved in lysosomal function, which supports the plausibility of this mechanism in RPE cells (Shu et al., 2023, pp. 16–17; Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 13–15).

Given that RPE cells are highly metabolically active and rely on efficient lysosomal degradation for the phagocytosis and recycling of photoreceptor outer segments, the expected outcome of GSK126 treatment would be an improvement in lysosomal clearance. This improvement could translate into a reduction of the toxic protein aggregates and lipofuscin accumulation that are hallmarks of dry AMD pathology. In vitro, one would anticipate observing an increase in TFEB nuclear translocation, upregulation of CLEAR network genes, enhanced lysosomal acidification (as measured by V-ATPase activity) and restored cathepsin D levels in treated RPE cells, thereby validating the hypothesized mechanism (Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 17–18; Abokyi & Tse, 2025, pp. 3–4). In vivo, similar effects might lead to improved RPE function and a potentially slower progression of dry AMD. However, it is important to note that while there is evidence for the role of EZH2 in regulating p16 and autophagy in various models, direct evidence linking GSK126 treatment to restored lysosomal gene networks in RPE cells remains to be generated.

Overall Evaluation:  
The proposal to repurpose GSK126 for dry AMD represents an innovative application of epigenetic therapy beyond its established role in oncology. One of the major strengths of this candidate is the robust preclinical and clinical safety data that have been accumulated in cancer studies. The availability of dosing and pharmacokinetic profiles from oncology clinical trials offers a significant advantage in terms of de-risking the development timeline for repurposing efforts (GlaxoSmithKline, 2014; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.). Moreover, the mechanistic rationale is scientifically sound: EZH2 is a well-characterized repressor of gene transcription via H3K27me3, and its inhibition could indeed lead to the derepression of genes critical for lysosomal maintenance (Abokyi & Tse, 2025, pp. 2–3; Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7).

However, there are several weaknesses and uncertainties that must be addressed. First, despite the compelling mechanistic hypothesis, there is a paucity of direct evidence demonstrating that EZH2 inhibition in RPE cells leads to upregulation of lysosomal genes, specifically those involved in the acidification machinery and cathepsin D expression (Coryell, 2019, pp. 48–53). Second, comprehensive target-disease association analyses using platforms such as Open Targets reveal a very weak connection between EZH2 and AMD, which raises the possibility that EZH2’s role in the pathogenesis of dry AMD may be limited, or that other compensatory pathways might diminish the impact of EZH2 inhibition in the retinal environment (Buniello et al., 2025). Third, while studies in cancer cell lines have indicated that EZH2 inhibition can upregulate V-ATPase subunits and lysosomal enzyme expression, cancer cells and RPE cells exhibit markedly different epigenetic landscapes and stress responses; therefore, extrapolation from oncology models to the RPE must be approached with caution (Shu et al., 2023, pp. 20–21, 22–23).

Furthermore, targeting epigenetic regulators always carries the risk of off-target effects since these enzymes regulate the expression of a broad spectrum of genes. In the context of the retina—an organ with complex cellular interdependencies—the potential for unintended consequences on RPE differentiation, survival, or interactions with photoreceptors must be thoroughly evaluated prior to clinical translation (Abokyi & Tse, 2025, pp. 7–8; Ferret, 2024, pp. 171–173).

Another point of consideration is the durability of the epigenetic modification induced by EZH2 inhibition. While durable enhancement of lysosomal capacity through chromatin-level changes is an attractive prospect, the reversibility and specificity of these modifications in the context of chronic degenerative diseases like dry AMD remain uncertain. It will be crucial to determine whether the epigenetic changes induced by GSK126 are sustained over time in RPE cells and whether they translate to meaningful improvements in visual function or retinal integrity in preclinical models.

From a translational perspective, the repurposing strategy for GSK126 should include comprehensive in vitro studies using RPE cell lines and primary cultures, with endpoints that directly assess lysosomal acidification, cathepsin D activity, and clearance of photoreceptor outer segment debris. Furthermore, in vivo studies in animal models of dry AMD are needed to evaluate whether EZH2 inhibition can restore lysosomal function and slow disease progression under physiologically relevant conditions (Abokyi & Tse, 2025, pp. 2–3, 9–10). Comparative studies with other epigenetic modulators and TFEB activators could also provide context regarding the relative efficacy of GSK126 in reactivating the CLEAR network.

In conclusion, the repurposing of GSK126 for dry AMD is a promising, yet exploratory, approach that leverages a clear mechanistic hypothesis: by inhibiting EZH2, GSK126 may relieve repressive histone marks at lysosomal gene promoters, thereby promoting TFEB-driven transcription of genes essential for lysosomal acidification and proteolytic activity. This approach could conceivably ameliorate the lysosomal defects observed in RPE cells in dry AMD. The strengths of this candidate lie in its well-defined molecular target, its established clinical safety profile in oncology studies, and the potential for a durable, chromatin-level correction of lysosomal dysfunction. However, significant challenges remain, including the need for direct evidence linking EZH2 inhibition to enhancements in the CLEAR gene network within RPE cells, the potential off-target effects inherent to epigenetic therapies, and the overall weak association between EZH2 and AMD pathogenesis as indicated by current target-disease databases.

Given these considerations, while the mechanistic rationale is robust and the repurposing strategy innovative, the current level of evidence is insufficient for immediate clinical application. It is imperative that future research generate direct preclinical data in ocular models of dry AMD to confirm that GSK126 can, in fact, restore lysosomal function in RPE cells via TFEB activation and increased cathepsin D and V-ATPase expression. Further investigation should also focus on clarifying the broader gene expression changes induced by GSK126 in RPE cells to ensure that the desired effects on lysosomal pathways are achieved without detrimental off-target consequences.

The forthcoming research should aim to delineate the dose-response relationships, optimize delivery to the ocular compartment, and ensure that sustained improvements in lysosomal capacity correlate with clinical endpoints relevant to AMD progression (Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 13–15; Sharif, 2015, pp. 68–72; Ferret, 2024, pp. 103–106).

In summary, while the repurposing of GSK126 for dry AMD is conceptually attractive and supported by a reasonable mechanistic framework, the endeavor is in its nascent stages. The existing literature does not yet provide direct evidence that GSK126 elicits the specific lysosomal benefits hypothesized in RPE cells. As such, this candidate represents a high-risk, high-reward opportunity that merits further in-depth investigation through rigorous preclinical studies, with a view toward eventual clinical translation if the mechanistic hypotheses are confirmed (Coryell, 2019, pp. 48–53; Sharif, 2015, pp. 68–72).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Tocilizumab (Actemra; Roche/Chugai) is a recombinant humanized monoclonal antibody that binds the human interleukin-6 receptor (IL-6R) and blocks IL-6 signal transduction, resulting in systemic anti-inflammatory effects characteristic of IL-6 pathway inhibition (class: humanized anti-IL-6R monoclonal antibody) (Shi, 2017a; Shi, 2017b; Zhujiang Hospital, 2025). In clinical development, tocilizumab has been administered intravenously at 8 mg/kg every 4 weeks and subcutaneously at 162 mg once weekly, with protocols reflecting the infectious, hepatic, hematologic, gastrointestinal, and reproductive safety considerations common to cytokine-targeted biologics (e.g., TB/hepatitis screening, neutrophil/platelet and transaminase thresholds, live-vaccine restrictions, diverticulitis history, and contraception requirements) (Shi, 2017b; University of Nebraska, 2016; Assistance Publique–Hôpitaux de Paris, 2017; Zhujiang Hospital, 2025). Ophthalmic interest in IL-6 blockade is evidenced by prospective trials in non-infectious uveitis and a withdrawn diabetic macular edema (DME) trial; those records establish feasible dosing, ophthalmic outcome collection, and safety oversight but do not provide efficacy data in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (Assistance Publique–Hôpitaux de Paris, 2017; University of Nebraska, 2016). At the disease-biology level, multiple clinical and literature-derived evidences associate IL-6 with AMD, including elevated ocular and systemic IL-6 in AMD populations and genetic associations in some cohorts; Open Targets ranks IL6 as the strongest among selected IL-6 pathway members for AMD relevance in the provided excerpt (Buniello et al., 2025).

Systemic uses and ophthalmic experience: Tocilizumab’s IL-6R blockade is well characterized clinically outside ophthalmology, and controlled ophthalmic trials have evaluated systemic tocilizumab as an investigational agent for posterior-segment, non-infectious uveitis (RUBI), using subcutaneous 162 mg weekly for 16 weeks with retinal structural and visual endpoints and active safety monitoring; the study is listed as completed in the registry excerpt but outcome data are not included here (Assistance Publique–Hôpitaux de Paris, 2017). A single-center, open-label Behçet’s uveitis trial planned to assess 6 months of tocilizumab while maintaining background immunosuppression, but it enrolled only three participants and was terminated early based on its measured outcomes, limiting inferences on efficacy; this protocol reiterates standard immunosuppression-related exclusions (active TB/hepatitis, malignancy, pregnancy) (Zheng, 2018). In DME, the READ-4 protocol designed a Phase 2 evaluation of monthly IV tocilizumab (8 mg/kg) alone or combined with monthly intravitreal ranibizumab through Month 6, with safety and OCT central retinal thickness as primary outcomes; the trial was withdrawn before enrollment due to loss of funding, yielding no clinical data (University of Nebraska, 2016). A registry query identified 10 ClinicalTrials.gov records linking “tocilizumab” with retina/macular degeneration terms, but no identifiers or results are available in the excerpt to inform AMD-specific evidence (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.). Beyond retinal disease, randomized and single-arm neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (NMOSD) studies used IV tocilizumab 8 mg/kg every 4 weeks (or every 4–6 weeks) and incorporated ocular structural and visual function endpoints among secondaries; these trials demonstrate feasibility of systemic dosing with ophthalmic measurements but are mechanistically distinct from retinal degenerations such as dry AMD (Shi, 2017b; Shi, 2017a). Collectively, the corpus establishes operational feasibility and safety monitoring frameworks for systemic tocilizumab in ophthalmic settings but contains no clinical evidence in dry AMD (University of Nebraska, 2016; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).

Mechanism of Action  
Drug mechanism: Tocilizumab is a humanized monoclonal antibody that binds to IL-6R and blocks IL-6 signaling, thereby attenuating inflammatory pathways downstream of IL-6R engagement; mechanistic rationales in non-retinal disease emphasize IL-6–dependent survival and differentiation programs (e.g., plasma cells and autoantibody production in NMOSD), with dosing typically at 8 mg/kg IV every 4 weeks or 162 mg SC weekly in the studies cited (Shi, 2017a; Shi, 2017b; Assistance Publique–Hôpitaux de Paris, 2017).

Retinal IL-6 biology and RPE sources/targets: Multiple lines of evidence link IL-6 to AMD: clinical reports of elevated serum and ocular IL-6 in AMD versus controls, genetic association signals in some cohorts, and IL-6’s role in inflammation and neovascularization in advanced disease; Open Targets assigns IL6 the strongest association among queried IL-6 pathway components in the excerpt, while evidence for STAT3 and IL6ST is comparatively weak (Buniello et al., 2025). Human retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells produce IL-6, secrete it in a polarized manner, and can engage autocrine/paracrine IL-6/IL-8 loops that drive RPE degeneration after inflammatory challenge (e.g., bacterial endotoxin), supporting the presence of IL-6–responsive circuits in retinal epithelia (Brandstetter, 2016).

AMD-relevant upstream injury nodes: The dominant mechanistic framework for dry AMD implicates chronic oxidative/photooxidative stress, age-related lysosomal decline, and intracellular clearance failure (autophagy/proteasome) in RPE, leading to lipofuscinogenesis, lysosomal membrane permeabilization (LMP), and activation of inflammasome pathways with downstream cytokine release and cell death (apoptosis vs pyroptosis depending on priming) (Brandstetter, 2016; Piippo, 2019). In primary human RPE and ARPE-19 cells, LMP induced chemically (Leu-Leu-OMe) or via blue-light irradiation of POS-derived lipofuscin activates the NLRP3 inflammasome with caspase-1–dependent maturation and release of IL-1β and IL-18; broader cytokine secretion includes IL-6, GM-CSF, and GRO, with IL-6 elevated ≈13.6-fold in a cytokine screen and partially suppressed by caspase-1 inhibition, indicating a secondary induction downstream of inflammasome activation (not direct inflammasome processing) (Brandstetter, 2016). Cytokine release is apically polarized, and conditioned media from inflammasome-activated RPE is chemotactic for microglia, linking RPE lysosomal injury to neuroretinal immune activation (Brandstetter, 2016). Complement C5a serves as a physiologically relevant priming agent in RPE by activating NF-κB and inducing pro-IL-1β, which permits subsequent LMP-triggered NLRP3 activation; C5a priming and IL-1α priming also shift cell death from apoptosis to pyroptosis after lipofuscin phototoxicity (Brandstetter, 2016). Lysosomal proteases are mechanistically implicated: inhibition of cathepsin B and L suppresses LMP-triggered inflammasome activation in RPE, and cytosolic cathepsins in general, including cathepsin D, can promote apoptosis when released from the lysosome, underscoring the importance of lysosomal integrity in RPE survival (Brandstetter, 2016).

Intracellular clearance failure and mitochondrial stress as alternative inflammasome drivers: Independent RPE models that combine proteasome inhibition (MG-132) with autophagy/lysosome blockade (bafilomycin A₁) activate NLRP3 via oxidative stress, producing caspase-1–dependent IL-1β secretion without evidence that lysosomal rupture/cathepsin leakage is the primary driver; Hsp90 stabilizes NLRP3 in this setting, and Hsp90 inhibition promotes autophagic degradation of NLRP3 when autophagy remains functional (Piippo, 2019). Mitochondrial dysfunction induced by antimycin A activates both NLRP3 and AIM2 inflammasomes in human RPE lines via mitochondrial ROS and cytosolic DNA, with AIM2 showing dominant control of IL-1β/IL-18 in some contexts, broadening the repertoire of upstream hazards beyond lysosomal damage (Korhonen, 2024).

Mechanistic gaps for IL-6R control of lysosomes/autophagy: Crucially, the provided materials do not furnish direct mechanistic or biochemical evidence that IL-6 or IL-6R signaling modulates RPE autophagic flux, lysosomal acidification (v-ATPase function), or cathepsin D enzymatic activity, and several excerpts explicitly note the absence of IL-6R blockade studies interrogating autophagy/lysosome endpoints in RPE/AMD models (Buniello et al., 2025; Brandstetter, 2016). Strengths

- Lack of mechanistic linkage to lysosomal rescue: No evidence in the corpus shows that IL-6/IL-6R signaling controls v-ATPase function, lysosomal pH, autophagic flux, or cathepsin D activity in RPE; multiple excerpts explicitly note the absence of IL-6R blockade studies addressing autophagy/lysosome endpoints in RPE models (Buniello et al., 2025; Brandstetter, 2016).
