- Given the current evidence, tocilizumab is not a priority candidate for slowing RPE atrophy in dry AMD via lysosomal preservation, because the mechanistic chain posited—IL-6R blockade preserving v-ATPase and cathepsin D activity—lacks experimental support in RPE/AMD models in this corpus, while disease-proximal injury nodes are driven by lysosomal/photooxidative damage, intracellular clearance failure, complement-driven NF-κB priming, and NLRP3/AIM2 activation (Brandstetter, 2016; Piippo, 2019; Korhonen, 2024).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Eltanexor (also known as KPT-8602, MedKoo 406829) is a synthetic small‐molecule compound belonging to the class of “selective inhibitors of nuclear export” (SINE). These agents were developed by medicinal chemists to target the nuclear export protein exportin-1 (XPO1, also known as CRM1), which mediates the transport of a wide range of proteins from the nucleus to the cytoplasm. Eltanexor, like its predecessor Selinexor (KPT-330), functions by binding within the nuclear export signal (NES) recognition site of XPO1—most notably involving interaction with a conserved cysteine residue (Cys528) in XPO1’s NES‐binding pocket—and thereby preventing export of many regulatory proteins. However, Eltanexor has been engineered with modifications that confer improved tolerability along with oral bioavailability and a favorable pharmacokinetic profile, making it an attractive candidate for repurposing. SINE compounds have been extensively studied in oncology, where their ability to cause the nuclear retention of tumor suppressors has led to approved indications in certain hematological malignancies; accordingly, the synthetic origin of Eltanexor is rooted in efforts to optimize the drug‐like properties of early XPO1 inhibitors and to improve their clinical safety profile (Newell et al., 2024).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, the SINE class has been primarily associated with anticancer applications. Early compounds such as leptomycin B (LMB) were the first to demonstrate that inhibition of XPO1 could induce nuclear retention of proteins; however, issues with toxicity limited their clinical utility. Subsequent development efforts led to the creation of SINE compounds including Selinexor (KPT-330) and more recently Eltanexor (KPT-8602), which have undergone both preclinical and early-phase clinical trials in various cancer types. In these settings, XPO1 inhibition was shown to result in the nuclear accumulation of proteins that typically support cell survival, thereby selectively promoting apoptosis in cancer cells (Newell et al., 2024; Tang et al., 2025). Outside the field of oncology, mechanistic studies have indicated that inhibiting nuclear export can also impact proteins critically involved in autophagy regulation and lysosomal homeostasis. For instance, preclinical work in neuronal and glioblastoma models has shown that XPO1 inhibitors trigger nuclear retention of the master autophagy regulator TFEB, thereby enhancing autophagic flux and lysosomal biogenesis (Abokyi & Tse, 2025; Tang et al., 2025). To date, however, there is no published study that directly employs Eltanexor or other XPO1 inhibitors as therapeutic agents for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or related retinal degenerative conditions. In retinal research, extensive efforts have focused on modulating TFEB activity through alternative strategies—such as using trehalose, metformin, or genetic approaches—to restore lysosomal function in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells (Ghosh et al., 2024; Abokyi & Tse, 2025). Although the direct use of XPO1 inhibitors in RPE or dry AMD models has not been experimentally demonstrated, the established efficacy of SINE compounds in other contexts of neurodegeneration and autophagy dysregulation provides a compelling rationale for their repurposing in ocular diseases (Abokyi & Tse, 2025; Falcão et al., 2025).

Mechanism of Action:  
Under normal cellular conditions, XPO1 mediates the nuclear export of a diverse set of proteins by recognizing nuclear export signals (NES) present on cargo proteins. One critical cargo is the transcription factor TFEB, which regulates the expression of lysosomal hydrolases and autophagy-related genes by binding to CLEAR (coordinated lysosomal expression and regulation) elements within gene promoters. In nutrient-rich or stress-dysregulated states, TFEB undergoes phosphorylation by kinases such as mTORC1, resulting in cytoplasmic sequestration mediated by binding to 14-3-3 proteins and subsequent export from the nucleus via XPO1 (Pan & Valapala, 2022; La Spina et al., 2021; Li, 2018). Eltanexor’s mechanism of action is to bind within the NES-binding pocket of XPO1 and disrupt its interaction with such cargo proteins. The inhibition is achieved through covalent and slowly reversible binding to the Cys528 residue in XPO1, thereby preventing the nuclear export of target proteins. When export is blocked, TFEB (and likely its paralog TFE3) accumulates in the nucleus where it is free to activate transcription of CLEAR network genes. The resulting upregulation of lysosomal genes leads to increased lysosomal biogenesis, a lowering of lysosomal pH, and enhanced activation of hydrolases such as cathepsin D—all of which are critical to maintaining proteostasis and clearing damaged proteins and organelles (Abokyi & Tse, 2025; Pan & Valapala, 2022). Published data in glioblastoma models have shown that other XPO1 inhibitors such as Selinexor induce this type of nuclear trapping of TFEB, which correlates with an increase in autophagic flux and enhanced clearance mechanisms (Tang et al., 2025). Importantly, unlike pharmacological treatments that rely on mTOR inhibition (which can have widespread metabolic effects), the SINE approach works directly at the level of nuclear export, thereby selectively increasing TFEB activity independent of upstream mTOR/AKT signaling (Abokyi & Tse, 2025; Li, 2018).

Expected Effect in Dry AMD:  
Dry age-related macular degeneration is characterized by dysfunction of the RPE, resulting in diminished autophagic flux, accumulation of lipofuscin, and impaired degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (POS). In healthy RPE cells, nuclear TFEB orchestrates a transcriptional program that maintains lysosomal homeostasis by upregulating genes involved in lysosomal biogenesis, acidification, and cargo degradation. However, in aging and diseased RPE, TFEB becomes increasingly phosphorylated and sequestered in the cytoplasm, leading to reduced CLEAR network activity (Ghosh et al., 2024; Abokyi & Tse, 2025). The hypothesis behind repurposing Eltanexor for dry AMD is that by inhibiting XPO1 in RPE cells, the drug will promote nuclear retention of TFEB and TFE3. This nuclear accumulation is expected to drive upregulation of lysosomal gene expression, resulting in the restoration of lysosomal acidification and proteolytic capacity, particularly cathepsin D activity. An effective increase in autophagic flux and lysosomal biogenesis should aid in the degradation of accumulated toxic compounds such as lipofuscin and undegraded POS debris, ultimately improving RPE function and potentially slowing or reversing progression of dry AMD (Ghosh et al., 2024; Abokyi & Tse, 2025). In addition, preclinical studies in neurodegeneration and retinal models have demonstrated that enhancing TFEB activity—whether by trehalose treatment, gene therapy approaches, or by upstream modulation of kinases such as AKT2—can protect cells from oxidative and proteotoxic stress (Abokyi & Tse, 2025; Ghosh et al., 2024). Although direct evidence in RPE cells is still pending, the large body of mechanistic work linking nuclear TFEB accumulation to improved lysosomal function provides a strong rationale for expecting similar outcomes with Eltanexor in the context of dry AMD.

Overall Evaluation:  
Eltanexor presents several attractive features as a potential therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, especially given its novel mechanism of action and its ability to modulate a fundamental cellular process that is impaired in the disease. One of the major strengths of Eltanexor lies in its targeted inhibition of XPO1, which has been well validated in oncology and neurodegeneration studies as a means to induce nuclear retention of regulatory proteins. By preventing the export of TFEB and TFE3, Eltanexor is expected to allow these key transcription factors to reactivate the CLEAR network, thereby restoring lysosomal function, lowering lysosomal pH, and boosting the activity of cathepsin D-mediated degradation. This mechanism is particularly compelling for dry AMD because RPE cell dysfunction in the disease has been closely linked to defective autophagy and impaired clearance of toxic aggregates (Ghosh et al., 2024; Abokyi & Tse, 2025). Moreover, the proposed therapeutic approach bypasses some of the limitations of mTOR-based interventions, as it directly affects nucleocytoplasmic transport rather than broadly inhibiting upstream signaling pathways. This specificity provides an additional level of mechanistic precision that could translate into a better safety profile for chronic applications in an aging population.

Nevertheless, several weaknesses and challenges must be acknowledged. First, while there is abundant evidence that XPO1 inhibitors such as Selinexor induce TFEB nuclear retention and autophagy in glioblastoma and other non-ocular models (Tang et al., 2025), there is currently a lack of direct preclinical data evaluating Eltanexor or related compounds in retinal pigment epithelial cells or in animal models of dry AMD. The extrapolation of data from cancer and neuronal models to RPE cells, while mechanistically plausible, remains to be experimentally validated. Second, because XPO1 regulates the nuclear export of a wide range of proteins—not only TFEB and TFE3—there is a potential for off-target effects that could disrupt other cellular processes. This issue is particularly critical in the context of chronic administration in elderly patients, who may be more susceptible to systemic side effects. Third, the pharmacodynamic properties required to achieve effective nuclear retention of TFEB in the RPE may differ from those established in oncology trials. For example, the concentration of Eltanexor required to affect TFEB nuclear localization and lysosomal gene expression in RPE cells might be higher than that used in cancer models, necessitating further optimization of dosing and delivery strategies. Finally, while the oral bioavailability and existing Phase I safety data of Eltanexor support its clinical feasibility (Tang et al., 2025), localized and retina-specific delivery might ultimately prove necessary to maximize its therapeutic window and minimize systemic exposure.

In summary, Eltanexor’s mechanism of inhibiting XPO1 to promote nuclear retention of TFEB/TFE3 aligns very well with emerging therapeutic strategies aimed at correcting lysosomal dysfunction in dry AMD. The extensive literature on the role of TFEB in regulating autophagy and lysosomal biogenesis in RPE cells provides a strong mechanistic foundation for this approach (Ghosh et al., 2024; Abokyi & Tse, 2025). Additionally, the demonstrated ability of XPO1 inhibitors to induce autophagy in other preclinical models (Abokyi & Tse, 2025; Tang et al., 2025) reinforces the potential for repurposing Eltanexor in an ocular setting. However, to move forward, it will be essential to generate direct experimental evidence in primary RPE cultures and in vivo dry AMD models to verify that Eltanexor indeed promotes TFEB nuclear retention, enhances CLEAR network activity, lowers lysosomal pH, and increases cathepsin D–mediated cargo degradation in the retinal environment. Addressing these issues will not only validate the therapeutic concept but will also help to optimize dosing, delivery, and safety profiles tailored for the treatment of dry AMD.

Overall, while Eltanexor shows promise as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD owing to its targeted mechanism of action and favorable preclinical attributes in other disease models, further studies focused explicitly on retinal cell biology and AMD pathology are imperative before clinical translation can be considered. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Recombinant human pro-cathepsin D (rhCTSD), as exemplified by R&D Systems product 1869-CD, is a bioengineered form of a naturally occurring lysosomal aspartyl protease that is synthesized as an inactive precursor (pro-cathepsin D) (Sharif, 2015, pp. 60–64). This therapeutic candidate belongs to the enzyme replacement therapy (ERT) class, a category of biotherapeutics developed to supplement or correct deficient lysosomal enzymes in various disorders. The natural cathepsin D enzyme is normally produced and processed intracellularly through the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and Golgi apparatus, undergoing critical post-translational modifications—including the removal of the N-terminal signal peptide, glycosylation, and addition of a mannose-6-phosphate (M6P) tag—that are essential for its subsequent targeting to the lysosome (Sharif, 2015, pp. 60–64). The recombinant version is produced under conditions aimed at ensuring high purity and biological activity conforming to GMP standards, thus making it an attractive candidate for repurposing in conditions where lysosomal proteolytic capacity is compromised. The candidate has been designed in the context of neurodegenerative and lysosomal storage disorders, where enzyme supplementation has been shown to restore proteolytic flux by directly replacing a rate-limiting hydrolase (Bassal et al., 2021; Marques et al., 2020).

Therapeutic History:  
Enzyme replacement therapies have been a cornerstone in the management of several lysosomal storage disorders since the early 1990s, with the first approved treatment for Gaucher’s disease setting a precedent for this therapeutic strategy (Saftig, 2005; Lerussi et al., 2025). In the specific case of cathepsin D, recombinant forms have been employed in preclinical models of neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis (NCL) and other neurodegenerative lysosomal storage disorders, where the administration of exogenous pro-cathepsin D was able to rescue functional deficits associated with genetic CTSD deficiency (Bassal et al., 2021; Marques et al., 2020). Animal studies using CTSD-deficient mouse models have demonstrated that both intracranial and localized injections of recombinant CTSD can correct defects in proteolysis and autophagy, leading to improvements in neuropathological markers and even extending lifespan in treated animals (Bassal et al., 2021; Liu, 2021; Marques et al., 2020). Although most of these studies have focused on neurodegenerative conditions of the central nervous system, similar principles of lysosomal dysfunction apply to retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells, which are critical for maintaining retinal homeostasis in the context of age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (Klettner et al., 2013). Notably, the literature suggests that cathepsin D is highly expressed in RPE cells and plays a vital role in the degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (POS), with its deficiency or reduced function being implicated in the accumulation of toxic deposits and drusen formation—a hallmark of dry AMD (Klettner et al., 2013; Sharif, 2015). Despite the absence of direct clinical trials in dry AMD using rhCTSD, the extensive preclinical evidence from both neurodegenerative and retinal disease models provides a compelling rationale for exploring the repurposing of this enzyme replacement strategy in dry AMD (Liu, 2021; Marques et al., 2020).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, the mechanism of action of recombinant human pro-cathepsin D is rooted in its ability to restore lysosomal proteolytic function, which is often impaired in disease states such as dry AMD. Under physiological conditions, pro-cathepsin D is synthesized in the rough ER as an inactive precursor that undergoes several post-translational modifications, including the cleavage of an N-terminal signal peptide, N-linked glycosylation, and critical mannose-6-phosphate (M6P) tagging in the Golgi apparatus (Sharif, 2015). The M6P tag facilitates the binding of pro-cathepsin D to M6P receptors within the trans-Golgi network (TGN), directing the enzyme to late endosomes and, eventually, to lysosomes where the acidic environment promotes its maturation into its active form (Sharif, 2015). Once active, cathepsin D contributes to the degradation of a wide range of substrates, including the photoreceptor outer segments in RPE cells, thereby playing a crucial role in maintaining cellular homeostasis and preventing the accumulation of deleterious debris that can lead to drusen formation (Klettner et al., 2013). The proposed therapeutic strategy involves subretinal delivery of the recombinant enzyme to bypass systemic limitations such as the blood-brain barrier and to achieve localized uptake into RPE cells via the M6P receptor-mediated endocytosis pathway (Liu, 2021; Marques et al., 2020; Sharif, 2015). Once internalized, the enzyme can replenish endogenous levels of cathepsin D, thereby enhancing autophagic flux and proteolytic degradation processes that are essential for the health and function of the RPE (Klettner et al., 2013; Sharif, 2015). This targeted mechanism is a direct, molecularly specific approach that aims not only to compensate for maturation defects in the enzyme but also to overcome upstream acidification abnormalities that often hinder proper activation of endogenously produced cathepsin D in aging RPE cells (Liu, 2021; Marques et al., 2020; Sharif, 2015).

Expected Effect:  
The anticipated outcome of employing recombinant human pro-cathepsin D for the treatment of dry AMD is multifaceted. First, the subretinal administration of the enzyme is expected to lead to efficient uptake by RPE cells via the M6P receptor, thereby supplementing or restoring the lysosomal pool of active cathepsin D where it is most critically needed (Sharif, 2015). This direct enzyme replacement should result in improved degradation of cellular waste such as spent photoreceptor outer segments, mitigating the build-up of lipofuscin and drusen that are characteristic of dry AMD pathology (Klettner et al., 2013). In animal models of CTSD deficiency—specifically those that mimic aspects of neurodegenerative lysosomal storage disorders—the administration of exogenous pro-cathepsin D has yielded significant improvements in proteolytic function, reduction of pathological markers, and even extensions in lifespan (Bassal et al., 2021; Marques et al., 2020), which suggest that similar therapeutic benefits might be achievable in the context of dry AMD. Enhancing the proteolytic flux within the lysosomes of RPE cells is expected to restore autophagy and maintain cellular homeostasis, thereby reducing the incidence of apoptotic cell death and preserving retinal structure (Klettner et al., 2013; Sharif, 2015). Additionally, by compensating for potential maturation deficits and bypassing defective acidification processes through localized delivery, the therapeutic candidate offers a targeted approach that is likely to be both efficacious and specific compared to more indirect modulators of lysosomal function (Liu, 2021; Marques et al., 2020; Sharif, 2015). Ultimately, the expected effect is an overall improvement in RPE health, which should translate into slowed progression of dry AMD, decreased drusen accumulation, and preserved visual function.

Overall Evaluation:  
In evaluating recombinant human pro-cathepsin D as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, several strengths emerge from the literature, though some challenges remain. One of the primary strengths of this candidate lies in its specificity; unlike indirect modulators of lysosomal function, the exogenous delivery of a rate-limiting hydrolase such as CTSD offers a mechanistically driven, targeted replacement therapy that directly addresses a known biochemical deficit in the retinal pigment epithelium (Klettner et al., 2013; Liu, 2021). The robust body of preclinical evidence supporting the efficacy of recombinant pro-cathepsin D in models of neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis, where similar lysosomal impairments are present, lends further credence to its potential applicability in AMD (Bassal et al., 2021; Marques et al., 2020). Moreover, the formulation's GMP-compatibility and prior demonstration of safety in the context of genetic CTSD deficiency are significant advantages that can accelerate its translational potential (Marques et al., 2020; Liu, 2021).

The enzyme’s molecular mechanism, which involves uptake via mannose-6-phosphate receptor-mediated endocytosis and subsequent activation in the lysosomal compartment, is well-characterized and aligns with the pathological requirements for restoring RPE function in dry AMD (Sharif, 2015). This targeted approach provides a direct means to enhance proteolytic activity and autophagic flux, crucial processes that are disrupted in the aging retina and contribute to drusen accumulation (Klettner et al., 2013). The ability of the exogenously delivered pro-cathepsin D to overcome defects in lysosomal maturation and acidification further reinforces its potential role in reversing or mitigating the deleterious effects of the disease (Liu, 2021; Marques et al., 2020).

On the other hand, several weaknesses or challenges must be acknowledged. Although the mechanistic rationale is robust, the translation of preclinical successes in neurodegenerative and lysosomal storage disorder models to the complex, multifactorial pathology of dry AMD remains uncertain (Benes et al., 2008; Liu, 2021). Dry AMD is influenced by a host of factors—including oxidative stress, chronic inflammation, and genetic predispositions—that may not be fully addressed by simply supplementing CTSD activity. Therefore, while the normalization of proteolytic flux in RPE cells is a critical component, it may not suffice on its own in the context of the broader pathophysiological milieu present in AMD (Klettner et al., 2013; Sharif, 2015).

Furthermore, delivery challenges inherent to subretinal injections must be considered. Although localized delivery methods help bypass systemic barriers such as the blood-brain barrier, subretinal injections are technically demanding, carry inherent risks of infection, and may provoke local immune responses due to repeated interventions (Marques et al., 2020; Liu, 2021). The emergence of neutralizing antibodies, as observed in some ERT studies when alternative routes of administration were explored, could compromise the long-term efficacy of the therapy if systemic leakage occurs or if repeated dosing is required (Marques et al., 2020; Liu, 2021). Additionally, the stability and persistence of the enzyme in the subretinal space represent important pharmacokinetic questions that must be addressed through rigorous preclinical pharmacodynamic studies.

Another potential shortcoming is the specificity of the enzyme’s action. While cathepsin D is indeed a critical protease in RPE cells, there is an intricate interplay between cathepsin D and other lysosomal enzymes such as cathepsins B, L, and S, as well as regulatory proteins like cystatin C, which modulate proteolytic activity (Sharif, 2015). This interdependence implies that augmenting CTSD activity alone might lead to compensatory changes in other proteases that could either enhance the therapeutic effect or, conversely, result in unforeseen off-target consequences. Moreover, given the complexity of the RPE cell’s lysosomal network and the multifactorial nature of dry AMD pathogenesis, combination approaches targeting several aspects of lysosomal dysfunction might be necessary to achieve optimal clinical outcomes.

In summary, recombinant human pro-cathepsin D presents a therapeutically attractive and mechanistically rational candidate for the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration. Its origins as a naturally occurring lysosomal precursor that, when supplemented exogenously, has been shown to restore enzyme activity in preclinical models of lysosomal dysfunction (Bassal et al., 2021; Marques et al., 2020) underscores its potential for addressing the proteolytic deficits seen in RPE cells affected by dry AMD (Klettner et al., 2013). The candidate’s well-defined molecular processing pathway—from synthesis as an inactive proenzyme to activation within the acidic environment of the lysosome—ensures that it is both functionally and biologically suited to compensate for endogenous maturation deficits (Sharif, 2015). This detailed understanding of its biochemistry and cellular uptake mechanisms via the mannose-6-phosphate receptor supports the hypothesis that subretinal delivery of rhCTSD could enhance proteolytic flux, reduce drusen accumulation, and ultimately contribute to the preservation of retinal function in patients with dry AMD (Liu, 2021; Marques et al., 2020).

Despite these promising attributes, the candidate’s clinical translation will require addressing several key challenges. Future studies must rigorously evaluate the pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic profiles of subretinally delivered rhCTSD, with particular emphasis on its stability, local retention time in the subretinal space, and potential immunogenicity. It will also be critical to determine whether augmenting CTSD activity alone is sufficient to counteract the multi-factorial processes underlying dry AMD or if the therapeutic strategy should be integrated into a broader, combination-based treatment regimen. Additionally, long-term safety studies are necessary to monitor for potential adverse effects, such as immune-mediated clearance or detrimental off-target proteolytic activity that might impair retinal structure and function (Marques et al., 2020; Thiessen, 2023).

Ultimately, the overall evaluation is cautiously optimistic. The mechanistic rationale is strong—supported by extensive preclinical data from related neurodegenerative and lysosomal storage disorder models—and the therapeutic candidate is produced under rigorous, GMP-compliant conditions, offering a level of quality assurance that is imperative for clinical advancement (Marques et al., 2020; Liu, 2021). The specificity of recombinant pro-cathepsin D in directly addressing a rate-limiting step in lysosomal degradation makes it an especially compelling candidate in a disease setting where impaired autophagy and proteolysis are central to pathology (Klettner et al., 2013). However, challenges related to effective subretinal delivery, the potential for immune responses, and the need to integrate its action within the broader context of AMD pathogenesis must be rigorously addressed in subsequent preclinical and clinical studies before a definitive therapeutic benefit can be confirmed (Marques et al., 2020; Benes et al., 2008). In light of these considerations, recombinant human pro-cathepsin D stands out as a promising avenue for therapeutic intervention in dry AMD, meriting further investigation to delineate its efficacy, safety, and long-term benefits in the appropriate animal models and ultimately in clinical trials.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN) is an endogenous intermediate in the mammalian NAD⁺ salvage pathway, generated by nicotinamide phosphoribosyltransferase (NAMPT) from nicotinamide (NAM) and 5-phosphoribosyl‐1‐pyrophosphate (PRPP) and converted to NAD⁺ by nicotinamide mononucleotide adenylyltransferases (NMNAT1–3) (Jadeja et al., 2020; Cimaglia et al., 2020). NMN belongs to the vitamin B3–derived NAD⁺ precursor class and is one of several precursors (others include nicotinamide [NAM], nicotinic acid [NA], and nicotinamide riboside [NR]) used to augment cellular NAD⁺ pools in aging and disease (Cimaglia et al., 2020). NMN was prioritized as a practical intervention because direct NAD⁺ delivery to tissues is not straightforward, whereas in vivo administration of NMN elevates tissue NAD⁺ and supports mitochondrial function and cellular stress defenses in multiple systems (Ebeling et al., 2020; Rahman et al., 2024). Transport and uptake mechanisms include the Slc12a8 transporter described in mouse small intestine, as well as extracellular dephosphorylation to NR followed by NR uptake via equilibrative nucleoside transporters; intracellular NR is re‐phosphorylated by NRK1 to NMN for resynthesis of NAD⁺ (Will‐Orrego, 2020a; Rahman et al., 2024). Notably for RPE models, ARPE‐19 cells have been reported to express transporters supporting NMN uptake but not NR uptake, favoring NMN over NR in this system (Will‐Orrego, 2020b). In RPE and retinal contexts, NMN and related precursors have been deployed preclinically to restore NAD⁺, improve mitochondrial function, modulate sirtuin‐dependent pathways, and mitigate features of neurodegeneration and cellular senescence (Jadeja et al., 2018; Ebeling et al., 2020; Lin, 2020).

Therapeutic History  
NAD⁺ decline with age is conserved across tissues, including the retina and RPE, and is mechanistically linked to impaired mitochondrial function, heightened oxidative stress, and increased susceptibility to degeneration (Jadeja et al., 2018; Cimaglia et al., 2020). In the outer retina, rod‐ or cone‐specific Nampt deletion produces NAD⁺ deficiency and photoreceptor degeneration; systemic NMN at 150 mg/kg i.p. restored retinal function by ERG and preserved photoreceptor structure, establishing that exogenous NMN can replenish retinal NAD⁺ and mitigate degeneration linked to impaired salvage (Lin, 2020). NMN also protected in models of acute retinal injury: daily systemic NMN reduced photoreceptor death and oxidative stress after retinal detachment and increased retinal SIRT1 and HO‐1, consistent with NAD⁺‐dependent sirtuin activation in vivo (Chen et al., 2020). In ischemia models, NMN administration protected against retinal dysfunction (Lee et al., 2022; Lee et al., 2024). In a cholesterol efflux–deficient murine model that recapitulates key dry AMD features driven by senescent subretinal macrophages (Abca1/g1‐deficient), systemic NMN reduced subretinal drusenoid deposits (SDDs), decreased lipofuscin‐positive macrophage burden, and improved electrophysiological and structural endpoints, supporting a role for NAD⁺ augmentation in reversing senescence‐driven outer retinal pathology in vivo (Terao et al., 2024). In RPE‐directed models, pharmacologic NAMPT inhibition with FK866 is widely used to mimic age‐related NAD⁺ decline; in ARPE‐19 and primary RPE, NMN co‐treatment preserved NAD⁺, SIRT1 protein, viability, and reduced senescence markers, and in vivo systemic NMN preserved RPE NAD⁺ and SIRT1 after subretinal FK866 (Jadeja et al., 2018). Oxidant injury with sodium iodate (NaIO₃) induced RPE senescence, NAD⁺ depletion, mitochondrial dysfunction, and subretinal inflammation; NMN restored RPE NAD⁺, reduced DNA damage and senescence markers, improved mitochondrial membrane potential and ATP in ARPE‐19, and reduced inflammatory cell recruitment in vivo, with intact Sirt1 signaling required for NMN benefit (Ren et al., 2022). Outside strictly RPE biology, NMN improved RPE phagocytosis and mitochondrial ultrastructure in the RCS rat model of retinal degeneration, with a mechanistic link to a NAD⁺/GAPDH axis that modulated actin/cytoskeletal phagocytosis machinery in RPE; GAPDH knockdown abrogated NMN’s benefits, supporting a causal chain from NAD⁺ repletion to enhanced RPE POS clearance via GAPDH‐dependent pathways (Zhang et al., 2024).

Clinical translation of NAD⁺ precursors has begun with nicotinamide and NR in ophthalmology-adjacent indications (e.g., glaucoma), demonstrating tolerability and retinal functional protection in mice, and documenting NAD⁺ elevation in adult humans, but direct clinical data for NMN in dry AMD are not available in the provided context (Cimaglia et al., 2020; Rahman et al., 2024). Long-term NMN treatment in mice mitigated age-associated physiological decline systemically and reportedly ameliorated eye function, but detailed ocular pharmacology and human NMN ocular safety are not established here (Rahman et al., 2024). Collectively, the preclinical record supports NMN as an NAD⁺ augmenting therapy with demonstrated efficacy in retina and RPE-relevant models of NAD⁺ deficiency, oxidative injury, and senescence; however, there is no direct published clinical trial evidence in dry AMD patients in this context set (Jadeja et al., 2018; Lin, 2020; Chen et al., 2020; Terao et al., 2024).

Mechanism of Action  
Core biochemistry  
- NAD⁺ salvage. In mammalian cells, the salvage pathway supplies most NAD⁺ (~80%), with NAMPT catalyzing NAM → NMN and NMNAT1–3 completing NMN → NAD⁺; this pool fuels redox reactions and serves as substrate for NAD⁺‐consuming enzymes including sirtuins, PARPs, and the NAD glycohydrolase CD38 (Cimaglia et al., 2020; Jadeja et al., 2020). NAMPT-mediated biosynthesis is essential for vision, and its decline in RPE with age causally links to reduced NAD⁺, reduced SIRT1 expression/activity, and enhanced cellular senescence (Jadeja et al., 2018).  
- Uptake and intracellular handling. NMN can enter cells via specific transporters (Slc12a8 shown in mouse gut) and/or after extracellular dephosphorylation to NR with re-phosphorylation by NRK1, routes that are cell type–dependent; ARPE-19 preferentially transport NMN in vitro, supporting the choice of NMN over NR in these RPE models (Will‐Orrego, 2020a; Will‐Orrego, 2020b; Rahman et al., 2024).

Downstream signaling nodes relevant to RPE and dry AMD  
- Sirtuins. NAD⁺ is an obligate co-substrate for sirtuins; increased NAD⁺ drives sirtuin deacetylase/deacylase activities across SIRT1–7 with consequences for mitochondrial function, antioxidant defenses, DNA repair, and autophagy/mitophagy (Cimaglia et al., 2020). In aging RPE, NAD⁺ and SIRT1 decline in parallel; restoring NAD⁺ with NMN rescues SIRT1 protein and activity in vitro and in vivo, and reduces senescence markers p16^INK4a and p21^Waf/Cip1 (Jadeja et al., 2018). SIRT3, the mitochondrial sirtuin, maintains mitochondrial integrity by deacetylating and activating SOD2 and coordinating antioxidant responses, mitophagy, and UPR^mt; retinal NAD⁺ deficiency impairs SIRT3, linking NAD⁺ loss to mitochondrial vulnerability (Cimaglia et al., 2020; Lin, 2020). In a retinal detachment model, systemic NMN increased SIRT1 protein and HO‐1, with mechanistic in vitro data supporting a SIRT1 → HO‐1 protective axis (Chen et al., 2020).  
- AMPK and NAMPT/SIRT1 crosstalk. AMPK upregulates NAMPT expression and thus supports NAD⁺ salvage; reciprocally, SIRT1 deacetylates/stabilizes LKB1 to activate AMPK, forming a positive feedback loop that coordinates energy sensing and catabolic responses (Luján et al., 2022). In RPE senescence induced by NaIO₃, AMPK activation occurs downstream of ATP depletion and is modulated by NMN treatment, though overactivation of Sirt1 by a direct agonist (SRT1720) produced mitochondrial hyperfusion and stress signaling, arguing for physiological NAD⁺‐driven Sirt1 activation rather than pharmacologic overdrive (Ren et al., 2022).  
- Autophagy/mitophagy and mitochondrial biogenesis. SIRT1 promotes autophagosome formation and Rab7‐dependent autophagosome–lysosome fusion; together with AMPK, it enhances expression of mitophagy effectors (PINK1, Parkin) and co-activates PGC‐1α to drive mitochondrial biogenesis programs via transcriptional partners (NRF‐1, ERRα, PPARα) (Luján et al., 2022). Reviews and preclinical observations indicate that NAD⁺ repletion can restore mitophagy, activate UPR^mt, and normalize mitochondrial metabolic profiles, including evidence that “NAD⁺ inhibits the metabolic reprogramming of RPE cells in early AMD by upregulating mitophagy,” supporting the hypothesis that NMN-driven NAD⁺ gain could favorably reprogram RPE mitochondrial quality control (Rahman et al., 2024; Jadeja et al., 2020). In primary AMD donor RPE, NMN improved mitochondrial function in vitro; the same study used mitophagy reporter assays (mKeima-mito), underscoring the feasibility of measuring NMN’s effects on mitophagy in human RPE although specific NMN → mitophagy data were not detailed in the excerpt (Fisher et al., 2022; Ebeling et al., 2020).  
- PARP and CD38 as NAD⁺ sinks. DNA damage and SASP/inflammation drive PARP and CD38 activities that deplete NAD⁺; CD38 in particular contributes to age-related NAD⁺ decline and mitochondrial dysfunction and is induced by LXR signaling and SASP, creating a self-reinforcing senescence–NAD⁺ depletion loop (Cimaglia et al., 2020; Terao et al., 2024). In photoreceptor cells, PARP inhibition partially rescues viability under NAMPT inhibition, highlighting the vulnerability of NAD⁺ pools to consumption pathways and the value of reducing NAD⁺ sinks in parallel with NMN supplementation (Lin & Apte, 2018).  
- Inflammation and inflammasome. NAD⁺ augmentation via NMN or increased NAMPT/NAD⁺ can reduce NLRP3 inflammasome activation and downstream IL-1β/IL-18 via a SIRT1‐dependent mechanism in RPE aging models, pointing to anti‐inflammatory benefits of the NAMPT/NAD⁺/SIRT1 axis (Wu et al., 2021). In the Abca1/g1 macrophage senescence model of dry AMD, NAD⁺ repletion (NMN or CD38 inhibition) eliminated senescent macrophages and reversed drusenoid pathology and RPE functional deficits, extending the anti‐senescence and anti‐inflammatory reach of NAD⁺ augmentation to subretinal immune cells central to AMD pathobiology (Terao et al., 2024).

Critically, although TFEB (a master regulator of lysosomal biogenesis) and lysosomal proteases such as cathepsin D (CTSD) are highly relevant to RPE oxidative‐debris clearance in dry AMD, the provided literature does not demonstrate direct NMN‐induced TFEB activation, lysosomal acidification, or increased CTSD activity in RPE or retina; these remain plausible but unproven links in this context set (Falcão et al., 2025; Will‐Orrego, 2020a; Ebeling et al., 2020; Cimaglia et al., 2020).

Expected Effect  
Assay-level expectations in RPE models of dry AMD  
- NAD⁺ repletion in RPE. In ARPE‐19 and primary RPE, co‐treatment with NMN restores cellular NAD⁺ reduced by NAMPT inhibition, with partial to robust recovery depending on media and dosing; in ARPE‐19, FK866 sharply lowers NAD⁺/NADH and ATP, while NMN rescues both metrics and normalizes OXPHOS/glycolysis balance measured by Seahorse assays (Will‐Orrego, 2020b, 2020c). ARPE‐19 cells express NMN but not NR transporters, predicting superior uptake and intracellular conversion for NMN in this model (Will‐Orrego, 2020b). In NaIO₃‐stressed ARPE‐19, 800–1,000 µM NMN restored NAD⁺, mitochondrial membrane potential, and ATP, reduced ROS and DNA damage, and reduced senescence markers, with Sirt1 activity required for these benefits (Ren et al., 2022).  
- Sirtuin engagement. In FK866‐inhibited RPE, NMN co‐treatment restored SIRT1 protein and activity in vitro and in vivo; in photoreceptor injury, NMN increased retinal SIRT1 and induced HO-1, suggesting a SIRT1‐dependent antioxidant arm (Jadeja et al., 2018; Chen et al., 2020). In primary AMD donor RPE, NMN improved mitochondrial function, consistent with engagement of mitochondrial sirtuins and/or PGC-1α programs, though specific sirtuin readouts were not reported in that excerpt (Ebeling et al., 2020).  
- AMPK and mitophagy. AMPK will be sensitive to changes in ATP/AMP driven by mitochondrial recovery after NMN; in RPE senescence models, AMPK activation was observed under oxidant injury and modulated by NMN, and the NAD⁺/Sirt1/AMPK network is positioned to restore mitophagy via ULK1 activation, mTORC1 attenuation, and PINK1/Parkin induction (Ren et al., 2022; Luján et al., 2022). The hypothesis that NAD⁺ supplementation restores RPE metabolic dysfunction by inducing mitophagy is supported conceptually and by limited preclinical data cited for NAD⁺ effects on RPE mitophagy, making mitophagy flux (e.g., mKeima‐mito) a reasonable expected readout under NMN treatment (Jadeja et al., 2020; Fisher et al., 2022).  
- Autophagy-lysosome system and debris clearance. TFEB governs lysosomal biogenesis and function and is a rational target in dry AMD; Sirt1 and AMPK facilitate autophagosome formation and autophagosome–lysosome fusion (Rab7) and thus could secondarily enhance lysosomal throughput after NMN (Falcão et al., 2025; Luján et al., 2022). However, direct evidence that NMN increases lysosomal number, lysosomal acidification, TFEB nuclear translocation, or CTSD activity in RPE is not provided here; these are testable but as yet unvalidated expectations (Falcão et al., 2025; Will‐Orrego, 2020a). By contrast, NMN increased RPE phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments and restored actin‐mediated phagocytic machinery in vivo in the RCS rat, revealing a complementary route by which NMN could improve outer segment turnover independent of direct TFEB activation (Zhang et al., 2024).  
- Anti‐senescence and anti‐inflammatory effects. In RPE and subretinal myeloid cells, NMN suppresses senescence phenotypes and reduces inflammatory mediators, which should reduce SASP‐driven bystander stress on RPE and photoreceptors and may indirectly lower CD38‐mediated NAD⁺ depletion in the subretinal compartment (Jadeja et al., 2018; Terao et al., 2024).

Collectively, in an RPE assay aligned to dry AMD pathophysiology, NMN is expected to: (1) restore NAD⁺ and ATP; (2) engage Sirt1/Sirt3 and normalize mitochondrial function; (3) reduce senescence and inflammatory signaling; and (4) enhance POS phagocytosis via cytoskeletal machinery, with plausible but unproven enhancement of lysosomal biogenesis/function via Sirt1/AMPK-mediated autophagy pathways and TFEB cross-talk (Will‐Orrego, 2020b; Jadeja et al., 2018; Ren et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2025; Luján et al., 2022).

Assay design notes  
- Use ARPE‐19 and primary human RPE including AMD donor–derived cultures for translational relevance; confirm NMN uptake advantages versus NR in each model (Will‐Orrego, 2020b; Ebeling et al., 2020).  
- Quantify NAD⁺ by enzymatic assay, SIRT1 activity fluorometrically, mitochondrial ATP production via Seahorse ATP rate assay, and senescence markers (SA‐β‐gal, p16, p21) per established protocols (Jadeja et al., 2018; Will‐Orrego, 2020b).  
- Test TFEB nuclear translocation (immunocytochemistry), lysosomal mass (LAMP1/2), acidification (LysoSensor/LysoTracker), and cathepsin D maturation/activity explicitly, recognizing these endpoints are not yet shown for NMN in RPE (Falcão et al., 2025).  
- Assay mitophagy flux (mKeima‐mito), PINK1/Parkin expression, and autophagosome–lysosome fusion (LC3‐II, p62, Rab7 localization) (Fisher et al., 2022; Luján et al., 2022).  
- Measure RPE phagocytosis of POS and handling of phototoxic bisretinoids/lipofuscin surrogates to capture clearance outcomes (Zhang et al., 2024).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Strong disease‐mechanism alignment. Dry AMD is characterized by RPE mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, impaired autophagy/lysosomal clearance, and chronic para‐inflammation; age‐associated NAD⁺ decline in RPE and retina connects this pathobiology to a targetable metabolic axis (NAMPT/NAD⁺), and restoring NAD⁺ is causally protective in multiple retinal models (Jadeja et al., 2018; Cimaglia et al., 2020; Lin, 2020). In vitro and in vivo, NMN replenishes NAD⁺ in RPE and retina, rescues SIRT1 and mitochondrial function, and reduces senescence and inflammation—key drivers of RPE failure in dry AMD (Jadeja et al., 2018; Ren et al., 2022; Chen et al., 2020).  
- Direct RPE benefits with functional readouts. Under NAMPT inhibition and oxidant stress, NMN restores NAD⁺/ATP, normalizes OXPHOS/glycolysis, rescues RPE gene expression, lowers ROS and DNA damage, and blunts senescence markers; in RCS rats, NMN enhances RPE POS phagocytosis through a NAD⁺/GAPDH-actin axis (Will‐Orrego, 2020c; Ren et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2024).  
- Reversal of senescence-driven dry AMD phenotypes in vivo. In the Abca1/g1 model where subretinal macrophage senescence drives SDDs and RPE dysfunction, NAD⁺ augmentation by NMN reduces SDDs, lipofuscin‐positive macrophages, and functional/structural pathology, demonstrating disease‐relevant efficacy in a model that captures hallmark dry AMD features (Terao et al., 2024).  
- Mechanistic tractability and biomarkerability. The NAMPT/NMN → NAD⁺ → sirtuin/AMPK network is well studied and offers clear pharmacodynamic biomarkers (NAD⁺ levels, SIRT1 activity, mitochondrial respiration) and pathophysiological readouts (senescence markers, mitophagy flux), supporting a high‐confidence translational path (Jadeja et al., 2018; Luján et al., 2022; Ebeling et al., 2020).  
- RPE uptake feasibility. ARPE‐19 transport NMN but not NR, favoring NMN for in vitro RPE work; broader literature identifies NMN transport and NR conversion pathways that together ensure NMN bioavailability in ocular cell types (Will‐Orrego, 2020b, 2020a).

Limitations and risks  
- TFEB/lysosome claims remain unproven for NMN in RPE. While TFEB‐driven lysosomal biogenesis/function is a compelling therapeutic target in dry AMD, direct evidence that NMN activates TFEB, increases lysosomal number/acidification, or enhances cathepsin D activity in RPE is not present in the provided literature; these are critical, testable hypotheses that should not be presupposed in development plans (Falcão et al., 2025; Will‐Orrego, 2020a; Ebeling et al., 2020; Cimaglia et al., 2020).  
- Context‐dependent AMPK/Sirt1 dynamics. In NaIO₃‐induced RPE senescence, AMPK activation accompanied ATP loss and was suppressed upon NMN treatment; further, pharmacologic Sirt1 overactivation caused mitochondrial hyperfusion and stress signaling, underscoring that pathway set points matter and that NMN’s benefits likely hinge on physiologic tuning rather than maximal activation (Ren et al., 2022). This complexity argues for careful titration of NMN exposure and for avoiding assumptions about AMPK activation being uniformly beneficial in all RPE contexts.  
- Model caveats. ARPE‐19 harbor genomic abnormalities and do not recapitulate all RPE functions (e.g., missing RPE65), and media composition strongly modulates metabolic readouts; corroboration in primary human RPE (including AMD donors) and in vivo models is essential (Will‐Orrego, 2020c; Will‐Orrego, 2020b; Ebeling et al., 2020).  
- Target competition with NAD⁺ sinks. PARPs and CD38 can drain NAD⁺; in photoreceptors and macrophages these sinks materially influence disease, suggesting that combining NMN with PARP/CD38 modulation may be superior to NMN alone in some settings, and that patient subgroups with high NAD⁺ consumption (e.g., inflammatory phenotypes) may require tailored strategies (Lin & Apte, 2018; Terao et al., 2024).  
- Translation and clinical data gaps. Although nicotinamide and NR have human safety/PK data, direct human ocular PK/PD and safety data for NMN are limited here, and no clinical testing in dry AMD is documented in the provided sources (Cimaglia et al., 2020; Rahman et al., 2024). Dosing translation must reconcile effective rodent exposures (150–1,000 mg/kg/day in various models) with human tolerability and ocular exposure (Lin, 2020; Chen et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2024).

Program implications and next steps  
- Mechanistic validation in RPE. Prioritize experiments that directly test the unproven parts of the hypothesis: TFEB activation (nuclear translocation), lysosomal biogenesis (LAMP1/2), acidification (LysoSensor), and cathepsin D maturation/activity after NMN in primary human RPE from AMD and non‐AMD donors, and in iPSC‐RPE, with parallel readouts of NAD⁺, SIRT1, SIRT3, and AMPK (Falcão et al., 2025; Ebeling et al., 2020).  
- Mitochondria–lysosome crosstalk. Quantify mitophagy flux (mKeima‐mito), autophagosome–lysosome fusion (Rab7 co‐localization), and PINK1/Parkin dynamics under NMN, leveraging assays already applied in AMD donor RPE studies (Fisher et al., 2022; Luján et al., 2022).  
- Functional clearance endpoints. Test NMN effects on RPE POS phagocytosis, lipofuscin/bisretinoid handling, and oxidative debris clearance in vitro and in vivo, building on the strong RCS rat evidence for NMN‐mediated enhancement of RPE phagocytosis via a GAPDH‐actin mechanism (Zhang et al., 2024).  
- Inflammation and senescence. Extend evaluation to subretinal macrophage phenotypes and SASP factors in RPE–macrophage co‐culture and in vivo, given NMN’s ability to eliminate senescent macrophages and reverse SDDs in the Abca1/g1 model (Terao et al., 2024).  
- Dosing/PD strategy. Calibrate NMN dose–response carefully: in ARPE‐19 and primary RPE, co‐treatment with 0.05–1.0 mM NMN rescued FK866‐induced NAD⁺ loss within 72 h, while NMN alone did not elevate ATP above baseline; in NaIO₃ ARPE‐19, 800–1,000 µM was required to adequately restore NAD⁺ (Jadeja et al., 2018; Will‐Orrego, 2020b; Ren et al., 2022). In vivo, effective rodent doses ranged from 150 mg/kg i.p. to 1,000 mg/kg oral depending on model and endpoint (Lin, 2020; Zhang et al., 2024). Engage PK/PD modeling to bridge to human‐equivalent dosing and to support ocular exposure.  
- Combination hypotheses. Consider rational combinations with PARP inhibition (to reduce NAD⁺ consumption) or CD38 inhibition in inflammatory phenotypes, consistent with partial rescue by PARP inhibitors in NAMPT‐deficient contexts and CD38’s role in macrophage senescence (Lin & Apte, 2018; Terao et al., 2024). Also consider pairing with agents that more directly activate TFEB where justified, while monitoring for unintended mTORC1 perturbations (Falcão et al., 2025).

Conclusion  
NMN is a biologically credible and mechanistically tractable candidate for dry AMD focused on RPE rescue through NAD⁺ repletion and sirtuin‐centric mitochondrial restoration, with strong preclinical support in RPE senescence, oxidant injury, and phagocytosis assays, and compelling in vivo evidence in retinal injury and senescence‐driven dry‐AMD–like pathology (Jadeja et al., 2018; Ren et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2024; Terao et al., 2024). The hypothesized downstream impacts on TFEB, lysosomal biogenesis, acidification, and cathepsin D activity are plausible given the Sirt1/AMPK/autophagy network architecture but remain unvalidated in RPE after NMN and should be explicitly de‐risked experimentally before clinical translation (Falcão et al., 2025; Luján et al., 2022; Ebeling et al., 2020). Strengths include a coherent disease‐mechanism target, measurable PD, multi‐compartment benefits (RPE, photoreceptors, subretinal macrophages), and favorable uptake in RPE models; weaknesses include reliance on models with limitations, the need to control for NAD⁺ sinks and pathway set points, and gaps in lysosome‐specific mechanistic evidence and human ocular PK/PD (Will‐Orrego, 2020b, 2020c; Lin & Apte, 2018; Rahman et al., 2024). Overall, NMN merits advancement to a rigorous preclinical validation package focused on lysosome‐mitophagy endpoints in primary human RPE and AMD‐relevant in vivo models, with a translational plan that integrates mitochondrial function, senescence/inflammation control, and debris clearance readouts as co‐primary pharmacology objectives (Ebeling et al., 2020; Fisher et al., 2022; Terao et al., 2024).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Eculizumab (Soliris, Alexion) is a humanized IgG monoclonal antibody derived from the murine anti–human C5 antibody m5G1 via CDR grafting and human framework engineering to reduce immunogenicity and extend serum half-life, designed to bind complement component C5 with high affinity and sterically prevent its cleavage by C5 convertases into C5a and C5b (thereby blocking terminal pathway activation and MAC assembly) (Park et al., 2019; Troutbeck et al., 2012; Yehoshua et al., 2014; Park et al., 2021). It belongs to the class of complement inhibitors that directly target an effector protein (C5) at the convergence of the classical, lectin, and alternative pathways, in contrast to upstream amplification-targeting agents (e.g., C3 or factor D inhibitors) (Park et al., 2019; Tzoumas et al., 2023). Systemically administered eculizumab has established clinical utility in complement-mediated hematologic and renal disorders, including paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria and atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome, and more recently generalized myasthenia gravis, reflecting a mature pharmacology and a well-characterized risk profile centered on increased susceptibility to encapsulated organisms (notably meningococcal infection) due to terminal pathway blockade (Park et al., 2019; Yehoshua et al., 2014).

Within ophthalmology, the terminal complement pathway is an attractive target for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) and geographic atrophy (GA) because C5a is a proinflammatory anaphylatoxin detected in drusen that can drive leukocyte recruitment and VEGF induction in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), and C5b nucleates formation of the membrane attack complex (MAC, C5b–C9), which accumulates with age and AMD in Bruch’s membrane and choriocapillaris and can lyse or sub-lytically activate choroidal endothelial and RPE cells (Kassa et al., 2019). The class of C5 inhibitors therefore aims to reduce both inflammatory signaling (via C5a) and cytolytic/proinflammatory MAC effects while preserving upstream opsonization and some host-defense functions mediated by C3b, potentially retaining aspects of immune competence relative to C3 inhibition (Halawa et al., 2021; Park et al., 2019).

Therapeutic History  
Approved indications and systemic pharmacology  
Eculizumab is FDA/EMA approved for paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria and atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome, where weight-based intravenous regimens achieve sustained trough serum concentrations and complete inhibition of hemolytic activity by blocking C5 cleavage; these regimens produce serum levels > 35 μg/mL and complete systemic C5 functional blockade, but require meningococcal vaccination to mitigate Neisseria risk inherent to terminal complement inhibition (Park et al., 2019; Yehoshua et al., 2014). In other complementopathies, clinical experience has highlighted a mechanism-consequent shift of pathology upstream (e.g., C3-loading and extravascular hemolysis in PNH under C5 blockade), underscoring that C5 inhibition leaves C3 activation intact (Hammadi et al., 2023).

Clinical investigation in geographic atrophy of dry AMD  
Eculizumab was investigated in the prospective, randomized, double-masked, single-center Phase 2 COMPLETE study that enrolled 30 participants with GA (primary cohort) plus an intermediate AMD/drusen cohort, randomized 2:1 to intravenous eculizumab versus saline over 24 weeks (with follow-up to 52 weeks) (Yehoshua et al., 2014). Two dosing regimens were tested: a low-dose arm (600 mg weekly × 4, then 900 mg every 2 weeks through week 24) and a high-dose arm with higher induction and maintenance dosing; all patients received meningococcal vaccination prior to first infusion (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Patel et al., 2022). Pharmacokinetically, systemic exposure and target engagement were confirmed: eculizumab concentrations were measurable at all assessed time points (mean ~ 65–189 μg/mL in low-dose and ~ 122–259 μg/mL in high-dose cohorts), with plasma C5 activity reduced to < 9% by week 1 and < 1% by week 2, indicating complete systemic terminal complement blockade sustained through treatment (Yehoshua et al., 2014).

Despite robust systemic pharmacodynamics, COMPLETE detected no effect on GA progression: at 26 weeks the change in square-root–transformed GA area was 0.19 ± 0.12 mm in eculizumab-treated eyes versus 0.18 ± 0.15 mm with placebo (P = 0.96), and at 52 weeks both arms exhibited ~ 0.37 mm enlargement (P ≈ 0.93), effectively excluding a large treatment effect (> 55% slowing) in this cohort (Yehoshua et al., 2014). Drusen volume endpoints in the intermediate AMD cohort were also negative (no participant achieved a 50% reduction), and fellow-eye analyses mirrored primary-eye results (Patel et al., 2022; Yehoshua et al., 2014). Visual function showed no durable benefit: a 26-week letter gain difference favoring eculizumab was attributed to a single outlier in placebo, and by 52 weeks there was no between-group difference; pooled estimates across small RCTs rated the certainty of BCVA effects as low-to-very-low with confidence intervals overlapping no effect (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Tzoumas et al., 2023). Safety was acceptable in the trial: no drug-related serious adverse events were identified through 52 weeks, and no eyes converted to neovascular AMD during the study; however, systemic C5 blockade requires vaccination and vigilance for meningococcal infection, and an independent systemic anti-C5 AMD trial was terminated early due to uncertainty about risk/benefit in light of reported meningococcal infections in real-world eculizumab users (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Tzoumas et al., 2023).

Interpretations from COMPLETE and subsequent reviews point to several plausible explanations for the null result: inadequate intraocular/RPE target engagement with systemic dosing due to blood–retinal and Bruch’s barriers; the possibility that C5 is the wrong target in GA given genetic associations that more strongly implicate proximal complement components (e.g., C3, CFH) rather than terminal pathway constituents; the short on-treatment window (24 weeks) and small sample size; and the biological reality that C5 inhibition preserves upstream C3a/C3b biology, which may continue to drive pathology (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Halawa et al., 2021; Hammadi et al., 2023; Tzoumas et al., 2023).

Comparative C5 and complement-targeting experience in AMD  
Intravitreal C5 inhibition has produced divergent results. LFG316 (tesidolumab), an anti-C5 monoclonal antibody administered intravitreally, failed to alter GA lesion growth or visual outcomes in a randomized phase 2 trial (Halawa et al., 2021; Park et al., 2019). By contrast, avacincaptad pegol (Zimura), an intravitreal C5 aptamer, reduced GA growth rates by approximately 27–30% over 12–18 months in pivotal trials, leading to FDA approval, although potential increased risk of macular neovascularization has been signaled and requires ongoing pharmacovigilance (Patel et al., 2022; Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023; Tzoumas et al., 2023). Upstream targeting at C3 with intravitreal pegcetacoplan (SYFOVRE) significantly slowed GA enlargement in phase 2–3 programs and achieved regulatory approval, but at the cost of increased rates of conversion to exudative AMD and, in the postmarketing setting, reports of occlusive retinal vasculitis, highlighting a target-dependent safety trade-off between efficacy and pro-angiogenic/immune-privilege perturbation risks (Halawa et al., 2021; Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023; Qin et al., 2024). Alternative-pathway inhibition via factor D (lampalizumab) produced a phase 2 signal but failed in two phase 3 trials, suggesting that partial pathway blockade may be insufficient in GA (Piri & Kaplan, 2023; Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023).

Taken together, these data place systemic eculizumab among C5-directed strategies where local delivery has demonstrated anatomic efficacy in GA, whereas systemic delivery has not, and they highlight that complement modulation can slow atrophy progression without improving visual function and may introduce target- and route-specific risks such as neovascularization or serious infection (Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023; Tzoumas et al., 2023).

Mechanism of Action  
Complement cascade biology and eculizumab target engagement  
Complement activation arises via classical, lectin, and alternative pathways, converging at the generation of C3 convertases that cleave C3 into C3a (anaphylatoxin) and C3b (opsonin/convertase component), with amplification by the alternative pathway accounting for the majority (80–90%) of downstream MAC generation in physiologic and pathologic settings (Tzoumas et al., 2023). C5 convertases (C4b2a3b for classical/lectin and C3bBbC3b for alternative pathway) cleave C5 into C5a, a potent anaphylatoxin that recruits/activates myeloid cells and stimulates RPE to produce VEGF and proinflammatory cytokines, and C5b, which seeds assembly of the terminal membrane attack complex (C5b–C9) on nearby membranes (Tzoumas et al., 2023; Kassa et al., 2019). Eculizumab binds C5 to prevent convertase-mediated cleavage, thereby abrogating both C5a generation and MAC formation independent of the initiating pathway; this preserves upstream C3 activation (C3a/C3b) and the alternative-pathway amplification loop while blunting terminal effector functions (Park et al., 2019; Halawa et al., 2021).

Ocular and RPE relevance of C5 and MAC  
Multiple lines of evidence implicate terminal pathway effectors in AMD pathophysiology at the RPE–choriocapillaris interface. Histopathology shows increasing MAC deposition with aging and AMD in Bruch’s membrane and the choriocapillaris; sub-lytic MAC on choroidal endothelial cells triggers pro-angiogenic/proteolytic responses (VEGF, MMPs), while high-level deposition can induce lysis of choroidal endothelial cells and bystander injury contributing to RPE atrophy (Kassa et al., 2019). C5a is present in drusen and is a strong inflammatory mediator that can recruit immune cells and induce VEGF release from RPE, linking terminal pathway activation to both atrophic and neovascular processes relevant to the AMD spectrum (Kassa et al., 2019). Additional experimental work demonstrates that sub-lytic C5b-9 can alter RPE function in ways consistent with AMD, including stress responses and secretory changes, reinforcing that terminal complement activation can be injurious to the RPE even in the absence of frank lysis (Park et al., 2019).

Complement production and regulation in the eye—and systemic versus local contributions  
Complement proteins are synthesized predominantly by the liver and circulate systemically, but they are also produced locally within ocular tissues (retina, RPE, choroid), with local activation and regulation shaped by cell-intrinsic complement regulatory proteins (e.g., CFH, CD46, CD59) and by oxidative stress effects that reduce cell-surface complement inhibition on RPE (Tzoumas et al., 2023; van Lookeren Campagne et al., 2016). Several studies highlight local complement expression and activation in retinal cells and macrophages, as well as increased local complement turnover preceding clinical disease, supporting the concept of an ocular complement “microenvironment” that can be dysregulated independent of systemic levels (Patel et al., 2022; Piri & Kaplan, 2023). Conversely, transcriptomic mapping suggests that posterior-pole tissues have limited local transcription of lectin and terminal pathway components (except C5 and C7), implying reliance on systemic sources for some terminal pathway proteins, which in principle could make systemic C5 blockade effective if sufficient intraocular penetration and target engagement are achieved (Troutbeck et al., 2012). These seemingly conflicting observations are reconciled by recognizing that both local production and systemic supply contribute to ocular complement biology, and that their relative importance likely varies by compartment (RPE, choriocapillaris, sub-RPE space), disease stage, and barrier integrity.

Genetic and biomarker context for C5 targeting in AMD  
GWAS and biomarker studies have repeatedly implicated complement dysregulation in AMD susceptibility and progression, including associations at CFH, C3, C2/CFB, CFI, and C9 loci, and elevated systemic and ocular concentrations of complement activation products (C3a, C5a, MAC) in AMD patients (Dascalu et al., 2024). However, the genetic signal is stronger and more consistent for proximal regulators (e.g., CFH, C3) than for C5, and at least one analysis noted C3 risk alleles do not necessarily correlate with GA progression (and in some contexts associated with decreased progression), emphasizing the complexity of translating susceptibility signals to progression biology and target selection in late AMD (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Halawa et al., 2021). Mechanistically, C5 blockade leaves upstream C3a/C3b biology intact; in extra-ocular diseases this can unmask C3-related pathophysiology under C5 inhibition, illustrating a general limitation of terminal pathway-only targeting (Hammadi et al., 2023). In GA, this implies that C3a/C3b-driven processes—chemoattraction, opsonization, and immune modulation—could continue in the outer retina/RPE even under complete C5 suppression, potentially blunting the benefit of C5-only therapy (Halawa et al., 2021; Tzoumas et al., 2023).

Therapeutic delivery constraints to ocular complement modulation with systemic C5 blockade  
Large biologics such as eculizumab face formidable physical barriers to ocular penetration, including the inner and outer blood–retina barriers and Bruch’s membrane/RPE tight junctions, whose permeability declines with increasing molecular weight and hydrophilicity (a profile characteristic of IgG antibodies), making intraocular access by systemic dosing uncertain without active transport mechanisms (Hammadi et al., 2023; Yehoshua et al., 2014). This is the most straightforward explanation for COMPLETE’s combination of complete systemic pharmacodynamic suppression with no effect on lesion enlargement: the effective intraocular concentration of antibody at relevant RPE–choroid interfaces was likely insufficient to inhibit terminal complement activation locally, a conclusion echoed by the trial investigators (Yehoshua et al., 2014).

Expected Effect  
Proposed pharmacologic and cellular effect  
Under the working hypothesis, systemic eculizumab would reduce MAC formation on RPE and choroidal endothelial surfaces and diminish C5a-driven inflammatory signaling, thereby protecting RPE cellular homeostasis and the RPE–choriocapillaris unit from complement-mediated injury and slowing expansion of GA lesions (Kassa et al., 2019; Park et al., 2019). Mechanistically, suppression of MAC would be expected to decrease lytic and sub-lytic injury to choroidal endothelial cells and RPE, attenuating downstream induction of VEGF and MMPs, and limiting bystander tissue damage around atrophic borders where complement activation is thought to be active (Tzoumas et al., 2023; Kassa et al., 2019). Reducing C5a generation could blunt recruitment and activation of myeloid cells and RPE proinflammatory cytokine production, decreasing local inflammatory amplification in the outer retina (Tzoumas et al., 2023; Kassa et al., 2019).

Expression and target presence in relevant cells/tissues  
C5 and terminal pathway components are present in the ocular compartments relevant to GA pathobiology: choriocapillaris/Bruch’s membrane deposition of MAC is well documented and increases with age and AMD, and C5a is detected within drusen; RPE-derived complement regulators (e.g., CD59) and choroidal endothelial susceptibility to MAC are described, establishing both target and downstream effectors within the disease-relevant tissues (Kassa et al., 2019). Complement components and regulators are expressed in retina, RPE, and choroid, with transcriptomic data indicating relatively higher choroidal expression and limited local transcription of some terminal components (except C5 and C7), consistent with both local and systemic sources contributing substrate for terminal pathway assembly (Troutbeck et al., 2012; Tzoumas et al., 2023).

Translational and clinical outcome expectations  
At the disease level, a therapy that meaningfully reduces local terminal complement activation in GA should slow the rate of GA lesion enlargement measured on fundus autofluorescence (FAF) and/or SD-OCT, endpoints accepted by the FDA/NEI and standard across GA trials; functional outcomes such as BCVA and low-luminance VA typically lag structural changes and may not improve even when lesion growth is slowed (Dascalu et al., 2024; Qin et al., 2024). In COMPLETE, these endpoints were precisely those evaluated; the absence of any measurable effect on square-root GA area at 26 and 52 weeks indicates that, at the tested systemic dosing regimens, eculizumab did not achieve sufficient intraocular target engagement to translate the mechanistic rationale into clinical benefit (Yehoshua et al., 2014).

Reasons for divergence between expected and observed effects  
Three non-exclusive explanations align with the totality of evidence:

  • Inadequate intraocular bioavailability from systemic dosing. Antibody size and hydrophilicity, combined with blood–retina and RPE–Bruch’s barriers, likely prevented sufficient drug from reaching the RPE–choriocapillaris compartment to inhibit local terminal pathway activation, despite verified systemic C5 suppression (Hammadi et al., 2023; Yehoshua et al., 2014; Tzoumas et al., 2023).

  • Target selection may be suboptimal for GA biology. The stronger genetic and pathophysiologic evidence for proximal complement dysregulation (e.g., C3, CFH) and the preservation of upstream activation under C5 blockade mean that C5-only inhibition may not adequately suppress the complement-driven processes that sustain GA border expansion, as supported by the comparatively stronger clinical signals with C3 inhibition and mixed-to-positive signals with intravitreal C5 inhibition (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Halawa et al., 2021; Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023).

  • Trial limitations. The COMPLETE cohort was small and on-treatment duration was six months, which may be insufficient to observe smaller effects on GA growth; however, confidence intervals excluded large effects, and lack of any trend over 52 weeks reduces the likelihood that longer dosing would have changed the outcome meaningfully (Yehoshua et al., 2014).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
  • Strong mechanistic rationale for terminal pathway blockade in AMD: C5a is proinflammatory and detected in drusen; MAC accumulates at the RPE–choriocapillaris interface with age/AMD and can injure choroidal endothelium and RPE via lytic and sub-lytic mechanisms, linking C5 effector functions directly to AMD pathophysiology (Kassa et al., 2019). Blocking C5 suppresses both MAC and C5a, targeting inflammatory and cytolytic arms while leaving upstream C3-mediated opsonization intact, an immunologic advantage over C3 blockade (Halawa et al., 2021; Park et al., 2019).

  • Mature systemic pharmacology with demonstrated ability to completely suppress plasma C5 activity at well-tolerated doses, including in AMD patients, making systemic development logistically straightforward and with known requirements (e.g., meningococcal vaccination) (Yehoshua et al., 2014).

  • Practical systemic-delivery advantages: single systemic therapy treats both eyes simultaneously and avoids intravitreal injection–related ocular risks (endophthalmitis, IOP spikes), which have nontrivial incidence in chronic IVT regimens (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Tzoumas et al., 2023).

  • External validation within the class: intravitreal C5 inhibition (avacincaptad pegol) has replicated GA-slowing effects in phase 2/3 programs, supporting the therapeutic value of suppressing terminal pathway activity in the outer retina if adequate local exposure is achieved (Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023).

Limitations  
  • Lack of efficacy in the definitive systemic eculizumab GA study. COMPLETE showed no reduction in GA lesion growth at 26 or 52 weeks despite complete systemic C5 blockade and adequate serum exposure, effectively excluding a large treatment effect and arguing strongly against systemic eculizumab as a viable GA therapy (Yehoshua et al., 2014).

  • Ocular pharmacokinetic barrier. The most parsimonious explanation for the COMPLETE result is inadequate intraocular target engagement from systemic dosing due to the blood–retina/RPE–Bruch’s barriers and the large size/hydrophilicity of IgG, an inherent limitation of systemic antibody delivery to the sub-RPE/choroidal compartment (Hammadi et al., 2023; Yehoshua et al., 2014).

  • Target-level uncertainties. Genetic and biomarker studies more consistently implicate proximal complement dysregulation (CFH/C3) than C5 in AMD susceptibility; moreover, C5 inhibition preserves upstream C3a/C3b activity, which may continue to drive border-zone inflammation and remodeling in GA (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Dascalu et al., 2024; Halawa et al., 2021). Clinical comparisons reinforce this: upstream C3 inhibition has produced larger and more consistent anatomic effects (with important safety trade-offs), whereas anti-C5 trials are split—systemic eculizumab negative; IVT LFG316 negative; IVT avacincaptad positive—pointing to delivery and target–context dependencies (Halawa et al., 2021; Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023).

  • Systemic safety constraints. While COMPLETE itself reported no drug-related serious adverse events over one year, terminal complement blockade carries a class risk of meningococcal infection requiring vaccination and risk mitigation; at least one planned AMD systemic anti-C5 trial was terminated early due to uncertainty regarding the systemic infection risk/benefit in this population (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Tzoumas et al., 2023).

  • Limited translatability of systemic complement activation to local disease control. Although systemic complement activation correlates with AMD and disease stage in several studies, the relative importance of local versus systemic complement sources—and the ability of systemic blockade to suppress complement activity at the RPE–choriocapillaris interface—is unresolved and likely unfavorable for large biologics, reducing the mechanistic plausibility of systemic C5 blockade for GA (Hammadi et al., 2023; Park et al., 2019).

Risk–benefit and competitive landscape assessment  
Eculizumab’s negative randomized, controlled data in GA, in the face of confirmed systemic pharmacodynamics, places a high bar against further systemic development for this indication, a conclusion explicitly drawn by the COMPLETE investigators who noted the linearity of GA growth and lack of signal as making additional systemic investigations with eculizumab unlikely (Yehoshua et al., 2014). In the evolving complement-therapeutic landscape, local (intravitreal) complement inhibitors have achieved regulatory approval (C3 inhibitor pegcetacoplan and C5 aptamer avacincaptad pegol), demonstrating that complement modulation can slow GA progression when adequate ocular exposure is achieved, albeit without functional vision improvement and with target-dependent safety liabilities (e.g., increased conversion to exudative AMD observed particularly with C3 inhibition) (Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023; Qin et al., 2024). Against this backdrop, systemic eculizumab offers no efficacy advantage, carries systemic infection risk and costs, and fails the core requirement of achieving ocular target engagement necessary for GA modification.

Operationally, even if one hypothesized that higher systemic dosing, longer exposure, or patient stratification could rescue efficacy, several facts weigh against that strategy: COMPLETE’s pharmacodynamics confirmed near-complete systemic C5 suppression within two weeks; genetic analyses within the trial found no association between at-risk alleles and GA growth or treatment response; and extended follow-up to a year showed no divergence in growth rates (Yehoshua et al., 2014). Moreover, retinal pharmacokinetics and barrier biology make it unlikely that increasing systemic doses would proportionally increase intraocular concentrations to therapeutic levels without exacerbating systemic risks (Hammadi et al., 2023). In addition, C5 may not be the optimal node for GA progression biology in many patients, given preserved upstream activity and the complex contributions of C3a/C3b, opsonization, and local complement production that may continue to drive border-zone degeneration independent of MAC inhibition (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Halawa et al., 2021; Piri & Kaplan, 2023).

Recommendation  
Based on the aggregate mechanistic, translational, and clinical evidence, eculizumab (systemic C5 inhibition) does not have compelling potential as a repurposed therapy for dry AMD/GA. The drug has a clear and relevant mechanism and an acceptable short-term tolerability profile in older adults, but it fails to slow GA lesion growth in a randomized, controlled trial despite complete systemic target engagement, and there are strong mechanistic and pharmacokinetic reasons to expect insufficient intraocular exposure with systemic delivery (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Hammadi et al., 2023). The therapeutic hypothesis—reducing MAC on RPE/choriocapillaris to preserve tissue integrity and slow atrophy—is supported conceptually and by local C5 inhibition successes; however, achieving that biology in vivo appears to require intraocular delivery or targeting upstream nodes, neither of which is compatible with systemic eculizumab administration (Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023; Halawa et al., 2021).

If complement-targeted strategies remain a program priority, resources should pivot to modalities with demonstrated ocular target engagement and anatomic efficacy (intravitreal C3 or C5 agents) while carefully managing known safety trade-offs (e.g., neovascularization risk), and to biomarker-driven questions (e.g., whether baseline low-luminance visual acuity deficit—correlated with faster GA growth in COMPLETE—can enrich for patients who derive greater anatomic benefit) (Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023; Tzoumas et al., 2023; Yehoshua et al., 2014). For systemic complement modulation in AMD more broadly, alternative targets with better ocular PK profiles (e.g., small-molecule systemic alternative-pathway inhibitors) and rigorous ocular target-engagement measurements would be required to justify late-stage development, but systemic C5 blockade with eculizumab itself should not be advanced further for GA (Hammadi et al., 2023; Tzoumas et al., 2023; Park et al., 2019).

In summary, while the mechanistic logic for terminal complement inhibition in AMD is robust, the totality of evidence argues against systemic eculizumab as a viable candidate to slow GA progression, and the development program should discontinue pursuit of this repurposing in favor of locally delivered complement inhibitors or alternative mechanisms better suited to the ocular compartment and GA pathobiology (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023).
