Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
SB216763 is a synthetic small‐molecule inhibitor originally discovered during GlaxoSmithKline’s dedicated program in developing GSK-3 inhibitors. It belongs to the bisarylmaleimide class of compounds, with its chemical structure based on a pyrrole-2,5-dione core that is further substituted by aryl and indole moieties. In its initial characterization, SB216763 was identified as an ATP-competitive inhibitor of glycogen synthase kinase 3 beta (GSK3β), a central serine/threonine protein kinase implicated in multiple intracellular signaling cascades. The chemical class to which SB216763 belongs – maleimides – has been widely exploited across medicinal chemistry due to their synthetic tractability and ability to serve as potent inhibitors of enzymes, particularly kinases. This group of compounds has previously been used in various preclinical studies targeting neurodegenerative diseases and cell proliferative disorders by modulating cell signaling pathways such as the Wnt/β-catenin cascade, which is ubiquitously expressed in many tissues including the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and the central nervous system (Gianferrara et al., 2022; Ruiz & Eldar-Finkelman, 2022; Alhassan et al., 2025).

Therapeutic History:  
SB216763 has a well-established history in preclinical research, particularly in models of neurodegeneration. Several studies have deployed this compound in rodent models of Alzheimer’s disease, Parkinson’s disease, and other neurological insults to demonstrate its neuroprotective potential. In these models, SB216763 was shown to reduce tau hyperphosphorylation, protect neurons against both β-amyloid-mediated toxicity and radiation-induced apoptosis in hippocampal neurons, and promote beneficial modulation of signaling pathways linked to PI3K–Akt (Gianferrara et al., 2022; Ruiz & Eldar-Finkelman, 2022). Beyond its neuroprotective effects, SB216763 has been applied as a tool compound in cellular studies to activate canonical Wnt signaling through stabilization of beta-catenin by inhibiting GSK3β. Importantly, a radiolabeled derivative, [11C]SB216763, has been developed as a positron emission tomography (PET) probe, which confirmed its ability to cross the blood–brain barrier in rodent and nonhuman primate models, although significant selectivity issues have been noted with respect to off-target kinase inhibition (Gianferrara et al., 2022; Benn & Dawson, 2020). In addition, there is documented evidence of its application in ocular contexts; for instance, in an experimental ischemic retinal neuron model in rats, SB216763 was found to promote DNA repair by upregulating DNA ligase IV transcriptional activity. However, while it has been evaluated extensively in neurological and in vivo rodent models for central nervous system diseases, formal clinical deployment or veterinary studies specifically targeting dry age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD) remain sparse, with no documented clinical trials registered on major platforms dedicated to AMD indications (Gianferrara et al., 2022; Ruiz & Eldar-Finkelman, 2022; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).

Mechanism of Action:  
The primary mechanism of action of SB216763 is centered on its potent inhibition of GSK3β. Under normal physiological conditions, GSK3β is a constitutively active kinase that phosphorylates a wide array of substrates, including beta-catenin, tau, and proteins critical to cellular metabolism and survival. One key substrate relevant to our hypothesis is the transcription factor EB (TFEB), a master regulator of the Coordinated Lysosomal Expression and Regulation (CLEAR) gene network. TFEB’s activity is tightly regulated by its phosphorylation state; when phosphorylated by kinases such as mTORC1 and possibly GSK3β, TFEB binds to cytosolic 14-3-3 proteins and is retained in the cytoplasm. Inhibition of GSK3β by SB216763 has been implicated in the dephosphorylation of TFEB, thereby allowing its translocation to the nucleus where it drives the transcription of CLEAR network genes. These genes are essential for lysosomal biogenesis, autophagic flux, and the expression of lysosomal proteases such as cathepsin D (Gianferrara et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2023). Detailed molecular studies in neuronal stem cells and N2a cells have demonstrated that SB216763 can inactivate GSK3β and thereby stimulate the nuclear accumulation of TFEB. In addition, the compound’s ATP-competitive mode of inhibition suggests it directly competes with ATP in the GSK3β active site, leading to rapid modulation of downstream substrates implicated in metabolic and autophagic processes (Gianferrara et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2023; Djajadikerta et al., 2020). From a biochemical standpoint, SB216763’s action not only stabilizes beta-catenin – thereby modulating Wnt signaling – but also appears to influence key regulatory nodes in autophagy. Activation of TFEB results in upregulation of lysosomal proteins, enhancement of lysosomal acidification via increased expression of components like the vacuolar-type ATPase (V-ATPase), and improved cathepsin D maturation and activity, all of which collectively promote the efficient clearance of intracellular aggregates and damaged organelles (Gianferrara et al., 2022; Ruiz & Eldar-Finkelman, 2022; Pan & Valapala, 2022).

Expected Effect in Dry AMD Context:  
The central hypothesis behind repurposing SB216763 for dry AMD rests on its ability to correct the cellular deficits observed in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) associated with aging and disease. Dry AMD is characterized by the accumulation of lipofuscin and other aggregate-prone materials within the RPE, coupled with impaired autophagic and lysosomal clearance mechanisms. The proposed pharmacological intervention with SB216763 is expected to inhibit GSK3β in RPE cells, leading to dephosphorylation and nuclear translocation of TFEB. Once in the nucleus, TFEB can activate the CLEAR network, thereby augmenting lysosome biogenesis and catalytic function. Enhanced lysosomal acidification, as mediated by the V-ATPase and corroborated by increased expression of lysosomal enzymes such as cathepsin D, should facilitate the degradation of accumulated lipofuscin, oxidized proteins, and lipid aggregates. In preclinical RPE models under oxidative stress, similar pharmacological modulation of TFEB (for example, via trehalose treatment or genetic induction) has been shown to improve lysosomal function and reduce the burden of autofluorescent granules analogous to lipofuscin (Falcão et al., 2025; Falcão et al., 2024). Therefore, SB216763 is hypothesized to recapitulate these beneficial effects by leveraging its upstream modulation of GSK3β. Given that RPE cells naturally express both GSK3β and TFEB, and considering the documented mechanistic role of GSK3β in regulating TFEB nucleo-cytoplasmic shuttling, the expected outcome is an enhancement of autophagic clearance and restoration of RPE homeostasis. This would theoretically slow or potentially reverse early degenerative changes in dry AMD by mitigating the cytotoxic accumulation of undegraded material (Gianferrara et al., 2022; Ruiz & Eldar-Finkelman, 2022; Yang et al., 2023).

Overall Evaluation:  
SB216763 exhibits several promising attributes as a candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry AMD. One major strength lies in its well-characterized and potent inhibition of GSK3β – a kinase that plays a central role in various signaling pathways implicated in both neurodegeneration and retinal pathology. The mechanistic rationale is underpinned by evidence that GSK3β inhibition facilitates the nuclear translocation of TFEB, the master regulator of lysosomal function. Through activation of TFEB, SB216763 can potentially stimulate the expression of the CLEAR gene network, leading to heightened lysosomal acidification and increased cathepsin D activity. These molecular events are directly relevant to mitigating the defective autophagic clearance that is a hallmark of dry AMD, and they align well with preclinical observations in other cell types where TFEB activation has been associated with improved degradation of accumulated toxic material (Gianferrara et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2023; Djajadikerta et al., 2020).

Further strengths include the extensive use of SB216763 in various preclinical models of neurodegeneration, wherein its ability to modulate key pathways such as beta-catenin/Wnt signaling has been repeatedly demonstrated. Its blood–brain barrier penetrance, as seen in rodent and nonhuman primate studies involving a radiolabeled derivative, suggests favorable pharmacokinetics that might also translate to ocular tissues with appropriate formulation strategies. The documented ocular application in rodent ischemic retinal neuron models – where SB216763 was shown to upregulate DNA repair mechanisms – provides additional indirect support for its potential in the ocular setting (Gianferrara et al., 2022).

Notwithstanding these promising aspects, there are notable weaknesses and gaps in the literature that warrant cautious interpretation. First, while preclinical evidence in neural and other cellular models supports the concept that GSK3β inhibition can drive TFEB-dependent transcriptional activation, direct evidence of SB216763’s efficacy in RPE cells under conditions of oxidative stress or in established dry AMD models is sparse. There is a lack of comprehensive studies that definitively link SB216763 treatment in RPE cells to enhanced lysosomal acidification, increased cathepsin D activity, and consequent reduction in lipofuscin accumulation. For example, while related studies using trehalose or mTOR inhibitors have shown clear benefits on TFEB activation and autophagic clearance in RPE models (Falcão et al., 2025; Falcão et al., 2024), SB216763-specific data in this context remain limited. 

Furthermore, concerns regarding kinase selectivity must be acknowledged. SB216763, being an ATP-competitive inhibitor, may exhibit off-target effects by inhibiting structurally related kinases, as indicated by the limited selectivity noted in studies involving its radiolabeled derivative [11C]SB216763 (Gianferrara et al., 2022; Benn & Dawson, 2020; Pan & Valapala, 2021). Off-target kinase inhibition could potentially disrupt other essential signaling pathways in the RPE and might lead to unforeseen adverse events upon clinical translation. This issue of specificity is particularly important in the context of chronic diseases like dry AMD, where long-term safety is paramount. 

Additionally, while its use in central nervous system models is encouraging, dry AMD pathophysiology has distinct features that may not be fully addressed by a therapeutic designed for neurodegeneration. The multifactorial etiology of dry AMD, which encompasses oxidative stress, chronic inflammation, and impaired autophagic degradation specific to the high metabolic and phagocytic demands of RPE cells, underscores the need for targeted evidence that SB216763 exerts its effects in these specialized cells. Moreover, the absence of any registered clinical trials on major platforms for SB216763 in the AMD space (as revealed by comprehensive searches on ClinicalTrials.gov) suggests that the translational path for this compound remains uncharted in the context of retinal disease (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.; Ruiz & Eldar-Finkelman, 2022).

Another consideration is the potential for conflicting actions of GSK3β inhibition. While inhibiting GSK3β does promote TFEB activation and lysosomal biogenesis, GSK3β also phosphorylates other substrates that could have deleterious effects if dysregulated in the RPE. For example, uncontrolled activation of the Wnt/β-catenin pathway may have proliferative effects or contribute to unwanted cell signaling changes. Thus, a delicate balance must be maintained in modulating GSK3β activity to elicit the desired autophagic responses without incurring off-target toxicity.

From a developmental perspective, the availability of SB216763 as a commercially sourced compound (Sigma S3442) is an advantage. Its established synthesis, reproducibility, and well-documented use in numerous preclinical studies allow for rapid deployment in early-stage in vitro and in vivo assays. However, the lack of formulation studies specifically for ocular delivery, and potential challenges in achieving therapeutic concentrations in the retina while minimizing systemic exposure, remain hurdles to overcome in advancing SB216763 as an AMD therapy.

In summary, SB216763 is a compelling candidate from a mechanistic standpoint, with a robust preclinical pedigree as a GSK3β inhibitor that can modulate TFEB and downstream lysosomal functions. Its synthetic origin as a bisarylmaleimide and proven in vitro potency provide a strong rationale for its repurposing. The proposed mechanism—wherein inhibition of GSK3β leads to enhanced nuclear localization of TFEB, activation of CLEAR genes, improved lysosomal acidification, and increased cathepsin D activity—directly addresses key pathogenic features of dry AMD, including the accumulation of lipofuscin and defective autophagy in RPE cells. This mechanistic alignment, supported by studies across neurodegenerative disease models and early ocular research, indicates that SB216763 has the potential to restore defective autophagic clearance in the RPE and slow AMD progression (Gianferrara et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2023; Djajadikerta et al., 2020).

Nonetheless, the overall success of SB216763 in the context of dry AMD will depend on addressing several critical issues. First, direct experimental validation in RPE cells exposed to oxidative stress is needed to confirm that SB216763 can indeed induce TFEB nuclear translocation and activate the CLEAR network in this specific cell type. Second, detailed pharmacokinetic and safety studies tailored for ocular administration are essential to determine whether the compound can reach effective concentrations in the retina without eliciting systemic toxicity or off-target kinase inhibition. Third, comprehensive in vivo studies in relevant animal models of dry AMD must be conducted to assess whether the biochemical improvements (e.g., enhanced lysosomal acidification and cathepsin D activity) translate into clinically meaningful outcomes, such as reduction in lipofuscin accumulation and preservation of RPE morphology and function.

Finally, while the theoretical framework is strong, the translational gap remains significant. The absence of clinical trials or robust preclinical data directly linking SB216763 to improvements in dry AMD phenotypes suggests that careful, incremental studies are required. These studies should ideally include dose–response evaluations, biomarker analyses of autophagic flux, and long-term safety assessments to establish the therapeutic window for SB216763 in the context of retinal disease (Ruiz & Eldar-Finkelman, 2022; Gianferrara et al., 2022; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).

Overall, SB216763 represents a promising mechanistic candidate whose ability to modulate GSK3β and, consequently, regulate TFEB activity offers a novel angle for addressing the autophagic deficits observed in dry AMD. Its well-defined synthetic origin, established preclinical usage in neurodegeneration, and documented biochemical effects in activating lysosomal and autophagic pathways suggest that it could, in principle, improve RPE function through enhanced clearance of toxic intracellular aggregates. However, the limitations regarding its selectivity, the need for targeted ocular studies, and the paucity of direct evidence in AMD models require that further rigorous investigations be conducted. A stepwise preclinical evaluation, starting with in vitro RPE models and advancing to in vivo AMD models, would be necessary to validate its efficacy and safety profile before considering clinical translation. In this regard, SB216763 should be advanced as a high-priority candidate for additional mechanistic studies and exploratory preclinical evaluations, albeit with cautious optimism given the potential for off-target effects and formulation challenges (Gianferrara et al., 2022; Ruiz & Eldar-Finkelman, 2022; Yang et al., 2023; Djajadikerta et al., 2020; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).

In conclusion, while SB216763 offers a robust mechanistic rationale for its repurposing in dry AMD based on its known capacity to inhibit GSK3β, promote TFEB-mediated lysosomal biogenesis, and potentially enhance autophagic clearance, careful attention must be paid to validating these effects directly in RPE cells under oxidative stress. The strengths of its preclinical performance and synthetic availability must be balanced against the challenges of kinase selectivity, ocular pharmacokinetics, and the absence of direct AMD-specific data. A systematic, comprehensive series of studies is warranted to firmly establish whether SB216763 can serve as a viable therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. The outcomes of these studies will significantly influence the strategic direction of the drug development program and may open the door to novel, mechanism-based interventions for a disease with substantial unmet clinical need (Gianferrara et al., 2022; Ruiz & Eldar-Finkelman, 2022; Yang et al., 2023; Djajadikerta et al., 2020; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Recombinant human pro-cathepsin D (rhCTSD), as exemplified by R&D Systems product 1869-CD, is a bioengineered form of a naturally occurring lysosomal aspartyl protease that is synthesized as an inactive precursor (pro-cathepsin D) (Sharif, 2015, pp. 60–64). This therapeutic candidate belongs to the enzyme replacement therapy (ERT) class, a category of biotherapeutics developed to supplement or correct deficient lysosomal enzymes in various disorders. The natural cathepsin D enzyme is normally produced and processed intracellularly through the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and Golgi apparatus, undergoing critical post-translational modifications—including the removal of the N-terminal signal peptide, glycosylation, and addition of a mannose-6-phosphate (M6P) tag—that are essential for its subsequent targeting to the lysosome (Sharif, 2015, pp. 60–64). The recombinant version is produced under conditions aimed at ensuring high purity and biological activity conforming to GMP standards, thus making it an attractive candidate for repurposing in conditions where lysosomal proteolytic capacity is compromised. The candidate has been designed in the context of neurodegenerative and lysosomal storage disorders, where enzyme supplementation has been shown to restore proteolytic flux by directly replacing a rate-limiting hydrolase (Bassal et al., 2021; Marques et al., 2020).

Therapeutic History:  
Enzyme replacement therapies have been a cornerstone in the management of several lysosomal storage disorders since the early 1990s, with the first approved treatment for Gaucher’s disease setting a precedent for this therapeutic strategy (Saftig, 2005; Lerussi et al., 2025). In the specific case of cathepsin D, recombinant forms have been employed in preclinical models of neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis (NCL) and other neurodegenerative lysosomal storage disorders, where the administration of exogenous pro-cathepsin D was able to rescue functional deficits associated with genetic CTSD deficiency (Bassal et al., 2021; Marques et al., 2020). Animal studies using CTSD-deficient mouse models have demonstrated that both intracranial and localized injections of recombinant CTSD can correct defects in proteolysis and autophagy, leading to improvements in neuropathological markers and even extending lifespan in treated animals (Bassal et al., 2021; Liu, 2021; Marques et al., 2020). Although most of these studies have focused on neurodegenerative conditions of the central nervous system, similar principles of lysosomal dysfunction apply to retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells, which are critical for maintaining retinal homeostasis in the context of age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (Klettner et al., 2013). Notably, the literature suggests that cathepsin D is highly expressed in RPE cells and plays a vital role in the degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (POS), with its deficiency or reduced function being implicated in the accumulation of toxic deposits and drusen formation—a hallmark of dry AMD (Klettner et al., 2013; Sharif, 2015). Despite the absence of direct clinical trials in dry AMD using rhCTSD, the extensive preclinical evidence from both neurodegenerative and retinal disease models provides a compelling rationale for exploring the repurposing of this enzyme replacement strategy in dry AMD (Liu, 2021; Marques et al., 2020).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, the mechanism of action of recombinant human pro-cathepsin D is rooted in its ability to restore lysosomal proteolytic function, which is often impaired in disease states such as dry AMD. Under physiological conditions, pro-cathepsin D is synthesized in the rough ER as an inactive precursor that undergoes several post-translational modifications, including the cleavage of an N-terminal signal peptide, N-linked glycosylation, and critical mannose-6-phosphate (M6P) tagging in the Golgi apparatus (Sharif, 2015). The M6P tag facilitates the binding of pro-cathepsin D to M6P receptors within the trans-Golgi network (TGN), directing the enzyme to late endosomes and, eventually, to lysosomes where the acidic environment promotes its maturation into its active form (Sharif, 2015). Once active, cathepsin D contributes to the degradation of a wide range of substrates, including the photoreceptor outer segments in RPE cells, thereby playing a crucial role in maintaining cellular homeostasis and preventing the accumulation of deleterious debris that can lead to drusen formation (Klettner et al., 2013). The proposed therapeutic strategy involves subretinal delivery of the recombinant enzyme to bypass systemic limitations such as the blood-brain barrier and to achieve localized uptake into RPE cells via the M6P receptor-mediated endocytosis pathway (Liu, 2021; Marques et al., 2020; Sharif, 2015). Once internalized, the enzyme can replenish endogenous levels of cathepsin D, thereby enhancing autophagic flux and proteolytic degradation processes that are essential for the health and function of the RPE (Klettner et al., 2013; Sharif, 2015). This targeted mechanism is a direct, molecularly specific approach that aims not only to compensate for maturation defects in the enzyme but also to overcome upstream acidification abnormalities that often hinder proper activation of endogenously produced cathepsin D in aging RPE cells (Liu, 2021; Marques et al., 2020; Sharif, 2015).

Expected Effect:  
The anticipated outcome of employing recombinant human pro-cathepsin D for the treatment of dry AMD is multifaceted. First, the subretinal administration of the enzyme is expected to lead to efficient uptake by RPE cells via the M6P receptor, thereby supplementing or restoring the lysosomal pool of active cathepsin D where it is most critically needed (Sharif, 2015). This direct enzyme replacement should result in improved degradation of cellular waste such as spent photoreceptor outer segments, mitigating the build-up of lipofuscin and drusen that are characteristic of dry AMD pathology (Klettner et al., 2013). In animal models of CTSD deficiency—specifically those that mimic aspects of neurodegenerative lysosomal storage disorders—the administration of exogenous pro-cathepsin D has yielded significant improvements in proteolytic function, reduction of pathological markers, and even extensions in lifespan (Bassal et al., 2021; Marques et al., 2020), which suggest that similar therapeutic benefits might be achievable in the context of dry AMD. Enhancing the proteolytic flux within the lysosomes of RPE cells is expected to restore autophagy and maintain cellular homeostasis, thereby reducing the incidence of apoptotic cell death and preserving retinal structure (Klettner et al., 2013; Sharif, 2015). Additionally, by compensating for potential maturation deficits and bypassing defective acidification processes through localized delivery, the therapeutic candidate offers a targeted approach that is likely to be both efficacious and specific compared to more indirect modulators of lysosomal function (Liu, 2021; Marques et al., 2020; Sharif, 2015). Ultimately, the expected effect is an overall improvement in RPE health, which should translate into slowed progression of dry AMD, decreased drusen accumulation, and preserved visual function.

Overall Evaluation:  
In evaluating recombinant human pro-cathepsin D as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, several strengths emerge from the literature, though some challenges remain. One of the primary strengths of this candidate lies in its specificity; unlike indirect modulators of lysosomal function, the exogenous delivery of a rate-limiting hydrolase such as CTSD offers a mechanistically driven, targeted replacement therapy that directly addresses a known biochemical deficit in the retinal pigment epithelium (Klettner et al., 2013; Liu, 2021). The robust body of preclinical evidence supporting the efficacy of recombinant pro-cathepsin D in models of neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis, where similar lysosomal impairments are present, lends further credence to its potential applicability in AMD (Bassal et al., 2021; Marques et al., 2020). Moreover, the formulation's GMP-compatibility and prior demonstration of safety in the context of genetic CTSD deficiency are significant advantages that can accelerate its translational potential (Marques et al., 2020; Liu, 2021).

The enzyme’s molecular mechanism, which involves uptake via mannose-6-phosphate receptor-mediated endocytosis and subsequent activation in the lysosomal compartment, is well-characterized and aligns with the pathological requirements for restoring RPE function in dry AMD (Sharif, 2015). This targeted approach provides a direct means to enhance proteolytic activity and autophagic flux, crucial processes that are disrupted in the aging retina and contribute to drusen accumulation (Klettner et al., 2013). The ability of the exogenously delivered pro-cathepsin D to overcome defects in lysosomal maturation and acidification further reinforces its potential role in reversing or mitigating the deleterious effects of the disease (Liu, 2021; Marques et al., 2020).

On the other hand, several weaknesses or challenges must be acknowledged. Although the mechanistic rationale is robust, the translation of preclinical successes in neurodegenerative and lysosomal storage disorder models to the complex, multifactorial pathology of dry AMD remains uncertain (Benes et al., 2008; Liu, 2021). Dry AMD is influenced by a host of factors—including oxidative stress, chronic inflammation, and genetic predispositions—that may not be fully addressed by simply supplementing CTSD activity. Therefore, while the normalization of proteolytic flux in RPE cells is a critical component, it may not suffice on its own in the context of the broader pathophysiological milieu present in AMD (Klettner et al., 2013; Sharif, 2015).

Furthermore, delivery challenges inherent to subretinal injections must be considered. Although localized delivery methods help bypass systemic barriers such as the blood-brain barrier, subretinal injections are technically demanding, carry inherent risks of infection, and may provoke local immune responses due to repeated interventions (Marques et al., 2020; Liu, 2021). The emergence of neutralizing antibodies, as observed in some ERT studies when alternative routes of administration were explored, could compromise the long-term efficacy of the therapy if systemic leakage occurs or if repeated dosing is required (Marques et al., 2020; Liu, 2021). Additionally, the stability and persistence of the enzyme in the subretinal space represent important pharmacokinetic questions that must be addressed through rigorous preclinical pharmacodynamic studies.

Another potential shortcoming is the specificity of the enzyme’s action. While cathepsin D is indeed a critical protease in RPE cells, there is an intricate interplay between cathepsin D and other lysosomal enzymes such as cathepsins B, L, and S, as well as regulatory proteins like cystatin C, which modulate proteolytic activity (Sharif, 2015). This interdependence implies that augmenting CTSD activity alone might lead to compensatory changes in other proteases that could either enhance the therapeutic effect or, conversely, result in unforeseen off-target consequences. Moreover, given the complexity of the RPE cell’s lysosomal network and the multifactorial nature of dry AMD pathogenesis, combination approaches targeting several aspects of lysosomal dysfunction might be necessary to achieve optimal clinical outcomes.

In summary, recombinant human pro-cathepsin D presents a therapeutically attractive and mechanistically rational candidate for the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration. Its origins as a naturally occurring lysosomal precursor that, when supplemented exogenously, has been shown to restore enzyme activity in preclinical models of lysosomal dysfunction (Bassal et al., 2021; Marques et al., 2020) underscores its potential for addressing the proteolytic deficits seen in RPE cells affected by dry AMD (Klettner et al., 2013). The candidate’s well-defined molecular processing pathway—from synthesis as an inactive proenzyme to activation within the acidic environment of the lysosome—ensures that it is both functionally and biologically suited to compensate for endogenous maturation deficits (Sharif, 2015). This detailed understanding of its biochemistry and cellular uptake mechanisms via the mannose-6-phosphate receptor supports the hypothesis that subretinal delivery of rhCTSD could enhance proteolytic flux, reduce drusen accumulation, and ultimately contribute to the preservation of retinal function in patients with dry AMD (Liu, 2021; Marques et al., 2020).

Despite these promising attributes, the candidate’s clinical translation will require addressing several key challenges. Future studies must rigorously evaluate the pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic profiles of subretinally delivered rhCTSD, with particular emphasis on its stability, local retention time in the subretinal space, and potential immunogenicity. It will also be critical to determine whether augmenting CTSD activity alone is sufficient to counteract the multi-factorial processes underlying dry AMD or if the therapeutic strategy should be integrated into a broader, combination-based treatment regimen. Additionally, long-term safety studies are necessary to monitor for potential adverse effects, such as immune-mediated clearance or detrimental off-target proteolytic activity that might impair retinal structure and function (Marques et al., 2020; Thiessen, 2023).

Ultimately, the overall evaluation is cautiously optimistic. The mechanistic rationale is strong—supported by extensive preclinical data from related neurodegenerative and lysosomal storage disorder models—and the therapeutic candidate is produced under rigorous, GMP-compliant conditions, offering a level of quality assurance that is imperative for clinical advancement (Marques et al., 2020; Liu, 2021). The specificity of recombinant pro-cathepsin D in directly addressing a rate-limiting step in lysosomal degradation makes it an especially compelling candidate in a disease setting where impaired autophagy and proteolysis are central to pathology (Klettner et al., 2013). However, challenges related to effective subretinal delivery, the potential for immune responses, and the need to integrate its action within the broader context of AMD pathogenesis must be rigorously addressed in subsequent preclinical and clinical studies before a definitive therapeutic benefit can be confirmed (Marques et al., 2020; Benes et al., 2008). In light of these considerations, recombinant human pro-cathepsin D stands out as a promising avenue for therapeutic intervention in dry AMD, meriting further investigation to delineate its efficacy, safety, and long-term benefits in the appropriate animal models and ultimately in clinical trials.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
SRT1720 is a first-generation synthetic small-molecule sirtuin 1 (SIRT1)–activating compound (STAC) originally discovered by high-throughput screening at Sirtris Pharmaceuticals and optimized around an imidazo[1,2-b]thiazole chemotype to yield higher apparent potency and selectivity than the natural product resveratrol in early assay systems (Chang et al., 2024; Mazzone, 2018). Subsequent mechanistic work across the STAC class resolved that many apparent activation signals were substrate/context dependent and, in some assay configurations, artifactual; nevertheless, later kinetic/biophysical and structural studies established that STACs can directly engage SIRT1 via an assisted allosteric mechanism that stabilizes the enzyme–substrate complex, with mutational data showing that E230K/A SIRT1 variants abolish both binding and activation by STACs (Lee et al., 2021; Mazzone, 2018). While most STACs are SIRT1-selective, SRT1720 exhibits notable polypharmacology, including reported inhibitory activity against Sirt3, highlighting potential off-target risks intrinsic to this first-generation class (Mazzone, 2018). As a class, STACs have been widely evaluated for metabolic, inflammatory, neurodegenerative, and aging phenotypes predicated on SIRT1’s broad substrate repertoire (for example, PGC-1α, NF-κB p65/RelA, FOXO family, p53), which link to mitochondrial biogenesis, anti-inflammatory signaling, oxidative stress responses, and cell survival programs (Chang et al., 2024; Mazzone, 2018).

Therapeutic History  
SRT1720 has extensive preclinical use, but there is no evidence in the provided corpus that it has been tested in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), in the eye, or in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) models (cellular or in vivo) (Ji et al., 2021; Ding et al., 2017; Bononi et al., 2022). In non-ocular systems, SRT1720 increased mitochondrial biogenesis and rescued mitochondrial function after oxidant injury in renal proximal tubule cells, providing proof-of-concept that STAC activation can drive PGC-1α–linked mitochondrial programs in mammalian cells under oxidative stress (Ji et al., 2021). In metabolic disease models, SRT1720 is reported to improve hepatic lipid metabolism via SIRT1-dependent pathways regulating PGC-1α, AMPK, PPARα, FOXO1, SREBP-1c and FGF21, with consistent decreases in lipogenesis and inflammation and increases in fatty-acid β-oxidation in NAFLD models (Ding et al., 2017). Multiple lifespan/healthspan studies reported benefits in mice—improved survival and healthspan in diet-induced obese animals and lifespan extension on standard diet—again consistent with systemic SIRT1-axis engagement (Mazzone, 2018). At the same time, substantial controversy surrounds both mechanism and safety. Pacholec et al. argued SRT1720 (and related first-generation STACs) are not direct SIRT1 activators under specific biochemical conditions, although later work provided structural and kinetic support for allosteric activation with specific substrates (Lee et al., 2021; Bononi et al., 2022). Importantly for repurposing risk, SRT1720 promoted tumor cell migration and lung metastasis in a breast cancer model, and SRT1720 can trigger SIRT1-independent cytotoxicity in some hematologic malignancy cells, underscoring unresolved off-target liabilities (Bononi et al., 2022; Chang et al., 2024). No pharmacokinetic (PK), ADME, or clinical tolerability data for SRT1720 are supplied in the present corpus; by contrast, the second-generation STAC SRT2104 has human PK/tolerability and multiple preclinical and clinical signals across diseases, including ocular/neurologic models (but those data cannot be extrapolated to SRT1720 without qualification) (Bononi et al., 2022; Chang et al., 2024). Collectively, the historical record supports that SRT1720 is a pharmacologically active first-generation STAC with broad preclinical use, mixed mechanistic interpretations, and safety concerns; critically, there is no published use in AMD or RPE models in the material provided here (Ji et al., 2021; Bononi et al., 2022).

Mechanism of Action  
- Biochemical pharmacology and target engagement: SRT1720 belongs to the STAC class that can directly activate SIRT1 through an assisted allosteric mechanism requiring specific substrate motifs; mutating SIRT1 E230 disrupts both activator binding and activation, and co-crystal structures of SIRT1 with SRT-like activators support an allosteric binding pocket that enhances deacetylation efficiency in a substrate-dependent manner (Lee et al., 2021; Mazzone, 2018). Early reports of direct activation were contested due to labeled peptide assay artifacts, but subsequent kinetic and structural data reconciled these findings with an allosteric model; nonetheless, the field recognizes pharmacological caveats including context-dependent activation and off-targets, such as reported Sirt3 inhibition by SRT1720 (Mazzone, 2018; Lee et al., 2021).  
- Canonical SIRT1 substrates and pathway biology: SIRT1 deacetylates transcriptional regulators and autophagy/mitophagy machinery that converge on mitochondrial quality control, oxidative stress defense, and inflammatory tone—each relevant to AMD pathogenesis. These include PGC-1α (mitochondrial biogenesis/oxidative metabolism), FOXO1/FOXO3a (antioxidant/autophagy transcription), NF-κB p65/RelA (inflammatory gene programs), p53 (apoptosis/senescence), and Nrf2 (antioxidant transcription), as well as autophagy proteins (e.g., ATG family members and LC3) and trafficking nodes such as Rab7 that promote autophagosome–lysosome fusion (Chang et al., 2024; Luján et al., 2022; Luo et al., 2025). In multiple cell types, SIRT1 activation or NAD⁺ elevation increases PGC-1α activity and mitochondrial biogenesis and can suppress NF-κB signaling via p65 deacetylation, consistent with anti-oxidative and anti-inflammatory effects that are therapeutically desirable in RPE (Ding et al., 2017; Luo et al., 2025).  
- RPE-specific SIRT1/autophagy linkage: In ARPE-19 cells under oxidative stress, PARP1 activation depletes NAD⁺, inhibits SIRT1 (elevated p53 acetylation), and selectively impairs late-stage autophagy by blocking autolysosome formation without preventing autophagosome formation; restoring NAD⁺ or inhibiting PARP1 preserves SIRT1 activity and rescues late autophagic flux, whereas PARP1 inhibition fails to rescue autophagy when SIRT1 is depleted—placing SIRT1 as the essential downstream effector for recovering autophagy in oxidatively stressed RPE (Jang et al., 2020). In vivo, PARP1 inhibition protected the retina in sodium iodate (SI) injury and the benefit was autophagy-dependent, reinforcing the PARP1→NAD⁺→SIRT1→autophagy axis as a mechanistic driver of RPE/retinal resilience (Jang et al., 2020). AMD donor RPE exhibits decreased NAD⁺, reduced SIRT1 levels, increased acetylated (inactive) PGC-1α, impaired AMPK signaling, and hyperactive mTOR—all changes expected to depress SIRT1-dependent autophagy and mitochondrial biogenesis and to contribute to lysosomal/autophagic abnormalities (Zhang et al., 2020).

In AMD/RPE-relevant literature, TFEB/CLEAR is positioned as a principal lever for lysosomal rejuvenation, and lysosomal acidity and calcium handling are identified as key determinants of autophagic flux and RPE health (Boya et al., 2023). Therapeutic biology of the disease target supports SIRT1 activation in RPE. Multiple AMD-relevant datasets show NAD⁺ depletion and SIRT1 downregulation in AMD RPE (primary donor-derived cultures and iPSC-RPE), accompanied by impaired PGC-1α activity, AMPK suppression, and mTOR hyperactivation, together with autophagy/lysosome structural and functional abnormalities; the PARP1-dependent late-autophagy block under oxidative stress in RPE is SIRT1-dependent for rescue, further bolstering SIRT1 as a target for restoring autophagic flux and organelle quality control (Zhang et al., 2020; Jang et al., 2020). - Scientific merit: Pursuing SIRT1 activation to normalize late-stage autophagy and mitochondrial quality control in RPE is well-justified by the PARP1→NAD⁺→SIRT1 axis in RPE and AMD donor biology; however, SRT1720 is not, on current evidence, the optimal first-in-class molecule to test this hypothesis in RPE (Jang et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2020).

- For in vivo progression, the SI model used to establish PARP1→SIRT1/autophagy dependency provides a tractable retinal degeneration context, but ocular delivery and safety (especially with first-generation STACs) will require localized dosing strategies (intravitreal/subretinal) and careful dosing to minimize systemic exposure (Jang et al., 2020).

Bottom Line  
- The hypothesis that SRT1720 can correct RPE proteostasis in dry AMD via SIRT1 activation is mechanistically credible with respect to autophagy/mitophagy restoration, but the specific claims of TFEB deacetylation, CLEAR network activation, and enhancement of lysosomal acidification/CTSD activity by SRT1720 in RPE are not supported by the present literature and must be treated as untested (Jang et al., 2020; Falcão et al., 2025; Boya et al., 2023).  
- Given the safety concerns and off-target profile of SRT1720, and the existence of a later-generation STAC (SRT2104) with human PK and ocular neuroprotection, SRT1720 should not be advanced beyond in vitro RPE validation until it demonstrates clear, on-target superiority in RPE assays and acceptable safety margins; otherwise, the team should prioritize either SRT2104 or NAD⁺ augmentation/PARP1 modulation for translational efforts (Chang et al., 2024; Bononi et al., 2022; Jang et al., 2020).  

Summary assessment  
- Pros: Strong disease–target alignment in RPE; robust class biology for SIRT1-driven autophagy/mitophagy; SRT1720 can activate SIRT1 pathways in other oxidative-stress contexts; feasible, discriminating assays exist to test the MoA (Zhang et al., 2020; Jang et al., 2020; Ji et al., 2021; Boya et al., 2023).

Decision guidance: Proceed with a narrowly scoped, mechanism-first in vitro validation of SRT1720 in human RPE focused on SIRT1 target engagement and late-stage autophagy rescue under oxidative/phagolysosomal stress, with explicit tests for TFEB/CLEAR activation and lysosomal acidification/CTSD activity; in parallel, benchmark against SRT2104 and NAD⁺ repletion, and use pre-specified go/no-go criteria tied to on-target mechanistic readouts and safety signals to decide whether SRT1720 merits in vivo exploration in retinal degeneration models (Jang et al., 2020; Chang et al., 2024; Boya et al., 2023).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Harmine is a naturally occurring β-carboline alkaloid that is abundant in Peganum harmala L., and has been investigated for neuropharmacological activities including acetylcholinesterase (AChE) inhibition, antioxidant activity, and anti-inflammatory effects, with related β-carbolines such as harmaline frequently studied alongside it (Singh et al., 2024). As an alkaloid, harmine belongs to a class of nitrogen-containing, basic, often polycyclic natural products that have historically provided a rich source of neuroactive scaffolds and approved therapeutics across neurodegenerative diseases (NDDs), with the literature situating harmine within a broader set of “neuroprotective alkaloids” considered for NDD drug discovery (Singh et al., 2024). In preclinical pharmacology, water-soluble salt forms such as harmine hydrochloride have been used, and medicinal chemistry analogs with higher potency than the parent have been reported, supporting tractability for formulation and structure–activity optimization (Singh et al., 2024).

The mechanistic disease context relevant to dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is dominated by lysosomal and autophagy dysfunction in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), where impaired lysosomal degradation, phagosome–lysosome fusion, and autophagic flux promote lipofuscin accumulation, oxidative stress, complement/inflammasome activation, and RPE death (Boya et al., 2023; Kaarniranta et al., 2023). Master regulators of lysosomal biogenesis and degradative capacity include TFEB/TFE3, which are controlled by mTORC1, AMPK, Ca2+/calcineurin, and lysosomal signaling nodes; TFEB drives expression of the CLEAR gene network to expand lysosomal/autophagy capacity and has been repeatedly highlighted as a central therapeutic axis for restoring RPE degradative function (Boya et al., 2023). The CLEAR program directly impacts lysosomal membrane proteins such as LAMP2 and proteases like cathepsins, and TFEB activity is constrained by nutrient-sensing mTORC1 signaling on the lysosomal surface (Boya et al., 2023). Because LAMP2 deficiency impairs photoreceptor outer segment (POS) degradation and yields AMD-like phenotypes, and cathepsin D (CTSD) is the primary POS protease in RPE, TFEB-mediated enhancement of these systems is mechanistically aligned with dry AMD pathobiology (Boya et al., 2023; Si et al., 2023; Kaarniranta et al., 2013). Note, however, that the provided evidence base contains no direct data linking harmine to TFEB activation, CLEAR gene induction, or DYRK1A inhibition in RPE or neural cells; those specific connections are absent in the cited retinal/lysosome literature excerpts (Boya et al., 2023).

Therapeutic History  
No registered clinical trials were identified on ClinicalTrials.gov for the search terms “Harmine retinal pigment epithelium” or “Harmine dry age-related macular degeneration,” indicating no publicly registered clinical evaluation of harmine for dry AMD or closely related RPE indications under those exact phrases (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.). The negative registry findings were reiterated in independent queries and associated summaries, which emphasize that these are specific to the exact search terms and this registry, and do not exclude preclinical studies, trials registered elsewhere, or studies indexed under alternative nomenclature; nonetheless, they demonstrate a lack of registered clinical activity for harmine in dry AMD on this platform (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).

Outside ophthalmology, harmine has a preclinical pharmacology history in neurodegenerative disease models, including antiparkinsonian activity comparable in some studies to levodopa, anti-cataleptogenic effects in haloperidol models at 2.5–5 mg/kg, and reduction of MPTP-induced oligokinesia, with some analogs achieving desired effects at 2 mg/kg compared with 20 mg/kg for harmine (Singh et al., 2024). Mechanistically, harmine promotes time- and dose-dependent degradation of α-synuclein species via upregulation of the PSMD1 subunit of the ubiquitin–proteasome system and enhanced PKA phosphorylation, supporting a proteostasis-modulating mechanism in CNS models (Singh et al., 2024). Additional pharmacology reported in the literature includes MAO and AChE inhibition in preclinical models, consistent with multi-target neuromodulatory activity of β-carbolines (Singh et al., 2024). The excerpts provided here do not document any prior use of harmine in ocular disease models or clinical settings for retinal disease, nor do they offer ocular pharmacokinetic/tissue exposure or ocular tolerability data (Singh et al., 2024).

Mechanism of Action  
Known pharmacology of harmine in the supplied materials centers on: (1) enhancement of proteasome-dependent clearance of aggregation-prone proteins through upregulation of the PSMD1 subunit and PKA-mediated mechanisms, leading to time- and dose-dependent degradation of α-synuclein species; and (2) inhibition of monoamine oxidase (MAO) and acetylcholinesterase (AChE), along with reported antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects in diverse preclinical systems (Singh et al., 2024). These activities position harmine as a multi-modal agent influencing proteostasis and neurotransmitter pathways in the CNS (Singh et al., 2024).

By contrast, the specific hypothesis under evaluation—that harmine will inhibit DYRK1A in RPE, increase TFEB dephosphorylation and nuclear translocation, and thereby promote CLEAR-driven lysosomal biogenesis, acidification, and CTSD activity—is not supported by direct evidence in the provided context; the retinal/lysosomal references explicitly discuss TFEB/TFE3 regulation, RPE lysosome biology, and autophagy dysfunction in AMD, but do not report DYRK1A involvement or link harmine to TFEB modulation (Boya et al., 2023). The mechanistic literature excerpts instead highlight established regulatory routes by which TFEB/TFE3 control lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy: mTORC1-dependent phosphorylation prevents TFEB nuclear import, whereas AMPK activation and lysosomal Ca2+/calcineurin signaling can promote TFEB/TFE3 dephosphorylation and nuclear translocation to induce the CLEAR program (Boya et al., 2023). In the RPE, upstream lysosomal amino-acid sensing via V-ATPase–Ragulator–Rag GTPases coordinates mTORC1 activity at the lysosomal membrane, and disruptions in these nodes (e.g., βA3/A1-crystallin deficits) impair TFEB/TFE3 nuclear translocation and CLEAR gene expression, contributing to AMD-like phenotypes (Boya et al., 2023; Sinha et al., 2016).

The RPE’s degradative workload is extraordinary—daily heterophagy of shed photoreceptor outer segments and continuous autophagy—so lysosomal membrane proteins and hydrolytic enzyme systems are critical to homeostasis: LAMP2 is a TFEB/CLEAR target whose deficiency delays POS degradation and produces AMD-like retinal changes, and CTSD is the principal lysosomal protease mediating POS/rhodopsin degradation; impaired phagosome–lysosome fusion and elevated lysosomal pH (e.g., due to A2E or lipofuscin) reduce cathepsin activity and drive lipofuscinogenesis and RPE degeneration (Boya et al., 2023; Si et al., 2023; Kaarniranta et al., 2013). Consequences of lysosomal failure include LMP with cytosolic release of cathepsins, DAMP emission, complement activation, and necroptotic cell death; interventions that stabilize lysosomal membranes (e.g., Hsp70 induction) or normalize pH have restored lysosomal function and reduced retinal degeneration in preclinical models, underscoring the therapeutic relevance of lysosome-centric strategies (Boya et al., 2023). Therapeutic interventions that restore lysosomal enzyme function (e.g., cathepsin D gene therapy) and enhance CMA or autophagy have also attenuated retinal degeneration and preserved visual function in vivo, further supporting this axis (Boya et al., 2023).

In summary, while TFEB activation and lysosomal rejuvenation are compelling, disease-relevant mechanisms for dry AMD, the materials provided do not document harmine as a DYRK1A inhibitor in RPE, or as an agent that increases TFEB nuclear translocation, CLEAR gene expression, LAMP1/2 abundance, or CTSD activity in ocular systems; these specific mechanistic links remain unsubstantiated in this evidence set (Boya et al., 2023).

Expected Effect  
If the hypothesized mechanism were correct—that harmine inhibits a TFEB-restraining kinase and thereby drives TFEB nuclear translocation and CLEAR gene activation in RPE—the expected cellular outcomes would include increased lysosomal biogenesis, improved lysosomal acidification and ion homeostasis, higher LAMP2/LAMP1 expression, augmented cathepsin content and activity (including CTSD), enhanced autophagic flux, and improved phagosome–lysosome fusion and degradation of POS, together leading to reduced lipofuscin burden, mitigation of LMP, and protection from necroptosis and chronic inflammation (Boya et al., 2023; Si et al., 2023). TFEB is the master transcriptional regulator of the CLEAR program, and its dephosphorylation/nuclear localization induces expression of genes that collectively increase lysosomal number and degradative competence; in the RPE, CLEAR-dependent targets include LAMP2, whose deficiency causes delayed POS clearance and AMD-like degeneration (Boya et al., 2023). A direct functional prediction is that promoting TFEB activity would increase lysosome number and cathepsin activity; indeed, pharmacologic Ezrin inhibition—through a distinct regulatory route—has been shown to increase lysosomal number and cathepsin activity in RPE, reduce vision loss, and thus serves as proof-of-concept that boosting lysosomal protease capacity is salutary in retinal disease models (Boya et al., 2023). Because CTSD is the primary POS protease in RPE and is inhibited by elevated lysosomal pH or phototoxic lipofuscin constituents such as A2E, a TFEB-driven program that improves acidification and enzymatic capacity would be predicted to restore POS processing and limit lipofuscin accumulation (Si et al., 2023; Kaarniranta et al., 2013; Boya et al., 2023).

Autophagy and mitophagy readouts should similarly improve: TFEB/CLEAR activation increases autophagosome formation and lysosomal fusion, restoring autophagic flux diminished with age and in AMD, and reducing SQSTM1/p62 accumulation and associated proteostatic stress (Kaarniranta et al., 2023). Enhanced lysosomal function is expected to reduce DAMP release and intracellular complement activation, attenuate inflammasome/ferroptosis cascades associated with reduced autophagy, and stabilize mitochondrial–lysosomal crosstalk via AMPK-dependent signaling and TFEB-induced biogenesis (Boya et al., 2023). Because mTORC1 hyperactivation in the RPE causes lysosomal dysfunction and AMD-like degeneration, an agent that indirectly reduces mTORC1 activity or relieves TFEB from mTORC1/AKT constraints could restore lysosomal-autophagic balance and improve RPE survival (Boya et al., 2023).

However, the materials provided include no experimental data demonstrating that harmine produces these outcomes in RPE or retina, nor do they show ocular pharmacokinetics or local tolerability; thus, in the proposed assays, any expected effects of harmine on TFEB/CLEAR, lysosomal acidification, LAMP1/2, CTSD, POS clearance, autophagic flux, or inflammatory readouts should be regarded as hypothesis-generating and require direct testing (Singh et al., 2024). In designing such assays, relevant endpoints and models include: TFEB nuclear translocation and CLEAR gene panels; Lysotracker-based pH measurements; LAMP1/LAMP2 abundance; total and active CTSD and cathepsin activity assays; live-cell phagosome–lysosome fusion kinetics with POS; A2E/lipofuscin-loaded RPE to model elevated lysosomal pH and LMP susceptibility; LC3-II turnover and SQSTM1/p62 levels to quantify autophagic flux; markers of LMP (cytosolic cathepsin activity) and necroptosis; complement activation and inflammasome markers (e.g., IL-1β) in stressed RPE—each aligned with disease-relevant mechanisms in the cited literature (Boya et al., 2023; Kaarniranta et al., 2013; Boya et al., 2023; Kaarniranta et al., 2023; Boya et al., 2023).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Mechanistic alignment with RPE pathobiology: The dry AMD literature strongly implicates lysosomal dysfunction, autophagy decline, impaired phagosome–lysosome fusion, and defective degradative capacity in RPE degeneration; TFEB-directed lysosomal biogenesis and restoration of lysosomal pH/ion homeostasis are repeatedly identified as rational therapeutic axes (Boya et al., 2023). CLEAR-dependent targets such as LAMP2 and cathepsins (including CTSD) are essential for POS processing and retinal homeostasis, and their failure yields AMD-like phenotypes—consistent with the proposed direction of effect (Boya et al., 2023; Si et al., 2023; Kaarniranta et al., 2013).  
- Proof-of-concept for lysosome-centric interventions: Stabilization of lysosomal membranes, normalization of lysosomal pH, enhancement of cathepsin activity, activation of CMA, and direct correction of lysosomal enzyme deficits each attenuate retinal degeneration and preserve function in preclinical models, providing a diverse set of precedents that validate the therapeutic strategy at the pathway level (Boya et al., 2023).  
- Proteostasis-modulating activity of harmine: In CNS models, harmine promotes clearance of misfolded/aggregation-prone proteins via the ubiquitin–proteasome system, upregulating PSMD1 and enhancing PKA-dependent proteasomal activity; this establishes harmine as a proteostasis-active scaffold with in vivo pharmacology, a potentially favorable feature for diseases characterized by toxic protein/lipid waste accumulation (Singh et al., 2024).  
- Formulation and medicinal chemistry tractability: A water-soluble hydrochloride salt has been used in vivo, and analogs with markedly improved potency over harmine have been reported, supporting a path for optimization if ocular exposure or target engagement proves limiting (Singh et al., 2024).

Weaknesses and Critical Gaps  
- No direct evidence for the central hypothesis: The provided evidence base lacks demonstrations that harmine inhibits DYRK1A, increases TFEB dephosphorylation/nuclear localization, induces CLEAR gene expression, or elevates LAMP1/2 and CTSD in RPE or neural cells; consequently, the core premise—DYRK1A→TFEB→CLEAR engagement by harmine in RPE—remains unsubstantiated here (Boya et al., 2023).  
- Absence of ophthalmic data: There are no ocular pharmacokinetics, retina/RPE exposure, or local ocular tolerability data for harmine in the materials provided, which constitute major translational risks for an ocular indication (Singh et al., 2024).  
- No registered clinical activity in dry AMD: Multiple ClinicalTrials.gov queries under relevant phrases returned zero trials, indicating an absence of publicly registered clinical development for harmine in RPE/dry AMD; this constrains assessment of clinical feasibility, ocular target engagement, and dose–response in humans for this indication (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).

- Unclear linkage to mTORC1/AMPK axes in RPE: The TFEB pathway in RPE is tightly regulated by mTORC1, AMPK, lysosomal Ca2+/calcineurin, and V-ATPase–Ragulator signaling; the provided materials do not show harmine’s effects on these nodes in ocular systems, leaving mechanistic plausibility at the level of generic TFEB activation rather than compound-specific evidence (Boya et al., 2023).

- Evidence-based conclusion: On the evidence provided here, harmine is not yet a validated candidate for dry AMD, because the central mechanism-of-action claims (DYRK1A inhibition leading to TFEB/CLEAR activation in RPE) are not supported by direct data in these materials, and there is no ocular PK/tolerability or registered clinical experience to de-risk translation (Boya et al., 2023; Singh et al., 2024; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).

Bottom Line  
Harmine presents as a proteostasis-active, neuropharmacologically tractable scaffold with preclinical in vivo CNS efficacy and formulation/medicinal chemistry precedent, but the specific mechanism-of-action proposed for dry AMD—DYRK1A inhibition leading to TFEB/CLEAR-mediated lysosomal rejuvenation in RPE—lacks direct support in the provided evidence base, and there is no ocular pharmacokinetic or tolerability information to enable translational planning (Singh et al., 2024; Boya et al., 2023). Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Genistein is a naturally occurring isoflavone that was first isolated from soybeans and other leguminous plants. As a member of the phytoestrogen class, genistein possesses structural similarities to mammalian estrogens and can bind to estrogen receptors, albeit with much lower intrinsic potency than endogenous steroids. It is typically obtained from dietary sources such as soy, red clover, and other legumes, but high‐purity formulations have been developed and are commercially available (for example, Sigma G6649). Genistein belongs to a broader class of natural bioactive compounds that have been studied over the past several decades for their modulating effects on various cellular processes including antioxidant defense, differentiation, apoptosis, and proliferation. Historically, phytoestrogens like genistein have been investigated both for their hormone‐like activity and as specific inhibitors of protein tyrosine kinases. The compound has been utilized in research ranging from hormone replacement strategies in menopausal women to anticancer studies, and its ability to modulate several cell signaling pathways—including those associated with PI3K/AKT/mTOR—has attracted interest in other fields such as neurodegeneration and ocular health (Albulescu & Popovici, 2007).

Therapeutic History:  
The therapeutic history of genistein spans multiple domains. Clinically, phytoestrogens have been examined largely as potential alternatives to traditional estrogen replacement therapies for the alleviation of menopausal symptoms, with some studies reporting modest effects on vasomotor symptoms, menstrual cycle regulation, and quality‐of‐life indices (Glazier & Bowman, 2001; Albulescu & Popovici, 2007). In the veterinary and preclinical realm, high doses of phytoestrogens have been associated with reproductive toxicity in livestock such as sheep (the classical clover disease), while rodent studies have similarly documented endocrine disruptions when exposed to high concentrations (Glazier & Bowman, 2001). For bone health specifically, preclinical data have shown that ovariectomized rats fed genistein exhibit reduced rates of bone loss; this finding parallels clinical trials using the synthetic isoflavone derivative ipriflavone—which is related to the parent compounds in the isoflavone class—and has demonstrated benefits in slowing bone loss and increasing bone mineral density when given for periods of up to two years in postmenopausal women (Glazier & Bowman, 2001). Regarding ocular applications, there is emerging preclinical work to improve the solubility and corneal penetration of genistein; for example, encapsulating genistein in hyaluronic acid–modified MPEG-b-PAE polymeric micelles has been shown to improve its corneal permeability by approximately 1.5-fold compared to a simple drug solution (Li et al., 2018). Although genistein has not yet been extensively evaluated in clinical trials specifically targeting dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD), its broad modulatory effects on tyrosine kinases and downstream signaling pathways provide a rationale for repurposing it to address dry AMD pathophysiology, particularly given the significant unmet therapeutic need in this area (Glazier & Bowman, 2001).

Mechanism of Action:  
Genistein is widely recognized for its ability to inhibit protein tyrosine kinases. This inhibitory action extends to several receptors and intracellular kinases, thereby modulating key signaling cascades including the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway—a pathway that is critical for cell survival, proliferation, and metabolism. In many cell-based studies, genistein has been shown to suppress PI3K/AKT signaling, leading to downstream inhibition of mTOR complex 1 (mTORC1) activity. Since mTORC1 coordinates cellular anabolic processes and suppresses autophagy under nutrient-rich conditions, inhibiting this complex can trigger autophagic clearance mechanisms (Albulescu & Popovici, 2007). One of the pivotal regulators downstream of mTORC1 is the transcription factor EB (TFEB), which, when dephosphorylated due to mTORC1 inhibition, translocates into the nucleus and promotes the transcription of genes involved in lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy. There is evidence that genistein can modulate lysosomal metabolism and promote TFEB activation, as reported in studies highlighting the ability of flavonoids to enhance the clearance of substrate accumulations via TFEB-mediated transcriptional programs (Xu et al., 2020). In retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells, which play a crucial role in maintaining photoreceptor health through phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments (POS), enhanced autophagy and lysosomal function are essential for the degradation and removal of cellular debris, including drusen components characteristic of dry AMD (Falcão et al., 2024). Moreover, experimental reports have suggested that in RPE-like models, treatment with compounds that suppress the PI3K/AKT/mTOR axis leads to increased LC3 turnover and upregulation of cathepsin D (CTSD), a lysosomal aspartic protease essential for phagolysosomal digestion (Albulescu & Popovici, 2007; Jahan et al., 2022). In this context, genistein is hypothesized to function by inhibiting upstream tyrosine kinases that feed into PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling, thereby promoting TFEB activation. TFEB then orchestrates the transcription of lysosomal genes, leading to enhanced lysosomal acidification and increased enzymatic activities, including that of cathepsin D, which is imperative for effective degradation within phagolysosomes (Falcão et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2025).

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis posits that administration of genistein to RPE cells will lead to measurable inhibition of the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway, resulting in dephosphorylation and nuclear translocation of TFEB. This transcriptional activation is expected to upregulate a battery of lysosomal and autophagy-related genes, including those responsible for the maintenance of lysosomal acidification and the synthesis of key proteases such as cathepsin D (Falcão et al., 2024). In functional assays, an increase in LC3 turnover—a marker of enhanced autophagic flux—would be anticipated, alongside elevated levels of CTSD, providing the biochemical basis for improved phagolysosomal digestion. Consequently, in an in vitro RPE cell model subjected to a photoreceptor outer segment (POS) feeding assay, genistein treatment is expected to facilitate the clearance of POS-derived debris and reduce the accumulation of autofluorescent lipofuscin-like granules. This outcome mimics the effects observed with compounds like rapamycin, where mTOR inhibition leads to a significant, approximately 30% reduction of POS-dependent autofluorescence by improving lysosomal processing (Falcão et al., 2024). Moreover, in light of published observations demonstrating that effective activation of TFEB can restore lysosomal biogenesis and enhance cellular clearance, genistein’s dual inhibition of kinase activity and subsequent autophagy upregulation is predicted to result in a favorable impact on drusen clearance and overall RPE function in dry AMD settings (Falcão et al., 2024; Xu et al., 2020).

Overall Evaluation:  
Overall, genistein presents as an intriguing candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry AMD, particularly given its established history as a natural product with a favorable oral safety profile and its documented ability to modulate critical signaling pathways involved in cell survival and autophagy. One of the major strengths of genistein lies in its dual mechanism: as a selective inhibitor of tyrosine kinases, it can suppress the upstream activation of the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway, and as a modulator of lysosomal metabolism, it facilitates TFEB activation. This mechanistic duality offers a targeted approach to enhance the autophagic clearance capacity of RPE cells, which is critical in preventing the accumulation of intracellular debris and drusen associated with dry AMD (Falcão et al., 2024; Xu et al., 2020). Furthermore, the existing literature on phytoestrogens indicates that compounds in this chemical class are generally well tolerated when administered orally, and formulation strategies (such as encapsulation in hyaluronic acid–modified polymeric micelles) enhance ocular bioavailability, potentially enabling effective local delivery with minimal systemic adverse effects (Li et al., 2018).

However, several challenges and weaknesses must be addressed before advancing genistein as a therapy for dry AMD. First, while there is a substantial body of evidence supporting the role of genistein in modulating PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling in non-ocular tissues, direct evidence in RPE cells and in the context of dry AMD is sparse. Most published studies in the ocular domain have focused on formulation and delivery aspects rather than on detailed mechanism-of-action studies within RPE cells. Second, the estrogenic activity of genistein, although weak, raises potential concerns regarding off-target endocrine effects, particularly during long-term administration in older populations who may be susceptible to hormone-related side effects. These aspects would require rigorous assessment in preclinical and early-phase clinical trials. Additionally, the pharmacokinetics of genistein when administered via ocular routes (either topically or systemically) remain incompletely characterized, and comprehensive data on tissue distribution, especially to the retina or RPE, is limited. Such pharmacokinetic studies are crucial to ensure that therapeutic concentrations can be achieved and maintained in the target tissues without eliciting adverse effects (Glazier & Bowman, 2001; Li et al., 2018).

In light of the above considerations, genistein is promising as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD based on its capacity to inhibit upstream tyrosine kinases and suppress the PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling cascade, thereby promoting TFEB-mediated enhancement of lysosomal acidification and cathepsin D activity. Such a mechanism is directly relevant to improving phagolysosomal function in RPE cells and facilitating the clearance of drusen components—a critical unmet need in the management of dry AMD (Falcão et al., 2024; Xu et al., 2020). The dual actions of genistein offer mechanistic clarity that may translate into a therapeutic edge when compared to broad-spectrum autophagy inducers. Nonetheless, the current evidence base is still largely circumstantial, and further direct investigations are necessary to confirm that genistein induces the expected autophagic and lysosomal responses in RPE cells. Preclinical studies employing appropriate RPE models (such as POS feeding assays and chronic oxidative stress paradigms) should be prioritized to solidify the link between genistein treatment and improved clearance of lipofuscin-like deposits. Ultimately, detailed pharmacokinetic, efficacy, and safety studies—ideally complemented by early-phase clinical trials—will be required before genistein can be confidently advanced as a therapeutic modality for dry AMD (Albulescu & Popovici, 2007; Falcão et al., 2024).

In summary, genistein’s natural origin, established safety in other contexts, and its dual ability to inhibit relevant tyrosine kinase–mediated signaling and upregulate autophagy through TFEB activation collectively support its potential for repurposing in dry AMD. However, critical gaps in direct efficacy data in ocular models and a precise understanding of its tissue pharmacokinetics necessitate further investigation. This combination of promising mechanistic rationale and some supportive preclinical data argues that genistein merits further preclinical exploration in RPE models of dry AMD, with the expectation that if such studies confirm improved clearance of lipofuscin and drusen markers, subsequent early-phase clinical trials can be pursued to evaluate its therapeutic benefit in patients suffering from this blinding disease (Falcão et al., 2024; Glazier & Bowman, 2001; Li et al., 2018; Xu et al., 2020).
