Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
ZLN005 is a synthetic, small-molecule benzimidazole identified by high-throughput screening of ~48,000 compounds using a HEK293 cell line harboring a human PGC-1α promoter–driven luciferase reporter; it was selected for its ability to transcriptionally induce the Ppargc1a (PGC-1α) gene and validated in follow-up orthogonal assays and cell types (Zhang et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2021). Chemically, ZLN005 is 2-(4-tert-butylphenyl)-1H-benzimidazole with a reported molecular weight of 250.3; it is repeatedly described as a “small-molecule PGC-1α transcriptional activator/agonist” and a “specific and selective transcriptional inducer of PGC-1α expression” (Bleckwehl et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2013; Maurice et al., 2022). The initial discovery campaign also yielded a related backbone compound (ZLN027) that showed cytotoxicity, whereas ZLN005 did not under the reported in vitro conditions, and ZLN005 was later found to inhibit luciferases—an assay interference red flag that necessitates careful interpretation of luciferase-based readouts (Zhang et al., 2013).

Pharmacologic class and precedent: ZLN005 belongs to the class of tool/investigational small molecules that transcriptionally upregulate PGC-1α and thereby stimulate mitochondrial biogenesis, oxidative phosphorylation, and fatty-acid oxidation in a tissue-selective fashion (Zhang et al., 2013). This class has been deployed broadly in preclinical systems—skeletal muscle, cardiomyocytes, neurons, kidney, lung epithelium, vascular smooth muscle, and retinal pigment epithelium (RPE)—to probe whether enhancing PGC-1α can restore mitochondrial capacity, reduce oxidative stress, and improve cell/tissue resilience (Zhang et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2020; Xu et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2021; Ma et al., 2023; Zou et al., 2025; Shu et al., 2021). A subset of studies emphasizes that ZLN005 acts upstream of AMPK→PGC-1α/MEF2 transcriptional circuits and engages canonical mitochondrial biogenesis regulators (NRF1/2, TFAM, ERRs), while in some tissues it promotes downstream fatty-acid oxidation via CPT-1α, aligning with the recognized role of PGC-1α as a master coactivator of oxidative metabolism (Zhang et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2020).

Therapeutic History  
ZLN005 has no reported clinical use. Its portfolio of preclinical applications includes:

- Metabolic disease: In diabetic db/db mice, chronic oral ZLN005 (15 mg/kg/day for 6 weeks) improved glucose tolerance, insulin sensitivity, and dyslipidemia, with induction of PGC-1α and mitochondrial/FAO gene programs in skeletal muscle and reduced hepatic gluconeogenic transcripts; AMPK/ACC phosphorylation rose in muscle but not liver, consistent with tissue selectivity (Zhang et al., 2013). Basic single-dose oral pharmacokinetics in db/db mice showed rapid plasma absorption and high initial liver exposure, with relatively stable muscle exposure over 4 hours (Zhang et al., 2013). A short-term rat safety study (75 mg/kg/day, 14 days) reported survival with no obvious changes in body weight gain or gross metabolic parameters (Zhang et al., 2013).

- Skeletal muscle cells: In L6 myotubes, ZLN005 dose-dependently increased PGC-1α mRNA, glucose uptake, and palmitate oxidation; AMPK and ACC phosphorylation increased, PGC-1α induction was AMPK-dependent (Compound C–sensitive), and MEF2 promoter integrity was required, consistent with a transcriptional mechanism (Zhang et al., 2013).

- Kidney ischemia–reperfusion injury (AKI): In mouse I/R models and H/R-injured renal tubular cells, ZLN005 restored PGC-1α and CPT-1α expression, improved mitochondrial ultrastructure/membrane potential, reduced ROS and lipid peroxidation (H₂O₂, MDA), lessened apoptosis, and required CPT-1α activity for benefit; high concentrations were toxic to HK2 cells (Wang et al., 2021).

- Neuronal injury: ZLN005 improved viability in OGD/R-injured PC12 cells, induced PGC-1α and antioxidant genes (SOD1/HO-1), and post-ischemia administration reduced infarct volume and neurological deficit in rat tMCAO, indicating neuroprotection likely via PGC-1α-driven mitochondrial and antioxidant programs; in a separate study, ZLN005 crossed the blood–brain barrier and protected against PBDE-47 neurotoxicity via PGC-1α-dependent mitochondrial biogenesis (Xu et al., 2018; Tian et al., 2023).

- Cardiomyocytes: In hESC-derived cardiomyocytes, brief ZLN005 exposure (10 μM, 48 h) increased PGC-1α and ERRγ, upregulated mitochondrial biogenesis and OXPHOS/FAO genes (NRF1, TFAM, respiratory subunits, CPT1b), increased mtDNA copy number, basal OCR and ATP, and drove structural/electrophysiological maturation (longer sarcomeres, more negative RMP, enhanced Ca²⁺ handling, increased CX43) (Liu et al., 2020).

- Lung epithelium/infection: In AECs (A549 and primary AEC2), ZLN005 increased PGC-1α and NRF1, improved mitochondrial bioenergetics, membrane potential, ATP, decreased ROS and senescence markers (p21, SA-β-gal), and these effects required PGC-1α (shPGC-1α attenuated benefit); in a P. aeruginosa pneumonia model, ZLN005 pretreatment (15 mg/kg × 3) reduced bacterial load and IL-1β and rescued SIRT3 in lung, consistent with PGC-1α–SIRT3 axis activation (Ma et al., 2023; Maurice et al., 2022).

- Vascular smooth muscle cells: ZLN005 increased PGC-1α, ESRRA, NRF1, mtDNA, and ATP, shifted mitochondrial dynamics toward fusion (↑MFN2, ↓DRP1), and dispersed perinuclear aggregates, indicating enhanced mitochondrial function (Zou et al., 2025).

- Retinal and RPE models: In ARPE-19, ZLN005 robustly increased PGC-1α, upregulated transcription factors, antioxidant enzymes and mitochondrial genes, improved basal/maximal respiration and spare capacity, and protected against oxidative insults (H₂O₂, oxLDL, NaIO₃); protection was PGC-1α-dependent; in primary human RPE (H-RPE), 10 μM ZLN005 selectively induced PGC-1α and blocked TGFβ₂-induced EMT and migration, with smaller fold-change than in ARPE-19 due to higher baseline PGC-1α (Tong et al., 2022; Shu et al., 2021). In ex vivo rd1 retinal explants (inherited photoreceptor degeneration), ZLN005 reduced overall calpain activity, shifted calpain isoform balance toward neuroprotective calpain-1 and away from calpain-2, and enhanced photoreceptor viability, supporting retinal neuroprotection via PGC-1α activation (Wang et al., 2025).

There are no reports that ZLN005 has been tested in dry age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD) animal models, nor direct demonstrations that it improves RPE phagosome clearance, lysosomal acidification, cathepsin D activity, lipofuscin burden, or drusen in AMD contexts; TFEB-targeted rescue of lysosomal function and cathepsin activity in RPE has been achieved with other agents (e.g., trehalose) or genetic TFEB activation, but ZLN005 has not been evaluated in those axes in RPE (Ghosh et al., 2024; Ghosh et al., 2023; Tong et al., 2022; Shu et al., 2021).

Mechanism of Action  
Transcriptional induction of PGC-1α. ZLN005 increases PGC-1α transcription via the PGC-1α promoter, requiring an intact MEF2 binding site; it increases PGC-1α mRNA and protein across multiple cell types where responsive, including myotubes, cardiomyocytes, lung epithelium, VSMCs, and RPE; reliance on MEF2 sites suggests ZLN005 engages upstream signaling and chromatin/transcriptional complexes that drive Ppargc1a expression (Zhang et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2020; Ma et al., 2023; Zou et al., 2025; Shu et al., 2021).

AMPK activation via mild mitochondrial uncoupling. In L6 myotubes, ZLN005 increases the cellular ADP:ATP ratio and mildly increases mitochondrial oxygen consumption in isolated mitochondria, consistent with weak uncoupling that activates AMPK; AMPK and ACC phosphorylation increase, and pharmacologic AMPK inhibition (Compound C) blocks PGC-1α induction and glucose uptake; the pathway is further modeled as AMPK-phosphorylated PGC-1α engaging MEF2C to amplify its own gene expression via positive feedback (Zhang et al., 2013). AMPK-dependence extends functionally: glucose uptake and PGC-1α induction in muscle cells require AMPK activation (Wang et al., 2021).

Downstream PGC-1α programs. Across tissues, ZLN005 induces the canonical PGC-1α program: coactivation of ERRs/PPARs/NRF1/2, upregulation of TFAM, increases in mtDNA copy number, OXPHOS complex gene products, fatty-acid oxidation enzymes (e.g., CPT-1, MCAD), and functional increases in basal/maximal OCR, ATP production, and mitochondrial content/number—data are robust in cardiomyocytes and skeletal muscle, and consistent in lung epithelial cells and RPE (Liu et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2013; Ma et al., 2023; Tong et al., 2022). In kidney I/R, PGC-1α induction by ZLN005 increased CPT-1α, restored mitochondrial FAO, reduced ROS and MDA, and decreased apoptosis; genetic or pharmacologic CPT-1α inhibition abrogated ZLN005 benefit, placing FAO downstream of PGC-1α as a necessary mediator of cytoprotection in that model (Wang et al., 2021).

PGC-1α–SIRT axis and anti-inflammatory effects. In lung infection models, ZLN005 activated the PGC-1α–SIRT3 axis, rescued SIRT3 expression, and lowered IL-1β expression in infected lungs, aligning with the role of SIRT3 in mitochondrial antioxidant function (activation of SOD2, glutathione system) and with PGC-1α’s coactivation of oxidative metabolism and antioxidant defense (Maurice et al., 2022).

Cell-type specificity and paradoxical tissue effects. ZLN005 shows a cell-type- and tissue-selective response: skeletal muscle and diverse non-hepatic cells robustly induce PGC-1α, whereas primary hepatocytes do not; in db/db mice, liver PGC-1α was paradoxically downregulated, with concurrent suppression of gluconeogenic genes, possibly via indirect systemic mechanisms (Zhang et al., 2013). In RPE, primary cells (H-RPE) exhibited modest PGC-1α fold-induction relative to ARPE-19 due to higher baseline PGC-1α expression, yet ZLN005 still blocked TGFβ₂-induced EMT and migration in H-RPE (Shu et al., 2021).

Assay caveats. ZLN005 potently inhibits luciferases, necessitating caution and orthogonal validation for any conclusions drawn from luciferase reporters, including those targeting TFEB/TFE3 or PGC-1α target promoters (Zhang et al., 2013).

Linking to TFEB/lysosomal axis: rationale vs evidence. AMPK primes lysosomal biogenesis and function partly by inducing TFEB/TFE3, while simultaneously regulating mitochondrial biogenesis via PGC-1α; a combined AMPK activation and mTORC1 inhibition strategy has been proposed as superior for mitochondrial disease contexts (Boya et al., 2023). In RPE/retina, genetic and pharmacologic activation of TFEB restores lysosomal hydrolases (CTSD, CTSL), improves autophagosome–lysosome fusion and catabolism, and reduces disease-relevant lipid accumulation; these TFEB-centered effects are well documented in RPE but have not been demonstrated for ZLN005 (Ghosh et al., 2024; Ghosh et al., 2023). Some evidence in non-retinal systems places PGC-1α upstream of TFEB-regulated lysosomal activity (e.g., in Huntington disease models), supporting a conceptual link between mitochondrial biogenesis and lysosomal/autophagy competence; however, ZLN005-specific co-activation of TFEB or enhancement of lysosomal acidification/CTSD in RPE has not been shown (Blasiak et al., 2021).

Expected Effect  
Dry AMD pathobiology—RPE mitochondrial–lysosomal dysfunction. Dry AMD features RPE oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction (mtDNA damage, reduced OXPHOS, fewer/disorganized mitochondria), defective mitophagy, impaired proteostasis, and lysosomal/autophagy defects that promote lipofuscin and drusen biogenesis (Hyttinen et al., 2023; Luján et al., 2022; Felszeghy et al., 2019). PGC-1α is highly expressed in retina/RPE and is a potent regulator of mitochondrial biogenesis and antioxidant defenses in these cells; genetic deficiency of PGC-1α (especially combined with NRF2 loss) fosters RPE degeneration with proteostatic/lysosomal stress reminiscent of dry AMD (Felszeghy et al., 2019; Hyttinen et al., 2018; Hyttinen et al., 2023). Mechanistically, AMPK→PGC-1α signaling induces mitochondrial biogenesis and interacts with NRF2/ARE antioxidant programs; reciprocally, AMPK can promote TFEB/TFE3-driven lysosomal biogenesis, providing a bidirectional mito–lyso coupling framework relevant to RPE homeostasis (Nita & Grzybowski, 2023; Boya et al., 2023).

What ZLN005 is expected to do in RPE assays. In ARPE-19 and H-RPE, ZLN005 selectively induces PGC-1α, improves mitochondrial respiration, upregulates mitochondrial/antioxidant gene expression, and protects against oxidative insults; PGC-1α dependence of cytoprotection has been demonstrated in ARPE-19 (Tong et al., 2022; Shu et al., 2021). In H-RPE, ZLN005 prevents TGFβ₂-induced EMT and migration, linking PGC-1α induction to preservation of epithelial phenotype and metabolic competence under stress (Shu et al., 2021). Based on these data, in RPE assays ZLN005 is expected to:

- Increase PGC-1α transcript/protein and downstream mitochondrial biogenesis (e.g., NRF1/TFAM/OXPHOS genes), raising basal/maximal respiration and spare capacity, and boosting ATP (Tong et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2020).  
- Lower ROS and improve mitochondrial membrane potential and structure, thereby reducing oxidative injury susceptibility (Tong et al., 2022; Ma et al., 2023).  
- Preserve epithelial features and reduce EMT/migration under profibrotic stress (TGFβ₂), maintaining RPE barrier function (Shu et al., 2021).

Hypothesized effects on lysosomes/TFEB/CTSD and phagosome clearance. The proposal posits that ZLN005 will “cooperate with TFEB to enhance lysosomal acidification and cathepsin D activity, thereby improving phagosome clearance” and that improved mito–lyso coupling will reduce lipofuscin. Available evidence supports the general biological framework—AMPK can activate TFEB/TFE3 and PGC-1α in parallel, PGC-1α/NRF2 promote mitochondrial homeostasis and antioxidant capacity in RPE, and TFEB activation restores lysosomal hydrolases and autophagic flux in diseased RPE—but there are no direct data that ZLN005 activates TFEB, increases lysosomal acidification, elevates cathepsin D activity, or enhances phagosome clearance in RPE (Boya et al., 2023; Ghosh et al., 2024; Tong et al., 2022; Shu et al., 2021). In fact, the TFEB-centric rescue of CTSD/LAMP1 and lysosome function in AMD-model RPE has been demonstrated with trehalose or genetic TFEB activation, not with ZLN005; therefore, any expectation that ZLN005 alone will enhance lysosomal acidification/CTSD or phagosome clearance is a plausible but unproven hypothesis that requires explicit testing with lysosomal pH probes, CTSD activity assays, and POS phagocytosis/phagosome clearance metrics in primary human RPE (Ghosh et al., 2024).

Important caveats for experimental design:  
- Reporter interference: ZLN005 inhibits luciferases and may confound TFEB/E-box luciferase or PGC-1α reporter assays; use non-luciferase readouts (e.g., immunoblots, qPCR, ChIP-qPCR, RNA-seq, proteomics, TFEB nuclear translocation imaging, LysoTracker/DQ-BSA/CTSD activity assays) (Zhang et al., 2013).  
- Primary vs cell line responsiveness: Primary H-RPE shows smaller PGC-1α fold-induction than ARPE-19 due to higher baseline PGC-1α; dosing windows and exposure times must be optimized in H-RPE to achieve functional gains without undue mitochondrial uncoupling (Shu et al., 2021).  
- Cross-talk assessment: If synergy with TFEB is a key aim, include a TFEB activator arm (e.g., trehalose) as comparator/combination and measure canonical TFEB outputs (CTSD/L, LAMP1/2, CLEAR network gene expression), while maintaining AMPK/mTORC1 pathway controls to dissect mechanism (Ghosh et al., 2024; Boya et al., 2023).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Direct RPE activity. ZLN005 selectively upregulates PGC-1α in ARPE-19 and primary H-RPE, enhances mitochondrial respiration, and protects ARPE-19 from oxidative stress in a PGC-1α-dependent manner; it also suppresses TGFβ₂-induced EMT/migration in H-RPE, linking mitochondrial competence to epithelial stability—both highly relevant to dry AMD pathophysiology (Tong et al., 2022; Shu et al., 2021).  
- Robust mitochondrial biogenesis/transcriptional program. Across cardiomyocytes, muscle, and lung epithelium, ZLN005 reproducibly induces PGC-1α and downstream transcriptional programs (NRF1/TFAM/OXPHOS/FAO), increasing mtDNA, OCR, and ATP, establishing a mechanistic basis for improving RPE mitochondrial deficits observed in dry AMD (Liu et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2013; Ma et al., 2023; Hyttinen et al., 2023).  
- Systems-level cytoprotection. In AKI and neuronal ischemia/toxicity models, ZLN005 reduces ROS and apoptosis, improves mitochondrial integrity, and requires key downstream effectors (CPT-1α in kidney), demonstrating that PGC-1α activation can translate to organ protection, which conceptually extends to RPE under oxidative/energetic stress (Wang et al., 2021; Xu et al., 2018; Tian et al., 2023).  
- Disease relevance of the target. Extensive genetic/pathophysiologic evidence places PGC-1α at the center of RPE mitochondrial biogenesis, antioxidant defense, and senescence control; PGC-1α or PGC-1α/NRF2 loss causes AMD-like degeneration, and AMPK→PGC-1α and NRF2/ARE axes are validated protective mechanisms in RPE (Felszeghy et al., 2019; Hyttinen et al., 2018; Hyttinen et al., 2023; Nita & Grzybowski, 2023).  
- Translational feasibility. ZLN005 has oral bioactivity with favorable metabolic endpoints in mice, rudimentary short-term rat safety, and a breadth of preclinical efficacy across tissues; it penetrates the CNS, implying some potential for ocular exposure via circulation, though eye PK is unknown (Zhang et al., 2013; Tian et al., 2023).

Limitations and risks  
- No direct evidence for TFEB/lysosomal activation by ZLN005. There are no data showing that ZLN005 increases TFEB activity, lysosomal acidification, cathepsin D activity, or phagosome clearance in RPE; TFEB-dependent improvements in lysosome function and CTSD have been demonstrated with other interventions (trehalose or genetic TFEB activation), not with ZLN005 (Ghosh et al., 2024; Tong et al., 2022; Shu et al., 2021). The hypothesized mito–lyso crosstalk is biologically plausible via AMPK signaling but remains to be demonstrated for this compound (Boya et al., 2023).  
- Potential pro-angiogenic signaling. PGC-1α/ERRα activation in RPE has been linked to VEGF upregulation under certain conditions; in a chronic retinal setting, inadvertent promotion of angiogenic signaling could be undesirable, especially near neovascular AMD thresholds; careful assessment of VEGF/angiogenic gene expression in RPE and choroid is warranted (Blasiak et al., 2021).  
- Dose window and uncoupling toxicity. ZLN005 acts at least partly via mild mitochondrial uncoupling to activate AMPK; while beneficial in moderation, uncoupling can exacerbate ROS and bioenergetic stress if overdosed; high ZLN005 concentrations were toxic in HK2 cells, underscoring the need for careful titration in primary H-RPE (Zhang et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2021).  
- Cell-type and species specificity. ZLN005 does not induce PGC-1α in primary hepatocytes and downregulated hepatic PGC-1α in db/db mice; responsiveness varies by cell context (e.g., smaller fold-change in H-RPE than ARPE-19), complicating dose translation and efficacy prediction in human RPE in vivo (Zhang et al., 2013; Shu et al., 2021).  
- Reporter assay interference. The compound inhibits luciferases; any reliance on luciferase readouts for PGC-1α or TFEB activity risks artifact and demands orthogonal assay confirmation (Zhang et al., 2013).  
- Ocular pharmacokinetics unknown. Oral PK demonstrates high liver exposure and moderate muscle exposure; there are no data on ocular distribution, RPE exposure, or retinal bioavailability, making formulation and dosing strategies for eye delivery an open question (Zhang et al., 2013).

Decision-critical gaps and suggested de-risking experiments  
- TFEB/lysosomal axis: Directly test whether ZLN005 increases TFEB nuclear translocation, CLEAR network gene expression, lysosomal pH acidification (ratiometric probes), CTSD/CTSL protein/activity, and autophagosome flux (LC3B-II/p62 turnover) in primary H-RPE; benchmark versus trehalose and/or genetic TFEB activation and evaluate additivity or synergy in ZLN005+trehalose combination, with AMPK/mTORC1 pathway readouts to mechanistically link signaling (Ghosh et al., 2024; Boya et al., 2023).  
- Phagosome processing: Quantify photoreceptor outer segment (POS) uptake and phagosome clearance kinetics, including cathepsin-dependent proteolysis and lipofuscinogenic adduct accumulation, under oxidative/complement stress ± ZLN005; include PGC-1α knockdown to confirm dependence (Tong et al., 2022; Felszeghy et al., 2019).  
- In vivo efficacy in AMD-relevant models: Test in complement/CFH risk allele iPSC-RPE xenograft or sodium iodate/aging mouse models focusing on RPE structure/function, lipofuscin proxies, sub-RPE deposit formation, and ERG endpoints; incorporate TFEB activation arms where possible to validate the dual-axis hypothesis (Ghosh et al., 2024; Luján et al., 2022).  
- Safety pharmacology: Titrate ZLN005 dosing in ocular delivery paradigms (intravitreal, periocular, or systemic) with eye PK, retinal/RPE exposure, retinal function (ERG), and VEGF expression profiling to exclude pro-angiogenic shifts; assess off-target mitochondrial stress at higher exposures in H-RPE (Blasiak et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2021).

Conclusion: fit for further evaluation with focused lysosome endpoints. ZLN005 has strong mechanistic and preclinical support as a PGC-1α activator that improves mitochondrial biogenesis and oxidative resilience in RPE and retina-adjacent systems, and it produces protective effects across diverse tissues via PGC-1α-dependent programs (Tong et al., 2022; Shu et al., 2021; Xu et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2021). However, the core elements of the present hypothesis—enhancement of TFEB activity, lysosomal acidification, cathepsin D activity, and phagosome clearance, plus reduction of lipofuscin and drusen—are not yet evidenced for ZLN005 and remain inferential based on pathway crosstalk (AMPK→TFEB/TFE3, PGC-1α–NRF2) and TFEB-targeted rescue in RPE by other agents (Boya et al., 2023; Ghosh et al., 2024). Consequently, ZLN005 is a promising mitochondrial-centric candidate for dry AMD that merits accelerated, targeted validation on lysosomal/phagosome endpoints and ocular delivery feasibility. The compound’s strengths—a validated mitochondrial biogenesis mechanism in RPE, demonstrated oxidative stress protection in ARPE-19, primary H-RPE EMT suppression, and broad cross-tissue efficacy—justify this investment, provided that the risks of off-target uncoupling, reporter assay interference, cell-type specificity, and potential pro-angiogenic signaling are actively managed in the experimental plan (Tong et al., 2022; Shu et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2013; Blasiak et al., 2021).

Candidate 1 (GSK126) is an EZH2 inhibitor with a well‐characterized MoA—competitive inhibition of the H3K27 methyltransferase—intended to derepress CLEAR network genes in RPE cells. Candidate 2 (Panobinostat) is a potent pan‐HDAC inhibitor that broadly increases histone and non‐histone acetylation, hypothesized to activate TFEB and enhance autophagy. Its clinical efficacy and detailed PK/safety data in oncology are robust, but systemic toxicity (thrombocytopenia, GI effects, QT prolongation) is significant. MoA is less specific to lysosomal gene repression and poses higher off‐target risk in nondividing RPE cells. Both require ocular delivery development and preclinical validation in RPE/AMD models. The evidence for EZH2’s role in AMD pathogenesis is weak, but the mechanistic rationale is more direct and potentially less toxic than broad HDAC inhibition.
Reasoning: GSK126 (Candidate 1) is favored because it offers a more targeted epigenetic approach—specific inhibition of EZH2 to relieve repression of lysosomal genes—minimizing the broad pleiotropic effects inherent to a pan‐HDAC inhibitor. It benefits from existing clinical safety and PK data, lowering development risk for repurposing. Although direct AMD data are currently absent, its mechanism aligns tightly with the core pathology of lysosomal failure in RPE cells. Panobinostat (Candidate 2) has stronger general efficacy in oncology but carries substantial systemic toxicity, less mechanistic specificity for lysosomal gene networks, and unknown ocular PK/toxicity, making it a higher‐risk candidate for dry AMD.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
GSK126 is a small‐molecule, synthetic compound originally developed as a selective inhibitor of the enhancer of zeste homolog 2 (EZH2) enzyme. As a S-adenosyl-L-methionine (SAM)-competitive inhibitor, GSK126 belongs to the class of epigenetic modulators that work by impairing the catalytic activity of EZH2, a methyltransferase that deposits H3K27me3 repressive marks on chromatin. These compounds were discovered and optimized initially for use in cancer, where aberrant EZH2 activity drives tumor progression through silencing of tumor suppressor genes. The chemical structure of GSK126 and its mode of synthesis have been well characterized in the oncology literature, and the compound has been extensively used in preclinical models and early phase clinical studies to assess its ability to relieve polycomb repressive complex 2 (PRC2)-mediated gene silencing (Shu et al., 2023, pp. 16–17). As such, GSK126 represents a prototypical member of a therapeutic class that has been used predominantly in oncology, with recent efforts to repurpose its epigenetic modulatory properties to other diseases where aberrant gene repression plays a role.

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, the development of EZH2 inhibitors such as GSK126 has been focused predominantly on oncological applications. Several clinical trials have evaluated EZH2 inhibitors in hematologic malignancies and solid tumors, where deregulated EZH2 activity supports cancer cell proliferation and survival. For example, while related compounds (e.g., GSK2816126) were investigated in dose escalation studies in patients with hematologic malignancies and solid tumors, GSK126 itself has been studied preclinically and in clinical contexts for its anti-proliferative effects in cancer models (GlaxoSmithKline, 2014). In addition, high-content screening initiatives in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells have identified EZH2 inhibitors among a range of epigenetic drug candidates, with studies reporting that GSK126 can upregulate p16 expression in RPE models as part of broader efforts to identify modulators of senescence (Coryell, 2019, pp. 48–53). However, there is no published record to date of GSK126 being deployed specifically for the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or for directly targeting lysosomal dysfunction in ocular tissues. Open Targets Platform data reveal a very weak association between EZH2 and AMD, with minimal documented evidence tying EZH2 activity directly to disease pathogenesis in the retina (Buniello et al., 2025). Thus, while extensive preclinical and clinical data substantiate the use of EZH2 inhibitors in cancer, their specific application to dry AMD remains an emerging hypothesis that has not yet been validated either in biochemical in vitro studies or in in vivo ocular models.

Mechanism of Action:  
The primary mechanism of action of GSK126 is based on its inhibition of EZH2 activity. EZH2 is the catalytic subunit of the polycomb repressive complex 2 (PRC2) that methylates lysine 27 on histone H3 (H3K27me3), a modification generally associated with transcriptional silencing of target genes. By competitively binding to the SAM-binding pocket of EZH2, GSK126 prevents the addition of methyl groups to H3K27, thereby reducing the global levels of H3K27me3 and leading to a derepression of genes normally silenced by this epigenetic mark (Shu et al., 2023, pp. 16–17). In cancer cells, this mechanism leads to reactivation of tumor suppressor genes such as p16, and similar findings have been observed in epigenetic drug screens using RPE cells where treatment with GSK126 resulted in upregulation of p16 expression (Coryell, 2019, pp. 48–53).

The repurposing hypothesis for dry AMD suggests that similar chromatin-level mechanisms could be exploited in RPE cells to relieve the suppression of the CLEAR (Coordinated Lysosomal Expression and Regulation) network, a collection of genes regulated by the master transcription factor TFEB responsible for lysosomal biogenesis and function. Under stress conditions, the epigenetic repression mediated by EZH2 via H3K27me3 may contribute to the diminished expression of lysosomal genes, including those coding for components of the acidification machinery such as vacuolar ATPase (V-ATPase) subunits and lysosomal proteases like cathepsin D (Abokyi & Tse, 2025, pp. 2–3; Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7). The rationale is that inhibition of EZH2 with GSK126 will alleviate H3K27me3 deposition at promoters of lysosomal genes, allowing TFEB to more effectively activate the transcription of these CLEAR genes. In cancer models, related observations have been made where EZH2 inhibition leads to increased expression of V-ATPase subunits and CTSD (cathepsin D) as well as enhancement of autophagy (Coryell, 2019, pp. 48–53; Shu et al., 2023, pp. 16–17, 22–23). Although most of these studies have been conducted in cancer or other non-ocular cell types, the underlying biochemical interactions between EZH2, histone modifications, and gene expression remain consistent and serve as the basis for the proposed mechanism in RPE cells. In summary, by reducing H3K27me3-mediated repression, GSK126 is expected to derepress genes that are essential for maintaining proper lysosomal acidification, proteolysis, and overall cell homeostasis, thereby addressing one potential pathogenic mechanism in dry AMD.

Expected Effect:  
The therapeutic hypothesis posits that in the context of dry AMD, RPE cells suffer from lysosomal dysfunction—manifested by aberrant acidification and insufficient activity of lysosomal proteases such as cathepsin D—that contributes to the accumulation of toxic protein aggregates and cellular debris. TFEB, a transcription factor known to drive the expression of the CLEAR network, plays a critical role in regulating lysosomal biogenesis and function. Notably, in aging retina and AMD, the activation of TFEB-mediated gene expression is impaired, leading to reduced levels of essential lysosomal enzymes and V-ATPase subunits, as well as the accumulation of lipofuscin-like material (Abokyi & Tse, 2025, pp. 9–10). The proposed effect of GSK126 in RPE cells is to inhibit EZH2 and relieve the epigenetic repression imposed by H3K27me3 at lysosomal gene promoters. This derepression should allow TFEB to more robustly activate the transcription of its target genes, thereby enhancing the expression of V-ATPase subunits and cathepsin D. Enhanced V-ATPase expression will improve lysosomal acidification—a key determinant of lysosome function—while increased levels of cathepsin D will bolster the degradative capacity of the lysosome. In other cellular contexts, such as in certain cancer cell lines, EZH2 inhibition has been shown to upregulate autophagy-related genes, including those involved in lysosomal function, which supports the plausibility of this mechanism in RPE cells (Shu et al., 2023, pp. 16–17; Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 13–15).

Given that RPE cells are highly metabolically active and rely on efficient lysosomal degradation for the phagocytosis and recycling of photoreceptor outer segments, the expected outcome of GSK126 treatment would be an improvement in lysosomal clearance. This improvement could translate into a reduction of the toxic protein aggregates and lipofuscin accumulation that are hallmarks of dry AMD pathology. In vitro, one would anticipate observing an increase in TFEB nuclear translocation, upregulation of CLEAR network genes, enhanced lysosomal acidification (as measured by V-ATPase activity) and restored cathepsin D levels in treated RPE cells, thereby validating the hypothesized mechanism (Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 17–18; Abokyi & Tse, 2025, pp. 3–4). In vivo, similar effects might lead to improved RPE function and a potentially slower progression of dry AMD. However, it is important to note that while there is evidence for the role of EZH2 in regulating p16 and autophagy in various models, direct evidence linking GSK126 treatment to restored lysosomal gene networks in RPE cells remains to be generated.

Overall Evaluation:  
The proposal to repurpose GSK126 for dry AMD represents an innovative application of epigenetic therapy beyond its established role in oncology. One of the major strengths of this candidate is the robust preclinical and clinical safety data that have been accumulated in cancer studies. The availability of dosing and pharmacokinetic profiles from oncology clinical trials offers a significant advantage in terms of de-risking the development timeline for repurposing efforts (GlaxoSmithKline, 2014; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.). Moreover, the mechanistic rationale is scientifically sound: EZH2 is a well-characterized repressor of gene transcription via H3K27me3, and its inhibition could indeed lead to the derepression of genes critical for lysosomal maintenance (Abokyi & Tse, 2025, pp. 2–3; Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7).

However, there are several weaknesses and uncertainties that must be addressed. First, despite the compelling mechanistic hypothesis, there is a paucity of direct evidence demonstrating that EZH2 inhibition in RPE cells leads to upregulation of lysosomal genes, specifically those involved in the acidification machinery and cathepsin D expression (Coryell, 2019, pp. 48–53). Second, comprehensive target-disease association analyses using platforms such as Open Targets reveal a very weak connection between EZH2 and AMD, which raises the possibility that EZH2’s role in the pathogenesis of dry AMD may be limited, or that other compensatory pathways might diminish the impact of EZH2 inhibition in the retinal environment (Buniello et al., 2025). Third, while studies in cancer cell lines have indicated that EZH2 inhibition can upregulate V-ATPase subunits and lysosomal enzyme expression, cancer cells and RPE cells exhibit markedly different epigenetic landscapes and stress responses; therefore, extrapolation from oncology models to the RPE must be approached with caution (Shu et al., 2023, pp. 20–21, 22–23).

Furthermore, targeting epigenetic regulators always carries the risk of off-target effects since these enzymes regulate the expression of a broad spectrum of genes. In the context of the retina—an organ with complex cellular interdependencies—the potential for unintended consequences on RPE differentiation, survival, or interactions with photoreceptors must be thoroughly evaluated prior to clinical translation (Abokyi & Tse, 2025, pp. 7–8; Ferret, 2024, pp. 171–173).

Another point of consideration is the durability of the epigenetic modification induced by EZH2 inhibition. While durable enhancement of lysosomal capacity through chromatin-level changes is an attractive prospect, the reversibility and specificity of these modifications in the context of chronic degenerative diseases like dry AMD remain uncertain. It will be crucial to determine whether the epigenetic changes induced by GSK126 are sustained over time in RPE cells and whether they translate to meaningful improvements in visual function or retinal integrity in preclinical models.

From a translational perspective, the repurposing strategy for GSK126 should include comprehensive in vitro studies using RPE cell lines and primary cultures, with endpoints that directly assess lysosomal acidification, cathepsin D activity, and clearance of photoreceptor outer segment debris. Furthermore, in vivo studies in animal models of dry AMD are needed to evaluate whether EZH2 inhibition can restore lysosomal function and slow disease progression under physiologically relevant conditions (Abokyi & Tse, 2025, pp. 2–3, 9–10). Comparative studies with other epigenetic modulators and TFEB activators could also provide context regarding the relative efficacy of GSK126 in reactivating the CLEAR network.

In conclusion, the repurposing of GSK126 for dry AMD is a promising, yet exploratory, approach that leverages a clear mechanistic hypothesis: by inhibiting EZH2, GSK126 may relieve repressive histone marks at lysosomal gene promoters, thereby promoting TFEB-driven transcription of genes essential for lysosomal acidification and proteolytic activity. This approach could conceivably ameliorate the lysosomal defects observed in RPE cells in dry AMD. The strengths of this candidate lie in its well-defined molecular target, its established clinical safety profile in oncology studies, and the potential for a durable, chromatin-level correction of lysosomal dysfunction. However, significant challenges remain, including the need for direct evidence linking EZH2 inhibition to enhancements in the CLEAR gene network within RPE cells, the potential off-target effects inherent to epigenetic therapies, and the overall weak association between EZH2 and AMD pathogenesis as indicated by current target-disease databases.

Given these considerations, while the mechanistic rationale is robust and the repurposing strategy innovative, the current level of evidence is insufficient for immediate clinical application. It is imperative that future research generate direct preclinical data in ocular models of dry AMD to confirm that GSK126 can, in fact, restore lysosomal function in RPE cells via TFEB activation and increased cathepsin D and V-ATPase expression. Further investigation should also focus on clarifying the broader gene expression changes induced by GSK126 in RPE cells to ensure that the desired effects on lysosomal pathways are achieved without detrimental off-target consequences.

The forthcoming research should aim to delineate the dose-response relationships, optimize delivery to the ocular compartment, and ensure that sustained improvements in lysosomal capacity correlate with clinical endpoints relevant to AMD progression (Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 13–15; Sharif, 2015, pp. 68–72; Ferret, 2024, pp. 103–106).

In summary, while the repurposing of GSK126 for dry AMD is conceptually attractive and supported by a reasonable mechanistic framework, the endeavor is in its nascent stages. The existing literature does not yet provide direct evidence that GSK126 elicits the specific lysosomal benefits hypothesized in RPE cells. As such, this candidate represents a high-risk, high-reward opportunity that merits further in-depth investigation through rigorous preclinical studies, with a view toward eventual clinical translation if the mechanistic hypotheses are confirmed (Coryell, 2019, pp. 48–53; Sharif, 2015, pp. 68–72).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Panobinostat (LBH589) is a fully synthetic small‐molecule compound originally developed by Novartis and characterized chemically as a cinnamic hydroxamic acid analogue formulated as its anhydrous lactate salt. This molecule belongs to the hydroxamate class of histone deacetylase inhibitors (HDACi), a group of compounds designed to inhibit the enzymatic activity of HDACs that regulate chromatin remodeling and transcription by catalyzing the removal of acetyl groups from histone proteins. Panobinostat’s chemical structure, defined by its hydroxamic acid moiety, is tailored to chelate the zinc ion in the catalytic domain of HDAC enzymes, thereby preventing deacetylation reactions that normally lead to a condensed chromatin state. In its initial development, panobinostat was formulated in multiple dosage forms, including oral hard capsules containing 10, 15, or 20 mg doses and earlier intravenous preparations, illustrating its versatility in administration routes for different clinical indications (Van Veggel, Westerman, & Hamberg, 2018; Libby et al., 2015; Dokmanovic, Clarke, & Marks, 2007). Compounds of this class have historically been employed in oncology, where their capacity to induce hyperacetylation of histone and non-histone substrates leads to altered gene transcription, cell cycle arrest, differentiation, and eventual apoptosis in malignant cells (Van Veggel et al., 2018; Cea et al., 2013). Moreover, the broad-spectrum inhibition of HDAC isoforms—spanning Classes I, II, and IV—distinguishes panobinostat as a “pan-HDAC inhibitor” with high potency at nanomolar concentrations, a characteristic that underlies its robust pharmacological profile and its subsequent regulatory approvals for certain cancer indications (Morabito et al., 2016).

Therapeutic History:  
Since its discovery, panobinostat has undergone extensive preclinical and clinical evaluation primarily targeting multiple myeloma and various hematologic malignancies. Early phase clinical trials established that, as a single agent, panobinostat had modest activity; however, its combination with proteasome inhibitors such as bortezomib and corticosteroids like dexamethasone produced synergistic effects that translated into significant improvements in progression‐free survival in relapsed and refractory multiple myeloma patients. This positive clinical efficacy culminated in its approval by both the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and the European Medicines Agency (EMA) in 2015 for the treatment of patients with multiple myeloma who had received at least two prior regimens (Van Veggel et al., 2018; Libby et al., 2015; Bondarev et al., 2021). Beyond multiple myeloma, panobinostat has been scrutinized in a variety of clinical settings—including cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, acute myeloid leukemia, diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, and several solid tumor malignancies—to explore its antitumor potential in combination therapies, given its capacity to potentiate the cytotoxic effects of other agents by modulating epigenetic regulation (Cea et al., 2013; Cinek & Karalı, 2021; Libby et al., 2015). Despite its demonstrated efficacy in cancer, there is no recorded use of panobinostat in ophthalmological diseases such as dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or in any similar degenerative condition. The extensive body of clinical research on HDAC inhibitors has predominantly focused on antineoplastic applications, and while some mechanistic parallels exist between the cellular processes targeted in cancer and those disrupted in degenerative retinal diseases, panobinostat’s utility in dry AMD remains an uncharted territory that has thus far not been explored in preclinical or clinical trials (Dokmanovic, Clarke, & Marks, 2007; Morabito et al., 2016; Libby et al., 2015).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, panobinostat exerts its biological effects primarily through the inhibition of histone deacetylase enzymes. The compound’s hydroxamic acid group binds with high affinity to the zinc ion located in the catalytic domain of HDAC enzymes, thereby blocking the deacetylation of lysine residues on histone tails as well as on several non-histone proteins. This blockade causes an accumulation of acetylated histones, which in turn results in a more open chromatin conformation that facilitates enhanced transcription of a multitude of genes, including those pivotal for cell cycle arrest, apoptosis, and cellular differentiation (Benedetti, Conte, & Altucci, 2015; Morabito et al., 2016). Beyond its classical role in modifying histone tail acetylation, panobinostat’s broad inhibition across HDAC classes implies that it can modulate the acetylation status of key transcription factors, chaperone proteins (such as heat shock protein 90), and structural proteins like α-tubulin. This wide-ranging impact on protein acetylation alters the functional activity of numerous signaling pathways and cellular processes, contributing to anti-proliferative and pro-apoptotic outcomes in cancer cells (Morabito et al., 2016). The pleiotropic nature of its action is further evidenced by the induction of autophagy in various tumor models, an effect thought to be mediated by the increased acetylation and transcriptional activation of master regulators of lysosomal biogenesis such as transcription factor EB (TFEB). Although the provided literature does not explicitly detail TFEB upregulation in response to panobinostat, the general tendency of HDAC inhibitors to enhance acetylation-dependent transcription supports the hypothesis that TFEB and its downstream lysosomal genes could be upregulated—thereby promoting autophagy and lysosomal clearance pathways (Cinek & Karalı, 2021; Libby et al., 2015). This complex interplay of molecular events not only underpins panobinostat’s established antitumor activity but also provides a rationale for its possible repurposing in degenerative diseases where enhanced cellular clearance mechanisms may be therapeutic (Van Veggel et al., 2018; Benedetti, Conte, & Altucci, 2015).

Expected Effect in Dry Age-Related Macular Degeneration (AMD):  
Dry age-related macular degeneration is characterized by the progressive dysfunction of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), which is responsible for the maintenance of photoreceptor health and the clearance of cellular debris. A central pathological hallmark of dry AMD is the accumulation of drusen deposits beneath the RPE, partly attributable to impaired lysosomal degradation and autophagy. In the context of this disease, the hypothesis proposes that localized ocular administration of panobinostat could inhibit HDAC activity in RPE cells, leading to a global increase in histone acetylation. This epigenetic modulation is expected to activate acetylation-dependent transcription factors such as TFEB—a master regulator of lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy—that, once activated, upregulates a network of genes involved in lysosomal acidification and cathepsin D expression (Van Veggel et al., 2018; Cinek & Karalı, 2021). Enhanced expression of these lysosomal components is anticipated to restore or improve the degradative capacity of the RPE, facilitating the clearance of drusen deposits and ameliorating the pathological buildup of cellular waste characteristic of dry AMD.

In preclinical oncology studies, panobinostat has consistently induced autophagy and promoted lysosomal function in cancer cells, leading to growth inhibition and apoptosis. The expression of cathepsin D—a lysosomal protease critical for the degradation of photoreceptor outer segments and other metabolic substrates—is well documented in RPE cells, and its activity is tightly regulated by lysosomal pH; thus, any intervention that improves lysosomal acidification is likely to have a favorable impact on RPE homeostasis (Mottamal et al., 2015; Morabito et al., 2016). These findings support the proposed mechanism whereby panobinostat’s inhibition of HDACs may indirectly enhance the transcriptional activation of TFEB, culminating in improved lysosomal biogenesis and function. This targeted approach aligns with current trends in ocular pharmacotherapy, which increasingly favor local drug delivery systems designed to maximize therapeutic efficacy while minimizing systemic toxicity (Bondarev et al., 2021; Van Veggel et al., 2018). Ultimately, the expected outcome in the proposed assay is that panobinostat treatment will lead to measurable upregulation of lysosomal gene expression, restoration of lysosomal acidification, and enhanced activity of cathepsin D within RPE cells, thereby reducing the burden of drusen deposits and potentially slowing the progression of dry AMD (Cea et al., 2013; Libby et al., 2015).

Overall Evaluation:  
The repurposing of panobinostat for dry age-related macular degeneration presents an intriguing and biologically plausible strategy that leverages the compound’s well-documented HDAC inhibitory properties to modulate critical intracellular degradation pathways. One of the foremost strengths of this therapeutic candidate is its potent, broad-spectrum inhibition of HDAC enzymes at low nanomolar concentrations, which has been repeatedly demonstrated in various preclinical and clinical studies in oncology (Van Veggel et al., 2018; Morabito et al., 2016). The resultant hyperacetylation of histones and non-histone proteins not only promotes cell cycle arrest and apoptosis in malignant cells but also facilitates the transcriptional activation of autophagy- and lysosome-related genes—a pathway that could be harnessed to restore faithful lysosomal degradation in retinal pigment epithelial cells affected in dry AMD (Benedetti, Conte, & Altucci, 2015; Cinek & Karalı, 2021).

In terms of mechanistic specificity, the broad inhibitory profile of panobinostat could be seen as an advantage in the context of dry AMD, where multiple deacetylation pathways may contribute to the impaired clearance of cellular debris. By simultaneously inhibiting several HDAC isoforms, panobinostat is likely to achieve a more robust activation of TFEB and other transcription factors central to lysosomal biogenesis, thereby amplifying the cellular clearance mechanisms required to remove drusen deposits (Morabito et al., 2016; Carafa, Nebbioso, & Altucci, 2011). Additionally, the existing clinical experience with panobinostat in oncology provides a rich repository of pharmacokinetic, pharmacodynamic, and safety data that can inform dose optimization and risk management strategies—albeit with the caveat that ocular tissues may respond differently to HDAC inhibition than cancer cells (Bondarev et al., 2021; Libby et al., 2015).

Nevertheless, several significant weaknesses must be acknowledged in evaluating panobinostat as a candidate for dry AMD treatment. Chief among these is the potential for systemic toxicity. Panobinostat’s clinical utilization in cancer has been limited by adverse side effects including gastrointestinal toxicity, thrombocytopenia, and cardiac complications, and although localized ocular delivery may attenuate these concerns, the safety profile of panobinostat in retinal tissues remains largely unexplored (Libby et al., 2015; Karol et al., 2020). Moreover, the pharmacokinetic behavior of panobinostat when administered locally to the eye is unknown; challenges such as drug solubility, stability, and diffusion across retinal layers must be addressed rigorously in preclinical models. Another point of concern is the translational leap from oncology to ophthalmology. While the mechanistic rationale for using panobinostat to enhance autophagy and lysosomal function is supported by its effects in cancer cells, RPE cells possess distinctive metabolic and regulatory pathways that may not respond identically to HDAC inhibition. The degree to which TFEB and other autophagy or lysosomal genes are modulated by panobinostat in RPE cells has not yet been directly demonstrated, and significant differences in chromatin structure and gene expression profiles between cancer cells and differentiated RPE cells could impact both efficacy and safety outcomes (Morabito et al., 2016; Carafa, Nebbioso, & Altucci, 2011). In addition, the chronic nature of dry AMD necessitates long-term treatment, and the potential cumulative effects of continuous HDAC inhibition in ocular tissues raise concerns regarding retinal integrity, visual function, and overall ocular health over extended periods—a consideration that remains entirely speculative without targeted preclinical studies (Dokmanovic, Clarke, & Marks, 2007; Morabito et al., 2016).

From a drug development perspective, the strategy of repurposing panobinostat for dry AMD is compelling because it integrates a well-characterized molecular mode of action with an unmet clinical need. However, critical translational challenges must be overcome. These include reformulating panobinostat for localized ocular delivery, establishing appropriate dosing regimens that maximize local efficacy while minimizing toxicity, and conducting comprehensive preclinical evaluations in relevant in vitro and in vivo models of dry AMD. The potential benefit of enhancing lysosomal clearance through increased TFEB activation is a particularly attractive aspect of this proposal, as impaired autophagy and lysosomal dysfunction are recognized contributors to the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Cinek & Karalı, 2021; Morabito et al., 2016). On the positive side, panobinostat is among the most potent HDAC inhibitors available, capable of eliciting profound changes in gene expression that might restore lysosomal function in RPE cells and thereby clear accumulated drusen deposits. In addition, modern advances in ocular drug delivery—such as intravitreal injections, biodegradable implants, or topical formulations enhanced by nanocarrier systems—offer promising routes to achieve the necessary drug concentrations in the retina while mitigating systemic exposure and toxicity (Van Veggel et al., 2018; Morabito et al., 2016).

Conversely, the risk of adverse effects related to HDAC inhibition, the unknown ocular pharmacokinetics, and the potential differences in cellular responses between cancerous and retinal cells represent significant hurdles that must be rigorously addressed through targeted preclinical research. Furthermore, given that panobinostat’s clinical track record is largely confined to oncology, its application in a degenerative ocular disease such as dry AMD would require new, dedicated studies to validate its safety, efficacy, and optimal delivery modality in this context (Libby et al., 2015; Afifi et al., 2015).

Overall, panobinostat emerges as a promising yet challenging candidate for repurposing in dry age‐related macular degeneration. Its ability to robustly inhibit multiple HDAC isoforms and thereby potentially activate TFEB and lysosomal gene networks aligns well with the therapeutic strategy of improving autophagic clearance in RPE cells. However, substantial gaps in knowledge remain regarding its direct effects on retinal cells and the feasibility of its long-term use in an ocular setting. Consequently, while the mechanistic rationale is strong and the preclinical evidence from oncology provides useful insights, extensive additional research is needed to assess the translational potential, determine safe and efficacious ocular dosing parameters, and ultimately validate this approach in models that reliably mimic the pathophysiology of dry AMD (Prince et al., 2009; Morabito et al., 2016; Benedetti, Conte, & Altucci, 2015; Bondarev et al., 2021).

In conclusion, panobinostat’s repurposing for dry AMD is grounded in a robust understanding of epigenetic regulation and lysosomal biology. Its established clinical use in oncology offers a wealth of pharmacological data and a precedent for potent HDAC inhibition, while the hypothesis that HDAC inhibitors can reactivate latent clearance pathways in RPE cells is both innovative and scientifically plausible. The strengths of panobinostat lie in its potency, broad-spectrum activity, and documented ability to elicit autophagic responses, which collectively suggest that, under the right conditions and with a carefully optimized ocular delivery system, it could address one of the major pathophysiological mechanisms underlying dry AMD. Nonetheless, the weaknesses, including potential off-target toxicity, uncertain ocular pharmacokinetics, and the need for a comprehensive reevaluation of its effects in non-malignant, differentiated cell types, must be thoroughly investigated before advancing into clinical studies. Therefore, data from directed preclinical experiments employing RPE cell cultures and animal models of dry AMD will be essential in determining whether the benefits of panobinostat can be safely and effectively harnessed to treat this common cause of vision loss in the elderly (Srinivas, 2017; Van Veggel et al., 2018; Bondarev et al., 2021; Carafa, Nebbioso, & Altucci, 2011).

At the molecular level, the mechanism of action of recombinant human pro-cathepsin D is rooted in its ability to restore lysosomal proteolytic function, which is often impaired in disease states such as dry AMD. Preclinical in vitro data have demonstrated that pharmacological inhibition of AKT using MK-2206 leads to decreased AKT phosphorylation, increased nuclear TFEB localization, and enhanced autophagy flux in RPE, rescuing some of the defects observed in these models (Karim et al., 2020). Although MK-2206 per se has not been directly tested in animal models of AMD, related preclinical evidence based on the modulation of the AKT–TFEB axis in RPE supports its potential utility in the AMD context (Karim et al., 2020). In addition, several patent reviews have discussed MK-2206 within the broader portfolio of AKT inhibitors that are being repurposed for indications beyond oncology, further reinforcing the plausibility of using MK-2206 to target cellular pathways implicated in AMD (Guo et al., 2021).

─────────────────────────────  
Mechanism of Action  
─────────────────────────────  
The established mechanism of MK-2206 is anchored in its ability to inhibit AKT signaling through an allosteric mechanism. Under normal conditions, the AKT kinase is activated by phosphorylation events – typically at threonine 308 and serine 473 – in response to upstream signals from receptor tyrosine kinases and phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K) pathways. AKT then phosphorylates a wide range of substrates that control cell survival, growth, and metabolism. One of the downstream effects of activated AKT is the phosphorylation of TFEB (and possibly other MiT/TFE family members such as TFE3) at specific serine residues (for example, S467). This phosphorylation event hampers TFEB’s capacity to translocate from the cytosol to the nucleus, thereby repressing its transcriptional activity on the CLEAR (Coordinated Lysosomal Expression and Regulation) network, a gene set that drives lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy (Karim et al., 2020).

MK-2206 exerts its effect by binding to an allosteric site on AKT, a mode of inhibition that distinguishes it from ATP‐competitive inhibitors. In doing so, it reduces the phosphorylation of AKT at Ser473, thereby lowering its kinase activity (Karim et al., 2020). In RPE cells – particularly under pathogenic conditions such as immunoproteasome deficiency that leads to AKT hyper‐phosphorylation – MK-2206 administration has been shown to result in a marked decrease in AKT activity. This decrease, in turn, permits the dephosphorylation of TFEB, facilitating its nuclear import (Karim et al., 2020). Once in the nucleus, TFEB upregulates the transcription of genes involved in lysosomal function, autophagosome formation, and the expression of critical enzymes such as cathepsin D and components of the V-ATPase, which are necessary for maintaining lysosomal acidification (Karim et al., 2020).

Although the research cited does not explicitly verify isoform‐specific inhibition of AKT2 by MK-2206, the underlying hypothesis – that AKT2 hyperactivity in RPE suppresses TFEB nuclear localization – provides a strong rationale for repurposing MK-2206 in AMD. Some studies have proposed that AKT2, among the three isoforms, may predominantly drive the inflammatory and autophagy‐related deficits encountered in RPE in AMD models (Ghosh et al., 2019). This hypothesis is further supported by evidence showing that AKT2 inhibition can attenuate inflammatory cascades (such as IFNλ–LCN-2–driven neutrophil infiltration) that contribute to early RPE pathology (Ghosh et al., 2019). Thus, the mechanism of action of MK-2206 – namely, its ability to allosterically inhibit AKT activity leading to increased nuclear translocation of TFEB and subsequent upregulation of lysosomal/autophagy pathways – directly addresses key pathobiological mechanisms implicated in dry AMD.

─────────────────────────────  
Expected Effect  
─────────────────────────────  
Based on the hypothesis under review, the administration of MK-2206 to RPE cells is expected to yield several critical downstream effects that are therapeutically desirable in the context of dry AMD. First, MK-2206 should decrease the hyper‐phosphorylation of AKT observed in stressed or disease‐impacted RPE, which is thought to be a major contributing factor to the suppression of TFEB nuclear localization in these cells (Karim et al., 2020). By relieving this inhibitory phosphorylation, MK-2206 should facilitate the dephosphorylation and subsequent nuclear translocation of TFEB. Once TFEB is allowed to enter the nucleus, it can promote the transcription of a broad array of genes responsible for lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy, including those involved in the expression of vacuolar H-ATPase (V-ATPase) components and cathepsin D (CTSD) (Karim et al., 2020).

The restoration of nuclear TFEB activity is expected to lead to several beneficial cellular effects. In the RPE – which relies on robust autophagy for the clearance of photoreceptor outer segments and maintenance of cellular homeostasis – enhanced TFEB‐driven gene expression should improve lysosomal acidification and enzymatic activity, including that of cathepsin D (a key lysosomal protease) (Karim et al., 2020). Improved lysosomal acidification is critical for the maturation and function of cathepsin D, which in turn is essential for the degradation of protein aggregates and lipofuscin. Since drusen and lipofuscin accumulation represent major pathological hallmarks of dry AMD, the normalization of cathepsin D function could help to clear these toxic deposits, potentially slowing or reversing disease progression (Karim et al., 2020; Ghosh et al., 2019).

Furthermore, other reports suggest that AKT activation in RPE not only hinders autophagy but also promotes pro‐inflammatory pathways that contribute to tissue degeneration (Ghosh et al., 2019). Thus, the inhibition of AKT signaling by MK-2206 is anticipated to diminish such inflammatory cascades (Ghosh et al., 2019). In aggregate, the expected net effect is a re‐establishment of cellular proteostasis within the RPE via two interrelated mechanisms: (1) an enhancement of autophagic flux and lysosomal clearance via the TFEB pathway, and (2) a reduction in deleterious inflammatory and stress responses mediated by aberrant AKT2 signaling. Given that RPE dysfunction, lipofuscin accumulation, and drusen formation underlie the pathogenesis of dry AMD, MK-2206 could thereby serve to counteract disease progression at a mechanistic level (Karim et al., 2020).

─────────────────────────────  
Overall Evaluation  
─────────────────────────────  
In evaluating MK-2206 as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, several key points emerge. On the strength side, MK-2206 is a well-characterized small-molecule allosteric inhibitor of the AKT pathway – a pathway increasingly implicated in the regulation of autophagy and lysosomal function in RPE cells. Preclinical studies in immunoproteasome-deficient RPE have demonstrated that MK-2206 can inhibit AKT phosphorylation, restore nuclear TFEB localization, and promote autophagic flux (Karim et al., 2020). This mechanistic link is especially relevant, as dry AMD is characterized by reduced autophagy, impaired lysosomal clearance, and resultant accumulation of drusen and lipofuscin. Moreover, the rationale that AKT2 hyperactivity in RPE cells suppresses TFEB function – thereby weakening the cell’s proteolytic capacity – is well supported by the available preclinical data (Ghosh et al., 2019). In addition, MK-2206 has already been through several Phase I oncology trials, meaning that its safety and pharmacokinetic profiles are largely established in humans, which dramatically de-risks its repurposing for a different indication such as AMD (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2008; 2010). This could accelerate the clinical development timeline, as much of the initial toxicity and dosing work has been completed.

Nonetheless, there are several challenges and potential weaknesses to be addressed. First, while the available studies support that MK-2206 can modulate the AKT–TFEB axis in RPE cells under preclinical conditions, many of these studies do not provide isoform‐specific data; our hypothesis hinges on the idea that AKT2 is the critical isoform to be inhibited. MK-2206 is generally described as a pan-AKT inhibitor, which means that it may also affect AKT1 and AKT3. The lack of isoform specificity could lead to unanticipated off-target effects or impact cellular processes in non-RPE tissues if systemic exposure is not tightly controlled (Karim et al., 2020). Second, although the mechanism of promoting nuclear TFEB activity through AKT inhibition is conceptually sound and supported by cellular data, direct measurements of downstream endpoints critical to AMD – such as lysosomal acidification (e.g., via V-ATPase activity assays) and cathepsin D maturation or activity – are limited or indirect in the current literature (Karim et al., 2020). Without robust evidence that MK-2206 improves these specific lysosomal functions in RPE cells, the link between restored autophagy and actual therapeutic benefit in terms of drusen clearance remains inferential. Third, previous clinical development of MK-2206 in oncology has encountered variable efficacy when used as a monotherapy, prompting its evaluation predominantly in combination regimens (Guo et al., 2021; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2009). The implications of these findings for a non‐oncologic, degenerative condition such as AMD are not straightforward, and careful attention must be paid to optimizing both delivery routes (for example, local versus systemic administration) and dosing strategies that are tailored to the ocular microenvironment.

Furthermore, while the literature provides a strong rationale linking AKT hyperactivation to impaired autophagy in RPE, dry AMD is a multifactorial disease with complex pathophysiology that includes oxidative stress, inflammation, and genetic risk factors such as CFH variants. It is not yet fully clear whether correcting the autophagy defect alone will suffice to produce clinically meaningful outcomes in all patients with dry AMD. In addition, toxicity concerns must be carefully revisited: although MK-2206’s safety profile is defined in the context of oncology, potential ocular toxicity – such as RPE cell toxicity, off-target retinal effects, or interference with normal retinal cellular turnover – must be rigorously evaluated via dedicated preclinical ocular studies before clinical translation. Finally, the intellectual property and regulatory landscape for repurposing a cancer drug to treat an ocular disease will require further scrutiny, although the existing clinical data on MK-2206 do provide an important head-start compared to wholly novel compounds (Guo et al., 2021; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2009).

In summary, the strengths of MK-2206 as a candidate for repurposing in dry AMD include:  
• A well-characterized mechanism of action that aligns with pathobiological insights from RPE autophagy studies, namely the inhibition of aberrant AKT signaling leading to enhanced nuclear TFEB activity and autophagy restoration (Karim et al., 2020).  
• Established clinical safety and PK data from multiple Phase I oncology trials, which reduce translational risk and may accelerate repurposing efforts (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2008; 2010).  
• A plausible hypothesis that links AKT2 hyperactivity in RPE (observed in CFH-risk models and immunoproteasome-deficient systems) to lysosomal dysfunction, drusen accumulation, and ultimately, AMD pathology (Ghosh et al., 2019).

Conversely, potential weaknesses include:  
• Limited evidence regarding isoform specificity toward AKT2, as MK-2206 is generally considered a pan-AKT inhibitor, which may inadvertently modulate other AKT isoforms and lead to systemic side effects (Karim et al., 2020).  
• Incomplete preclinical data linking MK-2206 directly to improvements in lysosomal acidification and cathepsin D activity in RPE, which remain key therapeutic endpoints predicted to counteract drusen formation (Karim et al., 2020).  
• The challenge of adapting systemic dosing regimens used in oncology to the ocular setting, where achieving therapeutic retinal concentrations without causing off-target toxicity is paramount (Guo et al., 2021; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2009).  
• The multifactorial nature of dry AMD that may require combination approaches, meaning that modulation of the AKT–TFEB axis alone might not be sufficient to achieve robust clinical benefit in all patients.

Overall, MK-2206 represents a promising candidate to repurpose for dry AMD based on its ability to allosterically inhibit AKT, a central node in a pathway that has been implicated in RPE autophagy and lysosomal dysfunction. The preclinical rationale – that inhibition of AKT releases the block on TFEB nuclear translocation, thereby improving lysosomal acidification and cathepsin D activity – is well founded in the literature (Karim et al., 2020). Moreover, the favorable clinical safety profile gleaned from its extensive evaluation in oncology serves as an important asset when considering repurposing strategies. However, critical questions remain regarding isoform specificity, the optimal route and dosing for ocular application, and whether restoring autophagy via this pathway is sufficient to reverse or halt the progression of dry AMD in patients. Future studies should focus on establishing robust preclinical data in AMD-relevant animal models —including direct measures of lysosomal acidification, cathepsin D function, and drusen clearance —as well as refining ocular delivery strategies that minimize systemic exposure. Addressing these gaps will be essential for de-risking MK-2206’s application in the AMD setting and for paving the way toward clinical trials specifically targeting the AKT–TFEB pathway in the context of retinal degeneration.

─────────────────────────────  
Conclusion  
─────────────────────────────  
In conclusion, our comprehensive literature review supports the repurposing of MK-2206 for dry AMD on the following grounds: it is a well‐studied allosteric AKT inhibitor with a known safety profile from Phase I oncology trials; preclinical investigations in RPE models implicate AKT hyperactivation in the suppression of TFEB nuclear localization and consequent lysosomal dysfunction; and mechanistic hypotheses derived from these models suggest that inhibiting AKT (and, by extension, AKT2) can restore autophagy, improve lysosomal acidification, boost cathepsin D activity, and potentially counteract drusen accumulation – a key driver of dry AMD pathology. While challenges remain, particularly with respect to isoform selectivity and the translation of dosing paradigms from oncology to ocular applications, the existing data provide a strong rationale for advancing MK-2206 into more focused preclinical studies for dry AMD. Such work should include detailed analyses of lysosomal pH, cathepsin D activity, and the overall impact on RPE proteostasis in in vivo models that recapitulate the human disease. With these additional studies, MK-2206 could emerge as a viable candidate in our therapeutic pipeline for addressing the unmet need in dry AMD (Karim et al., 2020; Ghosh et al., 2019; Guo et al., 2021).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Nicotinamide riboside (NR), marketed as ChromaDex Niagen, belongs to the vitamin B3 family and is a naturally occurring precursor of nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+). Originally discovered in trace amounts in milk and other food sources, NR has been isolated and subsequently synthesized to yield a high‐purity form for nutritional and pharmaceutical applications. As a member of a class of compounds designed to elevate intracellular NAD+ levels, NR has attracted significant attention in the fields of metabolism, aging, and neuroprotection. Its chemical structure—a combination of a nicotinamide moiety bound to ribose—enables it to enter salvage pathways in cells with minimal metabolic conversion losses. In this regard, NR is comparable to other NAD+ boosters such as nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN), though differences in bioavailability and cellular transporter expression have been noted in some studies. Preclinical research has documented retinal distribution of NR in rodent models, suggesting that it reaches ocular tissues in pharmacologically relevant concentrations, an essential prerequisite for any agent intended to treat dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) (Abokyi & Tse, 2025; Braidy et al., 2019).

Therapeutic History:  
NR has been extensively investigated for its potential to modulate cellular energy metabolism and mitigate the effects of aging in diverse tissues. Early studies revealed that supplementation with NR effectively elevates NAD+ levels in multiple cell types, including neurons, skeletal muscle, and retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells, thereby enhancing mitochondrial function and cellular stress resistance (Dovijarski, 2019; Pîrvu et al., 2021). In the context of ocular research, while much of the direct experimental work has been performed using NMN, the close biochemical relationship between NMN and NR—as NAD+ precursors—has led investigators to propose that NR could produce similar outcomes in RPE cells. Models of retinal degeneration, including glaucoma and optic nerve injury, have demonstrated that NAD+ boosting via NR administration can ameliorate mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress, indirectly supporting its potential repurposing for dry AMD (Kitaoka et al., 2020; Mehmel et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2024). Moreover, clinical studies investigating NR’s safety in humans have shown that it is well tolerated at doses that elevate systemic NAD+ levels; doses in the gram-range have been employed without significant adverse effects (Jadeja et al., 2020). Although direct clinical trials targeting dry AMD are still forthcoming, the overall therapeutic history of NR—encompassing robust preclinical ocular benefit across neurodegenerative models and a favorable safety profile in human subjects—strongly supports further investigation for eye diseases where NAD+ depletion is a central pathophysiological feature (Dovijarski, 2019; Braidy et al., 2019; Pîrvu et al., 2021).

Mechanism of Action:  
The proposed mechanism of NR in dry AMD centers on its capacity to elevate intracellular NAD+ levels, thereby fueling a cascade of beneficial biochemical events. After cell entry, NR is phosphorylated by nicotinamide riboside kinases (NRKs) to generate NMN, which is subsequently converted to NAD+ through the activity of NMN adenylyltransferase. The resultant increase in NAD+ acts as a vital cofactor for sirtuins—primarily SIRT1 and SIRT3—which are NAD+-dependent deacetylases involved in regulating numerous cellular processes. SIRT1, in particular, has been implicated in deacetylating key transcription factors such as peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator-1α (PGC-1α) and transcription factor EB (TFEB). TFEB is a master regulator of lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy; its deacetylation leads to its nuclear translocation and binding to CLEAR (Coordinated Lysosomal Expression and Regulation) elements in the promoter regions of autophagy and lysosomal genes. Such activation promotes lysosomal acidification and increases the activity of hydrolases like cathepsin D, which are critical for the degradation of damaged proteins and organelles. Concurrently, SIRT3, which localizes predominantly to mitochondria, enhances mitochondrial function by deacetylating enzymes crucial for mitochondrial bioenergetics and reactive oxygen species (ROS) detoxification. The overall effect of NR supplementation is therefore hypothesized to be a restoration of cellular homeostasis in RPE cells—improving both autophagic clearance and mitochondrial function, two processes known to be compromised in dry AMD (Kitaoka et al., 2020; Mehmel et al., 2020; Lin & Apte, 2018; Jadeja et al., 2020). Such a mechanism is consistent with a substantial body of literature demonstrating that the NAD+-sirtuin axis plays a critical role in regulating neuroprotective and anti-aging functions across various tissues (Dovijarski, 2019; Jadeja et al., 2018; Pîrvu et al., 2021).

At the molecular level, the cascade initiated by NR begins with its metabolic conversion to NAD+, which then serves as an essential substrate for SIRT1 activation. Activated SIRT1 deacetylates TFEB, facilitating its nuclear accumulation and binding to the CLEAR network promoters, thereby upregulating genes responsible for autophagy, lysosomal biogenesis, and lysosomal acidification. This process is expected to boost cathepsin D activity and overall lysosomal proteolytic function. Parallel activation of SIRT3 in mitochondria further strengthens cellular defenses by enhancing mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation and reducing ROS generation through deacetylation of key metabolic enzymes. These reconstructed pathways directly address the deleterious effects of oxidative stress and metabolic dysfunction that drive RPE cell death in dry AMD (Kitaoka et al., 2020; Mehmel et al., 2020; Jadeja et al., 2018). In the nucleus, TFEB binds to target gene promoters, thereby upregulating a suite of genes involved in lysosomal biogenesis and the autophagic process. An overall evaluation of NR as a candidate for treating dry AMD reveals both promising strengths and areas requiring further elucidation. Among the principal strengths is NR’s robust ability to elevate systemic and intracellular NAD+ levels, a key factor in numerous regulatory processes implicated in aging and cellular stress response. Its well-characterized pharmacokinetics, combined with documented safety in human supplementation studies, position NR as an attractive candidate for rapid clinical translation (Jadeja et al., 2020; Braidy et al., 2019). The underlying mechanism—that is, the activation of SIRT1 and SIRT3 leading to deacetylation and activation of TFEB—is supported by a breadth of biochemical and preclinical studies, albeit many of these have been performed with related compounds such as NMN. Restoration of lysosomal function, as evidenced by improved acidification and protease activity (e.g., cathepsin D), is a novel therapeutic target that addresses the accumulation of cellular debris—a key factor in the progression of dry AMD.
