Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Torin1 is a synthetic small‐molecule that belongs to the second‐generation, ATP‐competitive class of mTOR inhibitors, originally derived from a quinoline‐based scaffold. Its discovery originated from a high‐throughput compound library screen that identified quinolone hits with moderate mTOR activity, which were then optimized through iterative medicinal chemistry by introducing a six‐membered lactam to convert the initial quinolone into a tricyclic benzonaphthridinone scaffold (Guillem, 2015). This chemical modification yielded a molecule with exceptional biochemical potency—capable of inhibiting both mTOR complexes, mTORC1 and mTORC2, at very low (nanomolar to picomolar) concentrations—and with approximately 1000-fold improvement in cellular potency relative to the initial hits (Guillem, 2015). As an ATP-competitive inhibitor, Torin1 binds directly to the active (ATP-binding) site of mTOR, thereby circumventing the partial inhibition that is observed with first-generation mTOR inhibitors like rapamycin that act allosterically by binding FKBP12 (Liu et al., 2012). Torin1 has been widely used as a research tool to interrogate mTOR signaling in various cellular contexts, and its chemical lineage as a quinoline-derived molecule positions it within a well-characterized class of inhibitors that have been instrumental in expanding our understanding of mTOR-dependent regulation of autophagy and cellular metabolism (Liu et al., 2012).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, Torin1 has been employed predominantly as a research tool rather than as a clinical drug candidate. Extensive preclinical studies have demonstrated its robust ability to inhibit mTOR signaling in cancer models, autophagy-deficient systems, and metabolic studies. For instance, Torin1 was shown to potently inhibit mTOR signaling pathways in glioblastoma and prostate cancer cells, significantly reducing cell-cycle progression and inducing apoptosis in certain contexts (Gu, 2017; Liu et al., 2012). Its use as an autophagy inducer is well documented, as experiments utilizing Torin1 have demonstrated increased autophagic flux and elevated lysosomal activity in multiple cell lines (Li, 2018; Liu et al., 2012). Importantly, Torin1 is also used in studies with retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells, as evidenced by its ability to increase TFEB-driven luciferase reporter activity in ARPE-19 cells by effectively suppressing mTORC1 signaling (Huang et al., 2018). Despite these promising experimental findings, Torin1 has not advanced to clinical trials for any indication, including neurodegenerative disorders or dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD). Moreover, its intrinsic pharmacokinetic limitations—such as poor aqueous solubility, a short half-life, and low oral bioavailability—have been recognized in several studies, thereby limiting its potential as a direct therapeutic candidate without further structural optimization (Guillem, 2015; Wang et al., 2022).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, Torin1 functions by competing with ATP for binding to the catalytic domain of mTOR, effectively blocking the phosphorylation of downstream substrates. Its ATP-competitive nature allows Torin1 to inhibit both mTORC1 and mTORC2 complexes, thereby offering a broader inhibition profile than allosteric agents like rapamycin that primarily target mTORC1 (Guillem, 2015; Liu et al., 2012). Detailed molecular modeling and structure–activity relationship studies indicate that the tricyclic benzonaphthridinone core of Torin1 forms critical hinge-binding interactions with residues in the mTOR kinase domain (Liu et al., 2012). This interaction accounts for its high potency, as reflected in low nanomolar IC₅₀ values in cellular assays (Liu et al., 2012; Gros & Muller, 2014). Torin1 induces rapid dephosphorylation of canonical mTORC1 substrates, such as S6 kinase at Thr389 and 4E-BP1 at Thr37/46, which results in downregulation of protein synthesis and cellular growth signals (Misra & Pizzo, 2013). Moreover, by simultaneously inhibiting mTORC2, it reduces phosphorylation of Akt at Ser473—a site critical for full Akt activation—thus attenuating the feedback loops that typically reinvigorate upstream PI3K signaling in response to mTORC1 inhibition (Gu, 2017; Martina et al., 2014). A particularly notable feature of Torin1 is its slow off-rate, which leads to sustained inhibition of mTOR activity even after drug washout, a pharmacodynamic property that may confer prolonged downstream effects such as enhanced autophagic flux (Liu et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2013). The inhibition of mTOR by Torin1 correlates with dephosphorylation of transcription factors, particularly TFEB and TFE3; under normal nutrient-replete conditions, mTORC1 phosphorylates TFEB (e.g., on S211 in TFEB) and TFE3, sequestering them in the cytosol through binding with 14-3-3 proteins (Huang et al., 2018; Martina et al., 2014). Upon mTOR inhibition by Torin1, TFEB is dephosphorylated and translocates to the nucleus, where it induces the transcription of CLEAR (Coordinated Lysosomal Expression and Regulation) network genes that drive lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy (Li, 2018; Liu et al., 2013). This precise modulation of mTOR signaling and subsequent transcriptional reprogramming forms the biochemical basis for leveraging Torin1 as a candidate to ameliorate lysosomal clearance defects.

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis for repurposing Torin1 in the context of dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is that potent inhibition of mTORC1/2 in RPE cells can lift the repressive phosphorylation that normally limits the activity of TFEB and TFE3. In RPE cells, as demonstrated by studies in ARPE-19 cell models, mTOR inhibition via Torin1 not only leads to decreased phosphorylation of S6 kinase but also results in marked activation of TFEB-driven transcription (Huang et al., 2018). When TFEB translocates to the nucleus, it binds to CLEAR elements present in the promoters of genes responsible for lysosomal biogenesis, acidification (through the upregulation of V-ATPase subunits), and the maturation and activity of lysosomal enzymes such as cathepsin D (CTSD) (Huang et al., 2018; Li, 2018). In dry AMD, RPE cells exhibit a decline in lysosomal function along with accumulation of cellular debris and lipofuscin, which contribute to disease pathology. By inducing a robust CLEAR response, Torin1 is expected to restore lysosomal function through increased biogenesis, enhanced acidification, and elevated cathepsin D activity, thereby improving the clearance of toxic aggregates in RPE cells and ultimately mitigating the progression of dry AMD (Gu, 2017; Huang et al., 2018). Additionally, the sustained target engagement afforded by Torin1’s slow off-rate may provide prolonged therapeutic benefit even with intermittent dosing, an attractive feature given the chronic nature of AMD (Liu et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2013). Recent evidence from preclinical iPSC models and autophagy-deficiency studies underscores the potential translation of mTOR-targeted strategies in restoring cellular homeostasis in degenerative diseases, lending further credence to this expected mechanism (Guillem, 2015).

Overall Evaluation:  
In summary, Torin1 possesses a compelling mechanistic profile that aligns well with the therapeutic needs of dry AMD by targeting a fundamental pathway governing cellular homeostasis in RPE cells. Its origin from a quinoline-based scaffold and subsequent chemical optimization into a highly potent ATP-competitive mTOR inhibitor underline its status as a valuable chemical probe in preclinical settings (Guillem, 2015). The dual inhibition of both mTORC1 and mTORC2 by Torin1, combined with its slow off-rate and sustained downstream effects—including dephosphorylation and nuclear translocation of TFEB/TFE3—make it an ideal tool for inducing lysosomal biogenesis and enhancing autophagic clearance (Martina et al., 2014; Huang et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2012). In cellular models, including ARPE-19 RPE cells, Torin1 has already demonstrated the ability to activate TFEB and upregulate CLEAR gene expression, which is directly relevant to counteracting the lysosomal clearance defects observed in dry AMD (Huang et al., 2018; Li, 2018).

However, significant challenges remain regarding the translational applicability of Torin1 as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. Its reported poor aqueous solubility, short half-life, and low oral bioavailability present formidable barriers to clinical development unless addressed through formulation improvements or further medicinal chemistry optimization (Guillem, 2015; Wang et al., 2022). Moreover, while extensive preclinical literature supports its role as a robust mTOR inhibitor in cancer and autophagy research, there is a lack of direct in vivo evidence for its efficacy in ocular models, particularly in dry AMD or geographic atrophy (GA) mouse lines (Liu et al., 2013; Gu, 2017). Careful dosing will also be critical, as the broad and potent inhibition of mTOR can have unintended effects on cellular metabolism and protein synthesis beyond the intended enhancement of lysosomal function. Additionally, off-target effects have been observed in some biochemical screens at supraphysiologic concentrations, including binding to other PIKK family members such as ATR, ATM, and DNA-PK, although these are generally not manifested at the low nanomolar concentrations used in cellular assays (Settembre et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2012).

From the perspective of repurposing for dry AMD, Torin1’s deep mechanistic specificity is a double-edged sword: it offers a highly defined and robust approach to upregulating lysosomal biogenesis via the TFEB/TFE3 axis, yet its pharmacokinetic liabilities and the absence of any clinical history in ocular disease necessitate additional work. The promising in vitro data in RPE models (ARPE-19 cells) and iPSC-derived RPE systems provide valuable target validation, but before advancing to clinical trials a refined analog or an optimized delivery method (for example, local ocular administration to bypass systemic bioavailability issues) should be considered (Huang et al., 2018; Li, 2018; Wang et al., 2022).

In summary, Torin1 is an excellent candidate for preclinical proof-of-concept studies to validate mTOR inhibition as a strategy to combat lysosomal dysfunction in dry AMD; however, further optimization to improve its stability and bioavailability, alongside rigorous in vivo testing in relevant AMD models, will be essential prior to clinical development (Guillem, 2015; Gu, 2017). The strengths of Torin1 lie in its potent, dual mTOR inhibition and its ability to robustly induce TFEB activation, whereas its weaknesses center on its pharmacokinetic shortcomings and the current lack of efficacy data in ocular disease models. Overall, with focused optimization and targeted delivery strategies, Torin1 or its derivatives may offer a promising therapeutic avenue for ameliorating the lysosomal clearance defects that underlie dry AMD pathology (Liu et al., 2012; Huang et al., 2018).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
NSC19723 is presented by the team as a custom-synthesized small-molecule enhancer of cathepsin D (CTSD) activity, hypothesized to bind the zymogen (pro-CTSD) and accelerate its maturation within retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) lysosomes to restore proteolysis and debris clearance in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD). No peer-reviewed publications or preprints describing NSC19723’s structure, discovery, selectivity, or in vivo performance are present in the provided literature corpus; accordingly, this evaluation treats NSC19723 as a theoretical representative of the drug class “CTSD activity enhancers” and assesses the therapeutic hypothesis against the current substrate-specific and disease-relevant CTSD/RPE biology (Ng et al., 2024; Sharif, 2015; Liu, 2021; Buniello et al., 2025).

The stated drug class is mechanistically distinct from upstream autophagy enhancers or lysosomal pH modulators: a CTSD activity enhancer would operate at the level of CTSD protein maturation/activity, ideally in acidic lysosomes, rather than by globally raising autophagic flux or indirectly modulating lysosomal acidification (Frost et al., 2014; Boya et al., 2023; Ng et al., 2024). CTSD itself is an aspartic endoprotease synthesized as a pre-proenzyme with an N-terminal signal peptide (for ER entry) and a propeptide region that supports folding and prevents premature activity; post-translational maturation occurs in late endosomes/lysosomes after mannose-6-phosphate (M6P)-mediated trafficking, where acidic pH supports autocatalysis and protease processing to the mature, active two-chain enzyme (Sharif, 2015). The RPE expresses CTSD at high levels, with evidence for enriched CTSD protein/activity in central/macular RPE relative to periphery, consistent with the macula’s heavy daily photoreceptor outer segment (POS) phagocytic load that relies on lysosomal proteolysis (Sharif, 2015; Pay, 2017). These features nominate CTSD as a plausible therapeutic target for restoring RPE degradative capacity; however, a specific CTSD maturation enhancer such as NSC19723 has not been characterized in the provided literature, so all compound-level conclusions must remain contingent on experimental validation (Ng et al., 2024; Buniello et al., 2025).

Therapeutic History  
No published biochemical, veterinary, or clinical use of NSC19723 is documented in the provided sources, and the name does not appear in the referenced literature; consequently, there are no prior data on this molecule in dry AMD or retinal disease within the provided corpus (Buniello et al., 2025). By contrast, there is considerable disease-relevant literature on CTSD biology in RPE and on pharmacological strategies that indirectly restore CTSD function by correcting upstream lysosomal defects. In patient-derived RPE from Stargardt disease (STGD1, ABCA4 mutations), lysosomal pH is elevated, CTSD accumulates in immature forms, and CTSD proteolytic activity is reduced; pharmacologic re-acidification of lysosomes (e.g., via P2Y₁₂ antagonism with ticagrelor) reverses these defects by lowering lysosomal pH, reducing the immature pro-CTSD pool, and restoring CTSD proteolytic activity and POS degradation in vitro and in vivo (RPE cells and Abca4−/− mice) (Ng et al., 2024). While STGD1 is not AMD, these data show that CTSD maturation/activity in human RPE is drug-modifiable and that improving CTSD function can improve degradative endpoints relevant to lipofuscin-associated disease biology, a pathophysiologic axis shared with dry AMD (Ng et al., 2024; Boya et al., 2023).

In the RPE/AMD literature, multiple lines of evidence support CTSD as a major lysosomal protease necessary for POS degradation and proteostasis. CTSD deficiency or pharmacologic inhibition impairs POS proteolysis, provokes accumulation of debris reminiscent of drusen, and is linked to retinal dysfunction in animal models, reinforcing its centrality to RPE homeostasis (Mahmud, 2019). Advanced glycation end-products (AGEs), which accumulate with age and in AMD, downregulate CTSD activity or expression in RPE and exacerbate lysosomal/autophagic failure and lipofuscin formation, further tying CTSD deficits to AMD-like phenotypes (Sharif, 2015; Mahmud, 2019). More broadly, lysosomal/autophagic insufficiency in RPE is mechanistically and pathologically linked to dry AMD: decreased degradative capacity leads to lipofuscin accumulation, lysosomal membrane permeabilization (LMP), DAMP release, inflammasome activation (e.g., NLRP3), and eventual RPE atrophy that drives photoreceptor degeneration; re-acidifying lysosomes and strengthening lysosomal function ameliorate several of these pathologies in vitro and in vivo (Choi, 2019; Frost et al., 2014; Boya et al., 2023).

A second therapeutic precedent relevant to “enhancing CTSD function” is enzyme augmentation. Recombinant pro-CTSD administration has been reported to correct proteolysis and autophagy defects in neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis (CLN10/CTSD deficiency), and intravitreal enzyme replacement strategies in other lysosomal storage diseases (e.g., TPP1 in CLN2) have preserved retinal structure/function in preclinical models, supporting feasibility of increasing lysosomal enzyme function in ocular tissues (Liu, 2021). These studies, while not in AMD and not small molecules, validate the general concept that augmenting CTSD can rescue lysosomal degradative failure in retina-derived tissues.

In summary, there is no therapeutic history for NSC19723 itself in the provided sources; however, there is an increasingly robust therapeutic precedent that pharmacological manipulation which restores CTSD maturation/activity in RPE improves degradative capacity and disease-relevant readouts in lipofuscin-accumulating retinal disorders, and that enzyme augmentation of lysosomal hydrolases can be effective in ocular degenerations driven by lysosomal insufficiency (Ng et al., 2024; Liu, 2021).

Mechanism of Action  
CTSD biosynthesis and maturation provide the mechanistic backdrop for a CTSD maturation enhancer. CTSD is synthesized as pre-procathepsin D with a signal peptide (for ER translocation) and a propeptide that maintains the zymogen in an inactive, folding-competent state; the protein acquires N-linked glycans and an M6P tag in the Golgi for M6P-receptor–mediated trafficking to late endosomes/lysosomes, where acidic pH facilitates removal of the propeptide, proteolytic processing, and generation of the mature, active enzyme (heavy and light chains) (Sharif, 2015). As an aspartic protease, CTSD employs two Asp residues to activate and position a water molecule for nucleophilic attack on the scissile peptide bond, a chemistry that requires acidic conditions for optimal catalysis; in neutral or alkaline environments, activity falls sharply, explaining why lysosomal alkalinization in disease states compromises both maturation and steady-state activity (Sharif, 2015; Ng et al., 2024).

In RPE disease models, immature and intermediate CTSD forms accumulate when lysosomal pH is elevated, and total CTSD protein may paradoxically rise even as proteolytic activity falls, illustrating a maturation bottleneck rather than a transcriptional deficit; pharmacological re-acidification reduces immature CTSD, increases the mature enzyme, and restores proteolytic activity in RPE (Ng et al., 2024). Functionally, impaired CTSD maturation/activity correlates with delayed degradation of internalized POS and accumulation of aggregation-prone substrates such as α-synuclein, consistent with CTSD’s principal role in RPE proteolysis of rhodopsin and POS proteins; CTSD is reported to account for the majority of rhodopsin degradation in RPE and exhibits far higher proteolytic activity than cathepsin B against POS substrates (Ng et al., 2024). The RPE’s reliance on phagolysosomal degradation of POS and basal autophagy for proteostasis means that even partial reductions in CTSD activity can precipitate progressive accumulation of lipofuscin-like material and lysosomal residual bodies, which in turn further impair lysosomes and create a feedback loop of increasing oxidative and inflammatory stress central to dry AMD pathophysiology (Choi, 2019; Frost et al., 2014; Sharif, 2015).

The proposed mechanism for NSC19723—direct binding to pro-CTSD to accelerate maturation—aligns with the above biology and would target the specific rate-limiting step observed in RPE lysosomes under stress: conversion of immature pro-CTSD to the mature, active enzyme in the acidic lumen. If achieved without broad, off-target activation of other proteases or perturbation of lysosomal pH/ion homeostasis, this mechanism would distinguish NSC19723 from autophagy inducers (e.g., rapamycin) or pH re-acidifiers (e.g., ticagrelor), while being convergent on the same functional outcome: restored CTSD proteolysis and lysosomal degradative capacity (Frost et al., 2014; Ng et al., 2024).

Mechanistic cross-talk and constraints that are relevant for a CTSD maturation enhancer include:  
- pH dependence: CTSD maturation and catalysis require acidic lysosomes; in alkaline lysosomes (e.g., due to bisretinoid accumulation), pro-CTSD processing is impaired even if total CTSD protein increases, so a maturation accelerator may be insufficient without concurrent restoration of lysosomal pH in some disease states (Ng et al., 2024).  
- Protease networks: While CTSD is an aspartic protease, lysosomal proteases co-regulate one another’s maturation and substrate turnover; for example, denatured cathepsin L can be a substrate for CTSD, and changes in cysteine cathepsins (B/L/S) alter autophagic flux and POS degradation, implying that selective enhancement of CTSD maturation must be interpreted in the context of broader protease network homeostasis (Mahmud, 2019; Sharif, 2015).  
- Endogenous inhibitors: Cystatin C potently inhibits cysteine cathepsins (B, H, L, S) and is abundant in RPE; although it does not inhibit CTSD (aspartic protease), changes in cystatin C with age and AMD suggest that protease–inhibitor balance in the lysosome and extracellular space is dynamic and may modulate the consequences of altering one protease’s activity (Myerscough, 2015; Sharif, 2015).  
- Lysosomal membrane integrity: LMP releases cathepsins to the cytosol, where they can trigger apoptosis/inflammation; any intervention that modifies lysosomal protease activity must be vetted for unintended effects on LMP susceptibility or cytosolic protease activity under stress (Boya et al., 2023; Mahmud, 2019).  
- Extracellular exposure: RPE can secrete cathepsins; most cathepsins are inactivated at neutral pH, but acidic niches or heparan/ECM interactions can stabilize activity, raising potential off-tissue effects if a compound perturbs trafficking/secretion (Sharif, 2015).

Collectively, the mechanistic plausibility that a small molecule could stabilize a conformation of pro-CTSD that accelerates propeptide removal and activation in acidic lysosomes is strong, and a favorable on-target pharmacodynamic effect can be anchored to clearly measurable, disease-relevant biochemical endpoints in RPE (Ng et al., 2024). The key risk is that without correction of lysosomal pH, pro-CTSD processing bottlenecks may persist; therefore, a CTSD maturation enhancer may be best deployed in lysosomes that are sufficiently acidic or in combination with pH-restoring strategies (Ng et al., 2024).

Expected Effect  
Dry AMD pathophysiology features RPE lysosomal-autophagic insufficiency leading to accumulation of POS-derived material, lipofuscin, and AGEs, heightened oxidative stress, inflammasome activation, and progressive RPE atrophy; restoring lysosomal proteolysis is predicted to mitigate these processes (Choi, 2019; Frost et al., 2014; Boya et al., 2023). In RPE, CTSD is a principal protease responsible for POS/rhodopsin degradation, and its activity declines with aging and under stressors relevant to AMD (AGEs, lipids/oxidation, lysosomal alkalinization), producing immature CTSD accumulation and reduced proteolytic capacity (Mahmud, 2019; Sharif, 2015; Ng et al., 2024). Therefore, a compound that accelerates pro-CTSD maturation to increase mature CTSD abundance/activity in acidic lysosomes is expected to:

- Increase CTSD catalytic activity in RPE lysosomes, measurable by fluorogenic substrate assays and activity-based probes, with corresponding decrease in immature/intermediate CTSD species and increase in mature, active CTSD on immunoblot and imaging (Ng et al., 2024).

- Disease relevance: verify effects in hiPSC-RPE derived from dry AMD patients, which display altered lysosomal protease processing (e.g., immature CTSD increases under oxidative stress) and increased stress susceptibility; extend to macular-enriched RPE phenotypes given regional CTSD enrichment (Voisin et al., 2019; Sharif, 2015).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Strong target–disease mechanistic rationale: CTSD is the principal lysosomal protease for RPE POS protein degradation, with reported responsibility for the majority of rhodopsin proteolysis and markedly higher activity than cathepsin B; CTSD deficiency or inhibition impairs POS degradation and produces drusen-like debris, and genetic or pharmacologic CTSD impairment causes retinal dysfunction, aligning CTSD activation with a disease-modifying mechanism in dry AMD (Ng et al., 2024; Mahmud, 2019).  
- Convergent therapeutic precedent: Restoring lysosomal pH in patient-derived and mouse RPE models rescues CTSD maturation and activity, improves POS degradation, reduces lipofuscin-like autofluorescence, and protects photoreceptors, demonstrating that enhancing CTSD function is sufficient to improve disease-relevant outcomes in lipofuscin-associated retinal pathology (Ng et al., 2024).  
- Clear, measurable pharmacodynamic biomarkers: Mature CTSD abundance, CTSD activity, lysosomal pH, POS clearance, and lipofuscin/autofluorescence changes provide a rigorous framework for early de-risking of NSC19723 and for prioritizing compound optimization (Ng et al., 2024).  
- Disease context supports target engagement benefits: RPE lysosomal dysfunction, autophagy/heterophagy deficits, lipofuscin/AGE accumulation, inflammasome activation, and progressive atrophy are central features of dry AMD; a CTSD maturation enhancer directly addresses the degradative bottleneck at the lysosome (Choi, 2019; Frost et al., 2014; Boya et al., 2023).

Risks and gaps  
- Absence of public data on NSC19723: No structural, selectivity, potency, PK/PD, ocular disposition, or toxicology data are available in the provided corpus; thus, claims of pro-CTSD binding, selectivity for CTSD over other cathepsins, and in vivo rescue in CTSD-deficient retina remain unverified by the sources provided (Buniello et al., 2025). This is the major program risk at present.  
- Lysosomal pH constraint: If lysosomal alkalinization is a primary driver of immature CTSD accumulation (as in STGD1 and arguably in stressed AMD RPE), a maturation accelerator may not overcome the pH-dependent processing barrier; efficacy may require sufficient lysosomal acidity or combination with pH-restoring interventions (Ng et al., 2024).  
- Protease network and safety considerations: Enhancing lysosomal protease activity can exacerbate LMP-driven cytotoxicity under oxidative or lipofuscin stress; careful LMP and inflammasome assessments are required, alongside confirmation that NSC19723 does not perturb trafficking/secretion to increase extracellular protease activity where pH can be locally acidic (Boya et al., 2023; Sharif, 2015).  
- Disease heterogeneity and target linkage: Although CTSD biology is compelling in RPE and in lipofuscin-associated pathology, Open Targets curates only a low-confidence literature-based association between CTSD and AMD, reflecting limited direct genetic or clinical targeting data in AMD; translational success will depend on demonstrating benefit in dry AMD–relevant human RPE models and in vivo models that recapitulate AMD’s lysosomal/autophagic deficits (Buniello et al., 2025; Inana et al., 2018; Frost et al., 2014).  
- Off-target and network effects: Crosstalk between cathepsins (e.g., CTSD processing of denatured cathepsin L, altered cathepsin L/C3/NF-κB signaling), and modulation by AGEs/oxidative stress and endogenous inhibitors necessitate comprehensive off-target profiling and immune readouts to ensure that CTSD-specific maturation enhancement does not dysregulate broader proteostasis/inflammatory networks in RPE or at the RPE–Bruch’s membrane (BrM) interface (Sharif, 2015; Mahmud, 2019).

Program implications and recommended next steps  
Given the robust mechanistic case for CTSD restoration in RPE and the successful pharmacologic rescue of CTSD maturation/activity via lysosomal re-acidification in human patient–derived RPE, a selective CTSD maturation enhancer is a rational, high-potential approach for dry AMD—provided the compound is real, selective, and effective in acidic lysosomes (Ng et al., 2024). To advance NSC19723, the following de-risking package is critical:  

- Biochemical validation: Demonstrate pro-CTSD binding and acceleration of maturation at acidic pH using purified pro-CTSD and lysosomal-mimetic conditions; quantify catalytic activation and processing kinetics; confirm no activation or inhibition of cathepsins B/L/S and other lysosomal hydrolases (Sharif, 2015).  
- Cellular validation in RPE: In primary human RPE/hiPSC-RPE (including dry AMD lines), show increased mature CTSD and activity without altering lysosomal pH, improved POS degradation and reduced autofluorescence under chronic POS/AGE stress, restored clearance of α-synuclein aggregates, and normalization of autophagic flux using proper flux assays (Frost et al., 2014; Ng et al., 2024; Sharif, 2015).  
- Safety pharmacology in RPE: Demonstrate no increase in LMP susceptibility or NLRP3 activation under oxidative/bisretinoid stress; characterize secretion/trafficking effects and exclude extracellular protease activation under BrM-like conditions (Boya et al., 2023; Sharif, 2015).  
- In vivo proof of concept: In models featuring RPE lysosomal dysfunction and lipofuscin burden, measure retinal/RPE CTSD maturation/activity, RPE autofluorescence, drusen-like material, photoreceptor survival, and visual function; compare with or add to pH-reacidifying strategies (Ng et al., 2024).

Overall, while a CTSD maturation enhancer is scientifically well grounded for RPE-centered degenerations and could represent a differentiated, direct-restoration modality versus pH modulators or broad autophagy inducers, the current file lacks any external validation for NSC19723. Progressing NSC19723 is justified only with rapid, rigorous confirmation of selectivity, on-target activity in RPE lysosomes, and favorable safety in stressed RPE systems that model dry AMD’s lysosomal/autophagic failure (Frost et al., 2014; Boya et al., 2023; Choi, 2019).

In summary, the therapeutic concept—enhancing CTSD maturation/activity to restore RPE lysosomal proteolysis—has high mechanistic plausibility and encouraging precedent from pharmacologic re-acidification studies, but the specific candidate NSC19723 remains unsubstantiated in the provided literature and requires foundational biochemical and cellular validation to warrant preclinical development in dry AMD (Ng et al., 2024; Buniello et al., 2025).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Fenofibrate is a synthetic small‐molecule drug belonging to the fibrate class of compounds, originally developed and approved for the treatment of dyslipidemia. It acts predominantly as a peroxisome proliferator‐activated receptor alpha (PPARα) agonist. Fenofibrate itself is a prodrug that undergoes hepatic esterase hydrolysis to form its active metabolite, fenofibric acid, which binds to PPARα and modulates the transcription of genes involved in lipid metabolism. This drug class has historically been used for lowering serum triglycerides and increasing high‐density lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol, reflecting its well‐established lipid‐modulating properties. Although fenofibrate was not initially developed for ocular indications, its mechanism as a PPARα agonist has spurred interest for repurposing in retinal diseases. In particular, the broad class of fibrates has garnered attention because PPARα is expressed in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), and its activation can regulate lipid oxidation, autophagy, and inflammatory processes—all of which are critically disturbed in dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) (Fu et al., 2019; Falcão et al., 2025).

Therapeutic History:  
Fenofibrate has a robust clinical history in the management of dyslipidemia and cardiovascular risk reduction, with extensive use in millions of patients worldwide. Its ocular benefits became apparent with large clinical trials, such as the FIELD and ACCORD Eye studies, which demonstrated that fenofibrate can reduce the progression of diabetic retinopathy and decrease the need for retinal laser therapy in diabetic patients (Lu et al., 2014; Treacy & Hurst, 2012). Although these trials primarily addressed diabetic retinal disease, subsequent preclinical and clinical reports have indicated that the retina may benefit from the lipid‐modulatory, anti‐inflammatory, and neuroprotective actions of PPARα agonists. For instance, several studies have explored fenofibrate in animal models of retinal ischemia and neovascularization, showing protective effects on the retinal vasculature and RPE (Fu et al., 2020; Qiu et al., 2017). While the majority of these ocular studies have focused on diabetic retinopathy or neovascular AMD, emerging literature has pointed to the potential of targeting PPARα signaling to mitigate RPE dysfunction and lipid accumulation, which are hallmarks of dry AMD (da Ana et al., 2023; Dou & Duerfeldt, 2020). This history of fenofibrate in retinal disease, combined with its proven clinical safety for dyslipidemia and established ocular pharmacokinetics (including studies on topical delivery), provides a compelling rationale for its repurposing in dry AMD (Tomita et al., 2020; Lee et al., 2021).

Mechanism of Action:  
Fenofibrate’s mechanism of action is rooted in its role as a PPARα agonist. Upon conversion to fenofibric acid, the compound binds to PPARα—a nuclear receptor highly expressed in several tissues, including the liver and the retinal pigment epithelium. When activated, PPARα forms heterodimers with retinoid X receptors (RXR) and binds to peroxisome proliferator response elements (PPREs) within the promoters of target genes. This binding results in the upregulation of genes critical for fatty acid uptake, β-oxidation, and lipid catabolism. Key genes regulated by PPARα include those encoding enzymes that facilitate mitochondrial and peroxisomal fatty acid oxidation, which in turn reduces intracellular lipid accumulation and promotes energy homeostasis (Fu et al., 2019; Lee et al., 2023).

In the context of the RPE and dry AMD, the hypothesis is that fenofibrate will stimulate PPARα-mediated transcriptional programs that not only enhance lipid catabolism but also intersect with cellular degradative pathways. One of the central tenets of the proposed mechanism is the coactivation of transcription factor EB (TFEB). TFEB is recognized as a master regulator of lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy through the coordinated lysosomal expression and regulation (CLEAR) network. Under normal conditions, TFEB is kept inactive in the cytosol by phosphorylation mediated by mTORC1. Under stress conditions or when lysosomal function is impaired, TFEB translocates to the nucleus to upregulate genes involved in lysosomal acidification, autophagy, and lipid metabolism. The therapeutic hypothesis posits that fenofibrate, through PPARα activation in RPE cells, will indirectly coactivate TFEB. This may occur through changes in cellular metabolism that reduce mTORC1 activity or via direct transcriptional crosstalk between PPARα target genes and the CLEAR network (Falcão et al., 2025; da Ana et al., 2023).

Moreover, TFEB activation is expected to enhance lysosomal acidification—a process necessary for optimal degradation of phagocytosed outer segment debris and drusen precursors—and upregulate lysosomal hydrolases such as cathepsin D. In AMD, RPE cells often show lysosomal dysfunction characterized by deficient cathepsin D activity and lipofuscin accumulation. By improving lysosomal function, fenofibrate may facilitate the clearance of lipid-rich drusen precursors, thereby reducing RPE stress and preventing progression of dry AMD (Falcão et al., 2025; da Ana et al., 2023). In addition to these lysosome-centric effects, fenofibrate has anti-inflammatory properties, as PPARα activation suppresses NF-κB signaling, reduces the expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines (e.g., TNF-α and IL-1β), and alleviates oxidative stress—all of which are exacerbating factors in the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Lee et al., 2023; Treacy & Hurst, 2012). Furthermore, the modulation of the FGF21 pathway, occasionally observed with fenofibrate treatment, may contribute to neuroprotection and further support retinal homeostasis (Tomita et al., 2020; Lee et al., 2023). Taken together, the molecular interactions initiated by fenofibrate converge on restoring lipid homeostasis, enhancing autophagic flux, and mitigating inflammatory insults in RPE cells—a multifaceted approach that aligns with the pathophysiology of dry AMD (Treacy & Hurst, 2012; Lee et al., 2021).

Expected Effect:  
In the assays proposed to evaluate fenofibrate’s efficacy for dry AMD, one anticipates several measurable cellular and biochemical outcomes. First, treatment of RPE cells with fenofibrate should lead to a consistent activation of PPARα target genes, as demonstrated by upregulation of markers for fatty acid oxidation and lipid catabolism. Such molecular signatures can be quantified using gene expression analyses and reporter assays for PPRE activity (Fu et al., 2019; Tomita et al., 2021). Concurrently, it is expected that fenofibrate will enhance autophagic flux in RPE cells. This could be evident from increased LC3-II accumulation in the presence of lysosomal inhibitors and enhanced degradation of autophagic substrates, which would indicate an upregulation of the autophagic machinery (Falcão et al., 2025; da Ana et al., 2023).

A critical aspect of the proposed mechanism involves TFEB. Upon fenofibrate treatment, one should observe increased nuclear translocation of TFEB in RPE cells, which can be assessed by immunocytochemistry and subcellular fractionation. The activation of TFEB would then be expected to drive the transcriptional upregulation of genes encoding lysosomal proteins, such as lysosomal-associated membrane protein 2 (LAMP2) and various components of the V-ATPase complex, leading to enhanced lysosomal acidification. Lysotracker assays and measurements of intralysosomal pH could be deployed to confirm that fenofibrate-treated cells exhibit more acidic lysosomes (Falcão et al., 2025; da Ana et al., 2023).

Furthermore, increased cathepsin D activity is a pivotal expected outcome, serving as a surrogate marker for improved lysosomal enzyme function in degrading waste products, including drusen precursors. Biochemical assays to quantify cathepsin D activity, alongside immunostaining for its protein levels, would help to validate this aspect of the mechanism. Functionally, the cumulative effect of these molecular changes should be a reduction in the accumulation of lipofuscin and other drusen-associated lipid-protein aggregates within the RPE. This reduction could be observed using autofluorescence imaging techniques and electron microscopy to assess cytoplasmic inclusions (Falcão et al., 2025; Treacy & Hurst, 2012).

Additionally, given that fenofibrate has established anti-inflammatory properties, one might expect a decrease in the secretion or expression of inflammatory mediators in RPE cultures, as well as improved cellular resistance to oxidative stress challenges. Cytokine assays and measurements of reactive oxygen species (ROS) would serve as corroborative evidence for an anti-inflammatory and antioxidant effect. Importantly, because reduced autophagy and lysosomal dysfunction are central to dry AMD, the combined effect of enhanced lipid catabolism, improved lysosomal acidification, and increased cathepsin D activity should contribute to an overall reduction in cellular stress and preservation of RPE integrity (Falcão et al., 2025; Treacy & Hurst, 2012). Taken together, these expected effects would validate the therapeutic hypothesis and provide a strong rationale for advancing fenofibrate into further preclinical models of dry AMD.

Overall Evaluation:  
Fenofibrate emerges as a promising repurposed drug candidate for dry AMD based on several compelling lines of evidence. The drug’s long-established clinical safety profile and extensive use in dyslipidemia serve as major strengths in terms of its translational potential (Lu et al., 2014; Treacy & Hurst, 2012). Additionally, the documented success of fenofibrate in slowing the progression of diabetic retinopathy in large-scale clinical trials underscores its ability to exert beneficial effects in retinal tissues (Lu et al., 2014; Treacy & Hurst, 2012).

From a mechanistic standpoint, fenofibrate’s mode of action as a PPARα agonist is well characterized, and its ability to stimulate lipid oxidation and enhance fatty acid metabolism could directly address the lipid dysregulation observed in RPE cells in dry AMD (Fu et al., 2019; da Ana et al., 2023). Crucially, the hypothesis that fenofibrate may also coactivate TFEB, thereby promoting lysosomal biogenesis and function, positions it uniquely among therapeutic candidates. Improved lysosomal acidification and increased cathepsin D activity would facilitate the clearance of drusen precursors and reduce the cytotoxic accumulation of lipofuscin, which is a central pathogenic feature of dry AMD (Falcão et al., 2025; da Ana et al., 2023; Dou & Duerfeldt, 2020). The convergence of lipid catabolism enhancement, autophagy upregulation, and anti-inflammatory effects creates a multifaceted therapeutic profile that is particularly attractive for a complex, multifactorial disease such as dry AMD.

However, there are also notable weaknesses and challenges. Most of the current evidence supporting fenofibrate’s retinal benefits is derived from studies focusing on diabetic retinopathy or neovascular AMD rather than directly on dry AMD. Although there is supportive mechanistic rationale linking PPARα activation to improved lysosomal function in the RPE, direct evidence for fenofibrate’s efficacy in reducing drusen accumulation and alleviating RPE stress in dry AMD models remains sparse (Dou & Duerfeldt, 2020; da Ana et al., 2023). The specific involvement of TFEB activation by fenofibrate in RPE cells has not been fully elucidated in the existing literature, and further in vitro and in vivo studies are needed to validate this aspect of the mechanism. Additionally, while fenofibrate is generally safe when used systemically, there have been concerns regarding potential renal side effects, which may be particularly relevant in the elderly population that predominantly suffers from AMD (Treacy & Hurst, 2012; Tomita et al., 2021). Thus, optimizing the route of delivery—possibly via topical formulations or nanoparticle-based systems—may be necessary to ensure sufficient retinal bioavailability while minimizing systemic exposure (Huang et al., 2021; Lu et al., 2014).

Another potential limitation is the dose required to achieve sufficient PPARα activation in the RPE to modulate TFEB and lysosomal pathways effectively. Preclinical studies have sometimes required relatively high doses of fenofibrate to observe significant ocular effects, and the pharmacokinetic barriers posed by the blood-retinal barrier may further complicate translatability (Tomita et al., 2020; Lee et al., 2023). Moreover, the current body of literature underscores the need for more targeted studies to determine whether the benefits seen with fenofibrate in models of diabetic retinopathy and neovascular AMD can be replicated in models of dry AMD, where the pathogenic processes are distinct in their emphasis on lipid accumulation, oxidative stress, and RPE dysfunction (da Ana et al., 2023; Dou & Duerfeldt, 2020).

Despite these challenges, the overall evaluation remains cautiously optimistic. Fenofibrate’s mechanism of action aligns well with the pathophysiological features of dry AMD, particularly regarding the restoration of lipid homeostasis and the enhancement of lysosomal function. The dual potential for direct metabolic benefits via PPARα activation and indirect benefits through TFEB-mediated lysosomal enhancement represents an innovative therapeutic strategy that could fill a critical gap in the current treatment landscape for dry AMD (Falcão et al., 2025; Fu et al., 2019; da Ana et al., 2023; Dou & Duerfeldt, 2020; Lee et al., 2023). Additionally, the availability of various delivery platforms—including systemic administration, topical eye drops, and nanoparticle formulations—provides flexibility in addressing bioavailability challenges and minimizing adverse effects (Huang et al., 2021; Lu et al., 2014).

In conclusion, fenofibrate (Sigma F6020) possesses significant potential for repurposing as a drug candidate for dry AMD based on its well-established pharmacological profile, robust clinical safety record, and mechanistic actions that target key pathological processes in the RPE. While further preclinical studies specifically focused on dry AMD models are warranted to validate the hypothesized coactivation of TFEB and subsequent enhancement of lysosomal acidification and cathepsin D activity, the current literature provides a strong scientific basis for such investigations. The strengths of fenofibrate lie in its multifaceted mechanism—encompassing lipid catabolism, autophagy, anti-inflammatory, and possibly neuroprotective effects—which collectively offer a promising strategy to reduce drusen precursors and mitigate RPE stress. The primary weaknesses involve the need for direct evidence in dry AMD models, optimization of ocular delivery to overcome pharmacokinetic barriers, and careful monitoring of potential systemic side effects in an elderly population. Overall, fenofibrate represents a compelling and scientifically sound candidate that merits further exploration in the context of dry AMD, with the potential to significantly advance our therapeutic arsenal against this currently untreatable form of macular degeneration (Falcão et al., 2025; Fu et al., 2019; da Ana et al., 2023; Dou & Duerfeldt, 2020; Lee et al., 2023).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Nicotinamide riboside (NR), marketed as ChromaDex Niagen, belongs to the vitamin B3 family and is a naturally occurring precursor of nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+). Originally discovered in trace amounts in milk and other food sources, NR has been isolated and subsequently synthesized to yield a high‐purity form for nutritional and pharmaceutical applications. As a member of a class of compounds designed to elevate intracellular NAD+ levels, NR has attracted significant attention in the fields of metabolism, aging, and neuroprotection. Its chemical structure—a combination of a nicotinamide moiety bound to ribose—enables it to enter salvage pathways in cells with minimal metabolic conversion losses. In this regard, NR is comparable to other NAD+ boosters such as nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN), though differences in bioavailability and cellular transporter expression have been noted in some studies. Preclinical research has documented retinal distribution of NR in rodent models, suggesting that it reaches ocular tissues in pharmacologically relevant concentrations, an essential prerequisite for any agent intended to treat dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) (Abokyi & Tse, 2025; Braidy et al., 2019).

Therapeutic History:  
NR has been extensively investigated for its potential to modulate cellular energy metabolism and mitigate the effects of aging in diverse tissues. Early studies revealed that supplementation with NR effectively elevates NAD+ levels in multiple cell types, including neurons, skeletal muscle, and retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells, thereby enhancing mitochondrial function and cellular stress resistance (Dovijarski, 2019; Pîrvu et al., 2021). In the context of ocular research, while much of the direct experimental work has been performed using NMN, the close biochemical relationship between NMN and NR—as NAD+ precursors—has led investigators to propose that NR could produce similar outcomes in RPE cells. Models of retinal degeneration, including glaucoma and optic nerve injury, have demonstrated that NAD+ boosting via NR administration can ameliorate mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress, indirectly supporting its potential repurposing for dry AMD (Kitaoka et al., 2020; Mehmel et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2024). Moreover, clinical studies investigating NR’s safety in humans have shown that it is well tolerated at doses that elevate systemic NAD+ levels; doses in the gram-range have been employed without significant adverse effects (Jadeja et al., 2020). Although direct clinical trials targeting dry AMD are still forthcoming, the overall therapeutic history of NR—encompassing robust preclinical ocular benefit across neurodegenerative models and a favorable safety profile in human subjects—strongly supports further investigation for eye diseases where NAD+ depletion is a central pathophysiological feature (Dovijarski, 2019; Braidy et al., 2019; Pîrvu et al., 2021).

Mechanism of Action:  
The proposed mechanism of NR in dry AMD centers on its capacity to elevate intracellular NAD+ levels, thereby fueling a cascade of beneficial biochemical events. After cell entry, NR is phosphorylated by nicotinamide riboside kinases (NRKs) to generate NMN, which is subsequently converted to NAD+ through the activity of NMN adenylyltransferase. The resultant increase in NAD+ acts as a vital cofactor for sirtuins—primarily SIRT1 and SIRT3—which are NAD+-dependent deacetylases involved in regulating numerous cellular processes. SIRT1, in particular, has been implicated in deacetylating key transcription factors such as peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator-1α (PGC-1α) and transcription factor EB (TFEB). TFEB is a master regulator of lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy; its deacetylation leads to its nuclear translocation and binding to CLEAR (Coordinated Lysosomal Expression and Regulation) elements in the promoter regions of autophagy and lysosomal genes. Such activation promotes lysosomal acidification and increases the activity of hydrolases like cathepsin D, which are critical for the degradation of damaged proteins and organelles. Concurrently, SIRT3, which localizes predominantly to mitochondria, enhances mitochondrial function by deacetylating enzymes crucial for mitochondrial bioenergetics and reactive oxygen species (ROS) detoxification. The overall effect of NR supplementation is therefore hypothesized to be a restoration of cellular homeostasis in RPE cells—improving both autophagic clearance and mitochondrial function, two processes known to be compromised in dry AMD (Kitaoka et al., 2020; Mehmel et al., 2020; Lin & Apte, 2018; Jadeja et al., 2020). Such a mechanism is consistent with a substantial body of literature demonstrating that the NAD+-sirtuin axis plays a critical role in regulating neuroprotective and anti-aging functions across various tissues (Dovijarski, 2019; Jadeja et al., 2018; Pîrvu et al., 2021).

At the molecular level, the cascade initiated by NR begins with its metabolic conversion to NAD+, which then serves as an essential substrate for SIRT1 activation. Activated SIRT1 deacetylates TFEB, facilitating its nuclear accumulation and binding to the CLEAR network promoters, thereby upregulating genes responsible for autophagy, lysosomal biogenesis, and lysosomal acidification. This process is expected to boost cathepsin D activity and overall lysosomal proteolytic function. Parallel activation of SIRT3 in mitochondria further strengthens cellular defenses by enhancing mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation and reducing ROS generation through deacetylation of key metabolic enzymes. These reconstructed pathways directly address the deleterious effects of oxidative stress and metabolic dysfunction that drive RPE cell death in dry AMD (Kitaoka et al., 2020; Mehmel et al., 2020; Jadeja et al., 2018). While several studies using NMN have validated these pathways in RPE and retinal cells (Ren et al., 2022), the mechanistic rationale for NR’s effectiveness remains compelling given its similar mode of action and previously documented retinal distribution (Kitaoka et al., 2020; Jadeja et al., 2020).

Expected Effect:  
In the experimental setting, the administration of NR is expected to lead to a marked elevation of intracellular NAD+ levels within RPE cells, setting off a chain reaction of intracellular adjustments. The immediate consequence of increased NAD+ availability will be the enhanced activation of SIRT1 and SIRT3. Once activated, SIRT1 is anticipated to deacetylate TFEB, resulting in its translocation to the nucleus. In the nucleus, TFEB binds to target gene promoters, thereby upregulating a suite of genes involved in lysosomal biogenesis and the autophagic process. Critically, improvements in lysosomal acidification are expected to boost cathepsin D activity—a protease essential for the degradation of intracellular waste and damaged organelles. Simultaneously, SIRT3-mediated deacetylation events within the mitochondria are projected to improve mitochondrial respiratory capacity and enhance ATP production, while also reducing the production of ROS that ordinarily contribute to oxidative damage. The net effect of these cellular modifications should be an increase in RPE cell viability, particularly under conditions of induced oxidative stress (for example, H₂O₂ exposure), which mimics the pathological environment observed in dry AMD (Zhu et al., 2016; Tong et al., 2022).

Additionally, the NR-induced NAD+ boosting is hypothesized to initiate a beneficial feedback loop wherein improved mitochondrial function further supports cellular energy demands and sustains autophagic flux. This dual action—simultaneously targeting lysosomal and mitochondrial dysfunction—addresses two major hallmarks of dry AMD pathophysiology. RPE cells, which are crucial for the maintenance of photoreceptors, suffer from cumulative oxidative damage and impaired clearance of cellular debris as a result of aging and environmental stress. By restoring efficient autophagic processes and ensuring proper mitochondrial function, NR treatment is expected to reduce the accumulation of toxic protein aggregates and dysfunctional organelles, thereby staving off cellular senescence and death. This is especially salient given that recent studies have linked improved NAD+ metabolism to increased cellular resilience in models of age-related neurodegeneration (Jadeja et al., 2018; Jadeja et al., 2020). The expected outcomes in these assays include measurable increases in NAD+/NADH ratios, enhanced expression and nuclear localization of TFEB, elevated cathepsin D activity, and ultimately, improved cell survival following oxidative challenge. Such effects have been reported in various in vitro and in vivo studies employing NAD+ precursors, strengthening the biological plausibility of the NR hypothesis for treating dry AMD (Kitaoka et al., 2020; Mehmel et al., 2020; Dovijarski, 2019).

Overall Evaluation:  
An overall evaluation of NR as a candidate for treating dry AMD reveals both promising strengths and areas requiring further elucidation. Among the principal strengths is NR’s robust ability to elevate systemic and intracellular NAD+ levels, a key factor in numerous regulatory processes implicated in aging and cellular stress response. Its well-characterized pharmacokinetics, combined with documented safety in human supplementation studies, position NR as an attractive candidate for rapid clinical translation (Jadeja et al., 2020; Braidy et al., 2019). The underlying mechanism—that is, the activation of SIRT1 and SIRT3 leading to deacetylation and activation of TFEB—is supported by a breadth of biochemical and preclinical studies, albeit many of these have been performed with related compounds such as NMN. Nevertheless, the evidence suggests that the NAD+–sirtuin–TFEB axis is critical for autophagic and mitochondrial homeostasis in RPE cells—a process compromised in dry AMD (Kitaoka et al., 2020; Mehmel et al., 2020; Jadeja et al., 2018).

Further strengths include NR’s potential to confer dual-organellar benefit. Restoration of lysosomal function, as evidenced by improved acidification and protease activity (e.g., cathepsin D), is a novel therapeutic target that addresses the accumulation of cellular debris—a key factor in the progression of dry AMD. Concurrently, the enhancement of mitochondrial quality and bioenergetics through SIRT3 activation can mitigate oxidative stress and improve cell survival in metabolic stress conditions. Together, these actions provide a mechanistically coherent rationale for repurposing NR in a disease context that currently lacks effective treatments (Kitaoka et al., 2020; Mehmel et al., 2020).

However, several challenges and weaknesses must be acknowledged. First, while preclinical data offer promising insights, direct evidence of NR’s efficacy in RPE cells specifically challenged by dry AMD-like oxidative stress is still limited. Much of the supportive evidence comes from studies employing NMN or from models of other neurodegenerative conditions such as glaucoma and optic nerve degeneration (Lin et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2024). Given differences in uptake and metabolic processing between NR and NMN (Will-Orrego, 2020), it will be important to confirm that NR is adequately taken up by RPE and that its metabolic conversion is efficient in these cells.  

Furthermore, the full cascade—from NAD+ elevation through SIRT1/SIRT3 activation, subsequent TFEB deacetylation, and eventual lysosomal and mitochondrial improvements—remains to be validated within the specific context of dry AMD. Although the general biology of the NAD+–sirtuin axis is well established, its quantitative impact on TFEB activity and cathepsin D function in RPE under conditions of oxidative stress has not been directly demonstrated. This gap in the literature raises questions regarding the optimal dosing regimen, the timing of supplementation, and the potential for compensatory metabolic changes that might blunt the predicted benefits (Ren et al., 2022).

Another consideration is the heterogeneity inherent in dry AMD pathology. RPE cell dysfunction in AMD is multifactorial, involving not only oxidative stress and defective autophagy, but also inflammation, extracellular matrix alterations, and genetic predispositions. Whether NR’s NAD+ boosting effect alone can sufficiently address the multifaceted nature of dry AMD remains uncertain. There is also the possibility that chronic administration might lead to unforeseen metabolic imbalances or off-target effects, particularly if prolonged high-dose supplementation alters systemic NAD+ homeostasis or affects non-target tissues in unintended ways (Ghosh et al., 2023; Jadeja et al., 2018).

Despite these challenges, the candidate’s favorable safety profile and the mechanistic soundness of the NAD+–sirtuin–TFEB hypothesis underpin a strong case for further investigation. In vitro experiments using ARPE-19 cells and primary RPE cultures under oxidative stress conditions should be prioritized to determine whether NR supplementation can reproducibly induce TFEB nuclear translocation, enhance lysosomal acidification, and improve mitochondrial function. In addition, in vivo studies in animal models that recapitulate dry AMD pathology will be essential to assess the translational potential of NR. These studies might include detailed pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic analyses to ascertain the retinal bioavailability of NR, as well as dose-response studies to define the therapeutic window. Finally, controlled clinical trials in patients with early dry AMD would be necessary to confirm efficacy and to optimize treatment protocols (Martucci et al., 2025; Oshitari, 2024; Lin & Apte, 2018).

In summary, the current body of evidence suggests that NR is a promising repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. Its ability to efficiently elevate intracellular NAD+ levels, combined with the downstream activation of SIRT1 and SIRT3, provides a strong mechanistic rationale for improving both autophagic flux and mitochondrial function in RPE cells. These cellular processes are crucial for maintaining retinal health and combating the oxidative and metabolic stress that drives dry AMD progression. Moreover, the extensive preclinical investigation of NAD+ precursors and the favorable safety record of NR in human studies further support its potential for fast-tracking into clinical evaluation for retinal disorders (Kitaoka et al., 2020; Mehmel et al., 2020; Dovijarski, 2019; Jadeja et al., 2020; Pîrvu et al., 2021).

Nonetheless, key uncertainties remain regarding the direct applicability of NR’s effects to the complex microenvironment of the retina in dry AMD. Issues such as differential cellular uptake, the efficiency of NR’s metabolic conversion to NAD+ in RPE cells, and the precise threshold of NAD+ elevation required to trigger beneficial deacetylation of TFEB must be addressed. Furthermore, given the multifactorial nature of AMD pathology, combinatorial therapeutic approaches may ultimately be necessary to achieve clinically significant improvements. Therefore, while NR emerges as a highly promising candidate with a compelling mechanistic framework, rigorous experimental validation tailored specifically to the ocular setting is imperative. Future studies should elucidate whether the activation of the NAD+–sirtuin–TFEB axis translates into meaningful improvements in lysosomal acidification, cathepsin D activity, and RPE cell survival in both in vitro models of oxidative stress and in vivo models of dry AMD (Kitaoka et al., 2020; Jadeja et al., 2018; Will-Orrego, 2020).

Looking forward, systematic exploration through well-designed preclinical trials is recommended to confirm the predicted molecular events. These experiments should include detailed time-course and dose-response analyses of NAD+ levels, sirtuin activities, TFEB deacetylation status, and lysosomal function in retinal cells exposed to oxidative insults. Such data will not only clarify the effectiveness of NR in restoring cellular homeostasis but also help refine dosing strategies and identify potential biomarkers of response. Ultimately, if subsequent research affirms the predicted benefits of NR in improving RPE function and survival, this therapeutic candidate could represent a major advancement in the pharmacological management of dry AMD—a condition for which current treatment options remain notably limited (Kitaoka et al., 2020; Mehmel et al., 2020; Dovijarski, 2019; Jadeja et al., 2020; Pîrvu et al., 2021).

Overall, the promising preclinical evidence supporting the NAD+–sirtuin–TFEB pathway, combined with the safety profile demonstrated in human trials, renders NR a highly attractive candidate for drug development in dry AMD. While further direct experimental evidence is required to confirm its efficacy in retinal cells, the mechanistic insights gleaned from various studies provide a sound scientific basis for proceeding with additional preclinical and clinical investigations. Thus, repurposing nicotinamide riboside for dry AMD holds significant potential and merits further exploration as part of an integrated strategy to address the unmet therapeutic need in this degenerative retinal disease (Abokyi & Tse, 2025; Cimaglia et al., 2020; Ebeling et al., 2020; Jadeja et al., 2020; Pîrvu et al., 2021; Lin & Apte, 2018).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
BAY 11-7082 is a synthetic, small-molecule inhibitor originally discovered as an irreversible inhibitor of IκBα phosphorylation, which blocks NF-κB activation. Chemically, it is classified as a phenyl vinyl sulfone compound featuring an α,β-unsaturated moiety that functions as a Michael acceptor. This reactive electrophilic center enables the compound to covalently modify nucleophilic cysteine residues on target proteins. Early studies identified BAY 11-7082 for its capacity to inhibit NF-κB signaling in endothelial cells, and subsequent research expanded its profile to include inhibition of the NLRP3 inflammasome via cysteine alkylation of critical regulatory sites. In essence, BAY 11-7082 belongs to the class of covalent inhibitors that have been widely studied in the context of inflammatory and oncologic diseases, and its availability as Sigma B5556 has made it a common tool compound in preclinical research (Juliana et al., 2010; Marchetti, 2019; Yu et al., 2018).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, BAY 11-7082 has been utilized extensively in biochemical, cellular, and animal studies as an anti-inflammatory agent. Initial applications centered on its ability to block the phosphorylation and degradation of IκBα, thereby inhibiting downstream NF-κB–driven gene expression. This mechanism was exploited in models of endothelial inflammation and various cancer cell lines, including studies showing potent anticancer, neuroprotective, and anti-inflammatory effects (Lee et al., 2012; Melisi & Chiao, 2007). Furthermore, its repurposing has been explored in fields as diverse as hematologic malignancies, diabetes-related complications, and preclinical psoriasis models, where it served as a dual inhibitor of NF-κB and the NLRP3 inflammasome (Irrera et al., 2017; Kolati et al., 2015). Despite this broad research history, BAY 11-7082 has not been previously tested explicitly in the context of dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or diseases with a similar pathology in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE). However, its known capacity to reduce inflammatory cytokine production and preserve lysosomal integrity in nonocular cell types provides a rationale for evaluating its potential utility in dry AMD—a disease characterized by chronic inflammation, impaired lysosomal clearance, and inflammasome activation (Blevins et al., 2022; Irrera et al., 2017; Marchetti, 2019).

Mechanism of Action:  
BAY 11-7082 exerts its pharmacological effects predominantly through irreversible covalent inhibition. Its most well‐characterized mechanism is the blockade of NF-κB signaling by preventing the phosphorylation of the inhibitory protein IκBα. Under normal conditions, phosphorylation of IκBα triggers its degradation, thus allowing NF-κB (typically the p65/p50 heterodimer) to translocate into the nucleus and activate pro-inflammatory target genes. By inhibiting IκBα phosphorylation, BAY 11-7082 effectively sequesters NF-κB in the cytosol, thereby suppressing the expression of genes associated with inflammation such as IL-1β, TNF-α, and various chemokines (Marchetti, 2019; Melisi & Chiao, 2007).  

Moreover, BAY 11-7082 has been repurposed based on its ability to inhibit the NLRP3 inflammasome. Mechanistically, the compound forms covalent adducts with reactive cysteine residues on the NLRP3 protein, most likely within the ATPase domain—an essential activity domain required for inflammasome activation. This alkylation event, which proceeds via a Michael-type addition reaction, results in irreversible inactivation of NLRP3’s ATPase function, thereby preventing the assembly and subsequent activation of the inflammasome complex (Cocco et al., 2014; Juliana et al., 2010; Marchetti, 2019). In addition to these primary actions, BAY 11-7082 has been reported to inhibit other cysteine-dependent enzymes such as protein tyrosine phosphatases and even components like gasdermin D that contribute to pyroptosis. Consequently, the compound displays a broad-spectrum inhibitory profile that may diminish inflammatory cascades not only at the transcriptional (NF-κB) level but also at the inflammasome activation stage (Yu et al., 2018; Zahid et al., 2019).  

Expected Effect in Dry Age-Related Macular Degeneration:  
In the context of dry AMD, the hypothesis is that chronic inflammation in the RPE drives cellular dysfunction through mechanisms that include sustained NF-κB activation and priming of the NLRP3 inflammasome. Inflammatory cytokines and resultant oxidative stress contribute to lysosomal impairment, reducing the activity of v-ATPase and lysosomal proteases such as cathepsin D (CTSD), which are crucial for the clearance of cellular debris. BAY 11-7082 is expected to intervene at an early stage in this inflammatory cascade by inhibiting NF-κB signaling. In doing so, it would reduce the transcriptional upregulation of inflammasome components and pro-inflammatory cytokines, particularly IL-1β, a key mediator in inflammasome activation (Blevins et al., 2022; Marchetti, 2019).  

Experimental studies in macrophages and psoriasis models have demonstrated that NF-κB inhibition with BAY 11-7082 leads to a reduction in IL-1β production and preserves lysosomal integrity. Although these studies were conducted in nonocular tissues, the expression of NF-κB and NLRP3 inflammasome components in RPE cells is well-documented in the literature. Therefore, it is reasonable to propose that BAY 11-7082, when applied to RPE cell models, could diminish the priming of the NLRP3 inflammasome. This reduction in inflammasome activity is expected to mitigate downstream lysosomal damage, preserve v-ATPase function, and maintain cathepsin D–mediated clearance. Ultimately, these cellular improvements could slow the degenerative progression characteristic of dry AMD (Cocco et al., 2014; Irrera et al., 2017).  

The proposed testing strategy leverages the rapid on–off pharmacology observed in cell culture models, facilitating dose optimization to achieve sufficient anti-inflammatory activity while minimizing potential toxicity. Importantly, targeting an upstream event, namely NF-κB activation and inflammasome priming, distinguishes BAY 11-7082 from therapeutic strategies that focus on downstream caspase inhibition. In retinal cells, preservation of lysosomal function is critical; thus, preventing inflammasome-triggered lysosomal rupture could have a marked protective effect on RPE health (Ajetunmobi et al., 2023; Zahid et al., 2019).

Overall Evaluation:  
BAY 11-7082 presents a compelling therapeutic candidate for dry AMD based on its dual mechanism of action. One of its primary strengths is that it targets two key upstream pathways—inhibition of NF-κB signaling and direct inactivation of the NLRP3 inflammasome—which are critically implicated in the inflammatory processes that drive RPE dysfunction and subsequent retinal degeneration in dry AMD. This upstream intervention could, in theory, reduce the chronic production of pro-inflammatory cytokines and prevent lysosomal abnormalities that compromise the clearance of metabolic waste in RPE cells. The promising preclinical data from psoriasis, diabetic nephropathy, and other inflammatory disease models provide an encouraging foundation regarding its anti-inflammatory capacity (Blevins et al., 2022; Irrera et al., 2017; Marchetti, 2019).

However, there are several potential weaknesses and challenges to consider. First, BAY 11-7082 operates via irreversible covalent binding through its Michael acceptor; while this can yield sustained inhibition, it also raises significant concerns regarding off-target effects and general toxicity due to the potential for nonselective alkylation of other cysteine-containing proteins. Such promiscuous reactivity has been observed in studies involving diverse cell types, and cellular toxicity in contexts such as platelets or myeloma cells has been reported, albeit at higher concentrations (Coles et al., 2021; Paul et al., 2017; Rauert-Wunderlich et al., 2013). Second, although extensive preclinical data exist demonstrating its anti-inflammatory and anti-cancer activity, BAY 11-7082 has not been previously evaluated in ocular tissues. The unique physiology of the eye, particularly the retinal pigment epithelium, could result in significantly different pharmacokinetics and tissue-specific toxicity profiles. The documented rapid on–off pharmacology in cell culture is encouraging, yet extrapolation to an in vivo retinal environment must be approached cautiously (Paul et al., 2017; Zahid et al., 2019).  

Another consideration is the narrow therapeutic window that may exist; while doses in animal models have been optimized for systemic inflammation or cancer, achieving effective local concentrations in the RPE without compromising cell viability is a delicate balance. Previous studies in nonocular systems suggest that BAY 11-7082 can function without overt toxicity at concentrations up to 20 μM in cell culture and 20 mg/kg/day in animal models, but whether similar dosing regimens would be applicable for ocular delivery remains to be determined (Mabuchi et al., 2004; Paul et al., 2017). Additionally, because BAY 11-7082 modulates ubiquitin system components beyond NF-κB and NLRP3 inflammasome targets, there is a risk of unintended interference with normal protein turnover and cellular homeostasis, potentially exacerbating cellular stress in a tissue already vulnerable to degenerative processes, as seen in dry AMD (Coles et al., 2021; Strickson et al., 2013).

In summary, BAY 11-7082 shows promise as a candidate repurposed for dry AMD because it strategically targets early inflammatory events that have been implicated in RPE dysfunction, including NF-κB–mediated inflammasome priming and consequent lysosomal impairment. The compound’s established anti-inflammatory effects in various preclinical models lend strong support to the hypothesis that its use in RPE could preserve lysosomal function and enhance CTSD-mediated clearance. Nonetheless, the inherent risks associated with its covalent, irreversible mechanism demand rigorous ocular-specific toxicity and pharmacokinetics investigations. If dose optimization and targeted delivery—perhaps through localized ocular formulations—can mitigate off-target effects, BAY 11-7082 might offer a novel approach that differentiates itself from therapies focused solely on downstream caspase inhibition.
