Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
ML-SA1 is a synthetic, cell-permeable small-molecule agonist of the endolysosomal mucolipin/TRPML family, with primary pharmacological activity at TRPML1, the Ca2+-permeable cation channel encoded by MCOLN1 that resides on late endosome/lysosome membranes and mediates lysosomal Ca2+ efflux into the cytosol (Wang et al., 2023). ML-SA1 and chemically related “ML-SA” agonists emerged from small-molecule discovery programs aimed at pharmacologically restoring TRPML1 function; the compound is frequently referred to in the literature as “mucolipin synthetic agonist 1,” reflecting its origin as a tool compound class designed to activate TRPML channels rather than as a derivative of a natural product scaffold (Yan et al., 2021). Although the chemical structure and synthetic route for ML-SA1 are not detailed in the cited records, its provenance traces to a specialized small-molecule therapeutics effort at Calporta Therapeutics, a company subsequently acquired by Merck in 2019, signaling substantial translational interest in TRPML1 agonism for lysosomal storage and neurodegenerative disorders (Van Acker et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2023).

Functionally, ML-SA1 belongs to the broader class of TRPML1 agonists/activators that includes endogenous lipid ligands such as phosphatidylinositol-3,5-bisphosphate, PI(3,5)P2, and other synthetic small molecules (e.g., SF-22, MK6-83, and newer ML-SA chemotypes like ML-SA5), all of which gate TRPML channels to increase endolysosomal Ca2+ release (Wang et al., 2023; Más Gómez et al., 2018; Wünkhaus et al., 2024). Within this class, ML-SA1 is reported to activate TRPML1 with potency comparable to or greater than the endogenous PI(3,5)P2 under certain conditions and can act in conjunction with PI(3,5)P2 to potentiate channel opening, thereby rescuing endo-lysosomal morphology and function in cellular disease models that exhibit lysosomal stress (e.g., after PIKfyve inhibition) (Wang et al., 2023). Across preclinical research, TRPML1 agonists have been deployed as mechanistic probes and candidate therapeutics to restore lysosomal Ca2+ signaling, normalize lysosomal pH/acidification, promote autophagosome maturation and autolysosome formation, enhance lysosomal exocytosis, and induce TFEB-dependent lysosomal biogenesis in lysosomal storage and neurodegeneration models (Tedeschi et al., 2025; Pollmanns et al., 2022).

In ocular systems directly relevant to retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) biology, ML-SA1 has been used to interrogate TRPML1 function. In mouse primary RPE, human embryonic stem cell–derived RPE (hesRPE), and ARPE-19 cells, ML-SA1 produced rapid, robust, reversible increases in cytosolic Ca2+ that persisted in Ca2+-free external solutions and were blunted by lysosomal disruption, indicating a lysosomal Ca2+ source (Más Gómez et al., 2018). Critically, ML-SA1 failed to evoke Ca2+ signals in RPE from TRPML1 knockout mice, confirming channel specificity in this tissue (Más Gómez et al., 2018). The same study demonstrated that lysosomal lipid accumulation—induced pharmacologically or present in disease models—impairs ML-SA1-evoked TRPML1 Ca2+ release, mechanistically linking lysosomal lipidization to diminished TRPML1 function in RPE (Más Gómez et al., 2018). These data situate ML-SA1 squarely within a mechanistic toolkit for modulating RPE lysosomal physiology implicated in retinal degenerations associated with lipid/lipofuscin accrual (Más Gómez et al., 2018).

Therapeutic History  
There is no record in the provided corpus of ML-SA1 being used clinically in humans or specifically in trials for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or geographic atrophy (GA) (Más Gómez et al., 2018). However, extensive preclinical use across cell and animal models supports the biological rationale relevant to dry AMD. In RPE systems, ML-SA1 has been applied acutely to evoke TRPML1-dependent lysosomal Ca2+ release as described above (Más Gómez et al., 2018). In vivo, subretinal ML-SA1 administration in a rat retinal detachment model preserved outer nuclear layer thickness, reduced photoreceptor apoptosis, lessened cleaved caspase-3, increased autophagy markers (LC3-II/LC3-I and Beclin-1), decreased reactive oxygen species (ROS), and prevented TRPML1 degradation, collectively demonstrating functional rescue via autophagy activation and oxidative stress mitigation in injured retina (Yan et al., 2021).

Beyond the eye, multiple studies in neuronal and disease-model systems have used ML-SA1 to correct lysosomal/autophagy defects and proteostasis. In cultured neurons and HEK293T cells, ML-SA1 enhanced maturation of autophagosomes into acidic autolysosomes and reduced α-synuclein accumulation/aggregates; ML-SA1 could override bafilomycin-induced fusion/acidification blocks in both HEK293T cells and neurons, and these effects required lysosomal PI(3,5)P2 and cytosolic Ca2+ consistent with TRPML1 channel gating (Pollmanns et al., 2022). In primary cortical neurons, ML-SA1 rapidly acidified endolysosomes and prevented LDL-induced amyloidogenesis by reducing Aβ and BACE1 mislocalization/activity; TRPML1 knockdown abrogated ML-SA1’s effects and exacerbated LDL-driven Aβ production (Hui et al., 2019). In lysosomal storage disease (LSD) contexts, ML-SA1 was used as a TRPML1 activator to elicit lysosomal Ca2+ release responses that were impaired in Niemann–Pick type C (NPC1) patient fibroblasts; BK channel activation partially rescued the reduced ML-SA1 response, and BK upregulation lowered lipofuscin accumulation via lysosomal exocytosis, establishing pharmacological synergies that might be exploited in lipid storage states (Zhong et al., 2016).

Importantly for RPE-relevant lysosomal storage phenotypes, the more potent TRPML1 agonist ML-SA5 was used in ARPE-19 CLN3-knockout cells (a juvenile neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis model) to reduce lysosomal accumulation of subunit C of mitochondrial ATPase (SubC), Gb3, and lysosomal glycerophosphodiesters, accompanied by TFEB nuclear translocation and increased surface LAMP1 consistent with enhanced lysosomal exocytosis; however, BMP/LBPA lipid deficits and maturation of cathepsin D (CatD) and TPP1 remained impaired, indicating incomplete restoration of lysosomal hydrolase processing (Wünkhaus et al., 2024; Unknown Reference). Patch-clamp experiments in these cells confirmed that ML-SA1 variants evoke TRPML1 currents fully blocked by the antagonist ML-SI3, supporting pharmacological specificity in RPE lysosomes (Unknown Reference). Collectively, the body of preclinical work shows that TRPML1 agonism has repeatedly restored facets of lysosomal function (Ca2+ release, acidification, autophagosome–lysosome fusion, exocytosis, TFEB activation) across cell types and in injured retina, though complete correction of all lysosomal abnormalities (e.g., hydrolase maturation) is not assured in all disease contexts (Pollmanns et al., 2022; Yan et al., 2021; Unknown Reference).

No studies in the present corpus demonstrate ML-SA1 use in dry AMD animal models, in RPE models of drusen/lipofuscin accumulation specific to AMD, or in clinical AMD studies; however, in RPE, lipid accumulation was shown to blunt ML-SA1–evoked TRPML1 Ca2+ release, and TRPML1 KO RPE exhibited increased autofluorescence, mechanistically connecting TRPML1 functionality to handling of autofluorescent/neutral lipid material relevant to AMD pathophysiology (Más Gómez et al., 2018). The class of TRPML1 agonists (including ML-SA1) is being investigated preclinically for lysosomal storage and neurodegenerative indications, reinforcing translational plausibility even in the absence of AMD-specific studies (Wang et al., 2023).

Mechanism of Action  
TRPML1 is a lysosomal six-transmembrane TRP superfamily channel permeable to Ca2+ and other cations that localizes primarily to late endosomal/lysosomal membranes via cytosolic dileucine motifs, where it mediates lumen-to-cytosol ion efflux in response to endogenous and pharmacological gating (Wang et al., 2023; Unknown Reference). Physiological activation is conferred by the late endosomal/lysosomal phosphoinositide PI(3,5)P2, whose 3′ phosphate directly stabilizes an open-channel conformation; PI(4,5)P2 acts as an antagonist enriched at the plasma membrane, ensuring compartmental specificity (Wang et al., 2023). TRPML1-dependent lysosomal Ca2+ release acts as a master regulator of lysosomal/autophagic homeostasis via several calcium-sensitive effectors: calcineurin dephosphorylates TFEB to drive its nuclear translocation and induce the CLEAR network (lysosomal biogenesis and function genes), whereas CaMKKβ activation promotes autophagosome biogenesis; additional roles include regulation of vesicle trafficking, membrane fusion/fission, lysosomal reformation, exocytosis, and mitochondria–lysosome contacts (Wang et al., 2023; Tedeschi et al., 2025; Unknown Reference).

ML-SA1 is a synthetic agonist that binds TRPML channels and increases channel open probability, functionally mimicking or synergizing with PI(3,5)P2 to produce lysosomal Ca2+ efflux (Wang et al., 2023). In multiple cell systems, ML-SA1 triggers rapid lysosomal Ca2+ release measured by cytosolic Ca2+ reporters and genetically encoded TRPML1-proximal indicators; responses are abolished or blunted by TRPML1 gene knockout, lysosomal rupture, or pharmacological inhibitors, confirming that cytosolic Ca2+ rises originate from lysosomes through TRPML1 (Más Gómez et al., 2018). In RPE cells, ML-SA1-evoked Ca2+ signals were insensitive to extracellular Ca2+ removal and ER Ca2+ depletion with thapsigargin, but were eliminated by lysosomal disruption with GPN and absent in TRPML1−/− RPE, demonstrating the specificity and lysosomal source in the cell type of interest (Más Gómez et al., 2018).

Downstream of TRPML1 activation, ML-SA1 drives a coordinated set of lysosome-centric responses:  
- Autophagosome–lysosome fusion and maturation: ML-SA1 increases conversion of LC3-positive autophagosomes into acidic autolysosomes and shifts cargo (e.g., α-synuclein) into LAMP1-positive, acidified vesicles; notably, ML-SA1 can partially override bafilomycin A1 blocks on fusion/acidification, consistent with a Ca2+-dependent maturation/fusion mechanism (Pollmanns et al., 2022).  
- Lysosomal acidification: In primary neurons, ML-SA1 rapidly acidifies endolysosomes in a TRPML1-dependent manner, coincident with reduced LDL-induced amyloidogenesis and BACE1 localization/activity in endolysosomes (Hui et al., 2019).  
- TFEB signaling and lysosomal biogenesis/exocytosis: TRPML1 activation promotes TFEB nuclear translocation and transcription of lysosomal/autophagy genes; in ARPE-19 CLN3-KO cells, ML-SA5 triggered TFEB translocation and increased surface LAMP1 within 90 minutes, consistent with enhanced lysosomal exocytosis, and reduced lysosomal glycerophosphodiester loads (Tedeschi et al., 2025; Wünkhaus et al., 2024).  
- Proteostasis correction: ML-SA1 reduces α-synuclein protein/aggregates in cell models by steering cargo into maturing autolysosomes and promoting degradative flux; these effects require autophagy, PI(3,5)P2, and cytosolic Ca2+, aligning with TRPML1’s canonical signaling dependencies (Pollmanns et al., 2022).  
- Neuroprotection via autophagy induction and oxidative stress reduction: In vivo in retinal detachment, subretinal ML-SA1 increased LC3-II/LC3-I and Beclin-1, reduced cleaved caspase-3, decreased ROS, preserved photoreceptors, and prevented injury-induced TRPML1 degradation (Yan et al., 2021).

Two mechanism-linked constraints merit emphasis for AMD translation. First, lysosomal lipid accumulation impairs TRPML1 function in RPE: desipramine (ASM inhibition), PIKfyve inhibition (YM201636), and chloroquine/U18666A-induced neutral lipid/lipofuscin models decreased ML-SA1–evoked Ca2+ release without reducing TRPML1 mRNA or total lysosomal Ca2+, indicating functional channel inhibition by lipidized lysosomal membranes—an AMD-relevant condition (Más Gómez et al., 2018). Second, in CLN3-deficient RPE, TRPML1 activation improved substrate clearance and TFEB signaling but did not restore the mature, active forms of CatD and TPP1 despite increased transcripts and precursor/intermediate protein levels, pointing to persistent hydrolase processing defects not corrected by TRPML1 agonism alone (Unknown Reference). These observations suggest that while ML-SA1 should restore key steps (Ca2+ efflux, fusion/acidification, TFEB), lysosomal lipid environments typical of aged RPE may constrain efficacy, and hydrolase maturation deficits—if present in AMD—may not normalize solely via TRPML1 activation (Más Gómez et al., 2018; Unknown Reference).

- Lipid-dependent resistance: Lysosomal lipid accumulation diminishes ML-SA1 responses in RPE without reducing TRPML1 expression or total lysosomal Ca2+, implying that aged/AMD RPE may exhibit attenuated pharmacodynamics; combination strategies or higher potency agonists (e.g., ML-SA5) may be needed to overcome lipidized lysosomal membranes (Más Gómez et al., 2018; Wünkhaus et al., 2024).  
- Hydrolase maturation not universally rescued: In CLN3-deficient RPE, TRPML1 activation failed to restore mature CatD and TPP1 despite TFEB induction, indicating that some degradative deficits—potentially relevant to AMD—may not normalize solely via TRPML1 activation; this could limit improvements in cathepsin-dependent proteolysis of drusen precursors (Unknown Reference).  
- Selectivity considerations: ML-SA1 can activate other TRPML family members (e.g., TRPML3) in overexpression systems, and pan-TRPML agonism in RPE may have uncharacterized effects on lysosomal trafficking and axonal transport; selectivity profiling in RPE and concentration-response mapping are needed to de-risk off-target TRPML isoform engagement (Unknown Reference).  
- Context-dependent acidification: ML-SA1 acidifies neuronal endolysosomes and enhances degradative flux, but direct demonstrations of increased CatD activity in RPE after ML-SA1 are not provided here; given the CLN3-KO findings on hydrolase maturation, reliance on acidification alone may not guarantee improved protease activity in diseased RPE (Hui et al., 2019; Unknown Reference).

Development guidance  
Given the strong RPE target validation and consistent downstream biology, ML-SA1 (or a more potent TRPML1 agonist such as ML-SA5) is a credible mechanistic candidate for dry AMD; however, AMD-relevant pharmacology must be demonstrated directly. The most decision-informative steps are:  
- Establish efficacy in AMD-relevant RPE contexts: Test ML-SA1 in iPSC-derived human RPE from older donors and/or RPE cultured with A2E/lipofuscin and oxidized lipids to recapitulate lysosomal lipidization; quantify TRPML1 Ca2+ responses, TFEB translocation, lysosomal pH, autophagosome–lysosome fusion, and cargo clearance (e.g., ApoE/cholesterol-rich particles, complement-containing deposits), benchmarking against the lipid-impairment reported in RPE (Más Gómez et al., 2018).  
- Measure hydrolase activity and maturation: Directly assay CatD and other cathepsin activities and maturation states post-ML-SA1 in lipidized RPE; if maturation remains deficient, evaluate combinations with agents that restore hydrolase processing (e.g., modulators of endolysosomal trafficking or mannose-6-phosphate receptor pathways) (Unknown Reference).  
- Explore potentiation strategies: Consider co-targeting known TRPML1 modulators to overcome lipidized lysosomal membranes—examples include augmenting PI(3,5)P2 availability or adding BK channel activators, which rescued impaired ML-SA1 responses and reduced storage in NPC-related settings (Wang et al., 2023; Zhong et al., 2016).  
- Prioritize potency and exposure: Given blunted responses in lipidized RPE, evaluate higher-potency ML-SA chemotypes (ML-SA5 EC50 ~80 nM in a TFE3/TFEB-related translocation assay vs. ML-SA1 in the µM range) for superior pharmacodynamics; subretinal tolerability is supported by RD studies but needs AMD-model confirmation (Wünkhaus et al., 2024; Yan et al., 2021).  
- In vivo validation in AMD models: Move to aged/multiple-hit models that accumulate sub-RPE deposits (e.g., high-fat diet, light exposure, Abca4−/− backgrounds) to test whether TRPML1 agonism reduces drusen-like material, preserves RPE function, and slows GA-like endpoints; note that Abca4−/− RPE exhibited impaired TRPML1 Ca2+ release, making it a relevant sensitized background to assay pharmacological rescue (Más Gómez et al., 2018).

Conclusion  
ML-SA1 is a tractable, mechanistically well-supported TRPML1 agonist with direct RPE target validation and robust evidence that its downstream effects—lysosomal Ca2+ release, TFEB activation, autophagosome–lysosome fusion/acidification, and exocytosis—can correct core lysosomal deficits that plausibly drive drusen precursor accumulation in dry AMD (Más Gómez et al., 2018; Pollmanns et al., 2022; Wünkhaus et al., 2024). The principal risks are the lipid-dependence of TRPML1 dysfunction in RPE and the incomplete rescue of hydrolase maturation observed in CLN3-deficient RPE, both of which may attenuate the magnitude of effect on complex AMD cargoes and necessitate combination strategies or use of more potent agonists (Más Gómez et al., 2018; Wünkhaus et al., 2024). On balance, the mechanistic specificity, ocular proof-of-concept in retinal detachment, and extensive preclinical precedent for lysosomal restoration argue that ML-SA1 (or next-generation TRPML1 agonists) merits prioritized evaluation in AMD-relevant RPE assays and in vivo models, with an early focus on overcoming lipidized lysosomal resistance and verifying improvements in both acidification and hydrolase function (Yan et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2023; Tedeschi et al., 2025).

Strength of evidence for the dry AMD hypothesis: moderate, driven by strong RPE target biology and retinal neuroprotection data but constrained by the absence of AMD-specific in vivo studies and by lipid-imposed pharmacodynamic limits (Más Gómez et al., 2018; Yan et al., 2021). If forthcoming AMD-relevant experiments confirm that TRPML1 activation restores lysosomal Ca2+ signaling and degradative capacity in lipidized RPE, and that drusen precursors are reduced, ML-SA1/ML-SA5 would represent a differentiated, mechanism-based approach compared with broad mTOR inhibition, with the potential to correct proximal lysosomal defects underlying GA progression (Wang et al., 2023; Pollmanns et al., 2022).

Detailed, component-wise assessment  

- Target presence and engagement in RPE: TRPML1 expression and function are present in ARPE-19 and primary RPE; ML-SA1 evokes lysosomal Ca2+ release that is TRPML1-dependent (absent in TRPML1−/− RPE), establishing on-target engagement (Más Gómez et al., 2018).  
- Relevance of TRPML1 signaling to AMD pathobiology: Lysosomal lipid/lipofuscin accumulation impairs TRPML1 function in RPE and is germane to AMD; RPE autofluorescence increases in TRPML1 KO, linking the channel to handling of drusen-like material (Más Gómez et al., 2018).  
- Downstream mechanisms aligned with therapeutic hypothesis: ML-SA1 triggers calcineurin-TFEB signaling, augments autophagosome–lysosome fusion and acidification, and enhances exocytosis—mechanisms expected to improve clearance of drusen precursors (Wang et al., 2023; Pollmanns et al., 2022).  
- Evidence for improved degradative flux: In neurons, ML-SA1 acidifies endolysosomes and reduces Aβ/BACE1 pathology; in retina in vivo, ML-SA1 increases autophagy markers and preserves photoreceptors; in RPE disease models, TRPML1 activation decreases stored substrates and reduces lysosomal surface area (Hui et al., 2019; Yan et al., 2021; Wünkhaus et al., 2024).  
- Constraints/unknowns: Lipid-imposed TRPML1 inhibition in RPE may limit efficacy; CatD/TPP1 maturation not rescued in CLN3-KO RPE; no direct AMD data; potential TRPML3 co-activation (Más Gómez et al., 2018; Unknown Reference).

Recommendation  
Advance ML-SA1 (and evaluate ML-SA5 as a higher-potency comparator) into AMD-relevant RPE assays with lipidized lysosomes, incorporating quantitative readouts of TRPML1 Ca2+ signaling, TFEB translocation, lysosomal pH, hydrolase maturation/activity, and cargo clearance, and then proceed to in vivo testing in drusen-accumulating models if in vitro data are supportive; in parallel, explore combination strategies (e.g., BK channel activation) to overcome lipid-dependent resistance to TRPML1 agonism (Más Gómez et al., 2018; Wünkhaus et al., 2024; Zhong et al., 2016).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Genistein is a naturally occurring isoflavone that was first isolated from soybeans and other leguminous plants. As a member of the phytoestrogen class, genistein possesses structural similarities to mammalian estrogens and can bind to estrogen receptors, albeit with much lower intrinsic potency than endogenous steroids. It is typically obtained from dietary sources such as soy, red clover, and other legumes, but high‐purity formulations have been developed and are commercially available (for example, Sigma G6649). Genistein belongs to a broader class of natural bioactive compounds that have been studied over the past several decades for their modulating effects on various cellular processes including antioxidant defense, differentiation, apoptosis, and proliferation. Historically, phytoestrogens like genistein have been investigated both for their hormone‐like activity and as specific inhibitors of protein tyrosine kinases. The compound has been utilized in research ranging from hormone replacement strategies in menopausal women to anticancer studies, and its ability to modulate several cell signaling pathways—including those associated with PI3K/AKT/mTOR—has attracted interest in other fields such as neurodegeneration and ocular health (Albulescu & Popovici, 2007).

Therapeutic History:  
The therapeutic history of genistein spans multiple domains. Clinically, phytoestrogens have been examined largely as potential alternatives to traditional estrogen replacement therapies for the alleviation of menopausal symptoms, with some studies reporting modest effects on vasomotor symptoms, menstrual cycle regulation, and quality‐of‐life indices (Glazier & Bowman, 2001; Albulescu & Popovici, 2007). In the veterinary and preclinical realm, high doses of phytoestrogens have been associated with reproductive toxicity in livestock such as sheep (the classical clover disease), while rodent studies have similarly documented endocrine disruptions when exposed to high concentrations (Glazier & Bowman, 2001). For bone health specifically, preclinical data have shown that ovariectomized rats fed genistein exhibit reduced rates of bone loss; this finding parallels clinical trials using the synthetic isoflavone derivative ipriflavone—which is related to the parent compounds in the isoflavone class—and has demonstrated benefits in slowing bone loss and increasing bone mineral density when given for periods of up to two years in postmenopausal women (Glazier & Bowman, 2001). Regarding ocular applications, there is emerging preclinical work to improve the solubility and corneal penetration of genistein; for example, encapsulating genistein in hyaluronic acid–modified MPEG-b-PAE polymeric micelles has been shown to improve its corneal permeability by approximately 1.5-fold compared to a simple drug solution (Li et al., 2018). Although genistein has not yet been extensively evaluated in clinical trials specifically targeting dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD), its broad modulatory effects on tyrosine kinases and downstream signaling pathways provide a rationale for repurposing it to address dry AMD pathophysiology, particularly given the significant unmet therapeutic need in this area (Glazier & Bowman, 2001).

Mechanism of Action:  
Genistein is widely recognized for its ability to inhibit protein tyrosine kinases. This inhibitory action extends to several receptors and intracellular kinases, thereby modulating key signaling cascades including the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway—a pathway that is critical for cell survival, proliferation, and metabolism. In many cell-based studies, genistein has been shown to suppress PI3K/AKT signaling, leading to downstream inhibition of mTOR complex 1 (mTORC1) activity. Since mTORC1 coordinates cellular anabolic processes and suppresses autophagy under nutrient-rich conditions, inhibiting this complex can trigger autophagic clearance mechanisms (Albulescu & Popovici, 2007). One of the pivotal regulators downstream of mTORC1 is the transcription factor EB (TFEB), which, when dephosphorylated due to mTORC1 inhibition, translocates into the nucleus and promotes the transcription of genes involved in lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy. There is evidence that genistein can modulate lysosomal metabolism and promote TFEB activation, as reported in studies highlighting the ability of flavonoids to enhance the clearance of substrate accumulations via TFEB-mediated transcriptional programs (Xu et al., 2020). In retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells, which play a crucial role in maintaining photoreceptor health through phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments (POS), enhanced autophagy and lysosomal function are essential for the degradation and removal of cellular debris, including drusen components characteristic of dry AMD (Falcão et al., 2024). Moreover, experimental reports have suggested that in RPE-like models, treatment with compounds that suppress the PI3K/AKT/mTOR axis leads to increased LC3 turnover and upregulation of cathepsin D (CTSD), a lysosomal aspartic protease essential for phagolysosomal digestion (Albulescu & Popovici, 2007; Jahan et al., 2022). In this context, genistein is hypothesized to function by inhibiting upstream tyrosine kinases that feed into PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling, thereby promoting TFEB activation. TFEB then orchestrates the transcription of lysosomal genes, leading to enhanced lysosomal acidification and increased enzymatic activities, including that of cathepsin D, which is imperative for effective degradation within phagolysosomes (Falcão et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2025).

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis posits that administration of genistein to RPE cells will lead to measurable inhibition of the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway, resulting in dephosphorylation and nuclear translocation of TFEB. This transcriptional activation is expected to upregulate a battery of lysosomal and autophagy-related genes, including those responsible for the maintenance of lysosomal acidification and the synthesis of key proteases such as cathepsin D (Falcão et al., 2024). In functional assays, an increase in LC3 turnover—a marker of enhanced autophagic flux—would be anticipated, alongside elevated levels of CTSD, providing the biochemical basis for improved phagolysosomal digestion. Consequently, in an in vitro RPE cell model subjected to a photoreceptor outer segment (POS) feeding assay, genistein treatment is expected to facilitate the clearance of POS-derived debris and reduce the accumulation of autofluorescent lipofuscin-like granules. This outcome mimics the effects observed with compounds like rapamycin, where mTOR inhibition leads to a significant, approximately 30% reduction of POS-dependent autofluorescence by improving lysosomal processing (Falcão et al., 2024). Moreover, in light of published observations demonstrating that effective activation of TFEB can restore lysosomal biogenesis and enhance cellular clearance, genistein’s dual inhibition of kinase activity and subsequent autophagy upregulation is predicted to result in a favorable impact on drusen clearance and overall RPE function in dry AMD settings (Falcão et al., 2024; Xu et al., 2020).

Overall Evaluation:  
Overall, genistein presents as an intriguing candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry AMD, particularly given its established history as a natural product with a favorable oral safety profile and its documented ability to modulate critical signaling pathways involved in cell survival and autophagy. One of the major strengths of genistein lies in its dual mechanism: as a selective inhibitor of tyrosine kinases, it can suppress the upstream activation of the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway, and as a modulator of lysosomal metabolism, it facilitates TFEB activation. This mechanistic duality offers a targeted approach to enhance the autophagic clearance capacity of RPE cells, which is critical in preventing the accumulation of intracellular debris and drusen associated with dry AMD (Falcão et al., 2024; Xu et al., 2020). Furthermore, the existing literature on phytoestrogens indicates that compounds in this chemical class are generally well tolerated when administered orally, and formulation strategies (such as encapsulation in hyaluronic acid–modified polymeric micelles) enhance ocular bioavailability, potentially enabling effective local delivery with minimal systemic adverse effects (Li et al., 2018).

However, several challenges and weaknesses must be addressed before advancing genistein as a therapy for dry AMD. First, while there is a substantial body of evidence supporting the role of genistein in modulating PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling in non-ocular tissues, direct evidence in RPE cells and in the context of dry AMD is sparse. Most published studies in the ocular domain have focused on formulation and delivery aspects rather than on detailed mechanism-of-action studies within RPE cells. Second, the estrogenic activity of genistein, although weak, raises potential concerns regarding off-target endocrine effects, particularly during long-term administration in older populations who may be susceptible to hormone-related side effects. These aspects would require rigorous assessment in preclinical and early-phase clinical trials. Additionally, the pharmacokinetics of genistein when administered via ocular routes (either topically or systemically) remain incompletely characterized, and comprehensive data on tissue distribution, especially to the retina or RPE, is limited. Such pharmacokinetic studies are crucial to ensure that therapeutic concentrations can be achieved and maintained in the target tissues without eliciting adverse effects (Glazier & Bowman, 2001; Li et al., 2018).

In light of the above considerations, genistein is promising as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD based on its capacity to inhibit upstream tyrosine kinases and suppress the PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling cascade, thereby promoting TFEB-mediated enhancement of lysosomal acidification and cathepsin D activity. Such a mechanism is directly relevant to improving phagolysosomal function in RPE cells and facilitating the clearance of drusen components—a critical unmet need in the management of dry AMD (Falcão et al., 2024; Xu et al., 2020). The dual actions of genistein offer mechanistic clarity that may translate into a therapeutic edge when compared to broad-spectrum autophagy inducers. Nonetheless, the current evidence base is still largely circumstantial, and further direct investigations are necessary to confirm that genistein induces the expected autophagic and lysosomal responses in RPE cells. Preclinical studies employing appropriate RPE models (such as POS feeding assays and chronic oxidative stress paradigms) should be prioritized to solidify the link between genistein treatment and improved clearance of lipofuscin-like deposits. Ultimately, detailed pharmacokinetic, efficacy, and safety studies—ideally complemented by early-phase clinical trials—will be required before genistein can be confidently advanced as a therapeutic modality for dry AMD (Albulescu & Popovici, 2007; Falcão et al., 2024).

In summary, genistein’s natural origin, established safety in other contexts, and its dual ability to inhibit relevant tyrosine kinase–mediated signaling and upregulate autophagy through TFEB activation collectively support its potential for repurposing in dry AMD. However, critical gaps in direct efficacy data in ocular models and a precise understanding of its tissue pharmacokinetics necessitate further investigation. This combination of promising mechanistic rationale and some supportive preclinical data argues that genistein merits further preclinical exploration in RPE models of dry AMD, with the expectation that if such studies confirm improved clearance of lipofuscin and drusen markers, subsequent early-phase clinical trials can be pursued to evaluate its therapeutic benefit in patients suffering from this blinding disease (Falcão et al., 2024; Glazier & Bowman, 2001; Li et al., 2018; Xu et al., 2020).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Rapamycin (sirolimus), commercially available as Sigma R0395, is a macrocyclic lactone originally isolated from the bacterium Streptomyces hygroscopicus, a discovery that dates back to studies on soil samples from Easter Island. As a naturally derived compound now synthesized and purified for clinical use, rapamycin belongs to the macrolide class and is best known for its potent immunosuppressive properties, having been used extensively to prevent organ rejection in transplantation. Over time, its application expanded beyond transplantation to include areas such as oncology, neurodegeneration, and age-related diseases due to its ability to inhibit the mechanistic target of rapamycin complex 1 (mTORC1). The rationale for repurposing rapamycin in the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD), specifically geographic atrophy (GA), stems from its established pharmacological profile, extensive safety record, and well-characterized biochemical functions. Its clinical approval and long-term safety data in other contexts provide a solid foundation for exploring its potential in ocular indications, particularly given its capacity to modulate autophagy in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells (Wang et al., 2022).

Therapeutic History:  
Rapamycin’s development began with its use as an immunosuppressant in organ transplantation, and over the ensuing decades, its application has broadened considerably. Biochemical and preclinical studies have demonstrated that rapamycin is an effective inhibitor of mTORC1, a critical regulator not only of cell proliferation but also of autophagy and lysosomal biogenesis. Early investigations revealed that rapamycin could induce autophagy in various cell types, including RPE cells, by inhibiting mTORC1, thereby facilitating the clearance of toxic aggregates and damaged organelles. This mechanism has been explored extensively for neurodegenerative conditions, and more recently, there has been focused investigation into its utility for dry AMD. Clinical trials have tested rapamycin in forms ranging from intravitreal to subconjunctival injections in patients with GA; for example, a clinical trial by the National Eye Institute aimed to evaluate intravitreal injections of sirolimus for GA, although this study was terminated due to safety concerns (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2012). Similarly, other studies using subconjunctival injections demonstrated that while rapamycin appears safe and well-tolerated, significant benefits in terms of preventing GA progression have not been conclusively demonstrated (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2008, 2011). In animal studies and in vitro RPE models, rapamycin enhanced autophagic flux, increased the activity of cathepsin D (CTSD), and reduced the accumulation of toxic material such as A2E—an effect that is consistent with a potential for slowing GA progression (Wang et al., 2022; Falcão et al., 2024). Thus, rapamycin’s therapeutic history encompasses a combination of robust preclinical evidence supporting its mechanistic action and mixed clinical outcomes in ocular trials, setting the stage for further investigation into optimal dosing, delivery methods, and patient selection criteria (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2008, 2011).

Mechanism of Action:  
Rapamycin exerts its biological effects primarily through direct inhibition of mTORC1, a serine/threonine kinase complex that integrates signals from nutrients, growth factors, and cellular energy status to regulate cell growth, proliferation, and autophagy. In the absence of rapamycin, active mTORC1 phosphorylates downstream targets such as S6 kinase and 4E-BP1, thereby promoting anabolic processes and suppressing autophagy. When rapamycin binds to its intracellular receptor, FKBP12, the resulting complex interacts with the FKBP12-rapamycin binding (FRB) domain of mTORC1, leading to its inhibition. This inhibition results in dephosphorylation and subsequent activation of transcription factor EB (TFEB), a master regulator of lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy-related genes. Activated TFEB then translocates to the nucleus, where it enhances the expression of genes involved in lysosomal function, acidification, and the production of lysosomal enzymes such as cathepsin D (CTSD) (Falcão et al., 2025; Falcão et al., 2024; Sinha et al., 2016). In the context of dry AMD, the proposed mechanism hinges on rapamycin’s ability to restore cellular homeostasis in RPE cells by increasing autophagic flux and lysosomal clearance of accumulated drusen components, which include toxic aggregates like A2E. Preclinical studies have shown that treatment of RPE cells with rapamycin results in a marked reduction in the accumulation of autofluorescent granules (AFGs) that are indicative of impaired lysosomal degradation (Falcão et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2025). The cascade initiated by rapamycin—mTORC1 inhibition, TFEB activation, and enhanced expression of lysosome-associated proteins such as LAMP1 and pro-cathepsin D—forms the crux of its proposed therapeutic action in mitigating the progression of GA by promoting the dismantling and clearance of pathological deposits (Falcão et al., 2024).

Expected Effect:  
In RPE cells, the inhibition of mTORC1 by rapamycin is expected to release the inhibitory phosphorylation on TFEB, enabling its nuclear translocation and activation of a transcriptional program that drives lysosomal biogenesis, acidification, and the production of key lysosomal enzymes such as cathepsin D. This molecular shift is anticipated to markedly enhance the autophagic capacity of the RPE, leading to increased degradation of drusen components, including lipofuscin and A2E, which are hallmarks of dry AMD pathology. The activation of autophagy not only facilitates the clearance of accumulated toxic material but also mitigates oxidative stress by removing damaged mitochondria and other organelles that may contribute to reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation (Wang et al., 2022; Falcão et al., 2024). Moreover, preclinical evidence indicates that, in ARPE-19 cell models, rapamycin improves cellular viability in the face of oxidative injury and reduces markers of cellular senescence by enhancing autophagic flux. These cellular effects are directly linked to the expression of critical proteins in RPE cells; for example, TFEB is known to be expressed in these cells and its activation correlates with increased lysosomal gene expression and function (Falcão et al., 2024) while cathepsin D, a lysosomal protease, is vital for the degradation of phagocytosed photoreceptor outer segments (Chang et al., 2022; Sinha et al., 2016). The intended therapeutic outcome is to slow or potentially halt the progression of GA by reducing the burden of drusen and preserving RPE function, which could translate into better preservation of visual acuity over time. However, it is important to note that while these mechanisms are promising in vitro, clinical translation has encountered challenges related to dosing, delivery, and the stage of disease at which intervention occurs (Wang et al., 2022; Falcão et al., 2024).

Overall Evaluation:  
Rapamycin presents itself as a scientifically promising yet clinically challenging candidate for the treatment of dry AMD. One of the key strengths of rapamycin is its well-established mechanism of action: as a potent mTORC1 inhibitor, it leverages a well-characterized pathway involving TFEB activation that directly targets the core pathology observed in dry AMD—the accumulation of drusen components and impaired lysosomal function in RPE cells. Preclinical studies have consistently demonstrated that rapamycin can enhance autophagic flux, lower levels of toxic aggregates such as A2E, and increase the activity of lysosomal enzymes like cathepsin D, thereby supporting its target validation in the context of RPE health (Falcão et al., 2025; Falcão et al., 2024). Additionally, rapamycin has an extensive history of clinical use in other indications, and its safety profile, while not without concerns, is well documented from its use as an immunosuppressant in transplantation and in various oncology settings (Wang et al., 2022).

However, the clinical translation of rapamycin for dry AMD has not been straightforward. Multiple clinical trials have assessed its application using different routes of administration, such as intravitreal and subconjunctival injections, with mixed results. While safety and tolerability have generally been acceptable, the efficacy endpoints—specifically, the prevention or slowing of GA progression—have not been definitively met in these studies (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2008, 2011, 2012; Wang et al., 2022). Furthermore, some trials encountered complications such as sterile endophthalmitis or observed decreases in visual acuity relative to untreated eyes, suggesting that even if the underlying molecular mechanisms are engaged, the overall benefits in late-stage disease might be limited (Wang et al., 2022; Falcão et al., 2024).

Another potential weakness is the complexity inherent in mTOR signaling itself. The pathway plays a dual role in cellular homeostasis—while its inhibition can promote autophagy and lysosomal clearance, inappropriate or excessive inhibition could lead to adverse effects such as increased retinal neuron apoptosis, particularly in advanced stages of AMD where the cellular milieu is significantly altered (Wang et al., 2022; Chang et al., 2022). Moreover, the optimal dosing regimen and delivery method for achieving the desired ocular concentration without incurring systemic side effects remain unresolved. Some studies have suggested that modifications to the formulation, such as encapsulation in synthetic nanoparticles, could enhance ocular penetration and prolong the effective duration of rapamycin within the eye, thereby minimizing side effects and improving efficacy (Jo et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2022).

Despite these challenges, the strength of rapamycin’s mechanism—the inhibition of mTORC1 and consequent activation of TFEB leading to enhanced lysosomal biogenesis—remains compelling. The molecular rationale is robust, and the repeated demonstration of reduced levels of autofluorescent granules in RPE cells following rapamycin treatment is particularly encouraging (Falcão et al., 2024). The concept of using a repurposed, clinically approved drug to address a significant unmet need in dry AMD is attractive, especially given the limited treatment options currently available for this degenerative condition. In this light, further investigations—ideally, in earlier stages of AMD and with innovative delivery modalities—may reveal a niche where rapamycin can exert a clinically meaningful benefit (Wang et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2019).

In conclusion, while rapamycin has significant potential grounded in sound molecular pharmacology and extensive preclinical validation, its clinical application for dry AMD warrants careful optimization. The candidate’s strengths lie in its potent and well-understood mechanism of mTORC1 inhibition, the activation of TFEB, and subsequent improvements in lysosomal function and autophagic clearance in RPE cells. Conversely, clinical challenges including mixed efficacy outcomes in GA trials, potential adverse effects related to mTOR pathway modulation in vulnerable retinal neurons, and limitations in current dosing/delivery strategies represent hurdles that must be surmounted. Based on these comprehensive literature insights, rapamycin remains a promising candidate for further investigation, albeit with recommendations to explore its use in earlier disease stages and in combination with advanced ocular delivery systems to maximize its therapeutic benefit while minimizing risks (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2012; Wang et al., 2022; Falcão et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2025).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
NSC19723 is presented by the team as a custom-synthesized small-molecule enhancer of cathepsin D (CTSD) activity, hypothesized to bind the zymogen (pro-CTSD) and accelerate its maturation within retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) lysosomes to restore proteolysis and debris clearance in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD). No peer-reviewed publications or preprints describing NSC19723’s structure, discovery, selectivity, or in vivo performance are present in the provided literature corpus; accordingly, this evaluation treats NSC19723 as a theoretical representative of the drug class “CTSD activity enhancers” and assesses the therapeutic hypothesis against the current substrate-specific and disease-relevant CTSD/RPE biology (Ng et al., 2024; Sharif, 2015; Liu, 2021; Buniello et al., 2025).

The stated drug class is mechanistically distinct from upstream autophagy enhancers or lysosomal pH modulators: a CTSD activity enhancer would operate at the level of CTSD protein maturation/activity, ideally in acidic lysosomes, rather than by globally raising autophagic flux or indirectly modulating lysosomal acidification (Frost et al., 2014; Boya et al., 2023; Ng et al., 2024). CTSD itself is an aspartic endoprotease synthesized as a pre-proenzyme with an N-terminal signal peptide (for ER entry) and a propeptide region that supports folding and prevents premature activity; post-translational maturation occurs in late endosomes/lysosomes after mannose-6-phosphate (M6P)-mediated trafficking, where acidic pH supports autocatalysis and protease processing to the mature, active two-chain enzyme (Sharif, 2015). The RPE expresses CTSD at high levels, with evidence for enriched CTSD protein/activity in central/macular RPE relative to periphery, consistent with the macula’s heavy daily photoreceptor outer segment (POS) phagocytic load that relies on lysosomal proteolysis (Sharif, 2015; Pay, 2017). These features nominate CTSD as a plausible therapeutic target for restoring RPE degradative capacity; however, a specific CTSD maturation enhancer such as NSC19723 has not been characterized in the provided literature, so all compound-level conclusions must remain contingent on experimental validation (Ng et al., 2024; Buniello et al., 2025).

Therapeutic History  
No published biochemical, veterinary, or clinical use of NSC19723 is documented in the provided sources, and the name does not appear in the referenced literature; consequently, there are no prior data on this molecule in dry AMD or retinal disease within the provided corpus (Buniello et al., 2025). By contrast, there is considerable disease-relevant literature on CTSD biology in RPE and on pharmacological strategies that indirectly restore CTSD function by correcting upstream lysosomal defects. In patient-derived RPE from Stargardt disease (STGD1, ABCA4 mutations), lysosomal pH is elevated, CTSD accumulates in immature forms, and CTSD proteolytic activity is reduced; pharmacologic re-acidification of lysosomes (e.g., via P2Y₁₂ antagonism with ticagrelor) reverses these defects by lowering lysosomal pH, reducing the immature pro-CTSD pool, and restoring CTSD proteolytic activity and POS degradation in vitro and in vivo (RPE cells and Abca4−/− mice) (Ng et al., 2024). While STGD1 is not AMD, these data show that CTSD maturation/activity in human RPE is drug-modifiable and that improving CTSD function can improve degradative endpoints relevant to lipofuscin-associated disease biology, a pathophysiologic axis shared with dry AMD (Ng et al., 2024; Boya et al., 2023).

In the RPE/AMD literature, multiple lines of evidence support CTSD as a major lysosomal protease necessary for POS degradation and proteostasis. CTSD deficiency or pharmacologic inhibition impairs POS proteolysis, provokes accumulation of debris reminiscent of drusen, and is linked to retinal dysfunction in animal models, reinforcing its centrality to RPE homeostasis (Mahmud, 2019). Advanced glycation end-products (AGEs), which accumulate with age and in AMD, downregulate CTSD activity or expression in RPE and exacerbate lysosomal/autophagic failure and lipofuscin formation, further tying CTSD deficits to AMD-like phenotypes (Sharif, 2015; Mahmud, 2019). More broadly, lysosomal/autophagic insufficiency in RPE is mechanistically and pathologically linked to dry AMD: decreased degradative capacity leads to lipofuscin accumulation, lysosomal membrane permeabilization (LMP), DAMP release, inflammasome activation (e.g., NLRP3), and eventual RPE atrophy that drives photoreceptor degeneration; re-acidifying lysosomes and strengthening lysosomal function ameliorate several of these pathologies in vitro and in vivo (Choi, 2019; Frost et al., 2014; Boya et al., 2023).

A second therapeutic precedent relevant to “enhancing CTSD function” is enzyme augmentation. Recombinant pro-CTSD administration has been reported to correct proteolysis and autophagy defects in neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis (CLN10/CTSD deficiency), and intravitreal enzyme replacement strategies in other lysosomal storage diseases (e.g., TPP1 in CLN2) have preserved retinal structure/function in preclinical models, supporting feasibility of increasing lysosomal enzyme function in ocular tissues (Liu, 2021). These studies, while not in AMD and not small molecules, validate the general concept that augmenting CTSD can rescue lysosomal degradative failure in retina-derived tissues.

In summary, there is no therapeutic history for NSC19723 itself in the provided sources; however, there is an increasingly robust therapeutic precedent that pharmacological manipulation which restores CTSD maturation/activity in RPE improves degradative capacity and disease-relevant readouts in lipofuscin-accumulating retinal disorders, and that enzyme augmentation of lysosomal hydrolases can be effective in ocular degenerations driven by lysosomal insufficiency (Ng et al., 2024; Liu, 2021).

Mechanism of Action  
CTSD biosynthesis and maturation provide the mechanistic backdrop for a CTSD maturation enhancer. CTSD is synthesized as pre-procathepsin D with a signal peptide (for ER translocation) and a propeptide that maintains the zymogen in an inactive, folding-competent state; the protein acquires N-linked glycans and an M6P tag in the Golgi for M6P-receptor–mediated trafficking to late endosomes/lysosomes, where acidic pH facilitates removal of the propeptide, proteolytic processing, and generation of the mature, active enzyme (heavy and light chains) (Sharif, 2015). As an aspartic protease, CTSD employs two Asp residues to activate and position a water molecule for nucleophilic attack on the scissile peptide bond, a chemistry that requires acidic conditions for optimal catalysis; in neutral or alkaline environments, activity falls sharply, explaining why lysosomal alkalinization in disease states compromises both maturation and steady-state activity (Sharif, 2015; Ng et al., 2024).

In RPE disease models, immature and intermediate CTSD forms accumulate when lysosomal pH is elevated, and total CTSD protein may paradoxically rise even as proteolytic activity falls, illustrating a maturation bottleneck rather than a transcriptional deficit; pharmacological re-acidification reduces immature CTSD, increases the mature enzyme, and restores proteolytic activity in RPE (Ng et al., 2024). Functionally, impaired CTSD maturation/activity correlates with delayed degradation of internalized POS and accumulation of aggregation-prone substrates such as α-synuclein, consistent with CTSD’s principal role in RPE proteolysis of rhodopsin and POS proteins; CTSD is reported to account for the majority of rhodopsin degradation in RPE and exhibits far higher proteolytic activity than cathepsin B against POS substrates (Ng et al., 2024). The RPE’s reliance on phagolysosomal degradation of POS and basal autophagy for proteostasis means that even partial reductions in CTSD activity can precipitate progressive accumulation of lipofuscin-like material and lysosomal residual bodies, which in turn further impair lysosomes and create a feedback loop of increasing oxidative and inflammatory stress central to dry AMD pathophysiology (Choi, 2019; Frost et al., 2014; Sharif, 2015).

The proposed mechanism for NSC19723—direct binding to pro-CTSD to accelerate maturation—aligns with the above biology and would target the specific rate-limiting step observed in RPE lysosomes under stress: conversion of immature pro-CTSD to the mature, active enzyme in the acidic lumen. If achieved without broad, off-target activation of other proteases or perturbation of lysosomal pH/ion homeostasis, this mechanism would distinguish NSC19723 from autophagy inducers (e.g., rapamycin) or pH re-acidifiers (e.g., ticagrelor), while being convergent on the same functional outcome: restored CTSD proteolysis and lysosomal degradative capacity (Frost et al., 2014; Ng et al., 2024).

Mechanistic cross-talk and constraints that are relevant for a CTSD maturation enhancer include:  
- pH dependence: CTSD maturation and catalysis require acidic lysosomes; in alkaline lysosomes (e.g., due to bisretinoid accumulation), pro-CTSD processing is impaired even if total CTSD protein increases, so a maturation accelerator may be insufficient without concurrent restoration of lysosomal pH in some disease states (Ng et al., 2024).  
- Protease networks: While CTSD is an aspartic protease, lysosomal proteases co-regulate one another’s maturation and substrate turnover; for example, denatured cathepsin L can be a substrate for CTSD, and changes in cysteine cathepsins (B/L/S) alter autophagic flux and POS degradation, implying that selective enhancement of CTSD maturation must be interpreted in the context of broader protease network homeostasis (Mahmud, 2019; Sharif, 2015).  
- Endogenous inhibitors: Cystatin C potently inhibits cysteine cathepsins (B, H, L, S) and is abundant in RPE; although it does not inhibit CTSD (aspartic protease), changes in cystatin C with age and AMD suggest that protease–inhibitor balance in the lysosome and extracellular space is dynamic and may modulate the consequences of altering one protease’s activity (Myerscough, 2015; Sharif, 2015).  
- Lysosomal membrane integrity: LMP releases cathepsins to the cytosol, where they can trigger apoptosis/inflammation; any intervention that modifies lysosomal protease activity must be vetted for unintended effects on LMP susceptibility or cytosolic protease activity under stress (Boya et al., 2023; Mahmud, 2019).  
- Extracellular exposure: RPE can secrete cathepsins; most cathepsins are inactivated at neutral pH, but acidic niches or heparan/ECM interactions can stabilize activity, raising potential off-tissue effects if a compound perturbs trafficking/secretion (Sharif, 2015).

Collectively, the mechanistic plausibility that a small molecule could stabilize a conformation of pro-CTSD that accelerates propeptide removal and activation in acidic lysosomes is strong, and a favorable on-target pharmacodynamic effect can be anchored to clearly measurable, disease-relevant biochemical endpoints in RPE (Ng et al., 2024). The key risk is that without correction of lysosomal pH, pro-CTSD processing bottlenecks may persist; therefore, a CTSD maturation enhancer may be best deployed in lysosomes that are sufficiently acidic or in combination with pH-restoring strategies (Ng et al., 2024).

Expected Effect  
Dry AMD pathophysiology features RPE lysosomal-autophagic insufficiency leading to accumulation of POS-derived material, lipofuscin, and AGEs, heightened oxidative stress, inflammasome activation, and progressive RPE atrophy; restoring lysosomal proteolysis is predicted to mitigate these processes (Choi, 2019; Frost et al., 2014; Boya et al., 2023). In RPE, CTSD is a principal protease responsible for POS/rhodopsin degradation, and its activity declines with aging and under stressors relevant to AMD (AGEs, lipids/oxidation, lysosomal alkalinization), producing immature CTSD accumulation and reduced proteolytic capacity (Mahmud, 2019; Sharif, 2015; Ng et al., 2024). Therefore, a compound that accelerates pro-CTSD maturation to increase mature CTSD abundance/activity in acidic lysosomes is expected to:

- Increase CTSD catalytic activity in RPE lysosomes, measurable by fluorogenic substrate assays and activity-based probes, with corresponding decrease in immature/intermediate CTSD species and increase in mature, active CTSD on immunoblot and imaging (Ng et al., 2024).  
- Improve rate and completeness of POS degradation in RPE pulse–chase assays (e.g., rhodopsin clearance), reduce accumulation of lysosomal residual bodies, and decrease autofluorescent lipofuscin-like material formation in POS-challenged RPE under AGE/oxidative stress conditions (Ng et al., 2024; Frost et al., 2014; Sharif, 2015).  
- Reduce intracellular burden of aggregation-prone CTSD substrates (e.g., α-synuclein) and attenuate proteostasis stress, potentially normalizing vesicle trafficking defects tied to aggregate accumulation (Ng et al., 2024).  
- Rebalance autophagic flux by removing a degradative bottleneck at the lysosome, observable as improved degradation of autophagic cargo rather than simply altered LC3 abundance; careful flux assays with lysosome–autophagosome fusion inhibitors (e.g., bafilomycin A1) should be used for interpretation (Frost et al., 2014; Sharif, 2015).  
- Decrease downstream inflammatory signaling associated with lysosomal debris accumulation, including reduced NLRP3 inflammasome activation and cytokine release during chronic stress paradigms implicated in AMD pathogenesis (Choi, 2019; Boya et al., 2023).  
- With longer-term dosing, reduce subcellular and extracellular deposit biogenesis (lipofuscin, drusen-like material), preserve RPE morphology/mitochondrial health, and sustain photoreceptor function in models where lysosomal degradation is limiting, as seen when CTSD function is restored by lysosomal re-acidification (Boya et al., 2023; Ng et al., 2024).

The target is well expressed in the cell type of interest: CTSD is abundant in RPE, enriched in central/macular RPE, and directly linked to RPE’s POS degradation function; its activity is reduced by aging and AGE exposure, both highly relevant to dry AMD (Sharif, 2015; Pay, 2017; Mahmud, 2019). In lipofuscin-associated retinal disease models, restoring lysosomal acidity to rescue CTSD maturation/activity improved RPE degradative function and reduced pathological autofluorescence, underscoring the expected benefits of directly increasing CTSD maturation/activity via a selective small molecule (Ng et al., 2024).

Experimental considerations for robust readouts in RPE:  
- Biochemical: ratio of pro-/intermediate/mature CTSD by immunoblot in lysosomal fractions; CTSD activity in intact live cells and in isolated lysosomes at matched pH; selectivity profiling against other cathepsins (B/L/S) to confirm the putative specificity reported by the team; lysosomal pH measurements to control for off-target alkalinization/acidification effects (Ng et al., 2024; Sharif, 2015).  
- Functional degradative flux: POS pulse–chase assays (rhodopsin clearance kinetics), autophagy flux assays (LC3-II, p62/SQSTM1 degradation with and without bafilomycin A1), α-synuclein aggregation/clearance; quantify autofluorescence as a proxy for lipofuscin-like material (Ng et al., 2024; Frost et al., 2014; Sharif, 2015).  
- Cell health/inflammation: LMP susceptibility (galectin-3 puncta, cytosolic cathepsin immunostaining), NLRP3 inflammasome activation (caspase-1 activity), ROS and mitochondrial integrity (Boya et al., 2023; Choi, 2019).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Strong target–disease mechanistic rationale: CTSD is the principal lysosomal protease for RPE POS protein degradation, with reported responsibility for the majority of rhodopsin proteolysis and markedly higher activity than cathepsin B; CTSD deficiency or inhibition impairs POS degradation and produces drusen-like debris, and genetic or pharmacologic CTSD impairment causes retinal dysfunction, aligning CTSD activation with a disease-modifying mechanism in dry AMD (Ng et al., 2024; Mahmud, 2019).

- Absence of public data on NSC19723: No structural, selectivity, potency, PK/PD, ocular disposition, or toxicology data are available in the provided corpus; thus, claims of pro-CTSD binding, selectivity for CTSD over other cathepsins, and in vivo rescue in CTSD-deficient retina remain unverified by the sources provided (Buniello et al., 2025). This is the major program risk at present.  
- Lysosomal pH constraint: If lysosomal alkalinization is a primary driver of immature CTSD accumulation (as in STGD1 and arguably in stressed AMD RPE), a maturation accelerator may not overcome the pH-dependent processing barrier; efficacy may require sufficient lysosomal acidity or combination with pH-restoring interventions (Ng et al., 2024).

- Off-target and network effects: Crosstalk between cathepsins (e.g., CTSD processing of denatured cathepsin L, altered cathepsin L/C3/NF-κB signaling), and modulation by AGEs/oxidative stress and endogenous inhibitors necessitate comprehensive off-target profiling and immune readouts to ensure that CTSD-specific maturation enhancement does not dysregulate broader proteostasis/inflammatory networks in RPE or at the RPE–Bruch’s membrane (BrM) interface (Sharif, 2015; Mahmud, 2019).

Program implications and recommended next steps  
Given the robust mechanistic case for CTSD restoration in RPE and the successful pharmacologic rescue of CTSD maturation/activity via lysosomal re-acidification in human patient–derived RPE, a selective CTSD maturation enhancer is a rational, high-potential approach for dry AMD—provided the compound is real, selective, and effective in acidic lysosomes (Ng et al., 2024). To advance NSC19723, the following de-risking package is critical:  

- Biochemical validation: Demonstrate pro-CTSD binding and acceleration of maturation at acidic pH using purified pro-CTSD and lysosomal-mimetic conditions; quantify catalytic activation and processing kinetics; confirm no activation or inhibition of cathepsins B/L/S and other lysosomal hydrolases (Sharif, 2015).  
- Cellular validation in RPE: In primary human RPE/hiPSC-RPE (including dry AMD lines), show increased mature CTSD and activity without altering lysosomal pH, improved POS degradation and reduced autofluorescence under chronic POS/AGE stress, restored clearance of α-synuclein aggregates, and normalization of autophagic flux using proper flux assays (Frost et al., 2014; Ng et al., 2024; Sharif, 2015).  
- Safety pharmacology in RPE: Demonstrate no increase in LMP susceptibility or NLRP3 activation under oxidative/bisretinoid stress; characterize secretion/trafficking effects and exclude extracellular protease activation under BrM-like conditions (Boya et al., 2023; Sharif, 2015).  
- In vivo proof of concept: In models featuring RPE lysosomal dysfunction and lipofuscin burden, measure retinal/RPE CTSD maturation/activity, RPE autofluorescence, drusen-like material, photoreceptor survival, and visual function; compare with or add to pH-reacidifying strategies (Ng et al., 2024).

Overall, while a CTSD maturation enhancer is scientifically well grounded for RPE-centered degenerations and could represent a differentiated, direct-restoration modality versus pH modulators or broad autophagy inducers, the current file lacks any external validation for NSC19723. Progressing NSC19723 is justified only with rapid, rigorous confirmation of selectivity, on-target activity in RPE lysosomes, and favorable safety in stressed RPE systems that model dry AMD’s lysosomal/autophagic failure (Frost et al., 2014; Boya et al., 2023; Choi, 2019).

In summary, the therapeutic concept—enhancing CTSD maturation/activity to restore RPE lysosomal proteolysis—has high mechanistic plausibility and encouraging precedent from pharmacologic re-acidification studies, but the specific candidate NSC19723 remains unsubstantiated in the provided literature and requires foundational biochemical and cellular validation to warrant preclinical development in dry AMD (Ng et al., 2024; Buniello et al., 2025).

Historically, the development of EZH2 inhibitors such as GSK126 has been focused predominantly on oncological applications. Furthermore, in vivo studies in animal models of dry AMD are needed to evaluate whether EZH2 inhibition can restore lysosomal function and slow disease progression under physiologically relevant conditions (Abokyi & Tse, 2025, pp. 2–3, 9–10). Comparative studies with other epigenetic modulators and TFEB activators could also provide context regarding the relative efficacy of GSK126 in reactivating the CLEAR network.

In conclusion, the repurposing of GSK126 for dry AMD is a promising, yet exploratory, approach that leverages a clear mechanistic hypothesis: by inhibiting EZH2, GSK126 may relieve repressive histone marks at lysosomal gene promoters, thereby promoting TFEB-driven transcription of genes essential for lysosomal acidification and proteolytic activity. This approach could conceivably ameliorate the lysosomal defects observed in RPE cells in dry AMD. The strengths of this candidate lie in its well-defined molecular target, its established clinical safety profile in oncology studies, and the potential for a durable, chromatin-level correction of lysosomal dysfunction. However, significant challenges remain, including the need for direct evidence linking EZH2 inhibition to enhancements in the CLEAR gene network within RPE cells, the potential off-target effects inherent to epigenetic therapies, and the overall weak association between EZH2 and AMD pathogenesis as indicated by current target-disease databases.

Given these considerations, while the mechanistic rationale is robust and the repurposing strategy innovative, the current level of evidence is insufficient for immediate clinical application. It is imperative that future research generate direct preclinical data in ocular models of dry AMD to confirm that GSK126 can, in fact, restore lysosomal function in RPE cells via TFEB activation and increased cathepsin D and V-ATPase expression. Further investigation should also focus on clarifying the broader gene expression changes induced by GSK126 in RPE cells to ensure that the desired effects on lysosomal pathways are achieved without detrimental off-target consequences.

The forthcoming research should aim to delineate the dose-response relationships, optimize delivery to the ocular compartment, and ensure that sustained improvements in lysosomal capacity correlate with clinical endpoints relevant to AMD progression (Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 13–15; Sharif, 2015, pp. 68–72; Ferret, 2024, pp. 103–106).

In summary, while the repurposing of GSK126 for dry AMD is conceptually attractive and supported by a reasonable mechanistic framework, the endeavor is in its nascent stages. The existing literature does not yet provide direct evidence that GSK126 elicits the specific lysosomal benefits hypothesized in RPE cells. As such, this candidate represents a high-risk, high-reward opportunity that merits further in-depth investigation through rigorous preclinical studies, with a view toward eventual clinical translation if the mechanistic hypotheses are confirmed (Coryell, 2019, pp. 48–53; Sharif, 2015, pp. 68–72).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Trehalose is a naturally occurring non‐reducing disaccharide (molecular weight 342.3 Da) found broadly in microorganisms and invertebrates, widely used as a stabilizer and excipient in foods and pharmaceuticals, and formulated in ophthalmic solutions at 3% w/v (≈87.7 mM) for ocular surface applications (e.g., dry eye) (Cox et al., 2025, pp. 1–2). In mammalian cells, trehalose enters via fluid‐phase endocytosis at millimolar concentrations and has been repeatedly reported as an autophagy enhancer that can activate AMPK signaling, stimulate lysosomal activity, and augment autophagic flux across multiple tissues, including ocular tissues (RPE) and retina (Cox et al., 2025, pp. 1–2). In the context of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), trehalose has been deployed as a small‐molecule modulator of the lysosome–autophagy axis with proposed mTOR‐independent activation of TFEB, the master transcriptional regulator of lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy (CLEAR network), positioning it mechanistically distinct from direct mTORC1 inhibitors such as rapamycin (Ghosh et al., 2024, p. 6; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 10–11). Topical ophthalmic trehalose is generally well tolerated, and preclinical studies show no overt ocular toxicity at 3% or 9% w/v after twice-daily dosing for up to two weeks, supporting feasibility for posterior segment delivery strategies; Raman spectroscopy has detected trehalose in RPE/choroid after repeated topical dosing, although posterior penetration is variable (Cox et al., 2025, pp. 8–10).

Therapeutic History  
Preclinical evidence in RPE and retina  
- Human RPE cell line (ARPE-19) oxidative stress model: Trehalose upregulates autophagy markers (LC3-II, p62/SQSTM1), increases TFEB protein and autophagy gene transcripts (ATG5, ATG7), and elevates lysosomal markers including LAMP2 and Cathepsin D (CTSD) protein; importantly, trehalose pretreatment confers cytoprotection against hydroquinone (HQ)-induced oxidative injury, and this protection is abolished by ATG5 knockdown, demonstrating autophagy dependence (typical dosing 50 mM trehalose; HQ 50 μM) (Abokyi et al., 2020, pp. 1–2, 9–11, 11–12, 12–13, 15–16). Dose–response caveats were noted: higher trehalose concentrations (≥100 mM) lost cytoprotection and were associated with stronger LC3-II accumulation, suggesting risk from excessive autophagy activation (Abokyi et al., 2020, pp. 11–12, 15–16).  
- Primary murine RPE in vitro: A non‐toxic trehalose dose (12.5 mM) increased autophagic flux measured by tandem GFP–RFP-LC3B, increasing RFP+ autolysosomes and RFP:GFP ratios without accumulating GFP+ autophagosomes, with colocalization to LysoTracker+ acidic compartments; trehalose also attenuated H₂O₂-induced mitochondrial superoxide and restored maximal respiration (Cox et al., 2025, pp. 7–10). These data indicate trehalose enhances autophagosome–lysosome fusion and downstream degradative flux in RPE under oxidative stress (Cox et al., 2025, pp. 7–10).  
- iPSC-derived human RPE carrying the CFH Y402H risk allele (CFH (H/H)): Trehalose (100 mM, 20–48 h) restored levels and enzymatic activities of lysosomal hydrolases Cathepsin D and Cathepsin L and rescued LAMP1 in complement challenge models, phenocopying constitutively nuclear TFEB (TFEB-S467A) and AKT2 inhibition; these data support trehalose as an mTOR-independent TFEB activator that rejuvenates lysosomal function in AMD-relevant RPE (Ghosh et al., 2024, p. 6; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 10–11).  
- Ex vivo/in vivo lysosomal/autophagy disease models: In Cryba1 KO RPE explants with lysosomal defects, trehalose rescued CLEAR gene expression and autophagy flux; in Cryba1 conditional KO and Akt2 knock-in mice, a regimen of 1 mg/g/day intraperitoneal trehalose for 2 days followed by 2% w/v in drinking water for 3 months starting at 6 months of age restored lysosomal function in RPE, rescued CLEAR network gene expression, and prevented early Bruch’s membrane basal deposit formation that typically emerges by 9 months (Ghosh et al., 2023, pp. 11–15; Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 6–8).  
- Topical trehalose in mice with acute outer retinal stress: Twice-daily eyedrops of 9% trehalose for seven days before and after light-induced outer retinal degeneration (LIRD) reduced ONL thinning by ~53%, preserved RPE morphology and F-actin junctions, and increased LC3B and LAMP1 with decreased p62 in the RPE, consistent with enhanced autophagy-lysosome engagement in vivo (Cox et al., 2025, pp. 8–13). Raman spectroscopy detected trehalose in posterior ocular tissues (RPE/choroid > retina) after repeated dosing, supporting posterior segment exposure from topical application (Cox et al., 2025, pp. 8–10).

Broader retinal/lysosomal disease context and precedent  
- Trehalose reduced retinal degeneration, neuroinflammation, and storage burden in a lysosomal hydrolase deficiency retinal model, supporting disease modification in lysosomal storage–related retinal pathology, although model details are not provided here (Boya et al., 2023, pp. 17–18; Cox et al., 2025, p. 16).

Clinical use  
- No clinical trials or clinical case series for trehalose in atrophic AMD or geographic atrophy (GA) are reported in the provided context (Abokyi et al., 2020, pp. 1–2; Cox et al., 2025, pp. 1–2). AMD-relevant lysosome–autophagy context in RPE  
- The RPE is exceptionally reliant on lysosomal degradation for both autophagy and daily heterophagy of photoreceptor outer segments (POS), and lysosomal ion homeostasis, including proton pump activity, determines acidification and hydrolase function; age-related lipofuscin accumulation, often oxidized and crosslinked, compromises lysosomal integrity and can promote lysosomal membrane permeabilization (LMP), driving cathepsin release and cell death cascades (Boya et al., 2023, pp. 3–4, 4–6). The mTORC1–TFEB/TFE3 axis regulates lysosomal biogenesis; TFEB dephosphorylation and nuclear translocation induce CLEAR network genes, including lysosomal hydrolases and V-ATPase subunits, while pathological signals (amino acid–Ragulator–Rag GTPases, AKT, and mTORC1) can sequester TFEB/TFE3 in the cytoplasm, thereby undermining lysosomal biogenesis (Boya et al., 2023, pp. 3–4, 4–6). In AMD models, impaired lysosomal acidification (e.g., via βA3/A1-crystallin deficits) and hyperactive mTORC1 reduce TFEB/TFE3 nuclear translocation, LAMP2 function, and degradative capacity, phenocopying AMD-relevant delays in phagosome degradation and lipofuscin handling (Boya et al., 2023, pp. 4–6). In ARPE-19 cells, trehalose increased TFEB protein levels, autophagy genes (ATG5, ATG7), LAMP2, LC3, p62, and Cathepsin D protein, and protection from HQ oxidant injury required intact autophagy (ATG5-dependent), illustrating an autophagy-centric cytoprotective mechanism in human RPE cells (Abokyi et al., 2020, pp. 1–2, 11–13).

  - Directly quantify TFEB nuclear translocation (immunocytochemistry with nuclear segmentation; nuclear/cytosolic fractionation and immunoblotting) under trehalose vs. TFEB-S467A and vs. AKT2 inhibition, to confirm that trehalose’s phenotypic rescue is TFEB-dependent in RPE (Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 6, 10–11).  
  - CTSD/CTSL processing and activity: Extend the CFH (H/H) results by testing trehalose across primary human RPE and AMD-donor–derived RPE; relate CTSD activity rescue to autophagic flux endpoints (LC3 turnover, p62 degradation) and to substrate clearance (POS proteolysis kinetics) (Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 6, 10–11; Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7).  
  - Lipofuscin/A2E clearance: In A2E-loaded and POS-fed RPE, quantify autofluorescence granules and A2E mass spectrometry before/after trehalose, and test dependence on TFEB (siRNA/CRISPR) and lysosomal hydrolase inhibition (e.g., pepstatin-A for CTSD) (Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7, 7–9).  
- PK/PD and delivery optimization:  
  - For topical delivery, map trehalose concentration–time in RPE/choroid and retina with LC-MS or validated Raman signatures; explore permeation enhancers or sustained-release formulations to overcome low posterior bioavailability (Cox et al., 2025, pp. 8–10, 10–13, 15–16).  
  - Define an ocular PD biomarker panel (RPE LC3B/LAMP1 colocalization, p62 decrease, CTSD activity) and link to functional readouts (ERG, OCT metrics) in chronic complement- or lipofuscin-based models (Cox et al., 2025, pp. 10–13).  
- Comparative and combinatorial strategy:  
  - Benchmark trehalose against TFEB-centric comparators (e.g., rapalogs, Ezrin inhibitors) on shared endpoints (TFEB nuclear index, lysosomal pH, CTSD activity, lipofuscin clearance), given rapamycin’s ability to reduce A2E/lipofuscin via TFEB activation and the potential of ezrin blockade to increase lysosome number and cathepsin activity in RPE (Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7, 7–9; Boya et al., 2023, pp. 4–6).  
  - Consider combination with complement modulation where indicated, as complement stress contributes to AMD-relevant lysosomal dysfunction in CFH (H/H) RPE (Ghosh et al., 2024, p. 6).

Go/no-go criteria for advancement toward GA  
- Mechanistic Go: Demonstration in RPE that trehalose increases the TFEB nuclear index by >2-fold, lowers lysosomal pH toward physiological values, and increases CTSD activity by >30% over disease-state baseline, with concordant increases in LC3B–LAMP1 colocalization and p62 degradation; abrogation of effects by TFEB knockdown would confirm mechanism (Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 10–11; Cox et al., 2025, pp. 7–8; Boya et al., 2023, pp. 3–4).  
- Functional Go: Demonstrated reduction of A2E/lipofuscin by ≥25% in RPE models without cytotoxicity, and structural/functional rescue in a chronic AMD-relevant animal model (e.g., CFH-risk or complement-driven models) with durable effects beyond acute stress models (Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7; Cox et al., 2025, pp. 8–10; Ghosh et al., 2024, p. 6).  
- Safety Go: No evidence of autophagy-associated cytotoxicity at the intended exposure (maintained viability; absence of excessive LC3-II accumulation without flux; ocular histopathology clean) (Abokyi et al., 2020, pp. 15–16; Cox et al., 2025, pp. 8–10).

The totality of evidence supports trehalose as a plausible, repurposable modulator of the TFEB–lysosome/autophagy axis in the RPE with multiple independent signals of autophagy flux enhancement, lysosomal hydrolase restoration (CTSD/L), and cytoprotection in oxidative/complement stress contexts, delivered via mechanisms that appear mTOR-independent and therefore potentially safer than broad mTORC1 inhibition (Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 10–11; Cox et al., 2025, pp. 7–8; Abokyi et al., 2020, pp. 1–2; Ghosh et al., 2023, pp. 11–15). However, the hypothesis’s most stringent claims—quantitative restoration of lysosomal acidification, trehalose-driven TFEB nuclear translocation in RPE, and direct lipofuscin/A2E clearance leading to slowed geographic atrophy progression—are not yet demonstrated in the supplied literature and require targeted mechanistic and disease-model validation (Ghosh et al., 2024, pp. 10–11; Abokyi et al., 2020, pp. 16–17; Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7; Cox et al., 2025, pp. 8–10). Given strong biological plausibility and encouraging preclinical signals, a focused IND-enabling program that closes these gaps is justified, with early emphasis on mechanistic biomarkers (lysosomal pH, TFEB nuclear index, CTSD activity), pharmacokinetics of posterior delivery, and chronic AMD-relevant efficacy models before advancing to clinical study in GA (Boya et al., 2023, pp. 3–4; Cox et al., 2025, pp. 10–13; Ghosh et al., 2024, p. 6).
