Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
MCC950 (AdipoGen AG‐CRID3) is a synthetic small‐molecule inhibitor that belongs to the diarylsulfonylurea chemical class and was originally discovered during investigations aimed at identifying potent inhibitors of the NLRP3 inflammasome complex (Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018). Its chemical scaffold was designed to specifically interfere with the ATPase function of the NLRP3 NACHT domain, thereby preventing the oligomerization of NLRP3 and subsequent formation of the ASC speck complex that is essential for inflammasome activation (Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2025). This compound has been synthetically optimized for high potency, with reported effective concentrations in the nanomolar range in various disease models, and its structure–activity relationship has been refined in numerous preclinical studies over the past several years (Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018; Wooff et al., 2020). As a representative of its drug class, diarylsulfonylureas have been broadly explored in inflammatory contexts due to their capacity to modulate innate immune pathways; however, MCC950 has emerged as a prototype NLRP3-targeting agent with potential applications across inflammatory and degenerative diseases, including those affecting ocular tissues (Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018; Wooff et al., 2020).

Therapeutic History:  
MCC950 was initially characterized in systemic inflammatory disease models, where it demonstrated remarkable efficacy in reducing the production of proinflammatory cytokines, such as interleukin (IL)-1β and IL-18, by directly inhibiting the activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome (Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018; Wooff et al., 2020). Preclinical evaluations in nonocular contexts—such as experimental colitis, myocardial infarction, and atherosclerosis—have consistently shown that MCC950 can markedly mitigate pathology by blocking the inflammasome cascade (Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018; Wooff et al., 2020). In the ocular arena, several studies have examined MCC950’s impact in diverse rodent models of retinal disease. For example, in laser-induced choroidal neovascularization (CNV) models, MCC950 administration led to reductions in IL-1β mRNA and secreted protein levels, albeit with a paradoxical increase in overall CNV lesion volume, suggesting a complex interplay between inflammasome inhibition and immune cell recruitment (Dieckmann et al., 2024). Furthermore, intravitreal delivery of MCC950 in an OPTN(E50K) mouse model of normal-tension glaucoma (NTG) showed functional and structural retinal improvements through decreased expression of inflammasome components and glial activation markers (Wang et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2023). In vitro investigations using ARPE-19 and R28 retinal cell lines have also highlighted MCC950's ability to decrease NLRP3, caspase-1, IL-1β, and IL-18 levels, thus attenuating inflammasome-mediated inflammatory responses (Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018; Li, 2020). Despite these promising preclinical data in models of retinal inflammation and vascular dysfunction, MCC950 has not yet progressed into clinical trials for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or geographic atrophy (GA), and its use in ocular conditions remains primarily in the preclinical and exploratory phase (Wooff et al., 2020).

Mechanism of Action:  
MCC950 exerts its pharmacological effects by specifically targeting the NLRP3 inflammasome, a cytosolic multiprotein complex that mediates the innate immune response to both pathogen-associated and damage-associated molecular patterns (Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018). At the molecular level, MCC950 is believed to bind to the NACHT domain of NLRP3, thereby inhibiting its ATPase activity—a critical step required for the conformational changes and oligomerization that lead to the formation of the active inflammasome complex (Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2025). This blockade prevents the recruitment of the adaptor protein ASC, thus halting the maturation and activation of caspase-1 (Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018; Wooff et al., 2020). Consequently, the cleavage of pro-IL-1β and pro-IL-18 into their bioactive forms is suppressed, which results in diminished secretion of these potent proinflammatory cytokines (Wang et al., 2025; Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018). Importantly, MCC950’s mechanism is selective for NLRP3, as it does not interfere with the activation of other inflammasome platforms, such as those mediated by AIM2, NLRC4, or NLRP1 (Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018; Wooff et al., 2020). In the context of retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells—a cell type critical for the maintenance of the outer blood–retina barrier and implicated in the pathogenesis of dry AMD—NLRP3 activation has been linked to chronic inflammation, oxidative stress, and lysosomal destabilization. Inhibition of NLRP3 by MCC950 is postulated to preserve lysosomal integrity by preventing excessive caspase-1 activation, which is known to contribute to lysosomal membrane permeabilization and the subsequent loss of v-ATPase–dependent acidification along with aberrant cathepsin D (CTSD) activity (Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018; Korhonen, 2024). Although direct experimental evidence demonstrating the preservation of CTSD activity or v-ATPase function by MCC950 in RPE cells is not yet firmly established in the literature provided, the underlying rationale is supported by the well-documented role of caspase-1 in mediating pyroptosis and lysosomal dysfunction in models of RPE degeneration (Korhonen, 2024; Ildefonso et al., 2016).

Expected Effect:  
In a therapeutic scenario for dry AMD, the expected effect of MCC950 is to inhibit NLRP3 inflammasome activation within RPE cells, thereby reducing the downstream activation of caspase-1 and the cleavage of proinflammatory cytokines IL-1β and IL-18. This dampening of the inflammatory cascade is anticipated to prevent or attenuate the lysosomal membrane destabilization that is often observed in RPE cells under stress conditions such as those induced by Alu RNA accumulation secondary to DICER1 deficiency—an event that has been strongly implicated in geographic atrophy (Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018; Korhonen, 2024). With reduced caspase-1 activity, it is hypothesized that MCC950 will preserve the integrity of the lysosomal compartment by maintaining proper v-ATPase function and ensuring that cathepsin D is correctly matured and compartmentalized, thereby mitigating autophagic and lysosomal stress (Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018; Ildefonso et al., 2016). In preclinical RPE models, inhibitors of NLRP3 have been shown to decrease IL-1β/IL-18 release and reduce inflammatory cell death (pyroptosis), which in turn supports cellular homeostasis and may prevent the progressive loss of RPE cells that drives the clinical progression of dry AMD (Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018; Wooff et al., 2020). Although direct evidence of MCC950 restoring lysosomal enzyme activity or preventing v-ATPase dysfunction in the context of AMD is currently limited, the compound has demonstrated efficacy in reducing inflammatory biomarker levels in retinal cell cultures and animal models, which is consistent with the desired outcome in a dry AMD setting (Li, 2020; Wooff et al., 2020). In addition to its biochemical effects, it is anticipated that the suppression of chronic inflammation by MCC950 will translate into preserved retinal architecture and function, as observed in some glaucoma models where intravitreal administration improved retinal ganglion cell survival and visual behavioral outcomes (Wang et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2023). Therefore, integrating both molecular and functional endpoints, MCC950 is expected to mitigate the inflammatory processes that underlie RPE loss, preserve key lysosomal functions, and ultimately slow or prevent the progression of geographic atrophy in dry AMD (Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018; Wooff et al., 2020).

Overall Evaluation:  
MCC950 offers several notable strengths as a potential therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. Foremost among these is its high potency and selectivity as an inhibitor of the NLRP3 inflammasome, a central mediator of innate immune inflammatory responses that has been implicated in the pathogenesis of various retinal degenerative disorders, including AMD (Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018). Its mechanism of action—binding to the NACHT domain to inhibit ATPase activity and subsequently block caspase-1 activation—provides a targeted approach that directly addresses a proximal event in the inflammatory cascade (Wang et al., 2025; Wooff et al., 2020). Preclinical studies have demonstrated that MCC950 can successfully reduce the release of IL-1β and IL-18 in various cell types, including retinal endothelial cells and RPE-like cells, which underscores its potential to ameliorate the chronic inflammatory environment observed in dry AMD (Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018; Li, 2020). Moreover, the use of MCC950 in ocular models—albeit primarily in glaucoma and CNV studies—has yielded promising outcomes in terms of reducing retinal inflammation, glial activation, and, in the case of intravitreal delivery in aged mouse models, improving retinal morphology and visual function (Wang et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2023). This provides an encouraging proof-of-concept that NLRP3 inhibition can have beneficial effects on retinal structure and function.

However, several weaknesses and challenges must be considered before advancing MCC950 as a therapy for dry AMD. While the compound effectively reduces inflammasome activity in multiple settings, its performance in models that closely recapitulate dry AMD pathology, particularly those focusing on geographic atrophy and RPE degeneration, remains to be conclusively demonstrated (Wooff et al., 2020). In some preclinical models, such as the photo-oxidative damage study, MCC950 failed to rescue photoreceptor cell death or improve overall retinal function, and higher doses were associated with adverse functional effects, suggesting a narrow therapeutic window or model-specific limitations (Wooff et al., 2020; Zha et al., 2022). Furthermore, while the hypothesis that MCC950 will preserve lysosomal v-ATPase function and cathepsin D activity is compelling, the current literature does not present direct experimental evidence confirming that these specific endpoints are restored in RPE cells following NLRP3 inhibition by MCC950 (Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018; Ildefonso et al., 2016). This gap is critical, given that lysosomal dysfunction and impaired autophagy are central to the chronic inflammation and RPE loss observed in dry AMD. Additionally, there are reports of paradoxical effects in certain ocular models—such as increased lesion volume in laser-induced CNV models despite reductions in IL-1β levels—which hint at the complex biology of the inflammasome and suggest that blocking NLRP3 may have unintended consequences on immune cell recruitment and neovascular dynamics (Dieckmann et al., 2024).

A further limitation is the relative paucity of data regarding the pharmacokinetic properties and ocular bioavailability of MCC950 when administered via routes that would be clinically relevant for AMD, such as intravitreal or topical delivery. Although some studies have begun to characterize its ocular distribution and short-term safety in rodent models (Chen et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2025), comprehensive long-term toxicity profiles, dose–response evaluations, and assessments of potential off-target effects in the highly specialized environment of the eye have yet to be established. These studies are essential not only for confirming the anti-inflammatory efficacy of MCC950 in RPE cells but also for ensuring that long-term inhibition of NLRP3 does not inadvertently impair other cellular processes critical for retinal health.

In summary, the evaluation of MCC950 as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD is promising yet remains preliminary. Its well-characterized ability to selectively inhibit the NLRP3 inflammasome, reducing caspase-1 activation and downstream IL-1β/IL-18 release, aligns with the mechanistic rationale for targeting chronic inflammation in RPE cells—a key driver of geographic atrophy in dry AMD (Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018; Korhonen, 2024). The compound’s preclinical efficacy in reducing inflammatory biomarkers in various ocular and non-ocular models supports the hypothesis that MCC950 may alleviate the inflammatory milieu that underlies RPE degeneration and lysosomal dysfunction. However, mixed outcomes observed in certain retinal models, along with the absence of direct evidence linking MCC950 to improved lysosomal v-ATPase function and cathepsin D maturation in RPE cells, underscore the need for further detailed studies (Wooff et al., 2020). Moreover, optimizing the ocular delivery method, establishing a robust pharmacokinetic profile in the eye, and conducting dedicated preclinical trials in models that accurately mimic dry AMD pathophysiology are critical next steps before this candidate can be considered for clinical translation. 

Overall, while MCC950 exhibits significant mechanistic and pharmacological strengths that support its evaluation as a potential treatment for dry AMD, its clinical viability will depend on resolving several key uncertainties. These include (1) the demonstration of its capacity to restore and maintain lysosomal integrity and CTSD activity in stressed RPE cells, (2) the establishment of an optimal dosing regimen with minimal ocular toxicity, and (3) clarification of the complex immunological consequences of long-term NLRP3 inhibition within the retinal environment. Addressing these questions through a comprehensive series of biochemical, cellular, and animal studies will be essential for determining whether MCC950 can be effectively repurposed to combat the progressive RPE loss and chronic inflammatory state that drive geographic atrophy in dry AMD (Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018; Wooff et al., 2020; Ildefonso et al., 2016).

In conclusion, MCC950 is a highly attractive candidate from a drug development perspective due to its potent, selective inhibition of the NLRP3 inflammasome—a pathway increasingly implicated in the inflammatory cascade that underlies dry AMD. Its synthetic origins as a diarylsulfonylurea and its extensive preclinical evaluation in inflammatory disease models lend strong support to its potential utility. Nevertheless, the complex biology of the retinal environment and the conflicting preclinical results observed in some models necessitate cautious optimism. Further targeted studies that rigorously assess MCC950’s effects on RPE-specific endpoints—including lysosomal acidification, v-ATPase function, and cathepsin D maturation—will be pivotal in establishing its efficacy for dry AMD. Additionally, comprehensive ocular safety and pharmacokinetic studies are required to ensure that the benefits of MCC950 can be realized without incurring off-target toxicities in this delicate tissue. Based on the current literature, MCC950 holds promise as a means to directly address inflammasome-driven inflammation in dry AMD; however, its advancement into clinical trials will depend on the outcomes of these critical preclinical investigations (Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018; Wooff et al., 2020; Li, 2020; Ildefonso et al., 2016; Dieckmann et al., 2024).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Anakinra (brand: Kineret) is a recombinant, non-glycosylated form of the human interleukin-1 receptor antagonist (IL-1Ra) that competitively binds the type I interleukin-1 receptor (IL-1RI) and prevents signaling by IL-1α and IL-1β, thereby broadly antagonizing downstream IL-1–dependent signal transduction cascades (notably NF-κB and MAPK) in responsive cells (Dabouz, 2024; Dabouz et al., 2020). IL-1Ra belongs to the class of anti-cytokine biologics that block pro-inflammatory cytokine signaling, a therapeutic strategy that has been validated across systemic autoinflammatory and autoimmune diseases; Kineret has an extensive human safety and pharmacology dossier as an approved product, with prescribing information available for systemic use (Mesquida, Drawnel, & Fauser, 2019). Within ophthalmology, IL-1 pathway blockade has been investigated in multiple preclinical ocular models and has seen clinical use for inflammatory eye diseases; routes explored include systemic administration of anakinra for uveitis and scleritis, topical IL-1 antagonists for ocular surface disease (e.g., isunakinra/EBI-005), and experimental ocular gene therapy encoding IL-1Ra (Fabiani et al., 2017). In posterior segment disease models, intravitreal recombinant IL-1Ra (anakinra) inhibited laser-induced choroidal neovascularization (CNV) in rodents in a dose-dependent fashion, establishing local ocular pharmacologic activity of IL-1R antagonism in retina/choroid (Fabiani et al., 2017; Sandhu, Lambert, Xu, & Kaplan, 2018).

Therapeutic History  
Systemic indications and ocular inflammatory experience. Anakinra has long been employed systemically in rheumatology and has been repurposed for ocular autoinflammatory and autoimmune conditions such as Behçet uveitis, Blau syndrome/CAPS phenotypes, and refractory scleritis, with reported improvements in intraocular inflammation and steroid-sparing in case series and retrospective cohorts; dosing regimens reported include 100–150 mg daily or weight-based 1–3 mg/kg daily subcutaneous dosing, with acceptable tolerability profiles dominated by mild injection-site reactions in the ocular cohorts cited (Fabiani et al., 2017; Korhonen, 2024). A practical constraint is anakinra’s short systemic half-life that necessitates daily dosing, with relapse reported upon dose reductions in some inflammatory eye disease cases—an important consideration for chronic indications (Fabiani et al., 2017; Korhonen, 2024). Topical isunakinra/IL-1Ra formulations for ocular surface disease demonstrated clinically meaningful symptom and sign improvements in randomized trials, high ocular receptor occupancy (~97%) at low doses, minimal systemic exposure (plasma below detection), and a favorable local safety signal, although these outcomes pertain to the anterior segment and cannot be extrapolated directly to the posterior segment (Fabiani et al., 2017).

Posterior segment and AMD-relevant preclinical work. Multiple animal studies substantiate that IL-1 signaling is active and targetable in the posterior segment. In a rat CNV model, intravitreal anakinra led to dose-dependent reductions in neovascular area; related IL-1β-targeted interventions prevented CNV without exacerbating photoreceptor degeneration, arguing against gross phototoxicity from IL-1 blockade in that setting (Sandhu et al., 2018; Fabiani et al., 2017). In a blue light–induced retinal degeneration model, systemic IL-1R antagonism with anakinra mitigated inflammatory readouts, reduced accumulation of subretinal macrophages, preserved photoreceptor structure, and maintained ERG function; an allosteric IL-1R modulator (rytvela) was somewhat superior, but anakinra nonetheless produced protective effects (Dabouz et al., 2020; Dabouz, 2024). Mechanistically, these studies localized IL-1β production to inflammasome-active subretinal mononuclear phagocytes (MPs) and mapped Il1r1 expression mainly to astroglia and vascular cells in mouse retina, supporting paracrine IL-1 signaling to neurovascular targets in the outer retina (Dabouz et al., 2020; Dabouz, 2024).

Human clinical evidence in dry AMD/geographic atrophy. No published human trials of anakinra for dry AMD/geographic atrophy (GA) were identified in the provided materials; a registry search string returned 18 ClinicalTrials.gov hits combining anakinra with retinal keywords, but no trial-level information (indication, route, dose, status, outcomes) was provided, and no AMD/GA trials of anakinra are documented here (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.). Systemic IL-1β blockade with canakinumab showed no effect in a diabetic retinopathy exploratory clinical context, underscoring translational uncertainty of systemic IL-1 pathway modulation for posterior segment disease (Korhonen, 2024).

Mechanistic rationale in RPE/AMD. Extensive literature supports that in AMD-relevant stress contexts the RPE and subretinal myeloid cells exhibit NLRP3 inflammasome activation, caspase-1–dependent maturation of IL-1β and IL-18, lysosomal membrane permeabilization (LMP) with cathepsin release, and altered autophagy/heterophagy—mechanistic substrates for chronic para-inflammation and cell death (apoptosis → pyroptosis shift) in RPE (Treanor, n.d.; Yerramothu, Vijay, & Willcox, 2018; Kaarniranta et al., 2023). IL-1β levels are elevated in AMD vitreous and plasma, and microglia/MP-derived IL-1β can drive chemokine and cytokine production by Müller cells and RPE, linking IL-1 to retinal inflammatory amplification (Nashine et al., 2022; Korhonen, 2024). The RPE itself produces IL-1Ra and uses IL-1Ra to limit immune activation: IL-1Ra suppresses necrosis-induced release of IL-6, IL-8, and MCP-1 from ARPE-19 and reduces antigen-presenting functions in RPE cocultures, indicating that IL-1 signaling is operational in RPE and that IL-1R antagonism can blunt RPE-mediated inflammatory outputs in vitro (Fabiani et al., 2017; Kaur & Singh, 2021).

Mechanism of Action  
Receptor pharmacology. IL-1β and IL-1α bind IL-1RI and recruit IL-1 receptor accessory protein (IL-1RAcP) to form a signaling complex that initiates MyD88-dependent activation of IRAKs, TRAF6, TAK1, and downstream MAPKs (JNK/p38) and NF-κB, driving expression of inflammatory mediators and cell-type–specific responses (Dabouz, 2024). Anakinra is a competitive orthosteric antagonist of IL-1RI that prevents IL-1α/β binding and thereby blocks the formation of the signaling complex with IL-1RAcP, “non-selectively” inhibiting downstream IL-1–dependent pathways across cell types expressing IL-1RI (Dabouz, 2024; Dabouz et al., 2020). In the blue-light retinal injury model, orthosteric antagonism with anakinra and allosteric modulation with rytvela each prevented IL-1–driven retinal inflammation and photoreceptor injury; mechanistically, both agents protected neuroretinal compartments that express IL-1R while not necessarily reducing IL-1β produced in macrophage conditioned media, consistent with receptor-level antagonism in responder cells (Dabouz et al., 2020; Dabouz, 2024).

Cellular sources/targets in retina. In injury models, Il1b is upregulated primarily in infiltrating subretinal mononuclear phagocytes that co-express NLRP3 and caspase-1, whereas Il1r1 expression is detected predominantly in astrocytes, pericytes, endothelial cells, and bipolar cells, with little to no detection in photoreceptors or MPs by scRNA-seq; this places the critical pharmacodynamic target of anakinra on neurovascular/astroglial elements rather than on the IL-1β-producing cells themselves (Dabouz et al., 2020; Dabouz, 2024). IL-1β is elevated in AMD patients’ vitreous and is a recognized biomarker of retinal inflammation; microglia-derived IL-1β amplifies chemokine signaling by Müller and RPE cells, indicating that RPE can serve as an IL-1–responsive amplifier of inflammation even if Il1r1 detection varies by model and assay (Nashine et al., 2022; Korhonen, 2024). RPE-derived endogenous IL-1Ra provides further evidence that IL-1 signaling—and its antagonism—are biologically relevant in the RPE microenvironment (Fabiani et al., 2017).

Inflammasome context and limitations of IL-1R blockade. In RPE and adjacent retinal cells, NLRP3 inflammasome activation is triggered by AMD-relevant stimuli including A2E/lipofuscin photooxidation, drusen components, DICER1/Alu RNA accumulation, oxidized lipoproteins, complement/cofactors, ROS, and lysosomal membrane permeabilization with cathepsin release (Treanor, n.d.; Yerramothu et al., 2018). Inflammasome activation requires priming (e.g., TLR-NF-κB–dependent upregulation of NLRP3/pro-IL-1β) followed by an activation signal (e.g., mtROS, LMP), culminating in caspase-1 activation and secretion of mature IL-1β and IL-18; inflammasome priming can shift RPE death from apoptosis to pyroptosis, increasing inflammatory cytokine release and DAMP extrusion (Treanor, n.d.; Kaarniranta et al., 2023). Critically, IL-1 pathway blockers such as anakinra do not inhibit upstream inflammasome assembly, caspase-1 activation, or IL-18 production; thus, IL-1R antagonism will block IL-1 signaling but will not shut down inflammasome-dependent IL-18 release or pyroptotic execution, which may continue to drive disease biology (Korhonen, 2024). Moreover, in some experimental paradigms, IL-18 can have protective or context-dependent roles in AMD models, complicating network-level predictions when only IL-1 signaling is blocked (Lim et al., 2020).

Evidence gaps regarding lysosomal targets. The working hypothesis posits that anakinra will prevent IL-1β-driven inflammasome amplification and lysosomal destabilization in RPE, preserving vacuolar H+-ATPase (v-ATPase) function and cathepsin D (CTSD) maturation/activity; however, the provided materials contain no direct experimental evidence that IL-1R antagonism rescues v-ATPase activity, lysosomal pH, or CTSD processing in RPE, nor that anakinra reduces lysosomal membrane permeabilization in these systems (Lim et al., 2020; Treanor, n.d.). While lysosomal destabilization and cathepsin B/L release are well-documented inflammasome triggers in RPE, and bafilomycin A1 (a v-ATPase inhibitor) has been used to model lysosomal/autophagic impairment that activates NLRP3 and IL-1β release, there is no reported dataset here demonstrating that IL-1R blockade restores lysosomal acidification or cathepsin D maturation in RPE (Yerramothu et al., 2018; Piippo, 2019). Consequently, the proposed IL-1→lysosome preservation claims remain conjectural in the absence of targeted RPE lysosomal measurements following anakinra treatment in AMD-relevant paradigms (Lim et al., 2020; Treanor, n.d.).

Expected Effect  
Assay-level effects in retinal/RPE systems. Based on the presented literature, IL-1R antagonism with anakinra is expected to reduce IL-1–driven inflammatory signaling in neuroretinal and gliovascular compartments, attenuate subretinal macrophage accumulation/activation, and preserve photoreceptor structure/function in acute inflammatory injury paradigms; these effects have been demonstrated in the blue light model (reduced GFAP, Il1b/Il6/Ccl2 transcripts, fewer subretinal MPs, more preserved ONL and ERG amplitudes) (Dabouz, 2024; Dabouz et al., 2020). In explant co-culture systems where LPS/ATP-activated macrophages produce IL-1β, IL-1R antagonists and anti-IL-1β antibodies abrogate photoreceptor death, supporting a causal role for IL-1β and a direct cytoprotective effect of IL-1 pathway blockade on IL-1RI-expressing retinal cells (Dabouz, 2024). In vitro RPE models show that IL-1Ra can suppress necrosis-induced secretion of IL-6, IL-8, and MCP-1 (likely via NF-κB), suggesting that anakinra may dampen autocrine/paracrine amplification in RPE cultures challenged with danger signals—though definitive RPE IL-1RI expression patterns in vivo remain incompletely defined in the cited mouse scRNA-seq data (Fabiani et al., 2017; Dabouz et al., 2020).

Inflammasome priming versus activation. IL-1 can contribute to priming (NF-κB–dependent) of inflammasome components; therefore, anakinra might indirectly reduce NLRP3 priming in some contexts by interrupting IL-1 positive feedback loops, leading to lower pro-IL-1β and possibly reduced susceptibility to subsequent activation triggers (Fabiani et al., 2017). However, because anakinra acts downstream of inflammasome assembly, it will not prevent caspase-1 activation, gasdermin D pore formation, pyroptosis, or IL-18 maturation/secretion once NLRP3 is engaged—which are all relevant to RPE and subretinal myeloid biology in AMD (Korhonen, 2024; Treanor, n.d.; Kaarniranta et al., 2023). Consequently, anakinra’s benefit in dry AMD models that are dominated by RPE-intrinsic inflammasome activation and pyroptosis may be partial, favoring reductions in IL-1–driven chemokine/cytokine cascades and immune cell recruitment over direct prevention of inflammasome-executed cell death (Korhonen, 2024; Treanor, n.d.).

Lysosomal endpoints. The proposed preservation of v-ATPase function and cathepsin D activity is not currently supported by primary data in the provided sources; no reports demonstrate that anakinra normalizes lysosomal pH, protease maturation (including CTSD), or membrane integrity in RPE subjected to AMD-relevant stressors (Lim et al., 2020; Treanor, n.d.; Piippo, 2019). While inhibiting IL-1 signaling may lower NF-κB–driven transcription of inflammatory mediators (and thus lessen secondary stressors to lysosomes), the extent to which this translates into measurable correction of lysosomal biology in RPE remains to be tested experimentally (Fabiani et al., 2017).

Translational dosing and safety in the eye. In mice, systemic anakinra at 4 mg/kg twice daily for 3 days produced retinal protection in the blue light model; this regimen emphasizes short-term systemic exposures in an acute injury context rather than chronic degenerative settings (Dabouz, 2024). In CNV rodents, intravitreal IL-1Ra reduced neovascularization without aggravating photoreceptor degeneration, providing proof-of-concept for posterior segment delivery and a supportive safety signal in that animal model (Sandhu et al., 2018). Clinically, systemic anakinra has an established safety profile in inflammatory eye disease cohorts, but no intravitreal human anakinra safety data in AMD/GA are presented here; systemic IL-1β blockade (canakinumab) did not improve retinopathy outcomes in a separate context, and anakinra’s daily dosing requirement remains a burden for chronic use unless long-acting ocular delivery is engineered (Korhonen, 2024; Fabiani et al., 2017).

Overall Evaluation  
Merits  
- Biological plausibility in AMD. AMD-relevant stressors activate NLRP3 in RPE and subretinal myeloid cells, elevating IL-1β and IL-18 and driving para-inflammatory cascades and pyroptosis; IL-1β is increased in AMD vitreous and plasma, and IL-1–producing MPs are present at sites of pathology, establishing IL-1 as a rational target for modulating retinal inflammation (Treanor, n.d.; Nashine et al., 2022; Korhonen, 2024).  
- Pharmacologic validation in retinal models. Anakinra significantly reduced inflammation and preserved retinal structure/function in a light-damage model and intravitreally suppressed CNV in rodents, indicating target engagement and protective potential in the posterior segment; IL-1β neutralization prevented CNV without exacerbating photoreceptor degeneration, arguing for a non-toxic profile in those contexts (Dabouz et al., 2020; Dabouz, 2024; Sandhu et al., 2018).  
- RPE-relevant immunobiology. RPE naturally produces IL-1Ra, and exogenous IL-1Ra reduces necrosis-induced inflammatory mediator release from RPE and suppresses dendritic-cell activation in RPE co-cultures, suggesting that anakinra could attenuate RPE-mediated inflammatory amplification in dry AMD (Fabiani et al., 2017; Kaur & Singh, 2021).  
- Clinical and formulation precedents. Systemic ocular use of anakinra in uveitis and scleritis shows clinical feasibility and manageable safety; topical IL-1 antagonists have robust ocular safety signals; gene therapy encoding IL-1Ra and intravitreal administration have been explored preclinically, supporting a spectrum of delivery options that could be adapted for posterior segment disease (Fabiani et al., 2017).

Limitations and risks  
- Mechanistic incompleteness vis-à-vis inflammasomes. IL-1R blockade will not prevent upstream NLRP3 activation, caspase-1 activity, gasdermin-mediated pyroptosis, or IL-18 production; in RPE-intrinsic inflammasome-dominant pathophysiology, anakinra would be expected to blunt downstream IL-1–mediated amplification and leukocyte recruitment but not stop the execution machinery of inflammasome-driven cell death (Korhonen, 2024; Treanor, n.d.; Kaarniranta et al., 2023).  
- Unsubstantiated lysosomal rescue claims. There is no evidence here that anakinra preserves lysosomal acidification (v-ATPase function), cathepsin D maturation/activity, or prevents LMP in RPE under AMD-relevant stress; this is a critical gap because the proposed therapeutic specificity hinges on cytokine–lysosome cross-talk that remains to be demonstrated (Lim et al., 2020; Treanor, n.d.; Piippo, 2019).  
- Target expression uncertainties. In mouse retina, Il1r1 is enriched in astroglia and vascular cells and not detected in photoreceptors or MPs by scRNA-seq, complicating assumptions about direct photoreceptor or RPE targeting by anakinra in vivo; while RPE responds to IL-1 in vitro and produces IL-1Ra, spatial and species differences in IL-1RI distribution may shape efficacy and delivery decisions (Dabouz et al., 2020; Dabouz, 2024; Fabiani et al., 2017).  
- Mixed translational signals. Systemic IL-1β blockade did not improve diabetic retinopathy outcomes in the cited study, and anakinra’s systemic short half-life imposes burdensome daily dosing for chronic disease; there is no documented human safety/efficacy experience with intravitreal anakinra in AMD/GA in the provided sources (Korhonen, 2024; Fabiani et al., 2017; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).  
- Network complexity. NLRP3/IL-18 can exert context-dependent protective or detrimental effects in AMD models; while anakinra does not block IL-18 signaling, its selective inhibition of IL-1 may not suffice to rebalance inflammasome-driven pathology if pyroptosis and IL-18-dependent pathways remain active (Lim et al., 2020).

Go/No-Go considerations and critical experiments  
- RPE-centric validation. Test anakinra in human RPE models exposed to A2E/blue-light, drusen components, DICER1/Alu RNA, or oxidized lipoproteins; quantify NLRP3 priming (NLRP3, pro-IL-1β), activation (ASC specks, caspase-1 cleavage), downstream cytokines (IL-1β, IL-18), and execution (GSDMD cleavage/pyroptosis markers), with and without anakinra to define points of pathway modulation (Treanor, n.d.; Yerramothu et al., 2018).  
- Lysosomal endpoints. Directly measure lysosomal pH, v-ATPase activity, LMP (galectin-3 puncta), cathepsin D maturation/activity, and autophagic flux in the same RPE paradigms ± anakinra to test the hypothesis that IL-1R blockade preserves lysosomal integrity and protease processing (Piippo, 2019).  
- In vivo GA-relevant models. Move from acute light injury to RPE-atrophy models (e.g., chronic photooxidative stress, Alu RNA/DICER1 disruption, lipofuscin models) to assess whether anakinra reduces rates of RPE atrophy, outer retinal thinning, and visual function decline; include comparators targeting the inflammasome (e.g., NLRP3 inhibitors) to benchmark effect sizes and mechanistic depth (Treanor, n.d.; Kaarniranta et al., 2023; Lim et al., 2020).  
- Ocular delivery and PK. Develop and test intravitreal dosing and, preferably, sustained-release formats for anakinra to overcome systemic short half-life; establish vitreous/retinal PK and receptor occupancy, and evaluate ocular safety (IOP, ERG, histopathology) and immunogenicity (anti-drug antibodies) in large-eye species (Korhonen, 2024; Fabiani et al., 2017).  
- Biomarker strategy. Use vitreous/plasma IL-1β and retinal inflammatory transcript signatures as pharmacodynamic biomarkers; consider scRNA-seq to confirm target cell engagement (Il1r1-expressing compartments) pre- and post-treatment (Nashine et al., 2022; Dabouz, 2024).

Positioning relative to alternatives  
Because anakinra does not interrupt inflammasome activation or execution, proximal inhibitors of the NLRP3 inflammasome (e.g., MCC950-class) may provide deeper control of IL-1β/IL-18 production and pyroptosis in RPE-driven disease, at the cost of potentially suppressing beneficial IL-18 signaling in some contexts; preclinical literature shows NLRP3 blockade can be protective in retinal models, meriting parallel evaluation (Lim et al., 2020). Conversely, allosteric IL-1R modulators (rytvela-type) have shown superior protection to anakinra in the light-damage model and may offer functional selectivity (e.g., sparing NF-κB while inhibiting JNK/p38/AP-1) with improved distribution and immunogenicity profiles; these properties deserve consideration if an IL-1-targeting approach is pursued (Dabouz, 2024; Dabouz et al., 2020).

Conclusions  
- Strength of rationale. There is robust evidence that IL-1β is elevated and pathogenic in retinal neuroinflammation and that IL-1R antagonism—including anakinra—can protect retina in preclinical models by reducing inflammatory signaling and immune cell recruitment; RPE-relevant IL-1 biology further supports plausibility (Dabouz et al., 2020; Dabouz, 2024; Fabiani et al., 2017).  
- Weakness of hypothesis specifics. The central claim that anakinra preserves v-ATPase function and cathepsin D maturation in RPE lacks support in the provided literature; moreover, IL-1R blockade cannot prevent upstream inflammasome activation or pyroptosis, limiting its capacity to halt RPE-intrinsic degenerative processes central to GA (Lim et al., 2020; Korhonen, 2024; Treanor, n.d.; Piippo, 2019).  
- Translational readiness. No human AMD/GA trials of anakinra are documented here; systemic IL-1β blockade has shown limited efficacy in retinal vascular disease, and anakinra’s dosing logistics are unfavorable for chronic ocular therapy without dedicated ocular delivery systems (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.; Korhonen, 2024).

Overall Evaluation  
Anakinra is a mechanistically credible anti-inflammatory candidate to blunt IL-1–driven retinal inflammation and leukocyte recruitment, with reproducible preclinical efficacy signals in posterior-segment injury models and supportive RPE-centric immunobiology; however, the specific hypothesis that it will mechanistically preserve lysosomal v-ATPase function and cathepsin D activity in RPE is currently unsupported by direct evidence, and IL-1R antagonism is unlikely to arrest inflammasome activation, IL-18 signaling, or pyroptotic cell death that contribute to RPE atrophy in dry AMD (Dabouz et al., 2020; Dabouz, 2024; Fabiani et al., 2017; Korhonen, 2024; Lim et al., 2020). Given the absence of clinical data in GA and delivery constraints, anakinra merits consideration as an adjunct anti-inflammatory approach contingent on (1) generation of RPE-focused data demonstrating modulation of inflammasome priming and lysosomal integrity, and (2) development of sustained intraocular delivery; in parallel, more proximal interventions (NLRP3 inhibitors) and IL-1R allosteric modulators with superior preclinical efficacy should be benchmarked as potentially higher-leverage strategies for disease modification in dry AMD (Lim et al., 2020; Dabouz et al., 2020).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN) is an endogenous intermediate in the mammalian NAD⁺ salvage pathway, generated by nicotinamide phosphoribosyltransferase (NAMPT) from nicotinamide (NAM) and 5-phosphoribosyl‐1‐pyrophosphate (PRPP) and converted to NAD⁺ by nicotinamide mononucleotide adenylyltransferases (NMNAT1–3) (Jadeja et al., 2020; Cimaglia et al., 2020). NMN belongs to the vitamin B3–derived NAD⁺ precursor class and is one of several precursors (others include nicotinamide [NAM], nicotinic acid [NA], and nicotinamide riboside [NR]) used to augment cellular NAD⁺ pools in aging and disease (Cimaglia et al., 2020). NMN was prioritized as a practical intervention because direct NAD⁺ delivery to tissues is not straightforward, whereas in vivo administration of NMN elevates tissue NAD⁺ and supports mitochondrial function and cellular stress defenses in multiple systems (Ebeling et al., 2020; Rahman et al., 2024). Transport and uptake mechanisms include the Slc12a8 transporter described in mouse small intestine, as well as extracellular dephosphorylation to NR followed by NR uptake via equilibrative nucleoside transporters; intracellular NR is re‐phosphorylated by NRK1 to NMN for resynthesis of NAD⁺ (Will‐Orrego, 2020a; Rahman et al., 2024). Notably for RPE models, ARPE‐19 cells have been reported to express transporters supporting NMN uptake but not NR uptake, favoring NMN over NR in this system (Will‐Orrego, 2020b). In RPE and retinal contexts, NMN and related precursors have been deployed preclinically to restore NAD⁺, improve mitochondrial function, modulate sirtuin‐dependent pathways, and mitigate features of neurodegeneration and cellular senescence (Jadeja et al., 2018; Ebeling et al., 2020; Lin, 2020).

Therapeutic History  
NAD⁺ decline with age is conserved across tissues, including the retina and RPE, and is mechanistically linked to impaired mitochondrial function, heightened oxidative stress, and increased susceptibility to degeneration (Jadeja et al., 2018; Cimaglia et al., 2020). In the outer retina, rod‐ or cone‐specific Nampt deletion produces NAD⁺ deficiency and photoreceptor degeneration; systemic NMN at 150 mg/kg i.p. restored retinal function by ERG and preserved photoreceptor structure, establishing that exogenous NMN can replenish retinal NAD⁺ and mitigate degeneration linked to impaired salvage (Lin, 2020). NMN also protected in models of acute retinal injury: daily systemic NMN reduced photoreceptor death and oxidative stress after retinal detachment and increased retinal SIRT1 and HO‐1, consistent with NAD⁺‐dependent sirtuin activation in vivo (Chen et al., 2020). In ischemia models, NMN administration protected against retinal dysfunction (Lee et al., 2022; Lee et al., 2024). In a cholesterol efflux–deficient murine model that recapitulates key dry AMD features driven by senescent subretinal macrophages (Abca1/g1‐deficient), systemic NMN reduced subretinal drusenoid deposits (SDDs), decreased lipofuscin‐positive macrophage burden, and improved electrophysiological and structural endpoints, supporting a role for NAD⁺ augmentation in reversing senescence‐driven outer retinal pathology in vivo (Terao et al., 2024). In RPE‐directed models, pharmacologic NAMPT inhibition with FK866 is widely used to mimic age‐related NAD⁺ decline; in ARPE‐19 and primary RPE, NMN co‐treatment preserved NAD⁺, SIRT1 protein, viability, and reduced senescence markers, and in vivo systemic NMN preserved RPE NAD⁺ and SIRT1 after subretinal FK866 (Jadeja et al., 2018). Oxidant injury with sodium iodate (NaIO₃) induced RPE senescence, NAD⁺ depletion, mitochondrial dysfunction, and subretinal inflammation; NMN restored RPE NAD⁺, reduced DNA damage and senescence markers, improved mitochondrial membrane potential and ATP in ARPE‐19, and reduced inflammatory cell recruitment in vivo, with intact Sirt1 signaling required for NMN benefit (Ren et al., 2022). Outside strictly RPE biology, NMN improved RPE phagocytosis and mitochondrial ultrastructure in the RCS rat model of retinal degeneration, with a mechanistic link to a NAD⁺/GAPDH axis that modulated actin/cytoskeletal phagocytosis machinery in RPE; GAPDH knockdown abrogated NMN’s benefits, supporting a causal chain from NAD⁺ repletion to enhanced RPE POS clearance via GAPDH‐dependent pathways (Zhang et al., 2024).

Clinical translation of NAD⁺ precursors has begun with nicotinamide and NR in ophthalmology-adjacent indications (e.g., glaucoma), demonstrating tolerability and retinal functional protection in mice, and documenting NAD⁺ elevation in adult humans, but direct clinical data for NMN in dry AMD are not available in the provided context (Cimaglia et al., 2020; Rahman et al., 2024). Long-term NMN treatment in mice mitigated age-associated physiological decline systemically and reportedly ameliorated eye function, but detailed ocular pharmacology and human NMN ocular safety are not established here (Rahman et al., 2024). Collectively, the preclinical record supports NMN as an NAD⁺ augmenting therapy with demonstrated efficacy in retina and RPE-relevant models of NAD⁺ deficiency, oxidative injury, and senescence; however, there is no direct published clinical trial evidence in dry AMD patients in this context set (Jadeja et al., 2018; Lin, 2020; Chen et al., 2020; Terao et al., 2024).

Mechanism of Action  
Core biochemistry  
- NAD⁺ salvage. In mammalian cells, the salvage pathway supplies most NAD⁺ (~80%), with NAMPT catalyzing NAM → NMN and NMNAT1–3 completing NMN → NAD⁺; this pool fuels redox reactions and serves as substrate for NAD⁺‐consuming enzymes including sirtuins, PARPs, and the NAD glycohydrolase CD38 (Cimaglia et al., 2020; Jadeja et al., 2020). NAMPT-mediated biosynthesis is essential for vision, and its decline in RPE with age causally links to reduced NAD⁺, reduced SIRT1 expression/activity, and enhanced cellular senescence (Jadeja et al., 2018).  
- Uptake and intracellular handling. NMN can enter cells via specific transporters (Slc12a8 shown in mouse gut) and/or after extracellular dephosphorylation to NR with re-phosphorylation by NRK1, routes that are cell type–dependent; ARPE-19 preferentially transport NMN in vitro, supporting the choice of NMN over NR in these RPE models (Will‐Orrego, 2020a; Will‐Orrego, 2020b; Rahman et al., 2024).

Downstream signaling nodes relevant to RPE and dry AMD  
- Sirtuins. NAD⁺ is an obligate co-substrate for sirtuins; increased NAD⁺ drives sirtuin deacetylase/deacylase activities across SIRT1–7 with consequences for mitochondrial function, antioxidant defenses, DNA repair, and autophagy/mitophagy (Cimaglia et al., 2020). In aging RPE, NAD⁺ and SIRT1 decline in parallel; restoring NAD⁺ with NMN rescues SIRT1 protein and activity in vitro and in vivo, and reduces senescence markers p16^INK4a and p21^Waf/Cip1 (Jadeja et al., 2018). SIRT3, the mitochondrial sirtuin, maintains mitochondrial integrity by deacetylating and activating SOD2 and coordinating antioxidant responses, mitophagy, and UPR^mt; retinal NAD⁺ deficiency impairs SIRT3, linking NAD⁺ loss to mitochondrial vulnerability (Cimaglia et al., 2020; Lin, 2020). In a retinal detachment model, systemic NMN increased SIRT1 protein and HO‐1, with mechanistic in vitro data supporting a SIRT1 → HO‐1 protective axis (Chen et al., 2020).  
- AMPK and NAMPT/SIRT1 crosstalk. AMPK upregulates NAMPT expression and thus supports NAD⁺ salvage; reciprocally, SIRT1 deacetylates/stabilizes LKB1 to activate AMPK, forming a positive feedback loop that coordinates energy sensing and catabolic responses (Luján et al., 2022). In RPE senescence induced by NaIO₃, AMPK activation occurs downstream of ATP depletion and is modulated by NMN treatment, though overactivation of Sirt1 by a direct agonist (SRT1720) produced mitochondrial hyperfusion and stress signaling, arguing for physiological NAD⁺‐driven Sirt1 activation rather than pharmacologic overdrive (Ren et al., 2022).  
- Autophagy/mitophagy and mitochondrial biogenesis. SIRT1 promotes autophagosome formation and Rab7‐dependent autophagosome–lysosome fusion; together with AMPK, it enhances expression of mitophagy effectors (PINK1, Parkin) and co-activates PGC‐1α to drive mitochondrial biogenesis programs via transcriptional partners (NRF‐1, ERRα, PPARα) (Luján et al., 2022). Reviews and preclinical observations indicate that NAD⁺ repletion can restore mitophagy, activate UPR^mt, and normalize mitochondrial metabolic profiles, including evidence that “NAD⁺ inhibits the metabolic reprogramming of RPE cells in early AMD by upregulating mitophagy,” supporting the hypothesis that NMN-driven NAD⁺ gain could favorably reprogram RPE mitochondrial quality control (Rahman et al., 2024; Jadeja et al., 2020). In primary AMD donor RPE, NMN improved mitochondrial function in vitro; the same study used mitophagy reporter assays (mKeima-mito), underscoring the feasibility of measuring NMN’s effects on mitophagy in human RPE although specific NMN → mitophagy data were not detailed in the excerpt (Fisher et al., 2022; Ebeling et al., 2020).  
- PARP and CD38 as NAD⁺ sinks. DNA damage and SASP/inflammation drive PARP and CD38 activities that deplete NAD⁺; CD38 in particular contributes to age-related NAD⁺ decline and mitochondrial dysfunction and is induced by LXR signaling and SASP, creating a self-reinforcing senescence–NAD⁺ depletion loop (Cimaglia et al., 2020; Terao et al., 2024). In photoreceptor cells, PARP inhibition partially rescues viability under NAMPT inhibition, highlighting the vulnerability of NAD⁺ pools to consumption pathways and the value of reducing NAD⁺ sinks in parallel with NMN supplementation (Lin & Apte, 2018).  
- Inflammation and inflammasome. NAD⁺ augmentation via NMN or increased NAMPT/NAD⁺ can reduce NLRP3 inflammasome activation and downstream IL-1β/IL-18 via a SIRT1‐dependent mechanism in RPE aging models, pointing to anti‐inflammatory benefits of the NAMPT/NAD⁺/SIRT1 axis (Wu et al., 2021). In the Abca1/g1 macrophage senescence model of dry AMD, NAD⁺ repletion (NMN or CD38 inhibition) eliminated senescent macrophages and reversed drusenoid pathology and RPE functional deficits, extending the anti‐senescence and anti‐inflammatory reach of NAD⁺ augmentation to subretinal immune cells central to AMD pathobiology (Terao et al., 2024).

Critically, although TFEB (a master regulator of lysosomal biogenesis) and lysosomal proteases such as cathepsin D (CTSD) are highly relevant to RPE oxidative‐debris clearance in dry AMD, the provided literature does not demonstrate direct NMN‐induced TFEB activation, lysosomal acidification, or increased CTSD activity in RPE or retina; these remain plausible but unproven links in this context set (Falcão et al., 2025; Will‐Orrego, 2020a; Ebeling et al., 2020; Cimaglia et al., 2020).

Expected Effect  
Assay-level expectations in RPE models of dry AMD  
- NAD⁺ repletion in RPE. In ARPE‐19 and primary RPE, co‐treatment with NMN restores cellular NAD⁺ reduced by NAMPT inhibition, with partial to robust recovery depending on media and dosing; in ARPE‐19, FK866 sharply lowers NAD⁺/NADH and ATP, while NMN rescues both metrics and normalizes OXPHOS/glycolysis balance measured by Seahorse assays (Will‐Orrego, 2020b, 2020c). ARPE‐19 cells express NMN but not NR transporters, predicting superior uptake and intracellular conversion for NMN in this model (Will‐Orrego, 2020b). In NaIO₃‐stressed ARPE‐19, 800–1,000 µM NMN restored NAD⁺, mitochondrial membrane potential, and ATP, reduced ROS and DNA damage, and reduced senescence markers, with Sirt1 activity required for these benefits (Ren et al., 2022).  
- Sirtuin engagement. In FK866‐inhibited RPE, NMN co‐treatment restored SIRT1 protein and activity in vitro and in vivo; in photoreceptor injury, NMN increased retinal SIRT1 and induced HO-1, suggesting a SIRT1‐dependent antioxidant arm (Jadeja et al., 2018; Chen et al., 2020). In primary AMD donor RPE, NMN improved mitochondrial function, consistent with engagement of mitochondrial sirtuins and/or PGC-1α programs, though specific sirtuin readouts were not reported in that excerpt (Ebeling et al., 2020).  
- AMPK and mitophagy. AMPK will be sensitive to changes in ATP/AMP driven by mitochondrial recovery after NMN; in RPE senescence models, AMPK activation was observed under oxidant injury and modulated by NMN, and the NAD⁺/Sirt1/AMPK network is positioned to restore mitophagy via ULK1 activation, mTORC1 attenuation, and PINK1/Parkin induction (Ren et al., 2022; Luján et al., 2022). The hypothesis that NAD⁺ supplementation restores RPE metabolic dysfunction by inducing mitophagy is supported conceptually and by limited preclinical data cited for NAD⁺ effects on RPE mitophagy, making mitophagy flux (e.g., mKeima‐mito) a reasonable expected readout under NMN treatment (Jadeja et al., 2020; Fisher et al., 2022).  
- Autophagy-lysosome system and debris clearance. TFEB governs lysosomal biogenesis and function and is a rational target in dry AMD; Sirt1 and AMPK facilitate autophagosome formation and autophagosome–lysosome fusion (Rab7) and thus could secondarily enhance lysosomal throughput after NMN (Falcão et al., 2025; Luján et al., 2022). However, direct evidence that NMN increases lysosomal number, lysosomal acidification, TFEB nuclear translocation, or CTSD activity in RPE is not provided here; these are testable but as yet unvalidated expectations (Falcão et al., 2025; Will‐Orrego, 2020a). By contrast, NMN increased RPE phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments and restored actin‐mediated phagocytic machinery in vivo in the RCS rat, revealing a complementary route by which NMN could improve outer segment turnover independent of direct TFEB activation (Zhang et al., 2024).  
- Anti‐senescence and anti‐inflammatory effects. In RPE and subretinal myeloid cells, NMN suppresses senescence phenotypes and reduces inflammatory mediators, which should reduce SASP‐driven bystander stress on RPE and photoreceptors and may indirectly lower CD38‐mediated NAD⁺ depletion in the subretinal compartment (Jadeja et al., 2018; Terao et al., 2024).

Collectively, in an RPE assay aligned to dry AMD pathophysiology, NMN is expected to: (1) restore NAD⁺ and ATP; (2) engage Sirt1/Sirt3 and normalize mitochondrial function; (3) reduce senescence and inflammatory signaling; and (4) enhance POS phagocytosis via cytoskeletal machinery, with plausible but unproven enhancement of lysosomal biogenesis/function via Sirt1/AMPK-mediated autophagy pathways and TFEB cross-talk (Will‐Orrego, 2020b; Jadeja et al., 2018; Ren et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2025; Luján et al., 2022).

Assay design notes  
- Use ARPE‐19 and primary human RPE including AMD donor–derived cultures for translational relevance; confirm NMN uptake advantages versus NR in each model (Will‐Orrego, 2020b; Ebeling et al., 2020).  
- Quantify NAD⁺ by enzymatic assay, SIRT1 activity fluorometrically, mitochondrial ATP production via Seahorse ATP rate assay, and senescence markers (SA‐β‐gal, p16, p21) per established protocols (Jadeja et al., 2018; Will‐Orrego, 2020b).  
- Test TFEB nuclear translocation (immunocytochemistry), lysosomal mass (LAMP1/2), acidification (LysoSensor/LysoTracker), and cathepsin D maturation/activity explicitly, recognizing these endpoints are not yet shown for NMN in RPE (Falcão et al., 2025).  
- Assay mitophagy flux (mKeima‐mito), PINK1/Parkin expression, and autophagosome–lysosome fusion (LC3‐II, p62, Rab7 localization) (Fisher et al., 2022; Luján et al., 2022).  
- Measure RPE phagocytosis of POS and handling of phototoxic bisretinoids/lipofuscin surrogates to capture clearance outcomes (Zhang et al., 2024).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Strong disease‐mechanism alignment. Dry AMD is characterized by RPE mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, impaired autophagy/lysosomal clearance, and chronic para‐inflammation; age‐associated NAD⁺ decline in RPE and retina connects this pathobiology to a targetable metabolic axis (NAMPT/NAD⁺), and restoring NAD⁺ is causally protective in multiple retinal models (Jadeja et al., 2018; Cimaglia et al., 2020; Lin, 2020). In vitro and in vivo, NMN replenishes NAD⁺ in RPE and retina, rescues SIRT1 and mitochondrial function, and reduces senescence and inflammation—key drivers of RPE failure in dry AMD (Jadeja et al., 2018; Ren et al., 2022; Chen et al., 2020).  
- Direct RPE benefits with functional readouts. Under NAMPT inhibition and oxidant stress, NMN restores NAD⁺/ATP, normalizes OXPHOS/glycolysis, rescues RPE gene expression, lowers ROS and DNA damage, and blunts senescence markers; in RCS rats, NMN enhances RPE POS phagocytosis through a NAD⁺/GAPDH-actin axis (Will‐Orrego, 2020c; Ren et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2024).  
- Reversal of senescence-driven dry AMD phenotypes in vivo. In the Abca1/g1 model where subretinal macrophage senescence drives SDDs and RPE dysfunction, NAD⁺ augmentation by NMN reduces SDDs, lipofuscin‐positive macrophages, and functional/structural pathology, demonstrating disease‐relevant efficacy in a model that captures hallmark dry AMD features (Terao et al., 2024).  
- Mechanistic tractability and biomarkerability. The NAMPT/NMN → NAD⁺ → sirtuin/AMPK network is well studied and offers clear pharmacodynamic biomarkers (NAD⁺ levels, SIRT1 activity, mitochondrial respiration) and pathophysiological readouts (senescence markers, mitophagy flux), supporting a high‐confidence translational path (Jadeja et al., 2018; Luján et al., 2022; Ebeling et al., 2020).  
- RPE uptake feasibility. ARPE‐19 transport NMN but not NR, favoring NMN for in vitro RPE work; broader literature identifies NMN transport and NR conversion pathways that together ensure NMN bioavailability in ocular cell types (Will‐Orrego, 2020b, 2020a).

Limitations and risks  
- TFEB/lysosome claims remain unproven for NMN in RPE. While TFEB‐driven lysosomal biogenesis/function is a compelling therapeutic target in dry AMD, direct evidence that NMN activates TFEB, increases lysosomal number/acidification, or enhances cathepsin D activity in RPE is not present in the provided literature; these are critical, testable hypotheses that should not be presupposed in development plans (Falcão et al., 2025; Will‐Orrego, 2020a; Ebeling et al., 2020; Cimaglia et al., 2020).  
- Context‐dependent AMPK/Sirt1 dynamics. In NaIO₃‐induced RPE senescence, AMPK activation accompanied ATP loss and was suppressed upon NMN treatment; further, pharmacologic Sirt1 overactivation caused mitochondrial hyperfusion and stress signaling, underscoring that pathway set points matter and that NMN’s benefits likely hinge on physiologic tuning rather than maximal activation (Ren et al., 2022). This complexity argues for careful titration of NMN exposure and for avoiding assumptions about AMPK activation being uniformly beneficial in all RPE contexts.  
- Model caveats. ARPE‐19 harbor genomic abnormalities and do not recapitulate all RPE functions (e.g., missing RPE65), and media composition strongly modulates metabolic readouts; corroboration in primary human RPE (including AMD donors) and in vivo models is essential (Will‐Orrego, 2020c; Will‐Orrego, 2020b; Ebeling et al., 2020).  
- Target competition with NAD⁺ sinks. PARPs and CD38 can drain NAD⁺; in photoreceptors and macrophages these sinks materially influence disease, suggesting that combining NMN with PARP/CD38 modulation may be superior to NMN alone in some settings, and that patient subgroups with high NAD⁺ consumption (e.g., inflammatory phenotypes) may require tailored strategies (Lin & Apte, 2018; Terao et al., 2024).  
- Translation and clinical data gaps. Although nicotinamide and NR have human safety/PK data, direct human ocular PK/PD and safety data for NMN are limited here, and no clinical testing in dry AMD is documented in the provided sources (Cimaglia et al., 2020; Rahman et al., 2024). Dosing translation must reconcile effective rodent exposures (150–1,000 mg/kg/day in various models) with human tolerability and ocular exposure (Lin, 2020; Chen et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2024).

Program implications and next steps  
- Mechanistic validation in RPE. Prioritize experiments that directly test the unproven parts of the hypothesis: TFEB activation (nuclear translocation), lysosomal biogenesis (LAMP1/2), acidification (LysoSensor), and cathepsin D maturation/activity after NMN in primary human RPE from AMD and non‐AMD donors, and in iPSC‐RPE, with parallel readouts of NAD⁺, SIRT1, SIRT3, and AMPK (Falcão et al., 2025; Ebeling et al., 2020).  
- Mitochondria–lysosome crosstalk. Quantify mitophagy flux (mKeima‐mito), autophagosome–lysosome fusion (Rab7 co‐localization), and PINK1/Parkin dynamics under NMN, leveraging assays already applied in AMD donor RPE studies (Fisher et al., 2022; Luján et al., 2022).  
- Functional clearance endpoints. Test NMN effects on RPE POS phagocytosis, lipofuscin/bisretinoid handling, and oxidative debris clearance in vitro and in vivo, building on the strong RCS rat evidence for NMN‐mediated enhancement of RPE phagocytosis via a GAPDH‐actin mechanism (Zhang et al., 2024).  
- Inflammation and senescence. Extend evaluation to subretinal macrophage phenotypes and SASP factors in RPE–macrophage co‐culture and in vivo, given NMN’s ability to eliminate senescent macrophages and reverse SDDs in the Abca1/g1 model (Terao et al., 2024).  
- Dosing/PD strategy. Calibrate NMN dose–response carefully: in ARPE‐19 and primary RPE, co‐treatment with 0.05–1.0 mM NMN rescued FK866‐induced NAD⁺ loss within 72 h, while NMN alone did not elevate ATP above baseline; in NaIO₃ ARPE‐19, 800–1,000 µM was required to adequately restore NAD⁺ (Jadeja et al., 2018; Will‐Orrego, 2020b; Ren et al., 2022). In vivo, effective rodent doses ranged from 150 mg/kg i.p. to 1,000 mg/kg oral depending on model and endpoint (Lin, 2020; Zhang et al., 2024). Engage PK/PD modeling to bridge to human‐equivalent dosing and to support ocular exposure.  
- Combination hypotheses. Consider rational combinations with PARP inhibition (to reduce NAD⁺ consumption) or CD38 inhibition in inflammatory phenotypes, consistent with partial rescue by PARP inhibitors in NAMPT‐deficient contexts and CD38’s role in macrophage senescence (Lin & Apte, 2018; Terao et al., 2024). Also consider pairing with agents that more directly activate TFEB where justified, while monitoring for unintended mTORC1 perturbations (Falcão et al., 2025).

Conclusion  
NMN is a biologically credible and mechanistically tractable candidate for dry AMD focused on RPE rescue through NAD⁺ repletion and sirtuin‐centric mitochondrial restoration, with strong preclinical support in RPE senescence, oxidant injury, and phagocytosis assays, and compelling in vivo evidence in retinal injury and senescence‐driven dry‐AMD–like pathology (Jadeja et al., 2018; Ren et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2024; Terao et al., 2024). The hypothesized downstream impacts on TFEB, lysosomal biogenesis, acidification, and cathepsin D activity are plausible given the Sirt1/AMPK/autophagy network architecture but remain unvalidated in RPE after NMN and should be explicitly de‐risked experimentally before clinical translation (Falcão et al., 2025; Luján et al., 2022; Ebeling et al., 2020). Strengths include a coherent disease‐mechanism target, measurable PD, multi‐compartment benefits (RPE, photoreceptors, subretinal macrophages), and favorable uptake in RPE models; weaknesses include reliance on models with limitations, the need to control for NAD⁺ sinks and pathway set points, and gaps in lysosome‐specific mechanistic evidence and human ocular PK/PD (Will‐Orrego, 2020b, 2020c; Lin & Apte, 2018; Rahman et al., 2024). Overall, NMN merits advancement to a rigorous preclinical validation package focused on lysosome‐mitophagy endpoints in primary human RPE and AMD‐relevant in vivo models, with a translational plan that integrates mitochondrial function, senescence/inflammation control, and debris clearance readouts as co‐primary pharmacology objectives (Ebeling et al., 2020; Fisher et al., 2022; Terao et al., 2024).
