Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
NSC19723 is presented by the team as a custom-synthesized small-molecule enhancer of cathepsin D (CTSD) activity, hypothesized to bind the zymogen (pro-CTSD) and accelerate its maturation within retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) lysosomes to restore proteolysis and debris clearance in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD). No peer-reviewed publications or preprints describing NSC19723’s structure, discovery, selectivity, or in vivo performance are present in the provided literature corpus; accordingly, this evaluation treats NSC19723 as a theoretical representative of the drug class “CTSD activity enhancers” and assesses the therapeutic hypothesis against the current substrate-specific and disease-relevant CTSD/RPE biology (Ng et al., 2024; Sharif, 2015; Liu, 2021; Buniello et al., 2025).

The stated drug class is mechanistically distinct from upstream autophagy enhancers or lysosomal pH modulators: a CTSD activity enhancer would operate at the level of CTSD protein maturation/activity, ideally in acidic lysosomes, rather than by globally raising autophagic flux or indirectly modulating lysosomal acidification (Frost et al., 2014; Boya et al., 2023; Ng et al., 2024). CTSD itself is an aspartic endoprotease synthesized as a pre-proenzyme with an N-terminal signal peptide (for ER entry) and a propeptide region that supports folding and prevents premature activity; post-translational maturation occurs in late endosomes/lysosomes after mannose-6-phosphate (M6P)-mediated trafficking, where acidic pH supports autocatalysis and protease processing to the mature, active two-chain enzyme (Sharif, 2015). The RPE expresses CTSD at high levels, with evidence for enriched CTSD protein/activity in central/macular RPE relative to periphery, consistent with the macula’s heavy daily photoreceptor outer segment (POS) phagocytic load that relies on lysosomal proteolysis (Sharif, 2015; Pay, 2017). These features nominate CTSD as a plausible therapeutic target for restoring RPE degradative capacity; however, a specific CTSD maturation enhancer such as NSC19723 has not been characterized in the provided literature, so all compound-level conclusions must remain contingent on experimental validation (Ng et al., 2024; Buniello et al., 2025).

Therapeutic History  
No published biochemical, veterinary, or clinical use of NSC19723 is documented in the provided sources, and the name does not appear in the referenced literature; consequently, there are no prior data on this molecule in dry AMD or retinal disease within the provided corpus (Buniello et al., 2025). By contrast, there is considerable disease-relevant literature on CTSD biology in RPE and on pharmacological strategies that indirectly restore CTSD function by correcting upstream lysosomal defects. In patient-derived RPE from Stargardt disease (STGD1, ABCA4 mutations), lysosomal pH is elevated, CTSD accumulates in immature forms, and CTSD proteolytic activity is reduced; pharmacologic re-acidification of lysosomes (e.g., via P2Y₁₂ antagonism with ticagrelor) reverses these defects by lowering lysosomal pH, reducing the immature pro-CTSD pool, and restoring CTSD proteolytic activity and POS degradation in vitro and in vivo (RPE cells and Abca4−/− mice) (Ng et al., 2024). While STGD1 is not AMD, these data show that CTSD maturation/activity in human RPE is drug-modifiable and that improving CTSD function can improve degradative endpoints relevant to lipofuscin-associated disease biology, a pathophysiologic axis shared with dry AMD (Ng et al., 2024; Boya et al., 2023).

In the RPE/AMD literature, multiple lines of evidence support CTSD as a major lysosomal protease necessary for POS degradation and proteostasis. CTSD deficiency or pharmacologic inhibition impairs POS proteolysis, provokes accumulation of debris reminiscent of drusen, and is linked to retinal dysfunction in animal models, reinforcing its centrality to RPE homeostasis (Mahmud, 2019). Advanced glycation end-products (AGEs), which accumulate with age and in AMD, downregulate CTSD activity or expression in RPE and exacerbate lysosomal/autophagic failure and lipofuscin formation, further tying CTSD deficits to AMD-like phenotypes (Sharif, 2015; Mahmud, 2019). More broadly, lysosomal/autophagic insufficiency in RPE is mechanistically and pathologically linked to dry AMD: decreased degradative capacity leads to lipofuscin accumulation, lysosomal membrane permeabilization (LMP), DAMP release, inflammasome activation (e.g., NLRP3), and eventual RPE atrophy that drives photoreceptor degeneration; re-acidifying lysosomes and strengthening lysosomal function ameliorate several of these pathologies in vitro and in vivo (Choi, 2019; Frost et al., 2014; Boya et al., 2023).

A second therapeutic precedent relevant to “enhancing CTSD function” is enzyme augmentation. Recombinant pro-CTSD administration has been reported to correct proteolysis and autophagy defects in neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis (CLN10/CTSD deficiency), and intravitreal enzyme replacement strategies in other lysosomal storage diseases (e.g., TPP1 in CLN2) have preserved retinal structure/function in preclinical models, supporting feasibility of increasing lysosomal enzyme function in ocular tissues (Liu, 2021). These studies, while not in AMD and not small molecules, validate the general concept that augmenting CTSD can rescue lysosomal degradative failure in retina-derived tissues.

In summary, there is no therapeutic history for NSC19723 itself in the provided sources; however, there is an increasingly robust therapeutic precedent that pharmacological manipulation which restores CTSD maturation/activity in RPE improves degradative capacity and disease-relevant readouts in lipofuscin-accumulating retinal disorders, and that enzyme augmentation of lysosomal hydrolases can be effective in ocular degenerations driven by lysosomal insufficiency (Ng et al., 2024; Liu, 2021).

Mechanism of Action  
CTSD biosynthesis and maturation provide the mechanistic backdrop for a CTSD maturation enhancer. CTSD is synthesized as pre-procathepsin D with a signal peptide (for ER translocation) and a propeptide that maintains the zymogen in an inactive, folding-competent state; the protein acquires N-linked glycans and an M6P tag in the Golgi for M6P-receptor–mediated trafficking to late endosomes/lysosomes, where acidic pH facilitates removal of the propeptide, proteolytic processing, and generation of the mature, active enzyme (heavy and light chains) (Sharif, 2015). As an aspartic protease, CTSD employs two Asp residues to activate and position a water molecule for nucleophilic attack on the scissile peptide bond, a chemistry that requires acidic conditions for optimal catalysis; in neutral or alkaline environments, activity falls sharply, explaining why lysosomal alkalinization in disease states compromises both maturation and steady-state activity (Sharif, 2015; Ng et al., 2024).

In RPE disease models, immature and intermediate CTSD forms accumulate when lysosomal pH is elevated, and total CTSD protein may paradoxically rise even as proteolytic activity falls, illustrating a maturation bottleneck rather than a transcriptional deficit; pharmacological re-acidification reduces immature CTSD, increases the mature enzyme, and restores proteolytic activity in RPE (Ng et al., 2024). Functionally, impaired CTSD maturation/activity correlates with delayed degradation of internalized POS and accumulation of aggregation-prone substrates such as α-synuclein, consistent with CTSD’s principal role in RPE proteolysis of rhodopsin and POS proteins; CTSD is reported to account for the majority of rhodopsin degradation in RPE and exhibits far higher proteolytic activity than cathepsin B against POS substrates (Ng et al., 2024). The RPE’s reliance on phagolysosomal degradation of POS and basal autophagy for proteostasis means that even partial reductions in CTSD activity can precipitate progressive accumulation of lipofuscin-like material and lysosomal residual bodies, which in turn further impair lysosomes and create a feedback loop of increasing oxidative and inflammatory stress central to dry AMD pathophysiology (Choi, 2019; Frost et al., 2014; Sharif, 2015).

The proposed mechanism for NSC19723—direct binding to pro-CTSD to accelerate maturation—aligns with the above biology and would target the specific rate-limiting step observed in RPE lysosomes under stress: conversion of immature pro-CTSD to the mature, active enzyme in the acidic lumen. If achieved without broad, off-target activation of other proteases or perturbation of lysosomal pH/ion homeostasis, this mechanism would distinguish NSC19723 from autophagy inducers (e.g., rapamycin) or pH re-acidifiers (e.g., ticagrelor), while being convergent on the same functional outcome: restored CTSD proteolysis and lysosomal degradative capacity (Frost et al., 2014; Ng et al., 2024).

Mechanistic cross-talk and constraints that are relevant for a CTSD maturation enhancer include:  
- pH dependence: CTSD maturation and catalysis require acidic lysosomes; in alkaline lysosomes (e.g., due to bisretinoid accumulation), pro-CTSD processing is impaired even if total CTSD protein increases, so a maturation accelerator may be insufficient without concurrent restoration of lysosomal pH in some disease states (Ng et al., 2024).  
- Protease networks: While CTSD is an aspartic protease, lysosomal proteases co-regulate one another’s maturation and substrate turnover; for example, denatured cathepsin L can be a substrate for CTSD, and changes in cysteine cathepsins (B/L/S) alter autophagic flux and POS degradation, implying that selective enhancement of CTSD maturation must be interpreted in the context of broader protease network homeostasis (Mahmud, 2019; Sharif, 2015).  
- Endogenous inhibitors: Cystatin C potently inhibits cysteine cathepsins (B, H, L, S) and is abundant in RPE; although it does not inhibit CTSD (aspartic protease), changes in cystatin C with age and AMD suggest that protease–inhibitor balance in the lysosome and extracellular space is dynamic and may modulate the consequences of altering one protease’s activity (Myerscough, 2015; Sharif, 2015).  
- Lysosomal membrane integrity: LMP releases cathepsins to the cytosol, where they can trigger apoptosis/inflammation; any intervention that modifies lysosomal protease activity must be vetted for unintended effects on LMP susceptibility or cytosolic protease activity under stress (Boya et al., 2023; Mahmud, 2019).  
- Extracellular exposure: RPE can secrete cathepsins; most cathepsins are inactivated at neutral pH, but acidic niches or heparan/ECM interactions can stabilize activity, raising potential off-tissue effects if a compound perturbs trafficking/secretion (Sharif, 2015).

Collectively, the mechanistic plausibility that a small molecule could stabilize a conformation of pro-CTSD that accelerates propeptide removal and activation in acidic lysosomes is strong, and a favorable on-target pharmacodynamic effect can be anchored to clearly measurable, disease-relevant biochemical endpoints in RPE (Ng et al., 2024). The key risk is that without correction of lysosomal pH, pro-CTSD processing bottlenecks may persist; therefore, a CTSD maturation enhancer may be best deployed in lysosomes that are sufficiently acidic or in combination with pH-restoring strategies (Ng et al., 2024).

Expected Effect  
Dry AMD pathophysiology features RPE lysosomal-autophagic insufficiency leading to accumulation of POS-derived material, lipofuscin, and AGEs, heightened oxidative stress, inflammasome activation, and progressive RPE atrophy; restoring lysosomal proteolysis is predicted to mitigate these processes (Choi, 2019; Frost et al., 2014; Boya et al., 2023). In RPE, CTSD is a principal protease responsible for POS/rhodopsin degradation, and its activity declines with aging and under stressors relevant to AMD (AGEs, lipids/oxidation, lysosomal alkalinization), producing immature CTSD accumulation and reduced proteolytic capacity (Mahmud, 2019; Sharif, 2015; Ng et al., 2024). Therefore, a compound that accelerates pro-CTSD maturation to increase mature CTSD abundance/activity in acidic lysosomes is expected to:

- Increase CTSD catalytic activity in RPE lysosomes, measurable by fluorogenic substrate assays and activity-based probes, with corresponding decrease in immature/intermediate CTSD species and increase in mature, active CTSD on immunoblot and imaging (Ng et al., 2024).  
- Improve rate and completeness of POS degradation in RPE pulse–chase assays (e.g., rhodopsin clearance), reduce accumulation of lysosomal residual bodies, and decrease autofluorescent lipofuscin-like material formation in POS-challenged RPE under AGE/oxidative stress conditions (Ng et al., 2024; Frost et al., 2014; Sharif, 2015).  
- Reduce intracellular burden of aggregation-prone CTSD substrates (e.g., α-synuclein) and attenuate proteostasis stress, potentially normalizing vesicle trafficking defects tied to aggregate accumulation (Ng et al., 2024).  
- Rebalance autophagic flux by removing a degradative bottleneck at the lysosome, observable as improved degradation of autophagic cargo rather than simply altered LC3 abundance; careful flux assays with lysosome–autophagosome fusion inhibitors (e.g., bafilomycin A1) should be used for interpretation (Frost et al., 2014; Sharif, 2015).  
- Decrease downstream inflammatory signaling associated with lysosomal debris accumulation, including reduced NLRP3 inflammasome activation and cytokine release during chronic stress paradigms implicated in AMD pathogenesis (Choi, 2019; Boya et al., 2023).  
- With longer-term dosing, reduce subcellular and extracellular deposit biogenesis (lipofuscin, drusen-like material), preserve RPE morphology/mitochondrial health, and sustain photoreceptor function in models where lysosomal degradation is limiting, as seen when CTSD function is restored by lysosomal re-acidification (Boya et al., 2023; Ng et al., 2024).

The target is well expressed in the cell type of interest: CTSD is abundant in RPE, enriched in central/macular RPE, and directly linked to RPE’s POS degradation function; its activity is reduced by aging and AGE exposure, both highly relevant to dry AMD (Sharif, 2015; Pay, 2017; Mahmud, 2019). In lipofuscin-associated retinal disease models, restoring lysosomal acidity to rescue CTSD maturation/activity improved RPE degradative function and reduced pathological autofluorescence, underscoring the expected benefits of directly increasing CTSD maturation/activity via a selective small molecule (Ng et al., 2024).

Experimental considerations for robust readouts in RPE:  
- Biochemical: ratio of pro-/intermediate/mature CTSD by immunoblot in lysosomal fractions; CTSD activity in intact live cells and in isolated lysosomes at matched pH; selectivity profiling against other cathepsins (B/L/S) to confirm the putative specificity reported by the team; lysosomal pH measurements to control for off-target alkalinization/acidification effects (Ng et al., 2024; Sharif, 2015).  
- Functional degradative flux: POS pulse–chase assays (rhodopsin clearance kinetics), autophagy flux assays (LC3-II, p62/SQSTM1 degradation with and without bafilomycin A1), α-synuclein aggregation/clearance; quantify autofluorescence as a proxy for lipofuscin-like material (Ng et al., 2024; Frost et al., 2014; Sharif, 2015).  
- Cell health/inflammation: LMP susceptibility (galectin-3 puncta, cytosolic cathepsin immunostaining), NLRP3 inflammasome activation (caspase-1 activity), ROS and mitochondrial integrity (Boya et al., 2023; Choi, 2019).  
- Disease relevance: verify effects in hiPSC-RPE derived from dry AMD patients, which display altered lysosomal protease processing (e.g., immature CTSD increases under oxidative stress) and increased stress susceptibility; extend to macular-enriched RPE phenotypes given regional CTSD enrichment (Voisin et al., 2019; Sharif, 2015).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Strong target–disease mechanistic rationale: CTSD is the principal lysosomal protease for RPE POS protein degradation, with reported responsibility for the majority of rhodopsin proteolysis and markedly higher activity than cathepsin B; CTSD deficiency or inhibition impairs POS degradation and produces drusen-like debris, and genetic or pharmacologic CTSD impairment causes retinal dysfunction, aligning CTSD activation with a disease-modifying mechanism in dry AMD (Ng et al., 2024; Mahmud, 2019).  
- Convergent therapeutic precedent: Restoring lysosomal pH in patient-derived and mouse RPE models rescues CTSD maturation and activity, improves POS degradation, reduces lipofuscin-like autofluorescence, and protects photoreceptors, demonstrating that enhancing CTSD function is sufficient to improve disease-relevant outcomes in lipofuscin-associated retinal pathology (Ng et al., 2024).  
- Clear, measurable pharmacodynamic biomarkers: Mature CTSD abundance, CTSD activity, lysosomal pH, POS clearance, and lipofuscin/autofluorescence changes provide a rigorous framework for early de-risking of NSC19723 and for prioritizing compound optimization (Ng et al., 2024).  
- Disease context supports target engagement benefits: RPE lysosomal dysfunction, autophagy/heterophagy deficits, lipofuscin/AGE accumulation, inflammasome activation, and progressive atrophy are central features of dry AMD; a CTSD maturation enhancer directly addresses the degradative bottleneck at the lysosome (Choi, 2019; Frost et al., 2014; Boya et al., 2023).

Risks and gaps  
- Absence of public data on NSC19723: No structural, selectivity, potency, PK/PD, ocular disposition, or toxicology data are available in the provided corpus; thus, claims of pro-CTSD binding, selectivity for CTSD over other cathepsins, and in vivo rescue in CTSD-deficient retina remain unverified by the sources provided (Buniello et al., 2025). This is the major program risk at present.  
- Lysosomal pH constraint: If lysosomal alkalinization is a primary driver of immature CTSD accumulation (as in STGD1 and arguably in stressed AMD RPE), a maturation accelerator may not overcome the pH-dependent processing barrier; efficacy may require sufficient lysosomal acidity or combination with pH-restoring interventions (Ng et al., 2024).  
- Protease network and safety considerations: Enhancing lysosomal protease activity can exacerbate LMP-driven cytotoxicity under oxidative or lipofuscin stress; careful LMP and inflammasome assessments are required, alongside confirmation that NSC19723 does not perturb trafficking/secretion to increase extracellular protease activity where pH can be locally acidic (Boya et al., 2023; Sharif, 2015).  
- Disease heterogeneity and target linkage: Although CTSD biology is compelling in RPE and in lipofuscin-associated pathology, Open Targets curates only a low-confidence literature-based association between CTSD and AMD, reflecting limited direct genetic or clinical targeting data in AMD; translational success will depend on demonstrating benefit in dry AMD–relevant human RPE models and in vivo models that recapitulate AMD’s lysosomal/autophagic deficits (Buniello et al., 2025; Inana et al., 2018; Frost et al., 2014).  
- Off-target and network effects: Crosstalk between cathepsins (e.g., CTSD processing of denatured cathepsin L, altered cathepsin L/C3/NF-κB signaling), and modulation by AGEs/oxidative stress and endogenous inhibitors necessitate comprehensive off-target profiling and immune readouts to ensure that CTSD-specific maturation enhancement does not dysregulate broader proteostasis/inflammatory networks in RPE or at the RPE–Bruch’s membrane (BrM) interface (Sharif, 2015; Mahmud, 2019).

Program implications and recommended next steps  
Given the robust mechanistic case for CTSD restoration in RPE and the successful pharmacologic rescue of CTSD maturation/activity via lysosomal re-acidification in human patient–derived RPE, a selective CTSD maturation enhancer is a rational, high-potential approach for dry AMD—provided the compound is real, selective, and effective in acidic lysosomes (Ng et al., 2024). To advance NSC19723, the following de-risking package is critical:  

- Biochemical validation: Demonstrate pro-CTSD binding and acceleration of maturation at acidic pH using purified pro-CTSD and lysosomal-mimetic conditions; quantify catalytic activation and processing kinetics; confirm no activation or inhibition of cathepsins B/L/S and other lysosomal hydrolases (Sharif, 2015).  
- Cellular validation in RPE: In primary human RPE/hiPSC-RPE (including dry AMD lines), show increased mature CTSD and activity without altering lysosomal pH, improved POS degradation and reduced autofluorescence under chronic POS/AGE stress, restored clearance of α-synuclein aggregates, and normalization of autophagic flux using proper flux assays (Frost et al., 2014; Ng et al., 2024; Sharif, 2015).  
- Safety pharmacology in RPE: Demonstrate no increase in LMP susceptibility or NLRP3 activation under oxidative/bisretinoid stress; characterize secretion/trafficking effects and exclude extracellular protease activation under BrM-like conditions (Boya et al., 2023; Sharif, 2015).  
- In vivo proof of concept: In models featuring RPE lysosomal dysfunction and lipofuscin burden, measure retinal/RPE CTSD maturation/activity, RPE autofluorescence, drusen-like material, photoreceptor survival, and visual function; compare with or add to pH-reacidifying strategies (Ng et al., 2024).

Overall, while a CTSD maturation enhancer is scientifically well grounded for RPE-centered degenerations and could represent a differentiated, direct-restoration modality versus pH modulators or broad autophagy inducers, the current file lacks any external validation for NSC19723. Progressing NSC19723 is justified only with rapid, rigorous confirmation of selectivity, on-target activity in RPE lysosomes, and favorable safety in stressed RPE systems that model dry AMD’s lysosomal/autophagic failure (Frost et al., 2014; Boya et al., 2023; Choi, 2019).

In summary, the therapeutic concept—enhancing CTSD maturation/activity to restore RPE lysosomal proteolysis—has high mechanistic plausibility and encouraging precedent from pharmacologic re-acidification studies, but the specific candidate NSC19723 remains unsubstantiated in the provided literature and requires foundational biochemical and cellular validation to warrant preclinical development in dry AMD (Ng et al., 2024; Buniello et al., 2025).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Torin1 is a synthetic small‐molecule that belongs to the second‐generation, ATP‐competitive class of mTOR inhibitors, originally derived from a quinoline‐based scaffold. Its discovery originated from a high‐throughput compound library screen that identified quinolone hits with moderate mTOR activity, which were then optimized through iterative medicinal chemistry by introducing a six‐membered lactam to convert the initial quinolone into a tricyclic benzonaphthridinone scaffold (Guillem, 2015). This chemical modification yielded a molecule with exceptional biochemical potency—capable of inhibiting both mTOR complexes, mTORC1 and mTORC2, at very low (nanomolar to picomolar) concentrations—and with approximately 1000-fold improvement in cellular potency relative to the initial hits (Guillem, 2015). As an ATP-competitive inhibitor, Torin1 binds directly to the active (ATP-binding) site of mTOR, thereby circumventing the partial inhibition that is observed with first-generation mTOR inhibitors like rapamycin that act allosterically by binding FKBP12 (Liu et al., 2012). Torin1 has been widely used as a research tool to interrogate mTOR signaling in various cellular contexts, and its chemical lineage as a quinoline-derived molecule positions it within a well-characterized class of inhibitors that have been instrumental in expanding our understanding of mTOR-dependent regulation of autophagy and cellular metabolism (Liu et al., 2012).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, Torin1 has been employed predominantly as a research tool rather than as a clinical drug candidate. Extensive preclinical studies have demonstrated its robust ability to inhibit mTOR signaling in cancer models, autophagy-deficient systems, and metabolic studies. For instance, Torin1 was shown to potently inhibit mTOR signaling pathways in glioblastoma and prostate cancer cells, significantly reducing cell-cycle progression and inducing apoptosis in certain contexts (Gu, 2017; Liu et al., 2012). Its use as an autophagy inducer is well documented, as experiments utilizing Torin1 have demonstrated increased autophagic flux and elevated lysosomal activity in multiple cell lines (Li, 2018; Liu et al., 2012). Importantly, Torin1 is also used in studies with retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells, as evidenced by its ability to increase TFEB-driven luciferase reporter activity in ARPE-19 cells by effectively suppressing mTORC1 signaling (Huang et al., 2018). Despite these promising experimental findings, Torin1 has not advanced to clinical trials for any indication, including neurodegenerative disorders or dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD). Moreover, its intrinsic pharmacokinetic limitations—such as poor aqueous solubility, a short half-life, and low oral bioavailability—have been recognized in several studies, thereby limiting its potential as a direct therapeutic candidate without further structural optimization (Guillem, 2015; Wang et al., 2022).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, Torin1 functions by competing with ATP for binding to the catalytic domain of mTOR, effectively blocking the phosphorylation of downstream substrates. Its ATP-competitive nature allows Torin1 to inhibit both mTORC1 and mTORC2 complexes, thereby offering a broader inhibition profile than allosteric agents like rapamycin that primarily target mTORC1 (Guillem, 2015; Liu et al., 2012). Detailed molecular modeling and structure–activity relationship studies indicate that the tricyclic benzonaphthridinone core of Torin1 forms critical hinge-binding interactions with residues in the mTOR kinase domain (Liu et al., 2012). This interaction accounts for its high potency, as reflected in low nanomolar IC₅₀ values in cellular assays (Liu et al., 2012; Gros & Muller, 2014). Torin1 induces rapid dephosphorylation of canonical mTORC1 substrates, such as S6 kinase at Thr389 and 4E-BP1 at Thr37/46, which results in downregulation of protein synthesis and cellular growth signals (Misra & Pizzo, 2013). Moreover, by simultaneously inhibiting mTORC2, it reduces phosphorylation of Akt at Ser473—a site critical for full Akt activation—thus attenuating the feedback loops that typically reinvigorate upstream PI3K signaling in response to mTORC1 inhibition (Gu, 2017; Martina et al., 2014). A particularly notable feature of Torin1 is its slow off-rate, which leads to sustained inhibition of mTOR activity even after drug washout, a pharmacodynamic property that may confer prolonged downstream effects such as enhanced autophagic flux (Liu et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2013). The inhibition of mTOR by Torin1 correlates with dephosphorylation of transcription factors, particularly TFEB and TFE3; under normal nutrient-replete conditions, mTORC1 phosphorylates TFEB (e.g., on S211 in TFEB) and TFE3, sequestering them in the cytosol through binding with 14-3-3 proteins (Huang et al., 2018; Martina et al., 2014). Upon mTOR inhibition by Torin1, TFEB is dephosphorylated and translocates to the nucleus, where it induces the transcription of CLEAR (Coordinated Lysosomal Expression and Regulation) network genes that drive lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy (Li, 2018; Liu et al., 2013). This precise modulation of mTOR signaling and subsequent transcriptional reprogramming forms the biochemical basis for leveraging Torin1 as a candidate to ameliorate lysosomal clearance defects.

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis for repurposing Torin1 in the context of dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is that potent inhibition of mTORC1/2 in RPE cells can lift the repressive phosphorylation that normally limits the activity of TFEB and TFE3. In RPE cells, as demonstrated by studies in ARPE-19 cell models, mTOR inhibition via Torin1 not only leads to decreased phosphorylation of S6 kinase but also results in marked activation of TFEB-driven transcription (Huang et al., 2018). When TFEB translocates to the nucleus, it binds to CLEAR elements present in the promoters of genes responsible for lysosomal biogenesis, acidification (through the upregulation of V-ATPase subunits), and the maturation and activity of lysosomal enzymes such as cathepsin D (CTSD) (Huang et al., 2018; Li, 2018). In dry AMD, RPE cells exhibit a decline in lysosomal function along with accumulation of cellular debris and lipofuscin, which contribute to disease pathology. By inducing a robust CLEAR response, Torin1 is expected to restore lysosomal function through increased biogenesis, enhanced acidification, and elevated cathepsin D activity, thereby improving the clearance of toxic aggregates in RPE cells and ultimately mitigating the progression of dry AMD (Gu, 2017; Huang et al., 2018). Additionally, the sustained target engagement afforded by Torin1’s slow off-rate may provide prolonged therapeutic benefit even with intermittent dosing, an attractive feature given the chronic nature of AMD (Liu et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2013). Recent evidence from preclinical iPSC models and autophagy-deficiency studies underscores the potential translation of mTOR-targeted strategies in restoring cellular homeostasis in degenerative diseases, lending further credence to this expected mechanism (Guillem, 2015).

Overall Evaluation:  
In summary, Torin1 possesses a compelling mechanistic profile that aligns well with the therapeutic needs of dry AMD by targeting a fundamental pathway governing cellular homeostasis in RPE cells. Its origin from a quinoline-based scaffold and subsequent chemical optimization into a highly potent ATP-competitive mTOR inhibitor underline its status as a valuable chemical probe in preclinical settings (Guillem, 2015). The dual inhibition of both mTORC1 and mTORC2 by Torin1, combined with its slow off-rate and sustained downstream effects—including dephosphorylation and nuclear translocation of TFEB/TFE3—make it an ideal tool for inducing lysosomal biogenesis and enhancing autophagic clearance (Martina et al., 2014; Huang et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2012). In cellular models, including ARPE-19 RPE cells, Torin1 has already demonstrated the ability to activate TFEB and upregulate CLEAR gene expression, which is directly relevant to counteracting the lysosomal clearance defects observed in dry AMD (Huang et al., 2018; Li, 2018).

However, significant challenges remain regarding the translational applicability of Torin1 as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. Its reported poor aqueous solubility, short half-life, and low oral bioavailability present formidable barriers to clinical development unless addressed through formulation improvements or further medicinal chemistry optimization (Guillem, 2015; Wang et al., 2022). Moreover, while extensive preclinical literature supports its role as a robust mTOR inhibitor in cancer and autophagy research, there is a lack of direct in vivo evidence for its efficacy in ocular models, particularly in dry AMD or geographic atrophy (GA) mouse lines (Liu et al., 2013; Gu, 2017). Careful dosing will also be critical, as the broad and potent inhibition of mTOR can have unintended effects on cellular metabolism and protein synthesis beyond the intended enhancement of lysosomal function. Additionally, off-target effects have been observed in some biochemical screens at supraphysiologic concentrations, including binding to other PIKK family members such as ATR, ATM, and DNA-PK, although these are generally not manifested at the low nanomolar concentrations used in cellular assays (Settembre et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2012).

From the perspective of repurposing for dry AMD, Torin1’s deep mechanistic specificity is a double-edged sword: it offers a highly defined and robust approach to upregulating lysosomal biogenesis via the TFEB/TFE3 axis, yet its pharmacokinetic liabilities and the absence of any clinical history in ocular disease necessitate additional work. The promising in vitro data in RPE models (ARPE-19 cells) and iPSC-derived RPE systems provide valuable target validation, but before advancing to clinical trials a refined analog or an optimized delivery method (for example, local ocular administration to bypass systemic bioavailability issues) should be considered (Huang et al., 2018; Li, 2018; Wang et al., 2022).

In summary, Torin1 is an excellent candidate for preclinical proof-of-concept studies to validate mTOR inhibition as a strategy to combat lysosomal dysfunction in dry AMD; however, further optimization to improve its stability and bioavailability, alongside rigorous in vivo testing in relevant AMD models, will be essential prior to clinical development (Guillem, 2015; Gu, 2017). The strengths of Torin1 lie in its potent, dual mTOR inhibition and its ability to robustly induce TFEB activation, whereas its weaknesses center on its pharmacokinetic shortcomings and the current lack of efficacy data in ocular disease models. Overall, with focused optimization and targeted delivery strategies, Torin1 or its derivatives may offer a promising therapeutic avenue for ameliorating the lysosomal clearance defects that underlie dry AMD pathology (Liu et al., 2012; Huang et al., 2018).

Below is our comprehensive evaluation of VX-765 (Belnacasan; Selleckchem S2731) as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
VX-765 is an orally bioavailable small‐molecule agent belonging to the caspase-1 inhibitor class. It is a synthetically derived peptidomimetic prodrug that, once metabolized, yields an active derivative capable of selectively binding to and inhibiting caspase-1. Originally developed by Vertex Pharmaceuticals, VX-765 was designed to address the shortcomings of earlier peptide-based caspase inhibitors by improving bioavailability, stability, and selectivity. As a caspase-1 inhibitor, it falls within a broader category of agents that have been used to blunt excessive inflammasome responses in various inflammatory and immune-mediated conditions. In the context of drug discovery, caspase-1 inhibitors have been of keen interest because caspase-1 is the key enzyme responsible for converting pro-IL-1β and pro-IL-18 into their active cytokine forms, thereby playing a central role in mediating inflammation and the programmed cell death process known as pyroptosis. VX-765 has been evaluated primarily in systemic inflammatory and cardiovascular settings, where its favorable pharmacokinetic profile and excellent oral bioavailability have been demonstrated (Audia et al., 2018; MacKenzie & Schipper, 2010).

Therapeutic History:  
The therapeutic history of VX-765 underscores its extensive preclinical development and early clinical evaluation in several inflammatory settings. In preclinical cardiovascular models, for instance, VX-765 demonstrated significant cardioprotection when administered during reperfusion, reducing infarct size and preserving mitochondrial enzyme activities (Audia et al., 2018). It has undergone Phase I and Phase II clinical studies—its Phase II safety data indicate that it is well tolerated at doses that achieve a suppression of proinflammatory cytokines in plasma (MacKenzie & Schipper, 2010). Although the major clinical investigations with VX-765 have focused on disorders such as epilepsy and other inflammatory diseases rather than ophthalmic disorders, the rationale for its use in dry AMD stems from overlapping inflammatory mechanisms. Specifically, dry AMD shares underlying pathological processes such as chronic inflammation, oxidative stress, and lysosomal dysfunction in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells. Prior experimental studies in RPE models using caspase-1 inhibitors like Z-YVAD-FMK have demonstrated that inhibiting caspase-1 activity reduces IL-1β release and can influence cell death pathways (Brandstetter, 2016; Tseng et al., 2013). However, despite this promising mechanistic background, VX-765 itself has not yet been directly evaluated in preclinical models of dry AMD or in similar ocular diseases. This gap in ophthalmic precedent is notable, but given its established safety profile in nonocular clinical settings and robust anti-inflammatory activity, VX-765 remains an attractive candidate for repurposing into the dry AMD arena (Audia et al., 2018; MacKenzie & Schipper, 2010).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, VX-765 exerts its effect primarily through selective inhibition of caspase-1, a cysteine protease critically involved in the processing of pro-inflammatory cytokines. Under conditions of cellular stress—such as those occurring in RPE cells in response to lipofuscin accumulation and photooxidative damage—lysosomal destabilization can occur. This lysosomal membrane permeabilization (LMP) leads to the release of cathepsins and other proteases into the cytosol, which, in turn, can serve as an activator of the NLRP3 inflammasome. Once assembled, the inflammasome facilitates the autocatalytic cleavage of caspase-1 into its active p10/p20 subunits, thereby enabling it to convert pro-IL-1β and pro-IL-18 into their mature, secreted forms. VX-765 binds to the active site of caspase-1, thereby preventing this proteolytic cleavage and subsequent cytokine release. This action not only blunts the inflammatory cascade but, by inhibiting caspase-1–dependent processing, may also prevent the activation of gasdermin-D (GSDMD) which is responsible for forming membrane pores during pyroptosis (Brandstetter, 2016; Tseng et al., 2013).

The hypothesis for using VX-765 in dry AMD is that inhibition of caspase-1 will disrupt a pathological amplification loop. In RPE cells exposed to chronic oxidative stress and lipofuscin-related photooxidative damage, inflammasome activation has been shown to promote rapid pyroptotic cell death rather than a slower apoptotic process. This results in an autocrine/paracrine loop where secreted IL-1β further primes neighboring cells for inflammasome activation, exacerbating cell death and causing tissue dysfunction. By blocking caspase-1 activity, VX-765 is expected to prevent this destructive cascade, thereby preserving lysosomal function. More specifically, there is a hypothesized link between caspase-1 activity and alterations in lysosomal integrity—a process involving LMP that is associated with a loss of vacuolar (V-) ATPase activity and disturbances in cathepsin D maturation. The V-ATPase is critical for maintaining an acidic lysosomal environment necessary for optimal enzyme activity, including that of cathepsin D, which is involved in the degradation of photoreceptor outer segments. Some studies have shown that under conditions of inflammasome activation, RPE cells demonstrate not only an increase in cytokine secretion but also a decline in the functionality of lysosomal hydrolases, which may further compromise cell viability (Brandstetter, 2016). Although direct evidence linking VX-765 to the preservation of V-ATPase activity or cathepsin D function in RPE is currently lacking, the mechanistic framework provided by previous studies using other caspase-1 inhibitors supports the notion that caspase-1 blockade may confer lysosomal protection and attenuate pyroptotic RPE death (Brandstetter, 2016; Tseng et al., 2013).

Expected Effect:  
In the proposed in vitro and in vivo assays, VX-765 is expected to reduce the levels of active caspase-1 and consequently diminish the secretion of IL-1β and IL-18 from RPE cells stressed by inflammatory stimuli such as lipofuscin photooxidative damage. In validated ARPE-19 cell models that mimic the conditions of dry AMD—where priming with IL-1α and subsequent exposure to lysosomal stressors (for example, the photooxidative effects of lipofuscin components) lead to inflammasome activation and rapid pyroptotic cell death—treatment with caspase-1 inhibitors has been shown to reduce cell lysis and cytokine release (Brandstetter, 2016; Tseng et al., 2013). By extrapolation, VX-765 should produce similar results. Endpoints for such studies might include decreased levels of IL-1β and IL-18 measured by ELISA, preservation of cell viability as determined by metabolic assays (such as MTT or LDH assays), and a reduction in markers of pyroptosis including the cleavage of GSDMD.

Furthermore, because the hypothesis posits that caspase-1 activity contributes to inflammasome‐mediated lysosomal membrane permeabilization, VX-765 is anticipated to stabilize lysosomal integrity. This stabilization should help maintain the acid–base balance within lysosomes—reflected by sustained V-ATPase activity—which is critical for the proper maturation and function of cathepsin D. In healthy RPE cells, cathepsin D is a major lysosomal protease responsible for degrading photoreceptor outer segment debris. In the context of dry AMD, a decline in cathepsin D activity may contribute to the accumulation of undegraded material, exacerbating cellular stress and death. Although direct measurements of V-ATPase activity and cathepsin D maturation following VX-765 treatment have not yet been published, the overall expectation is that by interrupting the caspase-1–driven inflammatory signaling cascade, VX-765 can prevent the deleterious loss of lysosomal function and thereby reduce RPE cell death (Brandstetter, 2016; Gao et al., 2019; Tseng et al., 2013).

Additionally, in in vivo models of AMD (for example, those induced by Aβ₁₋₄₀ or other drusen mimetics), the inhibition of caspase-1 should theoretically reduce the incidence or severity of geographic atrophy by preserving RPE structure and function. This is of particular interest given that RPE degeneration is a critical event in the progression of dry AMD. Markers of efficacy would include improved retinal morphology on OCT imaging, better electrophysiological responses (as measured by ERG), and a decrease in inflammatory cellular infiltrates. Collectively, these anticipated outcomes support the hypothesis that VX-765’s inhibition of caspase-1 may interrupt the cascade of inflammasome activation, LMP, and lysosomal enzyme failure that leads to RPE death in dry AMD (Brandstetter, 2016; Tseng et al., 2013).

Overall Evaluation:  
Our overall evaluation of VX-765 as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD is cautiously optimistic but recognizes several critical hurdles. One of the major strengths of VX-765 is its well-characterized mechanism of action as a selective caspase-1 inhibitor, along with its demonstrated anti-inflammatory effects in non-ocular preclinical models. The clinical safety profile established in Phase I and II studies—particularly its ability to reduce circulating pro-inflammatory cytokines—lends support to its potential use in a chronic disease setting such as dry AMD (Audia et al., 2018; MacKenzie & Schipper, 2010). From a mechanistic standpoint, the centrality of caspase-1 in mediating inflammasome-driven cytokine maturation and pyroptosis is well established, and there is compelling evidence from RPE cell models that caspase-1 inhibition can reduce IL-1β secretion and potentially modify cell death pathways (Brandstetter, 2016; Tseng et al., 2013). These observations provide a strong rationale for the hypothesis that VX-765 could prevent the lysosomal destabilization and subsequent inflammatory cascade responsible for RPE degeneration.

However, there are also several weaknesses and gaps that must be addressed before VX-765 can be fully endorsed for dry AMD. Although the mechanistic data support the role of caspase-1 inhibition in reducing inflammatory cytokine release and possibly preserving lysosomal function, there is currently no direct evidence that VX-765 can stabilize lysosomal membrane integrity, preserve V-ATPase activity, or maintain proper cathepsin D function specifically in RPE cells. Most of the available literature has utilized generic caspase-1 inhibitors such as Z-YVAD-FMK as proof-of-principle tools rather than VX-765 itself in ocular models (Brandstetter, 2016; Tseng et al., 2013). Furthermore, although numerous studies have demonstrated that inflammasome activation and caspase-1–dependent pyroptosis are features of RPE injury in vitro and in some in vivo models of dry AMD, the translation of these findings into effective therapies has proven challenging. The eye’s unique anatomy and the need for adequate drug delivery to the retina raise additional concerns. For an orally administered agent like VX-765, it is not yet clear whether systemic dosing can achieve therapeutically relevant concentrations in the RPE, or whether intravitreal or alternative delivery methods would be necessary.

Another potential weakness lies in the multifactorial nature of dry AMD. In addition to inflammasome activation and lysosomal dysfunction, dry AMD pathogenesis involves complement dysregulation, oxidative stress, impaired autophagy, and other pro-inflammatory pathways. It remains possible that targeting caspase-1 alone may not be sufficient to arrest disease progression, and a combination approach might be necessary. Moreover, previous caspase inhibitor candidates (for example, pralnacasan) have encountered issues with liver toxicity or other off-target effects in long-term studies, raising concerns about the safety of chronic caspase-1 inhibition (MacKenzie & Schipper, 2010). These potential challenges underscore the need for rigorous preclinical studies in relevant dry AMD models that not only assess the anti-inflammatory and anti-pyroptotic effects of VX-765 but also directly measure lysosomal functional parameters such as V-ATPase activity and cathepsin D maturation.

In summary, while VX-765 offers a promising and mechanistically coherent approach to perturbing the detrimental caspase-1–mediated signaling cascade implicated in RPE degeneration, significant gaps remain in linking its action to improved lysosomal function and reduced RPE death in the specific context of dry AMD. The strengths of VX-765 include its established safety data, oral bioavailability, and selective inhibition of a central inflammatory enzyme; however, its application to AMD is currently supported only by indirect evidence extrapolated from non-ocular models and generic caspase-1 inhibitor studies (Audia et al., 2018; Brandstetter, 2016; MacKenzie & Schipper, 2010; Tseng et al., 2013). To move this candidate forward, we recommend that targeted preclinical studies be undertaken in sight-relevant in vitro systems (e.g., ARPE-19 or primary human RPE models) and in vivo models of dry AMD to assess whether VX-765 can indeed prevent or reverse lysosomal membrane permeabilization, sustain V-ATPase activity, and preserve cathepsin D function, in addition to reducing downstream cytokine release and pyroptotic cell death. Only with such data can we determine whether VX-765 holds true promise as a therapeutic for dry AMD.

Overall, while VX-765 has scientifically robust credentials as a caspase-1 inhibitor with proven anti-inflammatory potential in other systems, its repurposing for dry AMD will depend on demonstrating that its molecular actions translate into preservation of RPE function and structure in ocular models. The candidate is promising, but further focused studies are needed to address drug delivery, ocular pharmacokinetics, and the precise impact on lysosomal pathways within the RPE before clinical translation can be considered (Audia et al., 2018; Brandstetter, 2016; MacKenzie & Schipper, 2010; Tseng et al., 2013).

Fenofibrate itself is a prodrug that undergoes hepatic esterase hydrolysis to form its active metabolite, fenofibric acid, which binds to PPARα and modulates the transcription of genes involved in lipid metabolism. Fenofibrate has a robust clinical history in the management of dyslipidemia and cardiovascular risk reduction, with extensive use in millions of patients worldwide. While the majority of these ocular studies have focused on diabetic retinopathy or neovascular AMD, emerging literature has pointed to the potential of targeting PPARα signaling to mitigate RPE dysfunction and lipid accumulation, which are hallmarks of dry AMD (da Ana et al., 2023; Dou & Duerfeldt, 2020). This history of fenofibrate in retinal disease, combined with its proven clinical safety for dyslipidemia and established ocular pharmacokinetics (including studies on topical delivery), provides a compelling rationale for its repurposing in dry AMD (Tomita et al., 2020; Lee et al., 2021).

Mechanism of Action:  
Fenofibrate’s mechanism of action is rooted in its role as a PPARα agonist. Upon conversion to fenofibric acid, the compound binds to PPARα—a nuclear receptor highly expressed in several tissues, including the liver and the retinal pigment epithelium. When activated, PPARα forms heterodimers with retinoid X receptors (RXR) and binds to peroxisome proliferator response elements (PPREs) within the promoters of target genes. This binding results in the upregulation of genes critical for fatty acid uptake, β-oxidation, and lipid catabolism. Key genes regulated by PPARα include those encoding enzymes that facilitate mitochondrial and peroxisomal fatty acid oxidation, which in turn reduces intracellular lipid accumulation and promotes energy homeostasis (Fu et al., 2019; Lee et al., 2023).

One of the central tenets of the proposed mechanism is the coactivation of transcription factor EB (TFEB). TFEB is recognized as a master regulator of lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy through the coordinated lysosomal expression and regulation (CLEAR) network. Under normal conditions, TFEB is kept inactive in the cytosol by phosphorylation mediated by mTORC1. Under stress conditions or when lysosomal function is impaired, TFEB translocates to the nucleus to upregulate genes involved in lysosomal acidification, autophagy, and lipid metabolism. The therapeutic hypothesis posits that fenofibrate, through PPARα activation in RPE cells, will indirectly coactivate TFEB. Torin1 induces rapid dephosphorylation of canonical mTORC1 substrates, such as S6 kinase at Thr389 and 4E-BP1 at Thr37/46, which results in downregulation of protein synthesis and cellular growth signals (Misra & Pizzo, 2013). Moreover, by simultaneously inhibiting mTORC2, it reduces phosphorylation of Akt at Ser473—a site critical for full Akt activation—thus attenuating the feedback loops that typically reinvigorate upstream PI3K signaling in response to mTORC1 inhibition (Gu, 2017; Martina et al., 2014). A particularly notable feature of Torin1 is its slow off-rate, which leads to sustained inhibition of mTOR activity even after drug washout, a pharmacodynamic property that may confer prolonged downstream effects such as enhanced autophagic flux (Liu et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2013). The inhibition of mTOR by Torin1 correlates with dephosphorylation of transcription factors, particularly TFEB and TFE3; under normal nutrient-replete conditions, mTORC1 phosphorylates TFEB (e.g., on S211 in TFEB) and TFE3, sequestering them in the cytosol through binding with 14-3-3 proteins (Huang et al., 2018; Martina et al., 2014). Upon mTOR inhibition by Torin1, TFEB is dephosphorylated and translocates to the nucleus, where it induces the transcription of CLEAR (Coordinated Lysosomal Expression and Regulation) network genes that drive lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy (Li, 2018; Liu et al., 2013). This precise modulation of mTOR signaling and subsequent transcriptional reprogramming forms the biochemical basis for leveraging Torin1 as a candidate to ameliorate lysosomal clearance defects.

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis for repurposing Torin1 in the context of dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is that potent inhibition of mTORC1/2 in RPE cells can lift the repressive phosphorylation that normally limits the activity of TFEB and TFE3. In RPE cells, as demonstrated by studies in ARPE-19 cell models, mTOR inhibition via Torin1 not only leads to decreased phosphorylation of S6 kinase but also results in marked activation of TFEB-driven transcription (Huang et al., 2018). When TFEB translocates to the nucleus, it binds to CLEAR elements present in the promoters of genes responsible for lysosomal biogenesis, acidification (through the upregulation of V-ATPase subunits), and the maturation and activity of lysosomal enzymes such as cathepsin D (CTSD) (Huang et al., 2018; Li, 2018). In dry AMD, RPE cells exhibit a decline in lysosomal function along with accumulation of cellular debris and lipofuscin, which contribute to disease pathology. By inducing a robust CLEAR response, Torin1 is expected to restore lysosomal function through increased biogenesis, enhanced acidification, and elevated cathepsin D activity, thereby improving the clearance of toxic aggregates in RPE cells and ultimately mitigating the progression of dry AMD (Gu, 2017; Huang et al., 2018). Additionally, the sustained target engagement afforded by Torin1’s slow off-rate may provide prolonged therapeutic benefit even with intermittent dosing, an attractive feature given the chronic nature of AMD (Liu et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2013). Recent evidence from preclinical iPSC models and autophagy-deficiency studies underscores the potential translation of mTOR-targeted strategies in restoring cellular homeostasis in degenerative diseases, lending further credence to this expected mechanism (Guillem, 2015).

Overall Evaluation:  
In summary, Torin1 possesses a compelling mechanistic profile that aligns well with the therapeutic needs of dry AMD by targeting a fundamental pathway governing cellular homeostasis in RPE cells. Its origin from a quinoline-based scaffold and subsequent chemical optimization into a highly potent ATP-competitive mTOR inhibitor underline its status as a valuable chemical probe in preclinical settings (Guillem, 2015). The dual inhibition of both mTORC1 and mTORC2 by Torin1, combined with its slow off-rate and sustained downstream effects—including dephosphorylation and nuclear translocation of TFEB/TFE3—make it an ideal tool for inducing lysosomal biogenesis and enhancing autophagic clearance (Martina et al., 2014; Huang et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2012). In cellular models, including ARPE-19 RPE cells, Torin1 has already demonstrated the ability to activate TFEB and upregulate CLEAR gene expression, which is directly relevant to counteracting the lysosomal clearance defects observed in dry AMD (Huang et al., 2018; Li, 2018).

However, significant challenges remain regarding the translational applicability of Torin1 as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. Its reported poor aqueous solubility, short half-life, and low oral bioavailability present formidable barriers to clinical development unless addressed through formulation improvements or further medicinal chemistry optimization (Guillem, 2015; Wang et al., 2022). Moreover, while extensive preclinical literature supports its role as a robust mTOR inhibitor in cancer and autophagy research, there is a lack of direct in vivo evidence for its efficacy in ocular models, particularly in dry AMD or geographic atrophy (GA) mouse lines (Liu et al., 2013; Gu, 2017). Careful dosing will also be critical, as the broad and potent inhibition of mTOR can have unintended effects on cellular metabolism and protein synthesis beyond the intended enhancement of lysosomal function. Additionally, off-target effects have been observed in some biochemical screens at supraphysiologic concentrations, including binding to other PIKK family members such as ATR, ATM, and DNA-PK, although these are generally not manifested at the low nanomolar concentrations used in cellular assays (Settembre et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2012).

From the perspective of repurposing for dry AMD, Torin1’s deep mechanistic specificity is a double-edged sword: it offers a highly defined and robust approach to upregulating lysosomal biogenesis via the TFEB/TFE3 axis, yet its pharmacokinetic liabilities and the absence of any clinical history in ocular disease necessitate additional work. The promising in vitro data in RPE models (ARPE-19 cells) and iPSC-derived RPE systems provide valuable target validation, but before advancing to clinical trials a refined analog or an optimized delivery method (for example, local ocular administration to bypass systemic bioavailability issues) should be considered (Huang et al., 2018; Li, 2018; Wang et al., 2022).

In summary, Torin1 is an excellent candidate for preclinical proof-of-concept studies to validate mTOR inhibition as a strategy to combat lysosomal dysfunction in dry AMD; however, further optimization to improve its stability and bioavailability, alongside rigorous in vivo testing in relevant AMD models, will be essential prior to clinical development (Guillem, 2015; Gu, 2017). The strengths of Torin1 lie in its potent, dual mTOR inhibition and its ability to robustly induce TFEB activation, whereas its weaknesses center on its pharmacokinetic shortcomings and the current lack of efficacy data in ocular disease models. Overall, with focused optimization and targeted delivery strategies, Torin1 or its derivatives may offer a promising therapeutic avenue for ameliorating the lysosomal clearance defects that underlie dry AMD pathology (Liu et al., 2012; Huang et al., 2018).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Sulforaphane (SFN) is a naturally occurring isothiocyanate derived from glucoraphanin in cruciferous vegetables via myrosinase-mediated hydrolysis; as an electrophilic small molecule, SFN was identified through its unusually potent induction of phase II detoxification enzymes and antioxidant defenses in mammalian tissues via the KEAP1–NFE2L2/NRF2 stress-response axis (classically termed “phase 2 induction”) (Qin, 2007; Hyttinen et al., 2019). Isothiocyanates and related electrophiles covalently modify reactive cysteine residues on KEAP1, disrupting the KEAP1–NRF2 “hinge-and-latch” ubiquitin ligase complex and stabilizing NRF2 to drive ARE-dependent transcription of cytoprotective enzymes including NQO1, GCLM, HO-1, and glutathione pathway genes (Hyttinen et al., 2019; Qin, 2007). Beyond canonical NRF2 activation, SFN is now recognized to engage lysosome-centered adaptive transcription by inducing nuclear translocation and activation of TFEB/TFE3 through a mild, ROS-triggered Ca²⁺–calcineurin pathway that is largely MTOR-independent, thereby upregulating CLEAR-network genes controlling lysosome and autophagy biogenesis (Li et al., 2021). In ocular contexts, SFN has been used experimentally as a cytoprotective agent in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) models subjected to oxidative or phototoxic stress, and as a modulator of autophagy markers, situating SFN within a dual-modality class that can activate antioxidant defenses and augment lysosome-autophagy function (Yang et al., 2021; Li et al., 2021).

Therapeutic History  
SFN and other NRF2 activators have been widely studied as cytoprotective chemopreventive agents and as protectants in oxidative-stress paradigms across tissues; in RPE models, SFN has repeatedly demonstrated NRF2-dependent protection and modulation of stress and quality-control pathways, although direct clinical testing in dry AMD is not reported in the provided literature (Qin, 2007; Liu et al., 2016). In ARPE-19 cells exposed to blue light, SFN promoted NRF2 nuclear translocation, induced HO-1 and glutathione production, reduced oxidative stress and inflammation, and its cytoprotective effect was blocked by the NRF2 inhibitor ML385, indicating a mechanistic dependence on NRF2; SFN also increased LC3B-II and p62, and the autophagy inhibitor 3-MA blunted its protective action, linking SFN’s benefit to autophagy engagement in this RPE stress model (Yang et al., 2021). In a separate ARPE-19 inflammatory model (TGF-β), SFN (alone or combined with vitamin D) lowered ROS and VEGF and restored epithelial junction markers; in that system, the authors did not detect NRF2 pathway modulation and instead implicated ERK1/2 downregulation, underscoring context-dependence of the upstream signaling mediating protection (Bergandi et al., 2024). Reviews and experimental summaries further report that SFN protects retinal/epithelial tissues and can recover cone function in an NRF2-dependent manner in mice undergoing RPE oxidative stress, although primary data for those specific in vivo outcomes are not detailed in the provided text (Falcão et al., 2025). Mechanistically adjacent precedents in RPE include robust protection by the electrophilic NRF2 activator RTA 408 in primary human RPE subjected to H₂O₂, with genetic evidence for NRF2 dependence; while not SFN, this validates the KEAP1–NRF2 axis as druggable and protective in human RPE (Liu et al., 2016). With respect to lysosome-autophagy axes central to dry AMD, TFEB activation (via rapamycin or constitutively active TFEB) reduces photoreceptor outer segment–derived autofluorescent granules in RPE POS-feeding models, and TFEB-directed interventions (including trehalose or constitutively nuclear TFEB) restore cathepsin D/L abundance and activity and increase LAMP1 in AMD-relevant human RPE models, establishing the lysosome/transcriptional arm as therapeutically tractable in RPE; however, these TFEB-driven rescues have not been directly demonstrated with SFN in RPE in the supplied literature (Falcão et al., 2024; Ghosh et al., 2024).

Mechanism of Action  
- NRF2 engagement via KEAP1 cysteine sensing: SFN, as an electrophile, reacts with specific redox-sensitive cysteines on KEAP1 (notably Cys151 among others), impairing KEAP1-mediated ubiquitination of NRF2 and permitting NRF2 stabilization, nuclear accumulation, and heterodimerization with small Maf proteins to bind AREs and induce a large gene battery of antioxidant, detoxification, and proteostasis regulators (e.g., NQO1, HO-1, GCLM, GSTs), increasing GSH and related defenses (Hyttinen et al., 2019; Qin, 2007). In RPE and ocular tissues, SFN and related NRF2 activators have induced phase II enzymes and HO-1 and conferred resistance to photooxidative injury, with biochemical readouts that include increased NQO1, thioredoxin, GSH, and reduced ROS (Qin, 2007; Zhang et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2021). Aging impairs inducible NRF2 signaling in RPE under oxidative challenges (e.g., sodium iodate), supporting the rationale for exogenous NRF2 activation in older RPE (Sachdeva et al., 2014).

- TFEB/TFE3 activation and lysosome-autophagy biogenesis: SFN provokes a mild increase in ROS that sensitizes lysosomal MCOLN1/TRPML1 channels to agonist-evoked Ca²⁺ release; resultant cytosolic Ca²⁺ engages calcineurin to dephosphorylate TFEB, enabling its nuclear translocation and activation of CLEAR-network transcription independently of acute MTORC1 inhibition (TFEB activation is blocked by antioxidants, BAPTA-AM, and attenuated by FK506) (Li et al., 2021). The SFN-induced TFEB program upregulates autophagy and lysosome genes (SQSTM1, ULK1, LC3) and multiple lysosomal components including LAMP1, v-ATPase subunits (e.g., ATP6V1H), hydrolases (CTSB, TPP1), and MCOLN1, and increases LysoTracker and LAMP1 signals, consistent with enhanced lysosomal mass and acidotropic probe accumulation (Li et al., 2021). Critically, TFEB is necessary for SFN-induced upregulation of NFE2L2/NRF2 and for SFN-mediated suppression of ROS in mitochondrial and lysosomal stress models, documenting a TFEB→NRF2 dependency in SFN’s antioxidant protection (Li et al., 2021). Reviews synthesizing TFEB–NRF2 crosstalk add that TFEB can directly or indirectly promote NRF2 by repressing its E3 ligase (DCAF11) and via p62-mediated KEAP1 sequestration; reciprocally, NRF2 activation can induce TFEB-related gene sets and promote autophagosome–lysosome fusion, indicating bidirectional reinforcement (Falcão et al., 2025).

- RPE-specific TFEB/lysosome biology relevant to AMD: In human RPE-derived ARPE-19 cells, TFEB controls lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy; nutrient deprivation and lysosomal stress increase TFEB and MITF and induce CLEAR genes including LAMP1, CTSD, MCOLN1, and autophagy factors (BECN1), with calcineurin-mediated dephosphorylation regulating nuclear translocation (Pan et al., 2019). In AMD-relevant RPE models, TFEB activation (via mTORC1 inhibition or constitutively active TFEB) reduces POS-dependent lipofuscin-like autofluorescent granules through a hydrolase-dependent mechanism, and inhibition or genetic loss of CTSD increases autofluorescent burden and abrogates rapamycin’s benefit, tying TFEB-driven rescue to functional lysosomal proteolysis (Falcão et al., 2024). In human AMD donor RPE and CFH Y402H iPSC-RPE, elevated p-TFEB/p-TFE3 associates with reduced CTSD/CTSL abundance and activity; interventions that restore TFEB nuclear activity (AAV2-TFEB-S467A) or TFEB activators (trehalose) rescue CTSD/CTSL levels and activities and increase LAMP1, while AKT2 inhibition counters secretory-autophagy bias and improves degradative flux (Ghosh et al., 2024; Ghosh et al., 2023).

- Cathepsin D biochemistry and lysosomal pH: Cathepsin D (CTSD) is an abundant lysosomal aspartyl protease synthesized as an inactive proenzyme that undergoes maturation and activation in the acidic late endosome/lysosome; cathepsins generally require a reducing, mildly acidic lumen and lose activity at neutral pH, linking lysosomal acidification (v-ATPase function) tightly to CTSD proteolysis (Sharif, 2015). In AMD, lysosomal dysfunction (including LMP, impaired proton-pump function, and hydrolase inhibition by lipofuscin-derived oxidized products) is prominent, and CTSD leakage and reduced hydrolase activity are reported in AMD RPE, mechanistically supporting the therapeutic objective to normalize lysosomal pH and restore cathepsin activity (Falcão et al., 2025).

- Safety and pathway caveats: Constitutive or excessive activation of NRF2 or TFEB can carry oncogenic or maladaptive risks, and chronic KEAP1–NRF2 perturbation can yield accumulation of non-degradative organelles, emphasizing the need for cell-specific, dose-titrated modulation and rigorous safety assessment in the AMD context (Falcão et al., 2025).

Taken together, SFN stands out for concurrent engagement of NRF2 antioxidant programs and TFEB-driven lysosome/autophagy biogenesis—mechanisms that align with central oxidative and degradative defects in dry AMD RPE—yet it is important to note that direct biochemical evidence demonstrating SFN-mediated normalization of lysosomal pH and restoration of CTSD maturation/activity in RPE under AMD-relevant oxidative stress is not present in the supplied literature (Falcão et al., 2025; Li et al., 2021).

Expected Effect  
Under the stated hypothesis—SFN engages NRF2 and TFEB in oxidatively stressed RPE to normalize lysosomal pH and restore CTSD proteolysis—the expected proximate and downstream effects in rigorously designed assays are:  
- Antioxidant response and ROS control: SFN should increase NRF2 nuclear accumulation and ARE target expression (HO-1, NQO1, GCLM, Trx1, GSH biosynthesis enzymes) in RPE cells subjected to oxidative paradigms (e.g., blue light, sodium iodate, hydroquinone, or POS feeding with photooxidative stress), lowering ROS burden and oxidative damage; this is strongly supported in ARPE-19 under blue light (and in other epithelial systems), and the effect shows functional dependence on NRF2 (ML385-sensitive) (Yang et al., 2021; Qin, 2007). Aging-associated defects in inducible NRF2 signaling suggest exogenous NRF2 activation may be especially beneficial in aged RPE, further motivating this outcome measure (Sachdeva et al., 2014).

- TFEB activation and lysosome-autophagy program: SFN should induce TFEB nuclear translocation through ROS→Ca²⁺→calcineurin signaling, upregulate CLEAR-network transcripts (including LAMP1, CTSD, ATP6V1H, MCOLN1, ULK1, SQSTM1, LC3), increase lysosomal biogenesis and LysoTracker staining, and enhance autophagic flux; these outcomes are well documented for SFN in multiple human cell models and provide mechanistic plausibility for analogous effects in RPE (Li et al., 2021). In RPE specifically, TFEB is inducible and drives LAMP1 and CTSD expression under stress, while TFEB activation improves degradative capacity in AMD-relevant settings, supporting the assay logic to monitor TFEB localization and CLEAR targets in RPE (Pan et al., 2019; Falcão et al., 2024).

- Lysosomal acidification and CTSD proteolysis: If SFN increases v-ATPase subunit expression and lysosomal mass (as in other cells), one would expect improved lysosomal acidification (lower pH) and more efficient CTSD maturation (pro- to intermediate- to mature forms) and activity, read out by calibrated pH probes (e.g., LysoSensor or ratiometric genetically encoded sensors), Western blots for CTSD processing, and fluorometric CTSD activity assays. This is biologically plausible given SFN-induced lysosomal gene expression and LysoTracker increases in vitro, and given that TFEB activation rescues hydrolase-dependent POS processing in RPE; however, direct evidence that SFN normalizes lysosomal pH and increases CTSD maturation/activity in RPE under oxidative stress is not shown in the provided literature and must be generated (Li et al., 2021; Falcão et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2025).

- Functional RPE outcomes: Improved degradative clearance of POS-derived material and reduced accumulation of autofluorescent granules (lipofuscin-like AFG) are expected functional correlates. Rapamycin and constitutively active TFEB reduce AFG in RPE POS-feeding models in a hydrolase-dependent manner, and TFEB activation or AKT2 inhibition restores CTSD/CTSL activity and LAMP1 levels in human AMD RPE models; SFN could converge on these endpoints via TFEB activation, but this remains to be established experimentally (Falcão et al., 2024; Ghosh et al., 2024).

Assay implementation considerations:  
- Cell systems and paradigms: iPSC-derived human RPE (including CFH Y402H risk background) and ARPE-19, subjected to blue light, hydroquinone/cigarette smoke mimetics, sodium iodate, POS feeding, and/or complement challenge, to model oxidative and degradative stress relevant to dry AMD (Yang et al., 2021; Ghosh et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2024).

- Readouts: NRF2 nuclear translocation and ARE target induction; TFEB nuclear translocation and phosphorylation state; CLEAR-network gene expression (LAMP1, CTSD, ATP6V1H, MCOLN1, ULK1, SQSTM1); lysosomal pH (calibrated probes); lysosomal mass (LAMP1 immunostaining, LysoTracker); CTSD processing (pro/mature Western blots) and enzymatic activity; autophagic flux (LC3 turnover with and without lysosomal inhibitors); POS processing kinetics and AFG quantification (Li et al., 2021; Pan et al., 2019; Falcão et al., 2024).

- Controls and mechanism validation: Antioxidant blockade (NAC, catalase) to test ROS-dependence of TFEB activation; Ca²⁺ chelation (BAPTA-AM) and calcineurin inhibition (FK506) to probe TFEB activation pathway; NRF2 inhibitor (ML385) to test NRF2 dependence; TFEB loss-of-function (siRNA/CRISPR) to test TFEB dependence; rapamycin/trehalose/AAV-TFEB as positive controls for lysosomal biogenesis; cathepsin inhibitors and CTSD KO/knockdown to test hydrolase dependence; use of AKT2 pathway modulators to deconvolve TFEB repression in AMD-relevant models (Li et al., 2021; Yang et al., 2021; Ghosh et al., 2024).

- Dosing: Based on mechanistic studies, SFN at 5–15 µM for 4–9 h is effective for TFEB activation in several cell lines; in ARPE-19 blue-light studies, SFN modulated NRF2 and autophagy markers, and in TGF-β models, SFN was tested at 1–10 µM with ERK pathway modulation observed (Li et al., 2021; Yang et al., 2021; Bergandi et al., 2024).

- Interpretation caveats: In TGF-β–treated RPE, investigators did not detect NRF2 modulation with SFN, implying model-specific pathway engagement; this further justifies running multiple oxidative-stress paradigms and confirming pathway activation per condition (Bergandi et al., 2024).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Mechanistic alignment with AMD pathobiology: SFN targets two validated, convergent axes implicated in non-neovascular AMD—NRF2-mediated antioxidant defense and TFEB-driven lysosomal-autophagy competence—addressing both oxidative injury and impaired degradative capacity in RPE (Pinelli et al., 2020; Pan et al., 2019; Falcão et al., 2024). The KEAP1–NRF2 pathway is protective in RPE and becomes inducibly impaired with age, and TFEB activation restores lysosomal hydrolase function and reduces POS-derived autofluorescence in RPE models (Sachdeva et al., 2014; Ghosh et al., 2024).

- Robust cellular mechanism for dual-pathway engagement: High-quality mechanistic studies show SFN activates TFEB via ROS→Ca²⁺→calcineurin independent of acute MTORC1 inhibition, induces CLEAR genes, increases lysosomal mass and LysoTracker staining, and requires TFEB to drive NFE2L2 transcription and antioxidant protection; this dual activation positions SFN to coordinate detoxification and lysosomal biogenesis (Li et al., 2021).

- RPE-relevant efficacy signals: In ARPE-19 blue-light stress, SFN confers NRF2-dependent cytoprotection and requires autophagy; SFN also reduces ROS and preserves epithelial integrity in an inflammatory RPE model (albeit via ERK1/2 modulation), indicating protective breadth across RPE-relevant stressors (Yang et al., 2021; Bergandi et al., 2024).

- Translational plausibility: SFN (and class analogs) have measurable bioavailability in humans and have long been explored as chemopreventive agents, supporting feasibility of repurposing if ocular exposure and dosing can be optimized; as a comparator, RTA 408’s efficacy in primary RPE confirms the druggability of KEAP1–NRF2 in human RPE (Qin, 2007; Liu et al., 2016).

Weaknesses and Gaps  
- No direct evidence for lysosomal pH normalization or CTSD rescue by SFN in RPE: Although SFN upregulates lysosomal genes and LysoTracker signal in other cell types, the literature provided does not report calibrated lysosomal pH measurements, CTSD maturation patterns, or CTSD enzymatic activity in RPE after SFN under AMD-relevant oxidative stress; this is the critical gap relative to the stated hypothesis (Falcão et al., 2025; Li et al., 2021).

- Model-dependent pathway engagement: In TGF-β ARPE-19, SFN protection tracked with ERK1/2 modulation rather than detectable NRF2 activation, underscoring that the upstream route by which SFN confers benefit can vary with the stressor and cellular context; robust pathway biomarker panels will be required in each model (Bergandi et al., 2024).

- Safety and liability considerations: Persistent activation of NRF2 or TFEB may carry oncogenic or maladaptive risks; KEAP1–NRF2 dysregulation can drive accumulation of non-degradative organelles, and TFEB activation must be titrated to avoid excessive catabolic or proliferative shifts; this risk profile necessitates careful dose finding, exposure control, and long-term safety assessment (Falcão et al., 2025).

- Ocular delivery/exposure unknowns: The provided literature notes systemic bioavailability with detection in non-ocular tissues; however, data establishing therapeutic concentrations in the RPE/choroid following systemic or local administration are absent here and will need to be generated to support translational feasibility (Qin, 2007).

- Disease-network complexity: In AMD-relevant RPE, AKT2 upregulation suppresses TFEB/TFE3 and reduces cathepsin expression/activity, while complement dysregulation, iron overload, and lipofuscin-associated proton-pump/hydrolase inhibition further stress lysosomes; whether SFN’s TFEB activation suffices under these multi-hit conditions, or whether combination with AKT2/MTOR modulators is required, remains to be determined (Ghosh et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2025; Ghosh et al., 2023).

Programmatic recommendation  
- Proceed to focused preclinical validation with a decision gate on lysosomal biochemical rescue. The mechanistic case for SFN’s dual NRF2/TFEB action is strong, and RPE protection data exist; however, the program’s value hinges on demonstrating that SFN normalizes lysosomal acidity and restores CTSD maturation/activity in stressed human RPE—outcomes not yet shown (Li et al., 2021; Yang et al., 2021; Falcão et al., 2025).

- Experimental plan (key go/no-go criteria):  
  1) Pathway engagement: SFN dose–time response for NRF2 and TFEB activation in iPSC-RPE (±CFH Y402H) under blue light, hydroquinone, sodium iodate, POS feeding, and complement challenge; use ML385, FK506, BAPTA-AM, and TFEB LOF to assign mechanism (Yang et al., 2021; Li et al., 2021; Falcão et al., 2024).  
  2) Lysosomal function: Calibrated lysosomal pH; CTSD pro/mature processing and activity; LAMP1 and LysoTracker; autophagic flux; POS degradation kinetics and AFG load; requirement for CTSD confirmed by CTSD knockdown and cathepsin inhibitors (Falcão et al., 2024; Sharif, 2015).  
  3) Comparative controls: Rapamycin, trehalose, and AAV2-TFEB-S467A as positive controls for lysosomal rescue; AKT2 inhibition as a disease-relevant comparator; RTA 408 or DMF as NRF2-pathway comparators (Ghosh et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2016).  
  4) In vivo signal-seeking: Acute oxidative RPE injury (e.g., sodium iodate) and chronic stress models to test functional endpoints (ERG, OCT) and histology with RPE lysosomal markers and CTSD activity ex vivo; assess whether SFN improves cone/RPE function in an NRF2-dependent manner as suggested by prior reports (Sachdeva et al., 2014; Falcão et al., 2025).  
  5) Safety/tolerability: Proliferation, TFEB/NRF2 target overactivation, lysosomal membrane integrity (LMP markers), and non-degradative organelle accumulation with extended SFN exposure; aim for intermittent dosing to minimize chronic pathway hyperactivation (Falcão et al., 2025).

If SFN demonstrates robust TFEB/NRF2 engagement in human RPE, normalizes lysosomal pH, and restores CTSD maturation/activity with concomitant functional improvements in POS clearance and AFG reduction, it would represent a differentiated candidate addressing both oxidative and degradative lesions central to geographic atrophy; absent those biochemical rescues, SFN should be deprioritized in favor of TFEB-directed agents (e.g., trehalose or gene-based TFEB activation) or combinations that address AKT2–TFEB repression and complement-driven lysosomal injury (Ghosh et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2024; Ghosh et al., 2023).

In summary, sulforaphane is a scientifically credible, mechanistically dual-action candidate for dry AMD based on strong evidence of NRF2 activation in RPE and TFEB-driven lysosome-autophagy induction in multiple cell systems, with supportive RPE protection data; yet the decisive evidence that SFN normalizes lysosomal acidity and rescues cathepsin D proteolysis in oxidatively stressed human RPE is currently lacking in the provided literature and must be established to justify advancement (Yang et al., 2021; Li et al., 2021; Falcão et al., 2025).
